In this and the following verses up to 15, Brentius observes that the Son of God is setting forth the wrath of God by an enumeration of almost all the signs and arguments by which God has testified to the ineffable gravity of his wrath against the sins of men in the Prophetic Scriptures, such as in the flood (Genesis 6 and 7), in the conflagration of Sodom (chapter 19), in the promulgation of the Decalogue (Exodus 19), in the punishment of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram (Numbers 16), in the excision of the kings of the Amorites (Joshua 10) and of Sisera (Judges 5) and of the Philistines (1 Samuel 7), in the terror of the Israelites (1 Samuel 12), etc. Add also the suffocation of Pharaoh (Exodus 14). For since the Son of God undertook to expiate the sins of the entire human race, he also had to experience the sense of the most severe wrath of God. Blessed Bugenhagius refers these to the portents produced during the passion of Christ: (which are joined by Osiander with the former.) "Since it is clearer than light that Christ is speaking here, why do we seek things fetched from further away, when he himself says these miracles were done not in Egypt or at Sinai, but when he himself cried out to the Father with the desire of his heart in his greatest tribulation, when he seemed forsaken by God and all creatures in the sorrows of death and of the lower regions, in the trouble of iniquity and the snares of death? Do we still not know that every creature of God was troubled at the death of the Son of God, and that the wrath of God the Father, watching the death of his Son, was declared by a horrible and foul spectacle? Who doubts, if ever there was a horrible tempest of the air and a commotion of heaven and earth by a miracle, that here all things were most horrible? since you read in Matthew that the earth was moved, the rocks rent, the graves opened, and the lower regions opened to give back the dead, who rose with Christ and were seen in Jerusalem, and also darkness for three hours and the sun itself obscured, in the three Evangelists. Moreover, Peter in Acts 2, from Joel, adds the moon into blood, signs in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath, blood and fire and vapor of smoke, etc. Furthermore, at these such sad spectacles, signs indeed of an angry God at the death of his Son, the troubled minds of the people are read of, especially of the Gentiles, that is, of the Centurion and those who were with him, for they are written to have feared greatly and glorified God: then also of others of the people, as many as were present at that spectacle, who returned smiting their breasts. What if we interpret the horror of the people here also among the Gentiles and Jews, where the new law and the new testament, that is, the Gospel, was confirmed in the death and blood of Christ? If therefore you look diligently, you see that the Spirit of Christ, when speaking in this Psalm about the miracles performed during the passion of Christ, looked back and alluded to those things which we cited above from ancient history. For thus are the Prophets accustomed to see other things in other events. And certainly we ought to estimate those things by those which were done for the ancient people, namely that they were sufficiently and exceedingly horrible, which the very words here also declare.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

COMMOVETUR ET CONTREMISCIT TERRA.

In hoc & seqq. versibus usque ad 15. Filium DEI exponere iram Dei enumeratione omnium pæ- ne signorum & argumentorum, quibus DEUS ine- narrabilem iræ suæ gravitatem adversus peccata ho- minum in Scriptis Propheticis testificatus est, obser- vat Brentius, utpote in diluvio Genes. VI. & VII. in conflagratione Sodomæ cap. XIX. in promul- gatione Decalogi Exod. XIX. in punitione Coræ, Datham & Abiram Numer. XVI. in excisione Re- gum Amorrhæorum Jos. X. & Sisaræ Judic. V. & Philistæorum 1. Samuel. VII. in perterrefactione Israëlitarum 1. Sam. XII. &c. Adde & in suffoca- tione Pharaonis Exod. XIV. Quum enim Filius DEI susceperit peccata universi generis humani expianda, debuit etiam sensum severissimæ iræ Dei experiri. Beatus Bugenhagius hæc refert ad portenta in passione Christi edita: (quæ ab Osiandro cum prioribus conjunguntur.) "Cum luce clarius sit Christum hic loqui, quid longius petita quærimus, cum dicat ipse hæc miracula facta non in Ægypto aut in Sina, sed quando ipse ad Patrem clamavit desiderio cordis in tribulatione sui maxima, quando videbatur derelictus à DEO & omnibus creaturis in doloribus mortis & inferorum, in conturbatione iniquitatis & laqueis mortis? Num adhuc ignoramus ad mortem filii Dei omnem Dei creaturam turbatam, & horrendo tetroque spectaculo declaratam iram Dei Patris spectantis necem Filii sui? Quis dubitat, si unquam per miraculum fuit horrenda aëris tempestas & cæli terræque commotio, hic omnia fuisse horrendissima? quandoquidem legis in Matthæo, terram motam, petras scissas, monumenta aperta, inferos patuisse, ut redderent mortuos, qui cum Christo surrexerunt & visi sunt in Hierusalem, tenebras quoque per tres horas & ipsum solem obscuratum, in tribus Evangelistis. Insuper Petrus Actor. II. ex Joële addit lunam sanguineam, signa in cœlo sursum, & signa in terra deorsum, sanguinem & ignem & vaporem fumi &c. Porro ad hæc tam tristia spectacula, signa profecto irati DEI in morte filii sui, turbatos animos legis, imprimis gentilium, id est, Centurionis & qui cum eo erant, scribuntur enim timuisse valde & Deum glorificasse: deinde & de aliis legis quotquot aderant ad spectaculum istud, quod percutientes pectora sua reversi sunt. Quid si & hic horrorem legis in gentibus & Judæis interpretemur, ubi lex nova & testamentum novum, id est, Evangelium, confirmabatur in morte & sanguine Christi? Si diligenter itaque intuearis, vides Spiritum Christi cum in hoc Psalmo de miraculis in passione Christi factis loqueretur, ad illa quæ supra ex historia veteri citavimus respexisse & allusisse. Sic enim solent Prophetæ in aliis factis alia videre. Et certe ista ex illis quæ veteri populo facta sunt æstimare debemus, satis scilicet nimiumque horrenda fuisse, id quod & hic verba ipsa declarant.

## 18:10
Ver. 11. AND HE ASCENDED UPON THE CHERUBIM, AND DID FLY) It seems that formerly רכוב was written for כרוב, which signifies a chariot, as in the very similar passage 104 v. 3. Similar is that of Plato in the Phaedrus: the great leader in heaven Zeus, driving a winged chariot, goes first, ordering all things and taking care of them.

By no, or the slightest, indication can that transposition be proved. All codices, Hebrew, Chaldean, Greek, Latin, read in the same way, and the sense is clearer, he ascended upon the Cherubim, than upon a chariot; for what is that chariot, if not the Cherubim themselves? Just as they were like chariots 2 Kings 2 v. 11, ch. 6 v. 17. Nor is the description of God unusual, that he sits upon the Cherubim Psalm 21 v. 5 and 99 v. 1. The passage Psalm 104 v. 3, although in the latter member of the verse it is very similar to this one of ours, yet in the former it differs. For there it is said that God makes the cloud his chariot. But here no mention of a cloud is made. Nor of a chariot expressly: except that he is said to ascend upon the Cherubim as if it were a chariot. For both are rightly said of God, both that he sits by means of the Angels as his chariots, and that he has a cloud for his chariot: because he uses now Angels, now clouds and winds for a vehicle, as it pleases him.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET ADSCENDIT SVPER CHERVBIM, ET VOLAVIT) Videtur olim pro כרוב scriptum fuisse רכוב, quod currum significat, ut in loco persimili 104. v. 3. Simile Platonis illud in Phædro: ὁ μὲν δὴ μέγας ἡγεμὼν ἐν ὀυρανῷ Ζεὺς πτηνὸν ἅρμα ἐλαύνων, πρῶτος πορέυεται διακο- σμῶν πάντα καὶ ἐπιμελούμενος.

Nullo vel minimo indicio probari potest illa μετάθεσις. Codices omnes, Ebræi, Chaldæi, Græci, Latini eodem modo legunt, & luculen- tior sensus est, ascendit super Cherubim, quam su- per currum; quisnam enim ille currus, nisi Che- rubim ipsi? Sicut illi curruum instar fuere 2. Reg. 2. vers. 11. c. 6. versu 17. Nec inusitata est Dei de- scriptio, quod sedeat super Cherubim Psalm. 21. v. 5. & 99. v. 1. Locus Psalm. 104. vers. 3. etsi in poste- riori membro versus sit huic nostro persimilis, in priori tamen differt. Ibi enim dicitur Deus po- nere nubem currum suum. Hic vero nubis nulla mentio facta. Nec currus expresse: nisi quod ascendere super Cherubim velut currum dicatur. Utrumque enim de Deo recte dicitur, & quod sit per Angelos ceu currus suos sedeat, & quod nubem pro curru suo habeat: quia utitur modo Angelis, modo nubibus ventisque pro vehiculo, prout libet.

## 18:16 Addition
Vers. 16. HE SENT FROM ON HIGH &c.

By these and the following words the Son of God proclaims the help of God and his own deliverance, because God sent help from heaven, and as if by hand drew him out, already immersed and almost suffocated by the waters of afflictions, from the infernal enemy, that strong and armed one Luke XI, 21, and from all his enemies, who seemed more robust than he and to prevail over him, and brought him into a broad place: with the cause added; because he delighted in me, which properly befits the Son of God Is. XLII, 1. Matt. III, 17. chap. XVII, 5. which he explains in verse 20 and following. He rewarded me according to my righteousness &c. where that perfection of innocence and righteousness is described at length, which falls to no mortal, and must necessarily be explained concerning the righteousness of Christ and his most perfect fulfillment of the law.

With the holy, he says, verse 22, you will be holy, with the perverse, as it is held in the Vulgate, you will be perverse, which however Bellarmine amends thus, because the Hebrew word signifies that GOD will wrestle with the perverse with great effort. That concerning him, who is μονοτρόπως holy, Christ Jesus it will be permitted to accept as the author of all Holiness, just as on the opposite side that perverse one can be understood, ἐξαιρέτως perverse, and the author of all perversity: nor perhaps will it be irrelevant, in those things which follow in verse 23, to accept the afflicted people as the human race, truly most afflicted and most miserable, yet saved by GOD the proud, whom GOD humbles, when he fixes his own avenging eyes upon the high ones, which is held in the parallel 2 Sam. XXII, as the most proud devils, from whom pride first arose and was introduced. But how that defeat of the perverse, and the humiliation of the proud Spirits, about which Mary the Mother of God also sang in Luke 1, 51, is explained v. 28. For you light my lamp etc. "Concerning which it is pleasant to hear the blessed Brentius again: Darkness, if you take it metaphorically, signifies afflictions and tribulations. GOD therefore is said to illuminate the darkness, when he saves the afflicted in afflictions, and delivers him from tribulations. Therefore GOD then illuminated the lamp of Christ, and illuminated his darkness, when he saved him in death, and led him out of the sepulcher and hell, so that he might rise again and sit at the right hand of God his Father. By what light, by what glory, what can be more illustrious? Then: Through you, he says, I crush military forces, and through my God I leap over a wall, or I storm cities and fortified fortresses. Here again let us consider, such are the military forces, fighting with Christ, and the walls of his enemies, as is the king, namely, not worldly, but spiritual, not earthly, but heavenly. The armies therefore, and military forces, which resist Christ, and the walls of his enemies, are the rulers of the darkness of this world, and spiritual wickedness in heavenly places, and thus those principalities and powers, about which the Psalm and David speak: He led captivity captive. And Paul again: He showed the principalities and powers despoiled, triumphing openly over them through himself, for Satan is such a powerful prince in this age, that he is even called the GOD of this age by Paul. Sin dominates so widely, that it oppresses the entire human race. Death and hell are of such power, that not even the Monarchs of this earth can escape their tyranny. But Christ the son of GOD routed and put to flight all these military forces, and leaped over and overcame all these walls, however high. But through whom, and by whose power did Christ overcome these forces and walls? THROUGH YOU, he says, THROUGH MY GOD. For Satan is conquered, sin is expiated, and death and hell are stormed by Christ, not by earthly, but by heavenly, not by human, but by divine power.

"Regarding verse 30, Brentius has it thus: The way of God is the purpose and institution of GOD. And his word is his promise. This institution of GOD therefore concerning his son is not subject to change, is not corrupted by any vice, but is perfect, inviolate, fixed and stable. This promise of GOD concerning the mission of his Son is not like wood or stubble, which, seized by fire, are immediately consumed, but is like pure gold, which, thrown into the fire, is so far from being consumed that it is rather rendered more purified. Therefore it remains that as many as are stirred by this promise, conceive a certain hope of clemency

of the Lord, for the sake of his Son, to them the Lord truly becomes a shield, a buckler, a protection, and a bulwark in all dangers. Instructed therefore by this divine fortitude, I pursue, he says in verse 37, the children of God, my enemies, and I overtake them, etc. And persevering in the same metaphor taken from worldly wars, he describes his victory. Which Brentius interprets as spiritual enemies conquered through Christ, but Osiander as bodily enemies persecuting the Church to be destroyed by Christ. And verse 41 seems to have no light difficulty. They cried out, and there was none to save them, it must be said that sin, death, and hell are introduced by prosopopoeia, such as occurs in Hosea 13:14; how Brentius explains it, that the spiritual enemies are reduced by the victory of Christ to such great perdition that, even if they had some human sense and called upon God, they could not nevertheless emerge from their destruction and recover their strength, as if Christ were saying, I so cast down and crush my enemies, Satan, death, and hell, that they suffer extreme slaughter, etc. Yet the interpretation of those who wish it to be a matter here of the carnal enemies of Christ, and especially of the Jews, who not only afflicted him extremely in the days of his flesh and especially in his passion, but were finally supplanted and dispersed when Christ gloriously rose again and was exalted to the right hand of God, girded with divine virtue, and rejected by God, to whom they cried out in vain, and Christ himself crushed them like dust before the face of the wind, he wiped them away like the mire of the street, which happened in the extreme πανωλεθρίᾳ (total destruction) of Jerusalem and the extermination of the polity and the Jewish people. Just as immediately follows a most express prophecy concerning the rejection of the Jews and the assumption of the Gentiles. Verse 43. You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people, that is, you will free me from the contentious and stiff-necked Jewish people, so that I do not have to struggle any longer with their insane obstinacy. But you will set me as the head of the Gentiles, so that the Gentiles may acknowledge me as their King and head, and obediently submit themselves to me, see Genesis 49:10, Isaiah 11:10, chapter 42:1, chapter 49:6, Haggai 2:8, Ephesians 5:23. A people whom I have not known, that is, I have not held as my people, shall serve me, shall submit themselves to my rule, and shall render to me the due worship and obedience. Compare Hosea 1:10. Which are rashly snatched away by Calvin, Musculus, and the Dutch to the victories of David, the subjection of the Moabites, Ammonites, and other nations, since David was not the HEAD OF THE GENTILES, even if he made certain peoples tributary to himself; therefore the blessed Gesner himself acknowledges and proves that those words in verse 44 and following can by no means be explained concerning the earthly kingdom of David, even if he understood the preceding verses concerning David: For he says, David or any faithful monarch cannot and ought not to conceive in his mind the hope that he will enjoy such tranquility of his kingdom that he is immune from the contentions and disputes of the people: since empires were instituted for the purpose that they might hear and compose the disputes and contentions of their subjects. Furthermore, since David composed this song of victory when near to death, by what reasoning could he finally promise himself that he would be the head and king of the Gentiles, and indeed of those whom he had not known? Finally, it would be absurd, indeed far most absurd, for David to flatter himself so much that he does not hesitate to persuade his own mind that the Gentiles, alien to the Israelite religion, would spontaneously obey him and at the hearing of the Davidic name would render obedience; since he could scarcely subdue the peoples of the land of Palestine with arms and prisons. Blessed Gesner says these things: from which, since one and the same person speaks throughout the whole Psalm, it can be invincibly proven that the preceding parts are also to be understood concerning Christ, and not indeed concerning David. Jerome also explained the contentions concerning the contradictions by which the Jews opposed themselves to Christ and contradicted the doctrine of the Gospel and denied that he was the Messiah himself, and Augustine explained those things which were done concerning the passion of Christ, when even the wicked crowd mocked him while suspended on the cross: to whose explanation Gesner adds his approval. What is added in verse 45, 'At the hearing of the ear they will obey me,' the same man rightly explains concerning the mode and manner by which the nations would come from the service of their idols to the obedience of Christ: They will hear the Gospel and will believe: For faith is from hearing, Rom. 10. This praise of the nations is a great reproach to the Jews, says Cassiodorus: for they served who did not see: they obeyed, to whom the most sacred words did not sound from his mouth. And to those things which are further added, 'The alien sons lied to me': He calls them sons, he says, because of their carnal origin and birth: for they are the seed of Abraham; but because they rejected the faith of Abraham, he therefore names them sons of separation or of defection and degenerate. For although they boast that they are sons of Abraham and of God, nevertheless they justly hear from Christ, John 8, 'You are from your father the devil.' But he names the defection of the people and of his sons by a general term, Lying: 'Because just as the devil is their father, so they also did not stand in the truth.' The Chaldean interpreter rendered it thus: 'They lied in my presence': Which indeed exaggerates their sin; since they did not fear the sight of the Son of God himself: And they despised not only the prophets, as ambassadors, but even the Lord himself, and affixed him to the cross. Finally, what Christ prophesies here concerning the punishment of the Jews, 'The sons of separation will fade away and will tremble from their prisons,' Blessed Gesner explains thus, that the former indeed explain the temporal punishment, that they are to be cut off by the Romans, but the latter explain the spiritual and eternal, by the name of prisons and bonds, in which they will grieve eternally. Whence one must wonder that in verse 47 and the rest Blessed Gesner interprets concerning David, when he acknowledged that verses 44, 45, and 46 cannot be explained concerning David, and confessed that in verse 47 the Fathers with ONE voice refer it to the rising Christ, and that Augustine and the rest also attribute these words to Christ, i.e. From the Jews rising up against me as I suffer, you will exalt me as I rise again, but he also admits in verse 50, 'Therefore I will celebrate you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing to your name,' that it deals with the kingdom of Christ: because Paul interprets it the same way concerning the calling of the nations, Rom. 15, 9, and in the last verse, 'Magnifying the salvations of his king,' he understands Christ as King, and admits that the manifold salvation provided by Christ is designated. For what must be warned again, as it is most evident from the Psalm, there is only one person who speaks in this Psalm, who if in verses 44, 45, 46 is Christ, it will not be permitted to establish that David speaks in the rest: nor will the Apostolic demonstration hold together, Rom. 15, 9, brought forward from the present place for the calling of the nations in the New Testament, if it is asserted that David said these things about himself: For thus David, already near to death, would have received that he would celebrate the Lord among the nations, which does nothing to prove the calling of the nations, which was to happen in the time of the New Testament after the Jews were rejected. Whence others apply that Rule here, that Christ sometimes ascribes to himself those things which are of his faithful members, because of the mystical union of the head and the body, as Matt. 25, 40, Acts 9, 4, 5. But Lyranus and Thomas explain it thus: 'I will confess to you among the nations,' that is, I will cause through the Holy Spirit that the nations confess to you with a confession of faith, which would have no place unless Christ himself were speaking here.

Latin:

Vers. 16. MISIT DE SUMMO &c.

His & seqq. verbis auxilium Dei & ereptionem suam deprædicat Filius Dei, quod Deus de cœlo miserit auxilium, & jam immersum ac pæne suffocatum aquis afflictionum, quasi manu extraxerit, ab inimico infernali, forti illo & armato Luc. XI, 21. omnibusque suis hostibus, qui robustiores ipso videbantur, eidemque prævalere, liberarit, & in latitudinem deduxerit: addita causa; quoniam complacitum est ei in me, quæ proprie Filio Dei convenit Es. XLII, 1. Matth. III, 17. cap. XVII, 5. quam explicat vers. 20. seqq. Retribuit mihi secundum justitiam meam &c. ubi prolixe ea innocentiæ & justitiæ perfectio describitur, quæ in nullum mortalium cadit, & necessario de justitia Christi ac perfectissima ejusdem legis impletione explicanda est.

Cum sancto, inquit, vers. 22. sanctus eris, cum perverso, ut in vulgata habetur, perverteris, quod tamen ita emendat Bellarminus, quod vox Ebræa significet, DEUM cum perverso magno molimine luctaturum. Id de eo, qui μονοτρόπως sanctus est, Christo Jesu accipere licebit omnis Sanctitatis autore, quem- admodum ex adverso perversus ille intelligi pote- rit, ἐξαιρέτως perversus, & omnis perversitatis autor: nec alienum fortassis erit, in iis quæ vers. 23. sequuntur, uti populum afflictum de genere humano, afflictissimo sane ac miserrimo, à DEO tamen servato accipere, ita oculos superborum, quos humiliat DEUS, cum oculos suos vindi- ces in altos defigit, quod in parallelo 2. Sam. XXII. habetur, de diabolis superbissimis, à quibus su- perbia primum orta & invecta est, intelligere. Quomodo autem illa perversi debellatio, & su- perborum Spirituum humiliatio, de qua etiam cecinit Maria Deipara Luc. 1, 51. facta, exponi- tur v. 28. Quoniam tu illustras lucernam meam &c. „De quo audire iterum juvat B. Brentium: Te- „nebræ, si μεταφορικῶς accipias, significant af- „flictiones & tribulationes. DEUS ergo dici- „tur illuminare tenebras, cum servat afflictum „in afflictionibus, & liberat eum ex tribulatio- „nibus. Itaque DEUS tunc illustravit lucer- „nam Christi, & illuminavit tenebras ejus, cum „servavit eum in morte, & eduxit eum è sepul- „chro & inferno, ut resurgeret & sederet ad „dextram Dei Patris sui. Qua luce, qua glo- „ria, quid potest esse illustrius? Deinde: Per „te, inquit, contero copias militares, & per „Deum meum transilio murum, seu expugno ci- „vitates & arces munitas. Hîc iterum confide- „remus, tales esse copias militares, pugnantes „cum Christo, & muros hostium ejus, qualis „est rex, videlicet, non mundanus, sed spiri- „tualis, non terrenus, sed cœlestis. Exerci- „tus igitur, & copiæ militares, quæ Christo re- „sistunt, ac muri hostium ejus, sunt rectores te- „nebrarum hujus seculi, & spirituales astutiæ in „cœlestibus, adeoque principatus & potestates „illæ, de quibus Psalmus & David loquuntur: „Captivam duxit captivitatem. Et Paulus ite- „rum: Expoliatos principatus ac potestates „ostentavit palam triumphans de illis per semet- „ipsum, Satan enim tam potens est princeps in „hoc seculo, ut etiam DEUS hujus seculi à Pau- „lo dicatur. Peccatum tam late dominatur, ut „universum humanum genus opprimat. Mors „& infernus tantæ sunt virtutis, ut ne Monar- „chæ quidem hujus terræ possint tyrannidem eo- „rum evadere. Sed Christus filius DEI has „omnes copias militares fudit & fugavit, & hos „omnes muros, quamvis altissimos transilivit & „superavit. Per quem autem, & cujus virtute „superavit Christus has copias & muros? PER „TE, inquit, PER DEUM MEUM. Satan „enim victus est, peccatum expiatum est, & mors „ac infernus expugnata à Christo, non terrena, „sed cœlesti, non humana, sed divina virtute.

„Ad vers. 30. ita habet Brentius: Via Dei, est „propositum & institutum DEI. Et eloquium „ejus est promissio ejus. Hoc igitur institutum „DEI de filio suo, non est mutationi obnoxium, „non est ullo vitio corruptum, sed perfectum, „inviolatum, fixum & stabile. Hæc promissio „DEI de missione Filii sui non est sicut lignum „aut stipula, quæ ab igni arrepta, confestim „absumuntur, sed est velut purum aurum, quod „in ignem conjectum, tantum abest, ut absu- „matur, ut potius purgatius reddatur. Itaque „reliquum est, ut quotquot hac promissione ex- „citati, concipiant certam spem de clementia

Domini, propter filium suum, iis Dominus vere fit clypeus, scutum, protectio & propugnaculum in omnibus periculis. Hac ergo divina fortitu- dine instructus, persequor, inquit verf. 37. Filios DEI, inimicos meos, & apprehendo eos &c. Ac perseverans in eadem metaphora sumta a munda- nis bellis describit victoriam suam. Quæ de ho- stibus spiritualibus per Christum devictis Brentius, Ofiander vero de hostibus corporalibus Ecclesiam persequentibus a Christo delendis interpretatur. Et difficultatem videtur non levem habere verf. 41. Clamaverunt, nec erat, qui salvos faceret, nisi per prosopœiam peccatum, mortem & infernum in- duci, qualis Of. XIII, 14. occurrit, dicendum; quomodo Brentius explicat, significari hostes spirituales victoria Christi in tantam perditionem redactos, ut etiamsi aliquem humanum sensum ha- berent, & DEUM invocarent, non tamen pos- sent ex interitu suo emergere, & vires suas reci- pere, quasi dicat Christus, hostes meos Satanam, mortem & infernum ita dejicio & contundo, ut ex- trema internecione laborent, &c. Simplicior ta- men videtur eorum interpretatio, qui hic agi volunt de hostibus Christi carnalibus, & impri- mis de Judæis, qui eum non tantum in diebus carnis suæ & imprimis in passione extreme affli- xerunt, sed supplantati tandem & disperditi sunt Christo gloriose resurgente & ad dextram Dei evecto, divina virtute præcincto, & reprobati a Deo, ad quem nequicquam clamaverunt, & comminuit eos Christus ipse ut pulverem ante fa- ciem venti, ut lutum plateæ delevit eos, quod in extrema πανωλεθρίᾳ Hierosolymæ & exterminio politiæ & populi Judaici factum. Quemadmodum statim subjungitur vaticinium expressissimum de abjectione Judæorum & assumtione gentium. verf. 43. Eripies me de contradictionibus populi, id est, li- berabis me a populo Judaico contentioso, & duræ cervicis, ut non necesseum habeam diu- tius cum insana ipsius pertinacia conflictari. Con- stitues autem me in caput gentium, ita ut gentes me Regem & caput suum agnoscant, mihique obedienter se subjiciant, vid. Genes. XLIX, 10. Es. XI, 10. cap. XLII, 1 cap. XLIX, 6. Hagg. II, 8. Ephes. V, 23. Populus quem non cognovi, id est, non ha- bui pro populo meo, serviet mihi, meo regimini se submittet, debitumque mihi præstabit cultum & obsequium. Conf. Hos. 1, 10. Quæ temere a Calvino, Musculo, Belgis ad victorias Davidis, subjectionem Moabitarum, Ammonitarum, alia- rumque gentium abripiuntur, quum David non fuerit CAPUT GENTIUM, etsi populos quosdam sibi tributarios fecerit, ideo agnoscit B. Gesnerus ipse, ac probat verba illa verf. 44. seqq. minime exponi posse de terreno Davidis regno, etsi præcedentia de Davide intellexerit: Non enim, inquit, potest, neque debet David aut quispi- am fidelis monarcha, eam spem animo concipere, se tanta usurum regni sui tranquillitate, ut a conten- tionibus & litibus populi immunis sit: cum impe- ria in eum finem sint instituta, ut lites & contentio- nes subditorum audiant & componant. Præterea cum David morti vicinus ἐπινίκιον condiderit, qua ratione sibi demum polliceretur, se fore caput & regem gentium, & quidem earum, quas non nove- rit? Absurdum denique longe absurdissimum foret, Davidem adeo sibi blandiri, ut persuadere animo suo non dubitet, gentes ab Israelitica religione alie- nas, sponte sibi obtemperaturas & ad auditum nominis Davidici obsequium præstituras; cum vix armis & carceribus populos terræ Palæstinæ edomare potuerit. Hæc B. Gesnerus: è quibus quum una eademque persona per totum Psalmum loquatur, invicte probari potest, antecedentia etiam de Chri- sto, non vero de Davide intelligenda esse. Conten- tiones etiam Hieronymus de contradictionibus, qui- bus sese Christo opponebant Judæi, & doctrinæ Evan- gelii contradicebant, ipsumque Messiam esse per- negabant, Augustinus de iis, quæ circa passionem Christi facta sunt, exposuit, cum etiam in crucem suspenso scelerata turba illusit: quorum explicatio- ni calculum adjicit Gesnerus. Quod additur v. 45. Auditu auris obtemperabunt mihi, recte idem expo- nit de modo & ratione, qua gentes ab idolorum suorum servitio ad Christi obedientiam perventu- ræ sint: Audient Evangelium & credent: Fides enim est ex auditu, Rom. 10. Laus ista gentium ex- probratio magna est Judæorum, ait Cassiodorus: ser- vierunt enim, qui non viderunt: obtemperarunt, qui- bus ex ore ejus sacratissima minime verba sonuerunt. Et ad ea, quæ porro subjiciuntur, filii alieni mentiti sunt mihi: Filios, inquit, vocat Judæos propter ,,carnalem eorum ortum & nativitatem: sunt ,,enim semen Abrahæ; quia vero fidem Abrahæ ,,respuerunt, ideo nominat filios separationis seu ,,defectionis & degeneres. Quamvis enim glo- ,,riantur se esse filios Abraham & Dei, tamen juste ,,audiunt à Christo, Johann. 8. Vos ex patre dia- ,,bolo estis. Defectionem autem populi & filiorum ,,suorum nominat vocabulo generali, Mendacium: ,,Quia sicut diabolus pater ipsorum, ita ipsi quo- ,,que in veritate non steterunt. Chaldaicus in- ,,terpres ita reddidit: Mentiti sunt in præsentia ,,mea: Quod sane illorum peccatum exaggerat; ,,siquidem ipsius filii Dei conspectum non sunt ,,veriti: Et non modo Prophetas, tanquam lega- ,,tos, sed ipsum etiam Dominum contemserunt, & ,,cruci affixerunt. Denique quæ de pœna Judæo- rum hic vaticinatur Christus, Filii separationis dece- dent & expavescent è carceribus suis, ita explicat B. Gesnerus, quod priora quidem pœnam tempora- lem, quod exscindendi sint à Romanis, posteriora autem spiritualem & æternam exponant, nomine carcerum & vinculorum, in quibus æternum dole- bunt. Unde mirari oportet, quod vers. 47. & re- liquis B. Gesnerus de Davide interpretetur, quum non agnoverit tantum, vers. 44. 45. 46. non posse de Davide exponi, atque fassus sit, vers. 47. Patres UNO ore ad Christum resurgentem referre, Augusti- num etiam & reliquos hæc verba Christo tribuere, q. d. A Judæis insurgentibus in me patientem exalta- bis me resurgentem, sed etiam admittat vers. 50. Pro- pterea celebrabo te inter gentes Domine, & nomini tuo psallam, de regno Christi agere: quia de vocatio- ne gentium eundem Paulus interpretatur Rom. 15, 9. & versu ultimo, Magnificans salutes regis sui, per Regem Christum intelligat, & salutem multiplicem à Christo præstitam designari admittat. Nam quod iterum monendum, utpote è Psalmo eviden- tissimum, una tantum persona est, quæ in hoc Psal- mo loquitur, quæ si vers. 44. 45. 46. Christus est, in reliquis Davidem loqui statuere haud licebit: ne- que constabit sibi Apostolica demonstratio, Rom. 15, 9. pro gentium vocatione in N. Testam. adducta è præsenti loco, si hæc David de se dixisse asseratur: Nam ita recepisset David morti jam vicinus, se in- ter gentes Dominum celebraturum, quod nihil fa- cit ad vocationem gentium probandam, quæ Judæis reprobatis N. Test. tempore futura erat. Unde alii Regulam illam hic adhibent, quod Christus sibi quandoque adscribat ea, quæ fidelium membrorum suo- rum sunt, ob mysticam capitis & corporis unionem, ut Matth. 25, 40. Actor. 9, 4. 5. Lyranus vero & Thomas sic exponunt: Confitebor tibi in gentibus, id est, faciam per Spiritum S. ut gentes tibi confiteantur confessione fidei, quæ locum non haberent, nisi Christus ipse hic loqueretur.

## 18:21
Ver. 22. NOR HAVE I DONE WICKEDLY FROM MY GOD) That is, against my God. Thus the particle מ is sometimes taken for against, as in Cant. 3:8 and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 22. NEC IMPIE GESSI A DEO MEO) Id est, contra Deum meum. Sic particula מ sumitur interdum pro contra, ut Cant. 3, 8. & alibi.

## 18:26
Vers. 27. WITH THE ELECT YOU WILL BE ELECT, AND WITH THE PERVERSE YOU WILL BE PERVERTED) You act candidly with the candid, you walk obliquely with the one walking obliquely. From Levit. 26, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 27. CVM ELECTO ELECTVS ERIS, ET CVM PERVERSO PERVERTERIS) Cum candido agis candide, cum oblique incedente oblique incedis. Ex Levit. 26, 23.

## 18:34
Vers. 35. AND YOU HAVE PLACED AS A BRAZEN BOW MY ARMS) From the Greek ἔθε τόξον χαλκᾶν τὼς βραχίονας με. They read, of course, נחת, not as we do now נחתה.

But that it was written otherwise in approved Codices at the time of the LXX does not follow from the fact that they rendered it otherwise, which is a fallacy of Grotius we have often noted; Grotius seems to have been seduced here by Bellarmine in this passage, who likewise says the Hebrew reading is corrupt here. Felix rendered the Hebrew text thus: And the brazen bow is crushed by my arms, that is, by my strength the power of those who seemed invincible like a brazen bow was broken. Which sense Genebrardus also praises. Others explain the brazen bow as war instruments being crushed by the arms of David: Piscator, the Italian, the Genevan version, Sixtinus Amama, etc. Junius, Aldegond, and the English rendered it a steel bow: but Drusius in his Hebrew questions shows that steel was not in use at that time in the making of weapons. Concerning which see also Genebrardus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ET POSVISTI VT ARCVM ÆREVM BRA- CHIA MEA) Ex Græco ἔθε τόξον χαλκᾶν τὼς βραχίονας με. Legerunt nimirum נחת, non ut nos nunc נחתה.

At secus scriptum fuisse in Codicibus proba- tis tempore τῶν ὁ non sequitur ex eo, quod hi se- cus reddiderunt, quem paralogismum Grotii sæpe notavimus, seductus hic videtur à Bellarm. in hoc loco Grotius, qui pariter Ebræam lectio- nem corruptam hic dicit. Felix ita reddidit E- bræum textum: Et contritus est arcus æneus bra- chiis meis, id est, fortitudine mea fracta est potentia illorum, qui ut arcus æneus videbantur invicti. Quem sensum laudat etiam Genebrardus. De arcu æneo, instrumentis bellicis brachiis Davidis conterendis alii explicant: Piscator, Italic. Genev. versio, Sixt. Amama &c. Chalybeum arcum reddi- dere Jun. Aldegond. Angli: sed Drusius in quæst. Hebr. ostendit, in conficiendis armis chalybem in usu tum non fuisse. De quo etiam vid. Genebrard. ad hunc locum.

## 18:43
Vers. 44. THE SONS OF THE ALIEN HAVE LIED TO ME) They flattered me against their will.

Latin:

Vers. 44. FILII ALIENI MENTITI SVNT MIHI) Blanditi mihi sunt animo invito.

## 18:45
Vers. 46. AND THEY HAVE HALTED FROM THEIR PATHS) In the Hebrew: They will be terrified from their inner chambers. They will hold their own refuges suspect. Some prefer in the Hebrew, מסגרותיהם, that is, from their swords. For also below 35, 3, some translate סגור as sword: σαγάγεις or σάγαρος are Persian swords according to Herodotus, Xenophon, and others.

It is not in our power to change letters and consequently the words themselves, for the substitution or omission of one letter in place of another changes the word and the sense of Scripture. Nor is there any cause here for variation, although no sufficient cause can ever be found for varying the sacred text. The sense is plain in itself, whether you explain it with the Vulgate concerning the evil of fault, they have halted from their paths, or with Jerome concerning the evil of punishment, they will be contracted in their straits, or as Pagninus rendered it, they will be terrified from their prisons. And that same word occurs similarly in the parallel passage 2 Sam. 22, 46, in which, however, if it is compared with this Psalm, Abarbenel counted seventy-four differences, but without suspicion of error. See Buxtorf, Vindic. verb. Ebr. p. 475.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ET CLAVDICAVERUNT A SEMITIS SUIS) In Hebræo: Pavescent a penetralibus suis. Ipsa sua suffu- gia suspecta habebunt, Quidam malunt in Hebræo, מסגרותיהם, id est, a gladiis suis. Nam & infra 35,3. סגור quidam vertunt gladium: σαγάγεις vel σάγαρος gladii Persici Herodoto, Xenophonti & aliis.

Non est in nostro arbitrio literas & consequen- ter dictiones ipsas immutare, unius enim literæ loco alterius substitutio vel omissio dictionem & sensum Scripturæ mutat. Nec ulla causa hic est variationis, quamvis textum sacrum variandi nul- la unquam sufficiens causa inveniri possit. Sensus est per se planus, sive cum Vulgato de malo culpæ exponas, claudicaverunt à semitis suis, sive cum Hie- ronymo de malo pœnæ, contrahentur in angustiis suis, aut ut Pagninus reddidit, expavescent à carceribus suis. Et occurrit eadem illa vox similiter in loco parallelo 2. Sam. 22, 46. in quo tamen si cum hoc Psalmo conferatur, Abarbenel numeravit septua- ginta quatuor differentias, sed absque suspicione erroris. Vid. Buxtorff. Vindic. verb. Ebr. p. 475.

## 19:1 Argument
PSALM XIX. The universal proclamation of the Gospel and its eulogy.

Latin:

PSALMUS XIX. Universale Evangelii præconium ejusque elo- gium.

## 19:3
Ver. 4.

THERE ARE NO SPEECHES, NOR WORDS, WHOSE VOICES ARE NOT HEARD) Better: there is no speech for them, nor words: but without (these, of course) their voice is understood, namely the signification of divine wisdom.

The Latin translation here is corrected without cause. For the Hebrew words are rightly rendered, which κατὰ πόδα are thus: No speech, and no words (sc. there are) whose voice is not heard. And the LXX Interpreters render this sense. For the Hebrews are accustomed to understand the pronoun אשר: to whom also the particle בלי often signifies THAT NOT, or without; whence it can be explained, that their voice is not heard, or without hearing the voice. Chrysostom, Hom. 9 to the Antiochians: there is no nation, nor language, which cannot understand this voice. The interpretation of Grotius is plainly arbitrary, and interpolated. For in the former clause he adds the pronoun FOR THEM, which is not held in the Hebrew, as if the speech were about the heavens, when it is said absolutely, that there is no speech, no words, or no language under heaven, sc. In the latter, the pronoun THESE is added again, as if the heavens were said to be heard without speech, without words. Finally, the word נשמע which imports heard, is explained by understood: not to mention that there is a contradiction in the words. For that there are no words FOR THEM, and yet their words or voices are understood, do not agree well enough. But that exposition pleases Grotius, lest these things be understood of the proclamation of the Apostles, of which most of our people explain the words of the Psalmist, following the lead of Augustine and other Fathers of the Church. But we are about to speak of the true sense of the Psalm presently. Augustine has it thus regarding these words: Read the Acts of the Apostles, how when the Holy Spirit came upon them they were all filled with Him: and they spoke in the languages of all nations, as the Spirit gave them to pronounce. Behold, there are no speeches, nor words, whose voices are not heard. But they did not sound only there where they were filled, their sound went out into all the earth. Thus, therefore, Augustine explains these things particularly concerning the feast of Pentecost. In the former exposition of the Psalm, however, he accepts them generally: Through whom were the voices of the Evangelists not heard, when they preached the Gospel in all languages?

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NON SVNT LOQVELÆ, NEQVE SERMONES, QVORVM NON AVDIANTVR VOCES EORVM) Melius: non est illis sermo, neque verba: at sine (his scilicet) intelligitur vox eorum, nempe significatio divinæ sapientiæ.

TRanslatio Latina hic citra causam corrigitur. Recte enim Ebræa redduntur, quæ κατὰ πό- δα ita habent: Non sermo, & non verba (sc. sunt) quorum non audiatur vox illorum. Atque hunc sen- fum reddunt LXX. Interpp. Solent enim Ebræi subintelligere pronomen אשר: quibus & particula בלי significat sæpe UT NON, vel absq́;: unde ex- poni potest, ut non audiatur vox illorum, vel absque audire vocem. Chrysostom. Hom. 9. ad Antioch. non est gens, neque lingua, quæ hanc vocem intelligere non possit. Interpretatio Grotii plane arbitraria est, atque interpolata. Nam in priori inciso addit pro- nomen ILLIS, quod in Ebræo non habetur, ac si de cælis sermo sit, quum absolute dicatur, nullum esse sermonem, nulla verba, vel nullam linguam sub cœlo sc. In posteriori iterum additur pronomen HIS, ac si sine sermone, sine verbis cæli au diri dice- rentur. Denique verbum נשמע quod auditum im- portat, per intelligi explicatur: ut taceam, quod contradictio verbis insit. Nam non esse ILLIS ver- ba, & intelligi tamen ipsorum verba vel voces, non satis bene conveniunt. Placet autem illa expositio Grotio, ne hæc de præconio Apostolorum intelli- gantur, de quo verba Psaltis plerique nostrates ex- plicant, præeunte Augustino, & aliis Ecclesiæ Pa- tribus. Sed de vero sensu Psalmi jamjam dicturi sumus. Augustinus ad hæc verba ita habet: Legite Actus Apostolorum, quomodo veniente super eos Spir. Sancto omnes impleti sunt illo: & loquebantur linguis omnium gentium, sicut Spiritus dabat eis pro- nunciare. Ecce non sunt loquelæ, neque sermones, quo- rum non audiantur voces eorum. Sed non ibi tantum ubi impleti sunt, sonnerunt, in omnem terram exiit sonus eorum. Ita ergo explicat ista Augustinus pe- culiariter de festo Pentecostes. In priori tamen Psal- mi expositione generaliter ea accipit: Per quos non auditæ sunt Evangelistarum voces, cum omnibus lin- guis Evangelium prædicarent?

## 19:4
Ver. 5. INTO ALL THE EARTH THEIR SOUND WENT OUT) It appears there was once a double reading קום which we now have in the Hebrew, whence also κανὼν is with Aquila, a metaphor taken from architects: and קולם whence the LXX placed ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν, whom Paul follows, Rom. 10. v. 8, with a certain similarity taken from the stars to the Apostles, just as here the Syrian and the Arab, both Christians. Chrysostom, just as it is read here in the Greek, cites this whole passage, in a speech that Christ is God.

Latin:

Vers. 5. IN OMNEM TERRAM EXIVIT SONVS EO- RVM) Apparet olim duplicem fuisse lectionem קום quod nunc in Hebræo habemus, unde & κανὼν est apud Aquilam metaphorâ ab Architectis sumta: & קולם unde LXX. po- suere ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν, quos sequitur, similitudine quadam ab astris ad Apostolos desumta, Paulus Rom. 10. v. 8. quo- modo & hic Syrus & Arabs, ambo Christiani. Chrysosto- mus, ita ut hic in Græco legitur, citat totum hunc locum, ora- tione Christum esse Deum.

## 19:5
Ver. 6.

IN THE SUN HE SET HIS TABERNACLE) In the Hebrew: He set a tabernacle for the sun in them, supply heavens. He gave it a magnificent dwelling. A similar comparison Psalm 104. ver. 2.

AS A BRIDEGROOM PROCEEDING FROM HIS CHAMBER) From the nuptial bed, the likeness of which that canopy refers to, under which the bridegroom and bride receive the blessing in the Synagogue, thence called חפה.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

IN SOLE POSVIT TABERNACVLVM SVVM) In Hebræo. Soli posuit tabernaculum in eis, supple cælis. Magni- ficam ei habitationem dedit. Par similitudo Psalm. 104. vers. 2.

TANQVAM SPONSVS PROCEDENS DE THA- LAMO SVO) De lecto nuptiali, cujus similitudinem re- fert umbraculum illud, sub quo sponsus & sponsa benedictio- nem in Synagoga accipiunt, inde dictum חפה.

## 19:6
Ver. 7. HE EXULTED AS A GIANT TO RUN THE WAY) In the Hebrew: as a mighty one, that is, just as men who are princes run with swift horses.

Two things are to be noted here: First, concerning the reading; which Grotius establishes as double without sufficient cause. For it does not follow that, because the LXX translated it Φθόγγος (sound), the Hebrew text at that time had קולם: for the Greeks could have rendered it thus, having considered not the reading of the word, but the sense, and being moved by the other word מליהם which denotes a word, whether uttered by the mouth or written, Dan. 2. v. 9. Joh. 19. vers. 32. as observed by our Dn. D. Weller in his Commentary on Romans 10. vers. 18. For they did not always render the original text word for word, as is evident from innumerable examples. Concerning which we have treated copiously and diligently in the Critici Sacri. And because it made no difference to the sense which word was used, whether κανών or φθόγγος, Paul retained the received version, as was generally done in the New Testament, because the doctrine of the Apostles is the line, the plumb line, and the rule of all dogmas in the Church, as Genebrardus says here, whom the Syrian and Arab followed here in the Psalms. The Papists themselves acknowledge this. Let us hear Lorinus: It is possible, he says, that by looking to the sense, even if the LXX read קוָם they preferred to render it as sound, as Eugubinus and Genebrardus teach, and furthermore Titelmannus, Briedenbachius, and Malvenda, whom I read later. Similarly Martin Delrio Adag. 724. I do not think the LXX and Paul read קוֹלָם but called the sound itself the preaching, which is in truth the plumb line of the heavenly building. And it is the true Prophetic sense of that place. Simeon de Muis observes that this word קוָם also conveys the meaning of sound. Nor indeed, he says, does the Hebrew word קו which the Psalmist uses here differ: For among other things it also signifies that sound which a line or a level makes when it is extended by carpenters over wood and released. Whence he concludes against other Papists: Who therefore could bear what is commonly said, that the Greek interpreter, St. Jerome, the holy Apostle also, and Symmachus had קוֹלָם instead of קוָם in their codices. Isaac Levita, a German converted Jew, preceded Muysius, who although a Papist, opposed an erudite defense of the Hebrew truth to William Lindanus, Bishop of Utrecht, from which, because those things that pertain to this are very rare, it will not be a burden to bring forward: But perhaps you will object, how does it happen that the Apostle Paul, the Seventy, and St. Jerome translated: Their sound. Truly this matter, to confess frankly, sometimes tormented me too. But an annotation on the Psalter by a certain learned man, and as I hear, Vatablus, a Professor at Paris, removed the scruple from me in part, whose words are these: Or their level, that is, their structure made to a level, this is, in the furthest parts of the earth that fabric of the heavenly bodies is seen as if made to a level, which is in place of words. What is said here about the heavens, Paul at Rom. cap. 10. adapts by allegory to the Apostles, who did not otherwise celebrate and preach the power and majesty of GOD in the whole world than that most accurate structure of the heavens speaks and declares to men living everywhere on earth. This opinion of Vatablus, although it pleases me greatly, yet I think we have also found something else, from which it may easily appear why they expressed קו by sound or voice. If pious and learned men will consider the words of this Psalm, and examine them more exactly, they will discover in all the verses כֶפֶל לָשׁוֹן בְּמִלִּוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת that is, the same thing always repeated with a different word, which has almost the same meaning as the preceding, such as הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַפְּרִים The heavens declare, מַגִּיד הָרָקִיעַ The firmament announces, יַבִּיעַ אוֹמֶר It pours forth speech, יְחַוֶּה דָּעַת it indicates knowledge, etc. Therefore, since in all the verses an iteration of the same sentiment, but with different words, is discovered, it is necessary that here too קו should have some kinship with מִלָּה and conversely מִלָּה with קו. For if this were not so, that elegance which is seen in all the other little verses would seem to have been omitted here. It is necessary therefore that קו, besides other known meanings, should also have another one now unknown to many. But it is known and common that קו signifies hope, congregation, rule, standard, line and outline, small cord, plumb line, or the stone of the plumb line. Besides these, I say, it is necessary to have another notion, which may have קול, that is, a voice, or at least התוך דבר, that is, an expression of some voice. The Chaldean paraphrase in chapter 28 of Isaiah on the words קו לקו also confirms this opinion, if one weighs it more diligently. We see also that the plumb line, which consists of a cord, is not entirely lacking a voice. For architects and other craftsmen, when they wish to mark or measure something, while they extend the plumb line or cord, and then release it, are accustomed to emit a certain sound. From which fact it is confirmed that קו also has another notion, commonly not so well known to the Hebrews, and that it represents either קור, or certainly התוך קור, so that a relationship and affinity between קו and מקר may exist. But since this is known to few, they suspect that the Apostle, the LXX, and D. Jerome read it otherwise than קום by some error. and D. Jerome read it otherwise than קום by some error. This opinion of ours, if it has been approved by anyone, he may seize upon it; if not, we allow everyone their own free judgment, provided they do not dare to violate the text itself. See the Cœlum Orientis of B. D. Bangius, page 52, who makes the radical and common meaning of the words קו and Φθόγγος canonical, and the gnomonic drawing of a thing from one extreme to another, in which he elegantly teaches that this canon and sound agree: (1.) As a linear straight rule is drawn from one point through the middle to be measured to another as the limit of measurement, and as a sound emitted by a sounding object permeates various places before it ceases, so the proclamation of the saving Gospel, emitted by God through the voices of the Apostles and Disciples, flowed through all the ends and extremities of the world. (2) Just as a plumb line let down straight from the upper parts of buildings being constructed, by an equal balance of weight, ensures that their integrity and beauty remain for all, so that the structure suffers nothing crooked or disordered; indeed, just as sound emitted from colliding bodies, pneumatic organs, and other solid sounding objects is carried with speed and spontaneous motion to the ears, affects them in various ways, soothes, moves, and excites various emotions in the minds of men, which is recorded to have happened to Saul in 1 Sam. 17, verses 14, 15, 16, etc., who, troubled by an evil spirit, not only felt relief from the Davidic harp with its sweet melody (ibid. verse 23), but also, with David playing the strings, the vexation of the evil spirit ceased: So the sound of the Gospel and the divine word, having proceeded from the mouth of the men of God, not only tends straight to the wide-open gates of the ears, but also sweetly affects them. (3) Not otherwise than as a plumb line exists as a certain sign of things to be measured, and ὁ Φθόγγος is an indication of the thoughts and ideas which pre-existed in the mind of the craftsman before his hand was applied to the work: so the sound of the Evangelical doctrine claims this proper praise for itself, that it may sound forth a λόγον ἔυσημον (well-signifying word) to the ears and minds of the hearers, 1 Cor. 14, verse 9. (4) As a rule, for the sake of ἐυταξίας (good order), is not applied to buildings and all things to be measured at one moment, but is applied now to one part and soon to another to be inserted and combined ἐυκαίρως, καὶ ἐυτάκτως (opportunely and orderly): in like manner, the human voice recognizes its ordinary organs, first, middle, and last, and therefore consists of its own articulations, which instruments placed in or added to the mouth produce. (5) Architects gradually unroll their coiled linear plumb line from its casings, and once unrolled, they turn and apply it until the thread has δεικτικῶς (demonstratively) marked the gnomon, which furthermore, showing the obliquity of the work, provides the architect an opportunity to amend it and to begin thinking about finding the straightness of the structure. Sound, destined to serve the sense of hearing, by no means completes its task with the first impulse or the neighboring part of the air, but the impulse of further succeeding aerial parts will be needed before it can be perceived by empty ears. Beat. Bangius applies this to the perpendicular canon of the Evangelical sound, and excellently shows its revolving turns and series. Genebrardus imagines an apocope of קו for קולם, but without example, and Sim. de Muys also rejects it for that reason. It also seems possible to say that the LXX repeated the word φθόγγος from the preceding verse. That it was read formerly, as it is now, is testified not only by the version of Aquila, but also by the Chaldean translation, as the Masora itself teaches, which, by the note ל added to that word, indicates that it no longer exists, which could not be said of the word קולם. Add also Aben Ezra, who says of this word: That is, Scripture or direction: as in a book lines teach: so in the heavens the whole world reads the power of God. And R. David Kimchi, their line, that is, the structure, because a building is made by a line.

The other concerns the sense: about which there is a greater difficulty because of the Pauline passage. Grotius wishes that only a certain similarity was taken by Paul from the stars to the Apostles: which he explains thus at Romans 10, verse 18. The starry heaven is in one place, and yet its voice and words are heard everywhere, that is, its power is understood. In like manner, since the Apostles were in the more illustrious cities, and preached everywhere, and performed miracles, as in Jerusalem, Caesarea, Joppa, Antioch, Ephesus, Corinth, Thessalonica, from there the fame of such great things reached all the lands in which the Jews lived, and that is sufficient. This gloss is too cold. The Apostle is not doing this, to teach that it is sufficient that the Apostles preached in the more illustrious cities, or to compare the universal proclamation of the heavens in that way, that just as it, remaining in one place, seems to emit words everywhere, so the Apostles, subsisting in certain places, scattered the word of the Gospel everywhere with fame flying through the world. And what would be so exceptional about this compared to ancient times? For could not the same be said of the proclamation under the Old Testament, which, sounding from one place in Jerusalem or through Palestine, spread its fame from there through the whole world? The grace exhibited under the New Testament is described far differently, both in this and in other places of Scripture, in that not only the report about the Apostles, but the sound of the Apostles, or the word from which faith is conceived—which certainly cannot be conceived from report alone—has gone out into all the earth; and that no doubt may remain, it is immediately explained concerning the word of the Gospel, when it is added: καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκεμένης τὰ ῥήματα ἀυτῶν. And to the very ends of the world, or of the universe, their words, namely, the Apostles'. That the Gospel reached the whole world, and was preached to every creature which is under heaven Col. 1, 6. 23. just as Paul testifies concerning himself, that he preached the Gospel from Jerusalem through all the neighboring regions as far as Illyricum Rom. 15. verse 19. and Christ commanded the Apostles, whom He sent into the whole world, to announce the Gospel to every creature Matt. 28. verse 19. Mark 16. verse 15. The Fathers most close to the age of the Apostles also testified concerning this. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho, page 270: 'And yet there is not even one race of mortals, whether of barbarians or of Greeks, or even of all others by whatever name they are called, whether of Hamaxobii, or of Nomads lacking a home, or of those living in tents (Scenitae) and sustaining their life by cattle, among whom supplications and thanksgivings are not made to the Father and Maker of all things through the name of the crucified Jesus.' These things Justin wrote from the age of the Apostles. Irenaeus, in that age, in book 1, against Heresies, chapter 2, says that the Church, sown throughout the whole world even to the ends of the earth, is from the Apostles and from their disciples. And in chapter 3, he testifies that the Gospel was EVERYWHERE throughout the whole world, just as the sun shines in the whole world. This preaching, he says, and this faith, when the Church has received it, although disseminated throughout the WHOLE WORLD, she guards it diligently, as if inhabiting one house, and believes these things similarly, namely as if having one soul and one heart, and consonantly preaches and teaches and hands them down, as if possessing one mouth. For although in the world languages are different, yet the power of the tradition is one and the same. And neither do these Churches which have been founded in Germany believe otherwise, or hand down otherwise, nor those which are among the Iberians, nor those which are among the Celts, nor those which are in the East, nor those which are in Egypt, nor those which are in Libya, nor those which are established in the middle of the world: But as the sun, the creature of God, is one and the same in the whole world, so also the light, the preaching of the truth, shines EVERYWHERE, and illuminates all men who wish to come to the knowledge of the truth. Tertullian, who flourished a little later in Africa, against the Jews, c. 7. For whose right hand, he says, does God the Father hold, if not Christ his Son? whom all nations have heard, i.e., whom all nations have believed, whose preachers also the Apostles are shown to be in the Psalms of David: their sound, he says, has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. For in whom else have all nations believed, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Armenia, Pamphylia, Cappadocia, and the dwellers in Pontus, and Asia and Phrygia, those staying in Egypt and the region of Africa which is beyond Cyrene, the Romans and the inhabitants: then also in Jerusalem the Jews and other nations, so that now the varieties of the Gaetuli, and the many borders of the Moors, all the ends of the Spains, and the diverse nations of the Gauls, and the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans, but truly subject to Christ, and of the Sarmatians and Dacians and Germans, and Scythians and many hidden nations and provinces and many islands unknown to us and which we are less able to enumerate. In which ALL PLACES the name of Christ, who has already come, NOW REIGNS. This, in his own time, Tertullian already in the second century after the departure of the Apostles. We do not now bring forward others: It is sufficiently clear from these how falsely the universal proclamation is restricted to only certain and illustrious places, from whence fame might have penetrated into others. What of the fact that that proposition of comparison from the heaven is quite inept, that it, remaining in one place, announces the glory of God everywhere. For the heaven is diffused through the whole world, and encompasses the whole earth, and does not stick only in a certain part of the world, so that the remaining regions lack its sight, as they all enjoy it equally, whence everywhere in the same manner it is present to announce the glory of God.

But if it be asked, how the Apostolic allegation stands, and what is the proper sense of the words of the Psalmist? I find three main opinions concerning the Apostolic passage. The first is that the Apostle in Romans 10, verse 18, treats only of the knowledge of God revealed to the nations in the workmanship of the world, of which it is discussed in Romans 1 and Acts 14, and that he brings forward the Psalm for that reason, because the same thing is said in the same, that God had already in past ages revealed his glory in the most beautiful volume of the heaven, and that this was a prelude to a fuller doctrine. Which is the gloss of Calvin. But it is deservedly chastised by the blessed Gesner in Psalm 19, as a violent corruption of the Pauline text, as he discusses most openly the means and organ by which we obtain faith, which is the preaching of the Gospel. Mercerus, however, embraced it, nor did he hesitate to refer the relative OF THEM, in the Apostle, as in the Psalm, to the heavens, whose doctrine no one has not heard, but against the Apostolic text entirely; in which there is no mention of THE HEAVENS, but the pronoun OF THEM refers openly to the Apostles. Vasquez the Jesuit does not only approve that explanation, with this paraphrase given in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 10. Can it be said that the nations did not hear at all, so that recognizing at least one GOD they could call upon him? Since the heavens declare and preach the glory of God, and the firmament announces his works, and their sound has gone out into all the earth. But he contends also in the first part, Disp. 97, quest. 5, that it follows from thence that the nations cannot be destitute of sufficient aid for believing and for salvation. Nor is Jansenius alien to that explanation in this place of the Psalm. But it is too clear from the whole context that Paul is discussing the revelation of the Gospel, not natural knowledge, and therefore, so that this scope of the Apostle may not be neglected, Beza in Romans 10 and Rivetus in this Psalm explain the allegation a little differently; that Paul indeed understands the Davidic words concerning the universal vocation which is made through creatures, but concludes from thence, since God has revealed himself to all, however remote, through creatures, there is no doubt that the Jews also were called by God in suitable ways: or he connects an argument from a like case: if the voice of the heavens once went out into all the earth, why not also today the voice of the Gospel: or from the lesser, how much more the voice of the Gospel? But there is no evidence for that argument, so that another argument would be needed to show the consequence, if any consequence is in it, lest it be said that a begging of the question was committed, or that an obscure thing was proved from an equally obscure one. The explanation of others is more correct, who wish the Apostle to use this Davidic testimony through a certain accommodation to his purpose, so that it may be truly said of the preaching of the Gospel what David sang of the heavens and the expanse, namely that its sound and words had penetrated to the ends of the world and could be heard by all. But two things are opposed to this opinion by Rivetus. First, that such an accommodation or rather allusion, where especially there is a certain analogy and similarity, may indeed often be in use, but hardly where there is need of confirmation and argument as in this place. Then, that Paul would have spoken untimely then, that the voice of the Gospel had been heard in the whole world from the mouth of the Apostles, which had scarcely reached a few at that time. But to answer the καθ' ὕστερον πρότερον; the latter openly contradicts the Apostle here, asserting both in this place and in Colossians 1 that universal preaching had already been done at that time, and it accuses the Apostles of negligence, because they had not executed the command of Christ given in Matthew 28, verse 19: the former, however, can be easily resolved if it is said that Paul is not proving here that the Gospel has been preached to every creature, but is assuming it as notorious and illustrating it with Davidic words, having accommodated them to the voice of the Gospel, so that he may teach at the same time how illustrious the grace of the New Testament is, since the sound of the Apostles has gone out into all the earth just as the heaven announces the glory of God throughout all the earth. It can also be said that the Apostle uses the words of the present Psalm for this matter all the more willingly, because in it David moves from manifestation through the creature to revelation through the word

Comparing himself to the work of God, he might easily have hinted at a comparison, of which comparison instituted by the Prophet, or if not expressly, at least tacitly indicated, the Apostle acted as interpreter regarding this member, concerning the amplitude of the proclamation of the word, and thus at the same time taught how certainly the delineation and documents of the heavens went forth into all the earth, just as certainly in these times the doctrine of the Gospel has flowed into the whole world through the preaching of the Apostles. To which returns the explanation of Franc. Junius in his sacred parallels, not easily to be rejected: certainly in many ways to be preferred to the Calvinian glosses.

But thirdly, most think that Paul brought forward the words of David for the sake of proof, and accepted them concerning the universal proclamation of the Apostles: which opinion can be explained in two ways: First, that it may be said that David, according to the literal sense and directly intended, deals in this Psalm only with the doctrine of the Gospel: and by the heavens understands the Apostles through a figurative manner of speaking, since the pronoun THEIR refers itself in the word קוָם to the preceding noun, since no other occurs in the text, except of the heavens, and the words, THEIR LINE or SOUND, are understood of the Apostles and their proclamation, whence nothing seems more certain than that by the heavens the same Apostles are designated, and by the announcement of divine glory the announcement of the Gospel, in which the glory of divine wisdom, justice, and grace has been made manifest throughout the world. Induced by this argument, our blessed Luther, Bugenhagen, and Gesner in this Chair, Brentius in the Wurtemberg Church, and most others have expounded the words of the Psalm figuratively, along with Augustine and other ancient Doctors of the Church. The Psalm, says our Bugenhagen, speaks manifestly of the Gospel spread throughout the whole world. For Paul cites it in Romans 10, not concerning celestial spectacles, but very manifestly concerning the vocal word or the Gospel preached in the whole world: And in a later commentary; those visible heavens, stars, day, night, the Sun, are divine spectacles, in which we behold the glory of the creator and his admirable works, Romans 1. But why does he not add here the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, as he is accustomed, why is there mention here only of the heavens? Therefore the divine spirit plays here too with his figures, who also sometimes created all things and from eternity saw a new world, sometimes to be, and the kingdom of the heavens on earth, of which read Isaiah 65, verse 66, and you will rejoice: whence here this kingdom of the heavens is declared to be ruled by the word, while it is said of declaring the glory of God, of announcing the works of God, of the pouring forth of the word, of announcing knowledge, of hearing voices in all languages and in all lands, not to mention in the meantime what is added concerning the immaculate law of the Lord, etc. And Paul opened to us the meaning of this Psalm in Romans 10, where he cites the verse concerning the preachers of Christ: Their sound went into all the earth, etc. Therefore here you see a new world in the Spirit after Pentecost, which they call, when through the Spirit sent from the heavens, the glory of the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord was declared, and the wonders of God, the word, the Spirit, and the knowledge of the Scriptures were preached to all nations and languages, with illumination shining everywhere, and Christ, the Sun of justice, kindling through the Spirit, when that was fulfilled which he promised in the previous Psalm, therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord, etc. Then the law of the Lord, hitherto unbearable, became the sweet yoke of Christ, and a light burden, desirable above everything, both riches and delights, namely, the Spirit of Christ having been given by the Father into the hearts of believers. Who, because there still remains in them something of the flesh, and thus sin in the flesh, have need, even after having received grace, to always cry out, who understands his faults? Thus piously and elegantly our blessed predecessor summed up the sum of the Psalm: similarly blessed Brentius; these things indeed seem to be said concerning that narration and announcement by which the glory and majesty of God is made manifest and illustrated from the creatures of this world. But the authority of the Apostle Paul calls us elsewhere. Therefore what David says is this: the heavens, that is, the Apostles excited by a heavenly calling, adorned with the heavenly Spirit, declare the glory of GOD, namely, the Gospel concerning Christ: And the firmament (expansion) those same Apostles, by whose doctrine the Church has been founded and strengthened and extended or divulged into the whole world, announce the works of the hands of God, because through the Gospel of the Apostles the redemption of the human race from sin, death, and hell is announced through Christ the Son of God. Which work is no less a miracle than the creation of heaven and earth. Moreover, this work of redemption is announced through the Gospel, not only during the day, but day and night, etc. Isaiah also alludes to this (chapter 60) when he preaches concerning the Church of Christ: Your gates will be opened continually, they will not be shut day and night, etc. Mr. Brentius treats this at greater length, and thus also explains what is held concerning the sun: He has set a tabernacle for the sun in them, namely, in the Apostles. For the Apostles were divinely ordained for this purpose, that they might be the tabernacle or tent of the Sun, that is, in whose Gospel the true Sun, who is Christ, might dwell, and be carried around through the whole world. For the very same reason blessed Gesner interprets the whole Psalm concerning the preaching of the Gospel, and explains excellently everything that is said concerning the heavens, the firmament, and the Sun in an allegorical sense, and he proves that interpretation, both because most things in this whole Psalm stand in the way of our being able to accept the beginning of the Psalm according to the letter, and because the Apostle manifestly expounded the first part of the Psalm concerning the ministry of the preaching of the Gospel, and that there can be no doubt for anyone that the remaining parts deal with heavenly doctrine, and because the Jews themselves also, as Lyranus observes, accepted the beginning of the Psalm concerning the promulgation of the law on Mount Sinai. And thus Tertullian, book 5 against Marcion, chapter 19, teaches that these things were predicted concerning the preachings of the Gospel: Their sound went into all the earth, etc. And that the Apostles, the preachers of Christ, are shown here in the Psalms of David, in the book against Jud. c. 6. observes, and in that sense Augustine in both expositions of this Psalm interpreted the words of the Psalm. The Evangelists themselves (so the words of St. Augustine hold) in whom God dwells as if in the heavens, express the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is sung of Christ, which EVIDENTLY appears, because it is written there; he himself as a bridegroom proceeds from his chamber. Who is the bridegroom, except he to whom that bride is betrothed, for whom the chaste friend of the bridegroom fears, lest as Eve &c. (2 Cor. 11.) proceeding from the virginal womb, where the bridegroom God was joined to human nature. Which sense of the ancient Church we have expressed in the ancient hymn, Veni Redemtor gentium, recognized by Dr. Luther and approved in our Church, Er gieng aus der Kammer sein, &c. which also the ancient Bibles of the year 1483 expressed. published at Nuremberg, as also at Augsburg in the year 1518, in which this inscription is held: The summary of the Psalm: David recognized in the Spirit, when Christ would be born of his lineage, that the Holy Spirit would be sent to his disciples, who would teach them finally to speak all tongues, and would come into all the world, then he makes this Psalm, prophesying thereof.

But because Basil the Great and Ambrose explain the beginning of the Psalm concerning the declaration of the glory of God, which is through creatures, and that sense concerning the material heavens and the firmament, and also concerning the Sun itself, which by their wonderful magnitude, beauty, motion, and light declare the glory of God throughout the whole world, as Ecclesiasticus 43:2 explains, seems very clear; nor should one depart from the literal sense, unless that the beginning of the Psalm should be understood concerning the manifestation through the works of creation κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν (according to the letter). Whence also from this passage the natural knowledge of God is usually demonstrated against Socinus and his associates, which was also done by us at length in Tom. 2. sup. August. Confess. p. 116. seqq. Therefore, in order that the Apostolic allegation may retain its force and truth, and yet no strength may be lost from the argument which is drawn from this Psalm to bring forward the natural knowledge of God, both of those things can be joined together in explaining this oracle of David: both that the glory of God is announced to the world through nature and the intuition of the works of creation, and that this ought to have been done through the proclamation of the Gospel; not indeed that we should invent a double sense with the Papists, one literal, the other allegorical, and derive Paul's argument from the mystical and allegorical, since there cannot be but one meaning of a single statement, and the allegorical sense, as the trite Rule from Augustine's Epistle to Vincentius holds, is not argumentative, but that it may be said, by alluding to this figurative locution, that the Holy Spirit supposed that which is inferred according to the letter by the same words, in which way there will indeed be only one interpretation of the words of the Hieropsalt, and that is to be understood in a figurative sense from the intention of the Holy Spirit prophesying concerning the proclamation of the Apostles, but the foundation of the metaphor and allegory will here be tacitly supposed in that comparison, since the Apostles are compared to the heavens most of all for this reason, that just as the heavens by their wonderful workmanship everywhere declare the glory of God, so the Apostles and Evangelists by their wonderful Gospel and the proclamation of the Gospel are to announce the glory of God throughout the whole world: just as the Sun goes forth like a Bridegroom to his course, so the Sun of righteousness, Christ, is to go forth. Thus the πρότασις (proposition) will be taken from nature and the book of nature, but the ἀπόδοσις (application) is figured and indicated by this prophecy, so that the reason and foundation of the comparison may be an argument against the Socinians for natural θεογνωσίας (knowledge of God): but the thing itself signified by those figurative locutions is the universal proclamation of the Apostles, which the Apostle demonstrates from the Psalm. For when metaphors are taken from natural things, those things in which the foundation of the comparison is situated are presupposed in nature, and the comparison itself which is instituted strengthens those things and establishes their truth. You have a similar example in Psalm 84:4; indeed, similar examples occur everywhere. For by observing this analogy of explanation in similar places, light is shed upon many sayings of Scripture. And in this sense the interpretation of the Weimar Paraphrasts is to be accepted or admitted, lest anyone believe, in the manner of the Papists, that a double sense is posited in the same statement: Which, having been so accepted, I wish to have been entirely related here: It is helpful, however, to adduce some things from it for the sake of illustration. To verse 1, they have it thus: Just as a natural testimony of the honor, goodness, omnipotence, and wisdom of GOD is presented to us humans in the dear heaven above us: So and much more is it with the preaching office in the New Testament: There the honor of GOD is truly told, and the work of grace of his hands is proclaimed, Psalm 8, verse 4; Psalm 100, verse 3; Ephesians 3, verse 10. There his omnipotence and wisdom are gloriously to be recognized in the destruction of the devil's kingdom, and in the erection of his

Kingdom of Heaven, solely through the Word of the Gospel, without any external violence and power. To verse 5: Just as that which is in the heaven is, as it were, a certain plumb line ordained by GOD the LORD, according to which all creatures direct themselves in time, place, power, and effect: So is the sound of the Apostles, Romans 10, verse 18, and the written Word of GOD the most certain rule and plumb line of all doctrine, religion, faith, divine service, and Christian life among men on earth: And it seems that Mr. Brentius also intends this in the explanation of verse 1, when he discourses so copiously about the external Sun in his Paraphrase: Just as the external Sun dwells in the heaven as in its tabernacle, and rising in the morning, proceeds from the lower hemisphere over the earth, with great and illustrious adornment, the dawn as if golden, like a Bridegroom from his chamber, and walks and progresses to complete its course from the end of the heavens even to the end, that is from the east even to the west, nor is there any place on earth to which the Sun does not cast its rays, or at least its heat or power. It walks, however, not in a common and humble way, not after the manner of captive men, but with great, if I may say so, alacrity and majesty like a giant, or some hero, to whom nothing can stand in the way, which could hinder and delay it from its course. So also it is to be thought concerning Christ the true sun. For he is carried around by the preaching of the Apostles through the whole world, nor does he come in sordid and tattered clothing, but walks like a bridegroom, adorned with many gifts, which he liberally confers upon his Church: nor does he linger in one place only, but runs through the whole earth from the east to the west, nor is there any nation, any people, in which Christ has not been preached.
