And although both Jews and Gentiles contributed whatever strength they had to extirpate the name of Christ and to oppress his Gospel, yet he himself, even against the will of the gates of hell, always proceeds with the greatest alacrity and power like a hero feared by all and unconquered to propagate and defend his Gospel. The Weimar Paraphrase is double: Just as it is with the natural sun: So and much more gloriously is it with the Sun of righteousness, Malachi 4, verse 2. Provided for Christ JESUS: The same has his tabernacles or dwelling in the spiritual heaven of grace, the Christian Church, Psalm 132 v. 13, Isaiah 48 v. 35, 2 Cor. 6 v. 16. He goes out through his Word, and distributes divine light and radiance everywhere, through his saving knowledge, John 1 v. 8, 9, chap. 18 v. 12, Acts of the Apostles 13 v. 47. He is the wondrously beautiful bridegroom of his Christian Church, Psalm 45 v. 2, 3, John 3 v. 29. He is the joyful two-stemmed hero, Psalm 45 v. 4, who has performed his course from the Father into the world, and from the world back to the Father, John 16 v. 28, with willing obedience, and afterwards constantly accomplishes his swift course through the world in his Word, 2 Thessal. 3 v. 1. He is full of lovely warmth of grace, Luke 24 v. 32, from which all believers receive their strength and life-force. All of which we have wished to adduce so laboriously now not without cause, so that we may indeed learn to penetrate more correctly the force of the phrases and sayings of the Holy Spirit: nor, if in allegorical passages some thing is posited by the Holy Spirit, upon which the allegory is built, and in the explanation both are indicated, then the foundation of the allegory or figurative phrase of the Holy Spirit, as well as the sense directly intended by him there, should anyone invent for us a double sense of the same saying; which nowhere in the scriptures do we judge it must be admitted, or, with the sense retained under a figurative expression intended for comparison, and the foundation of the figurative expression, it might call into doubt the truth easily indicated or supposed. Both of which must be avoided. And thus the explanation of B. Luther, Bugenhagen, Brentius, Gesner, Osiander, and others of ours, as well as the ancients Tertullian and Augustine, is in excellent standing; indeed, the very citation of the Apostle himself, and rightly the whole Psalm (whose continuity is perpetual) will be accepted concerning the Gospel and the Prophetic sense, nor yet will the force of the proposition here supposed and tacitly indicated perish, which was developed by Basil and Ambrose and usefully and solidly employed by our theologians against the Socinians for natural knowledge of God: and thus also those things of Chrysostom will be correct, if they are employed to explain the foundation of the Davidic phrase, which are read in Tom. 5. Hom. 9. to the people of Antioch. are read: The heaven is silent, but its very appearance sends forth a voice clearer than a trumpet through the eyes, not through the ears, teaching us, for this sense is more certain and manifest than that one by nature. The Scythian, and the Barbarian, and the Indian, and the Egyptian, and every man walking upon the earth hears this voice of nature from the appearance of the heaven, and the stars, and this whole world. For it falls into our mind not through the ears, but through the eyes. Moreover, the participation of visible things is the same, and not different, like that of languages: both the unlearned and the wise will be able to look into this book equally, and the poor and the rich, and wherever one may have come, looking into the heaven he will take sufficient doctrine from the appearance. For there is no nation, nor language, which cannot understand this voice. But these things about that passage are indeed a little prolix, but not beside the point, nor, as I think, without utility. To which things, thus handed down eleven years ago, I see the opinion of Mr. Dr. Sebast. Schmied to correspond. in his Biblical college published the previous year 1671, p. 77, proposed: namely, that David in this beginning of the Psalm deals entirely according to the literal sense with the Apostolic preaching of the Gospel in the whole world, so much so that Paul cites the words of verse 5 according to the literal sense, not only an accommodative one, but has taken the whole phrase from the book of nature by tropical borrowing, so that the preaching of the Gospel and the preaching of nature are compared together, and one illustrates the other. Since it is known that Scripture very often calls the kingdom of Christ the kingdom of heaven, so that the comparison with the physical heavens may be the more convenient: and thus David lays down and supposes here the truth of the knowledge of the mind, just as every trope supposes a proper signification and the truth of the thing from which the translation is made, unless it is established concerning a fiction, from which, as if from a real thing, a word or phrase is taken, e.g., Chimera, Phaethon. See there more to this effect.

Latin:

Vers. 7. EXVLTAVIT VT GIGAS AD CVRREN- DAM VIAM) In Hebræo: ut potens, id est, sicut viri prin- cipes equis celeribus currunt.

Duo hic notanda: Primum circa lectionem; quam citra sufficientem causam geminam statuit Grotius. Non enim sequitur, LXX. verterunt Φθόγγος sonus, Ego tum Ebræus textus habuit קולם: potuere enim ita reddere Græci, pensi habita non vocis lectione, sed sensu, motique voce altera מליהם quæ verbum notat seu ore prolatum, seu scriptum Dan. 2. v. 9. Joh. 19. vers. 32. ut obser- vatum à Dn. D. Wellero nostro in Comment. ad Roman. 10. vers. 18. Non enim κατὰ πόδα semper originalem textum reddidere, ut ab innumeris exemplis constat. Quo de in Critico Sacro copio- se ac diligenter egimus. Et quia ad sensum ni- hil referebat, utra vox adhiberetur seu κανών, seu φθόγγος, versionem receptam, uti plerumque in Nov. Testam. factum, retinuit Paulus, quia do- ćtrina Apostolorum est linea, perpendiculum, ac re- gula omnium in Ecclesia dogmatum, ut hic Gene- brardus, quem Syrus & Arabs in Psalmis hic se- quuti sunt. Agnoscunt hoc ipsimet Pontificii. Audiamus Lorinum: Fieri, inquit, potest, ut ad sensum respiciendo, etsi legerent LXX. קוָם maluerint reddere sonum, ut docent Eugubinus & Genebrar- dus, præterea Titelmannus, Briedenbachius, & quem postea legi, Malvenda. Similiter Martinus Del- rio Adag. 724. Non puto LXX. & Paulum legisse קוֹלָם sed vocasse sonum ipsum prædicationem, quæ revera est perpendiculum ædificii cœlestis. Et est verus sensus Propheticus loci istius. Simeon de Muis observat, vocem etiam istam קוָם sonum inferre. Neque vero, inquit, abludit vox Hebraica קוּ quæ hic utitur Psalmographus: Nam inter alia significat etiam sonum illum, quem edit linea, aut amussis, dum à Fabris lignariis extensa super lignum remitti- tur. Unde concludit adversus alios Papistas: Quis ergo ferat, quod vulgo dicitur, Græcum inter- pretem, D. Hieronymum, Sanctum quoque Aposto- lum, ac Symmachum קוֹלָם pro קוָם in suis Codicibus habuisse. Præivit Muysio Isaacus Levita Ger- manus conversus Judæus, qui etsi Pontificius, Wilhelmo Lindano Episcopo Trajectensi defen- sionem Ebraicæ veritatis eruditam opposuit, è qua, quia rara admodum ea, quæ huc faciunt, afferre non pigebit: Sed fortasse objicies, quî fiat, quod Paulus Apostolus, Septuaginta & D. Hiero- nymus transtulerint: Sonus eorum. Profecto hæc res, ut ingenue fatear, me quoque aliquando torsit. Sed annotatio in Psalterium docti cujusdam viri, & ut audio Vabli Professoris Parisiensis ex parte scrupulum mihi exemit, cujus hæc sunt verba: Vel amussis eorum, id est, structura eorum ad amussim facta, hoc est, in extremis quibusque terræ parti- bus conspicitur illa fabrica corporum cœlestium quasi ad amussim facta, quæ est vice verborum. Quod hic dicitur de cœlis, Paulus ad Rom. cap. 10. accommodat Apostolis per allegoriam, qui non ali- ter in universo orbe potentiam & majestatem DEI celebrarunt, & prædicaverunt, quam illa accu- ratissima cœlorum structura eloquitur, & denun- ciat hominibus ubivis terrarum habitantibus. Hæc sententia Vatabli, etsi mihi valde arridet, tamen pu- to nos aliud quoque invenisse, ex quo facile appareat cur illi ק per sonum vel vocem expresserint. Si pii & docti viri hujus Psalmi verba considerabunt, & exactius examinabunt, in omnibus versibus de- prehendent כֶפֶל לָשׁוֹן בְּמִלִּוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת id est, eandem semper rem diverso vocabulo repeti, quod cum præcedenti eandem fere significationem habet, ut הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַפְּרִים Cœli enarrant מַגִּיד הָרָקִיעַ E- nunciat firmamentum, יַבִּיעַ אוֹמֶר Eructat sermo- nem יְחַוֶּה דָּעַת indicat scientiam &c. Proinde cum in omnibus versibus ejusdem sententiæ, sed diver- sis verbis iteratio deprehendatur, oportet hic quoque קו aliquam cum מִלָּה cognationem habere & con- tra מִלָּה cum קו. Nam si hoc non esset, ea certe elegantia, quæ in cæteris versiculis omnibus cerni- tur, hic prætermissa videretur. Necesse igitur est קו præter alias etiam significationes notas, aliam quo- que jam multis incognitam habere. Notum autem & Vulgatum est קו significare spem, congregatio- nem, normam, lineam & delineamentum, funiculum, amussim, vel lapidem amussis. Præter hos, inquam, aliam necesse est notionem habere, quæ קול, id est, vocem vel saltem התוך דבר, id est, expressio- nem alicujus vocis habeat. Hanc sententiam con- firmat etiam paraphrasis Chaldaica in cap. 28. Es super verba קו לקו, si quis diligentius perpendat. Vi- demus etiam, quod amussis, quæ funiculo constat, non omnino voce careat. Siquidem architecti & alii artifices, quando aliquid signare aut metiri vo- lunt, dum amussim vel funiculum extendunt, & de- inde remittunt, sonum quendam edere consueverunt. Quâ ex re confirmatur קו aliam quoque notio- nem, vulgo Hebræorum haud ita notam habere, eamque vel קור, vel certe התוך קור repræsen- tare, ut cognatio & affinitas inter קו & מקר con- stet. Hoc autem quoniam paucis notum est D. A- postolum, LXX. & D. Hieronymum aliter quam קום legisse errore quodam suspicantur. Hæc no- stra sententia, si alicui probata fuerit, eam arripe- re potest, sin minus, suum cuique liberum judicium permittimus, si modo ipsum textum violare non ausit. vid. Cœlum Orientis B. D. Bangii pag. 52. qui radicale & commune vocum קו & Φθόγγος significatum facit canonicum, & gnomonicum rei ductum ab uno extremo in aliud, in quo hæc ca- nonem & sonum convenire eleganter docet: (1.) Ut linearis Regula recta ducitur ab uno per medium mensurandum in aliud ceu terminum mensionis, & ut sonus à sonante editus varia loca permeat, ante- quam desinat, sic à DEO vocibus Apostolorum & Discipulorum editum salutaris Evangelii præconium per omnes orbis fines & extremitates dimanavit. (2) Sicut perpendiculum è superioribus recte con- struendarum ædium partibus recta demissum æquo ponderis libramento efficit, ut cunctis sua integritas & pulchritudo constet, ne quid tortuosum aut inor- dinatum structura patiatur, imo ut sonus è collisis corporibus, organis pneumaticis aliisque sonabilibus solidis emissus pernicios ac ultroneo motu fertur ad au- res, eas varie afficit, demulcet, movet, atque in ani- mis hominum varios motus excitat, id quod Sauli accidisse memoratur 1. Sam. 17. vers. 14. 15. 16. seq. qui turbatus malo genio, non modo levamen sentit è Davidica cythara suavi modulamine ibid. vers. 23. sed fidibus canente Davide etiam vexatio mali spiri- tus cessavit: Sic Evangelici & verbi divini sonus ab ore virorum Dei profectus, non modo ad aurium bipatentes fores recta tendit, sed & easdem suaviter afficit. (3) Non secus ac amussis rerum mensuran- darum certum signum existit, & ὁ Φθόγγος indici- um est noëmatum & idearum, quæ in mente artifi- cis præextiterunt, antequam manus operi fuit admo- ta: sic doctrinæ Evangelicæ sonus hanc propriam lau- dem sibi vendicat, ut λόγον ἔυσημον (bene significan- tem) insonet auditorum auribus & animis 1. Cor. 14. vers. 9. (4) Ut regula ἐυταξίας causa non uno momento adhibetur fabricis, rebusque omnibus meti- endis, sed nunc uni mox alteri parti ἐυκαίρως, καὶ ἐυτάκτως inserende atque combinandæ applicatur: pari modo vox humana sua agnoscit ordinaria orga- na, prima, media, ultima, ac proinde suis con- stat articulis, quos ori vel indita vel addita instru- menta conficiunt. (5) Architecti involutum li- neare suum perpendiculum sensim evolvunt ex in- volucris, evolutum tamdiu versant & applicant, donec filum δεικτικῶς signaverit gnomen, qui porro obliquitatem operis monstrans occasionem præbet ar- chitectoni eam emendandi, ac de rectitudine fabricæ invenienda suscipere cogitationem. Sonus auditui deserviturus neutiquam absolvit munus impulsa prima vicinave aëris parte, sed ulteriori succeden- te tium aëriarum partium impulsu opus erit, ante- quam à vacivis auribus percipi possit. Quæ ap- plicat Beat. Bangius ad canona perpendicularem Evangelici soni, ejusque revolubiles vices & se- ries eximie ostendit. Genebrardus fingit Apoco- pen קו pro קולם, sed sine exemplo, inde eam etiam rejicit Sim. de Muys. Videtur etiam dici posse, quod LXX. vocem φθόγγος è versu præcedente repetierint. Lectum autem fuisse o- lim, uti nunc, non tantum Aquilæ versio testatur, sed etiam Chaldaica translatio, ut & Masora ipsa docet, quæ ad vocem illam addita nota ל indicat non amplius extare, quod de voce קולם dici non poterat. Adde quoque Aben Ezra: qui ad hanc vocem ita: Id est, Scriptura vel directio: sicut in libro lineæ docent: sic in cælis totus mundus Dei po- tentiam legat. Et R. David Kimchi, linea eorum, id est, fabrica, quia ædificium fit per lineam.

Alterum concernit sensum: de quo major difficultas ob locum Paulinum. Grotius vult tantum similitudinem quandam ab astris ad Aposto- los desumptam fuisse à Paulo: quam ita explicat ad Roman. 10. vers. 18. Cœlum astriferum uno in loco est, & tamen ejus vox & verba ubique locorum au- diuntur, id est, vis ejus intelligitur. Pari modo cum Apostoli in illustrioribus urbibus fuerint, ubique & prædicaverint, & miracula fecerint, ut Hieroso- lymis, Cæsareæ, Joppe, Antiochiæ, Ephesi, Corinthi, Thessalonicæ, inde fama rerum tantarum pervenit ad omnes terras, in quibus habitabant Judæi, idque sufficit. Frigida nimis hæc glossa. Non id agit Apostolus, ut doceat sufficere, quod Apostoli in illustrioribus urbibus prædicarint, aut ea ra- tione cœli universale præconium conferat, quod quemadmodum illud uno in loco manens, verba ubique locorum emittere videtur, ita Apostoli certis locis subsistentes, ubique sparserint verbum Evangelii fama per orbem volitante. Et quid hoc eximii foret præ antiquis temporibus? Non- ne enim idem dici poterat de præconio sub Vete- ri Testamento, quod uno in loco Hierosolymis vel per Palæstinam sonans inde fama se diffuderit per totum orbem? Longe aliter gratia sub Novo Te- stamento exhibita describitur tum in hoc, tum in aliis Scripturæ locis, quod nempe non tantum fa- ma de Apostolis, sed sonus Apostolorum, vel ver- bum, ex quo fides concipitur, quæ utique è sola fa- ma concipi non potest, in omnem terram exiverit, quod ne dubium supersit ullum, de verbo Evan- gelii statim explicatur, cum additur: καὶ εἰς τὰ πέ- ρατα τῆς οἰκεμένης τὰ ῥήματα ἀυτῶν. Et ad extre- ma usque orbis, vel universi verba ipsorum, Apo- stolorum scilicet. Quod Evangelium ad totum mundum pervenerit, & omni creaturæ prædicatum fuerit, quæ sub cælo est Col. 1, 6. 23. quemadmodum Paulus de seipso testatur, quod Evangelium ab Hierosolymis per omnes vicinas regiones usque ad Il- lyricum prædicarit Rom. 15. vers. 19. jussitque Chri- stus Apostolos, quos in totum mundum emisit, omni creaturæ Evangelium annunciare Matth. 28. vers. 19. Marc. 16. vers. 15. Quo de testati etiam sunt Apostolorum ætati maxime vicini Patres. Ju- stlin. Martyr Dialogo cum Tryphone pag. 270. Atqui ne unum quidem genus est mortalium sive bar- barorum, sive Græcorum, seu etiam aliorum omnium quocunque appellantur nomine, vel Hamaxabiorum, vel Nomadum domo carentium, vel in tentoriis viventium (Scenitarum) & pecoribus vitam tole- rantium, inter quos per nomen crucifixi Jesu suppli- cationes & gratiarum actiones Patri & fabricatori rerum omnium non fiant. Hæc Justinus proximo ab Apostolis seculo. Irenæus ei ætate suppar lib. 1. contr. Hæres. cap. 2. Ecclesiam per universum or- bem usque ad fines terræ seminatam dicit, ab Aposto- lis, & ab eorum discipulis. Et cap. 3. testatur, per universum mundum UBIQVE fuisse Evangelium, sicut Sol in universo lucet mundo. Hanc, inquit, prædicationem cum acceperit & hanc fidem ¡ Eccle- sia, & quidem in UNIVERSUM MUNDUM DISSEMINATA diligenter custodit, quasi unam domum inhabitans, & similiter credit hic, videli- cet quasi unam animam habens, & unum cor, & consonanter hæc prædicat, & docet, & tradit, quasi unum possidens os. Nam etsi in mundo loquelæ dis- similes sunt, sed tamen virtus traditionis una & ea- dem est. Et neque hæ, quæ in Germania fundatæ sunt Ecclesiæ, aliter credunt, aut aliter tra- dunt, neque hæ, quæ in Hiberis sunt, neque hæ, quæ in Celtis, neque hæ, quæ in Oriente, neque hæ, quæ in Ægypto, neque hæ, quæ in Lybia, neque hæ, quæ in medio mundi sunt constitutæ: Sed sicut Sol creatura Dei in universo mundo unus & idem est, sic & lu- men, prædicatio veritatis UBIQVE lucet, & illu- minat omnes homines, qui volunt ad cognitionem veritatis venire. Tertullianus, qui paulo post floruit in Africa, adversus Judæos c. 7. Cui enim, inquit, dextram tenet Pater Deus, nisi Christo Filio suo? quem exaudierunt omnes gentes, i. e. cui omnes gentes credi- derunt, cujus & prædicatores Apostoli in Psalmis Da- vid ostenduntur: in universa, inquit, terra exiit sonus eorum, & usque ad terminos terræ verba eorum. In quem enim alium universæ gentes crediderunt, Par- thi, Medi, Elamitæ, & qui inhabitant Mesopota- miam, Armeniam, Pamphyliam, Cappadociam, & incolentes Pontum, & Asiam & Phrygiam, im- morantes Ægyptum & Regionem Africæ, quæ est trans Cyrenem, inhabitantes Romani & incolæ: tunc & in Hierusalem Judæi & cæteræ gentes, ut jam Ge- tulorum varietates, & Maurorum multi fines, His paniarum omnes termini, & Galliarum diversæ nationes, & Britannorum inaccessa Romanis loca, Christo vero subdita, & Sarmatarum & Dacorum & Germanorum, & Scytharum & abditarum mul- tarum gentium & provinciarum & insularum mul- tarum nobis ingnotarum & quæ enumerare minus possumus. In quibus OMNIBUS LOCIS Christi nomen, qui jam venit, NUNC REGNAT. Hæc suo tempore jam Tertullianus altero post exces- sum Apostolorum seculo. Alios jam non addu- cimus: Satis ex his liquet, quam falso universale præconium ad certa & illustria tantum quædam loca, unde fama in alia penetrarit, restringatur. Quid quod satis inepta sit illa πρότασις compara- tionis de cœlo, quod id in uno loco manens ubique annunciet gloriam Dei. Cœlum enim per uni- versum orbem diffusum est, terramque totam complectitur, non vero in certa parte orbis ter- rarum tantum hæret, ut reliquæ regiones ejus aspectu careant, utpote quo omnes æqualiter fruuntur, unde ubique eadem ratione præsto est ad annunciandam Dei gloriam.

Si autem quæratur, quomodo se habeat Apo- stolica allegatio, & quisnam proprius sit verborum Psaltis sensus? Tres præcipue invenio de Aposto- lico loco sententias. Prior est, quod agat Apo- stolus Roman. 10. vers. 18. solum de notitia Dei re- velata gentibus in opificio mundi, de quo Roman. 1. & Actor. 14. disseritur, eaque sententia Psalmum adducat, quod idem in eodem dicatur, quod De- us jam ante actis seculis patefecerit in pulcherri- mo cœli volumine suam gloriam, atque hoc am- plioris doctrinæ fuerit præludium. Quæ Calvini est glossa. Sed merito castigatur a Beat. Gesnero in Psalm. 19. ceu violenta Paulini textus corruptela, utpote qui apertissime de medio & organo, quo fi- dem consequimur, quod est Evangelii prædicatio, disserit. Amplexus tamen eam est Mercerus, neque dubitavit relativum EORUM, penes A- postolum, ut in Psalmo, ad cœlos referre, quo- rum doctrinam nemo non audierit, sed invito prorsus textu Apostolico; in quo nulla COE- LORUM mentio, sed aperte pronomen EO- RUM ad Apostolos se refert. Vasquez Jesuita non probat tantum illam explicationem, hac da- ta paraphrasi in Epist. ad Roman. cap. 10. Nun- quid dici potest, gentes omnino non audivisse, ut u- num DEUM saltem agnoscentes illum possent in- vocare? Siquidem cæli enarrant & prædicant glo- riam Dei, & opera ejus annunciat firmamentum, & in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum. Sed con- tendit etiam in prima parte Disp. 97. quæst. 5. quod sequatur inde, gentes auxilio sufficienti ad cre- dendum & ad salutem non posse destitui. Nec ab illa explicatione alienus est Jansenius in hunc Psal- mi locum. Sed nimis luculentum est e toto con- textu Paulum de revelatione Evangelii disserere, non de notitia naturali, ideoque ut hic scopus Apostoli non negligatur, aliter paulo Beza ad Roman. 10. & Rivetus ad hunc Psalm. allegatio- nem explicat; quod intelligat quidem Paulus Da- vidica verba de universali vocatione, quæ fit per creaturas, sed exinde colligat, quum Deus omni- bus quantumvis remotis, per creaturas se patefece- rit, non dubium esse, Judæos etiam a Deo fuisse vo- catos convenientibus modis: vel argumentum nectat a pari: si vox cælorum olim in omnem terram exivit, quidni etiam hodie vox Evangelii: aut a minori, quanto magis vox Evangelii? Sed argu- menti illius ideo nulla est evidentia, ut argumento alio ad consequentiam ostendendam, si qua inest illi consequentia, prorsus opus fuerit, ne princi- pii petitio commissa, vel obscurum ex æque ob- scuro probatum dicatur. Rectius sese habet alio- rum explicatio, qui Apostolum hoc testimonio Da- vidico utivolunt, per quandam ad institutum suum accommodationem, ut de prædicatione Evangelii ve- re dici possit, quod David de cælis & expanso ceci- nit, nempe sonum & verba ejus ad fines usque orbis penetrasse, & ab omnibus exaudiri posse. Cui ve- ro sententiæ duo opponuntur a Riveto. Primum, quod talis accommodatio seu potius allusio, ubi præ- sertim quædam est analogia & similitudo, sæpe qui- dem in usu sit, sed vix ubi confirmatione & argumen- to opus sit ut hoc loco. Deinde quod intempestive Paulus tunc dixisset, Evangelii vocem ex ore Apo- stolorum fuisse in toto mundo auditam, quæ vix tum ad paucos pervenerit. Sed ut καθ' ὕστερον πρότερον respondeam; Posterius hic palam contradicit A- postolo, cum hoc in loco, tum Col. 1. universa- lem prædicationem jam tum factam fuisse asse- renti, & Apostolos negligentiæ accusat, quod mandatum Christi Matth. 28. vers. 19. datum exequuti non fuerint: Prius vero expediri potest facile, si dicatur Paulum hic non probare, quod Evangelium omni creaturæ prædicatum sit, sed ceu notorium assumere, ac verbis Davidicis illustra- re, accommodatis iisdem ad vocem Evangelii, ut doceat simul, quam illustris gratia sit Novi Testa- menti, cum perinde in omnem terram sonus Apo- stolorum exiverit, uti per omnem terram cælum an- nunciat Dei gloriam. Dici etiam potest, eo li- bentius hanc in rem adhibere Apostolum verba Psalmi præsentis, quod in eodem David a patefa- ctione per creaturam ad revelationem per verbum

Dei factam sese conferens facile comparationem innuerit, cujus comparationis à Propheta institu- tæ vel si non expresse, tacite saltim indicatæ, quan- tum ad hoc membrum, de amplitudine præconii verbi interpretem egerit Apostolus, adeoque si- mul docuerit, quam certo in omnem terram cœlo- rum delineatio & documenta prodierunt, tam certo his temporibus doctrinam Evangelii in universum terrarum orbem dimanasse Apostolorum prædicatio- ne. Quo redit Franc. Junii explicatio in parall. sac. non facile reprobanda: multis certe modis Calvinianæ glossæ præferenda.

Tertio autem plerique censent, Paulum Da- vidica verba probationis gratia adduxisse, eaque de universali Apostolorum præconio accepisse: quæ sen- tentia duobus modis explicari potest: Primo ut dicatur, Davidem secundum sensum literalem ac directe intentum in hoc Psalmo de Doctrina Evan- gelii tantum agere: ac per cœlos intelligere figurata loquendi ratione Apostolos, siquidem pronomen EORUM sese refert in voce קוָם ad præcedens nomen, quum nullum aliud in textu occurrat, ni- si cœlorum, & verba, LINEA vel SONUS EO- RUM, de Apostolis eorumque præconio intelligan- tur, unde nihil certius videtur, quam quod per cœ- los iisdem Apostoli designentur, per annunciatio- nem gloriæ divinæ annunciatio Evangelii, in quo gloria divinæ sapientiæ, justitiæ, & gratiæ per or- bem patefacta est. Quo argumento inducti B. Lutherus noster, Bugenhagius & Gesnerus in hac Cathedra, Brentius in Wurtembergica Ecclesia, & alii plerique verba Psalmi figurate exposuerunt, cum Augustino & aliis veteribus Ecclesiæ Docto- ribus. Psalmus, inquit Bugenhagius noster, mani- seste dicit de Evangelio per totum mundum divulga- to. Nam Paulus citat eum Roman. 10. non de specta- culis cælestibus, sed valde manifeste de verbo vocali sive Evangelio prædicato in toto mundo: Et in po- steriori commentario; cæli isti visibiles, stellæ, dies, nox, Sol, divina sunt spectacula, in quibus gloriam creatoris & admirabilia opera intuemur Roman. 1. Sed cur non addit hic terram, mare & omnia quæ in iis sunt, ut solet, cur tantum de cælis hic sit mentio? Ludit ergo & hic divinus spiritus suis figuris, qui etiam quandoque creavit omnia & ab æterno vidit no- vum mundum, quandoque futurum, & regnum cœ- lorum in terris, de quo Es. 65. vers. 66. lege & gau- debis: unde hic regnum hoc cœlorum verbo regi de- claratur, dum de enarranda gloria Dei, de annun- ciandis operibus Dei, de eructatione verbi, de annun- cianda scientia, de audiendis vocibus in omnibus lin- guis & in omnibus terris dicitur, ut interim non di- cam, quæ adduntur de lege Domini immaculata &c. Et Paulus aperuit nobis sententiam hujus Psalmi Roman. 10. ubi citat de Christi prædicatoribus ver- sum: In omnem terram exivit &c. Igitur hic no- vum mundum in Spiritu vides post Pentecosten, quam vocant, quando per Spir. Sanct. è cælis missum declarata gloria resurrectionis Jesu Christi Domini nostri, & mirabilia Dei, verbum, Spiritus & sci- entia Scripturarum omnibus gentibus & linguis præ- dicata sunt, ubique affulgente illuminatione, & accen- dente per Spiritum Sole justitiæ Christo, quando im- pletum est, quod superiori Psalmo promisit, propterea confitebor tibi in nationibus, Domine &c. Tunc lex Domini hactenus importabilis facta est jugum Christi suave, & onus leve, desiderabilis super omne, & divitias & delicias, nempe donato Spiritu Christi à Patre in cordibus credentium. Qui quia adhuc in eis aliquid superest carnis, atque adeo in carne pec- catum, necesse habent, post susceptam etiam gratian semper clamare, delicta quis intelligit? Ita pie & ele- ganter complexus summam Psalmi B. antecessor noster: similiter B. Brentius; videntur quidem hæc dici de ea enarratione & annunciatione, qua gloria & majestas Dei patetfit & illustratur ex creaturis hu- jus mundi. Sed alio nos vocat Apostoli Pauli aucto- ritas. Quod ergo dicit David, illud est: cæli, hoc est, Apostoli cælesti vocatione excitati, cælesti Spiritu or- nati enarrant gloriam DEI, Evangelium videlic. de Christo: Et firmamentum (expansio) iidem illi A- postoli, quorum doctrina fundata & firmata est Ec- clesia & extensa seu divulgata in universum orbem, annunciant opera manuum Dei, quia per Apostolo- rum Evangelium annunciatur redemtio humani ge- neris à peccato, morte & inferno per Christum Filium Dei. Quod opus non minus miraculum est, quam creatio cæli & terræ. Annunciatur autem hoc re- demptionis opus per Evangelium, non interdiu tan- tum, sed diu noctuque &c. Huc alludit etiam Esaias (cap. 60.) cum de Ecclesia Christi concionatur: A- perientur portæ tuæ jugiter, die ac nocte non clau- dentur &c. Hæc prolixius exequitur Dn. Bren- tius, atque ita etiam quod de sole habetur explicat: Soli posuit tabernaculum in ipsis, videlic. Apostolis. Apostoli enim in hunc usum divinitus ordinati sunt, ut sint tabernaculum seu tentorium Solis, hoc est, in quorum Evangelio verus Sol, qui est Christus, com- moretur, & per universum orbem circumferatur. Eadem plane ratione B. Gesnerus totum Psalmum interpretatur de prædicatione Evangelii, & præcla- re omnia, quæ de cælis, firmamento, Sole dicun- tur, allegorico sensu explicat, eamque interpre- tationem probat, tum quod pleraque in toto hoc Psalmo obstent, quo minus principium Psalmi κα- τὰ τὸ ῥητὸν accipere possimus, tum quod Aposto- lus manifeste primam partem Psalmi de ministerio prædicationis Evangelii exposuerit, reliquas autem partes de doctrina cælesti agere nullum cuiquam dubium esse possit, tum quod ipsi quoque Judæi, observante Lyrano, principium Psalmi de promul- gatione legis in monte Sinai acceperint. Atque ita Tertullianus l. 5. contr. Marc. cap. 19. de Evange- lii prædicationibus hæc prædicta esse docet: In omnem terram exiit sonus eorum &c. Christique prædica- tores Apostolos in Psalmis David hic ostendi, libr. ad- vers. Jud. c. 6. observat, eoque sensu Augustinus in utraque Psalmi hujus expositione verba Psalmi interpretatus est. Ipsi Evangelistæ (ita habent S. Augustini verba) in quibus Deus tanquam in cælis habitat, exprimunt gloriam Domini nostri Jesu Chri- sti. Cantatur de Christo, quod EVIDENTER apparet, quia illic scriptum est; ipse tanquam spon- sus procedit de thalamo suo. Quis est sponsus, nisi cui desponsata est illa sponsa, cui timet castus sponsi a- micus, ne sicut Eva &c. (2. Cor. 11.) procedens de u- tero virginali, ubi sponsus Deus humanæ naturæ co- pulatus est. Quem sensum Veteris Ecclesiæ ex- pressum habemus in antiquo Cantico, Veni Re- demtor gentium, à D. Luth. recognito & in Ecclesia nostra probato, Er gieng aus der Kammer sein, &c. quem etiam expressere antiqua Biblia Ann. 1483. Norimbergæ edita, ut & Augustæ Anno 1518. in quibus hæc ἐπιγραφή habetur: Der Summa Psal- mi: David erkannt in dem Geist, wenn Christus gebohren würdt von seinem Geschlecht, daß der håylige Gåyst würde gesandt seinen Jüngern, der sie würde lehren endlich reden alle Zungen, und kåm in alle Welt, do machet er diesen Psalm, wåys- sagende darvon.

Quia vero Basilius M. & Ambrosius initium Psalmi de annunciatione gloriæ Dei, quæ per crea- turas sit, explicant, & perquam luculentus videtur sensus ille de cœlis materialibus, ac firmamento, nec non de Sole ipso, quæ mirabili magnitudine sua, venustate, motu ac lumine per totum orbem glo- riam Dei enarrant, quemadmodum explicat Ec- cles. 43, 2. neque à proprietate literæ discedendum, nisi cogat ipsa necessitas, non paucis interpretibus visum fuit, initium Psalmi de manifestatione per opera creationis intelligendum esse κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν. Unde etiam ex hoc loco demonstrari solet natura- lis Dei notitia, adversus Socinum ejusque Socios, quod à nobis quoque prolixe factum Tom. 2. sup. August. Confess. p. 116. seqq. Ut ergo allegationi A- postolicæ sua constet vis & veritas, neque tamen robur argumento decedat, quod ex hoc Psalmo ad adferendam notitiam naturalem Dei depromi- tur, utrumque illud conjungi potest, in explican- do hoc Davidis oraculo: tum quod per naturam & intuitum operum creationis gloria Dei orbi an- nuncietur, tum quod fieri hoc debuerit per præconium Evangelii; non quidem ut cum Pontificiis gemi- num fingamus sensum, literalem unum, allegoricum alterum, & è mystico & allegorico argumentum Pauli deducamus, siquidem unius dicti non possit nisi una esse sententia, & allegoricus sensus, ut Re- gula habet trita ex Augustini Epist. ad Vincent. argu- mentativus non sit, sed ut dicatur, alludendo hac figurata loquutione id supposuisse S. S. quod secundum literam verbis iisdem infertur, quo pacto unica qui- dem erit tantum verborum Hieropsaltis interpre- tatio, eaque sensu figurato intelligenda ex inten- tione Spiritus S. vaticinantis de Apostolorum præ- conio, sed fundamentum metaphoræ, & allegoriæ hic supponetur tacite in ista comparatione, quum cœlis vel ideo maxime comparentur Apostoli, quod uti cœli admirabili suo opificio ubique enarrant Dei gloriam, ita Apostoli & Evangelistæ admiran- do suo Evangelio & Evangelii præconio gloriam Dei per totum orbem annunciaturi sint: uti Sol instar Sponsi egreditur ad cursum suum, ita Sol justitiæ Chri- stus egressurus sit. Sic πρότασις è natura & libro na- turæ petita erit, ἀπόδοσις autem hac Prophetia fi- guratur & indigitatur, ut ratio & fundamentum comparationis argumentum sit adversus Socinianos θεογνωσίας naturalis: res autem ipsa figuratis illis loquutionibus significata sit præconium Apostolorum universale, quod è Psalmo demonstrat Apostolus. Cum enim Metaphoræ desumuntur à rebus natu- ralibus, res illæ in quibus fundamentum compara- tionis situm, in natura præsupponuntur, atque ipsa comparatio quæ instituitur, res illas firmat, ac ve- ritatem earum statuminat. Simile exemplum habes Psal. 84, 4. imo passim similia exempla occurrunt. Observata enim hac analogia explicationis in con- similibus locis multis Scripturæ dictis lux affundi- tur. Atque hoc sensu accipienda, vel admitten- da Vinariensium Paraphrastarum interpretatio, ne quis more Pontificiorum geminum poni sensum in eodem dicto credat: Quam ita acceptam huc to- tam relatam volo: Juvat autem nonnulla inde, illu- strationis gratia, adducere. Ad versum 1. ita ha- bent: Gleich wie am lieben Himmel über uns ein natürlich Zeugniß der Ehre, Gütigkeit, Allmacht und Weisheit GOttes uns Menschen dargestellet ist: Also und vielmehr ists mit dem Predigt-Amt im Neuen Testament beschaffen: Da wird rechtschaf- fen erzehlet die Ehre GOttes, und verkündiget sei- ner Hände Gnaden-Werck, Psalm. 8. vers. 4. Psalm. 100. vers. 3. Ephes. 3. vers. 10. Da ist herrlich zu er- kennen seine Allmacht und Weisheit, in Verstöhrung des Teuffels Reichs, und in Auffrichtung seines

Himmelreichs, allein durchs Wort des Evangelii, ohn alle äusserliche Gewalt und Macht. Ad vers. 5. Gleich wie aber das am Himmel gleichsam eine ge- wisse Richtschnur von GOTT dem HERRN geordnet ist, darnach alle Creaturen in Zeit, Ort, Krafft und Würckung sich richten: Also ist der Schall der Apostel Rom. 10. vers. 18. und das be- schriebene Wort GOttes die allergewisseste Regel und Richtschnur aller Lehre, Religion, Glaubens, Gottes-Dienstes, und Christlichen Lebens bey den Menschen auf Erden: Atque eo etiam intendere videtur in explicatione vers. 1. Dn. Brentius, cum tam copiose de externo Sole disserit in Paraphrasi sua: Sicut externus Sol hæret in cælo tanquam in suo tabernaculo, & mane oriens, procedit ex infe- riori hemisphærio super terram, magno & illustri or- natu, aurora quasi aurea, tanquam Sponsus de tha- lamo suo, & incedit ac progreditur ad perficiendum cursum suum ab extremo cælorum usque ad extre- mum, hoc est ab oriente usque in occidentem, nec est ullus locus in terra, ad quem Sol non projiciat radios, aut ad minus calorem seu virtutem suam. Incedit au- tem non vulgari & humili modo, non pro more homi- num captivorum, sed magna, ut ita dicam, alacri- tate & majestate tanquam gigas, aut heros quispiam, cui nihil potest obsistere, quod ipsum à cursu suo im- pedire, & remorari queat. Ita etiam de Christo ve- ro sole sentiendum est. Circumfertur enim predica- tione Apostolorum per omnem orbem, nec venit sordi- do ac lacerato vestitu, sed incedit sicut sponsus, multis donis ornatus, quæ in Ecclesiam suam liberaliter con- fert: nec commoratur in uno tantum loco, sed discur- rit per omnem terram ab oriente in occidentem, nec est ulla gens, ulla natio, in qua Christus non sit prædica- tus. Et quanquam tam Judæi, quam Ethnici contule- rint, quicquid habuerint virium ad exstirpandum no- men Christi ac opprimendum Evangelium ejus, tamen ipse semper invitis etiam inferorum portis pergit sum- ma alacritate & potentia tanquam heros omnibus formidatus & invictus Evangelium suum propaga- re ac tueri. Gemina est Vinariensis Paraphrasis: Gleich wie es mit der natürlichen Sonnen bewandt: Also und viel herrlicher ist es mit der Sonnen der Gerechtigkeit Malach. 4. vers. 2. Christo JESU beschaffen: Derselbe hat seine Hütten oder Woh- nung in dem geistlichen Gnaden-Himmel, der Christ- lichen Kirchen Psalm. 132. v. 13. Esa. 48. v. 35. 2. Cor. 6. v. 16. Er gehet aus durch sein Wort, und theilet al- lenthalben Göttliches Licht und Glantz aus, durch sein heilsames Erkanntniß, Joh. 1. vers. 8. 9. cap. 18. vers. 12. Apostel Geschicht 13. vers. 47. Er ist der wunderschöne Bräutigam seiner Christlichen Kir- chen Psalm. 45. vers. 2. 3. Joh. 3. vers. 29. Er ist der freudige zwenstämmige Held, Psalm. 45. vers. 4. welcher seinen Lauff vom Vater in die Welt, und von der Welt wieder zum Vater Johann. 16. vers. 28. mit willigem Gehorsam verrichtet hat, und her- nach stetiglich in seinem Worte durch die Welt sei- nen schnellen Lauff vollbringet, 2. Thessal. 3. vers. 1. Er ist voller lieblicher Gnaden-Wärme, Luc. 24. vers. 32. davon alle Gläubigen ihre Stärcke und Lebens-Krafft empfahen. Quæ omnia non absque causa tam operose nunc adducere voluimus, ut nempe in similibus oraculis penetrare rectius vim Phraseon & dictorum Spiritus S. discamus: neque si supponatur, in allegoricis locis, res aliqua à Spiritu Sancto, cui superstruitur allegoria, & in explica- tione utrumque indicetur, tum fundamentum alle- goriæ aut figuratæ phraseos Spir. S. tum sensus dire- cte ab ipso illic intentus, fingat nobis quis geminum ejusdem dicti sensum; quem nuspiam in scripturis admittendum censemus, aut retento sensu sub figurata locutione intento comparationis, ac fundamenti figuratæ locutionis, veritatem facile indicatam vel suppositam in dubium revocet. Quod utrumque cavendum. Atque ita optime sese habet B. Lutheri, Bugenhagii, Brentii, Gesne- ri, Osiandri ac aliorum nostrorum, tum veterum quoque Tertulliani, & Augustini explicatio, imo ipsi- us Apostoli allegatio, recte etiam totus Psalmus (cu- jus perpetua est συνέχεια) de Evangelio sensuque Prophetico accipietur, nec tamen peribit vis προ- τάσεως hic suppositæ, ac tacite indicatæ, à Basilio au- tem atque Ambrosio evolutæ & ab nostris Theolo- gis utiliter, ac solide, adversus Socinianos, pro θεο- γνωσίᾳ naturali adhibitæ: adeoque etiam recte Chrysostomi illa se habebunt, si ad explicandum fundamentum Davidicæ phraseos adhibeantur, quæ Tom. 5. Hom. 9. ad popul. Antioch. leguntur: Tacet cælum, sed ipsius adspectus vocem tuba clario- rem emittit per oculos, non per aures, nos docens, hic enim sensus à natura est illo certior, & manifestior. Scytha, & Barbarus, & Indus, & Ægyptius, & omnis homo super terram incedens hanc vocem naturæ ex cœ- li, & syderum, totiusque mundi hujus aspectu audit. Non enim per aures, sed per oculos in mentem incidit nostram. Visibilium autem participatio eadem, ne- que differens, sicut linguarum: in hunc pariter librum & idiota & sapiens intueri poterunt, & pauper & di- ves, & quocunque quis venerit, in cælum respiciens sufficientem capiet doctrinam ex aspectu. Non enim est gens, neque lingua, quæ hanc vocem intelligere non possit. Sed hæc de isto loco paulo prolixius qui- dem, non autem præter rem, nec, ut opinor, citra utilitatem. Quibus ita ante hosce undecim an- nos traditis video consonare sententiam Dn. D. Sebast. Schmied. in collegio suo Biblico priori an- no 1671. edito p. 77. propositam: quod nempe Da- vid omnino in hoc Psalmi initio juxta literalem sen- sum agat de prædicatione Evangelii Apostolica in uni- verso orbe, adeo ut Paulus verba vers. 5. juxta sen- sum literalem citet, non tantum accommodatitium, sed phrasin totam sumserit ex libro naturæ tropice mutuatione, ut prædicatio Evangelii, & prædicatio naturæ inter se simul comparentur, & una alteram illustret. Siquidem notum sit, quod sæpissime Scri- ptura regnum Christi appellet regnum cælorum, ut comparatio cum cælis corporeis Physicis eo sit commo- dior: adeoque substernat David & supponat hîc veritatem notitiæ mentis, quemadmodum omnis tro- pus supponit propriam significationem & rei, à qua fit translatio, veritatem, nisi sicubi constet de figmen- to, à quo quasi à re vera sumatur vox vel phrasis, e. g. Chimæra, Phaëtonte. Vide illic plura in hanc sententiam.

## 19:7
Verse 8. THE LAW OF THE LORD IS PERFECT.

The perfection of Holy Scripture, which David understands by the law of the Lord, is celebrated here with a sonorous voice. For תמימה is perfect, as Pagninus and Arias Montanus render it from תמם to perfect, to consummate, to complete. Genebrard explains: perfect properly, teaching not only things to be done, but also things to be believed, to be worshipped, and the rest. Lorinus, the Hebrew word signifies perfect, entire, absolute, to which nothing is lacking. The Chaldean explains שלימתא perfect. Compare what is said about the perfection and perspicuity of Scripture in verse 8 in the System of Theology.

Latin:

Vers. 8. LEX DOMINI PERFECTA.

Perfectio Scripturæ sacræ quam per legem Do- mini David intelligit, hîc sonora voce celebratur. Nam תמימה est perfecta, ut reddunt Pagninus & Ariemontanus à תמם perficere, consumma- re, absolvere. Genebrard. exponit: perfecta pro- prie, docens non tantum facienda, verum & creden- da, colenda & reliqua. Lorinus, Hebræa vox signi- ficat perfectam, integram, absolutam, cui nihil desit. Chald. explicat שלימתא perfecta. Conf. quæ de perfectione, & perspicuitate Scripturæ vers. 8. in Systemate Theol. dicta.

## 19:10
Verse 11. AND MUCH PRECIOUS STONE)

that here the interpreters take פז for gold, Job 28, verse 17. The Chaldean here [takes it for] Ophir gold, whence it is thought to be called Obrifum.

Jerome on Isaiah. But here the LXX translate it precious stone, in Psalm 119, 27, 126, topaz. Hence Hesychius: Pazion which is also topazion, a precious stone.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET LAPIDEM PRETIOSVM MVLTVM)

quod hîc פז pro auro sumunt interpretes Job. 28. vers. 17. Ophirinum hic Chaldæus, unde Obrifum dictum puta

Hieronymus ad Esaiam. At hic LXX. vertunt λίθον τίμιον, in Psalm. 119, 27. 126. τοπάζιον. Inde Hesychius: Πάζιον ὃ καὶ τοπάζιον, λίθος πολύτιμος.

## 19:12
Verse 13.

WHO UNDERSTANDS DELICTS? CLEANSE ME FROM MY HIDDEN ONES.

From these words Bellarmine and Reihing infer the uncertainty of grace, but Ambrose, Catharinus, and Vega expressly refute those who conclude it from there. See Vasquez, Tom. 2, in 1. 2, Disput. 710, cap. 5. In order that we may obtain pardon, and be certain of it, there is no need that we understand all our delicts, provided we flee with true confidence to the grace of God, and sigh, cleanse me from my hidden ones. Compare Psalm 31, v. 5, Psalm 103, James 1, v. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DELICTA QUIS INTELLIGIT, AB OC- CULTIS MEIS MUNDA ME.

Ex his verbis incertitudinem gratiæ colligit Bel- larminus & Reihingus, sed eos, qui inde eam conclu- dunt, Ambrosius, Catharinus & Vega ex professo re- fellunt. Vid. Vasquez. Tom. 2. in 1. 2. Disput. 710. cap. 5. Ut veniam consequamur, & de ea certi si- mus, non opus est, ut delicta omnia intelligamus, modo vera fiducia confugiamus ad Dei gratiam, & suspiremus, ab occultis munda me. Conf. Psalm. 31. v. 5. Psalm. 103. Jacob. 1. v. 6.

## 19:13
Verse 14.

AND SPARE THY SERVANT FROM STRANGERS) He reads זָרִים, where זֵדִים is more correct. The sense is, keep me from sins which are committed knowingly and willingly. For these are to the Hebrews זֵדִים, ὑπερήφανα in Symmachus. Thus some translate the word זִיד in Exod. 18, verse 11 as ὑπερηφανεύσαντο. And it is not otherwise in the received version in Dan. 5, verse 22, Nehem. 9, verses 10, 16, and elsewhere as ἀσεβεῖν, as in Deut. 17, verse 13, ch. 18, v. 20. There is also a place where it is translated by ἐπιτίθεσθαι, ἀνθίστασθαι, παραβιάζεσθαι, as in the said place Exod. 18, 11, Jerem. 50, 29, Deut. 1, 43. And the adjective which we have here זֵד or זֵדוֹן is translated as ὑπερήφανος, θρασὺς, ἄνομος, παράνομος.

IF THEY HAVE NOT HAD DOMINION OVER ME, THEN SHALL I BE BLAMELESS, AND I SHALL BE CLEANSED FROM THE GREATEST SIN) The sense is: If that pride or contumacy does not carry me away, then I shall be held as innocent by Thee, and I shall be free from at least the more serious sins.

And these things concerning Psalm 19. But it will not be irrelevant if we here subjoin a Program, in which we have in part expounded that Psalm, which is as follows:

About to receive with most faithful devotion the holy and desirable, glorious and singular solemnity, that is, the Nativity of the Lord Savior, we ought with all our strength, with His help, to prepare ourselves, and, as the great Bishop of the Hipponensians warns, diligently to examine all the hiding places of our soul, lest by chance there be in us some hidden sin, which both confuses and bites our conscience, and offends the eyes of the divine majesty. How happy is the soul, to quote St. Augustine again, which has studied to govern its life in such a way, with GOD assisting, that it deserves to receive Christ as guest and inhabitant: just as, on the contrary, how unhappy is that conscience, to be mourned with a whole fountain of tears, which has so stained itself with evil works that not Christ, but the devil, begins to hold dominion in it. For such a soul, if the medicine of repentance does not quickly come to its aid, is abandoned by the light, is occupied by darkness, is emptied of sweetness, is filled with bitterness, is invaded by death, is repudiated by life. Nor indeed did IMMANUEL come to us only as a guest, who might visit us, and rest in us, and dwell forever, but also as the bridegroom of our soul, who deigns to marry us to Himself in a sweet and indissoluble union. For on the birthday of the Lord, to express this again in the words of St. Augustine, Christ was joined to His Bride the Church as if in spiritual nuptials. Then TRUTH sprang from the earth, then JUSTICE looked down from Heaven; then THE BRIDEGROOM PROCEEDED from His chamber, that is, the WORD OF GOD from the virginal womb. For He proceeded with His Bride the Church, that is, He took on human flesh. Remaining in the bosom, as that Saint says elsewhere, He filled the womb of His mother. In which chamber, that is, the womb of the virgin, the divine nature coupled human nature to itself: where the word made flesh for us proceeding from the mother, prepares where we may dwell. Concerning which mystery in a similar way in these solemnities the holy

Church of God, led by St. Ambrose, is accustomed to sing: "She proceeds from her chamber, the royal hall of modesty, a twin great one of the substance eager to run the way." And again according to another hymn: "Creator of the stars, eternal light of believers, when the world’s evening declines," as the bridegroom comes forth from the chamber, the most honest enclosure of the virgin mother.

In these most sweet meditations, by which it still delights to bestow some holy garland, this excellent Psalmist of Israel supplied the cause, whose tongue was a reed of the most eloquent scribe at the court, the secretary and chancellor of the highest Spirit, when he sang the mystical glories of God, recounting them through the whole world, whose voices have been heard in all tongues, whose sonorous Canon and sonorous Canonical sound went out into all the earth, and whose words penetrated to the ends of the land, that is, the holy Apostles of Christ, as the Doctor of the Gentiles has interpreted, chief conductor of the hieropsalmist mind, most sure. For who else are the heavens that thus declare the glory of God, that day utters the word to day, and night shows knowledge to night, whose voices resound in all tongues, whose sound is Canon and rule of faith and life throughout the whole orb of the lands, whose doctrine undefiled, converting souls, bestowing wisdom to babes, enlarging hearts, enlightening eyes, remaining into the age of ages, justified in itself, desirable above gold and a very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb, wherein if guarded is great reward?

Such praises most aptly suit the Apostles and Apostolic doctrine, by their material heavens or by their proclamation resonant in nature, not at all. In those spiritual heavens the sun has placed his tabernacle, just as a most clear Hebrew fountain flows: which are in the streams the LXX. interpreters and the Vulgate versions thus have rendered, "he has placed his tabernacle in the sun."

But Christ did not place his tabernacle in the sun, nor is there the place of Christ's tabernacle if you understand the sun materially; rather the mystical sun is needed here, which the perpetual allegory of the hieropsalmist and of the whole hymn for which he asks, himself is Christ: For David sings of the Sun as Bridegroom, of the Sun as Hero, of the Sun as his Rock and his Redeemer and Goel.

Who indeed is that Sun, who is both Bridegroom and Hero and Rock and Goel of David, in whom alone the King of Israel placed his trust, but the Messiah of Jacob, of whom he himself was confirmed by the Holy Spirit? This Sun of righteousness, as by Malachi, the rising from on high, as by Zechariah the parent of the Forerunner, that great light which enlightens every man, as is called by St. John, whose aspect to Ezekiel was Hachashmal, the most noble Sun, and truly majestic, most illustrious Sun, and most serene, most beautiful and most pure Sun, in whom no spot, no darkness, a most efficacious and salutary Sun, fountain and spring of all light, of all life, of all spiritual warmth, of all virtue and vigour, of all joy and gladness. Nor is there anyone who hides himself from his heat whether enlivening, by which he desires to exhilarate all, or deadly (by accident) whereby the reprobate perish by their own fault.

For he himself is a consuming fire: Just as his Gospel is the odor of life to those believing unto life: the odor of death to those perishing unto death. The tabernacle of this Sun, the palace of this Hero, the hall and bed of this Bridegroom, the scene of this Goel is the Church, the house of the living God, formerly figured by the Mosaic tabernacle; but that is not the typical or shadowy tabernacle in which the solar Bridegroom, the Goelic Hero, the true Simphon (man of the Sun), the very rock of our salvation dwells: it is the Church. For the Lord chose Zion, he chose it for his habitation:

"This is my rest for ever and ever" (he says): here also Blessed Luther dwells, who here should first be heard.

Thus, however, he himself in his works on Psalm 19, Volume 3 of the Wittenberg Latin edition. That this Psalm is to be understood concerning the ministry of the Gospel, Paul also teaches and compels [us to believe] in Romans 10, saying: Have they not heard? And indeed their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Whence it is necessary to take the heavens, the firmament, the sun, days, nights, and similar things allegorically, by which pleasant veils the Spirit draws us from this visible world to the spectacle of a certain new world, in which there are other heavens, nights, and days, of which we see the figure and shadow in this world. Therefore, the very evident circumstance and evidence of the sayings, as well as the authority of the New Testament, compel us to grasp an allegory, which otherwise is to be avoided by an interpreter of the Scriptures as much as possible, lest the simplicity of the sense be lost and he wander in his mere dreams. The heavens, therefore, are the Apostles, and as many as perform the Apostolic ministry, that is, the office of the Word. For what is the Gospel, if not the announcement of the glory of God and his works? But the glory of God cannot be declared unless the ignominy of men is declared at the same time. From which it is gathered that the glory of GOD is twofold: that by which we glory in him, given by a pure conscience through his gratuitous mercy, and that by which he is glorified in us and by us. And that to declare the glory of God is nothing else than to preach that in which GOD is glorified and we glory, that is, all the wonders of his inestimable mercy, and the riches of the glory of his compassions poured out upon us, which is truly to teach Jesus Christ and the Gospel purely. Thus far B. Luther. Bartholomew Westhemmer followed him in these things, retaining the very words of the Great Man; B. Bugenhagen, our own, also followed, as did B. Lucas Osiander, and B. Gesner, our own, chastising the petulance of Calvin (to whom the Belgian paraphrasts agree), the Weimar paraphrasts, and others of our own. Which explanation John Baptist Folengo of Mantua did not disapprove of among the Papists, even though he desires the gloss of others concerning material heavens to be retained as well: which Bellarmine alone embraces here, even though he acknowledges that the Psalm is expounded by Augustine concerning Christ and the Apostles, and that it can be so expounded: nay, that according to Paul it ought to be so expounded.

But we must speak here primarily about the Sun, the bridegroom. Therefore, that Sun whom David sings is the Bridegroom of the Church and of our souls, Immanuel, our little Jesus, who, as a bridegroom adorned elegantly, proceeding from his chamber, is seen in great majesty, and rejoiced as a giant to run his course, not otherwise than the golden sun in the morning, with great and illustrious adornment, like a golden dawn, proceeding from the lower hemisphere, advances to complete his course.

Most people take the way of this mystical bridegroom concerning the course of his Gospel ministry, and not only the way, but also the going forth, which the prophet adds, from the end of heaven, and his circuit even to the end of heaven. Concerning which we sing thus in the ecclesiastical hymn: His going forth from the Father: His progress to the Father; His going down even to the underworld: His return to the seat of God. And in another prose the Church has been accustomed to sing that Christ made three huge leaps: One from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the virgin. The second from the womb of the virgin to the underworld: The third from the underworld to the right hand of God. It is the opinion of almost everyone, says Dr. Luther, that these two verses treat of the incarnation, conversation, and assumption of Christ. Although, indeed, the Great Man prefers that the way of the bridegroom should apply only to Christ reigning and preached and believed through the Gospel: yet, such is his modesty, he establishes this while leaving everyone else's better opinion without prejudice. But perhaps it would not be inconvenient to understand the way of the bridegroom proceeding from his chamber, with the Church, according to the customary hymn concerning the incarnation, conversation, and assumption. Even if what follows concerning the going forth from the end of heaven, and the circuit even to the end of heaven, are taken concerning those things which followed the ascension into heaven and the sitting at the right hand of God: where that Sun of righteousness, the circle of the redemptive office being completed, diffused himself through the whole world with the clearer light of the kingdom and the gifts of the Spirit, so that there is no one who hides himself from his heat. In this sense, therefore, the latter verse will not explain the former exegetically; but by these two verses a distinct course will be exhibited: the one of the economy of the Word in the assumption of flesh, earthly conversation, and exaltation to the right hand of GOD: the other in the going forth through the word of the Gospel, and the progress of the kingdom of Christ through the world; which is administered by the scepter of the Word. For there are also twofold nuptials of this bridegroom, both personal, in the conjunction of the Word and flesh in the womb of the virgin, whence the Giant of twofold substance went forth to run the course of our redemption; and spiritual, in the coupling of Christ the bridegroom with the Church through the Word and Sacraments, by whose grace, the course of redemption having been completed, the Sun of righteousness, the mystical bridegroom of the Church, went forth from the end of heaven to its extremity through the proclamation of the Gospel. From which course the Sun of righteousness has never ceased, and will never cease, while it is still the day of grace (which he effects by the rising of his light) until the consummation of the age, or until there shall be Sun and Moon; and until we shall no longer need the light of the sun, since the Lord God himself will illuminate us for ever and ever. Concerning the former course, St. Augustine says thus on this passage: And he himself as a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber; and he himself proceeding from the virginal womb, where God was coupled to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Likewise: he as a bridegroom, when the Word was made flesh, found a chamber in the virginal womb: and thence joined to human nature, as if proceeding from a most chaste bedchamber, humble in mercy below all, strong in majesty above all. For this is: The Giant rejoiced to run his course: he was born, he grew, he taught, he suffered, he rose again, he ascended. The chamber of Christ, says Dr. Luther (in Hebrew it signifies something hidden and veiled), all understand as the virgin Mary, from whose womb he came forth, just as the sun from the dawn, or rather from the hidden place of night. A beautiful sentiment, certainly, by which that ineffable birth is signified, in which alone the power of the Most High overshadowed the virgin, and in secret wrought this fruit of salvation, which nature knew not nor could attain. For just as the rising sun comes forth visible to all, and yet no one can know whence it comes: so Christ born came into the sight of all, and yet (as Isaiah foretold) had an indescribable birth, since to be born of a virgin without a man surpasses the use and grasp of nature. But how does the bridegroom proceed from his chamber? And why does he proclaim this Sun Christ by that comparison? Perhaps because the bridegroom proceeds adorned and crowned, exulting in the love of his bride. Thus Christ, for the love of the Church, proceeded from the womb of the virgin adorned and crowned in spirit, although according to the flesh he came in the greatest poverty and contempt. For he came full of the ornaments and crowns of the grace of God, exulting in the love of his Church; therefore he rejoiced as a strong man to run his course, that is, he grew, worked, and fought in the struggle with the Devil and our sins, suffered and died with great fortitude of charity and spirit. But we can no longer pursue these things. It remains that we conclude with the exhortation of St. Augustine, Sermon 2 de tempore: Invited therefore to such holy nuptials, and about to enter the banquet of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, see with what garments we ought to be adorned, and therefore let us cleanse as much as we can, with the help of God, our hearts and our bodies together, so that that heavenly inviter may find nothing sordid, nothing foul, nothing obscure, nothing unworthy in our eyes.

These things, therefore, we ought to attend to, not fleetingly, but with great trembling. For we have been invited to a wedding, where we ourselves, if we act well, shall be the bride. And therefore let us see to it, lest perhaps within the soul, where we ought to be adorned with the pearls of good works, we appear there wrapped in the old rags of vices: and when chastity renders those who are good white in the eyes of God, then may luxury render those who are evil soiled. Finally, we earnestly admonish that you piously recall these mysteries, that you holily frequent the temples of the Lord, in which the nuptial festival of the hypostatic union is celebrated, and the solemnity of our mystical union with Christ is adorned, and that, having deposited your offerings at the altar, you show gratitude with us, in the solemn manner, to the sacred paranymphs, who are also the ministers of the mystical union and the heralds of the word. P. P. Under the Seal of the Academy, Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, Year 1666.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ET AB ALIENIS PARCE SERVO TUO) Legit זָרִים, ubi rectius est זֵדִים. Sensus est, arce me a peccatis quæ scienter & volenter committuntur. Nam ea sunt He- bræis זֵדִים, ὑπερήφανα Symmacho. Sic verbum זִיד Exod. 18. vers. 11. vertunt quidam ὑπερηφανεύσαντο. Nec aliter in recepta versione Dan. 5. vers. 22. Nehem. 9. vers. 10. 16. alibi ἀσεβεῖν, ut Deut. 17. vers. 13. c. 18. v. 20. Est & ubi vertitur per ἐπιτίθεσθαι, ἀνθίστασθαι, παραβιάζεσθαι, ut dicto loco Exod. 18, 11. Jerem. 50, 29. Deut. 1, 43. Et adjectivum quod hîc ha- bemus זֵד vel זֵדוֹן vertitur ὑπερήφανος, θρασὺς, ἄνομος, παράνομος.

SI MEI NON FUERINT DOMINATI, TUNC IM- MACULATUS ERO, ET EMUNDABOR A DELI- CTO MAXIMO) Sensus est: Si illa superbia sive contu- macia me non abripiat, tunc a te pro innocenti habebor, li- berque ero a delictis saltem gravioribus.

Atque hæc de Psalm. 19. Non abs re autem fue- rit, si hîc subjecerimus Programma, in quo Psal- mum illum ex parte exposuimus, quod ita habet:

Sanctam & desiderabilem, gloriosam ac singula- rem solennitatem, hoc est, Nativitatem Domini Sal- vatoris, devotione fidelissima suscepturi, totis viri- bus nos debemus, cum ipsius adjutorio, præparare, & omnes latebras animæ nostræ, monente magno Hipponensium Antistite, diligenter aspicere, ne forte sit in nobis aliquod peccatum absconditum, quod & conscientiam nostram confundat, ac mor- deat, & oculos divinæ majestatis offendat. Quam felix est anima, ut iterum S. Augustinus, quæ vi- tam suam ita, DEO auxiliante, studuerit guberna- re, ut Christum hospitem & habitatorem mereatur excipere: sicut, è contrario, quam infelix est illa conscientia, toto lachrymarum fonte lugenda, quæ se ita malis operibus cruentavit, ut in ea non Chri- stus requiescere, sed diabolus incipiat dominari. Ta- lis enim anima, si medicamentum pœnitentiæ non ci- to subvenerit, à luce relinquitur, à tenebris occu- patur, vacuatur dulcedine, impletur amaritudine, à morte invaditur, à vita repudiatur. Nec vero tantum ad nos venit IMMANUEL, ut hospes, qui nos visitare, & in nobis requiescere atque in perpetuum habitare, sed etiam ut animæ no- stræ sponsus, qui suavi, & indissolubili conjugio nos sibi maritare dignatur. In natali enim Domi- ni, ut hæc denuo D. Augustini verbis exprima- mus, quasi in nuptiis spiritualibus Sponsæ suæ Ec- clesiæ Christus adjunctus est. Tunc VERITAS de terra orta est, tunc JUSTITIA de Cœlo prospexit; tunc PROCESSIT SPONSUS de thalamo suo, hoc est, VERBUM DEI de utero virginali. Processit enim cum Sponsa sua Ecclesia, id est, humanam car- nem suscepit. Manens in sinu, ut alibi Sanctus ille, implevit uterum matris. In quo thalamo, id est, vir- ginis utero, natura divina sibi copulavit humanam: ubi verbum caro factum pro nobis à matre proce- dens, ubi habitemus, præparet nobis. De quo mysterio simili modo hisce solemnibus sancta

Dei Ecclesia, praeeunte S. Ambrosio, canere solet: Procedit è thalamo suo Pudoris aula Regia Gemina gigas substantie alacris ut currat viam. Et rursus juxta alium hymnum: Conditor alme siderum Aeterna lux credentium, vergente mundi vespere,... ut sponsus de thalamo egressus honestissima virginis matris clausula.

Suavissimis istis meditationibus, quibus adhuc sanctam aliquam opellam impendere nunc juvat, causam praebuit egregius iste Psaltes Israel, cujus lingua calamus fuit foribae, velociter scribentis, cancellarii & secretarii summi, spiritus Sancti, cum caelos cecinit mysticos gloriam Dei enarrantes, per universum orbem, quorum voces in omnibus linguis audite sunt, quorum Canon sonorus & sonus Canonicus in omnem terram exivit, & verba in fines orbis terrae penetrarunt, hoc est, sanctos Christi Apostolos, uti interpretatus est Doctor gentium, mentis Hieropsaltis promus condus certissimus. Quinam enim alii sunt Caeli gloriam DEI sic enarrantes, ut dies diei verbum eruttet, & nox nocti indicet scientiam, quorum voces omnibus linguis resonant, quorum sonus Canon & norma sit fidei & vitae per universum terrarum orbem, quorum doctrina immaculata, convertens animas, sapientiam praestans parvulis, laetificans corda, illuminans oculos, permanens in seculum seculi, justificata in seipsa, desiderabilis super aurum & lapidem pretiosum multum, & dulcior super mel & favum, in qua custodita retributio multa?

Quae elogia Apostolis & doctrina Apostolica examussim conveniunt, caelis materialibus aut praeconio eorum, in natura resonanti, neutiquam. In illis caelis spiritualibus posuit sol tabernaculum, quemadmodum fons Hebreus limpidissimus fluit: quae in rivulos LXX.

Interpr. & Vulgate versionis ita traducta sunt, in sole posuit tabernaculum suum. At non in sole tabernaculum posuit Christus, nec ibi locus est tabernaculi Christi, si de materiali Sole intelligas; mysticus autem Sol hic indigetur, quod perpetua Hieropsaltis allegoria & tota Hymni cuius Qua poscit, Christus ipse est: Nam de Sole Sponsó, de Sole Heroe, de Sole Petra sua & Goele ac Redemptore suo canit David.

Quis vero Sol ille, qui & Sponsus, & Heros, & Petra, & Goel Davidis, in quo uno Rex Israelis fiduciam collocavit, nisi Messias Dei Jacob, de quo per Spiritum Sanctum ipse confirmatus fuit? Hic Sol justitiae, ut à Malachia, Oriens ex alto, ut à Zacharia Protobaptistae parente, lux ista magna, quae illuminat omnem hominem, ut à S. Johanne vocatur, cujus aspectus Ezechieli fuit Hachasmahl, Sol Nobilissimus, & vere majestaticus, Sol illustrissimus, & serenissimus, Sol pulcherrimus, & purissimus, in quo macula nulla, tenebra nulla, Sol efficacissimus, & saluberrimus, fons & scaturigo omnis lucis, omnis vitae, omnis caloris spiritualis, omnis virtutis & vigoris, omnis gaudii, & laetitiae. Nec est, qui abscondat se à calore ejus seu vivifico, quo exhilarare gestit omnes, seu mortifero, (ex accidente) quo propria culpa pereunt reprobi.

Est enim ipse ignis consumens: Quemadmodum Evangelium ejus est odor vitae ad vitam credentibus: odor mortis ad mortem pereuntibus. Huijus Solis tabernaculum, hujus Herois Regia, hujus Sponsi aula & cubile, hujus Goelis Scena est Ecclesia, domus Dei viventis, per tabernaculum Mosaicum olim figurata; Verum illud, non typicum aut umbratile tabernaculum, in quo moratur Sponsus Soleus, Heros Goelicus, verus Simson (vir Solis) ipsa salutis nostra Petra, est Ecclesia: Quoniam elegit Dominus Sion, elegit eam in habitationem sibi: Haec requies mea (inquit) in seculum seculi: hic habitatur etiam B.

Lutherus, qui hic imprimis

Ita autem ipse in oper. in Pf. 19. Tom. 3. Lat. Witte- bergens. Hunc Pfalmum esse de ministerio Evange- lico intelligendum, docet & cogit Paulus Rom. 10. di- cens: Numquid non audierunt? Et quidem in omnem terram exivit sonus eorum, & in fines or- bis terræ verba eorum. Unde cœlos, firmamentum, solem, dies, noctes & similia, allegorice oportet acci- pere, quibus jucundis involucris, nos spiritus trahit ab hoc visibili mundo ad spectaculum cujusdam novi mundi, in quo alii cœli, noctes, dies sunt, quorum in hoc mundo figuram & umbram videmus. Cogit ergo nos hic ipsa evidens circumstantia & evidentia dictorum, tum autoritas Novi Testamenti, allegoriam appre- hendere, quæ alioqui tractatori scripturarum fugien- da est, quantum fieri potest, ne simplicitate sensus amif- sa, vagetur in meris suis somniis. Cœli igitur sunt Apostoli, & quotquot funguntur Apostolico ministerio, id est, officio verbi. Quid enim est Evangelium, nisi annunciatio gloriæ Dei & operum ejus? Gloria autem Dei enarrari non potest, nisi simul ignominia homi- num enarretur. Ex quibus colligitur, gloriam DEI esse duplicem, eam, qua nos in ipso gloriamur, pura conscientia per misericordiam ejus gratuitam donata, & eam, qua ipse in nobis & a nobis glorificatur. Et enarrari gloriam Dei aliud non esse, nisi prædicari id, in quo DEUS glorificatur & nos gloriamur, hoc est, universa inæstimabilis misericordiæ suæ mirabilia, & divitias gloriæ miserationum suarum super nos effu- sas, quod est vere Jesum Christum & Evangelium pu- re doceri. Hactenus B. Lutherus. Quem secutus est in his, ipsis Megalandri verbis retentis, Bartho- lomeus Westhemmerus; sequutus & B. Bugenhagius Noster, nec non B. Lucas Osiander, & B. Gesnerus Noster, Calvini (cui paraphrastæ Belgici adstipulan- tur) castigans petulantiam, Vinarienses paraphra- stæ, aliique Nostrates. Quam explicationem nec inter Pontificios improbavit Johannes Baptista Fo- lengus Mantuanus: Etsi aliorum Glossam de cœ- lis materialibus etiam retentam cupiat: Quam Bel- larminus solam hîc amplectitur, utut agnoscat, ab Augustino de Christo & Apostolis Psalmum exponi, atque ita exponi posse: Imo juxta Paulum exponi debere.

Sed de Sole sponso hic imprimis nobis dicendum. Sol itaque ille, quem David canit, Sponsus est Eccle- siæ & animarum nostrarum, Immanuel, Jesulus no- ster, qui seu Sponsus egregie ornatus procedens de thalamo suo, in magna majestate conspectus est, ac gavisus ut gigas ad currendam viam, non secus atque mane sol aureus, magno & illustri ornatu, aurora quasi aurea, ex inferiori hemisphærio procedens, ad perficiendum cursum suum progreditur.

Viam sponsi hujus mystici plerique de curriculo muneris ejus Goëlici accipiunt, nec viam solum, sed etiam egressum, quem adjicit propheta, à summo Cœli, & circuitum ejus usque ad cœli summum. De quo in hymno Ecclesiastico ita canimus: Egressus ejus à patre: Progressus ejus ad Patrem; Excessus us- que ad inferos: Recursus ad sedem Dei. Et in prosa alia Ecclesia canere consuevit, quod Christus tres ingentes saltus dederit: Unum de sinu Patris in ute- rum virginis. Alterum de utero virginis ad inferos: Tertium ab inferis ad dextram Dei. Omnium fere sententia est, ait D. Lutherus, hos duos versus agere de incarnatione, conversatione, assumtione Christi. Quanquam vero malit Megalander viam sponsi non nisi regnanti & per Evangelium prædicato & credito Christo convenire: id tamen, quæ modestia ejus est, salva cujusque meliore sententia, statuit. Forte autem non incommodum fuerit, viam procedentis de thalamo sponsi, cum Ecclesia, juxta consuetum hymnum de incarnatione, conversatione, & assum- tione intelligere. Etsi, quæ sequuntur de egressione à summo cælo, & circuitu usq; ad cælum summum, de iis, quæ secuta sunt adscensum in cælum, & conses- sum ad dextram Dei, accipiantur: ubi sol ille justi- tiæ, circulo muneris redemtorii expleto, per or- bem universum, luce regni & donorum spiritûs cla- riore se diffudit, ut non sit, qui se abscondat à calore ejus. Hoc itaque sensu non exegetice versus poste- rior priorem explicabit; Sed duobus istis versibus distinctum curriculum exhibebitur: Alterum οἰκο- νομίας Verbi in assumtione carnis, conversatione ter- rena, & exaltatione ad dextram DEI: alterum in egressione per verbum Evangelii, & progressu regni Christi per terrarum orbem; quod admnistratur per sceptrum verbi. Nam & duplices sunt nuptiæ hu- jus sponsi, cum personales, in conjunctione λόγε & carnis in utero virginis, unde progressus est Gigas geminæ substantiæ ad currendam viam redemtio- nis nostræ; tum spirituales, in copulatione Christi sponsi cum Ecclesia per verbum & Sacramenta, cu- jus gratia peracto redemtionis curriculo, egressus est Sol justitiæ, sponsus mysticus Ecclesiæ, à summo cæli ad extremum ejus per præconium Evangelii. A quo curriculo nunquam destitit, nunquam desistet Sol justitiæ, dum adhuc dies est gratiæ, (quam ortu lucis suæ efficit) usq; ad seculi consummationem, vel donec erit Sol & Luna; & donec non egebimus amplius solis lumine, quoniam ipse Dominus Deus illuminabit nos in seculorum secula. De priori curriculo ita S. Au- gustinus in hunc locum: Et ipse tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo; & ipse procedens ex ute- ro virginali, ubi Deus naturæ humanæ tanquam spon- sus sponsæ copulatus est. Item: ille tanquam sponsus, cum verbum caro factum est in utero virginali thala- mum invenit: atque inde naturæ conjunctus humanæ, tanquam de castissimo procedens cubili, humilis mise- ricordia infra omnes, fortis majestate super omnes. Hoc est enim, Gigas exultavit ad currendam viam: natus est, crevit, docuit, passus est, resurrexit, adscendit. Thalamum Christi, ait D. Lutherus, (Ebraice, oc- cultum velatumque significat) omnes intelligunt vir- ginem Mariam, è cujus utero prodiit, sicut sol ex auro- ra, imo ex noctis occulto. Pulchra certe sententia, qua ineffabilis illa nativitas signatur, in qua sola virtus Al- tissimi obumbravit virginem, & in abscondito operata est hunc fætum salutis, quod natura nescivit nec attin- gere potuit. Sicut enim sol oriens prodit omnibus visi- bilis, & tamen nemo noscere possit, unde venit: ita Chri- stus natus ad omnium conspectum venit, & tamen nati- vitatem suam (ut Esaias prædixit) habuit inenarrabi- lem, cum nasci ex virgine sine viro, usum & captum superet naturæ. Sed quomodo procedit sponsus de tha- lamo suo? & cur hunc Solem Christum ea compara- tione prædicat? Forte quod sponsus ornatus & coro- natus procedit, gestiens amore sponsæ suæ. Ita Christus amore Ecclesiæ processit de ventre virginis ornatus & co- ronatus in spiritu, cum secundum carnem venerit in summa paupertate & comtemtu. Plenus enim orna- mentis & coronis gratiæ Dei venit, gestiens in amo- rem Ecclesiæ suæ, ideo exultavit ut fortis ad curren- dam viam, h. e. magna charitatis & spiritus fortitu- dine, crevit, operatus est, pugnavit in agone cum Dia- bolo, & peccatis nostris, passus & mortuus est. Sed hæc non possumus jam amplius prosequi. Superest, ut exhortatione S. Augustin. Serm. 2. de tempore con- cludamus: Ad istas ergo tam sanctas nuptias invita- ti, & ad convivium Patris, & Filii & Spiritus Sancti intraturi, videte, qualibus indumentis debemus orna- ri, & ideo mundemus quantum possumus, cum Dei adjutorio, corda simul & corpora nostra, ut cælestis ille invitator nihil in nobis sordidum, nihil fædum, nihil obscurum, nihil oculis suis deprehendat indignum.

Hæc ergo non transitorie, sed cum ingenti tremore de- bemus attendere. Invitati enim sumus ad nuptias, ubi nos ipsi, si bene agimus, sponsæ erimus. Et ideo videa- mus, ne forte intus in anima, ubi deberemus bonorum operum margaritis ornari, ibi appareamus vitiorum pannis veteribus involuti: & quando eos qui boni sunt in oculis Dei castitas reddet candidatos, tunc eos qui mali sunt, reddat luxuria sordidatos. Postremo sedu- lo monemus, ut mysteria hæc pie recolatis, templa Domini, in quibus nuptialis festivitas copulationis hy- postaticæ celebratur, & copulationis mysticæ nostri cum Christo solemnitas adornatur, sancte frequen- tetis, Paranymphis etiam sacris, iisdemque copulati- onis mysticæ ministris verbi præconibus, depositis ad aram muneribus, gratitudinem, solemni more, nobiscum exhibeatis. P. P. Sub Sigillo Academiæ, Vigilia Natalis Domini, Anno cIɔ. Iɔc. LXVI.

## 20:1 Argument
PSALM XX. A vow for the Magistrate.

It is a prayer and good wishes, with which the people accompany a king going into war.

Although, as R. Aben-Ezra testifies, some Hebrews accept it concerning Christ, and Coccejus wishes the faith of the Church to be represented here in its head, Christ, and a prayer to be made for the kingdom of Christ; the Psalm itself teaches that the vow and prayers are rather prescribed for the Magistrate: Coccejus rightly observed that in verse 10, 'King, hear us,' Christ is understood.

Latin:

PSALM. XX. Votum pro Magistratu.

PRECATIO est & bona omina, quibus regem in bellum euntem populus prosequitur.

ETsi R. Aben - Ezra teste Ebræi nonnulli de Christo accipiant, & Coccejus fidem Ecclesiæ in capite suo Christo hic repræsentari, & orationem pro regno Christi fieri velit; votum tamen & pre- ces potius pro Magistratu præscribi Psalmus ipse docet: Interim vers. 10. Rex exaudiat nos, Christum intelligi Coccejus recte observavit.

## 20:1 Addition
To Psalm 20, towards the end, p. 977.

Blessed Luther in his works on this Psalm indeed explained the present Psalm as a certain Litany, as he calls it, general for Magistrates, yet concerning the last verse he warned thus in the same place, Tom. III. Witteb. f. 360. In our translation this verse can be taken as an Epilogue, or a confirmation, but the Hebrew distinguishes it thus, 'Lord save, let the King hear us, on the day we call.' In which I know not what mystery lies hidden, for it is not said 'hear us' [imperative], but 'let him hear us' in the third person, just as in the beginning of the Psalm: 'May he hear you,' he said in the same person and with the same verb. 'King' is also placed in the nominative, not in the accusative, the pronoun 'you' is not had at the end of the verse: If it has any secret, I leave it to the spiritual, content with the simplest sense, by which I think God himself is called King here, in the third person, in the Hebrew manner, just as also in the beginning of the Psalm: 'May the Lord hear you.' And Moses, Numbers 14. Let the strength of the Lord be magnified, just as you swore, for 'your strength.' And Psalm 3, 'Salvation is of the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.' And Numbers 27, 'Let the Lord provide a man who may be over this multitude,' that is, provide, O Lord. And Genesis 30, Joseph to Pharaoh, 'Let the King provide a wise man.' So also here: 'Let that King hear us.' For the article is placed as a notable mark, that is, You hear us, who truly are that King of ours: For David, who ministers to you, is not King, nor does he reign his own kingdom, but yours; For we are your kingdom, and you are our King, by which affection he vehemently moves, that is, he teaches us to move God, who is then moved, when we are moved. For how should he not hear, when his kingdom, his affair, his glory is in danger? These things are from Blessed Luther. Junius and Coccejus in this place understand Christ as the King. What of the fact that B. Luther does not object to the whole Psalm being explained as concerning Christ: I would not dare, he says in the loc. cit., to deny that it should be understood of Christ, and that he speaks of banners in the Spirit. I am moved most of all, along with many others, by Ps. 110, in which Christ the King is commanded to sit and to rule in the midst of his enemies, and his scepter is to be sent forth from Zion, likewise the Kings of the earth are to be shattered, and the rest, which although they sound carnally, are nevertheless spoken and understood deeply in the Spirit. It is permitted to adduce similar things from Psalm 72, and Psalm 2. The iron rod is spoken of in the Spirit. Thus also here it would be easy to accept banners in the spirit. For nothing stands in my way to prevent me from expounding it of Christ, except that it is my intention to avoid allegory as much as possible, and also because this Psalm is not cited in the N. Testament, as are the others. Again, the following Psalm urges strongly that it be understood of Christ, and it is likely that it speaks of the same King of whom it speaks here, as we shall see. If you listen to Bellarmine, this Psalm seems to have been sung by David foreseeing the coming of Christ to overcome the powers of the air, to which the two following Psalms also pertain.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 20. sub finem p. 977.

B. Lutherus in operat. in hunc Psalm. exposuit quidem Psalmum præsentem ceu Litaniam quan- dam, ut vocat, generalem pro Magistratibus, de ul- timo tamen versiculo ita ibidem monuit, Tom. III. Witteb. f. 360. In nostra translatione hic versus pot- est, velut Epilogus, vel confirmatio haberi, sed Hebræus sic distinguit, Domine salva, Rex exaudiat nos, die qua vocabimus. In quo nescio quid mysterii lateat, non enim exaudi nos, sed exaudiat nos in tertia persona di- citur, sicut in principio Psalmi: Exaudiat te, eadem persona eodemque verbo dixit. Rex etiam in nomina- tivo ponitur, non in accusativo, Pronomen, te, in fine versus non habetur: Ego si quid secreti habet, spiritua- libus relinquo, simplicissimo sensu contentus, quo Deum ipsum hic Regem vocari arbitror, in tertia persona, more Ebraico, sicut & in principio Psalmi: Exaudiat te Dominus. Et Moses Numer. 14. Magnificetur for- titudo Domini, sicut jurasti, pro fortitudo tua. Et Psalm. 3. Domini est salus, & super populum tuum benedictio tua. Et Numer. 27.
