Provideat Dominus hominem, qui sit super hanc multitudinem, id est, pro- vide tu Domine. Et Genes. 30. Joseph ad Pharaonem, provideat Rex virum sapientem. Ita & hic: Exau- diat nos ille Rex. Ponitur enim articulus notæ insi- gnis, hoc est, Tu exaudi nos, qui vere es ille Rex noster: Nam David, qui ministrat tibi non est Rex, nec suum regnum regnat, sed tuum; Tuum enim sumus nos re- gnum, & tu Rex noster es, quo affectu vehementer mo- vet, hoc est, movere nos docet Deum, qui tunc move- tur, quando nos movemur. Quomodo enim non ex- audiat, quando regnum suum, res sua, gloria sua pe- riclitatur? Hæc B. Lutherus. Per Regem Christum intelligit Junius & Coccejus in h. l. Quid quod non repugnet B. Lutherus, explicari Psalmum totum de Christo: Non tamen ausim, inquit l. c. negare de Christo intelligendum, & de vexillis in Spiritu eum loqui. Movet me quam maxime cum multis aliis Ps. 110. in quo Christus Rex sedere jubetur & in medio ini- micorum dominari, & sceptrum ejus emitti ex Zion, item Reges terræ conquassari, & reliqua, quæ etsi car- naliter sonent, tamen penitus in Spiritu dicuntur & intelliguntur. Similia Psalm. 72. liceat adducere, & Psalm. 2. Virga ferrea, in Spiritu dicitur. Ita & hic vexilla facile fuerit in spiritu accipere. Nihil enim obstat mihi, quo minus de Christo exponam, nisi quod allegoriam vitare propositum est, quantum fieri potest, tum quod in N. Test. non allegatur hic Psalmus, quem- admodum cæteri. Rursus Psalmus sequens, valde ur- get se de Christo intelligi, & verisimile est eum de eo- dem Rege loqui, de quo hic loquitur, ut videbimus. Bel- larminum si audias, Psalmus hic videtur cantatus à Davide prævidente Christi adventum ad debellandas aereas potestates, quo etiam pertinent duo Psalmi sequentes.

## 20:3
Verse 4. AND MAY THY BURNT OFFERING BE FAT) Let it be held as fat, that is, let it be accepted, as in Dan. 3:40. Coccejus, with Vatablus, Buxtorf, and indeed also Kimchi, and the Belgians, rendered the Hebrew word as 'reduce to ashes': because burnt offerings were accustomed to be consumed by fire from heaven, and thus reduced to ashes. This sense of the word דשׁן, Mr. Dr. Geier seems to prefer, along with B. Glassius, lib. 5, Phil. p. 494, and Bochart, Tom. 1, Hieroz. lib. 2, c. 35, f. 360 and 539. But because he observes that that word in Ps. 23:5 and Prov. 15:30 means 'to make fat,' and thus not only the Vulgate, but also the Chaldean and the Syrian, and the LXX, πιανάτω (let it make fat), have explained it, we easily accede to Grotius, as our B. Luther also renders it, and Mr. Dr. Geier does not deny it.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET HOLOCAVSTVM TVVM PINGVE FIAT) Pro pingui habeatur, id est acceptum sit, ut Dan. 3, 40. Verbum Ebræum incineret, cum Vatablo, Bux- torf. imo & Kimchio Coccejus, & Belgic. reddidere: quia holocausta igne absumi de cælo solebant, & in cineres ita redigi. Quem sensum verbi דשׁן videtur præferre Dn. D. Geier. cum B. Glassio, lib. 5. Phil. p. 494. & Bochart. Tom. 1. Hieroz. lib. 2. c. 35. f. 360. & 539. Quia vero observat verbum illud Pf. 23, 5. Prov. 15, 30. esse pinguefacere, atque ita non vulg. tantum, sed Chald. & Syrus quoque ac LXX. πιανάτω pinguefaciat, exposuere, facile Grotio ac- cedimus, sic etiam reddente B. Luthero nostro, nec abnuente quoque Dn. D. Geiero.

## 20:5
Verse 6. WE SHALL BE MAGNIFIED) Μεγαλυνθησόμεθα. It appears they read נגדל, not נדגל. So also the Syrian and the Arab. The usual fallacy of the cause recurs for our author, so that he may introduce a discrepancy in the Hebrew Codices. But the Hebrew text is correct, whatever the Greeks may have seen, who often looked only to the sense, not the very words of the Hebrew source. Concerning the Latin, there is no reason for us to be anxious about what he himself read in the Hebrew. For he did not translate from the Hebrew. The sources flow thus: in the name of our Lord we shall raise banners, that is, we shall triumph. To which the Greek translation, as to the sense, agrees very well. The Midrash Tillim on this passage also proves that Hebrew reading.

Latin:

Vers. 6. MAGNIFICABIMVR) Μεγαλυνθησόμεθα. Appa- ret legisse eos נגדל non נדגל .Sic & Syrus & Arabs. Recurrit consueta Nostro causæ fallacia, ut discrepantiam in Ebræis Codd. ingerat. Sed recte se habet textus Ebræus, quicquid viderint Græci, qui sæpe sensum tantum respexerunt, non verba ipsa fontis Ebræi. De Latino non est, quod soliciti simus, quid ipse legerit in Ebræo. Non enim ex Ebræo transtulit. Fontes ita fluunt: in nomine Do- mini nostri vexilla erigemus, id est, triumphabimus. Quibus optime congruit, quod ad sensum, Græca translatio. Probat etiam illam lectionem Ebræam Midrasch Tillim in h. 1.

## 20:6
Verse 7. NOW I HAVE KNOWN THAT THE LORD HATH SAVED HIS CHRIST) That is, now I hold it for certain that it will come to pass that God will give victory to the King.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NVNC COGNOVI QVONIAM SALVVM FECIT DOMINVS CHRISTVM SVVM) Id est, nunc pro certo habeo futurum, ut Deus Regi det victoriam.

## 20:8
Verse 9. THEY THEMSELVES ARE BOUND AND HAVE FALLEN) They have slipped and fallen. For כרע, among other things, signifies to slip, as we said at 17:13. Moreover, these are past tenses in the Hebrew manner for future ones.

Latin:

Vers. 9. IPSI OBLIGATI SVNT ET CECIDERVNT) Prolapsi sunt & ceciderunt. Nam כרע inter alia prolabi significat, ut diximus 17, 13. Sunt autem hic præterita more Hebræo pro futuris.

## 20:9
Verse 10. AND HEAR US IN THE DAY THAT WE SHALL CALL UPON THEE) It appears the Greeks, whom he follows here, read תעננו, not יעננו as our Hebrew Codices have, although otherwise it is not infrequent for the Hebrews to pass from the second person to the third, and vice versa. You could also interpret that reading which we have in the Hebrew metaphorically: Let the King feel help from our prayers; for in the Hebrew that 'THEE' is not there.

The Hebrew Codices are in excellent condition, not so the Latin Vulgate: which here had to be amended by Grotius, not defended, because the Athnach accent does not permit the word המלך to be conjugated with the preceding, 'Lord save'; nor is the sign of the accusative present here. Therefore, המלך 'King' coheres with the following verb, and consequently it must necessarily be read as the Hebrew text now has it: 'King, hear us in the day in which we shall call.' Which the Hebrews interpret concerning the King of the world, God: for they retain the same reading, and they also approve it, so far is it from anyone having suspected a corruption. R. David Kimchi, 'Save, Lord, King of the world, GOD, hear us.' R. Aben-Ezra, 'King, let him hear,' that is, King of Kings: who nevertheless also applies it to the King thus: 'Let the King answer Amen to our prayers,' as in Deuteronomy 27, 'Let all the people say Amen.' Nor did Jerome render it otherwise, who faithfully translated the Hebrew text: 'Lord save, King hear us, etc.' Our B. Gesnerus attends to the emphasis of the demonstrative He: That King, the Messiah indeed, who is the only King over Zion, Psalm 2, let him hear us, as often as we have implored his help in our calamities. And thus also the Vinarienses explain it, as do Junius and Piscator: similarly also the Belgian interpreters, who nevertheless introduce a type here, namely, King David. Our Bugenhagius explains this whole Psalm concerning the Messiah: that the faithful themselves pray for all prosperous things for him, and in him hope to be saved through God. That there is no need for that metaphorical or metonymical explanation of Grotius, is readily evident. Which is also little consistent here.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ET EXAVDI NOS IN DIE QVA INVO- CAVERIMVS TE) Apparet Græcos, quos hic sequitur, le- gisse תעננו, non ut nostri Codices Hebræi habent יעננו, quanquam alioqui non infrequens Hebræis est, ut de secunda persona in tertiam transeatur, & contra. Posses etiam μετα- φορικῶς interpretari illam, quam in Hebræo habemus lectio- nem: Sentiat Rex opem à precibus nostris; nam in Hebræo non est illud TE.

Ebræi Codices optime se habent, non item Latina vulgata: quæ emendanda hic erat à Grotio, non defendenda, quia non permittit accentus Ath- nach, ut vox המלך conjugatur cum præcedenti, Domine salva: neque nota accusativi hic adest. Ideo המלך Rex cohæret cum sequenti verbo, ac proinde necessario id legendum, prout nunc Ebræus textus habet: Rex exaudiat nos in die, quo invocaverimus. Quod de Rege mundi Deo interpretantur Ebræi: Hi enim eandem lectionem retinent, eamque etiam probant, tantum abest ut suspicatus ullus fuerit corruptelam. R. David Kimchi, salva Domine, Rex mundi DEUS exaudiat nos. R. Aben-Ezra, Rex audiat, id est, Rex Regum: qui tamen etiam ad Regem applicat ita: Respondeat Rex Amen ad preces nostras: ut in Deuter. 27. Dicat omnis populus Amen. Nec aliter reddidit Hieronymus, qui fideliter vertit Ebræum textum: Domine salva, Rex audiat nos &c. B. Gesnerus noster attendit Emphasin He demonstrativi: Ille Rex, Messias nimirum, qui unicus est Rex super Zion Psalm. 2. exaudiat nos, quoties in calamitatibus nostris opem ejus imploraverimus. Atque ita etiam explicant Vinarienses, ut & Junius ac Piscator: similiter quoque Belgici Interpp. qui tamen hic typum inferunt, Regem nempe Davidem. Bugenhagius noster totum hunc Psalmum de Messia exponit: quod imprecentur ipsi fideles omnia prospera, inque eo se sperent per Deum salvandos. Metaphorica certe vel metonymica illa Grotii explicatione opus non esse, ultro constat. Quæ etiam parum hic concinna est.

## 21:1 Argument
PSALM XXI. Concerning the triumph of Christ, and the destruction of the enemies of Christ.

Latin:

PSALM. XXI. De triumpho Christi, & interitu hostium Christi.

## 21:1 Addition
On Psalm 21.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 21.

## 21:1 Addition
Ver. 1. O LORD, IN THY STRENGTH THE KING SHALL REJOICE.

Bellarmine connects the preceding and the present Psalm thus: That one, he says, was asking God to protect Christ the King, who was about to do battle with the enemy of the human race; This one gives thanks that He has protected, exalted, and crowned him. B. Luther, although he professes that he is not certain enough whether this Psalm should be understood of Christ alone or of any King, nevertheless, he says, it seems entirely to be a thanksgiving for those things which were requested in the preceding, that it be a certain Epinicion of Christ, and just as he interpreted the preceding Psalm primarily of the figurative King, so he interprets this one against the first of Christ the figurative King, since in truth David and any King whatsoever by his wars and victories has prefigured the passion and resurrection of Christ and the thing prefigured from one another. He adds, perhaps this Psalm also speaks in a general sense of both Kings at once, as was seen in the preceding. Not that he establishes a double sense, from which the blessed Luther greatly recoiled, as we warned in its place, but that things said generally of the King in common, apply to Christ the King of Kings, and to Kings who are under Christ, each in its own special way. According to the blessed Bugenhagen, the glory of our triumphant King Christ is described here, and the vengeance upon those who, hating him, persecuted him. The same is the opinion of the blessed Brentius, who urges verse 4 especially: He asked life of thee, and thou gavest him length of days for ever and ever. This, he says, properly applies to Christ and not to David: And verse 6: Thou makest him to be a perpetual blessing, of which he adds: this also pertains properly to the person of Christ; wherefore this Psalm, according to the literal sense, is to be understood of Christ and his kingdom or majesty, not of David. For he thinks this little verse is taken from that promise in Genesis 22:18: in thy seed shall all nations be blessed. Whence he assigns two parts to this Psalm: The former, he says, is an exposition of the glory and majesty of Christ: the latter is an exposition of the oppression and rejection of the Jews: to whom, although Christ was promised, yet there were no more virulent enemies and persecutors of Christ: inasmuch as they hastened to that very end, that they might depress and trample the majesty of Christ even to the underworld. Origen, Athanasius, Eusebius, and Augustine led the way, who likewise expounded the Psalm concerning the Messiah, which was also done by the Chaldean, and by the Calvinist Cocceius, although Junius and Piscator expound the Psalm concerning David, and the Dutch concerning David as the type and Christ as the antitype.

Latin:

Vers. 1. DOMINE IN VIRTUTE TUA LÆTABITUR REX.

Bellarmin. antecedentem & præsentem Psalmum ita connectit: Ille, inquit, petebat à Deo, ut Christum regem cum hoste generis humani præliaturum, prote- geret; Iste gratias agit, quod protexerit, exaltaverit, & coronaverit. B. Lutherus, etsi se non satis cer- tum esse profiteatur, de solo ne Christo an de quovis Rege hic Psalmus intelligi debeat, omnino tamen, in- quit, videtur esse gratiarum actio super acceptis his, quæ præcedente postulata sunt, ut sit Epinicion quod- dam Christi, atque ut Psalmum præcedentem inter- pretatus est primum de Rege figurato, ita hunc con- tra primum de Rege figurato Christo interpretatur, cum revera David & quivis Rex bellis & victoriis suis Christi passionem & resurrectionem figuraverit, & facile sit figuram & rem figuratam ex se invicem in- telligere. Addit, forte & hic Psalmus generali senten- tia de utroque Rege simul loquitur, sicut in præcedente visum est. Non quod geminum sensum statuat, a quo abhorruit maxime B. Lutherus, ut suo loco monuimus, sed quod generaliter dicta de Rege in communi, & Christo Regi Regum, & Regibus, qui sub Christo sunt, sua cuilibet speciali ratione, conveniant. Secundum B. Bugenhagium Megalan- dri præstatam gloria triumphantis Regis nostri Chri- sti hic describitur, & vindicta in eos, qui eum odien- tes persequuti sunt. Eadem B. Brentii est senten- tia, qui v. 4. præcipue urget, vitam petiit a te, dedisti ei longitudinem dierum in seculum & seculum. Hoc proprie, inquit, in Christum & non in Davidem com- petit: Et v. 6. Constituis eum, ut sit benedictio perpe- tua, de quo addit: pertinet & hoc proprie ad perso- nam Christi; Quare hic Psalmus juxta τὸ ῥητὸν de Christo, & regno seu majestate ejus, non de Davide in- telligendus est. Hunc enim versiculum sumtum putat ex illa promissione Genes. 22, 18. in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Unde duas partes assi- gnat hujus Psalmi: Prior, inquit, est expositio gloriæ & majestatis Christi: posterior est exposi- tio oppressionis & abjectionis Judæorum: quibus etsi Christus erat promissus, tamen non fuerunt virulentiores Christi hostes & persecutores: quip- pe quod ad illum tantum exitum properarunt, ut majestatem Christi ad inferos usque deprimerent & conculcarent. Præiverunt Origenes, Athana- sius, Eusebius, Augustinus, qui de Messia itidem ex- posuere Psalmum, quod & a Chaldæo factum, & a Coccejo Calviniano, etsi Junius & Piscator de Davi- de, Belgæ de Davide ut typo, Christo ut antitypo Psalmum exponant.

## 21:3
Ver. 4. FOR YOU HAVE PREVENTED HIM WITH THE BLESSINGS OF SWEETNESS) Better in the Hebrew: You have surrounded him with the benefits of goodness. For we have said above at 18, 6 that קדם is often used for to surround.

That this Psalm is to be understood of Christ, which is evident especially from ver. 5, is taught by Origen, Athanasius, Eusebius, Augustine, and the Chaldean: and Cocceius acknowledges it, against Piscator who explains it of David. How the desire of his heart is attributed to him can be seen in Psalm 2, 8 and John 11, 42. Cocceius teaches that the abundance and heap of benefits are noted from a comparison with Proverbs 24, 25 and Psalm 84, 7, with which the translation of Blessed Luther agrees. Compare 2 Cor. 9, 5, 6. How he asked for life is taught in Psalm 16. Eternity, moreover, is noted in ver. 5 by the addition of the word עד to the word עולם. Concerning his glory and majesty, Ps. 8 and Phil. 2, 9; how he is placed for a blessing, from Gen. 12, 3 and Eph. 1, 7; how he was gladdened with joy, is taught in Psalm 16, 11. Therefore he is called in ver. 7 המלך that King, Ps. 2, 6; concerning whose trust, Ps. 22, 10; concerning the cutting off of enemies (ver. 10, 11), one may read in Matt. 3, 10 and Luke 13, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVONIAM PRÆVENISTI EUM IN BENEDICTIONIBVS DVLCEDINIS) Melius in Hebræo: Circumdedisti eum beneficiis bonitatis. Nam sæpe קדם pro circumdare poni diximus supra 18, 6.

DE Christo Psalmum hunc accipiendum esse, quod è vers. 5. imprimis constat, docent Origenes, Athanas. Eusebius, Augustin. & Chaldæus: & agnoscit Coccejus, adversus Piscatorem de Davide explicantem. Desiderium cordis quomodo ei tribuatur, Psalm. 2, 8. Joh. 11, 42. videre est. Beneficiorum abundantiam & cumulum notari Coccejus e collatione Proverb. 24, 25. Psalm. 84, 7. docet, cui convenit translatio B. Lutheri. Conf. 2. Cor. 9, 5. 6. Quomodo vitam postularit, Psalm. 16. docet. Æternitatem autem notari v. 5. addito ad vocem עולם nomine עד. De gloria & majestate ejus Ps. 8. & Phil. 2, 9, quomodo in benedictionem ponatur è Genes. 12, 3. Ephes. 1, 7. quomodo lætitia exhílaretur Psalm. 16, 11. docetur. Ideo vocatur v. 7. המלך Rex ille, Ps. 2, 6. de cujus fiducia Psal. 22, 10. de excisione hostium (v. 10. 11.) Matth. 3, 10. Luc. 13, 7. legere est.

## 21:7 Addition
Verse 8. THY HAND SHALL FIND ALL THINE ENEMIES.

Brentius understands these things of the Jews and interprets verse 10 concerning the destruction of their seed. Thou shalt destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men. The fruit, he says, and the seed of the Jews are their descendants. The Psalm therefore sings that the Lord is so inflamed with anger against the Jews that he is going to oppress not only those very people who shouted, crucify, crucify, but also their posterity. For so they themselves wished, when they cried: His blood (that is) the vengeance of his blood come upon us, and upon our children. This punishment the Jews pay even to this day. For although they do not seem to have been removed from all these lands, yet those who are still survivors wander with uncertain homes, and not only have they been cast out from their ancestral possessions in these lands, but they have also been excluded from the heavenly inheritance. This truly is to be cast out from the company of the children of men. The blessed Luther expounded it similarly, whose operations on the first 21 Psalms, with the explanation of Psalm 22, contain many excellent things, and when compared with the commentaries of Brentius and Bugenhagen, can provide notable uses in many places. The blessed Gesner interprets it of the impious and the fighters against God in general, yet he understands verse 12 particularly of the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 8. INVENIT MANUS TUA OMNES INIMICOS TUOS.

De Judæis hæc intelligit Brentius & v. 10. de se- minis eorum excidio interpretatur. Fructum eorum de terra perdes, & semen ejus de filiis homi- num. Fructus, inquit, & semen Judæorum sunt posteri eorum. Canit igitur Psalmus, quod Do- minus tanta ira sit adversus Judæos inflammatus, ut non solum illos ipsos, qui vociferati sunt, cruci- fige, crucifige, verum etiam posteritatem eorum sit oppressurus. Sic enim voluerunt ipsi, cum clamarent: Sanguis (hoc est) ultio sanguinis ejus veniat super nos, & super filios nostros. Hanc pœnam adhuc hodieque dant Judæi. Etsi enim non videntur omnes ex his terris sublati, tamen qui adhuc sunt superstites, vagantur incertis sedi- bus, & non solum ejecti sunt ex avitis suis posses- sionibus in his terris, verum etiam exclusi sunt e cœlesti hæreditate. Hoc vere est e contubernio filiorum hominum ejici. Similiter exposuit B. Lutherus, cujus operationes in priores 21. Psalmos, cum explicatione Psal. 22. multa præclara continent, & cum Brentianis & Bugenhagianis commentatio- nibus collatæ in plusculis locis insignes usus præbe- re possunt. B. Gesnerus de impiis & θεομάχοις in communi interpretatur, versum tamen 12. peculia- riter de Judæis intelligit.

## 21:12
Ver. 13. YOU SHALL MAKE THEM A BACK. Vatablus, Junius, Piscator, the Belgian [translation], and Cocceius understand this of a mound which is like a shoulder, as if to say: you shall make them, consumed by fire, a mound of ashes. But the Vulgate is deservedly preferred by Mr. Dr. Geier, with which the Septuagint, the Ethiopic, and Luther agree, for whose marginal gloss see.

Latin:

Vers. 13. PONES EOS DORSUM. De tumulo qui humero similis est intelligunt Vatabl. Jun. Piscat. Belg. Coccejus, q. d. facies igne absumtos tumulum cinerum. Sed præfertur merito à Dn. D. Geiero vulg. cui consonant ó, Æth. & Luther. cujus Glossa marginal. vid.

## 22:1 Argument
PSALM XXII. A prayer of the hind exposed to the most grievous hunting, that is, of Christ suffering, containing the desertion of God, the reproach of all men, the besetting of wild beasts, the piercing of hands and feet, and the stripping of garments, with a vow of public thanksgiving.

FOR THE MORNING HELP) ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀντιλήψεως τῆς ἑωθινῆς, that is, to implore the help of God in the morning. The Greek interpreters seem, for that which we have אילת, to have read עוזר, for עזרתי ἀντίληψις is translated in this very Psalm, verse 20. If we now follow the received reading, אילת השחר seems to be the beginning of the dawn. For the Arabism related to the Hebraism leads us to that. This ode describes the calamities of David the fugitive. Yet it does not prevent it from looking toward the Messiah in a more sublime sense, which the Hebrew scholia, which they call Midrash, also indicate for this place. And it often happens that words in a mystical sense have a more open and less figurative meaning.

Thus Grotius corrupts both the title of the Psalm and its argument, and indeed the entire Psalm, for the sake of the Jews. The title was indeed subject to various expositions, yet no one, so far as I know, has been found who believed that עוזר had once been read in the Hebrew text. Which is a total change of the Hebrew word, with nothing left except the final servile letter. If it is permissible to invent such changes in the Hebrew text for the sake of some translation when it varies, what will finally remain that ought to be left intact in the Hebrew truth? This audacity argues for a spirit that is not good: one that seeks to render the foundation of saving doctrine (I refer to Holy Scripture) doubtful and uncertain, nay, to undermine it from the very foundation. But all the Hebrews, however much they differ in their exposition, retain the word אילת, and the author of the Midrash, R. Aben-Ezra, R. David Kimchi, R. Salomon Jarchi, R. Obadiah, confirm it. Gaon, and the rest. Which that notable work of the Masorah also confirms, observing unanimously that there are three places in which אילת is read: here, Jerem. 14, v. 5, and Proverbs 5, 19. The Jesuit Bellarmine is more modest here than Grotius, preferring to deduce the Greek from the Hebrew rather than to correct the Hebrew from the Greek, although he betrays his own ignorance when he wishes to prove that אילת signifies 'he took up,' from nowhere else than from a similarly bad version of Ps. 107, 15 in the Vulgate. It seems, therefore, in my opinion, that the LXX interpreters also read אילת entirely, but took the word to mean strength or virtue, as if it hints that the strength of divine help or divine virtue is to be implored in the morning: and that what Aben-Ezra observes about R. Menachem, who also rendered it as 'morning help,' confused different words: of which one is without a dagesh, the other, which occurs here, with a dagesh. But as for the meaning of the Hebrew word, it is not for us to deduce it from Arabism with Grotius, since that word occurs in the Hebrew text, and as the Masorah notes, it is read three times in the Sacred Scriptures as 'hind.' Which interpretation is not rejected by R. Kimchi, even though he also explains the title as the rising of the dawn. For he notes that the congregation of Israel is called a hind, and the word 'dawn' is added because of its beauty: Thus also R. Salomon Jarchi, even though he says the name of an instrument is noted, nevertheless adds: or concerning the morning hind, the congregation of Israel, beautiful as the hind of delights and looking forth as the dawn, which David foresaw would go into captivity. Furthermore, the title is not to be taken as referring to the beginning of the dawn, as if the Psalm had always to be sung at that time, even though it pleased some Hebrews and Junius, who render it 'to the strength' or 'the beginning of the dawn,' and in a convenient sense to denote the nobility of the Psalm, the dignity of the same argument to be constantly inculcated, the piety of the ancients, and its conformity with our faith, as Dr. Tarnovius seems to think; the reason for which we have already brought forward from R. Aben-Ezra. Strength is expressed by the word אֱיָלוּת, which is found in this Psalm, v. 20. But here we have אַיֶּלֶת, which word signifies nothing but a hind. But as for understanding it with Kimchi and R. Salomon as a musical instrument, or with Aben-Ezra as the beginning of a song to whose tune the Psalm is to be sung, no reason persuades us, especially where the Hebrew word itself can be retained in the proper sense which it yields, and it agrees very well with the argument of the Psalm. There is no reason for us to explain it as the morning STAR with some Hebrews; indeed, there is a sufficiently pregnant reason why it should not be so explained, because that word nowhere denotes a star in the Holy Code, but we have said that it was observed in the Masorah itself that it denotes a hind.

Blessed Luther expressed the argument of the Psalm very well from that title: 'Of the hind that is hunted early.' For in this Psalm, the passion of Christ is compared to a hunt, Christ himself to a hind, and his enemies to dogs, v. 17, and the passion of Christ and his consequent resurrection, and the act of the passion and resurrection, is clearly described. And thus that morning hunt, because he was dragged early in the morning from the house of Annas to Caiaphas, and thence to the praetorium of Pilate, or because the hunt began early from the beginning of the world, just as he is said to have been slain from the foundation of the world, can be indicated. For no one among Christians has doubted that there is a prophecy here concerning Christ; the matter is too clear, both from the words of the Psalm and from the explanation of the New Testament, so much so that even Calvin himself not only interprets those things which look to the amplitude of the kingdom of Christ and the conversion of the whole world as properly concerning Christ in the latter part of the Psalm, but also in the former part, where it deals with the passions, he affirms that a type of Christ is proposed in the person of David, nay, at v. 7 he is forced to confess that the Son of God ought ESPECIALLY to come to our mind here: our Grotius also asserts that the Psalm looks toward the Messiah in a MORE SUBLIME SENSE, which he then calls MYSTICAL, and brings the Jews themselves to that opinion. Moreover, since it is agreed that we must be entirely certain about the immediate, historical, and paraphrastic sense in the interpretation of Scripture, which, namely, flows from the words themselves and is intended by the Holy Spirit through them by the force of the context, regarding that, not only Calvin, but Grotius also, pressing here in the footsteps of Calvin, to whom he is otherwise sufficiently hostile, egregiously Judaizes: which, just as the blessed predecessor Dr. Aegidius Hunnius demonstrated to the eye for Calvin, so he convicted Grotius of the same Jewish error at the same time, and both ought to be considered to have been solidly refuted.

For is this not judaizing, when Grotius makes the argument of the Psalm the calamities of the fugitive David with the Jews? Which opinion of theirs R. David Kimchi reports in this place. Whence I wonder that Hackspan reproves the blessed Jac. Martini, because in book 3 of the Trib. Elohim he wrote that certain Jews accept the present Psalm concerning David, even though some have explained the same concerning the woman Esther in the Yalkut in this place, and the most recent ones concerning the Israelites established in exile. When likewise he invents with the Jews a double ancient reading of verse 18, so that that one concerning the crucifixion or piercing of the hands and feet, which can in no way be fitted to David, but only to Christ, may not be held as uniquely true, and so that the argument which Christians seek from thence may be rendered doubtful, nay, he asserts that the reading of the Jews can be defended: When finally, according to the perversity of the Jews, he contends with Calvin that that most clear prophecy concerning Christ, which is had in verse 19, they divided my garments among themselves, must be understood metaphorically concerning David, in this sense: they divided my fortunes among themselves as if confiscated. For thus the whole Psalm must be corrupted in the Jewish manner, and what was uniquely predicted concerning Christ must be twisted toward David; whereas all things in the Psalm cohere by a perpetual continuity of the text, and speak concerning the same subject. But how little is this, which Grotius leaves here to Christians, while explaining the Psalm in a proper, immediate, and primary sense concerning David in a Jewish spirit, he at least says that this does not prevent it from having regard in a more sublime sense to the Messiah? In this way, indeed, the Jews will triumph over the Christians: If the Psalm in its proper and immediate sense describes the calamities of the fugitive David, it cannot and ought not, according to the intention of the Holy Spirit, be explained of any other than David, not of the Messiah, because no other sense is intended by the Holy Spirit than the literal, proper one, and that which flows immediately from the words. The Jew will say that another, and a more sublime one, which looks to Christ, is intended is a mere begging of the question. And what, then, will remain for converting the same person, if those words have been so distorted by which the Jews could uniquely be constrained? Then, indeed, how false it is that one saying has many and most disparate senses intended by the Holy Spirit, and that only the historical and literal sense is genuine and native, has been said often. Nothing, therefore, will he gain for the Christian faith from another fictitious sense. And what certainty Grotius himself has, he testifies sufficiently, when he says that his own interpretation concerning David DOES NOT PREVENT, at least, that it be understood in a more sublime or mystical sense concerning the Messiah, that is, he concedes that it CAN be understood in some sense concerning the Messiah: But because the consequence from CAN to IS is not valid, the Jew will deny that these things in this place ought to be understood concerning the Messiah, and that that more sublime and mystical sense, which could underlie the words, was intended by the Holy Spirit. For it is certain that many senses of words are sometimes given and can be given, which nevertheless were not intended by the Holy Spirit, or concerning which at least it is not established beyond contradiction that they were intended. Add that the allegorical or mystical sense is not argumentative, and has no force of demonstration, by which method the nerve of the argument, which is accustomed to be drawn from this Psalm concerning the Messiah by Christians, will likewise be cut: nor will they profit much against the Jews. For these will always cry out: That the native and genuine sense is concerning David, but that they are not compelled to accept another sense, concerning a clearly different subject, or a mystical and more sublime one: That there is indeed no doubt that David was a type of Christ in many things, but since he was not his type in all things, the argument proceeds from a particular, and is therefore illogical: that in these things which are described in the Psalm, he was a type of the Messiah, and that those things also which are proposed in the Psalm, insofar as some more sublime and mystical sense of them can be found, according to which they look to Christ, were predicted here by the Holy Spirit concerning Christ, that, indeed, is the point in question. Therefore, that cannot be assumed as something agreed upon, but must be demonstrated before all else by invincible arguments. But how will it be demonstrated? From the interpretation of the New Testament? but the Jews reject that, nay, they affirm with Grotius that it is forced, or at least foreign, and that it goes into all other things from the native sense, which is concerning the calamities of the fugitive David. From other places of the Old Testament? But it will have to be proven that this Psalm is explained in those. Finally, from the context, or the very words of the Holy Spirit in this Psalm? But Grotius has already conceded to the Jews that the words themselves, in the native and literal, or paraphrastic sense, which is immediately intended by them, sing of David, and that the whole context deals with David. Nothing, therefore, remains but for Grotius to yield here to the Jews: that nothing can be proven from this most illustrious prophecy, which has hitherto been held by all Christians as invincible against the Jews; nay, that contrary to the opinion of the Holy Psalmist it is applied to Christ in the New Testament, and that the Evangelists, as Calvin says quite impiously of them, depart from the NATIVE SENSE by neglecting the figure. For to this point at last has progressed that man of profane slander, from whom Grotius learned his paraphrase, especially concerning verse 19. The passage, however (I recite the words of Calvin), which the Evangelists bring from Psalm 22, seems to be DRAWN UNSEASONABLY to the present case. For since David complains there that he was a prey to his enemies, he designates ALL HIS POSSESSIONS METAPHORICALLY under the name of GARMENTS, as if he had said in one word that he had been despoiled and stripped by the wicked. Which FIGURE, while the Evangelists NEGLECT, they DEPART FROM THE NATIVE SENSE.

Nor does it excuse Grotius that he himself confesses that it happens sometimes that words in the sense which he calls mystical (concerning the Messiah) have a more open and less figurative meaning. For so much the more is he himself to be blamed, because he does not hold the MORE OPEN AND LESS FIGURATIVE meaning for the native and proper sense of the passage, but prefers a FIGURATIVE AND METAPHORICAL sense; that is, he deflects from the propriety of the words to figures. Why does he not acknowledge that according to the native and paraphrastic, if I may so call it, sense, it is treated here concerning the Messiah, but contends that the discourse is thus concerning David? And what does Grotius finally leave here to the Christians, except this, that although the calamities of the fugitive David are described here historically, in them nevertheless CAN BE UNDERSTOOD the calamities of the Messiah prefigured by David: although the words concerning the division of garments are to be taken metaphorically, that David was a prey of his enemies, it CAN nevertheless, if the figure employed by the Holy Spirit is neglected and one departs from the native sense, BE UNDERSTOOD concerning the division of the garments of the Messiah instituted by the soldiers, according to the more open meaning of the words. But by what reason, since in the same place the same word CANNOT be understood simultaneously METAPHORICALLY and PROPERLY, nothing else will remain than that the thing itself, which was signified and indicated here by the native sense of the words, namely the depredation of David, bore the type of the future depredation and despoiling of the garments of the Messiah; the thing, I say, itself, signified there by those metaphorical words, was thus a type of the Messiah, but not the words of the Psalm, if we ought to be precise, to be understood concerning the Messiah in a typical or mystical sense: just as those things which are had in Exodus 12 concerning the Paschal Lamb are to be taken only historically, and do not have a double sense, even if under that history something concerning Christ was shadowed forth. To say it in a word, only the type will be left. Although not even that can be obtained against the Jews. That the Paschal lamb was indeed a type of the Messiah, along with the Levitical victims, was undoubted even among the Jews: But that David, in those things which are sung in this Psalm, was a type of the Messiah, cannot be proven from the O. T. I add that, even with the authority of the N. T. admitted, it cannot be demonstrated. For where is a type of this kind indicated in the N. T. in such a way as is established concerning the type of the Paschal lamb from the Apostolic declaration? Indeed, as the blessed Hunnius rightly warned, that notable Psalm (admitting the explanation of Calvin and Grotius) will prophesy of the Passion of Christ no differently than those Biblical chapters in the first and second book of Samuel, in which the afflictions of David are historically commemorated, and this will be the only difference in both cases, that other prophets described the history concerning David in the books of Samuel: but David himself proposed the same history in this Psalm, as it were reduced to a summary, under the form of a prayer to God. Just as therefore in the history of the books of Samuel, when it is narrated how Saul persecuted David, how he surrounded him with his armies in the cave of Maon, etc., the native, proper, and paraphrastic sense speaks of David, AND NOT OF CHRIST: but then in the place of doctrine, or a common place, it is added that David bore in these things a type of Christ: so if David in that Psalm historically recounts to the Lord what he himself suffered under Saul, as Calvin and

Grotius contends that then, in exactly the same way, the historical and paraphrastic sense, and the proper and genuine text, will relate to David, but the Psalm will relate to Christ in no other way than that in which the history of David described in 1 Sam. chapters 23, 24, 25, etc., is accustomed to be referred to him. Whether this is to keep such a famous oracle safe and sound, I leave to be estimated by the sound judgment of all who love the glory of Christ and cherish the truth, along with the blessed Hunnius.

But now let us show by arguments from the text and the infallible interpretation of the New Testament that this treats of the Messiah alone, and by no means of David, according to the native sense and that which is directly indicated by the words of the Psalmist.

But first, from the continuity of the whole Psalm, it is certain that it treats here of one and the same subject, as far as the native sense is concerned: But in the latter part of the Psalm, when he who had narrated his sufferings and his deliverance from them receives that he will celebrate the name of the Lord, David cannot be understood, but it must necessarily be confessed that a prophecy concerning the New Testament is held there, because that proclamation is to be preached in the GREAT Church and throughout the whole world: v. 26 ff. 'My praise shall be of thee in the great congregation: all the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the Lord: And all the families of the nations shall worship before thee: for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations: All they that be fat upon earth have eaten and worshipped: And my soul shall live unto him, and my SEED shall serve him.' As these things teach that the discourse is about the same subject who previously instituted the complaints, so they cannot be understood of David, nor were they fulfilled in any other than the Messiah in the time of the New Testament, which Calvin himself was forced to acknowledge: 'I confess indeed,' he says, 'that the name of David was great and famous among the neighboring nations; but how small a portion of the world was this? Add that he never brought the foreigners, upon whom he imposed the yoke of his rule, to the pure worship of God. Wherefore that forced servitude, which subjected profane nations to an earthly King, was far from the voluntary obedience of piety, which would gather them from their dispersion to the Lord.' And afterwards: 'For there is no DOUBT that this passage agrees with many other prophecies, by which the throne of God is raised, on which Christ may preside to govern the world.' And at verse 31. Whence we gather again that the glory of God is not celebrated here, which, born from a fleeting and vanishing rumor, reached the Gentiles, but that which will illuminate the WORLD with its RAYS until the end. These are Calvin's words: From which it is irrefutably concluded that in the first part, according to the native sense, it does not treat of David, but of Christ. By which argument the Jews can likewise be convinced, especially since they confess that seed is attributed to the Messiah here in v. 31, and that is so certain to them that they even urge it against Jesus of Nazareth, that, since he himself has no children, he should not be held as the Messiah. For they do not see, such is the blindness of the Jews, that these things are sung concerning the spiritual seed of the Messiah: which is also introduced in Is. 53:10, 11 and elsewhere throughout, and is explained by the Psalmist himself concerning believers throughout the whole world: 'A generation to come shall be reckoned to the Lord, and the heavens shall declare his righteousness unto the people that shall be born: that he hath done this.'

Furthermore, that complaint at the beginning of the Psalm, which is by far the most grave and most tragic, is nowhere read to have been repeated by David, and is nowhere explained of David: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' David never complained that he was forsaken by God, that he was far from his salvation, the words of his offenses, that he had cried out day and night, but was not heard. But Christ exclaimed with these very words on the Cross, Matt. 27:46, Mark 15:34, 'Eli, Eli, lama asabthani': so that with a loud voice, while he hung thus with his body expanded and his hands and feet pierced, he might appropriate this Psalm to himself, and indicate that those things had been predicted in the same. Therefore, it is not to be doubted at all that these things are proper to him who complained with these very words in his most grave suffering concerning divine desertion, and who alone among those acceptable to God had need to complain: I say that this complaint fits him alone, because he alone had to sustain the weight of divine wrath and the punishment of infernal torments, than which there is none greater, of divine desertion in our place. Whence all the faithful are free from the curse, because he was made a curse for us on the wood of the Cross, as the Apostle testifies, Gal. 3:13. It fits him alone, what is read here in v. 5, 6, 7, because the faithful hoping in the Lord were delivered, crying to the Lord they were saved: But he himself could not obtain what he so anxiously repeated several times, namely that the cup of sufferings to be drained for us might pass, so that consequently he had need to drink from that cup, and by exclaiming on the cross to complain, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'

Thirdly, he who complained here describes his affliction in such a way that it fits the Messiah in all things, but by no means David. He opposes himself and his suffering to the affliction of the Fathers, and testifies that his own evils are to be preferred far above theirs; and that there is no one who can be compared with him: indeed, that when compared with others, he is a worm, not a man: so that while the Fathers were treated as men, he himself is treated as a worm. Which the Messiah rightly professed concerning his own sufferings, who, made like even to the crimson worm (designated by the Hebrew word) in his bloody passion, had to be crushed like a worm and die in his own blood, and had to be suspended on the cross like a serpent. Cf. Num. 21:9, John 3:15.

Fourthly, while he calls himself the reproach of any man, and the contempt of the people, this again is less fitting for David, but in Christ it was clearly fulfilled, as the Evangelical History testifies: who was despised by men of every kind and rank. Whose contempt and gestures are graphically expressed here in v. 8 and words in v. 9. Which had their fulfillment not in David, but in Christ. For not all who saw David mocked him and shook their head. Where it is said to David, he trusted in the Lord, let him deliver him, and save him, since he desires him? But to Christ those things not only happened exactly so, just as the Spirit of Christ predicted here, as the history of the passion testifies, but the Evangelists also not obscurely intimate that this very prophecy was fulfilled in Christ according to its native and proper sense: Matthew c. 27. 37. And they that passed by blasphemed him SHAKING THEIR HEADS. And v. 43. Likewise also the chief priests mocking with the scribes and elders said: He trusted in God, let him deliver him now, if he desires him. Cf. Mark 15, 29. Luke 23, 35. where the emphasis of the Hebrew word לעג is expressed by the word ἐξεμυκτήριζον. Since the same sarcasms and gestures of those mocking are described here, which the Holy Spirit wished to express particularly through the Evangelists, there is no doubt that he signified with a voice as it were resonant that what was predicted in the Psalm was fulfilled in Christ. Nothing of such a kind is found anywhere concerning David. For he who speaks these things in his own person does not only complain that he is to be exposed to jeers and illusions in general, but he specifically describes the gestures, illusions, and sarcasms of the words: so that we may not err concerning the person who is being dealt with here.

Fifthly, that description of trust in v. 10 does not fit David, my hope from my mother's breasts, which is proper to the Messiah alone. For David confesses that he was conceived in iniquity, and had need of regeneration through the Sacrament of Circumcision, but he did not place his hope in God from the womb and from his mother's breasts. Christ, however, according to his human nature, is Holy from the womb Luke 1, 35. Not to mention here that it is intimated that God brought him forth miraculously from the womb, in a stable, where the services of other little women were absent: and that, although the mother was a virgin, yet he provided for him from the Milk in the mother's breasts, which was observed by B. Tarnovius.

Sixth, the description of the enemies in v. 13 and following is such that it does not sufficiently fit David, but in the Messiah it has obtained its fulfillment in all things: Many bulls have surrounded me, fat bulls have beset me: they have opened their mouth against me, like a ravening and roaring lion. He described the multitude of the enemies, their ferocity, the power of the bulls, their cruelty, and the ardor of doing harm by the likeness of a lion. That these things fit the enemies of Christ most exactly, the Evangelical History clearly testifies. Their multitude was great: From the Priestly order were the Chief Priests and Pharisees; from the Political, Herod and Pilate with their guards and a troop of executioners, and finally the untamed mob: Their ferocity was truly bovine and taurine, because like a young bull the enemies trusted beyond measure in their horns, and raged: Their power was notable, since they did not merely threaten from afar, but brought him into their own power, and surrounded him on all sides, so that he could not escape. They exhibited Leonine cruelty: because they opened their mouth against Christ, so that they might devour or tear him to pieces like prey.

Seventh, the thing itself teaches that Christ graphically depicted here the magnitude and multitude of his sufferings and torments in v. 15, 16. But how these things peculiarly agree with David does not appear. The sufferings which Christ endured in body and soul, how his Flesh, Bones, Heart, the moisture of his tongue, and finally he himself in his entirety wasted away, his hands and feet were pierced, all his bones and joints were stretched, are graphically described: I am poured out like water, he says in v. 15, by which the copious shedding of his blood is noted. Cf. Ps. 79. 3. And they have separated all my bones, by which the disjunction and dislocation of Christ's bones, done most especially in the crucifixion: My heart was like wax melted in the midst of my bowels: by which the deadly melting of Christ's heart, and the opening of the same by the lance, the failure of the internal organs, the liver, the lungs, and others is signified v. 6. My strength is dried up like a potsherd, by which the drying up of the powers of his soul and of the radical moisture itself: And my tongue cleaving to my jaws, by which the loss of voice on account of the heat of divine wrath and extreme consternation; And you have brought me into the dust of death: by which the total deprivation of life is designated. All these things exactly fit the sufferings of Christ: they do not fit David's, who neither shed his blood, nor felt the disjunction of bones, the melting of the heart, the drying up of strength, much less the total deprivation of life in the persecutions of Saul: but he escaped safe from them.

Eighth, the designation of the Crucifixion of Christ, which is subjoined in v. 17, is to be especially observed. According to B. Gefner, in v. 17, 18, 19, there is a brief description of the whole history of the Passion, which can be distributed into three acts according to three places: the Garden, the City, and the place of execution. The first is the betrayal and capture in the garden, concerning which he says: dogs have surrounded me, like the morning hind, so that the ministers of the Priests and the lictors are compared to hunting dogs. The second act in the city, partly before Annas and Caiaphas, the High Priest, and partly before Pilate the Governor, is expressed thus: The congregation of the malignant has surrounded me: because עדה denotes an assembly which meets by public edict, and is translated by the LXX as συναγωγὴ. The third is outside the city, in the place of Calvary, where they first pierced the hands and feet of Christ with nails, then stretched the most tender and most holy body of Christ on the cross to such an extent that one could count all his bones and ribs. Furthermore, with lurid eyes, burning spirits, and Diabolical gloating, they mocked him as he hung on the Cross. They themselves will look and stare at me. Finally, the soldiers divided his garments, and cast lots for his tunic. All of which provide peculiar proofs for the literal sense concerning Christ, against the literal sense concerning David: since all things have been fulfilled according to the native sense in the former, not in the latter. But above all, the kind of execution must be urged here. For it treats of that execution, of that suffering according to the native sense, which brings about the piercing of the hands and feet, and such an expansion of the whole body that all the bones can be counted: But David was not subject to such an execution or suffering, but Christ was: Wherefore it is certain that according to the native sense of the Psalm, it treats here not of David, but of Christ.

Ninth, an argument also arises here under our hand, and it is indissoluble. It treats here according to the genuine and native sense of the Psalmist of him whose garments the enemies divided among themselves, and for whose tunic they cast lots. For no necessity compels us to resort to metaphors here. But it is not to be granted to fix both senses, the metaphorical and the proper, in the same place, unless we wish to make Delphic oracles out of the scriptures. And the distinct denomination of the tunic and the remaining garments is to be noted here, and the distinct acts concerning the same are to be properly observed, which it is not permitted to distinguish in a metaphor: But it is not to be thought that such a distinction was made by the Holy Spirit in vain here, since nothing is placed in the Sacred Scriptures rashly. Now the enemies divided the garments of the Messiah among themselves; but the tunic, because it was seamless, they did not divide, but cast lots for it, as the Evangelical History testifies: something of which kind is nowhere commemorated concerning David. Strength is added to this argument by the explanation of the Holy Spirit itself: For lest anyone should still be able to doubt that this was fulfilled in the passion of Christ, behold witnesses superior to any exception, St. John c. 19, 23 sqq., and also St. Matthew c. 27, 35. The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified him, took his garments (and made four parts, to each soldier a part) and the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless and woven from the top throughout. They said therefore to one another: let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be. Why these little details so laboriously? Why was that division of garments and casting of lots for the tunic described by all four Evangelists, unless so that the prophecy of David might be recognized as fulfilled, which St. John therefore added expressly with Matthew, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, saying: they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots. When these things are narrated as having been so clearly fulfilled in Christ, is not the perversity of Calvin and Grotius to be detested, who understand figuratively the words which, according to the Rule of good interpretation and according to the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, are to be taken literally, and who twist those things which according to the Evangelists treat of Christ, to David, and peddle this metaphorical sense of theirs as the genuine and native one?

Tenth, the prayer which is appended to the narration of the sufferings suits Christ better than David, v. 20 seqq., in which he asks to be snatched from the sword in death, and to be delivered from the mouth of the infernal Lion, and also from the horns of the unicorns, that is, from the power of haughty and arrogant enemies. For it must be considered here that the subject is the hind of the morning, exposed then to the power of both the infernal lion and bodily enemies, and the extreme danger which is described here with such a great apparatus of words must be fixed in the mind, and it will be manifest that these things square far more rightly with the Messiah than with David, whose cross was a yoke and a light burden, if it is compared with the cross of Christ. Nor is David ever compared to a Hind: but it is certain that Christ is compared to a Hind from Canticles 2:9: My beloved is like a roe or a young hart. But the fact that David wished to introduce the hind here rather in the feminine gender, that was done without doubt, in the judgment of the blessed Gesner, because he wished to describe Christ as plainly weak, destitute of all help at the time of his passion, and wished to shadow forth his immense love toward the human race through the intense ςοργή (affection) of the hind. The Chaldean explained it concerning the morning burnt offering: that the passion of Christ was shadowed forth by this, is beyond doubt among Christians from the Epistle to the Hebrews; which, that they might cherish it with a faithful mind, the Jews are said to have recited this Psalm every morning, as being a prophecy concerning the passion of Christ, than which none more evident is found in the O.T., in which Cassiodorus warned that not so much a prophecy as a history is handed down, for which reason also the past is frequently used for the future in this Psalm, so that the sacred psalmist seems not so much to have looked forward by prophesying into the future, as to have fixed his eyes and pen upon a present matter.

Eleventh, the thanksgiving for the deliverance, which is subjoined in the second part of the Psalm, befits not David, but Christ: who receives that he will declare the name of the Lord to all his brethren, and will praise the Lord in the midst of the Church, exciting by his example and exhortation others to the same piety. Ye that fear the Lord, praise him, all ye the seed of Jacob, glorify him: Which pertain to the whole spiritual seed of Jacob Rom. 9, 7. 8. Gal. 4, 21. c. 6, 16. For David did not equally declare the name of the Lord to his brethren in the midst of the Church, and so excite all the seed of Jacob; and the matter of divine praises, which he here proposes, is universal, concerning all, because God has not despised, nor disdained the affliction of the afflicted, nor turned his face from him, which is deservedly proposed to all from the person of the Messiah, whether because this is the first and chief matter of divine praise for believers, which they have from the passion and deliverance of Christ, or because it is the foundation and meritorious cause of the hearing of all the afflicted. Then also that spiritual satisfying of the poor or meek, by which they are to be filled with the gifts of God to satiety. The poor shall eat and be satisfied, joined with the celebration of the Lord, is peculiarly vindicated to the kingdom of the Messiah Is. 55, 2. Matth. 5, 6. Joh. 4, 14. c. 6, 27. Rom. 14, 17. The most sweet feast of the faithful is from the flesh of this morning hind, which was exposed to death for the life of the world Joh. 6, 54. thence our hearts shall live for ever and ever. By this name is predicted here the conversion of the Gentiles, that all the fat ones of the earth may also eat and worship, with all who go down into the dust (the great and the lowly), that the spiritual seed, from Jews and Gentiles, may be reckoned to the Lord, in every generation even to the end of the world, and that he may come who shall announce the Evangelical righteousness to the people to be born and to be converted, which HE HIMSELF SHALL DO, because from him is the beginning, middle, and complement of salvation. Which exhibit the sum of Evangelical sermons, and the fruit of the passion of Christ, and can be seen explained among Orthodox Interpreters. But lest any doubt remain that Christ is set forth here as the herald of the praises of the Lord, we have the Apostle as a most abundant witness Heb. 2, 12. who explains these things not concerning David, but concerning Christ, openly among the Hebrews, whence it is not permitted to doubt but that at that time it was beyond doubt among the Hebrews that the present Psalm is to be understood concerning Christ. For which reason he is not confused to call them brethren, saying: I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the Church will I praise thee. R. Solomon also refers to the days of Christ at v. 29. The kingdom is the Lord's: In the days of Christ the kingdom shall return to the Lord, and it shall be made known to his people by deliverance.

Twelfth and lastly, we urge that which we do with the blessed Hunnius, that it cannot be proved by even one argument, even to appearance, that the Prophet here sings of his own adversities, which he suffered under Saul or other enemies, whence by common suffrage the ancient and recent interpreters refer the Psalm not to the afflictions of David, but without a type to the passion of Christ alone; the sum of which Theodoret thus comprehends: This Psalm predicts Christ's cross and resurrection, and the calling of the Gentiles, and the salvation of the whole world. That it treats solely of Christ and describes the passions not of David, but of the Messiah, the most ancient of the Fathers taught, among the Greeks Justin Dial. c. Tryph., among the Latins Tertull. advers. Jud. c. 10, whose words it is pleasing to transcribe: If you still seek, he says, the preaching of the Lord's cross, the twenty-first Psalm will already be able to suffice for you, containing the whole passion of Christ, singing even then his own glory. To Aurelius Cassiodorus the present Psalm seemed so clear in this cause, that he said it seemed to him a history written, not a prophecy. Nor will one easily be found in antiquity who moved a doubt, except Theodore of Mopsuestia, whom Leontius of Byzantium perhaps reports to have explained all the Psalms Judaically, with only three applied to Christ: But he was condemned for that reason in the V. Council of Constantinople, as also in the Roman Synod under Vigilius. For the rest, by unanimous opinion, Christian Interpreters explained the Psalm concerning Christ, and indeed in such a way that they believed only his passions, not David's, were described, both because of the evidence of the Psalm and because of the Apostolic testimonies: For these, as Brentius gravely says, ought to be more certain to us than if an Angel from heaven, let alone some vain and blinded Rabbi, should dream otherwise to us. The Jews, and our Judaizers, Calvin and Grotius, as resting on no foundation at all, but following an ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν (private interpretation), nay, openly contradicting Christ and the Apostles, and the very clearest words of the Psalm, no pious and sensible man will heed. Nor do they find in their commentaries where to fix their foot: Grotius wishes the calamities of David the fugitive under Saul to be described: Calvin, that not one persecution only, but whatsoever he suffered, is comprehended. But among the Jews, although some explain it concerning David, when he was fleeing from Saul, yet most acknowledge that these things do not befit David, and thus interpret them either concerning the persecution under Haman, or concerning the Babylonian captivity, or concerning the present Jewish Church, which now lies obscure and deserted, as is evident from R. David Kimchi. Again, when Calvin sees that some things must be referred entirely to Christ, he wishes David to be viewed as a type of Christ, explaining some things very absurdly as applying only to Christ, others to both: whereas there is only one subject of the Psalm. For the series of the discourse demands, as Piscator himself warns, that if any one particle is accommodated to David as a type, all the rest should be accommodated to the same, which the truth of history does not allow. Grotius indeed invents a double sense also, but how great an absurdity there is in this commentary has already been shown. Thus they can have no certainty who depart from the native sense of Holy Scripture, which alone is certain and produces immovable πληροφορίαν. But why say more, when the disciples of Calvin himself acknowledge that the Psalm treats of none but Christ. For us Christians, says Rivetus, it is not permitted in this Psalm to doubt, or with that Eunuch in Acts 8:34, to ask, of whom does the Prophet say all these things, of himself, or of some other? For the testimonies of all the Evangelists and of the Apostle Paul, and the words of the Psalm itself, most openly prove that whatever is said in it must be expounded of Christ our Lord: to say it in a word, if anyone compares what the holy Evangelists wrote concerning the passion of the Lord with those things which are contained in this Psalm, he will most openly recognize that ALL things square with Christ in such a way that there is NO OTHER to whom they can be accommodated, and he will discover that David, foreseeing by a most clear ray of illumination many ages before what was to come, described them as if they were past, and that indeed so perfectly and distinctly as if he himself, being present, had surveyed with his own eyes all things which were done afterwards. Although, however, he afterwards attempts to excuse the opinion of Calvin, or rather of Bucer, out of reverence, as it appears, for his teacher, he was nevertheless compelled by the force of truth to openly contradict the same: when he added this: 'But because, although IN SOME PART FROM CERTAIN VERSES THE argument of the Psalm CAN BE ADAPTED TO DAVID, there are nevertheless MANY things which CANNOT BE UNDERSTOOD of him, but point to Christ as if with A FINGER EXTENDED, I incline more to the former opinion, that the argument of the Psalm is SIMPLE, and is referred DIRECTLY TO CHRIST (without a type), so that his speech is of his own dereliction on the cross, complaining of the cruelty of his enemies, and recounting the magnitude of his own sufferings, afterwards asking for liberation, and for it promising to the Father thanksgiving and the preaching of his name among all nations, among whom he predicts the kingdom of God, and the true religion, will be illustrated and declared.' Thus, he who begins with a complaint, on account of the dereliction on the cross, ends in joy, on account of the conversion and multiplication of the faithful from his glorification. Thus Rivetus. Piscator confesses that this Psalm contains a prophecy concerning the passion and death of Christ, and likewise his resurrection and spiritual kingdom, and refutes others who understand it of David. Johannes Drusius, lib. 10. Observ. c. 3: 'I truly,' he says, 'believe without doubt that David, when he composed this Psalm, had in mind what the Holy Spirit had revealed to him περὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν. Why should I not believe it? Since I have as authors the Apostles themselves, who sometimes draw testimonies from it. Nay, the Savior himself, by using the beginning of this song, confirms it more fully, so that no one can or ought to doubt it unless he is PLAINLY IMPIOUS.' See also Rudolph Gualther and Franciscus Junius on this passage: to whom we most recently add the agreement of Grotius, that this treats of the Messiah, in his annotations on Luke 24:42.

Latin:

PSALM. XXII. Precatio cervæ venatui gravissimo expositæ, h. e. Christi patientis, Dei desertionem, hominum omnium opprobrium, ferarum obsessionem, manuum & pedum transfixionem, vestium spoliationem cum voto Eucharistiæ publicæ continens.

PRO SVSCEPTIONE MATVTINA) ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀντιλήψεως τῆς ἑωθινῆς, id est, ad implorandum mane Dei auxilium. Videntur Græci interpretes pro eo, quod habemus אילת legisse עוזר , nam עזרתי ἀντίληψις vertitur hoc ipso Psalmo commate 20. Si receptam nunc lectionem sequa- mur אילת השחר videtur esse initium auroræ. Eo enim nos ducit Arabismus cognatus Hebraismo. Ode hæc Da- vidis profugi calamitates describit. Neque tamen impedit, quo minus sensu sublimiore ad Messiam respiciat, quod & Hebæorum Scholia, quæ Midras vocant, ad hunc locum in- dicant. Et sæpe evenit, ut verba in sensu mystico significa- tionem habeant apertiorem, minusque figuratam.

SIc & titulum Psalmi & argumentum ejusdem, adeoque universum Psalmum in gratiam Judæ- orum corrumpit Grotius. Titulus variis quidem expositionibus obnoxius fuit, nemo tamen, quod sciam, inventus est, qui crediderit, in Hebræo textu lectum quondam fuisse עוזר. Quæ totalis est vocis Hebrææ immutatio, non relicta, nisi fi- nali servili litera. Cujusmodi immutationes si in gratiam translationis alicujus in textu Hebræo, cum ille variat, fingere liceat, quid supererit tan- dem, quod integrum relinqui debeat in Ebraica veritate? Arguit hæc audacia spiritum non bo- num: qui id quærit, ut fundamentum Doctrinæ salutiferæ (Scripturam Sacram indigito) dubium atque incertum reddat, imo ex ipso fundamento eandem subruat. Ebræi autem omnes, utut in expositione non parum discrepantes, vocem אילת retinent, ac confirmant, Autor Midras, R. Aben- Ezra, R. David Kimchi, R. Salomon Jarchi, R. Obad. Gaon, & reliqui. Quam etiam statumi- nat ὁμοθυμαδὸν insigne illud opus Masoræ obser- vans tria esse, in quibus אילת legatur, hic, Jerem. 14. v. 5. & Proverb. 5, 19. Modestior hic est Grotio Jesuita Bellarminus, qui ex Ebræo mavult deduce- re Græcum, quam Ebræum è Græco corrigere, quamvis inscitiam suam prodat, dum probare vult, quod אילת significet suscepit, non aliunde, quam ex mala itidem versione Ps. 107, 15. in Vulgata. Vi- detur ergo, mea quidem sententia, LXX. Interpp. omnino etiam legisse אילת, sed vocem de robore vel virtute accepisse, ac si robur auxilii divini vel divi- nam virtutem mane implorandam innuat: & quod Aben-Ezra de R. Menachem observat, qui etiam reddidit de auxilio matutino, confudisse voces di- versas: quarum una est sine dagesch, altera, quæ hic occurrit, cum Dagesch. Sensum autem vocis Ebrææ quod attinet, non est, ut cum Grotio ex A- rabismo eum deducamus, cum in Ebræo textu vox ea occurrat, & notante Masora ter in Sacris lega- tur de cerva. Quæ interpretatio à R. Kimchio, etsi is etiam de ascensu auroræ titulum explicet, non re- probatur. Notat enim Israelis congregationem vo- cari cervam, & vocem auroræ addi ob pulchritudi- nem: Sic etiam R. Salomo Jarchi, etsi nomen instru- menti notari dicat, addit tamen: vel de cerva matu- tina, congregatione Israel, pulchra sicut cerva deli- ciarum & prospiciente sicut aurora, quam prævidit David ituram in captivitatem. Porro nec de initio auroræ, quasi sub illud semper decantandus fuerit Psalmus, etsi Ebræis etiam nonnullis & Junio id placuit, reddentibus ad fortitudinem, seu primordi- um auroræ, ac sensu commodo ad denotandam Psal- mi nobilitatem, argumenti ejusdem jugiter inculcan- di dignitatem, veterum pietatem, & cum fide nostra conformitatem, ut videtur D. Tarnovio, explicari possit, accipiendus titulus; cujus rei causam jam è R. Aben-Ezra adduximus. Fortitudo exprimitur voce אֱיָלוּת, quæ hoc Psalmo v. 20. reperitur. At hic habetur אַיֶּלֶת quæ vox non nisi cervam signi- ficat. Ut autem cum Kimchio & R. Salomone in- strumentum Musicum, vel cum Aben-Ezra initium cantilenæ, ad cujus tonum decantandus Psalmus, in- telligamus, nulla suadet ratio, maxime ubi vox ipsa Ebræa sensu proprio, quem reddit, retineri potest, atque argumento Psalmi optime congruit. Per STELLAM matutinam ut cum Ebræis noñullis ex- plicemus, causa nulla est, imo causa satis prægnans est, cur ita explicari non debeat, quia nuspiam vox illa stellam notat in S. Codice, cervam autem eam notare in Masora ipsa observatum diximus.

Argumentum Psalmi B. Lutherus ex isto titulo optime expressit: Von der Hindin, die früh geja- get wird. In hoc enim Psalmo Christi passio vena- tioni, Christus ipse Cervæ, hostes ejus canibus v. 17. comparantur, ac passio Christi ejusque consequens resurrectio, ac passionis & resurrectionis actus lu- culenter describitur. Atque ita matutina illa vena- tio, quod mane summo ex domo Hannæ in Cai- phæ, & inde in Pilati prætorium abreptus fuerit, vel quod mane inde à mundi exordio venatio ce- perit, quemadmodum ab origine mundi mactatus dicitur, indigitari poterit. Quod enim de Christo hîc vaticinium habeatur, nemo inter Christianos dubitavit; res nimis clara est, cum è verbis Psalmi, tum è N. T. explicatione, adeo, ut Calvinus etiam ipse non modo in posteriori Psalmi parte, ea quæ spectant amplitudinem regni Christi totiusque mundi conversionem, de Christo proprie inter- pretetur, sed in priori etiam parte, ubi de passioni- bus agitur, in Davidis persona typum Christi pro- poni affirmet, imo ad v. 7. fateri cogatur, PRÆ- CIPUE hic Filium Dei in mentem nobis venire debe- re: Grotius quoque noster SENSU SUBLI- MIOR E, quem MYSTICUM deinde vocat, ad Messiam Psalmum respicere asserat, atque in eam sententiam Judæos ipsos adducat. Cæterum cum de immediato, historico & paraphrastico sensu certos nos omnino esse conveniat in Scripturæ interpre- tatione, qui scil. ex verbis ipsis fluat, & vi contex- tus per illa intendatur à Spiritu Sancto, circa illum non Calvinus tantum, sed Grotius etiam, presse hic Calvini, cui alias satis infensus est, insistens vesti- giis, egregie Judaizat: quod uti Calvino ad ocu- lum demonstravit B. Antecessor Dn. D. Ægidius Hunnius, ita in eodem simul Grotium Judaici er- roris convicit, ac utrumque solide refutasse cen- seri debet.

Annon enim hoc ἰυδαΐζειν est, quando Gro- tius cum Judæis argumentum Psalmi facit profugi Davidis calamitates? Quam eorum sententiam re- fert R. David Kimchi in h. l. Unde miror Hackspa- nium B. Jac. Martini reprehendere, quod lib. 3. de Trib. Elohim scripserit, Judæos quosdam Psalmum præsentem de Davide accipere, utut nonnulli eun- dem de fæmina Esther in Jalcut ad h. l. ac recen- tissimi de Israelitis in exilio constitutis exposuerint. Quando item cum Judæis duplicem antiquam lectio- nem v. 18. fingit, ne illa de crucifixione vel confos- sione manuum & pedum, quæ nullatenus Davidi, sed soli Christo aptari potest, unice vera habeatur, utque argumentum, quod inde Christiani petunt, dubium reddatur, imo Judæorum lectionem defendi posse asserit: Quando denique juxta στρεβλότητα Ju- dæorum, cum Calvino apertissimum illud vatici- nium de Christo, quod v. 19. habetur, diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, de Davide intelligendum esse με- ταφορικῶς contendit, hoc sensu: fortunas meas ut confiscatas inter se partiti sunt. Ita enim totum Psal- mum Judaico more corrumpi, ac quod de Christo unice prædictum, ad Davidem detorqueri oportet; quum omnia in Psalmo perpetua textus συνεχεία cohæreant, & de eodem subjecto loquantur. Quantillum vero hoc est, quod Christianis hîc re- linquit Grotius, dum Psalmum sensu proprio, imme- diato & primario de Davide Judaico Spiritu expo- nens saltem, id non impedire, ait, quo minus sensu- sublimiore ad Messiam respiciat? Ita profecto triumphabunt Judæi adversus Christianos: Si sensu proprio & immediato Psalmus calamitates profugi Davidis describat, non posse nec debere eundem, juxta intentionem Spiritus Sancti, de alio quam Davide, non de Messia explicari, quia nullus alius est sensus à Spiritu Sancto intentus, quam literalis, proprius & qui ex verbis immediate fluit. Alium, eumque sublimiorem, qui Christum respiciat, intendi, meram petitionem principii esse, dicet Judæus. Et quid tandem pro convertendo eodem supererit, si verba illa ita detorta fuerint, quibus Judæi unice constringi poterant? Tum vero, quam falsum sit, unius dicti plures & maxime disparatos à Spiritu S. intentos esse sensus, solumq; sensum Historicum & literalem genuinum & nativum esse, sæpius dictum. Nihil ergo ab altero fictitio sensu præsidii reportabit pro fide Christiana. Et quæ certitudo sit ipsi Grotio, satis ipse testatur, quando propriam interpretationem de Davide NON IMPEDIRE, saltem ait, ne intelligatur sensu sublimiori vel mystico de Messia, hoc est, POSSE intelligi aliquo sensu de Messia concedit: Sed quia à POSSE ad ESSE non valet consequentia, negabit ita Judæus, quod h. l. illa de Messia intelligi debeant, & quod sensus ille sublimior & mysticus, qui posset subesse verbis, à Spiritu S. intentus sit. Certum enim est, quod multi quandoque dentur & dari possint sensus verborum, qui tamen à Spiritu S. intenti non sint, aut de quibus saltem non constet ἀναντιῥῥήτως, eos intentos esse. Adde quod sensus allegoricus vel mysticus non sit argumentativus, nullamque demonstrandi vim habeat, quo pacto itidem nervus incidetur argumento, quod ex hoc Psalmo de Messia depromi à Christianis solet: neque multum adversus Judæos proficient. Hi enim semper clamabunt; Sensum nativum & genuinum esse de Davide, se autem alium sensum, de plane alio subjecto, aut mysticum & sublimiorem non cogi acceptare: Non dubium quidem esse, Davidem typum Christi in multis fuisse, sed quum in omnibus typus ejus non fuerit, argumentum à particulari procedere, adeoque ἀσυλλόγισον esse: quod in his quæ in Psalmo describuntur, typus fuerit Messiæ, & quod illa etiam, quæ in Psalmo proponuntur, qua inveniri potest eorum sensus aliquis sublimior, atq; mysticus, secundum quem Christum ea respiciant, à Spiritu S. de Christo hic prædicta sint, id vero esse τὸ κρινόμενον. Proinde id non posse assumi tanquam ὁμολογύμενον, sed ante omnia invictis argumentis demonstrandum esse. Quî vero demonstrabitur? Num è N. T. interpretatione? at illam reprobant Judæi, imo coactam esse, aut saltem alienam, & à sensu nativo, qui est de Davidis profugi calamitatibus, in alia omnia ire, cum Grotio affirmant. Num ex aliis Vet. Testam. locis? at in illis Psalmum hunc explicatum esse, probandum erit. Num denique è contextu, aut verbis ipsis Spiritus S. in hoc Psalmo? At verba ipsa nativo & literali, vel paraphrastico sensu, qui immediate illis intenditur, Davidem canere, totumque contextum de Davide agere, Grotius Judæis jam concessit. Nihil ergo superest, quam ut victas hic Judæis det manus Grotius: non probari posse quidquam ex hoc tam illustri vaticinio, quod ab omnibus Christianis hactenus pro invicto habitum fuit adversus Judæos; imo præter sententiam Hieropsaltis id in Nov. Test. ad Christum applicari, & Evangelistas ut impie satis de ipsis Calvinus, negligendo figuram à NATIVO SENSU discedere. Huc enim tandem progressus est prophanæ maledicentiæ is, à quo suam paraphrasin, maxime circa v. 19. didicit Grotius. Locus tamen (verba Calvini recito) quem ad- ducunt Evangelistae ex Psalm. 22. videtur INTEM- PESTIVE ad praesentem causam TRAHI. Nam cum illic queratur David, se hostibus praedae fuisse ME- TAPHORICE sub nomine VESTIUM SUA O- MNIA designat, ac si uno verbo dixisset, spoliatum se, ac nudatum ab improbis fuisse. Quam FIGU- RAM dum NEGLIGUNT Evangelistae, a NATI- VO SENSU DISCEDUNT.

Neque id excusat Grotium, quod fateatur ipse, evenire quandoque, ut verba in sensu, quem vocat, my- stico (de Messia) significationem habeant apertiorem, minusque figuratam. Tanto enim magis arguendus ipse est, quod APERTIOREM, MINUSQUE FIGURATAM significationem non habeat pro nativa & propria loci sententia, sed praeferat FI- GURATUM & METAPHORICUM sensum; hoc est, a proprietate verborum ad figuras deflectat. Cur non agnoscit secundum nativum & paraphra- sticum, ut ita vocem, sensum de Messia hic agi, sed de Davide ita sermonem esse contendit? Et quid hic denique Christianis relinquit Grotius, nisi hoc, quod etsi Davidis profugi calamitates hic historice describantur, in illis tamen INTELLIGI POS- SINT calamitates Messiae per Davidem praefigurati: etsi verba de divisione vestium μεταφορικῶς accipi- enda sint, Davidem hostium praedam fuisse, POSSE tamen, si neglecta figura a Spiritu S. adhibita, a nati- vo sensu discedatur, INTELLIGI de divisione vesti- um Messiae a militibus instituta, juxta apertiorem si- gnificationem verborum. Qua vero ratione, siqui- dem in eodem loco idem verbum NON POSSIT simul & METAPHORICE & PROPRIE intelligi, nihil aliud remanebit, quam rem illam, quae hic nativo verborum sensu significata, & indicata fuit a Spiritu S. depraedationem nempe Davidis typum gessisse futurae depraedationis & spoliationis vestium Messiae; Res, inquam, ipsa, illic per verba ista Meta- phorica significata, typus Messiae sic fuerit, non vero verba Psalmi sensu typico aut mystico, si ἀκριβολογεῖν debeamus, intelligenda de Messia : perinde ut ea quae Exod. 12. de Agno Paschali habentur, historice tantum accipienda sunt, non vero geminum sensum habent, etsi sub historia illa adumbratum aliquid de Christo fuerit. Verbo ut dicam, typus solum re- linquetur. Quanquam nec ille quidem adversus Ju- daos obtineri possit. Agnum sane Paschalem typum Messiae cum victimis Leviticis fuisse, indubitatum etiam apud Judaeos fuit: At Davidem in illis, quae hoc Psalmo decantantur, typum Messiae fuisse, e V. T. probari non potest. Addo, ne admissa quidem N. T. autoritate id demonstrari posse. Ubi enim ty- pus ejusmodi in N. T. ita indicatus, uti de Agni Pa- schalis typo e declaratione Apostolica constat? Imo, quod B.
