Pfeifferus in disp. de hac voce hic habita: ut & Altingius de integritate vocis כארי §. 39. Nec ullam videmus causam, cur eadem reprobanda sit, imprimis quia Philologi observant cum R. David Kimchi in Michlol. f. 35. א in verbis quiescentibus ע mediam radicalem esse, & in Kametz delitescere. Vid. Dn. Pfeifferus §. 37. l. c. Quo pa- cto non opus est statuere Nun Epentheticum, & so- lum apocope literæ Mem satis usitata relinquetur: atque hic sensus non modo simplicissimus est, sed etiam versionibus omnibus prædictis, præ aliis inter- pretationibus egregie consonat. (5.) Confirmatur Christianorum Interpp. explicatio e contextus συν- εχείᾳ atque ordine. Quum enim de consiliis actum fuerit v. 16. quæ in concilio malignantium instituta, ad crucifixionem directa fuisse Historia Evangelica testatur, consequens est, ut etiam de effectu agatur, & quum de antecedentibus & sequentibus crucifixionem, ipsa cumprimis vestium divisione, ac de tunicæ sortitione, tam luculenter tractetur, quomodo, quod præcipuum in passione, ac reliquorum pene caput est (externas indigito passiones) silentio involveretur, ac cruci- fixio ipsa, quæ peculiarem fidei articulum in Symbolo Apostolico constituit, plane præteriretur? Quæ vero quum optime perfossione ac perterebratione manuum ac pedum, utpote quæ in nullo alio supplicio conti- git, designetur, hic eam ita indicatam esse, creden- dum est. (6.) E complementi luce. Quum in recen- fione sione passionum Christi manuum ac pedum hic mentio fiat, ab ipso eventu satis constat, perfossionem ma- nuum ac pedum, in crucifixione factam, intelligendam esse. Quo de B. Luth. graviter ac præclare Tom. 2. Lat. Jen. Comm. in hunc Psalm. f. 252. Nobis, qui in Christum credimus, & HUNC Psalmum totum de Christo dictum auctoritate Evangelica tenemus, facile est pro- bare legendum, foderunt, non sicut Leo. Nos enim non rem gestam e Scripturarum mysteriis, sed Scripturarum mysteria e re gesta, h. e. veterem Scripturam Evangelio illustramus, & non e contra ad illius sensum hujus sensum comparamus, & in Christum, ceu duos Cherubim in pro- pitiatorium, spectare facimus, sicut dicit Jer. 23. in no- vissimis intelligetis consilium ejus. Et ad Mosen: Poste- riora mea videbis. Cum ergo certum habeamus, Christi manus & pedes esse perfossos in cruce, nec minus certum, hunc Psalmum in Christum quadrare, tum sensus mire consentiat, ac omnino exigat, FODERUNT legendum esse, præsertim cum nullus etiam Grammaticæ rigor huic resistat, absque contentione & commutatione legimus fo- derunt. Et cum περιστάσεις crucifixionibus Christi a Spriritu Christi, qui in Prophetis fuit, pleræque omnes exacte designatæ fuerint, quis credat, id, quod præ- cipuum in passione est, ipsam nempe crucifixionem, ab eodem haud significatam fuisse? (7.) E transla- tionum ὁμοψηφίᾳ & consensione. Non enim a Chri- stianis demum hæc ita translata sunt. Sed ab ipsis LXX. Interpp. qui reddiderunt ὤρυξαν. foderunt. Nec non a Chald. Interprete, qui in pretio apud Judæos est. Nec in nuperis solum translationibus, sed in an- tiquissimis, utpote Hieronymi, qui reddidit FIXE- RUNT, ut & vulgata versione, quæ habet, FODERUNT, quibus, quomodo Aquilæ translatio consentiat, antea dictum est. Nec Græci tantum, & Latini, sic explica- runt. Habent eandem interpretationem Arabes in sua paraphrasi: habent eam Syri, habent Æthiopes & alii. (8.) E Masoræ observatione. Quum enim in ipsa Masora, cujus magna apud Judæos auctoritas est, cer- tum habeatur, aliam significationem vocem כָּאֲרִי hic obtinere, quam Es.38,13. ubi citra controversiam notat, SICUT LEO, nulla autem alia significatio dari queat, quam illa a כּוּר FODERUNT, inhærendum utique eidem erit: aut melior danda explicatio. Si illa a כָּאַר defœdârunt suggeratur, quomodo ista nostræ interpre- tationi non adversa sit, sed consonet, jam ostensum. Ad- de quod ad Num. 24, 25. Masora notet in quibusdam Codd. scriptum fuisse כָּארוּ, quæ vox non potest exponi SICUT LEO. Nostra ergo Christianorum interpreta- tio juxta utramque lectionem locum habet, non item Judaica. Quibus denique accedit (9.) argumentum e loci paralleli collatione Zach. 12, 10. Videbunt, quem transfixerunt; qui ad crucifixionem Christi applicatur Joh. 19, 37. Hæc ergo etiam de isto insigni loco.

## 22:18
Vers. 19. THEY DIVIDED MY GARMENTS AMONG THEMSELVES) In David this is to be understood metaphorically, i.e., they divided my fortunes among themselves as if confiscated. Thus also the Latins say 'spolia' [spoils] of any thing whatsoever, when properly 'spolia' are garments, whence 'spoliarium' in a bath, and the French 'despoüiller'.

Latin:

Vers. 19. DIVISERUNT SIBI VESTIMENTA MEA) In Davide hoc intelligendum μεταφορικῶς, i. e. fortunas meas ut con- fiscatas inter se partiti sunt. Sic & Latini spolia dicunt de re quavis, cum proprie spolia sint vestes, unde spoliarium in balneo, & Gal- licum despoüiller.

## 23:1 Argument
Ps. XXIII. Christ the good shepherd.

Vers. 1. THE LORD RULES ME) The Chaldean thinks it is an ode made in the name of the Israelites who were in the desert. For poets are often accustomed to feign what could have been said in the past, such as the prophecy of Nereus in Horace.

It is not sufficiently piously compared, the Sacred ode with the fictions of profane poets. Moreover, that this ode was made in the name of the Israelites does not appear: nor is the authority of the Chaldean or of the Jewish Rabbis, destitute of Scripture, to be highly esteemed. Otherwise, R. D. Kimchi is to be heard, explaining it of Israel, of the captivity, or of David himself, since the discourse here is about affliction. But rightly our Bugenhagen: you will have understood the Psalm exactly then, if you have diligently meditated that God is the Shepherd, and you yourself the sheep, by whom being fed and refreshed, you will not be able to perish, even if at times nothing but death is set before your eyes. This is proven by similar passages in Is. 40, Jer. 23, Ezech. 34, Joh. 10, 1 Pet. 2; thus the sheep of God boasts, The Lord is my Shepherd, and I shall lack nothing. This, however, shines forth especially from those passages, that the Son of God is understood here in particular, who is called by himself, I am that good Shepherd Joh. 10, 1 Pet. 5, 4. ἀρχιποιμὴν &c. v. 25. ποιμὴν &c. Bishop of our souls Ebr. 13, 20. Shepherd of the sheep ὁ μέγας. Whatever the occasion may have been, says Brentius, for the comparison of this Psalm, it certainly appears that David received some notable revelation from the Holy Spirit concerning the kingdom and majesty of the promised Christ. Let us therefore take this Psalm as a brief compendium, in which are recited the greatest and highest benefits which befall the believer from the knowledge of the kingdom and majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ. For the same reason B. Gesner and our theologians, one and all, understand Christ by the Shepherd, and teach that his benefits are described here; B. Christianus Matthiæ in his Triad of Meditations on this Psalm says that it contains the rudiment of our entire Christianity: and that it describes under a double image the office of our Shepherd Christ, and his manifold benefit. The first of which is taken from the Shepherd and the little sheep; the second from the sumptuous banquet. So too the Orthodox Fathers. The Church speaks of Christ, says St. Augustine. Similarly, the commentary ascribed to Jerome, Chrysostom, and others explain it of Christ; all things in the Psalm also fit Christ perfectly, as our interpreters, especially Brentius, Gesner, and Christian Matthiæ, have shown.

Latin:

Ps. XXIII. Christus pastor bonus.

Vers. 1. DOMINVS REGIT ME) Chaldæus putat esse oden factam nomine Israelitarum, qui in deserto fuerunt. Nam solent sæpe Poetæ fingere, quæ olim dici potuerunt, quale est vaticinium Nerei apud Horatium.

NON satis pie confertur ode Sacra cum figmentis Poetarum prophanorum. Nomine autem Israeli- tarum hanc oden factam, non apparet: neque Chaldæi aut Judæorum Rabbinorum auctoritas, Scriptura desti- tuta, magni æstimanda. Alias R. D. Kimchi audiendus de Israele exponentis, de captivitate, vel de Davide ipso, cum de afflictione sermo hic est. Sed recte Bugenh. noster: Psalmum tunc exacte intellexeris, si diligenter meditatus fueris, Deum esse Pastorem, te vero ovem, quo pascente & reficiente perire non poteris, etsi quandoque nihil nisi mors ob oculos versetur. Quod probat e similibus locis Es. 40. Jer. 23. Ezech. 34. Joh. 10. 1. Pet. 2. sic gloriatur ovis Dei, Dominus est Pastor meus, & nihil mihi deerit. Id vero cumprimis ex locis istis elucescit, peculiariter hic intelligi Filium Dei, qui de seipso, Ego sum ille Pastor ille bonus Joh. 10. 1. Pet. 5, 4. vocatur ἀρχιποιμὴν &c. v. 25. ποιμὴν &c. Epi- scopus animarum nostrarum Ebr. 13, 20. Pastor ovium ὁ μέγας. Quæcunque fuerit occasio, inquit Brentius, hujus Psalmi comparatione, certe apparet Davidem insignem aliquam revelationem a S. S. de regno & majestate promissi Christi accepisse. Excipiamus igi- tur hunc Psalmum tanquam breve compendium, quo recitantur maxima & summa beneficia, quæ contin- gunt credenti ex cognitione regni & majestatis Do- mini nostri Jesu Christi. Eadem ratione B. Gesnerus & Theologi nostri ad unum omnes per Pastorem Christum intelligunt, ejusque beneficia hic describi docent, B. Christianus Matthiæ in Triad. Medita- tionum super hunc Psalmum, illum continere dicit rudimentum totius Christianismi nostri: ac describe- re sub duplici imagine Pastoris nostri Christi officium, atque multiplex beneficium. Quarum prima desumta a Pastore & ovicula; Secunda a convivio opiparo. Sic & Orthodoxi Patres. Ecclesia loquitur de Christo, in- quit S. Augustinus. Similiter de Christo explicat Hieronymo adscriptus commentarius, Chrysostomus & alii; omnia etiam in Psalmo apprime conveniunt Christo ut Interpp. nostri cumprimis Brentius, Gesnerus, & Christian. Matthiæ ostenderunt.

## 23:1 Addition
On Psalm 23.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 23.

## 23:5
Vers. 5. YOU HAVE PREPARED A TABLE IN MY SIGHT.) Not of wood or stone, but an easy one made of sods suddenly heaped up.

No one easily among the Jews themselves was so inept here. R. David Kimchi understood it thus: my enemies see my glory and affluence. But R. Aben-Ezra ascends higher; he says, it indicates the joy of the servants of God; in the hope of the future they despise the joys of this age; and thus among the Christians, Didymus explains it of the table of glory and heavenly delights, others of benefits both corporal and spiritual, others with the Hieronymian commentary of the table of the Holy Scriptures. To B. Gesner it seems that the Prophet looks to the table which had the showbread in the tabernacle of the Lord, Ex. 25, which he also explains concerning the calling to the knowledge and communion of Christ, which comes to us without our merits out of grace, as if to a table already prepared and set, so that all things in the doctrine of the Gospel and the business of our reconciliation with God are hinted at as being justly and wisely arranged. Which expositions are subordinate. Whence D. Matthiæ says a triple table is prepared for us: in the kingdom of power, Ps. 104, 14, to which refer also the table prepared for the Israelites in the desert, Ps. 78, 6; in the kingdom of grace, the word of the Gospel, Deut. 8, 3, Matth. 4, and the Holy Communion, 1 Cor. 10, 21, c. 11, v. 20, of which the table in the tabernacle was a type. Cf. Prov. 9, 2, Matth. 8, 11, Luc. 14, 16; and in the kingdom of glory, Ap. 2, 17, Luc. 22, 3; for that provision we congratulate ourselves in the Lord; leaving to Grotius and his like that easy table suddenly heaped up from sods.

YOU HAVE ANOINTED MY HEAD WITH OIL) For oil you will rightly translate, with fat things, as the Chaldean does here. For thus שמן is taken in Prov. 21, 20, Ps. 109, 24, Es. 5, 1. Understand here, however, with the Chaldean, those very fat birds with which the Israelites were fed in the desert, whether they were ὀρτυγομήτραι or others.

Thus he always chooses the worst things from the Rabbis or Targums, viz., according to that of the Apostle, 1 Thess. 5, 21, prove all things, hold fast that which is good. For how excellent is the sense: you have anointed my head with oil, that is, with very fat birds; was the head anointed with these like oil? The Chaldean has the head of my Priests כהני, therefore he understands it of sacred oil.

R. Solomon wishes the kingdom, to which David was anointed, to be looked to. But R. Aben-Ezra more correctly understands spiritual oil: with which the servants of God are anointed, with joy fixed in heavenly things. That there is an allusion to those fat and fluid ointments with which guests were accustomed to be perfumed at a banquet for the sake of sweetness and pleasure, there is no doubt, since the Lord is compared here to a liberal host, Luc. 7, 46, Joh. 12, 3. Therefore Augustine explains it: you have gladdened my mind with spiritual joy. Scripture itself exhibits this oil, the oil of gladness, Ps. 45, 7, of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ was anointed not by measure, Joh. 3, 34, but we are anointed according to the measure of the gift of Christ, Eph. 4, 8, Rom. 12, 13, 1 Cor. 12, 11, of which ointment St. John speaks in 1 Ep. 2, 20, and Paul in 2 Cor. 1, 12. Thus, therefore, since three things used to commend the preparation of banquets, the magnificence of the dishes, the fragrance of the oil, and the excellence of the wine, the doctrine of the Gospel is compared to feasts and magnificent dishes, or a table; the Holy Spirit to fragrant oil; and finally the benefits of the Lord, especially spiritual ones, to a cup full of the purest wine, or generous wine, if indeed spiritual provision is accustomed to be described through banquets, Es. 25, c. 55, Prov. 9, Matth. 22, Luc. 14. For that this deals with spiritual benefits is evident not only from the whole Psalm, but especially from v. 13 and the last. For there the holy Psalmist celebrates the conversion of the soul and the leading in the paths of righteousness: here he promises and vows mercy to himself, and a persevering dwelling in the house of the Lord or the Church. Whence also Rivetus is refuted, who in Decad. Psal. p. 199 makes the true and literal interpretation of this place concerning the table, ointment, and cup refer to the sustenance of David. He acknowledges, however, that v. 5 ought to be referred to spiritual benefits in addition to the literal.

Latin:

Vers. 5. PARASTI IN CONSPECTU MEO MEN- SAM.) Non ligneam, aut lapideam, sed facilem ex cespiti- bus subito aggestis.

Nemo facile e Judæis ipsis hic tam ineptus fuit. R. David Kimchi sic accepit: inimici vident gloriam & affluentiam meam. Altius vero ascendit R. Aben- Ezra; indicat, inquit gaudium servorum Dei; in spe futuri contemnunt gaudia hujus seculi; atque ita e Christianis Didymus, de mensa gloriæ & deliciarum cœlestium, alii de beneficiis cum corporalibus, tum Spiritualibus, alii cum Hieronymiano commenta- rio de mensa S. Scripturarum explicant. B. Gesnero videtur, Prophetam respicere ad mensam, quæ in ta- bernaculo Domini panes propositionis habebat Ex. 25. qui & de vocatione ad agnitionem & communionem Christi, quæ sine meritis nostris ex gratia, tanquam ad mensam jam paratam & instructam, nobis ob- tingit, explicat, ut omnia in Evangelii doctrina & negotio nostræ cum Deo reconciliationis juste & sa- pienter disposita innuantur. Quæ expositiones sub- ordinatæ sunt. Unde D. Matthiæ mensem triplicem nobis paratam dicit in regno potentiæ Ps. 104, 14. quo refer & mensam Israelitis in deserto paratam Ps. 78, 6. in regno gratiæ, verbum Evangelii Deut. 8, 3. Matth. 4. & Sacram Synaxin, 1. Cor. 10, 21. c. 11. v. 20. cu- jus typus fuerit mensa in tabernaculo. Conf. Prov. 9, 2. Matth. 8, 11. Luc. 14, 16. & in regno gloriæ, Ap. 2, 17. Luc. 22, 3. de illo apparatu nobis gratulamur in Do- mino; Grotio ejusque similibus facilem illam men- sam ex cespitibus subito aggestis relinquentes.

IMPINGVASTI IN OLEO CAPUT MEUM) Pro oleo recte verteris, pinguibus, ut hic Chaldæus. Sic enim שמן sumitur Prov. 21, 20. Ps. 109, 24. Es. 5, 1. Intellige autem hic cum Chaldæo aves illas pinguissimas, quibus pasti sunt in deserto Israelitæ, sive illæ ὀρτυγομήτραι fuere, sive aliæ.

Sic semper ille pessima quæque eligit e Rabbi- nis vel Thargumim, sc. juxta illud Apost. 1. Thess. 5, 21. πάντα δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε. Quam præclarus enim sensus: impinguasti caput meum oleo, id est, avibus pinguissimis, num his instar olei caput delibutum fuit? Chaldæus habet caput Sacer- dotum meorum כהני, de oleo ergo sacro intelligit.

R. Salomo regnum, ad quod unctus fuit David, re- spici vult. Sed rectius spirituale oleum R. Aben- Ezra intelligit: quo servi Dei unguntur, gaudio in coelestibus fixo. Alludi ad unguenta illa pinguia & fluida, quibus in convivio ob suaveolentiam & vo- luptatem solebant perfundi hospites, dubium nul- lum est, quum Dominus convivatori liberali hic comparetur Luc. 7, 46. Joh. 12, 3. Ideo explicat August. lætificasti lætitia spirituali mentem meam. Scriptura ipsa oleum hoc exhibet, oleum lætitiæ Ps. 45, 7. Spiritus Sancti, quo Christus unctus est non ad mensuram Joh. 3, 34. nos vero ungimur κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς χριστ̃ Eph. 4, 8. Rom. 12, 13. 1. Cor. 12, 11. de quo unguento S. Johannes 1. Ep. 2, 20. & Paulus 2. Cor. 1, 12. Sic ergo quum tria convivio- rum apparatum commendarint quondam, ferculo- rum magnificentia, olei fragrantia, & vini præstan- tia, doctrina Evangelii epulis & ferculis magnifi- cis, seu mensæ confertur, Spiritus S. oleo fragranti, beneficia denique Domini, maxime spiritualia, cali- ci vino meracissimo pleno, vel vino generoso com- parantur, siquidem spiritualis apparatus per con- vivia describi soleat Es. 25. c. 55. Prov. 9. Matth. 22. Luc. 14. de Spiritualibus enim beneficiis hic agi, cum e toto Ps. apparet, tum imprimis e v. 13. & ult. evidenter liquet. Ibi enim animæ conversionem & in semitis justitiæ deductionem celebrat Hieropsal- tes: hic misericordiam sibi pollicetur ac vovet, & perseverantem mansionem in domo Domini vel Ecclesia. Unde etiam Rivetus refellitur, qui in De- cad. Psal. p. 199. veram & literalem hujus loci in- terpretationem de mensa unguento & calice facit de Davidis sustentatione. Agnoscit tamen v. 5. ad Spiritualia beneficia ad literalem referri debere.

## 23:6 Addition
Verse 6. THY MERCY SHALL FOLLOW ME.

The Papists Bellarmine, Alvarez, and Coton wrongly snatch these things to the species of preventing and subsequent grace. For the Hebrew radaph is to pursue someone pressingly and greedily, and thus with the ardor of the grace of God is noted his inseparable assistance: and that false hypothesis of the Papists concerning preceding and subsequent grace, by which the subsequent is not ordered to the prior preventing grace, but is called grace either preventing or subsequent to the same with respect to the motion of free will, has nothing to do with this saying.

Latin:

Vers. 6. MISERICORDIA TUA SUBSE- QUETUR ME.

Perperam Pontificii Bellarm. Alvarez, Cotonus hæc ad species gratiæ prævenientis & subsequentis abripiunt. Nam Ebr. רָדַף est presse, avideque ali- quem insequi, adeoque cum ardore gratiæ Dei indi- vulsa assistentia ejus notatur: & falsa illa Papistarum de gratia præcedente & subsequente hypothesis, qua subsequens non ordinatur ad priorem gratiam præ- venientem, sed respectu motus liberi arbitrii dicitur gratia vel præveniens vel subsequens eundem, nihil habet cum hoc dicto commercii.

## 24:1 Argument
Ps. XXIV. Christ the King of glory.

Latin:

Ps. XXIV. Christus Rex gloriæ.

## 24:1 Addition
On Psalm 24.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 24.

## 24:2
Vers. 2. HE HIMSELF FOUNDED IT UPON THE SEAS] The Hebrew text has it, namely the earth. According to the nature of the matter, which Aben-Ezra says here בדרך התולדת, water ought to surround the whole earth. But God depressed the sea, so that the earth might stand out. See what we have brought from Strabo and others on this matter at the beginning of the Testimonies to book I of the Truth of the Christian Religion. See also Exod. 20, 4, and the opposite state in Genesis 7, 17, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 2. IPSE SVPER MARIA FVNDAVIT EVM] He- bræus textus eam, nempe terram. Secundum materiæ ratio- nem quod hic Aben-Esdra dicit בדרך התולדת, aqua deberet totam terram circumdare. At Deus depreffit mare, ut terra extaret. Vide quæ ex Strabone & aliis ad hanc rem attulimus initio Testimoniorum ad librum I. de Veritate Re- ligionis Christ. Vide & Exod. 20, 4. & oppositum statum Genes. 7, 17. 18.

## 24:3 Addition
v. 3. HE HATH FOUNDED IT UPON THE SEA.

From this passage Francis Valesius, with Augustine, gathers that the earth floats upon the waters; but the preposition 'al here is not to be rendered 'upon', but 'beside', as is manifest from the following clause, 'beside the rivers', in which meaning it also occurs in Psalm 137:1 and Psalm 1:3. Compare Genesis 1:9, Job 26:7.

At the end of verse 8, page 988, column b.

Those opinions of the Papists concerning the gates of hell being opened when Christ descended to the gates of Purgatory, or of Limbo, have arisen, as have also those of certain Fathers concerning the gates of heaven from the voice of the Vulgate, ETERNAL GATES. Moreover, that the name עוֹלָם denotes not only an age, but also the world, and thus the inhabitants of the world are addressed, has been proven by Dn. D. Geierus in this place, from Gen. 49:26, Job 22:15, Ps. 73:12, Ps. 139:24, Eccl. 3:11. Nor is there any evidence that the discourse here is about the entry of Christ into heaven; but that interpretation is merely precarious. Whence furthermore, from this fabricated Dialogism of the Angels, Who is this King of glory?, some of the ancients deduced that the mystery of redemption was unknown to the angels, and that that ascending king was the Messiah. But how can that ignorance be attributed to the holy angels, who, just as they were present at other acts of Christ, so also informed the Apostles themselves in his ascension, Acts 1. And who is ignorant that questions of this kind in the Scriptures are often signs not of wonder or ignorance, but of excellence, and are employed for the sake of explanation? see Jer. 30:21, Zech. 4:7, ch. 9:17.

Latin:

v. 3. SUPER MARE FUNDAVIT EAM.

Ex hoc loco innatare terram aquis Franc. Va- lesius cum August. colligit; At præpositio עַל hic non reddenda super, sed juxta, ut e sequenti com- mate, juxta fluvios, manifestum est, quo significatu etiam occurrit Ps. 137, 1. & Ps. 1, 3. Conf. Gen. 1, 9. Job. 26, 7.

Ad finem vers. 8. p. 988. b.

Enatæ sunt illæ opiniones Papistarum de portis inferni apertis, cum Christus descendit ad portas Pur- gatorii, vel limbi, ut & Patrum quorundam de portis cœlorum e voce Vulgatæ, PORTÆ ÆTERNA- LES. Nomen autem עוֹלָם non tantum seculum, sed etiam mundum notare, adeoque orbis incolas com- pellari, ex Gen. 49, 26. Job. 22, 15. Ps. 73, 12. Ps. 139, 24. Eccl. 3, 11. Dn. D. Geierus in h. l. probavit. Neque de ingressu Christi in cœlum sermonem hic esse ullo indicio constat; sed mere precaria est illa interpre- tatio. Unde porro e conficto hoc Angelorum Dialogismo, Quis est iste Rex gloriæ? deduxere ve- teres nonnulli angelis ignotum fuisse mysterium redemtionis, & regem illum ascendentem Messiam esse. Sed quomodo S. angelis ea ignorantia tribui potest, qui ut aliis Christi actibus præsto fuere, ita in ejusdem ascensione ipsos etiam Apostolos insor- marunt Act. 1. Et quis ignorat ejusmodi quæstiones in Scripturis sæpe non admirationis vel ignorantiæ, sed excellentiæ indicia esse, & explicationis gratia adhiberi? vid. Jer. 30, 21. Zach. 4, 7. c. 9, 17.

## 24:4
Ver. 4. WHO HATH NOT RECEIVED HIS SOUL IN VAIN. Some render it 'my soul,' as if God were speaking of His own soul. But the phrase is unusual; indeed, we are forbidden to take the name of God in vain, but not the soul of God. Others, therefore, like the Vulgate, explain it: 'who does not receive,' or rather 'lift up his soul,' which some interpret as: let us not lift up the soul to false doctrine, which is especially called שוא: others generally, that we should not lift up the soul to worldly things; but since this general prohibition is held in the other members, we judge with Blessed Luther that this is to be understood of false doctrine.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QUI NON ACCEPIT IN VANO ANIMAM SUAM. Nonnulli reddunt animam meam, quasi Deus de sua anima loquatur. Sed phrasis insolens est; no- men quidem Dei in vanum sumere prohibemur, non autem animam Dei. Alii ergo, ut Vulgata, expli- cant: qui non accipit, vel potius levat animam suam, quod interpretantur nonnulli, ne levemus animam ad doctrinam falsam, quæ ἐξαιρέτως שוא dicitur: alii generaliter ne ad res mundanas animam levemus; sed quum in cæteris membris hoc generale inter- dictum habeatur, cum B. Luthero de Doctrina salsa hoc intelligendum censemus.

## 24:7
Ver. 7. THE KING OF GLORY SHALL ENTER) The Ark. The history is 2 Sam. 6, 22. That the Ark in the nominative case is called the King of glory is unheard of. Nothing can be brought forward from Scripture for this opinion. This gloss was accepted from the Jews. Thus R. David Kimchi: The King of glory, i.e., the ark, because the King of glory dwelt upon it. An excellent reason. Because the Lord of glory dwelt upon the ark: Therefore the ark itself is the King of glory. He also dwells in the faithful. Is the faithful person himself, therefore, the King of glory? The text itself teaches who the King of glory is: The Lord strong and mighty: the Lord mighty in battle. And again, when it is asked a second time: Who is this King of glory? v. 10. The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. What could have been said more clearly? And yet it pleased Grotius to dream that the King of glory is the ark! If, therefore, these words were to be admitted in the highest degree at the entry of the ark, they are nevertheless not about the ark, but it is most manifest that they must be said and understood of the Lord, who sat above the ark. Vers. 8. LIFT UP YOUR HEADS, O YE GATES; AND BE YE LIFTED UP, YE EVERLASTING DOORS) In Hebrew: Lift up your heads, O gates, and be ye lifted up, O ye long-lived doors. Long-lived because they were made of cedar. Now these gates of Zion seem to have been of that kind which the Greeks call καταῤῥάκτας or ἐπιῤῥάκτας. Livy calls them hanging, falling, which, when they are to be moved, are lifted on high. Not unlike is the thought of Sappho: Raise high the roof, O carpenters; the bridegroom comes like Ares, much greater than a great man. He understands it only of material gates. But those who, according to the letter, refer these things with Calvin, Vatablus, Martyr, and Piscatus to the gates of Solomon's temple, wish them to be addressed prophetically because they did not yet exist, and to be called eternal because the tabernacle had already received firm seats, whereas before it had often changed locations: first through the desert, then in Gilgal, afterwards in Shiloh, thence in the land of the Philistines, from there in Beth-shemesh, further in the house of Obed-Edom, and from there it was carried into the City of David. Therefore, they are not firm because of cedar wood, as the gloss, which is too weak—nay, straw-like—of Grotius holds. But because their long-lasting stability is founded in the word of God; because, although the temple excelled in material, the highest excellence nevertheless lay in the fact that the promise of God was inscribed upon its building: This is my rest for ever and ever, Ps.

132, 14. But because this prophecy is about the Messiah, as most orthodox Fathers and more recent theologians explain, who is the Lord of glory 1 Cor. 2, 8, King of kings and Lord of lords Ap. 17, 14, c. 19, the strong Lord Is. 9, 6, and almighty Ap. 1, 8, the Lord mighty in battle Is. 49, 24, seqq. c. 63, 1, Hos. 13, 14, Mic. 5, 4, the Lord of hosts Is. 25, 6, Zach. 2, 8, who was prefigured by the ark of the covenant, Rom. 3, Ap. 12, 9, therefore they are everlasting gates; it is not a matter of the material gates of the Jerusalem temple, which had not yet been built in the time of David, but of the mystical gates of the Spiritual Jerusalem, and, to speak more correctly, the external lifting of the gates is not commanded, but the faithful reception of the Messiah is figuratively designated, so that that King of glory may be admitted by all worldly Kings, and may fix his royal seat and his spiritual kingdom in their kingdoms. The gates and doors of the world, says Brentius, are the kingdoms and principalities in this age, which are fortified with gates, walls, ramparts, and furthermore with laws and civil ordinances. The Psalm therefore admonishes the political magistrate not to close their gates and doors, but to open them wide to the glorious King, who is Christ: and to make the lintels of the gates high enough, so that Christ, together with His Gospel, may enter and be able to gather His Church from their regions. Some of the Ancients understood this of Christ's entry into heaven, Justin Dial. with Trypho, Basil l. 1 contr. Eunom. and others, and they understand the angels as speaking thus among themselves concerning the entry of Christ into heaven: Who is this King of glory? Some combine both the Princes of the age and the celestial dominations and principalities. Bugenhagen understands whatever power there is everywhere, so that it may be subjected to this power, and that the gates of hell may not prevail, nor the gates of the kingdoms of heaven be closed, so that all things may lie open to this triumphant king and victor over death. These things are to be admired, he says, in the words of both Angels and men. Hence that questioning of those who admire: Who is this King of glory? But the former explanation is simpler and more suitable to the text: which is also to be preferred to the allegory of Augustine and Pseudo-Jerome's explanation concerning the gates of the age, that is, of pleasures and sins, by which the approach to eternal salvation is precluded, which therefore must be removed. For in this Psalm is described both the universal kingdom of God, which He exercises in the whole world, and the peculiar one, which Christ has in the Church, and its citizens and subjects are defined, and the princes of the world are warned to admit this King of glory and to provide hospitality for Him in their kingdoms and cities. For since judgments were once exercised in the gates, by gates are understood empires, which according to some are called gates OF THE AGE, or EVERLASTING, because gates can thus flourish and endure for a long time, if indeed they have received Christ, Is. 60, v. 21. Others say that the souls of the faithful are called gates, as in Ap. 3, 20, which are commanded to lift up their heads, i.e., having left behind earthly things, to raise their mind upward: which are everlasting gates, because they are consecrated and dedicated to eternity, never to be overcome by the gates of hell. The Arabic paraphrase renders: O heads, or princes, lift up your gates, make gates and arches in honor of the Messiah. Aben-Ezra also admits that it looks to the Messiah, when he observes that the exhortation is repeated twice, so that the return of the glory of God and the captivity of the people might be shown. But the second time, mention is not made of the strong in battle, because in the days of Christ they shall not learn war anymore, Is. 2. And he understands the everlasting gates as those that would persist in the third house to the honor of God forever. But since the second house is the latest, the Jews wait in vain for another under the advent of their utopian and fictitious Christ. But concerning the heavenly house, which we await, and the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem, one may read in Ap. 21, 12. Those who understand by the gates of the age the doors of hell, and by the princes the powers of darkness, which are commanded to open their gates as the Lord approaches, so that He may lead a triumph over the power of the underworld, are unworthy of refutation.

Latin:

Vers. 7. INTROIBIT REX GLORIÆ) Arca. Historia est 2. Sam. 6, 22. Arcam in casu recto dici Regem gloriæ inauditum. Nihil in hanc sententiam e Scriptura adferri pote- rit. A Judaicis hæc glossa accepta. Sic R. David Kim- chi: Rex gloriæ, i. e. arca, quia super eam habitabat Rex gloriæ. Egregia ratio. Quia Dominus gloriæ ha- bitabat super arcam: Ergo arca ipsa Rex gloriæ est. Habitat etiam in fidelibus. Ergone ipse fidelis est? Textus ipse docet, quis sit Rex gloriæ, Dominus for- tis & potens: Dominus potens in prælio. Et rursus dum quæritur altera vice: Quis est iste Rex gloriæ? v. 10. Dominus exercituum ipse est Rex gloriæ. Quid clarius dici poterat? Et adhuc libuit Grotio somniare Re- gem gloriæ esse arcam! Si ergo maxime admittere- tur in ingressu arcæ hæc dicta, non tamen de arca, fed de Domino, qui super arcam sedebat, ea dici, atque intelligi debere, manifestissimum est. Vers. 8. ATTOLLITE PORTAS PRINCIPES VE- STRAS, ET ELEVAMINI PORTÆ ÆTERNALES) In Hebr. Attollite portæ capita vestra, & elevamini vos fores lon- gævæ. Longævæ quia ex cedro factæ. Videntur autem istæ portæ Sionis fuisse eo ex genere, quas καταῤῥάκτας aut ἐπιρ- ῥάκτας Græci vocant. Livius pendulas, recidentes, quæ ubi amovendæ sunt, attolluntur in sublime. Non dissimilis ἔννοια Sapphus: ὕψι δὴ τὸ μέλαθρον ἀείρατε τέκτονες ἄνδρες· Γαμ- βρὸς ἔρχεται ἴσος ἄρηι, ἀνδρὸς μεγάλω πολλῶ μείζων. De portis tantum materialibus intelligit. At, qui secundum literam ad portas templi Salomonei hæc cum Calvino, Vatablo, Martyre, Piscatore refe- runt, Prophetice eas, quia nondum extabant com- pellari, & æternas dici volunt, quia firmas jam sedes acceperat tabernaculum, cum antea sæpe loca mu- tasset, primo per desertum, tum in Gilgal, postea in Silo, exin in terra Philistæorum, inde in Bethsemes, porro in Kiriathjearim, ulterius in domum Obed- Edom, & exinde in Civitatem David delatum. Non ergo firmæ ob lignum cedrinum, ut habet glossa ni- mis infirma, imo straminea Grotii. Sed quia earum diuturna stabilitas in verbo Dei fundata; quia, etsi materia excelluit templum, summa tamen præstan- tia in eo sita fuit, quod ejus ædificio inscripta pro- missio Dei, Hæc requies mea in seculum seculi Psal.

132, 14. Verum quia Prophetia hæc de Messia, ut plerique orthodoxi Patres ac recentiores Theolo- gi exponunt, qui Dominus est gloriæ 1. Cor. 2, 8. Rex regum & Dominus dominantium Ap. 17, 14. c. 19. Dominus fortis Es. 9, 6. & omnipotens Ap. 1, 8. Dominus potens in prælio Es. 49, 24. seqq. c. 63, 1. Hos. 13, 14. Mich. 5, 4. Dominus exercituum Es. 25, 6. Zach. 2, 8. qui per arcam fœderis præfigura- tus fuit, Rom. 3. Ap. 12, 9. ideo portæ æternales; non de portis materialibus templi Hierosolymitani, quod tempore Davidis exstructum nondum fuit, sed de portis mysticis Spiritualis Hierosolymæ agi- tur, &, ut rectius dicam, non præcipitur portarum externa elevatio, sed figurate designatur Messiæ fidu- cialis susceptio, ut Rex ille gloriæ ab omnibus Re- gibus mundanis intromittatur, & in regnis ipso- rum sedem regiam, ac regnum suum spirituale fi- gat. Portæ & januæ mundi, ait Brentius, sunt regna & principatus in hoc seculo, qui muniti sunt portis, mu- ris, vallis, legibus præterea & civilibus ordinationi- bus. Admonet igitur Psalmus Politicum magistra- tum, ut non claudant portas & januas suas, sed late eas glorioso Regi, qui est Christus, aperiant: & superli- minaria portarum satis alta faciant, quo Christus una cum Evangelio suo ingredi, & ex regionibus eo- rum Ecclesiam suam colligere queat. Nonnulli Ve- teres de ingressu Christi in cælum acceperunt, Ju- stinus Dial. cum Tryph. Basil. l. 1. contr. Eunom. & alii, angelosque circa ingressum Christi in cæ- lum ita inter se colloquentes, quis est iste Rex gloriæ, intelligunt. Nonnulli conjungunt tum Principes seculi, tum dominationes & principatus cælestes. Bu- genbagius, quicquid ubique potentiæ est, intelli- git, ut id huic potentiæ subdatur, nec portæ infero- rum prævaleant, nec portæ regnorum cæli clau- dantur, ut omnia pateant huic regi triumphanti, & mortis victori. Admiranda hæc sunt, inquit, in verbis & Angelorum & hominum. Hinc est illa ad- mirantium interrogatio: Quis est hic Rex gloriæ? Sed prior explicatio simplicior, textuique convenien- tior est: quæ etiam præferenda allegoriæ Augustini & Pseudo-Hieronymi explicationi de portis seculi, hoc est, voluptatum & peccatorum, quibus aditus ad æternam salutem præcluditur, quæ proinde tol- lendæ sint. Describitur enim in hoc Psalmo tum re- gnum Dei universale, quod exercet in toto mundo, tum peculiare, quod Christus habet in Ecclesia, ejus- que cives ac subditi definiuntur, ac principes mun- di monentur, ut Regem hunc gloriæ intromittant, eique in regnis & urbibus suis hospitium præbeant. Quum enim in portis exercita olim sint judicia, per portas imperia intelliguntur, quæ juxta nonnullos dicuntur portæ SECULI, vel ÆTERNÆ, quod ita portæ diu florere, & perennare possint, si nem- pe Christum susceperint Es. 60. v. 21. Alii fidelium animas portas dici ajunt, ut Ap. 3, 20. quæ capita at- tollere, h. e. terrenis relictis sursum mentem erige- re jubeantur : quæ portæ æternæ, quia æternitati con- secratæ & dedicatæ sunt, in æternùm a portis in- ferorum non superandæ. Arabica paraphrasis red- dit : o capita, vel principes attollite portas vestras, fa- cite portas & arcus in honorem Messiæ. Ad Mes- siam respici fatetur etiam Aben-Ezra, cum obser- vat, bis repeti adhortationem, ut monstretur reditus gloriæ Dei & captivitatis populi. Secunda autem vi- ce non fieri mentionem fortis in prælio, quia in die- bus Christi non discent prælium amplius Es. 2. Et portas æternas intelligit in domo tertia perstituras ad honorem Dei in æternum. Sed quum Domus secunda novissima sit, aliam expectant frustra Judæi sub Christi sui utopici ac fictitii adventum. De do- mo autem cælesti, quam nos expectamus, & portis cælestis Hierosolymæ Ap. 21, 12. legere est. Qui per portas seculi fores inferni, per principes pote- states tenebrarum, quæ jubeantur portas suas Do- mino adventante referare, ut de inferorum pote- state triumphum ducat, intelligunt, refutatione in- digni sunt.

## 25:1 Argument
Ps. XXV. The desires of an anxious soul.

Vers. 1. UNTO THEE, O LORD, DO I LIFT UP MY SOUL) This Psalm is also alphabetical, like many others for the use of boys who were learning to write. But the verses are not well distinguished: for the second verse ought to begin there at בָךְ, and the fifth there at וְלַמְדֵנִי, and at the beginning of verse 17 the word קוּם, arise, is missing. But those words פְדֵה down to the end ought to be an addition to the preceding verse, not a new verse.

Latin:

Ps. XXV. Desideria animæ anxiæ.

Vers. 1. AD TE DOMINE LEVAVI ANIMAM ME- AM) Est & hic Psalmus Alphabeticus, ut multi alii in usum puerorum qui scribere discebant. Sed commata non bene distincta sunt : nam secundum comma debet incipere ibi בָךְ, & quintum ibi וְלַמְדֵנִי, & initio commatis 17. deest vox קוּם surge. Verba autem illa פְדֵה ad finem usque, accces- sio esse debent commmatis præcedentis, non novum comma.

## 25:5
Vers. 5. LEAD ME IN THY TRUTH) God illuminates more and more those who live well and pray solicitously (such as David shows himself here).

Latin:

Vers. 5. DIRIGE ME IN VERITATE TUA) Deus be- ne viventes, & sollicite precantes (qualem hîc se ostendit David) magis magisque illustrat.

## 25:11
Vers. 11. FOR THY NAME'S SAKE, O LORD, PARDON MINE INIQUITY; FOR IT IS GREAT.

This is not the cause of propitiation: but the reason for the prayer for pardon, because no salvation survives, unless God forgives our sins out of pure mercy. However, כִּי can also be taken adversatively, and you will spare my iniquity, although it is great. Cf. Gen. 8, 21.

Concerning v. 17, 18, see Eductionis Beatæ Desiderium, Conc. 13, in Memor. justor. Witteb.

Latin:

Vers. 11. PROPTER NOMEN TUUM, DOMINE PROPITIABERE PECCATO: MULTUM EST ENIM.

NOn hæc causa est propitiationis : sed ratio depre- cationis veniæ, quia nulla salus superat, nisi con- donante Deo ex mera misericordia peccata nostra. Potest tamen etiam כִּי accipi adversative, & parces iniquitati meæ, quamvis multa sit. Conf. Gen. 8, 21.

De v. 17. 18. vid. Eductionis Beatæ Desiderium Conc. 13. in Memor. justor. Witteb.

## 26:1 Argument
Ps. XXVI. Purgation of innocence.

Vers. 1. FOR I HAVE WALKED IN MY INNOCENCE.

Papists cannot draw these to the perfection of works. For the innocence of the cause is indicated, or certainly the pursuit of an innocent life, to which he had been devoted ἄνευ ὑποκρίσεως, as is clear from v. 11, and he betakes himself to the mercy of God. Cf. Ps. 143, 3.

Latin:

Ps. XXVI. Purgatio innocentiæ.

Vers. 1. QUONIAM EGO IN INNOCEN- TIA MEA INGRESSUS SUM.

NOn possunt hæc trahere Papistæ ad perfectio- nem operum. Innocentia enim causæ indicatur, aut certe innocentis vitæ studium, cui ἄνευ ὑποκρίσεως deditus fuerit, ut e v. 11. patet & ad misericordiam Dei sese recipit. Conf. Ps. 143, 3.

## 26:2 Addition
To Psalm 26:2.

PROVE ME, O LORD.

These do not treat of a desire for temporal afflictions, as Genebrardus, Lorinus, Estius, Schnepfius, and Arndius wish. David appeals to divine testimony, not concerning the integrity of his worship toward God, as Bellarmine explains, but concerning his innocence and justice in the criminal case of sedition and treason of which he was accused. Compare v. 1, 4, following, as also v. 10, 11, 12, whence the blessed Hülsemannus concludes that this Psalm was written during his flight from Saul, comparing here similar appeals in Ps. 7:4, 5, 9, 10, 11, Ps. 9:9, 10, Ps. 139:25.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 26, 2.

PROBA ME DOMINE.

Non de desiderio afflictionum temporalium hæc agunt, ut Genebrardus, Lorinus, Estius, Schnepfius, Arndius volunt. Ad testimonium divinum pro- vocat David, non de integritate cultus sui erga Deum, ut Bellarm. explicat, sed de innocentia & justitia in causa criminali seditionis & proditionis, cujus ar- guebatur. Conf. v. 1. 4. seqq. ut & v. 10. 11. 12. unde colligit B. Hülsemannus hunc Psalmum scriptum esse durante fuga a Saule, conferens hic similes pro- vocationes Ps. 7, 4. 5. 9. 10. 11. Ps. 9, 9. 10. Ps. 139, 25.

## 26:6
Vers. 6. I WILL WASH MY HANDS AMONG THE INNOCENT) In Hebrew: in innocence: that is, as an innocent person. The people would wash their hands when they testified themselves pure from crime, as in Deut. 21, 6. See also what was brought forward at Matth. 27, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 6. LAVABO INTER INNOCENTES MANUS MEAS) In Hebræo : in innocentia : id est, ut innocens. La- vabunt manus populi illi cum se puros a scelere testabantur, ut Deut. 21, 6. Vide & quæ allata ad Matth. 27, 24.

## 27:1 Argument
Ps. XXVII. The one thing necessary.

PSALM OF DAVID BEFORE HE WAS ANOINTED)

πρὸ τῦ χρισθῆναι [before he was anointed] the Greeks. The Hebrews do not have this. This pertains to the time about which 2 Sam. 2, 4.

They are read neither in the Chaldee nor in the Syriac. Therefore David glories especially in God as the light, salvation, and strength of his life against his enemies, because nothing is more pleasing and more desirable to him than if he could serve the Lord quietly and rejoice perpetually in His tabernacle. Whence he asks this one thing from the Lord, v. 4, אחת one, to wit, שאלה that petition, or rather the feminine placed for the neuter, this which Christ teaches is the one thing necessary, Luke 10:42. THEREFORE (thus we render the particle כי) HE HIDES ME, (he says trustfully, v. 5) in His hiding place, leaning upon divine protection, and certain that he will obtain that one thing, and so will even triumph and lift up his head above his enemies, v. 6.

Latin:

Ps. XXVII. Unum necessarium.

PSALMUS DAVID PRIUSQVAM LINIRETVR)

πρὸ τῦ χρισθῆναι Græci. Hebræi hoc non habent. Pertinet hoc ad tempus de quo 2. Sam. 2, 4.

Neque in Chald. nec Syro leguntur. Ideo impri- mis gloriatur David in Deo luce, salute, fortitudine vitæ suæ adversus inimicos suos, quod ipsi nihil gratius magisque desiderabile sit, quam si quiete Domino inservire ejusque tabernaculo perpetuo gaudere possit. Unde hoc unum petit a Domino v. 4. אחת unam sc. שאלה petitionem illam, vel potius fœmin. posito pro neutro hoc quod unum necessarium Christus docet Luc. 10, 42. IDCIRCO (sic particul. כי reddimus) OCCULTAT ME, (inquit fiducialiter v. 5.) in latibulo suo, innitens præsidio divino, ac certus unicum illud se impetra- turum, adeoque triumphaturum etiam, ac caput elevaturum super hostes suos. v. 6.

## 27:10 Addition
To Psalm 27:10.

FOR MY FATHER AND MY MOTHER HAVE FORSAKEN ME.

There is no need for us to explain it conditionally, if they have forsaken, but the word forsaking can be taken as the inability to help, to which is opposed the most powerful taking up by God. But those wander furthest from the scope, as the blessed Hülsemannus notes, who understand the forsaking comparatively as such, as parents are to be left for the sake of Christ, Matt. 19:29; for the discourse is clearly not about this.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 27, 10.

QVONIAM PATER MEUS, ET MATER MEA DERELIQUERUNT ME.

Non opus est, ut conditionaliter explicemus, si dereliquerint, sed de impotentia juvandi accipi po- test derelictionis verbum, cui opponitur potentissi- ma Dei assumptio. Maxime autem a scopo aber- rant, notante B. Hülsemanno, qui derelictionem comparative intelligunt de tali, quali deferendi sunt Parentes propter Christum Matth. 19, 29. de hac enim plane sermo non est.

## 27:13
Vers. 19. I BELIEVE THAT I SHALL SEE THE GOODNESS OF THE LORD IN THE LAND OF THE LIVING] That is, in the land of happy men, in Jerusalem, not in these caves and, as it were, sepulchers. In the Hebrew it is: Unless I had believed that I would see (that is, experience) the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living, by aposiopesis. For it is understood: I would have long since succumbed to these evils.

Augustine and other ancients prefer to understand it of the future life: I believe that I shall see (this is Augustine's paraphrase) but not in the land of the dying; I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living. Theodoret explains it thus: Not only in the present life shall I be superior to my enemies, but I shall also enjoy the expected goods. He calls the future life the land of the living, as being exempt from death and free from destruction and sadness. Which explanation is confirmed by the exhortation subjoined to confidence: because others can conceive a similar hope and confidence of the happiness of the future life, but not likewise of temporal happiness, which was proper to him, and concerning which he had been made more certain by the promise of the kingdom. And Tirinus observed that the Chaldee, Origen, Athanasius, Eusebius, and Didymus interpret it in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 19. CREDO VIDERE BONA DOMINI IN TER- RA VIVENTIVM] Id est, in terra hominum felicium, Hierosolymis, non in his speluncis, & quasi sepulchretis. In Hebræo est: Nisi credidissem visurum me (id est experturum) bonitatem Domini in terra viventium, per ἀποσιώπησιν. Adin- telligitur enim: pridem succubuissem his malis.

Augustinus, & alii Veteres, malunt de futura vita intelligere: Credo videre (paraphrasis Augusti- ni est) sed non in terra morientium; Credo videre bo- na Domini in terra viventium. Theodorethus ita ex- plicat: Non solum in præsenti vita superior meis ini- micis ero, verum etiam expectatis bonis perfruar. Terram autem viventium vocat futuram vitam, veluti mortis expertem, & ab interitu ac tristitia li- beram. Quæ explicatio e parænesi subjuncta ad fiduciam confirmatur: quia similem spem ac fidu- ciam felicitatis futuræ vitæ concipere possunt alii, non item felicitatis temporalis, quæ ipsi propria, & de qua peculiariter, per regni promissionem, ipse certior redditus erat. Atque ita interpretari Chal- dæum, Origenem, Athanasium, Eusebium, & Dydy- mum Tirinus observavit.

## 28:1 Argument
Ps. XXVIII. The retribution of the wicked. The hearing of the faithful.

Vers. 1. UNTO THEE O LORD WILL I CRY. Some of the Papists, such as Bellarmine, Genebrard, and others, wish these to be the words of Christ hanging on the cross and asking for a swift resurrection, and they appeal to the authority of Augustine and Jerome. But they have nothing to bring forward from the text to that effect, except that they drag in v. 10, and my flesh flourished again, which they judge to treat of the glorious resurrection. But there is nothing of the sort in the original text, which has it thus: my heart rejoiced, where Bellarmine vainly argues for corruption in the Hebrew source text, of which he can show no trace. But what is said in verse 3, do not draw me away together with the wicked, does not exempt the one praying from the number of sinners. But it must be taken concerning obstinate sinners, who work iniquity of set purpose, as the added epexegesis has it. Theodoret and Euthymius correctly interpret the Psalm concerning David, as do our B. Luther, Bugenhagen, Gesner, and others, and also Tirinus among the Papists, with Menochius not denying it.

Vers. eod. O MY GOD DO NOT BE SILENT TO ME) Better: Do not depart from me. How חרש is taken below 35:22, 1 Sam. 7:8. The Greeks translate it παρήπας, Esth. 7:4.

Latin:

Pl. XXVIII. Retributio impiorum. Exauditio fidelium.

Vers. 1. AD TE DOMINE CLAMABO. VErba esse Christi in cruce pendentis, ac postu- lantis celerem resurrectionem Bellarmin. Ge- nebrard. & alii volunt e Pontificiis, & ad Autorita- tem August. & Hieronymi provocant. Sed e textu nihil eam in rem adferre habent, nisi quod huc tra- hant v. 10. & refloruit caro mea, quem de gloriosa resurrectione agere censent. At nihil tale in textu originali, qui ita habet: gavisum est cor meum, ubi frustra corruptionem arguit in textu in fonte E- bræo Bell. cujus nullum monstrare potest vestigium. Quod vero vers. 3. dicitur, ne simul trahas me cum peccatoribus, non eximit precantem e numero pec- catorum. Sed accipiendum est de præfractis pecca- toribus, qui operantur iniquitatem data opera, uti habet addita ἐπεξήγησις. De Davide recte Psalmum interpretantur Theodoretus & Euthymius, ut & no- stri B. Lutherus, Bugenhagius, Gesnerus, alii, nec non e Pontificiis Tirinus, haud abnuente Meno- chio.

Vers. eod. DEVS MEVS NE SILEAS A ME) Melius: Ne recedas a me. Quomodo חרש sumitur infra 35, 22. 1. Sam. 7, 8. παρήπας vertunt Græci, Esth. 7, 4.

## 28:1 Addition
To Psalm 28:1.

AND I SHALL BE LIKENED TO THEM THAT GO DOWN INTO THE PIT.

Lorinus wrongly concludes from this an uncertainty concerning the present state of grace. For although we do not deny that eternal perdition is denoted, as appears from a comparison of v. 3 and Zech. 9:11, yet that uncertainty cannot be gathered from a prayer for preservation from eternal perdition. For is it not necessary to pray for preservation in the faith? But that prayer of the Papists

Ecclesiastical, free the souls of all the faithful departed from the pains of hell, and the explanation concerning the limbo of purgatory, which Bellarmine alleges here, does not fit here: and Bellarmine himself explains the Psalm with Augustine and Jerome concerning Christ, and makes this Psalm a compendium of Ps. 22. These words, however, he says are of Christ hanging on the cross and requesting a swift resurrection. But those things which Brentius, Pomeranus, and others of our side acknowledge to sound concerning David and those similar to David or the faithful. For those things in v. 10, 'my flesh has flourished again,' do not imply resurrection, Bugenhagen observing that it is to be explained thus: 'My flesh has been exhilarated again, consolation having been restored, because flesh also perishes when the mind is in anguish and affliction,' Prov. 27. 'A sad spirit dries up the bones.' In which manner the sense of the Vulgate does not differ much from the Hebrew text, in which it is, 'My heart has rejoiced.'

Latin:

Ad Psal. 28, 1.

ET ASSIMILABOR DESCENDENTI- BUS IN LACUM.

Incertitudinem de præsenti statu gratiæ perperam hinc concludit Lorinus. Nam etsi non negemus æternam perditionem notari, ut e collatione v. 3. & Zach. 9, 11. apparet, incertitudo tamen illa e preca- tione pro præservatione a perditione æterna colli- gi non potest. Annon enim orandum est pro con- servatione in fide? Oratio autem illa Papistarum

Ecclesiastica, libera animas omnium fidelium defun- ctorum de pœnis inferni, & explicatio de limbo purga- torii, quam allegat hic Belllarminus, huc non qua- drat: & explicat Bellarminus ipse Psalmum cum Au- gust. & Hieron. de Christo, facitque hunc Psalmum compendium Ps. 22. hæc vero verba dicit Christi esse in cruce pendentis ac postulantis celerem resurrectio- nem. Quæ vero Brentius, Pomeranus & alii è no- stris agnoscunt de Davide similibusque Davidi seu fidelibus sonare. Non enim resurrectionem illa v. 10. refloruit caro mea, inferunt Bugenhagio obser- vante ita explicanda : Rursum exhilarata est caro mea, reddita consolatione, quia caro perit quoque, ubi in angustia & afflictione mens est, Prov. 27. Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa. Quo pacto vulgatæ sensus ab E- bræo textu non multum discrepat, in quo est, Ga- visum est cor meum.

## 29:1 Argument
PSALM XXIX. The voice of the Lord thundering.

IN THE CONSUMMATION OF THE TABERNACLE) This is not in the Hebrew, just as not all Greek copies have ἐξοδίε σκηνῆς. It seems to pertain to that which is at the end of 2 Sam.

Vers. 1. GIVE UNTO THE LORD O YE SONS OF GOD, GIVE UNTO THE LORD THE SONS OF RAMS. In the Hebrew there is nothing more than give unto the Lord, O ye sons of the mighty; Bellarmine judges that other words crept into the Vulgate by error, perhaps written in the margin, which he attributes to a double interpretation of the word אֵלִים. But God is nowhere designated by the plural noun אֵלִים. Therefore, from that erroneous reading, the inept proof of the two-horned Episcopal miter arose, i.e., give unto the Lord the sons of rams, that is, Bishops, because אֵלִים denotes horns. Therefore, Bishops will be the sons of horns. But these are absurdities. Bellarmine and Genebrard wish the sons of rams, that is, lambs, to be indicated as to be offered. But the sons of rams are called Princes, as being the sons of the powerful. Therefore, the kingdoms of the world and the princes of the earth, who cannot but persecute the word of the Lord, are warned that, having laid aside their own glory, they should glorify the truly glorious God, as our Bugenhagen rightly says. The Hebrew phrase is customary, sons of the powerful, that is, the powerful themselves, just as sons of iniquity are said for the wicked themselves, and sons of death for those devoted to death.

Latin:

PSALMUS XXIX. Vox Domini tonans.

IN CONSVMMATIONE TABERNACVLI) Hoc in Hebræo non est, sicut nec omnia Græca habent ἐξοδίε σκηνῆς. Videtur pertinere ad id quod est in fine 2. Sam.

Vers. 1. AFFERTE DOMINO FILII DEI, AFFERTE DOMINO FILIOS ARIETUM. IN Ebræo nihil amplius est, quam afferte Domino filii fortium, per errorem irrepsisse alia verba in Vulgatam censet Bellarmin. forte in margine ad- scripta, quod duplici vocis אֵלִים interpretationi tribuit. At nomine אֵלִים plurali nuspiam Deus designatur. Ex illa ergo erronea lectione inepta orta est probatio bicornis mitræ Episcopalis, q. d. date Domino filios arietum, h. e. Episcopos, quod אֵלִים notent cornua. Episcopi ergo filii cornuum erunt. Sed hæ ineptiæ sunt. Bellarm. & Gene- brard. filios arietum, id est agnos offerendos indica- ri volunt. Verum filii arietum dicuntur Principes utpote filii potentum. Monentur ergo regna mundi & Principes terræ, qui non possunt non per- sequi verbum Domini, ut deposita gloria sua, vere gloriosum Deum glorificent, ut recte Bugenhagius noster. Usitata est Ebr. phrasis, filii potentum, id est, potentes ipsi, ut filii iniquitatis pro ipsis impiis, filii mortis, pro morti devotis dicuntur.

## 29:5
Vers. 5. THE LORD SHALL BREAK THE CEDARS OF LEBANON) The Syrians who are neighbors to Lebanon. These things were written at the time whose history is in 2 Sam. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 5. CONFRINGET DOMINVS CEDROS LIBA- NI) Syros Lybano vicinos. Scripta hæc eo tempore, cujus historia 2. Sam. 8.

## 29:6
Vers. 6. AND THE BELOVED AS THE SON OF THE UNICORNS) The sense is: And the mountain of Hermon as young unicorns. Thus he will make the inhabitants of Hermon flee, whom the Sidonians called Sarion. Deut. 3, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ET DILECTUS QVEMADMODVM FILIVS VNICORNIVM) Sensus est: Et Hermonem montem ut juve- nes monocerotes. Ita fugere faciet incolas Hermonis, quem Si- donii vocabant Sarion. Deut. 3, 9.

## 29:8
Vers. 8. AND THE LORD SHALL SHAKE THE DESERT OF CADES) That is, the Moabites.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET COMMOVEBIT DOMINUS DESER- TVM CADES) Id est, Moabitas.

## 29:9
Vers. 9. THE VOICE OF THE LORD PREPARING THE HINDS) In the Hebrew: you will afflict the hinds with pain: that is: he will terrify the Moabites as hinds. חול is usually translated now as ὠδίνειν, now as πονεῖν, κοπάζειν, ἀλγεῖν, φοβεῖσθαι.

IN HIS TEMPLE ALL SHALL SAY GLORY) Everyone in the temple will praise God with those words which he will now annex.

Latin:

Vers. 9. VOX DOMINI PRÆPARANTIS CERVOS) In Hebræo: cruciatu afficies cervas: id est: perterrebit Moa- bitas quasi cervas. חול verti solet modo ὠδίνειν, modo πονεῖν, κοπάζειν, ἀλγεῖν, φοβεῖσθαι.

IN TEMPLO EJVS OMNES DICENT GLORIAM) Quilibet in templo Deum laudabit verbis iis quæ jam an- nectet.

## 29:10
Vers. 10. THE LORD MAKETH THE FLOOD TO DWELL, AND THE LORD SHALL SIT FOR EVER] In the Hebrew word for word: The Lord sat at the flood, and the Lord shall sit King for ever. To sit is that of a judge. Therefore he says this: As God judged the human race at the time of the flood, so also he will continue to judge in the future.

Others explain it both of the universal flood and of a partial one when after thunder he pours down rains and showers in great abundance: such as Tirinus and Munster, and also R. Aben-Ezra. Bellarmine also explains it concerning a copious shower. The Chaldean indeed understands it of the flood, but so that the governance of mercy, not of wrath, is indicated: He sat on the throne of mercy and preserved Noah, and he reigns over the Sons of Noah for ever. Brentius wishes it to regard both judgment and grace. Just as the Lord once governed the flood, so that, although the wicked perished, the pious Noah with his family might be preserved in the ark: so also he will sit, govern, and protect his Church perpetually in the flood of Baptism. Gesner, as well as Osiander, considers that the flood of Baptism is also referred to here, whose paraphrase is as follows: The Lord (Jesus Christ) sits, that is, He contemplates instituting the flood of Baptism, in which the old Adam may be suffocated, and sin abolished, so that it may no longer be imputed to us in the sight of God. For that Baptism was prefigured by the flood, Peter testifies in 1 Epist. 3. And the Lord Jesus Christ shall sit, as the heavenly King, placed forever on the throne of His Majesty, namely at the right hand of the Father in divine glory, so that He may govern and protect His Church in a heavenly manner while present. Most all of our theologians agree, as does the Weimar paraphrase. B. Luther, T.I. Jen. Germ. f. 187: Baptism is a greater flood than that described by Moses, because more men are baptized than were suffocated in the flood. For the force of the thunder is not described here, which some Papist interpreters think, Bellarmine, Tirinus, Menoch., but the efficacy of the word of God; whence the power of the Sacrament of Baptism is conveniently subjoined. Nor is it about corporal enemies being overthrown, as Grotius understands here the Cedars of Lebanon as the Syrians, neighbors of Lebanon, and by the desert of Cades the Moabites, by the mountain of Hermon, the inhabitants of Hermon, but the spiritual power of the Gospel is celebrated: To bring to the Lord Messiah glory and honor, Kings and

Princes are commanded, not oxen or rams, but a sacrifice of praise in holy attire: Because the voice of the Lord is heard over the waters, contained in the clouds, like thunder, while he thunders with the voice of the word Marc. 3, 17. the glorious voice of the Lord, which breaks the cedars of Lebanon, like a lightning bolt it prostrates whatever is high and sublime in the world. Just as storms cast down the most lofty trees: so that just as calves and the foals of unicorns leap, so the branches of the highest cedars leap upon the earth: and the preaching of the Gospel may be effective among the nations, even through the horrid desert of Kadesh, so that they may be humbled under Christ, and submit themselves to him. Let the paraphrase of Osiander and the Vinariean be seen.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DOMINVS DILVVIVM INHABITARE FA- CIT, ET SEDEBIT DOMINVS IN ÆTERNUM] In Hebræo ad verbum: Dominus in diluvio sedit, & sedebit Do- minus Rex in perpetuum. Sedere est judicis. Hoc ergo dicit: Sicut Deus genus humanum judicavit tempore diluvii, ita & in posterum judicare perget.

Alii cùm de universali diluvio, tum de partiali cum post tonitrua pluvias & imbres magna copia perfundit, exponunt: ut Tirinus & Munsterus, nec non R. Aben-Ezra. De copioso imbre Bellarminus etiam explicat. Chaldæus de diluvio quidem intelli- git, sed ut regimen misericordiæ, non iræ innuatur: In throno misericordiæ sedebat & servabat Noa- chum, & regnat super Filios Noæ in æternum. Bren- tius & judicium & gratiam respici vult. Sicut Do- minus gubernavit quondam diluvium, ut, etsi impii perierint, pius Noah cum sua familia in arca conser- varetur: ita etiam sedebit, gubernabit, & tuebitur Ecclesiam suam perpetuo in diluvio Baptismi. Di- luvium Baptismi etiam hic respici censet Gesnerus, nec non Osiander: cujus hæc est paraphrasis: Do- minus (Jesus Christus) sedet, id est, meditatur in- stituere diluvium Baptismi, in quo suffocetur vetus Adam, & aboleatur peccatum, ut non amplius nobis in conspectu Dei imputetur. Per diluvium enim præ- figuratum esse Baptismum, testatur Petrus 1. Epist. 3. Et sedebit Dominus Jesus Christus, ut Rex cælestis, in throno Majestatis suæ in æternum collocatus, nimi- rum ad dextram Patris in divinam gloriam, ut præsens Ecclesiam suam gubernet, & tueatur cælesti modo. Consentiunt plerique omnes Theologi no- strates, ut & paraphrasis Vinariensis. B. Lutherus T.I. Jen. Germ. f. 187. Baptismus est majus diluvium, quam illud a Mose descriptum, quia plures homines baptizantur, quam in diluvio suffocati sunt. Non enim vis tonitrui hic describitur, quod nonnulli Pontificii Interpp. putant, Bellarminus, Tirinus, Me- noch. sed efficacia verbi Dei; Unde commode sub- jungitur vis Sacramenti Baptismatis. Neq; de hostibus corporalibus prosternendis, uti hic Cedros Libani Gro- tius Syros, Libani vicinos, intelligit, & per desertum Cades Moabitas, per Hermonem montem, incolas Her- monis, sed spiritualis virtus Evangelii celebratur: Af- ferre Domino Messiæ gloriam & honorem Reges ac

Principes jubentur, non boves aut arietes, sed sacrificium laudum in ornatu sancto: Quia vox Domini super aquas, in nubibus contentas, auditur instar tonitrui, dum tonat voce verbi Marc.3,17. vox Domini gloriosa, quæ confringit cedros Libani, tanquam fulmen prosternit, quicquid altum & sublime est in mundo. Sicuti tempestates dejiciunt arbores excelsissimas: ut quemadmodum vituli & pulli unicornium exiliunt, sic subsiliunt rami altissimorum cedrorum in terra: ac prædicatio Evangelii efficax sit apud gentes, etiam per horridum desertum Cades, ut sub Christo humilientur, & se illi submittant. Videatur paraphrasis Osiandri & Vinariensis.

## 29:10 Addition
To Ps. 29, 10. towards the end. p. 990. a.

Rightly the blessed Hülsemann in this place. The sitting of God at the flood is not alleged in this place as an argument of divine majesty from the past, namely, that it is to be venerated because He once punished the world, in the way that 'sitting for the age' not only denotes the duration of past time, but especially the present and the future. And this is evident from the remaining works of God, the condition of which is narrated in the present, not in the past. But especially that the discourse is about the present and future work of God is evident from the application to the eleventh verse, where the Psalmist concludes from this sitting that the blessing of the Church and eternal peace are to be conferred. Whence two things are evident: 1. that it is not a bare provocation to the majesty of God shown in the first flood; 2. that it is not a provocation to the power of God punishing crimes, but to the power conferring benefits. Therefore the Belgians and all Calvinists err when they think the flood is introduced in this place as an example of divine majesty shown in the past; either in the flood of Noah, or in the sending of daily rains and the opening of the cataracts. Better, not only the Greek and Latin Fathers, ignorant of Hebraisms, but Jerome also and Origen in chapter 45 of Isaiah explained it concerning the saving flood of divine grace and Baptism. In the way that also our Luther, Tom. I. Jen. Germ. sermon on preparation for Baptism and both Commentaries on Gen. 8, where he explains this saying concerning the drying up of the first flood and the substitution of another, wholesome flood. See also our Gerhard in the place on Baptism, page 597, and Gefner, rightly appealing here to 1 Pet. 3. The blessed Brentius, by 'the Lord,' to whom the sons of rams or heroes, the princes and powerful of this age, ought to bring glory, and to whom they ought to serve in holy attire, that is, true faith, by which alone, just as the heart is purified, so it is also adorned, understands Christ v. 1. His voice or the preaching of the Gospel thunders in many waters, that is, among many peoples v. 2. through the sons of thunder Mark 3. to break the cedars of Lebanon, and the trees of Mount Sirion, all the power, wisdom, justice, and sublimity of the world (conf. Ezech. 31, Ps. 37, 1 Cor. 10, 4, Isa. 60) so that just as a calf is accustomed to kick against the goad, and the foal of unicorns to leap, so also the branches of those trees, broken and dissipated by the voice of the Lord, might leap and skip here and there. His voice makes flames of fire, that is, to flash, to thunder, and to inflame whatever it has seized: and that it also moves the desert, indeed the horrible and most vast desert of Kadesh (Numbers 13, c. 20, Deut. 1), the voice of the Lord moves the hinds, which, even if in the times of their birth they retreat into places most removed from the company of men, so that they cannot be observed (Job 39), yet in storms they betake themselves, contrary to their nature, to paths trodden by human footsteps, and there give birth. (Aristot. lib. VI. de nat. anim. and Pliny.) In which manner the word of the Lord excites the nations, so that even if by nature they abhor all cultivation of humanity and piety, and lie hidden in vast barbarism, as if in a most secret desert, yet, moved and inflamed by the voice of the Gospel, they betake themselves to a gentle way of life, and to embracing true piety: The voice of the Lord strips the forests, see, the pathless, rendering them passable, that is, the nations, which were like forests. Conf. Isa. 19, ch. 43, 49. Concerning this Lord, therefore, Brentius judges: The Lord sat at the flood: which he understands indeed concerning the old flood as a type, but he judges that it is immediately transferred to the flood of Baptism as an antitype by the subsequent words: 'and the Lord shall sit as King forever,' where he compares Isa. 54, 1 Pet. 3. The sense of Brentius, therefore, comes back to the same as the former explanation, but it does not favor the interpretation of the Jews or the Calvinists.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 29, 10. sub finem. p. 990. a.

Recte B. Hülsemannus in h. l. Sessio Dei ad diluvi- um, non allegatur hoc loco, tanquam argumentum ma- jestatis divinæ à præterito, scil. venerandum esse, quia olim puniverit mundum, quomodo sedere in seculum non tantum notat durationem temporis præteriti, sed præsens maxime & futurum. Et hoc patet ex reli- quis operibus Dei, quorum conditio de præsenti narra- tur, non de præterito. Imprimis autem de præsenti & futuro opere Dei sermonem esse, patet ex applicatio- ne ad versum undecimum, ubi concludit Psalmista ex hac sessione conferendam esse Ecclesiæ benedictionem & æternam pacem. Unde duo patent 1. non esse nudam provocationem ad majestatem Dei in primo diluvio ostensam; 2. non provocari ad potentiam Dei vindi- cantem scelera, sed ad potentiam conferentem benefi- cia. Errant itaque Belgæ & Calvinistæ omnes, quan- do diluvium h. l. introduci censent, tanquam exem- plum majestatis divinæ olim ostensæ; vel in diluvio Noachi, vel in immittendis quotidianis imbribus & solvendis cataractis. Melius non Græci solum & La- tini Patres, Ebraismorum ignari, sed Hieronymus quoque & Origenes in cap. 45. Es. de salutari diluvio gratiæ divinæ & Baptismi exposuerunt. Quomodo etiam noster Lutherus Tom. I. Jen. Germ. serm. de præparat. ad Baptism. & utrog. Comment. in Gen. 8. ubi de exsiccatione primi diluvii & substitutione salu- bris alteriusg, diluvii hoc dictum exponit. Vide eti- am nostrum Gerhardum in loco de Baptismo pag. 597. & Gefnerum hîc recte provocantes ad 1. Petr. 3. B. Brentius per Dominum, cui filii arietum vel he- roum, principes & potentes hujus seculi gloriam ad- ferre, & cui in ornatu sancto, h. e. vera fide, qua sola, sicut cor purificatur, ita & ornatur, servire debeant, Christum intelligit v. 1. Ejus vocem vel prædicatio- nem Evangelii tonare in aquis multis, id est, inter po- pulos multos v. 2. per filios tonitrui Marc. 3. confrin- gere cedros Libani, arboresque montis Seiron, omnem mundi potentiam, sapientiam, justitiam & sublimi- tatem (conf. Ezech. 31. Ps. 37, 1. Cor. 10, 4. Esa. 60.) ut quemadmodum vitulus solet adversus stimulum calcitrare, & pullus unicornium exilire, ita & rami il- larum arborum voce Domini confracti & dissipati hinc inde exiliant & saltitent. Vocem ejus efficere flammas ignis, h. e. fulgurare, fulminare & inflama- re, quæcunque arripuerit : eamque etiam desertum, imo horribile & vastissimum desertum Cades (Nu- mer. 13. c. 20. Deut. 1.) commovere, vocem Domini commovere cervas, quæ etsi temporibus partus sui se recipiant in loca ab hominum contubernio remo- tissima, ut observari non possint (Job. 39.) in tem- pestatibus tamen conferant se contra ingenium su- um ad semitas humanis vestigiis tritas, ibique pa- riant. (Aristot. lib. VI. de nat. anim. & Plin.) Quo pacto verbum Domini excitet gentes, ut etsi natura abhorreant ab omni humanitatis & pietatis cultu, & in vasta barbarie, quasi in abditissimo deserto de- litescant, tamen commotæ & inflammatæ voce Ev- angelii conferunt sese ad mansuetum genus vitæ, & ad amplectendam veram pietatem: Vox Domini de- nudat sylvas vid. invias, reddens eas pervias, id est, gentes, quæ sylvarum instar erant. Conf. Es. 19. cap. 43, 49. De hoc ergo Domino censet Brentius: Do- minus sedit ad diluvium: quod de diluvio quidem veteri intelligit ceu typo, sed id transferri statim ad diluvium Baptismi ceu antitypum verbis subse- quentibus censet: & sedebit Dominus Rex in æternum, ubi confert Es. 54. 1. Pet. 3. Sensus ergo Brentii eodem recidit cum priori explicatione, non autem favet Judæorum aut Calvinianorum interpretationi.

## 30:1 Argument
PSALM XXX. Sadness turned into joy.

ON THE DEDICATION OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID) That is, when David purified his house defiled by Absalom.

Latin:

PSALMUS XXX. Tristitia in gaudium versa.

IN DEDICATIONE DOMVS DAVID) Id est, cum David domum suam ab Absolomo fœdatam repurgavit.

## 30:7
Ver. 8. YOU HAVE GRANTED STRENGTH TO MY BEAUTY) From the Greek: παρέσχες τῷ κάλλει μου δύναμιν. It appears they read not להררי, that is, on my mountain, but להדרי from רור or רוד which is to rule. You have added strength to my kingdom. Nor do the Syrian and Arab differ.

The Hebrew text is correct: you have placed strength upon my mountain, i.e., you have strengthened me in the kingdom, like a most strong and immovable mountain, as Munster has it, or rather you have placed, or given strength, or fortitude to my mountain, which is my beauty: because the palace of David was on Mount Zion. Therefore, as far as the sense is concerned, the Greek, Vulgate, Syrian, Arab, and Grotian interpretation comes to the same thing as the Hebrew text, so that there is no need for correction or a different reading. For who is ignorant that often the sense is expressed in versions, not precisely the words themselves, and that one translator followed another? If the words themselves were to be rendered, it should have been interpreted not as beauty, but as kingdom by the Vulgate, as also by the Greek interpreters, which Grotius thinks was read by them in the Hebrew.

Latin:

Vers. 8. PRÆSTITISTI DECORI MEO VIRTVTEM) Ex Græco: παρέσχες τῷ κάλλει μου δύναμιν. Apparet legisse eos non להררי, id est, in monte meo, sed להדרי à רור vel רוד quod est dominari. Regno meo vires addidisti. Nec aliter Syrus & Arabs.

Recte se habet Ebræus textus: collocasti fortitudinem super montem meum, h. e. roborasti me in regno, velut fortissimum & immobilem montem, ut habet Munsterus, vel potius posuisti, aut dedisti robur, vel fortitudinem monti meo, quod est decus meum: quia regia Davidis erat in monte Sion. Eodem ergo redit, quantum ad sensum, Græca, vulgata, Syri, Arabis & Grotiana interpretatio, cum textu Ebræo, ut correctione, vel diversa lectione opus non sit. Quis enim ignorat, sæpe sensum expressum in versionibus, non præcise ipsa verba, & unum translatorem sequutum esse alium? Si verba ipsa reddenda, non decus, sed regnum interpretandum fuisset Vulgato, ut & Græcis Interpp. quod ab illis in Ebræo lectum putat Grotius.

## 31:1 Argument
Ps. XXXI. Christ commends his Spirit to the Father. Ver. 1. IN YOU O LORD HAVE I HOPED.

Theodoret and Euthymius understand the present Psalm as being about David fleeing because of the persecution of Absalom. Most Papists, Bellarmine, Genebrard, Menochius, and others do as well; yet Genebrard admits it agrees with Christ. Bellarmine also applies it to the Church groaning amidst the straits of persecutions. But because we know the words of v. 5 are Christ's, who used the same on the cross, Luke 23, Father into your hands I commend my spirit, we think the whole Psalm should be claimed for Christ. For just as by using that exclamation from Ps. 22 on the cross, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, he taught that the whole prayer of that Psalm was his, and looked to his passion: so when he repeats the last word on the cross from this Psalm, he makes us equally certain that the whole of that Psalm is to be taken as being about no one else but himself; nor is there anything in the whole Psalm that does not fit Christ perfectly. Therefore Cassiodorus makes this the fourth passion Psalm. Nor is there any reason to object that Christ is the Redeemer, not the redeemed. For he is Redeemer with respect to us, who have been redeemed by him, but he is said to be redeemed with respect to God, by whom, on account of our sins, he was delivered into death, and on account of our justification was redeemed from death and resurrected, Heb. 5, 7. Rom. 4, 24. Whence he is also called SAVED, Zech. 9, 9. For the word פדה does not always denote redemption made by a price; sometimes it designates simple liberation, and is the same as σώζειν, to rescue, to save, where the discourse is not about redemption from sin, but about bare liberation from evil. But Pareus is inept, and [claims] that the word is taken here properly for redemption when understood of David, and improperly when understood of Christ. Just as the word 'is' in the institution of the Sacrament must hold and be taken properly in respect to the bread, and improperly in respect to the body of Christ. Which is ignorance and trickery. For a single word does not have more than one single meaning, which if it is taken properly, certainly cannot be taken improperly and metaphorically at the same time in the same place. Whence it is also clear from v. 1 that the Reformed wrongly conclude for the inamissibility of the faith of the reborn: since it in no way treats of the reborn. Nor is the opinion of Simon de Muis to be approved here, that it treats of the danger of David at Ziph and Keilah, v. 9, of which 1 Sam. 23. But as for those words in v. 23, I said in my excess of mind, the Hebrew has, in my trembling, the LXX, in my astonishment. Aquila, in my amazement. Symmachus, in my astonishment: how these fit Christ, Ps. 22 sufficiently teaches, along with Ps. 79. But Cocceius's application to the Reformed Church and its liberation from a cruel war is foreign.

Latin:

Ps. XXXI. Christus Spiritum suum Patri commendat. Vers. 1. IN TE DOMINE SPERAVI.

PSalmum præsentem de Davide intelligunt fugiente ob persequutionem Absalonis, Theodoret. Euthymius. Pontificii plerique Bellarmin. Genebrard. Menochius, alii; Christo tamen congruere fatetur Genebrard. Bellarm. etiam applicat Ecclesiæ inter persequutionum angustias gementi. Quia vero verba v. 5. Christi esse novimus, qui eadem in cruce usurpavit Luc. 23. Pater in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum, Psalmum totum Christo vendicandum existimamus. Quemadmodum enim illa exclamatione e Ps.22 in cruce usus, Deus meus, Deus meus, quare me dereliquisti, precationem totam istius Psalmi suam esse docuit, & ad passionem suam spectare: ita cum ex hoc Psalmo ultimum in cruce verbum repetit, pariter certos nos reddit, totum illum Psalmum non de alio, quam de sese accipiendum esse; Nec est quicquam in toto Psalmo, quod non apprime Christo conveniat. Ideo Cassiodorus hunc quartum facit Psalmum passionalem. Nec est, quod objiciatur, Christum Redemtorem esse, non redemtum. Nam Redemtor est respectu nostri, qui ab ipso redemti sumus, redemtus autem dicitur respectu Dei, a quo propter peccata nostra in mortem traditus, propter justificationem nostram e morte redemptus & resuscitatus est Ebr. 5, 7. Rom. 4, 24. Unde etiam SALVATUS dicitur Zach. 9, 9. Nec enim verbum פדה semper redemtionem notat pretio factam, quandoque liberationem simplicem designat, & idem est, quod σώζειν, eruere, servare, ubi non de redemtione a peccato, sed de nuda liberatione a malo sermo est. Ineptus autem Pareus est, & proprie vocem illam hic sumi ac pro redemtione, cum de Davide, & improprie, cum de Christo intelligitur. Ut obtineat verbum edite in Sacramenti institutione & proprie accipi ratione panis, & improprie ratione corporis Christi. Quæ est imperitia & κυβεία. Nam unius vocis non est, nisi unica tantum significatio, quæ si proprie accipiatur, certe in eodem loco improprie & metaphorice simul accipi non potest. Unde etiam constat e v. 1. Reformatos perperam pro fidei renatorum inamissibilitate concludere: quum nullatenus de renatis agat. Neque proinde probanda Simon de Muis sententia hic de Ziphæo & Ceilano Davidis periculo v. 9. agi de quo 1. Sam. 23. Quod vero ad illa v. 23. Ego dixi in excessu mentis meæ, Ebr. habent, in trepidando me, LXX. ἐν τῇ ἐκπλήξει μου. Aquila ἐν θαμβήσει μου. Symmachus ἐν τῇ ἐκπλήξει μου: quæ quomodo Christo conveniant Ps. 22. satis docet, cum Ps. 79. Aliena autem est Cocceji applicatio ad Ecclesiam Reformatam ejusque liberationem ex atroci bello.

## 31:1 Addition
To Ps. 31.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 31.

## 31:1 Addition
Vers. 1. IN THEE O LORD HAVE I HOPED.
