That David is not speaking of himself in this Psalm, which Bellarmine, as well as Bohlius, wishes with the Jews, but of Christ from Luke 23, 46, is sufficiently clear, who is that servant of God par excellence, verse 17 of this Psalm, and the just one v. 19, as Brentius rightly notes: into whom those who do not believe perish eternally, who v. 21 speaks of his trepidation in extreme affliction as if cast out from the sight of the Lord: just as he also complained in Ps. 22, 1, and verse 14 he expresses the cause of his affliction, whose Vulgate translation, 'my strength has been weakened in poverty' (with which Junius, Piscator, Musculus, Montanus agree), Brentius amends thus: 'My strength collapses because of iniquity': understanding the iniquity or sin of the human race, which Christ received into Himself. And that most rightly: because it had already been spoken of concerning punishment and affliction in verse 10, but nothing had yet been commemorated in the Psalm concerning sin or iniquity taken up by Christ: which is not neglected in the parallels Ps. 40, 13, Ps. 69, 5.6, Isa. 53, 5 seqq. Vatablus also explained it as iniquity.

Latin:

Vers. 1. IN TE DOMINE SPERAVI.

Non de se Davidem loqui in hoc Psalmo, quod cum Judæis Bellarm. ut & Bohlius volunt, sed de Christo è Luc. 23, 46. satis luculentum est, qui est servus ille Dei κατ’ ἐξοχὴν vers. Psalmi hujus 17. & ju- stus v. 19. ut recte Brentius notat: in quem qui non credunt, æternum pereunt, qui v. 21. de trepidatio- ne sua in extrema afflictione loquitur quasi projectus à conspectu Domini: uti etiam conquestus est Ps. 22, 1. & vers. 14. causam afflictionis suæ exprimit, cujus translationem vulgatam, infirmata est in paupertate virtus mea (cui consonat Junius, Piscator, Muscu- lus, Montanus) ita emendat Brentius: Collabitur præ iniquitate virtus mea: iniquitatem seu peccatum generis humani intelligens, quod in se recepit Christus. Idque rectissime: quia de pœna & af- flictione jam dictum erat vers. 10. de peccato seu iniquitate à Christo suscepta nihil adhuc in Psalmo commemoratum: quæ in parallelis non negligitur Ps. 40, 13. Ps. 69, 5.6. Esa. 53, 5. seqq. Vatablus etiam exposuit iniquitatem.

## 31:15
Vers. 16. IN THY HANDS ARE MY LOTS) In the Greek it was καιροί μου, which agrees with the Hebrew, as Apollinaris, the Arab, and the Ethiopian read: and in the old Roman Psalter, my times. Certain scribes wrote κλῆροι μου instead of καιροί μου, and from that comes this version.

Latin:

Vers. 16. IN MANIBVS TVIS SORTES MEÆ) In Græco fuit καιροί μου, quod Hebræo convenit, quomodo legerunt Apollinaris, Arabs, Æthiops: & in Psalterio Romano vetere, tempora mea. Librarii quidam pro καιροί μου scripsere κλῆροι μου, & inde hæc versio.

## 31:19
Vers. 20. HOW GREAT IS THE MULTITUDE OF THY SWEETNESS, O LORD, WHICH THOU HAST HIDDEN FOR THEM THAT FEAR THEE? THOU HAST PERFECTED IT FOR THEM THAT HOPE IN THEE IN THE SIGHT OF THE SONS OF MEN) The sense is: how great is the multitude of good things which Thou reservest for the pious, and in Thy own time displayest even before all? It is customary to translate צפן by φυλάττειν, τηρεῖν, θησαυρίζειν.

From this multitude of hidden divine sweetness or kindness, the Origenists conclude irrationally and theologically incorrectly that the same will be shown even to the damned. See Augustine, book 1, On the City of God, ch. 18. For cannot God be celebrated for the hidden and inscrutable kindness which He shows to the elect and the faithful, and which, as far as it depends on Him, He is prepared to show to all men, even if by the force of His justice He punishes eternally in the other world the impious who have spurned the treasures of divine kindness, and who have rendered themselves unworthy in this age, nay, have treasured up for themselves wrath against the day of wrath, Rom. 2, 5.

Regarding verse 15 of the present Psalm, see the Memorial of the Just of Wittenberg, Sermon 7.

Latin:

Vers. 20. QVAM MAGNA MVLTITVDO DVLCE- DINIS TVÆ, DOMINE QVAM ABSCONDISTI TI- MENTIBVS TE? PERFECISTI IIS QVI SPERANT IN TE IN CONSPECTV FILIORVM HOMINVM) Sensus est: quanta est multitudo bonorum, quæ reservas piis, ac suo tempore coram omnibus etiam exhibes? Solet verti צפן per φυλάττειν, τηρεῖν, θησαυρίζειν.

Ex hac multitudine suavitatis vel benignitatis divinæ absconditæ ἀλόγως & ἀθεολόγως concludunt Origenistæ eandem etiam damnatis exhibitum iri. Vid. August. l. 1. de civ. Dei c. 18. Annon enim ab occulta & imperscrutabili benignitate celebrari Deus potest, quam electis & fidelibus exhibet, & quantum in ipso est, omnibus hominibus exhibere paratus est, etiamsi vi justitiæ suæ impiis, qui thesauros benignitatis divinæ sprevere, quique semetipsos indignos reddidere in hoc seculo, imo thesaurizarunt sibi iram in diem iræ Rom. 2, 5. æternum puniat in altero seculo.

De vers. 15. Psalmi præsentis vid. memoria Justor. Witteberg. Conc. 7.

## 31:22
Vers. 23. BUT I SAID IN THE EXCESS OF MY MIND) While I am in fear: For חפז is translated δειλιάζειν in Ps. 104, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 23. EGO AVTEM DIXI IN EXCESSV MEN- TIS MEÆ) Dum paveo: Nam חפז vertitur δειλιάζειν Ps. 104, 7.

## 32:1 Argument
Ps. XXXII. The blessedness of the penitent, the remission of sin.

INTELLECTVS) משכיל The LXX translate it συνέσεως or εἰς σύνεσιν, that is, a song that is eminently didactic.

Vers. 1. BLESSED ARE THEY WHOSE INIQUITIES ARE FORGIVEN) The Psalm seems to have been composed so that it might be sung on the day of atonements. For at that time a certain general confession of sins was made.

Latin:

Ps. XXXII. Beatitudo pœnitentis, remissio peccati.

INTELLECTVS) משכיל LXX. vertunt συνέσεως vel εἰς σύνεσιν id est, carmen eximie διδακτικόν.

Vers. 1. BEATI QVORVM REMISSÆ SVNT INI- QVITATES) Videtur Psalmus esse in id factus, ut in die expiationum cantaretur. Eo enim tempore generalis quædam fiebat peccatorum confessio.

## 32:1 Addition
To Ps. 32.

V. 1. BLESSED ARE THEY WHOSE INIQUITIES ARE FORGIVEN.

The subject are those to whom iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered, those to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, nor is there guile in their spirit. The predicate is that they are blessed. Through the Apostolic interpretation in Rom. 4, these are drawn from the words of David both as regards the subject and as regards the predicate κυρίαι δόξαι: 1. That not only the reason for justification, but also for salvation and blessedness is described here, by which name the Apostle urges the word אַשְׁרֵי blessednesses, and μακαρισμὸν, differing concerning this, how we are both justified before God and obtain eternal salvation v. 5. 6. 7. Rashly therefore do the Papists and the Innovators Calixtus, Hornejus and their followers distinguish between justification and glorification, as if some things were necessary for the latter which are by no means necessary for the former, such as our good works. For here it is a matter of salvation, and yet good works are not urged as necessary for obtaining the same. And the Apostle uses this testimony to teach that our works are excluded no less from salvation than from justification. 2. The Apostle, pressing the words of the Holy Psalmist both as regards the form and manner of justification and glorification, and as regards the principal efficient cause, and the instrumental on our part, acknowledges no diversity; because he teaches that justification and blessedness or glorification alike consist in the remission, or non-imputation of sins, and the imputation of righteousness, not which is situated in our works, but which is imputed χωρὶς ἔργων without works: for the reason that in our Psalm there is no mention of works, but only of the non-imputation of sins in the description of blessedness made. Whence the Apostle concludes (3.) that David teaches that the blessedness of that man is [such], to whom God imputes righteousness without works: because, to wit, he does not require works by any little word: but only the non-imputation of sins. Since here the method of obtaining justification and blessedness is fully described, nor is any iota of charity, or infused righteousness, or works held, only are commemorated פשע transgression, חטאה sin, עון iniquity. Which three Cocceius distinguishes thus, that the former is the rejection of the law and the legislator, the latter the passing over of the highest end and good, the former the defect of some rectitude, which also adheres to a good work, and so all those things, that we may be blessed and justified, are said to be remitted, covered, not imputed. Therefore (4.) the Holy Spirit holds these for the same, not only the covering, non-imputation, and remission of sins and iniquities: but even the very imputation of righteousness, which he declares to be the very righteousness of Christ: because one's own righteousness has no place, since only iniquities for sins are found in the subject being justified: nor can our righteousness be thought of or feigned without works. (5.) Although David does not expressly add that the remission, covering, and non-imputation is done through faith, the Apostle nevertheless teaches with an Apostolic spirit that it is included in them, when he proves from thence that faith is imputed for righteousness. Concerning which Brentius rightly: Although in these verses there is no express mention of Christ, for whose sake alone sins are remitted through faith, nevertheless again from the very interpretation of Paul, nay from the whole doctrine of Christianity, it is known that to no man is sin pardoned, or iniquity covered, unless he believes in Jesus Christ, that for his sake alone sin is pardoned to us: It is not written, says Paul, that it was imputed to him for Abraham's sake only, but also for our sake, to whom it will be imputed, believing in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our sins, and was raised for our justification. And Peter: There is no other name given under heaven among men, in which it behooves us to be saved. And again: To him all the Prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him shall receive remission of sins through his name. Wherefore, when it is said in the Psalm: Blessed are they whose iniquities are remitted, or to whom transgression is pardoned, it is to be understood as through Christ by faith, for there is no pardon of transgression except through faith in Christ. So also when it is said: Whose sin is covered, it is to be understood as through Christ, for Christ alone is the true covering, by which sin is entirely hidden, nay, taken away from the sight of God. Similarly also that which follows, Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin, is to be expounded concerning non-imputation through Christ; for God is so severe an exactor of his law, that to all those who do not perfectly satisfy the law, he imputes sin, even if they have not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam: but to those only who believe in Christ, he does not impute sin, whence also it is added, in whose spirit there is no guile, (that is) who is not in his heart an Epicurean or a hypocrite, but who has true faith in Christ. He who truly and sincerely believes in Jesus Christ our Lord, that God pardons our sins, and covers our iniquities, and does not impute to us our transgressions, not on account of any merits of ours, either preceding or following, not on account of any virtues or dignities of ours, which we have either from the flesh or from the spirit, but only by his gratuitous liberality and clemency, on account of his only-begotten Son our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus he. But neither did David neglect faith: For when he explains in verse 10 whom grace or mercy, consisting in the remission, covering, and non-imputation of transgressions, sins, and iniquities, surrounds, and who those חסידי κεχαριτωμένοι are, whom God affects with his grace, he says in verse 6 that they are those who trust in the Lord; and so he teaches that we obtain divine grace only through faith: by which through a certain and firm trust in God we have our only refuge, and pray for the remission of sins with boldness: which guards us from distress, and surrounds us on every side with joy, and the shouts of escape; so that the righteous may rejoice in the Lord and be glad, and exult with an upright heart, verses 5, 6, 7, 10, 11. Whence it is clear that the whole Psalm looks to the righteous and blessed through faith, and acknowledges no other righteousness and blessedness than that of faith. But to those who are thus justified through faith and the remission of sins, the Lord promises in verse 8. I will give thee understanding, and I will instruct thee in the way in which thou shalt walk; because sanctification is the consequence of justification.

Moreover (7.) the Psalmist adds in the description of the one to be justified, in whose spirit there is no guile, so that hypocrisy may be removed from the acknowledgment of sin and faith in the penitent heart, since a true and sincere confession of sin and true and sincere faith are required in those to be justified. For here it is not yet a question of the consequences of the remission of sins, but the discourse is still about the antecedents. (8.) Rightly does the blessed Hülsemann here note the impudent exception of Lorinus and Bellarmine, lib. II. de Justif. cap. 7, as if to be covered and to be remitted in this place were the same as to have ceased entirely to exist in the nature of things, and not to be imputed were the same as to be unworthy of being imputed by God, whereas the Apostle expressly says that the matter or object not imputed is by its nature iniquity, and by this middle term commends the mercy of God, because that which by its nature is imputable to guilt and punishment, He does not impute through grace alone; for otherwise, he says, the Apostle would have had to say: Blessed is he to whom God does not impute that which does not exist in the nature of things. A great grace, forsooth, when adultery or homicide is not imputed to me, which I have not committed, or which I have sufficiently washed away by contrition and just satisfaction. Jansenius is more ingenuous in his Paraphrase: happy, etc. whose crimes have been pardoned by God, and whose sins have been hidden, so that God does not look upon them to punish them. Therefore, because the Apostle and the LXX not only translated that Hebrew word נשא, which sometimes denotes the abolition of the essence, here by ἀφιέναι or by remission, which is an act of the mind in the one remitting, but also add two synonyms, to cover and not to impute, to demonstrate quite evidently that they are speaking of actions in the mind of God concerning our sins. And therefore we invert the argument of the Papists in this way: That signification of the infinite word, such as כסה in the Davidic and Apostolic passage, is proper, such as it is when accompanied by declarative synonyms through their own proper signification. For if the exegetical words labored under the same indefiniteness, they could not be exegetical or declarative. Now indeed, from an induction of examples, it is certain that the proper signification of the exegetical words לא יחשב and כסה is such that it signifies a mental operation concerning an object, not an essential abolition of the object acted upon, which is proved from the Concordances, and the Jesuit Lorinus could not deny it, etc., with examples alleged concerning covering and uncovering while the substance of the thing covered and uncovered remains safe, Ps. 85, 3, Lam. 4, 22, Jer. 49, 10, Neh. 4, 5, Philem. v. 18, Ezek. 18, 22, cap. 33, 16, etc. See Kircher's Concordance. Therefore, the indefinite word כסה must be restricted in this place to the finite and proper signification of the added exegetical synonyms. Compare what we have said on Rom. 4 against Grotius concerning this Davidic testimony.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 32.

V. 1. BEATI QUORUM REMISSÆ SUNT INIQUITATES.

Subjectum sunt illi, quibus remissæ sunt iniqui- tates, & quorum tecta sunt peccata, illi quibus non im- putavit Dominus peccatum, nec est in spiritu eorum dolus. Prædicatum est, quod beati illi sint. Per in- terpretationem Apostolicam Rom. 4. hæ è verbis Davidis eruuntur cum quoad subjectum tum quo- ad prædicatum κυρίαι δόξαι: 1. Non tantum justi- ficationis rationem, sed etiam salutis & beatitudinis hic describi, quo nomine urget Apostolus vocem אַשְׁרֵי beatitudines, & μακαρισμὸν, de eo differens, quomodo coram Deo & justificemur, & salutem æ- ternam consequamur v. 5. 6. 7. Temere ergo Papi- stæ & Novatores Calixtus, Hornejus & asseclæ distin- guunt inter justificationem & glorificationem, ac si aliqua sint necessaria ad hanc, quæ ad illam neces- saria minime sint, utpote bona opera nostra. Nam hic de salute agitur, nec tamen bona opera urgen- tur, ceu ad eandem consequendam necessaria. Et Apostolus utitur hoc testimonio, ut non minus à salute quam justificatione opera nostra excludi do- ceat. 2. Apostolus Hieropsaltis verba premens tum quoad formam & modum justificationis & glo- rificationis, tum quoad causam efficientem principa- lem, & instrumentalem ex parte nostri nullam agno- scit diversitatem; quia justificationem pariter & bea- titudinem vel glorificationem docet constare remif- sione, vel non-imputatione peccatorum, & interpreta- tione justitiæ, non quæ in operibus nostris sita sit, sed quæ imputatur χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus: eo quod in Psalmo nostro nulla operum, sed solum non-imputa- tionis peccatorum in descriptione beatitudinis men- tio fiat. Unde 3. concludit Apostolus, quod Da- vid doceat, beatitudinem ejus hominis esse, cui Deus imputat justitiam sine operibus: quia scil. non requi- rit ullo verbulo opera: sed solum non-imputationem peccatorum. Siquidem hic plene describatur ratio consequendi justificationem & beatitudinem, nec ullum jota de charitate, vel justitia infusa, vel operi- bus habeatur, solum commemorentur פשע trans- gressio חטאה peccatum עון iniquitas. Quæ tria Coc- cejus ita distinguit, quod illud sit rejectio legis & le- gislatoris, istud præteritio summi finis & boni, hoc defectus rectitudinis alicujus, qui & bono operi ad- hæreat, adeoque illa omnia ut beati simus, & justifi- cemur, remitti, tegi, non imputari dicantur. Ideo (4.) hæc pro iisdem habet Spiritus S. non solum tectio- nem, non imputationem, & remissionem peccatorum, & iniquitatum: sed ipsam etiam justitiæ imputatio- nem, quam declarat esse ipsammet Christi justitiam: quia propria justitia locum non habet, cum solum iniquitates ad peccata in subjecto justificando inveni- antur: nec cogitari vel fingi potest justitia nostra si- ne operibus. (5.) Quamvis non addat diserte David, quod remissio, tectio, non imputatio fiat per fidem, A- postolus tamen spiritu Apostolico id illis includi do- cet, cum inde probat fidem imputari ad justitiam. »Quo de recte Brentius: Etsi in his versiculis non sit „expressa mentio Christi, propter quem solum re- „mittuntur peccata per fidem, tamen iterum ex ipsa „Pauli interpretatione, imo ex universa Christia- „nismi doctrina notum est, quod nulli hominum „condonatur peccatum, aut tegitur iniquitas, nisi „credat in Jesum Christum, quod propter ipsum „solum condonetur nobis peccatum: Non scri- ptum est, inquit Paulus, propter Abraamum tan- tum, imputatum fuisse illi, sed etiam propter nos, quibus imputabitur, credentibus in eum, qui exci- tavit Jesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis, qui tra- ditus fuit propter peccata nostra, & excitatus est propter justificationem nostram. Et Petrus: Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum inter homines, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. Et iterum: Huic o- mnes Prophetæ testimonium ferunt, quod remissio- nem peccatorum accepturus sit per nomen ejus, quisquis crediderit in eum. Quare, cum dicitur in Psalmo: Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, vel quibus condonatur prævaricatio, subintelligendum est propter Christum per fidem, nulla enim condona- tio prævaricationis, nisi per fidem in Christum. Sic & cum dicitur: Quorum tectum est peccatum, subin- telligendum est, per Christum, solus enim Christus est verum operculum, quo peccatum prorsus absconditur, imo tollitur à conspectu Dei. Similiter & illud quod sequitur, Beatus vir, cui Dominus non imputat pec- catum, exponendum est, de non-imputatione, propter Christum; Deus enim tam severus est legis suæ exactor, ut omnibus iis, qui legi non perfecte satisfaciunt, impu- tet peccatum, etiamsi ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam non peccaverint: solis autem illis, qui credunt in Christum, non imputat peccatum, unde & additur, in cujus spiritu non est dolus, (hoc est) qui non est in corde suo Epicuræus aut hypocrita, sed qui veram habet fidem in Christum. Qui vere & sincere cre- dit in Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, quod De- us nobis condonet peccata, & tegat nostras iniqui- tates, nec imputet nobis nostras prævaricationes, non propter ulla nostra merita, vel præcedentia vel sequentia, non propter ullas nostras virtutes aut di- gnitates, quas vel ex carne vel ex spiritu habemus, sed tantum gratuita sua liberalitate & clementia, pro- pter solum unigenitum Filium suum Dominum no- strum Jesum Christum. Hæc ille. Sed nec David fidem neglexit: Cum enim ex ponit verf. 10. quosnam gratia vel mifericordia con- sistente in remissione, tectione, non imputatione trans- gressionum, peccatorum, iniquitatum, circumdet, de quinam sint illi חסידי κεχαριτωμένοι, quos gratia sua afficit Deus, v. 6. dicit, eos illos esse, qui confi- dunt in Domino; adeoque nonnisi per fidem gratiam divinam nos consequi docet: qua per certam fir- mamque fiduciam in Deo unice habemus refugium, & pro remissione peccatorum μετὰ παῤῥησίας ora- mus: qui ab arcto nos custodit, & undiquaque nos cir- cumdat lætitia, & jubilis evasionis; ut justi lætari in Domino & gaudere, ac recto corde jubilare possint v. 5. 6. 7. 10. 11. Unde liquet, totum Psalmum justos & be- atos per fidem respicere, nec aliam quam fidei justi- tiam & beatitudinem agnoscere. Quibus vero ita per fidem & remissionem peccatorum justificatis promittit Dominus v. 8. Intellectum tibi dabo, & in- struam te in via, qua gradiaris; quia consequens ju- stificationis est sanctificatio.

Cæterum (7.) addit Hleropsaltes in subjecti justi- ficandi descriptione, in cujus spiritu non est dolus, ut removeatur hypocrisis ab agnitione peccati, & fide in corde pœnitenti, siquidem vera ac sincera peccati confessio, vera & sincera fides in justificandis requi- ratur. Nam hic nondum de consequentibus remis- sionis peccatorum agitur, sed adhuc de anteceden- tibus sermo est. (8.) Merito notat hic B. Hülseman- nus impudentem Lorini & Bellarmini lib. II. de Ju- stif. cap. 7. exceptionem, quasi tegi & remitti hoc loco idem sit, quod plane desiisse in rerum natura esse, non imputari, idem sit, quod indignum esse, ut possit à Deo imputari, quum Apostolus materiam seu objectum non imputatum expresse dicat sua natura esse ini- quitatem, atque hoc medio termino misericordiam Dei commendet, quod id quod sua natura est impu- tabile ad culpam & pœnam, per solam gratiam non imputet, alias enim, inquit, dicendum fuisset Aposto- lo; Beatus cui Deus id non imputat, quod non est in rerum natura. Magna scil. gratia, cum mihi non imputatur adulterium aut homicidium, quod non commisi, vel quod contritione justaq; satisfactione satis dilui. Magis ingenuus Jansenius in Paraphrasi: fe- lices, &c. quorum scelera à Deo sunt condonata, & quorum peccata abscondita sunt, ut ea non aspiciat Deus ad vindicandum. Proinde quia Apostolus & LXX. verbum illud Ebræum נשא quod aliquan- do abolitionem essentiæ notat, non solum hic verte- rint per ἀφιέναι seu per remissionem, quæ est actus mentis in remittente, sed addunt etiam duo synony- ma regere & non imputare, ut satis evidenter demon- strent se loqui de actionibus in mente Dei, circa pec- cata nostra. Ideoque invertimus argumentum Pa- pistarum hoc modo : Illa significatio infinitæ vocis qualis est כסה loco Davidico & Apostolico propria est, qualis inest adjectis Synonymis declarativis per si- gnificationem suam propriam. Nam si exegetica ea- dem indefinitudine laborarent, exegetica seu declara- tiva esse non possent. Jam vero ex inductione exem- plorum constat propriam significationem verborum exegeticorum לא יחשב & כסה eam esse ut signifi- cet mentalem operationem circa objectum, non essenti- alem abolitionem objecti passi, quod probatur ex Con- cordantiis, & Lorinus Jesuita diffiteri non potuit, &c. allegatis exemplis de tegendo & retegendo salva rei tectæ & retectæ substantia Ps. 85, 3. Thren. 4, 22, Je- rem. 49, 10. Nehem. 4, 5. Philem. v. 18. Ezech. 18, 22. cap. 33, 16. &c. Vide Kircheri concord. Ea propter indefinitum verbum כסה restringendum esse hoc loco ad finitam & propriam significationem adjunctorum synonymorum exegeticorum. Conf. quæ ad Rom. 4. contra Grotium circa hoc testimo- nium Davidicum diximus.

## 32:3
Vers. 3. MY BONES HAVE GROWN OLD) Aquila, κατετρίβη. So also the Syrian. And the same word בלה is translated by κατατρίβειν in Deut. 8, 4; 29, 5; for things that grow old are accustomed to be worn away and consumed.

Latin:

Vers. 3. INVETERAVERUNT OSSA MEA) Aquila, κατετρίβη. Sic & Syrus. Idemque verbum בלה per κατατρίβειν vertitur Deut. 8, 4. 29, 5. solent enim quæ vetustiscunt, atteri atque consumi.

Vers. 4. FOR DAY AND NIGHT THY HAND IS HEAVY UPON ME) He contrasts the past state with this present one.

Vers. 4. QVONIAM DIE AC NOCTE GRAVATA EST SVPER ME MANVS TVA) Opponit statum præteritum huic præsenti.

## 32:6
Vers. 6. FOR THIS SHALL EVERY HOLY ONE PRAY UNTO THEE IN A CONVENIENT TIME) In the Hebrew:

For this reason the pious man will pray to you at a time when you may be found. That is, as soon as possible, while God can still be found: For the time of finding him does not always remain, Is. 55:6. where Aben-Ezra says, while he can be found, i.e., before the condemnatory decrees are sealed. See what is said on Luke 19:44.

There seems to lurk here some hyperbole from the Socinian hypotheses, by which, with the Novatians, grace is denied to those who have fallen into habitual sins after regeneration. By this means, a smooth path is paved to despair for miserable sinners. For who is there who, after conversion, does not fall into this or that kind of sin, and contract in it some custom of sin, or even a certain habit? Not to mention the wicked habit of original concupiscence, which is common to all, the sin which so easily besets, which is never put off except with life itself, Heb. 13:1, Rom. 7. But enough has been said elsewhere against the Socinians and Arminians. God always wishes to be found by the penitent. He always invites us to repentance, while we act in this life, as long as it is called today, Heb. 4:13, Ps. 95:8. Wickedness will not harm the wicked man, on whatever day or hour he turns away from his wickedness, Ez. 33:11, which God also confirmed there by an oath. There are, therefore, no such condemnatory decrees by which anyone is simply reprobated from grace, with no hope of it left. The case of temporal judgments and punishments, which God has decreed for this or that nation or people when they have filled their measure, is different. For, regarding such decrees, we admit that there is sometimes a time when God does not wish to be found. To this pertain the passages Is. 55:6, Luke 19:44. But the door of grace is never so closed to any of mankind that he cannot, through repentance, return to God and obtain His mercy. Because God Himself calls all sinners to repentance, has ordained Sacraments for all as means of grace, and Christ has acquired grace for all by His blood, by which we are cleansed from all sin, 1 John 1:7.

Verse same. NEVERTHELESS] You would better translate that 'ach as 'certainly', in the way it is taken in Gen. 20:15, where the Greeks have 'ara', and 1 Kings 21:25.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PRO HOC ORABIT AD TE OMNIS SAN- CTVS IN TEMPORE OPFORTVNO) In Hebræo:

Ob id deprecabitur te pius quibis in tempore inveniendi. Id est, quam primum, dum adhuc inveniri Deus potest: Non enim semper manet inveniendi eum tempus Ef. 55, 6. ubi Aben-Esdra, dum inveniri potest, i. e. antequam decreta da- mnatoria obsignentur. Vide quæ dicta ad Lucam 19, 44.

Videtur hic latitare ὑπερβολόν τι ex Socinianis hy- pothesibus, quibus, cum Novatianis, prolapsis in peccata habitualia post regenerationem denega- tur gratia. Quo pacto ad desperationem plana ster- nitur via miseris peccatoribus. Ecquis enim est, qui post conversionem non in hoc, vel illud pec- cati genus incidens, in eo aliquam peccati consue- tudinem, vel etiam quendam habitum contrahat? Ut taceam habitum concupiscentiæ originalis pra- vum, qui omnibus communis, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, τὴν εὐπερίστατον, quæ nunquam nisi cum ipsa vita exui- tur Ebr. 13, 1. Rom. 7. Sed Socinianis & Arminia- nis alias factum satis. Semper Deus inveniri vult a pœnitentibus. Semper nos invitat ad pœnitentiam, dum in hac vita agimus ἄχρις ὅ τὸ σήμερον κα- λεῖται Ebr. 4, 13. Ps. 95, 8. Impietas non nocebit im- pio, quacunque die, vel hora se averterit ab impie- tate sua Ez. 33, 11. quod jurejurando etiam confir- mavit ibidem Deus. Nulla ergo sunt ejusmodi de- creta damnatoria, quibus quis simpliciter a gratia reprobetur, nulla ejusdem spe relicta. Temporali- um judiciorum & pœnarum, quas Deus huic aut illi nationi, vel populo decrevit, cum illi mensuram suam impleverunt, alia est ratio. Nam, quoad hu- jusmodi decreta, fatemur, tempus nonnunquam esse, quo Deus inviniri non velit. Quo pertinent lo- ca Ef. 55, 6. Luc. 19, 44. Nunquam autem ulli ho- minum janua gratiæ ita occlusa est, quin per pœni- tentiam redire ad Deum, ejusdemque misericor- diam consequi possit. Quia Deus ipse omnes pec- catores vocat ad pœnitentiam, omnibus ordinavit Sacramenta, ceu media gratiæ, omnibusq; gratiam acquifivit Christus sanguine suo, quo ab omni pec- cato mundamur 1. Joh. 1, 7.

Vers. eod. VERVNTAMEN] Illud אך melius vertas certe, quomodo sumitur Gen. 20, 15. ubi Græci ἄρα, & 1. Reg. 21, 25.

## 32:6 Addition
On Psalm 32, verse 6, towards the end.

However, the saints ought not only to pray against venial sins, as Bellarmine wishes, but also those concerning which David says that they afflicted his soul; and Jansenius, Lorinus, and Estius acknowledge that the words אל זאת are to be referred to what immediately precedes: for impiety and sins every saint will pray to you. But Salmero is inept, as is also Franc. Horantius, book III, Loc. Cath., chapter 21, while they prove from this saying the prayer of the saints in heaven for the Church.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 32. v. 6. sub finem.

Non autem deprecari tantum Sancti debent peccata venialia, ut Bellarmin. vult, sed etiam ea, de quibus David, quod afflixerint animam suam; & a- gnoscunt Jansenius, Lorinus & Estius voces אל זאת referendas esse ad immediate præcedentia: pro im- pietate & peccatis orabit te omnis sanctus. Ineptus autem est Salmero, ut & Franc. Horantius l. III. Loc. Cath. c. 21. dum ex hoc dicto orationem Sanctorum in cælis pro Ecclesia probant.

## 32:9
V. 9. WITH BIT AND BRIDLE CONSTRAIN THEIR JAWS WHO DO NOT APPROACH THEE] In the Hebrew: With a bit and bridle their mouth is to be constrained, because they do not approach thee: namely, of their own accord. That 'lamed' placed before the infinitive verb is explained by 'dei' or 'hoste', as appears in 2 Sam. 5:20. A similar 'lamed' is in Hosea 9:13 and elsewhere.

Latin:

V. 9. IN CAMO ET FRÆNO MAXILLAS EO- RVM CONSTRINGE QVI NON APPROXIMANT AD TE] In Hebræo: Lupato, & freno obstringendum illis os, quia non accedunt ad te: nempe sua sponte. Illud ל verbo infinitivo præpositum exponitur per deῖ vel ὥστε, ut apparet 2. Sam. 5, 20. Simile ל Oseæ 9, 13. & alibi.

## 33:6
Verse 6. BY THE WORD OF THE LORD THE HEAVENS WERE ESTABLISHED) In the Hebrew: were made, from Gen. 1:6.

AND BY THE SPIRIT OF HIS MOUTH ALL THEIR HOST) The stars are the Spirit of the mouth of God, 'qol pi Yah' to the Phoenicians. And concerning the Word, or the Reason that is the maker of things, and concerning this Spirit, those things which we said in Book 1 of the Truth of the Christian Religion can be seen.

By the Spirit of the mouth of God, the Holy Spirit is to be understood, who is so called from Job 33, Is. 11:1, 2 Thess. 2. Therefore, he is joined here with the WORD OF THE LORD, by which the 'logos hypostatikos' is understood. For this one, with the Holy Spirit, is the author of creation: to which interpretation light is added from Job 1:2, 3. Hence also the Chaldean often designated the Son of God by the name of the Word. By this means, we have here an illustrious testimony of the Holy Trinity, with the consent of antiquity, which the Holy Fathers frequently urge against the Arians. We treated of it more fully in Vol. III of the System of Theology. On Book I of the Truth of the Christian Religion, Grotius observes on p. 24 that 'qol pi Yah' is 'the wind of the mouth of God'. But who will be so inept as to believe that 'wind' is to be understood here, when the host of the heavens is said to be adorned by the Spirit of the mouth of God? However, when he brings in the 'logos' as the maker of things and the Spirit from the Gentiles, one cannot easily say whether he understands the persons of the Holy Trinity or not. He seems rather to speak of the 'logos prophorikos', or of the command by which things were created, section 16. By the Word of God, he says, all things were made, it is also declared by Epicharmus and the Platonists: and before them by the most ancient writer, not of those hymns which we have under that name, but of those poems which antiquity called Orphic, not because they were Orpheus's, but because they contained what was handed down by him. This is Grotius, Book I, in the annotations on verse 16. He praises Tertullian against the Gentiles, citing Zeno and other Gentile wise men who establish the 'logos' as the artificer of the universe. He brings these things forward in order to insinuate the 'logos hypostatikos', the Son of God, to the Gentiles. He also praises Amelius the Platonist concerning the 'logos' judged by John the Evangelist, whom he calls a Barbarian, since he said that he stood by God in the first founding of things, nay, even in the unformed state, and through whom absolutely all things were made. Since, therefore, John speaks of the Son of God, it could seem that Grotius attributes to Amelius and other Gentiles some light concerning the Son of God, the maker of things, which they received from Moses. Furthermore, Grotius not rarely confuses the 'logos hypostatikos', the Son of God, with the 'logos prostaktikos', the word of command: And what he understands by the word here in the Davidic oracle, he does not sufficiently explain. He seems only to have wished to render doubtful a passage which, until now, has been held as indubitable against the Anti-Trinitarians by the ancients and the moderns, if you except the pack of Arians and Socinians, and our innovators the Calixtines, who were indeed satisfied in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony. Let those things which we said above on Gen. 1:2, 3 be compared. Here it is only pleasing to observe a passage from the book of Psalms, in which the Rabbis also judged that the Word of the Son of God the Messiah was spoken of: which occurs in Ps. 107:20. He sent

His WORD, and healed them. This is the exposition of Libertus Cominetus (so the man's name is written) Hackspan, a converted Rabbi, skilled in fourteen languages, cited by Augustinus Justinianus in his Annotations to the Octapla Psalter, Geneva edition, year 1516, Ps. 148: it seems it must be said: He speaks His word, but He does not send His word; for it is more fitting for a word to be pronounced and brought forth than to be sent, which seems to be proper to an Orator. But it is resolved; for as far as I myself feel, David in this place prophesied the coming of the Messiah. Cominetus had these things from other Rabbis. For it is read thus in the Commentary of R. Isaac Arama on the book of Numbers, whose title is The Sacrifice of Isaac: R. Samuel the Levite said, the word of God is His messenger or Orator. The Word came to heal all, but He was not accepted, except by individuals who were considered among all the duller of wit, men who were fishermen, exercising themselves in the sea; And this is what was said (Ps. 107, 23) those going down to the sea in ships, doing work in great waters, they saw the work of God.

Hackspan, who willingly weakens the sayings of the O.T.

confirming the Most Holy Trinity, nor did he spare this passage; for that argument, that the word is really distinguished from Him whose word it is, and the Spirit really from Him whose Spirit it is, he therefore attempts to break, even though he himself ought to have confessed on p. 145 that He who is the Spirit of God is not that divine person whose Spirit it is, and he strives to prove by a collation with v. 9 that a created word is to be understood in this place. Nevertheless, he argues against the Socinians, Calvin, Sixtus of Siena, Cajetan, as also a certain M. Casp. Bolerus, that the H. H. Trinity is designated here, and he compares Job 26:13, that the uncreated Word is understood as the Son of God, as also Job 26:13, that the Spirit of God's mouth is the H. S., to whom creation is directly attributed there, which does not fall upon a created breath, but is a personal action. That this goes off into self-contradiction, everyone understands. But so that he may return to favor with himself, he observes through the word

that the spoken word is primarily noted here, but that under that sense there also lies a mediate signification, namely the Son of God; similarly, that by the breath of the mouth of God an immediately created breath is denoted, and mediately the Spirit, and that one is a symbol of the other. But this is a new method of explanation, and hitherto unheard of among the Orthodox, that by one word both a created thing and God the creator (a created thing immediately, God the creator mediately) should be hinted at, and both the symbol and that which is indicated by the symbol. If the word דבר denotes a created word here, how then does the same word simultaneously designate the Son of God? If רוח is some created breath in this place, by what means, I beseech you, does Hackspan himself refute Vatablus from this principle Ps. 45, 7. Solomon typically and improperly אלהים gods, but Christ truly and properly pag. 204. On account of the type, he says, who would concede that the same word once placed is taken both properly and improperly, and against the adversaries who would have proven even the slightest thing from this? Who therefore himself now asserts that the same word once placed obtains such diverse significations simultaneously, and what will he be able to prove from that against the adversaries? But what Hackspan says Gen. 1, that by saying likewise something created is understood immediately and primarily, while meanwhile the Son of God is also hinted at mediately, whose it is to bring forth speech, in that he is greatly mistaken. For that saying is not primarily something created: otherwise God would have first created the word, and the word would be the first creature, and then through this creature or by means of it he would have formed the light. No one would say that that word of God is a creature, since God created by a nod and a command, and by will alone, and it is not to be imagined that he emitted a word or a created breath of the mouth. Unless this is mitigated, it is Anthropomorphitic. Nor did the uncreated Word lie hidden there under the symbol of the created word. But because the Father did not speak thus except in the Son, with the Son, and through the Son, nor could he speak or work otherwise, therefore by the force of the underlying matter that אמר must be explained in such a way that the Father, speaking and working in the Son, made the light; and Hackspan himself refutes at Gen. 1, 3. that mediate sense which he proves here pag. 38. That mediate sense, he says, concerning the substantial Word of God is either literal or mystical; certainly it cannot be mystical, if indeed it has arisen from the equivocation of the word 'word'. The mystical and divine sense of scripture intended by the Holy Spirit, which D. Glassius establishes, is finally that which is designated in express words by the citation of the passage. But this passage is nowhere cited for a mystery. The consequence is good: all things were made through the word. Therefore also the light. But this is harsher: All things were made through the word. Therefore the substantial Word is connoted by that ויאמר. Likewise all things were made through the Son. Therefore the Son is also connoted under the aspect of the Son in that Vajomar; which no one says. Thus, therefore, he who strove to refute our theologians, especially the blessed Gerhard, did not remain consistent with himself. But we have already explained how our people say the substantial Word is connoted, and we have observed it at Gen. 1, 3. Indeed, they do not deny that a divine command is indicated, which the Psalmist expresses in this Psalm v. 9, and the holy Apostle 2 Cor. 4, 6. Which, however, is not explained badly by Maimonides in More Nebuch. p. 1. c. 65, R. Saadia, and R. Isaac Karo, as having been done not by a word spoken humanly or by the sound of a voice, but by the will and nod alone. Moreover, if any spoken word is understood here at all (which we do not deny in a right sense), that word nevertheless cannot be imagined without the internal and eternal hypostatic Word of God, whence it is not undeservedly said to be connoted by this word, especially because the Son exists in the mind of God after the manner of a word, and with God the Father saying here, and commanding that light be made, that saying and mandate was made in the Word or hypostatic Wisdom. There is no need here, therefore, for a mystical sense, nor is the matter proven by that bare collection, all things were made through the word, therefore.

the substantial Word is connoted. But because the Father possessed the hypostatic Word from eternity, and the Son is from the Father and in the Father, after the manner of a word, which is from the mind and in our mind, as Prov. 8 and John 1, 1 establish, and through this word, and not indeed without this hypostatic word, he willed, commanded, and said, as the parallelism of the passages indicates: that the Father willed to create in and with the Word and through the hypostatic Word, and commanded that light should be made. Which is more certain, safer, and holier than if you make that אמר a created word and a created breath of the mouth, and imagine a symbol of the Son created externally, which nevertheless will also have to be called a symbol of the Spirit. S. not without confusion of the divine Persons, and a duality of sense in the same word; for the confirmation of which, while the same author alleges Ex. 12, as if a double sense occurs there, and the paschal lamb were denoted immediately and Christ mediately John 19, 36, he confuses the diverse notion of a word, which we do not acknowledge here, with the typical adumbration of a thing expressed through words. The same word has only the same signification, you shall not break a bone of it (the lamb, for the text dealt only with it, not a jot of Christ occurs in it). Meanwhile, because the lamb was a type of Christ, it is adumbrated by this ceremony of the bones not being broken, or because the bones were left whole in the Paschal lamb, that the legs of Christ would not be broken: where anyone understands that it is one thing for a word or pronoun to denote Christ, and for that precept to be taken in a mediate sense concerning Christ: and another thing for the lamb, denoted solely by that pronoun, to have adumbrated Christ, and for the ceremony performed there (not the Mosaic words themselves) to have signified the thing to be fulfilled in the antitype, that the bones of Christ would be kept whole.

Latin:

Vers. 6. VERBO DOMINI COELI FIRMATI SVNT) In Hebræo: facti sunt ex Gen. 1, 6.

ET SPIRITV ORIS EJVS OMNIS EXERCITVS EO- RVM) Sidera Spiritus oris Dei קול פי יה Phœnicibus. Et de verbo, sive ratione rerum opifice, & de hoc Spiritu vi- deri possunt, quæ diximus ad librum 1. de Veritate Religio- nis Christianæ.

PEr Spiritum oris Dei Spiritus Sanctus intelli- gendus est, qui ita vocatur e Job. 33. Ef. 11. 1. Theff. 2. Ideo hic conjungitur cum VERBO DO- MINI, per quod λόγον ὑποστατικὸς intelligitur. Hic enim cum Spiritu Sancto autor est creationis: Cui interpretationi lux accedit è Job. 1, 2. 3. Inde etiam Chaldæus sæpe verbi nomine designavit Fi- lium Dei. Quo pacto S.S. Trinitatis illustre hic te- stimonium, consentiente antiquitate, habemus, quod adversus Arianos S. Patres frequenter ur- gent. Egimus de eo uberius Tom. III. Systemat. Theolog. Ad libr. I. de V. R. Christ. Grotius obser- vat p. 24. קול פי יה vocem oris Dei ventum esse. Quis autem tam ineptus erit, ut credat hic ventum intel- ligendum esse, quum ornatus Spiritu oris Dei exercitus cœlorum dicitur? Cum autem λόγον re- rum opificem & Spiritum è gentibus adducit, non facile dixeris, an personas S. S. Trinitatis intelligat, nec ne? Loqui potius de verbo προφορικῷ, aut man- dati, quo creatæ res sunt, videtur §. 16. Verbo Dei, inquit, facta omnia, etiam Epicharmo & Platonicis proditur: & ante eos scriptore antiquissimo non illo- rum hymnorum, quos nos sub eo nomine habemus, sed eorum carminum, quæ vetustas Orphica appellavit, non quod Orphei essent, sed quod ab eo tradita conti- nerent. Hæc Grotius lib. I. in annotatis v. ad §. 16. Tertullianum laudat advers. Gentes Zenonem ad- ducentem, & alios sapientes gentiles, qui λόγον ar- tificem universitatis constituere. Qui ea adfert, ut λόγον ὑποστατικὸν Filium Dei gentilibus insinuet. Laudat quoque Amelium Platonicum de λόγῳ a Jo- hanne Evangelista judicato, quem Barbarum vo- cat, quum in primo rerum conditu, imo & in incon- dito statu Deo adstitisse, & per quem omnia omnino facta dixit. Quum ergo Johannes de Filio Dei lo- quatur, videri posset, Grotium aliquid lucis de Fi- lio Dei, rerum opifice, ita Amelio & aliis gentibus tribuere, quod a Mose acceperint. Cæterum con- fundit non raro Grotius λόγον ὑποστατικὸν Filium Dei cum λόγῳ προστακτικῷ verbo mandati: Et quid per verbum hic intelligat in oraculo Davidico, non satis explicat. Locum solum videtur dubium red- dere voluisse, qui hactenus adversus Anti-Trinita- rios indubius, penes veteres & recentiores habitus fuit, si Arianorum & Socinianorum manipulum, ac Novatores nostros Calixtinos excipias, quibus vero in Harmonia Calixtino - Hæretica satisfactum. Conferantur quæ ad Gen. 1, 2. 3. supra diximus. Hic observare solum placet locum e Psalmorum libro, in quo Rabbini etiam censuere, Filium Dei Messiæ verbum dictum esse: qui occurrit Ps. 107, 20. Misit

VERBUM suum, & sanavit eos. Libertatis Coni- meti (sic habet nomen viri) Hackspani, Rabbini Con- versi, quatuordecim linguarum periti, citante Augu- stino Justinianeo in Annotat. ad Octapla Psalter. edit. Genevens. Ann. cIɔIɔXVI. Ps. 148. expositio hæc est: videtur dicendum: loquitur verbum suum, non autem mittit verbum suum; Verbo siquidem ma- gis convenit pronunciari, & proferri, quam mitti, quod videtur proprium esse Oratoris. Sed solvitur; Nam quantum ipse sentio, David hoc loco vaticina- tus est adventum Messiæ. Habuit ista Cominetus ab aliis Rabbinis. Nam ita legitur in Comment. R. Isaac Arama in libr. Numer. quibus titulus est Sacrificium Isaac: dixit R. Samuel Levita, verbum Dei est nuncius sive Orator ejus. Verbum venit sana- re omnes, verum non fuit acceptus, nisi a particula- ribus, qui censebantur inter omnes crassiores ingenii, viri piscatores, exercentes se in mari; Et hoc est, quod dictum est (Ps. 107, 28.) conscendentes in ma- re navibus, facientes opera in aquis magnis, ipsi vi- derunt opus Dei.

Hackspanius qui libenter enervat dicta V. T.

Sacrosanctam Trinitatem confirmantia, nec huic loco pepercit; argumentum enim illud, quod ver- bum realiter ab eo cujus est verbum, & Spiritus rea- liter ab eo cujus est Spiritus, distinguatur, ideo in- fringere conatur, etsi fateri ipse debuerit p. 145. cum qui est Spiritus Dei non esse illam personam di- vinam, cujus est Spiritus, & verbum creatum hoc lo- co intelligendum esse e v. 9. collatione probare ni- titur. Disputat tamen contra Socinianos, Calvinum, Sixtum Senensem, Cajetanum, ut & quendam M. Casp. Bolerum, designari hic S. S. Trinitatem, & confert Job. 1, 3. quod increatum verbum Filius Dei intelligatur, ut & Job. 26, 13. quod Spiritus oris Dei sit Sp. S. cui ibi directe creatio tribuatur, quæ in halitum creatum non cadit, sed actio personalis sit. Quæ in ἑαυτομαχίαν abire nemo non intelligit. Sed ut secum in gratiam redeat, observat per verbum

λόγον προφορικὸν h. l. primario notari, sub sensu au- tem illo latere etiam mediatam significationem sc. Fi- lium Dei; Similiter per Spiritum oris Dei immediate halitum creatum, mediate Spiritum denotari, & unum esse alterius Symbolum. Sed hæc nova jam est, atque hactenus inaudita penes Orthodoxos explicandi ratio, ut uno verbo innuatur & res creata, & Deus creator, (res creata immediate, Deus creator me- diate) & Symbolum, & id quod Symbolo indicatur. Si vox דבר hic verbum creatum notat, quomodo ergo simul Filium Dei eadem vox designat? Si רוח est halitus aliquis creatus hoc loco, quo pacto, obse- cro, redarguit ex hoc principio Hackspanius ipse Vatablum Ps. 45, 7. Salomonem typice & improprie אלהים dii, Christum autem vere & proprie pag. 204. Ob typum, inquit, eandem vocem semel positam cum proprie tum improprie sumi quis concesserit & contra adversarios quis hinc vel tantillum evicerit? Qui er- go ipse nunc vocem eandem semel positam tam di- versos significatus simul obtinere asserit, & quid contra adversarios inde evincere poterit? Quod vero Hackspanius ait Gen. 1. per dicere itidem im- mediate & primo intelligi creatum quid, interim me- diate etiam Dei filium innui, cujus est sermonem pro- ferre, in eo fallitur maxime. Non enim primo dice- re illud creatum quid est: alias Deus primo creasset verbum, & prima creatura foret verbum, ac tum per hanc creaturam vel mediante illa lucem formasset. Nemo dixerit verbum illud Dei creaturam esse, quum nutu & jussu, ac voluntate sola Deus crearit, non fingendus sit verbum, vel halitum oris creatum emisisse. Quod nisi mitigetur, Anthropomorphiti- cum est. Neque ibi sub symbolo verbi creati verbum increatum latuit. Sed quia non nisi in Filio, cum Fi- lio, per Filium ita dixit, nec aliter dicere, aut opera- ri potuit Pater, ideo vi materiæ substratæ illud אמר explicandum est ita, quod Pater in Filio loquens & operans lucem fecerit; & refellit ipse Hackspanius ad Gen. 1, 3. Sensum illum mediatum quem hic pro- bat pag. 38. Sensus, inquit, ille mediatus de verbo Dei substantiali vel literalis est, vel mysticus; certe non potest esse mysticus, siquidem est ex æquivocatione vo- cis verbi ortus. Mysticus & divinus scripturæ sensus intentus a Sp. S. quem D. Glassius statuit, is demum est, qui disertis verbis designatur per citationem loci. Hic locus autem pro mysterio nuspiam citatur. Bona est consequentia: omnia per verbum facta sunt. Er- go etiam lux. Sed hæc durior: Omnia per verbum facta sunt. E. verbum substantiale connotatur illo ויאמר Item omnia per Filium facta sunt. E. Filius etiam connotatur sub ratione Filii in illo Vajomar; quod nemo dicit. Ita ergo sibi non constitit ipse, qui Theologos nostrates, imprimis B. Gerhardum re- fellere sategit. At quo pacto connotari verbum substantiale nostri dicant, jam exposuimus, & ad Gen. 1, 3. observavimus. Nimirum non negant jus- sum divinum indicari, quem Psaltes hoc Psalmo v. 9. exprimit, & S. Apostolus 2. Cor. 4, 6. Qui vero non verbo ἀνθρωπίνως prolato, aut vocis sono fa- ctus, sed de voluntate ac nutu solo a Maimonide in More Nebuch. p. 1. c. 65. R. Saadia, & R. Isaac Ka- ro non male explicatur. Cæterum si omnino ali- quod verbum προφορικὸν hic intelligatur (quod dextro sensu non diffitemur) non tamen verbum illud fingi potest sine interno & æterno Dei verbo hypostatico, unde non immerito hoc ea voce con- notari dicitur, maxime quia per modum verbi Fi- lius in mente Dei sese habet, ac Deo Patre hic di- cente, ac jubente fiat lux, dictum & mandatum il- lud factum in verbo vel sapientia hypostatica. Non ergo opus hic sensu mystico, neque nuda illa colle- ctione res evincitur, omnia per verbum facta, E.

connotatur verbum substantiale. Sed quia Pater ab æterno verbum hypostaticum possedit, & Filius a Pa- tre, & in Patre est, per modum verbi, quod est a men- te & in mente nostra, ute Prov. 8. & Job. 1, 1. con- stat, atque per verbum hoc, non vero fine hoc verbo hypostatice voluit, præcepit & dixit, ut paralle- lismus locorum indicat: quod Pater in & cum verbo & per verbum hypostaticum creare voluerit, ac ut lux fieret jusserit. Quod certius, tutius ac sanctius est, quam si illud אמר verbum creatum halitumque oris creatum facias, ac Symbolum fingas ad extra creatum Filii, quod tamen etiam Symbolum erit di- cendum Sp. S. non absque confusione Personarum divinarum, & διπλότητι sensus in eadem voce; pro cujus confirmatione, dum idem autor allegat Ex. 12. quasi duplex ibi sensus occurrat, atque immediate agnus paschalis, mediate Christus denotaretur Joh. 19, 36. confundit diversam vocis notionem, quam hic non agnoscimus, cum rei per voces expressæ ty- pica adumbratione. Vox eadem eandem solum ha- bet significationem, os ipsi (agno, nam de eo solum textus egit, de Christo ne gry quidem in eo occur- rit) non frangetis. Interim quia agnus typus erat Christi, adumbratur hac ceremonia ossium non fra- ctorum seu quod ossa agno Paschali integra relicta sint, Christo haud fractum iri crura: ubi quilibet in- telligit, aliud esse, vocem vel pronomen Ipsi notare Christum, & sensu mediato de Christo illud præce- ptum accipi debere: Aliud, agnum pronomine illo unice notatum adumbrasse Christum, & ceremo- niam ibi impetratam (non verba ipsa Mosaica) si- gnificasse rem implendam in antitypo, integra ser- vatum iri ossa Christi.

## 33:7
Vers. 7. GATHERING AS IN A BOTTLE THE WATERS OF THE SEA) From the Greek συνάγων ὡσεὶ ἀσκον ὕδατα θαλάσσης. The interpreters read not כנד as we do, but more correctly כנאד or בנאד. And not only the Greeks, whom the Syrian and Arab mostly follow, but also the Chaldean. God constrained the sea in the shores as if in a bottle.

The Hebrew codices most correctly [read] כנד, he gathers AS INTO A HEAP the waters of the sea, and places the abysses (as if) in a treasury. On which words Munster: God is wonderful in his works, who gathered all the waters of the sea into one greatest mass, separating it from the earth, and from its natural position, into one place of the Ocean, where he placed the abysses as if in his treasuries. It is better to acknowledge the παροράματα of the interpreters than to derogate from the truth of the Hebrew reading. And what can be desired here in the sense of the Hebrew text? The style of Scripture agrees perfectly: For elsewhere also waters are said to be gathered into a heap, Ex. 15, 8. Job 3, 15. 16. Ps. 78, 13. But nowhere, as far as is known, is God said to have gathered the waters of the sea into a bottle. Nor does the word נד without a Nun in the middle signify a bottle anywhere. A new word is therefore invented, or one invented by Capellus is accepted. For Grotius seems to have followed him, against whom see Buxtorf's Defense of the Hebrew Truth. part II. c. 8. page 554.

Verse same. HE WILL PLACE THE ABYSSES IN TREASURIES) He places is more correct. The same thing is said by another comparison; for ἄβυσσος are the seas. These God holds locked up as if in storehouses. Thus he called the treasuries or storehouses of snow in Job 38, 22.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CONGREGANS SICVT IN UTRE AQVAS MARIS) Ex Græco συνάγων ὡσεὶ ἀσκον ὕδατα θαλάσσης. Legerunt Interpretes non כנד ut nos, sed rectius כנאד vel בנאד. Nec Græci tantum, quos plerunque sequuntur Sy- rus & Arabs, sed & Chaldæus. Deus mare in littoribus velut in utre constrinxit.

Rectissime Ebræi Codices כנד ipse congregat QVASI IN CUMULUM aquas maris, & ponit (velut) in thesauro abyssos. Ad quæ verba Munsterus: Mirabilis est Deus in operibus suis, qui omnes aquas maris in unam maximam congeffit molem, separans eam a terra, & a naturali situ suo, in unum Oceani locum, ubi abyssos posuit veluti in thesauris suis. Sa- tius est παροράματα interpretum agnoscere, quam derogare veritati lectionis Ebraicæ. Et quid in sensu Ebræi textus hic desiderari potest? Stylus Scripturæ apprime congruit: Nam & alibi in cu- mulum congregatæ aquæ dicuntur Ex. 15, 8. Job. 3, 15. 16. Ps. 78, 13. Nuspiam vero, quod constet, aquas maris in utrem collegisse Deus dicitur. Neque vox נד sine Nun in medio uspiam utrem significat. Nova ergo fingitur vox, aut a Capello ficta accipitur. Hunc enim sequutus videtur Grotius, adversus quem vi- deatur defens. verit. Ebrææ Buxtorff. part. II. c. 8. pag. 554.

Vers. eod. PONET IN THESAURIS ABYSSOS) Re- ctius ponit. Alia comparatione idem dicitur; nam ἄβυσσος sunt maria. Ea Deus velut in apothecis reclusa tenet. Sic the- sauros sive apothecas nivis dixit Job 38, 22.

Vers. 8. TIMEAT DOMINUM OMNIS TERRA) Nam quis dubitat, quin in terra faciat, quæ velit, qui tam indomi- tam naturam maris domat?

## 33:9
Verse 9. HE HIMSELF SPOKE AND THEY WERE MADE) As we say in Latin, said and done, with no delay interposed.

Latin:

Vers. 9. IPSE DIXIT ET FACTA SUNT) Ut latine dicimus, dictum factum, nulla mora interposita.

## 33:15
Verse 15. WHO FASHIONED THEIR HEARTS INDIVIDUALLY) The Greeks [read] Καταμόνας. They seem to have read יַחַד not יַחַד. The Hebrew יַחַד [means] equally, together, not concerning simultaneity of time, but concerning the parity of the work, namely that God fashioned all hearts equally and alike, is to be understood. For not all souls were created at once and together. Whatever, therefore, the Greeks may have read or seen, the Hebrew text is correct: But that from this passage the creation of souls is wrongly asserted, was stated in Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica p. 549.

Hackspan argues for it thus: I ask when God is said to create the heart, what kind of creation they understand, whether mediate or indeed immediate. If immediate. Therefore it is produced from nothing. If mediate, I ask, what is that medium by which the soul is created? You say parents. R. Parents cannot produce a soul proximately. You ask, seed. Resp. Seed cannot produce a Spirit, otherwise the cause would not be more excellent in its whole genus, but inferior to its effect. Here, however, we lack the force and vigor of proof. For the seed is not destitute of a soul, but animated, nor is a Spirit generated from seed, but a human; for a human generates not a spirit, but a human by means of seed, which we have discussed at length in the aforementioned Harmonia, where the origin of the soul was discussed expressly; and we showed that the Calixtines torture themselves in vain with the asserted creation of the soul regarding the existence of original sin. Nor is Hackspan more successful than the others: He objects to himself this argument: If in this place immediate creation is to be understood, it follows that God is the cause of sin. For it is asked, if God immediately creates the soul, that soul will either be immune from every stain, or not. If the former, whence then did the stain later accrue to it? If the latter, God will be the cause of sin. He responds, however, that it can be said that God forms a soul which is pure and immune from every stain. Meanwhile, as soon as that soul is joined to the body, and constitutes one thing with it, it is also simultaneously affected by the body, and hence that stain accrues. But how can the body infect the soul, since the soul is the πρῶτον δεκτικὸν of sin, and how does this accord with the justice of God, to unite and infuse an innocent and pure soul into a body contaminated by the stain of sin, or what finally is the cause of the soul’s sin, if indeed it cannot be infected by the body, but rather infects the body itself? He responds, sin is a defect; and therefore where there is a subject naturally apt, there, if the habit is absent, privation is present. The cause of this matter is therefore referred to the first parents, who are the cause not indeed physically, by producing the effect, but morally. But in this way the Psalmist will not be able to confess that he received his sin by inheritance from his immediate parents, while he professes himself to have been conceived in sins, Ps. 51. And since the soul is a subject naturally apt, does the soul, as it is founded by God, labor under that privation, and thus under sin before it is infused into the body (as far as the order of nature is concerned), or is it free from sin? If the latter, it will be pure when it is infused into the body. If, however, the former, sin must be from God, from whom the soul is, where indeed Hackspan cannot retreat with his teacher Calixtus to the state of pure naturals, as if the soul were created in that state by God. For he himself exploded this fiction on Ps. 34, p. 163. But what the Scholastics imagine, that a human in pure naturals is neither good nor evil, that is a fiction, for where a subject is capable, there it is necessary that either a habit or a privation be present. In a capable subject, therefore, such as the soul is as founded by God before it is sent into the body, it is necessary that a privation or a habit, or a vice or a virtue, be present. If, therefore, a habit is present, the soul will be holy not only through regeneration, but through creation, which is the view of the Calvinists: if a privation, it will be infected with sin by immediate creation: and thus God, its creator, will be the cause of sin. But these things, and what are imagined here concerning the mere privation of original sin, we have discussed by design in the cited place.

Latin:

Vers. 15. QUI FINXIT SIGILLATIM CORDA EO- RUM) Καταμόνας Græci. Legisse videntur יַחַד non יַחַד. Ebræum יַחַד Pariter, una, non de simultate tem- poris, sed de paritate operis, quod nempe pariter & ex æquo omnia corda finxerit Deus, intelligen- dum. Non enim simul & semel omnes animæ con- ditæ. Quicquid ergo legerint, aut viderint Græci, recte se habet Ebræus textus: Perperam autem ex- hoc loco creationem animarum adstrui, Harmonia Calixtino - Hæretica p. 549. dictum.

Pro ea ita pugnat Hackspanius: Quæro quando Deus dicitur creare cor, qualem creationem intelligant, an mediatam, an vero immediatam. Si immediatam. Ergo producitur ex nihilo. Si mediatam, quæro, quid sit illud medium, quo creatur anima? Dicis Parentes. R. Parentes animam producere proxime nequeunt. Inquis Semen. Resp. Semen non potest producere Spiritum, alias causa toto genere non esset præstantior, sed deterior suo effectu. Hic vero desideramus vim & nervum probandi. Non enim Semen animæ destitutum, sed animatum est, neque ex semine generatur Spiritus, sed homo, homo enim non spiritum, sed hominem generat mediante semine, quod prolixe adseruimus in Harmon. laudata, ubi ex professo de Origin. animæ disputatum; & ostendimus frustra Calixtinos se torquere asserta animæ creatione circa peccati originalis existentiam. Neque cæteris felicior est Hackspanius: Objicit sibi hoc argumentum: Si h. l. immediata creatio est intelligenda, sequitur Deum esse causam peccati. Quæritur enim, si Deus immediate creat animam, anima illa aut erit ab omni labe immunis, aut non. Si illud, unde igitur illi postea accessit macula? Si hoc, Deus erit causa peccati. Respondet vero dici posse, Deum formare animam, quæ pura & ab omni labe immunis est. Interim simul ac illa anima conjungitur corpori, cumque eo unum quid constituit, etiam simul a corpore afficitur, hincque labes illa accedit. Sed quomodo corpus inficere potest animam, quum anima sit πρῶτον δεκτικὸν peccati, & qui convenit hoc justitiæ Dei, animam innocentem & puram corpori peccati labe contaminato unire ac infundere, aut quænam tandem peccati animæ causa, siquidem illa a corpore infici nequeat, sed corpus ipsum potius inficiat? Respondet, peccatum est defectus; ideoque ubi est subjectum aptum natum ibi si habitus abest, adest privatio. Refertur itaque causa hujus rei ad primos parentes, qui causa sunt non quidem physica, producendo effectum, sed moraliter. Sed ita Hieropsaltes fateri non poterit, se a proximis parentibus peccatum suum hereditario accepisse, dum in peccatis conceptum se profitetur Ps. 51. Et cum subjectum aptum natum anima sit, num anima prout a Deo conditur laborat illa privatione, adeoque peccato prius quam infundatur corpori (quod ordinem naturæ attinet) aut expers est peccati. Si hoc, pura erit, cum infunditur corpori. Si vero illud, peccatum oportet esse a Deo, a quo est anima, ubi sane se recipere non potest Hackspan. cum præceptore suo Calixto ad statum primorum naturalium, quasi anima creetur in illo statu a Deo. Nam hoc commentum explosit ipse ad Ps. 34. p. 163. Quod autem Scholastici fingunt, hominem in puris naturalibus, nec bonum esse nec malum, id figmentum est, nam ubi subjectum capax est, ibi necesse est, adsit vel habitus vel privatio. In subjecto ergo capaci, qualis est anima, uti a Deo condita antequam immittatur in corpus, necesse est, adsit privatio aut habitus, vel vitium aut virtus. Si ergo habitus adest, sancta erit anima non per regenerationem demum, sed per creationem, quod Calvinianorum: si privatio, peccato eadem erit infecta per immediatam creationem: adeoque Deus creator ipsius erit causa peccati. Sed hæc & quæ de mera privatione peccati originalis hic finguntur, loco citato ex instituto discussimus.

## 34:1 Argument
PSALM XXXIV. A celebration of divine protection, and a school of piety.

WHEN HE CHANGED HIS COUNTENANCE) When he feigned that he was fleeing, 1 Sam. 21:13.

BEFORE ABIMELECH) In Hebrew Abimelech, which was an ancient name of the kings of that region, as appears in Gen. 20 and 26, whence it also adhered to successors, as the name of Caesar to the Roman Emperors. For the proper name of the King, who is treated here, was Achish.

Latin:

PSALMUS XXXIV. Celebratio divinæ tutelæ, & Scholæ pietatis.

CUM IMMUTAVIT VULTUM SUUM) Cum fugere se simulavit, 1. Sam. 21, 13.

CORAM ACHIMELECH) In Hebræo Abimelech, quod ab antiquo nomen regum illius tractūs, ut apparet Gen. 20, & 26. unde & succefforibus adhæsit, ut Cæsarum nomen Ro- manis Imperatoribus. Nam proprium Regis, de quo hîc agi- tur, nomen fuit Achis.

## 34:5
Ver. 6. DRAW NEAR TO HIM: AND BE ENLIGHTENED] That 'and' ought to have begun a new clause, which begins with the letter ו.

In Hebrew it is not an imperative, as the Vulgate, Syrian, Arab, and Ethiopian versions, following the LXX, have it. But an indicative: which the Chaldean also retained, they looked to him, so that they were enlightened. B. Luther understood the pronoun, whoever look to him. Nor is it a new clause, but the words are joined in the explanation of the subject, they looked to him and flowed together. For thus the Hebrew is more correctly rendered than 'they were enlightened.' See Is. 2:2, Jer. 31:12, Mic. 4:1, Is. 60:5. Compare the marginal gloss of Luther and Dn. D. in Geier in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ACCEDITE AD EUM: ET ILLUMINAMI- NI] Illud & debuit incipere novum comma, quod incipit a litera ו.

In Ebr. non imperativus est, uti cum Vulgata Syrus, Arabs, Æthiop. præeuntibus τοῖς ὁ. Sed in- dicativus: quem retinuit quoque Chaldæus, respe- xerunt ad eum, ut illuminati sunt. B. Luther. subin- tellexit pronomen, quicunque respiciunt eum. Ne- que novum est comma, sed conjunguntur verba in subjecti explicatione, respexerunt ad eum & conflu- xerunt. Ita enim Ebr. rectius redditur, quam illumi- nati sunt. Vid. Es. 2, 2. Jer. 31, 12. Mich. 4, 1. Es. 60, 5. Conf. Gloss. Luth. margin. & Dn. D. in Geier. in h. l.

## 34:7
Ver. 8. THE ANGEL OF THE LORD.

Aben-Ezra understands this as an angelic troop, as a soldier for soldiers, a hornet for hornets, Ex. 23:28, just as entire camps surrounded Jacob, Gen. 32:2, and Elisha, 2 Kings 6:17. Others understand a single angel, since even one angel can be to us like an entire camp, just as he can destroy one, 2 Chron. 32:21. But it can be taken indefinitely or for the angelic species, namely that an angel, whether one or many as it pleases God to ordain, now this one, now that one, or an entire angelic troop, surrounds us on all sides or pitches camp around us, where חנה, which is used here, means to pitch camp, 1 Sam. 26:5, whence the name מחנים for the angelic camps, Gen. 32:2. Some understand the uncreated angel, the Son of God, Exod. 23:20. But he is rather presented as the Prince of the host of the Lord, Josh. 5:14. And although the word חנה also occurs regarding God, Is. 29:14, here, however, the Lord, whose angel pitches camp around the faithful, is set before them by reason of His goodness, so that they may taste and see how sweet He is; who is the Son of God Himself, according to the interpretation of St. Peter, 1 Ep. 2:2. In the Vulgate, it is not rendered conveniently: 'The angel of the Lord shall send in the circuit of those who fear him.'

Latin:

Vers. 8. ANGELUS DOMINI.

De angelica turma intelligit Aben-Ezra, ut miles pro militibus, crabro pro crabronibus Ex. 23, 28. quomodo castra integra circumdedere Jacob Gen. 32, 2. & Elisæum 2. Reg. 6, 17. Alii angelum sin- gularem, siquidem unus etiam angelus ut integra castra destruere ita instar castrorum nobis esse potest 2. Par. 32, 21. Accipi autem ita potest indefinite vel pro specie angelica, quod nempe angelus vel unus, vel plures prout Deo ordinare placuerit, modo hic vel ille, modo integra turma angelica, nos undiqua- que circumvallet, aut castra metetur circa nos, ubi חנה quod hic adhibetur est castra metari 1. Sam. 26, 5. unde nomen מחנים de castris angelicis Gen. 32, 2. Nonnulli angelum increatum Filium Dei intelli- gunt Exod. 23, 20. Sed is ut Princeps exercitus Domini potius sistitur Jos. 5, 14. & quanquam etiam de Deo verbum חנה occurrat Es. 29, 14. hic tamen Dominus, cujus angelus castra metatur circa fideles, ratione bonitatis suæ iisdem proponitur, ut gustent & vi- deant, quam suavis sit; qui est ipse Filius Dei inter- prete S. Petro 1. Ep. 2, 2. In Vulg. non commode redditur immittet Angelus Domini in circuitu timen- tium eum.

## 34:8
Verse 9. TASTE AND SEE. To taste is to understand, to experience, to enjoy. Prov. 31:15, Heb. 6:5. Likewise, to see is to know accurately, to contemplate with the eyes of the mind; indeed, even to enjoy the thing known, Ps. 27:13, Eccl. 1:16.

Latin:

Vers. 9. GUSTATE ET VIDETE. Gustare est intelligere, experiri, frui. Prov. 31, 15. Ebr. 6, 5. Ita & videre est accurate cognoscere, oculis animi intueri; imo etiam frui re cognita Ps. 27, 13. Eccl. 1, 16.

## 34:10
Verse 11. THE RICH HAVE LACKED. So also the Syriac and Blessed Luther, following the Seventy Interpreters. In the Hebrew, it is 'young lions prevailing in strength and preying.' They therefore expressed the sense lying hidden under the metaphor, from the opposite member, 'those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good,' or 'shall not (be in need of) any good,' even if they do not prey upon others, indeed even if they are in bodily need, 1 Tim. 6:8; such promises, however, are to be taken with a grain of salt, or the tempering of the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 11. DIVITES EGUERUNT. Ita & Syrus, ac B. Luther. præeuntibus LXX. Int. In Ebr. est LEUNCULI viribus prævalentes ac præ- dantes. Sensum ergo illi expresserunt, sub meta- phora latentem, ex membro opposito, inquirentes Dominum non minuentur omni bono, vel non (indi- gent) omni bono, etsi alios non deprædentur, imo corporaliter egeant, 1. Tim. 6, 8. quales vero promissiones cum grano salis, seu temperamento crucis accipiendæ sunt.

## 34:11 Addition
On Psalm 34, verse 12. I WILL TEACH YOU THE FEAR OF THE LORD.

Bellarmine, in book 1 on Justification, chapter 13, wrongly understands by the fear of the Lord here the effect of contrition, distinguished from faith, hope, and charity, since the word יראת denotes not fear or dread, but any worship of God whatsoever, as Genebrardus, Lorinus, Saa, and Jansenius admit, and to it corresponds 'seeking God' in verse 11. Compare 1 Peter 3:13.

No less falsely does Bellarmine, in book II on Penance, chapter 2, explain verse 19 concerning voluntary and chosen and meritorious contrition of the heart, since it is evident from the context of the text that the discourse is not about an affection of the heart voluntarily elicited, but one commanded by extrinsic afflictions. Compare verse 18 and 20, Psalm 51:19, Isaiah 57:15, chapter 66, verse 2, chapter 61:12. Lorinus explains the contrite as the afflicted, to whom the Lord promises that He wishes to be present with them in tribulation, Psalm 91:15, Psalm 102:20, Isaiah 58:9.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 34. v. 12. TIMOREM DOMINI DOCEBO EOS.

Perperam Bellarmin. l. 1. de Justif. c. 13. per timorem Domini hic effectum contritionis, fidei, spei, & charitati contradistinctum intelligit, cum vox יראת non timorem vel metum, sed quemcunque cultum Dei notet fatente Genebrardo, Lorino, Saa, Jansenio, ei- que τὸ quærere Deum vers. 11. respondeat. Conf. 1. Petr. 3, 13.

Nec minus falso v. 19. Bellarm. l. II. de Pœnit. c. 2. de voluntaria & electa, ac meritoria contritione cordis exponit, quum e συνεχεία textus pateat, sermonem non esse de affectu cordis volun- tarie elicito, sed per afflictiones extrinsecas imperato. Conf. v. 18. & 20. Psal. 51, 19. Es. 57, 15. c. 66. v. 2. c. 61, 12. Lorinus contritos exponit tribulatos, qui- bus spondet Dominus, quod adesse ipsis velit in tribu- latione, Psal. 91, 15. Psal. 102, 20. Esa. 58, 9.

## 34:20
Verse 21. THE LORD KEEPS ALL THEIR BONES, NOT ONE OF THEM SHALL BE BROKEN) See what is said on John 19:36. The Rabbis trifle with wonderful things here concerning the bone which they call Lutz.

He mentions bones because they are as it were the foundation of the human body, as Aben-Ezra notes, yet synecdochically including skin and flesh; NOT ONE is not even one, or none, Matt. 10:29, Ps. 106:11. Therefore, there is no place for that Jewish fable about one little bone of the spine not being broken, by the aid of which the whole body is to be recalled to life. See Targ. Hieros. Cant. 8:5, and Rashi Gen. 47:19, Men. Ben-Israel, book 2, on the resurrection, ch. 15. Meanwhile, because God keeps the bones of both the living and the dead, the resurrection of the dead is not incorrectly proven from this. An entire, says Hilary on Ps. 52, and incorrupt hope of eternity being signified in the bones also there we recall, where it is said, The Lord keeps all the bones of the righteous: not one of them shall be broken: because according to the resurrection shown to Ezekiel, its mystery was revealed under the signification of bones. Nothing is broken to God, as Lorinus and Coccejus; for even the dead live to God, Matt. 22:32. Nothing is broken by a final breaking, according to Dionysius the Carthusian, so that bones crushed in passion or putrefaction remain such, and are not restored to wholeness by God who resurrects.

Latin:

Vers. 21. CUSTODIT DOMINUS OMNIA OSSA EORUM, UNUM EX EIS NON CONTERETUR) Vide quæ ad Johannem 19, 36. Rabbini de osse quod Lutz vocant, mira hîc nugantur.

Ossium meminit, quia corporis humani sunt veluti fundamentum, notante Aben-Ezra, Synecdo- chice tamen cutem & carnem comprehendens; U- NUM NON est ne unum quidem, vel nullum Matt. 10, 29. Ps. 106, 11. Non ergo locus illi fabulæ Judaicæ de uno ossiculo spinæ dorsi haud conterendo, cujus adminiculo in vitam revocandum sit totum cor- pus. Vid. Targ. Hieros. Cant. 8, 5. & Rasche Gen. 47, 19. Men. Ben-Israel. l. 2. de resurr. c. 15. Inte- rim quia & viventium & defunctorum ossa Deus custodit, non inrecte hinc resurrectio mortuorum probatur. Integram, inquit Hilar. in Ps. 52. & incor- ruptam spem æternitatis significari in ossibus etiam il- lie meminimus, ubi dicitur custodit Dominus omnia ossa justorum: unum ex his non contere- tur: quia secundum demonstratam Ezechieli resur- rectionem Sacramentum ejus sub ossium significatio- ne sit revelatum. Nullum frangitur Deo, ut Lorin. & Coccejus; vivunt enim Deo etiam mortui Matth. 22, 32. Nullum frangitur fractione finali, secundum Dionys. Carth. ita ut ossa in passione vel putrefa- ctione comminuta talia maneant, neque a Deo re- suscitante restituantur in integrum.

## 35:1 Argument
PS. XXXV. Defender of the innocent.

Latin:

PS. XXXV. Defensor innocentium.

## 35:1 Addition
On Psalm 35, verse 1. JUDGE, O LORD, THOSE WHO HARM ME.

Bellarmine acknowledges that the meaning is to be sought from the Hebrew text, rendering it thus: Judge those who judge me. But that David is not speaking about himself, which Theodoret, Euthymius, Mollerus, Musculus, and Cocceius wish, but about Christ, which St. Augustine and Jerome, B. Brentius, B. Gesnerus, B. Hülsemannus, and the Vinarieans teach, from a comparison of verse 11 with Matthew 26:60, and also verse 19 with John 15:25.

Nor do the things said in verses 13 and 14 stand in the way, provided that the manner of speaking is allegorical, and not to be taken literally even concerning David himself regarding the putting on of sackcloth: and it notes only the highest and most tender compassion even towards enemies and the envious. Mark 9:19. To which verse 18 of this Psalm seems to be favorable, compared with Psalm 22:26, Psalm 40:10.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 35. Vers. 1. JUDICA DOMINE NOCEN- TES ME.

Ex Ebræo textu sententiam petendam esse agnoscit Bellarm. eum ita reddens: Judica judican- tes me. Non autem de se loqui Davidem quod Theodoretius, Euthymius, Mollerus, Musculus, Coc- cejus volunt: sed de Christo, quod S. August. & Hie- ronymus, B. Brentius, B. Gesnerus, B. Hülsemannus & Vinarienses docent, ex collatione v. 11. cum Matth. 26, 60. nec non vers. 19. cum Johan. 15, 25.

Nec obstare, quæ v. 13. 14. dicuntur, siquidem allegorica sit loquendi ratio, neque vel de Davide ipso secun- dum literam de sacci induitione accipienda: notat- que solum summam & tenerrimam etiam cum ho- stibus & invidis compassionem. Marc. 9, 19. Qui- bus favere videtur Psalmi hujus vers. 18. collatus cum Psal. 22, 26. Psal. 40, 10.

## 35:3
Vers. 3. DRAW OUT THE SPEAR, AND STOP THE WAY) It can be translated, the spear and the battle-axe, as we warned above 18, 47.

Jerome, Augustine, Bugenhagen, Brentius, and Gesner deservedly explain this Psalm concerning Christ, with Christ himself leading the way, who in verse 19 interpreted it of himself, John 15, 25. In it is held a notable description of the passion of Christ, and of the frauds, calumnies, conspiracies, and violent persecutions which the Pharisees, the Priests, and the Jewish people plotted against him. Concerning the false witnesses in v. 11, the History of the Passion is well known. Concerning the gesture of mockery in v. 21, the same things are held as in Ps. 22, 8; concerning the conspiracy of the malignant in v. 15, the same as in Ps. 22, 17; and the complaint and prayer in v. 17 is entirely similar to that in Ps. 22, 20, 21, 22. Similar here in v. 18 is the vow of public preaching of the name of the Lord, which is there in v. 23 and 26, which we know from Heb. 2, 12 to be Christ's. Nor does that most grave συμπάθεια concerning the destruction of enemies suit anyone more than Christ, which v. 13 and 14 exhibit. Finally, who else are they, other than the faithful of Christ, of whom it is said in v. 27, let them shout and be glad, who delight IN MY RIGHTEOUSNESS?
