For this is the unique joy of the faithful, that they delight in the righteousness of Christ, Rom. 14, 17; nor can we solidly rejoice or boast in any other, 1 Cor. 1, 29, 30, 31; Jer. 9, 23; Is. 45, 24; who also for this reason continually proclaim God, Let the Lord be magnified, who delights in the peace of his servant v. 27, i.e., which his servant has procured, Is. 52, 13; c. 53, 5, in whom I am well pleased (εὐδόκησα), Matt. 3, 17; Col. 1, 19, 20. By THE QUIET OF THE LAND, Brentius rightly understands the Apostles in v. 20, who were not only quiet and tranquil, and rejoiced in the true tranquility which is through faith, but also, as messengers of peace, offered true and eternal salvation and tranquility to the land, or to men on earth, by their Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 3. EFFVNDE FRAMEAM, ET CONCLVDE) Verti potest, frameam & sagarim, ut admonuimus supra 18, 47.

PSalmum hunc de Christo merito explicant Hie- ronym. Augustinus, Bugenhagius, Brentius, Gesnerus, præeunte ipso Christo, qui vers. 19. de se interpretatus est Joh. 15, 25. habeturque insignis in eo descriptio passionis Christi, & fraudum, calu- mniarum, conspirationum, & violentarum perse- quutionum, quas adversum ipsum moliti sunt Pha- risæi, & Sacerdotes, populusque Judaicus. De testi- bus falsis v. 11. nota est passionis Historia. De gestu illusionis v. 21. eadem habentur, quæ Ps. 22, 8. de con- spiratione malignantium v. 15. quæ Ps. 22, 17. ac si- milis prorsus est querela, ac precatio v. 17. quæ Ps. 22, 20. 21. 22. Simile hic v. 18. votum publica præ- dicationis nominis Domini, quod illic v. 23. & 26. quod Christi esse ex Ebr. 2, 12. novimus. Neque illa gravissima συμπάθεια de hostium exitio ulli magis, quam Christo convenit, quam v. 13. & 14. exhibent. Denique quinam alii sunt, quam fideles Christi, de quibus v. 27. jubilent & lætentur, qui delectantur IN JUSTITIA MEA? Nam unicum hoc fide- lium est gaudium, quod in Christi justitia delecten- tur Rom. 14, 17. nec in alio vel lætari solide possu- mus, vel gloriari 1. Cor. 1, 29. 30. 31. Jer. 9, 23. Es. 45, 24. qui etiam ideo Deum jugiter deprædicant, Magnificetur Dominus, qui delectatur pace servi sui v. 27. h. e. quam servus ipsius comparavit Es. 52, 13. c. 53, 5. in quo ipsi εὐδόκησα Matth. 3, 17. Col. 1, 19. 20. PER QVIETOS TERRÆ recte Brentius Aposto- los intelligit v. 20. qui non tantum quieti & trans- quilli erant, veraque tranquillitate, quæ per fidem est, gaudebant, sed Evangelio etiam suo ceu nun- tii pacis veram & æternam salutem ac tranquilli- tem terræ, vel hominibus in terra offerebant.

## 35:7
Vers. 7. FOR WITHOUT CAUSE THEY HAVE HID FOR ME THE DESTRUCTION OF THEIR NET) The Greeks do not translate this badly: δωρεὰν ἔκρυψάν μοι διαφθορὰν παγίδος ἀυτῶν, here δωρεὰν is undeservedly. We have already noted above that שחת is translated as διαφθορὰν. Moreover, it is a Hebraism, διαφθορὰ παγίδος, for a destructive net. The similitude is taken from bird-catching.

THEY HAVE WITHOUT CAUSE REPROACHED MY SOUL) He said without cause, for without reason. But what he translates as reproached, in the Hebrew is חפרו. Moreover, חפר is properly to dig, and metaphorically to lie in wait, which the Chaldean placed here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVONIAM, GRATIS ABSCONDERVNT MIHI INTERITVM LAQVEI SVI) Non male sic Græ- ci: δωρεὰν ἔκρυψάν μοι διαφθορὰν παγίδος ἀυτῶν, hic δωρεὰν est immerito. שחת διαφθορὰν verti jam supra notavi- mus. Est autem Hebraismus διαφθορὰ παγίδος pro laqueo exitiali. Ab aucupio sumta similitudo.

SVPERVACVE EXPROBRAVERVNT ANIMAM MEAM) Supervacue dixit, pro sine causa. Quod autem vertit exprobaverunt, in Hebræo est חפרו. Est autem חפר proprie fodere & per metaphoram insidiari, quod hic posuit Chaldæus.

## 35:15
Vers. 15. AND AGAINST ME THEY REJOICED) In the Hebrew: In my miseries they rejoiced. For so is צלע usually taken, which properly is to limp.

THE SCOURGES WERE GATHERED AGAINST ME) Better: Vile men were gathered against me, with the punctuation removed in the Hebrew after עלי. That נכים is well translated as vile appears from a similar place in Job 30, 8.

AND I KNEW NOT, THEY WERE DISSIPATED, AND NOT CUT) You may translate it best thus: those whom I did not know tore me apart incessantly. קרע is to treat with reproaches among the Arabs. For that word appears in that sense several times in the Arabic version of this book. דמם is placed for to cease, and is translated πά- υσω. But the Chaldean and certain Rabbis say: if they tore me, they did not draw blood, namely because the body was bloodless from emaciation.

We do not disapprove of these interpretations. Yet there is no need for the punctuation in the Hebrew to be removed, or the text to be amended; since in the Psalms the accents do not always have their force. Moreover, Christ can be said to have been ignorant of his calumniators, because he had not even conversed with some of them, who nevertheless did not fear to tear him with reproaches, as if they had known him well, out of a mere lust for slandering. Coccejus and others render it: I KNEW NOT. They do this unexpectedly. Blessed Brentius rightly says: And not only do my manifest enemies and the High Priests do this, but also the lame, that is, those limping on both sides, who now applaud my Gospel, now approve of Pharisaical doctrine. They gather frequently, I say, they gather against me, beyond all expectation, and having been affected by no injury from me, together with actors, buffoons, jesters, parasites, and even with the vilest of scoundrels, who would allow themselves to be hired for a crust of bread to betray their very country. These gnash at me with their teeth, and tear me with extreme insults: for they see that by their execrations they are doing a service most pleasing to the High Priests. Moreover, there is no need for you to cast your eyes around for long, where these things were fulfilled in Christ: look for me at the history of his passion, and you will see not only a servant giving a blow to Christ, before the tribunal of the High Priest, to gratify his Lord, but also a crowd of those scoundrels and buffoons, to whom Christ was handed over at night to be mocked and spat upon, who also, with his eyes veiled and his cheeks struck, shout out: Prophesy to us, Christ, who struck you? &c.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ET ADVERSVM ME LÆTATI SVNT) In Hebræis: In miseriis meis lætati sunt. Nam ita sumi solet צלע quod proprie est claudicare.

CONGREGATA SVNT SVPER ME FLAGELLA) Melius: Congregati sunt adversus me homines viles: demta in Hebræo interpunctione post עלי. Bene autem נכים verti viles apparet ex loco simili Job. 30, 8.

ET IGNORAVI, DISSIPATI SVNT, NEC COM- PVNCTI) Optime sic vertas: ii quos ignorabam proscide- runt me indefinenter. קרע est probris afficere apud Arabes. Apparet enim id verbum eo sensu aliquoties in versione Ara- bica libri hujus. דמם pro definere ponitur, & vertitur πά- υσω. At Chaldæus & Rabbini quidam: si proscinderent me, non educerent sanguinem, nimirum quod macie factum exan- gue esset corpus.

Non improbamus has interpretationes. Non tamen opus est, ut dematur in Ebræo interpunctio, vel emendetur textus; quum in Psalmis semper vim suam non habeant accentus. Ignorasse autem Christus calumniatores dici potest, quod cum nonnullis ne conversatus quidem fuerit, qui etiam veriti haud sunt probris eum proscindere, ac si notitiam ejus probe habuissent, ex mera calumniandi libidine. Coccejus & alii reddunt: NESCIEBAM. Faciunt hoc inopinato. Recte B. Brentius: Nec id solum faciunt manifesti mei hostes & Pontifices, verum etiam claudi, hoc est, claudicantes in utramque partem, qui nunc meo Evangelio applaudunt, nunc Pharisaicam doctri- nam probant. Conveniunt frequentes, frequentes, in- quam, conveniunt adversus me, praeter omnem ex- spectationem, & nulla prorsus a me injuria affecti, una cum histrionibus, scurris, joculatoribus, parasitis, adeoque cum vilissimis quibusque nebulonibus, qui vel frustulo panis se ad prodendam patriam ipsam con- duci paterentur. Hi fundunt in me dentibus suis, & proscindunt me extremis convitiis: vident enim se execrationibus suis officium Pontificibus gratissimum facere. Non est autem opus, ut diu circumferas oculos, ubinam haec in Christo impleta sint: intuere mihi hi- storiam passionis ejus, & videbis non solum servum dare alapam Christo, ante tribunal Pontificis, ut Do- mino suo gratificaretur, verum etiam catervam illo- rum nebulonum & scurrarum, quibus traditus est Christus noctu illudendus & conspuendus, qui etiam velatis oculis & percussis maxillis ejus, vociferantur: Vaticinare nobis Christe, quis te percusserit? &c.

## 35:18
Vers. 18. IN A HEAVY PEOPLE I WILL PRAISE THEE) In a numerous people. עצום is translated by πολὺς Gen. 18, 18. Num. 14, 12. Deut. 7, 1. Joel 2, 5. Zach. 8, 22. and the verb עצם by πληθύνεσθαι Jer. 15, 8. 30, 14. 16.

The blessed Gesner rightly expressed the sense of this verse: Although the Jews reject me: nevertheless, after my resurrection and ascension, I will gather from the nations a huge Church through the Apostles, which will celebrate me throughout the whole world.

Latin:

Vers. 18. IN POPVLO GRAVI LAVDABO TE) In populo numeroso. עצום per πολὺς vertitur Gen. 18, 18. Num. 14, 12. Deut. 7, 1. Joel 2, 5. Zach. 8, 22. & verbum עצם per πληθύνεσθαι Jer. 15, 8. 30, 14. 16.

Recte sensum hujus versus expressit B. Gesne- rus: Etsi Judaei me rejiciunt: nihilominus ex gentibus ingentem Ecclesiam post resurrectionem & ascensio- nem meam per Apostolos colligam, quae me per totum terrarum orbem celebrabit.

## 35:21
Vers. 21. THEY HAVE WIDENED THEIR MOUTH OVER ME) They mocked with gaping lips, as above 22, 8. Otherwise, to widen the mouth is also to speak boldly. 1 Sam. 2, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 21. DILATAVERUNT SVPER ME OS SVVM) Irriserunt hiantibus labiis, ut supra 22, 8. Alioqui os dilatare etiam est audacter loqui. 1. Sam. 2, 1.

## 35:25
Vers. 25. LET THEM NOT SAY IN THEIR HEARTS) That is, with the whole affection of the mind. Thus Is. 47, 8. above 14, 1. Apoc. 18, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 25. NON DICANT IN CORDIBVS SVIS) Id est, toto animi affectu. Sic Es. 47, 8. supra 14, 1. Apoc. 18, 7.

## 36:1 Argument
PSALM XXXVI.

Hypocrisy reproved: The goodness of God toward the upright is proclaimed.

Latin:

PSALMUS XXXVI.

Hypocrisis reprobata: Bonitas Dei erga probos depraedicatur.

## 36:1
vers. 2. THE UNJUST SAID THAT HE MIGHT SIN IN HIMSELF &c.

The interpretation of Mr. Dr. Geier pleases me, in the midst of my heart (that is, or thus I determine with myself in my heart) the saying of the transgression of the wicked (thus the transgressing wicked man is accustomed to say and act) that there is no fear of God before his eyes: where, however, I judge that the former should be repeated ἀπὸ κοινοῦ with the blessed Luther in this manner: I also thus determine with myself, that there is no reverence for God before the eyes of the wicked.

Latin:

vers. 2. DIXIT INJUSTUS UT DELINQUAT IN SEMETIPSO &c.

PLacet Dn. D. Geieri interpretatio, in medio cordis mei (hoc est, vel ita in corde meo statuo mecum) dictum praevaricationis impii (ita dicere, ac agere solere praevaricantem impium) nullum Dei timorem esse coram ipsius oculis: ubi tamen illud prius ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repetendum censeo cum B. Luth. h. m. etiam ita statuo mecum, quod nulla coram impii oculis sit Dei reverentia.

## 36:1 Addition
On Psalm 36, verse 7. YOU WILL SAVE MEN AND BEASTS.

Genebrardus, Jansenius, Bellarmine, Lorinus, and the Belgians explain the beasts as carnal men living in the manner of beasts, along with certain Greek and Latin Fathers; this also seems to have been the opinion of Origen, with Jerome and Rufinus not dissenting, which others have truly accepted in such a way as if they determined that brute animals were to be saved, or even that the demons themselves were to be received into grace. Vatablus and Estius interpret it more correctly concerning the beneficence of God toward the brutes themselves, not as saving, but as a matter of common providence, because the Holy Psalmist teaches that the goodness of God extends to all the ends of heaven and earth. Cf. Ps. 147, 9.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 36. V. 7. HOMINES ET JUMENTA SAL- VABIS.

Jumenta de hominibus carnalibus, more ju- mentorum viventibus exponunt cum Græcis & La- tinis quibusdam Patribus Genebrardus, Jansenius, Bellarm. Lorinus, Belgæ, quæ etiam videtur Origenis sententia fuisse, non abnuente Hieronymo cum Ruf- fino, quam vero alii eo accepere, ac si animalia bruta salvanda statuerint, imo ipsos dæmones in gratiam recipiendos. Rectius Vatablus & Estius de bene- ficentia Dei ergo bruta ipsa non salutifera sed pro- videntiæ communis, interpretantur, quia bonita- tem Dei ad omnes fines cæli & terræ se extendere docet Hiero-Psaltes. Conf. Psal. 147, 9.

## 36:2
Vers. 3. FOR HE ACTED DECEITFULLY IN HIS SIGHT.

In Hebrew: He flatters himself in his own eyes to himself, to deceive himself: to find his sin, so that he may the more licentiously indulge in lusts, ἀπατῶν τὴν καρδίαν αὐτοῦ Jac. 1, 26: and especially, to have hatred, so that he may pursue the innocent with hatred, and satisfy his mind in it.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QUONIAM DOLOSE EGIT IN CONSPECTU EJUS.

In Ebr. Blanditur sibi in oculis suis ad seipsum, ad decipiendum semetipsum: ad inveniendum pec- catum suum, ut tanto licentius ἀπατῶν τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶ Jac. 1, 26. concupiscentiis indulgeat: & impri- mis, ad odio habendum, ut odio infontes prosequa- tur, & animum suum in eo expleat.

## 36:3
Vers. 4. HE WOULD NOT UNDERSTAND THAT HE MIGHT DO GOOD) We learn from this also that the will can do something to the intellect, namely, that it may command the intellect, so that it may occupy and labor itself in this or that matter.

Simplicius is rendered: he ceased to understand, or to attend to doing good. Conf. the version of B. Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NOLVIT INTELLIGERE VT BENE AGE- RET) Discimus hinc etiam voluntatem aliquid posse in in- tellectum, nempe ut imperet intellectui, ut is in hac vel illa re se occupet ac laboret.

Simplicius redditur : defiit intelligere, vel attendere ad bene agendum. Conf. versio B. Lutheri.

## 36:8
Vers. 9. THEY SHALL BE INEBRIATED WITH THE ABUNDANCE OF THY HOUSE.

They shall be copiously irrigated, as the word רוה occurs concerning thirsty land irrigated by rain, Ps. 65, 11. By the metaphor of fatness, that is, of rich foods, the benefits of God which delight in the highest degree are expressed: but by the name of the House of God, the domestics of God are understood, for whom that fatness is prepared, Piscator; R. Kimchi thinks heaven is insinuated: both can be comprehended; for here we are irrigated inchoatively, there we are to be irrigated completively. Concerning the torrent, conf. Job 20, 17. Concerning the fountain of life, John 4, 14. Ap. 21, 6. 22, 1. IN THY LIGHT, which is the word illuminating us, Ps. 19, 9. and refreshing us with the splendor of grace, Ps. 27, 1. Num. 6, 21. we see, we know in such a way that we simultaneously enjoy, LIGHT here of grace, there of glory. Through the light, Raimund in Pug. Fid. f. 33 understands Christ, who is the object, sum, scope, sun, and chief gem of the divine word. John 5, 39. c. 8, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 9. INEBRIABUNTUR AB UBERTA- TE DOMUS TUÆ.

Irrigabuntur copiose, ut verbum רוה de terra siticulosa imbre irrigata Ps. 65, 11. occurrit. Metapho- ra pinguedinis, id est, ciborum pinguium, beneficia Dei summe oblectantia exprimuntur: Domus au- tem Dei nomine respici domesticos Dei, quibus illa pinguedo parata est, Piscator, cœlum insinuari R. Kimchi censet : utrumq; comprehendi potest; nam hic irrigamur inchoative, ibi irrigandi completive. De torrente conf. Job. 20, 17. De fonte vitæ Joh. 4, 14. Ap. 21, 6. 22, 1. IN LUMINE TUO, quod est verbum nos illuminans Ps. 19, 9. gratiæque splendore resi- ciens Ps. 27, 1. Num. 6, 21. videmus, cognoscimus ita, ut simul fruamur, LUMEN hic gratiæ, illic gloriæ. Per lucem Raimund. in pug. fid. f. 33. intelligit Chri- stum, qui objectum, summa, scopus, sol, & gemma præcipua est verbi divini. Joh. 5, 39. c. 8, 12.

## 36:9 Addition
Ver. 10. FOR WITH THEE IS THE FOUNTAIN OF LIFE AND IN THY LIGHT SHALL WE SEE LIGHT.

Blessed Hülsemann explains it concerning the light of glory necessary for seeing God, along with the Scholastics, concerning the Father who is seen in the Son, as Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine do, and concerning the light of grace, both that which is offered to all and that which is offered to the elect, from the comparison of ver. 11 and the parallels in John 5, 14; 7, 38; Jer. 2, 13; 17, 13, as also Ps. 4, 7; Ps. 27, 1, and especially because of the subject matter and the consolation opposed to the snares of enemies.

Latin:

Vers. 10. QUONIAM APUD TE EST FONS VITÆ ET IN LUMINE TUO VIDE- BIMUS LUMEN.

De lumine gloriæ necessario ad videndum Deum Bellarm. cum Scholasticis, de Patre, qui in Filio vi- detur, Ambros. Hieron. Augustin. de lumine gratiæ, tum quæ offertur omnibus, tum quæ electis è col- latione v. 11. & parallelis Job. 5, 14. c. 7, 38. Jer. 2, 13. c. 17, 13. ut & Psal. 4, 7. Ps. 27, 1. exponit B. Hülse- mannus, & imprimis propter subjectam materiam & consolationem insidiis hostium oppositam.

## 37:1 Argument
Ps. XXXVII.

Indignation suppressed on account of the flourishing lot of the wicked.

Latin:

Ps. XXXVII.

Indignatio ob florentem impiorum sortem repressa.

## 37:2
Vers. 2. FOR AS GRASS THEY SHALL QUICKLY WITHER) He used grass, because in the Greek he finds ὡσεὶ χόρτος: but it is the custom for Jews speaking Greek to say χόρτον for herb. And so Peter I. 1, 24. and James 1, 10. said ἄνθος χόρτε the greenness of the herb. And thus the same thing is said twice here in the Hebrew manner.

Latin:

Vers. 2. QVONIAM TANQVAM FOENVM VELO- CITER ARESCENT) Fœnum posuit, quia in Græco repe- rit ὡσεὶ χόρτος: sed mos est Judæis Græce loquentibus χόρτον dicere pro herba. Itaq; Petrus I. 1, 24. & Jacobus 1, 10. dixere ἄν- θος χόρτε herbæ virorem. Sicque bis hic idem dicitur more Hebræo.

## 37:3
Vers. 3. AND THOU SHALT BE FED IN HIS RICHES] In the Hebrew it is רְעֵה אֱמוּנָה : רעה אמונה can indeed signify either faith or truth. But that רעה has a difficult and therefore varied signification. Some translate: strengthen yourself with truth: others: feed yourself in faith, just as in Habakkuk the just man is said to live from his faith: others: feed: that is, teach the faith. But the Syrian reads בְּעֵה, and renders a very easy sense: inquire for truth.

He leans toward a different reading and a correction of the text: that רעה was placed for בעה. But what will be the end of different readings, what method of amending the Hebrew Codex, if either various readings or emendations are to be sought from versions? For here too the Greeks and Latins translated otherwise, where in the Hebrew there is now אמונה, whence the Pseudo-Critic Ludovicus Capellus, similar to Grotius, divines that the Greeks read הָמוֹן. But Buxtorff rightly warns, vind. p. 632, that the Greeks did not read the word אמונה otherwise, but accepted it for riches, because המון is said in the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syrian language from אמן, because men for the most part trust in riches, and אמונה signifies faith just as much as riches, whence a convenient sense: Thou shalt be fed in riches. Other interpretations also, whether the word is taken concerning truth or concerning faith, agree. Münster renders: thou shalt be fed in truth, i.e. when sinners have perished, and have been destitute of their happiness, the just man who hopes in the Lord shall truly be fed by divine benefits that remain perpetually, when the rich man shall perpetually hunger and thirst. Pagninus renders transitively: feed on truth, i.e., in word and works pursue truth and candor, as the Chaldean: apply yourself to truth, feed yourself on truth, as if it were your food by which you are sustained. And thus also the Syrian expressed the sense, not the word: inquire for truth. R. David Kimchi: Feed others, wherever you dwell, with instruction in the ways of the Lord. Jerome: be fed by faith. Others: nourish yourself in faith, or in truth. Thus almost B. Luther, who took this noun adverbially: feed in truth, i.e., acquire your living not fraudulently and by evil arts, but in truth and honestly. Nähre dich redlich. To which also R. Aben-Ezra seems to incline: Feed yourself in truth, not from rapine, which sense the preceding Rule favors: Stay in the land; whence it is commonly approved by ours, and retained.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET PASCERIS IN DIVITIIS EJVS] In Hebræo est רְעֵה אֱמוּנָה : רעה אמונה quidem aut fidem signi- ficare potest, aut veritatem. Illud autem רעה difficilem ideoque variam habet significationem. Alii vertunt roborare veritate: alii nutri te in fide, sicut Abacuco justus dicitur ex fide sua vivere: alii pasce: id est, doce fidem. At Syrus legit בְּעֵה, & sensum reddit facillimum: inquire veritatem.

Propendet in diversam lectionem, & correctio- nem textus: רעה positum esse pro בעה. Sed quis finis erit lectionum diversarum, quis modus emen- dandi Ebræum Codicem, si e versionibus vel lectio- nes variæ, vel emendationes petendæ? Nam & hic aliter Græci & Latini transtulere, ubi in Ebræo nunc est אמונה unde similis Grotio Pseudo-Criticus Ludovicus Capellus הָמוֹן Græcos legisse divi- nat. Sed recte monet Buxtorff. vind. p. 632. Græcos vocem אמונה non aliter legisse, sed pro divitiis ac- cepisse, quia המון sic in lingua Hebræa, Chaldæa & Syra ab אמן dicatur, quod homines plerumq; divitiis confidant, & אמונה æque fidem, sicut divitias significet, unde sensus commodus: Pasceris in divitiis. Aliæ etiam interpretationes, sive vox accipiatur de veritate, seu de fide, congruunt. Münsterus reddit pasceris in veritate, h. e. cum peccatores perierint, & destituti fuerint felicitate sua, justus qui sperat in Do- mino, vere pascetur beneficiis divinis perpetuo manen- tibus, quando dives perpetuo esuriet & sitiet. Pagni- nus transitive reddit; pasce veritatem, h. e. in verbo & operibus veritatem & candorem sectare, uti Chal- dæus: operam nava veritati, te pasce veritate, ac si esset cibus tuus, quo sustentaris. Atque ita etiam Syrus sensum, non verbum expressit, inquire veritatem. R. David Kimchi, Pasce alios, ubicunq; habitas in- structione in viis Domini. Hieronymus, pascere fide. Alii, nutri te in fide, vel in veritate. Sic fere B. Lu- therus, qui hoc nomen adverbialiter sumsit, pasce in veritate, h. e. victum acquire non fraudulenter, & malis artibus, sed in veritate & honeste. Nähre dich redlich. Quo etiam abire videtur R. Aben-Ezra: Pasce te in veritate, non ex rapina, cui sensui ante- cedens Regula favet: Bleibe im Lande; unde com- muniter a nostris probatur, ac retinetur.

## 37:20
Vers. 20. BUT THE ENEMIES OF THE LORD AS SOON AS THEY SHALL HAVE BEEN HONORED AND EXALTED, FAILING AS SMOKE THEY SHALL FAIL)

That which is here in the Hebrew כרים often signifies lambs, sometimes leading men. Thus 2 Kings 11, v. 4, כרי others translate ἑκατοντάρχες, others ἡγεμόνας. Ezech. 22, 22, כרים the Chaldean translates אמרורין with an Arabic word, unless you rewrite אמרנין, which signifies lambs: but the simplest exposition is: And the enemies of the Lord as the fat of lambs vanishes in smoke, so they shall vanish. A comparison from holocausts to the wicked is frequent: we said this at Mark 9, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 20. INIMICI VERO DOMINI MOX VT HO- NORIFICATI FVERINT ET EXALTATI, DEFICI- ENTES QVEMADMODVM FVMVS DEFICIENT)

Quod hic in Hebræo est כרים sæpe agnos significat, interdum viros principes. Sic 2. Reg. 11. v. 4. כרי alii vertunt ἑκατοντάρχες, alii ἡγεμόνας. Ezech. 22, 22. כרים Chaldæus vertit אמרורין voce Arabica, nisi rescribas אמרנין, quod agnos significat: sed simplicissima expositio est: Et inimici Domini sicut pinguedo agnorum euanescit in fumo, ita evanefcent. Comparatio ab holocaustis ad impios frequens: diximus ad Marcum 9, 4.

## 37:23
Vers. 23. FOR THOSE WHO BLESS HIM SHALL INHERIT THE LAND: BUT THOSE WHO CURSE HIM SHALL PERISH) Thus the LXX: οἱ ἐυλογῶντες & καταρώμενοι. But Symmachus: οἱ ἐυλογημένοι ὑπ' ἀυτὲ, & καταρώμενοι ὑπ' ἀυτᾶ, so that the construction in Hebrew is such as מכה אלהים in Isaiah 53, 5. and in the language of the Hellenists, διδακτοὶ τᾶ Θεᾶ, διδακτὸς πνεύματος ἁγίε, ἐυλογημένοι τᾶ πατρὸς, where ὑπὸ is tacitly understood. See what is said at John 6, 45.

Vers. 23. BY THE LORD HIS STEPS SHALL BE DIRECTED, AND HE SHALL WILL HIS WAY] It is a Hebraism, for which common speech would say: God directs his steps, whose way he approves.

Latin:

Vers. 23. QVIA BENEDICENTES EI HEREDITABVNT TERRAM: MALEDICENTES AVTEM EI DISPERIBVNT) Sic LXX. οἱ ἐυλογῶντες & καταρώμενοι. At Symmachus: οἱ ἐυλογημένοι ὑπ' ἀυτὲ, & καταρώμενοι ὑπ' ἀυτᾶ, ut sit in Hebræo constructio talis, qualis מכה אלהים Esaiæ 53, 5. & in lingua Hellenistarum, διδακτοὶ τᾶ Θεᾶ, διδακτὸς πνεύματος ἁγίε, ἐυλογημένοι τᾶ πατρὸς, ubi ὑπὸ tacitè intelligitur. Vide quæ ad Joh. 6, 45.

Vers. 23. APVD DOMINVM GRESSVS EJVS DIRIGENTVR, ET VIAM EJVS VOLET] Hebraismus est, pro quo communis locutio diceret: Deus gressus ejus dirigit, cujus viam approbat.

## 37:24
Vers. 24. WHEN HE SHALL FALL HE SHALL NOT BE CRUSHED) His evils are temporary, Is. 22, 17. Rom. 11, 11. where this sentiment is adapted to those of the Jews who sinned more by error than by malice.

Latin:

Vers. 24. CVM CECIDERIT NON COLLIDETVR) Mala ejus sunt temporaria, Es. 22, 17. Rom. 11, 11. ubi hæc sententia aptatur illis Judæorum, qui errore magis quam malitia peccabant.

## 37:25 Addition
To Ps. 37, v. 26.

I HAVE NOT SEEN THE RIGHTEOUS FORSAKEN, NOR HIS SEED BEGGING BREAD.

Most, because of experience, which seems to teach the contrary, understand it restrictively concerning that which commonly happens, such as Vatablus, Jansenius, the Vinarieans, and Cramer: so that the promise is not derogated by the exception of a few. But because the truth of divine promises does not suffer such exceptions, it is better with Blessed Hülsemann to take the sense of this verse conjunctively, not separately, so that it is understood that the seed of the righteous is not forsaken in their very begging by the forsaking of grace, if, that is, they insist upon the pious footsteps of their parents: 1. because there is nothing in the text that compels these two predicates to be taken separately. Because in the preceding verses, generally all such predicates are taken conjunctively, not divisively, as in v. 6, 10, 11, 18, 19, 23, 24, 28, 29, 36, 37. 2. Then because the scope of the whole Psalm is to console the pious concerning both happiness, both temporal and eternal, and that conjoined, as is evident from the conjunction in v. 3, 4, 5, 18, 19, 21. and 22, but especially, however, concerning eternal happiness and the perpetual assistance of grace, of which only v. 6, 11, 18, 23, 24 speak; and therefore nothing is derogated from this divine promise, even if very many martyrs were killed by famine. Thus there is no need for us to betake ourselves, with Campensis, Lorinus, Estius, and Muis, to a trope concerning the heavenly bread that will not be lacking.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 37. v. 26.

NON VIDI JUSTUM DERELICTUM, NEC SEMEN EJUS QUÆRENS PANEM.

Intelligunt plerique, ob experientiam, quæ contrarium videtur docere, restricte de eo, quod communiter sit, utpote Vatablus, Jansenius, Vinarienses, Cramerus: ita ut promissioni non derogetur per paucorum exceptionem. Sed quia promissionum divinarum veritas tales exceptiones non patitur, præstat cum B. Hülsemann. sensum hujus versus conjunctim, non seorsim sumere, ut intelligatur semen justorum in ipsa mendicitate non derelictum derelictione gratiæ, si sc. parentum piis insistat vestigiis: 1. quia nihil est in textu, quod cogat ut duo hæc prædicata seorsim sumantur. Quia in antecedentibus plerumque omnia talia prædicata conjunctim non divisim sumuntur, ut v. 6. 10. 11. 18. 19. 23. 24. 28. 29. 36. 37. 2. Deinde quia universi Psalmi scopus est consolari pios de utraque quidem felicitate & temporali & æterna eaque conjuncta, ut patet ex conjunctione v. 3. 4. 5. 18. 19. 21. & 22. sed præcipue tamen de felicitate æterna, & assistentia perpetua gratiæ, de qua tantum loquuntur v. 6. 11. 18. 23. 24. ideoque nihil derogatur huic promissioni divinæ, si maxime multi martyres fame necati sunt. Ita non opus est, ut cum Campensi, Lorino, Estio & Muisio ad tropum de non defuturo pane cœlesti nos recipiamus.

## 37:27
Vers. 27. FOR EVER AND EVER) In Hebrew: for an age, that is, for a long time. Thus also below.

Latin:

Vers. 27. IN SÆCVLVM SÆCVLI) In Hebræo: in sæculum, id est, diu. Sic & infra.

## 37:28
Vers. 28. THEY SHALL BE PRESERVED FOR EVER) In Hebrew it is here also for an age, that is, for a long time. But a new clause ought to begin here, and the ל be taken away. Thus also Ps. 89, 3. עולם is placed for לעולם. He who annotates such things does no injury to the Masorete. Unless what we have said is admitted, this ע will be missing in the Alphabet, which who would believe?

The words, for an age, are rightly expressed by the Vulgate, for ever. For to the just, not so much a temporal as an eternal happiness is promised. But while Grotius corrects the text here, both as to accents and as to letters, who will believe that injury is not being done, I will not say to the Masoretes, but to the Biblical Code itself, and to the divinely inspired word? Even if, therefore, this ע is missing in the Alphabet here, that letter could have been omitted for a certain reason, however much we may perhaps be unable to render that reason. If the text is to be corrected for that reason, others will correct it differently: and they will deny that the correction of Grotius is necessary or certain: just as it is evident that to some it once seemed that these words, in Hebrew, began a new clause עוילים וענשו which the LXX rendered ἄνομοι δὲ ἐκδιωχθήσονται, if indeed Symmachus also acknowledges that addition. But these words neither any Hebrew Codes acknowledge, nor were they read by the Chaldean, or by Jerome. Agellius, Bishop of Acerno, conjectures that the words לעולם נשמרו they shall be preserved for ever, had been read in certain books עוילים נשמרו the unjust shall be punished, and from these two joined interpretations it happened that the same Hebrew words, read a little differently, were placed twice in Greek and Latin: And the unjust shall be punished. Others will devise something else. What then, finally, will be held as certain? Genebrardus thinks that David omitted the letter ע by euphemism, because he did not wish to contaminate his order with the mention of עולים or עווילים of the unjust, of the wicked. Jerome, who translated according to the Hebrew truth, has it as it is now read in the Hebrew. There is no necessity for an Alphabetic series, as is evident from Ps. 25. For there, no clause begins with ב, none with כ, none with ק, even though otherwise the series of the Alphabet is observed. Just as, therefore, there one must not invent some corruption of the text, or omission of verses, on account of those omitted letters, so neither is it permitted to invent it here. The order of the alphabet, whether regarding all, or almost all, or most of the letters in such things, was arbitrary for the Holy Spirit, not necessary, and it is not for us to insert it into the text as we please, but to venerate and esteem it as it is found.

Latin:

Vers. 28. IN ÆTERNVM CONSERVABVNTVR) In Hebræo est & hic in sæculum, id est, diu. Incipere autem hic debet novum comma, & ל auferri. Sic & Ps. 89, 3. est עולם positum pro לעולם. Talia qui annotat, nullam Masoretis facit injuriam. Nisi quod diximus admittatur, deerit in Alphabeto hoc ע, quod quis crediderit?

Verba, in seculum, recte exprimuntur a vulgata, in æternum. Justis enim non tam temporalis quam æterna felicitas promissa est. Dum autem textum hic corrigit Grotius tum qua accentus, tum qua literas, quis credet, non fieri injuriam non dicam Masoretis, sed ipsi Codici Biblico, & verbo θεοπνεύστῳ? Etiamsi ergo in Alphabeto hic ע desideretur, potuit certa de causa illa litera prætermitti, utut causam istam reddere forte nequeamus. Si ideo textus corrigendus, alii aliter corrigent: ac correctionem Grotii necessariam vel certam esse negabunt: quemadmodum constat, nonnullis videri olim hæc verba, in Ebræo, novum comma incepisse עוילים וענשו quæ LXX. reddiderunt ἄνομοι δὲ ἐκδιωχθήσονται, siquidem etiam Symmachus eam additionem agnoscit. Quæ vero verba neque ulli Ebræi Codices agnoscunt, neque a Chaldæo, aut Hieronymo lecta sunt. Agellius Episcopus Acernensis conjeciat, verba לעולם נשמרו in æternum conservabuntur, ita lecta fuisse in libris quibusdam עוילים נשמרו injusti punientur, atque ex his duabus interpretationibus junctis factum esse, ut eadem verba Ebraica paulo aliter lecta bis in Græco & Latino ponerentur: Et injusti punientur. Alii aliud excogitabunt. Quid ergo denique certi habebitur? Genebrardus putat per ἐυφήμησιν Davidem literam ע prætermisisse, quod nollet contaminare suum ordinem, mentione עולים vel עווילים injustorum, pravorum. Hieronymus, qui juxta veritatem Ebraicam transtulit, ita habet, uti nunc in Ebræo legitur. Nulla est necessitas seriei Alphabeticæ, uti constat e Ps. 25. Ibi enim nullum comma incipit a ב, nullum a כ, nullum a ק, etsi de cætero series observetur Alphabeti. Sicut ergo ibi non est propter omissas istas literas fingenda textus quædam corruptela, vel versuum omissio, ita neque hic eam fingere licet. Ordo alphabeti sive quoad omnes, seu pene omnes aut plerasque literas in talibus Spiritui S. arbitrarius fuit, non necessarius, neque nostrum est eum in textum, prout placet, inferre, sed prout invenitur, venerari & æstimare.

## 37:35
Vers. 35.

AND RAISED UP ABOVE THE CEDARS OF LEBANON) The Greeks read not as we do אזרח but ארוז, which does not depart as far as the fact that for רענן they read לבנן. Here again a double and different reading he invents without cause. For the Greeks did not explain the words precisely, but the sense. The Hebrew text is perfectly consistent with itself: I have seen the notable impious one, (thriving in opulence and prosperity, as the Hebrews explain) AND THE SUCCULENT ומתערה (which the Hebrews explain מתלולח as flourishing and growing in sap) כאזרח רענן like a leafy laurel. The Hebrews take אזרח for a tree that is always green and succulent, such as the laurel, box, cedar, and the like. Is it therefore right to pervert and change all the words in the Hebrew, because the Greeks explained them with other words while retaining the sense? Jerome rendered it, AND THE STRONGEST LIKE A NATIVE FLOURISHING. Therefore, the Hebrew Codex did not have Cedars of Lebanon then: but as it has now. Nor did the Hebrew interpreters R. Kimchi read or explain it otherwise, LIKE A GREEN TREE: a native is famous in his own country, from which his family arises (not so a stranger); thus a tree is known by its humidity and beauty, and surrounded by all. R. Aben-Ezra: Like a green tree growing in its own soil, or like a tree with many branches, that is, leaves, to which is opposed זר a stranger. R. Salomo, like a native reflourishing.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

ET ELEVATVM SVPRA CEDROS LIBANI) Legerunt Græci non ut nos אזרח sed ארוז, quod tam longe non abit, quam quod pro רענן legerunt לבנן. Geminam hic iterum & diversam lectionem fingit sine causa. Non enim verba præcise, sed sen- fum exposuere Græci. Ebræus textus optime sibi constat: vidi impium insignem, (proficientem in opu- lentia, & prosperitate, ut exponunt Ebræi) ET SUC- CULENTUM ומתערה (quod Ebræi exponunt מתלולח per virescentem, & in succo augefcentem) כאזרח רענן in morem lauri frondosæ. Ebræi אזרח accipiunt pro arbore semper viridi & succulenta, qua- lis est laurus, buxus, cedrus & similes. Num ideo omnia verba in Ebræo pervertere, & immutare fas est, quod sensu retento aliis verbis exposuerint Græci? Hieronymus reddidit,ET FORTISSIMUM SICUT INDIGENAM VIRENTEM. Non ergo tum habuit Ebræus Codex Cedros Libani: sed uti nunc habet. Neque aliter legerunt aut exposuerunt Ebræi Interpp. R. Kimchi, SICUT ARBOR VI- RIDIS: indigena sua patria celebris est, ex qua fami- lia oritur (non sic extraneus) sic arbor humiditate & pulchritudine sua nota est, & ab omnibus circumda- ta. R. Aben-Ezra: Sicut arbor viridis crescens in pro- prio Sole, vel sicut arbor cum multis ramis, id est, so- liis, cui opponitur זר extraneus. R. Salomo, sicut nativus reflorefcens.

## 37:36
Verse 36.

AND I PASSED BY) The Greeks, from whom this is taken, read ואעבר, whom the Syriac and Arabic follow as they almost always do. The sense here is better because of what follows.

The matter comes to the same thing. For when ויעבר is read, and he shall pass by, it is not necessary that the IMPIOUS one be understood, of whom it was before: but indefinitely, and someone passed by, and behold he was not, i.e., that impious one. No one of those passing by saw him anymore. Thus what follows agrees perfectly. I myself sought him, and he was not found. If, however, it is also referred to the impious one, the text will rightly hold, And the impious one passed by, and he was not. He is gone; thus the latter explains the former, what kind of passing it is: I sought him, and he was not found.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ET TRANSIVI) Græci, unde hoc sumptum est, lege- runt,ואעבר quos sequuntur ut ferme semper Syrus & Arabs. Sensus hic melior est ob sequentia.

Res eodem recidit. Nam cum legitur ויעבר & transibit, non est necessum, ut IMPIUS intelliga- tur, de quo antea: sed indefinite & transivit quis, & ecce non erat sc. impius ille. Nemo e transeuntibus ipsum videbat amplius.Sic optime conveniunt quæ sequuntur. Ego ipse eum quæsivi, & non est inventus. Si tamen ad impium etiam referatur, recte textus habebit, Et transivit impius, & non erat. Ist vergan- gen; sic posterius explicat prius, qualis sit transitus: Quæsivieum, & non est inventus.

## 37:38
Verse 38. BUT THE UNJUST SHALL PERISH TOGETHER) יחדו rather signifies utterly, as in Greek writers ἅπαξ ἅπαξ. The same Hebrew word has this sense above 4,9. 19, 10. below 49. v. 10. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 38. INJVSTI AVTEM DEPERIBVNT SIMVL) יחדו potius significat penitus, ut in Græcis scriptoribus ἅπα- ξάπαξ. Habet hunc sensum vox eadem Hebræa supra 4,9. 19, 10. infra 49. v. 10. & alibi.

## 38:1 Argument
PSALM XXXVIII. The great burden and evil of sin.

IN REMEMBRANCE OF THE SABBATH) That about the Sabbath is not in the Hebrew, but in the Greek. Nor indeed does this song pertain to the Sabbath, but to the perpetual inculcation in David of the memory of both his sin and the pardon granted.

Latin:

PSALMUS XXXVIII. Grande peccati onus & malum.

IN REMEMORATIONEM DE SABBATO) Illud de Sabbato in Hebræo non est, sed in Græco. Nec sane ad Sab- batum hoc carmen pertinet, sed ad inculcandam perpetuo Davidi & peccati sui & indultæ veniæ memoriam.

## 38:10
Verse 11. MY HEART IS TROUBLED) ἐταράχθη. Properly, it wanders away from me, as merchants are accustomed to do. See what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 11. COR MEVM CCNTVRBATVM EST) ἐταράχθη. Proprie, a me evagatur, ut mercatores facere so- lent. Vide quod sequitur.

## 38:11
Verse 12. MY FRIENDS AND NEIGHBORS HAVE DRAWN NEAR AGAINST ME) In the Hebrew: they stood afar off from my plague. Thus מנגד is taken 2 Sam. 18, 13. 2 Kings 2, 7. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 12. AMICI MEI ET PROXIMI ADVERSVM ME APPROPINQVAVERVNT) In Hebræo: eminus à plaga mea constiterunt. Sic sumitur מנגד 2. Sam. 18, 13. 2. Reg. 2, 7. & alibi.

## 38:17
Verse 18. FOR I AM PREPARED FOR SCOURGES) Ὅτι ἐγὼ εἰς μάστιγας ἕτοιμος, LXX, whom the Syriac and Arabic follow in their own way. צלע which is here, is noted above 35,15 to be put for miseries, where certain versions have ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ μου. Aquila there, ἐν σκασμῷ μου. Symmachus σκάζοντός μου. The same Symmachus here, εἰς τὸ σκάζειν.

It is well that Grotius now favors the Hebrew reading, to which he is otherwise accustomed to be less fair. For his associate Ludovicus Capellus also invents here that the LXX read something else, namely לפגע for a plague, for which now לצלע limping is read. But he saw that Symmachus agrees with the Hebrew, and that צלע is put for misery: whence the Greeks rendered it scourges, expressing the sense. Therefore he did not want to follow Capellus here.

Latin:

Vers. 18. QVONIAM EGO IN FLAGELLA PARA- TVS SVM) Ὅτι ἐγὼ εἰς μάστιγας ἕτοιμος, LXX. quos suo more sequuntur Syrus & Arabs. צלע quod hic est, pro mi- seriis poni notatum supra 35,15. ubi quædam versiones habent ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ μs. Aquila ibi, ἐν σκασμῷ με. Symmachus σκά- ζοντός με. Idem Symmachus hic, εἰς τὸ σκάζειν.

BEne, quod juvat nunc Grotius Ebræam lectio- nem, cui alias minus æquus esse solet. Socius enim ejus Ludovicus Capellus hic etiam aliud legisse LXX. fingit, nimirum לפגע plage, pro quo nunc le- gatur לצלע claudicatio. Sed vidit Symmachum con- venire Ebræo, ac צלע pro miseria poni: unde fla- gella reddiderunt Græci, sensum exprimentes. Ideo sequi Capellum hic noluit.

## 38:19
Vers. 20. BUT MY ENEMIES ARE ALIVE AND ARE STRENGTHENED OVER ME) The Syrian, for that which we have וידדו, seems to have read וירודו, so that the sense may be: My enemies, looking upon me, have swelled up. See a similar use of the verb דור in Micah 4:11.

He seems to think that the Greek, Latin, and others agree with the Hebrew text. Also Jerome, who rendered it: but my living enemies are strengthened. And because of a frivolous conjecture about the Syrian, who did not even institute his translation from the sources, he tries to detract from the sources of truth, וחס ושלום!

Latin:

Vers. 20. INIMICI AVTEM MEI VIVVNT ET CONFIRMATI SVNT SVPER ME) Syrus pro eo quod habemus וידדו videtur legisse וירודו ut sensus sit, Ini- mici mei ad me spectantes intumuerunt. Vide similem usum verbi דור Micheæ 4, 11.

Ebræo textui Græcum, Latinum, alios conso- nare videt. Hieronymum etiam, qui reddidit, inimi- ci autem mei viventes confortati sunt. Et ob frivo- lam de Syro, qui ne quidem e fontibus translatio- nem instituit, conjecturam fontibus veritatis de- rogare conatur, וחס ושלום!

## 39:1 Argument
Ps. XXXIX. Reproof of the tongue. Meditation on death.

TO THE END, FOR IDITHUN) To the leader of the singers, Idithun, whose mention is in 1 Chron. 16:42, 2 Chron. 5:12.

Latin:

Ps. XXXIX. Linguæ reprobatio. Mortis meditatio.

IN FINEM IPSI IDITHVN) Principi cantorum Idi- thuno, cujus mentio 1. Par. 16, 42. 2. Paral. 5, 12.

## 39:1
Vers. 2. I HAVE SET A GUARD TO MY MOUTH) A muzzle. Thus Symmachus well here.

WHILE THE SINNER STOOD BEFORE ME) Better: While sedition stood before me: namely, that which Absalom had stirred up. The verb רשע, as the Hebrews note, in its primitive meaning is to be restless. For לבגדי you have 'observed' also in Psalm 51:5.

Latin:

Vers. 2. POSVI ORI MEO CVSTODIAM) Capistrum. Ita hic bene Symmachus.

CVM CONSISTERET PECCATOR CORAM ME) Melius: Dum seditio obversabatur mihi: illa scilicet quam Absalomus suscitaverat. Verbum רשע ut notant Hebræi, primitiva significatione est inquietum esse. לבגדי pro ob- servatur habes & Pfal. 51, 5.

## 39:2
Vers. 3. I WAS SILENT FROM GOOD THINGS) I abstained from all joyful things. For the Hebrew words that signify to be silent are also taken in the sense of abstaining, ceasing, desisting: and thus this word is also translated by παρεώρω in Isaiah 57:11. We had a similar one above at 28:1.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SILVI A BONIS) Abstinui ab omnibus rebus lætis. Nam verba Hebræ quæ filere significant, sumuntur & in sensu abstinendi, cessandi, desinendi: itaque & per παρεώρω hoc verbum vertitur Ef. 57, 11. Simile habuimus supra 28, 1.

## 39:5
Vers. 6. BEHOLD THOU HAST MADE MY DAYS MEASURABLE) There was undoubtedly in the Greek παλαιστὰς instead of παλεσταιας, so small that they can be comprehended as if by a palm, which Symmachus translates otherwise, ὡς σπιθαμὰς. The Hebrew means the same. From this good reading flowed the corrupt παλαιὰς, which Ambrose, Apollinaris, the Roman Psalter, the Arabic, and the Ethiopic follow. Nor do Chrysostom and certain others take παλαιτὰς more correctly as 'full of struggle'.

Here it is permitted to observe how the Greek translation is corrupt, as Grotius admits. Which, although it has the ancients Ambrose, Apollinaris, and likewise the Roman, Arabic, and Ethiopic Psalters favoring it, he abandons. Such a corruption he also acknowledged above in Ps. 31:16, IN THY HANDS ARE MY LOTS. In the Greek it was καιροί με, which agrees with the Hebrew, as Apollinaris, the Arab, and the Ethiopian read. And in the old Roman Psalter, 'my times'. Certain scribes wrote κλῆροι με instead of καιροί με, and thence this version. But why does he not argue in other places as well that the Greek translation is so corrupt, as he does the sources of the Hebrew truth themselves? Why is he so greatly hostile to these? Doubtless, he wished to gratify the parasite of the Antichrist, the Jesuits and Papists, who defend the corruption of the Hebrew text for their own sake.

We also dealt with v. 5 and 6 in the Memor. Witteberg. justor. Conc. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ECCE MENSVRABILES POSVISTI DIES MEOS) Fuit haud dubie in Græco παλαιστὰς. pro παλεσται- ας, tam exiguos, ut palmo quasi comprehendi possint, quod Symmachus aliter vertit, ὡς σπιθαμὰς. Idem vult Hebræum. Ex hac bona lectione fluxit corrupta παλαιὰς, quam sequun- tur Ambrosius, Apollinaris, Psalterium Romanum Arabi- cum & Æthiopicum. Nec magis recte Chrysostomus, & alii quidam παλαιτὰς sumunt pro πλήρεις πάλης.

HIc observare licet, quomodo corrupta sit, fa- tente Grotio, Græca translatio. Quam etsi habeat faventes veteres Ambrosium, Apollina- rem, Psalteriam item Romanum, Arabicum, & Æ- thiopicum, deserit. Qualem corruptelam etiam agnovit supra Pf. 31, 16. IN MANIBUS TUIS SORTES MEÆ. In Græco fuit καιροί με, quod Hebræo convenit, quomodo legerunt Apollinaris, A- rabs, Æthiops. Et in Psalterio Romano vetere, tem- pora mea. Librarii quidam pro καιροί με, scripsere κλῆροι με, & inde hæc versio. Cur vero non in aliis etiam locis magis Græcam translationem tam cor- ruptam arguit, quam fontes ipsos Ebraicæ verita- tis? Cur his tantopere invisus est? Nimirum grati- ficari voluit Parasitus Antichristi Jesuitis & Papi- stis, corruptionem textus Ebraici in ejus gratiam propugnantibus.

De v. 5. & 6. egimus etiam in Memor. Witte- berg. justor. Conc. 26.

## 39:6
Vers. 7. NEVERTHELESS) אך you would translate better as 'certainly', as in Gen. 29:14 and elsewhere.

IN AN IMAGE, MAN PASSES BY) Other books have כצלם instead of בצלם. Man departs like the image of a dream. This interpretation is confirmed by the passage below at 73:20 and that of Sophocles in Ajax: 'For I see that we who live are nothing else but phantoms, or a light shadow.' The same meaning emerges, whichever way you read it, 'in an image' or 'like an image' man passes by: or as Münster explains, 'in an image', i.e., in a vain shadow. For he thinks the Hebrew צלם here is the same as צלמות, that is, the shadow of death. And what is the whole life of man other than a passing in an image, or in a shadowy and vanishing form, because life is frail and momentary, and more an image and shadow of life than true life.

Latin:

Vers. 7. VERVNTAMEN) אך melius vertas certe, ut Gen. 29. v. 14. & alibi.

IN IMAGINE, PERTRANSIT HOMO) Alii libri pro בצלם habent כצלם Abit homo velut imago somnii. Hanc interpretationem firmat locus infra 73, 20. & illud So- phoclis Ajace: Ὁρῶ γὰρ ἡμᾶς ὀὐὲν ὄντας ἄλλο, πλὴν Εἴδωλ᾽, ὅσοι περ ζῶμεν, ἢ κούφην σκιάν. Eadem sententia prodit, utrovis legas modo, in imagine vel instar imaginis pertransit homo:vel ut Münsterus exponit, in imagine, h. e. in umbra ina- ni. Putat enim Ebræum צלם hic idem esse, quod צלמות, id est, umbra mortis. Et quid vita tota ho- minis aliud est, quam transitus in imagine, vel for- ma umbratili & evanida, quia vita caduca est, & momentanea, magisque imago & umbra vitæ, quam vita vera.

## 39:11
Vers. 12. AND YOU HAVE MADE HIS SOUL WASTED AWAY LIKE A SPIDER (עש is understood as a moth by the Hebrews, and by this interpreter in Job 4:19 and 27:18. Therefore you will rightly translate: Thus you have consumed his life with wasting away just as a moth: supply, is accustomed to [consume] a garment. But the Syrian translates it as stubble.)

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET TABESCERE FECISTI SICVT ARA- NEAM ANIMAM EJVS( עש tinea intelligitur Hebræis, & huic interpreti Job 4, 19. & 27, 18. Recte ergo vertes: Ita vitam ejus tabe consumsisti quomodo tinea: supple, vestem so- let. At Syrus, ut stipulam vertit.

## 40:1 Argument
PSALM XL. Christ's obedience is our righteousness.

Latin:

PSALM. XL. Christi obedientia nostra justitia.

## 40:4
BLESSED IS THE MAN, WHOSE HOPE IS THE NAME OF THE LORD) From the Greek: ὧ ἐστὶτὸ ὄνομα κυρίου ἐλπὶς ἀυ- τᾶ. There was therefore for them perhaps a Schin with a tzere in the word שם, whereas the Hebrews have a soft Schin with a Camez, and explain it as 'he placed'.

Thus, indeed, not only is the point transposed in Schin, but another vowel is also substituted, so that שָׂם may be read in place of שָׂם. However, the Hebrew texts need no correction; Blessed is that man who has placed the Lord as his hope. Nor do the Greek or Latin versions differ regarding the sense and the matter itself: whose name is the Lord his hope. Jerome, in his own age, read it no differently than we read it. For he rendered it from the Hebrew: Blessed is the man who has placed the Lord as his confidence.

Latin:

BEATVS EST VIR, CVJVS EST NOMEN DOMI- NI SPES EJVS) Ex Græco: ὧ ἐστὶτὸ ὄνομα κυρίου ἐλπὶς ἀυ- τᾶ. Fuit ergo illis Schin forte cum tzere in voce שם, cum Ebræi Schin lene cum Camez habeant, & exponant posuit.

Ita vero non tantum in Schin punctum trans- ponitur, sed alia etiam vocalis substituitur, ut שָׂם loco שָׂם legatur. Ebræa autem correctionis nullius indigent; Beatus vir ille, qui posuit Dominum spem suam. Nec discrepant Græca, vel Latina, quoad sensum & rem ipsam: cujus est nomen Domi- ni spes ejus. Hieronymus sua ætate non aliter legit, quam prout nos legimus. Ex Ebræo enim reddi- dit, Beatus vir, qui posuit Dominum confidentiam suam.

## 40:6
Ver. 7.

BUT YOU HAVE PERFECTED EARS FOR ME) כָּרִיתָ properly signifies to dig, and sometimes to perfect. You have dug ears for me, that is, you hold me bound to you by perpetual right. An allusion to the custom mentioned in Deut. 15:16. It appears from this interpretation, which follows the LXX Elders, that in their version there was ὠτία, which many Scholia also show. Those who substituted σῶμα adapted the version to the passage of the divine Writer in Heb. 10:5. But that Writer, as well as others, often cites passages more according to the sense than according to the letter, unless one thinks that in certain copies there was פִגְרָא, which is body in Chaldean and Syriac.

As for the word כָּרִיתָ, both meanings can be retained: by digging you have perfected ears for me, and by perfecting you have dug. For even if it were alluding to the custom regarding servants in Exod. 21:6 and Deut. 15:6, yet because the discourse is about the Son of God, ears had to be perfected for him, or rather a body had to be adapted. Otherwise, he could neither have undergone servitude, nor could his ears have been pierced, nor could he himself have been bound to servitude. For this reason he assumed a human body and willed to be born a man, so that he might be subjected to the law for us (Gal. 4:4) and assume the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6). That ὠτία was once among the LXX cannot be gathered from the Latin Vulgate, since this was not taken from the LXX version, nor does it follow it, but rather some other Greek version, as we noted above at the beginning of the book of Psalms. However, it is likely that Paul cited this passage, as he was accustomed to do, according to the LXX elders: although we do not deny that those words σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι express the sense of the Hebrew text more than the letter. For they place the antecedent, the incarnation or the adaptation of a human body, in place of the consequent, the piercing of the ears, because the body was adapted to him for that end, that he might fulfill the service to God to which he was bound, which was prefigured by sacrifices. Therefore, God did not desire sacrifices in themselves, but the Son of God had to perform that which He desired and intended, and which He figured through sacrifices, for whose sake God adapted a body to him and pierced his ears. Unless one prefers to say that Paul concluded the whole body from an integral organic part. For when God perfected ears for the Son, He undoubtedly adapted the whole human body to him, even if special mention is made of the ears on account of obedience and service. Thus Rivetus, also bringing in Bellarmine to that opinion, says that the LXX changed a figurative expression into a literal one; for he who says, 'you have prepared ears for me,' signifies the whole by a part, which is not without cause signified by the ears rather than by another member, because the Holy Spirit wished to join the office of Christ, which he had to perform before God the Father, to the instrument of hearing, which is necessary for docility and ministerial obedience. He observes, however, that ears are said to be pierced for Christ not privatively, as if they were ever closed, but negatively, when the body was adapted to him by Him who planted the ears (Ps. 94:9). So that to pierce the ears is nothing other than to form them and make them so concave that they can receive sound. Therefore, in whatever way these are translated, whether 'you have adapted or prepared a body,' or 'you have pierced or perfected ears,' the matter comes to the same thing, that by the body or ears is understood synecdochically the whole nature assumed, so adapted to the Son

of God, that in it he came prepared to fulfill the will of God, for the salvation of the human race, through perfect obedience even to the death of the cross. These are the words of Rivetus. This synecdoche also pleases Genebrard, Franc. Riebera, Matth. Galen in his Epistle to the Hebrews, Cornelius a Lapide, and others. However, Rivetus does not approve here of the allusion to the Jewish custom of servants, about which he himself can be read in his commentary on the Decad of Psalms, p. 269. Let those things which we have said about this passage in Critico Sacr. p. 529 and Diatrib. 10, § 12 be compared. But Grotius acts as an inept conciliator when he takes the words of the Apostle in Heb. 10:5, σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, as: 'you have adapted me to the doorpost,' which was accustomed to be done according to the law of Deut. 15:17, so that they might agree with the Davidic words. For the Apostle does not say 'you have adapted to the doorpost,' but 'you have adapted a body to me.' Vain also is the suspicion that in place of אזנים, גויה was written in certain copies, which signifies body not to the Hebrews, but to the Chaldeans and Syrians. For what is the analogy of those letters? And from where will such a great change be proven in the highest consensus of codices—Hebrew, Chaldean, Latin Vulgate, and the Hieronymian translation, as well as the Hebrew interpreters R. Kimchi, R. Jarchi, R. Aben-Ezra, and also the Christian Doctors Eusebius, Cyril, and the Syriac version? The Chaldean Paraphrast rendered it: 'you have given me purged ears.' Jerome: 'you have dug ears for me.' Jerome renders the version of the LXX Interpreters: 'but you have perfected a body for me.' Therefore, Grotius did not examine him when he noted at Heb. 10:5 that he had placed in the version which he made from the LXX, 'but you have perfected ears for me': and from there he thought it clear that in the Greek books there was ὠτία. If it is permitted to invent, others will easily devise something else, and will contend with their fictions. Thus Johannes Morinus of Blois, a Papist, invents that formerly עצם was read. Jonas Schlichtingius, a Photinian, invents in his commentary on the Hebrews, p. 445, that גויה was written. Finally, it is worthy of observation that even the misographi themselves, and the enemies of the sources, most of the Pontificians, pronounce this passage in the Hebrew text to be free from corruption. But we refuted Morinus in the cited place. Nor did Capellus himself, who attacked the Hebrew Codices with the greatest zeal and more laboriously than the Pontificians themselves, wish to suspect a corruption here.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

AVRES AVTEM PERFECISTI MIHI) כָּרִיתָ per- fodere significat proprie, interdum & perficere. Perfodisti mihi aures, id est, me tibi perpetuo jure mancipatum tenes. Allusio ad morem, de quo Deut. 15, 16. Apparet ex hac in- terpretatione, quæ sequitur LXX. Senes, in eorum versione fuisse ὠτία, quod & Scholia multa ostendunt. Qui reposue- runt σῶμα; versionem aptarunt ad locum divini Scriptoris ad Hebr. 10, 5. At is Scriptor, ut & alii, sæpe loca citat ma- gis κατὰ διάνοιαν quam κατὰ λέξιν, nisi quis putet, in quibus- dam exemplaribus fuisse פִגְרָא; quod est corpus Chaldæ- is & Syris.

Quod ad vocem כָּרִיתָ retineri potest utra- que significatio, perfodiendo perfecisti mihi aures, & perficiendo perfodisti. Etsi enim ad morem de ser- vis Exod. 21, 6. Deut. 15, 6. alluderetur, tamen quia de Filio Dei sermo est, aures ei perficiendæ, imo cor- pus adaptandum erat. Alias neque servitium subi- re, neque aures ipsi perforari, vel ad mancipatum i- pse obstringi potuisset. Ideo enim corpus huma- num assumsit, nascique homo voluit, ut pro nobis legi subderetur, Gal. 4, 4. servique formam assume- ret Phil. 2, 6. Penes LXX. olim fuisse ὠτία e Lati- na vulgata colligi non potest, siquidem hæc tran- sumta non sit e LXX. versione, nec illam sequatur, sed aliam quandam versionem Græcam, ut supra sub initium libri Psalmorum monuimus. Paulum au- tem allegasse hunc locum, quemadmodum plerun- que consuevit, secundum LXX. senes, verisimile est: Etsi non diffiteamur, verba illa σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, magis διάνοιαν quam λέξιν textus Ebræi expri- mere. Ponunt enim antecedens, ἐνσωμάτωσιν, vel corporis humani adaptationem, loco consequentis, au- rium perfossionis, quia eo fine corpus ei adaptatum, ut servitio Dei mancipatus, id quod hostiis præfigu- ratum fuit, adimpleret. Ideo Deus sacrificia non voluit per se, sed id quod voluit atque intendit, quodque per sacrificia figuravit, præstare debuit Fi- lius Dei, cujus gratia corpus ipsi Deus adaptavit, au- resque perfodit. Nisi quis dicere malit, Paulum e parte integrali organica, totum corpus conclusisse. Quum enim Filio aures perfecit Deus, corpus totum humanum sine dubio ipsi adaptavit, etsi aurium pe- culiaris mentio fiat, ob obedientiam & servitium. Ita Rivetns, in eam sententiam etiam adducensBellarmi- num, LXX. ait, locutionem figuratam in propriam mu- tasse; qui enim dicit, aures parasti mihi, ex parte signi- ficat totum, quod non sine causa per aures potius, quam per aliud membrum significatur, quia voluit Spiritus Sanctus eadem opera ab instrumento auditus ad docili- tatem & obsequium ministratorium necessarii officium Christi, quod apud Deum Patrem præstare debuit, con- jungere. Observat autem aures dici perfossas Christo non privative, quasi clausæ unquam fuerint, sed ne- gative, quando corpus ei aptatum ab eo, qui aures plantavit Ps. 94, 9. Ut perfodere aures nihil aliud sit, quam eas formare & ita concavas reddere, ut so- num possint excipere. Quocunque igitur modo hæc transferantur, sive corpus aptasti, aut præpa- rasti, sive aures perfodisti, vel perfecisti, res eo- dem redit, ut per corpus, vel aures Synecdochice intelligatur tota natura assumta, ita aptata Filio

Dei, ut in ea paratus venerit ad implendum voluntatem Dei, pro humani generis salute, per obedientiam perfectam usque ad mortem crucis. Hæc Rivetus. Quæ Synecdoche placet etiam Genebrardo, Franc. Riebera, Matth. Galeno in Epist. ad Hebr. Cornelio a Lapide, aliisque. Non autem probat Rivetus hic allusionem ad Judaicum morem Servorum, de quo ipse legi poterit in comment. in Decad. Ps. p. 269. Conferantur quæ de hoc loco diximus Critico Sacr. p. 529. & Diatrib. 10. §. 12. Ineptum autem Conciliatorem agit Grotius, cum Ebr. 10, 5. verba Apostoli σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι ita accipit: aptasti me posti, quod fieri solitum secundum legem Deut. 15, 17. ut conveniant verbis Davidicis. Non enim Apostolus ait posti aptasti, sed corpus aptasti mihi. Vana etiam est suspicio loco אזנים in quibusdam exemplaribus scriptum fuisse גויה, quod non Ebræis, sed Chaldæis, & Syris corpus significat. Quæ enim istarum literarum analogia? Et unde tanta mutatio probabitur in summo Codicum consensu, Ebræorum, Chaldæorum, Latinorum vulgatorum, & Hieronymianæ translationis, nec non Interpretum Ebræorum R. Kimchi, R. Jarchi, R. Aben-Ezra, ut & Christianorum Dd. Eusebii, Cyrilli, ut & Syriacæ versionis. Chaldæus Paraphrastes reddidit, aures purgatas dedisti mihi. Hieronymus: aures fodisti mihi. Versionem autem LXX. Interpp. reddit Hieronymus corpus autem perfecisti mihi. Non ergo inspexit eum Grotius, cum ad Ebr. 10, 5. notaret, eum in versione, quam fecit ex LXX. posuisse, aures autem perfecisti mihi: atque inde liquere arbitraretur in Græcis libris fuisse ὠτία. Si fingere fas sit, facile alii aliud excogitabunt, & figmentis suis certabunt. Ita fingit Johannes Morinus Blesensis Papista olim lectum fuisse עצם. Jonas Schlichtingius Photinianus fingit, in comment. ad Ebræos p. 445. scriptum fuisse גויה. Denique observatione dignum est, quod ipsi etiam μισόγραφοι, & fontium hostes, Pontificii plerique, locum hunc in textu Ebræo immunem a corruptela pronuncient. Morinum autem loco cit. refutavimus. Nec Capellus ipse, qui summo studio, ac operosius, quam ipsimet Pontificii Ebræos Codices insectatus est, suspicari hic voluit corruptelam.

## 40:8
Ver. 9.

IN THE HEAD OF THE BOOK IT IS WRITTEN OF ME, THAT I SHOULD DO THY WILL) LXX. ἐν κεφαλίδι. Aquila & Symmachus more accurately ἐν ἰλήματι. It is the custom of the Hebrews to write their contracts on a rollable membrane, and to preserve them in the manner of a volume. Thence the similitude is taken, not from the book of the law, which they likewise bind into the form of a volume. He calls it a contract as it were written between himself and God, that he himself indeed might serve God, but God might protect him.

Of David, as it appears, Grotius explains it uniquely; yet in his Annotations on Hebrews 10:5, he applies it to Christ in a mystical sense. Our writer, he says, put σῶμα for ὠτία. He did this, however, to express the mystical sense more clearly; for in Christ the ear was not fastened to the doorpost, but the whole body was adapted to the cross as a testimony of obedience. These are merely arbitrary interpretations. For there is nothing here about an ear FASTENED TO A DOORPOST, nothing about a body ADAPTED TO A CROSS. Nor did God adapt the body to the cross as a testimony of obedience, so that he might serve thereafter, in the way that an ear was fastened to a doorpost for servants, so that they might remain servants: because on the cross the servitude was completed, not begun, nor did it need to be confirmed by a new testimony, or a new obligation. But above all Grotius is mistaken, while following the Jews, Kimchi, Aben-Ezra, and Solomon Jarchi, he takes the Psalm according to the letter concerning David; and not except as to the mystical sense, or Insofar as David bore the type of Christ, he thinks it pertains to Christ, which is also the opinion of Cornelius Jansen, Bishop of Ghent, and William Estius, Professor at Douai, in his Epistle to the Hebrews, as well as, among the Calvinists, David Pareus, and among the Neo-Photinians, Georg Enjed and Jonas Schlichting.

John Calvin, and following him, Augustine Marloratus, likewise maintain that the Prophet is here speaking of himself; indeed, they pronounce that it can be said in general of any of the elect, because it is written in the secret book of God only concerning them, that they might fulfill the will of God: where the Calvinists have read this secret, they neither teach, nor indeed can they teach: but it is written without doubt in the same book, and on the same page, where that horrible absolute decree is inscribed with a Rhadamanthine pen. Thus also Martin Bucer depraves the Prophetic words, that they were written concerning any of the Saints, but are applied to Christ, because what is written concerning any of the Saints pertains especially to Christ, and as Calvin says, where the community of the Church comes into the midst, it must necessarily descend to the head itself.

All those are vehemently mistaken. For the Psalm deals literally with Him who promises His coming here: Then I said, behold I come: who opposes His coming to sacrifices and burnt offerings, and intimates that they would cease at His coming; of whom it is written in the head of the book, in the volume of the sacred scriptures, and either in the beginning of that book, or in the principal chapters; who had to come according to Scripture, that He might fulfill the will of God, and most perfectly perform His law; that by performing the will of God He might fulfill the type of sacrifices, for which end God adapted a body to Him in an admirable way, for whom He perfected and pierced ears beyond all other men; who by the oblation of His body had to do the will of God, as it was prefigured by sacrifices, through whose obedience we are all uniquely sanctified; who was to announce the righteousness of God (Evangelical) in the GREAT Church, all of which are most manifest from the context of the Psalm and the allegation and application made by the Apostle in Hebrews 10. But these things cannot be said of David, but uniquely of the Messiah; therefore, the discourse here is not of David, but uniquely of the Messiah according to the letter. The scope of David is to set forth here the head of the primary τῶν θαυμασίων or wonders of God, and of His ineffable thoughts concerning us, which are ὑπὲρ νῶν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ κατάληψιν κτιςῆς Φύσεως: namely, the mystery of the divine will according to His good pleasure, Eph. 1:9, and not to relate the obedience and zeal for holiness of the elect or the faithful, and of himself. And it is clearer than it can be denied that the substance and body of those things, which consist in His coming and obedience, are here opposed to the figures of the sacrifices, of which it is written primarily in the volume of the Holy Scriptures. But neither is any other of the saints figured in the sacrifices, especially the expiatory ones, nor can David, nor any other elect, REJECTING the sacrifices instituted by God Himself, say: Behold I come. Nor is it written of David, nor of any faithful person in the volume of the book, that they fulfill that will of God, or perform exact satisfaction to the law of God. And why many words? The Apostolic commentary, Hebrews 10:5 ff., is written, as it is said, with the very rays of the Sun. For he teaches in the most explicit words that these things do not speak of David, the elect, or the Saints, but of Christ εἰσερχό- μενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον, entering or coming into this world; that a body was adapted not to David, or any of the elect, but to Christ, according to this prophecy, by whose oblation He might perfect the will of God: as it is altogether plain that we are sanctified not by the obedience of David or the elect, but by the righteousness of Christ alone, which the Apostle gathers from this fulfillment of the will of God. And Genebrardus, Archbishop of Aix, refutes the Popish interpreters in the same synagogue, as does Robert Bellarmine, Cardinal, in his commentary on Psalm 40, as well as Bartholomew Petri, successor to William Estius and interpolator of his commentaries. For all these accept this prayer as the voice of Christ Himself in the literal sense. The most learned Junius refutes his teacher Calvin in his Parallels. Sacr. lib. 3. on Hebrews 10, col. 1603. These things, he says, cannot properly be pronounced of David, that he denies God is delighted with sacrifice and offering, that he asserts his ear was pierced by God, that he confidently presents himself to the Lord, that he boasts that he looked to the law as to his end, that he promises he will do the will of God, and will perform all those things which could not be fulfilled by legal sacrifices, on account of their infirmity, and if there are any such things. Finally, even from the argument of the preceding verse, it is most evidently certain that these verses CANNOT be conveniently understood of David or any faithful person. Likewise, Johannes Piscator of Herborn refutes his master in his notes on Psalm 40, from the Apostolic allegation, and from the form and coherence of the prayer of the Psalm; add also Theodore Beza, who in his annotations on those words οὐκ ἠθέλησας, you did not will, Hebrews 10:5. This, indeed, he says, CANNOT apply to David, whatever subterfuges may be sought. For (as the most learned interpreter rightly observes) he had the command of sacrificing in common with the rest, and therefore he could not pass over what God had commanded him. By which words he refutes Calvin, if I am not mistaken, out of Calvin. But let Junius, who in the cited place infers thus, answer Pareus here in particular: But if those words do not pertain to David properly and simply (which he had previously proved), it is concluded that they pertained much less properly to David, so that they might be accommodated typically to Christ. But Pareus also refutes himself, when to the words brought up above, he adds: that the Messiah ALONE fulfilled the whole will of God, and abolished the sacrifices of the Law, whereas David often both sinned against the will of God, and offered legal sacrifices to God. Whence it is invincibly concluded that these words are to be understood of the MESSIAH ALONE, and not of David. For it can in no way be taught or admitted that David bore the type of Christ in those things which are said here concerning the Messiah: Whence Pareus, contradicting himself, confesses: David speaks there in the person of the Messiah, or introduces THE MESSIAH HIMSELF speaking.

Andreas Rivetus, however, when he acknowledged that some things did not at all fit David, yet did not wish to desert the footsteps of his teacher Calvin entirely, invented in his Psal. Prophet. page 252 that this speech should be ascribed to David, as the father of Christ according to the flesh, usurping by paternal right the words of his son. But this invention collapses by its own vanity: For no similar example can be brought forward from the Scriptures. And what will arise from that, if not a notable confusion? For thus David, as the Father of Christ, could testify that he himself was incarnate and had perfectly satisfied the divine law, and had been prefigured by expiatory sacrifices, and indeed that he himself had died and been crucified for the sins of men, and that he sanctifies us by his obedience, and whatever other things befit Christ the Son of David. What of the fact that Rivetus confesses on page 267 that these words were testified by the blessed Paul to have been uttered in the PERSON of Christ: who, since the sacrifices of the old law had no power to remit sins, himself put on a body, and that very thing, which he had assumed as a body, he offered to GOD the Father: thus to verse 10. 11. They announce righteousness in the great assembly &c. Rivetus page 277. it seems, he says, to look to that highest benefit of the redemption of the human race exhibited in Christ, which is more worthy of celebration than all others: and TO SPEAK IN THE NAME OF THE SON OF GOD about to come into the world, not only so that in the assumed body he might satisfy the Father through Sacrifice, but also so that he might announce the will and kindness of the same to the world, as the highest Prophet, and might impel others not only by his example, but also by his command and mandate to perform the same office. Add to these, what Rivetus has on page 252. It is certain that the Apostle in the Epist. to the Hebrews chap. 10. verses 7. 8. & 9. uses and applies to Christ words which it is a sin not only to say, but even to think, were violently twisted by him. But what would those be if not a violent twisting, if they spoke properly of David alone? We convince Schlichtingius of Bukoviz, a Socinian, and Grotius, who Judaizes with him, both from the sacred text and from the confession of Schlichtingius himself: If this discourse is to be claimed literally and in the proper sense for David, so that it is accommodated to Christ only typically and mystically, it follows that all those things which are contained in this discourse belong to David literally and in the proper sense, but to Christ only under a type and mystically. This reason for the consequence is invincible, because the discourse is brought forth with an equal thread and style, and because all the predicates in it cohere, and of whom one is predicated, of the same the others are also uttered: To whom one of them belongs according to the letter, to him the others ought to belong according to the letter. But it is certain that all things which are contained in this discourse belong primarily and according to the letter to Christ, as is evident most clearly both from the Apostolic explanation and as Schlichtingius himself is forced to acknowledge. For (1.) those words Sacrifice and offering you did not want, imply that Sacrifices do not please God AT ALL ANY LONGER, that God wants those things abrogated and antiquated, as Schlichtingius confesses, because the words of the Apostle, by which he interprets David, are by far the clearest verse 13. τότε εἴρηκεν, ἰδὲ ἥκω ποιῆσαι, ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ θέλη- μά σꙋ, ἀναιρεῖ τὸ πρῶτον, ἵνα τὸ δεύτερον στήσῃ. That indeed would have been entirely false concerning the time of David. (2.) Those words intimate that he who speaks here offers another sacrifice to God, different from the legal sacrifices, or offers himself, and thus thoroughly expiates the sins of the people, as Schlichtingius interprets. For the text is clear verse 10. in which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ, made once, which namely for that reason was adapted to him; Which again can in no way be understood of David. (3.) He who speaks here, among other things says thus: BEHOLD I COME, which words IN THE PROPER SENSE, as Schlichtingius says again, designate Christ's coming into the world, and appearance, so that he might execute the divine will. But for what purpose was David coming, when he said these words in the literal sense? But the Apostle teaches that they speak of Christ, who affirms that these were said by him as he was entering the world, or coming into the world. (4.) It COULD BE SAID PROPERLY by Christ, as Schlichtingius says, that it was written in the volume of the book specifically about him, as the one on whom the Holy Spirit everywhere and especially fixes his eyes. But how David could have said this properly of himself, Schlichtingius could not explain, however miserably he might twist himself here. Nor did Grotius explain it: and he did not even attempt to. (5.) Not only Eucharistic victims are commemorated here, which ALONE according to Schlichtingius pertained to David's institution, but also expiatory victims, or for sin, of which, if you look at David's purpose, no mention seems to have needed to be made here to Schlichtingius: Because namely he himself wanders from David's purpose: according to which it is certain, both from the context and from the Apostolic declaration, that they ought to have been commemorated entirely and especially. (6) Add that the Apostle Heb. 10, 10. commemorating the offering of the body of Christ, not obscurely looks to those things which he had brought from the Psalm, you adapted a body to me, as Schlichtingius confesses again: For the matter is clear. Therefore they cannot, except through remarkable violence, be drawn to David, whose body was not offered, much less does it make for our sanctification. (7) And since Christ had this discourse while entering the world, as the Apostle says, is it not the height of impudence, not to say anything harsher, to claim the same for David, and indeed according to the proper and literal sense? What of the fact that the Apostle could not have constrained the Hebrews with Prophetic words, if the same sounded properly and literally of David, even if it is finally established that the same belong to Christ in a mystical sense. Since a mystical sense of that kind would have been easily rejected by the Hebrews, and it seemed no less doubtful and obscure than the very thing being judged, which is treated here. Furthermore, they could consider it alien to the custom of Scripture that a sense so different be hidden under the same words; especially where the words and the purpose did not seem to fit either subject. Finally, since there is only one meaning for one statement, how could the same words be explained of Christ if a literal sense concerning David were admitted? Whoever desires the complete analysis and explanation of the Psalm, let him go primarily to Mr. Gesner and Tarnovius in the Passion Psalms, who explain it excellently concerning Christ.

What Grotius notes about the volume is new, nor does it rest on any probable reason; whence also it will be taught, that here regard is had to the contract entered into between God and David, and as it were written out? Furthermore, the name מגלת ספר, VOLUME OF THE BOOK, does not suit a contract: But it openly designates a book of Scripture, which comes by way of eminence under the name of the book. The name מגילה indeed occurs concerning an Epistle written in a cylinder for death, Zech. 5, 1. But when the word ספר is added, some entire volume is designated, because as the Hebrews observe, in ancient days books were not bound, but they used to roll them up. To which contributes that of Is. 34, 4. ונגלו כספר, and they shall be rolled up as a book. And so the Talmud also explains: The whole law entirely, that is, Holy Scripture, is called Megilla, as it is written: in the volume of the book it is written of me: which Joh. Henricus Hottingerus cites from the Talmud in thesauro Philolog. p. 101. Furthermore, there is no reason why we should here prefer the version of Aquila and Symmachus to the translation of the LXX Elders, which was approved by the Holy Spirit Himself, Heb. 10, 6. ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε: where Nicol. Fuller, l. 2. Miscell. c. 10, understands ספר כפול as βιβλίον διπλόμενον. And what is more manifest than that a book of Scripture is pointed out? Inasmuch as the discourse is about that book in which it was written down concerning the Messiah about to do the will of GOD, as it had been prefigured through the types of sacrifices: Whence Capillus observes, Spicileg. p. 122, since hardly any other sacred books had been written in David's time besides the Pentateuch of Moses, nor can any sacred book be called ספר βιβλίον more antonomastically than the book of the law, which even today is still called so by the Jews, and has always been called so, that in the volume of the law is to be sought the προσφοράν of the body of Christ, which is taught and hinted at clearly enough by the legal sacrifices, the shadows and figures of the true sacrifice. Alii

They take ἐν κεφαλίδι as if it were said ἐν μιᾷ or πρώτῃ κεφαλίδι, and they wish to refer to the Proto-Evangelium Gen. 3, 15. But because in the Hellenistic language κεφαλὶς is the same as מגלה Esdr. 6, 2. Ezech. 3, 9. and here, the volume or head of a book of Scripture is indicated, which treats especially of Christ, as of the primary Scope and argument.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

IN CAPITE LIBRI SCRIPTVM EST DE ME, VT FACEREM VOLVNTATEM TVAM) LXX. ἐν κεφαλίδι. Aquila & Symmachus magis accurate ἐν ἰλήματι. Mos est Ebræis contractus suos scribere in membrana volubili, & voluminis modo eos asservare. Inde sumta similitudo, non a libro legis, quem itidem in voluminis formam compingunt.
