Contractum velut perscriptum dicit inter se & Deum, ut ipse quidem Deo serviat, Deus autem ipsum tueatur.

De Davide, ut apparet, unice explicat Grotius; in Annot. tamen ad Ebr. 10, 5. sensu mystico ad Christum applicat. Scriptor noster, inquit, pro ὠτία posuit σῶμα. Fecit autem hoc, ut sensum mysticum magis exprimeret; non enim in Christo auricula posti, sed corpus totum cruci adaptatum est in obedientiæ testimonium. Quæ mere arbitraria interpretamenta. Nihil enim hic de auricula POSTI APTATA, nihil de corpore CRUCI APTATO. Nec aptavit Deus corpus cruci in obedientiæ testimonium, ut deinceps serviret, quemadmodum auricula posti aptata fuit servis, ut manerent servi: quia in cruce completa fuit servitus, non cœpit, neque novo testimonio confirmanda fuit, aut nova obligatione. Sed præprimis fallitur Grotius, dum Judæos, Kimchium, Aben-Ezra, & Salom. Jarchi sequutus, secundum literam Psalmum de Davide accipit; nec nisi quoad sensum mysticum, vel quatenus David typum gessit Christi, ad Christum pertinere putat, quæ etiam Cornelii Jansenii Episco- pi Gandavensis, & Guilb. Estii Duacens. Professoris in Epist. ad Ebræos, nec non e Calvinianis David Pa- rei, & Neophotinianis Georg. Enjed. & Jonæ Schlich- tingii est sententia.

Joh. Calvinus, & ex eo Augustinus Marloratus pariter volunt, Prophetam hic de sese differere, quin & in genere de quibusvis electis ea dici posse pronun- ciant, quod in arcano Dei libro non nisi de iisdem scri- ptum sit, ut Dei voluntatem compleant : quod arca- num ubi legerint Calviniani, nec docent, nec vero docere possunt : Scriptum autem procul dubio in eodem libro, folioque eodem, ubi horribile illud absolutum decretum Rhadmanteo stylo exaratum. Sic etiam depravat verba Prophetica Martinus Buce- rus, quod de quolibet Sanctorum ea scripta sint, ad Christum autem applicentur, quia quod de quolibet Sanctorum scriptum, præcipue Christo competat, & ut Calvinus ait, ubi in medium prodit Ecclesiæ communi- tas, ad caput ipsum descendere necessum est.

Falluntur omnes illi vehementer. De eo e- nim agit Psalmus secundum literam, qui adventum suum hic promittit : Tunc dixi, ecce venio : qui adventum suum opponit Sacrificiis & holocaustis, eaque in adventu suo desitura innuit ; De quo in capite libri scriptum est, in sacrarum literarum vo- lumine, & vel in initio libri istius, vel in præcipuis capitibus ; qui venire debuit juxta Scripturam, ut im- pleret voluntatem Dei, legemque ejus perfectissime præ- staret ; ut præstando voluntatem Dei sacrificiorum typum adimpleret, cui ea fini Deus corpus adaptavit admiranda ratione, cui aures præ aliis hominibus u- niversis perfecit, ac perfodit ; qui oblatione corporis sui voluntatem Dei, prout præfiguratum erat sacrificiis, facere debuit, per cujus obedientiam nos omnes uni- ce sanctificamur ; qui justitiam Dei (Evangelicam) in Ecclesia MAGNA annunciaturus erat, quæ omnia e contextu Psalmi & allegatione atque applicatione Apostoli Ebr. 10. facta longe manifestissima sunt. Hæc autem non de Davide, sed unice de Messia di- ci possunt ; Proinde non de Davide, sed de Messia sermo unice hic est secundum literam. Scopus Davidis est caput primarium hic sistere τῶν θαυ- μασίων seu mirabilium Dei, & cogitationum ejus de nobis ineffabilium, quæ ὑπὲρ νῶν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ κατάληψιν κτιςῆς Φύσεως : Mysterium sc. volunta- tis divinæ secundum beneplacitum ejus Eph. 1, 9. non autem referre electorum vel fidelium, & sui ipsius ob- sequium & sanctitatis studium. Et luculentius est, quam ut negari possit, figuris sacrificiorum hic op- poni substantiam & corpus eorum, quæ in adventu ejus & obedientia consistunt, de quo in volumine S. literarum præprimis scriptum est. At nec quis- quam alius sanctorum figuratus est in sacrificiis, præsertim expiatoriis, nec David, nec alius electus, REPROBATIS sacrificiis, a Deo ipso institutis, di- cere potest : Ecce venio. Nec de Davide, nec de ul- le fideli scriptum est in volumine libri, quod illam voluntatem Dei impleant, aut legi Dei exactam præstent satisfactionem. Et quid multis ? Ipsis, quod dicitur, Solis radiis scriptus est commenta- rius Apostolicus Ebr. 10. v. 5. seqq. Non enim Davidem, electos aut Sanctos, sed Christum εἰσερχό- μενον εἰς τὸν κόσμον ingredientem vel adventantem in hunc mundum, hæc de sese loqui ; non Davidi, vel electis quibusvis, sed Christo, secundum hoc vatici- nium adaptatum esse corpus, cujus oblatione volun- tatem Dei perficeret, verbis edocet longe diser- tissimis : uti planum omnino est, non Davidis aut electorum obedientia, sed unius Christi justitia nos sanctificari, quod ex hac voluntatis Dei adimple- tione colligit Apostolus. Et refellit Pontificios Interpp. in eadem Synagoga Genebrardus, Archi E- piscopus Aquens. ut & Robertus Bellarminus Cardina- lis in comment. ad Psal. 40. nec non Bartholomæus Petri Guilh. Estii successor ac commentariorum e- jusdem interpolator. Hi enim omnes Orationem hancce tanquam Christi ipsius vocem literali sensu accipiunt. Refellit Calvinum præceptorem do- ctissimus Junius Parall. Sacr. lib. 3. super Ebr. 10. col. 1603. Non possunt, inquit, ista proprie de Da- vide pronunciari, quod Deum sacrificio & munere delectari neget, quod aurem sibi a Deo perfossam asse- rat, quod seipsum sistat confidenter Domino, quod ad se respexisse legem, tanquam ad finem suum, glorietur, quod se facturum spondeat voluntatem Dei, & perfe- cturum ea omnia, quæ sacrificiis legalibus non poterant expleri, propter infirmitatem ipsorum, & si quæ sunt ejusmodi. Postremo vel ex præcedentis versus argu- mento evidentissime constat, NON POSSE hos versus commode de Davide aut ullo fideli intelligi. Pariter quoque Johannes Piscator Herbornensis refutat in notis ad Psalm. 40. Magistrum suum, ex allegatio- ne Apostolica, & e forma atque cohærentia ora- tionis Psalmi; Adde & Theodor. Bezam, qui in an- notatis ad verba illa οὐκ ἠθέλησας, noluisti, Ebr. 10, 5. Hoc vero, inquit, NON POTEST Davidi conveni- re, quæcunq́; subterfugia quærantur. Nam (ut recte prorsus observat doctissimus Interpres) habuit com- mune cum cæteris sacrificandi mandatum, itaque præ- terire, quod illi Deus mandarat, non potuit. Quibus verbis Calvinum, ni fallor, e Calvino refutat. Pareo vero peculiariter hic respondeat Junius, qui l. cit. sic infert : Quod si proprie & simpliciter verba illa ad Davidem minime pertinent (quod antea probarat) conficitur, multo minus ita proprie ad Davidem perti- nuisse, ut Christo typice accommodentur. Sed & Pa- reus semetipsum refellit, cum verbis superius ad- ductis, subjicit : quod Messias omnem voluntatem Dei SOLUS impleverit, & sacrificia Legis aboleverit, cum David sæpe & in voluntatem Dei deliquerit, & sacrifi- cia legalia Deo obtulerit. Unde invicte concludi- tur, de SOLO MESSIA, non autem de Davide ver- ba ista exaudienda esse. Nec enim in illis, quæ de Messia hic dicuntur, Davidem typum Christi ges- sisse ullatenus doceri aut admitti potest: Unde si- bi ipsi contradicens Pareus fatetur : loquitur ibi David in persona Messiæ, seu inducit IPSUM MES- SIAM loquentem.

Andreas Rivetus vero, quum agnoverit non- nulla haud quadrare in Davidem, nec tamen Præ- ceptoris Calvini vestigia penitus deserere voluerit, commentus est in Psal. Prophet. pag. 252. orationem hanc Davidi, ceu Patri Christi secundum carnem, filii verba paterno jure usurpanti adscribendam esse. Sed hoc commentum vanitate sua corruit: Nullum e- nim simile exemplum e Scripturis adferri potest. Et quid inde, nisi insignis orietur confusio ? Sic enim David, ceu Pater Christi, & incarnatum sese & legi divinæ perfecte satisfecisse, præfiguratum- que sacrificiis expiatoriis fuisse, testari posset, imo mortuum sese, ac crucifixum pro peccatis homi- num, & obedientia sua nos sanctificare, & quæ- cunque alia Christo Filio Davidis conveniunt. Quid quod fateatur Rivetus pag. 267. hæc verba B. Paulum testari in PERSONA Christi prolata fuisse : qui cum sacrificia veteris legis ad peccata re- mittenda nihil haberent virium, ipse corpus induit, & illud ipsum, quod assumserat corpus, DEO Patri ob- tulerit: ita ad vers. 10. 11. Annuntiant justitiam in cætu magno &c. Rivetus pag. 277. videtur, inquit, respicere summum illud beneficium redemtionis generis humani in Christo exhibitum, quod præ cæteris omni- bus celebratione dignissimum est: & LOQUI NO- MINE FILII DEI in mundum venturi, non solum ut in assumto corpore Patri per Sacrificium satisface- ret, sed etiam ut voluntatem & benignitatem ejusdem annuntiaret mundo, tanquam summus Propheta, a- liosque non solum exemplo suo, sed etiam jussu & man- dato ad idem officium præstandum impelleret. Adde his, quæ habet Rivetus pag. 252. Certum est Apo- stolum in Epist. ad Hebr. cap. 10. verba 7. 8. & 9. ver- suum usurpare & Christo applicare, quæ violenter ab ipso detorta fuisse, non solum dictu, sed etiam cogitatu nefas est. At quid illa nisi violenta detorsio es- sent, si proprie de uno Davide agerent? Schlichtin- gium a Bukoviz, Socinianum & Grotium, cum ipso Judaizantem cum e textu sacro, tum ex ipsius Schlichtingii confessione ita convincimus: Si ora- tio hæc literaliter & sensu proprio Davidi vindican- da, ita ut typice solum atque mystice ad Christum ac- commodetur, consequens est, omnia illa, quæ in hac oratione continentur, Davidi literaliter & sensu proprio competere, sub typo autem & mystice so- lum Christo. Ratio consequentiæ invicta hæc est, quod parili filo & stylo proferatur oratio, quodque omnia in ea prædicata cohæreant, & de quo præ- dicatur unum, de eodem efferantur quoque cæte- ra: Cui unum eorum secundum literam convenit, ei cætera secundum literam competere oporteat. Certum autem est, convenire omnia primo & secun- dum literam, Christo, quæ in hac oratione continen- tur, ut tum ex Apostolica explicatione constat evi- dentissime, tum agnoscere cogitur ipse Schlichtin- gius. Nam (1.) verba illa Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, id inferunt, Sacrificia Deo omnino non place- re AMPLIUS, Deum illa abrogata & antiquata velle, fatente Schlichtingio, quia verba Apostoli, quibus Davidem interpretatur, longe sunt clarissima vers. 13. τότε εἴρηκεν, ἰδὲ ἥκω ποιῆσαι, ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ θέλη- μά σꙋ, ἀναιρεῖ τὸ πρῶτον, ἵνα τὸ δεύτερον στήσῃ. Id vero utique falsum fuisset de tempore Davidis. (2.) Innuunt verba illa, eum, qui hic loquitur, aliud sacrificium offerre Deo, diversum a legalibus sacrificiis, vel seipsum offerre, & sic peccata populi penitus expia- re, interprete Schlichtingio. Textus enim lucu- lentus est vers. 10. in qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Christi, semel factam, quod scil. ideo ipsi aptatum fuit; Quæ iterum nullo mo- do de Davide intelligi possunt. (3.) Is qui hic lo- quitur, inter alia ita ait: ECCE VENIO, quæ ver- ba SENSU PROPRIO, dicente iterum Schlich- tingio, designant Christi in mundum adventum, & apparitionem, ut divinam voluntatem exeque- retur. Quorsum autem veniebat David, cum hæc verba sensu literali diceret? De Christo autem ea loqui Apostolus docet, qui hæc ab ipso mun- dum ingrediente, vel adveniente in mundum dicta affirmat. (4.) A Christo PROPRIE DICI PO- TUIT, dicente Schlichtingio, quod in volumine li- bri scriptum sit nominatim de ipso, utpote in quem ocu- los ubiq́; potissimum intendit Spiritus Sanctus. Quo- modo vero hoc David proprie de seipso dicere po- tuerit, explicare non potuit Schlichtingius, utut misere hic se torqueret. Neque id explicuit Gro- tius: ac ne tentavit quidem. (5.) Commemo- rantur hic non tantum victimæ Evcharisticæ, quæ SOLÆ secundum Schlichtingium pertinebant ad Davidis institutum, sed etiam victimæ expiatoriæ, seu pro peccato, quarum, si scopum Da- vidis spectes, nulla hic Schlichtingio videtur fieri debuisse mentio: Quia scil. aberrat ipse a Davidis scopo: juxta quem omnino ac potissimum eas com- memorari debuisse, tum e contextu, tum e decla- ratione Apostolica certum est. (6) Adde quod Apostolus Ebr. 10, 10. oblationem corporis Christi commemorans, haud obscure respiciat ad ea, quæ e Psalmo adduxerat, corpus adaptasti mihi, fatente iterum Schlichtingio: Res enim clara est. Non ergo possunt ea, nisi per insignem violentiam trahi ad Davidem, cujus corpus oblatum non fuit, multo minus ad sanctificationem nostram facit. (7) Et quum orationem istam habuerit Christus in mun- dum ingrediens, dicente Apostolo, annon summa impudentia est, ne quid gravius dicam, eandem vendicare Davidi, & quidem secundum proprium & literalem sensum? Quid, quod constringere non potuisset Ebræos Apostolus verbis Propheticis, si proprie eadem & literaliter de Davide sonarent, etsi tandem statuatur mystico sensu eadem Christo com- petere. Quandoquidem mysticus ejusmodi sen- sus ab Ebræis facile reprobatus fuisset, nec minus dubius atque obscurus videbatur, quam ipsum τὸ κρινόμενον, de quo hic agitur. Sensum præterea tam diversum sub iisdem verbis occultari, a consue- tudine Scripturæ alienum censere poterant; præ- sertim ubi verba scopumque utrique subjecto haud congruere videbant. Denique quum unius dicti non sit nisi una sententia, quomodo admisso literali de Davide sensu verba eadem de Christo explicari poterant? Integram Psalmi analysin & explicatio- nem, qui desiderat, adeat cumprimis Dn. Gesnerum & Tarnovium in Psalm. Passional. qui egregie illum de Christo explicant.

Quod de volumine notat Grotius, novum est, neque ulla probabili ratione nititur; unde etiam do- cebitur, quod hic ad contractum inter Deum & Davi- dem initum, ac velut perscriptum respectus habeatur? Adhæc non convenit nomen מגלת ספר VOLU- MEN LIBRI contractui: Sed aperte designat li- brum Scripturæ, qui κατ’ ἐξοχὴν libri nomine venit. Nomen quidem מגילה de Epistola cylin- dri in mortem scripta occurrit, Zach. 5, 1. Sed cum vox ספר additur, integrum aliquod volumen desi- gnatur, quia ut observant Hebræi, diebus antiquis li- bri non erant compacti, sed convolvebant eos. Quo fa- cit illud Es. 34, 4. ונגלו כספר, & convolventur ut li- ber. Atque ita explicat etiam Talmud; Tota omni- no lex, id est, Sacra Scriptura, vocatur Megilla, sicut scriptum est: in volumine libri scriptum est de me: quod e Talmude adducit Joh. Henricus Hottingerus in thesauro Philolog. p. 101. Porro non est, cur Aquilæ & Symmachi versionem hic præferamus LXX. Seniorum translationi, quæ ab ipso Spiritu S. probata est Ebr. 10, 6. ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε: ubi ספר כפול βιβλίον διπλόμενον intelligit Nicol. Fuller. l. 2. Miscell. c. 10. Et quid manifestius est, quam quod liber Scripturæ indigitetur? siquidem de eo libro sermo sit, in quo de Messia voluntatem DEI, prout per typos sacrificiorum præfiguratum erat, facturo perscriptum erat: Unde observat Ca- pillus, Spicileg. p. 122. quum vix alii libri sacri Da- vidis tempore præter Pentateuchum Mosi, scripti fuerint, neque ullus liber sacer ἀντονομασικω̃ς ma- gis ספר βιβλίον dicatur, quam liber legis, qui etiamnũ hodie a Judæis sic dicitur, semperque dictus est, in le- gis volumine quærendam esse corporis Christi προσ- φορὰν, quæ satis aperte doceatur, & innuatur sacri- ficiis legalibus, veri sacrificii umbris, ac figuris. Alii

ἐν κεφαλίδι accipiunt quasi dictum ἐν μιᾷ sive πρώ- τῃ κεφαλίδι, ac respici volunt Prot-Evangelium Gen. 3, 15. Sed quia lingua Hellenistica κεφαλὶς idem est, quod מגלה Esdr. 6, 2. Ezech. 3, 9. & hic, volumen capitatũ libri Scripturæ indicatur, quod præcipue de Christo tractat, tanquam de primario Scopo, atque argumento.

## 41:1 Argument
PSALM XLI.

The blessedness of one who receives the affliction and trampling of Christ with faith.

ver. 1.

Latin:

PSALMUS XLI.

Beatitudo Christi afflictionem & conculcatio- nem fide suscipientis.

vers. 1.

## 41:1
BLESSED IS HE WHO CONSIDERS THE POOR AND NEEDY.

Truly blessed is he who understands Christ, as He was attenuated and exhausted for our sake, and receives Him with true faith Is. 53, 11. Matth. 8, 20. 2 Cor. 8, 9. concerning whom in the last verse of the preceding Psalm he testifies to that blessedness of the faithful 1. deliverance from present evil v. 2. 2. preservation from future evil. 3. quickening. 4. success, prosperity, and blessing. 5. preservation from the greed of enemies. 6. sustenance in the bed of sickness, and the changing of the bed, v. 3. 4. Then indeed Christ is introduced in His poverty, or attenuation, or emptying, how He was afflicted as to His soul, whence He seeks the grace of God, be gracious to me, heal my soul, כי חטאתי לך B. Tarnov. in the passion Psalm rendered it, although I have sinned against thee, because He was made sin for us, 2 Cor. 5, 21. Coccejus, because I am held to thee for the punishment of sin: as that word concerning obligation and guilt occurs Gen. 43, 8. c. 44, 32. Num. 32, 23. how likewise He was afflicted by enemies: which are explained in v. 6 and following. B. Tarnovius makes the evils of affliction here both internal, such as are the imputation of the sins of the whole human race, and the struggle arising thence with eternal death itself v. 5. as well as external, brought upon Him both by outsiders and open enemies v. 6. as well as by clandestine and hidden hypocrites, the worst of all, from whom proceeded slanders v. 7. plots constructed against Him v. 8. most atrocious injuries inflicted upon Him v. 9. as well as by those of His own household, and one principal traitor Judas v. 10. who ate the bread of Christ, not only common, but also sacramental, and that peculiar morsel which pointed out the traitor himself John 13, 23. Matth. 26, 23. For in him this prophecy was fulfilled, and that properly, as John 13, 18 testifies. Finally, there is subjoined to the prayer of Christ a thanksgiving, both of Christ Himself, because He sustained Him in evils and placed Him at His right hand v. 12. 13. and the public and perpetual thanksgiving of all Christians v. 14. prescribed. Thus our B. Gesner also explains this Psalm, with Ambrose and Bugenhagius leading the way; Bellarmine notes that Jerome and Augustine also teach that the whole pertains to the passion of Christ, explaining likewise in this manner: Blessed is he who attentively considers the poor Christ, for he will find Him to be poor not by necessity, but by will, and poor by will, that He might enrich us by His poverty. So also Viccars from the Arabic makes the summary: A prophecy concerning the incarnation and concerning Judas, and from the Arabic MS. he considers the poor Christ, as also from the Syriac, and not least another author Sect. 8. Similarly Coccejus: Blessed is he who looks upon the humble Christ.

Latin:

BEATUS QUI INTELLIGIT SUPER E- GENUM ET PAUPEREM.

VEre beatus ille est, qui Christum uti nostri causa attenuatus & exhaustus fuit intelligit, veraque fide suscipit Es. 53, 11. Matth. 8, 20. 2. Cor. 8, 9. de quo in versu ult. Psalm. præced. Beatitudi- nem illam fidelium testatur 1. ex malo præsenti li- beratio v. 2. 2. a futuro præservatio. 3. vivificatio. 4. Successus prosperitas & benedictio. 5. a cupidi- tate hostium conservatio. 6. in sponda ægritudinis sustentatio, & lecti mutatio, v. 3. 4. Tum vero in- traducitur Christus in egestate, vel attenuatione aut exinanitione sua, quomodo afflictus fuerit, quoad animam, unde gratiam Dei expetit, gratio sus esto mi- hi, sana animam meam, כי חטאתי לך B. Tarnov. in Psalm. passional reddidit, quamvis peccaverim ti- bi, quia factus est pro nobis peccatum, 2. Cor. 5, 21. Coccejus, quia teneor tibi ad pœnam peccati: uti ver- bum illud de obligatione, & reatu occurrit Gen. 43, 8. c. 44, 32. Num. 32, 23. quomodo item ab inimicis afflictus fuerit: quæ v. 6. seqq. exponuntur. B. Tarnovius afflictionis mala hic facit tum interna, ceu sunt totius generis humani peccatorum imputatio, & hinc orta cum ipsa morte æterna colluctatio v. 5. tum externa illata cum ab exteris tam inimicis a- pertis v. 6. quam clandestinis, & opertis hypocritis pessimis, a quibus profectæ calumniæ v. 7. ipsi stru- ctæ insidiæ v. 8. ipsi afflictæ atrocissimæ injuriæ v. 9. tum domesticis, & præcipuo uno proditore Juda v. 10. qui comedit cibum Christi non tantum vulga- rem, sed & sacramentalem, & peculiarem illam buccel- lam, quæ ipsum proditorem demonstrabat Joh. 13, 23. Matth. 26, 23. Nam in eo impletum hoc vati- cinium idque proprie ut testatur Joh. 13, 18. Deniq; subjungitur precationi Christi gratiarum actio tum ipsiusmet Christi propria, quod eum in malis susce- perit, quodque ad dextram suam collocarit v. 12. 13. tum omnium Christianorum publica & perpetua v. 14. præscripta. Ita explicat etiam hunc Psalmum B. Gesnerus noster præcunte Ambrosio, & Bugenha- gio; totum ad Christi passionem pertinere Hierony- mum quoque & Augustinum docere monet Bellarm. exponens itidem h. m. Beatus, qui attente conside- rat Christum pauperem, inveniet enim esse paupe- rem non necessitate, sed voluntate, & pauperem voluntate, ut nos sua inopia locupletaret. Sic e- tiam Viccars. ex Arab. summam facit: Prophetia de incarnatione & de Juda, & ex Arab. MS. confi- derat pauperem Christum, ut & ex Syro, nec non a- lio autore Sect. 8. Similiter Coccejus: Beatus qui respicit humilem Christum.

## 41:6
HE WENT FORTH AND SPOKE) Namely in the crossroads, as the Latins say:

A story is spread everywhere at all the crossroads. and the Greeks: ἐπὶ τριόδοισιν ἀκούει. AGAINST ME ALL WHISPERED) In the Hebrew: it precedes: יחד together, namely gathered, in circles. Which word the Latin version attaches to the preceding words.

Latin:

EGREDIEBATVR FORAS ET LOQVEBATVR) Nempe in triviis, quomodo Latini dicunt:

Omnibus in triviis vulgatur fabula passim. & Græci : ἐπὶ τριόδοισιν ἀκούει. ADVERSVM ME SV SVRRABANT OMNES) In He- bræo : præcedit : יחד una, scilicet congregati, in circulis. Quam vocem Latina versio annectit verbis præcedentibus.

## 41:7
Ver. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

## 41:9
Ver. 10.

FOR EVEN THE MAN OF MY PEACE, IN WHOM I HOPED.

In the Hebrew it is, Even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted. Which word 'trusted' here is of effect, according to the interpreter Cocceius, not of affection. Tarnovius: to whom I entrusted the treasure of the oracles, and indeed even my goods and money, John 12:6. WHO ATE MY BREAD, in the Hebrew 'my bread', Cocceius: as often at other times, so at the last supper. B. Tarnovius: eating my food, both because what it was necessary for the others to take, he himself as a thief intercepted, John 12:6, and because he ate my bread at the supper, and indeed unworthily, and because he ate the morsel which I had dipped for him, by which I demonstrated him to be the traitor, John 13:26. He acknowledges, however, that because the traitor Judas is described generally in this way in Matthew 26:23, Mark 14:10, Ezra 22:21, even here one who was of the household and a table-companion, σύσσιτον καὶ ὁμοτράπεζον, is designated, and that the remaining explanations, which are the simplest, are subordinate to this one.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ETENIM HOMO PACIS MEÆ, IN QUO SPERAVI.

In Ebr. est, Etiam vir pacis meæ, in quo fidebam. Quod verbum fidebam hic effecti est, interprete Coccejo, non affectus. Tarnovius : cui thesaurum oraculorum concredebam, imo etiam mea bona & pecuniam Joh. 12, 6. QUI EDEBAT PANES MEOS, in Ebr. panem meum, Coccejus : cum sæpe alias, tum in ultima cœna. B. Tarnovius : come- dens cibum meum tum quia quod & reliquos cape- re oportebat, ipse ut fur intercipiebat, Joh. 12, 6. tum quia comedit panem meum in cœna imc me indigne, tum quia comedit buccellam, quam ipsi intinxeram, qua ipsum proditorem esse demonstra- bam Joh. 13, 26. Agnofcit tamen quia generatim ita describitur Matth. 26, 23. Marc. 14, 10. Esdr. 22, 21. proditor Judas, etiam hic ex domesticis ac con- victoribus unum σύσσιτον καὶ ὁμοτράπεζον desi- gnari, huic vero explicationi, quæ simplicissima, reliquas subordinatas esse.

## 41:10
Verse 11.

AND I WILL REPAY THEM.

From this it is evident that it is not David, who even forgave Shimei himself, but Christ, whose is the vengeance, Deut. 32:36, Rom. 12:19, who speaks these things, who repays enemies who are incapable of being corrected. Compare Psalm 69:23 ff., Psalm 109:6 ff.

Latin:

Versus 11.

ET RETRIBUAM EIS.

Hinc constat non Davidem, qui ipsi etiam Simei condonavit, sed Christum, cujus est vindicta Deut. 32, 36. Rom. 12, 19. hæc loqui, qui inimicis corripi nesciis retribuit. Conf. Psalm. 69, 23. seqq. Pfal. 109, 6. seqq.

## 41:11
Ver. 12.

BY THIS I HAVE KNOWN, THAT YOU HAVE DELIGHTED IN ME.

Tarnovius takes it in a twofold active sense: I make others know that you have delighted in me. Compare Matthew 3:17, Rom. 1:4.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

IN HOC COGNOVI, QUONIAM VO- LUISTI ME.

Dupliciter active accipit Tarnovius, cogno- scere alios facio, quod fueris me delectatus. Con- fer Matth. 3, 17. Rom. 1, 4.

## 41:13
Ver. 14.

BLESSED BE THE LORD &c.

The last psalms of each book have blessings of this kind: and especially they celebrate God for the benefits exhibited in Christ.

THE END OF THE FIRST BOOK OF PSALMS.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

BENEDICTUS DOMINUS &c.

Psalmi ultimi cujusque libri ejusmodi bene- dictiones habent : & imprimis Deum ob beneficia in Christo exhibita celebrant.

FINIS LIBRI PRIMI PSALMORUM.

## 42:1 Argument
BOOK TWO. PSALM 42. The stag thirsting for the waters of refreshment is recreated by the confidence of divine grace.

Verse of the same.

UNDERSTANDING TO THE SONS OF KORAH) In the Hebrew: To the chief musician, instructing the descendants of Korah: who had suitable melodies for cheering the soul,

Verse 1.

Latin:

LIBER SECUNDUS. PSALMUS XLII. Cervus sitiens lymphas refocillationis fiducia divina gratiæ recreatur.

Vers. eod.

INTELLECTVS FILIIS CORE) In Hebræo : Principi cantorum instruenti posteros Core: qui ad hilarandum ani- mum aptos modos habebant,

Vers. 1.

## 42:1
AS THE STAG DESIRES) In the Hebrew it is ערג, which is a word proper to stags. David seems to have renewed in this poem the memory of the evils which he had once endured while an exile, far from the city and the sacred rites, with Saul seeking him for his destruction.

The stag pants for the waters when it has been wounded by serpents, Oppian, Halieutica 2, and on account of the heat from having swallowed serpents, as Bochart teaches from Tertullian, Basil, Theophrastus, and others, T. 1. Hierozoicon, f. 884, and when it is wearied by the pursuit of dogs, it seeks security in the waters.

Latin:

QVEMADMODVM DESIDERAT CERVVS) In Hebræo est ערג, quæ vox propria cervorum. Videtur au- tem hoc carmine David sibi renovasse memoriam malorum; quæ olim pertulerat extorris, procul ab urbe & sacris, Saule eum quærente ad exitium.

CErvus anhelat ad aquas, cum a serpentibus vul- neratus est, Oppianus Halievt. 2. & ob æstum a deglutitis serpentibus, ut e Tertull. Basilio, Theophra- sto, aliisq; docet Bochard. T. 1. Hieroz. f. 884. & cum lassatus est a canum instantia in aquis securitatem quærit.

## 42:5
ver. 6. FOR I SHALL YET GIVE THANKS TO HIM: THE SALVATION OF MY COUNTENANCE.

In Hebrew, I will celebrate him (for) the manifold salvation of his face. Christ can be understood as the face of the Lord, Exod. 32, 14.

Latin:

vers. 6. QUONIAM ADHUC CONFITEBOR ILLI: SALUTARE VULTUS MEI.

In Ebræo, celebrabo ipsum (ob) multijugam fa- lutem faciei ejus. Intelligi potest Christus facies Domini Exod. 32,14.

## 42:6
ver. 7. FROM THE LAND OF JORDAN, AND HERMON FROM THE LITTLE MOUNT.

On Mount Mizar. Junius wishes three borders of Judea to be described, but Coccejus refutes this. Why, he says, would he have mentioned Hermon, which leans toward the East, rather than Lebanon? And the land of Jordan rather than the trans-Jordanic or Perea? And why would he not say the ends of the earth to the south, as is customary, but a small mountain or Mitzar? Likewise, why would he omit the western region? Coccejus adds his own opinion: Nor is it an enumeration of the places in which David wandered. For he omitted the Philistines, among whom he spent a long time. Nevertheless, certain principal places of David's exile can be understood. For he also spent time in the land of Moab, which is the land at or beyond the Jordan. And because he married the daughter of Talmai, King of the Geshurites, it seems he also approached the Geshurites, who are the Hermonites. Now, he undoubtedly spent time in the mountains of Judah and Engedi by the Dead Sea. Therefore, the mention of the Philistines here can be neglected, so that this prayer might be accommodated to an earlier time. Here, however, I consider that the land of Jordan is placed to indicate seclusion from the sanctuary: the Hermonites, to indicate expulsion to the nations outside the limits of the republic: Mount Mitzar, or Engedi, to signify either exclusion from men, because he lived in solitude, in the rocks of the wild goats, 1 Sam. 24, 1, 2, 3, or the terrifying memory of the judgment of God upon the Sodomites, as if to say, I live there where Lot, saved from the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, was finally barely secure: for Coccejus understands Mount Mitzar as the mountain near Zoar in the desert of Engedi near the Dead Sea, because Lot had called that Mitzar, Gen. 19, 20, and mention of that mountain was made ibid. 30.

Latin:

vers. 7. DE TERRA JORDANIS, ET HERMO- NIM A MONTE MODICO.

In monte Mizar. Terminos tres Judææ de- scribi Junius vult, sed hoc refellit Coccejus. Qua- re, inquit, potius Hermonis, qui vergit ad Orien- tem, quam Libani meminisset? & terræ Jordanis po- tius, quam ultrɔ-Jordanicæ sive Pereæ: & quare non diceret fines terræ ad meridiem, ut solet, sed mon- tem exiguum vel Mitzar? Item, quare plagam occi- dentalem omitteret? Addit autem mentem suam Coccejus: Neque est enumeratio locorum, in qui- bus vagatus est David. Nam Philistæos omisit, in- ter quos diu egit. Possunt tamen præcipua quæ- dam loca exilii Davidici intelligi. Nam & in Moa- bitide egit, quæ est terra ad vel ultra Jordanem. Et quia Talmæi Regis Gefuritarum filiam duxit, vide- tur etiam Gesuræos accessisse, qui Hermonitæ sunt. Jam in montanis Judæ, & Engedi apud mare mor- tuum sine dubio egit. Potest igitur hic Philistæo- rum mentio neglecta esse, ut accommodata esset an- teriori tempori hæc oratio. Hic tamen considero, terram Jordanis poni ad indicandam seclusionem a sanctuario: Hermonitas, ad indicandam expulsio- nem ad gentes extra reipublicæ limites: Montem Mitzar, sive Engedi ad significandam vel exclusio- nem ab hominibus, quia in solitudine, in rupibus rupicaprarum habitabat, 1. Sam. 24,1, 2. 3. vel terri- ficam memoriam judicii Dei in Sodomitas, q. d. ibi vivo, ubi Lot servatus ab incendio Sodomæ & Go- morrhæ vix denique securus fuit: Montem enim Mitzar intelligit Coccejus montem prope Zoar in deserto Engedi prope mare mortuum, quia illam Mitzar appellaverat Loth, Gen. 19, 20. & ejus mon- tis mentio facta est ibid. 30.

## 42:7
Ver. 8. DEEP CALLETH UNTO DEEP AT THE VOICE OF THY WATER-SPOUTS)

A comparison taken from the great flood, when the cataracts or sluices of heaven were opened, Gen. 7, 11, and the deep of the sea called, or drew, as it were another deep from the clouds. He compares his own calamities to this flood.

Coccejus thus: one part of the Ocean cries to another, i.e., it emits a sound, as if to say, the Northern Ocean calls to the Southern, meaning, each Ocean roars in such a way that the sound reaches the other, that is: The world is in an uproar. I prefer, however, the explanation of Grotius, to which the sense of B. Hopfner also agrees, that it alludes to the flood, where the deeps below and the windows of heaven above were opened.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ABYSSSVS ABYSSVM INVOCAT IN VOCE CA- TARRACTARVM TVARVM)

Comparatio sumta a ma- gno diluvio, cum apertæ sunt cataractæ sive emissaria cœli, Gen. 7, 11. & abyssus maris invocavit, sive attraxit, velut al- teram abyssum e nubibus. Huic diluvio suas calamitates comparat.

Coccejus ita: una pars Oceani ad aliam clamat, h. e. sonitum edit, q. d. Oceanus Borealis Austra- lem inclamat, pro, uterque Oceanus ita fremit, ut so- nus usque ad alterum pertingat, id est: Mundus tu- multuatur. Præfero tamen Grotii explicationem, cui accedit & sensus B. Hopfneri, alludi ad diluvium, ubi infra abyssi supra fenestræ cœli apertæ.

## 43:1 Argument
PSALM XLIII. God the deliverer of the troubled soul.

Ver. 1.

FROM A NATION NOT HOLY) He indicates the retinue of Saul. FROM A MAN UNJUST AND DECEITFUL) Saul. AND UNTO THY TABERNACLES) The tent and the Ark.

That the retinue of Saul cannot be understood is clear from ver. 3, where David asks to be led to the holy mountain, which in the time of Saul was not yet a place of divine worship. Others, therefore, more correctly understand it of the army of Absalom. But the interpretations of R. are foreign.

Salomon of Edom, Simon Muys of the Babylonians, as also Cocceius: who says that David perhaps could have said this concerning the ministers of Saul, but the nation nevertheless denotes something greater. Christ [is] best concerning the Jewish nation. Who also through the man of deceit later understands the Anti-Christ. Nor yet is Cocceius consistent with himself: For at verse 5 he annotates thus: The LXX translate περίλυπος εἶ. These Psalms can be explained concerning David; also concerning the Babylonian captivity. If, however, you look at the matter as a figure, and consider the emphasis of the words, and the distinction and order of the temptations, you will find primarily indeed that continuous and ἐκτενὲς desire of Israel to see the living God and the manifestation of the glory of GOD promised in Ps. 42, 23. then a complaint concerning the defection of many, and the mockery of his hope, v. 4. 5. 6. then a complaint concerning the as it were oblivion of God, and that indeed after the manifest grace shown amidst the reproaches and tribulation of enemies v. 7-12. finally a prayer, by which he seeks judgment from the defectors and the Pseudo-Prophet: with which is joined a complaint as if concerning the rejection of himself: and a petition for the sending of the light and truth of God, which may lead him to the mount of God, and his tabernacles, i.e., that through them the Church may be gathered again. Ps. 43. These are the words of Cocceius.

Latin:

PSALMUS XLIII. Deus liberator animæ turbatæ solatium.

Vers. 1.

DE GENTE NON SANCTA) Comitatum Saulis in- dicat. AB HOMINE INIQVO ET DOLOSO) Saule. ET IN TABERNACVLA TVA) Tentorium & Arcam.

NOn posse comitatum Saulis intelligi, patet e vers. 3. ubi David petit deduci in montem san- ctum, qui tempore Saulis nondum fuit cultus divi- ni locus. Rectius ergo alii de exercitu Absol. intel- ligunt. Alienæ autem sunt interpretationes R.

Salom. de Edom, Sim. Muys de Babyloniis, ut & Coc- ceji: qui David, inquit, forte de ministris Saulis hoc potuit dicere, sed gens tamen majus aliquid notat. Chri- stus optime de gente Judæa. Qui etiam per virum doli postea Anti-Christum intelligit. Neque tamen sibi constat Coccejus: Nam ad v. 5. ita annotat: LXX. vertunt περίλυπος εἶ. De Davide hi Psalmi ex- poni possunt; etiam de captivitate Babylonica. Si autem pro figura rem spectes, & emphasin verbo- rum, & distinctionem, ordinemque tentationum consideres, invenies imprimis quidem Israelis illud continuum & ἐκτενὲς desiderium videndi Deum vi- vum & manifestationem gloriæ DEI promissam Ps. 42, 23. deinde querimoniam de defectione multo- rum, & irrisione spei suæ, v. 4. 5. 6. tum querimo- niam de Dei quasi oblivione, & quidem post exhi- bitam gratiam luculentam inter opprobria & tribu- lationem hostium v. 7-12. denique orationem, qua petit judicium a defectoribus & Pseudo-Propheta: cum qua conjungitur querimonia tanquam super rejectione sui: & petitio mittendæ lucis, & veritatis Dei, quæ ipsum ducant ad montem Dei, & taberna- cula ejus, h. e. ut per ea recolligatur Ecclesia. Ps. 43. Hæc Coccejus.

## 43:3
Verse 3.

SEND OUT THY LIGHT, AND THY TRUTH.

St. Augustine understands Christ by the light and truth: What stands in the way of our understanding Christ by the light, since even R. Salomon interprets concerning the Messiah from Ps. 132, 17: and Christ has frequently professed himself to be the light, especially in John 8, 12. but by the truth the Holy Spirit, since it is the work of the mission of Christ, and likewise of the Holy Spirit, that we may be led to God John 14, 6. and there is no doubt that David greatly desired the mission of the Son of God, and also of the Holy Spirit, promised for the fullness of time. For he does not wish to be led only to the holy mount, to the tabernacles, and to the altar of God: but to God himself.

Latin:

Versus 3.

EMITTE LUCEM TUAM, ET VERITA- TEM TUAM.

S. Augustinus per lucem & veritatem Christum intelligit: Quid obstat, quo minus per lucem Chri- stum intelligamus, quum etiam R. Salomo de Messia e Ps. 132, 17. interpretetur: & Christus se lucem esse sæpius professus sit, imprimis Joh. 8, 12. per verita- tem autem Spiritum Sanctum, quandoquidem Chri- sti missione, pariter & Spiritus Sancti opus sit, ut ad Deum deducamur Joh. 14, 6. & dubium nullum sit missionem Filii Dei, nec non Spiritus Sancti pleni- tudini temporum promissam Davidem summopere desiderasse. Non enim tantum ad montem san- ctum, ad tabernacula, & ad altare Dei deduci vult: sed ad ipsummet Deum.

## 43:4
Ver. 4.

UNTO GOD, WHO GIVETH JOY TO MY YOUTH.

In the Hebrew it is, unto God the joy of my exultation, that is, of the greatest joy. Campensis renders it, unto God the author of joy ineffable to me. Rashly therefore did the Vulgate translate it with ὁ youth, even though the Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic also have it so.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

AD DEUM, QUI LÆTIFICAT JUVEN- TUTEM MEAM.

In Ebræo est, ad Deum gaudium exultationis meæ, hoc est, gaudii latissimi. Campensis reddit, ad Deum autorem inenarrabilis mihi lætitiæ. Temere ergo Vulg. cum ὁ juventutem exposuit, etsi etiam ita habeat Syr. Arabs, Æth.

## 44:1 Argument
PSALM XLIV. The sighs of the afflicted faithful and especially of the Martyrs.

Latin:

PSALMUS XLIV. Suspiria fidelium afflictorum & imprimis Martyrum.

## 44:19
v. 20. AND THOU HAST TURNED ASIDE OUR PATHS FROM THY WAY.

In the Hebrew it is held otherwise, which Bellarmine himself notes: St. Jerome most clearly translates from the Hebrew: 'And our paths have not turned aside from thy way.' The particle of negation is to be repeated from the former member, as in Ps. 9:19, Ezek. 11:11.

Latin:

vers. 20. ET DECLINASTI SEMITAS NOSTRAS A VIA TUA.

In Ebr. aliter habetur, quod notat Bellarm. ipse : S. Hieronymus clarissime vertit ex Hebræo : Et non declinaverunt semitæ nostræ a via tua. Repe- tenda est partic. negandi e priori membro, ut Psal. 9, 19. Ezech. 11, 11.

## 44:20
v. 21. BECAUSE THOU HAST HUMBLED US IN THE PLACE OF AFFLICTION.

Thus the Vulgate with the Septuagint. Jerome, however, from the Hebrew, [translates] 'into the place of dragons,' where such poisonous men dwell, so that they can be considered mere dragons. So R. Kimchi, Vatablus, and B. Luther in the margin, 'poisonous tyrants'; others [translate] 'into desert places,' where dragons are accustomed to dwell, Jer. 9:10, ch. 10:12. If you ask why God permits the innocent to be afflicted? I answer: That before God no one is entirely innocent; nor indeed are the saints punished, but only tested, and that He does this so that they may not cling to temporal goods, nor love the stable instead of the house, exile instead of the fatherland.

Latin:

vers. 21. QUONIAM HUMILIASTI NOS IN LO- CO AFFLICTIONIS.

Sic Vulg. cum τοῖς ὁ. Hieronym. vero ex Ebr. in locum Draconum, ubi tales degunt venenati ho- mines, ut mere Dracones haberi possint. Ita R. Kimchi, Vatabl. & B. Luth. in marg. gifftige Tyran- nen; alii in loca deserta, ubi dracones habitare solent Jer. 9, 10. cap. 10, 12. Si quæras, cur Deus innocentes affligi permittat? Resp. Apud Deum neminem esse prorsus innocentem; neque vero puniri sanctos, sed probari tantum, idque agere, ut non adhæreant bo- nis temporalibus, neque ament stabulum pro do- mo, exilium pro patria.

## 44:21
v. 22. WE ARE COUNTED AS SHEEP OF SLAUGHTER)

We are slaughtered as victims.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ÆSTIMATI SVMVS SICVT OVES OCCISIONIS)

Trucidamur ut victimæ.

## 44:22
Ver. 23.

THOU HAST SOLD THY PEOPLE WITHOUT PRICE AND THERE WAS NO MULTITUDE IN THEIR EXCHANGES) In the Hebrew: Thou hast sold thy people for nothing, and hast made no profit from their price. Thou hast so despised thy people, that without any profit to thyself thou didst deliver them into servitude, now to the Moabites, now to the Canaanites, now to the Philistines, which are histories in the book of Judges. Masters are accustomed to sell cheaply those whom they value at nothing, and not so much for the hope of profit as to be freed from useless slaves. Diodorus on this passage: πέπρακας ἡμᾶς τοῖς ἔθνεσι τῶ μηδενός. For this he says without price, as useless slaves and worth nothing. That which is here in the LXX ἐν τοῖς ἀλάγμασιν αὐτῶν, signifies in their price. For ἄλαγμα according to the idiom of the Scriptures is called a price, says Jerome on Amos 5. Some codices corruptly had, ἐν ἀλαλάγμασι, which error flowed into the Roman and Ethiopic Psalter, and into Augustine, who translates it with jubilations.

Junius also thought that the histories of the Judges were being looked to: others referred them to the time of the Babylonian captivity: Theodoret and Cyril to the persecutions under Antiochus, to which Calvin subscribes: but Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine judge that these pertain to the martyrdoms of Christians under the ten persecutions: Cocceius draws them to the tyranny of the Anti-Christ: the Hebrews distort them to their own, as they call it, modern captivity, which, however, they endure not for the glory of the divine name, but for the rejection of the Messiah and most stubborn impenitence. Blessed Luther and Vitus Theodor most excellently teach that the calamities of the faithful are generally represented here, but that primarily the persecutions under the New Testament are designated, by which method the interpretations of the Latin and Greek Fathers will easily be able to be reconciled. It is easily clear that these cannot be referred so conveniently to the sales of the people at the time of the Judges, or even to the Babylonian captivity: because it is not a matter of past events, such as those which had happened under the judges, and those calamities which the faithful endure, not because of their own iniquities and transgressions, but because of the glory of the divine name and their constant profession, are designated, v. 19 seqq. and are explained as the persecutions of Christians by the Apostle as interpreter, Rom. 8:36. The argument, however, is sought from the ancient works of God, which the Fathers have already celebrated v. 2 and seqq., whom He planted after the nations were expelled, a kingdom having arisen in Israel. What is held in v. 4, 'thy right hand, and thy arm, and the light of thy countenance' (He provided salvation for them), we understand concerning the Son of God, who is also the right hand of the Lord, Ps. 118:16, and the arm of the Lord, Is. 53:1, and the light of the countenance of the Lord, Heb. 1:3, and He provided salvation for the people, Josh. 5:14.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

VENDIDISTI POPVLVM TVVM SINE PRETIO ET NON FVIT MVLTITVDO IN COMMVTATIO- NIBVS EORVM) In Hebræo: Vendidisti populum tuum pro nihilo, neque lucrum fecisti ex pretio eorum. Adeo con- temsisti populum tuum, ut sine ullo lucro tuo eos in servitu- tem traderes modo Moabitis, modo Cananæis, modo Philisti- nis, quæ historiæ sunt in libro Judicum. Solent Domini, quos nullius faciunt servos, vili vendere, neque tam spe lu- cri, quam ut liberentur ab inutilibus mancipiis. Diodorus ad hunc locum: πέπρακας ἡμᾶς τοῖς ἔθνεσι τῶ μηδενός. Τοῦ- το γὰρ λέγει ἄνευ τιμῆς, ὡς ἀχρήστες δούλυς καὶ οὐδενὸς ἀξίυς. Quod hîc est in LXX. ἐν τοῖς ἀλάγμασιν αὐτῶν, significat in pretio eorum. Nam ἄλαγμα juxta idioma Scripturarum pretium dicitur, ait Hieronymus ad 5. Amosi. Corrupte quidam codices habuere, ἐν ἀλαλάγμασι, quod vi- tium in Psalterium Romanum & Æthiopicum fluxit, & in Augustinum, qui vertit jubilationibus.

Historias Judicum respici etiam Junius censuit: ad tempus vero captivitatis Babylonica retulere alii: Theodoretus & Cyrillus ad persequutiones sub Antio- cho, quibus subscribit Calvinus : at Ambrosius, Hiero- nymus, Augustinus hæc ad martyria Christianorum sub decem persequutionibus pertinere judicant : Coccejus ad Anti-Christi tyrannidem trahit : Ebræi ad suam, quam vocant, modernam captivitatem, quam vero non pro gloria divini nominis, sed pro repro- batione Messiæ & impoenitentia pertinacissima su- stinent, detorquent. Optime B. Lutherus & Vitus Theodor. generaliter hic calamitates fidelium exhi- beri, sed imprimis tamen persequutiones sub Novo Testam. designari docent, quo pacto facile Latino- rum & Græcorum Patrum interpretationes concilia- ri poterunt. Ad venditiones populi tempore Ju- dicum, vel etiam ad captivitatem Babylonicam non adeo commode referri hæc posse facile liquet : quia non de præteritis, qualia erant, quæ sub judicibus ac- ciderant, agitur, & calamitates illæ, quas non ob ini- quitates & prævaricationes suas, sed ob nominis di- vini gloriam & constantem professionem fideles susti- nent, designantur, v. 19. seqq. ac de Christianorum persequutionibus explicantur interprete Apostolo Rom. 8, 36. Argumentum vero petitur ab antiquis Dei operibus, quæ Patres jam celebrarunt v. 2. & seqq. quos expulsis gentibus plantavit regnum in Israel exortum. Quod v. 4. habetur dextra tua, & brachium tuum, & lux faciei tuæ (præstitit ipsis salu- tem) de Filio Dei intelligimus, qui & dextra Do- mini est Psal. 118, 16. & brachium Domini Ef. 53, 1. & lux faciei Domini Ebr. 1, 3. & salutem præstitit popu- lo, Jos. 5, 14.

## 45:1 Argument
PSALM XLV. An epithalamium of Christ.

FOR THE END, FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED) The LXX translate עַל־שׁשַׁנִּים as 'for those who shall be changed.' This word also signifies lilies, but the origin is from שׁשׁ, which signifies six: whence it seems to signify a hexachord, which has six strings, no less than a lily has six petals.

A SONG FOR THE BELOVED) In the Hebrew: A song of the beloved ones. Thus were called the virgins who surrounded the new bride: Just as he who was present with the new bridegroom is called 'the friend of the bridegroom,' John 3:29. This song, therefore, is sung to the melodies of the sons of Korah by the virgins, in honor of Solomon the new bridegroom, and the new bride, the daughter of the King of Egypt. For it was customary at weddings for songs to be sung both by virgins and by young men, even among the Greeks and Romans, as we learn from Catullus. Furthermore, the Chaldean Paraphrast also acknowledges that this song pertains mystically to the Messiah.

Grotius Judaizes vigorously here again, explaining the most excellent Prophetic Psalm concerning the Messiah according to the letter as concerning Solomon, and converting it into a worldly love song. He followed Calvin, and some of his disciples, as well as the Transylvanian Neophotinians in refut. lib. 2. Major. Enjedinus in Explic. locor. Vet. & Nov. Test. p. 70. 349. Socinus in animadv. ad Assert. Posn. pag. 81. Volckel. lib. 1. de ver. Relig. cap. 9. Crellius & Schlichting. in Epist. ad Ebr. 1, 9. For the argument which Grotius uses here is utterly worthless: It is called a song of the beloved. Therefore it was sung by virgins, surrounding a new bride, in honor of Solomon the new bridegroom, and the new bride, the daughter of the King of Egypt. For neither is the antecedent certain, nor the consequence firm. It is called in Hebrew שיר ידידות, which the Hebrews render, a song of loves, or of sweetnesses. And Aquila [renders it] ᾆσμα προσφιλίας, since ידידות signifies sweetness and love in the abstract, no less than the beloved or the dear one. And since the loves of the bridegroom are sung here, hence the Vulgate renders it, A song for the beloved, just as the LXX [renders it] ὑπὲρ ἀγαπητẽ. Those therefore who explain the song of loves as a hymn, understand it concerning the reciprocal loves of the Bridegroom and the Bride, or they judge that loves in the plural are said for excellence as the most ardent love, therefore Jerome rendered it: a song of the most beloved. For the kindnesses of God can be understood, just as love exhibited in Christ is accustomed to be described. Conf. Ps. 89, 2. Isa. 55, 3. Venerable antiquity, Theodoret, Cassiodorus, Remigius, understand that beloved one to be the Messiah, because the spiritual nuptials of the Son of God are referred to here, and the vows of the Epithalamium are celebrated with praise: τῷ ἀγαπητῷ τẽτ᾽ ἐςι τῷ χρισῷ, says Athanasius in fragm. Psalm. Conf. Orat. 5. contr. Arian. Augustine Orat. adv. Jews; Because it is read A song for the beloved, Christ is most openly shown. Whence Jerome says, This Psalm, he says, contains the Sacrament of spiritual Nuptials, that is, the conjunction of Christ with the Church. Which Andr. Rivetus, the hyperaspistes of Calvin, also acknowledges, explaining the title: A love song: And rightly, he says, the series of the discourse and the whole argument shows this to be the title, so that it is an Epithalamium, a song by which the mutual love of the spouses is described, composed long ago by the supreme artist of the Holy Spirit, the Son of God the Bridegroom, and the Church the Bride. Which also R. David Kimchi among the Jews acknowledged here, understanding the Messiah by the beloved. Then, if it were even rendered a song of the beloved [women], spiritual virgins could be understood, (just as the whole song will presently be taught to sing of spiritual things) singing a hymn in honor of the Messiah, and his Bride, the Church. Grotius says it was sung by virgins to the melodies of the sons of Korah, but the Sons of Korah are established as the authors of the Psalm in the title, just as elsewhere the author David is accustomed to be designated in this way מזמור לדוד, therefore Gabriel Sionita makes Asaph and Ethan the authors of the Psalm; which indeed the Syrian Church in the ἐπιγραφῇ testifies was sung in the days of the Mosaic Sanhedrin. And from there Genebrardus concludes, that there is no doubt that the sons of Korah, who in the times of Moses, that is 480 years before Solomon, prophesied those words by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, referred that prophecy rather to Christ than to Solomon, who in respect to Him was a manikin of absolutely no value. Nor is it said without reason that this didactic song is instructive שיר שכיל. For the Psalm persuades us at the beginning that for this reason there is need of a certain heavenly understanding, as Eusebius advises in book IV of the Demonstratio Evangelica, and Cassiodorus, because it contains the spiritual sacraments of future things.

But so that it may be more evidently established that this does not treat of Solomon's nuptials according to the literal sense, but of the spiritual nuptials of the Messiah, we urge first of all the very words of the Psalm and the entire συνέχειαν. And first, indeed, the magnificent entrance, which the θεόπνευστος author would by no means have made with such great apparatus if earthly loves were being celebrated. My heart has poured forth a good word, I say my works to the King, my tongue is the pen of a scribe, writing swiftly. A good word is spoken of the excellent and consolation-filled word in Isaiah 39:8. Zechariah 1:3. Therefore my heart pours forth a good word, is the same, as Rivetus admits, as if he were saying: my heart is eager to speak something excellent and pleasant, which might bring joy and delight to all, wipe away all sorrow, and soothe all hardships and griefs: and Calvin himself notes that by this Preface it is sufficiently shown that the subject matter of this Canticle is not common, because the author promises that he will speak about great and excellent things. And that it does not treat only of a perishable kingdom, but that something more excellent is being discussed. To say his works (Symmachus renders it τὰ ποιήματα) or this poem, he means to the King, or about the King, so called κατ' ἐξοχὴν, the King of Kings, whom he takes as the subject matter for speaking: But so that his tongue may be directed by the Holy Spirit and be the instrument and pen of this scribe, writing swiftly, since he was about to present a special prophecy about this King. Beautifully Basil the Great in his explanation on the Psalm. Vol. 1 of works, p. 207, concerning this scribe: Just as a pen is an instrument suitable for delineating writing, with the hand of a skilled man moving it to express the characters of those things which are to be written: so also the tongue of the just man, with the Holy Spirit moving it, inscribes the words of eternal life upon the hearts of believers, dyed indeed not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God. The scribe, therefore, is the Holy Spirit, since He is wise and teaches all things. Writing swiftly. For the movement of the mind is swift. Moreover, the Holy Spirit inscribes for us not on tablets of stone, but on the fleshy tablets of our hearts. However, one cannot, with Grotius, Calvin, and Rivetus, imagine a double object, so that the King is understood typically as Solomon, and then the true King Messiah as the one signified by the type: because he was eager to pour forth a good word about the King so called κατ' ἀντονομασίαν and μοναδικῶς, about that most loving or most beloved one whom he carried in his breast: whom he also describes in such a way that he is understood to have prophesied about no one but one subject, no one but the Messiah. Calvin admits that the name of King is attributed to this Bridegroom by excellence, so that we may know that the discourse is not held about just any King, but about that memorable King whose throne God promised would be established until the Sun and Moon shine, Psalm 72:5.

Therefore, secondly, the description of this King must be weighed a little more accurately. Whom he depicts (1.) by grace and form. Fair in form above the sons of men: which exhibit spiritual beauty. For even if the Messiah was most fair in external majesty, this eulogy nevertheless tastes of something more. Nor does it suit Solomon, or any mortal. For how is Solomon said to be fair above the sons of men, so that no one of the sons of men is to be compared to him, he who defiled himself with various and most grave sins? Calvin himself admits that Christ is here called fair in form because He was adorned with excellent gifts, by which He surpasses ALL OTHERS. Therefore, by whatever phrase the eminence of gifts ABOVE ALL OTHERS is noted, that by no means fits Solomon. Rivetus adds that he is called beautiful above others because of holiness, because all the other sons of men are all deformed and squalid regarding this innocence, polluted by sins, and lacking the glory of God, Romans 3. Therefore, that eulogy cannot belong to Solomon. It is manifest, says Basil the Great in the cited book, that the Prophet here, having inspected the clarity of the Son, and being copiously surrounded by the irradiation of the splendor rebounding from there, and having his soul struck and pierced by such great beauty, was moved to the divine love of that spiritual beauty, by which, once it has shone upon a human soul, all other things which were hitherto loved are seen to be base and rejected: and for that reason Paul, as soon as he saw this one fair in form, considered all things to be dung, that he might gain Christ.

(2.) Then that Bridegroom is described by the eloquence and sweetness of his mouth. Grace is poured out in thy lips. Which look to the most sweet word of the Gospel, which Christ, full of grace and truth, brought forth, John 1:14, 18, and they commend the sweetness of his mouth and his proclamation, Isaiah 61:1, Luke 4:22, John 3:17, concerning which Blessed Luther in his commentary on this Psalm, Vol. III of the Jena Latin works. Nor does he simply call them gracious lips, but grace poured out, so that he may signify that Christ is most abundant in his lips, from whose mouth, as if from some rich fountain, proceed most opulent promises and doctrines, by which he raises up and consoles souls. Nor does Calvin deny it: It is deservedly said that grace is poured out in his lips, because the Gospel by its nature breathes the odor of life. If, therefore, that is signified here, how could this be understood of Solomon? For it is evident, even by Calvin's own admission, that not just any eloquence, but that altogether admirable sweetness and grace of the proclamation of Christ and the Gospel is expressed here by that phrase. Incomparable eloquence and sweetness is designated here, just as is incomparable beauty. Because that, 'above the sons of men,' ἀπὸ κοινõ must be repeated here, so that it may extol the external eloquence no less than the internal beauty above all men.

Thirdly, a singular blessing is expressed, which is proper to our King; therefore God has blessed you forever. Because of those most eminent internal gifts, and the grace of the Evangelical proclamation, a blessing not temporary, but eternal, fell to our King in the office which he discharged, which again cannot be explained according to the letter concerning Solomon, but looks to the Messiah: Who is blessed forever, that we all may be blessed in Him forever: and from His fullness receive grace for grace, John 1, Eph. 1. We have here Rivet confessing: It is sufficiently evident from the history of chapter 3, he says, that God blessed Solomon abundantly. 1 Kings 12. But in Solomon these things were not ETERNAL, unless eternity is referred to the perpetuity of doctrine (which contributes little here), and therefore MUCH MORE PROPERLY this blessing is referred to Christ, IN WHOM ALONE all the families of the earth are blessed, and in whom resides the eternal truth and solidity of all promises. He ought to have inferred, if he had wished to speak consistently, that because this does not suit Solomon, this blessing is to be referred (not more properly, but) SOLELY to Christ; and therefore that the discourse here is about Christ ALONE. For the discourse is about Him whom God has truly blessed forever. Junius also explains this blessing thus: Therefore God has blessed you forever, namely, that you might surpass all in the elegance of graces, and rather be the author of elegance and grace to all. How do these things fit Solomon?

Fourthly, the highest fortitude and power of this King is shadowed forth. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty, with splendor and glory: which are understood either as glorious and splendid arms, by apposition, or they teach that arms are borne for the sake of glory and splendor, to be asserted against enemies. Calvin himself acknowledges that these things do not fit Solomon: How, he says, will it be fitting that warlike bravery is so greatly celebrated in Solomon, who was of a gentle disposition, and having attained a tranquil state, cultivated only the arts of peace, and never gave any specimen of himself in war that these things were typically fulfilled in Solomon? Junius explains the Royal arms, which in Solomon were carnal, but in Christ are the spiritual sword of the word proceeding from his mouth, of which Isa. 11:4, Heb. 4:12, and Rev. 1:16. But Calvin confesses that the very typification fails here, because Solomon cultivated only the arts of peace, did not use arms against enemies, nor had need to use them. For the Prophet speaks here, as Rivetus confesses, not only of strength and power, but also of the use of the same. And how can the sword be taken in the same place, both properly concerning arms, and improperly concerning the word of God? If, therefore, that figurative sense is only true concerning the sword of the spirit, it can BY NO MEANS be said that this discourse is about the bodily sword of Solomon. It is sufficiently evident that that word, which is understood by the sword, is, as Rivetus says, the glory and beauty of the Messiah, by which he attests and protects his Majesty. And Junius confesses that that address, O most mighty, in this verse 4, is not Solomon's, but an epithet of the Messiah, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, and by whose arms we overthrow all strongholds.

Fifthly, the virtues of the government are celebrated, Equity upon the word of equity, meekness, and justice. Although all Kings ought to strive for these, yet there is no one of them all who can be celebrated for these always and everywhere in all parts of his government. Sins are committed within and without the walls of Troy! While they wish to extend and fortify their power, their horses, to use the words of Calvin, and chariots are often ambition, pride, cruelty, exactions, rapine, violence. But to no one does that spiritual riding upon the word of meekness, virtue, and justice so well fit (these are the words of Rivetus) as to the Messiah. When he has explained these things at length, all these things, says Rivetus, are clearly manifested in the Gospel, the word of truth, concerning the King Messiah. Cf. Isa. 42:2, Dan. 9:24, Zech. 9:9, Matt. 21:5.

Sixthly, the most happy success against enemies: thy right hand shall lead thee wonderfully: thy arrows are sharp, the peoples shall fall under thee, in the hearts of the King's enemies. Which things certainly fit Solomon BY NO MEANS, but the Messiah alone. For did his right hand lead Solomon? He certainly had need of the right hand of the Lord: by his own right hand he could neither rule nor defend himself, which no mortal can do. And what peoples fell under Solomon? How were there sharp arrows in the heart of Solomon's enemies? It is indeed to be believed, says Rivetus again, that Solomon, if there had been need and use, would have come forth even against enemies, as a brave hero: But here the Prophet does not speak of power and strength only, but also of the use of the same, when that King exercised power, by girding on the sword, and acting prosperously, when he performed terrible works with his right hand, when he pierced the hearts of enemies with arrows, and peoples fell under him. These things certainly DO NOT SUFFICIENTLY FIT Solomon. Which confession of Rivetus is to be well noted. But where now is the literal sense concerning Solomon, if most things do not fit Solomon, and all the predicates regard the same subject? But concerning the Messiah he says: This is the same, he says, whose power performed wonders, whom his right hand taught wonderful things, and manifested openly to all, of whom Ps. 98:1, He hath done marvelous things, his right hand and his holy arm hath gotten him the victory: which place wonderfully illustrates this of ours. Both show that those wonders done by God, especially the redemption of men through the admirable victory reported over all our enemies, were done by his own virtue, not by the work of any other, and are the work of the divine arm and right hand. Therefore Isa. 59:19, explaining this sentiment, says, and God looked if there were an helper, and he wonders also that there is no one to intercede, therefore his own arm brought salvation unto him Isa. 63:5, etc. And a little later: Since this King of ours is not said, like Cyrus and Moses, to be led by another having taken his right hand (Isa. 45:1 and 63:12), but that his own right hand taught him wonderful things, that is, that he performed and brought them forth by that own right hand, it is certainly and clearly deduced that it is DIVINE, and above all created power. Cf. Job 40:5, etc. But what sane person will apply these to Solomon? Therefore the discourse is not according to the proper and literal sense concerning Solomon, but concerning him who said of himself, Matt. 12:42, Behold, more than Solomon is here. And thus he also understands concerning Christ what is said about the sharp arrows of this King in the hearts of the King's enemies, under whom the peoples fall, and about the administration of the Gospel, which penetrates into the mind and breast, comparing Isa. 49:2, ch. 6:12, and asserts that there will be enough strength in the hand of this King to break the stubbornness of all. We add the excellent explanation of Basil the Great, The sharp arrows are discourses skillfully and ingeniously devised, reaching the hearts of the hearers, and striking and wounding the souls that are well-disposed, for the words of the wise are as goads of the good (Eccl. 12). By these arrows, those souls that have embraced the faith are wounded, and those that have burned with the highest love for God, and at the same time say with that Bride: I am wounded by love. Basil adds another meaning in these very words: You may also understand the sharp arrows to be those who were sent to scatter the seed of the Gospel throughout the whole world. Because they had sharpened themselves, they shone with works of righteousness, and subtly broke into the minds of those whom they were instructing in the faith. These arrows, therefore, sent out in every direction, prepared the peoples to submit themselves to the yoke of Christ. He establishes a hyperbaton in these words, so that the sense may be: And the peoples shall fall under you, because your arrows are sharp in the heart of the King's enemies. No adversary of God, or contumacious or proud person, falls under God or is subjected to Him, except those who have undertaken obedience through faith. But the arrows falling into the hearts of the enemies of the King sometimes draw them to a desire for the truth and to the Lord Himself, so that those who were enemies of God may be reconciled to Him through doctrine. Luther explains it without a hyperbaton, and takes 'heart' as a Hebraism for 'midst': the peoples shall fall under you in the midst of the King's enemies.

Seventh, it is especially clear that what is said concerning the perpetuity of this Kingdom cannot be twisted to Solomon except by a remarkable act of perversity (σρεβλότητα). Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever. For the Psalmist also calls His kingdom eternal, and addresses the King of whom he speaks by the name אלהים, which in the singular is offered to none but the one God. Since, therefore, the kingdom of Solomon is not eternal, nor can he himself be called אלהים, these things can in no way be accepted as referring to Solomon, so that we cannot wonder enough here how Grotius still dares, with the Jews and Calvin, to explain these things as referring to Solomon according to the literal sense. For they understand the whole Psalm literally as referring to Solomon. The simple and genuine sense, says Calvin, is that Solomon does not rule tyrannically, as most kings do, but by right and equitable laws, and therefore his throne will be stable for all ages. He adds that Solomon is also called God, because upon kings God has inscribed some mark of His glory. Calvin speaks in such clear words, and yet his champion Pareus still denies that Calvin judaizes here. But Dn. D. Ægid. Hunnius bravely silences Pareus, that unhappy patron of Calvin; we, for our part, convict Calvin here out of Calvin himself. Nowhere, he says on v. 7, do we read that either man or Angel is adorned with this title אלהים, without any addition. Thus, indeed, both Angels and Judges are called by the plural number, but NO ONE SINGLE PERSON is called אלהים, without some restriction being added: just as when Moses is constituted as a God to Pharaoh, Exod. 7, 1. From which it may be gathered that this Psalm looks higher than to a shadowy kingdom. What audacity, then, or rather what impiety is it, that Calvin himself should here distort this plural name, placed absolutely, to one man, Solomon, and sell this sense as SIMPLE & GENUINE or literal? What he said to the Jews, he ought to have said to himself: however much the Jews may attempt to elude this verse with their CAVILS, thy throne O God is for ever and ever, it is nevertheless sufficiently valid to prove the eternal divinity of Christ, because while the name אלהים is ascribed to either angels or men, some note is usually added at the same time, which distinguishes them from the true and only God: Here, however, it is simply conferred upon Christ and without any exception. If it is used simply and without any exception, which the αὐτοψία (self-evidence) teaches, it cannot apply to anyone here, indeed not even to an Angel, by Calvin's own admission, and therefore there can be no discourse here about Solomon according to the letter. The evidence of this argument compelled Rivetus, otherwise a stubborn defender of Calvin, so that although he insisted on the footsteps of Calvin in the explanation of the Psalm, and began to explain the Psalm with him concerning Solomon in the literal sense, he was nevertheless forced to confess openly concerning these two verses 7. & 8. that they could by no means be understood of Solomon, and in the Jews and Arians at the same time he openly refuted his teacher Calvin: Against the sense of this appellation (he is dealing with the name of God) the Jews and Arians, or the more recent Photinians, rise up; the former wish this name to be understood here of Solomon: The latter, indeed, of Christ but improperly, in the way that, even if they do not agree on the person, the Jews also wish it to be understood: namely, that he is not called God here, who is truly God, but because in the Holy Scriptures princes and judges are sometimes called by this name: Which latter sense Calvin embraces here as the simple and genuine meaning, namely that Solomon is called God here because God has inscribed on kings some mark of His glory. Rivetus therefore replies, and indeed from Calvin himself: But neither can ever show the name אלהים said simply of one single person except of the one true God. For neither is Moses said simply to have been made Elohim, but to Aaron or Pharaoh: Furthermore, this IMPROPER SENSE here in the Psalmist is excluded by the following words: for whose earthly prince's seat is established forever? What of that which was said a little above, thy right hand shall teach thee wonderful things? Are these to be understood of an earthly prince, or rather of GOD Himself? Now therefore, as to the perpetuity of the kingdom, Calvin's ἑαυτομαχία (self-contradiction) will serve to convict even Grotius himself here. For it is clearer than light that an eternal throne is ascribed to this King, of whom it is treated according to the letter, which even R. David Kimchi of the Jews acknowledges: But Solomon's throne was by no means eternal. Let us hear Calvin himself; Nothing harsher can be brought forward than this testimony, where the perpetuity of the kingdom is asserted. For there is no doubt that the oracle in Psalm 7, 23 is noted. And the Jews themselves are even forced to refer this to the Messiah. Therefore the Prophet, although he had begun his discourse concerning the Son of David, yet ascending higher in the Spirit, he embraced the Kingdom of the true and perpetual Messiah. Ought we not therefore to detest Calvin's corruption, that it is still a question here of Solomon? For thus he says on v. 7. Thy throne. He commends other royal virtues in Solomon; that his throne is eternal: then that there is a just and right manner of governing. But those things are also ἀσύςατα (inconsistent); that the Prophet had begun concerning Solomon, but now ascends to the Messiah: because the whole Psalm treats of one person, of one King, of whom he had begun, he continues his hymn: whom he had called beautiful beyond the Sons of men, gracious in speech, mighty with a glorious sword, riding upon the word of equity, of meekness and of justice, he asserts that he himself also teaches his right hand terrible things, and sends arrows into the hearts of his enemies, and that his throne endures for ever: and he calls him God absolutely. Calvin, therefore, is here again refuted and convicted by Calvin, indeed even by himself, by Rivetus: The Prophet therefore wishes this kingdom to be so constituted by the strength of Christ God, that it is perpetual, and never to be taken away from its King: and that he will use his judicial power with such equity, that nothing which deviates from righteousness will ever appear in his whole administration. But the most manifest arguments prove that these things which are said here CANNOT properly apply to Solomon (which Calvin contends). To pass over other things, the kingdom of Solomon was neither perpetual, nor even long-lasting, since he reigned for only 40 years. But if anyone should wish to bring in his descendants, what follows concerning the scepter of righteousness will oppose it, since a most wicked son succeeded Solomon, nor were his grandsons any better, with a few exceptions. Nor would the straight rod fit even Solomon himself, except for a time, since he later shamefully fell away from God. These things, therefore, are to be referred to Christ, to whom the Psalmist also directs his speech when he calls him God. Which ἀναντιῥῥήτως we can now use to refute Rivet himself in this way: He who is called God by the Psalmist, and whose throne is eternal, and whose scepter is a rod of righteousness, is that King and Bridegroom of whom this epithalamium treats literally, and of whom the whole is also to be explained literally: But it is not Solomon, but solely the Messiah who is he who is called God by the Psalmist, whose throne is eternal, and whose scepter is a rod of righteousness. Therefore, it is not Solomon, but solely the Messiah who is that King and Bridegroom of whom it is treated here literally, and of whom this whole poem is to be explained according to the literal sense. The conclusion is entirely adverse not only to Calvin and Grotius, but also to Rivet. Moreover, the major proposition, however much it may be most evidently established by the συνεχείᾳ and συναφείᾳ of the text, is confirmed even by Rivet's own ἀνάλυσιν. Thus is our King described to us (I recite his words from p. 308) as a warrior and powerful, formidable to his enemies; the instruments of his power are described by metaphorical terms, which he uses against all the enemies of the human race. 1. Against those standing firm, as if in a stationary battle, armed with a sword. 2. Against those fleeing, as if by horse or chariot, by which he pursues and overtakes them, wherever they may be. Whom he finally destroys, at close quarters indeed with his right hand, which does wonderful things; from a distance with very sharp arrows. After he has been described as formidable and terrible to his enemies, in the following verses he is introduced as to be revered with the highest majesty, v. 7, 8. Which coherence Grotius could have learned even from the Jesuits (for he attributes much to them), especially from Cardinal Bellarmine, who renders this paraphrase at v. 4: Come, beloved of God, who are not only most beautiful and most gracious, but also most powerful and most robust, gird yourself with your weapons, and come, deliver your people. And at

Latin:

PSALMUS XLV. Epithalamium Christi.

IN FINEM PRO IIS, QVI COMMVTABVNTVR) LXX. עַל־שׁשַׁנִּים vertunt ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων. Significat hæc vox & lilia, sed origo est à שׁשׁ, quod sex si- gnificat : unde hexachordum significare videtur, quod sex fides habet, non minus quam lilium sex folia.

CANTICVM PRO DILECTO) In Hebræo : Carmen dilectarum. Ita vocabantur virgines, quæ novam nuptam cingebant : Sicut is, qui novo marito aderat, vocatur ὁ φίλος τοῦ νυμφίου Joh. 3, 29. Est ergo hoc carmen ad modulos filio- rum Core Cantatum a virginibus, in honorem Solomonis novi mariti, & novæ nuptæ, filiæ Regis Ægypti. Solebant enim in nuptiis tum a virginibus, tum ab Juvenibus cani carmina etiam apud Græcos & Romanos, ut ex Catullo di- scimus. Cæterum μυσικῶς hoc carmen ad Messiam pertinere etiam Chaldæus Paraphrastes agnoscit.

STrenue hic iterum Judaizat Grotius, Psalmum excellentissimum Propheticum de Messia, secun- dum literam explicans de Salomone, & in Canticum amatorium mundanum convertens. Sequutus Cal- vinum, ejusque discipulos nonnullos, nec non Neo- photinianos Transsylvanos in refut. lib. 2. Major. En- jedinum in Explic. locor. Vet. & Nov. Test. p. 70. 349. Socin. in animadv. ad Assert. Posn. pag. 81. Volckel. lib. 1. de ver. Relig. cap. 9. Crellium & Schlichting. in Epist. ad Ebr. 1, 9. Argumentum enim, quo utitur hic Grotius, prorsus ficulneum est: Dicitur carmen dilectarum. Ergo a virginibus, no- vam nuptam cingentibus, decantatum est in honorem Salomonis novi mariti, & novæ nuptæ, filiæ Regis Æ- gypti. Nam neque antecedens certum est, nec con- sequentia firma. Dicitur in Hebræo שיר ידידות, quod reddunt Hebræi, canticum amorum, vel sua- vitatum. Et Aquila ᾆσμα προσφιλίας, quum ידידות suavitatem & amorem in abstracto signifi- cet, non minus quam amatam, vel dilectam. Et quum amores sponsi hic decantentur, hinc vulgata reddit, Canticum pro dilecto, uti LXX. ὑπὲρ ἀγαπητẽ. Qui ergo exponunr canticum amorum hymnum, de amo- ribus reciprocis Sponsi & Sponsæ intelligunt, vel amo- res in plurali ob excellentiam dici amorem flagran- tissimum censent, ideo Hieronymus reddidit: canti- cum amantissimi. Possunt enim benignitates Dei intelligi, ut solet amor in Christo exhibitus descri- bi. Conf. Psal. 89, 2. Esa. 55, 3. Per dilectum il- lum Messiam intelligit veneranda antiquitas, Theo- doretus, Cassiodorus, Remigius, quod nuptiæ Filii Dei spirituales hic referantur, votaque Epithalamii lau- de celebrentur: τῷ ἀγαπητῷ τẽτ᾽ ἐςι τῷ χρισῷ, ait Athanas. in fragm. Psalm. Conf. Orat. 5. contr. Arian. Augustinus Orat. adv. Judæos; Quia legitur Canticum pro dilecto, apertissime Christus ostenditur. Unde Hieronymus, Psalmus hic, inquit, spiritualium Nuptiarum continet Sacramentum, hoc est, conjunctio- nem Christi cum Ecclesia. Quod agnoscit etiam Andr. Rivetus, Calvini hyperaspistes, titulum expo- nens: Carmen amatorium: Et recte, inquit, series o- rationis & totum argumentum ostendit, hunc esse titu- lum, ut sit Epithalamium carmen, quo mutuus conju- gum amor describitur, a summo artifice S. S. Filio Dei Sponso, & Ecclesiæ Sponsæ, olim conditum. Quod etiam e Judæis R. David Kimchi hic agnovit, per di- lectum intelligens Messiam. Tum, si redderetur etiam carmen dilectarum, virgines intelligi possent spirituales, (quemadmodum totum carmen spiri- tualia cantare jamjam docebitur) in honorem Mes- siæ, & Sponsæ ejus, Ecclesiæ, hymnum decantantes. Dicit Grotius ad modulos filiorum Core cantatum a virginibus, sed Filii Kora Autores Psalmi constitu- untur in titulo, perinde uti alias autor David ita de- signari solet מזמור לדוד, ideo Gabriel Sionita, As- saph & Ethan, autores Psalmi facit; quem vero in diebus Synedrii Mosaici decantatum Ecclesia Syria- ca in ἐπιγραφῇ testatur. Atque inde Genebrardus concludit, non esse dubium, quin filii Coreh, qui Mosis temporibus, hoc est 480. ante Salomonem annis, verba illa instinctu Spiritus S. vaticinati sint, vaticini- um illud potius ad Christum, quam ad Salomonem, qui illius respectu plane nullius pretii fuit homuncio, retule- rint. Nec abs re dicitur canticum hoc didacticum eruditorium שיר שכיל. Ideo enim intelligentia quadã superna op9 esse, Psalmus initio nobis persuadet, monente Eusebio libr. IV. Demonstr. Evangel. & Cassiodor. quod futurarum rerum Sacramenta Spiri- tualia contineat.

Sed ut evidentius constet, non de Salomonis nuptiis hic agi, secundum literalem sensum, sed de spiritualibus Messiæ nuptiis, urgemus cumprimis ipsa Psalmi verba, totamque συνέχειαν. Et pri- mum quidem magnificum ingressum, quem cum tan- to apparatu minime fecisset autor θεόπνευστος, si amores terreni decantarentur. Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum, dico ego opera mea regi, lingua mea ca- lamus scribæ, velociter scribentis. Verbum bonum de præclaro & consolatione pleno dicitur Esa. 39, 8.
