Zach. 1, 3. ideo eructat cor meum verbum bonum, idem est, fatente Riveto, ac si diceret, præclarum quidpiam ge- stit dicere cor meum & jucundum, quod omnibus læti- tiam & voluptatem afferat, mœrorem omnem abster- gat, omnes ærumnas ac mœrores leniat: notatque Cal- vinus ipse, hac Præfatione satis ostendi, non vulgare esse hujus Cantici argumentum, quia promittit autor, se de rebus magnis & præclaris verba facturum. Nec de caduco tantum regno agi, sed excellentius quid tra- ctari. Dicere opera sua (Symmachus τὰ ποιήμα- τα reddit) vel carmen hoc vult Regi, vel de Rege, κατ' ἐξοχὴν ita dicto, Regum Rege, quem pro dicen- di materia sumit: Sed ut lingua dirigatur a Sp. S. & scribæ hujus, velociter scribentis, instrumentum atque calamus sit, siquidem peculiarem prophetiam de hoc Rege exhibiturus erat. Pulchre Basilius M. in explicatione super Psalm. T. 1. oper. p. 207. de hoc scriba: Sicut calamus instrumentum est, deline- andæ Scripturæ accommodum ipsum manu viri periti promovente ad eorum, quæ scribenda sunt, characte- res exprimendos: Sic & lingva justi, Spiritu Sancto eam movente, cordibus credentium verba inscribit vi- tæ æternæ, tincta qvidem non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viventis. Scriba igitur Spiritus Sanctus, qvoniam sapiens est, & omnes docens. Velociter scribens. Ve- lox enim mentis motus est. Inscribit autem nobis Spi- ritus Sanctus non in tabulis lapideis sed tabulis cordis nostri carneis. Non potest autem cum Grotio, Calvino, Riveto, fingi geminum objectum, ut tum Rex typice Salomo intelligatur, tum typo significa- tus, verus Rex Messias: quia de Rege κατ' ἀντονομα- σίαν & μοναδικῶς ita dicto, de amantissimo vel di- lectissimo illo quem in pectore gerebat, eructare ver- bum bonum gestiebat: quem ita etiam describit, ut non nisi de uno subjecto, non nisi de Messia vatici- natus esse intelligatur. Fatetur Calvinus Regis no- men per excellentiam huic Sponso tribui, ut scia- mus, non de Rege quolibet haberi sermonem, sed me- morabili illo Rege, cujus solium Deus stativum promi- sit, donec fulgeant Sol & Luna Ps. 72, 5.

Proinde secundo Regis hujus descriptio expen- denda paulo accuratius. Quem (1.) a venustate ac forma depingit. Speciosus forma præ filiis homi- num: quæ spiritualem pulchritudinem exhibent. Etsi enim externa majestate speciosissimus fuerit Mes- sias, hoc tamen elogium aliquid amplius sapit. Ne- que Salomoni, aut ulli mortalium id convenit. Quo- modo enim Salomo speciosus præ filiis hominum dici- tur, ut nemo e filiis hominum ipsi comparandus sit, qui variis & gravissimis peccatis sese polluit? Calvi- nus ipse fatetur, Christum hic vocari speciosum forma, quia eximiis dotibus ornatus fuerit, quibus OMNES ALIOS supereminet. Qua ergo phrasi eminen- tia dotium SUPER ALIOS OMNES notatur, ea neutiquam in Salomonem quadrat. Rivetus addit pulchrum præ aliis dici ob sanctitatem, quia reliqui omnes filii hominum ad hanc in- nocentiam cuncti deformes sint, & squalidi, peccatis polluti, gloria Dei carentes Rom. 3. Non er- go id elogium Salomoni competere potest. Palam est, inquit Basilius M. lib. cit. quod Propheta hic in- specta claritate Filii, & illinc resilientis splendoris irra- diatione copiose circumfusus, animamque habens hac tanta pulchritudine perculsam atq; perstrictam, ad di- vinum amorem spiritualis illius pulchritudinis permo- tus est, qua ubi semel humanæ affulsit animæ, cætera o- mnia, quæ eatenus diligebantur, turpia esse conspiciun- tur & rejectitja: eoque Paulus simul ut vidit hunc spe- ciosum forma, omnia duxit stercora esse, ut Christum lucrifaceret.

(2.) Deinde describitur Sponsus ille ab oris facundia & suavitate. Diffusa est gratia illa in labiis tuis. Quæ suavissimum Evangelii verbum respi- ciunt, quod Christus plenus gratia & veritate protu- lit Joh. 1, 14. 18. & oris ac præconii ejus suavitatem commendant Esa. 61, 1. Luc. 4, 22. Joh. 3, 17, de quo B. Lutherus in com. hujus Psalm. Tom. III. oper. Latin. Jenens. Nec vocat simpliciter gratiosa labia, sed diffusa gratia, ut significet, Christum esse abundantissi- mum in suis labiis, ex cujus ore, ceu ex fonte quodam uberi procedant opulentissimæ promissiones & doctrinæ, quibus erigit, & consolatur animas. Nec abnuit Calvinus: Merito dicitur in labiis ejus diffusam esse gratiam, quia Evangelium vitæ odorem natura sua spirat. Si ergo id hic significatur, quomodo de Sa- lomone hoc intelligi poterit? Non enim quamcun- que facundiam, sed illam prorsus admirabilem sua- vitatem & gratiam præconii Christi & Evangelii hic exprimi ea phrasi, fatente ipso Calvino, constat. In- comparabilis facundia & suavitas hic designatur, æ- que, uti pulchritudo incomparabilis. Quia illud, præ filiis hominum, ἀπὸ κοινõ hic repetendum, ut externum eloquium non minus, quam internam venustatem supra omnes homines extollat.

Tertio singularis benedictio exprimitur, quæ Regi nostro propria est; propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum. Ob istas internas dotes eminen- tissimas, & gratiam præconii Evangelici benedictio Regi nostro in munere, quod obiit, non temporaria, sed æterna obtigit, quod iterum secundum literam de Salomone exponi nequit, sed ad Messiam spectat: Qui in æternum benedictus est, ut nos omnes in ipso benedicamur æternum: & de plenitudine ejus gra- tiam per gratiam accipiamus Joh. 1. Eph. 1. Habe- mus hic confitentem Rivetum: Salomoni, inquit, Deum abunde benedixisse satis constat ex historia capi- tis 3. Reg. 12. verum in Salomone hæc non fuerunt Æ- TERNA, nisi æternitas referatur ad doctrinæ perpetui- tatem (quæ huc parum facit) ac proinde MULTO MAGIS PROPRIE ad Christum hæc benedictio re- fertur, IN QUO SOLO omnes terræ familiæ sunt be- nedictæ, & in quo residet omnium promissionum æter- na veritas & soliditas. Inferre debebat, si conse- quenter loqui voluisset, quia Salomoni hæc non con- venit, de æterna benedictione (non magis proprie, sed) UNICE ad Christum hanc benedictionem referendam esse; Adeoque de Christo SOLO hic sermonem es- se. De eo enim est sermo, cui Deus vere in æter- num benedixit. Sic etiam explicat hanc benedi- ctionem Junius: Propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum, nimirum, ut omnes elegantia gratiarum su- perares, ac potius omnibus auctor esses elegantiæ & gra- tiæ. Qui hæc in Salomonem quadrant?

Quarto Regis hujus adumbratur summa for- titudo & potentia. Accingere gladio tuo super fe- mur tuum potentissime decore & gloria: quæ vel de armis gloriosis & decoris, per appositionem intelli- guntur vel arma ob gloriam & decorem geri docent, adversus hostes adserendum. Non convenire autem hæc Salomoni, ultro agnoscit Calvinus: Jam belli- cam fortitudinem, inquit, in Salomone tantopere ce- lebrari qui conveniet, qui & mansueto fuit ingenio, & tranquillum statum adeptus, pacis artes tantum co- luit, nullum unquam in bello edidit sui specimen? Qua ergo veritatis specie affirmari potest, in Salomone hæc typice impleta esse? Junius explicat arma Re- gia, quæ in Salomone fuerint carnalia, in Christo vero gladius spiritualis verbi procedentis ex ore ipsius, de quo Esa. 11, 4. Ebr. 4, 12. & Apoc. 1, 16. Sed ipsam etiam typirationem, fatetur Calvinus, hic deficere, quod pacis artes tantum coluerit Salomo, armis adver- sus hostes usus non fuerit, nec uti opus habuerit. Lo- quitur enim hic Propheta, quod fatetur Rivetus, non de viribus & potentia tantum, sed etiam de earun- dem usu. Et quomodo gladius cum proprie de ar- mis, tum improprie de verbo Dei, eodem loco acci- pi poterit? Si ergo sensus ille figuratus tantum ve- rus est de gladio spiritus, NULLATENUS dici po- test, quod de gladio corporali Salomonis hic sermo fit. Verbum illud, quod per gladium intelligitur, Rivetus gloriam & decorem Messiæ esse, qvo Majesta- tem suam testatam facit, & tuetur, satis constat. Et fatetur Junius, compellationem illam, o potentissi- me, versu hoc 4. non Salomonis esse, sed Messiæ Epi- theton, cui omnis potestas data in cælo & in terra, & cujus armis omnes munitiones subvertimus.

Quinto celebrantur virtutes regiminis, Eqvi- tas super verbum æquitatis, mansuetudinis, & justitiæ. Quibus utut Reges omnes studere debeant, nemo tamen omnium est, qui ab his semper & ubique in omnibus partibus regiminis sui celebrari possit. Iliacos intra muros peccatur & extra! Dum potentiam suam efferre & munire volunt, equi eorum, ut verbis Calvini utar, & qvadrigæ sæpe sunt ambitio, fastus, crudelitas, exactiones, rapinæ, violentiæ. Nulli au- tem ita convenit (Riveti verba sunt) eqvitatio illa spi- ritualis super verbo mansvetudinis, virtutis, & justi- tiæ, ut Messiæ. Quæ ubi prolixe exequutus est, hæc omnia, inquit Rivetus, in Evangelio, verbo veritatis, perspicue manifestantur de Rege Messia. Conf. Esa. 42, 2. Dan. 9, 24. Zach. 9, 9. Matth. 21, 5.

Sexto felicissimus successus adversus hostes: de- ducet te mirabiliter dextera tua: sagittæ tuæ acutæ, po- puli sub te cadent, in corda inimicorum Regis. Quæ Salomoni utique NULLATENUS conveniunt, sed Messiæ soli. Num enim Salomonem dextra sua deduxit? Opus utique habuit dextra Domini: sua dextra neque regere, neque defendere potuit semetipsum, quod nec ullus mortalium potest. Et qui populi ceciderunt sub Salomone? Quomodo acutæ sagittæ fuere in cor inimicorum Salomonis? Id qvidem credendum est, ait iterum Rivetus, Salo- monem, si opus & usus fuisset, etiam contra hostes, tan- quam fortem heroa, proditurum fuisse: Sed hic non lo- qvitur Propheta de potentia & viribus tantùm, sed etiam de earundem usu, cum Rex ille potentiam exer- cuit, gladium accingendo, & prospere agendo, cum e- didit opera terribilia dextera sua, cum transfixit sagit- tis hostium corda, & ceciderunt sub eo populi. Hæc certe Salomoni NON SATIS COMPETUNT. Quæ confessio Riveti probe notanda. Ubi vero nunc sensus literalis de Salomone, si in Salomonem ple- raque non conveniant, & omnia prædicata idem subjectum respiciant? De Messia vero ait: Hic idem est, inquit, cujus potentia miranda patravit, quem dextera sua mirabilia docuit, & omnibus palam ma- nifestavit, de qvo Ps. 98, 1. Mirabilia fecit, salutem peperit sibi dextera sua, brachio sanctitatis suae : qui locus nostrum hunc mire illustrat. Uterque ostendit mirabilia illa a Deo facta, praesertim hominum redem- tionem per victoriam admirabilem de cunctis hostibus nostris reportatam, factam esse propria ejus virtute, non alterius alicujus opera, esse opus brachii & dexterae divinae. Ideo Es. 59, 19. explicans hanc sententiam ait, & respexit Deus an esset auxiliator, miratur etiam ne- minem esse, qui intercederet, itaq́; salutem sibi fecit bra- chio suo Es. 63, 5. &c. Et paulo post : Cum hic Rex noster non dicatur ut Cyrus & Moses ab alio deduci ap- prehensa dextera (Esa. 45, 1. & 63, 12.) sed dextram ipsius docuisse illum mirabilia, id est, ea dextra propria perfecisse, & edidisse, deducitur certe & plane eam esse DIVINAM, & supra omnem creatam potentiam. Conf. Job. 40, 5. seqq. Quis autem sanus Salomo- ni haec applicabit ? Non ergo secundum sensum proprium & literalem de Salomone sermo, sed de eo, qui de seipso dixit, Matth. 12, 42. Ecce plus quam Salomo hic. Atque ita etiam de Christo intelligit, quae de sagittis Regis hujus acutis in corda inimicorum Regis, sub quo populi cadunt, dicuntur, & de Evange- lii administratione, quod in animum & pectus pene- trat, conferens Esa. XLIX, 2. cap. VI, 12. inque Re- gis hujus manu satis virium fore ad frangendum o- mnium contumaciam asserit. Addimus eximiam Basilii M. explicationem, Sagittae poteritis acutae sunt sermones solerter & ingeniofe excogitati, audientium corda pertingentes, animasque probe sensatas ferientis atq́; sauciantis, verba namq́; sapientum stimuli sunt bonorum (Eccl. XII.) His sagittis, quae fidem am- plexatae sunt, animae sauciantur, & quae summa in Deum exarserunt charitate, simulq́; cum Sponsa illa dicunt : vulnerata charitate ego sum. Subjungit & alium sensum Basilius his omnino verbis : Intelli- gere item possis sagittas acutas eos, qui ad spargendum per universum orbem Evangelii semen missi sunt. Hi quod se exacuissent, fulgebant operibus justitiae, & sub- tiliter in eorum dirumpebant animos, quos erudie- bant ad fidem. Hae igitur Sagittae imprimis, qua- quaverfum emissae, populos, se ut Christi jugo subster- nerent, praeparabant. Statuit autem in verbis his hyperbaton, ut sensus sit : Et populi sub te cadent, propterea quod Sagittae tuae acutae sunt in corde inimi- corum Regis. Nullus Deo adversarius aut contumax, aut superbus sub Deo cadit, vel ei subigitur, nisi illi, qui fide obedientiam susceperunt. Sagittae autem in corda cadentes inimicorum aliquando Regis trahunt eos ad veritatis desiderium & ad ipsum Dominum, ut inimici Dei existentes eidem per doctrinam conci- lientur. Lutherus sine hyperbato explicat, & cor per Ebraismum, pro medio accipit : populi sub te ca- dent in medio inimicorum Regis.

Septimo imprimis luculentum est, quae de perpetuitate Regni hujus dicuntur, non nisi per in- signem ad detestandam sρεβλότητα ad Salomonem detorqueri. Solium tuum Deus in Seculum, & usque. Nam & aeternum dicit regnum ejus Psaltes, & nomine אלהים, quod in singulari non nisi de uno Deo offertur, compellat Regem, de quo agit. Quum ergo nec aeternum sit regnum Salomonis, nec ipse אלהים vocari possit, nullatenus haec de Sa- lomone accipi possunt, ut mirari satis hic nequea- mus, quomodo adhuc Grotius ausit cum Judaeis & Calvino haec de Salomone, secundum literalem sen- sum explicare. Ad literam enim totum Psalmum de Salomone intelligunt. Simplex & genuinus sensus est, ait Calvinus, Salomonem non tyrannice dominari, ut plerosque Reges, sed rectis & aequis le- gibus, ideoq́; folium ejus omnibus seculis fore stabile. Addit, Salomonem etiam Deum vocari, quia Regibus aliquam gloriæ suæ notam Deus insculpsit. Hæc tam disertis verbis Calvinus, & adhuc negatum ìt hyperaspistes ejus Pareus, Calvinum hic judaizare. Sed Pareum, infelicem Calvini Patronum, fortiter ἐπισομίζει Dn. D. Ægid. Hunnius; nos Calvinum ex ipso Calvino solum hic convincimus. Nusquam, inquit ille ad v. 7. legimus vel hominem vel Angelum hoc titulo אלהים ornatum esse, absque ulla adjectione. Sic quidem plurali numero vocantur tam Angeli quam Judices, sed NEMO UNUS vocatur אלהים, quin addatur aliqua restrictio: sicuti dum Moses constituitur in Deum Pharaonis Exod. 7, 1. unde colligere licet, Canticum hoc altius quam ad umbratile regnum spectare. Quæ ergo, malum, audacia vel impietas potius est, quod Calvinus ipse ad unum hominem Salomonem hoc nomen plurale absolute positum hic detorqueat & hunc sensum pro SIMPLICI & GENUINO vel literali venditet? Quod Judæis dixit, sibi ipsi etiam dixisse debuit: utcunque versum hunc suis CAVILLIS eludere Judæi conentur, solium tuum Deus in seculum seculi, satis tamen valet, ad æternam Christi divinitatem probandam, quia dum nomen אלהים vel angelis vel hominibus adscribitur, simul addi solet nota aliqua, quæ discernat eos a vero & unico Deo: Hic autem simpliciter confertur in Christum & absque ulla exceptione. Si simpliciter & absque ulla exceptione, quod αὐτοψία docet, adhibetur, non potest ulli hic, imo ne Angelo competere, fatente Calvino, ideoque nec de Salomone secundum literam hic sermo esse potest. Quæ argumenti hujus evidentia coegit Rivetum, pertinacem alias Calvini defensorem, ut quamvis in explicatione Psalmi vestigiis Calvini institerit, ac de Salomone, literali sensu, cum eodem Psalmum explicare cœperit, de his tamen duobus versibus 7. & 8. fateri palam debuerit, illos neutiquam de Salomone intelligi posse, & in Judæis ac Arianis simul Præceptorem suum Calvinum aperte confutarit: Contra hujus appellationis, (de nomine Dei agit) sensum insurgunt Judæi & Ariani, sive Photiniani recentiores, illi volunt hoc nomen hic de Salomone intelligi: Hi de Christo quidem sed improprie, quomodo etsi de persona non consentiant, volunt etiam Judæi intelligi debere: nempe hic non vocari Deum, qui sit vere Deus, sed quia in Sacris literis hoc nomine quandoque principes ac judices appellantur: Quem posteriorem sensum, ceu simplicem & genuinam sententiam hic amplectitur Calvinus, quod nempe Salomo Deus hic vocetur, quia regibus Deus aliquam gloriæ suæ notam insculpsit. Respondet ergo Rivetus, & quidem e Calvino ipso: Sed neutri unquam possunt ostendere de uno solo nomen אלהים simpliciter dictum nisi de uno vero Deo. Neque enim Moses dicitur simpliciter factus Elohim, sed Aaroni vel Pharaoni: Deinde hic apud Psalmistam hic SENSUS IMPROBRIUS consequentibus verbis excluditur: cujus namque terreni principis sedes in æternum stabilita est? Quid illud quod paulo superius dicebatur, docebit te mirabilia dextera tua? An de terreno principe, num potius de DEO ipso hæc sunt intelligenda? Jam ergo, quod ad regni perpetuitatem, Calvini ἑαυτομαχία proderit ad ipsummet etiam Grotium hic convincendum. Æternum enim solium huic Regi, de quo secundum literam agitur, adscribi luce clarius est, quod agnoscit etiam e Judæis R. David Kimchi: Salomonis autem thronus æternus nullatenus fuit. Audiamus ipsum Calvinum; Nihil hoc testimonio durius afferri potest, ubi asseritur regni perpetuitas. Neque enim dubium est, quin notetur oraculum Psalm. 7, 23. Atque hoc Judæi etiam ipsi coguntur ad Messiam referre. Ergo Propheta, quam- quam- vis de Filio Davidis sermonem inchoaverat, Spiritu tamen altius afcendens Regnum veri & perpetui Messiæ complexus est, Annon ergo detestari opor- tet Calvini corruptelam, quod hic de Salomone adhuc agatur? Sic enim ille ad v. 7. Solium tuum. Alias regias virtutes in Salomone commendat; quod solium ejus æternum sit: deinde quod justa rectaque gu- bernandi ratio. Sed ἀσύςατα etiam illa sunt; Pro- phetam cepisse de Salomone, afcendere autem nunc ad Messiam: quia de una persona totus agit Pfalmus, de uno Rege, de quo ceperat, hymnum suum continuat: quem pulchrum præ Filiis homi- num, gratiosum eloquio, fortem gladio glorioso, equitantem super verbum æquitatis, mansuetudi- nis & justitiæ, dixerat, illum ipsum etiam terribilia dexteram suam docere, ac sagittas in corda inimi- corum immittere, foliumque ejus in seculum dura- re, asserit: eumque Deum absolute vocat. Cal- vinum ergo hic iterum e Calvino, imo etiam semet- ipsum refellit ac convincit Rivetus: Vult igitur Propheta hoc regnum ita comparatum esse Christi Dei fortitudine, ut perpetuum sit, & nunquam suo Regi auferendum: eumque potestate judiciaria sua cum tanta æquitate usurum, ut nihil unquam quod a rectitudine deviet, in tota ejus administratione appa- reat. Hæc autem quæ hic dicuntur, Salomoni pro- prie competere NON POSSE (quod contendit Cal- vinus) evincunt argumenta manifestissima. Ut a- lia taceam, regnum Salomonis nec fuit perpetuum, nec etiam diuturnum, cum 40. tantum annis regnave- rit. Quod si posteros ejus quis velit, repugnabit quod sequitur de sceptro rectitudinis, cum Salomoni successerit nequissimus filius, nec meliores fuerint ne- potes, exceptis paucis quibusdam. Ne ipsi quidem Salomoni conveniret virga recta, nisi ad tempus, cum turpiter postea a Deo defecerit. Sunt igitur hæc ad Christum referenda, ad quem etiam sermonem dirigit Psalstes, cum eum Deum appellat. Quæ ἀναντιῥ- ῥήτως jam ita ipsi Riveto refutando adhibere possu- mus: Is qui a Psalte Deus appellatur, & cujus thro- nus æternus est, ac sceptrum virga rectitudinis, est Rex ac Sponsus ille, de quo ad literam hoc Epitha- lamium agit, de quo ad literam etiam totum expli- candum est: At non Salomo, sed unice Messias est is, qui a Psalte Deus appellatur, cujus thronus æ- ternus est, ac sceptrum virga rectitudinis. Ergo non Salomo, sed unice Messias est Rex ac Sponsus ille, de quo hic ad literam agitur, & de quo totum hoc carmen secundum literalem sensum explican- dum est. Conclusio non Calvino tantum & Grotio, sed & Riveto prorsus adversa est. Major autem propositio, utut e συνεχείᾳ & συναφείᾳ textus e- videntissime constet, per Riveti etiam ἀνάλυσιν confirmatur. Sic descriptus est nobis (verba ejus recito e p. 308.) Rex noster bellator & potens, hosti- bus formidabilis, descripta sunt potentiæ ejus organa, metaphoricis vocibus, quibus utitur contra omnes ge- neris humani hostes. 1. Contra consistentes, stataria veluti pugna, armatus gladio. 2. contra fugientes ve- lut quasi equo vel curru, quo eos persequitur & asse- quitur, ubicunque sint. Quos tandem conficit, comi- nus quidem dextera, quæ mirabilia facit; eminus sagittis acutissimis. Postquam descriptus est hosti- bus formidabilis & terribilis, in sequentibus summa majestate verendus introducitur v. 7. 8. Quam co- hærentiam Grotius, vel e Jesuitis (his enim multum tribuit) didicisse poterat, imprimis e Cardin. Bel- larmin, qui ad v. 4. hanc paraphrasin reddit: Eja dilecte Deo, qui non solum speciosissimus & gratiosissi- mus, sed etiam potentissimus & robustissimus es, accinge- re armis tuis, & veni, libera populum tuum. Et ad

## 45:4
v. 5. With your splendor and your beauty, that is, with your comeliness, in splendor consists wisdom and in beauty justice, as if girded and equipped with sword and arms, press on, proceed prosperously, and reign, i.e., direct your course to the battle against the devil, prosper in the battle, and having conquered and defeated the prince of this world, acquire for yourself a kingdom, so that you may henceforth reign in the hearts of men through faith and charity, etc. Menochius, esteemed by Grotius, holds the same συνέχειαν (continuity), and explains everything throughout the whole Psalm literally as pertaining to only one subject. The minor proposition of Rivetus is likewise in the words immediately subjoined: Which two verses, 7 and 8, are to be diligently weighed, since the Apostle, Heb. 1:8, refers them IMMEDIATELY TO CHRIST, to whom they certainly belong ALONE. Those things which belong to Christ ALONE, and are to be referred to him IMMEDIATELY, do not suit Solomon in any way, nor do they pertain to Christ only MEDIATELY, insofar as Solomon was his type, but immediately to Solomon, or literally to him, and only mystically regard Christ. We see the force of the truth. For it is too evident that this prophecy deals uniquely with the Messiah, and admits no other subject, no other type.

Eighth, the justice of our King is to be peculiarly weighed. The rod of direction is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved justice and hated iniquity. Which is pronounced absolutely concerning our King, so that it is implied he never departs from the path of justice: Namely, that he, as Rivetus has confessed, will use his judicial power with such equity that nothing which deviates from rectitude will ever appear in his entire administration. For he renders this as the literal and paraphrastic sense of the words, which he openly testifies does not suit Solomon: Not even to Solomon himself, he says (let alone his descendants), does the straight rod belong, except for a time, since he later shamefully fell away from God. Therefore Bellarmine paraphrases thus: your throne, O Christ God, will not be temporal, as was that of David and Solomon, and it will remain for ever and ever. And the rod of your kingdom, that is, your scepter, will always be most straight and most just. For it is a Hebrew phrase, a rod of direction, for a most straight rod. So also Menochius, in these things an epitomizer of Bellarmine. Nor without merit does Jerome, at this place, refer the love of justice and the hatred of iniquity to the fulfillment of the commandments of God: Whence Estius, Comment. on Heb. 1:8, says: It is peculiar to Christ the King so to love justice that he is also for us the just author and bestower of justice, and so to hate iniquity that he sanctifies us, cleansed from all iniquity by his merit and power. In which things, certainly, Solomon was not his type.

Ninth, the anointing of our King, which is highly singular, confirms most clearly that no one but Christ the God-man is to be understood here. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. The Prophet again calls God by the vocative case. Therefore Solomon cannot be understood, who cannot be called God absolutely, nor has he ever been so called. Then he points out that anointing which in no way suits Solomon: Because this anointing is connected with the love of justice and the perennial and immutable hatred of iniquity: this anointing is made in a subject who is the God-man, who is God by nature, and has companions in his assumed humanity: this anointing is made ABOVE all companions, so that no one can be compared to this King by reason of it: anointing made so that he may reign forever, and bear the scepter of rectitude, which is always most straight and most just, loving justice and pursuing iniquity with hatred, so that he may perform wonders with his right hand, and pierce the hearts of any enemies with his sharp arrows; the anointing is made with the oil of gladness, that is, not material, but spiritual, and by the Holy Spirit himself, in whom is true gladness, Rom. 14, not according to measure, but in an immense and infinite manner, John 3:34. Therefore it imports a communication of infinite gifts: for which there was absolute need for that kingdom: on account of that anointing also, religious adoration is owed to this King, as the Holy Psalmist testifies, v. 42, whence this anointing cannot in any way square with Solomon. Rivetus indeed confesses that the anointing with the oil of gladness in this place is to be understood of the Messiah as being called Christ of God ἀντονομασικῶς (by antonomasia), p. 326. Junius provides this paraphrase: Therefore he anointed you, that is, to this end you have received the fullness of the Spirit, that you may perform these things, and from your fullness we all receive grace for grace, John 1:16. And at v. 1 he has it thus: A description of the majesty and justice and divine glory in Christ from the gifts and calling of God: For that these things pertain less to Solomon, both the very series of the words shows, and the Apostle, Heb. 1:8. But more fully on this place later. And these things concerning the second class of arguments from the description of the Bridegroom.

Third, we confirm our opinion from the description of the Bride. For since these are related, Bridegroom and Bride, they declare each other, and from the description of the Bride, we know who the Bridegroom is. The Bride here is spiritual, namely the Church, who is the one Bride of Christ, 2 Cor. 11, Eph. 5, Hos. 2, and not the Daughter of the King of Egypt, the Bride of Solomon: For even if it were granted in the highest degree that there is an allusion in certain metaphorical or allegorical locutions to Solomon's Bride, her retinue, clothing, and the like, just as in metaphors from natural things, allusion is made to things of that kind, and truth is supposed in them, and in the unfolding of the metaphor, it is deservedly brought forward: yet that Solomon's Bride is described as a type, and under the same the antitype, the Church, the Bride of Christ, is designated; that the literal and immediate sense concerns Solomon's Bride, but the mediate and mystical concerns the Church in the very words, that indeed is what must be flatly denied. Which differ even by what is called the whole heaven. For there, in metaphorical expressions, only a single sense underlies them, according to which the words are to be understood figuratively, and the metaphors are to be unfolded, and they have truth concerning the proper subject of which it is treated, not in a proper sense, but in a figurative and metaphorical one, which is uniquely intended by the Holy Spirit. Here, however, a double sense of the same words is established, and both are said to be intended by the Holy Spirit: both the immediate, as the type, concerning which the words are to be understood properly, without metaphor, and the mediate, as the antitype, concerning which those words are to be explained figuratively. By which arrangement the same word in the same place will have to be accepted both properly and improperly. Which is extremely absurd. Therefore, all the Ancients with unanimous consent understand the Church through the Bride, without a type. Basil expounded the entire Psalm, but made no mention of either Solomon or his spouse. But regarding the words, 'the Queen stood': He says it is now explained concerning the Church, about which we learned in the Canticles that she is the one perfect dove of Christ. And a little later: 'The Queen therefore stood,' namely the soul co-opted by the bridal word, no longer oppressed by the tyranny of any sin, but admitted into a share of the Kingdom of Christ: 'at the right hand,' I say, she stands by the Savior, in raiment of white, that is, in doctrines interwoven with spiritual understanding, and gravely composing herself, interspersed with flowers of variety,

& adorning religiously. With whom the rest agree.

Moreover, the honor & adornment of the Bride is described. Daughters of Kings are among your honorable ones: the consort stood at your right hand in gold of Ophir. Rivetus is entirely correct when he asks: who are these daughters of kings among the honored & dear ones of the Bridegroom? He observes: in earthly weddings they are not the same as those who accompany the Bridegroom, and the Bride herself: But in the spiritual marriage, all the friends, both male and female, of the Bridegroom and Bride constitute the Bride. Because the bride is a mystical body, and pertains to discrete quantity, not continuous. The Bride is called the whole body aggregated from the universal number of the faithful. The Daughters of Kings accompanying the Bride are the faithful considered separately, who in one body constitute the Bride, as members. And therefore the Church is described here 1. according to the whole. 2. According to the parts. According to the parts, the Daughters of Kings are among the honored ones of the Bridegroom. According to the whole, the Queen stands at your right hand. These things, I say, Rivetus [states] rightly & accurately after our blessed Gesner: Whence there will be no need to inquire, who are those daughters of Kings, differing from the Bride? concerning which Bellarmine among others is anxious: From which the daughters of Kings have delighted themselves in your honor (thus the Vulgate has it) that is, from which aromatics, which breathe from the garments and ivory houses of your humanity, the daughters of Kings, or souls of the Kingdom and exalted ones, or multitudes of peoples from various kingdoms have delighted you, while they run into the odor of your ointments. And at v. 16. virgins shall be brought to the King after her (the daughter, the Bride of the King) Her neighbors shall be brought to you: Although the Bride is unique to Christ, and she is uniquely beloved, that is, the universal Church, nevertheless after her there are also Brides of Christ, by a certain special prerogative beyond the other faithful, those souls who in the flesh have vowed their virginity to God, so that the sense may be: after the principal Bride the Church, or as Bellarmine has it then, after the mother of the Lord, all those souls who have dedicated their virginity to God shall also be brought to the nuptial chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom. These things he [says] in favor of the monastic vow. But do not those souls pertain to the universal Church itself, and are they its members? How then shall they be brought after her? To say nothing of the fact that that Monastic vow has no foundation in the Scriptures, let alone bringing a prerogative into the Church. Moreover, all the faithful are called virgins on account of the integrity of uncorrupted faith and confession, and the innocence of life 2. Corinth. 11. Apoc. 14. Matth. 25. That the discourse is here specifically, or even μοναδικῶς (uniquely) about the mother of the Lord, when the Bride of Christ is being described, can be taught neither from this passage, nor from elsewhere in the Scriptures. If, however, any distinction is to be established between the Bride and the Daughters of the King, and the virgins, the Vinarie Paraphrasts express it not badly, that the Daughters of Kings are the kingdoms and Provinces of Kings, which walk in the adornment of the Bridegroom, that is, are converted to the Bridegroom, and are adorned by him Is. 49, 18. 22. 23. But the Bride is the universal Church itself: And the companion virgins in verse 15 are the faithful, following the Church in Spirit, faith, and life, when she rightly teaches and proposes the word of God Matth. 25, 1. 4. Apoc. 14, 4. Others understand by the Daughters of Kings the churches from the gentiles, and by the Queen the Israelite consort, who will have them as companions. From these things, however, the Jewish opinion of Calvin and Grotius, and others, concerning the Daughter of the King of Egypt, and her harem, or even concubines, is easily refuted, in which Calvin is by no means consistent with himself: It must be known, he says, that it was not approved by GOD what is praised here in Solomon. And to say nothing of others, polygamy certainly displeased God immediately from the beginning. And yet concubines are placed among the BLESSINGS OF GOD: for there is no doubt that by honorable ones the Prophet signifies wives, of whom mention is made elsewhere. Thus there is no doubt for Calvin that concubines are praised here in Solomon, and placed among the blessings of God: and yet that his polygamy was not approved by God. Which are truly inconsistent. Similarly, one would not easily reconcile what is added in the same place: Although it was not lawful for Solomon to take a foreign wife: yet this too is deservedly numbered among the GIFTS OF GOD, that her affinity was sought by a most powerful King. And not undeservedly does Rivetus oppose the glosses of Calvin, because this passage deals only with a single Bride, and therefore the words of the Prophet cannot be taken concerning the other wives and concubines of Solomon. And how will what is said about many wives fit the antitype? For if more churches are imagined, the unity of the body of Christ will be torn apart: And speaking properly, there is a single Bride, who is gathered from the universal assembly of the pious, this very Calvin himself holds. But that which most strongly opposes Rivetus himself is that he takes these things κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν (by way of explanation), and considers them the same: The Daughters of Kings are among the honored ones of the Bridegroom, and the Queen stands at your right hand. For if the Daughters of Kings and the Queen are the same, it will certainly not be permitted to understand the Queen as the Daughter of Pharaoh, and the daughters of Kings as her harem, which however Rivetus contends here, and calls the Grammatical sense. He says, all these things can, and ought to be, referred to the retinue and most sumptuous cult of the Egyptian Bride of Solomon. For she had a splendid harem etc. Are the Egyptian Bride and her harem the same?

Moreover, the due office of the Bride is designated here (2.). Hear O Daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your Father's house. God the Father names her Daughter, whose exhortation this is, and thus designates the spiritual regeneration of the faithful, and requires both the diligent listening to and observation of the heavenly word, and the forgetting of one's own people: For those who have given their names to Christ, it behooves them to bid farewell to the world. Insipid is what Rivetus [says] here: This address sufficiently hints that the author of this Psalm was not a man from the common people, or some obscure person, but either a King, or one in whose court there was great authority. For otherwise these words would not befit a private man. For did not the Prophets speak in the name of God? Nor does the interpretation hold, which he pursues in favor of Calvin, concerning the daughter of Pharaoh, who ought to forget her people, and her father, and the customs and rites of her fathers, nor should she find it hard to be without her country, since her marital status brings her such a notable compensation. Those things which he relates on page 341 concerning the Church, the Bride of our King, are more correct. He calls her a daughter, who constitutes the body of the sons of God, who, having been spiritually reborn through his word, have received the adoption of sons. John 1, v. 13. He requires that she hear, which is the first among those things which pertain to the primary worship of Christ GOD. He interposes the commandment of seeing, which sight, since it is spiritual, denotes also the attention of the mind, but that for the most part which is aided by the very consensus and effect of experience. For then the kindness of God is, as it were, placed before the eyes. Finally, he adds an exhortation to the whole Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, whose also are the gifts and the promises which follow: Where, by the house of the Father, Rivet, with others, Calvin himself leading the way, understands whatever corruption we bring from the womb, or what- soever things afterwards adhere to us from a corrupt upbringing, as if transfused into us by hereditary right or education. But through the people [are signified] those things which are acquired from evil custom and conversation with the impious and idolaters, and which lead away from God, all of which must be put aside if we desire to be joined to Christ the Bridegroom. In these he follows our B. Gesner, just as in the previous explanation he followed his Calvin. For he saw that our sense was true, yet he did not wish to abandon his own Calvin, and therefore he assumed both explanations. But those cannot stand together. For who could believe that such disparate senses underlie the same words? If indeed all the words were to be understood in such clearly different significations that they could be accommodated both to the Daughter of Pharaoh and to the Church! If therefore the latter sense is correct, as Rivetus does not doubt, the former must be entirely dismissed here.

(3.) The promise is subjoined v. 12. And the King shall desire thy beauty: for he is the Lord thy God, and they shall worship him. Thus also the LXX rendered it, they shall worship him. Jerome observes in Epist. ad Princip. that the Hebrews in the Codex have, thou shalt worship him. With which Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion agree, as Theodoret reports, and likewise Augustine, Apollinaris, and the Roman Psalter. But that Solomon cannot be understood here by the King is most manifest: for it is said of the King, he is thy Lord, and they shall worship him. What therefore is more certain than that one Messiah is to be understood here, who is GOD blessed for ever, over all, whom all ought to worship Rom. IX, 5. Psalm. XCVII, 7. & LXXII, 17. Therefore these things cannot be accepted concerning the Bride of Solomon: but concerning the Church, the Bride of Christ: The King shall desire thy beauty. Although indeed the word God is not held in the Hebrew, yet the LXX and Jerome rendered it so, and it is gathered from the adoration that he is truly God, just as he was also expressly called so before. For by the word of worshipping, as Calvin does here, not only an external ceremony is noted, but by synecdoche the pious affection of rendering reverence and obedience; for just as by the name of Daughter (these are likewise Calvin's words) he gently and sweetly soothes the new Church: So also he entices with a reward, that she may willingly despise and leave whatever she has hitherto held dear for the sake of Christ. Nor is it a common consolation that we shall be in the highest delights with the Son of GOD, when we have put off our earthly nature. Here therefore the Church, which is Rivetus's explanation, hears a most sweet promise, namely that it will come to pass that she will show herself compliant, and having cast off all idolatry and profanity will dedicate herself to him alone, so that he may compensate for every trouble with his sweetest custom and most ardent love. Moreover, this Spiritual Bridegroom is truly the Lord of his Bride, because he not only created, but also acquired her with his own blood, she who came to him undowered. Which, as they are said most truly and according to the mind of the Holy Scriptures, so they can by no means consist with those things which the same Rivetus premised for the sake of his Calvin, that these things can be referred to Solomon as to a type. For if that Spiritual beauty consists in the faith and sincere charity of the mind, how is it to be understood only of external beauty? If the Lord is pointed out, who is Lord by right of creation and redemption, how is the name of Lord to be explained only of the dignity of a head of a household or a husband? If the religious adoration of the first table is commanded, how can it be explained as a command of civil adoration of the second table? Disparate senses are again heaped upon the same words, which is altogether alien to the simplicity and perspicuity of Holy Scripture.

(4.) The glory of the Bride is proclaimed, redundant from the Spiritual marriage, and some consortium of the Bridegroom's honor, namely that the Bride herself also as a Queen is to be gifted with presents: And the daughters of Tyre with gifts, all the rich of the people shall entreat thy face. Rivetus indeed says that these things agree with the happiness of Solomon, whose face the whole earth desired, and individuals brought him gifts, and among all the neighbors of Tyre 1 Kings 10, 14. 26. ch. 5, 1. But yet he is forced to acknowledge that all these things square most perfectly with Christ and the Church; for it is predicted that the peoples of Tyre and external nations will come to the Church with gifts, which they will offer to her, nay, because of her magnificence and glory communicated by Christ her Bridegroom, all the Princes of whatever people will venerate her, entreating her that she might be willing to join them to herself, and receive them united to herself into the communion of her Bridegroom. I ask therefore again, how can these be reconciled with the former? For if these words, as Rivetus confesses, are not to be restricted to the Tyrians properly so called, exclusively to other nations, but under Tyre it is necessary to understand all other regions and all Gentiles outside the Jewish people, how does Rivetus here understand only the Tyrians and King Hiram properly? Or did all the nations entreat the daughter of Pharaoh? If by the rich of the people are designated those who have been converted from the world to Christ from among the more powerful according to similar prophecies Isa. LX, 3. 10. 11. 16. ch. XLIX, 23. how can that be accepted concerning the submission of the richest peoples toward Solomon? For it is not a question of some allusion only, which I warn again, but of the grammatical and genuine sense of the words: which certainly can and ought not to be established as twofold, and since that concerning Christ must be admitted without controversy, that which those Judaizing Interpreters desire to foist upon us concerning Solomon must necessarily be dismissed.

(5.) The adornment of the Bride is celebrated in verse 15. All her glory, O daughter of the King, is from within, clothed in golden fringes, surrounded by varieties. Where Grotius, that admirer of the Jesuit Bellarmine, ought to have listened: Because David has often spoken of the beauty and adornment of the bride, lest anyone should perhaps think those things are corporeal, he meets such carnal thoughts in this place, and says, all her glory, whether of the beauty of her face or of precious garments, is from within, even if she is said to be adorned with golden fringes and surrounded by that variegated garment, all things are spiritual, are internal, and are to be sought in the heart. These things are in harmony with the text and other places of Scripture, but how jejune and cold is the commentary of Calvin throughout, whom Grotius preferred to follow, as often as he saw him adhering to the Jews, rather than any other interpreters whatsoever; even though they were otherwise esteemed by him? A double sense, he says, can exist: that the Queen is always magnificently dressed, not only when she comes into the sight of the people, but also when she sits in her chamber: or that the splendor of her adornment is not painted on to deceive the eyes of the simple, but consists of solid opulence. He also adds the explanation of certain others, which he himself also does not seem to disapprove of: Others They think (Isidorus Clarius and Vatablus) that the King invites her to himself familiarly, because soon a transition into the bedchamber is described with a great and splendid retinue. But who does not see how inept and foreign these things are to our sacred Epithalamium? Therefore, those things could not be to the palate of Rivetus, even if for the sake of his Preceptor he says they are NOT INCONVENIENTLY DEVISED, provided he acknowledges that they cannot be so conveniently adapted to the words of the Prophet. I would not wish, therefore, he says, to depart from the COMMON sense of the interpreters, referring that to the INTERIOR ornament of the Bride, that one indeed chief, even if something also appears externally which commends her: ALL interpreters, whether ANCIENT or more recent, suggest this understanding: as if he were saying, the chief SPIRITUAL ornaments are to be found internally in the heart. To which Peter seems to allude, 1 Epist. 2, v. 4. It is strange, however, that Rivetus dares to apply this remarkable description specifically to the Pharaoh's daughter. For what was so exceptional in her, by which she stood out above others regarding that interior glory? For as to the fact that Solomon looked primarily at morals, and did not marry unless he believed her to be well-behaved, and whose ornament he considered to be primarily hidden—in which choice, however, he could be mistaken—what has this to do with that INTERIOR GLORY, of which the Prophet speaks, which does not consist in certain moral virtues, such as even fall to the Gentiles, or is doubtful and ambiguous, but consists of the gracious gifts of the Holy Spirit, and is truly illustrious by the judgment of the Holy Spirit Himself? The whole, he says, is the glorious Daughter of the King within. Which is rightly said of the Bride of Christ, not likewise of the Bride of Solomon. For what is precious, as Rivetus says again, with which the Bridegroom did not adorn her, so that he might present her to himself not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing, Ephes. 5? What is not to be wondered at in her in the divisions of graces, of ministrations, of operations? St. Basil explains this without a type, concerning only the Spiritual decorum of the Church, whose words, which express the sense of the Ancient Church and are remarkable, seem worthy to be read here from T. 1. Oper. in h. Psalm. p. 225. After the soul, purged of the doctrines of old malice that are to be disapproved, has exhibited obedience to sound and salutary Doctrine, when it has already forgotten its people and its father's house, the Holy Spirit narrates those things which are about it, and since He saw its intimate purity: All, He says, the glory of the king is from within, that is, the glory of the Bride of Christ, who is henceforth adopted as the Daughter of the King, is within. This discourse clearly exhorts to the mysteries of Ecclesiastical glory to be grasped inwardly, because the decorum and beauty of the Bride is enclosed and hidden. For he who adorns himself properly, for Him indeed who sees in secret, namely the Father, and prays to Him as a suppliant, and strives for nothing but good works, not that he may be looked upon by men, but that he may deserve to become known to the eyes of God alone: this one has hidden all his glory just as the daughter of the King within. Moreover, the golden fringes, with which such a soul is entirely surrounded and variegated, are indeed stored up intimately. Do not you seek anything in this external gold, the variegated garment of the body, but rather understand that a certain cultivation is insinuated to me here, which is worthy to honor and redeem a man who was created in the image of his creator according to the word of the Apostle: Having put off the old man and put on the new, who is renewed unto knowledge according to the image of his creator. And he who puts on bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, long-suffering, meekness: such a one is redeemed with an interior garment, and is properly adorned and cultivated according to the interior man. Paul likewise warns: Put on the LORD JESUS, not according to the exterior man, but let our mind be surrounded by the memory of God. For I think that the spiritual garment is then woven through, when the operation is added as a companion to the word of doctrine. For just as a cloak is then revealed for covering the body, while the woof is woven into the warp: So when the word has obtained the first place in weaving, if actions consistent with the word are soon added, then a most decent garment of the soul, having much honesty, can be fashioned—of the soul, I say, completing its life according to virtue both in word and in deed. Thus far St. Basil.

(6.) The retinue of virgins is celebrated: The virgins shall be brought to the King after her, her neighbors shall be brought to you, they shall be brought in joy and exultation, they shall be brought into the palace (the Vulgate has temple) of the King. Although the Hebrews accept this concerning the concubines of the King, with Calvin not denying it, it does not please Rivetus, however; he says the comparison and type is much more honorable (A comparison might be admitted, or an allusion, but a type cannot be demonstrated; indeed, it is repugnant to the text, as has been shown thus far) if that whole retinue is referred to the virgin companions and attendants of the Bride. Which is to be accepted entirely concerning the Church, and concerning Spiritual virgins, and joy and exultation not worldly, but Spiritual and heavenly. St. Basil has it thus: but certain souls follow the Bride of the Lord, which have not at all received the seed of foreign Doctrines, and these indeed shall be brought to the King, following the Bride. Rivetus acknowledges this: But here is an Apostrophe to the King, to whom the Prophet turns his speech. But who is that King? Solomon? Certainly, here is more than Solomon! Let us return, therefore, to the King of Kings and his most dear Bride acquired by his own Blood. She is brought to the King, namely by ministers and spiritual paranymphs exercising the Sacred ministry; the chaste virgin is presented to her husband in garments embroidered with Phrygian needlework, that is, with the various gifts of the Spirit. Now, indeed, by the retinue or Gynaeceum, the multitude of the faithful called to the marriage of the lamb is denoted. They are called virgins, however, because of the integrity of uncorrupted faith and confession, and the innocence of life, 2 Corinth. 11, Apoc. 11, Matth. 25. They are brought to Christ, however, through the preaching of the Gospel and the Sacraments, by which they are betrothed to the one true [husband]. These things Rivetus [says] with our B. Gesner, and from the same. Which do not bear the carnal or typical sense of the Hebrews and Calvin. For where spiritual virginity is designated, in that letter the virginity of the body is not exhibited, much less are concubines indicated. It is not a question (he says of this passage, cutting his own vineyards) of the virginity of the body, but of the purity of the soul, necessary for all the faithful who are to live forever with the Lamb. Where there is talk of spiritual and heavenly joy and exultation, there certainly it is not a question of worldly joy. Where the word Palace is used metaphorically of the Church, or rather of heaven, there it ought not, nor can it, be explained properly of a material royal palace. For one and the same word, in the same place, cannot be taken at once both properly and figuratively, that is, improperly, unless one makes the Scriptures into Delphic Oracles.

(7.) The fruit of the marriage is predicted in verse 17: Instead of your fathers shall be your sons, and you shall make them princes in all the earth. These things, however, in no way fit Solomon, nor can the principle of a type have a place here. Calvin therefore twists the passage, and since he cannot understand it as referring to sons—of whom Solomon had none from his marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh—he distorts it to refer to posterity: Instead of your fathers shall be your sons. This also contributes to the excellence of the kingdom, that the posterity does not yield in dignity to the fathers, and thus the nobility of the lineage will not be diminished after the death of Solomon: because the sons who will be born from him will equal their ancestors in every excellence of virtues. Behold, ὀχεβλότητα! It is not a question now of the excellence of the kingdom, but of the fruit of the marriage, and indeed of that marriage which he has dealt with thus far, by laboriously describing the Bridegroom and the Bride. Calvin, however, wishes it to be about the marriage of the daughter of Pharaoh; yet from her Solomon received no children and left no posterity. Therefore, it is manifest, even from this verse, that the Bride cannot be understood as the daughter of Pharaoh. Nor is the discourse only about posterity, but about the very sons of the Bridegroom: nor about the dignity and excellence of the virtues of Solomon's posterity, which certainly cannot be compared with David in terms of power, nor with the Patriarchs in terms of the ornaments of virtue. And how were the sons of Solomon constituted princes by him in all the earth, i.e., according to Calvin's interpretation, with the empire so widely propagated that it can conveniently be distributed into many kingdoms? Calvin himself acknowledges that this cannot be understood of Solomon, nor could he find here anything in which Solomon typologically shadowed forth Christ alone, whence it is most manifest that our Psalm cannot be explained literally of Solomon as a type of Christ. This prophecy, says Calvin, is easily gathered to be about Christ: Because it is so far from the case that the sons of Solomon divided the provinces among themselves on account of the greatness of the kingdom, that his first heir retained only a small part, so that no one among his legitimate successors approached his power, but all were, as it were, confined to the straits of one tribe and a half. Therefore, no principle of a type holds here, neither in the children nor in the posterity of Solomon. What remains, therefore, but to acknowledge that this prophecy is simple, as Pareus calls it, and looks to Christ without a type, and that consequently the whole of this Psalm deals immediately with Christ the Bridegroom, and not under the type of Solomon: and since it is the same Person, the same King, to whom the discourse is directed and of whom the Prophet speaks, the whole Psalm is to be understood immediately of Christ, and not of Solomon as a type of Christ. Rivetus must also be added here; for he says (thus concerning this verse): It is an exposition of the fruit OF THIS MARRIAGE, namely, the most happy offspring to be born from it, which is to rule over the WHOLE WORLD. Although this could be said to Solomon and the Bride, by the law of an epithalamium, for the sake of a good omen (as if this epithalamium were written by human spirit, and not dictated by the Holy Spirit who is prescient of future things, or as if what COULD be said should be looked at here, and not rather what was certainly PREDICTED to be future by the Holy Spirit! yet in them the promise had no place, and therefore it is not to be understood of them), since it is read that the daughter of Pharaoh bore NO son to Solomon (where then is the principle of a type here?) so that in this place it is NECESSARY to look to the BRIDE THE CHURCH, once barren and afterwards made a joyful mother of children, to whom it also fits that her sons were placed as princes in all the earth. NOR indeed does THAT FIT THE POSTERITY of Solomon except in Christ. Isaiah also predicted this fruitfulness of the Church in ch. 49:18, ch. 54:1. For the former Patriarchs (says Cyril), Abraham is the father of many nations, Isaac and Jacob are the authors and propagators of their own people and their own tribes. The Church has children of many, each of whom exists as a patriarch of most numerous families, and generates entire peoples and most numerous nations for Christ and the Church. He explains it, therefore, of the Apostles, who were set over the whole World, and those who followed in the Sacred ministry, and since Christ deposited His Gospel with them, which is the scepter of His kingdom, he says with Calvin how they exercise its power. For Christ through His ministers subjected the World to Himself, and raised up for Himself as many principalities as there were Churches gathered in different regions, and through them it was brought about, which can belong to no temporal Monarch, that laws were given to the World. For, as Chrysostom notes, the Monarchs of the Romans could not give a law to the Persians, nor the Persians to the Romans. But the Apostles, in the name of Christ, gave a law to the Romans and Persians, and all other nations. And these things are concerning the Bride, and the arguments of the third class.

Fourth, a peculiar argument, and that again invincible, is supplied from the conclusion of the epithalamium. They will be mindful of your name, O Lord (in the Hebrew and Greek it is in the singular, I will be mindful, or rather I will make them mindful, so that the Vulgate may express the sense, and Jerome and Augustine, having it with her, will be mindful) unto all generations and generations; Therefore the peoples will confess to You forever and unto the age of the age. He promises, therefore, thanks to God for such innate benefits bestowed upon the whole human race, which he sang in this Psalm, to be continued until the consummation of the age, indeed unto all eternity. Which again teach that the subject of this epithalamium cannot be established as the marriage of Solomon, but that it is discussed solely concerning the spiritual marriage of Christ. We have here an adversary of Calvin confessing: THIS fits Solomon no more, who defiled the memory of his name with a base and unspeakable defection; for when he polluted the land sacred to God with the filth of superstitions, did he not bespatter himself with eternal disgrace and ignominy? Certainly he was worthy that perpetual oblivion should cover his name in burial. Rehoboam, who lost a good part of the kingdom through his foolish pride, deserved no more glory. Therefore, he could find no analogy of type here regarding the name of Solomon being commemorated in every generation: Therefore, concludes Calvin, so that the truth of the Eulogy may stand for the good, it is NECESSARY to pass to Christ (he ought to have said, to explain it immediately and in the literal sense concerning Christ, because it can be understood of no other literal sense), whose memory always flourishes and blooms. In vain does Rivetus here try to help Calvin; therefore in Solomon, he says, repeating those things which we have already brought forward from Calvin, Christ the Son of God is preached: or from him an easy transition is made to Christ the King without any interval, so that his marriage is a great mystery: which, even if it was said by the Apostle on the occasion of all conjugal love, Eph. 5. verse 15, yet in some it was more expressly adumbrated, especially in those who were peculiar types of Christ, such as Solomon was. If in Solomon as a type Christ the Son of God was preached in every generation, it is necessary that Solomon himself was preached, so that the type and the antitype may correspond.

But what Calvin denies, judging him worthy whose name perpetual oblivion should cover. Yet who will believe that a transition is made here from Solomon to CHRIST, if indeed the conclusion ought to correspond to the whole treatise, and his name is proclaimed to be commemorated here unto every generation, whose beauty, grace, fortitude, glory, marriage, and offspring the Psalmist has hitherto extolled; since the Epithalamium is continued to the end concerning one and the same subject. If, therefore, the name of the Messiah is signified here as to be proclaimed unto every generation, and not that of Solomon, it must be acknowledged that the Epithalamium was concerned with the Messiah, not with Solomon. That Conjugal love adumbrates the mystery of the Spiritual love of Christ does not prove any more that this Epithalamium in a literal and Grammatical sense respects Solomon, than any other faithful Royal spouses whatsoever. And although Solomon was a peculiar type of Christ, yet in his marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh it must be proven that he was a PECULIAR type of Christ: nay, it must also be shown that HE IS PROPOSED IN THIS PSALM as a type of Christ, and that it treats of him in the literal sense, in so far as he bore the type of Christ, which is the very thing in question, and is gratuitously assumed as certain and indubitable, by a mere begging of the question. That it does not treat here literally of Solomon, that the spiritual marriage of the Messiah is not described under him as a type, but that the Messiah himself and his nuptials are immediately the subject of this Psalm, has been demonstrated hitherto throughout the whole Psalm by invincible proofs, which show πρὸς ὄμμα (before the eyes) that Solomon cannot be understood here literally, nor the daughter of Pharaoh, nor the children of Solomon. Just as it is confessed that in this last verse the name of Solomon cannot be understood.

To which may now be added, Fifthly, the authority of the Apostle in Heb. verse 8, who clearly explains this Psalm concerning Christ, and indeed in such a way that it is most manifest that it applies to him alone and exclusively. For what the Apostle testifies was said of the Son of God and concerning the Son of God in the proper sense, cannot be affirmed to have been said of Solomon in the literal sense. What was said of the Son of God in such a way that, according to the Apostle, it applies not only to no other of men, but not even to any angel, cannot be explained of Solomon. What is said of the Son of God demonstrates that the Son of God is not only superior to the Angels, but is the true God; this in no way concerns Solomon, nor can it be understood of him. If this oracle were to apply to Solomon in the literal sense, the name of GOD would be taken improperly in it. How, therefore, can the eternal and infinite Deity of the Son of God be demonstrated from the name of God taken improperly and enunciated concerning Solomon? Thus, indeed, the illustrious prophecy concerning Christ is shaken, the signal testimony of the eternal Deity of Christ is overturned, the chief argument employed by the Apostle to demonstrate the Deity of Christ is rendered futile and useless: and what was indubitable among the Hebrews themselves (for this could not have been brought forward in proof among them if it had been exposed to doubt) is rendered most doubtful, nay, is utterly enervated. But that these things were said uniquely of the Son of GOD, the Apostle proclaims with a sonorous voice, so much so that they could not have been said of any Creature, nor of any Angel, but refer to God the Creator and his eternal throne, if we are willing to hear the Apostle: How, therefore, without impiety can those things be drawn to Solomon, or be accepted as if said of Solomon in the native and genuine sense? For thus the Apostle: And to the angels indeed he says; Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. But to the Son: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom, thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity, therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. And concerning whom those things were said in the proper and literal sense, of him the whole Epithalamium was sung; which cannot be so torn into parts that some parts treat of this Royal Spouse, and others of another, according to the letter, but as κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν (according to the letter) in the native and genuine sense it treats only of the Messiah in these two verses, so it celebrates one King and one Spouse, namely the Messiah, with his Spouse the Church, from the beginning of the hymn to the end of the same. Some refer to this concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ those words in John 12, verse 34: We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever, meaning that the present passage was there regarded.)

Which is further confirmed Sixthly from the comparison of the Song of Solomon. For since it is manifest that it treats everywhere of the same King and Spouse, and the same Queen and Spouse, from a pious and accurate consideration of the Song, we are more and more established that it has been treated in this Epithalamium of the Messiah alone, according to the paraphrastic sense, which they call Grammatical. Which will be evident in the annotations to the Song, ξὺν θεῷ (with God). Theodoret, in his preface to the Song, says: I think that Solomon wrote these things having been taught by the Father (as a Prophet, and a great Prophet indeed). For he had heard him singing thus: The Queen stands at Thy right hand, etc.

We now subjoin in the last place the consensus of Jewish and Christian Interpreters. For the Targum, which has the highest authority among the Jews, explains this Epithalamium concerning the Messiah. At verse 3: Thou art fairer, O Messiah, etc. The Spirit of Grace and Prophecy is on thy lips. And at verse 7: The throne of thy glory, O God, etc. The Jews also explain it concerning the Messiah, R. David Kimchi: The Song of the loves of the Lord to his Christ. At verse 4: The sword shall be thy glory, and although the days of Christ are peace, yet they will begin in the war of Gog, therefore he says, gird on the sword; he says the oil of gladness is called so: because the whole world will rejoice in the anointing of Christ and his mission. Concerning that, Ride upon the word of meekness, when he rides before his enemies, he will not be with pride, but will conduct himself with meekness, as in Zech. 9, he rides upon an Ass. He explains the whole Psalm according to the Grammatical sense concerning the Messiah, but by no means concerning Solomon. He mixes in carnal and impious trifles indeed concerning the Wives and Kingdom of the Messiah, but he has nothing regarding the type of Solomon; and he confesses that other, undoubtedly sounder Jews understand not the Wives of the Messiah, but by way of similitude the nations of the earth, as subjects of the Messiah. R. Aben Ezra teaches that this poem treats of King Christ the Son of David, of whom Ezek. 34. vers. 24 says, My servant David shall be King. He does indeed cite R. Gaon, who explains it concerning David, but he himself interprets it rather of the Messiah, and says that His Saints are called His companions here: but he does not explain it of Solomon in any way. R. Salomon Jarchi says, The King is God blessed be He, and through Him Kings rule, Prov. VIII. On vers. 10, They shall be brought with gladness, as Isa. LXVI. 20, The nations shall bring your brethren for an offering unto the LORD in chariots. It is false, therefore, what Grotius and Rivetus say, that the Jews understand this Epithalamium literally concerning Solomon as a type of Christ. Indeed, Nicolaus Lyranus notes regarding the Jews of his own time that they believed this Psalm was made by Mordecai about Ahasuerus for Esther. Riebera, however, in his Commentary on Hebrews 1, verse 9, observes that this Psalm is sung about the Messiah, and that the impious teachers of the Jews could not deny it, even though they take refuge in sacrilegious and violent expositions; and Genebrardus, in his Commentary on this Psalm, opposes to the Genevans, who interpret it concerning Solomon, not only the sense of all Christians, but even the more recent Rabbis. Bucer also grants us their consensus, even though he is of the same mind as Grotius and Calvin in perverting the Psalm. Bellarmine, in his explanation of this Psalm, says with the highest consensus that ALL expositors, Latin, Greek, and HEBREW, teach that this Psalm contains the praises of the Messiah and of his Spouse, the Church. Which Rivetus also confessed: Among ALL Interpreters. of the Psalms, not even excepting the HEBREWS, it is confessed that Psalm XLV is an Epithalamium poem, that is, a nuptial one, and that it is Spiritual, and therefore not to be understood σαρκικῶς (carnally), but μυστικῶς & πνευματικῶς (mystically and spiritually) concerning the Spiritual marriage between Christ and the Church. Therefore, we not unjustly oppose to Grotius, Calvin, and Rivetus the common consensus of both Jews and Christians, and even of the Syrian Church (which prefixes to the Psalm a title embracing this kind of argument and summary: A Psalm said by the Sons of Korah in the days of Moses; the birth of the Messiah: And concerning the Church and the glorious virtue of the Lord: or as Viccars has it from the Paris edition: A Psalm of the Sons of Korah written in the days of Moses concerning the resurrection of Christ and his power). Although Rivetus objects that, saving that consensus, the question is still agitated whether this Poem was written on the occasion of the nuptials of Solomon, so that under the type of Solomon the Bridegroom and the Egyptian Bride, to whom the Psalm is referred, κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν (according to the letter) in the FIRST LITERAL sense, the majesty and amplitude of the kingdom of Christ is depicted as if under an image; which he says is the COMMON opinion of the HEBREWS, which most Interpreters among the Reformed embrace, CALVIN, BUCER, JUNIUS, and others, and among the Papists, Jansenius; but as Rivetus himself admits in these matters that Calvin with his followers judaize, and depart from the common consensus of ancient and recent Interpreters, so it is by no means true that he asserts the COMMON opinion of the Jews stands on Calvin's side; the contrary is clear from what has already been said. A distinction had to be made between the ancient and the more recent Jews, although even among the latter some are sounder than Calvin: And Jansenius is undeservedly swept away into those parties; the explanation itself, however much Rivetus may apply a new crust to it, will not easily approve itself to anyone who has properly weighed the arguments adduced. The question is not about the occasion of the composed hymn, which it will by no means be proven to have been the nuptials of Solomon, nor could any foundation for this matter be produced thus far; indeed, the title itself is repugnant, making the sons of Korah the authors of the Epithalamium, as we observed before: but the question is about the argument of the Psalm and its literal sense. But that it is the nuptials of Solomon, there is nothing here in the whole Epithalamium that even obscurely teaches it, let alone clearly convinces it: indeed, the whole context powerfully convinces that it is not about the nuptials of Solomon. To say nothing of what some urge, that the nuptials of Solomon with the daughter of the Idolater Pharaoh would have been repugnant to the express command of GOD in Deut. VII, nor does the opinion of the Hebrews, that agreements were entered into concerning religion, so that according to the law of Moses the daughter of Solomon would worship JEHOVAH, stand on firm footing, or sufficiently agree with 1 Kings, chapter XI, verse 12. Where Beza thinks that marriage is expressly reproved in Chapter 1 to the Hebrews, whence Beza also went into all other things here from his teacher Calvin, to whom the whole Psalm seems merely allegorical, not typical: if indeed he wishes that the Psalmist looked to no history or past event, but only described the Spiritual marriage of Christ by words borrowed from the likeness of temporal nuptials between some King and a Queen, and proposed that sense to himself primarily and immediately, not what the words sound everywhere, but what agrees with Christ and the Church only in Spiritual conjunction, so that the literal and proximate sense is that which explains the whole matter spiritually. Similarly Amesius in his lectures on the Psalms of David. Although in the allegorical phrases, which are used in almost the whole Psalm, some respect is had to the glory of Solomon and his nuptials with the daughter of Pharaoh, there was nevertheless nothing either in the Daughter of Pharaoh, or in his Marriage with Solomon, which COULD SUSTAIN THE CHARACTER OF A TYPE in this mystery. Junius also, however much he constitutes Solomon as a type of Christ in his paraphrase or summary Biblical explanation, is nevertheless so far from admitting that type in his parallels, book III, to Hebrews I, that he even refutes it. For he says that almost every verse has things which no one could conveniently interpret concerning Solomon. And afterwards: What is it to the Church of GOD that the marriage of Solomon is celebrated in her assemblies, and celebrated at this time also, as the inscription demands? Certainly, since God is the author both of writing the Psalm and of delivering it in the Church and singing it in her Sacred assemblies and explaining it, we cannot in good faith but accept the PSALM concerning the eternal and not temporal marriage of Christ and NOT SOLOMON with the CHURCH; which marriage alone is salutary to the Church of God, and to be celebrated by her most religiously after all human memory. Finally, Pareus, although he attempted to defend his Calvin against B. Hunnius, nevertheless had to admit that most of the ancients wished for the Spiritual marriage of Christ with his Church to be sung literally under no type: nor could he disapprove of their opinion, both because almost every verse has something more divine or greater than what could apply to a natural King: and also, because the SOUNDER HEBREWS themselves admit that the Psalm treats of the Messiah, and the Chaldean Targum expressly names Christ several times. He acknowledges, therefore, that the sounder Hebrews did not establish Solomon as the type here, a point to be observed against Rivet. Although he adds that Calvin’s opinion is also not to be rejected, because Solomon bore the type of Christ, and many things can in some way agree with him according to history, and Calvin does not apply everything to Solomon, but only certain things, while certain things he applies to Solomon IN NO WAY: it is nevertheless entirely certain that he cannot but reject the opinion which explains the Psalm according to the letter concerning Solomon as the type of Christ, which maintains that nothing concerning Solomon is sung here, and that not the marriage of SOLOMON, but of Christ, is described according to the letter: while, however, it is admitted that certain things in no way agree with Solomon, it is most evident that in those things it is certainly not a matter of Solomon, and consequently that Solomon is not that King of whom it is sung according to the letter in this Psalm, because it is not of more than one King that it is treated according to the letter. Although Pareus spares the truth, when he says that that King is called God absolutely here, and has an eternal throne, and that he is anointed above his fellows, and that he has sons not yielding to their fathers in number and excellence: Calvin says that it applies IN NO WAY to Solomon; How Calvin adapted those things to Solomon, and perverted them, we have noted regarding each point. Finally, although Pareus says it is not only far more tolerable but also safer to refer the Psalm to Christ under a certain type, than to make the Psalm merely allegorical without a type and without a certain letter (which he imputes to Blessed Luther through Satanic calumny, as Blessed Hunnius demonstrated), and thinks that whichever opinion one follows, whether that of Calvin concerning Solomon, or that of the ancients concerning Christ, who explain the Psalm according to the letter, one will not err, in Calv. Orthod. p. 229. 234. yet in his Commentary on Hebrews c. 1. he produced second thoughts that are wiser, refuting Calvin's opinion among the Jews, and acceding to the opinion of the ancients: The Jews understand that Psalm as if it were an Epithalamium chanted for the wedding of Solomon with the daughter of Pharaoh. But that marriage contracted with an infidel spouse is not obscurely censured in sacred history. Nor indeed can those things which the Apostle brings forward apply to Solomon IN ANY WAY. Therefore it seems there should be NO DOUBT that the whole Psalm is an allegorical poem about the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church, of the same subject matter as the Song of Songs, which is ascribed to Solomon. Calvin indeed interpreted it concerning Solomon and Christ alike, under the aspect of a type; for which name he was most severely lacerated by Hunnius. But it has been solidly shown in Calvinus Orthodoxus l. 2. c. 31, that neither is Calvin alone in that opinion, nor is anything conceded to the Jews by this. But Blessed Hunnius evidently showed that he named no one else, besides Musculus, a follower of Calvin, than Cornerus, whose explanation, however, differs greatly from the inventions of Calvin, and that this one also Judaizes entirely, and greatly undermines the clear testimony and Apostolic demonstration of the Deity of Christ. If the name of God is taken improperly, according to the literal and genuine sense of the Psalmist, and the eternal throne is said to be so only regarding the long duration of the Solomonic Kingdom, how, I beseech you, will the eternal and immense Deity of the Son of God, most properly so called, be solidly and invincibly demonstrated from this oracle? Calvin indeed says that it always remains firm that Christ alone is this King, the Bridegroom of the Church, the eternal and true God, whether it is said that the spiritual marriage with the Church is celebrated here under no type, or under some type of Christ, provided that all things are fully and solidly referred to Christ. But how can those things which treat of Solomon according to the letter and the sense intended by the Holy Spirit, and describe his marriage, be fully and solidly referred to Christ, or to the spiritual marriage of Christ; how can they demonstrate Christ to be the eternal and true God, which according to the proper sense of the Holy Spirit speak metaphorically or improperly of the power and divinity of Solomon? How can Solomon, if he had been the greatest type of Christ, in his marriage with Pharaoh's daughter, which indeed cannot be taught by any, I say any, document from the Scriptures, be constituted a type of the eternal and true Deity of Christ?

Thus therefore Pareus pleaded the cause of Calvin, which is also that of Grotius. Rivetus, however, defends it no better: judging that neither opinion is improbable, nay rather, that a single one can and ought to be forged from the two, namely that of certain Jews and that of Calvin concerning Solomon, and that of all the Fathers and Christian Interpreters concerning Christ explaining the text according to the letter: which Rivetus also attempted in his commentary, with a great part of the explanation and words of both transcribed, concerning Solomon with Calvin, and concerning Christ with Blessed Gesner: but how unhappily he attempted that, has already been shown.
