In this life, however, we have these things under the shadow and under the covering of the wings of the Sun of righteousness, and we are righteous only by faith on account of him; then we shall also be truly righteous in ourselves. This scepter is therefore straight, because the doctrine of Christ and the laws of this kingdom are most straight and most pure, namely that we should believe in Christ and love him and our neighbor; in this law there is nothing of vice, but there is in us, because we do not believe enough, we do not love enough, we are not strong enough in tribulation, and yet because we are under that shadow of Christ, who is a pure lover of God and men, we therefore enjoy his benefit, and are accounted holy even in this life. Thus, first, in the law there is no vice, in the scepter there is no crookedness, for the word is pure, which promises grace and teaches to love God. This is the rectitude of the Scepter. Then, in us also there is nothing of vice, first as regards our head. For Christ absorbs our sins. Second, as regards the future life, in which the justice, which we now believe, will be revealed. This is blessed Luther, piously and solidly, according to his custom. One could also be warned about the fact that Grotius says the preaching of the Gospel was first predicted by Christ, which, said in the Socinian sense, is most false. Everywhere he sacrilegiously despoils the doctrine of the Old Testament of the Gospel: But there will be a more convenient place to speak of that elsewhere. Pareus on Hebrews 8: He calls it a straight scepter from the effect, because he directs his kingdom, that is, the citizens of the kingdom, to perfect equity and rectitude. He says, however, that this Scepter is both the omnipotence of the Son, who sustains and moderates all things, and the grace of the Spirit, which directs the citizens of his kingdom to justice, and finally the dispensation of the word and Sacraments, which kindles faith in the hearts of the elect and directs those justified by faith on the way of rectitude to eternal glory. By what right, therefore, could Calvin explain this Scepter literally concerning the Solomonic Scepter? With what conscience did Pareus undertake to defend Calvin?

Latin:

Vers. 7.

SEDES TUA DEUS IN SECULUM SECULI) Potest ex Hebræo verti : Sedes tua, Deus (durans in ) sæcula & æta- tes. Sedes, id est, firmitas.

Geminam ςρεβλότητα paucis verbis exhi- buit, utramque prorsus detestandam in Judæorum & Arianorum gratiam sine dubio excogitatam.Dum primo per sedem non Thronum intelligi vult, aut Re- gnum, prout vocis hujus ἔμφασις, & usus consue- tus, quo sedes de throno, & consequenter vel meto- nymice de Regno dici solet, nec non addita vox Sce- ptri, quæ regno convenit, & mentio unctionis, quæ ob Regnum fieri consvevit, ut & virtutum Regiarum illustrium, dilectionis justitiæ & odii iniquitatis, tum auctoritas etiam Apostoli Ebr. 1, 8. de throno & re- gno vocem accipientis, luculenter postulat : Et ab omnibus Interpp. hactenus consentienti suffragio vox illa accepta fuit: Sed FIRMITATEM signifi- cari ait: sine exemplo Scripturæ : sine ratione novæ interpretationis, qui nemini hactenus facile in mentem venit. Tum vero sensum testimonio il- lustri prorsus alium affingit Grotius, & quum communi Interpp. Christianorum calculo Deitas Christi ac Thronus ejus æternus hic stabiliatur, imo ab Apostolo ipso ad asserendam æternam Deitatem Christo hoc vaticinium adferatur, nova & hactenus inaudita versione hanc ei mentem eripere conatur, singula pervertens verba, sedem, uti dixi, in firmi- tatem transformans,nomen Dei,quod casu vocan- di est adhibitum, teste Apostolo, in casum nomi- nandi commutans, & duratione throni Regis hu- jus, qui in seculorum secula dicitur persistere, negle- cta, Dei durationem substituens; denique loco propriæ figuratam surrogans propositionem; cum sedes Regis hujus dicatur in æternum durare, sedem vel firmitatem Regis hujus Deum metonymice fa- cit, quia causa est firmitatis istius; atque ut hæc ita pervertere possit, de suo vocem ingerit παρενθετι- xῶς Deus (durans in) secula, quæ nec in textu appa- ret, nec colligi ex eodem potest. Quid enim lu- culentius, quam quod compellet Propheta hic Re- gem illum,ad quem hactenus sermonem suum di- rexit? quem pronominibus secundæ personæ no- tanter expressit, & in casu vocandi compellavit, Speciosus (sc. TU) forma præ filiis hominum: Diffu- sa est gratia in labiis TUIS, propterea benedixit TE Deus in æternum, ACCINGERE gladio TUO su- per femur TUUM POTENTISSIME (en ex- pressum vocandi casum!) Specie TUA, & pulchri- tudine TUA INTENDE, prospere PROCEDE, & REGNA, & deducet TE mirabiliter dextera TUA. Sagittæ TUÆ acutæ, populi sub TE ca- dent. Ut ergo hactenus ipsum compellavit, ita porro eundem nunc sic compellat: Sedes TUA, Deus, in seculum seculi. Deum vocans, quem an- tea POTENTISSIMUM in casu vocativo appel- lavit, & de cujus throno egit. Quid certius,quam quod hic non Deum Patrem, ejusque æternitatem describat, sed in descriptione Regis sui, quem cele- brare inceperat, pergat? cujus pulchritudinem, fa- cundiam, fortitudinem, successum, dexteram, sagittas hactenus descripsit, ejus nunc thronum exhibet; quod in seculum seculi duret, & sceptrum, quod re- ctissimum & mera rectitudo, & administrationem, & unctionem ac splendorem. Alienum ergo fuerit, cum antecedentia & consequentia occupentur in Rege describendo, hic ubi thronus ejus sistitur, nullo e- logio eundem ornari, nullumque addi ejus ἀξίω- μα, sed loco illius DEI περίφρασιν substitui: ac ἀπροσδιονύσως Dei Patris æternitatem ingeri,ubi de throni Sponsi duratione agendum erat. Quid e- videntius, quam quod non LXX. tantum Seniores, sed ipse etiam Spiritus Sanctus Ebr. 1, 8. in casu vo- cativo acceperit vocem Deus, ac Christi nostri Dei- tatem inde adstruxerit, thronique simul ejusdem æternitatem hic designari docuerit? Et ad Angelos quidem dicit: qui facit Angelos suos spiritus, & mi- nistros suos flammam ignis: Ad Filium autem: Thro- nus tuus Deus in seculum seculi. Filium sic compel- lari & nominari, ait: cum ad Filium illa dicta affe- rit. Et nomen ὁ θεὸς in casu vocandi, quoad sensum, adhibet, uti solent Græci sic adhibere. Atque ex hoc Oraculo demonstrat, Filium Dei Deum esse, quum Angeli creaturæ tantum Dei sint: Filium Dei thro- num æternum obtinere, quum Angeli ad ministe- rium creati sint. Detestatione dignum est, quod Grotius in Psalmo explicando magis Judæorum te- rat vestigia, & Arianorum, quam Christianorum & Catholicorum. Similem enim in modum sententi- am Judæi pervertunt R. Aben-Ezra cum R. Gaon: Thronum tuum Deus stabiliet; vel Thronus tuus est Thronus Dei: uti Salomon super thronum Dei sedisse dicitur 1. Par. 29, 23. Sed viderunt tamen probe Judæi, nomen אלהים hic debere accipi in casu vocativo: non tantum Rabbi David Kimchi, sed etiam R. Aben-Ezra: ideoque R. Aben - Ezra hanc notam adhibuit; Rex vocatur Deus, ut Exod. 22, 28. vocem Dei improprie accipiendam esse, uti judices Dii di- cuntur indigitans. Thargum certe Chaldaicum agnoscit, Messiam hic Deum vocari. Thronus glo- riæ tuæ ô Deus. Sed quanta execratione dignum ju- dicabimus, quod Grotius, in gratiam Judæorum, Apostolicam etiam Interpretationem hic perver- tere, & Argumentum Apostoli penitus evertere non veritus sit. Pro ô Deus, inquit annot. ad Ebr. 1, 8. in Hebræo est אלהים, quod nomen pluribus qui- dem sive Angelis, sive Judicibus dari solet: at cum uni tribuitur, Deo soli convenit: quia tunc oratio est ἐλλει- πτικὴ pro אלוה אלהים, ut alibi diximus (Nulla o- pus est ellipsi, nec probari ea potest solide: myste- rium autem subesse pluralitatis personarum, invicta demonstratione hujus mysterii cap. 1. evicimus) Sen- sus ergo est: Deus ipse est sedes tua perpetua: id est, si Salomonem respicimus: sicut sedes inconcussos tenet homines, ita Deus te semper in regno sustentabit: Si vero Christum: Deus ipse te sustentabit in regno nunquam desituro. Sic geminus & plane disparatus sensus iisdem verbis affingitur, ut verba in seculum seculi de Christo æternitatem notent: non autem æ- ternitatem, sed diuturnitatem notent de Salomone: quod de throno explicatur ab Apostolo, per Meta- phoram novam de sustentatione intelligitur, Deusque sedi comparatur, ob stabilitatem, sine exemplo Scri- pturæ, quia nuspiam Deus dicitur thronus vel sedes hominis, quem sustentat: ac prior glossa ad Psal- mos tradita deseritur. Hic enim sedi perpetuitas: ad Psalmum vero 45. Deo perpetua duratio tribui- tur. Et nomen אלהים ὁ θεὸς quod Apostolus Fi- lio Dei tributum esse disertis verbis docet, ex quo etiam ejus summam supra Angelos ὑπεροχὴν de- monstrat, non de Filio Dei, sed de Deo Patre ex- plicatur, totiq; probationi Apostoli nervus incidi- tur. Si Apostolus vocem ὁ θεὸς habuisset pro sub- jecto propositionis, & casu nominativo, non interpo- suisset commata, sed simpliciter dixisset ὁ θρόν- σχ ὁ θεὸς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: sed addita commata στρεβλότη- τα Grotii nullatenus ferunt, ὁ θρόν[ος] σχ ὁ θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Unde hactenus nemo inter Dd. & Interpp. inventus fuit, qui dubitaret saltim, quin casus vo- candi hic obtineat, & Apostolus Messiam voce Dei nuncuparit, atqs eo etiam argumento excellentiam supra Angelos, imo Deitatem, quam probare insti- tuerat, demonstrarit. Notissimum enim est, quod nominativum significatione vocativi adhibeant Græci per Atticismum κατ’ ἀντίπτωσιν, quod à LXX. Interpp. factum Psal. 51, 3. 60, 1. 22, 1. & in N.T. est. Matth. 22, 46. Luc. 18. 13. unde Aquila in Psalmo nostro evidentiæ causa vocem Elohim red- didit θεὲ ô Deus, Hieronymus vero in Latino trans- tulit Dee, cujus verba adscribere juvat ex Epist. ad Princip. virgin. Tom. 3. p. 108. Duas personas, ejus qui unctus est Dei, & qui unxit, intellige. Unde & Aquila Elohim אלהים verbum Hebraicum, non no- minativo casu, sed vocativo interpretatur, dicens, θεὲ, & nos propter intelligentiam Dee posuimus, quod Latina Lingua non recipit, ne quis perverse putet Deum dilecti & amantissimi & Regis bis Patrem no- minari. Quanquam enim Pater in Filio, & Filius in Patre: & alterutrum sibi & habitator & thronus sint, tamen in hoc loco ad Regem, qui Deus est, sermo dirigitur, & dicitur ei, quod imperium ejus (hoc e- nim intelligo thronum, juxta illud, quod scriptum est: De fructu ventris tui ponam super thronum tuum) finem non habeat: quod quidem & Mariæ nunciavit Angelus: Dabit ei Dominus Deus thronum David Patris sui, & regnabit super domum Jacob in sæcula, & regni ejus non erit finis. Et tam luculentum, hic compellari Messiam, ut Sociniani etiam ipsi, qui o- mnes fidiculas ad detorquenda testimonia Deita- tis Christi adhibere consueverunt, id agnoscere co- acti fuerint. Crellius lib. 1. de Deo & attribut. div. cap. 9. fatetur, illustre hic exemplum haberi, quod Christus Elohim appelletur. Racovienses in vers. Germ. ita reddunt: Dein Stul, O GOtt, bleibt in alle Ewigkeit: Conf. Comment. Schlicht. in Epist. ad Hebr. ad cap. 1, 8. Enjedinus quidem glossam illam primus hic protulit, in Expl. locor. V. & N.T. ad Ebr. 1, 8. p. 389. à quo eandem Grotius accepit, quam proinde, ut videas collusionem cum Arianis, adscribere juvat: Possunt, inquit, illa verba sic com- mode explicari, ut vox Deus nec de Salomone, nec de Christo dicatur, neque sit vocativi casus, sed nominati- vi, & intelligatur de Deo Patre tum Salomonis tum Christi, hoc sensu: Deus est thronus tuus in secu- lum: id est, Deus tibi thronum firmabit usque in se- culum. Sed eam glossam adeo inconvenientem ju- dicarunt cæteri, ut nemo Enjedinum sequi volue- rit,sed palam testati sint, hic Christum Deum vocari. Recte Rivetus: distortam esse expositionem quis non videt? Quis enim unquam sic loquitur, aut quod ex- emplum afferent, in quo verbum desit, quod maxime expressum oportuit? Quis etiam prohibebit, si quod- vis ex lubitu comminisci aut supplere liceat, ut ali- quis æque impius suppleat vocem, destruet, vel collidet.

Vers. eod. VIRGA DIRECTIONIS, VIRGA REGNI TUI) Per sceptrum Regium in Salomone μετωνυμικῶς intel- ligitur ratio regiminis: in Christo sermo Evangelii, ab ipso primum prædicatus.

Hæc, & quæ ad sequentem versum notamus, è Grotianis ad Ebr. 1, 8. annotatis hic adjicere visum fuit, ut eo plenius commenta ejus discutiantur. Sic vero geminus iterum fingitur sensus prorsus dis- paratus ejusdem propositionis. Et de Salomone explicatur, quod ipsi nullo pacto convenit. Nam de sceptro ejusmodi hic agitur, quod æternum est æterni Throni, quod cum virtute mirabilia patran- te, cum gladio & sagittis corda ipsa penetrantibus conjunctum, quod justissimum & æquissimum, nec ulla unquam injustitiæ labe contaminatum, quod amorem justitiæ & odium iniquitatis summum in- fert, ad quod gerendum donorum immensorum, communicatio requiritur, omnipotentiæ divinæ omniscientiæ & omnipræsentiæ, quia per totum or- bem gerendum: vi cujus principes super universam terram constituuntur : quod adorationis ἀξίωμα importat ; cujus gloria celebranda est in omnem ge- nerationem, imo in omnem æternitatem. Quæ certe nullatenus sceptro Salomoneo, sed unice Messiæ nostri sceptro conveniunt. Describitur potissimum hic regnum ab æternitate & rectitudine. Æternitas autem intelligitur non secundum quid dicta , sed vere infinita: Quia non tantum vox עֹולָם adhibetur, sed additur ei etiam particula עַד, quæ perpetuita- tem notat, & voci עֹולָם addita', absolutam æterni- tatem infert, ut Psal. 10, 16. & alibi, unde agnoscit Rivetus, hoc Salomoni proprie non competere, nec ulli regno terræ posse attribui, quia regna illa habent suas peridos & limites, quibus circumscripta sunt; Christo autem regnum hoc competere ex Es. 9, 7. Dan. 7, 14. Luc. 1, 33. constat. Atque in eo consentiunt omnes Christiani interpretes , æternum regnum hic describi; Unde ultro consequitur, non posse verba illa de Salomone explicari. Optime hic B. Luthe- rus noster Tom. 3. Jenens. Lat. in enarratione Psalmi hujus p. 454. Sedes tua , i. e. thronus tuus regius est æternus. Est libera confessio ac plena admirationis, quod ante revelatum Evangelium predicit ejusmodi Regem, cui non succedat alia persona, sed qui æternus administret regnum suum in secula. Non ergo potest intelligi Psalmus de regno temporali, aut de Rege, qui tantum sit homo. Et postmodum : Patet igitur ex hoc loco, Christum esse verum hominem (quia dicitur esse speciosus præ filiis hominum) & tamen esse quoque Regem non temporalem, sed æternum, hoc est, verum etiam Deum, qui quanquam mortuus , sit tamen re- surrexerit à morte. Nam mortem vincere non est ho- minis aut creaturæ. Sicut enim tota creatio unius Dei est, ita quoque vitam, quæ ipsa quoque creatura Dei est, nemo præter Deum creat. Consequitur igi- tur Christum verum esse Deum, quia vitam creat, & mortem devorat.

Alterum sceptri attributum est rectitudo sum- ma & absoluta: quia sceptrum dicitur rectitudinis, id est, summe rectum. Nullus est Regum, qui non quandoque à rectitudine deflectat, sive id sciens, prudens faciat, seu ex infirmitate, cui omnes ob- noxii sumus, labatur. At de hoc Rege simpliciter dici potest, sceptrum tuum, sceptrum rectitudinis, quod uni Christo convenit. Præclare iterum B. Lu- ther: Cætera regna, quantumcunque ea sint felicia & bene constituta, tamen habent infinita vitia, adeo ut impossibile sit unam Politiam invenire, in qua non hæ- reant plurima & maxima peccata. Sunt enim mix- ta tyrannide, insipientia, negligentia, omnibus cupidi- tatibus gloriæ, libidinis, vindictæ, avaritiæ, ita ut ne- cesse sit eum qui regit, multis facere injuriam. Sed in regno Christi non est ullum vitium, non sit ulla inju- ria, non toleratur injustitia, ne in puncto quidem. So- lus Christus in suo regno habet sceptrum rectum. Qua- re hoc ? Quia Rex noster habet verbum Dei, quod est purum, etiam PUNCTO MATHEMATICO. Christi regnum nullum patitur vitium, idque duplici ratione. I. Ratione Legis divinæ Quia patimur ar- gui & judicari peccata nostra. Quanquam enim Christus in vita nostra peccata tolerat, non tamen to- lerat in lege & doctrina. Sed lex est purissima, & pu- rissime occidit peccatum. II. Ratione capitis & Re- gis nostri, in quem credimus. Nam quoad Christum nihil in nobis est vitiosum, sed quoad nos sumus in- quinatissimi, & pleni concupiscentia, timore mortis desperatione. Christus autem non est talis, quia de e scriptum est: Non est inventus dolus in lingua ejus Quando igitur in eum credimus, reputamur propte eum absoluti, justi in fide; deinde post mortem huju carnis, in altera vita attingemus punctum Mathe maticum justitiæ, & habebimus in nobis illam abso lutam justitiam, quam jam credentes in Christum imputative habemus tantum merito Christi. Tum autem, cum ista revelabuntur in futura vita, aberit universa tyrannis mortis, ut nullus timor, pallor nul- lus in nobis hæreat, sed sint omnia suavissima & ju- cundissima. In hac autem vita habemus ista sub um- braculo, & sub velamento alarum Solis justitiæ, ac fide tantum justi sumus propter ipsum, tunc etiam in nobis vere justi erimus. Est igitur hoc sceptrum re- ctum, quia doctrina Christi, & leges regni hujus sunt rectissimæ & purissimæ, nempe ut credamus in Chri- stum & diligamus eum ac proximum; in hac lege ni- hil est vitii, sed in nobis est, quia nos non satis credi- mus, non satis diligimus, non sumus satis fortes in tri- bulatione, & tamen quia sumus sub isto umbraculo Christi, qui est purus dilector Dei & hominum, ideo fruimur ejus beneficio, & reputamur sancti etiam in hac vita. Sic primo in lege non est vitium, in sceptro nulla est curvitas, verbum enim est purum, quod pro- mittit gratiam, & docet diligere Deum. Hæc est re- ctitudo Sceptri. Deinde in nobis quoque nihil est vitii, primum quoad caput nostrum. Christus enim absor- bet peccata nostra. Secundo quoad futuram vitam, in qua justitia, quam nunc credimus, revelabitur. Hæc B. Lutherus pie ac solide pro more suo. Mo- neri etiam poterat de eo, quod a Christo primum dicat Grotius prædicatum sermonem Evangelii, quod sensu Sociniano dictum falsissimum est. Ubique Vet. Testam. doctrina Evangelii sacrilege spoliat: Sed de eo alias commodior erit dicendi locus. Pa- reus ad Ebr. 8. Sceptrum rectum ab effectu dicit, quia ad æquitatem & rectitudinem perfectam dirigit regnum suum, hoc est, cives regni. Hoc vero Sce- ptrum esse ait, tum omnipotentiam Filii, qui susten- tat & moderatur universa, tum Spiritus gratiam, quæ cives regni sui ad justitiam dirigit, tum denique verbi & Sacramentorum dispensationem, quæ fi- dem accendit in cordibus electorum & fide justifi- catos in via rectitudinis dirigit ad gloriam æter- nam. Quo jure ergo Sceptrum hoc ad literam de Salomoneo Sceptro Calvinus explicare potuit? Qua conscientia tueri Calvinum suscepit Pareus?

## 45:7
Verse 8.

THOU HAST LOVED RIGHTEOUSNESS, AND HATED INIQUITY, THEREFORE GOD, THY GOD, HATH ANOINTED THEE WITH THE OIL OF GLADNESS ABOVE THY FELLOWS) Solomon loved righteousness, and hated injustice, indeed from his early age, therefore above others, not only his fellow countrymen, but also his brothers, he was chosen by God as King 1 Chron. 28, which is signified by anointing 1 Kings 1, 34. Jesus, while He lived a mortal life, taught nothing else than all things just and honest by word and example, reproving things contrary to these. Therefore, after death, having been raised, He obtained a dignity above all men, nay even above the Angels, which dignity is here signified in human fashion by the word anointing. Thus God made Him Christ Acts 2, 36. There are, however, two nominatives אֱלֹהִים אֱלֹהֶיךָ that God, whom you worship. The Chaldean and many Rabbis interpret this passage concerning the Messiah.

There are many most perverse things in this gloss, which deserve detestation. First, that he again thrusts in Solomon, who can no more be thrust into this than the preceding verse, since the discourse is uniquely about Christ. Which Pareus also was forced to acknowledge, while he went to defend his Calvin. Certain things, he says, in NO WAY suit Solomon, such as that this King is called absolutely God, having an eternal throne, that he is anointed above his fellows, in Calv. Orthod. page 228. Which he executes more broadly in Epist. to Heb. 1, 8. Nor indeed can those things, which the Apostle brings forward, suit Solomon BY ANY REASON. For was Solomon God? But the Psalmist calls Him, whom he addresses, God. Kings indeed are called Gods, but not absolutely, as here: Your throne, O God. For was Solomon's throne eternal? It was scarcely forty years. In his son, his kingdom was soon most unhappily torn apart. Nor was the scepter of his kingdom always straight. For he oppressed the people with heavy and unjust exactions, which finally gave cause for complaints and seditions. But did Solomon always love justice and equity? Nay, being too woman-obsessed against the law, he variously violated divine and human law, and from the true worship of God he shamefully fell away into idolatry—which was the highest iniquity—by the seduction of women. This is Pareus: he adds that what is said about the anointing, above his fellows, applies to Solomon in some way, but in the explanation of v. 9 he corrects this and understands it of Christ alone: Our King, he says, is not indeed read to have been anointed with external oil, but imbued with the Oil of the Spirit without measure. ABOVE HIS FELLOWS, that is, his brothers, who are the faithful elect: For he has been made a FELLOW of these by the assumption of flesh and blood, as he will teach in chapter 2, where he will explain the reason for this etymology. For we are partakers (μέτεχοι) of Christ, because he himself partook (μετέσχε) of our flesh and blood in like manner (παραπλησίως). Above all these fellows, therefore, Christ the firstborn is anointed with his anointing, not only so that he might be happier, more powerful, and more glorious than all others, but especially so that he might pour out the Oil of his gladness upon his fellows, and that we all might receive from his fullness. Rivetus likewise acknowledges that these things apply to none but Christ. Which two verses, 7 and 8 of Psalm 45, must be diligently weighed. Since the Apostle in Hebrews 1:8 refers them IMMEDIATELY to Christ, to whom they certainly belong ALONE. Therefore they do not apply to Solomon, much less do they speak of Solomon in an immediate sense.

Furthermore, secondly, that gloss of Grotius is colder than ice itself, concerning the love of justice in Solomon from his earliest age. For however small these things are that can be predicated of him, they are for this PURPOSE ONLY, and such a sublime eulogy of a perfect love of justice and hatred of iniquity, which fails by no degrees and deviates in no way; for if it failed anywhere, or deviated, whether in love of justice or hatred of iniquity, it could not be absolutely predicated: you have loved justice and hated iniquity, much less could it be inferred that therefore your God has anointed you, because of the love of justice, and that Solomon was preferred to all others, even his brothers; this is nowhere taught in the Scriptures: because the promise was made to David concerning the Son as heir to the throne, therefore no one could be chosen from the other commoners, nor is it to be judged that because Solomon was chosen, he surpassed all other commoners in love of justice and hatred of iniquity. Nor indeed was Solomon preferred to his brothers by his own merit: But by the singular grace of God. Why many words? The Apostle clearly teaches that not Solomon, but Christ, is established as the subject here. "But to the Son" (πρὸς δὲ τὸν ὑιὸν) v. 9. To whose authority and proof Grotius here openly rebels. All Christian interpreters, therefore, with the highest consensus understand these things of Christ: and some indeed of the love of justice and hatred of injustice, as they belong to him by nature, others as they are seen in the administration of the kingdom: but most correctly those who understand them in both ways: because not only the internal propensity toward justice and the detestation of injustice, but also the exercise of it in this King carries us away into admiration and celebration.

Thirdly, Grotius's explanation of Christ is extremely meager, that he is said to have loved justice and hated iniquity because, while living his mortal life, he taught nothing but all things just and honest by word and example, arguing against things contrary to these; because it looks not only to his mortal life, but to his universal kingdom: nor would that be so singular and proper to Christ, since the Prophets also taught just and honest things by their word and example, and argued against things contrary to these. Grotius seems to imitate the Socinians and other heretics, who leave hardly anything divine to Christ here, just as Estius observes in this place regarding the Nestorians, that they derived an argument from this to prove that Christ is not the Son of God by nature, but that he earned the prerogative of adoption by the excellence of his works, which is also known regarding the Neo-Arians. But Catholic Doctors have received this eulogy in a far more illustrious manner, just as it is far more illustrious by the very sound of the words, and it is received by the Apostle in a most eminent manner, which surpasses the holiness of the Angels themselves. For the Apostle brings forward all these things to show the eminence of the Son above the Angels. For although some make the particle THEREFORE (PROPTEREA) here illative—for the reason that you have loved justice and hated iniquity, God has anointed you—they did not, however, constitute the merit of the anointing in it properly so called, but assigned it as a reward. Jerome in his Epistle to Principia the virgin, and Ambrose on this passage, certainly referred the cause of the anointing to a natural hatred of injustice and a divine love of justice. Concerning which also Basil the Great in his homily on this Psalm. Other men often attain a love of honesty and probity, and a detestation of all malice, by labor and exercise and attention, but to him, the property of pursuing the good is natural, and an alienation from the flight of iniquity is extremely familiar. Cyril in his Thesaurus, book 8, paraphrases it thus: Since all other things are mutable by nature, and mutable things cannot overcome the Devil. But you, O Jesus Christ, as the immutable Word of the immutable Father, always love justice and hate iniquity, therefore God has anointed you, so that in you first, human nature might achieve a perfect victory over the Devil. Athanasius, Oration 2 against the Arians. Rightly the Lord, who is always and by nature immutable, and loves justice and hates iniquity, is anointed and sent, so that, remaining the same and thus persisting, he might condemn sin in the flesh by assuming mutable flesh, and restore it, having been asserted as free, so that the justice of the law might thereafter be fulfilled in him. Gregory the Great explained this in his commentary on 2 Kings, chapter 11. It is an image and likeness to him, the illustrious one, to hate evil with hatred, and to love God with perfect love; whence also the Prophet, seeing that the brightness of the divine likeness had perished from the human race, looks to him who came from heaven with the illustrious light of our reparation, saying: You have loved justice, and hated iniquity.

Others, however, deny that the particle על כן, propterea (therefore) is taken here as referring to an efficient cause or a reason of nature, and they explain it finally, as Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury: 'Therefore,' that is, 'since you loved good and hated evil, God anointed you,' which is also the explanation of Anselm of Laon and Blessed Augustine, and others, and is almost common among the moderns Hunnius, Chemnitius, Gesner, Musculus likewise, Pareus, and among the Papists, Eman. à Saa, Cano, Estius, Schwarez, and others. Thus Rivetus: 'We explain the words על כן PROPTEREA, as above in v. 3, not as the cause of the consequent, but as the cause of the consequence, not that the love of justice is the cause why God anointed this King with the oil of gladness, but that the anointing is the cause of such great love and hatred. That is to say: He anointed you therefore, that is, to the end that you might love justice: or you loved justice because He anointed you with Oil.' Although, therefore, Rivetus and Musculus, along with Grotius, accept this also concerning Solomon, they do not, however, concede that a meritorious cause is hinted at here, but that he is said to be anointed above his fellows to the end that he might love justice and commend the loving of it to others; but that Christ received this singular anointing so that He might not only become for us the unique example of holiness and of justice to be cultivated, but also might engender the love of the same in our souls. since therefore this end of the anointing of Christ is indicated, that he might love righteousness and pursue iniquity with hatred; not only is the holiness of Christ noted, who cultivated righteousness in the highest degree and pursued sin with the highest hatred, from the first moment of his conception, and the fulfillment of the law, which he performed most perfectly in all parts and in all degrees and measures, but also the very restoration of righteousness itself, and the abolition of iniquity and sin; since righteousness had to be brought back by him, and iniquity abolished, which was done by his obedience, both active and passive, Dan. 9, 24. Rom. 8, 3. c. 10, 4. nay, even the donation of righteousness, that is, that he himself bestows it upon us, and constitutes us righteous by it, and takes away sin from us, and the renewal, through which we are reformed unto true righteousness, and injustice is mortified in us. Because this anointing looks to the threefold office of Christ: Priestly, by which he expiated sin and acquired righteousness: Prophetic, by which he offers us grace, that we may be freed from sin and made partakers of his righteousness through the Gospel: Kingly, by which he rules us with the scepter of righteousness and uprightness, so that, instructed by his righteousness and renewed by the Holy Spirit, we may be defended against iniquity and all our enemies, and attain the eternal crown of righteousness. All these things the love of righteousness and the hatred of iniquity in Christ the Bridegroom embrace or imply, which is explained throughout the Scriptures. And therefore it is very poorly reduced by Grotius to the Prophetic office alone. Fourthly, Grotius wrongly explains the anointing of Christ as his dignity. For although he is anointed for the sake of dignity and office, namely Prophetic, Priestly, and Royal: just as those were wont to be anointed in times past who were called by God to these duties, yet the anointing is not to be confused with the dignity itself: since ordination to an effect also differs from anointing: The latter took place in the Old Testament by the pouring of bodily oil, and at the same time signified and brought about, by God's bounty, the necessary concession of gifts for undertaking the office, which it is manifest was different from the designation and ordination to the office itself; since ordination was sometimes done without anointing, and anointing was sometimes prior in time to ordination and inauguration: for the former, oil was required, for the latter, it was not necessary. Furthermore, the anointing of Christ with the oil of gladness, that is, done by the Holy Spirit, brings about the concession of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, ἐκ μέτρου, not by measure, John 3, 34. Which differs entirely from the honor and dignity of Christ. The Calvinists indeed are accustomed to explain the anointing of Christ through ordination and the mediatorial office, and therefore refer the same to both natures. But by the common suffrage of the ancient Doctors, it pertains to the human nature, according to which he has companions, and it is explained through the communication of gifts which were necessary for the office, but it is not confused with the office itself, or the designation to the office, just as anointing, when it is applied to the faithful, denotes the collation of spiritual gifts, 2 Cor. 1, 21. 1 John 2, 20. These are the words of Athanasius, Orat. contr. Arian.: The flesh assumed by the Word is anointed and gladdened in him. Cyril, lib. de rect. fid. ad Regin.: That the anointing is according to humanity, no one who is accustomed to think rightly has doubted. And comment. in Es. 61. Christ, since he is God and the same is man, gives the Spirit to the creature by reason of his Deity, but receives it from God the Father by reason of his humanity: this we call anointing. And Irenaeus, who is much older than them, L. III. advers. haeret. cap. 10: According to that, that the Word of God was man from the root of Jesse and the Son of Abraham, according to this the Spirit of God rested upon him, and he was anointed to preach the Gospel to the humble. To say it in a word:

The Holy Fathers all agree here equally. Why then did Grotius not lend his ears here to antiquity, which he is so accustomed to harp upon?

Fifthly, a new and again unheard-of invention of the same man is that Christ was finally anointed after death, by which he attained dignity above angels and men when raised from the dead. For where is this in the Scriptures, where in ancient or recent theologians is it called anointing? And did he not receive or have the gifts of the Holy Spirit before death, was he not full of the Holy Spirit, did not the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge rest upon him? But then how could he perform miracles through the Spirit, how could he execute his divine office, if he was not yet anointed with the Spirit then? How could the Apostles receive from his fullness, if he himself was not yet anointed on this earth with the Holy Spirit? But what need is there of arguments, when it is established by the most manifest testimonies that Christ was anointed when he was sent to preach the Gospel, Es. 61, 1. therefore the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon him, Matth. 3. That he was full of grace and truth, John 1, 18. anointed with the Spirit and truth in the days of his flesh, Acts 10, 38. and thus he was anointed for the sake of his office, which he also executed in the days of his flesh. But there lurks in this opinion of Grotius a ὑπόλοιπόν τι, which he received from the Socinians: namely, that Christ was perfectly anointed only after the resurrection. To which end he brings forward with them the passage Acts 2, 36, otherwise expressly vindicated against the sophistries of the Socinians, namely in our Anti-Crellius, Tom. 2, on the Augustan Confession or Natural and Revealed Theology. But God is said to have made Jesus Christ in his exaltation, not that he was then finally anointed with the oil of gladness or the Holy Spirit, but that he then appeared, and it was made manifest, that he himself is the Christ. And the name of Christ is used, as is known, in the sense of office, because he was anointed for the sake of his office; and the Kingly office is designated most especially: not that he was made King only then, because he professed himself King when he lived on earth, and was born King, Matth. 2. Luc. 1. But that, placed upon his throne, he then fully administered his kingdom, when according to the flesh he was admitted to the full use of the divine prerogatives, with which he was anointed at the very moment of his conception.

Therefore, in the sixth place, Grotius very badly confuses the dignity of Christ, which he attained above men and Angels after the resurrection, with the anointing by which he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. The former he attained in a certain respect, namely regarding the plenary exercise of dominion over all things through his exaltation to the right hand of God. The latter, however, he received when he was conceived in his mother's womb: because he was filled with the Holy Spirit in his mother's womb from the first moment of his incarnation; since in him the whole fullness of the Deity dwelt σωματικῶς Col. 2, 9. And since Christ was born Lord & KING, and Ruler in Israel, Luke 2, Matt. 2, Micah 5, it is necessary that he was anointed with the Holy Spirit, because he is called Christ on account of the anointing, and without it he was not Lord, King, and Ruler in Israel; indeed, he was anointed for this and his other offices. But more on these things when the native majesty of Christ is defended against the Socinians. Rivetus rightly says on this passage: Since the anointed King is described here as about to make an expedition against his enemies, it does not seem so appropriate to explain the anointing by the resurrection, or to say that it happened after the resurrection; since the anointing is not said to have been done after the victory, or in the triumph itself. Thus, therefore, the pious ancients explained the time of the anointing, in that they referred it by common consent to the ἐνσάρκωσιν. Then the Greeks: and among them Chrysostom, Homily on the Spirit

Holy: Christ, from the time when the Savior deigned to assume our creature, was filled with the Holy Spirit. Then the Latins. August. lib. 15. de Trinit. c. 22. Christ was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit when he was baptized and it descended upon him like a dove. But he is to be understood as having been anointed with that mystical and visible anointing when the Word of God was made flesh. He adds an argument from John, who, although sown by the Father, nevertheless received the Holy Spirit while formed in the womb (Luke 1:15), whence it is to be understood, or believed, concerning the man CHRIST, whose very conception of flesh was not carnal, but spiritual. Hugo Eterian. lib. de Hæresibus, quas in Latinos Græci devolvunt, 3. c. 10. The flesh of Christ was anointed with a true anointing, namely, by the advent of the Holy Spirit in the very conception of the Son of God. To which also pertains that of Cyril, lib. de rect. Fide ad Theodos. When the Word was made flesh, then we also say that he himself was named CHRIST, since he was anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit by God the Father, and for that reason he was also named CHRIST.

I shall not inquire now what kind of dignity Grotius understands, whether finite as with the Calvinists, or truly infinite? Nor shall I investigate this: Why did he also make mention of the Angels in this comparison? Did he perhaps include them under the fellowship, before whom Christ is said to be anointed; just as Lyranus, Musculus, and Aretius also call the Angels into this fellowship? This anointing certainly imports not finite gifts, but infinite and immense ones: because οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου NOT BY MEASURE, that is, by an immense reason the Holy Spirit was given to Christ, John 3:34. Concerning which Theophyl. We all others receive the operation of the Spirit by measure. But to Christ himself he gave not by measure, one or two mighty works, but he has the Spirit himself entire substantially. And to Heb. 1. He did not receive the Holy Spirit by measure, nor as one who works miracles through the Spirit, but he was anointed by presence, and thus by the whole ointment, and by the whole anointer. And the anointing was done for the execution of the office, for which an infinite power was required, since to conquer sin, death, the Devil, to pierce the hearts of enemies, to rule with the scepter of the word, to appoint Princes over the whole earth, to adorn the Church as a Bride with internal and Spiritual beauty, and to govern the same entirely, are works of a truly divine and infinite power, to which divine omnipotence, divine omniscience, and καρδιογνωσία, divine omnipresence, which Scripture testifies were communicated to the flesh of Christ, Matt. 18:20, John 2 and 21, Matt. 28:20. That anointing brings with it the divine power of pouring out the Spirit κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς χριστοῦ Acts 2:35, Eph. 4:7. and the ordination to the possession of the divine and eternal throne, Apoc. 3:21, and therefore it cannot be completed by finite gifts. But then Christ was anointed not only before his fellows, but also for his fellows, so that from his FULLNESS WE ALL might receive, John 1:18. But what fullness would it be, and how would ALL receive from it throughout the whole World, if he were anointed with the Spirit only by finite gifts? Ambrose in Heb. 1. Christ is recognized to have received a blessing above the whole human race, so that, anointed singularly, he might anoint the others. For in him is the fountain of blessing, as it shall have seemed good to him, flowing forth competently through all the elect. August. Tract. 33. in John. The spiritual anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, whose Sacrament is in the visible anointing. And he anointed us for this reason, because he made us victors against the Devil. And from the Greeks Athanas. Orat. 2. contr. Arian. Our Savior is said to be anointed, so that he might again procure for us men the indwelling and intimacy of the Spirit. Cyrill. Alex. l. 8. Thes. Christ is exalted and anointed and sanctified for our sake, so that through him grace might run through to all men, given to the very nature of men, and communicated to the whole race. To which also pertains the explanation of those who interpret the prefix מ in the word מחבריך causally, BECAUSE OF your fellows: which sense I see also pleased our B. Luther: I do not disapprove, he says, Tom. 3. Oper. Latin Serm. 1. p. 460. ad h. l. that they translated, Before your fellows, so that it might signify excellence. Although it can also be translated, Because of your fellows. But whichever you read, it is a great consolation that the Prophet says that Christ was so gladdened and glorious that he has fellows, that that right Scepter does not pertain to him alone, but that he has fellows and partners, participants of that oil and gladness. It is therefore diligently to be observed that all things which Christ has are associated and communicated with his fellows who believe in him. They have the same love of justice, the same hatred of iniquity, the same oil of gladness, yet so that we do not contribute anything to Christ; but that we receive all things from him, just as the text says: From his fullness we all receive. Add here the confession of Wolfg. Muscul. ad h. Psalm. Christ as the Son of man was inaugurated with the oil of the Holy Spirit, and not according to measure, but by a full and perfect inauguration of divinity, with all power, and the fullness of blessings in heaven and on earth received from the Father.

Now as far as the fellows of Christ are concerned, it is easily evident that not all intellectual creatures, or Angels, are understood to be included, but only men, for he was made a partaker of our flesh and blood, not of the nature of Angels, Heb. 2:14. Nor is the grace of anointing attributed to Angels anywhere in the Scriptures; nor was the anointing in Christ done for the sake of Angels, but for the sake of men, Is. 61:1. Nor, however, are Priests and Kings only his fellows, which Episcopius wished, lib. 3. Instit. Sect. 2. cap. 2. Because as a spiritual anointing is understood here, so also is a spiritual fellowship; Kings and Priests are indeed called anointed, both because of an external anointing, and because of an internal collation of gifts for performing offices, and because of a typical prefiguration of Christ the King and Priest, but because Christ is said to be anointed with spiritual gifts, before his fellows and because of his fellows. All the faithful become partakers of spiritual gifts according to the measure of the gift, Eph. 4:7, who also receive the anointing, 2 Cor. 1:10, 1 John 2:20; therefore all the faithful are rightly constituted as partners of Christ, by the common consent of the Fathers: concerning which Cyprian, On the Anointing of Christ: As many as are partakers of Christ are partners of both the anointing and the name, and are called Christians from Christ, so that they may be Rulers and Leaders under Christ the Leader, and offer a daily sacrifice to God, ordained by God as Priests of holiness. For we have been made Priests and Kings through spiritual anointing, Apoc. 1 and 5; whence, since we are called partners of Christ in a double respect, according to the Orthodox Fathers, both regarding the communion of the same nature, Heb. 2:13, 14, and regarding the participation of the gifts of the Spirit: the former respect is common to all men, therefore he calls the sons of men partakers in this place. Augustine. But in the latter respect only the faithful are partakers, concerning which Theophylact on Heb. 1:9: All spiritual persons are partakers of Christ, as those who are sanctified by participation in him. And hence the name of Christians is proper to the faithful from Christ or our Anointed One, on account of the Spiritual anointing which they themselves have from Christ, of whom they become partners, concerning which Remigius on Heb. 1:9: The Apostles, Martyrs, confessors, and all who have been washed by the grace of Baptism are partakers of Christ, obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit, and are called Christians from Christ. And Augustine, Tractate on John, on chapter 1: Christ is anointed singularly, anointed preeminently, from whom all Christians are anointed: for all the saints are participants in him, but he is singularly the Holy of Holies, singularly Christ, singularly anointed. Seventh, it is to be rejected that Grotius makes those words אלהים אלהיך in this place two nominatives, and explains it thus: 'The God whom you worship.' For that the former אלהים here is not to be taken in the nominative, but in the vocative, is taught by (1) The address which the Psalmist institutes, directed to the Messiah; 'Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.' For without doubt he addressed the subject here, which was anointed, with the word 'God,' as in the preceding verses with the word 'mighty' in verse 4, and with the word 'God' in the verse immediately preceding, 7. (2) The custom of the Hebrew language. For when a repetition of some noun is made, for the sake of emphasis, it is accustomed to be repeated in exactly the same way: as may be observed in Psalm 22:1, 'My God, my God' (אלי אלי), not 'God, my God' (אלהים אלהי); see also Genesis 46:2, Exodus 3:4, 1 Samuel 3:10, Job 16:12. Thus, therefore, it should have been said here 'your God, your God' (אלהיך אלהיך) if the repetition had been made for the sake of emphasis. Furthermore, if a place were to be granted for emphasis, it should not have been applied so much to the anointer as to the anointed, as the context is occupied with his description. But that name 'your God' refers rather to the proclamation of paternal love than to a eulogy of the Son. Grotius indeed explains it as 'WHOM YOU WORSHIP,' but others, Ambrose, Cassiodorus, and others, prefer to understand it as the singular love of God the Father. (3) Apostolic explanation. For the Apostle took it not obscurely in the vocative case, when he also brought forward this verse in Hebrews 1 to prove the Deity of the Son of God; otherwise he would have brought forward only verse 7, in which he had already been called God. (4) The consensus of interpreters. For the Chaldean explains it by the vocative: 'And you, King Messiah, who have loved justice'; the Arabic Interpreter, Justin against Trypho, Irenaeus book 3, chapter 6, Tertullian against Praxeas chapter 13, Lactantius book 4 of the Institutes chapter 13, Hilary book 4 on the Trinity, Ambrose book 1 on the Faith chapter 2, Jerome in his Epistle to Principia the virgin, Augustine against the Jews 4, Hesychius book 2 on Leviticus 8, Fulgentius book 3 to Thrasimund: all of which Fathers also prove the Deity of the Son of God from this word in this place, which could not happen if the Father were being addressed here by the name of God, and the words were taken by apposition. The matter is so clear that even the Racovian Photinians themselves in their paraphrase thought it should be rendered no otherwise than in our sense: 'Darum hat dich, O GOtt, dein GOtt gesalbet' [Therefore has God, O God, your God anointed you], and the other Socinians have admitted the vocative case here. Crellius, in 'On God and Divine Attributes' chapter 9, says that an illustrious example is held here, where Christ is called Elohim, namely in verses 7 and 8 of Psalm 45.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

DILEXISTI JUSTITIAM, ET ODISTI INIQVITA- TEM, PROPTEREA VNXIT TE, DEUS, DEUS TU- US OLEO LÆTITIA PRÆ CONSORTIBUS TUIS) Dilexit Salomon justitiam, & odit injustitiam, nempe a prima ætate, ideo præ cæteris non popularibus tantum suis, sed & fratribus electus est a Deo in Regem 1. Par. 28. quod unctione significatur 1. Reg. 1, 34. Jesus, dum vitam egit mortalem, nihil aliud, quam justa & honesta omnia verbo & exemplo docuit, arguens his contraria. Ideo post mortem excitatus dignitatem supra omnes homines, imo & supra Angelos est consecutus, quæ dignitas hic humano more significatur un- ctionis vocabulo. Sic χριστὸν ἀυτὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε Actor. 2, 36. Sunt autem duo nominativi אֱלֹהִים אֱלֹהֶיךָ il- le Deus, quem tu colis. Locum hunc de Messia interpretatur Chaldæus, & Rabbini multi.

Multa sunt in hac glossa perversissima, quæ de- testationem mereantur. Primo quod Salomonem hic iterum ingerat, qui non magis in hoc, quam præcedenti versu ingeri potest, quum unice de Christo sermo sit. Quod agnoscere coactus est Pa- reus etiam, dum Calvinum suum defensum ivit. Quædam, inquit, Salomoni NULLO PACTO conveniunt, ut quod Rex iste absolute vocatur Deus, habens thronum æternum, quod unctus supra confor- tes suos, in Calv. Orthod. pag. 228. Quæ latius ex- equitur in Epist. ad Ebr. 1, 8. Neque vero possunt ea, quæ profert Apostolus, Salomoni ULLA RATIO- NE competere. Nunquid enim Salomon fuit Deus? Psaltes vero eum, quem alloquitur, vocat Deum. Re- ges quidem Dii dicuntur, sed non absolute, ut hic: Thronus tuus ô Deus. Salomonis enim thronus an fuit æternus? vix quadragenarius. In filio mox re- gnum ejus infelicissime laceratum fuit. Neque virga regni ejus semper recta fuit. Gravibus enim & ini- quis exactionibus populum pressit: quæ tandem que- relis, & seditionibus causam præbuerunt. An vero Salomon justitiam & æquitatem semper dilexit? Imo nimis mulierosus contra legem, jus divinum & huma- num varie violavit, à vero Dei cultu ad Idololatri- am, quæ summa fuit iniquitas, mulierum seductione, turpiter defecit. Hæc Pareus: addit, quod de unctio- ne dicitur, supra consortes, aliquo modo quidem in Salomonem competere, sed in explicatione v. 9. hoc corrigit, ac de solo Christo intelligit: Noster Rex, inquit, non quidem externo unctus oleo legitur, sed Oleo Spiritus perfusus sine mensura. PRÆ CON- SORTIBUS, hoc est, fratribus, qui sunt fideles ele- cti: Horum enim factus est CONSORS carnis & sanguinis assumtione, ut docebit cap. 2. ubi rationem hujus Etymologiæ explicabit. Sumus enim μέτεχοι Christi, quia ipse carne & sanguine nostro παρα- πλησίως μετέσχε. Supra hos ergo consortes omnes Christus primogenitus unctione sua est unctus, non mo- do ut sibi esset cunctis felicior, potentior, gloriosior, sed maxime ut Oleum lætitiæ suæ in consortes suos effunde- ret, nosque omnes de plenitudine ejus acciperemus. Ri- vetus pariter agnoscit, hæc non nisi Christo convenire. Qui duo versus 7. & 8. Pf. 45. diligenter sunt perpen- dendi. Quoniam Apostolus Ebr. 1, 8. eos ad Christum IMMEDIATE refert, cui certe SOLI competunt. Non ergo Salomoni conveniunt, nedum sensu im- mediato de Salomone loquuntur.

Porro Secundo glacie ipsa frigidior est illa Grotii glossa, de dilectione justitiæ in Salomone à prima ætate. Quantulacunque enim hæc sunt, quæ de ipso prædicari possunt, ad hoc TAN- TUM, & tam sublime elogium de perfecto justitiæ amore ac iniquitatis odio, quod nullis gradibus de- ficiat, nulla ratione exorbitet; nam si alicubi de- ficeret, vel exorbitaret, sive amore justitiæ, sive odio iniquitatis, non posset absolute prædicari; dilexi- sti justitiam, & odisti iniquitatem, nedum inferri, propterea te unxit Deus tuus, ob morem justitiæ, ac cæteris omnibus, etiam fratribus prælatum fuisse Salomonem nuspiam docetur in Scripturis: quia promissio erat Davidi facta, de Filio throni hærede, ideo ex aliis popularibus nemo eligi poterat, nec ideo quod Salomo electus, cæteros populares omnes justitiæ amore & iniquitatis odio superasse censen- dus est. Neque vero merito suo prælatus est fratribus suis Salomon: Sed ex singulari Dei gratia. Quid multis? non Salomonem, verum Christum subje- ctum hic constitui diserte Apostolus docet. πρὸς δὲ τὸν ὑιὸν v. 9. Cujus proinde autoritati & proba- tioni hic palam refragatur Grotius. Omnes ergo Interpp. Christiani summo consensu hæc de Chri- sto intelligunt: & alii quidem de amore justitiæ & odio injustitiæ, qua natura ipsi conveniunt, alii qua in administratione regni conspiciuntur: rectissime autem, qui utroque modo: quia non tantum inter- na propensio ad justitiam, & injustitiæ detestatio, sed etiam exercitium ejus in Rege hoc nos in admira- tionem & celebrationem abripit.

Tertio perquam jejuna Grotii est explicatio de Christo, quod is dilexisse dicatur justitiam, & o- dio habuisse iniquitatem, qua vitam agens mortalem, nihil aliud quam justa & honesta omnia verbo & ex- emplo docuit, arguens his contraria; quia non tan- tum ad vitam ejus mortalem respicitur, sed ad re- gnum ejus universum: neq; id singulare adeo ac pro- prium foret Christi, quum Prophetæ etiam justa ac honesta docuerint verbo & exemplo suo, & con- traria his arguerint. Videtur Grotius Socinos, & alios hæreticos, qui vix aliquid divini Christo hic re- linquunt, imitari, quemadmodum de Nestorianis observat h. l. Estius, quod argumentum hinc desum- serint, ut probarent Christum non natura Dei Filium esse, sed adoptionis prærogativam operum excellentia promeruisse, quod etiam de Neo-Arianis notum est. Longe vero illustriori ratione Catholici Dd. hoc elogium acceperunt, uti etiam ipso verborum sono longe illustrius est, & ab Apostolo eminen- tissima ratione, quæ ipsam Angelorum sanctitatem antecellat, accipitur. Omnia enim hæc adfert Apo- stolus, ut eminentiam Filii supra Angelos ostendat. Quamvis enim nonnulli particulam PROPTER- EA hic illativam faciant, ideo quia dilexisti justi- tiam & odio habuisti iniquitatem, Deus te unxit; non tamen meritum in eo constituerunt unctionis proprie dictum, sed pro præmio eam assignarunt. Hieronymus Epist. ad Princip. virg. & Ambros. in hunc locum certe ad naturale odium injustitiæ, ac divinum justitiæ amorem causam unctionis retule- runt. Quo de etiam Basilius M. hom. ad hunc Psalm. Reliqui homines labore & exercitatione & attentione sæpe numero assequuntur amorem honesti & probitatis, & malitiæ totius detestationem, ipsi au- tem naturalis est ad boni persecutionem proprietas, & ad iniquitatis fugam perquam familiaris aliena- tio. Cyrillus Thesaur. lib. 8. ita παραφράζει: Quo- niam cætera omnia mutabilia sunt secundum natu- ram, & mutabilia Diabolum superare nequeunt. Tu vero ô Jesu Christe, ut incommutabilis Patris incom- mutabile verbum semper justitiam diligis, & iniqui- tatem odio habes, propterea unxit te Deus, ut in te primo natura humana perfectam à Diabolo victo- riam consequeretur. Athanasius Orat. 2. cont. A- rian. Merito Dominus, qui semper & ex natura im- mutabilis est, diligitque justitiam, & odit iniquitatem, inungitur & emittitur, ut idem subsistens, adeoque per- manens mutabili carne assumta peccatum in carne condemnaret, liberum ipsum assertumque redderet, quæ deinceps justitia legis de eo adimpleatur. Grego- rius M. exposuit. l. 2. Reg. c. 11. Imago & similitudo ei est inclyto odio malum odire, & amore perfecto Deum diligere; Unde & Propheta claritatem divi- næ similitudinis ab humano genere periisse intuens, ad eum, qui cum incluta reparationis nostræ luce de cælo venit, respicit, dicens: Dilexisti justitiam, & odisti iniquitatem.

Alii vero particulam על כן, propterea negant hic de causa efficiente, vel ratione naturæ accipi, eam- que finaliter explicant, uti Anshelmus Cantuar. Episc. Propterea, id est, cum bonum diligeres & ma- lum odires, unxit te Deus, quæ Anshelmi etiam Lau- dunensis ac B. Augustini, & aliorum est explicatio, ac fere communis recentioribus Hunnio, Chemni- tio, Gesnero, Musculo item, Pareo, & è Pontificiis Eman. à Saa, Cano, Estio, Schwarez, aliisque. Ita Rivetus: Exponimus voces על כן PROPTEREA, ut supra v. 3. non de causa consequentis, sed de causa consequentiæ, non ut amor justitiæ sit causa, cur Deus unxerit hunc Regem Oleo lætitiæ, sed ut unctio causa sit tanti amoris & odii. q. d. unxit te propterea, id est, in eum finem, ut diligeres justitiam: vel dilexisti ju- stitiam, quia te unxit Oleo. Quamvis ergo Rivetus & Musculus cum Grotio de Salomone etiam hoc ac- cipiant, non tamen concedunt meritoriam causam hic innui, sed unctum dici præ fratribus eum in fi- nem, ut justitiam diligeret, eamque diligendam aliis commendaret; Christum autem singularem hanc unctionem accepisse, ut non solum unicum sanctita- tis & justitiæ colendæ exemplar nobis fieret, sed etiam ejusdem amorem animis nostris ingeneraret. Quum ergo finis hic indicitur unctionis Christi, ut justitiam diligeret, & odio prosequeretur iniquitatem, non solum sanctitas Christi notatur, quæ justitiam summe coluit, summoq; odio prosequutus est peccatum, inde à primo conceptionis momento, & impletio legis, quam omnibus partibus, omnibusque gradibus & numeris perfectissime præstitit, sed ipsa etiam justitiæ restitutio, ac iniquitatis & peccati abolitio; quandoquidem justitia per ipsum reduci, & iniquitas aboleri debuerit, quod obedientia ejus cum activa tum passiva factum, Dan. 9, 24. Rom. 8, 3. c. 10, 4. imo donatio etiam justitiæ, quod nempe ipse nobis eam donet, nosque eadem justos constituat, & peccatum a nobis tollat, ac renovatio, per quam ad justitiam veram reformamur, ac injustitia mortificatur in nobis. Quia hæc unctio ad trinum Christi officium spectat: Sacerdotale, quo expiavit peccatum, & acquisivit justitiam: Propheticum, quo offert nobis gratiam, ut liberemur à peccato, & justitiæ ejus participes reddamur per Evangelium: Regium, quo nos regit sceptro justitiæ, & rectitudinis, ut instructi ipsius justitia, & à Spiritu Sancto renovati, adversus iniquitatem, hostesque nostros universos defendamur, & æternum justitiæ coronam consequamur. Omnia hæc in Christo Sponso amor justitiæ, & odium iniquitatis complectuntur aut important, quod passim in Scripturis explicatur. Ideoque pessime ad solum officium Propheticum à Grotio reducitur. Quarto unctionem Christi de dignitate ejus perperam explicat Grotius. Ut enim unctus sit dignitatis & officii causa, Prophetici nempe, Sacerdotalis & Regii: quemadmodum illi ungi solebant quondam, qui ad hæc munera à Deo vocabantur, non tamen unctio cum ipsa dignitate confundenda est: Siquidem & ordinatio ad effectum ab unctione differat: Hæc fiebat in Vet. Testamento Olei corporalis effusione, simulque significabat, ac inferebat, Deo largiente, donorum ad officium subeundum necessariam concessionem, quam perinde ab ipsa ad officium destinatione ac ordinatione, diversam fuisse manifestum est; Siquidem & ordinatio absque unctione facta quandoque, & unctio nonnunquam ordinatione & inauguratione tempore prior fuerit: ad illam etiam oleum requisitum fuit, ad hanc necessarium non fuit. Porro unctio Christi oleo lætitiæ, hoc est, Spiritu Sancto facta, concessionem donorum Spiritus Sancti infert, ἐx ἐx μέτρε πon ad mensuram Joh. 3, 34. Quæ ab honore & dignitate Christi omnino differt. Calviniani quidem unctionem Christi explicare solent per ordinationem & officium mediatorium, ideoque eandem ad utramque naturam referunt. Sed communi veterum Dd. suffragio pertinet ea ad humanam naturam, juxta quam ipse consortes habet, & per donorum communicationem explicatur, quæ ad officium necessaria erant, non vero cum ipso officio, aut destinatione ad officium confunditur, quemadmodum unctio cum de fidelibus adhibetur, donorum spiritualium collationem notat 2. Cor. 1, 21. 1. Joh. 2, 20. Athanasii hæc sunt Orat. contr. Arian. Assumpta caro à λόγῳ & in eo inungitur & lætificatur. Cyrillus lib. de rect. fid. ad Regin. Quod unctio sit secundum humanitatem, nemo qui recte sapere solet, dubitavit. Et comment. in Es. 61. Christus Deus cum sit idemque homo, dat Spiritum creaturæ Deitatis ratione, accipit autem illum à Deo Patre ratione humanitatis: hanc unctionem dicimus. Et qui illis multum antiquior Irenæus L. III. advers. hæret. cap. 10. Secundum id, quod verbum Dei homo erat ex radice Jesse & Filius Abrahæ, secundum hoc requiescebat Spiritus Dei super eum, & ungebatur ad Evangelizandum humilibus. Verbo ut dicam:

Consonant hic S. Patres ex æquo omnes. Cur er- go antiquitati hic aures non præbuit Grotius, quam tantopere crepare solet?

Quinto novum iterum atque inauditum com- mentum ejusdem est, quod Christus unctus demum fuerit post mortem, qua dignitatem supra Angelos & homines a morte excitatus assequutus est. Ubi e- nim hoc in Scripturis, ubi in antiquis aut recentio- ribus Theologis unctio dicitur? Et annon dona Spiritus Sancti accepit, aut habuit ante mortem, an- non plenus Spiritu Sancto fuit, annon requievit su- per ipso Spiritus sapientiæ & scientiæ? Tum vero quomodo per Spiritum miracula patrare, quomo- do divinum officium exequi potuit, si Spiritu tum nondum unctus fuit? Quomodo de plenitudine e- jus accipere potuere Apostoli, si ipse inunctus non- dum fuit in his terris Spiritu Sancto? Sed quid ar- gumentis opus, quum manifestissimis testimoniis constet, unctum fuisse Christum, cum missus fuit ad Evangelizandum Es. 61, 1. ideo Spiritus S. dici- tur descendisse super ipsum Matth. 3. Plenus fuisse gratia & veritate Joh. 1, 18. unctus Spiritu & veri- tate in diebus carnis Act. 10, 38. atque sic unctus fuit officii causa, quod exequutus etiam est in die- bus carnis. Sed latet in hac Grotii sententia ὑπό- λόν τι, quod a Socinianis accepit : quod nempe Chri- stus perfecte unctus sit demum post resurrectionem. Quem in finem cum ipsis locum adducit Act. 2, 36. alias ex professo vindicatum adversus strophas So- cinianorum, in Anti-Crellio nempe nostro Tom. 2. super August. Confess. vel Theolog. Natural. & re- velat. Dicitur autem Deus in exaltatione Jesum Christum fecisse, non quod tum demum unctus sit oleo lætitiæ, aut Spiritu S. sed quod tum apparue- rit, ac palam factum fuerit, ipsum Christum esse. Et usurpatur nomen Christi, uti notum est, sensu officii, quia unctus est officii causa; Regiumque potissi- mum officium designatur: non quod Rex tunc de- mum factus sit, quia se Regem professus est, cum in terris ageret, ac Rex natus fuit Matth. 2. Luc. 1. Sed quod in throno suo collocatus tum plenarie re- gnum suum administrarit, cum secundum carnem ad usum plenarium divinorum αὐχημάτων, quibus in ipso conceptionis momento inunctus fuit, ad- missus est.

Pessime itaque Sexto confundit Grotius digni- tatem Christi, quam supra homines atque Angelos consequutus est post resurrectionem, cum unctio- ne, qua oleo lætitiæ supra consortes unctus est. Il- lam certo respectu, nempe quoad plenarium domi- nii super omnia exercitium per exaltationem ad dextram Dei consequutus est. Hanc vero accepit, cum in utero matris conceptus est: quia Spiritu S. in utero matris repletus fuit, a primo incarnationis momento; siquidem in ipso tota plenitudo Deitatis habitavit σωματικῶς Col. 2, 9. Et quum natus fuerit Christus Dominus & REX, ac Dominator in Israel, Luc. 2. Matth. 2. Mich. 5. unctum eum fuisse opor- tet Spiritu S. quia propter unctionem Christus di- citur, & sine eo Dominus, Rex ac Dominator in Israel non fuit, imo ad hoc & alia officia sua unctus est; Sed de his plenius, cum adversus Socinistas ma- jestas Christi nativa vindicatur. Recte Rivetus ad hunc locum: Cum hic describatur unctus Rex, ex- peditionem adversus hostes facturus, non ita congruum videtur, unctionem explicare per resurrectionem, aut dicere, factam post resurrectionem; Cum unctio non dicatur facta post victoriam, aut in ipso triumpho. Ita ergo tempus unctionis explicarunt pii veteres, ut ad ἐνσάρκωσιν communi consensu retulerint. Tum Græci: & inter eos Chrysostomus Homil. de Spiritu

Sancto: Christus ab eo tempore, quo Salvator digna- tus est assumere nostram creaturam, impletus est Spi- ritu S. Tum Latini. August. lib. 15. de Trinit. c. 22. Non tunc unctus Christus Spiritu S. est, quando super eum baptizatum velut columba descendit. Sed ista mystica & visibili unctione tunc intelligendus est un- ctus, quando verbum Dei caro factum est. Addit ar- gumentum à Johanne, qui quamvis seminatus à Pa- tre, tamen Spiritum S. in utero formatus acceperit (Luc. 1, 15.) unde de homine CHRISTO intelligen- dum est, vel credendum, cujus carnis ipsa conceptio non carnalis, sed spiritualis fuit. Hugo Eterian. lib. de Hæresibus, quas in Latinos Græci devolvunt, 3. c. 10. Caro Christi vera unctione uncta est, adventu scil. Spiritus S. in ipsa filii Dei conceptione. Quo fa- cit etiam illud Cyrilli lib. de rect. Fide ad Theodos. Quando verbum caro factum est, tunc & nomina- tum dicimus esse ipsum CHRISTUM, quoniam un- ctus est oleo exaltationis, hoc est, Spiritu S. à Deo Pa- tre, idcirco & CHRISTUS nominatus est.

Non disquiram nunc, qualem dignitatem in- telligat Grotius, finitamne cum Calvinianis, an ve- ro infinitam? Neque id indagabo: Cur Angelorum in hac comparatione mentionem etiam fecerit? Num illos forte sub consortium, præ quibus Chri- stus unctus dicitur, simul comprehendit; quemad- modum Lyranus, Musculus & Aretius etiam An- gelos in hoc consortium vocant? Unctio certe hæc non finita dona, sed infinita & immensa im- portat: quia ὐκ ἐκ μέτρε NON AD MENSU- RAM, hoc est, immensa ratione datus est Christo Spiritus S. Joh 3, 34. De quo Theophyl. Nos alii o- mnes ad mensuram accipimus operationem Spiritus. Ipsi autem Christo non ad mensuram dedit, unam vel duas virtutes, sed ipsum Spiritum integrum habet substantialiter. Et ad Ebr. 1. Non ex mensura acce- pit Spiritum S. Christus, neque ut is, qui per Spiritum operatur mirifica, verum inunctus est præsentia, ad- eoq; toto unguento, & toto ungente. Et facta est un- ctio propter exequutionem muneris, ad quod in- finita requirebatur virtus, quum peccatum, mor- tem, Diabolum vincere, corda inimicorum transfi- gere, sceptro verbi dominari, Principes in universa terra constituere, Ecclesiam ceu Sponsam interno & Spirituali decore exornare, eandemque totam guber- nare, opera sint vere divinæ & infinitæ virtutis, ad quæ divina opus omnipotentia, divina omniscientia, & καρδιογνωσία, divina omnipræsentia, unde illa Christi carni communicata esse Scriptura testatur Matth. 18, 20. Joh. 2. & 21. Matth. 28, 20. Unctio illa infert divinum effundendi Spiritum κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς χρισț potestatem Act. 2, 35. Eph. 4, 7. & ordinationem ad throni divini & æterni possessio- nem Apoc. 3, 21. ideoque non potest absolvi donis fi- nitis. Tum vero unctus est Christus non tantum præ consortibus, sed etiam propter consortes, ut ex ejus PLENITUDINE OMNES accipiamus Joh. 1, 18. Quæ vero PLENITUDO esset, & quo- modo ex ea OMNES acciperent per universum Orbem, si donis solum finitis Spiritus inunctus es- set? Ambrosius in Ebr. 1. Christus benedictionem su- pra omne genus humanum agnoscitur accepisse, ut unctus singulariter cæteros ungat. In illo enim fons benedictionis, prout ipsi visum fuerit, per universos electos competenter emanat. August. Tract. 33. in Joh. unctio Spiritualis ipse Spiritus S. est, cujus Sa- cramentum est in unctione visibili. Ideo autem nos unxit, quia victores nos contra Diabolum fecit. Et è Græcis Athanas. Orat. 2. contr. Arian. Salvator noster inungi dicitur, ut iterum nobis hominibus Spi- ritus ἐνοίκησιν καὶ ὀικειότητα conciliaret. Cyrill. A- lex. l. 8. Thes. Exaltatur Christus & ungitur & sancti- ficatur propter nos, ut per ipfum in omnes homines gratia percurrat ipsi hominum naturæ data, & toti generi communicata. Quo etiam pertinet eorum explicatio, qui præfixum מ in voce מחבריך caufa- liter exponunt, PROPTER confortes tuos: quem sensum video etiam placuisse B. Luthero nostro: Non improbo, inquit Tom. 3. Oper. Latin Serm. 1. p. 460. ad h. l. quod verterunt, Præ confortibus, ut significet excellentiam. Quanquam etiam potest ver- ti, propter confortes tuos. Utrum autem legas, ma- gna consolatio est, quod dicit Propheta, Christum sic esse lætificatum & gloriosum, ut habeat confortes, ut Sceptrum illud rectum non pertineat ad eum solum, sed ut habeat confortes & socios, participes istius olei & lætitiæ. Diligenter igitur est observandum, omnia quæ Christus habet, esse consociata & communicata cum suis confortibus, qui in ipsum credunt. Habent eandem dilectionem justitiæ, idem odium iniquitatis, idem oleum lætitiæ, sic tamen, ne nos aliquid in Chri- stum conferamus; sed ut accipiamus omnia ab eo, sic- ut dicit textus: De plenitudine ejus accipimus o- mnes. Adde hic confessionem Wolfg. Muscul. ad h. Psalm. Christus ut Filius hominis oleo Spiritus S. inauguratus est, atque non secundum mensuram, sed plena & perfecta divinitatis inauguratione, omni prorsus in cælo, & in terra potestatis, benedictionum- que plenitudine accepta à Patre.

Jam quod confortes Christi attinet, non intel- ligi omnes creaturas intellectuales, aut Angelos com- prehendi, sed solum homines facile constat, qui non Angelorum naturæ, sed carnis & sanguinis nostri μέτοιχ& consors factus est Ebr. 2, 14. Nec unctionis gratia uspiam in Scripturis Angelis tribui- tur; nec propter Angelos, sed propter homines fa- cta est in Christo unctio Es. 61, 1. Neque tamen Sa- cerdotes & Reges tantum confortes illi sunt, quod voluit Episcopius lib. 3. Instit. Sect. 2. cap. 2. Quia uti spiritualis unctio hic intelligitur, ita etiam spi- rituale consortium; dicuntur quidem Reges & Sacerdotes uncti, tum propter externam unctio- nem, tum propter internam donorum ad officia ob- eunda collationem, tum propter Christi Regis & Sacerdotis typicam præfigurationem, sed quia Chri- stus unctus dicitur spiritualibus donis, præ con- fortibus & ob confortes suos. Participes sautem donorum spiritualium κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς αὐτõ fiunt fideles omnes Ephes. 4, 7. qui etiam un- ctionem accipiunt 2. Cor. 1, 10. 1. Joh. 2, 20. ideo confortes Christi recte omnes fideles constituun- tur, communi Patrum consensu: de quo Cyprian. de unct. Christi: Participes Christi quotquot sunt, confortes sunt tam unctionis, quam nominis, & di- cuntur à Christo Christiani, ut sint sub Duce Christo Rectores & Duces, & offerant Deo quotidianum sa- crificium, ordinati à Deo sanctimoniæ Sacerdotes. Facti enim sumus Sacerdotes & Reges per spiri- tualem unctionem Apoc. 1. & 5. unde quum con- fortes dicamur Christi, duplici respectu, secundum Orthodoxos Patres, tum quoad communionem ejusdem naturæ, Ebr. 2, 13. 14. tum quoad donorum Spiritus participationem: prior respectus omnibus hominibus communis est, ideo filios hominum parti- cipes dicit in h. l. August. posteriori autem respectu soli fideles participes sunt, quo de Theoph. ad Ebr. 1, 9. Participes Christi sunt omnes spirituales, ut qui ejus participatione sunt sanctificati. Atque hinc no- men Christianorum à Christo vel uncto Nostro fide- lium est proprium, ob unctionem Spiritualem, quam ipsi à Christo habent, cujus confortes fiunt, de quo Remigius in Ebr. 1, 9. Participes Christi sunt Apostoli, Martyres, confessores, omnesque qui gratia Baptismi sunt abluti, donum Spiritus S. consequun- tur; & a Christo Christiani vocantur. Et Augustin. Tract. in Joh. ad cap. 1. Christus singulariter unctus est, præcipue unctus, unde omnes Christiani ungun- tur: Participes enim ejus omnes sancti, sed ille singu- lariter Sanctus Sanctorum, singulariter Christus, sin- gulariter unctus. Septimo reprobandum est, quod Grotius verba illa אל הים אלהיך in hoc loco duos nominativos faciat, & ita exponat: Deus ille quem tu colis. Nam prius אלהים hic non in nominativo ac- cipiendum esse, sed in vocativo, docet (1) Compel- latio, quam instituit Psaltes ad Messiam directa; Propterea unxit te, Deus, Deus tuus. Sine dubio enim subjectum, quod unctum est, voce Deus hic compellavit, ut in antecedentibus voce גבור vers. 4. & voce אלהים versu immediate præcedente 7. (2) Ebrææ linguæ consuetudo. Cum enim repetitio fit nominis alicujus, emphaseos causa, eodem prorsus modo id repeti solet: uti Psal. 22, 1. observare licet אלי אלי Deus mi, Deus mi, non אלהים אלהי, vide etiam Genes. 46, 2. Exod. 3, 4. 1. Sam. 3, 10. Job. 16, 12. Sic ergo ita dicendum hic fuisset אלהיך אלהיך si emphaseos gratia repetitio facta. Porro empha- si si locus concedendus esset, non tam ad ungentem quam ad unctum ea adhibenda fuisset, utpote in cu- jus descriptione contextus occupatur. At nomen illud Deus tuus præconium potius refert paternæ dilectionis, quam elogium Filii. Exponit quidem illud Grotius QUEM TU COLIS, sed alii ma- lunt de amore singulari Dei Patris id intelligere, Ambrosius, Cassiodorus, alii. (3) Apostolica explica- tio. Casu enim vocandi haud obscure accepit Apo- stolus, quum hunc versum etiam 8. ad probandum Deitatem Filii Dei adduxerit, alioquin solum v. 7. in quo Deus jam vocatus erat, adduxisset. (4) In- terpp. consensus. Per vocativum enim explicant Chaldæus: Et tu Rex Messia, qui dilexisti justitiam; Arabs Interpres, Justin. contr. Tryph. Iren. lib. 3. c. 6. Tertull. adv. Prax. c. 13. Lactant. lib. 4. Instit. c. 13. Hilarius lib. 4. de Trin. Ambrof. lib. 1. de Fid. c. 2. Hieronymus Epist. ad Princ. virg. Augustin. contr. Jud. 4. Hesychius lib. 2. in Levit. 8. Fulgentius lib. 3. ad Thrasim: qui Patres omnes etiam ex hac voce Filii Dei Deitatem hoc in loco probant, quod fieri non posset, si Pater hic nomine Dei appellare- tur, & per appositionem verba acciperentur. Res adeo luculenta, ut etiam ipsi Racovienses Photinia- ni in sua paraphrasi non aliter reddendum censue- rint, quam nostro sensu: Darum hat dich, O GOtt, dein GOtt gesalbet, cæterique Sociniani casum vo- cativum hic admiserint. Crellius de Deo & Attrib. Div. c. 9. exemplum hic illustre haberi ait, ubi Chri- stus Elohim appellatur, versu nempe 7. & 8. Psal. 45.

## 45:13
Verse 14.

ALL HER GLORY, O DAUGHTER OF THE KING, IS FROM WITHIN) She is endowed with native beauty, so that she has no need to be commended by garments and gems: which nevertheless are abundantly present with her, even to the fringes.

Again, a too jejune gloss, which did not even come into the minds of the Jews. R. Aben-Ezra says 'from within,' because it is not seen by everyone; and by great consensus the interpreters explained it concerning INTERNAL and SPIRITUAL glory. One who has taken it concerning external beauty has not yet been able to be found. Nor indeed does that explanation fit, either with the words or with the underlying subject matter. It is certainly openly repugnant to the words. For they exhibit glory from WITHIN or INTRINSIC and hidden. But that native beauty is not INTERIOR and hidden, but external and striking the senses. And it had been dealt with concerning beauty in verse 12: 'The King will desire your beauty': which the preceding words sufficiently indicate to be spiritual: 'Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people, and your father's house, and the King will desire your beauty.' For then she is beautiful in the eyes of the King, when she hears him and obeys him. Which Basil the Great elegantly explains, Volume 1. Works, p. 224, on this passage. He invites the Church and exhorts her to hear and at the same time to observe, and by that very appellation he adopts her into familiarity, while he calls her daughter, as if he had begotten her through charity. 'Hear, O daughter, and see.' He teaches her to direct her simple and naked mind to contemplation, from the fact that he says, 'see,' consider and weigh (he says) the creation, so that, aided by the order of nature, you may thus ascend higher to the contemplation of the creator. Then, bending the neck lifted with the pride of boasting, 'incline,' he says, 'your ear,' lest you run to external fables. But rather receive the humility of the voice, which is seen to be in the Evangelical discourse. Incline your ear to this precept, so that you may plainly forget that disapproved custom, and be made a participant in spiritual doctrine, and therefore 'forget your people and your father's house.' Everyone who commits sin is of the father the Devil. To which are also twin those things which Blessed Luther has in his enarrations: 'Nor indeed do those things which are added concerning the gilded fringes look to external adornment: since the Psalmist continues to describe that internal glory, and to render it more illustrious by phrases taken from external clothing.' These are Luther's words. Those fringes which depend from her loin in such a way are spiritual, and therefore they are asserted to be golden, says Basil again, whose long but most elegant paraphrase on this verse we brought forward above, where this glory was dealt with more fully. That gloss of Grotius must necessarily be consigned to the sponge, after it has now been proven that the subject matter or object of the treatment here is in no way the daughter of Pharaoh, concerning whose native beauty also nothing certain is held, but the Church, the Spouse of the Messiah.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

OMNIS GLORIA EJUS, FILIÆ REGIS, AB IN- TUS) Nativa pulchritudine prædita est, ita ut opus non ha- beat a vestibus & gemmis commendari: quæ tamen ipsi uber- tim adsunt, ad fimbrias usque.

Iterum nimis jejuna glossa, quæ ne Judæis qui- dem in mentem venit. R. Aben - Ezra, dicit intus, quia non videtur ab omnibus; Et magno consensu Interpp. de INTERNA ac SPIRITUALI glo- ria explicarunt. Qui de externa pulchritudine ac- ceperit, neminem adhuc invenire licuit. Neque vero congruit illa explicatio, vel verbis, vel materiæ substratæ. Verbis certe aperte repugnat. Ea enim gloriam ab INTUS vel INTRINSECAM & ab- sconditam exhibent. Pulchritudo autem illa nativa non est INTERIOR & abscondita, sed externa & in sensus incurrens. Et de decore v. 12. actum erat: Concupiscet Rex decorem tuum: quem vero Spiri- tualem esse antecedentia satis indicant: Audi filia & vide & intende aurem tuam, & obliviscere popu- lum tuum, & domum Patris tui, & concupiscet Rex decorem tuum. Tum enim decora in oculis Regis est, cum ipsum audit, eique obtemperat. Quæ eleganter explicat Basilius M. Tom. 1. Oper. p. 224. in h. l. Invitat Ecclesiam & exhortatur, ut audiat simul & observet, ipsaq́; appellatione sibi eam adsciscit in familiaritatem, dum filiam appellat, ac si per charitatem genuisset eam. Audi filia & vide. Docet ipsam simplicem nudamque mentem ad contemplationem gerere, ex eo quod ait, vide, considera & perpende (ait) creationem, ut ordine naturæ adjuta, sic ad creatoris contemplationem altius ascendas. Deinde flectens collum jactantiæ fastu sublatum, inclina, inquit, aurem tuam, ne curras ad externas fabulas. Quin suscipe potius vocis humilitatem, quæ in Evangelico conspicitur esse sermone. Inclina aurem tuam ad hanc præceptionem, ut plane obliviscaris improbatæ illius consuetudinis, & efficiare particeps spiritualis doctrinæ, eoq́; obliviscere populum tuum & domum Patris tui. Omnis, qui peccatum admittit, ex patre Diabolo est. Cui gemina etiam sunt, quæ B. Lutherus in enarrat. habet: Neque vero illa, quæ de fimbriis deauratis adduntur, externum ornatum spectant: Siquidem pergat Psaltes gloriam illam internam describere, ac phrasibus ab externo vestitu desumtis illustriorem reddere. Hæc Lutherus. Quæ a lumbo ejusmodi dependent fimbriæ, spirituales sunt, eoque adstruuntur esse aureæ, inquit iterum Basilius, cujus prolixam, sed elegantissimam paraphrasin ad h. v. supra adduximus, ubi plenius de hac gloria actum.
