In spongiam incumbat glossa illa Grotii necessum est, postquam jam probatum, materiam vel objectum tractationis hic nullo modo esse filiam Pharaonis, de cujus etiam nativa pulchritudine nihil certi habetur, sed Ecclesiam Sponsam Meffiæ.

## 45:16
Verse 17.

INSTEAD OF THY FATHERS) That is, instead of thy parents, Father and Mother, whom thou hast left; see above 11. For the Hebrews use masculine forms for common ones; thus also Heb. 11, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

PRO PATRIBUS TUIS) Id est, pro parentibus tuis, Patre & Matre, quos reliquisti; supra 11. Nam Hebræi masculinis utuntur pro communibus; sic & Hebr. 11,23.

## 45:17
THEY SHALL PRAISE THEE) That is, they shall laud thee.

There is no need that we should exchange Fathers with mothers. Nor in v. 11 was the Bride commanded only to leave her Parents, but to forget her own people, and her father's house. Therefore, by Fathers here are understood ancestors, not indeed parents; in which Interpreters easily agree. Why many words? Since this is not about the daughter of Pharaoh, who had no children, but about the mystical Bride, the Fathers also are to be understood spiritually, just as the children are. But that has already been dealt with above. And let these things suffice concerning Psalm 45, which will be further confirmed for the most part from the Song of Songs.

Latin:

CONFITEBUNTUR TIBI) Id est, laudabunt te.

Non opus est, ut Patres commutemus cum matribus. Nec v. 11. jubebatur Sponsa tantum Parentes relinquere, sed oblivisci populi sui, & domus patris sui. Proinde Patres hic intelliguntur majores, non vero parentes; in quo consentiunt facile Interpretes. Quid multis? Quum non agatur hic de filia Pharaonis, quæ filios non habuit, sed de Sponsa mystica, Patres etiam spiritualiter, perinde uti filii intelligendi. Sed de eo supra jam actum. Atque hæc sufficiant de Psal. 45. quæ è Cantico Canticorum pleraque confirmabuntur ulterius.

## 46:1 Argument
PSALM XLVI. A firm fortress for the Church in God.

FOR THE SECRETS] עַל־עֲלָמוֹת. I think the meaning is, those who were in charge of the maidens, that is, those who taught the choir of maidens to sing, as in 1 Chron. 15, 20.

Itranus takes the word עַלְמוֹת concerning the maidens of Korah. As for why the LXX and the Vulgate interpret it as 'for the secrets', some explain עֲלָמוֹת as concerning a secret matter known only to God regarding the future liberation of the Church. Blessed Luther interprets it 'Von der Jugend' [concerning youth], along with Chrysostom, as concerning the youth and adolescence, or rather the virginity of the Church and its hidden and wonderful liberation. Blessed Gesner and Backius, and most others, wish for a musical instrument to be designated by that name, to which Avenarius agrees in his Lexicon, which opinion is confirmed by the passage 1 Chron. 15, 20. Some Jews make the argument of the Psalm to be the fall of Sennacherib according to Aben-Ezra; this indeed concerns the battles of Jerusalem. Rabbi Solomon with the Chaldean [Targum] concerning the sons of Korah, since their father was swallowed up, but they remained alive and motionless, as they say, in the air. Rabbi David Kimchi concerning the wars of Gog. Some among the Christians interpret it concerning the victory of David over his enemies and the defense of the Israelite Church: in which manner Blessed Luther in the argument of the Psalm says it is a thanksgiving, which the people of Israel were singing at that time for those divine benefits and miracles, because God powerfully defended Jerusalem in the midst of the nations and enemies, etc. which, however, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Euthymius, and most of our own rightly apply to the liberation of the Christian Church from persecutions, concerning which Psalm Blessed Luther composed an ode full of the Spirit: Ein veste Burg ist unser GOtt; concerning which let the same be compared in the cited Tom. III. Witteb. Lat. fol. 413.

Verse 1. IN TRIBULATIONS, WHICH HAVE FOUND US EXCEEDINGLY.

In Hebrew it is: a helper in tribulations has been found exceedingly, that is, God has been found in tribulations a helper very powerful to intervene. To which sense, although excellent, Bellarmine undeservedly prefers the reading of the Vulgate and the LXX Interpreters, even though he does not know how to say what the LXX read. Thus, oversights of this kind produce for men readings found nowhere, which they are not even able to attain by guessing, so that they only render the Hebrew truth uncertain.

Latin:

PSALMUS XLVI. Arx in Deo firma Ecclesiæ.

PRO ARCANIS] עַל־עֲלָמוֹת. Sensum esse puto, qui puellis præerant, id est, qui chorum puellarum docebant canere, ut Paral. 15, 20.

ITranus vocem עַלְמוֹת de puellis Core accipit. Quid LXX. & Vulgat. pro arcanis interpretantur, עֲלָמוֹת quod de re arcana soli Dei nota futura liberatione Ecclesiæ nonnulli explicant. B. Lutherus Von der Jugend, cum Chrysostomo de juventute & adolescentia, imo virginitate Ecclesiæ ejusque occulta & mirabili liberatione interpretantur. B. Gesnerus & Backius, & alii plerique instrumentum Musicum isto nomine designari volunt, quibus adstipulatur Avenarius in Lexico, quam sententiam firmat locus 1. Paral. 15, 20. Argumentum Psalmi Judæi nonnulli faciunt à casu Sennacheribi apud Aben-Ezram; hic vero de præliis Jerusalem. R. Salomo cum Chald. de filiis Core, cum pater eorum absorptus, illi vero vivi & immobiles mansere, ut ajunt, in aëre. R. David Kimchi de bellis Gogi. E Christianis non- nulli de victoria Davidis ab hostibus suis & defensio- ne Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ interpretantur: quo pacto B. Luther. in argum. Psalm. est gratiarum actio, in- quit, quam eo tempore canebat populus Israel pro be- neficiis & miraculis illis divinis, quod Deus Jerusa- lem in medio gentium & hostium potenter defendebat &c. quam tamen recte Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Au- gustin. Chrysostom. Theodoret. Euthym. & nostri ple- rique ad liberationem Ecclesiæ Christianæ à persequu- tionibus applicant, de quo Psalmo B. Lutherus odam Spiritu plenam composuit: Ein veste Burg ist unser GOtt; qua de conferatur idem citato Tom. III. Witteb. Lat. fol. 413.

Vers. 1. IN TRIBULATIONIBUS, QUÆ INVE- NERUNT NOS NIMIS.

In Ebræo est: adjutor in tribulationibus inventus est nimis, id est, Deus in tribulationibus inventus est axiliator valde potens intervenire. Cui sensui, etsi optimo, immerito præfert Bellarminus lectio- nem Vulgatæ & LXX. Interpp. utut nesciat dicere quid legerint LXX. Ita παροράματα hominibus istius pariunt lectiones nuspiam repertas, quas ne divinando assequi valent, ut solum incertam red- dant veritatem Ebraicam.

## 46:1 Addition
On Psalm 46.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 46.

## 46:5 Addition
Verse 6. GOD IS IN THE MIDST OF HER, SHE SHALL NOT BE MOVED.

These things are said concerning the city of God, which is the Church, according to Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Basil, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Euthymius. Therefore, Bellarmine notes that the present Psalm is rightly placed after the former: for in that one, he says, the exaltation of the Church is predicted on account of the spiritual marriage with the King Christ the Lord: but in this one, persecution and deliverance from persecution are predicted. Therefore, these things are not to be understood as concerning Jerusalem being delivered long ago from Sennacherib, with Calvin, Musculus, and Moller, much less concerning the Israelite people saved in the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, with the Rabbis and Bohlius, but concerning the Church, especially of the New Testament. Cf. Psalm 93:3, 4; Hebrews 12:22.

But the Papists in vain infer from this the perpetuity of the flourishing and temporal happiness of the Church, or its perpetual visibility: because visibility and happiness of that kind are a mere accident of the Church, whose preservation is indeed asserted here, but not precisely under that quality, or in the same state of happiness. Cf. concerning the use of the Hebrew phrase, that it does not imply the same state perpetually, Psalm 16:8, Psalm 18:6, Psalm 30:7, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DEUS IN MEDIO EJUS, NON COMMOVEBITUR.

De civitate Dei hæc dicuntur, quæ Ecclesia est juxta Ambros. Hieron. August. Basil. Chrysost. Theo- dor. Euthymium. Ideo Psalmum præsentem recte subjungi superiori Bellarm. notat: In illo enim, inquit, prædicta est Ecclesiæ exaltatio ob nuptias spirituales cum Rege Christo Domino : in hoc autem prædicitur persecutio, & liberatio a persecutione. Non ergo de Hierosolyma à Sennacheribo olim liberanda cum Cal- vino, Musculo, Mollero hæc accipienda, nedum de populo Israelitico servato in rebellione Core, Dathan & Abiram cum Rabbinis & Bohlio, sed de Ecclesia, imprimis N. T. Conf. Psal. 93, 3. 4. Ebr. 12. v. 22.

Frustra autem Papistæ hinc colligunt perpetuitatem floris & felicitatis temporalis Ecclesiæ, aut visibilita- tem perpetuam: quia visibilitas & felicitas ejusmodi est merum accidens Ecclesiæ, cujus conservatio quidem, hic adseritur, sed non sub ista præcise qua- litate, vel in eodem felicitatis statu. Conf. de usu phraseos Ebraicæ, quod non inferat eundem per- petuo statum Psal. 16, 8. Psal. 18, 6. Ps. 30, 7. &c.

## 47:1 Argument
PSALM XLVII. The triumphant ascension of Christ.

Latin:

PSALM. XLVII. Ascensio Christi triumphatrix.

## 47:3
Verse 4. HE HAS CHOSEN FOR US HIS INHERITANCE.

Thus the LXX, which sentence Bellarmine calls clearer than that which is in the Hebrew: He has chosen for us our inheritance, for this can scarcely be understood. But the sense in the Hebrew is easy: whether you explain it thus with most, He has chosen for us our heavenly inheritance, which is also God's inheritance, because it is from God, and ours, because it was prepared for us, or whether you understand the people of God, the Church, as congratulating itself: i.e., God has chosen for us our inheritance, namely the possession of the nations for (or to) the magnificence of Jacob, which He loved, because He does not love this inheritance of the Jewish Church otherwise than the magnificence of Jacob itself. Thus it agrees with the preceding verse: He subdues the peoples under us and the nations under our feet.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ELEGIT NOBIS HÆREDITATEM SUAM.

ITa LXX. quam sententiam luculentiorem dicit Bellarminus, quam quæ in Ebræo est: Elegit no- bis hæreditatem nostram, hoc enim vix intelligi posse. At facilis est in Ebræo sensus: sive ita微 explices cum plerisque selegit nobis hæreditatem nostram cœle- stem, quæ & Dei est hæreditas, quia à Deo, & no- stra, quia nobis præparata, sive populum Dei Eccle- siam intelligas sibi quasi gratulari: q. d. Deus elegit nobis hæreditatem nostram gentium nempe possessi- onem in (vel ad) magnificentiam Jacob, quam di- lexit, quia non aliter diligit hanc hæreditatem Ec- clesiæ Judaicæ, quam ipsam magnificentiam Jacob. Sic congruit præcedenti versui: subjicit populos no- bis & gentes sub pedibus nostris.

## 47:4
Verse 5. GOD ASCENDS IN A JUBILEE.

The Hebrews and Lyranus understand it concerning the ascent of the Ark of the Lord, which Solomon caused to ascend, but it is one thing to cause to ascend, another to ascend, and the Ark is nowhere called the Lord, and the κέλευσμα (summons) of the nations to jubilee and applause teaches that these things pertain to the New Testament. Therefore, the Holy Fathers Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, and Euthymius interpret this prophecy concerning the ascension of Christ the Lord into heaven, by which the Holy Spirit was obtained and given to the nations, and on account of whom all nations together with the faithful from the people of Israel deservedly applaud and jubilate, to which sense the comparison of Psalm 68 and the very text of the present Davidic passage itself is favorable. For by the ascension into heaven the Lord was made King of all the earth, and He reigned over the nations, and sat upon His holy seat, verse 8, on the throne of majesty, at the right hand of God the Father in the highest. Thence the Princes of the peoples (of the nations) were gathered with the God of Abraham (the Messiah, who was God Himself, Genesis 15, verse 1, chapter 17), so that they also might have Him as God, and

they themselves might be His people. Here Bellarmine again chastises the Hebrew truth without merit. For what is it, he says, the Princes of the peoples are gathered to the people of the God of Abraham? But the sense is in the open, that namely the Princes of the peoples are likewise gathered to be the people of the God of Abraham, and pertain to the covenant entered into with Abraham. Thus the LXX and the Vulgate rendered the sense, they did not precisely express the words, or they believed that other points were to be placed underneath, as Bellarmine wishes. For the sense comes to the same thing.

FOR THE STRONG GODS OF THE EARTH ARE EXCEEDINGLY EXALTED.

Bellarmine again refutes the original text, which has it thus: For to the Lord belong the shields of the earth, who is exceedingly exalted. The Hebrew seems to the Cardinal to have no sense; but the sense is very open, that namely the shields of the earth or the Magistrates (Hosea 4, verse 18) owe all their axiom to the Lord, as some explain, therefore they deservedly submit themselves to Christ, to which Blessed Gesner agrees, or which is our opinion, that even the shields of the earth obey that Lord, of whose ascension the sacred psalmist sings, which is the reason why the people of the God of Abraham are also the Princes of the nations, and ought to be reckoned as such, who therefore is exceedingly exalted, as one to whom the shields of the earth submit themselves, but the sense in the Vulgate version is less fitting: The strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted. For the Psalm does not sing of the sublimity of the Princes, but of the eminence of the Prince of Princes, the Messiah. Nor does that version correspond in any way to the Hebrew text, in which אלהים is not found in the nominative case, but לאלהים in the genitive or dative, just as in the Greek LXX translation the genitive τῶ θεῶ is expressed. Nor does a plural verb occur, but a singular one, he is exalted, in the Hebrew. What sense, therefore, will it be, The strong gods of the earth he is exalted? And where is the word מגני left, which Jerome certainly read, and translated shields of the earth, just as in Hos. 4, verse 18, he rendered the same as protectors. Clearly, therefore, the Greek and Vulgate Latin translation is faulty. Genebrard wishes to assist the Vulgate, explaining it concerning the Holy Trinity, Gods the shields and protectors of the earth. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are vehemently exalted in this victory of the world, as if ל indicates the nominative emphatically as in Is. 32, verse 1. But there is no reason why one should depart from the customary meaning of the prefix ל, which even the LXX interpreters retained: nor are several persons in the divine essence ever expressed in the plural in this way by מגני shields, bucklers, or protectors of the earth, for there is one protector, one Lord, even if there are three Elohim: nor, finally, is this Psalm about the exaltation of the Holy Trinity, but about the exaltation of the Messiah, as even the Papal interpreters themselves admit along with the orthodox Fathers.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ASCENDIT DEUS IN JU- BILO.

Ebræi & Lyranus de ascensu arcæ Domini in- telligunt, quam ascendere fecit Salomo, sed aliud est, ascendere fecit, aliud ascendit, neque uspiam arca dicitur Dominus, & ad N. T. hæc pertinere κέλευ- σμα gentium ad jubilum & plausum docet. Ideo hoc vaticinium de ascensu Christi Domini in cœlum, quo impetratus & donatus & Spiritus Sanctus gen- tibus, & ob quem omnes gentes cum fidelibus è populo Israelis merito plaudunt & jubilant, inter- pretantur S. Patres Chrysostom. Hieronym. Augustin. Theodoret. & Euthymius, cui sensui favet collatio Psalm. 68. & ipsum τὸ ῥητὸν præsentis textus Davi- dici. Per ascensum enim in cœlum factus est Do- minus Rex omnis terræ, & regnavit super gentes, & sedit super sedem sanctam suam vers. 8. in throno ma- jestatis, ad dextram Dei Patris in excelsis. Inde Principes populorum (gentilium) cum Deo Abra- ham (Messia, qui erat ipsi Deus Genes. 15. vers. 1. cap. 17.) congregati sunt, ut & iis esset in Deum, &

ipsi populus ejus essent. Castigat hic iterum præ- ter meritum Bellarmin. Ebraicam veritatem. Quid enim est, inquit, Principes populorum congregati sunt populo Deo Abraham? At sensus in aprico est, quod nempe Principes populorum congregati itidem po- pulus Dei Abraham sint, & ad fœdus cum Abraha- mo initum pertineant. Sic sensum reddidere LXX. & Vulgatus, non præcise verba expresserunt, aut alia puncta substernenda esse, uti vult Bellarm. credi- derunt. Sensus enim eodem recidit.

QUONIAM FORTES DII TERRÆ VE- HEMENTER ELEVATI SUNT.

Redarguit denuo Bellarmin. textum origina- lem, qui sic habet: Quia Domino scuta terræ, qui valde exaltatus est. Sensum nullum Ebræa habere videntur Cardinali; at sensus est perquam aper- tus, quod nempe Domino scuta terræ vel Magistra- tus Hos. 4. vers. 18. omne suum axioma debeant, uti nonnulli exponunt, ideo merito Christo sese submittant, quibus adstipulatur B. Gesnerus, vel quæ nostra est sententia, quod Domino illi, de cu- jus ascensu canit Hieropsaltes, etiam scuta terræ pa- reant, quæ ratio est, cur populus Dei Abraham ipsi etiam Principes gentium sint, & censeri debeant, qui proinde valde elevatus est, utpote cui scuta ter- ræ se submittant, sensus vero in versione Vulg. mi- nus convenit: Dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt. Non enim de sublimitate Principum, sed de eminentia Principis Principum Messiæ Psalmus ca- nit. Neque congruit illa versio ullatenus textui Ebræo, in quo non אלהים in casu recto habetur, sed לאלהים in Genitivo, vel Dativo, uti etiam in Græca LXX. translatione Genitivus expressus est τῶ θεῶ. Neque verbum plurale occurrit, sed singu- lare, elevatus est, in Ebræo. Quis ergo sensus erit, Dii fortes terræ elevatus est? Et ubi relinquitur vox מגני, quam Hieronymus utique legit, & vertit scu- ta terræ, uti Hos. 4. vers. 18. reddidit eandem prote- ctores. Plane ergo vitiosa est Græca & Vulgata Lati- na translatio. Genebrardus Vulgatæ succurrere vult, explicans eam de S. S. Trinitate, Dii clypei & pro- tectores terræ. Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus ve- hementer elevati sunt in hac orbis victoria, quasi ל indicet nominativum emphatice ut Es. 32. vers. 1. Sed non est, cur ab usitata ל præfixi significatione recedatur, quam etiam LXX. Interpp. retinuere: neque uspiam personæ plures in essentia divina ita exprimuntur in plurali מגני scuta, clypei, vel prote- ctores terræ, unus enim est protector, unus Dominus, etfi tres Elohim: nec denique de elevatione S. S. Trinitatis, sed de exaltatione Messiæ in hoc Psalmo agitur, fatentibus id cum orthodoxis Patribus ipsis Interpretibus Pontificiis.

## 47:9
Verse 10.

THE PRINCES OF THE PEOPLES ARE GATHERED WITH THE GOD OF ABRAHAM) The Greeks read עם with a chireq, not as we do, with a patach. The sense in the Hebrew is: The leaders of the peoples joined themselves to the people of Abraham: that is: they sought our alliances. See also the following Psalm, and what we said regarding Psalm 2.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

PRINCIPES POPULORVM CONGREGATI SVNT CVM DEO ABRAHAM) Legerunt Græci עם cum chirec, non ut nos, cum patach. Sensus in Hebræo est: Pri- mores populorum adjunxerunt se populo Abraham: id est: fœ- dera nostra ambierunt. Vide & Psalmum sequentem, & quæ diximus ad Psalmum 2.

## 47:9 Addition
To Ps. 47, v. 17, near the end.

We only add those things which my blessed father-in-law, Dr. Hülsemann, [said] regarding this 17th verse: Although the commentator under the name of Jerome, Athanasius, Basil, Eusebius, and other Greek fathers refer these things as if spoken in the place of consolation to the bride, so that she might more easily leave her fathers and her kindred, because she herself is also about to receive sons, just as Boblius also interprets it: nevertheless, our Luther and Gesner observed that the expression varies here from the feminine to the masculine and the discourse is turned to the bridegroom, which was also observed by Vatablus and Jansenius. See the difference of construction from the comparison of v. 14 and 15 with this verse. Junius indeed and the Belgians acknowledge that the discourse is turned to Christ, but they take the preposition תחת participatively for the older and younger members of the Church, so that the continuous series of the faithful of the New Testament is understood; but from verse 11 and 12, it appears that by fathers and father's house is understood the state of the Old Testament and that it is distinguished from the condition of the future bride; therefore that [word] for fathers is to be taken adversatively, that is, in place of, instead of the forsaken fathers, not communicatively, and fathers and sons shall be born to you in the New Testament, just as elsewhere תחת is often taken for succession in the place of him who has ceased, not who reigns at the same time, or who shares in the state of succession. See examples in Gen. 36, 33, 34; Jos. 5, 7; 2, 15; 2 Sam. 17, 15, and passim, and compare Rom. 9, 5. Therefore this is a most clear testimony that not only the ceremonies, but the whole worship and axioms of the Old Testament and the manner of pursuing righteousness, which consisted in works according to Rom. 9, 31, are to be abrogated. Nor is it necessary, given this explanation, to understand by fathers only the impious of the Old Testament; we say that both the faithful and the hypocrites are to be understood in v. 11 and here. For although the faithful were saved by the same faith in Christ by which we are saved: Acts 15, 9, 10; nevertheless, their public pursuit consisted in holiness and external worship, Heb. 9, 9 seq., which public worship is said to be abrogated. The annotation of Saa is clearly inept, explaining fathers through prophets and apostles, and sons about to be born likewise through the apostles. Read our Luther, Vol. III, Jena, Latin.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 47. v. 17. sub finem.

Addimus solum ea, quæ ad versum hunc 17. B. Socer Dn. D. Hülsemannus: Quanquam commentator sub nomine Hieronymi, Athanasius, Basilius, Eusebius, aliiq́; Græci patres, hæc tanquam consolationis loco ad sponsam dicta referant, ut eo facilius relinquat Patres & cognationem suam, quia & ipsa susceptura est filios, quomodo etiam Boblius interpretatur: Observarunt tamen noster Lutherus & Gesnerus variare hic locutionem e fœminino in masculinum & converti sermonem ad sponsum, quod Vatablo etiam observatum fuit, & Jansenio. Differentiam constructionis vide ex collat. v. 14. & 15. cum hoc versu. Junius quidem & Belgæ agnoscunt sermonem converti ad Christum, sed præpositionem תחת sumunt participative pro adultioribus & junioribus membris Ecclesiæ, ut intelligatur fidelium Nov. T. continua series; sed ex versu 11. & 12. apparet, per Patres & paternam domum intelligi statum V. T. eumque contradistingui futuræ sponsæ conditioni; Itaque illud pro Patribus, adversative, id est, loco, vice desertorum Patrum, non communicative, & Patres & Filii nascentur tibi in Nov. Test. accipiendum est, ut alibi sæpe תחת pro successione in locum ejus, qui desiit, non qui simul regnat, vel comparticipat de statu successionis. Vide exempla Genes. 36, 33. 34. Jos. 5, 7. c. 2, 15. 2. Sam. 17, 15. & passim, & confer Rom. 9, 5. Itaque hic clarissimum testimonium est, non tantum ceremonias, sed totum cultum & axiomata V. T. modumque insectandi justitiam, qui consistebat in operibus ad Rom. 9, 31. abrogandum esse. Neque necessum est, posita hac explicatione per Patres solos impios V. T. intelligere; dicimus utrosque & fideles & hypocritas intelligendos esse v. 11. & hic. Quanquam enim fideles eadem in Christum fide salvati sint, qua nos salvamur: Actor. 15, 9. 10. publicum tamen eorum studium constitit in sanctitate & cultu externo Hebr. 9, 9. seq. qui publicus cultus dicitur abrogandus. Annotatio Saa plane inepta est, explicans Patres per Prophetas & Apostolos, filios nascituros identidem per Apostolos. Lege nostrum Lutherum T. III. Jen. Lat.

## 48:1 Argument
PSALM XLVIII. The City of the Lord.

THE SECOND OF THE SABBATH) It is not in the Hebrew: yet it is not noted in vain: for some Psalms were sung on feast days, others on certain days of the week.

Latin:

PSALM. XLVIII. Civitas Domini.

SECUNDA SABBATI) Non est in Hebræo: non ta- men id frustra annotatum est: nam alii Psalmi diebus festis, alii certis diebus hebdomadis canebantur.

## 48:1
Verse 2. MOUNT SION IS FOUNDED WITH THE EXULTATION OF THE WHOLE EARTH.

Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Euthymius explain this concerning the rebuilding of Jerusalem, but the things that are sung in this Psalm are too magnificent to

may gather at Jerusalem. And therefore Jerome and Augustine more correctly refer it to the Church, for which the whole earth rightly exults. Even the Rabbis themselves, Kimchi and Aben-Ezra, explain it concerning the days of the Messiah. But how Cassiodorus and Lyranus twist it to the birth of Christ, it is not relevant to say, much less how Comestor [twists it] to the ships by which the Magi came to Christ. Nor is it right to mention the trifles about the second SABBATH, which crept into the Greek title of the Psalm against the faith of the Hebrew Codices. Although it may indeed be conceded that the Holy Spirit alluded to the city of Jerusalem, which was often besieged but not taken, as in the time of Rehoboam 2 Chron. 12, [and] Jehoshaphat 2 Kings 16, it must not however be said with Bellarmine that the Holy Spirit intended a double sense, but the Psalm is to be explained according to the letter concerning the Church of Christ alone. Gesner himself, however much he made the argument of the Psalm a thanksgiving, because Jerusalem was preserved against the incursions of enemies, at v. 2 acknowledges that the spiritual Jerusalem is commended: he renders the Hebrew in this verse 2 thus: Beautiful in shoot, the joy of the whole earth, Mount Zion on the sides of the North, and by the shoot he understands Christ, who was about to preach and suffer at Jerusalem, whom D. Backius followed, but this mystery would have been indicated too concisely thus. B. Luther rendered: The Mount of Zion is like a beautiful little shoot, in which the whole land finds comfort. Felix, in Bugenhagen, explained it as a beautiful nymph, or bride, the joy of the whole world is Mount Zion, which Bugenhagen understands of the Church, the bride. Some explain it concerning beauty in climate or situation and the convenience of the air, with the Hebrews leading the way. Thus also B. Boblius: It lies pleasantly, beautifully, even more beautifully than Jerusalem. The explanation of our Forster in his Lexicon pleases me: פוֹז a shoot, which is tossed here and there and into all parts of the earth by the wind, and is taken figuratively for the doctrine of the Gospel to be propagated into all the earth by the agitation of the Holy Spirit Psalm 48. beautiful in shoot is the joy of the whole earth, Mount Zion. For this beauty is celebrated also in Psalm 72, verse 16. Genebrardus interprets these and the rest concerning Jerusalem thus: God is indeed praiseworthy everywhere, but especially in Jerusalem (the Church) appositively, in His holy mountain, the mountain dedicated and consecrated to His own worship. For it was situated on mountains to lift up the minds of the faithful to heaven: the topography of which he subjoins especially for the sake of Christ, whom God had determined to bring forth from it for the revelation of the Gentiles and the glory of His people. Let the rest be read there. But however much an allusion may be made to Jerusalem, to Mount Zion toward the south, where the citadel of David was situated, and to the sides of the North, where Mount Moriah and the temple of Solomon were built, the amplitude of the Church is nevertheless properly designated as diffused to the south and north. Compare verses 9, 11, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 2. FUNDATUR EXULTATIONE UNIVER- SÆ TERRÆ MONS SION.

DE reædificatione Hierusalem explicant Chryso- stom. Theodoret. & Euthymius, sed magnificen- tiora sunt, quæ in hoc Psalmo canuntur, quam ut

Hierosolymæ conveniant. Ideoque rectius Hie- ron. & August. eum ad Ecclesiam referunt, ob quam universa terra merito exultat. Etiam Rabbini ipsi, Kimchi & Aben-Ezra de diebus Messiæ exponunt. Quomodo autem Cassiodorus & Lyranus ad nativi- tatem Christi detorqueant, non attinet dicere, ne- dum quomodo Comestor ad naves, quibus magi ad Christum devenerint. Neque commemorare fas est nugas, de secunda SABBATI, quæ in titulum Græcum Psalmi irrepsit contra fidem Ebræorum Codicum. Quamvis vero concedi possit, allusisse Spir. S. ad urbem Hierusalem, quæ sæpe oppugna- ta, non expugnata fuit, utpote tempore Rehabeam 2. Paral. 12. Josaphat 2. Reg. 16. non tamen cum Bel- larmino geminum sensum intendisse Spir. S. dicen- dum est, sed de sola Ecclesia Christi, quoad literam Psalmus explicandus. Gesnerus ipse, utut argu- mentum Psalmi fecerit gratiarum actionem, quod conservata sit Hierusalem adversus incursiones hostium ad v. 2. commendari Hierusalem spiritualem agno- scit: Ebræa in hoc vers. 2. ita reddit: Pulcer surculo, gaudium totius terræ, mons Sion ad latera Aquilonis, & per surculum Christum intelligit, qui Hierosoly- mis concionaturus & passurus erat, quem sequutus est D. Backius, sed nimis concise sic indicatum fuis- set hoc mysterium. B. Luther. reddidit: Der Berg Sion ist wie ein schön Zweiglein, deß sich das gantze Land tröstet. Felix apud Bugenhagium ex- posuit formosa nympha, vel sponsa lætitia totius orbis mons Sion, quod de Ecclesia sponsa intelligit Bu- genhagius. Nonnulli de pulchritudine in climate vel situ aërisque commoditate exponunt, præeun- tibus Ebræis. Sic etiam B. Boblius: Sie lieget lustig, schön, noch schöner wie Jerusalem. Placet Forsteri nostri explicatio in Lexico: פוֹז surculus, qui hinc inde & in omnes terræ partes agitatur vento, & figu- rate sumitur pro doctrina Evangelii in omnem ter- ram agitatione Spir. S. propaganda Psalm. 48. pulcher surculo gaudium totius terræ est mons Sion. Nam hæc pulchritudo celebratur etiam Psalm. 72. vers. 16. Hæc & reliqua de Hierosolyma ita interpreta- tur Genebrardus: Deus quidem ubique laudabilis, sed præcipue in Hierusalem (Ecclesia) appositorie, monte sancto ejus, monte ipsius cultui dedicato & consecrato. Erat enim in montibus sita ad elevandas mentes fidelium in cælum: cujus topographiam subji- cit in gratiam præcipue Christi, quem ex ea statuisset Deus educere ad revelationem gentium, & gloriam plebis suæ. Cætera ibi legantur. Sed utut ad Hie- rosolymam ad montem Sion versus meridiem, ubi arx Davidis sita, & ad latera Aquilonis, ubi mons Moria & templum Salomonis conditum erat, allu- sio fiat, Ecclesiæ tamen amplitudo proprie designatur diffusa ad meridiem & septentrionem. Confer. vers. 9. 11. 12.

## 48:1 Addition
On Psalm 48.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 48.

## 48:1 Addition
Verse 1. IN THE CITY OF OUR GOD.

R. David says that this Psalm pertains to the days of the Messiah, but he refers the praise of Jerusalem to the Jerusalem to be rebuilt under the Messiah. Cocceius falsely dreams that it is permitted for them to hope for this; for nothing of the sort can be extracted from Luke 21:24, where the diametrically opposite is asserted. He acknowledges, however, that this city is to be understood as the Church of the New Testament: concerning which

Sion, Isa. 54 and ch. 60:10, 11, 18. He teaches that what is indicated here in verse 3 by a triple name—Sion, the northern sides, the city—refuting at length the opinion of those who think that Sion was situated in the northern part of the city, and observing the distribution of Jerusalem into 3 parts: Sion, the lower city, which is the northern region, and the house of the Lord or Moriah. Which he applies to the Church. But Alexander Carerius, de indulg. ch. 2, Sanderus de clave David b. 1, ch. 6, Bozius b. II de Sign. Eccl. are ridiculous, dragging those things which are in verses 5, 6, 7 to the basilicas, the towers of the city of Rome, the votive offerings and anathemas brought to this city: when it is clearer than light from verses 8 and 15 that the discourse is about the universal Church, which even the Papists themselves, Jansenius, Lyranus, Estius, admit.

Latin:

Vers. 1. IN CIVITATE DEI NOSTRI.

Ad dies Messiæ hunc Psalmum pertinere, ait R. David, sed encomium Hierosolymæ refert ad Hieroso- lymam sub Messia denuo ædificandam. Quod spe- rare ipsis licere Coccejus falso somniat; nihil enim tale è Luc. 21, 24. exsculpi potest, ubi e diametro contrarium asseritur. Agnofcit tamen de Eccle- sia N. T. hanc civitatem accipiendam esse: de qua

Sione Esa. 54. & cap. 60, 10. 11. 18. Quam vers. 3. triplici nomine hic indicari, Sionis, laterum Aquilonarium, civitatis, docet, prolixe refellens eorum sententiam, qui Sionem, parte urbis Aquilo- nari sitam fuisse putant, & observans distributio- nem Hierosolymæ in 3. partes Sionem, urbem inferio- rem, quæ est regio Aquilonaris, & domum Domini sive Morijah. Quæ ad Ecclesiam applicat. Ridiculi autem sunt Alexander Carerius, de indulg. cap. 2. Sanderus de clave David l. 1. c. 6. Bozius l. II. de Sign. Eccl. ea quæ v. 5. 6. 7. trahentes ad basilicas, tur- res urbis Romæ, donaria & anathemata huic urbi col- lata: quum luce clarius sit è v. 8. & 15. de universali Ecclesia sermonem esse, quod fatentur ipsimet quo- que Papistæ, Jansenius, Lyranus, Estius.

## 48:4
Vers. 5.

FOR THE KINGS OF THE EARTH HAVE GATHERED. Bellarmine noting this and the following two verses, the Latins Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine take it concerning the Gentiles converted to the faith. The Greeks, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Euthymius take it concerning the Gentiles attacking the faith. The Cardinal judges both these expositions to be true. But how can both the converted nations and the opposing nations be understood at the same time? How are the same words to be taken in this sense, they gathered together, that is, into the unity of the faith? and in this manner, they gathered against the Christian Church: likewise those were troubled by true repentance, and troubled partly by indignation and partly by grief. How can the vehement Spirit, and [the interpretation] concerning the Holy Spirit with vehement ardor of charity inflaming and breaking the ships of Tarshish, i.e., pride, luxury, and avarice, as the Cardinal explains the opinion of the Latins, and [the interpretation] concerning a strong wind breaking ships compared to an admirable manifestation of divine power, by which idolatry is to be crushed, just as a storm is wont to crush and dissipate ships in the sea in a very short time, as he later explains the mind of the Greeks, be taken at the same time? One and the same certain opinion must therefore be retained, which is this: concerning the enemies of the Church, the Kings of the earth gathering themselves against the city of the great King Christ, to be confounded and crushed by a vehement spirit, just as the ships of Tarshish, even great ones, such as are carried in the Mediterranean Sea, because Tarshish the son of Javan Gen. 10 inhabited the coastal places of that sea, (others wish India to be denoted by the word Tarshish 1 Kings 10, 2 Chron. 10.) driven by the wind with great force, are wont to be crushed by being dashed against rocks.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QUONIAM REGES TERRÆ CONGRE- GATi SUNT. Hunc & sequentes duos versus Bellarmin. no- tante, Latini Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus de gentilibus conversis ad fidem. Græci, Chrysostom. Theodor. Euthymius de gentilibus oppugnantibus fi- dem accipiunt. Quam utramque expositionem ve- ram esse judicat Cardinalis. At quomodo & gen- tes conversæ & gentes adversariæ simul intelligi pos- sunt? Quomodo eadem verba & hoc sensu acci- pienda, convenerunt in unum, id est, in unitatem fidei? & hoc pacto, convenerunt adversus Ecclesiam Christianam: item illa conturbati sunt per veram pænitentiam, & conturbati partim indignatione partim dolore. Quomodo Spiritus vehemens & de Spiritu S. vehementi ardore caritatis inflam- mante confringente naves Tarsis, h. e. superbiam, luxuriam & avaritiam, uti Latinorum sententiam Cardinalis explicat, & de vento valido naves con- fringente admirabili manifestationi divinæ poten- tiæ comparato, qua idololatria conterenda, uti so- let tempestas brevissimo tempore conterere, & dis- sipare naves in mari, ut postmodum Græcorum ex- ponit mentem, simul accipi potest? Una ergo ea- demque certa retinenda est sententia, quæ hæc est de hostibus Ecclesiæ Regibus terræ adversus civitatem Regis magni Christi sese congregantibus confun- dendis & spiritu vehementi conterendis, ficuti naves Tharsis magnæ etiam, quales feruntur in mari me- diterraneo, quia Tarsis filius Javan Genes. 10. lo- ca littoralia maris istius incoluit, (alii Indiam notari volunt voce Tharsis 1. Reg. 10. 2. Paralip. 10.) à vento magna vi impulsæ scopulis allisæ conteri solent.

## 48:14
Vers. 15.

HE SHALL RULE US FOREVER) Various readings have produced various versions in this place. The LXX and Symmachus read עלמות with a holem over the ayn, and thought it was for עלמים Ages, with the Lamed understood, as also elsewhere. Others [read] with the same letters, but with a patach under the ayn, and a shurech before the last, from youth. Others with the same letters, with other vowels, translate it in secret. Others divide the words על־מות and take על for עד and interpret it unto death. And Jerome follows this in his version from the Hebrew, as does Kimchi.

If the certainty of an authentic text is to be concluded immediately from various versions, what will be left? That is apparent even from this place, where such discrepant readings are invented. In the Hebrew there is על־מות unto death. And it appears that it was also held in the time of Jerome and R. David Kimchi, who interpreted it thus. Nor do the LXX or Symmachus seem to have read otherwise, even if they explain it otherwise, looking to the sense, not the words; which was also done by Don Aben-Jechijah, who explained: For He does not desert us in death, but accompanies us unto eternal life, and leads us. Add that the words על־מות can be rendered ABOVE death, as Ludov. de Dieu observes on this passage, just as the Syrian rendered it, i.e., into eternity, as the Arabs interpreted it; although David Kimchi observes that it can also be explained as one word, i.e. like adolescents, or youth, which sense Luther also expressed. R. Aben-Ezra joins both interpretations, who nevertheless does not therefore approve of a double reading. See Buxtorff against Capellus p. 706.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

IPSE REGET NOS IN SECULA) Variæ lectiones varias hoc loco & versiones peperere. LXX. & Symmachus legere עלמות per holem ad ayn, & putarunt esse pro עלמים Secula, subaudito, ut & alibi ל. Alii iisdem literis, sed cum patach sub ayn, & schurech ante ultimam, à pueritia. Alii iisdem literis, vocalibus aliis, vertunt in ab- scondito. Alii dividunt voces על־מות & על fumto pro עד interpretantur ad mortem. Et hoc in versione ex He- bræo sequitur Hieronymus, ut & Kimchi.

Si è variis versionibus diversitas lectionum sta- tim concludenda, quæ relinquetur textus authen- tici certitudo? Id vel ex hoc loco apparet, ubi tam discrepantes finguntur lectiones. In Hebræo habetur על־מות usque ad mortem. Atque ita Hieronymi & R. Davidis Kimchi tempore etiam ha- buisse apparet, qui sic interpretati sunt. Nec aliter legisse videntur LXX. vel Symmachus, etsi aliter ex- plicent, sensum respicientes, non verba; quod etiam factum à Don Aben-Jechijah, qui exposuit: Non enim in morte nos deserit, sed in vitam æternam usque nos comitatur, & ducit. Adde quod verba על־מות reddi possint SUPRA mortem, ut ob- servat Ludov. de Dieu ad h. l. quemadmodum Syrus reddidit, h. e. in æternitatem, ut LXX. in omnia secu- la, ut Arabs interpretati sunt; Quamvis David Kim- chi observet, quod exponi etiam possit ut una vox q. d. כעלמות ficut adolescentes, vel adolescenti- am, quem sensum expressit etiam Lutherus. Utram- que interpretationem conjungit R. Aben-Ezra, qui tamen non ideo geminam lectionem probat. Vid. Buxtorff. contra Capell. p. 706.

## 48:14 Addition
To verse 15, near the end.

Lyranus reads without a Makkaph: whom B. Luther followed; concerning which he warned in his Epist. vom Dolmetschen. B. Hülsemann says that his explanation is more suitable to the text; because the axioms of the city of God were to be revealed to the childhood or the subsequent age, verse 9.

Latin:

Ad v. 15. sub finem.

Sine Makkaph legit Lyranus: quem sequu- tus est B. Lutherus; de quo in Epist. vom Dolmet- schen monuit. Ejus explicationem textui conve- nientiorem esse ait B. Hülsemannus; quia axioma- ta civitatis Dei erant pueritiæ seu ætati subsequenti pro- palanda v. 9.

## 49:1 Argument
PSALM XLIX. The vanity of the men of the age: The redemption of the faithful.

Latin:

PSALM. XLIX. Vanitas hominum seculi: Redemtio fide- lium.

## 49:3 Addition
To Psalm 49, verse 4, near the end.

And these things we have said thus in the previous edition of the Anti-Grotian annotations. We do not deny, however, that various arguments now incline the mind toward the latter explanation: that the Lord of Gods himself spoke then αὐτοπροσώπως [in person], manifested in the flesh, verse 1; that all from the rising of the sun to its setting were called to his doctrine, verse 2 (Compare Ps. 102:23, Isa. 60:4, Mal. 1:11); that the Gospel had to go forth from Sion (Compare Isa. 2:3, Mic. 4:2, Luke 24:47, Acts 2:1, ch. 13:46); that the calling of the Gentiles is insinuated in verses 4 and 5, when by heaven and earth the breadth of those to be called under heaven seems to some to be designated: (where, however, the sense of an adjuration against his people before heaven and earth could not inconveniently be retained); that in verses 5 and 6 the segregation of the faithful from the unfaithful is noted as about to happen in the kingdom of grace, and that the opposition of true and imaginary righteousness is instituted in verse 6, and 8, which doctrine is proper to the Gospel, Matt. 5:20, Rom. 9:30, ch. 10:30, Heb. 9:9, 10; that finally, duties are prescribed here to the faithful in verses 14 and 23, opposed to the boasting of the sacrifices and ceremonies of the Old Testament, and thus the Christian faithful are described here: of whom this periphrasis is proper from the concession of divine grace. Compare Hos. 14:3, Heb. 13:5. The doubt concerning the fire preceding the coming of the Lord is dissolved by parallel passages speaking in a similar way about the first coming of Christ. Mal. 3:2, Joel 2:18 seqq., Acts 2:17 seqq.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 49. vers. 4. sub finem.

Atque hæc ita in priori editione annotatorum Anti-Grotianorum diximus. Non diffitemur au- tem argumenta varia jam mentem inclinare in po- steriorem explicationem : quod Dominus Deorum ipse tum αὐτοπροσώπως loquutus sit manifestatus in carne v. 1. quod ad ejus doctrinam omnes à Solis ortu usque ad occasum vocati vers. 2. (Conf. Psal. 102, 23. Esa. 60, 4. Malach. 1, 11.) quod è Sion egredi debuerit Evangelium (Conf. Esa. 2, 3. Mich. 4, 2. Luc. 24, 47. Actor. 2, 1. cap. 13, 46.) quod gentium vocatio insinuetur v. 4. & 5. quum per cælum & ter- ram, latitudo vocandorum sub cœlo designata qui- busdam videatur: (ubi tamen sensus obtestationis contra populum suum coram cælo & terra retineri non incommode potuit) quod v. 5. 6. segregatio fi- delium ab infidelibus notetur in regno gratiæ futura, quodque veræ & imaginariæ justitiæ oppositio vers. 6. & 8. instituatur, quæ doctrina propria est Evan- gelii, Matth. 5, 20. Rom. 9, 30. cap. 10, 30. Ebr. 9, 9. 10. quod denique præscribantur hic officia fidelibus v. 14. 23. opposita jactationi sacrificiorum & ceremo- niarum Vet. Testam. adeoque Christiani fideles hic de- scribantur: quorum hæc periphrasis propria est a concessione gratiæ divinæ. Conf. Os. 14, 3. Ebr. 13, 5. Dubium de igne antecedente adventum Domi- ni diluitur per loca parallela de adventu primo Chri- sti modo simili loquentia. Malach. 3, 2. Joel. 2, 18. seqq. Actor. 2, 17. seqq.

## 49:12
Vers. 13.

AND MAN WHEN HE WAS IN HONOR DID NOT UNDERSTAND) They read: יבין but our Codices read ילין, that is, he will not lodge, for he did not persist. Others more curiously infer from this that Adam sinned on the first day.

Our Codices are correct. For the sense flows very well, otherwise than Ludov. Capellus, the scourge of Hebrew Codices, judged, man when he was in honor, did not persist, (or will not remain) he was made (or will be made) like to the beasts, which perish, so that a comparison is instituted of the ungodly, even if honored, with the beasts, to which as he is similar regarding his beastly life, so it is certain that he will not remain in dignity forever, but will perish miserably a little later, and regarding his beastly destruction will turn out similar to the brutes: both because the memory of such men is abolished with death, who lived for themselves alone like a beast; and because they often meet a tragic end, and after death they are treated no more honorably than beasts, by the example of the impious King Jehoiakim and the impious Queen Jezebel, Jer. 23, 2 Kings 20, then especially also because they depart hence with a beastly end, who lived like the swine of Epicurus's herd, or like beasts, without God, without hope of life; some even with the Atheists and Epicureans believe that man is extinguished no differently than a beast, Wis. 2. The Greeks seem to have taken that יָבִין from the last verse (whom the Latin followed), which is however different, and in the last verse it is thus: man established in honor, if he does not understand, is like the beasts that are cut off. For here the sum of what had been said is briefly repeated; therefore that לֹא יָבִין pertains to the description of the subject. To verse 13, which we are now treating, it constitutes the predicate: but what subject ought to be understood had already been described before. There is therefore no diversity of readings to be invented in this place of ours, where there is the greatest consensus of the Codices: for no differing Codex could be produced thus far. And so also Jerome read with our Codices in his time, rendering it thus: Man will not remain in honor; nor did the Chaldean otherwise; the impious will not remain in honor with the just; or the Hebrews: R. David Kimchi and Kasvenaki, from whom he cites these things: He does not remain: he does not die with riches, which he considers his honor, but leaves them to others. And death is called an overnight stay, just as it is also called sleep: and he adds this explanation: of a man who pursues worldly vanities, his soul does not stay overnight in honor, but perishes. Thus also R. Aben-Ezra and R. Obad. read, as well as R. Salom. Jarchi, who, however, the latter not only more curiously but also more ineptly deduced from this that Adam did not remain one night in integrity, but fell at the end of the day. For nothing of the sort is held here: nor is this about Adam, the first man, but about any man whatsoever who trusts in riches.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ET HOMO CUM IN HONORE ESSET NON IN- TELLEXIT) Legerunt: יבין at nostri Codices ילין, id est, non pernoctabit, pro non perstitit. Alii curiosius hinc infe- runt Adamum primo die peccasse.

REcte habent nostri Codices. Nam sensus optime fluit, secus atque Ludov. Capellus, fla- gellum Codicum Ebræorum, judicavit, homo cum in honore esset, non perstitit, (vel non permanebit) similis factus est (vel fiet) bestiis, quæ intereunt, ut comparatio instituatur impii, etsi honorati, cum bestiis, quibus uti quoad vitam bestialem similis est, ita certum eundem non perpetuo in dignitate permanfurum, sed paulo post miserabiliter interi- turum, & quoad bestialem interitum brutis simi- lem evasurum: Tum quod memoria talium cum morte aboleatur, qui sibi solis tanquam bestiæ vi- xere; tum quod sæpe tragicum fortiantur exitum, & post mortem nihilo honestius, quam bestiæ tra- ctentur, exemplo impii Regis Joachim, & Reginæ impiæ Jesabelis Jerem. 23. 2. Reg. 20. tum imprimis etiam quod bestiali interitu, qui ut Epicuri de gre- ge porci, vel instar bestiarum, vixerunt, sine Deo, sine spe vitæ hinc decedant; nonnulli etiam cum Atheis & Epicureis hominem non aliter, quam ju- mentum extingui credant Sap. 2. Illud ergo יָבִין Græci videntur affumsisse ex postremo versu, (quos sequutus est Latinus) qui vero diversus est, atque ita habet in versu ultimo, homo in honore consti- tutus, si non intelligat, similis est jumentis, quæ exciduntur. Hic enim summa breviter repetitur eorum, quæ dicta erant; ideo illud לֹא יָבִין perti- net ad descriptionem subjecti. Ad vers. 13. quem nunc tractamus לֹא יָלִין prædicatum constituit: Subjectum autem quodnam intelligi debeat, jam antea descriptum erat. Nulla itaque in hoc nostro loco fingenda diversitas lectionum, ubi summa est Codicum consensio: Non enim produci potuit hactenus discrepans Codex. Atque ita etiam cum Codicibus nostris suo tempore legit Hieronymus, fic reddens: Homo in honore non commorabitur; Nec aliter Chaldæus; impius in honore cum justis permanebit; aut Ebræi: R. David Kimchi & Kasve- naki, ex quo ille hæc adducit: Non manet: non moritur divitiis, quas honorem suum reputat, sed eas aliis derelinquit. Et mors vocatur pernoctatio, uti etiam dicitur somnus: additque hanc explicatio- nem: hominis, qui persequitur vanitates munda- nas, non pernoctat anima in honore, sed perit. Sic etiam R. Aben-Ezra, & R. Obad. legerunt, nec non R. Salom. Jarchi qui postremus tamen non curio- sius solum, sed ineptius etiam hinc deduxit, Ada- mum non permansisse una nocte in integritate, sed in fine diei lapsum esse. Nihil enim tale hic habetur: nec de Adamo, primo homine, hic agitur, sed de homine quovis, in divitiis confidente.

## 49:15
Vers. 16.

NEVERTHELESS HE WILL REDEEM MY SOUL FROM THE HAND OF THE GRAVE, WHEN HE SHALL RECEIVE ME. Bellarmine rightly establishes here the prediction of the redemption of Christ made by the payment of the price of blood: because Christ is God our Redeemer, who redeemed us from the hand of hell, Hos. 13, ver. 14. (2.) This redemption is opposed to eternal condemnation, to which the impenitent are subject in hell, ver. 15. Since therefore death eternally feeds upon the unfaithful in hell, this is the undoubted comfort of the faithful on the contrary, that Christ redeemed their souls from the hand of hell, and by the virtue of that redemption they are free from eternal death. (3.) The Hierophaltes had taught in ver. 8 that a brother could not redeem a brother, nor give to God כָפְרוֹ his propitiation, because that redemption is too precious; here therefore he treats of the redemption which was made by God. For what a man could not perform for his brother, אִישׁ יְהוָה that man who is Jehovah, הָאֱלֹהִים that God, whom God the Father therefore anointed in the assumed flesh, Psalm 45, ver. 8, performed, inasmuch as he was indeed made our brother through the incarnation, for he is not a mere man, but God-man, and thus true God made a participant of our flesh and blood, that he might redeem us by his death from his death, Heb. 2, ver. 14, whom he is not ashamed to call his brothers, ver. 11. (4.) The reason which the Psalmist adds, because יִקָּחֵנִי HE WILL RECEIVE ME, fits this comfort perfectly, whether it be understood of the hypostatic reception of our flesh, or of the gracious reception of us into his protection, because he received us then, when he took not angels, but the seed of Abraham, that he might redeem us, Heb. 2, ver. 16. For he took our nature, and

became a participant of our flesh through that taking, ver. 14. Nor is our plenary redemption ambiguous, which we expect by the virtue of the redemption made by the blood of Christ, because he himself received us, and no one can snatch us from his hands, and he is about to give us eternal life, that we may not perish eternally, John 10, ver. 28. (5) Here is delivered true wisdom, which ought to be most highly commended to all, whether they be rich or needy, powerful or abject, ver. 2, lest they depart like cattle, deprived of the eternal light, ver. 18, 21; but what is that wisdom, by which we are freed from eternal destruction, and aspire to eternal light, if not that concerning the redemption of Christ from the hand of hell, Luke 1, ver. 77 seqq., John 8, ver. 12, 51? (6) Basil, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Chrysostom, Euthymius, and other Fathers explain this concerning the Redemption of Christ. Although indeed it treats of the redemption of Christ from the hand of hell, it is not, however, to be understood with Bellarmine concerning the liberation from the limbo of the Fathers through the descent into hell, as if he then received their souls and took them to himself, because there is no word here about the descent into hell, nor is to be redeemed from the hand of hell to be liberated from the limbo of the Fathers, about which there is not a jot in the Scriptures; but to be liberated from the power of hell, in which death feeds upon the damned unfaithful, as that to which we were all to be adjudged on account of sin, had we not been liberated through Christ, ver. 14; whence Bellarmine acknowledges that the passage can be understood of the lower hell, where the souls of the impious are tormented, so that the sense is: God will not suffer my soul to be snatched from the hand of hell, nor to be led down to the places of punishment, when he shall receive me from this world through the death of the body.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

VERUNTAMEN REDIMET ANIMAM MEAM DE MANU INFERI, CUM ACCE- PERIT ME. Recte hic statuit Bellarmin. prædictionem re- demtionis Christi persoluto pretio sanguinis factam: quia Christus est Deus Redemtor noster, qui nos de manu inferni redemit Hos. 13. vers. 14. (2.) Hæc redemtio opponitur æternæ condemnationi, cui ob- noxii sunt impœnitentes in inferno vers. 15. Quum ergo infideles mors in inferno æternum depascat, fidelium ex adverso hoc est indubitatum solatium, quod Christus animas suas de manu inferni rede- merit, ejusque redemtionis virtute liberi sint ab æterna morte. (3.) Docuerat Hierophaltes vers. 8. quod frater fratrem redimere non posset, nec dare Deo כָפְרוֹ propitiationem suam, quia nimis pretiosa est illa redemtio, hic ergo agit de redemtione, quæ à Deo facta est. Quod enim vir fratri præstare non potuit, אִישׁ יְהוָה vir ille qui Jehovah est, הָאֱלֹהִים Deus ille, quem ideo Deus Pater in carne assumta unxit Psalm. 45. vers. 8. præstitit, ut- pote qui frater quidem noster factus est per ἐνσάρ- κωσιν, non enim nudus homo est, sed θεάνθρωπος, adeoque verus Deus carnis & sanguinis nostri par- ticeps factus est, ut nos morte sua redimeret à mor- te sua Ebr. 2. vers. 14. quos appellare fratres suos οὐκ ἐπαισχύνεται vers. 11. (4.) Ratio quam addit Psal- tes, quia יִקָּחֵנִי SUSCIPIET ME apprime congruit huic solatio, sive de susceptione carnis nostræ hypo- statica intelligatur, sive de susceptione nostri in pa- trocinium gratiosa, quia tum nos suscepit, cum non angelos, sed semen Abrahæ assumsit, ut nos redimeret Ebr. 2. vers. 16. Suscepit enim naturam nostram, &

carnis nostræ particeps factus est per illam ἐπίληψιν vers. 14. Neque ambigua est plenaria nostri redem- ptio, quam virtute ἀπολυτρώσεως sanguine Chri- sti factæ expectamus, quia nos suscepit ipse, & nemo eripere nos potest de manibus ejus, ac daturus nobis est vitam æternam, ut non pereamus æternum Joh. 10. vers. 28. (5) Traditur hic sapientia vera, quæ o- mnibus debet esse commendatissima, sive divites sint, sive egeni, potentes aut abjecti vers. 2. ne instar pecudis decedant æterno privati lumine vers. 18. 21. quæ vero est illa sapientia, qua ab æterno interitu liberamur, & ad æternam lucem adspiramus, nisi illa de redemptione Christi à manu inferni Luc. 1. vers. 77. seqq. Joh. 8. vers. 12. 51? (6) De Redemptio- ne Christi explicant Basilius, Ambrosius, Hieronym. Augustin. Chrysost. Euthym. aliique Patres. Quan- quam vero de redemptione Christi è manu inferni agatur, non tamen ea cum Bellarm. intelligenda de liberatione è limbo Patrum per descensum ad inferos, quasi tunc animas eorum acceperit, & ad se assum- serit, quia nec de descensu ad inferos hic ullum ver- bum habetur, nec de manu inferni redimi est è lim- bo Patrum liberari, de quo nullum Jota in Sacris habetur; sed è potestate inferni, in quo mors depascit infideles damnatos, liberari, utpote cui ob pecca- tum omnes adjudicandi eramus, nisi liberati per Christum fuissemus vers. 14. unde agnoscit Bellarm. posse locum intelligi de inferno inferiori, ubi torquen- tur animæ impiorum, ut sensus sit: non patietur Deus animam meam rapi à manu inferni, nec deduci ad lo- ca pœnarum, cum de hoc mundo per corporis mortem accipiet me.

## 50:1 Argument
PSALM 50. The true worship of the Most High.

Latin:

PSALM. L. Verus cultus Altissimi.

## 50:2
Vers. 2.

OUT OF ZION THE BEAUTY OF HIS COMELINESS) In the Hebrew: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty (that is, the place), God will shine forth. For the perfection of beauty, the Syrian here placed a glorious crown.

The interpretation of Ludov. de Dieu is rather to be approved: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God has shone, or God has caused the perfection of beauty to shine. Thus the version of the Syrian and the Arab agrees.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

EX SION SPECIES DECORIS EJUS) In Hebræo: Ex Sione perfecta pulchritudinis (loco scilicet) Deus illuce- scet. Pro perfecta pulchritudine Syrus hîc posuit coronam gloriosam.

PRobanda potius Ludov. de Dieu interpretatio: E Zione perfectio pulchritudinis Deus splenduit, vel perfectionem pulchritudinis Deus splendere fecit. Sic Syri & Arabis versio congruit.

## 50:4
Verse 4.

HE SHALL CALL THE HEAVENS FROM ABOVE AND THE EARTH, TO JUDGE HIS PEOPLE] He will shut up the heaven: and he will condemn the earth to sterility, on account of the sins of men. This Psalm seems to recall the memory of that time, of which 2 Sam. 21. Mystically the Jews refer this to the soul and the body, which, since they have sinned together, will also be judged together.

The gloss of Grotius is too arbitrary. For where is it held that the heaven is to be shut up? Where is it held that the earth is to be condemned to sterility on account of the sins of men? God is said to be about to call heaven and earth into judgment: which most people explain as referring to the final judgment, because he will call both the angels from heaven, and all men from the earth, so that his people may be judged, and the elect may be separated from the reprobate, Matt. 13, just as Augustine explains it, or so that heaven and earth may be called as witnesses of the divine sentence, which is the opinion of the Greeks Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Euthymius. Others interpret it concerning the judgment which is made through the word, because they wish there to be a discourse here concerning the promulgation of the Gospel. To whom Mr. Brentius and our Mr. Dr. Gesner agree, as well as Osiander, whose paraphrase is this: he will call heaven and earth to witness, because he has that for which he may argue against his people for an age, and he will call them as if they were witnesses and inspectors; as do also the Weimar Paraphrasts, who nevertheless [interpret] the preceding clause concerning the advent as judgment, but here they think that heaven and earth are called to witness, because God judges the people rightly. The former seems simpler to us, which is also the explanation of most of the ancients, to which our Dr. Gerhard also added his vote, Vol. 9, on the final judgment, § 12. Conf. August. in b. l. & lib. 20. de Civit. Dei. cap. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ADVOGABIT COELVM DE SVRSVM ET TER- RAM, DISCERNERE POPULUM SVVM] Cœlum claudet: & terram sterilitate damnabit, propter hominum peccata. Videtur hic Psalmus memoriam recolere illius temporis, de quo 2. Sam. 21. Mysticè Judæi hoc referunt ad animam & corpus, quæ cum una peccaverint, una & ju- dicabuntur.

Glossa Grotii nimis arbitraria est. Ubi enim habetur quid de cælo claudendo? ubi de terra ste- rilitate damnanda propter hominum peccata? Cœ- lum & terram in judicium advocaturus Deus dici- tur: quod de extremo judicio plerique exponunt, quia & Angelos è cœlo advocabit, & è terra homi- nes universos, ut judicetur populus ejus, & electi à reprobis segregentur Matth. 13. quemadmodum Augustinus exponit, vel ut cælum & terra in testes divinæ sententiæ advocentur, quæ Græcorum Chry- sostomi, Theodoreti, Euthymii est sententia. Alii de judicio quod per verbum fit, interpretantur, quia hic de divulgatione Evangelii sermonem esse vo- lunt. Quibus Dn. Brentius & Dn. D. Gesnerus no- ster accedunt, nec non Osiander, cujus hæc est para- phrasis; contestabitur cælum & terram, quod ha- beat de quo arguat populum suum in seculum, & qua- si testes & inspectores vocabit; ut & Paraphrastæ Vi- narienses, qui tamen præcedens comma de adventu ad judicium explicant, hic vero INTEREA coelum & terram in testimonium, quod Deus recte judicet populum, vocari censent. Nobis simplicior vide- tur prior, quæ & plerorumque veterum est explica- tio, cui etiam calculum suum D. Gerhardus noster adjecit Tom. 9. de extr. jud. §. 12. Conf. August. in b. l. & lib. 20. de Civit. Dei. cap. 24.

## 50:13
Verse 13.

SHALL I EAT THE FLESH OF BULLS, OR DRINK THE BLOOD OF GOATS?) These were instituted, for that time, for the sake of men, not of God: Euripides: Δᾶται γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς, εἴπερ ἔς’ ὄντως Θεὸς, ὀδενός’ ἀοιδῶν οἵδε δύςηνοι λόγοι.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

NVMQVID MANDVCABO CARNEM TAVRO- RVM, AVT SANGVINEM HIRCORVM POTABO?) Instituta hæc fuere, pro eo tempore, hominum, non Dei cau- sa: Euripides: Δᾶται γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς, εἴπερ ἔς’ ὄντως Θεὸς, ὀδενός’ ἀοιδῶν οἵδε δύςηνοι λόγοι.

## 51:1 Argument
PSALM LI. The repentance of David the adulterer.

Latin:

PSALMUS LI. Poenitentia Davidis adulteri.

## 51:1
WHEN NATHAN CAME TO HIM) That is, written about this subject, although not at that time.

WHEN HE WENT IN TO BATHSHEBA) To be explained by the pluperfect: After he had had relations with Bathsheba.

Latin:

CVM VENIT AD EVM NATHAN) Id est, de hoc ar- gumento scriptus, quanquam non eo tempore.

QVANDO INTRAVIT AD BETH SABEE) Exponen- dum per plusquam perfectum: Postquam congressus esset cum Bethsabee.

## 51:3
Verse 5.

MY SIN IS BEFORE ME ALWAYS) In the Hebrew: My sin is before me daily: it shows itself to me, and terrifies me with the fear of punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

PECCATVM MEVM CONTRA ME EST SEM- PER) In Hebræo: Peccatum meum quotidie mihi obversatur: se mihi ostendit, & poenæ metu me exterret.

## 51:4
Verse 6.

AGAINST THEE ONLY HAVE I SINNED) From thee alone can I fear punishment. For Kings are free from the bonds of offenses, as Ambrose says on this passage. Harmenopulus: ὁ βασιλεὺς ἁμαρτάνων ὐ κολάζεται. See what we have brought forward on this matter in the book on the Law of War and Peace, book 1, chapter 3, § 1, where we also placed that saying of the Rabbis: No creature judges a King, but God blessed be He. Otherwise, he would have been a King in name, not in reality.

The words of David speak about the object of sin, upon whom it primarily redounds, or against whom we properly sin: namely, that sin is committed against God alone, who alone is the lawgiver, James 4:12, because every sin is ἄνομον, 1 John 3:4; for we sin against him whose law we transgress, and therefore it is the proper ἀξίωμα of God that we sin against him, against his majesty, glory, and also divine justice, since every sin is opposed to divine glory, inasmuch as God demands obedience and observance of his divine law, and sin is contrary to divine holiness. Although, therefore, by harming a neighbor we seem to sin against the neighbor; yet we properly sin against God alone, whose laws are those which the second Table presents, just as much as the precepts of the first Table. It is sinned against him alone as LAWGIVER, as the supreme avenger of the Law, from whom others have the power of punishing, indeed as the proper object of guilt as well, inasmuch as it redounds to the author of the law himself: for just as love of neighbor arises from love of God, so also injury to a neighbor redounds to God himself, and as it is sin, that is, the transgression of the law, it is committed against God, whose that law is. There is no need, therefore, for us to have recourse here to a metonymical and improper meaning, when the words can be taken properly. Nor does David grieve so much because he has to fear punishment from God, which is servile fear, as because he has offended God and sinned against Him; to whom ALONE he says he has sinned, not because he denies that he was injurious toward his neighbor when he killed Uriah and committed adultery with his wife, but because God alone perceives intimately the machinations of his heart and their atrocity, from which arise homicides, adulteries, and other sins (Matt. 15:19), and because He alone has made all men, the highest equally as the lowest, subject to the law, has inscribed the law upon all, and argues and convinces all in their conscience, so that the whole world may be silent; finally, because all sins and all injuries derogate from the Divine Majesty itself and redound upon God Himself. And this was what most gravely afflicted David's conscience, that he sinned against God Himself: Against Thee, Thee only have I sinned, and done evil in Thy sight. Although, he says, I killed Uriah and committed adultery with his wife, and by these offenses I sinned most gravely against my neighbor: Yet that does not torment my conscience as much as the fact that I offended God in this matter and provoked His wrath against me, as the explanation of the blessed Gesner holds.

Verse of the same.

THAT THOU MIGHTEST BE JUSTIFIED IN THY WORDS, AND MIGHTEST OVERCOME WHEN THOU ART JUDGED) That בדברך which is here translated 'in words,' you might best translate 'in actions': that is, that whatever You shall determine concerning me, both I and all others with me will profess that no injury is done to me. 'Overcome,' the LXX and the Syrian and Paul (Rom. 3:4) have. In the Hebrew it is 'be purged': for a verb in the Qal often signifies 'to appear' instead of 'to be'.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

TIBI SOLI PECCAVI) A te solo poenas metuere possum. Nam liberi sunt Reges à vinculis delictorum, ut ait Ambro- sius ad h. l. Harmenopulus: ὁ βασιλεὺς ἁμαρτάνων ὐ κολάζε- ται. Vide quæ in hanc rem protulimus de Jure Belli ac Pacis libr. 1. cap. 3. §. 1. ubi & dictum illud posuimus Rabbinorum: Nulla creatura judicat Regem, sed Deus benedictus. Alioqui nomine, non re Rex fuisset.

VErba Davidis de peccati objecto, in quemnam illud primario redundet, vel adversus quem- nam proprie peccemus, loquuntur: nimirum quod peccatum adversus solum Deum committa- tur, qui solus est legislator Jacob. 4, 12. quia omne peccatum est ἄνομον 1. Joh. 3, 4. in eum enim pecca- mus, cujus legem transilimus, ideoque ἀξίωμα Dei proprium est, quod ipsi peccemus, adversus maje- statem, gloriam, nec non justitiam divinam, siqui- dem divinæ gloriæ adversetur omne peccatum, quum Deus postulet obedientiam & observantiam legis suæ divinæ, & sanctitati divinæ contrarium sit peccatum. Quamvis ergo proximum lædendo vi- deamur adversus proximum peccare; soli tamen Deo proprie peccamus, cujus leges sunt æque illæ, quas secunda exhibet Tabula, atque primæ Tabu- læ præcepta. Peccatur ipsi soli ut LEGISLATO- RI, ut Legis summo vindici, à quo alii potestatem puniendi habent, imo ut proprio etiam objecto rea- tus, utpote qui redundat in ipsum legis autorem: ut enim dilectio proximi è dilectione Dei oritur, sic etiam injuria in proximum, in Deum ipsum re- dundat, & qua peccatum est, hoc est, legis trans- gressio, adversus Deum, cujus illa lex est, committi- tur. Non opus ergo est, ut ad metonymicam & impro- priam hic recurramus significationem, quum pro- prie verba accipi possint. Neque adeo dolet David, quod poenas metuere opus habeat à Deo, qui ti- mor servilis est, quam quod Deum offenderit, ipsi- que peccarit; cui SOLI se peccasse ait, non quod neget se adversus proximum injurium fuisse cum Uriam occidit, & uxorem ejus stupravit, sed quod Deus solus cordis sui machinationes & atrocita- tem earum intime perspiciat, è quo oriuntur homi- cidia, adulteria, & alia peccata Matth. 15, 19. quod- que ipse solus omnes homines, summos æque, ac infimos, legi obnoxios fecerit, omnibus legem in- sculpserit, omnes in conscientia arguat, & convin- cat, ut totus mundus fileat, denique quod ipsi Ma- jestati divinæ omnia peccata, omnes injuriæ de- rogent, & in Deum ipsum redundent. Atque hoc erat, quod gravissime angebat conscientiam Davi- dis, quod in ipsum Deum peccarit, Tibi, Tibi soli peccavi, & malum in oculis Tuis feci. Etsi, inquit, Uriam occidi & uxorem ejus stupravi, atque hisce delictis gravissime in proximum peccavi: Tamen id non adeo conscientiam meam torquet, quam quod Deum hac re offendi, ejusque iram in me concitavi, ut habet B. Gesneri explicatio.

Vers. eod.

VT JVSTIFICERIS IN SERMONIBVS TVIS, ET VINCAS CVM JVDICARIS) Illud בדברך quod hîc vertitur in sermonibus, optime vertas in actionibus: id est, ut quidquid de me statueris, & ego, & omnes alii mecum nul- lam mihi fieri injuriam sint professuri. Vincas, habent LXX. & Syrus, & Paulus Rom. 3. vers. 4. In Hebræo est purgeris: nam verbum in Cal sæpe pro esse, significat apparere.

## 51:5
Verse 7.

FOR BEHOLD I WAS CONCEIVED IN INIQUITIES, AND IN SINS DID MY MOTHER CONCEIVE ME) That 'for' is absent in the Hebrew. The sense is: Not now only, but also from my childhood, I have sinned more often. For it is a hyperbolic way of speaking, as the comparison of the passages Job 31:18, Psalm 22:9, Ps. 58:4, Ps. 71:5, 6, Isa. 48:8 shows. On the occasion of this grave crime, he remembers also the preceding ones, however less grave. For 'conceive' in the Hebrew it is 'cherish'.

Although the causal particle is not present in the Hebrew literally, it is present in sense, which the Vulgate interpreter expressed. But the sense which Grotius brings is mere distortion, which he drew from the school of Pelagius and Socinus. For he follows them in the denial of original sin. Therefore it is no wonder that he distorts the words of David in the same way, even though they are clearer than the sun. For thus Socinus in Praelect. Theol. cap. 5, p. 12, says of this passage: 'It can be sufficiently established that this is a figurative way of speaking, and HYPERBOLICAL, like that also in Psalm 58:4: The wicked are alienated from the womb: they have wandered from the belly speaking lies.' A similar passage is Isa. 48:8, by which ways of speaking sins are exaggerated and more effectively censured. Whence it is clear that Grotius sought even the parallel passages from Socinus. Although Socinus here still concedes more to Catholics than Grotius, formerly an adversary of Socinus. For he admits in the words subjoined that human frailty is hinted at in this passage, as if this sin were a thing clearly natural, but not that it is so in reality. Grotius, however, wishes nothing else to be hinted at than that David sinned from childhood. But this gloss is refuted by the very words of the Psalmist: He says not only that he sinned more often from childhood, but also that he was conceived in sins and infected with iniquity when his mother first cherished or warmed him: so that from the first native heat he was immediately corrupted by sin. Which is the very description of original sin, as it is defined by the Catholic Church. Then indeed there is no necessity to have recourse to a figurative way of speaking. But it is not right in the interpretation of Scripture to abandon the propriety of words without necessity, as the Socinians themselves admit, unless we wish to make a game and a joke of Scripture. Nor can a hyperbole be proven from the designated passages. For in Psalm 58:4 and Isa. 48:8, respect is likewise had to original sin. Christ is called Holy from the womb without hyperbole (Luke 1:35). In Ps. 71:5, 6, respect is had to the Sacrament of circumcision, through which faith is procured for infants regenerated from above on the eighth day from birth. Finally, if a hyperbole is admitted at all in Job 31:18, or even in Psalm 71:5, 6, what is this to the present passage? For there it can be said that the piety of Job and the trust of David are being exaggerated: but here, that sin is being exaggerated more than is just—under which appearance of truth will it be established, when that evil, so easily besetting our nature, intimately fixed as we are born flesh of flesh, and are by nature children of wrath, can never be sufficiently described, nor its gravity explained? And how, by this Grotian gloss, can it be reconciled with the present confession of sins and contrition for the sins of David, whom every single word testifies is here so vehemently distressed and so anxiously complaining about his sins, is it consistent that he should indeed only on the occasion of a grave crime remember others from childhood, however not grave? Not only is there a bare mention, but he is vehemently grieved and distressed about his sins, a contrite heart the iniquity in which he was conceived only on the occasion, but he reveals the same primarily as the fountain of all evil, and complains most gravely about the same: nor only the sins of infirmity and thoughtlessness designated in childhood, but that horrible depravation of nature, by which, warmed in sins and conceived in iniquities, he was subject to depraved lust and concupiscence in his mother's very womb, as soon as he obtained vital heat. Do these sound like NOT GRAVE sins? Behold, I was conceived IN INIQUITY, and in SINS my mother conceived me; Calvin more correctly: David, by the recognition of one sin, draws out a long examination of his whole life, until he finds nothing in himself except sin. Now he confesses himself guilty not only of one sin or even several, as hitherto, but he ascends higher, that he brought nothing else from his mother's womb than sin, and that he is naturally entirely corrupt, and as it were smeared with vices. For in the original text it is not without reason said in the singular, in INIQUITY AND SIN, because original sin, which we contracted in conception, is one, not many: as Bellarmine observes here. The LXX, however, translated in the number of the multitude, because that one sin is as it were the fountain of all other sins and in it all are concluded, as Menochius holds. Finally, David wishes to move the bowels of God's mercy; wherefore he makes mention not only on the occasion of the sins of childhood, which Grotius considers light, but he presents to God, as the words sound, the depraved concupiscence propagated by conception in the very womb of his mother, by the force of which man born of flesh is only inclined to sin, all the days of his life, so that the God and Father of all mercy may most graciously have mercy on this misery, and may deign propitiously to grant pardon for the sins into which he was precipitated by the law of sin adhering in his members. In this verse, as our blessed Gesner rightly says, the Prophet reveals the vicious fountain and poisonous spring of all sins, which is that innate corruption and depravation of human nature derived from Adam. David therefore accuses his whole nature, and all the faculties of soul and body, because they are vicious, and infected with the contagion of sin, and utterly dead to good as well. He speaks of birth, when he says that he was born in sins: he ascends beyond birth to the very conception itself, when he complains that he was conceived in sins by his mother. David therefore signifies by this verse that he did not become guilty of divine judgment only then when he took the wife of Uriah, but that this stain adhered to him at birth, nay even by repeating the matter higher, he confesses that malice and the corruption of nature were deeply fixed in the seed from which he was formed. Add that David therefore prays that God would be willing to create a new heart in him, so that the ancient depravity, which he contracted from his parents, may be mortified, and the spirit renewed in his bowels, so that he may not indulge the flesh, but may be able to resist it through the Spirit. Which R. Aben-Ezra also observed. Grotius could have learned here the true meaning of the Davidic words even from the Jesuits themselves, in whom he himself takes great delight, nay from any Roman Catholic interpreters whatsoever. For all here agree entirely that the Psalmist is dealing with original sin. The fourth reason, says Bellarmine,

is drawn from the first origin, and the sin of the first man transferred into us through generation, from which we have become infirm and inclined to sin, and on account of this as it were natural misery we are worthy of mercy. Whom Menochius follows, as he usually does in the Psalms: Tirinus explains it similarly, appealing to Athanasius, Jerome, Augustine, and Theodoret, and Gregory. Nor is there anyone, either among the Papists or the Calvinists, who explains it otherwise, or dreams of a hyperbole. The ancient Doctors of the Church also with unanimous suffrage accepted this passage concerning original sin, both before the controversies moved by Pelagius, and especially when Pelagius denied the sin of origin. St. Augustine produced the opinions of the ancients in book 1 against Pelagius, chapter 2, Vol. 7 of his works, page 939, and we from him in the Considerations on Arminianism, Chapter 12. of Cyprian, that he who is born carnally according to Adam contracted the contagion of ancient death by his first birth: of Hilary, who in his exposition of Psalm 118 says that he does not consider himself to be living in this life, since he had said: Behold I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me: He knows that he was born under the origin of sin, and under the law of sin. Of Ambrose from the Apology of David: Before we are born, we are stained with contagion, and before we enjoy the light, we receive the injury of origin itself, and we are conceived in iniquity. Of Gregory Nazianzen, who, dealing with Baptism, says: By this, he says, the stains of the first birth are purged, through which we are conceived in iniquities, and our mothers brought us forth in sins. There is no reason for us to bring forward the more recent writers who wrote against Pelagius and after him: for all agree that the sin in which David says he was conceived is original sin, which the Catholic Church defended against the Pelagian heresy. What of the fact that some have understood that even among the Jews themselves, the discourse here is about original sin? In R. David Kimchi on this passage, these things are held: He aggravates his sin from its duration, because concupiscence is fixed in the heart, and is as it were formed in it. And after that: or he says formed, because he was made from seed, just as a man who sows bitter seed brings forth similar fruits; therefore man inclines naturally to evil concupiscence above other sins: to which opinion Kasvenaki brings R. Solomon Jarchi: How, he says, should I not sin? My origin is corrupt, and hence those sins. Otherwise: my origin is from a man and a woman, who are full of iniquity. Aben-Ezra on this little verse: BEHOLD: Because of INNATE CONCUPISCENCE it is said to the human heart, I was born in iniquity: and the sense is: that from birth an evil figment is implanted in the human heart. But what he says, and in sin my mother warmed me, is a strange way of speaking, as if she was warmed by me. And there are those who say that he indicates here that Eve did not give birth until after she had sinned. On verse 12.
