The Vulgate is rightly amended: How rashly and vainly Bellarmine excuses this here, as if the desert of Judah were called the desert of Idumaea for the sake of amplification, which is clearly unusual in a historical inscription, and is joined with the confusion of Judaea and Idumaea: that therefore in verse 12 he calls himself King, but the King shall rejoice in GOD, is to be understood by reason of the designation, because this flight had been undertaken on account of Saul: but at that time he was not yet King in act: whereas Bellarmine less conveniently understands Christ by the King: since David speaks of himself in the third person (as Psalm 71, 6.) joining himself in religious acts with other faithful ones, who swear by GOD, just as he himself rejoices in GOD. But we do not deny to the Cardinal that, on the occasion of the desert in which he was then hiding, David here deplores his own pilgrimage and that of just men like him, and testifies to his desire to migrate sometime from the desert of this world to the heavenly fatherland. Yet so that the thirst to see GOD in the Sanctuary may directly look to the propitiatory, which was noted in the argument of the Psalm by B. Luther; who adds: that this Psalm can be used by those who, oppressed under tyrants, labor with hunger and thirst for the word of GOD, and meanwhile can nevertheless boast that they are sons and heirs of GOD, etc. Cf. Psalm 42, 1.

Latin:

PSALM. LXIII. Davidis in deserto Juda sitis spiritualis.

Vers. 1.

CVM ESSET IN DESERTO IDVMEÆ] Scribendum hîc & in exemplaribus Græcis Judæ, tum ex textu Hebræo, tum ex Historia 1. Sam. 22, 5. 23, 14. 15. REcte emendatur Vulgata: Quam temere & frustra excusat hîc Bellarmin. quasi desertum Judæ desertum Idumææ vocetur amplificandi gratia, quod in historica inscriptione plane insolens, & cum confusione Judææ & Idumææ conjunctum est: quod ergo vers. 12. se Regem vocat, Rex vero in DEO lætabitur, ratione designationis intelligen- dum, quia propter Saulem hæc fuga suscepta erat: tum autem actu nondum erat Rex: ubi vero Bellar- min. per Regem minus convenienter Christum in- telligit: quum de se in tertia persona loquatur Da- vid (ut Psalm. 71, 6.) conjungens se in actibus re- ligiosis cum aliis fidelibus, qui jurant in DEO, uti ipse in DEO lætatur. Occasione autem deserti, in quo tunc latebat, deplorare hîc Davidem peregri- nationem suam & sibi similium justorum, & desi- derium suum testari, migrandi aliquando ex deser- to mundi hujus ad patriam cœlestem, non abnui- mus Cardinali. Sic tamen ut sitis DEUM videre in Sancto propitiatorium directe respiciat, quod in ar- gument. Psalm. notatum B. Luthero; qui addit: hoc Psalmo uti posse, qui sub tyrannis oppressi, fame & siti verbi DEI laborant, & interea tamen gloriari possunt, esse filios & hæredes DEI &c. Conf. Psalm. 42, 1.

## 63:1
Verse 2.

MY SOUL HAS THIRSTED FOR THEE, HOW MANIFOLDLY FOR THEE MY FLESH] The LXX thought כמה to be composed of כ and מה. But the Hebrews better take it as one word, which signifies to desire. And so Aquila translated it ἐπετάτη, Symmachus ἱμείρεται. In the Hebrew the second part is to be rendered thus; my flesh has longed for thee. For it is not held as כמו, but כמה, a word ἅπαξ λεγομένη, as the Masora notes: concerning which it is thus in Michlol Jophi: the word כמה has a He with a Mappik, nor does it exist again in scripture, and its exposition is 'it will desire thee, and will groan.' Jerome himself translated it 'desired.' And it is also thus expounded by R. Nathan Mardochai, Pagninus, and Campensis, with the Chaldean and Syrian agreeing.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SITIVIT IN TE ANIMA MEA, QVAM MVLTI- PLICITER TIBI CARO MEA] Putarunt LXX. כמה esse compositum ex כ, & מה. At melius Hebræi pro uno verbo sumunt, quod desiderare significat. Itaque Aquila verti. ἐπετάτη, Symmachus ἱμείρεται. In Ebræo altera pars ita reddenda; appetiit ad te caro mea. Nam habetur non כמו, sed כמה vox ἅπαξ λεγομένη, ut notat Masora: de qua in Michlol Jophi ita: verbum כמה habet He cum Mappik, nec iterum extat in scriptura, ejusque expo- sitio est concupiscet te, atque ingemiscet. Hierony- mus ipse vertit desideravit. Atque ita exponitur etiam à R. Nathan Mardochai, Pagnino, & Campen- si, consonante Chaldæo, & Syro.

## 63:5
Verse 6. AS WITH FAT AND FATNESS SHALL MY SOUL BE FILLED, AND WITH LIPS OF EXULTATION SHALL MY MOUTH PRAISE. B. Luther rendered it otherwise, and more significantly, in the later translation of the Psalter now accepted, the reason for which he explained in the treatise 'vom Dolmetschen' [On Translating] in the year 1533, in the 6th Altenburg volume, folio 133, Psalm 65, in the 6th verse, where we previously according to the words had translated it thus: let my soul become full, as with marrow and fat, that my mouth may praise with joyful lips. Because no German understands such things, we have let the Hebrew words go, (marrow and fat, by which they mean joy, just as a healthy fat animal is joyful, and conversely a joyful animal becomes fat, a sad animal wastes away and becomes lean, and a lean animal is sad,) and have given it in clear German, thus: That would be my heart's joy and delight, if I should praise you with a joyful mouth. For such is indeed David's meaning, when he had to stay outside the city and flee from Saul, that he could not be at the divine service, nor hear the joyful Word of God, which comforts all troubled hearts etc. However, the parallel passages Ps. 36, 9 and Is. 55, 2 favor the former German translation and the Latin version, by which the Hebrew is rendered word for word, the sense of which Cocceius explains thus: God, being reconciled to me in Christ, has bestowed upon me through grace innumerable benefits, and has satisfied my desire, as a faithful shepherd, so that I lack nothing that pertains to spiritual joy. And therefore I enjoy full joy, and in that jubilation and triumph. More elegantly, Dr. Geier: I thirst for you so much, O Lord, and I desire you, because my soul experiences most abundantly in you pure delights, spiritual and ineffable, so that although I am hungry and dry in body, yet in mind I am wonderfully satisfied and sweetly fattened: The soul, refreshed within, subsequently reveals itself through lips full of jubilation, where both mouth and tongue and lips and whatever else can contribute anything to this duty, are most occupied.

Latin:

Vers. 6. SICUT ADIPE ET PINGUEDI- NE REPLEATUR ANIMA MEA, ET LA- BIIS EXULTATIONIS LAUDABIT OS ME- UM. B. Lutherus aliter, & significantius reddidit in posteriori translatione Psalterii jam recepta, cu- jus rationem exposuit tractat. vom Dolmetschen Anno 1533. Tomo 6. Altenburgensi fol. 133. Psalm 65. im 6. Vers, da wir vorhin den Wor- ten nach also gedolmetschet haben, laß meine See- le voll werden, wie mit Schmalz und Fettem, daß mein Mund mit frölichen Lippen rühme. Weil sol- ches kein Teutscher verstehet, haben wir lassen fahren die Ebräischen Worte, (Schmalz und Fett, damit sie Freude bedeuten, gleichwie ein gesund fett Thier frölich, und wiederum ein frölich Thier fett wird, ein traurig Thier abnimmet und mager wird, und ein mager Thier traurig ist,) und haben klar Teutsch gegeben, also: Das wäre meines Herzens Freude und Wonne, wenn ich dich mit frölichem Munde loben sollte. Denn solches ist doch Davids Mey- nung, da er ausser der Stadt bleiben und für Saul fliehen muste, daß er nicht seyn kunnte bey dem Got- tes-Dienste, noch das fröliche GOttes Wort hören, welches alle betrübte Herzen tröstet 2c. Priori ta- men translationi Germanicæ & versioni Latinæ, qua κατὰ πόδα Ebræa redduntur, favent loca pa- rallela Psalm. 36, 9. Es. 55, 2. cujus sensum ita ex- ponit Coccejus: Deus mihi placatus in Christo per gratiam innumerabilia beneficia donavit, meumque desiderium explevit, ut fidelis pastor, ut nihil deside- rem, quod ad lætitiam spiritualem pertineat. Ideo- que pleno gaudio fruor, inque eo jubilo & trium- pho. Concinnius Dn. D. Geierus: Tantopere te Domine sitio, desideroque, quia meras in te deli- tias, spirituales ac ineffabiles largissime experitur ani- ma mea, ita ut famelico licet aridoque sim corpore, mente tamen mire sim satur ac suaviter impinguatus: Anima interius refecta se postmodum prodit per labia jubilis plena, ubi & os & lingua & labia & quicquid modo conferre ad hoc officium aliquid potest, sunt oc- cupatissima.

## 63:8
Vers. 9. BUT THEY SOUGHT MY SOUL IN VAIN.

In Hebrew it is, as Bellarmine himself admits, but they sought to kill my soul; but what the Cardinal says, that the Hebrew word should be read with other letters, and the last letter removed so that instead of לשואת to kill, we have לשוא in vain, as the LXX and the Vulgate have, how vain that is, everyone sees: for even the added retaliation confirms the Hebrew truth: because they sought to kill my soul, they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword.

Latin:

Vers. 9. IPSI VERO IN VANUM QUÆSIERUNT ANIMAM MEAM.

In Ebr. est, fatente Bellarmin. ipso, ipsi vero in- terficere quæsierunt animam meam; quod autem Card. ait, vocem Ebræam cum aliis literis legen- dam esse, & tollendam ultimam literam ut loco לשואת interficere, habeamus לשוא in vanum, ut LXX. & Vulgatus habent, id quam vanum sit, nemo non videt: nam vel addita talio Ebraicam veritatem firmat: quia quæsierunt interficere ani- mam meam, ipsi tradentur in manus gladii.

## 63:10
THEY SHALL BE PORTIONS FOR FOXES.

Bellarmine explains it thus: they shall no longer rule over just men, but they themselves shall be subject to unjust demons as their portion and inheritance. But since one should not rashly depart from the letter, others more correctly say that their unburied bodies will be devoured by foxes and other carnivorous animals: because there was a great abundance of foxes in Judea, Judg. 15, 4, and nobler wild beasts, e.g., lions, would not deign to touch these ill-omened funerals, as Theodoret and Euthymius note. Cf. Rev. 19, 18.

Latin:

PARTES VULPIUM ERUNT.

Id ita exponit Bellarmin. non dominabuntur amplius super homines justos, sed ipsi subjecti erunt dæmonibus injustis quasi pars & hæreditas ipsorum. Sed quum à litera temere discedendum non sit, alii rectius corpora eorum inhumata à vulpibus aliis- que carnivoris animalibus devoratum iri dicunt: quia vulpium magna copia fuit in Judæa Judic. 15, 4. neque infausta hæc funera dignaturæ sint feræ nobiliores, v. g. leones, ut Theodor. & Euthym. no- tant. Conf. Apoc. 19, 18.

## 64:1 Argument
PSALM LXIV. The fall of those lying in wait. Vers. 1. HEAR MY PRAYER, O GOD.

Some make this prayer Christ's, some David's, Bellarmine both Christ's and David's, Cocceius the Church's, etc., but it is better to call it David's, even if we can also make it our own by use in persecutions with profit! Believe Rupert, who has experienced it. Our blessed Luther felt the same in the argument of the Psalm.

Latin:

PSALMUS LXIV. Insidiantium casus. Vers. 1. EXAUDI DEUS ORATIONEM MEAM.

Orationem hanc aliqui Christi faciunt, aliqui Davidis, Bellarmin. & Christi, & Davidis, Coc- cejus Ecclesiæ &c. sed præstat eam Davidis dicere, etsi eam quoque nostram τῇ χρήσει vel usu in per- sequutionibus cum fructu facere possimus! Exper- to crede Ruperto. Idem sensit in argum. Psalm. B. Lu- therus noster.

## 64:6
Vers. 7. THEY HAVE SEARCHED OUT INIQUITIES: THEY HAVE FAILED

SEARCHING WITH A SEARCH: MAN SHALL APPROACH TO A DEEP HEART, AND GOD SHALL BE EXALTED: THE ARROWS OF INFANTS HAVE BECOME THEIR WOUNDS) It appears the LXX read וירום and he was exalted for ירו and he pierced with arrows, and καὶ ὑψωθήσεται. Furthermore, since תמנו is read similarly in Lamentations 3, 22, where it signifies we are consumed, by an epenthesis of the letter נ which is not infrequent: the sense seems, by supplying the little words which are wont to be omitted, to be able to be repaired best thus: They searched out iniquities: (ways of harming us) we would have been consumed. But the most perfect investigation (supply, is God's, from what follows) and (supply reached) to the innermost and deep heart of man. God therefore finished them with a dart: suddenly their wounds appeared.

However the version of the LXX may be, Grotius is forced to acknowledge the agreement of the Hebrew text, which he rendered not unsuitably. And although Ludovicus Capellus thinks the LXX interpreters read תמנו, and it seems clearly harsh to him that תמנו is put for תמו, he did not, however, obtain the assent of Grotius here, who observes a similar reading in Lamentations 3, 22, and admits that the epenthesis of the letter נ is not infrequent. And the Masora openly contradicts Capellus, noting that that word is found four times in the Bible thus, here and in three other places, Numbers 17, 13, Jeremiah 44, 18, and Lamentations 3, 22, and all the codices acknowledge the Nun in the middle, all the interpreters, all the grammarians and lexicographers, Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, and all the grammarians of Spain, as Aben-Ezra warned. See Buxtorf in Vindic. part 2, book 13, page 983. It is therefore manifest here again, that it cannot be concluded immediately, where ancient versions vary from the text, that the authors of those versions read otherwise in their time, or that diverse readings of the Sacred text occur. This was acknowledged by Brian Walton, Professor at Cambridge, who, although in Volume 1 of the Polyglot Bibles, in the Apparatus, and in the special section of the Prolegomena of the same, b. prol. 6. page 38, he contends for Capellus, the inventor and unhappy champion of various readings, against Buxtorf and Bootius, the defenders of the integrity of the Hebrew Codices, is nevertheless forced to admit that not all discrepancies of interpreters from the original text are to be considered as various readings. For many things, he says, can arise from the lapse of the interpreter, while he may err either in the reading, or in the genuine sense of the passage, or in the true meaning of the words. He often also acts as a paraphraser, and adds certain words for the explanation of the passage, and also omits some which seem less necessary. Errors of scribes, which can creep into both the text and the version, are also not to be held as various readings. Therefore, the errors of copyists must be distinguished from the version itself, and in this, the lapses of the interpreter and paraphrastic expositions must be accurately distinguished from the varying readings of the original Codex. For there can be various causes why an interpreter read differently than he translated. Walton says these things most correctly: had either Capellus, or even our Grotius, attended to these, they would not have gone so easily and readily into the inventions of various readings, which they themselves devised and championed in huge abundance, relying on the authority of no Sacred Codex, and induced solely by the discrepancy of the versions from the text; whence I also marvel at Walton, who not only attributes much to the fictitious diverse readings of Capellus, but also wished to stuff into that distinguished London work, I point to the Polyglot Bibles, by the edition of which he otherwise earned for himself an eternal name, in Volume 6 and the last, all those things which occur in the Biblical Annotations of Grotius concerning diverse readings, without any examination and censure: which, however, are for the most part so constituted that they do not prove various readings, but present to us only the inventions of Capellus, or the conjectures or suspicions of Grotius himself, where the Interpreters seem to have read otherwise than the Hebrew Codices now have; which indeed conjectures, and those εὑρήματα which they hawk as genuine diverse readings, nay, they prefer a reading devised by their own ingenuity to one that is common and obvious in all the Codices: if Walton cannot see that this was done by the Papist Grotius to derogate from the praise of the purity and sincerity of the sources of Hebrew truth, and also from the dignity of their authentic authority he sees nothing. But these things are said παραφυαδικῶς, by occasion of the present passage.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SCRUTATI SVNT INIQVITATES: DEFECERVNT

SCRVTANTES SCRVTINIO: ACCEDET HOMO AD COR ALTVM, ET EXALTABITVR DEVS: SA- GITTÆ PARVVVLORVM FACTÆ SVNT PLAGÆ EORVM) Apparet LXX. pro ירו ו & telis confixit legisse וירום καὶ ὑψωθήσεται. Cæterum cum תמנו similiter le- gatur Threnorum 3, 22. ubi significat consumti sumus, per ἐπένθεσιν non infrequentem נ literæ: videtur sensus, sup- plendo voculas, quæ omitti solent, sic optime posse sarciri: Investigarunt illi iniquitates: (vias nobis nocendi) consumti essemus. Sed investigatio perfectedsima (supple, Dei est, ex se- quentibus) & ad intimum hominis & profundum cor (supple pervenit) Confecit igitur eos Deus telo: subito exstiterunt vul- nera eorum.

Quomodocunque se habeat versio LXX. In- terpp. agnoscere cogitur Grotius convenientiam textus Ebræi, quam non incommode reddidit. Et quanquam LXX. Interpp. תמנו legisse censeat Lu- dov. Capellus, planeque durum ipsi videatur, תמנו positum esse pro תמו, non obtinuit tamen hic à Grotio assensum, qui Thren. 3, 22. similem obser- vat lectionem, ac literæ נ epenthesin fatetur non infrequentem esse. Ac repugnat Capello aper- te Masora, annotans vocem illam quater in Bibliis ita reperiri, hic & in aliis tribus locis Numer. 17, 13. Jerem. 44, 18. & Thren. 3, 22. agnoscuntque omnes Codices Nun in medio, omnes Interpp. omnes Grammatici & Lexicographi, Aben-Ezra, Kim- chius, & omnes Grammatici Hispaniæ, ut Aben- Ezra monuit. Vid. Buxtorff. in Vindic. part. 2. lib. 13. pag. 983. Manifestum ergo hic iterum est, non statim, ubi à textu variant antiquæ versiones, concludi posse, autores versionum istarum suo tempore aliter legisse, aut diversas textus Sacri le- ctiones occurrere. Quod agnovit Brianus Wal- tonus Cantabrigiensis Professor, qui etsi in Tomo 1. Biblior. Polyglott. in Apparatu, & Prolegem. ejus- dem speciali b. prol. 6. pag. 38. pro Capello lectio- num variarum inventore, ac propugnatore infe- lici, adversus Buxtorffium, & Bootium, Vindices in- tegritatis Codicum Ebræorum, dimicet, fateri tamen cogitur, non omnes interpretum ab origina- rio textu discrepantias pro variis lectionibus haben- das esse. Multa enim, inquit, esse possunt ex inter- pretis lapsu, dum vel in lectione, vel in genuino loci sensu, vel in vera verborum significatione errare pos- sit. Sæpe etiam paraphrasten agit, & verba quæ- dam ad loci explicationem addit, quædam etiam, quæ minus necessaria videntur, omittit. Scribarum eti- am errores, qui tum in textum, tum in versionem irrepere possunt, pro variis lectionibus non habendi. Distinguendi itaque sunt errores librariorum ab ipsa versione, & in hac accurate distinguendi sunt inter- pretis lapsus, & expositiones paraphrasticæ à varian- tibus Codicis originarii lectionibus. Variæ enim cau- sæ esse possunt, cur interpres aliter legerit, quam ver- tit. Hæc rectissime Waltonus: quæ si attendisset vel Capellus, vel Grotius etiam Noster, non tam faciles, ac proni ivissent in commenta variarum lectionum, quas ingenti copia excogitarunt ipsi, ac propugnarunt, nullius Codicis Sacri auctorita- te nixi, solaque versionum à textu discrepantia in- ducti; Unde Waltonum etiam miror, qui non mo- do Capelli commentitiis lectionibus diversis mul- tum tribuit, sed etiam in opus illud insigne Lon- dinense, Biblia Polyglotta indigito, quorum editio- ne sibi æternum alioquin nomen peperit Tomo 6. & ultimo ea omnia, quæ in Annotatis Grotii Biblicis de diversis lectionibus occurrunt, sine ullo exami- ne, ac censura, infarcirc voluit: quæ tamen plera- que ita comparata sunt, ut non evincant varias le- ctiones, sed vel commenta solum Capelli, vel ipsiusmet Grotii Conjecturas, aut suspiciones no- bis exhibeant, ubi secus legisse videantur Inter- pretes, quam nunc habent Ebræi Codices; Quas vero conjecturas, & quæ εὑρήματα illi pro genui- nis diversis lectionibus venditant, imo lectionem ingenio proprio excogitatam plerumque commu- ni, & in Codd. omnibus obviæ præferunt: quod ad derogandam fontibus Ebraicæ veritatis puritatis ac sinceritatis laudem, nec non autoritatis authenti- cæ dignitatem à Papizante Grotio factum, si non vi- dere potest Waltonus, nihil videt. Sed hæc παρα- φυαδικῶς, ex occasione præsentis loci.

## 65:1 Argument
PSALM LXV. Spiritual and corporal blessing.

SONG OF JEREMIAH AND EZEKIEL TO THE PEOPLE OF THE TRANSMIGRATION, WHEN THEY BEGAN TO GO OUT) This is not in the Hebrew, nor in other interpreters, but in certain copies of the version of the LXX. Moreover, these complaints and prayers at the same time do not ill suit that time: and we noted at the beginning of the book that many things here are of an age after David.

But Jeremiah and Ezekiel were already dead at the time of the release from captivity, as Bellarmine admits.

Verse 1.

Latin:

PSALM. LXV. Benedictio spiritualis, & corporalis.

CANTICUM JEREMIÆ ET EZECHIELIS POPU- LO TRANSMIGRATIONIS, CVM INCIPERENT EXIRE) Non est hoc in Hebræo, nec Interpretibus aliis, sed in quibusdam exemplaribus versionis LXX. Cæterum non male conveniunt hæ querelæ, & simul preces isti tempori: & multa esse hîc ævi post Davidem initio libri notavimus.

At mortui sub solutionem captivitatis jam erant Jerem. & Ezechiel, fatente Bellarmino.

Vers. 1.

## 65:1
TE DECET HYMNUS) In the Hebrew: To thee silence, praise: That is: let all other things be silent, when it is a question of praising thee. Keep silence.

Latin:

TE DECET HYMNVS) In Hebræo: Tibi silentium, laus: Id est: sileant alia omnia, ubi de te laudando agitur. Fa- vete linguis.

## 65:3 Addition
To Psalm 65, verse 4, BLESSED IS HE WHOM YOU HAVE CHOSEN.

The question is not about election to salvation, as most Calvinists, and even B. Schnepfius and B. Gefnerus from among our own, maintain, but rather about election to grace, as B. Luther explains in Tom. VI. Jen. f. 126, along with Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine in De bono mortis chapter 12, as well as Lorinus and Genebrardus.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 65. v. 4. BEATUS, QUEM TU ELEGISTI.

Non de electione ad salutem agitur, ut pleri- que Calviniani, etiam e nostris B. Schnepfius & B. Gefnerus volunt, sed potius de electione ad gratiam, ut B. Lutherus explicat Tom. VI. Jen. f. 126. cum Hi- lario, Ambrosio & Augustino de bono mortis cap. 12, Lorino item, & Genebrardo.

## 65:4
Verse 5. BLESSED IS HE WHOM THOU HAST CHOSEN, AND TAKEN UNTO THEE] They proclaim those blessed before them whom the Chaldeans, as men of no use, had left in Judea. 2 Kings 25:11.

We have already said that these things are foreign: in this Psalm spiritual and corporal benefits are celebrated in general. There is nothing here about the Babylonian captivity.

Latin:

Vers. 5. BEATUS QVEM ELEGISTI, ET ASSUM- SISTI] Beatos præ se prædicant illos quos, ut nulli usui homines, Chaldæi in Judæa reliquerant. 2. Reg. 25, 11.

Aliena hæc esse jam diximus: celebrantur hoc Psalmo in genere beneficia spiritualia & corporalia. Nihil hic de captivitate Babylonica.

## 66:1 Argument
PSALM LXVI. Shout of those rescued.

SONG OF THE PSALM OF THE RESURRECTION) This is not in the Hebrew, nor was it in the Hexapla. The Greek Church seems to have added it.

Whosever it may be, it is a rash addition.

Latin:

PSALMUS LXVI. Jubilate ereptorum.

CANTICUM PSALMI RESURRECTIONIS) Non est hoc in Hebræo, neque fuit in Hexaplo. Videtur Græca Ec- clesia id addidisse.

Cujuscunque sit, temerarium est additamen- tum.

## 66:10 Addition
On Psalm 66, verse 10. WE WENT THROUGH FIRE.

This is ineptly applied to purgatory, which John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, acknowledges in article 37. Estius on 1 Corinthians 3 and Vasquez in part 3, Tom. disp. 238, and Lorinus admits that the phrase 'through fire and water' is proverbial, signifying great danger, as in Isaiah 43:2 and Job 24:19. In which manner Genebrardus, Saa, and Jansenius also explain it, as do Ribera on Zechariah 13:11, 17, and Bellarmine in this place, explaining it as the various calamities of this life. How, therefore, does the same Cardinal in book 1, De purgatorio, chapter 2, prove purgatory from that passage? When, however, the Fathers made mention of a fire of probation here, they followed allegories after their custom, but said nothing in favor of the fire of purgatory.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 66. v. 10. TRANSIVIMUS PER IGNEM.

Inepte hoc trahitur ad purgatorium, quod agnoscit Joh. Fischerus Episcop. Roffensis art. 37. Estius in 1. Cor. 3. & Vasquez in 3. part. Tom. disp. 238. & fatetur Lorinus phrasin per ignem & aquam proverbialem esse magnum periculum significantem, ut Esa. 43, 2. Job. 24, 19. Quo pacto etiam explicat Genebrardus, Saa, & Jansenius, ut & Ribera in Zachar. 13, 11. 17. ut & Bellarminus in h. l. de variis calamitatibus hujus vitæ exponens. Quî ergo idem Cardinalis l. I. de purg. cap. 2. purgatorium ex eo loco probat? Cum vero Patres ignis proba- tionis hic mentionem fecere, more suo allegorias prosequuti sunt, nihil autem pro igne purgatorii dixerunt.

## 66:18
Verse 18.

IF I HAVE REGARDED INIQUITY IN MY HEART, THE LORD WILL NOT HEAR] The sense is: if I had looked in my mind toward wicked counsels, the Lord would not have heard me. But now, since He has heard me, it is apparent to all that I was not of such a mind. Kimchi very poorly infers from this passage that God is not offended by evil thoughts, provided they are not carried out in act: which is the very opinion of Pharisaism, which both Christ and Paul often go about refuting.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

INIQVITATEM SI ADSPEXI IN CORDE MEO, NON EXAUDIET DOMINUS] Sensus est: si animo meo spectassem ad consilia improba, non exaudisset me Domi- nus. Nunc autem cum me exaudierit, apparet omnibus me non tali fuisse animo. Pessime hoc ex loco infert Kimchi, Deum cogitationibus malis, dum actu non impleantur, non offendi: quæ ipsa est sententia Pharisaïsmi, quam & Christus & Paulus sæpe repurgatum eunt.

## 67:1 Argument
PSALM LXVII. An Ecclesiastical Blessing.

Latin:

PSALM. LXVII. Benedictio Ecclesiastica.

## 67:6
Ver. 7.

LET ALL THE PEOPLES CONFESS THEE: THE EARTH HATH GIVEN HER FRUIT) All nations praise thee, the earth giving its fruit.

Thus Grotius, with the Rabbis, [interprets this] concerning the celebration of GOD on account of the fertility of the earth and a large harvest: but the argument of the Psalm is not about bodily goods and gifts; since it treats rather of the salvation and blessing to be brought through the Messiah, and the calling of the Gentiles, and therefore these things are to be explained concerning spiritual fruit, on account of which all nations exult and praise the Lord. Jerome and other ancients understood it of Christ, the sprout of David who was to come forth from the earth. The sense is pious. For that the Messiah is called the fruit of the earth, and that the earth has given its fruit, is not at all abhorrent to the phraseology of Scripture, Isa. 4:1, chap. 45:8. But the common interpretation concerning the fruit of the Gospel is more suitable. The salvation of the Lord, Christ, and the calling of the Gentiles have already been treated before; and therefore now the fruits are celebrated that are to arise from the proclamation of the word throughout the whole world. The whole Psalm is completed by a prayer, a celebration, and a blessing in honor of the Most Holy Trinity, chanted after the manner of the Ecclesiastical blessing in Num. 6:21, of which a commentary is held by some theologians. The prayer is directed to Elohim, God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that God the Father may have mercy on us, God the Son may bless us, God the Holy Spirit may make His face shine upon us, that the way and salvation of the Lord may be known: where, by apostrophe, the speaker turns to GOD the Father, that they may know Thy way, as also all nations [may know] Thy SALVATION. Because Christ is the salvation of GOD, Isa. 49:6, Luke 2:3.

The celebration of the divine name is likewise instituted in such a way that it can be applied to the individual persons in the Most Holy Trinity not inconveniently. Let the peoples confess Thee, O GOD (Father): Let all the peoples confess Thee. Let the nations exult and rejoice, because Thou (O Messiah, Son of God (in Evangelical equity, not according to the rigor of the Mosaic law)) judgest the peoples, and leadest the nations into the land (by Thy Spirit) Selah. Let the peoples confess Thee (Holy Spirit), let all the peoples confess Thee, because the earth has given its fruit. For the fruits of the word are to be attributed to the Holy Spirit: and therefore they are also called the fruits of the Spirit. Galat. 5. Ephes. 5.

Finally, a blessing is subjoined, instituted in the name of the same Most Holy Trinity, according to the custom of the solemn Ecclesiastical blessing in Numbers 6, as also the Patriarchal Jacobean [blessing] in Genesis 48:16. May GOD (the Father) bless us: may our God (Immanuel Christ, Isa. 7:14, who is God with us, Matt. 1:23, and is our God and Lord, on account of His special approach to us and appropriation, the communication of Himself, and our acquisition and redemption) bless us. May God (the Holy Spirit) bless us, and let all the ends of the earth fear Him (this triune GOD: so that by the triple repetition of the word GOD, the Trinity of persons is designated, but by this singular pronoun, the unity of essence is understood). The Seraphic doxology in Isa. 6:3 is twofold: Holy (God the Father), Holy (God the Son), Holy (Spirit of the Father and the Son), Jehovah Zebaoth (God one in essence), the whole earth is full of His glory.

Most refer this Davidic ode to the times of the New Testament, so that the prayer contains the sighing of the faithful Israelites for the sending of Christ, and for his manifestation to the whole world, which was the proper desire of the Old Church, panting for Him in whom the promised blessing was, and who had to come in order to bless them, Acts 3:26, and wishing that this salvation of GOD might be manifested to all nations, in whom all the nations of the earth were to be blessed. But the celebration (the other part of the Psalm) pertains to the times of the New Testament in such a way that the sacred singer does not so much institute a prophecy concerning the confession, joy, and jubilation of the faithful under the New Testament, as he views all those things as present. Let the peoples confess Thee, O GOD: the nations, whom Thou judgest as King and leadest as Shepherd with all equity and kindness, rejoice and jubilate in Thy rule (O Messiah). Let all the peoples confess Thee (O Holy Spirit), the whole earth giving fruit, which Thou makest fruitful and fertile by the word of the Gospel, when for the greatest part it was arid, sterile, and horrible. Isa. 32:15, chap. 35:7, chap. 44:3, seqq., chap. 55:10, 13. But just as the blessing made here in the name of the Holy Trinity, so also the prayer directed to the Holy Trinity, and indeed the celebration of the Holy Trinity, is, was, and will be for all times; although there is no doubt that the celebration and fuller exaltation is proper to the N. T.: but desires and sighs for the compassion of God the Father, the blessing of God the Son, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit were with the Church of the O. T. joined with the desires and sighs of the mission and advent of the Lord, and the calling of the Gentiles; just as the same are now with the faithful of the New Testament joined with the desires and sighs of the final advent of Christ and the glorious plenary illumination of the other life Ap. 22, 17. Tit. 2, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

CONFITEANTUR TIBI POPULI OMNES: TER- RA DEDIT FRUCTUM SUUM) Laudant te gentes omnes terra suum fructum dante.

ITa cum Rabbinis Grotius de celebratione DEI ob terræ fertilitatem, & largum proventum: sed argumentum Psalmi non est de corporalibus bonis ac donis: quum potius de salute ac benedictione per Messiam adferenda, & vocatione gentium agat, adeoque de spirituali fructu hæc explicanda, ob quem exultant, Dominumque prædicant omnes gentes. Hieronymus, & alii veteres, de Christo, germine Davidis è terra prodituro, accepere. Sen- sus pius est. Nam & Messiam fructum terræ dici, ac terram fructum suum dedisse à phrasi scripturæ haud abhorret, Esa. 4, 1. cap. 45, 8. Sed conve- nientior est communis interpretatio de fructu Ev- angelii. De salute Domini, Christo, & de vo- catione gentium antea jam actum: ideoque nunc celebrantur fructus è præconio verbi orituri per orbem universum. Psalmus totus absolvitur pre- catione, celebratione, ac benedictione in honorem S. S. Trinitatis decantatus ad Ecclesiasticæ benedi- ctionis Num. 6, 21. instar, cujus à nonnullis Theo- logis commentarius habetur. Precatio directa est ad Elohim Deum Patrem, Filium & Spirit. S. ut Deus Pater misereatur nostri, Deus Filius benedi- cat nobis, Deus Spiritus Sanctus illuminet faciem suam super nos, ut cognoscatur via & salus Domini: ubi per apostrophen se convertit orator ad DEUM Patrem, ut cognoscant viam Tuam, ut & omnes gen- tes SALUTEM tuam. Quia Christus est salus DEI Es. 49, 6. Luc. 2, 3.

Celebratio nominis divini itidem ita instituitur, ut singulis personis eadem applicari non incom- mode queat in S. S. Trinitate. Confiteantur Tibi DEUS (Pater) populi: Confiteantur tibi omnes po- puli. Gentes exultent, & jubilent, quod tu (o Mes- sia, Fili Dei (in æquitate Evangelica, non secun- dum rigorem legis Mosaicæ) judicas populos, & ducis gentes in terram (Spiritu tuo) Sela. Confite- antur tibi (Spiritus Sancte) populi, confiteantur ti- bi omnes populi, quia terra dedit fructum suum. Nam fructus verbi Spiritui Sancto accepti ferendi: atque ideo fructus Spiritus etiam dicuntur. Galat. 5. Ephes. 5.

Subjungitur tandem benedictio in nomine ejus- dem Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis instituta, juxta morem solemnis benedictionis Ecclesiasticæ Numer. 6. ut & Patriarchalis Jacobeæ Genes. 48, 16. Benedicat no- bis DEUS (Pater: benedicat nobis) Deus noster (Immanuel Christus Esa. 7, 14. qui Deus nobiscum Matth. 1, 23. & Deus ac Dominus noster est, ob specia- lem ad nos appropinquationem & ὀικείωσιν, sui communicationem, nostrique περιποίησιν, acqui- sitionem, & redemtionem) Benedicat nobis Deus (Spiritus Sanctus) & metuant Eum (hunc triu- num DEUM: ut trina vocis DEI repetitione per- sonarum Trinitas, hoc autem singulari prono- mine essentiæ unitas designata intelligatur) omnes fines terræ. Gemina est δοξολογία Seraphica Esa. 6, 3. Sanctus (Deus Pater,) Sanctus (Deus filius) Sanctus (Spiritus Patris & filii) Jehovah Zebaoth (unus essentiâ Deus) plena est gloria ejus universa terra.

Referunt plerique oden hanc Davidicam ad tempora Novi Testam. ut precatio suspirium con- tinuerit fidelium Israelitarum de mittendo Chri- sto, eodemque toti orbi manifestando, quod de- siderium Veteris Ecclesiæ proprium fuit, anhe- lantis eum, in quo benedictio promissa, quique venire debuit, ut ipsi benediceret, Actor. 3, 26. & exoptantis, ut omnibus gentibus hoc salutare DEI manifestetur, in quo omnes nationes terræ benedicendæ erant. Celebratio vero (altera pars Psalmi) ad tempora Novi Testamenti ita perti- neat, ut Hieropsaltes non tam vaticinium de Confessione, lætitia, & jubilo fidelium sub Novo Testamento instituat, quam ea omnia ceu præ- sentia intueatur. Confiteantur tibi DEUS omnes populi: lætantur & jubilant in tuo regimine (Mes- sia) gentes, quas judicas ut Rex, & ducis, ut Pastor cum omni æquitate ac benignitate. Confiteantur ti- bi (ô Sancte Spiritus) omnes populi, terra univer- sa dante fructum, quam verbo Evangelii fœcun- dam atque fertilem reddis, quum maximam par- tem arida, sterilis, & horrida esset. Esa. 32, 15. cap. 35, 7. cap. 44, 3. seqq. cap. 55, 10. 13. sed uti be- nedictio in nomine S. Trinitatis hîc facta, ita & precatio ad S. Trinitatem directa, nec non celebra- tio S. Trinitatis omnium est, fuit, eritque tempo- rum; tametsi dubium non sit celebrationem & ex- altationem pleniorem N. T. propriam esse: deside- ria vero ac suspiria pro miseratione DEI Patris, be- nedictione Dei Filii, ac illuminatione S. penes Ec- clesiam V. T. cum desideriis & suspiriis Missionis & adventus Domini, & vocationis gentium conjuncta fuisse; quemadmodum eadem nunc penes Fideles Novi Test, cum desideriis, & suspiriis adventus Christi novissimi ac illuminationis gloriosae plena- riae alterius vitae conjuncta sunt Ap. 22, 17. Tit. 2, 17.

## 68:1 Argument
PSALM LXVIII. The triumph and gifts of Christ, the joy and glory of the Church.

Ver. 1.

LET GOD ARISE) The subject matter of this song is the departure of the people out of Egypt.

Latin:

PSALMUS LXVIII. Triumphus & dona Christi, gaudium & gloria Ecclesiae.

Vers. 1.

EXURGAT DEUS) Argumentum hujus carminis est exitus populi ex Aegypto.

## 68:4
Ver. 5.

MAKE A WAY FOR HIM WHO ASCENDS ABOVE THE WEST) That is, prepare a way for him, ὁδοποιήσατε, as the LXX have it here. Above the west ἐπὶ δυσμῶν, in the Hebrew בערבות which Aquila translates in the uninhabited place, whence Jerome in another version [translates] through the deserts. Kimchi and others of the Hebrews understand the highest celestial sphere: and it is accepted hence among the Hebrews to use the word Araboth in that meaning. But since the most ancient of the Hebrews recognized no distinction of spheres in heaven, as we also learn from the Gemara at the beginning of Genesis, it is more true that by this word nothing else is signified than what Paul called ἀπρόσιτον 1 Tim. 6, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ITER FACITE EI QUI ASCENDIT SUPER OC- CASUM) Id est, viam ei munite, ὁδοποιήσατε, ut hic habent LXX. Super occasum ἐπὶ δυσμῶν, in Hebraeo בערבות quod Aquila vertit ἐν τῇ ἀοικήτῳ, unde Hieronymus in alte- ra versione per deserta. Kimchi, & Hebraeorum alii sum- mum orbem coelestem intelligunt: & receptum hinc apud Hebraeos in eo significatu uti voce Araboth. Sed cum vetu- stissimi Hebraeorum nullum orbium discrimen in coelo agno- verint, ut & ex Gemara discimus ad initium Geneseos, veri- us est hac voce nihil aliud significari, quam quod ἀπρόσιτον dixit Paulus 1. Tim. 6, 16.

## 68:8
Ver. 9.

THE EARTH SHOOK, THE HEAVENS ALSO DROPPED) That נטפו can best be translated were troubled. For it is the same word in Judg. 5, 4, where the Greek version [says] the heaven was troubled. AT THE PRESENCE OF GOD OF SINAI, AT THE PRESENCE OF THE GOD OF ISRAEL) It is better to join that first 'at the presence of God' with the preceding, so that 'Sinai at the presence of the God of Israel' may follow: supply ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, [it] was moved and troubled.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

TERRA MOTA EST, ETIAM COELI DISTILLA- VERUNT) Illud נטפו optime verti potest conturbati sunt. Est enim idem verbum Judic. 5, 4. ubi Graeca versio ὁ οὐρανὸς ἐταράχθη. A FACIE DEI SINAI, A FACIE DEI ISRAEL) Melius illud prius a facie Dei, conjungas cum praecedenti- bus, ut sequatur deinde Sinai a facie Dei Israel: supple ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, motus & conturbatus est.

## 68:9
Ver. 10.

A VOLUNTARY RAIN) A liberal one, as above §I, 14. FOR THINE INHERITANCE) For the people of Israel.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

PLUVIAM VOLUNTARIAM) Liberalem, ut supra §I, 14. HAEREDITATI TUAE) Populo Israel.

## 68:10
Ver. 11.

THY ANIMALS SHALL DWELL IN IT) The Hebrews understand the chief of the angels, who are the חיות to Ezekiel: But חיה can be understood as a congregation, just as below 31, חיה and עדה seem to be put for the same thing. For congregations for the sake of worshipping the true God were frequented only among the people of Israel.

Concerning the subject of this Psalm, various opinions are found, both among Jews and Christians. Among the Jews, some explain the whole of it as being about the departure of the people from Egypt, along with the Chaldean Interpreter and R. Solomon Jarchi, which opinion R. Aben-Ezra also cites at this place. Exegetes, he says, refer it to the law given at Sinai. Others explain it as being about the battles and victories of David against the uncircumcised, such as R. Aben-Ezra. Others, about the deliverance of Hezekiah from the army of Sennacherib, when he had besieged Jerusalem, along with R. David Kimchi. Others, about the Babylonian captivity and the redemption from it, which seems to be the explanation of R. Obadiah. Some, however, among the Jews acknowledge that a prophecy about the Messiah is held here, which R. Solomon Jarchi observes. Others say that this Psalm is about the future days of Christ. To this contributes what R. Obadiah has at verse 25: 'They saw your goings, O God,' that is, the prophets of God in visions foresaw you, O Christ. And what R. Solomon has at verse 34: 'Sing or chant praises after the advent of Christ.' Among Christian interpreters, the ancients interpret the Psalm with great consensus as being about the Messiah, about his resurrection and ascension into heaven; and although they sometimes differ in the paraphrase of certain parts of the Psalm, they easily agree, however, on this: that the subject of this Psalm is the resurrection and ascension of the Messiah. This explanation of the ancients is followed by our own Doctors: B. Luther, Bugenhagen, Brentius, Vitus Dietericus, Osiander, Aegid. Hunnius, Gesner, Hutter, Cramer, Gerhard, the Weimar Paraphrasts, and others, all to a man. Most Papists also follow it, as well as not a few from the Reformed.

However, some Zwinglians accede to the Jewish glosses, such as John Calvin, Bucer, Wolfgang Musculus, and others, as well as Enjedinus among the Neo-Photinians, appealing to the authority and consensus of Bucer, Musculus, and Calvin (Explic. locor. Vet. & Nov. Test. on Eph. 4:8, page 300). Grotius also embraced these here, in preference to the sense of Christian interpreters. Although, just as the Jews differ in their opinions regarding the true subject of the Psalm, even if most of them agree that it does not treat of the Messiah according to the letter, so those Judaizers easily agree on this: that according to the literal sense, the subject of the Psalm is not the Messiah; yet in explaining its genuine subject, some follow others among the Jews, whether in whole or in part. Grotius agrees with R. Solomon that this treats of the departure of the people from Egypt. Calvin, in the explanation of the subject, says that it was proposed to David in this Psalm to celebrate the victories he had obtained over his enemies by the grace of God, which is also the gloss of Enjedinus. Others interpret it as being about David bringing the Ark of the Covenant into the citadel of Zion, and they make this the historical sense of the Psalm; Pareus notes this opinion as being that of Musculus in his commentaries, of Beza in the Psalter, and of Junius in his Parallels (Calv. Orthod. book 2, chapter 32, page 241), and judges it most congruent. Others combine those two opinions about the departure from Egypt and the public festival of David. This was done by Rivet: 'I join those two occasions, by which David was moved to sing this Psalm, and which others tear apart, into one, yet in such a way that one proceeds from one to the other, and one is more remote, while the other is closer, and from which this enthusiasm, as it were, immediately arose.' I therefore judge that this Psalm was written by David when he had reported victories over neighboring enemies, especially the Philistines, which are treated in 2 Sam. 5; having subdued them and established the kingdom, he thought about transporting the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (2 Sam. 6). This, therefore, was the end proposed to David when he sang this Psalm to the Lord: that he might give thanks to God, who was coming into His Church through a visible sign of His presence, and in this order: that first, according to the type—that is, the Ark of the Covenant, which was being introduced into Jerusalem at that time—the celebration should be instituted; but then, according to the body and truth of the type, when Christ, after He was manifested in the flesh, joined Himself to His Church. This opinion is more tolerable because it does not deny, as it appears, the other part—as do the Jews and Calvin and his associates, as well as the Judaizing Grotius—that it prophesies of Christ according to the letter, but interprets it as a prophecy about Christ, as do the Christians. Even though, while he played the part of Calvin here, Rivet can in no way be excused, since he attacked with a petulant pen our most deserving theologian, B. Gesner, who with just zeal refuted Calvin here as a Judaizer. It is not the mark of a Christian heart, let alone theological piety, to patronize perverse glosses, which you yourself cannot prove, in such a way that you not only become angry at those who refute them with a due refutation, but also consign those who have died piously in the Lord to Satan on that account, and curse them. 'There is no reason,' says Rivet in his Commentary on the Prophetic Psalms, page 287, 'for certain Pseudo-Lutherans to lacerate Calvin, seeking calumny on every occasion.' intent, because he said that it was more subtly deflected by Paul to Christ, which he thinks should first be understood as a type, namely of the exaltation of the glory of God under David, which seemed to have lain dormant under Saul, showing nevertheless that the application of the Apostle agrees well with the mind of David, which, since he confirms it with many arguments and pursues it with more, it is a wonder that, from a few of his mutilated words, Gesner, a former Wittenberg Theologaster, dared to exclaim petulantly: Who therefore doubts that Calvin Judaizes, and obliquely carps at the Apostle Paul, and even the Holy Spirit himself? May the Lord rebuke you, O Satan! Does he seem to you to Judaize, who asserts that that principle can in no way be overturned, that David presided over the ancient people under such a law that under that figure Christ the eternal King might begin his empire; and affirms that the promise of eternal succession, which was finally sanctioned in the person of Christ, must always be held? Can he who laid that foundation build Judaism upon it? Or obliquely carp at the Apostle Paul for referring these things to Christ? Thus Rivetus. But that no injury was done here to Calvin, the genuinely Lutheran theologian, the blessed Ægidius Hunnius, our former predecessor, demonstrated to the eye in his Anti-Pareus, p. 212 et seqq., so that in such evidence of the matter, which has been exposed by that response of the blessed Hunnius in the very, as they say, disk of the Sun, one ought to detest Rivetus, because he does not hesitate to still defend Calvin, and at the same time to attack and disturb the shade of the blessed Gesner with such a slanderous pen. What is more evident than that Calvin Judaizes, and obliquely carps at Paul himself, by attributing to God the Father words which Paul openly testifies were spoken about the Son of God, along with the Jews, and by not accepting, but rather snatching away to a foreign meaning, what he teaches that he speaks about the ascension of Christ into heaven, along with the Jews, especially when he says that Paul 'more subtly deflects' this passage to Christ (Comment. in h. l.) and has 'twisted' this testimony not a little from its 'genuine sense' (Comment. ad Ephes. 4, 8). The fact that he constitutes David as a type of Christ does not contribute to a solid excuse for Calvin, because the Jews do not deny that David was a type of the Messiah, nor can it aid the Apostolic proof; indeed, if the victories of the God of Israel reported over enemies are types of the ascension of Christ into heaven, and for that reason the ascension was proved by the Apostle from the victory of David, that proof will certainly not be firmer than if the histories of the defeated Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and other enemies were brought forward for the sake of demonstrating the ascension, which, as those to whom preconceived opinions have not cast a fog and eaten away their eyes see very easily, contributes to obscuring the light of the prophecy, to infringing the strength of the proof, and to elevating the authority of the Apostolic allegation, just as the blessed Hunnius long ago warned from the truth. Rivetus therefore had no reason to harass the blessed Gesner so much, whom he now even calls a Theologaster out of contempt, so that you might understand, forsooth, the gratitude of a man who transcribed not a few things from Gesner's commentaries into his own, and thus ought to have acknowledged that he had made progress through our theologian!

But to Grotius: who indeed confesses that some things from this Psalm pertain mystically to Christ, yet accepts everything literally concerning the exodus from Egypt, and calls that the primary and obvious sense at Eph. 4, 8. Therefore, while he grants that some things were fulfilled more eminently in Christ, he makes the historical or paraphrastic sense far different, according to which, namely, some things are referred to here historically concerning certain people under the Old Testament, or are predicted prophetically concerning some, and in these were fulfilled under the Old Testament, whether they typified Christ, or otherwise have some similarity and convenience with the affairs of the New Testament, whence they can be referred to Christ in an eminent and mystical sense. Thus, what is had in v. 19 concerning gifts, Grotius explains concerning gifts accepted for the use of the Priests and Levites, according to the letter: mystically concerning the gifts distributed in Christ in the New Testament. He explains the dwelling among the rebellious according to the letter concerning the Gibeonites and those similar to them, who, having long been rebels against God, became proselytes; but he says that these were fulfilled more eminently through Christ. What is had in v. 32 concerning the ambassadors from Egypt, he understands according to the literal sense concerning those who brought a pact to Solomon: but he says they were fulfilled more eminently when the Egyptians offered oblations in the Church. Just as Calvin: Nor is there any doubt that he delineates under this type the magnificent glory of God, which finally appeared in Christ.

The question therefore is whether this Psalm, according to the literal sense, is a prophecy about Christ, or whether it only describes the affairs of the Old Testament? I say, it is not asked whether it can be applied in some way to those things which happened under the New Testament, or even now happen, either because it was at least a type there, and the thing itself is prefigured in the New Testament, or because the affairs of the New Testament respond by some similarity to those which happened under the Old Testament, or because they were indeed truly fulfilled in the Old Testament, but because the kingdom of Christ only began there, they obtained a more illustrious and eminent fulfillment in the New Testament: But whether the Psalmist prophesies solely about Christ and the affairs of the New Testament in an immediate and literal sense, Testament, even though in his phrases he may have alluded to things already past when he issued this prophecy, and recalled their similarity to future things to his mind, just as is wont to happen in allegorical matters, and it is especially solemn for the Holy Spirit to use words familiar to the Old Testament, as if taken from those things which were known at that time, to insinuate the mysteries of the New Testament, or even to have instituted a comparison in the things themselves, to illustrate those things about which he sings by design. In a word: The proper subject of the Psalm is being discussed: which Grotius constitutes as the exodus from Egypt, and Calvin as the Davidic victories, referring only certain things from the Psalm to Christ, and those only in a mystical sense. We, however, with most Christian interpreters, constitute Christ as the subject of the Psalm, according to the proper, immediate, and paraphrastic sense, rejecting the gloss of Grotius and Calvin as Jewish commentaries.

But first, because our business is with Christians, we lay down here as a foundation the Apostle’s explanation, as being above all exception: who in verse 19 clearly teaches in Eph. 4:8 that this is to be understood of Christ, and furthermore that the whole Psalm in its proper sense treats of Christ. For what is here acclaimed to the Lord, "You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive, you have received gifts in men," the Apostle interprets of Christ by merely changing the second person into the third, and explaining the purpose of the gifts received, as follows: "Grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." From which an invincible argument arises, against the Jews alike and other enemies of the divinity of Christ, whether Arians or

He who by ascending on high led captivity captive and gave gifts to men, is that God whom the Psalmist calls upon to arise, to whom to sing, and as to the Lord, and to make a journey, who leads out the bound with strength, who went forth in the sight of the people in passing through the desert, Jehovah who was about to give the word to those bringing good news, of whom the whole Psalm treats. But Christ is he who by ascending on high led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men, as the Apostle is witness and interpreter. The major proposition from the continuity of the text is most clear, but the words of Paul exhibit the minor. What then is more certain, than that a key is here provided, by which the mysteries of this Psalm may be unlocked, and that because of the perpetual coherence of the Davidic ode, the whole Psalm treats of Christ and explains his benefits. Which, among Christians receiving the Apostolic interpretation as infallible and divine, ought to have been indubitable, although it can also be demonstrated from the very bowels of the Psalm. Grotius, however, in order to help the Jews, explains it concerning God the Father and his ascent from the earth into heaven, and the condemnation of peoples to captivity, and among them the Midianites, and the acceptance of gifts for the use of the Priests and Levites, and affirms that Paul refers these things mystically to Christ alone. But Grotius could give no reason for this interpretation, new and hitherto unheard of, and merely arbitrary: Which is not a little unjust to the Apostle; for he says that he [Paul] DRAWS the words of the Psalmist to a mystical sense, Annot. on Eph. 4:8. Following Calvin, who pronounced that the Apostle deflects and distorts them from their genuine sense. Nor does it lightly oppose the Apostolic intention: Because the Apostle proves from the Psalm that the grace which has come to us in the New Testament is to be attributed to Christ, who gives it to each one according to the measure of his gift; because he ascended on high, and led captivity captive, that he might receive gifts for men, and having been raised to the right hand of God, might distribute the same to men, as he wills. This would be no proof if the Psalm did not treat of the ascension of Christ into heaven, but of the ascent of God from Mount Sinai: not of the donation of gifts, which Christ was to receive through his exaltation, in order to give them to men, but of the donation of God the Father, who received the same from no one, nor could receive them, just as he cannot be exalted: Not of gifts, which were distributed under the N.T., when Christ ascending above all heavens gave some Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, some Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the Saints for the work of the ministry; but of gifts, which tended to the use of the Levites and Priests under the Old Testament. Not of an ascent which had a preceding descent into the lowest parts, as the Apostle expressly says: But that he ascended, what is it, but that he also descended first into the lowest parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all heavens, but of an ascent from Mount Sinai, into which God had previously descended: as Grotius trifles: Not of such an ascent, which the fullness of all things follows, he ascended above all heavens, that he might FILL all things, says the Apostle; But of an ascent clearly different, by no means bringing with it this fullness of all things. Not of the majestic ascent of the triumphant one, by which spiritual captivity was led captive, hindering the distribution of gifts, which was to be captured for that reason, that gifts might be given to men, but of a certain metaphorical and improper ascent of God, of which nothing is held in the Scriptures, and to which the captivity of captivity cannot be imputed, in whatever way that may finally be explained. For is the ascension of God from Mount Sinai the cause of the captivity of the Midianites and other enemies, or how do those cohere? Whence that gloss neither agrees with the words themselves, nor with the context of the Psalm. For where is God said to have ascended from Mount Sinai? Did God receive gifts for men, and from whom did he receive them? How in the ascent from Mount Sinai did he lead captivity captive? How through that ascent did he either receive gifts for men or give them to the same? How through the same was it brought about that he should dwell among the rebellious? All those things are merely unwritten, incoherent, nay, inconsistent. If, however, they are explained with the Apostle concerning Christ's ascension into heaven, all things fit and cohere perfectly.

Calvin's invention, lest anyone should stick to it, is no better, who explains the Apostolic allegation in two ways: First, as if he had descended from the genus to a certain species, which explanation is found in the commentary on Eph. 4. Paul, when he saw the triumph of God and whatever victories he had brought about for the salvation of the Church celebrated by David, rightly accommodated this verse concerning the ascension of God to the person of Christ. For this is the chief triumph of God that God ever performed, when Christ, having overcome sin, subdued death, and routed Satan, was magnificently raised to heaven, that he might rule the Church with a glorious empire. Then, however, in the commentary on the Psalms, which is some years later than the commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, he judged a more convenient mode of explanation to be that Paul had more subtly deflected the words speaking of the type to the antitype. Just as God asserted his power through the hand of David, so that (God) raised on high might raise up his people, so in his only-begotten Son he showed his highest altitude. Neither explanation can be admitted: Not the former: For how inept would be the collection from genus to species: Because David celebrated the triumphs and victories of God, which he himself brought about for the salvation of the Church: Therefore he sang of that which Christ ascending into heaven was about to lead captivity captive, and receive gifts for men? For he who says the genus does not immediately express all species: and from genus to a certain species is to conclude from the undistributed to the distributed. How therefore could Paul, from the fact that God, raised by victories, receives gifts for men, as Calvin explains the words of David, infer that Christ had ascended on high, and had given gifts to men? When Calvin himself saw that this collection was an ἀνακόλυθον here, he finally despaired of the application of a literal exposition in his Commentary on Ephesians, and invented the idea that a mere allusion is being made by Paul here. He says, a scrupulously LITERAL EXPOSITION of the Psalm is not to be sought here, since he ONLY ALLUDES to the words of the Prophet: nay, he accused Paul of having TWISTED this testimony somewhat from its GENUINE SENSE. But the Pauline words themselves testify that it is not merely an allusion, but a proof, and that not only the words are being regarded, but the very subject matter of which the Psalmist had treated is, as it were, pointed out with the finger: to each one of us grace is given, according to the measure of the gift of Christ: WHEREFORE (it is a word of reasoning) he says: when he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men. Furthermore, what is that HE ASCENDED (of which David prophesied), unless that he had also DESCENDED INTO THE LOWER PARTS OF THE EARTH? David therefore prophesied concerning him, who had previously descended into the lower parts of the earth. Therefore, lest any doubt remain concerning the subject, Paul adds, HE WHO DESCENDED, IS THE SAME ONE who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things: most clearly pointing out Christ as the one designated by David, both in that he had to ascend above all the heavens, and in that he had previously to descend into the lower parts of the earth: THAT IT IS THE SAME ONE of whom David prophesied, not another. Finally, in order to elicit from this what he was intending, namely the fruit of the Lord's ascension, he adds that He GAVE Apostles, Prophets, etc., and instructed them with His gifts from heaven. And these things regarding the former explanation. Furthermore, there is no room for Calvin's latter explanation concerning a type, unless you wish to say that God raised up by victories is a type of Christ being raised on high in the ascension into heaven: which is absurd. If you say that the glory of God raised up in David was a type of the height of God shown in the Son, neither does the Psalmist have anything about the glory of God raised up in David, but about the ascension of the Lord on high or into heaven, nor is David anywhere in the Scriptures established as a type of Christ in that, or can be established more than any other of the Saints in the O.T. in whom the glory of God was raised up: nor does the Apostle demonstrate from the words of the Psalm only the height of God shown in the Son, but the ascension of the Son Himself into heaven: which are greatly different, because the height could be demonstrated in the Son of God in many ways, nor could an ascension into heaven be immediately concluded from that demonstrated height, unless you say that He ascended into heaven as many times as the height of God was demonstrated in Him. Whence Rivetus was forced here to desert his most learned interpreter Calvin, whom he openly contradicts on p. 387. But the things which are said in this place about the chariot of God, about the ascension on high, and the gifts conferred upon men, etc., can in no way be accommodated to the History of Sennacherib, nor do they even befit the bringing of the ark, and therefore it is NECESSARY that they be explained outside of EVERY TYPE RELATIONSHIP DIRECTLY CONCERNING GOD then to be manifested in the flesh, now manifested, to whom Paul also applied it in v. 19, Eph. 4, 8.

Now with this foundation laid, the exposition of the whole Psalm is easier: although it also shines with its own light. The entrance itself, which also provides the argument, Let God arise, and His enemies will be scattered: is instituted with those words which were used when the ark of the covenant, a type of the Messiah, was setting out, Num. 10, so that it might be indicated that the prophecy would treat of Him who was prefigured by that ark. Therefore, just as Moses prayed to God with those words, that as the ark arose and preceded the people, He Himself might also deign to arise, and render the people secure by His defense and protection: So David, imitating Moses and foreseeing the resurrection of Christ, through whom He Himself, as the ark of the covenant, was to be the leader to be elevated for the elect to the land of the true promise: says, Let God arise: as Bellarmine, Menochius, and others explain, along with the Fathers Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, and others. The sum of the vows, says Hilary in this place, is not from the uncertainty of one asking, but from the knowledge and understanding of one hoping. For he now desires the time of the resurrection in God: when, condemning sin in the flesh concerning sin, He makes the powers of this world a spectacle, triumphing with confidence in Himself. For He came into the world to conquer, and to fix the prince of the world with the law of sin, and to delete the decree of death by the remission of sin. The Prophet therefore expects this flight of His enemies. Theodoret has it thus: Let God arise, etc. It is time, he says, that You, O Lord, should arise, and that You should procure the salvation of men: for as soon as You have arisen, the whole army of enemies will be turned to flight, dissipated by the splendor of Your advent. Moreover, this word Arise, not only calls for the cessation of patience, but also for the resurrection of the Savior of the world after three days, when He most willingly underwent death for us. But those words: And let the just feast: He shows by these that he did not bring these prayers against men, but against the demons bringing war upon men, with whom dissipated and rendered vain, the nations exult, and praise God, who has bestowed salvation. Thus Blessed Bugenhagius makes this the SUM of the Psalm: Christ, having overcome death, is glorified, both in heaven and on earth. There because He sits at the right hand of God, here, the glory of Him who sits is preached everywhere: by whose ineffable joy both believers are glorified, and rebels are horribly cast away.

To this further pertains the exhortation to celebrate and receive this God of ours v. 3. Sing to God, sing psalms to His name, make a way for Him who ascends over the sunset, the Lord is His name, and exult in His sight. Which Hilary refers to the description of the raised Christ: To Him must be sung, and His way must be prepared, who ascends over all the sunset of death: that is, who has not departed from all sunset by the sunset itself. But to this One the name is Lord, who from the form of God emptying Himself and taking the form of a servant, made Himself obedient even to the death of the cross. On account of which God exalted Him, and gave Him a name which is above every name. To Him, therefore, a way must be prepared, according to that, prepare the ways of the Lord. Others explain the word בָעֲרָבוֹת, which the Vulgate rendered by sunset, as desert: as Aquila, in the uninhabited place. And Jerome: prepare the way for Him who ascends through the deserts. And so also Symmachus, whose version Theodoret praises, and by desert understands the nations, Is. 37 and elsewhere the nations are designated by solitude and deserts. He wishes, therefore, for the Apostles to be excited here, so that they may run to the nations with dances and hymns, and prepare a way for the Emperor of all. So also Felix Pratensis explained it, in Solitudes, and Mollerus, in the desert: nor are the deserts of the nations, to which the Apostles were sent through the resurrection of Christ, understood inconveniently: which seems to be confirmed from a similar passage Is. 40, 3. make straight in the desert (בָּעֲרָבָה) the paths of our God, where the Messiah is designated, for whom the way is to be prepared John 1, as Bugenhagius explains: you just, by the justice of faith, sing to God, preach everywhere the magnificence of Him who rose again, make a way for Him to the hearts of men through the preaching of the law and repentance, so that they may recognize themselves as sinners, and desire the Savior, and thirst for the Gospel: for Him, I say, who proceeds through the deserts of the nations, among whom before there was no grace. Others understand by עֲרָבוֹת pleasant places, as Tremellius and Junius: who resides in pleasant places, that is, He possesses all most pleasant things, and is the author of all pleasantness. Whence B. Luther rendered: der da sanfft herfähret, which the Weimar Bibles explain, der in der zuschlagenen Hertzen mit seinem Trost und Frieden sånstiglich einzeucht, Isa. 57, 15. John 14, 23. Nor does Osiander think otherwise in his Paraphr. Bibl. Others understand the highest heavens with the Hebrews, as Pagninus, who ascends above the heavens. Arias Montanus, who rides in the highest heavens, just as below v. 23, who ascends above the heavens of heavens: to whom the Genevans in the French Bibles agree, and Rivetus in his Commentaries. Boetius of Antwerp and Buchanan, and also from our own Mr. Brentius, who here compares the passages concerning the ascension of Christ above all heavens Eph. 4, Heb. 4, and 7. There follows an exhortation to commend and celebrate the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and an exposition of the majesty of his kingdom and the victory which he brought back from his conquered enemies, and of that triumphal procession which followed that victory before the assembly of all the heavenly citizens: Praise, he says, exalt, prepare the way, adorn, or receive honorably Christ, who ascends into the heavens, (that is) inhabits the heavenly and inaccessible light: which Grotius also thinks is signified here by ἀπρόσιτον from 1 Tim. 6, 16. We have no reason to depart from the interpretation of B. Luther, with which the Brentian one can be joined: who is carried with sweetness in his triumphal chariot, both in his ascension into heaven, and there through the ministry of the Gospel as if in a triumphal chariot he is carried through the world and into the hearts of the faithful, as palaces, which he desires to occupy, and wishes to dwell in them sweetly. For these are both his and our greatest delights, and the pleasures of all the faithful.

Thirdly, the description of this Lord, for whom the way is to be prepared in the desert, is found here from certain properties of his office, which teach not obscurely that the discourse is about the Messiah: namely (1.) from the protection of miserable persons, who are comprehended under the name of widows and orphans, Isa. 5, 17; Jer. 22, 3; because as pupils bereft of parents and widows bereft of husbands are necessarily destitute of protection, so the faithful, destitute of human protections, suffer various injuries. But Christ promised that he would not leave them orphans, John 14, 18; to whom, as the Father gave all judgment, so he himself is especially the judge of the afflicted and the Father of orphans, because he is the head of the whole Church as his own family, and the sole protection of those who labor with afflicted consciences.

Matt. 11, 28, 29. (2.) From the indwelling of the faithful: God, he says, is in the place of his holiness; in that seat which he chose especially among men; that is, in believers, of whom Christ speaks in John 14, 13. He is not only present to them for protection, but also dwells in them by his grace, just as God promised in Lev. 26, 12; 2 Cor. 6, 16; and Christ is said to be about to dwell in our hearts, Eph. 3, 17. (3.) From the blessing of the barren: Who makes the solitary to dwell in a house, i.e., who brings it about that those who lived childless and alone begin to have a family by procreating offspring; which, while Bellarmine adapts it to his monks, who prove themselves excellent males, what else does he do than refer that impurity to God, as one who grants that the solitary may rejoice in offspring? Cf. Psalm 113, 19; Exod. 1, 21. 1 Sam. 2, 5; which again fits Christ perfectly, both as he is one with the Father, God the author of all blessing and preservation of the human race, and as he is the cause of spiritual blessing in a peculiar way, as our Mediator, to whom it must be attributed not only that the curse is converted into a blessing and sterility into fertility, but also that the barren and solitary Gentile world rejoices in much spiritual offspring, Isa. 54, 1. For this is attributed to the Holy Redeemer in Israel, i.e., Christ, v. 5. (3.) From the release of the bound. This likewise is proper to Christ. Who brings out those who are bound in strength. He is the mighty God, Isa. 9, 6; that most mighty hero, Ps. 45, 4; who says to those who are bound, go forth, Isa. 49, 9; he procures and proclaims indulgence to the captives and opening to the blind, Isa. 61, 1; he sends forth the bound from the pit in which there is no water, Zech. 9, 11; he comes upon the strong armed man, conquers him, and distributes his spoils, Luke 11, 22. He who releases those bound by sins, and grants to others the power of releasing those spiritually bound, Matt. 18 and John 20. In the Hebrew it is בַּכּוֹשָׁרוֹת, he brings out the bound IN OPPORTUNITIES, or at an opportune time, as Bugenhagen and Brentius with Blessed Luther translate, which agrees with Isa. 49, 8, 9. (4.) From the casting out of the rebellious, concerning which the sacred psalmist says: But the rebellious dwell in a dry land, as the Hebrew text has it, from which the Vulgate differs as much as heaven from earth, and renders no sense, [saying] those who provoke, who dwell in tombs. This fits Christ as judge, who not only releases the penitent bound by sins, but also casts the rebellious and impenitent, [once] bound, where there is perpetual dryness, where there is not even a drop of refreshing water, Luke 16, 24; into the pit in which there is no water, Zech. 9, 11; which burns with sulfur and fire, Rev. 20, 1, 8; so that they may inhabit eternal dryness: being about to say to them one day: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels, Matt. 25, 14. Those who are rebellious and incredulous to the word of God dwell or remain in the arid [land], that is, they shall not be brought to the fountain of life and to the fruitful grace of Christ, even if they seem to themselves to dwell in paradise by their own righteousness, as our [author] paraphrases.

Bugenhagen the Pomeranian, called so by way of excellence. Thus also Blessed Luther rendered it, 'und lässest die Abtrünnigen bleiben in der Dürre' [and you let the apostates remain in the dryness], which the Vinarian Bible interprets concerning demons, and Osiander simultaneously concerning the impenitent. Therefore, all these predicates fit Christ peculiarly: which Brentius has summarized: In short, when Christ is preached as the Father of orphans, the judge of widows, the author of families, and the redeemer of captives, what else is preached about him than that he is the Father, Judge, author, and Redeemer of his elect and beloved Church, which is in these lands orphaned, deserted, barren, and captive?

Fourthly, the fruit of the resurrection and ascension of Christ is celebrated, namely (1.) the sending down of spiritual rain. O God, when thou wentest forth before thy people, when thou didst march through the wilderness, the earth shook, the heavens also dropped at the presence of God: even Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God, the God of Israel: thou, O God, didst send a plentiful rain, etc. These verses 8 and 9 can be understood either historically or prophetically: Historically, as they describe the manifestation of God on Mount Sinai in the promulgation of the law: in which manner those things which follow are considered to exhibit the doctrine of the Gospel κατ’ ἀντίθεσιν (by way of antithesis), to which sense the parallel passage in the Song of Deborah, Judg. 5:4-5, corresponds perfectly: Lord, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens and the clouds dropped water: The mountains flowed down from before the Lord, even that Sinai from before the Lord God of Israel. From the comparison of which passage it is also manifest that that 'Sinai' does not pertain to God, who is nowhere called the God of Sinai, but should be referred to the final clause and taken in the nominative case, which also seems to be approved by Grotius. And thus it is commonly believed that a comparison is instituted here between the past time, when the Son of God marched through the wilderness before his people, in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and promulgated the Decalogue with horrible majesty, when the earth was moved by immense thunders, and indeed the heavens also at the presence of God, and Mount Sinai was moved at the presence of the God of Israel, as Grotius explains, because in Judg. 5:4 it is written ὁ ὐρανὸς ἐταράχθη (the heaven was troubled), or as others render it, the heavens dropped (which most explain concerning the dropping of the doctrine of the law, Deut. 32:2), and the future time of the New Testament, in which the Son of God irrigated the Church with the preaching of the Gospel as with a most wholesome and fruitful rain. Theodoret, however, interprets even the former words concerning the time of the New Testament and wishes them to be spoken prophetically: When thou wast about to pass through that wilderness and uncultivated land, which had not yet received the ray of light, thou didst shake the earth and move it, and didst distil the dew of grace from heaven. He says that this happened particularly at the time of the crucifixion of Christ, when the earth shook and the rocks were rent, and when the grace of the Spirit was breathed upon the Apostles, which is similar to certain drops of dew, and therefore he thinks the same author is indicated by the words 'at the presence of God,' as if to say: He who appeared in greater majesty on Mount Sinai, this same one also shook the earth at the time of the cross and bestowed the grace of the Spirit. Thus, therefore, the Psalmist would have used words which befit the promulgation of the law, so that he might allude to the same, and by a tacit comparison of it, describe the grace of the New Testament; just as mention is also made of the shaking of heaven and earth at the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, Haggai 2:7. To this also tends the interpretation of Hilary: he says that in the past the earth was moved, the heavens dropped, and this at the presence of the God of Israel on Sinai, so that it might be known that when he performed those things which belong to the law, he also prefigured in them those things which are of the Gospel. The former interpretation, however, as it is more frequent, so it is also simpler: although both contribute to the fruit of the resurrection and ascension of Christ, whether to be illustrated by antithesis or to be explained directly, and adorned only by a tacit comparison. Now, what the Prophet sings concerning the voluntary rain (Grotius wishes it to be indicated as liberal, comparing Psalm 68:10, and we do not deny it), Orthodox interpreters with great consensus accept as referring to the time of the New Testament. Indeed, there are not lacking those among the Calvinists who understand these verses, 9 and 10, as referring to past benefits exhibited to the ancient people, an explanation which Rivetus has also recently followed, whence, while others understand the rain as manna in the desert, he himself interprets it as the rains of the earth moistened and rendered fruitful every year, or if it had been afflicted, restored again by divine generosity, and concerning the flock or people of God sustained in the land of Canaan, so that they might dwell in it, and when he was poor, bound to the harsh servitude of others in Egypt, and had nothing in the desert, having been enriched in the place of pasture, and refreshed with all necessary goods. But those things agree neither with the proper argument of the Psalm nor with the consequences, and they are too thin to satisfy the emphasis of the words.
