Most interpreters, therefore, accept them as referring to the spiritual benefits of the New Testament: just as the Prophet has used words of future time here, so that he might testify that he was prophesying about future benefits, namely, about the rain of the Gospel: You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance: BUT NOW (as it is held in the version of Blessed Luther, for the sake of explaining the antithesis, namely, in the New Testament) you send down a kindly rain of the evangelical proclamation and of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (for both are compared to rain and showers here and there in Prophetic Scripture, Isaiah 35, 55, Ezekiel 36 &c.) upon your people, which is the inheritance of the Lord, and you have confirmed what is languishing (so that believers may be refreshed in you, no differently than plants which had been languishing and are raised up again by rain: for thus the most sweet preaching of the Gospel refreshes languishing consciences and those near to despair) your animals (the sheep of your pasture or your flock) will dwell in it (in your Church) you confirm with your goodness the afflicted, O God, as the Hebrew text has it: so that they may not perish in the affliction of sin and the cross, but be sustained by the goodness of Christ, which the Gospel proposes. That this is the genuine meaning of the Psalmist's words is further confirmed by those things which are subjoined concerning those who are to be sent by the Messiah to evangelize. The Lord (he of whom there has been talk until now, namely the Messiah) will give the word to those evangelizing with great power (or will give the words of the Gospel), (he will give) Evangelists in a great army, in such number and order that they may go forth like an army sent out through the world to divulge the Gospel. Concerning the explanation of others and of Grotius, later. Now we will proceed in the text, and in confirming our opinion from the same.

(2.) The mutual agreement of the kings of the armies. Kings, he says in verse 13, love (one another) vehemently, as Osiander rendered it after Blessed Luther, they are friends among themselves, which interpretation the version of Symmachus favors, βασιλεῖς τῶν στρατιωτῶν ἀγαπήθησαν ἀγαπητοὶ ἐγένοντο. Jerome, The kings of the armies are leagued, are leagued: The Syriac translation: The kings of the virtues will be gathered, and the Arabic of the Maronites, The kings of the powerful will be gathered. Which most of our people explain concerning the Apostles with Blessed Luther, as those who are the kings of the spiritual army, concerning which army it was treated in the preceding verse, and they were about to conspire mutually, and thus with joined spirits were about to wage the wars of the Lord, Psalm 45:17, Isaiah 60:22, 2 Corinthians 10:4, whence the beauty of the house of the Church, which is like a mother of a family (for the Holy Spirit describes this as the ornament of the family Proverbs 31, divides the spoils which are brought back from the spiritual victory, and she herself can enjoy the same. For those spoils are given to the Church of Christ, the bride and spouse, and the mother of the faithful, so that not only may she herself rejoice in and enjoy them, but also distribute the same to others; which were acquired by death, the devil, and hell being conquered, and sin being taken away, such as are the remission of sins, justice, and eternal life. Bugenhagius, the beautiful wife of Christ or the Church will gain for herself spoils, that is, men snatched from the jaws of the devil and death, Luke 11, Ephesians 9. And thus those things about which the prophet sang here cohere very well: the promulgation of the Gospel, the gathering of the Church, the sending out of the teachers of the word through the world, the mutual conspiracy of the Apostles, who preside over the others, the distribution of spoils in the Church. Concerning which, because not only our own, but also the ancient doctors of the Church easily agree, and the continuity of the text no less than the harmony of the words favors the explanation, we do not see why it should be abandoned, and the words of the Psalmist be obliged to be taken concerning a bodily victory, with which neither the preceding nor the following things sufficiently agree, along with others who scarcely agree among themselves; who here does not weave a history, but is occupied in a prophecy, as the words teach, concerning future benefits, from verse 9 of this Psalm.

(3.) The beauty of the spiritual army. If you sleep among the dark places (as Grotius renders the word) you will be like the wings of a dove, which are as if covered with silver, and its feathers as if with gold (they shine). He speaks of the faithful or the spiritual army, who even in dark and gloomy places still shine with spiritual beauty; no differently than the weapons of worldly armies are accustomed to sparkle and shine with the sun's splendor, as if everything in the camps were silver and gold, like the feathers of doves when they are turned toward the sun. For the militant Church, which is engaged in camps and watches, and struggles and fights with the devil and the world, Ephesians 6:11, 12, 1 John 5:4, 5, shines with the gifts of the Holy Spirit and illustrious virtues: to which also the dove is compared in Song of Songs 2, to which Christ wishes the faithful to be similar, Matthew 10:16. Compare Matthew 5:16, Philippians 2:16. Grotius's annotation, which we append in its entirety, is correct here regarding the explanation of the word: that שפתים are cremathras, that is, hooks from which meat hangs, is apparent from Ez. 40, 43. Near them, those who lie down are accustomed to be defiled on all sides, and in such straits the Israelites had lived in Egypt. They shine, however, like doves: so beautifully distinguished and well-adorned was their army. שפתים in another sense signifies boundaries, as in Gen. 49, 14, looking to which meaning the LXX translated it as κλήρων. This is Grotius. We judge the Latin version, and what the commentators heap up concerning those two lots, unworthy of delaying us here. Let those who sleep among the middle lots in the Roman Catholic Church be concerned about such things, that is, between the Cardinalate attained and the Papacy hoped for, or between Jesuitism neglected and the red hat sought after, as Rivetus not undeservedly mocked Bellarmine and others here. Genebrardus certainly admits that the Hebrew here must be translated as, if you lie among the middle cauldrons, or tripods, or pots. Mariana explains it thus, if you sleep among the tripods, that is, in a low and sooty place. Del-Rio admits that Vatablus, following the opinion of R. Kimchi and Aben-Ezra, explains the sense correctly, even if you have lain among vessels full of soot, i.e., even if you have been oppressed by great calamity, squalid and blackened by the darkness of miseries. Sanctius admits that the Hebrew word, which the Vulgate rendered as lot, in no way allows for that sense. Sanctes Pagninus expressed the same more correctly, as did Arias Montanus in his poetic paraphrase, Joh. Bochius, Secretary of Antwerp, as well as Portæus in his French poetic paraphrase approved by the Parisian theologians, and Felix Pratensis, who interpreted it as among the tripods: that is, at the hearth: whose version was published at Venice in the year 1515 and by the Roman Pontiff was approved. Lud. de Dieu also translates it among the dross, but with a slightly different translation, which may be seen in his Animadversions on this passage.

The following verse also contributes to this, which Osiander rendered from the Hebrew thus: when the Almighty divides kings in it, then it becomes white as the snow of darkness, that is, when God distributes the Apostles and other pious ministers of the Gospel here and there in the world, then those things which had previously been dark and covered with shadows are illuminated by their ministry. And B. Luther also rendered the Hebrew thus in his German translation, just as the Weimar Bible illustrated the same sense. And Felix Pratensis, whose translation this is, when he extends the Almighty kings in it, as snow you will whiten the darkness, or it (the dove) itself will be whitened in Salmon: that is, in darkness; through those kings whom the Almighty God sends, it is ordered, and he extends over that dove, or Church, as Bugenhagius explains: with whom Gesner agrees. It is taught in this way whence the Church has its brightness: Not from itself, but from the grace of God: and the dignity and usefulness of the ministers is commended, according to Brentius. When the Almighty distributes and appoints kings in the Church, that is, Rulers, Administrators, or Preachers, then the Church shines forth from the darkness of sins and calamities. For thus Scripture is accustomed to describe those who are justified, that with the blackness of sin removed, they are whitened more than snow. The pronoun בָּהּ in it can be referred either to נַחֲלָתְךָ v. 10, inheritance, or to חַיָּתְךָ congregation v. 11. Others understand the mountain of Salmon, and wish to designate prosperity and salvation under the metaphor of whiteness, such as the brightness of snow on Mount Salmon; but the matter comes to the same thing. But if anyone wishes to say with Rivetus that בְּפָרֵשׂ must be taken in a bad sense as 'in scattering,' we deny that the force of the word implies this, inasmuch as it signifies 'he spreads out,' 'he extends,' and is used regarding the expansion of hands, the extension of clouds, and the distribution of bread, Isa. 1:15, Psalm 105:39, Exod. 40:19, Lam. 4:4. Nor do I see any reason why Rivetus should pronounce that Bellarmine most ineptly understands the Apostles by 'kings.' That is not the exposition of Bellarmine alone, but of the ancient Fathers, primarily Theodoret, Hilary, and Augustine, which not only have most interpreters in the Roman Catholic Church followed, but which is also commonly approved by our own Doctors, as being no less consonant with the words than with the context. The Apostles are also called kings and princes, v. 13 and Psalm 45:17.

(4.) The fertility of the mountain of the Church, and its perpetual habitation. The mountain of God is a fat mountain, a coagulated or high mountain is a fat mountain. The Church is like a great, most firm, most high mountain: But a most fruitful one, which bears fruit on every side: Which was also predicted of it in Isa. 2:1, Mic. 4:2, Isa. 35:1, and Psalm 49:3. For by fatness its fertility is designated. Therefore the Prophet addresses rival kingdoms by the name of mountains: Why do you leap, you (other) high mountains (envying the mountain of God, or opposing and boasting, and exalting yourselves against this mountain of God)? God desires this mountain, that He may dwell in it. And (indeed) the Lord will dwell (in it) forever. The other mountains devise various things against this mountain of God, the other kingdoms against the kingdom of the Church, for kingdoms are accustomed to be designated by mountains, and the Church is frequently expressed by this name, Psalm 15, Matt. 5, Gal. 4, Heb. 12. But in vain and with fruitless effort. Because it is God's good pleasure to dwell in it. God will dwell there forever. The kingdoms of the world will not prevail against the mountain of God, Dan. 2, nay, not even the gates of hell themselves, Matt. 16, 17. The Chaldean here designates the Messiah, when he renders: The Word of God desired to place His majesty in it. By the other mountains, Theodoret thinks the conventicles of heretics and the Jews are designated: and he institutes an opposition, that the Lord is not to dwell in this mountain for a fixed time, as among the Jews, but for eternity.

(5.) Having thus described the happiness and amplitude of the New Testament Church, which is to be attributed to both the resurrection and the ascension of Christ, because just as He rose for our justification, Rom. 4:24, so He ascended into heaven, that He might gather the Church to Himself by sending the Holy Spirit and sending forth the Apostles, and might rule in the midst of His enemies, and defend His own Church: now he describes the majesty and triumph of the Lord's ascension: The chariots of God, he says, are twice ten thousand, nay, many thousands; רבותים denotes two huge forces or myriads, אלפי שנאן thousands repeated, or more: whence Jerome rendered it according to the sense: The course of God is an innumerable multitude of those who abound. The Lord IS IN THEM (or among them and in the midst of them, so attended by chariots, by so many myriads of angels, 2 Kings 2 and 6:12. In Sinai (understand the particle of comparison AS in Sinai, when He promulgated the law among the ranks of angels and myriads, Deut. 32:2, Acts 7:38. Gal. 3:19.) in the sanctuary (which is designated by that holy thing that dwells in the Church) or as the particle of similitude is to be understood again, AS in the sanctuary, that the Lord is among those chariots, as He manifested His presence on Mount Sinai and in the Sanctuary, or that the same Lord, who was on Mount Sinai and in the sanctuary, is present in the midst of the chariots or myriads of angels, not only for the perpetual protection of the mountain of God, inasmuch as He is always present with it, attended by a heavenly ARMY (as Lord Brentius explains) but especially also because of that singular triumph which He was about to celebrate by His ascension into heaven, at which angels were present, not only appearing in visible form, Acts 1, but far more, nay, innumerable ones, whom there is no doubt accompanied Him, even if invisibly: since myriads of angels obey His nod, Matt. 26, and thousands of thousands serve Him, Dan. 7. Whence others by the Holy One understand the heavenly Sanctuary, which in that place presents itself no less magnificently, which appeared with many thousands of Angels on Sinai. Beautifully Cyprian, or whoever the author is of the Sermon on the Ascension, p. 469: He did not need angelic carriers, who, removing obstacles from the midst, would carry him in their hands, but those preceding and following applauded the victor, and singing together in jubilation modulated a new song, and the harmony of that consonance filled the heavens, with thrones and dominions preparing for the Son to be confessed next to the Father, with Cherubim and Seraphim surrounding his peaceful feet, radiating everywhere with divine brightnesses and supercelestial splendors, which neither persevering heat consumes, nor the blast of any whirlwind extinguishes, nor the interpolation of any darkness hides. The heavenly host, full of joy, celebrates the magnificence of such a triumph, and those who, when he was descending before the shepherds of Bethlehem, sang praises on high, now with more expressive efforts and more intense jubilation were paying more solemn homage to him returning to the Father; and with festive affections they venerated the man exalted above them: whom the Father had crowned with glory and honor, and placed at his right hand, with this singular privilege given to him, that at his name every knee should bow, and above every name his name should be worshipped as more excellent. Which seems to be confirmed by the fact that the Father, when he brought the firstborn into the world, said: And let all the Angels of God adore him, Heb. 1, v. 6.

There is no interpreter among Christians who doubts that in the following, namely in verse 18 and the following, the subject is the Son of God and the mystery of his exaltation, as Rivetus admits in this place, p. 387. And although Calvin refers these things to God in a general sense, Rivetus nevertheless acknowledges here that the discourse is not in a general sense about the magnificence and power of God, but about the majestic ascension of Christ into heaven, especially because of those things which are subjoined in verse 19. Therefore, having set forth Calvin's opinion, he subjoins this in the cited place: These things are elegant, as always. But the following things, which are said concerning the ascension of the Son of God, lead us to recognize in this statement a MOST CLEAR description of the majesty of Christ, ascending into heaven from the Mount of Olives, which matter the Prophet predicts, just as it happened in his own time, namely that after his resurrection, having trampled the devil and vanquished death, he was carried in the manner of victors and those who triumph in a magnificent chariot, not indeed a terrestrial and material one, but a heavenly and invisible one, namely that he sat among myriads of Angels and used their ministry, as much in the glorification of himself as in the protection of his Church; and that the magnificence of Christ ascending into heaven, so that from there he might provide for his own in all things necessary for salvation, would be no less than that of God was formerly on Mount Sinai, from where he promulgated the law given to his people by Moses. Rivetus also adds some observation concerning the word רכב and his ἐπίβασιν, which it is pleasing to note: Where someone, he says, says that the Hebrew and Chaldean word signifies the ascension of the Lord. And indeed רכב is to be carried over, to be carried upon, which verb is very often translated by the LXX as ἀναβάινειν and ἐπιβάινειν, which is to ascend, as in Isaiah 30:16, Isaiah 14:4, Genesis 24:6, and many times elsewhere. And the noun רכב is translated by ἐπίβασιν, ascension, in Psalm 103:4, Canticles 3:10. But it is better that it be taken for both, namely for vehicle and ascension, that is, for the chariot in which he was ascending, so that this action, prefigured in a certain way in Elijah, who was snatched into heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses (2 Kings 3:11), might more conform to the laws of triumphs. These are the words of Rivetus. Since he interprets these things concerning the New Testament without a type, it does not appear how the continuity of the context can be sufficiently consistent for him, unless he also understands the preceding things concerning the Church of the New Testament, just as we have explained.

Grotius easily agrees with us concerning the version, nor does he deny that by the chariots the Angelic armies are to be understood: To the words of verse 18, 'the chariots of God are ten thousand, thousands upon thousands.' From the Hebrew thus: 'The chariots of God are myriads and many thousands.' He compares the Angels to an army: but the most powerful part of the armies were chariots (Exodus 15:4, 2 Kings 2:2 and 6:17). 'THE LORD IS AMONG THEM IN SINAI IN THE HOLY PLACE.' By such an army God showed his majesty in Sinai. Thus far the annotations of Grotius; which, as far as the version is concerned, we do not disapprove. But that he wishes nothing else to be regarded than this history, and by no means believes that a prophecy is instituted here concerning the time of the New Testament, we judge that he is mistaken in that, from those things which have already been said: then indeed it is clear that what is immediately subjoined is a prophecy concerning the ascension of Christ, which we have previously demonstrated was explained by the Holy Scriptures themselves in the New Testament as referring to the same. The words themselves powerfully prove this, for they are clearer than the Sun: 'You have ascended on high.' They speak of God, and indeed of the second person of the divinity, of the Son of God, the Messiah. Who is that Lord, of whom it was treated in the preceding verses: the Lord, who was in the midst of the Angelic armies in Sinai, as the Proto-Martyr testifies in Acts 7:38, who ascended into heaven among the Angels. Which must be taken in a true and real sense concerning the ascension, since it is not permitted to abandon the proper sense at will and introduce figures. Theodoretus composes these with the preceding thus: 'He who showed himself to be seen by our ancestors on Mount Sinai, he himself will also rule these (in the New Testament). For it is not one person here and another there. For the Lord himself is rich to all who call upon him.' Thus, when the Prophetic discourse had demonstrated him who descended, and who overturned the host of enemies, it shows him ascending, and bestowing liberty upon those who were formerly captives. Which the Apostle also teaches in Ephesians 4, that the ascension shows the descension. The Prophet continues: 'You have led captivity captive.' How indeed did the Messiah, ascending on high, lead captivity captive, if not in the ascension into heaven? Where he led away his captives after the victory, which is accustomed to be noted by that phrase. Compare Deuteronomy 21:10, Numbers 21:2, Judges 5:12, 2 Chronicles 22:17, because with the enemies—the devil, sin, and death—vanquished, he led them as captives in the triumph of his ascension. Captivity, as the blessed Gesner has it, with the abstract put for the concrete, or the effect for the efficient cause, is said to be the devil, death, hell, and whatever is of the enemies, who held us bound. He led captivity captive in triumph, that is, everything, as Bugenhagius interprets, which had captivated the race of Adam, namely the devil, sin, death, hell (Hosea 13), and even the law itself exercising its tyranny in our conscience, which is the power of sin (1 Corinthians 15). But the law was a heavy captivity, and a heavy exaction and burden, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear (Acts 15, Isaiah 9, Colossians 2). Coccejus is somewhat different in his 'On the Last of Moses,' § 482: 'You have led captivity captive,' that is, you have liberated those who were bound by the chains of execration and thus given over to the enemy by the power of your satisfaction. We proceed further with the Psalmist: THOU HAST RECEIVED GIFTS IN MEN: With the ascension of the Messiah and the captivity of our enemies was joined the reception of gifts, because the Messiah had to receive gifts in men, so that he might indeed pour out the same upon them: which Peter testifies concerning Christ, Acts 2:33, that being exalted by the right hand of God he received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and poured it out. It cannot be said of God the Father that he received gifts, much less that he obtained them by ascending into heaven: but of Christ the Holy Spirit most truly predicted the same, with the event, the best interpreter of prophecies, as the primary witness, whence it is manifest that the prophecy here was made concerning the ascension of Christ, the defeat of enemies, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and his gifts. Coccejus U. S. Thou hast received gifts in men, by thy merit thou hast obtained righteousness, sanctification, life, etc. IN MEN, EVEN THE REBELLIOUS, THAT THE LORD GOD MIGHT DWELL. Which designate the conversion of the nations, who were strangers to the covenants of God, and of other rebels through the Gospel; since the gifts of the Holy Spirit are bestowed even upon them, and God is to dwell in them, as in temples of grace. Although some explain it thus: O Jehovah, God, thou shalt also subdue the otherwise rebellious and untamed, for dwelling, that is, that they themselves may dwell in thy Church. Cf. Is. 11:6.

To which is subjoined the congratulation of the triumphant faithful, on account of the benefits, and the constant celebration of the Messiah, the Savior: which the blessed Gesner thus excellently gathers into a summary from the preceding: In this description of the Church, and likewise of the ascension of Christ to the heavens, very many benefits of our Savior were comprised. First indeed, that he gave to this people the uncorrupted voice of the Gospel, of which v. 12. Then he adds a great abundance of faithful Teachers, v. same. Thirdly, he binds the minds of the teachers with a bond of concord, v. 13. Fourthly, the Church as a mother of a family faithfully distributes heavenly treasures through the Word and Sacraments: v. same. Fifthly, Christ protects the Church amidst the dangers of the raging devil and the cruelly insurgent world, v. 14. Sixthly, the Holy Spirit governs the faithful, that they may overcome the world, 1 John 5. Seventhly, God himself dwells in them, v. 17. Eighth, he surrounds the same with the firmest protections of the heavenly ministers, Psalm 34, Heb. 1, concerning which benefit, verse 18, he delivers them from the prison of eternal damnation: and finally, he abundantly provides the gifts of tongues and other mighty works. The Psalmist, therefore, pondering this in his mind, bursts into an exclamation, and concluding all the former things with these words, says: it is right that for such immense benefits of God toward us, we should daily celebrate his fatherly kindness. The Eucharistic words of the Psalmist are thus: Blessed be the Lord: daily God loads us for our salvation; as our blessed Luther renders it: He lays a burden upon us, but he also helps us. Which is also the explanation of Bugenhagen, Brentius, Osiander, Gesner, and others of our own: Because the word עמס signifies to be loaded, in which sense Rivetus confesses it is always taken in the Bible: But with some others he explains it: God, that salvation of ours, will load us, meaning that he is about to load, that is, to heap up with benefits. R. David Kimchi and Pagninus render it: God will bring salvation to us: Jerome: God of our salvation will carry us; the LXX: will guide, and the Vulgate: will make the journey prosperous. But since that word always has the meaning of loading, and that phrase of loading with benefits is unusual in the Scriptures, it is better to interpret it concerning the cross and the burden of calamity, which sense the following words also confirm: To the Lord God belong the exits from death; because he knows how to save not only from the burden of the cross, but also from death itself, and to open for us the exits of death. Cf. 1 Cor. 10, 13. The Chaldean renders it thus: God daily loads us, and helps us in carrying the burden. Which, therefore, ought to be added to the other benefits in the daily celebration of the name of God, namely, the divine deliverance from calamity and death, and indeed also the divine imposition of a burden and cross, because he imposes a burden for our salvation. Lud. de Dieu also explains it concerning the burden of affliction, rendering it thus: Blessed be the Lord daily, God our salvation imposes burdens upon us. Although he thinks this other translation is more apt: he imposes burdens upon us: God is our salvation: That is, if at any time he imposes burdens, he himself is nevertheless our salvation, which he confirms from the Reviab accent on the word לנו; and he proves from the Ethiopic language that the word עמס is referred to the burdens of calamities and evil things; where it signifies evil. But that this tends toward salvation, and that we are delivered from evil, and saved in death itself, and find exits to life, that is performed solely by Christ, who procured this benefit for us by his resurrection and ascension, and applies the fruit, and is therefore to be celebrated with perpetual blessing. For who is that הָאֵל God, who is our JESUS or OUR SALVATION? Who is God to us, God for saving, who is the Lord God, to whom belong the exits of death, if not God, of whom he has sung hitherto, Christ Jesus, our Savior and Immanuel, who has the key of death and hell, Apoc. 1, 18. And thus the Psalmist at the same time prepares an approach for himself to the opposite member, how Christ conducts himself against his enemies. For these things which we have had hitherto concern the faithful, who are partakers of the saving fruits of the Lord's resurrection and ascension.

Sixth, therefore, he commemorates the crushing or conversion of enemies, which will happen especially in the time of the New Testament. Nevertheless, God will crush the heads of his enemies, he will crush the hairy crown of those who walk in their transgressions, who persevere in them without repentance, and do not cease to persecute the Church. The Lord says: I will convert (some) from the fat ones, I will convert from the depth of the sea, (even if they seemed to be submerged in superstitions, hypocrisy, and impiety as if in the depth of the sea.) Which in those who were converted from the Priests to Christ

Acts 6, and from the princes of the world, had its fulfillment thereafter, and is still fulfilled today, if any such are converted. But because only some of the fat ones are converted, and many continue to resist, the prophet further explains the threats concerning the crushing of their heads: Therefore your foot will be dipped in the blood of your enemies, the tongue of your dogs will be dipped from the enemies (by the blood of the enemies) which they will lick. By which words the spiritual victory of Christ, by which he strikes down his enemies with the sword of the word, is described, according to Brentius. Others, however, wish the most true destruction of the Jews to be predicted, whose kingdom and priesthood might be designated by the head and the hairy crown. From whom, indeed, some fat ones and princes, and some also most deeply immersed in the depth of errors, are to be converted. Which is the explanation of blessed Luther in the marginal gloss and of others. Bugenhagen, explaining likewise concerning the Jerusalem destruction, has this to say concerning the conversion from Bashan: I will convert or I will return not only from Bashan and the lands. But also from the depth of the sea. The history of Josephus concerning the Jewish War, and of Hegesippus concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, holds that the Jews were attacked by both sea and land, and indeed, as the same histories hold, the Roman army first poured itself into the lands of the Jews in the region of Bashan, so that almost all of Galilee perished by fire and sword, and everything flowed with blood across the Jordan, until it came to the devastation of Jerusalem. Thus, he says, I will convert, or I will return to vengeance against you, O adversary people, so that your foot may be dipped in blood, so that you may be able to pass in the blood of the slain; and your enemies will cause your dogs to lick the blood of the slain. Cf. 1 Kings 21 and 22. Which harmonize with the histories and the fulfillment. Nor is there any reason why one should depart from the literal sense. And thus in a convenient order these prophecies follow the Ascension of Christ and the mission of the Holy Spirit.

Seventhly, there occurs here the assembly and communion of those who receive and celebrate Christ the King on account of his victory. 'They have seen thy goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, who is in the Sanctuary: the princes went before, joined with the singers, in the midst of the damsels playing with timbrels.' Some refer these words to the transportation of the ark of the covenant and the solemn applause, but even if it were alluded to in the highest degree, the context persuades us that these things must be accepted as referring to the entries of the Messiah prefigured by it, whom David addresses, whom he acknowledges as his God and Lord in Psalm 110:1, whom he worships as his King, who was in the Sanctuary symbolically, and is in the true Sanctuary with both a heavenly and a spiritual, or glorious and gracious presence, by which he enters through the Gospel and manifests himself. To him the princes, the singers, and the damsels playing with timbrels applaud. Most understand this simply as referring to men and women singing of the victory of Christ, just as virgins and consecrated women were accustomed to adorn a triumph with song and timbrels, as in Exodus 15, verse 5, and 1 Samuel 18, verse 6; others wish for the Apostles to be designated by the princes as leaders of the people of God under Christ the head. Mr. Gesner, following Mr. Brentius, rendered and explained it thus: 'The singers (the prophets, who were also sent to the Jews) went before, afterwards the harpists (the Evangelists and Apostles, called harpists because of the most beautiful harmony), in the midst of the virgins beating timbrels (the as yet tender churches, which the Apostles planted here and there throughout Samaria, Asia, and other regions).' And so he judges that it is hinted that the Jews have nothing with which to excuse themselves, since they saw the entry of Christ in the days of his flesh, heard his sermons, were spectators of his divine miracles, and had

Prophets formerly sent to them and Apostles. And thus also Osiander interpreted it from the Hebrew, they precede (in that procession) the Singers, the instrumental Musicians occupy the last place, in the middle are the damsels playing on timbrels. Because such processions existed among the Israelites. So also Jerome: The singers went before those who played behind, in the midst of the damsels. For it is held in the Hebrew שׁרים, which signifies Singers, not שׂרים which denotes princes, as the LXX and the Vulgate rendered. Which explanation of the blessed Gesner agrees very well with the preceding: if, however, it should perchance seem too subtle, everything will also hang together conveniently if it is only indicated in general as an assembly of faithful men and women singing of Christ's victories. There is now added the subject matter and summary of the Song, or as others prefer, the excitation of the Holy Spirit to these hymns: In the churches bless God the Lord: praise Christ, and that from the fountains of Israel, that is, with praises taken not from the human brain, but from the word of God. That phrase about the fountains of Israel indicating the lineage of the Hebrews, that they were born from Israel, which Rivetus desires, agrees neither with the manner of speaking of Scripture, nor with the text: For not only are the Hebrews excited to praises, but others also: Nor does Theodoret observe it beside the point: that it is said IN THE CHURCHES, so that the cessation of the Old Testament, where there was only one temple, might be hinted at, and the multitude of churches might be proclaimed: in which from the fountains of Israel, that is, from the books of the Prophets, we offer sweet song to God. The blessed Luther understands these objectively for the fountains of Israel, or because of the fountain, in the marginal gloss, 'for the fountain, that is, for the kingdom of Christ, which has begun, wells up and grows.' But the Psalmist seems to proceed in describing that procession of triumph: There (in that procession, or in the communion of the Church is) Benjamin the youth in an ecstasy of mind: The princes of Judah with their assembly: The princes (from the tribe) of Zebulun, and the princes (from the tribe) of Naphtali: Which some take concerning those tribes in the Old Testament, so that by the mention of the Benjaminites, who were neighbors to David, and the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali, which were most remote, the whole people might be indicated by Synecdoche. Junius interprets it thus, as if to say, let all the highest and lowest, those near and those far off be present, so that they may here perform their duty to God: But because from the connection of the text it is now manifest that everything looks to the times of the New Testament, be it that an allusion is made to those tribes, such as they once were, in a certain respect; according to the intention of the Holy Spirit, the things of the New Testament ought to be designated: which the Greeks and Latins, ancient and modern, if you except the Calvinists, who generally desire to be singular, have observed with excellent consensus. Theodoret connects and explains these things to the preceding thus: Since, however, besides the Prophetic fountains, He has also bestowed the Apostolic ones upon us; he deservedly adds: There is Benjamin the youth in an ecstasy of mind. But Aquila said, There is little Benjamin ruling them: According to Theodotion, however, Their preceptor. Furthermore, Benjamin the Youth is the blessed Paul, who was born from the tribe of Benjamin: Youth, as one called and summoned after all others. Besides, the history of the Acts calls him a youth. He rules the churches, and instructs the nations, and leads those who are willing to salvation. He was, however, in an ecstasy of mind, when he had learned that He was in the heavens whom he himself had persecuted, and whom he thought dead. But after not only the blessed Paul, but also the rest of the chorus of Apostles teaches the believers divine things; the prophetic discourse deservedly made mention of these also: The princes of Judah their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Naphtali. For from these tribes the other Apostles drew their origin, and those who were called the Brothers of the Lord drew their lineage from the tribe of Judah. But Peter,

and Andrew and James, and John, and Philip were from the town of Bethsaida. Matthew and James are said to dwell in Capernaum. Simon the Zealot is named the Canaanite, but all these places are of Galilee, Zebulun and Naphtali had their lot there, and there are two witnesses of this matter: One indeed the Prophet, the other the Evangelist, the latter predicting, the former bearing witness. He says thus, The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali and the rest inhabiting the maritime region beyond the Jordan of Galilee of the Gentiles, the people who sat in darkness, saw a great light, etc. Thus far Theodoret. So also Hilary, who uses that argument, that those tribes alone are expressed here, not without cause. Only that, he says, under the signification of Prophecy, has been mentioned from that universality of princes, which was to be fulfilled for the confirmation of the Gospel, both by the effects of things and by the election of the Apostles. It is certainly not without mystery that those alone are commemorated here. And that everything agrees so well, everyone sees. For the event is the best interpreter of prophecies. And since other more minute things of the New Testament have been predicted in the Old, what wonder if the Holy Spirit has predicted these singular things about the Apostles here also. For in this, the Psalms of David excel above other Prophetic books, that they predict most singular things about the matters of the New Testament.

Eighthly, the Psalmist subjoins a prayer, which likewise looks to the kingdom of the Messiah, and is conceived for the same. Thy God (God the Father, who is thy God) has commanded thy strength or power (O Messiah, John 20:20), that is, He has granted thee power: for the word of commanding when attributed to God denotes efficiency, Deut. 28:8, Psalm 42:9, Psalm 44:5, Psalm 133:3. By the power of the Messiah, the blessed Luther understands his kingdom, not badly, which God erected by commanding. Strengthen, O God (Holy Spirit, for this is the proper work of sanctification) what Thou hast wrought in us: from Thy temple over Jerusalem (Jerome: which is in Jerusalem) kings shall offer gifts to Thee. To Him, therefore, God granted power, to whom kings ought to bring gifts: to whom, as is predicted afterwards in verse 32, ambassadors were to come from Egypt for the sake of worship: who is no other than the Messiah. For that temple in Jerusalem is His own, Mal. 3, 1. to Him gifts in the New Testament were to be sent, to Him the nations were to convert themselves. Moreover, those gifts are said to be offered from the temple in Jerusalem (or because of Jerusalem, as others explain, that is, because of the Church, and the promises made to it); because there the Church began, which offered itself and its own to God, Acts 2 and 4, and from there it was propagated to the nations, and to kings themselves, and to the people in the New Testament, Luke 24, Acts 13. He prays, therefore, that God may confirm the kingdom of the Messiah, so that kings themselves may also offer gifts, which everyone sees pertain to the N. T. But on the contrary he asks: rebuke the wild beasts of the reed, the congregation of the Jews (the robust) among the cows of the peoples, so that they may exclude those who are tried with silver: (as the Vulgate renders it with the LXX) Scatter the nations, that desire wars. Most interpreters acknowledge that in these words there is a description of the enemies of the Church from their ferocity, pride, and hostile spirit, and a prayer against their attack. By the wild beast or company (as others render it from a comparison with 2 Sam. 23, 13, Ps. 68, 30) of the reed, Bellarmine understands wild beasts lurking among the reeds, and through these demons with Hilary and our Bugenhagen, others a barbarian army with Genebrard, others a reed-bearing battle line, or one armed and equipped with spears and lances, or the fierce enemies of the Church with Jansenius: Gesner understands by the wild beast of the reed hypocrites, by the bulls heretics and Jews, by the calves Epicureans, and by the peoples who stir up wars, he means to designate the tyrants and persecutors of the Church. Brentius understands all those as the Jews. Theodor. wishes to signify the Jews by the bulls, and the Gentiles by the calves of the peoples. For B. Luther, the wild reeds are false teachers: the congregation of bulls is the Antichristian assembly of tyrants. It seems difficult to distinguish these; therefore let us say in general that the enemies of the Church are described, and their ferocity, power, pride, and other things which befit those wild beasts are designated: whoever those enemies may be, Jews or Gentiles, heretics, hypocrites, tyrants, openly or secretly lying in wait for the Church. Which the Vulgate with the LXX renders: that they may exclude those who are tried with silver: Jerome, who kick against the silver wheels, others interpret as trampling on pieces of silver: (or glorying in them) or also, those who so abound in them that they can trample them with their feet, or who are proud because of some pieces of silver, so that they trample everything underfoot: Others, who trample because of the greed for silver: who venerate gold and silver in place of a deity, as Gesner explains. B. Luth. explains, Those who trample for the sake of money: as stallions (so the marginal gloss has it) trample the water and make it muddy, so that it is not fit to drink, so do all the sectarians trample and make the Scripture muddy. Conf. Ezek. 34, 18. 19. 2. Pet. 2, 13. 14. Grotius interpreted these things thus: REBUKE THE WILD BEASTS OF THE REED, that is, the archer-hosts, by whom he thinks the Ammonites are understood 2. Sam. 11, 20. But there is no reason why the Ammonites should be understood particularly or alone: The discourse is about the enemies of the Church, especially under the New Testament. CONGREGATION OF BULLS &c.) You might more correctly, he says, translate: The assembly of bulls, who glory in the calves of the peoples, that they may come with fragments of silver. Scatter the nations, who desire wars. By the bulls are to be understood the leaders, by the calves the soldiers who follow them, as in Psalm 22, 13. that they may come with fragments of silver, namely to redeem peace. But where is that THAT THEY MAY COME, and to redeem peace, found in the text? If the word מתרפס is rendered, those who make themselves walk (with fragments of silver) their pride, because they exalt themselves with silver, in their gait, will be designated: or if you prefer to render it at all, that they may come, or creep with fragments of silver, an offering will be hinted at, namely that they themselves also may offer their gifts, and consecrate the same to the Messiah.

Hence therefore in the ninth prophecy the Psalmist bursts forth concerning the calling and conversion of the Gentiles, verse 34. ambassadors shall come from Egypt: Ethiopia shall hasten her hands to God. Which Bugenhagius explains: He shall believe first, before the hands follow. Felix Ebræa interprets it thus; Ethiopia shall make her hands run to God. And so also Grotius: Her hands, that is, she shall hasten to bring gifts to God. Others more significantly, she shall stretch out her hands to God. The Egyptians are named particularly, as being most superstitious, and the Ethiopians, more famous for barbarity and rapine and cruelty, so that from this an omen might be made concerning the conversion of the rest of the less superstitious and barbarous. And this prediction was confirmed by the event, when the infant Christ fled into Egypt, Matt. 2. and the Egyptians were present at the Pentecostal assembly, Acts 2. and most illustrious Churches flourished there, especially at Alexandria, as Eusebius testifies, book 2, chap. 16, 17. book 8, c. 8. and the Prefect of the Queen carried the Gospel into Ethiopia, Acts 8. From which it is most manifest that the prophecy is instituted here concerning none other than the Messiah, nor concerning other matters than those which pertain to the N. T. For the discourse here is about Him, to whom Kings ought to offer gifts from the temple in Jerusalem, whose that temple is, to whom ambassadors from Egypt were to show worship, to whom the Ethiopians were to stretch out a hand, to whom the Gentiles were to be converted. That, however, is true of no earthly King, but solely of the Messiah, our Christ. Which Rivetus admits, therefore in his commentary on this place, p. 421. Both, he says, both the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, are known from sacred history to have brought aid to the people of Israel after the times of David: for we read that the Egyptians were allies of Hezekiah, chap. 36. of the Prophecies of Isaiah, and chap. 37 of the same book it is reported that Theraca, King of the Ethiopians, led an army against the King of the Assyrians, at which time Rabshakeh, in the name of Sennacherib, was soliciting Hezekiah to surrender. But these things do not pertain to the matter which is predicted here, whatever may have seemed so to some others; for neither can bringing aid, or fighting with the same enemies, be explained by this locution of stretching out one's hand to God. More correctly, therefore, others understand it of the faith of Christ and his empire accepted by the Gentiles, who also think that those nations were the first to hasten to receive the preaching of the Gospel, and they prove it concerning the Ethiopians from the history of the Eunuch of Queen Candace, who is handed down to have reigned on the island of Meroe, which the Nile creates, whose Eunuch's conversion is read in Acts, chap. 8. But what the increases of the Christian Church were in Egypt and especially in Alexandria, Eusebius reports, book 2, chap. 16, where he narrates that Mark the Evangelist preached there with great success. But that the rest were understood under those two peoples, has already been said by us. This is therefore in this place AN ILLUSTRIOUS PROPHECY concerning the calling of the Gentiles &c. Furthermore, if these things are to be explained concerning the conversion of the Gentiles to the Messiah, it is necessary that we understand the former things also concerning the Messiah. Because He, whose temple is in Jerusalem, and to whom Kings ought to offer gifts, is that same Lord, of whom it is said in the preceding: they have seen thy goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, who is in the Sanctuary: who as God and Lord has been proclaimed in the preceding. Which things certainly, because He himself acknowledges God the Father as his God, v. 29, cannot be accepted of any other than the Messiah.

Finally, to these, a tenth is added, an Epilogue, προκέλευσμα, inciting all nations to the praise of God, and exhibiting an ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν of the benefits of God, v. 33 seqq. Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth, sing psalms to the Lord: Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven to the east. Let us not believe that the Gospel will reach only Egypt and Ethiopia; all the kingdoms of the earth, that is, Kings and subjects in them, are incited to the praise of the Lord: and at the same time it is predicted that it will come to pass that the remaining kingdoms also will arrive at the acknowledgment of the Messiah, and celebrate him with praises. The causes of the hymns are (1.) the ascension of Christ into heaven; concerning which he had prophesied before. For the Lord Christ, as the explanation of Theodoret has it, not only ascended into this heaven which is seen, but also above that which is above this, and sits at the right hand of the Majesty in the high upper room, sending down the rays of his rising to all men. Our Gesner renders it 'To him who rides in the heavens of heavens from of old': Christ did not ascend into heaven in such a way that he might be enclosed by heaven, but he sits upon heaven and rides upon it: and he is superior not only to one heaven, but to all, having been elevated to the throne of the paternal right hand, Heb. 1, Eph. 1 and 4. The little word קדם is rendered by the LXX as κατ᾽ ἀνατολὰς, by the Vulgate as 'to the east': which others have referred to God the Father, because he ascended to him who is the rising and the beginning of all things, which is also the explanation of Bugenhagen; others wish to refer it to the Mount of Olives, from which he ascended

Christ into heaven, because he looks from the east to Jerusalem: others refer it to the east of heaven: Some render it QUONDAM [formerly], so that it may be an epithet of the heavens, which were formerly, that is, which were made long ago, and remain the same forever: as Deut. 33, 16. 27. which exposition pleases Rivet. It can also be an epithet of Christ ascending into heaven: because Christ is the ORIENS [Dayspring/Rising] from on high Luke 1. and αρχη εδων [the beginning of the ways] of the Lord is said in Proverbs 8, 22. where the same word occurs in the Hebrew: so that it may be implied that the same one who was with God from eternity and as the rising from on high visited us, has ascended again to God into the heavens of heavens. (2.) The propagation of the Word of God: Behold, he will give in his voice a voice of strength: which Calvin and his followers understand of the voice of thunder. But our people more correctly [understand it] of the voice or thunder of the Gospel, the propagation of which is celebrated here: for this voice is most strong, inasmuch as by it the kingdom of Satan is destroyed, the hearts of men are converted, and the minds of enemies also are softened. The voice from heaven, in which the Holy Spirit was given as the power of GOD Acts 2. Theodoret understands, which was done after the ascension into heaven; and Rivet, page 425, acknowledges that all the ancients and most of the recent ones refer this to the ascension of Christ and the efficacy of the preaching of the word, and he permits that in the first sense, which he wishes to be the Majesty of God in the heavens, and in the voice of thunder, while remaining, the words may be accommodated to Christian mysteries, that Christ after he ascended on high, sits at the fountain of light, whence all light arises, and thence gives to his voice a voice of strength, that is, causes the Gospel to penetrate into the hearts of men, etc. And this is the second. (3.) The magnificence exhibited to Israel and the Church of God: Ascribe strength to God, ascribe strength to Christ. B. Luther in his Scholium: Give GOD the power, that is, the kingdom: let him be LORD: Matt. 6. v. 13. acknowledge that all things in the kingdom of grace are from him, and that glory is owed to him: Over Israel (the faithful, who are the Israel of God Galat. 6. v. 16.) is his magnificence: which he made attested to the Church by sending his Son and pouring out the Holy Spirit, and never ceases to attest. For he magnificently adorns it with his gifts. And his strength is in the clouds, which likewise the pious ancients understand spiritually of those who fly like clouds Isaiah 6, from whom God rains the word of his Gospel, so that the earth everywhere may resound with the fruit of salvation, in whom he thunders and works wonders, so that the world itself is stunned with admiration, as our Bugenhagius explains with them. Although indeed some interpret it literally of the clouds in the air, they do not deny that a comparison is instituted with the wondrous works of the power of God in the Church, which are proclaimed in the following verse: as if to say, the strength of God is indeed conspicuous in the clouds; but God, who is wondrous in his Sanctuary, demonstrates his strength more in Israel his people, to whom he gives vigor and strength. Therefore is proclaimed (4.) The wondrous government and protection of the Church. Wondrous or tremendous and terrible is God from his Sanctuaries: He was not only wondrous from his sanctuary in the Old Testament, but is more wondrous from the Sanctuaries prefigured by it, namely from heaven and from the Church, on account of the wondrous and tremendous preservation, government, and defense of his Church; which he himself also instructs and arms with his power Ephes. 6. The God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people: so that they may be able to resist the enemies, both bodily and spiritual, in the power of God, and to overcome them, and to triumph in this strengthening of God forever: whence he concludes with a succinct doxology: Blessed be the Lord forever!

From this review of the Psalm it is manifest that it is best and most conveniently understood of the Messiah and the benefits of the New Testament, if you look at the whole continuity of the context. And that those who make the immediate sense of the same, either in some or in all its parts, to be things of the Old Testament, rely on no foundation; indeed, this mixture and confusion does not suit the text, which is woven throughout in the same tenor concerning the benefits of the New Testament: as has been shown thus far. If verse 18 is in the middle about the ascension of Christ, and again almost around the Epilogue verse 30 about the gifts to be offered to Christ by Kings and about his temple: then indeed in the Epilogue verses 34 and 36 again about the Messiah; but the rest in the Psalm are explained otherwise, what then will be the continuity of the text, what coherence? And how will it be permissible to invent diverse subjects, when the whole hymn is about the same Lord? Whence the Fathers with excellent consensus accepted the whole Psalm concerning the Messiah and his benefits. Augustine in this place. Let God arise and let his enemies be scattered. It has already been done, Christ has arisen, who is blessed above all forever: and his enemies have been dispersed through all nations, the Jews, in that very place where they exercised their enmities, were defeated, and from there dispersed through all [lands]. Rivet indeed thinks that Hilary and Jerome explain the Psalm concerning the mysteries of both Testaments, historically concerning the former, but prophetically concerning the latter: But that appears neither from Hilary's Commentary, nor from that which is attributed to Jerome. Hilary certainly makes Christ the subject of the Psalm, and does not wish the Sacraments of the law to be used otherwise than for the sake of comparison, so that through allegory and similitude they may illustrate the things of the New Testament. which his own explanation teaches, and indeed also the argument of the Psalm prefixed by him in the explanation of the title: Not a song of a Psalm, he says, but a Psalm of a song: so that in it the declaration of knowledge and Prophetic science might be taught. But it is itself the whole context of the sacraments of the law and the Gospels, and is filled with a great interpretation of allegorical sayings both from the past and from the future, which both contains the doctrine of the law given in itself, and brings the notion of the flesh assumed by the Lord, and reproaches the impiety of the former people, and announces the faith of our future knowledge, and embraces the Lord's ascension above the heavens, and comprehends the glory of his future kingdom. Thus also is the Hieronymian explanation: He understands the entrance, Let God arise, specifically of the Lord himself, so that he may arise from the dead and scatter his enemies, that is, The devil and his army, that they may exult in the sight of the righteous God, not only concerning vengeance, but also concerning eternal blessedness. To verse 7. He wishes to designate one author of the New and Old Testament, who went before the Israelite people in the desert, and in the Gospels visited the deserts of the Gentiles: To verse 17. He who formerly descending on Sinai distributed the law to the people, him now in the Holy, that is, in the assumed man, to have ascended the heights of the heavens etc. And so in others. Rivetus here gave credence to Bellarmine: if he had consulted Hilary and Jerome, he would have pronounced differently concerning their opinion. Furthermore, most recent interpreters agree with the fathers, if you except the Photinians and some Calvinists. However, we see no reason why we should depart with them, or with Grotius, from the common interpretation of the ancients and the moderns. We treated some things from this Prophetic Psalm in a Paschal Program in the year 1653, as also in another Paschal Program proposed here in the same place in the name of the Academic Rector in the year 1667, both of which we have thought fit to append here for the illustration of the same. The former reads thus:

Let GOD arise, and let his enemies be scattered: and let them that hate him flee from before his face: as smoke vanisheth, let them vanish; as wax melteth before the face of the fire, so let the sinners perish from before the face of GOD. And let the just feast and exult in the sight of GOD and be delighted in gladness. Sing to GOD, say a Psalm to his name: make a way for him, who ascendeth over the west, the Lord is his name. Thus did that excellent Psalmist of Israel stir up the Messiah, the man confirmed by the Christ of GOD of Jacob, thus he terrified and put to flight the enemies, thus he provoked the faithful to paschal joys! Let God arise and let his enemies be scattered: it is already done, exclaims St. Augustine: Christ has arisen, who is God blessed above all things for ever; and his enemies, the Jews, have been scattered through all nations, defeated in that very place where they exercised their enmities, and thence scattered through all things. The Lord has risen from the dead, as Jerome interprets; and his enemies are scattered, that is, the Devil and his armies. For the Prophet, providing, prays that upon his arising the Diabolical dominations may flee away. That was a solemn formula of praying, when the ark of the covenant was being lifted up, by which Moses addressed not the ark, but the Lord, who was peculiarly present beside it: Arise O Lord and let thy enemies be scattered, and let them that hate thee flee from before thy face, Num. 10. verse 35. As that was a type of Christ our Lord, so David applies it to the antitype through the Spirit of Christ, which was in him, and therefore he desires that the true ark of the covenant may arise, by which the enemies may be scattered. When that typical ark was in Ashdod in the midst of the enemies, the idol Dagon, truncated of head and hands, was cast down, and the Philistine enemies were struck with a most grievous plague, so that, touched by the hand of the Divinity, they were forced even against their will to let the ark go from their power 2. Samuel 5. The Devil and hell were by no means able to detain the true ark in their power; for it was impossible for Christ to be held by hell, Acts 2. v. 24. who, having become destruction to the infernal Dagon, crushed the head of the ancient serpent, and having overcome his enemies, broke through. Therefore, upon his arising, the enemies were scattered, but the just feast and exult in his sight. Death is swallowed up in victory, where is thy victory, O hell? where is thy sting, O death? Truly it has passed, perished, vanished utterly, and so you have labored here in vain. But the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to GOD, who has given us the victory, through our Lord Jesus Christ. These things he prays, as Gregory Nazianzen says in his oration. in the Passover, the feast of feasts and the celebration of celebrations, is so much superior to all others, not only human and fixed to the ground, but even to those which are of Christ himself and are celebrated on his account, as the Sun excels the stars. For Christ, raised from the dead, according to Athanasius in his homily on the Saturday in Albis, has rendered the whole life of mortals one feast. For by transferring the conversation of those dwelling on earth to heaven, he supplied abundant matter for celebrating feasts. This is the day which the Lord has made, higher than all, brighter than all, as St. Aug. judges in Sermon CLXIII. This day of the resurrection of Christ is life to the dead, pardon to sinners, glory to the saints; since by the prayer of virtue it lifts from the depths, raises from earthly things, places in the heights, perfects the just, strengthens the doubtful, condemns the incredulous. Let us therefore rejoice and exult in this day, in which the Lord, rising again, brought peace, brought salvation. But let us weigh a little more diligently the aforementioned Davidic oracle. The evidence of the text and the most lucid explanation of the Holy Spirit, Eph. 4. v. 8. seqq., does not permit one to doubt that this sixty-eighth Psalm is a triumphal song dedicated to the honor of Christ, powerfully rising from the dead and gloriously ascending into heaven. Wherefore he says, ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men. Now that he ascended, what is it, but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth: He who descended is the same, and who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. Here one must not listen to Antonius Agellius, who explains the Psalm with the Hebrews concerning the victory against the Assyrians and King Sennacherib, or more truly, corrupts it. The utterly Jewish distortion of Hugo Grotius is not to be borne, who makes the subject of this song the exit of the Jewish people from Egypt. The gloss of Calvin and his followers is not to be admitted, who refer this Ode according to the letter to the victories of David over his enemies, and especially the Philistines, Moabites, Syrians, Jews, and Ammonites 1. Par. 18. or with Beza, Musculus, Junius in the parallels, and Pareus against D. Hunnius, to the panegyrical deduction of the ark from the house of Obededom into the citadel of Zion described in 2. Sam. 6.: or to both with Andreas Rivetus. And indeed we do not wonder at the Jews because of the veil not being revealed; but who would not detest Hugo Grotius, perverting the words of the Holy Spirit with more than Jewish audacity? Who, to verse 22, The Lord will give the word to those evangelizing with great virtue, attaches this meaning; The Lord was giving the word, (that is, abundant matter for speaking) namely, that a great army of women preaching (victories) might say, i.e., those things which follow. Grotius is so blinded by Jewish commentaries that he cannot discern what are most clearly predicted as future from those which had already passed; and he drags the army of those evangelizing under the New Testament, concerning whom the Prophet prophesies, to the army of women singing at the exit from Egypt. Yet soon, constrained by the evidence of the prediction of a future thing, he interprets what is held in verse 32, Ambassadors will come from Egypt, Ethiopia shall prevent his hands to God, not of past history, but of future prosperity, truly with a Jewish Spirit: that men of the greatest dignity would come from Egypt into Judea, namely, when they were bringing the pact made with Solomon; Likewise: Ethiopia shall hasten to bring gifts to God, as the Queen of Sheba did. Where, however, it is permitted to discover the force of truth in Grotius himself. For he could not deny that these things were fulfilled MORE EVIDENTLY when the Egyptians and Ethiopians offered the oblations which Christians are accustomed to in the Church. But to what verse, finally, will he be able to affix a gloss not unlike the Jewish corruption to the words, 'You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts for men'? It was not unknown how greatly they torture themselves here, with some dragging those things which are most openly said of Jehovah to Moses ascending Mount Sinai, others to David raised on high through victories, others to the Ark of the Covenant being elevated: with others, along with R. Kimchi, explaining them indeed of God, but so that the ascent into heaven is nothing other than the withdrawal of Divine aid, which Grotius rightly noted agrees neither with the phrase, nor the scope or context, since the Psalmist sings of triumphs and victories, not dirges and complaints, and therefore he devised another but no less absurd opinion: 'You ascended on high,' from Sinai into heaven, as Kings are accustomed to ascend a tribunal to exercise judgment, Matt. 27 v. 19. 'You led captivity captive': you condemned many peoples to captivity, among them the Midianites, Num. 31. 'You received gifts in men,' that is, for the sake of men you received gifts for the use of the Priests and Levites. Could the infernal torturer himself have tortured scripture more? And from whom did God the Father, whom Grotius understands, receive gifts for the use of the Priesthood? Or did that Lord

Perhaps an angel is created, concerning which see verse 18. Grotius: The Lord among them in Sinai in the Holy: Through such an army GOD showed His majesty in Sinai. There was one angel representing GOD, many attendants were present with him. Thus, from the Lord, whom myriads and many thousands of chariots surround, he makes the Angel a minister representing the Lord, to whom many attendants are present, and again, forgetful of himself, he substitutes the Lord Himself, to whom without doubt he attributes that, you have led captivity captive. Furthermore, from the ascension of Christ into heaven, he fashions the ascension of a created angel from Mount Sinai, to the judgment of the glorious condemnation of the Midianites from the triumph of Christ ascending. Finally, from the Apostles and Pastors of the Church of the N.T., he forms the Priests and Levites of the Old Testament. Is this not to treat the scriptures piously? But does Grotius say that this sense is historical, but that the Apostle refers it mystically at least to Christ? Thus, through the Lord GOD, a certain created angel will be understood in the literal sense, but what was said historically about that created angel ascending from Mount Sinai and receiving gifts, will be referred mystically by the Apostle to Christ ascending into heaven and giving gifts to men? Surely it was not enough for the Scriptures to be twisted by Grotius, the Holy Spirit Himself had to be imagined to be twisting them as well. Which indeed Calvin did not disguise, being likewise struck with a Jewish blindness, drawing the Prophetic hymn to the victories of David: therefore he accused Paul of DEFLECTING this passage MORE SUBTLY to Christ in Eph. 4, in his commentary on this Psalm, nay, he blasphemed that Paul had DISTORTED this testimony somewhat from its genuine sense, so that he might accommodate it to his purpose, in his commentary. in Ephes. 4. whom, clearly Judaizing, and solidly convicted of that crime, Paraeus defends in vain, besmirching himself with the same, if not filthier, mud, while he interprets not only that 'let Jehovah arise and let his enemies be scattered' concerning the ark of the covenant, but also the rest, 'you ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts in men,' with a most absurd invention in his 'Calvinus Orthodoxus' page 241. To whom, moreover, B. Hunnius so stopped the mouth in his 'Anti-Pareus' that he was rendered completely speechless. And yet Andr. Rivetus did not fear to make his own Jewish glosses, and petulantly to attack B. Gesner in his commentary on the decade of the Psalms, p. 388. Gesner, formerly a Wittenberg Theologaster (behold theological modesty), who dared to exclaim petulantly: Who then doubts that Calvin Judaizes, and that he obliquely carps at the Apostle Paul himself, and even the Holy Spirit? Rivetus adds: May the Lord rebuke you, O Satan, so that, for instance, you may understand the spirit of gentleness: but what color of calumny does he cast over it? Does he not Judaize who makes David a figure of Christ? What? Does he not Judaize, who, when those things which were predicted concerning Christ according to the letter are interpreted by the Apostle, leaves this aside and, following a Jewish gloss, explains them according to the letter concerning David, not concerning Christ? But since the small exception of Rivetus was solidly prostrated by the response then given to Paraeus, come, let us recall that at least to the memory of obstinate men. Thus indeed B. Hunnius in his 'Anti-Pareus' p. 228. Nay, how will the argument of Paul deduced from this to assert the ascension of the Messiah into the heavens, and his exaltation to the right hand of GOD, hold up: if Paul only ALLUDES to those words of the Prophet speaking METAPHORICALLY, and deflects his testimony more subtly from its genuine sense, nay, DISTORTS it? Let heaven and earth judge here whether this wicked corruption can by any means subsist? Whatever Paraeus may bring forward from the conflict of Calvin against the Jews subjoined there: nevertheless, he who is not senseless and mad understands that the foundations of every solid response are not only shaken by those emblems of the commentator, but lie clearly demolished and overturned. And page 250. I see indeed that Calvin also remembers the type. I see that the same pleases Paraeus. But unless they prove their type, they will labor in vain. Let that distinguished defender of Calvin explain to us, who is that person who bears the type of the Savior in the words ('you ascended on high, you led captivity captive')? And to whom is that address directed? To God rising on high with His glorious victories, or indeed to David, through whose hands those victories, God favoring, happened to the people? If you say that David is addressed by this address as a type and that it is acclaimed to him: 'you ascended on high' etc., what will be falser than that assertion? What more absurd and inept? For did David thus ascend on high? Did he himself, having led captivity captive, receive gifts in men? But if, omitting David, you contend that Jehovah is addressed by that apostrophe, who is Jehovah as a type of Christ, what again will be more inconvenient? For types are accustomed to be less noble than the thing prefigured, which cannot be referred to Jehovah without palpable impiety. But the matter is well, his champion Rivetus deserts both Calvin and his Paraeus and confesses on page 387 that it is NECESSARY that the words of David be explained OUTSIDE of every notion of a type, directly concerning GOD then manifesting in the flesh, now manifested, to whom Paul also applied the verse 19. And after he had raved enough against the Pseudo-Lutherans and B. Gesner, because they said that Calvin Judaizes, he himself tears his Calvin to pieces regarding the Jews, whose glosses he followed, p. 395, while he affirms that they only obtrude their most alien glosses, referring what is said here to David, against the manifest words of the Prophet, who speaks clearly of Jehovah, when in the whole Psalm neither Moses is addressed, nor David, but GOD Himself. Trypho the Jew certainly, when the ascension of Christ into the heavens was demonstrated from this prophecy by Justin, acknowledged that it was abundantly demonstrated from it, he only sought that it be demonstrated that the same Christ, whom Justin preached as both crucified and returned into the heavens, is the Christ of GOD: see 'Dialog. cum Tryph.' in the works of Justin p. 200. And although Enjedinus, from among the enemies of the Deity of Christ, turns the glosses of Calvin, Bucer, and Musculus to his own advantage, in order to crush the most brilliant testimony of the Deity of Christ in the depraved passage on page 300, he was nevertheless forced to admit, as were Franciscus Davidis and Blandrata in the Alban disputation, and likewise Socinus himself in Antivvijeko page 75, that this prophecy must be accepted concerning Christ, and that He is pointed out here as GOD by the name Elohim. But it is not permitted to add more. We only subjoin the explanation of our excellent Pomeranus, which is in complete agreement with our own: What Moses had begun in figure, David pursues and desires, that the virtue and power of God may go before us, that we may be able to break through the wedges of the enemy, which virtue is Christ the Lord, now made our forerunner and leader. Therefore, that the ark of the New Testament and the mercy seat, in which dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily, not in a shadowing way, as formerly in that ark and mercy seat, that it may be lifted up, I say, that is, that He may rise from the dead, that He may come to our aid, and not always dissemble by permitting the impious Jews, and now the enemies of the Gospel, to do what they want, we provoke God, saying, Let God arise, etc. Let the disciples of Christ rejoice: let those glorious persecutors of the Gospel of Christ, who cannot endure the face of Christ, which is His presence in His preached word and the admirable operation of His Spirit in the saints, melt like wax, perish like smoke. But you, righteous by the righteousness of faith, sing to GOD, preach everywhere the magnificence of Him who rose again, make a way for Him to the hearts of men by the preaching of the law and repentance, that they may recognize themselves as sinners and desire the Savior, and let them hear the Gospel. Finally, let that man descending from the clouds, most sublime, whose face is as the face of an angel, and whose garment is as the splendor of lightning, whom Gregory the Theologian introduced crying out with a loud voice, acclaim us. Today the salvation of the world, as much visible as invisible. Christ is risen from the dead: rise together: Christ is returned to himself: Christ is out of the sepulcher, be released from the bonds of sin. The gates of hell are opened, and death is oppressed, and the old Adam is put off, and the new is perfected. If any new creature in Christ, be renewed! It is your duty to obey the heavenly warnings, and not to neglect the token of gratitude and public joy, the gift at the altar of the Lord, to whom such great SALVATION is announced, and provided you do not spurn it, is conferred. P. P. Wittenberg, Vigil of Easter in the Year of the Lord 1653.

This is the later Program: Let GOD arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let them that hate him flee from before his face. It has already happened, exclaims the Bishop of Hippo, Christ has arisen, who is God blessed above all things forever: and his enemies have been scattered among all nations, the Jews, in that very place where they exercised their enmities, defeated, and thence scattered through all things. And now they hate, and they fear; As smoke vanishes, they define; as wax flows from the face of the fire, so let sinners perish from the face of GOD. They lifted themselves up from the fires of their hatreds into a swelling of pride, and setting their mouth against heaven, and crying, crucify, they mocked the captive, they derided him hanging, and whence they swelled as victors, soon defeated they vanished. Since in this age, like smoke, by exalting themselves, that is, by being proud, they have vanished, there will come to them in the end extreme damnation, that they may perish from his face forever. Nor indeed did the Psalmist threaten only dissipation, flight, and destruction to those enemies; but primarily also to the devil, and his angels, by whose impulse they exercised enmity and hatred. For these bear implacable hatred and eternal enmities, and are the authors, torches, and trumpets of all enmity and hatred against GOD. Therefore, St. Jerome not undeservedly interpreted these things concerning the devil at the same time, and his army, that is, the Jews: The Prophet foreseeing prays that, as the Lord arises, the diabolical dominations may flee away. And Christ, having risen again, ought to have triumphed most of all over them; about to crush the head of the ancient serpent and his seed, by his death about to destroy him who had the power of death; that is, the devil: about to despoil principalities and powers, to lead them away confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself. Hence the Epinicion long ago sung by the Prophets, I will be thy death, O death, I will be thy bite, O hell: which he joyfully repeats in today's solemnity: Death is swallowed up in victory: Where is thy victory, O hell? where is thy sting, O death? For in this triumphal song (we point to the sixty-eighth Psalm) it is not sung either of the exodus of the people from Egypt, which most Hebrews, and with them Grotius, desire, or of the battles and victories of David against the uncircumcised, which R. Aben-Ezra, and Joh. Calvin's, and also the Samosatenian Enjedinus's gloss, or of the liberation of Hezekiah from the army of Sennacherib, which R. David Kimchi opined, or of the Babylonian captivity, and redemption from the same, which seems to be R. Obadiah's explanation; nor is the translation of the ark of the covenant into the citadel of Zion celebrated, which seemed so to Musculus, Beza, Junius, Pareus, and other Calvinists: But it is a prophecy about Christ, who was to triumph over his enemies, which, with the Holy Apostle leading the way, venerable antiquity in the Greek and Latin Church, with the whole assembly of orthodox interpreters, held as indubitable: nor could some heterodox, Reformed, Papists, and not even the Jews themselves deny it: R. Solomon at verse 34, Sing, or sing praises after the coming of Christ: Also R. Obadiah at verse 25. They saw thy goings, O GOD, that is, the Prophets of GOD in visions foresaw thee, O Christ; whence that Jarchian observation; Others say that this Psalm is about the future days of Christ. It is certainly a clear interpretation, and among all Christians deservedly superior to every objection, which the Apostle, by the divine Spirit, handed down, preaching from this triumphal song the victory of Christ and its fruit, Eph. 4, verse 8. For which reason he says (the Prophet) Ascending on high he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men: When Calvin pronounces that he (the Apostle) had bent this passage MORE SUBTLY to Christ, and had DISTORTED this testimony somewhat from the GENUINE SENSE, how, I ask, can he be absolved from impiety? Whence his defender, Andreas Rivetus, was himself forced to desert this patriarch of his, and to confess: What is said in this place about the chariot of GOD, about the ascension into heaven, and about the gifts conferred upon men, etc., CAN IN NO WAY be accommodated to the History of Sennacherib, nor does it fit the bringing of the ark, and therefore it is NECESSARY that they be explained, OUTSIDE OF ALL TYPICAL REASONING, directly about GOD then manifesting in the flesh, now manifested.
