The former brings in the words of the Vulgate, which make David—who was bound to describe the Law, and to turn it over and over again, and whom Bellarmine acknowledges to be cultivated in all divine and human doctrine—illiterate. That division, by which these words are drawn against the beginning of the new, does not agree with the Hebrew truth, according to which the same words pertain to the end of the preceding. We cannot, however, but marvel at the extreme impudence of Bellarmine, when he pronounces that the Hebrew punctuation is not to be heeded when it differs from the Greek, by an argument brought forward which consists only of a most empty begging of the question, because, forsooth, later Rabbis added the punctuation, who are in no way to be compared with the LXX elders. Since these matters have been dealt with by us at length elsewhere, this argument must be entirely inverted in this way: Because the LXX elders both erred themselves in countless places and were corrupted by scribes, it is a crime to examine the Hebrew truth, which has hitherto been able to be convicted of no error, not even in the punctuation, by a version. And to wish to render the fountain purer from the rivulets, which flows far more pure, and nowhere turbid. That error of the Greeks arose in this place from the fact that it confused the meanings of the words ספרות, which signifies numbers, and ספרים, which signifies books, whereas in the source the sense flows clear: 'My mouth told of thy righteousness, all the day thy salvation: for I have not known numbers': which the Chaldean expresses thus, 'because I have not known מנינהון the number of them,' namely, of thy righteousness and salvation: some take the particle כי in the more common sense: 'because in countless ways thy righteousness and salvation have come to me, whence deservedly and continually, and all the day, I proclaim it.' Vatablus explains it in an adversative sense, 'although thy salvation is incomprehensible to me, and exceeds the grasp of my mind.' Estius agrees with us, as does Sim. Muis, disapproving of the Vulgate. Cocceius loves to be singular, according to his custom, rendering it, 'I have not known fables.'

Latin:

Vers. 15. OS MEUM ANNUNCIABIT JUSTITIAM TUAM: TOTO DIE SALUTARE TUUM, QVONIAM

NON COGNOVI LITERATURAM) Melius; quam- bis numerum (nempe bonitatum tuarum) non novi: ut sensus fit idem qui 40, 6. Symmachus hic; ἐ γάρ ὄιδα ἐξαριθμῆ- σαι. Graeci ספרות sumfere pro arte numeraria qua utun- tur mercatores. Itaque verterunt πραγματείας, & inde Ro- manum Psalterium negotiationes. Alii γραμματείας. Utri- usque Graecae versionis mentio apud Augustinum.

Si vera haec versio, illiteratus fuerit Psaltes, oportet. Unde nonnulli eo abiere, ut pronuncia- rint Davidem non novisse literaturam, quoniam Pa- stor ovium fuit, quod refellit ipse Bellarmin. in h. l. Aliam ergo glossam quaerit Cardinalis, sed valde ineptam, non cognovi literaturam, id est, non co- gnovi sapientiam hujus mundi, non confido in huma- nis consiliis, non approbo astutiam & prudentiam seculi, sed introibo in potentias Domini, id est, ad- hærebo omnipotentiae Dei. At toto coelo diversa sunt, esse ἀγράμματον, non cognovisse literaturam, & non approbare prudentiam seculi. Prius Vulgatæ verba inferunt, quæ Davidem, qui tenebatur Le- gem describere, & jugiter volvere ac revolvere, quemque omni divina & humana doctrina excul- tum agnoscit Bellarm. illiteratum faciunt. Non convenit illa distractio, qua hæc verba adversus novi initium trahantur, Ebraicæ veritati, juxta quam adversus præcedentis finem eadem perti- nent. Non possumus autem non mirari extremam Bellarmini impudentiam, cum pronunciat distin- ctionem Ebraicam non esse attendendam, quando discrepat a Græca, Argumento adducto, quod va- nissima solum principii petitione constat, quia scilic. distinctionem addidere Rabbini posteriores, qui nullo modo comparandi sunt cum LXX. senioribus. Quæ quum prolixe alias a nobis expedita sint, inverten- dum omnino argumentum hoc modo : Quia LXX. Seniores innumeris in locis tum errarunt ipsi, tum corrupti sunt a Librariis, nefas esse Ebraicam veritatem, quæ nullius erroris, ne in distinctionibus quidem convinci hactenus potuit, ad versionem exa- minare. Et fontem e rivulis puriorem reddere velle, qui longe purissimus, nec uspiam turbidus fluit. Error autem ille Græcorum enatus est hoc loco in- de, quod fignificata vocum ספרות quæ numeros & ספרים quæ libros fignificat, confuderit, cum in fonte sensus fluat limpidus, os meum narrabat justi- tiam tuam, tota die salutem suam : quoniam non no- vi numeros: quod exprimit ita Chaldæus, quia non novi מנינהון numerum eorum, justitiæ scil. & salutis tuæ : particulam כי nonnulli sensu usitatiori acci- piunt: quia innumeris modis injustitia & salus tua mihi obtigit, unde merito jugiterque, ac tota die eam prædico. Vatablus adversario sensu exponit, quamvis salus tua mihi sit imcomprehensibilis, & ex- cedat mentis meæ captum. Annuit nobis & Estius ut & Sim. Muis improbantes vulgatam. Coccejus amat singularis esse, pro more, reddens, non novi fabulas.

## 71:18
Vers. 18. O GOD, THOU HAST TAUGHT ME FROM MY YOUTH.

See concerning these and the following, Memor. justor. Witeberg. Conc. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DEUS DOCUISTI ME A JU- VENTUTE MEA.

Vid. de his & seqq. Memor. justor. Witeberg. Conc. 9.

## 72:1 Argument
PSALM LXXII.

Solomon the heavenly Catholic King, blessed forever.

FOR SOLOMON) That is, of the celebration of the memory of that time when Solomon was first anointed, 1 Kings 1:39; yet an ancient Hebrew scholiast in this place, and R. Saadia Gaon on Dan. 7:14, and Solomon Jarchi acknowledge that these pertain in a more sublime sense to the Messiah.

Grotius again invents a double sense of the same sayings, along with some Zwinglians, Calvin, Junius and Tremellius and others, as also with the Papists.

But since a single saying can have only one sense, most Christian interpreters, both recent and ancient, explain the present Psalm as being about Christ, by no means about Solomon. The title, 'For Solomon,' does not contradict their opinion. For this must be explained according to the argument and the text of the Psalm itself: the whole context of which convinces us that it treats solely of Christ. Therefore, Solomon himself cannot be understood, whose kingdom was neither eternal, nor immense, nor blessed in every respect, but the Messiah, whose type Solomon is, and who is also called Solomon in Cant. 3:11 and 8:11, that is, according to the Midrash Shir HaShirim, the perfective King, who created all his creatures perfect, and is the King whose peace is peace. Which the ancient Rabbis also observed concerning this passage. Whence R. David Kimchi on this passage: 'Some explain this Psalm as being about Christ, who is called Solomon in Cant. 3:11.' But if the title is explained as being about Solomon himself, it may be said that the Psalm was dedicated and consecrated to Solomon, so that he might have the kingdom of the Messiah in constant memory, and propose his kingdom to himself as a norm. But that the Psalm must be explained as being about Christ without a type, in an immediate sense, its beginning, middle, and end confirm, because most things suit Christ ALONE, but can in no way be attributed to Solomon.

The Psalm is, however, partly euktikos (supplicatory), partly prophetikos (prophetic), partly eucharistikos (thanksgiving). First, the Psalmist prays: 'Give thy judgment, O God, to the King, and thy justice to the King's Son.' That King and the King's Son is Christ, because he is both God himself and the Son of God the Father, or because he is the Son of King David and King himself on David's throne, Luke 1:32, 33. That God gave his judgment to Christ is not obscure: since all judgment has been given to him by God the Father, John 5:22; whence he is not rarely described as administering judgment and justice. Tertullian indeed explains in book 5 against Marcion, ch. 9, those words, 'Give thy judgment, O God, to the King,' that is, to Christ who is to reign, 'and thy justice to the King's Son,' that is, to the people of Christ. For they are his children who are reborn in him: But the subject is monadikon and singular, 'the King's Son,' nor can it be taken as collective; indeed, the King's son and the King are the same, and the people of the Lord are clearly distinguished from the King's Son: for the former is to be judged, but the latter judges. R. David Kimchi explains the justice of God thus: that he judges and discerns what is right without witnesses, and he confesses that this is most plain if it is understood of Christ from a comparison with Isa. 11:3. 'He shall not judge by the sight of his eyes, nor decide by the hearing of his ears,' i.e., by witnesses. And what King judges the whole people of God, and all his poor, who judges in justice and judgment, so that he never departs from justice and judgment, and commits nothing unjust or iniquitous? This eulogy suits only the righteous branch of David, as Jeremiah testifies, ch. 23:5; for there it is introduced as proper to him, and here and there elsewhere. Thus, therefore, in this opening prayer of the Psalm, a prophecy is contained at the same time, indeed the argument of the whole prophecy subjoined. For since, as Theodoret holds, this Psalm prophesies the Messiah's rule and the peace brought by him, it indicates at the threshold that it proposes to sing of the justice and judgment of the Messianic King, and of the increase of his kingdom, as the fruit of such a rule, which is administered in justice and judgment. 'Give thy judgment to the King': Cause that King to arise at last, to whom all judgment is to be given, who will rule in judgment and justice. He therefore desires the advent of the Messiah.

of the King: and thus he prophesies first concerning the tenor of the rule which the Messiah was about to administer in justice and spiritual peace. 'The mountains shall receive peace for the people, and the hills justice. He shall judge the poor of the people and shall save the children of the poor and shall humble the slanderer.' By mountains and hills are understood either the kingdoms and the powerful of the world, or it is indicated that peace and justice will everywhere spring forth in the days of this King, wherever mountains and hills stand out; or the mountains and hills around Jerusalem are designated, so that it may be hinted that peace and justice would go forth from Jerusalem, which were to diffuse themselves into the whole world, Ps. 87:1, Ps. 125:2, Isa. 2:3, ch. 52:7. Augustine understands by them men eminent for excellent holiness, and by the hills their excellence following their obedience. These things, however, suit only the kingdom of the Messiah. Nor are those results, to judge the poor of the people and to save the children of the poor, of any other than our Savior, to whom all judgment has been given; who graciously regards the poor, especially those who are poor in spirit, Matt. 5:3, and alone always rightly discerns and judges, and alone can save in every necessity and truly redeem the miserable from the power of Satan, sin, and death, Matt. 1:21, Heb. 2:14. It is also his to humble and crush the slanderer, the Devil (as Augustine and Theodoret explain), and all enemies whatsoever. Therefore R. Obadiah Gaon explains it as being about Christ, who abolishes all perversity in the world.

Then the Psalmist also prophesies concerning the flourishing of the Kingdom of the Messiah: namely (1.) concerning its happy perpetuity v. 5. They shall fear thee as long as the Sun, and while the Moon endureth, throughout all generations. Which cannot be understood of Solomon's Kingdom: For how does that perpetual worship, as long as the Sun and Moon endure, from generation to generation, belong to Solomon or his Queen? Therefore Kimchi on this passage: They shall fear thee, that is, in his days they shall begin and shall remain forever. It is most plain concerning Christ Is. 11, 6. The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of God. (2) Concerning the perpetual fruitfulness of that kingdom. Which exerted itself most greatly in the advent of the Messiah: therefore concerning him: he shall come down like showers that water the earth. For the ancients understand these things concerning the advent of Christ, and either concerning the silent conception of the Son of God with Theodoret; just as the fleece receives the rain and the earth the dew without noise: or they interpret it concerning the advent destined first to the Jews, as the rain descended into the fleece in the time of Gideon Jud. 6, the earth remaining dry: then to the Gentiles, as it irrigated the earth on every side while the fleece remained dry, with Augustine. Righteousness shall spring up in his days (in the time of the New Testament under the advent of the Messiah), and abundance of peace: until the Moon be taken away. For then the eternal righteousness is to be brought back Dan. 9. v. 24. and true peace is to be restored, Luc. 2. Eph. 2. Col. 1. which goods endure forever, while the Moon is taken away, or until it is not. All of which are to be understood concerning the Messiah: because in the days of Solomon, or of any mortal King, there did not arise righteousness and abundance of peace which extends itself forever: Such righteousness and peace are proper to the Kingdom of Christ Is. 9. v. 6. Roman. 14. vers. 17. And these things are so clear that they deserve assent even from the Rabbis themselves. To those words, he shall come down like rain, R. David Kimchi: This King comes to the people for their good and salvation, like rain upon mown grass, which causes it to grow again: Thus Christ in his advent will cause Israel to multiply. And in Midrash Tillim: In his days, that is, in the days of Christ, as today the Sun and Moon, so the righteous will illuminate the world, as Is. 60. The Gentiles shall walk in thy light. (3) Concerning the fruitful amplitude of that kingdom v. 8. seqq. and he shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth. By which periphrasis the circuit of the whole world is accustomed to be designated in the Scriptures. For by the great sea, says Augustine here, the earth is surrounded, which is called the Ocean, therefore from sea to sea, from any end of the earth, unto any end he said he would have dominion, whose name and power was to be preached in the whole world, and would be of much avail. Which, so that it could not be understood otherwise, from sea to sea, he immediately added: And from the river even unto the ends of the earth. What he says, therefore, even unto the ends of the earth, he had said before, from sea even unto sea. But what he now says, from the river, he clearly expressed that he wished to commend his power from that place whence he also began to choose his disciples: namely, from the river Jordan, where, when the Lord had been baptized above and the Holy Spirit descended, a voice sounded from heaven, this is my beloved Son. Hence, therefore, his doctrine begins and the authority of his heavenly teaching is extended even unto the ends of the earth. These are the words of Augustine. Indeed, he will rule over all the ends of the earth, says Theodoret: For because there are great seas beyond the land which cannot be crossed, which some call the Atlantic, or the Eastern and Western Ocean, he rightly declared that the empire of the earth is surrounded on all sides by the sea. Bellarmine explains this thus: It seems that the habitable earth is described here according to its length from the Indian or Eastern sea, even unto the Gaditan or Western sea, and according to its breadth from the Northern river Tanais, even unto the ends of Ethiopia, which is the last province to the South. Bugenhagen provides another explanation, understanding the former part as referring to Judea and the latter to the Gentiles, and at the same time he shows the connection with the preceding: And he shall have dominion, etc. This is what we said about the miracle of Gideon, that all the kingdoms of the earth, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles, are subject to Christ. He shall have dominion, he says, from sea to sea, that is, he will be King of the whole land of the Jews. Read Num. 34. from the river, namely the Euphrates, even unto the ends of the earth, that is, he will be King of all the Gentiles. All agree that the whole earth is designated. And thus Remigius, Albertus, Hugo, Dionysius, Vatablus, and Montanus with Rupert, understand the East, West, South, and North: From sea (the southern Ocean) unto sea (the northern Ocean) and from the river (the Pishon which compasseth the whole land of Havilah in the east) unto the ends of the earth (the lands towards the Western sea, which are still being discovered). Nor is there any reason, as you might say with Christoph. de Castro, that the borders of Judea are described in this way in Gen. 15, 27. Exod. 23, 31. Deut. 11, 24. Jos. 14, for there the borders are named as the desert, Lebanon, the Sea, the Euphrates: but here, sea and sea, river and ends of the earth, a manner of speaking taken from the primordial joining together, because from earth and water one globe was made, so that the seas were received into the bays of the earth and surround the globe of the earth like a belt. In the same way, the amplitude of the kingdom of the Messiah throughout the whole world is also designated in Zech. 9, 10. However, Blessed Luther, with Augustine and Theodoret, judges that the river is also established as the beginning, so that it may be hinted that the beginning in the New Testament is to be made from the river Jordan: which is not to be rashly rejected. For he is accurate in the prophecies of the Holy Scriptures in every single word, which therefore should not be lightly passed over. It is certainly agreed among most Christian interpreters that the ends of the whole earth are designated. And we have here R. Aben Ezra from among the Jews agreeing: who explains it thus; from sea to sea, that is: from the southern sea, which is called the Red Sea, to the northern sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea: And from the river, i.e., from the river going out of Eden, which is from the beginning of the east, and even unto the ends of the earth, which are at the end of the west. Therefore, not only is there now special mention of various nations and peoples: The Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust. (Which R. Arama explains concerning the Messiah: the Messiah has no adversary except the serpent, whose food is dust, Is. 54. The kings of Tarshish and the Isles shall offer gifts: The kings of the Arabs of Sheba shall bring presents: But universally all peoples are also included, to worship this King and to serve him v. 11. And they shall worship him

ALL kings of the earth, ALL nations shall serve him: which both the preceding and the following context clearly teach are to be understood concerning religious adoration and service, and since no mortal is adored civilly by ALL the kings of the earth, nor have ALL nations ever served them, it is manifest again that the discourse here is not about a mere man, but about Christ, and that the calling of the Gentiles to the Gospel and the kingdom of Christ is openly predicted: Nor does R. David Kimchi and R. Aben-Ezra deny this here. The reason which is added for the adoration again designates the Messiah. For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth; and the poor also, and him that hath no helper; he shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor. The Messiah had to come to deliver man, who is truly poor after the fall, Rev. 3, 17, who had no helper, from the most powerful enemy, the Devil, and to save the souls of poor men. He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity (original sin is as it were a capital debt designated by iniquity, usury is actual sins, according to Bellarmine) and their name shall be honorable before him. Who can deliver souls from iniquity, except Christ alone, before whom our souls are precious, inasmuch as he deigned to redeem them with a precious ransom? Hence, therefore, the Messiah shall live, as the Psalmist further sings, and there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia (they shall offer him each their own, the Arabs gold, others will dedicate other things to his honor) and they shall worship concerning him (they shall worship before him, or through him, or because of him) they shall bless him all the day. In whom, I ask, could these things be completed, or have been completed, except in Christ alone? who is always worshipped, whom the faithful bless, praying to God through him and because of him all the day, doing all things in the name of Jesus, and celebrating him in all things Col. 3, 17. And thus the Psalmist concludes what he sang concerning the fruitful amplitude of the kingdom of Christ, with a notable similitude v. 16. There shall be a handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon, and they shall flourish in the City like the grass of the earth. Which again do not suit Solomon, but deal with the kingdom of the Messiah, because history hands down nothing about an extraordinary fertility of the earth in the time of Solomon, and the very sequence of the text compels that those things be understood concerning spiritual fertility and fruitfulness in the kingdom of the Messiah; of which hereafter.

Finally, in v. 17, he institutes a recapitulation of those things which the Prophet had predicted, comprehending them thus in summary: the perpetuity of the kingdom indeed in these words: His name (the Messiah's) shall be for an age: the fruitfulness of the same in the following words: His name shall sprout or be sonned, while the Sun lasts. Finally, the amplitude in this way: all nations shall be blessed in him, they shall call him blessed. Which again cannot be understood of any other than the Messiah. For in whom are ALL nations to be blessed, if not in that blessed SEED promised to the Patriarchs, which is uniquely described by this criterion or axiom, that in him all nations must be blessed Gen. 12, 3. and elsewhere passim.

This therefore is the prophetic part of the Psalm, which is finally concluded with a thanksgiving and a notable celebration of the God of Israel, which contains a silent repetition of the things said: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders, which certainly are the highest and most admirable in the coming and benefits of Christ 1 Tim. 3, 16. And blessed be the name of his majesty forever. For what will be celebrated more forever than the redemption of Christ Rev. 5, 9. 12. 13. 14. And all the earth shall be filled with his majesty. Amen, amen. When was this more fulfilled than in the coming of Christ under the New Testament through the calling of the Gentiles, with the Gospel propagated throughout the whole world, of which the Psalmist prophesied here? To which some also refer the fact that this last prayer of David is so called, because this Psalm was written last of all, and left as a kind of testament to his son Solomon, so that he might commend to him the faith and expectation of the Messiah, which we leave to its own place.

Everything clearly proves that the Psalm is to be understood solely of Christ. That Solomon is exhibited here as a type of Christ is supported neither by any document nor permitted by the text: because it is not a matter of anything but one subject throughout the whole Psalm, as far as the letter is concerned. Moreover, there are many predicates which by no means agree, according to the letter, with Solomon or his kingdom, such as those concerning the perpetual and immutable justice of the King of this kingdom, concerning the omnipotent liberation of all the oppressed throughout the whole world—for that kingdom extends itself that far—concerning the salvation of the poor, the trampling of the Devil, the eternity of the kingdom, the amplitude of the same extending itself through the whole world, the religious worship of this King, the adoration of all Kings, the subjection and servitude of all nations, the incredible fruitfulness and fertility, the eternal celebration of his glorious name, the blessing of all nations and tribes of the earth, which will be obtained in him, the name of his majesty, which is to be glorified in the heavens forever, and the majesty of the same, with which the whole earth is to be filled: For that same one, of whom the Psalmist prophesies in this way, his name will be forever, his name will be continued as long as the sun, all nations will be blessed in him, they will call him blessed, he is celebrated by the sacred Psalmist himself, so that he may lead the way by his own example in the manner of blessing or celebrating his name, and at the same time so excite and invite others, whether he exhibits a formula for using a hymn, or repeats, as we have said, those things which he had treated before, when he says: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel who alone does wonders, and blessed be the name of his majesty forever, and the whole earth will be filled with his majesty. Whence it is clear that the second person of the divinity, the Son of God, is celebrated in this way, of whom the sacred Psalmist had predicted all these things. Which I see also observed by Theodoret: Then the most holy Prophet, teaching more clearly his hidden divinity, added: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders. For this very one, he says, who was predicted, and who performed the predicted miracles, he himself is both the God of Israel and the Lord of all: so that these things are not to be twisted to Solomon, as far as the literal sense is concerned, except impiously. The Jews themselves, not to mention Christian interpreters, have openly acknowledged that these things are to be understood of the Messiah. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi indeed tries to twist the text to Solomon as well, whom our Judaizing Master followed: But David Kimchi observes that other Jews explain this Psalm of Christ according to the letter, as one who is called Solomon in Cant. 8:11, and although he explains certain things about Solomon as well, he does not rest in that explanation, but adds another about Christ, which he clearly saw to be more certain and more solid, however much he might have willingly wanted to adapt the Psalm to Solomon. He does not therefore make Solomon a type here (which I do not find in others either), but brings forward those two different expositions, yet in such a way that it is sufficiently clear that the palm is awarded to that one which understands the Psalm of Christ according to the letter. If it is understood of King Christ, he says at v. 1: it is most plain: And again at v. 5: it is MOST PLAIN concerning Christ. And at the same verse: before the moon, or rather during the moon: Properly, he says, it is said of Christ: and hyperbolically of Solomon. And so in others. Midrash Tillim likewise explains the Psalm according to the letter of the Messiah, even if it also brings forward another explanation about Solomon. Which Baal Hatturim also accepts concerning the Messiah at Num. 24:16, and

the following, and the Chaldean paraphrase at v. 1 of this Psalm, Give your justice to King Messiah, as also the Talmudists, who concluded from v. 17 that the name of the Messiah will be Yinnon in Cod. Sanhedr. c. ult. in Bereshith Rabba sect. 1. Nor does Lipman deny that v. 9 is to be accepted of the Messiah, where his dominion is said to extend far and wide. But R. Obadiah Gaon openly joins us, and interprets it of Christ in such a way that he teaches that the Psalm deals with the coming of Christ: that it is Christ who is said to abolish all perversity in the world: that Christ will be in the beginning like a handful of wheat, but afterwards a multitude of disciples will take increase like grass.

If anyone wishes to say with Bellarmino that the first four verses speak of Solomon, but the rest of Christ, he will manifestly contradict the most open text, because he for whom David prays for judgment and justice, so that the mountains may receive peace, and the hills justice, and the poor may be judged, and the sons of the poor may be saved, and the slanderer may be humbled; he speaks of the same, not of another, and he will remain with the sun and before the moon from generation to generation, as the Vulgate renders it, and what follows thereafter. Which the continuity of the words teaches more clearly than the sun. But this is said not of Solomon, but of Christ, as Bellarmino admits: For Bellarmino acknowledges in this place that these things CANNOT BE SAID of Solomon, and therefore the Holy Spirit compels us to understand these things of Christ. Therefore, those former things must likewise be understood of Christ, not of Solomon. Bellarmino indeed twists these also to Solomon in this way: King Solomon will remain in his Son (Christ) with the sun, or as long as the sun will be, but it will also have to be said in this way, that the former things are to be understood similarly, give your judgment to the King (in his son Christ) so that (in him) he may judge the people, so that the mountains may receive peace, and he may judge the poor of the people, and save the sons of the poor, and humble the slanderer (in his Son the Messiah), for whose kingdom is described by judgment and justice, his kingdom is said to remain with the sun, and to be diffused to the whole world. As therefore these things are to be understood of the kingdom not of Solomon himself but of the Messiah, as Bellarmino admits, so likewise it is necessary that that which is about the administration of the kingdom in judgment and justice, and about the kingdom, be explained not of Solomon, but of the Messiah. What need is there, therefore, for that monstrosity or absurdity concerning Solomon, not reigning in his own person, but in the Messiah? Since the text in no way treats of Solomon but of the Messiah, not of his kingdom but of the latter's. Which Ambrose urges in Apol. David. T. 4. oper. p. 394, to prove that those words, Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son, were not spoken to Solomon, but to Christ: How do you think it applies to Solomon, the son of David, what is written: that he shall remain with the sun and before the moon for ages of ages, when he, having obtained the use of a short life, passed the span of his living within narrow limits? How, moreover, is it said of him: he shall have dominion from sea to sea, when he, established within Syria, that is, within the province of one region, had circumscribed boundaries of empire: whereas Christ alone extended his empire to the ends of the world? For he alone is the one of whom the series of the Psalm prophesied well, that the Kings of the Arabs and Saba shall bring gifts, and all the Kings of the earth shall adore him: all nations shall serve him. For we know this one commanding all peoples and nations: with an uncircumscribed empire, with boundless power.

Latin:

PSALMUS LXXII.

Salomo cœlestis Rex Catholicus æternum benedictus.

IN SALOMONEM) Id est, celebrandæ memoriæ tem- poris illius, quo primum unctus est Solomon 1. Reg. 1, 39. sub- limiori tamen sensu pertinere hæ ad Messiam agnoscunt ve- tus Scholiastes Hebræus hoc loco, & R. Saadia Gaon ad Dan. 7, 14, & Salomon Jarchi.

ITerum geminum sensum fingit eorundem dicto- rum Grotius, cum Zwinglianis nonnullis, Cal- vino, Junio & Tremellio & aliis, ut & cum Papistis.

Sed quum unius dicti non possit esse nisi unus tan- tum sensus, Christiani Interpp. plerique, recentio- res & veteres, Psalmum præsentem de Christo ex- plicant, neutiquam de Salomone. Quorum sen- tentiæ non repugnat titulus; Pro Salomone. Hic e- nim explicandus est juxta argumentum & textum ipsum Psalmi: quem de Christo unice agere, tota e- jus συνέχειa convincit. Non ergo Salomo ipse in- telligi potest, cujus regnum nec æternum, nec im- mensum, nec ab omni parte beatum fuit, sed Mes- sias, cujus typus Salomo, quique Salomo etiam vo- catur Cant. 3, 11. & c. 8, 11. hoc est, secundum Mi- drasch Schir Haschirim, Rex perfectivus, qui creavit omnes creaturas suas שׁלמות perfectas, & Rex est, cujus pax est pax. Quod etiam circa hunc locum observarunt antiqui Rabbini. Unde R. David Kimchi ad h. 1. Aliqui exponunt Psalmum hunc de Christo, qui vocatur Salomo Cant. 3, 11. Quod si de ipso Salomone titulus explicetur, dici poterit Sa- lomoni Psalmum nuncupatum & consecratum fu- isse, ut in jugi memoria regnum Messiæ haberet, regnumque ipsius normæ loco sibi proponeret. De Christo autem sine typo, sensu immediato expli- candum esse Psalmum, initium, medium, & finis e- jusdem confirmant, quia pleraque SOLI Christo conveniunt, Salomoni autem nullatenus tribui possunt.

Est autem Psalmum partim εὐκτικὸς, partim προ- φητικὸς, partim εὐχαριστικὸς. Primum Psaltes pre- catur: Deus judicium tuum Regi da, & justitiam tuam Filio Regis. Rex ille & Regis Filius est Christus, quia & Deus ipse, & Dei Patris Filius, vel quia Davidis Regis Filius & Rex ipse in Davidis throno Luc. 1, 32. 33. Judicium autem suum dedisse Deum Christo, haud obscurum est: siquidem ei datum omne judi- cium à Deo Patre Joh. 5, 22. unde non raro ita de- scribitur, quod judicium & justitiam administret. Tertullianus explicat quidem l. 5. advers. Marc. c. 9. illa, Deus judicium tuum Regi da, id est, Christo re- gnaturo, & justitiam tuam Filio Regis, id est, populo Christi. Filii enim ejus sunt, qui in ipso renascuntur: Sed subjectum est μοναδικὸν & singulare, Filius Re- gis, nec ut collectivum accipi potest, imo idem est & Regis filius & Rex, ac distinguitur populus Domi- ni aperte à Filio Regis: ille enim est judicandus, hic autem judicat. Justitiam Dei sic explicat R. David Kimchi: quod judicet ac rectum discernat sine testibus, idq; planissimum esse fatetur, si de Christo intelligatur è collatione Ef. 11, 3. Non judicabit per visum ocu- lorum, nec per auditum aurium dijudicabit, i. e. per te- stes. Et quis Regum universum populum Dei judi- cat, omnesque pauperes ejus, quis judicat in justitia & judicio, ita ut nunquam migret justitiam, & judici- um, nihil injusti aut iniqui committat? Hoc elogium uni germini Davidis justo convenit, teste Jeremia c. 23, 5. ibi enim tanquam proprium ipsi introduci- tur, & passim alibi. Sic ergo in ista precatione auspi- cali Psalmi Prophetia simul continetur, imo argu- mentum totius Prophetiæ subjunctæ. Quum enim, ut Theod. habet, Messiæ regimen & pacem ab ipso alla- tam hic Psalmus vaticinetur, in limine indicat, quod constituat canere de justitia ac judicio Regis Messiæ, deq; incremento regni ejusdem, ceu fructu talis regi- minis, quod in justitia & judicio administratur. Da judicium tuum Regi: Fac, ut Rex ille oriatur tan- dem, cui omne judicium dandum, qui in judicio & justitia imperabit. Optat ergo adventum Messiæ

Regis: adeoque vaticinatur primum de regiminis tenore, quod administraturus erat Messias in justi- tia, & pace Spirituali. Suscipient montes pacem popu- li, & colles justitiam. Judicabit pauperes populi & salvos faciet filios pauperum & humiliabit calu- mniatorem. Per montes & colles vel regna & potentes mundi intelliguntur, vel indicatur, ubiq; pacem ac justitiam progerminaturam in diebus hujus Regis, quaqua montes & colles prominent; vel montes & col- les circa Jerusalem designantur, ut innuatur è Jeru- salem prodituram pacem ac justitiam, quæ se in to- tum mundum diffusura erat Pf. 87, 1. Pf. 125, 2. Es. 3. v. 3. c. 52. 7. Augustinus per viros excellenri sanctitate eminentes, per colles illorum excellentiam sua obedien- tia subsequentes intelligit. Hæc autem non nisi re- gno Messiæ conveniunt. Neque illa a̓ποτελέσματα, judicare pauperes populi salvos facere filios pauperum, alterius sunt, quam Salvatoris nostri, cui omne da- tum judicium; qui pauperes, imprimis qui Spiritu pauperes sunt Matth. 5, 3. gratiose respicit, ac solus semper recte discernit ac judicat, solus salvare po- test in omni necessitate & vere miseros è potestate Sathanæ, peccati & mortis redimit Matth. 1, v. 21. Ebr. 2, 14. Ejusdem etiam est humiliare & conterere calumniatorem Diabolum (ut August. & Theodorei. explicant) & hostes quoscunque. Ideo R. Obad. Gaon de Christo, qui perversitatem omnem in mundo abolet, explicat.

Deinde vaticinatur etiam Hierospaltes de Re- gni Messiæ flore: utpote (1.) de ejusdem felici peren- nitate v. 5. Reverebuntur te, quamdiu erit Sol, & du- rante Luna generatio generationum. Quæ de Salo- monis Regno accipi non possunt: Quomodo e- nim cultus ille perennis, quam diu Sol & Luna du- rat, de generatione in generationem, Salomoni aut Reginæ ejus competit? Ideo Kimchi in hunc loc. Timebunt te, id est, in diebus ejus incipient & permanebunt in æternum. Planissimum est de Chri- sto Es. 11, 6. Terra implebitur cognitione Dei. (2) De regni illius perenni fœcunditate. Quæ maxime in ad- ventu Messiæ sese exeruit: ideo de illo: descendet sicut stillicidia stillantia super terram. Hæc enim de adventu Christi intelligunt veteres, & vel de conce- ptione tacita Filii Dei cum Theodoreto; sicut lana imbrem & terra rorem suscipit sine fragore: vel de adventu primum ad Judæos destinato, uti in vel- lus descendit pluvia Gideonis tempore Jud. 6. terra manente arida: deinde ad gentes, uti terram undi- quaque irrigavit vellere arido manente, cum Augusti- no, interpretantur. Orietur in diebus ejus (tempore Nov. Test. sub adventum Messiæ) justitia, & abun- dantia pacis: donec auferatur Luna. Tunc enim æterna justitia reducendæ Dan. 9. v. 24. & pax vera restituenda, Luc. 2. Eph. 2. Col. 1. quæ bona durant in æternum, dum auferatur Luna, vel donec non sit. Quæ omnia intelligenda de Messia: quia in die- bus utique Salomonis, aut ullius Regis mortalis non orta est justitia, & pacis abundantia, quæ in æ- ternum sese porrigat: Justitia & pax talis Regni Christi propria sunt Es. 9. v. 6. Roman. 14. vers. 17. Atque hæc adeo perspicua sunt, ut ab ipsis etiam Rabbinis assensum mereantur. Ad illa, descendet sicut pluvia, R. David Kimchi: Hic Rex ad popu- lum in bonum & salutem ejus advenit, sicut pluvia in gramen excisum, quod illud efficit recrescere: Sic Christus in adventu suo multiplicare faciet Israel. Et in Midrasch Tillim: In diebus ejus, id est, in die- bus Christi, ut hodie Sol & Luna, sic futurum justi illuminant mundum, ut Es. 60. Ambulant gentes in lumine tuo. (3) De regni illius fœcunda amplitudine v. 8. seqq. & dominabitur a mari usque ad mare, & a flumine usq; ad terminos orbis terrarum. Qua περί- φράσει designari solet in Scripturis universi orbis ambitus. Mari quippe magno, ait Augustinus hic, cin- gitur terra, quæ vocatur Oceanus, proinde a mari us- que ad mare, a quolibet fine terræ, usque ad quemlibet finem dominaturum dixit, cujus nomen & potestas to- to orbe fuerat prædicanda, multumque valitura. Quod ne aliter posset intelligi, a mari usque ad mare, continuo subjecit: Et à flumine usque ad terminos orbis terræ. Quod ergo ait, usque ad terminos or- bis terræ, hoc ante dixerat, à mari usque ad mare. Quod vero nunc ait, à flumine, evidenter expressit inde voluisse Christum potestatem suam jam commen- dare, unde & Discipulos cœpit eligere: à flumine scil. Jordane, ubi supra baptizatum Dominum cum de- scenderet Spiritus Sanctus, sonuit vox de cœlo, hic est Filius meus dilectus. Hinc ergo doctrina ejus incipiens & magisterii cœlestis autoritas dilatatur usque ad ter- minos orbis terræ. Hæc Augustinus. Scilicet omnibus orbis finibus, inquit Theodor. dominabitur: Quo- niam enim trans terram magna sunt maria, quæ trans- mitti non possunt, quæ nonnulli Atlantica vocant, vel Eoum, & Hesperium Oceanum, merito orbis terræ imperium undecunque mari septum esse declaravit. Bellarminus hoc ita explicat: Videtur hîcc describi terra habitabilis secundum longitudinem à mari Indi- co, sive Orientali usŕ, ad mare Gaditanum sive Occi- dentale, & per latitudinem à flumine Tanai Septen- trionali, usŕ, ad fines Æthiopiæ, quæ est ultima pro- vincia ad Meridiem. Bugenhagius aliam tradit ex- plicationem, priora de Judæa, posteriora de gen- tibus intelligens, simulque monstrat connexionem cum præcedentibus: Et dominabitur &c. Hoc est quod diximus de miraculo Gedeonis, Christo subsunt omnia regna terræ sive Judæorum sive gentium. Do- minabitur, inquit, a mari solo, usque ad mare ma- gnum, id est, Rex erit totus terræ Judæorum. Lege Num. 34. à flumine, scilicet Euphrate, ab oriente usŕ, ad ter- minos orbis terrarum, hoc est, Rex erit omnium gen- tium. Conveniunt omnes totam terram designari. Atque ita Remigius, Albertus, Hugo, Dionysius, Va- tablus, & Montanus cum Ruperto, Orientem, Occi- dentem, Meridiem & Septentrionem intelligunt: A mari (Oceano meridiano) usque ad mare (Ocea- num Septentrionalem) & à flumine (Phison qui circumit omnem terram Hevilah orientalem) us- que ad fines terræ (terras versus mare Occiduum, quæ adhuc deteguntur.) Nec est, quod cum Christoph. de Castro dicas, terminos Judææ Gen. 15, 27. Exod. 23, 31. Deut. 11, 24. Jos. 14. ita describi, nam ibi termini no- minantur desertum, Libanus, Mare, Euphrates: hic vero mare & mare, flumen & fines terræ, modo lo- quendi ex primæva coagmentatione, quia ex terra & aqua unus factus est globus, ita ut maria in terræ sinus accepta sint, & cinguli instar ambiant orbem terrarum, desumto. Eodem modo etiam amplitu- do regni Messiæ per totum orbem designata est Zach. 9, 10. Flumen tamen initium constitui etiam ideo cum Augustino & Theodoreto censet B. Lu- therus, ut innuatur initium in N. T. faciendum à Jordanis flumine: quod non temere rejiciendum. Accuratus enim in vaticiniis S. S. est in singulis ver- bis, quæ proinde haud leviter transmittenda. Id sane penes plerosque Interpp. Christianos certum est terminos universæ terræ designari. Et habemus hic è Judæis R. Aben Ezram consentientem: qui sic exponit; à mari ad mare, hoc est: à mari meridio- nali, quod vocatur mare rubrum, ad mare septentrio- nale, quod est mare mediterraneum: Et à fluvio, h. e. à fluvio exeunte ex Eden, qui est ab initio orientis, & usque ad terminos terræ, qui sunt in fine occidentis. Id- eo non tantum variarum nationum & populorum nunc specialis fit mentio: Coram illo procident Æ- thiopes, & inimici ejus terram lingent. (Quod R. A- rama de Messia explicat: non habet Messias adver- sarium præter serpentem, cujus cibus est pulvis Es. 54. Reges Tharsis & Insulæ munera offerent: Reges Ara- bum de Saba dona adducent: Sed universaliter etiam omnes populi comprehenduntur, Regem hunc ado- raturi, eique servituri v. 11. Et adorabunt eum

OMNES Reges terræ, OMNES gentes servient ei: quæ de religiosa adoratione, & servitute intelligenda esse cum antecedentia, tum etiam consequentia luculenter docent, ac quum nemo mortalium ab OMNIBUS Regibus terræ adoretur civiliter, nec illi unquam OMNES gentes servierint, manifestum iterum est, non de ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, sed de Christo hic sermonem esse, ac vocationem gentium ad Evangelium & regnum Christi palam prædici: Neque hic diffitetur R. David Kimchi, & R. Aben-Ezra. Ratio quæ additur adorationis, iterum Messiam designat. Quia liberavit pauperem à potente, & pauperem cui non erat adjutor; parcet pauperi, & inopi, & animas pauperum salvas faciet. Hominem, qui vere pauper post lapsum Ap. 3,17. cui nullus adjutor fuit, a potentissimo hoste Diabolo liberaturus Messias, & pauperum hominum animas salvaturus, advenire debuit. Ex usuris & iniquitate redimet animas eorum (peccatum originale est velut debitum capitale per iniquitatem designatum, usuræ sunt peccata actualia, secundum Bellarminum) & honorabile nomen eorum coram illo. Quis ex iniquitate animas liberare potest, nisi solus Christus, coram quo pretiosæ sunt animæ nostræ, utpote quas dignatus est pretioso λύτρῳ redimere? Hinc ergo vivet Messias, uti canit porro Psaltes, & dabitur ei de auro Arabiæ (offerent ei quique sua, Arabes aurum, alii alia ejus honori dicabunt) & adorabunt de ipso (adorabunt ante eum, aut per eum, aut propter eum) semper tota die benedicent ei. In quo obsecro, ista completa, aut compleri potuere, nisi in uno Christo? qui semper colitur, cui benedicunt fideles, per eum & propter eum Deum orantes tota die, omnia in nomine Jesu peragentes, eumque celebrantes in omnibus Col. 3, 17. Atque ita concludit Psaltes, quæ de fæcunda amplitudine regni Christi cecinit, insigni similitudine v. 16. Erit pugillus in terra in vertice montium, perstrepent ut Libanus fructus ejus, & florebunt in Civitate, sicut horti terræ. Quæ iterum Salomoni non conveniunt, sed de Messiæ regno agunt, quia nihil historiæ de extraordinaria terræ fœcunditate, tempore Salomonis tradunt, cogitque ipsa συνέχεια textus, ut illa de spirituali fertilitate ac fœcunditate in regno Messiæ accipiantur; de quo postea.

Tandem v. 17. ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν instituit eorum, quæ prædixerat Vates συλλήβδην ea ita comprehendens: perennitatem quidem regni hisce: Erit nomen ejus (Messiæ) in seculum: fœcunditatem vero ejusdem sequentibus verbis: Sobolescet vel filiabitur nomen ejus, durante Sole. Amplitudinem denique hoc modo: benedicentur in eo omnes gentes, beatum prædicabunt eum. Quæ iterum non possunt de alio, quam de Messia intelligi. In quo enim OMNES gentes benedicendæ, nisi in SEMINE illo benedicto Patriarchis promisso, quod ab hoc κριτηρίῳ vel axiomate μοναδικῶς describitur, quod in ipso debeant omnes gentes benedici Gen. 12, 3. & alibi passim.

Hæc ergo est pars Psalmi προφητικὴ, quæ denique concluditur ἐυχαρισίᾳ & celebratione insigni Dei Israelis, quæ tacitam repetitionem dictorum continet: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israël, qui facit mirabilia solus, quæ certe summa & maxime admiranda in adventu & beneficiis Christi sunt 1. Tim. 3, 16. Et benedictum nomen majestatis ejus in æternum. Quid enim in æternum magis celebrabitur, quam redemtio Christi Ap. 5, 9. 12. 13. 14. Et replebitur majestate ejus omnis terra. Fiat, fiat. Quando hoc magis factum, quam in adventu Christi sub Nov. Test. per vocationem gentium, propagato Evangelio per universum orbem, de quo hic vaticinatus est Psaltes? Quo etiam referunt nonnulli, quod hæc precatio ultima Davidis dicatur, quod Psalmus iste postremo omnium conscriptus, & quasi testamen- to Salomoni filio relictus sit, ut fidem & expecta- tionem Messiae ei commendaret, quod suo loco nos relinquimus.

Omnia erga luculenter evincunt, Psalmum de Christo unice intelligendum esse. Salomonem ceu typum Christi hic exhiberi nec ullo documen- to constat, nec permittit textus: quia non agitur ni- si de uno subjecto per totum Psalmum, quantum ad literam. Multa autem praedicata sunt, quae nequa- quam conveniunt, quoad literam, Salomoni, aut regno ejus, utpote quae de regni hujus Regis perpe- tua, & incommutabili justitia, de omnipotenti libe- ratione oppressorum universorum per totum orbem, eousque enim sese porrigit illud regnum, de sal- vatione pauperum, de conculcatione Diaboli, de aeter- nitate regni, de ejusdem amplitudine extendente se per universum mundum, de cultu religioso hujus Regis, de Regum omnium adoratione, gentium omnium sub- jectione & servitute, de incredibili foecunditate & fertilitate, de nominis ejus gloriosi aeterna celebratio- ne, de benedictione omnium gentium & tribuum ter- rae, quae in ipso obtinebitur, de nomine majestatis ejus, quod in coelis in aeternum glorificandum, & de majestate ejusdem, qua universa terra replenda: Nam idem ille, de quo ita vaticinatur Psaltes, no- men ejus erit in seculum, filiabitur nomen ejus, du- rante Sole, benedicentur in eo omnes gentes, beatum praedicabunt eum, celebratur ab ipso Hiero-Pfalte, ut praeeat exemplo suo modum benedictionis, vel celebrationis nominis ejus, aliosque simul ita ex- citet & invitet, sive formulam etiam usurpandi hy- mni exhibeat, sive repetat, ut diximus ea, quae antea tractarat, cum ait: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel qui facit mirabilia solus, & benedictum nomen maje- statis ejus in aeternum, & replebitur majestate ejus omnis terra. Unde patet, secundam personam divi- nitatis, Filium Dei ita celebrari, de qua ista omnia praedixerat Hieropsaltes. Quod video etiam Theo- doreto observatum: Deinde sanctissimus Propheta manifestius ejus occultam divinitatem docens subjun- xit: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, qui facit mirabilia solus. Nam hic ipse, inquit, qui praedictus est, quique praedicta miracula perfecit, ipse est & Israel Deus, & omnium Dominus: ut non nisi impie ista ad Salomonem, quoad sensum literalem, detorque- antur. Judaei utique ipsi, ne de Christianis Interpp. dicam, agnoverunt palam, de Messia haec intelli- genda esse. Rabbi Salomo Jarchi conatur quidem ad Salomonem etiam textum detorquere, quem Ma- gistrum sequutus est noster Judaizans: Sed David Kimchi observat, alios Judaeos Psalmum istum de Christo quoad literam exponere, utpote qui Salo- mo vocatur Cant. 8,11. & quamvis quaedam de Salo- mone etiam explicet, non tamen in illa explicatio- ne acquiescit, sed alteram de Christo subjungit, quam probe vidit certiorem esse, ac solidiorem, ut- ut lubenter Salomoni Psalmum aptare voluerit. Non ergo Salomonem hic facit typum (quod nec in aliis invenio) sed duas illas diversas expositiones adducit, ita tamen ut satis constet, palmam tribui illi, quae de Christo secundum literam Psalmum in- telligit. Si intelligatur de Rege Christo, ait ad v. 1. pla- nissimum est: Et iterum ad v. 5. PLANISSIMUM est de Christo. Et ad versum eundem: ante Lunam, vel potius durante Luna: Proprie, inquit, dicitur de Christo: & hyperbolice de Salomone. Atque ita in aliis. Midrasch Tillim explicat itidem Psalmum quoad literam de Messia, etsi adducat etiam expli- cationem alteram de Salomone. Quem etiam de Messia accipit Baal Hatturim ad Num. 24, 16. &

seqq. & Chald. paraphrasis ad v. 1. Psalmi hujus, Jus tuum da Regi Messiæ, ut & Thalmudistæ, qui è v. 17. conclusere nomen Messiæ futurum ינון in Cod. Sanhedr. c. ult. in Beresch. Rabba sect. 1. Neque in- ficiatur Lipmanus v. 9. de Messia accipiendum esse, ubi dominium ejus longe lateque patere dicitur. R. Obad. Gaon vero nobis aperte accedit, & de Chri- sto ita interpretatur, ut doceat, Psalmum de adven- tu Christi agere: Christum esse, qui perversitatem omnem in mundo abolere dicatur: Christum fore in principio, sicut manipulum tritici, sed postea multitudi- nem Discipulorum instar herbæ incrementa sumturam.

Si quis cum Bellarmino dicere velit, primos quatuor versiculos de Salomone loqui, cæteros au- tem de Christo, textui apertissimo manifeste con- tradicet, quia cui precatur David judicium & justi- tiam, ut montes pacem, & colles justitiam suscipi- ant, ac judicentur pauperes, & salventur filii pau- perum, ac humilietur calumniator; de eodem, non de alio dicit, & permanebit cum Sole & ante Lunam à generatione in generationem, ut reddit Vulgata, & quæ porro sequuntur. Quod sole clarius συνέχεια verborum docet. At hoc non de Salomone, sed de Christo dicit, fatente Bellarmino: Hæc enim de Sa- lomone DICI NON POSSE adeoque nos cogere Spi- ritum S. ut hæc de Christo intelligamus, agnoscit Bel- larminus in h. l. Priora ergo illa pariter de Christo intelligenda erunt, non de Salomone. Torquet quidem & hæc Bellarm. ad Salomonem hoc modo: Permanebit Rex Salomo in Filio suo (Christo) cum Sole, vel quamdiu Sol erit, sed ita etiam dicendum erit, priora similiter intelligenda esse, da Regi ju- dicium tuum (in filio ejus Christo) ut (in illo) judicet populum, ut suscipiant montes pacem, & judicet pau- peres populi, & salvet filios pauperum, & humiliet calumniatorem (in Filio suo Messia) nam cujus re- gnum à judicio & justitia describitur, ejus regnum permansurum cum Sole, & ad totum orbem dif- fundendum dicitur. Sicut ergo hæc de Regno non ipsius Salomonis sed Messiæ intelligenda, fatente Bellarm. ita pariter necessum est, ut illud de admi- nistratione regni in judicio & justitia, ac de regno non Salomonis, sed Messiæ explicetur. Quid er- go illa τερατολογία vel sœελότητι opus, de Salomo- ne non in persona propria regnante, sed in Messia? quum nullo modo de Salomone sed de Messia, non de illius, sed de hujus regno agat textus. Quæ ur- get Ambrosius de Apol. David. T. 4. oper. p. 394. ut probet illa verba, Deus judicium tuum da regi, & justitiam Filio Regis, non Salomoni dicta esse, sed Christo: Quomodo in Salomonem Davidis Filium existimatis convenire, quod scriptum est: quia perma- nebit cum Sole & ante Lunam in sæcula sæculorum, cum ille brevis vitæ adeptus usuram, angustis terminis vivendi spatium transegerit? Quomodo autem de eo dicitur: dominabitur à mari usque ad mare, cum ille intra Syriam constitutus, h. e. intra unius regionis provinciam, circumscriptos fines habuerit imperii: so- lus autem Christus usque in orbis terminos suum pro- pagavit imperium? Solus enim iste est, de quo bene- Psalmi series prophetavit, quia Reges Arabum & Saba dona adducent, & adorabunt eum omnes Re- ges terræ: omnes gentes servient ei. Hunc enim novimus gentibus universis & nationibus imperantem: incircumscripto imperio, intermina potestate.

## 72:1 Addition
On Psalm 72, the final words.

Regarding those words of the Epilogue also: The prayers of David are ended, it is observed that Ambrose, Augustine, Rufinus, Apollinaris, Euthymius, Nicephorus, Cajetan, Lindanus, and Jansenius make them the beginning of Psalm 73, i.e., the prayers of David are ended, how good God is to Israel, meaning: David cannot attain this with his prayers; but we leave this opinion in its proper place.

Latin:

Ad Psal, 72. verba ultima.

De verbis etiam illis Epilogi: Defecerunt lau- des David, observatur, quod Ambrosius, Augusti- nus, Ruffinus, Apollinaris, Euthymius, Nicephorus, Cajetanus, Lindanus, Jansenius ea faciant initium Ps. 73. h. m. defecerunt laudes David, quam bonus Israeli sit Deus q.d. David hoc laudibus assequi non potest: sed hanc sententiam merito suo loco relinquimus.

## 72:5
Vers. 5. AND HE SHALL REMAIN WITH THE SUN, AND BEFORE THE MOON THROUGHOUT GENERATION AND GENERATION) In the Hebrew: They shall fear thee with the sun, and while the moon shall appear, offspring of offspring, that is, the descendants of Solomon. Similar is that of Ovid: With the sun and moon Aratus shall always be.

This is a manifest perversion: for it is most well known that the words דור דורים in the Scriptures signify perpetuity and continuation from generation to generation; and here they are all the more to be taken in this way, because the Holy Scripture is intent on emphatically expressing that perpetuity of the Messianic kingdom, in which they shall fear the Lord as long as the Sun shall be, and while the Moon shall appear from generation to generation. Nor did the Chaldean, or the LXX interpreters, or the Vulgate, or Jerome, or any other interpreter, whether of the Jews or of the Christians, accept those words otherwise. Certainly, that gloss about the descendants of Solomon came into no one's mind. Which also is plainly opposed to history. For what? Did the descendants of Solomon either remain or are they going to remain with the Sun, and while the Moon shall appear, or did they fear the Lord? Grotius seems to have been asleep while he smeared these things onto the pages.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ET PERMANEBIT CVM SOLE, ET ANTE LVNAM IN GENERATIONE ET GENERATIONEM) In Hebræo: Timebunt te cum Sole, & dum apparebit Luna soboles sobolis, id est, posteri Salomonis. Simile illud Ovidii: Cum Sole & Luna semper Aratus erit.

Manifesta hæc est perversio: verba enim דור דורים in Scripturis perpetuitatem & continuatio- nem de generatione in generationem fignificare, no- tiffimum est : atque hic eo magis ita accipienda, quod S. S. in eo sit, ut emphatice illam perpetuita- tem regni Messiani exprimat, in quo Dominum ti- mebunt, quam diu Sol erit, & dum apparebit Luna de generatione in generationem. Nec aliter acceperunt verba illa Chaldæus vel LXX. interpp. vel Vulgatus, vel Hieronymus, vel ullus Interpp. seu Judæorum, seu Christianorum alius. Nemini certe illa glossa de po- steris Salomonis in mentem venit. Quæ etiam hi- storiæ plane adversatur. Quid enim? Num posteri Salomonis vel mansere aut mansuri sunt cum Sole, & dum apparebit Luna, vel timuere Dominum? Dormitasse videtur Grotius, dum hæc chartis illevit

## 72:16
Verse 16. AND THERE SHALL BE A SUPPORT) He reads in the Greek στήριγμα: which reading has long prevailed, although it is corrupted from σίτου δράγμα, a handful of grain. For that is, פסת־בר, as the Chaldean has interpreted here, a particle of grain. We are accustomed, however, to designate the smallest quantity by the name of a handful, as appears in 1 Kings 18:44.

Verse same. IN THE EARTH ON THE TOPS OF THE MOUNTAINS) In the soil of a mountain summit, such places as are wont to be rocky and therefore sterile.

HIS FRUIT SHALL BE EXALTED ABOVE LEBANON) So also the Greeks: ὑπεραρθήσεται ὑπὲρ τὸν Λίβανον ὁ καρπὸς αὐτοῦ. But the Hebrew sounds more like: His fruit shall be moved like Lebanon. That is, so little grain sown in the most unhappy soil will produce a crop which, shaken by the wind, shall rustle no less than the trees of Lebanon. A description of the greatest fertility, which was to be under King Solomon. Thus Aben-Ezra and Kimchi. Homer in the description of a good King: - - - And the black earth bears wheat and barley, and the trees are laden with fruit.

AND THEY SHALL FLOURISH FROM THE CITY LIKE THE GRASS OF THE EARTH) From the city is said elliptically for men from the city: that is, citizens. And he said grass again, as the Greeks χόρτον, signifying green herb. See above 37, verse 2.

Grotius rightly corrects the Vulgate here, whose error he deduces from the depravation which crept into the Greek text. It is strange, however, that he did not also shout here that the Hebrew sources are corrupted. But with the same ease that the Greek translation could be depraved here, he ought to have thought that in other places also, mistakes and corruptions could have crept into it, thus he would not have had to accuse the sources themselves. He reads, he says of the Vulgate, from the Greek στήριγμα, which reading has long prevailed, although it is corrupted from σίτου δράγμα, a handful of grain. For that is פסת־בר, as the Chaldean has interpreted here, a particle of grain. We are accustomed, however, to designate the smallest quantity by the name of a handful, as appears in 1 Kings 18:44. These are the words of Grotius. We add also the rest, by which he explains this passage not inappropriately, which words are: IN THE EARTH ON THE TOPS OF THE MOUNTAINS. In the soil of a mountain summit, such places as are wont to be rocky, and therefore sterile. HIS FRUIT SHALL BE EXALTED ABOVE LEBANON. So also the Greeks ὑπεραρθήσεται ὑπὲρ τὸν Λίβανον ὁ καρπὸς αὐτοῦ, but the Hebrew sounds more like: His fruit shall be moved like Lebanon. That is, so little grain, sown in the most unhappy soil, will produce a crop which, shaken by the wind, shall rustle no less than the trees of Lebanon. Thus Grotius interpreted the words. Which interpretation we have also produced from R. David Kimchi in the Rostock Dissertations, in the first dissertation, or in our inaugural Disputation, page 71: In the days of this King there shall be enough blessing in the world, so that a man will sow a handful of grain even on the top of the mountains, from which shall arise ears so good and fat that, with the wind blowing, they shall make a rustling sound, such as the trees of Lebanon make. But regarding the application, Grotius is vehemently too much mistaken, while he takes those things concerning the time of Solomon, and brings in R. David Kimchi, along with Aben-Ezra, to that opinion. A description, he says, of the greatest fertility, which was to be under King Solomon. Thus Aben-Ezra and Kimchi. And yet neither hands down this application: Aben-Ezra applies it thus, that which is said about the handful of grain: the poor who were few shall be greatly multiplied through his mercy. R. David Kimchi, however, interprets it openly concerning the days of the Messiah. There shall be, he says, a blessing in the days of Christ: If a man sows a handful of grain for the poor, even on the top of the mountains, yet the ears shall be fat and full: THEY SHALL FLOURISH FROM THE CITY LIKE GRASS. Outside the city the fruits and inside the city the men shall be blessed, and shall be multiplied like grass. These are the words of R. Kimchi, who is more sound here than the Christian Grotius; and he saw that those things could not be accepted concerning Solomon, but were to be understood concerning the Kingdom of Christ, which even R. Obad. Gaon acknowledged: annotating these things to the words, a handful of grain: Christ shall be in the beginning like a handful of wheat, but afterwards the multitude of disciples shall grow like grass. And from where will Grotius prove their extraordinary fertility, which he says was in the time of Solomon? Certainly, the monuments of history have nothing about it. But then the following words are to be understood concerning men, not concerning the fruits of the earth: AND THEY SHALL FLOURISH FROM THE CITY LIKE THE GRASS OF THE EARTH. To which Grotius himself: from the city is said elliptically, for men from the city, that is, citizens. Therefore, the fertility of men, not of the fruits of the earth, is predicted in this kingdom, but a spiritual one, that they shall germinate with a great yield, and at the same time the word of God, which is the spiritual seed, Matthew 13. Mark 4. Luke 9. 1 Peter 1, 23. And under the name of grain, Jer. 23, 28, its power and efficacy is insinuated, because it is to unfold itself in such a way under the New Testament that it may produce a copious harvest not only in level places, but even on the highest mountain peaks, and in the midst of cities; that is, among the lowest, the highest, and those in between, outside cities and within cities: in short, that its Spirit may be felt everywhere. Bellarmine gathers this sense concerning the abundance of the word of God also from those words: And they shall flourish from the city, like the grass of the earth: explaining the same thus: and this fruit will not consist in bodily ears of corn, but in the multiplication of believers: for from the city of God, which is Jerusalem, of which it was said in Isaiah 2, out of Zion shall go forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, believers shall flourish and germinate in such abundance as grass is accustomed to germinate on the earth. And that it was so done, Luke teaches in Acts 6. And the word of GOD GREW, and the number of believers was multiplied greatly. But what of this saying: And men shall flourish from the city, that is, citizens like the grass of the earth, if they are taken with Grotius concerning bodily fecundity under Solomon? What peculiar and proper thing did the Solomonic times have in that matter?

Latin:

Vers. 16. ET ERIT FIRMAMENTVM) Legit in Græco στήριγμα : quæ lectio pridem invaluit, cum corrupta sit ex σί- του δράγμα, pugillus frumenti. Id enim, פסת־בר, ut Chal- dæus hic interpretatus est, particula frumenti. Solemus au- tem minimam quantitatem designare pugilli nomine, ut ap- paret 1. Reg. 18, 44.

Vers. eod. IN TERRA IN SVMMIS MONTIVM) In Solo verticis montani, qualia loca solent esse saxosa ac pro- inde sterilia.

SVPEREXTOLLETVR SVPER LIBANVM FRV- CTVS EJVS) Sic & Græci : ὑπεραρθήσεται ὑπὲρ τὸν Λίβα- νον ὁ καρπὸς αὐτοῦ. Sed Hebræum magis sonat: Movebi- tur ut Libanus fructus ejus. Id est, tam pauxillum frumenti satum in solo infelicissimo segetem producet, quæ concus- sa vento strepat non minus quam arbores Libani. Descriptio summæ fœcunditatis, quæ futura erat sub rege Solomone. Ita Aben-Esdra & Kimchi. Homerus in boni Regis descriptione: - - - Φέρῃσι δὲ γαῖα μέλαινα Πυροὺς καὶ κριθὰς, βρίθῃσι δὲ δένδρεα καρπῷ.

ET FLOREBVNT DE CIVITATE SICVT FOENVM TERRÆ) De civitate ἐκπιτικῶς dictum pro homines de ci- vitate : id est, cives. Et fœnum rursus dixit, ut Græci χόρ- τον, herbam virentem significans. Vide supra 37. vers. 2.

Recte hic corrigit Grotius vulgatam, cujus errorem è depravatione, quæ in Græcum textum irrepserit, deducit. Mirum autem, quod hic etiam non clamitarit fontes Ebræos corruptos esse. Qua vero facilitate depravari hic potuit Græca transla- tio, eadem, cogitare debuisset, in aliis etiam locis irrepere in eandem sphalmata & corruptelas po- tuisse, sic fontes ipsos non opus habuisset accusare. Legit, inquit de vulgato, è Græco στήριγμα, quæ le- ctio pridem invaluit, cum corrupta sit, ex σίτου δρά- γμα pugillus frumenti. Id enim פסת־בר ut Chal- dæus hic interpretatus est, particula frumenti. Sole- mus autem minimam quantitatem designare pugilli nomine, ut apparet 1. Reg. 18, 44. Hæc Grotius. Ad- dimus & reliqua, quibus hunc locum non incom- de, qua verba, explicat: IN TERRA IN SUM- MIS MONTIUM. In solo verticis montani, qua- lia loca solent esse saxosa, ac proinde sterilia. SUPER- EXTOLLETUR SUPER LIBANUM FRU- CTUS EJUS. Sic & Græci ὑπεραρθήσεται ὑπὲρ τὸν Λίβανον ὁ καρπὸς αὐτοῦ, sed Hebræum magis sonat: Movebitur ut Libanus fructus ejus. Id est, tam pauxil- lum frumenti, satum in solo infelicissimo segetem produ- cet, quæ concussa vento strepat, non minus quam arbo- res Libani. Sic interpretatus est verba Grotius. Qua- lem interpretationem è R. David Kimchi etiam in Dissertationibus Rostochiensibus dissertatione prima, vel Disputatione nostra inaugurali pag. 71. produximus : In diebus hujus Regis satis erit benedi- ctio in mundo, ut seminaturus sit homo pugillum fru- menti etiam in vertice montium, unde exorituræ spi- cæ adeo bonæ & pingues, ut flante vento strepitum edi- turæ sint, qualem edunt arbores Libani. Sed quoad applicationem vehementer nimium fallitur Gro- tius, dum illa de tempore Salomonis accipit, atque in eam sententiam etiam R. David Kimchium, cum Aben-Ezra adducit. Descriptio, inquit, summæ fœcun- ditatis, quæ futura erat sub Rege Salomone. Ita Aben- Ezra & Kimchi. Atqui neuter hanc applicationem tradit: Aben-Ezra ita applicat, quod de manipulo frumenti dicitur: pauperes qui pauci erant per mise- ricordiam ejus valde multiplicabuntur. R. David Kimchi vero aperte de diebus Messiæ interpreta- tur. Erit, inquit, benedictio in diebus Christi: Si se- minaverit homo pauperibus manipulum frumenti, licet in vertice montium, tamen spicæ erunt pingues & plenæ: FLOREBUNT DE CIVITATE SICUT GRAMEN. Extra urbem fructus & in- tra urbem homines benedicentur, & multiplicabun- tur ut gramen. Hæc R. Kimchi, qui hic magis sanus est, quam Grotius Christianus; viditque non posse illa de Salomone accipi, sed intelligenda esse de Re- gno Christi, quod etiam R. Obad. Gaon agnovit: ad verba, manipulus frumenti, hæc annotans: Id Chri- stus erit in principio sicut manipulus tritici, sed postea multitudo discipulorum sicut herba crescet. Et unde probabit Grotius extraordinariam illorum fœcun- ditatem, quam tempore Salomonis fuisse dicit? Nihil certe de ea historiarum habent monumenta. Tum vero de hominibus verba sequentia intelli- genda, non de fructibus terræ: ET FLORE- BUNT DE CIVITATE SICUT FOENUM TERRÆ. Ad quæ Grotius ipse: de civitate ἐλλει- πτικῶς dictum, pro homines de civitate, id est, cives. Hominum ergo, non fructuum terræ fœcunditas in hoc regno prædicitur, sed spiritualis, quod ma- gno proventu germinaturi sint, simulque verbi Dei, quod semen spirituale est, Matth. 13. Marc. 4. Luc. 9. 1. Petr. 1, 23. & frumenti nomine venit Jer. 23, 28. vis & efficacia insinuatur, quod ea ita se explicatu- ra sit sub N. T. ut non modo campestribus in locis, sed in summis etiam montium cacuminibus, inque mediis urbibus copiosam messem producat, hoc est, penes infimos, summos, & medioximos, extra civitates & in civitatibus: breviter: ut ubique Spiri- tus ejus sentiatur. Hunc sensum de abundantia ver- bi Dei colligit Bellarm. etiam ex illis verbis: Et flo- rebunt de civitate, sicut fœnum terræ: eadem ita ex- ponens: & hic fructus non consistet in spicis corpora- libus, sed in multiplicatione credentium: nam ex civi- tate Dei, quæ est Jerusalem, de qua dictum est Es. 2. de Sion exibit Lex, & verbum Domini de Jerusalem, florebunt & germinabunt credentes in tanta copia, ut fœnum in terra germinare solet. Et quod ita factum sit, docet Lucas Act. 6. Et verbum DEI CRESCEBAT, & multiplicabatur numerus credentium valde. Quid vero hoc dictum: Et florebunt homines de civitate, id est, cives sicut fœnum terræ, si de fœcunditate cor- porali sub Salomone accipiantur cum Grotio? Quidnam ea in re peculiare atque proprium ha- buere tempora Salomonea?

## 72:17
Verse 17. MAY HIS NAME BE BLESSED FOREVER, BEFORE THE SUN HIS NAME SHALL REMAIN) That 'blessed' is neither in the Hebrew, nor was it in the Hexapla. The sense of the Hebrew is: His name shall be perpetual before the Sun: (that is, while the Sun shall shine, by the same manner of speaking which we had above concerning the Moon) his name shall sprout, that is, his descendants shall be celebrated through his memory. נִין son. The word is Philistine, Gen. 21, 23, and Arabic, Job 18, v. 19. Hence the Egyptians took the name νίνις.

Although that BLESSED, as a word, is not found here in the Hebrew, nor in the Hexapla, which was observed also by Theodoret; yet as to the matter, it is held in the preceding, verse 11. All the kings of the earth shall adore him, verse 15. they shall adore before him always, all the day they shall bless him: it is held also in the following, verse 18. all nations shall call him blessed, that is, they shall glorify him, or his name shall be blessed among all nations: and also verse 20. blessed be the name of his majesty forever. Therefore it is expressed by the LXX Interpreters and The Vulgate, as well as the Arabic, as also in the commentaries of Jerome, Augustine, and Euthymius. Nor do the words, before the Sun, pertain to the former clause, but to the latter, in this way: His name shall be for ages: before the Sun his name shall flourish, or while the Sun shines. But this cannot be understood of Solomon; whose name is so far from having obtained unblemished and perennial praise, that he is very ill spoken of in Holy Scripture on account of idolatry. Nor were his descendants so celebrated for piety, which is the chief praise; most of them are highly distinguished for impiety. And how are his descendants celebrated through the name of Solomon, or his memory, or what did it matter that it should be celebrated in such a distinguished prophecy by the Holy Spirit with that apparatus of words? Certainly his descendants have a name more through the memory of David, for whose sake the Lord kept a lamp for himself in Israel. But interpreters accept these things concerning Christ with great consensus, as being he of whom both the preceding and the following things speak: just as that which is immediately subjoined, And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him, suits no one else but Christ. Those words are indeed liable to various explanations, but in this almost all agree, that they speak of Christ. The Chaldean Interpreter translates the same thus: קדם מהוי שמשא מזמן הוה שמיה, that is, from the existing of the Sun his name was prepared. Galatinus, book 4, ch. 13, p. 222, cites Jonathan's translation, which is this וַשְׁמֵיהּ דְּאִמַר מֶלֶךְ רַמִּין מִן קְמֵי עוֹלָמָא, the Syriac version has it thus: קדם שמשא איתוהי שמה: Before the Sun, or before the Sun, is his name. The LXX rendered it: πρὸ τo͂ῦ ἡλίε διαμένει τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτο͂ῦ. And the Vulgate: before the Sun his name remains. Certain Rabbis took יִנּוֹן as a proper name of the Messiah, and hence perhaps they referred the name of the Messiah among the seven things which they invented were created two thousand years before the foundation of the world. Thus in the Code Sanhedrin, ch. 2, they say, who from the School of R. Janna say the name of the Messiah is Jinnon, according to that, Jinnon is his name. Aben-Ezra rendered it יִקָּרֵא בֶן he shall be called Son. R. Solomon, He shall rule, he shall be magnified, etc. From this flowed an almost eightfold interpretation of this passage; some taking the word יִנּוֹן as a proper name, others as a verb: and these again rendering it either by the past or future, these finally either actively or passively. Thus also לפני־שמש some explained before the Sun, others at the face of the Sun, others above the Sun. Every difficulty, however, has arisen chiefly from the little word יִנּוֹן ἅπαξ λεγομένῃ. (1) The Talmudists understood the words of the Psalmist concerning the eternity of the proper name of the Messiah, Jinnon. (2.) Concerning the eternal propagation of the name of the Messiah (indefinitely and without mention of any certain name) R. Joseph the Blind in the Targum. (3.) Concerning the eternal constitution of the King Messiah, with Jonathan's TARGUM R. Salom. in the commentary on Micah 5. (4.) Concerning the pre-eternal existence of the Word of God, i.e., of Christ, Tertullian adv. Marc. book 5, ch. 9, on the occasion of the version of the LXX who explained it πρὸ τo͂ῦ ἡλίε before the Sun. Although I judge that for them the little word πρὸ here is the same as ἐνώπιον and ἔμπροσθεν, which is not infrequent among the Greeks; otherwise it would have been said very improperly, he shall remain before the Sun. (5.) Concerning the pre-eternal generation of the Son of God, Burgensis, Galatinus book 5, ch. 15, col. 141, with the Talmudists, to whom Mr. Helvicus adds his calculation, T. IV. Disp. 5. Giess. th. 23. p. 118. (6.) Concerning the perpetual propagation of the name of Christ, B. Luther, Gesner, Tremellius, Junius, Glassius, and very many others. (7.) Concerning the future resuscitation of the dead, again Galatinus from Midrash Tehillim on Ps. 93. (For thus he says in the loc. cit. p. 143. Jinnon signifies both born and making to be born: so that two things are hinted at in one word, viz., the eternal birth of the Messiah, by which he was eternally born from the Father, and the resurrection of the dead, whom he, raising up at the end of the world, will make to be born as it were anew.) (8.) Finally, concerning the sum of the name, i.e.

the virtue of the word of the Messiah, which surpasses the Sun in efficacy, which explanation I find in D. Justin Martyr in the Dialogue with Trypho, p. 274. πυρωδέστερος γὰρ αὐτοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ σοφίας λόγος, καὶ φωτεινότερος μᾶλλον τῶν ἡλίου δυνάμεων ἐστι, καὶ εἰς τὰ βάθη τῆς καρδίας καὶ τοῦ νοῦ εἰσδύνων, ὅθεν καὶ ὁ λόγος ἔφη ὑπὲρ τὸν ἥλιον ἀνατελεῖ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ i.e., more ardent is his word, namely of truth and wisdom, and much more lucid than the powers of the Sun, and it penetrates into the recesses of the heart and mind: whence it was also said: Above the Sun his name shall arise. But of these interpretations only the antepenultimate is conformable to the text, whether you look at the words or the underlying matter. For the words לפני־שמש are said in the same sense as in verse 5, לפני־ירח that is, as long as the Sun shall shine, as long as the Moon shall shine; Luther: So lange die Sonn währet, so lang der Mond währet. The same sense of this locution seems to be in Job 8:16. רטוב הוא לפני שמש he is green at the faces of the Sun. Nor is the passage Ps. 102:29 unlike it, where לפניך is before you, or at your faces. Which the LXX Interpreters rendered εἰς αἰῶνας Since God remains for eternity. And the Sons of God live eternally beside him. Just as R. Solomon in Ex. ch. 20, v. 3. You shall not have strange Gods על־פני before me, that is, as long as I shall be God, or for eternity. But most convenient is that passage which R. Aben-Ezra alleges at v. 5 of this 72nd Psalm לפני ירח כדרך ירכאוך לפני עש, At the faces of the Moon, according to the way, they shall fear you at the faces of Arcturus, i.e., until Arcturus shall be, just as it stands written in Job 4, verse 19. For here that duration or permanence is noted by this preposition. Thus therefore לפני ירח is, while the Moon shall be. Which is also expressed by another phrase in this Psalm thus עד בלי ירח until there is no longer a Moon v. 7. עם שמש. Aben-Ezra עד שלא יהי ירח and the meaning is, always, or perpetually. And again כל הימים שתעמוד השמש all the days that the Sun shall stand. Furthermore, the word ינון is not a proper noun, but a verb, and indeed of the third person future Niphal from נין son (which occurs in Gen. 21:23, Job 18:19, Is. 14:22), as is evidenced by the preformative letter Jod of the 3rd person and the Dagesh, which is a mark of the rejected characteristic Nun. Therefore, it signifies in this place, he shall be sonned, he shall have offspring, he shall be propagated, just as a family is accustomed to be propagated through a continuous series and succession of sons. Namely שמו His name, of the Messiah, concerning whom the whole Psalm prophesies. Thus the meaning of the prophecy is most evident: that the Messiah will have children, and will propagate his name as long as the Sun shall be: that he will preserve his Church perpetually until the consummation of the age, in which he will have offspring, and will generate sons spiritually, who will honor and venerate his name, and will adhere to him with true faith and sincere piety.

As for the context: not less than the consequences of this passage, the antecedents, and the entire argument of the Psalm demand this meaning. For this Psalm, as was said before, is partly εὐκτικὸς (precatory), partly προφητικὸς (prophetic), partly εὐχαριστικὸς (eucharistic). And as for the prophecy (of which this present pericope is a part), it prophesies both concerning the manner of the government which the Messiah was to administer in justice and spiritual peace, v. 2, 3, 4, and concerning the flourishing of his kingdom, namely, its perpetuity, happiness, and amplitude, v. 5 et seq. Therefore, what he had said in v. 5: They shall fear thee as long as the Sun shall be, and during the Moon, generation of generations: What in v. 7: The righteous shall flourish in his days, and the abundance of peace, until there be no Moon. What in v. 11: All nations shall serve him. What in the immediately preceding verse: There shall be a handful in the earth, on the top of the mountains, his fruit shall rustle like Lebanon, and they shall flourish in the city like the grass of the earth, that is, That which is smallest will be like a handful of grain, and even if sown in the most inconvenient place, it will grow with a copious yield, and its harvest will rustle with mutual friction, like the trees of Lebanon: these things, I say, all things, nay, that whole prophecy concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, the seventeenth Psalm comprises ὡς ἐν ἐπιτομῇ καὶ συλλήβδην (in summary and collectively). Concerning the happy perpetuity of the kingdom, he says: His (the Messiah's) name shall be for an age. Concerning the perennial fecundity: His name shall sprout or be sonned while the Sun lasts. Concerning the happy and fruitful amplitude, all nations shall be blessed in him, they shall call him blessed. Nothing here about the pre-eternal constitution of the King Messiah: Nothing about the pre-eternal existence of a certain name, or of Christ himself. Nothing about the divine generation of the Son of God. Since those words exhibit a prediction of that which is to be, as are almost all other prophetic things in this Psalm concerning future things; and they look to that, both the verb of future time יִנּוֹן, and the periphrasis of duration, with the Sun, and as long as the Sun shall be, and therefore it is explained rather concerning the perpetual propagation of the kingdom of Christ, that there will always be a Church, while the Sun and Moon shall be, in which Christ begets for himself sons through the word and sacraments, who celebrate him and propagate his name.
