The words immediately preceding our passage speak of this: His name shall be for an age, which prophesy of the future, and promise the perennial celebration of the name of the Messiah in the Church until the consummation of the age. The words immediately following, which seem to exhibit a certain ἐξήγησιν (exegesis) of our passage, hint at this no less obscurely: All nations shall be blessed in him. Which is the benefit of the Messiah. They shall call him blessed. Which is the duty of his sons. It comprises both, what precedes; while the Sun shall shine, he will have sons, or the Messiah shall sprout. Namely, both the blessing of the faithful in the Messiah, and the celebration and proclamation of the Messiah in them. That in him, who shall be blessed, they in turn shall bless him. So that the name of the sons of Christ is no less a name of honor and obedience than of love and benefit. For what else is it, that the Messiah will perpetually have sons, as long as the Sun shall be: than that in the Messiah all nations shall be blessed, and shall celebrate him with faith and worship? And therefore the Arab has these things likewise, nor does he render any other ἐξήγησιν (exegesis) of these words than that which is subjoined in the text. For thus he explains the entire verse: His name shall be blessed. All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed through him, and all nations shall magnify him. For our spiritual filiation is a blessing in Christ. Conf. Ephes. 1, 3. 5. These things concerning that place ennobled by various interpretations 28 years ago proposed in our inaugural disputation at Rostock, exhibited in the Anti-Crellian Parasceve, which we have deemed necessary to repeat here for the sake of illustrating the same, since that is no longer easily found in the workshops. But those things also teach that the interpreters have constantly understood the place concerning the Messiah, even if they have gone into different opinions regarding the explanation of the words.

Verse of the same. AND ALL THE TRIBES OF THE EARTH SHALL BE BLESSED IN HIM) For it shall be said among all nations: May your kingdom be like the kingdom of Solomon.

A very inept gloss, surpassing even the highest Rabbinical trifles. For does this suit all nations, or all the tribes of the earth, are all the nations and tribes of the earth Kings, and established in empire, so that they have need of such a vow? But here all the nations of the earth are said to be those who are to be blessed, who shall call this King blessed. Which certainly cannot be understood of kings only. For will only kings call this King blessed? are only kings all nations? Then indeed that, IN HIM they shall be blessed, does not denote a similarity with him; but expresses the origin and meritorious cause of the blessing, in him, that is, through him and on account of him. Nor is there any doubt that this is taken from the promises made to the Patriarchs concerning the Messiah, that in him all the tribes of the earth are to be blessed. But what do those promises have to do with this vow concerning the similarity of the Solomonic kingdom? Which all the interpreters without exception have observed. Theodoret in this place makes mention of the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: for to these three Patriarchs God promised that he would bless, sometimes indeed all the nations of the earth, but sometimes all the tribes of the earth: In different ways he calls the whole nature of men. The blessed Paul also interpreting this, says, But the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed: he does not say, And to seeds, as of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. And also in the Epistle to the Hebrews, for nowhere does he take hold of Angels. The Psalm proposed predicts concerning this through him, saying that he would bless all the Tribes. Thus all the rest. Finally, all nations are to be blessed in him, whom they shall magnify and call blessed or glorify. But that does not suit Solomon, but Christ. For do all nations glorify Solomon?

Latin:

Vers. 17. SIT NOMEN EJUS BENEDICTUM IN SE- CVLA, ANTE SOLEM PERMANET NOMEN EJUS) Illud benedictum neque in Hebræo est, neque fuit in Hexa- plo. Sensus Hebræi est: Nomen ejus erit perpetuum coram Sole: (id est, dum Sol lucebit, eodem loquendi genere, quod supra de Luna habuimus) sobolescet nomen ejus, id est, poste- ri ipsius per ipsius memoriam erunt celebres. נִין filius. Vox est Philistinorum Gen. 21, 23. & Arabum Job. 18. v. 19. Hinc Ægyptii sumsere nomen νίνις.

Etsi illud BENEDICTUM, qua vocem, hic in Ebræo non reperiatur, nec in Hexaplo, quod observatum etiam Theodoreto; quoad rem tamen habetur in antecedentibus, vers. 11. Adora- bunt eum omnes Reges terræ vers. 15. adorabunt ante eum semper, tota die benedicent ei: habetur etiam in consequentibus, vers. 18. omnes gentes beatum prædicabunt eum, id est, glorificabunt eum, vel be- nedictum inter omnes gentes erit nomen ejus: nec non vers. 20. benedictum nomen majestatis ejus in æternum. Ideo exprimitur à LXX. Interpp. & Vulgata, nec non Arabe, ut & in commentariis Hie- ronymi, Augustini, & Euthymii. Neque verba, coram Sole, ad prius comma pertinent, sed ad posterius, hoc modo: Nomen ejus erit in secula: coram Sole so- bolescet nomen ejus, vel dum Sol lucet. De Salomone autem id intelligi non potest; cujus nomen tantum abest, ut illibatam & perennem laudem obtinue- rit, ut propter idololatriam pessime audiat in Scri- ptura S. Neque posteri ejus adeo celebres a pietate, quae praecipua laus est; plerique impietate maxime insignes sunt. Et quomodo per nomen Salomonis, vel memoriam ipsius celebrantur posteri ejus, aut quid referebat isto verborum apparatu id in vati- cinio tam insigni celebrari a S. S. Magis certe per memoriam Davidis posteri ejus nomen habent, ob quem lucernam in Israel sibi servabat Dominus. De Christo autem ista magno consensu interpre- tes accipiunt, utpote de quo & antecedentia & con- sequentia loquuntur: quemadmodum id quod im- mediate subjungitur, Et benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terrae, nulli alii, quam Christo convenit. Verba ista variis quidem explicationibus obnoxia sunt, sed in eo pleriq; omnes conveniunt, quod de Christo loquantur. Chaldaeus Interpres eadem ita vertit: קדם מהוי שמשא מזמן הוה שמיה, id est, ab existendo Solem paratum fuit nomen ejus. Galatinus lib. 4. c. 13. p. 222. adducit Jonath. translationem, quae haec est וַשְׁמֵיהּ דְּאִמַר מֶלֶךְ רַמִּין מִן קְמֵי עוֹלָמָא, Syria- ca versio ita habet: קדם שמשא איתוהי שמה: Ante Solem, vel coram Sole, est nomen ejus. LXX. red- didere: πρὸ τo͂ῦ ἡλίε διαμένει τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτο͂ῦ. Et vul- gata: ante Solem permanet nomen ejus. Rabbini qui- dam accepere יִנּוֹן ut nomen proprium Messiae, & hinc forte nomen Messiae retulerunt inter septem res, quas per duo millia annorum ante mundi constitu- tionem creatas commenti sunt. Sic in Cod. Sanhedrin c. 2. dicunt, qui de Schola R. Janna Messiae nomen es- se Jinnon, juxta illud, Jinnon est nomen ejus. Aben- Ezra reddidit יִקָּרֵא בֶן vocabitur Filius. R. Salomon, Dominabitur, magnificabitur &c. Fluxit inde octu- plex fere hujus loci interpretatio; nonnullis vocem יִנּוֹן ut nomen proprium, aliis ut verbum: & his ite- rum vel per praeteritum vel futurum, his denique vel active vel passive reddentibus, Sic & לפני־שמש qui- dam ante Solem, alii ad faciem Solis, alii super Solem exposuere. Omnis tamen difficultas potissimum or- ta est a vocula יִנּוֹן ἅπαξ λεγομένῃ. (1) De nominis proprii Messiae Jinnon aeternitate verba Psaltis intelle- xere Talmudici. (2.) De nominis Messiae (ἀορίστως & citra mentionem alicujus certi nominis) aeterna propagatione R. Joseph Caecus in Tharg. (3.) De ae- terna regis Messiae constitutione, cum Jonath. תַּרְגּוּם R. Salom. in comment. Mich. V. (4.) De praeter- na existentia Sermonis Dei, h. e. Christi Tertul. adv. Marc. l. 5. c. 9. occasione versionis τῶν LXX. qui exposuere πρὸ τo͂ῦ ἡλίε ante Solem. Tametsi censeam eis voculam πρὸ heic idem esse quod ἐνώπιον & ἔμ- προσθεν, quod haud infrequens est apud Graecos; alioquin valde ἀκύρως dictum esset, permanebit ante Solem. (5.) De praeterna Filii Dei generatione Bur- gensis, Galatinus l. 5. c. 15. col. 141, cum Talmudist. quibus calculum suum addit Dn. Helvicus, T. IV. Disp. 5. Giess. th. 23. p. 118. (6.) De perpetua nomi- nis Christi propagatione B. Luther. Gesner. Tremell. Jun. Glassius, aliiq́; plurimi. (7.) De futura mortuo- rum resuscitatione iterum Galat. ex Midrasch The- hillim super Ps. 93. (Sic enim ille l. c. p. 143. Jinnon & natum significat & nasci facientem: ut duo in verbo uno innuantur, & aeterna scil. Messiae nativitas, qua aeternaliter a Patre natus est & mortuorum resurre- ctio, quos ipse in fine mundi resuscitans, quasi denuo nasci faciet.) (8.) Denique de summa nominis h. e.

verbi Messiæ virtute, quæ Solem superat efficacia, quam explicationem invenio apud D. Justin. Mar- tyr. in Dial. cum Tryph. p. 274. πυρωδέστερος γὰρ αὐτοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ σοφίας λόγος, καὶ φω- τεινότερος μᾶλλον τῶν ἡλίου δυνάμεων ἐστι, καὶ εἰς τὰ βάθη τῆς καρδίας καὶ τοῦ νοῦ εἰσδύνων, ὅθεν καὶ ὁ λόγος ἔφη ὑπὲρ τὸν ἥλιον ἀνατελεῖ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ h. e. ar- dentius ejus est, veritatis videlicet & sapientiæ, verbum, & lucidius multo, quam Solis virtutes, & in recessus cordis atq; mentis penetrat: unde & dictum est: Super Solem exorietur nomen ejus. Sed ex his interpreta- tionibus sola antepenultima textui conformis est, si- ve verba spectes, sive materiam substratam. Qua ver- ba לפני־שמש eodem sensu dicitur, quo vers. 5. לפני־ירח hoc est, quam diu lucebit Sol, quam diu lu- cebit luna; Lutherus: So lange die Sonn währet, so lang der Mond währet. Idem loquutionis hujus sen- sus videtur esse Job. 8,16. רטוב הוא לפני שמש viridis ipse ad facies Solis. Nec absimilis est locus Ps. 102, 29. ubi לפניך est coram te, vel ad facies tuas. Quod LXX. Interpp. reddidere εἰς αἰῶνας Quando- quidem Deus permaneat in æternum. Et Filii Dei juxta eum eo æternum vivant. Perinde ut R. Salomo in Ex. c. 20. v. 3. Non habebis Deos alienos על־פני co- ram me, id est, quamdiu ego Deus ero, vel in æternum Convenientissimus vero est locus ille, quem ad v. 5. Psalmi hujus 72. allegat R. Aben-Ezra לפני ירח כדרך ירכאוך לפני עש, Ad facies Lunæ, secundum viam, conterent eos ad facies Arcturi, h. e. donec fuerit Ar- cturus, quemadmodum scriptum extat Job. 4. vers. 19. Hic enim notatur ista præpositione duratio seu permanentiæ. Sic ergo לפני ירח est, dum fuerit Luna. Quod alia phrasi in hoc Psalmo ita quoque effertur עד בלי ירח donec non amplius Luna v. 7. עם שמש. Aben-Ezra עד שלא יהי ירח והטעם תמיד vel usq; dum non erit Luna, & sensus est, jugiter, aut perpetuo. Et rursus כל הימים שתעמוד השמש omnibus die- bus quibus stabit Sol. Porro vox ינון non est nomen proprium, sed verbum, & quidem tertiæ futuri Niphal à נין filius (quod occurrit Gen. 21, 23. Job. 18, 19. Es. 14. v. 22.) uti argumento est litera Jod præformativa 3. pers. & Dagesch, quod est nota abjectæ chara- cteristicæ Nun. Significat ergo hoc loco, filiabitur, sobolescet, propagabitur, sicut familia per continuam filiorum seriem & successionem propagari solet. Scili- cet שמו Nomen ejus, Messiæ, de quo vaticinatur totus Psalmus. Quomodo sensus vaticinii eviden- tissimus est: Messiam liberos habiturum, nomenque suum propagaturum, quoad usque Sol erit: Conserva- turum perpetuo Ecclesiam suam usque ad consumma- tionem seculi, in qua sobolescet, & filios generabit spiritualiter, qui nomen suum colant & venerentur, sibiq; vera fide & sincera pietate adhærescant.

Qua contextum: exposcunt hunc sensum non minus consequentia hujus loci, quam antecedentia, totumque adeo Psalmi argumentum. Etenim Psal- mus hic, quod antea dictum est, partim εὐκτικὸς, partim προφητικὸς, partim εὐχαριστικὸς est. Et qua Prophetiam, (cujus pars aliqua est præsens pericope) vaticinatur tum de regiminis tenore, quod Messias administraturus erat in justitia & pace spirituali v. 2. 3. 4. tum regni ejus flore, utputa de perennitate, feli- citate, & amplitudine v. 5. seqq. Quod ergo v. 5. dixe- rat Reverebuntur te, quamdiu erit Sol, & durante Luna generatio generationum: Quod v. 7. Florebit in diebus ejus justus & amplitudo pacis, donec non sit Luna. Quod v. 11. omnes gentes servient ei. Quod v. immedi- ate præcedente: Erit pugillus in terra, in vertice mon- tium, perstrepet ut Libanus fructus ejus, & florebunt in civitate, sicut herba terræ, h. e. Quod minimum erit instar pugilli frumenti, & vel in loco incommodissimo satum, crescet copioso proventu, segesque ejus mutuo confrictu perstrepet, sicut Arbores Libani: Hæc inquam, omnia, imo totam illam prophetiam de Messiæ regno ὡς ἐν ἐπιτομῇ καὶ συλλήβδην comple- ďtitur versus Psalmi decimus septimus. De regni felici perennitate ait: Erit nomen ejus (Messiæ) in seculum. De perenni fœcunditate: Sobolescet vel filiabitur nomen ejus durante Sole. De felici & fœcunda ampli- tudine, benedicentur in eo omnes gentes, beatum præ- dicabunt eum. Nihil hic de præeterna Regis Messiæ constitutione: Nihil de nominis cujusdam, vel de ipsius Christi præeterna existentia. Nihil de divina Filii Dei generatione. Quum verba ista exhibeant vaticinium de eo quod futurum est, ut sunt cætera fere in hoc Psalmo Prophetica de futuris; & respi- ciunt eo tum verbum futuri temporis יִנּוֹן, tum du- rationis περίφρασις, cum Sole, & quoadusῦ, Sol fue- rit, ideoque potius de perpetua regni Christi propa- gatione exponitur, semper fore Ecclesiam, dum Sol & Luna erunt, in qua Christus sibi gignit per verbum & sacramenta filios, qui se celebrent, nomenque suum propagent. Hoc loquuntur verba proxime perico- pam nostram præcedentia: Erit nomen ejus in secu- lum, quæ de futuro vaticinantur, perennemque no- minis Messiæ celebrationem in Ecclesia pollicen- tur usque ad consummationem seculi. Hoc itidem innuunt non obscure verba immediate sequentia, quæ videntur exhibere quandam ἐξήγησιν nostræ pericopes: Benedicentur in eo omnes gentes. Quod est beneficium Messiæ. Beatum prædicabunt eum. Quod est officium filiorum ejus. Utrumque comple- ďtitur, quod antecedit; dum Sol lucebit, habebit fi- lios, vel sobolescet Messias. Scilic. tum benedictionem fidelium in Messia, tum celebrationem & deprædicatio- nem Messiæ in iisdem. Quod in ipso, qui benedicen- tur, rursus benedicent ipsum. Ut ita nomen filiorum Christi non minus sit honoris & obsequii nomen, quam amoris & beneficii. Quid enim aliud est, Mes- siam perpetuo filios habiturum, donec Sol erit: quam in Messia benedictum iri, eumque celebraturas fide & cultu omnes gentes? Ideoque hæc perinde habet A- rabs, nec aliam reddit verborum istorum ἐξήγησιν, quam eam, quæ in textu subjungitur. Sic enim ex- ponit integrum versum: Benedictum erit nomen ejus. Benedicentur per eum omnes tribus terræ, & omnes gentes magnificabunt eum. Spiritualis quippe filiatio est nostra in Christo benedictio. Conf. Ephes. 1, 3. 5. Hæc de loco illo variis interpretamentis nobilita- to ante 28. annos in disputatione nostra inaugurali Rostochii proposita in Parasceve Anti-Crelliana exhibita, quæ hic ad eundem illustrandum, siqui- dem non facile amplius illa in officinis reperiatur, repetenda duximus. Docent autem etiam illa, quod de Messia Interpp. constanter locum intel- lexerint, etsfi qua explicationem verborum in di- versas itum sit sententias.

Vers. eod. ET BENEDICENTVR IN EO OMNES TRIBVS TERRÆ) Dicetur enim apud omnes gentes: Sit regnum tuum simile regno Salomonis.

Glossa perquam inepta, nugas etiam summas Rabbinicas superans. Num enim omnibus gentibus hoc convenit, aut omnibus terræ tribubus, num gen- tes & tribus terræ omnes Reges sunt, atque in imperio constituuntur, ut tali voto opus habeant? Atqui hic omnes gentes terræ dicuntur benedicendæ, quæ beatum prædicabunt hunc Regem. Quod cer- te non de regibus tantum intelligi potest. Num e- nim soli Reges hunc Regem beatum prædicabunt? num soli Reges sunt omnes gentes? Tum vero illud, IN IPSO benedicentur, non notat similitudinem cum ipso; sed originem & causam meritoriam benedictio- nis exprimit, in ipso, id est, per ipsum & propter ipsum. Neq; dubium est, desumtum hoc esse è promissio- nibus de Messia Patriarchis factis, quod in ipso bene- dicendæ sint omnes tribus terræ. Quid autem illæ pro- missiones ad votum istud de similitudine regni Sa- lomonei? Quod observarunt Interpp. ad unum omnes. Theodoretiis hoc in loco de promissionibus Abrahæ, Isaac, & Jacob factis, mentionem facit: his enim tribus Patriarchis promisit Deus se benedi- cturum, modo quidem omnes gentes terræ, modo vero omnes tribus terræ: Diversis modis omnem hominum naturam appellat. Hoc & beatus Paulus interpretans, inquit, Abrahæ autem dictæ sunt promissiones, & se- mini ejus: non dicit: Et seminibus, quasi in multis, sed quasi in uno, & semini tuo, qui est Christus. Atque etiam in Epistola ad Hebræos, nusquam enim Ange- los apprehendit. De hoc propositus Psalmus prædicit per ipsum, dicens omnes Tribus se benedicturum esse. Sic reliqui omnes. Denique in eo benedicendæ omnes gentes sunt, quem magnificabunt & beatum prædicabunt vel glorificabunt. Id autem non con- venit Salomoni, sed Christo. Num enim omnes gentes Salomonem glorificant?

## 72:20
Verse 20. THE PRAISES OF DAVID THE SON OF JESSE HAVE ENDED) In the Greek: ἐξέλιπον οἱ ὕμνοι Δαβὶδ τẽ ὑẽ Ιεσσαỳ. So also in the Hebrew: the prayers of David the son of Jesse end. That is, the collection of Psalms made by David himself ends here: those that follow, Asaph and others, and finally Ezra, added. There are, however, among them also some made by David, but after the volume of that collection was concluded.

End of Book II of the Psalms.

Latin:

Vers. 20. DEFECERVNT LAVDES DAVID FILII JESSE) In Græco: ἐξέλιπον οἱ ὕμνοι Δαβὶδ τẽ ὑẽ Ιεσσαỳ. Sic & in Hebræo: finiunt preces Davidis filii Isai. Id est, fini- tur hîc collectio Psalmorum ab ipso Davide facta: qui se- quuntur, eos Assaph aliiqve, postremo Esdras addiderunt. Sunt tamen inter eos etiam quidam a Davide facti, sed post conclusum volumen illius collectionis.

Finis Libri II. Psalmorum.

## 73:1 Argument
BOOK THREE. PSALM LXXIII.

Israel's consolation in the prosperity of the wicked.

The title and inscription of the Psalm do not allow us to doubt that it is a Psalm of Asaph, the son of Barachiah, who was not only an excellent Musician, but also endowed with a Prophetic Spirit, and composed several Psalms 2 Chron. 29, 30: which must be held equally concerning the following 10. Therefore, one should not agree with Augustine, book 17, De Civ. Dei, ch. 14, or Cassiodorus in the Preface to the Psalter, who, just as they establish that all the Psalms which are in the book of Psalms should be ascribed to David: so they refer this Psalm also with the following ones to David as the author. For Hezekiah ordered the Psalms of both David and Asaph the seer to be sung 2 Chron. 29, 30. He distinguished, therefore, between the Psalms of David and of Asaph, but our blessed Luther did not attribute all the Psalms to David, he also observed the diversity of style in both, and judged thus: that the style of Asaph is harder than that of David: that Asaph has the style of Persius, or Horace, that is, hard: But that the style of David is Attic and elegant. Which judgment of the great man B. Selneccer praised and approved in the Preface to the Holy Psalms, and he judged that learned men, who know how to discern style, judge no otherwise. And since the preceding Psalm is concluded thus: the prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended, it is sufficiently hinted that this one and the following ones, only a few, are not David's. Therefore B. Snepfius interpreted that clause thus: Hitherto we have heard sufficiently many Psalms of David: now I shall also add those of Asaph before I weave through the remaining Psalms of David.

HOW GOOD ISRAEL GOD) Certainly God is good to Israel. Thus the Hebrew has it.

Latin:

LIBER TERTIUS. PSALM. LXXIII.

Israelis solatium in prosperitate impiorum.

PSalmum Assaphi esse, filii Barachiæ, qui non solum excellens Musicus, sed etiam Prophetico Spiritu præditus fuit, & Psalmos aliquot condidit 2. Par. 29, 30. dubitare nos non sinit titulus & in- scriptio Psalmi: quod pariter de sequentibus 10. habendum. Non ergo Augustino l. 17. de Civ. Dei c. 14. aut Cassiodoro in Præf. Psalt. assurgendum, qui uti omnes Psalmos Davidi adscribendos esse sta- tuunt, qui in Psalmorum libro habentur: ita hunc etiam Psalmum cum sequentibus ad Davidem ceu autorem referunt. Jussit enim Ezechias & Davidis & Assaphi videntis Psalmos decantari 2. Par. 29, 30. Distinxit ergo inter Davidis Psalmos & Assaphi, non vero omnes Psalmos Davidi tribuit B. Luthe- rus noster, styli etiam diversitatem in utroque ob- servavit, atque ita judicavit: Assaphi stylum durio- rem esse, quam Davidis: Assaphum habere stylum Persii, vel Horatii, id est, durum: Sed Davidis sty- lum esse Atticum, & elegantem. Quod judicium Megalandri B, Selneccerus laudavit, & approbavit in Præf. ad S. Ps. nec aliter judicare doctos, qui sty- lum discernere norunt, censuit. Et quum præcedens Psalmus ita concludatur: finiunt orationes Davidis filii Isai, satis innuitur, hunc & sequentes, solum a- liquot, non esse Davidis. Ideo clausulam illam ita interpretatus est B. Snepfius: Hactenus satis multos Psalmos audivimus Davidis: jam subjiciam & Assaph antequam reliquos Psalmos Davidis pertexam.

Vers. 1. QVAM BONVS ISRAEL DEVS) Certe bonus Israeli Deus. Sic habet Hebræum.

## 73:2
THEIR INIQUITY HATH COME FORTH AS IT WERE FROM FATNESS.

So the Vulgate with the LXX Interpreters, whom also the Syrian and Arab follow, but against the Hebrew truth, which Bellarmine rashly accuses of corruption. For the sense is excellent: their eye has come forth from fatness, from their excessive fatness their eye protrudes, so they care for their skin; or if the eye is taken for the countenance and face, they are so fat and well-fed that the face swells with fatness: as Bugenhagius with Felix rendered it. But in the Greek and Latin Vulgate a suitable sense will hardly be given. For what is this: Pro- did their iniquity come out of fatness? Therefore it is a παρόραμα (oversight), because the LXX read עונמו instead of עינימו. Which indeed was correctly read by the Chaldean and thus rendered פרצופיהון, Their faces.

Latin:

Vers. 2. PRODIIT QVASI EX ADIPE INIQVITAS EORUM.

Ita vulgatus cum LXX Interpp. quos etiam Sy- rus & Arabs sequuntur, sed invita veritate Ebraica, quam temere corruptionis arguit Bellarm. Sensus enim optimus est, exiit præ adipe oculus eorum, ex nimia pinguedine eorum oculus eminet, ita cuti- culam curant; vel si oculus pro vultu & facie accipia- tur, adeo pingues sunt & bene pasti, ut facies pin- guedine intumescat: uti Bugenhagius cum Felice reddidit. In Græca vero & Vulgata Latina vix sen- sus conveniens dabitur. Quid enim hoc est: Pro- diit ex adipe iniquitas eorum? ideoque παρόραμα est, quod LXX. עונמו legerunt loco עינימו. Quod utique à Chaldaeo recte lectum atque ita redditum est פרצופיהון Vultus eorum.

## 73:24
Vers. 24. AND WITH GLORY THOU HAST RECEIVED ME) And with honor thou hast received me. Thou hast made me king. For Asaph composed these things in praise of David. אחר is translated by σὺν, above 49. v. 18.

But why could not Asaph, and any faithful Israelite, sing and consider this concerning himself, that he is to be assumed gloriously at last, if the ellipsis of the prefix ב is (in) glory, or if ל is (in) glory? Prov. 15. v. 33. c. 18. v. 12. Rom. 8. v. 18. 2. Tim. 3. v. 12. Conf. Grotius on Zach. 2. v. 8. Concerning v. 25. & 26. See what is in Sermon 16. on the memory of the just, Witteb.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ET CVM GLORIA SVSCEPISTI ME) Et cum honore suscepisti me. Fecisti me regem. Nam Asaphut haec composuit in laudem Davidis. אחר per σὺν vertitur, supra 49. v. 18.

Cur vero non Assaph, & quilibet fidelis Israe- lita de se hoc canere, ac considerare possit, quod as- sumendus sit tandem gloriose, si ellipsis praefixi ב sit, (in) gloria, vel si ל (in) gloriam? Prov. 15. v. 33. c. 18. v. 12. Rom. 8. v. 18. 2. Tim. 3. v. 12. Conf. Grotius in Zach. 2. v. 8. De v. 25. & 26. Vid. quae Concio- ne 16. in memor. justor. Witteb.

## 73:24 Addition
On Psalm 73, v. 24. WHAT HAVE I IN HEAVEN.

Piscator and Amama cavil at Luther here in vain. For the sense comes to the same thing; which Luther wished to express more emphatically, that there is nothing in heaven or on earth that delights one except God. In which manner Vatablus also rendered it, nor is the Belgian explanation different, but for these see Luther himself, Vol. V, Jena, German, f. 354.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 73. v. 24. QVID MIHI EST IN COELO.

Frustra Piscator & Amama Lutherum hic ca- villantur. Eodem enim sensus recidit; quem ma- gis emphatice exprimere voluit Lutherus, nihil esse in cœlo vel in terra, quod delectet præter Deum. Quo pacto etiam Vatablus reddidit, nec diversa est expli- catio Belgica, sed de his vid. ipse Lutherus Tom. V. Jen. Germ. f. 354.

## 74:1 Argument
PSALM. LXXIV. A miserable turtledove.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXIV. Turtur miserabilis.

## 74:1 Addition
On Psalm 47.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 74.

## 74:1 Addition
Verse 1. O CLAP YOUR HANDS, ALL YE NATIONS.

From this verse, and verses 9 and 10, compared with Matthew 8:10, 11, it is manifest that these things pertain to the conversion of the nations, and therefore are rashly snatched away by the Jews, Vatablus, Jansenius, Genebrardus, Sa, Calvin, Musculus, Moller, the Dutch, and Bohlius to the bringing in of the ark into Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:15, 1 Chronicles 13:8. Hence, with great consensus, they interpret verse 6 concerning the ascension of Christ: which was the efficient and promoting cause of the union of the nations with the people of God, Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 1. OMNES GENTES PLAUDITE.

E versu hocce, & 9. ac 10. collato cum Matth. 8, 10. 11. manifestum est, ad conversionem gentium hæc pertinere, adeoque temere a Judæis, Vatablo, Jansenio, Genebrardo, Saa, Calvino, Musculo, Molle- ro, Belgis, Bohlio ad inductionem arcæ in Jerusalem abripi 2. Sam. 6, 15. 1. Chron. 13. 8. Proinde magno consensu de ascensione Christi v. 6. interpretantur: quæ causa fuit efficiens, & promovens conjunctionem gentium cum populo Dei Abraham.

## 74:1 Addition
On Psalm 74, v. 1. O GOD, WHY HAST THOU CAST US OFF FOR EVER.

Regarding the argument of this Psalm, the blessed Hülsemann has it thus on v. 9: That calamity of which this Psalm speaks is not to be explained as the Babylonian captivity under the Assyrians, nor the calamity under Antiochus, which persecutions nevertheless had certain miraculous or prophetic or heroic events. (Although even our own people, Snepfius, Gesner, the Vinarieans, Arndt, in his Exposition of the Psalms, Boblius, and Luther himself in the marginal glosses to this Psalm, although these do not mention the Assyrian disaster in particular, seem to have explained it so) but as the final destruction of the temple under Titus, and the devastation of the synagogues throughout all Judea, as Jansenius, Agellius, Lorinus, Simon Muis, Jacob Valentia, and others do. For although the final destruction of the temple was indeed accomplished by fire, just as in the time of the Assyrians and Antiochus, yet images and idolatrous pictures were thrust into the temple before the final conflagration, from Dan. 9:26, 27. Matt. 24:15, before the final conflagration under Titus as well, Josephus expressly records that everything was first cast down with axes, and Egesippus in the history of the last temple. And therefore, since the total lack of prophecy belongs only to the final conflagration of the temple, and then also the total lack of gracious divine prodigies, we therefore side with those who say that David in this Psalm lamented the final destruction of the Jerusalem temple under the type of future calamities of the Church, which the Belgians do: extending some things to the disaster of the Babylonians and Antiochus, yet the whole Psalm to the imminent calamities of the New Testament Church.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 74. v. 1. UT QVID DEUS REPULISTI IN FINEM.

De argumento hujus Psalmi sic habet B. Hül- semann. ad v. 9. Calamitas illa, de qua hic Psalmus loquitur, non de captivitate Babylonica sub Assyriis, nec de calamitate sub Antiocho, quæ persecutiones quædam tamen miracula vel Prophetica vel heroica habuerunt. (Quanquam etiam nostrates Snepfius, Gesnerus, Vinarienses, Arndt, in Exposit. Psalmo- rum, Boblius, Lutherus ipse in glossis marginalibus „ad hunc Psalmum, etsi hæ cladem Assyriacam in „specie non commemorent, videntur exposuisse) „sed de ultima destructione templi sub Tito, & va- „statione Synagogarum per universam Judæam „exponenda, ut Jansenius, Agellius, Lorinus, Si- „mon Muis, Jacob. Valentia, & alii. Quanquam „enim ultima destructio templi facta fuerit igne, „perinde ut Assyriorum & Antiochi tempore, ima- „gines tamen & picturas idololatricas ante ultimam „conflagrationem fuisse templo obtrusas ex Dan. „9, 26. 27. Matth. 24, 15. ante ultimam conflagratio- „nem sub Tito quoque, primum securibus omnia „fuisse dejecta expresse Josephus commemorat, & „Egesippus in historia ultimi templi. Ideoque „cum totalis defectus Prophetiæ, soli ultimæ con- „flagrationi templi competat, deinde totalis etiam „defectus gratiosorum prodigiorum divinorum, „ideo facimus cum iis, qui Davidem hoc Psalmo „de ultimo excidio templi Hierosolymitani sub „typo futurarum calamitatum Ecclesiæ conque- „stum ajunt, quod Belgæ faciunt: Quædam exten- „dentes ad Babyloniorum & Antiochi cladem, to- „tum tamen Psalmum ad calamitates Ecclesiæ N. „T. imminentes.

## 74:6
Vers. 6. AS IN A FOREST OF TREES THEY CUT DOWN THE DOORS THEREOF WITH AXES: WITH AXE AND HATCHET THEY CAST IT DOWN) Namely the tabernacle of Shiloh, where the Ark was. The history which is in 1. Sam. 4. is represented here. פתוחיה its doors, not, as some say, its carvings. In Hebrew it is feminine, because it is understood from the aforementioned 4. מועד, which is of the feminine gender: and it signifies first a meeting, then indeed the place of meeting, as among the Greeks ἐκκλησία. These things, although, as I think, said about that time, nevertheless wonderfully agree with those things which happened under Nebuchadnezzar and Titus. The word כילפות which the Latin translates as hatchet, others better as hammer, is Philistine, to denote the time: it remains among the Arabs.

That these things were said about that time (namely David's), even if they were said at that time, is by no means clear; indeed, these things do not agree with that time: Therefore they are taken prophetically, and are explained by some directly concerning the devastation of Nebuchadnezzar; but they could not say at what time: He is no Prophet; by others concerning the destruction of Titus, such as Augustine, Theodoret, Euthymius, but then the Jews were not the sheep of the Lord's pasture: But they are most correctly taken concerning the time of Antiochus, with the favor of B. Luther in the argument of this and the 79th Psalm, Jansenius, Arias Montanus, Bellarmine, who may be compared here. Cocceius attributes it to the Church after the times of Solomon until the consummation of the age, urging this especially, that the temple was not burned in the time of Antiochus, as v. 8. is hinted. But that is to be understood μερικῶς (partially), as the gates of the temple were burned 1. Macc. 4. or that they cast fire into the Sanctuary and having burned its gates polluted it, the words of the context teach, for if they had burned the whole, they would not have polluted it. In Hebrew it is, they sent the sanctuary into the fire, by hypallage for they sent fire into the sanctuary. Even to the ground, that is, they profaned it to the last degree. Conf. Ps. 89. v. 40. Ps. 55. v. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 6. QVASI IN SILVA LIGNORVM SECVRI- BVS EXCIDERVNT JANVAS EAS IN IDIPSVM: IN SECVRI ET ASCIA DEJECERVNT EAM) Nempe tentorium Siloh, ubi erat Arca. Repraesentatur hic historia quae est 1. Sam. 4. פתוחיה januas ejus, non, ut quidam sculpturas ejus. Ejus in Hebraeo femininum est, quia sub- auditur ex superius dicto 4. מועד, quod est generis femi- nini: & primo quidem conventum, deinde vero & conven- tus locum significat, ut apud Graecos ἐκκλησία. Haec quan- quam, ut puto, de illo dicta tempore, mire tamen conveni- unt in ea quae sub Nabuchodonosoro & Tito evenerunt. Vox כילפות quam asciam transfert Latinus, alii meli- us malleum, est Philistina, ad notandum tempus: manet apud Arabas.

De illo (Davidis nempe) tempore ista dicta esse, etsi illo dicta sint tempore, minime liquet, imo non conveniunt haec isti tempori: Ideo prophe- tice accipiuntur, & de Nebucadnezaris à non- nullis directe explicantur devastatione; Quo vero tempore dicere non poterant: Non est Pro- pheta; ab aliis de eversione Titi, utpote August. Theodoreto, Euthymio, sed tum Judaei non erant oves pascuae Domini: Rectissime autem de tem- pore Antiochi accipiuntur, favente B. Luthero in argumento hujus & 79. Psalmi, Jansenio, Aria- montano, Bellarmino, qui hic conferantur. Cocce- jus Ecclesiae tribuit post Salomonis tempora usque ad consummationem seculi, hoc imprimis urgens, quod tempore Antiochi non sit combustum tem- plum, ut v. 8. innuitur. Sed id μερικῶς intelligen- dum esse, qua portas templi exustas 1. Macc. 4. vel quod injecerint ignem in Sanctuarium & portis ejus exustis id polluerint, contextus verba docent, nam si totum combussissent, non polluissent. In Ebr. est, miserunt in ignem sanctuarium per hypal- lagen pro ignem immiserunt sanctuario. Ad ter- ram usque, hoc est, ad extremum usque gradum profanarunt. Conf. Ps. 89. v. 40. Ps. 55. v. 21.

## 74:12 Addition
On verse 2. HE HATH WROUGHT SALVATION IN THE MIDST OF THE EARTH.

Jerome takes this as referring to Judea, which is situated in the midst of the earth, or to Jerusalem, which is in the midst of Judea, and thus also of the whole world: which location Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barbar. p. 508 teaches at length from Ezech. 38:12, because Jerusalem is called the navel of the earth, and from the German Patriarch, Casaubon, Josephus, Villalpando, and others. Augustine, Book XVII de civ. Dei c. 4, Eucherius in Questions of the O.T., and Thomas, Part III, q. 46, art. 10, explain it as the place of Christ's passion, with the approval of Tirinus and Genebrard, who nevertheless acknowledge with Euthymius, Bellarmine, and Saa that 'in the midst of the earth' means openly, in the sight of all men, and they take it as referring to the salvation provided for the Jews. See Estius and Jansenius on this passage.

Latin:

Ad vers. 2. OPERATUS EST SALUTEM IN ME- DIO TERRÆ.

Id de Judæa, quæ in medio terræ sita sit, vel de Hierusalem, quæ in medio Judææ, adeoque etiam orbis universi, Hieronym. accipit: quem situm ex Ezech. 38, 12. quod Jerusalem vocetur umbilicus ter- ræ, & e Germano Patriarcha, Casaubono, Josepho, Vi- talpando, aliisque prolixe docet Sixtin. Amama in Anti-Barbar. p. 508. Augustinus l. XVII. de civ. Dei c. 4. Evcher. in Quæstion. V. T. Thomas part. III. q. 46. art. 10. de loco passionis Christi explicant an- nuente Tirino, & Genebrardo, qui tamen agnoscunt cum Euthymo, Bellarm. & Saa in medio terræ esse propalam, in omnium hominum conspectu, & de salute Judæis præstita accipiunt. Videatur Estius & Jansenius in h. l.

## 74:13
Vers. 13. THOU HAST CONFIRMED IN THY STRENGTH THE SEA) That the Israelites might cross. THOU HAST BROKEN THE HEADS OF THE DRAGONS IN THE WATERS) The Egyptian king and princes. For it is the custom of Scripture to describe kings unmindful of humanity under the names of terrestrial or marine beasts. But here he preferred to name a marine beast, because the King of Egypt extended his empire to two seas.

Latin:

Vers. 13. TV CONFIRMASTI IN VIRTVTE TVA MARE) Vt transirent Israelitae. CONTRIBVLASTI CAPITA DRACONVM IN AQVIS) Regem & principes Aegyptios. Nam mos est Scripturae reges humanitatis immemores describere sub no- minibus ferarum terrestrium aut marinarum. Hic autem maluit marinam feram nominare, quia Rex Aegypti ad duo maria imperium suum protendebat.

## 74:14
Vers. 14. THOU HAST GIVEN HIM TO BE MEAT TO THE PEOPLES OF THE ETHIOPIANS) In Hebrew: to the dweller of the deserts: namely to those who occupied the shore of the Arabian gulf, and fed on fish, which fish are accustomed to feed on the flesh of drowned men. Jerome against Jovinian: Furthermore the Ichthyophagi, a wandering race on the shore of the Red Sea, roast fish on rocks heated by the heat of the Sun, and live on this food alone. Strabo also mentions it, book 15. The Junio-Tremellian version and interpretation is more correct here: Thou hast given food to the people themselves traveling through the deserts, or of the deserts: that is, Manna and quails; concerning which Exod. 16. & Num. 11. The series of words itself compared with history shows that this passage is to be taken in this way: For it follows further concerning the drink given to this people in the desert, v. 15. See a similar construction in Jos. 15. v. 19. Jud. 1. v. 15. In vain therefore does Cocceius say that it is twisted: whose gloss is both clearly foreign and sufficiently twisted: that God then gave the whale as food to the people, the desert-dwellers, when he gave the Roman empire to the Christians and barbarians. For the context clearly teaches that it refers to history in the desert. Who is therefore snatched away by time to the times of the New Testament. But to which peoples did the great Egyptian empire, when Pharaoh was drowned, fall as prey? For Cocceius acknowledges that it is treated here concerning the dividing of the Red Sea, just as Pharaoh is compared to a whale in Ezek. 29. v. 3. and that the following things speak of the cleft rock, from which the Lord caused water to flow, and of the drying up of the Jordan. But what he inserts, that it is treated here OF SIMILAR THINGS, is of a private and arbitrary interpretation, and besides it is altogether ἀσύςατον (inconsistent), that it is treated at the same time of past things, which happened to the Israelite people, and of future things, which are to happen to Christians, and indeed in the same words, and that the same words obtain a double, most disparate sense: which is certainly not infrequent in this interpreter, but is against the sound rule of interpreting.

Latin:

Vers. 14. DEDISTI EVM ESCAM POPVLIS AETHIOPVM) In Hebraeo: incolenti deserta: illis scilicet, qui oram Arabici sinus obtinebant, & piscibus vescebantur, qui pisces solent se pascere carnibus submersorum hominum. Hieronymus contra Jovinianum: Porro Ichthyophagi, gens errans in litto- re maris rubri, supra petras Solis calore ferventes assant pisces, & hoc solo alimento victitant. Meminit & Strabo lib. 15. Rectius hic se habet versio & interpretatio Junio-Tremelliana: Dedisti cibum ipsi populo per deserta proficiscenti, vel desertorum : id est, Man & coturnices; de quibus Exod. 16. & Num. 11. Hunc locum ita accipiendum esse ostendit ipsa verborum series cum historia comparata : Sequitur enim porro de potu in deserto huic po- pulo dato, vers. 15. Similem constructionem vi- de Jos. 15. v. 19. Jud. 1. v. 15. Frustra ergo id con- tortum dicit Coccejos : cujus glossa & aliena pla- ne, & satis contorta hæc est: DEUM tum dedisse balænam in cibum populo, eremicolis, quan- do imperium Romanum dedit Christianis & barba- ris. Ad historiam enim respici in deserto, con- textus luculenter docet. Qui tempore proinde abripitur ad tempora Nov. Testam. Quibus vero populis grande imperium Ægyptiacum, cum Pha- rao submergeretur, in prædam cessit ? De ma- ris enim rubri fiffione hic agi, uti Pharao balænæ comparatur Ezeh. 29. vers. 3. ac de rupe fissa, ex qua aquam effluere fecit Dominus, & de arefa- ctione Jordanis sequentia loqui agnoscit Cocce- jus. Quod vero inserit, DE SIMILIBUS hic simul agi, privatæ & arbitrariæ interpretatio- nis, adhæc ἀσύςατον omnino est, simul & de præ- teritis, quæ accidere populo Israelitico, & de futuris, quæ eventura sint Christianis, & qui- dem verbis iisdem tractari, eademque verba ita ge- minum, maxime disparatum, obtinere sensum: quod in hoc interprete non infrequens sane, at contra sanam interpretandi regulam est.

## 74:15
Vers. 15.

THOU DIDST CLEAVE FOUNTAINS AND TORRENTS) It is a μετάληψις for thou didst cleave rocks, so that fountains and torrents might flow forth. Note the history.

THOU DIDST DRY UP THE ETHAN RIVERS) The LXX elders are often accustomed to leave doubtful words in the Hebrew language. Otherwise, Aquila well rendered איתן as ςεῤῥὸς, that is to say, rapid rivers, such as the Jordan is.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

TV DIRVPISTI FONTES ET TORRENTES) Est μετάληψις pro dirupisti rupes, ut fontes ac torrentes emana- rent. Nota historia.

TV SICCASTI FLVVIOS ETHAN) Solent sæpe se- nes LXX. voces dubias in Hebræo sermone relinquere. Cæ- terum איתן bene Aquila reddidit ςεῤῥὸς, rapidos nimirum amnes, qualis est Jordanes.

## 75:1 Argument
PSALM LXXV. A cup in the hand of the Lord.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXV. Poculum in manu Domini.

## 75:2
Ver. 3.

WHEN I SHALL RECEIVE THE TIME I WILL JUDGE JUSTICES) Supply, God will say: when I shall have received the time, namely, the opportune one. When the measure of iniquities shall have been filled.

There is no need for this supplement, and the frequent permutation of persons which the interpreters invent, if we say that the Messiah speaks throughout the whole Psalm, who first joins himself to the faithful in the Eucharist, ver. 1, afterwards testifies that he will judge in his own time, inasmuch as all judgment has been given to him: And that he will strengthen the earth, especially that which is the seat of the Church, and its columns in the Political and Ecclesiastical state, Jer. 1, v. 18, Gal. 2, v. 8, but that the proud, others say the impious, will be humbled, he attributes to GOD the Father (for Christ the judge speaks of GOD the Father the judge, ver. 8, and the Lord, having the cup in his hand, ver. 9) and promises that he will therefore celebrate the GOD of Jacob, ver. 10, and lest there be any doubt that Christ is speaking, that same person, who professes that he will celebrate GOD, adds, ver. 11, that he will cut off the horns of the impious: which predicates sufficiently teach, inasmuch as they cohere in an inseparable connection, and are enunciated concerning the same person, that the God-man person speaks in this Psalm, and no other.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

CVM ACCEPERO TEMPVS EGO JVSTITIAS JV- DICABO) Supple, dicet Deus: cum accepero tempus, nem- pe opportunum. Vbi mensura iniquitatum fuerit impleta.

HOc supplemento, & crebra, quam Interpp. fingunt, personarum permutatione opus non est, si hic Messiam per totum Psalmum loqui di- camus, qui primum se jungit fidelibus in Eucha- ristia vers. 1. post se judicaturum suo tempore te- statur, utpote cui omne datum est judicium: Et terram, imprimis eam, quæ sedes Ecclesiæ est, ejusque columnas in statu Politico & Ecclesiasti- co se firmaturum Jer. 1. v. 18. Gal. 2. v. 8. super- bos vero, alii impios, humiliatum iri, DEO Pa- tri tribuit (loquitur enim Christus judex de DEO Patre judice vers. 8. & Domino, calicem in manu habente vers. 9.) ac promittit se ideo ce- lebraturum DEUM Jacob vers. 10. ac ne dubi- um sit Christum loqui, eadem illa persona, quæ DEUM sese celebraturam profitetur, addit vers. 11. se succisuram cornua impiorum: quæ prædi- cata satis docent, utpote indivulso nexu cohæren- tia, & de persona eadem enunciata, personam θεάνθρωπον in hoc Psalmo loqui, nec ullam aliam.

## 75:3
Ver. 4.

THE EARTH IS LIQUEFIED, AND ALL WHO DWELL IN IT) The whole State of Judea was disturbed by the faction of Ishbosheth.

It is not clear that those times are being referred to. Therefore, that is rashly introduced without scripture.

I HAVE STRENGTHENED ITS COLUMNS) I gave fortitude to David, to Joab, and to others of those parts.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

LIQVEFACTA EST TERRA, ET OMNES QVI HABITANT IN EA) Totus Status Judææ conturbatus fu- it factione Isbosethi.

Non liquet ea tempora respici. Temere ergo id ἄτερ γραφῆς ingeritur.

EGO CONFIRMAVI COLVMNAS EJVS) Ego for- titudinem dedi Davidi, Joabo aliisque earum partium.

## 75:5
Verf. 6. DO NOT LIFT UP YOUR HORN ON HIGH) Against David.

Latin:

Verf. 6. NOLITE ATTOLLERE IN ALTVM CORNV VE- STRVM) Contra Davidem.

## 75:8
Verf. 9. A CUP IN THE HAND OF THE LORD FULL OF PURE WINE MIXED]

As if to say, he has in that cup both good and evil. Wine, because it kindles wrath, signifies vengeance, Isaiah 51. v. 22. Jeremiah 25. v. 16. Apocal. 14. v. 10. chap. 16. v. 19. c. 18. v. 3. c. 19. v. 15. Not far from this is that of Homer: Δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς ἄδη, Κηρῶν ἔμπλειοι, ὁ μὲν ἐσθλῶν, ἀυτὰρ ὁ δειλῶν.

Latin:

Verf. 9. CALIX IN MANV DOMINI VINI MERI PLENVS MIXTO]

Quasi dicat, habet in eo calice & bonum & ma- lum. Vinum quia iram accendit, vindictam significat Esaia 51. v. 22. Jeremiae 25. v. 16. Apocal. 14. v. 10. cap. 16. v. 19. c. 18. v. 3. c. 19. v. 15. Non longe abit illud Homeri: Δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς ἄδη, Κηρῶν ἔμπλειοι, ὁ μὲν ἐσθλῶν, ἀυτὰρ ὁ δειλῶν.

## 76:1 Argument
PSALM. LXXVI. God is known in Judah.

A SONG TO THE ASSYRIANS) This is not in the Hebrew, nor was it in the old edition of the LXX, nor in many other editions, as the Greeks note at this place. The Psalm seems to have been written when the Ammonites were defeated: but Hezekiah used it afterwards when delivered from the Assyrians, a kind of thing we also noted above on Psalm LXX and LXXI.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXVI. Deus in Juda notus.

CANTICVM AD ASSYRIOS) In Hebraeo hoc non est, neque fuit in veteri editione LXX. neque in aliis multis edi- tionibus, ut notant Graeci ad hunc locum. Scriptus videtur Psalmus devictis Ammonitis: sed eo usus postea Ezechias li- beratus ab Assyriis, quale quid & supra annotavimus ad Psal. LXX. & LXXI.

## 76:3 Addition
On Psalm 76, v. 4. THE MIGHT OF THE BOWS.

In the Hebrew, 'coals of the bows,' fiery darts, or arrows flying like sparks, as the Chaldean, R. Solomon, Aben-Ezra, and the blessed Luther explain. Cf. Job 5:7, Ps. 91:5. Others, 'sparkling bows,' i.e., because of their brightness, or flashing.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 76. v. 4. POTENTIAS ARCUUM.

In Ebræo Carbones arcuum, jacula ignita, vel sagittas, instar scintillarum volitantes, ut Chald. R. Salomo, Aben-Ezra, & B. Lutherus explicant. Conf. Job. 5, 7. Ps. 91, 5. Alii arcus scintillantes q. præ ni- tore, seu coruscos.

## 76:5 Addition
On verse 6.

ALL THE MEN OF WEALTH FOUND NOTHING IN THEIR HANDS.

Regarding the Assyrians suddenly lulled into the sleep of death, who, although very wealthy, by desiring greater riches after a sudden death were thrust into hell and found nothing in their hands, neither from those things which they had, nor from those things which they hoped for, Bellarmine notes that it is commonly explained. He himself, however, explains it concerning the sleep of ignorance and concupiscence in general, and concerning the goods of the present life, that they are nothing but the mockeries of dreamers, because those devoted to them, when they awaken through death, find nothing. And thus most interpreters accept these words concerning the vain anxiety of the avaricious: but the Hebrew phrase, not to find one's hands, denotes finding no strength in one's own powers: and so it is not a matter of the vain pursuit of wealth, but of the weakness of strength for fighting, as B. Luther rendered it most excellently, and explained the Hebrew idiom in a marginal gloss. For when someone has the means to accomplish something, it is said that his hands find it, Lev. 12, 8. 1 Sam. 10, 7. whence a shortened hand, Isa. 59, v. 1.

Latin:

Ad vers. 6.

NIHIL INVENERUNT OMNES VIRI DI- VITIARUM IN MANIBUS SUIS.

De Assyriis somno mortis subito soporatis, qui etsi ditissimi majores divitias appetendo post mortem repentinam in infernum detrusi nihil invenerint in manibus suis, neque ex iis, quæ habebant, neque ex iis, quæ sperabant, communiter exponi notat Bel- larm. explicat autem ipse de sopore ignorantiæ & con- cupiscentiæ in genere, & de bonis præsentis vitæ, quod nil nisi ludibria sint somniantium, quod iis dediti, cum per mortem evigilant, nihil inveniant. Atque ita Interpp. plerique de vana sollicitudine avaro- rum hæc accipiunt: sed phrasis Ebræa, non invenire manus suas, notat nihil invenire roboris in viribus suis: adeoque non de inani studio opum, sed de infir- mitate virium ad pugnandum agitur, uti optime red- didit B. Lutherus, & in glossa marginali idiotismum Ebræum exposuit. Nam cum aliquid expediundi facultates quis habet, dicitur id invenire manus ejus Lev. 12, 8. 1. Sam. 10, 7. unde manus abbreviata Esa. 59. v. 1.

## 76:10
Verf. 11. FOR THE THOUGHT OF MAN SHALL CONFESS TO THEE) From the Hebrew: The fury of man shall yield to thy praise: if any residue of wrath remains, thou shalt restrain it. If any ill will still remains in the Ammonites, thou shalt easily hinder it. Hezekiah could have applied this very well to the Assyrians and their allies.

Although Hezekiah could have applied this to them, yet that the Psalm was composed by him, and not by David, which the Vulgate implies, not even Grotius dared to assert, referring the same to the defeated Ammonites and the times of David: Theodoret and Euthymius wish the victory of Hezekiah to be predicted in the same: whom many recent writers among the Papists follow: But Bellarmine has no doubt that the victory of the elect of GOD against all enemies, both visible and invisible, is rather predicted. B. Höpfner thinks that this deals with the defense and liberation of the Church of any time, yet B. Luther refers it to the times of David as the proper sense, although we can also make it our own by use: because he says it is a thanksgiving of the same argument, just as Psalm 46, because it preserves the word and worship of GOD in Jerusalem, and protects his people against Tyrants. The Grotian conjecture seems to be drawn from the Syriac inscription, but that rests on the same certainty as the Vulgate. Furthermore, the version of Grotius handed down in verse 11 concerning the residue of the enemies' wrath, Campensis and B. Luther have already handed down, concerning which see Kircher, use 2, Concord. Exempl. 14.

Latin:

Verf. 11. QVONIAM COGITATIO HOMINIS CONFITE- BITVR TIBI) Ex Hebraeo: Hominis furor in laudem tu- am cedet: si quid irarum residuum est, id constringes. Siquid adhuc in Ammonitis restat malae voluntatis, id facile impe- dies. Potuit Ezechias hoc optime aptare Assyriis eorumque sociis.

ETsi iis hoc aptare potuerit Ezechias, ab ipso tamen, non vero a Davide Psalmum concin- natum esse, quod Vulgatus innuit, nec ipse Gro- tius asserere ausus fuit ad Ammonitas devictos & tempora Davidis eundem referens: Theodoretus, & Euthymius praedici in eodem volunt victori- am Ezechiae: quos multi recentiores e Pontifi- ciis sequuntur: At Bellarm. dubium non est prae- dici potius victoriam electorum DEI adversus omnes hostes, tum visibiles, tum invisibiles. B. Höpfnerus censet agi hic de Ecclesiae defensio- ne, ac liberatione cujusvis temporis, B. Luthe- rus tamen ad Davidis tempora, qua sensum pro- prium refert, etsi usu eundem etiam nostrum face- re possimus: quia gratiarum actionem dicit ejus- dem argumenti, sicut Psalm. 46. quod verbum & cultum DEI in Jerusalem conservet, & popu- lum suum adversus Tyrannos tueatur. Grotia- na conjectura hausta videtur e Syriaca inscri- ptione, sed illa eadem nititur certitudine qua Vulgata. Caeterum versionem Grotii vers. 11. traditam de residuo irarum hostium Campensis & B. Luther. jam tradidere, de qua vid. Kircher. usu 2. Concord. Exempl. 14.

## 76:10 Addition
On v. 11.

FOR THE THOUGHT OF MAN SHALL CONFESS TO THEE, AND THE REMAINDERS OF THOUGHT SHALL KEEP A FEAST DAY TO THEE.

These are obscure: Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: because the wrath of man shall confess to thee, with the remainders of wrath thou shalt gird thyself. When the wrath of man is restrained, it confesses, providing an occasion and matter for confession, or even when an angry enemy is converted, he himself confesses and proclaims the Lord. Osiander explains: The fury of men yields to thy glory: if there shall be remainders (if they shall continue to rage) thou shalt gird thyself to oppress them.

Latin:

Ad v. 11.

QVONIAM COGITATIO HOMINIS CON- FITEBITUR TIBI, ET RELIQVIÆ CO- GITATIONIS DIEM FESTUM AGENT TIBI.

Obscura hæc: Ebræa sic reddidit Hieronym. quia ira hominis confitebitur tibi, reliquiis iræ accinge- ris. Ira hominis cum coercetur, confitetur, ἀφορ- μητικῶς occasionem, & materiam præbens con- fessioni, vel etiam cum convertitur hostis iratus, confitetur ipse & prædicat Dominum. Osiand. ex- ponit: Furor hominum cedit in gloriam tuam: si fue- rint reliquiæ (si perrexerint fuerere) accinges te ad opprimendum eos.

## 77:1 Argument
PSALM. LXXVII. The right hand of God changing all things.

UNTO THE END FOR IDITHUN.

This name is not of an instrument or a kind of song, as Aben-Ezra wishes, but of the person of the Prince of singers, to whom Asaph, inspired by the Holy Spirit, handed over the Psalm to be sung: that is, he entrusted it to the Symphonic Choir under his direction. 1 Chron. 16. verse 38. Compare Psalm 42 and 44. Therefore it does not deal with the Babylonian captivity, much less with the persecution of Antiochus, as some wish: but as Augustine notes, it deals with the misery which the faithful experience while panting for the heavenly Fatherland, from this exile of the world.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXVII. Dextra Dei omnia mutans.

IN FINEM PRO IDITHUM.

Nomen hoc non instrumenti est vel gene- ris cantici, ut Aben-Efra vult, sed personae Prin- cipis cantorum, cui Asaph a Spiritu S. inspira- tus Psalmum decantatum tradidit: hoc est, Choro Symphoniaco sub ejus directione com- mendavit. 1. Paralipp. 16. vers. 38. Conf. Psal. 42. & 44. Non ergo de captivitate Babylonica agit, nedum de persecutione Antiochi, ut volunt nonnulli: sed ut August. notat, de miseria quam fideles experiuntur anhelantes ad coelestem Pa- triam, ex hoc mundi exilio.

## 77:2
vers. 3. MY SOUL REFUSED TO BE COMFORTED.

Solecism of the Vulgate. Afterwards, instead of DELECTATUS SUM, in Hebrew it is I sounded, or I cried out; instead of EXERCITATUS, it is I spoke in a low voice, as Bellarmine admits; and verse 10, the Vulgate makes no sense, ET DIXI: NUNC CEPI, Bellarmine supplies to breathe, but who could have guessed this from the version? Jerome translates, my weakness: Cf. Jer. 10. v. 19. The Chaldean and Symmachus render the Hebrew likewise. See here Cloppenburg, Opusc. p. 263. Furthermore, concerning verses 8, 9, 10, 11, we treated them in Sermon 19, under the theme of the soliloquy of a soul provoking divine mercy and obtaining it, in Memor. justor. Witteberg.

Latin:

vers. 3. RENUIT CONSOLARI ANIMA MEA.

Solaecismus Vulgati. Postea loco DELE- CTATUS SUM in Ebr. est sonui, vel clama- vi, loco EXERCITATUS est summisse loquutus sum, fatente Bellarm. ac vers. 10. Vulgata nullo sen- su, ET DIXI: NUNC CEPI, supplet Bellarm. respirare, sed quis hoc ex versione divinare pote- rat? Hieronym. vertit, imbecillitas mea: Conf. Jer. 10. v. 19. Chaldaeus & Symmachus Ebraea pari- ter reddunt. Vid. hic Cloppenburg. Opusc. p. 263. Porro de vers. 8. 9. 10. 11. egimus in Concion. 19. Sub themate soliloquium animae misericordiam di- vinam provocantis, eamque impetrantis in Memor. justor. Witteberg.

## 77:16
Verse 17. THE WATERS SAW THEE AND THEY WERE AFRAID AND THE DEPTHS WERE TROUBLED) The thing itself speaks that these things also pertain to the exodus from Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 17. VIDERVNT TE AQVAE ET TIMVERVNT ET TVRBATAE SVNT ABTSSI) Etiam haec ad exitum ex Aegypto pertinere res ipsa loquitur.

## 77:18
Verse 19. THE VOICE OF THY THUNDER IN A WHEEL) A wheel here signifies the air, elsewhere the ether: because it is a common opinion that all these things are revolved around us.

The exposition of most people concerning the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots is simpler, unless one should rather prefer, as it seems, B. Luther's interpretation concerning a circular whirlwind. Cf. Psalm 83. v. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 19. VOX TONITRVI TVI IN ROTA) Rota hic aerem, alibi aetherem significat: quia haec omnia circum nos volvi communis est opinio.

SImplicior est plerorumque expositio de rotis curruum Pharaonis, nisi praeferenda potius, quod videtur, B. Lutheri interpretatio de turbine circulari. Conf. Psal. 83. v. 14.

## 78:1 Argument
PSALM LXXVIII. Ecclesiastical History.

verse 1. HEARKEN O MY PEOPLE TO MY LAW.

We learn from that passage of the Evangelist that these words are not Asaph's, as Grotius wishes at Matt. 13. v. 35, but the Son of God's. Because verse 2, I will open my mouth in parables, is openly explained concerning Christ. Nor indeed was Asaph the King of the people, nor could he claim for himself hearken O my people, much less call the law of the Lord his own law: hearken O my people to my law. Nor were the ears of the people to be inclined so much to a man as to God, to whom that great Prophet was promised, whom all ought to hear, Deut. 18, who could properly use this authoritative speech: incline your ear to the words of my mouth. And who that is, who says, I will open my mouth in parables, I will speak propositions from the beginning, we do not know more correctly than from the information of the Holy Spirit himself, who taught us about him thus in Matt. 13. verse 34. All these things Jesus spoke in parables to the crowds, and without parables he did not speak to them, THAT IT MIGHT BE FULFILLED which was said by the Prophet saying: I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world. Wherefore it is not to be doubted that the Son of God speaks these things, since we have as an interpreter the Holy Spirit himself, who is above all exception. But the things which follow in v. 3 seqq. contain the response of the people to the admonition of their King Messiah, as was properly observed by Cocceius in his Commentary on this passage. Let those things which we said on the passage of Matthew be compared.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXVIII. Historia Ecclesiastica.

vers. 1. ATTENDITE POPULE MEUS LE- GEM MEAM.

VErba haec non Assaphi esse, quod vult Gro- tius ad Matth. 13. v. 35. sed Filii DEI, ex eo Evangelistae loco discimus. Quia vers. 2. aperiam in parabolis os meum, de Christo aperte explica- tur. Nec vero Asaph Rex erat populi, aut eun- dem sibi vendicare poterat attendite populus meus, multo minus legem Domini legem suam dicere: attendite popule meus legem meam. Neque tam homini, quam DEO inclinandae aures populi, cui magnus ille Propheta erat promissus, quem audire debebant omnes Deut. 18. qui hac auto- ritativa oratione uti poterat proprie: inclinate aurem vestram in verba oris mei. Et quisnam il- le sit, qui ait, aperiam in parabolis os meum, lo- quar propositiones ab initio, non rectius cogno- scimus, quam ex informatione ipsius Spiritus S. Qui de eo ita nos edocuit Matth. 13. vers. 34. Haec omnia loquutus est Jesus in parabolis ad turbas, & sine parabolis non loquebatur eis, UT IMPLERE- TUR quod dictum erat per Prophetam dicentem: Aperiam in parabolis os meum, eructabo abscon- dita a constitutione mundi. Quapropter dubitan- dum non est Filium DEI haec loqui, quum inter- pretem habeamus omni exceptione superiorem ipsummet Spiritum S. Quae vero sequuntur v. 3. seqq. responsum populi continent ad admo- nitionem Regis sui Messiae, ut probe observatum Coccejo in Comment. ad h. l. Conferantur quae ad locum Matth. diximus.

## 78:12
verse 12. THE CHILDREN OF EPHRAIM.

The Chaldean, R. Solomon, Gefner, Dr. D. Geier, Moll on this passage, and B. Rungius in Exod. p. 5, Malvenda on 1 Chron. 7. v. 21, gather that this was done against the command of God before the leading out from Egypt, 1 Chron. 7. verse 21, namely that the Ephraimites, having gone out from Egypt to receive the promised land, waged war against the Gittites before God ordained it: but since the transgressions of the people are described here generally, and in the following verse the same children of Ephraim are said not to have kept the testament of God, and to have forgotten the wonders which He showed them, and which He did before their Fathers in the land of Egypt, others think that they happened to the children of Ephraim after the leading out from Egypt, that is, to the Israelites, who are so named because the tribe of Ephraim was the most numerous and most powerful, and refer to the history in 1 Sam. 4, where the Israelites were put to flight by the Philistines, as Aben-Ezra, from a comparison of v. 65 & 73, Tirinus, the Belgians, Coccejus, and others explain. Which sense seems not inappropriate. Bellarmine explains it thus, that the Sons of Ephraim, that is, the Israelites, were like soldiers beginning to fight and soon turning their backs, when they turned their backs on God. Which interpretation is less consistent.

Latin:

vers. 12. FILII EPHRAIM.

Id contra mandatum DEI factum ante edu- ctionem ex Aegypto e. 1. Par. 7. vers. 21. colligunt Chald. R. Salomo, Gefner. Dn. D. Geier. Moll. in h. l. & B. Rungius in Exod. p. 5. Malvenda ad 1. Par. 7. v. 21. quod nempe Ephraimitae antequam DEUS id ordinaret, bellum Gethaeis intulerint, ex Aegy- pto egressi ut terram promissam acciperent: sed quum generaliter hic populi praevaricationes de- scribantur, & vers. feqv. iidem filii Ephraim dican- tur non custodijsse testamentum DEI, & obliti mira- bilium quae ostendit iis, & quae fecit coram Patribus eorum in terra Aegypti, alii eas contigisse post edu- ctionem ex Aegypto filiis Epharim, id est, Israe- litis, qui ita nuncupantur, quia tribus Ephraim erat numerosissima, & potentissima, existimant, & respici historiam 1. Sam. 4. ubi Israelitæ à Phili- stæis in fugam dati sunt, ut Aben-Ezra è collatione v. 65. & 73. Tirinus, Belgæ, Coccejus, aliique ex- plicant. Qui sensus videtur non inconveniens. Bellarminus ita exponit, quod Filii Ephraim, id est, Israelitæ similes fuerint militibus incipien- tibus præliari & mox terga vertentibus, cum Deo terga verterunt. Quæ interpretatio minus con- sona.

## 78:24
Ver. 24. CAN HE ALSO GIVE BREAD?

The history here seems confused, because according to the Mosaic account the miraculous gift of manna and quails preceded the production of water from the rock, Exod. 16. v. 4, 8, 13, chap. 17. v. 6, seqq., as here after the water was drawn from the Rock in verse 17, the Israelites are said to have tempted [God] by demanding food in verse 18, and that with this kind of speech: Can GOD prepare a table in the wilderness? Because he struck the Rock, and the waters flowed and the torrents flooded? Can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people? vers. 22, 23, 24, as if the waters had flowed from the rock first, but afterwards at last bread had been given with the quails, concerning which it is reported in v. 27, seqq.: Whence Aben Esra on this passage says: Behold, Scripture speaks confusedly, for it has placed the following things first, and vice versa: nor was it concerned about that matter, because the order of the event is established for us in the law of Moses. Whom Coccejus followed. But in this way not only is confusion introduced, but also that speech will in no way be consistent: For how would the Israelites have said, he gave water, can he also give bread, when he had given bread before the water? Wherefore it must be said that by this expostulation, weary of manna, they desired bread, and called into doubt the power of GOD, that he could not furnish them in the wilderness with a table of food, and set before them barley or wheat loaves, and all kinds of meat: or if they simply demanded meat, it must be understood as concerning the concession of meat not for one day only, such as that gift of quails had been in Exod. 16. v. 13, made in one evening, but for many days, as can be gathered from the divine response in Num. 11, 19, 20, that not for one day, or two, or five or ten or twenty, but for an entire month would meat be granted to the people, which not even Moses himself could grasp, vers. 21, 22. But what is added here by Asaph in verses 27, 28, 29, must be rendered thus: that, namely, fire was kindled in Jacob, because they did not believe in GOD: ALTHOUGH he had commanded, as Piscator and B. Hopfner render: since the particle Vau also occurs sometimes in an adversative sense, and the Hebrews, R. Dav. Kimchi, and Aben-Ezra have also rendered the verb in the pluperfect: and thus the following verbs also in this verse 27 and the two following 28 and 29 must be taken in the pluperfect, so that the preceding gift of manna is referred to, and the quails described for the satiety of the whole people in Ex. 16, and by the word שְׂלָו not provisions in general, but quails are designated, which are otherwise caught by hunting עָוֹף, as Piscator rightly observed. This, therefore, is a description of distrust, that although the Israelites had already been sumptuously fed by a remarkable miracle from heaven and with the grain of heaven, bread, and that of the best, which is therefore called angelic according to some, or rather the bread of the great, and with quails, yet they still call into doubt the divine power, whether he can procure bread and meat for them? when it is as easy for GOD to give them barley loaves and meat for many days, as it was easy for him to rain manna upon them, and to give them quails for one day or for a supper. Now therefore verse 30 is explained further, how to that temptation described in Num. 11, the Lord did not indeed give them barley or wheat loaves at their pleasure, nor meat of every kind, yet he provided such an abundance of quails for an entire month that they were all greatly satisfied, and thus far granted them their concupiscence, but severely punished that distrust and concupiscence of theirs in verses 34, 35.

Latin:

Vers. 24. NUMQUID ET PANEM POTERIT DARE?

Historia hic videtur confusa, quia secundum relationem Mosaicam Mannæ & coturnicum mi- raculosa donatio aquæ è petra productionem an- tecessit, Exod. 16. v. 4. 8. 13. cap. 17. v. 6. seqq. ut hic post aquam è Petra elicitam vers. 17. tentasse di- cuntur Israelitæ cibum postulando vers. 18. idque hujusmodi oratione, nunquid poterit DEUS para- re mensam in deserto? Quoniam percussit Petram, & fluxerunt aquæ & torrentes inundaverunt? Num- quid & panem poterit dare aut parare mensam popu- lo suo? vers. 22. 23. 24. ac si prius aquæ è petra flu- xerint, postmodum vero demum panis datus fue- rit cum coturnicibus, de quo v. 27. seqq. refertur: Unde Aben Esra ad h. l. Ecce Scriptura, inquit, confuse loquitur, nam præposuit sequentia, & contra: neque ea de re solicita fuit, quia rei ordo nobis constat in lege Mosis. Quem sequutus est Coccejus. Sed ita non tantum confusio introducitur, verum et- iam oratio illa nullo modo consentanea erit: Quo- modo enim Israelitæ dixissent, aquam dedit, nun- quid & panem dare poterit, quum panem ante a- quam dederit? Quapropter dicendum, quod hac expostulatione, Mannæ pertæsi, panem desidera- rint, & in dubium vocarint DEI potentiam, quod nequeat ipsis in deserto Mensam ciborum apparatu instruere, & panes hordeaceos, vel tri- ticeos, omnisque generis carnes apponere: aut si simpliciter carnem postularint, intelligendum id de concessione carnis non ad unum tantum di- em, qualis fuerat illa coturnicum donatio Exod. 16. vers. 13. una vespera facta, sed ad plures dies quemadmodum è divina responsione Num. 11, 19. 20. colligere est, non ad unum diem, aut duos, aut quinque aut decem aut viginti, sed ad integrum men- sem populo carnes concessum iri, quod nec ipse Mo- ses capere poterat vers. 21. 22. Quæ vero hic ab Assapho adduntur vers. 27. 28. 29. ita reddenda sunt: quod sc. ignis accensus fuerit in Jacob, eo quod non crediderint in DEUM: QUAMVIS præce- perat, ut Piscator, & B. Hopfnerus reddunt: quum particula Vau etiam sensu adversativo quandoque occurrat, & verbum in plusquamperfecto reddi- derint quoque Ebræi, R. Dav. Kimchi, & Aben- Esra: atque ita consequentia etiam verba in plus- quamperfecto versu hoc 27. & seqq. duobus 28. & 29. accipienda, ut respiciatur Mannæ antegressa donatio, & coturnicum ad populi universi satietatem Ex. 16. descripta, & voce שְׂלָו non commeatus in genere, sed coturnices designentur, quæ עָוֹף ve- nando alias capiuntur, ut recte observavit Piscator. Hæc ergo est descripto diffidentiæ, quod etsi jam insigni miraculo cœlitus & frumento cœli, pane, eoque optimo, qui ideo angelicus dicitur juxta non- nullos, vel potius magnatum panis, & coturnicibus laute Israelitæ cibati fuerint, tamen in dubium ad- huc vocent divinam potentiam, anne sibi pa- nem & carnes procurare possit? quum tam fa- cile sit DEO panes hordeaceos, & carnes ad plu- rimos dies ipsis dare, quam facile Man super illos pluit, & coturnices ad diem unum vel ad cœnam ipsis donavit. Jam ergo vers. 30. exponitur por- ro, quomodo ad tentationem illam Num. 11. de- scriptam non quidem ad placitum eorum panes hordeaceos, aut triticeos, neque omnis generis carnes, tantam tamen copiam coturnicum per inte- grum mensem iisdem suffecerit Dominus, ut omnes valde satiati fuerint, & hactenus concupiscentiam ipforum ipsis præstiterit, sed illam diffidentiam, & concupiscentiam eorundem graviter puniverit vers. 34. 35.

## 78:26 Addition
On verse 26.

HE BROUGHT THE SOUTH WIND FROM THE HEAVENS, AND BY HIS POWER HE BROUGHT IN THE SOUTH-WEST WIND.

In the Hebrew it is 'he stirred up from the heavens, the East wind AND THE SOUTH,' etc., either because the East wind is referred to the Southern wind, as Bochart teaches at length in Hierozoicon 2. 1. 15, that the Hebrews take the words Kades and Theman indiscriminately; or because both the East wind and the South wind blew by turns and successively, so that they might carry quails not only from Egypt, but also from other parts of the land of Arabia or even beyond the Persian Gulf, as Poole conjectures in his Synopsis Criticorum on Numbers 11:31.

Latin:

Ad verf. 26.

TRANSTULIT AUSTRUM DE COELO, ET INDUCIT IN VIRTUTE SUA AFRICUM.

In Ebr. est excitavit e cœlo, Eurum ET AU- STRUM, &c. sive quod Eurus ad Australem ventum referatur, ut prolixe Bochart. in Hieroz. 2. 1. 15. do- cet, Ebræos voces Kades & Theman promiscue ac- cipere; sive quod & Eurus & Auster subinde & successive flarent, ut non ex Ægypto solum, sed etiam ex aliis vel Arabiæ vel etiam ultra sinum Persi- cum terræ partibus coturnices adveherent, ut conjicit Polus, in Synopsi Crit. ad Num. 11, 31.

## 78:29
Ver. 29. MAN ATE THE BREAD OF ANGELS.

In the Hebrew it is: the bread of אֲבִירִים the mighty, where R. Akiba understands angels, as does the Syrian. Others understand by the mighty the clouds, to which strength is attributed in Job 27. v. 18. Thus Bugenhagius also preferred to interpret it as the bread of the clouds, or the bread of the robust, which the robust eat, or from which the robust are made: as B. Bohlius also explained; jeder aß Brodt, das Stärcke geben kunte [everyone ate bread that could give strength]. Others interpret it as the bread of illustrious men, Herrenbrod, as Moller, Marinus, Muys, B. Walther, Bootius, etc. If, however, angels are understood, or with the Chaldean it seems to some that this bread is so called here, because it descended from the dwelling of the angels κατὰ δόξαν [according to glory], or because it was prepared through the ministry of the angels: or concerning most excellent bread, just as the tongues of angels are spoken of in 1 Cor. 13. v. 1. Cf. Wisd. 14. v. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 29. PANEM ANGELORUM MANDU- CAVIT HOMO.

In Ebræo est : panem אֲבִירִים fortium, ubi R. Akiba angelos intelligit, ut & Syrus. Alii per fortes nubes intelligunt, quibus robur tribuitur Job. 27. v. 18. Sic Bugenhagius etiam panem nubi- um maluit interpretari, vel panem robustorum, quem robusti comedunt, aut unde robusti fiunt: quomodo & B. Bohlius exposuit; jeder aß Brodt, das Stärcke geben kunte. Alii panem illustrium Herrenbrod interpretantur, ut Moller. Marinus, Muys, B. Walther. Bootius &c. Si tamen Angeli intelligantur, vel cum Chaldæo ita hic panis vocatus quibusdam videtur, quia descendit de habitaculo angelorum κατὰ δόξαν, vel quia per ministerium an- gelorum præparatus fuit: vel de pane excellentissimo, uti dicta lingua angelorum 1. Cor. 13. vers. 1. Conf. Sap. 14. v. 20.

## 78:54
Ver. 54. SENDINGS BY EVIL ANGELS] By the destroying angel in Exod. 12. v. 23. We said above that several were present to one Angel as attendants. Others understand the heralds of evils, Moses and Aaron, πάντης κακῶν [all evils].

But here the plagues are recounted, not the messengers of evils, therefore that opinion of Muis and Tarnovius in exerc. p. 338 does not deserve consideration. But we understand it entirely concerning evil angels with the Vulgate and B. Luther, as also with certain Hebrews and the Chaldean, even though Augustine, Theodoret, Euthymius, and others explain it concerning good ones.

Latin:

Vers. 54. IMMISSIONES PER ANGELOS MALOS] Per Angelum percussorem Exod. 12. v. 23. Vni Angelo plu- res adfuisse velut apparitores supra diximus. Alii intelli- gunt prænuntios malorum, Mosem & Aaronem, πάντης κακῶν.

Sed hic plagæ recensentur, non nuncii malorum, ideo calculum non meretur illa Muisii, & Tarno- vii in exerc. p. 338. sententia. De angelis autem malis cum Vulg. & B. Luthero omnino intelligi- mus, ut & cum Ebr. quibusdam & Chald. etsi Au- gustinus, Theodor. Euthymius, & alii de bonis ex- plicent.

## 79:1 Argument
PSALM LXXIX. The insolence of the enemies of the Church.

This Psalm seems to be of the same subject matter as the 74th. Salem or Jerusalem seems to have been in the first division made for the Israelite people, Joshua 15, v. 8. The Jebusites seem to have always held the citadel of Zion, 2 Sam. 5, v. 6, 7. Therefore, when the Philistines captured the Ark (which is here קֹדֶשׁ היכל), it is no wonder if they also captured Jerusalem, or Salem, a city at that time small and not well fortified. Furthermore, men of the times of Nebuchadnezzar could have very well adapted this Psalm to their own times.

The things that are said in this Psalm do not agree with that victory of the Philistines. For at that time the temple had not yet been built, nor was Jerusalem devastated. Therefore, Augustine, Theodoret, Euthymius, and Luther accept this Psalm concerning the things that happened to the Hebrews under Antiochus in the time of the Maccabees, who also not undeservedly made the present Psalm of the same subject matter as Psalm 74. Compare verses 2 and 3 of this Psalm with 1 Maccabees 7. Meanwhile, Augustine rightly applies this Psalm to the persecutions of the Church under the pagans. Lyra, Muys, Piscator, Hopfn, and Quistorp explain it concerning the state of the desolation of Babylon. Athanasius and Socrates, along with Justin, explain it concerning the devastation by the Romans; Cocceius concerning both. But if it is of the same subject matter as Psalm 74, which seemed so to Grotius and others, it looks rather to the times of Antiochus, which also pleased Eusebius, as well as Fr. Junius.

Vers. 1. THEY HAVE LAID JERUSALEM IN THE KEEPING OF ORCHARDS) LXX. εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον. And thus they are accustomed to translate

‘Iyyi, which others call heaps or mounds. Now, the keepers of great orchards were accustomed to keep watch on mounds.

Jerome, in his Epistle to Sunia, more correctly explained it as a heap of stones, and Aquila as λιθήγιον.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXIX. Insolentia hostium Ecclesiæ.

VIDETVR hic Psalmus esse ejusdem argumenti, cujus 74. Salem sive Hierosolyma videtur fuisse in divisione prima po- pulo Israelitico facta Josue 15. v. 8. Sionem arcem videntur semper tenuisse Jebusæi, 2. Sam. 5. v. 6. 7. Itaque cum Phi- listhini ceperunt Arcam, (quæ hic קֹדֶשׁ היכל) nihil mirum si & Hierosolyma, sive Salemum, urbem tunc exigu- am nec bene munitam, ceperint. Cæterum optime hunc Psalmum suis temporibus aptare potuerunt homines tempo- rum Nabuchodonosoris.

Non conveniunt, quæ hoc Psalmo dicuntur, illi Philistinorum Victoriæ. Tum enim nondum exstructum erat templum, nec Jerusalem vastata est. Ideo de iis, quæ Ebræis acciderunt sub An- tiocho Maccabæorum tempore hunc Psalm. accipi- unt August. Theodor. Euthym. Luther. qui etiam ejusdem argumenti Psalmum præsentem nec im- merito fecit cum Psal. 74. Confer vers. 2. 3. hu- jusce Psalmi cum 1. Maccab. 7. Interim applicat hunc Psalmum August. recte persequutionibus Ecclesiæ sub paganis. De statu Babylon. deso- lationis explicat Lyra, Muys. Piscator, Hopfn. Quistorp. De Romanorum devastatione Atha- nas. Socrat. cum Justino: de utraque Coccejus: Sed si argumenti ejusdem est cum Psalm. 74. quod Grotio & aliis visum, ad Antiochi potius tem- pora spectat, quod Eusebio quoque placuit, ut & Fr. Junio.

Vers. 1. POSVERVNT JERVSALEM IN POMORVM CV- STODIAM) LXX. εἰς ὀπωροφυλάκιον. Et sic solent vertere

עיי, quod alii acervos vel tumulos. In tumulis autem excubare solebant magnorum pomariorum custodes.

Rectius Hier. Epist. ad Suniam exposuit acer- vum lapidum, & Aquila λιθήγιον.

## 79:1 Addition
On Psalm 78, v. 1.

O GOD, THE GENTILES HAVE COME INTO THY INHERITANCE.

It is doubtful which times are being looked to. Lyranus, Piscator, and Höpfner refer it to the times of the Babylonian captivity; Augustine, Theodoret, Eusebius, Euthymius, and Junius to the times of the persecution of Antiochus; Justin, Athanasius, and Socrates to the most recent devastation, which was that of the Romans. B. Hülsemann has this to say about it: Most of our people also, by reason of the adequate object and chronology, determine that this Psalm is of the same subject matter as Psalm 74: namely, that it speaks of the calamity brought upon the Israelite people by Antiochus Epiphanes: but we showed above from v. 9 of that Psalm that it cannot be understood of that time, which the Belgians in their Bibles and the Weimar scholars also acknowledged. They indeed explain this Psalm as concerning those times and the future persecution of the Christian Church at the same time; but they explain Psalm 74 as concerning the final devastation of the city by Titus. Nor is there any relevant reason to restrict this Psalm to the Jewish people alone, because mention is made of Jerusalem: for it is confessed on both sides that under this proper name the Church is very often described by a synecdoche of the species, especially indeed in the prayers of David for the Church in general. Thus Psalm 51, 20; Psalm 125, 2. Thus, among the Papists, also Jacobus de Valentia, Genebrardus, and Jansenius. B. Brentius also makes it a general prayer formula in the calamities of the Church, as does Dn. D. Geier.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 78. v. 1.

DEUS VENERUNT GENTES IN HÆRE- DITATEM TUAM.

Quænam tempora respiciantur dubium est. Ad Babylonicæ captivitatis tempora referunt Lyranus, Piscator, Höpfnerus, ad tempora persequutionis An- tiochi, Augustin. Theodorets, Eusebius, Euthymius, Junius; ad novissimam devastationem, quæ Roma- norum fuit, Justinus, Athanasius, Socrates. B. Hülse- mannus ita de eo habet: Hunc Psalmum etiam ple- rique nostratium ratione Objecti adæquati & Chrono- logiæ, ejusdem argumenti esse statuunt cum Psal. 74. loqui videlicet de calamitate populi Israelitici ab An- tiocho Epiphane illata: sed ostendimus supra ex v. 9. ejus Psalmi, non posse de illo tempore intelligi, quod Bel- gæ in suis Bibliis & Vinarienses quoque agnoverunt. Hunc quidem Psalmum de istis temporibus & futura persecutione Ecclesiæ Christianæ simul; Psalmum au- tem 74. de ultima vastatione urbis per Titum expo- nentes. Nec ulla relevans ratio est, restringere hunc Psalmum ad solum populum Judaicum, quia Jeroso- lymorum fit mentio: est enim utrinque in confesso, sub hoc nomine proprio sæpissime describi Ecclesiam per Synecdochen speciei, imprimis vero in precibus Da- vidis pro Ecclesia generalibus.
