Sic Psal. 51, 20. Psal. 125, 2. Sic ex Papistis etiam Jacobus de Va- lentia, Genebrardus, & Jansenius. Formulam generalem precatoriam in calamitatibus Ecclesiæ etiam facit B. Brentius, ut & Dn. D. Geierus.

## 80:1 Argument
PSALM LXXX. The Sacred Vineyard.

Verse 1. WHO SITTETH ABOVE THE CHERUBIM) That is, who showest Thyself by oracles and splendor above the ark.

Some understand the angels by the Cherubim, and a seat in heaven: it pleases some to join these, like Bellarmine; who [understands] a seat in heaven above the angels, and as a type of this thing in the sanctuary. But GOD is described here first as the Shepherd of Israel, who feeds Joseph, which is added exegetically, so that it may be implied that the ten tribes are denoted by Israel: as in Ezek. 37. v. 16, 19; Am. 5. v. 6, 15; chap. 6. v. 6; Zech. 10. v. 15; or that the kingdom of Judah is denoted by the name of Israel, in which the Israelite men were, but the ten tribes are denoted by the name of Joseph. Then, from the revelation among the Jewish people, as His own peculiar possession, because He sits above the Cherubim. Afterward, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh are joined: they are the outermost who pertain to the ten tribes; Benjamin is established in the middle, by whom the Judean kingdom is designated. However, some think that the Son of God is addressed here, who is called the Shepherd of Joseph, and is introduced in Psalm 23. v. 1 as a Shepherd in a peculiar way: But because the same people wish for Christ to be denoted by the man of the right hand in verse 18, it is necessary in this place that they understand GOD the Father.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXX. Vinea Sacra.

Vers. 1. QVI SEDES SVPER CHERVBIM) Id est, qui te ostendis oraculis & splendore super arcam.

Nonnulli per Cherubim Angelos, & sedem in coelo intelligunt: quibusdam haec conjungere placet, ut Bellarmino; qui sedes in coelo super ange- los, & in typum hujus rei in sanctuario. Sed descri- bitur DEUS hic primum ut Pastor Israelis, qui Jo- sephum pascit, quod ἐξηγητικῶς additur, ut decem tribus per Israelem notari innuatur: ut Ezech. 37. v. 16. 19. Am. 5. v. 6. 15. cap. 6. v. 6. Zach. 10. v. 15. aut Israelis nomine Judae regnum, in quo viri Israe- litae erant, Josephi vero nomine X. tribus noten- tur. Deinde a revelatione in populo Juda, ceu peculio suo, quod sedeat super Cherubim. Post conjunguntur Ephraim, Benjamin, & Manasse: Extremi sunt, qui ad decem tribus pertinent, in medio constituitur Benjamin, quo regnum Judai- cum designatur. Compellari autem hic putant nonnulli Filium Dei, qui Pastor Joseph vocetur, & Psalm. 23. v. 1. ceu Pastor peculiariter introdu- catur: Sed quia iidem vers. 18. per virum dextrae Christum notari volunt, hoc loco necessum est DEUM Patrem intelligant.

## 80:1 Addition
On Psalm 80.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 80.

## 80:1 Addition
v. 1. GIVE EAR, O SHEPHERD OF ISRAEL.

The captivity, which is treated in this Psalm, according to Bellarmine, is both that which was first under the King of the Assyrians, Shalmaneser, who carried away the ten tribes, 2 Kings 17, and that which was later under King Nebuchadnezzar, who led the remaining people captive. Others, however, attribute the preceding Psalm to the Babylonian captivity of the Jews, but this one to that by which the ten Israelite tribes were abducted. Blessed Hülsemann has this to say about these matters: 'Just as the preceding Psalm, under the name of Jerusalem, also included the Christian Church, so it is false that by the vine brought over from Egypt in this Psalm only the Israelite Church is understood, and indeed such as it was in David's time, as Cajetan, Vatablus, Jansenius, Piscator, and Tremellius maintain. For because our Church is the same as that which was the Israelites', Acts 15:9, and therefore we or our Church are also rightly said to be brought over from Egypt, because our associates and fellow-citizens are brought over from there.' And just as it does not follow that David is not the author of this Psalm, who treats of the state of the Church not of his own time, but of a future time, so likewise it does not follow that for this reason he is not the author of the preceding Psalms 78 and 79, as Estius, Jansenius, Genebrardus, Muis, and others think.

Latin:

v. 1. QVI REGIS ISRAEL INTENDE.

Captivitas, de qua hoc Psalmo agitur, juxta Bellarminum est tum quæ primum fuit sub Rege Assyriorum Salmanassare, qui transtulit decem tri- bus 2. Reg. XVII. tum quæ deinde sub Rege Na- buchodonosore, qui captivum duxit reliquum popu- lum. Alii tamen præcedentem Psalmum tribuunt captivitati Babylonicæ Judæorum, hunc vero illi, qua abductæ decem tribus Israeliticæ. B. Hülsemannus „de his ita habet: Quomodo Psalmus antecedens „sub nomine Jerusalem etiam Christianam Eccle- „siam complexus est, ita falsum, per vineam ex „Ægypto traductam hoc Psalmo solam Ecclesiam „Israeliticam & quidem qualis Davidis tempore „fuit, intelligi, ut Cajetanus, Vatablus, Jansenius, „Piscator, Tremellius, statuunt. Quia enim eadem Ecclesia nostra est, quæ fuit Israelitarum Actor. 15, 9. Ideoque & nos seu nostra Ecclesia recte dicitur tradu- cta ex Ægypto, quia socii & ὁμόψηφοι nostri inde sunt traducti. Et quomodo non sequitur Davidem non esse autorem hujus Psalmi, qui de statu Ecclesiæ non sui, sed futuri temporis agit, ita pariter non se- quitur, quod hac de causa non sit autor anteceden- tium Psalmorum LXXIIX. & LXXIX. ut Estius, Jansenius, Genebrardus, Muis, aliique putant.

## 80:3
Verse 4. GOD CONVERT US, AND SHOW THY FACE.

That former word השיבנו is explained by some in this way: make us return, as if it were requested that those led away into captivity be brought back to their homeland: But Cocceius explains the reduction more correctly through conversion; and he takes that other phrase, show Thy face, in such a way that He wishes to show Himself appeased: Now this can be understood of Christ, who is the face of the Lord, by being exhibited: in whom alone is salvation, Acts 4. v. 12, which sigh is found sometimes afterward, v. 8, as also v. 10, to declare the desire for the coming of Christ: especially because in v. 18 the Prophet calls for the hand of the Lord to be upon the man of His right hand, by whom most understand Christ, who is next to God, Zech. 13. v. 7, the son of the right hand or most beloved, Gen. 35. v. 18. Precious like the right hand, as the Belgian Annotations have it: because it is declared by the son of man, which is a name of Christ, Ps. 8, Dan. 7, and by Arnobius, Jerome, Augustine, Athanasius, Cyril, Theodoret. Euthymius, it is explained concerning Christ. In the greatest emphasis, the man of the right hand, says Cocceius, is He who sits at the right hand of GOD, Ps. 110. v. 1, in whom the right hand of God works, even if afterward, departing from Himself (for those things cannot consist together), He makes Judah and his brothers men of the right hand. But the Belgians, Bellarmine, and indeed even Aben Ezra do not deny that the Messiah is understood, upon whom the hand of GOD was, when the work of redemption succeeded through Him. To say nothing of the fact that, according to some, even the words על־בן in verse 17 are explained thus: FOR THE SON, by understanding them of Christ Himself; the Vulgate has, upon the son of man, whom Thou hast confirmed for Thyself, to which sense Bellarmine brings the Chaldean Paraphrast, and from the Greeks Theodoret and Euthymius, and from the Latins Jerome and Augustine, because, namely, after the Babylonian captivity the Republic of the Jews was not better than before, so that this prophecy concerning the perfecting of the vineyard must necessarily be understood of Christ, so that, namely, GOD may look upon Him as the chief husbandman of His vineyard, the Leader and Prince of the Church. The explanation concerning the son, as it is handed down by Campensis, FOR THE SON, and by Junius and the Belgian Interpreters, AND THIS FOR THE SON, who, namely, is designated in Psalm 2. verse 7, Isaiah 9. verse 5, Daniel 9. verse 17, and is assumed by Mr. Dr. Geier because of the comparison with verse 18, does not seem entirely to be disapproved of, however much others may render it otherwise. Cocceius indeed joins what follows, and explains it as being for the shoot, burned with fire, etc. But these subsequent things pertain to verse 17 and look to the vineyard, which the Psalmist asks to be visited for the sake of the Son. It has been burned with fire, cut down; because of the rebuke of Thy countenance they perish, namely, the Israelites, denoted by the vineyard, or they will perish, unless Thou shalt assist. But it is doubtful to what times those calamities pertain. Cocceius refers the different clauses in this Psalm to distinct periods of time, but according to his custom, through his own interpretation and analysis. Blessed Luther takes it concerning the neighboring enemies, the Philistines, Moabites, Edomites, and Syrians, who seem to be designated in verse 7, concerning whom Cocceius also understands that clause. But the former things of verse 3, without cause, [pertain] to the abduction by Pekah, or [to] the remnants snatching away from the same. Furthermore, some refer the extermination of the boar from the forest in verse 14 to the King of the Assyrians, Shalmaneser, who led away the ten tribes, and to Nebuchadnezzar, who led away the two tribes; the Greek inscription favors them regarding the former in place of the Assyrians, and Cocceius agrees regarding the latter, and Bellarmine regarding both: the beginning of the Psalm is not alien to this opinion, nor is the description of GOD looking upon the Israelites and Jews, nor the scope, namely, the solicitation of grace to be exhibited through the coming of the Messiah.

Latin:

vers. 4. DEUS CONVERTE NOS, ET OSTENDE FACIEM TUAM.

Exponitur prius illud השיבנו a quibusdam h. m. fac nos redire, quasi petatur, ut in captivitatem abducti reducantur in Patriam: De reductione vero per conversionem rectius explicat Coccejus; & alterum illud, ostende faciem tuam, ita accipit; ut se placatum ostendere velit: Intelligi autem hoc potest de Christo, qui est facies Domini, exhibendo: in quo uno est salus Act. 4. v. 12. quod suspirium aliquo- ties postmodum reperitur, v. 8. ut & v. 10. ad decla- randum desiderium adventus Christi: maxime quia v. 18. vocet Propheta, ut manus Domini sit su- per virum dexterae ejus, per quem Christum intelli- gunt plerique Deo proximum Zach. 13. v. 7. dextrae filium seu charissimum, Gen. 35. v. 18. Instar dextrae pretiosum, ut Belgici Annotat. habent: quia decla- ratur per filium hominis, quod est nomen Christi Ps. 8. Dan. 7. & ab Arnob. Hieronym. August. Atha- nasio, Cyrillo, Theodor. Euthymio, de Christo expli- catur. In maxima emphasi vir dextrae, ait Coccejus, est is, qui sedet ad dextram DEI, Ps. 110. v. 1. in quo dextra Dei operatur, etsi postea a seipso discedens (non enim illa simul consistere possunt) Judam, & fratres ipsius viros dextrae faciat. Belgae autem, Bel- larminus, imo & Aben Ezra non abnuunt Messiam intelligi, super quem manus DEI fuit, quum per ipsum opus redemtionis succeffit. Ut taceam, quod juxta nonnullos etiam vers. 17. verba על־בן sic explicentur PROPTER FILIUM, de Chri- sto ipsomet ea intelligendo; Vulgata habet, super filium hominis, quem confirmasti tibi, in quem sen- sum adducit Bellarm. Paraphrasten Chaldaeum, & e Graecis Theodoretum, & Euthymium, e Latinis Hieron. & August. quia sc. post captivitatem Baby- lonicam non fuerit melior Resp. Judaeorum, quam antea, ut haec prophetia de perficienda vinea ita necessario intelligenda sit de Christo, ut nempe DEUS eum respiciat, ceu colonum praecipuum vineae suae, Ducem, & Principem Ecclesiae. Quae vero de filio explicatio uti a Campensi traditur, PROPTER FILIUM, & a Junio ac Belg. In- terpp. ET HOC PROPTER FILIUM, qui scil. designatus est Psalm. 2. vers. 7. Esai. 9. vers. 5. Dan. 9. vers. 17. & a Dn. D. Geiero ob collationem vers. 18. assumitur, ita non omnino improban- da videtur, utut alii aliter reddant. Jungit qui- dem Coccejus quae sequuntur, & exponit propter palmitem, crematum igne &c. Sed haec subsequen- tia ad vers. 17. pertinent ac vineam respiciunt, quam propter Filium visitari petit Psaltes. Com- busta est igne, succisa, ob increpationem vultus tui pereunt sc. Israelitae, per vineam notati, vel per- ibunt, nisi subveneris. Ad quaenam autem tem- pora calamitates illae pertineant dubium est. Coc- cejus ad distinctas temporum periodos diversa commata in hoc Psalmo refert, sed pro more suo, per ἰδίαν ἐπίλυσιν, & ἀνάλυσιν. B. Luther. de vicinis hostibus Philistaeis, Moabitis, Edomitis, Syris accipit, qui vers. 7. designati videntur, de quibus etiam Coccejus comma illud intelligit. Sed priora vers. 3. praeter causam ad abductionem per Pekah, vel reliquias ex eadem abripiens. Cae- terum exterminium apri de sylva vers. 14. ad Re- gem Assyriorum Salmanassarem, qui decem tri- bus, & ad Nebucadnezarem, qui duas tribus adduxit referunt nonnulli, quibus favet quoad pri- us inscriptio Graeca pro Assyriis, & accedit quo- ad posterius Coccejus, quoad utrumque Bellarmi- nus: a qua sententia non alienus est Psalmi ingres- sus, & descriptio DEI respiciens Israelitas, ac Ju- daos, neque scopus, solicitatio nempe gratiae per adventum Messiae exhibendae.

## 80:16 Addition
Verse 16.

BURNED WITH FIRE AND DUG UP, THEY SHALL PERISH AT THE REBUKE OF THY COUNTENANCE.

Vatablus, Musculus, Mollerus, Coppen, Piscator, Tremellius, the Belgian [translation], Jansenius, Saa, and Lorinus explain this as concerning the future conflagration of the city and temple, or the present danger of the excision of the vine, as in verses 13 and 14, and a greater one still to be feared, unless the enemies perish at the rebuke of the divine face; but because it is clear from the context that these things pertain to the consolatory part, that 'THEY SHALL PERISH' must be explained either as the destruction of the enemies burning the vine, or as the end of the devastation and affliction, as Blessed Luther rendered it. See Jeremiah 18:18, 49:7, Job 11:20.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

INCENSA IGNI ET SUFFOSSA AB IN- CREPATIONE VULTUS TUI PERIBUNT.

De conflagratione urbis & templi futura, vel de præsenti periculo excisionis vineæ, ut vers. 13. & 14. & majori adhuc metuendo, nisi hostes ab increpa- tione faciei divinæ pereant, exponunt Vatablus, Musculus, Mollerus, Coppen. Piscator, Tremellius, Belga, Jansenius, Saa, Lorinus, sed quia e συνεχείᾳ patet hæc pertinere ad partem Consolatoriam, illud PERIBUNT vel de interitu hostium incenden- tium vineam, vel de fine vastationis & afflictionis, ut B. Lutherus reddidit, explicandum. Vid. Jerem. 18, 18. c. 49, 7. Job. 11, 20.

## 81:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXI. The Feast of Tabernacles.

UPON THE WINEPRESSES] See above g. v. 1.

B. Luther correctly expressed the argument: It is a form of prayer, and a solemn canticle for that people sung annually at the feast of tabernacles to admonish the people, and to retain them in the true worship of God, namely the first commandment. For the feast בכסא which some render as at the new moon with Piscator, others as of the full moon, namely Dievius and Varenius, is explained by way of epexegesis concerning the notable day of the solemnity of the Hebrews, which was the feast of tabernacles Lev. 23. v. 34. Num. 29. falling on the 15th day of Tisri. Namely בחדש in the Month, on the Calends of the Month, the feast of trumpets, on the tenth day the feast of expiation was celebrated, but on the fifteenth that notable feast of tabernacles: whence most think that the feasts of this month are being referred to: and especially to the feast of tabernacles, which was a figure of the incarnation of the Son of GOD, by which He deigned to dwell in the tabernacle of the human body, that He might dwell in us. John 1. v. 14. chap. 14. v. 23. Cf. Psalm 118. v. 24.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXI. Festum tabernaculorum.

SVPER TORCVLARIBVS] Vide supra g. v. 1.

ARgumentum recte expressit B. Lutherus: Est formula precationis, & canticum solemne pro illo populo quotannis in festo tabernaculorum decan- tatum ad monendum populum, & retinendum in vero cultu Dei nempe primi praecepti. Nam festum בכסא quod aliqui reddunt in novilunio cum Pi- scat. alii de plenilunio, Dievius nimirum, & Vare- nius, explicatur κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν de insigni die sole- mnitatis Ebraeorum, quae erat tabernaculi festum Lev. 23. v. 34. Num. 29. in diem 15. Tisri inci- dens. Nimirum בחדש in Mense, Calendis Men- sis, festum tubarum, die decimo expiationis festum celebratum, decimo quinto vero festum illud infi- gne tabernaculorum: unde ad festa hujus mensis respici plerique putant: & maxime ad festum ta- bernaculorum, quod erat figura τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως Filii DEI, qua is habitare dignatus est in taberna- culo corporis humani, ut in nobis habitaret. Joh. 1. v. 14. cap. 14. v. 23. Conf. Psal. 118. v. 24.

## 81:1 Addition
On Psalm 81.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 81.

## 81:13
V. 14. THE ENEMIES OF THE LORD HAVE LIED UNTO HIM. The enemies of Christ: for the Lord speaks of the Lord, the Father of the Son: of whom it is also said, AND HE FED THEM: The former refers to the people, that they might lie to Him, that they might be forced to submit, even if hypocritically; not as some wish, the Lord, which the latter teaches, and had fed them.

Latin:

V. 14. INIMICI DOMINI MENTITI SUNT EI. Inimici Christi: loquitur enim Dominus de Domino, Pater de Filio: de quo etiam dicitur, ET CIBAVIT EOS: Prius respicit populum, men- tirentur ei, se submittere cogerentur, etsi hypocri- tice; non ut nonnulli volunt, Dominum, quod po- sterius docet, & cibasset eos.

## 81:13 Addition
v. 14. IF MY PEOPLE WOULD HEAR ME.

In Hebrew it is: O that my people would listen to me! This desire of God teaches the intimate will of God desiring the salvation of all. See B. Luther, Vol. IV, Jena, German, on Genesis 23, fol. 120, and on Zechariah 3, fol. 257, and the Arminians in the Hague Conference; it is not, however, an empty wish, such as those which are made about an impossible thing, as the Calvinist interlocutors perverted it in the same place, pp. 247, 383. For in verses 7, 8, 9, God has sufficiently testified concerning the exhibition of the means of salvation on His part.

Latin:

v. 14. SI POPULUS MEUS AUDIRET ME.

In Ebræo est: Utinam populus meus audiret me! Desiderium Dei hocce intimam Dei volunta- tem cupientem omnium salutem docet. Vid, B. Luther. Tom. IV. Jen. Germ. in Genes. XXIII. fol. 120. & in Zachar. III. fol. 257. & Arminianos in col- lat. Hagiensi; non autem votum inane est, qualia sunt, quæ de re impossibili fiunt, uti pervertebant ibi- dem Calviniani collocutores p. 247. 383. Nam v. 7. 8. 9. satis contestatus est Deus de exhibitione mediorum salutis ex parte sua.

## 82:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXII. Instruction for the Magistrate.

GOD STOOD IN THE SYNAGOGUE OF GODS) In the Hebrew: In the synagogue of God: that is His own, in the Hebrew manner. Thus Num. 10. v. 29. Thus also Luke 3. v. 19. and often elsewhere. The senate of judges is called the senate of God, because it exercises judgments in the name of God. 2 Chron. 19. v. 6. God in those first times punished the guilty severely by Himself, such as Cain, the age of the flood, the Sodomites, and others. Afterwards He substituted in His place judges legitimately appointed, especially in Judea.

False therefore with the LXX. Vulg. in the Assembly of gods, whom Bellarmine excuses in vain. BUT IN THE MIDST HE JUDGES THE GODS) That is, judges: for אלהים always has that meaning, even when it is used of God. We have taught in natural and revealed Theology and at the beginning of Genesis that the name אלהים is not derived from judging, but from the axiom of the cult of adoration. It is nevertheless attributed to Magistrates and judges, because they are vicars of GOD, and on account of the Lord, by whom they are set over others, they are to be honored.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXII. Informatio Magistratus.

DEVS STETIT IN SYNAGOGA DEORVM) In He- braeo: In Synagoga Dei: id est sua, more Hebraeo. Sic Num. 10. v. 29. Sic & Lucae 3. v. 19. & alibi saepe. Senatus Judicum, Senatus Dei dicitur, quia Dei nomine judicia exercet. 2. Pa- ralipp. 9. v. 6. Deus primis illis temporibus per se graviter fontes puniebat, ut Cainum, aetatem diluvii, Sodomitas, ali- os. Postea substituit suum in locum judices legitime con- stitutos, in Judaea maxime.

FAlso ergo cum LXX. Vulg. in Synagoga Deo- rum, quos nequicquam excusat. Bellarminus. IN MEDIO AVTEM DEOS DIJVDICAT) Id est judices : semper enim eam significationem habet אלהים, etiam cum de Deo ponitur. Nomen אלהים non à judicando, sed ab axiomate cultus adorationis dici in Theolog. nat. & revelat. & initio Geneseos docuimus. Tribuitur tamen Magistratibus & judicibus, quia illi vicarii DEI sunt, & ob Dominum, à quo aliis præfecti, sunt honorandi.

## 82:2
Vers. 2. HOW LONG DO YOU JUDGE INIQUITY?) As those who had followed Absalom.

Latin:

Vers. 2. VSQVEQVO JVDICATIS INIQVITATEM?) Vt illi qui Absolomum fuerant secuti.

## 82:6
Vers. 6. YOU ARE GODS) You are judges, established in eminent dignity according to my law.

AND ALL OF YOU ARE CHILDREN OF THE MOST HIGH) Those are called children who in some part are similar to someone.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DII ESTIS) Judices estis, eminenti in dignitate secundum legem meam constituti.

ET FILII EXCELSI OMNES) Filii dicuntur qui aliqua ex parte alicui sunt similes.

## 82:7
BUT YOU SHALL DIE LIKE MEN, AND LIKE ONE OF THE PRINCES YOU SHALL FALL) But that here signifies nevertheless. You shall die nevertheless: for this lot is common to the common people (for the word אדם in Hebrew often signifies such) and to the highest:

Pale death knocks with an impartial foot at the taverns of the poor and the towers of kings.

Latin:

VOS AVTEM SICVT HOMINES MORIEMINI, ET SICVT VNVS DE PRINCIPIBVS CADETIS) Illud au- tem hîc valet nihilominus. Moriemini nihilominus : hæc enim sors communis est plebejis (talem enim vox אדם in Hebreo sæpe significat) & summatibus :

Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas Regumque turres.

## 82:8
Vers. 8. ARISE O GOD JUDGE THE EARTH) Through King David.

It is rather a sigh toward Christ (which Cocceius and Bellarmine also acknowledge) to whom alone the inheritance of all nations is given, Psalm 2, v. 8, and who is the judge of all the earth, Gen. 18.

FOR YOU SHALL INHERIT AMONG ALL NATIONS) You shall extend your empire and your law far and wide through him.

Whoever desires the commentary of the blessed Luther on this Psalm, let him consult Volume III of the Wittenberg Latin edition.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SVRGE DEVS JVDICA TERRAM) Per re- gem Davidem.

Suspirium potius est ad Christum (quod etiam agnoscit Coccejus & Bellarminus) cui soli omnium gentium hæreditas data Psal. 2. v. 8. quique judex est universæ terræ Gen. 18.

QVONIAM TV HEREDITABIS IN OMNIBVS GENTIBVS) Tu per eum imperium legemque tuam lon- ge lateque proferes.

Commentationem B. Lutheri in hunc Psal- mum qui desiderat Tomum III. Latin. Witeber- gens. adeat.

## 83:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXIII.

The confederacy of the enemies.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXIII.

Confœderatio hostium.

## 83:1 Addition
On Psalm 83.

Latin:

Ad Psal. 83.

## 83:1 Addition
v. 1. O GOD, WHO SHALL BE LIKE UNTO THEE? DO NOT HOLD THY PEACE AND BE NOT STILL, O GOD.

Jerome translates the Hebrew thus: O God, do not hold thy peace, do not be silent, and do not rest, O God. Whence Vatablus, Jansenius, and Lorinus easily grant a παράπτωμα

of the Vulgate. Cf. Sixt. Amama. Regarding the argument of the Psalm, our blessed Hülsemann has it thus: Most of the Fathers, induced by the fifth verse, felt that this Psalm does not fit the age of David, and that the proper names which are commemorated from verse 6 onwards are hieroglyphics denoting various enemies of the Christian Church, just as the Apostle allegorizes under the name of Ishmael and Hagar in Galatians 4. But this exposition is a bad example. We judge that the discourse here is entirely about the condition of the Church in the time of David, but that it is nevertheless a prophecy concerning the future state of the Church. Which I think can be proven from verse 4, where the suffering subject is not only called the people of God, but they are also called the hidden ones of God; the Vulgate translates it as saints. But it has not attained the sense of the Hebrew word. For they are called hidden because of the singular and hidden grace which they have obtained from God. See the parallels Psalm 91:1, Psalm 31:21, Psalm 27:5, Psalm 36:8, Psalm 140:8. Colossians 3:3. Mollerus here points his finger at the invisible Church; but Gesner's interpretation is better, concerning the hidden and singular favor of GOD, towards which he cites that simile of the hen: See, however, the litigants concerning this Psalm, Forerus and D. Höe in the Apology for the sermon delivered at the Leipzig assembly of Princes in the year 1630. The blessed Höppfner maintains that it was completed by a prophetic spirit. Bellarmine, although he notes that some refer it to the times of Jehoshaphat (which Kimchi, Piscator, and Muis do) and that Theodoret and Euthymius wish it to look back to the wars of the nations after the return from Babylon in Nehemiah 4, and professes that it is more probable to him that these things pertain to the times of the Maccabees 1. Maccabees 5. But it is most probable that it looks to the times of the Anti-Christ, as Augustine judged, and he finally defines in this manner: whatever may be the case regarding the historical sense, it cannot and must not be denied that the principal intention of the Holy Spirit is directed toward Christ in the Church.

Latin:

v. 1. DEUS QVIS SIMILIS ERIT TIBI? NE TACEAS NEQVE COMPESCARIS DEUS.

Ebræa sic vertit Hieronymus: Deus ne taceas, ne sileas, & non quiescas Deus. Unde Vatablus, Jansenius, Lorinus, facile largiuntur παράπτωμα

vulgatæ. Conf. Sixt. Amama. De argumento autem Pfalmi sic habet B. Hülsemannus noster: Ple- rique Patrum versu quinto inducti senserunt Psal- mum hunc ætati Davidis non convenire, & nomi- na propria, quæ inde a vers. 6. seq. commemoran- tur esse hieroglyphica notantia diversos hostes Ec- clesiæ Christianæ, qualiter allegorizat Apostolus sub nomine Ismaëlis & Hagar Gal. 4. Sed hæc expositio mali exempli est. Cenfemus hic omni- no sermonem esse de conditione Ecclesiæ tempore Davidis: sed vaticinium tamen de futuro statu Ec- clesiæ. Quod probari posse puto ex vers. 4. ubi subjectum patiens non solum dicuntur populus Dei, sed dicuntur etiam occulti Dei; Vulgatus Sanctos vertit. Sed sensum vocis Ebrææ non est assecu- tus. Occulti enim dicuntur propter singularem occultamque gratiam, quam a Deo nacti sunt. Vi- de parallelos Psal. 91, 1. Psal. 31, 21. Psal. 27, 5. Psal. 36, 8. Psal. 140, 8. Coloss. 3, 3. Mollerus hic digitum intendit in Ecclesiam invisibilem; sed Gesneri inter- pretatio melior est, de occulto & singulari favore DEI, quorsum allegat similitudinem illam de galli- na: Vide tamen litigantes de hoc Psalmo Forerum & D. Höe in Apologia pro concione habita in con- ventu Principum Lipsico Anno 1630. Prophetico spiritu consummatum esse, B. Höppfnerus statuit. Bellarmin. etsi notet quosdam ad Josaphati tempo- ra eum referre (quod Kimchi, Piscator, Muis fa- ciunt) quodque Theodoretes & Euthymius bella gentium post reditum è Babylone Nehem. 4. respi- ci velint, & probabilius sibi esse profitetur, quod pertineant hæc ad tempora Maccabæorum 1. Mac- cab. 5. probabilissimum autem quod spectet ad An- ti-Christi tempora, uti Augustinus censuit, definit tan- dem h. m. quicquid sit de sensu historico, non potest nec debet negari, quod præcipua intentio Spiritus S. ad Christum in Ecclesiam dirigatur.

## 83:7
Ver. 8. THE TABERNACLES OF THE IDUMEANS AND THE ISHMAELITES, MOAB AND THE HAGARENES, GEBAL AND AMMON AND AMALEK, THE ALIENS WITH THE INHABITANTS (OF TYRE) I do not doubt that these pertain to the times which are described in 2 Sam. 8. Concerning Gebal or the Byblians, see 1 Kings 5, v. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 8. TABERNACVLA IDVMÆORVM ET ISMAELITÆ, MOAB ET AGARENI, GEBAL ET AMMON ET AMALEC, ALIENIGENÆ CVM HABI- TANTIBVS TTRVM) Non dubito quin hæc pertineant ad tempora quæ describuntur 2. Sam. 8. de Gebale sive Gy- bliis vide 1. Reg. 5. v. 18.

## 83:8
Ver. 9. FOR ASSUR ALSO IS COME WITH THEM) In the Hebrew, Also. Aquila and Theodotion καίγε, Symmachus ἔτι καὶ. History does not make special mention of these. But there is no doubt that they sought help from all their neighbors.

To which times this confederacy should be referred, there is no small doubt among the interpreters. B. Luther refers it to the times of David, and the enemies who were hostile to Judea from the neighborhood. Piscator and Muys, with Kimchi, refer it to the times of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20, with Cocceius not dissenting; Theodor. and Euthymius to the times after the return from the Babylonian captivity; Bellarmine to the times of the Maccabees; Cocceius to the conspiracy of the nations against the New Testament Church; St. Augustine to the battles of the Anti-Christ, etc. Of which opinions the former two are to be preferred; if the latter is accepted in such a way that Asaph here prophetically foresaw that confederacy which was to be in the time of Jehoshaphat: to which opinion B. Hopfner also acceded. For although in those armies in 2 Chron. 20 only the Ammonites and Idumeans with the Moabites are named, it is nevertheless likely that the others also who are named here conspired among themselves, and acted by common counsel, and if the beginnings had turned out well, the others would have contributed all their strength to suppress the kingdom of Judah. The land of Israel was a kind of center, toward which various enemies aimed from every side: from the south the Edomites, Ishmaelites, Amalekites; from the east Moab, Ammon, the Hagarenes; from the north the Assyrians; from the west the Philistines, Gebalites, Tyrians.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ETENIM ASSVR VENIT CVM ILLIS) In Hebreo, Etiam. Aquila & Theodotio καίγε, Symmachus ἔτι καὶ. Historia horum non specialiter meminit. Sed du- bitandum non est, quin ab omnibus vicinis auxilia petierint.

AD quæ tempora referenda sit hæc confœde- ratio, non exigua est dubitatio penes Interpp. Ad Davidis tempora, & hostes, qui circumcirca Judææ infesti erant è vicinia refert & B. Lutherus. Ad Josaphati tempora 2. Paralip. 20. Piscator, & Muys, cum Kimchio, non abnuente Coccejo : ad tempora post reductionem è captivitate Babylo- nica, Theodor. & Euthymius, ad tempora Mac- cabæorum Bellarminus, ad conspirationem genti- um contra Ecclesiam Nov. Testam. Coccejus, ad Anti-Christi prælia S. Augustin, &c. E quibus sententiis priores duæ præferendæ; si altera ita ac- cipiatur, ut hic Prophetice illam confœderatio- nem Josaphati tempore futuram præviderit As- saph : cui sententiæ etiam accessit B. Hopsne- rus. Quanquam enim in exercitibus illis 2. Par. 20. Ammonitæ tantum & Idumæi cum Moabitis nominentur, verisimile tamen est cæteros etiam qui hic nominantur conspirasse inter se, commu- nique egisse consilio, & si initia bene cecidissent, cæteras ad supprimendum regnum Judæ collatu- ras fuisse omnem opem. Terra Israelis erat quoddam quasi centrum, ad quod collineabant undiquaque varii hostes, à meridie Edomei, Is- maelitæ, Amalekitæ, ab oriente Moab, Ammon, Hagareni, ab Aquilone Assyrii, ab occasu Phili- stei, Gebalitæ, Tyrii.

## 83:10
Ver. 11. THEY PERISHED AT ENDOR) Supply 'who'. Endor is in the portion of Manasseh, Joshua 17, v. 11; 1 Sam. 28, v. 7; there were also Taanach and the waters of Megiddo mentioned in Judges 5, v. 19, as appears in the said place of Joshua and Judges 1, 27. Ver. 12. MAKE THEIR PRINCES LIKE OREB AND ZEB AND ZEBEE AND SALMANA) Judges 7, v. 25; ch. 8, v. 21. Ver. 14. O MY GOD, MAKE THEM LIKE A WHEEL) Roll them, like a wheel from a sloping place. Others interpret it as pappi, that is, the down of thistles.

Latin:

Verf. 11. DISPERIERVNT IN ENDOR) Supple qui. En- dor est in parte Manassis Josue 17. v. 11. 1. Sam. 28. v. 7. ibi- dem erant Thanach & aquæ Mageddo memoratæ Jud. 5. v. 19. ut apparet Josue dicto loco & Jud. 1, 27. Verf. 12. PONE PRINCIPES EORVM SICVT OREB ET ZEB ET ZEBEE ET SALMANA) Jud. 7. v. 25. c. 8. v. 21. Verf. 14. DEVS MEVS PONE ILLOS VT PROTAM) Devolve eos, ut rotam de loco declivi. Alii pappos, id est, lanuginem carduorum interpretantur.

## 84:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXIV. The tabernacles of the Lord.

IT IS BELIEVED) The Psalm was written in memory of that time when Absalom held the greater part of Judea.

That indeed seemed so to Piscator and Amama also: others refer that exile to Saul or to Babel with Kimchi, but it is more correctly considered to be a beatitude of the worshipers of GOD with B. Luther and B. Hopfner.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXIV. Tabernacula Domini.

CREDITVR) Scriptus Psalmus in memoriam ejus tem- poris, quo majorem Judææ partem tenebat Absolomus.

ID quidem Piscatori & Amamæ quoque visum: alii id exilium ob Saulem referunt vel in Babel cum Kimchio, sed rectius censetur esse μακαρι- σμὸς cultorum DEI cum B. Luther. & B. Hopfner.

## 84:1 Addition
On Psalm 84.

V. 1. HOW BELOVED ARE THY TABERNACLES. Some explain it as the desire to return to the earthly Jerusalem: Amama, along with Piscator, refers it to David as a fugitive from Absalom; R. Kimchi refers it to a fugitive from Saul, or even to the captives in Babylon; but there is no trace of these in the text; indeed, it is clear from verses 5 and 6 that it deals with the happiness of every believer, and Mr. Dr. Gejer testifies that this is taught at length by the blessed Höpffner. Most of the Fathers understand it as the desire for the heavenly tabernacle. Brentius explains it concerning the tabernacles of the Churches in the New Testament, to which we also accede.

Latin:

Ad Pfalm. 84.

V. 1. QUAM DILECTA TABERNACULA. De desiderio redeundi ad terrenam Hierusalem nonnulli exponunt: ad Davidem fugitivum ab Ab- solon refert Amama, cum Piscatore, ad fugitivum à Saule, vel etiam ad captivos in Babylonia R. Kimchi; sed de his nullum in textu vestigium; imo de felici- tate fidelis cujusq́; agi e v. 5. 6. patet, & prolixe doce- ri id a B. Höpffnero testatur Dn. D. Gejerus. Pleri- que Patres de desiderio cælestis tabernaculi intelli- gunt. De Ecclesiarum in Nov. Testam. tabernacu- lis Brentius exponit, cui & nos accedimus.

## 84:5
Ver. 6. BLESSED IS THE MAN WHOSE HELP IS FROM THEE, IN WHOSE HEART ARE THE ASCENTS.

In the Hebrew: whose strength is in Thee, who does not rely on his own virtue, his own merits, but trusts in Thee alone, and believes himself invincible against all the power of Satan and hell by Thy virtue) The paths (of Thee) in their heart: (they apply themselves with their whole heart to this, that they may walk in the way of Thy precepts.) The rest which follow here, the Vulgate distorted into an entirely different sense: he has disposed in the valley of tears in the place which he has set. For the lawgiver shall give a blessing: Which are foreign to the Hebrew source: But more foreign and contrary to the analogy of faith are the glosses of the Papists, Bellarmine, and Michael Ayguanus concerning meritorious acts, by which one ascends to glory, for which ascent the cooperation of our will with the grace and blessing of Christ the new lawgiver is required, so that we may proceed from virtue to virtue, as this Carmelite and Doctor of Paris explained: to which the aforementioned Cardinal also went: Nor do the interpretations of the Jews, Salvinus, Cocceius, and the Belgian Paraphrast agree, the empty expositions concerning the passage through the valley of weeping, (a horrible and thirsty place: which had to be crossed by those tending toward Jerusalem) with that alacrity with which another would cross places irrigated by perennial streams, or moistened by a large rain, and green: because they place it into a stream, considering that valley as a stream or a place abounding in rough spots, and which the rain covers in blessings, that is, bountifully and copiously; it is a matter of the Doctors, by whom one must pass through the valley of Habbacha, of tears: who place the arid valley, destitute of the waters of consolation, into a fountain or stream, bubbling with the purer waters of life-giving doctrine, and bringing consolation to the afflicted conscience: so that each one may overwhelm the hearers with the blessings of the Doctors, and as it were with a large rain of spiritual benefits, as B. Luther, Brentius, Osiander, the Vinarions, and others: even if they draw these things specifically to the Apostles: Brentius and Osiander. The Hebrew has it thus: Passing through the valley of tears, they shall make it a fountain: also (certainly, in truth) the Teacher shall cover (Arias Montanus rendered it SHALL BE COVERED) it with blessings. It is evident, however, from these verses that this Psalm is rashly drawn by Bellarmine, along with certain Fathers, to the heavenly tabernacles. Let us now add the Grotian ones:

Verse 6.

BLESSED IS THE MAN WHOSE HELP IS FROM THEE: HE HATH DISPOSED ASCENSIONS IN HIS HEART] Understand help as the ability to go to the temple. You may best translate the rest thus: The ways are paved in the midst of them. In all places in which they dwell, there are well-paved roads that lead to Jerusalem.

IN THE VALLEY OF TEARS IN THE PLACE WHICH HE HAS SET, FOR THE LAWGIVER WILL ALSO GIVE A BLESSING) There are many words here that are polysemous. But this seems to be the best interpretation: They who are to pass through the valley of mulberry trees will make it a fountain: (they will use it as a well-watered place) for a blessing (supply: divine) will cover it with rain. Mulberries grow in thirsty places. He says, therefore, even if thirsty places occur on the journey, God will give them rain instead of fountains. See Ezek. 34, v. 26.

Verse 18.

Latin:

Verf. 6. BEATUS VIR, CUJUS EST AUXILIUM ABS TE, ASCENSIONES IN CORDE SUO.

In Ebræo: cujus fortitudo est in Te, qui non sua virtute, suis meritis nititur, sed in Te uno con- fidit, tuaque virtute invictum se adversus omnem potestatem Satanæ & inferni credit) Semitæ (tuæ) in corde eorum: (toto corde in id incumbunt, ut in via præceptorum tuorum ambulent.) Reliqua quæ hic sequuntur, in alium prorsus sensum Vul- gatus detorsit: disposuit in valle lacrymarum in lo- co, quem posuit. Etenim benedictionem dabit legis- lator: Quæ aliena sunt à fonte Ebræo: Sed magis alienæ atque analogiæ fidei contrariæ sunt glossæ Pontificiorum, Bellarmini, & Michaelis Aygua- ni de actibus meritoriis, quibus ascendatur ad glo- riam, ad quem ascensum requiratur cooperatio no- stræ voluntatis cum gratia & benedictione Christi no- vi legislatoris, ut de virtute proficiamus in virtutem, ut hic Carmelita & Doctor Parisiensis exposuit: quo etiam abiit prædictus Cardinalis: Neque congruunt Judæorum, Salvini, Cocceji, Belgic. Paraphrast. inanes ἐκθέσεις de transitu per val- lemmori, (locum horridum & siticulosum: qui transeundus fuerit Hierosolymam tendentibus) cum ea alacritate, qua alius loca perennibus ri- vis irrigua, aut largo imbre humecta, & viren- tia transiret: quod in rivum ponant eam, repu- tando vallem illam pro rivo vel loco salebris ab- undante, & quem operit pluvia in benedictioni- bus, id est, largiter & copiosè; de Doctoribus agi- tur, quibus per vallem Habbacha, lacrymarum transeundum: qui vallem aridam aquis consola- tionum destitutam in fontem vel rivum ponunt, aquis purioribus vivificæ doctrinæ scaturien- tem, & afflictæ conscientiæ consolationem adfe- rentem: ut benedictionibus Doctorum quis- que obruat auditores, ac pluvia veluti larga be- neficiorum spiritualium, uti B. Lutherus, Bren- tius, Osiander, Vinarienses, alii: etsi ad Aposto- los speciatim hæc trahant: Brentius & Osiander. Ebræa ita habent: Transeuntes per vallem lacry- marum, fontem ponent eam: etiam (certe, pro- fecto) benedictionibus operiet (Arias Montanus reddidit OPERIETUR) Doctor. Patet au- tem ex his versibus temere hunc Psalmum à Bel- larm. cum Patribus quibusdam trahi ad cœlestia ta- bernacula. Addamus jam Grotiana:

Vers. 6.

BEATVS VIR CVI EST AVXILIVM ABS TE: ASCENSIONES IN CORDE SVO DISPOSVIT] Au- xilium intellige, facultatem eundi ad templum. Cætera sic optime vertas: Viæ sunt stratæ in medio eorum. In omnibus locis in quibus habitant, viæ sunt bene stratæ quæ Hierosoly- ma deducunt.

IN VALLE LACRYMARVM IN LOCO QVEM POSVIT, ETENIM BENEDICTIONEM DABIT LE- GISLATOR) Multæ hic voces sunt πολύσημοι. Sed opti- ma interpretatio hæc videtur esse: Transituri per vallem mo- rorum, fontem facient eam: (ea utentur tanquam aquoso lo- co) nam benedictio (supple divina) operiet eum imbre. Mori nascuntur in locis siticulosis. Dicit ergo etiam si in itinere oc- currant loca siticulosa, Deus illis pluviam dabit pro fonti- bus. Vide Ezech. 34. v. 26.

Vers. 18.

## 84:7
THEY SHALL GO FROM STRENGTH TO STRENGTH) From the Greek: πορεύσονται ἐκ δυνάμεως εἰς δύναμιν. But δυνάμεις for these writers, like the Hebrew חיל, signify troops. They will go divided into troops, as is accustomed to happen in great caravans.

Latin:

IBVNT DE VIRTVTE IN VIRTVTEM) Ex Græco: πορεύσονται ἐκ δυνάμεως εἰς δύναμιν. Sed δυνάμεις his scri- ptoribus, ut Hebræis חיל, agmina significant. Ibunt distincti in agmina, ut in magnis συνοδίαις fieri solet.

## 85:1 Argument
PSALM 85. A prayer against wrath, an imploring of blessing.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXV. Iræ deprecatio, benedictionis imploratio.

## 85:1
Verse 2.

THOU HAST TURNED AWAY THE CAPTIVITY OF JACOB) It is a description of the return to the city, after Absalom was defeated. He calls that exile beyond the Jordan captivity, where David and those who followed him were besieged, partly by their own popular adversaries, partly by hostile nations. This Psalm could very well have been used by Ezra and Nehemiah.

It is rash to drag these things to the exile of David: the captivity of Jacob is one thing, the exile of Jacob is another. Whence others more correctly interpret it concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity and the desire for the coming of the Messiah; or concerning the liberation granted to the Israelites, so that by that argument GOD might be moved to show His grace likewise to Christians; whence Blessed Luther says it is a prayer containing the affections of a heart fearing GOD and in most ardent words deprecates the terror of the wrath of God. Thus also Blessed Gesner. Cocceius calls it a prayer of those converted from among the Jews for the conversion of the rest, in which, however, he himself is ambiguous: If the Jews, he says, ever return to God, they will speak thus.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

AVERTISTI CAPTIVITATEM JACOB) Descriptio est reditus in urbem, devicto Absolomo. Captivitatem ap- pellat exilium illud ultra Jordanem, ubi David, & qui eum sequebantur obsessi erant, partim a popularibus adversariis suis, partim ab infestis gentibus. Optime potuit hic Psal- mus usurpari ab Esdra & Nehemia.

TEmere hæc ad exilium Davidis rapiuntur: aliud est captivitas Jacob, aliud exilium Ja- cob. Unde de liberatione è captivitate Babylonica, & desiderio adventus Messiæ alii rectius accipiunt; Vel de liberatione Israëlitis præstita, ut eo argu- mento moveatur DEUS Christianis itidem ex- hibendi gratiam suam; unde B. Luther. est oratio, inquit, continens affectus cordis timentis DEUM & ardentissimis verbis deprecatur terrorem iræ Dei. Sic & B. Gesnerus. Coccejus orationem dicit con- versorum ex Judæis pro reliquorum conversione, in quo tamen ipse ambiguus est: Si Judæi, inquit, unquam revertentur ad Deum, sic loquentur.

## 85:6
Verse 7.

GIVE US THY SALVATION.

That is JESUS, Luke 2, v. 30, in whom is peace, grace, and every happiness, both corporal and spiritual.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

SALUTARE TUUM DA NO- BIS.

Illud est JESUS, Luc. 2, v. 30. in quo pax, gratia, & omnis felicitas, cum corporalis, tum spiritualis.

## 86:1 Argument
PSALM 86. The conversion of the Gentiles. The turning away of enemies.

A PRAYER OF DAVID HIMSELF) Used, as the Hebrews advise us, by Hezekiah.

Be it so, that it was used by Hezekiah: it is nevertheless, as the inscription has it, a prayer of David himself, when, established in the agonies of his soul, he was in need of divine consolation, while at the same time predicting the conversion of the nations, verse 9.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXVI. Gentium conversio. Hostium aversio.

ORATIO IPSI DAVID) Vsurpata, ut Hebræi nos mo- nent, ab Ezechia.

SIt ita, usurpatam ab Ezechia fuisse: est tamen ut inscriptio habet oratio ipsius Davidis, cum in angoribus animi constitutus consolatione di- vina indigeret prædicentis simul conversionem gentium, vers. 9.

## 86:2
Vers. 2.

FOR I AM HOLY. Heb. חסיד others explain as a beneficiary or a fosterling. B. Franz. orac. 143. חסיד miserable: Thus also Montanus and Luther in the marginal gloss. In vain, therefore, do the Papists carve out the merits of works from this: See Bellarmine's own commentary on this place. The Arab and the Syrian refer it to GOD, in that you are good, but this is repugnant to the Hebrew text and the Chaldean and LXX interpreters.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

QUONIAM SANCTUS SUM. Ebr. חסיד alii exponunt beneficiarius vel alu- mnus. B. Franz. orac. 143. חסיד miserabilis: Sic & Montan. ac Luther. in gloss. marg. Frustra ergo hinc Pontificii operum merita exsculpunt: Vid. ipsius Bellarmin. Commentarius in h. l. Arabs & Syrus ad DEUM referunt, eo quod bonus tu (es) sed hoc textui Ebræo & Interpr. Chald. & LXX. repugnat.

## 86:13
Vers. 13.

THOU HAST DELIVERED MY SOUL FROM THE LOWEST HELL) ἐξ ᾅδε κατωτάτω. The sense is, from the deepest pit: that is, from the most grievous danger.

Feuardentius therefore ineptly proves purgatory from this. See B. Meisner on Purgatory, p. 137. That this happened to David while alive, his celebration teaches. Compare Crit. Sac. p. 683.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ERVISTI ANIMAM MEAM EX INFERNO IN- FERIORI) ἐξ ᾅδε κατωτάτω. Sensus est, ex specu pro- fundissima: id est, gravissimo periculo.

Inepte ergo hinc purgatorium probat Fevar- dent. Vid. B. Meisner. de Purg. p. 137. Vivo Da- vidi hoc contigisse, ejus celebratio docet. Conf. Crit. Sac. p. 683.

## 87:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXVII. A new generation in Zion.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXVII. Nova in Zion generatio.

## 87:4
Vers. 4.

I WILL MAKE MENTION OF RAHAB AND BABYLON TO THEM THAT KNOW ME: BEHOLD THE PHILISTINES, AND TYRE, WITH ETHIOPIA; THIS MAN WAS BORN THERE) Rahab is Egypt, so called on account of pride, as appears below 89, 11. Isaiah 51, 9. God, however, speaks and says: If I seek from the Egyptians or Babylonians, or Philistines, or Tyrians, or Ethiopians who among them have known me, they will say, these such were born among us.

These things, however, pertain to the New Testament. For this is a prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ and the future Church, as B. Luther has in his argument: which he understands by Zion. Bellarmine also says that all things agree with the triumphant Church: but will regeneration take place in the heavens?

Latin:

Vers. 4.

MEMOR ERO RAHAB ET BABYLONIS SCIEN- TIUM ME: ECCE ALIENIGENÆ ET TYRUS, ET POPULI ÆTHIOPUM, HI FUERUNT ILLIC) Rahab est Ægyptus, ob superbiam sic dicta, ut apparet infra 89, 11. Esaiæ 51, 9. Deus autem loquitur, & ait: Si quæram ex Ægyptiis vel Babyloniis, vel Palæstinis, vel Tyriis, vel Æthiopi- bus qui eorum me noverint, dicent, hi tales nati apud nos sunt.

PErtinent autem hæc ad Nov. Testam. Est enim hic Prophetia de regno Christi, & futura Ecclesia, ut B. Luth. in argum. habet: quam per Sion intelligit. Bellarm. etiam Ecclesiæ trium- phanti omnia convenire ait: sed num regenera- tio in cœlis locum habitura?

## 87:5
Vers. 5.

SHALL SION SAY: MAN AND MAN IS BORN IN HER?) Or will Jerusalem say in this manner, this one and that one (that is, one pious man and another) is born here?

Bellarmine rashly suspects the Hebrew text is corrupted here, as if Vau were written for מ. The sense is plain: And it shall be said of Sion, man and man is born in her, that is, many. For that repetition signifies a multitude, which Genebrard noted from Kimchi and Grotius acknowledged here.

AND THE HIGHEST HIMSELF ESTABLISHED HER) Nay rather, the Highest formed this whole city: he imbued it with his own customs. כון is accustomed to be translated as πλάττειν.

And so Bellarmine wrongly snatches these words for the temporal birth of Christ, relying on the erroneous Vulgate version, Man is born in her, and the Highest himself established her. That he (the Son of God) was born in her (Sion, which, however, he struggles vehemently to explain how it fits Christ, who was born not in Sion but in Bethlehem), who established her, the Highest: appealing to Tertullian, Euthymius, and Augustine, who indeed could not inspect the Hebrew text. The Cardinal also punctuates the text falsely and deceives others when he says that in the Hebrew text the former word איש refers to the preceding verb: since inspection shows by the force of the accentuation and the construction that איש ואיש cohere, and it is clear in the text that it treats of regeneration in the Church. Compare what is in Critic. Sacr. p. 657.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

NUMQVID SION DICET: HOMO ET HOMO NATUS EST IN EA?) An in eum modum dicent Hiero- solyma, hic & ille (id est, unus & alter pius) natus hic est?

Temere textum Ebr. hic corruptum suspica- tur Bellarm. quasi Vau pro מ scriptum sit. Sen- sus planus est: Et de Sion dicetur, vir & vir na- tus est in ea, id est, multi. Nam illa repetitio mul- titudinem significat, quod Genebr. è Kimchio notavit & hic agnovit Grotius.

ET IPSE FUNDAVIT EAM ALTISSIMUS) Imo vero hanc civitatem totam formavit altissimus: suis moribus im- buit. כון solet verti πλάττειν.

Perperam itaque Bellarm. hæc abripit ad na- tivitatem temporalem Christi erroneæ versioni Vulg. innitens, Homo natus est in ea, & ipse fun- davit eam altissimus. Quod in ea (Sione, quod tamen quomodo Christo non in Sione, sed in Bethlehem nato conveniat, in eo vehementer se torquet) natus sit, qui fundarit eam altissimus, FILIUS DEI: provocans ad Tertul. Euthym. & August. qui vero textum Ebræum inspicere non potuere. Falso etiam interpungit textum Car- din. & fallit alios, cum ait in textu Ebræo prio- rem vocem איש ad verbum præcedens referri: siquidem αὐτοψία doceat vi accentuationis & constructiones איש ואיש cohærere, & in textu luculentum est agi de regeneratione in Ecclesia. Conf. quæ in Critic. Sacr. p. 657.

## 87:6
Ver. 6.

THE LORD SHALL TELL IN THE WRITINGS OF THE PEOPLES AND OF THESE PRINCES WHO WERE IN HER) He repeats in other words what he had said: God in the register of the peoples easily counts (namely the pious, speaking from the preceding) this one and that one is born here.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

DOMINUS NARRABIT IN SCRIPTVRIS POPULO- RUM AC PRINCIPUM HORUM QVI FUERUNT IN EA) Repetit aliis verbis quæ dixerat: Deus in matricula po- pulorum facile numeret (nempe pios, ex superioribus dicens) hic ibi natus est.

## 87:7
AS THE HABITATION OF ALL WHO REJOICE IS IN THEE) In the Hebrew: As the precentor so the chorus: all my springs are in thee. The sense is: the matter stands far otherwise with thee, O Sion. As is the precentor, so is the chorus: this is proverbial, signifying that the greatest and the least are alike in this matter) my abundance (which is signified by waters) is with thee.

Blessed Luther rightly takes these words concerning the joyful voice of the Gospel, which all resound. Those words, all my springs are in thee, indicate that the reborn profess that they find in the Church everything that quenches thirst and refreshes the weary, which is more fitting than if one were to refer the voice in thee to Christ.

Latin:

SICUT LÆTANTIUM OMNIUM HABITATIO EST IN TE) In Hebræo: Sicut præcentor ita chorus : omnes scaturigines meæ in te. Sensus est: longe aliter apud te, ô Sion, res se habet. Qualis est præcantor, talis est chorus: proverbiale hoc, significans maximos minimosque in hac re esse similes) abundantia mea (quæ per aquas significatur) apud te est.

De læta voce Evangelii, quam omnes re- sonant, recte hæc accipit B. Luther. Illa, omnes fontes mei in te, indicant, quod renati profite- antur se in Ecclesia omnia reperire, quæ sitim restinguant, & fessos recreent, quæ magis con- veniunt, quam si quis vocem in te ad Christum referat.

## 88:1 Argument
PSALM LXXXVIII. The infernal anxiety of the Messiah.

A MASCHIL OF HEMAN THE EZRAHITE) This Heman is, if I am not mistaken, the one who is named among the singers or poets, 1 Chronicles 6:33, who seems to have composed this didactic song and handed it down to the descendants of Korah to be sung.

Augustine, Jerome, Euthymius, and Bellarmine wish for the Passion of Christ to be predicted here, with the blessed Luther, the blessed Pomeranus, and the blessed Brentius not denying it (although they also refer these things to spiritual temptations, which we concede can be done through a convenient application, because it is necessary for us to be made conformable to the image of the Son of God; yet we do not agree with Jansenius or Cocceius that these things apply to Christ, as prefigured by David, only in the fullest sense), along with the blessed Cramer and Dr. Geier.

Latin:

PSALM. LXXXVIII. Messiæ anxietas infernalis.

INTELLECTUS EMAN EZRAHITÆ) Hic Eman is est, ni fallor, qui nominatur inter cantores sive poetas, 1. Pa- ralipp. 6. v. 33. qui διδακτικὸν hoc carmen composuisse vide- tur, & canendum tradidisse Coræ posteris.

Passionem Christi hic prædici volunt August. Hie- ronym. Euthym. Bellarm. non abnuente B. Luther. B. Pomerano, B. Brentio (etsi etiam ad tentationes Spirituales hæc referant, quod per commodam ap- plicationem fieri posse concedimus, quia oportet nos conformes fieri imagini filii Dei; non tamen Jansenio, aut Coccejo accedimus, quod Christo ut per Davidem adumbrato hæc solum in plenissimo si- gnificatu conveniant) B. Cramero, Dn. D. Geiero.

## 89:1 Argument
PSALM 89. The kingdom of the Messiah, and the desire for it.

ETHAN) It seems that this Ethan lived at the time of the deportation. Verse 28. AND I WILL MAKE HIM MY FIRSTBORN) Namely, among kings, which the following words explain more clearly: Higher than the kings of the earth. Verse 32. IF THEY PROFANE MY STATUTES, AND DO NOT KEEP MY COMMANDMENTS, I WILL VISIT THEIR INIQUITIES WITH THE ROD AND THEIR SINS WITH STRIPES) The poet repeats those things which God had said concerning Solomon and his descendants, 2 Sam. 7:14, where see the stated words.

Grotius wrongly understood Solomon there: for the oracle speaks of Christ our Lord: and the present Psalm also treats of Him. For it is undoubted that this oracle is looked to here. Ethan sings of the future grace, whom Grotius judges to have lived at the time of the deportation: how then could he prophesy here about Solomon? Those things indeed in v. 28, 'I will make him my firstborn,' do not fit Solomon, who had long since finished his life? Most think that this Ethan was one of those four to whom Solomon is compared because of the excellence of his wisdom, 1 Kings 4:31, which indeed does not seem to Calvin to fit his age, unless perhaps, surviving Solomon, he laments the sad and disastrous dissipation which happened then, which was a prelude to the ruin. But do not the prophets also foresee future calamities from the revelation of the Holy Spirit? Grotius, however, seems to have followed Philo, who in book II of the Epitome of History refers him to the times of Jeconiah, who was cast into prison, concerning whom see the blessed Gesner on this Psalm. The notes of Junius-Tremellius on v. 39 are correct: This Psalm was given as a monument to the Church by a prophetic spirit, so that it might be sung to God in its own time, such as was the time of the Babylonian deportation. The proposition of the Psalm is had in v. 2, which is to celebrate the mercies of the Lord, and his faithfulness or

1. kindness in promising, and truth in fulfilling, looking back to that promise called by antonomasia, in which the kindness of God shines forth most, concerning the Messiah, as the foundation of all promises, 2 Cor. 1:16, Acts 4:12.

2. Then indeed he sings of the eternal grace that is to arise, which he also wishes to sing of eternally. Therefore, it is not the temporal grace which Solomon obtained in this age that is understood, but the spiritual grace which is promised to the faithful in Christ, which they will enjoy forever, and which they will celebrate forever. For through Him grace and truth came, John 1:16.

3. Thirdly, the promise made in 2 Sam. 7:12 ff. concerning the eternal seed and the establishing of the throne forever is repeated here, which was not fulfilled in Solomon and his descendants, but is explained in Christ and concerning Christ, Ps. 132:11, Acts 2:30. 'I have made a covenant with MY HOLY ONE' (Christ, Is. 42:1), 'I have sworn to David my servant,' concerning that covenant in the Messiah, I confirmed David, from whom He himself will be descended, by an oath, 2 Sam. 7:2, 23:1. For by the 'Elect' he then understands Christ in v. 20, whom he also distinguishes there from David the servant. Thus those things respond to each other best: 'I will establish your SEED FOREVER' (to you, my Elect) 'and I will build up YOUR throne from generation to generation': these things were fulfilled not in David, but in Christ, v. 30, 37.

And these are fourthly those faithful promises of David, or made to David, which are also established by Isaiah ch. 55:3 and are explained concerning Christ our Lord in Acts 13:34. This is fifthly that for which the heavens, that is, the heavenly hosts, the angels, celebrate and announce the admirable grace and truth of God; which happened at the time of the birth of Christ. Therefore, sixthly, the arm and the hand, and the right hand of God are celebrated here, whose power shone forth most in the liberation of the human race, as well as the justice and judgment, the mercy and truth of God, v. 14, 15, which are also especially conspicuous in this work, as the blessed Virgin testifies, Luke 1:50, as also St. Zechariah, v. 69 ff. Seventhly, according to the phrasing of Osiander, which is not inconvenient here, the eminence of Christ is celebrated: 'Who in the clouds shall be compared to the Lord?' (to our Christ) who will restore the human race in such a wonderful way, which could be done by no angel. God is powerful in the great council of the saints: (in the Church, which will consist not only of Jews, but also of Gentiles, He exercises admirable power) and He is terrible above all who are round about Him (He shows Himself terrible to the enemies of the Church, who for the most part dwell round about her). You rule the pride of the sea, You mitigate the tumult of its waves (the world being in the greatest tumult, the Lord can soon render all things tranquil). You crush the proud as one who is slain, with the arm of Your strength You have scattered Your enemies (the enemies of the Church). Yours are the heavens, and Yours is the earth (all things are in Your power, so that You may decree whatever You please concerning them). The north and the sea (the south) You have created, Tabor (towards the west) and Hermon (towards the east) shall exult in Your name (the kingdom of Christ Your Son, all enemies notwithstanding, will be propagated to the four corners of the world). Why mention is made here particularly of the mountains Tabor and Hermon, our blessed Bugenhagen gives this reason: because the Holy Spirit looked properly to those mountains, which are in Galilee, so that He might also designate a certain place of the grace about to appear to the world in Christ. For in those places Christ preached, performed miracles, fed a multitude of people even with bodily food, and furthermore it is said that the transfiguration of the Lord took place on Tabor in the middle of Galilee, Matt. 17. etc.) Your arm with power, the arm, hand and right hand of the Lord is the Messiah, Ps. 118. Eighth, the foundation of all spiritual joy of the people of God, nay, of blessedness, is established here; who therefore rejoices in the name of God, and glories in the righteousness of God: he walks confidently in the light of the face of God. But what is our blessedness and salvation, if not in the light of the face, or the grace of God shining upon us in Christ Jesus, Acts 4:12. What is the cause, what is the foundation of all our joy and exultation, if not Christ Jesus? Who, as He is Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. 23:6, so in Him alone do the faithful, who believe in Him, have righteousness and strength, Is. 45:26. In Thy good pleasure, says the Psalmist here, our horn shall be exalted. Which is the horn of salvation raised up in the house of David, Luke 1:67. For this was the εὐδοκία, that through Christ He might reconcile all things, Col. 1:20. Which is referred to God the Father as the fountain of all grace and salvation, by whose gracious good pleasure the horn of salvation has been raised and exalted for us, from whom is our shield, and our King, in whom we trust, Christ Jesus, who is also the horn of David, Ps. 132:17, and the shield of the faithful, Gen. 15:1, and our King appointed for us by God, Ps. 2:6. Others, and we heretofore, thus: Because the Lord is our shield and the Holy One of Israel is our King, v. 19. Which things, said to God the Father concerning another divine person, are to be understood of the Son of God. For he addresses God the Father in v. 17. The glory of their strength, and then also in Thy good pleasure our horn shall be exalted. And again in v. 19, with immediately subjoined words: Then you spoke in a vision to your saints. But since in the Hebrew it is not the nominative case, but the oblique case that is held, [the] Lord or [to the] Lord, is our shield, and [the] holy or [to the] holy of Israel (is) our King, the sense already handed down is to be preferred. Which was therefore observed by our B. Bugenhagen from the translation of Felix; concerning which translation he himself also said in the Preface to Frederick, Duke Elector of Saxony: we have stated the meaning of the Psalms from the Hebrew according to the translation of Felix the Hebrew, than which today THERE IS NONE BETTER. For it was necessary that we should look to the Hebrew, so that we might not interpret what the Hebrew Prophet had not said. But he rendered it in this place thus: Because from the Lord is our shield, and from the Holy One of Israel our King, that is, the Messiah is given to us by God, who sanctifies Israel, a shield, redemption, justice, sanctification. It follows, then you spoke in a vision to your saints, i.e., to Nathan and David. For the Lord spoke these things first to Nathan and through him to David. Whence it is clear that this Psalm is not to be ascribed to David, but to another, namely, as the inscription has it, to Ethan the Ezrahite.

Ninth, that hero whom God had promised in 2 Sam. 7 as the Savior of the people, chosen from the people, the servant David, can by no means be understood as Solomon, of whom Grotius interprets the Psalm, nor as David; for the things that follow do not befit him; but Christ is thus indicated in Is. 9:6, ch. 42:1, whom some also understand by the name David, because he is called David throughout the Prophets, as in Jer. 30:9, Ez. 34:23, 24, & 37:24, 25. But since the holy Apostle interpreted these things concerning David the son of Jesse in Acts 13:22, it must be believed that the Holy Spirit wished to make mention both of Christ, that HERO and ELECT LORD to be exhibited from the Israelite people according to the flesh, and of his servant David, from whose loins that HERO was to come forth and on whose throne he was to sit, and who was his notable type, but afterwards, having dismissed David, to weave his song concerning Christ that Hero. For the following words of the text cannot be explained partly of David and partly of Christ, as the Papists do. The continuation of the words is repugnant to this exposition: For all the words are so woven together and continued that they pertain to the same person, as Bellarmine admits here. Which argument must be opposed even to Bellarmine himself, and those who side with him: for he explains the same preceding things as concerning David, but acknowledges that the subsequent things are to be understood of Christ, noting thus at v. 27: Here indeed the Prophet speaks most openly of Christ: and so also in others. But the Cardinal is inept when he says that ALL things are to be explained literally of David, but are to be fulfilled FOR THE MOST PART through Christ: For in that part in which they are fulfilled solely through Christ, they certainly cannot and ought not to be explained of David: and therefore it is false that ALL things are to be explained of David. Furthermore, that that HERO, concerning whom the Holy Spirit continues to prophesy, S. is not David, but our Christ, who is anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, Ps. 45:8, is taught both by the success of that hero against his enemies; the enemy shall accomplish nothing in him, and I will cut down his enemies from his face, which are true of Christ in every respect, but not so of David, as Bellarmine himself admits: however they may be explained of David, he says, yet they are explained far more truly of Christ. Then the power of Christ and the amplitude of his dominion v. 24. And my truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn, or his power, be exalted, which Bellarmine acknowledges was scarcely adumbrated in David but most perfectly fulfilled in Christ. And I will set his hand in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers. From this place, he says, almost all agree, Augustine, Jerome, Theodoret, and many of the moderns, that the Psalm cannot be explained EXCEPT OF CHRIST: For David did not have power in the sea, but only on land, and that sufficiently narrow. For the land of promise extended as far as the sea of Palestine, and as far as the river Euphrates, and beyond. But concerning this our King it is said: I will set his hand in the sea, that is, I will give him power even in the sea itself, and in all the rivers, and through this in the whole world: for the sea is at the ends of the earth, surrounding the whole earth, but the rivers are in the middle of the earth. Therefore, by the sea and the rivers are understood all things, the ends, and the center; which is said in other words in Ps. 72: he shall have dominion from sea even to sea, i.e., from one extreme to the other. That hand and right hand denote power and dominion is most well-known from the Scriptures, Ex. 14, last, ch. 15:6, Num. 11:23, Ps. 18:36. Ps. 63:9, Ps. 77:11, Ps. 108:7, Ps. 139:5, 10. Therefore the dominion of the Messiah must extend beyond the sea and all the rivers of the world, which cannot be understood of David or Solomon, whose empire the islands of the sea never obeyed: But it must be accepted solely of the kingdom of Christ, as the parallel passage Ps. 72:8 clearly teaches.

Tenth, the naming of the Father is especially to be observed, concerning which v. 27: He shall call me: You are my Father. For there is no reason why we should depart from the propriety of this naming, which is never to be rashly set aside in Scripture. And the Apostle himself explains it in Heb. 1:5 concerning the Father properly so called, namely, that he himself calls God Father, not as the Angels, but as he who alone is begotten from the substance of the Father, and is the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person: to whom alone it was said in Psalm 2:7, You are my Son, today I have begotten you, and 2 Sam. 7:14, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son. For as this Psalm looks to the passage of Samuel alleged, so the Epistle to the Hebrews interprets the same, so that it may at the same time lend light to this our text, that it ought to be understood not of David or Solomon, but of the Messiah. Which the appellation of firstborn also affirms v. 28. I also will make him my firstborn, higher than the Kings of the earth. Where the distinction of natures in Christ is to be observed: For as in the preceding verse that which must be attended to comes: He shall call upon me: Thou art my Father: my God, and the rock of my salvation. For he is Father, by reason of the eternal generation, of the Son: he is his God and the rock of his salvation, by reason of his human nature: So in this verse, the former appellation of the correlatives, And I will make him my firstborn, concerns the divine nature; according to which he himself is πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως the firstborn of every creature Col. 1, 15. But the other, higher than the Kings of the earth, pertains to the human nature, according to which he himself is exalted above all things. Nor is it an objection that he is said to be made firstborn: because that making can be understood as the manner of manifestation, since things are often said to come to be when they are declared, or if he is said to be truly made, regard may be had to the incarnation: by which the Holy thing, which is born of Mary, was called the Son of God Luke 1, 35. He was indeed the firstborn from eternity in himself, but when he was made flesh he was constituted the firstborn Son of God, and became that firstborn Son of Mary. The illustrious passage Heb. 1, 6 can be compared here, where the name πρωτότοκος is applied to Christ on account of his eternal generation from the Father. For that appellation seems to be taken from nowhere else than from this Oracle of the Psalm, namely from the Greek version. The Syrian and Arab likewise retain the word בבר. Bellarmine in his commentary on this passage acknowledges that the Prophet is speaking most openly of Christ, and he confesses that the epithet, Higher than the Kings of the earth, can in no way be said of David and Solomon: inasmuch as they not only were not the highest absolutely; but even inferior to many Kings of the earth, and especially to the Kings of the Assyrians, who at that time held the Monarchy.

Eleventh, one must also observe the eternity of the Kingdom of this Hero: concerning which the Psalmist says in v. 28: I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant shall be faithful to him. For this pact was about an eternal Kingdom, 2 Sam. 7, which is also promised here to be kept for him without end: but of whom can this be understood, if not of him whom Gabriel announced in Luke 1, who would sit upon the throne of David, and whose kingdom would have no end? Which is also explained in v. 29 and following: And I will set his seed for the age of the age, and his throne as the days of heaven. Which seed Augustine rightly interprets as the spiritual children of the Messiah: who are themselves generated through the word of the Gospel: so that the perpetuity of the kingdom, and the continuous and perennial propagation of the spiritual seed of the Messiah, and the eternity of his royal throne are designated. For although the disobedient Sons of the Messiah are to be chastised with rods, the grace of the Messiah shall not be taken away, nor will the truth of the divine promise be endangered thereby: or the covenant of God be rendered void, which he had sanctioned by means of an oath: The kingdom of Christ shall not be overturned on that account, the Church shall not be cast away or destroyed, just as other kingdoms are extirpated because of their crimes: indeed, even all the elect, however gravely they may have sinned, shall not be so cast away that they perish eternally in their sins: And thus the Hieropsalmist returns again to David and the oath sworn to him: Once have I sworn by my Holy One, or by my holiness, (the Chaldean: in my holy name) if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the Sun in my sight, and as the perfect Moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven. Some refer the pronoun HIS to David: to whom the promise was made. But it can most conveniently be referred to the Messiah, because the discourse throughout the whole Psalm is about the same subject, and the eternal spiritual seed and perpetual throne of the Messiah were promised to the same; even if that promise was related to David, it was made not about David, but about the Messiah; nor does it seem to be about the seed of David, but about the seed of the Messiah, as is clear from verse 29, which is entirely similar: I will set his seed for the age of the age, and his throne as the days of heaven: as well as from verse 30, where that seed of the Messiah is explained as his children. If, however, anyone should contend that by the pronoun HIS in v. 35 David must be understood, then the seed of David shall remain forever, it must then be taken μοναδικῶς (uniquely) concerning the Messiah, the seed of David: whose eternal throne is described in the following verses: Unless perhaps the seed of the Messiah is also in some respect called the seed of David, just as believers (who are called the seed of the Messiah) are considered the children of Abraham, the Father of believers, as appears from verse 5. Or it must be said with Dr. Lucas Osiander, that by David here Christ is understood. I will not lie to David, to my Son Jesus Christ: For the Lord God the Father swore to his Son Christ and he will not repent of it, Ps. 110, 4. It is manifest that this cannot be understood of the children and grandchildren of David. But the former explanation is simpler, for the discourse is not about the oath made concerning Christ for the sake of his eternal Priesthood, but about the oath by which he confirmed the covenant to David, which is therefore truly ἀμεταμέλητον (irrevocable): concerning which he began to sing at the beginning: I have sworn to David my servant, etc., verse 5.

And these things concerning the first, Prophetic part of the Psalm: which we believe it is now clear concerns the Messiah and his kingdom in its entirety. In the other part, a complaint is woven concerning the miserable and calamitous state of the Jewish kingdom, so that God, the Father of all mercy, may most graciously have mercy on it, and finally send the Messiah

as Redeemer, who might liberate the human race from all evils, and erect his spiritual kingdom in the world. But thou hast repelled and despised (us, or thy people), thou hast deferred thy Christ. Augustine understands this as the mission of our Lord Jesus Christ being delayed; others understand it as the King of Judah, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, who translate from the Hebrew with St. Jerome, thou art angry against thy anointed. Osiander in his paraphrase thinks the Psalmist is prophesying and complaining about the Anti-Christ, because this kingdom of Christ is terribly harassed, torn apart, and all but overturned by the same and similar enemies, so that before human reason it appears that God has forgotten all his promises (concerning the durability of the Kingdom of Christ), and finally concludes the Psalm with an act of thanksgiving, to show that the kingdom of Christ will nevertheless be invincible against all the gates of hell. That complaint is prolixly continued, and then a prayer is subjoined for the acceleration of the Messiah, so that the promised oath of God may be fulfilled, as Bellarmine explains, How long, O Lord, wilt thou turn away thy face, or hide thyself unto the end, or shall thy wrath burn like fire unto destruction? Remember what my time (and that of other men) is, (how short a time man lives on these earths) why shouldst thou have created the children of men in vain? (For if thou dost not send thy Christ, or add all care for the preservation of thy Church, wilt thou not seem to have created the human race in vain? Thus not only the Latin paraphrase of Dr. Lucas Osiander, and the German one of Weimar, but also other ancient and more recent Interpreters. August. book 17 de C. D. ch. 11, and most Pontificals.) Bellarmine says, I think the Prophet, who was spiritual, because of the brevity of human life and the caducity of human affairs, burned with a desire for the future life of the earth in the heavens, and wished to pray to God that he might quickly send the Messiah, the Father of the future age, who would open the kingdoms of the heavens to believers. For unless at least some part of the human race were to arrive at that eternal and blessed life through Christ, God would seem to have created all the children of men truly in vain.) Who is the man that shall live, and shall not see death, shall deliver his soul from the hand of the grave? Where are thy ancient mercies, O Lord, which thou didst swear to David in thy truth. Since this sworn promise had been made concerning the Messiah, it is manifest again that the Psalmist perseveres in the same argument concerning the Messiah ('Remember, O Lord, the reproach of thy servants, which I have borne (or carried until now) in my bosom'—these are the words of the complaining Church—'wherewith thine enemies have reproached, O Lord, wherewith they have reproached the footsteps of thine anointed' (they hiss at and mock the progress of the kingdom of Christ, and the delay of his coming, or they have reproached the slowness of the footsteps of the Messiah, as the Chaldean interprets it). But since the Prophet foresees that the fulfillment of the promise will follow in his own time through the coming of the Messiah and the propagation of his kingdom, he exclaims in the Spirit: Blessed be the Lord! Amen; Amen! Thus, therefore, the whole structure of the Psalm exhibits Christ and his kingdom, which will be more correctly revealed from the praised paraphrase of Osiander, if it is considered piously and attentively, which is convenient in most parts of the explanation of this Psalm (as a comparison with these meditations of ours will reveal), and because of the single literal sense retained, it is to be preferred here and in other Prophetic Psalms to the paraphrase of the Weimar theologians, even if the latter also deserves its own praise.

Add to these now, finally, the confession of the Jews, who are themselves compelled to acknowledge that this promise must be understood concerning the Messiah. R. Nathan in Midrash on Ex. 13:2 interprets 'the firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth' as concerning the Messiah. And those which v. 37.

38. are held, his throne like the Sun before me, etc., are explained concerning the Messiah in Bereschith Ketanna on chap. 49, 8. R. Aben-Ezra on this Psalm: It is concerning God's covenant with David, and concerning the coming of the Messiah, in whom the Psalmist believes. And at v. 40. Thou hast made void the covenant: He speaks in the person of the adversaries, who were mocking the coming of the Messiah. At the last v.: Blessed be the Lord for the light of the coming of the Messiah. R. Anonymous in Genebrard here at v. 51. they reproach the footsteps, or the goings forth of thy Christ, they call him slow-footed or bandy-legged and lame, etc. And Grotius could have been instructed about this whole Psalm by those whom he had chosen as his teachers in Theology, I point to the Jesuits, namely by Bellarmine, Tirinus, and Menochius, whom he esteems. For these, to say nothing of others now, acknowledge that this Psalm contains the desire of the people of God placed in captivity, that Christ, promised so long before, might quickly arrive. Others in his School, especially Joh. Cocceius in the last things of Moses §. 990.
