Not only is some application instituted in Heb. 1, 6, but a demonstration: since the Apostle proves from this passage the eminence and Deity of Christ. But what kind of proof would that be if the Psalm were about God the Father, as Grotius wishes? For then the Apostle's inference would be thus: Christ is true God, because God the Father, according to the Psalmist, is to be adored by the Angels. Nor does it help that inference, what Grotius says at Heb. 1, 6, that it had long been accepted among the Hebrews that God would dwell in the Messiah in a singular way, and would be (as the Talmudists speak) demonstrable by the finger, and therefore whatever was said about the honor of God was accustomed to be applied to the Messiah. Because, how will it be taught that this was accepted among all Hebrews at that age, or at least among most? And how could the Jews themselves have accused the Messiah of blasphemy and impiety, when he applied to himself those things which are of God, if that common opinion about the Messiah was then held among them? Besides, what need would there have been for a proof among the Hebrews, which the Apostle institutes so prolixly here, of that thing which had already long since been accepted among them? But who does not see that something more sublime is demonstrated here, not only the singular inhabitation of God, but the very divine nature of Christ, and that not only an application is made, but a confirmation of the Deity of Christ is instituted from our Psalm? The nerve of which is clearly cut by the gloss of Grotius, that the Psalm is about God the Father, not about the Messiah. But then the Apostle testifies that those words were openly spoken when the firstborn was introduced into the world. Therefore, the same things were said about the firstborn, or the Son of God. Whence it is clear that in our Psalm the firstborn is introduced into the world, or the coming of the Son of God into the world, in which he was about to occupy the kingdom through the whole world, through the proclamation of the Gospel, is described. Whence others understand the heaven by οἰκουμένην, so that the exaltation of Christ may be defined, because it was then said that the Angels should adore him, Phil. 2. Therefore, it is a discourse about the kingdom of Christ, and indeed about the kingdom of grace. Which the beginning of the Psalm, exhibiting its argument or proposition, immediately indicates: The Lord reigns: Let the earth exult, let many isles rejoice, i.e., the inhabitants of the earth and the isles, for from thence is solid and true joy, when the Messiah reigns through the preaching of the Gospel. But first the Majesty and glory of the Lord is described; which, even if he is as it were covered by a cloud and darkness, and his government is hidden from us, (for who has known the ways of the Lord? Rom. 11.) yet the basis of his rule is justice and judgment, so that it does not rely on Tyranny, but is administered most justly, and just rewards are rendered to the faithful and pious, and just punishments to the incredulous and impious: whence as it were fire before him, by which his enemies are consumed, are exterminated, and when his lightnings have shone, the earth trembles, and the mountains (the kingdoms of the earth) flow like wax from the face of the Lord. So great is his power, so great his zeal against the enemies of his kingdom, or of the Church: which things pertain to the judgment of God, to which allusion is made regarding that tremendous apparition which took place on Mount Sinai, as it was that by which the judgment of God was exhibited as extremely horrible to the contemners of the law, so that the same Lord, who manifested himself there in the promulgation of the law, is hinted to be the one who is to reign through the whole world by the scepter of the Gospel. But the heavens announce his justice, i.e., the Apostles, so named because of their heavenly doctrine and life: Conf. Ps. 19, 1. Namely that which was revealed in the Gospel: whence all peoples see his glory, which is clearly known, having been manifested to all peoples through the Apostolic announcement: (Others understand by the heavens the Angels, who announced the coming of Christ, Luke 2, 13. But here the announcement made to all peoples is understood; because these things are related, the announcement of the justice of Christ and the knowledge of his glory, and this arises from that) And on the contrary, all who worship graven images (or any idols whatsoever) must be confounded; but it is necessary that not only all peoples throughout the earth, but also all his Angels in heaven, should uniquely worship and adore this King. Some wish the second coming of Christ to be described here, which opinion is also approved by Theod. and in the Syr. version, approved, although then judgment against enemies will be exercised most of all, and so that terrible apparatus may even extend to that, yet this announcement of justice and the proclamation of the Gospel, so that all peoples may recognize the glory of God from it, pertain to the kingdom and the time of grace. Is. 40, 5. And the Apostle also explains this introduction and investiture, if I may so call it, through which Christ was proposed to the world, so that he is to be adored by all the Angels of God, the ruler of all the earth, whose divine majesty, justice, and power, as once manifested on Mount Sinai: so in no less illustrious a manner is it to be manifested, announced, and adored in the kingdom of the Messiah. Nothing, therefore, is more certain than that all those things are to be understood of Christ, and that he is described here as the true and supreme God, Jehovah, the Lord of all the earth, to be adored by all; Which also among the Hebrews: It must have been in confession, otherwise no confirmation of the Deity of the Messiah could have been established from thence among them. Now, therefore, further, secondly, the joy and gladness of the people of this King is also described, which they conceive through this proclamation of evangelical righteousness and the administration of the reign of Christ: Sion heard and was glad: and the daughters of Judah rejoiced because of thy judgments, O Lord: the Church did not tremble, as Mount Sinai, but exulted for joy, both the universal Church designated by Sion, and each particular one designated by the daughters of Judah, as Theod. observed, having seen especially also the judgments of God against enemies and idolatrous cults, which are overturned by the proclamation of the word. Wherefore, for joy and admiration, she exclaims: For thou art Jehovah, the most high over all the earth (who reignest most gloriously in the whole world), greatly exalted above all gods. For from the proclamation of the Gospel, the supreme majesty of Christ shone forth in such a way that the glory of all idols collapsed, or, as those who are called gods are known to be subject to this Lord. But that this joy in the Lord may be solid and constant, the Psalmist finally warns that whoever loves the Lord Jesus Christ should hate evil (any idolatrous cult whatsoever) and every wickedness (by which the glory of God and the profession of the Gospel are profaned), being certain of the preservation of God against any persecutions whatsoever: because the Lord preserves the souls of the saints, he will deliver them from the hand of sinners (the violence of heretics and tyrants). Who alone can also bring it about, and is about to bring it about, that light may arise for the righteous and the upright in heart, joy (after the darkness of persecutions: and that in any darkness in this age the light of grace and joy may never not arise for them), in the Spirit. Wherefore rejoice, you righteous, (the sacred Psalmist concludes) and give thanks to the memory of his holiness, i.e., as D. Luc. Osiand. not badly [interprets], praise him on account of his revealed Gospel, in which is commemorated his innocence, purity, fulfillment of the law performed for us, the most holy sacrifice of his death, and his immense charity toward the human race. Or if you prefer, with the Vinarian theologians, so that the parenetic conclusion may correspond even more openly to the argument and the treatment: continually recollect the memory of his holiness, and give thanks, which shines forth most greatly in the preaching of the Gospel and the propagation and preservation of his kingdom: on account of which also the Holy Angels celebrated the holiness of this Lord with their heavenly trisagion, Is. 6,3. John 12, 11. It is manifest, however, at the same time from this exposition of the Psalm, in the Greek and

The title added to the same in the Latin codices: 'To David, when his land was restored,' which is not found in the Hebrew, is in vain approved by Grotius: as if this Psalm were written in memory of that time when, after Absalom was dead, he recovered the whole kingdom: unless you excuse it in such a way that, on the occasion of the recovered whole kingdom, he prophesied of the Catholic Kingdom of the Messiah, who did not ignore that he was acting as a type of the Messiah. Concerning which Theodoret also warned: the inscription is not of the prophecy itself: for the sense of the Psalm does not square with this argument: since the Prophet speaks of the order and constitution of the whole world, and not of Judea alone.

Although the Apostle's exposition is most clear, that this discourse is about Christ the firstborn, not about David, Grotius nevertheless attempts to obscure the Apostle's illustrious passage with his comment about a double sense, but not without significant impiety, annot. on Heb. 1, 6. τὸν πρωτότοκον: in an INFERIOR sense he signifies David, who is called by that name, as being eminent among Kings, Ps. 89, 27. and that ὀικυμένην [means] the land of Judea, which also appears from the Greek inscription of that Psalm, namely the 97th: But in an EXCELLENT sense πρωτότοκος is Christ Rom. 8, 29. Col. 1, 15. 18. Rev. 1, 5. and ὀικυμένη is that supreme region which is inhabited by Angels, as our Writer himself, looking back to these words of his, says soon after 2, 4. Nothing in this whole Psalm of ours [can be applied] to David, nor can the predicates of this kingdom or King which are contained in this Psalm be applied to David in any way. Nor is it manifest that the land of Judea can be understood by ὀικυμένην. We have already said what is to be held regarding the Greek inscription. We taught in the explanation of Ps. 89, 22 that not David, but the Messiah is called the firstborn. Nor does that name denote EXCELLENT only there, since there is no reason why, having abandoned the propriety of the word which fits perfectly, we should depart to a figurative sense. And Grotius contradicts himself: For he had explained the passage Ps. 89, 22 in his annotations on that Psalm as referring to Solomon: but now he wishes the same to be understood of David. Thus he judges that David is designated by 'firstborn' at one time, and Solomon at another. But by what document will he obtain that Paul used this name here in a double sense, and understood by πρωτότοκον both David in an inferior sense and the Messiah in a more excellent one? Or by what reasons will he convince [us] that ὀικυμένην was accepted here by the Apostle in a double sense, so that it might denote both Judea and the supreme angelic region? Of which thing neither a trace nor a footprint appears in the Apostolic passage. Indeed, how can such disparate senses be attached to the same word and saying? How can this be applied to David without idolatry: 'Let all the Angels of God adore him'? What, finally, would be that proof of the Apostle that Christ is the true and eternal God, because all Angels ought to adore him, if this were suitable in any sense to David himself, a mere man (ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ)? But that inept and profane gloss deserves detestation rather than refutation. The Jews themselves acknowledged that the days of Christ are looked to in the present Psalm, R. David Kimchi and R. Obadias, and Grotius also reports, on Heb. 1, 6, that all the Psalms from 93 to 101, according to David Kimchi, contain the mystery of the Messiah. But none of them explains the present Psalm as being about David, or attributes a double sense to it, an inferior and a sublime one, as Grotius does.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ADORATE EVM OMNES ANGELI EJVS) Hic est locus, quo scriptor ad Ebræos utitur applicans Chri- sto, ut sit in Novo Fœdere, id quod de Deo dictum est in Vete- re, προσκυνήτωσαν αυτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεᾶ, mutata persona, quod in allegandis locis nihil refert. Nam in Græco hic est προσκυνήσατε αυτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι ἀυτᾶ. Sæpe LXX. אלהים vertunt ἀγγέλους, ut supra 8, 6. & infra 138. 1. Cæterum hoc loco legerunt non אלהים sed cum affixo אלהיו.

NOn applicatio solum aliqua instituitur Ebr. 1, 6. sed demonstratio: siquidem Apost. ex h. l. probet emi- nentiam ac Deitatem Christi. Quænam autem illa foret probatio, si in Psalmo de Deo Patre ageretur, ut vult Grotius? Tum enim ita haberet illatio Apostoli: Chri- stus est verus Deus, quia Deus pater juxta Psalten ado- randus est ab Angelis. Neque juvat istam illationem, quod Grotius ad Ebr. 1, 6. apud Hebr. pridem receptum fuisse, ait, Deum singulari modo in Messia habitaturum, & fore (ut Thalmudici loquuntur) digito demonstrabilem, ideo quæcunq; de honore Dei dicebantur, eadem applicari solere ad Messiam. Quia id apud omnes Ebræos ista ætate, aut saltim apud plerosque receptum fuisse, unde doce- bitur? & quomodo blasphemiæ & impietatis postula- re potuissent Messiam Judæi ipsi, cum ea, quæ Dei sunt, sibi applicabat, si pervulgata illa de Messia sententia penes ipsos tum fuit? Adhæc quid opus fuisset proba- tione penes Ebræos, quam Apostolus tam prolixe hic instituit, ejus rei, quæ penes eosdem jam pridem rece- pta fuerat? Sed quis non videt, hic sublimius quid de- monstrari, non tantum inhabitationem Dei singularem, sed ipsam divinam naturam Christi neq; applicationem tantum fieri, sed confirmationem Deitatis Christi insti- tui e Psalmo nostro? cui nervus plane inciditur, per glossam Grotii, quod in Psalmo de Deo Patre agatur, non de Messia. Tum vero aperte verba illa dicta esse testatur Apostolus, cum introduclus est in orbem primo- genitus. Deprimogenito ergo, vel Filio Dei eadem dicta. Unde liquet in Psalmo nostro primogenitum in orbem introduci, vel adventum Filii Dei in mundum, in quo regnum occupaturus erat per totum orbem, per præconium Evangelii, describi. Unde alii per oi- κουμένην cælum intelligunt, ut exaltatio Christi definia- tur, quia tum dictum est, ut Angeli adorent eum Phil. 2. De regno ergo Christi & quidem de regno gratiæ fer- mo est. Quod initium Psalmi argumentum ejusdem, vel propositionem exhibens, statim indicat: Dominus regnat: Exultet terra, latentur Insulæ multæ, i. e. habitatores terræ ac insularum, inde enim solida & vera est lætitia, cùm regnat Messias per prædicationem Evangelii. De- scribitur autem primo Domini Majestas & gloria; quod etsi ipse veluti nube & caligine obtectus, & occulta ejus nobis sit gubernatio, (quis enim vias Domini co- gnovit? Rom. 11.) basis tamen regiminis ejus sit justitia & judicium, ut non Tyrannide nitatur, sed justissime ad- ministretur, ac fidelibus & piis præmia, incredulis & impiis supplicia justa reddantur:unde velut ignis ante ipsum, quo inimici ejus consumuntur, exterminantur, ac cum fulgura ejg illuxerint, terra contremifcit, montesq; (regna terræ) sicut cera fluunt a facie Domini. Tanta ejus est potentia, tantus Zelus adversus hostes regni sui, vel Ecclesiæ: quæ faciunt ad judicium Dei, quibus ad tre- mendam illam apparitionem, quæ in monte Sinai facta est, utpote qua judicium Dei comtemtoribus legis sum- me horribile exhibebatur, alluditur, ut idem Dominus, qui illic se manifestavit in legis promulgatione, innua- tur esse, qui per Evangelii sceptrum regnaturus est per totum orbem. Justitiam vero ejg annunciant cæli, i. e. A- postoli, sic propter cœlestem doctrinam & vitam nun- cupati: Conf. Ps. 19, 1. Eam nempe, quæ in Evangelio pa- tefacta: unde omnes populi gloriam ejus vident, quæ per annunciationem Apostolicam omnibus populis manifestata luculenter cognoscitur: (Alii per cœlos Angelos intelligunt, qui adventum Christi annuncia- runt Luc. 2, 13. Sed hic annuntiatio intelligitur popu- lis omnibus facta; quia relata hæc sunt, annunciatio ju- stitiæ Christi & cognitio gloriæ ejusdem, & hæc ex illa oritur) Et ex adverso confundi oportet omnes, qui colunt sculptilia (vel quæcunque idola;) necessum ve- ro est, ut hunc Regem unice colant & adorent non tantum omnes populi per terram, sed etiam omnes An- geli ejus in cœlo. Nonnulli adventum secundum Christi hic describi volunt, quæ sententia etiam a Theod. & in versione Syr. probatur, quanquam tum vel maxime ju- dicium adversus hostes exercebitur, adeoque iste ap- paratus terribilis eo etiam sese porrigat, hæc tamen annunciatio justitiæ & præconium Evangelii, ut Dei glo- riam inde omnes populi agnoscant, ad regnum & tem- pus gratiæ pertinent. Es. 40, 5. Et de hac introductione ac investitura, ut ita vocem, explicat quoq; Apostolus, per quam orbi terrarum Christus propositus est, ut ab omnibus etiam Angelis Dei adorandus, dominator omnis terræ, cujus majestas divina, justitia & potentia uti olim patefacta in monte Sinai: sic non minus illustri ratione in regnum Messiæ manifestanda, annuncianda, atque adoranda. Nil E. certius, quam de Christo illa omnia intelligenda esse, ipsumq; ut verum & summum Deum, Jehovam, Dominum omnis terræ ab omnibus adoran- dum hic describi; Quod etiam apud Hebr: in confesso fuisse oportet, alias nulla inde penes ipsos institui po- tuisset Deitatis Messiæ confirmatio. Jam itaq; porro Se cundo describitur etiam populi Regis hujus gaudium & lætitia, quam per hanc justitiæ Evangelicæ annuntia- tionem & Regiminis Christi administrationem conci- pit: Audivit & lætata est Sion: & exultaverunt Filiæ Juda propter Judicia tua Domine: non tremuit, ut mons Sinai, sed exultavit præ gaudio Ecclesia, cum universalis per Sion, tum particularis quæque per filias Judæ designata, ut observavit Theod. visis imprimis etiam judiciis Dei adversus hostes, & cultus idololatricos, qui evertuntur per præconium verbi. Quapropter præ gaudio & ad- miratione exclamat : Quoniam tu es Jehovah, altissimus super omnem terram (qui in universo mundo glorio- sissime regnas) valde exaltatus super omnes Deos. E præ- conio enim Evangelii majestas Christi summa ita efful- sit, ut omnium idolorum gloria concideret, vel, ut, quæ Dii vocantur, huic Domino subesse cognoscantur. Ut autem hæc in Domino lætitia solida & constans sit, mo- net postremo Psaltes, ut quicunque diligunt Dominum Jesum Christum odio habeant malum (idololatricum quemcunque cultum,) & omne scelus, (quo prophana- tur gloria Dei, & professio Evangelii,) certi de conser- vatione Dei adversus quascunque persecutiones: quia Dominus custodit animas Sanctor. a manu peccatorum (hæretic.& tyrannorum violentia) liberabit eos. Qui ef- ficere etiam solus potest, atq; effecturus est, ut lux oria- tur justis & rectis corde lætitia (post tenebras persequu- tionum: & nunquam non in quibusvis tenebris in hoc seculo lux gratiæ & lætitiæ ipsis exoriatur) in Sp. S Quare lætamini vos justi, (concludit Hieropsaltes) & consitemini memoriæ sanctitatis ejus, i. e. ut non male D. Luc. Osiand. laudate eum propter revelatum Evangelium ejus, in quo commemoratur ejus innocentia, puritas, im- pletio legis pro nobis præstita, sacrificium mortis ejus san- ctissimum, & immensa ejus charitas erga genus human. vel si malis, cum Theologis Vinariens. ut conclusio pa- rænetica argumento, & tractationi adhuc apertius congruat : memoriam sanctitatis ejus jugem recolite, ac confitemini, quæ in Evangelii prædicatione, & regni ejus propagatione ac conservatione maxime effulget: ob quam etiam S. Angeli tris hagio suo cœlesti sanctitatem Do- mini hujus celebrarunt Es. 6,3. Job. 12, 11. Manifestum autem simul ex hac Psalmi enarratione, in Græcis &

Latinis Codd. adjectum eidem titulum : Huic David, quando terra ejus restituta est, qui in Hebræo non habetur, nequicquam ab Grotio probari : quasi scriptus hic Psalmus sit in memoriam ejus temporis, quo Absolomo mortuo regnum recuperarit totum: nisi eundem ita excuses, quod occasione recupe- rati regni integri de Regno Messiæ Catholico vati- cinatus fuerit, qui typum se gerere Messiæ non ignoravit. De quo etiam monuit Theodoretus : inscriptio non est ipsius vaticinationis : neque enim sensus Psalmi huic argumento quadrat : quandoqui- dem totius orbis terrarum ordinem & constitutionem, & non Judææ tantum Propheta fatur.

Quanquam autem luculentissima sit Apostoli ex- positio, quod de Christo primogenito, non de Davi- de hic sermo sit, obscurare tamen illustrem locum Apostoli conatur Grotius, commento suo de sensu gemino, sed non absque insigni impietate, annot. ad Ebr. 1, 6. τὸν πρωτότοκον: sensu INFERIORE signi- ficat Davidem, qui eo nomine, ut inter Reges exi- mius, vocatur Ps. 89, 27. & illud ὀικυμένην terram Ju- dæam, quod etiam ex Græca Psalmi illius, nempe 97. in- scriptione apparet: Sensu autem EXCELLENTIORE πρωτόκῶ est Christus Rom. 8, 29. Col. 1, 15. 18. Ap. 1, 5. & ὀικυμένη est regio illa suprema, quæ ab Angelis inhabitatur, ut ipse mox Scriptor noster ad hæc sua verba respiciens dicit 2, 4. Nihil in toto hoc nostro Psalmo de Davide nec ullatenus prædicata regni aut Regis hujus Davidi applicari possunt, quæ in hoc Psalmo habentur. Neque per ὀικυμένην terram Ju- dæam intelligi posse manifestum est. Quid haben- dum sit de inscriptione Græca, jam diximus. Ps. 89, 22. non David, sed Messiam primogenitum vocari, in ejusdem explicatione docuimus. Neque nomen illud EXIMIUM tantum ibi notat, quum nulla cau- sa sit, cur relicta vocis proprietate optime congru- ente, ad figuratum sensum discedamus. Et contra- dicit sibi ipsi Grotius: Nam locum Ps. 89, 22. in annot. ad istum Psalmum de Salomone exposuerat: nunc vero de Davide eundem intellectum vult. Ita modo Davidem, modo Salomonem per primogenitum designari judicat. Sed quo documento obtinebit, Paulum nomen hoc duplici sensu hic adhibuisse, & per πρωτότοκον tum inferiori sensu Davidem, tum excellentiore Messiam intellexisse? aut quibus ratio- nibus convincet ὀικυμένην duplici sensu hic acce- ptam esse ab Apostolo, ut & Judæam, & regionem supremam Angelicam notaret? Cujus rei nec vola, nec vestigium in loco Apostolico comparet. Imo, quo- modo tam disparati sensus eidem voci & dicto affin- gi possunt? Quomodo citra idololatriam Davidi ap- plicari hoc potest: Adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei? Quæ deniq; esset illa probatio Apostoli, quod Chri- stus sit verus & æternus Deus, quia adorare eum de- bent omnes Angeli, si hoc ipsi etiam Davidi ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ullo sensu conveniret? Sed inepta atque prophana illa glossa detestationem magis quam re- futationem meretur. Judæi ipsi agnovere, quod hic dies Christi respiciantur in præsenti Psalmo, R. David Kimchi & R. Obadias, refertque etiam Grotius, ad Ebr. 1, 6. Psalmos omnes a 93. ad 101. secundum Da- vid Kimchium mysterium Messiæ continere. Nemo au- tem ex iisdem explicat Psalmum præsentem de Da- vide, aut sensum geminum illi tribuit, inferiorem & sublimiorem, quemadmodum Grotius.

## 97:10 Addition
To Psalm 97. Verse 10. HE SHALL JUDGE THE WORLD IN JUSTICE.

For the sake of consensus and agreement, I add the opinion of the blessed Hülsemann, for our opinion has already been set forth before: The judgment to which Christ is said to come here and in Ps. 96 does not signify that final condemnatory one, but an intermediate and gracious one. And although these passages can also be extended to the final judgment of Christ, which Eusebius already indicated long ago, dealing with both advents of Christ in l. VI. Demonstrat. Evangel. c. 6. against the gentiles, which the Belgians also note in their annotations, yet because this advent is alleged here as the cause of universal joy for the sea, mountains, rivers, and the whole world, v. 7. & 8. whereas the second advent will bring joy only to the elect, we therefore understand the letter formally concerning the judgment of the Holy Spirit, which He exercises in the preaching of the Gospel, John 16, 8. as above Ps. 96, 12. Jer. 2, 4. &c. and similar prophecies concerning Christ.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 97. Vers. 10. JUDICABIT ORBEM TERRARUM IN JUSTITIA.

Consensus & ὁμοψηφίας causa addo senten- tiam B. Hülsemanni, nam nostra sententia jam antea exposita est: Judicium, ad quod Christus hic & Ps. 96. dicitur venire non extremum illud condemna- torium, sed intermedium & gratiosum significat. Et quanquam extendi hæc loca etiam possint ad ulti- mum Christi judicium, quod jam olim indicavit Eusebius de utroque adventu Christi agens l. VI. Demonstrat. Evangel. c. 6. adversus gentiles, quod etiam Belgæ in annot. monent, quia tamen hic ad- ventus allegatur tanquam causa universalis lætitiæ, mari, montibus, fluminibus, toti orbi terrarum v. 7. & 8. Secundus autem adventus solis electis læti- tiam afferet, ideo literam formaliter intelligimus de judicio Spiritus S. quod exercet in prædicatione Evangelii Joh. 16, 8. ut supra Ps. 96, 12. Jer. 2, 4. &c. & similibus de Christo vaticiniis.

## 97:11
Vers. 11. LIGHT IS RISEN FOR THE RIGHTEOUS.

Bellarmino and Pelican rashly argue for a corruption of the Hebrew text, in which it is held: light is scattered, or sown for the righteous. For the Masoretic note ז at the word זרע teaches that it is uncorrupted. Nor is there any reason why light should not be said to be scattered, if there is not greater emphasis in the scattering of light than in the mere rising: therefore Genebrardus dissents here from Bellarmino: It is risen, sown and scattered properly, so that he may gather it widely, loosely, and copiously. Lest anyone explain it as 'emerged, appeared,' which was hiding itself before. Light and gladness are scattered in this world for the righteous and the upright in heart, which they will reap later in the future advent of Christ. Kimchi, [says] the light and gladness of future beatitude [is] here sown in our souls and conceived, [which they] will gather in heaven, enjoying the blessed sight of God, and immortal joys and pleasures. Or it is the past for the future: Then light and gladness will arise, be carried, be scattered, and be copiously bestowed by God upon the upright in heart. Some explain it concerning the eternal [light], about which [is] Is. 35 and 51. This [is] Genebrardus.

Latin:

Vers. 11. LUX ORTA EST JUSTO.

Temere Bellarminus & Pelican. Ebræum tex- tum corruptionis arguunt, in quo habetur: lux spar- sa, vel seminata est justo. Nam eum incorruptum esse Masoret. nota ז ad vocem זרע docet. Neque causa ulla est, cur non lux spargi dicatur, si non in sparsione lucis major emphasis, quam in solo ortu: ideo dissentit hic Genebrardus a Bellarmino: Orta est, sata & sparsa proprie, ut eam late, laxe & copiose colligat. Ne quis exponat emersit, apparuit, quæ se an- tea occultabat. Lux & lætitia sparsa sunt in hoc mun- do justis & rectis corde, quæ postea metant in futuro Christi adventu. Kimchi, Lucem & lætitiam futuræ beatitudinis hic seminatam in animis nostris & con- ceptam colligent in cælo, beato Dei conspectu, & im- mortalibus gaudiis, voluptatibusque perfruentes. Vel est præteritum pro futuro: Tum a Deo orietur, fere- tur, spargetur, copiose tribuetur lux & lætitia re- ctis corde. De æterna aliqui exponunt, de qua Es. 35. & 51. Hæc Genebrardus.

## 98:1 Argument
Ps. 98. A new song about the salvation of God announced to all.

THIS Psalm seems briefly written, to be of the same argument as the greater song Ex. 15.

The scope of the Psalm is thus very badly perverted, which exhibits a notable prophecy concerning the conversion of the Gentiles. Nor is there anything in this whole hymn that teaches that it pertains to the crossing through the Red Sea. For what is held in v. 7, 'let the sea be moved, and the fullness thereof,' is to be understood of the islands of the sea, and those descending into the sea, as R. David Kimchi also observed; which the words subjoined teach: 'the world and those who dwell in it.' It is too clear that the Psalmist is prophesying about the time of the N.T. and the universal preaching of the Gospel. Therefore he bids [them] sing to the Lord a new song, which R. Solomon Jarchi, warning on Ps. 46, says is everywhere to be explained as a Song to be sung in the days of Christ, and he makes the matter of the song the wonders of the Lord in the work of redemption Ps. 40, 6, when His right hand saved for Him, and His holy arm, which in Is. 63, 5 is preached concerning Christ in the work of redemption: who is also called the right hand of the Lord. Therefore Jerome rightly says: The new song is, the Son of God is crucified: which has never been heard. Because of those wonders therefore preached through the Gospel, he excites [us] to celebrate the Lord. The Lord has made known his salvation, in the sight of the nations he has revealed his justice. The salvation of the Lord and his justice are interchanged, because Christ has been made for us by God both into justice and into salvation. He has remembered his mercy and his truth to the house of Israel. What is that mercy, if not that which was so greatly preached by David, and through the whole Scripture, namely the mercy exhibited in Christ? Which, as it was promised to the Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, so it was performed to the house of Israel, when the Lord remembered his mercy and his truth Luc. 1, 54. 55. 72. 73. But he did not exhibit it to the house of Israel only: all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. How can it be doubted that these things pertain to the conversion of the nations? Therefore not only the Jews, but all peoples are excited to Canticles and Psalms: Shout to God all the earth, sing and exult, and play the psaltery. Shout in the sight of the King the Lord (the Messiah). Let the sea be moved, and the fullness thereof, the world and they that dwell therein. The rivers shall clap their hands, the mountains shall exult together; so that whatever is in the world of lands may shout with the tongue, be moved in spirit, clap with the hand, exult, and leap as if with feet for joy, from the sight of the Lord. Because he has come to judge not now Judea, but the whole earth: he is about to judge the world in justice and the peoples in equity. These things cannot be restricted to the Jewish people. Which the collation of the parallel Psalm, which is most similar to this one, 96, also confirms. Therefore all interpreters, Jewish and Christian, acknowledge that this concerns the calling and conversion of the nations. R. David Kimchi on v. 4, all the earth: Even the nations rejoice, because then there will be the salvation of the whole world. Es. 2, 4. R. Aben-Ezra teaches that this concerns the coming of Christ. R. Obadias in the days of Christ after the day of judgment: Theodoretus He explains concerning both advents of Christ, whom Bellarmine and Menochius follow. Tirinus concerning the eternal kingdom of Christ and the renewal of the world through Christ. Dn. D. Osiander expressed his argument most excellently: This Psalm also celebrates Christ and his kingdom, and teaches that it will be propagated into the whole world, and exhorts that all should rejoice and give thanks on account of the benefits of Christ bestowed upon the Church. Our B. Pomeranus proposes the summary thus: These are new things (in this new canticle). By the wonderful power of his divinity, the Lord God raised him himself from the dead: the kingdom of death having been conquered. For then he was declared the Son of God in power Rom. 1. That which is said here, his right hand and his holy arm saved him, just as God also speaks in Is. 63. And my arm saved me, and my indignation itself helped me. Then, having sent the Spirit from the heavens, he made known his salvation to the world, and his justice to the nations, indeed without the law, but yet testified to by the law and the Prophets, as this of the law Rom. 3. And this for the showing of his mercy, and the truth promised to the family of Jacob, as of the law Rom. 15. To which our other countrymen here assent, and others of the better sort of interpreters. And these things also regarding this Psalm.

The Lord Ez. 18, 31. c. 36, 36. There is need of a new life, which is not except from the Lord Rom. 6, 4. Gal. 2, 20. Let us be a new lump through Christ 1. Cor. 5, 7. The new man according to God. Eph. 2, 15. c. 4, 24. Col. 3, 10. A new creature in Christ Jesus 2. Cor. 5, 17. Gal. 6, 15. Inserted into the new covenant on account of Christ Jer. 31, 31. Matth. 26, 28. 1. Cor. 11, 26. 2. Cor. 3, 6. Heb. 8, 16. c. 9, 5. Gifted with a new name by Christ Is. 62, 2. Instructed with new strengths by the Lord Is. 40, 31. Let us walk in a new way through him, who is the way, is the truth, is the life. Heb. 10, 10. John 14, 6. so that at length we may be led to a new heaven and a new earth Is. 65, 17. c. 66, 22. 2. Pet. 3, 13. Acts 21, 27. Where we shall again receive a new name, Rev. 2, 17. where there will be nothing which is not new c. 21, 5. where finally without end we shall sing a new canticle, which no one could learn except those who have been bought from the earth Acts 14, 3. But what is that new canticle? The Lord will go forth like a Giant, as a man of wars awakening he will shout with Zeal, nay he will exult, he will prevail over his enemies. A truly new canticle, and so singular and wonderful; because it exhibits that New thing, which the Lord creates Jer. 31, 27. the newest of all new things, which alone is new under the sun. THE LORD, who is from eternity, comes forth in time. The immortal Jehovah is born a mortal man, so that he may go forth as a Giant of dual substance. Jehovah himself is a man of wars: That man, the Lord expected by the mother of all living, comes to the aid of all the living ἀπὸ μηχανῆς. He stirs up Zeal, so that he may run forth to defeat the kingdom of sin and the Demon; so that the stronger one himself, coming upon that strong armed Prince of the world, may drive him from the world, and either confound, or destroy, or convert all his followers. The seed of the woman is present, so that he may crush the head of the Serpent. He exults in victory over his enemies, so that we, who had been conquered, may eternally exult over them conquered 1. Cor. 15, 14. A truly new canticle, which ought never to grow old, but always to flourish in the Church Ps. 33, 3. Lam. 3, 21. Job 13, 24. which has always been new and solemn to all, as many as have ever existed as new men in the Church. For JESUS CHRIST is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Heb. 13, 8. This new canticle that Jessean prophet frequently sang before others, confirmed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, pleasant in the Psalms in Israel: Exult in the Lord, O ye just, praise becomes the upright. Sing to him a new canticle, play well to him with shouting. Because our heart will rejoice in him, and we have hoped in his name. Ps. 33, 3. Which name is no other under heaven, than that in which alone is the salvation of all Acts 4, 12. Sing to the Lord a new canticle, sing to the Lord all the earth. Sing to the Lord and bless his name, announce from day to day his SALVATION. Ps. 96, 1, 2. Sing to the Lord a new canticle, because he has done wonderful things. His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him. The Lord has made known his SALVATION, in the sight of the nations he has revealed his justice. He has remembered his mercy and his truth to the House of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the SALVATION of our God. Ps. 98, 2, 3. What other SALVATION of the Lord is that, than our Lord Jesus, whose name ישועה SALVATION is expressed here in the fountains? For by this name the Messiah was already celebrated by the Patriarchs, Gen. 49, 18. by Moses Ex. 15, 2. by Isaiah c. 12, 2. 49, 6. c. 52, 16. c. 62, 11. and no less by David Ps. 14, 7. Ps. 53, 7. Ps. 68, 14. Ps. 119, 81. My soul desires thy SALVATION v. 166. I have waited for thy SALVATION O Lord v. 177. I have longed for thy SALVATION O Lord. Whence the proper [description] of the faithful under the Old Testament. this was the description, who wait. We have dealt with this Psalm in the public program for the birthday festival of Christ, which, because it adds light to the same, it pleases to add here.

The much-desired and long-awaited birth of Christ is here, the renowned solemnity is here, and in the presence of the Savior the holy Church throughout the world renders thanks and praises to its visitor. Joys are announced to us from heaven, gladness is commanded; that night conscious of the sacred birth is illuminated with new splendors. The heavenly ones glory in the heights, peace is confirmed on earth to men of good will. Sing to the Lord a new canticle: his praise from the end of the earth, you who descend into the sea and its fullness: Let the islands and their inhabitants lift up their voice, the desert and its cities, the villages which Kedar inhabits. Let the inhabitants of Petra sing, and let them shout from the top of the mountains. Let them give glory to the Lord, and announce his praise in the islands. Thus long ago the most eloquent of the grandsons of Eber intimated the birthday joy. Words are lacking for immense things, the tongue even consecrated by Seraphic touch fails here. Yet the soul, kindled by the zeal for the glory of God, appears more ardent than any fire; the Spirit, not knowing how to be contained within itself, wanders over the whole world, provoking the joy of all. To both ends of the earth: to the sea of the West, to the desert of the East, it cries out: Sing. Praise. Lift up your voice. Chant. Acclaim. Ascribe praise to the Lord. Earth. Sea. Islands. Desert. Rocks. Summits of the mountains. The voice of joy penetrates to the ends of the earth. Because joy has been prepared for the whole earth. Even those who are in danger in the very abyss of the sea exult in the Lord. Because now they rejoice in the firm anchor of hope. The desert rejoices, joy and gladness are found in it, thanksgiving, and the voice of psalmody. Because the voice of one crying is heard in the desert. And the desert shall be as Carmel: the Lord disposes the desert like Eden and its solitude like the garden of Jehovah. The Kedarites, the most impious worshippers of idols, ascribe praise to the Lord. Wild men, and especially barbarians, compose themselves entirely for His glory: Because the loftiness of idols vanishes utterly on account of the terror of the Lord, and on account of the beauty of His excellence. Every mountain and hill is brought low, and goes into a plain, and what is crooked into a valley, that the glory of the Lord may be revealed. Sing to the Lord a new song. A new song is intimated, which the old man does not know, nor does the old earth and heaven grasp. Here there is need of a new spirit, which alone He bestows upon those waiting for the consolation of Israel, the SALVATION of the Lord, Luke 2:25, 30. For which reason also the first herald of the Lord's Nativity wished to announce the joy so greatly expected in no other words than those with which the faithful of the Old Testament sharpened their desires: Unto you is born this day a SAVIOR, who is Christ the Lord in the city of David. For the heavenly Evangelist proclaims that the SAVIOR, who is the Lord, was born in the City of David for this reason: that He had been promised to David, and that that Lord of Lords, the Lord of glory, the great God, God blessed forever above all, and to say it in a word, JEHOVAH, had to be born from his family. Which is most manifest from the first and most ancient promise made to David, 2 Sam. 7 and 1 Chron. 17; as it is the one from which, in the judgment of Blessed Luther, all other prophecies concerning Christ as God and man, of David himself and of the subsequent Prophets, flowed. For what could be said more clearly than what the Lord taught concerning the son of David who was to be born after his death: I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son? That this is to be understood solely of Christ was so placed beyond all risk of controversy among the Hebrews in the age of the Apostles, that the Apostle not only built his demonstration of the eternal Deity of Christ among them upon that promise, but also held it as indubitable and ἀναντιῤῥήτως (irrefutably) certain that this could apply to no angel, let alone any man. For to which of the angels said He at any time, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son? Heb. 1:5. Nor is it to be doubted that David, in whom was the Spirit of Christ, understood this well, who not only delivered a double testimony concerning the eternal Son of God in Ps. 2:7, but, being turned into total astonishment by this promise—that such grace should befall him and his house—exclaimed: This is the form, manner, or mode of the man of the Lord God (Adonai Jehovah). You have looked upon me according to the manner or form of the Man, who is the height or the high Jehovah Elohim, the Lord God? This was a clear profession of that great Mystery of godliness; concerning the Messiah θεανθρώπῳ (God-man), he therefore proclaims this grace with the highest admiration of a devout soul: Who am I, O Lord God, and what is my house, that You have brought me thus far? But even this seemed a small thing in Your sight, O Lord God! He considers it a small thing that he was translated from the sheepfold to the scepter, where he compares this grace with this axiom: that the eternal Son of God must proceed from his womb! Then indeed, he declares eloquently that God spoke to him concerning those things which were to be in the future, and that because of them he breaks forth into these words full of admiration: You have spoken also to the house of Your servant for a great while to come. And this is the manner or form of the man of the Lord God. Nor do these words suffer any other sense, if you attend to their proper and native force. He does not say, this is the human disposition, or a mode of acting familiar to men, as some pervert it, taking the word 'man' collectively, which the He Hajediah does not support; but this is the disposition of that Lord God, and lest any doubt remain that the God-man, or θεάνθρωπον (God-man), is designated, the parallel passage renders it thus: You have looked upon me according to the manner or form of that Man, who is that high Lord God. Whence it may be concluded that the Son of God, as He showed Himself to the Patriarchs in human form, so also here presented Himself to be looked upon by David, the man after God's own heart, in human form. And whence, I beseech you, will those words be explained more correctly than from the preceding revelation, which exhibits this, and no other, form or manner by which God deigned to look upon him, or which He revealed to him: namely, that those things of which the Lord speaks to the house of David for a great while to come concern the seed of David, to be raised up after his death, and that the same is the Son of God ὁμοόσιον (consubstantial), the eternal king; that is, true man and at the same time Jehovah Elohim, the Lord God. What else does David celebrate in his Eucharistic declaration of this promise in Ps. 89, than that his Seed shall be the Son of God? Nor do the θεοδίδακτοι (God-taught) observe it without reason that those names, as if of the same Person, are here interchanged: 'servant of the Lord,' which respects the human nature, 1 Chron. 17:19, 'O Lord, for Your SERVANT'S sake, and according to Your own heart, have You done all this greatness'; and 'Word of the Lord,' which expresses the divine nature, 2 Sam. 7:21, for Your Word's sake, and according to Your own heart, have You done all these great things. Because it cannot be doubted that this grace was done to David for the sake of Christ the θεάνθρωπον (God-man). Our Megalander explains this excellently in his work on the last words of David, Vol. 8, Jena, German, f. 144, whose words are worthy to be read here. 'Here David indicates that he understood the words well, when God promised him through Nathan: I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son; I will set him in my house and in my kingdom forever. Therefore he says: What am I? What is my house, that You bring me there? It is indeed too high and too glorious a thing that You promise me, that my house, I, my son, should come to the point that he shall sit in Your eternal kingdom, and be Lord and King. Lord God, whither do You bring me! He cannot repeat it for great wonder, and names it until then, whither, whither!' 'My dear God, shall I (that is, my flesh and blood) sit equal to You in Your eternal kingdom? Then my flesh and blood, my son, and Your Son, must be the right, true God, who sits equal to You; Ah God! whither do You bring me? You have looked upon me as in the form of a man, who in the height is God the Lord.' Almost all Hebraists translate this much differently here, but some, like Bernhard Ziegler, give me information that it can and should, according to grammar, be translated as I have now translated it into German. With this, David now clearly confesses that his son the Messiah shall certainly be a true man, in all form, manner, and measure, like another man, Philip. 2, and yet above, and in the height, where there is no human manner, but only God, and he shall be God the Lord who reigns. That is (I say) clearly the opinion of David, stated in dry words. In which explanation, as being solid and evident from the words and the whole context, we prefer to acquiesce, rather than to lend our ears to Julian the Innovator, who rashly denies that any open testimony of the Deity of Christ is found in the books of Kings and earlier ones, Refutation, Num. 87. For is not this testimony written with the rays of the sun, that the Messiah is the son of David, and that God is his Father? Which, I think, the Innovators will hardly deny must be accepted concerning the Father and the Son of the same essence! Did not David here issue a manifest confession of the divine and human nature of the Messiah, that he is a true man about to come forth from his family, and at the same time true God in the highest? Which ὁμολόγησις is that of all the faithful concerning the seed of David, that he is JEHOVAH, if it pleases one to hear Jeremiah ch. 23, 6. ch. 33, 15. And therefore Osiander rightly advises in his paraphrase that this Davidic testimony concerning the person of Christ must be diligently observed, that he is true man, and at the same time also Jehovah and true and eternal God consubstantial with the Father. Victor Strigelius agrees, in Comment. on this place. D. Helvicus T. 4. Giessens. disp. 5. Dan. Cramer in Schol. propheticis, class. II. Vatic. 2. B. Gerhard in the διηγήσει of the Academy concerning the advent of the Messiah, the authors of the textual paraphrase of the Weimar Bibles, and most other Orthodox.

B. Luther also observes that the Nativity of the Messiah from a virgin is indicated here, T. 8. Germ. de Christo Jesu natu Judæo f. 241, for the reason that the Son of God could not have been generated through carnal propagation: which Julianus in his most recent treatise on the covenants that God entered into with men, n. 38, confessed had already been revealed in the proto-Evangelium itself, while he explained it thus: The seed of the woman, that is, born of a virgin woman without the copulation of a man, shall crush thy head, that is, he will dissolve and destroy thy works, by which thou art uniquely intent and occupied in destroying men. So that he might in vain otherwise, yielding his own vineyards, deny that the pious ancients believed the Messiah would be the Son of God, and true God, by this argument, namely, that they were ignorant that he would be the Son of a virgin, Widerlegung n. LXXI. Verantwortung n. XIIX. But having dismissed such portents of errors concerning the gross ignorance of the believers of the O.T. and true unbelief, let us seek our Savior, true man and true God (a mere man, whom you do not believe to be God, can neither be held, nor honored, nor adored as the Savior of the human race) in the Prophetic Scriptures: And let it be our study to foster and maintain communion in faith, not with the Roman harlot, or the patrons of the horrible Rhadamanthine decree, but with the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and believers of the O.T.: Let the highest joy and sole pleasure be to sing together the new song, with sweet harmony with them, the heavenly choir leading, because CHRIST THE LORD is born; Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men. Let everyone strive that the mind of the tongue, and the life of both, may harmonize. Perfect is the music of him whose tongue, and acts, and life, and thought all cry out. The heralds of the New Song will excite to it those who piously esteem the benefits of the Savior, who are about to offer devoted attention in sacred assemblies and due gratitude in the customary offerings at the altar. P.P. On the eve of the Nativity solemnity. In the year of the birth of Christ 1654.

Latin:

Pl. XCIIX. Canticum novum de salutari Dei omnibus an- nunciato.

VIDETVR hic Psalmus breviter scriptus, ejusdem ar- gumenti esse, cujus majus carmen Ex. 15.

Pervertitur ita pessime scopus Psalmi, qui insigne vaticinium, de conversione gentium, exhibet. Nec est quicquam in toto hoc hymno, quod doceat ad traductionem per mare rubrum eundem pertinere. Nam quod v. 7. habetur, moveatur mare, & tota ple- nitudo ejus, de insulis maris, & descendentibus in mare intelligendum, ut etiam R. David Kimchi observavit; quod verba subjuncta docent: orbis terrarum & qui habitant in eo. Nimis luculentum est de tempore N. T. & prædicatione universali Evangelii vaticinari Hie- ropsalten. Ideo cantare jubet Domino canticum no- vum, quod R. Salomone Jarchi ad Ps. 46. monente, ubiq; exponendum de Cantico in diebus Christi can- tando, & materiam cantici facit, mirabilia Domini in opere redemtionis Ps. 40, 6. cum salvaret sibi dextra ejus, & brachium sanctum ejus, quod Es. 63, 5. de Chri- sto in opere redemtionis prædicatur: qui etiam dextra Domini dicitur. Ideo recte Hieronymus: Can- ticum novum est, Dei Filius est crucifixus: quod nun- quam auditum est. Ob illa ergo mirabilia per Evan- gelium prædicata excitat ad celebrandum Domi- num. Notum fecit Dominus salutare suum, in conspectu gentium revelavit justitiam suam. Salutare Domini & justitia ejus permutantur, quia & in justitiam, & in sa- lutem nobis factus est a Deo Christus. Recordatus est misericordiæ suæ, & veritatis suæ Domui Israel. Quæ- nam illa misericordia, nisi quæ tantopere prædicata a Davide, & per totam Scripturam, misericordia nempe in Christo exhibita? Quæ uti Patriarchis, Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo promissa, ita domui Israel præstita est, cum recordatus est Dominus miseri- cordiæ & veritatis suæ Luc. 1, 54. 55. 72. 73. sed non domui Israel tantum eam exhibuit: viderunt omnes termini terræ salutare Dei nostri. Quomodo am- bigi potest, ea pertinere ad conversionem gentium? Ideo non Judæi tantum, sed omnes populi ad Can- tica & Psalmos excitantur: Jubilate Deo omnis terra, cantate & exultate, & psallite. Jubilate in conspectu Regis Domini (Messiæ) Moveatur mare, & plenitudo ejus, orbis terrarum & qui habitant in eo. Flumina plaudent manu, simul montes exultabunt; ut quic- quid in orbe est terrarum jubilet lingua, moveatur animo, plaudat manu, exultet, ac subsiliat quasi pe- dibus præ gaudio, a conspectu Domini. Quoniam venit judicare non jam Judæam, sed universam ter- ram: judicaturus orbem terrarum in justitia & popu- los in æquitate. Non possunt hæc restringi ad popu- lum Judaicum. Quod collatio etiam Psalmi pa- ralleli, qui huic maxime similis est 96. confirmat. Ideo agnoscunt omnes Interpp. Judæi & Christiani, agi hic de vocatione & conversione gentium. R. Da- vid Kimchi ad v. 4. tota terra: Etiam gentes lætan- tur, quia tunc erit salus totius mundi. Es. 2, 4. R. Aben- Ezra docet, de adventu Christi hic agi. R. Oba- dias in diebus Christi post diem judicii: Theodoretus de utroque adventu Christi explicat, quem sequitur Bellarminus & Menochius. Tirinus de regno Chri- sti æterno & renovatione mundi per Christum. Opti- me argumentum ejus expressit Dn. D. Osiander: Celebrat etiam hic Psalmus Christum & regnum ejus, & docet propagatum illud iri in universum orbem terrarum, ac hortatur, ut omnes propter beneficia Christi in Ecclesiam collata gaudeant, & gratias agant. B. Pomeranus noster summam ita proponit: Nova sunt hæc. (in cantico hoc novo) Mirabili di- vinitatis suæ potentia Dominus Deus in Christo ipsum suscitavit a mortuis: regno mortis devicto. Tunc enim declaratus est Filius Dei in virtute Rom. 1. Id quod hic dicitur, salvavit eum dextera sua, & brachium sanctum suum, quemadmodum & Deus loquitur Es. 63. Et salvavit me brachium meum, & indigna- tio mea ipsa auxiliata est mihi. Tunc misso e cælis Spi- ritu notificavit orbi salutare suum, & gentibus ju- stitiam suam, fine lege quidem, sed tamen testificatam a lege & Prophetis, ut hæc legis Rom. 3. Atque hoc ad ostendendam misericordiam suam, & veritatem pro- missam familiæ Jacob,ut legis Rom.15. Quibus hic ad- stipulantur nostrates cæteri, & alii melioris com- matis interp. Atque hæc etiam ad istum Psalmum.

Dominus Ez. 18, 31. c. 36, 36. Nova opus est vita, quæ non est nisi a Domino Rom. 6, 4. Gal. 2, 20. Nova simus conspersio per Christum 1. Cor. 5, 7. Novus homo secundum Deum. Eph. 2, 15. c. 4, 24. Col. 3, 10. Nova creatura in Christo Jesu 2. Cor.5, 17. Gal. 6, 15. Novo inserti fœderi propter Chri- stum Jer. 31, 31. Matth. 26, 28. 1. Cor. 11, 26. 2. Cor. 3, 6. Ebr. 8, 16. c. 9,5. Novo donati nomine a Chri- sto Esa. 62, 2. Novis instructi viribus a Domino Esa. 40, 31. Nova incedamus via per eum, qui via est, veritas est, vita est. Ebr. 10, 10. Joh. 14, 6. ut tandem perducamur ad novum cœlum novamque terram Esa. 65, 17. c. 66, 22. 2. Pet. 3, 13. Act. 21, 27. Ubi denuo recipiemus novum nomen, Ap. 2,17. ubi nihil erit,quod non sit novum c. 21, 5. ubi deni- que sine fine decantabimus canticum novum, quod nemo discere poterat præter eos, qui empti sunt e terra Act, 14, 3. Quodnam vero est canticum illud novum? Dominus tanquam Gigas prodibit, quasi vir bellorum evigilans Zelo vociferabitur, imo jubilabit, super inimicis suis prævalebit. Canticum vere no- vum, adeoque singulare ac mirabile; quia exhibet Novum illud, quod creat Dominus Jer. 31, 27. novo- rum omnium novissimum, quod solum est sub sole no- vum. DOMINUS, qui ab æterno est, prodit in tempore. Jehovah immortalis nascitur homo mor- talis, ut Gigas prodeat geminæ substantiæ. Jeho- vah ipse vir bellorum est: Vir ille dominus a matre omnium viventium expectatus ἀπὸ μηχανῆς vi- ventibus omnibus succurrit. Exuscitat Zelum, ut procurrat ad debellandum peccati &Dæmonis re- gnum; ut fortem illum armatum mundi Principem fortior ipse superveniens mundo depellat,& omnes ejus asseclas vel confundat, vel deleat, vel conver- tat. Adest semen mulieris, ut conterat caput Serpen- tis. Jubilat in victoria de hostibus, ut nos, qui devi- cti eramus, æternum de illis devictis jubilemus 1. Cor. 15, 14. Canticum vere novum, quod nunquam antiquari, semper vigere debet in Ecclesia Ps. 33,3. Thren. 3, 21. Job. 13, 24. quod semper novum, ac so- lenne fuit omnibus, quotquot unquam novi exti- tere homines in Ecclesia. JESUS CHRISTUS enim heri, hodie idem & in secula. Ebr. 13, 8. Canti- cum hoc novum præ aliis frequenter decantavit vates ille Jesseus, confirmatus de Christo Dei Ja- cob, jucundus Psalmis in Israel: Exultate justi in Domino, rectos decet collaudatio. Cantate ei canti- cum novum, bene psallite ei in vociferatione. Quia in eo lætabitur cor nostrum, & in nomine ejus spera- vimus. Ps. 33, 3. Quod nomen aliud non est sub cœ- lo, quam in quo uno salus est omnium Act. 4, 12. Cantate Domino canticum novum, cantate Domino omnis terra. Cantate Domino & benedicite nomini ejus, annunciate de die in diem SALUTARE ejus. Ps. 96, 1, 2. Cantate Domino canticum novum, quia mirabilia fecit. Salvavit sibi dextra ejus & brachium sanctum ejus. Notum fecit Dominus SALUTARE suum, in conspectu gentium revelavit justitiam suam. Recordatus est misericordiæ suæ & verita- tis suæ Domui Israel. Viderunt omnes termini terræ SALUTARE Dei nostri. Ps. 98, 2, 3. Quod- nam illud SALUTARE Domini aliud, quam Do- minus Jesus noster, cujus hic in fontibus expressum est nomen ישועה SALUTARE? Hoc enim nomine celebratus jam fuit Messias a Patriarchis, Gen. 49, 18. a Mose Ex. 15, 2. ab Esaia c. 12, 2. 49, 6. c. 52, 16. c. 62, 11. nec minus a Davide Ps. 14, 7. Ps. 53, 7. Psal. 68, 14. Ps. 119, 81. Desiderat SALU- TARE tuum anima mea v. 166. Expectavi SA- LUTARE tuum Domine v. 177. Concupivi SA- LUTARE tuum Domine. Unde fidelium propria sub Vet. Testam. hæc erat descriptio, qui expecta- De hoc Psalmo egimus in Programmate pu- blico festo Christi genethliaco, quod quia lucem addit eidem, hic adjicere placet.

Adest Christi multum desiderata, & diu expe- ctata nativitas, adest solennitas inclyta, & in præ- sentia Salvatoris grates & laudes visitatori suo per orbem terrarum sancta reddit Ecclesia. Gaudiono- bis cœlitus nunciantur, lætitia imperatur; Nox ista sacri partus conscia novis fulgoribus illustratur. Gloriantur in Cœlestibus superi, pax in terra bonæ voluntatis hominibus confirmatur. Cantate Domi- no canticum novum: laudem ejus ab extremo terræ, qui descendunt in mare & in plenitudinem ejus: In- sulæ & habitatores earum attollant vocem, desertum & civitates ejus, villæ, quas inhabitat Kedar. Ca- nant habitatores Petræ, & de vertice montium cla- ment. Tribuant Domino gloriam, & laudem ejus in Insulis nuncient. Ita jam olim Genethliacum inti- mavit gaudium disertissimus Eberi nepotum. Ver- ba defunt rebus immensis, Lingua Seraphico etiam consecrata attactu hic deficit. Animus tamen Zelo gloriæ Dei accensus igne quovis apparet arden- tior, Spiritus intra se contineri nescius totum ob- errat orbem, lætitiam provocans omnium. Ad utrosque terræ fines: ad mare Occidentis, ad defer- tum Orientis exclamat: Cantate. Laudate. Vocem attollite. Psallite. Acclamate. Tribuite laudem Do- mino. Terra. Mare. Insulæ. Desertum. Petræ. Ver- tices montium. Penetrat vox gaudii ad extrema terræ. Quia terræ universæ comparatum est gau- dium. Exultant in Domino etiam qui in ipsa Ma- ris periclitantur voragine. Quia jam firma gaudent spei anchora. Jubilat desertum, gaudium & lætitia invenitur in illo, gratiarum actio, & vox Psalmodi- cæ. Quia vox clamantis auditur in deserto. Et erit desertum in Charmel: Dominus disponit desertum tanquam Eden & solitudinem ejus tanquam hortum Jehovah. Laudem tribuunt Domino Kedareni, cul- tores idolorum summe impii. Gloriæ ejus totos se- se componunt homines feri, maximeque barbari: Quia idolorum celsitudo evanescit penitus propter pavorem Domini, & propter decorem excellen- tiæ ejus. Mons collisque omnis deprimitur, & in pla- num abit, quod curvum est, & salebrosa in convallem, ut reveletur gloria Domini. Cantate Domino can- ticum novum. Novum intimatur Canticum, quod nescit vetus homo, neque capit terra cœlumque vetus. Novo hic opus est spiritu, quem solus indit bant consolationem Israel, SALUTARE Domini Luc. 2, 25.30. Quam etiam ob causam non aliis verbis primus Nativitatis Domini præco gaudium tanto- pere expectatum annunciare voluit, quam quibus sua acuerunt fideles Vet. Testam. desideria: Natus est vobis hodie SALVATOR, qui est Christus Domi- nus in civitate David. Ideo namque natum in Civitate Davidis prædicat Cœlestis Evangelista SALVA- TOREM, qui est Dominus, quod Davidi promissus fuerit: & e familia ejus nasci debuerit Dominus ille Dominantium, Dominus gloriæ, Deus magnus, Deus benedictus in secula super omnia, & ut verbo dicam, JEHOVAH. Quod e prima, & antiquissima, Da- vidi facta promissione 2. Sam. 7. & 1. Par. 17. ma- nifestissimum est; utpote, e qua, B. Luthero judice, profluxerunt omnia alia de Christo Deo & homine vaticinia, Davidis ipsius & subsequentium Pro- phetarum. Quid enim disertius dici poterat, quam quod de filio David post mortem nascituro edo- cuit Dominus: Ego ero ei in Patrem & ipse erit mihi in Filium? Quod de Christo unice intelligendum esse adeo apud Ebræos, Apostolorum ætate, extra omnem controversiæ aleam positum erat, ut Apo- stolus demonstrationem æternæ Deitatis Christi penes eosdem illi promissioni non tantum super- struxerit, sed & pro indubio ac ἀναντιῤῥήτως cer- to habuerit, nemini angelorum, nedum hominum hoc convenire posse. Cui enim dixit Angelorum, Ego ergo illi in Patrem, & ipse erit mihi in Filium? Ebr. 1, 5. Neque ambigendum Davidem, in quo Spiritus Christi erat, id probe intellexisse, qui non modo Pf. 2, 7. de æterno Dei Filio gemina tradidit: sed hac promissione totus in stuporem conversus, quod ista gratia sibi, & domui suæ obtingat, excla- mavit: Hæc est forma, ratio vel modus hominis Do- mini Dei (Adonai Jehovah) Aspexisti me secundum ra- tionem vel formam Hominis, qui excelsitas vel excelsus Jehovah Elohim, Dominus Deus? Luculenta hæc fuit professio magni illius pietatis Mysterii; de Mes- sia θεανθρώπῳ, ideo tantopere cum summa ani- mi devoti admiratione deprædicat hanc gratiam: Quis ego sum Domine Deus, & quæ Domus mea, quia adduxisti me hucusque? sed & hoc parum visum est in conspectu tuo Domine Deus! Parum æstimat, quod ab ovili ad sceptrum translatus fuit, ubi hanc gratiam cum isto axiomate componit, quod æter- nus Dei Filius de utero suo prodire debeat! Tum vero de iis, quæ olim futura erant, Deum sibi lo- quutum esse, & ob ea se in hæc verba admirationis plena prorumpere, diserte perhibet: Locutus es etiam ad domum servi tui in longinquum. Et hæc est ratio vel forma hominis Domini Dei. Nec alium sen- sum patiuntur hæc verba, si propriam & nativam eorum vim attendas. Non dicit, hæc est dispositio hu- mana, vel modus agendi hominibus familiaris, ut nonnulli pervertunt, vocem hominis collective ac- cipientes, quod non fert He Hajediah; sed hæc est dispositio illius Domini Dei, ac ne dubium supersit hominem Deum, vel θεάνθρωπον designari, paralle- lus locus ita reddit; aspexisti me secundum rationem vel formam hominis illius, qui est excelsus ille Domi- nus Deus. Unde concludi possit, Filium Dei, uti Patriarchis in forma humana sese exhibuit, sic quo- que Davidi viro secundum cor Dei se in forma hu- mana hic conspiciendum præbuisse. Et unde obse- cro rectius verba illa explicabuntur, quam e reve- latione præcedanea, quæ formam vel rationem, qua Deus ipsum aspicere dignatus est, vel quam eidem patefecit, hanc, non aliam exhibet, quod nempe illa, de quibus in longinquum Domui Davidis lo- quitur Dominus, concernant semen Davidis, post fata ejus excitandum, idemque Filium Dei ὁμοό- σιον, æternum regem; hoc est, verum hominem simul & Jehovam Elohim, Dominum Deum. Quid aliud David in Eucharistica promissionis hujus de- claratione Pf. 89. celebrat, quam quod Semen suum futurum sit filius Dei? Nec præter rem observant θεοδίδακτοι, quod illa ceu ejusdem Personæ nomina inter sese hic commutentur, servus Domini, quod respicit humanam naturam, 1. Par. 17, 10. Domine propter SERVUM tuum secundum cor tuum fecisti omnem magnificentiam hanc; & Verbum Domini, quod divinam naturam exprimit, 2. Sam. 7, 21. pro- pter Verbum tuum, & secundum cor tuum fecisti omnia magnalia ista. Quia dubitari non potest, pro- pter Christum θεάνθρωπον hanc gratiam Davidi fa- ctam esse. Explicat hæc egregie Megalander noster de noviss. verb. David. T. 8. Jenens. Germ. f. 144. cujus verba digna sunt, quæ hic legantur. Hie zeigt David an, daß er die Wort wohl verstanden hat, da GOtt durch Nathan ihm verhieß, ich will sein Vater seyn, und er soll mein Sohn seyn, ich will ihn setzen in mein Haus und in mein Königreich ewiglich. Darum spricht er: Was bin ich? Was ist mein Haus, daß du mich dahin bringest? Es ist ja zu hoch, und zu herrlich Ding, das du mir verheißt, daß mein Haus, ich, mein Sohn, soll dahin kommen, daß er in deinem ewigen Reich sitzen, HErr und König seyn soll. HErr GOtt, wohin bringst du mich! Er kans für grossem Wunder nicht nachsagen, und nennets biß dahin, wohin, wohin! Mein lieber GOtt soll ich, (das ist, mein Fleisch und Blut) dir gleich sitzen, in deinem ewigen Reich? So wird mein Fleisch und Blut, mein Sohn, und dein Sohn, rechter warhafftiger GOtt seyn müssen, der dir gleich sitzet; Ach GOtt! wo bringst du mich hin? du hast angesehen mich, als in der Ge- stalt eines Menschen, der in der Höhe GOtt der HErr ist. Fast alle Ebraisten dolmetschen hie viel anders, etliche aber, als Bernhard Ziegler, geben mir Kund- schafft, daß es kan und solle, nach der Grammatica, also verdolmetschet werden, wie ich itzt verdeutschet habe. Hiermit bekennet nun David klärlich, daß sein Sohn Messia solle gewißlich ein rechter Mensch seyn, in aller Gestalt, Weise und Masse, wie ein ander Mensch, Philip. 2. und doch überwärts und in der Höhe, da keine Menschen-Weise, sondern allein GOtt ist, und regiert, soll er GOtt der HErr seyn. Das ist (sag ich) klärlich die Meynung Davids, mit dürren Worten heraus gesaget. In qua explicatione, utpo- te solida, e verbis ac contextu toto luculenta ma- lumus acquiescere, quam aures Juliano Novatori præbere, temere neganti, quod in libris Regum & an- terioribus ullum testimonium Deitatis Christi aper- tum reperiatur, Widerlegung, Num. 87. Annon enim testimonium hoc solis radiis scriptum, quod Messias Davidis filius sit Dei Filius, quodque Deus pater ipsius sit? Quod de Patre, Filioque ejusdem essentiæ accipi debere haud, opinor, negabunt No- vatores! Annon manifestam divinæ & humanæ naturæ Messiæ confessionem hic edidit David, quod verus homo sit e familia sua proditurus, & simul verus in excelsis Deus? Quæ ὁμολόγησις omnium est fidelium de germine Davidis, quod sit JEHOVAH, si Jeremiam audire lubeat c. 23, 6. c. 33, 15. Ideoque recte monet Osiander in paraphrasi, diligenter ob- servandum esse Davidicum hoc testimonium de per- sona Christi, quod sit verus homo, & simul etiam Jehovah & verus & æternus Deus Patri consub- stantialis. Adstipulatur Victor. Strigelius, in Comment. in h. l. D. Helvici T. 4. Giessens. disp. 5. Dan. Cramerus in Schol. propheticis, class. II. Vatic. 2. B. Gerhard. διηγήσει Academiæ de Messiæ adventu, Autores paraphraseos textualis Bibliorum Vinariensium & plerique alii Orthodoxi.

Observat quoque B. Lutherus Messiæ Nativitatem e virgine hic indicatam T. 8. Germ. de Christo Jesu na- tu Judæo f. 241. eo quod filius Dei per carnalem propa- gationem generari non potuerit: quod in ipso etiam prot - Evangelio jam patefactum fuisse Julianus no- vissimo, de pactis quæ Deus cum hominibus iniit, tra- ctatu n. 38. fassus est, dum ita istud exposuit: Semen mulieris, id est, natus ex muliere virgine absque copula viri, conteret caput tuum, id est, opera tua, quibus ad perdendos homines unice intentus es & incumbis, dis- solvet & destruet. Ut frustra alias, vineta propria cedens, pios veteres Messiam Filium Dei, & verum Deum fore credidisse, hoc inficiatus sit argumen- to, quod nempe ignorarint, eundem futurum vir- ginis Filium Widerlegung n. LXXI. Verantwor- tung n. XIIX. Sed missis talibus errorum portentis de crassa fidelium V.T. ignorantia, veraque ἀπιστίᾳ quæramus Salvatorem nostrum, verum hominem verumque Deum (merus homo, quem Deum esse non credas, Salvator humani generis, nec haberi, nec coli aut adorari potest) in Scripturis Prophe- ticis: Studiumque nobis sit, communionem in fide, non cum Romana meretrice, aut Rhadamantei horribilis decreti Patronis, sed cum sanctis Patriar- chis, Prophetis, ac fidelibus V.T. fovere actueri: Gaudium summum & unica voluptas sit Canticum novum, suavi cum iisdem συμφωνίᾳ, præeunte cho- ro cœlesti, ob natum CHRISTVM DOMINVM concinere; Gloria in excelsis Deo, & in terra pax, ho- minibus bona voluntas. Operam autem quisque det, ut linguæ mens, & utrique vita consonet. Illius per- fecta est Musica, cujus & lingua clamat, & actus, & vita, & cogitatio. Excitabunt ad eam Novi Cantici præcones, quibus devotam attentionem in sacris conventibus, debitamque gratitudinem in consue- tis ad altare muneribus præbituri sunt, qui beneficia Salvatoris pie æstimant. P.P. Profesto solemnitatis Genethliacæ. Anno χριστογονίας cIɔ Iɔc LIV.

## 98:6 Addition
To Psalm 98. Verse 6. MOSES AND AARON AMONG HIS PRIESTS.

Moses is not constituted a Priest, but they are commemorated with the Priests in the fellowship of those worshipping: whence the Papists, in Lorinus and Estius, litigate in vain here among themselves concerning the Priesthood of Moses. Conf. Sixtin. Amam. in Collat. Bbl.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 98. Vers. 6. MOSES ET AARON IN SACER- DOTIBUS EJUS.

Non constituitur Moses Sacerdos, sed com- memorantur illi cum Sacerdotibus in consortio ad- orantium: unde frustra hic inter se litigant Papistæ apud Lorinum & Estium de Mosis Sacerdotio. Conf. Sixtin. Amam. in Collat. Bbl.

## 99:1 Argument
PSALM XCIX. Christ the Great King.

Latin:

PSALM. XCIX. Christus Rex Magnus.

## 99:5
Ver. 5. WORSHIP AT HIS FOOTSTOOL, FOR IT IS HOLY) That is, turn yourselves toward the Ark, as is the custom for the Israelites. Ps. 138, 2. 1 Kings 8, 44. Daniel 6, 10. and in this very Psalm 9. The Ark is indeed called the footstool of God. 1 Chron. 28, 2. below Ps. 132, 7. by comparison with heaven, namely, in respect to which even the earth, but especially Judea, is called the footstool of God, Isaiah 66, 1. Matt. 5, 35. Lam. 2, 1.

A double error of the Vulgate. They are not commanded to worship the footstool in the Hebrew: But at the footstool, as Bellarmine admits. From which error of the Vulgate, therefore, the worship of saints is wrongly established, that sacred things are worthy of adoration because of their relation to God. For the footstool of the Lord was not to be adored, but at the footstool, by which most understand the ark of the covenant: some, however, with the Chaldean, taking the lamed for the kaph, wish the temple to be signified, worship in the temple, which is his footstool, as Vatablus. The discourse throughout the whole Psalm is not about the adoration of the footstool, but of the Lord, therefore it is added, FOR HE IS HOLY: and not, as the Vulgate has it: FOR IT IS HOLY, referring that epithet to the footstool, which is another of its errors. For in the last verse it is expressed who that Holy One is; where likewise they are commanded to worship at his holy mountain, but not to worship the holy mountain, For the Lord our God is holy. But what Bellarmine observes, that the Hebrew can be rendered prostrate yourselves at the footstool, does nothing for its religious adoration, because a chair is not immediately adored when someone prostrates himself before it: nor is there any doubt that external honor of reverence can be shown to sacred symbols, such as the ark of the covenant was.

But it is entirely foreign that Bellarmine understands by the footstool the human nature of Christ, which is nowhere so called, nor can it be conveniently said. The Cardinal is most inept, when he further concludes from that that the humanity of Christ must be adored under the sacramental species in the Eucharist. For will they set up the footstool of the divinity under the color of bread? And what commerce does that fictitious body, which they pretend is present through transubstantiation, have with the ark of the covenant?

Latin:

Vers. 5. ADORATE SCABELLVM PEDVM EJVS, QVONIAM SANCTVM EST) Id est, vertite vos versus Arcam, ut mos Israelitis. Ps. 138, 2. 1. Reg. 88, 44. Daniel 6, 10. & hoc ipso Psalmo 9. Arca vero dicitur scabellum pedum Dei. 1. Paralip. 28, 2. infra Psal. 132, 7. comparatione cœli sc. cujus respectu & terra, maxime vero Judæa, scabellum pe- dum Dei dicitur, Esaiæ LXVI, 1. Matth. 5, 35. Thren. 2, 1.

DUplex erratum Vulgatæ. Non scabellum ado- rare jubentur in Ebræo: Sed ad scabellum ut fatetur Bellarm. Ex quo proinde Vulgatæ errore ἁγιολατρεία male stabilitur, res sacras propter rela- tionem ad Deum adoratione dignas esse. Non enim scabellum pedum Domini erat adorandum, sed ad scabellum, per quod arcam fœderis plerique intelli- gunt: nonnulli tamen cum Chald. ל pro כ accipien- tes, templum notari volunt, adorate in templo, quod est scabellum pedum ejus, uti Vatablus. Non de ado- ratione scabelli, sed Domini sermo est per totum Psalmum, ideo additur, QUONIAM SANCTUS EST: non vero, ut Vulgata habet: QUONIAM SANCTUM est, ad scabellum id elogium refe- rens, qui est alter ejusdem error. Nam versu ultimo exprimitur, quisnam ille Sanctus sit; ubi itidem in monte sancto, non vero montem sanctum adorare jubentur Quoniam sanctus Dominus Deus noster. Quod vero Bellarm. observat, Ebræa reddi posse prosternite vos ad scabellum, nihil facit ad ejusdem religiosam adorationem, quia non adoratur sta- tim Sella, cum quis coram ea prosternitur: neque dubium est externum reverentia honorem sacris Symbolis exhiberi posse, quale arca fœderis erat.

Id autem plane alienum est, quod Bellarm. per sca- bellum pedum intelligit humanam Christi naturam, quæ ita nuspiam dicitur, neque commode dici potest. Ineptissimus vero est Cardinalis, cum ex eo porro concludit humanitatem Christi sub specie- bus sacramentalibus in Eucharistia adorandam esse. Num enim sub colore panis statuent scabellum pe- dum divinitatis? Et quid illud fictitium corpus, quod per μεταμόρφωσιν adesse fingunt, commercii habet cum arca fœderis?

## 99:6
Ver. 6. MOSES AND AARON AMONG HIS PRIESTS) Among his ministers. For the word kohen is very general, even if it is mostly used by a certain antonomasia for Priests. See 2 Sam. 8, 19.

From these words the Papists gather that Moses was a Priest, even though he was the Prince of the people, Bell. lib. 3. de V. D. c. 4. l. 5. de R. P. c. 9. Becanus in tortur. torti refut. p. 57. Nor do some of the Jews deny it, Aben-Ezra on Ex. 28, 1. from the Reformed, Jac. Capellus on Heb. 1, 3. Joh. Selden. de Success. Pontific. c. 1. from the Fathers, Jerome Tom. II. Epist. l. c. against Jovinian. Furthermore, Augustine in this place and other ancients say that Samuel was a Priest, which however Jerome denies in book 2 against Jovinian and Bellarmine refutes in this place. It certainly does not fit that two high priests should be established at the same time, Moses and Aaron. Nor did Moses enter the holy of holies, but Aaron. Whence not Moses, but Aaron alone is to be held for Pontiff and high priest. For it was his duty to enter the Holy of Holies. Nor do the words of the present Psalm prove that we should believe Moses was called a Priest. Which Tremellius and Junius render thus: Moses and Aaron with his priests. Samuel finally with those calling upon his name, calling upon Jehovah, he immediately heard them. From which you will never extract that Moses was a Priest, even if he is joined with the Priests calling upon Jehovah. Others prefer the more general meaning of the word kohen, since Kimchi on Is. 61, 10. warns concerning the word priesthood; and Pineda himself admits on Job 12, 19. that the name of Priest is not always an ecclesiastical office in Holy Scripture. But sometimes a mark of honor and dignity, to imply any Prince, or excellent man. In which way 2 Sam. 8, 18. the sons of David are called kohenim, i.e.

Pagnino and Vatablo as interpreters [render it] 'Princes', the Chaldean and R. Solomon 'magnates' (1 Chron. 18:17, 'first at the hand of the King'), as in 1 Kings 4:2, 'Azariah the son of Zadok', 2 Sam. 20:last, 'Ira the Jairite', etc. Yet it may be a matter of doubt whether this more general signification has a place here? Since Samuel would also have to be included under this name. And therefore it is better to say that Moses is indeed placed before, but without a περιφράσει (periphrasis) and absolutely, who was most eminent by himself; but that that periphrasis pertains only to Aaron with his priests, i.e., 'his priest', just as it is said of Samuel alone in 'those who call upon his name', i.e., 'calling upon his name', in the Hebrew phrase, just as in Ps. 54:6, 'The Lord is in sustaining the soul' is 'The Lord is the sustainer of the soul'. However, the conjunction of Moses with Aaron the Priest does not make Moses a Priest. Moses is joined to Aaron the Priest, not because he himself was also a Priest, but because he was most powerful in prayer with him, or rather before him, at the same time: and because he is not to be considered a stranger to that kind, who indeed did not ordinarily perform the Priesthood, nor was anointed and inaugurated to it, yet out of the ordinary course he undertook some things which were of the Priest, and consecrated Aaron himself, Lev. 8, just as Samuel, although he was not a Priest, offered a sucking lamb according to Bellarmine (which, however, Augustine denies), and especially regarding the sacrifice of Elijah, the matter is free from doubt, 1 Kings 18:23, 33, who certainly, originating from the tribe of Gad, was not a Priest, inasmuch as they had to be taken from the tribe of Levi.

Blessed Luther in the argument of this Psalm has it thus: He mentions by name, however, Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, etc., indeed the greatest men among that people, who sustained not mediocre, but both domestic and external afflictions for the sake of the name of God. As far as the argument of the Psalm pertains, Luther has it thus: But for us now in the Church there is a clear prophecy concerning Christ, who governs and rules that true Zion in the spirit, in the whole world, and sitting at the right hand of Majesty on high, is unceasingly our propitiator and propitiatory, for the sake of which Christ the whole world rages and fumes against the people of God and the Church, kills the pious, and infests them with all kinds of afflictions.

Latin:

Vers. 6. MOSES ET AARON IN SACERDOTIBVS EJVS) Inter ministros ejus. Nam vox כהן valde generalis est, etsi plerumque per ἀντονομασίαν quandam de Sacerdoti- bus usurpatur. Vide 2. Sam. 8, 19.

Ex his verbis colligunt Papistæ Mosen Sacerdo- tem fuisse, etiamsi Princeps populi fuerit, Bell. lib. 3. de V. D. c. 4. l. 5. de R. P. c. 9. Becanus in tortur. torti refut. p. 57. Neque abnuit e Judæis Aben - Ezra ad Ex. 28, 1. e Reformatis Jac. Capellus ad Ebr. 1, 3. Joh. Selden. de Success. Pontific. c. 1. e Patribus Hier. Tom. II. Epist. l. c. adversus Jovinian. Porro August. in h. l. aliique veteres Samuelem Sacerdotem fuisse dicunt, quod tamen negat Hier. l. 2. c. Jovin. & re- fellit Bellarm. ad h. l. Non convenit certe, ut sta- tuantur duo simul Sacerdotes summi, Moses & Aa- ron. Neque ingressus est sanctum sanctorum Moses, sed Aaron. Unde non Moses, sed Aaron solus pro Pontifice & Sacerdote summo habendus. Hujus enim erat Sanctum Sanctorum ingredi. Nec vero id verba præsentis Psalmi convincunt, Mosen ut credamus Sacerdotem vocatum. Quæ Tremellius & Junius ita reddunt: Mosen & Aaronem cum Sa- cerdotibus ipsius. Samuel denique cum invocantibus nomen ipsius, inclamantes Jehovam, ipse illico exaudi- vit eos. E quibus nunquam exsculpes Mosen Sa- cerdotem fuisse, etsi cum Sacerdotibus inclaman- tibus Jehovam jungatur. Aliis placet generalior vocis כהן significatio, quum Kimchio ad Es. 61, 10. monente circa vocem כהנד Sacerdotii; Et Pi- neda ipso fatente ad Job. 12, 19. Sacerdotis nomen non semper in Scriptura Sacra sit Ecclesiastici officii. Sed interdum honoris & dignitatis nota, ut innuat quemcunque Principem, aut excellentem virum. Quo pacto 2. Sam. 8, 18. filii Davidis כהנים dicuntur, h. e.

Pagnino & Vatablo interprete Principes, Chald. & R. Salome magnates (1. Par. 18, 17. Primi ad manum Regis) ut 1. Reg. 4, 2. Azarias filius Zadock, 2. Sam. 20. ult. Hira Jarithes &c. Dubium tamen esse queat, num hæc generalior significatio hic locum habeat? Siquidem Samuel etiam ita hoc nomine compre- hendendus fuerit.
