Ideoque præstat dicere, Mosen quidem præponi, sed sine περιφράσει & absolute, qui per se eminentissimus fuit; Ad Aaronem autem solum pertinere illam περίφρασιν cum Sacerdotibus ejus, i. e. Sacerdos ejus, uti de uno itidem Samuele dicitur in invocantibus nomen ejus, i. e. invocans no- men ejus, phrasi Ebræa, quemadmodum Ps. 54, 6. Dominus in sustentandum animam est Dominus su- stentator animæ. Conjunctio autem Mosis cum Aa- rone Sacerdote non facit Mosen Sacerdotem. Jungi- tur autem Aaroni Sacerdoti Moses, non quod Sacer- dos ipse etiam fuerit, sed quod cum ipso, imo præ ipso eodem tempore maxime precibus valuerit: quodq; alienus ab eo genere non censendus sit, qui ordinarie quidem Sacerdotio functus non est, nec ad id unctus & inauguratus fuit, extra ordinem tamen nonnulla quæ Sacerdotis erant, subierit, Aaronemq; ipsum consecrarit Lev. 18. quemadmodum & Sa- muel, etsi Sacerdos non fuerit, agnum lactantem ob- tulit juxta Bellarm. (quod tamen negat August.) ac imprimis de sacrificio Eliæ res dubio vacet 1. Reg. 18, 23. 33. qui utique e tribu Gad oriundus Sacerdos non fuit, utpote qui e tribu Levi assumi debuerunt.

B. Lutherus in Ps. hujus argumento ita habet: No- minatim autem exprimit Mosen, Aaron & Samue- lem &c. nimirum summos viros in illo populo, qui non mediocres, sed & domesticas & externas afflictio- nes propter nomen Dei sustinuerint. Quod ad argumentum Psalmi attinet, ita Lu- therus habet: Nobis autem jam in Ecclesia est clara Prophetia de Christo, qui Ecclesiam illam veram Zion in spiritu, in toto mundo gubernat & regit, & sedens ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis, indefinenter est propitiator & propitiatorium nostrum, propter quem Christum totus mundus adversus populum Dei & Ecclesiam furit & fremit, pios occidit, & omnis generis afflictionibus infestat.

## 100:1 Argument
PSALM 100. The Lord is our maker.

THIS PSALM IS FOR CONFESSION) That is, accustomed to be used for sacrifices of תּוֹדָה, which the Greeks translate as praise. See Leviticus 7, 2 Chronicles 2, 9. Grotius has these things from Rabbi Solomon. But the Psalm without doubt looks to the times of the New Testament, because it calls the whole world to confession: Shout to God, all the earth. Therefore it cannot be restricted to the Jewish people. Rightly Blessed Luther: It is a prophecy concerning Christ, and he commands all to rejoice and exult, to give thanks, to shout, to enter his gates in praise, his courts and tabernacle in hymns and songs, with joy, etc. For through the Gospel and this word of the remission of sins, the Kingdom is constituted and established, which remains forever, for which thanks must also always be given.

Latin:

PSALMUS C. Dominus factor noster.

HIC PSALMVS IN CONFESSIONE) Id est, adhiberi solitus sacrificiis תּוֹדָה, quod αἰνέσεως vertunt Græci. Vide Levit. 7. 2. Paralip. 2, 9. HEc ex R.Salomone habet Grotius. Respicit au- tem Psalmus sine dubio tempora N. T. quia to- tum mundum ad confessionem vocat: Jubilate Deo omnis terra. Non ergo ad populum Judaicum re- stringi potest. Recte B. Luth. Est prophetia de Christo, & jubet omnes lætari & exultare, gratias agere, jubi- lare, introire portas ejus in laude, atria ejus & taber- naculum in hymnis & canticis, cum gaudio &c. Nam per Evangelium & hoc verbum remissionis peccato- rum constituitur & stabilitur Regnum, quod in æter- num manet, pro quo semper etiam agendæ gratiæ.

## 100:3 Addition
To Psalm 100. Verse 3. HE MADE US.

It is not a matter of creation, but of generation, as is evident from v. 2: his people, and the sheep of his pasture. Whence that is rightly urged by the blessed Chemnitz against the Papists, who assert the disposition of the unregenerate man toward his own justification. Nor did St. Augustine explain this passage otherwise, even though he brought forward diverse reasons for the divine making.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. C. Vers. 3. IPSE FECIT NOS.

Non agitur de creatione, sed de generatione, ut e v. 2. patet: populus ejus, & oves pascuæ ejus. Unde recte id à B. Chemnitio adversus Pontificios, dispositionem hominis irregeniti ad sui justificatio- nem adstruentes urgetur. Nec aliter exposuit S. Augustinus hunc locum, etsi diversas facturæ divi- næ rationes adduxerit.

## 101:1 Argument
PSALM 101. Mirror of a good Prince.

Latin:

PSALMUS CI. Speculum boni Principis.

## 101:2
I WILL SING AND I WILL UNDERSTAND IN A BLAMELESS WAY, WHEN WILL YOU COME TO ME) That 'I will sing' more correctly, if I am not mistaken, the Masoretic reading refers to the preceding clause. 'I will understand in a perfect way,' that is, I will direct the strength of my mind to the integrity of life. 'When will you come to me' is placed here for 'until you come to me,' that is, until you free and exalt me. For this is David's vow concerning the manner of reigning, which he had proposed to himself in his mind, by far the best, and the manner of which few kings fulfill, even those who owe more to God than David, that is, Christians. The Masoretic reading is rashly called the text of the Holy Spirit himself. That: 'When will you come to me,' Stephanus, Piscator, and the Dutch explain more correctly: 'When you will have exalted me to the promised kingdom'; see Lord Dr. Geier on this passage. Verse 8. IN THE MORNING I WAS DESTROYING ALL THE SINNERS OF THE EARTH) It is in the Hebrew future, as the preceding, I will cut off. This is said because in the morning judgments were exercised, as we said on Job 38:13. Timely vigilance in eradicating harmful men is indicated, even if it is established that judgments were celebrated in the morning, as Maimonides notes in Yad, Sanhedrin, fol. 229. For that pertains to a good prince, to encounter evils quickly and in time. Resist the beginnings; medicine is prepared too late.

Latin:

PSALLAM ET INTELLIGAM IN VIA IMMACV- LATA, QVANDO VENIES AD ME) Illud psallam re- ctius ni fallor, Masoretica lectio ad comma præcedens refert. Intelligam in via perfecta, id est, animi vim intendam ad vitæ integritatem. Quando venias ad me positum hic pro donec ad me venias, id est, me liberes atque evehas. Est enim hoc votum Davidis de ratione regnandi, quam sibi in animo proposue- rat, longe optimam, & cujus modum pauci implent reges, et- iam ii qui plus Deo debent quam David, id est, Christiani. Masoretica lectio temere dicitur ipsius Spiritus Sancti textus. Illa: Quando venies ad me, Stephan. Piscator, & Belgæ rectius exponunt: Quando ad regnum promissum me evexeris; vid. Dn. D. Geier. hoc loco. Vers. 8. IN MATVTINO INTERFICIEBAM OMNES PECCATORES TERRÆ) Est in Hebræo futurum, ut præ- cedentia, excidam. Hoc ideo dictum, quia mane judicia ex- ercebantur, ut diximus ad Job. 38, 13. Vigilantia tempestiva in eradicandis homini- bus noxiis indicatur, etsi constet, mane judicia ce- lebrata esse, ut notat Maimonides Jad. Sanhedr. f. 229. Id enim ad bonum principem spectat cito & in tempore malis occurrere. Principiis obsta, sero medicina paratur.

## 102:1 Argument
PSALM 102. An afflicted soul desiring the coming of the Lord.

Verse 1. PRAYER OF THE POOR) לְעָנִי properly signifies him who is established in miseries. This poem seems to have been written in the Babylonian exile. Verse 21. THAT HE MIGHT LOOSE THE SONS OF THE SLAIN) From the Greeks who translated it thus above, where the same words are in 79:11, but in both places in the Hebrew it is better 'sons of death.' By that manner of speaking are signified those who are already destined for death by others, whether well or ill. That appears in 2 Samuel 12:5, John 17:12, 2 Thessalonians 2:3. Similar is 44:22, צאֹן טִבְחָה, where the LXX say 'as sheep of slaughter,' and the Apostle no differently in Romans 8:36. Grotius applies this prayer, as far as it appears, only to the misery in the Babylonian exile. But most interpreters have believed that it looks to a more sublime liberation and the coming of the Messiah, which the pious of old, established in miseries, anxiously sought. Augustine and Gregory understood Christ himself by the 'poor man,' who speaks partly in his own person, partly in the person of his body. Although indeed it can be admitted that by the 'poor man' is understood the people, or rather any outcast from the people, established in exile and misery, as Theodoret and Euthymius wish, who seek the forgiveness of sins and the removal of committed evils, whence this Psalm has been numbered by the Church among the penitential ones; yet that prayer is also specially directed to this, that with the captivity loosed, Jerusalem and the whole polity of the people may be raised up in turn, in which the Messiah may be exhibited, to which the nations may be called, and from which the glory of God may be propagated; or, as others prefer, that a spiritual Jerusalem may be built up through the coming of the Messiah and the propagation of the Gospel. And the interpreters agree in this. unanimously, that a prophecy is had here concerning the Messiah, and concerning the calling of the Gentiles, nay, that God, to whom the Psalmist sighs, is the Messiah himself, the second person of the divinity: although others with Augustine believe the coming of the Son of God is immediately vowed, to whom among the Pontificians Genebrardus, Bellarmine, and Menochius, and among ours Bugenhagius, Gesnerus, and Luc. Osiander in his paraphrase accede: others, however, [believe it is vowed] through the mediation of the solution of the Babylonian captivity, which is here wished for and sought, so that with the Messiah coming and Zion rebuilt, the law might be able to go forth into the whole world, according to the prophetic prophecies of Isaiah 2:2 and Micah 4:2, which opinion of Theodoret pleases the authors of the Weimar paraphrase, Lord Dr. Tarnovius in the penitential Psalms among ours, and among the Pontificians, Tirinus the Jesuit, and others, as well as among the Reformed, John Calvin, Piscator, Junius and Tremellius, the authors of the Dutch notes, and most of the rest. Each exposition is not inappropriate; according to the former, however, all things cohere more correctly, which are had concerning the set time, the calling of the Gentiles, and the building of Zion in verse 13 and following. Nor, however, is it worth the effort to contend about the time and occasion of this supplication being written, as Blessed Gesnerus opportunely warned; for it is certain that this was the common desire of all the faithful in the Old Testament, that the promised Messiah might be exhibited, whence the prayer fits every time, whether under the Babylonian captivity or after it. We also think it matters little whether the Church of the Old Testament is said to pray for the coming of the Messiah, as Osiander wishes, or some one of the faithful from the Old Testament: although this latter explanation is simpler, because of those things which are had in verse 3 and following: 'My days have vanished like smoke, and my bones are burned like a firebrand.'

Moreover, in the second part of the Psalm, which is not only εὐκτικὴ but also προφητικὴ from v. 13 to the end, an accurate investigation of the words and the context of the συνεχείας teaches that the Psalmist, struck by the sense of tribulations and calamities, and of a miserable and frail life, betakes himself to the grace of Christ, and raises himself up by the divine promises concerning the advent and redemption of the Messiah, and at the same time seeks the same with most ardent vows and sighs: where first he opposes to the fugacity and misery of life the perpetuity of the Lord Redeemer, and the immutability of the promises of grace: But thou, O Lord (Messiah), shalt endure for ever; and thy memorial unto all generations, i.e., just as thou art eternal and immutable, so also thy memorial endures, in the active sense, by which thou thyself art mindful of thy promises made to the Patriarchs: or in the passive sense, by which the memory of thy name is celebrated in the Church, or thy Gospel, which is a μνημόσυνον of thy benefits, which is propagated to all posterity, from which alone all my consolation redounds. That, however, the Son of God is addressed by these words is manifest from v. 24, 25, 26, 27, where likewise eternity and immutability of the Son of God is contrasted with the brevity of our life and the mutability of the whole world. Because he addresses the same one in v. 14, 'You, O Lord, sit eternally,' whom he addresses in v. 27, 'But You are the same, and Your years will not fail': indeed, it is certain that throughout the whole Psalm one and the same divine person is addressed. That the Son of God is addressed in v. 27, Paul clearly teaches in Heb. 1:10, 'And You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of Your hands. They will perish, but You remain, and they will all grow old like a garment. And like a mantle You will fold them up, and they will be changed. But You are the same, and Your years will not fail.' In obscuring this passage, one must marvel at the truly profane audacity of Grotius: for what is clearer than that the Apostle asserts that those things were said to the Son, and indeed that from them he demonstrates the Son's supreme excellence above the Angels, and His eternal and immutable Deity? Grotius, however, contends to the contrary that whatever had been said about God is here applied only to the Messiah: as if such an accommodation truly had the force of a demonstration, or as if such an accommodation alone could have availed anything to convince the Hebrews of the eminence of the Son of God: for if it were sufficient, any other countless sayings that are read in the Old Testament about God the Father could have been applied with the same ease. But the Apostle does not apply to the Messiah what was said by the Psalmist about God, but testifies that it was said by the Psalmist about the Messiah and to the Messiah; and from such a great eulogy of the Psalmist, he proves the Deity of the Messiah. But Grotius said in vain that these things could easily be applied to the Messiah, because it was agreed among the Hebrews that this world was founded for the sake of the Messiah, and that it would come to pass that a new and better world would be founded through Him. For in these verses of the Psalmist there is not a single word about a new world; indeed, so that it might be clear that the discourse is about the ancient world, the Apostle repeats the words of the Greek text: 'at the beginning You founded the earth': where in the Hebrew it is 'lephanim' (long ago), explaining with the LXX Interpreters this place of the beginning of Genesis 'bereshith,' as Grotius admits: just as it is also manifest from the analysis of the text in v. 2 that the Apostle is occupied in proving what he had said, that the ages were founded through the Son. And what does that opinion of the Hebrews—which Grotius invents, not proves, and which is not only unwritten but contrary to what is written—that this world was founded for the sake of the Messiah, contribute either to the words of the Psalmist or to the proof of the Apostle, since both the Psalmist and the Apostle are dealing not with the final cause of the founded world, but with the efficient cause and author of creation? Grotius indeed distorts the word 'ethemeliosas' (You founded) to mean 'you were the cause why it was founded,' and 'works of your hands' to mean 'done on your account.' But who would not detest such a distortion? For the word 'ethemeliosas' speaks of an efficient cause producing, 'YOU FOUNDED THE EARTH'; not of a moving cause: 'you were the cause why it was founded.' For thus it would be said more correctly of man (for the world was founded for his sake, not the Messiah's): 'YOU FOUNDED the earth: and the heavens are the works of your hands'; that is, for your sake the earth was founded, for your sake the heavens were formed. But no one will admit that these things can be said of man in this way. Then, indeed, who is ignorant that the works of someone's hands are said to be, not those for whose sake they were produced, but those by whose hands or power they were produced? And what, I ask, does that distortion contribute, that 'al yad' among the Hebrews and Chaldeans also signifies 'BECAUSE OF'? For in the sources it is thus held: 'u-ma'aseh yadecha shamayim' (and the heavens are the works of your hands); which make the Lord, who is being discussed, the efficient cause of creation, or the creator of the heaven, by whose hand the heavens were produced. Finally, since Grotius acknowledges that the Lord who is addressed here is the Messiah, even though he trifles that they are called the works of his hands because they were made for his sake, we have from his own confession that the Son of God is addressed here by the Psalmist, whom, if he still denies is established as the cause of creation, he sees nothing at midday. And this is the first comfort, by which he who is afflicted raises himself, taken from the perpetuity of the Messiah the Redeemer, and the stability and certainty of the promises. The second is from the compassion and building up of Zion, and it is thus: 'You will have compassion on Zion, for the time to have compassion on her: for the appointed time has come.' Which again sound of the Messiah: that is to say, arise, Messiah, who seem to lie prostrate before the impious nations, and show yourself present in the flesh, and declare your mercy to Zion, or to your people: for it is time that you come and heal our calamities, the appointed time is imminent: which Augustine understands of the fullness of time, and similarly James understands of the time determined in Gen. 49: 'For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and will have compassion on her earth,' or as in the Hebrew, 'and have had compassion on her dust': Which some indeed explain of the rebuilding of Jerusalem done by the servants of God, and it is understood more correctly of the Prophets and other faithful of the Old Testament who had compassion on the tearing apart of the Church and the Jewish Polity, and who were seeking a spiritual construction, as the following words confirm not obscurely: 'And the nations will fear your name, O Lord, and all the Kings of the earth your glory.' For did the nations of the earth fear the name and glory of the Lord, or of the Messiah, when Jerusalem was rebuilt; do not those things clearly designate the times and statutes of the New Testament? For those words are not to be explained only 'telikos' (as a final cause), that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt for that end, so that the nations may fear the name of the Lord, but 'prophetikos' (prophetically), because they prophesy what is truly to happen, whence this very conversion of the nations and Kings of the earth pertains to the special rebuilding of Zion, and is joined to the advent of the Messiah, because these are wont to be frequently joined in the promises, Isa. 2, Psalm 72, Zech. 9:9-10, Hag. 2:8. 'For the Lord has built Zion, and he is seen in his glory,' which likewise exhibit the Messiah: For he is the Lord on Mount Zion, Psalm 2:7, who builds and constructs the Church, Matt. 16:16. and he had to be seen in his glory Isa. 40, 5. partly in the days of his flesh under the auspices of that building John 1, 14. partly in his exaltation when he was about to manifest his glory to the world, to build up Zion throughout the whole world Ephes. 4. verse 12. The nations will speak and confess, he has looked upon the prayer of the humble, and has not despised their petitions. For R. David Kimchi, even among the Jews, explains that the nations will speak thus after the redemption. Junius, in his notes on this passage, admits that all those things, so that the nations may revere the name of the Lord v. 16. and following, pertain to the restoration of the Catholic Church.

Thirdly, the afflicted one raises himself in this Psalm by the gracious redemption of the Messiah, which is to be the subject of all the praises of the Lord v. 19. and following. These things will be written for the next generation, (or later, and most recent, as Tarnovius and Junius interpret) and the people who shall be created will praise the Lord: that these pertain to the times of the N. Testament is clear, nor do the interpreters easily doubt it. For what else is the next generation, what is the people who were then to be created, the Holy Spirit admonishing in express words here what is written in 1 Pet. 1, 11, so that the Jews might not attribute these things to themselves, and so that the preceding things might not perhaps be understood concerning the release from the Babylonian captivity: Bellarmine admits this here. The Rabbis themselves seem to acknowledge it: R. Obadiah interprets it concerning the time of the Messiah, concerning the people being created in the image of God. R. David Kimchi: the people of the age following the redemption, when they see it written, will praise God for it. But what indeed is that new subject matter of the people's praises? Because He looked down from His holy height, the Lord looked down from heaven to earth: which looking is not that of one absent, but of one present. Thus He looked down from heaven to earth, so that He might truly descend from heaven to earth, and there work salvation, so that indeed the groans of the prisoners might at length be heard (who were held bound by spiritual chains Is. 49, 1. ch. 61, 1, 2. Tim. 2, 26.) so that He might loosen and lead forth the sons of death: such as we all were: But we have been redeemed and led forth from the hand of hell and death by Him Hos. 13, 14. Zach. 9, 11. Heb. 2, 14. Bellarmine is not bad here, He looked down from heaven to earth, not with an idle gaze, but so that from the height He might become humble, and be seen on earth, and dwell with men. By the prisoners he understands men, bound by the works of the devil to their own concupiscences: by the sons of the slain, as the Vulgate has it, the sons of Adam and Eve, who were the first killed by the cunning of the serpent. But in the Hebrew it is held, sons of death, that is, those who were given over to death. Compare Ps. 79, v. 19, just as they are also called sons of wrath Eph. 2, 3.

is about to return to Tohuvabohu: Aben-Ezra says that the heaven and earth which now are, are about to perish, but that a new heaven and a new earth are to be created. D. D. Sebast. Schmied. in his former Biblical College, page 404, observes that none of the Hebrews here dare to take the words only as a change according to Qualities, but all explain them as a substantial change; nor is there any place in the Scriptures where the word אבד is used otherwise than for essential destruction; and since men are excepted here in the last verse, who truly cannot be excepted from a change according to quality, a substantial change of heaven and earth must necessarily be understood.

Verse 29. THE CHILDREN OF THY SERVANTS SHALL DWELL AND THEIR SEED SHALL BE ESTABLISHED FOREVER.

By servants, Brentius understands the Patriarchs, others in general rather the faithful of the O.T. from v. 15, compared with Luke 10, 24, whose children are the faithful of the N.T., both Jews and Gentiles, or rather the Church of the N.T., insofar as it has been propagated from the faithful of the O.T., nor yet are the ancient faithful so excluded from that dwelling; but by parity of reasoning they are included, indeed it is taught that the faithful in the N.T. will also be partakers of the promises made to the ancients. Moreover, they are said to dwell and to be stable BEFORE THE LORD, not with a dwelling restricted to a certain time, but absolutely, therefore Kimchi rightly explains, they shall dwell forever (although he wrongly distorts it to an earthly kingdom;) which that absolute stability of theirs also demands. For their seat is before the Lord, who will remain forever, whose years shall not be consumed, when heaven and earth shall perish.

Fourthly, the universal Church also raises itself by gathering together, which is the end of Christ's redemption v. 22, so that they may announce the name of the Lord in Sion, and His praise in Jerusalem, in gathering the peoples into one, and Kings, so that they may serve the Lord. Which cannot be understood otherwise than of the time of the N. Testament, and of the Church or assembly of the faithful called and united from all nations through Christ, as Junius and Tarnovius also explain here, understanding a spiritual Sion, as in Psalm 2, 6, and Jerusalem, which is born from above Gal. 4, 26, when from Jews and Gentiles one body was made Eph. 2, 14, 15, to worship the Lord the deliverer, Jesus Christ 1. Cor. 12, 3.

Latin:

PSALMUS CII. Anima angustata desiderans adventum Domini.

Vers. 1. ORATIO PAVPERIS) לְעָנִי proprie eum si- gnificat, qui in miseriis est constitutus. Videtur scriptum hoc carmen in exilio Babylonico. Vers. 21. VT SOLVERET FILIOS INTEREMTO- RVM) Ex Græcis qui supra sic transtulerunt, ubi eædem voces 79, 11. sed utrobique in Hebræo melius filios mortis. Eo loquendi genere significantur ii, qui jam ab aliis bene aut male morti destinati sunt. Apparet id 2. Sam. 12, 5. Joh. 17, 12. 2. Thess. 2, 3. Simile 44, 22. צאֹן טִבְחָה, ubi LXX. ὡς πρό- βατα σφαγῆς, nec aliter Apostolus Rom. 8, 36. Orationem hanc, quantum apparet, soli mi- seriæ in exilio Babylonico applicat Grotius. Sed eam sublimiorem liberationem & adventum Messiæ, quem in miseriis constituti pii veteres anxie expe- tebant, respicere, plerique interpp. credidere. Au- gustinus & Gregorius ipsum Christum per pauperem intellexerunt, qui partim in sua persona, partim in persona corporis sui loquatur. Quanquam vero admitti possit, per pauperem intelligi populum, aut potius quemcunque abjectum e populo, in exilio & mi- seria constitutum, ut vult Theodoreus, & Euthy- mius, qui peccatorum condonationem, & malo- rum commissorum ablationem petat, unde Psal- mus hic pœnitentialibus ab Ecclesia annumeratus est, oratio tamen illa etiam specialiter eo directa est, ut soluta captivitate, Hierosolyma, & politia tota populi vicissim erigatur, in qua Messias exhi- beatur, ad quam gentes vocentur, & e qua gloria Dei propagetur; Vel, quod alii malunt, ut spiritua- lis Hierosolyma per adventum Messiæ, & propaga- tionem Evangelii exstruatur. Et consentiunt in eo Interpp. ὁμοθυμαδὸν, de Messia hic vaticinium ha- beri, ac de vocatione gentium, imo Deum, ad quem suspirat Psaltes, ipsum Messiam esse, secundam divi- nitatis personam: Etsi alii cum Augustino immediate voveri adventum Filii Dei credant, quibus e Pon- tificiis Genebrardus, Bellarminus & Menochius, e no- stris Bugenhagius, Gesnerus, Luc. Osiander in para- phrasi accedunt: alii vero mediante solutione capti- vitatis Babylonicæ, quæ hic optetur & expetatur, ut ad- veniente Messia, Zione iterum exstructa, lex prodi- re in orbem terrarum possit, secundum vaticinia Prophetica Es. 2, 2. Mich. 4, 2. quæ sententia Theo- doreti placet autoribus paraphraseos Vinariensis, Dn. D. Tarnovio in Psalmis pœnitentialibus, e no- stris, & e Pontificiis, Tirino Jesuitæ, aliisque, nec non e Reformatis Joh. Calvino, Piscatori, Junio & Tremellio, autoribus notarum Belgicarum, & reliquis plerisque. Utraque expositio non inconcinna est, juxta priorem tamen omnia cohærent rectius, quæ de statuto tempore, vocatione gentium & exstru- ctione Zionis v. 13. seqq. habentur. Neque tamen, quod opportune monuit B. Gesnerus: de tempo- re & occasione conscriptæ hujus supplicationis, vel de autore operæ pretium est contendere; certum enim est, commune hoc fuisse desiderium omnium fidelium in V. T. ut promissus Messias exhiberetur, unde omni tempori, sive sub captivitate Babyloni- ca, seu post eandem congruit Oratio. Parum etiam interesse arbitramur, sive Ecclesia V. T. orare dica- tur pro adventu Messiæ, uti vult Osiander, seu fide- lium quispiam e Veteri Testamento: quanquam hæc posterior explicatio simplicior sit, ob ea quæ v. 3. & seqq. habentur: defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei, & ossa mea sicut titio exusta sunt.

Cæterum in altera Psalmi parte, quæ non εὐκτικὴ solum, sed etiam προφητικὴ est a v. 13. ad finem us- que Psalten sensu tribulationum & calamitatum, ac miseræ, & caducæ vitæ perculsum ad gratiam Chri- sti se recipere, ac promissionibus divinis de adven- tu ac redemtione Messiæ sese erigere, simulque ar- dentissimis votis & suspiriis eandem expetere, ac- curata verborum & συνεχείας contextus ἐρεύνησις docet: ubi primum vitæ fugacitati ac miseriæ oppo- nit Domini Redemtoris perennitatem, & promissionum gratiæ immutabilitatem: Tu autem Domine (Messia) in æternum permanes, & memoriale tuum in genera- tionem, & generationem, i. e. sicut tu æternus es & im- mutabilis, ita permanet etiam memoriale tuum, sensu activo, quo ipse memor es promissionum tuarum Patriarchis factarum: vel passivo, quo celebratur memoria nominis tui in Ecclesia, vel Evangelium tuum, quod est μνημόσυνον beneficiorum tuo- rum, quod ad omnem posteritatem propagatur, ex quo unice omne solatium meum redundat. Quod autem his verbis compelletur Filius Dei e v. 24. 25. 26. 27. manifestum est, ubi pariter æternitas & im- mutabilitas Filii Dei opponitur vitæ nostræ brevitati ac totius mundi mutabilitati. Quia eundem com- pellat v. 14. Tu Domine æternum sedes, quem v. 27. Tu autem idem ipse es, & anni Tui non deficient: imo per totum Psalmum unam eandemque divinam personam compellari, certum est. Filium autem Dei v. 27. compellari Paulus aperte docet Ebr. 1, 10. καὶ σὺ κατ’ ἀρχὰς, κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σε εἰσὶν οἱ ἰρανοί. Αὐτοὶ ἀπολῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις, καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται. καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐ- τὰς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σε ἐκ ἐκλείψεσι. In quo loco obfuscanndo mirari oportet audaciam Grotii vere profanam: Quid enim clarius, quam quod illa πρὸς τὸν ὑιὸν, ad Filium dicta asserat Apostolus, imo quod ex iis Filii præ Angelis summam ὑπεροχὴν, & æternam ac immutabilem Deitatem demonstret: Grotius ta- men ex adverso contendit, Messiæ tantum hic aptari, quiquid de Deo dictum fuerat: quasi vero talis ac- commodatio vim demonstrationis habeat, aut quic- quam ad evincen dam aput Ebræos eminentiam Filii Dei facere potuerit sola ejusmodi accommo- datio: quæ si sufficiens erat, eadem facilitate quæ- vis alia dicta, quæ de Deo Patre in V. Testamento leguntur innumera, aptari potuissent. Apostolus ve- ro non aptat hoc Messiæ, quod a Psalte de Deo dictum, sed de Messia & ad Messiam dictum a Psalte fuisse, testatur; atque ex tanto Psaltis elogio Deita- tem Messiæ probat. Nequicquam vero dixit Gro- tius, aptari hæc facile potuisse Messiæ, quia constabat inter Ebræos, & mundum hunc conditum Messiæ causa, & fore, ut novus meliorœ mundus condatur per ipsum. Nam de novo mundo in his quidem versibus Psaltis nullum verbulum habetur, imo ut de antiquo mun- do sermonem esse constaret, Apostolus verba Græ- ci textus repetit: κατ’ ἀρχὰς a principio fundasti ter- ram: ubi in Hebr. est לפנים jam olim, exponens cum LXX. Interpp. hunc locum Geneseos initio בראשית ut fatetur Grotius: quemadmodum etiam ex ana- lysi textus v. 2. manifestum est, Apostolum occu- pari in probando eo, quod dixerat, per Filium esse se- cula condita. Et quid vel ad verba Psaltis, vel ad probationem Apostoli facit opinio illa Ebræorum, quam fingit, non probat Grotius, quæ non modo ἄγραφος est, sed ἀντίγραφος, quod mundus hic Messiæ causa conditus sit, quum non de causa finali mundi conditi, sed de causa efficiente, & autore creationis & Psaltes & Apostolus agant. Detor- quet quidem Grotius verbum ἐθεμελίωσας, causa fuisti, cur fundaretur, & ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σε opus manuum tuarum, id est, propter te factum. Sed quis ejusmodi σρεβλότητα non detestaretur? Verbum enim ἐθεμελίωσας de causa efficiente producente lo- quitur, FUNDASTI TERRAM; non de causa mo- vente: causa fuisti, cur fundaretur. Sic namque de homine (hujus enim causa mundus conditus est, non Messiæ) rectius id diceretur, FUNDASTI terram: & opera manuum tuarum cœli; id est, propter te terra fundata est, propter te cœli formati. Hæc autem de homine ita dici nemo admittet. Tum vero quis ignorat opera manuum alicujus dici, non cujus causa illa producta sunt, sed cujus manibus vel potentia illa producta: Et quid, obsecro, ad σρεβλότητα illam facit, quod על יד Ebræis & Chaldæis etiam PRO- PTER significet: In fontibus enim ita habetur: ומעשה ידיך שמים & opera manuum tuarum cœli; quæ Dominum, quo de agitur, causam efficientem creationis, vel creatorem cœli faciunt, cujus ma- nu cœli producti sint. Denique quum Dominum illum, qui hic compellatur, Messiam esse, a- gnoscat Grotius, etsi opera manuum ejus dici nugetur, quia propter ipsum facta sunt, ex ipsiusmet confessione habemus, Filium Dei a Psalte hic com- pellari, quem proinde causam creationis constitui, si adhuc negat, in meridie nihil videt. Atque hoc primum est, quo se afflictus hic erigit, solatium, a Messia Redemtoris perennitate, ac promissionum gratia stabilitate, & certitudine desumtum. Alterum a Sionis commiseratione & ædificatione, ita habet: Tu misereberis Sion, quia tempus miserendi ejus: quia ve- nit statutum tempus. Quæ iterum Messiam sonant: q. d. surge Messia, qui impiis gentibus jacere videris, & præsentem te in carne exhibe, ac misericordiam tuam Sioni, vel populo tuo declara: quia tempus est, ut venias & calamitatibus nostris medearis, tempus sta- tutum imminet: quod de temporis plenitudine Augu- stinus, ac similiter de tempore a Jacobo Gen. 49. de- terminato intelligunt: Quoniam placuerunt servis tuis lapides ejus, & terræ ejus miserebuntur, vel uti in Ebræo, & pulveris ejus sunt miserti: Quod nonnulli quidem de reædificatione Hierosolymæ a servis Dei facta explicant, ac rectius de Prophetis aliisque fi- delibus Veteris Testamenti misertis dilacerationis Ecclesiæ & Politiæ Judaicæ, atque expetentibus spi- ritualem exstructionem, intelligi, verba sequentia haud obscure confirmant: Et timebunt gentes nomen tuum Domine, & omnes Reges terræ gloriam tuam. Num enim gentes terræ nomen & gloriam Domini, vel Messiæ, timuere, cum reædificata est Hierso- lyma; annon ista clare Novi Testamenti tempora & statuta designant? Non enim verba illa tantum τελικῶς exponenda, quod ea fini sit reædificanda Hierosolyma, ut timeant gentes nomen Domini, sed προφητικῶς, quia quod revera futurum sit, va- ticinantur, unde hæc ipsa gentium & Regum terræ conversio ad reædificationem specialis Zionis per- tinet, & adventui Messiæ subjungitur, quia hæc in promissionibus frequenter conjungi solent Esa. 2. Psalm. 72. Zach. 9, 9. 10. Hagg. 2, 8. Quoniam ædi- ficavit Dominus Sion, & conspicitur in gloria, quæ iti- dem Messiam exhibent: Nam is est Dominus in monte Zion Psalm. 2, 7. qui ædificat & exstruit Ec- clesiam Matth. 16, 16. & conspici debuit in gloria sua Esa. 40, 5. partim in diebus carnis sub auspicium illius ædificationis Joh. 1, 14. partim in exaltatione cum gloriam mundo erat manifestaturus, per or- bem totum Sionem exstructurus Ephes. 4. vers. 12. 幅icent ac fatebuntur gentes, respexit in orationem hu- milium, & non sprevit preces eorum. Sic enim di- cturas gentes post redemtionem, exponit etiam e Judæis R. David Kimchi. Illa omnia, ut reverean- tur gentes nomen Domini v. 16. & seqq. ad instauration nem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ pertinere, fatetur Junius in notis ad hunc locum.

Tertio erigit sese afflictus in hoc Psalmo Mes- siæ gratiosa redemtione, quæ materia futura omnibus laudum Domini v. 19. & sequentibus. Scribentur hæc in generatione altera, (vel postera, & novissima, ut interpretatur Tarnovius & Junius) & populus, qui creabitur, laudabit Dominum: quæ ad N. Test. tem- pora pertinere, luculentum est, neque facile ambi- gunt Interpp. Quæ enim alias est generatio altera, quis populus, qui tum creandus erat, disertis verbis hic admonere Spiritum S. quod 1. Pet. 1, 11. scriptum est, ne Judæi ista sibi tribuant, & ne forte intelligerentur su- periora de solutione captivitatis Babylonicæ: fatetur hic Bellarminus. Rabbini ipsi videntur id agno- scere: R. Obadias de tempore Messiæ interpretatur, de populo creando in imagine Dei. R. David Kimchi: populus seculi redemtionem subsequentis, quando vident eam scriptam, ob eam laudabunt Deum. Quænam vero illa laudum populi nova materia? Quia prospexit de excelso sancto suo, Dominus de cœlo in terram aspexit: qui aspectus non est absentis, sed præsentis. Ita in terram aspexit de cœlo, ut vere de cœlo in terram descenderet, ibique salutem operatus sit, ut nempe tandem exaudirentur gemitus compeditorum (qui vinculis spiritualibus constricti tenebantur Es. 49, 1. cap. 61, 1, 2. Tim. 2, 26.) ut solveret & educeret filios mortis: quales nos omnes fuimus: Sed e manu in- ferni & mortis per ipsum redemti & educti sumus Hos. 13, 14. Zach. 9, 11. Ebr. 2, 14. Non male hic Bellarminus, de cœlo in terram aspexit, non otioso in- tuitu, sed ut de excelso fieret humilis, & in terris vide- retur, & cum hominibus versaretur. Per compedi- tos intelligit homines, opera diaboli alligatos propriis concupiscentiis: per filios interemtorum, ut vulgata ha- bet, filios Adami & Hevæ, qui fuerunt primi occisi ab astutia serpentis. Sed in Hebræo habetur, filii mor- tis, id est, qui morti dediti erant. Cons. Ps. 79. v. 19. uti filii iræ etiam dicuntur Eph. 2, 3.

Tohuvabohu rediturus sit: Aben-Ezra cælum & ter- ram quæ nunc sunt, peritura ait, creanda autem novum cælum, & novam terram. Dn. D. Sebast. Schmied. in Colleg. priori Biblico pag. 404. observat nullum Ebræorum hic audere verba accipere tantum de muta- tione secundum Qualitates, sed omnes de mutatione substantiali exponere; neq; in Scripturis ullum dari lo- cum, in quo verbum אבד aliter quam de interitu es- sentiali adhibeatur; & quum hic excipiantur homi- nes v. ult. qui vero a mutatione secundum qualita- tem excipi nequeunt, necessario substantialem cœli & terræ mutationem intelligendam esse.

Vers. 29. FILII SERVORUM TUORUM HA- BITARUNT ET SEMEN EORUM IN SECU- LUM DIRIGETUR.

Per servos Brentius Patriarchas, alii in genere potius fideles V. T. e v. 15. collato cum Luc. 10, 24. in- telligunt, quorum liberi sunt fideles N. T. tum Ju- dæi, tum gentiles, vel potius Ecclesia N. T. siquidem ea propagata sit inde a fidelibus V. T. nec tamen ita ab habitatione illa excluduntur prisci fideles; sed ob paritatem rationis includuntur, imo docetur ita promissionum antiquis factarum etiam consortes fore fideles in N.T. Habitare autem dicuntur & sta- biles fore CORAM DOMINO, non restricta habi- tatione ad certum tempus, sed absolute, ideo recte explicat Kimchi, habitabunt in æternum (quanquam male ad terrenum regnum detorqueat;) quod etiam postulat absoluta illa eorum stabilitas. Sedes enim eorum est coram Domino, qui manebit in æternum, cujus anni non consumentur, cum cœlum & terra peribunt.

Quarto erigit etiam sese Ecclesia universalis co- agmentatione, quæ finis est redemtionis Christi v. 22. ut annuncient in Sion nomen Domini, & laudem ejus in Jerusalem, in conveniendo populos in unum, & Re- ges, ut serviant Domino. Quæ aliter, quam de tem- pore N. Test. intelligi non possunt, & de Ecclesia sive cœtu fidelium ex omnibus gentibus convocato adunato- que per Christum, ut explicat etiam hic Junius & Tar- novius, Sionem spiritualem intelligens, uti Psalm. 2, 6. & Hierosolymam, quæ superne nata est Gal. 4, 26. cum ex Judæis & gentibus factum est unum corpus Eph. 2, 14. 15. ad colendum Dominum liberatorem, Jesum Christum 1. Cor. 12, 3.

## 103:1 Argument
PSALM CIII. A celebration of the mercy of the Lord.

Latin:

PSALMUS CIII. Celebratio misericordiæ Domini.

## 103:3
Verse 3. WHO FORGIVETH ALL THINE INIQUITIES, WHO HEALETH ALL THINE INFIRMITIES) In the Hebrew that 'thine' and 'thine' is not דְּ which smacks of Chaldaism.

See concerning v. 1, 2, Sermon 23 in the Memory of the Just, Witteberg.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QVI PROPITIATVR OMNIBVS INIQVI- TATIBVS TVIS, QVI SANAT OMNES INFIRMI- TATES TVAS) In Hebræo illud tuis & tuas non est דְּ quod redolet Chaldaismum.

Vid. de v. 1. 2. Concio 23. in Memoria Justor. Witteberg.

## 103:5
Verse 5. THY YOUTH SHALL BE RENEWED LIKE THE EAGLE'S) For eagles take on new feathers, Isaiah 40, 31, where the Greeks say, πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί.

Latin:

Vers. 5. RENOVABITVR VT AQVILÆ JUVENTVS MEA) Aquilæ enim novas pennas assumunt, Esaiæ 40, 31. ubi Græci, πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί.

## 103:12 Addition
To Psalm 103. Verse 12. AS FAR AS THE EAST IS FROM THE WEST. The Papists abuse this saying to prove a total renewal and a plenary abolition of every vicious habit; but what is removed from us does not entirely perish, nor is it abolished: and this word must be explained according to the subject matter and the scope of the discourse; which here is about the non-imputation or vindication of sins v. 10, about the affection of a Parent toward a son v. 13, which is an affection of pity, not an effect of the eradication of every evil. Finally, from the occasional or προκαταρκτικῇ cause which is brought forward in v. 14 concerning natural and innate vice, it easily shows that the pity of God is praised here, not for a plenary purging of vice in this life, but for a connivance regarding adherent infirmity, such as is the connivance of a Father toward a Son.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 103. Vers. 12. QUANTUM DISTAT ORTUS AB OCCIDENTE. Abutuntur hoc dicto Papistæ ad probandam totalem renovationem & plenariam abolitionem omnis habitus vitiosi; sed quod elongatur a nobis non plane interit, nec aboletur: & explicandum hoc verbum secundum subjectam materiam, & scopum dicendi; qui hic est de non imputatione vel vindicatione peccatorum v. 10. de affectu Parentis erga filium v. 13. qui est affectus miserationis non effectus eradicationis omnis mali. Denique e causa occasionali vel προκαταρκτικῇ quæ v. 14. affertur de naturali & connato vitio, facileque ostendit, laudari hic miserationem Dei, non a plenaria expurgatione vitii in hac vita, sed a conniventia circa adhærentem infirmationem, qualis est conniventia Patris erga Filium.

## 103:17
Verse 17. BUT THE MERCY OF GOD IS FROM EVERLASTING, AND EVEN UNTO EVERLASTING UPON THEM THAT FEAR HIM) That is, it lasts for a very long time, as in Exodus 20, 6, yet the words are such that they are rightly applied in a more sublime sense to eternity by Aben-Ezra and others.

Fifthly, our afflicted one raises himself up, [seeking] the mercy of the Lord from affliction, v. 24. He afflicts (God indeed with various calamities) in the way (in this valley of miseries, which is the way to the heavenly Fatherland) my strength, as Jerome renders the Hebrew, he shortened my days, so that they do not reach the days of my ancestors: but I do not cease to pray and to say μετὰ παῤῥησίας: My God, do not take me away in the midst of my days by an untimely death, before I have lived enough for myself, i.e., before I have prepared myself for a blessed death, (which is also the explanation of the Blessed Osiander, as well as of Rob. Bellarm. and others) relying on certain confidence, because you are my God, O Lord (Messiah), as He Himself is eternal, Creator of heaven and earth, immutable in essence and purpose, who always remain the same, even if heaven and earth should perish: so you are entirely able to bring it about, and by the power of your promises you will bring it about, that the children of your servants (the Patriarchs, who are such according to the promise, and their spiritual children, may dwell eternally) and their seed may persevere, or be established, before your face: So that he may be preserved here in the kingdom of grace, and endure in the kingdom of glory, which happiness I also hope to enjoy, because I do not doubt that I am included under that spiritual seed. Therefore, although heaven and earth may perish, yet your word and promise to the spiritual seed, and not to me, will not perish, but just as you will change and destroy those, so you will preserve these forever. From which paraphrase it is again manifest that the Messiah is addressed here, and his benefits are proposed as a consolation to the afflicted: which had to be demonstrated against Grotius.

Why does he here again double the meaning? Since the discourse is most openly about simple eternity and all-encompassing mercy, which lasts from eternity to eternity. For thus absolute eternity is described, from the part before, as they say, and from the part after. If from the part after only a long duration is designated, and from the part before only a long pre-existence, eternity will certainly not be noted, and thus a certain mutability would be inferred in God. Therefore, not only according to the literal sense is a long and lasting duration signified, but true eternity: nor is the mercy of God said to endure forever only according to the mystical sense, which Grotius calls the more sublime, but believers, according to the proper and native, and the only, sense of this saying, enjoy the eternal mercy of God. Which is also the mind of Aben-Ezra; for he believes that not only a lasting, but an eternal enjoyment of God's mercy is indicated here.

Latin:

Vers. 17. MISERICORDIA AVTEM DEI AB ÆTER- NO, ET VSQVE IN ÆTERNVM SVPER TIMENTES EVM) Id est, diutissime durat, ut Exod. 20, 6. verba tamen sunt talia, quæ in sensu sublimiori ad æternitatem recte ap- plicentur ab Aben-Ezra, & aliis.

Quinto erigit sese afflictius noster, misericordi Domini ex afflictione liberatione v. 24. Affligit (qui- dem Deus variis calamitatibus) in via (in hac mise- riarum valle, quæ via est ad cœlestem Patriam) for- titudinem meam, ut Ebræa reddit Hieronymus, ab- breviavit dies meos, ut non attingant dies majorum: sed ego non desisto precari ac dicere μετὰ παῤῥησίας: Deus mi, ne auferas me in medio dierum meorũ inten- pestiva morte, priusquam satis mihi vixerim, h. e. me ad beatum obitum composuerim, (quæ etiam B. Osiandri est explicatio, ut & Rob. Bellarm. & a- liorum) certa fiducia fretus, quia Deus meus es tu Do- mine Messia) uti æternus ipse est, Creator cœli & ter- ræ, immutabilis in essentio, & sententia, qui semper idem manes, etsi cœli & terra intereant: ita efficere omnino potes, & vi promissionum tuarum efficies, ut filii servorum tuorum (Patriarcharum, qui secun- dum promissionem, & spirituales ipsorum filii sunt, habitent, æternum) & semen eorum ante faciem tuam perseveret, vel stabiliatur: Sic ut conservetur hic in regno gratiæ, & perennet in regno gloriæ, qua feli- citate ego etiam me fruiturum spero, quia sub semi- ne illo spirituali me comprehensum esse non dubi- to. Licet ergo cælum & terra pereant, non tamen verbum & promissio tua semini spirituali, non mihi, peribit, sed uti illa tu immutabis, ac destrues, ita hæc servabis in æternum. E qua paraphrasi iterum ma- nifestum est, Messiam hic compellari, ejusque be- neficia in solatium afflictis proponi: quod contra Grotium demonstrandum erat.

Cur hic iterum sensum geminat? quum aper- tissime de æternitate simplici & omnimoda miseri- cordia sermo sit, quæ ab æterno in æternum durat. Sic enim absoluta æternitas describitur, a parte ante, ut loquuntur, & a parte post. Si a parte post longa tantum duratio designatur, a parte ante etiam longa præexistentia solum, utique non notabitur æterni- tas, atque ita mutabilitas quædam in Deum infere- tur. Non ergo tantum secundum sensum litera- lem duratio longa & diuturna significatur, sed vera æternitas: neque solum secundum sensum mysticum, quem sublimiorem vocat Grotius, in æternum durare dicitur Dei misericordia, sed credentes juxta proprium & nativum, eumque unicum hujus dicti sensum, æ- terna misericordia Dei fruuntur. Quæ etiam Aben-Ezræ mens est; Non enim tantum diuturnam, sed æternam misericordiæ Dei fruitionem hic indicari credit.

## 104:1 Argument
PSALM CIV. A celebration of the Creator, and of the works of creation.

But that the discourse is about substantial, not accidental, destruction, the emphasis of the words and the reason for the opposition teach, concerning which the gloss of the Jews, converting a categorical into a hypothetical, 'they themselves would perish, if you willed,' as being too violent, needs no refutation. And Kimchi reports that some of the Jews take these words to mean that the world [returns] to its ancient [state].

TO DAVID) It is not in the Hebrew: but whoever the author of this Psalm is, he is an excellent poet.

As if, indeed, either some poet, even if moved by the Holy Spirit, were not excellent, or something could be in the Canon which did not proceed from the Holy Spirit.

Calvin is deservedly deserted by Tremellius, Junius, Piscator, and the Belgian interpreters. The words of David are certainly clear; for he does not say, 'who makes the winds his angels, and flaming fire his ministers,' but in the inverted order: 'who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire.' Nor is it consistent that winds and fire, as meteors, should be compared with angels, spirits, and ministers standing before God; and in the judgment of Piscator himself, it is an inept expression that a flaming fire is called not a minister, but in the plural, ministers of the Lord. Moreover, there does not even seem to be a need for some to assume an ellipsis of the particle of similitude, and the former words should be taken properly, since no necessity compels otherwise, 'who makes his angels spirits,' as they are of spiritual essence (Heb. 1:7, 14); and in the latter member, 'a flaming fire' can likewise be explained concerning the most subtle and pure nature of angels, whence some are called Seraphim, i.e. burning fires; 'He makes his ministers such that their nature is a certain flaming fire.' But we leave these things in the middle. See D. D. Sebast. Schmied. in Colleg. Bibl. prior. on this passage, page 195.

Latin:

PSALMUS CIV. Celebratio Creatoris, & operum creationis.

De interitu autem substantiali, non acciden- tali sermonem esse, verborum ἔμφασις & opposi- tionis ratio docet, de qua alias Judæorum glossa Categoricam in hypotheticam convertens, ipsi per- irent, si velles, ceu nimis violenta, nulla indiget re- futatione. Et refert Kimchius quosdam e Judæis hæc verba eo accipere, quod mundus in antiquum

IPSI DAVID) Non est in Hebræo: sed cujuscunque est hic Psalmus, est Poetæ egregii.

QUasi vero vel a Spiritu Sancto agitatus Poeta aliquis non sit egregius, vel in Canone esse pos- sit, quod non sit a Spiritu S. profectum.

Tremellio, Junio, Piscatore & Belgis Interpp. Cal- vinus merito deseritur. Verba utique Davidis clara sunt; Non enim ait, qui facit ventos angelos suos, & ignem flammantem ministros suos, sed inversa ra- tione; qui facit angelos suos spiritus & ministros suos ignem flammantem: Nec consentaneum est, ventos & ignem ceu meteora componi cum angelis, spiriti- bus & ministris coram Deo stantibus, ac Piscatoris ipsius judicio ineptus sermo est ignem flammantem non ministrum, sed in plurali ministros Domini dici. Cæterum ne opus quidem videtur nonnullis ellipsi particulæ similitudinis, & proprie accipienda esse verba priora, cum nulla necessitas aliud cogat, qui facit angelos suos spiritus; utpote qui spiritualis es- sentiæ sunt Ebr. 1, 7. 14. & in posteriori membro, ignem flammantem de natura angelorum subtilissima & purissima itidem explicari posse, unde Seraphim nonnulli vocati q. d. ignes ardentes; Facit ministros suos tales, ut natura illorum sit quidam ignis flammans. Sed hæc in medio relinquimus. Vid. Dn. D. Se- bast. Schmied. in Colleg. Bibl. prior. ad hunc loc. pag. 195.

## 104:3
Verse 3.

EXTENDING THE HEAVEN LIKE A CURTAIN) ὡς δέρριν in the Greek here: nor does the writer of the Dialogus Philopatris, which is added to the works of Lucian, cite it otherwise; although he seems to be older, and written in the times of Trajan. Moreover, יריעה is a part of a tent, which used to be made from skins. Hence the Greeks said δέρριν. Such parts used to be supported by ropes. Thus also God supports the Heaven in mysterious ways. See Gen. 1:6 and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

EXTENDENS COELUM SICVT PELLEM) ὡς δέρριν in Græco hic: nec aliter citat scriptor Dialogi Philopatridis, qui additur Luciani operibus: quanquam antiquior videtur esse, & scriptus temporibus Trajani. Est autem יריעה pars tentorii, quod ex pellibus fieri solebat. Hinc δέρριν di- xere Græci. Tales partes funibus sustineri solebant. Sic & Cœlum Deus sustinet arcanis modis. Vide Gen. 1, 6. & ibi dicta.

## 104:4
Verse 4.

WHO MAKES YOUR ANGELS SPIRITS, AND YOUR MINISTERS A BURNING FIRE) For there are some angels of the air, others of fire, who, both good and evil, are called Seraphim. That angels have bodies, but most subtle ones, not only the school of Pythagoras and Plato felt, but also the ancient Jews and the ancient Christians. Aristotle is the maker of intelligences separated from all matter, whom many follow too much προστάς in theological matters.

Those tenets of the Pythagoreans and Platonists, or even of the Jews, are to be corrected by Scripture, not opposed to Scripture. Add also those of the ancient Christians: to some of whom Pythagorean and Platonic opinions had clung. For not only did Aristotle recognize from the light of nature that angels are incorporeal and immaterial as to their essence: but Holy Scripture also testifies clearly about this, while it teaches that angels are πνεύματα, spirits (Heb. 1:14), and it is reported that entire legions of angels have sometimes been in one subject: which could not happen if they were corporeal and material substances. And what is to be thought about the human soul? For if angels are bodies, it will also be necessary for the soul to be a body, or corporeal; which certainly cannot be constituted simpler and more secret from all matter than angels. Will man therefore consist of a soul or a more subtle body, and of an organic body, or a coarser body? Furthermore, what commerce have angels with air and fire, which are elements of natural bodies? Finally, if some angels are airy and others fiery, as Grotius trifles, will not angels differ in species? But these inventions are more fully refuted in the System of Theology. That evil angels are called Seraphim cannot be proven from Scripture. Some observe that Seraphim signifies 'burning with charity,' but the name Cherubim 'full of knowledge.' Because, therefore, the devil lost charity by sinning, and yet retained knowledge, he is indeed called Cherub (Ezek. 28:14), but not Seraph. It is certain that angels are compared to winds and fire because of their speed, agility, and lucid nature; but to construct an airy or fiery essence from that is no more permitted than when Cherubim are said to have a bovine essence, or similar, by which Cherubim are figured; metaphorical expressions are very poorly confused with proper ones. Moreover, Grotius approaches the error of the Sadducees, who even denied spirits (Acts 23). He follows those among the ancient Hebrews, but who were held by others as heretics: not, however, those who followed Holy Scripture. For the Jews themselves, Maimonides and others with the Chaldean interpreters, understand the כ of similitude, 'who makes his angels like the winds, his ministers like a flaming fire,' concerning which let Hackspanius be compared on this passage. Which things hold more correctly than the explanations of other Jews, R. Solomon, Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, and those who follow them, Calvin, Diodati, and the Genevans, as if the discourse were about winds, which God uses as messengers, even though Calvin himself acknowledges that the Greek and Latin interpreters explain it concerning angels, from whom, therefore, one departs rashly, and without regard for the Apostolic interpretation. Whence by the Socinians and others of his

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QVI FACIES ANGELOS TVOS SPIRITVS, ET MINISTROS TVOS IGNEM VRENTEM) Sunt enim Angelorum alii aërei, alii ignei, qui tam boni quam mali, di- cuntur Seraphim. Esse Angelis corpora, sed subtilissima, non Pythagoræ tantum & Platonis Schola sensit, sed & Ju- dæi veteres, & veteres Christiani. Intelligentiarum ab omni materia secretarum faber est Aristoteles, quem nimis προσ- τᾶς in rebus Theologicis multi sequuntur.

Placita illa Pythagoricorum & Platonicorum, vel etiam Judæorum e Scriptura corrigenda, non Scripturæ opponenda. Adde & Christianorum veterum: e quibus nonnullis Pythagoricæ & Plato- nicæ opiniones hæserant. Non enim Aristoteles solum e naturæ lumine agnovit, Angelos incorporeos esse, & immateriales, quantum ad essentiam: Sed testatur etiam de eo Scriptura S. luculenter, dum Angelos πνεύματα, Spiritus esse docet, Ebr. 1, 14. ac legiones integras Angelorum in uno subjecto quandoque fuisse perhibetur: quod fieri non pos- set, si corporeæ & materiales essent substantiæ. Et quid de anima humana sentiendum erit? Si enim Angeli corpora sunt, animam etiam oportebit cor- pus esse, aut corpoream; quæ certe non simplicior & magis secreta ab omni materia constitui potest, quam Angeli. Num ergo homo constabit ex ani- ma seu corpore subtiliori, & ex corpore organico, seu corpore crassiori? Porro quid commercii Angelis cum aëre, & cum igne, quæ elementa corporum na- turalium sunt? Denique si Angeli alii aërei, alii ignei sunt, uti nugatur Grotius, annon specie different Angeli? Sed ista commenta in Systemate Theolo- giæ plenius profligantur. Seraphim angelos malos dici e Scriptura probari nequit. Observant non- nulli Seraphin significare ardentem charitate, no- men vero Cherubim plenum scientia. Quia ergo diabolus peccando perdidit caritatem, & tamen re- tinuit scientiam, ideo vocari quidem Cherub, Ezech. 28, 14. non autem Seraph. Ventis, & igni, compa- rari Angelos ob celeritatem, agilitatem, ac lucidam naturam certum est; at essentiam aëream, vel igneam inde extruere non magis licet, quam cum Cheru- bim dicuntur essentiam bovinam habere, aut similem, qua Cherubim figurantur, Metaphoricæ loquutio- nes pessime cum propriis confunduntur. Acce- dit autem Grotius ad errorem Saducæorum, qui etiam Spiritus negarunt Actor. 22. Illos e veteri- bus Ebræis sequitur, sed qui ab aliis pro hæreticis habiti sunt: non vero eos, qui Scripturam S. sequu- ti sunt. Subaudiunt enim ipsi Judæi, Maimonides & alii cum Chaldæo Interpp. כ similitudinis, qui faciat angelos similes ventis, ministros suos sicut ignem flagrantem, de quo conferatur Hackspanius ad hunc locum. Quæ rectius se habent, quam aliorum Judæorum, R. Salom. Aben - Ezræ, Kimchi, & qui hos sequuntur, Calvini, Diodati, & Geneven- sium explicationes, quasi de ventis sermo sit, quibus Deus utatur tanquam nunciis, utur Calvinus ipse agnoscat Interpp. Græcos & Latinos de Angelis exponere, a quibus proinde temere, fusque deque habita etiam interpretatione Aposto- lica, disceditur. Unde a sociennis aliis suis

## 104:15
Verse 15.

AND WINE MAY GLADDEN THE HEART OF MAN: TO MAKE THE FACE SHINE WITH OIL) These are great gifts, the cultivators of which the Greeks referred to the gods. Pliny 14:22: 'There are two liquids most pleasing to human bodies, wine internally, oil externally, both the most excellent of the kind of trees, but oil is necessary.' Compare those things which are in Judg. 9:8, 9, 12, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ET VINVM LÆTIFICET COR HOMINIS : VT EXHILARET FACIEM IN OLEO) Magna hæc dona, quorum excultores Græci in deos retulere. Plinius 14, 22. Duo sunt liquores corporibus humanis gratissimi, intus vini, fo- ris olei, arborum e genere ambo præcipui, sed olei necessarius. Confer ea, quæ sunt Jud. 9, 8. 9. 12. 13.

## 104:26
Verse 26.

THIS DRAGON] Leviathan. Concerning whom see Job.
