Vers. 26.

DRACO ISTE] Leviathan. De quo Jobum vide.

## 104:29
Verse 29.

YOU WILL TAKE AWAY THEIR SPIRIT) Thus the Greeks. But in the Hebrew it is: My spirit. All life is from God, Heb. 12, 9. When He takes it away, He is said to receive it back to Himself, Eccles. 12, 7. Job 34, 14.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

AVFERES SPIRITVM EORVM) Sic Græci. At in Hebræo est: Spiritum meum. Omnis vita a Deo, Hebr. 12, 9. eam ubi adimit, dicitur eam ad se recipere Eccles. 12, 7. Job. 34, 14.

## 104:30
Verse 30.

YOU WILL SEND FORTH YOUR SPIRIT, AND THEY SHALL BE CREATED) That is, they shall be born. A similar manner of speaking, as that which preceded, and from the part the cause. In a more sublime sense, the Hebrews also refer this to the resurrection.

Some of the Ancients explain this not of life or a created Spirit, but of the Holy Spirit, the creator and author of life. Because here it is called the Spirit of God. But life or a created spirit would scarcely be called absolutely the Spirit of God: But by that appellation, the Holy Spirit is ordinarily and perpetually designated. Which we have shown elsewhere by an induction of passages. Then indeed, by sending forth His Spirit, God is said to create, because creation is a work ad extra: just as by the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord the hosts of the heavens are said to have been made, Ps. 33, 6, and by the breath of the Almighty we are enlivened, Job 33, 4; conversely, when He takes away His Spirit, it is necessary that we perish: because by the Spirit of God they are created, by the Spirit of God they are sustained and preserved. See our blessed Gerhard's Exegesis, Vol. I, loc. cit., page 1963.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

EMITTES SPIRITVM TVVM, ET CREABVNTVR) Id est, nascentur. Par loquendi genus, ut id quod præcessit, & ex parti causa. Sublimiori sensu ad resurrectionem hoc referunt etiam Hebræi.

Non de vita aut Spiritu creato, sed de Spiritu Sancto vitæ creatore & autore, Veteres nonnulli ex- plicant. Quia vocatur hic Spiritus Dei. At vita aut creatus Spiritus, vix absolute Dei Spiritus voca- bitur: Sed appellatione illa, ordinarie & perpetuo Spiritus S. designatur. Quod ex inductione loco- rum alibi ostendimus. Tum vero emittendo Spiri- tum suum creare dicitur Deus, quia creatio est opus ad extra: uti Spiritu oris Domini exercitus cælorum facti dicuntur Pf. 33, 6. & per Spiraculum omnipoten- tiæ nos vivificamur Job. 33, 4. vicissim cum aufert Spi- ritum suum, interire nos oportet: quia Spiritu Dei creantur, Spiritu Dei sustentantur, & conservan- tur. Vid. B. Gerhardi nostri Exeges. Tom. I. LL. CC. pag. 1963.

## 104:30 Addition
On Psalm 104, v. 30, toward the end.

We add what the blessed Hülsemann handed down concerning this saying: Athanasius, he says, in his Epistle to Serapion and others disputing about the divinity of the Holy Spirit, Irenaeus book V, ch. 33, Jerome in Questions on Genesis, question 3, Ambrose in Hexaemeron, and others whom you may see in great number in Lorinus, use this saying here to prove the Deity of the Holy Spirit, for which our Gesner rightly judges it to be brought forward. See also Gerhard in Exegesis, p. 1063. Conversely, Calvin, Musculus, Moller, Coppen, Amama, and among the Papists, Jansenius himself, explain it concerning the vigor or the very soul of created things. But the Belgians judge that it should be explained solely concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, alleging the parallels Job 33:4, Psalm 33:6. Which opinion is true. For that not the soul or vigor of created things itself, but something opposed to this is understood, is clear from the relative opposites of this and the preceding verse: you will take away their spirit, and you will send forth your spirit: Therefore the spirit of God and of creatures is not the same. Then it is clear from the immediately consequent effects of this Spirit in v. 31, that they do not pertain to created spirits or souls. And finally, the sum of the whole Psalm is to demonstrate the magnificence of the Creator from the variety of created things, which is clear from the proposition in verses 1 and 2. See the corruptions of the Photinians in Volkel and Crellius on God and the attributes of God, book 1, ch. 23 and 31. However, it is no obstacle that some, both of the Fathers and also of our own, explain the renewal of the face of the earth as the restoration to come on the last day: for the same efficient cause remains, namely, the Holy Spirit. But that the natural life of man, to be inspired again when bodies are raised, is called the Spirit of God here, which Jansenius and others cited before wish, is most false. For the whole argument deals with the creation, origin, and destruction of species according to their individuals. But it is by no means about an imaginary restoration of the world at the last judgment, or about the glorification of the elect alone.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 104. v. 30. sub finem.

Addimus quæ de hoc dicto tradidit B. Hülsemannus: Athanasius, inquit, in Epistola ad Serapionem aliique de divinitate Spiritus S. disputantes Irenæus l. V. c. 33. Hieron. quæst. in Genes. quæst. 3. Ambrosius in Hexaemer. aliique quos longo numero vide apud Lorinum hic utuntur hoc dicto ad probandam Deitatem Spiritus S. pro qua recte afferri censet noster Gesnerus. Vide etiam Gerhard. in Exeg. p. 1063. Contra Calvinus, Musculus, Mollerus, Coppen. Amama, atque ex Papistis ipse Jansenius de vigore seu ipsa anima rerum creatarum, explicant. Sed Belgæ unice de Spiritus S. persona exponendum censent, allegantes parallelos Job. 33, 4. Psalm. 33, 6. Quæ sententia vera est. Namque non ipsam animam seu vigorem rerum creatarum, sed aliquid huic oppositum intelligi patet ex oppositis relativis, hujus & antecedentis versus: auferes spiritum eorum, & emittes spiritum tuum: Ergo non est idem Dei & creaturarum spiritus. Deinde patet ex immediate consequentibus effectis hujus Spiritus v. 31. eos non competere spiritibus seu animabus creatis. Et denique totius Psalmi summa est, ex varietate rerum creatarum magnificentiam creatoris demonstrare, quod patet ex propositione vers. 1. & 2. Photinianorum corruptelas vide apud Volkel. & Crellium de Deo & attributis Dei l. 1. c. 23. & 31. Non obstat autem quod quidam tum Patrum tum etiam nostratium renovationem faciei terræ de restauratione in die novissimo futura exponunt: manet enim eadem causa efficiens, Sanctus videl. Spiritus. Vitam autem naturalem hominis suscitatis corporibus denuo tunc inspirandam vocari hic Spiritum Dei, quod Jansenius, aliique antea citati volunt, falsissimum est. Totum enim argumentum de creatione, ortu & interitu specierum secundum individua sua agit. Nequaquam vero sive de imaginaria mundi restauratione in novissimo judicio, sive de solorum electorum glorificatione.

## 105:1 Argument
PSALM 105. Hallelujah on account of the benefits shown to Israel.

Latin:

PSALMUS CV. Halleluja ob beneficia Israeli exhibita.

## 105:4
Verse 4.

SEEK THE LORD AND BE STRENGTHENED. In the Hebrew it is: And His strength. Bellarmine says the LXX Interpreters, whom the Latin followed, read עוז whereas in the Hebrew it is עזו, but the Masora teaches that this reading is erroneous and that this one is genuine, with the letter ו added, testifying that in four places this noun occurs with the prefix Vav and the suffix. If, however, the passage ought to be taken not nominally, but verbally, that observation would fail. Jerome himself reads it nominally, and rendered it, and His strength.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QUÆRITE DOMINUM ET CONFIR- MAMINI. In Ebræo est: Et virtutem ejus. Bellarmin. di- cit LXX. Interpretes, quos sequutus est Latinus, le- gisse עוז quam in Ebræo sit עזו, sed erroneam il- lam lectionem, hanc genuinam esse Masora docet, adscripta litera ו testata quatuor in locis nomen hoc cum præfixo Vav & suffixo occurrere. Si au- tem locus accipi deberet, non nominaliter, sed ver- baliter falleret illa observatio. Hieronymus ipse nominaliter legit, & reddidit, & virtutem ejus.

## 105:24 Addition
On Psalm 105, Verse 24. HE TURNED THEIR HEART TO HATE HIS PEOPLE.

Bellarmine on this passage: "God is said to have turned the heart of the Egyptians into hatred and the ruin of the Hebrews; not by infusing an evil will into their hearts (for God is not the cause of sin), but by doing good to His people, and by granting them unusual fertility, He in a way provided an occasion for the perverse hearts of the Egyptians to envy the happiness of others, and from that to desire to oppress them; but God did good to His people, foreknowing that envy and hatred would arise in the Egyptians from that occasion, because He could, and wished to, make good use of their evil will, which He Himself had not made, to punish the sins of the Egyptians and to liberate His people from captivity." Thus St. Augustine explains it. Cocceius himself here praises the opinion of Prosper: "God did not deprave the heart of the Egyptians from the right, but, since they were spontaneously evil, and such that they could envy the happy, He turned them into hatred of the Hebrews by His beneficence, by which He was multiplying His people; but by doing good to His own, He incited the Egyptians to their enmities, not by making them evil themselves, but by bestowing on His own goods which would burn the evil." Cocceius indeed adds: "but yet there is something more here." For if there were nothing but an occasion, he would have said, having explained the benefit causing envy, "and their heart was turned." But what is more here? "He changes," says Cocceius, "the heart by justly taking away the gift of good pleasure and love for His own." But he does not stop at these. For he adds that God elicits the depravity of a corrupt man through internal and external occasions, and adds strength of mind in evil to him who is inclined toward evil things. These are his words, who nevertheless does not wish to appear to establish God as the cause of sin! But the word הפך does not always, as the blessed Hülsemann notes, signify a direct influence, persuasion, or positive command, but more often an occasional or accidental conversion, or overturning; sometimes even involuntary, as above in Ps. 78:9, seq. In this place, however, it is clear from the preceding verse 24 that God is said to have turned the heart of the Egyptians to hatred occasionally, namely by blessing the Israelites and strengthening them, which words are uttered in Hiphil, but this in Kal: it can be explained neutrally concerning the heart perverting itself, as the words of the third person are accustomed to be, see Glass, book III, Grammar, tract. 3, can. 23, if nevertheless we explain it according to Luther's version concerning God, occasionally and objectively, God perverts, or turns, the hearts of the Egyptians to hatred, by the scandal received by them from the beneficence; how Alvarez, among the Papists, explains it better in disp. 24, treating this place concerning aids, than Bellarmine, book IV, on the loss of grace, ch. 13, explaining the same concerning the positive inclination of the heart from a greater evil to a lesser, e.g., from homicide to theft.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 105. Vers. 24. CONVERTIT COR EORUM UT ODIRENT POPULUM EJUS.

Bellarm. ad h. l. „Deus dicitur convertisse „cor Ægyptiorum in odium, & ruinam Hebræorum; non inferendo in cordibus eorum malam „voluntatem (Deus enim non est causa peccati) „sed benefaciendo populo suo, & fœcunditatem „insolitam illi donando, occasionem quodammodo præbuit perversis cordibus Ægyptiorum, ut „inviderent alienæ felicitati, & inde illos opprime- „re desiderarent, benefecit autem Deus populo „suo, præsciens invidiam & odium in Ægyptiis ea „occasione nascitura, quia poterat, & volebat ma- „la eorum voluntate, quam ipse non fecerat, be- „ne uti ad punienda peccata Ægyptiorum, & ad „populum suum de captivitate liberandum. Sic „exponit S. August. Laudat Coccejus ipse hic Pro- „speri sententiam: Cor Ægyptiorum non Deus de- „pravavit à recto, sed, cum sponte mali essent, & „tales, ut possent invidere felicibus, in odium il- „los Hebræorum convertit beneficentia sua, qua „populum suum multiplicabat; Benefaciendo au- „tem suis Ægyptios ad eorum inimicitias incitavit, „non ipsos malos faciendo, sed istis bona, quæ „malos urerent, largiendo. Addit quidem Cocce- „jus: sed tamen amplius hic quicquam est. Nam „si nihil esset nisi ἀφορμὴ, explicato beneficio „invidiam faciente dixisset, & versum est cor ipso- „rum. Quid vero hic amplius est? Mutat, inquit Coccejus, cor auferendo juste donum εὐδοκίας & amoris suorum. Sed in hisce non sistit. Subji- cit enim, Deum occasionibus internis & externis ho- minis corrupti pravitatem elicere, eique ad prava inclinato animi robur addere in malo. Hæc ille, qui tamen non vult videri Deum statuere causam peccati! Sed verbum הפך non semper, notante B. Hülsemanno, directam influentiam, persuasionem vel mandatum positivum, sed sæpius occasionalem seu accidentalem conversionem, vel eversionem si- gnificat, nonnunquam etiam involuntarium ut su- pra Ps. 78, 9. seq. Hoc loco autem patet ex an- tecedente versu 24. Deum dici convertisse Ægy- ptiorum cor ad odium occasionaliter, benedicendo scil. Israelitis eosque fortificando, quæ verba in Hiphil efferuntur, hoc autem in Kal: potest neu- traliter de corde seipsum pervertente, exponi, ut solent verba tertiæ personæ, vide Glass. l. III. Grammat. tract. 3. can. 23. si tamen juxta Lutheri versionem de Deo exposuerimus, occasionaliter & objective, Deus pervertit, seu convertit Ægyptio- rum corda ad odium, scandalo ab ipsis ex benefi- centia accepto; quomodo ex Papistis melius ex- ponit Alvarez disp. 24. de auxiliis tractans hunc locum, quam Bellarm. l. IV. de amiss. grat. c. 13. idem exponens de positiva inclinatione cordis a malo majori ad minus, v. g. ab homicidio ad furtum.

## 105:25
Verse 25.

HE TURNED THEIR HEART, THAT THEY MIGHT HATE HIS PEOPLE] That is, he turned the heart of the Egyptians into hatred of his people. God did this, however, by multiplying his people. Just as the minds of men are, so do the works of God make them better or worse: As mud hardens here and as wax melts here by one and the same fire.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

CONVERTIT COR EORUM, UT ODIRENT PO- PULUM EJUS] Id est, vertit cor Ægyptiorum in odium populi sui. Fecit autem hoc Deus, multiplicando populum suum. Prout sunt animi hominum, ita Dei opera eos me- liores vel pejores faciunt: Limus ut hic durescit & hac ut cera liquescit Vno eodemque igni.

## 105:28 Addition
Ver. 28. AND HE DID NOT EXACERBATE HIS WORDS.

Bellarmine says that in the Hebrew it is held thus: and they did not exacerbate his words, or as Jerome translates, and they were not incredulous to his words, that is, Moses and Aaron boldly fulfilled the commands of the Lord. In the Greek, however, it is held ὅτι παρεπίκραναν τὰς λόγυς ἀυτẽ, namely the Egyptians, of whom that must be understood entirely. For what need was there to indicate that Moses and Aaron, those faithful servants of God, had not rebelled against God? Although indeed a negation is added in the Hebrew, the sense nevertheless comes back to the same thing if the interrogative ה is understood, which is accustomed to be done elsewhere, i.e., and (did) they not rebel (further) against his word? See B. Glass. Gram. S. p. 606.

Latin:

Vers. 28. ET NON EXACERBAVIT SER- MONES SUOS.

Bellarm. in Ebræo, inquit, sic habetur: & non exacerbaverunt sermones ejus, vel ut Hiero- nymus vertit, & non fuerunt increduli verbis ejus, id est, Moses & Aaron audacter impleverunt man- data Domini. In Græco vero habetur ὅτι παρε- πίκραναν τὰς λόγυς ἀυτẽ, Ægyptii scil. de quibus omnino id intelligendum. Quid enim opus erat indicare Mosen & Aaronem fideles illos Dei servos non rebellasse Deo? Quanquam vero negatio in Ebræo addita sit, sensus tamen eodem recidit, si ה interrogativum subintelligatur, quod alias fieri so- let, h. m. & (an) non rebellarunt (porro) contra ver- bum ejus. Vid. B. Glass. Gram. S. p. 606.

## 106:1 Argument
PSALM 106. Hallelujah continued with the desire of the Messianic congregation.

Latin:

PSALMUS CVI. Hallelujah continuatum cum desiderio congre- gationis Messianæ.

## 106:20
Verse 20.

THEY CHANGED THEIR GLORY INTO THE SIMILITUDE OF AN OX THAT EATETH GRASS] Τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν. And thus it is now in the Hebrew כבודם. But the ancient Hebrews testify that it was once כבודו, his glory. Furthermore, it was changed because in later centuries כבוד began to signify something conspicuous, referring to the majesty of God: lest, forsooth, that word should become cheapened by this comparison.

No ancient codex can be brought forward in which כבודו, his glory, is read. Nor did the Chaldeans, or the Greeks, or Jerome, or the author of the Vulgate version read it so. If words in Scripture were changed because of other meanings that prevailed in later times, what certainty would it have? But Grotius's conjecture is so frivolous that it does not deserve to be refuted.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

MUTARUNT GLORIAM SUAM IN SIMILITUDI- NEM VITULI COMEDENTIS FOENUM] Τὴν δόξαν αὐτῶν. Et sic nunc in Hebræo est כבודם. At testan- tur Hebræi veteres olim fuisse כבודו, gloriam ejus. Cæte- rum mutatum id est, quia posterioribus seculis כבוד cœ- pit significare conspicuum quid, Dei majestatem referens: ne scilicet ea vox hac comparatione vilesceret.

Nullus Codex vetustus adferri potest, in quo כבודו gloriam ejus legatur. Nec ita vel Chaldæi, vel Græci, vel Hieronymus, vel Autor vul- gatæ versionis legerunt. Si ob alias significationes, quæ posterioribus temporibus obtinuere, immuta- tæ voces in Scriptura, quæ ejus certitudo erit? Sed ita frivola est Grotii conjectura, ut refutari non me- reatur.

## 106:20 Addition
To Psalm 106, v. 20, towards the end.

Moreover, from this word of change it cannot be inferred that Aaron's idolatry did not have the true God as its object, but that he changed the object of adoration, so that they did not intend to adore Jehovah through a likeness as it were, but instead of Jehovah they adored the calf, which Gregor. de Valent. opusc. de Idolol. contr. Heerbr. Hartus in the conference with Reinold, fol. 105. Bellarmine, Genebrard, Lorinus, Estius contend; for who would believe that Aaron and the Israelites were so brutish that, stripped of all knowledge of the true God, they believed this golden calf, which they themselves had formed, to be the eternal and infinite Being? And therefore Augustine, quest. 146 in Exod., book XIX of the City of God, ch. 11, Bernard, sermon 32 on the Song of Songs, Sanchez on Acts VII, 4, [argue that] they only held that calf as a likeness of the true God, by means of which they wished to worship God, just as Papists say they worship the true God through images. Nor indeed does every change signify the abolition of a prior object or the negation of another, but change is also made through alteration, mental change, through addition or subtraction, whether real or mental.

Latin:

Ad Psalm. 106. v. 20. sub finem.

Cæterum ex hac mutationis voce inferri non potest, Aaronis idololatriam non habuisse pro ob- jecto verum Deum, sed commutasse objectum adorationis, ita ut non per similitudinem veluti inten- derent adorare Jehovam, sed loco Jehovæ adora- rint vitulum, quod Gregor. de Valent. opusc. de Idolol. contr. Heerbr. Hartus in coll. cum Reinol- do fol, 105. Bellarm. Genebrard. Lorin. Estius con- tendunt; nam quis credat, tam brutos fuisse Aaronem & Israelitas, ut omni notitia veri Dei exuta, crediderint hunc aureum vitulum, quem ipsi formarant, esse Ens æternum & infinitum? ideoque August. quæst. 146. in Exod. l. XIX. de Civ. Dei c. 11. Bernhard. serm. 32. in Cantic. Sanchez. in Actor. VII, 4. eos tantum illum vitu- lum habuisse pro simulachro veri Dei, quo median- te Deum colere voluerint, uti Papistæ se per imagines verum Deum colere dicunt. Nec ve- ro omnis mutatio significat abolitionem prioris objecti aut alterius negationem, sed mutatio fit etiam per alterationem, mentalem mutationem, per additionem vel detractionem sive realem sive mentalem.

## 106:31
Verse 31. AND IT WAS COUNTED UNTO HIM FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS UNTO GENERATION AND GENERATION.

From this the Papists conclude that works of faith are useful for justification, Genebrardus at this place and others. But this is not about justification. For Phinehas had already been justified before; furthermore, the discourse is about righteousness, which extends unto generation and generation. Justification, however, does not pass to children. The just shall live by his faith, Hab. 2:4. Therefore, one must distinguish between the righteousness of the person and of the deed; the former is referred to in Gen. 15:6, and is attributed to faith alone. The latter is of the present passage, as Bellarmine himself admits, who renders this meaning: by God, who searches the hearts, and who well knows the inner intention of Phinehas, this deed was counted, not as an unjust slaughter, but as a just punishment, which deserves not punishment, but praise and reward.

End of Book IV of the Psalms.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ET REPUTATUM EST EI IN JU- STITIAM IN GENERATIONEM ET GENE- RATIONEM.

Concludunt hinc Pontificii opera fidei utilia esse ad justificationem, Genebrardus h. l. & alii. Sed hic non agitur de justificatione. Jam antea enim justificatus erat Phinehas: adhæc de justitia, quæ in generationem se porrigit, sermo est, Justificatio au- tem non transit in liberos. Justus sua fide vivet Hab. 2, 4. Ideo distinguendum inter justitiam per- sonæ & facti; illa Gen. 15, 6. respicitur, ac fidei soli tribuitur. Hac præsentis est loci, fatente ipfomet Bellarm. qui hanc reddit sententiam: a Deo, qui scrutatur corda, & qui probe novit intimam inten- tionem Phinees, reputatum est hoc factum, non in- juxta cædes, sed justa punitio, quæ non pœnam me- retur, sed laudem & præmium.

Finis Libri IV. Psalmorum.

## 106:33 Addition
On Psalm 106:33. AND HE SPOKE UNADVISEDLY WITH HIS LIPS.

Some wish it to be indicated that Moses did not command the rock absolutely, but hesitated in dividing his words, and they note that Augustine, Theodoret, and Euthymius understood it thus, Bellarmine notes. He himself, however, as also Jansen, following R. Solomon, refers it to God, and he spoke unadvisedly with his lips, that is, God openly pronounced and rebuked the Hebrews because they had not exterminated the nations. But because a continuation of the sins of the Israelites is made here, the former explanation is more correct, which is also that of Hilary and Hesychius, and the Hebrew word is rendered properly by others, and he blurted out or pronounced with his lips, or as Tremellius, and he pronounced with his lips, namely, his exasperation. See Num. 20:11. The word בטא denotes an inconsiderate or rash opening of the mouth: Campensis rendered it, and he wavered somewhat with his lips. The version of B. Luther, Cocceius, etc., agrees with these.

ONLY!

IM T HAT

ver. 16.

BECAUSE HE HAS BROKEN THE BRONZE GATES. Although indeed the same Bellarmine subjects this liberation, and the other benefits proclaimed in this Psalm, to a mystical sense, as he calls it, of liberation from spiritual miseries (which is repugnant to the unity of the sense of Scripture), he nevertheless made no mention here of the descent of Christ into hell.

vers. 16.

Ver. 25.

## 108:1 Argument
PSALM 108. The desire for the expansion of the kingdom of Christ.

THE SAME subject matter as Psalm 60. The same words also from that place: that your beloved may be delivered. The introduction only has been changed, and taken from Psalm 57:8. Changed, as I believe, and the measures.

The present Psalm exhibits the Davidic desire for the advent of the Messiah: therefore it is not to be considered a ταυτολογίᾳ and vain repetition, that what was contained in Psalms 57 and 60 recurs here. For he wished to testify by that repetition how ardently he desired his Lord: whom he thus confesses and calls in Ps. 110:1. For he wishes here that the time may arrive when it is permitted to give thanks to God among the peoples and nations, and to celebrate his name in that great assembly v. 4. Cf. Ps. 22:23, 28, 32. He proclaims the grace and truth of God extending itself, by which heaven is opened, (which was made to us in Christ Jesus John 1:17, and announced to all under heaven in the New Testament Col. 1:23) he excites the Lord, and vows, Be exalted, O God, above the heavens, and let your glory be (or shall be) over ALL THE EARTH, which was fulfilled when Christ the Lord, God blessed forever, according to the flesh was exalted above all the heavens: for then his glory filled the whole earth; Cf. Isa. 6:3, John 12:41, Eph. 4:10, Phil. 2:11. Nor can anyone doubt that these things pertain to the times of the New Testament. And by that very thing his beloved are delivered, when, the work of redemption having been accomplished, he himself converts them from darkness to light, from the power of Satan to God Acts 26:18, Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:13, 14. Which was the highest vow and desire of David 2 Sam. 23:5, Ps. 14:7. Therefore, when he has prayed these things, as if heard by the Lord, in the spirit he is certain of the coming of the Lord and exults, no otherwise than if he already heard him present, God, he exclaims, speaks in his sanctuary, therefore I rejoice, and exults concerning the Lord, who was to be manifested in the flesh, and was to come into the tabernacle of the flesh 1 Tim. 3:16, Heb. 9:11, John 2:21. For he longed to hear him with other holy Kings and Prophets Luke 10:24. he rejoices greatly, as if he were hearing the same one now present in the days of his flesh speaking, and preaching the words of eternal life at close range: A certain symbol of whose presence and manifestation was held in

Sanctuary, when oracles were being delivered. Therefore, with joy concerning the distribution and possession of his lands, in which was prefigured the inheritance of the whole earth of his son the Messiah, as the successor to his throne and a far more eminent heir, 2 Sam. 7:14, Isa. 9:7, Luke 1:32, he concludes: I will rejoice, and I will divide Shechem, and I will measure out the valley of Succoth. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head, Judah is my lawgiver, Moab is my washpot, over Edom will I cast out my shoe, etc., concerning which see Ps. 60:6 ff. Among our own countrymen, Pomeranus and Selneccerus acknowledge that the former part of the Psalm pertains to Christ; in the latter, they teach that David is to be considered as a type of Christ. Nor does the argument of Ps. 57, from which these earlier parts of the Psalm are repeated, stand in the way: because there David prays that he may be saved from Saul v. 1, since, being certain of deliverance, he rouses himself to thanksgiving, and, carried away by the sublimity of the spirit, he desires and seeks in addition the happiness of the time of the New Testament, the exaltation of the Messiah, and the divine glory to be celebrated throughout the whole world v. 6, 8, et seqq. If the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, what indeed did he cherish more in his heart than the Messiah promised to him, the man confirmed concerning the Messiah of the God of Jacob?

Latin:

PSALMUS CVIII. Desiderium ampliationis regni Christi.

EADEM materia, quae Psalmi 60. Eadem quoque verba ab illo loco: ut liberentur dilecti tui. Anteloquium dun- taxat mutatum est, sumtumque ex Psalmo 57,8. mutati, ut cre- do, & moduli.

Psalmus praesens exhibet desiderium Davidicum adventus Messiae: ideo non pro ταυτολογίᾳ & inani repetitione habendum, quod quae Psal. 57. & 60. habebantur, hic recurrant. Testari enim vo- luit ea repetitione, quam flagranter desiderarit Do- minum suum: quem ita confitetur & vocat Ps. 110, 1. Optat enim hic, ut adveniat tempus, quo Deo inter populos & gentes gratias agere, ejusque nomen ce- lebrare in magna illa panegyri liceat v. 4. Conf. Ps. 22, 23. 28. 32. Psal. 42. depraedicat gratiam & ve- ritatem Dei sese porrigentem, qua patet coelum, (quae in Christo Jesu nobis facta Job. 1, 17. & omni- bus sub coelo in Novo Testamento annunciata est Coloss. 1, 23.) excitat Dominum, ac vovet, Exaltare Deus super caelos, & super OMNEM TERRAM glo- ria tua (sit, vel erit) quod impletum, cum Christus Dominus Deus benedictus in secula, secundum car- nem exaltatus super omnes coelos fuit: tum enim gloria ejus plena fuit universa terra; Conf. Esa. 6, 3. Job. 12, 41. Ephes. 4, 10. Phil. 2, 11. Neque dubita- re quisquam potest, haec ad tempora Novi Testam. pertinere. Atque eo ipso liberantur dilecti ejus, cum opere redemtionis peracto ipse eos convertit a tenebris ad lucem, a potestate Satanae ad Deum Act. 26,18. Eph. 1, 7. Col. 1, 13. 14. Quod fuit summum votum ac desiderium Davidis 2. Sam. 23, 5. Ps. 14, 7. Ideo quum haec precatus, velut a Domino exaudi- tus in spiritu certus de adventu Domini exultat, non secus ac si jam praesentem audiret, Deus, exclamat, loquitur in sanctuario suo, idcirco laetor, & exultat de Domino, qui in carne manifestandus erat, & in carnis tabernaculum venturus 1. Timoth. 3, 16. Ebr. 9, 11. Joh. 2, 21. Nam audire gestiit cum aliis S. Regibus & Prophetis Luc. 10, 24. oppido gaudet, quasi eundem jam praesentem in diebus carnis suae loquentem, & verba vitae aeternae praedican- tem cominus audiret: Cujus praesentiae & mani- festationis symbolum quoddam habebatur in

Sanctuario, cum oracula redderentur. Ideo cum gaudio de distributione, & possessione terrarum suarum, in qua præfigurata fuit hæreditas universæ terræ filii sui Meffiæ, ceu throni sui successoris & hæredis longe eminentioris, 2. Sam. 7, 14. Esa. 9, 7. Luc. 1, 32. perorat: lætabor, & partibor Sichimam, & convallem tabernaculorum metibor. Meus est Galaad, & meus est Manasses, & Ephraim fortitudo capitis mei, Juda rex meus, Moab olla spei meæ, in Idumæam extendam calceamentum meum &c. de quibus vid. Pf. 60, 6. seqq. Ad Christum priorem partem Psalmi pertinere e nostratibus Pomeranus, Selneccerus agnoscunt; in posteriori Davidem ut typum Christi considerandum esse, docent. Neque officit Pf. 57. argumentum, ex quo priora hæc Psalmi repetita sunt: quod illic David precetur, ut a Saulo servetur v. 1. quia certus de liberatione excitat sese ad gratiarum actionem, ac spiritus sublimitate provectus altius concupiscit, atque expetit insuper felicitatem temporis Novi Testamenti, exaltationis Messiæ & gloriæ divinæ per totum orbem celebrandæ v. 6. 8. seqq. Si ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, quid vero magis in corde fovebat, quam Messiam sibi promissum, vir confirmatus de Messia Dei Jacob?

## 109:1 Argument
PSALM 109. Curses of Judas and his accomplices.

We may call this poem curses, or, as Virgil does, imprecations: it has much of the spirit of the Law. In the Gospel and the Apostles there is nothing of the sort: indeed, for that passage ἀποδώη αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος in 2 Tim. 4:14, manuscripts of the highest antiquity and authority have ἀποδώσει. Nevertheless, the Church has employed these expressions in the depositions of Bishops, in a sense that is forbidden, and in order to strike a salutary horror into the sinners themselves: and it has called this Psalm the Iscariotic Psalm, because it was written, as is credible, against Ahithophel, who had much in common with Judas Iscariot, to whom therefore the Apostles applied the words which are set down here in verse 8, Acts 1:20.

Latin:

PSALMUS CIX. Maledictiones Judæ & complicum.

HOc carmen possumus appellare ἀρὰς, sive, ut Virgilius, diras: multum habet hoc de Spiritu legis. In Evangelio & Apostolis nihil tale: quin & pro illo ἀποδώη αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος 2. Timoth. 4, 14. summæ vetustatis & auctoritatis manuscripti habent ἀποδώσει. Usurpavit nihilominus & has voces Ecclesia in depositionibus Episcoporum, sensu ἀπηγορευμένῳ, & ut peccatoribus horrorem incuteret ipsis salutarem: vocavitque hunc Psalmum Iscarioticum, quod in Achitophelem, ut credibile, scriptus esset, cui multa cum Juda Iscariote communia, cui propterea verba, quæ hîc posita sunt commate 8. aptarunt Apostoli Actor. 1, 20.

## 109:6
verse 6. over him the wicked, and let the devil stand at his right hand (because the discourse is specifically about Judas, who being a guide to the others, when Christ was being dragged away to his passion Acts 1, 16. The Jews also stood as one person in their conspiracies, and are introduced as one person, and it is vowed that they be delivered into the power of wicked men, and of Satan himself) when he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer be turned into sin (Their teaching, life, learning, praying must all be damned, as the marginal gloss of B. Luther has, to which words Christ seems to have looked John 17, 12.) Let his days be few, and his bishopric (which interpretation Grotius approves: פקד among other things signifies to care for, to inspect, hence פקדה which the LXX translated as ἐπισκοπὴν both here and elsewhere. The Latin interpreter retained the Greek word itself, just as Cicero did the word ἐπισκόπη, when he says he was appointed by Pompey as overseer of the maritime coast) let another take; Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow (and indeed such, that there is no one to take care of them: which curses the Holy Spirit testifies were fulfilled in Judas Acts 1, 20. For having been delivered into the power of Satan, he was so agitated by him in his conscience that he ended his life with a noose.) That what follows has been completed in the Jews, the children of Judas, regarding the imitation of impiety and impenitence, the event and experience openly testify: nor can any nation or posterity be designated, in which all those things have been so clearly and adequately fulfilled in the sight and judgment of the whole world. So that one must wonder that Grotius still understands these imprecations as being about Ahithophel (whom he does not indicate he wishes to join to them): that Beza and Tremellius interpret them as being about Doeg and the sons of Saul. The emphasis of the words teaches that they look much further, and pertain to the whole nation and posterity of the Jews, and the event itself proves it. Let his children wander about, and beg: and let them seek (their food) because of their poverty (as Osiander renders it) Let the extortioner draw all his substance to himself, and let strangers plunder his labors; (predators: whatever remains, let it all be snatched away, either by the extortioner through fraud, or by the predator through violence) Let there be no helper for him, nor let there be any to have pity on his orphans. Let his offspring be for destruction (let his posterity perish) in the next generation let his name be blotted out, let the iniquity of his fathers (of each one of them) be in memory before the Lord (Compare Matthew 23, 35.) and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out, let (those sins) be in the sight of the Lord always, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth. Experience likewise proves that these things happened to the Jews, by the force of the imprecation of the Jews themselves Matthew 27, 25. and the prediction of Christ Luke 23, 27. seqq. Matthew 23, 38. 39. Theodoret, regarding those words, in one generation let his name be blotted out, has it thus: For not yet forty years having passed, the people of the Jews underwent extreme slaughter, and they no longer administer a Republic by themselves, nor do they have their own Kings and Princes, nor that most famous metropolis, nor do they perform worship according to the law, but all those things are vain. Certainly no nation can be designated in which all these things are seen or have been fulfilled, as the Jewish nation: they are forced to suffer perpetual exile, they have been stripped of all their faculties by the Romans, and all day long they are drained by the Magistrates who tolerate them, they are hated by all peoples, and no one is moved by their mercy: their posterity is devoted to perpetual destruction, their name is inglorious, and their memory is detestable, and the same iniquity of their fathers is punished, just as they themselves vowed for their children, and the posterity itself, insisting on the impious footsteps of their fathers, deserves it. There are not read in the whole Code such great curses as are vowed here, or rather predicted: nor has a nation ever been found, besides the Jews, which has been subject to such great and such long-lasting curses. The causes indeed of such great curses of the people are rendered by Christ himself (1.) Neglect of mercy and justice v. 16. For the reason that he did not remember to show mercy, and persecuted the afflicted and poor, and thought to deliver to death the one crushed in heart: i.e., I was poor, needy, afflicted in many ways, but they doubled my miseries by pursuing them, wherefore let them also perish without commiseration: as Osiander's paraphrase has it. (2.) Contempt of divine grace v. 17. And he loved, (he voluntarily summoned) cursing (let his blood be upon our children Matthew 27, 25.) and it shall come to him. And he did not want blessing (for whose sake Christ was first sent to them Acts 3, 26. John 1, 11. Acts 13, 46.) and it shall be far from him. And he clothed himself with cursing, as with a garment etc. (3.) Perverse and wicked affection. This will be their reward from the Lord, who oppose me, and speak evil against my soul, they say and do those things by which they may take away my life. Which it is possible to see were fulfilled in Judas and the Jews just as exactly as they were predicted in the Evangelical History. The third part is a prayer for deliverance v. 21. and following. And you Lord, Lord do for me for your name's sake (be present to me with your help, that your name may be celebrated) because your mercy is sweet: deliver me, because I am afflicted and poor (destitute of all human aids), and my heart is sick within me (it is all but consumed by the sickness of both soul and body John 12, 29. Matthew 27, 37. 38.) as the shadow when it declines, I am forced to depart. (Compare Psalm 102, 12.) I am shaken, or driven away like a locust (that timid little animal, which flees even at the sight of a man, and has no place where it may rest for long: Compare Psalm 22, 78. By these things he demonstrated death, says Theodoret here: for like a shadow declining and failing, he met his end.) My knees are weak through fasting, and my flesh is lean from fat (exhausted of fatness. Cf. Ps. 109, 24.) And I became a reproach to them, they saw me, and shook their heads. Which complaints could all be more rightly repeated by whom, than by the Messiah? (Compare Psalm 22, 8. Matt. 27, 39. 40. Mark 15, 29.) Help me O Lord, save me for thy loving-kindness (Cf. Ps. 69, 1.) and raise me from the dead to glory: see Ps. 16. & 22. And let them know, that this is thy hand (Eph. 1, 18. 19.) that thou alone (willed and were able) to effect it. (Theodoret on these things thus: let them learn, he says, that he did not deliver him to the cross unwillingly, but it was the work of thy dispensation: For through my cross thou didst wish to bestow salvation upon all.) The fourth part finally is the thanksgiving from the promise of help v. 24. For also with undoubted confidence he promises himself to be heard: They will curse, and thou wilt bless, those who rise up against me shall be put to shame, but thy servant (Is. 53, 1. Christ is so called) shall rejoice: let those who oppose me be clothed with shame, and let them be covered with confusion as with a mantle: and for this reason he promises gratitude to God, (But I) will greatly praise the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many (in the great Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles) I will praise him. (Cf. Psalm 16. v. 9. 22, 23. 25. 69, 31.) because he stands at the right hand of the needy (Psalm 16. v. 1.) to save him from those who judge his life: that is, who condemn him. Thus from the analysis of the whole Psalm, no less than from the exegesis of the New Testament, we judge it to be manifest that the discourse here is not about Ahithophel, but about Judas and the Jews, and that the whole prayer is of none other than Christ, whose curses he who misinterprets, undoubtedly incurs a curse. The pious ancients agree in this explanation, Chrysostom,

Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, and Euthymius, who explain the passage about Judas and the Jews simply: whose authority Grotius ought not to have postponed for the sake of not so much Calvin and his Socinians, Beza, Piscator, and Tremellius (to whom are added also the authors of the Belgian notes added to the new translation) as for the sake of the Jews, especially because all things are so clear that they could not be clearer. The more recent ones agree with the ancients ὁμοθυμαδὸν, not only all of ours to a man, but also most of the Papists; Genebrard, Emanuel Saa, Bellarmine, Menochius, and others. Tirinus the Jesuit, however, here and in other Psalms, seduced by the Calvinists as it appears, preferred to Judaize than to adhere to his own associates. Although, as it does not agree among the Jews themselves, with R. David Kimchi and others interpreting the Psalm concerning the enemies of David, R. Solomon with the author of Midrash Tillim interpreting it concerning Isaiah, and R. Obadiah referring it to the times of the captivity: Thus neither does Calvin's school agree with itself. To Calvin there is no doubt that David complained about injuries brought upon him, but he does not name his adversary specifically; most think the Psalm deals particularly with Doeg; others with Ahithophel. We note here the confession of Calvin: who says at verse 8 that Peter takes in Acts 1:20 that principle, that David spoke in the person of Christ. If this is true, the Psalm will have to be understood not of David, but of Christ, in whose person David speaks. It is one thing for David to have borne the type of the Messiah, and to speak of himself, but as a type of Christ, of which there is no trace here, indeed most things are contrary: it is another thing for David to speak in the person of Christ, which Calvin grants.

Latin:

vers. 6. super eum impium, & diabolus stet a dextris ejus (quia de Juda peculiariter sermo est, qui cæteris γενόμενο̂ς ὀδηγὸς, cum Christus ad passionem ab- riperetur Act. 1, 16. Judæi etiam in conspirationi- bus suis pro una stabant persona, & introducuntur ceu persona una, ac vovetur ut in impiorum homi- num, ipsiusque Satanæ potestatem tradantur) cūm judicatur, exeat condemnatus, & oratio illius vertatur in peccatum (Ihr Lehr, Leben, Lernen, Beten müsse alles verdammt seyn, ut glossa marginalis B. Luthe- ri habet, ad quæ verba respexisse videtur Christus Joh. 17, 12.) Fiant dies ejus pauci, & Episcopatum ejus (quam interpretationem probat Grotius: פקד inter alia significat curare, inspicere, inde פקדה quod ἐπισκοπὴν tum hic, tum alibi verterunt LXX. Ipsam vocem Græcam retinuit Latinus Interpres, sicut vocem ἐπισκόπη Cicero, cum se dicit maritimæ oræ Episco- pum a Pompejo constitutum) accipiat alter; Fiant filii ejus orphani, & uxor ejus vidua (& quidem tales, ut non sit, qui eorum curam suscipiat: quas execra- tiones in Juda impletas esse Spiritus S. testatur Act. 1, 20. Traditus enim in potestatem Satanæ, ita ab eodem in conscientia exagitatus est, ut vitam la- queo finiverit.) Quæ sequuntur, in Judæis, Judæ filiis, quoad impietatis & impœnitentiæ imitatio- nem, completa esse, eventus & experientia palam testatur: nec ulla gens aut posteritas designari pote- rit, in qua ista omnia tam luculenter & adæquate in conspectu & judicio totius orbis adimpleta sint. Ut mirari oporteat, Grotium adhuc istas imprecatio- nes de Achitophele (cui quos adjungere velit, non in- dicat) intelligere: Bezam & Tremellium de Doego, ac Saulis filiis interpretari. Multo longius ea pro- spicere, & ad totam gentem & posteritatem Judæo- rum pertinere, verborum Emphasis docet, ac even- tus ipse comprobat. Vagando vagentur filii ejus, & mendicent: & quærant (victum) propter inopiam suam (sicut reddit Osiander) Attrahat ad se fœnerator o- mnem substantiam ejus, & diripiant alieni labores ejus; (prædatores: quicquid superfuerit, id omne eripiatur, vel a fœneratore per fraudulentiam, vel a prædatore per violentiam) Non sit illi adjutor, nec sit, qui misereatur pupillis ejus. Fiant nati ejus in interitum (posteritas ejus intereat) in generatione al- tera deleatur nomen ejus, in memoria sit iniquitas ma- jorum illius (uniuscujusque eorum) apud Dominum (Conf. Matth. 23, 35.) & peccatum matris illius non deleatur, sint (illa peccata) in conspectu Domini sem- per, ut exscindat e terra memoriam eorum. Hæc Ju- dæis evenisse, vi imprecationis Judæorum propriæ Matth. 27, 25. & prædictionis Christi Luc. 23, 27. seqq. Matth. 23, 38. 39. experientia itidem compro- bat. Theodoretius ad illa, in generatione una delea- tur nomen ejus, ita habet: Nam nondum quadragin- ta annis elapsis Judæorum populus extremam interne- cionem subivit, & non amplius per seipsos Rempubli- cam administrant, neque proprios habent Reges & Principes, neque celeberrimam illam metropolim, neq; secundum legem cultum perficiunt, sed vana illa omnia sunt. Nulla certe gens designari poterit, in qua ista omnia conspiciantur, aut impleta sint, uti Judæa gens: exilium perpetuum pati coguntur, a Romanis exuti sunt facultatibus omnibus, & tota die a Magistrati- bus, qui eosdem tolerant, exhauriuntur, exosi sunt omnibus populis, nec ullus misericordia eorum duci- tur: posteritas eorum exitio perpetuo devota est, no- men inglorium, & memoria detestabilis est, & puni- tur in eadem majorum iniquitas, quemadmodum ipsi voverunt filiis suis, ac posteritas ipsa majorum insistens impiis vestigiis meretur. Non leguntur in Codi- ce toto tantæ execrationes, quantæ hic vo- ventur, vel prædicuntur potius : nec inventa præter Judæos unquam gens est, quæ tantis & tam diutur- nis maledictionibus obnoxia fuerit. Caufæ vero tantarum maledictionum populi, hæ redduntur ab ipso Christo (1.) Neglectus misericordiæ & justitiæ v. 16. Pro eo, quod non est recordatus misericordiam facere, & persequutus est afflictum & pauperem, & con- tristatum corde cogitavit morti tradere: q. d. fui pau- per, egenus, afflictus multis modis, sed illi meas mi- serias etiam prosequendo duplicarunt, quare & illi sine commiseratione pereant : ut habet Osiandri pa- raphrasis. (2.) Contemtus divinæ gratiæ v. 17. Et dilexit, (ultro accersivit) maledictionem (sanguis ejus sit super filios nostros Matth. 27, 25.) & veniet ei. Et noluit benedictionem (cujus gratia ad ipsos primum missus erat Christus Actor. 3, 26. Joh. 1, 11. Actor. 13,46.) & elongabitur ab eo. Et induit maledictio- nem, sicut vestimentum &c. (3.) Pravus & iniquus affectus. Hoc præmium erit eorum a Domino, qui adversantur mihi, & loquuntur mala adversus ani- mam meam, ea dicunt & agunt, quibus vitam mihi eri- piant. Quæ exactissimie itidem in Juda & Judæis ita impleta, ut prædicta sunt, cernere licet in Histo- ria Evangelica. Tertia pars est precatio pro libera- tione v. 21. & seqq. Et tu Domine, Domine fac mihi propter nomen tuum (adesto mihi auxilio tuo, ut no- men tuum celebretur) quia suavis est misericordia tua: libera me, quia afflictus & pauper (omnibus hu- manis præsidiis destitutus) ego sum, & cor meum æ- grum est intra me (ægritudine & animi & corporis tantum non conficitur Joh. 12, 29. Matth. 27, 37. 38.) sicut umbra cum declinat ipsa, abire cogor. (Conf. Pf. 102, 12.) exagitor, vel abigor ut locusta (timidum illud animalculum, quod vel ad conspectum homi- nis fugit, nec locum habet, ubi diu quiescat: Conf. Pf. 22, 78. Per hæc mortem demonstravit, inquit Theod. hic : instar enim umbræ vergentis & deficientis finem obivivit.) Genua mea labant pro jejunio, & caro mea macilenta est a pingui (exhausta pinguedine. Conf. Pf. 23, 15. 16.) Et ego factus sum opprobrium illis, viderunt me, & moverunt capita sua. Quæ que- relæ omnes a quo rectius ingeminari potuere, quam a Messia ? (Conferatur Psalm. 22, 8. Matth. 27, 39. 40. Marc. 15, 29.) Auxiliare mihi o Domine, salva me pro benignitate tua (Conf. Psal. 69, 1.) & resuscita me ex mortuis ad gloriam : vid. Pf. 16. & 22. Et sciant, quod manus tua hæc (sit, Ephes. 1, 18. 19.) quod tu id (solus volueris & valueris) efficere. (Theodoretus ad hæc ita : discant, inquit, non invitum cruci tradi- disse, sed tuæ dispensationis opus : Per meam enim cru- cem salutem omnibus largiri voluisti.) Quarta pars denique est ex pollicitatione auxilii gratiarum actio v. 24. Nam & indubitata fiducia sibi exauditionem promittit : Maledicent illi, & tu benedices, qui insur- gunt in me, confudentur, servus autem tuus (Es. 53, 1. Christus sic vocatur) lætabitur : induantur, qui mihi adversantur, pudore, & operiantur sicut pallio confu- sione: & Deo eo nomine pollicetur gratitudinem, (Ego autem) confitebor Domino valde ore meo, & in medio multorum (in magna Ecclesia ex Judæis & gentibus collecta) laudabo eum. (Conf. Psal. 16. v. 9. 22, 23. 25. 69, 31.) quia astatit a dextris egeni (Psalm. 16. v. 1.) ad salvandum ab iis, qui judicant vitam illi : hoc est, qui condemnant illum. Ita e totius Psalmi ἀναλύσει, non minus quam e Novi Testamenti ἐξηγήσει manifestum esse arbitramur, non de Achitophele, sed de Juda & Judæis hic ser- monem, orationemque totam non alterius, quam Christi esse, cujus execrationes qui traducit, exe- crationem indubie incurrit. Consentiunt in hac explicatione pii veteres, Chrysostomus,

Hieronymus, Augustinus, Theodoretus, & Euthymius, qui de Juda & Judæis simpliciter exponunt: quorum autoritatem in gratiam non tam Calvini, & Socien- norum ejus, Beza, Piscatoris ac Tremellii (quibus ac- cedunt etiam autores notarum Belgicarum novæ translationi additarum) quam Judæorum posthabe- re non debuit Grotius, maxime quia tam clara sunt omnia, ut clariora esse non possint. Veteribus re- centiores ὁμοθυμαδὸν astipulantur, non solum no- stri ad unum omnes, sed etiam plerique Pontificii; Genebrardus, Emanuel Saa, Bellarminus, Menochius, alii. Tirinus tamen Jesuita hic & in aliis Psalmis a Calvinianis, ut apparet, seductus, Judaizare maluit, quam sociis suis adhærere. Quanquam ut Judæis non convenit inter se, R. David Kimchio & aliis Psal- mum de hostibus Davidis, R. Salomone cum Autore Midrasch Tillim de Esaia interpretantibus, R. Obad vero ad tempora captivitatis referente: Ita neque Calvini Schola sibi constat. Calvino dubium non est, quin de illatis sibi injuriis conquestus sit David, non autem exprimit nominatim adversarium ejus; ple- rique de Doeg; alii de Achitophele peculiariter Psal- mum agere opinantur. Confessionem Calvini hic notamus: qui ad v. 8. ait, sumere Petrum Actor. 1, 20. principium illud, Davidem in Christ. persona locutum esse. Si hoc verum, non de Davide, sed de Christo, in cujus persona loquitur David, Psalmus intelligen- dus erit. Aliud est Davidem gessisse typum Mes- siæ, & de se, sed ut typo Christi loqui, cujus hic nul- lum vestigium, imo contraria pleraque: Aliud Da- videm in Christi persona loqui, quod largitur Cal- vinus.

## 109:8
Ver. 8. AND HIS BISHOPRIC LET ANOTHER TAKE

פקד among other things signifies to take care of, to inspect. Hence פקדה, which the LXX have translated as ἐπισκοπὴν both here and elsewhere. The Latin translator has retained the Greek word itself, just as Cicero retained the word ἐπίσκοπος when he says that he was appointed by Pompey as an ἐπίσκοπος of the maritime coast.

A very unjust, nay profane, censor of the sacred odes which were dictated by the Holy Spirit. There is no difference between the times of the Law or the Old Testament and the Gospel or the New Testament, as far as the Spirit, the director of spiritual actions, is concerned. The ancients were directed by the same Spirit by whom we are governed, which is manifest from the passages Neh. 9, 20. Ps. 51, 13. 143, 10. Isa. 63, 12. and others. Therefore we are said to have the same Spirit of faith as David, 2 Cor. 4, 13. In sum, there is one Spirit, Eph. 4, 4, who inspired no curses against enemies to the faithful in the Old Testament, just as He does not inspire them in the New Testament. We must by all means distinguish between a carnal imprecation, which proceeds from a desire for vengeance and can in no way be attributed to the Spirit of God, whether under the Law or under the Gospel, and a Prophetic curse, which proceeds not from man, but from the very Spirit of God, by whom the holy men of God were moved to speak. For just as God in His righteous judgment sends all manner of dire things upon the wicked, so He can also threaten and predict them: since the Scriptures are inspired by Him, all pious men ought to detest the profane censure of Grotius, passed here against the Hiero-Psalten, certainly not in a good spirit. But whatever may be the case regarding the use and meaning of this Psalm in the Roman Catholic Church, (the sacrilegious abuse of which Calvin notes in Tom. I. V. T.

The more detestable, therefore, is the sacrilege that monks, and especially Franciscans, commit by profaning this Psalm. For it is a matter by no means hidden that if anyone has a mortal enemy whom he wishes to see destroyed, he may hire one of those scoundrels to recite this Psalm daily. Indeed, in the kingdom of France, I know of a certain noblewoman who had hired Franciscans to imprecate her only son in this manner.t) This Psalm is deservedly called the Iscariotic, not because it was spoken against Ahithophel, the twin of Judas Iscariot, of which we have no evidence, but because it was predicted of Judas himself, as the Apostolic explanation in Acts 1:20 also testifies. For Peter declares in clear words in verse 16 that this prediction was fulfilled in him: ἔδει πληρωθῆναι τὴν γραφὴν ταύτην, ἣν προεῖπε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον διὰ σόματος Δαβὶδ περὶ ἰὔδα. Peter openly testifies that the Psalm is about Judas, and says that the Holy Spirit foretold concerning Judas through the mouth of David: he pronounces that this Scripture was fulfilled in Judas. To this also tend the words of Christ himself in John 17:12: ὅς δέδωκάς μοι ἐφύλαξα, καὶ ὀδεὶς ἐξ ἀυτῶν ἀπώλετο, εἰ μὴ ὁ γὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας, ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ. Who, therefore, would admit that those things were said about Ahithophel? For the whole structure of the Psalm, when this light is brought to it from the New Testament, teaches this: that Christ complains grievously of the slanders, deceits, injuries, and malice not of one adversary alone, but of many enemies, the Jews, yet especially of the traitor Judas, and by imprecating, foretells that many evils, but especially those of Judas, would redound both upon them and upon their family on account of their connected impenitence, and that he prays for himself and his Church, and promises thanksgiving. Whence 4 parts are not inconveniently established. The first is the lamentation of Christ, v. 1, et seqq. O God of my praise, do not keep silent: for the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful have opened (he denotes the Jews, full of impiety, deceit, and hypocrisy, pouring out wagonloads of calumnies with open mouth, who conspired among themselves as if they were speaking with one voice) they have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue, (which was also done especially by Judas, when he greeted him while betraying him with a kiss, Hail Rabbi) And with words of hatred (hateful and poisonous) they have encompassed me, nay rather, they have surrounded me, just as a city is accustomed to be encircled by a siege, and they have attacked me without cause (cf. Ps. 59, 15; Joh. 15, 25.) In return for my love (for them) they have opposed me (as the very שׂטן, as the Hebrew word renders it) And I am prayer (thus I am devoted to prayer alone, and I pray with all my strength, as if I were becoming entirely prayer; thus are emphatically noted continuous, most ardent, and most holy supplications). Certainly no mortal can say that he is entirely prayer, since no one is so holy that he is not sometimes distracted in prayer itself, so far is it from the case that he has his mind perpetually directed toward God. Conf. Dn. D. Glassii dedicat. Epist. Orat. Christi τερωαγονίς) And they have repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love. In which he comprehends the causes of being heard from the person of God, and of his adversaries, and of their both wickedness and iniquity, and also from his own person, or his innocence and patience; which certainly suit no one as they do our Messiah.

The second part of the Psalm is Christ's imprecation v. 6. et seqq. by which both the punishment is designated, then the vexation constantly prepared by the adversary denounced against the enemy of the Messiah v. 6. condemnation and reprobation v. 7. the shortening of life and office v. 8. then the bereavement of the family, wife and children, beggary, desolation, the injustice of those plundering, the unmercifulness of friends, the abolition of the name v. 9. et seqq. and the guilt is recounted, the neglect of mercy and justice v. 16. as also the contempt of divine grace v. 17. and the depraved affection v. 20. I have determined, he says,

Latin:

Vers. 8. ET EPISCOPATUM EJUS ACCIPIAT ALTER)

פקד inter alia significat curare, inspicere. Inde פקדה quod ἐπισκοπὴν tum hîc tum alibi verterunt LXX. Ipsam vocem Græcam retinuit Latinus interpres, sicut vocem ἐπίσκοπος Cicero, cum se dicit maritimæ oræ ἐπίσκοπον à Pompejo constitutum.

VAlde iniquus, imo prophanus censor sacrarum odarum, quæ a Spiritu Sancto dictatæ sunt. Nulla inter legis vel Veteris Testamenti & Evangelii, vel Testam. Novi tempora est diversitas, quantum ad Spiritum, actionum Spiritualium directorem. Ab eodem Spiritu directi sunt veteres, quo nos regimur, quod e locis Nehem. 9, 20. Pf. 51, 13. 143, 10. Esa. 63, 12. & aliis manifestum est. Ideo nos eundem Spiritum fidei cum Davide habere dicimur 2. Cor. 4, 14. Summa, unus est Spiritus Ephes. 4, 4. qui nullas in Vet. Testamento diras adversus hostes fidelibus inspiravit, uti nec in Novo Testamento inspirat. Distinguendum omnino inter carnalem imprecationem, quæ ex vindictæ cupiditate proficiscitur, nec Spiritui Dei, sive sub lege, sive sub Evangelio ullatenus tribui potest, & Propheticam maledictionem, quæ non ab homine, sed ab ipso Dei spiritu, quo agitati loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines, proficiscitur. Deus enim uti justo judicio impiis dira quæque immittit, ita minari quoque & prædicere illa potest: a quo quum inspiratæ sint Scripturæ, detestari omnes pios oportet prophanam Grotii censuram, adversus Hiero-Psalten hic latam, spiritu certe non bono. Quicquid vero fit de usu, & sensu hujus Psalmi, in Ecclesia Romano-Catholica, (cujus abusum sacrilegum notat Calvinus Tom. I. V. T.

Quo magis detestabile sacrilegium est, quod Psalmum hunc Monachi profanant, & maxime Franciscani. Res enim minime occulta est, si quis hostem capitalem habeat, quem velit perditum, conducere ex illis nebulonibus aliquem, qui quotidie Psalmum hunc recitet. Imo in regno Galliæ scio primariam quandam fœminam conductitios ex Franciscanis habuisse, qui unigenito Filio hac forma imprecareturt ) Iscario- ticus utique hic Psalmus merito vocatur, non quod in Achitophelem, Judæ Ischarioti geminum dictus sit, quo de nullum habemus documentum, sed quod de Juda ipso prædictus, quod ipsa etiam Apostolica explicatio Actor. 1, 20. testatur. Nam in illo impletam esse hanc prædictionem verbis luculentis perhibet Petrus vers. 16. ἔδει πληρωθῆναι τὴν γραφὴν ταύτην, ἣν προεῖπε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον διὰ σόματος Δαβὶδ περὶ ἰὔδα. De Juda Psalmum agere palam testatur Petrus, de Juda prædixisse Spiritum S. hac per os Davidis ait: In Juda hanc Scripturam impletam esse pronunciat. Quo etiam tendunt ipsius Christi verba Joh. 17, 12. ὅς δέδωκάς μοι ἐφύλαξα, καὶ ὀδεὶς ἐξ ἀυτῶν ἀπώλετο, εἰ μὴ ὁ γὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας, ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ. Quis ergo admitter, quod illa de Achitophele dicta sint? Tota enim Psalmi structura, cum hæc ipsi fax e N. Testamento præfertur, id docet: Christum de calumniis, dolis, injuriis & malitia non unius solum adversarii, sed hostium plurium, Judæorum, cumprimis tamen proditoris Judæ graviter conqueri, inque ob connexam impœnitentiam mala plurima, sed maxime Judæ, tum in ipsos, tum in familiam eorum redundatura imprecando prædicere, pro se autem & Ecclesia sua precari, & gratiarum actionem polliceri. Unde 4. partes non incommode constituuntur. Prima est Christi ejulatio v. 1. seqq. Deus laudis meæ ne tacueris: quia os peccatorum & os dolosorum aperuerunt (Judæos impiis & dolis ac hypocrisi plenos notat, plaustra calumniarum ore aperto effundentes, qui inter se conspirabant, quasi uno ore loquerentur) loquuti sunt mecum lingua dolosa, (quod cumprimis etiam a Juda factum, cum eum osculo prodens salutavit, Ave Rabbi) Et sermonibus odii (odiosis & venenatis) me circumvenerunt, imo circumdederunt, veluti obsidione urbs cingi solet, & oppugnaverunt me immerito (conf. Ps. 59, 15. Joh. 15, 25.) Pro eo quod dilexi (eos) ipsi adversati sunt mihi (ut ipse שׂטן, ut vox Ebræa reddit) Et ego oratio (sic uni orationi vaco, atque omnibus viribus oro, ac si totus oratio efficerer; notantur ita emphatice continuæ, ardentissimæ, & Sanctissimæ precationes. Nemo certe mortalium dicere potest, se totum orationem esse, quum nemo tam sanctus sit, quin in oratione ipsa distrahatur nonnunquam, tantum abest, ut perpetuo mentem ad Deum directam habeat. Conf. Dn. D. Glassii dedicat. Epist. Orat. Christi τερωαγονίς) Et reposuerunt mihi malum pro bono, & odium pro dilectione mea. Quibus causas exauditionis a persona Dei, & adversariorum, eorumque tum improbitate tum iniquitate, nec non a sua persona, vel innocentia, & patientia sua comprehendit; quæ certe nulli sic conveniunt, ut Messiæ nostro.

Altera pars Psalmi est Christi imprecatio v. 6. seqq. qua & pœna designatur, tum hosti Messiæ denunciata, jugis ab adversario parata vexatio vers. 6. condemnatio atque reprobatio v. 7. vitæ ac officii decurtatio v. 8. tum familiæ, uxori & liberis orbitas, mendicitas, vastitas, deprædantium injustitia, amicorum immisericordia, nominis abolitio vers. 9. seqq. & culpa recensetur, neglectus misericordiæ & justitiæ vers. 16. ut & contemtus divinæ gratiæ vers. 17. & pravus affectus vers. 20. Constitui, inquit,

## 109:11
Verse 11.

LET THE USURER SEARCH OUT ALL HIS SUBSTANCE) Let him seek everywhere for goods into the adjudged matter. It appears the Greeks read ינקש, when they translated it ἐξερευνάτω. We today read with a very similar spelling ינקש, that is, let him hold bound.

Grotius followed Bellarmine here again, who does not fear to say that the Hebrew text is corrupted by the fault of the scribes. But the Hebrew Codices consistently report our reading: Let the usurer ensnare all that is his: which fits very well and has the emphasis of the ancients, because this way of speaking is taken from bird-catchers, or from those who catch wild animals with snares. Symmachus also favors our reading, rendering it thus, let the exactor crush those things which are his. Nor is it indeed necessary that we believe the Greeks read something else in their Codex: since it can be said that they, deceived by the affinity of the letters, snatched one for the other, which Jerome often notes in them; or confused different words, as Buxtorf thinks in Vind. Verit. Ebr. part 2, c. 8, p. 648. Finally, if with B. Tarnovius in this place a different reading is entirely admitted, no universal corruption of the Hebrew Codex can be inferred from it, because the true reading being found in only some codices, all cannot be judged corrupted.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

SCRUTETUR FENERATOR OMNEM SUBSTAN- TIAM EJUS) Quærat undique bona in rem judicatam. Apparet legisse Græcos ינקש, cum verterunt ἐξερευνάτω. Nos hodie legimus scriptione valde vicina ינקש, id est tene- at obstrictum.

Sequutus hic iterum Grotius Bellarminum, qui vitio librariorum Ebræum textum corruptum dicere non veretur. Nostram autem lectionem constanter referunt Codices Ebræi: Illaqueet fœne- rator omnia quæ sunt ipsius: quæ optime congruit ac majorum emphasin habet, quia modus hic loquen- di ab aucupibus desumitur, aut ab illis, qui capiunt tendiculis feras. Symmachus etiam nostræ lectioni favet, reddens ita, collidat exactor ea, quæ sunt ipsi. Nec vero necesse est, ut aliud legisse in Codice suo Græcos credamus: quum dici possit, eosdem affi- nitate literarum deceptos, unam pro altera arripu- isse, quod sæpius in illis notat Hieronymus; aut di- versas voces confudisse, ut censet Buxtorfius Vind. Verit. Ebr. part. 2. c. 8. p. 648. Denique si cum B. Tarnovio in h. l. omnino admittatur diversa lectio, nulla inde Codicis Ebræi inferri potest universalis corruptio, quia vera lectione in aliquibus solum co- dicibus reperta, omnes corrupti censeri non pos- sunt.

## 110:1 Argument
PSALM 110. Christ King and Priest.

PSALM OF DAVID) In Hebrew לדוד, as often above. And to whom it is ascribed, the Hebrews accept them as Psalms made by David, or approved by him: because the particle ל often signifies the genitive, as לרגליך the Greeks translate τῶν ποδῶν σου, which this Latin interpretation follows. Thus in Malachi 1:2 ליעקב the Greeks translate τῷ Ἰακὼβ; and 1 Sam. 1:3, for ליהוה in Greek is τῷ κυρίῳ, and many such things elsewhere.

He rightly proves it to be the genitive case, but that Grotius praises the opinion of the Hebrews also, as if a Psalm so inscribed לדוד could be understood as one that is not indeed David's, but approved by David, it is not obscure for what purpose this is done, namely, that he may gratify the Jews, that the Psalm was not sung by David in honor of the Messiah, but by another for the sake of another. And in that, Grotius was unmindful of those things which he had annotated at Matthew 22:43, which, because we judge them to stand on sufficiently firm footing, we ourselves not undeservedly oppose here. Thus indeed it holds in the aforementioned place: Christ names David as the writer of Psalm 110, who would never have taken that upon himself, unless it had then been beyond controversy. And indeed the ἐπιγραφὴ in the Hebrew Codices themselves is מזמור לדוד: which alone ought to have sufficed, so that the writer of that hymn would not be believed to be of the times of Eliezer or Hezekiah. For even if we grant that the titles were not added by the authors themselves, yet it is certain that they are very ancient, whose credibility it is the work of men insane with a desire for contention to tear down now, not by any arguments, but by the whim of the mind. The Septuagint are accustomed to translate that לדוד as τῷ Δαβίδ: But the other paraphrasts otherwise, and the Hebrews themselves who accept ל both in the inscriptions of the Psalms and in many other places in that signification which we express by the second case. And indeed if we interpret it otherwise, there will be no Psalm that is David's, or at least which is certain to be David's, when yet they themselves also confess that many Psalms, and indeed those having the same ἐπιγραφὴν, were written by David. These are the things of Grotius, which teach that that לדוד cannot be accepted as if the Psalm were only approved by David. Add that Peter, along with Christ, makes David the author of the Psalm, Acts 2:34, 35.

Verse 1.

THE LORD SAID TO MY LORD) The Jews interpret this Psalm in various ways, so that they may snatch its meaning from the Christians, concerning which matter we dealt with in Matthew 22:42 and following. Furthermore, R. Saadia Gaon interprets this concerning the Messiah to Daniel.

That is the only Psalm which Grotius seems to leave to Christians to be explained solely as a prophecy concerning the Messiah, since in all other prophetic passages he openly goes in entirely different directions. For it is too clear that this Psalm treats of Christ, to whom alone all those things which are predicted in the Psalm apply, namely that he is the Lord of David: for whom else did David acknowledge as his Lord, except God, from which Christ demonstrated his own Deity from these words in Matt. 22:45 ff., Mark 12:36, Luke 20:42-43 (which argument, from its intrinsic evidence, had the power of conviction from the special grace of Christ working in hearts, where Hackspan, in his Philological and Theological Notes, part 2, p. 321, recently attempted to elide such testimonies of the Old Testament, which were brought forward by Christ himself and the Apostles for the Deity of Christ, for the sake of his Calixtus): that he sits at the right hand of God (for it was once confessed among the Hebrews themselves that this was said to none of the angels, much less a man, Heb. 1:13; therefore, that this was said concerning the Messiah, with the Pharisees themselves acknowledging it, Christ testified in Matt. 22:44, which Paul also assumed as indubitable in 1 Cor. 15:25, Heb. 1:13, ch. 10:13); that the rod of his power was sent forth from Zion in such a way that he might rule in the midst of his enemies and place all his enemies as a footstool for his feet (in whom was that fulfilled, if not in the Messiah, as our Christ himself and the holy Apostle testify in the places previously cited); that he has a people as spontaneous worshippers in holy array, venerating him with spiritual sacrifices, namely his spiritual sons, filling the whole earth in an innumerable multitude, like the dew, begotten from the womb of the dawn. Who was ever, or could ever be, both King and Priest at the same time in Zion, saving the divine constitution, except this spiritual King in Israel? Who is a Priest after the order of Melchizedek, if not our Christ? Who is the Pontiff forever besides this unique Pontiff of the New Testament? It will never be taught that these things can be said of anyone, certainly not even according to the type or likeness of a shadow and figure, nor that they were even slightly adumbrated in anyone. Therefore, the Jews themselves in John 12:34 accepted these things concerning the Messiah: ἡμεῖς ἠκέσαμεν ἐκ τῶ νόμο ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς μένει εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα. And Paul, to the Hebrews themselves, places this beyond controversy, that it was said of Christ alone, ch. 5:6: Καθὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει, σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ. And ch. 7:17: Μαρτυρεῖ γὰρ, ὅτι σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ. And so also v. 12. Furthermore, who is that Lord who, in the day of his wrath, breaks whatever kings are adversaries, exercises judgment among the nations, shatters the head over much land, who drinks from the torrent in the way, and therefore has exalted his head, if not the Messiah? For all these things are said of one and the same Lord in v. 5, 6, 7. are said, with a προσφώνησις, directed to God the Father: The Lord, says the sacred psalmist, at your right hand (sitting) will break kings in the day of his wrath, will exercise judgment, etc. Concerning which see the Disputation on this saying by our Lord D. Dorscheus, § 46 et seqq. In such great light, Grotius is forced to desert the Jews, to whom he otherwise adheres too rashly, since he found nothing certain among them, and Calvin himself, who otherwise strenuously Judaizes, and in whose footsteps our author loves to insist in such matters, has deserted them here. For the blinded Apellae vary too much, nor do they find what to choose, since they are unwilling to leave room for the truth: some, among Aben-Ezra with the author of Midrash Tillim, by the Lord to whom it is said, 'sit at my right hand,' understand Abraham, to whom his servant Eleazar acclaimed it as an Epinicion, or as others wish, Melchizedek, when he was returning from the victory against the four kings. Others with R. David Kimchi, understand Moses, the Lord and Priest of the Prophets, as he says: others David, whose royal and prophetic excellence some one of the singers described. R. Solomon Jarchi understands both Abraham and David; others Solomon, whom some prophet honored with this poem; some the dignity of Zerubbabel; finally, some wish the guardian angel of David to be described: to none of whom, however, do the ἀξιώματα and praises, or the παθήματα, which are attributed to this Lord in the Psalm, correspond; all things most explicitly designate the Messiah. That he is described here, according to the ancient Hebrews, and in the time of Christ and the Apostles, was beyond all controversy, so much so that not even the Pharisees themselves dared to mutter against it, Matthew 22. And Isaiah Ben-Arama acknowledged this on Gen. 47: 'We never find any of the prophets whose birth was prophesied before the birth of the Father and Mother, except the Messiah, who is our righteousness.' To this also he looked, who said, 'from the womb, from the belly to you,' that is, before the womb of your conception was created, your birth was prophesied. He was sitting, however, at the right hand of God, and he looked to that when he said, 'sit at my right hand.' Thus in the book Midrash Tillim on Ps. 18, it is read that R. Joden in the name of R. Hama said: 'It is to be that the holy and blessed God will make King Messiah sit at his right hand, as it is written in Ps. 110.' And on Ps. 2, the mysteries of the King are said to be narrated in Ps. 110: 'The Lord said to my Lord,' etc. Genebrardus, a Parisian theologian, notes on this Psalm that the ancient Rabbis Barachia and R. Levi are brought to this opinion by R. Moses Nahmanides on Gen. 18. Johannes Viccarsus, an Englishman, in his Decapla on the Psalms, presented R. Obadiah on this Psalm, interpreting it concerning Christ. Grotius himself praises here R. Saadia Gaon on Daniel, and in his Annotations on Matth. 22:48, he has it thus: That this Psalm pertains to the Messiah, the ancient Hebrews acknowledged:

whom Isaac Ben-Arama follows on Gen. 47; those who were after the rise of Christianity began to deny this very thing, out of mere hatred of Christianity: although David Kimchi himself, and others with him, and among Justin, Trypho, interpret Psalm 2 concerning the Messiah, where the same thing is said about the scepter going out from Zion as in this Psalm. Nor can what is said here about the Priesthood be fitted to any of the Hebrew Kings. For while the Law of Moses remained, the Priesthood could not be transferred from the family of Aaron: whence it was decreed to King Uzziah, who is also named Azariah, 'it is not for you to offer incense, but for the Aaronites,' and the punishment was divinely inflicted, nor did he obey. But the one objection Kimchi makes, that no battles were fought by Jesus, is easily solved, since they themselves cannot deny that there are many things, especially in the Prophets, said figuratively. For, not to speak of the members of God, those among them who are of a slightly more refined nose understand that the mountain of the Lord will be raised above other mountains, and that wild beasts will stable with cattle, otherwise than the words sound: just as Albo also interprets the banquets in the heavenly kingdom. Among Christians, both ancient and more recent, no one has doubted that this Psalm pertains to Christ. Calvin himself acknowledges here that both the Kingdom and the Priesthood of Christ are celebrated in the argument of Psalm 1, and he begins the explanation thus: 'Since Christ testifies that this Psalm was composed concerning himself, certainty must be sought from nowhere else than from his own mouth: but even if his authority were to cease, and even the testimony of the Apostles, the Psalm itself cries out that it admits no other exposition.' For even if we have a struggle with the most obstinate of all Jews, we will extort by firm reasons that what is said here applies neither to David nor to any other person, except the Mediator alone. I confess indeed that in the person of David an image of the kingdom of Christ was adumbrated: but he could not assert of any successors that a King would rule widely who would at the same time be a Priest, not legal, but according to the order of Melchizedek, and indeed eternal. For a new and unusual dignity of Priesthood could not be erected then, unless the honor were taken away from the Levites. Nor indeed could the eternity, which is mentioned here, apply to a mortal man: because for any other besides this one, the honor is finished in a short and fleeting course of life. And to v. 4: 'This verse proves that the discourse is held about no one else than Christ.' Since Grotius therefore followed him in corrupting other Psalms, in the present Psalm also, which more than any other he vindicated for Christ, he did not wish to disregard his authority: whose very words he even retained in certain places, so that it can be doubtful to no one that he chose him as a leader in his glosses and kept him before his eyes. With him also he explains quite coldly the most eminent ἀξιώματα [axioms] and other predicates in this Psalm designating the Messiah, so that not even here could the Judaizing spirit of Calvin fully hide itself: inasmuch as he corrupts those words, SIT AT MY RIGHT HAND, with this jejune gloss: be secure in the confidence of my help. And at verse 4, those words, THOU ART A PRIEST FOREVER, he explains as MINISTER OF THE LORD. And what follows, AFTER THE ORDER OF MELCHIZEDEK, he renders thus from the Hebrew: According to my constitution, O my just King; and at verse 5. THE LORD AT THY RIGHT HAND, that is, he is a helper to you, and as it were a παραστάτης [supporter]. For in this way, to say nothing of the rest, the entire strength of three arguments, and those the principal ones, which invincibly vindicate this Psalm for the MESSIAH ALONE, is cut, so that they no longer have any force against the Jews. For if to sit at the right hand of God is nothing other than to be secure in the confidence of God's help, no one will doubt that it applies to David and other ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις [mere men].

If the name of Priest here implies only a minister of God, there is nothing to prevent the King from having been a Priest at the same time, even under the law. If the words 'according to the order of Melchizedek' mean only this in the sources, 'according to my constitution, O my just King,' it is undoubted that they also apply to David. Nor will the divine ἀξιώματα (axioms) which are held in verses 5 and 6 stand in the way of that explanation. For those must be understood as being about the Lord, at whose right hand he sits, of whom the discourse is, not about the Lord sitting at the right hand of God, according to Grotius. Thus, nothing at all in the whole Psalm will stand in the way of it fitting David according to the Grotian glosses. Nor can anything else be taught from the title, since, according to the Hebrews—with Grotius not dissenting in these later writings of his and his annotations on this Psalm—it can be accepted in such a way that the Psalm is understood as having been sung by another (in honor of David) and only approved by David. When I weigh all these things with an accurate balance of mind, I cannot conclude otherwise than that Grotius, when he was smearing these annotations on the Psalms onto paper, whatever his mind and opinion may have been before—namely, in his earlier writings and commentaries on the Gospels (for many things will prove that Grotius moved far from himself in his later works, not only regarding the controversies stirred up among Christians themselves, but also regarding the oracles of Scripture hitherto invincibly opposed to the Jews by the common calculation of all Christians, which is also evident regarding this passage from his annotations on John 12:34)—believed that the Psalm should still be explained concerning Christ, but in a mystical and more eminent sense, while at the same time tacitly suggesting another sense, namely the literal and first obvious one, which we have hitherto observed to have been done by him in other Psalms. The blessed Lord D. Hunnius noted an almost identical corruption in Calvin.
