Our Hunnius [noted this] in Calvin, and that without any injury (as he taught πρὸς ὄμμα [before one's eyes] from Calvin's commentary in the second Anti-Pareus, page 447) regarding verse 1 of this Psalm, namely that those words, 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand,' to some extent also correspond to David before all the monarchs of the whole world, insofar as he is sanctified by holy anointing to be the vicar of Christ, insofar as he is also, before all others, the IMAGE (and type) of the only-begotten Son of God, and insofar as it is established that he arrived at the kingdom by the voice, command, and order of God, even if they cannot be applied to him IN EVERY RESPECT: But one must seek in whom this dignity solidly resides, of which dignity (in the first verse of this Psalm) only a small spark shone forth in David, but the perfect brightness shone forth in Christ. Whence Calvin was deservedly noted here by the Lord D. Hunnius: whose ἐπίκρισιν (judgment) I make my own here from the second Anti-Pareus, p. 440. Certainly, whoever as a Doctor of the Church accommodates Psalm 110 entirely to Christ, and does so sincerely without the admission of a contrary error, does not contaminate the interpretation with such affirmations about David that lead back to Judaism rather than Christianity: an example of which Calvinian gloss I believe can hardly be found in any ancient or modern Christian writer. Musculus, however, followed his teacher; perverting the illustrious prophecy in the same way when he says: that an imperfect type preceded in David in that he defeated the neighboring nations, struck down their Kings, forced the Syrians to pay tribute, and finally killed the head of the city and land of Rabbah, namely the King, and captured the city (2 Sam. 12), and accomplished all these things from Zion: for he could in some way also be called a Priest, both because of his notable zeal for divine worship and because he is read to have blessed the people (2 Sam. 6:18), and in this way, according to the order of Melchizedek, he was both King and Priest. Rivetus is more sound here, who, while he acted as Calvin's defender in other matters, not only does not deny him his patronage in this place, but even destroys his opinion with arguments: For it is more certain than certain, says Rivetus in the argument of this Psalm, that what is said here CANNOT BE UNDERSTOOD of David or any other mere man. For what was not given to the Angels—to which of the Angels did He say, 'Sit at my right hand' (Heb. 1:5)—could it apply to any mere man? Who among men can be a Priest forever? And that it cannot be attributed to David is proven by the argument drawn from the fact that the Aaronic Priesthood was in force in his time; at which time no unusual and new dignity of Priesthood could be established. Therefore, since this concerns that King who was to be both King and Priest at the same time, not of a legal but of another order, and that forever, and no one can ever be such except the Messiah promised to the fathers, since the eternity of the Priesthood cannot apply to a mortal man, there is no reason for us to doubt about the θεανθρώπῳ (God-man) object. But one must entirely confess that this Psalm is perverted far worse by Grotius than by Calvin. For while the latter says that at least the first verse corresponds to David to some extent, Grotius not only renders a gloss of those words, 'sit at my right hand,' which fits David fully and in every respect, but also [perverts] the Priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, and the ministry of the King justly according to the constitution of God, in a most perverse manner, having disregarded no less the authority of the holy Apostle, who explained it concerning the eternal Priesthood of the Messiah among the Hebrews themselves, and held it to be ὁμολογουμένως (confessedly) certain and undoubted that it must be explained as such, rather than interpreting it by the proper meaning of the words and the confession of the Jews themselves; lest, forsooth, it should conflict with David. Who will not detest, who will not execrate with his whole heart this Cacoethes (bad habit) of sailing with the wind of Jewish corruptions? But he seems to have been seduced here primarily by Enjedinus, the Neophotinian, who likewise makes a double sense of the Psalm: a literal one about David and a mystical one about the Messiah. He gathers the former from the inventions of the Rabbis, and asserts that the Empæcta (mockers) existed not yesterday, but before Jesus Christ was born, and says that David, according to that sense, sat at the right hand of God, that is, had God at his right hand: that the word כהן can be taken so as to denote not a Priest, but a prince, that the word Melchisedech can be taken as an appellative noun, so that it may be said David is King of righteousness, or a just King, so that the sense may be: You, David, will be King forever, not like Saul, in that you are a just King. Which opinion, however, Enjedinus alone brings forward, so that he may prove himself a craftsman at twisting the Scriptures, and in that he was more sober and sound than Grotius, in that he did not dare to approve it: he added only this ἐπίκρισιν: But it is not safe for us to follow this interpretation, nor is it right. For the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews affirms that by the word Cohen a Priest is denoted: and it cannot be denied that it is often used in that way in sacred writings. Furthermore, that author builds and confirms the Pontificate and eternal Priesthood of Jesus Christ, especially from this passage. Therefore, let it be certain that this treats of a Priest.

And Grotius himself had once acknowledged, when he was preparing annotations on the Evangelists at Luke 24, v. 47, that this Psalm treats of Christ and the proclamation of the Gospel in the time of the N.T., the beginning of which was predicted to be in Jerusalem in v. 2, indeed in De Verit. Relig. Christ. lib. 5, § 22, he had taught that this Psalm CANNOT be explained otherwise. The latter, he says, (namely Psalm CX) CANNOT be explained of any other than the MESSIAH. For the things which some more recent Jews invent about Abraham, others about David, others about Hezekiah, are frivolous. The Psalm itself is David's, as the Hebrew inscription teaches. Therefore, what David says was said to his Lord, that neither

It cannot be applied to David himself, nor to Hezekiah, who among the descendants of David was in no respect more excellent than David. Abraham, however, did not have any preeminent priesthood; indeed, Melchizedek prayed for him as for one lesser than himself. But both this, and what is added concerning the scepter about to arise from Zion and to reach the furthest shores, clearly applies to the Messiah, as similar passages undoubtedly dealing with the Messiah make plain: nor did the older Hebrews and paraphrasts accept it otherwise. From whom R. Saadia brought it forward in particular. By what spirit of dizziness, therefore, was he carried away when he was writing the annotations on the Psalms, that, having abandoned the solid explanation of the ancient Hebrews, he did not hesitate to prefer the most inept distortion of the moderns, which is utterly repugnant both to the text and to the interpretation of the New Testament?

Same verse.

SIT AT MY RIGHT HAND) Be secure in the confidence of my help.

Hardly has a more jejune and cold explanation of this most illustrious passage been heard among Christians. In which there is no doubt that Grotius Judaizes thoroughly. For thus Aben-Ezra on 'sit at my right hand': Trust in the right hand of GOD for the subduing of enemies. Thus also Solomon Jarchi: Sit, that is, rest in my power. But it is no wonder that the blind Jews interpret it thus, since Aben-Ezra wishes this to be said to David, and Solomon Jarchi to Abraham. Grotius, however, acknowledges that these things were said to the Messiah: and therefore I cannot wonder enough that he himself interprets the session of the Messiah at the right hand of God so coldly: namely, that it is at least to rest securely in the confidence of divine help. For perhaps with Francis Davidis he determines that Christ now, while he sits at the right hand of God, lies hidden and rests at least, and does nothing, but only enjoys security under divine protection? For thus that Semi-Christian, as he is called by Socinus himself in his own [work] attacking the Holy Trinity, in the Theses on the office of Christ published with the Antitheses of Socinus, with the added disputation on the adoration of Christ by F. Socinus and Christ. Francken p. 184, when he denies that Christ now does anything, where he sits at the right hand of God, he interprets this session as meaning that he rests safely in the protection of God, from which he further infers that we, with him being permitted to dwell placidly in his rest, must believe that we can be helped by him in nothing now. Which Turkish impiety Socinus himself rejects. But he refutes that Jewish-Mahometan gloss with the force of the phrase 'session at the right hand of God,' which implies divine rule, to which the Messiah has been raised, of immense and infinite virtue and power, inasmuch as he has been made σύνθρονος to God, and exalted to the throne of the immense Majesty of God, he rules with the same virtue and power as the Father; which has been most clearly demonstrated hitherto by our people in the Commonplaces concerning the explanation of this article, and in the disputations against the Calvinists: As well as the Apostolic explanation of St. Paul, who expounds that session through divine Lordship and rule, 1 Cor. 15, v. 25. And also that of St. Peter, demonstrating that this session at the right hand of God does not befit David, but Christ alone, Acts 2:33 seqq., and that it implies the highest exaltation, which came to Christ through his ascension into heaven, and which therefore does not befit David, by the power of which he obtained the power of pouring out the Holy Spirit, and was made Lord over all, and Christ: indeed, the interpretation of David himself: because he speaks of that session at the right hand of God, through which the Messiah was made Lord, so that by David the King, who acknowledged no superior on earth, he was also to be held as Lord: by the power of which all enemies are to be placed as a footstool for his feet, the Scepter of the word is to be sent forth from Zion into the whole world, through which session at the right hand of God he rules in the midst of his enemies, begets and consecrates spiritual sons for himself in an innumerable multitude, shatters Kings in the day of his wrath, whoever opposes themselves to him, etc. which effects and divine axioms most openly designate divine rule. What of the fact that Grotius himself acknowledges that those words, 'until I make your enemies your footstool,' are to be understood in the Messiah concerning sin, the devil, many empires, and finally concerning death itself, 1 Cor. 15:25, 26? Although while he says these things are to be understood thus in the Messiah, he tacitly hints at another sense concerning David, though he does not express how those things are to be understood in David. Thus, therefore, when the session at the right hand of God is understood concerning the Messiah (as it is to be understood concerning him alone), it implies such a lordship, by which he rules not only over many empires, but also over the devil, sin, and death itself, to which no sane person can deny that divine and infinite power is required. Who, therefore, will admit that by that phrase only security under the confidence of divine help is designated? Our people, and Dr. Dorscheus and others, refute that detestable depravation at greater length in other places. Compare also the fourth fascicle of the Dissertations of Dr. Feurborn, page 106 seqq.

Same verse.

UNTIL I MAKE YOUR ENEMIES YOUR FOOTSTOOL) It was the custom in the East that victors should subject the vanquished to their feet. Josh. 10:24. These things are to be understood in the Messiah concerning sin, the devil, many empires, and finally concerning death itself, as we learn from 1 Cor. 15:25, 26.

Thus he wishes these things to be understood in the Messiah: but otherwise in David. Wherefore he not only introduces a genuine subject here, where the continuity of the Psalm convinces that it is a matter of only one subject, and Christ himself demonstrated against the Pharisees in Matt. 22, so that they could answer no word. But they would have had something to reply if the Grotian opinion had prevailed: But he also takes the same predicates, uttered in the same words, in a different sense, which is to overturn, or at least to render doubtful, the single, proper, and genuine meaning intended by the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

PSALMUS CX. Christus Rex & Sacerdos.

PSALMUS DAVID) In Hebræo לדוד, ut supra sæpe. Et quibus id adscriptum est, eos pro Psalmis a Davide factis, aut ab eo approbatis accipiunt Hebræi: quia ל particula sæpe genitivum significat, ut לרגליך Græci vertunt τῶν ποδῶν σου, quos hæc Latina interpretatio sequitur. Sic Malachiæ 1. v. 2. ליעקב Græci vertunt τῷ Ἰακὼβ; & 1. Sam. 1, 3. pro ליהוה in Græco est τῷ κυρίῳ, & multa alibi talia.

REcte Genitivi casus esse probat, sed quod E- bræorum etiam sententiam, quasi Psalmus ita inscriptus לדוד intelligi possit, qui non Davidis quidem, sed a Davide approbatus sit, laudat Gro- tius, haud obscurum est, quo fine id fiat, ut nempe gratificetur Judæis, Psalmum non a Davide in ho- norem Messiæ, sed ab alio alterius gratia decanta- tum esse. Et immemor in eo fuit Grotius eorum, quæ ad Matth. 22, 43, annotarat, quæ quia firmo sa- tis talo consistere arbitramur, ipsimet non immeri- to hic opponimus.. Ita vero habet loco prædicto: Scriptorem Psalmi CX. Davidem nominat Christus, nunquam id sibi sumturus, nisi id tum fuisset extra con- troversiam. Et sane ἐπιγραφὴ ipsis Hebræorum Codicibus est מזמור לדוד: quod vel solum sufficere de- bebat, ne Eliezer aut Ezechiæ temporum, scriptor ejus hymni crederetur. Ut enim demus, titulos ab ipsis Scriptoribus non additos, tamen antiquissimos esse con- stat, quorum nunc fidem convellere non argumentis ul- lis, sed animi lubidine, hominum est contentionis studio insanientium. Illud לדוד Septuaginta interpretari solent τῷ Δαβίδ: Sed aliter cæteri Paraphrastæ, He- bræique ipsi qui ל tum in Psalmorum inscriptionibus, tum aliis multis in locis ea significatione accipiunt, quam nos casu secundo exprimimus. Et sane si aliter inter- pretemur, nullus erit Psalmus, qui sit Davidis, aut cer- te quem Davidis esse constet, cum tamen Psalmos pluri- mos & quidem eandem habentes ἐπιγραφὴν a Davi- de scriptos ipsi quoque fateantur. Hæc Grotius, quæ docent, non posse illud לדוד accipi, ac si tantum a Davide approbatus sit Psalmus. Adde quod cum Christo Petrus etiam Davidem Psalmi auctorem fa- ciat Act. 2, 34. 35.

Vers. 1.

DIXIT DOMINUS DOMINO MEO) Varie inter- pretantur Judæi hunc Psalmum, ut ejus sensum Christianis eripiant, qua de re egimus Matth. 22, 42. & sequentibus. Cæ- terum de Messia hunc interpretatur ad Danielem R. Saadia Gaon.

Unicus ille Psalmus est, quem Christianis ceu vaticinium de Messia solo explicandum relinquere videtur Grotius, quum in cæteris Propheticis omni- bus in alia omnia aperte eat. Nimis enim luculen- tum est, Psalmum hunc de Christo agere, cui uni omnia illa conveniunt, quæ in Psalmo prædicantur, quod sit Dominus Davidis: quem enim alium David pro Domino suo agnovit, præter Deum, unde Dei- tatem suam ex his verbis demonstravit Christus Matth. 22, 45. seqq. Marc. 12. 36. Luc. 20, 42. 43. (quod argumentum ab intrinseca evidentia vim convin- cendi habuit a gratia speciali Christi in corda ope- rantis, ubi Hackspanius talia testimonia V. T. quæ pro Deitate Christi ab ipso Christo & Apostolis al- lata sunt, in gratiam Calixti sui nuper elidere cona- tus est in notis Philol. Theol. part. 2. p. 321: quod sedeat ad dextram Dei, (nulli enim Angelorum hoc dictum esse, nedum hominem, penes Ebræos ipsos quondam in confesso erat Ebr. 1, 13. ideo hoc de Messia dictum esse, agnoscentibus ipsismet Phari- sæis, Christus testatus est Matth. 22, 24. quod & Pau- lus 1. Cor. 15, 25. Ebr. 1, 13. c. 10, 13. velut indubium as- sumsit) quod virga virtutis ejus e Zion ita emissa, ut dominaretur in medio inimicorum suorum: poneretque inimicos omnes scabellum pedum suorum: (in quo illa impleta, nisi in Messia, teste ipso Christo nostro, sanctoque Apostolo, locis antea laudatis) quod po- pulum tam spontaneum cultorem habeat in sanctis or- natibus, spiritualibus sacrificiis ipsum venerantem, filios nempe suos spirituales, innumerabili multitu- dine terram universam replentes, instar roris, ex u- tero auroræ procreati. Quis & Rex simul in Zion, & Pontifex fuit unquam, aut esse potuit, salva constitu- tione divina, præter hunc spiritualem Regem in Isra- el? Quis Pontifex secundum ordinem Melchisedech, nisi Christus noster ? Quis Pontifex in æternum præter hunc unicum N. Testamenti Pontificem ? De nullo certe ista ne secundum typum vel instar umbræ & figuræ dici possunt, in nullo vel leviter saltim adumbrata ea fuisse , unquam docebitur. Ideo Judæi ipsi Joh. 12,34. hæc de Messia accepere ἡμεῖς ἠκέσαμεν ἐκ τῶ νόμο ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς μένει εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα. Et Paulus ad ipsos E bræos id extra con- troversiam ponit, de solo Christo dictum c. 5,6. Ka- θὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει, σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα κα- τὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ. Et c.7,17. Μαρτυρεῖ γὰρ, ὅτι σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισε- δέκ. Atque ita etiam v. 12. Porro quis est Dominus ille, qui in die iræ suæ Reges quoscunque adversarios frangit , judicium inter gentes exercet , caput in terra multa frangit,qui de torrente in via bibit, & ideo caput exaltavit,nisi Messias? De uno enim eodemqueDo- mino hæc omnia v. 5. 6. 7. dicuntur, cum προσφω- νήσει, ad Deum Patrem directa: Dominus, inquit Hieropsaltes , ad dextram tuam (sedens) franget in die iræ suæ Reges ,judicium exercebit &c. Quo de vid. Disp.de hoc dictoDn.D.Dorschei nostri §.46.seqq. In hac tanta luce Judæos , quibus alias nimis προ- πετῶς adhærefcit , deserere coactus est Grotius, quum nihil certi penes eos invenerit, ac Calvinus ipse strenue alias Judaizans , cujus vestigiis in tali- bus insistere amat Noster, eosdem hic deseruerit. Variant enim nimis Apellæ excæcati, nec quod eli- gant, inveniunt, cum veritati locum relinquere no- lint: nonnulli apud Aben-Ezram cum autore Mi- drasch Tillim,per Dominum,cui dictum, sede a dex- tris meis, Abrahamum intelligunt, cui id acclama- rit velut Epinicion servus Eleazar , aut ut alii vo- lunt, Melchisedech, cum a victoria adversus quatuor Reges reverteretur. Alii cum R. David Kimchio, Mosen, Prophetarum,ut ait, Dominum & Sacerdotem: alii Davidem, cujus Regiam & Propheticam excel- lentiam aliquis e cantoribus descripserit. R. Salo- mon Jarchi & Abrahamum & Davidem; alii Salomo- nem, quem Propheta aliquis hoc carmine honora- rit; nonnulli Zorobabelis dignitatem, quidam deni- que Angelum custodem Davidis describi volunt : quorum vero nulli vel ἀξιώματα & elogia, vel παθήματα, quæ huic Domino in Psalmo tributa sunt, conveniunt, omnia disertissime Messiam de- signant. Quem proinde hic describi penes anti- quos Ebræos, & Christi & Apostoli tempore, extra omnem controversiam fuit,adeo ut nec ipsimetPha- risæi contrahiscere ausi fuerintMatth.22. Agnovitq; id Esaias Ben-Arama ad Gen. 47. Nusquam inveni- mus quenquam etiam Prophetarum , cujus nativitas sit prophetata ante nativitatem Patris & Matris , nisi Messia , qui est justitia nostra. Ad hocq; respexit,qui di- xit,a vulva ex utero tibi , hoc est , antequam crearetur uterus conceptus tui,prophetata fuit nativitas tua. Se- debat autem ad dexteram Dei, idque respexit, cum di- xit, sede a dextris meis. Sic in libro Midrasch Til- lim ad Ps. 18. legitur R. Joden in nomine R. Hama dixisse: Futurum est, ut Deus sanctus & benedictus se- dere faciat Regem Messiam ad dextram suam,sicut scri- ptum est Ps. 110. Et ad Ps. 2. narrata dicuntur myste- ria Regis in Ps. 110. Dixit Dominus Domino meo &c. Genebrardus Theologus Parisiens. ad hunc Psal- mum notat , veteres Rabbinos Barachia , & R. Le- vi, a R. Mosi Nahmanide Genes. 18. in hanc senten- tiam adduci. R. Obadiam in hunc Psalmum , de Christo eum exponentem Johannes Viccarsus An- glus in Decaplis suis in Psalmos exhibuit. Grotius ipse laudat hic R. Saadia Gaon ad Daniel. & in An- not. ad Matth. 22, 48. ita habet : Ad Messiam perti- nere hunc Psalmum agnoverunt Hebræi veteres :

quos sequitur Isaac Ben-Arama ad Genes. 47. qui post ortum Christianismum fuerunt , negare id ipsum cœ- perunt, solo odio Christianismi : cum tamen ipse David Kimchi, & cum eo alii, & apud Justinum, Tryphon. Psalmum 2. de Messia interpretentur, ubi de sceptro ex Sione exituro idem dicitur,quod hoc Psalmo. Ne- que vero potest ulli Regum Hebræorum aptari, quod hic dicitur de Sacerdotio. Nam manente Mosis Lege,Sa- cerdotium ab Aaronis familia transferri non poterat : unde Regi Oziæ , qui & Azarias nominatur , edictum est, non tuum est adolere, sed Aaronidarum, & pœna divinitus inflicta est, nec obedienti. Quod autem u- num objicit Kimchi, nulla prœlia ab Jesu pugnata, fa- cile solvitur, cum ipsi negare non possint,multa esse, in Prophetis præsertim, dicta figurate. Nam ut de membris Dei nihil dicam, montem Domini elevatum iri supra montes alios , & feras cum pecudibus stabula- turas aliter, quam verba sonant, intelligunt, qui in- ter ipsos naris sunt paulo emunctioris: quomodo & con- vivia in regno cœlesti interpretantur Albo. Inter Christianos , tam veteres quam recentiores nemo dubitavit Psalmum hunc ad Christum pertinere. Calvinus ipse agnoscit hic celebrari Christi tam Regnum quam Sacerdotium in argumento Psalmi 1 & explicationem ita orditur : Quum de se composi- tum fuisse hunc Psalmum testetur Christus , non ali- unde quidem nobis, quam ex ejus ore petenda est certi- tudo : verum ut cesset ejus autoritas , atque etiam A- postoli testimonium, Psalmus ipse clamat, se non aliam expositionem admittere. Nam ut nobis certamen sit cum pervicacissimis quibusque Judæis, firmis rationibus extorquebimus , neque in Davidem neque in alium quempiam, excepto solo Mediatore, competere quæ hic dicuntur. Fateor quidem in Davidis persona fuisse adumbratam effigiem regni Christi : sed neque de ullis successoribus asserere potuit , Regem late dominatu- rum, qui simul Sacerdos esset, non legalis, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedech & quidem æternus. Neque enim nova & insolita Sacerdotii dignitas erigi tunc potuit, nisi ablato a Levitis honore. Nec vero in ho- minem mortalem competere potuit æternitas , cujus hic fit mentio: quia alius præter hunc unum brevi & fluxo vitæ curriculo statim honor finitur. Et ad v. 4. Versus hic evincit , non de alio quopiam haberi sermonem, quam de Christo. Hunc ergo quum in depravandis aliis Psalmis sequutus sit Grotius , in præsenti quoque Psalmo magis quam ullum alium Christo vindicando, auctoritatem ejus posthabere noluit:cuj9 etiam verba ipsa in quibusdam retinuit, ut nemini dubium esse queat, quin ipsum in glossis suis Ducem elegerit, ac præ oculis habuerit. Cum illo etiam frigide satis eminentissima in hoc Psalmo ἀξιώματα, & prædicata alia Messiam designantia explicat, ut ne hic quidem Spiritus Calvini Judai- zans sese penitus occultare potuerit : utpote quod verba illa , SEDE A DEXTRIS MEIS , hac je- juna glossa corrumpat ; securus esto fiducia mei au- xilii. Et ad vers. 4. illa , TU ES SACERDOS IN ÆTERNUM , explicet DOMINI MINI- STER. Et quæ sequuntur SECUNDUM OR- DINEM MELCHISEDECH , ita reddat ex He- bræo: Secundum meam constitutionem o Rex mi ju- ste; ac vers. 5. DOMINUS A DEXTRIS TUIS, id est , adjutor tibi est, & velut παραστάτης. Hoc enim pacto, ut reliqua taceam, argumentis tribus, iisque præcipuis, quæ invicte Psalmum hunc UNI MESSIÆ vindicant, nervus omnis inciditur , ut nullum amplius adversus Judæos robur habeant. Nam si sedere ad dextram Dei , nihil aliud est, quam securum esse fiducia auxilii Dei,Davidi,aliisque ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις id convenire , nemo ambiget.

Si Sacerdotis nomen hic ministrum Dei tantum impor- tat, Regem simul fuisse Sacerdotem etiam sub lege nihil repugnat. Si verba secundum ordinem Mel- chisedech, hoc tantum sibi volunt in fontibus, secun- dum meam constitutionem, o Rex mi juste, Davidi ea etiam competere indubium est. Neque illi ex- plicationi tum obstabunt quæ v. 5. & 6. habentur ἀξιώματα divina. Ea enim de Domino, ad cu- jus dextram sedet is, de quo sermo est, non de Do- mino ad dextram Dei sedente intelligenda erunt, juxta Grotium. Ita nihil omnino obstabit in toto Psalmo, quo minus Davidi id juxta gloffemata Gro- tiana conveniat. Neque e titulo aliud doceri po- terit, quum is juxta Ebræos, non repugnante in his quidem posterioribus suis scriptis & annotatis ad h. Psalmum Grotio, sic accipi possit, ut Psalmus ab a- lio (in honorem Davidis) cantatus, a Davide solum approbatus intelligatur. Quæ omnia cum accurata mentis trutina mecum expendo, aliter statuere non possum, quam quod Grotius, cum hæc in Psalmos annotata chartis illineret, cujuscunque antea fue- rit mentis & sententiæ, in scriptis nempe prioribus, & commentariis ad Evangelia (multum enim abs se in posterioribus migrasse Grotium nimis multa evincent non solum qua controversias inter ipsos Christianos motas, sed etiam qua oracula Scriptu- ræ communi omnium Christianorum calculo Ju- dæis invicte hactenus opposita, quod etiam de hoc loco patet ex annotatis ejus ad Joh. 12,34.) de Chri- sto quidem adhuc explicandum esse Psalmum cre- diderit, sed sensu mystico & eminentiori, simul autem alium sensum, literalem nempe, & primo obvium ta- cite ingesserit, quod expresse in aliis Psalmis ab ipso factum esse, hactenus observavimus, Geminam fere corruptelam notavit B. Dn. D. Hunnius noster in Calvino, idque citra ullam injuriam (ut e Calvi- ni commentario πρὸς ὄμμα docuit in Anti-Pareo altero pag. 447.) circa vers. 1. hujus Psalmi, quod nempe illa, Dixit Dominus Domino meo, sede a dex- tris meis, aliquatenus etiam præ cunctis totius mun- di Monarchis Davidi congruant, quatenus videli- cet ipse est sacra unctione sanctificatus, ut sit vicarius Christi, quatenus item præ universis cæteris IMAGO (& typus) est unigeniti Filii Dei, & quatenus constat, illum voce & mandato, & jussu Dei ad regnum perve- nisse, etsi NON OMNI EX PARTE illa ei aptari possint: Sed quærendus sit, in quem solide competat hæc dignitas, cujus dignitatis (versu primo Psalmi hujus expresse) exigua tantum scintilla emicuit in Davide, perfecta autem claritas enituit in Christo. Unde me- rito suo hic notatus fuit Calvinus a Domino D. Hunnio: cujus ἐπίκρισιν hic meam facio ex Anti- Pareo altero p. 440. Certe qui Doctor Ecclesiæ Psal- mum 110. Christo in solidum accommodat, idque facit sincere absque contrarii erroris admissione, is talibus affirmatis de Davide Judaismum magis, quam Chri- stianismum reducentibus interpretationem non conta- minat: quemadmodum istius Calvinianæ glossæ exem- plum apud ullum scriptorem Christianum veterem aut Neotericum credo, minime reperiri posse. Sequutus tamen Præceptorem suum Musculus est; eodem modo pervertens illustre vaticinium, cum ait: in Davide imperfectum quendam typum præcessisse in eo, quod gentes finitimas devicerit, Reges eorum percusse- rit, Syros quo᾿, ad tributa reddenda coegerit, ac tandem caput urbis ac terræ Rabbah, Regem videl. occiderit, & urbem ceperit 2. Sam. 12. atque hæc omnia e Zion per- fecerit: posse enim aliqua ratione Sacerdotem quoque dici, cum propter insigne studium divini cultus, tum propterea quod populo benedixisse legitur 2. Sam. 6,18. atque hoc modo secundum ordinem Melchisedech & Rex fuerit & Sacerdos. Sanus magis hic est Rivetus, qui quum in aliis hyperaspisten Calvini egerit, pa- trocinium ei suum hoc in loco non denegat modo, sed argumentis etiam sententiam ejus profligat: Certo enim certius est, ait Rivetus in argumento hujus Psalmi, quæ hic dicuntur, de Davide, aut alio puro ho- mine INTELLIGI NON POSSE. Quod enim Angelis datum non est, cui Angelorum dixit sede ad dextram meam Ebr. 1, 5 an alicui puro homini compe- teret? Quis inter homines Sacerdos potest esse in æter- num? Davidi autem non posse tribui, evincit argumen- tum ductum ab eo, quod ejus tempore vigebat Sacerdo- tium Aaronicum; quo tempore nulla insolita & nova Sacerdotii dignitas erigi potuit. Ergo cum hic aga- tur de eo Rege, qui simul futurus esset Rex & Sacerdos, non legalis sed alterius ordinis, idque in æternum, nec talis unquam possit aliquis esse præter Messiam patribus promissum, cum in hominem mortalem non possit com- petere Sacerdotii æternitas, non est quod de objecto θεανθρώπῳ dubitemus. Omnino autem fateri o- portet, longe deterius perverti a Grotio hunc Psal- mum, quam a Calvino. Quum enim hic saltim versum primum aliquatenus Davidi convenire di- cat, Grotius non tantum eam reddit verborum illo- rum, sede a dextris meis, glossam, quæ plene & omni ex parte Davidi competat, sed Sacerdotium secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech, & de ministerio Regis juste secundum constitutionem Dei perversissima ratione, posthabita non minus S. Apostoli auctoritate, qui id de æterno Sacerdotio Messiæ penes Ebræos ipsos exposuit, & exponendum esse ceu ὁμολογουμένως certum, atque indubitatum habuit, quam propria vocum significatione, ipsorumque Judæorum con- fessione, interpretatur; ne scil. id Davidi repugnet. Quis hoc Judaicis corruptelis velificandi Cacoe- thes non detestabitur, non execrabitur toto pecto- re? Seductus autem imprimis videtur hic ab Enje- dino, Neophotiniano, qui pariter duplicem Psalmi sensum facit literalem de Davide & mysticum de Messia. Illum ex Rabbinorum commentis colligit, & non heri, sed ante Jesum Christum natum esse Em- pæcta asserit, ac Davidem dicit juxta istum sensum sedisse ad dextram Dei, id est, habuisse Deum a dextris: vocem כהן posse accipi ut non Sacerdotem, sed princi- pem notet, vocem Melchisedech posse sumi pro nomine appellativo, ita ut dicatur David Rex justitiæ, seu Rex justus, ut sit sensus: Tu David eris Rex in perpetuum, non sicut Saul, eo quod es Rex justus. Quam tamen sententiam adfert solum Enjedinus, ut artificem se detorquendi Scripturas probet, inque eo magis so- brius ac sanus fuit, quam Grotius, quod eam pro- bare ausus non fuerit: una hanc ἐπίκρισιν adjecerit: Sed hanc interpretationem nobis sequi non est tutum, neque fas. Auctor enim Epistolæ ad Hebræos voce Cohen Sacerdotem denotari affirmat: & negari non potest, sæpe eam ita in sacris usurpari. Præterea Je- su Christi Pontificatum, & Sacerdotium æternum, præ- sertim ex hoc loco, auctor ille extruit & confirmat. Ergo certum esto, hic agi de Sacerdote.

Et agnoverat olim Grotius ipse, cum annota- tiones ad Evangelistas adornaret ad Luc. 24. v. 47. Psalmum hunc de Christo & præconio Evangelii tempore N. T. cujus initium Hierosolymis futu- rum esse v. 2. prædictum sit, agere, imo in de Verit. Relig. Christ. l. 5. §. 22. docuerat aliter hunc Psalmum exponi NON POSSE. Posterior vero, inquit, (Psalm. nempe CX.) de alio quam de MESSIA exponi NON POTEST. Nam quæ recentiores Judæi alii de Abrahamo comminiscuntur, alii de Da- vide, alii de Ezechia, frivola sunt. Psalmus ipse Davidis est, ut docet Hebræa inscriptio. Quod ergo David Domino suo dictum dicit, id nec

Davidi ipsi, nec Ezechia, qui inter posteros Davidis fuit Davide nulla re excellentior, aptari potest. Abraha- mus autem sacerdotium aliquod eximium non ha- buit, imo Melchisedecus ei tanquam se minori bene precatus est. Sed & hoc, & quod additur de sceptro ex Sione orituro & perventuro in oras ultimas, plane in Messiam competit, ut loci similes de Messia haud dubie agentes patefaciunt: nec aliter acceperunt ve- tustiores Hebrai & paraphraste. E quibus addu- xit imprimis R. Saadia. Quo ergo vertiginis abre- ptus fuit spiritu, cum annotata in Psalmos scribe- ret, ut relicta veterum Ebræorum explicatione tam solida, recentiorum ineptissimam detorsionem præferre non dubitaret, & textui & interpretationi N. T. prorsus refragantem?

Vers. eod.

SEDE A DEXTRIS MEIS) Securus esto fiducia mei auxilii.

Vix audita est inter Christianos magis jejuna & frigida loci hujus tam illustris explicatio. In qua Grotium penitus Judaizare, dubium non est. Sic enim Aben-Ezra sede ad dextram meam: Confide in dextram DEI ad subjugandos hostes. Sic etiam Salomo Jarchi: Sede, id est, acquiescas in potentia mea. Sed non mirum cæcos Judæos ita interpre- tari, quum Aben - Ezra Davidi, Salomo Jarchi Ab- rahamo id dictum velit. Grotius vero agnoscit, hæc Messiæ dicta: ideoque mirari satis non possum, tam frigide ipsum sessionem Messiæ ad dextram Dei interpretari: quod sc. saltim sit, secure quiescere fi- ducia divini auxilii. Nam forte cum Francisco Davidis statuit Christum nunc, qua sedet ad dextram Dei, delitescere acquiescere saltim, nihilque operari, sed frui solum securitate sub divina protectione? Sic enim Semi-Christianus ille, uti ab ipso Socino pro- prio in oppugnanda SS. Trinitate Socienno, voca- tur, in Thesibus de munere Christi cum Antithes. Socin. editis, adjunctis disputat. de adoratione Christi F. Socir. & Christ. Francken p. 184. quum neget, Christum nunc quicquam agere, ubi ad dextram Dei sedet, interpretatur hanc sessionem, quod tuto in pro- tectione Dei quiescat, unde porro infert, nobis, ipso in quiete sua placide versari permisso, nihil ab eo nunc juvari nos posse, credendum esse. Quam impieta- tem Turcicam reprobat ipse Socinus. Refellit autem glossam illam Judaico - Mahometanam cum vis phraseos sessionis ad dextram Dei, quæ infert re- gimen divinum, ad quod evectus est Messias, vir- tutis & potestatis immensæ, atque infinitæ, utpote qui factus est Deo σύνθρονος, & in thronum Majesta- tis immensæ Dei exaltatus, eadem cum Patre vir- tute ac potestate dominatur; quod in locis Commu- nibus circa explicationem articuli hujus, & in di- sputationibus adversus Calvinianos luculentissime hactenus a nostris demonstratum est: Tum expli- catio Apostolica S. Pauli per Dominium & regi- men divinum eam sessionem exponentis 1. Cor. 15. v. 25. Nec non S. Petri, demonstrantis Davidi non convenire hanc sessionem ad dextram Dei, sed uni Christo Act. 2, 33. seqq. eamque inferre summam exaltationem, quæ per ascensionem in cœlum Christo obtigit, quæque Davidi proinde non con- veniat, vi cujus potestatem effundendi S. S. consequu- tus, & Dominus super omnia, ac Christus factus est: imo ipsius Davidis interpretatio: quia loquitur de ea sessione ad dextram Dei, per quam Messias est Dominus factus, ut a Davide Rege nullum superio- rem in terris agnoscente, pro Domino etiam ha- bendus fuerit: vi cujus omnes inimici in scabellum pedum ejus ponendi, Sceptrum verbi e Zione in totum orbem emittendum, per quam sessionem ad dex- tram Dei in medio hostium dominatur, filios spiri- tuales innumera multitudine sibi procreat, & con- secrat, Reges in die iræ, quicunque ipsi se opponunt, confringit, &c. quæ effecta, & axiomata divina divi- num regimen apertissime designant. Quid, quod Grotius ipse agnoscat verba illa, donec ponam inimi- cos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum, intelligenda esse in Messia de peccato, diabolo, imperiis multis, postremum de morte ipsa 1. Cor. 15, 25. 26. Quanquam dum hæc ita in Messia intelligenda dicit, innuat tacite fer- sum alium de Davide, licet non exprimat, quomodo illa in Davide intelligenda. Sic ergo cum de Mes- sia sessio ad dextram Dei intelligitur, (uti omnino de illo solo intelligenda est) tale dominium infert, quo non imperiis solum multis, sed etiam diabolo, peccato & morti ipsi dominatur, ad quod divinam & infinitam virtutem requiri, nemo sanus inficiari po- test. Quis ergo admittet, phrasi illa solum securi- tatem sub fiducia auxilii divini designari? Pluribus detestandam illam depravationem in aliis refellunt nostrates, & Dn. D. Dorscheus & alii. Conf. etiam fascisc. Quart. Diss. III. Dn. D. Feurbornii pag. 106. seqq.

Vers. eod.

DONEC PONAM INIMICOS SCABELLVM PE- DVMTVORVM) Mos erat in Oriente, ut victores victos pedibus suis subjicerent. Jos. 10, 24. Intelligenda hæc in Messia de peccato, diabolo, imperiis multis, postremo de morte ipsa, ut discimus 1. Cor. 15, 25. 26.

Ita hæc in Messia intelligi vult: aliter vero in Davide. Quapropter non modo genuinum subje- ctum hic introducit, ubi de uno tantum subjecto agi & Psalmi συνέχεια convincit, & Christus ipse con- tra Pharisæos Matth. 22. demonstravit, ut nullum verbum respondere possent. Habuissent autem quod reponerent, si sententia Grotiana obtinuerit: Sed & prædicata eadem iisdem verbis prolata diver- so sensu accipit, quod est unicam, propriam & ger- manam a Sp. S. intentam sententiam evertere vel certe dubiam reddere.

## 110:2
Verse 2.

THE ROD OF THY STRENGTH) That is, the scepter, in the way the Greeks translated the word מטה 1 Sam. 14, 44 Hab. 3, v. 8. RULE THOU IN THE MIDST OF THINE ENEMIES) That is, you shall rule within hostile borders. Because the discourse is uniquely about Christ, the dominion is to be understood not of finite strength and power, but of infinite and immense, not within the borders of an earthly province, but in the midst of enemies, both spiritual and bodily, whosoever they may be, to which Christ was raised through his exaltation to the right hand of God, inasmuch as this sublimity is so great that it leaves behind it by a long interval all the dignity of angels and archangels, as the Holy Scriptures interpret in Heb. 1, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

VIRGAM VIRTVTIS TVÆ) Id est, sceptrum, quo- modo Græci vocem מטה transtulerunt 1. Sam. 14, 44 Abac. 3. v. 8. DOMINARE IN MEDIO INIMICORVM TVORVM) Id est, dominaberis intra fines hostiles. Quia de Christo unice sermo est, Dominium non finitæ virtutis & potestatis, sed infinitæ & im- mensæ, non intra fines provinciæ terrenæ, sed in me- dio hostium tum spiritualium tum corporalium quorumcunque intelligendum, ad quod Christus evectus est per exaltationem ad dextram Dei, ut- pote quæ sublimitas tanta est, ut omnem angelorum & archangelorum dignitatem longo post se relin- quat intervallo, interprete S. S. Ebr. 1, 6.

## 110:3
Verse 3.

WITH THEE IS THE PRINCIPALITY IN THE DAY OF THY POWER IN THE SPLENDORS OF THE SAINTS: FROM THE WOMB BEFORE THE MORNING STAR HAVE I BEGOTTEN THEE) Ἡ ἀρχὴ, which is here in the Greek, signifies both principality and beginning. Therefore, this interpreter took one meaning for the other here, unless he said beginning for principality, just as pontificium is said. Furthermore, the Greeks read עמך with a chirek under the first letter, which we read with a patach. That word חיל sometimes indeed signifies strength, but more often an army. The sense from the Hebrew will be best expressed thus: Thy people shall be most ready, in the day of battle most beautifully prepared. The dew (that is, the seed) of thy offspring (that is, from whence offspring shall be born to thee) shall be as the dew from the womb of the dawn. Thy seed shall be no less fruitful than the morning dew. קדש signifies not only to sanctify, but also to prepare, as in Num. 11, 18, and it is used specifically for preparation for war in Jer. 6, 4, where the Greeks translate קדשו as παρατάξασθε. By the name of dew, the Hebrews call seed by an elegant metaphor: hence that noble κρύσις in Cant. 5, 3. See also Isa. 26, 29. The same people, by a no less apt metaphor, attribute a womb to the dawn, as they do to other things in Job 38, 8 and 28.

We do not much disapprove of this explanation: yet, so that it may be more fully established, it is helpful to bring here what we once commented on regarding this verse in our inaugural dissertation, Rostock, page 77. Concerning this passage, there exist very diverse opinions, especially regarding the latter words: which the ancient Doctors of the Church interpreted concerning the birth of Christ himself. Tertullian indeed concerning the temporal birth from the Virgin Mary; but almost all other Greeks and Latins concerning the eternal birth from the substance of the Father. But most modern Doctors explain the same regarding the spiritual birth of the mystical Christ. Isaac Amama agrees with Tertullian, explaining the same thus in chapter 47, 19. קודם שיברא שחם יולדתך נתנבא יולדתך i.e., before the womb of your mother was created, your birth was prophesied. And Galatinus, who cites these things in book 3, de arc. Cath. verit. c. 17, understanding the Mother of Christ through the dawn, and Christ through the dew coming forth from the womb of the dawn; and B. Meisner follows the same opinion in his Commentary on Hosea, c. 14, p. 1245. Bellarmine and Genebrardus, among others, embrace the second exposition from the Papists; Jos. Simlerus from the Reformed; D. Gesnerus, etc., from our own. Luc. Osiander joins both in this way: From the womb, before the dawn, (you were begotten from eternity according to the Deity: but by reason of humanity) is to you the dew of birth (you were conceived in the womb of the Virgin just as the dew once descended onto the fleece of Gideon) so that the incarnation of the eternal Son of God is treated here. The patrons of the third interpretation are D. Luther, Dn. Bugenhagius, and Tilem. Heshusius, etc. The first relies solely on the Greek version, which is the LXX, and the Latin, which is commonly ascribed to Jerome: the former of which renders the Hebrew words thus: ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσφόρε ἐγγένησά σε. It expresses these same things thus: From the womb before the Morning Star I have begotten you. The second is defended furthermore from the authentic text, but with unequal success. Bellarmine, for his own authority, removes two words from these five, and changes two words, both as to letters and as to vowels, so as to extort a sense conformable to the LXX and the Vulgate version. Genebrardus leaves the Hebrew words in their place, and strives to prove that the LXX merely followed their sense. Gesnerus, our own, demonstrates this somewhat more accurately from the sources, who may be seen in his Commentary on the Psalms, p. 741. The Syriac and Arabic versions also seem to support this interpretation. For the former has it thus: from the beginning (from eternity) I have begotten you as a child. But the latter thus: From the womb before the morning star I have begotten you. The third flows from the sources: But Bugenhagius also strives to prove that it agrees with the Greek version, p. 653, Commentary on the Psalms.

Before this is confirmed, I add yet another, peculiar to Vatablus; concerning the communication of divine grace with the human nature of Christ; that is, that the dew of his birth is that grace which was given to him by the Father while he was assuming flesh, even from the womb and from the beginning of his birth. Perhaps he followed the Chaldean interpreter, who rendered these words thus: רחמין דאלהא יסתהדבון לך היך נחתת טלא יתבון לרווחצן תולדתך : i.e., The mercies of God will delight in you, like the descent of dew, they will reside for the confidence of your generation, or your descendants. For grace befell Christ as a man, so that we all might receive from his fullness through faith in him χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτος, John 1:16. Thus, the interpretation would indeed be clever and pleasant, but less suitable to the text than that of B. Luther. Who, according to the letter, has it thus, if it is explained entirely according to the proper force of the words: Your people (will be) liberalities or voluntary offerings; or a people of voluntary offerings, of liberalities, of spontaneous acts, in the day of your strength (or of your army and your forces) in the ornaments (or in the places of beauty) of holiness, from the matrix of the dawn, or before the womb of the dawn: To you (will be) the dew of your youth: (or from the womb of the dawn to you the dew of your youth) whence it is clear that two things are predicted here concerning the Messiah. For to interpret this Psalm concerning anyone other than Christ is to contradict Christ and his Apostles to their faces, who wished to guard against that more than ten times by their own authority. See Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:36, Luke 20:42, 45, Acts 2:34, 35, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 1:13, chapter 5:6, chapter 7:17 and 21, chapter 10:13, so that it is a wonder that Calvin departs into a different view here. For whose sake we append the censure of the Calvinist Erasmus Rudingerus, who says: This Psalm, without any type and expressly, is a prophecy concerning the person and kingdom of Christ. And I do not think one should even attempt to refer anything historically to David in this Psalm by any interpretation. Nor can anything be said in this genre that could be glorious for such an interpreter. With which we also agree. And so that we may return to where we digressed, we assert that two things are said here concerning the Messiah, insofar as he is King. The first is the promptness of the people: The second is the multitude of those born. For on one side the duty of the subjects is noted, on the other the benefit of the King. The former consists in prompt obedience and due reverence for the King: The latter is hinted at by paternal affection and the august expansion of the kingdom.

Regarding the duty and obedience of the subjects in the first clause of this passage, three things are indicated: (1.) the voluntary principle, a most prompt and devoted spirit. Your people shall be spontaneous acts and voluntary offerings; or your people shall be spontaneous acts, that is, according to the Hebrew phrasing, most prompt and voluntary for obedience (the abstract placed for the concrete, and the plural for the singular, which has a peculiar energy for denoting excellence: See concerning the abstract Gen. 3:6, c. 12:3, c. 26:35, c. 46:34, 1 Sam. 15:6, Ps. 39:6, Ez. 35:15, Luke 16:15, Job 17:17, Rom. 1:16, 2 Cor. 5:21, Eph. 5:8, etc.; concerning the plural, see Gen. 19:11, Ps. 42:6, Ps. 43:5, Ps. 45:16, Ps. 49:4, Ps. 89:2, Lam. 3:2, Rom. 12:1, 2 Cor. 1:3, Ps. 90:10, Prov. 1:20, c. 11:14, c. 9:1, Eccles. 5:6, Mic. 5:1, Nah. 2:6, Matt. 2:20, c. 9:8, 1 Pet. 3:2, Jas. 1:17; concerning the abstract and plural together, see Ps. 5:11. Ps. 87, 6. Cant. 4, 16. Dan. 9, 23. &c.) which are most pleasing offerings to God: 1. Sam. 15, 22. Jer. 7, 22. 23. Hos. 6, 6. & Ps. 1, 14. following, and endowed with a most liberal spirit, such as it befits Princes to have; according to that of Isa. 32, 8. נדיב נדיבות יעץ cf. Exod. 19, 6. 1. Pet. 2, 9.

Joh. Coccejus in the last [chapter] of Moses §. 1024. thus renders v. 3. Thy people is a voluntary offering in the day of thy strength: The people of Christ, he says, is a sacrifice. For this is altogether a simpler explanation than any other, Cf. Isa. 18. a gift shall be offered to the Lord, a people Isa. 66, 28. They shall offer your brethren out of all nations as a gift to the Lord Hos. 14. ver. 3. Rom. 12, 1. (II.) The time of obedience, the day of the strength of the Messiah, or of his army and forces. That respect is had to the N. T. there is no doubt: Whether the time of exaltation and glory is described in general in this way: as Mr. Bugenhagen explains it, while meanwhile the enemies are unwilling to be subject, with thee, O Christ, shall be the Principality: i. e. The people of thy kingdom shall be with thee. Spontaneous, not forced, (for thus he explains the Greek version from the sources; thy people shall be spontaneous offerings, or shall be liberal offerings) in the day of thy power, i. e. in the time of thy strength and kingdom. For in the time of thy infirmity, i. e. in thy mortal life thou shalt rather be a servant, and shalt appear the last of men, than a Prince: Whether in particular the time of the primitive

Of the Church, which B. Luth.'s version Nach deinem Sieg seems to imply, looking not so much at the words as at the sense: For after Christ had fought most fiercely with his spiritual enemies in his bloody passion, and had gloriously triumphed over them in his victorious resurrection, then at last his strength shone forth, and the day of his power arose; where he sent forth into the whole world a huge army of evangelizers Ps. 68, 11. Mark 16, 15. who would enlist spiritual soldiers and lead out their forces as leaders, under the auspices of the supreme Emperor, to do battle against the devil, the world, and the flesh. For there they flocked in crowds from the whole world, to profess their names for the sacred militia in great numbers, and to form huge forces and most well-equipped armies: see Acts 2, 21.

(III.) The manner of subjection and obedience is insinuated by the words בהדרי־קדש and consists in faith and holiness. For these are the sacred garments which befit a holy and royal priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ 1 Pet. 2, 5. 9. Rev. 5, 10. Cf. Ez. 17, 14. Mic. 2, 9. where this same word הדרי is said of priestly adornment. This is the most holy adornment with which spiritual soldiers, led out into battle and armed by the supreme Emperor, the Messiah, with the powerful word of God, are adorned, inasmuch as he clothes them with his own righteousness and endues them with the beauty of most holy virtues. See Isa. 61, 10.

Gal. 3, 27. Eph. 4, 22. Col. 3, 10. 12. Rev. 19, 8. etc. From the womb of the dawn, which R. Aben-Ezra interprets מעת עלות השחר from the time of the ascent of the dawn: from which light first shone forth in the heart of each one from the darkness 2 Cor. 4, 6. and the morning star arose for him, 2 Pet. 1, 19. just as the day approaches when the darkness of night is dispelled. Rom. 13, 11. 12. Cf. Eph. 5, 8. 1 Thess. 5, 4. and thus from the first time of anyone's regeneration. Or definitely concerning the first time of Apostolic preaching, which with respect to the subsequent day was like the dawn; or before the womb of the dawn, so that regard may be had for the splendor of holiness, which surpasses the splendor of the dawn, at its very beginning, where, namely, the dawn blushes as the stars are put to flight, as Virgil speaks in Aeneid III. Thus Mic. 6, 3. The going forth of the Lord is said to be כשחר like the dawn; indeed, the rise of the preaching of the Gospel is like the dawn, not only by reason of speed, because it arises suddenly: Cf. Isa. 58, 8. and by reason of the increase of light, because it increases continuously, so that no one can hinder it, although he can deprive himself of it: but also by reason of beauty: as D. Luth. rightly says, He will break forth like the beautiful dawn. Cf. Ps. 19, 6. Thus, therefore, the people of the Messiah shine with the splendors of holiness more than the splendor and beauty of the ascending dawn.

And thus stands the first clause, if indeed the accent Athnach here performs its distinctive office. Which, however, others neglect, because it sometimes does not distinguish in the Psalms: e.g., Psalm 113, 1. 2. and because here more regard ought to be had for the thing itself, and since in the other clause mention is made of birth, therefore what is said about the womb should be joined; who therefore read thus: from the womb of the dawn to you is the dew of your birth. Furthermore, they demonstrate by no single example that the word ילדות is taken for birth; which it is established is used for boyhood and youth. Eccles. 11, 9. 10. Elsewhere, however, it does not occur in this form. But that the womb must be taken metaphorically here is manifest. Whence it remains that there is no reference here to birth properly so called.

The latter clause speaks, however, as I said, of the office of the King Messiah, the august expansion of his kingdom, and his fatherly affection toward his subjects, where mention is made of the multitude of his sons. For that a multitude is denoted metaphorically by the word dew is clear from 2 Sam. 17, 12. We will fall upon him, as the dew is wont to fall upon the ground, i.e., with a huge army and a very great multitude of soldiers. But the abstract word יַלְדוּת is taken for the concrete, in a manner most customary to the Hebrews, just as nations are called ἀκροβυσία, and Jews περιτομή. Rom. 2, 26. ch. 3, 11. 20. and it is also customary among the Latins for youth to be used for a youth, or collectively for a group of youths, as prince of youth, all the youth. Thus, therefore, the dew of youth will be the multitude of youths or boys, born and sons of the Messiah, namely; יַלְדֻתֶךָ who are born of your youth, O Messiah, (which the word ילד and the relative particle imply). Therefore, for the sake of greater emphasis, the pronoun לְךָ to you is added, which looks partly to the origin which the faithful have from Christ, as his sons and seed Psalm 22, 31. Isaiah 53, 10. partly to the end for which they are regenerated by Christ, by the power of the Spirit, namely, that they may be his own and his people. To you the dew of your youth, or of your sons, O Messiah! To you and to your worship they are regenerated. Cf. Isa. 8, 18. Heb. 2, 13. The sense, therefore, is briefly this: An innumerable multitude of the sons of the Messiah will be born to him, and will appear dispersed throughout the whole world, no differently than dew falling from heaven is wont to cover the whole earth in great abundance. Cf. Isa. 55, 1. Those who join the preceding words explain this clause not unaptly thus: Just as dew is born in a wonderful way from the womb of the dawn, or from the dawn as if pregnant and bringing forth this offspring, and falls at dawn, covering the whole earth, so will an innumerable multitude of sons be born to the Messiah from the womb of the Church, throughout the whole earth. Whom he himself as Father will cherish and embrace as sons, and will keep for himself eternally. How well Luther: Your children will be born to you, like the dew from the dawn. But if one should wish to refer it again specifically to the time of the primitive Church, the fulfillment will be had in Acts 2, 41. ch. 4, 32. Colos. 1, 6. Thus, therefore, it is clear that not only is the universal Church asserted to be the Messiah's as King, as his own people, but also that all the faithful are his children, whom he begets for himself in a spiritual and wonderful way, so that he is deservedly called their Father.

We further advise this; that B. Luther and several other interpreters understand the words 'womb of the dawn' as the womb of the Church, especially that which existed at the beginning of the New Testament: so that by Christ the Spiritual Father, the mother, the Church, is designated: inasmuch as she is the Bride and spouse of Christ. Psalm 45:10. Psalm 68:13. Isaiah 54:5, chapter 62:4-6. Hosea 2:16, 19. John 3:28. Ephesians 5:26. Revelation 19:7, and the mother of the faithful, Psalm 45:17. Isaiah 60:4. Galatians 4:26. 'Christ's wife and bride,' says B. Luther in his commentary on this passage, T. 8. Germ. Witteb. fol. 578, 'and queen is called the dawn, that is, the Christian Church; from that same mother or body his children come to him.' To which may be referred that which is said in Canticles 6:9, that the Church of the New Testament advances like the rising dawn. As the dawn receives its splendor from the Sun, so the Church receives its splendor from Christ; as from the womb of the dawn, or while it is pregnant, dew is generated in a wonderful way: so the Church, rendered fruitful by the grace of God, generates children for Christ in a wonderful way. John 1:13. Isaiah 66:8. Whence Luther, loc. cit., 'He calls these same children the dew, because no soul is converted and transformed from the sinful childhood of Adam into the grace-filled childhood of Christ by human work, but solely through the operation'

God's from heaven down, like the dew. They therefore render this meaning: From the womb of the Church, especially at the beginning of the New Testament, as if at dawn, when after the darkness of ignorance and sins the light of the Gospel will first reach the nations, there shall be generated for you (O Messiah) the dew of your mystical youth, that is, a great multitude of spiritual children, or recent Christians, like dew: so that thus the primitive Church of the New Testament may be called the dawn, and similarly the primitive Christians may be designated by the name of childhood or youth. See D. Christoph. Schlegel's Regium Christi Sacerdot. or explanation of Psalm 110, p. 192 et seqq.

These things concerning a most difficult passage: of which many other interpretations are still found. Among the Jews, R. Moses indeed thinks that the vigor of David and the richness of the sap or the succulence of his body in old age, still green and vigorous, is compared to dew; thus rendering it: from the eruption of the dawn is left to you the sap of your youth. Aben-Ezra cites this explanation: from a humble and dark place you have received the lot of your youth, as if he were saying, you, a youth, have been advanced from an obscure condition to the royal pinnacle. But Arnold Bootius rightly says of these glosses in his Sacris Animadversionibus on the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, book II, chapter X, II. 1. These two expositions are so forced, and so poorly consistent with the Hebrew words, nay, so foolish and insipid, that they in no way deserve to be mentioned. Unless it were to appear to what insipid and ridiculous glosses and inventions the doctors of the faithless nation are often reduced; where they attempt to elude the most illustrious testimonies concerning Christ our Savior, and are unwilling to open their eyes or yield to the clearest truth. Not much better is the gloss of R. Aben-Ezra, who, taking the Psalm concerning David, renders these things thus: When the dawn rises, (your people) will come like the dew, which you were accustomed to see in your youth, when you bore the care of pasturing the flock: or R. David Kimchi, who likewise interprets it concerning David in this way; from the womb you came forth to the kingdom and the dew of blessing was yours at that very dawn (with which R. Jehu's explanation agrees); or Solomon Jarchi, who explains it concerning Abraham in this way; with holy adornments from the womb, from the projection; this will happen to you by merit of the holy adornment, which was in you from your mother's womb (for he had knowledge of the Creator here, when he was only three years old) from the womb, (from the projection) from which you fell from the womb: To you the dew of your childhood, that is, your childhood will be imputed to you: the upright morals and virtues, to which you accustomed yourself in your childhood, will be for your recreation, just as dew recreates and is sweet. However, there is no reason to linger in refuting these trifles of the Jews. For it is too clear from the Psalm that it cannot be taken either of David or of Abraham, neither of whom was raised to the right hand of GOD, neither of whom was of such power as is celebrated here, neither of whom performed the priesthood, let alone has an eternal Priesthood. Among Christian interpreters, however, R. Kimchi's explanation was approved by some, but in such a way that they accepted these things concerning the Messiah: August. Steuchus: From the womb from the dawn to you the dew of your nativity. But the sense according to many Hebrews is from the womb, that is, from birth and from the dawn, that is, from that light by which you came forth, was the dew of your nativity, that is, you were bedewed with the dew of heaven, with heavenly grace, from the day you were born and conceived you were anticipated with happy dew and blessing, the abundance of heavenly graces descended upon you. To which we have previously said Vatablus's explanation also tends. Nor does Marianus's interpretation differ much regarding the sense: From the dark (or shadowy) womb to you the dew of your childhood: that is, when you were conceived in the matrix of the virgin, which place, being filled with no light, is wont to be most dark, nevertheless the dew, that is, divine grace, was present to you. Arnold Bootius boasts of a new explanation, and says that no interpreter, at least of the more recent ones, has yet attained the mind of this oracle, as far as the whole is concerned. Concerning which he is very laborious in book II of his Animadversions, chapter VIII, book X, XI, XII. The whole interpretation, however, comes to this: You will have voluntary soldiers, when you gather an army in the citadel of Zion. Because he wants the word 'am to mean soldiers: but he takes the words 'be-yom chayil' as 'on the day of the army,' not when the troops are led on an expedition, as the Tigurines, Tremellius, and Piscator do, or when they are reviewed, as others do; but when they are conscripted, with the old English, both French versions, and Agellius, Schindler, Genebrard, and Kimchi; through the words 'be-hadre qodesh' he understands not the adornment of holiness, but the holy place or sanctuary, not indeed the temple, but either the city of Jerusalem or rather the citadel of Zion: and he wants these words to be an epexegesis of the preceding ones: the scepter of your power Jehovah will send forth from Zion, as if he were saying, from Zion having set out for war you will defeat all your enemies with the greatest prosperity, and with them subjugated to you, you will extend your power and dominion far and wide, as one leading valid troops and a voluntary soldier, who by no means gave his name to you forced or unwillingly, but offered himself to you of his own accord and promised his service, when, preparing for war in that holy place, the citadel, I say, of Zion, you conscripted an army after a selection was announced. And thus he wants the first clause to be understood: but he explains the other thus and joins it to the preceding, as if he were saying: You had such voluntary troops, because you were never, not even in your first age, involved in the ignorance of men on account of humility and obscurity, but from earliest infancy you acted in the clearest light, and those things happened around you and were seen in you, which would turn the minds of all and fill the mouths of all with the fame of your name. He therefore renders the sense of the words of the latter clause thus: from the beginning you had the highest clarity and your infancy was dewy. But this interpretation of Bootius, who has recalled the interpretations of all under the censor's rod, deserves censure altogether. Which is suspect first of all by its very novelty: for he judges that no interpreter, at least of the more recent ones, has attained the mind of David, therefore he departs from all recent interpreters. He has no one among the ancients who has interpreted it in this way. Furthermore, it does not agree with the words of the Prophet: Bootius acknowledges that the noun עמ in its common and most well-known meaning denotes a people: why then does he introduce for it another, doubtful and less customary meaning, contrary to the opinion of all interpreters, so that it denotes not a people, but soldiers? Nor is any reason given why this should not be understood as the day on which troops are led on an expedition, and why Kimchi’s explanation, "on the day you shall assemble the army," should be preferred: or why the words of David should not be explained as referring to the ready obedience of the subjects of the Messiah, rather than the exposition of Rivet, Junius, Moller, and Calvin himself, given the force of the word נדבות, which he acknowledges that it agrees very well and sufficiently represents the principal scope of the Prophet. But that the Metaphor used is taken not from the prompt obedience which subjects show to a king, but from the promptness and alacrity with which men give their names to a leader gathering an army and desire and undertake military service under him, is asserted without any proof. What of the fact that it is not so consistent with the analogy of faith; nay, what that about the promptness of giving names to the Messiah savors of Pelagianism, and Bootius seems to have been incautiously seduced to that sense by the Jews, R. Solomon in particular, who rendered it thus: when you gather an army to pursue them, your people will offer themselves to you willingly, and those who love you. And indeed those things which Bootius has at length about the allegory of volunteer soldiers cannot easily be applied to the sacred militia without suspicion of Pelagianism. Furthermore, as הדרי קדש is entirely new, so it is extremely forced to understand it in this place as the magnificent fortress of Zion. For although Bucer also understands the splendors or magnificences of the sanctuary and through them Jerusalem, as does Vatablus in the splendors of holiness, that is, in the splendid city of Jerusalem, to which Deodatus also adds: yet no one believed that the fortress of Zion was designated here by קדש, and Bootius judges that almost all Interpreters have been deceived by the ambiguity of this word, so that they did not attain the sense of this clause. And why would the Prophet call the fortress of Zion here by that excellent epithet, a decorous sanctuary; if indeed that pertains nothing to the choice itself here, as Bootius admits, since individual words in this Prophetic Psalm have been used with the greatest choice. Then indeed who will believe that these sound the same, and were said κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν, Jehovah will send forth the scepter of your power from Zion, and your people [will be] voluntary in the day of your army, in the decor of holiness or of the sanctuary? Furthermore, the Athnach accent is not only neglected by Bootius, but the latter part, which that author constitutes as a hemistich, is also torn apart against the opinion of the remaining Interpreters, for he affirms that it consists of two distinct members, contrary to what ALL OTHERS have thought hitherto, who unanimously took it for one colon: so that the former is מרחם משחר לך, but the latter is טל ילדותך. Moreover, most take those words מרחם משחר in the state of regimen and understand the dawn. But this new Interpreter constructs and explains it thus: from the first rising, splendor, or clarity of the dawn for you: and further he thinks it is taken metaphorically here for the celebrity of fame and the amplitude and clarity of a name. But where is the word משחר ever taken thus in the sacred writings? And how does such a great celebrity of fame and amplitude of name suit the first rising of the Messiah, who was born in poverty? Certainly that splendid and most clear fame does not agree with the state of humiliation, which was not so clear and illustrious from the first rising, much less conspicuous and remarkable. Which sense Bootius wishes to be here. Now as for the latter member, according to the Bootian distinction, but one no less repugnant to Hebrew Codices than to all Interpreters: that טל ילדותך has this sense, your infancy was dewy, and by that it is signified that Christ from his earliest infancy flourished with all graces and gifts, just as plants bathed in abundant dew widely grow green and mature, whence will it be taught? Who will allow himself to be persuaded that that מרחם משחר לך is in some way the same as טל ילדותך, which he himself asserts on page 262, unless perhaps he was born under a Bootian sky? And how will those glosses agree with the text or the scope of the Prophet, who prophesied about King Messiah sitting at the right hand of GOD and fighting against enemies, and about his subjects; but not about the first rising or infancy of Christ? Thus therefore ὀδὲν ὑγιὲς in that new interpretation of the Doctor Physician: who undertook that Luther, the Old English and Spanish version, what? The interpretations of all should not be cared for, but agitated, little mindful of that Vulgate: Physicians promise, smiths handle smith's work.

We must return to Grotius the Jurist. In whose translation we find these things lacking. First, that he interprets the day of the army as the day of battle: when nevertheless he wishes to seem to render word for word. Then that he takes the word קדש, which is a noun, as a verb or Participle: and renders it by a new interpretation prepared, when it denotes holiness or a sanctuary, and since the preceding word בהדרי is placed in the state of construction, it must necessarily be rendered in the ornaments of humility. Furthermore, that he takes those בהדרי adverbially; as if he were saying, most beautifully. Furthermore also, that he explains the name of dew, once placed, in two ways; as if it were taken once properly of the dawn and then also used through translation for seed: dew, that is, the seed of your offspring shall be, as dew from the womb of the dawn. Nor has it been shown yet where seed is understood by the name of dew. Certainly in the place of Canticles 5, verse 2, this meaning does not fit at all. For what sense would it be, my head is full of dew, that is, of seed? Nor is seed designated by the name of dew in Isaiah 25, verse 19. The dew of lights is your dew. No sense would emerge from this again: the seed of lights is your seed. The discourse is not about seed for him, but the name of dew is taken once properly; then indeed metaphorically, as if he were saying, just as dew falling upon herbs (for אורות denotes herbs and green vegetables) makes them grow, so the dew of grace falling upon dry bones will make them revive, as it is said in Isaiah 66, verse 14: Your bones shall germinate like an herb.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

TECVM PRINCIPIVM IN DIE VIRTVTIS TVÆ IN SPLENDORIBVS SANCTORVM: EX VTERO ANTE LVCIFERVM GENVI TE) Ἡ ἀρχὴ quod hic in Græco est, & principatum significat & principium. Sumsit ergo hic interpres significationem alteram pro altera, nisi principium dixerit pro principatu, sicut pontificium dicitur. Præterea legerunt Græci עמך cum chirek sub prima litera. quod nos cum patach legimus. Illud חיל inter- dum quidem fortitudinem, sed sæpius exercitum significat. Sensus ex Hebræo sic optime exprimetur: Populus tuus promptissimus erit, in die prælii pulcherrime præparatus. Ros (id est, semen) prolis tuæ (id est, unde proles tibi nascetur) erit ut ros ab utero auroræ. Non minus erit fœcundum se- men tuum, quam ros matutinus. קדש non sanctificare, tan- tum, sed & præparare significat, ut Num. 11, 18. & speciatim de præparatione ad bellum usurpatur Jerem. 6, 4. ubi קדשו Græci vertunt παρατάξασθε. Roris nomine semen ele- ganti translatione appellant Hebræi: inde σεμνὴ illa κρύ- σις Cantic. 5, 3. Vide & Esa. 26, 29. Iidem non minus apta translatione uterum tribuunt auroræ, ut & rebus aliis Job. 38, 8. & 28.

Non multum improbamus hanc explicatio- nem: ut tamen de ea plenius constet referre huc ju- vat, quæ de hoc versu commentati olim sumus in Dissert. nostra inaugurali dissertat. Rostoch. 1. pag. 77. Super hoc loco diversissimæ extant sententiæ, præ- sertim quoad posteriora verba: quæ veteres Eccle- siæ Dd. de ipsius Christi nativitate interpretati sunt. Tertullianus quidem de temporali e virgine Maria; cæteri vero pene omnes Græci & Latini de æterna e Patris substantiâ. At de Christi mystici nativitate spirituali eadem exponunt plerique Dd. moderni. Cum Tertulliano facit Isaac Amama, eadem sic ex- ponens in cap. 47, 19. קודם שיברא שחם יולדתך נתנבא יולדתך h. e. antequam crearetur uterus genitricis tuæ, prophetata fuit nativitas tua. Et Galat. qui hæc allegat lib. 3. de arc. Cath. verit. c. 17. per auroram Matrem Christi, per rorem ex utero auroræ prodeuntem Christum intelligens; sequitur que eandem sententiam B. Meisnerus in Comment. in Hos. c. 14. p. 1245. Alteram expositionem ample- ctuntur e Pontificiis Bellarminus & Genebrardus, alii- que: e Reformatis Jos. Simlerus: e nostris D. Ges- nerus &c. Luc. Osiander utramque conjungit, hoc modo: De utero, ante auroram, (ab æterno genitus es secundum Deitatem: ratione autem humanita- tis) es tibi ros nativitatis (perinde conceptus es, in utero Virginis, sicut ros descendit olim in vellus Gi- deonis) ut ita de incarnatione Filii Dei æterni hic agatur. Tertiæ interpretationis Patroni sunt D. Lutherus, Dn. Bugenhagius, & Tilem. Heshusius, &c. Prima nititur unice versione Græca, quæ LXX. & Latina, quæ Hieronymo vulgo adscribitur: quarum illa sic reddit verba Hebræa: ἐκ γαστρὸς πρὸ ἑωσ- φόρε ἐγγένησά σε. Hæc eadem ita exprimit: Ex utero ante Luciferum genui te. Altera defendi- tur insuper e textu authentico, sed dispari successu. Bellarminus pro autoritate sua e quinque istis verbis duo demit, duo verba immutat, qua literas, qua vocales, ut sensum extorqueat versioni LXX. & vul- gatæ conformem. Genebrardus vocibus Ebraicis suum relinquit locum, earumque sensum duntaxat sequutos esse LXX. probare annititur. Quod paulo accuratius demonstrat Gesnerus noster e fon- tibus, qui videatur in Comment. super Pf. p. 741. Pro qua interpretatione etiam facere videtur ver- sio Syriaca & Arabica. Illa enim habet ita: a prin- cipio (ab æterno) tibi puerum genui te. Hæc vero ita: Ex utero ante stellam matutinam genui te. Ter- tia fluit ex fontibus: Sed & Græcæ versioni eam convenire probare satagit Bugenhagius pag. 653. Comm. in Psalm.

Quæ antequam firmetur, addo adhuc aliam, Vatablo propriam; de gratiæ divinæ cum humana na- tura Christi communicatione; quod scil. ros nativita- tis ejus sit gratia illa, quæ donata ipsi est a Patre, dum carnem assumeret, jam inde ab utero, & a principio nativitatis ejus. Fortean sequutus est Chaldæum interpretem, qui hæc verba ita reddidit רחמין דאלהא יסתהדבון לך היך נחתת טלא יתבון לרווחצן תולדתך : h. e. Misericordiæ Dei delecta- buntur tibi, ut descensio roris, residebunt ad confi- dentiam generationis tuæ, vel posteriorum tuorum. Nam gratia obtigit Christo homini, ut nos omnes per fidem in ipsum acciperemus de plenitudine e- jus χάριν ἀντὶ χάριτο Joh. 1, 16. Sic arguta quidem & jucunda foret interpretatio, sed textui minus conveniens, quam B. Lutheri. Qui κατὰ ῥητὸν ita habet, si integre exponatur secundum propriam verborum δεινότητα: Populus tuus li- beralitates vel oblationes voluntariæ (erit; seu ob- - lationum voluntariarum, liberalitatum, spontaneita- tum populus) in die fortitudinis tuae (vel exercitus, & copiarum tuarum) in ornatibus (vel in decoris locis) sanctitatis, e matrice aurorae vel prae utero aurorae: Ti- bi (erit) ros juventutis tuae: (vel ab utero aurorae tibi ros juventae tuae) unde liquet duo hic praedici de Messia. Nam de alio quam Christo hunc Psal- mum interpretari, est Christo, ejusque Apostolis in os contradicere, qui plus quam decies id cavere voluerunt autoritate sua. Vid. Matth. 22, 24. Marc. 12, 36. Luc. 20, 42. 45. Actor. 2, 34. 35. 1. Cor. 15, 25. Ebr. 1, 13. cap. 5, 6. cap. 7, 17. & 21. cap. 10, 13. ut mirum sit Calvinum heic in diversum abire. In cujus gratiam apponimus Erasmi Rudingeri Calvi- niani censuram, qui, Hic Psalmus, ait, sine ullo typo & ex professo est prophetia de persona & regno Christi. Et ad Davidem aliquid historice referre in hoc Psalmo ne conandum quidem existimo quacunque interpreta- tione. Neque dici in hoc genere quicquam potest, quod gloriosum esse possit tali interpreti. Quibus & nos acquiescimus. Atque ut redeamus eo, unde digressi sumus, duo hic de Messia dici asserimus, quatenus Rex est. Primum est populi promptitudo: Alterum natorum multitudo. Nam ex una parte notatur subditorum officium, ex altera Regis benefi- cium. Illud consistit in prompto obsequio, debitaque Regis veneratione: Hoc vero innuitur paterno affe- ctu, & augusta regni dilatatione.

De Subditorum officio & obsequio in priori hu- jus pericopes inciso tria indicantur (1.) principium ἑκούσιον animus promptissimus & devotissimus. Erit populus spontaneitatum & oblationum voluntariarum; vel populus tuus erit spontaneitates, id est, secundum λέξιν Ebraicam, summe promptus & voluntarius ad obsequium (abstracto pro concreto, & plurali pro singulari posito, quod peculiarem habet ἐνέργειαν ad denotandum ὑπεροχὴν: Vide de abstracto Gen. 3, 6. c. 12, 3. c. 26, 35. c. 46, 34. 1. Sam. 15, 6. Ps. 39, 6. Ez. 35, 15. Luc. 16, 15. Job. 17, 17. Rom. 1, 16. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Eph. 5, 8. &c. de plurali V. Gen. 19, 11. Ps. 42, 6. Ps. 43, 5. Ps. 45, 16. Ps. 49, 4. Ps. 89, 2. Thr. 3, 2. Rom. 12, 1. 2. Cor. 1, 3. Ps. 90, 10. Prov. 1, 20. cap. 11, 14. c. 9, 1. Eccles. 5, 6. Mich. 5, 1. Nah. 2, 6. Matth. 2, 20. cap. 9, 8. 1. Pet. 3, 2. Jac. 1, 17. de abstracto & Plurali simul, vide Ps. 5, 11. Ps. 87, 6. Cant. 4, 16. Dan. 9, 23. &c.) quae sunt Deo gratissimae oblationes: 1. Sam. 15, 22. Jer. 7, 22. 23. Os. 6, 6. & Ps. 1, 14. seqq. animoque praeditus liberalissi- mo, quali decet esse Principes; juxta illud Esa. 32, 8. נדיב נדיבות יעץ conf. Exod. 19, 6. 1. Pet. 2, 9.

Joh. Coccejus in ult. Mosis §. 1024. ita reddit v. 3. Populus tuus voluntaria oblatio est in die stre- nuitatis tuae: Populus Christi, inquit, sacrificium. Nam haec est omnino simplicior explicatio, quam ulla alia, Conf. Esa. 18. offeretur munus Domino populus Esa. 66, 28. Offerent fratres vestros ex o- mnibus gentibus munus Domino Hos. 14. vers. 3. Rom. 12, 1. (II.) Tempus obsequii, dies fortitudinis Messiae, vel exercitus & copiarum ejus. Quo respectum haberi ad N. T. dubium non est: Sive in genere ita describatur tempus exaltationis & gloriae: ut exponit Dn. Bugenhagius, dum interim inimici subjecti esse nolunt, tecum, ô Christe, erit Principatus: i. e. Populus regni tui erit tecum. Spontaneus, non contrate, (sic enim explicat Graecam versionem ex fontibus; populi tui spontanei obferent, vel erunt oblationes liberales) in die virtutis tuae, i. e. in tempore fortitudinis & regni tui. Nam in tempore infirmitatis tuae, h. e. in vita mortali servus potius eris, & videberis novissimus virorum, quam Princeps: Sive in specie notetur temp9 primitivae

Ecclesiae, quod innuere videtur B. Luth. versio Nach deinem Sieg, non tam verba, quam sensum respiciens: Nam postquam Christus acerrime cum hostibus Spiritualibus depugnasset, in cruenta sua passione, & glorioso de iisdem triumphasset, in victoriosa resurrectione, tum demum emicuit fortitudo ejus, & exortus est dies virtutis ejus; Ubi in totum terrarum orbem emisit ingentem Evangelizantium exercitum Ps. 68, 11. Marc. 16, 15. qui milites spirituales conscriberent, copiasque eorum ceu ἡγέμενοι educerent, sub auspiciis summi Imperatoris, adversus diabolum, mundum, carnem, militaturas. Ibi enim confluere turmatim ex universo mundo, nomina sua profiteri sacrae militiae magno numero, ingentesque facere copias, & exercitus instructissimos: vide Act. 2, 21.

(III.) Modus subjectionis & obsequii insinuatur vocibus בהדרי־קדש & consistit in fide & sanctitate. Haec enim sunt vestes sacrae, quae decent ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον καὶ βασίλειον, ad offerendum πνευματικὰς θυσίας, εὐπροσδέκτες τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ 1. Petr. 2, 5. 9. Ap. 5, 10. Conf. Ez. 17, 14. Mich. 2, 9. ubi haec eadem vox הדרי de ornatu Sacerdotali dicitur. Hic est ornatus Sanctissimus, quo milites spirituales in aciem educti, & verbo Dei potenti armati ab Imperatore summo, Messia, exornantur, quippe qui sua ipsius justitia eosdem vestit, & virtutum sanctissimarum decore induit. Vid. Esa. 61, 10.

Gal. 3, 27. Ephes. 4, 22. Col. 3, 10. 12. Apoc. 19, 8. &c. Ab utero aurorae, quod R. Aben-Ezra interpretatur מעת עלות השחר a tempore adscensus Aurorae: ex quo primitus in corde cujusque e tenebris lux effulserit 2. Cor. 4, 6. & exorta ei fuerit Stella matutina, 2. Pet. 1, 19. uti noctis tenebris discussis dies appropinquat. Rom. 13, 11. 12. Conf. Eph. 5, 8. 1. Thess. 5, 4. adeoque a primo regenerationis cujusvis tempore. Sive definite de primo Apostolicae praedicationis tempore, quod respectu subsequentis diei instar aurorae fuit; vel prae utero aurorae, ut respectus habeatur ad splendorem sanctitatis, quod superet splendorem aurorae, sub primum ejus initium, ubi sc. rubescit stellis aurora fugatis, ut loquitur Virgilius III. Aeneidos. Ita Mich. 6, 3. Egressus Domini dicitur esse כשחר instar aurorae; nimirum ortus praedicationis Evangelii instar aurorae est, non tantum ratione celeritatis, quod subito exoriatur: Conf.
