Blessed Gesner in this place and those things at Prov. 1, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 10. INITIUM SAPIENTIÆ TIMOR DOMINI.

BEllarm. lib. 1. de Justif. c. 13. colligit inde, timo- rem Domini esse initium justificationis. Remon- strantes in Actis Synod. Dordr. p. 64. concludunt dispositiones quasdam in homine requiri, per quas idoneus redditur ad finem vel apprehendendum Ev- angelium. Respondent nonnulli ראשׁית esse idem, quod caput, vel notare id, quod primum est ratione dignitatis suæ, præstantissimum, ut Num. 24, 2. Am. 6, 6. atque ita Mariana: est prima & politissima scientia; sed quia in loco parallelo Prov. 9, 10. ex- plicite per תְּחִלַּת initium redditur concedunt nonnulli timorem servilem initium esse veræ sapien- tiæ & conversionis, ex quo vero concludi non po- test, timorem initium justificationis, aut disposi- tionem esse ad justificationem vel fidem, nam licet ordine temporis timor ille antecedat, nullum ta- men initium in justificationem vel fidem habet. Malunt tamen plerique de timore filiali hanc gno- men accipere (non abnuente Bellarm. in Com- mentar.) quia timor filialis Domini veræ ac solidæ sapientiæ initium est, quod Spiritus sapientiæ ani- mam malignam non ingrediatur. Sapientiæ, in- quam, ejus, quæ omnia consilia in rebus fecundis & adversis gubernat. B. Luther. Gloss. marginal. Wer wohl will lernen, der muss zum ersten gottfürch- tig seyn. Conf. Sirac. 19, 19. 20. Sap. 1, 4. Unde hæ- retici, qui timorem Domini ac reverentiam verbi cœlestis ex oraculis removent, ne initium quidem veræ sapientiæ habent. Conf. B. Gesner. in h. l. & quæ ad Prov. 1, 7.

## 112:1 Argument
PSALM CXII. The blessedness of the pious to be envied by the impious.

This Psalm is such as the one which precedes it, and is to be directed in an equal manner.

But the judgment of Bellarmine is too arbitrary, to whom it seems that David here in the spirit foresaw that Haggai and Zechariah returned to the people after the completed time of the captivity and admonished them how great is the happiness of a man who is just and fears God, so that by this example he might exhort others to probity, so that they might not walk into a similar captivity. Blessed Luther more correctly observes that the pious and the constancy of faith are praised here in general, and hypocrites are reproved. See his argument in Vol. 3, Wittenberg Latin, fol. 428. Thus also Blessed Gesner, Cocceius, and others: in Cocceius, however, it is to be disapproved that at verse 1, 'This man is,' he says, 'Christ' (Isa. 11, 2) 'and the Church,' although this is conveniently understood through his seed in verse 2. But the Church also has seed. By such explanations Scripture is only rendered ambiguous. It cannot be understood that both Christ and the Church are meant by the word 'man'. Nor is it a matter here of Christ, but of any faithful person fearing God, to whose seed, which the Psalmist himself explains through the generation or lineage of the upright, a blessing is promised: in whose house are wealth and riches: and those fearing the Lord who are in verse 4 is explained, namely the upright or just, and in verse 5, the beneficent: who in verse 6 are said not to fear from an evil report. Which do not so well agree with Christ.

Latin:

PSALM. CXII. Beatitudo piorum invidenda impiis.

EThic Psalmus talis est, qualis qui præcedit, parique mo- do dirigendus.

NImis autem arbitraria est crisis Bellarmini, cui videtur hic David in spiritu prævidisse Aggæ- um & Zachariam post expletum tempus captivita- tis rediisse ad populum eumque admonuisse, quan- ta sit felicitas viri justi & timentis Deum, ut hoc ex- emplo exhortetur alios ad probitatem, ut non in- cedant in similem captivitatem. Rectius B. Lu- therus observat, in genere hîc laudari pios, fidei- que constantiam, reprobari hypocritas. Vid. ejus- dem argumentum T. 3. Witteb. Lat. f. 428. Sic & B. Gesnerus, Coccejus, aliique: in Coccejo tamen im- probandum, quod ad v. 1. Vir hic est, inquit Chri- stus Esa. 11, 2. & Ecclesia, quanquam hæc per semen ipsius commode intelligitur vers. 2. Sed & Ecclesia se- men habet. Qualibus explicationibus tantum am- bigua redditur Scriptura. Non potest & Christus & Ecclesia voce viri intelligi. Nec de Christo hîc agitur, sed de fideli quovis Deum timente, cujus se- mini, quod Psaltes ipse per generationem vel prosapiam rectorum explicat, benedictio promittitur: in cujus domo opes & divitiæ sunt: & timentes illi Dominum qui sint v. 4. exponitur, nimirum recti vel justi, & v. 5. benefici: qui v. 6. dicuntur non timere à fama mala. Quæ non adeo conveniunt in Christum.

## 112:4
Verse 4. MERCIFUL AND COMPASSIONATE AND JUST. Some posit an ellipsis of the prefix ל here and render it 'from the merciful,' etc., which may have been omitted because of the series of letters of the alphabet, as Piscator, Walther, 40 questions, page 779. Others explain it in the dative as 'to the clement, pious, and just,' such as Kimchi, R. Solomon, Campensis, Bucer, Ludov. de Dieu. But it can entirely be retained with the LXX and Vulgate as a nominative, so that LIGHT is expressed, which arises for the just, namely that God himself is gracious, compassionate, and just, as Bellarmine and Cocceius explain: which seems the simplest exposition here, since there is no need for an ellipsis in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 4. MISERICORS ET MISERANS ET JUSTUS. Nonnulli ellipsin præfixi ל hic statuunt & reddunt à misericorde, &c. quod omissum sit ob seriem literarum alphabeti, ut Piscator, Walther. quadrag. quæst. pag. 779. alii exponunt in Dativo clementi, pio, & justo, utpote Kimchi, R. Salomo, Campensis, Bucer. Ludov. de Dieu. Sed retineri omnino potest cum LXX. & Vulg. nominativus, ut exprimatur LUX, quæ oritur justis, quod nempe sit Deus ipse gratiosus, miserator, & justus, ut Bellarm. & Coccejus explicant: quæ ἔκθεσις simplicissima hic videtur, quum ita nulla opus sit ellipsi.

## 113:1 Argument
PSALM CXIII. The exaltation of the humble.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXIII. Exaltatio humilium.

## 113:4
Ver. 4. HIS GLORY IS ABOVE THE HEAVENS) ἐν τοῖς ὑπερανίοις, as Paul sometimes speaks. RAISING THE NEEDY FROM THE EARTH) These things are taken from the song of Hannah, to whose history also belongs the verse which closes this Psalm.

That the times of the New Testament are regarded here appears from verses 3 and 4: where a universal proclamation throughout the world is designated, and God is said to be high above all nations, because all nations are to be subjected to Him, as Chrysostom rightly observed. Whence the argument is deservedly established by the Blessed Luther thus: It is a notable and most joyful prophecy, both concerning the kingdom of Christ being propagated from the rising of the sun even to its setting, into all the kingdoms of the world, into all nations, He commands to praise God and to preach the riches of grace, that is, the remission of sins through Christ. For He Himself is the God of the humble, the God of the afflicted, the God of those crying out and weeping, a truly lovable and pleasant σωτὴρ and God, who sits at the right hand of the majesty on high, and loves and regards the humble, the afflicted, the oppressed, the fearful, and the contrite in heart. For this is the proper office of Christ, and the work of the Kingdom of Christ, to cast down the proud, to put the wise to shame, to condemn the hypocrites and the holy. On the contrary, to exalt and lift up the humble, to enlighten the foolish, to sanctify sinners, to make the barren fruitful, to console the orphans, that is, the sorrowful and those afflicted in any way.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SUPER COELOS GLORIA EJUS) ἐν τοῖς ὑπερανίοις, ut interdum Paulus loquitur. SUSCITANS A TERRA INOPEM) Hæc sumta sunt ex Annæ cantico, ad cujus historiam pertinet & is, qui hunc Psalmum claudit versus.

REspici autem hîc tempora Novi Testamenti è v. 3. & 4. apparet: ubi præconium universale per orbem designatur, & excelsus super omnes gentes Deus dicitur, quod omnes gentes ipsi subjiciendæ sint, ut recte Chrysoft. observavit. Unde argumentum à B. Luthero merito ita constituitur: Est insignis & lætissima Prophetia & de regno Christi propagando à solis ortu, usque ad occasum, in omnia Regna orbis terrarum, in omnes Gentes, jubet laudare Deum & prædicare divitias gratiæ, id est, remissionem peccatorum per Christum. Ipse enim est Deus humilium, Deus afflictorum, Deus clamantium & lachrymantium, vere amabilis & jucundus σωτὴρ & Deus, qui ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis sedet, & amat ac respicit humiles, afflictos, oppressos, pavidos & contritos corde. Hoc enim est proprium officium Christi, & opus Regni Christi, deprimere superbos, sapientes pudefacere, damnare hypocritas & sanctos. E contra exaltare & evehere humiles, illuminare stultos, sanctificare peccatores, fœcundare steriles, consolari orphanos, id est, contristatos & quovis modo afflictos.

## 113:6
Ver. 6. RAISING THE POOR FROM THE DUNGHILL. Hence the Papists establish their so-called 'stercorary' chair, which they are accustomed to use in the election of a new Pope, but that application is most inept, and another reason for that chair is usually given, which they conceal because it is more foul than any dung, if you will pardon the expression.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DE STERCORE ERIGENS PAUPEREM. Hinc suam, quam vocant, stercorariam sellam adhiberi solitam in electione novi Papæ Papistæ staboliunt, sed & ineptissima est illa applicatio, & causa sellæ illius alia reddi solet, quam quia magis fœtida est, quam salva venia stercus ullum, dissimulant.

## 114:1 Argument
PSALM CXIV. The Jubilee of the Exodus.

Latin:

PSALM. CXIV. Jubilus Exodi.

## 114:2
Ver. 2. JUDAH BECAME HIS SANCTIFICATION. In the Hebrew, Judah is held, as a little later Israel: whence there is no reason why we should restrict it to the tribe of Judah, since by the name of Judah and Israel the whole people of God is designated, and therefore Rabbi Kimchi is not to be heard concerning Judah, that this tribe was held as the principal one because it was the first to betake itself into the Red Sea under the leadership of Nahshon.

Latin:

Vers. 2. FACTA EST JUDÆA SANCTIFICATIO EJUS. IN Ebr. Judas habetur, ut paulo post Israel: unde non est quod ad Judæ tribum restringamus, quum Judæ & Israelis nomine totus Dei populus designetur, adeoque audiendus non est R. Kimchi de Juda, quod præcipua habita sit hæc tribus, quia prima duce Nahasson se in mare rubrum contulerit.

## 114:4
Ver. 4. THE MOUNTAINS SKIPPED. In Hebrew it is 'they leaped', and Bellarmine admits that a trembling is indicated here, both because the same was the cause for the sea to flee, and the following words 'the earth was moved at the presence of the Lord' indicate terror; that, however, refers to the descent of God onto Mount Sinai from Exod. 19, v. 18. Most foolishly, however, it is taken by Mahomet to mean that God compelled the mountains to join with David in praising. See Hotting. Hist. Or. p. 62.

Latin:

Verf. 4. MONTES EXULTAVERUNT. In Ebr. est subsilierunt, & tremorem hic indicari fatetur Bellarm. tum quia idem causa maris fuit, ut fugeret, tum verba seqq. à facie Domini mota est, terrorem indicant, id autem ad descensum Dei in montem Sinai refertur è c. 19. Exod. v. 18. Insulsissime voro à Mahumeth eo accipitur, quod Deus coëge- rit montes cum laudante Davide se conjungere. Vid. Hotting. Hist. Or. p. 62.

## 114:7
Ver. 7.

THE EARTH WAS MOVED AT THE PRESENCE OF THE LORD) An answer to the question that preceded. Nay, it is rather a prosopopoeia: for it exhorts the earth to tremble also thereafter before the presence of the Lord. And it must be rendered in the imperative: tremble, O earth. See Jerem. 2, 12; c. 22, 29.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

A FACIE DOMINI MOTA EST TERRA) Respon- sio ad quæstionem quæ præcessit. Imo Prosopopœia potius est: adhortatur enim terram, ut deinde quoque coram facie Domini contremiscat. Et in Imperativo reddendum est: contremisce ô terra. Vid. Jerem. 2, 12. c. 22, 29.

## 115:1 Argument
PSALM CXV. To the only glory.

Latin:

PSALM. CXV. Uni gloriæ.

## 115:3
Ver. 3. HE HATH DONE ALL THINGS WHATSOEVER HE WOULD) And therefore man has freedom, because God willed it. The sacred psalmist speaks of an absolute will, not a conditional one, and he distinguishes the true God from the idols of the nations, in that they are able to do nothing, but God can do, and does, all things whatsoever He would. This distinction does not please the Calvinists; nay, it seems a contradiction if things happen which God does not will, or things do not happen which He does will. But the matter is clear from the Scriptures. For God does not will sins, which nevertheless happen, Ps. 5, 5; and God wills many things which do not happen, Is. 65, 12; c. 66, 4; Matth. 23, 37. Nor indeed does the will of God depend on a condition for that reason, for it is one thing for the divine will to regard a condition, and another to depend on a condition, as if, forsooth, God only then wills if the condition has been fulfilled. The effect of such a kind depends on a condition, and does not follow unless that has been fulfilled, but the divine will itself does not depend on it. On which matter more fully elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3. OMNIA QUÆCVNQVE VOLVIT FECIT) Et ideo homo libertatem habet, quia Deus voluit. LOquitur Hieropsaltes de voluntate absoluta, non de conditionata, & ab idolis gentium ve- rum Deum discernit, quod illa nihil valeant; Deus vero facere possit & faciat, omnia quæcunque vo- luit. Calvinianis hæc distinctio non placet, imo con- tradictio videtur, si quæ fiant, quæ Deus non ve- lit, aut non fiant, quæ velit. At res luculenta est è Scripturis. Peccata enim Deus non vult, quæ fiunt tamen Ps. 5, 5. & multa vult DEus, quæ non fiunt Es. 65, 12. cap. 66, 4. Matth. 23, 37. Nec vero ideo voluntas Dei dependet à conditione, aliud enim est, voluntatem divinam respicere conditionem, aliud dependere à conditione, quasi scil. tum demum Deus velit, si conditio fuerit præstita. Dependet à con- ditione ejusmodi effectus, nec sequitur nisi illa fue- rit impleta, non autem dependet ipsa voluntas di- vina. Qua de re alibi plenius.

## 115:16
Ver. 16.

THE HEAVEN OF HEAVENS IS THE LORD'S: BUT THE EARTH HE HATH GIVEN TO THE CHILDREN OF MEN) God is said to dwell in heaven in an eminent way, because the sun and the stars wondrously demonstrate His majesty. But the use of the earth is granted to men.

Beware of concluding with the heretics from this, as if God were confined to heaven and were not present on earth, or with the Epicureans, to whom the impious are similar, with Nicanor in 2 Maccab. 15, that God cares for heavenly things and leaves earthly things to men. Because God fills heaven and earth, Jerem. 23, and is nowhere absent, Ps. 139, 7; 89, 12, and thus the true God is distinguished from the idols of the nations; He is the Lord of heaven and earth, while they have no dominion either in heaven or on earth. Furthermore, the heaven of heaven is the Lord's, in which and from which He especially manifests His glory: but He is also the Lord of the earth, which He assigns to the children of men as He pleases, Acts 17, 23. For the empyrean heaven is not understood here, as Becanus feigns: because in the Hebrew there is not a construct state, but the name of heaven is repeated twice for the sake of emphasis.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

COELVM COELI DOMINO: TERRAM AVTEM DEDIT FILIIS HOMINVM) In cœlo eximie habitare dicitur Deus, quod Sol & sidera majestatem ejus mirifice de- monstrent. Terræ autem usus concessus hominibus.

Cave concludas cum hæreticis inde, quasi Deus cælo compescatur, nec in terris præsens sit, aut cum Epicureis, quibus similes sunt impii, cum Nicanore 2. Maccab. 15. Deum cœlestia curare, hominibus terrestria relinquere. Quia Deus cælum & ter- ram implet Jerem. 23. nec uspiam abest Ps. 139, 7. 89, 12. & distinguitur ita verus Deus ab idolis gen- tium; ille cœli & terræ Dominus est, hæc nullum vel in cœlo vel in terra habent Dominium. Porro cælum cælum est Domino, in quo & ex quo impri- mis gloriam suam manifestat: idem vero & terræ Dominus est, quam pro lubitu filiis hominum assi- gnat. Act. 17, 23. Non enim cœlum intelligitur hic empyræum, uti Becanus fingit: quia in Ebræo non est status constructus, sed bis repetitur nomen cæli emphaseos causa.

## 116:1 Argument
PSALM CXVI. The chalice of salvation. Ver. 1.

I HAVE LOVED) Namely the Lord, which is understood from what follows. BECAUSE HE HATH HEARD) The future for the past: because He has heard. I give this psalm as a sermon, to whomsoever it pleases, in the memory of the Witteb. justorum n. 10, under the title 'Davidic Enchiridion of Divine Offices' exhibited, one will be able to compare.

Latin:

PSALM. CXVI. Calix salutaris. Vers. 1.

DILEXI) Nempe Dominum, quod ex sequenti intel- ligitur. QUONIAM EXAVDIET) Futurum pro præterito: quia exaudivit. Do hoc Psalmo concionem, cui libet, in me- moria Witteb. justorum n. 10. sub Tit. Enchiri- dion divinorum officiorum Davidicum exhibitam conferre poterit.

## 116:10
Ver. 10.

I BELIEVED, THEREFORE I HAVE SPOKEN) Because I had firm hope in God, therefore I said, that which now precedes, that it would come to pass that I would return to Jerusalem safe and flourishing. BUT I HAVE BEEN HUMBLED EXCEEDINGLY] In the Hebrew: I was afflicted (supply then I was) exceedingly. I kept that hope in the greatest calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

CREDIDI, PROPTER QVOD LOQVVTVS SVM) Quia firmam in Deo spem habui, ideo dixi, id quod jam præcedit, fore ut redirem Hierosolyma sospes ac florens. EGO AVTEM HVMILIATVS SVM NIMIS] In Hebræo: Ego afflictus (supple tunc eram) valde. Spem il- lam servavi in maximis calamitatibus.

## 116:11
Ver. 11.

I SAID IN MY EXCESS) The Hebrew word פחז signifies dread. Even in the highest dread I retained trust in God. EVERY MAN A LIAR] That is, every hope placed in man can deceive. Understand from the opposite: but that which is placed in God cannot deceive.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

EGO DIXI IN EXCESSV MEO) Vox Hebræa פחז pavorem significat. Etiam in summo pavore retinui fiduciam in Deum. OMNIS HOMO MENDAX] Id est, omnis spes in ho- mine posita fallere potest. Intellige ex opposito: at quæ in Deo posita est, nequit fallere.

## 116:12
Ver. 12. I WILL TAKE THE CUP OF SALVATION) He calls the cup of salvation the cup of thanksgiving for salvation received, which the head of a household was accustomed to drink to his household. כוס הלל cup of blessing. See what is at Matt. 26, 27.

Latin:

Vers. 12. CALICEM SALVTARIS ACCIPIAM) Cali- cem salutis vocat calicem gratiarum actionis pro accepta sa- lute, quem paterfamilias solebat familiæ suæ προπίνειν. כוס הלל ποτήριον ἐυλογίας. Vide quæ ad Matth. 26, 27.

## 116:15
Ver. 15.

PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD IS THE DEATH OF HIS SAINTS) The sense is: God does not easily grant to the wicked that they should kill the pious. We do not easily give away things that are precious. If you take it otherwise, it will not cohere with the prior parts.

The words of David are not to be understood as a simple assertion, or of hope, and a profession of a return to Jerusalem: But as faith and the Davidic confession of faith. Namely, that he professed faith, just as it is right not only to believe in God, but also to profess one's faith, even if persecution and affliction follow that profession, as David immediately adds: But I have been humbled exceedingly: whence the Holy Apostle 2 Cor. 4, 13 teaches that those who are endowed with the Spirit of faith, like David, ought not to become more sluggish in the confession of faith because of calamities and dangers, but rather be rendered much more eager by his example, as one who in the midst of the danger of death testified: I believed, therefore I have spoken. There is nothing in the Psalm about a return to Jerusalem: unless perhaps you wish to seize upon those words, I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living, with the Jews, just as R. David Kimchi wishes the land of Canaan to be called the land of the living, because its air is the most healthy of all lands. Which, however, the blessed Gesner and other interpreters more correctly understand as the other life, along with Basil, Augustine, and Jerome. Because David could not take such joy from an earthly region: which, on account of the greatest calamities, should be called the land of the dead rather than the living: but in the other life is the true land of the living, in which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live, gathered with all the Elect, Luke 20, 38, in the bundle of the living 1 Sam. 25, 29, whence St. Basil on this Psalm says: For my part, he says, compare death with birth, and it is defined to mourn him who is withdrawn from this ignobility. And thus they follow one another in the second part of the Davidic Enchiridion of divine offices, which is a fiducial confession, first the stirring up of the soul ver. 7, then the proclamation of God, on account of the liberation of the soul from death, of the eyes from tears, of the feet from a fall: and also on account of the certainty of eternal life. v. 8, 9. Afterwards the declaration of trust, so that partly faith itself, partly the confession of the same, partly the tolerance of affliction on account of faith and confession, and partly finally the vanity of men being acknowledged, confidence in the one God is expressed v. 10, 11. For when, as if carried away into an ecstasy of divine economy, we weigh in the sanctuary of the Lord the counsel of God in sending or promising temptations, we acknowledge the truth of the word of God, even if all men desire that we be persuaded of something else, just as the Apostle Rom. 3, 4 brings out this opposition of the truth of God and the falsehood of men tacitly indicated by the words of David. All adversities are to be overcome by faith, because we know that God cannot deceive in His promises, which He gave concerning our final liberation and salvation, but that all the promises of men are vain and fallacious. The blessed Bugenhagen has summarized these things in this way.

The Christian affection and life, which is in the cross, is described here; I believed, he says, with my heart, and therefore I have confessed, and I have preached that which I believed, according to that which is believed with the heart unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. But this faith and confession suffers great insults, and is compelled to bear the cross through persecutions and horrible temptations even to the point of despair, either of the life of the body or of the salvation of the soul. In which ecstasy, or as it is in the Hebrew, precipitation, man sees that whatever is of human effort is vanity, and a lie, and hypocrisy, and folly. Finally, that acceptance of the cup promised in the thanksgiving, verse 13, also looks to this. By the acceptance of the cup, says St. Basil, he indicates tolerance, and the sweat of struggles for the sake of defending piety, and the persistent effort by which we resist sin even unto death. Grotius understands the cup of salvation as the cup of thanksgiving for salvation received, which the head of a household was accustomed to offer to his family. Although the eucharistic cup was indeed used in sacrifices and the eating of the Paschal lamb, here, however, it seems rather to be the cup of sorrow and calamity, and a patient and prompt submission to accepting the same is indicated, which also the blessed Gesner and others of our own have judged to be more consistent with what follows. For that use of the cup is frequent in the sacred writings, Ps. 75:9, Is. 51:17, 18, Jer. 25:17, Matt. 20:22, ch. 26:39, and it is right that we should not only patiently bear the cross imposed upon us, but also, like Job, celebrate the name of God for the same, Job 1:21, and hold the cup of the cross as the cup of salvation, Rom. 8:28, 1 Cor. 11:32. And thus that verse 15 also coheres very well: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints: even if you explain it with Grotius: God does not easily allow the wicked to kill the pious. For the Prophet celebrates God by the acceptance of the cup of salvation: because he knows, both that God can preserve him in the midst of calamities and persecutions, Zech. 2:8, Matt. 10:30, Psalm 34:2, and if he must die entirely by the divine will, that the death of the saints is precious in the eyes of God, and that they are bought with the price of the blood of the Lord, as Augustine says in this place, and that the saints are kept by God after death like pearls and precious gems, just as St. Basil explains in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

PRETIOSA IN CONSPECTV DOMINI MORS SANCTORVM EJVS) Sensus est: Non facile Deus impiis concedit ut pios occidant. Quæ pretiosa sunt non facile lar- gimur. Si aliter sumas, non cohærebit cum prioribus.

Verba Davidis non de simplici asseveratione qua- dam, aut de spe, ac professione reditus in Jerusalem: Sed fide ac fidei confessione Davidica intelligenda sunt. Quod nempe fidem professus fuerit, quem- admodum par est non solum credere in Deum, sed fidem etiam suam profiteri, etiamsi professio- nem illam sequatur persecutio & afflictio, uti a- ctutum subjicit David: Ego autem humiliatus sum nimis: unde S. Apostolus 2. Cor. 4, 13. docet, eos qui Spiritu fidei, Davidis instar, præditi sunt, non de- bere calamitatibus & periculis in fidei confessione segniores evadere, sed multo alacriores ipsius ex- emplo reddi, utpote qui in medio mortis discrimi- ne testatus est: credidi, propterea loquutus sum. Ni- hil in Psalmo de reditu in Jerusalem: nisi forte ver- ba illa, ambulabo coram Domino in terra viven- tium, cum Judæis eo arripere velis, uti R. David Kimchi Cananæam terram viventium dici vult, quia aër illius super omnes terras est saluberrimus. Quam vero de altera vita cum Basilio, Augustino, & Hieronymo, B. Gesnerus aliique Interpp. rectius intelligunt. Quia tantum gaudium David è terre- na regione capere non poterat: quæ propter cala- mitates summas potius mortuorum, quam viven- tium terra dicenda: in vita autem altera vera est viventium terra, in qua Abraham, Isaac, & Jacob vivunt, cum omnibus Electis, Luc. 20, 38. collecti in fasciculo viventium 1. Sam. 25, 29. unde S. Basi- lius in hunc Psalmum: Mihi sane, inquit, confer mortem cum nativitate, eumque definito lugere, qui huic ignobilitati subducitur. Atque ita se conse- quuntur in Enchiridii divinorum officiorum Davidici parte altera, quæ est fiducialis confessio, primum ani- mæ excitatio vers. 7. tum Dei deprædicatio, ob libera- tionem animæ à morte, oculorum à lacrymis, pe- dum à lapsu: nec non ob certitudinem æternæ vitæ. v. 8. 9. Postea fiduciæ declaratio, ut partim fides ipsa, partim confessio ejusdem, partim afflictionis tolerantia ob fidem & confessionem, partim denique agnita hominum vanitate in uno Deo confidentia exprima- tur v. 10. 11. Quum enim velut in ἔκστασιν divinæ ὀικονομίας abrepti expendimus in sanctuario Do- mini, consilium Dei, in tentationibus immitten- dis, aut promittendis, verbi Dei veritatem agno- scimus, etiamsi omnes homines aliud nobis per- suasum cupiant, quemadmodum hanc oppositio- nem veritatis Dei, & falsitatis hominum verbis Da- vidis tacite indicatum eruit Apostolus Rom. 3, 4. Superandæ sunt omnes adversitates fide, quod scia- mus Deum in promissionibus suis, quas de finali liberatione & salute nostra dedit, fallere non pos- se, hominum autem promissa omnia vana esse, & fallacia. B. Bugenhagius hæc ita complexus est.

Christianus affectus & vita, quæ est in cruce, hic de- scribitur, credidi, inquit, corde, & propterea confes- sus sum, & prædicari illud, quod credidi, secundum illud, quod corde creditur ad justitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. Verum hæc fides & confessio ma- gnos patitur insultus, & crucem cogitur ferre perse- quutionibus & horrendis tentationibus ad despera- tionem etiam usque vel vitæ corporis, vel salutis ani- mæ. In qua ecstasi, sive ut est in Hebræo præcipita- tione videt homo vanitatem esse, & mendacium, & hypocrisin, & stultitiam, quicquid est humani cona- tus. Huc denique spectat etiam illa in gratiarum actione promissa calicis acceptio vers. 13. Acceptilatio- ne calicis, inquit S. Basilius, tolerantiam subindicat, sudoremque certaminum in gratiam tuendæ pietatis, & pertinacem conatum quo ad mortem usque adver- sus peccatum resistamus. Grotius calicem salutis de calice gratiarum actionis pro salute accepta intelli- git, quem Paterfamilias solebat familiæ suæ προπί- νειν. Quamvis vero calix εὐχαριστήριος in sacrifi- ciis, esuque agni Paschalis usitatus fuerit, hic tamen videtur potius calix doloris & calamitatis, ac pa- tiens & prompta ad eundem acceptandum submis- sio indicari, quod etiam B. Gesnerus, & alii nostra- tes censuere sequentibus magis consentaneum. Nam frequens est illa calicis usurpatio in sacris Ps. 75, 9. Es. 51, 17. 18. Jerem. 25, 17. Matth. 20, 22. cap. 26, 39. & par est ut crucem impositam non modo patienter feramus, sed etiam ob eandem cum Jo- bo nomen Dei celebremus Job. 1, 21. ac calicem crucis pro calice salutis habeamus Rom. 8, 28. 1. Co- rinth. 11, 32. Atque ita cohæret etiam illud vers. 15. optime: Pretiosa in conspectu Domini mors sancto- rum ejus: Etiamsi exponas cum Grotio: Non fa- cile Deus impiis concedit ut pios occidant. Nam ce- lebrat Deum Propheta acceptione calicis salutis: quia scit, tum quod Deus conservare ipsum possit in mediis calamitatibus & persequutionibus Zachar. 2, 8. Matth. 10, 30. Psalm. 34, 2. tum si moriendum omnino sit divina voluntate, quod mors sancto- rum pretiosa sit in oculis Dei, & quod pretio emta sanguinis Domini, ut Augustin. h. l. & quod sancti ceu margaritæ & gemmæ pretiosæ à Deo adserventur post mortem, quemadmodum explicat S. Basilius in h. l.

## 117:1 Argument
PSALM CXVII. Hallelujah of the Gentiles and the Jews.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXVII. Hallelujah gentium & Judæorum.

## 117:2
Vers. 2.

HIS MERCY IS CONFIRMED OVER US) In the Hebrew it is 'excelled': He has done more good to us than to other nations.

R. Kimchi acknowledges from the Jews that the present Psalm looks to the times of the Messiah: and here the Gentiles and Jews are joined in the celebration of the Lord; the Gentiles by the word goyim, the Jews by the word ammim, whom Cocceius observes to be men of one kind, as if from one mother, and by that pact the twelve tribes are seen in some places to be distinguished from the Gentiles: as in Ps. 2. Which appears from the Apostle, Rom. 15:8, 9, 10, 11. But that the Apostle attributes an abundance of grace to the Gentiles and the constancy of divine truth to the Jews is not to be taken exclusively, since the promises made to the Fathers proceeded not from their merits, but from mere mercy, as Bellarmine himself admits, and grace and truth were made in Christ for both Gentiles and Jews, John 1:17. But compare, because however much promises may also exist concerning the Gentiles, those made to the people of God are nevertheless more solemn, and more frequently and illustriously established for them, whence they are judged to be the promises by way of excellence, Rom. 9:4, and similarly the grace is more illustrious which, after the people of God were rejected and the Gentiles were taken into God's possession throughout the whole world, fell to those who were once not a people: whence it is clear that these things are to be understood comparatively. That hillel or to celebrate God, as Cocceius warns, implies setting God as the highest good, preferring nothing to Him, or equating anything to Him, and even considering oneself far below God, indeed unworthy of God: Which is attributed to the Gentiles, and in this the Apostle places a remarkable mercy, that even to those whom God had allowed to go their own ways, and who had been outside the promise of the covenant and the polity of God, the LORD is preached as their good to be received by faith, who until now were without God in the world, Eph. 2:12. By which pact the distinction of nations and lands and the place of the worship of God is also removed. Mal. 1:11, John 4:21, Rom. 3:22, Gal. 3:26, 28. The word shabach is to approve something as good and to praise it: in which the duty of justifying God and His wisdom is completed, as the same Cocceius holds. Whence the Jews especially ought to acknowledge and celebrate the fulfillment of the promises, who, however, do nothing of the sort. Compare Luke 1:55, 73, John 1:11.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

CONFIRMATA EST SVPER NOS MISERICOR- DIA EJVS) In Hebræo est excelluit: plus nobis boni fecit, quam gentibus aliis.

PSalmum præsentem tempora Messiæ respicere è Judæis agnoscit R. Kimchi: & conjunguntur hic gentes ac Judæi in celebratione Domini; Gen- tes voce גוים, Judæi voce אמים, quos homines esse unius generis, quasi ab una matre, observat Cocce- jus, eoque pacto τὸ δωδεκάφυλον tribus duodecim alicubi videri à gentibus distingui: ut Ps. 2. Quod ex Apostolo Rom. 15, 8. 9. 10. 11. apparet. Quod autem Apostolus gentibus abundantiam gratiæ, Judæis ve- ritatis divinæ constantiam tribuat, non exclusive accipiendum, siquidem promissiones Patribus fa- ctæ non ex meritis eorum, sed ex mera misericor- dia processerint, fatente ipsomet Bellarmino, & gratia ac veritas in Christo & gentibus & Judæis facta sit Joh. 1, 17. Sed comparate, quia utut de gen- tibus etiam extent promissiones, solemniores ta- men sint, quæ populo Dei factæ, & frequentius at- que illustrius eidem stabilitæ, unde ἐξοχικῶς eju- dicuntur esse αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι, Rom. 9, 4. ac similiter illustrior est gratia, quæ rejecto populo Dei genti- bus per totum orbem assumtis in Dei peculium, ut- pote quæ erant olim non populus, obtigit: unde li- quet hæc συγκριτικῶς intelligenda esse. Illud הִלֵּל vel celebrare Deum, monente Coccejo, infert, Deum statuere pro summo bono, nihil ipsi præferre, vel æqua- re, etiam seipsum longe infra Deum, imo indignum Deo ducere: Quod gentibus tribuitur, & in eo insignis misericordia locatur ab Apostolo, quod & illis, quos Deus siverat ire vias suas, quique extra pro- missionem fœderis & politiam Dei fuerant, DO- MINUS tanquam bonum suum fide excipiendum prædicetur, qui hactenus fuere sine Deo in mundo Ephes. 2, 12. Quo pacto tollitur etiam discrimen gentium & terrarum & loci cultus Dei. Mal. 1, 11. Joh. 4, 21. Rom. 3, 22. Galat. 3, 26. 28. Vox נִשְׁבַּח est quid approbare tanquam bonum & laudare: in quo absolvitur officium justificandi Deum & sapientiam ejus, ut idem Coccejus habet. Unde impletionem promissionum imprimis Judæi agnoscere, & celebra- re debebant, qui vero nihil minus faciunt. Confer Luc. 1, 55. 73. Joh. 1, 11.

## 118:1 Argument
PSALM CXVIII. Confess the grace of God, and Christ the cornerstone of the Church.

Latin:

PSALM. CXVIII. Confitemini de gratia Dei, & lapide angulari Ecclesiæ Christo.

## 118:12
Ver. 12. AND THEY BLAZED UP LIKE FIRE AMONG THORNS.

So also the LXX. ἐξεκαύθησαν ὡς πῦρ ἐν ἀκάνθαις. But Aquila, Symmachus, the Syriac, Jerome, Ezra, Kimchi, Pagninus, Cajetan, Felix, Piscator, Junius, Coccejus, [render it] they are extinguished like the fire of thorns. But Capellus tries in vain to claim the LXX Elders read otherwise: with whom the Targum also agrees, rendering: דְלִקוּ they burn, than is now held, especially because the Masora also confirms the modern reading: nor does Buxtorf observe inconveniently in Anti-Crit. p. 680, that it seems the LXX interpreters took the verb דָעַךְ in this Pyhal conjugation in a contrary meaning, as happens in certain other verbs, so that what in Kal signifies to be extinguished, to extinguish, in Pyhal and Pihel is to burn and be consumed. Mr. Dr. Geier gathers the sense of this verse from a comparison of the preceding v. 10. & 11, where the first member in both verses expresses the hostile attempt, the latter the courageous purpose of the Messiah (others will say of David), [he gathers] the sense of this verse: they surrounded me like bees, nay, like the fire of thorns, which, when extinction is attempted, is rather increased, they blazed up. B. Luther in his first version had translated: They are extinguished / but in the later one he rendered: They quench / which is to run up and extinguish, as the marginal scholion has: Which sense Megalander also handed down regarding active extinction in the explanation of Psalm 118, Year 1530, Vol. 5, Jena, German, and especially defended in the Year 1533, treatise on translating, Vol. 6, Altenburg, p. 136. But he, as far as the matter itself is concerned, comes back to the same thing as the interpretation of Mr. Dr. Geier just praised, even if he departs from the points, and does not express the very words of the authentic text: in which is held LIKE FIRE in the nominative, which the preceding simile they surrounded me like bees also demands, not in the accusative LIKE FIRE. For he renders this sense in the cited place: That the great wrath of the adversaries against the righteous may be expressed: and in the explanation of v. 12, Vol. 5, Jena, fol. 55. They quench / or extinguish / like a fire in thorns. When someone teaches God's Word, he has (as they say in the German lands) set the Rhine on fire / (which in Hebrew is called / the

fences or hedges ignited,) there one must run up and extinguish, such heretics and rebels kill etc.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ET EXARSERUNT SICUT IGNIS IN SPINIS.

ITa & LXX. ἐξεκαύθησαν ὡς πῦρ ἐν ἀκάνθαις. At Aquila, Symmachus, Syrus, Hieronymus, Esra, Kimchi, Pagninus, Cajetanus, Felix, Piscator, Ju- nius, Coccejus, extincti sunt ut ignis spinarum. Fru- stra autem Capellus aliter legisse vult LXX. Senes: quibus etiam consonat Targum, reddens: דְלִקוּ ar- dent, quam nunc habetur, cumprimis quia moder- nam lectionem etiam confirmat Masora: nec in- commode observat Buxtorf. in Anti-Crit. p. 680. videri LXX. Interpp. verbum דָעַךְ in conjugatione hac Pyhal contraria significatione, ut in aliis qui- busdam verbis fit, accepisse, ita ut quod in Kal si- gnificat extingui, extinguere, in Pyhal & Pihel sit ar- dere & comburi. Dn. D. Geierus hunc ex collatio- ne antecedentium v. 10. & 11. ubi prius membrum in utroque versu exprimit hostilem conatum, posterius Messiæ (alii Davidis dicent) propositum animosum, colligit hujus versus sensum, circumdederunt me, ut apes, imo, ut ignis spinarum extinctione tentata ma- gis auctus exarserunt. B. Lutherus in prima versio- ne transtulerat: Sie sind verloschen / sed in poste- riori reddidit: Sie dämpffen / quod est accurrere & extinguere, ut Scholion marginale habet: Quem sensum etiam de extinctione activa Megalander tradidit in explicatione Psalm. 118. Anno 1530. Tom. 5. Jen. Germ. & imprimis defendit Anno 1533. tr. vom Dollmetschen Tom. 6. Altenb. p. 136. Sed is, quantum ad rem ipsam eodem redit cum interpre- tatione Dn. D. Geieri modo laudata, etsi à punctis abeat, nec verba ipsa textus authentici exprimat: in quo habetur SICUT IGNIS in nominativo, quam poscit etiam præcedens similitudo circum- dederunt me sicut apes, non in accusativo SICUT IGNEM. Sensum enim hunc reddit l. c. Daß mit ausgedrücket werde der grosse Grimm der Widersa- cher gegen die Gerechten: & in explicat. v. 12. T. 5. Jen. fol. 55. Sie dämpffen / oder leschen / wie ein Feur in Dornen. Wenn iemand GOttes Wort lehret / der hat (wie man in Teutschen Landen sagt /) den Rhein entbrannt / (welches im Ebräischen heißt / die

Zaͤune oder Hecken entbrannt,) da muß man zulauf- fen und daͤmpffen, solche Ketzer und Auffruͤhrer toͤdten 2c.

## 118:22
Vers. 22.

THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED) Saul & his court.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

LAPIDEM QVEM REPROBAVERVNT ÆDIFI- CANTES) Saul & aula ejus.

## 118:25
Vers. 25.

O LORD, SAVE ME) In Hebrew: Lord, save I pray: namely the King. For the first parts of the Psalm are of a king recently anointed 2 Sam. 2, the latter parts of the people and Priests wishing well to the king. From this place the word ὠσαννὰ was taken, Matthew 21, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

O DOMINE SALVVM ME FAC) In Hebræo: Domi- ne serba quæso: nempe Regem. Nam prima Psalmi sunt, regis recens uncti 2. Sam. 2. posteriora, populi ac Sacerdotum bene ominantium regi. Ex hoc loco sumta vox ὠσαννὰ Matth. 21, 9.

## 118:26
BLESSED IS HE WHO COMES IN THE NAME OF THE LORD) May the king given to us by God be happy.

Latin:

BENEDICTVS, QVI VENIT IN NOMINE DOMI- NI) Felix sit rex a Deo nobis datus.

## 118:26
WE HAVE BLESSED YOU FROM THE HOUSE OF THE LORD) We also who are of the house of the Lord, that is, the priests, pray for good things for the king and the people.

Our Hugo judaizes again with Calvin and his accomplices, as if the Psalm were about David. He is, however, completely silent about the interpretation of the New Testament: which he does not touch upon with a single word, except that he notes the word ὠσαννὰ, Matthew 21, 9, taken from this place. He followed R. David Kimchi among the Jews most of all, although he is still more sound than our Grotius. For he notes that others interpret this Psalm concerning the days of Christ, and that this is correct, and he explains the same now concerning Christ, now concerning David. R. Solomon Jarchi, although he also understands by the stone David rejected by Israel in the days of Saul, and also in another sense the contemptible Church among the nations, nevertheless refers the word of joy in v. 15 to the times of the Messiah, and indeed in v. 22 he explains the stone rejected in his commentary on Micah 5, 7 as the Messiah. Among the Christians he followed Calvin, Bucer, and Moller, who understand David by the rejected stone, although Calvin affirms that these things also properly apply to Christ, because when David was created King, the foundations of the eternal kingdom were laid, which was finally revealed by the advent of Christ. And that temporal throne, on which the descendants of David sat, was an image of the perpetual empire with which Christ was gifted by the Father. Junius and Tremellius understand the kingdom to be typically established in the person of David, and perfectly and absolutely instituted in Christ: and they say the typical stone was David, rejected by the nobles both in the times of Saul and of Ish-bosheth. Which is also the gloss of Piscator, and of the authors of the Belgian notes, as well as of Rivet, who says that David speaks about himself and about his own affairs, but in such a way that he saw by the Prophetic Spirit and prophesied about those things which were to be fulfilled most of all in Christ, of whom he himself was a type and future Father. Nor does Vatablus deny it. Rivet also brings into this opinion Antonio Agellius, as well as Jansenius and Simon de Muys from the Papists, because here the discourse is literally about David even in v. 22, but insofar as he bore the type of Christ. Otherwise, invincible arguments confirm that David cannot be understood by that rejected stone, but only Christ according to the literal and proper sense of the words, and that David is not proposed here as a type of Christ, since the discourse is about the stone rejected by the builders, but which was made the head of the corner: First from the Psalm itself, then from its explanation given in the New Testament. The Psalm is completed in these parts: The first is an exhortation to the celebration of the eternal mercy of God, which ought to be done by Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the Lord, vers. 1, 2, 3, 4. For what is that mercy of God, which is to be celebrated forever, which all the pious of all times ought to confess, if not the mercy which was exhibited to us in Christ? The second is a commemoration of the grace which befell Christ in his passions from God: namely, the divine hearing in vers. 5, by which he confidently raised himself in vers. 6, 7 (cf. Heb. 5, 7), whence he exhorts others to place their trust not in men, but in God alone in vers. 8, 9, his assistance against various enemies in vers. 10 seqq. (Cf. Psalm 2, 1, 2. Psalm 22, 17, 22. Psalm 69, 6.) and his erection when he was struck and afflicted in vers. 13. On account of which he himself then celebrates GOD, verse 14. Then an ἐπινίκιον [song of victory] concerning the victory of the right hand of GOD will be sung in the Church, verses 15, 16, and of [his] vivification: for indeed he is not to perish in eternal death, but is to live forever, to announce the works of the Lord in the Church, verses 17, 18. What, I ask, is that victory, which in the tabernacles of the righteous, in the assemblies of the Church, is so greatly sung and must be sung concerning the exaltation of the right hand of God, if not that victory which Christ brought back from infernal enemies for the salvation of the whole human race, which is celebrated throughout the universal Church? The third part is the prediction of the entry of Christ into Jerusalem, and in what manner he is to be received there, if indeed he himself, continuing the prayer, rouses the Jerusalemites so that the gates of righteousness may be opened to him, verses 19, 20, 21; compare Psalm 40:9, Zechariah 9:9, Matthew. 21:10.) And he celebrates God again on account of the liberation to be provided in the state of emptying and supreme humiliation, verse 21. Elegant here is the Commentary of the blessed Tarnovius on verse 19, p. 98. I, the King of righteousness and glory, Psalm 24, come, Ps. 40:8, so that I may now do the very will of the Father by suffering, nor does death terrify me, other evils do not deter me, I approach fearlessly, and because now the day of the New Testament has dawned (below v. 24), come, open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter this city, and in it recover the righteousness lost to the human race, full of good hope that I shall successfully accomplish all things, I shall enter through those gates, and I shall celebrate Jah, I shall enter the city with pomp, I shall enter the temple with power, I shall illuminate it, I shall reform and purge it, but in both places I shall celebrate the Father, preparing praise for him from the mouth of infants, casting out those who sell, teaching others the truth, refuting and convicting the Pharisees, Scribes, and Sadducees. And to verse 20. Open to me first, O Savior, so that afterwards this gate may be open to the faithful assembly, because this very gate is, and leads to, Jehovah; this passion of mine, satisfaction, merit, and thus I, the whole Christ, applied by faith, am that true door through which access is open to the Father, John 10:7; for in the Church they are made partakers of the lot of the saints in light through Christ, John 14:6; the righteous shall enter through that gate from the kingdom of grace into the kingdom of glory, from darkness into light, from the Kingdom of the Devil into the Kingdom of the Son of God. To verse 21. What will you do, Christ, when those gates were opened, both of the Jerusalem Temple, and of the typical city, and of the New Testament in the antitype? What will I do? You ask: I will take care that the Gospel be preached concerning me, emptied and suffered and exalted and glorified. I will celebrate you, O Father, I myself, as I have exhorted others, verse 1. and I will give thanks, celebrating through the public proclamation of the Gospel your wondrous way, by which you redeemed the human race through me, namely that in the state of emptying you heard me crying out and invoking you, above verse 5, and helped me, and thus became for me into salvation, or [my] salvation, above verses 13, 14. Furthermore, the Church or the faithful are introduced with admiration and exultation celebrating the οἰκονομίαν [economy/dispensation] of salvation, by which that stone rejected by the architects was made the head of the corner by the Lord in the day of salvation and liberation of the human race, verses 22, 23, 24 (compare Is. 49:8), whence there is perennial joy for all the faithful; they are introduced especially in the Church, that people, and the children who were about to congratulate their King Messiah as he was arriving, verses 25, 26. (Cf. Matt. 21.) Finally, the fourth part is a mutual exhortation of the faithful to celebrate these solemnities with Eucharistic sacrifices, throughout the world wherever there is a temple and altar of the Lord, i.e., the true Church, Isa. 56:7, Heb. 13 Lord God, who illuminates us (concerning which see B. Luther, Vol. 5, Jena, German, p. 169, on this passage, and B. Tarnov on this passage), so that thus the entire Church may sing with one mouth in true faith: You are my God, I will confess you: You are my God and I will exalt you, verse 28. To which, in the last place of the conclusion, is added the repetition of the command of the Lord, from whom the Psalm had begun: Confess to the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy is forever. Thus everything coheres beautifully and concisely, as has been excellently observed in the Paraphrase of Osiander, and the Weimar [Paraphrase], and the Commentaries of B. Tarnov. There are indeed also some among the Fathers, such as Theodoret and Augustine, who maintain that the Church speaks in the earlier parts of the Psalm: Bellarmine says that it can be explained literally concerning David, and is explained by Chrysostom. But perhaps everything coheres more conveniently if the whole Psalm is explained literally concerning Christ: just as Osiander, Gesner, Tarnov, and the authors of the Weimar paraphrase think that it speaks entirely of Christ, even if what happens to the head can also be accommodated to the members, if it is done in a right and due manner, provided that every faithful person can also profess: I shall not die, except by the will of God, not by the lust of men, I shall not die entirely, but I shall live in death, in eternal life I shall praise God: concerning which see B. Tarnov on this passage, just as B. Luther applied this verse 17 especially to himself, and inscribed it on the walls of his study, for the sake of encouraging himself, when a great danger threatened the true religion and himself: as witnessed by Matthesius, Conc. 8, on the Life of Luther, p. 90. Furthermore, whatever may be the case regarding the earlier parts, and even if it were conceded that they should be taken concerning David, and all things which were uttered in the first person, verse 5: in my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard me; verse 6: the Lord is my helper: and I will despise my enemies; verse 10: all nations surrounded ME, and so on, v. 11, 12, 13, 14, as well as verses 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, concern the person of David: Nor should there be any doubt, regarding those words which are found in the final verses, such as verses 27, 28, 29, that the Psalmist speaks of himself at the same time, when he says in the plural, we have blessed you, and the Lord has shone upon US: and particularly proclaims of himself, YOU ARE MY GOD, and I will confess you, etc., yet that victory, which he predicts in the latter part, v. 15 and 16, will be celebrated in the tabernacles of the righteous (even if he speaks in the past tense, in the Prophetic manner) and the prophecy concerning the cornerstone, verses 22, 23, and the exultation and votive exclamation, verses 24, 25, pertain to the Messiah: finally, the exhortation to the celebration of the solemn feast looks to the times of the New Testament, which David foresaw in the spirit. Certainly, when he speaks in the third person concerning the cornerstone, verse 22 and following, it is undoubtedly agreed among all Christian interpreters, if you except Calvin and his accomplices who stand here on the side of the Jews, that the discourse is about Christ, not about David, not about the Church. For these things fit no one else but Christ. What other stone is there, which, having been rejected by the architects, was made into a cornerstone by the admirable economy of God? Even if David was rejected by Saul and his court, he was not, however, rejected by the spiritual architects, especially or by the Priests who were in charge of building the house of the Lord, by whom the stone, concerning which the Holy Spirit here prophesies, was especially to be rejected. But then, how would David here excite the whole people of Israel, how would he excite the house of Aaron specifically to celebrate the Lord with all the pious, if he was rejected by the architects or ecclesiastical nobles from the house of Aaron or by the politicians in Israel? How would he here bless those who are of the house of the Lord, as pious and faithful, if he was rejected by them especially? verse 26. Moreover, although the admirable economy of the Lord shines forth also in David, it is not, however, that stupendous work of God which all the faithful, by virtue of this Psalm, ought to admire, so that they exclaim, This is the Lord's doing, and it is wonderful in our eyes, and for which all the faithful ought to rejoice and be glad so greatly: This is the day which the Lord has made, let us rejoice and be glad in it. Nor is it read that the feast of tabernacles was celebrated specifically because of the restoration of David, or that any other solemn feast was instituted: by which the altar of burnt offerings was either burdened or honored with victims accumulated extraordinarily at the horns, which he requests here, verse 27. Furthermore, the discourse here is about another benefit of the Lord, namely, a Spiritual one, verse 24, so that it ought to be a matter of religion for us to interpret these things as concerning the bodily benefit of the restoration of David and the worldly joy that arose from it. Nor was David established as a cornerstone, or as the head of the corner, containing and joining two peoples into one, as a cornerstone joins two walls. If you say that he ruled both peoples of Israel and Judah, which is the explanation of Jansenius, also approved by Rivet: I answer, that then they had not yet been split into two peoples, but constituted one people, one body of the Republic. Therefore, with respect to them, he could not be called a cornerstone. Add that David was neither the first nor the only one to hold both under his rule; for both before him Saul, and after him Solomon, was established as King over both peoples, if it pleases you to call them so. Theodoret urges this argument as invincible: Although the Jews may impudently deny this a thousand times, yet they cannot refer it to another: For Zerubbabel was the leader of the divided tribes, but he does not persist for long, whereas the Lord Christ, when He had brought together into one the two walls standing diametrically apart from each other, I mean those who believed from the Jews and those from the Gentiles, the former serving impiety, the latter bearing the yoke of the law, He joined those things which were separated, and fashioned one Church out of both, imitating a certain corner-stone, binding together two walls; this stone, therefore, which the Pharisees and Sadducees and Priests and Scribes once rejected and affixed to the cross, has become the head of the corner, or according to Symmachus, the Corner-stone. What of the fact that in the Old Testament that stone, chosen by God and precious, is expressly designated as the Messiah, Isa. 28, 16. (Cf. 1 Pet. 2, 6. Rom. 9, 33. ch. 10, 11.) who became for the Jews a stone of stumbling, Isa. 8, 14. (Compare Luke 2, 34. Rom. 9, 39. 1 Pet. 2, 8.) who is also signified by the name of a stone, Dan. 2, 45. Zech. 3, 9. Add that Jerome testifies that this Psalm was at that time frequently read to the Jews, chanted in the synagogues, and accustomed to be expounded concerning the coming of the Messiah, whence it was known even to the children themselves, who knew well that it treated of the Messiah, and therefore they shouted Hosanna to the Son of David. Doubtless it was then most well known to all that in its literal sense it treated not of David, but of the Son of David, the Messiah, in whose honor they celebrated the feast of tabernacles with palm branches, and to whom this Psalm was to be sung as they had learned from their ancestors the Jews, from which they were accustomed to sing with great joy at that festival. When, therefore, they now understood that Christ was celebrating his arrival and wished to present himself as the Messiah, by the instinct of the Holy Spirit they sang their Hosanna to Christ their King, contrary to the custom of the Passover festival, and for that reason were defended by Christ. From all of which we think it is established that the Messiah is understood here by the stone: which is so certain that R. Solomon Jarchi, among others pointed out by R. David Kimchi, acknowledged it even from the Jews themselves; indeed, so much so that no Jew dared to contradict Christ, who applied this passage to himself.

Now, therefore, if we approach the New Testament, the truth shines forth most clearly like the morning star: that it is to be understood of no one else but Christ. For Christ himself most openly referred to himself what the sacred psalmist had predicted concerning the rejected stone, and indeed in such a way that he convinced the Jews themselves of that testimony, in the forum of contradiction, as they call it, and among them the chief priests and scribes, and reduced them to silence, Matt. 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17. Have you never read in the Scriptures, the stone which the builders rejected, the same has become the head of the corner? This is the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. Saint Peter also openly confessed before the princes and elders and scribes and priests that Jesus of Nazareth, and no other, is this stone, that the priests themselves are the builders who rejected it: nor could the Jews answer even a word. If, however, these things had been said in any way about David, that objection would have been ready for them: but that was indubitable, and was assumed by Peter as admittedly certain, that Christ, and no other, is that stone of which the Psalmist speaks: therefore he did only this, that he applied it to Jesus of Nazareth, and asserted that he is the Messiah, or Christ. Let it be known, he says, to all of you, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of our Lord Jesus of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, in this very one he stands before you whole. This IS THE STONE, which was rejected BY YOU BUILDERS, which has become the head of the corner. Who, therefore, when Peter wishes this to be openly testified to all: This IS THE STONE, which was rejected by you builders, would still dare to say that that stone is David, rejected by Saul and his court? Is this not to contradict Peter to his face? Let the Church of Christ judge whether Grotius is far worse than the Jews themselves, who could not deny that opinion of David's words, while he, having admitted the authority of the New Testament, interprets as concerning David what, with the Jews themselves not dissenting, had been predicted solely of the Messiah? There is, therefore, no reason for Grotius to object that the Jews accepted the Psalm concerning the affairs of the Messiah only in a more mystical sense, which is his opinion at Matt. 21:42. For neither Christ nor Peter indicate in their speech who that cornerstone is in a mystical sense: for what trace is there here that they looked only to a mystical sense? They convince the Jews from the Scriptures that it had been predicted by the Holy Spirit himself that the Messiah would indeed be rejected by the priests, but chosen by God to be the head of the corner. It is necessary, therefore, that it be contained in that passage. If that mystical sense is the only one, since it is nowhere explained in the Scriptures, how could the Jews have been convinced by it? Shall we believe that Christ and the Apostles betook themselves to traditions, and wished to convince their adversaries from the same, or to a sense of Scripture not explained in the Scripture of the Old Testament itself, but which had been propagated through tradition? And from where could it be established to Grotius that that was only a mystical sense, or even that the Jews of old accepted those things in a literal sense concerning David, but in a mystical sense concerning Christ? Those Rabbis, David Kimchi and Solomon Jarchi, are too recent for you to seek or expect from them the opinion of the ancient Jews of the time of Christ. And who will believe that in the Scriptures of the New Testament this notable oracle is found explained by Christ and the Apostles not once, but several times in a mystical sense, but nowhere, either in the Old or in the New Testament, is its proper sense expressly explained? I pass over the fact that that invention, concerning a double sense of Scripture, literal and mystical, rests on no examples, and is entirely contrary to the clarity and simplicity of Scripture, which is free from equivocations and ambiguities; indeed, it even takes away and overturns the certainty of faith. For from where could that have been had of old, or could it even now be had, if Prophetic Scripture is so ambiguous and doubtful, and subject to diverse senses? For it will always be doubtful which of them should be admitted as the genuine sense of the Holy Spirit, since in equivocal and ambiguous things there is no certainty. Whence the blessed Luther gravely warns in Tom. 2. Jenens. Latin works on Psalm 8, fol. 98, that there ought to be one, simple, and constant sense of Scripture and the word of God, lest (as they say) we make a wax nose out of the sacred letters.

Furthermore, not only in that apologetic speech before the Sanhedrin, but also in his Catholic Epistle, St. Peter explained this passage in this way, and, which is again to be well observed, he joined with it other things which likewise treat of this mystical stone, prophetic oracles, so that they might mutually illuminate each other, 1 Epist. 2:4, 7. To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious, you also as lively stones are built up a spiritual house: wherefore it is contained in the Scripture (Isa. 28:16), Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner (Psalm 118:21), and a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence (Isa. 8:14) to those who stumble at the word: from which it is manifest that Isaiah in both places, and David here, speak of the same living stone according to the mind of the Apostle: and that this was indubitably certain at that time, since Peter assumes this sense as genuine and indubitably certain. This was likewise done by Paul, who also explained in what manner Christ was made the head of the corner, or the ἀκρογωνιαῖον stone, and wrote, as it were, a commentary on those words in Ephesians 2:14 et seqq., namely, that He contains the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, and joins them into one, just as a corner-stone joins two walls, so that it is only rashly, and against the Apostle himself, that Grotius denies that the meaning of this word γωνίας refers to the juncture τῆς ἐκλογῆς τῶν ἰυδαίων & of the people of the Gentiles (even though he readily admits that this relation is not inappropriate); and wishes to indicate by that word only that power which is accustomed to be in corners, of supporting the building: Annotat. ad Matth. 21:42. For what is more evident than that

Eph. 2, 20. The cornerstone, should it have regard to the joining together of the saints from the Jews and Gentiles? To which is added, that that people, who received Christ entering Jerusalem with joy, the Holy Spirit thus directing, sought from this Psalm their Hosanna, and blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Matt. 21, 9. Mark 11, 9. John 12, 13. Which acclamatory voices David perceived in the Spirit in his own time, when he foresaw that, while the leaders were rejecting Christ, some believers nevertheless would receive the same: just as he had learned from the revelation of the Spirit the very words which Christ was to use on the cross, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me! All of which, just as they most clearly convince that the Psalm must be understood of Christ, so the great Doctors of the Church, both ancient and modern, have interpreted these things, which are held here concerning the cornerstone and the votive acclamation made to the same, of Christ, and indeed in the literal sense, not merely the mystical. Nay, Hilary, Theodoret, Augustine, and others accepted it of Christ alone, excluding the type, or without regard to the type: as did our blessed Luther, Tom. 5. Jen. Germ. p. 65. seqq., and our theologians to a man, and finally even most of the Papists. Genebrardus: Which stone (Christ metaphorically) the builders (the Jews, especially the Priests and Pharisees, the constructors of the old Church because of the duty of teaching and governing it) rejected and cast away, here has been made the cornerstone of that ecclesiastical building. For Christ, having been disapproved, rejected, and expelled, as a useless stone, and fit for nothing, nevertheless emerged as King, and excelled as a cornerstone. That the Church is compared to a building is not new, as 1 Cor. 3, Is. 18; concerning this passage see Matt. 21, Mark 1, Luke 20, Acts 4, 1 Pet. 2. Into the head of the corner, into the better and more worthy place of the building. He is called in Is. 28 a cornerstone, as one who contains the whole building of the Church, and has joined together two walls, Jews and Gentiles, into one corner, into one body of the Church, of which he himself is the head, Eph. 2. For thus the cornerstone not only fills its own place, but also connects and contains the two walls. A prophecy concerning Christ having suffered, and having been made the head of the Church after the resurrection. Menochius follows Genebrardus, explaining it likewise of Christ alone. Tirinus, although he brings forward an explanation concerning David according to the opinion of the Chaldean, nevertheless teaches that the present passage is better understood of Christ. Estius and Eman. Saa interpret it simply of Christ. Bellarmine openly rejects the opinion of those who understand it of David according to the letter, as a type of Christ, as being more recent, and opposes to it the consensus of the ancients and reasons from the text and the collation of the N.T., and interprets it solely of Christ. These verses, he says, SOME MORE RECENT AUTHORS explain of David according to the letter, whom they say was made the head of the Corner when he was made King over Israel and Judah. But David bore the figure of Christ, who was made the head of the corner when he was made the head of the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles. Moreover, the Holy Fathers explain it absolutely of Christ, with no mention made of David. Nay, St. John Chrysostom, who explains the earlier parts concerning David according to the letter, writes in this place: That the Prophet unexpectedly changed the subject, and prophesied of Christ. Add that Christ himself publicly alleged this passage as pertaining properly to himself, Matt. 21, Mark 12, and Luke 21, nor did anyone answer that these words were to be understood of David. Saint Peter also, Acts 4, again alleged this passage before all the people as written properly of Christ, and no one contradicted. Saint Paul also to Rom. 9 and St. Peter 1 Epist. cap. 2 allege

Isaiah cap. 28 concerning this cornerstone, supreme, elect, approved, etc. Finally, the same Apostle Paul to the Ephesians 2 calls Christ the supreme cornerstone. Certainly, I would not dare to communicate in any way with the person of David a Scripture so famous and celebrated, explained by Christ and the Apostles. It is added that David was not the first, nor the only King over Israel and Judah, so that he deserved to be called a cornerstone: for before him Saul was King over both peoples, and after him Solomon: nor were Israel and Judah properly two peoples, or two different nations, as are the Hebrews and Gentiles. This is Bellarmine. Add the annotations of Grotius to Matt. 21, 22. Who are the builders? They are so called, the Elders of the great Sanhedrin, to whom was entrusted the care of the Republic no less than of religion. Peter teaches this, who, addressing the same, says, before you, the builders, Acts 4, 2. How therefore can Saul and his court be understood by the builders? Did they constitute the great Sanhedrin, or were they senators of the same? Rivetus confesses that there is hardly another passage in the whole O.T. so often cited in the New, and adapted to Christ, and if we look to the primary sense of the Prophecy, to which the Holy Spirit looked, it cannot be referred to ANOTHER, nor should it be stopped at David. If it cannot be referred to ANOTHER according to the primary sense of the Holy Spirit, how therefore is the literal sense concerning David? For the literal sense must be the primary, nay, the proper and genuine, I add, and the only one, if indeed Scripture ought not to be dragged into diverse senses. There is one thing which Rivetus objects: that nothing at all is detracted from the mystical sense, which looks to Christ, if these things are explained of David as a typical stone, nay, that it is more illustrated, if this dignity of the Son of God is shadowed forth not only by words, but also by things. Resp. The question is not about things which we admit by certain reasoning to be typical, and by which we also allow prophecy to be illustrated, as types are wont to be added to prophecies to illustrate them: But the inquiry in this oracle is concerning the proper and genuine sense of the words, because it is the passion of Christ and his exaltation, it certainly cannot be that the genuine sense is about David. Since therefore Rivetus confesses that, according to the primary sense, it CANNOT BE referred to ANY OTHER than Christ, is he not absurd, while he pronounces those morose who deny that these things are to be accepted concerning David as a typical stone? For it is not being inquired whether David can in some way be called a stone, and whether he was a type of Christ, but whether here by the Holy Spirit the name of stone, as a type of Christ, is signified according to the letter of the oracle; which we have already shown to be falsely said, nay, Rivetus himself is forced to acknowledge it, when he explains what it is to be the head of the corner, Tom 3. p. 342. in Dodec. Psalm. ad h. l. For a stone is said to become the head of the corner when it is placed in that position where it sustains the joint of the whole building, whence the Apostle translates it ἀκρογωνιαῖον, which not only sustains the weight of the whole building (as Grotius wished) but also joins both walls, that is, gathers the Church from Jews and Gentiles united in himself Ephes. 2, 14. 15. which rightly in no way suits David, and not even as a type, so far is it from being the case that this is expressed here concerning David. Finally, Rivetus confesses that the Prophet looked, even in v. 25. 26., to the truth in Christ, to whom this Prophecy is applied by the Jerusalemite people, with Christ approving and defending it Matth. 21, 9. And in which place it is clear, in the judgment of Rivetus, that Christ did not reject this honor, and defended the act of the children's acclamations as if directed by God. But it is certain, says Rivetus, that the words were taken from this our Psalm, which it is probable were often read in the synagogues of the Jews, and understood concerning the Messiah who was to come. Therefore they were used by the acclaiming people, as being customary and recognized. And afterwards: There is no doubt, he says, but that God by his providence directed the deed, and the words of the people applauding Christ in these words, as a King sent by God. If, therefore, in the ancient Synagogues of the Jews before the times of Christ those words of this Psalm were understood concerning the Messiah who was to come, and that was also known to the people, and familiar, and held as valid by Christ himself, and thus by divine providence also directing that acclamation from David to Christ it ought to have been made, are not the Zwinglian Judaizers, who accept the same concerning David according to the letter and the immediate, as they call it, sense, to be considered less sane than the ancient Church of the Jews rightly understanding the words of David in this part, and the very boys of Jerusalem? Indeed, even though R. Salomo Jarchi on Micah 5:2 confesses that this stone is not David, but Christ the son of David; And thou Bethlehem, out of thee shall come forth unto me etc. the Messiah, i.e., the son of David, according to that, the stone which they rejected etc. are they not more blind than the blind Jews, who boast themselves to be teachers of a purer Christian doctrine? Conf. on v. 13, 14. Sermon 29, and on v. 17, 18, 19. Sermon 14, in Memor. Justor. Witteberg.

We add Johannes Cocceius: who not only praises Kimchi, who refers this Psalm to the Messiah along with other Rabbis, but also, explaining his own opinion, says that the words of the Psalm can partly be of Christ speaking for himself and his members, and partly of the Church, as in the last verses: and on v. 5, I called upon Jehovah out of distress, he answered me in the breadth of Jah, he has it thus; The words are of CHRIST: who is also to be understood as commanding Israel, the Aaronites, those who fear

God, the proclamation of the goodness of God: but on verse 6, Jehovah is mine, I will not fear: he says, Christ speaks, but not only for himself, but also for his body.

Although indeed, according to his custom, Cocceius adds various private interpretations in the following verses, v. 10 et seqq., concerning the congregations of the nations against Christ 1. under the idolatrous Roman Emperors. 2. after Constantine, of the Arians and Saracens. 3. Under the Anti-Christ, 4. after the reformation of the Church persecuted by the Anti-Christ like Pharaoh: and takes verse 17, 18, as the said protestation against the nations drawing [men] into the second death: I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of Jah, and thanksgiving for preservation: Jah has chastened me severely, but has not delivered me to death; verse 19, 20, against the nations closing the gate of righteousness, but in verses

21, 22, 23, 24, he wishes the Church to give thanks to God for salvation from the hand of the persecutors: where he wrongly snatches the rejection of Christ made by the builders, who however is to be established as the head of the corner, to the times of the Anti-Christ and to the reformation of the Church, when these things treat of the passion and ascension of Christ into heaven: yet it is clear from the Cocceian interpretation that he acknowledged the text to be so clear that the Psalm cannot be understood concerning David, or referred to his times, as far as the literal sense is concerned; But it ought to be referred to Christ and the times of the New Testament. But what is to be thought of those Cocceian interpretations is clear from the above. The author maintains his old habit in devising wonderful and unheard-of glosses. Such as are also sprinkled here, from which it pleases me to produce a few by the way as an example. Christ, he says, is called a stone, and Gen. 49:24, thence, where he is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel: from heaven, where he is the Angel and Mediator of the Testament, who, as he vindicates his sheep, feeds, sustains, protects Israel, and is his rock. Is. 28:16, Behold, I am he who has founded in Zion a stone, a stone of probation, a corner of a most founded foundation. Dan. 2:34, 45, a stone was cut out, which was not or was not carried in hands, and struck the image. There is signified not only the rejection of Christ, but also his being cut out from the land of the living: which was done by unjust hands: which stone, not moved by the hands of men, but as if moved by its own force and power, struck and crushed the idol. Zech. 3:9, Behold the stone which I have given before Joshua, and which I have proposed to him to be looked upon in confidence, upon it shall be seven eyes, i.e. of many nations and indeed in seven times: Behold I will engrave its engravings, I will make it distinguished by every name and all its signs and characters, and I will wipe away the iniquity of THAT Land in one day. But setting aside those merely precarious interpretations, such as he inserts here and there in his Commentaries on Scripture, the author does not bring forth truly wonderful things from Scripture: it is worth observing one thing still concerning the present Psalm: That it is indeed not inelegantly accepted by some of our Interpreters as being entirely about Christ, if however all things are weighed more accurately, the opinion of our Blessed Luther seems to be preferred, in his golden and cedar-worthy explanation of this Psalm 118. Vol. 5. Jena edition, fol. 44 et seqq., approved by the preface of D. Cruciger the Elder, in which the Megalander judges that in the former verses David speaks of himself, as one who sets himself as an example to all the faithful, who also suffer such things, but finally conquer; that in verse 19 he desires the times of the N.T. and the manifestation of the Gospel, and that the gates of righteousness are called by a Hebrew phrase, by which Courts, Schools, Synagogues are called, because in the N.T. the Evangelical doctrine concerning the remission of sins and righteousness flourishes: but that in verse 22 it treats of Christ the head, and his humiliation and exaltation: in verse 24, This is the day which the Lord has made, explaining it excellently concerning the day of the N.T. which the Lord makes with the splendor and light of the sun of righteousness, Mal. 4:1. Which opinion the Blessed Luther repeats, appealing to his own commentary, in the Arguments of the Psalms Vol. III. Witteberg. Lat. on this Psalm. It is a thanksgiving, and that Psalm, Confitemini, which I uniquely admire, and pronounce to be golden, which has often lifted me up and comforted me in my temptations. It gives thanks at the same time and prophesies concerning Christ, who entered into glory through passion, who is that rejected Stone, made the head of the corner, as Christ also cites in Matthew 21. And it describes with wondrous affections the joyful day of the Gospel, the day of salvation and peace, the day of joy and consolation, that truly festive day, etc. Among other things, it shows that the Church and the children of God are to be rendered conformable to the image of the Son. To be surrounded on all sides by afflictions, and to be glorified through the cross and death; a brief summary does not embrace the most weighty matters of this chosen Psalm, my Commentary provides a full explanation. Which deserves to be consulted here entirely.

Moreover, those words of verse 22, the stone which the builders rejected, the Targum rendered thus: The boy whom the architects abandoned, who deserved to be constituted King: From that perverse interpretation, as if the discourse were about the boy David, and not from a different reading of the Hebrew codex, as if they had found אבן in the same, as Capellus contends, explaining it with an Arabic and Rabbinic signification concerning a boy, about which one may read Buxtorf in Anti-Crit. p. 717.

Latin:

BENEDIXIMVS VOBIS DE DOMO DOMINI) Et- iam nos qui de domo Domini sumus, id est, sacerdotes, fau- sta precamur regi ac populo.

Iterum judaizat cum Calvino, & complici- bus Hugo noster, ac si Psalmus de Davide agat. Mutus vero prorsus est de interpretatione Novi Testamenti: quam nullo attingit verbo, nisi quod vocem ὠσαννὰ Matth. 21, 9. ex hoc loco desumtam notet. Sequutus autem potissimum est R.
