## 120:7
MY SOUL HAS LONG BEEN A SOJOURNER. WITH THOSE WHO HATE PEACE I WAS PEACEFUL: WHEN I SPOKE TO THEM THEY ATTACKED ME WITHOUT CAUSE) The Hebrew punctuation makes this sense: My soul has long dwelt (that is, seemed to dwell) with those who hate peace. I (a man) of peace, (supply: I was) and when I spoke (peaceful things) to them (they spoke, that is) for war.

Some understand this of the exile of the faithful in these lands, where they are pilgrims and exiled from the heavenly fatherland: with Bellarmine, others understand it of the exile of David, when he had to stay among barbarians and idolaters, among the Moabites and Philistines, who are similar to Mesech and the Kedarenes or Muscovites and Arabs when comparing them in terms of their customs: although he also had such people in the court of Saul, concerning whom Wigand, Gesner, and Arcularius accept these things: The explanation of Blessed Luther in the argument of the Psalm is pleasing. Mesech are the neighboring nations which are to the north of Jerusalem itself, where the Tartars now are; Kedar are the Arabs to the east of Jerusalem. However, they are a type of all enemies and heretics who oppose the true Church.

Latin:

MVLTVM INCOLA FVIT ANIMA MEA. CVM HIS QVI ODERVNT PACEM ERAM PACIFICVS: CVM LOQVEBAR ILLIS IMPVGNABANT ME GRA- TIS) Hebræa distinctio hunc sensum facit: Multum sibi ha- bitavit (id est habitare visa est) anima mea cum his qui ode- runt pacem. Ego (vir) pacis, (supple eram) & cum loque- bar (pacifica) illi (loquebantur scilicet) ad bellum.

De exilio intelligunt nonnulli fidelium in his terris, ubi peregrini sunt, & a patria cœlesti exulant: cum Bellarmino, alii de exilio Davidis, ubi commo- randum ipsi fuit inter Barbaros, & idololatras, apud Moabitas, & Philistæos, qui similes Mesech & Keda- renis vel Moscovitis & Arabibus morum ratione il- lis conferendis: quanquam & in aula Saulis tales habuerit, de quibus Wigand. Gefneri Arcular. hæc accipiunt: Placet B. Lutheri explicatio in argum. Psalm. Mesech sunt vicinæ gentes, quæ ad septentrio- nem sunt ipsi Jerusalem, ubi jam sunt Tartari, Kedar sunt Arabes Jerosolymæ ad Orientem. Typus autem sunt omnium hostium, & hæreticorum, qui adversan- tur veræ Ecclesiæ.

## 121:1 Argument
PSALM 121. The Keeper of Israel who does not slumber.

I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES TO THE MOUNTAINS) Toward Zion. The Psalm seems to have been written at the time when there was war with Absalom.

To the mountains of the Scriptures or the Apostles, Augustine and others, and to the Saints and their invocation, some Papists snatch these things; but against the mind of David, who expects help solely from Him who made heaven and earth. By the mountains, the Weimar Paraphrasts understand heaven, in which sense the holy mountain seems to be taken in Psalm 3, 5. Not a few understand the mountains literally, partly by taking the preposition אל for על, because he who was established upon the mountains lifted up his eyes, as with R. Kimchi, Stephanus, Bucer, Calvin, Campensis, and also B. Glassius, Gramm. S. p. 498; partly by retaining the sense AD, interpreting it as the mountains of Zion and Moriah, which was done by the Dutch and others. Better is B. Tarnovius: Shall I lift up my eyes to these mountains, and to the inhabitants of this mountainous land, by metonymy, because Judea was mountainous, v. Exod. 15, 17. Deut. 11. v. 11. Psalm 125. v. 2. Luke 11. v. 39. From which interpretation the explanation of Piscator, Junius, B. Gesner, as also that of Mr. D. Gejer, does not depart much, in whose work the various explanations of others may also be seen. And although Bellarmine wishes to console David by promising the perpetual protection of God to pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem: yet it is more correctly established as an example of trust, with B. Luther leading the way, as to where and how it should be directed when we are in need of help, whence also his explanation (Tom. III. Witeb. Lat. fol. 583) is approved by us more than others; This place, he says, and similar ones (such as 'may He send you help from the Sanctuary') pertain properly to our Theology, which teaches that God wishes to be heard, worshipped, expected, and invoked according to His word, and not according to our thoughts. Thus He says in Deuteronomy: In whatever place I shall make a memorial of my name, I will come to you, and I will bless you. Therefore all the Jews were bound, in whatever place or region they were, to the Jerusalem temple, so that even when praying at home, they would turn their eyes toward Zion. God indeed accepted the prayer of the good in Babylon far from the temple and Jerusalem, but in such a way because they were singing and praying to that God who dwelt on Mount Zion, and had fixed His tabernacle there. And further: David fixes his prayer to the holy place, established in Jerusalem, in which was the memorial of the name of God, which He had made for Himself. Before that time it had been in Shiloh and Gibeah, where the tabernacle had been. In these places He heard prayers, He accepted sacrifices. In other places, however, He accepted neither prayers nor sacrifices. For there was not there the memorial of the name of the Lord, which He had made for Himself, but the memorial of the name of idolatry, which the impious Jews had fixed for themselves. Now, however, in the New Testament, the name of God dwells in Christ, and the Church, which is one body with Christ, where there are the word of God, baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the exercise of obedience toward God. These are B. Luther's words. It will be permitted, however, to understand by the mountain God Himself, as the added epexegesis teaches in v. 2: 'My help is from the Lord,' who is to us a Mountain of refuge and help; so that the plural used may be considered either for the sake of reverence, as Luther wishes, or also because of the antithesis, which cause Megalander also thinks has a place, i.e., 'Idolaters recur to their mountains, but I will remain at my mountains,' that is, at that one auxiliary mountain, my God, who is in the place of all things to me. It is known that empires are designated by mountains: why should not God, whose empire is over all things, be indicated by that name?

Latin:

PSALM. CXXI. Custos Israelis non dormitans.

LEVAVI OCVLOS MEOS IN MONTES) Versus Sionem. Videtur scriptus Psalmus de tempore, quo bellum erat cum Absolomo.

AD montes scripturarum vel Apostolos Augusti- nus & alii, ad Sanctos, eorumque invocationem Papistæ nonnulli hæc abripiunt; sed contra men- tem Davidis, qui auxilium unice expectat ab eo, qui cœlum & terram fecit. Per montes cœlum intelli- gunt Vinarienses Paraphrastæ, quo sensu mons san- ctus accipi videtur Psal. 3, 5. De montibus proprie non pauci intelligunt, partim præpositionem אל pro על accipiendo, quod super montes constitutus oculos levarit, ut cum R. Kimchi, Stephanus, Buce- rus, Calvinus, Campensis, nec non B. Glassius Gramm. S. pag. 498. partim retento sensu AD de montibus Sion & Moriæ interpretando, quod a Belgis & aliis factum. Melius B. Tarnovius: At- tollamne oculos meos ad hosce montes, & ad hujus ter- ræ montosæ incolas, per metonymiam, quia Judæa montoso erat, v. Exod. 15, 17. Deut. 11. vers. 11. Psal. 125. vers. 2. Luc. 11. vers. 39. A qua interpretatio- ne non multum abit Piscatoris, Junii, B. Gesneri, ut & Dn. D. Gejeri explicatio, apud quem & aliorum variæ explicationes videri poterunt. Et quanquam Bellarm. velit consolari Davidem peregrinos ascen- dentes in Jerusalem promittendo perpetuam Dei custodiam: rectius tamen constituitur exemplum fiduciæ præeunte B. Luthero, quorsum & quomo- do ea dirigenda sit, cum auxilio indigemus, unde & nobis præ aliis magis probatur ejusdem Tom. III. Witeb. Lat. fol. 583. explicatio; Hunc locum, in- quit, & similes (ut mittat tibi auxilium de Sancto) pertinere proprie ad nostram Theologiam, quæ docet, quod Deus velit audire, coli, expectari, invocari, se- cundum verbum suum, & non secundum nostras co- gitationes. Sic dicit in Deuter. In quocunque loco fe- cero ego memoriam nominis mei, veniam ad te, & be- nedicam tibi. Erant igitur omnes Judæi alligati, in quocumq; loco seu regione essent, ad templum Jerosoly- mitanum, ut etiam domi suæ orantes, verterent oculos ad Zion. Placuit quidem Deo oratio bonorum in Ba- bylone procul a templo & Jerusalem, sed ita, quia can- tabant & orabant ad illum Deum, qui in monte Sion habitabat, atque ibi suum tabernaculum fixerat. Et porro: Figit David orationem ad locum sanctum, constitutum in Jerusalem, in quo erat memoria nomi- nis Dei, quam ipse sibi fecerat. Ante id tempus fue- rat in Silo & Gibea, ubi tabernaculum fuerat. In his locis audiebat preces, accipiebat sacrificia. In aliis locis autem neque preces, nec sacrificia accipiebat. Erat enim ibi non memoria nominis Domini, quam ipse sibi fecerat, sed memoria nominis idololatriæ, quam impii Judæi sibi ipsis fixerant. Nunc autem in novo Testamento, habitat nomen Dei in Christo, & Ecclesia, quæ unum cum Christo corpus est, ubi sunt verbum Dei, baptismus, cœna Domini, & exercitium obedientiæ erga Deum. Hæc B. Luther. Licebit ta- men per montem intelligere Deum ipsummet, ut ἐπεξήγησις addita docet vers. 2. Auxilium meum à Domino: qui Mons refugii & auxilii nobis est; ut pluralis adhibitus censeatur sive reverentiæ gratia, ut Luther. vult, vel etiam ob antithesin, quam cau- sam etiam Megalander locum habere censet, q. d. Idololatræ recurrunt ad suos montes, sed ego manebo apud meos montes, h. e. unico illo auxiliari monte, Deo meo, qui est mihi loco omnium. Montibus imperia designari notum est: Quidni Deus cujus impe- rium est super omnia, isto nomine indigitetur.

THE LORD IS THY PROTECTION) σκέπη σου. In Hebrew: thy shadow.

## 121:6
Vers. 6.

BY DAY THE SUN SHALL NOT BURN THEE, NOR THE MOON BY NIGHT) In Hebrew it is: shall strike thee. The sun burns, the moon moistens beyond measure: concerning which matter see Macrobius, Saturnalia 7, near the end.

PER DIEM SOL NON VRET TE, NEQVE LVNA PER NOCTEM) In Hebræo est: percutiet te. Sol urit, Lu- na supra modum humectat: qua de re vide Macrobium Sa- turnalium 7. circa finem.

THE LORD KEEPS THY COMING IN AND THY GOING OUT) He prospers thy actions at home and abroad. Thus Num. 27. v. 17. 1 Kings 3. v. 7. 2 Chron. 1, 10.

DOMINVS CVSTODIT INTROITVM TVVM ET EXITVM TVVM) Actiones tuas domi forisque prospe- rat. Sic Num. 27. vers. 17. 1. Reg. 3. v. 7. 2. Paralip. 1, 10.

## 122:1 Argument
PSALM CXXII. The happiness of Jerusalem.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXII. Felicitas Jerusalem.

## 122:5
Vers. 5.

FOR THERE SAT SEATS IN JUDGMENT: SEATS UPON THE HOUSE OF DAVID) There is the great Sanhedrin judging the whole kingdom, which is as it were the house of the king.

Bellarminus refers the present Psalm both to the earthly and to the heavenly Jerusalem, yet primarily to the latter; but as a single sense must necessarily be established, so the predicates which are here attributed to Jerusalem sufficiently teach that it is not the heavenly, but the earthly that is regarded, for which he rejoices, because it is permitted there to hear the word of God and to preach the name of the Lord, for whose sake he prays for peace for it. Some think this congratulatory Psalm was composed on account of the ark of the covenant being carried to Mount Sion: and it seems probable to some that it was subsequently used when they ascended to solemn feasts with jubilation and song, Psalm 42, verse 5, Isaiah 30, verse 29. As we readily admit the latter, so concerning the time when the hymn was composed, nothing certain can be defined. B. Luther in Ps. grad. he judges that the temple had not yet been built at that time, yet its building by Solomon had been promised, whence he congratulates himself and all the people of David concerning a certain and firm place of the true worship of God in Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QVIA ILLIC SEDERVNT SEDES IN JVDICIO: SEDES SVPER DOMVM DAVID) Ibi est magnum Sy- nedrium jus dicens toti regno, quæ est velut domus regis.

BEllarminus Psalmum præsentem refert & ad terrenam, & ad cœlestem Jerosolymam, ad hanc tamen primario; sed uti unicus necessario statuen- dus est sensus, ita prædicata, quæ Hierosolymæ hic tribuuntur, satis docent, non cœlestem, sed terre- nam respici, ob quam lætatur, quod illic verbum Dei audire, & nomen Domini prædicare liceat, cu- jus gratia pacem eidem precatur. Nonnulli gratu- latorium huncce Psalmum concinnatam putant ob deportatam arcam fœderis in montem Sion: & pro- babile videtur quibusdam eundem usurpatum de- inceps, cum ad festa solemnia cum jubilis, & cantu ascenderunt Psalm. 42. vers. 5. Efa. 30. vers. 29. Quod posterius uti faciles admittimus, ita de tem- pore quo compositus est hymnus, nihil certi defini- re licet. B. Luther. in Ps. grad. censet tum non- dum fuisse conditum templum, promissam tamen ejus ædificationem per Salomonem, unde gratu- letur sibi, & toti populo David, de certo & firmo loco veri cultus Dei in Jerusalem.

Vers. 7.

LET THERE BE PEACE IN THY VIRTUE) In Hebrew: in thy bulwark: which certain Greeks translated ἐν προτειχίσματί σε. ABUNDANCE IN THY TOWERS) ἐν πυργοβάρεσί σε, which Jerome says is how houses built like towers are called. The Hebrews also explain ארמנות as palaces.

## 123:1 Argument
PSALM CXXIII. The hoping eye.

Vers. 5.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXIII. Oculus sperans.

Vers. 5.

## 123:4
FOR OUR SOUL IS EXCEEDINGLY FILLED: WITH THE REPROACH OF THE ABUNDANT, AND THE CONTEMPT OF THE PROUD) Better from the Hebrew thus: For our soul is affected with weariness by the reproach of the abundant and the contempt of the proud. The LXX translate שאננים as the wealthy, Isaiah 32:9, c. 33:20.

B. Luther in the argument of the Psalm teaches that it is an ardent prayer against the secure and most proud contemners of the word and of the ministers of the word: Which is more convenient than when the Hebrews refer it to the person of a captive in Babel. Bellarminus attributes it to a person suffering the pressure of the world in exile, but nothing is held here concerning exile. The servants of God are specifically the ministers of the word: in general, however, all the faithful serve God as their Lord; these, therefore, afflicted by contumely and reproach, look solely to the grace and mercy of their Lord and ardently seek it here. As for the final words of this Psalm, Tremellius and Junius accept them not as an ἐπιμονή, by which the same sentiment is repeated, but more fully, which is the interpretation of most, including Piscator and the Belgians, but by way of imprecation; which sense B. Tarnovius also embraces; Let this mockery be for those who are at ease (Am. 6, 1. who, confident in their present tranquility, abuse it, and mock us bitterly in our outcries) and let this contempt be (may it come hereafter) for the proud themselves. But those three things, the He Hajediah and the accentuation with others, which B. Tarnovius urges, do not at all stand in the way of the received interpretation, since the sense flows thus: Our soul is indeed abundantly sated: this insult (is) of the tranquil, this contempt (is) of the proud: and thus the Vulgate, the LXX Interpreters, the explanation of St. Augustine, and the Hieronymian version agree well, as far as the sense is concerned: our soul is much filled with the reproach of those who abound and the contempt of the proud, even if the punctuation varies: Compare Bellarm. in h. l.

of the preceding: as Jerusalem is surrounded on all sides by mountains, so the people of the Lord, the Church of GOD, is fortified on all sides by divine protection Zach. 2, 5. Matth. 16, 18. Psal. 34, 8. The Vulgate with the LXX Interpreters deviates from the Hebrew truth by rendering it thus, he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever. For the word Jerusalem belongs to the following verse.

Latin:

QVIA MVLTVM REPLETA EST ANIMA NO- STRA: OPPROBRIVM ABVNDANTIBVS, ET DE- SPECTIO SVPERBIS) Melius ex Hebræo sic: Tædio enim affecta est anima nostra opprobrio abundantium & despectu superborum. שאננים πλουτίους vertunt LXX. Esaiæ 32, 9. c. 33, 20.

B. Luther. in arg. Ps. docet, esse ardentem preca- tionem adversus securos & superbissimos con- temtores verbi & ministrorum verbi: Quod con- venientius est, quam cum Ebræi referunt ad perso- nam captivi in Babel. Bellarminus personæ in exilio mundi pressuram patienti tribuit, sed de exilio nihil hic habetur. Servi Dei speciatim sunt ministri verbi: in genere tamen Deo ut Domino suo omnes fideles serviunt; hi ergo contumelia & opprobrio afflicti unice gratiam & misericordiam Domini sui respiciunt eamque ar- denter hic expetunt. Quod a. ad postrema hujus Psalmi verba, Tremellius & Junius accipiunt non ut ἐπιμονὴν, qua repetatur eadem sententia, sed ple- nius, quæ plerorumque, etiam Piscatoris & Belga- rum est interpretatio, sed per modum imprecationis; quem sensum amplectitur etiam B. Tarnovius; Ista sanna sit tranquillis istis (Am. 6, 1. qui præsenti tranquillitati suæ confidentes ea abutuntur, & lu- disicantur nos acerbe in clamitatibus nostris) & iste contemtus sit (obveniat deinceps) ipsis super- bis. Sed tria illa He Hajediah & accentuatio cum aliis, quæ urget B. Tarnovius, nihil obstant rece- ptæ interpretationi, quum sensus ita fluat: Mul- tum profecto saturata est anima nostra: hæc autem insultatio (est) tranquillorum, hic contemtus (est) superborum: atque ita congruit probe vul- gata, LXX. Interpp. S. Augustini explicatio, & Hie- ronymiana versio, quantum ad sensum: multum repleta est anima opprobrio abundanium & despe- ctione superborum, etsi distinctio variet: Confer Bellarm. in h. l.

fus præcedentis: ut montibus undiquaque ambi- tur Jerusalem, sic populus Domini Ecclesiæ DEI undiquaque munitur præsidio divino Zach. 2, 5. Matth. 16, 18. Psal. 34, 8. Vulgata cum LXX. In- terpp. deflectit à veritate Ebr. ita reddendo, non commovebitur in æternum, qui habitat in Jeru- salem. Vox enim Jerusalem ad sequentem ver- sum pertinet.

PSALM CXXIV.

Vers. 7.

THE SNARE IS BROKEN) It is shattered.

Which Bellarmine understands both of the liberation from the Babylonian captivity and the enemies resisting the construction of the temple, and of the liberation of the martyrs from the persecutions of the pagans; for others, including B. Luther, it is more correctly an act of thanksgiving of the faithful in general for divine aid in all dangers.

Vers. 7.

LAQVEVS CONTRITVS EST) Ruptus est.

QUod intelligit Bellarmin. tum de liberatione è captivitate Babyl. & hostibus templi exstructio- ni resistentibus, tum de liberatione martyrum à perse- quutionibus paganorum; aliis, etiam B. Luthero re- ctius est gratiarum actio fidelium in genere pro di- vina ope in omnibus periculis.

## 125:1 Argument
PSALM CXXV.

Peace upon Israel.

They do not deserve consideration who, with Bellarmine, say this Psalm gives advice to pilgrims ascending to their homeland, both earthly and heavenly, nor does Cocceius, who says it is preached here as restricted to the Church of the New Testament and its firmness and preeminence. Which he wishes to be distinguished from Mount Zion, inasmuch as it could be moved and is not always inhabited; but it is a general description of the faithful and of the Church of any times: and the firmness of the faithful is preached, because they remain eternally, as is the divine custody of the Church which is to be freed from the pressure of the wicked: with a prayer for the faithful and the Church, and a commination against the impious. Those trusting in the Lord (are) as Mount Zion, i.e., so peculiarly beloved by GOD, and elected by Him, Ps. 78:68, 87:2, and therefore under the protection of GOD: (none of them) shall be moved, he shall remain forever: not that the faithful cannot fall from faith nor lose the Holy Spirit, can, as Crocius, Wendelinus, and Maffonius gather from this, but that the covenant of GOD on the part of GOD is ἀμεταμέλητον (irrevocable), Rom. 11:29, ch. 3:3, and that while the faithful themselves remain, they are never destitute of grace and divine custody: for Mount Zion indeed enjoyed the custody of GOD, and was beloved by GOD, as long as the Jewish people adhered to GOD: but that the faithful can turn away from GOD is indicated in verse 5, Musculus himself being the interpreter, not to mention Benefeld, who understands this predicate, he shall not be moved, not of individual members separately, but of the whole Church, which does not fail, but is invincible, Matt. 16:18. (Compare B. Barthol. Battus on the Apostasy of the Saints.) JERUSALEM (as far as it pertains, as Ps. 32:10, 41:13, 59:9, 90:10) mountains are around it; the Lord is around His people from now and even forever. It is a comparison, by the force of the

Latin:

PSALM. CXXV.

Pax super Israël.

NOn merentur calculum, qui cum Bellarmin hunc Psalmum ajunt consilium dare peregrinis ascendentibus in Patriam tum terrenam tum cœle- stem, nec Coccejus, qui restringit ad Ecclesiam Nov. Testament. ejusque firmitatem & præeminentiam hic prædicari, ait. Quam ille à monte Sion distin- gui vult, utpote qui & commoveri potuit & non semper habitatur; Est autem generalis descriptio fi- delium, & Ecclesiæ quorumvis temporum: & præ- dicatur firmitas fidelium, quod æternum maneant nec non custodia divina Ecclesiæ quæ liberanda à pressura improborum: cum precatione pro fidelibus, & Ecclesia & comminatione adversus impios. Confi- dentes in Domino (sunt) ut mons Sion, DEO sc. ita peculiariter dilecti, & electi ab eo Psal. 78, 68. 87, 2. ideoque sub protectione DEI: non commo- vetur (ullus eorum) in seculum manebit: non quod fideles excidere nequeant fide nec amittere Spir. Sanct. possint, ut Crocius, Wendelinus, Maffonius hinc colligunt, sed quod fœdus DEI ex parte DEI sit ἀμεταμέλητον, Rom. 11, 29. cap. 3, 3. quodque dum ipsi fideles manent, nunquam destituantur gratia & custodia divina: nam mons Sion fruebatur quidem custodia DEI, & dilectus erat DEO, quousque populus Judaicus adhære- bat DEO: quod autem declinare à DEO possint fideles verf. 5. indicatur, ipso Musculo interpre- te, ut taceam Benefeldum hoc prædicatum, non commoverur, non de membris singulis seorsim, sed de tota Ecclesia intelligere, quæ non deficit, sed invicta est Matth. 16, 18. (Confer. B. Barthol. Bat- tus de Apostasia Sanctor.) JERUSALEM (quod attinet, ut Psal. 32, 10. 41, 13. 59, 9. 90, 10.) montes circa ipsam sunt; Dominus circa populum suum à nunc usque in seculum. Comparatio est, vi ver-

## 125:3
ver. 3.

FOR THE LORD SHALL NOT LEAVE THE ROD OF SINNERS UPON THE LOT OF THE JUST.

In Hebrew: For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest upon the lot of the just, which some understand specifically of Pseudo-Prophets and fanatics, but tyrants are not to be excluded; for both heretics and tyrants sometimes rule over the just, by the judgment and permission of GOD, for a time; but it shall not remain or rest upon them, inasmuch as they are the Lot of the Lord himself 1. Petr. 5, 3. the scepter of wickedness: nay, those declining into their perversities, into ways both of doctrine and of life that are perverse, the Lord shall drive away from himself with the workers of vanity, or as את may be a sign of the accusative, WORKERS, because those who decline into perverse ways work vanity or iniquity. For און is pain of soul, and metaleptically iniquity bringing pain.

Latin:

verf. 3.

QUIA NON RELINQUET DOMINUS VIRGAM PECCATORUM SUPER SOR- TEM JUSTORUM.

In Ebr. Nam non quiescet sceptrum improbi- tatis super sortem justorum, quod de Pseudo-Pro- phetis & fanaticis nonnulli speciatim intelligunt, sed excludendi non sunt tyranni; Nam & hæretici, & tyranni dominantur quandoque, judicio & per- missione DEI, justis, ad tempus; sed non mane- bit aut quiescet super ipsis, utpote qui Sors sunt ipsius Domini 1. Petr. 5, 3. sceptrum improbiia- tis: imo declinantes in perversitates suas, in vias tum doctrinæ tum vitæ perversas, abiget à se Dominus cum operariis vanitatis, vel ut את Maneat nota ac- cusativi, OPERARIOS, quia qui declinant in vias perversas operantur vanitatem vel iniquitatem. Nam און dolor animi est, & metaleptice iniquitas afferens dolorem.

## 125:5
Ver. 5.

BUT THOSE WHO TURN ASIDE INTO OBLIGATIONS) In Hebrew: Those turning aside to crooked things. Symmachus: εις σκολιότητας (into crookednesses). Theodotion: εις διεστραμμένα (into perverted things).

The Vulgate is deservedly emended: The LXX have στραγγαλίας (perplexities): The Syrian, who twist their paths. The Papists twist themselves here, and yet they cannot free the Vulgate, which the Pope has canonized, from a blunder: In this place, says Cardinal Bellarmine, there is a great question about that word OBLIGATIONS; and indeed others say other things, but just as I allow everyone to abound in his own sense, so if this little verse must cohere with the previous one, and if the Latin codices are to be reconciled with the Greek and Hebrew, I have no doubt that the Latin interpreter wrote obligations, not so much looking to the thing which is bound and tightened by an obligation, as to the very obliquity which is seen in a rope while something is being bound, for nothing can be bound unless a rope that is otherwise straight is twisted and led into circles. What subtlety, worthy of a Jesuit, not to say a Cardinal! Naturally he does not dare to say, because of the Papal thunderbolt, that obligations ought to be read; hence he so ineptly twists those things which are straight and leads them into circles, so that in the end the Jesuitical obliquation, or obliquity, is felt.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

DECLINANTES AVTEM IN OBLIGATIONES) In Hebræo: Declinantes ad tortuosa. Symmachus: εις σκολιότητας. Theodotio: εις διεστραμμένα.

Merito emendatur Vulgata: LXX. habent στραγγαλίας perplexitates: Syrus, qui contorquent semitas suas. Torquent se hic Papistæ, nec tamen à sphalmate liberare possunt vulgatam, quam ca- nonizavit Pontifex: Hoc loco, inquit Cardin. Bel- larm. magna est quæstio de verbo illo OBLIGATIO- NES; & quidem alii alia dicunt, sed ego ut permit- to unumquemque abundare in sensu suo, ita si debeat cohærere hic versiculus cum superiore, & si concilian- di sunt codices Latini cum Græcis & Hebraicis, ni- hil dubito, quin Latinus interpres scripserit ob- ligationes, non tam respiciens ad rem, quæ ligatur, & stringitur per obligationem, quam ad ipsam ob- liquitatem, quæ cernitur in fune, dum aliquid liga- tur, neque enim obligari potest aliquid, nisi funis a- lioqui directus torqueatur, & in circulos ducatur. Hèm subtilitatem Jesuita, ne dicam Cardinali dignam! Nimirum non audet dicere ob fulmen Papale, obligationes legi debere, hinc tam in- epte ea quæ directa sunt contorquet, & in circu- los ducit, ut in fine palpetur Jesuitica obliquatio, vel obliquitas.

## 126:1 Argument
PSALM CXXVI.

The joyful harvest of those who weep.

Ver. 1.

WHEN THE LORD TURNED BACK THE CAPTIVITY OF ZION) It seems to be of Ezra, or someone contemporary. WE BECAME AS THOSE CONSOLED) ὡσεὶ παρακεκλημένοι (as those comforted). Like those who suddenly grow old from sickness. The Chaldean here interprets it as those recovering. For כּחלמין has that meaning in Isaiah 38:16, where the Greeks (say) παρακληθεὶς ἔζησε (having been comforted, he lived). The same word has the same sense in Job 39:4, and among the Syrian interpreter of the New Testament several times. The Syrian here: who rejoice.

This Vulgate in one verse commits two Solecisms, which Bellarmine miserably excuses with this Scheme: that he wished to render the Greek words word for word, and therefore spoke less Latinly. But was he therefore obliged to render it barbarously? Could it not have been translated: we have become as those affected by consolation? And he ought to have followed the Hebrew, not the Greek text. He says that St. Jerome followed the meaning, not the words, by rendering it in this way: When the Lord turned again the captivity of Sion, we became as dreamers; undoubtedly because Jerome did not wish to commit solecisms. But ought he not to be censured for having followed the words more, when he rendered כחלמים as dreamers? Bellarmine admits that the word signifies that, explaining the sense thus: As soon as the decree of release and return to the fatherland was heard by us, we could scarcely believe for excessive joy what was being said, and we seemed not to see and hear, but to dream. Which meaning of the Hebrew word is more accepted than the Grotian one, and is retained by most interpreters. Moreover, although the blessed [Psalm] present... Luther, in the arguments of the Psalms, refers it to the Babylonian captivity, yet in his explanation of the Psalms of Degrees, he thinks it looks to the redemption accomplished through Christ. For the Prophet, he says, uses far more serious language than to befit those particular and one-time captivities. For what great thing is it that this handful of the Jewish people was liberated, compared to that splendid and greatest liberation by which the entire human race was liberated, not from temporal enemies, but from eternal ones, from death, Satan, and hell? Wherefore we establish that this Psalm is a prophecy about the redemption to come through Christ, and the promulgation of the Gospel, through which the kingdom of Christ is propagated, death and Satan are conquered, and all evils are abolished. With this general meaning standing, it is afterwards free to apply the Psalm to any liberation, both bodily and spiritual.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXVI.

Flentium messis læta.

Vers. 1.

IN CONVERTENDO DOMINVS CAPTIVITA- TEM SION) Esdræ videtur esse, aut alicujus coævi. FACTI SVMVS SICVT CONSOLATI) ὡσεὶ παρα- κεκλημένοι. Vt illi qui ex morbo subito senescunt. Chal- dæus hic interpretatur convalescentes. Nam כּחלמין eam significationem habet Esaiæ 38, 16. ubi Græci παρακληθεὶς ἔζησε. Eundem sensum habet idem verbum Jobi 39, 4. & apud Syrum Novi Testamenti interpretem aliquoties. Sy- rus hic: qui lætantur.

Vulgatus hic in uno versu duos committit Solœcismos, quos misere excusat hoc Schemate Bellarm. quod verba Græca voluerit ad verbum reddere, & ideo minus Latine loquutus sit. At num ideo barbare reddere debuit? Annon verti potuit: facti sumus sicut consolatione affecti? Et Ebræum non|Græcum textum sequi debebat. S. Hierony- mum vero sententiam, non verba sequutum dicit hoc modo reddendo: Cum converteret Dominus captivitatem Sion, facti sumus sicut somniantes; ni- mirum quia solæcismos committere noluit Hiero- nymus. Annon vero magis verba sequutus cen- fendus est, cum כחלמים reddidit somniantes? Id utique verbum illud significare fatetur Bellarmi- nus, sensum ita exponens: Cum primum audi- tum est à nobis decretum relaxationis & reversionis in patriam, prægaudio vix credere potuimus, quid dicebatur, & nobis non videre & audire, sed somnia- re videbamur. Quæ significatio vocis Ebrææ receptior est, quam Grotiana, & a plerisque In- terpretibus retinetur. Cæterum Psalmum præ- sentem etsi B. Lutherus in argumentis Psalmorum ad captivitatem Babylonicam referat, in explica- tione tamen Psalmorum graduum spectare censet ad redemptionem per Christum factam. Nam Propheta, inquit, longe graviore oratione utitur, quam ut istis particularibus & unius temporis captivitatibus con- veniat. Quid enim magnum est, hunc quasi pugil- lum populi Judaici liberatum esse, præ illa splendida & maxima liberatione, qua universum genus hu- manum liberatum est, non à temporalibus hostibus, sed æternis, a morte, Satana, & inferno? Quare sta- tuimus hunc Psalmum esse Prophetiam de redemptio- ne per Christum futura, & invulgatione Evangelii, per quod regnum Christi propagatur, mors & Satan vincitur, & abolentur omnia mala. Stante hac ge- nerali sententia, postea liberum est, Psalmum ap- plicare cuilibet liberationi, tum corporali, tum spi- rituali.

## 126:5
ver. 5. TURN AGAIN, O LORD, OUR CAPTIVITY AS A TORRENT IN THE SOUTH.

Bellarmine explains it thus, so that the reduction is full and swift, such as is wont to be of those things which a torrent snatches up with it and rolls down, when it is filled by the South wind blowing and the rains and snows melting: others more correctly, that they are thus restored to their channels or beds, just as dried-up and empty channels are wont to be filled by rains IN SOUTHERN PLACES, because the Hebrew word denotes not the wind, but the region; Jud. 1, 9. 15. See Mr. Dr. Gejer on this passage.

Latin:

vers. 5. CONVERTE DOMINE CAPTIVITA- TEM NOSTRAM SICUT TORRENS IN AUSTRO.

Bellarm. ita explicat, ut plena sit & velox re- ductio, qualis solet esse earum rerum, quas torrens secum abripit, & devolvit, quando flante Austro pluviis & nivibus liquefactis impletur: alii rectius, ut ita restituantur alveis seu sedibus suis, uti pluviis im- pleri alvei arefacti atque vacui solent IN LOCIS MERIDIONALIBUS, quia non ventum, sed pla- gam vox Ebræa denotat; Jud. 1, 9. 15. Vid. Dn. D. Gejer. in h. l.

## 127:1 Argument
PSALM CXXVII. Good household management.

Ver. 1. A SONG OF DEGREES OF SOLOMON.

This Psalm, says Bellarmine, has always seemed to me beyond measure obscure, and even now after long study I confess that I do not perfectly grasp the literal sense. But what, I ask, is obscure in this Psalm? Undoubtedly the Cardinal does not attend to the words of Holy Scripture, but to the explanation of the Fathers, in which, since he found nothing certain, he rashly complained about the obscurity of the Psalm. He says the exposition of Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Euthymius seems more probable, that an exhortation to the Hebrew people is contained here, after the return from the Babylonian captivity, when they were laboring in building the house of GOD, and restoring the city of Jerusalem. Therefore he thinks Solomon is introduced, admonishing Zerubbabel how he ought to conduct himself in this building, drawing everything in the whole Psalm to that; yet also feigning a higher sense, about the true Solomon, Christ, who might admonish those who aspire to true peace, and by aspiring ascend from the valley of tears to the vision of peace, the heavenly Jerusalem, how they ought to build and guard the house or city of the Church, and then also how each one ought to build a house for himself in heaven. But this duality of sense regarding the temple, both material and mystical, is alien to the simplicity of Scripture, which being eliminated, no obscurity remains in the Psalm. Nor indeed is it about the temple of the Lord, as Coppenius and the blessed Tarnovius wish with Kimchi, but about a private house, family affairs, and politics that is treated here; there is certainly no indication that the temple of the Lord is being treated. Mention is made generally of a house, but not of the House of the Lord: nor with the He Hajediah. And it is known what it is in Scripture to build a house, see Exod. 1, 21. Deut. 25, 9. 1 Sam. 2, 35. 2 Sam. 7, 11. 16. 26. 1 Kings 2, 24. 11, 38. Prov. 14, 1. 11. c. 24, 3. therefore Vatablus rightly explains it concerning the whole economic matter. With whom most all interpreters agree; which opinion is confirmed by what the Holy Psalmist handed down concerning vain solicitude in the acquisition of daily bread, unless the Lord has blessed, and concerning the God-given gift of children, which the Cardinal ineptly twisted to the temple or the Church, but which the blessed Luther most correctly explained in his lectures on the Psalms of Degrees as concerning family affairs. Meanwhile, we easily concede that the Psalm was written by Solomon, which the Vulgate and Campensis with Eusebius and Origen hint, and the blessed Tarnovius teaches on this passage, although others explain it as 'for Solomon' or 'in favor of Solomon,' as Cajetan, Vatablus, Piscator, and Junius have interpreted with Kimchi: The blessed Luther also adopted the former opinion, from whom we subjoin some things also illustrating the argument of the Psalm: This Psalm has the title of Solomon, and indeed it is likely that Solomon is its author: for we see in all of Solomon's books that he is almost a political teacher, and he does not treat the principal article of his father David, concerning justification, or concerning Christ the heir and descendant of David, but he treats those things in which he was engaged and was appointed by God, namely, politics. But he does that in such a way that no philosopher, indeed no man, has ever taught about politics in this way. For he transfers the whole polity to faith, and whatever is done either in the Republic or in the Economy, he refers it to divine administration, which other writers, whether they were philosophers or orators, do not do. For although laws dictate and reasons prescribe by which a Republic may be rightly administered and a family beautifully governed, yet they do not know whence success is to be sought, so that those things which have been rightly consulted may succeed, but they experience themselves to be destitute of success. For they know only the material and formal cause of both Politics and Economics; but they do not know the final and efficient cause, that is, they do not know whence Politics and Economics come, and by whom they are preserved, likewise whither they tend. Aristotle therefore in his Ethics and on the Republic, likewise Xenophon, Plato, Cicero, and others, although they wrote excellently about the Republic, yet they do not touch upon the true efficient and final cause; for they think the best and chief final cause to be political peace, honesty, glory, etc. But they constitute the efficient cause to be a wise man, or a prudent Magistrate, or as they themselves speak, a good man and citizen. But we shall hear Solomon disputing otherwise and more properly. Thus Megalander, who has executed those things excellently.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXVII. Oeconomia bona.

Vers. 1. CANTICUM GRADUUM SALOMO- NIS.

PSalmus hic, inquit Bellarm. semper mihi visus est supra modum obscurus, & nunc etiam post longum studium fateor me non perfecte assequi sensum literalem. Quidnam vero, obsecro, in hoc Psal- mo obscuri? Nimirum non attendit verbis Scri- pturæ Sacræ Cardinalis, sed explicationi Patrum, in qua cum nihil certi inveniret, de obscuritate Psalmi temere questus est. Probabiliorem videri ait Chrystost. Theodor. & Euthymii expositionem, quod contineatur hic exhortatio ad populum Ebræum, post reversionem e captivitate Babylonica, quando laborabat in ædificanda domo DEI, & restauranda civitate Jerusalem. Ideo Salomonem introduci pu- tat, Zorobabelem admonentem, quomodo se in hac æ- dificatione gerere debeat, omnia in toto Psalmo eo trahens; altiorem tamen etiam fingens sensum, de vero Salomone Christo, qui admoneat eos, qui ad veram pacem adspirant, & adspirando adscendunt de valle lachrymarum, ad visionem pacis, Hierusa- lem cœlestem, quomodo debeant ædificare & custodire domum sive civitatem Ecclesiæ, tum etiam unus quis- que sibi domum ædificare in cœlo. Sed hæc διπλότης sensus de templo tum materiali, tum mystico aliena est à simplicitate Scripturæ, qua eliminata nulla relinquitur in Psalmo obscuritas. Nec vero de templo Domini, ut cum Kimchio, Coppenius & B. Tarnovius volunt, sed de domo privata, re familia- ri, & Politia hic agitur; Nullum certe indicium est de templo Domini tractari. Mentio fit gene- ratim domus, non vero Domus Domini: nec cum He Hajediah. Et notum est, quid in Scriptura sit, Domum ædificare, vid. Exod. 1, 21. Deut. 25, 9. 1. Sam. 2, 35. 2. Sam. 7, 11. 16. 26. 1. Reg. 2, 24. 11, 38. Prov. 14, 1. 11. c. 24, 3. ideo de tota re œconomica re- cte explicat Vatablus. Cui consonant plerique omnes interpretes; Quam sententiam firmant, quæ de frustranea solicitudine in acquisitione panis quo- tidiani, nisi benedixerit Dominus, & de liberorum dono θεοσδότῳ tradidit Hiero-Psaltes, quæ inepte detorsit ad templum, vel Ecclesiam Cardinalis, rectissime autem B. Lutherus prælectionibus in Psalm. graduum exposuit de re familiari. Interim facile concedimus à Salomone Psalmum conscri- ptum esse, quod vulgata & Campensis cum Eusebio & Origene innuit, ac B. Tarnovius docet in h. l. licet alii exponant pro Salomone, vel in gratiam Sa- lomonis, ut Cajetanus, Vatabl. Piscator, Junius cum Kimchio interpretati sunt: Assumpsit priorem sen- tentiam etiam B. Lutherus, e quo nonnulla subji- cimus argumentum etiam Psalmi illustrantia: Ha- bet hic Psalmus titulum Salomonis, & sane verisi- mile est Salomonem autorem ejus esse: Videmus enim in omnibus Salomonis libris, quod fere est doctor po- liticus, nec tractat principalem articulum patris sui David, de justificatione, vel de Christo hærede, & ne- pote Davidis, sed ea tractat, in quibus versatus & à Deo constitutus fuit, nempe politica. Id autem fa- cit eo modo, ut nullus Philosophus, imo nullus homo unquam sic de politicis docuerit. Transfert enim to- tam politiam ad fidem, & quidquid vel in Republ. vel in Oeconomia geritur, id refert ad divinam ad- ministrationem, quod alii scriptores, sive Philosophi, sive Oratores fuerunt, non faciunt. Quanquam enim leges dictant, & rationes præscribunt, quibus recte administrari Respublica, & familia pulchre gubernari possit, tamen non sciunt, unde successus petendus sit, ut illa, quæ recte consulta sunt, succe- dant, sed experiuntur se successu destitui. Nam ma- terialem & formalem causam solum tum Politiæ, tum Oeconomiæ norunt; finalem autem & efficien- tem causam non norunt, hoc est, nesciunt unde ve- niant Politia & œconomia, & à quo conserventur, item quo tendant. Aristoteles igitur in Ethicis & de Republica, item Xenophon, Plato, Cicero, & alii, quamquam de Republica præclare scripserunt, tamen veram efficientem, & finalem causam non attin- gunt; Causam enim finalem optimam & præci- puam putant esse pacem Politicam, honestum, glo- riam &c. Efficentem autem causam constituunt virum sapientem, seu prudentem Magistratum, vel ut ipsi loquuntur, virum & civem bonum. Sed Sa- lomonem audiemus aliter & proprie magis disputan- tem. Hæc Megalander, qui illa præclare exequutus est.

## 127:3
Vers. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

## 127:4
AS THE ARROWS OF A MIGHTY MAN, SO THE SONS OF THOSE SHAKEN OUT) That indeed הנעורים allows for this exposition, which the LXX translate as ἐκ τετιναγμένων, others as τῶν παιδητῶν, while some explain it as ἠκοντίστων νεῶν. But the best interpretation is that of Symmachus, who translates it as τῆς νεότητος. We have the opposite in Gen. 35:18 & 37:3. Sons born in youth are accustomed to be more robust.

Latin:

SICVT SAGITTÆ POTENTIS, ITA FILII EXCVS- SORVM) Illud quidem הנעורים hanc expositionem patitur, quam LXX. vertunt ἐκ τετιναγμένων, alii τῶν παιδητῶν, nonnulli exponunt, ἠκοντίστων νεῶν. Sed optima est inter- pretatio Symmachi, qui vertit τῆς νεότητος. Oppositum habemus Genes. 35, 18. & 37,3. Filii in juventute geniti ro- bustiores esse solent.

## 127:5
Verse 5.

HE SHALL NOT BE ASHAMED, WHEN HE SPEAKS WITH HIS ENEMIES IN THE GATE) No one will dare to impose unjust lawsuits upon him, for fear of so many avengers. These are the Spirit of the Law of the Old [Testament].

A twin accusation recurs from the school of Pelagius and Socinus, as if the faithful of the Old Testament did not possess the Spirit of adoption just as the faithful of the New Testament did, and as if vengeance in the Old Testament were of such a kind that it was lawful, which now under the New Testament is prohibited and illicit. Which we have already noted several times with just censure. Therefore, I do not wish to do what has been done (τὸ πραχθὸν πράττειν).

Latin:

Vers. 5.

NON CONFVNDETVR, CVM LOQVETVR INI- MICIS SVIS IN PORTA) Nemo illi audebit injustas li- tes impingere, præ metu tot ultorum. Hæc sunt Spiritus legis Veteris.

Recurrit ἔγκλημα geminum è Pelagii & So- cini Schola, ac si fideles Veteris Testamenti Spiritum adoptionis non perinde habuerint, uti fideles N. Test. & ultio in Veteri Testam. talis licita fuerit, quæ nunc sub N. T. sit prohibita, & illicita. Quod aliquoties justa censura jam notavimus. Nolo ergo τὸ πραχ- θὸν πράττειν.

## 128:1 Argument
PSALM CXXVIII. A blessed marriage.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXVIII. Conjugium benedictum.

## 128:2
Verse 2.

FOR THOU SHALT EAT THE LABOURS OF THINE HANDS) You shall live by honest labor acquired, suppliant to no one.

What Cocceius introduces here concerning the hidden manna in Rev. 2:7, 17, and in the following verse 3, concerning Christ the bridegroom of the Church, and how the Church of the Gentiles has been made as it were a spouse to the Church of the Jews, as well as concerning the feeding of many by the doctrine and type of life acquired, are both twisted and foreign (ἀλλότρια), as are many other things in this author, passively.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

LABORES MANVVM TVARVM QVIA MANDV- CABIS) Vives honesto labore partis, nemini supplex.

QUæ hic ingerit Coccejus de manna abscondito Ap. 2, 7. 17. & vers. 3. sequenti, de Christo sponso Ecclesiæ, & quomodo Ecclesia gentium quasi conjux Ecclesiæ Judæorum facta sit, nec non de ciba- tione multorum doctrina & typo vitæ acquisitorum, & contorta sunt, & ἀλλότρια, ut multa alia apud hunc autorem passivitus.

## 129:1 Argument
PSALM CXXIX. The persecutors of Israel cursed.

Verse 1.

MANY A TIME HAVE THEY AFFLICTED ME) He meant to say they fought against me, ἐπολέμησάν με.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXIX. Persequutores Israelis maledicti.

Vers. 1.

SÆPE EXPVGNAVERVNT ME) Voluit dicere oppu- gnaverunt, ἐπολέμησάν με.

## 129:3
Verse 3.

UPON MY BACK THE SINNERS HAVE BUILT) In Hebrew, they plowed. Aquila and Theodotion well [translated it] ἠροτρίασαν [they plowed]. They lacerated me like land that is broken up.

THEY HAVE PROLONGED THEIR INIQUITY) The LXX read למעלותם. In Hebrew, it is better as למענותם, a continued metaphor: they have drawn out their furrows: they have long vexed me.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SVPRA DORSVM MEVM FABRICAVERUNT PECCATORES) In Hebræo arabarunt. Aquila & Theo- dotion bene ἠροτρίασαν. Laceraverunt me ut terram quæ proscinditur.

PROLONGAVERVNT INIQVITATEM SVAM) Le- gerunt LXX. למעלותם. In Hebræo melius למענותם continuata metaphora: protraxerunt sulcos suos: diu me ve- xarunt.

## 129:4
Verse 4.

THE JUST LORD HATH CUT THE NECKS OF SINNERS] He tamed their ferocity.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

DOMINVS JVSTVS CONCIDIT CERVICES PEC- CATORVM] Domuit eorum ferociam.

## 129:6
Verse 6.

LET THEM BE AS THE GRASS OF THE ROOFTOP) Let them be like the herb (for that is what the Hellenists call χόρτον [grass]) which grows on roofs: and being destitute of moisture, it perishes very quickly.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

FIANT SICVT FOENVM TECTORVM) Fiant simi- les herbæ (id enim χόρτον vocant Hellenistæ) quæ in tectis nascitur: & humore destituta, cito admodum perit.

## 129:8
Verse 8.

AND THEY THAT PASSED BY DID NOT SAY: THE BLESSING OF THE LORD BE UPON YOU) As was the custom in the fields, Ruth 2:4.

Cocceius does not refer this Psalm to the nation of Israel according to the flesh, but to the covenantal Israel, the faithful friend of GOD and His people, in which are also contained those who, although they are not of Israel according to the flesh, are nevertheless participants in the covenant of the Israelites through faith. He makes the childhood of Israel that condition in which it was until the προθεσμίας [appointed] time set by the Father under curators and tutors: so that the first childhood is established in Egypt, the second under the judges, the third under the Kings, and the last after the Babylonian captivity; he understands verses 3 and 4 as referring to the time after childhood, as soon as the Church was made free, its back was given to be plowed by enemies. But that οἰκονομία [economy] and ἐξήγησις [exegesis] of the text is merely arbitrary. Israel is said to have been afflicted from its childhood. The time of affliction is therefore established from childhood, but it is not merely childhood, completed by distinct stages. We, with the blessed Luther, distinguish the application from the explanation of the text itself, and we subjoin its argument, and indeed its sense and use, as proposed in the argument of this Psalm, Tom 3. Lat. Witteb. f. 431. It is, he says, a thanksgiving, by which the people of God, Israel, give thanks to God for all kinds of consolations and liberations, just as from the beginning He often wonderfully and powerfully liberated them from the hand of enemies, just as it is written in the Books of Judges and Kings that the Israelites were often pressed by harsh empires and the tyranny of the Gentiles, who afflicted them for a long time, and by plowing as it were on their backs, drew long furrows with the harshest plows, and treated them most savagely under a hard yoke, until God sent them a deliverer, and liberated them from the plowmen and the plows and those yokes alike. In the end, he prays for them (that is, he prophesies) that they may perish, and that they may wither like the grass of the rooftops, just as it also happened. For all the enemies and hostile nations of Israel perished, but Israel remained, and was repeatedly raised up by new consolations. Thus, even now, all the impious and enemies of God and the Word are like the grass of the rooftops, which indeed luxuriates in a copious forest, as if it were going to last, but before it matures, it withers, and is of no use. So too the enemies of the Word, all heretics, when they are very proud and boast magnificently against God, suddenly wither away like falling grass, but Christians and the Church remain forever.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET NON DIXERVNT QVI PRÆTERIBANT: BE- NEDICTIO DOMINI SVPER VOS) Vt mos erat in agris Ruth. 2, 4.

COccéjus hunc Psalmum non ad gentem Israel secundum carnem, sed Israelem fœderatum fi- delem amicum DEI & populum ipsius refert, in quo etiam contineantur illi, qui licet secundum carnem non sunt ex Israele, tamen fœderis Israelitarum par- ticipes sunt per fidem. Pueritiam autem Israelis eam ejus conditionem facit, in qua fuit usque ad προθε- σμίας tempus à Patre præfixum sub curatoribus, & tutoribus: ut prima pueritia in Ægypto, altera sub judicibus, tertia sub Regibus, ultima post Babylo- nicam captivitatem constituatur; Versum v. 3. & 4. intelligit de tempore post pueritiam, statim atque libera facta est Ecclesia tergum ejus perarandum est datum hostibus. Sed ea textus οἰκονομία, & ἐξή- γησις mere est arbitraria. A pueritia afflictus dicitur Israel. Tempus afflictionis ergo constistuitur inde à pueritia, non vero mera est pueritia, absoluta di- stinctis gradibus. Nos cum B. Luthero applicatio- nem, ab ipsa explicatione textus distinguimus, ejus- que argumentum imo & sensum & usum in argu- mento hujus Psalmi Tom 3. Lat. Witteb. f. 431. pro- positum subjungimus. Est, inquit, gratiarum a- ctio, qua populus Dei Israel Deo agit gratias, pro o- mnis generis consolationibus & liberationibus, sicut inde ab initio sæpe mirabiliter & potenter libera- vit eos de manu hostium, sicut in Libris Judicum & Regum scriptum est, Israelitas sæpe esse duris impe- riis & tyrannide Gentilium pressos, qui eos longo tempore afflixerunt, & quasi in tergo ipsorum aran- do, asperrimis aratris longos sulcos duxerunt, & sub duro jugo sævissime tractarunt, donec Deus mitte- ret eis liberatorem, & ab arantibus simul & aratris, ac jugis illis, eos liberaret. In fine precatur eis (id est prophetat) ut pereant, & ut fænum tectorum exarescant, sicut etiam factum est. Nam omnes hostes, & gentes inimicæ Israelis perierunt, Israel au- tem mansit, & subinde erectus est novis consolatio- nibus. Ita adhuc omnes impii & hostes Dei & ver- bi sunt sicut gramen tectorum, quod quidem copiosa sylva luxuriat, quasi duraturum, sed antequam maturescat, exarescit, & nullius est usus. Ita & hostes verbi, omnes hæretici cum valde superbiunt, & magnifice se jactant adversus Deum, repente velu- ti caducum gramen deflorescunt, Christiani autem & Ecclesia perpetua manet.

## 130:1 Argument
PSALM 130. Crying from the depths.

Verse 1.

OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED UNTO THEE) That is, Sunk in evils. Psalm 69, 1 & 2 confirms this interpretation.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXX. Clamans de profundis.

Vers. 1.

DE PROFVNDIS CLAMAVI AD TE) Id est, Mersus malis. Hanc interpretationem confirmat Psal. 69, 1. & 2.

## 130:3
Verse 3.

IF THOU, O LORD, SHOULDST MARK INIQUITIES, O LORD, WHO SHALL STAND?) Many things in that time, as being more imperfect, were overlooked, which God would not overlook under the covenant of Christ, where there is such certainty of eternal life, such holiness of examples and precepts, such power of the Spirit; But in both times, with a distinction, it is nevertheless true what Philo says in his book ὅτι ἄτρεπτον τὸ θεῖον, aptly to this matter: 'For if God should wish to judge a mortal without mercy, He will bring a condemning vote, since no man from birth until death has run a life faultless of himself, but has used both voluntary and involuntary slips in his path.'

These again are Pelagian-Socinian absurdities, inasmuch as 1. The time of the Old Testament was more imperfect, as far as the laws were more imperfect: that in the New Testament more perfect laws were delivered. For the mortal law was perfect, μηδεμίαν πρόσθεσιν καὶ ἀφαίρεσιν ἀπεκδεχόμενος, as Varinus describes a perfect rule: Deut. 4, 2. chap. 12, 32. Nor in the New Testament has it been rendered more perfect in any way: nay, it is the eternal rule of justice, and a mirror of true perfection. Christ did not come as a new νομοθέτης: But that He might provide grace and truth, which could not be expected from the law requiring of us, after the fall, a rigid observance impossible to perform John 1, 18. Rom. 8, 4. 5. That God overlooked many things under the Old Testament which Christ did not overlook under the new Covenant. Where is there even a trace or footprint of this thing in the Holy Scriptures? Does God show Himself more rigid and severe to the faithful under the new Covenant, [and] show Himself more kind and easy in the time of the Old Testament? How then has χάρις σωτήριος now shone forth under the new Testament? How is the Gospel of grace now preached throughout the world far more sweetly, to preach which Christ Himself was anointed and sent Is. 61, 1. seqq. How is it now the time of grace, the day of salvation, the day which the Lord has made, in which we can rejoice and be glad in the Lord? Innumerable praises of this kind are available for the time of the New Testament, which can in no way consist with that heresy concerning rigor under the New Covenant. And is it not likewise under the New Testament that we must pray with David, if you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand? Must we not pray with the Publican, O Lord, be merciful to me a sinner, Luke 18:13. And with John we must confess: if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, 1 John 1:8. And with St. James ch. 3:4, in many things we all stumble. The pages of the New Testament are full of such things, nor do they propose any other method of justification than that which was under the Old Testament, which they also prove and derive from the Old Testament itself, situated in the gratuitous remission of sins, Rom. 4:6. Indeed, the holy Apostle proclaims publicly under the N.T., Acts 13:38: Be it known unto you, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins, and by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses. (3.) The certainty of eternal life we under the N.T. have, and that the ancients did not have the same. Which Pelagian error we have already refuted several times. (4.) And that the times of the New Testament excel in the holiness of examples and precepts. But are not the precepts repeated from the Old Testament in the New? What greater holiness can there be than that which the precepts of the O. Testament demand, namely, that we love God with all our heart, with all our mind, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves, Matt. 22:37, Deut. 6:5, Lev. 19:18; that we be holy, as God is holy, 1 Pet. 1:16, Lev. 29:2. Are not the examples of the Saints of the O. Testament proposed to us for imitation under the N.T., Heb. 11, James 5, and elsewhere? (5.) That a greater power of the Spirit comes to us than to the Patriarchs and the faithful under the O.T., regarding, namely, the Spirit of adoption and sanctification. Which likewise is not only ἄγραφον [unwritten], destitute of any document of Scripture, but also ἀντίγραφον [a copy/contradiction], because the faithful under the O.T. had the same Spirit; we must have the same Spirit of faith with David, 2 Cor. 4:13. As there is one faith in both places, Heb. 11, one grace of salvation, Acts 15:10, so also one Spirit, Eph. 4:4. But more fully on these things elsewhere against the Socinians.

Regarding the words, If you should mark iniquity, it is finally to be noted, not only venial sins, which Genebrardus and Lorinus wish, but mortal sins, which the word iniquities implies, 1 Sam. 20:8, Ps. 38:5, etc., namely those which plunge a man into the deep hell, of which Augustine and Lorinus, verse 1, accept it to be understood, as even Bellarmine himself admits in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SI INIQVITATES OBSERVAVERIS DOMINE, DO- MINE QVIS SVSTINEBIT?) Multa in illo tempore ut imperfectiori, dissimulabantur, quæ non dissimularet Deus sub fœdere Christi, ubi tanta est certitudo vitæ æternæ, tanta exemplorum & præceptorum sanctitas, tanta vis Spiritus; Sed in utroque tempore, cum distinctione, tamen verum est quod dicit Philo libro ὅτι ἄτρεπτον τὸ θεῖον, ad hanc rem apposite: εἰ γὰρ βουληθείη ὁ θεὸς δικάσαι τῷ θνητῷ χωρὶς ἐλέου, τὴν καταδικάζουσαν ψῆφον οἴσει, μηδενὸς ἀνθρώπων τὸν ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι, τελευτῆς βίον ἄπταιστον ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ δρα- μόντος, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἑκουσίοις, τὰ δὲ ἀκουσίοις χρησαμένου τοῖς ἐν ποσὶν ὀλισθήμασιν.

HÆc iterum Pelagio-Sociniana sunt ἀκόσμα- τα, utpote 1. Tempus Veteris Testamenti imper- fectius fuisse, quantum ad leges imperfectiores: in No- vo Testamento perfectiores leges traditas esse. Lex mortalis enim perfecta fuit μηδεμίαν πρόσθεσιν καὶ ἀφαίρεσιν ἀπεκδε χόμενος, ut Varinus perfectam regulam describit: Deut. 4, 2. cap. 12, 32. Neque in Novo Testamento ullatenus ea perfectior red- dita est: imo est æterna regula justitiæ, veræque perfectionis speculum. Christus non venit ut novus νομοθέτης: Sed ut gratiam & veritatem præstaret, quæ a lege rigidam observantiam nobis post lapsum præstitu impossibilem requirente, ex- pectari non poterat Joh. 1, 18. Rom. 8, 4. 5. Deum dissimulasse multa sub Vet. Testam. quæ non dissimu- lavit Christus sub novo Fœdere. Ubi hujus rei vel vola vel vestiguum in S. literis? Num rigidiorem ac severiorem se fidelibus præbet Deus sub novo Fœdere, benigniorem ac faciliorem se præbuit tempore Veteris Testamenti? Quomodo ergo nunc χάρις σωτήριος effulsit sub novo Testamen- to? Quomodo nunc Evangelium gratiæ per or- bem prædicatur longe svavius, ad quod prædican- dum Christus ipse unctus & missus fuit Es. 61, 1. seqq. Quomodo nunc est tempus gratiæ, di- es salutis, dies, quam fecit Dominus, in qua læ- tari & exultare possumus in Domino? Innume- ra ejusmodi elogia suppetunt temporis Nov. Test. quæ cum hæresi illa de rigore sub Novo Fœdere nullatenus consistere possunt. Et annon perinde sub Nov. Test. nobis precandum est cum Davide, si iniquitates observaveris Domine, quis sustinebit? Nonne cum Publicano orandumi, Domine propitius sis mihi peccatori Luc. 18, 13. Et cum Johanne fa- tendum: si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere, mentimur, & veritas non est in nobis 1. Joh. 1, 8. ac cum S. Jacobo c. 3, 4. in multis labimur omnes. Plenæ talibus sunt tabulæ N. Testamenti, neque aliam justificationis rationem proponunt, quam quæ sub Veteri Testamento fuit, quam è Veteri etiam Te- stamento probant, ac deducunt, sitam in gratuita peccatorum remissione Rom. 4, 6. imo proclamat sub N. T. publice S. Apostolus Act. 13, 38. Notum sit vobis, viri fratres, quia per hunc vobis remissio pec- catorum annunciatur, & ab omnibus, quibus non po- tuistis in lege Mosis justificari, in hoc omnis qui credit justificatur. (3.) Certitudinem vitæ æternæ nos sub N. T. habere, non item habuisse eandem veteres. Quem errorem Pelagianum aliquoties jam profligavimus. (4.) Et exemplorum & præceptorum sanctitate tem- pora Novi Testam. excellere. At annon præcepta è veteri Testamento repetuntur in Novo? Quæ ma- jor sanctitas esse potest illa, quam postulant præce- pta V. Testam. ut nempe Deum diligamus ex toto cor- de, ex tota mente, ex tota anima, & totis viribus, & proximum sicut nosmetipsos Matth. 22, 37. Deut. 6, 5. Lev. 19, 18. ut sancti simus, sicut Deus sanctus est, 1. Pet. 1, 16. Lev. 29, 2. Annon exempla Sanctorum V. Test. nobis ad imitationem proponuntur sub N. T. Ebr. 11. Jac. 5. & alibi? (5.) Majorem Spiritus vim nobis obtingere, quam Patriarchis, ac fidelibus sub V. T. quoad adoptionis nempe & sanctificationis Spiri- tum. Quod itidem non ἄγραφον modo, omni do- cumento Scripturæ destitutum, sed etiam ἀντίγρα- φον, quia eundem Spiritum habuere fideles sub V. T. eundem Spiritum fidei cum Davide nos habe- re oportet 2. Cor. 4, 13. Ut una fides utrobique Ebr. 11. una salvationis gratia Act. 15, 10. ita unus etiam Spiritus Eph. 4, 4. Sed de his alibi plenius contra Socinianos.

Circa verba, Si iniquitatem observaveris, deni- que observandum, non venialia tantum peccata, quod Genebrardus & Lorinus volunt, sed peccata mortalia, quæ vox iniquitatum importat 1. Sam. 20, 8. Psal. 38, 5. &c. ea sc. quæ hominem in profun- dum infernum mergunt, de quo Augustin. & Lorin. vers. 1. accipiunt, intelligi, fatente etiam ipfomet Bellarmino in h. l.

## 130:4
Verse 4. FOR WITH THEE THERE IS FORGIVENESS) כי [ki] often means but: and it is right that it be taken so here. הסליחה [has-selichah] is pardon, indulgence.

AND FOR THY LAW I HAVE WAITED FOR THEE O LORD) They connect the end of verse 4 with the beginning of the fifth, as it is in the Hebrew, and for תורתך [toratecha - thy law] they read יראתך [yiratecha - thy fear]. The sense of the Hebrew is, that thou mayest be feared: (as if he were saying, for not undeservedly are you good: for despair of pardon would draw men away from repentance) I have waited for the Lord, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 4. QVIA APUD TE PROPITLATIO EST) כי sæpe valet sed: & ita hic sumi par est הסליחה est venia, in- dulgentia.

ET PROPTER LEGEM TVAM SVSTINVI TE DO- MINE) Connectunt finem commatis 4. cum initio quinti, ut est in Hebræo, & pro תורתך legerunt יראתך. Sensus He- bræi est, ut timearis: ( quasi dicat, non immerito enim bonus es: qui desperatio veniæ homines à pœnitentia abstraheret) Exspectavi Dominum, &c.

## 130:6
Verse 6. FROM THE MORNING WATCH EVEN UNTO NIGHT) In the Hebrew this does not begin a new verse, but coheres with the preceding ones, nor is there mention of night, but the words are thus: My soul (is intent) toward the Lord more than the morning watchmen, the watchmen (I say) of the morning: who, namely, attentively await the day, so that they may be relieved from the labor and sleeplessness of the watch. The repetition of words, however, has a certain sweetness in songs.

Latin:

Vers. 6. A CUSTODIA MATUTINA VSQVE AD NOCTEM) Hoc in Hebræo non novum commma incipit, sed cum superioribus cohæret, neque noctis est mentio, sed sic habent verba: Anima mea (intenta est) ad Dominum ma- gis quam excubitores matutini, excubitores (inquam) matutini: qui scilicet attenti diem exspectant, ut ab excubiarum labo- re & insomnia leventur. Repetitio autem vocum in canticis suavitatem quandam habet.

## 130:8
Verse 8.

AND HE SHALL REDEEM ISRAEL) He shall deliver Israel. FROM ALL HIS INIQUITIES) From the punishments of sins. God forgives the sins of the whole people more easily. Pardon is necessary where the whole army has sinned.

Not only from the punishments of sins, but also from the sins themselves does God deliver. For He pardons sins, blots them out, casts them behind His back, and into the depth of the sea, Ps. 103:3, Is. 43:25, Mic. 7:18; and justification is defined by David through the remission of sins, Ps. 32:1. Cf. Rom. 4:7. Nor is the discourse here only about the whole people of Israel, or about sins committed by the whole people, but also about each one in the people; He wishes to pardon sins not only to a repenting people, but to anyone performing repentance: indeed, by Israel are understood not so much the Israelites according to the flesh, as according to the promise and the Spirit, Rom. 9:8, Gal. 6:16. It is also false that God forgives the sins of the whole people more easily. Where is this in Scripture? God is equally prepared to forgive anyone performing true repentance, just as to a whole repenting people, whence He calls not less any sinner than whole peoples to repentance, with the offer of grace and the remission of sins. The whole Holy Scripture is full of such invitations.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET IPSE REDIMET ISRAEL) Liberabit Israelem. AB OMNIBVS INIQVITATIBVS EJVS) A pœnis peccatorum. Peccatis populi totius facilius ignoscit Deus. Necessaria venia est, ubi totus peccavit exercitus.

Non tantum à pœnis peccatorum, sed etiam à peccatis ipsis Deus liberat. Condonat enim pec- cata, delet eadem, post tergum ea projicit, & in profundum maris Psal. 103, 3. Es. 43, 25. Mich. 7, 18. ac justificatio definitur à Davide per peccatorum remissionem Psal. 32, 1. Conf. Rom. 4, 7. Neque tantum hic de populo integro Israelis sermo est, aut de peccatis ab integro pupulo commissis, sed de unoquoque etiam in populo; non tantum populo pœnitenti, sed cuivis pœnitentiam agenti condo- nare vult peccata: imo per Israelem non tam Israe- litæ intelliguntur secundum carnem, quam secun- dum promissionem & Spiritum Rom. 9, 8. Gal. 6, 16. Falsum etiam, quod Deus facilius peccatis totius populi ignoscat. Ubi hæc Scriptura? Æque para- tus est Deus ignoscere cuivis veram pœnitentiam agenti, uti populo integro pœnitenti, unde non minus quemvis peccatorem, quam integros popu- los vocat ad pœnitentiam, cum oblatione gratiæ, ac remissionis peccatorum. Plena talium invita- tionum est tota Scriptura Sacra.

## 131:1 Argument
PSALM 131. The overthrow of pride.

This Psalm draws much from the Evangelical Spirit. And indeed, among David's virtues was a certain great modesty.

The error noted just above regarding Psalm 127 and often elsewhere. Shall we deny David the Evangelical Spirit, or virtues of that kind, with which the faithful in the New Testament ought to shine? His praise is so great in the Scriptures, that he was a man according to God's heart (Acts 13:22), that he loved God with his whole heart (1 Kings 14:8). Do not his Psalms and his deeds abundantly report that David was endowed with the Evangelical Spirit? Shall we believe that he was not heard when he sought to be confirmed with a Spirit (נדיבה), that is, as Grotius renders it, a liberal [spirit] and one liberally poured out into him (Psalm 51:14), or when he sought to be led into the land of righteousness by a good Spirit (Psalm 143:10)? And what is contained in this Psalm 131 that was not required of all the faithful under the Old Testament? The sacred singer proposes himself as an example of humility, patience, and trust in such a way that he requires the same virtues in everyone. Therefore he concludes in verse 3. Let Israel hope in the Lord from this time forth and even for evermore.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXXI. Profligatio fastus.

MULTUM de Evangelico Spiritu trahit hic Psalmus. Et sane inter Davidis virtutes fuit magna quædam modestia.

ERror proxime notatus ad Psal. 127. & alias sæ- pe. Num Davidi denegabimus Spiritum Ev- angelicum, aut virtutes ejusmodi, quibus fideles in Nov. Testam. coruscare debent? cujus laus tan- ta est in Scripturis, quod fuerit vir secundum cor Dei Act. 13, 22. quod toto corde dilexerit Deum. 1. Reg. 14, 8. Annon Davidem Spiritu Evangeli- co præditum fuisse affatim Psalmi ejus, & res gestæ referunt? Num credemus, eum non exauditum, cum Spiritu (נדיבה) id est, uti Grotius reddit, li- berali & liberaliter in se effuso, confirmari Psal. 51, 14. aut cum Spiritu bono in sententia justitiæ deduci expetiit Psal. 113, 10. Et quid in hoc Psal. 131. habe- tur, quod non requisitum fuerit sub Vet. Testam. ab omnibus fidelibus? Humilitatis, patientiæ & fi- duciæ exemplum ita se proponit Hieropsaltes, ut easdem virtutes in quibusvis requirat. Ideo con- cludit v. 3. Israel speret in Domino ex hoc nunc & us- que in seculum.

## 131:2
Verse 2. NEITHER HAVE I WALKED IN GREAT MATTERS NOR IN WONDROUS THINGS ABOVE ME) In the Hebrew: I have not arrogated to myself great and forbidden things. That is, I did not affect the kingdom by my own impulse. Theodotion: ἐν μεγαλωσύναις, ὐδὲ ὑπερβάλλουσιν ὑπὲρ ἐμέ.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NEQVE AMBULAVI IN MAGNIS NEQVE IN MIRABILIBVS SVPER ME) In Hebræo: Non arro- gavi mihi magna & inconcessa. Id est, non affectavi regnum meopte instinctu. Theodotio: ἐν μεγαλωσύναις, ὐδὲ ὑπερβάλ- λουσιν ὑπὲρ ἐμέ.

## 131:3
Verse 3. IF I HAVE NOT HUMBLY FELT, BUT HAVE EXALTED MY SOUL.

Verse 4. AS A WEANED CHILD IS UPON HIS MOTHER: SO IS MY RECOMPENSE IN MY SOUL.

Bellarmine acknowledges that the original text speaks more significantly here, explaining these things from it thus: If I have not composed myself to equality with others, but have exalted myself above others. As a weaned child is upon his mother; that is, as an infant recently weaned remains in the bosom, or upon the knees of his mother, sad and weeping, because he is deprived of the sweetness of milk, which for that time were his greatest delights: so let the recompense be in my soul, that is, thus let my soul be deprived of the sweetness of divine consolation, which is my greatest, and almost only, delight. But Bellarmine rashly prefers the Septuagint Interpreters, who explained it concerning exaltation, where in the Hebrew text it is a matter of the calming of the soul, and according to Jerome's version, and concerning recompense, where it is a matter of weaning. Most understand an imprecation, along with Kimchi, such as Stephanus, Campensis, Piscator, Mollerus, Coccejus, the Dutch, the new Tossanus Bible interpolated and published at Frankfurt am Main in the year 1668: Muis, Tirinus, B. Quistorpius, and B. Tarnovius; who explained it thus: if I have not composed and calmed my soul like a weaned child with his mother, to whom, however, he is present, and commits himself entirely to her, since he has nowhere else to flee; nay, I say, if he is not as one weaned here and conducts himself as such, so was my soul before me, punish me O GOD: Such an ellipsis indeed occurs in Gen. 14:23 and elsewhere throughout. But in truth, there is no need for such an ellipsis here; for the sake of avoiding which, the text is not to be expounded interrogatively, as with Junius (whose opinion the new Toussaint Bible also praises), because in that way, as Piscator observes, it should have been said הֲלֹא not אִם־לֹא: But just as the authentic text flows, everything can be rendered most simply in this manner: When I have not set (that is, composed) and made my soul silent, (it was the same) as a weaned child with its mother: as a weaned child here (truly) is my soul within me. And thus the version of the blessed Luther, as well as his interpretation, in Psal. Grad. Tom. 3. Witteb. Lat. page 661, holds itself most correctly. When I did not make my soul silent, that is, when I did not humble myself, when I did not abstain from the presumption and confidence of my own righteousness, of the law, nay even of GOD worshipped through the law, when I did not humble myself, and profess that I had indeed kept the law in some way, but nevertheless wished that the Lord would not enter into judgment with His servant. These things, I say, when I did not do them, then I was truly like a weaned child. And a little later: When I was seized by a spirit of pride and security, and lost that breast of divine grace, of the remission of sins and propitiation, I was truly like a child who has lost its mother, and cannot live without the benefit of the mother. To which interpretation the Osiandrian paraphrase is a foster-sibling: When I have not set, and made my soul silent (then) as one weaned from its mother, so was my soul weaned (i. As often as I did not place all my trust in the sole mercy and goodness of God, so as to render my soul tranquil through the meditation of it, then I was just like an infant to whom the breast is denied, who cannot yet live without maternal milk: therefore I would have had to pine away and perish.) (For the one Gospel of Christ, concerning the mercy of God, can pacify our conscience and restore true tranquility of soul; but with the Gospel lost, the breast of all true consolation is lost.) Nor is the Weimar paraphrase, or the interpretation of Dr. D. Gejer, foreign to this. Cf. Is. 66:11, 1 Pet. 2:7, Luke 18:14. Thus the final admonition fits best: Let Israel wait for Jehovah from this time forth, from this moment even unto eternity; which Rudingerus illustrated thus with a paraphrase praised by the blessed Tarnovius: Do thus, think thus of yourselves, all of you (Phil. 2:5.) this is salutary, let all your hope and all your trust be placed in the goodness and mercy of God, O Israel, trust and lean upon this alone, and on nothing else, expect all things from this alone, and attribute nothing to yourselves and your own affairs, O countrymen and holy ones of the universe, at all times. Thus also the preceding parts fit properly, that David did not act proudly in his heart before God, nor were his eyes lifted up, nor did he walk in great and wonderful things above himself: which the blessed Luther observes in hypocrites by the example of the Pharisee in Luke 18, when they please themselves because of their holiness, and seem to themselves to sit in the bosom of GOD, and yet know nothing of propitiation and the remission of sins, even though he confesses that theologians have not unlearnedly used these words according to the general sentiment against all pride: and he warns that the present Psalm speaks of almost the same matter as the preceding one had dealt with, except that it expresses the antithesis a little more clearly, whence, having abandoned the general sentiment, he interprets the Psalm concerning spiritual pride, which consists in the opinion of Wisdom and Righteousness.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SI NON HUMILITER SEN- TIEBAM, SED EXALTAVI ANIMAM MEAM.

Vers. 4. SICUT ABLACTATUS EST SUPER MATRE SUA: ITA RETRIBU- TIO IN ANIMA MEA.

Bellarm. textum originalem agnoscit signifi- cantius hic loqui, ex eodem hæc ita explicans: Si non composui me ad æqualitatem cum cæteris, sed supra cæteros me extuli. Sicut ablactatus est super matre sua; id est, sicut infans recens ablactatus ma- net in sinu, vel super genua matris suæ, mæstus & plorans, quia privatus est dulcedine lactis, qua pro il- lo tempore summæ delitiæ ipsius erant: ita retributio in anima mea sit, id est, sic anima mea privetur dulce- dine consolationis divinæ, quæ mea potissime, ac pene sola delicia sunt. Sed temere præfert Bellarminus LXX. Interpp. qui de exaltatione exposuere, ubi de sedatione animæ agitur in Ebræo textu, & jux- ta Hieronymi versionem, & de retributione, ubi de ablactatione: plerique subintelligunt execrationem, cum Kimchio, utpote Stephanus, Campensis, Pisca- tor, Mollerus, Coccejus, Belgæ, nova Biblia Tos- sani interpolata Francofurti ad Mœnum anno 1668. edita: Muis, Tirinus, B. Quistorpius, & B. Tarnovius; qui sic exposuit: si non compo- sui & sedavi animam meam sicut ablactatus a- pud matrem suam, cui tamen adest, seque ei totum committit, quum quo alias confugiat, non habeat, imo inquam, si non tanquam hic abla- ctatus est & se gerit, ita apud me fuit anima mea, punias me o DEUS: Qualis ellipsis quidem Gen. 14, 23. & alibi passim occurrit. Verum enim vero hic tali ellipsi opus non est; ob quam declinandam non quidem cum Junio (cujus sententiam etiam laudant Biblia nova Tossani) interrogative textus exponendus est, quia ita, Piscatore observante, di- cendum fuisset הֲלֹא non אִם־לֹא : Sed sicut fluit tex- tus authenticus reddi possunt omnia simplicissime h. m. Cum non posui (id est, composui) & silere feci animam meam, (fuit eadem) sicut ablactatus apud matrem suam: sicut ablactatus hic (vere) in me est anima mea. Atque ita rectissime se habet B. Luthe- ritum versio, tum interpretatio, in Psal. Grad. Tom. 3. Witteb. Lat. pag. 661. Cum non facerem silere animam meam, hoc est, cum non humiliabam, cum non abstinerem, a præsumptione & fiducia pro- priæ Justitiæ, legis, imo etiam DEI per legem culti, cum non humiliarem me, ac profiterer me quidem ser- vasse aliquo modo legem, sed tamen optare, ne intret Dominus in judicium cum servo suo. Hæc, inquam, cum non facerem, tum eram vere sicut ablactatus. Et paulo post : Cum spiritu superbiæ & securitatis arriperer, & amitterem illam mammillam divinæ gratiæ, remissionis peccatorum & propitiationis, ve- re similis eram puero, qui matrem amisit, & sine be- neficio matris non potest vivere. Cui interpretatio- ni collactea est paraphrasis Osiandrina : Quando non posui, & silere feci animam meam (tunc) quasi ablactatus a matre sua, sic fuit ablactata anima mea (i. Quoties non omnem meam fiduciam posui in sola misericordia & bonitate Dei, ut ejus meditatione tranquillum redderem animum meum, tum perinde fui quasi infans, cui denegatur mamma, qui sine la- cte materno vivere nondum potest: itaque mihi ta- bescendum & pereundum fuisset.) (Unum enim Christi Evangelion, de misericordia Dei, potest con- scientiam nostram pacificare, & veram animi tran- quillitatem restituere; Amisso vero Evangelio, amis- sa est mamma omnis veræ consolationis.) Ne- que aliena est Vinariensium paraphrasis, aut Dn. D. Gejeri interpretatio. Conf. Es. 66, 11. 1. Petr. 2, 7. Luc. 18, 14. Ita optime convenit admonitio fina- lis: Expectet Israel Jehovam ex hoc nunc, ab hoc mo- mento usque in seculum; quam sic illustravit Rudin- gerus paraphrasi à B. Tarnovio laudata : Sic faci- te, sic sentite de vobis universi (Phil. 2, 5.) hoc salu- tare est, in bonitate & misericordia collocetur omnis spes & fiducia omnis tua, o Israel, hoc solo fidite & nitimini, & nulla re alia, ab hoc solo expectate o- mnia, vobisque & rebus vestris nihil tribuite ô popu- lares & sancti universi, omni tempore. Ita etiam an- tecedentia probe congruunt, quod neque corde superbierit David apud Deum, nec elatis fuerit oculis, nec ambularit in rebus magnis & mirabilibus supra se : quod in hypocritis exemplo Pharisæi Luc. 18. observat B. Lutherus, cum sibi placent ob san- ctitatem, ac videntur sibi sedere in sinu DEI, & ta- men nihil norunt de propitiatione, & remissione pec- catorum, etsi fateatur non inerudite Theologos usos esse his verbis secundum generalem sententiam contra omnem superbiam: monetque, Psalmum præsen- tem fere de eadem materia loqui, de qua præcedens egerat, nisi quod antithesin paulo clarius exprimat, un- de relicta generali sententia Psalmum interpreta- tur de spirituali superbia, quæ in opinione Sapien- tiæ & Justitiæ consistit.

## 132:1 Argument
PSALM CXXXII. The Rest of the Lord in Zion.

Vers. 1. REMEMBER O LORD DAVID AND ALL HIS MEEKNESS) It is a song of Solomon fulfilling what was destined for his father. See 2 Sam. 7. Cf. verse 8 with 2 Chron. 6:41. You will see that they are the same words.

So also Bellarmine on this passage. These are the words of Solomon, he says, who prays to God through the merits of his father David. Yet he himself is not certain that Solomon composed the Psalm, and he doubts whether it was composed rather by David and given to Solomon to sing after the building of the temple: and that David himself is speaking here is the opinion not only of Kimchi, Aben-Ezra, Piscator, Polanus T. 2. Synt. col. 2835, the blessed Asselm. de invoc. Sanct. c. 3. th. 15, the blessed Gerh. T. 8. LLCC. p. 877, the blessed Glass. l. 3. Ph. S. p. 175, but also of Prosper, Ayguanus, and also Guilh. Estius, and Simon de Muis and others.
