Moreover, we easily admit with the Weimar theologians and the Belgians that Solomon is speaking here, but the Vulgate rashly translated it as meekness with the LXX Interpreters, when mention is made of the source of affliction; just as also Hieronym. rendered it Remember O Lord David, and all his affliction, which Thomas and Eman. Saa, with Jerome and Arnobius, understand specifically as the affliction under Saul, but Agathius Gredacerius, Lorinus, and Estius explain it as the insults brought by Michal after the carrying away of the ark, 2 Sam. 6:21, as noted by D. Gerhard in Confess. Cathol. Although the Psalmist calls to God's mind the memory of all of David's afflictions; yet he undoubtedly designates specifically those which he sustained for the sake of religion, Ps. 119:25, 50, 61, 107. For he makes mention of the merits of David in no word; but only of the vow by which he bound himself with an oath to the Mighty One of Jacob or Jehovah concerning the building of the temple in His honor, to whom Jacob had made a similar vow, Gen. 28:17, praying that the execution of this vow, which Solomon had undertaken, might be blessed and salutary. Rightly the blessed Luth. The circumstances argue that the Psalm speaks of David, who suffered much on account of the divine promise. But that Solomon the son, or the whole people, remembered these things in prayer and in the sight of GOD, does not happen in the way that the Papists think, that David intercedes for them; but they speak of David as having the promises, and they remind God through David of those promises, just as Paul also speaks of Abraham. Wherefore the name of David is not to be taken absolutely, as if it speaks only of his person, for it speaks of David not simply, but according to something, that is, of David the promise-bearer, if I may say so, or as having the promises, and clothed with divine promises. Thus also v. 10 was explained by Blessed Luther: For the sake of David thy servant, turn not away the face of thine anointed. This is a new prayer, which it institutes entirely on the confidence of the promises. For here, as also above, the word David does not signify properly that substance, but rather a quality, that is, David clothed and adorned with the promises concerning the kingdom. As if he were to say, I pray thee that thou wouldst also preserve our kingdom, and bless it, and be present with us; but I pray this not simply for my own sake, as if I were worthy that thou shouldst bestow these things upon me, but in confidence of the promises which thou madest to my father David, when thou saidst, the lamp shall not be wanting to the house of David, etc. But if the Monks wish to prove their vows from this, even though they differ as much as heaven from earth from David's vow, the Junian note on this passage is correct: David was not so arrogant as to think that by his vow he could prescribe a law to God, so that it would come as soon as he pleased, nor so rash as to promise that he would live under the open sky and spend sleepless nights until the ark was brought, or rather until he had built a tabernacle for the God of Jacob; what then? Bellarmine himself explained this: Nor indeed, if David swore that he would not enter into his house until he had built a temple, was there a danger that he would spend too long a time under the open sky; for the words of that oath contain, familiar with divine scripture: but they properly signify great solicitude for a thing to be done. Blessed Luther likewise explains it concerning the will or mind with which David was affected to complete this work; Since, he says, David thought it unworthy if he himself should dwell in a cedar house, while the ark was under skins, this figure explains the HIGHEST WILL, with which he desired to remove this indignity.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXXII. Requies Domini in Zion.

Vers. 1. MEMENTO DOMINE DAVID ET OMNIS MANSVETUDINIS EJUS) Salomonis est carmen patri destinata implentis. Vide 2. Sam. 7. Conf. versum 8. cum 2. Paralip. 6, 41. Videbis eadem esse verba.

ITa etiam Bellarminus ad h. l. Verba Salomonis haec sunt, inquit, qui Deum orat per merita patris sui David. Salomonem tamen Psalmum composuisse ipse certus haud est, & anne compositus potius a Da- vide sit, ac Salomoni ad concinendum post templi aedi- ficationem datus, ambigit: & Davidem ipsum hic lo- qui non Kimchi tantum, Aben-Ezra, Piscator, Pola- nus T. 2. Synt. col. 2835. B. Asselm. de invoc. Sanct. c. 3. th. 15. B. Gerh. T. 8. LLCC. p. 877. B. Glass. l. 3. Ph. S. p. 175. sed etiam Prosper, Ayguanus, nec non Guilh. Estius, & Simon de Muis aliique censent. Cæterum faciles cum Vinariensib. & Belgis admittimus Salo- monem hic loqui, temere autem vulgatus cum LXX. Interpp. mansuetudinem transtulit, quum affli- ctionis in fonte mentio fiat; sicuti etiam Hieronym. reddidit Memento Domine David, & omnis afflictionis ejus, quam speciatim de afflictione sub Saule, cum Hieronymo & Arnobio Thomas & Eman. Saa intelli- gunt, de contumeliis autem a Michole post arcae de- portationem 2. Sam. 6, 21. illatis explicant Agathius Gredacerius, Lorinus & Estius notante D. Gerhardo in Confess. Cathol. Etsi vero cunctarum afflictio- num Davidis memoriam in mentem Deo revocet Psaltes; peculiariter tamen eas sine dubio designat, quas religionis causa sustinuit, Ps. 119, 25. 50. 61. 107. Nullo enim verbo meritorum Davidis mentionem facit; Sed voti tantum, quo juramento sese obstrin- xit forti Jacobi vel Jehovae de aedificatione templi in honorem ejus, cui Jacob simile votum fecerat, Gen. 28, 17. precatus, ut hujus voti exequutio, quam su- sceperat Salomo, benedicta sit & salutaris. Recte B. Luth. Circumstantiae arguunt Psalmum loqui de Da- vide multa passo propter promissionem divinam. Quod autem horum sive Salomon filius, sive totus po- pulus in oratione & conspectu DEI meminerunt, non fit eo modo, quo Papistae putant, ut David pro ipsis in- tercedat; Sed loquuntur de Davide habente promis- siones, ac Deum per Davidem illarum promissionum commonefaciunt, sicut Paulus quoque loquitur de Ab- rahamo. Quare nomen Davidis non est accipien- dum absolute, tanquam loquatur solum de persona e- jus, loquitur enim de Davide non simpliciter, sed secun- dum aliquid, hoc est, de Davide promissario, ut sic di- cam, seu habente promissiones, & vestito divinis pro- missionibus. Sic etiam v. 10. exposuit B. Luther. Pro- pter David servum tuum non avertas faciem Chri- sti tui. Haec est nova precatio, quam totam instituit fi- ducia promissionum. Hic enim, sicut supra quoq́, vocabu- lum David, non significat proprie substantiam illam, sed qualitatem potius, hoc est, Davidem indutum & or- natum promissionibus de regno. Quasi dicat, Oro te, ut etiam regnum nostrum serves, & benedicas, & no- bis adsis, hoc autem oro non simpliciter mea causa, quasi dignus sim, cui ista largiaris, sed fiducia promis- sionum, quas fecisti patri meo David, cum dixisti, non defuturam lucernam domui David, &c. Si autem vota hinc sua Monachi probare velint, etsi ea toto coelo a Davidis voto distent, recte Juniana nota ad h. l. non fuit adeo arrogans David, ut putaret voto suo legem se posse Deo praescribere, ut quamprimum veni- ret arbitratu ipsius, neq́; adeo temerarius, ut sponderet se sub dio habitaturum, & noctes insomnes ducturum, donec apportetur arca, vel potius donec tabernacu- lum Deo Jacob extruxerit; Quid ergo? Exposuit hoc Bellarm. ipse: Neque vero si David juravit, se non ingressurum in domum suam, donec extrueret tem- plum, periculum erat ne nimis diu pernoctaret sub dio; verba enim illius juramenti amplificationem continent, scripturæ divinæ familiarem: proprie au- tem significant sollicitudinem magnam rei faciendæ. B. Lutherus itidem de voluntate seu animo explicat, quo David ad hoc opus perficiendum affectus fuit; Quoniam, inquit, David indignum esse ratus est, si ipse habitaret in Cedrina domo, arca autem sub pel- libus esset, explicat hæc figura SUMMAM VO- LUNTATEM, qua optavit hanc indignitatem tol- lere.

## 132:6
Verse 6.

BEHOLD WE HEARD OF IT IN EPHRATHA) We heard of it (supply: the tabernacle) in Ephratha: that is, when I was a boy in Bethlehem I had heard where the ark was kept. These words are David's, which Solomon repeats.

WE FOUND IT IN THE FIELDS OF THE WOOD) In Hebrew: In the fields of Iahar: that is, in the city called from wooded places Cariathiarim, where Abinadab dwelt. 1 Chron. 13, 6.

Latin:

Verf. 6.

ECCE AUDIVIMUS EAM IN EPHRATA) Audivi- mus de eo (supple tabernaculo) in Ephrata: id est, Bethleemi puer cum essem audiveram ubi asservaretur arca. Verba hæc sunt Davidis quæ Salomo repetit.

INVENIMUS EAM IN CAMPIS SILVÆ) In He- bræo: In campis Iahar: id est, in urbe a locis silvosis dicta Cariathiarim, ubi habitabat Abinadab. 1. Paralip. 13, 6.

## 132:11
Verse 11.

OF THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB I WILL SET UPON THY SEAT] That is, someone born from one of your wives. For בטן in this sense is accustomed to be said of women. Moreover, the womb of a wife pertains to the husband with all its fruit.

Thus Grotius accepts this promise indefinitely concerning some offspring of David. But we know from the infallible interpretation of the Holy Scriptures (Acts 2:30) that it is to be understood solely of the Messiah. Being therefore a PROPHET, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath concerning the fruit of his loins (in the Greek is added τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, by which the flesh or human nature of Christ is indicated) to sit upon his seat, he foreseeing spoke (Ps. 16) of the resurrection of Christ. Which words teach that a PROPHETIC prediction is held here, and that it is to be understood not as the Reformed, and among them Cocceius in ult. Mos. §. 991, do indefinitely concerning the distinct seed of David, that is, both concerning his descendants who were heirs of the kingdom, and concerning the Lord Jesus, but uniquely concerning the blessed seed, whose lineage and origin is restricted by this promise to the Davidic stem, that is, concerning Christ. Then it is also certain that the promise of 2 Sam. 7 is being looked back upon. made, which does not concern Solomon, as the same Cocceius §. 989 wishes, but Christ alone, as was shown when we treated that place and concerning the exegesis of the same Psalm 99 proposed. St. Augustine observes that this Son is also called the fruit not of the seed, but of the womb, for the reason that Christ was born from a virgin's womb without male seed. That by בטן or womb a woman is understood, so that the fruit of thy womb is a son born to thee from a woman, cannot be proven by any example from the Scriptures or elsewhere. Add now to these things which are held in v. 17: There I will make the horn of David to bud, I will order a lamp for my anointed. For that horn of David is Christ, who is said by Zacharias (Luke 1:69) to have raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, a metaphor taken from animals, which have their strength primarily in their horns. The same is also hinted at by the word of budding: which at the same time designates the time of the coming of Christ and the miserable condition of the royal stock, as if to say: the posterity of David will be like a dry trunk, yet from there, beyond all hope, I will produce a green shoot: Compare Is. 11:1, Jer. 23:5, Zach. 6:12. Similarly, by the name of a Lamp, Christ is expressed, as that true light illuminating every man (John 1:9), and at the same time it is designated that all the splendor of the Davidic stock, as if buried in the dense darkness of calamities, would perish, but suddenly from that soot a new and perpetually enduring light would shine forth in Christ. Which observation of our blessed Gesner is to be preferred entirely to the gloss of Grotius: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ: that is, descendants who will reign, who are called the lamp of their progenitors, because they draw light, that is, dignity, from them (1 Kings 11:36, 15:4). For here the prophecy is concerning a singular lamp, and so called uniquely, and

that lamp is called the horn of David, which it is established from the interpretation of Zacharias is Christ. Nor does Cocceius deny it: This is an absolute promise, a declaration of a testament, and of an immutable will: there shall arise from David, and as a Sprout (by himself without a Father in this age, from whom he might receive priesthood or kingdom, and by nature according to the power of an indissoluble life, so that to this one and no other can this priesthood and kingdom be given) shall sprout a seed or son, who will be a horn (why not in truth? and the only horn? and the horn of salvation? Psalm 19:3. For it is said antonomastically and by way of excellence) and a lamp to illuminate the eyes of the blind and of all hoping in God, so that in him they may see light, among whom David himself is (Psalm 110:1, 2 Sam. 23:5); for he says a lamp for my anointed. And without this lamp there would be no light for David, nor for David's; because his faith and hope would be nothing and vain. What of the fact that the Jews themselves acknowledged that the Messiah was designated here by the reflourishing horn of David. For thus R. David Kimchi, to those words, after it long withered, as Jer. 23:5: I will raise up to David a righteous branch; and this is Christ. Our blessed Bugenhagius provides still other arguments from the text from verses 8 and 9. Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification. The prophets, he says, when they speak of spiritual things, willingly allude to visible things, and it is established that this Psalm was sung in the temple for many years, when certainly it was not a sin for the ark to come into the temple. Therefore, while it is written about a visible thing, it looks toward another temple, as was said above. You can therefore accept that David, who was certified by the promise and oath of God, as is said in this Psalm, concerning Christ who was to be born from him, desired to know the place and habitation of the conversation of Christ the King, just as Solomon desired the same, and it was revealed by God that his first place would be in Bethlehem, where he would be born (according to verse 6: For we heard in Ephratha, i.e., Bethlehem) according to another prophecy also, and then in the fields of the Wood (we found him in the fields of the Wood), that is, among the nations, to whom he came in the Spirit after he was glorified. Thus elsewhere: Then all the trees of the woods will exult, etc., so that the faithful here may glory that they will enter into the holy Church of Christ, which is the true temple of God, and will adore at the mercy seat Christ, through whom the Father grants the remission of sins. For he is the throne of grace (Heb. 4, Rom. 5). And let them pray, that God himself may come into this rest of his temple with the ark, that is, the humanity of Christ, in which is his sanctification, i.e., all the fullness of the divinity bodily, by which we are sanctified. Then, he says, your priests, and your saints, that is, the believers, who are a royal priestly race, shall be clothed with justice, not the garments of Aaron, not those external pomps; it must be an internal garment, where there is a spiritual, not a carnal, or visible priesthood, and they shall exult, having been made joyful by yours, viz., the justice which is through faith. Although we indeed acknowledge that these things treat of the finding of the ark in Beth-shemesh and in that field, concerning which 1 Sam. 6, and that the prayer taken from 2 Chron. 6:41 ought not to be referred elsewhere than where Solomon repeats it κατὰ λέξιν: yet it is not without mystery, which the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon, does not say the ark was found in Beth-shemesh, but in Ephrathah, using a general name by which the borders of Bethlehem might be designated, because the true ark of the covenant, Christ, was found in Bethlehem Ephrathah, and announced in the fields there by the angel to the shepherds, Luke 2. Furthermore, what follows in verse 10, some even of the Ancients understand concerning the Christ of the Lord, and so also does the blessed Bugenhagen. For the sake of David your servant do not turn away the face of your Christ. Not because of the merits or holiness of David, but because of the promise made to him (as the following verses have it), we ask you that you do not turn away from us the face of your Christ, but send him to us to be seen by faith, so that seeing his song we may recognize him. For it is written in Isaiah 53, his countenance was hidden because of the forms of the cross. See 3 Kings 11, how often the Lord says that he will not take away all mercy because of David his servant. And it is promised to all in Isaiah 55: And I will make an everlasting covenant with you, the faithful mercies of David. Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a Leader and Commander to the nations. Behold, a nation you did not know, etc. In the confidence of this promise the people pray here, and urge God with the promise made, as we said in Psalm 88. (Junius and Tremellius explain the words 'because of David your servant' as 'because of Christ the Son of David,' who is often called David in the Prophets, as in Hosea 3:5; but the following verse teaches that David himself is understood, to whom God swore.) Moreover, a comparison of this Psalm with 2 Chronicles 6:42 teaches sufficiently that by 'Christ' or 'anointed' the Lord Jesus is not understood, but Solomon, who asks that the Lord not turn away his face, or that he might be willing to look upon him, i.e., 'do not allow your face to be turned away from me,' as Bellarmine does not poorly interpret here. The blessed Bugenhagen adds to verse 18 and the last: 'All his enemies,' that is, the adversaries of the Gospel, 'will be clothed with confusion,' while those who are saints in the kingdom will be clothed with righteousness and salvation, as said above: 'but upon him the glory of the kingdom of God will shine forever.' Whence the blessed Pomeranus concludes: Therefore, from that place where it is said, 'The Lord swore,' and up to the end of the Psalm, you have a manifest promise and oath of God concerning the eternal temple, priesthood, and kingdom in the seed of David, Christ. These are the words of the blessed Bugenhagen. The blessed Luther, in his commentary on the Psalms of Degrees, Tom. 4, Jena, on this Psalm, fol. 424, understands the Psalm simply concerning the kingdom of David up to Christ; yet he does not strongly object if anyone wishes to transfer all these things to Christ, and he confesses that this can be done without difficulty. For otherwise, he says, it is customary in the Prophets to append at the end prophecies concerning Christ, who is the true shoot or germ, and the true Nazarene prepared by God for this purpose, that he might be a perpetual lamp, which Satan cannot extinguish.

It is not to be denied that certain things are said concerning the Davidic kingdom promised to his descendants under a condition, as in verse 12, and that to the same end is added the promise concerning the temple being preserved until the end of the polity, verses 13 and 14, until the body succeeds the shadows. But since the promise concerning placing the fruit of the womb on the throne of David was made ἀμεταμελήτως (irrevocably) and fulfilled in Christ, as St. Peter interprets in Acts 2:30, and his own seat bears no other meaning in 2 Samuel 7:19, those things interposed concerning the earthly kingdom of the heirs of David are so that it might be established to them also that the throne would be preserved perpetually, if they had persisted in the covenant of the Lord, i.e., the Lord swore to David that the Messiah would come forth from his loins, whose throne will be eternal. But the Lord would also preserve the earthly kingdom itself forever for his descendants, if they kept his covenant and his testimony. The former promise, therefore, is the principal, absolute, and categorical one concerning the blessed seed, the fruit of David's womb, and his spiritual and eternal kingdom, verse 11. The latter, concerning the heirs of the earthly and temporal throne from the stock of David, is conditional and made under the hypothesis of observing the covenant, verse 12, to which is added the conversation of the Lord's dwelling in Zion, and the temporal blessing of the people, verse 15, and also the preservation of the priesthood until the true kingdom and priesthood, verse 18. From there, therefore, Solomon returns to that principal promise made to David concerning the Messiah and his kingdom, verse 17.

I will cause the horn of David to sprout, I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. By which, first, the place of the birth of the Messiah is designated, שם THERE is looked to, namely the place of which he had said above: 'We heard of it (the ark) in Ephrata, we will find it in the fields of the forest.' These things concerning Christ found in Bethlehem, with Jerome preceding, rendering the pronoun in the masculine, 'we heard him,' are accepted by the blessed Bugenhagen previously, and also by the blessed Reinhard Backius. But since in the source the pronoun is of the feminine gender, and the ark is looked to, found in the borders of Ephrata or Bethlehem: now Solomon informs us, verse 17, how the antitype corresponds to the type: THERE (in the Ephratite or Bethlehemite borders), says the Lord, 'I will cause the horn of David to sprout.' Cf. Micah 5:2, Matthew 2:4. Next, the birth of the Messiah is insinuated, 'I will cause the horn of David to sprout.' Because his temporal birth is accustomed to be designated in this way; see Jeremiah 23:6, chapter 33:15, Zechariah 6:12, Malachi 4:1. Luke 1:78. Thirdly, the Messiah is adorned with excellent names, expressing both his person and his office. For he is called a horn, that is, the strength and power of David, in which David boasted and placed his trust, Psalm 18:3, just as Zechariah also does in Luke 1:69, when he calls him the horn of salvation. By which name, therefore, his divine nature is exhibited, since God alone is our horn in whom we can trust, and also his office, because he is the horn of our salvation. He is also called a lamp prepared for the Lord's anointed, David, who desires to be illuminated only in this lamp, outside of which no light shines for either David or any mortal, but there is only darkness, Isaiah 23:5, Psalm 119:81, 105, Isaiah 9:1, chapter 60:1, Luke 1:19. Finally, the fate of those opposing the kingdom of the Messiah and the kingdom itself is added, verse 18. I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him, the Messiah, the King or his kingdom, which is the Kingdom of salvation, his diadem will flourish, because the Church, which is his kingdom, and the faithful are crowned with the diadem of his glory in this, and especially in the coming age, when his enemies will be clothed with eternal ignominy and confusion, Psalm 70:4, 5, Daniel 12:2, Wisdom 4:17.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

DE FRUCTU VENTRIS TUI PONAM SUPER SE- DEM TUAM] Id est, aliquem natum ex aliqua uxorum tuarum. Nam בטן in hoc sensu de fœminis dici solet. Uterus autem uxoris ad maritum pertinet cum omni suo fructu.

Ita accipit Grotius hanc promissionem ἀορί- στως de nato aliquo Davidis. Quam vero intelligen- dam esse unice de Messia ex interpretatione S. S. Act. 9, 30. infallibili novimus. PROPHETA igitur cum esset, & sciret, quia jurejurando jurasset illi Deus de fructu lumbi ejus (in Græco additur τὸ κατὰ σάρ- κα, quo caro vel humana Christi natura indigitatur) sedere super sedem ejus, providens locutus est (Pf. 16.) de resurrectione Christi. Quæ verba docent, vatici- nium hic haberi PROPHETICUM, idque acci- piendum esse non ut Reformati & inter hos Cocce- jus in ult. Mos. §. 991. indefinite de distincto semine Davidis, puta tum de posteris ejus regni hæredibus aliis, tum de Domino Jesu, sed μοναδικῶς de bene- dicto semine, cujus prosapia & origo hac promif- sione ad stemma Davidicum restricta, hoc est, de Christo. Tum certum etiam est, respici promissio- nem 2. Sam. 7. factam, quam non Salomonem ut i- dem Coccejus §. 989. vult, sed Christum solum con- cernere, cum locum istum tractavimus, & circa ἐξή- γησιν ejusdem Pf. 99. propositam, ostensum fuit. S. Augustinus observat, etiam Filium hunc appellari fructum non seminis, sed ventris, eo quod Christus è virginis alvo absque virili semine natus est. Per בטן vel ventrem mulierem intelligi, ut fructus ventris tui sit filius ex muliere tibi natus, nullo è Scripturis exem- plo, aut aliunde probari potest. Adde jam his, quæ habentur v. 17. Illic germinare faciam cornu Davi- dis, ordinabo lucernam uncto meo. Cornu enim illud Davidis Christus est, qui cornu salutis in domo Da- vidis excitatum dicitur à Zacharia Luc. 1, 69. sumta metaphora ab animantibus, quæ potissimum ro- bur habent in cornibus. Idem etiam germinandi verbo innuitur: quod simul tempus adventus Chri- sti, & conditionem regiæ stirpis miseram designat, q. d. Davidis posteritas trunco arido similis erit, inde ta- men præter omnem spem surculum viridem produ- cam: Conf. Es. 11, 1. Jerem. 23, 5. Zach. 6, 12. Simili- ter Lucernæ nomine exprimitur Christus, ceu lux illa vera illuminans omnem hominem Joh. 1, 9. simul- que designatur, omnem splendorem Davidicæ stirpis densis calamitatum tenebris quasi obrutum periturum, sed subito ex illa fuligine novam & per- petuo duraturam lucem effulsuram in Christo. Quæ observatio B. Gesneri nostri præferenda o- mnino glossæ Grotii: paravi lucernam Christo meo: id est, posteros regnaturos, qui dicuntur genitorum lucerna, quod ab eis lucem, id est, dignitatem tra- hant 1. Reg. 11, 36. 15, 4. Hic enim de lucerna sin- gulari, & μοναδικῶς ita appellata Prophetia est, &

lucerna illa cornu Davidis vocatur, quod Chri- stum esse ex interpretatione Zachariæ constat. Ne- que diffitetur Coccejus: Absoluta hæc est promif- sio, declaratio testamenti, & immutabilis volun- tatis: orietur ex Davide, & ut Germen (abs sese sine Patre in hoc seculo, à quo sacerdotium vel re- gnum accipiat, & natura secundum potentiam in- dissolubilis vitæ, ut huic soli & nulli alii sacerdo- tium hoc, & regnum possit dari) germinabit se- men aut filius, qui erit cornu (quidni in veritate? & solus cornu? & cornu salutis? Psal. 19, 3. Anto- nomastice enim & κατ' ἐξοχήν dicitur) & lucerna ad illuminandum oculos cæcorum & omnium spe- rantium in Deum, ut in ipso videant lucem, inter quos ipse David est (Psal. 110, 1. 2. Sam. 23, 5.) dicit enim lucernam uncto meo. Et sine hac lucerna neque Davidi esset lux; neque Davidis; quia nulla esset & vana fides, & spes ipsius. Quid quod Ju- dæi ipsimet agnoverint hic Messiam designatum per cornu Davidis reflorefcens. Sic enim ad verba illa R. David Kimchi, postquam diu exaruit, ut Jerem. 23, 5. Excitabo Davidi germen justitiæ; & hoc est Christus. B. Bugenhagius noster alia adhuc subministrat è textu argumenta è vers. 8. 9. Exur- ge Domine in requiem tuam tu & arca sanctificatio- nis tuæ. Prophetæ, inquit, ubi de Spiritualibus lo- quuntur, libenter alludunt ad visibilia, & hunc Pfalmum cantatum constat in templo ad multos an- nos, quando certe non peccatum est, ut arca veniret in templum. In aliud ergo templum dum de visibi- li scribitur, respicitur, ut supra dictum. Potes er- go accipere, quod David, qui promissione & jura- mento Dei, ut in hoc Psalmo dicitur, certificatus e- rat de Christo ex se nascituro, desideraverit scire lo- cum & habitationem conversationis Christi Regis, ut idem desideraverit Salomon, & revelatum sit à Deo, quod ejus locus primus futurus esset in Bethle- hem, ubi nasceretur (secundum vers. 6. Audivi- mus enim in Ephrata h. e. Bethlehem) secundum a- liam quoque Prophetiam, & deinde in campis Sylvæ (invenimus eum in campis Sylvæ) id est inter gen- tes, ad quas Spiritu venit, postquam est glorificatus. Sic alibi: Tunc exultabunt omnia ligna sylva- rum, &c. ut fideles hic glorientur se ingressuros in Ec- clesiam sanctam Christi, quæ est verum Dei templum, & adoraturos ad propitiatorium Christum, per quem Pater remissionem tribuit peccatorum. Est e- nim thronus gratiæ Hebr. 4. Rom. 5. Et orent, ut Deus ipse in hanc requiem sui templiveniat cum arca,id est, humanitate Christi, in qua est sanctificatio ejus,i.e.o- mnis plenitudo divinitatis corporaliter, qua sanctifi- camur. Tunc Sacerdotes, inquit, tui, & sancti tui, id est, credentes, qui sunt genus regium sacerdo- tale, induent justitiam, non vestes Aaron, non pom- pas illas externas, internam vestem oportet esse, ubi spirituale est, non carnale, sive visibile sacerdotium, & exultabunt, tua, sc. justitia, quæ est per fidem, lætificati. Quanquam vero agnoscamus hæc de inventione arcæ in Bethsemes & in agro illo agere, de qua 1. Sam. 6. ac precationem 2. Chron. 6, 41. de- promptam alio referri non debere, quam hic Salo- mo κατὰ λέξιν repetit: non tamen mysterio caret, quod Spir. Sanct. per Salomonem loquens non ait inventam arcam in Bethsemes, sed in Ephrata, u- tens nomine generali, quo confinia Bethlehem designentur, quia vera arca fœderis Christus in Bethlehem Ephrata inventa, & in campis ibidem annunciata per angelum Pastoribus est Luc. 2. Quæ porro vers. 10. sequuntur, nonnulli etiam è Veteribus de Christo Domini intelligunt, atque ita etiam B. Bugenhagius. Propter David servum tuum non avertas faciem Christi tui. Non propter merita aut sanctitatem David, sed propter promissio- nem illi factam (ut sequentia habent) te rogamus, ut non avertas a nobis faciem Christi tui, sed mittas eum nobis videndum fide, ut carmen ejus videntes agnosca- mus. Esa. enim 53. scribitur, absconditus vultus e- jus propter formas crucis. Vide 3. Reg. 11. quam sæ- pe dicat Dominus se non ablaturum omnem misericor- diam propter David servum suum. Et omnibus pro- mittitur Es. 55. Et feriam vobiscum pactum sem- piternum, misericordias David fideles. Ecce te- stem populis dedi eum, Ducem ac Præceptorem gentibus. Ecce gentem, quam nesciebas &c. Hujus promissionis fiducia hic orat populus, & urget Deum promissione facta, sicut diximus Psalm. 88. (Ju- nius & Tremellius verba, propter David servum tuum explicant, propter Christum Filium Davidis, qui subinde in Prophetis appellatur David, ut Hos. 3, 5. sed Davidem ipsum intelligi, cui Deus juravit, versus sequens docet.) Cæterum collatio hujus Psal- mi cum 2. Paral. 6, 42. docet satis per Christum vel unctum non intelligi Dominum Jesum, sed Salomo- nem, qui petit ne avertere faciem suam, vel respi- cere velit Dominus, q. d. ne sinas verti a me faciem tuam, ut hic non male Bellarmin. Addit B. Bugen- hagius ad vers. 18. & ultimum: Inimici ejus omnes, id est, adversarii Evangelii induentur confusione, dum qui in regno sunt sancti, vestientur justitia & sa- lute, ut supra dictum: super ipsum autem gloria re- gni Dei fulgebit in æternum. Unde concludit Pomeranus ὁ μακαρίτης: Itaque ab illo loco, quo di- citur, juravit Dominus, & usque in finem Psalmi ha- bes manifestam Dei promissionem & juramentum de æterno templo, Sacerdotio, & regno in Davidis semine, Christo. Hæc B. Bugenhagius. B. Lutherus enar- rat. in Psalm. grad. Tom. 4. Jen. ad h. Psalm. f. 424. Psalmum simpliciter intelligit de regno Davidis usque ad Christum: nec tamen valde repugnat, si quis ista omnia ad Christum transferre velit, idque sine negotio fieri posse, fatetur. Nam alioqui, inquit, in Prophe- tis usitatum est, ut in fine attexant Prophetias de Chri- sto, qui est verus surculus seu germen, & verus Naza- rænus a Deo in hoc paratus, ut sit lucerna perpetua, quam non possit extinguere Satan.

Id negandum non est de Regno Davidico po- steris sub conditione promisso quædam loqui, utpote vers. 12. eademque fini subjungi promissionem de templo conservando usque ad finem politiæ v. 13. 14. donec umbræ succedat corpus. Sed quum pro- missio de fructu ventris ponendo in solio Davidis, & ἀμεταμελήτως facta, & in Christo impleta sit S. Petro interprete Actor. 2, 30. nec aliud ferat sedes ejus propria 2. Sam. 7, 19. interjecta illa de regno ter- reno hæredum Davidis sunt, ut constaret etiam il- lis perpetuo conservatum iri solium, si perstiterint in fœdere Domini, q. d. juravit Davidi Dominus ex lumbis ejus proditurum Messiam, cujus solium æter- num erit. Sed & ipsum terrenum regnum in perpe- tuum conservaret posteris ejus Dominus, si illi serva- rent fœdus & testimonium ejus. Prior ergo pro- missio est præcipua, absoluta & categorica de semine benedicto, fructu ventris Davidis, & regno ejus spi- rituali atque æterno vers. 11. Posterior de hæredi- bus solii terreni & temporalis e stirpe Davidis est con- ditionata & sub hypothesi observandi fœderis facta, vers. 12. cui adjungitur conversatio habitationis Do- mini in Zion, & benedictio populi temporalis vers. 15. nec non sacerdotii usque ad verum regnum & Sa- cerdotium conservatio vers. 18. Inde ergo ad principem illam de Messia ejusque regno Davidi factam promissionem redit Salomo vers. 17.

efficiam, ut germinet cornu Davidis, paravi lucer- nam uncto meo. Quo primum locus designatur nativitatis Messiæ שם IBI respicitur nempe locus de quo supra dixerat: Audivimus eam (arcam) in Ephrata, inveniemus eam in agris campi. Quæ de Christo invento in Bethlehem præeunte Hie- ronymo, pronomen in Masculino reddente, au- divimus eum, B. Bugenhagius antea nec non B. Reinhard. Backius accipiunt. Sed quum in fon- te pronomen fœminei generis sit, & arca respicia- tur in confinibus Ephratææ vel Bethlehemais in- venta: nunc typo respondere concinne antitypum Salomo informat nos, vers. 17. ILLIC (in confi- nibus Ephratæis, vel Bethlehemitis) faciam, in- quit Dominus, germinare cornu Davidis. Conf. Mich. 5, 2. Matth. 2, 4. Deinde nativitas Messiæ insinuatur, faciam germinare cornu Davidis. Quia ita solet temporalis ejus nativitas designari; vid. Jer. 23, 6. cap. 33, 15. Zach. 6, 12. Mal. 4, 1. Luc. 1, 78. Tertio nominibus egregiis ornatur Messias, ejus tum personam, tum officium exprimentibus. Nam dicitur cornu, id est, robur ac potentia Davidis, in qua David gloriatus est, & fiduciam suam collo- cavit Ps. 18, 3. quemadmodum & Zacharias Luc. 1, 69. Cum vocat cornu salutis. Quo nomine pro- inde divina ejus natura, quum solus Deus cornu nostrum sit, in quo confidere queamus, nec non officium ejus, quia cornu est salutis nostræ, exhi- betur. Dicitur & lucerna parata uncto Domini, Davidi, qui in hac lucerna solum illuminari gestit, extra quam nullum etiam vel Davidi, vel ulli mor- talium fulget lumen, sed meræ sunt tenebræ Esa. 23, 5. Psal. 119, 81. 105. Es. 9, 1. cap. 60, 1. Luc. 1, 19. Postremo additur fors oppugnantium regnum Mef- siæ & regni ipsius vers. 18. inimicos ejus induam con- fusione, super ipsum vero Messiam, Regem vel re- gnum ejus, quod est Regnum salutis, florebit Dia- dema ejus, quia Ecclesia, quæ regnum ejus est, & fideles coronantur Diademate gloriæ ejus in hoc, & imprimis in venturo seculo, quum æterna ignomi- nia & confusione vestiantur inimici ejus Psal. 70, 4. 5. Dan. 12, 2. Sap. 4, 17.

## 132:15
Verse 15.

I WILL SURELY BLESS HER WIDOW) Better, Her food. Aquila: her provision. Symmachus: her sustenance. The Hebrew word צידה signifies both food and hunting. The LXX took it in the latter sense, and translated it as hunting, as Jerome cites. But the scribes, by changing one letter, made it widow, which Hilary, Apollinaris, the Arab, the Ethiopian, the Roman and Gallican Psalters follow. So easily do errors flow.

This has been rightly observed: but why, in other places, is the Greek version not equally accused rather than the Hebrew source? For what happened to one could have happened to any place: Grotius has no reason why he should almost always be more favorable to the Greek version than to the Hebrew sources: indeed, there is more than one reason at hand why we ought to assert the purity of these over any versions whatsoever: concerning which, elsewhere, professedly.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

VIDUAM EJUS BENEDICENS BENEDICAM) Me- lius, Esca ejus. Aquila ἐπισιτισμὸν αὐτῆς. Symmachus τὴν σίτησιν αὐτῆς. Vox Hebræa צידה & escam & venatio- nem significat. LXX. in posteriori significatu sumserunt, & verterunt θήραν, ut citat Hieronymus. Sed librarii litera una mutata fecerunt χήραν, quod sequuntur Hilarius, Apol- linaris, Arabs, Æthiops, Psalterium Romanum &Gallicum. Tam facile fluunt errores.

Recte hoc observatum: cur vero in aliis pari- ter non accusatur potius Græca versio, quam fons Ebræus? Quod enim uni contigit, cuivis contin- gere potuit loco: Non habet causam Grotius, cur æquior sit semper fere Græcæ versioni, quam fon- tibus Ebræis: imo causa in promptu est non una, cur horum puritatem adserere præ quibusvis ver- sionibus debeamus: de quo alias ex professo.

## 132:16
Verse 16.

AND HIS SAINTS SHALL SHOUT FOR JOY) Christ seems to refer to this passage in John 5:35.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

ET SANCTI EJUS EXULTATIONE EXULTA- BUNT) Ad hunc locum videtur respicere Christus apud Johannem 5, 35.

## 132:17
Verse 17.

I HAVE PREPARED A LAMP FOR MY ANOINTED) That is, descendants who will reign; who are called the lamp of their progenitors, because they draw light, that is, dignity, from them. 1 Kings 11:36, 15:4.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

PARAVI LUCERNAM CHRISTO MEO) Id est, po- steros regnaturos; qui dicuntur genitorum lucerna, quod ab eis lucem, id est, dignitatem trahant 1. Reg. 11, 36. 15, 4.

## 133:1 Argument
PSALM 133. A Sacred Irenicon.

BEHOLD HOW GOOD AND HOW PLEASANT IT IS FOR BRETHREN TO DWELL TOGETHER IN UNITY) Menander: Ὡς ἡδύ γ᾽ ἐν ἀδελφοῖσιν ὁμονοίας ἔρως.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXXIII. Sacrum Irenicum.

ECCE QVAM BONVM ET QVAM JUCUNDUM HABITARE FRATRES IN UNUM) Menander: Ὡς ἡδύ γ᾽ ἐν ἀδελφοῖσιν ὁμονοίας ἔρως.

## 133:3
Verse 3.

Verse 3.

AS THE DEW OF HERMON, WHICH DESCENDS UPON MOUNT ZION) But Hermon is far from Zion, no less than Πόἤῥω τὰ Μυσῶν καὶ Φρύγων ὁρίσματα [Far are the boundaries of the Mysians and Phrygians]. Zion is in Jerusalem: Hermon is near the Sea of Galilee: how therefore does the dew flow from here to there? Learned men think it probable that the less frequent word שיאן [Si'on] was changed into the word of similar sound ציון [Zion]. Moreover, the mountain שיאן is the same as Hermon, Deut. 4:48. Twice, therefore, he said the same thing here, as the Hebrews often do. Concerning dew on the summit of mountains, see Deut. 33:13, 14, 15.

There is no necessity here to invent a change; nor is there need, as with others, to seek out reasons how the dew of Mount Hermon descends upon Mount Zion, or to say with Bellarmine that this is expressed in a poetic manner, as if Mount Hermon, being higher and having a great abundance of dew, communicates with the lower and more arid mountains of Zion, and it is implied that the mountains or hills of Zion are irrigated by Christ, the highest mountain and most full of heavenly dew. For the mountains are compared among themselves, not with Christ. From the Syriac translation, Viccars renders this sense: Zion, although an arid mountain, was more blessed by God than if the dew of Hermon had fallen upon it, because the temple was built there. Our Bugenhagen says that the dew is designated not as the same in number, but in kind, that is, equally fruitful. And thus the Weimar paraphrasts understand that dew of the same kind fertilizes the mountains of Judea, for the sake of a more expressive sense, understanding a copulative conjunction: The dew of Hermon AND that which descends upon Mount Zion; which is also the interpretation of B. Gerhard, Comment. on Deuteronomy, p. 234, and of Glassius, Philologia Sacra, book 4, tract 1, observation 7. It can also be said that the particle of comparison must be repeated from the prior member, as is sometimes done in comparisons, and ellipses of nouns, verbs, and particles to be repeated from the preceding member occur elsewhere. Which opinion I also see is that of R. Aben-Ezra here: As the dew, he says, is taken twice like אל in Prov. 30:3, that is, as the dew which descends upon Mount Zion. Which also pleased Junius and Tremellius, as well as the authors of the Belgian Notes, as also Sixtinus Amama, in Anti-Barbarus, p. 56, 3. Gesner says that Hermon is the summit of Mount Lebanon, whose ridges surround the holy land and the hills in it, whence the dew is said to slide down from there, because a very great quantity of vapors exhales from those very high mountains, which subsequently slides down by its own gravity into the sloping places. But the former explanation, as being simpler, is to be preferred.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Vers. 3.

SICVT ROS HERMON, QVI DESCENDIT IN MONTEM SION) At longe Hermon a Sione, non minus quam Πόῤῥω τὰ Μυσῶν καὶ Φρύγων ὁρίσματα. Sion est Hierosolymis: Hermon prope lacum Galilææ: quo- modo ergo ros hinc illuc defluit? Eruditi probabile putant, vocem minus frequentem שיאן mutatam in vocem similis soni ציון. Est autem mons שיאן idem qui Hermon Deut. 4, 48. Bis ergo hic idem dixit, ut sæpe Hebræi. De rore in ver- tice montium vide Deut. 33, 13. 14. 15.

NUlla hic necessitas fingendi mutationem; Nec opus est, ut cum aliis rationes conqui- rantur, quomodo ros montis Hermon descendat in montem Sion, aut ut cum Bellarmino dicatur, more Poetico hoc ita efferri, quasi communicet mons Hermon sublimior, in quo magna roris abundantia, cum montibus Sion humilioribus, & aridioribus, ac innuatur, a Christo monte altissimo, & rore cœ- lesti plenissimo montes sive colles Sion irrigari. Nam conferuntur montes inter se, non cum Christo. E Syriaca translatione hunc sensum reddit Viccar- sus: Sion, quanquam mons aridus, magis a Deo be- nedictus fuit, quum si ros Hermonis super eum ceci- disset, quoniam ibi ædificatum erat templum. Bu- genhagius noster rorem non eundem numero, sed specie, id est, æque fœcundum designari, ait. At- que ita Vinarienses paraphrastæ ejusdem generis rorem montana Judææ fœcundare, intelligunt, sen- sus expressioris causa copulativam subaudientes; Ros Hermon & qui descendit in montem Sion; quæ etiam B. Gerhard. Comment. in Deuteron. p. 234. & Glassii est interpretatio Grammat. Sacr. lib. 4. Tract. 1. observ. 7. Dici etiam potest, particulam similitudinis ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetendam esse e priori membro, quemadmodum fieri quandoque solet in comparationibus, & ellipses nominum, verbo- rum, & particularum, e præcedenti membro re- petendarum alias occurrunt. Quam etiam video sententiam hic esse R. Aben-Ezra: Sicut ros, in- quit, bis sumitur ut אל in Prov. 30, 3. id est, sicut ros qui in montem Sion descendit. Quæ Junio quo- que ac Tremellio, nec non Autoribus Notarum Bel- gicarum placuit, ut & Sixtino Amama, in Anti- Barbar. p. 56, 3. Gesnerus Hermon dicit esse verti- cem montis Libani, cujus juga terram sanctam & colles in ea cingant, unde ros inde delabi dicitur, quia maxima vaporum copia ex istis præaltis mon- tibus exhalat, quæ sua postmodum gravitate in lo- ca declivia delabitur. Sed prior explicatio ceu sim- plicior præferenda.

IN THE NIGHTS LIFT UP YOUR HANDS) For many Israelites continued days and nights in the temple, as appears above 92:3 and 119:147. See what is said on Luke 2:37. For their sake this Psalm was made, and the following one.

## 135:1 Argument
PSALM CXXXV. Celebration of the benefits of God. Detestation of Idols.

That is, from every part of the horizon. Indeed, winds are produced by GOD so suddenly as if they were brought forth from the treasuries of GOD, that is, from the most secret and most rich power of GOD, which can never be exhausted. Conf. Job 3:8, Deut. 28:12, Job 38:22.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXXXV. Celebratio beneficiorum Dei. Detestatio Ido- lorum.

Id est, ab omni parte horizontis. NImirum ita repente producuntur a DEO ven- ti, quasi educerentur de thesauris DEI, id est, de potentia DEI secretissima, & ditissima, quæ nun- quam exhauriri potest. Conf. Job. 3, 8. Deut. 28, 12. Job. 38, 22.

## 135:21
Verse 21. BLESSED BE THE LORD FROM ZION, WHO DWELLS IN JERUSALEM.

Some explain it from Sion, so that every blessing may go forth from Sion by the inhabitants of Sion; to some this ἐξήγησις pleases: Blessed be the Lord from Sion (spreading glory or bringing aid) who dwells in Jerusalem. But because of the accentuation we prefer the former sense.

Latin:

Vers. 21. BENEDICTUS DOMINUS EX SION, QUI HABITAT IN JERUSALEM.

Nonnulli ex Sion ita exponunt, ut ex Sion prodeat omnis benedictio ab incolis Sionis; qui- busdam hæc placet ἐξήγησις: Benedictus sit Dominus ex Sion (gloriam propagans vel opem ferens) habi- tat in Jerusalem. Sed ob accentuationem præferi- mus priorem sensum.

## 136:23
Vers. 23.

FOR IN OUR HUMILIATION) In our misery. WHO GIVETH FOOD TO ALL FLESH] To every living creature.

Ver. 27. FOR HIS MERCY ENDURETH FOR EVER.

We add the ἀξιομνημόνευτον (memorable) admonition of B. Luther, delivered in the argument of this Psalm: It is a notable and general act of thanksgiving for the infinite, ineffable, never-failing bodily and spiritual benefits of God, and in this golden and excellent Psalm, he wished as it were to summarize and prescribe to the priests what the subject matter of all sermons, all exhortations, and all songs among the people ought to be, so that all impious doctrine and all false worship of God may be avoided, and God may be truly worshipped with that worship which the first commandment of the Decalogue demands. For this ought to be the sum: Let us praise the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is for an age, that is, give thanks incessantly, preach and celebrate the infinite amplitude of grace, learn from the word that just as he promised, so he is present to us, and incessantly accumulates benefits upon benefits, and the riches of his goodness are inexhaustible. Therefore, against the Devil, who does nothing else but extinguish faith and the knowledge of goodness and mercy in hearts, and cast us into sadness and doubt, he repeats the same sentiment through individual lines with this intercalary verse, 'for his goodness is incessant for ever,' by which verse, repeated so often, he wishes as it were to fix and inculcate the doctrine of grace, the worship of the first Commandment, as if to say: The immense goodness of God has done these wonders in you, not the works of men, not your merits. It is the mere and ineffable amplitude of grace and goodness that pours all these things upon you, and thus pours them gratuitously upon the unworthy. And by this verse he also alludes, in the manner of the Prophets, to the promise concerning the future Christ, for the promise of grace was not made to the Fathers out of any merits, in that seed of Abraham, etc. Learn to repeat and inculcate this intercalary verse to yourself and to others against the Devil, who always yaps as if it were not his goodness, but his cruelty, that is incessant. Hypocrites and Fanatics do not sing, nor can they sing this verse: For his mercy endureth for ever; But they sing, because our merit is unending &c. But you hold fast to this doctrine of the Davidic spirit, truly heavenly and divine, of the unending remission of sins, and conquerable by no sin; which alone overcomes against the Devil and all heresies, and alone makes the conscience rest in temptations and the agonies of death.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

QVIA IN HVMILITATE NOSTRA) In miseria nostra. QVI DAT ESCAM OMNI CARNI] Omni animanti.

Vers. 27. QUONIAM IN ÆTERNUM MISERI- CORDIA EJUS.

ADdimus monitum B. Lutheri ἀξιομνημόνευτον, in argumento hujus Psalmi traditum: Est in- signis & generalis Gratiarum actio, pro infinitis, in- effabilibus, nunquam deficientibus beneficiis Dei corporalibus & spiritualibus, & hoc aureo & egre- gio Psalmo, quasi summatim complecti & præscri- bere voluit Sacerdotibus, cujus argumenti esse de- beant omnes Conciones, omnes Exhortationes, omnia- que cantica in populo, ut vitetur omnis impia doctri- na, omnis falsus cultus Dei, & Deus vere colatur cultu illo, quem exigit primum præceptum decalogi. Nam hæc debet esse summa, Laudemus Dominum, quoniam bonus, quoniam in seculum misericordia ejus, id est, indefinenter gratias agite, prædicate & celebrate infinitam amplitudinem gratiæ, discite ex verbo, quoniam sicut promisit, ita præsens adest no- bis, & indefinenter beneficia accumulat beneficiis, & inexhaustæ sunt divitiæ bonitatis. Ideo contra Diabolum, qui nihil aliud agit, quam ut in cordibus extinguat fidem & cognitionem bonitatis ac miseri- cordiæ, & nos conjiciat in tristitiam & dubitatio- nem, versu hoc intercalari per singulas lineas repetit eandem sententiam, quoniam indefinens bonitas ejus in æternum, quo versu toties repetito, quasi insigere vult & inculcare doctrinam gratiæ, cultum primi Præcepti, q.d. Immensa bonitas Dei fecit hæc mira- bilia in vobis, non opera hominum, non merita ve- stra. Mera & ineffabilis amplitudo gratiæ est & bonitas, quæ hæc omnia in vos effundit, adeoque gra- tuito indignos effundit. Atque hoc versu alludit etiam more Prophetarum, ad promissionem de futuro Christo, neque enim ex ullis meritis facta est Patribus promissio gratiæ, in semine illo Abrahæ &c. Hunc intercalarem disce repetere & inculcare tibimet- ipsi, & aliis contra Diabolum, qui semper obgannit, quasi non bonitas, sed sævitia ejus sit indefinens. Hy- pocritæ & Fanatici non canunt, nec canere possunt hunc versum: Quoniam in æternum misericordia ejus; Sed canunt, quoniam indefinens meritum no- strum &c. Verum tu retine hanc doctrinam Davidi- ci spiritus, vere cælestem & divinam remissionis pec- catorum indefinentis, & nullo peccato superabilis; quæ sola contra Diabolum & omnes hæreses vincit, solaque in tentationibus & agonibus mortis acquie- scere facit conscientiam.

PSALM CXXXVII. The Weeping of the Babylonians.

## 137:9
Verse 9.

BLESSED IS HE THAT SHALL TAKE AND DASH THY LITTLE ONES AGAINST THE ROCK) According to the custom of that age, which was sufficiently harsh, but which was excused for that time by the hatred of impious nations. See what we have said about the Law of War and Peace, book 3, chapter 4, section 9.

It is in vain that a custom of that age more harsh than usual is imagined to exist among the people of God; it is in vain that the Psalmist is excused in the Hebrew; nay, it is nothing but an impious attribution to the Holy Spirit, by whose authority he himself brought these things forth. It has been said often enough that there were no other moral laws under the Old Testament than under the New, and that no other custom of the people of God was divinely granted or approved in that age than now. Here is predicted prophetically the just judgment of God and the sentence of the Holy Spirit himself, and those who are blessed are proclaimed, or a blessing and success in the execution of the judgments of God is vowed by the Hierosolymitan Psalmist; namely, to those who were about to take vengeance upon impious Babylon, just as a happy success in that matter was promised to Cyrus also by Isaiah, Isaiah 44, and can be wished and promised today to all Magistrates fighting with zeal for the glory of the Lord against idolaters and the enemies of the Church. On the contrary, however, those are pronounced cursed who execute the work of the Lord in punishing impious peoples fraudulently, Jeremiah 48:10, and therefore these things are piously applied to the kingdom of the Anti-Christ, and the vows of the faithful against the same, by our Bugenhagen: Blessed, that is, let that people be blessed, whom God has sent for this purpose, that it may render to you your due; may God help his hands, that you may so perish by the raging of enemies, that not even the little ones, who are usually spared in war, may be spared, so that there may be no hope left for you, all being killed, so that you may no longer rise up and grow into a Kingdom. So also must we pray, that the kingdom of Anti-Christian impiety, which has miserably oppressed us, with its great and lesser scandals, may perish through the revealed Gospel, so that not even the little ones may remain, by whom it might again grow and multiply against us, but let that happen which is written in Psalm 9: His sin shall be sought, and it shall not be found; you shall perish, O nations, from his land; man shall no longer set himself to magnify himself upon the earth, Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

BEATVS QVI TENEBIT ET ALLIDET PARVV- LOS TVOS AD PETRAM) Ex more illius seculi satis inclemente, sed qui odio impiarum gentium pro illo tem- pore excusabatur. Vide quæ diximus de Jure Belli ac Pacis libro 3. c. 4. §. 9.

FRustra fingitur mos seculi istius inclementior, penes populum Dei; Frustra is in Hebræo Psal- te excusatur; imo non nisi impie affingitur Spiritui Sancto, quo auctore ipse hæc protulit. Non fuisse alias leges morales sub Vet. Test. quam sub Novo, non alium divinitus concessum aut probatum mo- rem populi Dei ista ætate, quam nunc, sæpius di- ctum. Prædicitur hic Prophetice justum Dei judi- cium ac sententia ipsius Spiritus Sancti beati præ- dicantur, vel benedictio ac successus in exequutio- ne judiciorum Dei ab Hiero-Psalte ipsis vovetur; qui nempe supplicium de impia Babylone sumturi erant, quemadmodum Cyro felix successus ea in re etiam ab Esaia promissus est, Es. 44. omnibus- que Magistratibus Zelo pro gloria Domini adver- sus idololatras & hostes Ecclesiæ pugnantibus ho- dieque optari & promitti potest. Ex adverso vero maledicti pronunciantur, qui opus Domini in pu- niendis impiis populis fraudulenter exequuntur Jerem. 48, 10. ideoque pie hæc ad regnum Anti- Christi, ac vota fidelium adversus eundem appli- cantur a Bugenhagio nostro: Beatus, id est, bene- dictus sit ille populus, quem ad hoc miserit Deus, ut vi- cem tibi reddat; Deus adjuvet manus ejus, ut ita pereas sævientibus hostibus, ut ne parvulis quidem, quibus in bello parci solet, parcatur, ut non sit tibi spes reliqua, omnibus occisis, quo amplius exurgas & crescas in Regnum. Sic & nobis orandum, ut impietatis Anti-Christiana regnum, quod nos misere pressit, cum magnis suis & minoribus scandalis, per revelatum Evangelium intereat, ut ne parvuli quidem supersint, quibus rursum crescat & multiplicetur contra nos, sed fiat quod Psal. 9. scribitur: Quæretur peccatum illius, & non invenietur, peribitis gentes de terra illius, non opponet ultra se magnificare homo super terram, Amen.

## 138:1 Argument
PSALM 138. The sanctification of the name of GOD.

HERE in the Greek is added that which is neither in the Hebrew nor in the Latin: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαβὶδ Ἀγγαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου: signifying that this is a Psalm of David, but used also by Haggai and Zechariah: such inscriptions as we have had above.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXXVIII. Sanctificatio nominis DEI.

HIC in Græco additur, quod nec in Hebræo est, nec in Latino: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαβὶδ Ἀγγαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου: significans hunc Davidis esse Psalmum, sed usurpatum etiam Aggæo, & Zachariæ: quales inscriptiones & supra habuimus.

## 138:1
IN THE SIGHT OF THE ANGELS I WILL SING PSALMS UNTO THEE) אלהים, which is here in the Hebrew, can signify both the Angels and the Senators of the great Sanhedrin. I would prefer the latter.

Felix Pratensis translates it as 'of gods', so that judges and princes may be understood. Whence our blessed Bugenhagius observes that this is the nature of faith, that a believer should fearlessly confess before princes whatever he cherishes in his heart. The Chaldean explains it also as referring to judges and Rabbis, which sense is also approved by the blessed Backius and Hackspanius, who here weighs the opinion of the Walenburgians, that angels are hinted at as knowing our prayers and as being to be invoked as intercessors; even if the angels understand the pious singing before the angels, they are not on that account to be invoked so that they may intercede for us: for this is nowhere commanded. That certainly appears sufficiently, that it is not to be taken only concerning David singing before the Sanhedrin. For although it is a Psalm of David, as the title indicates, it does not treat only of the benefits shown to David, but of those which have been provided in Christ to all the kingdoms of the earth, according to the clear meaning of verse 4. Which was rightly observed by our blessed Gesner.

Latin:

IN CONSPECTU ANGELORUM PSALLAM TIBI) אלהים, quod hic in Hebræo est & Angelos potest significare, & magni Synedrii Senatores. Ego hoc præferam.

Felix Pratensis reddit Deorum, ut judices & principes intelligantur. Unde B. Bugenhagius noster observat, hanc fidei naturam esse, quod confiteatur coram principibus intrepide fidelis, quicquid corde fovet. Chaldæus explicat etiam de judicibus & Rabbinis, qui sensus probatus quoque B. Backio & Hackspanio, qui Walenburgicorum sententiam, quod angeli innuantur preces nostras novisse, & ut intercessores invocandos esse hic expendit, etiamsi coram angelis psallentes pios intelligant angeli, non tamen ideo ut intercedant pro nobis, invocandi: hoc enim nuspiam mandatum est. Id utique satis apparet, non de Davide tantum coram Synedrio psallente accipiendum. Etsi enim Davidis Psalmus est, quod titulus indicat, non agit tamen de beneficiis solummodo Davidi exhibitis, sed de iis, quæ in Christo omnibus terræ regnis sunt præstita, juxta perspicuam vers. 4. sententiam. Quod recte observatum B. Gesnero nostro.

## 138:2
Verse 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

## 138:4
Verse 4. LET ALL THE KINGS OF THE EARTH CONFESS TO THEE BECAUSE THEY HAVE HEARD.

In vain do Piscator, Junius, Amama, and the Dutch reject this version along with the German and prefer a hypothetical sense, 'if' or 'when they have heard'. For the particle כי is ordinarily causal, and so it must be taken here and in verse 5; therefore it is also translated thus, and the present passage is taken by Cocceius as a categorical prophecy concerning the calling of the Gentiles: The matter is clear from the emphasis of the words and the truth of the thing, but then especially from the fourth verse that this Psalm treats of the Kingdom of Christ. For there it is said: All the kings of the earth shall confess the Lord, because they have heard the words of the mouth of GOD. Moreover, that a universal calling is described is evident from a comparison of similar passages, Psalm 67:6, 7; Psalm 68:30 ff.; Psalm 72:10, 11; Psalm 111:23; Psalm 149:8.

Latin:

Vers. 4. CONFITEANTUR TIBI OMNES REGES TERRÆ QUIA AUDIERUNT.

Nequicquam Piscator, Junius, Amama, & Belgæ versionem hanc juxta cum Germanica reprobant & hypotheticum præferunt sensum, si vel cum audiverunt. Nam particula כי ordinarie causalis est, atque ita etiam hic & v. 5. accipienda; ideo etiam ita redditur, & locus præsens ut vaticinium de vocatione gentium categoricum accipitur a Coccejo: Res aperta est ex verborum emphasi & rei veritate, tum vero maxime ex versu quarto agi in hoc Psalmo de Regno Christi. Ibi enim dicitur: Omnes reges terræ confiteri Dominum, quia audiverint verba oris DEI. Vocationem autem universalem describi e collatione locorum similium patet Psal. 67, 6. 7. Psal. 68, 30. seqq. Psal. 72, 10. 11. Psal. 111, 23. Psal. 149, 8.

Verse 6.

AND THE HIGH HE KNOWS FROM AFAR) Better: and the high one knows from afar: so that the same thing is said twice in other words.
