Vers. 6.

ET ALTA A LONGE COGNOSCIT) Melius: & altus e longinquo cognoscit: ut bis idem dicatur aliis vocibus.

## 139:1 Argument
PSALM CXXXIX. The omniscience, omnipresence, and most just providence of God.

Latin:

PSALM. CXXXIX. Providentia Dei omniscientia, omnipræsentis, & justissimi.

## 139:2
Verse 2.

THOU HAST KNOWN MY SITTING AND MY RISING AGAIN) The sense is, whether I sit, or rise to the same: that is, thou knowest all my leisure and my business.

These are words not of Christ, concerning whom the Papists chant them from the Breviaries in the second vespers under the matins of Easter, as if they sounded of the resurrection of Christ, as Estius has in this place, but of David, uttered concerning himself, as Vatablus, Cajetan, Jansenius, and Lorinus acknowledge: therefore the Pontificians wrongly seek arguments from verses 6, 7, and 8 to deny to Christ, according to his human nature, omniscience and divine omnipresence: see Sixtus Senensis, book 5, Bibl. ann. 269, Bellarmine, book 3, on the Incarnation, chapter 11. The sense is, as Estius confesses, thou hast me thoroughly explored and known. And literally the individual parts can be applied thus: Thou hast known my sitting and my rising again, that is, all my actions which I perform, whether I sit, or rise, or whatever else I may do. So he. But that which the Roman Catholic Churches excuse by a mystical sense as an interpretation of the resurrection of Christ is frivolous, for how can a sense concerning the resurrection of Christ lie hidden in these words, which speak of the common actions of men?

Latin:

Vers. 2.

TV COGNOVISTI SESSIONEM MEAM ET RESVRRECTIONEM MEAM) Sensus est, sive sedeam, sive ad eundem surgam: id est, omnia mea otia & negotia mea nosti.

VErba sunt non Christi, de quo Papistæ e Bre- viariis in secundis vesperis sub matutinum Pa- schatos ea decantant, quasi de resurrectione Christi sonent, uti Estius in h. l. habet, sed Davidis, de se- metipso prolata, ut Vatablus, Cajetanus, Janse- nius, Lorinus agnoscunt: ideo perperam e vers. 6. 7. 8. argumenta petunt Pontificii ad denegandam Christo secundum humanam naturam omniscien- tiam & omnipræsentiam divinam: vid. Sixt. Sen. l. 5. Bibl. ann. 269. Bellarm. lib. 3. de Incarnat. cap. 11. Sensus est, fatente Estio, tu me penitus explora- tum & cognitum habes. Et ad literam singula sic applicari possunt: Tu cognovisti sessionem & resur- rectionem meam, id est, omnes actiones meas, quas ago, sive sedeam, sive surgam, sive quodcunque aliud agam. Hæc ille. Quod vero per sensum mysticum ex- cusant Ecclesiæ Romano - Catholicæ de resurre- ctione Christi interpretationem, frivolum est, nam quomodo in istis verbis latere potest sensus de re- surrectione Christi, quæ de communibus hominum actionibus loquuntur?

## 139:3
Verse 3.

AND THOU HAST INVESTIGATED MY LINE) רבעי signifies lying down. Therefore it is credible that the LXX translated it as κοίτον, for which the scribes wrote σχοῖνον, whence this version.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ET FVNICVLVM MEVM INVESTIGASTI) רבעי cubatum significat. Itaque LXX. credibile est κοίτον ver- tisse, pro quo librarii σχοῖνον scripserint, unde hæc versio.

## 139:4
Verse 4.

FOR THERE IS NO SPEECH IN MY TONGUE: BEHOLD O LORD THOU HAST KNOWN ALL) You may translate it best: When there is not yet speech in my tongue, behold already thou hast known all things. There is no need that I should utter thoughts: thou seest them already conceived in the mind. Here also the LXX wrote λόγῳ, as Jerome teaches us how it should be read in his epistle. Aquila wrote λαλιὰ, but the scribes wrote δόλος instead of λόγῳ, which the old Psalter, Hilary, and Augustine follow.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QVIA NON EST SERMO IN LINGVA MEA: EC- CE DOMINE TV COGNOVISTI OMNIA) Optime vertas: Cum nondum sermo in lingua mea, ecce jam omnia tu novisti. Non opus est ut cogitationes eloquar: jam in ani- mo conceptas tu vides. Hic quoque λόγῳ scripserunt LXX. quomodo legendum nos docet Hieronymus in epistola. Aquila λαλιὰ sed librarii pro λόγῳ scripsere δόλος, quod se- quuntur Psalterium vetus, Hilarius, Augustinus.

## 139:5
Verse 5.

THE LAST AND THE ANCIENT: THOU HAST FORMED ME) In the Hebrew: Behind and before thou hast formed me, or besieged me. For צור signifies both: and the latter meaning is more suitable to this place. The Rabbis who interpret it as 'thou hast formed' refer this to their pre-existence of souls which they dream of.

In the Hebrew these things are otherwise: for the former pertain to verse 4, in this manner: Behold O Lord thou hast known the whole of it, the latter to verse 5, sounding thus in Pagninus's version: Behind and before thou hast formed me, and hast placed thy palm upon me. Junius and Tremellius render it, (when there is not yet thus speech in my tongue) Thou O Jehovah hast known the whole of it. Behind and before thou dost besiege me, and dost lay thy hand upon me. For צור in its customary meaning is to besiege. To which also the Chaldean, Aben-Ezra, and Buxtorf go, and the German translation of Luther does not differ much, even if it assumes another meaning of the word צור, by which it denotes to form. But the Vulgate, when it refers these to the formation of man, is more alien; the discourse is not about the formation of man, but about the direction of all the actions of man, therefore the passage Job 10:8 is not conveniently compared here. But the Hebrews are inept who dream from this that Adam was formed in the beginning as an androgynous being having two faces, because it is said 'behind and before thou hast formed me,' such as R. Jeremias, and certain ones in the Epitome Talmud. En Israel p. 80, and Menasse Ben-Israel. For the Psalmist speaks of himself, not of Adam.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

NOVISSIMA ET ANTIQVA: TV FORMASTI ME) In Hebræo: Retro & ante tu me formasti, vel circumsedisti. Nam צור utrumque significat: & posterior significatio ma- gis huic loco convenit. Rabbini qui formasti interpretantur, referunt hoc ad suam quam somniant animarum προϋπαρξιν.

In Ebræo aliter hæc habent: priora enim ad v. 4. pertinent h. m. Ecce Domine tu nosti totum ipsum, posteriora v. 5. sequenti ita sonante Pagnini versione: Retro & ante formasti me, & posuisti su- per me volam tuam. Junius & Tremellius reddunt, (quum nondum est ita sermo in lingua mea) Tu o Jehova nosti ipsum totum. Retro & ante obsides me, & imponis mihi manum tuam. Nam צור usitata si- gnificatione est obsidere. Quo abit etiam Chaldæus, Aben-Esra, Buxtorfius, nec multum discrepat Lu- ther. Germanica translatio, etsi aliam significatio- nem verbi צור, qua notat formare, assumat. Vulga- ta autem cum refert hæc ad formationem hominis alienior est; non de formatione hominis, sed de re- ctione omnium actionum hominis sermo est, ideo nec commode hic confertur locus Job. 10, 8. Ebræi au- tem inepti sunt, qui hinc Adamum androgy num duas facies habentem initio formatum somniant, quod dicatur retro & ante formasti me, utpote R. Jeremias, ac quidam in Epitome Talmud. En Israel p. 80. & Menasse Ben-Israel. De se enim loquitur Psaltes non de Adamo.

## 139:6
Ver. 6.

THY KNOWLEDGE IS BECOME WONDERFUL FROM ME) For from me; you might more correctly place before me: so that the sense may be: Thy knowledge is more wonderful than that I should be hidden from it. This agrees excellently with what follows.

Ver. the same.

WHITHER SHALL I GO FROM THY SPIRIT?

The orthodox commonly prove the omnipresence of the Holy Spirit from this passage. This does not please Hackspan, because by רוח the same thing is denoted as by the word פנים. But whence will that be proved? There is, he says, no reason why the Holy Spirit should be distinguished from the divine face. But there is no lack of reason, not indeed why it should be distinguished (which does not happen here), but why these two should be joined. Because, namely, the Spirit of the Lord is the Spirit of judgment, and His wrath can apprehend us everywhere, which is indicated by the word פנים in this place; or the face of the Lord, which they feel to be angry, is joined with the Spirit of the Lord pursuing men, whithersoever they betake themselves. Although he adds: if I hide in the heavens, thou art there, yet from that it is not permitted to conclude that nothing else is understood by the Spirit of God than God Himself, as R. Solomon thought, because, where the Spirit of the Lord is, there the Lord is entirely. Hackspan adds that, just as for the Hebrews τὸ שם and for the Chaldeans τὸ מימרא דיי is God Himself, so it is not to be thought that wherever רוח אלהים is read, the Holy Spirit is immediately denoted. See 1 Sam. 18:10, ch. 19:9, Job 33:4. But as he is again, according to his custom, singular in this, that he wishes that Chaldean term to denote nothing else than God Himself, whereas most theologians judge that a hypostatic word is expressed by that term, which the blessed Selneccer showed in a special book, so the word Spirit of the Lord does not occur absolutely in the former passages cited, but an evil spirit from the Lord (permitting it) is said to have irritated Saul. In the last passage of Job, however, the Holy Spirit is entirely understood. Finally, the same author disapproves that our people prove the divine presence from this passage by calling it formally an action, because thus the categories of where and of action are confounded. But being somewhere is not confounded with divine action (which are wrongly reduced to the categories of where and of action, since God transcends all categories); it is only joined in an adequate description of divine omnipresence with the adestentia, as they call it, or the divine energy or operation, inasmuch as Holy Scripture nowhere speaks of the divine presence without including action at the same time. Nor indeed is the sense of the Biblical style to be drawn from Logic, but from the interpretation of the Holy Spirit Himself. Are the categories of substance and relation confounded, or does the Biblical style prejudice Logic, because God, according to Scripture, is not described without personal relations? Nor is there any reason why those words, thou art there, and, behold thou, should be urged with Thummius: for they do not denote a simple presence, but also import action. God is present in the heavens, He is present in hell, not by a simple presence but by an efficacious energy, so that no one can escape His hand, whether he ascends into the heavens or makes his bed in hell. It is too manifest from the text that it is not a matter of bare presence, which is deduced more broadly in the Saxon Decisions and by the Giessen doctors.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

MIRABILIS FACTA EST SCIENTIA TVA EX ME) Pro ex me; rectius ponas præ me: ut sensus sit: Admirabilior est scientia tua, quam ut ego ei lateam. Hoc optime convenit cum sequentibus.

Vers. eod.

QVO IBO A SPIRITU TUO?

Communiter orthodoxi ex hoc loco probant omnipræsentiam Spiritus Sancti. Non placet hoc Hackspanio, quia per רוח idem notetur quod per פנים vocem. Sed unde id probabitur? Nulla, inquit, ratio est, cur Spir. Sanct. contradistinguatur faciei divinæ. At non deest ratio, non quidem cur contradistinguatur, (quod hic non fit) sed cur conjungantur hæc duo. Quia sc. Spiritus Domini est Spiritus judicii, & ubivis ira sua nos apprehendere potest, quod voce פנים indicatur h. l. aut conjungitur cum Spiritu Domini insectante homines facies Domini, quam iratam sentiunt, quocunque se recipiant. Licet vero addat: si abscondere in cælos, ibi tu, ex eo tamen non licet concludere, nihil aliud per Spiritum Dei, quam Deum ipsum intelligi, uti putavit R. Salomo, quia, ubi est Spiritus Domini, ibi omnino Dominus est. Addit Hackspanius, uti Hebræis τὸ שם & Chaldæis τὸ מימרא דיי est ipse Deus, ita non ubicunque רוח אלהים legitur, illico Spir. Sanct. notari, putandum est. Vid. 1. Sam. 18, 10. cap. 19, 9. Job. 33, 4. Sed ut in eo iterum, pro more, singularis ipse est, quod Chaldæum illud nihil aliud, quam Deum ipsum notare velit, quum plerique Theologi voce ista verbum ὑποστατικὸν exprimi censeant, quod B. Selneccerus peculiari libro ostendit, ita vox Spiritus Domini in locis prioribus adductis absolute non occurrit, sed spiritus malus a Domino (permittente) Saulem irritasse dicitur. In postremo autem Jobeo omnino Spiritus Sanct. intelligitur. Denique improbat idem autor, quod nostrates ex hoc loco probant præsentiam divinam formaliter dicere actionem, quod ita prædicamenta, ubi & actionis, confundantur. At non confunditur τὸ esse alicubi cum actione divina (quæ perperam ad prædicamenta ubi & actionis rediguntur, quum Deus transcendat omnia prædicamenta) solum conjungitur in adæquata omnipræsentiæ divinæ descriptione cum ἀδιαστασίᾳ vel adessentia, quam vocant, ἐνέργεια vel operatio divina, siquidem Sacra Scriptura nuspiam de præsentia divina loquatur, quin actionem simul includat. Nec vero e Logica hauriendus est sensus styli Biblici, sed ex ipsa interpretatione Spirit. Sanct. Num ideo, quia Deus, juxta scripturam, non describitur sine relationibus personalibus, confunduntur prædicamenta substantiæ & relationis, aut stylus Biblicus præjudicat Logicæ? Neque est, quod cum Thummio urgeantur illa, ibi tu, &, ecce tu: nam ea non simplicem παρουσίαν notant, sed actionem etiam important. Adest in cœlis, adest in inferno Deus non simplici παρουσίᾳ sed efficaci ἐνεργείᾳ, ut nemo manum ejus effugere queat, sive in cælos ascendat, sive in inferno stratum faciat. Nimis manifestum est e textu, non agi de nuda adessentia, quæ latius in Decision. Saxon. & a Dnn. Giessensibus deducuntur.

## 139:15
Ver. 15.

MY BONE IS NOT HIDDEN FROM THEE WHICH THOU HAST MADE IN SECRET, AND MY SUBSTANCE IN THE LOWER PARTS OF THE EARTH) Understand my bone as bones. For the Hebrew has it so, although it can also be translated as body. The LXX read רכשי instead of רקמתי. But רקמתי agrees well with this place. For it signifies as if I were embroidered. He compares the most beautiful distinction of the members to Phrygian work. That in the lower parts of the earth signifies in the womb: as Eph. 4:9. It is a mutual metaphor. For both the lower parts of the earth and the heart of the earth are called the womb.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

NON EST OCCVLTATVM OS MEVM A TE QVOD FECISTI IN OCCVLTO, ET SVBSTANTIA MEA IN INFERIORIBVS TERRÆ) Os meum intellige ossa. Ita enim habet Hebræum, quanquam & corpus verti potest. LXX. pro רקמתי legere רכשי. At רקמתי bene huic loco convenit. Significat enim velut acu pictus sum. Distinctionem pulcherrimam membrorum comparat operi Phrygionico. Illud in inferioribus terræ significat in utero: ut Eph. 4, 9. Est mutua metaphora. Nam & inferiora terræ uterus dicuntur & cor terræ.

## 139:17
Ver. 17.

BUT THY FRIENDS ARE EXCEEDINGLY HONOURED UNTO ME O GOD: EXCEEDINGLY STRENGTHENED IS THE PRINCIPALITY OF THEM) Οἱ φίλοι σου, thus they translated רעיך

And the word indeed bears that meaning. But your thoughts bear another, which seems to suit this place better: so that the sense may be, how sublime are your thoughts above me, how numerous are their sums? For רָאשֵׁיהֶם which the Greeks translate αἱ ἀρχαὶ is translated by number. Num. 1, 49. sum Exod. 30, 12. Grotius admits that the version of others, YOUR THOUGHTS, is more suitable. But he ought rather to have said that this version alone is sound. And that the Vulgate does NOT AT ALL agree. He wished to excuse the Vulgate, as also the Greek translation, as if the words also bore that meaning. Because it was not unknown to him that the Papists attempt to prove the invocation of Saints from this passage. Alphonsus a Castro against heresies. Eccius in Enchir. chap. 15. Costerus the Jesuit in Ench. chap. 12. Which is indeed most absurd. For if that word רֵעֶיךָ is even translated as your friends, from where will it be proven that by them the deceased saints are to be understood, from where will it be shown that יָקְרוּ means to be honored, and that this in turn means to be religiously worshipped? And what does that mean, their principality is too strengthened? Must that be accepted with Coton, that the deceased Saints administer this world? Whence perhaps that distribution among the Saints in the Roman Church, that Elisha presides over the smiths, Blaise over the carders, Lucy over the tailors. But for a just censure of these trifles, see, if you please, in Sixtinus's Antibarbarus Biblicus, book 3, at this place, p. 462.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

MIHI AVTEM NIMIS HONORIFICATI SVNT AMICI TVI DEVS: NIMIS CONFORTATVS EST PRINCIPATVS EORVM) Οἱ φίλοι σου, ita verterunt רעיך

& fert quidem vox illum sensum. Sed alterum cogitationes tuae, quod loco huic magis convenire videtur: ut sensus sit, quam sunt sublimes supra me cogitationes tuae, quam nume- rosae sunt earum summae? Nam רָאשֵׁיהֶם quod Graeci vertunt αἱ ἀρχαὶ vertitur per ἀριθμὸν. Num. 1, 49. συλλογι- σμὸν Exod. 30, 12. Fatetur Grotius, magis convenire aliorum versionem COGITATIONES TUAE. Sed di- cere potius debebat, solam hanc versionem pro- bam esse. Vulgatam autem NULLATENUS congruere. Excusare Vulgatam voluit, ut & Grae- cam translationem, quasi sensum etiam illum ver- ba ferant. Quia non ignotum erat ipsi, quod Pa- pistae ex hoc loco invocationem Sanctorum proba- re conentur. Alphonsus a Castro advers. haeres. Eccius in Enchir. cap. 15. Costerus Jesuita in Ench. c. 12. Quod vero ineptissimum. Si enim maxime vox illa רֵעֶיךָ ita vertatur, amici tui, unde proba- bitur, per eos sanctos defunctos intelligendos, un- de ostendetur יָקְרוּ esse honorificari, & hoc rursus esse religiose coli? Et quid illud sibi vult, nimis con- fortatus est principatus eorum? Num id cum Coto- no eo accipiendum, quod Sancti defuncti hunc mundum administrent? unde forte illa inter San- ctos distributio in Romana Ecclesia, quod Eliseus praesit fabris, Blasius carminatoribus, Lucia sartori- bus. Sed justam nugamentorum istorum censu- ram vide sis in Antibar. Bibl. Sixtini libr. 3. ad h. l. p. 462.

## 139:18
Verse 18. I WILL COUNT THEM AND THEY SHALL BE MULTIPLIED ABOVE THE SAND) It is the future for the subjunctive: If I should count, namely those thoughts of yours, they will exceed the number like the sands.

Latin:

Vers. 18. DINUMERABO EOS ET SUPRA ARENAM MULTIPLICABUNTUR) Est futurum pro subjunctivo: Si numerem, nempe illas cogitationes tuas, numerum supera- bunt ut arenae.

## 140:1 Argument
PSALM 140. The practice and punishment of hypocrites.

Latin:

PSALM. CXL. Hypocritarum praxis, & poena.

## 140:3
Verse 4. THE POISON OF ASPS UNDER THEIR LIPS] Rom. 3, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VENENUM ADIPSUM SUB LABIIS EORUM] Rom. 3, 13.

## 140:9
Verse 10. THE HEAD OF THEIR CIRCUIT, THE LABOR OF THEIR OWN LIPS SHALL COVER THEM] רֹאשׁ signifies both head and poison. The sense will agree well with the preceding as follows: May the poison of those surrounding me, the work of their own lips, cover them. That is, may the calumnies by which they plot my destruction fall back upon themselves.

Bellarmine is therefore mistaken that the reading of the LXX Interpreters and the Vulgate is truer: THEIR CIRCUIT, than the Hebrew my circuit. He acknowledges that Jerome also read as it is in the Hebrew, because he rendered it, the bitterness of my guests. Junius, Piscator, and Mr. Dr. Gejer also understood it concerning poison, to which explanation verse 4 is favorable.

Latin:

Vers. 10. CAPUT CIRCUITUS EORUM, LABOR LABIORUM IPSORUM OPERIET EOS] רֹאשׁ & ca- put & venenum significat. Sensus superioribus bene con- gruet talis: Venenum circumbenientium me, opus labiorum ipsorum ipsos operiat. Id est, in ipsos recidant calumniae, qui- bus exitium mihi struunt.

FAllitur ergo Bellarm. quod lectio LXX. Interpp. & Vulgatae verior sit: CIRCUITUS EO- RUM, quam Ebraea circuitus mei. Agnoscit, Hie- ronymum etiam legisse, ut in Ebraeo est, quia red- didit, amaritudo convivarum meorum. De vene- no etiam intellexit Junius, Piscator, Dn. D. Gejer. cui explicationi favet v. 4.

## 140:10
Verse 11. THEY SHALL FALL UPON THEM COALS) May they fall, namely as they fell upon the Sodomites.

Latin:

Vers. 11. CADENT SUPER EOS CARBONES) Cadant, nempe ut ceciderunt super Sodomitas.

## 141:1 Argument
PSALM 141. A sacrifice of prayers.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLI. Sacrificium precum.

## 141:5
Verse 5. BUT LET NOT THE OIL OF THE SINNER ANOINT MY HEAD] The LXX seem to have read רָשָׁע for רֹאשׁ, and for יָנִי they seem to have read יְנַיֶּה. As we now read the Hebrew, this interpretation seems best: Let the righteous strike me (with his corrections:) and kindness (will be held by me:) let him rebuke me and (it will be as) the best oil: it will not break my head (it will not grieve me) indeed my prayer (namely to God will persist) in their evils: that is, while they speak evils to me. שֶׁמֶן רֹאשׁ here is the most excellent ointment, as in Cant. 4, 14. רָאשֵׁי בְשָׂמִים and in Ezekiel 27, 22. רֹאשׁ כָּל־בֹּשֶׂם the chief of spices.

It is a mere suspicion concerning the different reading of the LXX, such as also Capellus's regarding the last word of this verse, in which, however, Grotius did not wish to follow him, corrected by Buxtorf in his Vindications p. 645.

THEY SHALL HEAR MY WORDS FOR THEY HAVE BEEN ABLE: AS THE THICKNESS OF THE EARTH HAS BROKEN FORTH UPON THE EARTH.

There is no sense here. In the Hebrew, however, it is held far otherwise, whence Jerome translated it thus: They shall hear my words, for they are comely: as the farmer, when he cleaves the earth, &c. Compare the version of B. Luth. The Chaldean and Syrian: As the plowshare cleaving the earth, my bones are scattered.

Latin:

Vers. 5. OLEUM AUTEM PECCATORIS NE IMPINGUET CAPUT MEUM] Videntur LXX. pro רֹאשׁ legisse רָשָׁע, & pro יָנִי legisse יְנַיֶּה. Vt nos nunc Hebraeum legimus, vi- detur haec interpretatio optima: Contundat me justus (casti- gationibus suis:) & benignitas (a me habebitur:) increpet me & (erit ut) oleum optimum: non franget caput meum (non do- lebit mihi) imo oratio mea (nempe ad Deum perstabit) in malis eorum: id est, dum mala mihi dicent. שֶׁמֶן רֹאשׁ hic unguentum praestantissimum, ut Cant. 4, 14. רָאשֵׁי בְשָׂמִים & Ezechielis 27, 22. רֹאשׁ כָּל־בֹּשֶׂם praecipuum aro- matum.

MEra est suspicio de diversa lectione τῶν ó. qua- lis etiam Capellae circa vocem postremam hujus versus, in qua tamen Grotius ipsum sequi no- luit, castigata a Buxtorfio in vindiciis p. 645.

AUDIENT VERBA MEA QUONIAM POTUERUNT: SICUT CRASSITUDO TERRÆ ERUPTA EST SUPER TERRAM.

Nullus hic est sensus. In Ebr. autem longe aliter habetur, unde Hieronym. sic transtulit: Audient verba mea, quoniam decora sunt: sicut agricola, cum scindit terram, &c. Conf. B. Luth. versio. Chaldæus & Syrus; Sicut vomer scindens terram, dispersa sunt ossa.

## 142:1 Argument
PSALM CXLII. The lamentation of David from the cave.

WHEN HE WAS IN THE CAVE A PRAYER) So also in the Hebrew and in the Greek. The history which is in 1 Sam. 24 is represented.

Kimchi, Rashi, Genebrardus, and Coccejus wish for this to be looked to as well. Others refer it more correctly to the cave of Adullam, 1 Sam. 22: because in the cave of Engedi, Saul was in danger of his life rather than David.

Verse 1.

I CRIED WITH MY VOICE UNTO THE LORD.

Bellarmine, although he acknowledges that it must be accepted as being about David, on account of the inscription, nevertheless wishes it to pertain to Christ in a higher sense: and in the Roman Church the Psalm is sung on the day of Christ's passion, as if it were dealing with the guarding of Christ's body in the sepulcher, v. 8: But this is irrelevant, nor does any trace appear that it is dealing here with Christ, or with the liberation of Christ's body from the sepulcher, or of his soul from hell, as Bellarmine has in book 4 of Christ's soul, chapters 11 and 12. Nor is that custody, from which David seeks to be liberated, correctly understood by Origen and Cajetan as the binding of the soul in the body, but it is dealing solely here with David in the cave, as if shut up in a prison, concerning which Jansenius, Genebrardus, and Lorinus explain.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLII. Ejulatus Davidis ex antro.

CUM ESSET IN SPELUNCA ORATIO) Ita & in Hebræo & in Græco. Repræsentatur historia quæ est 1. Sam. 24.

EO etiam respici vult Kimchi, Rasche, Genebrardus, Coccejus. Rectius ad speluncam Odullam 1. Sam. 22. referunt alii: quia in spelunca Engeddi Saul potius in periculo vitæ fuit, quam David.

Vers. 1.

VOCE MEA AD DOMINUM CLAMAVI.

Bellarm. etsi agnoscat de Davide accipiendum esse, ob inscriptionem, tamen altiori sensu ad Christum pertinere vult: & in Romana Ecclesia canitur Psalmus die passionis Christi, ac si de custodia corporis Christi in sepulcro v. 8. ageretur: Sed hoc impertinens est, nec ullum apparet vestigium, quod de Christo hic agatur, aut de liberatione corporis Christi e sepulchro, aut animæ ex inferno, ut Bellarm. l. 4. de Christ. anim. habet cap. 11. 12. neque custodia illa, e qua liberari petit David, recte ab Origene & Cajetano de ligatione animæ in corpore accipitur, sed de Davide in spelunca, ceu in custodia concluso, unice hic agitur, quo de explicant Jansenius, Genebrardus, Lorinus.

## 142:4
Verse 5.

I LOOKED ON THE RIGHT HAND, AND BEHELD) Supply: on the left. I was looking in every direction, whether there was any helper for me: there was none.

But in the Hebrew text there is not, AND BEHELD, but AND BEHOLD, and indeed the preceding is also in the imperative mood: Look to the right: where supporters are accustomed to be (not to the left) and behold, so that you may know more accurately that there is no one who acknowledges me. Compare Lamentations 1:11. Therefore there is no need for any supplement.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

CONSIDERABAM AD DEXTRAM, ET VIDEBAM) Supple ad sinistram. Respectabam in omnem partem, num quis mihi esset adjutor: nemo erat.

Atqui in textu Ebræo non est, ET VIDEBAM, sed ET VIDE, imo & antecedens est imperativi modi: Considera ad dextram: ubi solent esse parastatæ (non ad sinistram) & vide, ut eo accuratius cognoscas, non esse qui agnoscat me. Conf. Thren. 1, 11. Nullo ergo opus supplemento.

BRING MY SOUL OUT OF PRISON) Out of this dungeon. Thus he calls the cave in which he was hiding.

The Papists therefore ineptly prove purgatory from this: See B. Meisner on purgatory, p. 144.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

EDUC DE CUSTODIA ANIMAM MEAM) De carcere hoc. Ita appellat specum in qua latebat.

## 143:1 Argument
PSALM 143. The desire for divine grace and the guiding Spirit.

WHEN ABSALOM HIS SON PERSECUTED HIM] The Greeks have appended this argument quite appropriately.

With the same ease that this is asserted, it is also rejected, because it is not found in the Hebrew.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLIII. Gratiæ divinæ & Spiritus ductoris desiderium.

QVANDO PERSEQVEBATUR EUM ABSOLOM FILIUS EJUS] Græci hoc argumentum satis convenienter apposuerunt.

Qua facilitate hoc asseritur, eadem etiam rejicitur, quia in Ebræo non habetur.

## 143:2
verse 2.

ENTER NOT INTO JUDGMENT WITH THY SERVANT, FOR NO LIVING MAN SHALL BE JUSTIFIED IN THY SIGHT.

This passage teaches that no one can be justified before God by their own righteousness, nor can anyone perfectly fulfill the law, for otherwise they would be justified by the law. Which David denies: therefore it is not to be maintained that here human righteousness is denied only in comparison to the perfection of God, as in Job 25:4.

This exception is Bellarmine's in book 4 of his work on Justification, and others'; likewise Lindanus in book 3 of his Panoplia, chapter 15, who says the meaning is that no man is just by that justice which is God's. But Jansenius himself not undeservedly rejects that answer. For it is a question of such an imperfection, on account of which a man is deservedly called into the judgment of God. But he is not called into judgment because he is not as just as God. And Jansenius teaches from the context that David is not comparing himself to God, but to the ferocity of his enemies, and is confessing that he has deserved evils, but is praying for pardon, because even if he is innocent before men, he is not so before God: as Estius, Genebrardus, and Lorinus also observe. And therefore the same Jansenius rightly noted that this phrase, 'not to enter into judgment with anyone,' does not signify a contention as to who is more just, but whether either one is just at all and in the due manner. Tirinus explains it thus: that there is no man who, during the whole time of his life, does not commit some sin. But if that explanation stands, no one will perfectly fulfill the law. For where there is sin, there is ἀνομία (lawlessness). But it is not the case that one can say that after conversion and justification the law can be fulfilled, for even in the reborn and justified, the flesh struggles against the spirit and resists the law of the mind (Gal. 5:17, Rom. 7:23), and all the saints freely confess that they are still far from the perfect fulfillment of the law, and therefore they seek the remission of sins (1 Kings 8:46, Job 9:2-3, Ps. 19:13, Ps. 32:6, Prov. 20:9, Isa. 64:6, Dan. 9:5, Jas. 3:2, 1 John 1:8). Who in this life, says Gregory the Great in Homily 22 on Ezekiel, can live without fault after faith, when John says: 'If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,' with whose words James agrees, saying, 'In many things we all offend.' If past sins were dismissed at the reception of faith, and yet after faith one declines into sins, what presumption of justice will we have, what hope of a lasting life? Estius brings forward many sayings of the ancients on this matter in 1 John 1:8, that there is no one who does not have sin, because he does not live without daily and frequent sins. Nor is there any reason for Bellarmine to say that everyone indeed has venial sins, but that those do not prevent a man from being just, nor are they against the law, but beside the law. For every sin is ἀνομία (lawlessness), and therefore against the law; and although venial sins do not hinder the justice of faith, because they are not imputed on account of accompanying repentance, they do nevertheless act against one's own justice, whether actual or habitual, so that it is not a perfect fulfillment of the law (for where there is sin, there is not a perfect fulfillment of the law); indeed, by their nature they are mortal sins and deserve death.

Latin:

vers. 2.

NON INTRES IN JUDICIUM CUM SERVO TUO, QUIA NON JUSTIFICABITUR IN CONSPECTU TUO ULLUS VIVENS.

Docet hic locus, neminem coram Deo justificari posse propria justitia, neque quenquam posse perfecte legem implere, alias enim per legem justificaretur. Quod negat David: non ergo statuendum, quod hic tantum denegetur homini justitia in comparatione ad perfectionem Dei, ut Jobi 25, 4.

quæ exceptio est Bellarmini l. 4. de Justific. & alio- rum; item Lindani l. 3. Panopl. c. 15. qui ait sensum esse, quod nullus hominum justus sit illa justitia, quæ Dei est. Sed eam responsionem reprobat ipse Janse- nius non immerito. De tali enim imperfectione agitur, ob quam merito in judicium Dei homo vo- catur. At non vocatur in judicium, quod non ita justus sit ut Deus. Et docet Jansenius e contextu Davidem non se Deo, sed hostium ferociæ comparare, & fateri mala promerita, sed precari veniam, quia etsi coram hominibus sit innocens, non tamen coram Deo: uti etiam Estius, Genebrardus & Lorinus observant. Ideoq; recte idem Janseniq notavit phrasin istam, non intrare cum aliquo in judicium, non significare con- tentionem, uter sit magis justus, sed an alteruter omni- no & modo debito justus sit? Tirinus ita explicat, nul- lum esse hominem, qui toto vitæ suæ tempore nullum admittat peccatum. Verum stante illa explicatio- ne nemo legem perfecte implebit. Ubi enim pec- catum, ibi ἀνομία. Non vero est, quod dicatur post conversionem & justificationem legem impleri pos- se, nam etiam in renatis & justificatis caro luctatur adversus spiritum & repugnat legi mentis Gal. 5, 17. Rom. 7, 23. & confitentur ultro omnes sancti, se pro- cul adhuc abesse a perfecta legis impletione, adeo- que remissionem peccatorum expetunt 1. Reg. 8, 46. Job. 9, 2. 3. Ps. 19, 13. Psal. 32, 6. Prov. 20, 9. Esa. 64, 6. Dan. 9, 5. Jac. 3, 2. 1. Joh. 1, 8. Quis in hac vita, in- quit Gregor. M. Hom. 22. super Ezech. valeat post fidem sine culpa vivere, cum Johannes dicat: si dixe- rimus, quia peccatum non habemus, nos seducimus, & veritas in nobis non est, cujus verbis Jacobus con- cordans ait, in multis offendimus omnes. Si pecca- ta præterita in fidei perceptione dimissa sunt, & adhuc post fidem ad peccata declinatur, quæ nobis erit præ- sumtio justitiæ, quæ spes vitæ permanentis? Estius mul- ta veterum dicta eam in rem adducit in 1. Joh. 1, 8. quod nemo sit, qui peccatum non habeat, quia non vi- vit sine quotidianis ac frequentibus peccatis. Neque est, quod dicat Bellarmin. Venialia peccata quidem omnes habere, sed illa non impedire, quo minus homo sit justus, neque esse contra legem, sed præter legem. Nam omne peccatum est ἀνομία, adeoque contra le- gem; & quamvis venialia peccata non impediant ju- stitiam fidei, quia non imputantur ob comitantem pœ- nitentiam, faciunt tamen adversus justitiam pro- priam, sive actualem, sive habitualem, quo minus ea perfecta sit legis impletio (ubi enim peccatum, ibi non est perfecta impletio legis) imo natura sua sunt peccata mortalia, & merentur mortem.

## 144:1 Argument
PSALM 144. The Lord is a stronghold and a fountain of blessing.

AGAINST GOLIATH) It is not in the Hebrew. But it was once in the Hexapla, and is now in the Greek which we use. David later celebrated the memory of that danger with this poem.

They are also found in the Arabic and Ethiopic; but Theodoret denies that they proceeded from the LXX. The Syrian understands it of Asaph, who killed the brother of Goliath. But whence will such things be taught? From verses 7, 8, and 21, something far different appears. For the enemies from whom he seeks to be delivered are designated as 'sons of the stranger' (whether that people be a stranger, or any foreigner whatsoever), whose mouth speaks vanity or lying, and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood. And that these things pertain to David now established in the kingdom and having gained victories against various enemies is gathered not obscurely from verse 1: 'Blessed be the Lord my rock, who trains my hands for conflict.' Verse 2: 'who subdued my people under me.' Vers. 10. You who have given salvation to kings, who have delivered David your servant from the evil sword; whence he exclaims with wonder: What is man, that you acknowledge him: the son of man, that you esteem him? vers. 3. which he indeed understands of himself, acknowledging his own unworthiness, but because he prophesied in the same words concerning Christ, the seed promised to him, and His exaltation Ps. 8, 5. there is no doubt but that he tacitly hints at the same time κατ' ἐπαίνεξιν or at least has embraced the Messiah in his mind, on account of whom all grace comes to us, which does come to us. Therefore it seems most akin to the truth that David composed this Psalm during the persecution of Absalom, who was the son of a foreign people, inasmuch as he was begotten from the daughter of Talmai, King in Geshur 2. Sam. 3:3, with whom other sons of strangers without doubt joined themselves and conspired; or if you understand 'strangers' with some, as Israelites degenerate and utterly alien from the virtue of their ancestors (which explanation is also that of B. Luther in the argument of this Psalm), were not Absalom and his accomplices truly such? The Dutch explain it of those who refused to acknowledge David as the genuine King, such as were indeed all those adhering to Absalom. Now, did not Absalom speak mere lies, did he not draw Israel to himself by mere falsehoods, was not his right hand a right hand of falsehood (2 Sam. 15:3, 4, 5, 6)? R. Obadiah agrees with our opinion, understanding this Psalm of the deliverance from Absalom, even though the same man also joins the rebellion of Sheba to the sedition of Absalom. But those who say that either the victory of the Maccabees against Antiochus with Theodoret, or the victory of Christ against the devil with Hilary, or the victory of the Church likewise against Satan with Augustine, or both the victory of David against Goliath literally and the victory of Christ and the Church against the devil spiritually with Bellarmine are described, depart from the words and the scope of the text.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXLIV. Dominus præsidium & fons benedictionis.

ADVERSVS GOLIATH) In Hebræo non est. Sed fuit olim in Hexaplis, & est nunc in Græco quo utimur. Memo- riam istius periculi hoc carmine postea celebravit David.

HAbentur & in Arabe, & Æthiope; Sed a LXX. profectum esse negat Theodoretes. Syrus de Asapho. qui fratrem Goliath interfecerit intelligit. Sed unde talia docebuntur? E v. 7. 8. & 21. longe a- liud apparet. Hostes enim, a quibus liberari ex- petit, designantur filii peregrini (sive peregrinus ille sit populus, sive alienigena quicunque) quorum os vanitatem seu mendacium loquitur, & dextra est dextra falsitatis. Et pertinere hæc ad Davidem jam in regno constitutum, & victoriis potitum ad- versus hostes varios haud obscure colligitur e v. 1. Benedictus sit Dominus rupes mea, qui assuefacit ma- nus meas ad conflictum. Vers. 2. qui subjecit populum meum mihi. Vers. 10. qui dedisti salvationem regi- bus, qui liberasti Davidem servum tuum a gladio malo; unde exclamat cum admiratione: Quid est homo, quod agnoscis eum: filius hominis, quod æstimas eum? vers. 3. quæ de sese intelligit quidem, indignitatem suam agnoscens, sed quia iisdem verbis vaticinatus est de Christo semine sibi promisso, ejusque exal- tatione Ps. 8, 5. non est dubium, quin tacite innuat simul κατ' ἐπαίνεξιν aut certe mente complexus fuerit Messiam, ob quem nobis omnis gratia obtin- git, quæ obtingit. Vero itaque maxime affine vi- detur, quod hunc Psalmum David composuerit in persequutione Absolomi, qui filius erat peregrini populi, utpote e filia Thalmai, Regis in Gesur pro- creatus 2. Sam. 3, 3. cum quo alii peregrinorum filii sine dubio sese conjunxerunt & conspirarunt; aut si peregrinos intelligas cum quibusdam, peregrinis si- miles Israelitas degeneres a majorum virtute pror- sus alienos (quæ explicatio etiam est B. Luther. in argumentum hujus Psalmi) annon vere tales Abso- lom cum complicibus suis? Belgæ de iis explicant, qui Davidem pro Rege genuino agnoscere detre- ctabant, quales utique erant omnes Absolomo ad- hærentes. Jam annon mendacia mera loquutus Absolom est, annon meris falsiloquiis ad se Israe- lem attraxit, annon dextra ejus dextra fuit falsita- tis 2. Sam. 15, 3. 4. 5. 6. Annuit nostræ sententiæ R. Obadias, de liberatione ab Absolomo Psalmum hunc intelligens, etsi etiam rebellionem Sebæ Sedi- tioni Absolomi idem jungat. Qui vero vel cum Theodoreto victoriam Maccabæorum adversus Antio- chum, vel cum Hilario victoriam Christi adversus diabolum, vel cum Augustino victoriam Ecclesiæ iti- dem adversus Satanam, vel cum Bellarm. tum victo- riam Davidis adversus Goliat ad literam, tum spiri- tualiter victoriam Christi & Ecclesiæ adversus diabo- lum describi ajunt, a verbis & scopo textus rece- dunt.

verse of the same.

## 144:13
Verse 13.

WHOSE SONS ARE AS NEW PLANTS IN THEIR YOUTH: THEIR DAUGHTERS ARE COMPOSED AND ADORNED AS THE LIKENESS OF A TEMPLE.

In the Critici Sacri, page 804, we said that this translation of the LXX and the Vulgate should be amended, and that Jerome expressed the Hebrew text more successfully in this manner: that our sons may be as a plant growing in their youth, our daughters as corners, etc. Not only do Pagninus, Campensis, Piscator, and Cocceius favor this explanation with their versions, but almost the common interpretation does as well, since this is held to be a vow and prayer of David, desiring the perpetuity of divine blessings. The rebellion of his son was greatly hindering this, and thus the happiness of the Lord's people, which was being not lightly endangered, both earthly and bodily, and especially spiritual and heavenly. For Bellarmine also concedes that the Hebrews interpret that אשר in this way, nor is that acceptance of it as ἵνα, 'that,' unusual in the sacred writings, for which matter Mr. D. Gejerus has cited Deut. 11:10, ch. 32:46, Ruth 3:1, Nehem. 8:15, 16, ch. 13:1. and that David in that affliction brought about by his degenerate son prayed then for his own house, and for the people of the Lord, a better lot, so that, being delivered from the same, he may see the happier increase of his sons and daughters, and may be able to enjoy the fruits of peace, which prosperity He Himself promised to those who fear the Lord, Psalm 128, 1. seqq. is by no means alien to the argument of the Psalm. Nor does the common interpretation suit the pronoun of the Hebrew text: in which OUR SONS, & OUR DAUGHTERS are held, and not indeed their sons and daughters. But if they are thought to be introduced boasting of earthly happiness, there will be need of an ellipsis besides, with the pronouns of the first person retained, which cannot be changed, whatever Bellarmine may pretend. Furthermore, Cocceius's interpretation concerning spiritual food and that by sheep are understood catechumens, by fat oxen those bearing the burdens of the Church, diverges too much from the letter of the text.

Latin:

Versus 13.

QUORUM FILII SICUT NOVELLÆ PLANTATIONES IN JUVENTUTE SUA: FI- LIÆ EORUM COMPOSITÆ CIRCUMOR- NATÆ UT SIMILITUDO TEMPLI.

In Critico Sacro pag. 804. diximus hanc LXX. & vulg. translationem emendandam esse, & Ebræ- um textum felicius expressisse Hieronymum h. m. ut sint filii nostri quasi plantatio crescens in adolescentia sua, filiæ nostræ quasi anguli, &c. Cui explicationi non tantum Pagninus, Campensis, Piscator, & Coc- cejus suis versionibus favent: sed communis fere interpretatio, quum habeatur hæc pro voto & pre- catione Davidis exoptantis perennitatem divina- rum benedictionum. Seditio filii multum inter- vertebat, adeoque felicitatem populi Domini, quæ non leviter periclitabatur, tum terrenam & corpo- ralem, tum imprimis spiritualem & cœlestem. Nam & Ebræos illud אשר ita interpretari largi- tur Bellarminus, nec insolens est ea acceptio in sa- cris pro ἵνα ut, in quam rem Dn. D. Gejerus ad- duxit Deut. 11, 10. cap. 32, 46. Ruth. 31, 1. Nehem. 8, 15. 16. cap. 31, 1. & Davidem in ista afflictione a degenere filio conciliata precatum esse tum domui suæ, tum populo Domini meliorem sortem, ut nempe liberatus ab eadem videat filiorum & fi- liarum suarum feliciora incrementa, & fructibus pacis gaudere possit, quam prosperitatem ipse pro- misit timentibus Dominum, Psalm. 128, 1. seqq. ab argumento Psalmi minime alienum est. Neque convenit vulgata interpretatio pronomini textus Ebræi: in quo FILII NOSTRI, & FILIÆ NO- STRÆ habentur, non vero filii, & filiæ eorum. Si autem introduci censeantur felicitatem terrenam jactantes, ellipsi insuper opus erit retentis prono- minibus primæ personæ, quæ mutari non possunt, quicquid prætendat Bellarminus. Cæterum Coc- ceji interpretatio de cibo spirituali & quod per oves Catechumeni, per boves obesos onera Eccle- siæ portantes intelligantur, a litera textus nimium divaricatur.

## 144:15
Vers. 15.

THEIR STOREHOUSES FULL, POURING FORTH FROM THIS INTO THAT) Thus the Greeks: ἐκ τᾶτε εἰς τᾶτο. That is, from kind to kind, as Aben-Ezra and David Kimchi interpret best here. The Chaldean prefers from year to year. For that pouring forth, in Hebrew it is, emitting, or bringing forth from itself.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

PROMTVARIA EORVM PLENA, ERVCTANTIA EX HOC IN ILLVD) Sic Græci: ἐκ τᾶτε εἰς τᾶτο. Id est, de specie in speciem, quomodo optime hic interpretantur Aben-Esdra & David Kimchi. Chaldæus mavult de an- no in annum. Pro illo eructantia, in Hebræo est, emittentia, sive de se edentia.

## 145:1 Argument
PSALM CXLV. The glorious and beneficent Lord, whom the eyes of all await.

IT IS Alphabetic by individual verses.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXLV. Dominus gloriosus & beneficus, quem omnium oculi expectant.

EST Alphabeticus per versus singulos.

## 145:9
Vers. 9. HIS MERCIES ARE OVER ALL HIS WORKS.

Hilary explains it thus: that it excels all the works of God: and the Scholastics dispute from that, how is mercy more excellent than all virtues? see Thomas and Cajetan in 2. 2. q. 30. art. 4. but these arise from ignorance of the Hebrew language: for there is no comparison held here, but על in or over; OVER all his works, as Jerome translates and Chrysostom and Augustine explain.

Latin:

Vers. 9. MISERATIONES EJUS SUPER OMNIA OPERA EJUS.

HIlarius ita exponit: quod excellat omnibus ope- ribus Dei: & disputant inde Scholastici, quomodo misericordia excellentior sit omnibus virtu- tibus? vid. Thomas & Cajet. in 2. 2. q. 30. art. 4. sed hæc oriuntur ex ignorantia Ebrææ linguæ: non enim hic habetur comparatio, sed על in vel super; IN omnia opera ejus, ut vertit Hieronym. & explicant Chrysost. & August.

## 145:13
Vers. 13.

THE LORD IS FAITHFUL IN ALL HIS WORDS, AND HOLY IN ALL HIS WORKS) From the Greek πιστὸς κύριος ἐν τοῖς λόγοις ἀυτῶ κὰι ὅσιος ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις ἀυτῶ. The Syrian and the Arab have the same. It is not to be doubted that this verse fell out of the Hebrew Codices by the fault of the scribes: for the verse that should begin with the letter Nun is missing. And that would have been: נאמן יהוה בדבריו וקדוש במעלליו How will those who order us to stand by the decrees of the Masoretes in all things answer to this?

The answer has already been sufficiently given by Buxtorf to Ludovicus Capellus, whom Grotius followed here, as in many other things. I have nothing to add: I will only transcribe the Buxtorfian response from Vindic. verit. Hebr. part. II. Cap. 2. p. 437, because the book is in the hands of few here. A double foundation is brought forward here, that the verse was omitted in Ps. 145, 1. because the order of the Alphabet requires a verse beginning with the letter Nun here. 2. That the LXX. and certain Interpreters express that verse. But those do not seem to me solid enough to undermine the Hebrew text. For we have also seen above that that order is not so strictly observed. Nor is it probable that this verse either fell out by chance or was expunged on purpose: it could not have happened by chance, because the error due to the interrupted series of the Alphabet would have been too manifest and easily detected. Why would it have been expunged on purpose, when there is nothing in it that could have offended the Jews or moved them to erase it? If the Septuagint had found it in their own or in another approved Codex, without doubt that exemplar would have become known to others also, or other similar exemplars would have existed elsewhere, and from that a various reading would have arisen in Hebrew books. But in this place nothing of the sort was ever seen or heard, or noted by the Masoretes. Therefore, someone else seems to have invented this verse and inserted it there to complete the Alphabet. That some others also acknowledge that verse is no wonder to me; because they all drew it from that Greek version, as being more recent. On the contrary, neither St. Jerome, nor Aquila, nor Theodotion, nor the Chaldean Paraphrast, nor the Masoretes, nor the Talmudists, nor any Hebrew Interpreters acknowledge it. Is it credible that St. Augustine had a different exemplar of the Hebrew Bibles than St. Jerome? I do not think so. And yet he acknowledges that verse; but this one does not. Kimchi writes thus: David composed this Psalm according to the alphabetical order, but he did not compose Nun: but we do not know why. Our Rabbis allegorize on this: Why, they say, is Nun not written? Because in that letter is the ruin of the enemies of the Israelites, just as it is written, the virgin of Israel has fallen, and shall rise no more, Amos 5, 2. It is pleasing to append here what Genebrardus, otherwise hostile to the Hebrew text, wrote about this matter in his commentaries: Because, he says, Nun was missing in the Hebrew, they (the LXX. Greeks, and the Latin) inserted a verse similar to the eighteenth, having changed צדיק just, into נאמן faithful, and ways into words, so that the Psalm might be whole and consist of its numbers, just as they had behaved in Psalm 36, verse 31. From which someone might think that the Hebrew Codices are defective. For while other verses follow the order of the letters, here the Nun is clearly skipped. I know that R. Solomon and the Talmudists have recourse to a reason and a mystery; namely, that the acrostich Nun was omitted, because through that letter the final overthrow of the children of Israel would have been expressed, when it is written in Amos 5, 'She has fallen, and the virgin of Israel shall not rise again' (i.e., the ten tribes). And so the Psalmist rather inverted it for the sake of a good omen, and through the Holy Spirit added, 'The Lord lifts up all who are falling' (נופלים). But that reason does not satisfy me. Wherefore Kimchi also prefers to confess that he does not know the cause; if there is any room for conjecture, I would prefer that the Psalmist, having conceived by divine inspiration the mystery of the reprobation of the Jews, and having recognized the oracles concerning it, wished indeed to sing what is expressed in this verse, that God is indeed faithful in His words and predictions: but that, being troubled, he passed over it; 'For I would wish,' he says, 'that this faithfulness and constancy did not have place and force in the rejection of my people, for whom I myself even wish to be anathema from God, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, whose is the adoption of sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the legislation, and the service, and the promises, and the Fathers, from whom will be Christ, etc.,' with the Apostle in Romans 9. And thus I would have thought that the LXX prophetically restored this verse, as they did many others, concerning which Jerome is therefore rightly in his second preface to the book of Chronicles. The LXX added some things, either for the sake of elegance or by the authority of the Holy Spirit. For thus the contemplation of the Talmudists is confirmed at the same time, and the prophetic faculty of our interpreters is established, who in turn may have had it by tradition that this acrostich of the Psalmist was to be completed by the context of the words. So far he. But what is to be thought of that opinion, which attributes divine authority to the LXX interpreters, we have explained at length in the Critico Sacro. Lorinus and Cajetanus admit that there was no reason here why the Jews should erase these words, but rather why they should insert them, because they love such testimonies about the faithfulness of God in keeping promises, so that they may foster their own foolish hopes about the restoration of a temporal kingdom. And therefore Lorinus thinks that either the LXX or some other interpreter added this verse out of untimely solicitude, or rather repeated it by tautology, for it exists in verse 17.

of this Psalm, except that an insipid interpreter has placed נאמן here for צדיק. But the reasoning is invalid, as if in those acrostic Psalms it were not necessary for any of the Hebrew consonants to be missing. See Psalm 25, and you will see three consonants missing: ב. ו. ק. In Psalm 33, ו is missing; in 37, ע. And who shall give a law to the Holy Spirit, that wherever He begins with acrostic verses, He may not omit or transpose any consonant at all at the beginning of individual verses? As B. Hülseman does here. Furthermore, as to the argument of the Psalm, the opinion of Hilary, Augustine, B. Luther, B. Cramer, and others pleases me, that this treats of Christ the King; for whose sake it is helpful to bring forward some things from the argument of this Psalm by our B. Luther: It is, he says in Vol. III, Witeb. Lat. f. 435, a very excellent thanksgiving for the kingdom of Christ, which God was about to raise up in that people. For on account of Christ that whole people was chosen from the beginning before all nations, the Law was given, the whole Mosaic worship was established, etc. And this Psalm strongly urges that highest and most excellent good work, the chief and most grateful worship of God, which the first table demands, namely, the sacrifice of praise. For it proclaims with magnificent words the power of God and His infinite mercy, which is over all His works. And the whole Psalm is a notable rhetoric of the Holy Spirit, and an amplification through various affections and ornaments of words and sentences of the first commandment of the Decalogue, and of that voice, I am the Lord your God. And it desires that men should know the kingdom of Christ, so that, as it says, your power and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom may be made known to the sons of men, that is, that it may be made known through the Gospel that there is a liberation from the power of the devil, from eternal death, from sin, etc. than through faith in the word of mercy and grace granted to us in Christ. And afterwards: But this which he says in verse 14 properly pertains to the kingdom of Christ, which raises up the crushed, lifts up all the fallen. For Christ is that King of the afflicted, the poor, the fallen, justifying sinners, raising the dead, etc., through whom God is appeased toward us, hears us paternally, does all the will of those who fear Him, feeds and clothes those whom the world hates. He guards and defends against the gates of hell, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

FIDELIS DOMINVS IN OMNIBVS VERBIS SVIS, ET SANCTVS IN OMNIBVS OPERIBVS EJVS) Ex Græco πιστὸς κύριος ἐν τοῖς λόγοις ἀυτῶ κὰι ὅσιος ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔργοις ἀυτῶ. Idem habent & Syrus & Arabs. Non est dubi- tandum, quin versus hic in Hebræis Codicibus librariorum culpa exciderit: nam deest versus qui à littera Nun incipiat. Is autem fuerit: נאמן יהוה בדבריו וקדוש במעלליו Quomodo ad hoc respondebunt, qui nos jubent per omnia Masoretarum stare decretis?

Responsum jam satis est a Buxtorffio Ludo- vico Capello, quem hic, ut in aliis multis, sequutus est Grotius. Non habeo quod addam: Solum re- sponsionem Buxtorffianam e Vindic. verit. Hebr. part. II. Cap. 2. p. 437. quia liber in paucorum ma- nibus hic versatur, adscribam. Duplex hic funda- mentum affertur, quod versus sit omissus in Ps. 145, 1. quod ordo Alphabeti versum a littera Nun inci- pientem hic requirat. 2. Quod LXX. & quidam In- terpretes eum versum exprimant. At ista mihi non videntur solida satis ad textum Hebræum labefa- ctandum. Nam supra quoque vidimus, ordinem illum non ita stricte observari. Nec est probabile, vel casu hunc versum excidisse, vel studio expun- ctum esse: casu fieri non potuit, quia error ob in- terruptam seriem Alphabeti nimis manifestus, & facile deprehensus fuisset. Studio cur expunctus esset, cum nihil in eo sit, quod Judæos offendere, vel ad eum eradendum permovere potuisset? Si Se- ptuaginta vel in suo, vel in alio probato Codice eum invenissent, procul dubio illud exemplar aliis quo- que innotuisset, vel ei similia alia exemplaria alibi etiam extitissent, & inde varia in libris Hebraicis lectio orta fuisset. At in hoc loco nihil tale un- quam visum vel auditum, vel a Masorethis nota- tum. Itaque aliquis alius hunc versum videtur fin- xisse, & ibi inseruisse, ad Alphabetum complendum. Quod alii nonnulli illum versum quoque agno- scunt, non est apud me mirum; Quia ex Græca illa versione illi omnes eum hauserunt, tanquam recen- tiores. Contra est, quod nec D. Hieronymus, nec Aquila, nec Theodotion, nec Paraphrastes Chaldæus, nec Masorethæ, nec Talmudici, nec ulli Interpretes Hebræi eum agnoscunt. An credibile est, S. Augusti- num aliud exemplar Hebræorum Bibliorum ha- buisse, quam D. Hieronymum? Non puto. Et ta- men ille versum istum agnoscit; hic vero non. Kimchi scribit sic? David composuit hunc Psalmum secundum ordinem Alphabeticum, sed non composuit Nun: nescimus autem quare. Rabbini nostri super hoc allegorizant: Quare, inquiunt, non est scriptum Nun? Quia ei litteræ inest ruina hostium Israelita- rum, sicut scriptum est נפלה cecidit, & non addet surgere virgo Israelis Amos. 5, 2. Placet hic appo- nere, quæ Genebrardus, textui Hebræo alias infen- sus, hac de re scripsit in suis commentariis: Quia, inquit, desiderabatur Nun in Hebræo, interfuerunt (LXX. Græci, & Latinus) versum similem decimo octavo, mutato צדיק justus, in נאמן fidelis, & viis in verbis, ut Psalmus esset integer, ac constaret suis nu- meris, quomodo se gesserant Psal. 36. vers. 31. Ex quo aliquis putaret Codices Hebraicos esse mancos. Cum enim alii versus sequantur ordinem literarum, hic Nun plane transilitur. Scio R. Salomonem & Tal- mudicos recurrere ad rationem & mysterium; præ- termissum videlicet acrostichon Nun, quod per illam literam expressa fuisset extrema filiorum Israel ever- sio, quando scriptum Amos 5. נפלה & non adjiciet ut resurgat virgo Israel (i. e. decem tribus.) Itaque Psalten invertisse potius bene ominandi causa, ac per Spiritum Sanctum subjecisse, allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt (נופלים) Verum illa ratio mihi non satisfacit. Quare & Kimchi se nescire causam confiteri mavult; Si locus sit aliquis conjecturæ, mal- lem, Psalten concepto divinitus reprobationis Judæo- rum mysterio, & agnitis de ea oraculis, voluisse qui- dem canere, quod hoc versu exprimitur, Deum fide- lem quidem esse in suis verbis, & prædictis: at pertur- batum prætercurrisse; Quoniam vellem, inquit, ne hæc fidelitas & constantia haberet locum & vim, in mei populi rejectione, pro quo vel optem ego ipse esse anathema a Deo, qui sunt cognati mei secundum car- nem, qui sunt Israelitæ, quorum adoptio est filiorum, & gloria, & testamenta, & Legislatio, & obsequium, & promissa, & Patres, e quibus erit Christus &c. cum Apostolo ad Rom. 9. Atque ita LXX. versum hunc putaverim prophetice restituisse, ut pleraque alia, de quibus proinde recte Hieronymus secunda præfatione in librum Paralipomenon. LXX. addiderunt aliqua, vel ob decoris gratiam, vel ob Spiritus Sancti au- ctoritatem. Nam sic confirmatur Talmudicorum contemplatio simul, & stabilitur nostrorum Interpre- tum prophetica facultas, qui rursum per traditionem habere potuerunt, Psaltis acrostichon hoc verborum contextu esse perficiendum. Hactenus ille. Quid vero de sententia ista, quæ auctoritatem divinam LXX. Interpretibus tribuit, sentiendum sit, expo- suimus prolixe in Critico Sacro. Fatentur Lorinus & Cajetanus, hic nullam fuisse causam, cur Judæi verba ista eraderent, sed potius ut infererent, quia amant ejusmodi testimonia de fide Dei in servan- dis promissis, ut ineptas suas spes, de instauratione regni temporalis foveant. Ideoque censet Lorinus, sive LXX. seu alium quendam inrerpretem ex in- tempestiva sollicitudine adjecisse hunc versum, vel potius repetivisse per tavtologiam, extat enim v. 17.

hujus Psalmi, nisi quod insulsus, quidam interpres pro צדיק hic posuit נאמן. Invalida vero ratio est, quasi in Psalmis illis acrostichis non oporteat de- esse ullam ex consonis Ebraicis. Vide Psal. 25. & vi- debis deesse tres consonas ב. ו. ק. in Pf.33.deest ו. in 37. ע. Et quis legem dabit Spiritui S. ut ubicunque cæpit a versibus acrostichis nullam omnino consonam initio singulorum versuum vel omittat vel transpo- nat? ut hic B. Hülseman. Cæterum quod ad Psal- mi argumentum, placet Hilarii, Augustini, B. Lu- theri, B. Crameri & aliorum sententia, quod hic de Christo Rege agatur; cujus gratia quædam ex ar- gumento hujus Psalmi B. Lutheri nostri adducere juvat: Est, inquit T. III. Witeb. Lat. f. 435. valde egregia Gratiarum actio, pro regno Christi, quod Deus in illo populo suscitaturus erat. Nam propter Christum totus ille populus ab initio præ omnibus gen- tibus est electus, Lex data, totus Mosaicus cultus constitutus &c. Et hic Psalmus valde urget sum- mum illud & excellentissimum bonum opus, præ- cipuum & gratissimum cultum Dei, quem exigit pri- ma tabula, scilicet sacrificium laudis. Magnificis enim verbis prædicat Dei potentiam, & infinitam misericordiam, quæ est super omnia opera ejus. Et totus Psalmus est insignis Rhetorica Spiritus Sancti, & amplificatio per varios affectus, & ornamenta verborum & sententiarum primi præcepti decalogi, & illius vocis, Ego Dominus Deus vester, Et optat, ut regnum Christi homines cognoscant, ut nota, inquit, fiat filiis hominum potentia tua & gloria magnificen- tiæ regni tui, id est, ut notum fiat per Evangelium, quod non sit liberatio a potestate diaboli, ab æterna morte, a peccato &c. quam per fidem in verbum mise- ricordiæ & gratiæ nobis donatæ in Christo. Et postea: Hoc autem quod versu 14. dicit, proprie pertinet ad regnum Christi, quod erigit elisos, allevat omnes lapsos. Nam Christus est Rex ille afflictorum, paupe- rum, lapsorum, justificans peccatores, suscitans mor- tuos &c. per quem Deus placatus est nobis, exaudit nos paterne, facit omnem voluntatem timentium se, pascit & vestit eos, quos mundus odit. Custodit & de- fendit adversus portas inferorum. &c.

## 146:1 Argument
PSALM CXLVI. The works of the magnificence and beneficence of the Lord.

ALLELUIA] This word was as it were the stimulus of those singing in the highest joy. Tobit 13, v. 20. Rev. 19, verses 1, 3, 4, 6.

OF HAGGAI AND ZECHARIAH] This also is from the Greek. And it was in the Hexapla.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLVI. Opera magnificentiæ, & beneficientiæ Domini.

ALLELVJA] Hæc vox erat velut suscibulum cantantium in summa lætitia. Tobiæ 13. v. 20. Apoc. 19. verf. 1. 3. 4. 6.

AGGÆI ET ZACHARIÆ] Hoc quoque ex Græco. Et fuit in Hexaplis.

## 146:7
Verse 7.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

## 146:8
THE LORD LOOSES THE PRISONERS; THE LORD ENLIGHTENS THE BLIND: THE LORD RAISES UP THE CRUSHED] These wonderfully agree with the times of Christ: for those are called prisoners who are held by diseases. Luke 13:16. For crushed in Hebrew it is bowed down, such as are the paralytics, likewise the woman who was bent over, Luke 13:11, and others.

Similarly, Grotius understands these things as predicted of Christ in his annotations on Matthew 11:4. While he otherwise corrupts the prophecies concerning the Messiah that sound with the suffrage of all, he transfers this one, which does not treat of the advent of Christ, to a foreign sense by dragging the words. Genebrardus and Lorinus even call it a dream and delirium, when the Rabbis accept these things concerning the infernal shackles to be loosed at the time of the Messiah. The same must also be held concerning the gloss of the Papists, by which they snatch those things away to a liberation from Purgatory. But what Bellarmine himself explains in his commentary on this passage concerning the shackles of evil concupiscence: and the parallels teach what kind of shackles and what kind of loosening are understood. Psalm 79:11, Psalm 102:21, Psalm 107:14.

Isa. 61:1. Cf. Psalm 147:3. See what we said on Matthew 11, v. 4.

Latin:

DOMINVS SOLVIT COMPEDITOS; DOMINVS ILLVMINAT CÆCOS: DOMINVS ERIGIT ELISOS] Mire hæc congruunt in Christi tempora: nam compediti di- cuntur, qui morbis tenentur. Luc. 13, 16. Pro elisos in He- bræo est curvatos, quales sunt παραλυτικοὶ, item ἡ συγκύπ- τουσα Luc. 13, 11. & alii.

Similiter hæc de Christo intelligit prædicta Gro- tius in annot. ad Matth. 11, 4. Quum alias vati- cinia de Messia omnium suffragio sonantia corrum- pat, hoc, quod de adventu Christi non agit, verbis etiam in alienum sensum pertractis eo transfert. Somnium etiam & delirium vocant Genebrardus, & Lorinus, cum Rabbini hæc de compedibus inferna- libus tempore Messiæ solvendis accipiunt. Idem etiam habendum de Pontificiorum glossa, qua illa ad liberationem e Purgatorio abripiunt. Quæ vero Bellarminus ipse in comment. ad h. l. exponit de compedibus concupiscentiæ malæ: & parallela fatis docent, quales compedes, qualisve solutio intelli- gantur. Psalm. 79, 11. Psalm. 102, 21. Psal. 107, 14.

Esa. 61, 1. Conf. Psal. 147, 3. Vid. quæ ad Matth. 11. v. 4. diximus.

## 147:1 Argument
PSALM CXLVII. Divine providence in nature and in the Church.

Verse 1. BUILDING JERUSALEM HE WILL GATHER THE DISPERSIONS OF ISRAEL] It agrees very well with the times of Nehemiah.

Although it may agree with the times of Nehemiah, and indeed with others, before and after the birth of Christ, it does not however agree with the LXX, with which the Arab, Syrian, and Ethiopian versions concur, as their inscription has it, Ἀλληλούϊα Ἁγ- γαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου; either the Psalm must be vindicated for these Prophets, or it must be restricted to their times, whether as a prophecy or as a hymn, since such an inscription is found neither in the authentic text, nor in the Targum, nor in the Vulgate; although we do not deny that the Psalmist, having foreseen the time and the benefit of the restoration of the people by a prophetic spirit, included it among those things for which Hallelujah is to be sung. v. 2. For it is a general exhortation and thanksgiving, as has been rightly observed by the blessed Luther and others.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLVII. Providentia divina in natura, & in Ecclesia.

Vers. 1. ÆDIFICANS JERUSALEM DISPERSIONES ISRAELIS CONGREGABIT] Optime congruit in tempo- ra Nehemiæ.

ETsi congruat Nehemiæ temporibus imo & aliis, ante & post Christum natum, non tamen cum LXX. quibus consonant Arabs, Syrus, & Æthiops, ut habet eorum inscriptio, Ἀλληλούϊα Ἁγ- γαίου καὶ Ζαχαρίου, vel his Prophetis vindicandus est Psalmus, vel ad tempora eorum seu ut vaticinium, seu ut hymnus restringendus, siquidem talis inscri- ptio nec in textu authentico, nec in Thargum, nec in vulgata reperiatur; Etsi non diffiteamur, quod Psaltes tempus, & beneficium reductionis populi prævisum spiritu Prophetico etiam inter ea, ob quæ Hallelujah cantandum est, comprehenderit. v. 2. Est enim generalis parænesis, & gratiarum actio, ut recte B. Luthero, aliisque observatum.

## 147:10
Vers. 10. NOR IN THE LEGS OF A MAN WILL HE TAKE PLEASURE] He does not care for swift runners.

Our Lord Dr. Gejerus explained these things more correctly: that God is not moved by the strength of men to love one more than another, and always to employ the same person for great tasks in preference to others who are weaker. Cf. Deut. 7, 7; 9, 4. And he observed that the legs of a man are joined with horses, because both of these are wont to be the chief defenses of earthly kings in wars, for which they also take the greatest care.

Latin:

Vers. 10. NEC IN TIBIIS VIRI BENEPLACITVM ERIT EI] Non curat celeres cursores.

Rectius hæc exposuit Dn. D. Gejerus noster: Deum non moveri hominum robore, ut unum diligat præ altero, eundemque semper ad grandia adhibeat ne- gotia præ aliis infirmioribus. Conf. Deut. 7, 7. c. 9, 4. & conjungi crura viri equis observavit, quia ambo hæc Regum mundanorum præcipua solent esse in bellis præsidia, pro quibus etiam vel maxime curam gerunt.

## 147:20
Vers. 20. HE HATH NOT DEALT SO WITH ANY NATION.

That is, with none. From this, Calvinists gather their absolute decree regarding the preterition of the greater part of mankind. But besides the fact that these words sound only in a comparative sense—He did not deal SO—from which an absolute preterition cannot be concluded, the statement of Augustine has its place: He did it, but He did not do it thus: this economy can be referred partly to the consequent will of God, from which it does not derogate from the universal calling according to the antecedent will (see the blessed Aegidius Hunnius, Tom. I. oper. f. 802), and partly to the free, yet just, dispensation of grace, without, however, an absolute preterition of others. For although He did not deal SO with other nations as He did with the Jewish people, in whom He had His seat, His hearth, and His fire, He did not however exclude other nations, but through His people, and indeed in their Fathers, He called them—not only in Adam after the fall the whole human race, in Noah after the flood the whole new world, just as He deigned to call the whole world again in the Apostles after the resurrection of Christ—but He also invited all other nations to the enjoyment of grace, blessing, and salvation in Abraham and other Patriarchs through the promise made to them in Gen. 12, 3; 22, 18, etc. and the sacrament of circumcision, from which foreigners and those bought with money were not excluded (Gen. 17), as also through instruction and the preaching of the word among the Philistines, in Egypt, and in other places of their sojourning; to which were added later the solemn invitations of all nations (Ps. 9, 12; 33, 8; 49, 2; 57, 10; 66, 1; 77, 1; 116, 1 ff.; 117, 1; 126, 2. Cf. Ps. 126, 2) and the sermons of the Prophets directed to the nations and delivered among the nations, as well as the examples of those who were eminent among the nations, such as are recounted: Melchizedek, Abimelech (Gen. 20), Ephron, the King in Gerar (Gen. 26), the King of Egypt in the time of Joseph, Job the Idumean, Jethro the Midianite, the Kenites, the Gibeonites, the Nethinim, the Queen of Sheba, Naaman the Syrian, along with a notable multitude of those who from Egypt with the Israelites departed, or afterwards joined themselves to the same as proselytes: for whose sake laws were specifically enacted, Lev. 17. verse 8. Num. 15. verse 15. just as also a specific court was ordained for the Gentiles at Jerusalem: Finally, the proclamations and public edicts of the most powerful Monarchs and Kings concerning the worship of the one God, Nebuchadnezzar, Darius the Mede, Cyrus, Darius Hystaspis, Artaxerxes Longimanus, in Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah: the translation of the Bibles into the Greek language under Ptolemy Philadelphus, and others, and then subsequently into other languages as well: concerning which see what we have said in Triga selectarum Exercitationum Exerc. 1. on John 8. v. 58. Th. 59. Add to these the most celebrated fame of the Israelite Church and the Jerusalem temple; on account of the miracles performed among the people of God, especially those which were done in the sun in the time of Joshua and Hezekiah, which could not but be notorious to the whole world; through which those who rejoiced only in the book of Nature and of the creature could altogether be led to the Church: so that no one has cause to complain that he was excluded or passed over by an absolute decree, since neither is preterition nor pre-damnation ever attributed in the Holy Scriptures to the simple good pleasure of God, but to the unbelief of men.

Latin:

Vers. 20. NON FECIT TALITER OMNI NATIONI.

Id est, nulli. Colligunt inde Calvin. suum ab- solutum decretum in præteritione maximæ partis hominum. Sed præterquam quod hæc comparate tantum sonent, non fecit TALITER, unde abso- luta præteritio concludi non potest, sed dictum Augustini locum habet: fecit, sed non fecit sic: refer- ri ista οἰκονομία partim potest ad voluntatem Dei consequentem, unde vocationi universali juxta vo- luntatem antecedentem non derogat (vid. B. Ægid. Hunn. Tom. I. oper. f. 802.) partim ad liberam, ju- stam tamen gratiæ dispensationem, citra vero ab- solutam præteritionem aliorum. Quamvis enim non ITA fecerit aliis nationibus, uti populo Judai- co, in quo sedem suam, focum & ignem suum ha- buit, non tamen exclusit alias nationes, sed per po- pulum suum, imo in Patribus eorum easdem voca- vit, non solum in Adamo post lapsum totum genus humanum, in Noacho post diluvium totum mun- dum novum, uti in Apostolis post resurrectionem Christi orbem universum iterum vocare dignatus est, sed invitavit etiam omnes alias gentes ad gratiæ, benedictionis, & salutis fruitionem in Abrahamo aliisque Patriarchis per promissionem ipsis factam Gen. 12, 3. c. 22, 18. &c. & circumcisionis sacramentum, a quo non excludebantur alienigenæ & emtitii Gen. 17. ut & per informationem & verbi præconium apud Philistæos, in Ægypto, aliisque peregrinationis ipsorum locis; quibus postmodum accessere so- lemnes invitationes omnium gentium Psal. 9, 12. 33, 8. 49, 2. 57, 10. 66, 1. 77, 1. 116, 1. seqq. 117, 1. 126, 2. Conf. Pf. 126, 2. & conciones Prophetarum ad gentes directæ, & inter gentes habitæ, nec non exempla eo- rum, qui inter gentes eminuere, quales recensentur Melchisedech, Abimelech Gen. 20. Ephrom, Rex in Gerar Gen. 26, Rex Ægypti tempore Josephi, Job Idumæus, Jethro Midianita, Kenæi, Gabaonitæ, Na- thinæi, Regina Sabæ, Naaman Syrus, cum insigni eorum multitudine, qui ex Ægypto cum Israelitis egressi, aut iisdem ceu proselyti postmodum se ad- junxere: quorum causa peculiariter leges sancitæ Lev. 17. verf. 8. Num. 15. verf. 15. quemadmodum & atrium peculiare gentibus Hierosolymis ordina- tum: Denique programmata, & edicta publica Mo- narcharum & Regum potentissimorum de cultu unius Dei, Nebucadnezaris, Darii Medi, Cyri, Darii Hystaspis, Artaxerxis Longimani, in Daniele, Esdra, & Nehemia: translatio Bibliorum in linguam Græ- cam sub Ptolemæo Philadelpho, & aliis, tum dein- ceps in alias etiam linguas: de quibus vid. quæ dixi- mus in Triga selectarum Exercitationum Exerc. 1. ad Joh. 8. v. 58. Th. 59. Adde hisce famam Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ & templi Hierosolymitani celebratissi- mam; ob miracula in populo Dei patrata, imprimis quæ in sole tempore Josuæ & Ezechiæ facta sunt, to- tique orbi non poterant non esse notoria; per quam illi, qui solo Naturæ, & creaturæ libro gaudebant, deduci omnino poterant ad Ecclesiam: ut nemo conqueri habeat, se absoluto decreto exclusum, aut bræteritum, siquidem nec simplici Dei beneplacito vel præteritio vel prædamnatio uspiam in S. literis tribuatur, sed hominum incredulitati.

## 148:1 Argument
PSALM CXLVIII. Choirs of creatures praising God.

Latin:

PSALMUS CXLVIII. Chori creaturarum Deum laudantes.

## 148:5
Ver. 5. ALL WATERS THAT ARE ABOVE THE HEAVENS) For even this lowest air is heaven to the Hebrews. See Gen. 1, 7.

BUT we have taught in Tom. III. System. Theol. that neither here, nor in Genesis, is the air designated by the word heaven, but the firmament, and that the super-celestial waters are asserted in both places. The arguments brought forward there can be read. R. Aben-Ezra seems to give assent to the Waters above the heavens, noting this: The globe of Waters is the boundary of the superior world, in which he (the Psalmist) begins from the principal (creature, the Angels,) and concludes in the less principal; but it is the contrary in the inferior world.

Ver. same. HE COMMANDED AND THEY WERE CREATED) All things which have now been named. Even the Angels: contrary to what certain Rabbis think. Therefore in the Nicene Synod it was added: creator of things visible and invisible.

Latin:

Vers. 5. AQVÆ OMNES QVÆ SVPRÆ COELOS SVNT) Nam etiam aër hic infimus, cœlum Hebræis. Vid. Gen. 1, 7.

AT neque hic, neque in Genesi aërem, sed firma- mentum voce cœli designari, & aquas supra- cœlestes utrobique adseri docuimus Tom. III. Sy- stem. Theol. Argumenta adducta ibi legi poterunt. Assensum præbere videtur R. Aben - Ezra ad Aquas supra cœlos hæc annotans: Globus Aquarum est limes seculi superioris, in quo incipit (Psaltes) à prin- cipali (creatura, Angelis,) & in minus principali concludit; sed est e contrario, in seculo inferiori.

Vers. eod. IPSE MANDAVIT ET CREATA SVNT) Omnia quæ jam nominata sunt. Etiam Angeli: contra quam sentiunt Rabbini quidam. Ideo in Nicena Synodo additum est: creatorem visibilium & invisibilium.

## 149:1 Argument
PSALM CXLIX. Exultation of the Church in Christ the King and avenger.

Latin:

PSALM. CXLIX. Exultatio Ecclesiæ in Christo Rege & vindice.

## 149:2
Ver. 2. CHILDREN OF ZION.

This is, inhabitants; as Ef. 11, 14. Children of the East, that is, inhabitants of the East, or Eastern peoples. Ez. 16, 26. children, i.e., inhabitants of Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 2. FILII SION.

HOc est, incolæ; ut Ef. 11, 14. Filii Orientis, id est, incolæ Orientis, seu Orientales populi. Ez. 16, 26. filii, h. e. incolæ Ægypti.

## 149:5
Ver. 5. THE SAINTS SHALL EXULT IN GLORY.

The Jesuit Coturius drew this to the deceased Saints, so that from the following, two-edged swords in their hands to execute vengeance upon the nations, he might teach that they are presidents and governors of human affairs, and on that account to be invoked. Similarly Bellarmine, who likewise in his commentary on this place explains these things not of the modern presidency of the Saints, but of the judicial power by which they will strike their persecutors on the last day. In

Latin:

Vers. 5. EXULTABUNT SANCTI IN GLORIA.

Ad Sanctos defunctos traxit Coturius Jesuita, ut e sequentibus gladii ancipites in manibus eorum ad faciendam vindictam in nationibus, doceat eos esse præsides & gubernatores rerum humanarum, eoque nomine invocandos. Similiter Bellarminus, qui iti- dem in comment. ad h. l. non de moderno Sancto- rum præsidio, sed de potestate judiciaria, qua in die novissimo persequutores suos ferient, hæc explicat. In

## 149:8
Verse 8. TO BIND KINGS IN THEIR FETTERS) As was done to Adonibezek, Jud. 1, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 8. AD ALLIGANDOS REGES IN EORVM COMPEDIBVS) Vt factum Adonibeseco Jud. 1, 7.

## 149:9
Verse 9. TO EXECUTE UPON THEM THE WRITTEN JUDGMENT) A similitude taken from sentences which were accustomed to be recited after being written down. God is said to write down what He decrees. Jude 4, Rev. 13, 8, 20, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 9. VT FACIANT IN EIS JVDICIVM CON- SCRIPTVM) Similitudo sumta ex sententiis, quæ descri- ptæ recitari solebant. Deus describere dicitur, quod decer- nit. Judæ 4. Apoc. 13, 8. 20, 15.

## 150:1 Argument
PSALM 150. The cause and instruments of divine praise.

PRAISE THE LORD IN HIS HOLY PLACES) In His sanctuary: that is, in the temple. He rightly corrects the Vulgate here, which is snatched away by Papists for the invocation of Saints, concerning which Sixtinus Amama, Antibarb. page 568, may be consulted. Since we have Grotius agreeing here, we do not wish to cling to those. Estius and Jansenius also agree, as does Bellarmine himself: Praise the Lord in His holy places, that is, O you elect and holy ones, praise the Lord dwelling in the heavenly sanctuary. For the Hebrew word Chodes properly signifies holiness and a sanctuary. Therefore, literally, by the word in His holy places, it seems that the heavenly sanctuary must be understood, which Heb. 9 calls the holy places. So he.

Verse same. PRAISE HIM IN THE FIRMAMENT OF HIS POWER. Because of the expanse of His strength, that is, the expanded strength which is expended and diffused upon all created things, according to the interpretation of Glassius, l. 3. Phil. S. p. 26. It is taken more simply as an explanation of the previous clause: or if that is understood of the sanctuary of the Church, this may be explained of heaven with Osiander; celebrate God dwelling in the heavens, which He created to show us His immense power. For thus the word רקיע is taken in the scriptures everywhere, Gen. 1, v. 6, 7, 8, 14, 15, 17, Ps. 19, v. 1, Is. 1, 22, Dan. 12, 3, etc., namely nominally, and of heaven or the air, but never participially, of some other thing diffusing itself, or diffused.

Latin:

PSALM. CL. Laudis divinæ causa & instrumenta.

LAVDATE DOMINVM IN SANCTIS EJVS) In sanctuario ipsius: id est, in templo. MErito hic corrigit vulgatam, quæ a Papistis ad Sanctorum invocationem abripitur, de quo conferri poterit Sixtinus Amama, Antibarb. pag. 568. Quum habeamus Grotium hic consentientem, in- hærere istis nolumus. Consentit & Estius, ac Janse- nius, ut & Bellarm. ipse: Laudate Dominum in San- ctis ejus, id est, o vos electi & sancti laudate Domi- num in sanctuario cœlesti habitantem. Nam vox Hebrea Chodes sanctitatem proprie & sanctuarium significat.---Ideo ad literam videtur omnino per vo- cem in sanctis ejus intelligendum esse sanctuarium cœ- leste, quod Hebr. 9. vocatur sancta. Hæc ille.

Vers. eod. LAUDATE EUM IN FIRMA- MENTO VIRTUTIS EJUS. Ob expansum roboris ejus, id est, expansum ro- bur, quod ad omnes res creatas expenditur, & dif- funditur, interprete Glaffio l. 3. Phil. S. p. 26.
