Sim- plicius accipitur, ut ἐξήγησις prioris commatis: vel si illud de sanctuario Ecclesiæ intelligatur, hoc de cœlo explicetur cum Osiandro; celebrate Deum habi- tantem in cælis, quos creavit ad monstrandam nobis immensam suam potentiam. Ita enim vox רקיע ac- cipitur in scripturis passim Gen. 1. v. 6. 7. 8. 14. 15. 17. Psal. 19. v. 1. Esa. 1, 22. Dan. 12, 3. &c. nominaliter nem- pe, & de cœlo vel aere, nuspiam autem participia- liter, de re aliqua alia sese diffundente, vel diffusa.

## 150:4
Verse 4. AND ORGANS) In Hebrew עוגב: concerning which word see what is at Gen. 4, 23.

LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE JEHOVAH HALLELUJAH. The end of the 5th and last Book of Psalms.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ET ORGANA) In Hebræo עוגב : de qua voce vide quæ ad Gen. 4, 23.

OMNIS SPIRITUS LAUDET JEHOVAM HALLELUJAH. Finis Libri Psalmorum 5. & ultimi.

# Proverbs

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
TO THE BOOK AT THE PRESS

The Solomonic books, by the opinion of all, both Hebrews and Christians, are three: PROVERBS, ECCLESIASTES, & THE SONG OF SONGS. Yet not long ago, Ludovicus de la Cerda dared to increase this number by adding a fourth book of Solomon, whose manuscript he claims to have found in the Augustan Library, namely the PSALMS OF SOLOMON, 18 in number, which he appended to his sacred adversaries; but in Canon law they are referred to the power of excommunication. l. 6. decret. cap. 1. 2. 3. de excommunicatis. Therefore, the same Bellarmine elsewhere, contr. Barclaj. c. 7. and Baronius in Paraen. adv. Venet., ineptly apply these very things to the power of the Roman Pontiff to brandish the temporal sword against Kings and princes, and others to his judgment and power over infernal princes, to liberate those held in Purgatory from their power; see Chamier, Panstrat. T. III. l. 4. c. 3. For it concerns the vengeance and victory of the spiritual sword of the divine word, Eph. 6. verse 17, Heb. 4, 12, 2 Cor. 10, verse 4, Rev. 1, verse 16, not external victories, even if those are proposed in the form of victors who insult captives at the beginning, then bind the same captives in fetters so as to lead them in triumph, and so they do not slip away, etc., as Brentius rightly says. Conf. Is. 45, 14, c. 60, 12, seqq.

OF PROVERBS. [FRAGMENT].

cit, and presented them endowed with Latinity according to the translation made from the Hebrew with the Greek. But all antiquity knew only three books of Solomon: nor is it in any way probable that for so many centuries all the Rabbis of the Hebrews, as well as Christian Doctors, should have missed a book proceeding from the wisest of mortals, which only now at last had to be brought to light. If it be said to have proceeded from the Holy Spirit, it would have to be added to the Canon of the Old Testament. But thus

Would the Jewish Church, to which the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. 3:4), have had an imperfect Canon of Scripture? Or if it was perfect in the time of Christ and the Apostles, and that book of the Psalms of Solomon was not then desired, how did it happen that neither a trace nor a vestige of it is to be seen in the entire New Testament Scripture, nor likewise in the entire Ecclesiastical History and antiquity? Is it to be believed that a book dictated by the Holy Spirit fell out of the Canon of Scripture, or remained in hiding for over fifteen hundred years, and was entrusted to moths and bookworms? Our Grotius attributes the diminished number of Solomonic books, and assigns Ecclesiastes not to Solomon, but to other, I know not what, compilers who brought it together from diverse writings. He also ascribes the sentences in Proverbs to others who lived before Solomon, and does not specify who collected them. Although there were not lacking those who believed that all these books—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—were put together by another, namely by the Prophet Isaiah, they nevertheless assigned their subject matter to Solomon, and thought that they were collected into order and a certain system by Isaiah, at least from the Solomonic Sentences and Songs preserved in the Church. But since no proof of that matter can be brought forward, and the contrary is quite clearly evident from the text itself, partly because they are openly attributed to Solomon, and partly because certain indications designate the same author, it was not without reason believed by a great consensus, among Jews and Christians alike, that those books originated from Solomon. But we must return to Grotius, whose commentaries on the book of Proverbs we shall now weigh, having added, however, those things which contribute to the sense of the sacred text, from notes of a better sort and from a scrutiny of both the words and the context.

The structure of the whole book of Proverbs is this: namely, it can be divided into an inscription and preface, a preparation, or general preparation, and a narrative, or special treatment of the sentences. The title and preface are contained in the first six verses: the former presents the object and author in the first verse; the latter sets forth the ends and uses of this book in verse 2 and following.

The preparation, which you might perhaps not inappropriately call the general part, first exhibits in summary the requirements of wisdom and its supreme Master inviting us to the same, in chapter 1. Then, indeed, with those things explained individually through the five following chapters, it introduces the same supreme Master instructing us in it—namely, hypostatic wisdom—in chapters 8 and 9. Those requirements are: I. Prayer. II. The investigation of true wisdom, with the flight from adulterous wisdom, chapter 2. III. The observance of divine laws, some of which are brought forward according to the first and second tables, chapter 3. IV. The acceptance of Solomonic instruction, both in general, so that we may insist upon the ways of wisdom which he shows and flee the path of the wicked, chapter 4; and in particular, so that we may avoid harlots, chapter 5; furthermore, that we may free ourselves from pledges, fleeing idleness and vices, and keep paternal precepts, lest we be seduced into adulteries, chapters 6 and 7. Furthermore, the Son of God, the hypostatic Wisdom of God, commends his doctrine and offers himself to be acknowledged, chapter 8; and with the house of wisdom built and the means adorned, he invites us to its enjoyment, at the same time dissuading us from false doctrine shadowed forth by the foolish woman, chapter 9. The special narrative of the proverbs exhibits: I. Proverbs arranged by Solomon himself, chapter 10 up to 25 exclusive, through 15 chapters. II. Proverbs of Solomon added in the time of Hezekiah, comprised in five chapters, namely 25, 26, 27, 28, 29. III. The mystical words of Agur, chapter 30. IV. Finally, the admonitions of Lemuel received from his mother, chapter 31 and the last. In these, although because of the variety of the sentences, as regards the first and second section, a certain method can hardly or scarcely be established, yet so that the order may be designated in some way as regards the principal contents, in the first section of Proverbs 1, concerning justice and impiety or justice, chapters 10, 11, 12. 2. Concerning discipline and the contempt of the same, chapter 13. 3. Concerning prudence and folly, chapters 14 and 15. 4. Concerning divine providence, chapter 16. 5. A comparison of the wise and the foolish, where also concerning anger in particular, and enmity, chapters 17, 18, 19. 6. Concerning drunkenness and idleness, chapter 20. 7. Concerning pride, chapter 21. 8. Concerning a good name, chapter 22. 9. Concerning temperance, chapter 23. 10. Concerning patience and fortitude, chapter 24, is treated most especially. And therefore: I. Concerning the condition and properties of the just. II. Concerning the causes contributing to justice, discipline, and prudence, which is in the word of God: where also concerning God directing all things. III. Concerning adversities and opposing things, such as 1. Anger. 2. Drunkenness and Idleness. 3. Pride. IV. Concerning adjuncts. 1. A good name and 2. temperance. 3. patience and fortitude are discussed through proverbs. In the second section, it is treated: 1. Concerning the prudence of rulers and others, chapter 25. 2. Concerning men worthy of no honor, such as the foolish, the idle, and the deceitful, chapter 26. 3. Concerning self-praise and anger: and friendship, chapter 27. 4. Concerning an evil conscience, chapter 28. 5. Finally, chapter 29, political and economic admonitions alternate: and it is concluded with moral admonitions.

The third section concerning the true knowledge of God, likewise idolatry and false doctrine, concerning self-sufficiency, concerning manifold perversity as also natural ignorance, chapter 30.

In the fourth section are contained maternal admonitions concerning the seduction of women and avoiding drunkenness, helping the deserted and the poor, as also a description and praises of the virtuous wife.

There have certainly not been wanting those who have attempted to hunt down the order more laboriously and to arrange the individual items in Proverbs methodically: a task which the blessed Lord SAMUEL BOHLIUS, Professor at Rostock, a theologian and formerly my singular friend, pursued with particular zeal, and whose Commentaries on Proverbs, snatched away by his premature death, were continued under the title SACRED ETHICS, according to the information of the blessed one, by Lord Georg Wizlebius, now Royal Theologian of the Copenhagen Academy, dividing the whole book into five orations and into two parts: the Common part, which deals with the highest and ultimate end of this wisdom, Fear, or the FOLLOWING of God, and with the means and principles leading to it, which he establishes as seven, and distributes according to three grades of subjects, namely, both of BEGINNERS, for whom he makes I. דעת knowledge, or the complex of all things which the most wise Lord wished us to know in Scripture, chap. 1, from verse 20. II. בינה discretion, by which those things which have been accepted from Scripture are rightly applied, so that we may begin to uncover the deception in some measure and to determine rectitude and justice in acting. c. 2, from verse 5 to the end. III. שכל happy and prudent information of actions according to prior knowledge, chap. 3, verse 4 up to 13. Then of those CONTINUING, for whom he likewise requires three particles, as it were, which are IV. תושיה confirmation and constancy in the work begun, chap. 3, from verse 22 up to the end of the chapter, so that the will may more readily choose and desire the good and turn away from evil. V. מוסר foundation and binding, so that in all external conversation one may be rendered holy and blameless before God and men, c. 4, from v. 13 up to the end of the chapter. VI. מזמות accurate circumspection, which is called the more perfect habit of the intellect, so that a man may not only be more abundant in the knowledge of spiritual things, but may also be able to discern good from evil and rightly define the way of rectitude in all things, c. 5. To these, according to Lord Wizlebius, is added the accidental means of wisdom, which is necessary on account of human infirmity, namely, repentance. chapter 6. And finally, the 7th requirement is subjoined, which he refers to the third degree of those to be PERFECTED in the following of God, under the name ערמה, the leading of a matter upon a matter, chapter 8 & 9, and he defines it as the most perfect habit of all the powers of man, gifted by essential Wisdom, so that he may be like unto Him in all things. He judges these seven requirements to be the seven pillars of the house of wisdom, chapter 9, and he determines that all these, together with the opposite of Wisdom, the STRANGE WOMAN or FOLLY, are exhibited in those nine preceding chapters by a most accurate order and method; which he says complete the FIRST DISCOURSE: and he thinks that the two final discourses, the one of AGUR chapter 30, the other of THE MOTHER chapter 31, although in other words, are nevertheless described and comprehended in the same sense and order. He teaches, however, that the two intermediate discourses contain a proper part, and in particular determine those things which were placed generally in the first part, and thus accommodate the same to the state of each person, and above all deal most accurately with actions and virtues in particular: which part he says begins at chapter 10 and ends at chapter 24, so that those chapters contain one discourse within themselves, and confirm one proposition, with which the other, brought together by the servants of Hezekiah, which is also of the same tenor, coheres. This is their οἰκονομία.

But not a few things stand in the way of our applauding this arrangement. First, because those seven means were ingeniously devised rather than proposed by the Holy Scriptures in this book: since they are not even enumerated in that order in the preface, but far otherwise, where 1. חכמה. 2. מוסר. 3. בינה. 4. שכל. 5. ערמה. 6. דעה. 7. מזמה occur, and these three latter ones are destined for the simple and for children, and thus for beginners: nor is that order preserved in the progress: but with דעת knowledge, תוכחת correction chapter 1, v. 22, 23, and עצה counsel v. 25 are joined: and דעת is interchanged with יראת יהוה the fear of the Lord verse 29, chapter 2, 5: and furthermore חכמה & תבונה chapter 2, 2 seem to be held in the same sense; and since בינה ought to be treated there, according to that method, and יראת יהוה, and דעת, and חכמה and מזמה and תושיה are treated almost indiscriminately, that distinction of the means or pillars of the house of wisdom is by no means observed in verses 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 2. That this third so-called medium שכל is not primarily intended in verse 4, chapter 3, or proposed as a medium, but is promised to them as an end together with the grace of God, who observe the divine precepts. 3. That מוסר chapter 3, 11 is placed before, and not only תושיה chapter of the same verse 22, but also מזמה, and indeed is required in a like manner. 4. That מוסר is similarly joined with בינה chapter 4, 1. 5. And no less is it commanded in the same tenor with תבונה & מזמות & דעת chapter 5, 1. 6. What is held concerning suretyship for a friend chapter 6, 1, is to be taken as it sounds, and not to be dragged to a fall, for which there is need of repentance, i.e., If you have become surety for YOUR NEIGHBOR, that is, the Devil. It is harsh to understand the Devil by the name of Neighbor. 7. When ערמה is demanded, c. 8, 5, the speech is directed not to the more advanced, but to the simpler: and דעת knowledge is likewise commended v. 9, nay even מוסר is enjoined verse 10, and חכמה is celebrated verse 11. 8. That the seven pillars in chapter 9 are those seven means of Wisdom is asserted without proof. 9. But the comparison which is instituted in chapter 30 with those seven means is very forced: and no less that Parallelism in chapter 31 with the same; of which, indeed, no indication appears in the text. 10. That one continuous discourse is held from chapter 10 to 24, or even 11 from chapter 24 to 29, no one would rashly admit: nor could that be taught thus far. For the sentences are too disparate, which are sometimes heaped together, as is wont to happen in such a book of Proverbs. Whence Hugo on chapter 10 says: This chapter, he says, just as the following ones up to c. 25, has as many parts as it has parables, wherefore a connection is not to be sought here, nor can the chapters be divided into certain sections, so far is it from being the case that one continuous and coherent discourse is held. 12. That those seven means of Wisdom are contained in these specifically stated Parables of Solomon, or even in those which were collected by the ministers of Hezekiah, is a μέγα λίαν ἄιτημα. For nothing of the sort appears in that arbitrary accumulation of various sentences. But enough of these.

The interpreters of the book of Proverbs, who have illustrated it with commentaries, are celebrated especially these: among the Ancients 15. Greek Fathers in the Catena of Theod. Peltan., Apollinar., Basil, Chrysost., Cyril of Alex., Didym., Diodor., Epiphan., Evagr., Euseb., Eustachius, Hippolytus, Julian, Origen, Olympiod., Polychron. Add to these Honor. Augustod. from the Latins: from the more recent Robert Holcot, William of Paris, Lyran, Hugo, Dionys. Carthuf., and Osorius: as also Joh. Mercer, Draconites, Anton. Fajus, Lavather, Thomas Cartwright, Theodor. Peltanus, Sixtus Senensis, Cajetan, Lorinus, Jansen, Salazar, Cornel. a Lapide, and he who is easily worth all of them, our Dn. D. Geier: nor are the Paraphrases, Osiandrina and Ernestina, to be despised here. From the writings of B. Luther, excellent explanations can be gathered for all the chapters, if you follow the indices of his Volumes, chapter 3, in Vol. 10, Altenburg. Of the Hebrews, R. Jarchi, Aben-Ezra, and R. Levi Ben-Gerson, a chain was edited by Antonius Giggeus. But these things in place of a prologue.

Latin:

AD LIBRUM PR PRÆLO

LIbri Salomonei omnium tam Ebræorum, quam Christianorum sententia tres sunt: PROVERBIA, ECCLESIASTES, & CANTICUM CANTICORUM. Numerum tamen hunc augere non ita pridem ausus fuit Lu- dovicus de la Cerda, addito Quarto Salomonis libro, cujus manuscriptum se in Bibliotheca Augustana invenisse ait, nimirum PSALMORUM SALOMO- NIS, numero 18. quos suis adversariis sacris subje- jure autem Canonico ad potestatem excommunica- tionis referuntur. l. 6. decret. cap. 1. 2. 3. de excom- municatis. Inepte itaque hæc ipsa idem Bellarm. alibi, contr. Barclaj. c. 7. & Baronius in Paræn. adv. Venet. ad Potestatem Romani Pontificis tempora- lem vibrandi gladium in Reges & principes, alii ad judicium & potestatem ejusdem in principes infer- nales, liberandi detentas in Purgatorio ex potestate ipsorum, adducunt: Vid. Chamier. Panstrat. T. III. l. 4. c. 3. De vindicta enim & victoria gladii spiri- tualis verbi divini agitur Eph. 6. vers. 17. Ebr. 4, 12. 2. Cor. 10, vers. 4. Apoc. 1. vers. 16. non de exter- nis victoriis, etsi illa proponantur ad formam vi- ctorum, qui captivis initio insultant, eosdem dein- de captivos constringunt compedibus, ut in trium- pho ducant, & ne elabantur &c. ut recte Brentius. Conf. Es. 45, 14. c. 60, 12. seqq.

ROVERBIORUM. OQVIUM.

cit, & juxta cum Græca ex Ebræo facta translatione Latinitate donatos exhibuit. Sed universa antiqui- tas non nisi tres libros Salomonis novit: neque ulla- tenus probabile fit, per tot secula omnes tum Ebræo- rum Rabbinos, tum Christianos Doctores librum a Sapientissimo mortalium profectum fugisse, qui nunc demum in lucem protrahendus fuerit. Qui si a Spiritu Sancto profectus dicatur, ad Cano- nem Veteris Testamenti adjiciendus fuerit. Ita vero

Canonem Scripturæ imperfectum habuisset Ecclesia Judaica, cui credita sunt τὰ λόγια τῦ θεῦ Rom. 3, 4? aut si perfectus tempore Christi & Apostolorum fuit, neque desideratus tum liber ille Psalmorum Salomonis, quî factum, quod ejus nec vola, nec ve- stigium in universa Nov. T. Scriptura, in universa item Historia & antiquitate Ecclesiastica conspi- ciatur? Num credendum, librum a S. S. dictatum Canone Scripturæ excidisse, aut ultra sesquimille annos in abscondito mansisse, ac blattis atque ti- neis creditum fuisse? Grotius Noster imminui numerum librorum Salomoneorum, & Ecclesiasten non Salomoni, sed aliis, nescio quibus, eclogariis, qui e diversis scriptis illum comportarint, tribuit. Sententias etiam in Proverbiis aliis adscribit, qui ante Salomonem vixerint, neque exprimit, quis il- las collegerit. Quanquam vero non defuerint, qui libros istos omnes Proverbiorum, Ecclesiasten, & Canticum ab alio concinnatos credidere, nimirum ab Esaia Propheta, materiam tamen eorum Salo- moni assignarunt, eosque e Sententiis &CanticisSa- lomoneis in Ecclesia conservatis saltim in ordinem & certum Syntagma collectos ab Esaia, putarunt. Cæterum quum nullum ejus rei documentum ad- ferri possit, ac contrarium ex ipso textu haud ob- scure liqueat, partim quod aperte Salomoni tri- buantur, partim quod indiciis quibusdam eundem auctorem designent, magno consensu creditum non immerito fuit, penes Judæos pariter & Chri- stianos, libros illos a Salomone profectos esse. Sed ad Grotium redeundum, cujus commenta in li- brum Proverbiorum nunc expendemus, additis ta- men illis, quæ ad sensum textus sacri faciunt, e me- lioris commatis notis & vocum & contextus scru- tinio.

Oeconomia totius libri Proverbiorum hæc est: nimirum dispesci potest in ἐπιγραφὴν, & præfa- tionem:παρασκευὴν, seu generalem præparationem, & διήγησις seu specialem sententiarum tractationem. Titulus, & præfatio sex prioribus versibus contine- tur: ille primo versiculo objectum & autorem: hæc fines & usus hujus libri sistit v. 2. seqq.

Parasceve, quam etiam partem generalem for- te non incommode dixeris, primo summatim sa- pientiæ requisita, ejusque summum Magistrum nos ad eandem invitantem exhibet cap. 1. tum vero si- gillatim illis per quinq; capita seqq. expositis,paulo prolixius eundem summum Magistrum ad eam nos instruentem, sapientiam nempe hypostaticam, in- troducit cap. 8. & 9. Requisita illa sunt I. Oratio. II. Indagatio veræ sapientiæ, cum fuga adulterinæ cap.2. III. Legum divinarum observatio, quarum nonnullæ juxta primam & secundam tabulam ad- ducuntur cap. 3. IV. Institutionis Salomoneæ susce- ptio tum in genere, ut viæ sapientiæ,quam monstrat, insistamus, & impiorum semitam fugiamus cap. 4. tum in specie, ut meretrices vitemus cap. 5. adhæc sponsionibus nos liberemus, otium, & vitia fugien- tes, præcepta paterna custodiamus, ne ad adulteria seducamur cap. 6. & 7. Porro Filius Dei, Sapien- tia Dei hypostatica, commendat suam doctrinam, & seipsum agnoscendum præbet cap. 8. domoque sapientiæ exstructa, ac mediis adornatis, ad ejus fruitionem invitat, a falsa doctrina per stolidam mu- lierem adumbrata simul dehortans. cap. 9. Specialis proverbiotum διήγησις exhibet I. Proverbia a Salo- mone ipso digesta c. 10. usque ad 25. exclusive, per 15. capita. II.Proverbia Salomonis tempore Hiskiæ ad- jecta, capitibus quinque, nimirum 25. 26. 27. 28. 29. comprehensa. III. Verba Aguris mystica cap. 30. IV. Denique monita Lamuelis a matre accepta, cap. 31. & ultimo. In quibus etsi ob varietatem senten- tiarum, quoad primam & secundam sectionem vix ac ne vix quidem certa methodus constitui potest, ut tamen aliqua ratione ordo designetur, quoad præcipua contenta, in prima sectione Proverbiorum 1. de justitia & impietate vel justitia cap. 10. 11. 12. 2. De disciplina, & contemtu ejusdem cap. 13. 3. De prudentia, & stultitia c. 14. & 15. 4. De divina providentia cap. 16. 5. Collatio sapientis & stulti, ubi etiam de ira peculiariter, & inimicitia c. 17. 18. 19. 6. De ebrietate, & otio cap. 20. 7. De superbia cap. 21. 8. De bona fama cap. 22. 9. De temperantia, cap. 23. 10. De patientia & fortitudine, c. 24. potissimum tractatur. Ideoque I. de justorum conditione & proprietatibus. II. De causis ad justitiam facientibus, pædia, ac prudentia, quæ in verbo Dei est: ubi & de Deo omnia dirigente. III. De adversis & repugnantibus, utpote 1. Ira. 2. Ebrietate & Otio. 3. Superbia. IV. De adjunctis. 1. Bona fama & 2. temperantia. 3. patientia & fortitudine per paræmias disseritur. In secunda sectione agitur 1. de prudentia Regentum & aliorum. c. 25. 2. De hominibus nullo honore dignis, utpote stultis, otiosis, & dolosis, cap. 26. 3. De περιαυτολογία & ira: atque amicitia. cap. 27. 4. De mala conscientia cap. 28. 5. Tandem c. 29. alternant monita Politica, & Oeconomica: & concluditur monitis moralibus.

Sectio Tertia de vera notitia Dei, idololatria item & falsa doctrina, de αυταρκεία, de perversitate multiplici ut & naturali ignorantia c. 30.

Sectione quarta monita materna de seductione mulierum, & ebrietate vitanda, desertis & pauperibus juvandis, ut & descriptio, atque elogia uxoris virtuosæ continentur.

Non defuerunt sane, qui ordinem operosius venari, & methodice disponere singula in Proverbiis conati sunt: quod imprimis studiose egit B. Dn. SAMUEL BOHLIUS, Professor Rostoch. Theologus, amicus quondam meus singularis, & qui ejusdem præmatura morte abrepti Commentationes super Proverbia, sub titulo ETHICÆ SACRÆ, juxta informationem τῶ μακαρίτη continuavit, Dn. Georg. Wizlebius jam Regius Haffniensis Academ. Theologus, in quinque orationes dispescens totum librum, & in partes duas: Communem, quæ agit de fine summo & ultimo hujus sapientiæ, Timore, vel SEQUELA Dei, & de mediis, ac principiis eo deducentibus, quæ septem constituit, & juxta tres gradus subjectorum distribuit, utpote tum INCIPIENTIUM, ad quos faciant I. דעת scientia, seu complexio rerum omnium, quas nos in Scriptura scire voluit Dominus sapientissimus cap. 1. a vers. 20. II. בינה discretio, qua ea quæ ex Scriptura accepta sunt, recte applicantur, ut aliqualiter detegere fucum, & rectitudinem & justitiam in agendo determinare incipiamus. c. 2. a vers. 5. ad finem. III. שכל felix & prudens secundum præviam cognitionem actionum informatio, cap. 3. vers. 4. usque ad 13. tum CONTINUANTIUM, ad quos itidem tres quasi particulas requirit, ut sunt IV. תושיה confirmatio & constantia in opere incepto cap. 3. a vers. 22. usque ad finem cap. ut voluntas promtius bonum eligat, appetat, & malum aversetur. V. מוסר fundatio & colligatio, ut in omni conversatione externa sanctus & inculpabilis quis, coram Deo & hominibus, reddatur c. 4. a v. 13. usq; ad finem cap. VI. מזמות accurata circumspectio, quæ habitus dicitur intellectus perfectior, ut homo non tantum abundantior sit scientia rerum spiritualium, sed etiam bonum a malo discernere, & rectitudinis viam in omnibus rite definire possit, c. 5. Quibus juxta Dn. Wizlebium additur medium sapientiæ per accidens, quo ob humanam infirmitatem opus, pœnitentia scil. cap. 6. ac subjungitur denique 7. requisitum, quod ad gradum tertium PERFICIENDORUM in sequela Dei refert, sub nomine ערמה ductus rei super rem cap. 8. & 9. ac definit, quod sit habitus perfectissimus omnium virium hominis, do- natus a Sapientia essentiali, ut juxta omnia ei similis sit. Quæ septem requisita esse septem columnas domus sapientiæ cap. 9. censet, atque hæc omnia una cum opposito Sapientiæ, UXORE PEREGRI- NA vel STULTITIA novem illis capp. priori- bus ordine, ac methodo accuratissima exhiberi sta- tuit; quæ ORATIONEM PRIMAM absolve- re ait: & duabus postremis orationibus altera AGU- RIS cap. 30. altera MATRIS cap. 31. etsi verbis aliis, sensu tamen atque ordine eodem describi, & comprehendi existimat. Duas autem intermedias orationes partem propriam continere docet, & in specie determinare ea, quæ in prima parte generali- ter posita erant, adeoque ad cujusque statum eadem accommodare, & imprimis accuratissime agere de actionibus, & virtutibus in specie : Quam partem inchoari dicit cap. 10. & terminari cap. 24. ita ut il- la capita unam orationem in se contineant, & unam confirment propositionem, cum qua cohæreat al- tera, a servis Hiskiæ comportata, quæ ejusdem etiam sit tenoris. Hæc illorum est οἰκονομία.

Sed quo minus isti dispositioni applaudamus, non pauca obstant. Primum quod illa septem media ingeniosè potius excogitata, quam a S. S. in hoc li- bro proposita sint: quum nec in præfatione eo ordi- ne ista recenseantur, sed longe aliter, ubi 1. חכמה. 2. מוסר. 3. בינה. 4. שכל. 5. ערמה. 6. דעה. 7. מזמה. occurrunt, & tria hæc posteriora simplicibus & pue- ris, adeoque incipientibus destinantur: nec in pro- gressu ordo ille servetur: sed cum דעת scientia תוכחת correptio cap. 1. v. 22. 23. & עצה consilium v. 25. conjugatur: & דעת cum יראת יהוה timore Domini verf. 29. cap. 2, 5. permutetur: ac porro חכמה & תבונה cap. 2, 2. eodem sensu haberi videa- tur; & quum illic de בינה tractari, juxta istam me- thodum, debeat, de יראת יהוה, & דעת, & חכמה & מזמה & תושיה fere promiscue agatur, nullatenus vero illa distinctio mediorum vel columnarum do- mus sapientiæ observetur vers. 2. 3. 5. 6. 10. 11. 2. Quod tertium istud ita dictum medium שכל non primario vers. 4. cap. 3. intendatur, aut ut medium proponatur, sed instar finis una cum gratia Dei illis promittatur, qui præcepta divina observant. 3. quod מוסר cap. 3, 11. præmittatur, neque תושיה cap. eodem vers. 22. solum, sed etiam מזמה, & quidem parili ratione requiratur. 4. Quod מוסר similiter cum בינה cap. 4, 1. conjugatur. 5. Nec minus cap. 5, 1. cum תבונה & מזמות & דעת eodem tenore im- peretur. 6. Quæ de sponsione pro amico cap. 6, 1. ha- bentur, uti sonant accipienda, non vero ad lapsum, ob quem pœnitentia opus sit, trahenda, h. m. Si spoponderis PROXIMO TUO, h. e. Diabolo. Durum est Proximi nomine Diabolum intelligere. 7. Cum ערמה postulatur, c. 8, 5. non ad provectiores, sed ad simpliciores sermo dirigitur: & דעת scientia pariter commendatur v. 9. imo etiam מוסר præci- pitur vers. 10. & חכמה celebratur vers. 11. 8. Colu- mnas septem cap. 9. esse illa septem media Sapientiæ precario asseritur. 9. Quæ vero 30. capitis cum il- lis septem mediis instituitur collatio, valde contor- ta est: Nec minus ille Parallelismus cap. 31. cum iisdem; de quo utique nullum apparet in textu in- dicium. 10. Orationem unam continuam haberi a cap. 10. ad 24. aut etiam 11. a cap. 24. ad 29. nemo temere admiserit: neque id doceri hactenus potuit. Sententiæ enim nimis disparatæ sunt, quæ quando- que congeruntur, uti fieri amat in ejusmodi Pro- verbiorum libro. Unde Hugo ad cap. 10. Hoc ca- put, inquit, æque ac fequentia usque ad c. 25. tot habet partes, quot parabolas, quare hic connexio non est quærenda, nec capita in certas sectiones dividi queunt, tantum abest, ut una continua & cohærens oratio habeatur. 12. Septem illa Sapientiæ media in hisce speciatim dictis Parabolis Salomonis, vel etiam in illis, quæ ab Hiskiæ ministris collecta, contineri, μέγα λίαν ἄιτημα. Nihil enim tale in illa arbitraria coacervatione variarum sententiarum apparet. Sed hæc de istis.

Interpretes libri Proverbiorum, qui eum com- mentariis illustrarunt, celebrantur hi imprimis: in- ter Veteres 15. Græci Patres in Catena Theod. Pel- tan. Apollinar. Basilius, Chrysost. Cyrillus Alex. Didym. Diodor. Epiphan. Evagr. Euseb. Eusta- chius, Hippolytus, Julian. Origenes, Olympiod. Poly- chron. Adde his Honor. Augustod. e Latinis: e recentioribus Robert. Holcoth. Guilhelm. Parisienf. Lyran. Hugo, Dionys. Carthuf. & Osorius: ut & Joh. Mercerus, Draconites, Anton. Fajus, Lavatherus, Thomas Cartwrightus, Theodor. Peltanus, Sixtus Se- nens. Cajetanus, Lorinus, Jansenius, Salazar, Cor- nel. a Lapide, & qui facile instar omnium est Dn. D. Geierus noster: neque contemnendæ hic sunt Para- phrases, Osiandrina, & Ernestina. E B. Lutheri scriptis præclaræ explicationes in omnia capita colligi possunt, si sequaris indices Tomorum ejus, cap. 3. in Tom. 10. Altenburg. Ebræorum R. Jar- chi, Aben-Ezr. & R. Levi Ben-Gerson catenam edidit Antonius Giggeus. Sed hæc προλεγομένων loco.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

The title having been premised, and in place of a preface an eulogy of the book, the requirements of wisdom are summarized: the fear of God, obedience toward parents, and the avoidance of evil company are handed down, and the supreme Master of wisdom, the Son of God, invites one to look toward the same, with the punishment of those who despise it and the fruit of obedience.

Verse 1. THE PARABLES OF SOLOMON. In Greek this book is called παροιμίαι: indeed the Hebrew מָשָׁל properly signifies a comparison or παραβολή. And because proverbs were for the most part made from shortened comparisons, from there it began to be taken in the meaning of παροιμία: then more broadly, as happens, with the use of the word extending itself, every γνώμη began to be called thus. We will not repeat here what we have said about that matter, both in the prolegomena to the sayings of the Poets from Stobaeus, and to Matt. 13, 3. However, this book seems to be an ἐκλογὴ of the best sentences from many writers who were before Solomon, such ἐκλογαὶ as many of the emperors of Constantinople caused to be written for their own uses. Moreover, the things that are here are all ethical, pertaining either to the precepts of morals or of prudence, yet in such a way that these and those always look toward the worship of God: which virtue produces all the others from itself: neglected by many nations: but held in the highest regard by the wise Hebrews, as is noted by Josephus. And from this the beginning of this book is drawn.

Grotius thinks too meanly of Solomon, the wisest of kings and mortals who lived in his age, and a divinely inspired author, while he makes him only a collector of the maxims of other writers, perhaps even of profane ones not borne along by the Holy Spirit, as if the Holy Spirit had need of such things, or would devote effort to them so that they might be destined for the canonical use of the Church, just as the Greek Emperors caused selections to be written for their own uses or for public ones. And what obscure indication at least will Grotius bring forward that Solomon here collected the maxims of other writers? The title does not permit us to doubt who is the author of the book, which the title does not permit us to doubt, not added by others, as was done in certain other books, but inserted by the author himself at the beginning of the first chapter, of which it constitutes a part: and since in chapter 15, 1, it is stated thus concerning the subsequent Proverbs: These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out, it is gathered not obscurely from there that the preceding sentences are not only of Solomon as author, but were also arranged and written down by Solomon himself in that order, just as the others from chapter 26 to 30 indeed have Solomon as author, but were collected and consigned by those to whom Hezekiah gave that task by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, the same Spirit directing. Therefore the LXX translated, which they COPIED, which the Vulgate rendered, they carried over, Grotius explains, they gathered together. But here Grotius seems to have followed R. Levi, who said that the sentences of chapter 25 and following were plucked from the sects and enunciations of the wise, not seeing that the title openly contradicts him: These also are proverbs of Solomon. Whence other Hebrews and most interpreters gather that those were not once joined to the others, but were written on various membranes, and were finally added by Hezekiah, lest they should lose the name and strength or authority of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah King of Judah העתיקו strengthened, as some render: Lyranus translates: they fortified by placing them in an authentic book. Hippolytus the Martyr believed them to be chosen from the number of the others as being more distinguished, since Solomon is read to have dictated three thousand proverbs, 1 Kings 4, verse 32, which opinion is favored by the fact that in the whole book of Proverbs not even a thousand are found, and that Hippolytus in the LXX interpreters' version read these are the proverbs of Solomon the distinguished, although in the Roman edition it is now read undistinguished. Grotius makes those collectors Eliakim, Shebna, Joah, but others believe that Isaiah was their chief. Whoever he may have been, one must confess that he was directed by the Holy Spirit, since all Scripture is God-breathed. Although Grotius perhaps was not much removed from the opinion of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who taught that Solomon dictated the Proverbs only by human wisdom, and did not receive the grace of prophecy when he wrote them: whom, however, he could not have been ignorant was condemned for this in the 5th Council of Constantinople, Act 4. Certainly among the Doctors of the Church there was no doubt concerning the canonical authority and divine origin of this book, who religiously accepted the Canon of the Hebrews, to which Josephus is the author, in Eusebius book 3, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 10, that the four books of Hymns and Precepts of human life, i.e. the Psalms of David, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon belonged; following Melito Bishop of Sardis unanimously. Who called this book proverbs and Wisdom in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 25, called by the name of Wisdom also by Cyprian to Quirinus, book 3, chapters 21 and 56, Clement, book 1, Constitutions, chapter 10, Nazianzen in the praises of Gorgonia: as also by Eusebius himself, book 4, chapter 21. Where he observes that this book is called by Hegesippus, Irenaeus, and the whole choir of the ancients, all-virtuous Wisdom, wisdom full of every kind of virtue. By which name it is honored also by Basil the Great in the beginning of Proverbs. But of that elsewhere.

Moreover, the word משלים does not mean parables, but sententious sayings, or rounded aphorisms comprising many things in few words, whether that is done by proper or figurative words, which for that reason is called from משל, dominion, because they are as it were predominant and more excellent than the others, full of wisdom, gravity, utility, acuteness, authority, he notes here, even if at other times it is sometimes used for Parables, Ezekiel 17, verse 2, chapter 24, verse 3, and thus it is more correctly expressed by Blessed Luther, the sayings of Solomon, than by proverbs and PARABLES, or even PROVERBS, because not so much proverbs as gnomes and distinguished sentences are comprehended here in almost every verse, containing absolute and perfect doctrine. For a proverb, according to Didymus in the Catena, is a speech showing truth in a hidden way; a Parable, according to Donatus, is a comparison of things of different kinds: a Proverb, as a proverb is wont to describe, covers a manifest speech with obscurity: which therefore are all narrower than the Hebrew word.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Præmisso titulo, & præfationis loco elogio libri, summatim requisita sapientiæ, timor Dei, ob- sequium erga parentes, & vitatio pravi soda- litii traduntur, & summus Magister sapien- tiæ Filius Dei ad eandem prospiciendam cum pæna contemtorum & fructu obedientiæ in- vitat.

Verf. 1. PARABOLÆ SALOMONIS. Græce dicitur hic liber παροιμίαι: nimirum Hebræum מָשָׁל proprie comparationem sive παραβολὴν significat. Et quia ex comparationibus curtatis plerumque fiebant proverbia, inde cœpit sumi in significatu παροιμίας: deinde latius, ut fit, protendente se vocis usu, omnis γνώμη sic cœpit dici. Non repetemus hîc quæ ea de re diximus, tum in prole- gomenis ad dicta Poëtarum è Stobæo, tum ad Matth. 13, 3. Videtur autem hic liber esse ἐκλογὴ optimarum sententia- rum ex plurimis, qui ante Salomonem fuere scriptoribus, quales ἐκλογὰς multi imperatorum Constantinopolitano- rum conscribi in suos usus fecere. Sunt autem quæ hîc sunt ἠθικὰ omnia, pertinentia aut ad morum, aut ad prudentiæ præcepta, fic tamen ut hæc & illa semper ad Dei cultum re- spiciant: quæ virtus cæteras omnes ex se parit: neglecta mul- tis gentibus: maximi autem facta ab Hebræis sapientibus, ut Josepho notatum est. Atque hinc initium ducitur hujus libri.

NImis abjecte de Salomone Regum & morta- lium, qui ætate ipsius vivebant, sapientissimo, & autore θεοπνεύστῳ sentit Grotius, dum eum Colle- ctorem tantum facit sententiarum, aliorum fcripto- rum, forte etiam parophanorum ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁ- γίε μὴ φερομένων, ac si Spiritus Sanctus opus haberet talibus, aut operam in iis collocaret, ut ea in usum Ecclesiæ Canonicum destinarentur, quemadmodum Imperatores Græci, in usus suos, aut publicos, ἐκλο- γὰς conscribi curarunt. Et quodnam vel obscurum saltim indicium proferet Grotius, Salomonem hic aliorum scriptorum congessisse sententias? Quem auctorem libri esse titulus nos dubitare non per- mittit, mittit, non ab aliis additus, ut in aliis libris quibus- dam factum, sed ingressui capitis primi, cujus par- tem constituit, ab ipso auctore infertns : & quum cap. 15, 1. ita habeatur de subsequentibus Prover- biis: Haec quoque parabola Salomonis, quas transtu- lerunt viri Ezechia regis Juda, haud obscure inde colligitur, sententias praecedentes non Salomonis tantum autoris esse, sed ab ipso Salomone etiam isto ordine digestas & conscriptas, uti caeterae a cap. 26. ad 30. Salomonem quidem auctorem habent, sed ab his, quibus id negotii S. S. instinctu Ezechias dedit, eodem Spiritu dirigente collectas, & con- signatas esse. Ideo LXX. verterunt, quas TRAN- SCRIPSERUNT, quod vulgata reddidit, trans- tulerunt, Grotius exponit, congesserunt. Sequu- tus autem hic videtur Grotius R. Levi, qui senten- tias cap. 25. & seqq. decerptas dixit ex sapientum sc- ctis, & enunciatis, non videns, quod aperte illi refra- getur titulus: Haec quoque sunt Parabola Salomonis. Unde Ebraei caeteri ac Interpp. plerique colligunt, conjunctas olim illas non fuisse caeteris, sed in va- riis membranis conscriptas, ab Ezechia demum, ne nomen & robur, vel auctoritatem Salomonis amitte- rent, adjectas fuisse, quas העתיקו roborarunt viri Ezechia Regis Juda, ut nonnulli reddunt: Lyranus vertit: fortificarunt imponendo eas in libro authen- tico. Electas illas e numero caeterarum tanquam insigniores, Hippolytus Martyr credidit, siquidem tria millia Parabolarum dictasse legatur Salomo 1. Reg. 4. vers. 32. cui opinioni favet, quod in toto Proverbiorum libro ne mille quidem reperiantur, & quod Hippolytus in LXX. Interpp. versione legerit ἀυταὶ αἱ παροιμίαι Σαλομῶντος οἱ διάκριτοι, quam- vis in Romana editione nunc legatur ἀδιάκριτοι. Eclogarios illos Eliacim, Sobna, Joahe Grotius fa- cit, sed alii praecipuum eorum fuisse Esaiam cre- dunt. Quisquis fuerit, a Spiritu S. directum esse, fateri oportet, siquidem tota Scriptura sit θεόπνευ- στος. Quamvis Grotius fortassis non multum alie- nus fuerit a Theodori Mopsvesteni sententia, qui Salomonem Proverbia tantum humana sapientia dictasse, neque Prophetia gratiam, cum ea scri- beret, accepisse, docuit: quem vero in Synodo 5. Constantinop. Act. 4. ob id damnatum fuisse, ipse ignorare non potuit. Penes Doctores certe Ec- clesiae de Canonica auctoritate, & origine divina hujus libri dubium nullum fuit, qui Canonem Ebraeorum, ad quem quatuor Hymnorum ac Praece- ptorum vita humana libros h. e. Psalmos Davidis, Proverbia, Ecclesiasten, ac Canticum Salomonis spe- ctasse, Josephus autor est, apud Eusebium l. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 10. religiose susceperunt; Melitonem Sardicensem Episcop. ὁμοθυμαδὸν sequuti. Qui hunc librum παροιμίας, καὶ Σοφίαν dixit apud Euseb. lib. 4. cap. 25. nomine Sapientiae etiam a Cypriano ad Quirin. lib. 3. cap. 21. & 56. Clemente lib. 1. Con- stit. cap. 10. Nazianz. in laudibus Gorgon. nun- cupatum: ut & ab ipsomet Eusebio lib. 4. cap. 21. Ubi observat, hunc librum ex Hegesippo, Irenaeo, & universo veterum choro dictum πανάρετον Σοφίαν Sa- pientiam omnis generis virtute plenam. Quo nomine honoratur etiam a Basilio M. in princip. Proverb. Sed de eo alias.

Caeterum vox משלים non parabolas, sed dicta sententiosa, vel aphorismos rotundos paucis verbis multa complectentes, sive propriis seu figuratis id fiat vocibus, quae ob id a משל dominatus est, di- cuntur, quod quasi praedominantes & excellentio- res sint caeteris, plenae sapientiae, gravitatis, utilita- tis, acuminis, auctoritatis, hic notat, etsi alias quan- doque de Parabolis adhibeatur, Ezech. 17. vers. 2. cap. 24. vers. 3. adeoque rectius exprimitur a B. Lu- thero, die Sprüche Salomonis, quam per παροιμίας & PARABOLAS, vel etiam PROVERBIA, quia non tam proverbia quàm gnomæ & sententiæ insignes singulis pene versibus hic comprehenduntur, absolutam & perfectam doctrinam continentes. Parœmia enim juxta Didymum in Catena, est oratio, occulto modo veritatem ostendens; Parabola juxta Donatum est rerum genere dissimilium comparatio: Proverbium, ut parœmia describit solet, sermonem manifestum obscuritate tegens: quæ proinde omnia angustiora sunt Ebræa voce.

## 1:2
verse 2.

TO KNOW WISDOM AND DISCIPLINE.

The end and utility of these sentences are expressed by these and the following words, both in general and in particular: In general 1. for the knowledge of true Wisdom and erudition: the didactic use of the former is insinuated, since they contribute to an accurate knowledge of divine and human things, which is true wisdom: but the latter is the paideutic use, because they conduce to παιδείαν and the correction of morals and life, as 2 Tim. 3:16 treats of these distinct ends of Holy Scripture. Cornelius a Lapide also understands wisdom here in almost the same way, which he calls practical, which is the knowledge of God and the ultimate end and the means leading to it, but discipline is the correction and chastisement of passions and vices. Solomon explains both these ends further, both from the means leading to it and from the resulting fruit, to which this wisdom and erudition is subordinated. As for those things, the understanding of the sayings pertains to true wisdom, namely the intelligence which is comprehended in the sacred letters, which if they are properly understood, then at last we may believe we possess true wisdom: the reception of the erudition of prudence contributes to erudition, which is likewise drawn from the word of God alone: for we cannot progress toward the amendment of life unless we receive and admit this παιδείαν of the Holy Spirit. As for the fruit, Solomon expressed the same in three words, namely through justice and judgment and uprightness: because we both understand and receive through this wisdom and erudition the justice of faith, and the judgment of our condemnation according to the law, and also the uprightness of life and of our actions: all of which are required for spiritual perfection and constitute a true Christian. For the justice of faith could not be omitted here, where we are instructed unto salvation by true wisdom, 2 Tim. 3:15, the hypostatic wisdom itself undertakes to inform us. Cf. Prov. 8:35. But in particular, what benefit these sentences bring: it is explained partly to the simpler, verse 4, partly also to the more perfect, verses 5 and 6, that they give to the simple, unskilled, or as the Vulgate renders it, the little ones, Symm. νηπίοις (the LXX have ἀκάκοις) עַרְמָה prudence, so that the unskilled may learn what should be omitted and what should be done; and to every youth knowledge and understanding, so that he may seek from here what is necessary to be known; so that this knowledge and understanding may be disposed toward wisdom, but that prudence of the simple toward more perfect practical erudition. Whence, as far as the wise and more perfect are concerned, Solomon teaches that they also find here what contributes to a greater τελείωσιν of wisdom: the wise man will hear and will add doctrine; and that the provident will have counsels here in managing affairs, by which they may enrich their own prudence. The Vulgate rendered it 'and the understanding man shall possess the helm': with the LXX, ὁ δὲ νοήμων, κυβέρνησιν κτήσεται: but in the Hebrew it is, 'and the understanding man shall possess counsels': the word תַּחְבּוּלוֹת, derived from חֹבֵל, a ship's pilot, Jonah 1:6, according to some introduces the governing prudence, necessary in directing the helm of the Republic, in governing the ship of the Church, the School, the Republic, or the house, and in the direction of life and all actions, concerning which Cornel. a Lap. speaks at length. Kimchi, however, notes that the word signifies reasonings and pressed considerations: which, because of the sequence, fits not badly: for understanding the sentence and eloquence, the words of the wise, and their enigmas: because through this Solomonic book the more perfect ones progress toward reasonings and pressed considerations in the intellect of sharp sentences, and in perceiving the senses of eloquence or of the words of Scripture, nay even toward the enigmatic words of the wise (by hendiadys), namely of Moses and the Prophets, to be understood, those things which can seem to be enigmas because of their difficulty. חידה according to Mr. Dr. Gejer is an involved and knotty discourse, such as wise men are usually accustomed to use to veil their wisdom, and to enclose it like a nut and an almond within a hard shell, lest the same, becoming too exposed, eventually become worn out and cheapened. In the word מליצה, interpreters note an emphasis on מלץ, which in Niphal is to become cheap, because just as sweet food, like honey, tastes sweetly to the mouth, so may the interpretation of an enigma and of an obscure matter taste to the mind, and be sweet and pleasant. That which is sought with more difficulty, says St. Augustine, in Ps. 105, conc. 2, is usually found more sweetly, nor should you think these things were withheld from you by obscurity, but seasoned by difficulty. And Jerome, Epist. to Paulinus: Everything that we read in divine books shines and gleams indeed even in the shell, but it is sweeter in the marrow. Osiander and the Vinariensis Paraphrase also understand these things concerning the wisdom of the word of God and divine utterances. Vinariensis, to the perception and wholesome use of which these Solomonic sentences contribute not a little.

Latin:

vers. 2.

AD SCIENDAM SAPIENTIAM ET DISCIPLINAM.

Exprimitur his, & sequentibus verbis finis & utilitas harum sententiarum cum in genere, tum in specie: In genere 1. ad cognitionem veræ Sapientiæ, & eruditionis: quarum illa usus didacticus insinuatur, quum faciant ad accuratam rerum divinarum & humanarum notitiam, quæ vera est sapientia: hæc vero usus pædevticus, quod ad παιδείαν & correctionem morum & vitæ conducant, uti 2. Tim. 2. v. 16. de his Scripturæ S. distinctis finibus egit S. S. Ita fere etiam Cornelius a Lapide Sapientiam hic intelligendam, quam vocat practicam, quæ est cognitio Dei & ultimi finis ac mediorum eo ducentium, disciplinam vero passionum vitiorumque esse correctionem & castigationem. Quem utrumque finem explicat Salomo ulterius tum a mediis eo conducentibus, tum a fructu consequente, ad quem subordinatur hæc sapientia & eruditio. Quantum ad illa, ad sapientiam veram pertinet intellectus eloquiorum nempe intelligentia, quæ sacris literis comprehensa, quæ si probe intelligantur, tum demum veram nos possidere sapientiam credamus: ad eruditionem facit susceptio eruditionis prudentiæ, quæ itidem e solo Dei verbo hauritur: non enim ad vitæ emendationem proficere possumus, nisi hanc Spiritus S. παιδείαν suscipiamus & admittamus. Quod ad fructum, tribus verbis expressit eundem Salomo, per justitiam nempe & judicium, & rectitudines: quia justitia fidei, & judicium damnationis nostri secundum legem, nec non rectitudines vitæ, & actionum nostrarum & intelligimus, & accipimus per hanc sapientiam & eruditionem: quæ omnia ad perfectionem spiritualem requiruntur, verumque Christianum constituunt. Non enim omitti poterat hic fidei justitia, ubi de vera sapientia, qua ad salutem instruimur 2. Tim. 3. vers. 15. ipsa sapientia hypostatica nos informare instituit. Conf. Prov. 8. vers. 35. In specie vero quid emolumenti adferant hæ sententiæ: partim simplicioribus vers. 4. partim etiam perfectioribus vers. 5. 6. exponitur, quod dent simplicibus imperitis, vel ut Vulg. reddit parvulis, Symm. νηπίοις (LXX. ἀκάκοις habent) עַרְמָה prudentiam, ut imperiti discant, quæ omittenda, quæ facienda; & puero cuique scientiam & cognitionem, ut necessaria cognitu hinc petere possit; ut ita hæc scientia & cognitio dispositia sit ad sapientiam, illa vero simplicium prudentia ad eruditionem Practicam perfectiorem. Unde quod ad sapientes & perfectiores attinet, Salomo docet, invenire eos hic etiam, quod ad majorem sapientiæ τελείωσιν faciat: audiet sapiens, & addet doctrinam; & providos in rebus gerendis consilia hic habituros, quibus suam prudentiam locupletare possint. Vulg. reddidit & intelligens gubernacula possidebit: cum LXX. ὁ δὲ νοήμων, κυβέρνησιν κτήσεται: sed in Ebræo est, & intelligens consilia possidebit: vox תַּחְבּוּלוֹת, a חֹבֵל gubernatore navis Jon. 1. vers. 6. deducta, secundum quosdam prudentiam gubernatricem, in dirigendo clavo Rei- publicæ, gubernanda navi Ecclesiæ, Scholæ, Rei- publicæ, vel domus, vitæ, & actionum omnium di- rectione necessariam infert, quo de fuse Cornel. a Lap. Kimchius tamen ratiocinationes, & pressas con- siderationes vocem significare notat: quod ob se- quentia non male convenit : ad intelligendam sen- tentiam & eloqutionem, verba sapientum, & ænigma- ta eorum: quia per hunc Salomoneum librum per- fectiores proficiunt ad ratiocinationes & pressas considerationes in intellectu sententiarum acuta- rum, & sensibus eloqutionis vel verborum Scri- pturæ percipiendis, imo etiam ad verba sapientum ænigmatica (per hendyaden) Mosis nempe & Pro- phetarum intelligenda, ea quæ ænigmata videri possunt ob difficultatem. חידה juxta Dn. D. Gejerum est sermo involutus, & nodosus, quali plerum- que viri prudentes solent suam velare sapientiam, & tanquam nucem & amygdalum duro cortici includere, ne eadem nimium patescens protrita tandem fiat ac vi- lescat. In voce מליצה interpretes ad מלץ quod in Niphal est vilescere, emphasin notant, quod sicut dulcis cibus, ut mel, ori suaviter sapit, sic menti sa- piat, dulcis & jucunda sit interpretatio ænigmatis, & rei obscuræ. Quod difficilius quæritur, ait S. Au- gustinus, in Ps. 105. conc. 2. solet dulcius inveniri, nec putetis ista vobis obscuritate subtracta, sed difficultate condita. Et Hier. Epist. ad Paulin. Totum quod legimus in divinis libris nitet quidem & fulget etiam in cortice, sed dulcius est in medulla. De sapientia verbi Dei & eloquiorum divinorum intelligunt e- tiam hæc Osiander, & Paraphr. Vinariensis, ad quo- rum perceptionem & usum salutarem hæ sententiæ Salomoneæ non parum conducunt.

## 1:3
Vers. 3.

JUSTICE AND JUDGMENT AND EQUITY) צדק is that which conforms to goodness. משפט is commutative justice, which is usually exercised regarding contracts and offenses. Whatever is right besides these, and pertains to some virtue, comes under the name משרים.

What is understood by these words, we have already said. The Holy Spirit, when He names justice and judgment, is accustomed to indicate not Ethics or Politics, but something more sublime. Cf. Isa. 9:7, Jer. 23:6.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

JUSTITIAM ET JUDICIUM ET ÆQUITATEM) צדק est id quod bonitati convenit. משפט Jus συναλλακτι- κὸν, quod circa contractus & delicta exerceri solet. Quic- quid præter hæc rectum est, & ad aliquam virtutem pertinet, venit sub nomine משרים.

Quid per hasce voces intelligatur, jam dixi- mus. Spiritus S. cum justitiam & judicium nominat, non Ethica aut Politica, sed sublimius quid indica- re solet. Conf. Esa. 9, 7. Jer. 23, 6.

## 1:6
Vers. 6.

THEIR ENIGMAS) ἄινιγμα are very frequent among the Orientals. See what is in the prolegomena already mentioned, and in the annotations to book 3 of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

In the Annotations to book 3 of the Truth of the Christian Religion, to which he refers us, p. 125, he had adduced from Josephus, book 7 of the Antiquities, ch. 6, and the first against Apion, a passage from the Phoenician history of Dius concerning Hiram, King of Tyre: They say also that Solomon, who then reigned in Jerusalem, sent certain enigmas to Hiram and desired to receive others from him. But Hiram, since he could not solve those enigmas, paid a great sum of money as a fine: but afterwards Abdemon, a Tyrian man, solved those which had been proposed, and proposed others in turn, which when Solomon could not solve, great sums of money were paid by him to Hiram. And from Menander of Ephesus: At this age lived the youth Abdemon, who was the victor in explaining the problems sent by Solomon, King of Jerusalem. Concerning the friendship of King Solomon with Hiram, King of Tyre, the matter is certain, but that he was defeated by the youth Abdemon in the wisdom of solving enigmas, I do not think that faith should be so easily given to foreign and profane writers, whether they were extending the glory of their own people, or were carried away by affection or false reasoning. For I do not know whether those things are sufficiently consistent with the judgment of the Holy Spirit concerning the wisdom of Solomon, that he surpassed the wisdom of all the Orientals and Egyptians, and was wiser than all men, or with the report of Scripture, that they came from all peoples to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the Kings of the earth, who heard his wisdom: if indeed God gave Solomon wisdom and exceeding much prudence, and largeness of heart as the sand that is on the seashore, 1 Kings 4:29 seqq. However, that the word for enigmas is used in this place of ours in such a strict signification, as Grotius wishes, is not probable: since that word does not easily occur in the Scriptures with such a meaning. But let it be applied generally to any things said sharply and usefully (just as the name חִידָה has a correspondence with the verb חָדַד to be sharp) and perhaps no enigma strictly so called may be found in the Scriptures. For as to what is brought forward from Judg. 14:14, proposed by Samson, Vossius, l. 4. institut. orat. c. 2, denies that it was an enigma with that word taken strictly, because it was unknown to the Philistines that a lion had been killed by Samson and honey taken from its carcass. An enigma seems properly to be a discourse signifying a KNOWN THING by the obscurity of an allegory.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ÆNIGMATA EORUM) ἄινιγμα multum frequentes Ori- entalibus. Vide quæ in dictis jam prolegomenis, & in anno- tatis ad librum 3. de Veritate religionis Christianæ.

In Annotatis ad librum 3. de veritate religio- nis Christianæ, ad quæ nos remittit, p. 125. e Josepho lib. 7. Historiæ Antiquæ c. 6. & priore contra Ap- pionem adduxerat locum ex Dii historia Phænicia de Iramo, Tyri Rege: Ajunt & qui Hierosolymis tunc regnabat Salomonem ad Iromum ænigmata misisse quædam, & cupiisse ab ipso alia accipere. Sed Iro- mum, cum ænigmata illa solvere nequiret, magnam pe- cuniæ vim pro multa pependisse: postea vero Abdeno- mum hominem Tyrium solvisse ea, quæ proposita fue- rant, ac proposuisse vicissim alia, quæ cum solvere Salo- mon nequiffet, Iromo ab eo magnas pecunias persolutas. Et e Menandro Ephesio: Hac ætate Abdenomus vixit juvenis, qui victor fuit explicando problemata missa a Salomone Hierosolymorum Rege. De amicitia Regis Salomonis cum Hiram Rege Tyri res certa est, sed quod illa ab Abdemono juvene sapientia solvendi ænigmata victus fuerit, exteris ac prophanis Scriptoribus, sive gloriam suorum extendenti- bus, seu affectu aut falsa ratione abreptis, tam facile fidem adhibendam non arbitror. Nescio enim an ea satis consentanea sint τῇ ἐπικρίσει Spiritus San- cti de sapientia Salomonis, quod omnium orientalium & Aegyptiorum sapientiam superarit, & cunctis homi- uibus sapientior fuerit, aut relationi Scripturæ, quod venerint de cunctis populis ad audiendam sapientiam Salomonis, & ab universis Regibus terræ, qui audie- bant sapientiam ejus: siquidem dederit Deus sapien- tiam Salomoni & prudentiam multam nimis, & lati- tudinem cordis quasi arenam, quæ est in littore maris 1. Reg. 4, 29. seqq. Ænigmatum autem vocem tam stricta significatione, ut vult Grotius, usurpari in hoc nostro loco, non est probabile: quum vox illa in Scripturis non facile tali significatu occurrat. Sed generaliter de quibusvis acute & utiliter dictis ad- hibeatur (uti nomen חִידָה convenientiam habet cum verbo חָדַד acutum esse) neque fortassis ullum ænigma stricte dictum in Scripturis reperiatur. Nam quod e Jud. 14, 14. affertur, a Simsone propositum, Vossius l. 4. institut. orat. c. 2. ænigma voce illa presse sumta fuisse negat, quia ignotum erat Philistæis, leo- nem a Samsone interemtum, ac mel a cadavere ejus ex- emtum. Ænigma proprie esse videtur oratio, obscu- ritate allegoriæ REM NOTAM significans.

## 1:7
vers. 7. THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS THE BEGINNING OF WISDOM.

Solomon, about to explain in summary how we may aspire to true and solid wisdom, praises the fear of the Lord above all things, since it does not happen except to those who fear the Lord, nor does it have a place without the fear of the Lord.

The first requirement of wisdom, therefore, is the fear of the Lord: concerning which Basil, Homily 1 on the Hexaemeron, says: For this fear of reverence toward GOD is like a foundation for one striving toward perfection. Which Blessed Luther expressed succinctly and clearly in a marginal gloss: he who wishes to learn well must first be godly. And in the Wittenberg Tome 3, fol. 195: Holy Scripture wants to have a humble heart. Whoever holds God's Word in honor, loves and values it, and also prays constantly, 'Teach me, O LORD, thy ways, and thy laws.' Since wisdom does not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins, Wis. 1:4, he who indulges in sins and does not strive for true piety can by no means attain true wisdom. For heavenly wisdom is not carnal, but spiritual and holy, James 3:15. Its beginning, therefore, is the fear of the Lord, Ps. 111:10, Prov. 1:7, ch. 9:10. Although some understand this regarding preeminence, that the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom and the first and chief wisdom, it should rather be understood as the beginning, because it is explained by the word תְּחִלַּת (beginning) in Prov. 9:10, and the discourse here is about wisdom, not about the first elements of knowledge: but in order that we may aspire to true and solid wisdom, the fear of the Lord is certainly required: and nothing else is evident from the antithesis, FOOLS DESPISE WISDOM AND INSTRUCTION. For just as the impious, and those destitute of the fear of the Lord, despise wisdom and therefore do not attain it, so the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, since the pious both fear and revere the Lord, and obtain and attain wisdom, with diligent study accompanying it. Pious men, says Olympiodorus, eagerly pursue discipline and wisdom: but those who, by the fear of God (which is of the interior the root cause of sense) are destitute, they draw no taste of discipline or wisdom, but rather are averse to the study of both.

Latin:

vers. 7. TIMOR DOMINI PRINCIPIUM SAPIEN- TIÆ.

Quomodo adspirare ad veram & solidam sa- pientiam possimus, summatim expositurus Salomo, ante omnia timorem Domini laudat, siquidem non nisi timentibus Dominum ea contingat, nec sine ti- more Domini locum habeat.

Requisitum ergo Sapientiæ primum est timor Domini: de quo Basilius homil. 1. Hexaem. Est enim hic reverentiæ erga DEUM timor ad perfectionem con- tendenti velut fundamentum. Quod succincte ac præclare B. Lutherus in glossa marginali expresit: wer wohl lernen will, der muß zum ersten Gottselig seyn. Et Tom. Witteberg. 3. fol. 195. Die Heilige Schrifft will ein demüthig Hertz haben. Wer GOt- tes Wort in ehren hat, lieb und werth hält, auch stets ummerdar bittet, lehre du mich HERR deine Wege, und deine Rechte. Quum sapientia non intret in animam malignam, nec in corpore peccatis subdito ha- bitet, Sap. 1, 4. Sapientiam veram consequi, qui peccatis indulget, nec veræ pietati studet, minime potest. Sapientia enim cœlestis non carnalis est, sed spiritualis, & sancta Jac. 3, 5. Ejus ergo princi- pium timor Domini est Ps. 111, 9. Prov. 1, 7. c. 9, 10. Quod etsi de principatu intelligant nonnulli, quod caput Sapientiæ, & prima ac præcipua sapientia ti- mor Domini sit, de initio tamen potius accipien- dum, quia per תְּחִלַּת initium explicatur Prov. 9, 10. & de sapientia hic sermo est, non de primis ele- mentis cognitionis: ut autem ad veram & solidam sa- pientiam adspiremus, timor Domini utique requi- ritur: nec aliud ex antithefi constat, SAPIEN- TIAM ATQUE DOCTRINAM STULTI DE- SPICIUNT. Uti enim impii, & timore Domi- ni destituti sapientiam despiciunt, adeoque eam non consequuntur, ita timor Domini sapientiæ ini- tium est, siquidem pii & Dominum timentes & re- vereantur, & obtineant ac consequantur, acceden- te studio sedulo, sapientiam. Pii homines, inquit Olympiodorus, disciplinam & sapientiam avide consectantur: qui autem Dei timore (qui interioris sensus radix causa est) destituuntur, illi nullum disci- plinæ aut sapientiæ gustum hauriunt, quin potius studio utraque aversantur.

## 1:8
verse 8.

HEAR MY SON THE DISCIPLINE OF THY FATHER.

The second requirement of true wisdom is obedience toward parents, and teachers, who are in their place, and Doctors of the Church ch. 10, 1. ch. 15, 20. ch. 20, 20. ch. 23, 22. seqq. ch. 28, 24. ch. 29, 15. ch. 30, 14. Cf. a fuller explanation of this requirement declared by a proper example in ch. 4.

Latin:

vers. 8.

AUDI FILI MI DISCIPLINAM PATRIS TUI.

Alterum requisitum veræ sapientiæ est obedien- tia erga parentes, & præceptores, qui eorum loco sunt, Doctoresque Ecclesiæ cap. 10, 1. c. 15, 20. c. 20, 20. c. 23, 22. seqq. c. 28, 24. c. 29, 15. c. 30, 14. Conf. plenior explicatio hujus requisiti exemplo proprio decla- rati c. 4.

## 1:9
verse 9.

THAT GRACE MAY BE ADDED TO THY HEAD.

In Hebrew: FOR A BINDING OF GRACE THEY SHALL BE TO THY HEAD: The Chaldean explains it as beauty and grace, the LXX as στέφανος χαρίτων, B. Luther as ein schöner Schmuck; Solomon explains it by a crown in ch. 4, 9, and Lyranus has interpreted it here as a crown, just as לוית is derived from לוה, to adhere inseparably, and לויות are girdles in 1 Kings 7, 29. 30. but in the following verse it denotes ענקים, ornaments of the neck. Cf. Cant. 4, 9. Jud. 8, 20. The Vulgate rendered it here as chains. The LXX as κλοιὸν χρύσεον, a golden collar. Cartwrightus says of these: Just as chains and diadems procure grace for the man wearing them in the eyes of the common people: so this doctrine [procures grace] for the one who possesses it in the minds of the wise. For it causes both the counsels, which have their seat in the head from the brain, to be sharper and more considered; and the speech, which flows from the throat, to be sweeter and more pleasant.

Latin:

vers. 9.

UT ADDATUR GRATIA CAPITI TUO.

In Ebr. QVIA COPULATIO GRATIÆ ERUNT CAPITI TUO: Chald. explicat pulchritudo, & gratia, LXX. στέφανος χαρίτων, B. Luther. ein schöner Schmuck; Salomo per coronam c. 4, 9. exponit, & Lyranus de corona hic interpretatus est, uti לוית a לוה indivulsæ adhæsit deducitur, & לויות cin- cturæ sunt 1. Reg. 7, 29. 30. at in commate sequenti ענקים ornamenta colli notat. Conf. Cant. 4, 9. Jud. 8, 20. Torques reddidit hic Vulgata. LXX. κλοιὸν χρύσεον collare aureum. De his ita Carth- wrightus: Quemadmodum torques, & Diademata homini illa gestanti gratiam conciliant in oculis vulgi: ita hæc doctrina ejusdem compoti in animis sapientum. Nam efficit ut & consilia, quæ ex cerebro in capite se- dem habent, acutiora & magis consulta sint; & ut ser- mo, qui e gutture fluit, suavior sit, & jucundior.

## 1:10
verse 10.

MY SON, IF SINNERS ENTICE THEE, DO NOT CONSENT TO THEM.

This third requirement of Wisdom is the flight from evil company, as if he were to say, Let a pious mother suckle thee, but let not the impious suckle thee. Receive with natural milk the moral and spiritual milk of maternal doctrine, not the adulterated [milk] of robbers, as Cornel. [says] here. Cf. 2 Tim. 1, 5. 1 Pet. 2, 2. But the Hebrew יפתוך means to entice with speech or a bland and sweet gesture, Exod. 22, 16. Jud. 14, 46. By sinners, however, are understood those who give themselves to wickedness, and exist as persuaders to others so that they might do the same, Gen. 13, 13. Psalm 1, 1. Ps. 26, 9.

Latin:

versus 10.

FILI MI, SI TE LACTAVERINT PEC- CATORES, NE ACQUIESCAS EIS.

Tertium hoc requisitum Sapientiæ est fuga pravi sodalitii, quasi dicat, Lactet te mater pia, non vero lactent te impii. Suscipe cum lacte naturali lac morale & spirituale doctrinæ maternæ, non adulte- rinæ prædonum, ut hic Cornel. Conf. 2. Tim. 1, 5. 1. Pet. 2, 2. Sed Ebr. יפתוך est allicere sermone vel gestu blando & suavi, Exod. 22, 16. Jud. 14, 46. Peccatores autem intelliguntur, qui improbitati se dedunt, & aliis, ut idem faciant, suasores existunt Gen. 13, 13. Psalm. 1, 1. Ps. 26, 9.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

LET US SWALLOW HIM UP, AS HELL [DOES] THE LIVING.

Some understand the word שאול as the sepulcher, which indeed properly denotes hell, and is explained here as such by the LXX, Chald., Vatablus, Pagninus, and others, which sense has greater emphasis: because hell not only devours unexpectedly, but so consumes and absorbs (soul and body, because the wicked will one day feel the swallowing of both) all who live securely, that it can never be satisfied, but is always gaping for more; so that that allusion is made to the history of Korah, Num. 16. Cf. Ps. 123, 3. To swallow is clearly to destroy, or to abolish utterly, as noted by Olympiodorus. Cf. Wis. 2, 13. seqq.

Latin:

Versus 12.

DEGLUTIAMUS EUM, SICUT INFER- NUS VIVENTEM.

Vocem שאול de sepulcro intelligunt non- nulli, quæ vero proprie infernum notat, & a LXX. Chald. Vatabl. Pagnino, aliis de eo hic explicatur, qui sensus majorem emphasin habet: quia infernus non insperato tantum, sed ita devorat, ac absorbet (anima, & corpore, quia utriusque deglutitionem im- pii olim sentient) omnes secure viventes, ut nun- quam tamen exatiari possit, semper pluribus inhiet; ut illa allusio fiat ad historiam Coræ Num. 16. Conf. Ps. 123, 3. Deglutire est plane perdere, vel funditus ab- olere, ut Olympiodoro notatum. Conf. Sap. 2, 13. seqq.

## 1:17
Vers. 17.

BUT IN VAIN IS THE NET SPREAD BEFORE THE EYES OF THE WINGED.

Not inappropriately, with R. Solomon and Aben-Ezra, Eman. Saa explains it thus: as birds fall into a net spread before them, so these, seeing their destruction, perish. And Vatablus: As birds, even though they see the net spread before them, do not therefore fly away and escape the danger, being intent upon the food, and that food is their destruction. Cartwright: As a net spread out does not make birds more cautious, so that they do not run to the food; and in that respect regarding the birds it can truly be said to be placed in vain: so these, caught by the desire for prey, do not notice the snare which either GOD himself or the magistrate sets for them. It is a proverb, says Cornel., signifying that punishment is shown to the wicked in vain, and that it is in vain to threaten thieves with prison and the gallows. Mercer, Lavater, Piscator, and the Vinariens. explain it similarly, to which, as far as the sense is concerned, the exposition of Salazar also tends, even though he takes it interrogatively. Is the net spread in vain before the eyes of the winged? As if he were to say, not at all: for however freely winged birds may fly through the air, they nevertheless sometimes let themselves down to the ground and are entangled in the nets.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

FRUSTRA AUTEM JACITUR RETE AN- TE OCULOS PENNATORUM.

Non incommode cum R. Salomon. & Aben- Efra, Eman. Saa ita explicat: ut aves in rete cadunt ante ipsas expansum, sic isti videntes perniciem per- eunt. Et Vatablus: Sicut aves, tametsi sparsum rete ante se videant, non propterea avolant & periculum effugiunt, escæ nimirum attentæ, illisque est exitio earum esca. Cartvvrightus: Ut cassis explicatus avibus illas cautiores non facit, quo minus ad escam accurrant; eoque avium respectu frustra collocari ve- re dici potest: sic isti cupiditate prædæ capti non anim- advertunt laqueum, quem vel DEUS ipse, vel magistratus illis tendit. Proverbium est, inquit Cor- nel. significans frustra impiis ostendi supplicium, frustra furibus comminari quempiam carcerem & patibulum. Similiter explicant Mercerus, Lavaterus, Piscator, Vinariens. quo etiam, quantum ad sensum, abit ex- positio Salazaris, etsi is interrogative accipiat h. m. Frustrane jacitur rete ante oculos pennatorum? quasi dicat, minime vero: nam quantumvis libere per ae- ra pennatæ aves ferantur, aliquando tamen sese ad terram demittunt, & cassibus implicantur.

## 1:18
verf. 18. THEY ALSO LIE IN WAIT AGAINST THEIR OWN BLOOD, AND DEVISE FRAUDS AGAINST THEIR OWN SOULS.

R. Aben-Ezra, R. Levi, and the Tigurina take 'their' blood relatively, i.e., of the winged or of the travelers for whom the net is spread: But it is more correctly taken reciprocally: because those snares prepared were already treated in verse 11, and the reciprocal sense fits the simile better, that by those snares they harm themselves, and precipitate their own souls into the danger of temporal and eternal salvation. This sense is favored by the Vulgate, the LXX, the interpreters of Piscator and Junius, Mariana, Menochius, as well as the interpretation of Mercer and B. Luther. Cf. Ps. 7, 16.

Latin:

verf. 18. IPSI QUOQUE CONTRA SANGUINEM SUUM INSIDIANTUR, ET MOLIUNTUR FRAUDES CONTRA ANIMAS SUAS.

R. Aben-Ezra, R. Levi & Tigurina relative acci- piunt sanguinem ILLORUM, pennatorum scil. vel viatorum, quibus rete panditur: Sed rectius accipi- tur reciproce: quia de insidiis illis paratis jam vers. 11. actum, & similitudini magis reciprocus sensus con- venit, quod insidiis illis sibi ipsis noceant, & animas suas in discrimen temporalis & æternæ salutis præci- pitent. Cui sensui favet cum Vulgata LXX. In- terpp. Piscatoris & Junii, Mariana, Menochii, ut & Merceri, & B. Lutheri interpretatio. Conf. Ps. 7, 16.

## 1:19
vers. 19. SO ARE THE PATHS OF EVERY ONE THAT IS GREEDY OF GAIN, WHICH TAKETH AWAY THE SOULS OF THE OWNERS THEREOF.

That such also are the paths of everyone greedy for gain (whom he makes similar to such ensnarers and robbers), and with a similar outcome, the GAIN is taught to take away the souls of its owners, according to the Hebrew truth. Thus Aben-Ezra; that the things taken by robbery take the robber himself. Similarly Beda, Lyranus, Mercer, Junius, Vatablus, Menochius, Tirinus, and others. For avarice kills the soul, and often the body of the avaricious man. Cf. 1 Tim. 6, 10.

Latin:

vers. 19. SIC SEMITÆ OMNIS AVARI ANIMAS POSSIDENTIUM RAPIUNT.

Tales quoque semitas esse omnis lucro inhian- tis, (quem similem talibus insidiatoribus & prædo- nibus facit) similique exitu LUCRUM animarum Dominorum illius rapere docetur, juxta Ebræam veritatem. Sic Aben-Ezra; quæ rapina sublata sunt, raptorem ipsum rapiunt. Similiter Beda, Ly- ranus, Mercerus, Junius, Vatablus, Menochius, Tiri- nus & alii. Avaritia enim occidit animam, sæpe & corpus avari. Conf. 1. Tim. 6, 10.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. WISDOM CRIETH WITHOUT.

That hypostatic wisdom is to be understood as the Son of God himself is evident from the predicates, for actions belong to subjects: nor is a prosopopoeia to be invented without cause: that speech in verse 24 seqq. argues primarily for hypostatic Wisdom, where mention is made of imitation, the extension of the hand, counsel, laughter, and derision: and verse 28, Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer: which befit a divine Person, not an essential attribute of God: Compare Isa. 58, 9; c. 65, 1. 7. 10. And the ancients explain this as referring to the Son of God. Hilar. in Ps. 118, Tertul. in Scorpiaco, Salvianus lib. 4 ad Eccles. Cathol., Beda, and others: of the recent interpreters, Hugo, Dionys., Lyranus, Lavater, Tremell., Piscator, Cartwright, Osiander, Vinariens., and others. See what has been said regarding Prov. chap. 8. But the fact that the plural noun חָכְמוֹת is used, is done on account of the manifold cry; because wisdom thus cries out in the streets, in the doorways, at the head of the bustling crowds, and through the whole world, as if in each individual place a peculiar invitress were uttering her voice, and thus there were not one preaching wisdom, but many: just as the seven spirits sent out into all the earth, Apoc. 5, 6, denote the Holy Spirit, who is one τῇ ὑποστάσει, exerting himself in the seven Asiatic churches, nay, everywhere throughout the whole world by his power, not otherwise than if a peculiar Spirit were present to the churches and to individual believers. The sum of this proclamation, which is made publicly everywhere, so that it may reach everyone, is the sum of the sermon preached more explicitly by Christ in the days of his flesh: He who will have believed, will be saved, he who will not have believed shall be condemned. Wisdom proposes this latter clause more lengthily here, so that it might, if possible, snatch the unbelievers from condemnation, who refuse to hear it, and spurn the counsel of its salvation, Luke 7:30. But it embraces the former clause succinctly in v. 32. For it preaches, gives voice, cries out, speaks its own utterances, then the accumulation also of places outside, in the streets, at the head of the tumultuous (of the streets, which resound and roar from the noise of trumpets), in the openings of the gates, in the city, or through the whole world, and the specification of the objects, that to the simple, to the mockers, and to the foolish or stubborn, and the impious, the Ruchlosen, as blessed Luther emphatically says, Wisdom cries out to those who hate wisdom: Turn (from sins) to hear and admit my rebuke, or chastisement, with the promise in v. 23. אַבִּיעָה ἀναβλύσω as Aquila and Theodot. rightly explain as 'I will cause to gush forth' (from נָבַע which brings about fruitful irrigation. Cf. Prov. 18:4, Isa. 35:7) my spirit to you (cf. John 7:38). I will make you know my words, and what else does the whole speech and invitation of Hypostatic Wisdom cry out, than a most serious will, and an internal, ardent desire for conversion and salvation in the calling of the impious, and a universal calling, with a benevolent intention of communicating grace for salvation? In what way the Son of God refutes with a clear voice that absolute Calvinistic decree of election and preterition, and openly confounds the impious doctrine concerning the will of good pleasure, and the internal [will], different and discrepant from the will of the sign, and the external.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SAPIENTIA FORIS PRÆDICAT.

Hypostaticam sapientiam intelligendam esse ipsummet Filium Dei e prædicatis constat, actiones enim suppositorum sunt: neque prosopopœia fingen- da est sine causa: arguit imprimis hypostaticam Sa- pientiam illa oratio vers. 24. seqq. ubi imitationis, extensionis manus, consilii, risus, subsannationis men- tio fit: & vers. 28. Tunc invocabunt me, sed non exaudiam: quæ Personæ divinæ conveniunt, non attributo Dei essentiali: Confer Esa. 58, 9. c. 65, 1. 7. 10. idque e veteribus de Filio Dei explicant. Hi- lar. in Psal. 118. Tertul. in Scorpiaco, Salvianus lib. 4. ad Eccles. Cathol. Beda & alii: e recentioribus in- terpretibus Hugo, Dionys. Lyranus, Lavater. Tre- mell. Piscator, Cartwrightus, Osiander, Vinariens. alii. Vid. quæ ad Prov. 8. cap. dicta. Quod au- tem plurale adhibitum nomen חָכְמוֹת, factum est multiplicis clamoris causa; quia sapientia ita in plateis, in ostiis, in capite tumultuantium, & per totum orbem clamat, ac si singulis in locis peculiaris invita- trix vocem suam ederet, adeoque non una esset sa- pientia prædicatrix, sed plures: quemadmodum septem spiritus emissi in omnem terram Apoc. 5, 6. Spi- ritum S. qui unus est τῇ ὑποστάσει notant, in septem Ecclesiis Asiaticis, imo ubique per totum terrarum orbem sese exerentem virtute sua, non secus, ac si Ecclesiis & fidelibus singulis peculiaris adesset Spi- ritus. Summa hujus præconii, quod publice passim fit, ut ad omnes penetrare possit, summa est concionis a Christo in diebus carnis explica- tius prædicatæ: Qui crediderit, salvus erit, qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Quod posterius membrum prolixius hic proponit sapientia, ut con- demnatione si fieri possit, eripiat incredulos, qui audire ipsam renuunt, & consilium salutis ipsius spernunt Luc. 7, 30. Prius autem membrum suc- cinte complectitur v. 32.
