Illa vero, prædicat, dat vocem, clamat, eloquia sua dicit, tum accumulatio e- tiam locorum foris, in plateis, in capite tumultuan- tium (platearum, quæ perstrepunt, ac reboant ex strepitu tubarum) in ostiis portarum, in urbe, vel per totum orbem, & specificatio objectorum, quod ad sim- plices, ad derisores, & ad stultos vel pervicaces, & im- pios, die Ruchlosen, ut emphatice B. Lutherus, odio habentes sapientiam clamitet sapientia: Convertimi- ni (a peccatis) ad increpationem, vel castigationem meam audiendam & admittendam, cum promissio- ne v. 23. אַבִּיעָה ἀναβλύσω ut Aquila & Theodot. recte exponunt scaturire faciam (a נָבַע quod fœcun- dam irrigationem infert. Conf. Prov. 18, 4. Esa. 35, 7.) vobis spiritum meum (conf. Joh. 7, 38.) Scire vos faciam verba mea, & tota oratio & invitatio sapien- tiæ Hypostaticæ quid aliud clamant, quam maxime seriam voluntatem, & internum, ardensque deside- rium conversionis, & salutis in vocatione impio- rum, & universalem vocationem, cum benevola intentione communicandæ gratiæ ad salutem? Quo pacto refellit Filius Dei λευκάδι φωνῇ absolutum illud Calvinisticum electionis & præteritionis decre- tum, & confundit palam impiam doctrinam de vo- luntate beneplaciti, & interna, diversa & discrepante a voluntate signi, & externa.

## 1:26
v. 26.

I ALSO WILL LAUGH AT YOUR DESTRUCTION.

These things pertain to the consequent and judiciary will, and things said anthropopathically must be understood theopathically. To laugh, says Gregory the Great, Morals, bk. 9, ch. 20, is to be unwilling to pity human affliction: wherefore I also will laugh at your destruction, that is, I will not sympathize with your affliction with any pity. But this expression introduces something more, namely that God wishes to punish them sharply, and to expose them to be mocked and derided by all, indeed to rejoice in their destruction, because of justice exercised against his mockers and contemners, who disparaged all his correction, as is had in v. 30, where the LXX have ἐμυκτήριζον, they as it were turned up their noses, or mocked my reproofs.

Latin:

vers. 26.

EGO QUOQUE IN INTERITU VESTRO RIDEBO.

Pertinent hæc ad voluntatem consequentem, & judiciariam, & ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicta θεοπρεπῶς intelligenda sunt. Ridere Dei, inquit Gregor. M. l. 9. Moral. c. 20. est humanæ nolle afflictioni misereri: quare ego quoque in interitu vestro ridebo, hoc est, af- flictioni vestræ nulla pietate compatiar. Sed amplius quid infert hæc loquutio, quod nempe Deus acri- ter ipsos punire, omnibusque irridendos, & subsan- nandos objicere, imo in ipsorum interitu gaudere velit, ob justitiam adversus irrisores, & contemto- res suos exercitam, qui detraxerunt universæ corre- ptioni ejus, ut habetur v. 30. ubi LXX. habent ἐμυ- κτήριζον quasi naso adunco suspenderunt, vel subsan- narunt meas redargutiones.

## 1:32
v. 32.

THE AVERSION OF THE PEOPLES WILL KILL THEM, AND THE PROSPERITY OF FOOLS WILL DESTROY THEM) The interpreter took this from Symmachus: ὅτι ἀποστροφὴ νηπίων ἀνελεῖ ἀυτοὺς, where ἀποστροφὴ is that which is called by more elegant Greeks ἀπροσεξία. פְּתָיִם are ἄνοι. Cf. 7:11, πεπωρωθέντες below 7:22. And because children are wont to be such, therefore it is often translated νήπιοι.

By מְשׁוּבַת, an aversion from good, from counsel, from the proclamation of God of the simple, who prefer to persist in their ignorance and damnable simplicity than to lend ears to wisdom, and therefore remain in aversion, nor are they converted to rebuke: thus by aversion, which is the customary meaning of the word, the Chaldean, Zurich, Mercer, Lavater, Piscator, the Dutch, the Vinarienses, and Dr. Geier explain it. Symmachus himself said ἀποστροφὴν, and why it should be taken otherwise than in the customary sense of aversion does not appear, even if it pleased some to render the Hebrew word as 'rest', but this is contrary to the usage of Scripture. Cf. Jer. 2:19, 3:22, 5:6, 8:5, Hos. 11:7. Blessed Luther correctly expressed the sense: 'what the foolish lusts for, kills them'.

v. same. AND THE PROSPERITY OF FOOLS WILL DESTROY THEM.

Thus also Aquila, Symmachus, Pagninus, Vatablus, Münster, Cartwright, and blessed Luther render it 'prosperity' and 'fortune'. The Chaldean explains it by 'error', and Aben Ezra by 'guilt', R. Levi by 'idleness', Junius by 'tranquillity', which thus far agree as to the sense, because the abuse of prosperity and fortune is regarded, and culpable tranquillity, Isa. 16:49. Prosperity, says Bernard, Sermon 3 on Palm Sunday, will destroy not all, but the foolish, because the wise know how to use their prosperity modestly for their own benefit and progress. For the most part, to use favorable circumstances beyond merit provides the beginning of greater calamities for foolish men. Cf. Deut. 32:15, and blessed Luther, Vol. 3, Lat. Jena, fol. 513, preface to Amos.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

AVERSIO POPULORUM INTERFICIET EOS, ET PROSPERITAS STULTORUM PERDET EOS) Hoc ex Symmacho sumsit interpres: ὅτι ἀποστροφὴ νηπίων ἀνελεῖ ἀυ- τοὺς, ubi ἀποστροφὴ est id, quod Græcis elegantiioribus dicitur ἀπροσεξία. פְּתָיִם sunt ἄνοι. Of. 7, 11. πεπφωθέντες infra 7, 22. Et quia tales esse solent pueri, ideo sæpe vertitur νήπιοι.

Per מְשׁוּבַת aversio a bono, a consilio, a præconio Dei simplicium, qui malunt in sua insci- tia, & damnabili simplicitate persistere, quam sa- pientiæ aures præbere, ideoque in aversione perma- nent, nec ad increpationem convertuntur: ita per aversionem, quæ usitata vocis est significatio, expli- cant Chald. Tigur. Mercer. Lavat. Piscat. Belgæ, Vi- nariens. Dn. D. Geier. Symmachus ipse ἀποσρο- φὴν dixit, quæ cur aliter quam consueto aversionis sensu accipi debeat, non apparet, etsi per requiem nonnullis placuerit vocem Ebræam reddere, sed præter usum Scripturæ. Conf. Jer. 2, 19. c. 3, 22. c. 5, 6. c. 8, 5. Hos. 11, 7. B. Lutherus sensum recte ex- pressit: was den Albern gelüstet, tödtet sie.

vers. eod. ET PROSPERITAS STULTORUM PER- DET EOS.

Sic etiam Aquila, Symmachus, Pagnin. Vata- blus, Münsterus, Cartwright, B. Lutherus reddunt prosperitas & fortuna. Chald. per errorem explicat & Aben Ezra per culpam, R. Levi per otium, Junius per tranquillitatem, quæ hactenus quoad sensum conveniunt, quia prosperitatis & fortunæ abusus respicitur, & tranquillitas culpabilis Es. 16, 49. Pro- speritas, inquit Bernhard. Serm. 3. in Dom. Palm. non omnium, sed stultorum perdet illos, quia sapientes norunt prosperitate sua uti modeste ad suum commo- dum & profectum. Plerumque secundis rebus præter meritum uti stolidis hominibus majorum calamita- tum initium præbet. Conf. Deut. 32, 15. & B. Luth. Tom. 3. Lat. Jen. fol. 513. præfat. in Amos.

## 1:33
v. 33. BUT HE WHO HEARS ME SHALL REST WITHOUT TERROR, AND SHALL ENJOY ABUNDANCE, WITH THE FEAR OF EVILS REMOVED.

In Hebrew it is, 'but whoever hears me, shall dwell confidently, and shall rest from the fear of evil.' By this antithesis the Son of God teaches that whoever hears him crying out and preaching, and obeys him through faith, and receives his cry and proclamation with true faith, he shall dwell confidently, shall enjoy true tranquility, and shall be free from all evil, nay, even from the fear of evil. Cf. Jer. 23, 6. ch. 33, 6. Rom. 5, 3. The fruit and consequence of faith is, along with true liberation from evil, tranquility, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit Rom. 14, 17. Which true and solid tranquility of the faithful is opposed to the unhappy rest and security of the impious.

Latin:

Vers. 33. QUI AUTEM ME AUDIERIT ABSQUE TERRORE REQUIESCET, ET ABUNDAN- TIA PERFRUETUR TIMORE MALORUM SUBLATO.

In Ebr. est, qui autem me audierit, habitabit confidenter, & requiescet a timore mali. Hac anti- thesi Filius Dei docet, quisquis ipsum audierit cla- mantem, & prædicantem, eique per fidem obedie- rit, ac clamorem & præconium ejus vera fide susce- perit, eum fiducialiter habitaturum, tranquillitate vera fruiturum, & a malo omni, imo a timore etiam mali liberum futurum. Conf. Jer. 23, 6. cap. 33, 6. Rom. 5, 3. Fructus & consequens fidei est cum ve- ra liberatione a malo tranquillitas, pax & gaudium in Spiritu Sancto Rom. 14, 17. Quæ vera & solida tranquillitas fidelium impiorum infelici quieti & securitati opponitur.

## 2:1-2 Argument
CHAPTER II.

For true wisdom there is need of attention, that we may obtain the same through pious prayer and diligent investigation: because it is granted by God for our salvation, that we may aspire to true justice, judgment, and uprightness, and be guarded from evil, from perverse ways, and from the strange woman, who leads to nothing but destruction.

ver. 1. 2. MY SON, IF YOU RECEIVE MY WORDS, AND HIDE MY COMMANDMENTS WITHIN YOU, SO THAT YOUR EAR HEARS WISDOM, INCLINE YOUR HEART TO KNOW PRUDENCE.

In the Hebrew, the two verses are rightly expounded by the blessed Luther in such a way that it is taught that there is need of pious attention if divine words are to be received through faith and kept; and therefore, for the sake of a clearer sense, Osiander inserted 'DEVOTE EFFORT,' that your ear may hear wisdom. For the discourse is completed in verses 1 and 2: this, therefore, is what is commanded and required in general, that you make your ear attend to wisdom, and incline your heart to understanding. There appears no reason why one should depart from the version of the blessed Luther.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Ad veram sapientiam opus est attentione, ut pia precatione & diligenti indagatione ean- dem obtineamus: quia a Deo conceditur ad nostram salutem, ut ad veram justitiam, ju- dicium & rectitudinem adspiremus, & a malo, viis perversis, & extranea muliere custodiamur, non nisi ad exitium perdu- cente.

vers. 1. 2. FILI MI, SI SUSCEPERIS SERMO- NES MEOS, ET MANDATA MEA ABSCON- DERIS PENES TE, UT AUDIAT SAPIEN- TIAM AURIS TUA INCLINA COR TUUM AD COGNOSCENDAM PRUDENTIAM.

IN Ebræo duo versus recte a B. Luthero ita expo- nuntur, ut attentione pia opus esse doceatur, si suscipiendi per fidem & custodiendi sint sermones divini; ideoque sensus evidentioris causa Osiander interposuit OPERAM DA, ut audiat sapientiam auris tua. Absolvitur enim versu 1. & 2. oratio: hoc ergo est, quod præcipitur & requiritur in uni- versum, ut attendere facias sapientiæ aurem tuam, & inclines cor tuum intelligentiæ. Non apparet cau- sa, cur a B. Lutheri versione discedendum sit.

## 2:3
ver. 3. FOR IF YOU CALL UPON WISDOM, AND INCLINE YOUR HEART TO PRUDENCE.

That 'ki', introducing a cause in its proper meaning, teaches that the former verses presented a complete discourse: which is now explained and further confirmed; as also the LXX rendered it with the Vulgate, the blessed Luther, Münster, and others: Therefore there is no reason why Mercer's 'nay rather,' or Pagninus's 'nay if,' or Let us also prefer Junius when expounding. Here is shown first the special means of acquiring wisdom, which is PRAYER. For if you cry out for understanding, which Bede expounds, if you call upon the Son of GOD, B. Luther, Osiander, the Vinarienses, Dn. D. Gejer. If you cry out to obtain understanding, or call upon GOD, and have given your voice to prudence (or to obtain prudence) (if you have prayed for it: therefore the Vulgate is to be corrected here) because the first and chief thing here is prayer, by which Solomon also obtained wisdom 1 Kings 3:6 ff. Cf. Ps. 119 and those to the same B. Luther, as also James 1:5, Wis. 6:6, Sir. 39:1. Capellus here, from the Chaldean, rendering it 'if you call understanding MOTHER', accuses the Hebrew text of corruption, as if for אִם־לַבִּינָה it now reads אֵם לַבִּינָה, but Grotius did not wish to follow him in that. For there is no suspicion of corruption underlying the constant consensus of the Hebrew Codices.

Latin:

vers. 3. SI ENIM SAPIENTIAM INVOCA- VERIS, ET INCLINAVERIS COR TUUM PRUDENTIÆ.

Illud כי causam significatu proprio inferens, docet priora orationem completam exhibuisse: quæ nunc explicatur, & confirmatur ulterius; uti etiam cum Vulgata, B. Luthero, Münstero, aliis- que LXX. reddidere : Non ergo est, quod Mercerum quin imo, vel Pagninum, imo si, vel Junium quinetiam exponentes præferamus. Mon- stratur hic primum medium speciale sapientiæ ac- quirendæ, quod est ORATIO. Si enim ad intel- ligentiam clamaveris, quod Beda exponit, si Filium DEI invocaveris, B. Luther. Osiander, Vinariens. Dn. D. Gejer. Si pro consequenda intelligentia cla- maveris, vel DEUM invocaveris, & ad prudentiam, (vel pro impetranda prudentia) vocem tuam dede- ris (si pro ea precatus fueris: corrigenda ergo hic vulgata) quia primum & præcipuum hic est preca- tio, qua Salomo etiam consequutus est sapientiam 1. Reg. 3, 6. seqq. Conf. Ps. 119. & quæ ad eundem B. Luther. ut & Jac. 1, 5. Sap. 6, 6. Syr. 39, 1. Capellus hic ex Chaldæo, reddente si MATREM intelligen- tiam vocaveris, corruptionis arguit Ebræum textum quasi pro אִם־לַבִּינָה nunc legatur אֵם לַבִּינָה, sed eum sequi in eo noluit Grotius. Nulla enim subest in con- stante Codicum Ebræorum consensu corruptelæ suspicio.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

IF YOU SEEK HER AS MONEY.

In Hebrew, as silver: for the metaphor is taken from silver in metallic mines, sought with great care, which also occurs in the word ἐρευνᾶτε John 5:39: just as it is added here, AND AS TREASURES YOU SHALL DIG HER, or rather you shall have searched her out: חָפַשׂ is to search out with all attention and zeal, even that which is intimately hidden, Gen. 31:35, Psalm 64:8, Proverbs 20:27. Chrysostom in the Greek Catena: As the greedy seek silver, so you [seek] wisdom. Cf. Matt. 13:44.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

SI QUÆSIERIS EAM QUASI PECU- NIAM.

In Ebr. quasi argentum: nam ab argento in fodinis metallicis magna cura quærendo desumta est metaphora, quæ etiam in verbo ἐρευνᾶτε Job. 5, 39. occurrit: quemadmodum hic additur, ET SICUT THESAUROS FODERIS ILLAM, vel potius scrutatus fueris illam: חָפַשׂ est omni attentio- ne & studio, etiam intime reconditum scrutari, Gen. 31, 35. Psalm. 64, 8. Proverb. 20, 27. Chrysost. in Caten. Græcor. Sicut avari quærunt argentum, ita tu sapien- tiam. Conf. Matth. 13, 44.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

THEN YOU SHALL UNDERSTAND THE FEAR OF THE LORD, AND FIND THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD.

The fruit of pious attention, that is, of prayer and the investigation of wisdom, is the perception of true religion (the fear of the Lord) and the true knowledge of God, in which eternal life consists John 17:3. Then it is confirmed (which Solomon says here) by prayers and the investigation of wisdom in the Word of God, in whose chambers true religion and the true knowledge of God, hidden away, must be brought forth by diligent scrutiny.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

TUNC INTELLIGES TIMOREM DOMI- NI, ET SCIENTIAM DEI INVENIES.

Fructus piæ attentionis, hoc est, precationis, & indagationis sapientiæ, est perceptio veræ religionis (timoris Domini) & veræ Dei cognitio, in qua vita æterna consistit Joh. 17, 3. Tunc confirmatur (quod hic dicit Salomo) precibus & indagatione sapientiæ in Verbo Dei, in cujus thalamis abscondita sedulo scrutinio eruenda est, vera religio, vera Dei cogni- tio.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

BECAUSE THE LORD GIVES WISDOM, AND FROM HIS MOUTH [COME] PRUDENCE AND KNOWLEDGE.

For because the Lord gives wisdom, the same must be sought from the Lord by prayers, Job 36:8, Dan. 2:20, James 1:5; because from his mouth is prudence and knowledge, it must be sought and drawn from his word. Cf. Is. 1:20, ch. 40:5, ch. 58:14, John 5:39, 2 Tim. 3:15.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

QUIA DOMINUS DAT SAPIENTIAM, ET EX ORE EJUS PRUDENTIA ET SCIEN- TIA.

Quia enim Dominus sapientiam dat, a Do- mino eadem precibus petenda est, Job. 36, 8. Dan. 2, 20. Jac. 1, 5. quia ex ore ejus est prudentia & scien- tia, e verbo ejus quærenda, & haurienda ea est. Conf. Es. 1, 20. c. 40, 5. c. 58, 14. Joh. 5, 39. 2. Tim. 3, 15.

## 2:7
Verse 7.

HE WILL GUARD THE SALVATION OF THE UPRIGHT.

He now pursues the fruit of the study of wisdom more abundantly: In Hebrew it is 'he will hide' or 'he will preserve' (cf. Cant. 7:13 and Prov. 1:11, ch. 2:1) for the upright, that is, the just, Psalm 32:2. תּוּשִׁיָּה which Osiander renders WORK, Junius whatever truly is: others more specifically wisdom, from a comparison of Prov. 3:21, ch. 8:21. I do not see why one should not adhere to the general meaning of the word, which, however, is viewed here not in an absolute state, but a respective one: namely, it is guarded through the study of wisdom for the just and upright to be what they themselves have, so that they may persevere in the state of justice: and thus salvation is preserved for them, as the LXX and Vulgate rendered it: whence some, as Cornelius notes, explain it thus: God will guard the essence, that is, the solidity and constant perseverance in good of the just, which is a huge treasure, for it leads straight to heavenly glory. For perseverance is the highest gift of God: Where the aforementioned Jesuit orthodoxly adds what follows: Therefore the great gift of perseverance is in the hand of GOD alone, which the just man cannot merit by condignity, but can only demand and obtain from Him by suppliant prayers.

verse of the same.

AND HE WILL PROTECT THOSE WALKING IN INTEGRITY. In Hebrew, A shield (he will be) to those walking uprightly. He not only preserves the just in justice, but is also a shield to them against the fiery darts of Satan of every kind. Cf. Gen. 15:1, Deut. 33:29, Ps. 84:12.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

CUSTODIET RECTORUM SALUTEM.

Fructum jam uberius exequitur studii sapien- tiæ: In Ebr. est recondet vel asservabit (conf. Cant. 7, 13. & Prov. 1, 11. c. 2, 1. rectis hoc est, justis Psalm. 32, 2. תּוּשִׁיָּה quod Osiander reddit OPUS, Junius quicquid revera est: alii specialius sapientiam, e col- latione Prov. 3, 21. c. 8, 21. Non video, cur non ge- nerali vocis significatui inhærendum sit, quod ta- men non in statu absoluto, sed respectivo hic specta- tur: nimirum custoditur per sapientiæ studium justis & rectis esse quale ipsi habent, ut in statu justitiæ per- severent: adeoque ita conservatur ipsis salus, ut cum LXX. Vulg. reddidit: unde nonnulli, notante Cor- nelio, sic exponunt: Deus custodiet essentiam, hoc est soliditatem, & constantem in bono perseverantiam ju- storum, quæ ingens est thesaurus, recta enim ducit ad gloriam cœlestem. Perseverantia enim est summum De donum: Ubi Jesuita praedictus orthodoxe addit, quae sequuntur: Igitur magnum perseverantiae donum in manu solius DEI est, quod justus mereri de condigno nequit, sed tantum supplicibus precibus ab eo flagitare & impetrare.

vers. eod.

ET PROTEGET GRADIENTES SIMPLI- CITER. In Ebr. Scutum (erit) ambulantibus integre. Non tantum conservat justos in justitia, sed scutum illis etiam est adversus omnis generis ignita Satanae tela. Conf. Gen. 15, 1. Deut. 33, 29. Psal. 84, 12.

## 2:8
verse 8.

PRESERVING THE PATHS OF JUSTICE AND GUARDING THE WAY OF HIS SAINTS. In Hebrew, that they may guard the paths of judgment, and the way of his mercies (Junius, of those whom he has received kindly; Chaldean, צדיקין of the just) he will preserve. The sense is that God so guards the upright in the state of justice and protects those walking in integrity like a shield, that they may be able to observe accurately the paths of equity and justice: Cf. v. 11 seqq., ch. 17:23, Gen. 18:19, Ps. 27:11. Therefore, God himself, the keeper of Israel, will guard with singular care the way of those whom he has received kindly, Ps. 121:4, Ps. 4:4, Ps. 30:5, Ps. 31:24, Ps. 32:6, Ps. 86:2.

Latin:

vers. 8.

SERVANS SEMITAS JUSTITIAE ET VIAM SANCTORUM CUSTODIENS. In Ebr. ut custodiant semitas judicii, & viam mi- sericordium ejus (Junius, eorum quos benigne accepit, Chald. צדיקין justorum) conservabit. Sensus est, quod Deus ita custodiat rectos in justitiae statu & in- star scuti protegat integre ambulantes, ut accurate observare queant semitas aequi justique: Conf. v. 11. seqq. c. 17, 23. Gen. 18, 19. Ps. 27, 11. Ideo viam eorum quos benigne accepit, singulari cura Deus ipse, cu- stos Israelis, custodiet, Ps. 121, 4. Ps. 4, 4. Ps. 30, 5. Ps. 31, 24. Ps. 32, 6. Ps. 86, 2.

## 2:9
verse 9.

THEN YOU WILL UNDERSTAND JUSTICE, AND JUDGMENT, AND EQUITY, AND EVERY GOOD PATH. Before, he had promised, then, when you have performed those things which I said concerning the invocation and investigation of wisdom, you will know the fear of God, and you will find the knowledge of God: now he illustrates that further by way of explanation, then you will understand, not only theoretically and by bare knowledge, but practically, true justice, which is of faith, and the judgment which God requires, while we judge ourselves, lest we be judged by the Lord 1 Cor. 11:31, John 16:10, 11, and rectitudes, whatever things are right before God and consistent with the rules of the divine word, and thus every good path. Cf. Prov. 1:3, Psalm 23:3, Ps. 140:6, Prov. 4:11, 26, Isa. 26:5, 7.

Latin:

vers. 9.

TUNC INTELLIGES JUSTITIAM, ET JU- DICIUM, ET AEQUITATEM, ET OMNEM SEMITAM BONAM. Antea promiserat, tunc, cum praestiteris ea, quae dixi, de invocatione, & investigatione sapien- tiae, cognosces timorem Dei, & invenies cognitionem Dei: nunc id κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν illustrat amplius, tunc intelliges, non tantum theoretice, & nuda cognitione, sed practice justitiam veram, quae est fidei, & judicium quod Deus requirit, dum nos ipsos judicamus, ne ju- dicemur a Domino 1. Cor. 11, 31. Joh. 16, 10. 11. & recti- tudines, quaecunque recte coram Deo, & regulae di- vini verbi congrua sunt, adeoque omnem semitam bonam. Conf. Prov. 1, 3. Psalm. 23, 3. Psal. 140, 6. Prov. 4, 11. 26. Esa. 26, 5. 7.

## 2:10
verse 10.

IF WISDOM ENTERS YOUR HEART. There follows another fruit of the study of Wisdom; inasmuch as by it we are not only instructed and preserved in the fear of God and the true knowledge of God, but we are also guarded and preserved from evil and the perversity of life and doctrine: we are not only led in every good path, but we are also rescued from the evil and dark way. And therefore כִּי here is taken for WHEN, as Proverbs 21:22, Gen. 4:12, as Aben Ezra and R. Levi, the Vulgate, B. Luther, and others interpret: when wisdom has entered your heart, if you have admitted wisdom into the inner chambers of your heart, AND KNOWLEDGE HAS BEEN PLEASANT TO YOUR SOUL, or rather, has been charming and sweet, as the love of women is wont to be sweet, 2 Sam. 1:26, where the same word נָעַם is used: for it is not just a momentary entry, but such an admission, as Dr. Geier notes, is marked, so that such a guest may be cherished with the greatest delight and applause. Compare Psalm 19:11. Psalm 119:103. COUNSEL (thought or prudence, to which this is attributed as a secondary cause, which had been attributed before to God as the primary cause) WILL GUARD YOU, PRUDENCE (intelligence) WILL PRESERVE YOU, THAT YOU MAY BE RESCUED FROM THE EVIL WAY, to rescue from the evil way, as if from the most present danger, which the word הִצִיל implies 1 Sam. 17:32, Psalm 18:1. It is very well known that 'way' denotes a manner of living and actions: whence it has been rightly observed by Mr. Dr. Geier that a perverse manner of life as well as of doctrine, or an aberration from the true and the good, is indicated here. Compare Psalm 1:1, Psalm 119:29, 101, Prov. 8:15, ch. 16:29, ch. 28:10, Ezek. 3:18. I would prefer, however, that it be rendered here as 'from the life of an EVIL man,' because the following member of this verse 12 is explanatory of the present one, along with the others that follow in verses 13, 14, and 15, which deal with an evil man straying from the true and the good: just as afterwards in verse 16 and following, it deals with a strange woman, from whom we are likewise rescued by means of this divine wisdom: which therefore guards us so that we may be safe both from the manifest and violent seductions of any EVIL MAN, and from the hidden and flattering enticements and deceptions of a STRANGE WOMAN. Safe from the seductive words of an evil man, because he speaks perversely (verse 10), and from his scandalous works, by which he abandons the paths more rightly shown in the Holy Scriptures (Gal. 6:16), so that he walks through dark ways, partly of errors and ignorance (Isa. 9:2, Eph. 5:8), and partly of crimes and malice (Rom. 13:15, Eph. 5:2, 1 Thess. 5:4), which lead down into eternal darkness (Matt. 8:12, ch. 22:13, Jude 7:6. Compare Job 3:19, 20), and from his most perverse pursuits and counsels, inasmuch as he rejoices to do evil and exults in the perversities of evil, whence the PATHS of such (he notes a custom and a habit of sinning) are perverse: or as Junius more rightly expresses it, 'who, I would prefer because [they] are perverse in their windings,' which sense the following member demands, 'and are stubborn in their orbits,' so that the preposition ב is to be understood in the former member, which is expressed in the latter. The LXX render it καμπόλαι, their paths are bent. Rashi explains it through tortuosity and obliquity, but the Vulgate less conveniently explains it as 'infamous.' A deflection in doctrine and life is noted: as Blessed Luther says, 'folgen dem Abwege' [follow the wrong path].

Latin:

versus 10.

SI INTRAVERIT SAPIENTIA COR TUUM. Sequitur alter fructus studii Sapientiae; utpote qua non tantum in timore Dei & vera Dei agnitione erudimur, & conservamur, sed etiam a malo & per- versitate vitae & doctrinae custodimur, & praeservamur: non tantum in omni semita bona deducimur; sed e- tiam a via mala & tenebricosa eruimur. Ideoque כִּי hic accipitur pro QUANDO, ut Proverb. 21, 22. Gen. 4, 12. ut Aben Esr. & R. Levi, Vulgat. B. Luther. & alii interpretantur: quando sapientia intraverit cor tuum, si sapientiam in penetralia cordis tui admise- ris, ET SCIENTIA ANIMAE TUAE PLACUE- RIT, vel potius, amoena & dulcis fuerit, quam dul- cis solet esse amor foeminarum, 2. Sam. 1, 26. ubi idem verbum נָעַם: non enim ingressus tantum momentaneus, sed ejusmodi admissio, observante Dn. D. Geiero notatur, ut summa cum delectatione, applausuque talis foveatur hospes. Confer Psalm. 19, 11. Psalm. 119, 103. CONSILIUM (cogitantia vel prudentia, cui id tribuitur ceu causae mediae, quod Deo ante tributum erat ceu causae principali) CU- STODIET TE, PRUDENTIA (intelligentia) CONSERVABIT TE, UT ERUARIS A VIA MALA, ad eripiendum a via mala, velut e prae- sentissimo periculo, quod verbum הִצִיל importat 1. Sam. 17. vers. 32. Psalm. 18. vers. 1. viam notare vivendi consuetudinem, & actiones no- tissimum est: unde hic tam vitæ quam doctrinæ per- versam rationem aut aberrationem a vero & bono in- dicari recte Dn. D. Geiero observatum. Confer Psalm. 1, 1. Psal. 119, 29. 101. Prov. 8, 15. cap. 16, 29. cap. 28, 10. Ezech. 3, 18. Malim tamen hic reddi a vita MALI, quia membrum sequens hujus v. 12. præ- sentis ἐξηγητικὸν cum cæteris, quæ sequuntur vers. 13. 14. 15. de viro malo aberrante a vero & bono agit: quemadmodum postea v. 16. seqq. de muliere ex- tranea agitur, a qua itidem eruimur mediante hac divina sapientia: quæ proinde ita nos custodit, ut tuti simus tum a manifestis & violentis MALI cujus- que VIRI seductionibus, tum a tectis, ac blandienti- bus MULIERIS EXTRANEÆ illecebris & dece- ptionibus. Tuti a viri mali tum sermonibus sedu- ctoriis, quia perversa loquitur vers. 10. tum operibus scandalosis, qua derelinquit semitas rectius in S. Li- teris monstratas Gal. 6, 16. ut ambulet per vias te- nebrosas partim errorum, ac inscitiæ, Esa. 9, 2. Eph. 5, 8. partim scelerum ac malitiæ: Rom. 13, 15. Eph. 5, 2. 1. Thess. 5, 4. quæ in æternam caliginem deducunt Matth. 8, 12. cap. 22, 13. Jud. 7, 6. Conf. Job. 3, 19. 20. tum studiis & consiliis perversissimis, utpote qui lætatur facere malum & exultat in perversitatibus mali, unde SEMITÆ talium (consuetudinem no- tat, & habitum peccandi) perversæ sunt: vel ut re- ctius Junius exprimit, qui, malim quia vel quar-, ti- neribus suis perversi sunt, quem sensum postulat se- quens membrum, & præfracti in orbitis suis, ut sub- audiatur præpositio ב in priori membro, quæ ex- pressa est in posteriori. LXX. reddunt καμπόλαι inflexæ sunt semitæ eorum. Rasche per tortuosita- tem & obliquitatem explicat, minus autem conve- nienter Vulg. infames exponit. Deflexio in doctri- na & vita notatur: ut B. Luth. folgen dem Abwege.

## 2:16
Verse 16.

THAT YOU MAY BE RESCUED FROM A STRANGE WOMAN, AND FROM A FOREIGNER) That is, from a woman who is not a Hebrew, such as almost all were who were alien to true piety, and could easily corrupt the minds of young men, as the Midianite women did of old.

Thus Grotius with certain Hebrews. But other interpreters more rightly understand in general any woman, a harlot and an adulteress; 'strange,' that is, who is not yours (ch. 5:10, 17, ch. 22:14, ch. 32:33), and 'foreigner,' by which word likewise for the sake of emphasis, so that the reason may penetrate more deeply, is understood she who is placed outside your bed, just as those two synonyms are joined in Prov. 5:20, ch. 7:5, and are commonly used of an adulteress in ch. 23:27. Therefore the most learned Mercerus in this place: 'I, because mention has been made of a man speaking perversely, think that an adulteress is now understood, who is external and strange to the adulterer, since she is not his wife.' Some of the Hebrews understand 'strange' as a foreigner, who was forbidden to the Israelites, but I think there is no need for this. An adulteress is to an adulterer as if from another nation, and tribe, and lineage, since she does not belong to him. Nor is there any reason why it should be restricted in this place to a non-Hebrew woman; indeed, since mention is added of a covenant with God in verse 17, namely with the living One, who is none other than the God of Israel, the discourse is rather about a Hebrew woman than about a Gentile. For in vain does Grotius understand this covenant as the precepts given to Noah, to whom Scripture teaches no precepts were peculiarly given, and those which Grotius recounts, concerning the worship of one God, the avoidance of adulteries and homicides, were inscribed upon nature itself from the primeval creation, and are not read as having been newly promulgated to Noah and his children in Rabbinical traditions. But the Israelites entered into a covenant with the GOD of Israel immediately in their first infancy, by means of the Sacrament of Circumcision, the force of which covenant extended itself even to women, although circumcision itself was not destined for them.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

UT ERUARIS A MULIERE ALIENA, ET AB EX- TRANEA) Id est, à fœmina non Hebræa, quales fere omnes à vera pietate alienæ erant, & facile juvenum animos pote- rant corrumpere, ut olim Madianitides.

Sic Grotius cum Ebræis quibusdam. Rectius autem alii Interpretes in genere quamvis mulierem intelligunt, Scortatricem, ac adulteram; Aliena, id est, quæ tua non est cap. 5, 10. 17. c. 22, 14. cap. 32. 33. & extranea, qua voce itidem emphaseos causa, ut ratio magis penetret, intelligitur ea, quæ extra tho- rum tuum constituta est, quemadmodum duo illa synonyma conjunguntur Prov. 5, 20. c. 7, 5. & de ad- ultera communiter usurpantur cap. 23, 27. Ideo doctissimus Mercerus in h. l. Ego quia viri perver- sa loquentis mentio facta est, simpliciter puto adulte- ram nunc intelligi, quæ adultero externa est, & aliena, quum ejus uxor non fit. Hebræorum nonnulli alie- nam intelligunt alienigenam, quæ Israelitis erat prohi- bita, sed nihil puto necesse esse. Adultera adultero velut ex alia gente est, & tribu ac prosapia, quum ad eum non spectet. Nec causa est, cur hic loci restrin- gatur ad fœminam non Ebræam, imo cum addatur mentio pacti cum Deo v. 17. vivo nempe, qui non est nisi Israelis Deus, de Ebræa potius muliere, quam de gentili sermo est. Frustra enim Grotius hoc pactum de præceptis Noah datis intelligit, cui nulla peculiariter data præcepta docet Scriptura, & quas recenset Grotius, de unius Dei cultu, fuga adulte- riorum & homicidiorum, naturæ ipsi insculpta sunt a primæva creatione, neque noviter promul- gata leguntur Noah, & liberis ejus in traditioni- bus Rabbinicis. Pactum autem cum DEO Israelitæ statim in prima infantia inivere, mediante Sacramento Circumcisionis, cujus pacti vis etiam se ad foeminas porrigebat, etsi circumcisio ipsa illis destinata non fuerit.

## 2:17
Verse 17.

AND FORSAKES THE GUIDE OF HER YOUTH) Of her adolescence. God, who gave her life and sustenance from her earliest age.

Others take these things not of God, but of a spouse, because of the preceding and following context, which softens its own utterances, 'who forsakes the guide of her youth': and has forgotten the covenant of her God, violating the covenants and connubial rights sanctioned by God (Gen. 2:24), to which she bound herself in the most holy name of God. For Aben-Ezra also noted in this place that women enter into the covenant of God with their husbands, so that the husband may not become perfidious, and vice versa. Which covenant Scripture itself respects in Mal. 2:14. Compare Joel 1:8. Not to mention that Ludovicus de Dieu translates it thus: 'The friend of HER YOUTH': deriving the meaning of the Hebrew word אלוף from the cognate Arabic language, in which a friend is thus denoted: see his notes on the places of the Old Testament on Psalm 55:14.

Verse of the same.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ET RELINQVIT DUCEM PUBERTATIS SUÆ) Adolescentiæ suæ. Deum, qui ipsi vitam dedit, & alimenta à prima ætate.

Non de Deo, sed de conjuge hæc alii accipiunt, ob antecedentia & consequentia, quæ eloquia sua e- mollit, quæ deserit ducem adolescentiæ suæ : & pacti Dei sui oblita est, violans pacta, & jura connubialia à Deo sancita Gen. 2, 24. ad quæ sese in Sacrosancto Dei nomine obstrinxit. Nam & Aben-Ezra nota- vit ad h. l. mulieres cum viris intrare fœdus Dei, ne vir fiat perfidus, & vice versa. Quod fœdus respicit ipsa Scriptura Mal. 2, 14. Conf. Joel. 1, 8. Ut taceam, quod Ludovicus de Dieu sic vertat: Amicum ADO- LESCENTIÆ SUÆ: vocis Ebrææ אלוף significationem e lingua cognata Arabica eruens, in qua amicus ita denotatur: vid. animadvers. ad loca V. T. ad Psalm. 55, 14.

Vers. eod.

## 2:18
AND HAS FORGOTTEN THE COVENANT OF HER GOD) The covenant which God entered into with Noah and his descendants, in which covenant is included the worship of one God, the avoidance of adulteries, homicides, and other things of that kind.

Regarding these matters, as far as concerns the commentaries of Grotius, we have already said enough, insisting upon the common explanation which takes these words about the adulterous woman in their literal sense, just as Cornelius, along with Bede, connects these words to the preceding ones in this way: He warned that one must beware of the company and conversation of the wicked; now he warns that one must beware of the alluring and unchaste woman. For nothing is so contrary to wisdom as an alluring woman. But when I examine more accurately the comparison of this passage with Proverbs 9:13, I am easily led to that opinion which I see pleased Vatablus and the Hebrews: that the adulterous woman is to be taken improperly and figuratively, in a manner most familiar to parables; which they explain (inadequately) as false doctrine or heresy: Bede himself not denying it: By the strange woman, the depravity of heretics can be understood, alien to the members of Christ and the Church: which is accustomed to deceive the hearts of the innocent by the softness of its eloquence and the blandishments of its tongue. Adequately, the FOOLISH WOMAN, or FOLLY, is opposed to WISDOM, which is both that of heresy and false doctrine, and that of pleasure and depraved concupiscence, by which we are ensnared either through the example or seduction of others, or through innate malice: παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτὸς James 1:22. For both are opposed to heavenly wisdom, both are mere folly, both deviate from and lead away from the straight path and the rule of divine truth, and both lead those who follow them to destruction. And this description of foolishness is especially fitting: Which (1) is deservedly distinguished by the name of STRANGE and foreign WOMAN, because wisdom is betrothed to us by divine right, which must be received into the bridal chamber of our heart, and must uniquely please our soul, verse 10, whom we ought to love intimately and embrace sweetly like a most choice bride, ch. 4:6, 8, whence we are warned in ch. 7:4. Say to wisdom, you are my sister: which name the Bridegroom attributes to the Bride, Canticles 4:9, 10, ch. 5:2, 3. But FOLLY entices us toward itself and insinuates itself into our heart like a strange woman, drawing us away from that most sweet bride and longing to occupy her bridal chamber: just as also in ch. 5:3. The Fathers take STRANGE to mean fallacious, painted human wisdom; Rabbi Solomon takes it to mean idolatry or heresy. (2.) How heresy softens its speech, χρησότης, καὶ ἐυλογίας teach, by which it deceives innocent souls, as the Apostle testifies, Romans 16:18. And no less does depraved concupiscence ensnare us, with various blandishments and enticements, so that we even do that which we do not want, and so that it renders us captives to the law of sin Rom. 7, 23. not otherwise than Delilah ensnared Samson with soft words. Conf. Jac. 1, 14. (3) This adulteress abandons the Guide of her puberty or adolescence, not he who only gave corporal life and nourishment, but he who from earliest infancy received us into grace through the sacrament of initiation, and takes care of us, as Jer. 3, 4. she whose forehead has become that of a harlot woman, called to repentance is commanded by God to say, My father, you are the guide of my virginity (adolescence): where exactly the same words occur in the source as in this place. For the soul betrothed to God through the sacrament of regeneration, enticed by concupiscences and false doctrine, while it consents to them, abandons its God, and the guide of its puberty, when through heresy, or even any other sin, having forgotten the covenant entered into with God, it breaks the faith given to God, and conceives a new love and offspring of illicit delight. (4) The covenant of our God pertains properly to this. For it is said to have forgotten not the covenant with a husband, but with its God, Jer. 2, 2. Ezech. 16, 60. (5) All of which are confirmed by a similar passage in Prov. 9, which a comparison clearly teaches to be parallel to this.

Vers. 18. FOR HER HOUSE IS INCLINED UNTO DEATH) Thus, God has not promised anything good to those living in this way, not even in this life.

Vers. eod. AND HER PATHS UNTO THE DEAD) In the Hebrew: And unto the Rephaim her path. That is, she runs to idols in which there is no life.

This is a purely precarious interpretation. That it does not deal specifically with an idolatrous woman has already been shown: because of which preconceived hypothesis it pleased Grotius to twist the words of Solomon to that end. Its sense is clear from the preceding member, for they explain each other: Her house is inclined unto death, and her paths unto the dead. Although Grotius perverts the first member as well, rendering this sense: Thus, God has not promised anything good to those living in this way, not even in this life. But the words of the Holy Scriptures are clear, not only that such people have nothing good to promise themselves, but also that they precipitate themselves into destruction. The Chaldean renders: in the depth of death is her house. The LXX: She has placed her house near death. Aben Ezra: this very woman declines to death her house. Mercerus, as if to say, it is like a certain valley leading to hell, and her house is leaning; as if to say, those who approach it summon certain destruction upon themselves: And unto the DEAD (Rephaim) her paths lead, that is to say: to follow her, to associate with her, is a certain way to destruction. To which Ambrose referred in book 1, de Cain c. 5. Instead of the dead, her house leading you into the retreat of death. The matter is evident from the parallel passage Prov. 5, 5. her feet go down to death, and her steps take hold on hell. Therefore, by Rephaim are not designated idols or the gods of the gentiles, but dead men, and especially the very slaves of eternal death. See Prov. 9, 18. to which passage Grotius: Rephaim signifies rather the lifeless in this place, and others. See what is said on the passage c. 21, 16. below. Clement of Alexandria, book 2, Paedagog. c. ult. teaches that the pleasure of the flesh is punished in three ways: because it deprives the carnal man of a triple life through a triple death, namely, the life of grace through sin, the life of nature through premature death, the life of glory through the eternal death of hell. St. Cyprian, de singular. Cleric. at the end: through infinite disgraces it brings multiple deaths into the ruin of the lost. Jose son of Jochanan in Pirke Aboth cap. 1. Do not multiply conversation with a woman. For thence the Sages said, every time that a man multiplies conversation with a woman, he summons, or multiplies evil for himself, and is hindered from the words of the law, and finally descends into hell. These things Jose says of women properly so called. But erroneous paths are understood in a general sense, both heretical doctrines and the depravity of life, all of which lead to hell. Matth. 7, 13. 21. 23. Rom. 6, 21. 23. 2. Pet. 2, 1.

Latin:

ET PACTI DEI SUI OBLITA EST) Pacti ejus quod Deus cum Noa & posteris ejus iniit, in quo pacto compre- henditur unius Dei cultus, fuga adulteriorum, homicidio- rum, & alia ejusmodi.

De his quantum ad commenta Grotii satis jam di- ximus, communi insistendo explicationi, quæ de muliere adultera sensu proprio hæc accipit, quemad- modum cum Beda hæc ita superioribus connectit Cornelius: Monuit cavendum a consortio & colloquio improborum, nunc monet cavendum a muliere illice & impudica. Nihil enim ita contrarium sapientiæ, ac mulier illex. Ubi vero collationem hujus loci cum Proverb. 9, 13. accuratius expendo, facile deducor in eam sententiam, quam Vatablo, & Ebræis placuisse video: quod improprie & figurate more parabolis maxime familiari, mulier adultera accipienda sit : quam illi de falsa doctrina, vel hæresi (inadæquate) explicant: non abnuente ipsomet Beda: Potest per mulierem extraneam hæreticorum pravitas intelligi, a Christi & Ecclesiæ membris aliena: quæ mollitia diser- titudinis, & blandimentis linguæ corda decipere inno- centium solet. Adæquate SAPIENTIÆ opponi- tur MULIER STOLIDA, vel STULTITIA, quæ tum hæreseos est, & falsæ doctrinæ, tum voluptatis, & pravæ concupiscentiæ, qua vel per aliorum exemplum vel seductionem, vel per congenitam malitiam ine- scamur: παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτὸς Jac. 1, 12. Utra- que enim opposita est cœlesti sapientiæ, utraque mera est stultitia, utraque a semita recta & regula di- vinæ veritatis deviat, & abducit, utraque ad exitium sequentes inducit. Et convenit hæc descriptio stoliditatis apprime: Quæ (1) MULIERES ALIE- NÆ & extraneæ nomine insignitur merito, quia sa- pientia desponsata nobis est, de jure divino, quæ in thalamum cordis nostri recipienda, unice animæ nostræ placere debet, vers. 10. quam intime amare, ac instar sponsæ lectissimæ suaviter amplexari debe- mus c. 4, 6. 8. unde monemur cap. 7, 4. Dic sapien- tiæ soror mea es: quod nomen Sponsæ tribuit Spon- sus Cantic. 4, 9. 10. cap. 5, 2. 3. Allicit autem contra nos ad sese, ac insinuat se cordi nostro INSIPIEN- TIA, instar alienæ mulieris, nos ab illa dulcissima sponsa abstrahens, ejusque thalamum occupare ge- スティens: quemadmodum etiam cap. 5, 3. EXTRA- NEAM Patres de humana sapientia fallace, fucata, R. Salomo de idololatria, aut hæresi accipiunt. (2.) Quomodo sua eloquia emolliat hæresis χρησότης, καὶ ἐυλογίας docent, quibus innocentes animas decipit, teste Apostolo Rom. 16, 18. Nec minus in- escat nos concupiscentia prava, blandimentis & illecebris variis, ut etiam id quod nolumus agamus, utque captivos nos reddat legi peccati Rom. 7, 23. non secus atque Delila Simsonem molli- bus verbis inescavit. Conf. Jac. 1, 14. (3) Re- linquit haec adultera Ducem pubertatis vel adolescen- tiae suae, non qui tantum vitam corporalem & ali- menta dedit, sed qui a prima infantia nos in gra- tiam recepit per sacramentum initiationis, nostri- que curam gerit, uti Jer. 3, 4. illa cui frons mulieris meretricis facta, vocata ad poenitentiam Deo jube- tur dicere, Pater meus, dux virginitatis (adolescen- tiae) meae tu es: ubi prorsus eadem verba in fonte oc- currunt, quae hic loci. Anima enim Deo despon- sata per sacramentum regenerationis, concupiscen- tiis & falsa doctrina illecta, dum eis consentit, relin- quit Deum suum, & ducem pubertatis suae, cum per haeresin, vel etiam aliud quodvis peccatum, oblita pacti cum Deo initi, fidem Deo datam infringit, no- vumque amorem & foetum illicitae delectationis concipit. (4) Huc proprie pactum Dei nostri per- tinet. Non enim pacti cum marito, sed cum Deo suo initi oblita esse dicitur, Jer. 2, 2. Ezech. 16, 60. (5) Quae omnia confirmantur e loco simili Prov. 9. quem huic parallelum esse, collatio luculenter docet.

Vers. 18. INCLINATA EST ENIM AD MORTEM DOMUS EJUS) Ita viventibus Deus ne in hac quidem vi- ta, quicquam boni est pollicitus.

Vers. eod. ET AD INFERNOS SEMITAE EJUS) In Hebraeo: Et ad vita caffos semita ejus. Id est, currit ad idola in quibus nihil est vitae.

Mere precaria haec est interpretatio. Non agi in specie de muliere idololatra jam ostensum: ob quam praeconceptam hypothesin verba Salomonis eo torquere placuit Grotio. Sensus ejus e membro praecedente liquet, explicant enim se mutuo: Incli- nata est ad mortem domus ejus, & ad inferos semitae ejus. Quamvis prius membrum etiam pervertat Grotius, hunc reddens sensum: Ita viventibus Deus ne in hac quidem vita quicquam boni est pollicitus. Ve- rum verba S. S. luculenta sunt, non tantum quod ni- hil boni sibi polliceri habeant tales, sed & quod in exitum sese praecipitent. Chaldaeus reddit: in pro- funditate mortis domus ejus. LXX. Posuit juxta mor- tem domum suam. Aben Ezra, declinat ipsa haec mu- lier ad mortem domum suam. Mercerus, q. d. est velut vallis quaedam ad gehennam ducens, & propen- dens ejus domus; q. d. qui eam adeunt, certum sibi exi- tium accersunt: Et ad MORTUOS רפאים ואל ducunt scilicet נתיבותיה semitae ejus: eam sectari, cum ea versari certa est ad interitum via. Quo respexit Ambrosius l. 1. de Cain c. 5. Vice inferorum domus ejus deducens vos in secessum mortis. Res evidens est e parallelo loco Prov. 5, 5. pedes ejus descendunt ad mortem, & ad inferos gressus ejus penetrant. Non ergo per רפאים idola sive Dii gentilium, sed ho- mines mortui designantur, & imprimis ipsa aeternae mortis mancipia. Videatur Prov. 9, 18. ad quem locum Grotius: רפאים potius exanimes significat hoc loco, & aliis. Vid. quae ad locum c. 21, 16. infra. Clemens Alexand. lib. 2. Paedagog. c. ult. docet vo- luptatem carnis tripliciter lui: quia carnalem ho- minem triplici vita per triplicem mortem privat, nimirum vita gratiae per peccatum, vita naturae per citam mortem, vita gloriae, per mortem gehennae aeternam. S. Cyprianus de singular. Cleric. in fine: per infinita dedecora multiplices mortes in- vehit in perniciem perditorum. Jose filius Jo- chanam in Pirke Aboth cap. 1. Ne multiplices ne sermonem cum fœmina. Inde enim dixerunt Sapien- tes, omne tempus, quo homo multiplicat colloquium cum fœmina, accersit, vel multiplicat sibi ipsi malum, & im- peditur a sermonibus legis, & tandem descendit in ge- hennam. Hæc Jose de mulieribus proprie dictis. Sed semitæ erroneæ in genere intelliguntur, tum he- reticæ doctrinæ, tum pravitatis vitæ, quæ omnes ad inferos deducunt. Matth. 7, 13. 21. 23. Rom. 6, 21. 23. 2. Pet. 2, 1.

## 2:20
verf. 20. THAT YOU MAY WALK IN THE GOOD WAY.

In the way of the GOOD in Hebrew, as also in the following member, AND KEEP THE PATHS OF THE JUST. Some wish this sentence to depend on v. 11, so that two fruits of wisdom are assigned: to turn away from evil, and to do good. But since those two fruits have already been treated in reverse order, here we have a summary combination of them, and at the same time we are referred to the examples of the just: that you may walk, (I say) through the way of the good and have the same goal set before you as they have, Phil. 3, 14. and thus there is involved at the same time frequent conversation with the pious, by which we are mutually stirred up, so that we may insist on straight paths, adhering to the glorious footsteps of the just, and not turning aside to the dark dens of the sons of the adulteress: with the cause of the epiphonema added for the sake of both v. 21 and 22.

Latin:

verf. 20. UT AMBULES IN VIA BONA.

In via BONORUM in Ebr. uti etiam in mem- bro sequenti, ET CALLES JUSTORUM CU- STODIAS. Pendere hanc sententiam nonnulli volunt a v. 11. ut duo fructus assignentur sapientiæ, declinare a malo, & facere bonum. Sed cum duo illi fructus jam pertractati sint ordine inverso, jam hic summaria eorum complexio habetur, & simul ad exempla justorum remittimur: ut ambules, (in- quam) per viam bonorum & eundem cum ipsis sco- pum tibi præfixum habeas, Phil. 3, 14. adeoque in- volvitur ita simul crebra cum piis conversatio, qua mutuo excitamur, ut semitis rectis insistamus, vesti- giis justorum gloriosis inhærentes, nec ad tenebri- cosa filiorum adulteræ lustra divertentes: addita e- piphonematis causa ratione utriusque v. 21. & 22.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. FOR THE UPRIGHT SHALL DWELL IN THE LAND, AND THE SIMPLE SHALL REMAIN IN IT.

This promise is to be understood of the land both present and especially future, made to the upright and the whole, that is, in a word, to the just Psalm 15, 1. Psal. 16, 9. Ps. 37, 9. 11. seqq. Matth. 5, 5. 2. Pet. 3, 13. Conf. 1. Tim. 4, 8. In which sense, therefore, the cutting off of the wicked from the land, and the plucking up of the transgressors, is also to be understood in the antithesis, Psalm 37, 36. Matth. 3, 10. Job 15, 6. Conf. Gen. 17, 14. Exod. 12, 15. cap. 30, 33. 38. Lev. 17, 4. 9. Job 18, 17. Ps. 73, 9. To which also the interpretation of Osiander and Mr. Dr. Geier tends.

Latin:

Vers. 21. QUI ENIM RECTI SUNT HABITABUNT IN TERRA, ET SIMPLICES PERMANEBUNT IN EA.

De terra tum præsenti, tum imprimis futura hæc promissio accipienda, rectis & integris, hoc est, uno verbo, justis facta Psalm. 15, 1. Psal. 16, 9. Ps. 37, 9. 11. seqq. Matth. 5, 5. 2. Pet. 3, 13. Conf. 1. Tim. 4, 8. Quo sensu proinde etiam in antithesi accipienda impiorum de terra succisio, & prævaricatorum electio, Psalm. 37, 36. Matth. 3, 10. Job. 15, 6. Conf. Gen. 17, 14. Exod. 12, 15. cap. 30, 33. 38. Lev. 17, 4. 9. Job. 18, 17. Ps. 73, 9. Quo abit etiam Osiandri & Dn. D. Geieri in- terpretatio.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

The third means of true wisdom is proposed as the observance of divine laws, both in general, along with the fruit of this obedience: and in particular regarding GOD, where trust, fear of GOD, gratitude, patience, and love of wisdom are commended, which brings happiness, long life, glory, and peace: as well as regarding one's neighbor, toward whom is required a zeal for beneficence and a hatred of maleficence.

Ver. 1. MY SON DO NOT FORGET MY LAW.

The Holy Spirit speaks (through Solomon), whose children and disciples we all are, and exhorts in general to the observance of divine laws; that we do not forget his law: inasmuch as it is not the law of Solomon, but of the Holy Spirit, even though it is proposed and inculcated through Solomon as a ministerial cause: and that our heart may keep his precepts: with the promise of longevity of life, Deut. 8, 1. chap. 30, 23. Cf. Job 12, 12. Psalm 21, 5. Ps. 91, 16. Prov. 3, 16. c. 4, 10. and of peace or all-encompassing happiness, which is accustomed to be comprehended under the name of peace, as also of mercy, and divine faithfulness, and grace, and good understanding in the eyes of God and men.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Tertium medium veræ sapientiæ, legum divina- rum observatio proponitur, tum in genere, cum fructu hujus obedientiæ: tum in specie quoad DEUM, ubi commendatur fiducia, ti- mor DEI, gratitudo, patientia, & amor sa- pientiæ, quæ beatitudinem, vitam diuturnam, gloriam & pacem adfert: nec non quoad proximum, erga quem requiritur studium beneficentiæ, odiumque malificentiæ.

Vers. 1. FILI MI NE OBLIVISCARIS LEGIS MEÆ.

LOquitur Spiritus S. (per Salomonem) cujus filii & discipuli omnes sumus, & hortatur in genere ad observationem legum divinarum; ne obliviscamur legis suæ: utpote quæ non Salomonis, sed Spiritus S. lex est, etsi per Salomonem ceu causam ministeria- lem proponatur, & inculcetur: & ut præcepta sua cor nostrum custodiat: cum promissione longævitatis vi- tæ, Deut. 8, 1. cap. 30, 23. Conf. Job. 12, 12. Psalm. 21, 5. Ps. 91, 16. Prov. 3, 16. c. 4, 10. & pacis vel felicitatis o- mnigenæ, quæ pacis nomine comprehendi solet, ut & misericordiæ, & fidelitatis divinæ, ac gratiæ, & intel- ligentiæ bonæ in oculis Dei & hominum.

## 3:3
Verse 3. LET MERCY AND TRUTH NOT FORSAKE THEE.

It is more correctly rendered THEY SHALL NOT FORSAKE, so that a continuation of the promise is held here: because special precepts are not yet being handed down, and these things sound more conveniently concerning the mercy of the Lord, and the truth or faithfulness in fulfilling the promises which have been made to the pious: nor is it evident that that signification of the word אל for NOT is unusual, or from v. 25. And therefore this promise is accepted by the Syrian, R. Levi, Aben-Ezra, Mercerus, Munsterus, B. Lutherus, Osiander, the Vinarienses, Jansenius, and others. For we are not commanded to bind mercy and truth to the throat, and to write them on the tablet of the heart, as Chrysostom in the argument of the epistle to the Philippians, Cornelius, and Cartwright wish: But the precepts of the Lord, as is evident from Deuteronomy 6:6, seqq., Proverbs 7:3. And therefore, by way of explanation and for the sake of further amplification, it is added, so we shall find grace and good understanding in the eyes of God and men: because we find favor not only in the eyes of God, but also of men Luc. 2, 52. and understanding or intelligence or prudence Prov. 13, 15. c. 19, 11. Ps. 111, 10. that which is good no less in the eyes of God than of men: for to both in verse 4. the antecedent of the former clause, here the προσδιορισμὸς of the latter clause is most correctly referred, according to the custom received in the Proverbs.

Latin:

Versus 3. MISERICORDIA ET VERITAS TE NON DESERANT.

Rectius redditur NON DESERENT, ut promissionis continuatio hic habeatur: quia non- dum specialia præcepta traduntur, & de misericordia Domini, & veritate vel fidelitate in præstandis pro- missis, quæ piis facta sunt, hæc convenientius so- nant: neque inusitatam esse illam vocis אל pro NON significationem vel e v. 25. liquet. Ideoque ut promissio hæc a Syro, R. Levi, Aben-Ezra, Mercero, Munstero, B. Luthero, Osiandro, Vinariensibus, Jan- senio, aliis accipiuntur. Non enim misericordiam & veritatem ad guttur ligare jubemur, & in tabula cordis scribere, ut Chrysostom. in argum. epist. ad Phi- lipp. Cornel. & Carthwrightus vult: Sed præcepta Domini ut e Deuteronom. 6,6. seqq. Prov. 7,3. con- stat. Ideoque κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν & ulterioris am- plificationis gratia additur, ita nos inventuros gra- tiam & intellectum bonum in oculis Dei & hominum: quia & gratiam non tantum in oculis Dei, sed & ho- minum invenimus Luc. 2,57. & intellectum vel intelli- gentiam aut prudentiam Prov. 13, 16. c. 19, 11. Ps. 111, 10. eam, quæ bona sit non minus in Dei, quam homi- num oculis: ad utrumque enim in vers. 4. commati priori antecedens, hic προσδιορισμὸς posterioris commatis rectissime refertur, more in Proverbiis recepto.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. HAVE TRUST IN THE LORD WITH ALL THY HEART, AND DO NOT LEAN UPON THY PRUDENCE) As if, forsooth, all events depended upon that, and not upon God.

This first special precept is to be kept holily: Lean above all things upon the Lord, and upon divine grace, and trust in Him with all thy heart: but do not lean upon thy prudence, as if it were a staff, and rest upon it: which the Hebrew ישען implies. Compare Isaiah 36:6, Ezekiel 29:7, Jeremiah 17:7. Beautifully Basil the Great, oration 20: Just as it is right to attribute worship to no one else except to God alone, so also we ought to place our hope in no other thing than in God, the Lord of all things. For hope, as the same says in oration 7 on virtue and vice, which is placed in God, does not allow itself to be placed in another, nor does it wish for help to be brought to itself, but it is necessary to truly acquiesce in the help of God.

Latin:

Vers. 5. HABE FIDUCIAM IN DOMINO EX TOTO CORDE TUO, ET NE INNITARIS PRUDENTIÆ TUÆ) Quasi scilicet omnes eventus inde pendeant, & non a Deo.

Primum hoc speciale præceptum sancte custo- diendum: Innitere ante omnia Domino, & divinæ gra- tiæ, eique ex toto corde confide: ne autem prudentiæ tuæ, velut baculo, innitaris, & incumbas: quod infert Ebr. ישען. Conf. Es. 36,6. Ez. 29,7. Jer. 17,7. Pulcre Basil. M. orat. 20. Sicut nulli alii nos præter quam Deo soli cultum tribuere par est, sic etiam in nulla alia re spem nostram constituere debemus, quam in Deo omni- um rerum Domino. Spes enim, ut idem orat. 7. de virtut. & vit. quæ in Deo collocatur, non sinit se in alio constituere, neque sibi auxilium ferri vult, sed oportet vere in Dei auxilio acquiescere.

## 3:6
Vers. 6.

IN ALL THY WAYS THINK OF HIM.

The second precept concerning the reverence and fear of God is completed by its three requirements: The first is, that we always have Him in our mind and before our eyes: thinking always of His presence, Ps. 139:2, seqq., so that we do not undertake anything evil in His sight: concerning which Boethius says, a great necessity of probity is imposed upon us, since we do all things in the eyes of God who sees all things: and always representing to ourselves the will of God, as the norm of our actions, Gen. 17:1, 1 Thess. 4:3. Thus Bernard: the instruction of an honest life warns that each one should understand God to be always present, just as if he saw Him, who is present, in His own essence: and thus should fear and revere Him, and be carried toward Him with intense love, and enjoy Him as much as he can in life, and rest in Him, not in another. For thus HE SHALL DIRECT THY STEPS, Ps. 25:4, 5, 9, Ps. 119:35. The second is, that we do not abandon the rule of divine wisdom through the persuasion of our own wisdom: BE NOT WISE IN THINE OWN EYES, Rom. 12:16, so that you may say boastfully, With my wisdom as a guide I shall take the right path, as Aben-Ezra has interpreted here. Which is truly the source of all errors and heresies. Compare James 3:17, 1 Cor. 3:18, Isaiah 5:21. The third is, that we depart from evil through the fear of GOD. FEAR GOD AND DEPART FROM EVIL. Which is connected with the preceding, Rom. 11:20, Sir. 25:14.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

IN OMNIBUS VIIS TUIS COGITA ILLUM.

Alterum præceptum de reverentia & timore Dei tribus ejus requisitis absolvitur: Primum est, ut ipsum semper in animo, & ante oculos habeamus: ejus præsentiam semper cogitantes, Ps. 139,2. seqq. ne in ejus conspectu quicquam mali suscipiamus: de quo Boëthius, magna nobis indicta est necessitas probitatis, cum omnia agamus in oculis Dei cuncta cernentis: Dei- que voluntatem semper nobis repræsentantes, ceu normam actionum nostrarum, Gen. 17, 1. 1. Thess. 4, 3. Ita Bernhardus: informatio honestæ vitæ monet, ut quisque sic Deum semper præsentem intelligat, ac si ipsum, qui præsens est, in sua essentia videret: sicque eum timeat & revereatur, & intenso amore in eum fe- ratur, eoque prout potest in vita fruatur, & in ipso, non in alio requiescat. Sic enim IPSE DIRIGET GRESSUS TUOS, Ps. 25, 4. 5. 9. Ps. 119,35. Al- terum est, ne sapientiæ propriæ persuasione regulam divinæ sapientiæ relinquamus: NE SIS SAPIENS APUD TEMETIPSUM Rom. 12,16. ut jactabundus dicas, Sapientia mea duce rectum iter capiam, ut A- ben-Ezra hic interpretatus est. Qui vere fons est omnium errorum & hæresium. Conf. Jac. 3, 17. 1. Cor. 3,18. Esa. 5,21. Tertium est, ut metu DEI a malo recedamus. TIME DEUM ET RECEDE A MALO. Quod cum præcedente connexum est Rom. 11,20. Syr. 25, 14.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. BE NOT WISE IN THINE OWN EYES) Do not be δοκησίσοφος (wise in one's own conceit).

Latin:

Verf. 7. NE SIS SAPIENS APUD TEMETIPSUM) Ne sis δοκησίσοφος.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. FOR IT SHALL BE HEALTH TO THY NAVEL, AND MOISTURE TO THY BONES.

Spiritual health is insinuated by the description of bodily health: for the health of the body depends greatly upon the health of both the more tender parts lacking bone, namely the vital ones, the heart, the liver, the spleen, the viscera, which are near the navel, and the navel itself: and of the harder ones, for instance the bones, which are as it were the base and columns of our house and microcosm. Compare Job 21:24, Ps. 52:4. The author of the Greek Catena says, the bones of the soul are its more robust and firmer powers, which, so that each may properly perform its duty, need singular care and diligence.

Latin:

Verf. 8. SANITAS QUIPPE ERIT UMBILICO TUO, ET IRRIGATIO OSSIUM TUORUM.

Sanitas spiritualis descriptione sanitatis corpo- ralis insinuatur: sanitas enim corporis maximè de- pendet ex sanitate tum teneriorum partium osse ca- rentium, vitalium sc. cordis, epatis, splenis, visce- rum, quæ sunt juxta umbilicum, & ipsius umbilici: tum duriorum, puta ossium, quæ sunt quasi basis & columnæ domus nostræ & microcosmi. Conf. Job. 21, 24. Ps. 52, 4. Auctor Caten. Græc. animæ ossa, inquit, sunt robustiores firmioresque illius vires, quæ singulæ ut suo munere probe fungantur, singulari cura & diligentia egent.

## 3:9
Vers. 9. HONOR THE LORD WITH THY SUBSTANCE, AND GIVE TO HIM OF THE FIRSTFRUITS OF ALL THY PRODUCE.

The third precept concerning gratitude regards not only the sustenance of the Sacred ministry, for which the firstfruits were destined, but the contribution of our gifts and goods to the honor of God: since indeed firstfruits were to be offered primarily to GOD, even if something from them also went to the use of the priests, and that likewise for the honor and glory of God, which is propagated through the sacred ministry. Conf. Rom. 12, 1. Therefore, this is not to be understood, as with some Hebrews, Cajetan, and Jansenius, concerning only sacrifices and firstfruits to be offered according to the law, nor concerning only the sustenance of the Ministry, or the granting of Alms: But if you look at the force of the Proverb, it concerns gifts received divinely being spent in turn for the honor of God, even if they also looked to the offerings of sacrifices and firstfruits in the O. Test. For he, as the author of the Cat. Gr. has it, offers firstfruits to God, who humbly and with a submissive mind attributes the cause and praise of all rightly done things to Him as the primary author, or who from any kind of diligent action offers something to Him as a firstborn. That this honor, by which God is honored in His ministers with gratitude, and Christ in His needy mystical members, is thus simultaneously comprehended, there is no doubt. Conf. 1 Sam. 2, 30. Prov. 14, 31. c. 21, 27. Isa. 61, 8. Mal. 3, 10. Matt. 10, 4. ch. 25, 45. Therefore, the mystical sense which Cornelius makes here is the true and rather literal sense: that a pious man ought to worship God with holy works, so that he may refer all his gifts of mind and body, which he has received from God (I add also his riches and wealth), to His honor, and expend them for His praise and glory.

Latin:

Verf. 9. HONORA DOMINUM DE TUA SUB- STANTIA, ET DE PRIMITIIS OMNIUM FRUGUM TUARUM DA EI.

Tertium præceptum de gratitudine non tan- tum Sacri ministerii respicit sustentationem, cui pri- mitiæ destinatæ erant, sed donorum & bonorum no- strorum ad Dei honorem collationem: siquidem præ- primis DEO offerendæ erant primitiæ, etsi etiam de illis quid cesserit in usum sacerdotum, idque pariter ad honorem & gloriam Dei, quæ per ministerium sacrum propagatur. Conf. Rom. 12, 1. Non ergo cum Ebræis nonnullis, Cajetano, Jansenio, de solis sacrificiis & primitiis juxta legem offerendis, hæc in- telligenda, nec de sola Ministerii sustentatione, vel Eleemosynarum concessione: Sed si vim Proverbii spectes, de donis divinitus acceptis Dei vicissim honori impendendis agitur, etsi ea etiam spectarint sacrificiorum & primitiarum oblationes in V. Test. Is enim, ut autor Cat. Gr. habet, Deo offert primitias, qui omnem recte factorum causam, & laudem illi tan- quam primario autori humiliter, submissoque animo tribuit, aut qui ex quovis studiosæ actionis genere ali- quid illi tanquam primogenitum offert. Compre- hendi autem ita simul honorem illum, quo Deus honoratur in ministris suis gratitudine, & Christus in membris suis mysticis egentibus, dubium nullum est. Conf. 1. Sam. 2, 30. Prov. 14, 31. c. 21, 27. Esa. 61, 8. Mal. 3, 10. Matth. 10, 4. cap. 25, 45. Quem ergo mysticum sensum hic facit Cornelius, verus & litera- lis potius sensus est: quod vir pius Deum sanctis o- peribus colere, ut omnes suas dotes mentis, ac cor- poris, quas a Deo accepit, (addo & divitias & opes suas) ad ejusdem honorem referre, ad ejusque lau- dem & gloriam expendere debeat.

## 3:11
ver. 11. MY SON, DO NOT REJECT THE DISCIPLINE OF THE LORD, NOR FAINT WHEN YOU ARE REPROVED BY HIM.

The Syriac, as also Pagninus, rendered the latter word more conveniently, 'do not be affected with weariness,' with the Chaldean 'do not be nauseated,' and Theod. 'do not disdain.' Therefore, fourthly, patience is required when God chastises us, since it is done out of fatherly love toward us, and for our benefit and salvation v. 12. Heb. 12, 5. seqq. Rev. 3, 19. Job 5, 17. 1 John 5, 3. James 1, 2. Discipline, says St. Augustine, tr. de bon. disc. T. IX., is the teacher of religion, the teacher of true piety, which does not rebuke in order to harm, nor chastise in order to injure, etc. is now accepted. But the LXX read not וְכָתַב, but וְיִכְתּב : for that is μασιγοῖ & between בֶּן & יְרַצֶּה they understood 'whom', such ellipses are frequent among the Hebrews.

Latin:

verf. 11. DISCIPLINAM DOMINI, FILI MI, NE ABJICIAS, NEC DEFICIAS CUM AB EO CORRIPERIS.

Syrus, ut & Pagninus posterius verbum conve- nientius reddidit, ne tædio afficiaris, cum Chaldæo ne nausees, & Theod. ne fastidias. Quarto itaque re- quiritur patientia, cum Deus nos castigat, siquidem id ex amore paterno adversus nos fiat, & in nostri commodum ac salutem v. 12. Ebr. 12, 5. seqq. Apoc. 3, 19. Job. 5, 17. 1. Joh. 5, 3. Jac. 1, 2. Disciplina, inquit S. August. tr. de bon. disc. T. IX. magistra est reli- gionis, magistra veræ pietatis, quæ nec ideo increpat, ut lædat, nec ideo castigat, ut noceat, &c. nunc recepta est. At LXX. legerunt non וְכָתַב, sed וְיִכְתּב : id enim est μασιγοῖ & inter בֶּן & יְרַצֶּה subintellexerunt quem, quales ἐλλείψεις frequentes Hebræis.

## 3:13
Verse 13. BLESSED IS THE MAN WHO FINDS WISDOM.

Fifthly, the love of Wisdom is now commended up to verse 27. 'Who finds', that is, after pious investigation attains wisdom, just as 'attains' (יָפִיק) corresponds to 'finding' (τῷ εὑρεῖν), according to the interpretation of B. Luther, which the Vulgate renders less conveniently as 'who abounds in prudence'. What follows, 'her acquisition is better than the negotiation of silver', is brilliant. Yet there may be a doubt concerning this: whether these things are to be understood of hypostatic Wisdom, or rather of the Wisdom of divine knowledge, which is had from the Holy Scriptures? Certainly not a few of the Fathers understand it of the Son of GOD Himself: such as Clem. Alex. l. 5. Strom. Origen on Rom. 6. Gregory of Nyssa on this passage. Hilary on Hos. 1. Ambrose l. de Parad. c. 1. Jerome on Isa. 65. Augustine l. 13. de Civ. Dei c. 21. & in Ps. 120. Gregory the Great l. 12. Mor. c. 48. Bede, the author of the Greek catena, Hugo, and others. Nor does the text gainsay it. For (1) the primary cause of blessedness is the Son of God, whom he who finds has eternal life 1 John 5:12. (2) Which the same testifies of Himself in a parallel passage Prov. 8:35. 'He who finds me, finds life.' (3) Her acquisition is not inappropriately compared with the negotiation of silver, by virtue of the comparison in Matt. 12:44. (4) Nor is her produce or fruit compared with gold or pearls here in v. 14, 15, otherwise than in a similar passage Prov. 8:10, 11, where hypostatic Wisdom treated of her fruit and produce, namely, the Wisdom which she communicates to us. (5) What is said about her right hand and left in verse 16, St. Augustine in Ps. 120 compares with those things which are held in Cant. 8:3 concerning the right and left hand of the Bridegroom: with this commentary added: 'That length of days is eternity. For Scripture calls that long in a proper sense, which is eternal. For whatever has an end is short. Long life is in her right hand.' But truly riches and glory, that is, the sufficiency of this life which is considered good by men, is the left hand. (6) The ways and doctrines of the hypostatic Wisdom, the Son of God, are altogether beautiful, and her paths are peaceful: concerning which Bede says, 'ways', that is, the actions of Christ and the doctrine which are contained in the Gospels, are beautiful, because they are divine, and have far transgressed the manner of a pure man, and all His commands lead to eternal peace: All things which He did in the flesh to reconcile mortals to God, to pacify the human race with the angels, to demonstrate to His own examples of peace and love to be kept toward one another, pertain to this. (7) The Son of God is the tree of life to those who apprehend Him through faith. Apoc. 2:7, c. 23:2. Thus Jerome l. c. understands the tree of life to be the Son of God, who is set up in the midst of Paradise, that is, the Church, as a vital tree bestowing life upon all who believe in Him. Bede, just as the tree of life gave life to Adam, so through the Wisdom of God, that is, Christ, the Church is given life: which even now receives the pledge of life by His sacraments and blood, and in the future is blessed by His present sight. Add also Augustine l. 1. contr. advers. leg. & Proph. cap. 15. & Gregory the Great l. c. (8) Of this tree of life, that is, of Christ, it is well said, 'he who fears Him, is blessed.' Cf. John 3:16. Apoc. 22:14. Thus in the Greek Catena: 'The tree of life is for all who adhere to Him, and who firmly lean upon Him as upon the Lord Himself.' Similarly also Hilary in Psalm 1. 'The tree of life is for all who embrace her (wisdom) and who lean upon her as upon the Lord.' Augustine in Ps. 32. 'Do not think that wisdom itself, because Scripture called it your possession, is something that is inferior to you,' he follows

and adds, 'and to those leaning upon her as in a safe house: Behold, your Lord is to you as a staff, the secure man leans, because He does not succumb.' Therefore from where shall we be blessed? By possessing God. (9) For that reason it fits very well, what is subjoined in verse 19, 'The Lord in wisdom founded the earth': which seems to fit less well if the preceding things are explained concerning the wisdom of the word or Holy Scripture. For it hardly appears what those things, that God created the earth in wisdom, have to do with the wisdom which we draw from the Holy Scriptures, or how they cohere with its praises. Therefore Didymus in the Greek Catena accepted those things also concerning hypostatic wisdom: 'And this also,' he says, 'is the tree of life, which is indeed nourishment to those who apprehend it, but to those who lean upon it, a firm and stable column, and which cannot be shaken. But by both I understand the Lord, for He Himself is life and the fulcrum and foundation.' Moreover, power is included with her other praises, so that the praise of the beauty of Wisdom may be fulfilled through all good things: for 'GOD', he says, 'by Wisdom founded the earth.' Furthermore, what follows further in v. 21, 'My son, let not these depart from your eyes,' as they contain a new instruction and exhortation, so there is no doubt that they pertain to the wisdom and counsel of the revealed word. Namely, he progresses from hypostatic Wisdom, in the finding of which blessedness is situated John 17:3, and which is a tree of life to those who apprehend her, to the Wisdom communicated to us by the same through the word, and expressed in the word of God, from the archetype to the ectype: and just as he had already warned that she must be received through faith to attain blessedness, so he further teaches that this also must be diligently guarded, because in it we have life through faith in Christ 2 Tim. 3:15. For in the Wisdom of the Word revealed we uniquely find hypostatic Wisdom, John 5:39. We now add the Grotius notes on these:

Latin:

Vers. 13. BEATUS HOMO QUI INVENIT SAPIEN- TIAM.

Quinto jam commendatur amor Sapientiæ us- que ad vers. 27. Qui invenit, id est, post piam in- dagationem consequitur sapientiam, uti τῷ inveni- re respondet יָפִיק consequitur, interprete B. Lu- thero, quod minus commode Vulgat. qui affluit pru- dentia. Quæ sequuntur, melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione argenti, luculenta sunt. De eo tamen dubium esse possit: num hæc de Sapientia Hyposta- tica accipienda sint, an vero de Sapientia agnitionis divinæ, quæ habetur e Sacris literis? Patres certe non pauci de ipso DEI Filio intelligunt: utpote Clem. Alex. l. 5. Strom. Origenes in Rom. 6. Gregorius Nyssenius in h. l. Hilar. in Os. 1. Ambrof. l. de Parad. c. 1. Hieron. in Esa. 65. August. l. 13. de Civ. Dei c. 21. & in Psal. 120. Gregor. M. l. 12. Mor. c. 48. Beda, Au- ctor cat. Græc. Hugo, alii. Neque abnuit textus. Nam (1) Beatitudinis causa præcipua est Filius Dei, quem qui invenit, vitam habet æternam 1. Joh. 5, 12. (2) Quod testatur idem de se in loco parallelo Prov. 8, 35. Qui me invenit, vitam invenit. (3) Acquisitio ejus cum negotiatione argenti non inconcinne con- fertur, vi collationis Matth. 12, 44. (4) Nec pro- ventus vel fructus ejus cum auro vel margaritis ali- ter hic v. 14, 15. comparatur, quam in simili loco Prov. 8, 10. 11. ubi Sapientia hypostatica de fructu & proventu suo, Sapientia nempe, quam nobis com- municat, egit. (5) Quæ de dextra & sinistra ejus vers. 16. dicuntur S. August. in Ps. 120. componit cum illis quæ Cant. 8, 3. de dextra & sinistra Sponsi haben- tur: addito hoc Commentario: Longitudo illa die- rum æternitas est. Hoc enim proprio modo longum dicit Scriptura, quod æternum est. Nam quicquid finem habet, breve est. Longa vita est in dextera ejus. At vero divitiæ & gloria, id est, fufficientia vitæ hujus ea quæ bona existimatur ab hominibus, sinistra est. (6) Viæ & doctrinæ Sapientiæ hypostaticæ Filii Dei pul- cræ omnino sunt, & semitæ ejus pacificæ : de quo Beda, viæ, inquit, id est, actiones Christi & doctrina, quæ in Evangeliis continentur, pulcræ sunt, quia divi- næ, ac puri hominis modum longe transgressæ, & omnia ejus jussa ad pacem ducunt æternam: Omnia quæ in carne gessit ad reconciliandum Deo mortales, ad pacifi- candum cum angelis genus humanum, ad demonstran- da suis servandæ ad invicem pacis, & dilectionis exem- pla pertinent. (7) Lignum vitæ est Filius Dei his, qui apprehendunt eum per fidem. Apoc. 2, 7. c. 23, 2. Ita de Filio Dei Hieron. l. c. lignum vitæ intelligit, qui in medio Paradisi, id est, Ecclesiæ quasi arbor vita- lis vitam omnibus in se credentibus largiens erigitur. Beda, sicut lignum vitæ vivificabat Adamum, ita per Sapientiam Dei, id est, Christum vivificatur Ecclesia: cujus & nunc Sacramentis ac sanguine pignus vitæ ac- cipit, & in futuro præsenti beatificatur aspectu. Adde & August. l. 1. contr. advers. leg. & Proph. cap. 15. & Greg. M. l. c. (8) De hoc vitæ ligno, hoc est de Christo, optime dicitur, qui timuerit eum, beatus est. Conf. Joh. 3, 16. Apoc. 22, 14. Ita in Caten. Græc. Lignum vitæ est omnibus qui adhærent illi, quique fir- miter illi tanquam ipsimet Domino innituntur. Simi- liter & Hilarius in Psalm. 1. Lignum vitæ est omni- bus qui complectuntur eam (sapientiam) & qui incum- bunt in eam sicut in Domino. August. in Ps. 32. Ne putes ipsam sapientiam, quia possessionem tuam dixit Scriptura, aliquid esse, quod sit te inferius, sequitur

& adjungit, & incumbentibus in eam velut in domo tuta: Ecce Dominus tuus est tibi quasi baculus, securus homo incumbit, quia ille non succumbit. Ergo unde beatierimus? Deum possidendo. (9) Ea ratione optime congruit, quod verf. 19. subjungitur, Domi- nus in sapientia fundavit terram: quod minus con- venire videtur, si de sapientia verbi vel Scripturæ Sa- cræ antecedentia explicentur. Nam vix apparet, quid illa, quod in sapientia Deus terram creavit ad sapientiam, quam e sacris literis haurimus, faciant, aut quomodo cum ejus elogiis cohæreant. Ideo Dydimus in Caten. Græcor. illa etiam de hypostatica sapientia accepit: Et hæc quoque, inquit, est lignum vitæ, quod est quidem nutrimentum iis, qui eam ap- prehendunt, iis autem qui innituntur, columna firma ac stabilis, & quæ non potest labefieri. Per utram- que autem intelligo Dominum, ipse enim est vita & fulcrum ac firmamentum. Comprehenditur autem cum cæteris ejus quoque laudibus potentia, ut per omnia bona impleatur laus pulchritudinis Sapien- tiæ: DEUS enim, inquit, Sapientia fundavit terram. Cæterum quæ porrò v. 21. sequuntur, Fili mi, ne ef- fluant hæc ab oculis tuis, uti novam informationem & parænesin continent, ita dubium nullum est, ea- dem ad verbi revelati sapientiam & consilium perti- nere. Nimirum progreditur a Sapientia Hypostati- ca, in cujus inventione beatitudo sita est Johan. 17. vers. 3. quæque apprehendentibus eam lignum vitæ est, ad Sapientiam nobis ab eadem per verbum communicatam, & in verbo Dei expressam, ab ἀρ- χετύπῳ ad ἔκτυπον: & uti illam ad beatitudinem consequendam per fidem suscipiendam jamjam monuerat, ita porro etiam hanc sedulo custodien- dam esse docet, quia in ea vitam habemus per fidem in Christum 2. Tim. 3, 15. Nam in Sapientia Verbi revelata Sapientiam Hypostaticam unice inveni- mus, Joh. 5, 39. Addimus jam de his Grotiana:

## 3:15
Verse 15.

MORE PRECIOUS IS SHE THAN ALL RICHES, AND ALL THINGS THAT ARE DESIRED CANNOT BE COMPARED TO HER] פנינים, which he translated here as riches, to others are pearls, to others gems. The passage Lam. 4:7 makes me believe it is a kind of red gem. LENGTH OF DAYS IN HER RIGHT HAND) Wisdom bestows good things upon men with both hands. And first, through prudence many dangers are avoided. Above. 2. AND IN HER LEFT HAND RICHES AND GLORY) Thus the Greeks: Menander: 'He who excels in reason has everything.' Chaeremon: 'For he who thinks well has everything gathered together.'

Latin:

Vers. 15.

PRETIOSIOR EST CUNCTIS OPIBUS, ET OMNIA QUÆ DESIDERANTUR HUIC NON VALENT COM- PARARI] פנינים, quod hic opes transtulit, aliis sunt mar- garitæ, aliis gemmæ. Facit locus Thren. 4, 7. ut gemmæ ru- bentis genus esse credam. LONGITUDO DIERUM IN DEXTRA EJUS) Amba- bus manibus sapientia hominibus bona largitur. Ac primum per prudentiam multa evaduntur pericula. Supra. 2. ET IN SINISTRA ILLIUS DIVITIÆ ET GLORIA) Sic Græci: Menander: Ο διαφέρων λογισμῷ πάντ' ἔχει Chæremon: Ὁ γὰρ φρονῶν εὖ πάντα συλλαβὼν ἔχει.

## 3:18
Verse 18.

A TREE OF LIFE IS IT TO THEM THAT LAY HOLD UPON IT) The tree of life in paradise preserved not only from death, but also from diseases. Compare what is below in chapter 13, verse 12, and chapter 15, verse 4.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

LIGNUM VITÆ EST HIS QVI APPREHENDERINT EAM) Arbor vitæ in paradiso non à morte tantum, sed & à morbis servabat. Confer quod infra 13. vers. 12. c. 15. v. 4.

## 3:21
Verse 21.

LET NOT THESE DEPART FROM THINE EYES: KEEP SOUND WISDOM AND DISCRETION.

Mr. Dr. Geier rightly observes that the nominative, transposed by hyperbaton, must be sought from the other clause, as in Deut. 32:5 and elsewhere in this manner. Let solid wisdom and shrewdness not depart from your eyes, but rather guard them diligently.
