By wisdom, however, is understood that which we conceive from the word of God: in Hebrew it is תושיה, which the blessed Boblius explains as a thing consistent with itself from Job 5:12, and says its nature is true confidence and constancy of action, in Eth. Sacr. p. 37. Which can be illustrated from Heb. 11:1, where faith is described by ὑπόςασιν. By מזמה he understands thought with motion, or accurate circumspection, so that in all actions we may consider what is to come.

Mr. D. Gejerus translates the diligence of the mind as discussion, when a matter is weighed now on this side, now on that, at ch. 1, 4. He derives it from דמם, he has meditated, he has deliberated: but he interprets the preceding word תושיה as solid Wisdom, just as Mercerus interprets it as solid knowledge of things, which Pagninus with the Vulgate rendered as law: so that the sense is that whatever things pertain to Wisdom, promote it, or are in any other way required for it, are to be thought upon from time to time, eagerly embraced, and tightly retained. The fruit promised from this is that they will be LIFE TO THE SOUL 2 Tim. 3, 15. AND GRACE TO THE THROAT: because it will give a taste and savor of divine things, so that we may say with the Psalmist: How sweet are your words to my throat. Psalm 119, 103. and our FOOT SHALL NOT STUMBLE, since we can walk in confidence on our way Ps. 91, 11. 12. Prov. 15, 19. ch. 28, 18. OUR SLEEP SHALL BE SWEET, so that we do not fear when we sleep, Ps. 3, 6. Ps. 4, 9. Job 11, 19. Prov. 6, 22. FOR THE LORD SHALL BE AT THY SIDE, is found in the Vulgate, which in Hebrew is, Because Jehovah shall be for your confidence: Der HErr ist dein Trutz, as B. Luther rendered it, because כסל denotes an unmoved and firm confidence and a reliable protection Job 31, 24. Psalm 78, 7.

Latin:

Versus 21.

NE EFFLUANT HÆC AB OCULIS TUIS: CUSTODI LEGEM ATQUE CONSILIUM.

Recte observat Dn. D. Geier. nominativum per Synchysin trajectum ex altero commate petendum esse, uti Deut. 32, 5. & alibi h. m. Sapientia solida & solertia ne recedant ab oculis tuis, quin potius easdem custodi sedulo. Sapientia autem intelligi- tur, quam e verbo Dei concipimus: In Ebr. est תושיה, quam B. Boblius exponit rem sibi constan- tem e Job. 5, 12. ejusque naturam dicit esse veram confidentiam, & actionis constantiam, in Eth. Sacr. p. 37. Quod illustrari potest ex Ebr. 11, 1. ubi fides per ὑπόςασιν describitur. Per מזמה intelligit cogita- tionem cum motu, seu accuratam circumspectionem, ut in omnibus actionibus cogitemus quid futurum sit.

Dn. D. Gejerus reddit industriam animi discussionem, cum res libratur modo in hanc modo in illam partem ad c. 1, 4. a דמם in animum inducit, meditatus est, deliberavit: vocem vero antecedentem תושיה Sapientiam solidam interpretatur, uti Mercerus so- lidam rerum notitiam, quam Pagninus cum Vulgata legem reddidit: ut sensus sit, subinde cogitanda, avide amplectenda, arcteque retinenda esse, quæcunque Sa- pientiam attinent, promovent, aliove modo ad illam re- quiruntur. Fructus inde promissus est, quod futu- ra sint VITA ANIMÆ 2. Tim. 3, 15. ET GRATIA GUTTURI: quia datura gustum & saporem divi- norum, ut dicamus cum Psalte: Quam dulcia fauci- bus meis eloquia tua. Psalm. 119, 103. & PES noster NON IMPINGAT, quum ambulare in fiducia possimus in via nostra Psal. 91, 11. 12. Prov. 15, 19. cap. 28, 18. SOMNUS NOSTER SUAVIS sit, ut non ti- meamus, cum dormimus, Psal. 3, 6. Psal. 4, 9. Job. 11, 19. Prov. 6, 22. DOMINUS ENIM ERIT IN LATERE TUO, habetur in Vulgata, quod in Ebr. est, Quia Jehova erit in fiduciam tuam: Der HErr ist dein Trutz, ut B. Luther. reddidit, quia כסל immotam firmamque fiduciam & fiduciale præsidium notat Job. 31, 24. Psalm. 78, 7.

## 3:24
Vers. 24. DO NOT SAY TO THY NEIGHBOR) To your neighbor, that is, to any man in need of your help. GO AND RETURN, TOMORROW I WILL GIVE TO THEE) Do not be the one who gives. Many always delay benefits, and even if they do not always delay, A grace that is slow-footed is a graceless grace.

Latin:

Vers. 24. NE DICAS AMICO TUO) Proximo tuo, id est, homini cuivis tuæ opis egenti. VADE ET REVERTERE, CRAS DABO TIBI) Ne sis ὁ δώσων. Multi semper differunt beneficia, & ut non semper differant, Α χάρις ἁ βραδύπους ἄχαρις χάρις.

## 3:27
Vers. 27.

DO NOT WITHHOLD DOING GOOD TO HIM WHO CAN; IF YOU ARE ABLE, DO GOOD YOURSELF.

After the precepts of true piety pertaining to God follow the precepts of sincere charity, which pertain to one's neighbor: and first indeed of beneficence. In Hebrew it is: do not withhold good from its owners or masters, Junius from those who have need. Among the LXX it is needy. But he is called the master of our goods more wittily than conveniently, namely the needy neighbor: and therefore it seems the Vulgate expressed the sense more conveniently: to which also agrees what is added in the other clause: when there is power in your hand to do it: when you are able either to withhold or to promote the distribution of goods, or that liberality of the rich: do not withhold it out of envy or avarice: for the avaricious do not even look at that with equal eyes, when others show themselves to be beneficent, certainly they are not accustomed to promote it, intent only on their own wealth. For it is about the liberality which is to be exercised from one's own resources that is treated in the following verse 28: do not say to your neighbor, go and return, tomorrow I will give to you, when you can give immediately: in the Hebrew: WHEN WHAT HE SEEKS IS WITH YOU, as the LXX and Luther explain.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

NOLI PROHIBERE BENEFACERE EUM, QUI POTEST; SI VALES ET IPSE BENE- FAC.

Post præcepta veræ pietatis Deum attinentia sequuntur præcepta sinceræ charitatis, quæ proxi- mum attinent: & primo quidem beneficentiæ. In Ebr. est: ne prohibeas bonum ab heris vel dominis suis, Junius ab iis, qui opus habent. Apud LXX. est ἐνδεής. Sed ille argute magis, quam commode Dominus dicitur bonorum nostrorum, proximus nem- pe indigus: ideoque sensum convenientius videtur expsessisse Vulgatus: cui etiam congruit, quod ad- ditur in altero commate: quum fuerit facultas manui tuæ ad faciendum: quum vel prohibere queas vel promovere distributionem bonorum, vel liberali- tatem illam divitum: ne prohibeas ex invidia vel avaritia: nam avari ne id quidem æquis oculis in- tuentur, cum alii beneficos se exhibent, certe id promovere non solent, suis tantum intenti opibus. De liberalitate enim quæ de propriis exercenda est facultatibns, sequenti demum versu 28. agitur: ne dicas amico tuo, vade & revertere, cras dabo tibi, cum statim possis dare: in Ebræo: CUM QUOD PETIT APUD TE SIT, uti LXX. & Luther. exponunt.

## 3:29
vers. 29.

DO NOT DEVISE EVIL AGAINST THY NEIGHBOR, WHEN HE HAS CONFIDENCE IN THEE.

After beneficence is commended, he restrains maleficent behavior, that we should not devise evil, that we should not litigate in vain, that we should not emulate the unjust v. 29. 30. 31. with the reason subjoined, that such are abominable to God, are punished with poverty, and yield to mockery and ignominy verse 32. seqq. Drusius translates DO NOT PLOW EVIL l. 1. Observat. cap. 12. comparing Proverbs 22, 8. Hos. 10, 13. Syr. 7, 13. What it is, DO NOT EMULATE THE UNJUST, Solomon explains immediately according to his custom, DO NOT IMITATE HIS WAYS. Therefore Junius does not translate it conveniently as DO NOT ENVY any violent man. Who the man of violence is, the explanations comprehended in the reasons in verses 32 seqq. also teach. נלוז perverse, LXX lawless, R. Levi who deviates from the straight path. Vulg. inconveniently MOCKER, through wicked, and mockers, as also fools, HE SHALL MOCK THE MOCKERS: where the LXX says, The Lord resists the proud, which is repeated in James 4, 6. 1 Pet. 5, 1. with the sense observed, even if the words vary: because proud men are truly mockers, who despise everyone with a haughty brow, and laugh at those who advise rightly; and God resists the proud, and by resisting them mocks them, by eluding and frustrating their schemes, and by deposing them from their seat, he renders them contemptible, which is the property of one who deposes, as B. Gerhard has in 1 Pet. 5: just as the antithesis teaches that proud mockers are noted, because they are opposed to the same humble ones. Conf. Proverbs 16, 19.

Latin:

vers. 29.

NE MOLIARIS AMICO TUO MALUM, CUM ILLE IN TE HABEAT FIDUCIAM.

Post beneficentiam commendatam cohibet maleficentiam, ne malum moliamur, ne frustra litige- mus, ne injustum æmulemur v. 29. 30. 31. subjuncta ra- tione, quod tales abominati Deo sint, egestate punian- tur, irrisioni & ignominiæ cedant vers. 32. seqq. Dru- sius reddit NE ARATO MALUM l. 1. Observat. cap. 12. conferens Proverb. 22, 8. Hos. 10, 13. Syr. 7, 13. Quid sit, NE ÆMULERIS INJUSTUM explicat statim Salomo pro more, NE IMITERIS VIAS E- JUS. Non ergo commode Junius ne INVIDE- TO ulli violento. Quis sit איש חמס docent etiam ἐξηγήσεις in rationibus comprehensæ vers. 32. seqq. נלוז perversus, LXX. παρανόμῷ, R. Levi qui a recta via deviat. Vulg. incommode ILLUSOR, per רשע impius, & לצים illusores, ut & כסילים stulti, IPSE DELUDET ILLUSORES: ubi LXX. Κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, quod repetitur Jac. 4, 6. 1. Petr. 5, 1. sensu observato, etsi verba varient: quia homines superbi vere illusores sunt, qui omnes alto contemnunt supercilio, & recta monentes rident; & Deus resistit superbis, ac resistendo eos deludit, eludendo atque frustrando eorum molimina, & de sede eos deponendo, reddit eos contemptibiles, quod proprium est deponentis, ut B. Gerhard. in 1. Pet. 5. habet: quemadmodum antithesis docet per illusores superbos notari, quia opponuntur iisdem ענוים humiles. Conf. Proverb. 16, 19.

## 3:30
Vers. 30. DO NOT CONTEND AGAINST A MAN IN VAIN, WHEN HE HAS DONE YOU NO HARM) Do not be a quarrelsome person.

Latin:

Vers. 30. NE CONTENDAS ADVERSUS HOMINEM FRUSTRA, CUM IPSE TIBI NIHIL MALI FECERIT) Noli esse vitilitigator.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Solomon requires attention to his admonitions, recalling the admonitions of his Father concerning the acquiring of wisdom with the magnificent promises made to him: and he dissuades from the way of the wicked, which he depicts alongside the path of the just, and commands that ears be inclined to him, the heart be guarded, and the mouth and lips be kept far from perversity, the eyes be directed to what is right, and the path of the feet be carefully weighed.

ver. 1. HEAR, O CHILDREN, THE DISCIPLINE OF A FATHER. The father here is Solomon, who testifies to his fatherly affection for his disciples as if they were his own children. This is clear from v. 2: I will give you a good gift, do not forsake my law, Prov. 1, 5; for he speaks of himself. לקח טוב is good doctrine or instruction, Is. 29, 24. He uses the example of the instruction of his own father David in v. 3 and following: FOR I WAS MY FATHER'S SON, TENDER. He says he was instructed immediately in his tender age, which the word רך implies, Gen. 33, 13.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Requirit Salomo attentionem monitorum suorum, commemorans monita Patris sui, de acquirenda sapientia cum magnificis sibi factis promissis: & dehortatur a via malorum, quam cum semita justorum depingit, & aures sibi inclinari, cor custodiri, & os & labia a pravitate elongari, oculos ad rectum dirigi, pedumque semitam probe ponderari, jubet.

vers. 1. AUDITE FILII DISCIPLINAM PATRIS. Pater hic est Salomo: qui paternum affectum testatur discipulis informandis ceu filiis suis. Quod e v. 2. liquet: Donum bonum tribuam vobis, legem meam ne derelinquatis Prov. 1, 5. de se enim loquitur. לקח טוב est doctrina vel informatio bona Es. 29, 24. Exemplo autem utitur informationis Patris sui Davidit v. 3. seqq. NAM ET EGO FUI FILIUS PATRIS MEI TENELLUS. In tenella ætate statim se informatum dicit, quam vox רך infert, Gen. 33, 13.

## 4:3
Vers. 3. AND AN ONLY SON BEFORE MY MOTHER) That is, as if an only son, most tenderly beloved. For Bathsheba had more children by David. The signs of comparison are often left unexpressed.

In Hebrew it is יחיד, which does not denote an only-begotten, but an only or uniquely dear one, Gen. 22, 2. 12. 16. Jud. 11, 34. Jer. 6, 26. Am. 8, 20. Zach. 12, 10. Therefore there is no need for a sign of comparison. The Socinians otherwise abuse that Vulgate translation when they dispute about the word μονογενὴς. But Solomon does not say that he was μονογενὴς, which is said of the Son of God, and teaches that He is the ONLY-BEGOTTEN, or the only Son by generation from the essence of the Father. Nor does he call himself the only one in any other way, since he had four sons by Bathsheba, 1 Chron. 3, 5, than that he was uniquely dear, and indeed ἐν προσώπῳ μητρὸς before the face of his mother: or if you wish to understand a sign of comparison at all, as if an only one, in view of the others who were not so beloved.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ET UNIGENITUS CORAM MATRE MEA) Id est, quasi unigenitus, tenerrime dilectus. Nam plures ex Davide liberos habuit Bethsabea. Notæ comparationis sæpe subticentur.

In Ebræo יחיד est, quod non unigenitum notat, sed unicum vel unice carum Gen. 22, 2. 12. 16. Jud. 11, 34. Jer. 6, 26. Am. 8, 20. Zach. 12, 10. Non ergo opus est comparationis nota. Abutuntur illa translatione vulgata alias Sociniani, cum de voce μονογενὴς disputant. Sed non dicit, Salomo, quod μονογενὴς fuerit, quod de Filio Dei dicitur, eumque SOLIGENITUM, vel solum per generationem e Patris essentia Filium esse docet. Nec aliter unicum dicit, quia e Bethseba quatuor habuit filios 1. Par. 3, 5. quam quod unice ille charus fuerit, & quidem ἐν προσώπῳ μητρὸς coram facie matris suæ: vel si comparationis notam omnino subintelligere velis, quasi unicus, intuitu reliquorum, qui ita dilecti non fuere.

## 4:5
Vers. 5. GET WISDOM, GET UNDERSTANDING.

In Hebrew it is acquire or get in the manner of merchants, who spare no labors to acquire riches: because wisdom is more excellent than all riches, ver. 7, Prov. 16, 16. Thus the word קנה is used for acquisition made by a price, Is. 24, 2, Ezech. 7, 12. On possessing, holding, and cherishing acquired wisdom, v. 6 follows.

Latin:

Vers. 5. POSSIDE SAPIENTIAM POSSIDE PRUDENTIAM.

In Ebr. est acquire vel compara more mercatorum, qui nullis laboribus parcunt, ut acquirant divitias: quia sapientia omnibus divitiis præstantior est vers. 7. Prov. 16, 16. Ita verbum קנה de comparatione pretio facta adhibetur Esa. 24, 2. Ezech. 7, 12. De sapientia acquisita possidenda, tenenda, & dili- genda v. 6. sequitur.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. THE BEGINNING OF WISDOM, POSSESS WISDOM] Better: Through the beginning of wisdom (that is, the fear of the Lord, above, 1, 7.) acquire wisdom.

AND WITH ALL THY POSSESSION ACQUIRE PRUDENCE) Redeem at any price.

The interpretation of others is still more suitable: The beginning of wisdom, i.e., is: acquire wisdom: as Em. Saa, wisdom is the chief thing, and therefore buy it. Aldegond, Lud. de Dieu, and the Belgian version agree. The explanation of Dionys. Hugo, Cajetan, Jansenius, and the passage Wisd. 6, 18, agree with B. Luther's version. That the discourse is about the dignity of wisdom, for which it is deservedly to be obtained, the things that follow sufficiently teach. Therefore it is added, and with all thy substance acquire understanding: Cf. Matt. 12, 44, which the Vulgate rendered obscurely and ambiguously. AND WITH ALL THY POSSESSION acquire prudence. For the ב indicates the ablative of price, Isa. 34, 24, whence Grotius rightly amends the Vulgate, explaining it thus: redeem at any price.

Latin:

Vers. 7. PRINCIPIUM SAPIENTIÆ, POSSIDE SAPI- ENTIAM] Melius: Per principium Sapientiæ (id est, timo- rem Domini, supra, 1, 7.) acquire sapientiam.

ET IN OMNI POSSESSIONE TUA ACQVIRE PRUDENTIAM) Quovis pretio redime.

Convenientior adhuc aliorum interpretatio est: Principium Sapientiæ sc. est: acquire sapientiam: uti Em. Saa, principatus est Sapientia, ideoque eme. Consonat Aldegondus, Lud. de Dieu, & versio Belgica. B. Lutheri versioni congruit explicatio Dionys. Hu- gonis, Cajetan. Jansenii & locus Sap. 6, 18. De di- gnitate sapientiæ, ob quam merito ea comparanda, sermonem esse, ea quæ sequuntur satis docent. Ideo additur, & omni substantia tua acquire intelligenti- am: Conf. Matth. 12, 44. quod obscure & ambigue reddidit Vulg. ET IN OMNI POSSESSIONE TUA ac- quire prudentiam. Nam ב ablatīvum pretii indi- cat Esa. 34, 24. unde recte emendat Vulgatam Gro- tius ita exponens, quovis pretio redime.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. HEAR O MY SON.

With the Davidic instruction completed, Solomon now continues his own, and especially warns that we should hold fast to his מוסר discipline or erudition, and decline the way of the wicked, as being dark, and indeed cleave to the ways of the righteous as being splendid.

Latin:

Vers. 10. AUDI FILI ME.

Absoluta informatione Davidica, Salomo jam suam pertexit, & inprimis monet, ut מוסר discipli- nam vel eruditionem ipsius teneamus, viamque im- piorum, utpote tenebricosam declinemus, justorum vero viæ ceu splendidæ inhæreamus.

## 4:11
Vers. 11.

I WILL SHOW THEE THE WAY OF WISDOM.

In the Hebrew it is the past tense: He taught thee to walk in the way of wisdom. When thou hast walked (in it) thy step shall not be straitened, as צר is taken in Num. 33, 58, Ps. 129, 1, 2: the widening of steps is opposed in Psalm 18, 37. Moreover, steps denote actions, pursuits, endeavors, Prov. 16, 9, Job 14, 16, Jer. 10, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

VIAM SAPIENTIÆ MONSTRABO TIBI.

In Ebræo præteritum est: Per viam sapientiæ do- cuit te incedere. Quum ambulaveris (illam) non ar- ctabitur gressus tuus, uti צר Num. 33, 58. Ps. 129, 1. 2. accipitur: opponitur dilatatio gressuum Psal. 18, 37. Notant autem gressus actiones, studia, conatus Prov. 16, 9. Job. 14, 16. Jer. 10, 23.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. FOR THEY SLEEP NOT UNLESS THEY HAVE DONE EVIL) Virgil: And if he had not harmed someone, he would have died.

That restlessness of theirs is not only explained and confirmed, but also intensified, when he adds, AND SLEEP IS TAKEN AWAY FROM THEM UNLESS THEY HAVE SUPPLANTED or unless they have caused to fall, i.e., they not only cannot sleep because of their zeal for doing evil, but if sleep should steal upon them at all, it is soon shaken off again, so that they may be awake and intent upon the arts of harming. THEY EAT THE BREAD OF INIQUITY, in the Hebrew the particle כי because is prefixed, rashly omitted by the Vulgate. For the cause of that restlessness is given, because they are eager to eat the bread of iniquity, they live from plunder, chap. 1, 12, as Salazar, Mariana, Drusius, and before them Lucifer Calaritanus in Apol. They are fed with the foods of impiety: and Vatabl. For they live on food wickedly acquired. R. Levi, Their food and drink consist of crimes and rapine. The explanation of others by hypallage is harsher, which indeed pleased Bede and Hugo, they eat impiety greedily as if it were bread, but it does not suit the text so well.

Latin:

Vers. 16. NON ENIM DORMIUNT NISI MALE FE- CERINT) Virgilius: Et si non aliqua nocuisset, mortuus esset.

Illa eorum inquietudo non tantum explica- tur & confirmatur, sed intenditur etiam, cum addit, ET RAPITUR SOMNUS AB EIS NISI SUP- PLANTAVERINT vel nisi ruere fecerint, q. d. non modo non possunt dormire præ studio malefacien- di, sed si somnus iis omnino obrepat, mox excuti- tur ille iterum, ut vigilare & intenti esse possint ar- tibus nocendi. COMEDUNT PANEM INI- QUITATIS, in Ebr. præmittitur particula כי quia, temere a Vulg. prætermissa. Nam causa redditur istius inquietudinis, quia student comedere panem ini- quitatis, e rapto vivunt cap. 1, 12. ut Salazar, Maria- na, Drusius, & ante illos Lucifer Calarit. in Apol. Ci- bantur cibis impietatis: & Vatabl. Victitant enim cibo impie acquisito. R. Levi, Cibi ipsorum & potus cri- minibus & rapina constant. Aliorum explicatio per hypallagen durior est, quæ Bedæ & Hugoni qui- dem placuit, comedunt avide impietatem quasi pa- nem, non autem adeo textui convenit.

## 4:18
Verse 18.

BUT THE PATH OF THE JUST IS AS THE SHINING LIGHT THAT PROCEEDS.

Some understand it as the light of knowledge (Job 3:20, Eph. 5:8), which Cornelius a Lapide does not deny; some as the light of virtue, with Gregory the Great and Canon Law (de poenit. dist. 2, cap. 10); others as the light of happiness (Isa. 58:10, 11, Prov. 13:9, Psalm 97:11): which latter explanation is confirmed by the antithesis, namely the danger or ruin of the wicked stumbling and falling in darkness, in verse 19. Although we do not deny that the increase of the light of knowledge and holiness is simultaneously included, because the path of the just is said to proceed and grow like the shining light, insofar as the Word of God shines before them in the darkness of the world, where all things are confused by errors, vices, and miseries, even unto the day of perfect knowledge and holiness, and consummated happiness. 2 Peter 1:19. Some, as R. Immanuel testifies, citing Mercer, interpret the word נֹגַהּ as Lucifer; but it is more correctly understood as the splendor of the dawn, because it is said to go and to shine, that is, to shine more and more in its progress, even unto the perfect day. But Cornelius a Lapide in vain mocks our faith here regarding imputed righteousness, that it does not grow but is equal in all: because we do not deny the increase of virtue, even if we acknowledge the imputed righteousness of Christ to be so perfect that it does not admit of increase: nor indeed is this a matter of the righteousness by which they are constituted just, which is nothing but the obedience of Christ alone, as the Apostle testifies (Rom. 5:19), but of the path and course of the just, in which, namely, those already justified proceed; which path of the just, according to Dionysius, is the conduct of the good and virtuous, in which the light of grace, the splendor of wisdom, and the purity of the heart shine forth. Furthermore, we do not deny that we progress in virtue until the end of life, as Canon Law teaches from Gregory (Homily 5 on Ezekiel), even if we are justified solely not by our own virtue, but by the most perfect obedience of Christ: nor do we teach, as the Jesuits slander, that the virtues of all are equal, as Jovinian did. And Cornelius himself confesses that we teach that a just man CAN GROW in virtue. With what face, therefore, does he attribute a contrary opinion to us?

Latin:

Vers. 18.

JUSTORUM AUTEM SEMITA QUASI LUX SPLENDENS PROCEDIT.

Nonnulli de luce cognitionis Job. 3, 20. Eph. 5, 8. quibus Cornel. a Lap. non abnuit, quidam de luce virtutis cum Gregorio M. & jure Canon. de pœnit. dist. 2. cap. 10. alii de luce felicitatis Esa. 58, 10, 11. Pro- verb. 13, 9. Psalm. 97, 11. accipiunt: quæ posterior explicatio ex antithefi, periculo nempe vel damno impiorum in tenebris impingentium, & ruentium versu 19. firmatur. Quanquam non abnuamus incrementum lucis cognitionis & sanctitatis simul comprehendi, quia semita justorum quasi lux splen- dens procedere, & crescere dicitur, quatenus illis quæ in mundi tenebris, ubi omnia erroribus, vitiis, & miseriis confusa sunt, verbum Dei prælucet, usque in diem perfectæ cognitionis & sanctitatis, ac feli- citatis consummatæ 2. Petr. 1, 19. vocem נֹגַהּ qui- dam R. Immanuel, teste Mercero, de Lucifero inter- pretatur; sed de auroræ splendore rectius intelligitur, quia ire & lucere, id est, in progressu magis ac magis lucere dicitur, usque ad perfectum diem. Frustra autem Cornel. a Lap. hic nostram fidem de justitia imputata, quod non crescat, sed in omnibus æqualis sit, sugillat: quia virtutis incrementum non negamus, etiamsi imputatam Christi justitiam adeo perfectam agnoscamus, ut incrementum non capiat: Neque vero hic de justitia qua justi constituuntur, quæ non est nisi unius Christi obedientia, teste Apostolo Rom. 5, 19. sed de justorum semita & curriculo, in quo scil. jam justificati pergunt, agitur, quæ semita justorum, interprete Dionysio est conversatio bonorum atque virtuosorum, in qua lux gratiæ, splendor sapientiæ, puritas cordis relucent. De cætero non inficiamur, usque ad finem vitæ nos proficere in virtute, uti e Gre- gor. homil. 5. in Ezech. jus Canonicum docet, etsi non virtute nostra, sed perfectissima Christi obedi- entia unice justificemur: neque cum Joviniano o- mnium virtutes pares esse docemus, uti Jesuitæ calu- mniantur. Et fatetur ipse Cornelius, nos docere, POSSE justum CRESCERE in virtute. Qua ergo fronte nobis contrariam sententiam affingit?

## 4:19
verse 19.

THE WAY OF THE WICKED IS DARK; THEY KNOW NOT WHERE THEY STUMBLE.

Cornelius acknowledges that the Hebrew has it more vigorously in this manner: the way of the wicked is thick darkness, they know not at what they stumble; even if they seem to themselves most sharp-sighted, perceptive, and wise, it is nevertheless certain that they walk in the thickest darkness of errors, sins, and miseries, so much so that they do not know at what they stumble, for sudden ruin will come upon them, which they will not be able to avoid (Prov. 1:27), and thus in that darkness they finally precipitate themselves into the eternal darkness of Gehenna (Matt. 8:12); just as the light in the path of the just progresses unto the perfect day, so the darkness in the way of the wicked progresses unto the perfect darkness of eternal night (2 Peter 2:17). Compare Isaiah 8:27.

Latin:

vers. 19.

VIA IMPIORUM TENEBROSA; NE- SCIUNT UBI CORRUANT.

Nervosius Ebr. habere agnoscit Cornel. h. m. via impiorum caligo, nesciunt in quod impingant; etsi sibi maxime oculati, perspicaces & sapientes videntur, certum tamen est, eos in crassissimis tenebris erro- rum, peccatorum & miseriarum versari, adeo ut ne- sciant, quo impingant, ruina enim repentina illis superveniet, quam cavere non poterunt Prov. 1, 27. adeoque in caligine illa præcipitant se tandem in æ- ternas gehennæ tenebras Matth. 8, 12. ut lux in justo- rum semita proficit in diem perfectam, ita caligo in via impiorum proficit in perfectam æternæ noctis caliginem 2. Petr. 2, 17. Conf. Esa. 8, 27.

## 4:21
Verse 21. LET THEM NOT DEPART FROM THINE EYES.

The LXX wrongly [translates] ὅπως μὴ ἐκλίπωσί σε αἱ πηγαί σου, so that your fountains may not leave you. There is no mention of fountains here, but of eyes and heart: KEEP THEM IN THE MIDST OF THINE HEART: which is an explanation of the preceding: for there the eyes of the mind are understood: for thus the Word of the Lord will always be before the eyes of the mind, if it has been kept in the midst of our heart, in the innermost recesses of the heart. Compare chapter 3:3.

Latin:

Vers. 21. NE RECEDANT EA AB OCULIS TUIS.

LXX. perperam ὅπως μὴ ἐκλίπωσί σε αἱ πη- γαί σου, ut ne derelinquant te fontes tui. Nulla hic fontium mentio, sed oculorum & cordis: CUSTODI EA IN MEDIO CORDIS TUI: quæ ἐξήγησις est præcedentium: Nam illic oculi intelliguntur mentis: ita enim semper Verbum Domini ante oculos mentis versabitur, si in medio cordis nostri custoditum fue- rit, in intimis cordis penetralibus. Conf. cap. 3, 3.

## 4:22
Verse 22. AND HEALTH TO ALL THEIR FLESH.

Truly, the sayings of the Lord are life to those who find them, Prov. 4:22, in that they bring a remedy and healing to all flesh—that is, to the whole man, who is entirely corrupt in his whole extent—since we are in absolute need of them after the fall. To all His flesh, that is, to each one of them, as Mercerus notes: which pronoun the Vulgate wrongly omits. Therefore, that this panacea may conduce to the health of the whole man, Solomon now teaches how to apply it to the individual parts, primarily to the heart, the mouth, the lips, and the eyes, and the feet, as being most weakened by sin, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 3:11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ET UNIVERSÆ CARNI SANI- TAS.

Scilicet ita eloquia Domini vita sunt inve- nientibus ea Proverb. 2, 22. ut medelam & sanatio- nem, siquidem ea nobis post lapsum omnino opus sit, adferant universæ carni, id est, toti homini, qui totus, quantus quantus est, corruptus est. Toti carni Ejus, id est, uniuscujusque eorum, ut notat Mercerus: quod pronomen perperam omittit Vul- gatus. Ut ergo hæc panacea toti homini condu- cat ad sanitatem, applicare eam partibus singulis jam docet Salomo, cordi imprimis, ori, labiis, & ocu- lis, pedibusq́;, utpote maxime per peccatum debilita- tis, teste Apostolo Rom. 3, 11. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18.

## 4:23
ver. 23. KEEP THY HEART WITH ALL DILIGENCE, FOR OUT OF IT PROCEEDETH LIFE.

The Vulgate, B. Luther, and Münster rightly express the sense thus: with all diligence: although in the Hebrew there is a comparison מכל PRÆ OMNI CUSTODIA, that the heart is to be kept more than any custody, as Kasvenaki, R. Aben-Ezra, and Drusius, book 2, quæst. & resp. 10, and also the Belgians κατὰ πόδα explain: Junius, above all observation. Mercer's interpretation is more alien from all that which must be guarded against, who seems to have followed R. Solomon. That reason, FOR OUT OF IT ARE THE ISSUES OF LIFE, Mercer refers not to the heart, but to the keeping of the heart, from that, namely, that if you keep your heart from all transgression, life arises: but it is more rightly referred by others to the heart, which must be kept before all things. Because there is an allusion to natural life, which proceeds from the heart, upon the injury of which death follows; which [proceeds] from the heart, if indeed it has been quickened by Christ Gal. 2, 20, and restored to spiritual health by the Holy Spirit Psalm 51, 12. Ezech. 36, 26. spiritual life diffuses itself through all the members, and all their functions Matth. 15, 19. That life proceeds from the heart, Bernh. serm. 46, teaches among the small, because with the heart man believeth unto righteousness (Rom. 10) and the just shall live by faith (Rom. 1) and by faith the heart is purified (Act. 15) and with a pure heart GOD is seen (Matth. 5), that is, is acknowledged, and this is eternal life Joh. 17, 3. Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, says Cassian, book 6, de instit. renunt. c. 2, murders, adulteries, etc. That, therefore, is primarily to be expiated, whence the fountain of life and death is known to flow, Solomon saying, with all diligence, etc. For the flesh serves its will and command. Just as, says Dionysius, the life of nature depends upon and arises from the corporeal heart: so from the spiritual heart, which is the mind, depends and sprouts the life of grace, and progress in it. Therefore the Savior says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. And in Deuter. Keep thyself and thy soul solicitously. For invisibly enemies besiege the heart itself as the most precious castle: therefore the most intense custody is necessary for a man desiring to escape.

Latin:

vers. 23. OMNI CUSTODIA SERVA COR TUUM, QUIA EX IPSO VITA PROCEDIT.

Sensum ita Vulg. B. Luther. & Münster. recte exprimunt mit allem Fleiß: etsi in Ebr. compara- tio מכל PRÆ OMNI CUSTODIA habeatur, cor magis, quam ullam custodiam servandum esse, uti Kasvenaki, R. Aben-Ezra & Drusius l. 2. quæst. & resp. 10. ut & Belgæ κατὰ πόδα exponunt: Junius supra omnem observationem. Alienior est Merceri inter- pretatio ab omni eo, quod cavendum, qui sequutus vi- detur R. Salomonem. Rationem illam, QUIA EX IPSO SUNT EGRESSUS VIT ARUM Mer- cerus refert non ad cor, sed ad custodiam cordis, ex eo, sc. ut cor tuum ab omni transgressione serves, vita oritur: sed rectius ad cor, quod ante omnia custo- diendum est, refertur ab aliis. Quia allusio est ad vitam naturalem, quæ a corde procedit, quo læso mors sequitur; quod a corde, siquidem vivificatum sit per Christum Gal. 2, 20. & sanitati spirituali resti- tutum per Spiritum S. Psalm. 51, 12. Ezech. 36, 26. vi- ta spiritualis se diffundat per omnia membra, o- mnesque eorum functiones Matth. 15, 19. Vitam a corde procedere Bernh. serm. 46. inter parvos do- cet, quia corde creditur ad justitiam (Rom. 10.) & justus ex fide vivit (Rom. 1.) & fide mundatur cor (Act. 15.) & mundo corde DEUS videtur (Matth. 5,) id est, agnoscitur, & hæc est vita æterna Joh. 17, 3. De cor- de exeunt cogitationes malæ, ait Cassian. l. 6. de instit. renunt. c. 2. homicidia, adulteria &c. Illud ergo est primitus expiandum, unde fons vitæ & mortis manare cognoscitur, dicente Salomone, omni custodia &c. Ca- ro enim ejus arbitrio atque imperio famulatur. Quem- admodum, inquit Dionys. ex corporeo corde dependet & oritur vita naturæ : ita a corde spirituali, quod est mens, pendet ac pullulat vita gratiæ, ac profectus in ea. Ideo ait Salvator: Beati mundi corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Et in Deuter. Custodi temet- ipsum & animam tuam solicite. Invisibiliter nam- que hostes ipsum cor tanquam pretiosissimum obsident castrum: idcirco intensissima custodia est necessaria ho- mini evadere cupienti.

## 4:24
Vers. 24. REMOVE FROM THEE A FROWARD MOUTH.

Thus the Vulgate wrongly: therefore some with Hugo have accepted it concerning the removal of another's froward mouth, as of a detractor: But in the Hebrew it is remove from thee the perversity of the mouth, as Theodot. translates. Conf. Proverb. 6, 12. because after the keeping of the heart, the work is primarily the keeping of our mouth Jac. 3, 8. Psal. 39, 2. and this sense is demanded by the exegesis, which Solomon adds according to his custom: AND PERVERSE LIPS BE FAR FROM THEE: which in the Hebrew is more general: And the perversity of lips put far from thee. The word לוּת, occurring nowhere else, receded from לות, is rendered by the Chaldean עותא iniquity, perversity, by which we recede from the law of God. The LXX have ἄδικα χείλη unjust lips, Aquila & Theod. ςρεβλότητα ςόματος. Cornel. acknowledges this sense to be the best and proves it thus: For just as, he says, he commanded the keeping of ONE'S OWN HEART: so also he commanded the keeping of one's own mouth: for great is the sympathy and connection of the heart and mouth.

Latin:

Vers. 24. REMOVE A TE OS PRAVUM.

Ita perperam vulgata: ideo nonnulli cum Hugone de remotione oris pravi alieni accepere, utpo- te detractoris: Sed in Ebr. est remove a te oris perver- sitatem, ut Theodot. vertit. Conf. Proverb. 6, 12. quia post cordis custodiam opus imprimis est custo- dia oris nostri Jac. 3, 8. Psal. 39, 2. & hunc sensum postulat ἐξήγησις, quam pro more suo Salomo addit: ET DETRAHENTIA LABIA SINT PROCUL A TE: quod in Ebr. generalius est: Et pravitatem labiorum elonga a te. Vox לוּת nuspiam alias occurrens, a לות recessit a Chaldæo redditur עותא iniquitas, pravitas, qua recedi- mus a lege Dei. LXX. habent ἄδικα χείλη inju- sta labia, Aquila & Theod. ςρεβλότητα ςόματος. Agnoscit hunc sensum optimum esse Cornel. eum- que ita probat: Sicut enim, inquit, CORDIS PRO- PRII custodiam præcepit: sic & oris proprii custodiam præcepit: magna enim est cordis & oris Sympathia & connexio.

## 4:25
Vers. 25. LET THINE EYES LOOK RIGHT ON, AND LET THINE EYELIDS LOOK STRAIGHT BEFORE THEE.

In the Hebrew it is, let thine eyes look into the direct, and let thine eyelids direct (the way) before thee, or let them be directed, as the Chaldean has. The LXX more alienly, Let thine eyelids nod just things. After the keeping of the heart and mouth, he ordains the keeping of the eyes: for eyes in love (of virtue or vice) are leaders, and that you may keep the heart, it is necessary above other senses and members to keep the eyes equally as the tongue, 1. Joh. 2, 16. Conf. Matth. 6, 22. Others prefer to take it of the eyes of the mind, that they may always look back at the set goal, by which we may strive straight to it Phil. 3, 14, that they may always be directed to the Lord Psalm 123, 2, not wander hither and thither. Mercerus, I think, he says, that it is simply commanded in the three last verses of this chapter, that we should depend in all things on the rule of the divine word, not receding from it even by a broad nail, that the way once proposed by the Lord is to be held, that eyes are always to be cast straight into it, not deflected hither or thither. Moreover, there is altogether need for the eyes of the mind to be enlightened, so that we do not turn ourselves with the eyes of the body to the vanities of the world Psalm 19, 9, from which Solomon here properly wishes the eyes of the body to be averted, as Ambros. lib. de Bon. mort. c. 9. Let thine eyes look right on: Which would not be said unless they frequently wandered. For the leader, says Basil. M. lib. de S. Virg., and the forerunner and matchmaker of the eyes is that, of which the hands and touch are ministers. He now demands the government of the eyes, where before he demanded that of the tongue and lips. Conf. c. 6, 13. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 25. OCULI TUI RECTA VIDEANT, ET PAL- PEBRÆ TUÆ PRÆCEDANT GRESSUS TUOS.

In Ebr. est, oculi tui in directum aspiciant, & palpebræ tuæ dirigant (viam) coram te, vel dirigan- tur, ut Chald. habet. LXX. alienius, Palpebræ tuæ annuant justa. Post cordis & oris custodiam san- cit custodiam oculorum: oculi enim in amore (virtu- tis aut vitii) duces sunt, atque ut custodias cor, opus est præ cæteris sensibus & membris custodire oculos æque ac linguam, 1. Joh. 2, 16. Conf. Matth. 6, 22. De oculis mentis alii accipere malunt, ut semper re- spiciant scopum præfixum, quo recta ad eum con- tendamus Phil. 3, 14. directi sint semper ad Domi- num Psalm. 123, 2. non vagentur huc, illuc. Mer- cerus, puto, inquit, simpliciter tribus extremis versicu- lis hujus capitis præcipi, ut in omnibus ex regula verbi divini pendeamus, ab ea ne latum quidem unguem re- cedentes, viam a Domino semel propositam tenendam, in eam recta conjiciendos semper oculos, non huc aut il- luc deflectendum. Cæterum oculis mentis illustra- tis omnino opus est, ut ne oculis corporis ad mundi vanitates nos convertamus Psalm. 19, 9. a quibus hic oculos corporis averti proprie vult Salomo, ut Ambrof. lib. de Bon. mort. c. 9. Oculi tui recta vi- deant: Quod non esset dictum nisi frequenter erra- rent. Dux enim, ait Basil. M. l. de S. Virg. & præ- vius ac pronubus oculorum jactus est ejus, cujus mini- stræ sunt manus, tactus. Oculorum gubernationem jam poscit, ubi antea linguæ & labiorum. Conf. c. 6, 13. 17.

## 4:26
vers. 26.

PONDER THE PATH OF THY FEET.

In the Hebrew פלס is more emphatic, weigh, and adjust the path to thy feet to the level of right reason. Symmach. & Theodot. prepare; Pagninus weigh, LXX. Make straight paths τροχιὰς for your feet, which the Apostle cites Ebr. 12, 13.

AND ALL THY WAYS SHALL BE ESTABLISHED.

It is more correctly rendered as a precept, LET THEM BE STABLE, so that it may be a kind of exposition of the former: just as v. 27 confirms this sense: which Mercerus, Mariana, and the Belgians have also embraced; for how the path is to be directed, and the ways ought to be stable, is further explained in the last verse: DECLINE NOT TO THE RIGHT, NOR TO THE LEFT: TURN AWAY THY FOOT FROM EVIL. All of which pertain to the instruction of the feet in the literal sense: just as the preceding things had been delivered for the instruction of the tongue and the eyes. Although indeed the right and left denote extremes, which are to be avoided, and the path of the commandments of God is prescribed to us to be observed as a royal road, as is certain from parallel passages Deuteronomy 5, verse 32, Isaiah 30, verse 21, etc. here, however, the direction and governance of our feet according to the Word of the Lord, and the way of His commandments, is regarded; not the feet of the mind, or of the affections, because Solomon had previously warned about governing the heart, but of the body, lest they hasten to evil and deviate from the way of the divine law, Proverbs 1:16, Isaiah 59:7, 8, Romans 3:16. But the things which both the LXX and the Vulgate add, For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right: but those that are on the left are perverse, but He Himself will make thy courses straight, and will bring thy journeys to pass in peace, although they are cited by some Fathers from the LXX Interpreters, they are not read in the Hebrew source, nor in the Chaldean, indeed not even in the Complutensian or Royal Latin, nor in Cajetan, nor in some manuscripts, as Cornelius admits. Therefore they are foreign and interpolated. Nor, however they may be reconciled with the preceding, do they cohere with the same; since a reason ought rather to be given for the way to be declined to the right and left alike, than for the way to be chosen to the right, and to be fled to the left.

Latin:

vers. 26.

DIRIGE SEMITAM PEDIBUS TUIS.

In Ebræo פלס est ἐμφατικώτερον libres, & ad libellam rectæ rationis adæques semitam pedibus tuis. Symmach. & Theodot. ἑτοίμαζε; Pagninus pondera, LXX. Gressus rectos τροχιὰς facite pedibus vestris, quod adducit Apostolus Ebr. 12, 13.

ET OMNES VIÆ TUÆ STABILIENTUR.

Rectius redditur ceu præceptum, STABILES SINT, ut prioris sit quædam expositio: quemad- modum v. 27. hunc sensum confirmat: quem etiam Mercerus, Mariana, Belgæ amplexi sunt; nam quo- modo dirigenda semita sit, & viæ stabiles esse de- beant, ulterius explicatur versu ultimo: NE DE- CLINES AD DEXTERAM, NEQUE AD SI- NISTRAM: AVERTE PEDEM A MALO. Quæ omnia ad informationem pedum sensu literali spectant: quemadmodum præcedentia ob infor- mationem linguæ & oculorum tradita erant. Quan- quam enim dextra & sinistra extrema notent, quæ vitanda, & semita mandatorum Dei ceu via regia ita observanda nobis præscribatur, ut e locis parallelis certum est Deuteronom. 5. versu 32. Esa. 30. versu 21. &c. hic tamen pedum nostrorum directio & guber- natio juxta Verbum Domini, & via mandatorum ejus respicitur; non pedum animi, vel affectuum, quia de corde gubernando antea monuerat Salomo, sed corporis, ne ad malum properent & a via legis divinæ devient, Proverb. 1, 16. Esa. 59, 7. 8. Rom. 3, 16. Quæ vero & LXX. & Vulg. addunt, Viæ enim quæ a dextris sunt novit Dominus: perversæ vero sunt quæ a sinistris sunt, ipse autem rectos faciet cursus tuos, itinera autem tua in pace producet, etsi a Patribus nonnullis e LXX. Interpp. adducuntur, in fonte Ebræo non leguntur, nec in Chaldæo, imo nec in Com- plutensi vel Regia Latina, nec in Cajetano, nec in MM. SS. nonnull. fatente Cornelio. Aliena ergo sunt & irreptitia. Neque, utcunque concilientur cum antecedentibus, cohærent cum iisdem; quum ratio potius reddi debeat viæ ad dexteram pariter & sinistram declinandæ, quam viæ ad dextram eligendæ, ad sinistram fugiendæ.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. He teaches that the harlot is to be fled from like a plague, on account of the most present dangers, and suggests the love of one's own wife as a remedy for flight.

Latin:

CAPUT V. Meretricem fugiendam esse ut pestem, ob peri- cula præsentissima docet, ac remedium fu- gæ dilectionem uxoris propriæ suggerit.

## 5:2
Ver. 2. DO NOT HEED THE DECEITFULNESS OF A WOMAN.

The LXX and the Vulgate added these: for they are not contained in the Hebrew: nor can this προσθήκη be excused, because they are tacitly understood in the Hebrew: because it is not right to add anything to the word of God, and to pass off as the words of the Holy Spirit those which did not proceed from Him: nor was there need for that inference, since the Holy Spirit Himself added the conclusion in verses 8 and 20.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NE ATTENDAS FALLACIÆ MU- LIERIS.

HÆC LXX. & Vulgatus addidere: In Ebræo enim non habentur: nec excusari hæc προσ- θήκη potest, quod tacite in Ebr. subintelligantur: quia fas non est aliquid verbo Dei adjicere, & pro verbis Spirit. S. venditare, quæ ab eo profecta non sunt: neque illatione ista opus erat, quum versu 8. & 20. conclusionem adjecerit ipse Spi- ritus Sanct.

## 5:3
Ver. 3. FOR THE HONEYCOMB DISTILLING ARE THE LIPS OF A HARLOT) For harlot in the Hebrew is זרה, that is, strange, namely, a wife. See below 18, 19, 20, 6, 29.

Lyranus takes this harlot to be idolatry; Beda, Cyril of Jerusalem (Catech. 4), Cyril of Alexandria (book 15 on adoration), and Olympiodorus and Polychronius (as also Jerome in Ez. 6) take it to be heresy; others take it to be pleasure and concupiscence: and indeed most things can be adapted to the STRANGE WOMAN, of whom in chapter 2, 16, who embraces all those things in her own way, and deceives like a harlot with flatteries sweeter than honey: but because all things flow more aptly if you adhere to the letter, and one must not depart from the letter unless necessity compels, furthermore in the preceding verses Solomon taught generally to direct the heart, tongue, eyes, and feet, now he informs us how we ought to govern ourselves primarily so that we are not seduced by women, inasmuch as they can easily occupy our heart (ver. 12), ensnare us with lips distilling mere honey (v. 3), and drag the unwary into their paths, even if they are the worst, and seduce them with their arts. And how would Solomon have suddenly jumped to fleeing from human Wisdom, or heresy, idolatry, or base concupiscence in general, regarding the fleeing of suretyships and sloth in chapter 6? Since those who explain the harlot improperly understand that this does not fit, they are forced in the following chapter to betake themselves to I know not what figurative senses concerning suretyship and liberation from the same through repentance, or concerning human intellect standing surety before God for appetite, etc. Nor indeed is it without cause that Solomon warns specially about avoiding harlots, he who had most experienced the seduction of women, to his own great harm, if indeed, as Augustine has in his book on the honesty of women, chapter 1, among the other struggles of Christians, only the battles of chastity are hard, where the fight is daily and victory is rare. For chastity has been allotted a grave enemy, which is resisted daily and is always feared. Jerome. Book 1 against Jovinian, near the end: It is the voice of a most learned man that modesty is to be retained above all, for when it is omitted every virtue collapses. In this is the primacy of feminine virtues, etc.

Moreover, Cartwright does not interpret נפת, which explains the honeycomb, badly as honey most choice, which distills of its own accord from the comb, by which the flattering speech of a harlot is expressed: Chrysostom (homily 14 to the people) refers the honeycomb of the lips to bland kisses, but it is more correctly referred by others to the words of harlots, which sweeten in such a way that they seem to drip honey: Let the sweetness of the voice, says Jerome to Gaudentius, which wounds the soul through the ears, flee away: and Saint Cyprian on the Singularity of Clerics: Now the harlot exhibits flatteries, now soft words, and what is more poisonous than all, she delights to sing, by whose singing it is more tolerable to hear a hissing basilisk.

AND SMOOTHER THAN OIL IS HER THROAT. In the Hebrew and Chaldean, smoother than oil is her palate; the Syriac, her words are softer than oil: the LXX, more strangely: for a time she fattens your throat. Hugo the Cardinal refers oil to the ointments of women: but that this explains the preceding gnome, there should be no doubt: for thus women soften their words so that they seem smoother than oil, which is therefore attributed by metonymy to the throat, from which smooth words and flatteries emanate like oil.

Latin:

Vers. 3. FAVUS ENIM DESTILLANS LABIA MERETRICIS) Pro meretricis in Hebræo est זרה, id est, alienæ, scilicet uxoris. Vide infra 18. 19. 20. 6, 29.

De idololatria hanc meretricem Lyranus, de humana sapientia Beda, Cyrill. Hieros. Catech. 4. Cyrill. Alexand. l. 15. de ador. de hæresi Olympiod. & Polychron. ut & Hieron. in Ez. 6. de voluptate & concupiscentia alii accipiunt: & accommodari sane pleraque possunt MULIERI EXTRANEÆ, de qua cap. 2, 16. quæ omnia illa suo modo comple- ctitur, & instar meretricis melle dulcioribus blan- ditiis decipit: sed quia omnia aptius fluunt, si li- teræ inhæreas, nec a litera discedendum, nisi co- gente necessitate, adhæc in antecedentibus cor, linguam, oculos, & pedes dirigere generatim docuit Salomo, jam quomodo imprimis, ne a mulieribus seducamur, nos gubernare debeamus, informat, utpote quæ cor nostrum facile occupare, vers. 12. labiis mera mella destillantibus nos inescare, v. 3. & in semitas suas, etsi pessimas incautos abripere, ac seducere artibus suis possunt. Et quomodo ad sponsiones & pigritiam fugiendam c. 6. transiliret Sa- lomo actutum, si hic de fugienda Sapientia huma- na, vel hæresi, idololatria, aut concupiscentia pra- va in genere monuisset? Quod cum non conve- nire intelligant, qui meretricem improprie ex- plicant, capite sequenti etiam ad nescio quos figu- ratos sensus de sponsione, & liberatione ab eadem per pœnitentiam, vel de intellectu humano spondente apud Deum pro appetitu &c. se recipere coguntur. Nec vero absque causa specialiter Salomo de cavendis meretricibus monet, qui mulierum seductionem maxime expertus erat, magno suo malo, siquidem ut August. libr. de honest. mulier. cap. 1. habet, inter alia certamina Christianorum sola dura sunt prælia castitatis, ubi quotidiana est pugna, & rara victoria. Gravem namq́; sortita est castitas inimi- cum, cui quotidie resistitur & semper timetur. Hie- ronym. l. 1. contra Jovian. sub finem: Doctissimi viri vox est pudicitiam imprimis esse retinendam, qua omissa omnis virtus ruit. In hac muliebrium virtutum principatus est, &c.

Cæterum נפת quod favum explicat com- muniter Cartwright. mel longe lectissimum, quod ex favo sponte destillat, non male interpretatur, quo blandiloquentia meretricis exprimitur: Chry- sostom. homil. 14. ad popul. favum labiorum ad oscula blanda refert, sed rectius ad verba meretri- cum refertur ab aliis, quæ ita edulcorant, ut mel stillare videantur: Vocis dulcedines, inquit Hieronym. ad Gaudent. per aures animam vulne- rantes fugiant: & Sanct. Cyprian. de Singul. Cle- ric. Nunc blanditias exhibet meretrix, nunc verba mollia, & quod venenosius est super cuncta, psallere delectatur, cujus cantu tolerabilius est audire basi- liscum sibilantem.

ET NITIDIUS OLEO GUTTUR EJUS. In Ebr. & Chald. lenius oleo palatum ejus, Syrus, molliora oleo verba ejus: LXX. alienius: ad tempus impinguat fauces tuas. Hugo Card. oleum refert ad unguenta mulierum: sed quod præceden- tem gnomam hæc explicet, dubium esse non de- bet: ita enim mulieres verba emolliunt, ut oleo le- niora videantur, quod proinde gutturi per meto- nymiam tribuitur, e quo verba lenia & blanditiæ instar olei emanant.

## 5:4
Ver. 4.

But her end is bitter as wormwood, and sharp as a two-edged sword.

To the honeycomb and honey of the lips is opposed bitter wormwood, and to the smooth oil, a sharp sword. Cf. Psalm 55, verse 22, that the end of the harlot's loves ends in most bitter and painful destruction. Which final bitterness, with the pains arising from that sharp sword, Solomon soon describes, that the feet of the harlot go down to death, and her steps penetrate to the underworld, and those who allow themselves to be seduced by them are also precipitated there, since fornicators are excluded from the kingdom of God 1 Cor. 6, verse 9, Galat. 5, 19, that the blandishments of the harlot bring damage to beauty, life, strength, and faculties, so that we may at length grieve too late. Beautifully St. Cyprian, de singul. Cleric.: Through infinite disgraces she brings multiple deaths to the destruction of the lost. Grotius on v. 5 has these words: HER FEET GO DOWN TO DEATH) Menander: There is no matter more precious than an adulterer, for it is bought with death.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NOVISSIMA AUTEM ILLIUS AMARA QVASI ABSYNTHIUM, ET ACUTA QVASI GLADIUS ANCEPS.

Favo & melli labiorum dulci amarum absyn- thium, leni vero oleo acutus gladius opponitur. Conf. Psalm. 55. versu 22. quod novissime amo- res meretrici in amarissimam, & dolorosam perni- tiem desinant. Quam novissimam amaritudinem cum doloribus ab acuto isto gladio oriundis mox describit Salomo, quod pedes meretricis in mortem descendant, & ad inferos gressus illius penetrent, eoque etiam præcipitentur, qui ab illis seduci se patiuntur, quum scortatores a regno Dei exclu- dantur 1. Cor. 6. vers. 9. Galat. 5, 19. quod damnum adferant blanditiæ meretriciæ decoris, vitæ, roboris, facultatum, ut nimis sero tandem doleamus. Pul- cre S. Cyprian. de singul. Cleric. Per infinita dede- cora multiplices mortes invehit in perniciem perdi- torum. Grotius ad v. 5. hæc habet: PEDES EJUS DESCENDUNT AD MORTEM) Menander: Ουκ ἔστι μοιχẽ πρᾶγμα τιμιώτερον Θανάτε γάρ ἐστιν ὤνιον.

## 5:6
Vers. 6.

HER STEPS ARE WANDERING AND UNTRACEABLE.

Mercerus renders the Hebrew thus: Her steps are wandering, so that you do not know, to wit, whither she tends. So also Münster. Dr. Gejer prefers to refer it to the preceding, that he may not know, to wit, the true path of life, which is compared here: Osiander refers it to the harlot in this manner, nor shall she know (she herself, the harlot, to wit) the way of salvation, by which she might escape damnation.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

VAGI SUNT GRESSUS EJUS ET IN- VESTIGABILES.

Ebræa ita reddit Mercerus: Vagi sunt gressus ejus, adeo ut nescias, quo scil. illa tendat. Sic etiam Münsterus. Dn. D. Gejer. mavult ad præceden- tia referre, ne sciat, veram scil. vitæ semitam, qui hic conferatur: ad scortum refert Osiander h. m. neque cognoscet (ipsa, meretrix scil.) viam saluti, qua damnationem effugere possit.

## 5:9
Vers. 9.

GIVE NOT THY HONOR TO STRANGERS, AND THY YEARS TO THE CRUEL ONE.

Mercerus, Cajetan, and Salazar understand it of the flower of age, the ornament of both body and soul; others think the beauty of integrity and chastity is designated; Cornelius a Lapide of public dignities, as well as of the honor of things done excellently; Osiander of faculties, which expose us as honored, and Dr. Gejer, with the blessed Luther, interprets it even of wealth and reputation. However, all those things can in our judgment be included together under the word honor, insofar as they contribute to honor. By the name CRUEL ONE, most understand the adulteress, who as if in play exhausts the life of her lover, with Mercerus, who is expressed in the masculine gender because of her masculine audacity: but it can be understood indefinitely as anyone, for example, either that harlot, or the jealous husband of the adulteress, or another coming upon them, ignorant of pity: so that the danger impending over him, whether from the Magistrate or from another, may be designated.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

NE DES ALIENIS HONOREM TUUM, ET ANNOS TUOS CRUDELI.

De flore ætatis, ornamento & corporis & animi intelligunt Mercerus, Cajetan. Salazar, integrita- tis castitatisque decus alii designari censent; de di- gnitatibus publicis, ut & de honore rerum præclare gestarum Cornel. a Lap. de facultatibus, quæ nos honoratos exponunt, Osiander, adeoque de opi- bus etiam & existimatione cum Beat. Luthero Dn. D. Gejerus interpretatur. Possunt autem illa omnia nostro judicio simul voce honoris compre- hendi, quatenus sc. ea ad honorem faciunt. CRU- DELIS nomine Adulteram intelligunt plerique, quæ per lusum quasi exhaurit vitam amasii, cum Mercero, quæ masculino efferatur genere ob masculam audaciam: intelligi autem potest qui- cunque indefinite, puta seu meretrix illa, seu maritus adulteræ Zelotypus, seu alius superve- niens, ignarus miserationis: ut designetur illi periculum sive a Magistratu, seu ab alio immi- nens.

## 5:10
Verse 10.

LEST PERCHANCE STRANGERS BE FILLED WITH THY STRENGTH, AND THY LABORS BE IN THE HOUSE OF A STRANGER.

It treats specifically of the loss of resources, which is designated by 'strength': as Vatablus [says], lest perchance strangers be satisfied with those things which thou hast prepared by thy strength, and thy labors be in the house of a stranger, so that the latter hemistich may be an interpretation of the former. Compare Proverbs 10, verse 15; Luke 15, verse 17. So also Cajetan and Salazar on this passage, as well as John Alba, Elector, chapter 87.

Latin:

Verf. 10.

NE FORTE IMPLEANTUR EXTRA- NEI VIRIBUS TUIS, ET LABORES TUI SINT IN DOMO ALIENA.

Speciatim de damno facultatum agitur, quod viribus designatur: uti Vatabl. ne forte satientur alieni iis, quæ viribus tuis parasti, & labores tui sint in domo aliena, ut posterius hemistichion prioris sit interpretatio. Conf. Proverb. 10. v. 15. Luc. 15. versu 17. Sic etiam Cajetan. & Salaz. hoc loc. ut & Joh. Alba Elector. cap. 87.

## 5:11
Verse 11.

AND THOU GROAN IN THE END WHEN THOU HAST CONSUMED THY FLESH, AND THY BODY.

In the Hebrew it is: nerugias, like a famished lion, in the end, exhausted, to wit, not only of wealth, but also of flesh; because lust emaciates the whole body and exhausts all the vigor of the body. The latter word שאר, which Forster interprets as flesh, which is the remaining part of an animal after the soul, Osiander interprets as the remains of wealth; some explain it as juice and radical and native moisture; Junius understands it of the whole body even consumed down to the bones and marrow, so that it may be an amplification. It can also be rendered as whatever is still remaining to you, whether as flesh, or as resources, or even honors, so that the preceding [verses] may be regarded in this way. Namely, when all those things of which he had spoken shall have been consumed.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

ET GEMAS IN NOVISSIMIS QUAN- DO CONSUMSERIS CARNES TUAS, ET CORPUS TUUM.

In Ebr. est: nerugias, instar leonis famelici, in novissimis, exhaustus scil. non modo opibus, sed etiam carnibus; quia libido totum corpus ema- ciat, & omnem corporis vigorem exhaurit. Po- steriorem vocem שאר quam Forsterus carnem, quæ est reliqua pars animalis post animam, Osian- der reliquias opum interpretatur, nonnulli succum & humorem radicalem & nativum exponunt: Ju- nius de corpore toto etiam exeso ad ossa & medullas usque, intelligit, ut auxesis sit. Reddi potest & quicquid reliquum adhuc tibi est, seu qua carnes, seu qua facultates, seu honores etiam, ut ita supe- riora respiciantur. Quando nempe omnia illa, de quibus dixerat, consumta erunt.

## 5:14
Verse 14.

I HAVE BEEN ALMOST IN ALL EVIL, IN THE MIDST OF THE CHURCH AND THE SYNAGOGUE.

In all evil, both of fault, because lust is the origin and cause of every fault and sin, as Chrysostom [says], and of punishment, to which infamy also pertains, of which Polychronius interprets these things, nay even Gehenna, in which is every evil: whence Rabbi Solomon [says], there was only a step between me and Gehenna; he says, however, that he fell into almost every evil in the midst of the assembly and congregation, that is, openly and with others looking on, which brings greater grief.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

PENE FUI IN OMNI MALO, IN ME- DIO ECCLESIÆ ET SYNAGOGÆ.

In omni malo tum culpæ, quia libido est origo & causa omnis culpæ & peccati, ut Chrysost. tum pœnæ, ad quam etiam infamia spectat, de qua Po- lychronius hæc interpretatur, imo & gehenna, in qua omne malum est: Unde R. Salomo, passus tan- tum inter me & gehennam interfuit; in medio autem cœtus & congregationis se in omne pene malum incidisse, h. e. palam & aliis inspectantibus, ait, quod majorem adfert dolorem.

## 5:15
Verse 15.

DRINK WATER FROM THY CISTERN, AND THE STREAMS OF THY WELL) Enjoy lawful pleasure. It is called a cistern here modestly, as a sealed fountain, Canticles 4, verse 12. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion have 'pit' here. Diphilus of Gnathaena, 'cool the pit for the vessels.' See also below, verse 23.

Some interpret this regarding the waters of Wisdom to be drawn from Holy Scripture, along with R. Sal. Jarchi, Lyranus, and Gregory the Great, who explain the former as human and adulterous wisdom: others interpret it regarding faculties to be spent for our own uses, along with Basil the Great in Psalm 40, as also Philip Melanchthon, Osiander, and B. Franzius on the Interpretation of Scripture, 45. But most, along with Chrysostom, hom. 1 on Matthew, Jerome on Malachi 3, Bede, and Hugo, interpret it regarding one's own wife, who is like a domestic fountain for quenching the heats of lust, 1 Cor. 7, verses 2, 9. Cf. Isa. 51, 1; Sir. 26, 15. This explanation is confirmed from verse 18. The simple sense, says Mercerus, is that he should return to that from which he had digressed, when he brings in the mimesis of one wailing late: Do not therefore follow a harlot, but be content with your wife, enjoy her, from her satisfy your thirst. For he will also soon say, rejoice with the wife of your youth. Moreover, he expressed the work of marriage הבעילה, as the Hebrews call it, with most honest and sweetest words, through the drinking of waters, as he calls מים גנובים, waters stolen by theft, below in the ninth chapter (says Kabvenaki here), clandestine intercourse and fornications.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

BIBE AQVAM DE CISTERNA TUA, ET FLU- ENTA PUTEI TUI) Fruere voluptate licita. Cisterna hîc di- citur σεμνῶς, ut fons signatus. Cant. 4. vers. 12. λάκκον hic habent Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion. Diphilus Gna- thenæ, ψυχρὸν ὄχοις τὸν λάκκον. Vide & infra 23. versu 23.

Hoc nonnulli de aquis Sapientiæ è Scriptura S. hauriendis accipiunt cum R. Sal. Jarchi, Lyrano, & Gregor. M. qui scil. priora de sapientia humana, & adulterina explicant: alii de facultatibus ad no- stros usus impendendis, cum Bafil. M. in Psalm. 40. ut & Philipp. Melancht. Osiandro, & B. Fran- zio de Interp. Scriptur. 45. Plerique autem cum Chrysost. hom. 1. in Matth. Hieron. in Mal. 3. Beda & Hugone de uxore propria, quæ est instar fontis domestici ad restinguendos æstus libidinis 1. Cor. 7. versu 2. 9. Conf. Es. 51, 1. Syr. 26, 15. interpretan- tur. Quæ explicatio è versu 18. confirmatur. Sim- plex sensus est, inquit Mercerus, ut eo redeat, unde digressus fuerat, cum Mimesin sero ejulantis affert: Ne ergo meretricem sequere, sed uxore tua esto con- tentus, hac fruere, hinc sitim exple. Nam & mox dicet, lætare cum uxore pueritiæ tuæ. Honestissimis autem & suavissimis verbis opus expressit conjugii הבעילה, ut appellant Hebræi, per potum aqua- rum, ut est infra nono capite מים גנובים aquas furto ablatas appellat (ait hic Kabvenaki) clandestinum coitum & scortationes.

## 5:16
Ver. 16.

LET YOUR FOUNTAINS BE DISPERSED ABROAD) There, almost where you measure your offspring.

Some explain it regarding liberality, so that the following things are for you alone regarding parsimony, so that he may command it to be a benefit, lest you be cast out from your estate: but so derive your fountains to others, that you yourself retain their ownership for yourself, and remain their Lord. Mercerus, along with R. Abraham, refers it to numerous offspring: as also Dn. D. Geierus: (which are more suitable than the Grotian explanation) because from this fruitful spring of marriage, sons and daughters proceed like rivulets through God's blessing, who, being well educated, in turn serve others, Psalm 128, verse 3, from whom also this Capellus is deservedly chastised for preferring the negative reading of the LXX and Aquila to the fountains. Those things can also be taken by way of a promise, as the fruit of marriage promised by God to the chaste: just as the following things, HAVE THEM TO YOURSELF, that is, THEY SHALL BE FOR YOU ALONE, are taken by Mercerus: you will claim them for yourself by your own right. Mercerus adds: associating with a harlot, you will be in danger if you have children by her, lest they be common to you with other adulterous progenitors; here they will be yours alone from the wife with whom you have chaste intimacy, you will have no reason to doubt. So also Cornelius à Lap. SHALL BE or WILL BE YOUR FOUNTAIN or spring BLESSED, AND REJOICE WITH THE WOMAN, or WIFE OF YOUR YOUTH. So Vatablus, Pagninus, Jansenius, and others. Cf. Deut. 28, 4. The Belgic version renders it rejoice in your wife, so that the D denotes the object, as if he were saying, That domestic fountain and spring of yours will be blessed, and you will rejoice only in the wife of your youth, concerning which latter phrase cf. Malachi 2, 15, and concerning this chaste joy, Proverbs 6, v. 26. Eccl. 9. v. 9. A MOST DEAR HIND AND MOST PLEASANT FAWN. LET HER BREASTS INEBRIATE YOU AT ALL TIMES, DELIGHT IN HER LOVE CONTINUALLY. That all these things look toward marriage is clear. Cf. Cant. 2, 9; chap. 1, 2. Continually with respect to others; so that we may never delight with others, but always with our own wife alone. The love of harts for hinds is most ardent, and hinds are faithful, chaste, and sweet to their mate; for harts and hinds lack gall, whence they are also long-lived. Thus he calls her wife, says Mercerus, whom he wishes to be loved intensely, and to be to her husband as a beloved hind and a grateful ibex to her mate, in which kind of animal there is great simplicity, a sincerity of love not suspicious, not morose nor fastidious, nor painted, and between both the ardor of love is highest, as Oppian describes when dealing with harts. Thus he wishes spouses themselves to be toward one another, to acquiesce in mutual love, even if he is dealing with the love of the husband properly toward the wife. There are those who think that mention is made of these animals for the reason that they were among the delights of kings. I believe it is rather an allusion to their nature, which I have mentioned. I add what Grotius says about these:

Latin:

Verf. 16.

DERIVENTUR FONTES TUI FORAS) Ibi fere ubi prolem metas.

De liberalitate nonnulli explicant, ut sequen- tia sint tibi soli de parsimonia, ut ita beneficium esse jubeat, ne de fundo tuo excutiaris : sed ita fontes tuos in alios derives, ut ipse tibi eorum proprie- tatem retineas, & eorum Dominus maneas. Mer- cerus cum R. Abraham ad prolem numerosam re- fert : ut & Dn. D. Geierus: (quæ commodiora sunt Grotiana explicatione) quia ex fœcunda hac scaturigine conjugii filii filiæque ceu rivuli per Dei benedictionem procedunt, qui bene educati aliis vicissim inserviunt Psalm. 128. vers. 3. à quo etiam merito castigatur hic Capellus negativam Lectio- nem LXX. & Aquilæ fontibus præferens. Possunt etiam illa accipi per modum promissionis, ceu fru- ctus conjugii castis à Deo promissus: uti & sequen- tia HABETO EAS SOLUS, id est, ERUNT TIBI SOLI à Mercero accipiuntur : tuo tibi jure eos vindicabis, Addit Mercerus : cum meretrice versans periclitabere, si ex ea liberos susceperis, ne tibi cum aliis progenitoribus adulteris essent communes, hic tui solius erunt de uxore cum qua castam habes consuetudinem, dubitare non habebis. Sic etiam Cor- nelius à Lap. SIT vel ERIT VENA vel scaturigo TUA BENEDICTA, ET LÆTARE CUM MULIERE, vel UXORE ADOLESCEN- TIÆ TUÆ. Sic Vatablus, Pagninus, Jansenius & alii. Conf. Deut. 28, 4. Belgica reddit lætare de uxore, ut D objectum denotet, quasi dicat, Erit be- nedicta illa vena & scaturigo tua domestica, & læta- beris solum de uxore adolescentiæ tuæ, de qua poste- riori phrasi conf. Malach. 2, 15. & de casta hac læti- tia Proverb. 6, v. 26. Eccl. 9. v. 9. CERVA CHA- RISSIMA ET GRATISSIMUS HINNULUS. UBERA EJUS INEBRIANT TE IN OMNI TEMPORE, IN AMORE EJUS DELE- CTARE JUGITER. Quæ omnia ad conjugium spectare luculentum est. Conf. Cant. 2, 9. cap. 1. 2. Jugiter respectu aliarum; ita ut nunquam cum aliis, semper cum propria solum uxore delectemur. Cervorum in cervas amor ardentissimus est, suntque cervæ mari suo fidæ, castæ & suaves; nam cervi & cervæ felle carent, unde & vivaces sunt. Sic uxo- rem appellat, ait Mercerus, quam impensè amari vult, & viro esse ut amatam cervam & ibicem gra- tam suo mari, in quo genere animantium magna est simplicitas, amoris sinceritas non suspicax, non mo- rosa nec fastidiosa, nec fucata, & inter utrumque ar- dor amoris summus, ut Oppianus de cervis ageus de- scribit. Sic conjuges ipsos invicem esse vult, in mutuo amore acquiescere, etsi de amore proprie viri erga uxo- rem agit. Sunt qui ideo putent horum animantium fie- ri mentionem, quod essent regibus in deliciis. Ego ad eorum naturam, quam dixi, allusum potius credo. Addo quæ de his Grotius:

## 5:17
Vers. 17. HAVE THEM TO YOURSELF, AND LET NOT STRANGERS BE PARTAKERS WITH YOU) Those waters, namely, that is, your wife. Be a diligent guardian of your marriage. The Rabbis interpret allegorically regarding the hidden Theology, which they call מַרְכָבָה, verse 19.

Latin:

Vers. 17. HABETO EAS SOLUS, NEC SINT ALIE- NI PARTICIPES TUI) Eas nempe aquas, id est, uxorem. Diligens esto tui matrimonii custos. Rabbini ἀλληγορικῶς interpretantur de abscondita Theologia, quam מַרְכָבָה vocant vers. 19.

## 5:19
A MOST DEAR HIND, AND MOST PLEASANT FAWN) For many have such animals among their delights. Hence those similarities in Cant. 2, 9.

LET HER BREASTS INEBRIATE YOU) The Hebrews call breasts דּוֹד, as the seat of loves.

Vers. eod. DELIGHT IN HER LOVE CONTINUALLY) In the Greek, ἐν γὰρ τῇ ταύτης φιλίᾳ συμπεριφερόμενος, πολλοστὸς ἔσῃ. It appears the Seventy Elders read שגג, with a dot on the left in the first letter. For thus it signifies to be multiplied. But with a dot on the right, it signifies to be delighted among other things. And thus some translate: שִׁגְיוֹנַוֹת delights, Hab. 3, 1.

If the LXX. Interpreters, among whom παροράματα are not infrequent, had seen anything else, yet to recall the fountains of Hebrew truth, with Lud. Capellus, l. 6. Critic. S. cap. 4. §. 6., to impure rivulets,

& from these purge, for us religion. The fountains flow here excellently: Nor does the version of the LXX Elders depart from them, as far as the sense is concerned. For תשגה denotes to wander, Ez. 34, 6. so that the sense may be, in her love you may wander continually, to which the Greek word περιφερόμενος corresponds well, and because that is of delight, and an amiable object, as to the sense, it is rightly rendered by delighting, by Vatablus, Pagninus, Luther: Mercerus illustrates that word excellently in this place. He adds a notable hyperbole to describe excellent love, in her love you may wander assiduously, so that you are as it were outside yourself, and forget other things because of your love for her. He wishes one to be worth all, and if one must wander in love, one should rather wander in a wife than with a strange woman, as he subjoins. Others of the Hebrews explain תשגה, you shall wander, from the Talmudic תעסוק, you shall be occupied, you shall be at leisure, in which way they say it is also taken in the Arabic language: others, you shall be delighted, as they wish it to be taken in Psalm 7, in the title. Thus also our Interpreter renders, be delighted, which seems somewhat harsh, for Solomon to command one to wander in the love of a wife. But it is nothing else than a notable hyperbole of excellent love towards a wife, by which you may as it were wander, and in other matters be little wise, having forgotten all things by the force of love, whence also lovers are almost lunatics. If you refer this to the study of wisdom and the Law with others, it fits most aptly, so that because of your mind intent upon it, you are not with yourself. R. Solomon tells of a certain R. Eleazar, who, teaching in one village, because of the affection of teaching, had left his tunic elsewhere, where it was found wrapped in a serpent. The Greeks learnedly expressed the sense ἐν τῇ ταύτης Φιλίᾳ περιφερόμενος πολλοστὸς ἔσῃ, in her love you will be circumvolved and as it were carried hither and thither and wandering, you will be much: This is Mercerus.

Latin:

CERVA CARISSIMA, ET GRATISSIMUS HIN- NULUS) Multi enim talia animalia in deliciis habent. In- de illæ similitudines Cant. 2, 9.

UBERA EJUS INEBRIANT TE) Hebræi ubera דּוֹד vocant, ut amorum sedem.

Vers. eod. IN AMORE EJUS DELECTARE JUGI- TER) In Græco, ἐν γὰρ τῇ ταύτης φιλίᾳ συμπεριφερόμε- νος, πολλοστὸς ἔσῃ. Apparet legisse LXX. Senes שגג, cum sinistro puncto in prima littera. Sic enim significat multipli- cari. At cum puncto dextro inter alia delectari significat. Et sic vertunt quidam: שִׁגְיוֹנַוֹת delectationes Hab. 3, 1.

Si omnino aliud vidissent LXX. Interpp. pe- nes quos non infrequentia sunt παροράματα fon- tes tamen Ebraicæ veritatis cum Lud. Capello l. 6. Critic. S. cap. 4. §. 6. ad rivulos impuros revocare,

& ex iis repurgane, nobis religio. Fluunt hic opti- me fontes : Neque ab illis, quantum ad sensum, abit versio LXX. Seniorum. Nam תשגה notat di- vagari Ez. 34, 6. ut sensus sit, in amore ejus divageris jugiter, cui congruit probe verbum Græcum περι- φερόμενος, & quia id delectationis est, ac objectum amabile, qua sensum, recte redditur, per delecta- ri à Vatablo, Pagnino, Luthero: Eximie illustrat vo- cem illam Mercerus in h. l. Addit insignem hyperbo- len ad eximium amorem describendum, in amore ejus erres assidue, ut velut extra te sis, & rerum aliarum obliviscare præ ejus amore. Vult unicam instar omnium esse, & si in amore errandum est, in uxore potius er- randum, quam cum aliena, ut subjungit. Alii He- bræorum תשגה erres ex Thalmudicis exponunt תעסוק occuperis, vaces, quo modo & in lingua A- rabica sumi dicunt: alii, delecteris, ut volunt sumi Psalm. 7. in titulo. Sic & noster Interpres reddit, de- lectare, quod duriusculum videtur, jubere Salomo- nem in uxoris amore errare. Sed nihil est aliud, quam insignis hyperbole amoris eximii erga uxorem, quo velut erres, & in rebus aliis parum sapias, præ amoris vi omnium oblitus, unde & amantes fere sunt amen- tes. Hoc si ad sapientiæ & Legis studium cum aliis referas, aptissime quadrat, ut præ intento in eam ani- mo apud te non sis. De quodam R. Eleazar narrat R. Salomo, qui in uno vico docens præ affectu docendi ali- bi tunicam reliquisset, ubi inventa fuerit serpente in- voluta. Græci docte sensum expresserunt ἐν τῇ ταύτης Φιλίᾳ περιφερόμενος πολλοστὸς ἔσῃ in ejus amore circumvolutus & velut huc illuc delatus ac oberrans multus eris: Hæc Mercerus.

## 5:22
Vers. 22.

HIS OWN INIQUITIES CAPTURE THE WICKED, AND HE IS BOUND WITH THE ROPES OF HIS OWN SINS.

Since he has said that God looks upon the ways of man, or that they are before the eyes of God, as is held in the Hebrew, to terrify adulterers, of which see Syr. 23, verse 25, he now teaches how unexpectedly God's all-seeing eye captures those who put aside the judgment of God, and the guilt of punishment, so that they are dragged to punishment (Compare Job 18, verse 10): nay, he threatens that stubborn prevaricators will be more and more bound by the ropes of lust, so that they cannot extricate themselves from them, and they precipitate themselves into other sins immediately, 2 Pet. 2, verse 19, 2 Tim. 2, 26, until at length they perish eternally. While one serves lust, says Aug. lib. 6, Conf. cap. 12, a habit is made, and while habit is not resisted, a necessity is made. Concerning the various ropes of sins bound to lust, see Gregor. Magn. lib. 31, Moral. cap. 2. From luxury are generated blindness of mind, inconsideration, inconstancy, precipitation, love of self, hatred of God, affection for the present age, but horror or despair of the future. And Hieron. lib. 1, contr. Jovinian, love of beauty is an oblivion of reason, and next to insanity, a foul vice, and one by no means becoming a suspended mind; it disturbs counsels, breaks high and generous spirits, draws down from great thoughts to the most humble, makes one querulous, irascible, rash, harshly imperious, servilely flattering, useless to all, and to love itself. For when it burns with an insatiable desire of enjoying, it wastes more time in suspicions, tears, and complaints, it makes hatred for whom it loves, and finally is a hatred to itself.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

INIQUITATES SUÆ CAPIUNT IM- PIUM, ET FUNIBUS PECCATORUM SUO- RUM CONSTRINGITUR.

Quum dixerit Deum respicere vias hominis, vel coram oculis Dei eas esse, ut in Ebr. habetur, ad terrendos mœchos, de quo vid. Syr. 23. versu 25. jam quomodo ἀπροσδοκήτως capiat impios ejus- modi Dei παντεποψίαν posthabentes judicium Dei, & reatus pœnæ, ut ad supplicium rapiantur (Conf. Job. 18. vers. 10.) docet: imo minatur, ita contumaces prævaricatores magis magisque funi- bus libidinis constrictum iri, ut se expedire iisdem nequeant, & in alia peccata præcipitent subinde 2. Petr. 2. versu 19. 2. Timoth. 2, 26. donec tandem æternum pereant. Dum servitur libidini, ait Aug. lib. 6. Conf. cap. 12. facta est consuetudo, & dum consuetudini non resistitur, facta est necessitas. De va- riis peccatorum funibus libidini colligatis Gregor. Magn. lib. 31. Moral. cap. 2. De luxuria cæcitas mentis, inconsideratio, inconstantia, præcipitatio, amor sui, odium Dei, affectus præsentis seculi, horror autem vel desperatio futuri generantur. Et Hieron. lib. 1. contr. Jovinian. amor formæ rationis oblivio est, & insaniæ proximus, fœdum, minimeque conve- niens animo suspensi vitium; turbat consilia, altos & generosos spiritus frangit, a magnis cogitationibus ad humillimas detrahit, querulos, iracundos, temerarios, dure imperiosos, serviliter blandos, omnibus inutiles, ipsi amori facit. Nam cum fruendi cupiditate insa- tiabilis flagrat, plura tempora suspicionibus, lachry- mis, conquestionibus perdit, odium cui facit, & ipsi novissime sibi odio est.

## 5:23
vers. 23.

HE HIMSELF SHALL DIE, BECAUSE HE HAD NO DISCIPLINE, AND IN THE MULTITUDE OF HIS FOLLY HE SHALL BE DECEIVED.

Which can be understood of the frequency both of whoring and of sinning in general, because we are led down into hell by those ropes, 1 Tim. 6, verse 9. It happens by the just judgment of God, as Augustine says, that the sinner, who in life has forgotten God, in death forgets also himself. But Solomon warned of this specifically concerning fornication so prolixly: because according to Isidor. l. 2, de summ. bon. cap. 39, the devil dominates the human race principally by these two vices, that is, pride of mind and luxury of the flesh.

Latin:

vers. 23.

IPSE MORIETUR, QUIA NON HA- BUIT DISCIPLINAM, ET IN MUL- TITUDINE STULTITIÆ SUÆ DECI- PIETUR.

Quod de frequentia tum scortandi, tum in genere peccandi accipi potest, quia funibus istis deducimur in infernum 1. Tim. 6. versu 9. Justo Dei judicio fit, dicente Augustino, ut peccator, qui in vita oblitus est Dei, in morte obliviscatur & sui. De fornicatione autem speciatim hæc monuit tam pro- lixe Salomo: quia juxta Isidor. l. 2. de summ. bon. cap. 39. principaliter his duobus vitiis diabolus hu- mano generi dominatur, id est, superbia mentis, & lu- xuria carnis.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. Concerning dissolving the bond of suretyship, prudent diligence to be learned from ants, six marks of perverse men, and as many abominations to be avoided, pious warnings of parents to be diligently observed, and especially the harlot to be avoided, as well as the foulness and ruin of adultery.

Vers. 1. MY SON, IF YOU HAVE GIVEN SURETY FOR YOUR FRIEND, YOU HAVE STRUCK YOUR HAND WITH A STRANGER)

In the Hebrew: you have struck together. For by that rite among the Hebrews suretyships were made. Below 17, 18. 22, 26.

That this concerns a surety made for a friend, so that the surety may take pains to free himself again from the surety, both the letter and the consequence of the text teach. When he has instructed concerning the observation of the sixth commandment, he now delivers some admonitions concerning the seventh and eighth; and since the transgression against the sixth commandment is too common, he institutes a comparison of the same with the transgression of the seventh; diligent and assiduous labor and the avoidance of idleness also make for the dissolution of that bond of surety: certainly it coheres not inconveniently with the same. But the interpretations of certain others, diverging from this received and native sense of the words, are less suitable, such as those of the Hebrews, R. Levi concerning the human intellect, taking GOD for the appetite promising, Lekach Tob concerning the surety of the Israelites regarding the observation of the commandments of GOD at Mount Sinai, and of certain ancients, Gregory the Great, Part 3, Pastoral Admonitions, chapter 3, and Thomas on chapter 13. The Hebrews [speak] of the surety of ministers of the Church, or of magistrates concerning the procuring of the salvation of those who have been entrusted to their faith.
