Mr. Witzleben [speaks] of a surety made to the Devil and of penance to be done. Basil the Great understands by the friend the body, and by the liberation from the snares of the surety, amendment, so that we may bravely raise ourselves above the snares of adversaries, lifted on high by the wings of virtues; certain Papists draw these things to religious and Monastic vows, which they have fabricated; If you have vowed chastity, poverty, and obedience to God for a friend, that is, for the saving of your soul, etc. Whom, however, others refute: For the sense is, as the Jesuit Cornelius admits, if for the crime or debt of another you have pledged your faith and yourself, that is, that you will take care that the guilty party purges the crime, or satisfies for him, and so pays the fixed penalty, or as a debtor pays a debt, you have fastened, that is, by the stipulation and the fastening of your hand into the hand of the creditor you have obligated yourself. Whence the Chaldean translates, you have clearly promised to pay for a stranger with your hand; the Syrian, you have extended your hand to a stranger; the Septuagint, you will deliver your hand to an enemy. This is Cornelius. What have these things to do with vows made to GOD? Is He that stranger? Or do the Papist religious perhaps consider GOD to be an enemy? Concerning rash suretyship Cornelius says that Solomon exhorts: Let him acknowledge therefore that monastic vows are rash, since he applies these to those.

Moreover, although the word ערב signifies he has pledged, he has interposed faith in a general sense, although it denotes a sponsorship, here however it treats properly of a pecuniary debt, when for a friend or partner, or neighbor לרעה for the sake of a neighbor one interposes faith: Conf. Proverb. 10. verse 15. chap. 20. vers. 16. chap. 22. v. 26. 27. c. 27. verse 13. the word תקע expresses the gesture of one giving security by fixing hand to hand Job 17. verse 3. Proverb. 17. v. 18. chap. 22. verse 26. The sense however hangs on this verse, therefore the following must be added, If you have pledged for your friend, If you have struck with a STRANGER (a creditor, who with respect to the debtor and the sponsor is a stranger זר) with your hand, YOU ARE ENSNARED BY THE WORDS OF YOUR MOUTH, so bound as a bird by nets or snares Psalm 141. verse 9. Jerem. 50. verse 24. AND CAPTURED BY YOUR OWN SPEECHES, the utterances of your mouth. What Solomon warns about to avoid a rash sponsorship, not indeed against the duty of charity, which we are sometimes bound to perform for the needy in a case of necessity, by the force of the law of nature Matth. 7, 12. Grotius on this passage has it thus:

Latin:

CAPUT VI. De vinculo sponsionis dissolvendo, prudenti se- dulitate à formicis addiscenda, sex notis perversorum hominum, & totidem abo- minationibus vitandis, piis parentum monitis diligenter observandis, & im- primis cavenda scortatrice, nec non de adulterii fœditate, ac pernicie.

Vers. 1. FILI MI SPOPONDERIS PRO AMICO TUO, DEFIXISTI APUD EXTRANEUM MANUM TUAM)

In Hebræo: complosisti. Eo enim ritu apud Hebræos fie- bant sponsiones. Infra 17, 18. 22, 26.

DE sponsione pro amico facta agi, ut sponsor satagat, quo iterum sponsione se liberet, & li- tera, & consequentia textus docent. Quum in- formarit de sexti præcepti observatione, jam de se- ptimo & octavo nonnulla tradit monita; & quum nimis communis sit prævaricatio contra sextum præceptum, comparationem ejusdem cum trans- gressione septimi instituit; ad illam etiam nexus sponsionis dissolutionem facit diligens & sedulus labor, & fuga otii: certe non incommode cum ea- dem cohæret. Minus autem conveniunt alio- rum quorundam interpretationes à recepta hac & nativa verborum sententia divaricantes, utpote Ebræorum, R. Levi de intellectu humano, apud DEUM pro appetitu spondente, Lekach Tob de sponsione Israëlitarum quoad observationem præce- ptorum DEI ad montem Sinai, quorundam vete- rum Gregorii Magni P. 3. adm. Pastor. cap. 3. Thom. in c. 13. Ebr. de sponsione ministrorum Eccle- siæ, vel Magistratuum de procuranda salute eo- rum, qui fidei ipsorum crediti sunt. Dn. Witzle- bii de sponsione Diabolo facta & agenda pœniten- tia. Basilius M. per amicum corpus, per libera- tionem à sponsionis laqueis emendationem intelligit, ut supra adversariorum laqueos fortiter nos effera- mus, virtutum alis in altum sublati; Pontificii quidam hæc ad vota religiosa ac Monastica, quæ confinxere, trahunt; Si voveris Deo castitatem, paupertatem, obedientiam pro amico, id est, pro anima tua salvanda &c. Quos tamen alii refel- lunt: Sensus enim est fatente Jesuita Cornelio, si pro crimine vel debito alterius fidem tuam, & teipsum obligaris, sc. te curaturum, ut reus crimen pur- get, vel pro eo satisfaciat, adeoque pœnam statam luat, aut quasi debitor debitum exolvat, defixisti, id est, stipulatione & defixione manus tuæ in ma- num creditoris obligasti teipsum. Unde Chald. ver- tit clare promisisti solvere extraneo manu tua, Sy- rus porrexisti manum tuam extraneo, LXX. tra- des manum tuam inimico. Hæc Cornelius. Quid hæc ad vota DEO facta? Num ille extra- neus? An forte pro inimico religiosi Papistici ha- bent DEUM? A temeraria fidejussione de- hortari Salomonem ait Cornelius: Agnoscat ergo monastica vota temeraria esse, cum ad illa hæc applicat.

Cæterum quamvis verbum ערב spopondit, fi- dem interposuit in genere quamvis sponsionem no- tet, hic tamen de debito pecuniario propriè agitur, cum pro amico vel socio, aut proximo לרעה in gra- tiam proximi quis fidem interponit: Conf. Pro- verb. 10. versu 15. cap. 20. vers. 16. cap. 22. v. 26. 27. c. 27. vers. 13. verbum תקע infexit gestum fideju- bentis manum manui infigendo exprimit Job. 17. vers. 3. Proverb. 17. v. 18. cap. 22. versu 26. Sensus autem pendet in hoc versu, ideò sequens adden- dus, Si spoponderis pro amico tuo, Si percussisti A- LIENO (creditori, qui respectu debitoris & sponsoris זר alienus est) manu tua, ILLAQUE- ATUS ES VERBIS ORIS TUI, ita constri- ctus ut avis retibus vel laqueis Psalm. 141. versu 9. Jerem. 50. versu 24. ET CAPTUS PROPRIIS SERMONIBUS, eloquiis oris tui. Quod mo- net Salomo ad vitandam temerariam sponsionem, non verò contra charitatis officium, quod nonnun- quam indigentibus præstare tenemur in casu ne- cessitatis, vi legis naturæ Matth. 7, 12. Grotius ad h. l. ita habet:

## 6:2
YOU ARE ENSNARED BY THE WORDS OF YOUR MOUTH) The Greek sentiment, ἐγγύα πάρα δ' ἄτα. below 11, 15.

Latin:

ILLAQVEATVS ES VERBIS ORIS TUI) Græca sententia, ἐγγύα πάρα δ' ἄτα. infra 11, 15.

## 6:3
vers. 3. YOU HAVE FALLEN INTO THE HAND OF YOUR NEIGHBOR.

Into the hand that is the power Jerm. 12. verse 7. Of your partner, whom some wish to be the creditor here, since the Hebrew word denotes him with whom we have business, but Salazar and Dr. Gejerus more correctly understand the debtor from the preceding, for whom one makes the sponsorship: if he is negligent or deceitful and ungrateful, he can easily ruin the sponsor. Counsel therefore is given to the sponsor, that he may free himself: FREE YOURSELF, so that, namely, he may not rest until he renders himself free from that sponsorship in any way whatsoever: and therefore he is warned particularly to approach and prostrate himself, RUN HASTEN the Vulgate renders. But Münster with Aben-Ezra, R. Levi, and Mercer more correctly Go, prostrate yourself, by humbling yourself before the creditor: which is the sense of the word התרפס, as the Lexicons note: STIR UP, Aquila and Theodotion παρόξυνησον, incite, Luther treibe, (which seem to agree more with the use of the Hebrew word רהב Efa. 3. verse 5.) YOUR FRIEND, for whom, namely, you have interposed faith, so that he may solicit the creditor with prayers, and the debtor also with compelling ways and means, and drive him, so that the former may not urge his right so strictly, and the latter may truly free the faith. Grotius explains that stir up your friend thus:

Latin:

vers. 3. INCIDISTI IN MANUM PROXIMI TUI.

In manum hoc est potestatem Jerm. 12. vers. 7. Socii tui, quem hic creditorem esse nonnulli vo- lunt, quum vox Ebræa eum notet, cum quo no- bis res est, sed rectiùs è præcedentibus debito- rem, pro quo sponsionem quis facit, intelligit Salazar, & Dn. D. Gejerus: iste si negligens vel dolosus & ingratus sit, facile sponsorem perdere po- test. Consilium ergo sponsori datur, ut se liberet: LIBERA TEMETIPSUM, ut sc. non quiescat, donec se ab ista sponsione quomodocunque libe- rum reddat: ideoque monetur peculiariter, ut adeat & prosternat se, DISCURRE FESTINA reddit Vulgat. Sed Münsterus cum Aben-Ezra, R. Levi, & Mercero rectiùs Vade, prosterne te, humiliando te coram creditore: qui vocis התרפס sensus est, notantibus Lexicis: SUSCITA, A- quila & Theodotio παρόξυνησον, incita, Lutherus treibe, (quæ magis convenire videntur usui verbi Ebr. רהב Efa. 3. versu 5.) AMICUM TUUM, pro quo scil. fidem interposuisti, ut ita creditorem precibus, debitorem autem modis etiam & me- diis cogentibus solicitet, & adigat, ut ille non ita strictè jus suum urgeat, hic vero fidem liberet. Grotius illa suscita amicum tuum ita explicat:

## 6:3
STIR UP YOUR FRIEND) Call upon your mandator. For it was permitted, if that were not done, for the creditor to convene the surety without having convened the principal, below 20. verse 16. chap. 27. verse 13.

Moreover, this surety himself is instructed, and not indeed the debtor. GIVE NO SLEEP TO YOUR EYES, NOR LET YOUR EYELIDS SLUMBER, until you have rendered yourself free, and have rescued yourself from the bond of the sponsorship. No otherwise than fawns or young goats strive to rescue themselves as quickly as possible from the hands of hunters, and birds from the nets of fowlers, which is added in verse 5: as in the former clause it is held simply by the hand, but in the latter the name יקוש of him who spreads nets is supplied, Psalm 91. v. 2. 3. Psalm 141, 9. such as with respect to the fawn is the hunter, but with respect to the bird is the fowler.

GO TO THE ANT O SLUGGARD) Horace: The tiny ant (for it is an example) of great labor, drags with its mouth whatever it can, and adds to the heap which it builds, not ignorant, and not incautious of the future. Which as soon as Aquarius saddens the inverted year, does not crawl out anywhere, but uses those things previously gathered, being patient. WHICH HAVING NO LEADER) Just as nature has fashioned a form of kingdom in bees, so in ants a democracy.

Conveniently, from rash suretyship, lest one's family estate suffer detriment, one passes to the flight of sloth, and the pursuit of labors and diligence, by which (if no other way is permitted) we can free ourselves from the bonds of suretyship, and each can provide for himself and his family. The meaning is clear. We note only from Basil the Great, homily 9, p. 98 of the Hexaemeron, the prudent skill of the ant: Will you not, O man, apply the same diligence to yourself? Will you not fashion a house for yourself? Will you not in this present time store up fruits for yourself, and prepare rest for the future by the example of the ant? The ant diligently stores up food for the winter time in summer, and does not pass the time idly because the inconveniences of winter are not yet present: but with a certain restless and intent zeal for gathering seeds, it applies itself until it stores up sufficient nourishment for itself in its cells. Nor does it do this through carelessness, but with a certain wise providence, so that the food may persist and be preserved for itself for as long a time as possible. For it cuts the middle of the fruits with its little claws, and stores them bitten: lest they sprout again into plants from the earth, and thus become useless to it for the purpose of nourishment. When it senses that they have been moistened by rain, it brings them out and dries them. And it does not do this at all times, but when it has foreseen that the air is held in a serene state, and the sky is clear. For you will never have seen rain flow down from the clouds during the time that the grain is exposed by the ants. Cf. Pliny, book 30, chapter 2; Ambrose, book 6 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 4. We also add the application of Saint Augustine, book against Adimantus, chapter 24: Thus let every Christian in the tranquility of affairs, which summer signifies, gather the word of God, so that in adversity and tribulations, which are noted by the name of winter, he may have wherewith to live spiritually. The ant, says Alvarez de Paz, book 1, on the extinction of life, part 2, signifies the provident man and the Egyptian strenuous in conducting business.

Moreover, there is added among the LXX after this verse about the ants a similar one about the bees: or go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is: and the venerable operation she performs, whose labors Kings and commoners bring to health. But she is desirable and dear to all; even though she is weak in strength, she is exalted by honoring Wisdom. But however much Jerome in Ezekiel 3 and Ambrose in book 5 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 21, with Clement of Alexandria, book 4 of the Stromata, bring forward similar things, those are nevertheless, without doubt, interpolated and spurious: because they occur neither in the Hebrew source, nor in the Chaldean, nor in the Latin Vulgate.

Latin:

SVSCITA AMICVM TVVM) Appella mandatorem tuum. Licebat enim, ni id fieret, creditori convenire fidejus- sorem non convento principali, infra 20. versu 16. cap. 27. versu 13.

Cæterum instruitur hic ipse fidejussor, non vero debitor. NE DEDERIS SOMNUM O- CULIS TUIS, NEC DORMIENT PAL- PEBRÆ TUÆ, donec te liberum reddideris, & nexu sponsionis erueris. Non secus atque damulæ vel capreoli student quam celerrime venatorum, aves vero aucupum manibus & retibus sese erue- re, quod versu 5. additur: uti commate priori sim- pliciter habetur מיד, sed e posteriori suppletum est nomen יקוש ejus qui retia tendit, Psalm. 91. v. 2. 3. Psalm. 141, 9. qualis respectu capreæ est venator, respectu avis vero auceps.

QVADE AD FORMICAM O PIGER) Horatius : Parvula (nam exemplo est) magni formica laboris, Ore trahit quodcunque potest, atque addit acervo Quem struit, haud ignara, ac non incauta futuri. Quæ simul inversum contristat Aquarius annum Non usquam prorepit, at illis utitur ante Quæsitis patiens. QVÆRAM CUM NON HABEAT DUCEM) Sicut in apibus regni formam molita natura est, ita in formicis δημοκρατίας.

Commode à sponsione temeraria cavenda, ne res familiaris detrimentum patiatur, transitur ad fugam inertiæ, & studium laborum ac diligentiæ, quæ etiam (si alia non licet via) nos exolvere ne- xibus fidejussionis possumus, & quisque sibi & fa- miliæ suæ providere. Sensus luculentus est. No- tamus solum è Basil. M. homil. 9. p. m. 98. hexaëm. prudentem solertiam formicæ : Non tute tibi eau- dem o homo diligentiam adhibebis? non tute tibi ipsi domum elaborabis? non hoc tempore præsenti fruges tibi recondes, requiemque ad futurum formicæ exem- plo parabis? Formica temporis hyberni pabulum æsta- te sibi sedulo condit, & non quod hyemis incommoda nondum adsunt, otiosa tempus traducit : sed incesla- bili quodam intento que studio legendi semina tantisper incumbit, dum sufficiens alimentum in cellulis sibi recondat. Neque id incuria facit, sed sapienti qua- dam providentia, ut quam plurimo tempore pabulum sibi persistere conservarique possit. Secat enim un- guiculis fructus medios, arrososque condit: ne rursus in fruges exeant è terra, atque inutiles inde sibi ad usum alimoniæ fiant. Cum senserit eos madefactos imbre profert atque exsiccat. Nec omni tempore id agit, sed cum præsenserit aërem serena in statione teneri, serenumque cælum. Etenim nunquam ex nubibus imbrem defluxisse conspexeris, quanto tem- pore a formicis expositum est frumentum. Conf. Plinius lib. 30. cap. 2. Ambrosius lib. 6. Hexaëm. cap. 4. Addimus & accommodationem Sanct. Au- gustini l. contr. Adim. cap. 24. Sic unusquisque Christianus in rerum tranquillitate, quam signi- ficat æstas, colligat verbum DEI, ut in adversitate & tribulationibus, quæ hyemis nomine notantur, ha- beat unde spiritualiter vivat. Formica, inquit Al- varez de Paz l. 1. de extinct. vit. part. 2. hominem providum & in negotiis gerendis strenuum Ægy- ptium significat.

Cæterum additur apud LXX. post hunc ver- fum de formicis simile de apibus: aut vade ad apem, & disce quomodo operaria est: operationem quoque quam venerabilem facit, cujus labores Re- ges & idiotæ ad sanitatem afferunt. Appetibilis autem omnibus est & chara; etiam cum sit robore infirma, Sapientiam honorans erecta est. Sed utut si- milia adferat Hieronym. in Ez. 3. & Ambros. l. 5. Hexaëm. cap. 21. cum Clem. Alex. l. 4. Strom. ἐμ- βολιμαῖα tamen illa, sine dubio, & irreptibilia sunt: quia nec in fonte Ebræo, nec apud Chal- dæum, nec in vulgata Lat. occurrunt.

## 6:4
Vers. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

## 6:10
Verse 10. A LITTLE YOU WILL SLEEP) ἐκ ὀλίγου τὸ παρ’ ὀλίγον.

From a heavier and more frequent sleep, noted by the plural שֵׁנֹוֹת, he descends to slumber. Cf. this chapter, verse 4, and from there to the folding of the hands, which is a habit or gesture of those composing themselves for sleep, who are accustomed to knot their hands and arms over their chest, as Salazar notes: as the Syrian rendered it, put your hands over your chest: or he joins to those slumbering the vigilant ones folding their hands, which meaning could seem consistent from a comparison with Ecclesiastes 4:5, but because לִשְׁכַּב FOR LYING DOWN is added, the former explanation is to be preferred.

Latin:

Vers. 10. PAVLVLVM DORMIES) ἐκ ὀλίγου τὸ παρ’ ὀλίγον.

A somno graviori & crebriori plurali שֵׁנֹוֹת notato, ad dormitationem descendit. Conf. capit. hujus vers. 4. & inde ad complicationem manuum, qui habitus vel gestus est ad somnum se compo- nentium, qui solent manus & brachia innodare su- per pectus, notante Salazar: uti Syrus reddidit po- nes manus super pectus tuum : vel dormitantibus subjungit vigilantes manus complicantes, qui sen- sus videri possit congruus e collatione Eccl. 4, 5. sed quia additur לִשְׁכַּב AD CUBANDUM, prior explicatio præferenda.

## 6:11
Verse 11. AND POVERTY WILL COME TO YOU LIKE A TRAVELER.

Roa, book 3, singular, chapter 2, and Cornel. here explain the traveler as a lictor, but Delrio, Vol. 2, Adag. 157, refutes this. Aben-Ezra correctly expresses the sense: Poverty will turn aside to you like a stranger, whose arrival is unknown until he stands there, and poverty like one who approaches to conquer another, armed with a shield.

But what is added here in the Vulgate: IF HOWEVER YOU ARE DILIGENT, YOUR HARVEST WILL COME LIKE A FOUNTAIN, AND POVERTY WILL FLEE FAR FROM YOU, although they may have been inserted into the edition of the 70 Interpreters amended at Rome, they are nevertheless entirely spurious: because they occur neither in any Hebrew Codex, nor in the Chaldean or Syriac translations, nor indeed even in the Complutensian LXX.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET VENIET TIBI QUASI VIATOR EGESTAS.

Roa l. 3. singul. c. 2. & Cornel. hic viatorem explicant de lictore, sed refellit hoc Delrio Tom. 2. Adag. 157. Sensum recte Aben-Ezra exprimit : Ad te divertet egestas tanquam peregrinus, cujus adven- tus, donec astet, ignoratur, & paupertas tanquam qui clypeo munitus ad alium expugnandum accedit.

Quæ vero hic subjunguntur in Vulgata: SI VE- RO IMPIGER FUERIS, VENIET UT FONS MESSIS TUA, ET EGESTAS LONGE FUGIET A TE, etsi editioni LXX. Interpp. Romæ emendatæ inserta sint, notha ta- men omnino sunt: quia nec in ullo Ebræo Codice, nec in Translationib. Chald. Syr. imo nec in LXX. Complut. occurrunt.

## 6:12
Verse 12. AN APOSTATE MAN, A USELESS MAN, WALKS WITH A PERVERSE MOUTH.

From idleness to describing a perverse man: because these things cohere, and idleness gives rise to vices, and he proceeds to abominations hateful to God, according to the members or parts of a man. In Hebrew it is אָדָם בְּלִיַּעַל, that is, according to the interpreter Aquila and Jerome, who is WITHOUT A YOKE, he rejects or has cast off the yoke of divine law, a wicked man, or one of impiety, as is evident from similar places in Deuteronomy 13, verse 13, 1 Samuel 10, 27, etc.: whence the Devil himself, as the author of impiety, comes by this name in 2 Corinthians 6, 15. AND אִישׁ אָוֶן A man of iniquity, see Psalm 5, verse 6. He notes (1.) A perverse mouth: because he abuses his tongue for frauds and any wicked things, he walks with a perverse mouth, as if accustomed to such things. (2.) Eyes: because he is accustomed to give a sign to his other accomplices with his nod, which nodding is fraudulent according to R. Salomon. (3.) Feet: because he is also accustomed to trample with his feet and indicate his intention, and thus TO SPEAK as the Hebrew word מֹלֵל sounds. (4.) Fingers, because he speaks or teaches with them also, so that his accomplices may understand what he wants. (5.) Heart: because he fosters perversities within it. (6.) Mind: because he plots evil at all times. (7.) External act: because he sows quarrels, or as in the Hebrew, introduces contentions. Compare chapter 10, 12. To which is added the Punishment: TO HIM (in Hebrew and Syriac it is THEREFORE) HIS DESTRUCTION WILL COME IMMEDIATELY AND SUDDENLY HE WILL BE CRUSHED (broken) AND HE WILL NO LONGER HAVE A REMEDY, so that no one can heal him. Compare 2 Chronicles 21, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 12. HOMO APOSTATA VIR INUTILIS GRADITUR ORE PERVERSO.

Ab otio ad describendum hominem perver- sum: quia hæc cohærent, & otia dant vitia, & ad abominationes Deo exosas, juxta membra vel partes hominis, progreditur. In Ebr. est אָדָם בְּלִיַּעַל, hoc est interprete Aquila, & Hieronymo, qui est SI- NE JUGO, legis divinæ jugum respuit, vel abjecit, homo impius, vel impietatis, ut è similibus locis Deuteronom. 13. vers. 13. 1. Sam. 10, 27. &c. constat: unde Diabolus ipse ut impietatis autor hoc nomi- ne venit 2. Cor. 6, 15. ET אִישׁ אָוֶן Vir iniquitatis, Vid. Psalm. 5. vers. 6. Ejus notat (6.) Os perver- sum: quod lingua abutatur ad fraudes, & iniqua quævis, ore perverso ambulet, ceu ad talia asvetus, (2.) Oculos: quod aliis complicibus suis signum nutu suo dare soleat, quæ nutatio fraudulenta est se- cundum R. Salomon. (3.) Pedes: quod etiam pedibus suis terere soleat, & intentionem suam indicare, adeoque LOQUI uti verbum Ebr. מֹלֵל sonat. (4.) Digitos, quod illis quoque loquatur vel do- ceat, ut quid velit, complices intelligant. (5.) Cor. quod perversitates in eodem foveat. (6.) Men- tem: quod omni tempore malum machinetur. (7.) Actum externum: quod jurgia seminet, vel ut in Ebr. contentiones immittat. Conf. cap. 10, 12. Quibus subjungitur Pœna: HUIC (in Ebr. & Syro est IDEO) EXTEMPLO VENIET PERDI- TIO SUA (ejus) ET SUBITO CONTE- RETUR (confringetur) NEC HABEBIT UL- TRA MEDICINAM, ut nemo mederi queat. Conf. 2. Chron. 21, 18.

## 6:16
Verse 16. THERE ARE SIX THINGS WHICH THE LORD HATES, AND THE SEVENTH HIS SOUL DETESTS.

These seven abominations are added to the preceding seven vicious gestures of the impious man, and to his ἀνομίαις as if analogous: For here too members and parts and similar acts are noted: namely 1. HAUGHTY EYES, to express arrogance and pride, Psalm 101, 5, 131, 2, Isaiah 3, 16. 2. A LYING TONGUE; or of a lie, because of the perversity of the mouth, situated specifically in lying words. 3. HANDS SHEDDING INNOCENT BLOOD: which is sometimes the detestable effect of those who speak with their fingers. 4. A HEART PLOTTING THE WORST THOUGHTS: which is placed here in the middle, as if situated in the middle of the body like some royal palace. אָוֶן denotes iniquities of any kind. 5. FEET SWIFT TO RUN INTO EVIL, which by promising indicates an inveterate habit: just as he had said before that the wicked man tramples with his feet, to trample upon his neighbor. 6. BRINGING FORTH

LIES, A DECEITFUL WITNESS: which pertains especially to the malignant mind, which is prone to false testimonies. 7. AND HIM WHO SOWS DISCORD AMONG BROTHERS: such as he had also designated before. God is said to detest this last one especially, because from whispering there follow indeed not one, but many slaughters, Sirach 28, verse 15, and all the members, and all the faculties of man, eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet, the spirit or mind of man, contribute their ἐπιβάλλον μέρός (appropriate share) to disseminating contentions. As for the seven abominations that are enumerated, it is not that more are not found against the first and second table, but that Solomon is here occupied chiefly with the abominations against the second table, and for the sake of memory and elegance he wished to join these seven separately, especially because he had intended to treat separately and at greater length of obedience regarding the fourth commandment and of adultery regarding the sixth, whence it pleased him to present here in summary those things which pertain to the remaining commandments of the second table.

Latin:

Vers. 16. SEX SUNT QUÆ ODIT DOMI- NUS, ET SEPTIMUM DETESTATUR ANIMA EJUS.

Hæ septem abominationes præcedentibus septem vitiosis hominis impii gestibus, & ἀνομίαις ceu ana- logæ subjunguntur: Nam & hic membra & partes, actusque similes notantur: utpote 1. OCULI SUBLINES, ad fastum & superbiam exprimendam Psalm. 101, 5. 131, 2. Es. 3, 16. 2. LINGUA MEN- DAX; vel mendacii, ob perversitatem oris, sitam speciatim in verbis mendacibus. 3. MANUS EF- FUNDENTES INNOXIUM SANGUINEM: qui quandoque detestandus est effectus eorum qui digitis loquentes sunt. 4. COR MACHI- NANS COGITATIONES PESSIMAS: quod in medio hic ponitur, utpote in medio corporis instar Regiæ cujusdam situm. אָוֶן iniquitates notat quascunque. 5. PEDES VELOCES AD CUR- RENDUM IN MALUM, quæ promittendo in- veteratum habitum indicat: quemadmodum an- tea virum iniquum dixerat terere pedibus, ad pes- fundandum proximum. 6. PROFERENTEM

MENDACIA TESTEM FALLACEM: quod ad mentem malignam imprimis pertinet, quæ pro- clivis est ad falsa testimonia. 7. ET EUM QUI SEMINAT INTER FRATRES DISCOR- DIAS: qualem etiam antea designarat. Ultimum hoc imprimis abominari dicitur Deus, quia ex su- surratione sequuntur sane cædes non una, sed mul- tæ Syr. 28. v. 15. & conferunt ad disseminandas contentiones suum ἐπιβάλλον μέρός, omnia pro- pemodum membra, omnesque faculates hominis, oculi, lingua, manus, cor, pedes, animus vel mens hominis. Quæ vero septem abominationes recensen- tur, non quod plures haud reperiantur adversus primam & secundam tabulam, sed quod hic præci- pue in abominationibus adversus secundam tabu- lam occupetur Salomo, & memoriæ ac elegantiæ causa seorsim hasce septem conjungere voluerit, imprimis quia de obedientia ad quartum, & adulte- rio ad sextum præceptum spectante seorsim, & prolixius agere instituerat, unde compendio illa, quæ ad reliqua tabulæ secundæ præcepta pertinent, hic exhibere ipsi placuit.

## 6:20
Vers. 20. KEEP, MY SON, THE COMMANDMENTS OF THY FATHER.

He therefore now exhorts to filial obedience and to the observation of the commandments of parents, inasmuch as it is their duty to dissuade their children from those and other abominations. He wishes these commandments to be bound to the heart, to be attached to the throat: and he warns that we should meditate upon them in our mind, so that they may lead us when we walk, and guard us when we sleep: since by that method we can properly govern our heart, tongue, feet, and mind, and abstain from those abominations: nay, even that the commandment of the Father shall be to our eyes like a lantern or lamp (as נר is taken in Num. 8. vers. 2.), and the law of the mother like a light, inasmuch as they are consistent with the word of God, which is a lantern and light to us, Psalm 19. vers. 9. 119. v. 105, or contain the very word of God, Deuteronomy 6. verse 7. Thus the reproofs of instruction or παιδείας of parents will be to us the way of life, vers. 23. Moreover, three times are expressed for remembering and observing discipline and the law: the time of walking or of the day, of sleeping or of the night, and of waking or of the morning, or that we should observe it whether we sleep or wake, by day and by night. Polychr. The sense, he says, is: whenever you shall meditate on anything, or speak, or work, always do and perform all things according to the law predetermined by Christ. The word of flattery, however, contains within itself the force and reason of all these things. For he who studiously searches the mysteries of the law discovers that the whole law is a certain light.

Whence the perspicuity of Scripture, from which parents draw that παιδείαν, is rightly established against the Papists from this passage. And this very Cornelius the Jesuit acknowledges that Solomon alludes to, or rather cites, that saying of David his father, Psalm 119. v. 105: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths: and that a lamp is named from light, because it diffuses and spreads its light through the lumen: and he praises the exposition of Ambrose on the cited Psalm: it shines before us in this night of the world, lest, walking as if in darkness, we stumble with uncertain steps and be unable to find the true way. And that saying of Cassiodorus: The same word is a lamp to the feet in the night entangled by various offenses, and a light to the paths: for through it, indeed, while we are instructed for the course of a good life, we walk with clarified hearts and directed steps.

Latin:

Vers. 20. CONSERVA FILI MI PRÆCE- PTA PATRIS TUI.

Hortatur ergo jam ad filialem obedientiam, & ad observationem præceptorum parentum, ut- pote quorum est dehortari filios ab illis, aliisque abominationibus. Quæ præcepta cordi alligari, gutturi annecti vult: & ut nos deducant cum deambu- lamus, nos custodiant cum dormimus, eandem animo meditemur, monet: quum ea ratione cor, linguam, pedes, animumque nostrum probe gubernare, & ab abominationibus istis nos abstinere possimus: quin etiam oculis nostris instar lucernæ vel lampa- dis (uti נר accipitur Num. 8. vers. 2.) mandatum Pa- tris, & instar lucis lex matris futura sint, utpote verbo Dei, quod nobis lucerna & lux est, Psalm. 19. vers. 9. 119. v. 105. consentanea, seu ipsummet Dei verbum continentia Deuteronom. 6. versu 7. Ita nobis via vitæ erunt increpationes eruditionis vel παιδείας parentum vers. 23. Exprimuntur autem tria tempora memoranda & observandæ discipli- næ, & legis, tempus ambulandi seu diei, dormiendi seu noctis, & evigilandi seu mane, vel ut dies, & no- ctes seu dormiamus, seu evigilemus, illam obser- vemus. Polychr. Sensus, inquit, est, quandocunque aliquid meditaberis, aut loqueris, aut operaberis, omnia semper secundum legem à Christo præfinitam facito, & operare. Adulationis autem vox horum ominum vim & rationem in se continet. Qui enim legis mysteria studiose rimatur, universam legem lu- men quoddam esse deprehendit.

Unde Scripturæ, è qua hauriant illam παιδείαν parentes, necessum est, perspicuitas adversus Pon- tificios ex hoc loco recte adstruitur. Et agnoscit hic ipse Cornelius Jesuita, alludere, imo citare Sa- lomonem illud Davidis Patris sui Psalm. 119. v. 105. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen semitis meis: ac lucernam dici à luce, quia lucem suam per lumen diffundit & spargit: laudatque Am- brosii ἔκθεσιν in Psal. cit. prælucet nobis in hoc mun- di nocte, ne sicut in tenebris ambulantes, incertis ti- tubemus vestigiis, & viam veram invenire nequea- mus. Et Cassiodori illud: Idem verbum est lucerna pedibus in nocte diversis offensionibus irretita, & lu- men semitis: per ipsum siquidem dum ad vitæ bonæ cursum instruimur, clarificati corde directis gressi- bus ambulamus.

## 6:22
Vers. 22. WHEN THOU WALKEST, THEY SHALL GO WITH THEE: WHEN THOU SLEEPEST, THEY SHALL KEEP THEE, AND WHEN THOU WAKEST, TALK WITH THEM) In the Hebrew, these are of the singular number, and of the future tense in this sense: When you walk, it will go with you: (namely the law of God which you will learn from father and mother) when you sleep it will guard you: and when you have awakened it will speak to you. In every act of life it will profit you. Furthermore, the book Pirke Avoth understands these three times, of this life, of death, and of the resurrection.

They are not so much words of promise as of command, nor do they treat of death or resurrection, but of the different times of life, whether one walks, or sleeps, or keeps watch.

Latin:

Vers. 22. CUM AMBULAVERIS GRADIANTUR TECUM: CUM DORMIERIS CUSTODIANT TE, ET EVIGILANS LOQVERE CUM EIS) In Hebræo sunt singularis numeri, & futuri temporis hoc sensu : Cum ambulaveris, tecum ibit: (nempe lex Dei quam à patre & ma- tre disces) cum dormieris custodiet te : & cum experrectus fue- ris te alloquetur. In omni actu vitæ tibi proderit. Cæte- rum liber Pirke Avoth intelligit hæc tria tempora , vitæ hu- jus, mortis & resurrectionis.

Non tam verba promissi sunt, quam mandati, nec de morte aut resurrectione agunt, sed de tempo- ribus vitæ diversis, sive ambulet quis, sive dormiat, sive vigilet.

## 6:24
Vers. 24.

THAT THEY MAY GUARD YOU FROM THE EVIL WOMAN, AND FROM THE SMOOTH TONGUE OF THE STRANGER.

Symmachus explained 'evil woman' as 'harlot,' not badly: because the other hemistich indicates that meaning. Solomon returns again, however, to the flight from fornication, and he pursues it at length now in this and the following chapter: because this is the snare which the demon stretches for every race of men, but especially for incautious youth full of that lust. He warns, however, that the smooth tongue must be guarded against, and beauty not coveted: because according to August. serm. 83. de Temp., the first arrows of adultery are of the eyes, the second of words. Conf. Syr. 25. verse 28. Job 31. verse 1. He commands to guard against the glances of the eyes, lest we be captured by them. By the word לקח a certain violence is inflicted; the likeness of which is when a woman vibrates the rays of her eyes, by the casting of which she shoots arrows of love into those looking, by which with a certain force they are captured. The Syrian rendered it: do not be the prey of the hunting of her eyes, and may she not make you a captive with your eyelids. Ambrof. l. 1. de pœnit. cap. 14. Many nets are stretched by the Devil, many nets there are: the eye of a harlot is the snare of the lover.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

UT CUSTODIANT TE A MULIE- RE MALA, ET BLANDA LINGUA EX- TRANEÆ.

Malam mulierem Symmachus per meretri- cem exposuit non male: quia sensum illum alte- rum hemistichium indicat. Redit autem iterum Salomo ad fugam fornicationis, eamque prolixe jam persequitur hoc & sequenti capite : quia la- queus hic est, quem dæmon tendit omni hominum ge- neri, imprimis vero juventuti incautæ & ejus libi- dinis plenæ. Cavendam autem monet linguam blandam, nec concupiscendam pulchritudinem : quia secundum August. serm. 83. de Temp. prima adul- terii oculorum tela sunt, secunda verborum. Conf. Syr. 25. versu 28. Job. 31. vers. 1. Cavere jubet oculo- rum nutus, ne illis capiamur. Voce לקח violentia quædam infertur ; cujus instar est, cum mulier ra- dios vibrat oculorum, quorum jactibus sagittas amoris in aspicientes jaculatur, quibus vi quadam illi capiuntur. Syrus reddidit: ne sis præda vena- tionis oculorum ejus, & palpebris tuis captivum te faciat. Ambrof. l. 1. de pœnit. cap. 14. Multa retia tenduntur a Diabolo, multa retia sunt: oculus mere- tricis laqueus amatoris est.

## 6:26
Vers. 26.

FOR THE PRICE OF A HARLOT IS SCARCELY ONE LOAF OF BREAD) In the Hebrew: Because of a harlot (that is, an adulteress, as the preceding and following show) to a morsel of bread (that is, to extreme poverty: supply, one comes.) BUT THE WOMAN TAKES THE PRECIOUS SOUL OF A MAN) The woman of a man, that is, married to another. That is often the reason why an adulterer loses his life. And conversely the adulterer [loses] the adulteress, as we just heard Menander saying.

Not only natural life, but also spiritual and heavenly life does the woman of a man, or of another, and thus an adulteress, snatch away. See Galat. 5. verse 19. A precious soul, says Solomon, because it was redeemed with a great price 1. Corinth. 6. verse 20. than which we also have nothing more precious.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

PRETIUM ENIM SCORTI VIX EST VNIVS PA- NIS) In Hebræo: Propter scortum (id est, adulteram, ut præcedentia & sequentia ostendunt) ad buccellam panis (id est, ad summam egestatem : supple, devenitur.) MVLIER AVTEM VIRI PRETIOSAM ANIMAM CAPIT) Mulier viri, id est alteri nupta. Ea causa sæpe est cur adulter vitam amittat. Ac vicissim adulter adulteræ, ut modo dicentem Menandrum audivimus.

Non vitam tantum naturalem, sed etiam spi- ritualem ac cœlestem rapit mulier viri, seu alterius, adeoque adultera. Vid. Galat. 5. versu 19. Animam pretiosam, inquit Salomo, quia magno redemta est pretio 1. Corinth. 6. versu 20. qua nihil etiam ha- bemus pretiosius.

## 6:27
Vers. 27.

CAN A MAN HIDE FIRE IN HIS BOSOM.

These things are explained concerning the avoidance of conversation with women because of the burning of the flame of love by Chrysost. Epist. 7. ad Olymp., and Basilius tr. de virgin., with Cyprian leading the way, who in tract. de singul. Cleric. says: Uncertain, he says, is the victory to fight among hostile arms. And impossible is the liberation to be surrounded by flames and not to burn. More correctly, however, it is taken concerning penal inflammation, as is evident from the application of the similitude in v. 29: HE WILL NOT BE CLEAN (more correctly innocent) when he has touched her. Just as fire in the bosom burns up the whole body with the garment, nor can anyone walk upon coals so that his soles are not burned, so he who commits adultery (for this is to go in to the woman of his neighbor Genes. 6, 4. cap. 19, 31. c. 38, 9. Psalm. 51, 2.) burns up his conscience, fame, life, and soul just as much as his body with the fire of lust. Conf. Ez. 20, 7. Jerem. 30, 12. 1. Corinth. 6, 10. Negation is used for the affirmative for the sake of emphasis; he will not be innocent, that is, he will be most guilty, and he will be punished most severely.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

NUNQUID POTEST HOMO ABSCON- DERE IGNEM IN SINU SUO.

Hæc de conversatione cum mulieribus vitanda propter flammæ amoris incendium explicant Chrysost. Epist. 7. ad Olymp. Basilius tr. de virgin. præeunte Cypriano, qui tract. de singul. Cleric. In- certa, inquit, victoria est inter hostilia arma pugna- re. Et impossibilis liberatio est flammis circumdari, nec ardere. Rectius tamen de inflammatione pœna- li accipitur, ut ex applicatione similitudinis v. 29. constat: NON ERIT MUNDUS (rectius inno- cens) cum tetigerit eam. Sicut ignis in sinu totum corpus cum veste exurit, nec ambulare quis super prunas potest, ut non comburantur plantæ ejus, sic qui adulterium committit (hoc enim est ingredi ad mulierem proximi sui Genes. 6, 4. cap. 19, 31. c. 38, 9. Psalm. 51, 2.) igne libidinis conscientiam, famam, vitam & animam æque ac corpus suum exurit. Conf. Ez. 20, 7. Jerem. 30, 12. 1. Corinth. 6, 10. Ne- gatio pro affirmativa emphaseos causa adhibetur, non erit innocens, id est, maxime nocens erit, & pu- nietur gravissime.

## 6:30
THE GUILT IS NOT GREAT, WHEN SOMEONE HAS STOLEN) In the Hebrew: A thief is not affected by disgrace; he is not beaten with whips, but is compelled to make restitution with an increase. But an adulterer is put to death.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected; in the Hebrew it is THEY DO NOT DESPISE A THIEF, they do not affect a thief with disgrace, if he has stolen to satisfy his soul and he has been hungry. Theft is not extenuated, but it is taught that the disgrace and punishment of adultery are more grievous than those of theft: concerning which Chrysostom, homily 10 to the people: A thief is indeed a grievous thing, but not as grievous as an adulterer. For the former, even if he has a cold cause, can nevertheless pretend necessity from poverty: but the latter, with no necessity compelling him, rushes into the abyss of sin out of mere madness.

Latin:

NON GRANDIS EST CVLPA, CUM QVIS FU- RATUS FUERIT) In Hebræo: Non afficitur probro fur: non cæditur flagris, sed compellitur ad restitutionem cum augmento. At adulter occiditur.

Recte corrigitur Vulgata, in Ebr. est NON SPERNUNT FUREM, non afficiunt probro furem, si furatis fuerit, ut impleat animam suam & esuriverit. Non extenuatur furtum, sed pro- brum & supplicium adulterii gravius esse, quam fur- ti docetur: quo de Chrysost. homil. 10. ad pop. Gravis quidem res etiam fur, sed non tam gravis quam adulter. Ille enim etsi frigidam causam habet, tamen ex pauperie necessitatem prætendere potest: hic verò nulla ipsum cogente necessitate præ dementia sola in pec- cati voraginem corruit.

## 6:31
Verse 31.

IF HE IS CAUGHT HE WILL ALSO RENDER SEVENFOLD) From the Hebrew you might translate better: If caught he will repay sevenfold: that is, even if he is convicted of theft seven times, he is not held to more than the restitution of which we have already spoken. Thus the word שבעתים is taken in Psalm 12:7.

AND HE WILL HAND OVER ALL THE SUBSTANCE OF HIS HOUSE) As long as he has property from which he may pay, he is not led into prison.

From the Vulgate translation a contradiction has arisen, since in Exodus 22:1, a fourfold or fivefold, but not a sevenfold, restitution was ordained, by which the Papist interpreters torment themselves. But in vain, if the Hebrew text is rendered as was done by Grotius; or if this interpretation concerning theft repeated seven times does not please, sevenfold could be explained indefinitely, or as concerning perfect restitution, since Solomon does not precisely define how much is to be restored, which was done by Moses, but only hints at this, that the restitution of theft can be made in the highest degree and most perfect rigor, but that the damage brought about by adultery is impossible to repair.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

DEPREHENSVS QVOQVE REDDET SEPTU- PLUM) Ex Hebræo melius vertas: Deprehensus rependet se- pties: id est, etiamsi septies furti convincatur, non ultrà te- netur quam ad restitutionem, qualem jam diximus. Sic vox שבעתים sumitur Psalm. 12, 1.

ET OMNEM SUBSTANTIAM DOMUS SUÆ TRA- DET) Quamdiu res habebit unde solvat, non ducitur in nervum.

E vulgata translatione contradictio suborta, cum Exod. 22, 1. quadrupli, vel quintupli, non au- tem septupli restitutio sancita sit, qua se macerant Pontificii Interpp. Sed frustra, si ita reddatur E- bræus textus, ut à Grotio factum; aut si non pla- ceat hæc de furto septies iterato interpretatio, septu- plum explicari poterit indefinite, vel de perfecta restitutione, quum non definiat præcise Salomo, quantuplum restituendum sit, quod à Mose fa- ctum, sed id solum innuat, quod restitutio furti in summo gradu, & rigore perfectissima fieri pos- sit, damnum autem per adulterium illatum resar- cire impossibile sit.

## 6:32
Verse 32.

BUT HE WHO IS AN ADULTERER, BECAUSE OF THE LACK OF HEART, WILL DESTROY HIS OWN SOUL.

Which is to be understood both of temporal and of eternal destruction. Compare Genesis 38:24, Leviticus 20:10, chapter 21:9, Deuteronomy 22:13 ff., Proverbs 5:7, chapter 7:22, chapter 9:18, chapter 22:14, 1 Corinthians 6:9, Galatians 5:21, Ephesians 5:5, Revelation 21:8.

Latin:

Vers. 32,

QVI AUTEM ADULTER EST, PRO- PTER CORDIS INOPIAM PERDET ANI- MAM SUAM.

Quod tum de temporali, tum de æterno exitio intelligendum. Conf. Genes. 38. vers. 24. Lev. 20. vers. 10. cap. 21. vers. 9. Deut. 22. v. 13. seqq. Prov. 5. vers. 7. cap. 7, 22. cap. 9, 18. cap. 22, 14. 1. Cor. 6. v. 9. Gal. 5. vers. 21. Ephes. 5, 5. Ap. 21, 8.

## 6:33
Verse 33. A WORSE DISGRACE NOT DUE.

It is not a question of not blotting out the guilt, but of not blotting out the infamy, and therefore Tertullian in his book on modesty, chapter 18, rashly concluded from this that adulterers are not to be received back into favor, who, out of excessive love of modesty, as Cornelius says, fell into heresy.

Latin:

Vers. 33. OPPROBRIUM PEJUS NON DEBITUM.

Non de non delenda culpa, sed de non delen- da infamia agitur, ideoque Tertul. lib. de pudic. cap. 18. temere hinc conclusit, non recipiendos esse mœchos in gratiam qui nimio pudicitiæ amore, ut lo- quitur Cornelius, in hæresin lapsus est.

## 6:34
Verse 34. FOR JEALOUSY AND FURY OF A MAN WILL NOT SPARE IN THE DAY OF VENGEANCE) Either from grief, perhaps upon discovering the adulterer:

Yet that grief sometimes demands more than any law has permitted to grief. As Juvenal says in Satire 10. Or even when the matter is brought to judgment, where the convicted adulterer will not repeat the crime, which thieves sometimes do, but will immediately pay with his life.

It is rightly noted, however, by Cornelius, that among the Jews a husband could not kill an adulterer by his own hand, but had to accuse him before a judge, by whom he was condemned to stoning: See Num. 5, verse 12. That the punishment for adultery was strangulation is taught in the Talmud, Sanhedrin, chapter 10, but that it was stoning is gathered from John 8, verse 5, which is also observed by R. Kimchi on Ezekiel 16, verse 40.

Latin:

Vers. 34. QVIA ZELVS ET FVROR VIRI NON PARCET IN DIE VINDICTÆ) Sive ex dolore, de- prenso forte adultero:

exigit autem Interdum ille dolor, plus quam lex ulla dolori Permisit. Vt ait Juvenalis Satyra 10. Sive etiam re in judicium addu- cta, ubi convictus adulter non repetet crimen, quod fures interdum faciunt, sed statim capite luet.

Recte tamen notatum à Cornelio, quod apud Judæos per se maritus adulterum occidere non potuerit, sed accusare eum apud judicem debue- rit, a quo condemnabatur ad lapidationem: Vid. Num. 5. vers. 12. Pœnam adulterii strangulationem fuisse in Thalmud. Sanhedr. cap. 10. docetur, lapi- dationem vero fuisse è Johan. 8. vers. 5. colligitur, quod etiam à R. Kimchio in Ezech. 16. versu 40. ob- servatum.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. Solomon presents both the harlot enticing to fornication, and the outcome of the seduction, which is utterly destructive.

Ver. 1. MY SON KEEP MY WORDS, AND LAY UP MY PRECEPTS.

He again puts forward a general admonition about keeping his words as a precious treasure, and diligently storing them up in the chest of the mind. The things added here by the LXX, My son honor the Lord & worship him, fear no other, although they are cited by Lucifer of Cagliari & Ephrem the Syrian, do not occur in the Hebrew nor in the Chaldean, and are rejected by the Papists themselves, since they have been omitted even in the Vulgate.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. Exhibet Salomo tum meretricem ad fornica- tionem allicientem, tum eventum fedu- ctionis penitus exitialem.

Vers. 1. FILI MI CUSTODI SERMONES MEOS, ET PRÆCEPTA MEA RECONDE.

ITerum admonitionem generalem præmittit de custodiendis sermonibus suis veluti thesauro pretioso, iisdemque in arca mentis studiose re- condendis. Quæ apud LXX. hic adduntur, Fili mi honora Dominum & cole eum, ne timueris alium, etsi à Lucifero, Calarit. & Ephrem Syro adducan- tur, nec in Ebr. nec in Chald. occurrunt, & à Papi- stis ipsis reprobantur, quum in vulgata etiam præ- termissa sint.

## 7:2
Ver. 2. SON KEEP MY COMMANDMENTS, AND LIVE.

These things teach that, not only on account of the special precept concerning the avoiding of adulteries, but for the sake of all the commandments which Solomon proposed to the candidates of wisdom as his sons, it is inculcated that one should not only keep and store them up with the greatest zeal, but also observe and fulfill them: therefore Solomon, with Moses, promises life under the condition, if, namely, the same have been kept, Lev. 18, 5, which indeed is impossible for us to perform after the fall, Romans 8, verse 3, Acts 15, verse 11. Therefore those things which are commanded concerning the law in Deuteronomy 6. v. 8. that it is to be bound as a sign on the hand, and ought to be moved between the eyes, the same are commanded concerning these divine Solomonic precepts, that, namely, we ought to keep his law as the apple of the eye, and bind it on the fingers, which, so that we do not understand it in a crude way like the Jews, who affix the law of the Decalogue written on small membranes to the arm and forehead, is rendered here: WRITE IT UPON THE TABLES OF THY HEART: for this, according to the letter, as it sounds, certainly cannot be done. Nothing else is noted, therefore, than that we should continually have the law before our eyes and in our mind, and strive to observe it holily. This sense is acknowledged here by the Jesuit Cornelius, while he ineptly says that his more religious ones, as he calls them, who bind the law with thread, paper, or the like to their fingers, observe the warning of Moses and Solomon plainly to the letter: which he himself confesses is not to be observed to the letter, and on that account criticizes it in the Jews, which he praises in his own religious ones not without ἑαυτομαχίᾳ (self-contradiction).

Latin:

Vers. 2. FILI SERVA MANDATA MEA, ET VIVES.

Docent hæc, non tantum ob speciale præce- ptum de cavendis adulteriis, sed in gratiam omnium mandatorum, quæ Salomo Candidatis sapientiæ ceu filiis suis, proposuit, inculcari, ut summo stu- dio ea non tantum custodiat & recondat, sed etiam servet, atque impleat: ideo Salomo cum Mose vi- tam pollicetur sub conditione, si scil. eadem ser- vata fuerint Lev. 18, 5, quæ vero nobis post lapsum præstitu impossibilis est Roman. 8. versu 3. Actor. 15. versu 11. Ideo quæ de lege præcepta sunt Deu- teronom. 6. v. 8. quod nempe liganda ea sit quasi si- gnum in manu, & inter oculos moveri debeat, ea- dem de his præceptis divinis Salomoneis juben- tur, quod scil. servare legem ejus debeamus, ceu pupillam oculi, & ligare in digitis, quod ne crasso modo cum Judæis intelligamus, qui legem Deca- logi membranulis inscriptam brachio, & fronti affigunt, redditur hic: SCRIBE ILLAM IN TABULIS CORDIS TUI: hoc enim secun- dum literam, ut sonat, utique fieri non potest. Ni- hil ergo aliud notatur, quam ut legem jugiter præ oculis & in mente habeamus, sancteque observare studeamus. Quem sensum agnoscit hic Cornelius Jesuita, interim religiosiores suos, quos vocat, le- gem filo, charta, similive digitis alligantes monitum Mosis, & Salomonis plane ad literam servare, ine- pte ait: quod ad literam non esse servandum ipse fatetur, eoque nomine in Judæis reprehendit, quod in suis religiosis non sine ἑαυτομαχίᾳ laudat.

## 7:4
Ver. 4. SAY TO WISDOM THOU ART MY SISTER, AND CALL PRUDENCE THY FRIEND.

We ought to have wisdom not only as a sister, and be joined to her, as Bede speaks, by a preliminary love, but as a bride: i.e., If you seek a bride, seek wisdom. For friend is taken for bride, because the bride is the most intimate and beloved friend. Here, therefore, Solomon makes wisdom a bride, and wants us to be her suitors, so that, namely, we may betroth to ourselves the wisdom of the divine word. In the Canticle, however, he establishes the archetype itself, the Son of God, as Hypostatic Wisdom, as our Bridegroom, whose bride is every faithful soul. Because, in order that that heavenly bridegroom might betroth himself to us, he deigned to communicate to us the ectype wisdom through the word, in which we have his image, so that we may embrace the same with intimate love, and have her as a uniquely beloved bride. What of the fact that Hypostatic Wisdom herself is also depicted in the likeness of a Bride, of whom Solomon says, Wisd. 8, 2. I have loved her from my youth, and

sought to take her to myself as a bride and I became a lover of her beauty. The reason for this exchange in this mystery is the intimate communion, by which he is everything to us, and thus both Bridegroom and Bride: Bridegroom because of the origin of love, the acquisition of the bride, and the communication of all goods and honors, because he first loved us, and acquired us for himself by the price of his own blood, and gives and communicates his goods and his honors to us: Bride because of the sweetness, grace, and magnitude of love.

Latin:

Vers. 4. DIC SAPIENTIÆ SOROR MEA ES, ET PRUDENTIAM VOCA AMICAM TUAM.

Non ut sororem tantum habere debemus sa- pientiam, eique, ut Beda loquitur, previa dilectio- ne conjungi, sed ut sponsam: q. d. Si sponsam ambis, ambi sapientiam. Amica enim pro sponsa accipi- tur, quia sponsa maxime intima, & dilecta est ami- ca. Hic ergo sapientiam sponsam facit Salomo, ejusque procos nos esse vult, ut scil. verbi divini sapientiam nobis desponsemus. In Cantico vero ἀρχέτυπον ipsummet, Filium Dei, ceu Sapientiam Hypostaticam, Sponsum nostrum constituit, cujus sponsa est anima quæque fidelis. Quia ut cœle- stis ille sponsus se nobis desponsaret, sapientiam ἔκτυπον per verbum nobis communicare dignatus est, in quo ejus habemus effigiem, ut eandem in- timo amore complectamur, & ceu sponsam unice dilectam habeamus. Quid quod ipsa Sapientia hypostatica etiam depingatur instar Sponsæ, de qua Salomo Sap. 8, 2. Hanc amavi à juventute mea, &

quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere & amator factus sum formæ illius. Cujus commutationis in hoc mysterio ratio est intima communio, qua ille omnia nobis est, adeoque & Sponsus & Sponsa: Sponsus ob amoris originem, Sponsæ acquisitionem, bonorumque & honorum omnium communicationem, quia prior ipse dilexit nos, sibique nos acquisivit pretio sanguinis proprii, & bona sua, honoros- que suos nobis donat, & communicat: Sponsa ob suavitatem, venustatem, & amoris magnitudinem.

## 7:5
Ver. 5. THAT SHE MAY KEEP THEE FROM THE STRANGE WOMAN, AND FROM THE FOREIGNER, WHO MAKES HER WORDS SWEET.

In the Hebrew, 'who softens her words.' The Septuagint, 'who attacks you with gracious words.' By this strange woman some understand pleasure, with Ambrose, book 1, On Cain, ch. 4, or depraved concupiscence with R. Levi: but there is no reason why we should depart from the literal meaning of the word to a figurative signification, or admit a prosopopoeia here throughout the whole chapter, but rather that the dissuasion from harlots is continued, not only with the preceding chapter, but all the words of the present chapter also testify, in which the manners of harlots, and the arts of enticing and seducing, and also the danger which arises from thence, are described by the example subjoined in ver. 6 and following, whether it was truly done, or rather composed by art to illustrate the matter. Furthermore, Ambrose beautifully depicts the manners and gestures of a harlot: She, he says, is bold in her harlot-like movement, with a gait broken by delights, with wavering eyes, and casting nets with playful eyelids, by which she captures the precious souls of young men (for the eye of a harlot is a snare for the sinner), whoever she sees passing by who is lacking in sense, she attacks with gracious speeches in the corner of the passage of her house, making the hearts of young men fly, restless at home, wandering in the streets, prodigal with kisses, vile in modesty, rich in clothing, painted on the cheeks.

Latin:

Vers. 5. UT CUSTODIAT TE A MULIERE EXTRANEA, ET AB ALIENA, QUÆ VERBA SUA DULCIA FACIT.

In Ebr. quæ verba sua lenificat. LXX. quæ te verbis adoritur gratiosis. Per hanc mulierem alie- nam nonnulli voluptatem intelligunt, cum Ambr. l. 1. de Cain c. 4. vel concupiscentiam pravam cum R. Levi: sed non est cur à proprietate vocis ad figu- ratam significationem abeamus, vel prosopopæiam hic admittamus per totum serme caput, quin con- tinuari potius dehortationem à meretricibus non συνέχεα cum præcedenti capite tantum, sed omnia etiam verba præsentis capitis testantur, quo gra- phice mores meretricum, & artes illiciendi, ac se- ducendi, nec non periculum quod inde oritur, ex- emplo subjuncto v. 6. seqq. seu vere id gestum sit, seu potius arte ad rem illustrandam compositum describuntur. De cætero pulcre Ambrosius me- retricis mores & gestus depingit: Illa, inquit, me- retricio procax motu, infracto per delicias incessu, nutantibus oculis, & ludentibus jaculans palpebris retia, quibus pretiosas juvenum animas capit (ocu- lus enim meretricis laqueus est peccatoris) quemcun- que viderit sensu indigum prætereuntem, in angulum in transitu domus suæ, sermonibus adoritur gratio- sis, faciens juvenum volare corda, domi inquieta, in plateis vaga, osculis prodiga, pudore vilis, amictu di- ves, genas picta.

## 7:10
Ver. 10. PREPARED TO CAPTURE SOULS.

In the Hebrew, 'guarded in heart': Syriac and Septuagint, 'who makes the hearts of young men fly': But לְבֻבָה is 'guarded,' or as R. Solomon, 'fortified in heart,' whose heart is fortified by cunning on every side.

GARRULOUS AND WANDERING) Thus Horace called a wandering harlot.

In the Hebrew, 'tumultuous,' as Pagninus, or 'noisy,' as Vatablus and Junius. By 'tumultuous' her garrulity is noted: And 'perverse' or 'refractory,' by which name the indomitable contumacy of the woman is expressed. Cf. Deuteronomy 21, verse 18. Psalm 78, verse 8. For the harlot is described by (1.) impudence, because she goes out to meet the young man. (2.) external habit, harlot-like adornment, (3.) singular cunning, ver. 10. (4.) garrulity, (5.) contumacy. (6.) restless wandering, ver. 11, 12. (7.) immodesty in kissing, ver. 17. (8.) a brazen forehead: she coaxes with a bold face: In the Hebrew it is, 'she strengthened her face,' or 'hardened her countenance' for an immodest address. (9.) enticing speech, and instructed with arguments for seduction, ver. 14 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 10. PRÆPARATA AD CAPIEN- DAS ANIMAS.

In Ebr. custodita corde: Syr. & LXX. quæ facit juvenum volare corda: Sed לְבֻבָה est custodita, vel ut R. Salomo munita corde, cujus cor astutia unde- quaque communitum est.

GARRVLA ET VAGA) Sic vagum scortum di- xit Horatius.

In Ebr. tumultuosa, ut Pagninus, vel strepe- ra, ut Vatablus & Junius. Tumultuosa garrulita- te notatur: Et perversa vel refractaria, quo nomi- ne contumacia indomita mulieris exprimitur. Conf. Deuteronom. 21. vers. 18. Psalm. 78. versu 8. Describitur nempe meretricis (1.) impudentia. quod prodeat in juvenis occursum. (2.) externus habitus, ornatus meretricius, (3.) calliditas singu- laris vers. 10. (4.) garrulitas, (5.) contumacia. (6.) inquieta divagatio, vers. 11. 12. (7.) impudicitia in deosculatione vers. 17. (8.) frons perfricta: proca- ci vultu blanditur: In Ebr. est. roboravit vultum suum, vel obfirmavit faciem suam ad impudicum alloquium. (9.) sermo allectans, & argumentis ad seductionem instructus v. 14. seqq.

## 7:12
Ver. 12. NOW NEAR THE CORNERS LYING IN WAIT)

In all the crossroads and alleys: as Catullus says.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NVNC JVXTA ANGVLOS INSIDIANS)

Cunctis in triviis & angiportis: ut ait Catullus.

## 7:14
Ver. 14. I HAVE VOWED VICTIMS FOR MY SAFETY] For your safety.

In the Hebrew, 'Victims of peace-offerings are with me.' Under the guise of piety she entices, because she has already offered Eucharistic sacrifices, from a vow made long ago, and a sacred banquet she has prepared according to custom, to which she desires to invite the young man who happens upon her: and she wishes to persuade him thus, that she is not so alienated from piety, and that God, now appeased, will not much concern Himself with these venial sins, just as our Mr. Dr. Gejer does here.

Latin:

Vers. 14. VICTIMAS PRO SALVTE VOVI] Pro tua salute.

In Ebr. Victimæ pacificarum apud me. Sub schemate pietatis allicit, quod sacrificia Eucharistica, ex voto pridem facto, jam obtulerit, & convivium sacrum pro more inde appararit, ad quod juve- nem sibi occurrentem invitatum cupiat: & per- suadere ei ita vult, se a pietate non adeo alienam, Deumque jam placatum peccatilla haec venialia non adeo curaturum esse, ut hic Dn. D. Gejerus no- ster.

## 7:16
Verse 16.

I HAVE WOVEN MY BED WITH CORDS, I HAVE SPREAD IT WITH PAINTED TAPESTRIES FROM EGYPT. Heb. מרבדים which the Vulgate renders as cords, Piscator as coverlets, Pagninus & Sixt. Amama as tapestries, Aquila & Theod. explained not unsuitably as περισρώμασιν, i.e., περισρώμασιν περιέστρωσα with tapestries, and I have spread it with hangings, others with ornaments I have adorned. Cornelius likewise explains the word חטבות as tapestries, cut into various figures of flowers and animals; but because the sense of this word as such cannot be proven, the interpretation of Mercer, rather, and of R. Levi Gers. and of him who follows Kimchi, to which also Mariana and Vatablus accede, seems to be admissible, concerning the boards or beams of the bed cut out and artfully sculpted: so that it may be understood that the bed consists of skillfully carved wood; ואטון מצרים & with Egyptian cord: which Mercer and Mariana understand as the cords supporting the bed, others with Junius as linen made of flax, which were most precious in Egypt, to be preferred to all others for whiteness and softness, according to Pliny, book 18, chapter 1. Beda: beds which are woven from cords, or according to another translation from bands, are wont to be softer than those which are constructed from wood or horn or any other material.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

INTEXUI FUNIBUS LECTULUM MEUM, STRAVI TAPETIBUS PICTIS EX ÆGYPTO. Ebr. מרבדים quod Vulg. funibus, Piscator stragulis, Pagninus & Sixt. Amama tapetibus red- dunt, Aquila & Theod. exposuere περισρώμασιν non inconcinne, h. m. περισρώμασιν περιέστρωσα tapetibus, & aulaeis stravi, alii ornamentis ornavi. Vocem חטבות itidem per tapetes, variis florum & animalium figuris incisos exponit Cornelius; sed quia sensus talis hujus vocis probari nequit, Mer- ceri potius, R. Levi Gers. & Kimchium sequentis interpretatio, cui etiam accedit Mariana & Va- tablus, admittenda videtur, de asseribus vel trabi- bus lecti excisis & artificiose sculptis: ut innustur lectum constare lignis affabre incisis; ואטון מצרים & fune Ægyptio: quod Mercerus & Maria- na de funibus lectum sustinentibus, alii cum Ju- nio de linteis xylinis, quae in Ægypto pretiosissima erant, omnibus candore & mollitie praeferenda Plinio teste lib. 18. cap. 1. intelligunt. Beda: so- lent lecti, qui ex funibus, vel juxta aliam transla- tionem institis texuntur, molliores fieri, quam qui ex ligno vel cornu vel qualibet alia materia substruun- tur.

## 7:17
Verse 17.

I HAVE SPRINKLED MY BED WITH MYRRH AND ALOES AND CINNAMON) I have perfumed it. אהלים which is translated here as aloes, the Jews interpret as sandalwood. The word נפת I have distilled denotes to sprinkle drop by drop the sides of the bed: Ps. 68, v. 10. But the word אהלים is more correctly rendered by aloes than, with R. Kimchi, Junius, and Piscator, as sandalwood, which is a certain Indian wood used for incense, because the name fits better, and aloes contributes more to the scent. See Plin. book 27, chapter 4. Conf. Ps. 45, v. 9. Cant. 4, v. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ASPERSI CUBILE MEUM MTRRA ET ALOE ET CINNAMOMO) Odoravi illud. אהלים quod hic aloë vertitur, sandalum interpretantur Judæi. Verbum נפת destillavi notat guttatim con- sperse cubilis latera: Pf.68. v. 10. Vox vero אהלים rectius per aloën redditur, quam cum R. Kimchi, Junio & Piscatore, Santalis, quod est lignum quod- dam Indicum ad suffitum faciens, quia & no- men magis convenit, & plus ad odorem con- ducit aloë, Vid. Plin. lib. 27. cap. 4. Conf. Pfal. 45. v. 9. Cant. 4. v. 14.

## 7:20
Verse 20.

ON THE DAY OF THE FULL MOON HE HAS RETURNED TO HIS HOUSE) Thus Jerome translates this word from the Hebrew in Ps. 80, v. 4, in the version from the Greek, as new moon. And in the same way Aben-Ezra interprets it here. But it is closer to be from כסא to calculate and to signify a calculated, or certain, agreed-upon, appointed time. This the adulteress says, lest the adulterer fear being caught.

In this way indeed Pagninus, the Tigurines, Junius, Cajetanus, and Baynus render it: concerning a fixed solemnity, Buxtorf from the Rabbis and Luther explain it as aufs Fest: and that interpretation concerning the new moon seems altogether more remote, even if R. Levi Ben Gerson also agrees with it: but the exposition of the Vulgate concerning the full moon is even more alien: because if כסא is derived from כסה to cover, the moon is covered at the new moon, but not at the full moon. For then it is entirely illuminated.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

IN DIE PLENÆ LUNÆ REVERSUS EST IN DO- MUM SUAM) Sic vocem hanc vertit ex Hebræo Hiero- nymus Psal. 80. v. 4. in versione ex Græco, neomeniam. Et eodem modo hic interpretatur Aben-Esdra. Propius vero est esse a כסא supputare & significari tempus supputatum, sive certum, condictum, constitutum. Hoc dicit mœcha, ne adulter deprehendi metuat.

Hoc sane modo reddunt Pagninus, Tigurini, Junius, Cajetanus, Baynus: de solemnitate fixa e Rabbinis Buxtorff. & Lutherus aufs Fest expli- cant: & videtur omnino remotior illa de novilu- nio interpretatio, etiamsi ei etiam accedat R. Le- vi Ben Gerson: alienior autem adhuc Vulgatae ex- positio de plena luna: quia si כסא deducatur a כסה texit, luna in novilunio operitur, non vero in plenilunio. Tum enim tota illuminatur.

## 7:22
Verse 22.

AND AS A WANTON LAMB. The Vulgate added these words of its own: just as the LXX add a comparison to a dog with the Chaldean. For those are not contained in the Hebrew: where only mention of an ox is made, suddenly led away to the victim and the slaughter. For whatever the LXX or the Vulgate saw or read here, it was a παρόραμα. Just as also the LXX and the Chaldean in the following verse, 23, added a simile, AS A STAG struck by a dart in the liver, when in the source it is only held, until the arrow cleaves his liver: and the sense is consistent for itself, without that addition. But the arrow is noted not so much of love as of pain: because the liver is the source of blood, and with it pierced, a man must die. Through darts and arrows, divine wounds are wont to be designated. See Job 6, verse 4; chapter 34, verse 6; Ps. 38, verse 3; Ps. 64, v. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ET QUASI AGNUS LASCIVIENS. Hæc de suo addidit Vulgatus: quemadmodum LXX. similitudinem de cane cum Chald. adjiciunt. Illa enim in Ebræo non habentur: ubi solum bo- vis mentio fit, subito abrepti ad victimam, & la- nienam. Quicquid enim hic viderint, aut lege- rint seu LXX. seu Vulgatus, παρόραμα fuit. Sic- uti etiam LXX. & Chald. versu sequ. 23. addide- re simile, SICUT CERVUS telo percussus in Epate, quum in fonte tantum habeatur, donec fin- dat sagitta jecur ejus : & constet sibi sensus, sine illo additamento. Sagitta autem non tam amo- ris quam doloris notatur : quia jecur est fons san- guinis, eoque transfixo moriendum est homini. Per tela & sagittas solent designari plagæ divinæ. Vid. Job. 6. vers. 4. cap. 34. vers. 6. Psal. 38. vers. 3. Psal. 64. v. 8.

## 7:27
THE WAYS OF HELL ARE HIS HOUSE.

The word שאול here denotes hell; the house of adulterers is there: chap. 2. v. 18. She (the adulteress) declines to death her house, where the Chaldean says, in the depth of death is her house: chap. 5. v. 5. her steps penetrate to the underworld. Conf. Gal. 5. v. 21. Eph. 5. v. 5. Heb. 13. v. 4.

Latin:

VIÆ INFERI DOMUS EJUS.

Vox שאול hic infernum notat; domus ibi est adulterorum : cap. 2. v. 18. Declinat (adulte- ra) ad mortem domum suam, ubi Chaldæus, in profunditate mortis domus ejus : cap. 5. v. 5. ad in- feros gressus ejus penetrant. Conf. Gal. 5. v. 21. Eph. 5. v. 5. Ebr. 13. v. 4.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

Hypostatic Wisdom is brought forward, calling us from the ways of sinners and of hell to itself and inviting the seduced, with a promise of truth, justice, wisdom, and the fear of GOD, as the cause and origin of prudence, counsel, riches, and glory: and its eternal generation, the production of the world, and its delight with the human race are described; the reception of whose instruction brings life, while its neglect brings death.

Ver. 1.

DOES NOT WISDOM CRY OUT) The Hebrews explain these things concerning that wisdom which appears in the law, and indeed these attributes belong not to it alone, but especially to it.

Grotius here again prefers the gloss of the Jews to the interpretation of the Holy Fathers: but the passage is worthy of being weighed a little more accurately, since in this chapter especially the mysterious Wisdom of the wisest of Kings and mortals, which he had concerning the true origin of Wisdom from the inspiration of the Spirit by whom he was moved, and then both at the beginning of the wisest Proverbs, and especially in this and the following chapter, he opened to the people over whom he ruled, and indeed even to us, for whose sake also ancient monuments were written Rom. 15. v. 4. so that we might be instructed unto salvation by faith in Christ. 1. Tim. 3. v. 18. Although not a few explain this crying Wisdom otherwise: for instance, either generally concerning wisdom abstracted from divine and human, or as it is common to GOD and men, which is the interpretation of Cornelius à Lapide and Menochius: or concerning the Essential Wisdom of GOD, which is that of certain Jews and Photinians, or concerning the wisdom of the Word of GOD, contained in the Holy Scriptures, and announced at all times through the public ministry of Teachers, which is the explanation of Mercer and others, or specifically concerning the wisdom delivered in the law, as R. Solomon Jarchi and Le Kach Tob interpret, as also with them Salazar and our Grotius, or concerning the habitual wisdom of men, which Solomon preferred to other goods 1. Reg. 3. v. 11. (to pass over in silence the mystical, and in large part impious, distortions of the Papists Salazar, Cornelius à Lapide, and others toward the holy Virgin Theotokos: Tirinus says that the Roman Church applies these to the Mother of God in an accommodative sense) it is nevertheless certain to us that Solomon is speaking of hypostatic Wisdom, the eternal Son of God, the author and source of all Wisdom; not of some divine attribute, not of the Word of God, not of some accidental habit in us, but of an eternal, most wise, omnipotent, divine person, the Creator, Preserver, and Governor of all things, the Savior of the human race, the cause of our eternal salvation, crying out in the word, and through the ministry of the word, and all inviting to true wisdom and the fruits of the same, and thus to eternal blessedness. And indeed, it is no wonder regarding the Jews that they could not see that hypostatic Wisdom here, who rejected Christ the Wisdom of God (Matt. 23:34) and acknowledge no hypostatic Wisdom in GOD; nay, they hold the doctrine concerning the eternal ears to them here. Nor is it a wonder regarding the Photinians, who impugn the προϋπαρξιν of the Son of God before his temporal birth. But that Christian interpreters, admitting the mystery of the Holy Trinity, should accept it concerning the Word of God προφορικῷ and the Wisdom which is exhibited by the same, the cause seems to be chiefly that they have observed that the Wisdom of the Word of God is adorned with similar eulogies, and that not a few things occur which are to be understood properly of it here and in the parallel in Wisdom 1. and 2, and that other things, folly and pleasure, are introduced in antithesis through prosopopoeia, whence they believed that it also has a place here, and that the discourse is about the Wisdom expressed by the Word of God or at least about the essential wisdom of God. But when we have weighed the matter more deeply, it will by no means be obscure that it is accurately distinguished by Solomon, and that this inviting Wisdom is defined by those epithets and predicates so that it cannot be accepted otherwise than of the Son of God. For (1) the inviting Wisdom is openly distinguished from that wisdom which is to be learned from it and by it: concerning that, it is thus held: Does not WISDOM cry out, and PRUDENCE give its voice, and what follows concerning the change of the same and what kind it is, what its ὕπαρξις is, what its attributes and effects are, are explained. But that hypostatic Wisdom proposes this, inviting us to learn and embrace Wisdom, v. 5: understand, O simple ones, ASTUTENESS, and you fools, pay attention; listen, for I will speak of excellent things, and my lips shall be opened so that they may proclaim RIGHT things. My palate shall speak TRUTH, all MY WORDS are just, there is nothing crooked or perverse in them, they are right to those who understand, and equitable to those who find knowledge: receive MY INSTRUCTION and not silver, and KNOWLEDGE rather than chosen gold: because Wisdom is better than all most precious things. Who does not see here that it is one thing to be the Wisdom that cries out and gives forth its voice, which is our confirmer and Teacher: and quite another to be the precepts and doctrine which are handed down by it, namely, the ASTUTENESS which the simple ought to understand: those excellent things which can be learned from its mouth: those right things for the sake of proclaiming which it opens its own lips: that truth which its palate speaks: its words which it speaks: the instruction, and also the knowledge, which it proposes and commends, and which it wishes to be drawn solely from itself. Whoever does not distinguish these must necessarily confuse that supreme Doctor with the Doctrine, that unique Master with his Precepts, the author of wisdom, who is wisdom itself, with the knowledge and wisdom which he himself hands down, the Wisdom communicating with the Wisdom to be communicated, which, however, are so clearly discriminated here that they could not be more clearly. Furthermore, with distinct eulogies, the communicating and communicated wisdom is called archetype and ectype here. For hypostatic Wisdom commends first its doctrine, then to the simple and foolish, who can learn from it pious astuteness and Wisdom, and also to the learned, who can learn all most excellent things and true rectitude, v. 5, 6; and it celebrates the same, because sacred astuteness brings a remedy to our stupidity and folly, v. 5; and because it hands down most excellent mysteries and most certain precepts, informing us about divine truth and true piety, v. 6, 7; and in every way just, and sufficiently obvious and perspicuous, v. 8, 9; finally, because it is far more precious than gold and silver and pearls and all desirable things, v. 10, 11. Then indeed, hypostatic wisdom describes itself, v. 12 and following: I, Wisdom, dwell in astuteness, etc. which everyone sees is done in such a way that it openly distinguishes itself again from the astuteness with which it wishes to instruct us, in which it dwells, and the knowledge of knowledges which it finds, or provides so that we may find: from the Wisdom whose beginning is the fear of the Lord, so that pride and arrogance and the evil way may be fled: which hypostatic wisdom testifies that it hates, and which it wishes to generate and reconcile in its worshippers, along with the fear of the Lord: Mine, says hypostatic wisdom, is counsel, תושיה (which the LXX ἀσφάλειαν, the Vulgate equity, Junius WHATEVER IS, the Hebrews, conveniently enough with the other words, explain as wisdom, so called because of its solidity:) mine is intelligence, mine is strength, so that it thus distinguishes itself from counsel, wisdom, intelligence, and virtue, which are attributes, as the subject to which those attributes belong, or if those are understood κατ’ ἔξω, as the cause from the effects of which it is the author: And thus it speaks thereafter about itself through the entire chapter, not neglecting that distinction which is hinted at again in v. 33: listen to DISCIPLINE and be wise, and do not cast it away; and c. 9, 6: leave infancy and live, and walk through the ways of prudence. v. 10: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and the knowledge of the Holy Ones is prudence. Which, when it had professed concerning the wisdom communicated by itself, it calls us back again to itself, the author and source of the same: v. 11. FOR BY ME your days shall be multiplied, and the years of your life shall be added to you. Which can likewise be seen in the parallel passage c. 2, 20 seqq. For there WISDOM, preaching outside, giving its voice in the streets, openly discriminates itself from the knowledge which it hands down, and from its correction, to which it wishes all to be converted, and from the word of its doctrine or institution, and from its counsel and rebukes, so that it can be a doubt to no one that by that WISDOM is not understood the Word of God itself, the doctrine or law, and the precepts of God, but that these are entirely distinct from the mind of the Holy Spirit.

That this Wisdom is truly a hypostasis and a person is testified, first, by the personal predicates in the genus. Because it speaks as a person, and claims for itself those things which are proper to a person, and no one doubts that it is introduced here as a person: although those from the opposition take refuge in the figure of prosopopoeia. But because there is no necessity in such a prolix and exquisite description of a person to desert the proper mode of speaking and leap to the figurative; nor is it right for us to depart from the propriety of words where necessity does not compel, unless we wish to make a game and a joke out of the Scriptures, which Schmalcius himself even warned among the Socinians, we understand these things concerning a person and hypostatic wisdom without the fiction of a person. Nor indeed, if folly and pleasure are introduced as persons through fiction, must it be concluded that the same applies to wisdom, because we know from the Scriptures that a hypostatic Wisdom is given, the supreme cause and teacher of wisdom, to whom all these things most rightly correspond, and therefore those things are deservedly explained concerning it in a proper sense, and without figure. On the other hand, it is again indubitable from the Scriptures that folly and pleasure are not hypostatic, and therefore that what is said of them as a person cannot be understood properly: whence the thing itself necessarily demands that we determine that this one is introduced only through prosopopoeia in the likeness of a person. Therefore, the reason for these opposites is very different. I pass over the fact that some understand the Devil by the foolish woman: who is indeed a person.

See what is said regarding chapter 9, verse 13. Now if the names, attributes, and predicates are considered specifically, it will appear that the fiction of a person has no place here, but that a true person is introduced. That the name of wisdom itself belongs to the Son of God is undoubted from the New Testament, since in Luke 11, verse 29, he is expressly called σοφία τꭢ θεꭢ, to which also Matthew 11, verse 29 and Luke 7, verse 35 pertain, concerning wisdom justified by her children, on which passage see the Rostock dissertations, p. 88, and 1 Corinthians 1, verse 24: We preach Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Which name is attributed to Christ the Son of God both κατ' ἔσω (internally) because of his eternal generation, just like the name λόγꭢ: because he is the Wisdom and Word of the Father, proceeding from him from eternity, and remaining in him eternally, just as the internal Word and wisdom is from the mind and remains in the mind: as a certain offspring and daughter of the mind.
