Har præessè conciliis in nomine ejus erectis, præessē sanctis consiliis & cogitationibus, præessē eruditis, & erudi- tioni cuilibet ad v. 12. ait Cornelius : Hanc reginam mundi esse, & in Christum jus habere maternum, quo ei quasi filio possit præcipere atque imperare ad v. 16. blaspheme asserit: & quod Filius Dei sapientia hy- postatica v. 19. pronunciat, Fructus meus melior au- ro, ad Mariam detorquet, quod illa hæc de se pro- fiteri possit, quia Christus fructus est Mariæ: quam ideo Mediatricem & auctricem redemtionis salu- tisque nostræ vocat: eique tribuit, quod cruci astans Christi filii sui vitam, dolores & mortem atrocissi- mam Deo obtulerit ardentissima charitate in holo- caustum, & ut victimam pro peccatis totius mundi, imo quod seipsam cum eodem offerens Patri, quan- tum potuit, COOPERATA sit Christi sacrificio, & consequenter redemtioni nostræ: quæ vere impia sunt, quia honorem uni Christo Θεανθρώπῳ debi- tum ad ψιλάνθρωπον transferunt. Quæ de genera- tione æterna Filii Dei dicuntur, abripit & detorquet pariter Jesuita Lapideus ad Mariam, quod Deus eam ab æterno possederit: quam ab æterno ordinatam etiam dicit Sacerdotem mysticam, ut Christum suum in holocausto pro peccato offerret Deo ad redemtionem generis humani, ut in ipsa & per ipsam inveniret reus veniam, peccator justitiam, justus perseveran- tiam. Ad illam trahit etiam, quod Sapientia hypo- statica vers. 3. de se profitetur CUM EO ERAM CUNCTA COMPONENS, & ut uno dicam verbo, omnia quæ de se filius Dei hic testatus est, obtorto collo detorquet, non sine idololatria, & blasphemiis, ad S. Mariam Jesuita ille cum Salaza- ro suo, nihil metuens fulmina maledictionum in eos vibrata, qui in homine confidunt, & gloriam creatoris creaturæ tribuunt.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

To the gift of the hypostatic Wisdom building the Church, and adorning a mystical banquet, and inviting all to it, despised by the impious, loved by the faithful, threatening rewards to the former and punishment to the latter, is opposed stupidity, in the form of a foolish, wild, and garrulous woman, enticing men to herself everywhere, but to their eternal destruction.

Verse 1.

WISDOM HATH BUILT HERSELF A HOUSE) The human body.

SHE HATH HEWN OUT SEVEN PILLARS) As many as there were posts in the temple under the treasuries. He understands, however, the five senses, and two besides which others add, voice and memory.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

Sapientiæ Hypostaticæ donum Ecclesiæ extruenti, & convivium mysticum adornanti, & ad illud omnes invitanti, ab impiis contemtæ, a fidelibus adamatæ, his præmia, illis pœnam minitanti, opponitur stoliditas, sub forma mulieris insipientis, feræ, & garrulæ, passim homines ad sese allicientis, sed ad æter- num eorum interitum.

Vers. 1.

SAPIENTIA ÆDIFICAVIT SIBI DOMVM) Cor- pus humanum.

EXCIDIT COLVMNAS SEPTEM) Quot erant po- stes in templo sub gazophylaciis. Intelligit autem quinque sensus, & duos præterea quos addunt alii, vocem & memo- riam.

## 9:2
Verse 2. SHE HATH SLAIN HER VICTIMS) She has prepared many good things for men, if they know how to use them. These things are best referred in a more eminent sense to the Gospel. Matt. 22, 4.

Grotius is too much delighted with inventions and Rabbinical trifles. There is nothing here about the creation of the human body: nor did Wisdom create only the body, but the soul also: And how shall we understand human senses by seven pillars? To elicit which sense, he posits not only five senses, which has been the common doctrine of philosophers until now, but seven; counting voice and memory among the senses. It is a discourse about a house of refreshment and a banquet, in which Wisdom receives and refreshes her guests. And therefore by that house the Church is understood; in which we are refreshed and exhilarated by spiritual food and drink. For there the table is prepared, Ps. 23, 5. There a sumptuous banquet is set out, Is. 25, 6. And we are invited by the Son of God, Is. 55, 1. 2. eat what is good and your soul shall delight itself in fatness. There we are received with food and drink: Eat, O friends, and drink, be inebriated, O beloved, Cant. 5, 2. There we taste how sweet the Lord is Ps. 34, 9. and we are inebriated by the abundance of the house of the Lord, and are made to drink of the torrent of his pleasure Ps. 36, 9, there the bread of life John 6. and the water of life is offered, which may be in us a fountain of water springing up into life everlasting c. 4, 14. And this discourse concerning this banquet in the Church of God is not here in a more eminent sense only, but according to the letter. For no other literal sense can be brought forth from Scripture. But Rabbinical fables are not to be listened to. And how will that more eminent sense, which he says is used in the Gospel, square with that sense, if it be established as literal, concerning the formation of the human body, and the concession of the five senses, and the preparation of goods which a man ought to use? How will either that house, or the columns understood as the senses, agree with the mystical sense? Now because it pleased [Solomon] Jarchi to follow, who explains it concerning the creation of the world, why does he not understand the whole universe created by God rather than the human body by the house, and by the seven columns the seven days in which the world was created, or the works of the seven days, as he foolishly thought, adding the day of the Sabbath, on which God rested, to the hexaemeron of creation, to complete the septenary number. For thus he would not have had need, against the opinion of all philosophers, to multiply the senses and invent seven senses. Or why does he not, with Aben-Ezra, understand the seven liberal arts, upon which as columns wisdom has established her house? Is it not sufficiently known that the septenary is accepted for the number of perfection and fullness? Whence the sense is plain and obvious, with the approval of Gregory, many columns hewn out, and which are abundantly sufficient for propping up so noble a house. Furthermore, since others among the Hebrews understand by this house the temple of Solomon, in which Jerome, Pradus, and Villalpando, as also Grotius himself here, establish seven principal columns; which Cornelius a Lapide takes up in such a way that he wishes the Church to be represented typically at the same time, I do not see the reason why, having abandoned this, which approaches more closely to the mind of Solomon, he should have snatched at that inept opinion concerning the seven senses. If he had consulted Christian interpreters and especially the ancient Doctors, he would certainly have observed that it is understood by great consensus that the Church is the house built by Wisdom, by Athanasius, Orat. V. against the Arians, Ambrose, l. 1. on the Faith c. 7, Augustine, l. 17. on the City of God c. 4, Caesarius of Arles, hom. 7 on Easter, Chrysostom, hom. 50 and the imperfect work on Matthew, Anastasius of Nicaea, q. 40 on Holy Scripture, Gregory the Great, 33 Morals c. 15, Bede in his Commentary, Isidore, l. 8 Etym. c. 1, and the author of the questions of the Old and New Testament among the works of Augustine, Vol. 4. Thomas 3. p. q. 37. art. 5. and in the Greek Catena, etc. Although they cherish diverse opinions concerning the columns, Augustine understanding particular Churches, Chrysostom and Bernard the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, Bede the universality of Doctors, who are called columns c. 12, 11, to which many others agree, Menochius, Tirinus, Estius, Philippus, Osiander: Gregory the Great leads the way, l. 1. The house of Wisdom is called the Church: which hewed out seven columns for itself; because it raised up the minds of preachers, separated from the love of the present age, to carry the fabric of the same Church. Which, because they are supported by more perfect virtue, are designated by the septenary number. Following whom, Salianus says, The columns of this house are the holy Doctors, which columns are well said to be seven, because the holy Doctors are filled with the septiform grace of the Holy Spirit. How then did Wisdom hew out these columns? Because she separated the minds of preachers from the love of the present age as if from their stoniness, and raised them up to carry the fabric of the Church. Mercerus understands by the seven columns of wisdom all things upon which Wisdom relies, and through which it is taught, or the principal heads of the same. It is certain that columns are called for to indicate primarily the solidity of the house, although the beauty of the same is also insinuated at the same time, and since the Church is sustained by the Word, concerning which Chrysostom speaks excellently in 1 Timothy 3. the truth is the column and foundation of the Church, therefore most rightly the Holy Scriptures, upon which it most firmly leans, are understood, so that the number of perfection may designate the perfection of the Holy Scriptures, that they are abundantly sufficient for sustaining the house of the Church, and from the word of God primarily the principal and fundamental heads of faith, upon which it is established that faith and the house of the Church, and even eternal salvation itself, lean, are indicated. And since the word of God, through the mediation of the holy ministry, is placed under to sustain the Church, thence the teachers of the word are also called columns of the Church, not by reason of themselves, and of themselves, but because of the Word, through which it is sustained, which is propagated by them, guarded, and placed under to prop up and sustain the Church: nor undeservedly are they understood here for that reason. For although by the name of the handmaids, who are said to be sent forth, the ministers of the Word are signified, nothing nevertheless prevents us from understanding them also as columns: since they perform both duties, as heralds and messengers sent forth calling and gathering the Church, and as columns carrying and sustaining the gathered Church by the power of the divine Word, but ministerially and as servants, so that that power is proper to the Word, whose ministry they perform: not properly and principally; for thus who, unless demented by the Anti-Christ, who sells himself as God and the Vicar of Christ, would doubt that only God, and Wisdom itself hypostatic, the Son of God, sustains the house of the Church?

Latin:

Vers. 2. IMMOLAVIT VICTIMAS SVAS) Plurima bona præparavit hominibus, si uti norint. Hæc sensu emi- nentiore ad Evangelium optime referuntur. Matth. 22, 4.

NImis delectatur Grotius commentis, nugisque Rabbinicis. Nihil hic de creatione humani corporis: Neque corpus tantum, sed animam etiam creavit sapientia: Et quomodo per septem columnas sensus humanos intelligemus? Quem sensum ut eli- ciat, non quinque solum sensus, quæ Philosopho- rum hactenus communis fuit doctrina, sed septem constituit; vocem & memoriam sensibus annume- rans. De domo refectionis & convivii sermo est, in quo Sapientia hospites suos excipit ac reficit. Ideoque per domum illam Ecclesia intelligitur; in qua cibo ac potu spirituali reficimur, atque exhila- ramur. Ibi enim mensa parata est Psal. 23, 5. Ibi convivium lautum instructum Es. 25, 6. Et invita- mur a Filio Dei Es. 55, 1. 2. comedite bonum & dele- ctabitur in crassitudine anima vestra. Ibi excipimur esculentis & potulentis: Comedite amici, & bibite, inebriamini, charissimi, Cant. 5, 2. Illic gustamus, quam suavis sit Dominus Pf. 34, 9. & inebriamur ab ubertate domus Domini, ac torrente voluptatis ejus potamur Pf. 36, 9, illic panis vitæ Joh. 6. & aqua vitæ præbetur, quæ in nobis sit fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam c. 4, 14. Atque de hoc convivio in Ecclesia Dei non sensu eminentiori tan- tum hic sermo est, sed secundum literam. Nullus enim alius literalis sensus e Scriptura proferri potest. Rabbinicæ vero fabulæ audiendæ non sunt. Et quomodo ad illum sensum, si is literalis statuatur, de formatione corporis humani, & quinque sensuum concessione, ac bonorum præparatione, quibus homo uti debeat, eminentior, quem in Evangelio adhibe- ri dicit, sensus quadrabit? Quomodo vel domus il- la, vel columnæ de sensibus intellectæ congruent mystico sensui? Jam quia placuit Salomonem Jar- chi sequi, qui de mundi creatione explicat, cur non totum universum a Deo conditum potius, quam corpus humanum per domum, & per septem colu- mnas septem dies intelligit, quibus creatus mundus, aut opera septem dierum, ut ille ineptiit, diem Sab- bathi, quo quievit Deus, hexaëmero creationis ad- dens, ad complendum numerum septenarium. Ita enim non opus habuisset contra omnium Phi- losophorum sententiam sensus multiplicare, & se- ptem sensus fingere. Aut cur non cum Aben-Ezra septem artes liberales, super quas tanquam colu- mnas domum suam stabilierit sapientia intelligit? Annon satis notum, septenarium pro numero perfe- ctionis & plenitudinis accipi? unde sensus planus & obvius, annuente Gregorio, multas columnas ex- cisas, & quæ abunde sint ad tam præclaram domum fulciendam. Porro quum alii ex Ebræis per do- mum hanc intelligant templum Salomonis, in quo septem columnas præcipuas constituunt Hierony- mus Pradus, & Vilalpandus, ut & Grotius ipse hic; quod Cornelius a Lapide ita suscipit, ut typice re- præsentatatam Ecclesiam simul designari velit, cau- sam non video, cur hac, quæ propius accedit menti Salomoneæ, relicta, ineptam illam de septem sensi- bus arripuerit sententiam. Christianos si consuluif- fet Interpp. & præcipue Doctores Veteres, observaf- fet utique magno consensu Ecclesiam per domum a Sapientia exstructam intelligi, ab Athanas. Orat. V. contra Arian. Ambros. l. 1. de Fid. c. 7. August. l. 17. de Civ. Dei c. 4. Cæsario Arelat. hom. 7. de Pasch. Chrysost. hom. 50. & oper. imperf. in Matth. Anastasio Nicen. q. 40. in Script. S. Gregorio M. 33. Moral. c. 15. Beda in Comment. Isidoro l. 8. Etym. c. 1. Auctore quæst. V. & N. T. apud August. Tom. 4. Thoma 3. p. q. 37. art. 5. & in Græc. Ca- ten. &c. Quamvis de columnis diversas foveant sententias, Augustino particulares Ecclesias, Chry- sostomo & Bernhardo septem S. S. dona, Beda uni- versitatem Doctorum, qui columnæ dicuntur c. 12, 11. intelligente, cui plerique adstipulantur alii, Menochius, Tirinus, Esthius, Philippus, Osiander: Præit Gregorius M. l. 1. Domus Sapientiæ Ecclesia vocatur: quæ septem sibi columnas excidit; quia ab amore præsentis seculi disjunctas ad portandam ejus- dem Ecclesiæ fabricam mentes prædicantium erexit. Quæ pro eo, quod perfectiori virtute subnixæ sunt, septenario numero designantur. Quem sequutus Sa- lianus, Columnæ, inquit, domus hujus sunt sancti Doctores, quæ columnæ bene septem esse dicuntur, quia sancti Doctores referti sunt septiformi gratia Spiritus Sancti. Quomodo ergo excidit Sapientia has columnas? Quia mentes prædicatorum ab amore præsentis seculi velut a sua lapidisina separavit, & ad portandam Ecclesiæ fabricam erexit. Mercerus per septem columnas sapientiæ omnia, quibus ni- titur Sapientia, & per quæ docetur, vel præcipua ejusdem capita intelligit. Certum est, columnas vocari ad soliditatem cumprimis domus indican- dam, quamvis etiam pulchritudo ejusdem simul in- sinuetur, & quum Ecclesia sustentetur per Ver- bum, de quo præclare Chrysost. in 1. ad Tim. 3. ἡ ἀλήθειά ἐστι στύλος κὴ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἐκκλησίας veri- tas est columna & firmamentum Ecclesiæ, ideo re- ctissime Scripturæ Sacræ, quibus illa innititur fir- missime, intelliguntur, ut perfectionis numerus perfectionem S. literarum, quod abunde sufficiant ad sustentandam domum Ecclesiæ designet, & e verbo Dei cumprimis capita fidei præcipua ac fun- damentalia, quibus fidem ac domum Ecclesiæ, ipsam etiam salutem æternam inniti constat, indi- centur. Et quum verbum Dei, mediante sancto mi- nisterio, Ecclesiæ sustentandæ substernatur, inde columna Ecclesiæ etiam Doctores verbi dicuntur, non ratione sui, & per se, sed propter Verbum, per quod illa sustentatur, quod ab ipsis propagatur, custoditur, & Ecclesiæ fulciendæ ac sustentandæ substernitur: nec immerito ea ratione illi hic intel- liguntur. Quamvis enim nomine ancillarum, quæ emitti dicuntur, Verbi ministri significentur, nihil tamen obstat, quo minus eosdem etiam per colu- mnas intelligamus: siquidem utrumque munus præstent, ut præcones & nuncii emissi Ecclesiam convocantes, & congregantes, & ceu columnæ convocatam virtute Verbi divini portantes & su- stentantes, sed διακονικῶς ac ministerialiter, ut Ver- bi ea virtus sit propria, cujus ministerio funguntur: non κυρίως & principaliter; sic enim solum Deum, ac Sapientiam ipsam hypostaticam Filium Dei sustentare domum Ecclesiæ quis, nisi ab Anti- Christo, qui se pro Deo & Vicario Christi vendi- tat, dementatus ambigat?

## 9:6
Vers. 6. FORSAKE INFANCY AND LIVE. In the forsaking of stupidity, errors, and sins, the term from which, in the walking through the ways of understanding, the term to which of conversion is insinuated, and the consequent, or the fruit of it, is designated by the word of life, which is promised here to the faithful. For it is not a word of command, but of promise וַחְיוּ AND YOU SHALL LIVE. Cf. c. 4, 4. c. 7, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 6. RELINQVITE INFANTIAM ET VIVITE. In relictione stoliditatis, errorum & peccato- rum terminus a quo, in incessu per vias intelligen- tiæ terminus ad quem conversionis insinuatur, & consequens, vel fructus ejus voce vitæ designatur, quæ fidelibus hic promittitur. Non enim verbum est mandati, sed promissi וַחְיוּ ET VIVETIS. Conf. c. 4, 4. c. 7, 2.

## 9:7
Vers. 7. HE WHO TEACHES A SCOFFER, DOES AN INJURY TO HIMSELF. These things are advised for the sake of those INVITING, lest, to wit, they cast pearls before swine. Matt. 7, 6. For he who wishes to inform a scoffer exposes himself and his own things to laughter and mockery, nay, he brings upon himself a certain mark of imprudence Sir. 32, 6. But for the scoffer, there is at least a cause that he sins more gravely, while he strives to defend his sin, and in it hardens himself, disparages the one advising these things, murmurs against him, and mocks him.

Latin:

Vers. 7. QVI ERUDIT DERISOREM, IPSE INJURIAM SIBI FACIT. Hæc in gratiam INVITANTIUM monen- tur, ne sc. margaritam porcis projiciant. Matth. 7, 6. Qui enim derisorem informare vult, ipse se & sua risui & ludibrio exponit, imo imprudentiæ quandam sibi accersit notam Sir. 32, 6. Derisori au- tem saltim causa est, ut gravius peccet, dum pecca- tum suum tueri satagit, in eoque se obfirmat, hæc monenti detrahit, obmurmurat, eumque deridet.

## 9:8
Vers. 8. DO NOT REPROVE A SCOFFER) Clearly an impious one. Medicine is not to be applied to the desperate, says Hippocrates. See what is at Matt. 7, 6. Greg. M. lib. 8. Moral. c. 24. He is rendered worse by reproof, because he esteems the word of purity as if it were the dart of a dire striking. Whence, exasperated, he immediately rises into insults, and inquires what evils he may exaggerate against the life of the corrector.

Latin:

Vers. 8. NOLI ARGVERE DERISOREM) Plane im- pium. Desperatis non adhibendam medicinam, ait Hippo- crates. Vide quæ ad Matth. 7, 6. Gregor. M. l. 8. Moral. c. 24. Redargutione deterior redditur, quia quasi diræ percussionis æsti- mat jaculum puritatis verbum. Unde exasperatus protinus in contumelias surgit, & quæ mala exagge- ret, contra vitam correptoris, inquirit.

## 9:13
Vers. 13.

A FOOLISH AND CLAMOROUS WOMAN] Pleasure. More correctly, folly is said to be introduced here under the figure of a harlot, inasmuch as it is opposed to WISDOM, and embraces under itself not only pleasure, but also depraved doctrine and heresy, by which we are seduced no less than by pleasure Rom. 16, 18. whence these things are accepted by Jerome, Polychronius, Evagrius concerning FALSE WISDOM, which is diametrically opposed to true wisdom, which concerning pleasure Ambrose explains specifically, following Philo, in book 1 on Cain and Abel, chapter 4. She is called that WOMAN OF FOLLY, as if to say: She is folly itself personified and dressed in female attire, AND CLAMOROUS or tumultuous she is called, because from heresy and false doctrine, just as from pleasure, the greatest tumults arise; indeed, from them all things are tumults; they are the true and adequate causes of tumults. Nor perhaps does Mr. Dr. Geier judge unsuitably that Satan is described under the figure of a shameless and highly seductive harlot, just as, conversely, the Son of God had been represented under the countenance of a most chaste and most wealthy Queen, just as that male ὁ ἀντικείμενός or Antichrist is also produced under the figure of a harlot, Apoc. 1, 2.

AND FULL OF ALLUREMENTS, AND KNOWING NOTHING AT ALL.

In Hebrew, פתיות is governed by the word אשת, which occurs in the preceding hemistich: woman of folly, bringing about folly, or infatuating: knowing nothing at all, i.e., of truth and good: for what would stupidity know? The LXX interpreted the former word as 'lacking bread,' the latter as 'who does not know shame.' The Chaldean more correctly says 'does not know good,' the Syrian, 'does not know useful things.'

Latin:

Vers. 13.

MULIER STULTA ET CLAMOSA] Voluptas. Rectius insipientia hic sub mulieris meretri- cis figura introduci dicitur, utpote quæ opposita est SAPIENTIÆ, & sub se complectitur non vo- luptatem tantum, sed etiam pravam doctrinam & hæresin, a qua non minus quam voluptate seduci- mur Rom. 16, 18. unde de FALSA SAPIENTIA, quæ veræ sapientiæ e diametro opponitur, hæc ac- cipiunt Hieronym. Polychron. Evagr. quæ de volu- ptate fpeciatim explicat Ambrofius Philonem fequu- tus l. 1. de Cain & Abel c. 4. Vocatus autem illa MULIER STULTITIÆ, q. d. Est ipfa ftultitia perfonata, & habitu muliebri veftita, ET CLA- MOSA vel tumultuofa dicitur, quia ab hærefi, & falfà doctrinà, æque ut a voluptate tumultus ma- ximi oriuntur, imo ab illis omnes funt tumultus; illæ veræ & adæquatæ tumultuum caufæ funt. Neque forte inconcinne Dn. D. Geierus cenfet Sa- tanam fub Schemate fcorti impudici fummeque blan- dientis defcribi, ficuti e diverfo Filius Dei fub ami- co caftiffimæ ditiffimæque Reginæ vultu fuerat repræ- fentatus, quemadmodum fub meretricis quoque fchemate ὁ ἀντικείμενός ille mafculus vel Antichri- ftus producitur Apoc. 1, 2.

PLENAQVE ILLECEBRIS, ET NIHIL OMNINO SCIENS.

In Ebr. פתיות regitur a voce אשת, quæ in he- miftichio præcedente occurrit: mulier fatuitatis, fatuitatem inferens, vel infatuans: nihil quicquam fciens, veri fc. bonique: quid enim ftoliditas fciat? LXX. aliene priorem vocem indiga panis, pofte- riora quæ non novit pudorem interpretati funt. Re- ctius Chald. nefcit bonum, Syrus, nefcit utilia.

## 9:17
Verse 17.

STOLEN WATERS ARE SWEETER, AND HIDDEN BREAD IS MORE PLEASANT.

The foolish woman indeed imitates wisdom by inviting everyone, but this one to wine, that one to waters: because whatever the world or the flesh displays is watery, that is, insipid, juiceless, and cold: this one invites to her bread, that one to stolen or surreptitiously taken things, and to clandestine bread, to be eaten in secret: this one openly proposes her well-furnished table, that one insinuates that her table is hidden. For adulterers burn with the stolen lust of another's wife. Whence Clem. Alex. lib. 3. Paed. c. 12 calls stolen Venus 'sweet stolen water.' But whence that sweetness? Because the desire for stolen things is greater: For whatever is not permitted is more desired, as Jerome says in Hosea 13. However, that water is stolen, although in these places it is perhaps less sweet, in the hotter regions of Palestine, due to the lack of water, it is not so surprising that it seems sweet and desirable; which must also be held regarding stolen bread. Cf. Prov. 20, 17. Which indeed pertain not only to stolen Venus, but to every pleasure and secret desire. For we always strive for what is forbidden and desire what is denied.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

AQVÆ FURTIVÆ DULCIORES SUNT, ET PANIS ABSCONDITUS SVAVIOR.

Mulier ftulta imitatur quidem fapientiam, omnes invitando, fed hæc ad vinum, illa ad aquas: quia aqueum, id eft infipidurn, exuccum & frigi- dum eft, quicquid mundus aut caro oftentat: hæc ad panem fuum, illa ad furtiva vel furto fubtracta, & panem clandeftinum, in abfcondito edendum invitat: hæc menfam fuam bene inftructam palam proponit, illa fuam menfam occultam effe infinuat. Mœchi enim ardent furtiva libidine alienæ uxo- ris. Unde Clem. Alex. lib. 3. Pæd. c. 12. Dulcem furti aquam furtivam dicit Venerem. Unde autem illa dulcedo? quod furtivorum majus fit defide- rium: Quicquid enim non licet, magis defideratur, dicente Hieronymo in Of. 13. Aquam autem fur- to fubduci, etfi his in locis forte minus dulce fit, in calidioribus tamen Paleftinæ oris, ob defectum aquæ, fuave, & amabile videri, non adeo mirum; quod etiam de pane furtivo habendum. Conf. Prov. 20, 17. Quæ vero non folum ad Venerem fur- tivam, fed ad omnem voluptatem & cupiditatem clanculariam pertinent. Semper enim nitimur in vetitum cupimusque negata.

## 9:18
Verse 18.

AND SHE KNEW NOT THAT GIANTS ARE THERE)

רפאים rather signifies the lifeless in this place, and others. LXX: γηγενεῖς, earth-born: R. Levi and the Tigurine: mortals. Cf. c. 2, 18. It is absurd that some understand demons by giants. The other hemistich renders the sense: AND HER GUESTS ARE IN THE DEPTHS OF HELL. For, as Basil has it on the Holy Virgin: The way that leads to her (the harlot's) house tends straight to hell and the abyss of death: but he, meanwhile, blinded by luxury and given to flesh and gluttony, does not consider, etc. The things which the LXX add here in the Roman edition: 'But retreat, do not linger in the place, nor cast your eye upon her: for so you will pass by strange water: but abstain from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain, that you may live a long time, and years of life may be added to you,' are absent from the Hebrew text, as well as from the Latin Vulgate, and indeed even from the Greek Complutensian. Which, therefore, Cornelius a Lapide not undeservedly rejects.

THE SECOND AND SPECIAL PART OF THE BOOK OF PROVERBS.

SECTION I. EXHIBITING THE PROVERBS COMPILED BY SOLOMON HIMSELF.

THE PARABLES OF SOLOMON) Those which preceded are general exhortations to wisdom and its leader, piety. There follow now special precepts, for the most part by antitheses: because opposites compared among themselves shine more brightly.

It is not therefore denied that the former are Solomon's: but since those were general, and completed a whole discourse, it is now intimated that maxims and sententious sayings delivered by aphorisms follow.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

ET IGNORAVIT QVOD IBI SVNT GIGANTES)

רפאים potius exanimes fignificat hoc loco, & aliis. LXX. γηγενεῖς terrigenæ: R. Levi, & Tigur. mortales. Conf. c. 2, 18. Ineptum eft, quod per gi- gantes Dæmones intelligunt nonnulli. Senfum reddit alterum hemiftichium: ET IN PRO- FUNDIS INFERNI CONVIVÆ EJUS. Etenim, ut Bafil. habet de S. Virgin. Via quæ ad domum ejus (meretricis) ducit, recta ad infernum mortisque barathrum tendit: at ille interim luxu ob- tæcatus, carnique & gulæ deditus haud confiderat, &c. Quæ hic LXX. in Rom. edit. addunt: Sed refili, ne moreris in loco, neque injicias oculum tuum ad eam: ita enim transibis aquam alienam: Ab aqua autem aliena abftine te, & de fonte alieno ne biberis, ut lon- gum vivas tempus, adjiciantur etiam tibi anni vitæ, ab Ebræo textu abfunt, ut & Latina vulgata, imo & a Græca Complut. Quæ proinde non immerito reprobat Cornel. a Lap.

ALTERA ET SPECIALIS PARS LIBRI PROVERBIORUM.

SECTIO I. PROVERBIA A SALOMONE IPSO DIGESTA EXHIBENS.

PARABOLÆ SALOMONIS) Quæ præcefferunt ex- hortationes sunt generales ad sapientiam & ducem ejus pie- tatem. Sequuntur nunc præcepta specialia, pleraque per antitheta: quia opposita inter se comparata magis lu- cescunt.

Non ergo negatur, priora Salomonis esse: sed quum illa generalia fuerint, & orationem inte- gram absolverint, jam gnomas, & dicta sententiosa per aphorismos tradita sequi, innuitur.

## 10:1
ver. 1. A WISE SON MAKETH A GLAD FATHER; BUT A FOOLISH SON IS THE SORROW OF HIS MOTHER.

Because he had hitherto stirred up those whom he had undertaken to instruct toward wisdom under the name of sons, the wisest of Kings now begins his maxims to be delivered by antithesis from a comparison of the wise and the foolish son; that the former brings joy to his parents, the latter sorrow, so that he may intimate immediately at the beginning what fruit the wise and obedient, and what the foolish and disobedient, may expect from the observation or neglect of individual things. Under Father, however, mother is understood, and under mother, Father is understood at the same time. In the first place, therefore, he establishes this maxim, by which he warns parents to instruct their children in true wisdom, so that they may be a joy to them, not a sorrow. And since in this instruction justice excels toward Wisdom, he treats before all things of the just and the unjust or impious, inserting immediately sentences concerning wisdom, because without it justice cannot exist, whence also the wise man is everywhere called just and upright, but the foolish man unjust and wicked. He attributes joy to the Father, however, and sorrow to the mother, because Fathers educate children more severely, whence they are exhilarated, while mothers do so more gently, whence they themselves are the cause of sorrow through excessive indulgence. Furthermore, by wisdom is primarily understood that by which we are instructed through faith unto eternal salvation, 2 Tim. III, 15, which, as it is the fountain and spring of every virtue, so it can finally bring true joy: whereas those destitute of it, however much they may excel in worldly wisdom, are more a sorrow than a joy to faithful and pious parents. Conf. Jer. IX, 14. 1. Cor. 1, 21. Therefore rightly does Dn. D. Geier [say] that a fool is not so much one who labors under a natural weakness of judgment, as one who behaves himself altogether ineptly regarding heavenly things or the salvation of his soul, not striving to know them, nor solicitously pursuing the known way of salvation, but most foolishly contaminating himself with crimes, petulant, contumacious, and behaving himself before God, the angels, and the pious as equally fatuous as a man bereft of his senses or delirious. For with what spirit, with what eyes can parents look upon such a son as a future firebrand of hell?

Latin:

vers. 1. FILIUS SAPIENS LÆTIFICAT PATREM; FILIUS VERO STULTUS MOESTITIA EST MATRIS SUÆ.

QVia ad sapientiam hactenus quos informan- dos susceperat, sub nomine filiorum excitarat, jam gnomas suas per antithesin tradendas orditur Regum sapientissimus a comparatione filii sapientis & stolidi; quod ille Parentibus lætitiam, hic mœsti- tiam afferat, ut quem fructum sapiens, & obediens, quem stolidus & inobediens expectare e singula- rum observatione, vel neglectu habeat, initio sta- tim innuat. Sub Patre autem mater, & sub matre Pater simul intelligitur. Primo ergo loco hanc gnomen constituit, quo moneat parentes, ut ad veram sapientiam liberos instruant, ut gaudio ipsis sint, non mœrori. Et quum in hac informatione ad Sapientiam justitia præemineat, de justis & inju- stis vel impiis ante omnia agit, infertis subinde sen- tentiis de sapientia, quia sine illa esse nequit justitia, unde etiam passim sapiens justus, & probus, stultus vero injustus & improbus dicitur. Patri autem læti- tiam, matri mœstitiam tribuit, quia Patres severius educant liberos, unde exhilarantur, matres blan- dius, unde nimia indulgentia mœroris causa ipsæ sunt. Cæterum sapientia imprimis ea intelligitur, qua instruimur nos per fidem ad æternam salutem, 2. Tim. III, 15. quæ uti fons est & scaturigo omnis virtutis, ita veram demum afferre potest lætitiam: quum contra illa destituti, utcunque mundana pol- leant sapientia, fidelibus & piis parentibus magis mœrori sint, quam gaudio. Conf. Jer. IX, 14. 1. Cor. 1, 21. ideo recte Dn. D. Geier. quod stultus sit non tam qui imbecillitate judicii naturali laboret, quam qui circa cælestia, vel animæ salutem prorsus inepte se ge- rit, eadem nec cognoscere satagens, - nec cognitam salu- tis viam solicite premens, sed stolidissime sceleribus se contaminans, petulans, contumax, & coram Deo, angelis, piisque æque fatuum se gerens, quam homo mente captus aut delirans. Quo enim animo, quibus oculis intueri talem possunt filium parentes ceu futurum titionem ignis infernalis?

## 10:2
Vers. 2. TREASURES OF WICKEDNESS WILL PROFIT NOTHING, BUT JUSTICE WILL DELIVER FROM DEATH.

Here again by a Rhetorical aposiopesis, as they call it, [it is] to be supplied from the latter member: i.e., they will profit nothing for deliverance, viz., from death: whence the sense is clear, that they will profit nothing in the day of wrath, c. 11, 4. they will profit nothing in the other world, Matt. 16:26; Luke 12:20; Wisd. 5:8; nay, that they are harmful, because of the impiety with which they are acquired and amassed: for such negative statements affirm emphatically that to be of no use is to be harmful, 1 Tim. 6:9. Therefore, such treasures are to be gathered as are not harmful, do not bring death, but are useful and deliver from death, Matt. 6:20; 1 Tim. 6, 17. 19. This maxim is therefore to be understood concerning Evangelical righteousness, which is the best treasure, and alone is useful for life, alone delivers from death, Is. 45, 24. ch. 53, 11. Jer. 23, 6. Dan. 9, 24. Phil. 3, 9. namely, from death both temporal, so that it may be free from the curse itself, and at least a transition to true life may be made, Job 5, 24. and eternal, so that it may never be felt, Joh. 11, 26. Which Paraphrase of the Vinarieans is not disapproved by Mr. Dr. Geier, although he judges the opinion of those who take righteousness for beneficence not to be incongruous.

Latin:

Vers. 2. NIL PRODERUNT THESAURI IM- PIETATIS, JUSTITIA VERO LIBERABIT A MORTE.

Hic iterum per aposiopesin Rhetoricam, ut vo- cant, e membro posteriori prius supplendum: h. m. nil proderunt ad liberationem, sc. a morte: unde sensus patet, quod nil in die iræ prosint, c. 11, 4. nil pro- fint in altero seculo Matth. 16, 26. Luc. 12, 20. Sa- pient. 5, 8. imo quod obsint, ob impietatem, qua acquiruntur & congeruntur : nam negativæ tales emphatice affirmant, ut nil prodesse sit obesse, 1. Tim. 6, 9. Thesauri itaque tales colligendi, qui non obsint, non inferant mortem, sed prosint, & a morte liberent, Matth. 6, 20. 1. Tim. 6, 17. 19. De justitia ergo Evangelica hæc gnome accipienda, quæ est thesaurus optimus, ac sola ad vitam prodest, sola a morte liberat Es. 45, 24. c. 53, 11. Jer. 23, 6. Dan. 9, 24. Phil. 3, 9. a morte nempe tum tempo- rali, ut maledictione ipsa careat, saltemque transitus ad vitam veram fiat Job. 5, 24. tum æterna, ne un- quam sentiatur Joh. 11, 26. Quam Vinariensium Paraphrasin non reprobat Dn. D. Geierus, etsi non incongruam eorum judicet sententiam, qui justi- tiam pro beneficentia accipiunt.

## 10:3
Ver. 3. THE LORD WILL NOT AFFLICT THE SOUL OF THE RIGHTEOUS WITH FAMINE: BUT HE WILL SUBVERT THE SNARES OF THE WICKED.

In Hebrew: Jehovah will not allow the soul of the righteous to hunger: but the wickedness of the wicked, that is, the wicked who are depraved and perverse, he will unexpectedly and utterly subvert; such was the subversion of the Canaanites, Jos. 13, 5. and elsewhere, noted by the word הות. For there is an opposition between the righteous who is to be preserved in need, and the wicked who is to be subverted with unjustly acquired riches. And therefore Solomon now proceeds from eternal salvation to the temporal sustenance of the body, because the righteous are not to be forsaken, but sustained in need, whereas the wicked, even if rich, must not only eventually lack, but are to be utterly subverted. Ps. 34, 11. Although the righteous may sometimes lack for a time, yet not constantly, or at least not to their destruction, but for a salutary end, and so that a momentary lack may be followed by a more generous and perennial abundance, if not in this life, yet in the other, Luc. 6, 20. ch. 16, 25. Rev. 7, 16, 17. Ps. 17, 14. 15. Is. 65, 13. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NON AFFLIGET DOMINUS FA- ME ANIMAM JUSTI : ET INSIDIAS IM- PIORUM SUBVERTET.

In Ebr. Non sinet esurire Jehovah animam ju- sti : pravitatem autem impiorum, id est impios pra- vos & perversos insperato ac penitus subvertet ; qualis fuit subversio Cananæorum Jos. 13, 5. & alibi, voce הות notata. Oppositio enim est inter ju- stum in egestate conservandum, & impium cum divi- tiis injuste acquisitis subvertendum. Ideoque a salute æterna ad temporalem corporis sustentatio- nem jam progreditur Salomo, quod justi non de- serendi, sed sustentandi sint in egestate, impii ve- ro, etsi divites non modo carere tandem debeant, sed plane subvertendi sint. Ps. 34, 11. Etsi ad tem- pus quandoque etiam careant justi, non tamen constanter, vel certe non in perniciem ipsorum, sed fine salutari, & ut momentaneam carentiam se- quatur largior, & perennior abundantia, si non in hac, in altera tamen vita, Luc. 6, 20. c. 16, 25. Ap. 7, 16, 17. Ps. 17, 14. 15. Es. 65, 13. 14.

## 10:4
Ver. 4.

A SLACK HAND HAS WROUGHT POVERTY, BUT THE HAND OF THE STRONG PREPARES RICHES.

Now concerning the cause of poverty and the means of solid riches. Labor produces wealth, idleness poverty. Although we are sometimes reduced to poverty even through misfortunes, yet ordinarily, and in opposition to industry, poverty is deservedly said to be induced by idleness. ראש with the epenthesis of the letter א is also found in 2 Sam. 12, 1. 4. which is commonly written רש Poor. Compare with this maxim Prov. 12, 24. 27. ch. 19, 15. as also Gen. 3, 29. But those things which are added here in the Vulgate are alien: He who relies on lies, this one feeds on winds; the same one also follows flying birds: whence Cornelius is rash, when he professes that they once existed in the Hebrew and have Canonical authority, only because they are read in the Roman Latin edition in Clem. Alex. and August.: since they appear in no Hebrew Codex: nor even among the Chaldeans, or in the edition of the LXX. in the Complutensian, nor were they found in all Latin editions, as Cornelius himself admits. The allegation of one or another Father does not suffice for the demonstration of Canonical authority: for the maxims could have crept into the Greek and Latin Codices which they used. And the LXX of the Roman edition has that maxim, not in this place, but in the preceding chapter after v. 12, along with two other maxims equally alien: an evident sign of interpolation. But it coheres best with the former one concerning idleness and labor, which follows immediately after that inserted maxim in the source, for prudence in labor must be joined with industry, so that the cause may not be neglected.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

EGESTATEM OPERATA EST MANUS REMISSA, MANUS AUTEM FORTIUM DI- VITIAS PARAT.

Jam de causa inopiæ, & medio solidarum divitia- rum. Labor parit opes, otium inopiam. Etsi per infortunia etiam ad paupertatem redigamur quan- doque, ordinarie tamen, & in oppositione ad indu- striam paupertatem otio induci merito dicitur. ראש cum Epenthesi literæ א habetur etiam 2. Sam. 12, 1. 4. quod communiter scribitur רש Pauper. Conf. cum hac sentenria Prov. 12, 24. 27. c. 19, 15. ut & Gen. 3, 29. Aliena autem sunt, quæ adduntur hic in Vulgata : Qui nititur mendaciis, hic pascit ven- tos ; Idem autem ipse sequitur aves volantes : unde temerarius est Cornelius, cum olim in Ebræo ea exti- tisse, & Canonicam habere autoritatem profitetur, solum quia in Romana Latina editione apud Clem. Alex. & August. leguntur : Siquidem in nullo Co- dice Ebræo ea compareant : neque etiam apud Chaldæos, aut in editione LXX. Complutensi, nec in omnibus Latinis editionibus, fatente ipsomet Cornelio, reperta sint. Unius vel alterius Patris al- legatio non sufficit ad autoritatis Canonicæ demon- strationem : irrepsisse enim potuere sententiæ in Græcos, & Latinos Codices, quibus illi usi sunt. Et habent illam gnomen LXX. Rom. edit. non hoc loco, sed cap. præced. post v. 12. cum aliis etiam dua- bus gnomis æque alienis : evidenti νοθείας indicio. Optime autem cohæret priori de otio & labore, quæ proxime fine illa insititia in fonte sequitur senten- tia, cum industria enim conjuncta esse debet in la- bore prudentia, ut ne negligatur caussa.

## 10:5
Ver. 5. HE WHO GATHERS IN HARVEST IS A WISE SON: BUT HE WHO SLEEPS IN SUMMER IS A SON WHO CAUSES SHAME.

In Hebrew, in the former member there is summer instead of harvest, in the latter there is harvest instead of summer. They explain each other: for one must gather in summer, in the harvest. But under the name of summer and harvest, every opportune time is comprehended: e.g., that one must labor in youth, so that one may provide for old age. Compare Prov. 6, 6. But a SON WHO CAUSES SHAME or puts to shame, i.e., himself, or is said to be despised, because such a one sleeping is not only not wise himself, but also exposes himself to the contempt of others. Compare ch. 12, 4. ch. 14, 35. ch. 17, 2. ch. 19, 26. ch. 29, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 5. QUI CONGREGAT IN MESSE FILIUS SAPIENS EST: QUI AUTEM STERTIT ÆSTATE FILIUS CONFUNDENS.

In Ebr. in priori membro loco messis æstas, in posteriori loco æstatis messis est. Explicant illa se mutuo: nam in æstate colligendum, in messe. Sub æstatis autem messisque nomine tempus oportunum omne comprehenditur: v. g. laborandum esse in adolescentia, ut prospiciatur senectuti. Conf. Prov. 6, 6. FILIUS vero CONFUNDENS vel pudefaciens sc. semetipsum, vel despectus dicitur, quod stertens ejusmodi non modo non ipse sit sa- piens, sed etiam despectui sese aliis exponat. Conf. c. 12, 4. c. 14, 35. c. 17, 2. c. 19, 26. c. 29, 15.

## 10:6
CHAPTER X.

He alternates discourses concerning the wise and the foolish, and especially concerning the just and the impious, as regards their salvation, sustenance, reputation, mouth, tongue, life, hope, and fruits.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Alternat sermones de sapiente & stolido, & im- primis de justo & impio, quantum ad salu- tem, sustentationem, famam, os, linguam, vitam, spem, fructus eorum.

## 10:6
Ver. 6. THE BLESSING OF THE LORD IS UPON THE HEAD OF THE RIGHTEOUS: BUT INIQUITY COVERS THE MOUTH OF THE WICKED.

In Hebrew: Blessings are upon the head of the righteous, but violence will cover the mouth of the wicked: the opposition teaches that a violent punishment is understood: which covers the head and the face indicated by the name of the mouth. He now promises an all-encompassing blessing, both temporal and eternal, to the righteous: against the wicked he threatens that a curse will cover the face of the oppressed, Ps. 109, 17. But their mouth is said to be covered, according to the interpreter Cartwright, because violence or curses, which are inflicted by God upon the unwilling wicked, also concur, and so stun them that, deceived by the vain hope of prosperity, they have nothing to answer to those who reproach them, as if confused and oppressed by shame.

Latin:

Vers. 6. BENEDICTIO DOMINI SUPER CAPUT JUSTI: OS AUTEM IMPIORUM OPERIT INIQUITAS.

In Ebr. Benedictiones sunt super caput justi, os au- tem impiorum operiet violentia: Pœnam violentam intelligi oppositio docet: quæ caput & vultum no- mine oris indicatum operit. Omnigenam ergo be- nedictionem tum temporalem tum æternam justis jam promittit: maledictionem contra vultum op- pressorum obtecturam, impiis minatur, Pf. 109, 17. Os autem eorum obtegendum dicitur Cartwrighto interprete, quia violentia seu maledictiones, quæ in- vitis improbis a Deo inferuntur tum etiam concur- sant, & eos ita obstupefaciunt, ut vana spe prosperi- tatis falsi tanquam confusi, & pudore oppressi quid exprobantibus respondeant, non habeant.

## 10:7
Ver. 7. THE MEMORY OF THE RIGHTEOUS IS WITH PRAISES: BUT THE NAME OF THE WICKED SHALL ROT.) A frequent maxim in the mouth of the Hebrews, which they write abbreviated thus: ז. ל. ש.

In Hebrew: The memory of the just is for a blessing: concerning a good reputation even after death. The LXX also render it μετ' εγκωμι's. For blessing is sometimes taken for praise or honor, 2 Sam. 8, 14. Job 31, 20. Ps. 62, 5. And the opposition teaches this: because rottenness indicates a reputation not praiseworthy, but rotten, and joined with a stench, and therefore detestable. From rottenness is understood corruption, from corruption a stench, from a stench abomination, and infamy, and the detestation of the infamous. Cf. Mark 2, 62. For morals have their colors, they have also their odors. Color in the conscience: odor in reputation, as Bernard says in homily LXXI on the Song of Songs.

Latin:

Vers. 7. MEMORIA JVSTI CVM LAVDIBVS: ET NOMEN IMPIORVM PVTRESCET.) Frequens in ore Hebræorum sententia, quod breviatum sic scribunt ז. ל. ש.

In Ebr. Memoria justi in benedictione: de bona fama etiam post mortem. LXX. etiam reddunt μετ' εγκωμι's. Benedictio enim pro encomio vel ho- nore quandoque accipitur 2. Sam. 8, 14. Job. 31, 20. Pf. 62, 5. idque oppositio docet: quia putredo famam non laudabilem, sed putridam, & cum fœtore con- junctam, adeoque detestandam indicat. Ex putredi- ne intelligitur corruptio, ex corruptione fœtor, ex fœtore abominatio, & infamia, infamisque detesta- tio. Conf. Marc. 2, 62. Habent enim mores suos colo- res, habent & odores. Colorem in conscientia: odorem in fama, dicente Bernhardo hom. LXXI. in Cant.

## 10:8
Vers. 8. THE WISE IN HEART RECEIVES COMMANDMENTS: BUT THE FOOLISH SHALL BE BEATEN WITH LIPS.

From the Hebrew and the collation of both opposites, this sense emerges: The wise in heart, or he to whom the heart is wise, and who manifests by mouth and lips the wisdom lying hidden in the heart, will receive (divine and salutary) commandments more and more, and therefore will not fall, but will be saved: But the foolish in lips (who betrays the folly of the heart by speech) will altogether fall. Thus the word ילבט is used in Hos. 4, 14. Solomon therefore pursues the properties and adjuncts of the just, who alone are wise in heart (as the wicked truly are foolish, Ps. 14, 1) and strive for integrity, nor do they deprave their ways, and therefore they walk with trust, or confidently, not fearing destruction v. 9. They also abstain from the gestures and speeches of the wicked and foolish, who wink with the eye and betray themselves with their lips, bringing grief and destruction to themselves no less than to others, and they take the greatest care for themselves, v. 10, whence the mouth of the just is a vein and fountain of life, when on the contrary the mouth of the wicked covers them with violence, who offer an ear to them: these also, burning with hatred, stir up strifes: while those, on the contrary, covering all the transgressions of their neighbor with sincere charity, and abhorring strifes v. 12, since wisdom is found in the lips of the wise, but he who is lacking in heart (the foolish) procures a rod for his back with his lips, or punishment and penalty, v. 13. Let the wise store up and cherish saving knowledge in their heart, and bring it forth with their mouth: But the foolish (lacking a heart and destitute of wisdom) hasten destruction for themselves and others with their mouth or their words v. 14. and therefore the wise and the just can walk CONFIDENTLY (which he had said above) the bodily riches of the rich are as a city of his strength, while the poverty of the poor is mere consternation to them; how much more will the wise be able to rely on their spiritual riches, to the wicked destitute of which nothing remains but consternation, v. 15. since the work of the wise and the just is for life (terminatively, not meritoriously Rom. 6, 22.), but the produce or fruit of the impious is for sin and death (as again Rom. 6, 21. Apostle: where, however, he teaches that the principle of merit intervenes v. 23.) he who keeps saving correction according to Solomon, keeps the path to life, but he who rejects reproof, strays from the path of life v. 17. Solomon discourses primarily about the produce of the lips of the impious: that lying lips of the foolish cover hatred: who nevertheless sometimes betray themselves as foolish, while they make or utter detraction v. 18. and since in a multitude of words transgression is not lacking, he warns that everyone should restrain his lips, which he teaches is the mark of those who understand v. 19. and thus he implies that those who are talkative or loquacious are not understanding, but foolish: and just as the tongue no less than the heart of the just is as choice silver, that is, by Metonymy speeches of the tongue approved, indicators of a prudent heart, are excellent, so the heart and speeches of the impious are to be held as nothing, כמעט for a little, or a thing of that kind, which is of no value v. 20. as the lips of the just feed many with doctrine and information, whether public or private Jer. 3, 15. Ps. 78, 70. Heb. 10, 24. Jas. 5, 20. so that they may be delivered from death: so the foolish, lacking justice that avails before God, and destitute of the acknowledgment of the Messiah, 1 Cor. 1, 30. not only cannot provide saving information, because they lack a heart, but they themselves are also deprived of salvation, and are subject to death, because of the defect of heart and true wisdom and justice v. 21. For the blessing of the Lord alone makes rich in that blessed one Eph. 1, 3. 7. 1 Cor. 1, 5. the faithful, and the just: nor does (Jehovah) add sorrow or anxious labor to it (the blessing) v. 22. so that we have need to contribute some ἐπιβάλλον μέρος of ours, our laborious or painful works to it: Jer. 9, 23. 1 Cor. 1, 30. 31. Gal. 6, 14, Eph. 2, 6. seqq. just as the foolish are persuaded, relying on their own works: for here too there is a certain tacit opposition of the truly wise and faithful, and the foolish and unfaithful, which is observed in these verses.

Furthermore, the fruits and consequences of both the wicked and the just are subjected κατ᾿ ἀντίθεσιν: that to the fool indeed it seems to be an abomination to do, but a man of understanding not only abhors it, but heavenly wisdom is his sole concern v. 23. whence it happens at length to the impious, what he fears, but to the just God gives whatever they desire, v. 24. and as the whirlwind passes, so the impious must pass quickly and without any trace left: but for the just there is an everlasting foundation, as those who rely in true faith on God alone as an immovable Rock, v. 25. What follows in v. 26. concerning the sluggard, who harms those who send him, no differently than vinegar to the teeth, smoke to the eyes, is to be understood concerning the lazy and slothful or negligent in perceiving and caring for those things which make for the salvation of the soul, concerning those lazy in intellect or the rude and stupid: which meanings of the word עָצֵל are assigned by Schindler in Lex. Pentagl. who not only harm themselves, but also others, who use their services: to which sense the LXX and the Syrian in some way approach: As sour grapes are harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes: So is iniquity to those who use it. Solomon therefore proceeds in recounting the fruits of piety, κατ’ ἀντίθεσιν of the impious, v. 27. The fear of Jehovah makes for μακροβιότητα, adds days: but the years of the impious are shortened (Cf. Prov. 3, 2. c. 4, 10. Ps. 34, 13. Lev. 26, 25. Deut. 4, 25. Ps. 55, 24.) The expectation of the just is joy, but the hope of the impious will perish v. 28. The way of the Lord is strength to the upright, and terror to those who work iniquity v. 29. The just will not be moved forever: but the impious will not dwell in the land, v. 30. Finally, some things are also brought forward concerning the fruits of the mouth of the just and the impious v. 31. The mouth of the just will bring forth wisdom like a tree or fertile land, and it will not be cut down, but will always germinate and be guarded: but the tongue of perversities, like a pestilent tree, will be cut down: and v. 32. the lips of the just know what is well-pleasing (to the Lord) (they know how to propose it rightly) but the mouth of the impious delivers nothing but perverse things, or can bring forth nothing else.

Latin:

Vers. 8. SAPIENS CORDE PRÆCEPTA SUSCIPIT: STULTUS CÆDITUR LABIIS.

Ex Ebr. & collatione utriusque ἀντιθέτε hic sen- sus emergit: Sapiens corde, vel cui cor sapiens est, quique ore & labiis Sapientiam in corde latentem manifestat, præcepta (divina & salutaria) magis ma- gisque suscipiet, ideoque non corruet, sed servabitur: Stultus autem labiis (qui sermone stultitiam cordis prodit) omnino corruet. Ita verbum ילבט adhibetur Hos. 4, 14. Justorum ergo proprietates & adjuncta persequitur Salomo, qui soli sapientes sunt corde (uti improbi vere desipiunt Pf. 14, 1.) & integritati student, nec depravant vias suas, ideoque cum fidu- cia, seu confidenter ambulant, non metuentes contri- tionem v. 9. a gestibus etiam, ac sermonibus impro- borum & stolidorum, qui oculo annuunt, & labiis se produnt, sibi non minus quam aliis afferentes dolorem, & interitum, abstinent, sibique maxime cavent, v. 10, unde vena & scaturigo vitæ os justi, quum contra os impiorum violentia operiat eos, qui ipsis aurem præbent: hi etiam odio flagrantes rixas suscitent: Illis contra sincera charitate univer- sas prævaricationes proximi operientibus, & a rixis abhorrentibus v. 12. fiquidem in labiis sapientis in- veniatur sapientia, ille autem qui corde indigett, (sto- lidus) labiis suis conciliet virgam in dorso suo, seu pœnam & fupplicium, v. 13. sapientes condant & fo- veant in corde scientiam salutarem, eamque ore pro- mant: Stulti autem (corde indigentes & destituti sapienti) contritionem ore vel verbis suis sibi aliisque accelerent v. 14. ideoque CONFIDENTER (quod supra dixerat) ambulare possunt Sapientes & justi, non item insipientes, & improbi: nam si divitiæ corporales divitis sunt ut urbs fortitudinis ejus, cum egestas pauperum mera ipsis sit consternatio; quanto magis niti poterunt sapientes spiritualibus divitiis suis, quibus destitutis improbis nihil superest ni- si consternatio, v. 15. siquidem opus sapientis & ju- sti sit ad vitam (terminative, non meritorie Rom. 6, 22.) proventus vero vel fructus impii sit ad pecca- tum & mortem (ut iterum Rom. 6, 21. Apostolus: ubi tamen meriti rationem intervenire docet v. 23.) qui salutarem correctionem custodit secundum Salomonem, custodit semitam ad vitam, qui vero increpationem respuit, aberrat a vitæ semita v. 17. De proventu imprimis labiorum impii disserit Sa- lomo: quod odium operiant labia mendacia stolido- rum: qui tamen se produnt stolidos quandoque, dum faciunt vel proferunt detractionem v.18. & quum in multitudine verborum non desit prævaricatio, mo- net, ut coerceat quisque labia sua, quod intelligentium esse docet v. 19. adeoque non intelligentes, sed stultos esse τοὺς πολυλόγους vel multiloquos innuit: & uti lingua non minus quam cor justi velut argen- tum selectum est, hoc est, per Metonym. sermones lingua probati, cordis prudentis indices, præstan- tes sunt, sic cor & sermones impiorum nihili habendi, כמעט pro pauxillo, vel re ejusmodi, quæ nullius serme est pretii v. 20. uti labia justi multos pascunt doctrina & informatione seu publica seu privata Jer. 3, 15. Ps. 78, 70. Ebr. 10, 24. Jac. 5, 20. ut a morte liberentur: ita stulti justitia coram Deo valente ca- rentes, & agnitione Messiæ destituti, 1. Cor. 1, 30. non solum non possunt salutarem informationem præstare, quia corde carent, sed ipsi etiam salute privantur, & morti obnoxii sunt, ob defectum cordis & veræ sapientiæ ac justitiæ v. 21. Nam sola benedictio Domini in benedicto illo ditat Eph. 1, 3. 7. 1.Cor. 1, 5. fideles, & justos: nec apponit (Jehovah) do- lorem vel laborem anxium ei (benedictioni) v. 22. ut nostrum quoddam ἐπιβάλλον μέρος, nostra la- boriosa aut dolososa opera ad id conferre opus ha- beamus: Jer. 9, 23. 1. Cor. 1, 30. 31. Gal. 6, 14, Eph. 2, 6. seqq. quemadmodum stolidi persuasi sunt, suis ope- ribus nitentes: nam & hic tacita quædam opposi- tio est vere sapientum & fidelium, ac stultorum & infidelium, quæ in hisce versibus observata.

Porro ulterius fructus & consequentia tum im- proborum tum justorum subjiciuntur κατ᾿ ἀντίθε- σιν: quod stulto quidem veluti visus sit abominatio- nem facere, vir autem intelligentiæ non modo ab- horreat ab eo, sed curæ ei unicæ sit cælestis sapientia v. 23. unde impio evenit tandem, quod timet, justis autem donat Deus quicquid desiderant, v. 24. & ut transit turbo, sic celeriter & sine ullo relicto vesti- gio transire oportet impium: justis autem est funda- mentum perpetuum, utpote qui solo Deo ceu Petræ immobili vera fide innituntur, v. 25. Quod vers. 26. sequitur de pigro, qui officiat mittentibus eum, non secus atque acetum dentibus, fumus oculis nocet, de pigris & segnibus vel negligentibus in iis perci- piendis & curandis, quæ ad salutem animæ faciunt, de pigris ingenio vel de rudibus & stupidis acci- piendum: quæ vocis עָצֵל significata assignantur a Schindlero in Lex. Pentagl. qui non modo sibi no- cent, sed & aliis, qui opera eorum utuntur: cui sen- sui LXX. & Syrus quodammodo accedunt: Sicu uva acerba dentibus noxia est & fumus oculis : Sic iniquitas his qui ea utuntur. Pergit itaque Salomo in fructibus pietatis, κατ’ ἀντίθεσιν impiorum, recen- sendis, v. 27. Timor Jehova facit ad μακροβιότητα, apponit dies : anni autem impiorum abbreviantur (Conf. Prov. 3, 2. c. 4, 10. Pf. 34, 13. Levit. 26, 25. Deut. 4, 25. Pf. 55, 24.) Expectatio justorum est læti- tia, at spes impiorum peribit v. 28. robur est integro via Domini, & pavor operantibus iniquitatem v. 29. justus in seculum non commovebitur : impii autem non habitabunt in terra, v. 30. Denique de fructibus oris justorum & improborum etiam nonnulla addu- cuntur v. 31. Os justi proferet instar arboris vel ter- ræ fœcundæ sapientiam, neque succidetur, sed ger- minabit semper ac custodietur : lingua autem per- versitatum, ceu arbor pestilens succidetur : & v. 32. labia justi cognoscunt quod beneplacitum (Domino) est (sciunt illud dextre proponere) at os impiorum nil nisi perversa tradit, aut proferre potest.

## 10:12
Vers. 12.

LOVE COVERS ALL TRANSGRESSIONS) It forgives whatever can be forgiven, 1 Pet. 4, 8. 1 Cor. 13, 7.

Therefore our love is not established as the cause of the forgiveness of sins before God, but a certain proper affection of our love is designated in covering the transgressions of a neighbor: for as hatred uncovers sins, not its own, but a neighbor's: stirs up quarrels not with itself but with those hated, so love of a neighbor covers transgressions, not its own, but those of him whom it sincerely loves. Just as hatred covers no transgressions, but reveals them, nay, where there are none, it invents them, and thus knows how to stir up nothing but quarrels, so love not only extremely detests quarrels, but also hides even great and many transgressions and perversities, and labors to cultivate peace, as the learned Dr. Geier rightly explains, composing that antithesis between them, pitting the Cadmean brothers the Jesuits against each other: as for instance on one side Salazar, who says this is the common exposition, and observes that it is approved by Jansenius, Rudolph, Hugo, Cajetan and others, and that the passage is not to be taken concerning sins of guilt in general 1. 1 Pet. 4:8. Where this maxim is cited, it teaches, but concerning injuries, which provide the causes and harvest of contentions and quarrels; and on the other side Salmeron, Lorinus, Tirinus, who snatch this passage toward purification before God: as if charity covers our sins in divine judgment; of which there is clearly no discussion here, but it is taught what kind of people the righteous should show themselves toward their neighbors in forgiving their injuries. Cf. Prov. 17:9, Matt. 19:22, 1 Cor. 13:7, Gal. 6:2, Jas. 5:20. Which sense Lorinus himself acknowledges to have been handed down by Chrysostom, Homily 5 on the Acts of the Apostles; Ambrose, Homily 16 on Ps. 118; Augustine, Book 1 on Baptism, ch. 17; Bernard, Epistle 7; the Council of Lérida, ch. 7; Lyranus on this passage. Just as hatred, he says, through anger manifests the defects of others, so charity conceals them, unless fraternal correction requires otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

VNIVERSA DELICTA OPERIT CHARITAS) Con- donat quicquid condonari potest, 1. Pet. 4, 8. 1. Cor. 13, 7.

Non ergo charitas nostra causa constituitur con- donationis peccatorum coram Deo, sed propria quæ- dam charitatis nostræ affectio designatur in ope- riendis delictis proximi : ut enim odium retegit pec- cata non sua, sed proximi : suscitat rixas non secum ipso sed cum exosis, sic amor proximi operit delicta, non sua, sed ejus, quem sincere diligit. Sicut odium delicta nulla tegit, sed revelat, imo ubi nulla sunt, fingit, atque sic nil nisi rixas excitare novit, ita cha- ritas rixas non modo extreme detestatur, sed delicta etiam ac prævaricationes grandes, atque multas ce- lat, pacemque colere laborat, ut recte ἀντίθεσιν illa inter se componens explicat Dn. D. Geierus, com- mittens h. l. cadmæos fratres Jesuitas inter sese : ut- pote ab una parte Salazarum, qui communem hanc expositionem dicit, & Jansenio, Rudolpho, Hugoni, Ca- jetano aliisque eam probari observat, nec de delictis culpæ in universum accipiendum esse locum 1. Petr. 4, 8. ubi hæc gnome citatur, docet, sed de injuriis, quæ contentionum & jurgiorum causas, & segetem subministrant ; & ab altera parte Salmeronem, Lori- num, Tirinum, qui hunc locum ad purificationem coram Deo abripiunt : quasi charitas tegat nostra peccata in judicio divino ; de quo hic plane non agitur, sed quales se justi præbeant erga proximos in condonandis ipsorum injuriis docetur. Conf. Prov. 17, 9. Matth. 19, 22. 1. Cor. 13, 7. Gal. 6, 2. Jac. 5, 20. Quem sensum Lorinus ipse agnoscit traditum esse a Chrysost. hom. V. in Act. Apost. Ambros. hom. 16. in Pf. 118. August. l. 1. de Bapt. c. 17. Bernardo Epist. 7. Concilio Ilerdensi c. 7. Lyranus in h. l. Sicut odium, inquit, per iram manifestat defectus aliorum, sic charitas celat, nisi quantum correctio fraterna re- quirit.

## 10:25
Verse 25.

BUT THE RIGHTEOUS IS AS AN EVERLASTING FOUNDATION) Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος, θεμέλιος αἰώνιος. Maimonides understands it as the foundation of the world, and says the world stands because of the righteous.

Some, with Piscator, explain it: To the righteous, indeed, there is an everlasting foundation, with the dative sign ל added. Cf. Matt. 7:24. It can, however, be said that the righteous is as the foundation of the age, or everlasting (in a metaphorical sense) because he is so immovable, he does not waver: just as, on the contrary, the wicked is like a passing whirlwind, and easily vanishes, even if he causes no disturbances in the state or the Church, he nevertheless passes away suddenly, so that he leaves no trace behind him. Ps. 37:35, Ps. 33:19.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

JVSTVS AVTEM QVASI FVNDAMENTVM SEM- PITERNVM) Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion : ὁ δὲ δί- καιος, θεμέλιος αἰώνιος. Maimonides intelligit fundamen- tum mundi, & dicit mundum stare ob justos.

Nonnulli cum Piscatore exponunt : Justo vero est fundamentum perpetuum, nota Dativi ל addita. Conf. Matth. 7, 24. Dici tamen potest justum esse velut fundamentum seculi, vel perpetuum (sensu metaphorico) quod ita immobilis sit, non vacillet : quemadmodum contra impius est sicut turbo tran- siens, ac facile evanescit, etsi nullas turbas det in po- litia, vel Ecclesia, subito tamen transit, ut nullum etiam post se relinquat vestigium Psal. 37, 35. Psal. 33, 19.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

Again it contains various antitheses concerning the just and the unjust, regarding their business, mind, success, end, applause, fruit, blessing, and retribution.

Ver. 1.

A DECEITFUL BALANCE IS AN ABOMINATION BEFORE THE LORD, AND A JUST WEIGHT IS HIS WILL) Similar things below XX, 10. and 23. in one species every kind of injustice is forbidden. For all injustice is ἀνισότης (inequality).

From the tongue of the just it proceeds to works and the justice necessary in contracts: and to the perversity of the tongue it subjoins the perversity of work or of hands, of those deceiving their neighbor with a deceitful weight and measure: A balance of deceit or a deceitful one is an abomination to the Lord, or extremely adverse to God and itself as an abomination in the abstract: See Lev. 19, 35. Deut. 25, 13. Prov. 20, 13. Ezech. 45, 10. Am. 8, 3. Mich. 6, 11. But on the contrary a just weight is his will, i.e., of God. A stone is used for a weight, which was accustomed to be used in weighing in the places already cited from Lev. Deut. Prov. and Mich. Ambrose, concerning the weighing of words, explains how this gnome does not ill agree with the former. Let everyone, he says in book 7, Epist. 44 to Constantius, weigh his own words, not with fraud and deceit. A fallacious and reprobate balance before God: I do not mean that balance which weighs another's merchandise, and indeed in cheap things fallacy is rarely found; but the balance of words itself before God is execrable, which pretends the weight of sober gravity, and subjoins the wiles of fraudulence. This God condemns most of all, if anyone deceives his neighbor with the kindness of promises, and oppresses the one who has been impoverished by deceitful iniquity, profiting nothing for himself by the arts of his cunning.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Iterum varias antitheses habet de justis & in- justis, qua eorum negotiationem, animum, successum, exitum, applausum, fructum, be- nedictionem, & retributionem.

Vers. 1.

STATERA DOLOSA ABOMINATIO EST APVD DOMINVM, ET PONDVS ÆQVVM VOLVNTAS EJVS) Similia infra XX, 10. & 23. in una specie omne genus injustitiæ vetatur. Omnis enim injustitia ἀνισότης.

A Lingua justorum progreditur ad opera & ju- stitiam in contractibus necessariam: ac perversitati linguæ subjungit operis vel manuum perversitatem, doloso pondere ac mensura proximum decipien- tium: Statera doli vel dolosa abominatio Domino, vel extreme Deo adversa & ipsa velut abominatio in abstracto: Vid. Lev. 19, 35. Deut. 25, 13. Prov. 20, 13. Ezech. 45, 10. Am, 8, 3. Mich. 6, 11. At ex adverso pondus æquum voluntas ejus, Dei sc. Lapis pro pon- dere usurpatur, qui in ponderando adhiberi solebat locis jam citatis e Lev. Deut. Prov. & Mich. Am- brosius de ponderandis sermonibus explicat, quo pacto hæc gnome prioribus non male congruit. Ponderet, inquit l. 7. Epist. 44. ad Constant. unus- quisque sermones suos, non cum fraude & dolo. Statera fallax & improbabilis apud Deum: non illam state- ram dico, quæ mercem appendit alienam, & in vili- bus quidem rebus raro constat fallacia; sed statera verborum ipsa apud Deum est execrabilis, quæ præ- tendit pondus gravitatis sobriæ, & subnectit versutias fraudulentiæ. Hoc maxime condemnat Deus, si de- cipiat aliquis proximum suum promissorum benigni- tate, & subdola iniquitate defœneratum opprimat, nihil sibi profuturus astutiæ suæ artibus.

## 11:2
Ver. 2.

WHERE THERE SHALL BE PRIDE, THERE SHALL BE ALSO CONTUMELY: BUT WHERE THERE IS HUMILITY, THERE ALSO IS WISDOM.

In the mind of the just, pride does not dwell, but humility, and therefore even if he is affected by contumely, he is little affected, because he thinks humbly of himself and is truly wise: and therefore he is honored, he is not moved by contumely; but the proud man by presumption and pride brings upon himself the contempt of others, and contumely, nor is he to be considered wise, but foolish because of that elation of mind. Just as true humility is wisdom, so pride is mere foolishness. St. Augustine in Matthew, sermon X. You wish to be great, he says, begin from the least. You are thinking of constructing a great building of loftiness, think first of the foundation of humility.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

UBI FUERIT SUPERBIA, IBI ERIT ET CONTUMELIA: UBI AUTEM EST HUMI- LITAS, IBI ET SAPIENTIA.

In animo justi non superbia habitat, sed humili- tas, ideoque etiamsi contumelia afficiatur, parum afficitur, quia humiliter ipse de se sentit vereque sa- piens est: atque ideo honoratur, non commove- tur contumelia; at superbus sibi per præsumtio- nem & superbiam ipse accersit contemtum alio- rum, & contumeliam, nec sapiens, sed stolidus ob illam elationem animi censendus est. Sicut humi- litas vera est sapientia, ita superbia mera est infi- pientia. S. August. in Matth. serm. X. Magnus, in- quit, esse vis, a minimo incipe. Cogitas magnam fa- bricam constituere celsitudinis, de fundamento prius cogita humilitatis.

## 11:3
Ver. 3. THE SIMPLICITY OF THE JUST SHALL DIRECT THEM: AND THE SUPPLANTING OF THE PERVERSE SHALL DESTROY THEM.

The proper affection of the just is simplicity; because they are devoid of hypocrisy and fraud, and strive for integrity and true sincerity. The LXX render it perfection, which is also sometimes opposed to hypocrisy and deceit. Whence such just ones are directed by God, who loves simplicity and sincerity: they have success by their integrity; they are not destroyed; but the perverse, given to the supplantings of others, to deceits, and to frauds, destroy themselves, Syr. 27, 28. the word סלף is said from perverting Exod. 23, 8. Prov. 19, 3. But the treacherous are the broken and rebellious, who are opposed to the upright, just as perversity is to integrity without hypocrisy. The simple, says Jerome, Ep. to Pammachius, are safe among sorrows.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SIMPLICITAS JUSTORUM DIRI- GET EOS: ET SUPPLANTATIO PERVER- SORUM VASTABIT ILLOS.

Justorum propria affectio est simplicitas; quod hypocriseos & fraudis expertes sint, & integritati veræque sinceritati studeant. LXX. reddunt perfe- ctionem, quæ etiam τῇ ὑποκρίσει, & dolo quandoque opponitur. Unde justi tales diriguntur a Deo, qui simplicitatem & sinceritatem amat: successus ha- bent integritate sua; non vastantur; perversi autem supplantationibus aliorum, dolis, & fraudibus de- diti semetipsos vastant, Syr. 27, 28. vox סלף a per- vertendo dicitur Exod. 23, 8. Prov. 19, 3. בגדים vero sunt præfracti, & rebelles, qui rectis opponuntur, uti perversitas integritati ἀνυποκρίτῳ. Simplices, ait Hieron. Ep. ad Pammach. tuti sunt inter dolores.

## 11:4
Ver. 4.

RICHES WILL NOT PROFIT IN THE DAY OF WRATH: BUT RIGHTEOUSNESS SHALL DELIVER FROM DEATH.

The fruits of righteousness are now being recounted, κατ᾿ ἀντίθεσιν, then 1. regarding the righteous themselves: (1.) that it delivers from death, whereas on the contrary, for the unfaithful and perverse, riches can profit nothing in the day of wrath, nor are they themselves delivered from death, being destitute of faith and righteousness, Ps. 83, 49. Ez. 7, 19. Zeph. 1, 18. Job 3, 18. 36. (2.) that righteousness directs the way of the simple, so that he does not fall, but remains in the way of God's commandments, and attains the goal; whereas on the contrary, the wicked must necessarily fall by their own impiety v. 5. (3.) that the righteousness of the upright delivers them, to whatever snares or dangers they may be exposed, especially from eternal condemnation; but the iniquitous are caught in their own snares, Job 5, 13. indeed, when the wicked man is dead, there is no further hope, and the expectation of the wicked (or rather the iniquitous) perishes, and so they must perish eternally: and when the righteous is delivered from distress or misery, the wicked is to be handed over in his stead, or is forced to undergo temporal and eternal distress in his place because of his impiety: then 2. regarding others: that the wicked hypocrite deceives his friend with his mouth, or corrupts him with speech, as much as lies in him; but the righteous are delivered by their knowledge, so that they are not deceived, and can profit others with counsel; so that they themselves also may be rescued, and not only will they not corrupt with their mouth, but they will not be corrupted by others, and they provide by their knowledge that others may not be corrupted, v. 9. and furthermore, that the goods of the righteous redound not only to private individuals, but to the good of the entire Republic: the pursuits of the wicked do harm: In the goods of the righteous (which God grants to them, especially the goods of soul and body), says Solomon, the city shall exult, or rather rejoice, and in the destruction of the wicked there shall be praise, or exultation: there shall be no συμπάθεια, or commiseration. The reason is added v. 11. By the blessing of the righteous the city shall be exalted, because they will bless it, they will pray for it, and they will obtain glory and exaltation for it by their prayers, and it will not be exalted by the mouth of the wicked, by perverse speeches, against the first and second table, but it will be subverted, Eccl. 28, 16. For the wicked is so far from being concerned for others that he even despises his friends, being senseless and lacking heart: but the righteous, as a prudent man, or a man of knowledge, does not despise others, but rather remains modestly silent, out of true humility and love for his neighbor, v. 12. As the wicked walks fraudulently, so he reveals secrets to the fraud and ruin of his neighbor: but the righteous, as one who is sincere and of a faithful spirit, conceals what is entrusted by a friend, v. 13. Compare c. 20, 19. c. 25, 9. These things look to the benefits which redound from the righteous to his neighbor: now as to those which redound to the Republic. the knowledge or wisdom of the righteous is hinted to profit it much v. 11: where there is no governor, i.e., wise and just, for he who is not such is to be held as nothing, (in the Hebrew it is, where there shall be no counsels, less correctly Grotius, without a driver) the people shall fall: but where there are many counsels, which have a place only among the wise and righteous, for wisdom without righteousness is cunning rather than wisdom, the safety of the Republic flourishes. Safety, he says, or preservation (of the Republic or the people) is in the multitude of counselors, who are such not only in title, but in reality, who watch not for their own interests, but for public uses. Finally, as to those things which concern the righteous and prudent themselves: they avoid the snares of suretyship, so that they may be secure. For he is crushed with destruction when he has pledged his faith for a stranger, as it is in the Hebrew, but he who hates hands that stipulate rash suretyship, acts tranquilly.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NON PRODERUNT DIVITIÆ IN DIE ULTIONIS: JUSTITIA AUTEM LIBERA- BIT A MORTE.

Fructus jam recensentur justitiæ, κατ᾿ ἀντίθεσιν, tum 1. quoad justos ipsos: (1.) quod liberet a morte, quum ex adverso infidelibus, & perversis nihil prodesse queant divitiæ in die ultionis, nec a morte liberentur ipsi, utpote fide ac justitia destituti, Ps. 83, 49. Ez. 7, 19. Zeph. 1, 18. Job. 3, 18. 36. (2.) quod viam simplicis dirigat justitia ejus, ne corruat, sed in via mandatorum Dei maneat, ac metam assequatur; quum contra impii sua impietate corruere necessum habeant v. 5. (3.) quod justitia rectorum liberet eos, quibuscunque exponantur insidiis, aut periculis, imprimis a condemnatione æterna; iniqui autem insidiis suis capiantur, Job. 5, 13. imo mortuo homine impio nulla ultra spes sit, & expectatio solicetorum (vel potius iniquorum) pereat, adeoque æternum ipsis pereundum sit: & quum liberetur justus de angustia vel miseria, impius pro eo tradendus sit, seu ejus loco angustias temporales & æternas subire cogatur ob impietatem suam: tum 2. quoad alios: quod improbus simulator ore decipiat amicum suum, vel corrumpat sermone, quantum in ipso est; justi autem liberentur scientia sua, ut ne decipiantur, aliisque prodesse consilio possint; ut ita ipsi quoq; eruantur, & ore suo non modo non corrumpent, sed nec ab aliis corrumpantur, & ne alii corrumpantur, præstent scientia sua, v. 9. quodque porro non privatis tantum, sed integræ Reipublicæ bono cedant justorum bona: noceant impiorum studia: In bonis justorum (quæ Deus ipsis concedit, animæ imprimis & corporis bonis) inquit Salomon, exultabitur, vel potius lætabitur civitas, & in perditione impiorum illi erit laudatio, vel exultatio: nulla erit συμπάθεια, aut commiseratio. Ratio additur v. 11. Benedictione justorum exaltabitur civitas, quia ei benedicent, pro ea precabuntur, eique gloriam & exaltationem precibus suis impetrabunt, & ore impiorum, sermonibus pravis, contra primam, & secundam tabulam, non exaltabitur, sed subvertetur, Eccl. 28, 16. Nam impius tantum abest ut de aliis sollicitus sit, ut etiam amicos suos despiciat, utpote amens & corde indigens: justus autem ceu vir prudens, vel vir scientiarum alios non despiciat, sed potius modeste taceat, ex vera humilitate, & proximi amore, v. 12. Impius uti fraudulenter ambulat, ita in fraudem & perniciem proximi arcana revelet: justus autem ceu sincerus, qui fidelis est animi, amici commissum celet, v. 13. Confer. c. 20, 19. c. 25, 9. Hæc ad commoda quæ redundant a justo in proximum spectant: jam quod ad ea, quæ redundant in Rempubl. scientiam vel sapientiam justi multum ei prodesse v. 11. innuitur: ubi non est gubernator sc. sapiens & justus, qui enim talis non est, pro nullo habendus, (in Ebr. est, ubi non fuerint consilia, minus recte Grotius, sine impulsore) populus corruet: ubi autem multa consilia, quæ penes sapientes & justos solum locum habent, nam sapientia sine justitia astutia potius, quam sapientia est, salus efflorescit Reipublicæ. Salus inquit vel conservatio (Reipubl. vel populi) est in multitudine consultorum, qui non solo titulo, sed reipsa tales sunt, non propriis commodis, sed publicis usibus invigilant. Quod denique ad ea, quæ justos & prudentes ipsos concernunt: cavent ipsi laqueos sponsionis, ut securi sint. Nam contritione conteritur, quum fide jusserit (quis) pro extraneo, ut in Ebr. est, at qui odit manus stipulantes temerariæ fidejussionis, tranquille agit.

## 11:10
Vers. 10.

IN THE GOODS OF THE RIGHTEOUS THE CITY SHALL EXULT) Euripides Hecuba: For why do many cities suffer, when some man who is noble and zealous gains nothing more than the worse ones.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

IN BONIS JVSTORVM EXVLTABIT CIVITAS) Euripides Hecuba: Εἰ τῷ δὲ γὰρ κάμνεσιν αἱ πολαὶ πόλεις Ὅταν τις ἐσθλὸς καὶ πρόθυμος ὢν ἀνὴρ Μηδὲν φέρηται τῶν κακιόνων πλέον.

## 11:14
Verse 14.

WHERE THERE IS NO GOVERNOR, THE PEOPLE WILL FALL) In the Hebrew: Without industry the people will fall. - - - οὐ γὰρ οἱ πλατεῖς, Οὐδ᾽ εὐρύνω τοιφῶτες ἀσφαλέστατοι, Ἀλλ᾽ οἱ φρονῦντες εὖ κρατῦσι πανταχῦ, says Sophocles in Ajax.

Latin:

Verf. 14.

VBI NON EST GVBERNATOR, POPVLVS COR- RVET) In Hebræo Sine industriis corruet populus. - - - ὀὰ γὰρ ὁἱ πλατεῖς, Οὐδ᾽ εὐρύνω τοιφῶτες ἀσφαλέστατοι, Ἀλλ᾽ ὁἱ φρονῦντες ἐὖ κρατῦσι πανταχῦ, Ait Sophocles Ajace.

## 11:16
Verse 16.

A GRACIOUS WOMAN SHALL FIND GLORY: AND THE STRONG SHALL HAVE RICHES.

He designates a new attribute and fruit of the righteous by way of antithesis: graciousness; and he names a woman, both to teach that this extends also to women, and because it adorns women especially and renders them pleasing if they are gracious in words and deeds, the fruit of which thing is honor and glory: in the antithesis, however, he names men עריצים, not so much strong and robust as abusing their strength and power, and formidable to others, whence Blessed Luther rendered it 'tyrant', he seizes riches, but more by force and injustice, or through wickedness, than justly and as is right, namely with the oppression of others, to whom he is so far from showing himself gracious that he rather strives to unfold and oppress them: he seizes riches, therefore, indeed, but he does not bring back glory or honor from them, but ignominy and detestation. But what riches might profit such a person, Solomon had already indicated: they cannot deliver him in the day of wrath, v. 4.
