Furthermore, just as the righteous and prudent are gracious to others, so they also do good to themselves: whereas, on the contrary, the impious and those lacking heart are cruel to their own flesh. 'The merciful man does good to his own soul, but he who is cruel even casts off his relatives,' the Vulgate has in v. 17. In the Hebrew it is, 'A man of grace rewards (good) to his own soul: but the cruel troubles his own flesh.' Grotius explains it less correctly: 'he has no regard for kinship,' comparing Deut. 23, 7. For the antithesis yields our sense.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

MVLIER GRATIOSA INVENIET GLO- RIAM : ET ROBVSTI HABEBVNT DIVI- TIAS.

Novum justorum attributum, ac fructum κατ᾽ ἀντίθεσιν designat, gratiositatem; ac mulierem no- minat, tum ut ad mulieres se etiam hæc porrigere doceat, tum quia mulieres imprimis ornet, & gra- tas reddat, si gratiosæ sint in verbis, & factis, cujus rei fructus honor est, & gloria: in antithesi autem nominat viros עריצים non tam fortes & robustos, quam fortitudine, ac potentia sua abutentes, aliis- que formidabiles, unde B. Lutherus, tyrannus, red- didit, apprehendit, sed vi magis, & injustitia, vel per nefas, quam juste, & uti fas est, divitias, cum alio- rum nempe oppressione, quibus tantum abest, ut gratiosum se præbeat, ut eos potius explicare, & op- primere studeat: divitias ergo apprehendit qui- dem, at non gloriam, vel honorem inde reportat, sed ignominiam & detestationem. Quid autem ta- li prosint divitiæ, jam indicarat Salomo: non pof- sunt illum liberare in die iræ, v. 4. Porro justi & pru- dentes uti gratiosi sunt aliis, ita etiam sibi ipsis be- nefaciunt: quum ex adverso impii, & corde caren- tes in carnem propriam crudeles sint. Benefacit, habet vulgata v. 17. animæ suæ vir misericors, qui au- tem crudelis est, etiam propinquos abjicit. In Ebræo est, Retribuit (bonum) animæ suæ vir gratiæ: at crudelis turbat carnem suam. Minus recte exponit Grotius: rationem nullam habet propinquitatis, conferens Deut. 23, 7. Antithesis enim nostrum sensum reddit.

## 11:17
Verse 17.

BUT BECAUSE HE IS CRUEL, HE EVEN CASTS OFF RELATIVES) In the Hebrew: 'But the cruel troubles his own flesh': that is, he has no regard for kinship. See Deuteronomy 23, 7, and what was brought forward by us concerning the Law of War and Peace, book 2, chapter 7, § 10, and in the Annotations.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

QVIA AVTEM CRVDELIS EST, ETIAM PROPIN- QVOS ABJICIT) In Hebræo: Crudelis vero carnem suam turbat: id est, rationem nullam babet propinquitatis. Vide Deuteron. 23, 7. & quæ allata nobis de Jure Belli ac Pacis 2. cap. 7. §. 10. & in Annotatis.

## 11:18
Verse 18.

THE IMPIOUS MAN DOES UNSTABLE WORK: BUT TO HIM WHO SOWS JUSTICE THERE IS A FAITHFUL REWARD.

He further pursues the work and fruits of the righteous: inasmuch as the works of the impious are lies, while those of the faithful are just and bring back a stable reward. The impious man does a lying work, whence he can have no reward except that which a lie brings: Prov. 22, 8; Gal. 6, 7. (But to the righteous) sowing justice there shall be a stable and faithful reward, v. 18 h.l., so that justice is for life, but he who pursues malice (let him pursue it) for his death, v. 19; Rom. 6, 19; because the perverse in heart are an abomination to Jehovah; but those of perfect way, who walk in the ways of the Lord with a sincere heart (Vulg. who walk simply), are his good pleasure, v. 20. The evil man shall not be innocent, even if hand to hand, though he gathers both hands and strives with every effort, he shall not escape danger: but the seed of the righteous shall escape danger, v. 21. (As) A GOLDEN RING IN HIS NOSTRILS, (so is) A BEAUTIFUL AND FOOLISH WOMAN (lacking in counsel), v. 22. How much more must this be judged concerning a foolish man, even if he is most instructed in the gifts of the body? Grotius says, 'Women used to have nose-rings.' See Job 42, 11 and what is said there. But he is most foolish who is destitute of divine wisdom and the justice which is from God, 1 Cor. 1, 30. 'What a pig is in the figures of things, that a fool is in the genus of things,' says St. Augustine, book VI against Faustus, ch. 7. THE DESIRE OF THE RIGHTEOUS IS ALL (in the Hebrew: ONLY) GOOD, THE EXPECTATION OF THE IMPIOUS IS FURY (the indignation and wrath of the Lord), i.e., the desire of the righteous is carried only toward good, and it obtains good, namely the grace of the Lord: the desire of the impious is carried only toward evil, and what else can it have to expect but evil, namely the fury of the Lord? Cf. v. 7.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

IMPIUS FACIT OPUS INSTABILE: SE- MINANTI AUTEM JUSTITIAM MERCES FIDELIS.

Vlterius prosequitur opus, & fructus justorum: utpote quod opera impii mendacia, fidelis justa sint, & mercedem stabilem reportent. Impius fa- cit opus mendax, unde mercedem nullam habere potest, nisi quam mendacium importat: Prov. 22, 8. Gal. 6, 7. (justo autem) seminanti justitiam erit merces stabilis & fidelis v. 18. h. l. ut ita justitia ad vi- tam sit, qui vero sectatur malitiam (sectetur eam) ad mortem suam v. 19. Rom. 6, 19. quia abominatio Jehovah sunt perversi corde; at perfectivia, qui sin- cero corde viis Domini incedunt, (Vulg. qui sim- pliciter ambulant,) beneplacitum ejus. v. 20. Non in- nocens erit malus, etiamsi manus ad manum, licet am- bas congerat manus, omnique annitatur ope, non evadet periculum: Semen autem justorum evadet pe- riculum. v. 21. (Sicut) CIRCULUS (inauris) AU- REUS IN NARIBUS SUIS, (ita) MULIER PULCHRA ET FATUA (deficiens consilio) v. 22. Quanto magis id censendum de viro fatuo, etsi doti- bus corporis instructissimo? Grotius, Habebant, in- quit, fæminæ monilia ἐπίῥῥινα. Vid. Job. 42, 11. & ibi dicta. Fatuus autem maxime est, qui sapientia divi- na, & justitia, quæ ex Deo est, destituitur, 1. Cor. 1, 30. Quod in rerum figuris porcus, hoc in rerum gene- re stultus, ait S. August. l. VI. contra Faust. c. 7. DE- SIDERIUM JUSTORUM OMNE (in Ebræo TANTUMMODO) BONUM EST, PRÆ- STOLATIO IMPIORUM FUROR (indigna- tio & ira Domini) q. d. ad bonum tantum fertur defiderium justorum, & bonum confequitur, gra- tiam nempe Domini: ad malum tantum fertur impiorum defiderium, & quid præstolari aliud ha- beat nifi malum, furorem nempe Domini? Conf. v. 7.

## 11:22
v. 22.

A GOLDEN RING IN HER NOSTRILS) That is, a nose-ring. Women used to have nose-ornaments: See Job 42, 11. and what is said there.

Latin:

Verf. 22.

CIRCVLVS AVREVS IN NARIBVS SVIS) Id est, Dorca. Habebant foeminæ monilia ἐπιῤῥίνια: Vide Jobum 42, 11. & ibi dicta.

## 11:24
v. 24.

OTHERS DISTRIBUTE THEIR OWN, AND BECOME RICHER; OTHERS SEIZE WHAT IS NOT THEIRS, AND ARE ALWAYS IN WANT) For those who wish to take the things of their neighbors, Often fail, being overcome; And they add their own things to the things of others, Menander.

Latin:

Verf. 24.

ALII DIVIDVNT PROPRIA, ET DITIORES FI- VNT; ALII RAPIVNT NON SVA, ET SEMPER IN EGESTATE SVNT) Οἱ γὰρ θέλοντες προσλαβεῖν τὰ τῶν πέλας, Αποτυγχάνουσι πολλάκις νικώμενοι˙ Τὰ δ' ἴδια προστιθέασι τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις, Menander.

## 11:26
v. 26.

HE WHO HIDES GRAIN, SHALL BE CURSED AMONG THE PEOPLE) That is, he who drives up the price of grain, a forestaller.

BUT BLESSING IS UPON THE HEAD OF THOSE WHO SELL) In the Hebrew, of him who breaks: that is, of him who shares with others at a fair price. An example in Joseph, the governor of Egypt.

In the Hebrew v. 24 there is, he who scatters, and it is added (to him) more: and there is one sparing his property more than is right, but only to poverty. Where the righteous man is described by munificence and liberality, and its fruit, that he feels no want from it, but is enriched. Ps. 112, 9. Prov. 19, 17. For as Chrysostom deduces in a special homily, almsgiving is the most profitable of all arts. The unrighteous man on the contrary spares his property, he does not scatter, and that מיושר from rectitude, that is, so that it is not rectitude; but he is not enriched for that reason, but rather is reduced to poverty by the just judgment of God. The soul that blesses, by distributing its own 1. Sam. 25, 27. c. 30, 26. 2. Cor. 9, 5. 6. v. 25. shall be made fat; and he who waters, he himself also shall be watered. יוירא from רוה he watered. The contrary sense is clear both from the member of the antithesis, which is passed over in silence, and from the subjoined sentiment v. 26. he who hides grain, shall be cursed among the people: But blessing is upon the head of those who sell. And because he dealt with the manner of becoming rich, those things which follow pertain neatly to this: v. 27. HE RISES EARLY IN THE MORNING, WHO SEEKS GOOD: BUT HE WHO IS A SEARCHER OF EVILS, SHALL BE OPPRESSED BY THEM. In the Heb. he who seeks in the morning (that is, diligently and eagerly) good (as that which the antecedents and consequents imply, that he may do good to others, and promote the good of his neighbor, which sense is approved also by Salazar, and Mr. Dr. Geier) he acquires for himself the benevolence, or good pleasure of God and men: which is proper to the righteous: But he who seeks evil (the destruction of his neighbor, that he may fleece him, and depress him) to him himself it will happen, viz. the evil, which he intends for his neighbor. And v. 28. He who trusts in his riches shall fall; but the righteous (who do not trust in their riches, but in God alone Ps. 62, 51. 1. Tim. 6, 17.) shall flourish like a green leaf, Jer. 17, 7. seqq. Ps. 92, 13. Chrysostom on that saying of the Apostle, there must be heresies, As a root, he says, planted in rich soil brings forth timely fruits and leaves every year, so also money planted in the hands of the poor produces for us not only every year, but even every day spiritual fruits and leaves; viz. confidence in God, departure from sins, a good conscience, spiritual joy, pleasant hope, and the good things which God has prepared for those who love him.

Furthermore, v. 29 also pertains to the same subject. He who troubles his own house, shall possess

(HE SHALL INHERIT) the winds; and he who is foolish shall serve the wise (HEART), which is not inappropriately explained regarding the covetous. For these are so eager for riches that they even disturb their own house with quarrels, curses, lashes, the continuous imposition of labors, and the denial of wages, food, and drink, as the Tirugini explain. Grotius, who observes neither order nor measure in the administration of family affairs, instead of the hoped-for abundant profit, inherits the wind, his hope being frustrated, c. 10, 24. Eccl. 1, 14. 17. Prov. 15, 17. And such a fool shall finally be compelled to serve the wise: so far is he from becoming great through his hardness that he can even more easily be reduced to extremities, and he who treated others as slaves shall himself, by the law of retaliation, become the slave of others; namely, of those who act wisely and justly.

The Ἀντίθεσις (antithesis) therefore of this is to be sought in the following verse 30: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise. The wise and the righteous, indeed, act far differently; they do not disturb their own, but they attract the souls not only of their own, but also of others, and they wisely bind them to themselves, and offer themselves as a tree of life to others, and serve and benefit others by delighting, nourishing, and informing them, as the marginal gloss says. B. Luther, 'What the righteous do, that comes to everyone for good?'

Latin:

Verf. 26.

QVI ABSCONDIT FRVMENTA, MALEDICE- TVR IN POPVLIS) Id est, qui flagellat annonam, dar- danarius.

BENEDICTIO AVTEM SVPER CAPVT VEN- DENTIVM) In Hebræo frangentis: id est, aliis communi- cantis non iniquo pretio. Exemplum in Josepho Ægypti præside.

In Ebræo v. 24. est, qui dispergit, & additur (ei) amplius: & est parcens rei suæ plus æquo, sed tantum ad egestatem. Ubi justus describitur a munificentia & liberalitate, ejusque fructu, quod nullam inde inopiam sentiat, sed ditetur. Pf. 112, 9. Prov. 19, 17. Nam ut Chrysost. peculiari homilia deducit, elee- mosyna ars est omnium quæstuosissima. Injustus con- tra parcit rei suæ, non dispergit, idque מיושר a recti- tudine, id est, ut non sit rectitudo; ille vero non dita- tur ideo, sed præ justo Dei judicio ad inopiam po- tius redigitur. Anima, quæ benedicit, distribuendo sua 1. Sam. 25, 27. c. 30, 26. 2. Cor. 9, 5. 6. v. 25. impin- guabitur; & qui inebriat, ipse quoque inebriabitur. יוירא a רוה inebriavit. Contrarius sensus tum e mem- bro ἀντιθέσεως, quod tacetur, tum e sententia sub- juncta liquet v. 26. qui abscondit frumenta, maledi- cetur in populis: Benedictio autem super caput ven- dentium. Et quia de modo ditescendi egit, ea quæ sequuntur, concinne huc faciunt: v. 27. BENE CONSURGIT DILUCULO, QUI QUÆRIT BONA: QUI AUTEM INVESTIGATOR MALORUM EST, OPPRIMETUR AB EIS. In Ebr. qui mane quærit (id est, sedulo & alacriter) bonum (ut quod antecedentia & consequentia in- nuunt, benefaciat aliis, proximique bonum promo- veat, qui sensus probatur etiam Salazari, & Dn. D. Geiero) is acquirit sibi benevolentiam, vel benepla- citum Dei & hominum: quod justorum propri- um est: Qui autem quærit malum (proximi interi- tum, ut eum emungat, & deprimat) ei ipsi eveniet, sc. malum, quod proximo intendit. Et v. 28. Qui confidit in divitiis suis corruet; justi autem (qui non in divitiis suis, sed in solo Deo confidunt Pf. 62, 51. 1. Tim. 6, 17.) quasi virens folium germina- bunt, Jer. 17, 7. seqq. Pf. 92, 13. Chrysost. in illud Apostoli, oportet hæreses esse, Sicut radix, inquit, in pingui plantata solo singulis annis tempestivos affert fructus & folia, sic & pecunia in manibus pau- perum plantata non solum in singulos annos, sed etiam in singulos dies spirituales nobis fructus, foliaque pro- ducit; fidentiam sc. in Deum, peccatorum abscef- sum, conscientiam bonam, lætitiam spiritualem, spem jucundam, & bona quæ preparavit Deus diligenti- bus se.

Porro ad eandem materiam facit quoque v. 29. Qui conturbat domum suam, possidebit

(HÆREDITABIT) ventos; & qui stultus est, serviet sapienti (CORDE) quod de avaris non incommode explicatur. Hi enim ita student divi- tiis, ut domum etiam suam ideo conturbent jurgiis, execrationibus, flagris, continua laborum imposi- tione, mercedis, cibi & potus denegatione, uti Ti- rugini exponunt. Grotius, qui neque ordinem neque modum servat in administratione rei familiaris, lo- co sperati copiosi proventus hæreditat ventum spe sua frustrata, c. 10, 24. Eccl. 1, 14. 17. Prov. 15, 17. & stul- tus talis cogetur denique sapienti servire: tantum abest, ut duritie sua magnus evadat, ut facilius etiam ipse ad incitas redigi possit, & qui alios pro mancipiis tractavit, ipse jure talionis aliorum ser- vus evadat; eorum sc. qui sapienter & juste agunt.

Ἀντίθεσις ergo hujus versu sequenti 30. quærenda: Fructus justi lignum vitæ, & qui suscipit animas, sa- piens est. Sapientes nempe ac justi longe aliter agunt, non conturbant suos, sed alliciunt animas non suorum tantum, verum etiam aliorum, eosque sibi sapienter devinciunt, aliisque arborem vitæ se præbent, aliis inserviunt, ac prosunt, delectando, alendo, informando, uti glossa margin. B. Luthe- rus, was die Gerechten thun, das kömmet jeder- mann zu gut?

## 11:29
Vers. 29.

HE WHO TROUBLES HIS OWN HOUSE, SHALL INHERIT THE WINDS) He who observes neither order nor measure in the administration of family affairs.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

QVI CONTVRBAT DOMVM SVAM, POSSIDE- BIT VENTOS) Qui neque ordinem neque modum ser- vat in administratione rei familiaris.

## 11:31
Vers. 31. IF THE RIGHTEOUS IN THE EARTH RECEIVES, HOW MUCH MORE THE UNGODLY AND THE SINNER?

Solomon finally subjoins the retribution and punishment of the ungodly by a comparison of the afflictions of the righteous: as the LXX explain, and St. Peter 1 Ep. 4, 18. If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear? For what is more evident, says St. Augustine c. 20 against Faustus, than that (God) does not spare the righteous, correcting them with a variety of tribulations: and in Ps. 93, if the sons are scourged, what ought the most wicked servants to hope for? Cf. Jer. 25, 29. c. 49, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 31. SI JUSTUS IN TERRA RECIPIT, QUANTO MAGIS IMPIUS, ET PECCA- TOR?

Subjungit tandem Salomo retributionem & pœnam impiorum, comparatione afflictionum justo- rum: uti LXX. exponunt, & S. Petrus 1. Ep. 4, 18. Si justus quidem vix salvatur, impius & peccator ubi comparebunt? Quid enim evidentius, ait S. August. c. 20. contra Faust. quod nec justis parcat (Deus) emendans eos varietate tribulationum: & in Psal. 93. Si flagellantur filii, quid sperare debent servi nequissi- mi? Conf. Jer. 25, 29. c. 49, 12.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. He teaches how the righteous man loves discipline, being devoted to virtue, justice, and mercy, is diligent, and studies truth, describing the heart, tongue, and hands of the righteous in opposition to the ungodly.

Vers. 1.

WHO LOVES DISCIPLINE, LOVES KNOWLEDGE: BUT HE WHO HATES REPROOFS, IS FOOLISH.

Because he had commemorated the afflictions of the righteous, he teaches that they do not turn away from them, but love discipline, whether it be done by words or by lashes and stripes, as that by which they are more instructed. Cf. Ps. 141, 15. Concerning which Chrysostom, homily on bearing reproof: In sins, he says, reproofs effect what remedies do in wounds. Therefore, just as he is foolish who rejects medicines, so also is he a fool who does not receive reproofs with a grateful mind. Augustine, book on correction and grace, c. V. Whoever you are who do not wish to be corrected, you are for that very reason to be corrected, because you do not wish to be corrected. For you do not wish your vices to be shown to you; you do not wish them to be struck, and for a useful pain to be made for you, by which you might seek a physician. To which the following verse also refers: He who is good shall draw grace (benevolence) from the Lord: as one humbly admitting discipline: because God gives grace to the humble 1 Pet. 5, 1. Jas. 4, 7. Concerning which Antiochus hom. LXVIII. The humble man is filled with incredible joy, silent regarding private reproof and contempt more than for honor shown and the celebrity of his own name. But he who (Solomon continues) trusts in his own thoughts, acts impiously. In Hebrew it is: A man of thoughts (who indulges only in his own thoughts, machinations, imaginations) shall be condemned for impiety. But what the success and outcome is for the righteous man who loves discipline, and what for the wicked man who opposes it, is taught in v. 3. A man shall not be strengthened by impiety (or rather, he shall not be stable in the impiety which he loves and pursues, having neglected discipline, he shall not endure, but shall quickly perish), but the root of the righteous shall not be moved or removed: On the contrary, the righteous stand immovable in any adversities whatsoever, as being firmly rooted. Matt. 7, 24. Is. 27, 6. c. 28, 16. Jer. 17, 8.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. Docet, quomodo Justus disciplinam diligat, vir- tuti, justitiæ, misericordiæ deditus, diligens sit, & veritati studeat, cor, linguam & manus justi cum oppositione ad impium describens.

Vers. 1.

QUI DILIGIT DISCIPLINAM, DILIGIT SCIENTIAM: QUI AUTEM ODIT INCRE- PATIONES, INSIPIENS EST.

Quia justorum afflictiones commemorarat, eos non aversari illas, sed disciplinam, correptio- nem sive verbis fiat, seu plagis & verberibus, dili- gere docet, utpote qua magis erudiuntur, Conf. Ps. 141, 15. Quo de Chrysost. homil. de ferend. repre- hens. In peccatis, inquit, id efficiunt reprehensiones, quod in Vulneribus remedia. Idcirco sicut insipiens est, qui Pharmaca rejicit, ita & stultus est, qui non grato animo suscipit reprehensiones. August. lib. de cor- rept. & grat. c. V. Quicunque corripi non vis, ex eo sane corripiendus es, quia corripi non vis. Non vis enim tua tibi vitia demonstrari; non vis, ut feriantur, fiatque tibi utilis dolor, quo medicum quæras. Quo etiam refertur versus sequens: Qui bonus est, hau- riet gratiam (benevolentiam) a Domino: utpote humiliter admittens disciplinam: quia humilibus Deus dat gratiam 1. Petr. 5, 1. Jac. 4, 7. Quo de An- tiochus hom. LXIIX. Vir humilis incredibili lætitia perfunditur, tacitus super correptione privata & contemtu magis, quam pro exhibito honore, & pro- j prii celebritate nominis. Qui autem (pergit Salo- mo) confidit in cogitationibus suis, impie agit. In Ebr. est: Vir cogitationum (qui suis tantum indulget co- gitationibus, machinationibus, imaginationibus) impietatis condemnabitur. Quis autem successus & eventus sit justi disciplinam diligentis, quis impro- bi adversantis, docetur v. 3. Non roborabitur homo ex impietate, (vel potius non erit stabilis in impietate, quam amat, & persequitur, posthabita disciplina non perdurabit, sed cito peribit,) at radix justo- rum non commovebitur, vel dimovebitur: Ex adverso justi immobiles consistunt in quibus- vis etiam adversitatibus, utpote firmiter radicati Matth. 7, 24. Es. 27, 6. c. 28, 16. Jer. 17, 8.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. A DILIGENT WOMAN IS A CROWN TO HER HUSBAND: AND ROTTENNESS IN HIS BONES, IS SHE WHO ACTS IN A MANNER WORTHY OF CONFUSION.

Virtue becomes not only men, but also women: and these are like a crown to their husbands themselves, and they greatly adorn them, when they are virtuous and honest, and diligently and cheerfully care for the family estate. A WOMAN חיל that is of virtue, strenuousness, and cheerfulness. Cf. Ex. 28, 21. Ruth 3, 11. Prov. 31, 10. 11. But she who is not given to virtue, nay, who is מבישה, shaming her husband by her life and morals, is as rottenness in his bones, even if she does not appear so externally, Syr. 25, 25. 31. c. 26, 10. Cf. Zehner in Adag. p. 71.

Latin:

Vers. 4. MULIER DILIGENS CORONA EST VIRO SUO: ET PUTREDO IN OSSIBUS EJUS, QUÆ CONFUSIONE RES DIGNAS GERIT.

Virtus non tantum viros decet, sed etiam mu- lieres: & hæ coronæ instar ipsis maritis sunt, eos- que valde ornant, quum virtuosæ & honestæ, ac rem familiarem sedulo & alacriter curant. MU- LIER חיל id est virtutis, strenuitatis, & alacritatis. Conf. Ex. 28, 21. Ruth. 3, 11. Prov. 31, 10. 11. Quæ vero virtuti dedita non est, imo מבישה pudefaciens vita & moribus suis maritum, est quasi putredo in ossibus ejusdem, utut externe talis non appareat, Syr. 25, 25. 31. c. 26, 10. Conf. Zehner. in Adag. p. 71.

## 12:5
Vers. 5. THE THOUGHTS OF THE RIGHTEOUS ARE JUDGMENTS, AND THE COUNSELS OF THE WICKED ARE FRAUDULENT.

In Hebrew JUDGMENT, & FRAUDULENCE in the abstract: judgment, not of God, as the author of the Greek Catena [says], although the righteous often revolve these things in their minds, but that which is to be exercised toward one's neighbor, as is evident from the opposite; just as the wicked think of and plot deceits, so the righteous [think of] that which is just, so that they may do injury to no one, and may render to each his own, according to the norm of all justice, the Word of God, Mic. 6, 8. Zech. 7, 9. 10. From internal thoughts Solomon descends to external words: THE WORDS OF THE WICKED LIE IN WAIT FOR BLOOD, the wicked lie in wait for others not only with thoughts, but also with words: but the mouth of the righteous not only does not lie in wait for others, but also SHALL DELIVER THEM, whose reputation and life are being plotted against. For indeed their virtue is of strength, as is held in the Greek Catena, so that it not only helps and defends itself, but also champions others, and brings aid to those destitute of aid. Rightly, however, in the decree VI. quest. V. final chapter, it is warned concerning this sentence: It is one thing to report the crimes of others out of charity, so that those whom we cannot correct by secret admonition may be corrected by the sentence of a judge once convicted: and it is another thing to object false things by lying in wait, or to easily reproach true things by insulting. The former is a duty of charity, but the latter is a duty of impiety. But what the outcome is for such wicked men, who lie in wait for others with counsels and words, is explained in v. 7. OVERTURN THE WICKED (or rather GOD WILL OVERTURN THE WICKED) AND THEY SHALL NOT BE. Cf. c. 10, 25. BUT THE HOUSE OF THE RIGHTEOUS SHALL REMAIN. Not only will the righteous man himself stand, but also his house. And v. 8. A MAN SHALL BE KNOWN BY HIS DOCTRINE. In Hebrew, according to the measure of his intelligence, or his prudence, as each shall have conducted himself prudently and justly toward others, he shall be praised and exalted: BUT HE WHO IS VAIN AND HATED SHALL BE EXPOSED TO CONTEMPT: In Hebrew, Perverse of heart, who is destitute of salutary intelligence, and deviates from the rule of justice, shall be in contempt, however much he may exalt himself and boast of himself. Whence it is added v. 9. BETTER IS THE POOR MAN WHO IS SELF- sufficient than he that is glorified and lacketh bread. In Heb. The ignoble man who has a servant is more excellent than the boaster, not only destitute of servants, but also lacking bread, or those things which are most necessary for the sustenance of life. Nor indeed does the faithful man prove himself to others only prudent and just, but also merciful and kind: since the just man knows even the soul of his beast, with a practical knowledge, joined with an affection of love, Prov. 29, 2. Ps. 1, 6. On the contrary, however, the impious man is cruel even when he most wishes to seem to exercise mercy, v. 10. The very mercies of the impious are cruel.

Latin:

Vers. 5. COGITATIONES JUSTORUM JU- DICIA, ET CONSILIA IMPIORUM FRAU- DULENTA.

In Ebr. JUDICIUM, & FRAUDULENTIA in abstracto: judicium, non Dei, ut autor Caten. Græcor. etsi ea omnino mente crebro versent justi, sed quod erga proximum exercendum, ut ex oppo- sito constat; uti impii dolos cogitant, & machi- nantur, ita justi id quod justum, ut nulli faciant in- juriam, unicuique suum tribuant, juxta omnis ju- stitiæ normam Verbum Dei, Mich. 6, 8. Zach. 7, 9. 10. A cogitationibus internis descendit Salomo ad sermones externos: VERBA IMPIORUM INSI- DIANTUR SANGUINI, non tantum cogita- tionibus, sed etiam sermonibus insidiantur aliis impii: os justorum vero non modo non insidiatur aliis, sed etiam LIBERABIT EOS, quorum famæ & vitæ insidiæ struuntur. Enim vero virtus earum est virium, ut habetur in Catena Græc. ut non modo seipsam adjuvet, atque defendat, sed alios propugnet, opemque ope destitutis ferat. Recte autem in decreto VI. quæst. V. cap. fin. monetur circa hanc senten- tiam: Aliud est ex charitate aliorum crimina defer- re, ut quos secreta admonitione corrigere non possu- mus, convictos judicis sententia corripiat: atque aliud insidiando falsa objicere, vel insultando vera facile exprobrare. Illud charitatis, hoc autem impietatis est officium. Quis autem eventus sit talium impiorum, qui aliis consiliis, & verbis insidiantur, exponitur v. 7. VERTE IMPIOS (vel potius EVERTET DEUS IMPIOS) ET NON ERUNT. Conf. c. 10, 25. DOMUS AUTEM JUSTORUM PER- MANEBIT. Non stabit tantum justus ipse, sed etiam domus ejus. Et v. 8. DOCTRINA SUA NOSCETUR VIR. In Ebr. pro ratione intelligen- tiæ, vel prudentiæ suæ, prout sese prudenter & juste erga alios gesserit, laudabitur quisque & evehetur: QUI AUTEM VANUS ET EXOSUS EST PATEBIT CONTEMTUI: IN Ebr. Perversus corde, qui salutari intelligentia destituitur, & a ju- stitiæ regula deflectit, erit in contemtum, quomo- docunque etiam se efferat, & de se glorietur. Un- de additur v. 9. MELIOR EST PAUPER, ET SUF- FICIENS SIBI QVAM GRATIOSUS ET INDIGENS PANE. In Ebr. Præstantior est ingnobilis cui est ser- vus, quam jactabundus, non modo servis destitutus, sed etiam pane carens, vel iis, quæ ad vitæ sustenta- tionem maxime sunt necessaria. Nec vero tantum prudentem, & justum se aliis probat fidelis, sed etiam misericordem & benignum : siquidem justus etiam animam jumenti sui cognoscat, practica notitia, cum affectu amoris conjuncta, Prov. 29, 2. Ps. 1, 6. Ex adverso vero impius etiam tum crudelis est, cum maxime misericordiam exercere videri vult, v. 10. Miserationes ipsæ impiorum crudeles.

## 12:10
Vers. 10. THE JUST MAN KNOWS THE SOULS OF HIS BEASTS) He knows, that is, he takes care, as Ps. 1, 6. It is also praiseworthy to use some kindness toward many living creatures, by which one may abstain further from savagery toward men. See what we have said at Deut. 25, 4. and at Lev. 22, 28.

Latin:

Vers. 10. NOVIT JVSTVS JVMENTORVM SVO- RVM ANIMAS) Novit, id est, curam gerit, ut Ps. 1, 6. Lauda- bile est etiam adversus animantia multa aliqua uti bonitate, quo longius à feritate in homines abstineatur. Vide quæ di- ximus ad Deuteron. 25, 4. & ad Lev. 22, 28.

## 12:11
Vers. 11. HE WHO WORKS HIS LAND, SHALL BE SATIATED WITH BREAD: BUT HE WHO FOLLOWS IDLENESS IS MOST FOOLISH.

But because mention was made of the poor man needing bread, now it is taught how it is permitted to escape poverty, so that one may be satiated with bread: while, namely, he works or tills his land, does not follow idleness, but diligently does his duty: for he who does not do this, but indulges in idleness (in Heb. following empty things or empty men) will not only lack bread, but will also be failing in heart, as it is in the Heb.: since folly and the lack of bread follow idleness, when idleness gives vices, and makes the mind dull: Human nature, says Cassiodorus, just as it is instructed by hard labors, so it is made foolish by sluggish idleness. What else is idleness than the burial of a living man? says the Philosopher. What the Vulgate adds here: He who is pleasant in the moderations of wine, leaves reproach in his strongholds, are spurious: Because they do not occur in the source. But what follows v. 12. THE DESIRE OF THE IMPIOUS IS A STRONGHOLD OF THE WORST: BUT THE ROOT OF THE JUST SHALL FLOURISH, pertains to the unjust acquisition of bread. THE IMPIOUS DESIRES (so it is in the Heb.) THE HUNTING or THE NET OF EVILS: which R. Solomon explains thus; the impious desire this most, that they may feed on those things, and sustain their life, which the wicked have hunted through fraud and rapine. Cajetan, Vatablus, Pagninus, Mercerus, Salazar, Lavater take it thus: the impious man lacking the fear of God always desires the nets of other evils, i.e., methods of deceiving, wicked arts of scraping together riches, and oppressing the resisting just, to which also the version of B. Luther goes. For avarice is the root of all evil 1 Tim. 6, 9. 10. BUT THE ROOT OF THE JUST (God) SHALL GIVE, as the Heb. rightly explains from the comparison of c. 10, 24. Dd. D. Geierus. The just have no need of evil arts, for from God is given to them what suffices, for whose sake they strike deeper roots than the impious with their tricks. Ps. 37, 18. 20. 35. 36. 37.

Latin:

Vers. 11. QUI OPERATUR TERRAM SUAM, SATIABITUR PANIBUS: QUI AUTEM SE- CTATUR OTIUM STULTISSIMUS EST.

Quia vero pauperis indigentis pane mentio facta est, jam quomodo effugere paupertatem liceat, do- cetur, ut quis satietur panibus : dum sc. operatur vel colit terram suam, non sectatur otium, sed sedulo facit officium suum : qui enim id non facit, sed otio indulget (in Ebr. vacuos vel vacua sequens) non modo pane carebit, sed etiam deficiens erit corde, ut in Ebr. est : siquidem vecordia cum defectu panis otium sequantur, quum otia dent vitia, mentemque hebescere faciant: Natura humana, ait Cassiodo- rus, sicut duris laboribus instruitur, ita per otia tor- pentia infatuatur. Quid aliud est otium, quam vivi hominis sepultura? ait Philosophus. Quæ hic addit Vulgata: Qui suavis est in vini moderationibus, in suis munitionibus relinquit contumeliam, notha sunt: Quia in fonte non occurrunt. Quod autem sequitur v. 12. DESIDERIUM IMPII MUNIMENTUM EST PESSIMORUM : RADIX AUTEM JUSTORUM PROFICIET, ad injustam panis acquisitionem perti- net. DESIDERAT IMPIUS (ita in Ebr. est) VENA- TIONEM vel RETE MALORUM: quod ita explicat R. Salomo; impii hoc maxime optant, ut iis vescantur, vitamque sustentent, quæ scelerati per fraudem & ra- pinam venati fuerint. Cajetanus, Vatabl. Pagninus, Mercerus, Salazar, Lavater. ita accipiunt: impius ti- more Dei carens appetit semper malorum aliorum re- tia, h. e. modos decipiendi, artes pravas corradendi divitias, opprimendique obsistentes justos, quo etiam abit B. Lutheri versio. Avaritia enim est radix omnis mali 1. Tim. 6, 9. 10. RADICEM AUTEM JUSTO- RUM DABIT (Deus) ut Ebr. recte explicat e colla- tione c. 10, 24. Dd. D. Geierus. Justi non opus ha- bent malis artibus, a Deo enim ipsis datur, quantum sufficit, cujus gratia radices firmiores ipsi agunt, quam impii suis technis. Ps. 37, 18. 20. 35. 36. 37.

## 12:13
Vers. 13. BECAUSE OF THE SINS OF THE LIPS RUIN APPROACHES THE EVIL: BUT THE JUST SHALL ESCAPE FROM DISTRESS.

Now he returns to where he had digressed on the occasion of poverty, namely to the deceits of the tongue. In the Heb. these and the following have it thus: in the transgression of the lips is a snare (of a man) of evil. (conf. c. 18, 7.) But the just shall go out from distress, or he will not be involved in a snare, or he will extricate himself happily. v. 14. from the fruit of the mouth everyone shall be satiated with good, if, namely, he gives wholesome advice, he will experience God and men as kind, Conf. c. 11, 30. c. 13, 2. c. 18, 20. and (God) will render to him the retribution of a man's hands, which can be taken antithetically concerning those who not only do not advise useful things, but also work evil and harmful things, Conf. Is. 3, 11. as as THE WAY

OF THE FOOL IS RIGHT IN HIS EYES, when on the contrary the Wise man does not rely on his own ingenuity, but obeys the Counsel of the prudent, and of God Himself in the revealed word, v. 15. whence the Fool indulging only his own Affections Immediately Indicates His Anger (as the Vulgate has it, in the Heb. it is: as for the fool, in the very day his anger will be known:) when on the contrary ערום the circumspect and prudent man covers shame, or as the Vulg. explains, dissimulates an injury. For this, as Cassian says Coll. 16. c. 27. is the nature of anger, that when delayed it languishes and perishes, but when brought forth it burns more and more.

And so Solomon now proceeds in the Antithesis of the goods and evils of the tongue of a truthful man, and a false-speaker. v. 17. He who speaks truth (thus these have it in the Heb., and what follows, that is, he who is truthful, as is evident from the antithesis) announces justice; and a lying witness (announces) deceit: because the former strives for justice, so that he may not bring forth anything to the harm of the innocent, or the scandal of the hearers, but the latter is devoted to falsehoods, harmful and damaging to his neighbor. v. 18. There is who brings forth words, (which are) like the piercings of a sword, Conf. Ps. 55, 22. Ps. 57, 5. Ps. 70, 8.) But the tongue of the wise not only does not harm his neighbor, but if that other has been injured or pierced by the tongue of another, it is also health, or medicine. Therefore (what is added v. 19.) the lip of the truthful is firm forever; but the tongue of the liar (is) for a moment (only), the liar will not be established Ps. 101, 7. Ps. 140, 12. For not only does a lie betray itself, but the liar himself also brings destruction upon himself: especially because he devises evil in his heart, and lies in wait for his neighbor, as is taught v. 20. For there is deceit in the heart of those thinking evil, (which is the source of false testimonies and calumnies Matt. 15, 19.) but in the heart of those counseling peace there is no deceit, but joy, i.e., metonymically what brings joy to men. Nor indeed do the fraudulent impious harm others so much by deceitful machinations, and speeches, as especially themselves, v. 21. For to the Just No Iniquity will happen, so that he may be exposed either to the lust of the impious, or to the punishments of iniquity: But the Impious Are Filled With Evil. The reason is added v. 22. Lying lips are an abomination to Jehovah: (i.e., lying men) but in those who do truth is his good pleasure.

Latin:

Vers. 13. PROPTER PECCATA LABIO- RUM RUINA PROXIMAT MALO : EFFU- GIET AUTEM JUSTUS DE ANGUSTIA.

Jam eo redit unde digressus ex occafione pau- pertatis erat, nimirum ad dolos linguæ. In Ebr. hæc & sequentia ita habent: in prævaricatione labiorum laqueus (hominis) mali. (conf. c. 18, 7.) Egredietur autem de angustia justus, aut laqueo non involve- tur, aut sese expediet feliciter. v. 14. de fructu oris quisque saturabitur bono, si sc. salutaria suadeat, De- um hominesque experietur benignos, Conf. c. 11, 30. c. 13, 2. c. 18, 20. & retributionem manuum homi- nis reddet ei (Deus) quæ ἀντιθετικῶς accipi possunt de iis, qui non modo non suadent utilia, sed etiam mala & noxia operantur, Conf. Es. 3, 11. ut ut VIA

Stvlti Recta Sit In Ocvlis Ejus, quum ex ad- verso Sapiens non suo nitatur ingenio, sed pru- dentum, Deique ipsius in verbo revelato, Obtem- peret Consilio, v. 15. unde Fatuus suis indul- gens tantum Affectibus Statim Indicat Iram Suam (ut vulgata habet, in Ebr. est: quod ad stul- tum attinet, in ipsa die cognoscetur ira ejus:) quum ex adverso ערום circumspectus ac prudens operiat ignominiam, vel ut Vulg. explicat, injuriam dissimu- let. Hæc enim, dicente Cassiano Coll. 16. c. 27. natura est iræ, ut dilata languescat & pereat, prolata vero magis magisque conflagret.

Atque ita pergit jam Salomo in Antithesi bono- rum & malorum linguæ hominis veracis, & falsilo- qui. v. 17. Qui loquitur veritatem (sic in Ebr. ha- bent hæc, & quæ sequuntur, id est, qui verax est, ut ex antithesi constat) annunciat justitiam; & testis mendax (annunciat) dolum: quod ille studeat, ju- stitiæ, ne cum damno innocentis, vel scandalo au- dientium quid proferat, hic vero falsitatibus dedi- tus sit, proximo noxiis & damnosis. v. 18. Est qui profert verba, (quæ sunt) veluti confossiones gladii, Conf. Ps. 55, 22. Ps. 57, 5. Ps. 70, 8.) Lingua autem sa- pientum non modo non nocet proximo, sed si læsus vel consossus ille alterius lingua sit, sanitas etiam est, vel medicina. Ideo (quod additur v. 19.) labium veracis firmum in perpetuum; sed ad momentum (tantum est) lingua mendacis, non stabilietur men- daciloquus Ps. 101, 7. Ps. 140, 12. Non enim tantum mendacium seipsum prodit, sed & mendax ipse sibi interitum accersit: imprimis quia corde suo moli- tur malum, & insidiatur proximo, ut v. 20. docetur. Dolvs enim est in corde cogitantium malum, (quod fons est falsorum testimoniorum & calu- mniarum Matth. 15, 19.) at in corde consulentium pa- cem non dolus est, sed lætitia, h. e. metonymice quod hominibus gaudium adferat. Neque vero tam aliis nocent impii fraudulenti dolosis machinatio- nibus, & sermonibus, quam imprimis sibi ipsis, v. 21. Justo enim non accidet Vlla Iniqvitas, ut exponatur vel impiorum libidini, vel iniquitatis pœnis: Impii Vero Repleti Svnt Malo. Ra- tio addita est v. 22. Abominatio Jehovæ sunt labia mendacia: (h.e. homines mendaces) at in facien- tibus veritatem est beneplacitum ejus.

## 12:16
Vers. 16. BUT HE WHO DISSIMULATES AN INJURY IS CUNNING) In the Hebrew rather thus: The cautious man dissimulates an injury. Among the powerful that is most necessary, where one does not reach old age, except by accepting injuries, and dissimulating. But also among others, Expressed hatreds lose the place of vengeance.

Latin:

Vers. 16. QVI AVTEM DISSIMVLAT INJVRIAM CALLIDVS EST) In Hebræo sic potius: Cautus injuriam dissimulat. Apud potentes id maxime necessarium, ubi ad se- nectutem non pervenitur, nisi accipiendo injurias, & dissi- mulando. Sed & apud alios, Professa perdunt odia vindictæ locum.

## 12:20
V. 20. THEY WHO ENTER INTO THE COUNSEL OF PEACE, JOY FOLLOWS THEM) Thus Euripides bids us think: Ὅσῳ τε πολέμꙋ κρεῖττον εἰρήνη βροτοῖς, Ἡ πρῶτα μὲν Μέσαισι προσφιλεστάτη, Γόοισι δ' ἐχθρὰ, τέρπεται δ' εὐπαιδίᾳ, Χαίρει δὲ πλέτῳ.

Latin:

V. 20. QVI PACIS INEVNT CONSILIVM, SEQVI- TVR EOS GAVDIVM) Sic Euripides cogitari jubet: Ὅσῳ τε πολέμꙋ κρεῖττον εἰρήνη βροτοῖς, Ἡ πρῶτα μὲν Μέσαισι προσφιλεστάτη, Γόοισι δ' ἐχθρὰ, τέρπεται δ' εὐπαιδίᾳ, Χαίρει δὲ πλέτῳ.

## 12:23
Vers. 23. A CRAFTY MAN CONCEALS KNOWLEDGE: AND THE HEART OF FOOLS PROVOKES FOLLY.

This also pertains to the government of the tongue. ערום is not 'crafty' in this place, but 'prudent,' and 'cautious,' and 'circumspect,' for it is opposed to the foolish: the former conceals, he does not boastfully parade his knowledge: the latter, however, יקרא proclaims folly; although he intends to show wisdom, he nevertheless betrays the folly of his heart: or also the former conceals what he knows or has heard, but the latter immediately manifests it, and like a herald publicly proclaims it.

Latin:

Vers. 23. HOMO VERSUTUS CELAT SCI- ENTIAM: ET COR INSIPIENTIUM PRO- VOCAT STULTITIAM.

Pertinet & hoc ad gubernationem linguæ. ערום non versutus est hoc loco, sed prudens, & cautus, ac circumspectus, opponitur enim insipienti: celat ille, non jactat gloriabundus scientiam: hic autem יקרא prædicat stultitiam; quamvis sapientiam ostentare intendat, stultitiam tamen cordis sui pro- dit: vel etiam celat ille, quod scit, vel audivit, hic vero illico manifestat, & præconis instar publice proclamat.

## 12:24
Vers. 24. THE HAND OF THE MIGHTY SHALL RULE, BUT THAT WHICH IS SLACK SHALL SERVE UNDER TRIBUTE. רמיה, he did not translate 'slack' badly. For רמה is to cast away. Thus 'cast away patience' in Tacitus. Erinna in the hymn of Fortitude. Σοὶ μόνα πρέσβιστα δέδωκε μοῖρα Κῦδος ἀῤῥήκτω βασιλῆϊον ἀρχᾶς.

Just as previously Solomon had joined the diligence of the tongue with the prudence of governance in the works of the hands, so now, after he has treated more fully those things which pertain to governing the tongue, he further commends diligence and industry, because indeed the hand of the חרוצים (diligent) (Conf. c. 10, 4.) shall rule, whereas on the contrary (the hand) of רמיה (sloth) or deceitful labor shall become tributary, or be for tribute, or as Vatabl. explains, those who strenuously perform their duties are accustomed to be masters of others, whereas against them the sluggards are tributaries of the just, and thus are compelled to serve them. Furthermore, v. 25 is added: anxious solicitude (דאגה) (such as the solicitude concerning famine was in Jer. 42, 16.) in the heart of a man (if it shall be) shall depress (avert by whatever means) it: for both the feminine suffix, and the reason for the placement, and the context demand this sense; lest we be tormented by the solicitude of poverty concerning our sustenance, Matt. 6, 25. For A GOOD WORD (but what is a good word, if not the word of God?) shall gladden it, shall convert it into joy, or shall not only console it, but shall cause joy to follow. Conf. Job 41, 13. Deut. 8, 3. Matt.

4, 4. Such a good word is consolatory and exhilarating, which is subjected in v. 26. The just (is) an abundance to his neighbor, not only does nothing fail him, but he even abounds beyond others: (where the Vulg. wrongly says: he who neglects damage for the sake of a friend is just) but the way of the impious shall cause them to err, not to attain their end, inasmuch as they intend abundance, but fail, and experience penury, Ps 34, 11. For it concludes nothing (the meaning of the word יתר, which has no brother in scripture, Fuller observed in Miscell. l. 6. c. 13., with the approval of Dr. Geier) SLOTH (or a slothful man, the abstract for the concrete) (TO HIS NET: Nets are spread in vain by the slothful, not applying just diligence: BUT THE SUBSTANCE (or faculty) OF A MAN (sc. of a diligent and strenuous one, as appears from the antithesis) IS PRECIOUS חרוץ (shall be) gold, as it is taken in Prov. 3, 14. c. 8, 19.: which sense of the word Avenarius also posits here in his Lexicon, and the Chald. and Vulg. have followed.

Latin:

Vers. 24. MANVS FORTIVM DOMINABITVR, QVÆ AVTEM REMISSA EST, TRIBVTIS SERVIET( רמיה non male transtulit remissa. Nam רמה est projicere. Sic pro- jecta patientia apud Tacitum. Erinna in hymno Fortitudinis. Σοὶ μόνα πρέσβιστα δέδωκε μοῖρα Κῦδος ἀῤῥήκτω βασιλῆϊον ἀρχᾶς.

Ut antea Salomo cum prudentia guberna- tionis linguae diligentiam in operibus manuum con- junxerat, ita nunc postquam fusius ea quae ad lin- guam gubernandam faciunt, exequutus est, dili- gentiam & industriam ulterius commendat, quod nempe manus חרוצים sedulorum (Conf. c. 10, 4.) dominetur, cum ex adverso רמיה (manus) desidiae vel dolosi laboris tributaria evadat, vel in tributum sit, aut uti explicat Vatabl. qui strenue obeunt munia sua, soleant esse Domini aliorum, contra cessato- res sint tributarii justorum, adeoque servire iis co- gantur. Additur porro v. 25. solicitudo anxia (דאגה) qualis solicitudo de fame erat Jer. 42, 16.) in corde viri (si fuerit) deprimat (avertat quibus- cunque modis) illam: hunc enim sensum postulat & foemininum suffixum, & ratio positus, & contex- tus; ne solicitudine inopiae angamur de sustentatio- ne nostri, Matth. 6, 25. Nam VERBVM BO- NVM, quod vero bonum verbum, nisi verbum Dei?) laetificabit illam, convertet eam in laetitiam, vel solabitur illam non tantum, sed efficiet ut suc- cedat laetitia. Conf. Job. 41, 13. Deut. 8, 3. Matth.

4, 4. Tale verbum bonum consolatorium & exhi- laratorium est, quod subjicitur v. 26. Abundantia (est) proximo suo justus, non modo nihil ei deficit, sed abundat etiam prae aliis: (ubi perperam Vulg. qui negligit damnum propter amicum justus est) via autem impiorum errare faciet eos, non assequi fi- nem suum, utpote qui intendunt abundantiam, sed deficiunt, & penuriam experiuntur Ps 34, 11. Nam non concludit quicquam (quam vocis יתר, quae non habet fratrem in scriptura, significationem Fulle- rus Miscell. l. 6. c. 13. observavit, approbante Dn. D. Geiero) IGNAVIA (vel vir ignavus, abstra- ctum pro concreto (RETI SUO: Frustra retia expanduntur ab ignavis, non justam adhibentibus diligentiam: SVBSTANTIA AVTEM (vel facultas) HOMINIS (sc. gnavi, & strenui, ut ex antithesi apparet) PRETIOSA חרוץ (erit) au- rum, uti Prov. 3, 14. c. 8, 19. accipitur: quem vocis sensum hic etiam ponit Avenarius in Lex. & sequu- tus est Chald. & Vulg.

## 12:28
Ver. 28. IN THE PATH OF JUSTICE IS LIFE: BUT A DEVIATING WAY LEADS TO DEATH. The sentences of this chapter concerning the just and justice are concluded, with the outcome and end being indicated, or the outcome of his life, and life is promised to justice, and for the sake of greater βεβαιώσεως (confirmation) a negative is added: And the way of his path is not death, as is held in the Hebrew. Capellus, in Critico S. lib. 5. c. 2. f. 326, urges another reading for the Vulgate, אל instead of לא, to death. But neither the Hebrew Codices, nor the interpreters agree. See Buxt. Anti-Crit. page 717.

Latin:

Vers. 28. IN SEMITA JUSTITIAE VITA: ITER AUTEM DEVIUM DUCIT AD MORTEM. Concluduntur sententiae hujus capitis de ju- sto, & justitia, indicato exitu & fine, vel exitu vi- tae ejus, ac promittitur justitiae vita, majorisque βεβαιώσεως gratia additur negativa: Et via semita ejus non est mors, ut in Ebr. habetur. Capellus pro Vulgata lectionem aliam urget אל pro לא ad mor- tem, in Critico S. lib. 5. c. 2. f. 326. Sed nec Codices Ebraei, nec interpp. annuunt. Vid. Buxt. Anti-Crit. pag. 717.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

The necessity of discipline, regarding the custody of the mouth, sloth, lying, injustice, pride, contempt of the word, flight; and the fruit of the same.

Ver. 1.

A WISE SON (HEARS) THE DOCTRINE OF THE FATHER: BUT HE WHO IS A SCORNER, DOES NOT HEAR WHEN HE IS REBUKED.

There is no sense in the former member according to the vulgate: but the verb must be supplied from the latter, i.e., A wise son hears the discipline or instruction of the Father; but a scorner does not hear rebuke.

CHAP. XIII. v. 1. - 8.

- Therefore, he does not obtain the name and praise of a wise Father who does not listen to rebuke, but is a mocker and a buffoon. Whence the necessity of correction shines forth, which Solomon pursues in parts: 1. Regarding the custody of the mouth, which is necessary if one wishes to be satisfied with good things, v. 2. From the fruit of his mouth a man shall be satisfied with good things (everyone eats good, ch. 12, 14), but the soul of the treacherous is wicked (shall eat, or rather, injury). בֹּגְדִים are the treacherous, holding divine and human things in contempt, rashly blaspheming with their mouth, putting forth scandalous and injurious things. By 'injury,' however, metonymically, the antithesis teaches that the punishment of injury is understood: he shall not eat good, or enjoy good things, but shall feel and experience the punishments of injury and violence. Cf. ch. 1, 31. Hos. 10, 13. Which he further explains in v. 3. HE WHO GUARDS HIS MOUTH, GUARDS HIS SOUL, (Cf. Matt. 12, 36.) BUT HE WHO IS INCONSIDERATE IN SPEAKING, SHALL FEEL EVILS. To him who opens (namely, when he ought not to open his lips, but guard his mouth, and thus rashly opens them), there shall be destruction. Cf. Sir. 28, 29. Ps. 141, 3. Ps. 39, 2. 2. Regarding the flight from laziness, v. 4. THE SLUGGARD WANTS, AND WANTS NOT: BUT THE SOUL OF THE DILIGENT SHALL BE MADE FAT. In the former member, the Hebrew text has it thus: He desires, and the soul of the sluggard is not. Idleness makes him desire many things, but inertia prevents him from obtaining them: because he always sticks in idle desires, and does not progress further; so that, indeed, he might apply his hand to work and labor, by which he might obtain those things which he desires, Cf. ch. 20, 4. 3. Regarding the flight from lying, v. 5. A WORD OF A LIE THE JUST MAN WILL DETEST (holds in hatred) BUT THE IMPIOUS MAN CONFOUNDS AND SHALL BE CONFOUNDED. In the Hebrew, as Corn. a Lap. acknowledges, it is: but the impious man shall make to stink (himself, as B. Luther, Jun., Piscator, the Belgians) and shall be affected with shame. Do you not see, says Chrysost. hom. 32 to Antioch, pigs eating and wallowing in mud? So too are these detractors. For what is more foul than the words which the abusive speak? 4. Regarding the flight from injustice, v. 6. JUSTICE GUARDS THE WAY OF THE INNOCENT (perfect or whole in way) BUT IMPIETY SUPPLANTS THE SINNER (shall subvert): R. Salom. shall devastate and humiliate. 5. Regarding the flight from pride, v. 7. THERE IS AS IF RICH, WHEN HE HAS NOTHING: AND THERE IS AS IF POOR, WHEN HE IS IN MANY RICHES. The Hebrew, word for word, has it thus: There is who shows himself rich, and there is nothing to him; (there is) who shows himself poor, and many riches (are to him), which sense the Chaldean, Syrian, R. Levi, Vatablus, Pagninus, Mercerus, and others follow. The disease of riches, says August. serm. 212 de temp., is great pride. For a great soul is one that is not tempted by this disease among riches. A soul greater than its riches which overcomes them not by desiring, but by despising. The reason, however, why such ostentation is to be fled is this, v. 8. because he who shows off riches is compelled to redeem his soul; THE REDEMPTION OF A MAN'S SOUL IS HIS RICHES: whereas, on the contrary, he who humbly carries poverty before him, does not even need to hear a rebuke: BUT THE POOR MAN DOES NOT HEAR A REBUKE: and in this sense we approve the explanation of Grotius in his tract on the satisfaction of Christ: that the rich man pleases the angry, the poor man is less subject to the thing of another, etc. Cf. Socinism. proflig. page 497. The naked man does not fear thieves, says S. Hilarion in S. Jerome in his life: The poor man does not fear the noise of a man, says Theodor. Orat. 7 on Providence, nor does he dread the voice of the herald nor is he terrified by the grim countenance of a judge, and eyes breathing fire.

But just as pride is to be avoided in wealth, so also in the vain pursuit of fame, which the ungodly affect in vain. For THE LIGHT OF THE RIGHTEOUS REJOICES: the fame and glory of the pious is like a broad light, which illuminates, exhilarates, and gladdens: BUT THE LAMP OF THE WICKED (to whom not a brief and meager fame, not light, but a lamp is ascribed, and thus immediately) SHALL BE EXTINGUISHED, nor can it bring solid brightness and joy. Cf. Job 8, 5. The LXX add yet another sentence, deceitful souls wander in sins, but the righteous are merciful and show mercy: which the Vulgate stitches onto verse 13; but that is foreign, since it is not found in the source.

Moreover, it is added concerning the effect of pride in v. 10. AMONG THE PROUD THERE ARE ALWAYS QUARRELS: In the Hebrew, truly or only in pride does contention emerge. It is no wonder, says Augustine, if pride begets dissension: for this is its own genuine offspring. BUT THOSE WHO DO ALL THINGS WITH COUNSEL ARE RULED BY WISDOM. In the Hebrew, But with those who consult, or take the counsel of others (which is of humility) there is wisdom from above, which is peaceable, Jas. 3, 17. The proud do not listen to or follow the counsels of others, they are wise only to themselves; but the humble seek out and embrace the judgments and counsels of others: and therefore to these wisdom is attributed, to those it is tacitly denied: again, to these the pursuit of peace is tacitly ascribed, just as contention thrives among those.

It is added in v. 11 concerning riches, about which Solomon had said some are proud, how they either take a decrease, namely from vanity, when they are spent on vain things, or an increase, when indeed one does not lose them to vanities, or squander them, but gathers them with his own hand, and daily adds a little to a little. Riches from vanity shall be diminished, but he who gathers with (his) hand shall multiply (them:) the latter clause of which the Vulgate rendered not badly as to the sense, but it perverted the mind of the former by interpreting it thus: substance hastened shall be diminished: but that which is gathered little by little by hand shall be multiplied.

What is subjoined in v. 12. HOPE WHICH IS DEFERRED AFFLICTS THE SOUL: A DESIRE COMING IS A TREE OF LIFE, although it may have a general sense concerning things expected and desired, that those deferred bring sickness to the heart, and those obtained bring life, like the tree of life, which served to sustain health, yet it can provide a tacit admonition to the rich, that they should succor the needy who are panting and expecting aid from them, without delay when they are able, and not sustain them with hope alone.

6. Concerning contempt of the word: v. 13. He who despises the (divine) word destroys or loses for himself whatever he has of happiness or faculty: but to him who fears the (divine) commandment it shall be repaid, or he who fears will truly receive retribution, as not only the Chaldean, R. Solomon, but also Vatablus, Pagninus, and Mercerus render, from which sense, however, the Vulgate wrongly departs: He who detracts from anything binds himself for the future: but he who fears the commandment shall dwell in peace. Cf. Dn. D. Geier. Commentary on this passage.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

Disciplina necessitas, quoad oris custodiam, pi- gritia, mendacii, injustitia, superbia, con- temtus verbi fugam; & fructus ejusdem.

Vers. 1.

FILIUS SAPIENS DOCTRINA PATRIS: QUI AUTEM ILLUSOR EST, NON AU- DIT CUM ARGUITUR.

Nullus sensus est in priori membro juxta vul- gatam: supplendum autem verbum est e posteriori h. m. Filius sapiens audit disciplinam vel eruditio- nem Patris; at derisor non audit increpationem.

CAP. XIII. v. 1. - 8.

- Sapientis ergo Patris nomen & laudem non con- sequitur, qui non audit increpationem, sed derisor est, & scurra. Unde necessitas correptionis effulget, quam prosequitur Salomo per partes, 1. Quoad custodiam oris, qua opus est, si quis bonis satiari ve- lit, v. 2. De fructu oris sui homo satiabitur bonis (quisque comedit bonum c. 12, 14.) anima autem prævaricatorum iniqua (comedet, vel potius inju- riam.) בֹּגְדִים sunt prævaricantes, divina ac humana fusque deque habentes, ore suo temere blasphe- mantes, scandalosa, injuriosa protrudentes. Per injuriam vero metonymice pœnam injuriæ intel- ligi antithesis docet : non bonum comedet, aut bonis fruetur, sed pœnas injuriæ & violentiæ sen- tiet, & experietur. Conf. c. 1, 31. Hos. 10, 13. Quod explicat porro v. 3. QUI CUSTODIT OS SUUM, CUSTODIT ANIMAM SUAM, (Conf. Matth. 12, 36.) QUI AUTEM INCON- SIDERATUS EST AD LOQUENDUM, SENTIET MALA. Aperienti (sc. cum non ape- rire labia, sed os custodire debebat, adeoque te- mere aperienti) labia sua, erit contritio. Conf. Sir. 28, 29. Ps. 141, 3. Ps. 39, 2. 2. Qua fugam pigritiæ, v. 4. VULT, ET NON VULT PIGER: ANIMA AUTEM OPERANTIUM IMPINGUABI- TUR. In priori membro Ebr. textus ita habet; Concupiscit, & non est anima pigri. Otium facit eum multa desiderare, sed inertia prohibet eum illa consequi: quia hæret semper in otiosis desideriis, nec ultra progreditur; ut nempe manum adhibeat operi, & labori, quo ea, quæ desiderat, adipiscatur, Conf. c. 20, 4. 3. Qua fugam mendacii v. 5. VER- BUM MENDACII JUSTUS DETESTABI- TUR (odio habet) IMPIUS AUTEM CON- FUNDIT ET CONFUNDETUR. In Ebr. agnoscente Corn. a Lap. est, impius autem fœtere faciet (seipsum, uti B. Luther. Jun. Piscat. Belgæ) & pudore afficiet. Non cernitis, inquit Chrysost. hom. 32. ad Antioch. porcos cænum edentes ac volventes? Sic & isti detractores. Quid enim fœtidius verbis, quæ contumeliosi loquuntur? 4. Qua fugam inju- stitiæ, v. 6. JUSTITIA CUSTODIT INNO- CENTIS VIAM (perfectum vel integrum via) IMPIETAS AUTEM PECCATOREM SUP- PLANTAT (subvertet:) R. Salom. deva- stabit & humiliabit. 5. Qua fugam superbiæ v. 7. EST QUASI DIVES, CUM NIHIL HA- BEAT: ET EST QUASI PAUPER, CUM IN MULTIS DIVITIIS SIT. Ebr. κατὰ πόδα ita habent: Est qui se divitem ostentat, & non est ei quic- quam, (est,) qui pauperem se ostentat, & divitiæ multæ (sunt ei,) quem sensum sequuntur Chald. Syrus, R. Levi, Vatabl. Pagninus, Mercerus, aliique. Morbus divitiarum, ait August. serm. 212. de temp. est superbia magna. Nam grandis animus est, qui inter divitias isto morbo non tentatur. Major animus divitiis suis qui eas vincit non concu- piscendo, sed contemnendo. Causa autem cur fu- gienda sit talis ostentatio hæc est, v. 8. quia redi- mere cogitur animam suam, qui divitias ostentat; REDEMTIO ANIMÆ VIRI DIVITIÆ EJUS: quum ex adverso, qui paupertatem præ se fert humiliter, ne increpationem quidem audire opus habeat: PAUPER AUTEM NON AU- DIT INCREPATIONEM: atque hoc sensu Grotii tract. de satisfact. Christi explicationem probamus: quod dives iratum placet, pauper alienæ re minus sit obnoxius &c. Conf. Socinism. pro- flig. pag. 497. Nudus latrones non timet, inquit S. Hilarion. apud S. Hieronym. in vit. ejus: Pau- per non metuit strepitum viri, ait Theodor. Orat. 7. de Provident. nec præconis vocem reformidat, nec judicis torvo vultu, & oculis ignem spirantibus eerretur.

Uti autem in opibus superbia fugienda, ita etiam in vana famæ aucupatione, quam nequicquam affectant impii. Sola enim LUX JUSTORUM LÆTIFICAT: fama & gloria piorum amplæ luci similis est, quæ illustrat, exhilarat & lætificat: LUCERNA AUTEM IMPIORUM (quibus non nisi brevis & exigua fama, non lux, sed lucerna adscribitur, adeoque illico) EXTINGUETUR, nec solidam claritatem, & lætitiam afferre potest. Conf. Job. 8, 5. LXX. addunt adhuc aliam sententiam, animæ dolosæ errant in peccatis, justi autem misericordes sunt & miserentur: quam vulgata versui 13. assuit; Sed ea aliena est, quum in fonte non habeatur.

Additur autem de superbiæ effectu v. 10. INTER SUPERBOS SEMPER JURGIA SUNT: In Ebr. vere vel tantum in superbia emergit contentio. Non mirum, inquit Augustinus, si superbia parit dissensionem: hæc enim ejus germana soboles est. QUI AUTEM AGUNT OMNIA CUM CONSILIO, REGUNTUR SAPIENTIA. In Ebr. At cum consultis, vel aliorum consilium capientibus (quod humilitatis est) sapientia est ἡ ἄνωθεν, quæ εἰρηνικὴ Jac. 3, 17. Superbi aliorum non audiunt, vel sequuntur consilia, sibi solis sapiunt; at humiles expetunt, & amplectuntur aliorum judicia & consilia: ideoq; his sapientia tribuitur, illis tacitē derogatur: rursus his tacitē pacis studium adscribitur, uti inter illos contentio viget.

Additur v. 11. de divitiis, quibus nonnullos superbire dixerat Salomo, quomodo illæ vel decrementum capiant, nimirum ex vanitate, cum rebus vanis impenduntur, vel incrementum, cum nempe quis eas non perdit vanitatibus, aut prodigit, sed manu sua congregat, & quotidie parvum parvo addit. Divitiæ præ vanitate minuentur, at qui manu (sua) congregat, multiplicabit (eas:) quorum posterius membrum non male quoad sensum reddidit vulgatus, prioris autem mentem pervertit, ita interpretando: substantia festinata minuetar: quæ autem paulatim colligitur manu, multiplicabitur.

Quod subjungitur v. 12. SPES QUÆ DIFFERTUR, AFFLIGET ANIMAM: LIGNUM VITÆ DESIDERIUM VENIENS, etsi generalem sensum habeat de rebus expectatis & desideratis, quod dilatæ ægritudinem cordi, obtentæ vitam adferant, instar ligni vitæ, quod ad sanitatem sustentandam conducebat, tacitam tamen præbere divitibus admonitionem potest, ut egenis anhelantibus, & expectantibus ab iisdem subsidia, sine cunctatione, quum possint, succurrant, nec spe sola eos sustentent.

6. Qua contemtum verbi: v. 13. Contemnens verbum (Dei) destruit vel perdit sibi ipsi, quicquid sc. habet felicitatis, vel facultatis: Timenti vero præceptum (divinum) retribuetur, vel timens vere retributionem accipiet, ut non Chald. tantum, R. Salomo, sed Vatablus etiam, Pagninus & Mercerus reddunt, a quo vero sensu perperam abit Vulgata: Qui detrahit alicui rei, ipse se in futurum obligat: qui autem timet præceptum, in pace versabitur. Conf. Dn. D. Geier. Commentar. in h. l.

## 13:7
Verse 7.

IS AS IF RICH WHEN HE HAS NOTHING) In the Hebrew: There is one who enriches himself (that is, boasts and proclaims himself rich) and there is nothing to him. These are those whom the Greeks call poor-boasters. See Theophrastus, on boastfulness: and the character of the ostentatious man in book IV of Ad Herennium.

AND IS AS IF POOR WHEN HE IS IN MUCH WEALTH) This is the dissembler to Aristotle: the dissimulator of his own wealth to Horace.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

EST QVASI DIVES CVM NIHIL HABEAT) In Hebræo: Est qui ditat se, (id est, ditem jactat & prædicat) & non est ei quicquam. Hi sunt quos Græci πτωχαλάζονας vocant. Vide Theophrastum, περὶ ἀλαζονείας: & oftentatoris characterem in libro IV. ad Herennium.

ET EST QVASI PAVPER CVM IN MVLTIS DIVITIIS SIT) Hic est εἴρων Aristoteli: dissimulator opis propriæ Horatio.

## 13:8
THE RANSOM OF A MAN'S SOUL IS HIS RICHES: BUT HE WHO IS POOR DOES NOT SUSTAIN REBUKE) These last words among the LXX are thus: but the poor does not withstand a threat. Others: he does not bear a reprimand. They seem to have read for שׁמע, חסך in this sense: A rich man, if any danger threatens him from an enemy, averts it from himself with money: and a poor man, if anyone threatens him, does not remain, but flees. The Vulgate reading can also be explained thus: he does not hear, that is, he does not sustain hearing.

Latin:

REDEMTIO ANIMÆ VIRI DIVITIÆ IPSIVS: QVI AVTEM PAVPER EST, INCREPATIONEM NON SVSTINET) Postrema hæc apud LXX. sic sunt: πτωχὸς δὲ ὐχ ὑφίστατη ἀπειλήν. Alii. ἰ φέρει ἐπιτίμησιν. Vi- dentur pro שׁמע legisse חסך hoc sensu: Vir dives, si quid ei ab inimico periculum immineat, pecuniis id a se avertit: & pauper si quis ei minetur, non manet, sed fugit. Potest & vulgata lectio sic exponi: non audit, id est, non susti- net audire.

## 13:14
Verse 14.

THE LAW OF THE WISE IS A FOUNTAIN OF LIFE TO TURN ASIDE FROM THE RUIN OF DEATH.

There follow now the advantages and fruits of discipline, παιδείας or instruction, and of salutary correction, which is done through the word of God, inasmuch as (1.) from it comes life and a turning aside from the ruin, or snares, and trap (as it is in the Hebrew) of death. (2.) that it gives, or procures, grace before God and men, whereas on the contrary the way of the contemptuous is rough and therefore deformed in the eyes of God and men. Good understanding gives grace: but the way of the contemptuous is hard. (3.) that it ensures that all things are done with knowledge, or counsel, and not after the manner of fools, who by their actions only manifest folly v. 16. Every clever (circumspect and cautious) person acts with knowledge (counsel). But a fool spreads folly; and that we may be able to serve others as faithful envoys, who are health or medicine to the republic, and to those whom they serve: as on the contrary a bad messenger because of his malice falls himself, so far is he from bringing medicine to others, v. 17. A WICKED MESSENGER SHALL FALL INTO EVIL: BUT A FAITHFUL ENVOY (is as) MEDICINE. (4.) that it brings honor and riches v. 18. POVERTY AND DISGRACE TO HIM WHO ABANDONS CORRECTION: BUT HE WHO KEEPS REPROOF SHALL BE HONORED. (5.) that it causes us to obtain our desires, which is sweet to the soul Ps. 145, 19. whereas fools, shunning discipline, to whom it is an abomination to depart from evil, are frustrated in their desire, and grieve eternally v. 19. DESIRE FULFILLED IS SWEET TO THE SOUL: BUT IT IS AN ABOMINATION TO FOOLS TO DEPART FROM EVIL, concerning which compare Mr. Dr. Geier. (6.) that it provides wisdom. For he who walks with the wise shall be wise: but he who is a friend to fools shall not only be made a fool, but shall also be crushed after the manner of fools, v. 20. (7.) that it brings good things v. 21. for when affliction pursues sinners, the righteous (God) renders good: verse 21. and indeed in such a way that the good man makes his children's children inherit (his wealth), not so the sinner, but rather the substance of the sinner is reserved for the righteous verse 22. and that there is much food in the field of the poor, or of him who is of abject lot, in the manner of farmers, if there is not lacking to him מִשְׁפָּט justice, but to his labor there is added just possession, and operation, as the second clause indicates: and there is he who perishes, בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט because there is no justice for him. B. Luth. But those who do wrong, perish. verse 23. Whence Solomon concludes verse 24. He who withholds his rod, in παιδείᾳ or discipline, hates his son: but he who loves him, seeks correction for him, even by applying the rod where it is needed. With the promise added in verse 25, by which he promises the righteous the tranquil possession of the goods of this life, so that they may always have wherewith to satisfy their soul, or the ordered appetite of the soul, whereas on the contrary cursed poverty presses upon the wicked. The righteous eats to the satisfying of his soul: but the belly of the wicked shall want.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

LEX SAPIENTIS FONS VITÆ UT DE- CLINET A RUINA MORTIS.

Sequuntur jam commoda & fructus discipli- næ, παιδείας vel informationis, & correptionis sa- lutaris, quæ fit per verbum Dei, utpote quod (1.) inde vita & declinatio a ruina, vel laqueis, & ten- dicula (ut in Ebr. est) mortis. (2.) quod gratiam det, vel conciliet, coram Deo & hominibus, quum ex adverso contemtorum via aspera adeoque de- formis sit in oculis Dei atque hominum. Intelligen- tia bona dat gratiam: at via contemtorum est dura. (3.) quod præstet, ut omnia cum scientia, vel con- silio agantur, non autem more stultorum, qui actionibus suis tantum manifestant stultitiam v. 16. Omnis callidus (circumspectus & cautus) agit cum scientia (consilio) Stultus autem expandit stultitiam; utque aliis inservire possimus ceu fideles legati, qui sanitas vel medicina sunt reipublicæ, & iis, quibus inserviunt: uti contra nuncius malus propter malitiam suam ruat ipse, tantum abest, ut aliis medicinam adferat, v. 17. NUNTIUS IMPIUS CADET IN MALUM: LEGA- TUS AUTEM VERAX (est velut) MEDI- CINA. (4.) quod honorem & divitias adferat v. 18. PAUPERTAS ET IGNOMINIA DESERENTI CORRECTIONEM: SED QUI CUSTODIT INCREPATIONEM HONORABITUR. (5.) quod faciat nos po- tiri desideriis nostris, quod dulce est animæ Ps. 145, 19. quum stulti disciplinam aversantes, quibus abo- minatio est recedere a malo, desiderio suo frustren- tur, æternum doleant v. 19. DESIDERIUM FACTUM DULCE EST ANIMÆ: AT ABOMINATIO STULTORUM EST RE- CEDERE A MALO, de quo Conf. Dn. D. Geierus. (6.) quod sapientiam præstet. Qui enim cum sapientibus graditur, sapiens erit: at qui stultis amicus, non modo stultus efficietur, sed etiam more stultorum conteretur, v. 20. (7.) quod bona adferat v. 21. quum enim peccatores insecta- tur afflictio, justus reddit (Deus) bonum: vers. 21. & sic quidem, ut bonus hæreditare faciat (opes suas) filios filiorum, non item peccator, quin reservetur potius justo substantia peccatoris vers. 22. utque multus cibus sit in agro pauperis, vel ejus, qui abje- ctæ sortis est, colonorum more, si non desit ei מִשְׁפָּט jus, sed ad laborem ejus accedat justa posses- sio, & operatio, uti comma alterum indicat: & est qui perit, בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט quod non sit ei jus. B. Luth. Aber die unrecht thun, verderben. vers. 23. Unde concludit Salomo vers. 24. Qui subtrahit vir- gam suam, in παιδείᾳ vel disciplina, odit filium suum: sed qui diligit eum, quærit ei correctionem, etiam adhibita, ubi opus est, virga. Addita pro- missione vers. 25. qua justis pollicetur tranquillam bonorum hujus vitæ possessionem, ut habeant semper unde animam, vel appetitum animæ ordi- natum expleant, quum contra impios maledicta premat egestas. Justus comedit ad saturitatem ani- mæ suæ: venter autem impiorum egebit.

## 13:20
Ver. 20. HE THAT WALKETH WITH WISE MEN SHALL BE WISE) As the Greeks say: Wise men are the tyrants of the wise by their company. Theognis: For from the good you shall learn good things; but if you mingle with the bad, you will destroy even the mind that you have. A COMPANION OF FOOLS SHALL BE DESTROYED) For Evil communications corrupt good manners, which the Apostle Paul took from Menander.

Latin:

Verf. 20. QVI CVM SAPIENTIBVS GRADITVR, SAPIENS ERIT) Vt Græci dicunt: Σοφοὶ τύραννοι τῶν σοφῶν συνουσίᾳ. Theognis: Εσθλῶν μὲν γὰρ ἀπ' ἐσθλὰ μαθήσεαι· ἢν δὲ κακοῖσι Συμμιχθῇς, ἀπολεῖς καὶ τὸν ἐόντα νόον. AMICVS STVLTORVM SIMILIS EFFICIETVR) Nam Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρήσθ' ὁμιλίαι κακαί. quod ex Menandro desumpsit Paulus Apostolus.

## 13:24
Ver. 24. HE THAT SPARETH HIS ROD HATETH HIS SON) That is, he has the same outcome as if he had hated him. Thus we are said to will many things, not because we properly will them, but because we do those things from which such consequences follow. See examples in Matt. 26:12, John 12:7, Luke 11:48, Ezek. 18:31, ch. 33:11, where 'why will ye die' is put for 'why do you wish to die.' Similar is Ps. 106:23, above here ch. 8:36, below ch. 17:19.

Latin:

Vers. 24. QVI PARCIT VIRGÆ ODIT FILIVM SVVM) Id est, eundem habet exitum quasi eum odisset. Sic multa dici- mur velle, non quod proprie ea velimus, sed quod ea agi- mus, unde talia consequuntur. Exempla vide Matth. 26, 12. Joh. 12, 7. Luc. 11, 48. Ezech. 18, 31. c. 33, 11. ubi moriemini est positum, pro vultis mori. Simile Ps. 106, 23. supra hic c. 8. v. 36. infra c. 17. v. 19.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV. The attributes of the wise and the foolish according to various states, regarding the mind, speech, works, and affections, as also successes and events.

Ver. 1. EVERY WISE WOMAN BUILDETH HER HOUSE: BUT THE FOOLISH PLUCKETH IT DOWN WITH HER HANDS) A wise woman increases the household property. Thus the Hebrew בנה is often taken.

Because the economic care belongs primarily to the woman, the first part deals with her works and advantages, or disadvantages, according to whether she is wise or foolish: The wise of women buildeth, that is, every wise woman, by a common Hebraism: or the wise among women, that is, among women; for which wisdom not only skill in economic matters, but primarily also the knowledge of divine things is required: since the building of a house also extends to the education of children, and ought to be done in the fear of the Lord, Eph. 6:4, Ps. 127:1, Ps. 128:1, seqq. For 'house' here denotes the family, and 'building' is taken improperly for the adorning, instruction, and amplification of the household property: just as also from the verb בנה are called בנים children, through whom the house is built, Ruth 4:11. Conf. Prov. 24,

3. Since there is a certain conspiracy of mind and works, and the mind of each shines forth in his works, the wise, as those in whose minds the fear of the Lord dominates, are taught to walk in uprightness, but the foolish, who despise the Lord, to pervert their ways, v. 2. And since speech is also an index of the mind, v. 3, it deals with the mouth, tongue, and speech of the wise and the foolish. In the mouth of the foolish is a rod (a staff for striking, for inflicting, namely injuries) of pride: but the lips of the wise shall preserve them, through the governance of Wisdom, so that, namely, they do not harm others. The fool, because he is proud, lashes others with his mouth and tongue as if with a proud rod; that this may not happen, Wisdom provides for the wise.

Moreover, diligence and labor are commended above all, which is necessary in all states, v. 4, to which all who are wise are devoted; because WHERE NO OXEN ARE (laboring ones, whose use is necessary in economy and the cultivation of fields) THE CRIB IS CLEAN: BUT MUCH INCREASE IS BY THE STRENGTH OF THE OX: In the Hebrew, because there is an abundance of crops in the strength of the ox. Conf. ch. 28:19. Which is applied to the Ecclesiastical state, with the Apostle leading the way, 1 Cor. 9:9, from Deut. 25:4, and is transferred to the use of the tongue by Gregory the Great, lib. 3, Registr. Ep. 30, to Eulogius: where there is much increase, there is the strength of the oxen. For if the strong ox had not driven the plow of the tongue into the soil of the heart of the hearers, such a great harvest of the faithful would not have sprung up.

Solomon continues to discuss the use of the tongue, v. 5. A faithful witness will not lie, but a false witness will utter lies: and since wisdom has no place among scorners; for the scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not, just as knowledge is easy to find for the intelligent person who seeks with proper piety and industry, and who lends his ears to wise Teachers, v. 6, therefore Solomon warns, v. 7. Go from the presence of a foolish man; since you do not know (in him) the lips of knowledge, if indeed the wisdom of the prudent is to understand his own way (the rationale of his duty, both regarding the common rule of piety and regarding the special state of his office), and thus even to show it to others, but such cannot be expected from fools: because the stupidity of fools is only deceit, occupied with deceit and frauds v. 8. nay, fools mock or despise sin: but among the upright and those endowed with true wisdom and integrity, not sin, but good pleasure, namely piety worthy of all favor, is found: as those disparage words, so on the contrary, these proclaim and extol the pursuit of piety. This is the gloss of Grotius:

Latin:

CAPUT XIV. Sapientis & stulti attributa secundum varios status, qua animum, sermones, opera, & affectus, ut & successus & eventus.

Vers. 1. SAPIENS MVLIER ÆDIFICAT DOMVM SVAM: INSIPIENS EXSTRVCTAM QVOQVE MANIBVS DESTRVIT) Sapiens mulier auget rem familiarem. Sic sæpe sumitur Hebræum בנה.

QUia mulieris imprimis est cura œconomica, de ejus operibus & commodis, vel incommodis, prout sapiens ea est, vel stolida primum agitur: Sa- pientes mulierum ædificat, id est, unaquæque sapiens mulier, Ebraismo usitato: vel Sapientes mulierum, id est, inter mulieres; ad quam sapientiam non tan- tum peritia rei œconomicæ, sed imprimis etiam notitia rerum divinarum requiritur: quum ædifi- catio domus etiam ad educationem liberorum se porrigat, & in timore Domini fieri debeat Eph. 6, 4. Ps. 127, 1. Ps. 128, 1. seqq. Domus enim hic fami- liam notat, & ædificatio improprie accipitur pro rei familiaris adornatione, instructione, amplificatio- ne: uti etiam a verbo בנה dicuntur בנים liberi, per quos domus ædificatur Ruth. 4, 11. Conf. Prov. 24,

3. Quum vero animi & operum conspiratio quæ- dam sit, & in operibus effulgeat cujusque animus, sapientes, utpote in quorum animis dominatur ti- mor Domini, in rectitudine ambulare, stultos autem qui despiciunt Dominum, vias suas pervertere doce- tur v. 2. Et quum sermo etiam index sit animi v. 3. agitur de Sapientis & stulti ore, lingua, & sermoni- bus. In ore stulti virga (baculus ad feriendum, in- fligendum, nempe injurias) superbiæ: labia autem sapientium custodiunt illos, per Sapientiæ regimen, ne sc. aliis noceant. Stultus, quia superbus est, ore suo & lingua quasi virga superba flagellat alios, quod ne fiat, penes sapientes præcavet Sapientia.

Commendatur autem imprimis sedulitas & labor, quo opus est in omnibus statibus, v. 4. cui dediti sunt quicunque sapiunt; quia UBI NON SUNT BOVES (laborantes, quorum in œconomia & agrorum cultura usus necessarius est) PRÆSEPE VACUUM EST: UBI AUTEM PLURIMÆ SEGETES, IBI MANIFESTA EST FOR- TITUDO BOVIS: In Ebr. quia copia frugum est in fortitudine bovis. Conf. c. 28, 19. Quod statui Ecclesiastico applicatur, præeunte Apostolo 1. Cor. 9, 9. e Deut. 25, 4. & ad linguæ usum transfertur a Gregor. M. l. 3. Registr. Ep. 30. ad Evlog. ubi plurimæ segetes, ibi manifesta est fortitudo boum. Si enim bos fortis aratrum linguæ in terra cordis audientium non transfixisset, tanta fidelium seges minime surrexisset.

Pergit autem de linguæ usu disserere Salomo v. 5. Testis verax non mentitur, loquitur autem menda- cia testis mendax: & quum penes derisores locum non habeat sapientia; quærit enim derisor sapien- tiam, & non (invenit) uti contra intelligenti, decen- te pietate atque industria quærenti, & Doctoribus sapientibus aures præbenti, facilis est (inventu) scientia v. 6. ideo monet Salomo v. 7. Vade a con- spectu viri stulti; quum non noveris (in eo) labia scientiæ, siquidem sapientia prudentis quidem sit viam suam (officii sui rationem, tum quoad com- munem pietatis regulam, tum quoad specialem statum muneris) intelligere, adeoque aliis etiam ostendere, sed a stultis tale expectari non potest: quia stoliditas stultorum solum dolus, circa dolum & fraudes occupatur v. 8. imo stulti illudunt vel vili- pendunt peccatum: inter rectos autem vera sapien- tia & integritate præditos non peccatum, sed bene- placitum, pietas nempe omni favore digna reperi- tur: ut illi extenuant dicta, ita contra, hi depræ- dicant, & extollunt pietatis studium. Grotii hæc est glossa:

## 14:9
Vers. 9. A FOOL WILL MOCK AT SIN, BUT AMONG THE RIGHTEOUS THERE IS GOODWILL)

Fools excuse one another's sins, and among the righteous there is (truly, that is) benevolence. To wish the same and to refuse the same is faction among the wicked, but friendship among the good: the similarity of vices joins the former; an equal pursuit of the honorable joins the latter. Τελεία δ' ἐςιν ἡ τῶν ἀγαθῶν φιλία καὶ κατ' ἀρετὴν ὁμοίων. Aristot. Ethic. 8, 4.

In Hebrew: The heart knows the bitterness of its own soul: and in its joy a stranger will not intermingle. The heart itself, which feels them, is hinted at as the most certain arbiter of the affections of sadness and joy. See 1 Cor. 2, 17. Since (as conscience dictates) not only the wicked, but also their families are destroyed, as is held in v. 11: the house of the wicked shall be destroyed, but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish, Ps. 92, 14. nor does feigned piety have this happiness or joy of heart as its companion: but sincere piety does: For what Solomon says in v. 12: There is a way that is right before a man (i.e., in the eyes of a fool, ch. 12. 15.) but the end thereof are the ways of death: Whence also IN LAUGHTER THE HEART IS SORROWFUL, when conscience is awakened, or we foresee danger, AND THE END OF MIRTH IS HEAVINESS v. 13. because THE BACKSLIDER IN HEART SHALL BE FILLED WITH HIS OWN WAYS, BUT A GOOD MAN (shall be satisfied from himself, which is to be repeated from the common source) v. 14.
