Thus, with Mercer and the Belgians, Mr. Dr. Gejerus renders it: Buxtorf in his Anti-Crit. p. 579, who should be consulted, satisfied Capellus, who was here suspecting a corruption of the text.

Latin:

Vers. 9. STVLTVS ILLVDET PECCATVM, ET INTER JVSTOS MORABITVR GRATIA)

Stulti excusant alii aliorum peccata, & inter justos est (vere scilicet) benevolentia. Idem velle atque idem nolle inter malos factio, inter bonos amicitia est: illos jungit vitiorum similitudo: hos par ho- nesti studium. Τελεία δ' ἐςιν ἡ τῶν ἀγαθῶν φιλία καὶ κατ' ἀρετὴν ὁμοίων. Aristot. Ethic. 8, 4.

In Ebr. Cor cognoscit amaritudinem animæ suæ: & in lætitia ipsius non immiscebitur alienus. Affe- ctus tristitiæ, & lætitiæ cordis arbiter certissimus cor ipsum, quod eosdem sentit, innuitur. Vid. 1. Cor. 2, 17. Siquidem (conscientia dictitante) non impii tantum, sed etiam familiæ eorum deleantur, uti v. 11. habetur: domus impiorum delebitur, taber- naculum autem rectorum florebit, Ps. 92, 14. neque pietas fucata hanc felicitatem vel lætitiam cordis comitem habeat: sed sincera: Nam quod v. 12. ait Salomo: Est via recta coram viro (in oculis sc. stul- ti c. 12. 15.) at exitus ejus viæ mortis: Unde etiam IN RISU DOLET COR, cum excitatur con- scientia, vel periculum præsentiscimus, ET EXI- TUS LÆTITIÆ TRISTITIA v. 13. quia VIIS SUIS SATURABITUR AVERSUS CORDE, AT EX SESE (viis itidem suis sa- turabitur, quod ἀπὸ κοινῶ repetendum) VIR BONUS v. 14. Ita cum Mercero, & Belgis reddit Dn. D. Gejerus: Capello de textus corruptio- ne hic suspicanti satisfecit Buxtorff. Anti-Crit. p. 579. qui videatur.

## 14:15
Vers. 15. THE SIMPLE BELIEVETH EVERY WORD: BUT THE PRUDENT MAN LOOKETH WELL TO HIS GOING.

Cornelius rightly corrects the Vulgate, since פתי signifies an inexperienced and unwise person, whose excessive ease and levity is relaxed toward believing anything, whereby it happens that he allows himself to be led by the fraudulent and enemies into destruction and ruin, whereas on the contrary, the cautious and prudent man by no means believes every word and counsel, but considers his steps, where he may securely plant the foot of his action. The Vulgate adds a sentence from the LXX Interpreters, but which is not held in the Hebrew: To a deceitful son there shall be nothing good: but to a wise servant there shall be prosperous acts, and his way shall be directed. But in the source, it follows more conveniently: A WISE MAN FEARETH and is prudent, lest he be seduced to evil, v. 16. A wise man feareth and departeth from evil, but a fool rageth, or rather makes himself transgress the prescribed limits of the laws (Conf. ch. 22, 3. Hab. 1, 11.) and does not fear, but is confident. Rashly does Capellus from the Chaldean and the LXX contend that the text is to be amended, or read otherwise: whom Buxtorf refutes in Anti-Crit. p. 647.

Latin:

Vers. 15. INNOCENS CREDIT OMNI VERBO: ASTUTUS CONSIDERAT GRESSUS SUOS.

Recte corrigit Vulg. Cornelius, siquidem פתי imperitum, & insipientem significet, cujus nimia facilitas & levitas ad credendum quodvis laxetur, quo fit, ut sinat se a fraudulentis & inimicis in per- niciem & ruinam duci, quum ex adverso cautus & prudens minime credat omni verbo & consilio, sed gressus suos consideret, ubi secure actionis suæ pe- dem figat. Addit Vulgata sententiam ex LXX. In- terpp. sed quæ non habetur in Ebræo: Filio doloso nihil erit boni: servo autem sapienti prosperi erunt actus, & dirigetur via ejus. Sequitur autem in fonte convenientius SAPIENTIS METUS & prudentia ne ad malum seducatur, v. 16. Sapiens timet & recedit a malo, sed stultus transilit, vel po- tius transgredi seipsum facit præscriptos legum ter- minos (Conf. c. 22, 3. Hab. 1, 11.) nec metuit, sed confidit. Temere Capellus e Chald. & LXX. con- tendit emendandum, vel aliter legendum esse tex- tum: quem refellit Buxtorff. in Anti-Crit. p. 647.

## 14:17
Vers. 17. THE IMPATIENT MAN WILL WORK FOLLY; AND A CRAFTY MAN IS HATEFUL.

These things concern the emotion of anger. In the Hebrew they are thus: He who is quickly angered, commits folly: and a man of machinations is held in hatred: he who indeed knows how to repress anger outwardly, but in his heart meditates revenge, who is hateful to God, and when he betrays himself, to all good men. Mercerus says he compares two contrary vices, headlong anger and long-meditated malice. Solomon adds in v. 18 that this is as it were the proper inheritance of the ignorant and foolish, folly, because they retain the same perpetually, and do not leave their stupid custom, but cherish and guard it like a possession, whereas the prudent are crowned with knowledge, they seek and embrace knowledge as a crown with which they are adorned, by which consequently they are also girded and decorated.

Latin:

Vers. 17. IMPATIENS OPERABITUR STULTITI- AM; ET VIR VERSUTUS ODIOSUS EST.

Hæc affectum iræ concernunt. In Ebr. ita ha- bent: Qui cito irascitur, facit stultitiam : & vir machinationum odio babetur: qui iram quidem ex- trinfecus reprimere novit, sed corde suo meditatur vindictam, qui Deo, & cum se prodit, bonis omni- bus exosus est. Mercerus, confert, inquit, duo vitia contraria, iram præcipitem, & diu meditatam ma- litiam. Addit Salomo v. 18. quod imperitorum & insipientium hæc veluti propria sit hæreditas stulti- tia, quod eandem perpetuo retineant, & stolidam suam consuetudinem non relinquant, sed uti pof- sessionem foveant, & custodiant, prudentes autem scientia coronentur, scientiam ceu coronam, qua ornentur, ambiant, & amplectantur, qua conse- quenter etiam cinguntur & decorantur.

## 14:19
Vers. 19. THE EVIL SHALL LIE BEFORE THE GOOD: AND THE WICKED BEFORE THE GATES OF THE JUST.

There follow therefore now the successes and outcomes of the wise, who are good and upright, and of the wicked, who are foolish, that although the latter may pant after riches, it happens nevertheless that the evil are forced to bow themselves before the good, and the wicked to wait at the gates of the just, which humiliation will not only happen in the future age, as R. Solomon, Bede, and Hugo interpret, but also not rarely occurs in this age: when the pious are exalted by God, and the wicked are overturned, Luke 1:52. And although it is the custom of this age, as the following proverb v. 20 has it, that the poor man is hateful even to his friend, piety being set aside, while the rich man is loved by many, James 2:2, yet whoever despises his neighbor (especially the miserable) sins, but blessed is he who has mercy on the poor: Cf. v. 31, chap. 19:17, Psalm 37:25, 26, Matthew 5:7, whom God cherishes and embraces with His grace, when they are upright, and exalts in His own time, 1 Peter 5:6. The Vulgate adds. He who believes in the Lord, loves mercy: but these words are not found in the LXX, Chaldean, or Syriac, nor, which is the main thing, in the Hebrew, and they are also disapproved of by Cajetan.

riches are not a crown, but because they cannot use them, they are a loss and a disgrace, as the Chaldean translates, and the glory of fools is their folly. A fool with all that he has, is, and remains a fool, as B. Luther rendered it. An ape is an ape, even if it wears golden insignia.

Latin:

Vers. 19. JACEBUNT MALI ANTE BONOS: ET IMPII ANTE PORTAS JUSTORUM.

Sequuntur ergo jam sapientum, qui boni & in- tegri, & impiorum, qui insipientes sunt, successus, & eventus, quod etsi hi divitiis inhient, eveniat tamen ut incurvare se mali coram bonis, & impii præstolari cogantur ad fores justi, quæ humiliatio non tantum in futuro seculo continget, ut R. Salomo, Beda, & Hugo interpretantur, sed etiam non raro in hoc se- culo sit: cum pii à Deo exaltantur, impii deturban- tur, Luc. 1, 52. & quamvis hujus seculi mos sit, quod paræmia sequens v. 20. habet, ut pauper etiam ami- co suo odio sit, posthabita pietate, dives autem à mul tis diligatur, Jac. 2, 2. peccat tamen quisquis proxi- mum suum (miserum imprimis) contemnit, at bea- tus ille est, qui pauperum miseretur: Conf. v. 31. cap. 19, 17. Pfalm. 37, 25. 26. Matth. 5, 7. quos Deus gratia sua fovet, & amplectitur, cum probi sunt, suoque tempore exaltat, 1. Petr. 5, 6. Addit Vulg. Qui cre- dit in Domino, misericordiam diligit: sed hæc ver- ba nec apud LXX. Chald. Syr. nec quod præcipuum est, in Ebræo habentur, & à Cajetan. etiam impro- bantur.

divitiæ non sunt corona, sed quia iis uti nequeunt, damno & dedecori, ut Chald. vertit, & decus stui- torum stultitia eorum. Stultus cum omnibus quæ ha- bet, est, & manet stultus, ut B. Luther. reddidit. Simia est simia, etiamsi aurea gestet insignia.

## 14:22
Vers. 22. THEY ERR WHO WORK EVIL: BUT MERCY AND TRUTH PREPARE GOOD THINGS.

The latter colon, by the force of the words and the opposition, is to be rendered thus: but grace and truth to those who think on good. Wisdom, which is according to God, looks to these fruits, those endowed with which do not meditate or work evil, but good: and they obtain the grace of God and perceive the truth of the divine promises: whereas, on the contrary, the foolish, by machinating evil, err not only from the divine law, and therefore from God himself, by an error both of judgment and speculative, and also of appetite and practical, but also from the prefixed end of happiness, and they are rendered liable to the divine wrath and the evils of punishment which God threatens to transgressors.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ERRANT QUI OPERANTUR MALUM: MISERICORDIA ET VERITAS PRÆPARANT BONA.

Posterius colon vi verborum, & oppositionis ita reddendum: at gratia & veritas cogitantibus bonum. Ad fructus hos spectat sapientia, quæ est secundum Deum, qua præditi non malum medi- tantur, vel operantur, sed bonum: ac gratiam Dei consequuntur & promissionum divinarum verita- tem sentiunt: quum ex adverso insipientes malum machinantes errent non solum à lege divina, adeo- que à Deo ipso, errore tum judicii & speculativo, tum appetitus quoque & practico, sed etiam à fine præfixo felicitatis, iræque divinæ & malis pœnæ, quæ minatur prævaricatoribus DEus, obnoxii red- duntur.

## 14:23
Vers. 23. IN EVERY WORK THERE SHALL BE ABUNDANCE, BUT WHERE THERE ARE MANY WORDS, THERE IS FREQUENTLY WANT.

Latin:

Vers. 23. IN OMNI OPERE ERIT ABUN- DANTIA, UBI AUTEM VERBA SUNT PLURIMA, IBI FREQUENTER EGESTAS.

## 14:25
Vers. 25. A FAITHFUL WITNESS DELIVERS SOULS: AND A DECEITFUL ONE UTTERS LIES.

Or A WITNESS OF DECEIT, that is, deceitful. The fruit of truthfulness and the consequence of lies, because Solomon had warned about the use of the tongue, is thus inculcated, that a truthful witness rescues souls, i.e., delivers men from death and other dangers: for soul is put for man by synecdoche: but a deceitful man breathes out lies, and by them subjects others to dangers, v. 5, chap. 12, v. 17. To the consequences and fruits of the fear of the Lord, which is proper to the wise man according to God, pertains also v. 26. In the fear of Jehovah is the confidence of strength, and to his (i.e., the Lord's) children there will be hope. For what is added in v. 27, the fear of the Lord is as a fountain of life, chap. 13, v. 14, chap. 10, v. 11, Jeremiah 17, v. 13, so that one may depart from the snares of death. Which is not to be drawn to justification, as if we were justified dispositively through the fear of the Lord, as is done by the Papists, but because the fear of the Lord embraces faith primarily, since in the fear of the Lord there is confidence, as Solomon had said before, it must be believed that this is attributed to the fear of the Lord for its sake, provided that we are justified by faith alone, not by holiness and reverence toward God. For therefore those who fear God, says this Jesuit Cornelius here, are strong and robust, because they have placed all their confidence in God almighty.

Latin:

Vers. 25. LIBERAT ANIMAS TESTIS FIDELIS: ET PROFERT MENDACIA VERSIPEL- LIS.

Vel TESTIS DOLI, id est, dolosus. Fructus veracitatis, & consequens mendaciorum, quia de linguæ usu monuerat Salomo, ita inculcatur, quod testis verax animas eruat, h. e. homines è mortis aliisque periculis liberet: anima enim pro homine per Synecdochen ponitur: dolosus autem menda- cia efflet, iisque alios periculis subjiciat, v. 5. cap. 12, v. 17. Ad consequentia & fructus timoris Domi- ni, qui sapienti secundum DEum proprius est, pertinet quoque v. 26. In timore Jehovæ est fiducia fortitudinis, & filiis ejus (Domini scil.) erit spes. Nam quod v. 27. additur, timor Domini est velut vena vitæ, cap. 13. v. 14. cap. 10, v. 11. Jerem. 17. v. 13. ut recedatur à laqueis mortis. Quod non trahen- dum ad justificationem, quasi per timorem Domi- ni dispositive justificemur, uti à Papistis fit, sed quia timor Domini fidem imprimis complectitur, quum in timore Domini fiducia sit, uti antea Salomo di- xerat, ejus gratia timori Domini hoc tribui cre- dendum est, siquidem sola fide justificemur, non sanctitate & reverentia erga Deum. Ideo enim timen- tes Deum, inquit hic Cornelius Jesuita, sunt fortes, & robusti, quia omnem suam fiduciam collocarunt in Deo omnipotente.

## 14:28
Vers. 28. IN THE MULTITUDE OF THE PEOPLE IS THE KING'S DIGNITY; AND IN THE FEWNESS OF THE PEOPLE THE DISGRACE OF THE PRINCE] The author of the questions to the Orthodox: πικροτάτη τιμωρία ἡ ἡμαρτηκότων βασιλέων ἡ τιμωρία τῷ λαοῦ. See 2 Sam. 24.

These things also can be referred to the consequences of wisdom. For the discourse is about a multitude rightly instructed and composed, which alone brings honor and strength to a prince, nor does it have a place without true wisdom. chap. 11. v. 14. In the Hebrew, in the second member, there is the attrition of the prince: whence to a King governing the people wisely and preserving the multitude, not only dignity but also the preservation of the kingdom is attributed; but to him whose subjects are reduced to fewness by his foolishness, both disgrace and destruction are attributed by way of opposition. There follows v. 29. Slow to anger, (because long-suffering and patience especially befit princes if they wish to rule happily: for he who does not know how to dissemble, does not know how to rule) of much understanding, and he who is short of spirit exalts folly, (conf. Eccles. 7. v. 8. makes the same conspicuous, as if placed on high) and v. 30. The life of the flesh is a mild heart (the fruit and consequence of mildness is the life and prosperity of the flesh or of man) and envy is the rottenness of the bones, i.e., the vehemence of anger, which is a synecdoche of the species for the genus. Therefore, in order to dissuade especially Princes and Magistrates from this, he adds v. 31. He who oppresses the poor, insults his maker, the author of his misery (which cannot but result unhappily. Conf. chap. 17. v. 5. chap. 22. v. 2. 1 Sam. 2. v. 7.) just as, on the contrary, he who has mercy on the poor, honors him.

Latin:

Vers. 28. IN MULTITUDINE POPULI DIGNITAS REGIS; ET IN PAUCITATE PLEBIS IGNOMINIA PRINCI- PIS] Scriptor quæstionum ad Orthodoxos: πικροτάτη τι- μωρία ἡ ἡμαρτηκότων βασιλέων ἡ τιμωρία τῷ λαοῦ. Vide 2. Sam. 24.

Hæc etiam ad sapientiæ consequentia referri pof- sunt. Sermo enim de multitudine rite instructa, composita, quæ sola decus & robur affert prin- cipi, nec sine sapientia vera locum habet. cap. 11. v. 14. In Ebr. in membro altero est Attritio prin- cipis: unde Regi sapienter populum gubernanti, & multitudinem conservanti non tantum dignitas, sed etiam regni conservatio, illi autem cujus in- sipientia subditi ad paucitatem rediguntur, & igno- minia, & interitus, vi oppositionis, tribuitur. Se- quitur v. 29. Tardus ira, (quia longanimitas & pa- tientia imprimis decet principes, si feliciter impe- rare velint: qui enim nescit dissimulare, nescit imperare) multus intelligentia, & brevis spiritu ex- altat stultitiam, (conf. Eccles. 7. v. 8. conspicuam eandem reddit, ceu in sublimi collocatam) & v. 30. Vita carnium est cor lene (fructus & consequens lenitatis vita & prosperitas carnis vel hominis) & putredo ossium Zelotypia, i. e. iræ vehementia, quæ Synecdoche speciei pro genere. Ab hac ergo ut dehortetur imprimis etiam Principes & Magistra- tus, subjicit v. 31. Qui opprimit pauperem, probris afficit factorem ejus, autorem miseriæ ejus (quod non potest non cedere infeliciter. Conf. cap. 17. v. 5. cap. 22. v. 2. 1. Sam. 2. v. 7.) uti contra qui misere- tur pauperis, honorat eum.

## 14:30
Vers. 30. ENVY IS THE ROTTENNESS OF THE BONES] Rottenness in Hebrew is a general noun, under which is also included the woodworm. Menander:

In the Hebrew, in all labor there is abundance, but the word of the lips is destined for want. Because the wise are commended before for their industriousness, abundance is promised to them as fruit from it, just as on the contrary, want follows the empty verbosity of the lips, which is opposed to strenuous labor. Cf. chap. 11, 24.

Young man, whom you seem to me to observe, that each thing is corrupted by its own vice, and all things that harm are within: just as rust is to iron, if you look,

Whence according to v. 24, the crown of the wise is their riches, but the folly of fools is folly, that is, all the glory of fools is folly, even if they are rich,

So that it is a worm, like moths; but the consumption, wood. And the worst of all evils is envy; it has made, and makes, and will make the consumptive, ungodly attendant of a wicked soul.

Latin:

Vers. 30. PUTREDO OSSIUM INVIDIA) Putredo in Hebræo nomen est generale, sub quo comprehenditur & teredo. Me- nander:

In Ebræo, in omni labore est abundantia, sed verbum labiorum sancitum est ad inopiam. Quia à laboriositate sapientes commendati antea, fructus illis inde promittitur abundantia, uti ex adverso inanem labiorum verbositatem, quæ labori stre- nuo opponitur, inopia sequitur. Conf. cap. 11, 24.

Μειράκιον ὅ μοι κατανοεῖν δοκεῖς, ὅτι Ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἕκαςα κακίας σήπεται, Καὶ πάντα τὰ λυμαινόμεν᾽ ἔνεςι ἔνδοθεν· Οἷον ὁ μὲν ἰὸς τὸν σίδηρον, ἂν σκοπῆς,

Unde juxta v. 24. corona sapientum divitiæ eorum, stultitia autem stultorum stultitia, id est, omne decus stultorum est stultitia, stultis etiamsi divites sint,

Ὤστ᾿ ἐνικάτιον, ὡς σῆτες· ἡ δὲ φθὺψ, ξύλον. Ὁ δὲ τὸ κάκισον ὧ κακῶν πάντων φθόνος· Φθισικὸν πεποίηκε κὰι ποίησ᾽ κὰι ποιεῖ Ψυχῆς πονηρᾶς δυσσεβὴς παραστάτης.

## 14:31
Vers. 31.

HE WHO OPPRESSES THE NEEDY, INSULTS HIS MAKER. BUT HE HONORS HIM WHO HAS MERCY ON THE POOR. THE WICKED WILL BE DRIVEN OUT IN HIS MALICE: BUT THE JUST MAN HOPES IN HIS DEATH. Understand 'malice' here as adverse circumstances, as in Matthew 6:34. Nor is anything else understood here by the name of death, although a more sublime sense lies hidden, which Christians understand very well.

It is a consequence of impiety that the wicked man, in his misfortune—as the blessed Luther rightly, along with R. Levi, Piscator, and the Belgians, holds—does not stand firm, nor does he know how to sustain himself with hope, but collapses; whereas, on the contrary, the just man hopes and trusts even in his very death, that he will either struggle through or certainly not perish even while dying. Psalm 68:21; John 5:24. Grotius also accepts it thus: 'Understand malice here,' he says, 'as adverse circumstances, as in Matthew 6:34.' He adds: 'Nor is anything else understood here by the name of death, although a more sublime sense lies hidden, which Christians understand very well.' But why should the name of death not be understood literally? Why should the sense regarding the hope of eternal life be restricted to the New Testament (which is what Grotius wants), when the faithful in the Old Testament, who had the same hope of salvation as we do, were by no means destitute of it? He hints that this hope belongs to the truly wise in the following verses, 33: wisdom rests in the heart of the intelligent: but in the midst of fools it is known, not folly, which the Chaldean Junius, Piscator, and the Belgians rashly insert, but wisdom itself, which is hidden in the heart of the wise man, exerts itself in the midst of fools (as in a theater for the exercise of virtue), and is recognized there; and it also instructs the unlearned, to which the Vulgate and the version of the blessed Luther incline: whence, just as a wise man often delivers a city through his wisdom, Ecclesiastes 9:14, 16, 17, it is taught in the following verse, that the justice of the wise exalts a whole nation: understand justice both in general, or universal, and especially distributive, which gives to each his own right: but that sin (which is the opposite of justice) is a reproach to peoples: because it cannot be denied that חסד sometimes denotes ignominy or reproach, even if that acceptance is rarer, and the antithesis demands this sense, to which the Belgians, as well as the blessed Luther, accede along with the Chaldean, Syriac, Vulgate, and Piscator. If you listen to Grotius, this is the best version: beneficence is the expiation of a people, which renders this meaning: that by those works which are not owed, I do not now say by natural law, but not even by the law of Moses, which otherwise enjoined many duties toward fellow countrymen, many sins are expiated. Although the Jesuit Cornelius brings this meaning from Vatablus, he nevertheless grants that the Vulgate renders it more aptly: nor is there need that we descend to an improper meaning of the word חסד, when there is a place for the proper one: not to mention that, since mercy cannot properly be called an expiatory sacrifice before God, it is only metaphorically implied that by mercy those are also reconciled to such a people who were otherwise hostile to it. And because Solomon had dealt with the King and the kingdom, he concludes with this sentence in verse 35: the good pleasure of the king is toward a servant who acts with understanding, but his fury will be against one who causes shame, who is stupid, and therefore does not know how to preserve the King's reputation, but affects him with shame.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

QVI CALVMNIATVR EGENTEM, EXPROBRAT FACTORI EJVS. HONORAT AVTEM EVM, QVI MISERETVR PAVPERIS. IN MALITIA SVA EXPELLETVR IMPIVS: SPERAT AVTEM JVSTVS IN MORTE SVA) Malitiam hîc intellige res adversas, ut Matth. 6, 34. Nec aliud hîc intelligitur mortis nomine, quanquam latet sensus sublimior, quem Christiani optime intelligunt.

Consequens impietatis est, quod impius in suo infortunio, ut recte B. Lutherus cum R. Levi, Piscatore, & Belgis, non consistat, neque spe sustentare se norit, sed corruat, quum ex adverso justus etiam in ipsa morte sua speret, & confidat, se, vel eluctaturum, vel certe morientem etiam non periturum Pfalm. 68, 21. Joh. 5, 24. Sic etiam Grotius accipit: Malitiam hîc intellige, inquit, res adversas, ut Matth. 6, 34. Addit: Nec aliud hîc intelligitur mortis nomine, quanquam latet sensus sublimior, quem Christiani optime intelligunt. Sed cur non mortis nomen intelligendum proprie? cur ad N. Test. (quod vult Grotius) sensus de spe vitæ æternæ restringendus, quum eo destituti minime fuerint fideles in V. Test. qui eandem nobiscum spem salutis habuerunt? Hanc autem spem vere sapientis esse vers. seqq. 33. innuit: in corde intelligentis requiescit sapientia: at in medio stultorum cognoscitur, non stultitia, quam Chald. Junius, Piscator, Belgæ temere ingerunt, sed ipsa sapientia, quæ abscondita in corde sapientis, sese in medio stultorum (ceu theatro exercendæ virtutis) exerat, ibique agnoscatur: & indoctos quoque erudiat, quo Vulgata abit, ac B. Lutheri versio: Unde uti sapiens per sapientiam suam urbem sæpe liberat, Eccles. 9, 14. 16. 17. docetur versu sequenti, justitiam sapientum exaltare gentem integram: intellige justitiam tum in genere, seu universalem, tum imprimis distributivam, quæ unicuique jus suum tribuit: peccatum autem (quod justitiæ est oppositum) populis esse opprobrium: quia חסד nonnunquam ignominiam, vel opprobrium notare, negari nequit, etsi rarior sit illa acceptio, & sensum istum postulat ἀντίθεσις, cui accedunt cum Chald. Syr. Vulgat. Piscat. Belgæ, ut & B. Lutherus. Grotium si audias, optima versio hæc est: beneficentia expiatio est populi, qui hunc sensum reddit: operibus illis, quæ non debentur, non jam dico lege naturali, sed nec lege Mosis, quæ alioqui multa officia in populares præcepit, multa peccata expiari. Quem sensum etsi Cornelius Jesuita è Vatablo adferat, magis tamen apposite Vulgatum reddere largitur: neque opus est, ut ad impropriam vocis חסד significationem descendamus, quum propriæ locus sit: ut taceam, quod quum proprie sacrificium expiatorium coram Deo dici non possit misericordia, metaphorice sic tantum innuatur, tali genti etiam eos reconciliari per misericordiam, qui ei infensi alias erant. Et quia de Rege, & regno egerat Salomo, concludit hac sententia vers. 35. beneplacitum regis est erga servum intelligentem, furor autem ejus erit contra pudefacientem, qui stupidus est, adeoque Regis existimationem conservare nescit, sed pudore eum afficit.

## 14:34
Verse 34.

JUSTICE EXALTS A NATION, AND BENEFICENCE IS THE EXPIATION OF A PEOPLE) This is the best version: Justice exalts a nation: and beneficence is the expiation of a people. The former clause is the same as that which is in the old Greek oracle:

The offspring of a man who keeps his oath is better hereafter. The latter means this, that by those works which are not owed, I do not now say by natural law, but not even by the law of Moses, which otherwise enjoined many duties toward fellow countrymen, many sins are expiated. For expiation no less than crime is signified by the word חטאת. Concerning the distinction of the word צדק and חסד we said some things in De Jure Belli ac Pacis 2. c. 14, 6. so that we may not repeat the same, see what we said on Luke 11, 41.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

JVSTITIA ELEVAT GENTEM, ET MISERICORDIA POPVLORVM PECCATVM) Optima versio hæc est: Justitia exaltat gentem: & beneficentia expiatio est populi. Prius comma idem est cum illo, quod est in veteri oraculo Græco:

Ἀνδρὸς δ' εὐόρκε γενεὰ μετόπισθεν ἀμέινων. Alterum hoc vult, operibus illis, quæ non debentur, non jam dico lege naturali, sed nec lege Mosis, quæ alioqui multa of- ficia in populares præcepit, multa peccata expiari. Nam ex- piatio non minus quam crimen significantur voce חטאת. De discrimine vocis צדק & חסד diximus quædam de Jure Bel- li ac Pacis 2. c. 14, 6. ne idem repetamus, vide quæ diximus ad Luc. 11, 41.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV.

Again he pursues some affections of the wise and the foolish, as also the advantages and disadvantages, regarding the moderation of the tongue, the admission of doctrine, and the condition, character, and pursuits of the heart.

Verse 1.

A SOFT ANSWER BREAKS WRATH: A HARSH WORD STIRS UP FURY.

To the moderation of the tongue (1.) pertains the softness or gentleness of words, which is necessary in a response, that is (by Synecdoche) in any speech, as is clear from the other member, especially for averting anger. Cf. Sirach 38:14, Judges 8:2, Chrysostom, homily 3 on David and Saul. Just as if you blow into a spark of fire, you excite a conflagration, if you spit upon it, you extinguish it: the same is true in the enmity of a neighbor; if you introduce puffed-up and senseless words, you excite a fire, but if you introduce mild and moderate ones, you will have extinguished the anger entirely. (2.) Cautious speech: THE TONGUE OF THE WISE WILL ADORN KNOWLEDGE, both so that it may be occupied with such things as pertain to knowledge, and so that it may render it pleasing and lovable, and instill it sweetly, and it may be seasoned with grace: and so that it may propose each thing in its own time and place. Cf. here what is said concerning the tongue and eloquence of the Doctors of the Church from Jerome, Plato, Cornelius à Lapide. THE MOUTH OF FOOLS BUBBLES OVER WITH FOLLY. For as Jerome according to the quality of the food, a belch erupts from the stomach, and it is an indication of a good or bad odor: so the words of a man bring forth his inner thoughts, and out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. From foolish conversations, scurrilities, and vanities, the meditation on the omnipresence of the Lord can especially recall us; therefore it is added in verse 3: the eyes of the Lord are in every place, contemplating the good and the evil, and observing their gestures, speeches, and works. Job 34:20, Psalm 11:4, Psalm 34:15, since according to Thales, not even the thoughts, much less the deeds of men, escape God. God is all sense, all sight, all hearing, or Pliny, book 2, chapter 7. (3.) Wholesomeness, or health of the tongue, so that it proposes nothing but what is wholesome and sound: The health of the tongue is a tree of life: and perversity in it is a breaking of the Spirit or of the mind, v. 4. Sound here is not the Vulgate version, while it renders: a placable tongue, likewise, but that which is immoderate.

Latin:

CAPUT XV.

Iterum affectiones sapientum & stultorum nonnullas, ut & commoda & incommoda persequitur, qua linguæ moderationem, admissionem doctrinæ, & cordis conditio- nem, indolem, ac studia.

Vers. 1.

RESPONSIO MOLLIS FRANGIT IRAM: SERMO DURUS SUSCITAT FUROREM.

AD linguæ moderamen (1.) verborum pertinet mollities vel lenitas, qua opus est in respon- sione, h. e. (per Synecdochen) quovis sermone, ut ex altero membro liquet, imprimis ad averten- dam iram. Conf. Sirac. 38, 14. Judic. 8, 2. Chry- sostom. hom. 3. de Davide & Saul. Sicut si infles in scintillam ignis, excitas incendium, Si inspuis, ex- tinguis: idem sit in inimicitia proximi, si inflatos ac vecordes ingeras sermones, excitas ignem, sin mites ac moderatos, iram omnino extinxeris. (2.) Sermo cautus: LINGUA SAPIENTUM ORNABIT SCIENTIAM, tum ut circa talia, quæ ad scien- tiam faciunt occupetur, tum ut eam gratam red- dat & amabilem, ac instillet suaviter, & gratia condita sit: tum ut suo quæque tempore & loco proponat. Conf. hîc, quæ de lingua & eloquen- tia Doctorum Ecclesiæ ex Hieron. Plat. Cornel. à Lapid. OS FATUORUM EBULLIT STUL- TITIAM. Nam ut Hieronym. juxta qualitatem ciborum ê stomacho ructus erumpit, & boni, vel ma- li odoris indicium est: ita interiores hominis cogita- tiones verba proferunt, & ex abundantia cordis os lo- quitur. A stultis autem sermocinationibus, scur- rilitatibus & vanitatibus imprimis nos omnipræsen- tiæ Domini meditatio revocare potest, ideo addi- tur vers. 3. in omni loco oculi Domini: contemplantes bonos & malos, eorumque observantes gestus, ser- mones, & opera Job. 34, 20. Psalm. 11, 4. Psalm. 34, 15. siquidem juxta Thaletem ne cogitata quidem, ne- dum facta hominum Deum lateant. Deus totus est sensus, totus visus, totus auditus, aut Plinius lib. 2. cap. 7. (3.) Salubritas, vel sanitas linguæ, ut non nisi ea, quæ salubria & sana sunt proponat: Sani- tas linguæ est lignum vitæ: & perversitas in ea est confractio Spiritus vel animi v. 4. Sana hîc non est versio vulgata, dum reddit: lingua placabilis, item, quæ autem immoderata est.

## 15:5
Verse 5.

A FOOL MOCKS THE DISCIPLINE OF HIS FATHER: BUT HE WHO KEEPS REPROOFS WILL BECOME MORE ASTUTE.

As for the admission of doctrine (1.) He is judged a fool who despises the correction or chastisement of a Father, or of one who is in the place of a Father, inasmuch as he indulges in brutish desires: but he who observes reproof attains true wisdom. The Vulgate adds with the LXX Interpreters: In abundant justice there is greatest virtue, but the thoughts of the wicked will be rooted out. But these are found neither in the Hebrew, nor in the Chaldean, nor in the ancient Latin Codices, and for that reason they are spurious. Added is (2.) the fruit of the admission of doctrine among the righteous v. 6. In the house of the righteous is great treasure, but in the income of the wicked is not treasure, but mere disturbance. And (3.) the reason why one must adhere to the wise, v. 7. because the lips of the wise spread knowledge, but the heart of fools not so: (since lips and heart cohere most tightly) which prefers to be occupied with trifles and vanities: and especially, because we learn the true worship of God from the wise θεοδιδάκτοις, which sacrifices are pleasing to God, which prayers are acceptable, since not every sacrifice is pleasing to God, not every prayer acceptable before God. The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, inasmuch as it is not joined with faith Gen. 4, 4. Heb. 11, 4. Psalm 50, 8. Isa. 1, 11. But the prayer of the upright is his good pleasure. Concerning which sentence in the Canon Law 3. quest. 7. c. 5. this observation is deduced: For in the judgment of the Almighty it is not looked at what is given, but by whom it is given: Hence it is that it is written: The Lord looked upon Abel, and upon his gifts: but upon Cain and upon his gifts he did not look. For intending to say that the Lord looked upon the gifts, he carefully premised that he looked upon Abel. From which thing it is patently shown that the gifts did not please because of the offerer, but the offerer because of the gifts. For the Most High does not approve the gifts of the iniquitous, nor does he look upon their oblations. Where it is highly ἄτοπον, καὶ ἀθεόλογον that Cornelius, along with his Bellarmino, insists that faith is indeed required for sacrifices, but not for moral works: since for a moral work to be done well it is not required that it be done with detestation of sins, or with a pure conscience. For the axiom of the Apostle is universal Rom. 14, 23. Whatever is not of faith, is sin. The example concerning alms to a poor person, which has for its end nothing but to bring aid to the needy, to the attainment of which end the purity or impurity of the life or conscience of him who gives the alms pertains to nothing, is equally ἀθεόλογον: for alms is not a good work unless it proceeds from faith, and it has not only to do good to the needy as its end, but also to render due obedience to God, and thus not only the utility of the neighbor, but primarily the glory of God: to which, if it perhaps suits Jesuitical Theology that the purity or impurity of life and conscience pertains to nothing, it is certainly most alien to the Theology of the Holy Scriptures. For ABOMINATION, which Solomon adds here v. 9. is the way of the wicked to the Lord, but he is finally loved by him who follows justice: concerning which sentence Cornelius himself teaches that the reason for the former is rendered in this way: Therefore God execrates the victims of the wicked, (to which also belong Alms, Phil. 4, 18. Heb. 13, 16.) because he execrates their way, that is, their manner of living and acting. But they follow justice who, having been reputed righteous through faith in the Messiah, devote effort to true holiness and justice as much as is in them, and with every zeal pursue it like a fleeing wild beast.

(4.) With what mind we ought to hear rebuke or correction is taught v. 10. namely not incorrigible: because correction is indeed troublesome to one leaving the path, but he who hates rebuke will die chap. 5, 23. and lest we doubt that our mind lies open to God, Solomon adds v. 11. hell and destruction (the state of the dead and the damned) are before the Lord, how much more the hearts of the sons of men? If those things which do not seem to be of such concern to the Lord are before the Lord, how much more those things which the Lord cares for most, whose eyes are always intent upon the sons of men? The connection is rendered here by R. Aben-Ezra and R. Levi, the Lord to whom nothing is hidden, tests the thoughts and hearts of the sons of men, who leave the way of discipline, and hate chastisement, and he will give them a reward, that they may die before their day, and perish, verse 12. A SCORNER DOES NOT LOVE ONE REBUKING HIM: and therefore he does not approach the wise. LXX. he does not associate with the wise.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

STULTUS IRRIDET DISCIPLINAM PA- TRIS SUI: QUI AUTEM CUSTODIT IN- CREPATIONES ASTUTIOR FIET.

Quod ad admissionem doctrinæ (1.) Stultus judi- catur, qui contemnit Patris, vel ejus, qui Patris lo- co est, correctionem vel castigationem, utpote bru- tis indulgens cupiditatibus: qui autem observat in- crepationem, sapientiam veram consequitur. Vulga- tus addit cum LXX. Interpp. In abundanti justitia virtus maxima est, cogitationes autem impiorum eradicabuntur. Sed ea nec in Ebræo, nec in Chald. nec in Vetustis Codicibus Latinis reperiuntur, ad- eoque adulterina sunt. Additur (2.) fructus admis- sionis doctrinæ penes justos v. 6. In domo justi est thesaurus magnus, at in proventu impii non thesau- rus, sed mera perturbatio. Et (3.) causa, cur sapien- tibus adhærescendum sit, v. 7. quia labia sapientum spargunt scientiam, cor autem stultorum non sic: (quum labia cum corde arctissime cohæreant) quod amat potius circa ludicra & vana occupari: & imprimis, quia verum Dei cultum à sapientibus θεοδιδάκτοις discimus, quænam Deo grata sacrifi- cia, quænam orationes acceptæ, siquidem non omne sacrificium Deo gratum, non omnis oratio accepta coram Deo. Sacrificium impiorum est abo- minatio Domino, utpote quod cum fide conjunctum non est Genes. 4, 4. Ebr. 11, 4. Psalm. 50, 8. Esa. 1, 11. Oratio autem rectorum beneplacitum est ejus. De qua sententia in Jure Canonico 3. quæst. 7. c. 5. hæc de- ducitur observatio: Neque enim in omnipotentis judicio quid, sed à quo datur, inspicitur: Hinc est enim, quod scriptum est: Respexit Dominus ad Abel, & ad munera ejus: ad Cain autem & ad munera ejus non respexit. Dicturus quippe, quia Dominus re- spexit ad munera, præmisit solicite, quia respexit ad Abel. Ex qua re patenter ostenditur, quia non offe- rens à muneribus, sed munera ab offerente placue- runt. Dona quippe iniquorum non probat Altissimus, nec respicit in oblationes eorum. Ubi perquam ἄτο- πον, καὶ ἀθεόλογον est, quod cum Bellarmino suo Cornelius ingerit fidem ad sacrificia quidem requiri, non autem ad opera moralia: siquidem ut fiat bene opus morale non requiratur, ut fiat cum detestatione peccatorum, vel cum conscientia pura. Nam universale est axioma Apostoli Rom. 14, 23. Quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est. Exemplum de eleemosyna in pauperem, quæ pro fine non habeat nisi egenti opem ferre, ad quem finem consequendum nihil pertineat puritas vel impuritas vitæ vel conscientiæ ejus, qui elee- mosynam facit, æque ἀθεόλογον est: nam eleemo- syna bonum opus non est, nisi ex fide proficiscatur, nec solum pro fine habet egenti benefacere, sed etiam Deo obedientiam debitam præstare, adeoque non proximi solum utilitatem, sed imprimis glo- riam Dei: ad quam nihil pertinere puritatem vel impuritatem vitæ & conscientiæ, Theologiæ Je- suiticæ si forsitan conveniat, à Theologia certe S. S. alienissimum est. ABOMINATIO enim, quod hîc addit Salomo v. 9. est Domino via impii, is au- tem demum diligitur ab eo, qui justitiam sequitur: qua sententia prioris rationem hoc modo reddi tradit ipse Cornelius: Ideo Deus execratur victimas impiorum, (ad quas etiam pertinent Eleemosynæ, Phil. 4, 18. Ebr. 13, 16.) quia execratur eorum viam, id est, vivendi, agendique rationem. Sectantur au- tem justitiam, qui per fidem in Messiam justi repu- tati, operam navant veræ sanctitati & justitiæ quan- tum in ipsis est, omnique studio eam instar feræ fu- gientis insequuntur.

(4.) Quo animo audire increpationem vel cor- rectionem debemus docetur v. 10. nempe non in- corrigibili: quia correctio molesta quidem relin- quenti semitam, sed qui odio habet increpationem mo- rietur cap. 5, 23. neve dubitemus animum nostrum Deo patere, addit Salomo v. 11. infernus & perditio (status mortuorum & damnatorum) sunt coram Domino, quanto magis corda filiorum hominum? si illa quæ non adeo curæ videntur Domino, coram Domino sunt, quanto magis ea, quæ maxime curat Dominus, cujus oculi semper intenti sunt in filios hominum? Nexus à R. Aben-Ezra, & R. Levi hîc redditur, Dominus cui nihil est absconditum, probat cogitationes, & corda filiorum hominum, qui relin- quunt viam disciplinæ, & odio habent castigationem, ac dabit illis mercedem, ut moriantur ante diem suum, & pereant, vers. 12. NON AMAT ILLUSOR INCREPANTEM SE: ideoque ad sapientes non accedit. LXX. cum sapientibus non conversatur.

## 15:8
Vers. 8.

THE VICTIMS OF THE WICKED ARE ABOMINABLE TO THE LORD) Plato in Alcibiades 2. For I do not think that the nature of the gods is such that they are led astray by gifts, like a base usurer. But we also say a foolish thing, claiming to surpass the Lacedaemonians in this way. For it would be terrible if the gods looked to our gifts and sacrifices, and not to the soul, if someone happens to be holy and just. Much more, I think, than to these expensive processions and sacrifices, which nothing prevents a man or a city from having to perform every year, having sinned much against the gods and much against men. But they, as not taking bribes, despise all these things, as the god and prophet of the gods says. At any rate, it is likely that both among the gods and among men who have sense, justice and prudence are honored in a distinguished way.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

VICTIMAE IMPIORVM ABOMINABILES DOMI- NO) Plato Alcibiade 2. Οὐ γὰρ (οἶμαι) τοιοῦτόν ἐσι τὸ τῶν θεῶν, ὥςε ὑπὸ δώρων παράγεσθαι, οἷον κακὸν τοκιστὴν. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡμεῖς εὐήθη λόγον λέγομεν, ἀξιοῦντες Λακεδαιμονίων ταύ- τῃ περιεῖναι. καὶ γὰρ ἂν δεινὸν εἴη εἰ πρὸς τὰ δῶρα καὶ τὰς θυ- σίας ἀποβλέπεσιν ἡμῶν οἱ θεοὶ, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς τὴν ψυχήν, ἄν τις ὅσιος καὶ δίκαιος ὢν τυγχάνῃ. Πολλῷ μᾶλλον, οἶμαι, ἢ πρὸς τὰς πολυτελεῖς ταύτας πομπάς τε καὶ θυσίας, ἃς οὐδὲν κωλύει πολλὰ μὲν εἰς θεοὺς, πολλὰ δ᾽ εἰς ἀνθρώπως ἡμαρτηκότας, καὶ ἰδιώτην καὶ πόλιν ἔχειν ἄν ἑκαστον ἔτος τελεῖν. Οἱ δὲ, ἅτε οὐ δω- ροδοκοῦντες, καταφρονοῦσιν ἁπάντων τούτων, ὥς φησιν ὁ θεὸς καὶ θεῶν προφήτης. Κινδυνεύει γοῦν καὶ παρὰ θεοῖς καὶ παρ᾽ ἀν- θρώποις τοῖς νοῦν ἔχουσι δικαιοσύνη τε καὶ φρόνησις διαφερόν- τως τετιμῆσθαι.

## 15:11
Vers. 11. HELL AND DESTRUCTION BEFORE THE LORD) Those things which are said to be ἐν ἄδῃ, because they do not appear to our eyes, are nevertheless conspicuous to God.

Latin:

Vers. 11. INFERNVS ET PERDITIO CORAM DO- MINO) Ea quæ dicuntur esse ἐν ἄδῃ, quia oculis nostris non apparent, tamen Deo sunt conspicua.

## 15:13
Vers. 13. A GLAD HEART MAKES A CHEERFUL COUNTENANCE, BUT BY SORROW OF HEART THE SPIRIT IS BROKEN.

In Hebrew: A glad heart adorns the face: but in the sorrow of the heart the spirit is crushed: so that all cheerfulness falls away, and the spirit is broken and unarmed, as if it were fleeing from all the limbs. Cf. c. 17, 22. c. 18, 24. Isa. 66, 2. Vatablus: the spirit is broken, obscured, or perishes, and grows old. A rejoicing heart not only rejoices in itself, but also transfuses its joy through natural sympathy into the body, and especially into the face: for it makes this cheerful, rosy, decorous, and flourishing, so that it seems to breathe out a spirit of cheerfulness: conversely, a sad and sorrowful heart or mind casts down the sad and sorrowful spirit, and consequently consternates the face and countenance, and makes it cloudy, lurid, and dark, since the spirit is accustomed to reveal its affections most of all with the countenance. But the true cause of joy, as the author of the Greek Catena says, is justice and the pursuit of virtues, just as the true cause of sadness is an evil life and conscience. Therefore it is added v. 14. A heart that understands seeks knowledge, so that, namely, it may possess true joy; but the mouth of fools (just as the heart) is fed on folly, on the vain and stupid delights and joys of the world: which it prefers to enjoy rather than solid pleasure in the true knowledge of God and justice, Rom. 14, 17. whence Solomon proceeds v. 15. All the days of the afflicted (on account of an evil conscience, which is a true and mere affliction) are evil, but he who is of a good heart (having a good conscience is as if he were in) a continual feast. Which is the explanation of R. Levi and Vatablus. Concerning which Chrysostom, hom. 15 in Matthew: when the evil mind is pricked by no stings of conscience, it always enjoys joy, so that no one can explain it in speech. For what seems pleasant and sweet to you in the present life? A delicious table? But this, compared to that pleasure which follows virtue, seems bitter and full of sadness. Clem. Alex. lib. 7. Strom. The whole life of the just man is a certain celebrated and holy feast day. To which the following verse 16 also contributes. Better is a little with the fear of the Lord, than a great treasure, and trouble or confusion therein. The author of the Greek Catena understands this of headstrong audacity. The fear of God makes the mind quiet, and content with its lot, glad and cheerful: which quietness of mind and joy is better than all riches. Cf. cap. 16, 8. c. 17, 1. 1 Tim. 6, 6. And v. 17. better is a dinner of herbs, where there is love (namely, of the host who prepared that dinner for us, especially the heavenly one, from whom comes every virtue Ps. 104, 27. Ps. 145, 15.) than (a meal of) a stalled ox, in which there is hatred. Grotius on these things thus:

Latin:

Vers. 13. CONGAUDENS EXHILARAT FA- CIEM IN MOERORE ANIMI DEJICITUR SPIRITUS.

In Ebr. Cor lætum decorat faciem : at in dolore cordis spiritus attritus est : ita ut concidat omnis ala- critas & spiritus fractus & inermis, quasi ex omni- bus membris emicet. Conf. c. 17, 22. c. 18, 24. Esa. 66, 2. Vatablus: frangitur, obscuratur, aut perit, & obsolescit spiritus. Cor gaudens non tantum in seipso gaudet, sed & suum gaudium per naturalem sympa- thiam in corpus, ac præsertim in faciem transfun- dit: hanc enim facit hilarem, roseam, decoram, flo- rentem, ut spiritum hilaritatis efflare videatur: vi- ce versa cor sive animus tristis & mœstus tristem mœstumque dejicit spiritum, & consequenter fa- ciem & vultum consternat, eumque nubilum, luri- dum & atrum efficit spiritus, cumque vultu maxime affectus suos patefacere solet. Vera autem lætitiæ causa, ut autor Caten. Græc. est justitia & virtu- tum studium, sicut vera tristitiæ causa est mala vita & conscientia. Ideo additur v. 14. Cor intelligens quærit scientiam, ut scil. vera potiatur lætitia; at os stultorum (æque ac cor) pascitur stultitia, vanis ac stolidis mundi delitiis, & gaudiis : quibus potius frui mavult, quam solida, in vera Dei notitia, & ju- stitia, voluptate, Rom. 14, 17. unde pergit Salomo v. 15. Omnes dies afflicti (ob malam conscientiam, quæ vera & mera est afflictio) mali, sed bonus corde (bonam habens conscientiam est, ac si esset in) con- vivio jugi. Quæ R. Levi & Vatabli est explicatio. Quo de Chrysost. hom. 15. in Matth. cum nullis sti- mulis conscientiæ animus pungitur malus, semper fruitur gaudio, adeo ut nemo id oratione possit expo- nere. Quid enim tibi videtur in præsenti vita jucun- dum, atque suave? Mensane delitiosa? Sed hæc illi voluptati, quæ virtutem consequitur, collata amara & tristitiæ plena videtur. Clem. Alex. lib. 7. Strom. universa vita justi est quidam celebris ac sanctus dies festus. Quo facit etiam versus sequens 16. Melius est parum cum timore Domini, quam thesaurus ma- gnus, & contritio vel confusio in eo. De præfracta au- dacia intelligit autor Caten. Græc. Timor Dei fa- cit mentem quietam, & sua sorte contentam, lætam & hilarem : quæ mentis quies, & lætitia omnibus opibus prior est. Conf. cap. 16, 8. c. 17, 1. 1. Tim. 6, 6. Et v. 17. melius est convivium oleris, ubi sit dilectio (hospitis scil. qui convivium illud nobis appara- vit, imprimis cœlestis, à quo omnis virtus Ps. 104, 27. Ps. 145, 15.) quam (esca) bovis saginati, in qua sit odium. Grotius ad hæc ita :

## 15:16
Ver. 16 BETTER IS A LITTLE WITH THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THAN GREAT TREASURES AND INSATIABLE) Hence seems to be taken that of Paul 1 Timothy 6:6. But godliness with contentment is great gain. See below 16:8 and 17:1.

Latin:

Verf. 16 MELIVS EST PARVM CVM TIMORE DO- MINI, QVAM THESAVRI MAGNI ET INSATIA- BILES) Hinc sumtum videtur illud Pauli 1. Timoth. 6, 9. ἔστι δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἐυσέβεια μετ' ἀυταρκείας. Vide in- fra 16, 8. & 17, 1.

## 15:17
Ver. 17. BETTER IS IT TO BE CALLED TO HERBS WITH CHARITY THAN TO A STALLED OX WITH HATRED) In Hebrew word for word thus: Better a feast of herbs and love there, than an ox stalled and hatred there. That 'and' and 'there' are for 'where'. A dinner of herbs is the food of the poor. As Apelles set forth a dinner having sacrificed a garden, thinking to feed sheep instead of friends. The radish, endive, fenugreek, lettuces, leeks, bulb, basil, marjoram, rue, asparagus. On the contrary, an ox or a stalled calf is among the best of feasts, Luke 15:23.

After the information concerning the joy and sadness of the heart follows that concerning anger and patience v. 18. A wrathful man stirs up strife but he that is slow to anger appeases strife: and concerning the love of labor or leisure, and the consequence of each, v. 19. the way of the slothful is as an hedge of thorns, (because he does not overcome the thorns of difficulties) but the path of the righteous is made plain, Vulgate without stumbling block. Compare Isaiah 57:14, chapter 62:10, and especially concerning the pursuit of wisdom v. 20. A wise son makes a glad father: but a foolish man despises his mother; whence nothing but the sadness of parents can arise: and v. 21. For foolishness (vanity, or worldly pleasure) is joy to him that is destitute of heart, chapter 10:23, but a man of understanding (has it for joy, if) he will direct (or make plain his way according to the line of the divine will) to walk.

Moreover where there is wisdom, there is counsel: whence it is subjoined v. 22. concerning counsels, thoughts are dissipated, when there is no counsel, but in the multitude of counselors (wise and pious) they are established. Therefore counsels are praised, because they bring prosperous successes, and bring joy, and also are useful to others in the time of being brought forth, concerning which v. 23. Joy is to a man in the answer of his mouth, and a word in its time, how good it is. Grotius thus concerning these:

Latin:

Verf. 17. MELIVS EST VOCARI AD OLERA CVM CHARITATE QVAM AD VITVLVM SAGINATVM CVM ODIO) In Hebr. ad verbum fic: Melius convivium oleris & dilectio ibi, præ bove saginato & odium ibi. Illa & ibi sunt pro ubi. Olerum cœna pauperum est. Ὡς κῆπον τεθυκὼς δεῖπνον παρέθηκεν Ἀπελλῆς, Οἰόμενος βόσκειν ἀντὶ φίλων πρόβατα. Ἡ ῥαφανὶς, σέρις ἦν, τῆλυς, θρίδακες, πράσα, βολβὸς, Ὤκιμον, ἡδύοσμον, πήγανον, ἀσπάραγος. Contra bos aut vitulus saginatus inter optimas epulas, Luc. 15, 23.

Post informationem de lætitia & tristitia cordis sequitur de ira & patientia v. 18. Vir iracundus miscet lites at tardus ad iram sedat litem: & de amore labo- ris vel otii, ac utriusque consequenti, v. 19. via pigri est quasi sepes spinosa, (quia difficultatum spinas non superat) semita autem rectorum est complanata, Vulg. absque offendiculo. Conf. Es. 57, 14. c. 62, 10. & impri- mis de sapientiæ studio v. 20. Filius sapiens lætificat pa- trem: at stultus homo vilipendit matrem; unde non nisi tristitia parentum oriri potest: & v. 21. Stultitia enim (vanitas, vel voluptas mundana) est lætitia so- liam ei, qui corde deficit, cap. 10, 23. at vir intelligens (pro gaudio habet, si) ordinabit (vel complanabit viam suam juxta lineam voluntatis divinæ) ad am- bulandam.

Cæterum ubi sapientia, ibi consilium: unde subjungitur v. 22. de consiliis, dissipantur co- gitationes, quando non est consilium, sed multitudine consiliariorum (sapientum & piorum) firmantur. Id- circo consilia prædicantur, quod prosperos succef- sus consuenti, ac lætitiam adferant, nec non aliis utilia sint in tempore prolatæ, quo de v. 23. Lætitia est viro in responsione oris sui, & verbum in tempore suo, quam bonum est. Grotius ita de his:

## 15:23
A MAN REJOICES IN THE SENTENCE OF HIS MOUTH: AND A WORD IN DUE SEASON IS BEST) And for 'but'. The sense is: everyone easily pleases himself because of those things which he has said: but those things are truly well said, which are said in season.

And wisdom is commended v. 24. because to the truly intelligent the way of life pleases upward, Colossians 3:1, 2, that he may decline from hell, which is downward, by reason of status, not location. Grotius on this v. 24. has it thus: Ver. 24. THE PATH OF LIFE IS ABOVE TO THE WISE, THAT HE MAY DEPART FROM HELL BENEATH) In the Hebrew: The way of life to the things above (supply tends) to the intelligent, that he may deflect from hell, which is underneath. That is, a wise man in all his actions looks to God, that he may be kept from danger.

And since pride, malice, avarice, wicked and scandalous speeches are opposed to true wisdom, there are subjoined concerning them in order apothegms v. 25. The Lord will destroy the house of the proud, but he will establish the border of the widow who is depressed, and the humble, and thus of all the humble v. 26. The thoughts of the wicked man are an abomination to the Lord (the heart of the wicked man) thinking only evil, such as are errors in faith, contempt of God and good laws, plotting against a neighbor, meditation of fraud, of revenge, of pleasures etc. Matthew 15:19. indeed thoughts also break forth outwardly, when out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks Matthew 12:34. but to the pure (as the heart is pure, so also) the speeches are beautiful, or rather because of the nature of the antithesis, they are pure (if they please) pleasant speeches overflowing from a faithful and pure heart. v. 27. He troubles his own house, who greedily pursues avarice. chapter 11:17, 29. But he who turns away from gifts, (which are offered, so that the mind may be recalled from the rule of justice, a species of avarice, gift-eating, is taken for the genus) shall live, shall enjoy prosperity, then he himself, but indeed also shall preserve his own house: which is to be elicited from the former by way of antithesis. (Those things which are added here according to the LXX and Vulgate: by mercy and faith sins are purged: but by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil, are not held in the Hebrew, and thus they do not acknowledge Solomon as the author) v. 28. The heart of the righteous will meditate on what it should answer, or speak, (words twice to the file before once to the tongue, as Bernard advises) so that, of course, the righteous person may bring forth or advise nothing but what is pleasing to God, and wholesome for the republic or his neighbor: but the mouth of the wicked will speak evil, without due premeditation, against God and his neighbor: whence it is added in v. 29 that God is far from the wicked, and does not hear their desires and prayers, but hears the prayer of the righteous, and is ready with His grace for them, Ps. 145, 18, and that the righteous obtain applause and a good reputation: concerning which v. 30. The light of the eyes, i.e., the serenity of the countenance, makes the heart glad: we are indeed exhilarated when others deem us worthy of a serene countenance, and show themselves gentle and kind to us: a good reputation, by which we hear our good deeds proclaimed among others, both exhilarates the heart and fattens the bones, c. 3, 8. c. 17, 23. For an emotion, as being a more vehement joy or sadness, so affects the soul that it overflows and abounds into the body: but in order that we may become wise, and obtain these things, it is necessary that we admit reproofs and discipline, the necessity of which, as Solomon had inculcated before, so now toward the end of the chapter he repeats again. v. 31. The ear that hears the reproof of life, or that which is directed toward a blessed and happy life, will dwell in the midst of the wise, and thus will be able to have a good reputation among others. A disciple, says Bede, who obediently assents to the reproofs of teachers, for the most part by progressing ascends even to the Chair of the Teacher. v. 33. He who neglects discipline despises his own soul, himself, he neglects the cultivation of his soul and his own salvation: but he who hears reproof acquires, or gains, a heart, i.e., a wise one, as Luther says: Der wird klug. But the way or the order of arriving at the summit of both wisdom and glory Solomon makes in v. 33 the fear of the Lord, and depression, and humility. The fear of the Lord, he says, is the instruction of wisdom, chap. 1, 2. c. 9, 10. and before glory is humility, or affliction, c. 3, 14. which in disciples who hear reproof also precedes, and glory and exaltation follow. Syr. 11, 1. We now subjoin the Grotian notes which remain in this chapter:

Latin:

LÆTATVR HOMO IN SENTENTIA ORIS SUI: ET SERMO OPPORTUNUS EST OPTIMUS) Et pro at. Sensus est: facile quilibet sibi placet ob ea, quæ dixit: sed illa vere bene dicta sunt, quæ dicta sunt ἐν καιρῷ.

Et commendatur sapientia v. 24. quod vere in- telligenti placeat via vitæ sursum versus Col. 3, 1. 2. ut declinet ab inferno, qui deorsum est, ratione status, non situs. Grotius ad hunc v. 24. ita habet: Verf. 24. SEMITA VITÆ SUPER ERUDITUM, VT DECLINET DE INFERNO NOVISSIMO) In Hebræo: Via vitæ ad superna (supple tendit) intelligenti, ut deflectat ab inferno, qui subter est. Id est, homo sapiens in omnibus actio- nibus suis Deum respicit, ut a periculo servetur.

Et quum veræ sapientiæ adversetur superbia, malitia, avaritia, pravi & scandalosi sermones, sub- junguntur de illis ordine apophthegmata v. 25. Do- mum superborum demolitur Dominus, stabilit autem terminum viduæ depressæ, & humilis, adeoque omnium humilium v. 26. Abominatio sunt Domino cogitationes viri mali (cor viri mali) mala tantum cogitantis, ut sunt errores in fide, Dei legumque bo- narum comtemtus, machinatio contra proximum, meditatio fraudis, vindictæ, voluptatum &c. Matth. 15, 19. cogitata vero etiam prorumpunt foras, quum ex abundantia cordis os loquatur Matth. 12, 34. at mundis (uti cor mundum, ita &) eloquia sunt pul- chra, vel potius ob antitheseos indolem, munda sunt (si placent) eloquia jucunda è corde fideli & mundo redundantia. v. 27. Turbat domum suam, qui avare sectatur avaritiam. c. 11, 17. 29. Sed qui aversa- tur dona, (quæ offeruntur, ut animus à justitiæ regu- la revocetur, species avaritiæ δωροφαγία sumitur pro genere) vivet, prosperitate fruetur, tum ipse, tum vero etiam domum suam conservabit: quod è priori κατ' ἀντίθεσιν eruendum. (Quæ hîc adduntur apud LXX. & Vulg. per misericordiam & fidem pur- gantur peccata : per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis à malo, in Ebræo non habentur, adeoque Salomonem non agnoscunt autorem) v. 28. Cor justi meditabitur quid respondeat, vel loquatur, (verba bis ad limam antequam semel ad linguam, ut monet Bernhardus) ut nimirum justus non nisi quæ Deo grata, reipublicæ vel proximo salubria, proferat, vel consulat: os autem impiorum loquetur mala, sine debita præmeditatione, contra Deum & proximum: unde additur v. 29. quod Deus longinquus sit ab impiis, eorumque desideria & preces non audiat, justorum vero orationem exaudiat, iisque gratia sua præsto sit, Ps. 145, 18. quodque justi applausum & famam bonam consequantur : de qua v. 30. Lumen oculorum, i. e. serenitas vultus cor lætificat: exhilaramur nempe cum alii nos sereno vultu dignantur, nobisque se blandos, & benignos præbent: fama bona, qua audimus benefacta nostra apud alios prædicari, & cor exhilarat, & ossa impinguat c. 3, 8. c. 17, 23. affectus enim utpote lætitia & tristitia vehementior ita afficit animum, ut redundet & exuberet in corpus : ut autem sapientes evadamus, & hæc consequamur, opus est, ut increpationes & disciplinam admittamus, cujus rei necessitatem uti antea inculcarat Salomo, ita nunc sub finem capitis denuo repetit. v. 31. auris, quæ audit increpationem vitæ, vel ad vitam beatam ac felicem directam, in medio sapientum commorabitur, adeoque audire bene apud alios poterit. Discipulus, inquit Beda, qui increpationibus docentium obedienter annuit, plerumque proficiendo ad Cathedram usque Doctoris ascendit. v. 33. Qui negligit disciplinam, spernit animam suam, seipsum, animæ suæ culturam & salutem suam negligit: sed qui audit increpationem, comparat, vel acquirit cor, sapiens scil. ut Luther. Der wird klug. Via autem vel ordinem deveniendi tum ad sapientiæ tum ad gloriæ culmen facit Salomo v. 33. timorem Domini, & depressionem, ac humilitatem. Timor Domini, inquit, eruditio sapientiæ cap. 1, 2. c. 9, 10. & ante gloriam humilitas, vel afflictio, c. 3, 14. quæ in discipulis increpationem audientibus etiam præcedit, & sequitur gloria & exaltatio. Syr. 11, 1. Subjungimus jam Grotiana, quæ in hoc capite restant:

## 15:27
Vers. 27. HE TROUBLES HIS OWN HOUSE, WHO PURSUES AVARICE: BUT HE WHO HATES GIFTS, SHALL LIVE) He shall live, that is, he shall flourish. Hesiod: Never does famine accompany men of straight justice, nor ruin; but they feast on the works they have cared for. For them the earth bears much livelihood, and on the mountains the oak bears acorns at the top, and bees in the middle. Wool-bearing sheep are weighed down with fleeces; women bear children like their parents; they flourish with good things continuously. But afterwards: Keeping these things in mind, O kings, make your judgments straight, you gift-eaters, and forget crooked judgments altogether. The man who works evil for another works evil for himself; and an evil plan is most evil for the one who planned it. The eye of Zeus, seeing all and knowing all, looks upon these things too, if he wishes, and it does not escape his notice what kind of justice the city keeps within itself.

Latin:

Vers. 27. CONTVRBAT DOMVM SVAM, QVI SECTATVR AVARITIAM: QVI AVTEM ODIT MVNERA, VIVET) Vivet, idest, florebit. Hesiodus: Οὐδέποτ' ἰθυδίκοισι μετ' ἀνδράσι λιμὸς ὀπηδεῖ, Οὐδ' ἄτη· θαλίῃς δὲ μεμηλότα ἔργα νέμονται. Τοῖσι φέρει μὲν γαῖα πολὺν βίον, ὄρεσι δὲ δρῦς Ακρη μέν τε φέρει βαλάνες, μέσση δὲ μελίσσας. Εἰροπόκοι δ' ὄϊες μαλλοῖς καταβεβρίθασι· Τίκτουσιν δὲ γυναῖκες ἐοικότα τέκνα γονεῦσιν· Θάλλεσιν δ' ἀγαθοῖσι διαμπερές. Postea vero: Ταῦτα φυλασσόμενοι βασιλεῖς ἰθύνετε μύθες, Δωροφάγοι, σκολιῶν δὲ δικῶν ἐπιπάγχυ λάθεσθε Οἷ αὐτῷ κακὰ τεύχει ἀνὴρ ἄλλῳ κακὰ τεύχων· Ἡ δὲ κακὴ βουλὴ τῷ βουλεύσαντι κακίστη. Πάντα ἰδὼν Διὸς ὀφθαλμὸς καὶ πάντα νοήσας, Καί νυ τάδ' αἴκ' ἐθέλησ', ἐπιδέρκεται, ὐδὲ ἐλήθει Οἵην δὴ κἀι τήνδε δίκην πόλις ἐντὸς ἐέργει.

## 15:33
Vers. 33. THE FEAR OF THE LORD, THE INSTRUCTION OF WISDOM: AND BEFORE GLORY IS HUMILITY) Humility here signifies modesty. Glory follows the one who flees it. The interpreter here has followed the Hebrew reading such as we have it, not the Greeks, who translate ἀποκριθήσεται ἀυτῇ, from ענה, which is to answer. But then also the chapters among the Greeks in this book are distinguished differently, and many sentences are either omitted or added, as is wont to happen in Eclogues, which is the reason why the same sentence is found placed in different locations in this book, because they could be referred to several titles, as it were.

But such omissions, or additions, or transpositions of sentences can in no way be approved or excused in a book which is not of man, but of the Holy Spirit Himself.

Latin:

Vers. 33. TIMOR DOMINI, DISCIPLINA SAPIENTIÆ: ET GLORIAM PRÆCEDIT HVMILITAS) Humilitas hic modestiam significat. Gloria fugientem sequitur. Hebraam lectionem qualem nos habemus secutus hic est interpres, non Græcorum, qui vertunt ἀποκριθήσεται ἀυτῇ, ab ענה, quod est respondere. Tum vero & capita apud Græcos in hoc libro distincta aliter, & multæ sententiæ aut omissæ aut additæ, ut in Eclogis fieri solet, quæ causa est cur & eadem sententia in hoc libro diversis in locis inveniantur posita, quia ad plures quasi titulos referri poterant.

Minime autem vel probati vel excusari possunt tales omissiones, vel additiones, vel trajectiones sententiarum in libro, qui non hominis est, sed ipsius Spiritus Sancti.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI.

The success of the wise and the pious, even of Kings, from the Lord: as well as concerning the successes or outcomes of the impious.

Vers. 1. IT IS FOR MAN TO PREPARE THE SOUL: AND FOR THE LORD TO GOVERN THE TONGUE.

In general, it is first taught that all success is from God and divine providence. The preparations of the heart, he says, are of man, what he wishes to speak or do, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord, so that we do not even speak that which we proposed, God often moderating the tongue otherwise. Therefore, the Pelagians foolishly gather from this that it is for man to prepare the soul, and that the beginning of Salvation is from man: since we cannot even think anything good, much less utter it from ourselves 2 Cor. 3, 5. Nor is this passage about spiritual things, but about those which concern the present life: and in the verse immediately following, Solomon teaches that we can neither understand our ways, much less prepare or dispose ourselves for spiritual goods and salvation. All the ways of a man, he says, are clean in his own eyes, chap. 14, 12. but the Lord is the one who weighs or examines the spirits or hearts v. 2. Whence we are warned that we should commit all things to God, v. 3. Roll your works unto the Lord, because, namely, the answer of the tongue is from the Lord, and He alone tests and confirms hearts, and your thoughts shall be established. For God works all things for His own answer v. 4. concerning which we must now speak further.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI.

Successus Sapientum & piorum, etiam Regum à Domino: nec non de successibus, vel even- tibus impiorum.

Vers. 1. HOMINIS EST ANIMAM PRÆPA- RARE: ET DOMINI GUBERNARE LIN- GUAM.

IN genere primum omnem successum à Deo & di- vina providentia esse docetur. Hominis, inquit, sunt præparationes cordis, quid loqui vel agere velit, sed à Domino est responsum linguæ, ita ut ne id qui- dem loquamur, quod proposuimus, Deo sæpe lin- guam aliter moderante. Inepte ergo hinc Pelagiani colligunt, hominis esse animam præparare, ac initi- um Salutis ab homine esse: quum ne quidem cogitare aliquid boni possimus, nedum eloqui ex nobismet ipsis 2. Cor. 3, 5. neque hîc de spiritualibus agatur, sed de iis, quæ vitam præsentem concernunt: & versu statim sequenti doceat Salomo, nos nec intelligere vias nostras, nedum ad spiritualia bona, & salutem nos præparare aut disponere posse. Omnes, inquit, viæ viri mundæ sunt in oculis ipsius cap. 14, 12. sed qui ponderat vel examinat spiritus vel corda est Dominus v. 2. Unde monemur, ut omnia Deo committamus, v. 3. Devolve ad Dominum opera tua, quia scil. à Do- mino est responsum linguæ, & ipse solus probat, confirmatque corda, & firmabuntur cogitationes tuæ. Omnia enim operatur Deus ad responsum ipsi- us v. 4. quo de jam porro dicendum.

## 16:4
Vers. 4. THE LORD HATH MADE ALL THINGS FOR HIMSELF, EVEN THE WICKED FOR THE EVIL DAY) The sense is not bad if you understand 'for himself' not that God has need of anything, but that He might make His properties known, and that the impious is not made such by God (far be this), but is made, or set, for evils. But this interpretation will be better: God makes (i.e., ordains) individual things for that which is fitting for each. Even the impious for the calamitous day (supply: ordained by God). For עָנָה among other things, as also the Latin word for answering, signifies τὸ συστοιχεִν [to correspond]; thus Eccl. 10, 19. וְהַכֶּסֶף יַעֲנֶה אֶת־הַכֹּל compensates. Nor indeed did the LXX take this passage otherwise: πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ κυρίου μετὰ δικαιοσύνης, φυλάσσεται δὲ ὁ ἀσεβὴς εἰς ἡμέραν κακήν [All the works of the Lord are with justice, but the impious is kept for an evil day].

The former explanation seems to be praised for the sake of the Vulgate version, whose sense he says is not bad. But to work or make the impious for an evil day is not to set or ordain him, who is already impious, for evils, just as to work all things for Himself is not to ordain all things, which have already been produced, for His own glory, but to produce them for Himself. Therefore, the Vulgate cannot easily be helped, unless the cause of sin is established in God, which dogma we know Grotius detested as Calvin's. Nor does that fit the Hebrew text; for in it the preposition לְמַעַן [for the sake of] is not held, as it always retains a Scheva under the first letter, nor does it admit the suffix וֹ, which is only attached to nouns ending in He preceded by a Sægol; whence the Hebrew word which is held here לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ cannot be rendered FOR HIMSELF. However, it is manifest that the noun מַעֲנֶה occurs here, from עָנָה to answer, which verb, because it sometimes also signifies to resound praise, sometimes to answer in testimony or to testify, R. Solomon explains it as 'for his praise': others 'for his testimony': because every work of the Lord testifies of Him, and praises His power, goodness, and wisdom: and thus it would be readier to assist the Vulgate, if it be said that the sense, not the words, is precisely rendered here: But because the word מַעֲנֶה denotes an answer, it will be rendered κατὰ πόδα [word for word], according to his answer. Which Grotius also acknowledged, abandoning the Vulgate and substituting another interpretation. Others had preceded, but in different ways. For most have referred the suffix pronoun to God: the Lord works all things for His answer, i.e.

that all things may answer to God and the divine will, and perform that for which they were made, and which they are commanded by their Maker; and thus God created the impious man himself, so that he might do, namely, what God willed, who nevertheless is drawn by his own malice to the evil day, i.e., to deserved punishments. Which opinion, asserted by the blessed Dr. Joh. Tarnovius in Exercit. Bibl. p. 130, our late Dr. Glassius approved in Grammatic. Sacr. p. 588. As also Dr. Walther in Harm. Script. S. Dr. Georg. Konig in Vindic. Sacr. locor. Script. c. 74 gives a similar sense in the former member: God works all things for His answer, i.e., that all things may humbly answer to the will of the heavenly Father: but in the latter member he thinks that either it should not be read in the accusative, and the impious also, but by ellipsis thus: And the impious for the day of evil, supply, shall fall, as Vatablus noted; or it must be said that God also worked the impious for the day of evil, not absolutely, for that reason, namely, because God so willed, but so that he might not harm the pure, as Aben-Ezra interprets: and this to answer to the divine will, so that such an impious person may be punished in the day of evil, or misfortune Psalm 41, 2. Ps. 69, 6. Prov. 15, 15. To which opinion the LXX Interpreters also lead: Πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ ταπεινοῦ φανερὰ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ· οἱ δὲ ἀσεβεῖς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κακῇ ὀλοῦνται [All the works of the humble are manifest before God; but the impious shall perish in an evil day]: thus explaining: all works in humility are manifest to God: but the impious perish in an evil day. For thus it is read in the Basel edition of the LXX Interpreters, which appeared in the year 45 of the previous century: but the Roman one, according to the Vatican exemplar brought here by Grotius, differs not a little from that. The Chaldean seems to have accepted the Hebrew word in a similar manner: All the works of God are for these, that they may obey Him, and the impious is kept for an evil day דְמִשְׁתַּמְעִין לֵיהּ [that they may be obedient to Him], that he may obey Him, or His will. Others, however, prefer to refer the suffix to the works of God, that God works all things and each thing for their response, or so that they may respond to one another: Marcus Marinus in Arca f. 396. It is formed for the verse from עָנָה for its response, in a truly very elegant Hebraism, according to how they correspond to one another and bring help to one another. Which sense Franciscus Junius also chooses in his notes to this place. I do not know whether an interpretation from the Hebrew context would be better: Jehovah works everything for that which may respond to Him, and even the wicked for the day of evil. For it is an etiology from the providence of God, by whose most wise power and ordination all things are so disposed that each preceding deed and thought responds to its consequences, and each consequence to its antecedents. In which sense also the Grotian version can be accepted: (God makes/ordains each thing) for that which is suitable to each thing: if the suffix pronoun is thus referred to the things which are ordained by God πρὸς τὸ συστοιχεῖν so that they may respond to one another and among themselves. But he himself seems to take 'that which is suitable to each thing' according to ἀνταποδοτικήν (retributive) justice: therefore he says that the Greek version renders the same sense, πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ κυρίου μετὰ δικαιοσύνης: and in the parallel place Eccles. 10:19, he takes the word יַעֲנֶה concerning compensation: That which is suitable to them, by the power of the justice of God; not, indeed, that it is suitable to them among one another, on account of mutual harmony. However, not inappropriately, Mr. Dr. Geier explains that mutual, if I may so say, correspondence in his Commentary on this place. God is said to work all things and each thing for the response, or in the response of them, that is, so that each and all may respond to one another, or observe a mutual harmonic order, which the most wise arbiter of all things once decreed. By which very reason that which follows coheres elegantly: namely, that such a concert is discovered not only among good things, but also among evil things, where, according to the reason of the most just decree, the evil of fault permitted responds to the evil of punishment sent into it, and the echo of misfortune results from the outcry of the impious. Cf. Sir. 16, 25. c. 40, 9. 10. c. 33, 14 Wis. 11, 12. Ps. 104, 24. 1 Cor. 14, 13. None of these interpretations is dissonant with the analogy of faith, or foreign to the words of Solomon. Nor is the Grotian sense to be disapproved, if indeed the words are rendered thus: God works or disposes individual things for their response, or as it responds and is fitting for them, or for that which responds and is suitable to individuals, according to the law of divine justice. Even the impious is ordained by God for the evil day, for that is owed to him by the same law. And thus that interpretation might seem to be preferred as simpler and more expeditious. Nor is this commentary of R. Levi foreign: Behold all things which God does, they (are directed) to perfection and utility or good, even if you see that the impious is punished for the evil day, this very thing is also for good, because in this consists the good, that the impious receives correction.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VNIVERSA PROPTER SEMETIPSVM OPERATVS EST DOMINVS, IMPIVM QVOQVE AD DIEM MALVM) Sensus non est malus, si propter se- metipsum intelligas, non quod opus quoquam Deus habeat, sed ut proprietates suas notas faciat, & impium non fieri ta- lem à Deo, (absit hoc) sed fieri, sive poni ad mala. Verùm melior erit hæc interpretatio: Singula Deus facit (i. e. ordi- nat) ad id, quod singulis convenit. Etiam impius ad diem ca- lamitosum (supple ordinatus a Deo) Nam עָנָה inter alia, ut & vox respondendi Latina, significat τὸ συστοιχεῖν: sic Eccl. 10, 19. וְהַכֶּסֶף יַעֲנֶה אֶת־הַכֹּל compensat. Neque sane aliter sumsere hunc locum LXX. πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ κυρίου μετὰ δικαιοσύνης, φυλάσσεται δὲ ὁ ἀσεβὴς εἰς ἡμέραν κακήν.

Prior explicatio in gratiam vulgatæ versionis laudari vidètur, cujus sensum non malum dicit. At impium operari vel facere ad diem malum, non est eum, qui jam impius est, ad mala ponere, aut ordi- nare, sicut universa propter semetipsum operari, non est universa, quæ jam producta sint, ad sui gloriam ordinare, sed producere ea propter semetipsum. Non ergo juvari facile potest vulgata, nisi Deo con- stituatur causa peccati, quod dogma Calvini dete- statum esse Grotium novimus. Neque congruit illa Ebræo textui; in eo enim non habetur præpositio לְמַעַן PROPTER, utpote, quæ sub prima litera semper Scheva retinet, nec affixum וֹ , quod solum nominibus in He præcedente Sægol definentibus annectitur, suspicit; unde vox Ebræa, quæ hic ha- betur לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ reddi non potest PROPTER SE- METIPSUM. Manifestum autem est, nomen מַעֲנֶה hic occurrere, ab עָנָה respondere, quod verbum quia interdum etiam significat resonare laudem, in- terdum respondere in testimonio vel testificari, R. Sa- lomo exponit ob laudem suam: alii ob testimonium su- um: quia unumquodque Domini opus testatur de eo, & laudat ejus potentiam, bonitatem, & sapienti- am: atque ita promtius foret fuccurrere vulgatæ, fi sensu, non verba præcise hic reddi dicatur: Sed quia vox מַעֲנֶה responsum notat, κατὰ πόδα reddetur, se- cundum responsum suum. Quod agnovit etiam Gro- tius, Vulgatam deserens, & aliam interpretationem substituens. Præiverant alii, sed diverfimode. Pleri- que enim pronomen sufixum ad Deum retulerunt: omnia operatur Dominus ad responsum suum, i. e.

ut respondeant Deo, & divinæ voluntati omnia, ac id præstent, ad quod facta sunt, & quod jubentur à suo factore; atque ita creavit Deus impium ipsum, ut faceret nempe, quod Deus voluit, qui tamen propria malitia ad diem malum, h. e. promeritas pæ- nas trahitur. Quam sententiam à B. Dn. D. Joh. Tarnovio in Exercit. Bibl. p. 130. assertam Dn. D. Glassius noster ὁ μακαρίτης probavit Grammatic. Sacr. p. 588. Ut & Dn. D. Walther. in Harm. Script. S. D. Georg. Konig. in Vindic. Sacr. locor. Script. c. 74. similem reddit sensum in priori membro: Deus operatur omnia ad responsum suum, i. e. ut cun- cta voluntati Patris cælestis humiliter respondeant: in posteriori vero membro putat, aut non legendum in accusativo, & impium etiam, sed per ellipsin sic: Et impius in diem mali, supple, corruet, prout nota- vit Vatablus; aut dicendum, Deum etiam opera- tum esse impium ad diem mali, non absolute, ob id scilicet, quia Deus fic voluit, sed ne noceat puro, ut interpretatur Aben-Ezra: & hoc respondere volunta- ti divinæ, ut talis impius in die mali, seu infortunii Psalm. 41, 2. Pf. 69, 6. Prov. 15, 15. puniatur. In quam sententiam etiam adducit LXX. Interpp. Πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ ταπεινοῦ φανερὰ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ· οἱ δὲ ἀσεβεῖς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κακῇ ὀλοῦνται: sic exponens: omnia opera in humilitate patent Deo: impii autem in die mala pereunt. Sic enim legitur in editione LXX. Interpp. Basilensi, quæ Anno superioris seculi 45. prodiit: Romana vero juxta Vaticanum exemplar hic adducta à Grotio, non parum ab illa discrepat. Chaldæus parili ratione vocem Ebræam accepisse videtur: Omnia opera Dei ad istos, ut obediant ei, & impius servatur in diem malum דְמִשְׁתַּמְעִין לֵיהּ ut obtemperet illi, vel voluntati ejus. Alii tamen affixum malunt ad opera Dei referre, omnia atque singula operari Deum ad responsum ipsorum, vel ut sibi invicem respondeant: Marcus Marinus in arca f. 396. Versui formatur à עָנָה responfioni sua, E- braismo sane perquam eleganti, prout sibi correspon- deant, & invicem opem ferant. Quem sensum eli- git etiam Francisc. Junius in not. ad h. l. Haud scio, annon melior sit futura ex Hebræo contextu interpre- tatio: Omne operatur Jehovah ad id, quod re- spondeat ipsi, etiamque improbum ad diem mali. Est enim ætiologia à providentia Dei, cujus sapientis- sima vi, & ordinatione sic disponuntur omnia, ut sin- gula antecedentia facta cogitationesque suis conse- quentibus, & singula consequentia suis antecedenti- bus respondeant. Quo etiam sensu accipi potest Grotiana versio: (singula Deus facit) (ordinat) ad id quod singulis convenit: si ita referatur prono- men suffixum ad res, quæ ordinantur à Deo πρὸς τὸ συστοιχεῖν ut respondeant sibi invicem & inter se. Sed ipse videtur id quod singulis convenit, accipere se- cundum justitiam ἀνταποδοτικήν: ideo Græcam versionem eundem sensum reddere dicit, πάντα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ κυρίου μετὰ δικαιοσύνης: & in loco pa- rallelo Eccles. 10, 19. vocem יַעֲנֶה de compensatione accipit: Quod convenit ipsis, vi justitiæ Dei; Non ve- ro, ut conveniat ipsis, inter se invicem, ob mutuam harmoniam. Non inconcinne autem illam mutuam ut ita dicam, correspondentiam explicat Dn. D. Geierus Commentar. in h. l.
