Operari dicitur Deus universa atque singula ad responsionem, vel in re- sponsione ipsorum, hoc est, ut singula & universa re- spondeant invicem sibi ipsis, vel ordinem harmoni- cum observent mutuum, quem semel sapientissimus rerum cunctarum arbiter decrevit. Qua fane ra- tione eleganter cohæret id quod sequitur: nimirum non inter res bonas tantum talem deprehendi concen- tum, verum etiam inter res malas, ubi pro ratione de- creti justissimi malo culpæ permisso respondet malum pœnæ immissum, atque ad vociferationem impii resul- tat echo infortunii. Conf. Sir. 16, 25. c. 40, 9. 10. c. 33, 14 Sap. 11, 12. Ps. 104, 24. 1. Cor. 14, 13. Nulla istarum in- terpretationum vel analogiæ fidei dissona, vel à ver- bis Salomonis aliena. Neque improbandus Gro- tianus sensus, si nempe sic verba reddantur: Sin- gula operatur, vel disponit Deus ad responsum ipso- rum, vel uti respondet atque convenit ipsis, aut ad id quod respondet ac congruit singulis, secundum legem justitiæ divinæ. Etiam impius ad diem malum or- dinatur à Deo, id enim ipsi debetur eadem lege. Atque ita videri possit ea interpretatio, ut simpli- cior, & expeditior, præferenda. Nec alienus hic est commentarius R. Levi: Ecce omnia, quæ facit De- us, illa ad perfectionem & utilitatem seu bonum (di- recta sunt) etiamsi videris, quod plectitur impius ad diem malum, hoc ipsum etiam ad bonum est, quia in hoc bonum consistit, quod impius accipit corre- ctionem.

## 16:5
Ver. 5. EVERY ARROGANT PERSON IS AN ABOMINATION TO THE LORD: EVEN IF HAND TO HAND IT SHALL BE, HE IS NOT INNOCENT.

Since the Lord works all things, and our successes are from him alone, there is no reason for anyone to exalt himself 1 Cor. 4, 7. indeed every one who is proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord. Even if hand to hand, or if he has many allies, he will not be innocent: he will not escape punishments, whatever conspiracies he may enter into: or rather, although he joins both hands, he will not expiate his sin; which agrees with the following verse. The Vulgate indeed adds with the LXX Interpreters, but which are foreign to the text and the Hebrew source and the Chaldean version, to do justice is the beginning of a good way: it is more acceptable to God than to sacrifice victims. But Solomon proceeds thus in the sources: BY MERCY AND TRUTH INIQUITY SHALL BE REDEEMED. Which the Weimar Paraphrasts, Glassius l. 3. Phil. S. tr. 3. c. 26. B. Quistorpius on this passage, D. Zeemannus carnif. Esav. p. 67. and also Fr. Jun. T. 1. Oper. f. 817. rightly accept concerning divine mercy and truth. id. Sibr. Lubbertus against Socin. p. 151. and others: See John 1, 17. Rom. 3, 24. AND IN THE FEAR OF THE LORD ONE TURNS AWAY FROM EVIL: in which manner, with the expiation of past sin shown, we are consequently warned to avoid sins in the future, by the fear of the Lord, i.e., by his sincere and filial worship, c. 3, 7. c. 14, 16. c. 16, 17. and thus Solomon promises desired successes further v. 7. When the ways of a man please the Lord, he makes even his enemies at peace with him: and he simultaneously inculcates αὐτάρκειαν v. 8. better is a little with justice, than a multitude of revenues without right chap. 15, 16. and he again commands that all things be committed to divine direction: because the heart of man, he says, devises his way, but God directs his steps. Jerem. 10, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ABOMINATIO DOMINO EST O- MNIS ARROGANS: ETIAMSI MANUS AD MANUM FUERIT, NON EST INNOCENS.

Quum omnia operetur Dominus, & ab ipso so- lo successus nostri sint, non est, quod quis sese ef- ferat 1. Cor. 4, 7. imo abominatio Domino est omnis elatus corde. Etiamsi manus ad manum, seu multi ejus sint socii, non erit innocens: non effugiet pœ- nas, quascunque etiam conspirationes ineat: vel potius, licet ambas congerat manus, non expiabit pec- catum suum; quod convenit sequenti versui. Addit quidem Vulgata cum LXX. Interpretibus, sed quæ aliena à textu, & fonte Ebræo, ac versione Chaldaica sunt, initium viæ bonæ facere justitiam: accepta est apud Deum magis, quam immolare victimas. Sic au- tem pergit in fontibus Salomo: MISERICOR- DIA ET VERITATE REDIMETUR INI- QUITAS. Quod de divina misericordia & veri- tate recte accipiunt Vinarienses Paraphrastæ, Glas- sius l. 3. Phil. S. tr. 3. c. 26. B. Quistorpius ad h. l. D. Zeemannus carnif. Esav. p. 67. nec non Fr. Jun. T. 1. Oper. f. 817. it. Sibr. Lubbertus contra Socin. p. 151. & alii: Vid. Joh. 1, 17. Rom. 3, 24. ET IN TIMO- RE DOMINI RECEDITUR A MALO: quo pacto ostensa peccati præteriti expiatione conse- quenter in futurum peccata vitare monemur, ti- more Domini, h. e. sincero & filiali ejus cultu, c. 3, 7. c. 14, 16. c. 16, 17. atque ita porro successus exoptatos promittit Salomo v. 7. Quum placuerint Domino viæ viri, etiam inimicos ejus pacatos reddit ei: & αὐ- τάρκειαν simul inculcat v. 8. melius est parum cum justitia, quam multitudo proventuum absq; jure cap. 15, 16. & divinæ directioni omnia committi iterum jubet: quia cor hominis, inquit, excogitat viam suam, Deus autem dirigit gressus ejus. Jerem. 10, 23.

## 16:7
Ver. 7. WHEN THE WAYS OF A MAN PLEASE GOD, HE WILL CONVERT EVEN HIS ENEMIES TO PEACE) An example in Joseph and his brothers.

Latin:

Vers. 7. CVM PLACVERINT DEO VIÆ HOMINIS, INIMICOS QVOQVE EJVS CONVERTET AD PA- CEM) Exemplum in Josepho & fratribus.

## 16:10
Ver. 10. DIVINATION IS IN THE LIPS OF THE KING, HIS MOUTH SHALL NOT ERR IN JUDGMENT) קסם is a middle word, and differs from prophecy, as appears in Is. 3, 2. The sense is, that God bestows upon kings, i.e., pious ones, a remarkable ἀγχίνοιαν (acuteness of mind), so that they may find the truth in judgments in wonderful ways. See an example 1 Kings 3, 16. and following. Hesiod in the Theogony about a king: - - - and all the people look to him as he decides cases with straight judgments, and he, speaking securely, quickly and skillfully puts an end to even a great quarrel.

He treats more specifically of the success of Kings: Let there be prophecy in the lips of the King: thus Aben-Ezra, Lyranus, Isidor, Clarius interpret imperatively, let him observe the word of the Lord; let not his mouth prevaricate in judgment: or as if this were a consequence of the antecedent, as Vatablus, then he will not prevaricate in judgment. For although God endows Kings and their intimate council with special ἀγχινόιᾳ, this however is neither perpetual, nor does it come under the name of divination, much less is it joined with infallibility in judgment. Lyranus says divination, i.e., let the reading of divine things be in the eyes and lips of the King. Which etymology seems ridiculous and foreign to Cornelius, but Lyranus was not so inept as to explain the etymology of the word in that way, without doubt more correctly than Cornelius understanding the force of the word קסם, being a Jew: he therefore wished to render only the sense (not the words themselves), which Cornelius acknowledges to be agreeable to the divine law Deut. 17, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 10. DIVINATIO IN LABIIS REGIS, IN JVDI- CIO NON ERRABIT OS EJVS) קסם vox est media, & differt a prophetia, ut apparet Es. 3, 2. Sensus est, Deum regibus, piis scil. insignem largiri ἀγχίνοιαν, ut in judiciis mi- ris modis verum reperiant. Exemplum vide 1. Reg. 3, 16. & se- quentibus. Hesiodus in Theogonia de rege: - - - οἱ δέ νυ λαοὶ Πάντες ἐς αὐτὸν ὁρῶσι διακρίνοντα θέμιςας Ἰθείησι δίκῃσιν, ὃ δ᾽ ἀσφαλέως ἀγορεύων, Αἶψά τε καὶ μέγα νεῖκος ἐπισταμένως κατέπαυσε.

De successu Regum specialius agit: Sit prophe- tia in labiis Regis: ita imperative exponunt Aben- Ezra, Lyranus, Isidor. Clarius, observet verbum Domini; in judicio non prævaricetur os ejus: vel ut consequens hac antecedentis sit, ut Vatablus, tunc in judicio non prævaricabitur. Quanquam enim ἀγχινόιᾳ speciali Reges, eorumque senatum inti- mum donet Deus, haec tamen neque perpetua est, nec divinationis nomine venit, nedum cum infalli- bilitate in judicio conjuncta est. Lyranus divinatio, inquit, i. e. divinarum rerum lectio sit in oculis & la- biis Regis. Quod etymon ridiculum & alienum Cornelio videtur, sed Lyranus non tam ineptus fuit, ut etymologiam vocis ita exponeret, rectius fine dubio quam Cornelius vim vocis קסם intelli- gens, utpote Judaeus: sensum ergo solum (non ver- ba ipsa) reddere voluit, quem convenientem esse legi divinae Deut. 17, 18. agnoscit Cornelius.

## 16:11
Ver. 11. THE WEIGHT AND BALANCE OF JUDGMENT ARE THE LORD'S: AND ALL THE WORKS OF HIS BAG) The balance of judgment here is a just balance. The Hebrews and neighboring peoples used stones for weights, and they stored them in bags. Deut. 25, 13. Theodotion here: all weights are of the bag. The sense is, the knowledge of justice is given to men by God as an excellent gift, as Hesiod also said: and he gave justice to men.

Furthermore, the love of justice is commended to the King, so that he may have happy success. Let the balance and scales be the Lord's judgment, i.e., let them be as just as the Lord's, and let them be used according to the prescription of the Lord, so that they may be approved by the Lord: (the Vulgate version, 'The weight and balance are the Lord's judgments,' agrees neither with the accentuation nor with the words of the text, therefore Grotius inverts it) let all the weights of the bag be his work. Compare Deut. 25, 13. It is not a question of God's judgments, or divine justification, as Cornelius, following the Vulgate, does entirely strangely with Lyranus and Dionysius, but of just weights and measures to be used in worldly commerce according to the divine prescription: whence for that purpose the standard of shekels and weights was kept in the temple. And thus, by the specifically named justice, which the King ought to observe and guard, justice in general is commended to him, as is clear from v. 12: let it be an abomination to Kings to do wickedness, so that he neither admits it himself, nor permits it among his own: because the royal throne shall be established in justice: and v. 13. Let just lips be the pleasure of Kings, and they shall love him who speaks right things. How much the King's favor is to be valued is taught from the contrary: v. 14. The wrath of the King is as a messenger of death: But a wise man will overcome it: which no one but a wise man will be able to appease: just as Joab and Abigail appeased David's wrath with their wisdom, 2. Sam. 24. 1. Sam. 25, 35. The fruit and advantage of royal favor is also added v. 15. When the face of the King shall shine, there shall be life, or prosperity of every kind. And his benevolence shall be as a cloud pouring forth the latter rain. Compare Job 29, 23. Prov. 19, 12. Joel 2, 22. Concerning which verses Grotius says thus:

Latin:

Vers. 11. PONDVS ET STATERA JVDICII, DOMI- NI SVNT: ET OPERA EJVS OMNES LAPIDES SACCVLI) Statera judicii hic est statera justa. Lapidibus Hebraei & vicinae gentes utebantur pro ponderibus, & eos re- ponebant in sacculos. Deut. 25, 13. Theodotion hic: πάντα στάθμια μαρσίππγ. Sensus est, justitiae cognitionem homini- bus a Deo, ut eximium munus datam, ut & Hesiodus dixit: ἀνθρώποισι δ᾽ ἔδωκε δίκην.

Commendatur autem porro Regi, ut successus habeat felices, amor justitiae. Statera & bilances ju- dicii Domini sint, h. e. tam justa sint, ceu Domini, & juxta praescriptum Domini adhibeantur, ut a Do- mino approbentur: (versio Vulgata, Pondus & sta- tera judicia Domini sunt, neque accentuationi, neque verbis textus convenit, ideo invertit eandem Gro- tius) opus ejus sint omnia pondera crumene. Confer Deut. 25, 13. Non de Dei judiciis, vel justificatione divina, ut e Vulgata Cornelius aliene prorsus cum Lyrano, & Dionysio, sed de justis ponderibus & men- suris in mundanis commerciis adhibendis juxta praescriptum divinum, agitur: unde eo fine asser- vabatur norma siclorum & ponderum in templo. Atque ita specie nominata justitiae, quam observare & custodire Rex debebat, in genere justitia eidem commendatur, ut e v. 12. liquet: abominatio Regi- bus sit facere impietatem, ita ut nec ipse eam admit- tat, nec in suis eam permittat: quia in justitia firma- bitur solium Regium: & v. 13. Beneplacitum Regum sint labia justa & loquentem recta diligent. Quanti autem gratia Regis aestimanda a contrario docetur: v. 14. Ira Regis est ut nuntius mortis: At vir sapiens superabit eam: quam nemo nisi sapiens placare po- terit: uti Joab & Abigail Davidis iram sapientia sua placarunt, 2. Sam. 24. 1. Sam. 25, 35. Additur etiam gratiae Regiae fructus, & commodum v. 15. Quum il- luxerit facies Regis erit vita, vel prosperitas omnige- na. Et benevolentia ejus erit veluti nubes effundens serotinam pluviam. Conf. Job. 29, 23. Prov. 19, 12. Joel. 2, 22. De quibus versibus ita Grotius:

## 16:14
Vers. 14. THE INDIGNATION OF THE KING, MESSENGERS OF DEATH) Whose wrath nothing opposes, to whose more severe sentence those who perish themselves assent, whom no one is about to question, nay, if he has flared up more vehemently, not even one about to entreat. These are Seneca's words in the first book of On Clemency, chap. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 14. INDIGNATIO REGIS, NVNTII MORTIS) Cujus ira nihil obstat, cujus graviori sententia ipsi, qui pereunt assentiuntur, quem nemo interrogaturus est, imo, si vehementius excanduit, ne deprecaturus quidem. Senecae haec sunt libro de Clementia primo cap. 5.

## 16:15
Vers. 15. IN THE CHEERFULNESS OF THE KING'S COUNTENANCE IS LIFE) He fills everyone with good hope. It does not come forth, but arises, says Seneca.

AS THE LATTER RAIN) See Deut. 11, 14. Jas. 5, 7. מלקוש is the harvest time. יורד or מורה is the spring time, the definition of which is in Amos 4, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 15. IN HILARITATE VVLTVS REGIS VITA) Bona spe omnes implet. Non prodit, sed oritur, ait Seneca.

QVASI IMBER SEROTINVS) Vide Deut. 11, 14. Jac. 5, 7. מלקוש est messis tempore. יורד vel מורה ve- ris tempore, cujus circumscriptio Amosi 4, 7.

## 16:16
Vers. 16. POSSESS WISDOM, BECAUSE IT IS BETTER THAN GOLD: AND ACQUIRE PRUDENCE, BECAUSE IT IS MORE PRECIOUS THAN SILVER.

For the happy success of affairs, the acquisition of wisdom and prudence is required, first of all, both among all people and especially among those shining with royal dignity: for whom it is more excellent to acquire and possess wisdom than to acquire precious gold, and to acquire intelligence than silver, or to accumulate great heaps and treasures of gold or silver: but heavenly wisdom is joined with piety and humility: whence the most wise Solomon inculcates both: Concerning the former v. 17. The way of the upright is to depart from evil: he who guards his way guards his soul.

Cf. ch. 3, 7. ch. 13, 19. ch. 16, 6. The LXX add some things here, but which did not proceed from Solomon, nor are they found in the Hebrew text, and therefore they have also been omitted in the Vulgate, for they read thus: He who receives discipline will abound in all good things: So he who observes rebukes will make progress in wisdom. He who guards his ways guards his soul: but he who loves his life must spare his mouth. Concerning this v. 18. Pride is before destruction, and an uplifting of spirit before ruin: And v. 19. It is better to be humbled in spirit with the humble, than to divide spoils with the proud. Cf. Obad. v. 4. Dan. 5, 20. Sir. 10, 15. Luke 14, 11. They are lifted on high, that they may fall with a heavier crash, says Claudian. Verse 20. THE LEARNED IN THE WORD SHALL FIND GOOD: AND HE WHO HOPES IN THE LORD IS BLESSED.

The happy success of the wise, the upright, and the humble is now subjoined: He who attends to the word of wisdom, the norm and form of uprightness and true humility, will find good, ch. 13, 13. and he who trusts in the Lord is blessed: which trust, or confidence in the Lord, is the cause not only of every happy success, but also of true and eternal blessedness, Jer. 17, 7. Ps. 2, 12. Estimation and fame also contribute to success, concerning which v. 21. the wise in heart is called, is proclaimed intelligent: And he who is sweet in speech will perceive greater things; Thus the Vulgate: which Grotius rendered and explained more correctly from the Hebrew: Verse 21. HE WHO IS WISE IN HEART SHALL BE CALLED PRUDENT, AND HE WHO IS SWEET IN SPEECH SHALL PERCEIVE GREATER THINGS) In the Hebrew: The sweetness of the lips will add learning, that is, will make learning more precious, will add weight to it. Euripides in Hecuba: Πειθὼ δὲ τὴν τύραννον ἀνθρώποις μόνην.

Furthermore, what is subjoined in verse 22 contributes to happy success regarding the information of others, concerning the wholesomeness of doctrine: intelligence is a fountain of life to its possessor: but the instruction or erudition of fools is folly. The sense according to Jansenius is: Erudition, wisdom, and intelligence is to those who truly have it, a fountain of life: because like a spring always flowing, and never failing, it supplies them assiduously with that from which they themselves may live in soul, and others through their doctrine: But on the contrary, the doctrine of fools, by which they teach both themselves and others about things to be done or believed, is nothing other than fatuity. Osiander's explanation pleases: The intelligence of the word of God is like a most wholesome fountain, from which flow waters (or doctrines refreshing and recreating man, lest he fall from eternal life) but the doctrine of impious men is full of errors, and leads to death. Thus he. From the belly of fools flow rivers of dead water: but from the belly of the wise according to God flow rivers of living water, says the author of the imperfect Work on Matthew, homily 20. And v. 23. THE HEART OF THE WISE WILL TEACH HIS MOUTH, so that he knows what must be said, and does not blurt out whatever comes into his mouth, and will add grace (in Hebrew: learning) to his lips. Where the heart is illuminated by the salutary knowledge of the word of God, there a man will speak useful things and will teach wholesome things, v. 24. A honeycomb (or rather honey already extracted from the comb) are pleasant words: sweetness to the soul, and health to the bones. Pleasant discourses from the word of God, such as Evangelical consolations, are most sweet and most grateful to an afflicted and perturbed man, they wonderfully recreate his soul, and in a way restore his bones, Ps. 19, 11. Ps. 119, 103.

These are now illustrated from the contrary, by the unhappy events and successes of the foolish and impious, as follows: with a general gnome premised, rather repeated from ch. 14, 12. that many promise themselves happy successes, but hasten to unhappiness and death. There is a way which seems right to a man, and its ends lead to death. It happens that a man thinks he is entering a right way, and does not allow himself to be led away from it, when nevertheless that purpose tends to his bodily or eternal destruction.

Latin:

Vers. 16. POSSIDE SAPIENTIAM, QUIA AURO MELIOR EST: ET ACQUIRE PRU- DENTIAM, QUIA PRETIOSIOR EST AR- GENTO.

Ad felicem rerum successum requiritur impri- mis sapientiae & prudentiae comparatio cum penes omnes, tum imprimis apud Regia coruscantes di- gnitate: quibus acquirere, & possidere sapientiam praestantius sit quam acquirere aurum pretiosum, & acquirere intelligentiam, quam argentum, vel ma- gnos auri argentive cumulare acervos, & thesauros: sapientia autem superna conjuncta est cum pietate et humilitate: unde utramque inculcat Salomo sapien- tissimus: De illa v. 17. Via rectorum est declinare a ma- lo: custodit animam suam, qui custodit viam suam.

Conf. c. 3, 7. c. 13, 19. c. 16, 6. Addunt hic LXX. non- nulla, sed quæ à Salomone profecta non sunt, nec in Ebræo textu reperiuntur, ideoque etiam in vulgata omissa sunt, ita enim habent: Qui recipit discipli- nam, bonis omnibus affluit: Sic qui observat increpa- tiones in sapientia progressus faciet. Qui custodit vias suas, custodit animam suam: qui autem vitam suam di- ligit, ori suo parcat, oportet. De hac v. 18. Ante contri- tionem est superbia, & ante ruinam elatio spiritus: Et v. 19. Melius est humiliari spiritu cum humilibus, quam dividere spolia cum superbis. Conf. Obad. v. 4. Dan. 5, 20. Sir. 10, 15. Luc. 14, 11. Tolluntur in altum, ut lapsu graviore ruant, ait Claudian. Vers. 20. ERU- DITUS IN VERBO REPERIET BONA: ET QUI SPERAT IN DOMINO BEATUS EST.

Successus felix sapientum, rectorum & humilium, jam subjungitur: Qui attendit ad verbum sapien- tiæ, rectitudinis & humilitatis veræ normam & formam, inveniet bonum, cap. 13, 13. & confidens in Domino beatus est: quæ fiducia, vel confidentia in Domino non tantum omnis felicis successûs, sed etiam veræ & æternæ beatitudinis causa est, Jerem. 17, 7. Psalm. 2, 12. Ad successum facit etiam æstima- tio & fama, de qua v. 21. sapiens corde vocatur, præ- dicatur intelligens: Et qui dulcis eloquio, majora per- cipiet; Ita Vulgatus: quæ rectius ex Ebræo Gro- tius reddidit & exposuit: Vers. 21. QVI SAPIENS EST CORDE, APPELLABI- TVR PRVDENS, ET QVI DVLCIS ELOQVIO, MA- JORA PERCIPIET) In Hebræo: Dulcedo labiorum addet doctrinam, id est, doctrinam faciet pretiosiorem, pondus ei adjiciet. Euripides in Hecuba: Πειθὼ δὲ τὴν τύραννον ἀνθρώποις μόνην.

Porro ad successum felicem quoad informatio- nem aliorum faciunt quæ subjunguntur vers. 22. de doctrinæ salubritate: vena vitæ est intelligentia pos- sessori suo: at institutio vel eruditio stultorum stul- titia. Sensus secundum Jansenium est: Eruditio, sapientia, & intelligentia est illis, qui vere habent eam, fons vitæ: quia velut scaturigo semper profluens, nec unquam deficiens subministrat eis assidue unde & ipsi in anima vivant, & alii per eorum doctrinam: At contra doctrina stultorum, qua & seipsos & alios de agendis rebus aut credendis docent, nihil aliud est, quam fatuitas. Placet Osiandri explicatio: Intelli- gentia verbi Dei est instar fontis saluberrimi, unde promanant aquæ (seu doctrinæ reficientes, & re- creantes hominem, ne vita æterna excidat) sed im- piorum hominum doctrina plena est errorum, & du- cit ad mortem. Ita ille. De stultorum ventre exeunt flumina aquæ mortuæ: de ventre vero sapientum se- cundum DEum exeunt flumina aquæ vivæ, ait au- tor imperf. Oper. in Matth. hom. 20. Et v. 23. COR SAPIENTIS ERUDIET OS EJUS, ut sciat quid loquendum sit, nec quicquid in buccam venit effu- tiat, & labiis ejus addet gratiam (in Ebr. doctrinam) ubi cor illuminatum est salutari cognitione verbi Dei, ibi homo loquetur utilia & docebit salubria, v. 24. Favus mellis (vel potius mel à favo jam ex- cretum) sunt jucunda verba: dulcedo animæ, & sani- tas ossium. Sermones jucundi è verbo Dei, quales sunt Evangelicæ consolationes, dulcissimi & gratif- simi sunt homini afflicto & perturbato, animum ejus mirifice recreant, & ossa quodammodo refi- ciunt, Ps. 19, 11. Ps. 119, 103.

Hæc à contrario jam illustrantur, eventibus ac successibus infelicibus stolidorum & impiorum, uti sequitur: præmissa gnoma generali, repeti- ta potius è c. 14, 12. quod multi sibi successus pro- mittant felices, sed ad infelicitatem & mortem pro- perent. Est via quæ videtur homini recta, & no- vissima ejus ducunt ad mortem. Accidit ut homo rectam se ingredi viam putet, nec ab ea deduci se patiatur, cum tamen id propositum vergat ad ejus interitum corporalem vel æternum.

## 16:26
Verse 26.

THE SOUL OF THE LABORER LABORS FOR HIMSELF, BECAUSE HIS MOUTH HAS COMPELLED HIM.

From this foreign version a proletarian sense is commonly gathered, that we are driven by hunger to labor, which no one ignores: But the Hebrew text is to be rendered thus: the soul that shows trouble (to another) shows trouble to itself: because his mouth bends such a one: that is, according to Osiander's interpretation, he who strives to create danger for others by his perverse tongue, will prepare destruction for himself by his poisonous tongue, and will be cast into the pit which he had made for others, as is added v. 27. An impious man digs evil, and in his lips there is a burning fire. Cf. James 3, 6. Angry men are also commonly said to breathe fire, v. 28. A perverse man sends forth strife, and a whisperer separates princes, v. 29. An iniquitous man seduces (Vulg. entices) his neighbor: and makes him walk through a way that is not good: he entangles him in his crimes, so that he may subsequently pay the penalty together with him. For 'iniquus' (wicked) in Greek is παράνομος, and for 'lactat' (entices), Aquila and Theodotion have ἀπατήσει, as Grotius observes here, citing Critias and Plutarch on how a flatterer and a friend are distinguished, v. 30. He who thinks of evil things with astonished (or rather closed) eyes, biting his lips, accomplishes evils. Those who signal with eyes and lips are perverse men, not at all candid; who meditate on evils and attempt to accomplish them. It is not inconveniently said, however, that the signs of the depravity of the angry are specifically handed down here, because of the comparison with verse 32: indeed, the angry and truculent are accustomed to meditate on destruction with eyes as if drawn inward, and in a certain way closed by the clouding of a dense, wrinkled forehead and contracted eyelids, and they bite their lips, as the LXX and Vulgate render it, as Horace lib. 1. Carm. says: 'He impressed a memorable mark on his lips with his tooth.' Solomon can promise no success to such perverse and truculent men; indeed, he tacitly threatens the abbreviation of life with David in Psalm 55:24: since one must arrive at old age through justice, as R. Solomon and Jansenius correctly interpret the following verse: 'The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.' Old age, says Ambrose lib. 51. de Cain & Abel. c. 3, is venerable, not white with years, but with morals. Wisd. 4:4. And verse 32 is better: 'He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty (truculent), and he that ruleth his spirit (and is not at all truculent) than he that taketh a city.' Truly, he is stronger who conquers himself than he who conquers the strongest walls, nor can virtue go higher, as Ovid sings. The victory of cities is lesser, says Gregory the Great, part 3, Pastor. adm. cap. 10, because those things which are subdued are outside; but it is a much greater thing which is conquered through patience: because the mind itself is overcome by itself, and subjects itself to itself, when patience compels it to be bridled within itself. We now append the Grotian notes:

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ANIMA LABORANTIS LABORAT SIBI, QUIA COMPULIT EUM OS SUUM.

Ex hac aliena versione sensus proletarius vul- go colligitur, fame nos adigi ad laborandum, quod nemo ignorat: At Ebræus textus ita reddendus: anima quæ molestiam exhibet (alteri) molestiam sibi ipsi exhibet: quia incurvat talem os ejus: id est, Osi- andro interprete, qui perversa sua lingua aliis peri- culum creare nititur, sibi ipsi exitium venenata lin- gua sua parabit, & in foveam, quam alii fecerat, præ- cipitabitur, uti additur v. 27. Vir impius fodit malum, & in labiis ejus ignis ardescit. Conf. Jacob. 3, 6. Ignes spirare irati vulgo etiam dicuntur, v. 28. Vir perver- sus immittit litem, & susurro separat principes, v. 29. Vir iniquus seducit (vulg. lactat) proximum suum: & ambulare facit eum per viam non bonam: impli- cat eum suis sceleribus, ut deinceps una cum ipso pœnas luat. Pro iniquus in Græco est παράνομος, & pro lactat, Aquila & Theodotion habent ἀπα- τήσει, ut hîc observat Grotius, Critiam & Plutar- chum adducens, quomodo adulator & amicus in- ternoscantur, v. 30. Qui attonitis (vel potius clau- sis) oculis cogitat ad (excogitandum) prava, mor- dens labia sua perficit mala. Qui oculis, & labiis innuunt, sunt homines perversi, minime candidi; qui mala meditantur, & perficere conantur. Non incommode tamen dicitur speciatim iracundiæ pra- vorum signa hîc tradi, ob vers. 32. collationem: si- quidem irati truculenti oculis intro quasi reductis, densaque frontis rugatæ, ac palpebrarum contracta- rum obnubilatione quodammodo occlusis per- nitiem meditari soleant, & labia sua mordeant, uti LXX. & Vulg. reddunt, ut Horat. lib. 1. Carm. Im- pressit memorem dente labris notam. Talibus per- versis & truculentis nullum successum promittere potest Salomo, imo tacite vitæ abbreviationem cum Davide Psalm. 55, 24. minatur: siquidem per justitiam perveniendum sit ad senectutem, ut R. Sa- lomo & Jansenius versum sequentem recte interpre- tantur: Corona gloriæ canities, in via justitiæ repe- rietur. Senectus, inquit, Ambrof. lib. 51. de Cain & Abel. c. 3. venerabilis est, non annis cana, sed moribus. Sap. 4, 4. ac melior sit v. 32. tardus ad iram, quam fortis (truculentus) & is qui dominatur spiritui suo, (minimeque truculentus est) quam is qui capit ur- bem. Nimirum fortior est qui se, quam qui fortissi- ma vincit mænia, nec virtus altius ire potest, uti ca- nit Ovidius. Minor est victoria urbium, ait Gregor. M. part. 3. Pastor. adm. cap. 10. quia extra sunt, quæ subiguntur; valde autem majus est, quod per pa- tientiam vincitur: quia ipse a se animus superatur, & semetipsum sibimet ipsi subjicit, quando eum pa- tientia intra se frenari compellit. Subnectimus jam adhuc Grotiana:

## 16:29
Vers. 29.

A WICKED MAN ENTICES HIS FRIEND, AND LEADS HIM BY A WAY THAT IS NOT GOOD) For 'iniquus' (wicked) in Greek is παράνομος: and for 'lactat' (entices) Aquila and Theodotion have ἀπατήσει. Critias: 'Whoever associates with friends by doing everything for their favor, makes the immediate pleasure an enmity for the later time.' See Plutarch on how a flatterer and a friend are distinguished.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

VIR INIQVVS LACTAT AMICVM SVVM, ET DV CIT EVM PER VIAM NON BONAM) Pro iniquus est in Græco παράνομος: & pro lactat Aquila & Theodotion habent ἀπατήσει. Critias: Ὅςις δὲ τοῖς φίλοισι πάντα πρὸς χάριν Πράσσων ὁμιλεῖ, τὴν παρ᾿ αὐτίχ᾽ ἡδονὴν Ἔχθραν καθίστης εἰς τὸν ὕστερον χρόνον. Vide Plutarchum, quomodo adulator & amicus interno- scantur.

## 16:32
Vers. 32.

BETTER IS THE PATIENT MAN THAN THE STRONG MAN, AND HE WHO RULES HIS SPIRIT THAN THE CONQUEROR OF CITIES) He says the same thing as Ovid: 'He is stronger who conquers himself than he who conquers the strongest walls, nor can virtue go higher.'

Latin:

Vers. 32.

MELIOR EST PATIENS VIRO FORTI, ET QVI DOMINATVR ANIMO SVO EXPVGNATORE VR- BIVM) Idem dicit quod Ovidius: Fortior est qui se quam qui fortissima vincit Mænia, nec virtus altius ire potest.

## 16:33
Verse 33.

LOTS ARE CAST INTO THE LAP, BUT THEY ARE DISPOSED BY THE LORD) Namely the lots which the law prescribes, as in the division of inheritances, or the Prophets, as Samuel in the election of a King. Likewise in the election of an Apostle Acts 1. verses 24. 25. 26.

As he had begun, so he also finishes the chapter, namely that success is from God; all things, even those which can seem fortuitous, are ruled by God, for all things are subject to divine providence. It appears, however, that there was formerly a custom that lots were collected into the lap of someone, from where afterwards each person's own was drawn out, just as now they are accustomed to be collected into a pot or any vessel whatsoever: unless perhaps the lap is called an urn, or a hollow and curved vessel, as here Cornelius à Lapide.

PSALM XVII.

Again the wise and upright are compared with the foolish and wicked, along with the inconveniences of foolishness and wickedness.

Latin:

Verf. 33.

SORTES MITTVNTVR IN SINVM, SED A DO- MINO TEMPERANTVR) Nempe sortes quas lex præci- pit, ut in hæreditatum divisione, aut Prophetæ, ut Samuel in electione Regis. Item in electione Apostoli Act. 1. vers. 24. 25. 26.

Ut ceperat, ita etiam finit caput, successum nempe à Deo esse; omnia, etiam quæ fortuica vide- ri possunt, à Deo regi, omnia enim subjacent divinæ providentiæ. Apparet autem olim morem fuisse, ut sortes in sinum alicujus colligerentur, unde postea cuique sua educeretur, sicut jam in ollam aut vas quodlibet colligi solent: nisi forte sinus vocetur urna, aut vas cavum, & sinuatum, ut hic Cornelius à Lapide.

PSALM. XVII.

Iterum conferuntur sapientes ac probi cum stul- tis, & improbis, cum incommodis stultitiæ & improbitatis.

## 17:1 Argument
Verse 1.

BETTER IS A DRY MORSEL WITH JOY, THAN A HOUSE FULL OF SACRIFICES WITH STRIFE.

Understand solid joy, which is not except among the wise and just Rom. 14, 17. Even if they live on vile food, and even live under the open sky, they are nevertheless far happier than those in whose houses, however splendid they may be, and filled with the flesh of slaughtered animals or sumptuous foods, contention reigns, which is proper and familiar to those destitute of heavenly wisdom. James 3, 13. et seqq. It is better to lead a poor life in the grace of God than a luxurious one in sin and the offense of God, as is held in the Catena Graeca. Conf. c. 15, 12. Peace with God and tranquility of conscience excludes internal contention and perturbation of the mind: of which the companion is external peace with one's neighbor, c. 16, 7.

Latin:

Verf. 1.

MELIOR EST BVCCELLA SICCA CVM GAUDIO, QUAM DOMUS PLENA VICTI- MIS CUM JURGIO.

INtellige gaudium solidum, quod non est nisi pe- nes sapientes & justos Rom. 14, 17. Etiamsi illi vili victitent cibo, ac sub dio etiam agant, longe felicio- res tamen sunt iis, in quorum domibus, utut splen- didæ sint, carnibusque mactatorum animalium, vel opiparis eduliis repletæ, contentio regnat, quæ sa- pientia superna destitutis propria & familiaris est. Jac. 3, 13. seqq. Præstat pauperem vitam agere in Dei gratia, quam lautam in peccato, Deiq; offensa, ut ha- betur in Caten. Græc. Conf. c. 15, 12. Pax cum Deo & tranquillitas conscientiæ excludit internam con- tentionem & perturbationem animi: cujus comes est pax externa cum proximo, c. 16, 7.

## 17:2
Verse 2.

A WISE SERVANT SHALL HAVE DOMINION OVER FOOLISH SONS) A manumitted tutor shall be left to the sons. Gal. 4, 1. 2. τὸ ἄρχειν κρεῖσσον, the philosophers say.

AND HE SHALL DIVIDE THE INHERITANCE AMONG BRETHREN) By the office of a tutor. The Hebrew text has 'a wise servant shall have dominion over a son that causeth shame (to his father).' But it is not a matter of obtaining a hereditary portion IN THE MIDST of brothers, as the word חלק is taken in Jos. 18, 2; Job 27, 17. Cf. Sirach 10, 28.

Latin:

Verf. 2.

SERVVS SAPIENS DOMINABITVR FILIIS STVL- TIS) Manumissus tutor filiis relinquetur. Gal. 4, 1. 2. τὸ ἄρχειν κρεῖσσον, ajunt Philosophi.

ET INTER FRATRES HÆREDITATEM DIVIDET) Tutorio officio. Servus intelligens, habet Ebræus textus, domina- bitur filio pudore afficienti (Patrem suum.) Non au- tem de adeptione portionis hæreditariæ IN ME- DIO fratrum agitur, uti verbum חלק Jos. 18, 2. Job. 27, 17. accipitur. Conf. Sirac. 10, 28.

## 17:3
Verse 3.

AS SILVER IS TRIED BY FIRE AND GOLD BY THE FURNACE: SO THE LORD TRIETH THE HEARTS.

In Hebrew, 'as the refining pot (as Pagninus, or the refiner, smelter, or purifier, as the Tigurines) tries silver and the furnace gold, so the Lord tries the hearts'; most exactly knowing, and by the sharp examination of His divine mind, as if by a most effective fire, searching, examining, and perceiving the innermost thoughts and volitions of our mind, and the individual scruples, price, and value of them and of the heart: which is the proper sense. Cf. Ps. 17, 3; Jer. 6, 27; Prov. 16, 2. Furthermore, concerning the fire of tribulation and temptation, by which the nature of our heart is manifested to ourselves, Sir. 2, 5.

Wisdom 3, 6. But those things concerning the fire placed by God before heaven, so that souls before entering, passing through the same, might be purged, are Cornelius's, and are unwritten (ἄγραφα) and foreign (ἀλλότρια). Since heavenly wisdom is joined with faith and integrity of mind, it is hinted that it is known intimately by God alone, and that the truly pious are distinguished from hypocrites only by God, who searches the hearts and reins. 1 Chron. 29, 17; Jer. 11, 20; ch. 17, 10; ch. 20, 12. Moreover, some things are added

marks (γνωρίσματα) by which the evil and wicked can be recognized even by men, when they betray themselves like a sewer: For the wicked man attends to an iniquitous lip, or is occupied with a vain and pernicious tongue, not with salutary doctrines. A man of lies listens to a tongue of perversities and thus delights in perverse speeches, and eagerly drinks them in v. 4. He mocks the poor, heaping reproaches upon his Maker (Cf. ch. 14, 31); he rejoices in the destruction (of another, and thus) he shall not be unpunished. v. 5. For the wicked are delighted by these things, namely, by the misery and destruction of others, both by mocking them and by rejoicing in their calamity through epichairekakia (ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν), which is a truly diabolical vice. These are connected, however, according to the custom of this book, so that the apophthegms may be presented as a whole. He who despises the poor, reproaches his Maker, (which is the height of impiety) and he who rejoices at the ruin of another, shall not be unpunished: where the LXX add from their own, but he whose bowels are moved, shall obtain mercy: who also insert another sentence before this one, which is found neither in the Hebrew text, nor in other versions, Chaldean, Syriac, or Latin: Of him who is faithful, the whole world is of riches, but of him who is unfaithful, not even an obol.

Moreover, Solomon here subjoins the reward of true piety for both parents and children, assigning to the former old age as a crown of a well-spent and holy life, and to the latter this happiness, that they may see their fathers and grandfathers surviving: for this glory God is accustomed to bestow upon upright and obedient children: indeed, Solomon thus gives a stimulus to parents as well as to children toward all probity, in that the honor and glory of probity of both does not stop in themselves, but flows over to one another: The crown of old men are the children's children, and the glory of children are their fathers, v. 6.

Latin:

Verf. 3.

SICUT IGNE PROBATUR ARGENTUM ET AURUM CAMINO: ITA CORDA PRO- BAT DOMINUS.

In Ebr. sicut conflatorium (ut Pagninus, vel con- flans, liquans, aut excoctor, ut Tigurini) probat ar- gentum & caminus aurum, sic corda probat Domi- nus; exactissime cognoscens, & acri examine men- tis suæ divinæ quasi igne efficacissimo scrutans, exa- minans, & perspiciens intimas mentis nostræ cogi- tationes, & volitiones nostras, earum & cordis scru- pulos singulos, pretium & valorem: qui sensus pro- prius est. Conf. Pf. 17, 3. Jer. 6, 27. Prov. 16, 2. Cæte- rum de igne tribulationis & tentationis, quo nobis- mes ipsis manifestatur cordis nostræ indoles Sir. 2, 5.

Sap. 3, 6. Quæ vero de igne à Deo posito ante cælum, ut animæ ante ingressum, eundem transeuntes purgentur Cornelius, & ἄγραφα, & ἀλλότρια sunt. Quum sapientia superna conjuncta sit cum fide, & integri- tate animi, eam à solo Deo intime cognosci, & ve- re pios ab hypocritis non nisi à Deo corda & renes scrutante discerni innuitur. 1. Par. 29, 17. Jerem. 11, 20. cap. 17, 10. cap. 20, 12. Adduntur autem aliqua

γνωρίσματα quibus mali & improbi etiam ab homi- nibus agnosci possint, cum se foricis instar produnt: Malus enim attendit labio iniquo, seu linguæ vanæ, ac perniciosæ vacat, non doctrinis salutaribus. Vir mendacii auscultat linguæ pravitatum adeoque pra- vis delectatur sermonibus, eosque avide haurit v. 4. subsannat pauperem, probris afficiens factorem ejus (Conf. cap. 14, 31.) lætatur in contritione (alterius, adeoque) non erit impunitus. v. 5. hisce enim oble- ctantur pravi, miseria nempe & contritione aliorum cum subsannando eosdem, tum gaudendo de ca- lamitate eorum per ἐπιχαιρεκακίαν, quod vitium vere diabolicum. Connectuntur tamen hæc pro more hujus libri, ut apophthegmata integra exhibe- antur. Qui despicit pauperem, exprobrat factori ejus, (quæ summa est impietas) & qui ruina lætatur alte- rius, non erit impunitus: ubi LXX. de suo addunt, ille autem cujus viscera commoventur, misericordiam con- sequetur: qui etiam ante hanc sententiam aliam in- ferunt, quæ nec in Ebræo textu, nec in versionibus aliis, Chaldaica, Syra, Latina reperitur: Ejus qui fidelis est, totus mundus divitiarum est, illius autem qui infidelis est, neque obulus.

Subjungit autem Salomo hic præmium veræ pie- tatis tum parentum, tum filiorum, illis senium ceu coronam bene actæ sanctæque vitæ assignans, his eam felicitatem, ut patres & avos videant supersti- tes: hanc enim gloriam filiis probis & morigeris Deus tribuere solet: imo dat Salomo ita stimulum parentibus æque ac filiis ad omnem probitatem, eo quod probitatis decus & honos utrorumque non sistat in ipsis, sed ad alterutros promanet: Coro- na senum filii filiorum, & gloria filiorum Patres eo- rum, v. 6.

## 17:7
Vers. 7. COMPOSED WORDS DO NOT BEFIT A FOOL, NOR A LYING LIP A PRINCE.

There follow now sentences expressed concerning the fool and the perverse or wicked: that (1.) grandiloquence does not befit the fool, just as conversely, vain-speaking or false-speaking does not befit a prince, or one conspicuous for chief dignity, to which wise men, not foolish ones, are appointed: It is not becoming for a fool to have an excellent lip, how much less for a prince (it is becoming) to have a שקר [lying] or deceitful lip. Lying is a vice of slaves, as Aristotle says. (2.) That the perverse easily allow themselves to be blinded by gifts. A precious stone is a gift in the eyes of its owners: to everyone, to whom it (that gift) turns, it will prosper. v. 8. The perversity of men makes it so that there is nothing so holy that it cannot be violated by the corruption of gifts. These are the customs, says Osiander, of this age, that gifts and presents make him who is furnished with them (to corrupt others) gracious: so that wherever he turns, he is held to be wise and good, even if he is foolish, or is pleading a bad cause. Conf. Exod. 23, 8. Deut. 16, 19. That 'to prosper' is therefore to be understood relatively with respect to that which he who offers the gift has proposed to himself, namely, that he may obtain his cause, although it would be more honorable to have lost the cause than to have given cause for a corrupted judgment. B. Luther, with Aben-Ezra and Mercer, refer the word בעליו to him who gives the gift: because he, wherever he turns with his gift, acts prosperously. Others prefer to refer it to him who receives the gift, because the gift is precious in his eyes, as with the Chaldean, such as Pagninus, Vatabl. Jun. Cartwright, and Mr. Dr. Geier: whose mind is fixed on the gift, no less than his eyes on the precious gem which is presented. The Vulgate here renders no sense.

they do not bring love, but bring discords, because they do not cover the sins of their neighbor, but uncover them, and repeatedly object to them, or divulge them. ver. 9. He that covereth a transgression, seeketh love: but he that repeateth a matter, separateth a prince or the chief among friends, as Mercerus explains, who was chief to us in love, honor, and assistance. Conf. chap. 16, 28. (4.) That they are not amended by correction, ver. 10. A reproof entereth more into an intelligent man (it will settle deeper in the mind) than if you strike a fool a hundred times. To which Grotius says thus:

Ver. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NON DECENT STULTUM VERBA COMPOSITA, NEC PRINCIPEM LABIUM MENTIENS.

Sequuntur nunc expressæ de stulto & perver- so vel iniquo sententiæ: quod (1.) non deceat stultum grandiloquentia, sicut contra non decet virum principem, vel præcipua dignitate conspi- cuum, ad quam sapientes, non stolidi adhibentur, vaniloquium, aut falsiloquium: Non est decorum stulto labium excellens, quanto minus principi (de- corum est) labium שקר vaniloquum aut Mendax. Mendacium vitium est servorum, dicente Aristo- tele. (2.) Quod perversi facile se patiantur mu- neribus excæcari. Lapis pretiosus est munus in oculis dominorum ejus: ad omnem, ad quem se vertit (munus illud) prosperabitur. v. 8. Hominum per- versitas facit, ut nihil tam sanctum sit, quod mune- rum corruptela non violari possit. Hi sunt mores, ait Osiander, hujus seculi, ut dona & munera eum, qui iis instructus est (ad corrumpendos alios) gratio- sum reddant: ut quocunque se vertat, sapiens & bonus habeatur, etiamsi stolidus sit, aut malam causam agat. Conf. Exod. 23, 8. Deut. 16, 19. Illud prosperari ergo intelligendum σχετικῶς respectu ejus, quod qui munus offert, sibi proposuit, ut nempe causam suam obtineat, licet præstabilius foret causa cecidisse, quam constuprati judicii causam dedisse. Ad eum qui dat munus referunt vocem בעליו B. Luther. wer zu schencken hat, cum Aben-Ezra & Mercero: quia hic, quocunque se verta munere suo, prospere agit. Alii malunt referre ad eum qui accipit mu- nus, quia in ejus oculis pretiosum est munus, cum Chald. utpote Pagninus, Vatabl. Jun. Cartwright. Dn. D. Geierus: cujus animus in munere defixus est, non minus quam oculi in gemmam pretiosam quæ exhibetur. Vulgata hic nullum sensum reddit.

lant dilectionem, sed discordias ferant, quia pec- cata proximi sui non tegunt, sed retegunt, & ite- rato objectant, aut propalant. vers. 9. qui tegit præ- varicationem, persequitur charitatem: qui vero ite- rat rem, separat principem vel præcipuum inter amicos, ut Mercerus explicat, qui in amore, ho- nore, auxiliisque nobis fuit præcipuus. Conf. cap. 16, 28. (4.) Quod correptione non emendentur, vers. 10. Descendit increpatio in intelligentem magis (altius animo insidebit) quam si percutias stultum centies. Ad quæ ita Grotius:

Vers. 30.

## 17:10
A REPROOF ENTERETH MORE INTO A PRUDENT MAN, THAN A HUNDRED STRIPES INTO A FOOL) In the Hebrew, for 'entereth' it is 'descendeth': that is, it penetrates into the mind. A word is enough to the wise.

The sum is, says Cartwright, that the pious profit by the smallest correction and the mildest chastisement unto repentance: whereas the impious do not soften under the most severe threats or judgments of God, but are rather hardened. Conf. Jerem. 5, 3. There follows ver. 11. Surely, or only the rebellious seeketh evil: but a cruel messenger (intimating the sentence and the punishment due to him, or executing it against him) shall be sent against him. The wicked, whether in rebellion against God or men, at length receives a just reward: to which Grotius says thus:

Latin:

PLVS PROFICIT CORRECTIO APVD PRVDEN- TEM, QVAM CENTVM PLAGÆ APVD STVLTVM) In Hebræo pro plus proficit est descendit: id est, in animum penetrat. Sapienti dictum sat est.

Summa est, inquit Cartwrightus, pios minima correotione, & lenissima castigatione ad resipiscenti- am proficere: cum impii severissimis Dei aut commi- nationibus, aut judiciis non mollescant, sed obdu- rentur potius. Conf. Jerem. 5, 3. Sequitur vers. 11. Profecto, vel tantum rebellis quærit malum: sed nun- tius crudelis (sententiam ac supplicium debitum ei intimans, vel adversus eum exequens) mittetur contra eum. Improbus sive in Deum vel homines rebellionis tandem justam accipit mercedem: ad quæ ita Grotius:

## 17:11
BUT AN EVIL ANGEL SHALL BE SENT AGAINST HIM) A messenger, who may announce death to him.

(5.) That they are worse than wild beasts. vers. 12. Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man (who has lost her young) and not a fool in his folly, (let him meet) that is, rather let that one meet someone than this one, there is less danger to be feared from the former. (6.) That they are ungrateful. Whence vers. 13. He who returns, he says, evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house. He teaches that the ferocity of returning evil for good is at length avenged by God himself. (7.) That they are the authors of contentions vers. 14. As he who opens (a way) for waters is the beginning (or head) of contention (which B. Luther rightly expressed: Wer Hader anfähet, ist gleich als der dem Wasser den Damm ausreiffet.) Conf. Sirac. 28, 14. therefore before you involve yourself, that is, before you plunge yourself more deeply into those restless whirlpools of quarrels, (as it is said of the fool in chap. 20, 3: Every fool will be meddling) leave off contention. Grotius thus to this place.

Latin:

ANGELVS AVTEM MALVS MITTETVR CON- TRA EVM) Nuntius, qui ei mortem denuntiet.

(5.) Quod deteriores feris sint. vers. 12. Occur- rat ursus orbus alicui (qui suos fœtus amisit) & non stultus in stultitia sua, (occurrat) id est, potius il- le, quam hic occurrat alicui, minus ab illo me- tuendum periculi. (6.) Quod ingrati sint. Un- de vers. 13. Reddens, inquit, malum pro bono, non recedet malum de domo ejus. Docet feritatem ma- lum pro bono retribuendi Deum ipsum tandem ulcsci. (7.) Contentionum autores sint vers. 14. Ut is, qui aperit (viam) aquis, est principium (vel caput) contentionis (quod B. Lutherus recte ex- presit: Wer Hader anfähet, ist gleich als der dem Wasser den Damm ausreiffet.) Conf. Sirac. 28, 14. igitur ante miscere se, hoc est, antequam profundius inquietis illis jurgiorum gurgitibus te immergas, (uti cap. 20, 3. de stulto dicitur: Omnis stultus immiscet seipsum liti) litem dimitte. Grotius ita ad h. l.

## 17:14
HE THAT LETTETH OUT WATER IS THE HEAD OF STRIFE, AND BEFORE HE SUFFERETH REPROACH, HE LEAVETH JUDGMENT) Better thus from the Hebrew: He opens the waters, who is the beginning of contention: therefore before the strife is mixed, leave off: As he who makes a trench in a river bank does not know how far the river will penetrate, so he who begins quarrels: wherefore before they grow hot, they must be cut off.

Latin:

QVI DIMITTIT AQVAM CAPVT EST JVRGIO- RVM, ET ANTEQVAM PATIATVR CONTVME- LIAM, JVDICIVM DESERIT) Melius sic ex Hebræo: Aperit aquas, qui principium est contentionis: propterea ante- quam lis commisceatur, desere: Vt qui incile facit in ripa amnica, nescit quousque amnis sit penetraturus, ita qui jur- gia incipit: quare priusquam incalescant, incidenda sunt.

## 17:15
Ver. 15.

HE THAT JUSTIFIETH THE UNGODLY) That is, he absolves him, or adjudges an unjust cause to him. To justify is to treat as just.

(8.) Given to injustice is verse 15. He that justifieth the ungodly, (that is, he absolves him, or adjudges an unjust cause to him, as Grotius here) and he that condemneth (in Hebrew, maketh ungodly) the just, both of them are an abomination to the Lord. But when God is said to justify the ungodly, Rom. 4, 5, he is to be understood as justifying not him as such, but as he believes in Christ, and apprehends his righteousness, even though he brings nothing of himself to the tribunal of God but mere impiety.

(9.) That riches profit the fool nothing, or bring him any good: v. 16. why is there a price in the hand of a fool? to acquire wisdom? But he has no heart. The LXX and Vulgate add a sentence, but one which is not in the Hebrew, as Grotius also notes:

HE THAT MAKETH HIS HOUSE HIGH, SEEKETH RUIN, AND HE THAT AVOIDETH LEARNING, SHALL FALL INTO EVIL) This is from the Greek, not from the Hebrew.

(10.) That a fool easily pledges for another. For although, as is said in verse 17, a friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity, (that is, according to Grotius, a friend appears in adverse circumstances like a brother, indeed more than a brother, ch. 28, 24. Is born, that is, shows himself. Cf. Sirach 6, 7. 14.) yet it is only of a senseless and improvident man to rashly interpose himself as a sponsor for another's debt, or to make others' dangers his own. A MAN DESTITUTE OF HEART strikes his hand (promises by a stipulated hand, ch. 6, 1. ch. 11, 15.) pledging a pledge in the face or presence of his friend, or of the debtor for whom he interposes his credit, verse 18. Cf. 2 Corinthians 8, 13. (12.) That he loves quarrels, verse 19, he loves transgression who loves strife: he that exalteth his door (this is a description of a proud man, from the affected height of buildings, as Kimchi, Cajetan, Peltarius, Jansenius, Vatablus, or from the arrogant and swollen elation of the mouth, which is the door of the mind, when one speaks proudly and haughtily, as R. Solomon, R. Aben-Ezra, Lyranus, Mercerus, Lavaterus, Baynius prefer to explain: which pride is the cause of contention) seeks contention, or ruin. If we listen to Grotius, the sense will cohere better if you translate from the Hebrew: He loves iniquity, that is, every kind of sin, who loves strife, and widens his door, (namely, of iniquity) who seeks a fracture, that is, dissensions. Discord opens the way to many sins. Thus also Cartwright: In the words 'he widens his door,' it is an allegory for the fact that he spreads defection far and wide, just as one who widens a door opens a way to bring more into the house. We subjoin what Grotius says on these verses:

Latin:

Vers. 15.

QVI JVSTIFICAT IMPIVM) Id est, eum absolvit, aut illi causam injustam adjudicat. Justificare est tractare ut justum.

(8.) Injustitiæ deditus est vers. 15. Justificans im- pium, (id est, eum absolvit, aut illi causam injustam adjudicat, ut hic Grotius) & qui condemnat (in Ebr. impium facit) justum, abominatio Domino sunt etiam ambo ipsi. Cum autem Deus impium ju- stificare dicitur Rom. 4, 5. non ipsum qua talem, sed qua credit in Christum, ejusque justitiam appre- hendit, etsi de se nihil ad tribunal Dei nisi meram impietatem adferat, justificare intelligendus est.

(9.) Quod stulto nihil prosit, vel boni adferant di- vitiæ: v. 16. ut quid est pretium in manu stulti? ad acquirendam sapientiam? At non est cor ei. Addunt LXX. & Vulg. sententiam, sed quæ in Ebræo non est notante etiam Grotio:

QVI ALTAM FACIT DOMVM SVAM, QVÆRIT RVINAM, ET QVI EVITAT DISCERE, OCCIDET IN MALO) Hoc ex Græco est, non ex Hebræo.

(10.) Quod stultus facile spondeat pro alio. Quanquam enim, quod vers. 17. dicitur, omni tem- pore diligit amicus, & frater in afflictione nasci- tur, (id est, juxta Grot. amicus in rebus adversis velut frater apparet, imo plusquam frater cap. 28, 24. Nascitur, id est ostendit se. Conf. Syrac. 6, 7. 14.) tamen non nisi vecordis & improvidi est, se temere pro ære alieno sponsorem interponere, aut aliena pericula sua facere. HOMO DE- FICIENS CORDE percutit manum (manu stipu- lata promittit, cap. 6, 1. cap. 11, 15.) spondens spon- sionem in facie vel præsentia amici sui, vel debi- toris, pro quo fidem suam interponit, vers. 18. Conf. 2. Corinth. 8, 13. (11.) Quod rixas diligat vers. 19. diligit prævaricationem, qui diligit litem: qui elevat ostium suum (descriptio est hominis su- perbi, ab eminentia ædium affectata, uti Kim- chius, Cajetanus, Peltarius, Jansenius, Vatablus, vel ab arroganti tumidaque oris, quod animi est janua, elatione, quum quis superbe ac fastuose loquitur, uti explicare malunt R. Salomo, R. A- ben-Ezra, Lyranus, Mercerus, Lavaterus, Bay- nius: quæ superbia causa est contentionis) quærit contentionem, vel ruinam. Grotium si audiamus, sensus melius cohærebit si ex Hebræo vertas: Diligit iniquitatem, id est, omne peccati genus, qui diligit jurgium, & ampliat januam ejus, (nempe iniquita- tis) qui quærit fracturam, id est, dissidia. Discor- dia multis peccatis viam aperit. Sic etiam Cart- wrightus: In verbis januam ejus ampliat, est allego- ria pro eo, quod est defectionem longe lateque pro- pagat, sicut qui januam dilatat, viam plus in domum inferendi aperit. Subjungimus, quæ Grotius ad hos versus:

## 17:17
Ver. 17.

A FRIEND LOVES AT ALL TIMES) He who truly loves does not desert a friend when fortune changes. Menander: Χρυσὸς μὲν οἶδεν ἐξελέγχεσθαι πυρὶ Ἡδ’ ἐν φίλοις ἔυνοια καιρῷ κρίνεται. AND A BROTHER IS PROVEN IN DISTRESS) A friend appears like a brother in adverse circumstances: indeed, more than a brother, as is said shortly in ch. 18, 24. Euripides thinks no differently in Orestes: Ὡς ἀνὴρ, ὅςις τρόποισι συντακῇ, θυραῖος ὢν Μυρίων κρείσσων ὀμαίμων ἀνδρὶ κεκτῆσθαι φίλος. Well, however, 'in distress.' Namely, as yellow gold is tested in fires, so faith is to be tested in hard times; says Ovid. For 'is proven' in the Hebrew it is 'is born,' for 'shows himself.'

Latin:

Vers. 17.

OMNI TEMPORE DILIGIT, QVI AMICVS EST) Qui verè amat, mutata fortuna amicum non deserit. Me- nander: Χρυσὸς μὲν οἶδεν ἐξελέγχεσθαι πυρὶ Ἡδ’ ἐν φίλοις ἔυνοια καιρῷ κρίνεται. ET FRATER IN ANGVSTIIS COMPROBATVR) Amicus in rebus adversis velut frater apparet : imo plus- quam frater, ut mox dicitur c. 18, 24. nec aliter censet Eu- ripides Oreste: Ὡς ἀνὴρ, ὅςις τρόποισι συντακῇ, θυραῖος ὢν Μυρίων κρείσσων ὀμαίμων ἀνδρὶ κεκτῆσθαι φίλος. Bene autem, in angustiis. Scilicet ut fulvum spectatur in ignibus aurum, Tempore sic duro est experienda fides; ait Ovidius. Pro comprobatur in Hebræo est nascitur, pro ostendit se.

## 17:19
Ver. 19.

HE WHO MEDITATES DISCORDS, LOVES QUARRELS, AND HE WHO EXALTS HIS DOOR, SEEKS RUIN) The sense will cohere better if you translate from the Hebrew: He loves iniquity (that is, every kind of sin) who loves strife, and he widens his door (namely, of iniquity) who seeks a fracture, that is, dissensions. Discord opens a way to many sins.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

QVI MEDITATVR DISCORDIAS, DILIGIT RI- XAS, ET QVI EXALTAT OSTIVM, QVÆRIT RVI- NAM) Sensus melius cohærebit, si ex Hebræo vertas: Diligit iniquitatem, (id est, omne peccati genus) qui diligit jurgium, & ampliat januam ejus (nempe iniquitatis) qui quæ- rit fracturam, id est dissidia. Discordia multis peccatis vi- am aperit.

## 17:20
Ver. 20.

HE WHO IS OF A PERVERSE HEART, SHALL NOT FIND GOOD: AND HE WHO PERVERTS HIS TONGUE SHALL FALL INTO EVIL. Let it be rendered, 'he who perverts his tongue.' The effects or inconveniences of perversity and folly are explained. (1.) That they do not have prosperous successes, both those who have a malignant mind, and those who have a perverse mouth, and who more plot and speak things that harm than those which are profitable. (2.) That they create grief for their own: He who begets a fool (begets him) to his own grief, and the father of a fool will not rejoice, verse 21. From foolish and impious children, parents perceive nothing but grief. Verse 22 is added, a sentence concerning the resulting joy of the soul: A joyful mind makes a flourishing age (in Hebrew it will be a sad spirit dries up the bones. A joyful heart keeps a man safe and healthy, but a sad mind consumes life. Which is to be understood concerning joy in a lawful matter, and one pleasing to God, since otherwise it is better to grieve than to rejoice, Eccles. 2, 2. 2. Cor. 7, 10. (3.) That they pervert judgment, verse 23. The impious man receives a gift from the bosom (which the offerer hides in his bosom), (therefore liable to the judgment of God, chap. 15, 27. Deuter. 16, 19. chap. 27, 25.) to pervert the paths (processes and ways) of judgment. Grotius on this passage at least says this:

Latin:

Vers. 20.

QVI PERVERSI CORDIS EST, NON IN- VENIET BONUM: ET QVI VERTIT LIN- GUAM INCIDET IN MALUM. Reddatur, qui pervertit linguam. Effecta vel in- commoda perversitatis & stultitiæ exponuntur. (1.) Quod non habeant prosperos successus, tum qui malignum habent animum, tum qui perversum os, & magis machinantur & loquuntur quæ obsunt, quam quæ prosunt. (2.) Quod dolorem creent suis: Gignens stultum in dolorem suum (gignit) & non gaudebit pater fatui, vers. 21. Ex stultis & impiis liberis parentes non nisi dolorem percipiunt. Additur v. 22. sententia de lætitia animi consequenti: Animus gaudens ætatem floridam facit (in Ebr. erit bona medicina) Spiritus autem tristis exsiccat ossa. Cor lætum incolumem & sanum conservat hominem, tristis autem animus absumit vitam. Quæ de gaudio in re licita, ac Deo placente accipienda, quum alias dolere præstet, quam lætari, Eccles. 2, 2. 2. Cor. 7, 10. (3.) Quod pervertant judicium vers. 23. Munus è sinu (quod offerens in sinu occultat) accipit impius, (obnoxius ideo judicio Dei cap. 15, 27. Deuter. 16, 19. cap. 27, 25. ad pervertendum semitas (processus & vias) judicii. Grotius ad h. l. hæc saltem:

## 17:23
Verse 23. THE IMPIOUS MAN RECEIVES GIFTS FROM THE BOSOM, TO PERVERT THE PATH OF JUDGMENT) See what is above 15, 27. & Deut. 16, 19.

(4.) That they always wander with an uncertain mind, verse 24. Wisdom is in the sight of the intelligent: that which he may look upon and perform wisely is obvious to him: but the eyes of a fool are at the end of the earth: inasmuch as a fool wanders here and there uncertain in mind, nor has anything certain which he may follow, now applying his mind to this thing, soon affected by weariness of it he flees to another, and fluctuates like a Euripus in all his counsels, as Cartwright explains.

(5.) That they bring bitterness to their parents, verse 25. A foolish son is an indignation to his father, and bitterness to his mother, that is, a cause of indignation and cares, nay, of bitterness and most grievous acerbity to both parents, so that nothing more bitter can happen to them. Which is more than what was said in verse 21, and is repeatedly inculcated, so that greater care may be applied in the education of children.

(6.) That they contract a grave guilt, especially by the condemnation of the just, verse 26. Also to condemn the just is not good, (it is a μείωσις, by which little is said, and more is signified, it is a great evil, and carries with it a grave guilt of punishment) by striking the noble נדיבים for righteousness. Compare the Weimar Paraphrase & Dn. D. Geier on this passage.

(7.) That fools betray themselves by much speaking: which is taught from the contrary in verse 27, he who knows knowledge restrains his words: a man of understanding is precious in spirit; whereas a fool brings forth all his spirit, chap. 29, 11. Solomon adds in verse 28, Even a fool, when he is silent, is counted wise (Conf. chap. 25, 28. Job 13, 5.) and he who shuts his lips is intelligent. Grotius: Just as it was said to someone: If you had been silent, you would have been a philosopher. Cartwright says we are taught by this Proverb to be of such a calming of the spirits, which restrains all sudden motions and perturbations of the mind, as of anger, so of love; as of joy, so of sorrow, fear, etc. We are also forbidden, lest, driven by these motions of the mind, we blurt out anything rashly, whether in praise or in blame, or whether it be to testify to our joy, or to betray our grief, etc. Then indeed the silence of a fool is most of all to his credit, when, with a consciousness of his own weakness and ignorance, he is silent, so that he may be informed by others who excel in wisdom. For as St. Gregory says, the wicked, just as they are light in sense, so are they precipitate in speech: because what a light mind conceives, a lighter tongue immediately brings forth. Therefore, let us perpetually guard our mouth, as Chrysostom warns in Psalm 50, applying reason to it as a key.

Latin:

Vers. 23. MVNERA DE SINV IMPIVS ACCIPIT, VT PERVERTAT SEMITAM JVDICII) Vide quæ supra 15, 27. & Deut. 16, 19.

(4.) Quod incerti animo semper vagentur, vers. 24. in conspectu intelligentis est sapientia: obvium ei est, quod suspiciat & peragat sapienter: at oculi stulti sunt in extremo terræ: siquidem stultus huc illuc animo incertus vagetur, nec certi quid habeat, quod sequatur, nunc animum ad hanc rem adjiciat, mox illius tædio affectus ad aliam transfugiat, & tanquam Euripus in omnibus consiliis suis fluctuet, ut explicat Cartwrightus.

(5.) Quod amaritudinem adferant parentibus vers. 25. Indignatio est Patri suo filius stultus, & amaritudo matri suæ, id est, indignationis & curarum, imo amaritudinis, & acerbitatis gravissimæ causa utrique parenti, ita ut non possit acerbius quid iisdem accidere. Quod plus est, quam vers. 21. dixerat, & iterato inculcatur, ut eo major cura in liberorum educatione adhibeatur.

(6.) Quod gravem reatum contrahant, imprimis condemnatione justi, vers. 26. Etiam contemnare justum non est bonum, (μείωσις est, qua parum dicitur, & plus significatur, grande malum est, & gravem reatum pœnæ secum trahit) percutiendo ingenuos נדיבים propter rectitudinem. Conf. Vinariens. Paraphr. & Dn. D. Geier. in h. l.

(7.) Quod multiloquio se prodant fatui: quod à contrario docetur vers. 27. cohibet eloquia sua, qui scit scientiam: pretiosus spiritu est vir intelligens: quum contra stultus omnem spiritum suum proferat, cap. 29, 11. Addit Salomo vers. 28. Etiam stultus, cum tacet sapiens reputatur (Conf. cap. 25, 28. Job. 13, 5.) & qui obturat labia sua intelligens. Grotius: Sicut cuidam dictum fuit: Si tacuisses, Philosophus fuisses. Cartwrightus docemur, inquit, hoc Proverbio, ea animorum sedatione esse, quæ omnes subitos animi motus & perturbationes cohibeat, ut iræ, sic amoris; ut gaudii, sic mœroris, metus &c. Una etiam prohibemur, ne his animi motibus impulsi aliquid temere effutiamus, sive in laudem, sive in vituperium, sive sit ad gaudium nostrum testandum, sive ad prodendum dolorem, &c. Tum vero silentium stulti vel maxime in laude est, cum conscientia imbecillitatis & inscitiæ suæ silet, ut ab aliis, qui sapientia pollent, informetur. Nam ut S. Gregor. ait, pravi sicut in sensu sunt leves, ita in locutione præcipites: quia quæ levis mens concipit, levior lingua protinus prodit. Os ergo nostrum monente Chrysostomo in Psalm. 50. perpetuo custodiamus, rationem ei tanquam clavem adhibentes.

## 17:28
Verse 28. EVEN A FOOL, IF HE IS SILENT, SHALL BE COUNTED WISE) Just as it was said to someone: If you had been silent, you would have been a philosopher.

φιλαυτία (self-love), προσωποληψία (respect of persons), the mouth of fools, as also sloth, vain hope, and likewise pride are noted; and the moderation of the tongue, and the utility of marriage and friendship are inculcated.

Latin:

Vers. 28. STVLTVS QVOQVE SI TACVERIT, SAPIENS REPVTABITVR) Sicut cuidam dictum est: Si tacuisses, Philosophus fuisses.

Notatur φιλαυτία, προσωποληψία, os stulto- rum, ut & desidia, spes vana, nec non super- bia; & inculcatur linguæ moderatio, conju- gii, & amicitiæ utilitas.

## 18:1 Argument
Verse 1.

HE WHO WISHES TO WITHDRAW FROM A FRIEND SEEKS OCCASIONS, HE WILL BE REPROACHABLE AT ALL TIMES) The sense of the Hebrew words here seems to be: He who withdraws himself from the crowd inquires as much as he pleases (supply: into the nature of things, from what follows): in every nature of things he mixes himself. Now follows the ἀντίθετον (antithesis).

Latin:

Verf. 1.

OCCASIONES QVÆRIT QVI VVLT RECEDERE AB AMICO, OMNI TEMPORE ERIT EXPROBRA- BILIS) Hebræorum verborum sensus hic videtur esse: Quantum lubet inquirit (supple rerum naturam, ex sequen- tibus) is qui subducit se turbæ: in omni rerum natura miscet se. Sequitur jam ἀντίθετον.

## 18:2
Verse 2.

A FOOL DOES NOT RECEIVE THE WORDS OF PRUDENCE, UNLESS YOU SAY THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE IN HIS HEART) From the Hebrew thus: A fool does not love intelligence, unless it be to manifest his heart. The sense of these two ἀντίθετα (antitheses) here is: that a philosopher does not seek things by which he may boast, but is delighted by the knowledge of things for their own sake: but that vain men learn nothing, unless it be to show themselves off to others as they please.

And the Vulgate, which Cornelius à Lapide tries in vain to reconcile with the Hebrew text, and Grotius, with the Belgians and Vatablus, departs from the true sense. Solomon is not dealing with an unfaithful friend who recoils and casts reproaches (thus Cornelius wishes 'exprobrabilem' to be said barbarously), nor with a philosopher investigating sciences solely out of a love of nature: but he notes Φιλαυτίαν [self-love] and ambition: by which whatever the ambitious man does, he does for the sake of his own desire, pleasing himself alone, and thereby separating himself from others: FOR THE SAKE OF HIS OWN DESIRE, THE SEPARATED ONE WILL SEEK, separating himself from others through ambition, MIXING HIMSELF IN ALL WISDOM, as if affecting a monopoly of wisdom, desiring to reform all others as if they were shadows: The sum is, says Cartwright, that a man delighting in his own studies, and despising others in comparison to himself, while he follows those things which are pleasing to his own mind, rashly thrusts himself upon everyone as a busybody. THE FOOL IS NOT DELIGHTED BY SOLID AND HEAVENLY INTELLIGENCE 1 Cor. 2:14. BUT IN THE REVEALING OF HIS OWN HEART, when he can scatter the folly which he fosters in his heart, as B. Luther and the Weimar theologians [Vinarienses] do, with the approval of Mr. Dr. Geier: so that the fool's itch for informing others, or for exposing the inept inventions of his own heart, may be noted. Fools do not listen to the intelligent, but they themselves desire to be heard. She applauds herself with clattering stork-beak. WHEN THE WICKED COMES, CONTEMPT ALSO COMES, AND WITH A MAN OF DISGRACE, REPROACH, verse 3. That is the property of Φιλαυτία [self-love], to despise others; as if he were saying, the wicked man (pleasing only himself) is accustomed to bring these things along with him, these things accompany him, because it is his property to despise others, to affect and drench them with disgrace and reproach, as much as lies within him, as Mercerus explains with Aben-Ezra and R. Levi. The Vulgate, having followed the LXX interpreters, departs here into entirely different matters: when the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he despises, but disgrace and reproach follow him: which it is manifest depart from the Hebrew text (more correctly expressed by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodoret in 'when the wicked comes, contempt comes'): whence Cajetan, Jansenius, Baynus, and others leave the Vulgate here and accede to the handed-down explanation. Now, in contrast, the eulogy of the speech of the wise is subjoined, verse 4: as deep waters are the words of the mouth of a man, who truly deserves to be called איש [a man], namely a prudent one, as is gathered from the other hemistich: as a redundant torrent is the fountain of wisdom. From a mind furnished with wisdom speeches gush forth, not vain or boastful, but reflecting the vein of wisdom, the force and weight of which you cannot easily examine. The words of a wise man are born not in the mouth, but in the heart: and as a fountain never dries up, but pours forth perennial waters, so the heart of a wise man pours forth perennial doctrines of wisdom.

Latin:

Verf. 2.

NON RECIPIT STVLTVS VERBA PRVDENTIÆ, NISI EA DIXERIS QVÆ VERSANTVR IN CORDE EJVS) Ex Hebræo sic: Non amat stultus intelligentiam, nisi ut manifestet se cor ejus. Duorum horum ἀντιθέτων hic sen- sus est: Philosophum non quærere quibus se jactet, sed dele- ctari rerum cognitione per se: at vanos homines nihil addi- scere, nisi ut pro lubitu se ostentent aliis.

Et Vulgata, quam nequicquam cum Ebræo textu conciliat Cornelius à Lapide, & Grotius cum Belgis & Vatablo à vero sensu abeunt. Non de amico infido resiliente, & probra jaciente (ita bar- bare exprobrabilem dici, vult Cornelius) nec de Philosopho solas scientias amore naturæ indagan- te agit Salomo: sed Φιλαυτίαν, & ambitionem notat: qua quicquid agit homo ambitiosus, ob cupiditatem propriam agat, sibi soli placens, ad- eoque se ab aliis separans: OB CONCUPISCEN- TIAM SUAM carnalem QUÆRET SEPA- RATUS, per ambitionem se ab aliis separans, IN OMNI SAPIENTIA MISCENS SE, qua- si monipolium sapientiæ affectans, cunctos alios tanquam umbras reformare gestiens: Summa est, inquit Cartwrightus, hominem studiis suis delectan- tem, & alios præ se spernentem, dum illa sequitur, quæ animo suo collibita sunt, se omnibus temere tan- quam πολυπράγμονα ingerere. NON DELE- CTATUR STOLIDUS INTELLIGENTIA SOLIDA & superna 1. Corinth. 2, 14. SED IN DETECTIONE CORDIS SUI, cum stultitiam suam, quam in corde fovet, spargere potest, uti B. Luther. & Vinarienses, approbante Dn. D. Geie- ro: ut notetur stolidus informandi alios, aut ine- ptas proprii cordis adinventiones exponendi pru- ritus. Non audiunt stolidi intelligentes, sed ipsi audiri cupiunt. Ipsa sibi plaudit crepitante ciconia rostro. QUANDO VENIT IMPIUS, VENIT ETIAM CONTEMTUS, ET CUM VIRO IGNOMINIÆ OPPROBRIUM, vers. 3. id τῆς Φιλαυτίας proprium est, alios contemnere; qua- si dicat, hæc una secum afferre solet impius (sibi so- li placens) hæc eum comitantur, quod ejus propri- um sit alios contemnere, ignominia & probro, quan- tum in eo situm est, afficere, & perfundere, ut expo- nit Mercerus cum Aben-Ezra & R. Levi. Vulgatus sequutus LXX. Interpp. hic in alia omnia abit: im- pius cum in profundum venerit peccatorum, conte- mnit, sed sequitur eum ignominia & opprobrium: quæ ab Ebræo textu (rectius ab Aquila, Symma- cho, & Theodoreto expresso in veniendo impium ve- nit contemtus,) abire manifestum est: unde Vulga- tam hic relinquunt, & traditæ explicationi acce- dunt Cajetanus, Jansenius, Baynus, aliique. Sub- jungitur jam ex adverso elogium sermonis sapien- tum, vers. 4. ut aquæ profundæ sunt verba oris viri, qui vere איש meretur dici, prudentis nempe, ut ex altero hemistichio colligitur: ut torrens redun- dans est vena sapientiæ. Ex animo sapientia in- structo sermones scaturiunt, non vani, aut jactabundi, sed venam sapientiæ referentes, quorum vim & pondus non facile perscruteris. Verba sapientis non in ore, sed in corde nascuntur: & uti fons nunquam arescit, sed perennes fundit aquas, sic cor sapientis perennes fundit sapientiæ doctrinas.

## 18:5
Verse 5.

TO ACCEPT THE PERSON OF THE WICKED IS NOT GOOD, THAT YOU MAY DECLINE FROM THE TRUTH OF JUDGMENT) To accept a person, or, as the Hebrews say, a face, is said of one who is moved by qualities not pertaining to the case, for instance, wealth, friendship, or kinship. For these are apparent: the case must be examined.

In the Hebrew, as Cornelius notes, it is, to cast down the just in judgment. It is not good, that is, it is most evil and wicked, according to the interpretation of R. Levi. Bernard, book 2, On Consideration, to Eugenius: Do not consider yourself guilty of a small sin if you take the faces of sinners, and not rather the causes. Compare Exod. 23, 3. Levit. 19, 18. Deut. 1, 17. chap. 10, 17. chap. 16, 19. 2. Paralip. 19, 7. Job 32, 2. chap. 34, 9. James 2, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ACCIPERE PERSONAM IMPII NON EST BONVM, VT DECLINES A VERITATE JVDICII) Personam, sive, ut Hebræi loquuntur, faciem accipere dicitur qui qualitatibus ad causam nihil pertinentibus movetur, puta divitiis, amicitia, propinquitate. Hæc enim apparent: causa scrutanda est.

In Ebr. notante Cornelio est, ad dejiciendum justum in judicio. Non est bonum, id est, pessimum est, & nefarium interprete R. Levi. Bernhardus lib. 2. de consider. ad Eugen. Non parvi te reum peccati existimes, si facies peccatorum sumis, & non potius causas. Conf. Exod. 23, 3. Levit. 19, 18. Deut. 1, 17. cap. 10, 17. cap. 16, 19. 2. Paralip. 19, 7. Job. 32, 2. cap. 34, 9. Jac. 2, 1.

## 18:6
Verse 6.

THE LIPS OF A FOOL MINGLE THEMSELVES IN STRIFE: AND HIS MOUTH PROVOKES QUARRELS.

The Hebrew, as Cornelius admits, is thus: The lips of a fool come into (with) strife, and his mouth will call for blows. For the striking of himself, as Luther rightly says: for this is the outcome of the pursuit of contention: as R. Solomon Jarchi says, he is a craftsman for himself, so that he may be beaten: which sense the following verse, which can be seen as an exegesis of this saying, confirms, unless one prefers to say that in this clause the cause is explained, and in the following verse 7 the consequent inconvenience is added, so that in both hemistichs the same thing is expressed: the mouth of the fool will be a confusion to himself, and his lips a snare to his soul, as Cartwright says on verse 6. The sum, he says, is that by the intemperance of the tongue peace is violated, and it comes to blows: on verse 7, the sum is that the foolish man often brings evil, and even death, upon himself by his imprudent and litigious railings. To the speeches of fools also pertains verse 8. The words of a double-tongued man (in Hebrew, a whisperer, a flatterer) are as simple, in the Hebrew. מִתְלַהֲמִים which occurs only here and in Proverbs 26, 22, and there the LXX render it as the speeches of flatterers, κερκώπων (of tailed ones), that is, of those fawning with their tails, μαλακοὶ (soft). Aquila explains it as the speeches of a whisperer, γοητικοὶ (enchanting), apt for deceiving. So also R. Mardochai Nathan interprets it, namely by חלקים (smooth things), soothing, flattering, dividing, where words are divided, so that one thing is in the mouth, and another is cherished in the heart: which explanation is to be preferred to the others. Compare Psalm 55, 22. BUT THEY DESCEND INTO THE INNERMOST PARTS OF THE BELLY, the innermost recesses of the heart: because belly stands for heart in chap. 22, 18. Job 32, 19. Hab. 3, 16. because the calumnies of whisperers remain stored in the deep mind: according to that saying, slander boldly, something always sticks. Others say, the words of a flatterer are smooth and thin like oil, but they carry with them poison, which quickly penetrates the innermost parts of the body and heart: since poison put into oil, carried by the smoothness and slipperiness of the oil, immediately penetrates into the innermost parts of the body.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

LABIA STULTI MISCENT SE RIXIS: ET OS EJUS JURGIA PROVOCAT.

Ebræa, fatente Cornelio, sic habent, Labia stulti veniunt in (cum) lite, & os ejus ad percussiones vocabit. Ad sui ipsius percussionem, ut recte Lutherus: hic enim eventus est studii contentionis: uti R. Salomo Jarchi, opifex est sibi, ut verberetur: quem sensum sequens versus, qui videri potest ἐξήγησις hujus dicti, confirmat, nisi quis malit dicere hoc commate prius exponi, & versu sequenti 7. consequens incommodum subjungi, ita ut utroque hemistichio idem exprimatur: os stulti erit confusio sibi, & labia ipsius laqueus animæ ejus, quomodo Cartwrightus ad vers. 6. Summa est, inquit, linguæ intemperantia pacem violari, & ad manus venire: ad vers. 7. summa est, stolidum suis imprudentibus & ligitiosis convitiis sæpe sibi malum, atque adeo mortem consciscere. Ad stultorum sermones pertinet quoque vers. 8. Verba bilinguis (in Ebr. susurronis adulatoris) quasi simplicia, in Ebræor. מִתְלַהֲמִים quod non nisi hîc, & Proverb. 26, 22. occurrit ibique LXX. reddunt sermones assentatorum κερκώπων caudatorum, id est, cauda blandientium, μαλακοὶ molles. Aquila exponit sermones susurronis, γοητικοὶ incantatorii, ad decipiendum apti. Sic etiam interpretatur R. Mardoch. Nathan, nimirum per חלקים lenientes, blandientes, dividentes, ubi verba dividuntur, ut aliud sit in ore, aliud foveatur corde: quæ explicatio cæteris præferenda. Conf. Psal. 55, 22. SED IPSA DESCENDUNT AD INFERIORA VENTRIS, recessus intimos cordis: quia venter pro corde cap. 22, 18. Job. 32, 19. Hab. 3, 16. quod calumniæ susurronum maneant alta mente repostæ: juxta illud calumniare audacter, semper aliquid hæret. Alii, verba adulatoris sunt blanda & tenuia instar olei, sed vehunt secum venenum, quod cito penetrat intima corporis & cordis: siquidem venenum oleo inditum olei lenitate & lubricitate vectum illico in intima corporis penetret.

## 18:9
Verse 9.

HE WHO IS SOFT AND DISSOLUTE IN HIS WORK, IS BROTHER TO HIM WHO WASTES HIS OWN WORK) In the Hebrew: Even he who is lazy in his work, is a brother (that is, is equal) to a master who wastes (his own). The lazy man and the prodigal have the same outcome: they come to poverty.

A maxim is prefixed in the Latin Roman Codex. Fear casts down the lazy, but the souls of the effeminate shall hunger: but that is neither held in the authentic text, nor transcribed in the Complutensian Latin from the LXX, who took the following Hebrew verse as ambiguous, and thus expressed it with a double meaning, as Cornelius excuses. But Grotius expressed the sense of the words, which are by no means ambiguous, more correctly. Compare chapter 10, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QVI MOLLIS EST ET DISSOLVTVS IN OPERE SVO, FRATER EST SVA OPERA DISSIPANTIS) In Hebræo: Etiam qui piger est in opere, frater est, (id est, par est) domino (sua) dissipanti. Eundem exitum habent piger & prodigus: ad egestatem deveniunt.

Præmittitur gnome in Codic. Latin. Roman. Pigrum dejicit timor, animæ autem effœminatorum esurient: sed ea nec in textu authentico habetur, nec in Latin.
