Complut. transcripta ex LXX. qui se- quentem versum Hebræum ut ancipitem accepe- runt, adeoque duplici sententia expresserunt, ut ex- cusat Cornelius. Rectius autem sensum verbo- rum, quæ minime ambigua sunt, expressit Grotius. Conf. cap. 10, 4.

## 18:10
Verse 10. THE NAME OF THE LORD IS A MOST STRONG TOWER: THE JUST RUNS TO IT, AND SHALL BE EXALTED.

That we may be taught how vain the hope of the wicked is, and that trust must be placed solely in God, whose name—or rather, who, for by the name of God, God himself designated by name is understood by metonymy with relation to acknowledgment, naming, and invocation—is as a most strong tower (or tower of strength), to which the just man runs with the trust of his heart, because he desires to surrender himself entirely to God and to enclose himself in his grace and power as if in a most strong tower: where he is certainly exalted, so that he may emerge superior to his adversaries and be able to look down upon them with a joyful heart. Regarding the wicked man, however, it is hinted by way of antithesis that he trusts in his riches in vain, and finds no safe protection or refuge there, nor any exaltation against enemies, but that that city or citadel of strength is only imaginary. v. 11. The riches of the rich man are as a city of his strength, and as a wall raised in his own imagination, which wall indeed suddenly and easily collapses, Isa. 30, 13. And since pride is an adjunct of the rich, Solomon adds concerning the outcome v. 12. Before he is broken, the heart of man is exalted (lifted up). Before a man is glorified, he is humbled. Compare c. 11, 2. c. 16, 18. To which the proverb of the Arabs contributes, Centur. 1. n. 3. If you do not know how to ascend by a ladder, you will not walk upon the roof.

Latin:

Vers. 10. TURRIS FORTISSIMA NOMEN DOMINI: AD IPSUM CURRIT JUSTUS, ET EXALTABITUR.

Ut quam vana sit spes impii, unice in Deo fiduciam collocandam esse docemur, cujus nomen, vel qui, nam per nomen Dei DEus ipse nomine designatus intelligitur per metonym. cum relatione ad agnitionem, nomi- nationem & invocationem, est velut turris fortis- sima, (vel turris roboris) ad ipsum currit justus cor- dis fiducia, quod totum se Deo concedere, ejus- que gratiæ & potentiæ veluti turri fortissimæ in- cludere gestit: ubi certo exaltatur, ut superior adversariis suis evadat, eosque læto corde despi- cere possit. De impio autem vi antirheseos innui- tur, eum frustra in divitiis suis confidere, nullum- que ibi tutum præsidium, aut refugium, nullam exaltationem adversus hostes invenire, sed imagi- nariam tantum esse illam fortitudinis urbem vel ar- cem. v. 11. Opes divitis sunt ut urbs fortitudinis ejus, & sicut murus elevatus in imaginatione ipsius, qui vero murus subito & facile corruit Esa. 30, 13. Et quum divitum adjunctum sit superbia, addit Salo- mo de eventu v. 12. Antequam conteratur, exaltatur (elevatur) cor hominis. Homo antequam glorifice- tur, humiliatur. Conf. c. 11, 2. c. 16, 18. Quo facit Arabum proverbium Centur. 1. n. 3. Si nescis ascen- dere per scalam, non ambulabis super tectum.

## 18:13
Verse 13. HE WHO ANSWERS BEFORE HE HEARS, SHOWS HIMSELF TO BE A FOOL, AND WORTHY OF CONFUSION.

Solomon now proceeds to the moderation of the tongue. In the Hebrew it is folly to him, and shame. The haste of fools in answering is noted, where one does not hear, that is, understand (Genesis 42, 23. Deuteronomy 28, 49) first his mind, to whom the answer is to be made. Compare Syr. 11, 8. To pass judgment on matters not fully perceived is both foolish and shameful.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QUI PRIUS RESPONDEt QUAM AU- DIAT, STULTUM SE ESSE DEMONSTRAT, ET CONFUSIONE DIGNUM.

Ad linguæ moderationem jam accedit Salomo. In Ebr. stultitia est ei, & pudor. Notatur stultorum præcipitantia in responsione, ubi non auditur, id est, intelligitur (Genes. 42, 23. Deuter. 28, 49. prius mens ejus, cui responsio sit. Conf. Syr. 11, 8. De re- bus non plane perceptis sententiam ferre simul cum stultum tum ignominiosum est.

## 18:14
Ver. 14. THE SPIRIT OF A MAN SUSTAINS HIS OWN INFIRMITY: BUT A SPIRIT EASY TO ANGER WHO SHALL BE ABLE TO SUSTAIN?

In the Hebrew it is not 'easy to anger,' but נכאה, 'sorrowful,' as Osiander says, 'shaken by pain,' as the Syriac, from כאב 'pain,' or 'struck, crushed, broken,' Theodotion from נכה, the LXX 'faint-hearted': to which is opposed the spirit of a man, a generous and manly mind: which can sustain, bear, and support infirmity, whether shaking the body or the soul: as Jerome relates of Paula in her life, that she sustained the diseases of the body with a strong spirit. Cf. Rom. 8:32, 2 Cor. 4:8, 9. But who shall lift up, raise up (sustain, from the former clause) a spirit broken and crushed? If, however, it pleases one to understand 'shaken' generally with the Tigurines as affected by passions, the sense of the Vulgate will also be comprehended: for a spirit can be crushed by anger, and by pain, or by a blow: and a magnanimous, vigorous, and joyful spirit can sustain not only its own infirmity, but another's as well. In what way this aphorism coheres with the preceding: because a fool is no less headlong in anger than in response is: Thus Bede: He who is easy to anger, and cannot sustain himself, so that being angry he often says those things which soon, when he is calm, because he said them, he regrets, and often does not even know if he said them. Therefore, what is added in v. 15, A prudent heart possesses or acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks knowledge, Aben-Ezra joins thus: A broken spirit, and one easy to anger, does not attain wisdom, but the mind of a prudent man, bearing his sickness patiently, will be accumulated with knowledge by the aid of his prudence. But the heart of the prudent acquires (and acquires, and by acquiring possesses) knowledge: Because (thus the particle Vav is not rarely taken in a causal sense) his ear seeks the same, chap. 15. Regarding the gift of wisdom, perhaps it will also not be inappropriately taken for the sake of connection in verse 16, with the author of the Greek Catena: THE GIFT OF A MAN, namely that chief one and called by way of excellence, which is primarily to be sought, acquired, and requested by prayers, James 1:5, as being better and more excellent than all gold, it widens his way, makes a broad place for him, nay, before Princes it makes space for him, or, as in the Hebrew, it will lead him before the great, when it will procure their favor, and will promote him to their familiarity and similar dignity. In almost the same manner Bede and Salonius: What is the gift that widens this way, and what makes space for him before princes? This gift is the gift of charity, or of other virtues, which the faithful receive from the Lord. Regarding the gifts and offerings which are offered to the great, they are commonly and generally explained, yet not those which are for overturning justice, but those which are offered for an honest and useful purpose, whether public or private. The sum is, says Cartwright, that a gift has the greatest moment for accomplishing that which we desire. For a gift is a means to instruct; and therefore, according as it is applied to honest or dishonest causes, so it is in praise or blame. For it is counted to the praise of Jacob, that he instructed and prepared a gift to calm the fury of his brother Esau: likewise Abigail, that she sent her gift ahead to bend David. On the contrary, the gift of Ziba, by which he drew David's mind to accept a calumny against Mephibosheth, is counted for blame. For the abuse of gifts does not take away their legitimate use.

Latin:

Vers. 14. SPIRITUS VIRI SUSTENTAT IMBECIL- LITATEM SUAM: SPIRITUM VERO AD IRASCENDUM FACILEM QUIS POTERIT SUSTINERE?

In Ebr. non est ad irascendum facilem, sed נכאה, mæstum, ut Osiander, dolore concussum, ut Syrus, à כאב dolore, vel percussum, attritum, fra- ctum, Thodot. à נכה, LXX. ὀλιγόψυχον: cui op- ponitur Spiritus viri generosus & virilis animus: qui sustinere, portare & sustentare potest infirmita- tem, seu corpus seu animam concutientem: uti Hie- ronym. de Paula in vita ejus refert, quod morbos corporis valido spiritu sustentarit. Conf. Rom. 8, 32. 2. Cor. 4, 8. 9. Quis autem attollet, eriget (sustenta- bit, è priori membro) spiritum fractum & attritum? Si tamen libeat concussum cum Tigurinis generali- ter intelligere affectum passionibus, etiam Vulgatæ sensus comprehendetur: nam & ira conteri potest Spiritus, & dolore, vel plaga: ac spiritus magnani- mus, vegetus, & lætus non suam modo, sed alienam etiam infirmitatem sustentare potest. Quo pa- cto cohæret hic aphorismus cum præcedente: quia stultus non minus ira, quam responsione præceps est: Ita Beda: Qui ad irascendum facilis est, nec se- ipsum potest sustinere, ita ut iratus sæpe dicat ea, quæ mox, cum placidus est, quia dixerit, pœnitet, plerumq; etiam an dixerit, ignorat. Quod ergo additur v. 15. Cor prudens possidet vel acquirit scientiam, & auris sapientum quærit scientiam, Aben-Ezra ita jungit: Spiritus quassatus, & ad irascendum facilis sapienti- am non adipiscitur, prudentis autem animus ægritu- dinem suam patienter ferens prudentiæ suæ ope scien- tiæ cumulabitur. Cor autem prudentis comparat (& comparat, & comparando possidet) scientiam: Quia (sic particula Vav non raro accipitur sensu causali) auris ejus quærit eandem cap. 15. De sapientiæ dono forte etiam non inconcinne ob συνέχειαν accipietur vers. 16. cum autore Catenæ Græcæ: DONUM HOMINIS, præcipuum scil. illud & ἐξοχικῶς nun- cupatum, quod imprimis quærendum, comparan- dum, precibusque expetendum est, Jac. 1, 5. utpote auro omni potius, & præstantius, dilatat viam ejus, latum ei facit locum, imo ante Principes spa- tium ei facit, vel, ut in Ebr. ante magnates dedu- cet, cum favorem eorum conciliabit, ad familia- ritatem eorum & dignitatem similem provehet. Ad eundem fere modum Beda & Salonius: Quod est donum quod dilatat viam hanc, & quod ante prin- cipes illi facit spatium? Donum hoc donum est cha- ritatis, sive aliarum virtutum, quas à Domino fide- les accipiunt. De donis & muneribus quæ offe- runtur magnatibus vulgo & communiter explican- tur, non tamen quæ ad evertendam justitiam, sed quæ ad honestam, & utilem bono publico vel privato offeruntur. Summa est, inquit Cartwrightus, mu- nus plurimum momenti habere ad illud, quod cu- pimus, efficiendum. Nam munus instruere ἐκ τῶν με- σῶν est; & proinde, prout adhibetur ad causas hone- stas, aut inhonestas, ita in laude, aut vituperio est. Laudi enim ducitur Jacobo, quod ad sedandum fra- tris Esavi furorem donum instruxit & apparavit: item Abigail, quod ad flectendum Davidem munus suum præmisit. Contra vero Zibæ munus, quo Da- vidis animum ad calumniam adversus Mephibose- thum accipiendum pertraxit, vituperio ducitur. Ne- que enim donorum abusus legitimum eorum usum tollit.

## 18:17
Ver. 17.

THE JUST MAN IS THE FIRST ACCUSER OF HIMSELF: HIS FRIEND COMES AND WILL INVESTIGATE HIM) The sense is from the Hebrew: He who speaks his case first, (the Greeks here say in the first-speaking) he is just (that is, he seems so) in his own case: but soon another comes, and inquires into him: that is, he weighs all his words, and refutes them as much as he can. For this precept, as also the following, pertains to lawsuits.

They have handed down this sense with R. Levi, and Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, Mercerus, Jansenius, Junius, Piscator, Cartwright. The Belgians and among our own Franz. de interpret. script. p. 594, as if it were about a political forum: Others, however, prefer to understand it of the spiritual, which is in the conscience, with the Vulgate: the just man is the first accuser of himself: with which the LXX agree: the just man is his own accuser in the beginning of his speech: the Chaldean and Symmachus: in his own judgment: In the Hebrew it is: the just man is first in his own lawsuit, or of himself, which he has not with another, but with himself, when he is viewed both as acting and judging as a just man, and as suffering or undergoing judgment, and in him there are two distinct principles, flesh and spirit, which foster a perpetual fight and contention between themselves. In this lawsuit, the just man is deservedly first before he judges others. Luke 6:41. then at last if his companion, or his neighbor, also comes into the contention, he investigates him and explores whether he himself is worthy of censure or not. HIS FRIEND COMES, AND WILL INVESTIGATE HIM. Thus Ambrose, lib. 1.

offic. c. 25. The just man accuses himself before others. And Bede: Everyone who is truly just, when he sees the errors of sinners, first turns the eye of consideration toward himself, and while he has anxiously accused his own frailty, thus at last he kindly exerts his tongue to correct others. Cf. Osiand. and Dn. D. Geier, as also Cornel. à Lapide. Which pertains to avoiding the precipitation about which Solomon had begun to speak. The author of the Greek Catena illustrates it by antithesis, according to the LXX Interpreters, in this way: The just man at the beginning of his speech is the accuser of himself: but the adversary and the unjust man begins his speech with insults and rebukes. He who begins to act justly, he says, accuses himself before all things. And thus those things which follow also cohere: For by avoiding precipitation, many contentions are either avoided or expire: But if they should flourish at all, and the case be uncertain and doubtful, Solomon suggests a means of composing them in v. 18. The lot makes lawsuits cease, and divides between the powerful, namely, the matter about which there is litigation. Vulgate, decides. For then no other way of calming lawsuits is available, unless the lot should settle and define them. For just as reason dominates in certain and manifest things, so in uncertain, doubtful, obscure, and fatuous things, the lot and chance dominate. Cf. Josh. 15. Grotius h. l. thus:

Latin:

Vers. 17.

JUSTUS PRIOR EST ACCUSATOR SVI: VENIT AMICUS EJUS ET INVESTIGABIT EVM) Senfus eft ex Hebræo: Qui prior causam dicit, (ἐν πρωτολογίᾳ Græci hic) is justus est (id est videtur) in causa sua: sed mox venit al- ter, & inquirit in illum: id est, omnia illius dicta expendit, & quantum potest refellit. Hoc enim præceptum, ut & se- quens, ad lites pertinet.

Sensum hunc tradidere cum R. Levi, & Aben- Ezra, Vatablus, Mercerus, Jansenius, Junius, Pi- scator, Cartwright. Belgæ & è nostris Franz. de in- terpret. script. p. 594. quasi de foro agatur politico: Alii tamen de spirituali, quod in conscientia est ma- lunt intelligere, cum Vulgato: justus prior est accu- sator sui: cui consonant LXX. justus sui ipsius est accusator in principio sermonis: Chald. & Symma- chus in judicio suo: In Ebræo est: justus prior est in lite sua, vel sui ipsius, quam habet non cum alio, sed cum semetipso, cum & ut justus agens, ac judicans, & ut patiens, vel subiens judicium spectetur & in eo duo sint distincta principia, caro & spiritus, quæ perpetuam inter se pugnam & contentionem fo- vent. In hac lite justus merito prior est antequam de aliis judicet. Luc. 6, 41. tum autem demum si ve- niat etiam socius, vel proximus ejus, in contentio- nem, investigat eum & explorat, num ipse dignus sit censura, nec ne. VENIT AMICUS EJUS, ET INVESTIGABIT EUM. Ita Ambros. lib. 1.

offic. c. 25. Justus seipsum prius, quam alios accusat. Et Beda: Omnis qui vere justus, ubi peccantium er- rata conspicit, primum ad seipsum oculum conside- rationis inflectit, dumque suam fragilitatem solicitus accusaverit, sic demum ad corripiendos alios linguam benignus exerit. Conf. Osiand. & Dn. D. Geier. ut & Cornel. à Lapide. Quod pertinet ad præcipitantiam fugiendam, de qua dicere occœperat Salomo. Illu- strat autem per antithesin autor Catenæ Græc. juxta LXX. Interpp. hoc modo: Justus initio sermonis est accusator sui: adversarius autem & injustus à con- vitiis & increpationibus orationem auspicatur. Qui juste operari orditur, ait, ante omnia seipsum accusat. Atque ita cohærent etiam quæ sequuntur: Nam vitata præcipitantia contentiones multæ vel vitan- tur, vel expirant: Si autem omnino vigeant, & cau- sa anceps & dubia sit, easdem componendi medi- um suggerit Salomo v. 18. Lites cessare facit sors, & inter potentes dividit litem scil. vel rem de qua litiga- tur. Vulgata, dijudicat. Tunc enim non alius lites sedandi suppetit modus, nisi ut eas dirimat, & defi- niat sors. Sicut enim in rebus certis & manifestis dominatur ratio, sic in incertis, dubiis, obscuris & fatuitis dominatur sors & casus. Conf. Jos. 15. Gro- tius h. l. ita:

## 18:18
Ver. 18. THE LOT SUPPRESSES CONTRADICTIONS, AND ALSO DECIDES BETWEEN THE POWERFUL) Lawsuits are kindled between many not so much by a desire of having as because one is unwilling to yield to another. For that matter, the lot is the best remedy. We have spoken about this matter in book 2 of the Law of War and Peace, chap. 23, § 9, and in the Annotations,

Moreover, in the midst of settling disputes, there is added an almost impregnable bitterness, especially between brothers and kinsmen, v. 19. A brother offended, or having suffered a transgression (as R. Levi, the Tigurines, Lavater, Junius, Piscator, and B. Luther, Osiander, and Mr. Dr. Geier explain more correctly than Mercer, Vatablus, and Jansenius, who with Aquila [take it as] actively rebelling) [is like] a strong city, where there is an ellipsis, namely: is stronger: And contentions (of brothers) [are] like the bar or bolts of a palace, because they close the approach to reconciliation. Grotius attempts to carve out a different reading from the Greek and Vulgate version, along with Cornelius à Lapide and other Papists:

Latin:

Vers. 18. CONTRADICTIONES COMPRIMIT SORS, ET INTER POTENTES QVOQVE DIJUDICAT) Lites accenduntur inter multos non tam habendi studio quam quod alter alteri nolit cedere. Ad eam rem optimum est remedium sors. Diximus hac de re libro 2. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. 23. §. 9. & in Annotatis,

Medio autem componendarum litium subjun- gitur inter fratres præcipue & cognatos inexpu- gnabilis ferme asperitas v. 19. Frater læsus, vel præ- varicationem passus, (uti R. Levi, Tigurini, Lava- ter. Jun. Piscat. & B. Lutherus, Osiander, Dn. D. Geierus rectius exponunt, quam Mercerus, Vata- blus & Jansenius cum Aquila active rebellans) civi- tate forti, ubi ellipsis est, scil. fortior est: Et lites (fratrum) velut vectis vel repagula palatii, quia oc- cludunt reconciliationi aditum. Grotius diver- sam lectionem è Græca & Vulgata versione exscul- pere conatur cum Cornelio à Lapide & aliis Papi- stis:

## 18:19
Vers. 19. A BROTHER WHO IS HELPED BY A BROTHER IS LIKE A STRONG CITY) From the Greek: ἀδελφὸς ὑπὸ ἀδελφῦ βοηθούμενος.. They seem to have read not נפשע, but נפדה, with the sound being similar.

But since no manuscript of the authentic text favors this reading, no room is left for such a suspicion. Nor is it to be approved that he explains the word מדינים with the Vulgate as 'judgments,' and with Aquila as δικασία, since 'contentions' denotes it more, and the comparison in v. 18 and the antithesis confirm this. Now Solomon proceeds in v. 20, 21 to discourse concerning the fruit of the mouth, the continuity of which is sufficiently manifest, repeating previous admonitions because of the supreme necessity of rightly governing the tongue, but in another matter and application to contentions and judgments: With the fruit of a man's mouth his belly shall be satisfied: with the produce of his lips he shall be filled, chap. 12, 14; chap. 13, 2. Death and life are in the hand (or power. Conf. Psalm 22, 28; 49, 16; Hos. 13, 14; Is. 47, 14) of the tongue, and he who loves it shall eat its fruits: he who delights to use the tongue and exercises it frequently, whether by speaking well or ill (as Vatablus, the Dutch, the Weimar edition, Mr. Dr. Geier,) shall eat its fruits. We can speak those things which either preserve life for us or others, or harm it. The tongue is almost the only door of death, says Chrysostom in Psalm 140. To which also goes the Arabic proverb: Beware lest the tongue strike its own neck.

AND JUDGMENTS AS BARS OF CITIES) He translated ברינים judgments well, like Aquila, καὶ δικαιόα.

Latin:

Vers. 19. FRATER QVI ADJUVATUR A FRATRE QVASI CIVITAS FIRMA) Ex Græco: ἀδελφὸς ὑπὸ ἀδελφῦ βοηθούμενος.. Videntur legisse non נפשע, sed נפדה fono accedente.

Sed quum nullus Codex textus authentici huic lectioni faveat, suspicioni tali locus nullus relin- quitur. Neque probandum, quod vocem מדינים cum Vulgat. judicia, & cum Aquila δικασία ex- ponat, quum lites potius eam denotare & colla- tio v. 18. & antithesis confirmat. Jam pergit Sa- lomo v. 20, 21. de fructu oris disserere, quæ συνέχεια satis manifesta est, ob summam linguæ recte guber- nandæ necessitatem repetens priores commonitio- nes, sed in alia materia & applicatione ad conten- tiones, & judicia: De fructu oris viri satiabitur venter ipsius: proventu labiorum suorum saturabi- tur cap. 12, 14. cap. 13, 2. Mors & vita in manu (vel potestate. Conf. Psalm. 22, 28. 49, 16. Hos. 13, 14. Es. 47, 14.) linguæ, & qui diliget eam comedet fructus ejus: qui lingua uti gestit eamque exercet frequen- ter, sive bene sive male dicendo, (ut Vatabl. Belgæ, Vinariens. Dn. D. Geierus,) comedet fructus ejus. Possumus ea proloqui, quæ vel nobis vel aliis vi- tam conservent vel noceant. Mortis unicum fere ostium lingua est, ait Chrysost. in Psalm. 140. Quo abit etiam proverbium Arabicum Cave ne lingua fe- riat collum suum.

ET JUDICIA QVASI VECTES URBIUM) Bene transtulit ברינים judicia, sicut Aquila, καὶ δικαιόα.

## 18:22
Ver. 22.

HE WHO FINDS A GOOD WOMAN, FINDS A GOOD THING] Supply: rare & excellent: below 31, 10. AND SHALL DRAW PLEASURE FROM THE LORD. Because especially in marriage precipitation & contention are to be avoided, where the Lord has given a good companion of life, that good thing is to be rightly valued: not inappropriately is this sentence added: He who finds אשה a woman, that is, a strenuous & sensible wife, as a man Eccl. 7, 28. for a good man, a King for a good King Prov. 16, 10. (whence the LXX. & Vulgate added GOOD) finds a good thing & draws benevolence from the Lord. Therefore, one must hold fortune reverently. The Vulgate adds some things with the LXX. but beyond the authentic text, which alone is Canonical, even if adduced in Canon law or Canonical 32. quest. 1. c. 2. He who expels a good woman, expels a good thing, but he who keeps an adulteress, is a fool, & impious.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

QVI INVENIT MVLIEREM BONAM, INVENIT BONUM] Supple : rarum & eximium : infra 31, 10. ET HAURIET VOLUPTATEM A DO- MINO. Quia imprimis in conjugio præcipitantia & contentio cavenda est, ubi bonam vitæ consortem Dominus donavit, bonum illud recte æstimandum : nonJAincommode hæc adjicitur sententia : Qui inve- nit אשה viram, id est, uxorem strenuam & corda- tam, uti homo Eccl. 7, 28. pro homine bono, Rex pro Rege bono Prov. 16, 10. (unde BONAM addidere LXX. & Vulgata) invenit rem bonam & haurit bene- volentiam a Domino. Fortunam ergo reverenter habeat, oportet. Addit nonnulla Vulgata cum LXX. sed præter textum authenticum, qui solus Canonicus, etiamsi adducta in jure Canonico seu Canonica 32. quæst. 1. c. 2. Qui expellit mulierem bonam, expellit bonum, qui autem tenet adulteram, stultus est, & impius.

## 18:23
Ver. 23.

THE POOR MAN SPEAKS WITH SUPPLICATIONS, AND THE RICH MAN WILL SPEAK RIGIDLY. These likewise pertain to the use of the tongue. For the poor man, being needy & destitute, everywhere timidly & suppliantly speaks: but the rich man, abounding in wealth & presiding, everywhere breathes pride, and thus acts imperiously, & speaks. Conf. Syr. 13, 4. Finally, verse 24 also pertains to this. A man of friends, that is, amicable for making friends (as Baynus translates) or for mingling himself, or for keeping intimate, i.e., he ought to be inclined to exercise friendship both by mouth & utterance, and by work & effect. Since a friend (sincerely loving) is more joined than a brother or adheres (often) more than a brother, chap. 17, 17. Syr. 6, 11. 15. if indeed the favor of brothers is also rare.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

CUM OBSECRATIONIBUS LOQUITUR PAUPER, ET DIVES EFFABITUR RIGIDE. Hæc itidem ad usum linguæ spectant. Pauper enim, utpote egens & inops, ubique timidus timide & suppliciter loquitur : dives vero opibus abundans & præsidens ubique timidus spirat fastum, adeoque imperiosê agit, & loquitur. Conf. Syr. 13, 4. De- nique eo etiam spectat v. 24. Vir amicorum, id est, amicabilis ad amicandum (ut Baynus vertit) vel ad commiscendum se, aut ad intimus conservandum, sc. propensus esse debet ad exercendam amicitiam tum ore & effatu, tum opere, & effectu. Quum amicus (sincere amans) magis conjunctus sit quam fra- ter vel adhærescat (sæpe) præ fratre, cap. 17, 17. Syr. 6, 11. 15. siquidem & fratrum quoque gratia rara.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

Concerning the wise poor man, the foolish rich man, & the use and abuse of the tongue, and the precipitation of anger, and long-suffering, diligence, piety, beneficence, & discipline, and the instruction of children.

Ver. 1.

BETTER IS THE POOR MAN WHO WALKS IN HIS SIMPLICITY) That is, in integrity. THAN THE RICH MAN TWISTING HIS LIPS] Perverse in his lips. AND FOOLISH) In Hebrew: and he himself is foolish. He thinks he is wise, but he is foolish, as all the wicked are. Antiphanes: Καλῶς πένεσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ πλουτεῖν κακῶς. Euripides: - - ἐγὼ δὲ πολλάκις σοφωτέρες Πένητας ἄνδρας εἰσορῶν τ͂ πλουσίων.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

De paupere sapiente, divite stulto, & usu at- que abusu linguæ, iraque præcipitantia, ac lon- ganimitate, sedulitate, pietate, beneficentia, & disciplina, ac informatione liberorum.

Vers. 1.

MELIOR EST PAVPER QVI AMBULAT IN SIM- PLICITATE SVA) Id est, in integritate. QVAM DIVES TORQVENS LABIA SVA] Per- versus labiis. ET INSIPIENS) In Hebræo : & ipse desipit. Putat se sapere, sed desipit, ut improbi omnes. Antiphanes : Καλῶς πένεσθαι μᾶλλον, ἢ πλουτεῖν κακῶς. Euripides : - - ἐγὼ δὲ πολλάκις σοφωτέρες Πένητας ἄνδρας εἰσορῶν τ͂ πλουσίων.

## 19:4
Ver. 4.

WEALTH ADDS MANY FRIENDS) Ovid: Donec eris felix, centum numerabis amicos. Sophocles Aleadis: Τὰ χρήματʼ ἀνθρώποισιν εὑρίσκει φίλες. Because he had thrown in some things about the poor & rich, as well as about the use & abuse of the tongue, as also about precipitation, and its flight, he continues this matter through apothegms: Better is the poor man, who walks in his integrity (so the Hebrew has it) than the perverse in lips (i.e., the rich man, chap. 28. verse 6.) and he himself foolish; who can indeed insinuate himself with crafty speeches, but is wicked, & senseless, Matt. 16, 26. WHERE THERE IS NO KNOWLEDGE OF THE SOUL (which the accentuation teaches is placed, that is, the true understanding of the Word of God) there is no good: and he who is hasty with his feet acts precipitately & inconsiderately) HE SHALL OFFEND, or rather shall sin, v. 2. Greater, says August. tract. de Vit. beat. And there is no more miserable poverty than to lack wisdom: and he who does not lack wisdom can lack nothing at all.

Ignorance, therefore, and rashness are here established as the principles of errors and of unfortunate outcomes. v. 3. THE FOOLISHNESS of a man will pervert his way (that is, his whole manner of living, it reduces him to crimes and the punishments of crimes) and his heart (namely, the foolish man's) will rage against the Lord, when he will blame God himself for his own errors and sins. Whence Augustine reads or rather understood this gnome in Ep. CV. thus: the foolishness of a man violates his ways, but he blames God in his heart.

Solomon now proceeds concerning riches v. 4. wealth adds many friends. Conf. Syr. 6, 8. c. 37, 4. But the poor man is separated from his friend: he not only does not obtain friends, but he is also separated from him to whom he is joined by the right of consanguinity or affinity.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

DIVITIÆ ADDUNT AMICOS PLURIMOS) Ovi- dius : Donec eris felix, centum numerabis amicos. Sophocles Aleadis : Τὰ χρήματʼ ἀνθρώποισιν εὑρίσκει φίλες. Quia de paupere & divite injecerat nonnulla, nec non de usu & abusu linguæ, ut & præcipitantia, ejusque fuga, pergit hanc materiam per apophthe- gmata : Melior est pauper, qui ambulat in integritate sua (sic habent Ebræa) quam perversus labiis (sc. dives, cap. 28. versu 6.) & ipse stultus; qui ver- sutis sermonibus se quidem insinuare potest, sed nequam est, & vecors, Matth. 16, 26. UBI NON EST SCIENTIA ANIMÆ (que m positum accentuatio docet, id est, verus Verbi Dei intelle- ctus) non est bonum: & qui festinus est pedibus præci- pitanter & inconsiderate agit) OFFENDET, vel po- tius peccabit, v. 2. Major, ait August. tract. de Vit. beat. & miserabilior egestas non est, quam egere sapientia: & qui non eget sapientia, nulla re omnino egere potest.

Ignorantia ergo & præcipitantia errorum & succef- suum infaustorum principia hic constituuntur. v. 3. STULTITIA hominis pervertet viam ejus (id est, to- tam vivendi rationem, redigit eum in scelera, & sce- lerum pœnas) & contra Dominum indignabitur cor ejus (stulti nempe hominis) cum errorum & pecca- torum suorum ipsummet Deum blasphemia arguet. Unde Augustin. ita legit vel potius intellexit hanc gnomen Ep. CV. insipientia viri violat vias ejus, Deum autem causatur in corde suo.

Pergit jam Salomo de divitiis v. 4. opes adjungunt amicos multos. Conf. Syr. 6, 8. c. 37, 4. At pauper ab amico suo separatur: non modo non consequitur amicos, sed separatur quoque ab eo, cui jure consanguinitatis, vel affini- tatis conjunctus est.

## 19:5
Vers. 5.

A FALSE WITNESS SHALL NOT BE UNPUNISHED: AND HE WHO SPEAKS LIES SHALL NOT ESCAPE.

In the Hebrew it is 'he shall not be innocent,' as Aquila, Theodotion, and the Chaldean render it, that is, he shall not be unpunished Exod. 20, 7. and he who BREATHES OUT or expires lies, SHALL NOT ESCAPE. Aquila and the Syrian, he shall not escape safe, that is, he shall not escape punishment. Since he has dealt with the poor man separating himself from his friend, while friends easily happen to the rich, he warns that no one should join himself to another in a bad cause, and speak false testimony, or lie for the sake of another. For it almost always happens that when things are flowing according to one's will, everyone promises their faithful and perpetual service to those who abound in wealth. Which, however, they afterwards treacherously fail, when riches have flown away as if having seized wings. Whence it appears that this sentiment is not inculcated here and in v. 9 for the same reason.

But he adds v. 6. Many pray to or suppliantly court, or honor (conf. Job 11, 19.) the face of a prince, and every man is a friend to a man of gifts, or to one who bestows a gift. (The Chaldean and the LXX wrongly change the word, and read 'evil' instead of 'friend')

Latin:

Vers. 5.

TESTIS FALSUS NON ERIT IMPUNI- TUS: ET QUI MENDACIA LOQUITUR, NON EFFUGIET.

In Ebr. non erit innocens, ut Aquila, Theod. & Chald. reddunt, id est, non impunitus erit Exod. 20, 7. & qui mendacia EFFLAT vel expirat, NON E- VADET. Aquila & Syrus, non evadet salvus, id est, non effugiet pœnam. Quum de paupere se ab amico separante, quum diviti facile amici contin- gant, egerit, ne quis se jungat alteri in causa mala, falsumque testimonium dicat, aut mentiatur in gra- tiam alterius, monet. Fere enim fit, ut rebus ad voluntatem affluentibus omnes suam operam his, qui opibus abundant, fidelem & perpetuam polli- ceantur. Quam tamen post perfide fallunt, cum divitiæ tanquam arreptis alis avolarunt. Unde non eadem ratione hanc sententiam hic & v. 9. inculca- ri, apparet.

Addit autem v. 6. Multi precantur vel suppliciter ambiunt, aut venerantur (conf. Job. 11, 19.) faciem principis, & omnis amicus est viro doni, vel donum tribuenti. (perperam autem vocem im- mutant Chald. & LXX. & pro amico malum legunt)

## 19:7
v. 7. All the brothers of the poor man hate him: how much more will his friends distance themselves from him? He (the poor man) pursues words (which brothers and friends have given) and they are not: he discovers himself deceived. Which the Vulgate less correctly drags to the following, when they pertain to the preceding, to which they better agree, as Cornelius admits: who furthermore of these v. 8.

But he who is a possessor of a mind, loves his own soul, and the keeper of prudence will find good things, this he renders συνέχειαν: He opposes the one pursuing words to the possessor of a mind, and the keeper of prudence, that is, him who is fed by mere words, to him who through wisdom possesses a heart, and he prefers the latter to the former by far, as if to say: he who is fed by words is fed by wind: for words, as soon as they are uttered, depart into the wind and vanish: therefore he will have nothing: but he who is fed by wisdom will possess it, nay, through it he will become a possessor of the heart, that is, of the mind, so that he may wisely rule and compose all its affections, actions, and motions according to the dictate of right reason and divine law. Wherefore such a one loves his own soul, because he consults for it in the best way, and procures eternal happiness and glory. Therefore the keeper of wisdom and prudence will find good things, both present on earth and eternal in heaven. The scope is, as Cartwright says, to say that the safest and firmest possession is the fear of God, with which, when he is imbued (when other things cease), he enjoys the good.

Moreover, he warns again about avoiding false speech v. 9, as not being suitable for a possessor of a mind and a guardian of prudence, or for one who loves his own soul: a false witness will not go unpunished: and he who speaks lies will perish. He repeats, therefore, the same sentiment, so that he may implant in us love, truth, and a hatred of vanity, which does not consist at all with the fear of the Lord. Conf. c. 6, 19. c. 14, 6.

Latin:

v. 7. Omnes fratres pauperis oderunt eum: quanto magis amici illius elongabunt se ab eo? Persequitur (pauper) verba (quæ dedere fratres & amici) & non sunt: deprehendit se delusum. Quæ minus recte ad sequentia abripit Vulgata, quum ad præceden- tia pertineant, quibus melius conveniunt, fatente Cornelio: qui porro istorum v. 8.

Qui autem pos- sessor est mentis, diligit animam suam, & custos pru- dentiæ inveniet bona, hanc reddit συνέχειαν: Opponit sectantem verba possessori mentis, & custodi prudentiæ id est, eum qui solis verbis pascitur, illi qui per sapien- tiam possidet cor, huncque illi longe præfert, q. d. qui pascitur verbis, pascitur vento: verba enim mox ut pro- lata sunt, in ventum abeunt & evanescunt: nihil ergo habebit: at qui pascitur sapientia, possidebit eam, imo per eam fiet possessor cordis, id est mentis, ut omnes ejus affectiones, actiones, motus sapienter juxta dictamen rectæ rationis & legis divinæ regat componatque. Quare talis diligit animam suam, quia illi optime consulit, ac felicitatem & gloriam æternam conci- liat. Igitur custos sapientiæ & prudentiæ inveniet bona tum præsentia in terris, tum æterna in cælis. Scopus est, dicente Cartvvrighto, dicere, tutif- simam & firmissimam possessionem esse Dei timorem, quo imbutus (cum alia desinunt) bono perfruitur.

Iterum autem monet de cavendo falsiloquio v. 9. ceu non convenienti possessori mentis, & custodi prudentiæ, aut ei qui diligit animam suam: falfus te- ftis non erit impunitus: & qui loquitur mendacia peri- bit. Repetit ergo eandem sententiam, ut implan- tet nobis amorem, veritatem & odium vanitatis, quæ cum timore Domini minime consistit. Conf. c. 6, 19. c. 14, 6.

## 19:8
Vers. 8.

HE WHO IS A POSSESSOR OF A MIND LOVES HIS OWN SOUL) That is, himself. In this sense, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8, c. 8: 'Therefore, the good man ought to be a lover of self; for he himself will be benefited by doing noble deeds, and he will benefit others; but the wicked man ought not to be. For he will harm both himself and his neighbors, following base passions. For in the wicked man, there is a disagreement between what he ought to do and what he does. But the upright man does those things which he ought to do. For every mind chooses what is best for itself.'

Latin:

Vers. 8.

QVI POSSESSOR EST MENTIS DILIGIT ANI- MAM SVAM) Id est, semetipsum. Hoc sensu Aristoteles Nicomacheorum 8. c. 8. ὥστε τῆς ἀγαθὸν δεῖ φίλαυτον εἶναι· καὶ γὰρ αὐτός ὀνήσεται τὰ καλὰ πράττων καὶ τὺς ἄλλυς ὠφε- λήσει· τὸν δὲ μοχθηρὸν, ὀὐ δεῖ. βλάψει γὰρ καὶ ἑαυτὸν κὶ τὺς πέλας, φαύλοις πάθεσιν ἑπόμενον. τῷ μοχθηρῷ μὲν ἐν δια- φωνεῖ ἃ δεῖ πράττειν καὶ ἃ πράττει. ὁ δὲ ἐπιεικὴς ἃ δεῖ ταῦτα καὶ πράττει. πᾶς γὰρ νοῦς αἱρεῖται τὸ βέλτισον ἑαυτῷ.

## 19:9
Vers. 9.

A FALSE WITNESS WILL NOT GO UNPUNISHED, AND HE WHO SPEAKS LIES WILL PERISH) The sense is the same; it differs little in words from that which is above v. 5. Many such things are found in Stobaeus.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

FALSVS TESTIS NON ERIT IMPVNITVS, ET QVI LOQVITVR MENDACIA PERIBIT) Sensus idem est, verbis parum differt ab eo quod supra v. 5. Talia multa apud Stobæum.

## 19:10
verse 10.

DELIGHTS ARE NOT BECOMING TO A FOOL, NOR FOR A SERVANT TO RULE OVER PRINCES.

In the Hebrew it is: How much less is it becoming for a servant to rule over princes? Since there is great need of wisdom and long-suffering, no less than wisdom, both in all stations and especially in the political state, Solomon teaches that it is inconvenient for a fool to be affected with delights and honors, or for one who ought to serve to rule over others whom it is fitting to command (which is most becoming to the wise). Conf. c. 10, 13. c. 26, 3. Men who are foolish and impious are not to be treated delicately (so the Osiandrian paraphrase has it). Because the more kindly they are cherished, the more insolent and worse they become. Nor is it to be permitted that those who ought to serve should take authority for themselves over their masters. For the more such people are exalted, the more intolerable they become. Nothing is harsher than a base man when he rises to a high place. Conf. cap. 30, 21. The fool is compared to a servant: because a servant is of a servile, that is, a dull and stupid disposition, like a fool; conversely, a fool is a servant to his own folly and foolish desire. 2 Pet. 2, 21. Furthermore, long-suffering contributes especially to government; concerning which it is handed down in v. 11 according to the Hebrew source: the intelligence of a man makes him long-suffering, and it is his glory to pass over wrongs. Undoubtedly, the doctrine of the word of God renders a man slow to anger, so that by his long-suffering he may correct many things, or at least not make them worse, and it is to his praise that he can overlook and forgive injuries received for the sake of God and for the public good. He who does not know how to overlook, does not know how to rule. Not to take revenge makes one equal to God, says Chrysostom, homily 41 on Acts.

But how pernicious the anger of a King is, Solomon teaches in v. 12: the anger (indignation) of a king is like the roaring of a vigorous lion, being angry and seething against a subject because of an offense, whether grave or light, whether real or imaginary. Conf. Am. 3, 8. However, the roaring is attributed to the King himself because he roars like a lion out of anger and indignation, and indeed like a vigorous lion, which is of middle age between a cub and an old one. Jud. 14, 5. Ez. 19, 5. Hos. 5, 14. 1 Pet. 5, 18. Whereas, on the contrary, the benevolence of a king is like dew upon the grass: because just as dew tempers the heat and exhilarates, and provides vital sap so that the grasses may grow and mature, and by bedewing it fattens and makes fertile, so the grace of a king refreshes and exhilarates his subjects, and makes them grow and heaps them with all good things. Conf. Hos. 14, 6. Subjects are therefore taught to revere the King, counselors are taught not to excite him to anger, and to restrain the king's anger themselves, lest if they allow it to be untamed, they rage like lions, but Kings themselves are taught to strive for gentleness. A savage and inexorable anger is not becoming to a King, says Seneca, book 1 of De Clementia, chapter 5. We add the Grotian [notes];

Latin:

versus 10.

NON DECENT STVLTUM DELITIÆ, NEC SERVVM DOMINARI PRINCIPIBUS.

In Ebræo est: Quanto minus decet servum do- minari principibus? Quum sapientia & longanimita- te non minus quam sapientia tum in omnibus stati- bus, tum imprimis in statu politico peropus sit, in- conveniens esse docet Salomo, ut stultus delitiis, & honoribus afficiatur, aut qui servire debet, aliis quibus imperare convenit (quod sapientes maxime decet,) dominetur. Conf. c. 10, 13. c. 26, 3. Non delicate tractandi sunt (ita habet paraphasis Osian- drina) homines vecordes & impii. Quia quanto be- nignius foventur, tanto fiunt insolentiores, & deterio- res. Nec committendum est, ut qui servire debent, imperium sibi in Dominos sumant. Quo enim magis exaltantur tales, tanto fiunt intolerabiliores. Aspe- rius nihil est humili, cum surgit in altum. Conf. cap. 30, 21. Comparatur stultus servo: quia servus servili, id est, hebeti & stolido est ingenio instar stulti: vi- cissim stultus est servus suæ stultitiæ, stultæque cupi- ditati. 2. Pet. 2, 21. Cæterum ad regimen imprimis facit longanimitas; qua de ita v. 11. juxta fontem E- bræum traditur, intelligentia hominis longanimem fa- cit eum, & gloria ejus est, iniqua prætergredi. Ni- mirum doctrina verbi Dei reddit hominem tardum ad iram, ut longanimitate sua multa corrigat, aut certe non deteriora reddat, & hoc ipsi laudi est, quod dissimulare & condonare potest injurias ac- ceptas propter Deum, & propter bonum publicum. Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit imperare. Non ulcisci Deo facit æqualem, ait Chrysost. homil. 41. in Acta.

Quam pernitiosa vero sit ira Regis v. 12. Salomo docet, rugitus sicut vegeti leonis est ira (indignatio) regis, ob offensam seu gravem, seu levem, sive ve- ram, sive imaginariam succensens subdito, & æstu- ans. Conf. Am. 3, 8. Tribuitur autem ipsi Regi rugitus, quod præ ira & indignatione instar leonis rugiat, & quidem instar leonis vegeti, qui ætatis inter catulum & vetulum est mediæ. Jud. 14, 5. Ez. 19, 5. Hos. 5, 14. 1. Pet. 5, 18. Quum ex adverso sicut ros super herbam benevolentia regis sit: quia sicut ros æstum temperat & exhilarat, per succum vitalem sufficit, ut herbæ crescant & adolescant, & irrorando im- pinguat, ac fœcundat, ita gratia regis reficit, & exhi- larat subditos, eosq; crescere facit, bonisq; omnibus cumulat. Conf. Hos. 14, 6. Docentur itaque sub- diti Regem vereri, consiliarii eundem non ad iram excitare, ipsique regis iram compescere, ne si indo- mitam eam sinant, quasi leones sæviant, Reges au- tem ipsi lenitati studere. Non decet Regem sæva & inexorabilis ira, ait Seneca l. 1. de Clement. cap. 5. Addimus Grotiana;

## 19:12
AS THE ROARING OF A LION, SO ALSO IS THE ANGER OF A KING) The beast, that is, the lion, signifies a king, Zeno in the Lion Iconomachus. Thus Nebuchadnezzar is a lion in Amos 5, 19. Nero is a lion to the Apostle Paul in 2 Timothy 4, 17. And Seneca, whose saying the Scholiast recites on Juvenal's fifth satire. Concerning the anger of a king, see what we said above 16, 14.

Latin:

SICVT FREMITVS LEONIS, ITA ET REGIS IRA) Τὸ θηρίον, id est leo, βασιλέα δηλοῖ, Zeno in leone Ico- nomacho. Sic Nabuchodonosor leo Amoso 5, 19. Nero Paulo Apostolo 2. Timoth. 4, 17. & Seneca, cujus dictum recitat Scho- liastes ad Iuvenalis Satyram quintam. De ira regis vide quæ di- ximus supra 16, 14.

## 19:13
Verse 13.

THE GRIEF OF A FATHER IS A FOOLISH SON) Euripides in Oenomaus: Αμηχανῶν δ᾽ ἔγωγε κ' ἐκ ἔχω μαθεῖν, Εἴ τ' οὖν ἄμεινόν ἐστ' γίγνεσθαι τέκνα Θνητοῖσιν, εἴτ' ἄπαιδα καρποῦσθαι βίον. Ὁρῶ γὰρ οἷς μὲν ἐκ ἔφυσαν, ἀθλίως· Οτοισι δ' εἰσὶν, οὐδὲν εὐτυχεςέρες· Καὶ γὰρ κακοὶ γεγῶτες, ἐχθίση νόσ@·

ROOFS CONTINUALLY DRIPPING, A CONTENTIOUS WOMAN.

Just as Solomon requires wisdom and gentleness in the state, so too in the household. In the Hebrew it is: A foolish (unwise and wicked) son is (manifold) griefs to his father, and the contentions of a woman are (like) a continual dripping. (Cf. ch. 21, 9. 10. ch. 25, 24. ch. 27, 15.) which gradually and step by step wear away her husband, just as a drop wears away a stone and drippings wear away beams, flooring, and pavements. Whence Solomon warned in v. 14 that a prudent wife is to be held as a signal gift of the Lord: house and riches (are) the inheritance of parents (who can leave lands and ample patrimonies to their children), but a prudent wife (is) from the Lord, Cf. ch. 18, 22. Syr. 26, 3. Buxtorf in Anti-Crit. p. 737 rightly corrects Capellus, who reads משכרת (hired) instead of משכלת (prudent) because the LXX have ἁρμόζεται (is joined/hired for a price). Grotius, whose footsteps he gladly follows, has not followed him here. He notes only that it is said properly from the Lord that a wife is prudent, that is, by the special providence of God, Tob. 6, 22. but in the Hebrew that word PROPERLY is not present. Meanwhile, the special providence of God has a place entirely. But since in the household there is the greatest need for labor and diligence, if one wishes, I will not say to amass wealth, of which mention has already been made, but to ward off hunger: Solomon adds in v. 15. Sloth makes one fall into a deep sleep (renders one somnolent) but a slack soul (a lazy, torpid man) shall hunger. Ch. 6, 11. ch. 10, 3. These are the words of Grotius on v. 14:

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DOLOR PATRIS FILIVS STVLTVS) Euripides Oenomao: Αμηχανῶν δ᾽ ἔγωγε κ' ἐκ ἔχω μαθεῖν, Εἴ τ' οὖν ἄμεινόν ἐστ' γίγνεσθαι τέκνα Θνητοῖσιν, εἴτ' ἄπαιδα καρποῦσθαι βίον. Ὁρῶ γὰρ οἷς μὲν ἐκ ἔφυσαν, ἀθλίως· Οτοισι δ' εἰσὶν, οὐδὲν εὐτυχεςέρες· Καὶ γὰρ κακοὶ γεγῶτες, ἐχθίση νόσ@·

TECTA JUGITER PERSTILLANTIA, LITIGOSA MULIER.

Uti sapientiam & lenitatem in Politia requirit Salomo, ita & in Oeconomia. In Ebr. est: Contri- tiones (multiplices) Patri suo est filius stultus (insi- piens & improbus) & (sicut) stillatio continua (sunt) contentiones mulieris. (Conf. c. 21, 9. 10. cap. 25, 24. c. 27, 15.) quæ sensim & pedetentim virum suum, ut gutta lapidem & stillicidia trabes, tabulatum, pavi- menta exedunt. Unde pro insigni dono Domini habendam esse prudentem uxorem Salomo monuit v. 14. domus & divitiæ (sunt) hæreditas parentum (qui liberis fundos, & ampla patrimonia relinquere pos- sunt) sed a Domino (est) uxor prudens, Conf. cap. 18, 22. Syr. 26, 3. Capellum pro משכלת intelli- gente legentem משכרת eo quod LXX. habeant ἁρμόζεται conducitur mercede, corrigit, ut par est Buxtorff. in Anti-Crit. p. 737. Non sequutus illum hic Grotius est, cujus vestigia libenter premit. Notat tantum proprie a Domino dici uxorem esse prudentem, id est, peculiari Dei providentia, Tob. 6, 22. sed in Ebr. illud PROPRIE non habetur. Interim omni- no peculiaris Dei providentia locum habet. Quum vero in Oeconomia opus maxime sit labore & sedu- litate, si non dicam opes congerere, quarum mentio jam facta, sed famem pellere quis velit: adjicit Sa- lomo v. 15. Pigredo cadere facit soporem (reddit somnolentum) at anima remissa (homo piger, tor- pidus) esuriet. Cap. 6, 11. c. 10, 3. Grotii ad v. 14. hæc sunt:

## 19:14
Verse 14.

HOUSE AND RICHES ARE GIVEN BY PARENTS: BUT A PRUDENT WIFE PROPERLY FROM THE LORD) In the Hebrew: House and wealth are the inheritance of fathers. Properly, that is, by the special providence of God. Tob. 6, 22.

To these political and economic admonitions are now subjoined common apophthegms concerning the observance of the Lord’s commandments and beneficence toward the poor: He that keepeth the commandment, keepeth his own soul (life). Cf. ch. 13, 3; ch. 16, 12; ch. 21, 23; ch. 22, 5; but he that despiseth his ways (prescribed to him by God) shall die. Cf. ch. 13, 1. He who institutes his life (thus Osiander paraphrases) piously according to the commandments of God, to him God will prolong this life, and such a man shall not fall from the grace of God, nor shall he lose eternal life. But he who does not observe his own conduct, but indulges his own desires and rushes into crimes, he both draws upon himself corporal punishments and falls into eternal death, Rom. 8:13. On beneficence v. 17. He lends, he says, or rather gives on loan to the Lord, who has pity on the poor, (he shows himself gracious to the needy) and He returns his vicissitude (more correctly retribution) to him. He has placed himself, says Chrysostom in hom. 38, as a kind of mediator, a sponsor to the poor, but a pledge or mortgage to the creditor. I do not have, you say, trust in this man because of his poverty; trust in me because of my abundance. If anyone, says Basil on Ps. 14, Sermon 11 against usury, in the city, a rich man, should stand surety for you to others, you accept his guarantee: but you do not admit God, who promises that He will pay back so much more for the sake of the poor.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

DOMUS ET DIVITIÆ DANTVR A PARENTI- BVS: A DOMINO AVTEM PROPRIE UXOR PRU- DENS) In Hebræo: Domus & opes hereditas patrum. Pro- prie, id est, peculiari Dei providentia. Tob. 6, 22.

Hisce Politicis & œconomicis monitis subjun- guntur jam communia apophthegmata de observa- tione mandatorum Domini, & beneficentia erga pau- peres: Qui custodit mandatum, custodit animam (vi- tam) suam. Conf. cap. 13, 3. c. 16, 12. c. 21, 23. c. 22, 5.) sed qui contemnit vias suas (sibi a Deo præscriptas) morietur. Conf. c. 13, 1. Qui vitam suam (ita παρα- φράζει Osiander) pie juxta mandata Dei instituit, huic Deus prorogabit hanc vitam, & talis homo non excidet gratia Dei, nec amittet vitam æternam. At qui non observat suos mores, sed indulget pro- priis suis cupiditatibus, atque in scelera ruit, is & corporales pœnas sibi attrahit, & in mortem æter- nam incidit Rom. 8, 13. De beneficentia v. 17. fœne- ratur, inquit, vel potius mutuo dat Domino, qui mi- seretur pauperis, (gratiosum se exhibet egeno) & vi- cissitudinem (rectius retributionem) suam reddit ei. Medium, inquit Chrysost. in hom. 38. se & quasi se- questrem præstitit, pauperi quidem sponsorem, pignus autem vel hypothecam creditori. Non habeo, inquis, huic fidem propter inopiam, mihi crede propter copiam. Si quis, ait Basilius Ps. 14. Serm. 11. contra fœnerat. in civitate dives tibi pro aliis spondeat, fidejussionem il- lius accipis: Deum vero non admittis, tanto se plura persoluturum pauperum causa pollicentem.

## 19:17
Ver. 17. HE LENDS TO THE LORD, WHO HAS PITY ON THE POOR) Mercy procures good safeguards.

Latin:

Vers. 17. FOENERATVR DOMINO, QVI MISERETVR PAVPERIS) Bona comparat præsidia misericordia.

## 19:18
Ver. 18. DISCIPLINE THY SON, LEST THOU DESPAIR: BUT DO NOT SET THY SOUL UNTO HIS DESTRUCTION. HE WHO IS IMPATIENT, SHALL SUFFER LOSS, AND HE WHO SHALL HAVE SNATCHED, SHALL ADD ANOTHER)

From the Hebrew the version may best be made thus: Chastise thy son while there is hope, but do not raise thy thought to his destruction. He who is very angry bears the penalty: but if thou leavest him unpunished, he will add still more. (that is, he will continue to sin.) The sense is, a mean must be applied, which is between Manlian severity and dissolute leniency.

For 'lest thou despair' in Hebrew it is, 'while there is hope.' After the rules concerning diverse states, and common admonitions, he subjoins special ones pertaining to the instruction of sons, first regarding parents, to whom the instruction and chastisement of sons is enjoined, but moderate, cf. Sir. c. 30, 12. because as v. 19 in the Hebrew text is added, A great anger (who easily and vehemently, or even for a long time flares up) sustains or bears the penalty or loss of every kind: Even if thou shalt have rescued (such an angry person from one penalty) he will still add, or his anger will continue, and consequently because of his flaring up, he will be forced to sustain a new penalty, as with R. Levi, Cornel. a Lap. and others: or if you prefer to explain it with Pagninus and Vatablus, it is allowed: If thou shalt be too severe (in chastisement) thou shalt receive loss: if thou shalt have rescued, thou shalt again add to chastise him, and perhaps thou wilt amend him, to which also the version of B. Luther, and the Weimar and Osiander paraphrase tend. For he persists in this matter concerning the chastisement of sons; and

now furthermore Solomon exhorts sons first in general to receive discipline v. 20. Hear counsel and receive correction: that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end, in thy old age, or even at the end of thy life. Syr. 25. v. 8. The crown of the aged is much experience. For there are, as v. 21 has, many thoughts in the heart of every man: but the will of the Lord (whose counsel he had admonished to be received) shall remain, Ps. 33, 11. Isa. 14, 24. 27.

1. John 2, 17. Then he instructs more specially, namely (1) on liberality v. 22. The desire of a man is his mercy, that is, a pious man (following the counsel of GOD) rejoices to do good to the miserable, he wishes and seeks that he may be able to exercise mercy: but a poor man (needy of mercy, or even bestowing alms out of his poverty Luke 21, 3.) is more excellent than (if he be opulent) a man of lying, who may offer help profusely, but provides none. (2) On the fear of the Lord v. 23. The fear of the Lord is to life, and he shall dwell satisfied, he shall not be visited by evil. The fear of the Lord is therefore commended by the prosperity of life, tranquil satiety, and true immunity from evils, cf. ch. 3, 18. 22. ch.

10, 11. 27. chap. 14, 25. (3) On sloth & the avoidance of idleness, v. 24. The sluggard hides his hand in his bosom, (the Hebrew word signifies a pot, and metaphorically it can be understood of the bosom, referring to the cavity of the side) after the manner of the idle, & for the avoidance of labor. He does not even bring it to his mouth (because of laziness). Osiander, retaining the meaning of a pot, renders this sense: such is the sloth of the lazy man, that if you set before him a pot with food, and he inserts his hand to eat: yet because of laziness he does not bring his hand back to his mouth. This is: lazy men shamefully neglect even the most excellent opportunities (by which their own affairs could be beautifully managed); as if someone, with food placed before him, would rather perish from hunger than move his hand to his mouth. Cf. the marginal gloss of B. Luther. Furthermore, it is added concerning the fruit of correction v. 25. If you strike a scoffer, the simple will become shrewd: But if (someone) reproves an intelligent man, he will understand knowledge. When the simple, even if a mocker, is struck with blows, he becomes shrewd, but when an intelligent man, in need of correction, is reproved with words, he will profit more and more in knowledge. And concerning the punishment of a disobedient son: A son wastes his father, puts his mother to flight, by affecting them with shame, & with reproachful speeches (or words), parents v. 26. And therefore he warns v. 27. Cease, my son, to hear instruction for wandering from knowledge. Do not listen to those who teach you things that conflict with the word of God, & are alien to true piety. The Vulgate clearly differs from the sources, rendering it thus: You do not cease, my son, to hear doctrine, nor are you ignorant of the words of knowledge. In place of a reason, there can be that which is added concerning an impious Master who cares nothing for divine judgment, who is called עד, testifying or witnessing, just as Christ is called in Is. 55, 4, a Master given to the peoples. v. 28. A witness of Belial (an impious man) mocks (divine) judgment & the mouth of the impious devours iniquity. Cf. Job 15, 16. Matth. 23, 24. But judgments are (certainly) prepared for mockers, and beatings for the body (or back) of fools v. 29. Beda says, the reprobate mock the judgment of divine command or dominion: yet the judgments of damnation await them, which, like a red-hot iron hammer, so beat them in the furnace of Gehenna without end.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ERVDI FILIVM TVVM, NE DESPERES: AD IN- TERFECTIONEM AVTEM EJVS NE PONAS ANI- MAM TVAM. QVI IMPATIENS EST, SVSTINE- BIT DAMNVM, ET QVI RAPVERIT, ALIVD AP- PONET)

Ex Hebræo sic optime fiat versio: Castiga fili- um tuum, dum spes est, sed ad exitium ejus ne erigas cogitatio- nem tuam. Qui plurimum irascitur fert pœnam: quod si im- punitum eum reliqueris, adhuc addet. (id est, perget peccare.) Sensus est, modum adhibendum, qui inter Manlianam severi- tatem & dissolutam lenitatem sit medius.

Pro ne desperes in Ebræo est, dum spes est. Re- gulis de statibus diversis, & communibus monitis spe- cialia ad informationem filiorum spectantia subjicit, primo quoad parentes, quibus injungitur informa- tio & castigatio filiorum, sed moderata, conf. Sir. c. 30, 12. quia ut v. 19. in Ebræo textu additur, Magnus ira (qui facile & vehementer, vel etiam diu excan- descit) sustinet vel portat pœnam aut damnum omnis generis: Etiam si erueris (ex una pœna talem iracun- dum) adhuc tamen addet, vel perget ira, & conse- quenter ob excandescentiam, pœnam novam susti- nere cogetur, ut cum R. Levi, Cornel. a Lap. & alii: vel si malis cum Pagnino & Vatablo exponas, licet: Si nimium severus fueris (in castigatione) damnum accipies: si erueris, rursum addes castigare eum, & for- tasse emendabis, quo etiam abit B. Lutheri versio, ac Vinariens. & Osiandr. paraphrasis. Persistit enim in hac materia de filiorum castigatione; &

nunc porro filios hortatur Salomo primum in gene- re ad suscipiendam disciplinam v. 20. Audi consilium & suscipe correctionem: ut sis sapiens in novissimo tuo, in senecta tua, vel etiam in fine vitæ tuæ. Syr. 25. v. 8. Corona senum multa peritia. Multæ enim, ut v. 21. habet, cogitationes sunt in corde cujusque: volun- tas autem Domini (cujus consilium suscipiendum monuerat) permanebit, Ps. 33, 11. Esa. 14, 24. 27.

1. Joh. 2, 17. Deinde informat specialius, utpote (1) de liberalitate v. 22. Desiderium hominis misericor- dia ejus, id est, pius homo (sequens consilium DEI) gaudet miseris benefacere, optat & expetit, ut mi- sericordiam exercere possit: at præstantior est pau- per (misericordia indigus, vel etiam pro pauperta- te sua stipem largiens Luc. 21, 3.) quam (opulentus si sit) vir mendacii, qui prolixe opem offerat, nul- lam autem præbeat. (2) De timore Domini v. 23. Timor Domini ad vitam, & satur commorabitur, non visitabitur malo. Commendatur itaque timor Domini a vitæ prosperitate, tranquilla satietate, vera a malis immunitate, conf. cap. 3, 18. 22. cap.

10, 11. 27. cap. 14, 25. (3) De desidia & otii fuga, v. 24. Abscondit piger manum suam in sinu, (vox Ebr. ollam significat, ac metaphorice de sinu cavi- tatem lateris referente accipi potest) more otioso- rum, & ob fugam laboris. Etiam ad os suum non adducit eam (præ pigritia.) Osiander ollæ signi- ficatum retinens hunc reddit sensum : tanta est igna- via hominis pigri, ut si ollam cum cibo illi proponas, & manum inserat, ut edat : tamen præ pigritia manum non reducat ad os suum. Hoc est : homines ignavi etiam præclarissimas occasiones (quibus ipsorum rebus pulchre consuli posset) turpiter negligunt; ac si quis cibo apposito, fame perire, quam manum ad os admovere mallet. Conf. glossa margin. B. Lutheri. Porro additur de fructu correctionis v. 25. Derisorem si percusseris, simplex efficietur astutus : At si increpaverit (quis) intelligentem, intelliget scientiam. Cum sim- plex etsi delusor plagis percutitur, astutus evadit, at cum verbis corripitur intelligens, correctionis in- digus, scientia magis magisque proficiet. Et de pœna filii immorigeri : Devastat patrem, fugat ma- trem filius pudore, & probris afficiens eloquiis (vel ver- bis) eosdem, parentes v. 26. Ideoque monet v. 27. Cessa fili, audire institutionem ad aberrandum a scien- tia. Noli auscultare iis, qui te ea docent, quæ pu- gnant cum verbo Dei, & a vera pietate sunt aliena. Vulgata plane discrepat a fontibus ita reddens : Non cessas fili audire doctrinam, nec ignores sermones scien- tiæ. Rationis loco esse potest, quod additur de Magistro impio nil curante divinum judicium, qui עד dicitur obtestans, vel contestans, uti Christus Ef. 55, 4. vocatur Magister populis datus. v. 28. Testis Belial (impius) deridet judicium (divinum) & os im- piorum devorat iniquitatem. Conf. Job. 15, 16. Matth. 23, 24. Sed parata sunt (certo) illusoribus judicia & contritiones corpori (vel tergo) stultorum v. 29. Beda reprobi, inquit, jussionis vel dominationis divinæ judi- cium derident : parata tamen eos expectant judicia da- mnationis, quæ ut mallei ferrum candens, ita eos in fornace gehennæ fine fine verberant.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

Miscellanea concerning drunkenness, the prudent and just man, avoiding suretyship, iniquity, the precipitation of counsels, and revelation, ingratitude, vengeance, injustice, the violation of vows, as also concerning the office of Kings.

Ver. 1.

WINE IS A LUXURIOUS THING, AND DRUNKENNESS IS TUMULTUOUS: WHOEVER DELIGHTS IN THESE WILL NOT BE WISE.

IN Hebrew. Wine (namely, consumed immoderately) makes a scoffer, strong drink makes one tumultuous: (concerning which Jerome in his Epistle to Nepotian says: Strong drink is any beverage that can intoxicate, whether it is made from grain, or from the juice of apples, or when honeycombs are boiled into a sweet and harsh drink, or the fruit of palms is pressed into a liquid, and water is colored with certain fruits, etc.) The positive effects of drunkenness are delusion and tumult, the privative is the lack of wisdom. Cf. Hos. 4, 18. Ephes. 5, 18. According to Aristotle, book 6 of the Ethics, chap. 5, σωφροσύνη is called as if it were σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν, and according to Socrates in Plato, q. σωτηρία τῆς φρονήσεως. But because scoffers and tumultuous people provoke the wrath of the Magistrate, who are so insane that they attack anyone with reproaches and quarrels, and do not even spare Kings themselves, it is not inappropriately added v. 2. The roaring as of a young lion (is) the terror of the King: in which place the terror of the King is not passive, but active, which a king stirred up by anger (or any Magistrate, the species being put for the genus) strikes into others: he who is enraged against him (thus it must be rendered in Hebrew. Compare Psalm 89:39. but not with the LXX & Vulgate or the Syriac, which say 'provokes him' or 'inflames with anger') sins against his own soul, or by a customary Hebraism (See Isaiah 5:24, ch. 46:2, Jer. 51:14) against himself. Compare 1 Kings 2:23, Prov. 16:14. And since mention has been made of tumult, it is added in v. 3: It is glory for a man to cease from strife: but every fool (such as drunkards certainly are) meddles with strife. To quarrel is unworthy of a magnanimous man, as Grotius says here. Furthermore, because leisure and drunkenness are joined, and drunkards are GIVEN TO LEISURE, the damage of sloth is designated in v. 4: the sluggard does not plow by reason of the winter, (he does not perform the parts of his duty because of the cold, or any inconvenience whatsoever:) therefore he shall beg in harvest time, (when farmers gather the fruits of their labors) Compare ch. 13:4, Sirach 6:19, 2. Thess. 3:10.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

Miscellanea de ebrietate, viro prudente & ju- sto, vitanda sponsione, iniquitate, consiliorum præcipitantia, ac revelatione, ingratitudine, vindicta, injustitia, votorum violatione, ut & de Regum officio.

Vers. 1.

LUXURIOSA RES VINUM, ET TUMUL- TUOSA EBRIETAS : QUICUNQUE HIS DE- LECTATUR NON ERIT SAPIENS.

IN Ebr. Derisorem (efficit) vinum (scil. immode- ratius haustum) tumultuantem sicera : (de qua Hie- ronymus Epist. ad Nepot. Sicera est omnis potio, quæ inebriare potest, sive illa, quæ frumento conficitur, seu pomorum succo, aut cum favi decoquuntur in dul- cem & barbaram potionem, aut palmarum fructus ex- primuntur in liquorem, certisque frugibus aqua pin- guior coloratur &c.) Effectus positivi vinolentiæ sunt delusio & tumultuatio, privativus est sapientiæ defe- ctus. Conf. Hos. 4, 18. Ephes. 5, 18. Secundum Aristotelem lib. 6. Eth. cap. 5. σωφροσύνη dicitur quasi σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν, & secundum Socra- tem apud Platonem q. σωτηρία τῆς φρονήσεως. Quia vero derisores & tumultuantes iram Magistra- tus provocant, qui ita vesani sunt, ut quoslibet probris & rixis appetant, nec vel ipsis Regibus parcant, non imcommode subjungitur v. 2. Ru- gitus tanquam leunculi (est) terror Regis : quo loco terror Regis non passivus, sed activus, quem rex ira concitatus (vel quivis Magistratus, specie pro genere posita) aliis incutit: qui excandescit adversus eum (ita Ebr. reddendum. Conf. Psal. 89, 39. non vero cum LXX. & Vulg. aut Syro, qui provocat eum vel ira inflammat) peccat contra animam suam, vel Ebraismo consueto (V. Esa. 5, 24. c. 46, 2. Jer. 51, 14.) contra semet ipsum. Conf. 1. Reg. 2, 23. Prov. 16, 14. Et quum tumultus mentio injecta sit, additur v. 3. Gloria est viro quiescere a lite: at omnis stultus (quales profecto ebrii sunt) admiscet se liti. Rixari indignum est viro magnanimo, ut hic Grotius. Porro quia otium, & ebrietas conjuncta, & ebriosi OTIO DEDITI sunt, damnum pigritiae designatur v. 4. propter hyemem piger non arat, (officii partes ob frigus, aut qualemcunque incommoditatem non peragit:) idcirco mendicabit messis tempore, (ubi laborum fructus agricolae percipiunt) Conf. cap. 13, 4. Syr. 6, 19. 2. Thess. 3, 10.

## 20:3
Verse 3.

IT IS AN HONOR FOR A MAN TO SEPARATE HIMSELF FROM CONTENTIONS) To quarrel is unworthy of a magnanimous man.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

HONOR EST HOMINI QUI SEPARAT SE A CONTENTIONIBUS) Rixari indignum est viro magnanimo.

## 20:5
Verse 5.

AS DEEP WATER, SO IS COUNSEL IN THE HEART OF A MAN: BUT A WISE MAN WILL DRAW IT OUT.

The intelligence of a man, or the sagacity of an intelligent and prudent person, is shown in investigating the counsels, thoughts, designs, and machinations of others, even if they lie in the deep: but not, as Mercerus with R. Solomon Jarchi and Aben-Ezra wishes, a prudence always teeming with manifold counsel. Thus in the Greek Catena: Although the counsel of a crafty man is deep like a whirlpool or a certain well, nevertheless a prudent man will draw it out, and bring it into the clear light. Another thing seems to be taught concerning the depth of the human heart in Ps. 64:7, Jer. 17:9, where it is said to be searchable by God alone; how then does an intelligent person draw it out? I answer: he draws it out partially, and in a certain respect, as far as human prudence can penetrate, not totally, or universally, regarding all things that are hidden in the mind of a man: nor in such a way that he knows it infallibly and intuitively, which belongs to God alone, but conjecturally, probably, and discursively, e.g., from one's gait, Eccl. 10:3, from bodily gestures, endeavors, Prov. 13:20, and finally from his own questions prudently proposed, by which, as if doing something else, he fishes out what he desires.

Furthermore, it is added in verse 6: MANY MEN ARE CALLED MERCIFUL: BUT A FAITHFUL MAN WHO SHALL FIND? so that the rarity of truly pious and faithful men, and the difficulty of discerning them, may be designated, even if many are commonly celebrated as pious and kind. To whom the counsel in the heart of a man is hidden, the faith of a man is much more hidden, so that even the most prudent of all can hardly discern who is truly faithful, whose heart corresponds to his words and deeds? A multitude of men (or as it pertains to a multitude of men, as it is customary in Hebrew for the nominative to be used thus) proclaims each one his own kindness or piety: but a man of faithfulness or truth who shall find in that multitude of men, which boasts itself with that title? For all wish to seem truthful, faithful, and truly pious, but who will discern, or find those who are truly such? Since nothing is more frequent than hypocrisy. Aben-Ezra has not poorly expressed that sense. But the interpretation of the LXX is different, man is a great thing, and Hilary on Psalm 118, letter Jod: A man is great and a merciful man is precious: but it is necessary to find a faithful man.

num

The fruit of integrity is suggested in v. 7. The just man who walks in his simplicity (integrity), will leave behind him blessed children, cf. Ex. 20, 5. Tob. 7, 7. Solomon the Magistrate threatens wickedness with punishment, and thus much rather divine vengeance: Since not even a Magistrate on earth should tolerate evil. The King who sits on the throne of judgment, dissipates all evil with his look. Whence the Author of the Greek Catena: The King sitting on the throne of judgment is God; who, residing in the heavenly court, from there foresees, corrects, and dissipates all evil. Similarly August. book on correction and grace, ch. 13. Bede, Salonius, and Hugo. Grotius explains these things thus:

Latin:

Vers. 5.

SICUT AQUA PROFUNDA, SIC CONSILIUM IN CORDE VIRI: SED HOMO SAPIENS EXHAURIET ILLUD.

Exhibetur viri intelligentia, seu intelligentis & prudentis sagacitas in aliorum consiliis, cogitatis, institutis, & machinationibus, etsi in profundo lateant, indagandis: non vero ut Mercerus cum R. Salom. Jarchi & AbenEzra vult, prudentia multiplici semper consilio scaturiens. Ita in Caten. Graec. Etsi hominis versipellis consilium instar gurgitis vel putei cujusdam sit altum, nihilo minus vir prudens exhauriet, & in manifestam lucem proferet illud. Aliud tradi videtur de profunditate cordis humani Pf. 64, 7. Jer. 17, 9. ubi illa soli Deo perscrutabilis dicitur, quomodo ergo intelligens eam exhaurit? Resp. exhaurit μερικῶς partialiter, & secundum quid, quousque penetrare potest humana prudentia, non ὁλικῶς totaliter, aut universaliter, quoad omnia, quae in mente hominis recondita sunt: nec ita ut infallibiliter & intuitive cognoscat, quod solius Dei est, sed conjecturaliter, probabiliter & discursive v. c. ex incessu Eccles. 10, 3. e corporis gestibus, conatibus, Prov. 13, 20. e suis denique quaestionibus prudenter propositis, quibus tanquam aliud agens, quid cupit, expiscatur.

Additur porro vers. 6. MULTI HOMINES MISERICORDES VOCANTUR: VIRUM AUTEM FIDELEM QUIS INVENIET? ut ita raritas vere piorum, & fidorum hominum, & difficultas eosdem dignoscendi designetur, etsi multi communiter celebrentur pii, ac benigni. Quibus occultum est consilium in corde viri, multo magis abscondita est fides hominis, ut dignoscere etiam prudentissimi quique aegre possint, quisnam vere fidus sit, cujus dictis & factis cor ipsum respondeat? Multitudo hominum, (vel quod attinet multitudinem hominum, ut solemne est in Ebraeo nominativum ita adhiberi) praedicat quisque benignitatem vel pietatem suam: at virum fidelitatis vel veritatis quis inveniet in ista hominum multitudine, quae se eo elogio jactitat? Omnes enim volunt veraces, fidi & vere pii videri, sed quis dignoscet, aut inveniet vere tales? Siquidem nihil hypocrisi frequentius sit. Sensum illum non male expressit Aben-Ezra. Aliena vero LXX. interpretatio, res magna est homo, & Hilarii in Psalm. 118. litera Jod: Grande homo & pretiosum vir misericors: virum vero fidelem opus est invenire.

num

Fructus autem integritatis insinuatur v. 7. Justus qui ambulat in simplicitate (integritate) sua, beatos post se filios derelinquet, conf. Ex. 20, 5. Tob. 7, 7. improbitati vero minatur Salomo Magistratus poenam, adeoque multo potius divinam vindictam: Siquidem ne Magistratus quidem in terris malum ferat. Rex qui sedet in solio judicii, dissipat omne malum intuitu suo. Unde Autor Caten. Graec. Rex sedens in solio judicii est Deus; qui in curia cælesti residens inde omne malum prospicit, corrigit, & dissipat. Simiter August. l. de corrept. & grat. c. 13. Beda, Salonius, & Hugo. Grotius hæc ita explicat:

## 20:8
THE KING WHO SITS ON THE THRONE OF HIS JUDGMENT, DISSIPATES ALL EVIL WITH HIS LOOK) He encourages kings to judge justly themselves, not through others. For thus they would find remedies for all evils, since they are well known to them. Herodotus said that kings were first established for the sake of enjoying justice, and Cicero approves that saying. But Hesiod had also said much earlier:

Τἕνεκα γὰρ βασιλῆες ἐχέφρονες, ἕνεκα λαοῖς Βλαπτομένοις ἀγορῆφι μετάτροπα ἔργα τελεῦσι.

Furthermore, Solomon also shows the origin of true piety, that it is not of our own ability, but of divine grace: as well as the imperfection of our holiness, that no one is immune from sin v. 9. Who can say my heart is clean, which in Hebrew is, as Cornelius admits, who will say I have cleansed my heart, I am pure from my sin? Which are therefore wrongly snatched away to the uncertainty of grace by Baynus in this place, as also by Bellarmine, book 3 on justification, ch. 4. For neither justification, nor the certainty of justification and the grace of the remission of sins, depends on our integrity, or purity, or holiness: but holiness and the pursuit of sincere piety follow justification rather. No one is entirely immune from sin, on account of the root and tinder of sin, namely depraved concupiscence, Rom. 7, 14. seqq. Heb. 12, 1, as well as on account of the sins of daily incursion, and human frailty, 1 Kings 8, 45. 1. John 1, 8. although the justified are immune from sin, as regards the guilt of sin, on account of the full remission of all sins, as also as regards the dominion of sin, as they struggle against the flesh, lest they be subjected under the servitude of sin. Therefore, the universal contamination of all men is taught here, and the impurity and imperfection of proper and inherent justice: where Papists distinguish in vain between being pure from sin, and saying, or boasting of someone, that he is pure: for who is truly pure, why should he not also be able to say it truly? Cf. B. Hæpffner. Disp. 6. Anti-Majer. aph. 8. but that we may acknowledge our imperfection, there is need of a just measure: For which reason a weight and a weight, a measure and a measure (namely diverse weights, one greater, the other smaller) both are even called an abomination to the Lord v. 10. which Gregory the Great rightly explains in this place from the order and sequence, hom. 4. on Ezekiel. A weight and a weight &c. We know that in the double weight of merchants one is greater, the other smaller: for they have one weight by which they weigh for themselves, and another weight by which they weigh for their neighbor: they prepare lighter weights for giving, but heavier ones for receiving: therefore every man, who weighs the things that are his neighbor's in one way, and his own in another, has a weight and a weight, therefore both are abominable before God: because if he were to love his neighbor as himself, he would judge him in good things, just as he would love himself: and if he were to look at himself as his neighbor, he would judge himself in bad things just as he would his neighbor. Cf. Cassian. collat. 21. c. 12. In another place and with another intention see the same sentiment c. 11, 1. c. 16, 11. above. Regarding hypocrisy and simulation, which is difficult to distinguish, not Gesner refers also to v. 11. Even a boy (not an adult only) feigns (or conducts himself as another, as the verb נכר in Hithpael is taken, Gen. 42, 7. 1 Kings 14, 5. 6.) in his actions, (so that it is difficult to distinguish) whether his work is pure, and whether it is right, so that the innate malice of men is noted. See Mr. Dr. Gejer on this passage, whence furthermore, as he observes, v. 12 explains the origin and cause of obedience toward God and superiors, that it is not to be attributed to corrupted nature, but to God alone, the giver of every good: The hearing ear (the obedient one. Cf. ch. 15, 31. ch. 25, 12.) and the seeing eye (observing divine works Deut. 6, 7. Isa. 5, 12.) the Lord has made even both of these. Of which two senses, as Polychronius notes, he makes mention because sight and hearing only receive admonition, or are the senses of discipline.

Which are commonly taken, as regards v. 11, concerning the preludes of manly actions in youth, but as regards v. 12, concerning the ear of an obedient people, and the eye of a prince, or a Magistrate wholesomely providing. Grotius annotated these things on those verses:

Latin:

REX QVI SEDET IN SOLIO JVDICII SVI, DISSIPAT OMNE MALVM INTVITV SVO) Excitat reges, ut ipsi jus dicant, non per alios. Ita enim omnibus malis, quippe sibi percognitis, remedia inventuros. Justitiæ fruendæ causa primum reges constitutos dixit Herodotus, & probat id dictum Cicero. Sed & multo ante Hesiodus dixerat:

Τἕνεκα γὰρ βασιλῆες ἐχέφρονες, ἕνεκα λαοῖς Βλαπτομένοις ἀγορῆφι μετάτροπα ἔργα τελεῦσι.

Porro veræ etiam pietatis originem monstrat Salomo, quod ea non sit nostræ facultatis, sed divinæ gratiæ: nec non sanctitatis nostræ imperfectionem, quod nemo immunis sit a peccato v. 9. Quis potest dicere mundum est cor meum, quod in Ebr. est fatente Cornelio, quis dicet mundavi cor meum, purus sum a peccato meo? Quæ proinde perperam ad incertitudinem gratiæ abripiuntur a Bayno in h. l. ut & Bellarm. l. 3. de justif. c. 4. Non enim ab integritate, aut puritate, vel sanctitate nostra dependet seu justificatio, seu justificationis, & gratiæ remissionis peccatorum certitudo: sed justificationem consequitur potius sanctitas & pietatis sinceræ studium. Nemo a peccato immunis prorsus est, ob peccati radicem & fomitem, pravam nempe concupiscentiam, Rom. 7, 14. seqq. Ebr. 12, 1, nec non ob peccata quotidianæ incursionis, & humanæ fragilitatis, 1. Reg. 8, 45. 1. Joh. 1, 8. etsi justificati a peccato immunes sint, qua peccati reatum, ob plenam peccatorum omnium remissionem, ut & quoad peccati dominium, qua luctantur contra carnem, ne subigantur sub peccati servitutem. Docetur ergo hic universalis omnium hominum contaminatio, propriaque & inhærentis justitiæ impuritas, & imperfectio: ubi frustra Papistæ distinguunt inter esse purum a peccato, & dicere, seu gloriari alicujus, quod purus sit: qui enim vere purus est, quidni etiam id dicere possit vere? Conf. B. Hæpffner. Disp. 6. Anti-Majer. aph. 8. ut autem imperfectionem nostram agnoscamus, justa opus est mensura: Quo nomine pondus & pondus, mensura & mensura (diversa sc. pondera, unum majus, alterum minus) abominatio etiam Domino ambo ipsa dicuntur v. 10. quæ ex ordine ac συνεχείᾳ recte Gregor. M. hoc loco explicat hom. 4. in Ezech. Pondus & pondus &c. Scimus quia in negotiatorum duplici pondere aliud majus, aliud minus est: nam aliud pondus habent ad quod pensant sibi, & aliud pondus ad quod pensant proximo: ad dandum quidem pondera leviora ad accipiendum vero gravia præparant: omnis itaque homo, qui aliter pensat ea, quæ sunt proximi, & aliter ea, quæ sua sunt, pondus & pondus habet, utrumque ergo abominabile apud Deum: quia si sic proximum, ut se diligeret, hunc in bonis, sicut se amaret: & si sic se, ut proximum adspiceret, se in malis sicut proximum judicaret. Conf. Cassian. collat. 21. c. 12. Alio loco & alia intentione vide eandem sententiam c. 11, 1. c. 16, 11. supra. Ad hypocrisin & simulationem difficulter dignoscendam non Gesneri refertur etiam v. 11. Etiam puer (non adultus solum) simulat (vel alium se gerit, ut verbum נכר in Hithpael accipitur, Gen. 42, 7. 1. Reg. 14, 5. 6.) in actionibus suis, (ut diffi- cile sit dignoscere) num purum, & num rectum sit opus ejus, ut congenita ita malitia hominum notetur. Vid. Dn. D. Gejer. in h. l. unde porro eodem observante v. 12. exponitur origo & causa debiti erga Deum & superiores obsequii, quod id non naturæ transferi- bendum sit corruptæ, verum soli Deo datori omnis boni: Aurem audientem (obsequentem. Conf. c. 15, 31. c. 25, 12.) & oculum videntem (observantem di- vina opera Deut. 6, 7. Esa. 5, 12.) Dominus fecit etiam ambo ista. Quorum duorum sensuum, notante Po- lychronio ideo meminit, quia visus & auditus tantum recipiunt admonitionem, vel sensus sunt disciplinæ.
