Quæ vulgo, quod ad v. 11. de præludiis actionum viri- lium in juventute, quod vero ad v. 12. de aure popu- li obsequentis, & oculo principis, vel Magistratus sa- lubriter providentis accipiuntur. Grotius hæc ad versus illos annotavit:

## 20:11
Verse 11.

BY HIS STUDIES A BOY IS UNDERSTOOD) From those things in which he most delights.

IF HIS WORKS BE PURE AND RIGHT) Whether his actions, which are to be, when he has grown up, are pure and upright.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

EX STVDIIS SVIS INTELLIGITVR PVER) Ex eis quibus maxime delectatur.

SI MVNDA ET RECTA SINT OPERA EJVS) An munda & integra actiones ejus, supple futuræ sint ubi ado- leverit.

## 20:12
Verse 12.

THE HEARING EAR AND THE SEEING EYE THE LORD HAS MADE BOTH OF THEM) He added this so that from their first age boys might both hear and see honorable things.

But because there is need of labor and industry also for acquiring knowledge no less than for acquiring those things which make πρὸς τὰ ἄλφιτα, Solomon warns in v. 13. Do not love sleep, lest you be made poor: open your eyes, be satisfied with bread itself. Diligence and vigilance are opposed to sleepiness: just as sleeping is a matter of necessity, so loving sleep is a matter of pleasure and laziness. But by the opening of the eyes, not mere contemplation, but the diligent and laborious care of the thing seen is noted, as is clear from 2 Kings 19, 17. Job 14, 3. Jer. 32, 19. Dan. 9, 18. Zech. 12, 4. One must be vigilant, however, not only for the acquisition of wealth, but primarily for the acquisition of wisdom: one must be vigilant not only for the body, but primarily for the nourishment and salvation of the soul, Eph. 5, 14. 1. Pet. 5, 8. Just as Solomon demanded a hearing ear and a seeing eye, so he now requires the shaking off of sleep and the opening of the eyes, without which neither the hearing ear nor the seeing eye has a place. Aben-Ezra connects these verses in almost the same way, as if he were saying, ears are ordained for listening to instruction, but eyes for contemplating those things by which we are corrected, and therefore do not love sleep. These are the words of Grotius in this place:

Latin:

Vers. 12.

AVREM AVDIENTEM ET OCVLVM VIDEN- TEM DOMINVS FECIT VTRVMQVE) Hoc ideo adjunxit, ut à prima ætate pueri & audiant, & videant honesta.

Quia vero labore opus est, & industria etiam ad comparandam scientiam non minus quam ad ac- quirenda ea, quæ faciunt πρὸς τὰ ἄλφιτα, monet Salomo v. 13. Ne diligas somnum, ne forte efficiaris pauper: aperi oculos tuos, saturare ipso pane. So- mnolentiæ opponitur sedulitas & vigilantia: uti dormire necessitatis est, ita somnum diligere volupta- tis & pigritiæ. Per apertionem vero oculorum non nudam contemplationem, sed sedulam & opero- sam rei conspectæ curam notari e 2. Reg. 19, 17. Job. 14, 3. Jer. 32, 19. Dan. 9, 18. Zach. 12, 4. liquet. Vi- gilandum autem non tantum pro opum acquisitione, sed imprimis pro sapientiæ comparatione: vigilandum non solum pro corpore, sed imprimis pro animæ nu- trimentis & salute, Eph. 5, 14. 1. Pet. 5, 8. uti aurem au- dientem, & oculum videntem postulavit Salomo, sic excussionem somni, & apertionem oculorum nunc requirit, sine qua nec auris audiens, nec ocu- lus videns locum habet. Similiter fere Aben-Ezra hos versus nectit, quasi dicat, aures ad institutionem auscultandam, oculi vero ad ea contemplanda, quibus corrigimur, ordinati sunt, ideoque ne diligas somnum. Grotii hoc loco hæc sunt:

## 20:13
Verse 13.

DO NOT LOVE SLEEP, LEST POVERTY OVERWHELM YOU.

For no idle person, having a god in his mouth, could gather a living without toil, says Euripides in Melanippe.

Furthermore, verse 14 follows: Bad, bad, says the buyer (concerning the subject matter of wisdom: concerning which Solomon frequently warns that it must be bought, acquired, and procured: it is bad to shake off sleep and devote oneself to wisdom: the root of studies is bitter, but the fruits are sweet) but when he has gone away (that apparent evil) then he will boast: Grotius retains the common interpretation, having this to say on this passage:

Latin:

Vers. 13.

NOLI DIGILERE SOMNVM, NE TE EGESTAS OPPRIMAT)

Ἀργὸς γὰρ οὐδεὶς θεὸς ἔχων ἀνὰ στόμα, Βίον δύναιτʼ ἂν συλλέγειν ἄνευ πόνου, ait Euripides Melanippa.

Sequitur porro v. 14. Malum, malum, dicit emtor (de materia substrata sapientiæ: de qua emen- da, acquirenda & comparanda sæpius monet Salo- mo: malum est somnum excutere, & sapientiæ se de- dere: amara est studiorum radix, fructus autem dul- ces) at cum abiit (malum illud apparens) tunc glo. riabitur: Grotius vulgarem interpretationem reti- net, ita ad hunc locum habens:

## 20:14
IT IS BAD, IT IS BAD, SAYS EVERY BUYER, AND WHEN HE HAS DEPARTED, THEN HE WILL BOAST. It is vile, he says: But when he has bought it, he boasts that he has bought it well. This is καπηλεύειν, to play the huckster. The buyer, bearing the wish to acquire it more cheaply, and the seller, to sell it more dearly, approach this contract, and scarcely after many contentions, with the seller gradually subtracting from what he had asked, and the buyer adding to what he had offered, do they agree on a certain price, says L. Si voluntate. C. de rescindenda venditione.

However, the context favors the interpretation which we have given: from which R. Levi is also not alien: For he says, no one considers wisdom useful to himself, unless he has attained it. Baynus explained it similarly, and Cornelius a Lapide from the same: Those who persist in virtues and wisdom experience many arduous and difficult things at the beginning, but afterwards they congratulate themselves that they have produced virtue and wisdom by their own labors. Whence also the Chaldean connects this gnome to the following one, in which the study of wisdom is preferred to riches and gold, v. 15. There is gold and a multitude of gems (in great price, to wit) but as a precious vessel are the lips of knowledge, for the lips full of knowledge like a vessel ought to be considered much more precious. Such were the lips of Chrysostom, of Peter Chrysologus, called golden for that reason. Conf. c. 3, 13. c. 8, 19. Job 28, 15.

Latin:

MALVM EST MALVM, DICIT OMNIS EMTOR, ET CVM RECESSERIT, TVNC GLORIABITVR) Vile est hoc, dicit: At ubi emerit, jactat se bene emisse. Hoc est καπηλεύειν, cauponari. Emtor viliore comparandi, venditor cariore distrahendi votum gerentes ad hunc contractum accedunt, vixque post multas contentiones, paulatim venditore de eo quod petierat detrahente, emtore autem huic quod obtulerat addente, ad certum consentiunt pretium, ait L. Si voluntate. C. de rescindenda venditione.

Illi tamen quam dedimus interpretationi contextus favet: a qua etiam aliena non est R. Levi: Nec enim, inquiens, sapientiam quis sibi utilem arbitratur, nisi cum illam sit adeptus. Similiter exposuit Baynus, ac Cornel. a Lapide ex eodem: Qui virtutibus & sapientiae insistunt, initio ardua multa & difficilia experiuntur, at postea sibi gratulantur, quod virtutem & sapientiam suis laboribus pepererint. Unde & Chaldaeus hanc gnomen nectit sequenti, in qua studium sapientiae opibus & auro antefertur v. 15. Est aurum & multitudo gemmarum (in magno sc. pretio) at ut vas pretiosum sunt labia scientiae, multo nempe pretiosiora censeri debent labia instar vasis plena scientiae. Qualia fuere labia Chrysostomi, Petri Chrysologi, aurea inde dicta. Conf. c. 3, 13. c. 8, 19. Job. 28, 15.

## 20:16
verse 16.

TAKE THE GARMENT OF HIM WHO HAS BECOME SURETY FOR ANOTHER: AND FOR STRANGERS TAKE A PLEDGE FROM HIM.

Now Solomon warns of those things which must be avoided by prudent men who take counsel for themselves: namely (1.) Inconsiderate suretyship: take his garment, who has stood surety for another (which, even if it could not be taken in place of a pledge from a needy neighbor, Deut. 24:17, was nevertheless justly taken from others also, when they have pledged their faith for others) and take a pledge for a stranger: that is, take the garment of him who stands surety for another, and retain it in place of a pledge. Cf. Mercer and Dr. Geier. (2.) Iniquity, the beginning of which is flattering, the outcome torturous, v. 7. The bread of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterwards his mouth will be filled with sand. Bread that is gritty (or mixed with pebbles and small stones) appears sweet, but if you chew it, it will create annoyance and danger. Which is discovered in every pleasure; whence Aristotle warned that we should contemplate pleasures not as they come, but as they depart, that is, not from the front, but from the back. For as they come, they flatter with a painted appearance, but as they depart, they leave behind repentance and pain. Cf. c. 9, 17. Job 20, 12. (3.) Precipitation and revelation of plans, v. 18. Thoughts (endeavors, designs) are confirmed by counsel (which is altogether necessary in arduous matters, as when one dares to undertake a war, whence it is added) and with counsels wage war. Cf. c. 24, 6. Luke 14, 31. Grotius corrects the Vulgate, which renders it 'wars are to be managed by steering,' thus: In the Hebrew, 'by industries.' There follows v. 19. He who reveals a secret walks deceitfully (c. 11, 13) and do not associate with him who errs or is seduced by his lips. He who, without regard for place, time, or persons, wanders indiscriminately with his speech, revealing secrets or even things not sufficiently verified. One must flee the company of him who is full of cracks. (4.) Ingratitude toward benefactors, especially one's own parents, v. 20. He who curses his father and mother, his lamp (of happiness and joy) will be extinguished in the darkness of shadows. Such an impious and ungrateful son will suddenly depart from a happy state into horrible calamities, so that wherever he turns, he does not know. Cf. chap. 13, 9. 11. c. 18, 6. chap. 29, 3.

Latin:

verf. 16.

TOLLE VESTIMENTUM EJUS QUI FIDEJUSSOR EXSTITIT ALIENI: ET PRO EXTRANEIS AUFER PIGNUS AB EO.

Jam de iis quae cavenda sunt viris prudentibus & sibi consulentibus monet Salomo: utpote (1.) Sponsio inconsiderata: tolle vestimentum ejus, qui fidejussit pro alieno (quod etiamsi pignoris loco a proximo egeno accipi non poterat, Deut. 24, 17. ab aliis tamen etiam, cum pro alienis fidem interposuere, juste accipiebatur) & pro extraneo pignus accipe: id est, accipe vestem ejus qui spondet pro alio, & pignoris loco eam retine. Conf. Mercer. & Dn. D. Geierus. (2.) Iniquitas, cujus initium blandens, exitus crucians v. 7. Suavis est viro panis falsitatis, at postea implebitur os ejus arena. Panis calculosus (vel scrupulis & lapillis mixtus) suavis apparet, sed si masticaveris, molestiam & periculum creabit. Quod in omni voluptate deprehenditur; unde monuit Aristotel. ut voluptates contemplemur non venientes, sed abeuntes, hoc est, non a fronte, sed a tergo. Venientes enim fucata specie blandiuntur, abeuntes vero poenitudinem, ac dolorem relinquunt. Conf. c. 9, 17. Job. 20, 12. (3.) Consiliorum praecipitantia ac revelatio, v. 18. Cogitationes (conatus, instituta) consilio confirmantur (quo omnino opus est in rebus arduis, utpote cum bellum quis suscipere audet, unde additur) & consiliis fac bellum. Conf. c. 24, 6. Luc. 14, 31. Vulgatam quae reddit, gubernaculis tractanda sunt bella sic corrigit Grotio: In Hebraeo per industrias. Sequitur v. 19. Qui revelat secretum, incedit fraudulenter (c. 11, 13.) & ei qui errat vel seducitur labiis suis ne admisceto te. Qui citra observationem loci, temporis aut personarum indiscriminatim sermone suo citra arcana, aut etiam non satis comperta vagatur. Fugiendum est ejus consortium, qui plenus rimarum est. (4.) Ingratitudo erga benefactores, imprimis parentes suos, v. 20. Qui maledicit patri suo & matri, extinguetur lucerna ejus (felicitatis, & laetitiae) obscuritate tenebrarum. Talis impius & ingratus filius subito excedet e felici statu in horribiles calamitates, ut quoquo se vertat, nesciat. Conf. cap. 13, 9. 11. c. 18, 6. cap. 29, 3.

## 20:18
Verse 18.

WARS ARE TO BE MANAGED BY STEERING) In the Hebrew: by industries. The Greeks: Γνῶμαι πλέον κρατῦσιν ἢ σθένος χερῶν, And Euripides: Γνώμη γὰρ ἀνδρὸς εὖ μὲν οἰκεῖται πόλις, Εὖ δ' οἶκος, εἶς τ' αὖ πόλεμον ἰσχύει μέγα, Σοφοὶ γὰρ ἔν βύλευμα τὰς πολλὰς χέρας, Νικᾷ.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

GVBERNACVLIS TRACTANDA SUNT BELLIA) In Hebræo: per industrias. Græci: Γνῶμαι πλέον κρατῦσιν ἢ σθένος χερῶν, Et Euripides: Γνώμη γὰρ ἀνδρὸς εὖ μὲν οἰκεῖται πόλις, Εὖ δ' οἶκος, εἶς τ' αὖ πόλεμον ἰσχύει μέγα, Σοφοὶ γὰρ ἔν βύλευμα τὰς πολλὰς χέρας, Νικᾷ.

## 20:21
Verse 21.

AN INHERITANCE WHICH IS HASTENED TO IN THE BEGINNING, WILL LACK A BLESSING IN THE END) He calls an inheritance, in the Hebrew manner, every right that can be transmitted to children. The sense is the same as above 13, 11. Nor did Menander mean anything else when he said: Οὐδεὶς ἐπλύτησε ταχέως δίκαιος ὢν. To which sentiment a comparison is below here 28, 20. Add, so that you may have the full sentiment, which is here, that Hesiodic one: Μὴ κακὰ κερδαίνειν· κακὰ κέρδεα ἶσ' ἄτῃσι. Euripides in Erechtheus: ὄυτε γὰρ πλῦτός ποτε Βέβαιος ἄδικος.

The sense is, if children or relatives have wished for the death of parents or relatives (from whom they expect some inheritance), and have gaped after the inheritance (while the parents are still alive), or have even importunately extorted it, let them know that those riches will not be happy or durable. This pertains to the preceding member concerning ingratitude. (5.) Vengeance v. 22. Do not say I will return evil: wait for the Lord, and He will save you. Cf. Rom. 12, 17. 1 Pet. 2, 23. Sir. 28, 1. 7. Therefore, it was not only by Christ that vengeance was forbidden, as the Socinians wish, which Solomon already prohibited here, and Moses long before Lev. 19, v. 18. (6.) Injustice in buying and selling, v. 23. Diverse weights are an abomination, and a deceitful balance is not good. Cf. ch. 11, 1. ch. 16, 11. (7.) Rash presumption v. 24. For therefore, to God guiding our steps v. 24, is opposed a man without strength not even understanding his own way, so that we may commit our steps (as far as concerns the success and outcome of our actions and ways) solely to God, and not institute our way except according to God or His word: Man's steps (are directed) by the Lord, but how shall a man understand his own way? Cf. ch. 16, 9. 25. Jer. 10, 23. Job 14, 16. ch. 31, 3. ch. 34, 21. (8.) Profane violation of vows, because those things which are either consecrated to God by others, or destined by us by a vow. It is a snare to a man (an ensnaring of the conscience, and a snare of perdition, and a man's misfortune) to devour what is sanctified, which is dedicated to God and sacred uses, and after vows to inquire whether they ought to be performed or not, or to seek reasons for retracting and violating them. Under that species of devouring consecrated things, the rest are also comprehended. Concerning the absurd reading of the Vulgate, to devour holy things, and after vows to retract, we have spoken in Crit. Sacr. p. 587. Grotius himself corrects it v. 25 in this way:

Latin:

Verf. 21.

HÆREDITAS AD QVAM FESTINATUR IN PRIN- CIPIO, IN NOVISSIMO BENEDICTIONE CAREBIT) Hæreditatem vocat more Hebræo omne jus quod ad liberos transmitti potest. Est sensus idem qui supra 13, 11. Nec ali- ud voluit Menander, cum dixit: Οὐδεὶς ἐπλύτησε ταχέως δίκαιος ὢν. Cui sententiæ compar infra est hic 28, 20. adde, ut plenam sententiam, quæ hic est, habeas, Hesiodēum illud: Μὴ κακὰ κερδαίνειν· κακὰ κέρδεα ἶσ' ἄτῃσι. Euripides Erechtheo: ὄυτε γὰρ πλῦτός ποτε Βέβαιος ἄδικος.

Sensus est, si liberi aut cognati parentum aut cognatorum (a quibus aliquid hæreditatis exspe- čtant) mortem optaverint, & hæreditati (vivis ad- huc parentibus) inhiaverint, vel eam etiam impor- tune extorserint, sciant eas opes non fore felices, aut durabiles. Pertinet hoc ad præcedens mem- brum de ingratitudine. (5.) Vindicta v. 22. Ne di- cas reddam malum: expecta Dominum, & salvum fa- ciet te. Conf. Rom. 12, 17. 1. Pet. 2, 23. Syr. 28, 1. 7. Non ergo a Christo demum interdičtum vindictæ accessit, quod Socinistæ volunt, quam hic jam prohibuit Sa- lomo, & Moses longe antea Lev. 19. v. 18. (6.) In- justitia in emtione & venditione, v. 23. Abominatio sunt diversa pondera, & bilanx dolosa non est bona. Conf. cap. 11, 1. c. 16, 11. (7.) Præsumtio temeraria v. 24. Ideo enim Deo gressus nostros gubernanti v. 24. opponitur homo imbellis viam suam ne qui- dem intelligens, ut Deo & gressus nostros (quantum ad successum & eventum ačtionum & viarum no- strarum) unice committamus, nec nisi juxta Deum vel verbum ejus viam nostram instituamus: A Do- mino gressus viri (diriguntur) homo autem quomodo intelliget viam suam? Conf. c. 16, 9. 25. Jer. 10, 23. Job. 14, 16. c. 31, 3. c. 34, 21. (8.) Votorum violatio pro- phana, quod ea quæ vel ab aliis Deo consecrata, vel a nobis voto destinata sunt. Laqueus est homini (illaqueatio conscientiæ, & laqueus perditionis, & infortunium hominis) deglutire sančtificatum, quod Deo, sacrisque usibus dicatum est, & post vota inqui- rere, an ea præstari debeant, nec ne, vel quærere causas eadem retračtandi, & violandi. Sub illa autem specie deglutitionis rerum consecratarum reliqua etiam comprehenduntur. De Vulgatæ absurda lečtione devorare sančta, & post vota retra- here, diximus Crit. Sacr. p, 587. Corrigit eam Gro- tius ipse v. 25. hoc modo:

## 20:22
Verse 22.

DO NOT SAY: I WILL RETURN EVIL: WAIT FOR THE LORD, AND HE WILL DELIVER YOU) There are many admonitions in these books which are divine precepts in the Gospel: some vengeance is also forbidden in the law, but not all.

Why should admonitions of this kind not be considered divine precepts in these books? Were they not written by divine instinct through the Holy Spirit? Are they not brought forward in the manner of commanding, just like other precepts? But a hidden error is fostered here concerning new precepts of the Gospel, which, if they are found in the books of the Old Testament besides the law, are to be held only as admonitions, not to be accepted as precepts. Thus, therefore, no divine precept will be held to be among the Prophets, none in the books of David and Solomon, which is most false. All vengeance which is in the New Testament is also forbidden in the law, namely private vengeance: but public vengeance is prohibited neither in the Old Testament nor in the New. Paul himself proves the precept about not taking revenge from Solomon, and from this book of Proverbs, repeating in Romans 12:20 the very words of Solomon, not in the place of some admonition, but as a precept from Proverbs 15:21. But that error of Grotius has already been chastised several times, which he shares in common with the Pelagians, Photinians, and Anabaptists. Let those things also be seen here which he said at the beginning of this book.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

NE DICAS: REDDAM MALUM: EXPECTA DO- MINVM, ET LIBERABIT TE) Multa sunt in his libris monita, quæ in Evangelio sunt divina præcepta: aliqua ultio & in lege vetita, sed non omnis.

Cur non monita ejusmodi divina habenda præcepta sint in his libris? Annon e divino instin- &u illi scripti sunt per Spiritum Sanctum. Annon modo imperandi proferuntur, perinde uti alia præ- cepta? Sed ὕπυλον hic fovetur de novis Evangelii Præceptis, quæ si reperiantur in libris V. T. præter le- gem, pro monitis tantum habenda sint, non ut præcepta accipienda. Sic ergo nullum præceptum divinum habebitur penes Prophetas, nullum in libris Davidis, & Salomonis, quod falsissimum. Ultio omnis, quæ in Novo Testamento, etiam in lege vetita est, priva- ta nempe: Publica autem neque in Veteri Testa- mento prohibita, neque in Novo. Probat ipse Paulus præceptum de non ulciscendo e Salomone, & ex hoc Prov. libro Rom. 12, 20. repetens ipsissima Salomonis verba non loco moniti alicujus, sed instar præcepti e Prov. 15, 21. Sed error iste Grotii jam ali- quoties castigatus est, quem cum Pelagianis, Photi- nianis, Anabaptistis communem habet. Videan- tur etiam hic ea, quæ sub ingressum libri hujus dixit.

## 20:25
IT IS THE RUIN OF A MAN TO DEVOUR THE HOLY, AND AFTER VOWS TO RETRACT) You translate this best thus: It is a snare for a man to devour what is sanctified, and after vows to be perplexed. Many men fall into grave evils because they turn to their own uses things dedicated to God, or when they have vowed something, having obtained what they hoped for, they infringe or diminish the vow by quibbling. Consider this, princes.

Latin:

RVINA HOMINIS EST DEVORARE SANCTOS, ET POST VOTA RETRACTARE) Optime sic vertes: Tendicula est homini devorare sanctificatum, & post vota per- plexari. Multi homines in mala gravia incidunt, quod Deo dedicata in suos usus vertant, aut ubi quid voverint, adepti quod sperabant votum cavillando infringant aut imminu- ant. Cogitate principes.

## 20:26
Verse 26.

A WISE KING SCATTERS THE WICKED: AND BENDS OVER THEM THE WHEEL.

In Hebrew: and brings over them the wheel. He is now dealing with the office of the Magistrate: that a pious and sensible Magistrate should punish the wicked, so that the honest and good may enjoy peace and tranquility in the Republic, Romans 13:4. Which sentiment coheres with the preceding, so that the impious may fear lest they be scattered or find it necessary to come under the wheel. Concerning the wheel, see Jerome on Amos, book 3; Fuller, book 3, Miscellanies, chapter 12. Compare Isaiah 28:27, chapter 41:5. By the bringing of the wheel, he understands a rigorous investigation and examination, with the Vinarie Paraphrase of Lord Dr. Gejer, comparing Jeremiah 15:7, Matthew 3:12, Luke 3:17; most others understand the infliction of punishment, such as Martin de Roa, part 2, singular, page 97; Mariana, Menochius, Vatablus, Lavaterus, Mercerus, Piscator, the Belgians, Osiander, etc. The context of verse 27 seems to favor the former explanation. For if the King is to be feared, bringing the wheel, winnowing and examining the impious, certainly the Lord is more to be feared, to whom the very mind of man is open: The light of the Lord is the spirit of man, he (the Lord) searches all the innermost parts of the belly: LXX. The light of the Lord is the breath of men, which searches the chambers of the belly; the light of the Lord is the soul of man, which (the Lord) searches the hiding places of the belly. It is signified, according to the author of the Greek Catena, that nothing in man is so hidden that it lies concealed, which is obscure to God: since even the soul itself, when He searches it, is light to Him, i.e., it is as open to Him as light itself. However, the coherence does not disagree with another exposition: If you take the lamp or light of the Lord as the favor of God with the blessed Luther: The grace of God or to be exhilarated by GOD is the spirit and life of man, and it penetrates the whole body; which sense Cornelius a Lapide also handed down. In such a way that, just as punishment was previously declared for the impious, so conversely grace and joy were promised here for the pious. Furthermore, the supports of the Royal throne are subjoined in verse 28, clemency and truth. Mercy (kindness, clemency) and truth will guard the King: and he will support his throne through mercy (clemency): so that by the same not only life, but also Royal dignity is guarded and preserved. Compare Psalm 51:1. By truth, in the phrase of Scripture, justice is rightly understood. These two, therefore, are the defenders, clemency and justice, who keep watch for the King night and day, and perpetually protect and guard him, as Cornelius not badly says. Moreover, just as the glory of young men is their strength, and the dignity of old men is gray hair, verse 29 (if, namely, they grow white not only with gray hair, but also with merits, and old age is gray not only in years, but also in character, as Ambrose speaks), and it is fitting for Princes to cherish the glory of young men flourishing in the strength of mind and body: so on the contrary, the wicked must be restrained by the stripes of a wound, and by blows (penetrating) to the inner parts of the belly; for as clemency, so also severity should have its time and place. Concerning which see the last verse. The blueness of a wound for evil; and stripes in the inner parts of the belly.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

DISSIPAT IMPIOS REX SAPIENS: ET INCURVAT SUPER EOS FORNICEM.

In Ebr. & inducit super eos rotam. De Magistra- tus jam agit officio: quod pius & cordatus Magistra- tus sceleratos supplicio afficiat, ut honesti, & boni pace, ac tranquillitate in Republ. frui possint, Rom. 13, 4. Quæ sententia superioribus cohæret, ut im- pii metuant, ne dissipentur aut sub rotam venire necesseum habeant. De rota vid. Hier. ad Am. I. 3. Fuller. lib. 3. Miscell. c. 12. Conf. Esa. 28, 27. cap. 41.5. Per rotæ inductionem rigorosam inquisitionem & exanima intelligit cum Vinariensibus Paraphr. Dn. D. Gejer. conferens Jer. 15, 7. Matth. 3, 12. Luc. 3, 17. alii plerique supplicii illationem, utpote Martin. de Roa, part. 2. singul. p. 97. Mariana, Menochius, Vatablus, Lavaterus, Mercerus, Piscator, Belgæ, O- siander &c. Priori explicationi favere videtur συν- έχεια v. 27. Si enim metuendus Rex est, rotam inducens, ventilans & examinans impios, magis certe metuendus Dominus, cui patet ipse homi- nis animus: Lux Domini spiritus hominis, perscruta- tur (Dominus) omnia penetralia ventris: LXX. Φῶς κυρίου πνοὴ ἀνθρώπων ὃς ἐρευνᾷ ταμιεῖα κοι- λίας, lux Domini est anima hominis, qui (Domi- nus) scrutatur latebras ventris. Significatur jux- ta autorem Caten. Græc. nihil in homine usque adeo abditum latere, quod Deo sit obscurum: quippe cum ipsa etiam anima, ubi eam scrutatur, lux ipsi existat, h. e. æque illi pateat, atque lux ipsa. Non discon- gruit tamên cohærentia etiam alteri expositioni: Si lucernam vel lucem Domini de favore Dei cum B. Luthero accipias: Gratia Dei vel exhilarari a DEO spiritus & vita est hominis, & penetrat totum corpus; quem sensum tradidit etiam Corn. a Lap. Quo pa- cto ut impiis pœna antea indicta, ita contra gratia piis, & lætitia hic promissa fuerit. Subjunguntur porro v. 28. stabilimenta throni Regii, clementia, & veritas. Misericordia (benignitas, clementia) & veritas custodient Regem: & fulciet per misericordiam (clementiam) solium suum: quod eadem non vita solum, sed & dignitas Regia custodiatur & confer- vetur. Conf. Pf. 51, 1. Per veritatem phrasi scriptu- ræ justitia recte intelligitur. Hi ergo duo sunt hyper- aspistæ clementia & justitia, qui nocte dieque pro Rege excubant, eumque perpetim tuentur & cu- stodiunt, ut non male Cornelius. Cæterum uti gloria juvenum est fortitudo eorum, & dignitas senum est canities vers. 29. (si scil. non solum ca- nis, sed meritis etiam albescant, & senectus non annis modo, sed & moribus cana sit, ut loquitur Ambrosius), ac gloriam juvenum animi & corporis fortitudine florentium fovere decet Principes: ita contra plagis vulneris coercendi sunt mali, & verberibus (penetrantibus) ad interiora ventris; ut enim clementia, sic etiam severitas suum tempus & locum habeat. Quo de vers. ult. Livores vulneris medicina in malo; & plagae in interioribus ventris.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. Still concerning Kings. Concerning the manner of growing rich. Concerning the perverse and impious, and especially unjust judges: concerning foolishness, and pride: and the evils thereof: and the advantages of the wise man.

Vers. 1.

AS THE DIVISIONS OF THE WATERS, SO IS THE HEART OF THE KING IN THE HAND OF THE LORD, WHITHERSOEVER HE WILL HE SHALL INCLINE IT) Themistius calls this an Assyrian maxim. The Hebrews note that this does not treat of that more common providence which pertains to all men, but of that more special one, by which He directs the thoughts of kings, both good and bad, in such a way that He uses them for the events which He has proposed to Himself. See Jer. ch. 10, near the end. A similitude taken from a farmer, who leads streams through meadows wherever he wishes.

In Hebrew: as the rivulets of waters. The heart of a king, viewed in respect of the operations and affections of the soul, such as to think, to will, to love, to hate, is in the power of the Lord, who directs it just as farmers or gardeners are accustomed to derive rivulets of water through channels into fields or gardens. The LXX refer it to God: as if to say, just as God derives rivers, like the Nile, through rivulets into certain parts of the earth, etc. See Ezra 7:28, ch. 9:9, Nehem. 2:8, Psalm.

33:15. Rev. 17:17. However, these things are not to be dragged by the Calvinists to fatal necessity, or to inclinations of the heart toward evil: for it is one thing to incline the heart, another to necessitate it: and that [the former] does not comprehend everything that He wills, but excludes evils: for God does not will, and indeed cannot even will, the evils of fault. Psalm 5:5. Deut. 32:4. 1 John 1:5. James 1:13. Now what he had said in general in ch. 16:2 concerning any men whatsoever, he here specifically applies and adapts to Kings: Vers. 2. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, (and thus that happens even in persons shining in purple) but the Lord weighs the hearts: whence he specifically warns Kings that they should do justice and judgment: v. 3. To do justice and judgment is more chosen by the Lord than sacrifice. For this is proper to kings 2 Sam. 15:15, 1 Kings 10:9, 1 Chron. 18:14, Jer. 22:3, Eccl. 1:5, 7. Which Philip explains: to do justice is to approve what is to be approved: to do judgment is to judge what is to be condemned. Similarly, it is perhaps not without reason said that humility is here specifically commended to kings, even if the general sense is not excluded, but because of the application, by the force of the saying concerning all and none, it is necessary, v. 4. The exaltation (pride) of the eyes and the breadth of the heart, when one dilates the heart excessively out of pride and excessive confidence because of a flourishing state, the lamp (for thus the Hebrew word is frequently taken 1 Kings 11:36, ch. 14:4, 2 Kings 8:19, 2 Chron. 21:7, and is explained as Lamp by the Chaldean, Elias Levita, LXX, Vulg., and B. Luth., by which indeed prosperity is designated, cf. ch. 13:9, ch. 24:20. However, the preposition ב seems to be understood, in light or prosperity) of the wicked is sin.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. Adhuc de Regibus. De modo ditescendi. De perversis & impiis, & imprimis judicibus injustis: de insipientia, ac superbia: illiusque malis: & sapientis commodis.

Vers. 1.

SICVT DIVISIONES AQVARVM, ITA COR REGIS IN MANV DOMINI, QVOCVNQVE VOLUERIT INCLINABIT ILLUD) Assyriam sententiam hanc vocat Themistius. Notant Hebræi non de communiore illa providentia, quæ ad omnes homines pertinet, hic agi, sed de specialiore illa, qua regum & bonorum & malorum cogitata ita dirigit, ut eis utatur ad eos, quos sibi proposuit eventus. Vide Jer. c. 10. circa finem. Similitudo ab agricola sumta, qui rivos per prata quo vult ducit.

INEbr. velut rivuli aquarum. Cor regis spectatum ratione operationum, & affectuum animæ, ceu sunt cogitare, velle, amare, odisse, in potestate Domini, qui id æque dirigit, ac coloni, vel hortulani rivulos aquarum per canales in agros, vel hortos derivare solent. LXX. ad Deum referunt: q. d. sicut Deus flumina, ut Nilum, derivat per rivos in certas terræ partes &c. V. Esdr. 7, 28. c. 9, 9. Nehem. 2, 8. Psal.

33, 15. Apoc. 17, 17. Non autem hæc trahenda cum Calvinianis ad fatalem necessitatem, aut ad inclinationes cordis ad malum: Aliud enim est cor inclinare, aliud necessitare: & illud ad omne, quod vult, non comprehendit, sed excludit mala: Deus enim non vult, ac ne potest quidem velle mala culpæ. Psal. 5, 5. Deut. 32, 4. 1. Job. 1, 5. Jac. 1, 13. Jam quod in genere c. 16, 2. de hominibus quibusvis dixerat, hic speciatim adhibet & applicat Regibus: Vers. 2. Omnis via viri recta est in oculis ejus, (adeoq; id contingit etiam in personis purpura coruscantibus) ponderat autem Dominus corda: unde peculiariter Reges monet, ut justitiam & judicium faciant: v. 3. facere justitiam & judicium magis electum est Domino, quam sacrificium. Hoc enim regum proprium est 2. Sam. 15, 15. 1. Reg. 10, 9. 1. Chron. 18, 14. Jer. 22, 3. Eccl. 1, 5. 7. Quod explicat Philippus: facere justitiam est probare probanda: facere judicium est judicare damnanda. Similiter speciatim regibus hic commendari humilitatem, non abs re fortassis dicitur, etsi generalis sensus non excludatur, sed ob applicationem, vi dicti de omni & nullo necessarius sit, v. 4. exaltatio (elatio) oculorum & latitudo cordis, cum cor præ fastu nimiaque confidentia ob statum florentem nimiopere quis dilatat, lucerna (ita enim vox Ebr. frequenter accipitur 1. Reg. 11, 36. c. 14, 4. 2. Reg. 8, 19. 2. Par. 21, 7. & de Lucerna a Chald. Elia Levita, LXX. Vulg. & B. Luth. explicatur, qua vero prosperitas designatur, conf. c. 13, 9. c. 24, 20. Subintelligenda autem videtur præpositio ב in luce vel prosperitate) impiorum peccatum sunt.

## 21:5
V. 5. THE THOUGHTS OF THE DILIGENT ARE ALWAYS IN ABUNDANCE: BUT EVERY SLUGGARD IS IN WANT.

In place of 'diligent' in the Hebrew is 'industrious', and in place of 'sluggard' is 'hasty'. He who diligently performs the works of his calling, to him there will be abundance, from the divine blessing.

He who hastens too much, and wishes to grow rich at once and all at once, and is not so eager to do his duty as to scrape together wealth, this man will hinder himself, and instead of abundance will gain lack (conf. c. 10,4. c. 12,24. c. 13, 4.) v. 6. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue (is) a vanity tossed to and fro (or like smoke dissipated Ps. 68, 3. Job. 13, 15.) of them that seek death: for while they solicitously seek riches, they seek their own destruction 1. Tim. 6, 9.

Latin:

V. 5. COGITATIONES ROBUSTI SEMPER IN ABUNDANTIA: OMNIS AUTEM PIGER IN EGESTATE EST.

Loco robusti in Ebræo sedulus, & loco pigri festinans est. Qui sedulo facit opera vocationis suæ, huic supererit, ex benedictione divina.

qui nimium festinat, & vult simul & semel ditescere, neque tam studet officium suum facere, quam opes corradere, hic seipsum impediet, & pro abundantia defectum lucrabiur (conf. c. 10,4. c. 12,24. c. 13, 4.) v. 6. opus thesaurom in lingua mendacii (est) vanitas propulsata (vel instar fumi dissipati Ps. 68, 3. Job. 13, 15.) quærentium mortem: dum enim solicite divitias quærunt, suum ipsorummet quærunt exitium 1. Tim. 6, 9.

## 21:7
Vers. 7.

THE RAPINE OF THE WICKED SHALL DRAG THEM AWAY: BECAUSE THEY REFUSED TO DO JUDGMENT.

Warnings are given concerning the wicked (1) Those who devastate others: v. 7. The devastation (the rapine by which they devastate others) of the wicked shall terrify them: (there shall be continual consternation for them) because they refuse to do judgment, which is a persistent rejection of what is equitable and just. Isa. 56, 1. c. 58, 2. (2) Those who are perverse v. 8. The way of a man who is perverse is strange (far from God and the Church, truly profane, according to that saying, let him be to you as a Gentile Matth. 18, 17.) but the work of the pure (man) is right. (3) Particularly concerning a quarrelsome woman v. 9. Because quarrelsomeness is more of women than of men. It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a contentious woman and in a wide house. Mention is made of the corner of the roof, because in Palestine, where the roofs were flat, they were accustomed to sleep, 2. Sam. 11, 2, cap. 16, 22. (4.) concerning those who are devoid of charity: v. 10. The soul of the wicked desires evil: his neighbor is not favored in his eyes. Matth. 7, 12. (5.) concerning scoffers v. 11. when (one) punishes (or chastises) a scoffer, the simple becomes wise: and when they instruct a wise man, he receives knowledge. The scoffer needs punishment: the wise man, if still subject to weaknesses, only instruction. The Vulgate version introduces something else here: When the pestilent man is punished, the little one will be wiser: and if he follows the wise man, he will receive knowledge: especially in the following verse.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

RAPINÆ IMPIORUM DETRAHENT EOS: QUI NOLUERUNT FACERE JUDICIUM.

De impiis monita traduntur (1) Qui alios va- stant: v. 7. Vastitas (rapina, qua alios vastant) im- piorum terrebit eos: (continua ipsis erit consterna- tio) quia renuunt facere judicium, quæ pertinax est æqui & justi excussio. Efa. 56, 1. c. 58, 2. (2) Qui perversi sunt v. 8. Perversus via vir alienus est (procul a Deo & Ecclesia, vere prophanus, juxta illud, sit tibi velut Ethnicus Matth. 18, 17.) mundi autem (viri) rectum est opus. (3) Peculiariter de muliere rixosa v. 9. Quia rixositas mulierum potius est, quam virorum. Melius est habitare in angulo tecti, quam cum muliere contentiosa & in domo ampla. Anguli tecti mentio fit, quia in tectis, quæ erant plana, dor- mire consueverant in Palæstina, 2. Sam. 11,2, cap. 16, 22. (4.) de his, qui charitatis expertes sunt: v. 10. Anima impii desiderat malum: non est gratus in oculis ejus amicus ejus. Matth. 7, 12. (5.) de derisoribus v. 11. cum (quis) mulctat (vel punit) derisorem, simplex efficitur sapiens: & cum instituunt sapientem, accipit scientiam. Derisor indiget pœna: Sapiens si adhuc imbecillitatibus obnoxius, solum informatione. Aliena hic ingerit Vulgata versio: Mulctato pesti- lente sapientior erit parvulus: & si sectetur sapientem, sumet scientiam: imprimis versu sequente.

## 21:12
verse 12.

THE RIGHTEOUS MAN CONSIDERS THE HOUSE OF THE WICKED: THAT HE MAY DRAW THE WICKED AWAY FROM EVIL.

In the Hebrew it is held far otherwise; The righteous man conducts himself wisely, as to the house of the wicked: but the wicked (each one of the wicked) subverts (devises overthrows and damages) to evil. Which sense B. Luther and Osiander express. Concerning judges or Magistrates he now delivers some things, namely that unjust judges pervert all things. The righteous Magistrate, says Osiander: prudently treats the family of the wicked, lest on account of the wickedness of the head of the household he destroy those who are good in his posterity, or at least curable. But the wicked apply themselves solely to this, that they turn all things (without distinction of persons) upside down, and spare no one. (2.) That they neglect the poor v. 13. He who shuts his ear to the cry of the poor, he himself also shall cry, and shall not be heard. It is the duty of judges and Magistrates to hear the cry of the poor Job 31, 16. Isa. 1, 17. Jer. 22, 3. Isa. 58, 9. Jas. 2, 13. (3.) That they regard gifts in judgment. Ver. 14. A HIDDEN GIFT EXTINGUISHES (calms) ANGER, AND A GIFT IN THE BOSOM THE GREATEST INDIGNATION. But on the contrary, the joy of the righteous is to do judgment. and terror (to cause or to cast) to those who work iniquity v. 15. Cf. Osiander's paraphrase.

Latin:

versus 12.

EXCOGITAT JUSTUS DE DOMO IM- PII: UT DETRAHAT IMPIOS A MALO.

In Ebr. longe aliter habetur; Sapienter se gerit justus, qua domum impii: at impii (unusquisque im- piorum) subvertit (eversiones ac damna machina- tur) ad malum. Quem sensum B. Luther. & Ofian- der exprimunt. De judicibus vel Magistratibus jam nonnulla tradit, quod nempe omnia pervertant ini- qui judices. Magistratus justus, ait Osiander: pru- denter tractat familiam impii, ne propter Patrisfami- lias improbitatem perdat eos, qui in ipsius posteritate sunt boni, aut certe sanabiles. Impii vero in id unice incumbunt, ut omnia (sine personarum discrimine) sur- sum deorsumque vertant, & nemini parcant. (2.) Quod pauperes negligant v. 13. Qui claudit aurem suam ad clamorem pauperis, etiam ipse clamabit, & non exaudietur. Judicum & Magistratuum est paupe- ris clamorem audire Job. 31, 16. Efa. 1, 17. Jerem. 22, 3. Efa. 58, 9. Jac. 2, 13. (3.) Quod munera respiciant in judicio. Vers. 14. MUNUS ABSCONDI- TUM EXTINGUIT (sedat) IRAS, ET DONUM IN SINU INDIGNATIONEM MAXIMAM. At ex adverso gaudium justorum est facere judicium. & pavorem (facere vel immittere) operantibus iniqui- tatem v. 15. Conf. Osiandrina paraphrasis.

## 21:16
ver. 16.

THE MAN, WHO HAS WANDERED FROM THE WAY OF DOCTRINE SHALL DWELL IN THE ASSEMBLY OF GIANTS.

He treats of the foolish, who wander from the way of understanding, having left the word of God to follow their own desires, because namely (1) they rest in the assembly of the dead (i.e., the damned), by the word רפאים not giants, but dead are here designated by רפה, he failed. (For the letters א & ה are εὐμετάβολοι [easily changeable]) because in them every vital power fails. Cf. chap. 2, 18. (2) That those who indulge in pleasures cast themselves into poverty, v. 17. He will be a man of poverty who loves joy (cf. c. 6, 11. c. 14, 23. c. 21, 5.) who loves wine & oil, fat and delicate foods, Ezek. 16, 13. or even balsam, or fragrant oil, with which the Israelites used to anoint the heads of those dining, Psalm 23, 5. and made the skin shiny, Ps. 104, 15. Cf. Prov.

7, 17. Eccles. 7, 1. chap. 9, 8. (3) That the wicked are to be given for the righteous in public calamities, so that when these are snatched away, those must perish: The wicked (will be) a ransom for the righteous & the transgressor (will be) in the place of the upright, v. 18. Cf. 2 Sam. 21.

(4) Solomon seems to indicate evils even domestic for the foolish: such as a house full of contention, and the dissipation of goods, v. 19. It is better to dwell in a desert land (even if horrid and vast) than (in a house ample and furnished with equipment) with a contentious and angry woman: For in this respect, because such wives easily fall to the foolish, as they are accustomed to seek those furnished with riches and immovable goods and soft things, rather than those pious and well-educated, this proverb seems to be repeated in this place, so that those about to take wives may learn to shop more cautiously, especially since this evil is no less grave than it is frequent (cf. v. 9. & c. 19, 13. c. 25, 24. c. 27, 15.) And v. 20. A desirable treasure and oil is in the dwelling of the wise, (who diligently performs the works of his calling, not only can he acquire necessary things by divine blessing, but also those things which can serve for honest recreation, indicated by oil, the granting of which is placed even among the chief benefits of God, Deut. 7, 13. c. 11, 14. Hos. 2, 22.) but the foolish man will dissipate (or rather devour) it, he will absorb it by gluttony and other ways.

It is added v. 21. concerning the wise man following justice and mercy: He who follows justice (in giving to each those things which we owe) and mercy (in bestowing upon the wretched especially those duties which are not owed) will find life, justice, and glory. Cf. c. 12, 28. c. 3, 16. 36. c. 8, 18. He finds, that is, he obtains not by merit, but as a gratuitous reward. And the wise man is commended not only for all-encompassing happiness, but also for the excellence of his strength, v. 22. The wise man will ascend into the city of the mighty, and casts down the strength of its confidence. Cf. 1 Sam. 14, 1. 2 Sam. 20, 22. Eccl. 9, 14. Furthermore, because the foolish do not know how to moderate their tongue, which the wise truly guard holily, Ps. 39, 2. the wisest of Kings adds v. 23. WHO GUARDS HIS MOUTH, AND HIS TONGUE, GUARDS HIS SOUL FROM DISTRESS. Which Aben-Ezra and Lyranus wrongly take concerning gluttony and drunkenness: since they treat of speech, so that the mouth may be guarded, lest it betray a secret, lest it defame someone, lest it lie, lest it bear false witness, lest it perjure itself, lest it blaspheme, etc. Put a bridle on your door, and you will not fear your enemies, has the Arabic proverb Cent. I. n. 37.

And because folly and pride are very closely related, Solomon now warns specifically about the proud in verse 24: the proud and arrogant man, scoffer is his name (empæcta, who is led by no love of religion or honesty, ch. 1, v. 22; ch. 3, 34; ch. 9, 7; ch. 8, 12; ch. 13, 1; ch. 15, 12; ch. 19, 25, 29; ch. 22, 10; ch. 24, 9; ch. 29, 8; 2 Pet. 3, 3. The Vulgate did not render it well, he is called unlearned) acting (his deeds or works) in the wrath of pride. Aben-Ezra explains it thus: the proud and arrogant man shall be allotted the name of scoffer, because in his wrath he will exceed the limits of modesty, charity, and justice, and will break out into insulting words and deeds, and injury to others. Cf. Sir. 10, 7. The proud mind, says Evagrius, is an inn for thieves.

Latin:

vers. 16.

VIR, QUI ABERRAVIT A VIA DOCTRI- NÆ IN CŒTU GIGANTIUM COMMORA- BITUR.

De insipientibus agit, qui a via intelligentiæ ab- errant, relicto Dei verbo suas sectati cupiditates, quod scil. (1) in cœtu mortuorum (sc. damnatorum) requiescant, Voce רפאים non gigantes, sed mortui hic designantur a רפה defecit. (Nam literæ א & ה sunt εὐμετάβολοι) quia in illis omnis virtus vitalis deficit. Conf. cap. 2, 18. (2) Quod illi, qui voluptatibus indulgent, in egestatem se præcipitent vers. 17. Vir egestatis erit, qui diligit lætitiam (conf. c. 6, 11. c. 14, 23. c. 21, 5.) qui diligit vinum & oleum, cibos pingues & delicatos, Ezech. 16, 13. vel etiam balsamum, aut oleum fragrans, quibus perfundebant Israëlitæ capita cœnantium Psalm. 23, 5. & nitidam efficiebant cutem Pf. 104, 15. Conf. Prov.

7, 17. Eccles. 7, 1. cap. 9, 8. (3) Quod impii pro justis dandi sint in publicis calamitatibus, ut his ereptis illis pereundum sit: Redemtio justi impius (erit) & loco rectorum (erit) prævaricator v. 18. Conf. 2. Sam. 21.

(4) Insipientibus mala etiam domestica indicare videtur Salomo: utpote domum contentione plenam, & dissipationem bonorum, v. 19. Melius est habitare in terra deserti (etsi horridi ac vasti) quam (in domo ampla, & apparatu instructa) cum muliere contentiosa & iracunda: Hoc enim respectu, quod tales insipientibus facile obtingant conjuges, utpote qui divitiis, & bonis immobilibus, ac mollibus instructas magis, quam pias probeque educatas ambire solent, repeti videtur hoc loco paræmia, ut uxores ducturi cautius mercari discant, maxime quum malum hoc non minus grave, quam frequens sit (conf. v. 9. & c. 19, 13. c. 25, 24. c. 27, 15.) Et v. 20. Thesaurus desiderabilis & oleum est in habitaculo sapientis, (qui sedulo opera vocationis peragit, non modo necessaria benedictione divina acquirere potest, sed ea etiam quæ honestæ recreationi inservire queant per oleum indicata, cujus concessio etiam inter præcipua Dei beneficia collocatur Deut. 7, 13. c. 11, 14. Hos. 2, 22.) at stultus homo dissipabit (vel potius devorabit) illud, helluationibus aliisque modis absorbebit.

Additur v. 21. de sapiente justitiam & misericordiam sectante: Qui sectatur justitiam (in tribuendis cuique illis, quæ debemus) & misericordiam (in conferendis misero potissimum officiis indebitis) inveniet vitam, justitiam & gloriam. Conf. c. 12, 28. c. 3, 16. 36. c. 8, 18. Invenit, id est, consequitur non ex merito, sed ut præmium gratuitum. Nec tantum a felicitate omnigena, sed etiam a roboris præcellentia commendatur sapiens, v. 22. In civitatem fortium ascendet sapiens, & dejicit robur fiduciæ ejus. Conf. 1. Sam. 14, 1. 2. Sam. 20, 22. Eccl. 9, 14. Porro quia insipientes nesciunt moderari linguam suam, quam vero sancte custodiunt sapientes Psal. 39, 2. subjungit Regum sapientissimus v. 23. QUI CUSTODIT OS SUUM, ET LINGUAM SUAM, CUSTODIT AB ANGUSTIIS ANIMAM SUAM. Quæ de gula & crapula perperam Aben-Ezra & Lyranus accipiunt: quum de sermone agant, ut os custodiatur, ne prodat secretum, ne quem infamet, ne mentiatur, ne falsum testetur, ne pejeret, ne blasphemet &c. Appone januæ tuæ frenum, & non timebis inimicos tuos, habet proverbium Arabicum Cent. I. n. 37.

Et quia stultitia & superbia valde cognata sunt, de superbis jam peculiariter monet Salomo vers. 24. superbus arrogans, derisor est nomen ejus (empæcta, qui nullo religionis vel honestatis amore ducitur, cap. 1. v. 22. cap. 3, 34. cap. 9, 7. cap. 8, 12, cap. 13, 1. cap. 15, 12. cap. 19, 25. 29. cap. 22, 10. cap. 24, 9. cap. 29, 8. 2. Petr. 3, 3. Vulgat. non bene reddidit, vocatur indoctus) faciens (facta vel opera sua) in ira superbiæ. Aben-Ezra ita exponit: superbus arrogans derisoris appellationem sortietur, quia in ira excedet limites modestiæ, charitatis & justitiæ, ac prorumpet in verba, & facta contumeliosa, aliisque injuria. Conf. Syr. 10, 7. Super- biæ, bus animus, inquit Evagrius, diversorium est latro- num.

## 21:25
Verse 25.

THE DESIRES OF THE SLUGGARD KILL HIM: FOR HIS HANDS REFUSED TO WORK. ALL THE DAY HE COVETS AND DESIRES: BUT THE RIGHTEOUS MAN GIVES AND WILL NOT CEASE) The sluggard desires to have and does not have, because he does not want to work. The Hebrews not inappropriately apply this to those who want to know, but do not want to apply the diligence required for learning.

Furthermore, because idleness is the pillow of Satan, and as St. Bernard says to the Brothers of the Mount of God, idleness is the sewer of all temptations and evil and useless thoughts: idle sloth is the greatest malice of the mind: Therefore Solomon here opposes the sluggard to the righteous man, and dissuades him from idleness and sloth, v. 25. The desire, he says, of the sluggard kills him, (both by tormenting him, because he always desires, but does not work, so that his desires may be fulfilled. Cf. Luther's marginal gloss and ch. 13, 4; Sir. 14, 9; and by accelerating death, since the sluggard does not find the means to sustain himself, 2 Thess. 3, 12.) because his hands refused to do anything: And v. 26. There is one who all the day covets with covetousness (but attains nothing, his covetousness remains naked and empty, so that he does not obtain those things which he might enjoy himself, let alone what he might distribute to others) but the righteous man (not only acquires by his labors, with which he sustains himself, but also to the poor) gives, and does not withhold (he does not deny those things which it is fitting to give, whether to those of his household or to strangers) Cf. Ps. 37, 25, 26; Eph. 4, 28; 1 Thess. 4, 6; 2 Thess. 3, 10 ff.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

DESIDERIA OCCIDVNT PIGRVM: NOLVERVNT ENIM QVICQVAM MANVS EJVS OPERARI. TO- TA DIE CONCVPISCIT ET DESIDERAT: QVI AVTEM JVSTVS EST TRIBVET ET NON CESSA- BIT) Cupit habere & non habet piger, quia laborare non vult. Hebræi non male aptant eis, qui scire volunt, nolunt autem diligentiam adhibere ad discendum requisitam.

Ulterius quia otium pulvinar Satanæ est, & ut S. Bernhard. ad Fratr. de monte Dei ait, omnium tentationum & cogitationum malarum & inutilium sentina otium est: summa mentis malitia est otium iners: Idcirco opponit hic Salomo pigrum justo, ac dehortatur illum ab otio & segnitie v. 25. Deside- rium, inquit, pigri interficit eum, (tum excruciando ipsum, quia semper desiderat, non vero laborat, ut desideria impleantur. Conf. Lutheri glossa mar- gin. & c. 13, 4. Sir. 14, 9. tum mortem accelerando, quum non inveniat piger, unde viam sustentet 2. Thess. 3, 12.) quia renuerunt manus ejus facere quic- quam: Et v. 26. Est, qui tota die concupiscit concupi- scentiam (sed nihil consequitur, nuda tantum & ina- nis manet concupiscentia ejusdem, ut nec ea quibus ipse fruatur, obtineat, nedum quæ aliis eroget) justus autem (non modo laboribus suis acquirit, quibus se sustentet, sed pauperibus etiam) tribuit, nec cohibet (non denegat ea, quæ dari convenit seu domesticis seu extraneis) Conf. Ps. 37, 25. 26. Eph. 4, 28. 1. Thess. 4, 6. 2. Thess. 3, 10. seqq.

## 21:27
Verse 27.

THE SACRIFICES OF THE WICKED ARE ABOMINABLE, WHICH ARE OFFERED OUT OF WICKEDNESS.

To the evils which the folly of the wicked brings with it, it also pertains that their religious worship is a mere abomination before God. The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination (cf. ch. 15, 8.) כִּי בְזִמָּה in that (according to Schindler in Voc. זִמָּה. See Job 35, 14; Ez. 23, 4; Hab. 2, 1, as in this place also that particle the LXX, Aquila, and B. Luther have rendered) in wickedness (or iniquity) he brings it.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

HOSTIÆ IMPIORUM ABOMINABILES, QUÆ OFFERUNTUR EX SCELERE.

Ad mala, quæ secum fert insipientia impiorum id etiam pertinet, quod cultus ipsorum religiosus mera sit coram Deo abominatio. Sacrificium im- piorum abominatio est (conf. c. 15, 8.) כִּי בְזִמָּה eo quod (juxta Schindl. in Voc. זִמָּה. Vid. Job. 35, 14. Ez. 23, 4. Hab. 2, 1. ut h. l. etiam particulam illam LXX. Aquila, B. Luther. reddidere) in scelere (vel nequi- tia) adducit illud.

## 21:28
Verse 28.

A LYING WITNESS SHALL PERISH: AN OBEDIENT MAN SHALL SPEAK OF VICTORY.

In the Hebrew: But the man who hears, namely what is testified, and always speaks, (not only shall he not perish, but he shall always be admitted, so that he may speak both publicly and privately without shame, with credibility and good reputation) cf. James 3:1 seqq. He treats specifically of the foolish and wicked witness, because very many such are found.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

TESTIS MENDAX PERIBIT: VIR OBE- DIENS LOQUETUR VICTORIAM.

In Ebræo: At vir, qui audit, quæ scil. testatur, & semper loquitur, (non modo non peribit, sed semper admittetur, ut scil. tum publice, tum privatim lo- quatur citra pudefactionem, cum fide, & bona exi- stimatione) conf. Jac. 3, 1. seqq. Speciatim de teste insipiente, & improbo agit, quia plurimi tales inveniuntur.

## 21:29
Verse 29.

A WICKED MAN BOLDLY HARDENS HIS FACE: BUT HE WHO IS UPRIGHT, CORRECTS HIS WAY.

The former proceeds impudently and stubbornly, perseveres contumaciously in error or sin, and does not strive to correct his way; the latter, however, arranges all things cautiously and prudently, so that he may undertake or plot nothing against God, nothing against his neighbor, and if he has strayed or sinned anywhere, he allows himself to be warned and corrects his error. Cf. Isa. 8:9. Jer. 5:3. For there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord v. 30. In the Hebrew אֵין there is nothing. Cf. Job 5:12, 13. Ps. 21:12. Ps. 33:10. Isa. 8:10. Luke 1:51. But as wisdom is invincible and incomparable, so also from God alone is all salvation, power, and victory, and that again in comparison to human defenses, v. 21. The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the salvation itself is of the Lord. Cf. 1 Sam. 11, 9. 13. ch. 19, 5. 2 Sam. 19, 3. 1 Chron. 29, 11. 1 Macc. 15, 21. Ps. 3, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

VIR IMPIUS PROCACITER OBFIRMAT VULTUM SUUM: QUI AUTEM RECTUS EST, CORRIGIT VIAM SUAM.

Ille impudenter & præfracte pergit, in errore aut peccato contumaciter perseverat, nec viam suam corrigere studet, hic vero caute, ac prudenter cuncta instituit, ut nihil contra Deum, nihil contra proximum suscipiat, vel moliatur, ac si alicubi ab- erravit, aut deliquit, moneri se patitur, & erratum corrigit. Conf. Esa. 8, 9. Jerem. 5, 3. Non enim est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium con- tra Dominum v. 30. In Ebr. אֵין nihil est. Conf. Job. 5, 12. 13. Psal. 21, 12. Ps. 33, 10. Esa. 8, 10. Luc. 1, 51. Ut autem invicta est, & incomparabilis sapientia, ita etiam a Deo solo omnis est salus, virtus, ac vi- ctoria, idque rursus in comparatione ad præsidia humana, v. 21. Equus paratus est ad diem belli, sed Domini est ipsa salus. Conf. 1. Sam. 11, 9. 13. c. 19, 5. 2. Sam. 19, 3. 1. Par. 29, 11. 1. Macc. 15, 21. Ps. 3, 9.

## 22:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXII.

On good reputation, and riches, with rules to be observed by those studious of a good reputation and by the wealthy.

Verse 1.

A GOOD NAME IS BETTER THAN MUCH RICHES: FOR GOOD GRACE IS ABOVE SILVER AND GOLD] A good name is a good reputation. Eccl. 7, 1. Ovid. If you lose everything, remember to preserve your reputation.

Latin:

CAPUT XXII.

De bona fama, & divitiis, cum regulis bonæ famæ studiosis & divitibus observandis.

Vers. 1.

MELIUS EST NOMEN BONUM, QUAM DIVI- TIÆ MULTÆ: SUPER ARGENTUM ENIM ET AU- RUM EST GRATIA BONA] Bonum nomen est bona fama. Eccl 7, 1. Ovid. Omnia si perdas famam servare memento.

## 22:2
Verse 2.

THE RICH AND THE POOR HAVE MET TOGETHER) They are useful to one another

And yet the small without the great are a shaky defense for a tower; for the small are best with the great, and the great are upheld by the small; but it is not possible to teach the foolish the judgment of these things. says Sophocles in Ajax.

In the former member it is held simply in the Hebrew as NAME, but it is taken by way of eminence for a good name, or from the latter member it is mentioned with GOOD grace, it must be supplied: A good reputation, and the benevolence of good men, which is its companion, is to be preferred far above riches or gold and silver. Cf. Sir. 41, 15. But so that no one may be anxious on account of poverty, or exalt himself on account of riches, but rather that all may have regard for a good name, Solomon adds that it has been so disposed by God, who most wisely orders all things, that the rich and the poor meet together, and that not all are rich, nor all poor, v. 2. The rich and the poor have met together: the Lord is the maker of them all. Cf. ch. 10, 22. ch. 14, 31. ch. 17, 5. ch. 30, 8. Sir. 11, 14. The rich man, says Augustine, sermon 25 on the Words of the Lord, was made for the sake of the poor man, and the poor man was made for the sake of the rich man. It is for the poor man to pray,

and for the rich to distribute. But because a good reputation and grace are acquired by prudence and virtue, Solomon treated here of prudence no less than of the fear of the Lord and humility v. 3. The prudent man sees the evil, and hides himself (so that he may avoid it) but the simple pass on

and are fined (or afflicted.) c. 14, 15. And v. 4. The reward of humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and glory and life, c. 15, 33. c. 18, 12. If therefore anyone wishes to grow rich, let him study piety and humility. On the contrary, however, thorns, which follow in v. 5, and snares are in the way of the perverse (c. 4, 19. c. 15, 9.) he who guards his soul will distance himself from them, that is, he who cares more for true and solid salvation than for the pleasures of the world c. 19, 16. c. 8, 36. c. 15, 32. And therefore Solomon warns v. 6. train a child according to his way, which, that is to say, is suitable for him, and which he ought to tread thereafter (the Vulgate ineptly prefixes: IT IS A PROVERB, about which there is nothing in the authentic text) Even when he has grown old, he will not depart from it. Theodoric, King of the Wise, in Cassiodorus, l. 1. Ep. 24, says: bring up your young men in martial discipline: for what is not learned in youth is not known in mature age. Jerome. Ep. 7, to Laeta, on the instruction of a daughter: it is difficult to eradicate what raw years have drunk in: who can recall the purple dyes of wool to their original whiteness? A fresh jar long retains both the flavor and the odor with which it was first imbued.

On the diverse lot of the rich and the poor v. 7. The rich man rules over the poor: and the borrower will be a servant to the lender. For a debtor is the chattel of the creditor. But since poverty and subjection do not in the least hinder a good name or favor before God and men, provided that iniquity and impiety are avoided, Solomon adds v. 8. He who sows iniquity will reap evils (or as Vatablus says, calamity) and he will perish by the rod of his anger. Which is the punishment of retaliation, as B. Luther rightly rendered, which Osiander explains: He who applies himself to this, that he may fulfill his carnal desires and perpetrate evils, he will not escape grave divine punishments, and while he prepares misfortune for others with a violent mind, he himself will perish in the same evil. Thus even the rich who rule over others are warned not to be iniquitous and to oppress others; but rather to exercise mercy and kindness. For as it is held in v. 9: A kind eye itself will be blessed, because he gave of his bread to the poor. Sir. 31, 28. c. 35, 21. 2 Cor. 9, 7. Rom. 12, 8. Because to him who gives, it will be given in turn by the Lord Luc. 6, 38. Where the Dative is excluded, the Ablative dominates. The Vulgate adds a related sentiment, but one which does not occur in the Hebrew, He will acquire victory and honor who gives gifts: but he will take away the soul of the recipients. The LXX, however, have added two other apophthegms of their own: God blesses a cheerful man and a giver: He has consumed the vanity of his works. He who has mercy on the poor is himself nourished in turn, as one who has shared his bread with the needy: but those are held neither in the Hebrew text, nor in the Vulgate, and other versions. To v. 7, Grotius says this:

Latin:

Vers. 2.

DIVES ET PAUPER OBVIAVERUNT SIBI) Utiles sunt alter alteri

Καί τοι σμικροὶ μεγάλων χωρὶς, Σφαλερὸν πύργε ῥῦμα πέλονται· Μετὰ γὰρ μεγάλων βαιὸς ἄρις ἂν, Καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ᾽ ὑπὸ μικρῶν· Ἀλλ᾽ οὐ δυνατὸν τοὺς ἀνοήτους Τούτων γνώμας προδιδάσκειν. ait Sophocles Ajace.

IN priori membro simpliciter habetur in Ebræo NOMEN, sed id ἐξοχικῶς pro nomine bono ac- cipitur, vel e membro posteriori cum gratia BONA commemoratur, supplendum est: Fama bona, & be- nevolentia bonorum, quæ illius comes est, longe præ- ferenda divitiis vel auro, & argento. Conf. Sir. 41, 15. Ne autem vel ob paupertatem quis solici- tus sit, vel ob divitias sese efferat, sed nominis boni rationem potius omnes habeant, addit Salomo, sic a Deo, qui sapientissime ordinat omnia, disposi- tum esse, ut dives & pauper sibi obvient, nec omnes divites sint, nec pauperes omnes, v. 2. Dives & pauper obviarunt sibi: faciens omnes ipsos Dominus (est.) Conf. cap. 10, 22. cap. 14, 31. cap. 17, 5. cap. 30, 8. Sir. 11, 14. Dives, inquit Augustin. serm. 25. de Verb. Dom. propter pauperem factus est, & pau- per propter divitem factus est. Pauperis est orare,

& divitiis erogare. Quia vero bona fama & gra- tia prudentia & virtute comparatur, de prudentia non minus, quam timore Domini, & humilitate hic egit Salomo v. 3. Prudens videt malum, & abscondit se (ut id evitet) imperiti autem transeunt

(secure) & mulctantur (vel affliguntur.) c. 14, 15. Et v. 4. Præmium humilitatis & timoris Domini divitiæ, & gloria & vita, c. 15, 33. c. 18, 12. Si ergo ditescere quis velit, pietati studeat, & humilitati. Ex ad- verso vero spinæ, quod v. 5. sequitur, & laquei sunt in via perversi (c. 4, 19. c. 15, 9.) qui custodit animam suam, elongabit se ab illis, hoc est, qui plus curat sa- lutem veram, & solidam, quam voluptates mundi c. 19, 16. c. 8, 36. c. 15, 32. Ideoque monet Salomo v. 6. imbue puerum juxta viam suam, quæ sc. illi con- venit, & quam calcare deinceps debet (vulgata in- eptè præmittit: PROVERBIUM EST, quo de nihil in textu authentico) Etiam quum senuerit, non recedet ab ea. Theodoricus Sophorum Rex apud Cassiodor. l. 1. Ep. 24. producite, inquit, juvenes ve- stros in Martiam disciplinam: nam quod in juventute non discitur, in matura ætate nescitur. Hieronym. Ep. 7, ad Lætan. de instit. filiæ: difficulter eraditur, quod rudes anni perbiberunt: lanarum conchylia quis in pristinum candorem revocet? recens testa diu & sapo- rem retinet, & odorem, quo primum imbuta est.

De diversa divitum & pauperum forte vers. 7. Dives pauperibus dominatur : & servus erit mutuum accipiens mutuanti. Debitor enim est creditoris mancipium. Quum vero paupertas, & subjectio nomini bono aut gratiæ coram Deo & hominibus minime officiant, modo vitetur iniquitas & impie- tas, subjungit Salomo v. 8. Qui seminat iniquita- tem, metat mala (vel ut Vatablus calamitatem) & in virga iræ suæ peribit. Quæ pœna talionis est, ut re- cte reddidit B. Lutherus, quod explicat Osiander : Qui in hoc incumbit, ut desideria sua carnalia impleat, & mala perpetret, is graves pœnas divinas non effugiet, & dum aliis animo violento infortunium parat, in eo- dem malo ipse peribit. Sic monentur etiam divites aliis dominantes, ne iniqui sint, aliosque oppri- mant; sed misericordiam potius & benignitatem exerceant. Nam ut v. 9. habetur: Benignus oculus ipse benedicetur, quia dedit de pane suo pauperi. Sir. 31, 28. c. 35, 21. 2. Cor. 9, 7. Rom. 12, 8. Quia ei qui dat, vicissim dabitur a Domino Luc. 6, 38. Ubi Da- tivus excluditur, Ablativus dominatur. Addit Vul- gata cognatam sententiam, sed quæ in Ebræo non occurrit, Victoriam & honorem acquiret, qui dat mu- nera : animam autem auferet accipientium. LXX. vero duo adhuc alia apophthegmata adjecerunt de suo: Virum hilarem & datorem benedicit Deus : Va- nitatem operum ejus consummavit. Qui miseretur pauperis ipse vicissim enutritur, ut qui egeno de pani- bus suis impertitus sit : sed illa nec in Ebræo haben- tur textu, nec in Vulgata, aliisque versionibus. Ad vers. 7. hæc Grotius:

## 22:7
HE WHO ACCEPTS A LOAN IS A SERVANT OF THE LENDER) As if a servant: for Δάνεια δούλυς τοὺς ἐλευθέρυς ποιεῖ. which the Mime translated thus: Another's debt is a bitter servitude to a free man.

In the Hebrew, and strife and ignominy will cease. To maintain a good reputation, communion with Lucianic scoffers is to be avoided, for whom it is a pleasure to mock the word of God and to delude men, which brings nothing but quarrels, strife, and reproaches. But with a good reputation is joined a pure conscience. Therefore, Solomon adds some things here about the purity of the heart v. 11. He who loves the cleanliness of the heart, his lips are grace (that is, remarkably gracious), (Eccl. 10, 12.) the King will be his friend. Cf. c. 16, 13. For Kings are delighted not by parasites, informers, and unclean and filthy gluttons, but by men of heart and noble character: as here Mr. Dr. Geier. There follows v. 12, concerning the grace of the Lord: since the cleanliness of the heart and sincerity renders one pleasing not only to Kings, but also to the Lord Himself, the King of Kings. The eyes of the Lord guard knowledge, and (the Lord) perverts the affairs of the transgressor. The Vulgate errs here, rendering the second member: and the words of the iniquitous are supplanted. The LXX also err, explaining: But the iniquitous man disparages words.

Furthermore, for preserving a good reputation and a pure conscience, it helps both to flee sloth and idleness, which according to Basil is the beginning of wickedness, about which v. 13. The sluggard says there is a lion outside: I shall be killed in the middle of the streets. A lazy man excuses himself, so that he cannot go out to work, affirming that I know not what dangers threaten him outside. For Judea had lions and other fierce beasts: and also to flee fornication v. 14. The mouth of strange women is a deep pit (for they deceive and seduce most of all with their mouth) he who is hated by the Lord will fall into it. The flatteries of harlots are like a deep pit, which is so covered that it is not noticed, until someone has fallen into it: by which they are deceived and ensnared, whom God hates, and wishes to punish with just judgment c. 7, 5. seqq. But because from childhood that foolishness clings to us, so that we are inclined toward contempt of laws, idleness, and base lust, it is added v. 15. foolishness is bound in the heart of a child (conf. Gen. 6, 5. c. 8, 21.) the rod of correction will make it depart from him (because it clings most tightly, the rod of correction is needed, so that it may be expelled from him) conf. c. 13, 24. c. 23, 23. Sir. 30, 1. 8. By anger and desires, says Chrysost., young men are more easily led and conquered: wherefore they require greater custody and a harder bridle.

tant, see 1 Kings 4, at the end. Those things which have been gathered into this book, and Ecclesiastes, pertain to Ethics: the books on fates and animals to Physics: the Song of Songs in an allegorical sense to Theology.

This division has nothing to do with the matter. For here Solomon refers to the present instruction: not indeed to the books which he wrote on Physics, or the Song of Songs. And what do Physics have to do with that end which he designated in v. 19, that your trust may be in Jehovah? What of those Ethics, which are distinguished from Theological matters, for which neither this book nor Ecclesiastes is intended? For they do not treat purely of morals, as is wont to be done in Ethics, but of true and solid Theology; therefore Solomon especially urges faith in God, and attributes blessedness to faith. Not much unlike the Grotian gloss is that of Bungus on the mystery of numbers, p. 163, concerning the triple wisdom: heavenly, moral, natural, and contemplative. Equally alien are the glosses of others, who understand the three Canonical books of Solomon: Proverbs for beginners, Ecclesiastes for those making progress, the Song for the perfect: as also those of the Hebrews, the Author of the Midrash, and R. Solomon, through the triple books of the Old Testament, the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, are thought to be designated: [those] of Origen and Jerome, who carve out a triple sense of Scripture from this: literal, allegorical, tropological: Finally, [those] of them who snatch these three away to words, deeds, and thoughts. Although indeed the Chaldean explains the word שלישים as תלת זמנין three times, and the LXX as τρισσῶς, as the Vulgate [does] tripliciter, yet that exposition does not admit a triple mode of teaching, or that three books are noted, since the Papist interpreters themselves explain it as 'in many ways' or 'manifoldly,' such as Eman. Saa, Tirinus, Menochius, in which way also B. Luther rendered it, mannichfältig. Furthermore, since in Hebrew the word שלישים is found with a Cametz, not שלישים (tertiani); and in the singular שליש is a great Leader or Prince, therefore others explain it more correctly: Have I not written to you great or principal things in counsels and knowledge; understanding the word דברי (words): Have I not written to you the words of Leaders, or Princes: that is, distinguished and excellent things, worthy of princes, which as κυρίας δόξας, nay, like leaders, can govern life, which are called נגידים, the words of princes or principal things, c. 8, 6. because they are chief and most excellent, and hold the principate among sentences, whence also משלים, parables, are named from the verb of ruling. Thus they explain from the Hebrews themselves, R. Levi Ben Gerson, R. David Kimchi, and R. Mardochai Nathan, as 'admirable and honorable.' Similarly Mercerus, Franc. Junius, B. Glaffius, and others. They are undoubtedly excellent, says Mercerus, and truly Royal, which Solomon taught in these proverbs: so that all orders of men, ages, and sexes may have [something] by which to form their life and compose their morals. Therefore, having reviewed the various opinions, 'To me,' he says, 'it pleases most that שלישים be explained as distinguished and excellent.'

Latin:

QVI ACCIPIT MVTVVM SERVVS EST FENE- RANTIS) Quasi servus : nam Δάνεια δούλυς τοὺς ἐλευθέρυς ποιεῖ. quod Mimus sic transtulit : Alienum æs homini ingenuo acerba servitus.

In Ebr. cessabitque lis, & ignominia. Ad bonam famam sustinendam vitanda communio cum deri- soribus Lucianis, quibus volupe est Dei verbum ir- ridere, & hominibus illudere, quæ nil nisi jurgia, li- tes, & opprobria affert. Cum fama autem bona conjuncta sit pura conscientia. Ideo de cordis pu- ritate hic nonnulla addit Salomo v. 11. Qui diligit munditiem cordis, gratia (id est insigniter gratiosa) sunt labia ejus, (Eccl. 10, 12.) amicus ejus erit Rex. Conf. c. 16, 13. Delectantur enim Reges non para- sitis, quadruplatoribus, immundisque ac spurcis lurconibus, sed viris cordatis ac ingenuis: ut hic Dn. D. Geierus. Sequitur v. 12. de gratia Domi- ni : siquidem mundities cordis, & sinceritas non Re- gibus tantum gratos reddit, sed etiam ipsimet Do- mino Regi Regum. Oculi Domini custodiunt scien- tiam, & pervertit (Dominus) res prævaricatoris. Aberrat hic Vulgatus, alterum membrum reddens: & supplantantur verba iniqui. Aberrant & LXX. exponentes : Vilipendit autem verba iniquus.

Porro ad bonam famam, & conscientiam pu- ram conservandam facit tum fuga socordiæ & otii, quod juxta Basilium est maleficii principium, de qua v. 13. Dicit piger leo est foris : in medio platearum occidar. Homo ignavus excusat se, quo minus ad labores exire possit, affirmans sibi foris imminere nescio quæ pericula. Judæa enim habebat leo- nes, aliasque truces belluas: tum etiam fuga forni- cationis vers. 14. Fovea profunda est os extranearum (ore enim maxime decipiunt, & seducunt) exosus Domino cadet illuc. Blanditiæ meretricum sunt instar profundæ foveæ, quæ ita contecta est, ut non animadvertatur, donec aliquis inciderit: quibus decipiuntur & irretiuntur, quos Deus odit, & justo judicio punire vult c. 7, 5. seqq. Quia vero a puero ea stultitia nobis adhæret, ut propenfi fimus in comtemtum legum, otium, & pravam libidinem, additur v. 15. stultitia colligata est in corde pueri (conf. Gen. 6, 5. c. 8, 21.) virga correctionis elongari faciet eam ab eo (quia arctissime adhæret, opus est virga correctionis, ut ab eo expellatur) conf. c. 13, 24. c. 23, 23. Sir. 30, 1. 8. Ira & cupiditatibus, inquit Chrysost. facilius juvenes ducuntur, & vincuntur: quare majorem custodiam requirunt, & frenum durius.

tant, vid. 1. Reg. 4. in fine. Quæ in hunc librum congesta sunt, & Ecclesiastes, ad Ethica pertinent: libri de fatis & animalibus ad Physica: Canticum Canticorum sensu allegorico ad Theologica.

Nihil hæc divisio ad rem facit. Respicit enim hic Salomo præsentem institutionem: non vero libros, quos scripsit in Physicis, aut Canticum Canticorum. Et quid Physica ad illum finem, quem designavit v. 19. ut sit in Jehovah fiducia tua? Quid Ethica illa, quæ a Theologicis distinguuntur, qualibus neque hic liber, neque Ecclesiastes destinatus est? Non enim pure moralia tractant, ut in Ethicis fieri amat, sed veram solidamque Theologiam, ideo præprimis urget Salomo fidem in Deum, ac beatitudinem fidei tribuit. Non multum abfimilis Grotianæ glossæ est illa Bungi de myster. numer. p. 163. de triplici sapientia cœlesti, morali, naturali, inspectiva. Æque alienæ sunt glossæ aliorum, qui tres libros Canonicos Salomonis intelligunt, Proverbia pro incipientibus, Ecclesiasten pro proficientibus, Canticum pro perfectis: ut & Ebræorum, Autoris Midrasch, & R. Salomonis, per triplices libros Vet. Testam. legem, Prophetas & Hagiographa, designari putant: Origenis & Hieronymi, qui triplicem Scripturæ sensum hinc exsculpunt, literalem, allegoricum, tropologicum: Denique eorum, qui ad dicta, facta, & cogitata hæc trina abripiunt. Quanquam vero Chaldæus vocem שלישים exponat תלת זמנין tribus vicibus, & LXX. τρισσῶς, uti vulgata tripliciter, non tamen admissa illa expositione triplex modus docendi, vel tres libri notantur, fiquidem ipsi Pontificii Interpp. explicent, multivarie, multipliciter, utpote Eman. Saa, Tirin. Menochius, quo pacto etiam B. Lutherus reddidit, mannichfältig. Cæterum cum in Ebræo vox שלישים cum Cametz habeatur, non שלישים tertiani: ac in singulari שליש sit magnus Dux vel Princeps, ideo rectius alii exponunt: Nonne scripsi tibi magna vel principalia in consiliis, & scientia; fubaudiendo דברי verba: Nonne scripsi tibi verba Ducum, vel Principum: hoc est insignia & præstantia, principibus digna, quæ tanquam κυρίας δόξας imo instar ducum gubernare possunt vitam, quæ נגידים principum verba vel principalia dicuntur c. 8, 6. quod præcipua sint ac præstantissima, & principatum inter sententias obtineant, unde etiam משלים parabolæ a verbo dominandi dictæ. Sic exponunt ex ipsis Ebræis, R. Levi Ben Gerson, R. David Kimchi, & R. Mardochai Nathan, per admiranda & honorabilia. Similiter Mercerus, Franc. Junius, B. Glaffius & alii. Sunt haud dubie eximia, inquit Mercerus, & vere Regia, quæ in his proverbiis docuit Salomon: uti omnes hominum ordines, ætates, sexus habeant, quo vitam forment, & mores componant. Ideo recensitis variis sententiis, Mihi, inquit, maxime placet שלישים insignia exponi, & eximia.

## 22:16
Vers. 16.

HE WHO OPPRESSES THE POOR TO INCREASE HIS RICHES) That is, oppresses by force. See Luke 3, 14. HE HIMSELF WILL GIVE TO THE RICHER AND WILL BE IN NEED) He will be forced to give. Expect from another what you have done to another. And in Seneca: Whatever the lesser fears from you, the greater master threatens you with this. In the Hebrew, v. 16 has it thus: He who suppresses the poor or takes from him, will give (by the just judgment of God, or will be forced to give, or will give willingly) to the rich, surely to poverty, seeking gain, but losing the whole sum) conf. Isa. 33, 1. Jer. 30, 16.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

QVI CALVMNIATVR PAVPEREM, VT AVGEAT DIVITIAS SVAS) Id est, vi opprimit. Vid. Luc. 3, 14. DABIT IPSE DITIORI ET EGEBIT) Cogetur dare. Ab alio exspectes, alteri quod feceris. Et apud Senecam: Quisquid a vobis minor extimescit, Major hoc vobis dominus minatur. In Ebr. v. 16. ita habet: Qui fupprimit pauperem vel aufert ab eo, dabit (justo Dei judicio, vel dare cogetur, vel dabit ultro) diviti, profecto ad egestatem, lucrum quærens, sed summam universam amittens) conf. Esa. 33, 1. Jerem. 30, 16.

## 22:17
vers. 17.

MY SON, INCLINE YOUR EAR, AND HEAR THE WORDS OF THE WISE: BUT APPLY YOUR HEART TO MY DOCTRINE.

Cornelius a Lapide says these were inserted to excite the readers, after he delivered wisdom in the manner of the ancients through short and grave gnomes in a long speech, and is about to deliver more in this way, as if to say: sharpen your ears, and apply them more closely, so that you may better hear and attend more to those things which I am about to say and teach. But since for acquiring a good reputation and preserving the purity of conscience there is need for the study of wisdom and virtue, the closer connection is in the open: incline your ear (that προσφώνησις, MY SON, does not appear in the Hebrew) and hear the words &c. that is, diligently and attentively hear those teaching you the wisdom of the Word of God, and admit that doctrine into your heart. v. 18. Because it is pleasant (or beautiful) if you keep them (the words) in your belly, that is, in the innermost recesses of your soul. Conf. c. 18, 8. c. 20, 27. 30. Job 15, 35. Job 7, 38. (if you keep them inside in your mind and outside) let them be directed equally (sc. not some things mutilated, but equally and fairly all things, as much those that pertain to God as those that pertain to men, as much those that pertain to the Polity as those that pertain to the Economy) on your lips, or in your speech. Whence the end of this wisdom is subjoined v. 19. that your trust may be in the Lord, I have made you know (these) today, even you, or you, I say. Conf. concerning this Hebraism Gen. 37, 34. Psalm 9, 7. Zech. 7, 5. By which name also Solomon commends his faithfulness in inculcating saving doctrine v. seq. 20 and 21. Have I not written to you three times in counsels and knowledge to answer the words of truth to those who send you (Vulg. to those who sent you) that is, as Osiander interprets, so that you may conduct yourself wisely in whatever business may have been committed to you.

Latin:

vers. 17.

FILI MI INCLINA AUREM TUAM, ET AUDI VERBA SAPIENTUM: APPONE AUTEM COR AD DOCTRINAM MEAM.

Cornelius a Lapide hæc inserferit ait ad excitandos lectores, postquam longa oratione sapientiam more veterum per breves, gravesque gnomas tradidit, ac porro ita traditurus est, q. d. aures acue, & propius adhibe, ut melius audias, magisque attendas iis, quæ dicturus, & docturus sum. Sed quum ad bonam famam comparandam & puritatem conscientiæ servandam sapientiæ & virtutis studio opus sit, συνέχεια propinquior in aprico est: inclina aurem tuam (προσφώνησις illa, FILI MI, in Ebræo non comparet) & audi verba &c. hoc est, diligenter & attente audi docentes te sapientiam Verbi Dei, & eam doctrinam in cor tuum admitte. v. 18. Quia jucundum (vel pulcrum) si custodieris ea (verba) in ventre tuo, id est, in intimis recessibus animæ tuæ. Conf. c. 18, 8. c. 20, 27. 30. Job. 15, 35. Job. 7, 38. (si intus servaveris ea in mente & foris) dirigantur pariter illa (sc. non mutilate nonnulla, sed pariter & ex æquo omnia, tam quæ ad Deum, quam quæ ad homines, tam quæ ad Politiam, quam quæ ad Oeconomiam spectant) in labiis tuis, vel sermone tuo.
