Unde finis sapientiæ hujus subjungitur v. 19. ut sit in Domino fiducia tua, scire te feci (hæc) hodie, etiam te, vel te, inquam. Conf. de hoc Ebraismo Gen. 37, 34. Psalm. 9, 7. Zach. 7, 5. Quo etiam nomine suam fidelitatem in inculcanda doctrina salutari commendat Salomo v. feq. 20. & 21. Nonne scripsi tibi ter in consiliis & scientia ad respondendum eloquia veritatis mittentibus te (Vulgat. illis, qui miserunt te) hoc est interprete Osiandro, ut sapienter te gerere possis in quocunque negotio, quod tibi commissum fuerit.

## 22:20
Vers. 20.

BEHOLD, I HAVE DESCRIBED IT TRIPLE-FOLD) Wisdom among the Hebrews is divided into משלים, into בושים, into מרכבה, which in Greek you would call εἰς ἠθικα, φυσικὰ, θεολογικὰ; concerning all these Solomon wrote very many things, which now not ex-

crush the wretched at the gate (that is, in judgment. Deut. 21, 19. Amos 5, 15. Zach. 8, 16. Job 5, 4.) because the Lord will judge their cause, and will snatch them from those who snatch them by the punishment of retaliation, compare Is. 33, 1.

(2) Concerning familiarity with an irascible person, v. 24. Do not become a friend with a master of anger (an irascible person) and do not go with a man of fury (a furious person). v. 25. Lest perhaps you learn his paths, and receive a snare into your soul, and be ensnared by his traps. Compare Prov. 1, 15. ch. 11, 9. ch. 13, 20. Sir. 13, 1. 1 Cor. 15, 33. Prov. 29, 6. There are certain vices, says the author of the book on friendship, Tom. 4 of the works of Augustine, by which if anyone is entangled, he will not long observe the laws or rights of friendship: for those who are overly irascible, unstable, suspicious, and talkative are not suitable for friendship. It is difficult for him whom the fury of anger often agitates not to rise up against a friend at some time.

(3) Concerning rash suretyship v. 26. Do not be among those striking the hand (clapping with the hand, that is, by giving surety; for those who pledge are usually forced to pay the debt in the end. The exegesis subjoined teaches this meaning.) Nor among those giving surety for debts v. 27. If you do not have wherewith to pay (which words seem to introduce a condition, unless, that is, you have an abundance from which you can free your pledge, or if you prefer a reason taken from the inconvenience;) Why should your bed be snatched away from you, which is under you? i.e., what reason is there for you to throw yourself into this danger, so that a creditor, because of another's debts, might take away even your bed, or those things which are most necessary to you? which, even if it is contrary to the rule of charity and the divine law, Ex. 22, 26. 27. Deut. 24, 12. 13. Ex. 18, 7. 12. yet it often happens in fact.

(4) Concerning not moving ancient boundaries. Which the rich and those powerful in force not rarely attempt. Do not transgress (in Hebrew, do not transfer) the ancient boundaries, which your fathers have set. Osiander explains: Do not tear down those things which have been piously, rightly, and wisely established by your ancestors. Others speak of preserving the boundaries of immovable goods, and in general of the pursuit of justice, so that to each his own may be left. Eccl. 10, 9. These explanations can be joined if you take it concerning any boundaries whatsoever established by ancestors, whether of arts, or of polity, or of lands and other immovable goods, and from here gather the genus from the species of immovable goods, so that this rule may be extended to other goods as well. Compare Deut. 19, 14. Jerome in Hos. 5, 10. Princes transfer the boundaries which their fathers have set, when they change the truth into a lie, and preach something other than what they received from the Apostles.

(5) Finally, concerning alacrity in performing our parts v. 29. Have you seen a man swift in his work? he will stand before Kings; he will not stand before the obscure. An example in David 1 Kings 16, 21. ch. 17, 48. Daniel, Mordecai, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ECCE, DESCRIPSI EAM TRIPLICITER) Sapientia apud Hebræos dividitur in משלים,in בושים in מרכבה,quod Græcè dicas εἰς ἠθικα, φυσικὰ, θεολογικὰ, de his omnibus plurima scripsit Salomon, quæ nunc non ex-

conteras miserum in porta (hoc est in judicio. Deut. 21, 19. Amos 5, 15. Zach. 8, 16. Job. 5, 4.) quia Dominus judicabit causam illorum, & rapiet a rapientibus eos per pœnam talionis, confer Es. 33, 1.

(2) De familiaritate cum iracundo, v. 24. Ne fias amicus cum Domino iræ (iracundo) & cum viro furoris (furibundo) ne eas. v. 25. Ne forte discas semi- tas ejus, & accipias laqueum in animam tuam, insidiis ejus illaqueeris. Conf. Prov. 1, 15. cap. 11, 9. c. 13, 20. Sir. 13, 1. 1. Cor. 15, 33. Prov. 29, 6. Sunt vitia quæ- dam, ait auctor l. de amicit. Tom. 4. oper. Aug. qui- bus si quis fuerit involutus, non diu leges amicitiæ vel jura servabit: non enim ad amicitiam sunt idonei nimis iracundi, instabiles, suspiciosi, verbosi. Difficile est eum, quem sæpe iracundiæ furor exagitat, non aliquan- do insurgere in amicum.

(3) De temeraria fidejussione v. 26. Ne sis inter percutientes manum (complodentes manu, fideju- bendo sc. qui enim spondent, plerumque tandem debitum solvere coguntur. Sensum hunc docet ἐξήγησις subjuncta.) Neque inter fidejubentes pro debitis v. 27. Si non sit tibi ad reddendum (quæ ver- ba videntur conditionem inferre, nisi scil. abunde suppetat tibi, unde fidem tuam liberare possis, vel si mavis rationem ab incommodo petitam;) Quare abripietur tibi lectus tuus, qui est subter te? q. d. quid causæ est, ut te in hoc periculum conjicias, ut credi- tor propter aliena debita etiam lectum tuum, vel quæ maxime tibi necessaria sunt, auferat? quod etsi regulæ charitatis, & legi divinæ adversum sit, Ex. 22, 26. 27. Deut. 24, 12. 13. Ex. 18, 7. 12. tamen de facto sæ- pe fit.

(4) De antiquis limitibus non movendis. Quod divites & vi pollentes non raro tentant. Ne transgrediaris (in Ebr. ne transferas) terminos anti- quos, quos posuerunt Patres tui. Osiander exponit: Ne convellas ea, quæ pie, recte, & sapienter constituta sunt a majoribus tuis. Alii de servandis bonorum immobilium limitibus, & in genere de studio justitiæ, ut unicuique suum relinquatur. Eccl. 10, 9, Possunt hæ explicationes conjungi, si accipias de quibuscun- que terminis a majoribus constitutis, sive artium, seu Politias, seu fundorum aliorumque bonorum im- mobilium, & hinc e specie bonorum immobilium genús colligas, ut ad alia quoque bona hæc regula extendatur. Conf. Deut. 19, 14. Hieronymus in Os. 5, 10. Transferunt Principes terminos, quos po- suerunt Patres eorum, quando immutant in mendacio veritatem, & aliud prædicant, quam ab Apostolis acce- perunt.

(5) Denique de alacritate in perfungendis partibus nostris v. 29. Vidisti virum velocem in ope- re suo? coram Regibus stabit; non stabit coram obscu- ris. Exemplum in Davide 1. Reg. 16, 21. cap. 17, 48. Daniele, Mardochai, &c.

## 22:22
Vers. 22.

DO NOT DO VIOLENCE TO THE POOR, BECAUSE HE IS POOR: NOR CRUSH THE NEEDY IN THE GATE.

Solomon had spoken concerning the rich and the poor, and concerning the study of divine Wisdom: now therefore he instructs the rich, and prescribes several Rules from the storehouse of divine wisdom (1) concerning the oppression of the poor: Do not despoil, as it is held in the Hebrew, the exhausted or the needy, because he is needy, destitute of the means to repel force and injustice, as Osiander holds, or because he is already exhausted and afflicted, and to the afflicted, affliction is not to be added: or if you prefer, with Blessed Luther, you may take the little word כי as 'although': nor

Latin:

Vers. 22.

NON FACIAS VIOLENTIAM PAUPERI, QUIA PAUPER EST: NEQUE CONTERAS EGENUM IN PORTA.

Dixerat de divitibus & pauperibus Salomo, & de Sapientiæ divinæ studio: jam ergo instruit divitem, & Regulas e sapientiæ divinæ penu nonnullas præscribit (1) de oppressione pauperum: Ne spolies, ut in Ebræo habetur, exhaustum vel egenum, quia egenus est, facultatibus destitutus ad vim, & injustitiam depellendam, ut Osiander habet, vel quia jam exhaustus & afflictus est, afflicto autem non est addenda afflictio: aut si mavis, cum B. Luthero, accipias licet, voculam כי quamvis: neque

## 23:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIII.

Concerning the avoiding of the banquets of Tyrants, the immoderate desire for becoming rich, the foods of those who invite, concerning the defrauding of orphans, concerning the benefit of discipline: the damages of harlots, and of drunkenness. Vers. 1. WHEN YOU SIT TO EAT WITH A PRINCE, DILIGENTLY ATTEND TO WHAT IS SET BEFORE YOUR FACE.

Because dignity is promised to the eager in courts, and among princes, Solomon instructs how one ought to converse with them, but especially with tyrants: namely, that there is need for circumspection when it is most needed. v. 1. When you sit to eat before a tyrant (thus the word מושל is accepted in Dan. 11, 3. 39. and the context teaches that this sense of the word holds here) considering, consider who is before you, what kind of man you have before you. The Vulgate is therefore to be corrected here: for it is not the food set before you, but the persons with whom one must eat, that are designated: v. 2. And set a knife to your throat, if you are master of your soul, that is, of your life itself, that is, as Osiander with Blessed Luther, if you wish to retain your way. Vulgate: if yet you have your soul in your power. The meaning of the word שכין, which occurs nowhere else, is sought by some from the Chaldean סכין to be in danger: since סכין in the Targum denotes a knife and a sword, Gen. 22, 6. 10. Jud. 19, 29. Zach. 11, 17. But to put a knife to the throat is to watch the words, for the forming of which the throat serves, no differently than if a sword were applied to inflict a wound, unless they were suitably formed to the pleasure of the tyrant. Conf. Ps. 39, 2. Sir. 9, 18. c. 31, 12. 13. The explanation of others concerning governing the appetite in food or drink seems more alien. Concerning that rather v. 3. Do not desire his delicacies (thus the Hebrew word is used in Gen. 27, 4. seqq.) that is, in general, whether eatables or drinkables, a common synecdoche. Because (vav is causal, as c. 4, 28. Gen. 20, 3.) the food itself is of lies, or deceitful, set before one not with a good mind, but with a treacherous one. Syr. 13, 8. 15.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII.

De fugiendis Tyrannorum conviviis, immodico ditescendi studio, cibis invitorum, de frauda- tione pupillorum, de bono disciplinæ: damnis meretricum, & ebrietatis. Vers. 1. QUANDO SEDERIS, UT COMEDAS CUM PRINCIPE, DILIGENTER ATTENDE, QUÆ APPOSITA SUNT ANTE FACIEM TUAM.

QUia alacribus promissa dignitas in aulis, & penes principes, quomodo cum his conver- sari oporteat, imprimis vero cum Tyrannis, in- struit Salomo : quod nempe circumspectione opus sit cum maxime. v. 1. Cum sederis, ut edas coram Ty- ranno (sic vocabulum מושל accipitur Dan. 11, 3. 39. & hunc vocis sensum hic obtinere,contextus do- cet) considerando considera quis ante te, quem virum ante te habeas. Corrigenda ergo hic Vulgata : non enim cibi propositi, sed personæ, cum quibus come- dendum est, designantur : v. 2. Et statue cultrum in gutture tuo, si Dominus animæ, id est, vitæ ipse, hoc est, ut Osiander cum B. Luthero, si vis retinere viam tuam. Vulgata, si tamen habes in potestate animam tuam. Vocis שכין, quæ nuspiam alias occurrit, si- gnificatio e Chaldaico סכין periclitari a nonnullis petitur: quum סכין in Targum cultrum & gladium notet Gen. 22, 6. 10. Jud. 19, 29. Zach. 11, 17. Po- nere autem cultrum in guttere est sermones, quibus formandis inservit guttur, observare, non secus ac si appositus sit gladius, ad infligendum vulnus, nisi convenienter illi ad Tyranni placitum formati fue- rint. Conf. Ps. 39,2. Sir. 9,18. c. 31,12. 13. Aliorum explicatio de appetitu in cibo potuve gubernando alienior videtur. De eo potius v. 3. Ne concupi- scas cupedias ejus (ita vox Ebr. Gen. 27, 4. seqq. ad- hibetur) hoc est in genere sive esculenta sive potu- lenta, usitata Synecdohe. Quia (vav causale est, ut c. 4,28. Genes. 20,3.) ipse cibus mendaciorum, vel fallax, animo non bono, sed doloso appositus. Syr. 13, 8. 15.

## 23:4
Vers. 4. DO NOT LABOR TO BE RICH, BUT SET A LIMIT TO YOUR PRUDENCE) For labor, you would more correctly translate to be fatigued. For thus יגע is often taken. Aquila here μὴ κοπία. And understand prudence as the plans for increasing wealth. It is the same sense as that in Lucillius in the Greek Epigram:

If you live a long time like a stag or a crow, / Forgiveness is yours for gathering much wealth. / But if you are one of the mortals, whom old age soon strikes, / Do not you take a burden of infinite possessions; / Lest you destroy your spirit in unbearable pains, / And others use your goods without restraint.

The Vulgate is deservedly corrected; because not labor, but anxious fatigue is prohibited: which that word in 2 Sam. 23, 10. Ps. 6, 7. implies. The following words have this sense: cease from your consideration or understanding, lest you wear yourself out by constantly devising one thing after another, as if your riches were acquired by your own prudence and not rather by divine blessing. The latter colon therefore declares what kind of fatigue is prohibited; not the labor incumbent by divine ordinance, which enriches with divine blessing c. 10, 4. 22. but that by which we have persuaded ourselves that we can become rich by our own sagacity and prudence. Which sense Blessed Luther neatly rendered with the word Fündlein. Conf. c. 3, 5. Eccl. 9, 11. Deut. 8, 17. Psal. 127, 2. Ez. 28, 45. Nor will you cast (you will make to fly) your eyes (Solomon continues v. 5.) to that which is not: since by making it makes for itself wings (that, namely, which you desire) like an eagle it will fly away into heaven, i.e. If you are swift in desiring, certainly riches will be even swifter in receding, so much so that the eyes can at last not follow them penetrating through the clouds, as Dr. Geier correctly expressed the emphasis: and when you will seem to have approached as closely as possible to seizing them, they will soon flee from you again, so that you can no more attain them than an eagle flying into heaven. The Chaldean in v. 4 and 5 still understood this as concerning the avoiding of the banquets of the rich: Do not approach the rich man, but by your understanding withdraw from him: if you fix your eyes upon him, he will not appear to you, since making he will make for himself wings, that is, if you fix your hope upon him, he will look down upon you from on high as if you were lying on the ground. Thus also generally the LXX and the Syrian. But the Hebrew sense does not agree.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NOLI LABORA RE, VT DITERIS, SED PRV- DENTIÆ TVÆ PONE MODVM) Pro laborare rectius, verteris fatigari. Ita enim sæpe sumitur יגע. Aquila hic μὴ κοπία. Et prudentiam intellige, consilia rei augendæ. Est idem sensus, qui apud Lucillium in Græco Epigrammate :

Εἰ μὲν ζῇς ἐλάφκ ταναὸν χρόνον ἠὲ κορώνης, Συγγνώμη πλεῖϛον πλοῦτον ἀγειρομένῳ. Εἰ δέ τις ἐπὶ βροτῶν, οὓς αὐτίκα γῆρας ἰάπτει, Μὴ σὺγ᾽ ἀπειρεσίων οἶστον ἔλῃ κτεάνων· Μὴ σὺ μὲν ἀτλήτοισιν ἐν ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ὀλέσσης, Χρήσωνται δ᾽ ἄλλοι σοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἀνέδην.

Merito corrigitur Vulgata; quia non labor, sed anxia defatigatio prohibetur: quam verbum il- lud 2.Sam. 23,10. Ps. 6,7. importat. Verba sequen- tia hunc habent sensum: a consideratione vel intelli- gentia tua desine,ne te maceres subinde aliud ex alio excogitando, quasi propria tua prudentia & non potius benedictione divina divitiæ comparentur. Posterius ergo colon declarat, qualis fatigatio pro- hibeatur; non labor ex ordinatione divina incum- bens, qui cum benedictione divina ditat c. 10, 4. 22. sed quo propria nostra sagacitate ac prudentia nos ditescere posse persuasi sumus. Quem sensum concinne Beat. Lutherus voce Fündlein reddidit. Conf. c. 3,5. Eccl. 9,11. Deut. 8,17. Psal. 127,2. Ez. 28, 45. Num conjicies (volare facies) oculos tuos (per- git Salomo v. 5.) ad id, quod non est: quoniam facien- do facit sibi alas (illud scil. quod. appetis) sicut aqui- la avolabit in cælum, q. d. Si velox fueris in appe- tendo, certe velociores adhuc erunt opes in rece- dendo, adeo ut oculi tandem sequi nequeant per nubes penetrantem, ut emphasin recte expressit Dn. D. Geierus: & cum quam proxime ad eas capien- das accessisse tibi videberis, mox rursus te fugient, ut eas non magis assequi possis, quam aquilam in cœlum volantem. Chaldæus v. 4. & 5. adhuc de conviviis divitum fugiendis intellexit: Ne accedas ad divitem, sed intelligentia tua recede ab eo: si allega- veris oculos tuos in eum, non comparebit tibi, quoniam faciens faciet sibi alas, id est, si spem tuam in ipsum defiges, te velut humi jacentem ex alto despiciet. Sic fere etiam LXX. & Syrus. Sed non congruit sons Ebræus.

## 23:6
Ver. 6.

EAT NOT WITH AN ENVIOUS MAN, AND DESIRE NOT HIS DAINTIES ] In the Hebrew: Eat not the bread of an evil eye. See what is at Matt. 20, 15. Association with the envious is discouraged: eat not the bread, (that is, do not take food) of him who is evil of eye (that is) an envious and covetous man. Cf. c. 28, 27. Eccl. 4, 8. Sir. 14, 8. And do not covet his delicacies. The etiology follows in v. 7. Because just as (the envious man) attentively observes in his mind (no differently than a doorkeeper at a gate: namely, that you might covet, vehemently desire his delicacies, and gape at them greatly) so is he himself (evil of eye, the more he observes you gaping, the more he envies you.) Eat and drink, he will say to you (in words) but his heart is not with you. With his mouth he invites you, in his heart he envies you. Cf. Jud. 16, 15. The Vulgate can in no way be reconciled with the sources here, while it renders: For like a guesser and a soothsayer he estimates what he does not know.

Furthermore, a reason is added from the subsequent repentance in v. 8. The morsel (which) you have eaten you will vomit up (by your wish: i.e., you would wish it vomited up: as those who understand that they have swallowed something harmful) and you will lose your words of sweetness, that is, you will grieve that you gave so many good words to a very wicked man, and uttered so many pleasant speeches in his presence.

And therefore Solomon immediately warns in v. 9. In the ears of a fool (such as covetous men entirely are) do not speak, because he will despise the wisdom of your words. In the presence of depraved and foolish men do not speak of great and serious matters: because they will mock you and your wise speeches. Cf. 25, 20. Sir. 22, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NE COMEDAS CVM HOMINE INVIDO, ET NE DESIDERES CIBOS EJVS ] In Hebræo : Ne come- das panem oculi mali. Vide quæ ad Matth. 20, 15. Convictus invidorum diffuadetur : ne comedas panem, (id est, ne cibum capias) ejus qui malus oculo (est) hoc est, invidi & avari. Conf. c. 28, 27. Eccl. 4, 8. Sir. 14, 8. Et ne concupiscas cupedias ejus. Sequi- tur ætiologia v. 7. Quia sicut (invidus) attente ob- servat in animo suo (non secus atque janitor ad por- tam : quod sc. tu concupiscas, vehementer deside- res cupedias ejus, iisque valde inhies) sic est ipse (ma- lus oculo, quo magis inhiare te observat, eo magis inwidet.) Comede & bibe, dicet tibi (verbis) sed cor ejus non est tecum. Ore te invitat, corde invidet tibi. Conf. Jud. 16, 15. Vulgata nullatenus cum fontibus hic conciliari potest, dum reddit: Quoniam in similitudinem conjectoris & arioli æstimat, quod ignorat.

Additur porro ratio a pœnitudine subse- qua v. 8. buccellam (quam) comedisti evomes (voto tuo : i. e. optares evomitam : ut qui noxium quid se deglutiisse intelligunt) & perdes verba tua dulcedi- nis, id est, dolebis, quod tot bona verba homini pes- simo dederis, tot jucundos sermones coram ipso protuleris.

Ideoque actutum monet Salomo v. 9. In auribus stulti (quales avari omnino sunt) ne lo- quaris, quia contemnet prudentiam eloquiorum tuo- rum. Coram pravis & stolidis hominibus ne lo- quaris de rebus magnis, & gravibus : quia deride- bunt te tuosque sapientes sermones. Conf. 25, 20. Sir. 22, 7.

## 23:10
Ver. 10.

DO NOT TOUCH THE BOUNDARIES OF THE LITTLE ONES) In the Hebrew: Do not move the boundary of the age. That is, the ancient one: as Ovid to Terminus: Every field will be litigious without you. It is added in the text: and (that is, especially) do not enter into the fields of orphans (with the intention, namely, of alienating or seizing them. See a similar expression Jud. 9, 52. 2 Sam. 5, 6.) Because their redeemer is strong: He himself will judge their cause against you v. 11. Cf. Deut. 10, 18. Ps. 10, 14. 18. Ps. 68, 6. Ps. 146, 9. Jer. 50, 34. Hos. 14, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

NE ATTINGAS PARVULORUM TERMINOS) In Hebræo : Ne moveas terminum seculi. Id est, veterem : ut Ovidius ad Terminum : Omnis erit sine te litigiosus ager. Additur in textu : & (id est, imprimis) in agros pupillorum ne introeas (animo sc. abalienandi, vel rapiendi eosdem. Vide similem loquutionem Jud. 9, 52. 2. Sam. 5, 6.) Quia vindex eorum fortis : Ipse judicabit causam eorum adversus te v. 11. Conf. Deut. 10, 18. Ps. 10, 14. 18. Ps. 68, 6. Ps. 146, 9. Jer. 50, 34. Os. 14, 3.

## 23:12
Ver. 12.

LET YOUR HEART ENTER INTO INSTRUCTION: AND YOUR EAR TO THE WORDS OF KNOWLEDGE.

In Hebrew, apply your heart to instruction, and your ears to the words of knowledge. Cf. ch. 2, 2. ch. 4, 20. Now, therefore, concerning the Good of information or discipline, both as regards us, so that indeed everyone may strive to acquire true knowledge, and thus may devote both his ears and his mind to information, so that he may listen attentively and meditate continually on those things which make for learning: and as regards our boys or children, the following verses.

Do not withhold correction from a boy: For if you strike him with a rod, he will not die, v. 13. He will not incur the death of soul and body through the vices to which nature is prone, as the ἐξήγησις

added teaches v. 14. You shall strike him with a rod, and you will deliver his soul (life) from hell. Whence Solomon turns himself in the person of a father to his son, sweetly exciting him to the study of wisdom: My son, if your heart is wise, my heart will rejoice, I, I say, will rejoice. Cf. for the reason of the phrase ch. 22, 19. And my reins will exult, when your lips speak what is right v. 16. When the wisdom of the heart is commended by the speech of the mouth, so that parents may rejoice over their son by the grace of both. They attribute feelings to the reins because of the remarkable sympathy with the heart, about which Physicians and Natural Philosophers speak. The LXX [Septuagint] differently: and your lips will linger on my lips, if they are right. He further exhorts to the flight of sin,

and the true fear of the Lord, v. 17. Let not your heart envy sinners: (ch. 1, 10. Ps. 37, 1.) but rather be in the fear of the Lord all the day. v. 18. Because in truth (thus Aben-Ezra takes the particle אֵם, others take it as expletive) there is a reward (the word אַחֲרִית is so taken in Ps. 37, 37, and the following verse suggests that sense) and your hope will not be cut off. v. 19. Listen, my son, and you will be wise, and walk in this way with your heart. That walking implies unwearied continuation, and indeed that we should remain in that way, and not turn aside to an evil way, ch. 4, 14. But because communion with gluttons is most opposed to this wisdom and way, Solomon dissuades from it v. 20. Do not be with wine-drinkers (nor) with gluttons of flesh. The word לָמוֹ is added by an elegant pleonasm for themselves, as in ch. 20, 14, because gluttons serve their own gullets. Whence it appears that in the Old Testament also, pleasures of food and drink were already prohibited, which the Socinians rashly deny, as we have warned more fully in its proper place. But a peculiar reason is added here from ignominious poverty v. 21. Because a drunkard and a glutton (the Vulgate wrongly giving 'Symbola') will be made poor, and drowsiness will clothe (a man) with tattered garments. For somnolence is the companion of gluttony. Cf. Luke 15, 22.

That these paternal admonitions may be more effective, Solomon inculcates filial obedience, and at the same time reminds [him] of the duty of compliance and reverence: v. 22. Hear thy father, who begat thee; and despise not when thy mother is old. For often a mother growing old is despised by her grown-up sons. This παραίνεσις can also be referred particularly and primarily to the next admonition with Osiander: Do not listen to those frivolous men who invite you to drinking bouts and revelries, and who strive to lead you away from performing your calling: but rather obey your father, whom God has commanded you to honor: and do not despise the admonitions of your mother, although she has grown old, who calls you away from revelries to the salutary labors of your calling.

To obedience toward parents is joined the pursuit of wisdom, to which Solomon exhorts his son in the person of a father v. 23. Buy the truth (that is, the true and solid knowledge of things, just as salutary doctrine is distinguished by the name of truth, Ps. 26:3, Zech. 8:3, John 8:40, 45, Tit. 1:1) and do not sell it, (acquire it with the greatest zeal, and retain it, but do not alienate it as if it were a useless thing) Wisdom (I say) and instruction and understanding. Therefore, the pleasures or vanities of the world are not to be preferred to this treasure of the soul, nor is heavenly wisdom to be exchanged for them, c. 3:14.

The fruit resulting from this is the joy of parents, v. 24. The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him. v. 25. Let thy father (therefore) rejoice, and thy mother: and let her that bare thee exult: who endured and sustained many troubles and heavy sorrows for thy sake. Whence it is just that she should be cheered by thee in her old age, and not be afflicted with sadness.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

INGREDIATUR AD DOCTRINAM COR TUUM : ET AURIS TUA AD VERBA SCIEN- TIÆ.

In Ebr. applica eruditioni cor tuum, & aures tuas eloquiis scientiæ. Conf. c. 2, 2. c. 4, 20. Jam er- go de Bono informationis vel disciplinæ tum quoad nos, ut nempe quisque studeat veram scientiam adi- pisci, adeoque informationi dedat & aures & ani- mum suum, ut attente audiat, & jugiter meditetur, quæ ad eruditionem faciunt : tum quoad pueros, vel liberos nostros vers. seqq.

Ne subtrahas a puero correctionem : Nam si percusseris eum virga, non mo- rietur, v. 13. animæ & corporis mortem non incur- ret vitiis, ad quæ natura proclivis est, ut ἐξήγησις

addita docet v. 14. Tu virga percuties eum, & ani- mam (vitam) ejus ab inferno erues. Unde conver- tit se in persona patris Salomo ad filium, suaviter eum excitans ad sapientiæ studium : Fili mi, si sa- piens fuerit cor tuum, lætabitur cor meum, ego, inquam, lætabor. Conf. ratione phraseos c. 22, 19. Et ex- ultabunt renes mei, cum labia tua loquentur recta v. 16. Cum sapientia cordis eloquium oris commendatur, ut utriusque gratia lætentur de filio parentes. Re- nibus affectus tribuunt ob insignem cum corde Sym- pathiam, de qua Medici & Physici. LXX. alienè: & immorabuntur sermonibus tua labia ad labia mea, si recta fuerint. Adhortatur porro ad fugam peccati,

& verum timorem Domini, v. 17. Ne æmuletur cor tuum peccatores: (c. 1, 10. Ps. 37, 1.) imo potius in timo- re Domini esto omni die. v. 18. Quia revera (sic par- ticulam אֵם accipit Aben-Ezra, alii pro expletiva habent) est præmium (vox אַחֲרִית ita accipitur Ps. 37, 37. eumque sensum comma sequens suggerit) & spes tua non succidetur. v. 19. Audi tu fili mi, & sapiens eris, & incede per hanc viam corde tuo. In- cessus ille continuationem indesessam importat, & quidem ut in via ista maneamus, nec ad malignam viam declinemus, c. 4, 14. Quia vero huic sapien- tiæ & viæ adversatur maxime communio cum belluo- nibus, ab ea dehortatur Salomo v. 20. Ne sis cum potatoribus vini (neque) cum voratoribus carnis. Ad- ditur eleganti pleonasmo vox לָמוֹ sibi, ut c. 20, 14. quia gulæ suæ inserviunt epulones. Unde apparet in Vet. etiam Test. jam prohibitas fuisse voluptates cibi & potus, quod temere negant Sociniani, ut suo loco uberius monuimus. Subjicitur autem pecu- liaris hic ratio ab ignominiosa pauperie v. 21. Quia bibax & epulo (vulgat. perperam dantes Symbola) pauperes efficientur, & vestibus laceris induet (homi- nem) dormitatio. Somnolentia enim comes est gulæ. Conf. Luc. 15, 22.

Ut efficaciores sint istæ monitiones paternæ, obedientiam filialem inculcat Salomo, & de obsequio ac reverentia debita simul commonefacit: v. 22. Audi Patrem tuum, qui genuit te; & ne contemnas cum senuevit mater tua. Sæpe enim mater senescens a filiis grandescentibus contemnitur. Referri etiam peculiariter & imprimis ad proximam monitionem hæc παραίνεσις potest cum Osiandro: Noli auscul- tare levibus istis hominibus, qui te ad pocula & comes- sationes invitant, teque a vocatione tua obeunda abdu- cere student: sed obtempera potius patri tuo, quem Deus te honorare jussit: & non contemnas monita matris tuæ, licet senuerit, quæ te a comessationibus ad salutares la- bores vocationis avocat.

Obedientiæ erga Parentes adjungitur sapientiæ studium, ad quod in persona patris hortatur filium Salomo v. 23. Veritatem (hoc est, veram solidam- que rerum notitiam, quomodo salutaris doctrina veritatis nomine insignitur Ps. 26, 3. Zach. 8, 3. Joh. 8, 40. 45. Tit. 1, 1.) eme & ne vendas, (acquiras summo studio, & retineas, non vero tanquam rem inuti- lem abalienes) Sapientiam (inquam) & eruditionem & intelligentiam. Non ergo voluptates vel vanita- tes seculi huic thesauro animæ præferendæ, vel sa- pientia cœlestis cum illis commutanda, c. 3, 14.

Fructus inde redundans est gaudium paren- tum, v. 24. Exultando exultabit Pater justi: & ge- nerans sapientem lætatur in eo. v. 25. Lætetur (ergo) Pater tuus, & mater tua: & exultet, quæ genuit te: quæ multas molestias & graves dolores tui causa ex- antlavit, & sustinuit. Unde æquum est, ut ea ite- rum in senectute tua per te exhilaretur, non tristitia afficiatur.

## 23:26
vers. 26. MY SON, GIVE ME THINE HEART, AND LET THINE EYES OBSERVE MY WAYS.

In the Hebrew: And let thy eyes delight in my ways. To the special dissuasion from harlots and drunkenness is prefixed an excitation to receive the doctrine of the Parent; so that the heart may be given to him with devoted attention and prompt obedience: and the eyes, both of the body and of the mind, may be directed to observing the right way; v. 26. Give, my son, thy heart to me, and let thy eyes observe my ways, lest, to wit, they be captured by the sight of harlots, or the color of wine, or look back to the ways of harlots and gluttons v. 27. For a deep pit is a harlot (chap. 22, 14.) and a narrow well is a strange woman, that is, one who is not yours. Because of the difficult exits, as Grotius here v. 28. She herself also lies in wait like a predator (chap. 7. v. 12.) and adds prevaricators among men, she increases their number. Eccl. 7. v. 27. But a strange woman, Vulg. and she will kill those whom you see to be incautious. These are the words of Grotius on v. 27: Verse 27. FOR A HARLOT IS A DEEP PIT) See what is above c. 5. v. 15. Anaxilaus. Does Phryne not make Charybdis not far off? Having taken the shipmaster, she has swallowed him with his ship. A NARROW WELL IS A STRANGE WOMAN) An adulteress. Difficult exits.

But because drunkenness is for the most part the cause of lust, Solomon depicts it here with vivid colors from its effects, that is, and its harms v. 29. To whom woe? אוי which is an interjection of one complaining 1 Sam. 4, 7. as also the following according to R. Solomon, and R. Kimchi, to whom אבוי Alas! which however Aben-Ezra and others prefer to render as poverty from אביון needy. The Vulgate ineptly explained it as to whom is the father of woe, as if it were composed of אב father, and וי woe: because drunken sons create a thousand sorrows for their parents according to Cornelius. To whom STRIFE, or contentions? Conf. chap. 22, 10. c. 20, 1. Syr. 31, 38. For by wine spirits are heated and inflamed, which easily kindle the brain and bile to anger, so that contention arises from a very slight cause: just as oil, as Chrysostom says, [inflames] a lamp, so wine inflames anger. To whom COMPLAINT? (as Job 7, 13. C. 10, 1. c. 23, 2. others explain it as murmuring: the Vulgate wrongly rendered it as pit, as if שוח were read) To whom WOUNDS WITHOUT CAUSE? which from contentions, falls, and other occasions drunkards draw upon themselves beyond measure. Basil, Tome on Drunkenness: Hey, what are you doing, O man! The servant flees from the master who is beating and wounding him: but you remain with wine, which strikes or beats your head every single day. Ambrose, book on Elijah and fasting, c. 12, says: in one day they drink the labors of many days, they rise to arms from drunkenness, weapons succeed the cups, blood is shed for wine, and wines have shed that very blood. TO WHOM REDNESS (Vulg. suffusion) OF EYES? whose deformity and weakness arises when, from the excessive effusion of humors, and from the abundance of fiery vapors exhaling thence, redness and blear-eyedness are brought upon the eyes. Clement of Alexandria, book 2, Pedagogue, c. 2. With immoderate wine the eyes are distorted and turned aside, when because of the multitude of humor the sight swims as if in a pool, and so, being forced to lie, some think everything is being turned in a circle, but they cannot count things that are far off, as if they were one. And I seem to myself to see two suns, that Theban old man used to say when drunk. In a word, the more liberal use of wine, says Chrysostom, hom. 10 in Gen., is the cause of infinite evils. Verse 30. To those who linger (stay a long time, Is. 5, 11. Eccl. 4, 3.) by (thus על is taken Ps. 1, 3. Isa. 23, 7. & c. 37, 1.) wine. To those going to search out mixed [drink] (chap. 9, 2. 5. or strong drink Isa. 5, 22.) Vatabl. who come to investigate where wine is mixed. The LXX and B. Luther expressed the sense, not the words: they render it thus: do they not track down where drinking parties are held? Here, that one comes to drink up what is poured out. verse 31.

Do not look upon wine, because it is red, because it gives its color in the cup (עינו its eye, a pleasant and glowing appearance: which word occurs metonymically also for color, Lev. 13, 5. 37. and for the brightness of color Ezech. 1, 4. 27. chap. 8, 2. Dan. 10, 6.) it enters smoothly (as the Vulg. and B. Luther. Lud. de Dieu in animadv. on this place IN STRAIGHTNESSES, or easinesses, because that which proceeds rightly without windings and impediments is moved easily, for RIGHTLY and easily: See similar things Eccl. 1, 13. c. 2, 21. c. 4. verse 2.) in the end like a serpent (or rather a viper, as Mart. de Roap. 2. singul. script. l. 1. chap. 9. 10. teaches) it will bite, and like a basilisk (or a basilisk killing by sight alone) it will afflict with pain, (the word יפרש for it stings, or afflicts with pain, is expressed by B. Luther, Vatablus, Mercer, because פרש a horseman uses פרישים spurs to stimulate a horse, as Aben-Ezra notes in this place) verse 32. Among the LXX, some things are added in v. 31 which are not held in the Hebrew, do not get drunk with wine, but converse with just men, and converse in walkings.

Latin:

vers. 26. PRÆBE FILI MI COR TUUM MIHI ET OCULI TUI VIAS MEAS CUSTODIANT.

In Ebr. Et oculis tuis viæ meæ placeant. Spe- ciali a meretricibus & ebrietate dehortationi præ- mittitur excitatio ad suscipiendam doctrinam Pa- rentis; ut ei cor præbeatur devota attentione, prom- taque obedientia: & oculi tum corporis tum animi intendantur ad custodiendam viam rectam; v. 26. Præbe, fili mi, cor tuum mihi, & oculi tui vias meas ob- servent, ne scil. capiantur oculi meretricum aspectu, vel colore vini, aut meretricum & heluonum vias refpiciant v. 27. Fovea enim profunda est meretricis (cap. 22, 14.) & puteus angustus aliena, quæ sc. tua non est. Ob difficiles exitus, ut hic Grotius vers. 28. Etiam ipsa tanquam prædator insidiatur (cap. 7. vers. 12.) & prævaricatores in hominibus addit, nu- merum eorum auget. Eccl. 7. vers. 27. Aliene au- tem Vulg. & quos incautos videris interficiet. Gro- tii ad v. 27. hæc sunt: Vers. 27. FOVEA ENIM PROFUNDA EST MERE- TRIX) Vide quæ supra c. 5. v. 15. Anaxilaus. Ἡ δὲ Φρύνη τὴν χάρυβδιν ἐχὶ πόῥῥω ποιεῖ; Τόν τε νάυκληρον λαβῦσα καταπεπωκ’ αὐτῷ σκάφει. PVTEVS ANGUSTUS ALIENA) Adultera. Difficiles exitus.

Quia vero libidinis causa ebrietas plerumque est, coloribus vivis eam depingit hic Salomo ab ef- fectis sc. & damnis ejusdem v. 29. Cuinam væ? אוי quæ querulantis interjectio 1. Sam. 4, 7. ut & se- quens juxta R. Salomonem, & R. Kimchi, cuinam אבוי Eheu! quam tamen Aben-Esdra & alii reddere malunt egestas ab אביון egenus. Vulg. inepte expo- suit cujus Patri væ, quasi componeretur ex אב Pa- ter, & וי Væ: quia filii ebriosi parentibus mille lores creant secundum Cornelium. Cui RIXÆ, vel contentiones? Conf. cap. 22, 10. c. 20, 1. Syr. 31, 38. Vino enim incalescunt & inflammantur spi- ritus, qui cerebrum & bilem facile accendunt ad iram, ut contentio ex levicula causa oriatur: sicut oleum, ut Chrysost. ait lucernam, sic vinum iram inflammat. Cui שיח QUERIMONIA? (uti Job. 7, 13. C. 10, 1. c. 23, 2. alii exponunt murmur: Vulg. foveam reddidit perperam, ac si legeretur שוח) Cui VULNERA SINE CAUSA? quæ ex conten- tionibus, lapsibus, aliisque occasionibus ebrii sibi ipsis ultra attrahunt. Basil. Tom. de Ebr. Hem quid agis, inquit, o homo! Famulus fugit Dominum cædentem ac vulnerantem: tu autem permanes cum vino, quod singulis diebus caput ferit seu percellit tuum. Ambrof. lib. de Elia & jejun. c. 12. uno, in- quit, die bibunt multorum dierum labores, de ebrieta- te ad arma consurgunt, calicibus tela succedunt, pro vino sanguis effunditur, & ipsum sanguinem vina fuderunt. CUI RUBOR (Vulg. suffusio) OCU- LORUM? quorum deformatio & debilitas ori- tur, cum e nimia humorum effusione, & inde ex- halantium fumorum igneorum copia rubor & lip- pitudo oculis conciliatur. Clemens Alex. lib. 2. Pæ- dag. c. 2. Vino immodico oculi detorquentur, ac di- vertuntur, cum præ humoris multitudine visus tan- quam in piscina natitet, atque adeo mentiri coacti exi- stimant quidam omnia in orbem circumagi, nume- rare autem non possunt quæ procul sunt, tanquam sint unica. Atque duos soles videre mihi videor, ebrius di- cebat ille Thebanus senex. Verbo, vini largior usus, inquit Chrysost. hom. 10. in Gen. infinitorum est causa malorum. Vers. 30. His qui immorantur (diu commorantur, Es. 5, 11. Eccl. 4, 3.) juxta (sic על accipitur Psal. 1, 3. Efa. 23, 7. &c. 37, 1.) vinum. Euntibus ad indagandum mistum (cap. 9, 2. 5. vel si- ceram Esa. 5, 22.) Vatabl. qui veniunt scrutatum ubi vinum misceatur. LXX. & B. Luther. sensum exprefžere, non verba: illi sic reddunt: nonne ve- stigantibus ubi compotationes fiunt? Hic da man kommt auszusuuffen was eingeschencket ist. vers. 31.

Ne intuearis vinum, quod rubrum sit, quod det in ca- lice colorem suum (עינו oculum suum, aspectum ju- cundum & rutilantem: quæ vox metonymice etiam pro colore occurrit, Lev. 13, 5. 37. & coloris fulgore Ezech. 1, 4. 27. cap. 8, 2. Dan. 10, 6.) ingre- diatur blande (ut Vulg. & B. Luther. Lud. de Dieu in animadv. ad h. 1. IN RECTITUDINIBUS, vel facilitatibus, quia quod recte procedit sine amba- gibus & impedimentis, id facile movetur, pro RE- CTE & facile: Vid. similia Eccl. 1, 13. c. 2, 21. c. 4. vers. 2.) in fine velut serpens (vel potius vipera, ut Mart. de Roap. 2. singul. script. l. 1. cap. 9. 10. do- cet) mordebit, & velut regulus (vel basiliscus solo necans aspectu) dolore afficiet, (vox יפרש per pun- git, vel dolore afficit, a B. Luthero, Vatablo, Mercero exprimitur, quia פרש eques utitur פרישים calcari- bus ad equum stimulandum notante Aben-Esr. h. l.) vers. 32. Apud LXX. adduntur v. 31. nonnulla, quæ in Ebr. non habentur, ne inebriamini vino, sed con- versamini cum hominibus justis, & conversamini in deambulationibus.

## 23:33
Verse 33.

YOUR EYES WILL SEE STRANGE WOMEN] Better, a strange woman. You will seem to yourself to see wondrous things: And a twin sun and double Thebes to rise. The Vulgate is corrected without cause, with which the LXX, R. Solomon, R. Aben-Ezra, B. Luther, the Tigurines, Junius, Piscator, and the Belgian interpreters agree. Grotius, however, followed the Chaldean, as did Corn. à Lap. and others, and R. Levi, Mercer, Vatablus, Cajetan, Jansenius. The Hebrew word nowhere denotes strange sights, but occurs concerning a strange woman, alien to our bed, c. 7, 5. c. 22, 14. etc., and among the evil consequences of drunkenness, lust was not to be rashly omitted. For the belly boiling with wine quickly foams into lust, says Jerome to Eustochium. In repletion is Venus, says Athenaeus l. 6. chap. 7. Solomon adds: AND YOUR HEART WILL SPEAK PERVERSE THINGS. Speaking is attributed to the heart, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Matt. 12. verse 34. Drunkards and wine-bibbers have their heart on their tongue, according to Plutarch in his Morals, whereas sober men have their tongue in their heart.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

OCVLI, TVI VIDEBVNT EXTRANEAS] Melius extranea. Res miras videre tibi videberis: Et geminum solem & duplices consurgere Thebas. Citra causam corrigitur Vulgata, cum qua consentiunt LXX. R. Salomo, R. Aben-Ezra, B. Lu- therus, Tigurini, Junius, Piscator, Belgici Interpp. Chaldæum a. sequutus Grotius est, Corn. à Lap. aliique & R. Levi, Mercerum, Vatablum, Cajeta- num, Jansenium. Vox Ebræa nuspiam notat alie- na visa, sed de extranea muliere, à thoro nostro alie- na occurrit c. 7, 5. c. 22, 14. &c. & inter ebrietatis mala consequentia non temere omittenda erat li- bido. Venter enim mero æstuans cito despumat in li- bidinem, ait Hieron. ad Eustach. In repletione Ve- nus, inquit Athenæus l. 6. cap. 7. Addit Salomo: ET COR TUUM LOQUETUR PER- VERSA. Cordi loquutio tribuitur, quia ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Matth. 12. vers. 34. Ebriosi & vinolenti cor habent in lingua, secundum Plutarchum in Moral. cum sobrii linguam habeant in corde.

## 23:34
Verse 34.

AND YOU SHALL BE AS ONE SLEEPING IN THE MIDST OF THE SEA, AND AS A SLEEPY PILOT WHO HAS LOST THE RUDDER] In the Hebrew: And you shall be as one sleeping in the midst of the sea (that is, on an island shaken on all sides by waves) or as one lying at the top of the mast: that is, as they now say, in the crow's nest of the ship, where the agitation is greatest.

There is no mention here of an island: but of one sleeping in the heart of the sea, and thus in a ship, which the second clause teaches: As one sleeping at the head, or top of the mast, or in the crow's nest, who is violently tossed, and is in the greatest danger. It is added in v. 35 by mimesis in the person of a drunkard, as the Vulgate explains: And you shall say (which words are not explicitly in the Hebrew) they have beaten me, but I did not feel pain: they have dragged (in the Hebrew, struck) me, and I did not perceive it. When shall I awake, and find wines again? In the Hebrew: I will add and seek it (wine) again. Thus a huge, and almost incredible and incorrigible stupor of the drunkenness of drunkards is depicted. Cf. Is. 56, 12. However great the danger may be, even if they are awakened, beaten, struck, they do not wake up: and when they have awakened, freed from danger, they return again to drinking bouts. Just as a sleeping shipmaster allows the ship to be driven into rocks, Scyllas, and Charybdes, by which it is shattered, or spun around, and submerged: so the drunkard allows himself to be swept away into a thousand dangers of fortune and life. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Paedag. cap. 2. You see the danger of shipwreck. The heart is indeed overwhelmed by much drink, but he has compared much drunkenness to the threats of the sea, in which the body, like a ship submerged, has undergone a depth of baseness and disgrace, overwhelmed by the tenth waves of wine. The pilot, however, namely the human mind, is driven around by the wave of oncoming drunkenness, and while moving in the sea, grows dizzy, and because of the darkness of the storm, wanders away from the port of truth, until, rushing into rocks hidden in the sea, he has destroyed himself, having been driven into pleasures.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ET ERIS SICVT DORMIENS IN MEDIO MARI, ET QVASI SOPITVS GVBERNATOR AMISSO GLA- VO] In Hebræo: Et eris sicut dormiens in medio mari (id est, in insula fluctibus undique concussa) aut sicut jacens in summo mali: id est, ut nunc loquuntur, in galea navis, ubi maxima est agitatio.

De insula nulla hic mentio: sed de dormien- te in corde maris, adeoque in navigio, quod comma alterum docet: Sicut dormiens in capite, vel sum- mitate mali, vel in carchesio, qui vehementer jacta- tur, & in summo periculo versatur. Additur v. 35. per Mimesin in persona ebrii, ut Vulg. explicat: Et dices (quæ verba διαῤῥήδην in Ebr. non haben- tur) verberaverunt me, sed non dolui: traxerunt (in Ebr. percusserunt) me, & ego non sensi. Quando evigilabo, & rursus vina reperiam? In Ebr. adji- ciam & quæram illud (vinum) amplius. Ita stupor ingens, ac pene incredibilis atque incorrigibilis te- mulentia ebriorum depingitur. Conf. Es. 56, 12. Quantumcunque sit periculum, etiamsi excitentur, tundantur, percutiantur, non evigilant: & quum evigilarunt, periculo liberati iterum ad compo- tationes redeunt. Sicut nauclerus dormiens sinit navim agi in rupes, scyllas, & charybdes, quibus eliditur, vel circumrotatur, & mergitur: sic ebrius in mille fortunarum & vitæ pericula se abripi sinit. Clem. Alex. lib. 2. Pædag. cap. 2. Videtis naufragii periculum. Cor quidem multo potu obruitur, mul- tam autem temulentiam minis maris comparavit, in qua corpus tanquam navis demersum turpitudinis ac dedecoris profundum subiit, decumanis vini fluctibus obrutum. Gubernator autem, mens scil. huma- na supervenientis ebrietatis fluctu circumagitur, & in mari versans caligat, & propter procellæ tene- bras à portu veritatis aberrat, donec in saxa mari latentia irruens seipsum in voluptates impactum per- diderit.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV.

On patience in the success of the wicked, and fortitude in the day of distress, both our own and that of other righteous people. And on these things to be observed both by Magistrates in particular, and in common life.

Ver. 1. DO NOT ENVY EVIL MEN, DO NOT DESIRE TO BE WITH THEM.

It pertains first to patience that we conduct ourselves rightly when we see that the wicked, who are called men of malice, succeed in everything, neither envying them their temporary happiness (chap. 3, ver. 31 and chap. 23, ver. 17) nor mixing ourselves in impiety and participating in their malignant works: the reason for which matter is rendered both from the internal conscience and from the external harm of lips or speeches (ver. 2), because their heart meditates on plunder (or devastation, chap. 21, ver. 7, or injuries of every kind to be inflicted on a neighbor) and their lips speak of labor (troubles of every kind): because they deceive others with their speeches, or offer scandals: but if anyone seeks solid happiness and the increase of domestic affairs, Solomon shows him the means (ver. 3): By wisdom a house shall be built (whereas, on the contrary, the house of the impious is to be destroyed, chap. 11, ver. 14, even if it is built for a time by iniquity, Jer. 22, ver. 13, Am. 5, 11. Mich. 3, ver. 10.) and by understanding it shall be established (so that it may remain firm: Compare Isa. 54, ver. 15, Luke 14,

ver. 28.) ver. 4. And by knowledge the inner rooms (of the house, or chambers, chap. 7, ver. 27) shall be filled with all precious and pleasant riches. Whence, contrary to fanatics, the private possession of houses and faculties is approved.

Then, however, fortitude is required for the patience of the pious, by which not only are temptations overcome, but also, if wisdom is added, victory is obtained against enemies and in wars (ver. 5): A wise man is in fortitude: (wisdom not only contributes to opulence, but also to opposing fortitude against an unjust invader. Compare chap. 14, ver. 26, chap. 30, ver. 10.) And a skilled man strengthens his powers (wisdom excels strength) Compare chap. 21, ver. 12, Eccl. 9, ver. 16.) Perfect virtue remains always, as Ambrose says in his book on Jacob and the blessed life, chap. 8, among adversities and delights, nor do these add to life: nor do they diminish anything from its interest, nor do delights add to perfection. Ver. 6. Because by counsels you shall wage war, and (there shall be) safety (that is, victory) in the multitude of counselors. (Wars indeed seem to be waged more by force than by counsel. And yet safety and victory cannot be hoped for where everything is done rashly, nor are counselors skilled in military affairs at hand. (Compare C. 11, 14. C. 15, 22. Eccl. 8, 11.

And as divine wisdom must be joined with true Christian fortitude, so by antithesis to folly, Solomon discourses here on wisdom (ver. 7): High (or arduous, which he does not attain, Compare Ps. 139, ver. 6) are the wisdoms to a fool; (and therefore) in the gate (that is, in judgment, or public assemblies) he will not open his mouth. A foolish man, devoid of true wisdom, is not easily admitted to public judgments or into the senate, and once admitted, he does not dare to state his opinion, or at least he finally ruins his credit and authority through his speech, so that he may not dare to open his mouth easily thereafter. Ezek. 16, ver. 63. And that we may understand whom he points out as a fool, namely not only one rude in knowledge, but also a contemner of the divine word, some apophthegms are added, such as from public fame and the contempt of such men (ver. 8). He who plots to do evil, who is intent on evil, and performs evil with purpose, they will call him a man of evil thoughts; he will publicly receive this eulogy from everyone: so far is he from being called to public honorable assemblies. Ver. 9. (For) the thought of folly (or of a man of folly) is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to men. As the thoughts and counsels of such are sin before God, so they themselves, as scoffers and contemners of the Word of God, are an abomination to the pious and the wise, indeed to any men whatsoever, since no one willingly converses with such a buffoon and mocker. Compare chap. 3, ver. 32, chap. 11, ver. 1, 20, chap. 12, ver. 22, chap. 16, ver. 5, chap. 20, ver. 10, chap. 29, ver. 27. Fortitude and patience, of which Solomon continues to discourse, also do not fall at all upon such men (ver. 10): If you are slack, he says, (Vulg. [explicat si desperaveris lapsus] in the day of distress, your strength will be narrow, Vulg. will be diminished. He is not to be considered a brave and constant man who is too dejected in spirit during affliction, Psal. 27. last verse. Cf. Rom. 4. verses 18. 20. 1. Pet. 5. verse 8. Plato, when asked how one ought to be disposed regarding adverse circumstances, replied: in such a way that one takes care by foresight not to fall into them, but if through imprudence one has fallen into them, one should care nothing for them.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV.

De patientia, in successu improborum, & forti- tudine, in die angustiæ, cum nostræ, tum alio- rum justorum. Et de his tum Magistratibus imprimis, tum in vita communi observanda.

Vers. 1. NE ÆMULERIS VIROS MA- LOS, NE DESIDERES ESSE CUM EIS.

AD patientiam pertinet primum, ut recte nos geramus, cum improbis, qui homines dicuntur malitiæ, omnia succedere videmus, iis nec inviden- do temporariam felicitatem cap. 3. v. 31. & cap. 23. vers. 17. nec admiscendo nos in impietate, & com- municando malignis eorum operibus: cujus rei ratio redditur cum ab intrinseca conscientia, tum ab externa labiorum sermonumve noxa v. 2. quia rapinam meditatur cor eorum (vel devastationem, cap. 21. vers. 7. seu omnis generis injurias proximo inferendas) & laborem (omnis generis molestias) labia eorum loquuntur: quia sermonibus suis alios decipiunt, aut scandala præbent: si vero felicita- tem solidam & incrementum rei domesticæ quis expetat, medium ei monstrat Salomo vers. 3. Sa- pientia ædificabitur Domus (quum contra impiorum domus destruenda sit cap. 11. vers. 14. utut ad tem- pus iniquitate ædificetur Jer. 22. vers. 13. Am. 5, 11. Mich. 3. vers. 10.) & intelligentia stabilietur (ut firma maneat: Conf. Esa. 54. vers. 15. Luc. 14.

vers. 28.) vers. 4. Et scientia interiora (domus, vel conclavia cap. 7. vers. 27.) replebuntur, omni- bus opibus pretiosis & jucundis. Unde contra fana- ticos propria domuum & facultatum possessio pro- batur.

Deinde vero ad patientiam piorum requiri- tur fortitudo, qua non tantum tentationes superan- tur, sed etiam adversus hostes, & in bellis, si accedat sapientia, victoria obtinetur, vers. 5. Vir sapiens est in fortitudine: (sapientia non tantum conducit ad opulentiam, sed etiam ad fortitudinem injusto invasori opponendam. Confer. cap. 14. vers. 26. cap. 30. vers. 10.) Et vir peritus roborat vires (sa- pientia præstat viribus) Confer. cap. 21. vers. 12. Eccl. 9. vers. 16.) Manet semper, Ambrosio dicen- te libro de Jacob. & vita beat. cap. 8. inter adversa & delectabilia virtus perfecta nec is ad vitam: neque fœnori ejus quicquam minuunt, neque delectabilia ad- jungunt perfectioni. vers. 6. Quia consiliis facies bel- lum, & (erit) salus (id est, victoria) in multitu- dine consiliariorum. (Bella videntur quidem ma- gis vi quam consilio geri. Et tamen non potest spe- rari salus & victoria, ubi omnia temere aguntur, nec præsto sunt consiliarii rei bellicæ periti. (Conf. C. 11, 14. C. 15, 22. Eccl. 8, 11.

Uti vero divinam sapientiam cum fortitudine vera Christiana conjunctam esse oportet, ita per antithefin stultitiæ, de sapientia hic disserit Salomo vers. 7. Excelsæ (vel arduæ, quas non assequitur, Conf. Pf. 139. v. 6.) sunt stulto sapientiæ; (ideoque) in porta (id est in judicio, vel publicis consessibus) non aperiet os suum. Homo vecors, expers veræ sa- pientiæ nec ad judicia publica, vel in senatum facile admittitur, & admissus non audet sententiam dice- re, vel certe per sermonem tandem decoquit fi- dem, & autoritatem, ut deinceps non facile os suum aperire ausit. Ezech. 16. vers. 63. Et ut quemnam stultum indigitet, intelligamus, nimirum non so- lum rudem scientia, sed & contemtorem verbi divi- ni, adduntur adhuc apophthegmata nonnulla, ut- pote à fama publica & contemtu talium hominum v. 8. Qui machinatur male facere, qui intentus ad malum, & cum proæresi malum patrat, illum virum cogitationum malarum vocabunt, publice hoc elo- gium ab omnibus reportabit: tantum abest ut ad publicos honoratos consessus vocandus sit. V. 9. Cogitatio (enim) stultitiae (vel viri stultitiae) pec- catum est, & abominatio hominum derisor. Ut co- gitata & consilia talium coram Deo peccatum: ita ipsi ceu derisores & contemtores Verbi Dei abo- minationi sunt piis, & cordatis, imo quibusvis ho- minibus, siquidem nemo libenter cum tali scurra & empaecta conversetur. Conf. cap. 3. vers. 32. cap. 11. vers. 1, 20. cap. 12. vers. 22. cap. 16. vers. 5. cap. 20. vers. 10. cap. 29. vers. 27. In tales etiam minime cadit fortitudo ac patientia, de qua disserere pergit Salomo vers. 10. Si remissus, inquit, fueris, (Vulg. explicat si desperaveris lapsus) in die angustiae, an- gusta erit, Vulg. imminuetur, fortitudo tua. Non est pro forti & constante homine habendus, qui in afflictione nimium dejecto est animo Psal. 27. vers. ult. Conf. Rom. 4. vers. 18. 20. 1. Pet. 5. vers. 8. Pla- to interrogatus, quomodo animatum esse oporteat circa res adversas, respondit: ita ut quis providen- do caveat, ne in eas incidat, quod si per imprudentiam in eas inciderit, nihil curet.

## 24:11
Vers. 11. DELIVER THOSE WHO ARE BEING LED TO DEATH) Those who are dragged to death by force, as in Ps. 82:4.

It pertains to fortitude, in the day of distress, not only to endure with a generous and constant spirit those things which befall us, but also to liberate a neighbor who is unjustly oppressed, concerning which it is said here in verse 11: "Deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain" (such as were Joseph, Gen. 37, verse 20; David, 1 Sam. 20, verse 31; the Prophets, 1 Kings 18, verse 13, etc.) "and do not forsake them!" Whence Ambrose, lib. 1, Offic., cap. 36, teaches that this liberation of the innocent is an act of true fortitude: "The law of virtue consists not in inflicting injury, but in warding it off; for he who does not repel an injury from his companion, if he can, is as much in fault as he who commits it." Whence St. Moses began here by first repelling the excuses of a weak fortitude. Verse 12: "If thou sayest, behold, we knew not this" (Vulgat. wrongly, the strength is not sufficient: because ignorance, not a defect of power or strength, is pleaded) does not He who weighs the hearts understand it himself? (that this πρόφασιν is of no account) and does He who observes your soul (chap. 22. vers. 12. chap. 23. vers. 25.) not know it himself, and will He not render to man according to his work? (according to his work, so that the standard may be indicated, not the meritorious cause. Conf. c. 16. vers. 14. Apoc. 20. vers. 12. chap. 22. vers. 12. and what we have said at Rom. 2, 6. There follows therefore an exhortation to the pursuit of wisdom, without which that fortitude in the Lord is not obtained: which he compares to honey for its sweetness in vers. 13. Eat, my son, honey, because it is good: (Conf. Jud. 14. v. 18. Ezech. 3, 13. Ap. 10, 9.) and the honeycomb which is sweet to your palate: so the knowledge of wisdom (will be sweet) to your soul. Conf. Psalm. 19. vers. 11. Ps. 119, verse 103: just as utility is innate in honey along with sweetness, because it is beneficial to cold temperaments and the elderly, and is turned into the best blood: so also the knowledge of wisdom is not only pleasant, but also most healthful. 2 Tim. 3, verse 15; v. 14: If you have found it, then there will be a reward, or recompense: and your expectation will not be cut off. Compare chapter 23, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ERVE EOS QVI DVCVNTVR AD MORTEM) Qui per vim ad mortem trahuntur, ut Pf. 82, 4.

Ad fortitudinem pertinet, in die angustiae non ea modo animo generoso & constante sustinere, quae nobis eveniunt, sed proximum etiam injuste oppressum liberare, quo de hic vers. 11. erue eos, qui raptantur ad mortem, & num eos qui divertunt ad occifionem (quales erant Joseph. Gen. 37. vers. 20. David 1. Sam. 20. vers. 31. Prophetae 1. Reg. 18. vers. 13. &c.) deseres! Unde Ambros. lib. 1. Offic. cap. 36. hanc innocentis liberationem actum esse verae fortitudinis docet: Non in inferenda sed de- pellenda injuria lex virtutis est: qui enim non re- pellit a socio injuriam, si potest, tam est in vitio, quam ille qui facit. Unde S. Moses hinc prius orsus est ten- tamenta imbecillis fortitudinis repellere. Vers. 12. Si dixeris, profecto ignoravimus istud (Vulgat. perpe- ram, vires non suppetunt: quia ignorantia, non v. defectus potentiae vel virium praetexitur) nonne qui ponderat corda, ipse intelliget? (nihili esse hanc πρόφασιν) & qui observat animam tuam (cap. 22. vers. 12. cap. 23. vers. 25.) ipse cognoscet, reddetque homini secundum opus suum? (secundum opus, ut norma indicetur, non causa meritoria. Conf. c. 16. vers. 14. Apoc. 20. vers. 12. cap. 22. vers. 12. & quae ad Rom. 2, 6. diximus. Sequitur ergo exhortatio ad studium sapientiae, sine qua ista fortitudo in Domi- no non obtinetur: quam melli ob suavitatem comparat vers. 13. Comede, fili mi, mel, quia bonum est: (Conf. Jud. 14. v. 18. Ezech. 3, 13. Ap. 10, 9.) & favum qui dulcis est palato tuo: sic cognitio sa- pientiae (suavis erit) animae tuae. Conf. Psalm. 19. vers. 11. Pf, 119. vers. 103. ut in melle cum dulcedine connata est utilitas, quia frigidis naturis & senibus commodum est, & in optimum vertitur sangui- nem: sic etiam sapientiae cognitio non jucunda modo, sed & saluberrima est 2. Tim. 3. vers. 15. v. 14. Si inveneris eam, tunc (erit) merces, vel prae- mium: & expectatio tua non excidetur. Confer. cap. 23, 18.

## 24:15
Ver. 15. NOR LAY WASTE THE REST

With the reward, however, security against the snares of the wicked is promised at the same time, and a raising up from former falls, ver. 15. Lie not in wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous, nor plunder his resting place (where the righteous has his rest like a beast, Isa. 65, 10. Jer. 50. ver. 6.) ver. 16. For the righteous falls seven times into spiritual temptations, or worldly and bodily misfortune, c. 11, 5. 14. c. 13, 12. c. 17, 20. 25. 27. c. 28, 10. Ps. 37, 24. 34, 20. Job 5, 19.) and shall rise again. But the wicked fall into evil, so that, to wit, they do not rise again. Jer. 21, 3. Ps. 18, 39. Jer. 8, 4. Grotius has it thus: FOR THE JUST MAN SHALL FALL SEVEN TIMES AND SHALL RISE AGAIN: BUT THE WICKED SHALL FALL INTO EVIL] Another proverb of the same sense exists among the Hebrews: Seven pits for the peaceful man: supply, are built, which he escapes) but one for the worker of evil, supply, is enough: he falls immediately: for to fall here is to be oppressed by adversities. A similar sentiment is in Ps. 34, 20 and 37, 23. Beware of taking these as referring to sins. For nowhere among the Hebrews is נָפַל to sin. But נָפַל and קוּם are opposed to each other when it is a matter of calamities. Mic. 7, 8. Amos 8, 14. Jer. 25, 27. Isa. 24, 20.

Which must be opposed to certain Papists, especially Bellarmine, who take it as referring to a fall into sin, from whom, however, they depart, and side with us: Isidor Clarius, Jansenius, Saa, Salazar, Delrio, etc.; then to the Calvinists, such as the Leideners in Censur. Conf. Rem. p. 180, and others who likewise explain it as referring to the frequent sins of the just: whom most Reformed interpreters here desert, Lavater, Junius, Piscator, Amama, the Dutch Annotations, etc., with St. Augustine, l. 11, de Civ. Dei c. 31, B. Luther, and others of our own who interpret the present passage as referring to a fall of calamity, not of prevarication. The number seven, says St. Augustine, is often put for the whole, just as it is written: the just man shall fall seven times, and shall rise again: as often as he shall have fallen, he shall not perish. Which he wished to be understood not of iniquity, but of tribulations leading to humility: And Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges that the Hebrew text favors this exposition, even though he prefers to take it as referring to the fall of the just into guilt for the sake of his Vulgate, wrongly dragging it along with others to indefectible justice: which truly just men can indeed lose, and fall into deliberate and mortal sins, as both the examples of Scripture and clear testimonies teach. See Exegema Aug. Conf. art. 13.

Furthermore, on this occasion of the ruin of enemies, Solomon dissuades the pious from ἐπιχαιρεκακία (rejoicing in evil) v. 17. When your enemy falls, do not rejoice. Conf. Isa. 15, 2. Amos 7, 8. Obad. v. 12.) and when he stumbles, let not your heart exult: lest perhaps (Solomon continues v. 18.) the Lord see, and it displease (or be evil) in his eyes (inasmuch as he looks upon the heart 1 Sam. 16, 7. Ps. 11, 4.) and turn his favor away from him: and so, as Pagninus rightly says, turn the law of retaliation upon you. Conf. Prov. 17, 8. Job 31, 20. Ezek. 25, 3. Obad. v. 12, 13.

Finally, the prior dissuasion from impatient emulation of the wicked is repeated, equipped and fortified with new arguments and necessary warnings: Do not be inflamed (inflame yourself) with anger, the ellipsis of which word is to be supplied here. Conf. Ps. 18, 8. Symmachus rendered it μὴ παροργίζου (do not be provoked). B. Luther: erzürne dich nicht (do not be angry): (which sense, following the clause, the interpretation of Aquila and Theodotion μὴ διαμάχου (do not fight), and the Vulgate 'do not contend', as also that of Aben-Ezra and Pagninus, 'do not have dealings with the wicked', teaches is to be preferred: for it is added for the sake of explanation) and do not emulate the wicked (conf. v. 1.) as also v. 20, because there will be no reward for the evil man: For thus the reason is given why we should not be inflamed on account of the success of the wicked, from their unhappy end. Conf. Ps. 37, 9 and 73. THE LAMP OF THE WICKED SHALL BE EXTINGUISHED. Conf. c. 13, 32. c. 20, 20. c. 3, 32. Job 18, 5. These are the newest warnings, containing as it were the sum of the others by way of recapitulation, v. 21. Fear the Lord, my son, and the King (Conf. Eccl. 12, v. 13. Rom. 13, 4, 5. 1 Pet. 2, 13. (with those who dissent (who fear neither God nor the King, which force of the word שׁוֹנִים is gathered from Esth. 3, 8 and the preceding member) do not mix yourself: Conf. 1 Cor. 5, 9, 11. 2 Thess. 3, 14. Since, as v.

22. it is added, their destruction shall rise suddenly (where it is not rashly observed by Dr. Geier that their punishment is noted as unexpected, impetuous, certain, and horrible) And the destructions of both (both of God and of the King) who knows? namely, when it shall be. Thus the author of the Greek Catena from the LXX Interpreters. For suddenly God and the King exact vengeance and punishment from wicked men: but who understands the manner and reason of the punishments of both? Thus Aben-Ezra, Jansenius, Bainius, Dr. Geier, and others. What some codices of the LXX Interpreters add here, see in Cornelius à Lapide; we pass them by as not being Solomon's.

Latin:

Vers. 15. NEQVE VASTES REQVIEM EJVS) Id est, ne tur- bes ejus quietem.

Cum praemiatione autem promittitur simul securitas adversus impiorum insidias, & erectio a lapsibus priorum, vers. 15. Ne insidieris, ô impie, ha- bitaculo justi, nec diripias accubitum ejus (ubi ju- stus instar jumenti suam habet requiem Esa. 65, 10. Jer. 50. vers. 6.) vers. 16. Quia septies cadit justus in tentationes spirituales, aut infortunium munda- num, & corporale, c. 11, 5. 14. c. 13, 12. c. 17, 20. 25. 27. c. 28, 10. Psal. 37, 24. 34, 20. Job. 5, 19.) & resurget. Im- pii autem corruunt in malum, ut sc. non resurgant. Jer. 21, 3. Psal. 18, 39. Jer. 8, 4. Grotius ita habet: SEPTIES ENIM CADET JVSTVS ET RESVR- GET: IMPII AVTEM CORRVENT IN MALVM] Ejusdem sensus proverbium est alterum apud Hebræos: Se- ptem foveæ pacifico: supple struuntur, quas evadit) at una ope- ranti malum, supple sufficit: statim ruit: nam cadere hic est adversis premi. Similis sententia Psalm. 34, 20. & 37, 23. Ca- ve de peccatis hæc accipias. Nusquam enim Hebræis נָפַל est peccare. Sed נָפַל & קוּם inter se opponuntur ubi de calamitatibus agitur. Mich. 7, 8. Amos 8, 14. Jerem. 25, 27. Esaiæ 24, 20.

Quæ opponenda cum Papistis quibusdam, imprimis Bellarmino de prolapsu in peccatum acci- pientibus, a quibus tamen discedunt, & nobiscum faciunt Isidor. Clarius, Jansenius, Saa, Salazarus, Delrio, &c. tum Calvinianis, utpote Leidenfibus in Censur. Conf. Rem. p. 180. aliisque itidem de justo- rum frequentibus peccatis explicantibus: quos de- serunt hic Interpretes plerique Reformati, Lavater. Junius, Piscator, Amama, Belgici Annotat. &c. cum S. August. l. 11. de Civ. Dei c. 31. B. Luthero, aliis que nostratibus de lapsu calamitatis, non prævari- cationis locum præsentem interpretantibus. Septe- narius numerus inquit S. August, pro universo sæpe ponitur, sicut scriptum est: septies cadet justus, & re- surget: quoties cum cediderit, non peribit. Quod non de iniquitate, sed de tribulationibus ad humili- tatem perducentibus intelligi voluit: Atque huic ex- positioni favere textum Ebræorum agnoscit Cor- nelius à Lapide, etsi in gratiam Vulgatæ suæ de casu justi in culpam accipere malit, perperam id cum aliis ad justitiam inamissibilem abripiens: quam utique vere justos etiam amittere, & in peccata proæretica, & mortalia incidere cum exempla Scripturæ, tum luculenta testimonia docent. Vid. Exegema Aug. Conf. art. 13.

Cæterum hac de ruina hostium occasione, de- hortatur Salomo pios ab ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ v. 17. Cum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne læteris. Conf. Esa. 15, 2. Amos 7, 8. Obad. v. 12.) & cum impegerit, ne exul- tet cor tuum: ne forte (pergit Salomo v. 18.) vi- deat dominus, & displiceat (aut malum sit) in oculis ejus (utpote qui cor intuetur 1. Sam. 16, 7. Pf. 11, 4.) & avertat ab eo favorem suum: adeoque, ut recte Pagninus, vi talionis in te convertat. Conf. Prov. 17, 8. Job. 31, 20. Ezech. 25, 3. Obad. v. 12. 13.

Tandem repetitur prior dehortatio ab impa- tiente impiorum æmulatione novis argumentis, & monitis necessariis instructa, & stipata: Ne accen- daris (inflammes teipsum) ira, cujus vocis ellipsis hic supplenda. Conf. Psal. 18, 8. Symmachus red- didit μὴ παροργίζε. B. Luther. erzürne dich nicht: (quem sensum sequens comma interpretationi A- quilæ & Theod. μὴ διαμάχου ne pugnes, & Vulgatæ ne contendas, ut & Aben-Ezræ & Pagnini, ne commer- cium habeas cum malignis, præferendum esse docet: additur enim ἐξηγήσεως gratia) & ne æmuleris im- pios (conf. v. 1.) ut & v. 20. quia non erit præmium ho- mini malo: Ita enim ratio redditur, cur non inflam- mari debeamus ob successum impiorum, ab infeli- ci eorum exitu. Conf. Psal. 37, 9. & 73. LUCER- NA IMPIORUM EXTINGUETUR. Conf. c. 13, 32. c. 20, 20. c. 3, 32. Job. 18, 5. Monita novissi- ma hæc sunt summam veluti cæterorum per ἀνακε- φαλαίωσιν continentia, v. 21. Time Dominum fili mi, & Regem (Conf. Eccl. 12. vers. 13. Rom. 13, 4. 5. 1. Petr. 2, 13. (cum discrepantibus (qui nec Deum timent nec Regem, quæ vocis שׁוֹנִים vis ex Esth. 3, 8. & membro præcedenti colligitur)ne admisceas te: Conf. 1. Cor. 5, 9. 11. 2. Thes. 3, 14. Quoniam, ut v.

22. additur, repente consurget contritio eorum (ubi pœnam ipsorum notari, ceu inopinatam, impetuo- sam, indubiam, & horrendam, non temere observat Dn. D. Geierus) Et contritiones amborum (tum Dei, tum Regis) quis scit? quando nempe ea futu- ra sit. Ita auctor Cat. Græc. ex LXX. Interpp. Re- pente namque de impiis hominibus vindictam & pœ- nam exigunt Deus & Rex: modum autem & ratio- nem suppliciorum utriusque quis intelligit? Sic Aben- Ezra, Jansenius, Bainius, Dn. D. Geierus, & alii. Quæ hic addunt nonnulli Codices LXX. Interpp. vid. apud Cornel. a Lap. nos ea ceu non Salomonea præterimus.

## 24:21
v. 21. FEAR THE LORD, MY SON, AND THE KING] Sophocles in Ajax: For in the future we shall know to yield to the gods, and we shall learn to revere the Atreidae; they are rulers.

Latin:

Vers. 21. TIME DOMINVM, FILI MI, ET REGEM] Sophocles Ajace: Τοὶ γὰρ τὸ λοιπὸν εἰσόμεσθα μὲν θεοῖς Εἴκειν, μαθησόμεσθα δ᾽ Ἀτρείδας σέβειν· Ἄρχοντές εἰσιν.

## 24:23
Ver. 23. THESE ALSO TO THE WISE) It is better to translate the ל as a genitive, as is often done. These also of the Wise, as, καὶ τάδε Φωκυλίδεω. The sentences which follow were added from the books of the Wise after Solomon and before the times of Hezekiah.

It is not asserted that they are from the books of the Wise, which were added after Solomon. Grotius assumes this precariously, indeed contrary to the force of the particle גם also: which implies that these are not of a different condition, but makes them equal to the others and of the same kind: because they contribute equally to the strengthening of the wise. Nor is there a reason why he should desert the Vulgate here, rendering it in the Dative, with which the Chaldean version and the LXX Interpreters agree, who interpret the Hebrew thus: I say these things to the Wise, as the Vulgate: These also to the Wise, i.e., let them be spoken. In a similar sense others say the prefix ל is a preposition, which signifies TO or FOR: Even these (pertain) to the Wise or (are handed down) for the Wise, or if the genitive is retained, it could be explained in the same sense: Even these (are) of the Wise, that is, they are suitable for them, as in chapter 31, 1. it is not of Kings, or it is suitable for Kings. Then even if you explain it most with Rasvenaki: These also are sentences of the Wise added here to the previous ones, which, namely, are contained in the 12 verses up to the end of the chapter, it is not however to be concluded therefore that they are not Solomon's: For they can be called the Wise's, because they were added by the Wise collected from the writings of Solomon, but not by the men of Hezekiah, as are those which follow in c. 25, 1. sqq. But Mercerus rightly observes that the former sense is more correct: When he had brought forward very many sentences, both at the beginning of the chapter and up to this place for informing the Wise, and for instructing them in every manner of life, as Solomon was wonderful and excellent, he now adds that the Wise ought to attend also to these things which follow up to the end of the chapter, and be warned about them. Thus also Junius, the Italian, English, and Genevan versions, and Sixtinus Amama: Even these pertain to the Wise. Cornelius a Lapide agrees; and Menochius, who has it thus: The sentence is: these things also which follow are said to the Wise, for it will profit the foolish nothing to be taught. Cartwright on this passage: The preface prefixed to these verses is common to the rest up to the end of this chapter, indicating that they all (which embrace the duties of men of any order and condition) look to the Wise. Whoever therefore does not attend to these, and thinks they do not pertain to him, is held to be a fool not so much by the judgment of Solomon, the wisest man, as by that of God, who alone is wise.

Ver. same. TO RECOGNIZE A PERSON IN JUDGMENT IS NOT GOOD.

Moreover, sentences both Political and Economic are handed down here, likewise pertaining to the wise. The first is Political concerning the avoiding of respect of persons: To recognize a face or person (namely, his external condition, dignity, wealth, kinship, by which as if by a face visible from the outside one is distinguished by others) is not good. Conf. c. 18, 5. That this may not happen, it is added v. 24. to the one saying to the wicked (out of such προσωποληψίᾳ) you are righteous, the peoples will curse. (Conf. c. 17, 15. Isa. 5, 33. ch. 24, 24.) the nations will detest him: with the antithesis subjoined v. 25. But to those who rebuke (the wicked) it will be pleasant, and upon them will come the blessing of good. From the antithesis it is clear that this is to be understood concerning the praise and blessing of the people: yet such public blessings are not void, for divine blessings follow them. The remaining sentences pertain to domestic prudence and to common life: (1.) Concerning right answers v. 26. He will kiss the lips, who answers right words, or in justice. c. 8, 8. 9. he is so grateful, namely, for right speeches, which dispel errors or doubts, instruct usefully, and console sweetly, just as one kisses the lips of a friend, which are accustomed to be sweet and pleasant. Gen. 27, 26. c. 48. 10. 1. Reg. 19, 20. Cant. 1, 2. c. 8, 1.

(2.) Concerning due industry and prudence in family affairs, so that, namely, the more necessary things are done first, and then those things follow which make for greater convenience: v. 27. Dispose your work outside, and prepare it in the field for yourself (to which the care both of livestock c. 27, 23. 26. and of agriculture c. 12, 12. is recommended above all: which are to be handled outside and in the field, not under a roof or within walls: since the Israelites were for a great part either shepherds or farmers:) and afterwards you will build a house. For they used tents in olden times, to which houses succeeded later: and thus Solomon means this, that they should be content with huts or tents and attend to their livestock and agriculture first, before they build houses and buildings for themselves; because through those means those things must first be acquired by which a house can be built. (3.) Concerning avoiding false testimony. v. 28. Do not be a witness rashly (that is, rash or lying. See B. Glass. b. 3. Phil. S. tr. 1. c. 10.)

against your neighbor, (whether in private meetings, or in public judgments c. 6, 19. c. 12, 17. c. 14, 5. 25. c. 19, 5. 9. 28. c. 21, 28.) and do not deceive with your lips, which Cornelius understands as concerning those who slander, with Bede, Hugo, Lyranus, and Jansenius; but more correctly with B.

Luther, according to the received meaning of the word פתה, it is understood as concerning seduction. (4.) Concerning private vengeance v. 29. Do not say, as he did to me, so I will do to him: I will render to the man according to his work,

Compare Deut. 32, 35. Rom. 12, 19. (5.) Concerning the losses of sloth, which Solomon recounts from his own experience v. 30. I passed by the field of the slothful man, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding (void of heart c. 7, 7. c. 9, 4. c. 11,

12.) And behold (as is added v. 31.) there had grown up (over) the whole of it thorns (Compare Gen. 3, 18. Drusius in his praeterita on Matt. 13, 7. renders it, the whole of it grew up with nettles) Its surface was covered with nettles: and the stone wall thereof was broken down, (so that it lay open to wild beasts and animals. Compare Ps. 80, 13.) And when I looked I applied my heart (c. 22, 17.) I saw, I say, and received instruction (lest, that is, I should be concerned about such sloth of mine. For happy is he whom the dangers of others make cautious) v. 33. a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep (compare c. 6, 10. 11.) v. 34. and thy poverty shall come (as) a traveler, and thy want as an armed man. Those who by sleeping and doing nothing neglect their calling, and by procrastinating lead their life from day to day, shall be overwhelmed by destitution: it will arrive to them swiftly like a traveler, who day by day draws some miles nearer: and want invades the slothful so powerfully, that they can no more repel it than an unarmed man can a well-armed man.

Latin:

Vers. 23. HÆC QVOQVE SAPIENTIBVS) Melius ל per genitivum transferas, ut sæpe. Hæc quoque Sapientum, ut, καὶ τάδε Φωκυλίδεω. Quæ sequuntur sententiæ adjectæ sunt è Sapientum libris post Salomonem ante Ezechiæ tem- pora.

Id non asseritur quod è Sapientum libris, qui post Salomonem adjectæ sint. Precario hoc assumit Grotius, imo contra vim particulæ גם etiam: quæ non disparis conditionis hæc esse innuit, sed cæteris paria & ejusdem generis facit: quod æque ad sa- pientes firmandos conducant. Neque causa est, cur hic Vulgatum deserat, in Dativo reddentem, cui consonat Chaldaico versio & LXX. Interpp. qui ita interpretantur Ebræa: hæc Sapientibus dico, uti Vulgata: Hæc quoque Sapientibus sc. dicta sunto. Si- mili sensu alii præfixum ל præpositionem esse ajunt, quæ significat AD vel PRO: Etiam hæc ad Sapi- entes (pertinent) vel pro Sapientibus (traduntur) vel si genitivus retineatur, eodem sensu explicari poterit: Etiam hæc Sapientum (sunt) id est, illis conveniunt, ut cap. 31, 1. non Regum est, vel Regibus convenit. Tum si maxime cum Rasvenaki expo- nas: Etiam hæ sunt sententiæ Sapientum hic ad su- periores additæ, quæ sc. 12. versiculis usque ad finem capitis continentur, non tamen statuendum ideo, quod Salomonis non sint: Nam Sapientum dici possunt, quod à Sapientibus collectæ è Salomonis scriptis adjectæ sint, sed non à viris Ezechiæ, uti quæ sequuntur c. 25, 1. seqq. Sed priorem sensum rectio- rem esse, merito observat Mercerus: Quum quam plurimas sententias attulisset, & initio capitis ad hunc usque locum ad informandos Sapientes, & instituendos in omni vitæ ratione, uti mirus fuit, & eximius Salo- mo, nunc subdit, etiam ad hæc quæ sequuntur usq; ad finem capitis advertere oportere Sapientes, & de his esse monitos. Sic etiam Junius, Ital. Angl. Genev. versio, & Sixtinus Amama: Etiam hæc ad Sapien- tes pertinere. Annuit Cornelius à Lapide; & Me- nochius, qui ita habet: Sententia est: hæc etiam quæ sequuntur, dici Sapientibus, nam insipientibus nihil profuerit doceri. Cartwrightus in h. l.
