Præfa- tio hisce versibus præfixa, reliquis ad ultimum hujus capitis communis est, eos omnes (qui hominum cujus- libet ordinis & conditionis officia complectuntur) ad Sapientes spectare, indicans. Quicunque igitur his non attendit, nec ad se pertinere opinatur, insipiens non tam Salomonis sapientissimi viri, quam Dei, qui solus sapiens est, judicio habetur.

Vers. eod. COGNOSCERE IN JUDICIO PERSONAM NON EST BONUM.

Traduntur autem hic sententiæ tum Politicæ, tum Oeconomicæ, ad sapientes itidem spectantes. Prima est Politica de vitanda prosopolepsia: Agno- scere faciem vel personam (externam sc. ejus con- ditionem, dignitatem, opulentiam, cognationem, quibus quasi vultu foris conspicuo dignoscitur quis ab aliis) non est bonum. Conf. c. 18, 5. Quod ne fiat additur v. 24. dicenti impio (ex ejusmodi προσωπο- ληψίᾳ) justus es, maledicent populi. (Conf. c. 17, 15. Esa. 5, 33. cap. 24, 24.) detestabuntur eum natio- nes: subjuncta antithefi v. 25. Sed corripientibus (impium) fuavis erit Dominus, & super eos veniet benedictio boni. Ex antithefi patet de laude ac be- nedictione populi hoc accipiendum esse: publicæ tamen ejusmodi benedictiones non sunt irritæ, se- quuntur enim easdem divinæ benedictiones. Cæ- teræ sententiæ ad prudentiam Oeconomicam, & ad vitam communem spectant: (1.) De responsis re- ctis v. 26. Labia deosculabitur, qui respondet verba recta, seu in justitia. c. 8, 8. 9. adeo sc. gratus est ser- monibus rectis, errores aut dubia dispellentibus, utiliter instruentibus, suaviter consolantibus, ut qui amici labia osculatur, quæ suavia & grata esse solent. Gen. 27, 26. c. 48. 10. 1. Reg. 19, 20. Cant. 1, 2. c. 8, 1.

(2.) De debita in re familiari industria, & pruden- tia, ut nempe prius magis necessaria agantur, se- quantur deinde ad commoditatem majorem facien- tia: v. 27. Dispone foris opus tuum, & præpara illud in agro tibi (quibus cura tum fœturæ c. 27, 23. 26. tum agriculturæ c. 12, 12. ante omnia commenda- tur: quæ foris & in agro tractanda, non sub tecto, vel intra mœnia: siquidem Israëlitæ magnam par- tem vel pastores erant, vel agricolæ:) & postea ædi- ficabis domum. Utebantur enim olim tabernaculis, quibus postmodum successêre domus: adeoque id vult Salomo, ut tuguriolis vel tabernaculis conten- ti suæ rei pecuariæ & agriculturæ prius vacent, ante- quam sibi domos & ædificia extruant; quia pri- mum per illa media ejusmodi acquirenda sunt, qui- bus domus ædificari possit. (3.) De falso testimonio vitando. v. 28. Ne sis testis temere (id est, temerarius vel mendax. Vid. B. Glass. l. 3. Phil. S. tr. 1. c. 10.)

contra proximum tuum, (seu in privatis congressi- bus, seu in publicis judiciis c. 6, 19. c. 12, 17. c. 14, 5. 25. c. 19, 5. 9. 28. c. 21, 28.) & ne decipias labiis tuis, quod de calumniantibus cum Beda, Hugone, Ly- rano, Jansenio accipit Cornelius; sed rectius cum B.

Luthero secundum receptam verbi פתה significa- tionem de seductione intelligitur. (4.) De privata vindicta v. 29. Ne dicas, quemadmodum fecit mihi, sic faciam ei: reddam ipsi viro secundum opus suum,

Conf. Deut. 32, 35. Rom. 12, 19. (5.) De damnis pi- gritiæ, quæ e propria experientia recenset Salomo v. 30. Juxta agrum hominis pigri transivi, & juxta vineam carentis corde (vecordis c. 7, 7. c. 9, 4. c. 11,

12.) Et ecce (ut additur v. 31.) ascenderant (per) totum ipsum spinæ (Conf. Genes. 3, 18. Drusius in præter. ad Matth. 13, 7. reddit, ascendit totus ipse ur- ticis) Tegebatur superficies ejus urticis: & clausu- ra lapidum ejus destructa erat, (ut pateret feris ac be- stiis. Conf. Pf. 80, 13.) Et cum intuerer ego apposui cor meum (c. 22, 17.) Vidi, inquam, & accepi eru- ditionem (ne sc. tali socordia mea curarem. Felix enim quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum) v. 33. pufillum somni, pusillum dormitationum, pusillum complicationis manuum ad dormiendum (conf. c. 6, 10. 11.) v. 34. & veniet (tanquam) viator pauper- tas tua, & penuria tua tanquam vir scutatus. Qui dormiendo & nihil agendo vocationem suam ne- gligunt, & procrastinando diem ex die ducunt, ege- state obruentur: ea velociter illis aderit instar viatoris, qui in dies aliquod milliaria propius acce- dit: & inopia tam potenter desides invadit, ut eam non magis repellere queant, quam homo inermis virum optime armatum.

## 25:1 Argument
SECTION II. SENTENCES COLLECTED BY THE HEZEKIANS. CHAPTER XXV. Moral admonitions concerning Kings and political conduct, as well as common conduct with one's neighbor, even an enemy, and the resulting good name.

Verse 1.

THESE ALSO ARE PARABLES WHICH THEY TRANSLATED) That is, gathered together.

THE MEN OF HEZEKIAH KING OF JUDAH) The collectors, Eliakim, Shebna, Joah, mentioned in 2 Kings 18, 26.

It is not said there that they gathered them: but whoever these men of Hezekiah were, among whom Isaiah is believed to have been the chief, that they gathered them by the divine Spirit, and not from writings adorned by human prudence, or even of various authors, as Grotius thinks, but from the Solomonic ones, is convinced both by the origin and authority of the Canonical Scripture, of which these chapters are a certain part: and by the inscription of this chapter: These also are Parables of Solomon. Compare what was said at the beginning of the book.

Latin:

SECTIO II. SENTENTIÆ AB HISKIANIS COLLECTÆ. CAPUT XXV. De Regibus & conversatione Politica, nec non de conversatione communi cum proximo, etiam inimico, & consequente nomine bono, moralia monita.

Vers. 1.

HÆC QVOQVE PARABOLÆ QVAS TRANSTV- LERVNT) Id est, congesserunt.

VIRI ERECHIÆ REGIS JVDÆ) Eclogarii, Eliacim, Sobna, Joahe, memorati 2. Reg. 18, 26.

ILlos congessisse ibi non dicitur: Quicunque autem isti viri Ezechiæ fuerint, inter quos præcipuus creditur fuisse Esaias, divino Spiritu eosdem con- gessisse, nec e Scriptis humana prudentia adornatis, vel variorum etiam auctorum, uti putat Grotius, sed e Salomoneis, tum Scripturæ Canonicæ origo & au- ctoritas, cujus hæc capita pars quædam sunt: tum capitis hujus ἐπιγραφὴ: Etiam hæ sunt Parabolæ Sa- lomonis, convincunt. Conf. quæ sub initium libri dicta sunt.

## 25:2
Verse 2.

IT IS THE GLORY OF GOD TO CONCEAL A THING) A thing, that is, a matter, for instance His nature and many decrees. For it is holier to believe concerning God than to know, to speak with Tacitus. Philemon: Θεὸν νόμιζε καὶ σέβυ· ζήτει δὲ μή· Πλέον γὰρ ἐδὲν ἄλλο τῆ ζητεῖν ἔχεις. The same: Τί ἐςιν ὁ θεὸς, ὐ θέλησε μανθάνειν. Pindar: Τὰ θεῶν βυλεύματα ἐρευνῆσαι Βροτείᾳ φρενὶ δύσκολον. θνατᾶς Δ' ἀπὸ ματρὸς ἔφυς. Sophron: Ὡς μᾶλλον ὅςις εἰδέναι τὰ τῶν θεῶν Ζητεῖ, τοσύτῳ μᾶλλον ἧσσον εἴσεται. See Rom 11, 33.

AND THE GLORY OF KINGS IS TO SEARCH OUT A MATTER) That is, the affairs of their subjects: wealth, actions, counsels.

The government and judgments of God, the King of Kings, and of earthly kings are compared; because the οἰκονομία of divine government and the judgments of God are hidden and occult. Rom. 11:33, Is. 40. But worldly kings ought not only to scrutinize more accurately themselves those things which pertain to the administration of their kingdoms and to judgments, but they also ought not to conceal them, so that by prior just exploration they may administer justice in the public light, and openly prove to others the reasons for their judgments and deeds: which contributes to conciliating the love of subjects toward kings. For the antithesis demands this sense. But the former member is ineptly snatched away by Socinus to the obscurity of divine oracles in lection. sacr. p. 50, because דבר here signifies not a word, but a thing. Also inept is the explanation of Cornelius a Lapide: it pertains to the glory of God that priests and doctors conceal some of his words, so that the common people, not understanding them, may admire and worship. This admiration is blind if the τὸ ὅτι (the 'that') is not understood: just as, on the contrary, admiration is pious when we do not understand the τὸ διότι (the 'why'). What we are completely ignorant of, and about which we know or understand nothing at all, how can we either admire or worship it? Nor is it the duty of doctors to conceal, but to explain the Word of God, by the example of Paul, Acts 20:27. And Cornelius later confesses that the antithesis of God and kings more strongly persuades one to refer the concealing to God, not to man, and adds his vote to our explanation: It is the glory of God to conceal the reasons for his decrees and judgments, so that he may show his eminent majesty, dominion, and power: but indeed, for kings, to decree nothing, to judge nothing, unless by a prior exact examination, so that it may be established that the law or sentence is just, honest, and useful: because they ought to manifest why they judge or decree thus. To this also returns the explanation of Jansenius: Just as it makes for the glory of God that he ought not to inquire about any matter, but that, since he knows all things, he nevertheless conceals very many: so on the contrary it makes for the glory of Kings that, although they ought to admit that as men they do not know most things, they diligently scrutinize matters necessary to be known, so that they may discover and direct those things that have been investigated. Therefore, those things which are held in Tob. 12:7 do not conflict with such an opinion: It is good to hide the secret of a King: but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God. For there it is a matter of the concealment of the King's counsels, which he does not wish to be known publicly, and of the public proclamation of the works of God, which he himself wishes to be revealed to all: but here it is a matter of the occultation of divine judgments and decrees, which he hides within himself, and of the investigation and manifestation of those things which it concerns both Kings and others to know.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

GLORIA DEI EST CELARE VERBVM) Verbum, id est, rem, puta naturam suam & decreta multa. Sanctius enim de Deo credere quam scire, ut cum Tacito loquar. Philemon: Θεὸν νόμιζε καὶ σέβυ· ζήτει δὲ μή· Πλέον γὰρ ἐδὲν ἄλλο τῆ ζητεῖν ἔχεις. Idem: Τί ἐςιν ὁ θεὸς, ὐ θέλησε μανθάνειν. Pindarus: Τὰ θεῶν βυλεύματα ἐρευνῆσαι Βροτείᾳ φρενὶ δύσκολον. θνατᾶς Δ' ἀπὸ ματρὸς ἔφυς. Sophron: Ὡς μᾶλλον ὅςις εἰδέναι τὰ τῶν θεῶν Ζητεῖ, τοσύτῳ μᾶλλον ἧσσον εἴσεται. Vide Rom 11, 33.

ET GLORIA REGVM INVESTIGARE SERMO- NEM) Id est, res subditorum suorum: opes, actiones, consilia.

Conferuntur Dei Regis Regum, & terreno- rum Regum gubernatio & judicia; quia regiminis divini οἰκονομία, & judicia Dei abscondita & occul- ta sunt. Rom. 11, 33. Es. 40. Reges autem mundani ea, quæ ad regnorum suorum administrationem, & judicia pertinent, non tantum scrutari accuratius ipsi, sed ea etiam non celare debent, ut prævia justa exploratione in luce publica justitiam admini- strent, rationes judiciorum factorumque suorum aliis palam probent: quod facit ad amorem subdi- torum erga Reges conciliandum. Hunc enim sen- sum antithesis postulat. Inepte autem prius mem- brum a Socino abripitur ad obscuritatem oraculo- rum divinorum in lection. sacr. p. 50. quia דבר non verbum hic, sed rem significat. Inepta etiam est ex- plicatio Cornelii a Lap. ad gloriam Dei pertinet, quod Sacerdotes & Doctores nonnulla ejus verba ab- scondant, ut vulgus ea non intelligens admiretur, & colat. Cæca est hæc admiratio, si non intelligatur τὸ ὅτι: quemadmodum contra pia admiratio, cum τὸ διότι non intelligimus. Quod plane ignoramus, & de quo nihil omnino scimus, vel intelligimus, quomodo vel admirari, vel colere possumus? Ne- que Doctorum est abscondere, sed explicare Dei Verbum, exemplo Pauli Actor. 20, 27. Et fatetur postea Cornelius antithesin Dei & Regum magis suadere τὸ celare Deum referre, non hominem, no- stræque explicationi calculum adjicit: Gloria Dei est decretorum & judiciorum suorum rationes cela- re, ut eminentem suam majestatem, dominium & po- testatem ostendat: at vero Regum nihil decernere, nihil judicare, nisi prævio exacto examine, ut constet legem vel sententiam esse justam, honestam, utilem: quia manifestare debent, quare sic judicent, aut de- cernant. Quo etiam redit Jansenii explicatio: Sic- ut ad gloriam Dei facit, quod non debeat inquirere de re aliqua, sed quod cum omnia sciat, celet tamen plurima: ita e contrario ad gloriam Regum facit, quod cum fateri debeant se pleraque ut homines nescire, diligenter scrutentur res scitu necessarias, ut investi- gatas detegant, & dirigant. Non ergo tali sententiæ repugnant illa, quæ Tob. 12, 7. habentur: Sacra- mentum Regis abscondere bonum est: opera autem Dei revelare & confiteri honorificum est. Ibi enim de consiliorum Regis, quæ publice sciri non vult, celatione, & operum Dei quæ omnibus ipse reve- lari vult, publica deprædicatione agitur: hic vero de judiciorum & decretorum divinorum, quæ pe- nes se abscondit, occultatione, & de illorum, quæ scire & Reges & alios interest, indagatione, & ma- nifestatione sermo est.

## 25:3
Verse 3.

THE HEAVEN ABOVE AND THE EARTH BELOW, AND THE HEART OF KINGS IS UNSEARCHABLE] Just as neither the height of the heavens nor the depth of the earth can be comprehended by us, so neither can the secrets of Princes. To inquire into the hidden thoughts of a prince, and if he prepares anything more secretly, is illicit, dangerous, and you will not attain it thereby. Tacitus, Annals 6.

This seems to be a limitation of the previous opinion: Although Kings do not conceal their administration, as is done in great part by the Lord, yet it is scarcely, or indeed not at all, permitted to penetrate their counsels: As no one can touch the sky with a finger, nor reach to the center of the earth: so no one can search out the heart of a King. Silence is the soul of counsel.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

COELVM SVRSVM ET TERRA DEORSVM, ET COR REGVM INSCRVTABLE] Sicut nec cæli altitudo, nec terræ profunditas comprehendi à nobis potest, ita nec Principum arcana. Abditos principis sensus, & siquid occul- tius parat, exquirere illicitum, anceps, nec ideo assequare. Ta- citus Annal. 6.

Limitatio hæc videtur superioris sententiæ: Quamvis non celent Reges suam administrationem, uti magnam partem à Domino fit, consilia tamen ipsorum vix ac ne vix quidem penetrare licet: Ut cœ- lum nemo digito attingere potest, neque ad centrum terræ pertingere: ita nemo cor Regis perscrutari po- test. Anima consilii silentium.

## 25:4
Verse 4.

TAKE AWAY THE RUST FROM THE SILVER, AND A MOST PURE VESSEL SHALL COME FORTH.

What the Latin called rust, in Hebrew is dross. But the following verse must be added, so that the sense may be full: take away impiety from the face of the King, and his throne shall be established in justice: that is: Just as dross must be removed from silver, so that a pure vessel may be formed from it, which may withstand examination: so the impious and reprobate must be removed, so that the court and the Republic may be pure: thus the Royal throne shall be stabilized by the work of pious counselors and by justice, c. 20:8.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

AUFER RUBIGINEM DE AR- GENTO, ET EGREDIETUR VAS PURIS- SIMUM.

Quod Latinus rubiginem dixit, in Ebræo sco- ria est. Addendus autem versus sequens, ut plenus sit sensus: aufer impietatem de vultu Regis, & fir- mabitur justitia thronus ejus: id est: Quemad- modum ab argento scoria removenda est, ut inde formetur vas purum, quod examen sustineat: ita impii & reprobi removeri debent, ut pura sit aula, & Respublica: ita stabilietur thronus Regius pio- rum consiliariorum opera & justitia c. 20, 8.

## 25:6
Verse 6.

DO NOT APPEAR GLORIOUS BEFORE THE KING: AND DO NOT STAND IN THE PLACE OF GREAT MEN.

Let humility and modesty be inculcated in courtiers and those conversing with Kings or Princes: do not magnify yourself (whether by gestures, or by speech, or by external pomp) before the King (in the sight of those who wish the majesty granted to them from heaven to shine alone, who wish to be an object of admiration to others, not others to themselves, who love submissive modesty, and are accustomed to be indignant at braggarts) And in the place of the great (who are established in eminence, and thus obtain a more eminent place and seat on account of the dignity of their office) do not stand (whether by the occupation of the first seat or an incompetent place, or by affection) because it is better that, as v.

7. it is held, that it may be said to you ascend hither, rather than that (someone) should humble you before a Prince, whom your eyes have seen, when, to wit, you have moved yourself closer to him, from whom, however, when you are cast further away with ignominy, as rightly with

Mercerus interprets R. Levi. Cf. Luke 14:8, since pride and ostentation are indeed hateful to all, but especially to Kings and Princes.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NE GLORIOSUS APPAREAS CO- RAM REGE: ET IN LOCO MAGNORUM NE STETERIS.

Aulicis, & cum Regibus vel Principibus con- versantibus inculcetur humilitas & modestia: ne ma- gnifices te (sive gestibus, sive sermone, sive externa pompa) coram Rege (in conspectu eorum, qui ma- jestatem cœlitus sibi concessam splendescere vo- lunt solam, qui admirationi esse volunt aliis, non alios sibi, qui submissam amant modestiam, & thra- sonibus indignari solent) Et in loco magnatum (qui ἐν ὑπεροχῇ constituti sunt, adeoque locum & sedem eminentiorem ob dignitatem muneris obtinent) ne steteris (sive πρωτοκλισίας aut loci incompetentis occupatione, seu affectione) quia melius est, ut v.

7. habetur, ut dicatur tibi ascende huc, quam ut hu- miliet te (aliquis) coram Principe, quem viderunt oculi tui, cum sc. te propius ipsi admovisti, a quo ve- ro cum ignominia longius rejiceris, ut recte cum

R. Levi interpretatur Mercerus. Conf. Luc. 14, 8. siquidem superbia & ostentatio omnibus quidem exosa sit, sed maxime Regibus, & Principibus.

## 25:8
Verse 8. WHAT YOUR EYES HAVE SEEN, DO NOT BRING FORTH IN HASTY STRIFE] Do not betray even what you have seen: much more what you have not seen. The interpreter connects this well, which others divide badly.

It is wrongly preferred in this way to the authentic Vulgate text, in which everything coheres most correctly, as has already been explained: and these words render a full sense, according to the Hebrew truth: do not go forth into contention quickly. The discourse is not about hiding those things which we have seen, but about avoiding strife. Namely, we are instructed here how we ought to conduct ourselves in common life, and first indeed by fleeing judicial and public contention in this verse 8 and following, so that we do not quickly go forth to contend, with the causes and moments of the circumstances not sufficiently weighed: lest an ignominious outcome perhaps follow for us. Lest (you know not) what you may do in the end of it (the strife) when your neighbor has put you to shame. The Vulgate inverts the sense: lest you be unable to be corrected afterwards: when you have dishonored your friend. Cornelius acknowledges that it can be translated from the Hebrew thus, when your friend has dishonored you, with this added explanation: a friend injured by you will injure you in turn, and returning reproach for reproach will lay bare your secrets and shameful things. But he could not teach that it could be translated as the Vulgate rendered it. Whence Baynus rendered those words: lest your friend put you to shame.

Latin:

Vers. 8. QVÆ VIDERVNT OCVLI TVI, NE PRO- FERAS IN JVRGIO CITO] Etiam quæ videris noli pro- dere: multo magis quæ non videris. Bene interpres hoc connectit, quæ alii male dividunt.

Male ita præfertur Vulgatæ textui authentico, in quo cohærent omnia rectissime, uti jam exposi- tum: & sensum plenum reddunt hæc, juxta verita- tem Ebraicam: ne egrediaris in contentionem cito. Non de celandis illis, quæ vidimus, sed de vitanda lite sermo est. Nimirum instruimur hic, quomodo nos gerere in communi vita debeamus, & primo quidem fugiendo contentionem judicialem & publi- cam versu hoc 8. & seqq. ne cito prodeamus ad con- tendendum, causis & circumstantiarum momentis non satis ponderatis: ne eventus forte nobis igno- miniosus sequatur. Ne (nescias) quid facias in no- vissimo ejus (litis) quando pudore affecerit te proxi- mus tuus. Vulgata invertit sensum: ne postea emendari non possis: cum dehonestaveris amicum tuum. Agnoscit Cornelius ex Ebræo sic verti pos- se, cum dehonestaverit te amicus tuus, hac addita ἐξη- γήσει: amicus a te læsus te vicissim lædet, & probrum probro regerens secreta & verenda tua nudabit. Sic autem, ut vulgata reddidit, verti posse, docere non potuit. Unde Baynus illa reddidit: ne pudefaciat te amicus tuus.

## 25:9
Verse 9.

TREAT YOUR CAUSE WITH YOUR FRIEND] That is, see to whom you entrust counsels that you wish to remain hidden. It is not about the cautious and circumspect communication of counsels, but about the treatment of a private lawsuit with a neighbor: just as it was warned before, that one should not rashly go to public courts. Plead your cause (litigate your lawsuit privately) with your neighbor, Matt. 5:25, ch. 18:15, so that, to wit, you do not go forth immediately into public: and do not reveal the secret of another: For things that are hidden are not easily to be dragged into public. The translation of the Vulgate, do not reveal the secret to a stranger, does not agree with the accentuation. For the reason added in v. 10 confirms our explanation: lest perhaps the hearer (the neighbor) should affect you with reproaches and your infamy be not averted. Therefore, judgments or forensic actions are not disapproved, as is done by the Anabaptists, but we are warned that private correction should precede, and that composition ought to be attempted, before a judicial process is instituted.

Moreover, it also especially contributes to private correction that it be done in time: since a timely word is always more pleasing and pleasant, verse 9. Golden apples (quince apples) in silver beds (in Hebrew it is in a sculpture or silver figure, or some vessel adorned with figures, or beautifully latticed) who speak a word in its time. In Hebrew: A word spoken according to its modes, or convenient circumstances. The things which interpreters bring forward here allegorically about wheels and charioteering do not agree with the rules of grammar, which admit no sense of wheels. But the things which R. Moses invents here about a double literal and mystical sense are utterly inept, explaining a word spoken to its faces; however much Isidorus Clarius and other Papists all err on the same string. Most of the Hebrews, as Mercerus notes, prefer to explain אפניו, so that the Aleph is adventitious, according to its modes, that is, a word as it is convenient: The Hebrews, he says, everywhere use the word אופן metaphorically from this passage for circumstance and mode. Some of whom he also observes to join this wisdom with the preceding in such a way that, because he had spoken about a blameworthy word, when another's secret is uncovered, now he warns on the contrary about a praised word, how much grace it has. But the connection already handed down concerning opportune and timely correction (even if this reason is general, since every word ought to be timely and opportune, and instituted according to its modes, but then especially that is to be observed in Elenctic, or Epanorthotic, as well as pedagogical discourse) is confirmed by the following verse 12. (Those things which are inserted from the Greek into the Vulgate, they free from thanks and friendship, which you should keep for yourself lest you become blameworthy, are not Solomonic, because they are not held in the Hebrew sources) as a golden earring and an ornament (feminine Cant. 7, 1. Of. 11, 13. of refined gold, of most excellent gold) is he who reproves a wise man (or by metonymy, the correction of a wise man) upon, or to an ear that hears (c. 15, 31.) with the due manner, place, and time observed, sc. Ps. 141, 5. Let us not therefore turn away from corrections: for he who corrects us, he places a golden necklace around our neck. Concerning the untimely speech of a fool, see Syr. 20, 22.

But when the Holy Spirit has touched upon the benefits of speech, He now pursues them further, v. 13. regarding messengers: As the cold of snow (a simile of the cold of snow, as being a very cold drink refreshing and reviving reapers in the heat. Conf. v. 25.) in the day of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; and he refreshes the soul of his Lord, who longs for his expedition, and burns with desire.

The boasting of a braggart and a false promise also pertain to speech, concerning which he warns in v. 14. Clouds, and wind, and no rain, (or as the Vulgate, and rains not following;) a man who boasts of a lying gift, that is, a man who promises many things liberally, yet does not perform them, is like clouds and winds, often bringing hope of rain to the wise when the land is dry, even though no shower follows. Concerning windy men, Job 6. verse 26. chap. 8. verse 2. chap. 16. verse 3. Hos. 9. verse 7. concerning clouds without water, Jude v. 12. On the contrary, a kind and gentle tongue, but one consistent with the mind, is celebrated. By long-suffering is a Prince (not only every common person, but even) persuaded: and a soft tongue (gentle, chap. 15. verse 1.) breaks bones. For soft words break or soften the bones or the hardness of anger (or rather of an angry man) by soothing, according to R. Levi. Conf. 1 Sam. 25, 24. the example of Abigail and David.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

CAVSAM TVAM TRACTA CVM AMICO TVO] Id est, consilia quæ velis latere, vide cui credas. Non de cauta & circumspecta consiliorum com- municatione, sed de privatæ litis cum proximo tra- statione agitur: quemadmodum antea monebatur, non temere ad publica eundum esse judicia. Cau- sam tuam age (litem tuam litiga privatim) cum pro- ximo Matth. 5, 25. c. 18, 15. ut sc. non prodeas statim in publicum: & secretum alterius ne reveles: Non enim facile ea, quæ occulta sunt, in publicum pro- trahenda. Vulgatæ translatio, secretum extraneo ne reveles, non congruit accentuationi. Confirmat enim explicationem nostram ratio v. 10. addita: ne forte probris afficiat te audiens (proximus) & infa- mia tua non avertatur. Non ergo improbantur judicia, vel actiones forenses, quemadmodum ab Anabaptistis fit, sed privatam correptionem præce- dere, & compositionem tentari debere monemur, antequam processus judicialis instituatur.

Ad privatam autem correptionem imprimis etiam facit, ut ea in tempore fiat: siquidem sermo tempestivus gratior & jucundior semper sit, vers. 9. Mala aurea (poma Cydonia) in lectis argenteis (in Ebr. est in sculptura vel figura argentea, vel vase ali- quo figuris exornato, aut pulcre cancellato) qui lo- quuntur verbum in tempore suo. In Ebr. Verbum di- ctum secundum modos suos, vel circumstantias con- venientes. Quæ de rotis & aurigatione hic allegori- ca afferunt interpretes, non conveniunt Gramma- ticæ Regulis, quæ nullum rotarum sensum admit- tunt. Inepta vero prorsus sunt, quæ R. Moses de duplici sensu literali & mystico hic comminiscitur, exponens verbum dictum ad facies suas; utut Isido- rus Clarius, aliique Papistæ eadem omnes errent chorda. Pleriq; Hebræorum, Mercero notante אפניו exponere malunt, ut Aleph ascititium sit, juxta mo- dos suos, id est, dictum ut convenit: Hebræi, inquit, passim ex hoc loco metaphorice nomine אופן pro cir- cumstantia & modo utuntur. Quorum nonnullos etiam observat hanc sapientiam ita cum præceden- ti jungere, ut quia de sermone vituperando dixerat, cum detegitur alterius arcanum, nunc de sermone laudato e contrario moneat, quantam ille habeat gra- tiam. Sed συνέχειαν jam traditam de oportuna & tempestiva correptione (etsi ratio hæc generalis sit, quum omnis sermo tempestivus & oportunus esse debeat, & secundum modos suos instituendus, tum vero imprimis id observandum in sermone Elencti- co, vel Epanorthotico, ut & pædeutico) confirmat se- quens verficulus 12. (Quæ è Græco inferciuntur in Vulgata, gratia & amicitia liberant, quas tibi serva ne exprobrabilis fias, Salomonea non sunt, quia in Ebræis fontibus non habentur) ut inauris aurea & ornamentum (muliebre Cant. 7, 1. Of. 11, 13. obryzi, auri præstantiffimi) est qui arguit sapientem (vel metonym. correptio sapientis) super, vel ad aurem audientem (c. 15, 31.) debito sc. observato modo, loco, & tempore Psal. 141, 5. Non ergo aversemur correptiones: qui enim nos corrigit, is torquem aureum collo nostro circumponit. De stulti vero sermone intempestivo vid. Syr. 20, 22.

Quum vero sermonis commoda attigerit Spir. S. jam ea prosequitur ulterius, v. 13. quantum ad legatos: Sicut frigus nivale (simile nivis frigori, utpote potus valde frigidi meffores in æstu refrigerantis & refocillantis. Conf. v. 25.) in die messis, fic legatus fidelis mittentibus illum; & animam Domini sui recreat, qui anhelat expeditionem ejus, & præ desiderio æstuat.

Ad sermonem etiam pertinet gloriatio jactabundi, & fallax promissio, de qua monet v. 14. Nubes, & ventus & pluvia non est, (vel ut Vulg. & pluviæ non sequentes;) vir qui se jactat de dono mendaci, id est, homo qui multa liberaliter promittit, nec tamen ea præstat, similis est nubibus & ventis, spem sæpe sapientibus pluviæ, cum arida est terra, tametsi nullus sequatur imber. De viris ventosis Job. 6. vers. 26. cap. 8. vers. 2. cap. 16. vers. 3. Ose. 9. vers. 7. de nubibus sine aqua Judæ v. 12. E contrario benigna placidaque lingua, sed menti consonans celebratur. Longanimitate flectitur (non solum vulgaris quisque, sed etiam) Princeps: & lingua mollis (placida cap. 15. vers. 1.) confringit ossa. Verba enim mollia iræ (vel potius hominis irati) ossa seu duritiem demulcendo infringunt secundum R. Levi. Conf. 1. Sam. 25, 24. exemplum Abigail & Davidis.

## 25:16
Verse 16.

YOU HAVE FOUND HONEY: EAT WHAT IS SUFFICIENT FOR YOU, LEST PERCHANCE BEING SATIATED YOU VOMIT IT UP] One must philosophize, but in few words. Thus Maimonides explains this passage.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

MEL INVENISTI: COMEDE QVOD SVFFICIT TIBI, NE FORTE SATIATVS EVOMAS ILLVD] Philosophandum, sed paucis. Ita hunc locum explicat Maimonides.

## 25:17
Verse 17.

WITHDRAW YOUR FOOT FROM THE HOUSE OF YOUR NEIGHBOR, LEST AT ANY TIME BEING SATIATED HE HATE YOU] The LXX interpret well: σπάνιον ἔπαγε τὸν πόδα πρὸς σεαυτῶ φίλον. The Arabs say: Visit rarely and you will increase love. Martial: Make yourself too much of a companion to no one.

That this simile is to be understood not of Philosophy, but of conversation with a neighbor, the apodosis of v. 17 teaches, and thus R. Levi, R. Solomon, Bede, Strabus, Cajetan, Corn. à Lap., Tarnov. Exercit. Bibl. p. 241 understand it: as the moderate use of honey is sweet and refreshes, but on the contrary its excessive consumption is unpleasant, creating vomiting and generating mere bile; so also the liberal use of friendship in moderation refreshes, but in excess it satiates and makes one hateful, according to that saying, too much familiarity breeds contempt. Χρὴ τῶ μέλιτος ἄκρῳ δακτύλῳ, ἀλλὰ μὴ κοίλῃ χειρὶ γένεσθαι. Honey is to be tasted with the tip of the finger, not with the hollow hand, says Dionysius Milesius. When your friend is honey, do not eat him all up, warns the Arab proverb. And the Persian in Warner's Persian Proverbs p. 3. It is not unseemly to visit men, provided it does not happen so often that they say: it is enough. It is necessary to be rare, if you wish to be dear for a long time, says Seneca lib. 1. de beneficiis, cap. 15. In the Hebrew it is: make your foot precious in the house of your neighbor. B. Glassius notes that the preposition מ signifies 'in', l. 4. Phil. p. 621.

To the maintaining of friendship belongs entirely the avoidance of false testimony against a neighbor, both in judgment and outside of judgment, which strikes and harms the neighbor, just as if one were to crush the neighbor's head with a club or hammer, or pierce him through with a sword, or slaughter him, or transfix his heart with an arrow, which three were formerly the most used weapons, verse 18. Compare Jer. 51. verse 20. Psalm 59. verse 8. Psalm 64. verse 4. Prov. 30. verse 14. Also Psalm 120. verse 4. Psalm 57. verse 5. as a hammer (the LXX explain it as a club) & a sword, & a sharp arrow is a man who speaks false testimony against his neighbor. chap. 6. v. 19. chap. 14. verse 5. chap. 19. verse 5. 9. 28. chap. 21. v. 28. c. 24. v. 28.

We are further warned not to place confidence in friends, verse 19. as a broken tooth (which we cannot use for crushing and chewing, the Vulgate wrongly called it a rotten tooth) & a wavering foot (not supporting the body because of a dislocation, so that it may not totter or slip, Psalm 18, 37. Job 12, 5.) So is confidence (which one places in patrons and worldly things) a prevaricator in the day of distress: Zeph. 1. verse 18. James 5. verse 1. since most copies, as Mercer testifies, have מֹבטַח with Kametz, and the observation of the Masora also requires this, it is more correctly rendered a prevaricating confidence, such as it certainly is, which is placed in men, Jer. 17. verse 5. than a prevaricator's: since the word is not placed in that way in the state of regimen. However, the Vulgate does not agree: he who hopes upon an unfaithful man. Cornelius himself admits more elegantly that confidence itself is compared in this way: namely, that such confidence abandons a man in a time of need, just as a rotten tooth and a slipped foot abandon a man in a necessary matter, namely in eating and walking. Compare Psalm 26. verse 1. Psalm 71. verse 5. Jer. 17. verse 7.

Finally, the apophthegm which is had in verse 20 also contributes to conversation and timely speech, and decent correction: namely, that we should not flatter a perverse man: as the Osiandrian Paraphrase explains: Taking away a garment in the day of cold, and vinegar upon alum (or nitre poured on) is he who sings songs or ditties to a very bad heart: that is: he who flatters a depraved and perverse man does just as one who strips a garment from someone in winter, he increases the cold for the miserable man, so that he may be colder: and he who pours vinegar upon alum (nitre) makes a bitter thing more bitter: for thus a depraved man is rendered worse than he had been, while his vices are even sweetly stroked. Thus Cornelius a Lapide explains from Gregory the Great, book 1 in Ezech. hom. 9, and he brings in R. Solomon to the same sentiment, and praises a similar gnome from R. Simeon in Pirke aboth: Do not try in vain to soothe with flattering words one in whom the spirit of anger still boils. If, however, songs are not to be taken as sweet ditties, but are understood because of those similar things by which bitter and not at all pleasing things are regarded, as biting songs, or those by which someone is sharply criticized or corrected, just as to pour upon vinegar is to sharply criticize and bite: such songs as are designated in Ezech. 33. verse 32. Lam. 3. verse 14. 63. Gregory does not deny this, or Beda who followed him: If vinegar is poured into nitre, the nitre immediately effervesces and boils up: so also a perverse mind, when it is corrected by rebuke, or when good things are persuaded to it through the sweetness of preaching. For it becomes worse from correction, and is thence kindled into the iniquity of murmuring, from which it ought to have been restrained from iniquity. According to the Vulgate, the former words still pertain to the preceding verse, by reason of the sense: and he loses (he who hopes upon an unfaithful man) his cloak in the day of cold: but wrongly, and against the authentic text. Nor did the verse proceed from Solomon, which is stitched on here from the LXX Interpreters in the Vulgate, but without a number, as are many others, so that their νοθεία [spuriousness] may be evident: as a moth to a garment, and a worm to wood, so the sadness of a man harms the heart. That being sent away, therefore, we proceed to other things.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

SVBTRAHE PEDEM TVVM DE DOMO PROXIMI TVI, NE QVANDO SATIATVS ODERIT TE] Bene interpretantur LXX. σπάνιον ἔπαγε τὸν πόδα πρὸς σεαυτῶ φίλον. Arabes dicunt: Visita raro & augebis amorem. Martialis: Nulli te facias nimis sodalem.

Non de Philosophia, sed conversatione cum proximo hoc simile accipiendum esse ἀπόδοσις v. 17. docet, atque ita intelligunt R. Levi, R. Salomo, Beda, Strabus, Cajetanus, Corn. à Lap. Tarnov. Exercit. Bibl. pag. 241. ut mellis usus moderatus suavis est, & reficit, contra vero nimius ejus esus insuavis est vomitum creans, merumque fel generans; ita usus quoque amicitiæ liberalis modicus recreat, nimius vero saturat, odiosumque facit, juxta illud, nimia familiaritas parit contemtum. Χρὴ τῶ μέλιτος ἄκρῳ δακτύλῳ, ἀλλὰ μὴ κοίλῃ χειρὶ γένεσθαι. Mel summo digito, non cava manu delibandum est, ait Dionysius Milesius. Cum fuerit amicus tuus mel, ne comedas eum totum, monet Arabum proverbium. Et Persicum in Warneri Persic. Proverb. p. 3. Homines invisere indecorum non est, modo toties non fiat, ut dicant: sat est. Rarum esse oportet, quod diu charum velis, ait Seneca lib. 1. de beneficiis, cap. 15. In Ebræo est: pretiosum fac pedem tuum in domo proximi tui. Præpositionem מ valere in notat B. Glassius l. 4. Phil. p. 621.

Ad Amicitiam retinendam pertinet omnino vitatio falsi de proximo testimonii, tum in judicio tum extra judicium, quod proximum ferit ac laedit, perinde ac si clavo vel malleo proximi caput con- tunderet, aut gladio eundem confoderet, vel jugu- laret, aut sagitta cor ejus transfigeret, quae tria olim fuere arma maxime usitata, vers. 18. Conf. Jer. 51. vers. 20. Psalm. 59. vers. 8. Psalm. 64. vers. 4. Prov. 30. vers. 14. Item Psalm. 120. vers. 4. Psalm. 57. vers. 5. ut malleus (clavum exponunt LXX.) & gladius, & sagitta acuta est vir, qui loquitur contra proximum suum falsum testimonium. cap. 6. v. 19. cap. 14. vers. 5. cap. 19. vers. 5. 9. 28. cap. 21. v. 28. c. 24. v. 28.

Monemur porro, ne fiduciam in amicos col- locemus vers. 19. ut dens confractus (quo ad com- minuendum & masticandum uti non possumus, Vulg. perperam dentem putridum dixit) & pes va- cillans (ob luxationem corpus non sustinens, quo minus nutet, vel prolabatur Psal. 18, 37. Job. 12, 5.) Sic est fiducia (quam in patronis, rebusque munda- nis collocat) praevaricatrix in die angustiae: Zeph. 1. vers. 18. Jac. 5. vers. 1. quum pleraque Exemplaria teste Mercero מֹבטַח cum Kametz habeant, idque etiam requirat observatio Masorae, rectius fiducia praevaricatrix redditur, qualis utique est, quae in ho- mines collocatur Jer. 17. vers. 5. quam praevarica- toris: quum vox ita non ponatur in statu regimi- nis. Non convenit autem Vulgata: qui sperat su- per infideli. Fatetur ipse Cornelius elegantius fidu- ciam ipsam ita comparari: quod nempe fiducia ta- lis in tempore necessario hominem destituat, sicut dens putridus & pes lapsus hominem destituit in re neces- saria, nempe in manducatione, & ambulatione. Conf. Psalm. 26. vers. 1. Psalm. 71. vers. 5. Jer. 17. vers. 7.

Denique ad conversationem & sermonem oportunum, ac decentem correptionem etiam facit apophthegma, quod vers. 20. habetur: ne sc. homi- ni perverso blandiamur: ut explicat Paraphrasis Osiandrina: Vestem auferens in die frigoris, & ace- tum ad alumen (vel nitrum affusum) qui cantat carmina seu cantilenas cordi pessimo: id est: qui homini pravo & perverso blanditur, perinde facit ut qui in hyeme vestem alicui detrahit, is auget mi- sero frigus, ut magis algeat: & qui acetum infun- dit alumini (nitro) rem acerbam reddit acerbio- rem: Sic enim redditur homo pravus pejor quam fuerat, dum ejus vitia suaviter etiam palpan- tur. Ita e Gregor. M. lib. 1. in Ezech. hom. 9. ex- ponit Corn. a Lap. & in eandem sententiam R. Salo- monem adducit, similemque gnomam laudat e R. Si- meone in Pirke aboth: Noli frustra conari, ut cum blandis sermonibus lenias, in quo adhuc fervet ira- cundiae spiritus. Si tamen carmina non de suavi- bus cantilenis accipiantur, sed ob similia illa, quibus acerba, minimeque grata respiciuntur, carmina mordacia, aut quibus acriter quis perstringitur, vel corripitur, intelligantur, uti aceto perfundere est acriter perstringere & mordere: qualia carmina de- signantur Ezech. 33. vers. 32. Thr. 3. vers. 14. 63. non abnuit Gregorius, aut eundem sequutus Beda: Ace- tum si in nitrum effunditur effervescit nitrum pro- tinus & ebullit: sic & perversa mens, quando per in- crepationem corripitur, aut cum ei per praedicationis dulcedinem bona suadentur. De correptione enim fit deterior, & inde in murmurationis iniquitatem succenditur, unde debuit ab iniquitate compesci. Juxta Vulgatam priora verba ad versum praece- dentem adhuc pertinent, ratione sensus: & amit- tit (qui sperat super infideli) pallium in die fri- goris: sed perperam, & contra textum authenti- cum. Neque a Salomone profectus est versus, qui ex LXX. Interpretibus hic assuitur in Vulgata, ast sine numero, ut alii plures, quo pateat eorum νοθεία: sicut tinea vestimento, & vermis ligno, ita tristitia viri nocet cordi. Eo ergo misso ad alia pro- gredimur.

## 25:21
Ver. 21. IF THY ENEMY BE HUNGRY, FEED HIM: IF HE BE THIRSTY, GIVE HIM WATER TO DRINK.

Now he teaches what kind of people we ought to show ourselves to be toward enemies in common conversation: to whom evil is not to be returned for evil, but rather benefits are to be bestowed, so that we may overcome evil with good. For under bread and wine, not only all kinds of food, and

drink, but any benefits whatsoever are understood by synecdoche. Rom. 12, 20. But he seems to allude, as Cornelius à Lapide notes, to physicians, who, for those suffering from frenzy or apoplexy due to cold, being stiff and numb, apply warm poultices to the head to dissolve this cold, and from time to time apply a pot or a censer of coals. In a similar way, enemies who are cold and stiff with hatred are to be warmed by a heap of benefits as if by a censer of coals, so that they may change the cold of hatred into the heat of love. Whence St. Augustine, sermon 163, on the Season: Thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head. For when, he says, he begins to do penance, the sense of reason, that is his head, begins to be kindled by the fire of charity: and he who previously, as if cold and frenzied, had been accustomed to retain anger against you, kindled by spiritual heat from your goodness, begins to love with his whole heart. It is evident, however, from this Solomonic warning and the Apostolic allegation, that it is false what the Socinians say, that the precept concerning the love of neighbor was extended to enemies in the New Testament. Cf. Luke 10, 27. 37. It is added: AND THE LORD SHALL REWARD THEE, lest anyone think that benefits conferred upon enemies are lost: since God himself is willing to repay them. 1 Sam.

24, 18. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 21. SI ESURIERIT INIMICUS TUUS CI- BA ILLUM: SI SITIERIT DA EI AQUAM BIBERE.

Jam quales nos inimicis in conversatione com- muni exhibere debeamus, docet: quibus non ma- lum malo reddendum, sed beneficia potius præ- standa, ut malum bono vincamus. Sub pane enim & vino non tantum omnis generis esculenta, &

potulenta, sed quævis beneficia conveta Synec- doche intelliguntur. Rom. 12, 20. Alludere au- tem, Cornelio à Lap. notante, videtur ad Medi- cos, qui phrenesi vel apoplexia ex frigore laboranti- bus, rigentibus & torpentibus, ad frigus hoc solven- dum capiti fomenta calida, ac subinde testam vel a- cerram pranarum adhibent. Simili modo inimici qui frigent, rigentque odio, beneficiorum congerie velut prunarum acerra calefaciendi sunt, ut frigus odii mutent in calorem amoris. Unde S. August. serm. 163. de Tempore: Carbones ignis congeres super caput ejus. Nam cum, inquit, pœnitentiam cœperit agere, sensus rationis, hoc est caput ipsius, incipit charitatis igne succendi: & qui prius quasi frigidus & phreneticus contra te consueverat ira- cundiam retinere, spirituali calore de tua bonitate succensus, incipit toto corde diligere. Liquet au- tem ex hoc monito Salomoneo, & allegatione Apostolica, falsum esse, quod Sociniani ajunt, præceptum de dilectione proximi in Nov. Testam. extensum esse ad inimicos. Conf. Luc. 10, 27. 37. Additur: ET DOMINUS REDDET TIBI, ne quis arbitretur perdi beneficia inimicis col- lata: siquidem Deus ipse retribuere ea velit. 1. Sam.

24, 18. 26.

## 25:23
Ver. 23. THE NORTH WIND DISPELS RAIN: AND A SAD FACE A BACKBITING TONGUE.

In the Hebrew it is: an angry face (ch. 24, 24) and secretly backbiting. As clouds are dispelled and rain ceases when the North wind blows, so are secret informers driven away if those to whom flatterers report others do not listen to them with a placid countenance, but look severely upon those whisperers, so that they may understand that they are bringing them a thing that is by no means pleasing. This also pertains to the same subject, how we ought to conduct ourselves toward enemies, so that, namely, we do not lend our ears to those who flatter us while slandering or reporting them, much less traduce them ourselves or publish their vices. On the same occasion, an apophthegm about a hostile woman is subjoined, even though it was delivered on another occasion before, ch. 21, 9. It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop (or roof) than with a litigious woman, and in a common house. It is better for a husband to dwell in a narrow corner of the house, even on the roof, than in a most spacious house with a quarrelsome wife. For such a wife gnaws away the life of her husband.

The consequence and fruit of good conversation is a good reputation: which is proclaimed in verse 24. Cold water to a knowing soul, and a good messenger (in Hebrew, a good report, or good reputation) from a far country. A good messenger in verse 13 was compared to cold water, but now a good reputation is compared with the same: as cold water is very pleasing to a man who is thirsty and weary, so a good reputation, which comes from distant shores and is spread abroad, wonderfully refreshes the soul, chapter 15, 30. We must take care that we strive for this reputation and good name, lest we be precipitated into sin and squander a good name. Concerning which in verse 26: A troubled fountain and a corrupted spring of water, the just man falling before the wicked: when, namely, he is precipitated into sin, both because wholesome information can no longer spring forth from him, and because he offers a wicked example to others: and because the wicked man publishes his fall, and procures infamy for him and scandal for others. In this sense, Bede and the Ordinary Gloss connect this sentence to the following one thus: it often happens that those who shone, endowed with greater knowledge, at the last, wishing to know more than is granted to human frailty, fall into the pit of foolishness: whence he adds: as he who eats much honey, it is not good for him: so he who is a searcher of majesty shall be oppressed by glory. Aben-Ezra also joins these verses, but for another reason, as will be said in the following verse. Osiander, Baynus, and Jansenius explain the damage resulting to the Republic from the oppression of the just man.

Latin:

Vers. 23. VENTUS AQUILO DISSIPAT PLU- VIAS: ET FACIES TRISTIS LINGUAM DETRAHENTEM.

In Ebr. est: facies iracunda (c. 24, 24.) & oc- cultè se detrahentem. Ut nubes dispelluntur, & cessat pluvia, flante vento Aquilonari, ita abigun- tur occulti delatores, si ii quibus adulatores defe- runt alios, non placido vultu eos audiant, sed se- vere susurrones illos intueantur, ut intelelligant, se illis rem minime gratam ferre. Pertinet & hoc ad eandem materiam, quomodo erga inimicos nos gerere debeamus, ut sc. nec iis, qui nobis adulan- tes illos calumniantur, vel deferunt, aures præ- beamus, nedum ipsi eosdem traducamus, vel eo- rum vitia propalemus. Eadem quoque occasio- ne de muliere hostili subjungitur apophthegma, et- si alia occasione antea traditum cap. 21, 9. Melius est sedere in angulo domatis (seu tecti) quam cum muliere litigiosa, & in domo communi. Satius est marito in augusto angulo domus, etiam in tecto, habitare, quam in domo amplissima cum uxo- re rixosa. Talis enim uxor abrodit vitam ma- riti.

Consequens & fructus bonæ conversationis est bona fama: quæ deprædicatur vers. 24. Aqua frigida animæ scienti, & nuncius bonus (in Ebr. nuntium bonum. vel bona fama) e terra longin- qua. Nuncius bonus vers. 13. aquæ frigidæ com parabatur, jam vero bona fama cum eadem com- ponitur: ut aqua frigida pergrata est homini sitien- ti, & lasso, sic bona fama, quæ e longinquis oris venit & spargitur, animum mirifice recreat, cap. 15, 30. Huic famæ & nomini bono ut studeamus cavendum est, ne in peccatum præcipitemur, no- menque bonum decoquamus. Quo de vers. 26. Fons turbatus & vena aquæ corrupta, justus cadens coram impio: cùm sc. in peccatum præcipitatur, tum quod amplius aquæ salutaris informationis inde scaturire nequeant, & quod exemplum pra- vum aliis propinet: tum quod impius lapsum ejus evulget, eique infamiam, aliis scandalum con- ciliet. Quo sensu Beda & Glossa ordinaria sen- tentiam hanc sequenti ita connectunt: evenit sæpe, ut qui majore præditi scientia fulgebant ad ultimum plus volentes sapere, quam fragilitati humanæ concessum est, in insipientiæ foveam incidant: unde adjungit: sicut qui mel multum comedit, non est ei bonum: sic qui scrutator est maje- statis, opprimetur à gloria. Conjungit etiam A- ben-Ezra hosce versus, sed alia ratione, ut sequen- ti versu dicetur. De damno ex justi oppressione redundante in Rempubl. exponunt Osiander, Baynus, & Jansenius.

## 25:27
Verse 27.

AS HE WHO EATS MUCH HONEY, IT IS NOT GOOD FOR HIM, SO HE WHO IS A SEARCHER OF MAJESTY SHALL BE OPPRESSED BY GLORY] This version approaches the Hebrew more closely: As eating much honey is not sweet, so neither is hunting for honor an honor to them, namely, to those hunting. Here I have added the negative particle in the latter member, because it is often the custom for the Hebrews to understand it from the preceding, apo koinou, as the Greeks say. And here, as elsewhere, is for than. Glory follows him who flees it.

Concerning the former member, there is no doubt that it should be rendered thus: To eat much honey is not good, or even sweet. Although honey in itself may be good and sweet, yet the excessive use of honey is neither good nor sweet. The latter member, however, has produced diverse interpretations, both because it appears obscure to what the pronoun suffix in the word refers, and especially because it seemed to most that a comparison of similar things is instituted here, whence they took it concerning excessive scrutiny or excess in the investigation of things, which is not equally good: and for that reason they believed the negative was to be repeated from the preceding member. Some refer the pronoun to the just, in the preceding verse: The investigation of their (the just's) glory is glory: Thus Aben-Ezra: He who is at leisure to investigate the glory of the just shall bring back glory. In almost the same way, Ludovicus de Dieu in his animadversions on this passage, who connects these to the preceding thus: Since the just are forced to move aside before the wicked, that it is harmful to the human race, just as when fountains are troubled and springs of water are corrupted: yet that their glory does not perish, but remains so great always that even to pursue their glory is glorious, and better than eating much honey. But who does not see that the present verse completes a separate sentence, and that this coherence with the preceding verse, which is sought in vain in these proverbs, is assumed only precariously: and that the number does not correspond, because in verse 16 mention is made of the just man in the singular, but not of the just in the plural. Cajetanus, their glory is the glory of the people or the community: that it is honorable to seek the glory or honor of the Republic. But this is twisted. Junius, the Genevans, the English, and B. Tarnovius in his Biblical Exercises, as also Sixtinus Amama in Anti-Barb. p. 590. they understand the pronoun reciprocally: Thus the investigation of his own honor, of them (it is not) honor, i.e., περιαυτολόγοις. Which explanation, however, will hardly sustain an accurate examination. For, not to speak of others, it is one thing to investigate the honor of oneself, but it is another thing to trumpet the same among others in a Thraso-like manner, whence the word חקר is by no means appropriate to grandiloquence. Others, therefore, more correctly gather from the protasis what is indicated by that pronoun. Thus Mercerus: I simply think the suffix in כבדם of their glory refers to honeys in the plural, even though דבש honey is not read in the plural, which is done so because by the name of honeys he understands in the plural those things which he wished to be signified by honey, namely divine things, the investigation of which has the appearance of honey: & I repeat the negation: And to inquire into their glory, of things, I say, which are like honey, of sublime things; it is not glorious, since they exceed the grasp of our mind. Thus also Piscator: To eat too much honey is not good, so the investigation of the glory of the same things, which are like honey, is no honor. To which also, as far as the meaning is concerned, the version of B. Luther returns, even though he took the words otherwise: Whoever investigates heavy things, it becomes too heavy for him. For since כבד signifies to be heavy, and is thence transferred to dignity, he took the word כבוד concerning heaviness: just as Osiander also rendered it: he who searches into heavy things is burdened: or the scrutiny of heavy things is heavy.) Which sense Jansenius also embraces, and Cornelius a Lapide does not disapprove. For Avenarius, Schindl. in Lexic., and Kircher in Concord. rightly observe that כבוד denotes heaviness. However, therefore, where it is used concerning the heaviness of weight in sacred writings, perhaps no other passage may be available, yet that signification agrees with the etymology, and it is not rare for some word to occur only once in its proper signification, but to be used in other places in a figurative sense. Thus, therefore, this rivulet of B. Luther's version will be best deduced from the sources, indeed it will be derived from there far more expeditiously than the preceding versions. For there will be no need to sub-understand the particle of negation, or to repeat it, nor must a foreign sense of the pronoun be sought, but it will be involved, in a manner not infrequent among the Hebrews, in the noun, so that this sense may emerge; as to eat much honey is not good, (even though honey is good & sweet) So the scrutiny of the heaviness of those things which are heavy, or of heavy things: when we strive to search through and thoroughly investigate by inquiry the heaviness itself, and of heavy things, and of those exceeding our grasp, and what is most heavy in them) is a heaviness, oppressing us; and therefore it is not good for us, even though a pious and moderate investigation of heavy things may be good and pleasant. To which sense the Vulgate version can also be recalled: The searcher of majesty will be oppressed by glory: or the excessive scrutiny of glory (of glorious things) will burden, or will oppress the searcher himself with heaviness or with the very glory of glorious things, not otherwise than those who look directly at the splendor of the Sun with twisted eyes are blinded by that splendor, the light of the sun oppressing the light of the eyes. Although B. Luther's version is more convenient, which rendered the same word כבד not with a different, as the Vulgate, but with the same signification of heaviness: But if this is urged at all, that the word כבוד here must be explained as glory, the sense overflowing spontaneously from the words, just as they have them in the source, will be clear, provided the comparison is taken antithetically: To eat much honey is not good. The scrutiny of glory (namely of glorious things, as being divine things especially, which are most glorious) is glory, i.e., honey, even though it be sweet and good, yet not so much of it can be taken, lest perhaps you be sated with it, and vomit it, which he said in v. 16. But the scrutiny of divine things, which are more pleasant to us than honey itself, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb Psalm 19:11, Psalm 119:103, is so constituted that we can never be sated with it. Honey, however sweet, is not sweet when we are sated with it: but divine glorious things, when we piously meditate upon and search into them, are the greatest glory to us; the more diligently we weigh their glory, with the greater glory they affect us. Come to me all, cries Wisdom Syr. 24:16. For my spirit is sweet above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb. Those who eat me will still hunger: they can never be sated enough, and to the point of nausea Prov. 24:13, 14. Eat, my son, honey, because it is good, and the honeycomb is sweetest to your throat, so also is the doctrine of wisdom to your soul. Cf. Sap. 19:16, 18. Prov. 4:8, 9. Nor is it necessary that we say similar things are compared here, since even dissimilar things are compared among themselves, as in this very chapter 24:1, it is the glory of God to conceal a word, BUT the glory of Kings to search out a word: and the LXX Interpreters, Aben-Ezra, Cajetanus, Ludov. de Dieu, and the recent Belgian Interpreters recognize an antithetical sense here. In this way, therefore, there will be no need to inject a particle of negation into the text, or to attribute a foreign sense to the pronoun, or even to depart from the customary signification of the word כבוד. Nor is the interpretation of the LXX so foreign. To eat much honey is not good, but one ought to hold glorious words in esteem, τιμᾷν δὲ χρὴ τὰς ἐνδόξες λόγες. For they are held in esteem when we search into the same piously and diligently in the due manner. Ludovicus de Dieu renders the same sense, but exhibits another translation with the word אשר sub-understood, and the scrutiny of those things whose glory is (that is, of glorious things) is glory: i.e., to eat honey is good and sweet, but one easily sins there in excess, if you eat much, it will be a disgust and a harm. The scrutiny of glorious things is not so, one hardly sins there in excess, the diligent investigation of them is glory. The Belgian Interpreters, however, render it in almost the aforementioned manner: But the inquiry of the glory of such things (which are like honey, which are sweet and pleasant to perceive) is glory. Dn. D. Gejerus in his commentary. He transfers to this passage by a similar line of reasoning: The searching of their glory (which are things most arduous, splendid, glorious, placed above our grasp) is glory; but he understands an excessive searching, and such a searcher like a glutton greedy for honey, and he says that he experiences the same outcome as him, which is to say not a good one, because from that searching a new glory emerges, namely from the profane destruction or ruin of this rash searcher, and that results in the glory not indeed of the one investigating, but of the thing investigated, just as the gaze of glorious sunlight ends in the glory not of the one looking, but of the Sun looked upon, yet it blunts the senses of the searcher, and extorts from him a confession of his own dullness and infirmity, so that the common version is also saved in this way, he that searches the majesty shall be oppressed by the glory, and likewise the paraphrase of B. Luther: Wer schwere Ding forschet, dem wirds zu schwer.

As regards the Grotian interpretation, which he seems to have received from Cartwright: in it we find wanting that he not only repeats the negative without necessity: but converts the noun חקר into a verb, and when the investigation of a thing is denoted by it, he carries it off to the hunting for honor, without example from scripture, and contrary to the meaning of this word; finally, he even transposes the words: when he renders it: so neither is hunting for honor an honor to them, namely to those hunting, just as if it were written effect וְחֹקֶר כְּבֹוֹד כָּבֹוֹד to pass over the fact that this ἀπόδοσις does not seem to correspond to the τῇ προτάσει sufficiently conveniently.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

SICVT QVI MEL MVLTVM COMEDIT, NON EST EI BONVM, SIC QVI SCRVTATOR EST MA- JESTATIS, OPPRIMETVR A GLORIA] Propius ad Hebræum accedit hæc versio: Vt comedere multum mellis non est suave, ita nec venari honorem est honor illis, nempe venan- tibus. Hic negativam particulam in posteriore membro ad- didi, quia mos sæpe est Hebræis eam intelligere ex præcedenti, απο κοινοῦ, ut Græci loquuntur. ו hic ut alibi est pro מן. Gloria fugientem sequitur.

De priore membro non est dubium, quod ita reddendum sit: Comedere multum mellis non est bonum, vel etiam suave. Etsi mel in se bo- num & svave sit, minus tamen usus mellis ne- que bonus est, neque svavis. Posterius autem membrum diversas peperit interpretationes וחקר כבודם כבוד tum quia obscurum apparet, quo- nam se referat pronomen suffixum in voce כבודם, tum imprimis, quia visum fuit plerisque com- parationem similium hic institui, unde de nimio scrutinio, vel excessu in rerum indagatione id ac- ceperunt, qui æque bonus non est: atque ea de causa negativam è præcedenti membro repeten- dam crediderunt. Nonnulli pronomen ad ju- stose referunt, versu præcedente: Inquisitio glo- riæ eorum (justorum) gloria: Sic Aben-Ezra: Qui justorum gloriæ investigandæ vacat, gloriam reportabit. Eadem pene ratione Ludovicus de Dieu in adnimadv. ad h. l. qui hæc præcedentibus ita connectit: Quum justi coguntur dimoveri ante impios, noxium id esse generi humano, sicut quando fontes conturbantur, & venæ aquarum cor- rumpuntur: Eorum tamen gloriam non interire, sed tantam manere semper, ut etiam sectari eorum gloriam, gloriosum sit, & melius quam multum mel- lis comedere. Sed quis non videt, versum præ- sentem separatam absolvere sententiam, ac pre- cario tantum affumi istam cum versu præceden- te cohæsionem, quæ frustra in his parœmiis quæ- ritur: neque numerum respondere, quia justi in singulari fit mentio vers. 16. non vero justorum. Cajetanus, gloria eorum est gloria populi vel com- munitatis: quod honorificum sit, gloriam vel ho- norem Reipubl. quærere. Sed hoc contortum est. Junius, Genevenses, Angli, & B. Tarnovius Exer. Bibl. ut & Sixtin. Amama in Anti-Barb. p. 590. pronomen reciproce intelligunt: Ita pervestiga- tio honoris sui, ipsorum (non est) honor sc. περιαυ- τολόγοις. Quæ vero explicatio vix accuratum exa- men sustinebit. Nam ut de aliis non dicam, aliud est sui ipsius honorem investigare, aliud vero est eun- dem penes alios Thrasonice ebuccinare, unde vox חקר grandiloquentiæ nullatenus convenit. Rectius ergo alii e προτάσει colligunt, quid per pronomen illud indigitetur. Ita Mercerus: Ego simpliciter puto affixum in כבדם gloriæ eorum ad mella plura- liter referri, etsi דבש mellis pluraliter non lega- tur, quod ideo sic fit, quia mellium nomine plura- liter intelligat ea, quæ per mel significari volebat, nempe res divinas, quarum investigatio mellis spe- ciem habet: & repeto negationem: Ac inquirere eorum gloriam, rerum, inquam, quæ melli sunt similes, rerum sublimium; non est glorio- sum, quum nostræ mentis captum excedant. Sic & Piscator: Zu viel Honig essen, ist nicht gut, also die Erforschung der Herrlichkeit derselben Ding, die wie Honig sind, ist kein Ehr. Quo etiam, quantum ad sententiam, redit B. Lutheri versio, etsi verba aliter acceperit: Wer schwere Ding forschet, dem wirds zu schwer. Quum enim כבד gravem esse significet, atque inde ad dignitatem transferatur, vocem כבוד de gravitate accepit: quemadmodum & Osiander reddidit: scrutans gra- via gravatur: vel scrutinium gravium grave est.) Quem sensum etiam amplectitur Jansenius, ne- que improbat Cornelius a Lapide. Nam כבוד gra- vitatem notare Avenarius, Schindl. in Lexic. Kir- cherus in Concord. recte observant. Utut ergo, ubi de gravitate ponderis in sacris adhibeatur, for- te non suppetat alius locus, significatio tamen illa etymo congruit, neque rurum est, vocem ali- quam significatione propria semel tantum occur- rere, alias autem tralatitio sensu adhiberi. Sic ergo è fontibus optime hic rivulus versionis B. Lutheri deducetur, imo longe expeditius inde de- rivabitur, quam præcedentes versiones. Nam neque opus erit particulam negandi subintellige- re, aut repetere, neque peregrinus sensus prono- minis quærendus, sed involvetur id, more E- bræis non infrequenti, in nomine, ut sensus iste prodeat; ut comedere mellis nimium, bonum non est, (etsi mel bonum & svave) Sic scrutatio gra- vitatis eorum quæ gravia sunt, vel rerum gra- vium: cum ipsam gravitatem, & rerum gravium, captumque nostrum superantium, & quod in il- lis gravissimum est, indagatione prorsus perscru- tari, & exquisite pervestigare contendimus) gra- vitas est, nos opprimens; ideoque bona nobis non est, etiamsi pia ac moderata gravium rerum indagatio bona atque jucunda sit. Ad quem sensum revocari etiam potest Vulgata versio: Scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria: vel scru- tinium nimium gloriæ (rerum gloriosarum) gra- vabit, vel opprimet ipsum scrutatorem gravitate vel gloria ipsa rerum gloriosarum, non secus at- que illi, qui Solis splendorem oculis irretortis directe intuentur, à splendore illo excæcantur, opprimente Solis luce lumen oculorum. Quan- quam convenientior B. Lutheri versio, quæ vocem eandem כבד non diversa, ut vulgatus, sed eadem gravitatis significatione reddidit: Si vero omnino hoc urgeatur, quod vox כבוד hic gloria explicanda sit, sensus è verbis ultro re- dundans, prout eadem in fonte habent, lucu- lentus erit, modo ἀντιθετικῶς accipiatur com- paratio: Comedere mel multum non est bonum. Scrutinium gloriæ (rerum nempe gloriosarum, utpote divinarum cumprimis, quæ maxime glo- riofae sunt) gloria, q. d. mel etsi svave sit, ac bo- num, non tamen multum adeo de ipso assumi po- test, ne forte satieris eo, & evomas illud, quod v. 16. dixit. At scrutinium rerum divinarum, quae no- bis melle ipso jucundiores sunt, & dulciores supra mel & favum Psalm. 19, 11. Psalm. 119, 103. ita comparatum est, ut nunquam eo satiari possi- mus. Mel utut svavissimum non est suave, cum eo satiamur: res autem divinae gloriosae, cum eas pie meditamur, & scrutamur, summa nobis gloriae sunt, quo diligentius gloriam eorum ex- pendimus, eo majori gloria nos afficiunt. Tran- site ad me omnes, clamat Sapientia Syr. 24, 16. Spi- ritus enim meus super mel dulcis, & hereditas mea super mel & favum. Qui edunt me, adhuc esu- rient: nunquam satis, & ad nauseam satiari pos- sunt Prov. 24, 13. 14. Comede mi fili mel, quia bonum est, & favum dulcissimum gutturi tuo, sic & doctri- na sapientiae animae tuae. Conf. Sap. 19, 16. 18. Prov. 4, 8. 9. Neque vero necessum est, ut similia hic conferri dicamus, quum etiam dissimilia inter se componantur, utpote hoc ipso cap. 24, 1. gloria Dei est celare verbum, AT gloria Regum scru- tari verbum: ac sensum ἀντιθετικὸν hic agnoscant LXX. Interpp. Aben-Ezra, Cajetanus, Ludov. de Dieu, & Belgici Interpp. nuperi. Hoc ergo pacto opus non erit particulam negandi textui in- gerere, aut pronomini alienum sensum tribuere, aut etiam a consveta vocis כבוד significatione abi- re. Neque aliena ita est interpretatio LXX. Co- medere mel multum non bonum, in pretio autem oportet habere sermones gloriosos, τιμᾷν δὲ χρὴ τὰς ἐνδόξες λόγες. Habentur enim tum in pretio, dum easdem pie ac sedulo modo debito scrutamur. E- undem sensum reddit Ludovicus de Dieu, sed aliam exhibens translationem subintellecta vo- ce אשר & scrutatio eorum, quorum est gloria (id est rerum gloriosarum) gloria est: q. d. mel come- dere bonum est, & svave, sed facile ibi in excessu peccatur, si multum edas, fastidio & nocumento erit. Non ita se habet scrutatio rerum gloriosarum, vix ibi in excessu peccatur, diligens earum inve- stigatio gloria est. Interpretes autem Belgici prae- dicta fere ratione reddunt: Sed inquisitio gloriae talium rerum (quae similes sunt melli, quae svaves & jucundae perceptu sunt) est gloria. Dn. D. Gejerus in comment. ad hunc locum simili ratione transfert: Scrutatio gloriae eorum (quae sunt ma- xime ardua, splendida, gloriosa, supra captum no- strum posita) gloria; Sed scrutationem nimiam intelligit, talemque scrutatorem similem avido mellis lurconi, eundemque cum ipso eventum, qui sc. non bonus, experiri dicit, quia scrutatione il- la gloria emergat nova, ex profana nempe bujus ac temerarii scrutatoris pernitie vel clade, eaque in glo- riam non quidem investigantis, sed rei investigatae, uti gloriosi luminis Solis intuitus in gloriam non in- spicientis, sed Solis inspecti desinit, scrutatoris autem sensus obtundit, eique hebetudinis ac infirmitatis pro- priae confessionem extorqueat, ut vulgata versio et- iam ita salvetur, scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria, nec non B. Lutheri metaphrasis: Wer schwe- re Ding forschet, dem wirds zu schwer.

Grotianam interpretationem quod attinet, quam videtur a Cartwrighto accepisse: in ea desi- deramus, quod non modo citra necessitatem ne- gativam repetat: Sed nomen חקר in verbum con- vertat, & quum rei indagatio ea notetur, ad honoris aucupium abripiat, sine scripturae exemplo, & con- tra vocis hujus significationem; deniq; voces etiam transponat: cum reddit: ita nec venari honorem est ho- nor illis, nempe venantibus, non secus, ac si scriptum effet וְחֹקֶר כְּבֹוֹד כָּבֹוֹד ut taceam quod non satis commode ἀπόδοσις ista τῇ προτάσει respon- dere videatur.

## 25:28
Vers. 28. AS A CITY THAT IS OPEN, AND WITHOUT THE CIRCUIT OF WALLS, SO IS A MAN WHO CANNOT RESTRAIN HIS SPIRIT IN SPEAKING.

Cornelius admits that 'in speaking' is not in the Hebrew, Chaldean, and LXX, and that the Hebrew reads thus: 'a city broken down without a wall, a man to whom there is no restraint of his spirit.' Moreover, this is also a huge impediment to acquiring a good name, when someone is unable to restrain his spirit, or the ὁρμὴν and heat of the affections in general, or even specifically his anger, which works no good. Jas. 1:20. For he who cannot restrain and curb his affections with the bridle of reason and spirit is like a city whose walls are broken down, so that anyone can freely enter and exit, and it lies open to the depredation of enemies. The soul, says Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, part 3, admonition 15, exposes itself entirely to the wounds of the lurking enemy, which no fortification of guard surrounds. Which he applies specifically to the guard of the tongue: Because it does not have the wall of silence, the city of the mind lies open to the darts of the enemy, and when it casts itself outside itself through words, it shows itself open to its adversary, which it overcomes with as little labor as the city itself, which is conquered, fights against itself through talkativeness. So also Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epistle 309, to Cassian: 'Not to restrain the tongue is to leave the gate open to the enemy.' Cf. Gen. 5:17, 24; Sir. 20:7, ch. 28:28.

Latin:

Vers. 28. SICUT URBS PATENS, ET ABS- QUE MURORUM AMBITU, ITA VIR QUI NON POTEST IN LOQUENDO CO- HIBERE SPIRITUM SUUM.

Fatetur Cornelius illud in loquendo non esse in Ebræo, Chald. & LXX. & Ebræa sic habere,\urbs dirupta sine muro, vir cui non est cohibito spiri- tui ejus. Est autem hoc etiam ingens boni nominis comparandi impedimentum, cum quis cohibere spiritum non valet, vel ὁρμὴν & æstum affectuum in genere, vel etiam speciatim iram suam, quæ nil bo- ni operatur. Jac. 1, 20. Qui enim affectus suos fre- no rationis & spiritus cohibere ac coërcere nequit, similis est urbi cujus muri dirupti sunt, ut quis libe- re ingredi, & egredi possit, ac hostium deprædatio- ni patet. Anima, inquit Gregor. M. Pastor. part. 3. admon. 15. totam se insidiantis hostis vulneribus de- tegit, quam nulla munitio custodiæ circumcludit. Quod applicat specialiter ad custodiam linguæ : Quia murum silentii non habet, patet inimici jaculis civitas mentis, & cum se per verba extra semetipsum ejicit, apertam se adversario suo ostendit, quam tanto ille sine labore superat, quanto ipsa quæ vincitur, con- tra semetipsam per multiloquium pugnat. Sic etiam Isidor. Pelus. l. 1. Epist. 309. ad Cassian. Non cohibe- re linguam est relinquere hosti portam apertam. Conf. Gen. 5, 17. 24. Syr. 20, 7. c. 28, 28.

## 26:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVI. On men worthy of no honor: on fools, the idle, and the deceitful.

Vers. 1. AS SNOW IN SUMMER, AND RAIN IN HARVEST, SO GLORY IS UNBECOMING TO A FOOL.

Things repugnant to a good name are now brought forward in order, which, namely, are most contrary to it, such as folly, laziness, and fraudulence, which procure not a good, but a bad reputation. Therefore, he teaches first in v. 1 that honor does not befit a fool. As snow in summer, and rain in harvest (in eastern places; where Jerome says he never saw rain in the month of June and July, cf. 1 Sam. 12:17 seq., it is not fitting, which is to be sought from the following clause), so neither is glory or honor fitting for a fool, such as an honored office or name, Ez. 6:6, 9; Prov. 4:8. By a fool, however, he understands the imprudent, the dull-witted, the impious, and the profane, as is evident from what precedes, whom, just as depression, not eminence, so ignominy and vituperation, not glory or honor, befit.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVI. De hominibus nullo honore dignis: de stultis, otiosis & dolosis.

Vers. 1. QUOMODO NIX IN ÆSTA- TE, ET PLUVIÆ IN MESSE, SIC INDE- CENS EST STULTO GLORIA.

REpugnantia bono nomini jam ordine adducun- tur, quæ sc. maxime eidem contrariantur, ceu sunt stultitia, pigritia, fraudulentia, quæ non bo- nam, sed malam conciliant famam. Stulto ergo non convenire honorem primum docet v. 1. Sicut nix in æstate, & pluvia in messe (in locis orientali- bus; ubi nunquam se mense Junio, & Julio pluviam vidisse Hieronymus ait, Conf. 1. Sam. 12, 17. seq. non convenit, quod e sequenti commate petendum) sic nec conveniens est stulto gloria, vel honor, puta hono- ratum officium, aut nomen, Ez. 6, 6. 9. Prov. 4, 8. Per stultum autem intelligit imprudentem, vecor- dem, impium, ac prophanum, ut ex antegressis con- stat, quem ut depressio, non eminentia, ita ignominia & vituperium, non gloria, vel honor decet.

## 26:2
Vers. 2. AS A BIRD FLYING TO HIGH PLACES AND A SPARROW GOING ANYWHERE, SO A CURSE UTTERED IN VAIN WILL COME UPON SOMEONE) It will be best translated thus: As it is for a bird to wander, and for a swallow to fly, so a curse made without cause will not have an outcome. In like manner, as birds, it goes off into the winds. The Hebrews refer this to unjust ἀναθεματισμὺς (anathemas), which they say fall back upon the head of those who are cursing.

It treats of the (1.) vain cursing of fools, v. 2, as a bird flying to high places (in Heb. as a sparrow is accustomed to wandering) and a sparrow going anywhere (in Heb. and as a swallow to flying, to flying past swiftly, Wis. 5:11). So a curse uttered in vain against someone will come upon him (in Heb. so a curse without cause, or undeserved, such as fools are accustomed to cast at others) will not come upon him, namely, the one at whom it is cast, but will fly past, will vanish into the air, will be void. There is no reason, therefore, for the pious to be terrified by the curses and imprecations of the impious: whom God easily knows how to turn into blessings, Num. 23:21, 24; 2 Sam. 16:12. (2.) Of their necessary restraint, v. 3. A whip for a horse (namely, a raw and untamed one) and (a halter) for an ass (a slow, stupid, and indocile animal is fitting) and (so) a rod for the back of fools (is necessary), ch. 10:13, ch. 19:29, Sir. 33:25. (3.) Of the comparison of the prudent with the fool, verse 4, do not answer a fool according to his folly (namely, with similar foolish talk: therefore it is better to be silent, or not to answer according to the folly of his conversation, lest we repay insults with insults, trifles with trifles, Sir. 8:13, 14) lest you be made like him (lest you put on manners like his, or be considered like him). V. 5, answer a fool according to his folly (not by emulating his folly, but by manifesting and refuting it, and in such a way that the response does not transcend his grasp, but is tempered to convict and amend him), lest he seem wise to himself. Lyranus observes that the first 'as' here is of imitation, the latter of requirement, so that we answer him as his folly demands. Treat a foolish and impious man in such a way (yet with decent gravity and moderation) that, once convicted, he may even feel that he is a depraved and foolish man, so that hereafter he may cease to be troublesome to himself and others. St. Jerome, lib. 1 in Ezech.: 'Both,' he says, 'agree according to the diversity of times and persons, while the fool is despised because he did not receive wisdom, and foolish pride is shaken off by another folly, according to what the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 12: I have become a fool; you have compelled me.' The sum is that for one living among the wicked, the time for speaking and for keeping silent must be observed with the highest judgment and prudence, as this Cartwright says: Conf. Zehner. Cent. 1. Adag. 66. But just as a discussion with a fool is to be prudently avoided, so no communication or business should be easily established with a dullard. Concerning which we are warned in verse 6; and thus, just as we should not speak with a dullard, so we must take care not to speak through a dullard, lest we use him as a messenger. As one cutting off (for himself, which sense the following commemoration demands) his feet, and drinking in violence (those things which are violent and harmful to himself) is he who sends business (of great moment) by the hand of a fool. Here Cornelius himself prefers the Hebrew text to the Vulgate, which has 'lame in feet': whence Aben-Ezra and Cajetan render this sense not inappropriately: Just as one cutting off his feet deprives himself of the ability to walk, so also one handling his affairs through a fool deprives himself of the ability to carry them out; for a fool so entangles and perverts them that they can hardly be extricated and restored to their integrity by anyone. He likewise drinks in iniquity, because he derives upon himself the deeds and actions done iniquitously and foolishly, and their damages. Furthermore, just as it is absurd for a wise man to use foolish words, verse 4, so it is equally absurd to want to treat the words of the wise with a fool, concerning which in verse 7: As it is fitting for a lame man to dance (as the Hebrew is translated by B. Luther and Osiander). so is a parable, or wise speech, in the mouth of fools. Conf. verse 9 and Syr. 20, 21. Regarding the word דליו, the opinion of Mr. D. Gejer pleases me, that it is a noun of the form שתו, 'swimming,' from דלה, 'he lifted up,' so that the lifting of the feet, which is for rhythm or song, or dancing, may be understood. As sitting befits a lame man, so silence most befits the wicked, says this Cartwright. But the interpretation of the Vulgate does not walk with straight feet at all, in how it has 'beautiful legs' in vain, for where are those beautiful legs in the Hebrew? Now, just as it teaches that it is absurd to bestow honor upon a fool and an impious man, verse 8, so it declares it harmful to have a noble saying in the mouth of a wicked man, v. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 2. SICVT AVIS AD ALIA TRANSVOLANS ET PASSER QVOLIBET VADENS, SIC MALEDI- CTVM FRVSTRA PROLATVM IN QVEMPIAM SV- PERVENIET) Optime sic vertetur: Sicut avis est vagari, & hirundinis volare, sic exsecratio sine causa facta eventum non habebit. Pari modo, ut aves, in ventos abit. Hebræi hoc ad injustos ἀναθεματισμὺς referunt, quos ajunt in caput ἀνα- θεματιζόντων recidere.
