De stultorum agitur (1.) frustanea maledictio- ne, v. 2. ut avis ad alta transvolans (in Ebr. sicut pas- ser assvetus est ad vagandum) & passer quolibet va- dens (in Ebr. & ut hirundo ad volandum, velociter prætervolandum Sap. 5, 11.) Sic maledictum frustra prolatum in quempiam superveniet (in Ebr. sic ma- ledictio sine causa, vel immerita, qualem stulti in a- lios jactare solent) non veniet in eum, sc. in quem ja- ctatur, sed prætervolabit, in auras evanescet, irrita erit. Non ergo est, quod pii maledictionibus & im- precationibus impiorum terreantur : quos Deus facile novit in benedictiones convertere, Num. 23, 21. 24. 2. Sam. 16, 12. (2.) De necessaria eorum coër- citione, v. 3. Flagellum equo (rudi sc. & indomito) & (capistrum) asino (animali tardo, stupido & in- docili convenit) & (sic) virga dorso stultorum (ne- cessaria est) c. 10, 13. c. 19, 29. Syr. 33, 25. (3.) De prudentis cum stulto collatione, vers. 4. ne respondeas stulto juxta stultitiam ejus (parili sc. stultiloquio: proinde tacendum potius, aut non respondendum juxta stultitiam sermocinationis ejus, ne convitia convitiis, nugas nugis reponamus Syr. 8, 13. 14.) ne efficiaris ei similis (ne mores ei similes induas, aut similis ei censearis) v. 5. responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam (stultitiam ejus non æmulando, sed manifestando & confutando, idque ita, ut non transcendat responsum captum ejus, sed ad eum convincendum, emendandumque attemperatum sit) ne sibi sapiens esse videatur. Lyranus Caph prius hic imitationis, posterius exigentiæ esse ob- servat, ut respondeamus ei sicut stultitia ejus po- stulat. Sic tracta hominem stolidum & impium (cum decenti tamen gravitate & moderatione) ut convictus vel palpare possit se esse hominem pravum, & fatuum, quo posthac sibi aliisque mo- lestus esse desinat. S. Hieronym. lib. 1. in Ezech. utrumque, inquit, pro temporum & personarum di- versitate concordat, dum & stultus contemnitur, quia non recepit sapientiam, & stulta superbia alia decutitur stultitia, juxta quod Apostolus dicit 2. Corinth. 12.) factus sum insipiens, vos me coëgi- stis. Summa est, inter improbos versanti tempus loquendi, & tacendi summo judicio & prudentia ob- servandum esse, ut hic Cartwrightus: Conf. Zeh- ner. Cent. 1. Adag. 66. Ut autem prudenter decli- nanda cum stulto collatio, ita nulla cum stolido fa- cile instituenda communicatio, vel negotiatio. De quo vers. 6. monemur; adeoque sicut cum stolido, ita etiam per stolidum ne loquamur, cavendum, ne eodem ceu legato utamur. Sicut præcidens (sibi, quem sensum sequens commemoratio po- stulat) pedes, & imbibens violentiam (ea quæ vio- lentia, & noxia sibi sint) est, qui mittit negotia (momenti magni) per manum stulti. Præfert hic Cornelius ipse Ebræum textum Vulgatæ, quæ habet claudus pedibus: unde Aben-Ezra, & Caje- tanus hunc reddunt sensum non incommode: Sic- ut pedes sibi succidens privat se facultate ambulan- di, sic quoque res suas tractans per stolidum privat se facultate easdem peragendi: stultus enim ita eas in- tricat, & pervertit, ut vix a quopiam extricari, & in integrum restitui possint. Idem bibit iniqui- tatem, quia inique & stulte facta & gesta, & da- mna eorum in se derivat. Porro sicut absurdum sapientem stolidis uti sermonibus, vers. 4. ita æ- que absurdum stolidum tractare velle verba sa- pientum, quo de vers. 7. Sicut claudo (convenit) saltare (ut Ebræa B. Luther. & Osiander. vertunt) sic in ore stultorum est parabola, vel sermo sapiens. Conf. vers. 9. & Syr. 20, 21. De voce דליו placet Dn. D. Gejeri sententia, nomen esse formæ שתו natatio, a דלה extulit, ut elatio pedum, quæ ad numerum cantumve sit, vel saltatio intelligatur. Sicut clau- dum sessio, sic improbos silentium maxime decet, ait hic Carthwrightus. Nullatenus vero rectis in- cedit hic pedibus Vulgati interpretatio, quomodo pulcras frustra habet claudus tibias, ubi enim in Ebræo illæ pulchræ tibiæ? Jam ut absurdum do- cet esse stulto & impio honorem deferre, vers. 8. ita noxium perhibet dictum præclarum in ore impro- bi, v. 9.

## 26:4
Ver. 4.

DO NOT ANSWER A FOOL) But it follows: answer a fool. Thus the Pythagoreans used to say 'to walk on the public road' and 'not to walk on the public road.' Such sentences are contradictory, but they are easily reconciled by the application of discretion regarding times and things. See what we have said on Matt. 12:30.

Latin:

Verf. 4.

NE RESPONDEAS STVLTO) At fequitur: refponde stulto. Sic Pythagorici dicebant λεωφόρῳ βαδίζειν & λεωφόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν. Sunt tales sententiæ ἐναντιοφανεῖς, sed quæ ad- hibita temporum & rerum discretione facile conciliantur. Vi- de quæ diximus ad Matth. 12, 30.

## 26:8
Ver. 8.

AS HE WHO THROWS A STONE INTO A HEAP OF MERCURY, SO IS HE WHO GIVES HONOR TO A FOOL) Such heaps, into which every traveler would throw a stone out of superstition, are called by the Greeks Ἑρμαῖοι λόφοι, as in Homer's Odyssey 11, with Didymus as interpreter: ἕρμαια, as in Strabo book 17, or ἕρμακες, which the Scholiast of Nicander interprets as 'stones heaped up in honor of Hermes.' And just as those words are from a Greek name, so from a Latin word the term used by the Rabbis in the same sense, מרקולים, occurs in the Talmud in the titles concerning idolatry and the Sanhedrin. Anyte in an epigram: 'Passing by, men heaped up a holy stone pile for Hermes.' There is also mention of these heaps in the Sibylline Oracles. Vincent of Beauvais notes that this custom existed among the Indians and Arabs. Acosta observes the same custom in America.

Who would believe that such superstition, and heaps of Mercury, already had a place in the time of Solomon, or are indicated here by Solomon? Since the superstitions of earlier times, which Grotius notes from the Greeks, which were among the Indians and Arabs (as from Placentius Bellovacensis), which were in America (as from Acosta), which were once also among the Gentiles, have been brought in; and how they are called מרקולים by the Rabbis in the Talmud from the Latin name of Mercury, is 'nothing to the point' when the meaning of the Holy Spirit is being discussed, and the meaning of the purely Hebrew word, not corrupted from the Latin word, מרגמה, which occurs here. We are not unaware that a similar superstition has been noted by others concerning the heap of Mercury, who was called ἐνόδιος and believed to be the guardian of roads, whence travelers desiring him to be propitious increased such a heap of stones in his honor: concerning which see Selden, Synt. 2, de Diis Syris, ch. 15, and Corn. à Lapide on this passage. But how will Mercurius be formed from מרגמה, and whence is it certain that that superstition was also accepted in Judea, so that Solomon looked to it here? The verb רגם, from which this name is derived, denotes to overwhelm with stones, which happens to criminals subjected to the extreme penalty (Lev. 20:2, Num. 15:5, Jos. 7:25); therefore that name is rightly understood as a 'polyandria,' or a deadly and abominable pile of stones, or in general as a collection of common stones, into which to throw a precious stone—as such are designated by the word אבן κατ' ἐξοχήν (Exod. 39:10, 1 Chron. 29:8)—is absurd and harmful; and thus it is also inconvenient, indeed joined with loss and damage, to give glory to a fool. Most understand by the word מרגמה, which occurs here only in Scripture, a ballista or sling; the LXX, the Chaldean, the Syrian, the Arab, R. Solomon, R. Levi, Lyranus, Cajetanus, Vatablus, Pagninus, Baynus, Junius, Buxtorfius, Piscator, the Belgian Interpreters, the Blessed Lord D. Quistorpius, i.e., just as a precious stone is not to be placed in a sling so that it may be thrown away, so honor is not to be conferred upon a fool, or as Ambrose explains: 'He who binds a stone in a sling is like him who gives brightness to a fool; he wounds himself, and rather brings danger upon himself while he whirls the missile.' Although you might say this is the meaning of the Amama, Pagnini, and English translations—that it would be foolish if one were to bind a stone to a sling, for how could it be thrown if firmly bound? This explanation he also says is Drusius's, and prefers it to others. However, the former interpretation seems to be preferred here, as it agrees with the etymology of the word. Which the Blessed Luther also followed in his version, as did Osiander in his paraphrase, as well as the authors of the Italian and Genevan translations. Thomas Cartwright agrees on this passage. Just as a pearl is not to be placed among common stones (than which what is more worthless? 1 Kings 10:27): so honor is not to be granted to fools. For this is not only to put a saddle on an ox, but to hand a sword to a madman. Blessed Luther looks to this: 'He who bestows honor on a fool, that is as if one were to throw a precious stone onto the gallows-hill.'

Latin:

Verf. 8.

SICVT QVI MITTIT LAPIDEM IN ACERVVM MERCVRII, ITA QVI TRIBVIT INSIPIENTI HONO- REM) Acervi tales, in quos per superstitionem viatorum quisque lapidem mittebat, Græcis dicuntur Ἑρμαῖοι λόφοι, ut Homero Odyffeæ 11. Didymo interprete: ἕρμαια, ut Straboni libro 17. aut ἕρμακες, quos Scholiastes Nicandri interpreta- tur λίθες σεσωρευμένες εἰς τιμὴν τὲ Ἑρμᾶ. Ac sicut eæ vo- ces a Græco funt nomine, ita a Latino vox Rabbinis eodem sensu usitata מרקולים occurrit in Thalmude titulis de ido- lolatria, & de fynedrio. Anyta in Epigrammate: Ἱερὸν ἑρμάη κε παραςείχοντες ἔχευσαν Ἄνθρωποι λίθινον σωρόν. Est & in fastis Sibyllinis mentio horum acervorum. Apud Indos, & Arabes fuiffe hunc morem notat Vincentius Bello- vacenfis. In America eundem morem obfervat Acosta.

Ejusmodi superstitionem, & acervos Mer- curii, tempore Salomonis jam locum habuisse, aut à Salomone hic indigitari ecquis credet? Quum superiorum temporum superstitiones, quæ apud Indos & Arabes, quod è Placentio Bellovacenfi, quæ in America, quod ex Acosta, quæ olim etiam apud gentiles, quod è Græcis notat Grotius, invexere; & quomodo à Latino Mercurii nomine Rabbinis in Thalmude מרקולים dicuntur ἐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος, cum de sententia Spiritus Sancti disquiritur, & de vocis pure Ebrææ, non ex Latina voce corruptæ מרגמה, quæ hic occurrit, fignificatione. Non ignoramus etiam ab aliis fimilem superstitionem notatam de acervo Mercurii, qui ἐνόδιος dictus, viarum præses credebatur, unde illum propitium cupientes viatores, acervum ejusmodi lapidum ja- ctu in honorem ejusdem augebant: Quo de Sel- denus Synt. 2. de Diis Syris cap. 15. & Corn. à Lapi- de h. l. Sed quomodo ex מרגמה efformabitur Mercurius, & unde constat, illam superstitionem in Judæa etiam receptam fuisse, ut ad eam hic re- spexerit Salomo? Verbum רגם unde hoc nomen deductum notat lapidibus obruere, quod facinoro- sis supplicio extremo affectis accidit Lev. 20, 2. Num. 15, 5. Jos. 7, 25. ideo nomen illud de polyandria, sive strue lapidum funesta, ac abominabili recte accipi- tur, vel in genere de congerie lapidum vulgarium, in quam lapidem pretiosum, ut voce אבן κατ' ἐξο- χὴν tales defignantur Exod. 39, 10. 1. Paralip. 29, 8. projicere absonum, ac damnosum; atque ita etiam inconveniens, imo cum jactura & damno conjunctum, stulto dare gloriam. Plerique per vocem מרגמה quæ hic solum occurrit in Scriptu- ra, balistam seu fundam intelligunt, LXX. Chaldæus, Syrus, Arabs, R. Salomo, R. Levi, Lyranus, Ca- jetanus, Vatablus, Pagninus, Baynus, Junius, Buxtorfius, Piscator, Belgici Interpp. B. Dn. D. Quistorpius, q. d. sicut lapis pretiosus non est ponen- dus in funda, ut abjiciatur, sic non conferendus ho- nor stulto, vel ut Ambrosius explicat: qui alligat la- pidem in fundiculo, similis est ei, qui dat insipienti claritatem, seipsum vulnerat, atque sibi potius dum intorquet jaculum, affert periculum. Quamvis Amama Pagniniæ & Anglicanæ translationis, hanc dicas mentem, stultum fore si quis alliget lapidem fundæ, quomodo enim alligatum firmiter posset ejaculari. Quam explicationem etiam Drusii esse dicit, aliisque præfert. Cæterum prior in- terpretatio hic præferenda videtur, utpote quæ vocis etymo congruit. Quam etiam B. Luthe- rus in versione sua sequutus est, ac Osiander in paraphr. ut & Italicæ ac Genev. translationis au- tores. Annuit Thomas Cartwrightus in h. l. Quemadmodum Margarita inter vulgares lapides (quibus quid vilius? 1. Reg. 10, 27.) non est collocan- da: Sic honor stultis non est concedendus. Hoc enim est non modo ephippium bovi apponere, sed fu- rioso gladium in manum tradere. Respicit huc B. Lutherus: Wer einem Narren Ehre anlegt, das ist, als wenn einer einen Edelstein auf den Raben- stein würffe.

## 26:9
Ver. 9. AS IF A THORN GROWS IN THE HAND OF A DRUNKARD: SO IS A PARABLE IN THE MOUTH OF FOOLS.

The fool is compared to a drunkard, because each is devoid of reason, and is driven not by judgment, but by fantasy and desire. But a parable and wise speech in the mouth of a fool is a thorn, because like a thorn it pricks, wounds, and harms both the wicked and foolish person himself, and others. For a sentence, however excellent, in the mouth of an impious person is like a thorn in the hand of a drunkard, with which he brings harm to himself or to those standing by, while he does not apply them correctly, brings them forth at an inopportune time, or perversely distorts them, not without scandal. For 'grows' in the hand, in the Hebrew it is 'enters' into the hand.

The Wise Man continues the subject begun, warning now that we should not entrust those things which must be done to a foolish and inept craftsman. רב Master (whence the name Rabbini, who excels in much learning or art) fashions all things skillfully (which, to wit, pertain to his art): But he who hires (thus the word שכר is taken everywhere, Gen. 30, 16. Deut. 23, 5. Jud. 9, 4. 2. Sam. 10. 6. &c.) a foolish (craftsman) hires also transgressors, for he hires a transgressor: for he corrupts the work in more than one way, so that several ἁμαρτήματα are noted in the same by the wise man, transgressing the laws of the art in various ways, and sinning shamefully against them, or performing everything superficially and as if in passing, whence Osiander rendered it, he who hires (something to be done) to a fool, hires it to a superficial person. Others explain it concerning God, as Kimchi, Jarchi, Lavater, Jansenius, that He creates all things, and gives a reward to the fool, and gives a reward to transgressors: some concerning Tyrants with R. Levi, Mercerus, Piscator, Cartwright, the Belgians, that a Prince afflicts anyone, and hires foolish, unskilled men, and hires transgressors as prefects; but these things are foreign to the present treatment and the nature of these proverbs. But the Vulgate dissents from the words of the Hebrew text even by the whole heaven, as Cornelius himself admits: Judgment determines causes, and he who imposes silence on a fool, mitigates anger.

Now concerning the property of the foolish and wicked man, that he is not easily correctable, and is very impudent, repeatedly returning to his nature, verse 11. As a dog that returns to its vomit; so is the imprudent (foolish) man who repeats (when the occasion is given, and where the old desire of the untamed flesh stimulates) his folly, which he had vomited up. Conf. 2. Pet. 2, 23. Why do you turn again to your vomit? If a dog doing this is horrible in your eyes, what will you be in the eyes of God? says August. in Ps. 83. These are the words of Grotius on this verse:

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVOMODO SI SPINA NASCITUR IN MANU TEMULENTI: SIC PARABO- LA IN ORE STULTORUM.

Stultus ebrio comparatur, quia uterque ra- tionis impos est, nec judicio, sed phantasia & cu- piditate agitur. Parabola vero & sermo sapiens in ore stulti spinæ, quia instar spinæ pungit, sauciat & lædit tum ipsum improbum & stultum, tum alios. Sententia enim quamlibet excellens, in ore impii instar spinæ in manu ebrii est, qua si- bi aut astantibus damnum infert, dum eas non recte adhibet, inoportuno tempore profert, aut perperam detorquet, non absque scandalo. Pro nascatur in manu in Ebræo est, ingrediatur in manum.

Pergit autem materiam cœptam Sapiens, ad- monens jam ne committamus ea, quæ efficien- da sunt, stolido, & inepto artifici. רב Magister (unde Rabbini nomen, qui multa doctrina, vel arte pollet) efformat affabre omnia (quæ sc. ad artem ejus spectant:) Conducens autem (sic verbum שכר accipitur ubique, Gen. 30, 16. Deut. 23, 5. Jud. 9, 4. 2. Sam. 10. 6. &c.) stolidum (ar- tificem) conducit etiam transgressores, pro trans- gressorem: corrumpit enim opus non uno modo, ut plura in eodem à sapiente notentur ἁμαρτή- ματα, varie artis leges transgrediens, & in eas- dem turpiter delinquens, vel superficialiter & ve- ut in transitu omnia efficiens, unde Osiander red- didit, qui autem locat (aliquid faciendum) stul- to, locat illud superficiario. Alii de Deo expli- cant, uti Kimchius, Jarchi, Lavaterus, Janse- nius, quod creet omnia, & mercedem det stulto, & mercedem det transgressoribus: nonnulli de Ty- rannis cum R. Levi, Mercero, Piscatore, Cart- wrighto, Belgis, quod Princeps affligat quemlibet, & conducens stultos imperitos, & conducens transgressores præfectos; sed hæc aliena sunt a tra- ctatione præsenti, & indole harum paræmiarum. A verbis autem textus Ebræi toto etiam cœlo, fa- tente ipsomet Cornelio, dissentit Vulgata: Judi- cium determinat causas, & qui imponit stulto silen- tium, iras mitigat.

Jam de stulti & improbi proprietate, quod non facile corrigibilis, valdequi impudens sit, subinde rediens ad ingenium, vers. 11. Sicut canis qui revertitur ad vomitum suum; sic est imprudens (stultus) qui iterat (occasione data, & ubi anti- qua stimulat carnis indomitæ cupiditas) stulti- tiam suam, quam evomuerat. Conf. 2. Pet. 2, 23. Quid rursus converteris ad vomitum tuum? Si ca- nis hoc faciens horret in oculis tuis, tu quid eris ocu- lis Dei? ait August. in Psal. 83. Grotii ad hunc ver- sum hæc sunt:

## 26:11
Vers. 11. AS A DOG THAT RETURNS TO ITS VOMIT, SO IS THE IMPRUDENT MAN WHO REPEATS HIS FOLLY] You have the same similitude in 2. Peter 2, 22. where he calls it a true proverb.

But finally he compares the conceit of wisdom with stupidity: and he teaches that he who seems wise to himself is less corrigible than a fool, verse 12. You have seen a man wise in his own eyes. (chap. 3, 7.) There is more hope for a fool than for him, both because of his own fault, who by a vain persuasion of wisdom reject the instruction of others, and think they are in no need of it, and because of divine punishment, since God resists the proud, and permits the minds of those who are further blinded by Satan, but gives grace to the humble 1. Pet. 5, 5. even to the stupid and the wicked, who, that is, allow themselves to be taught, and humbly commit themselves to divine grace through true repentance. It is more credible that a foolish man will one day be prudent, than he who already seems to himself to be most beautifully wise. For such a one does not easily allow himself to be taught. Whence it is commonly said: He who is wise to himself, is most foolish. Compare Is. 5, 21. Rom. 12, 16. 1. Cor. 8, 2. Great is the evil of pride, says Chrysost. hom. 39. to the Antiochians. It is better to be a fool than insolent. For there it is only folly and slowness of mind, but here folly is worse and is fatuity with madness. A fool is an evil to himself, the proud man is a plague to others also: this vice is born from madness. He cannot be proud who is not fatuous: but the proud man is full of folly. The maxim which the LXX have here, there is confusion bringing sin, and there is confusion that is glory and grace, that is neither in the Hebrew, nor the Chaldean, nor even in the Vulgate Latin, nor indeed in the Complutensian edition of the LXX Interpreters.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SICVT CANIS QVI REVERTITVR AD VOMI- TVM, SIC IMPRVDENS QVI ITERAT STVLTITI- AM SVAM] Eandem similitudinem habes 2. Petri 2,22. ubi vocat ἀληθῆ παροιμίαν.

Tandem vero componit δοκησισοφίαν cum stoliditate: & eum qui sibi ipsi videtur sapiens in- fipienti minus corrigibilem esse docet vers. 12. Vi- disti virum sapientem in oculis suis. (cap. 3, 7.) Spes est de stulto magis, quam de eo, tum ob culpam pro- priam, qui vana sapientiæ persuasione aliorum in- formationem respuunt, eaque se minime indige- re putant, tum ob pœnam divinam, siquidem Deus superbis resistat, & Satanæ mentes eorum ulterius excæcari permittat, humilibus autem gratiam dat 1. Petr. 5, 5. stolidis etiam & improbis, qui sc. sese doceri permittunt, & humiliter se vera pœnitentia divinæ gratiæ committunt. Cre- dibilius est hominem insipientem aliquando pru- dentem fore, quam eum qui sibi pulcherrime jam sapere videtur. Talis enim doceri se non facile permittit. Unde vulgo dicitur: Qui sibi sapit, summe desipit. Confer Es. 5, 21. Rom. 12, 16. 1. Corinth. 8, 2. Magnum est elationis malum, ait Chrysost. hom. 39. ad Antioch. stultum esse melius est, quam insolentem. Illic enim stultitia tantum est, mentisque tarditas, hic autem stultitia pejor est & fatuitas cum furore. Stultus sibimet ipsi ma- lum est, elatus & aliis pestis: ex amentia hoc vi- tium nascitur. Non potest esse superbus, qui fa- tuus non sit: stultitia vero plenus est superbus. Quam hic habent LXX, gnomam, est confusio adducens peccatum, & est confusio gloria & gratia, ea nec in Ebræo, nec Chaldæo est, neque etiam in Vulg. Latin. ac ne quidem in edit. Complut. LXX. In- terpp.

## 26:13
Verse 13.

THE SLUGGARD SAYS: A LION IS IN THE WAY: AND A LIONESS IN THE STREETS.

Another thing repugnant to a good reputation is sloth, under which respect this sentence concerning the sluggard is repeated in this place, proposed in chap. 22, 13, because a sluggard of this kind, who sits idle at home, and does not wish to go out to necessary labors, using bald excuses, has no hope of any glory: he who in his bed only turns his side now this way, now that, and does not rise to those things by which he might acquire a good reputation for himself, verse 14. As a door turns on its hinge, so does the sluggard on his bed, so far is he from wishing to go out into the field or the streets, or to go out to work, that he does not even desire to rise from his bed. As a door, although it may be opened now, is soon closed, yet it is not torn from its hinge: so the sluggard turns and rolls himself from one side of the bed to the other, yet does not depart from it. Compare chap. 6, 10. 11. chap. 20, 13. With the love of leisure and the pretexts of the sluggard's inertia, the wise man further joins slothful hands verse 15. The sluggard hides his hand in his bosom, he is fatigued to bring it back to his mouth, he not only does not apply his hand to his mouth, as he had said in chap. 19, 14, but he also feigns or acts as if he were weary and completely destitute of strength for work that is highly necessary, as one who cannot even move his hand to his mouth, but has need that food be thrust into his mouth, which is accustomed to be done for infants. Finally, he teaches how difficult the sluggard is to treat and amend through vain conceit of wisdom verse 16. The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven (that is, very many, chap. 6, 3. chap. 24, 16.) who answer with counsel (savory and judicious, which is the emphasis of the Hebrew word, chap. 11, 22.) and therefore he does not admit instruction, he does not suffer correction.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

DICIT PIGER: LEO IN VIA: ET LEÆNA IN ITINERIBUS.

Alterum repugnans bonæ famæ est pigritia, sub quo respectu hæc de pigro hoc loco iteratur sententia, cap. 22, 13. proposita, quod piger ejus- modi, qui domi desidet iners, nec ad labores ne- cessarios, calvis excusationibus usus, egredi vult, non sperare habeat ullam gloriam: qui in lectulo solum modo in hoc, modo in aliud volutat se la- tus, nec ad ea quibus sibi bonam famam compa- rare queat, consurgit, vers. 14. Sicut ostium ver- titur in cardine suo, ita piger in lectulo suo, tantum abest ut in agrum aut plateas prodire, aut ad opus foras egredi velit, ut nec e lecto suo surgere cu- piat. Sicut janua, quamvis nunc aperiatur, mox claudatur, a suo tamen cardine non avellitur: sic piger ab uno lecti latere in aliud se vertit, volutat- que, inde tamen non recedit. Confer cap. 6, 10. 11. cap. 20, 13. Cum amore otii & prætextibus inertiæ pigri, somnique amore conjungit porro sapiens manus desides vers. 15. Abscondit piger ma- num suam in sinum, fatigatur reducere eam ad os suum, non modo non applicat manum ad os suum, ut cap. 19, 14. dixerat, sed & fessum pla- ne viribusque destitutum se simulat aut gerit ad la- borem summe necessarium, ut qui nec manum ori admovere queat, sed opus habeat, cibum sibi in os ingeri, quod infantibus fieri solet. Deni- que docet, quam difficilis tractatu & emendatu sit piger per vanam δοξοσοφίαν vers. 16. Sapientior est piger in oculis suis, quam septem (id est plurimis cap. 6, 3. cap. 24, 16.) respondentibus consilium (sa- pidum & judiciosum, quæ emphasis vocis Ebrææ est cap. 11, 22.) ideoque informationem non admit- tit, correctionem non patitur.

## 26:17
Verse 17.

AS HE WHO TAKES A DOG BY THE EARS, SO IS HE WHO PASSES BY IMPATIENT, AND MEDDLES IN ANOTHER'S QUARREL.

In the Hebrew there is not that word 'impatient': nor 'meddles'; but 'flares up' in a strife or quarrel not his own, which does not concern him or his. While he approaches the third thing repugnant to a good reputation, fraudulence, which is often employed in the unexpected and hasty intervention between quarreling and contending parties, while indeed one brings help to one party for the oppression of the other, the wise man dissuades from the same, having proposed the danger of that matter. For just as he who takes a dog by the ears, an impatient and biting animal, which has delicate ears, and is irritated by nothing more than if it is taken by the ears, rashly provokes the dog against himself to bark, to rise up, and to bite, and easily brings danger upon himself: so he who rashly mixes himself in a cause not his own among those contending with each other, easily provokes spirits already irritated and angry against himself, and is not free from danger. Compare Syr. 28, 10. If you prefer, refer this maxim still to the preceding ones concerning sloth with Cartwright: for that curiosity in the affairs of others, and the lust for contending, is born almost from idleness 1. Tim. 5, 13. 1. Thess. 4, 11. Also that word PASSING BY seems to look to that. For he who does his own business, either does not walk about in such a way that he falls into such things, or if he falls into them, he passes them by, hastening to his own affairs, and leaving the affairs of others, and not mixing himself in them.

Now he warns first concerning the deceitful and fraudulent, verses 18-19, because under the pretext of a joke and play they secretly harm their neighbor: As he hides himself (as Pagninus and Luther, not badly, render it with R. Immanuel) throwing sparks, arrows, and death, (mortal weapons) so is the man who defrauds his friend (secretly, or hiding himself with his frauds) and says, am I not playing? when indeed that deceit is betrayed or noticed. Hidden malice, says Basil, is more pernicious than open. Then concerning not bearing or admitting whisperers, verse 20. When there is no wood, the fire will be extinguished, so when there is no whisperer, contention will be silent, chap. 16, 28. chap. 17, 14. chap. 22, 10. To which also the following gnome pertains, verse 21. A coal to embers and wood to fire, and a contentious man to (kindle) strife, causes greater fires of anger and contention to arise immediately. And verse 22. The words of a whisperer are as if smooth (Vulg. SIMPLE: Osiander Wounds) and they themselves reach to the innermost parts of the belly, See chap. 18, 8, where the same sentiment is held: which according to Cartwright is repeated for this reason, that when compared with other proverbs of the same kind it may shine more, but especially that it may be taught that this sin is not easily separated from the idle, or rather the fraudulent, concerning whom he is here by design, and that it is proper and perpetual.

Thirdly, concerning the false pigments of words, verse 23. Silver of dross (still mixed with and full of dross, or which deserves the name of dross rather than silver, as a rod of iron is iron, referring to the form of a rod Ps. 2, 9.) overlaid upon a potsherd (which is of vile price, fragile, and of no use Is. 30, 4. Lam. 4, 2. because it is not called an earthen vessel, which could be used, but a potsherd, an abject and useless fragment, as Pagninus rendered it) burning lips (inflaming minds, kindling strifes. Chald. burning lips, called Φλεγόμενα by Symmachus, κασόμενα by Aquila and Theodoret. B. Luther. poisonous mouth: so also Osiander:) and a wicked heart (devoid of true piety, and truly wicked.) For however lips of this kind may seem similar to silver, yet because they burn with anger kindled from hell Jas. 3, 6, and inflame others, they are nothing but dross, or mere impurity, dregs and filth: Whence

Osiander explains it thus: as there is nothing of excellence in such an earthen vessel either inside or outside, so there is nothing of good in a man whose heart is malignant, but his mouth is cursed. Likewise Zehner, Similitudes LXX, page 128. Similarly Jansen: i.e., a lid worthy of the pot is the evil mouth of an evil heart, just as dross of silver overlaid on an earthen vessel. For a perverse mouth aptly corresponds to a perverse heart, and dross is a fitting covering for a potsherd. Others understand it of hypocrisy, because the LXX translate it as smooth and deceitful lips, Clarius as flattering lips, the Belgians also think that those burning with love can be understood: and thus most Papists explain the Vulgate's swelling lips, which swell outwardly in the mouth with simulation and feigned love, but in such a way that they flicker from time to time, and thus show signs of internal hatred: as Corn. à Lap. has it. and Cartwright; Just as the vileness and filthiness of a potsherd is hidden by reprobate silver, when yet it itself is of no account: so the malice of the mind is concealed by the flattery of words, which yet themselves are of no value. But the Hebrew word is not found in the sense of the ardor of love, nor can it here be taken at the same time of the seat of anger and the ardor of love, as it perhaps seemed to Cornelius. Of almost similar meaning is what follows in verse 24. By his lips he is known (ינכר which word in Niphal is to be known, Job 34:19, Lam 4:8, as Luther with the Vulgate, but not as Mercer, Junius, Piscator, Lavater, the Belgians, Cartwright, who translate it as 'he feigns himself to be another, he acts as another': It therefore sounds: he betrays himself by his speech: he cannot hide hatred at all with his lips:) hating: but in the midst of his (heart) he will put (he will carefully store up) deceit. Thus this is referred to insidious flattering speech, the simulation of which, however, might be detected by no obscure signs. Nor is that inappropriate. For, as the dross of silver, and a lightly coated potsherd, is easily distinguished from pure silver: so it is not difficult to judge of a hostile mind from burning lips, i.e., from gestures, (Sirach 19, penultimate verse) or certainly from bitter and biting taunts, which sometimes escape imprudent adversaries in feigned speech, as Zehner has it in his Similitudes, page

128. Therefore in verse 25 we are warned: when he has made his voice gracious, do not believe him (Sirach 12:10) because seven abominations (that is, very many, verse 16, chapter 24:16) are in his heart. Compare chapter 14:15, Eccles 7:22. He continues the same subject in verse 26. Hatred covers itself in deception (or deceptive simulation, or for deception, or to the end that he may deceive) his malice will be manifest in the congregation (it will be publicly uncovered) or in the assembly of the Magistrate, or of judges, or otherwise, so that it may become known to all, or certainly in the future judgment,

Luke 12:2, 1 Corinthians 4:5. And that such insidious hypocrisy will not go unpunished is taught in verse 27: He who digs a pit for another will fall into it, (just as wilder beasts are wont to fall into a pit incautiously. Cf. Ezek 19:4. Concerning such pits prepared, see Job 6:27, Ps 35:7, Ps 119:80, Jer 18:20, 21, and how those who prepare them for others fall into them, Ps 7:16, Ps 9:16, Ps 57:7, Eccles 10:8, Sirach 27:28. For examples see Dan 6:25, Esth 7:10, and he who rolls a stone, it will return to him, Ps 7:16, Sir 27:28. Κακὴ βυλὴ τῷ βυλεύσαντι κακίςη. Harmful to others, as is commonly said, harmful to himself. An arrow against you, an arrow to you, or for you, the Arab proverb has it. Which matter Solomon pursues in verse 28. A tongue of falsehood (or a lying tongue) hates those who crush, or strike it (as B. Luther and the Belgians, Vatablus 'those who repress it'. Cf. here Mr. Dr. Gejer on the Hebrew word. In sense the Vulgate agrees: it does not love truth; and therefore neither does it love one who reproves it for a lie) and (therefore) a flattering (soft, or smooth) mouth will cause an impulse: Vulgate: a slippery mouth works ruins: because deceitful flatteries, like slippery oil, glide into the minds of the hearers, and anoint, soothe, and deceive them. Because a lying tongue admits no reproof, while it tries to precipitate others by fallacious flattery, it will work ruin and destruction for itself. For just as the preceding verses are about the vices of a lying tongue, so verses 27 and 28 are about the punishment of the same. If, however, one prefers to understand the ruin of one's neighbor, the explanation handed down by Osiander will not be inelegant: If you convict a vain-talking man of a lie, do not doubt that he will hate you. But a flatterer is not to be listened to: because he will cause harm by exasperating the minds of friends against one another. Therefore, both liars and flatterers are to be avoided. Flatterers are worse than the former in this, that they make men who are not sufficiently known to themselves more insolent and worse than they had been.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

SICUT QUI APPREHENDIT AU- RIBUS CANEM, SIC QUI TRANSIT IM- PATIENS, ET COMMISCETUR RIXÆ ALTERIUS.

In Ebræo non est illud impatiens: nec com- miscetur; sed excandescit in lite vel rixa non sua, quæ se suosque non attinet. Dum aggreditur ter- tium bonæ famæ repugnans, fraudulentiam, quæ sæpe adhibetur in insperato & præcipiti interven- tu inter partes rixantes, & contendentes, dum nempe alteri parti quis suppetias fert ad alterius oppressionem, dehortatur ab eadem sapiens, proposito ejus rei periculo. Sicut enim qui ap- prehendit auribus canem animal impatiens, & mordax, quod aures habet delicatas, nec alia re magis irritatur, quam si auribus apprehendatur, temere contra se canem provocat ad oblatrandum, insurgendum & mordendum, ac facile periculum sibi conciliat: ita qui aliis temere in causa non sua se immiscet inter se contendentibus, animos jam irritatos & iratos facile adversus se provocat, nec expers periculi est. Conf. Syr. 28, 10. Si mavis, refer hanc gnomam adhuc ad præcedentes de pi- gritia cum Cartwrighto: curiositas enim illa in rebus alienis, & libido contendendi ex desidia fe- re nascitur 1. Tim. 5, 13. 1. Thess. 4, 11. Etiam illud PRÆTERINS eo spectare videtur. Qui enim sua agit, aut non ita obambulat, ut in tales in- cidat, aut si incidat in eos, præterit illos, ad sua properans, & aliena relinquens, nec immiscens se iisdem.

Jam de dolosis, & fraudulentis primum mo- net vers. 18. 19. quod sub prætextu joci & lusus oc- culte proximo noceant: Sicut abscondit se (ut cum R. Immanuele Pagninus & Lutherus non ma- le reddunt) jaciens scintillas, sagittas & mortem, (tela mortalia) sic vir, qui fraudat amicum suum (occulte, vel abscondens se cum fraudibus suis) & dicit, nonne ludo ego? cum nempe dolus ille pro- ditur vel animadvertitur. Occulta malitia, ait Basilius, pernitiosior est, quam aperta. Deinde de non ferendis vel admittendis susurronibus vers. 20. Cum non fuerint ligna, extinguetur ignis, sic cum non fuerit susurro, silebit contentio, cap. 16, 28. cap. 17, 14. cap. 22, 10. Quo facit etiam se- quens gnoma vers. 21. Carbo ad prunas & ligna ad ignem, & vir contentiosus ad (succendendam) litem facit, ut subinde majora oriantur irarum & contentionum incendia. Et vers. 22. Verba susur- ronis quasi blanda (Vulg. SIMPLICIA: Osiander Vulnera) & ipsa perveniunt ad intima ventris, Vid. cap. 18, 8. ubi eadem habetur sententia: quæ jux- ta Carthwrightum ideo repetitur, ut cum aliis proverbiis ejusdem generis collata splendescat magis, maxime vero ut doceatur, hoc peccatum ab otioso non facile divelli, vel potius fraudulen- to, de quo hic ex instituto, esse propriam & per- petuam.

Tertio de falsis verborum pigmentis, vers. 23. Argentum scoriarum (scoriis adhuc permixtum & plenum, aut quod scoriarum potius, quam argenti nomen meretur, ut baculus ferri ferrum est, baculi formam referens Ps. 2, 9.) superinductum testæ (quæ vilis est pretii, fragilis, & nullius usus Es. 30, 4. Thr. 4, 2. quia non vas testaceum, quod adhiberi pos- set, sed testam, fragmen abjectum & inutile no- minatur, ut Pagninus reddidit) labia urentia (ani- mos inflammantia, lites succendentia. Chald. la- bia incensa, Φλεγόμενα Symmacho, κασόμενα A- quilæ & Theodor. dicta. B. Luther. gifftiger Mund: sic & Osiander:) & cor malum (veræ pietatis ex- pers, vereq; improbum.) Nam utut labia ejusmodi argento videantur similia, tamen quia accensa ab in- ferno Jac. 3, 6. ira ardent, & inflammant alios, nil sunt nisi scoriæ, vel mera impuritas, fex & sordes: Unde

Ofiander ita explicat: ut nihil præstantis est in ta- li vafe fictili neque intus neque extra: ita nihil boni est in homine, cujus cor malignum, os vero ejus maledictum est. Sic & Zehnerus fimilit. LXX. pag. 128. Similiter Jansenius: q. d. dignum patella operculum est os malum cujus cordis mali, æque ac scoria argenti vasi fictili superinducta. Pravum enim os respondet apte pravo cordi, & scoria congruum est tectorium testæ. Alii de hypocry- si intelligunt, quia LXX. vertunt labia levigata & dolosa, Clarius labia blandientia, Belgæ etiam ardentia amore intelligi posse arbitrantur: atque ita vulgatæ labia tumentia plerique Papistæ expo- nunt, quæ exterius in ore tument simulatione & simulato amore, sed ita ut intermicent subinde, itaque ostendant interni odii signa: ut habet Corn. à Lap. & Carthwrightus; Sicut reprobo argento te- stæ vilitas & turpitudo occultatur, cum tamen i- psum nihili sit: sic animi malitia verborum assenta- tione celatur, quæ tamen ipsa nullius pretii sunt. Sed Ebræa vox non reperitur de amoris ardore,ne- que hic simul de sede iræ & de amoris ardore accipi potest, uti Cornelio forte visum. Similis fere sententiæ est quod sequitur vers. 24. Labiis suis agnoscitur (ינכר quod verbum in Niphal est agno- sci Job. 34, 19. Thren. 4, 8. ut Lutherus cum Vulg. non vero ut Mercerus, Junius, Piscat. Lavat. Belgæ, Carthwrigt. alienum se simulat, alium se gerit: Id ergo sonat: forex seipsum prodit: occultare o- mnino non potest labiis suis odium:) odio habens: at in medio (cordis) sui ponet (cum cura recon- det) dolum. Ita refertur hoc ad insidiosam blandi- loquentiam, cujus tamen simulatio non obscuris in- diciis deprehendi possit. Neque id inconvenienter. Nam, ut spuma argenti, & testa leviter obducta, fa- cile a puro argento dignoscitur: ita de hostili animo haud difficulter judicari potest ex labiis ardentibus, h. e. è gestibus, (Sirach. 19. vers. penult.) vel certe ex amaris & mordacibus dicteriis, quæ nonnun- quam adversariis imprudentibus, in fucata oratione, simul excidunt, ut habet Zehnerus in simil. pag.

128. Ideo vers. 25. monemur: cum gratiosam præ- buerit vocem suam, ne credideris illi (Syrach. 12, 10.) quoniam septem abominationes (id est longe plurimæ vers. 16. cap. 24, 16.) sunt in corde illius. Confer cap. 14, 15. Ecclef. 7, 22. Pergit eandem materiam vers. 26. Operit se odium in deceptione (vel deceptoria simulatione, vel in deceptionem, seu eo fine, ut decipiat) manifesta erit malitia e- jus in congregatione (publice retegetur) sive in consessu Magistratus, aut judicum, seu alias, ut innotescat omnibus, aut certe in futuro judicio,

Luc. 12, 2. 1. Corinth. 4, 5. Neque impunitam fo- re ejusmodi insidiosam hypocrisin vers. 27. doce- tur: Qui alteri fodit foveam, in eam cadet, (uti feræ sæviores in foveam incautæ incidere solent. Conf. Ezech. 19, 4. De foveis talibus paratis vid. Job. 6, 27. Ps. 35, 7. Psal. 119, 80. Jerem. 18, 20. 21. & quomodo in easdem cadant, qui aliis eas parant Pfal, 7, 16. Psal. 9, 16. Psal. 57, 7. Eccles. 10, 8. Syrach. 27, 28. Exempla vid. Dan. 6, 25. Esth. 7, 10. & qui volvit lapidem, ad eum revertetur, Psal. 7, 16. Syr. 27, 28. Κακὴ βυλὴ τῷ βυλεύσαντι κακίςη. Damnosus aliis, ut vulgo dicitur, damnosus sibi. Sagitta con- tra te, sagitta tibi, vel pro te habet Arabum dicte- rium. Quam rem persequitur Salomo v. 28. Lin- gua falsitatis (vel fallax) odio habet atterentes, vel percutientes se (uti B. Luther. & Belgæ, Vatablus reprimentes se. Conf. hic Dn. D. Gejerus de voce Ebræa. Sensu convenit Vulg. non amat veritatem; adeoque nec arguentem se ob mendacium) & (ideoque) os blandum (molle, vel glabrum) faciet impulsionem : Vulg. os lubricum operatur ruinas : quia blanditiæ fallentes instar olei lubrici illabuntur in mentes audientium, easque inungunt, deliniunt, & fallunt. Quia lingua mendax nullam admittit reprehensionem, dum alios blandiloquio fallaci præcipitare conatur, sibi ipsi ruinam & perditionem operabitur. Nam uti de linguæ fallacis vitiis versibus præcedentibus, ita vers. 27. & 28. de pœna ejusdem agitur. Si tamen ruinam proximi quis malit intelligere, non inconcinna erit explicatio ab Osiandro tradita : Si conviceris hominem vaniloquum mendacii, ne dubites, quin te sit osurus. Adulatori vero non est auscultandum : quia damnum dabit, animos amicorum erga invicem exasperando. Utrique igitur, & mendaces & adulatores, sunt fugiendi. Adulatores prioribus hoc sunt deteriores, quod homines sibi ipsis non satis notos, faciant insolentiores, & pejores, quam fuerant.

## 26:25
Verse 25.

BECAUSE SEVEN WICKEDNESSES ARE IN HIS HEART) Seven, that is, very many, as above v. 16 and ch. 24:16.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

QVONIAM SEPTEM NEQVITIAE SVNT IN CORDE EJVS) Septem, id est plurimæ, ut supra v. 16. & c. 24, 16.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII. On avoiding self-glorification. On anger, and love, as also friendship: Certain Economic admonitions.

verse 1.

DO NOT BOAST ABOUT TOMORROW, IGNORANT OF WHAT THE COMING DAY MAY BRING FORTH.

In Hebrew: Do not exalt yourself (ch. 20, 14; ch. 21, 1) concerning the morrow (by metonymy, concerning the matter to be performed on the morrow, Jas. 4, 13. Cf. Deut. 4, 31) because you do not know what the day is about to bring forth. It is foolishly inferred from this, however, that there is uncertainty regarding salvation or perseverance. Osiander correctly expresses the sense of the proverb: Do not insolently boast of how much you might be able to accomplish or obtain in the future time. For you do not know what evil or impediment might still happen to you this very day. Therefore, one must live modestly, in the fear of the Lord, especially since it is uncertain whether we shall live to see tomorrow's light. Metaphorically, childbirth is here attributed to the day. Therefore, just as no one knows, as long as a woman carries a womb, what the offspring will be like: so neither does one understand what the day is about to bring forth. The second verse is of a similar argument. This proverb, says Cartwright, seems to be related to the former and to include a certain prolepsis: the refutation of which is tacit; although it is not permitted for a man to boast of things not yet brought forth, yet it will be permitted to proclaim one's own praises concerning things acquired: the subjection is expressed in this verse. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. For one's own praise is foul. And he also detracts much from his true praises who proclaims his own deeds himself: ὀυδὲν ὕτως ἀπὸσμα φορτικὸν, ὡς ὁ κατ᾽ ἀυτõ ἔπαινον, no narrative is as odious as the encomium of oneself, says Themistius in Stobaeus.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII. De fugienda περιαυτολογίᾳ. De ira, & amore, ut & amicitia: Monita quædam Oeconomica.

vers. 1.

NE GLORIERIS IN CRASTINUM, IGNORANS QUID SUPERVENTURA PARIAT DIES.

IN Ebr. Ne extollas teipsum (cap. 20, 14. cap. 21, 1.) de die crastino (metonym. de re crastina die peragenda, Jac. 4, 13. Conf. Deut. 4, 31.) quia nescis quid paritura sit dies. Inepte autem hinc colligitur incertitudo de salute, vel perseverantia. Recte sensum parœmiæ exprimit Osiander : Noli insolenter jactare, quanta in tempore futuro efficere aut consequi valeas. Nescis enim, quid mali aut impedimenti tibi adhuc hodierno die evenire possit. Vivendum igitur modeste, in timore Domini, præsertim cum incertum sit, crastinane luce simus victuri. Metaphorice hic diei tribuitur puerperium. Sicut igitur quam diu fœmina uterum fert, nemo scit, qualis futura sit proles : ita nec intelligit quid paritura sit dies. Similis argumenti est secundus versus. Hoc proverbium, inquit Cartwrightus, superiori videtur affine esse, & prolepsin quandam complecti : cujus occupatio tacita est ; tametsi non liceat homini de nondum partis gloriari, tamen de acquisitis licebit suas laudes prædicare : subjectio in hoc versu exprimitur. Laudet te alienus, & non os tuum, extraneus, & non labia tua. Propria enim laus sordet. Et multum etiam de veris suis laudibus detrahit, qui sua facta ipse prædicat : ὀυδὲν ὕτως ἀπὸσμα φορτικὸν, ὡς ὁ κατ᾽ ἀυτõ ἔπαινον, nulla narratio tam odiosa est, quam sui ipsius encomium, ait Themistius apud Stobæum.

## 27:3
Ver. 3.

A STONE IS HEAVY, AND SAND IS BURDENSOME, AND THE WRATH OF A FOOL IS HEAVIER THAN BOTH.

The subject now is wrath, and first indeed the wrath of a fool, not that which he draws upon himself, provoking the vengeance of God, as R. Solomon wishes, but that with which he himself is inflamed. For when a senseless and impious man rages with wrath and is armed with some power, he knows not how to keep any measure in taking revenge. Sir. 22, 10. As a stone and sand press upon the one carrying them, so the indignation of a fool is very heavy and troublesome to the one against whom he is indignant. This is confirmed in verse 4, since if all the wrath and envy of a man is heavy to carry, how much more so is the wrath, as also the envy, of fools? Nor is it inappropriately said that envy is compared with anger, since the latter passes, while the former persistently clings and insidiously lies hidden, and is therefore more grievous. Cruelty of heat (or fury) and the impulse of anger: And (but) who shall stand before envy? No one will escape its hidden darts unharmed. Cf. 1 Corinthians 3:3, James 3:14, Mark 7:22. The fury of an angry man designs cruel deeds: the anger of the unjust is like a sudden flood, which causes huge damage: and where someone has once labored under envy, especially among the powerful, he will not easily be able to stand, as Osiander's paraphrase has it. Nothing among all goods is so firm that it perpetually resists envy, says Josephus. According to Cleobulus, two things are especially to be avoided: the envy of friends and the plots of enemies. Furthermore, v. 5. A comparison is instituted between open correction and tacit dissimulation, and v. 6. between the chastisement of a friend and the kisses of an enemy. Better is manifest correction than hidden love, i.e., love that reveals itself by correcting the faults of a friend, is better than latent love, which does not carp at, but dissimulates faults, or covers and hides them. Matthew 18:15. For reproof, according to Clement of Alexandria, lib. 1, Paedagogus, cap. 5, is like a certain surgery of the soul. Admonition is like a certain diet for a sick soul, verse 6. BETTER (in Hebrew, faithful) ARE THE WOUNDS OF A FRIEND THAN THE DECEITFUL (in Hebrew, to be deprecated, as Junius, Piscator, and the Belgians render it) KISSES OF AN ENEMY, that is, when your friend chastises you even rather harshly (for an admitted error), know that this is far more wholesome for you than if he who secretly hates you should flatter you greatly. These things are not said because we ought to treat friends importunately and harshly: but so that we do not take it ill if friends deal with us a little more severely, because they wish us well. Not everyone, says Augustine, Epist. 48 to Vincent, (in Canon Law, S. quest. 5, with in the beginning) who spares is a friend, nor is everyone who strikes an enemy: better are the wounds of a friend than the voluntary kisses of an enemy; it is better to love with severity than to deceive with leniency. And he who binds a madman, and he who rouses a lethargic person, is troublesome to both, yet loves both. Who can love us more than God? And yet He does not cease to lead us not only sweetly, but also wholesomely to fear, often adding to the gentle poultices with which He consoles us, the most biting medicine of tribulation. Confer Psalm 141:5, Proverbs 26:27, 2 Samuel 20:9-10, Matthew 26:48. But in order that it may be clear to whom friendly reproofs are pleasing and sweet, namely not to a man overflowing with pleasures, who scorns a honeycomb of this kind, but to a hungry soul craving information and correction, verse 7 is added: a satisfied soul will trample on a honeycomb, and a hungry soul will take even the bitter for the sweet. It is evident, it is said in Cassian, Collat. 14, cap. 13, that it is an indication of a lukewarm and proud mind if it fastidiously and negligently looks down upon the medicine of wholesome words, even if it is ingested with the zeal of excessive assiduity. The following proverb can also be referred to the same scope, concerning a man who, out of levity and inconstancy of mind, changes the seat of his habitation induced by any trouble whatsoever: as one who can neither sustain the correction of friends nor swallow any bitterness, and therefore, with a hope shining a little brighter, is easy in changing his place, not without danger and loss. For in pilgrimage, as Seneca says, this happens to those living their lives: that they have many lodgings, but no friendships. Ephrem Syrus in the place says, remain willingly in the habitation which you have received as assigned by God, repelling idleness and sloth from yourself, since it is not situated in the change and distance of a place that we repress our passions, but in the attention and care of the mind. Grotius has it thus in verse 8: AS A BIRD WANDERING FROM ITS NEST, SO IS A MAN WHO ABANDONS HIS PLACE. A bird flying away from its nest is easily caught: so also he who, having left his home, travels far, exposes himself to many dangers. Confer Sirach 29:31. Change in all things except in evils is dangerous, says Plato in Dialogue 7 of the Laws.

Furthermore, it is discussed concerning the sweetness of friends in verse 9: the heart is delighted by ointment, that is, fragrant oil, balsam, and various odors, and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend, in Hebrew: and (thus) the sweetness of a friend for the sake of counsel (proceeding from a sincere heart) cheers the heart. Confer cap. 12:15, cap. 13:10, 15, cap. 15:22, cap. 17:17, cap. 25:16. Therefore he warns further in verse 10: Do not abandon your friend and the friend of your father (therefore an old friend, whom we have received as if by inheritance, he means, Sirach 9:14), and do not enter the house of your brother in the day of your affliction (which is said comparatively, i.e., not so much a brother, who is not also a friend, but joined only by blood, not by affection of mind, cap. 17:17, cap. 18:14), for a neighbor who is near (i.e., a friend) is better than a brother who is remote, either in place or even in affection of mind, who either cannot or will not bring help. Herodotus says, a prudent and benevolent friend is a most precious treasure and excels all riches. Benevolence is of such value, says Ambrose, lib. 1, Offic. cap. 34, that it often overcomes the pledges of nature. Grotius on this verse says these things:

Latin:

Vers. 3.

GRAVE EST SAXUM, ET ONEROSA ARENA, ET IRA STULTI UTROQUE GRAVIOR.

De ira jam agitur, & primo quidem de ira stulti, non quam in se derivat, Dei provocans vindictam, ut R. Salomo vult, sed qua incenditur ipse. Vecors enim & impius cum ira furit & potentia aliqua est armatus, nescit modum ullum tenere in ulciscendo. Syr. 22, 10. Sicut lapis & arena portantem premunt, sic indignatio stulti ei, cui indignatur, gravis admodum & molesta est. Confirmatur hoc vers. 4. siquidem omnis ira hominis & invidia portatu gravis sit, quanto magis ira, ut & invidia stul- torum? Neque incommode dicitur comparari invidia cum ira, siquidem hæc transeat, illa per- tinaciter hæreat, & insidiose lateat, adeoque gra- vior sit. Crudelitas excandescentiæ (vel furori) & impetus iræ: Et (at) quis stabit coram invidia? Nemo illæsus ejusdem evadet occulta spicula. Conf. 1. Corinth. 3, 3. Jacob. 3, 14. Marc. 7, 22. Fu- ror hominis iracundi, crudelia facinora designat: ira injusti est instar subitæ inundationis, quæ ingen- tia dat damna: & ubi quis semel invidia laborave- rit, præsertim apud potentes, is non facile subsistere poterit, ut habet Osiandri paraphrasis. Nihil in- ter omnia bona tam firmum est, quod invidiæ per- petuo resistat, ait Josephus. Duo juxta Cleobulum maxime sunt cavenda, amicorum invidia & inimi- corum insidiæ. Porro v. 5. Comparatio instituitur apertæ correctionis, & tacitæ dissimulationis, ac v. 6. castigationis amici, & osculorum inimici. Melior est manifesta correctio, quam amor absconditus, h. e. amor qui se prodit corripiendo vitia amici, præstat amore latenti, qui non carpit, sed dissi- mulat vitia, vel ea tegit, & abscondit. Matth. 18, 15. Reprehensio enim juxta Clement. Alexandr. lib. 1. pædag. cap. 5. est velut quædam chirurgia animæ. Admonitio est veluti quædam diæta ægrotantis ani- mæ vers. 6. MELIORA (in Ebr. fidelia) SUNT VULNERA DILIGENTIS QUAM FRAU- DULENTIA (in Ebr. deprecanda, uti Junius, Piscator, Belgæ reddunt) OSCULA ODIEN- TIS, id est, cum amicus tuus etiam asperius te (ob admissum erratum) castigat, scias id tibi lon- ge salubrius esse, quam si is qui te occulte odit, maxime blandiatur. Hæc non dicuntur, quod debeamus amicos importune & aspere tractare: Sed ut non ægre feramus, si paulo severius amici nobiscum agant, quia bene nobis cupiunt. Non omnis, inquit Augustin. Epist. 48. ad Vincent. (in jure Canon. S. quæst. 5. cum in princ.) qui parcit amicus est, neque omnis qui verberat inimicus: me- liora sunt vulnera amici, quam voluntaria oscula ini- mici, melius est cum severitate diligere, quam cum lenitate decipere. Et qui phreneticum ligat, & qui lethargicum excitat, ambobus molestus, ambos amat. Quis nos potest amplius amare, quam Deus? & ta- men nos non solum ducere suaviter, verum etiam salubriter terrere non cessat, fomentis lenibus qui- bus consolatur, sæpe etiam mordacissimum tribula- tionis medicamentum adjungens. Confer. Psalm. 141, 5. Proverb. 26, 27. 2. Samuel. 20, 9. 10. Matth. 26, 48. Ut autem constet, cuinam gratæ sint, & sua- ves amicæ reprehensiones, nimirum non homi- ni voluptatibus affluenti, qui favum ejusmodi asper- natur, sed animæ famelicæ informationem, & cor- reptionem esurienti, additur vers. 7. anima satu- rata calcabit favum, & anima esuriens etiam ama- rum pro dulci sumet. Evidens, dicitur apud Cas- sian. collat. 14. cap. 13. est tepidæ & superbæ mentis indicium, si verborum salutarium medicinam, quamvis studio nimiæ assiduitatis ingestam, fastidio- se negligenterque suspiciat. Referri ad eundem scopum potest etiam sequens paræmia de viro ex animi levitate & inconstantia, qualicunque molestia inducto sedem habitationis suæ mutante: ut qui nec amicorum correptionem sustinere, nec qualem- cunque amaritiem devorare potest, ideoque afful- gente spe paulo pinguiori facilis est in mutando lo- co, non absque periculo & damno. In peregrinatio- ne enim, dicente Seneca, vitam agentibus hoc evenit: ut multa hospitia habeat, nullas amicitias. Ephrem Sy- rus in loco, inquit, habitationis tuæ vel quem à Deo as- signatum accepisti, lubens permaneto, otium atque de- sidiam à te repellens, cum neque in loci mutatione, atque distantia situm sit, ut passiones nostras repri- namus, sed in attentione & cura mentis. Grotius ita habet vers. 8. SICVT AVIS TRANSMIGRANS DE NIDO SUO, SIC VIR QVI DERELINQVIT LOCUM SVVM) Facile capitur avis à nido avolitans: Sic & qui domo reli- cta longe peregrinatur, multis se objicit periculis. Confer Sirac. 29, 31. Mutatio omnibus in rebus præterquam in malis est periculosa, ait Plato Dia- logo 7. de Legibus.

Porro de amicorum dulcedine vers. 9. disseri- tur: unguento, id est, oleo fragranti, balsamo) & variis odoribus delectatur cor, & bonis amici consi- liis anima dulcoratur, in Ebr. & (ita) dulcedo ami- ci propter consilium animæ, (ex sincero corde pro- fectum) scil. exhilarat cor. Confer. cap. 12, 15. cap. 13, 10. 15. cap. 15, 22. cap. 17, 17. cap. 25, 16. Idcir- co monet ulterius vers. 10. Amicum tuum & ami- cum Patris tui (veterem ergo amicum, quem hæ- reditate quasi accepimus intelligit, Sirac. 9, 14.) ne derelinquas, & domum fratris tui ne ingrediaris in die afflictionis (quod συγκριτικῶς dictum, h. m. non tam fratris, qui scil. non amicus simul est, sed sanguine tantum junctus, non animi affectione cap. 17, 17. cap. 18, 14.) nam melior est vicinus pro- pinquus (amicus scil.) quam frater remotus, seu loco, seu etiam animi affectu, qui opem ferre aut non potest, aut non vult. Herodotus, pretiosis- simus, inquit, thesaurus est, & omnibus opibus an- tecellit amicus prudens, & benevolus. Tantum va- let, inquit Ambros. lib. 1. Offic. cap. 34. benevolen- tia, ut plerumque pignora vincat naturæ. Grotius ad hunc versum hæc:

## 27:10
Verse 10. BETTER IS A NEIGHBOR NEARBY THAN A BROTHER AFAR OFF) Hesiod:

Call him most of all who dwells near you. For if even any local matter should arise, neighbors come ungirded, while kinsmen gird themselves. A bad neighbor is a bane, as much as a good one is a great blessing.

When he has treated of a friend gladdening the heart, turning to his son he exhorts him to devote himself to the study of wisdom, by which parents especially may be gladdened by him, and may be able to answer or meet enemies who are railing or reproaching them with some matter, verse 11. Be wise my son, and let it gladden (or you shall gladden, from chap. 23, 15. 24.) my heart, and I will answer him who reproaches me. Conf. Psalm 119, 42. Ps. 127, 5. For if anyone should slander either the Father or the son, the Father will be able to answer both himself and through his wise son, and to repel every reproach: who can also assist the parent in public judgment and in a case to be argued against adversaries. Moreover, to this exhortation is added the benefit of wisdom, verse 12. The prudent man sees the evil, and hides himself (conf. chap. 22, 3.) the simple pass on, and are punished. A pious, prudent, and sensible man, having been warned by the word of God, perceives in good time the evils that are hanging over him, and acts circumspectly, and escapes: but a foolish man proceeds in blind security, and falls into calamities.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit continues in the warnings concerning friends (1.) that we should so serve them as not to expose ourselves to quarrels, which happens especially by suretyships, according to that saying, be surety and harm is present: verse 13. And this proverb coheres with the preceding, because they are altogether simple who do not foresee those evils hanging over from suretyships, and thus are punished by their own fault, therefore it is repeated what had been said in chap. 20, 16: take his garment, because he has become surety for a stranger, etc. Then that in the praises of a neighbor we should not exceed, nor should we hunt for or suspect excessive praises, and thus we should flee flatterers. verse 14. He who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early (untimely, too early in the morning, before he has sufficiently explored him) it shall be reckoned as a curse to him, namely by wise men; it will not even result in praise for the one being praised, and an untimely commendation will therefore be held as a curse. Bede says, he blesses his neighbor with a loud voice who extols him with the favor of superfluous praise, either by favoring his evil acts against justice, or by praising good things more than is just: but this man is likened to one cursing, because he harms him greatly: since by praising him he grants him confidence in an evil action, or diminishes the simplicity of a pure heart in a right work, so that, namely, he may finish with the love of transitory praise the good which he had begun with a view to heavenly virtue.

Thirdly, concerning a quarrelsome woman, not to be further exasperated, v. 15, 16, 17. Who is therefore first depicted in verse 15. A continual dripping in the day of a violent rain (the Vulgate has leaking roofs in the day of cold) and a woman of contentions are equal. Compare chap. 19, 13. Drops, says Zehner, similit. page 130, which drip through tiles or broken roof-tiles during rainy weather, are not only annoying to tenants because of the frequent repetition of the sound and the unpleasant spray, but also bring extreme ruin to the buildings themselves in the passage of time. In the same way, a quarrelsome woman not only causes much annoyance to her husband, but also delays the growth of the family estate by her importunity, nay, she miserably dissipates all that had been previously acquired, and all but overturns and ruins the whole house. For in that lust for arguing, neither can prayers be seriously poured out to God, nor the blessing of the divine Majesty be obtained, nor the concord of souls be nourished for long, nor finally can the same household staff be constantly retained, but it is necessary that new workers be introduced daily. Each of these things brings a panolethrian or universal destruction to domestic affairs, Prov. 11, 29.

Furthermore, it is taught that the malice of a quarrelsome woman cannot be repressed by violence, and that therefore there is need for gentleness, verse 16. He who hides her hides (or strives to conceal) the wind (with vain effort: Compare Sirach 34, 2. just as no one can repress the roaring wind, or shut it in prisons so that it may not strike and rage against the ears, so neither can one a roaring woman.) But the oil of his right hand shall call (the husband's blandishments and soothing words will summon her, entice her, and turn her to her husband. For these things soothe and soften the hardness of a rigid woman far better than the severity and bitterness of a man. Cornelius notes that R. Aben-Ezra explains it thus: and oil is accustomed to be compared to blandishments. See Psalm 55, 22. and thus the following verse 17 agrees, and iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his neighbor: which Baynus and others apply thus: just as iron is sharpened by iron, so if a rigid man falls in with a rigid and quarrelsome wife, one will sharpen the other to anger and quarreling: and therefore, so that this may not happen, let the gentleness and patience of one receive, blunt, and dull the asperity and anger of the other like a file, nay, let it soothe and soften it, and render his face calm and serene. Vatablus translates, and (hides) the oil which shall call. Whence the proverb, as Cornelius notes: Three things cannot be hidden, because they betray themselves and make themselves felt, namely, a woman, the wind, an ointment: a woman by her voice, the wind by its force, an ointment by its scent. But the LXX version is entirely foreign: The North wind is a hard wind, but it is called by the name of the right hand, even though the Chaldean, the Syrian, Aquila, and Symmachus render it in a nearly similar way.

Now, verse 18 teaches how, in particular, servants ought to conduct themselves toward their Masters, and conversely Masters toward their faithful servants: He who keeps the fig tree shall eat its fruit, and he who is a guardian of his Master shall be glorified, that is, just as he who diligently cares for a fruitful tree, so that it may not wither, and does all those things which seem to pertain to the fruitfulness and longevity of the tree, he also enjoys its fruits for a long time and in abundance: so a servant who diligently (as far as in him lies) and faithfully procures the safety and happiness of his Master, will long and abundantly enjoy the benefits which can proceed from his Master. And faithful ministers, who watch zealously for the safety of their superiors, will be raised to happiness, dignity, and honors, as the Osiandrian Paraphrase has it. But he brings the example of the fig tree, as Mercer notes, because this tree would abound in Judea, and bears a most sweet fruit: likewise according to Kabvenaki, because all its fruits do not ripen at once, but one after another in succession. Whence he perceives an advantage from its custody again and again. Thus he who faithfully and zealously obeys his master, etc. By the mention of honor, however, by synecdoche, according to the custom accepted by Solomon, every kind of compensation is understood: and the discourse is of right, even if in fact it often happens otherwise, as is evident from the example of Jacob serving under Laban.

Mutual conformity of souls also pertains to friendship: concerning which, therefore, verse 19 treats: As water (or as regards waters) face to face (of the one looking is formed in them as in a natural mirror) so the heart of man to man (who converses with him, responds, and is conformed, and shines forth in the same) so that a friend is as it were another self. Hence, just as the grave and destruction (death, which is the destruction of all) are not satisfied, so the eyes of men are not satisfied with the sight of such a friend: but they always desire to enjoy the same, verse 20. But so that a friend may be rightly tested, a means is suggested for exploring his secret qualities, verse 21. whether the pursuit of virtue, or indeed a foolish love of self and of vices is with him: as the refining pot for silver and the furnace for gold (v. chap. 17, 3.) so is the mouth of one praising him to a man. Just as silver and gold are tested in the fire, and it is discovered whether those metals are pure, or impure and mixed: so if you praise a man in his presence, you will easily discover whether folly is in him: for he will not be able to conceal it, but provoked by his own praises, he will boast magnificently of great things. A wise man, however, when praised, is suffused with a bashful and modest blush, and does not acknowledge as much in himself as is proclaimed about him. For just as if gold and silver remain intact and yield no dross, it is a sign that they are pure: but if they yield dross, it is a sign that they are impure; so likewise if anyone becomes proud and swells up from praise, it is a sign that the man is of less upright and solid virtue. The Vulgate adds another sentence, but without a number, and without the authority of the Hebrew and Greek text, which is also missing in certain Latin codices: the heart of the wicked seeks evil, but the heart of the upright seeks knowledge. The sentence which follows in the sources, verse 22, coheres with the verse 21 already expounded, because such people who are rendered swollen by praise are truly foolish: concerning whom it is held thus: If you pound a fool in a mortar, in the midst of crushed wheat with a pestle, his folly will not depart from him. It seems to contradict chapter 22, 15. But in that passage the discourse is about a tender mind, which like a tender tree is easily corrected: here it is about men of advanced age, in whom the seeds of vices strike deep roots, nor can they be easily plucked out. Gregor. M. in Pastoral. part. 3. adm. 14. Those are to be admonished in one way who fear the lash, and therefore live innocently; and those are to be admonished in another way who have so hardened themselves in iniquity that they are not corrected even by the lash. Compare Sirach 21:17, chapter 22:7. However, this proverb is not to be taken as if nothing should be attempted that might contribute to the amendment of wicked men; but so that we do not torment ourselves with vain cares if it does not succeed according to our desire. For some wicked men are clearly incurable.

Latin:

Vers. 10. MELIOR EST VICINUS JUXTA, QVAM FRA- TER PROCUL) Hesiodus:

Τὸν δὲ μάλιστα καλεῖν ὅςις σέο ἐγγύθι ναίει. Εἰ γάρ τοι καὶ χρῆμ᾽ ἐγχώριον ἄλλο γένηται, Γείτονες ἄζωστοι ἔκιον, ζώσαντο δὲ πηοί. Πῆμα κακὸς γείτων, ὅσσον τ᾽ ἀγαθὸς μέγ᾽ ὄνειαρ.

Quum de amico cor exhilarante egerit, con- versus ad filium hortatur, ut studio sapientiæ vacet, quo ab ipso imprimis exhilarari possint parentes, & inimicis convitiantibus, vel rem aliquam ex- probrantibus respondere, aut occurrere vers. 11. Sis sapiens fili mi, & lætificet (vel lætificabis ê cap. 23, 15. 24.) cor meum, & respondebo rem expro- branti mihi. Conf. Psalm. 119, 42. Ps. 127, 5. Si quis enim vel Patrem vel filium calumnietur, responde- re Pater tum ipse, tum per filium sapientem pote- rit, ac probrum omne propellere: qui parentem etiam in publico judicio & causa contra adversa- rios disceptanda adjuvare potest. Additur autem huic adhortationi commodum sapientiæ vers. 12. Prudens videt malum, & abscondit se (conf. cap. 22, 3.) simplices transeunt, & mulctantur. Pius prudens & cordatus homo admonitus verbo Dei tempestive impendentia mala animadvertit, & cir- cumspecte agit, atque effugit: homo autem vecors, cœca securitate pergit, & in calamitates incidit.

Pergit autem Spirit. Sanct. in monitis de ami- cis (1.) ut ita iis inserviamus, ne ipsimit nos rixæ exponamus, quod imprimis fit sponsionibus juxta illud, sponde præsto noxa est: vers. 13. Et cohæret hæc paræmia cum præcedenti, quia simplices o- mnino sunt, qui ista mala è sponsionibus impen- dentia non prævident, adeoque culpa sua mulctan- tur, ideo repetitur, quod cap. 20, 16. dictum erat: tolle vestimentum ejus, quia fidejussit pro extra- neo, &c. Deinde ut in laudibus proximi ne exce- damus, neque laudes nimias aucupemur, vel suspi- piamus, adeoque adulatores fugiamus. vers. 14. Qui benedicit amico suo voce magna mane surgendo (in- tempestive, mane nimis, antequam satis eum ex- ploravit) maledictio reputabitur ei, à viris sscil. cor- datis ipsi etiam laudato non cedet in laudem, com- mendatio intempestiva proinde habebitur ut ma- ledictio. Beda, voce grandi, inquit, proximo be- nedicit, qui eum favore superfluæ laudis extollit, vel malis actibus ejus contra justitiam favendo, vel bona plus justo laudando: sed hic maledicenti assimi- latur, quia plurimum lædit: quum eum laudando sive in mala actione confidentiam tribuit, seu in ope- re recto simplicitatem puri cordis imminuit, ut vi- delicet bonum, quod supernæ virtutis intuitu inchoa- rat, transitoriæ laudis amore consummet.

Tertio de muliere rixosa, non ulterius exa- speranda, v. 15. 16. 17. Quæ proinde primum de- pingitur vers. 15. Stillatio assidua in die imbris ve- hementis (Vulg. habet tecta perstillantia in die fri- goris) & mulier contentionum æquantur. Confer. cap. 19, 13. Guttæ, inquit Zehner. similit. pag. 130. quæ pluvia tempestate per tegulas aut imbrices fra- ctas destillant, non tantum inquilinis, ob crebram sonitus iterationem & ingratam asperginem molestæ sunt, verum etiam ipsis ædibus progressu temporis per- niciem extremam afferunt. Eodem pacto mulier ri- xosa non solum marito plurimum exhibet molestiæ, sed etiam importunitate sua rei familiaris augmen- tum remoratur, imo omnia, quæ prius parta erant, misere dissipat, ac tantum non totam domum evertit ac pessundat. Nam in ista altercandi libidine nec preces serio ad Deum fundi, nec divini Numinis be- nedictio impetrari, nec animorum concordia diuti- us ali, nec denique idem famulitium constanter re- tineri potest, sed indies novas operas induci necesse est. Quæ singula rei domesticæ πανωλεθρίαν vel in- teritum universalem afferunt, Prov. 11, 29.

Porro malitiam mulieris rixosæ violentia re- primi non posse, adeoque lenitate opus esse doce- tur vers. 16. Abscondens eam abscondit (vel occulta- re studet) ventum (conatu irrito: Confer. Sirac. 34, 2. uti nemo ventum frementem reprimere, vel ne aures feriat furiatque, carceribus includere potest, ita nec frementem mulierem.) At oleum dextræ ejus vocabit (blandimenta & delinimenta mariti evocabunt ipsam, allicient, & ad virum convertent. Hæc enim longe melius fœminæ rigidæ duritiem demulcent, atque emolliunt, quam severitas & acerbitas viri. Sic explicare R. Aben-Ezram notat Cornelius: & solet oleum blan- dimentis conferri. Vid. Psalm. 55, 22. atque ita con- gruit vers. sequens 17. ferrumque ferro acuitur, & vir exacuit faciem proximi sui: quem Baynus & alii sic applicant: sicut ferrum ferro acuitur, sic vir rigidus si in rigidam & rixosam uxorem incidat, alius alium ad iram rixamque exacuet: ideoque ne hoc fiat, lenitas, & patientia unius asperitatem, iram- que alterius ceu lima excipiat, hebetet, & obtun- dat, imo leniat, & emolliat, faciemque ejus pla- cidam & serenam reddat. Vatablus vertit, & (re- condit) oleum quod clamabit. Unde proverbium notante Cornelio: Tria celari nequeunt, quia se ipsa produnt, faciuntque sentiri, sscil. mulier, ven- tus, unguentum: mulier voce, ventus impetu, un- guentum odore. Aliena vero prorsus est LXX. versio: Aquilo durus ventus, nomine autem dexter vocatur, etsi Chald. Syrus, Aquila & Symmachus fe- re simili modo reddant.

Jam quomodo in specie servi erga Dominos, & vicissim Domini erga servos fideles sese gerere debeant, vers. 18. docet: Qui servat ficum, comedet fructus ejus, & qui custos est Domini sui, glorificabitur, id est, quemadmodum qui arborem fœcundam diligenter curat, ne exareat, & omnia ea facit, quæ ad arboris fœcunditatem & diuturnitatem pertinere videntur, is etiam diu & multum fruitur ejus fructibus: ita servus, qui Domini sui incolumitatem & felicitatem diligenter (quantum in se est) & fideliter procurat, diu multumque fruetur beneficiis, quæ à Domino suo proficisci possunt. Et fideles ministri, qui sedulo vigilant pro salute suorum Præcipum, ad felicitatem, dignitatem, & honores evehentur, ut habet Osiandrina Paraphrasis. Ficus autem exemplum, notante Mercero, affert, quod hæc arbor in Judæa abundaret, & dulcissimum fructum ferat: item juxta Kabvenaki, quod non simul omnes ejus fructus maturescant, sed alii subinde post alios. Unde identidem ex ejus custodia commodum percipit. Sic qui fideliter & sedulo hero suo obsequitur, &c. Mentione vero honoris Synecdochice pro more Salomoni recepto omnis generis compensatio intelligitur: & de jure sermo est, etsi de facto non raro aliter contingat, ut exemplo Jacobi apud Labanum servientis constat.

Ad amicitiam etiam pertinet mutua animorum conformatio: de qua proinde vers. 19. agitur: Sicut aquæ (vel quod ad aquas) facies ad faciem (intuentis efformatur in iisdem ceu speculo naturali) sic cor hominis homini (qui cum ipso conversatur, respondet, & conformatur, ac resplendescit in eodem) ut amicus sit quasi alter ego. Hinc sicut sepulcrum & perditio (mors, quæ omnium perditio est) non saturantur, sic oculi hominum non saturantur aspectu amici talis: quin semper eodem frui cupiant, vers. 20. Ut autem recte probetur amicus, medium suggeritur arcanas ejus qualitates explorandi vers. 21. num studium virtutis, an vero amor stultus sui ac vitiorum penes eum sit: ut conflatorium argento & fornax auro (v. cap. 17, 3.) sic est viro os laudantis eum. Quemadmodum argentum & aurum in igne examinantur, & deprehenditur, an pura sint illa metalla, an impura, & mixta: ita si hominem in præsentia laudaveris, facile deprehendes an in eo sit stultitia: non enim eam celare poterit, sed laudibus suis provocatus, magnifice gloriabitur de rebus magnis. Sapiens vero vir laudatus, verecundo & modesto rubore suffunditur, neque agnoscit tanta in se, quanta de ipso prædicantur. Sicut enim si aurum & argentum perstet integrum, nullamque det scoriam, signum est esse purum: sin scoriam det, signum est esse impurum; sic pariter si quis ex laude superbiat & intumescat, signum est hominem esse minus probæ, & solidæ virtutis. Vulgata addit aliam sententiam, sed sine numero, & citra Ebræi & Græci Codicis autoritatem, quæ etiam in Latinis quibusdam Codicibus desideratur: cor iniqui inquirit mala, cor autem recti inquirit scientiam. Cohæret autem quæ in fontibus sequitur vers. 22. sententia cum jam exposita vers. 21. quia tales qui laude tumidi redduntur, vere stulti sunt: de quibus ita habetur: Si contuderis stultum in mortario, in medio triticorum contusorum pistillo, non recedet ab eo stultitia. Contrariari videtur cap. 22, 15. Sed in eo de animo tenello sermo est, qui instar arboris teneræ facile corrigitur: hic de provectæ ætatis hominibus, in quibus vitiorum semina altas gerunt radices, nec facile evelli possunt. Gregor. M. in Pastoral. part. 3. adm. 14. Aliter admonendi sunt, qui flagella me- tuunt, & propterea innocenter vivunt; atque aliter admonendi sunt, qui sic in iniquitate duruerunt, ut neque per flagella corrigantur. Confer. Sirac. 21. v. 17. cap. 22. v. 7. Non autem eo accipienda haec paroemia, quasi nihil tentandum sit, quod ad emen- dationem hominum pravorum faciat; sed ut nos non torqueamus vanis curis, si id non ex animi sententia successerit. Quidam enim impii plane sunt insanabiles.

## 27:20
Verse 20.

HELL AND DESTRUCTION ARE NEVER FILLED) In the same sense, the poets call the kingdom of Dis insatiable.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

INFERNUS ET PERDITIO NVNQVAM IM- PLENTVR) Eodem sensu regnum Ditis insatiabile vocant Poetae.

## 27:23
Verse 23.

DILIGENTLY KNOW THE FACE OF THY CATTLE, AND CONSIDER THY FLOCKS.

There follow economic admonitions, directed primarily to livestock matters, because wealth in former times consisted almost entirely in that: whose knowledge, therefore, (1.) is required here of the householder: and thus the Papists are ridiculous, who snatch this verse away to auricular confession. For literally, as Cornelius admits, Solomon commands the head of a household, or farmer, and shepherd, that he should have diligent care of his cattle: Consider, consider the face of thy cattle: set thy heart to the flocks. So also Lyranus, Bannes, Jansenius, Menochius, and others. For he adds concerning the instability of riches, verse 24: Because riches are not to last for an age: will the crown (dignity and preeminence) be from generation to generation? And concerning the manner of caring for the flocks with herbs both flowering and dried, collected at the proper time, verse 25. The grass comes forth, and the herb appears, or the sprout (which, when it exists, the flocks are to be led out in early spring) and the herbs of the mountains are collected (which are to be collected even from the mountains, not only from the valleys, for the future necessity of winter.) But there are subjoined in verse 26 the benefits of the flocks, both as to clothing: The wool of the sheep is for thy garments (Job 31:20, Heb 11:37) and as to food, in the same verse: and the price of the field are the goats (which can be sold so that a field may be bought, from which grain and bread are prepared. Compare Ezek 27:21) as also in verse 27: and the sufficiency of the milk of the goats for thy food, and for the food of thy house, and for the sustenance of thy maidens: whom he mentions here particularly: because their own duties in the fields also belonged to them separately. Ruth 2:8, 22, chapter 3:2, Proverbs 31:15. He signifies that from the care of a flock of cattle, all things can be had which contribute to the necessities of life. 1 Tim. 6:8.
