The LXX wrongly render the words for milk as strong words: Son, you have received from me strong words, by which you sustain the life of yourself and your ministers.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

DILIGENTER AGNOSCE VULTUM PE- CORIS TUI, TUOSQUE GREGES CON- SIDERA.

Sequuntur monita Oeconomica, ad rem im- primis pecuariam directa, quia in illa fere divi- tiae olim constetere: cujus proinde (1.) cognitio ab Oeconomo hic requiritur: ideoque ridiculi sunt Papistae, qui hunc versum ad confessionem auri- cularem abripiunt. Ad literam enim, fatente Cornelio, jubet Salomon Patrifamilias, sive agri- cola, & pastori, ut curam diligentem habeat peco- ris sui: Considerando considera vultum pecoris tui: pone cor tuum ad greges. Sic etiam Lyranus, Ban- nes, Jansenius, Menochius, aliique. Addit nam- que de instabilitate divitiarum, vers. 24. Quia non in seculum divitiae sunt duraturae: num co- rona (dignitas & praeeminentia) erit in genera- tione & generatione? Et de modo greges curandi her- bis tum florentibus tum arefactis, debito tempo- re collectis, vers. 25. Prodit gramen, & apparet herba, vel germen, (quod cum sit, primo ve- re educendi sunt greges) & colliguntur herbae mon- tium (quae ex montibus etiam colligendae, non tantum e convallibus, ad futuram hyemis ne- cessitatem.) Subjunguntur autem vers. 26. com- moda gregum, tum qua amictum: Ovium lanae sunt pro indumentis tuis (Job. 31, 20. Ebr. 11, 37.) tum qua victum, eodem versu: & pretium agri sunt hirci (qui vendi possunt, ut ager coëma- tur, ex quo frumentum ac panis paratur. Con- fer. Ezech. 27, 21.) ut & vers. 27. & sufficientia la- ctis caprarum in cibum tuum, & in cibum domus tuae, & ad victum puellarum tuarum: quarum hic peculiariter meminit: quia illis seorsim sua quo- que in agris competebant munia. Ruth. 2, 8. 22. cap. 3, 2. Proverb. 31, 15. Significat ex gregis peco- rum cura haberi posse omnia, quae προς τα άλφι- τα faciunt 1. Timoth. 6, 8. LXX. perperam pro lac verba fortia reddunt: Fili accepisti a me verba for- tia, quibus tuam & tuorum ministrorum vitam su- stentes.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning an evil conscience, the cause of which is impiety, the oppression of the poor and iniquity, and especially the tyranny of magistrates: with analogous moral admonitions.

Verse 1.

THE WICKED FLEES, WITH NO ONE PURSUING, BUT THE JUST SHALL BE AS A CONFIDENT LION, WITHOUT TERROR.

In the Hebrew: They have fled, although no one pursues the wicked (that is, everyone of the wicked, agitated by the furies of conscience) and (but) the just (everyone of the just) will be confident like a young lion. Cf. Job 15:21, Prov. 28:1. A young lion is mentioned, which is clearly fearless, far more so than an older lion: both because it has not yet experienced hunters and enemies like a lion; and because sharp hunger, with which it is continually afflicted, and the greed for blood, which it has recently tasted and therefore thirsts for, sharpens its spirits and angers; and because it has sharper and firmer teeth; for through age, the teeth of lions are not rarely worn down or fall out. Whence that of Job 4:10: The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the young lions are broken: and because it rests secure under the wings of its father and mother, that is, the lion and the lioness. Thus the just rest under the wings of God, Psalm 91:1. As here Cornel. a Lapide. The wicked and the impenitent (Osiander explains) tremble and flee even at the rustling of a leaf. The pious, however, even if they themselves have sinned and still carry about a weak flesh, yet because they have a conscience pacified by the word of the Gospel, overcome dangers with a great spirit.

These things concern the confidence of the just in their own calamities: Now the fruit redounding to the Republic from the just is designated in verse 2, because on account of the transgression of (the wicked indeed in the region, or of a certain) region, many are its princes (may they become, especially as the best Princes die off successively due to the fault of the subjects, Isa. 57:2), but on account of an intelligent and knowing man (or a populace of subjects intelligent not only theoretically, but also practically, as to what true piety is, which is opposed to transgression), thus its Prince, namely of the land or region, prolongs his days, so that there is no need for many princes. When the people are wicked and criminal, the Lord punishes the ingratitude of the subjects with frequent changes of Princes. For changes of governments disturb the Republic for some time; like a certain earthquake: But when the subjects are intelligent and lovers of the word of God and of piety, God prolongs the life of the Princes for many years, so that the Republic may flourish and remain tranquil and quiet. Osiander. Grotius thus:

Latin:

CAPUT XXIIX. De mala conscientia, cujus causa impietas, op- pressio pauperum & iniquitas, ac Tyrannis imprimis Magistratuum: cum monitis mo- ralibus analogis.

Vers. 1.

FUGIT IMPIUS, NEMINE PERSEQUEN- TE, JUSTUS AUTEM QUASI LEO CON- FIDENS, ABSQUE TERRORE ERIT.

IN Ebr. Fugerunt, tametsi nemo persequatur impius, (id est, quisque impiorum conscientiae furiis agitatus) & (at) justi (justorum quisque) instar leunculi confidet. Conf. Job. 15, 21. Jac. 17, 8. Leunculus autem commemoratur, qui plane impavidus est, longe magis quam leo senior: tum quia necdum venatores & hostes expertus est ut leo: tum quia fames acris, qua assidue laborat; & aviditas sanguinis, quem recens degustavit, ideoque sitit, acuit ei animos & iras: tum quia dentes habet acutiores & firmiores; nam per aetatem leonibus dentes non raro conteruntur vel excidunt. Unde illud Job. 4, 10. Rugitus leonis, & vox leænæ, & dentes catulorum leonum contriti sunt: tum quia suæ alis patris & matris, id est, leonis & leænæ, securus requiescit. Ita justi requiescunt sub alis Dei, Psalm. 91, 1. Ut hic Cornel. a Lapid. Impii & impœnitentes (explicat Osiander) vel ad strepitum folii trepidant & fugiunt. Pii vero etsi ipsi peccarunt, & adhuc circumferunt carnem imbecillem, tamen quia habent conscientiam pacatam verbo Evangelii, magno animo superant pericula.

Hæc de justorum fiducia in propriis calamitatibus: Jam fructus ad Rempublicam redundans a justis designatur vers. 2. quod propter (improborum quidem in regione, vel cujusdam) regionis prævaricationem multi principes ejus (fiant, imprimis successive decedentibus ob culpam subditorum optimis Principibus Esa. 57, 2.) at propter hominem intelligentem & scientem (aut plebem subditorum non theoretice solum, sed & practice, quæ vera sit pietas, prævaricationi opposita, intelligentem) sic prolonget dies Princeps ejus, terræ scil. vel regionis, ita ut opus non sit multis principibus. Cum populus impius est & sceleratus, punit Dominus ingratitudinem subditorum crebris mutationibus Principum. Mutationes enim imperiorum perturbant aliquandiu Rempublicam; quasi terræ motus quidam: Quando vero subditi sunt intelligentes, & amantes verbi Dei & pietatis, Deus prorogat Principibus vitam in multos annos, ut Respublica floreat, maneatque tranquilla & quieta. Osiander. Grotius ita:

## 28:2
Verse 2.

ON ACCOUNT OF THE SINS OF THE LAND MANY ARE ITS PRINCES) Governments are transferred from family to family through seditions, conspiracies, and slaughters, as often happens in the ten tribes.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

PROPTER PECCATA TERRÆ MULTI PRINCIPES EJVS) Transferuntur imperia de familia in familiam per seditiones, conjurationes, cædes, ut sæpe evenit in decem tribubus.

## 28:3
Verse 3.

A POOR MAN OPPRESSING THE POOR IS LIKE A VIOLENT RAIN, IN WHICH FAMINE IS PREPARED.

In the Hebrew it is: A poor man (if he sits at the helm, or obtains power: גבר properly denotes one powerful in strength, ch. 24:5) and one who by force despoils the poor (ch. 22:16, ch. 30:22, Eccl. 4:1) is an inundating rain (sweeping away, driving forward or prostrating, as the word סחף is taken in Jer. 42:5, as Dievius notes, the crops of the fields, and other things) and there is no bread (so that there is no food, otherwise hoped for from the earth) just as such rain is to the land, so he who oppresses the poor by force brings want and famine upon him: whereas, on the contrary, rain ought to fertilize the land, and the powerful ought to help the poor with their authority. Nothing is harsher than a lowly person when he rises to the heights.

Furthermore, since the powerful, especially those who have emerged from poverty to honors, ought to succor the pious but needy and oppressed, it is on the contrary customary for the impious who abandon the law not to promote and assist the pious, but to praise and love the impious, concerning which v. 3: They that forsake the law praise (& magnify) the wicked (as such, and therefore the pursuits and arts, machinations and practice of the wicked) but keeping the law contend with them (against individuals and all the impious companions.) Compare 1 Kings 18, verse 14. Psalm 119, verses 136, 139. The reason is: because evil men (in Hebrew, men of malice, having neglected the dictates of conscience) do not 'think (do not care about) judgment (which is just and fair or consistent with divine law;) but those who inquire of the Lord, notice everything that is just or unjust (which, namely, pleases or displeases God, Deuteronomy 4, verse 6. Whence such a person, even if he is poor, is deservedly preferred to the perverse rich man, verse 6. better is the poor man who walks in his integrity than the perverse in his ways, (tortuous, turning from good ways now to the right, now to the left, Isaiah 30, verse 21.) who is himself rich, and abuses his riches for wickedness, chapter 19, verse 1. For while the latter enjoys a tranquil and happy conscience, the former has no rest, nor any joy because of an evil conscience, chapter 15, verses 15, 16. The method of aspiring to true wisdom is also taught, and the fruit of keeping the law is illustrated by the contrary, verse 7. He who keeps the law (or doctrine, preserving it with a mindful heart, and observing it) is an understanding son (to be numbered among prudent men) but he who is a friend (or companion) of gluttons (loving carousers instead of teachers, and drinking bouts instead of instruction, and thus following wicked associations) brings shame upon his Father: those indeed who covet riches are warned not to attempt it by illicit means: whence no success, verse.

8. He who multiplies his riches by usury (biting, which the Hebrew word from נשׁך, bit, like a serpent, implies) and interest (prohibited in Leviticus 25:36, Ezekiel 18, verse 8) gathers them for one who is generous to the poor, since a third heir does not enjoy them, but God knows how to divert them in wondrous ways and means for the benefit of the poor, so that in this way the usury, by which the very needy neighbor is plundered, may return again to such an exhausted person: that is to say, what was snatched from them by fair means or foul will at last return to the poor. Compare chapter 13, verse 22. Job 27:15. Ecclesiastes 2:26. Grotius thus:

Latin:

Vers. 3.

VIR PAUPER CALUMNIANS PAUPEREM SIMILIS EST IMBRI VEHEMENTI, IN QUO PARATUR FAMES.

In Ebræo est: Vir pauper (si ad clavum sedeat, vel potestatem obtineat: גבר proprie notat viribus pollentem, c. 24, 5.) & vi spolians pauperes (c. 22, 16. c. 30, 22. Eccl. 4, 1.) est pluvia inundans (everrens, propulsans aut prosternens, uti vox סחף Jer. 42, 5. accipitur notante Dievio, sata agrorum, & alia) & non est panis (ut nullus sit cibus, e terra alias speratus) sicut pluvia talis terræ, ita qui pauperem vi opprimit, eidem inopiam & famem inducit: quum contra pluvia terram fœcundare, & potentes pauperem juvare debeant autoritate sua. Asperius nihil est humili cum surgit in altum.

Porro quum potentes, imprimis qui e paupertate emerserunt ad honores, piis at egenis, & oppressis succurrere debeant: solemne ex adverso est impiis legem derelinquentibus non pios promovere, eosque juvare, sed impios laudare & amare, quo de v. 3. Derelinquentes legem laudant (& magnifaciunt) impium (qua talem, ideoque studia & artes, machinationes & praxin impii) at custo- dientes legem decertant cum eis (contra singulos ac universos impii sodales.) Confer. 1. Reg. 18. vers. 14. Psalm. 119. vers. 136. 139. Causa est: quia viri mali (in Ebr. Viri malitiæ, posthabito conscientiæ dictamine) non 'cogitant (non curant) judicium (quod justum & æquum vel legi divi- næ consentaneum est;) qui autem inquirunt Dominum, animadvertunt omnia, quæ justa vel injusta sunt (quæ scil. Deo placent, aut displi- cent Deuter. 4. vers. 6. Unde merito præfertur talis, etsi pauper sit, diviti perverso, vers. 6. præstantior est pauper, qui ambulat in integritate sua, quam perversus viis, (tortuosus viarum bonarum modo ad dextram, modo ad sinistram declinans Esa. 30. vers. 21.) qui ipse dives est, & divitiis suis abutitur ad nequitiam cap. 19. vers. 1. Quum enim tranquilla & læta ille fruatur conscientia, hic nullam habet requiem, nec ullum gaudium ob malam conscientiam cap. 15. vers. 15. 16. Docetur etiam modus adspirandi ad veram sapientiam, ac fructus custodiæ legis à contrario illustratur vers. 7. Qui custodit legem (vel doctrinam, eam memori mente asservans, & observans) filius est intelligens (viris prudentibus annumerandus) qui autem amicus (vel socius est) comedonum (loco Doctorum lurcones, loco informationis comessationes & compotationes amans, adeoque prava sodalitia sectans) pudore afficit Patrem suum: illi vero qui divitias affectant, monentur ne illicitis id mediis tentent: unde nullus successus vers.

8. Multiplicans divitias suas usura (mordace, quod vox Ebræa à נשׁך momordit instar serpentis, importat) & fœnore (prohibito Levit. 25, 36. Ezechiel. 18. vers. 8.) ad largiendum pauperibus congregat eas, quum illis non gaudeat tertius hæres, sed Deus miris modis & viis easdem derivare novit in commodum pauperum, ut ita usura, qua proximus maxime tenuis expilatur, iterum ad ejusmodi exhaustum devolvatur: q. d. ad pauperes tandem rediturum, quod illis per fas & nefas ereptum. Confer. cap. 13. vers. 22. Job. 27, 15. Eccles. 2, 26. Grotius ita:

## 28:8
Verse 8.

HE WHO HEAPS UP RICHES BY USURY AND INTEREST, GATHERS THEM FOR ONE WHO IS LIBERAL TO THE POOR) Wealth wickedly acquired, for instance by interest, the king takes away from those who have thus produced it, and gives it to those who are charitable.

But that we may be more and more deterred from impiety toward God and fraud toward our neighbor, the Holy Spirit subjects the punishment of both, verse 9. He who turns away his ear from hearing the law (the word of God, or God teaching in the word (Psalm 58, verse 5. Acts 7, verse 54. 2 Timothy 4, verse 4.) even his prayer is an abomination (God will also turn away His ears from his prayer, and will not hear, nay, He will abominate the same. Compare chapter 1, verse 28. chapter 21, verse 27. Sirach 34.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

QVI COACERVAT DIVITIAS VSVRIS ET FOENORE, LIBERALI IN PAVPERES CONGREGAT EAS) Opes improbe partas, puta fœnore, rex aufert iis qui sic eas peperere, datque eas beneficiis.

Ab impietate autem erga Deum & fraudulentia erga proximum ut magis magisque deterreamur, pœnam utriusque subjicit Spiritus Sanctus vers. 9. Qui removet aurem suam ne audiat legem (verbum Dei, vel Deum in verbo docentem (Psalm. 58. vers. 5. Actor. 7. vers. 54. 2. Timoth. 4. vers. 4.) etiam oratio ejus abominatio (Deus etiam aures suas avertet ab ejus precatione, nec audiet, imo abominabitur eundem. Confer. cap. 1. vers. 28. cap. 21. vers. 27. Sirac. 34.

## 28:13
Verse 13.

BUT WHOEVER SHALL HAVE CONFESSED) And indeed specifically, as Maimonides says.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

QVI AVTEM CONFESSVS FVERIT) Et quidem speciatim, ut ait Maimonides.

## 28:15
Verse 15. A ROARING LION AND A HUNGRY BEAR IS A WICKED PRINCE OVER A POOR PEOPLE.

Since he spoke of the rich despoiling the poor in verse 3, he now particularly warns Princes and Magistrates not to tyrannically rage against the bodies or goods of their subjects: for such are like wild beasts, not men: roaring lions, who ferociously invade and tear apart: and bears running about for hunger and desire of prey (Isaiah 29:8). A leader lacking understanding (Solomon continues in verse 16) has multiplied robberies (the cause of that cruelty and rapacity is a defect of true wisdom). He who hates avarice (not only is he truly intelligent, but in place of a reward he will also have τὴν μακροβιότητα) will prolong his days, (as opposed to those multiplying robberies, they do not multiply, but shorten their days. Micah 3:6, chapter 7:3. Psalm 55:24.) Nor does he only threaten the shortening of life to such, but the perpetual restlessness of conscience, with a general rule proposed concerning murderers in verse 17. A man who is oppressed (whether κατ' ἔξω by others, or κατ' ἔσω by the furies and afflictions of his own conscience: for it is a passive עָשׁוּק, not active, whence it is rendered passively by R. Levi, and R. Joseph, Cartwright, the Dutch, Glassius, Dr. Geier, and others) in blood (or because of the blood) of a soul (or of a man shed, Genesis 9:4, 5. Leviticus 17:11, 14.) will flee even to the pit (agitated by perpetual stings and lacerations of conscience, he will have no rest all the days of his life until the grave) they will not hold him (no one will free him from this trepidation, Genesis 4:14, or render his conscience tranquil.) Yet, it is not therefore to be despaired of by such with Cain, since GOD denies His grace to no one who performs penance. And therefore all are warned (even those established in the highest dignities) that they walk innocently and uprightly, and perform their duty without the oppression and robbery of others, by which they may enjoy the protection and blessing of God, with joyful tranquility of mind.

Latin:

Vers. 15. LEO RVGIENS ET URSUS ESURIENS PRINCEPS IMPIUS SUPER POPULUM PAU- PEREM.

Quum de divitibus pauperes spoliantibus di- xerit vers. 3. jam peculiariter Principes & Magi- stratus monet, ne tyrannice grassentur in subdi- torum corpora, vel bona: tales enim feris simi- les, non homines sunt: leones rugientes, qui truculenter invadunt, & dilacerant: & ursi dis- cursantes præ fame & desiderio prædæ (Es. 29. vers. 8.) Dux carens intelligentiis (pergit Salomo vers. 16.) multiplicavit rapinas (Causa crudelitatis, & ra- pacitatis istius defectus est veræ sapientiæ.) Qui odio habet avaritiam (non tantum vere est intel- ligens, sed præmii loco etiam habebit τὴν μα- κροβιότητα) prolongabit dies, (uti contra rapinas multiplicantes, non multiplicant, sed abbrevi- ant dies suos. Mich. 3. vers. 6. cap. 7. vers. 3. Psalm. 55. vers. 24.) Nec vero tantum vitæ decurtatio- nem minatur talibus, sed perpetuam conscientiæ in- quietudinem, generali de homicidis proposita re- gula vers. 17. Homo, qui oppressus est (sive κατ' ἔξω ab aliis, sive κατ' ἔσω à propriæ conscientiæ furiis, ac afflictionibus: passivum enim est עָשׁוּק, non activum, unde passive à R. Levi, & R. Joseph, Cartwrighto, Belgis, Glassio, Dn. D. Geiero & aliis redditur) in sanguine (vel propter sanguinem) animæ (aut hominis effusum Genes. 9. vers. 4. 5. Le- vit. 17. vers. 11. 14.) usque ad sepulcrum fugiet (per- petuis conscientiæ stimulis & lancinationibus ex- agitatus nullam habebit, usque ad foveam, re- quiem omnibus vitæ suæ diebus) non retinebunt eum (nemo eum ab hâc trepidatione liberabit Genes. 4. vers. 14. aut conscientiam ejus tranquil- lam reddet.) Non tamen ideo cum Caino talibus desperandum, cum nemini pœnitentiam agenti gratiam suam deneget DEUS. Ideoque monen- tur omnes (etiam in summis constituti dignitati- bus) ut innoxie & integre ambulent, & citra aliorum oppressionem & rapinas suo munere fun- gantur, quo protectione & benedictione Dei fru- antur, læta animi tranquillitate.

## 28:17
Verse 17.

A MAN WHO IS OPPRESSED BY THE BLOOD OF A SOUL, IF HE SHALL HAVE FLED EVEN TO THE PIT, NO ONE WILL SUSTAIN HIM) The sense is: he who oppresses others by force, so that he even sheds innocent blood, if he shall have run even to hidden pits, no one will hold him back, no one will take care of him. For by the enormity of his crimes he has lost all mercy.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

HOMINEM QVI CALVMNIATVR ANIMÆ SAN- GVINEM, SI VSQVE AD LACVM FVGERIT, NE- MO SVSTINET) Sensus est: qui alios per vim opprimit, ita ut & fundat sanguinem innoxium, si adusque latentes fo- veas cucurrerit, nemo eum retinebit, nemo ejus curam ge- ret. Immanitate enim flagitiorum omnem misericordiam perdidit.

## 28:18
Verse 18.

HE WHO WALKS UPRIGHTLY SHALL BE SAVED: HE WHO WALKS IN PERVERSE WAYS SHALL FALL AT ONCE.

Whoever walks uprightly, without guile, in the way of God's commandments, him God will protect: but he who studies evil arts and acts deceitfully, when he least expects it, will fall into destruction, verse 19. HE WHO WORKS HIS LAND SHALL BE SATISFIED WITH BREAD: BUT HE WHO FOLLOWS IDLENESS (Hebrew: a thing of nothing) SHALL BE FILLED WITH POVERTY. How this maxim, delivered in chapter 12, verse 14, is repeated here, has already been stated. Which sense and scope is confirmed by verse 20. A FAITHFUL MAN SHALL BE MUCH PRAISED (blessed) BUT HE WHO HASTENS TO BE RICH SHALL NOT BE INNOCENT (he shall not only not feel a blessing, but even punishment and a curse, who, hastening to gather wealth, does not deal faithfully or justly with his neighbor, but is given to injustice and impostures. Compare chapter 13, verse 11; chapter 20, verse 2; 1 Tim. 6, verses 9, 17. Similarly, it appears from verse 21 that these things, although general, especially regard the Magistrate in this place, and pertain to the continuation of the subject concerning Princes and Magistrates. To acknowledge a face (in judgment) is not good (chapter 18, verse 5; chapter 24, verse 27) and for a morsel of bread (namely, a gift of small moment, chapter 17, verse 1) a man transgresses, a man powerful in strength or dignity, chapter 24, verse 5. Finally, it is added concerning those who hasten to be rich, and are besides of an evil eye, or envious, that they are to be punished with poverty, verse 22. A man of an evil eye hastens to riches; he who so hastens to riches that he envies his neighbor his gain, and desires to derive everything to his own advantage, much less has pity on his neighbor, or bestows anything of his own upon him, and does not know that poverty will come upon him. Compare verse 8, and chapter 13, v. 11; chapter 20, v. 21.

For God punishes the impious, the unmerciful, and the greedy.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

QUI AMBULAT SIMPLICITER SALVUS ERIT: QUI PERVERSIS GRADITUR VIIS CONCIDET SEMEL.

Quisquis simpliciter, sine dolis, in via man- datorum Dei ambulaverit, hunc Deus prote- get: at qui malis artibus studet, & dolose agit, is ubi minime cogitaverit, in exitium ruet, vers. 19. QUI OPERATUR TERRAM SUAM, SATIATUR PANIBUS: QUI AUTEM SE- CTATUR OTIUM (Ebraic. res nihili) RE- PLEBITUR EGESTATE. Quæ sententia cap. 12. vers. 14. tradita quomodo hîc repetatur, jam dictum. Quem sensum & scopum confirmat vers. 20. VIR FIDELIS MULTUM LAUDA- BITUR (benedicetur) QUI AUTEM FESTI- NAT DITARI, NON ERIT INNOCENS (non modo non benedictionem, sed pœnam & maledictionem etiam sentiet, qui ad opes colligen- das festinans non fideliter aut juste cum proximo suo negotiatur, sed injustitiæ & imposturis dedi- tus est. Conf. cap. 13. vers. 11. cap. 20. vers. 2. 1. Tim. 6. vers. 9. 17. Similiter è vers. 21. apparet, hæc etsi ge- neralia, imprimis respicere hoc loco Magistratus, & ad continuationem materiæ de Principibus & Ma- gistratibus pertinere. Agnofcere faciem (in judicio) non est bonum (cap. 18. vers. 5. cap. 24. vers. 27.) & ob buccellam panis (nempe munus exigui momenti cap. 17. vers. 1.) prævaricatur vir גֶבֶר potens viribus vel dignitate cap. 24. vers. 5. Tandem additur de illis, qui ditari festinant, ac præterea mali oculi, vel invidi sunt, quod egestate puniendi sint, vers. 22. Festinat ad divitias vir mali oculi; qui ita festi- nat ad divitias, ut proximo lucrum suum invi- deat, & omnia in suum commodum derivare cu- piat, multo minus misereatur proximi, aut de suo quicquam ei eroget, nec cognoscit quod inopia eveniet ei. Conf. vers. 8. & cap. 13. v. 11. cap. 20. v. 21.

Punit enim Deus impios, immisericordes, & avaros.

## 28:21
Vers. 21. HE WHO RECOGNIZES A PERSON IN JUDGMENT, DOES NOT DO WELL: THIS MAN EVEN FOR A MORSEL OF BREAD DESERTS THE TRUTH) He who was previously induced by a large price to violate the laws, has arrived at such a point through the habit of sinning, that he does the same thing when the slightest opportunity for gain is given. We have already had the former part of this sentence twice, chap. 18, 5. c. 24, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 21. QVI COGNOSCIT IN JVDICIO FACIEM, NON BENE FACIT: ISTE ET PRO BVCCELLA PANIS DESERIT VERITATEM) Qui prius magno pretio indu- ctus jura violavit, consuetudine peccandi eo devenit, ut mi- nima data lucrandi occasione idem faciat. Partem priorem hujus sententiæ jam bis habuimus cap. 18, 5. c. 24, 23.

## 28:23
verse 23. Proverbs 9, verse 31.) And verse 10. He who causes the upright (who do not deserve this, but rather should have been helped in every way because of their piety and uprightness) to err (whether he seduces by act, or only attempts to seduce) through an evil way, he himself will fall into his own pit: But since men are seduced in two ways, as Cartwright warns, either when they are driven from piety and justice into sin; or when they are driven from the way that looks to peace and utility into the punishment of danger and loss; that the latter is meant here is clear from the fact that he who leads into error is said to be about to fall into the pit which he has dug for another. For he who draws another into sin is already in the pit before he prepares it for another. Whence the Paraphrase of Osiander is correct: If anyone cunningly wishes to lead and precipitate pious men into destruction, he himself will rush into destruction. AND (but) THE SIMPLE (the upright) SHALL POSSESS (shall receive by inheritance) GOOD THINGS (they will not so fall into a desperate pit, nay, in the end good things will happen to the pious, even if snares are laid for them, or they themselves are sometimes involved in dangers) For the Lord takes care of the pious, 2 Peter 2, verse 9. Romans 8, verse 28. Compare Proverbs 26, verse 27. chapter 24, verse 16. The Vulgate adds 'his' good things, but Cornelius acknowledges that 'His' is not in the Hebrew, Chaldean, LXX, Aquila, Theodotion, nor in many Latin versions.

Now again he teaches that the prudent poor man (informed by the word of God and following its guidance) is to be preferred to the imprudent rich man, however much he may be wise in his own conceit, verse 11. The rich man seems wise to himself: but the prudent poor man will examine him. Naturally, riches add spirit to the rich, and inflate them, so that they seem to themselves to be beautifully wise, especially because they are proclaimed by the common people as great and excellent, and are called prudent and happy by flatterers. But the poor man, yet one who is wise, despising their pride, examines them through conversations, questions, and actions, to see whether they possess true wisdom, and easily detects the foolishness of the rich: and thus he prefers to be wise and needy, than to possess riches and be foolish. Compare James 2, verse 5.

How much good accrues to the public good when truly prudent and just men are raised to dignities is taught in verse 12: when the just exult (when they are extolled, flourish, and have cause for exultation, chap. 11, verse 10), there is much glory (much honor, and thus also a cause for exultation for the people when the just rule and flourish, chap. 29, verse 2). But when the wicked rise (or are raised up and reign, 2 Kings 23, verse 25; Numbers 24, verse 17), man is searched out (because he is forced to hide himself, it is necessary that he be searched out), as R. Levi explains: when the wicked are exalted, the pious flee and hide themselves in secret places; wherefore the wicked search them out and track them down, so that they may bring them out from there into the light to themselves. Vatablus translates, and when the wicked rise, man shall be explored; then the virtue and constancy of man is explored. For to be good among the wicked is of immense goodness, as Gregory the Great says, lib. 1 in Job, chap. 1.

Moreover, since no one lives without sinning, a remedy for obtaining grace is also shown: confession and the forsaking of sin, that is, true and serious repentance: verse 13. He who covers his crimes shall not prosper (meiosis: he shall be punished; or he shall not escape punishment, he shall not obtain mercy), but he who confesses (and has truly performed repentance) shall obtain mercy. Psalm 32:5; Hosea 1:8, 9. From which, however, Papal auricular confession can in no way be established, as indeed Hugo and Cajetan thought; since in the Old Testament the sacrament of repentance, which they invent, did not yet exist, by the very confession of the Papists themselves: whence Cornelius reprobates Hugo's opinion (although he later says it was foreseen here by the Holy Spirit as an anachronism), nor is the special confession of all sins prescribed anywhere, indeed it is not even possible by David's judgment, Psalm 19:13. Furthermore, it contributes to the avoidance of sin that we always live in the fear of God, not indeed a servile fear, which is that of the faithless, who doubt or despair of the grace of God; but a filial one, which is proper to the faithful, who although they are made certain of the remission of sins and the grace of God, in the fear of God and true piety they diligently take care lest they commit anything by which they might offend God and fall from His grace, Philippians 2:12. For he had already excluded the fear of doubt and Papistic diffidence, by the indubitable promise of mercy made to the penitent: and therefore Solomon, verse 14, demands only the fear of caution and reverence, lest we lose grace. Blessed, he says, is the man who fears always, but he who hardens his heart will fall into evil, so that we may indeed flee rashness, audacity, and the hardness that despises sin and carnally trusts in justice, Nehemiah 9:17, Jeremiah 7:25, Ezekiel 33:13. and in the fear of God let us take care lest torpor or sloth invade, lest petulance creep in, lest the flesh triumph against the spirit, Psalm 119:120, 161, lest we lose grace and fall from eternal salvation, Proverbs 8:12, chapter 14:16. We also add the fear of punishment, as the Holy Spirit also deters us from sin by it, Matthew 10:28, Luke 12:4, and it is also good to fear punishment, provided that not only the punishment, but also, and indeed primarily, the offense of God and separation from Him as a friend and spouse of the soul is feared. The LXX render: Blessed is the man who fears all things δι εὐλάβειαν, on account of reverence for God, or because of the caution by which evil is declined, as Ariasmont explains, or who fears all things which could bring some contagion or detriment, as the author of the Greek Catena interprets. Such fear of God and caution against sins does not destroy confidence, but properly consists with it: because confidence trusts against the evil which the fear of God dreads. Therefore, the Papists vainly abuse this saying to construct diffidence regarding the remission of sins. This fear, as Cornelius himself says, does not destroy, but effects security, confidence, and magnanimity: citing Bernard, Epistle 87 to Ogerius, explaining this fear, not as one that is a snare of desperation, but one that acquires the hope of blessedness. Cassander in Consult. de A. C. article 4 explains it concerning the filial fear of God, by which the faithful are always solicitous, lest they have received the grace of God in vain, and lest by their own injury and arrogance they fall again from the received grace into their former filth, according to the Apostle's warning, standing in faith do not be high-minded, but fear.

Latin:

vers. 23. Proverb. 9. vers. 31.) Et vers. 10. Qui errare facit (sive actu seducat, seu tantum seducere conetur) rectos (qui id non merentur, sed juvandi potius erant omnibus modis ob pietatem & rectitudinem) per viam malam, in foveam suam ipse corruet: Quum autem bifariam seducantur homines, monente Cartwrighto, vel cum à pietate, & justitia in peccatum; vel cum à via, quæ pacem, & utilitatem spectat, in periculi, & damni pœnam impelluntur; de posteriore hîc agi inde liquet, quia in errorem ducens, in foveam, quam alteri defoderit, casurus affirmetur. Qui enim in peccatum trahit, ipse prius in fovea est, quam al- teri eam paret. Unde recte se habet Paraphra- sis Osiandri : Si quis callide homines pios in exiti- um abducere & præcipitare volet, is ipse in exiti- um ruet. ET (at) SIMPLICES (inregri) POS- SIDEBUNT ( hæreditate accipient ) BONA (non ita ruent in desperatam foveam, imo tan- dem bona piis evenient, etiamsi insidiæ iis stru- antur, aut periculis etiam ipsi aliquando invol- vantur) Dominus enim curam agit piorum, 2. Petr. 2. vers. 9. Rom. 8. vers. 28. Confer Proverb. 26. vers. 27. cap. 24. vers. 16. Addit Vulgata bona ejus, sed agnoscit Cornelius τὸ Ejus non esse in Ebræo, Chaldæo, LXX. Aquila, Theodot. nec in multis Latinis.

Jam iterum pauperem prudentem ( ê verbo Dei informatum, & ejusdem ductum sequen- tem) diviti imprudenti, utut δοκησισόφῳ præfe- rendum esse docet vers. 11. Sapiens sibi videtur vir dives : pauper autem prudens scrutabitur eum. Nimirum addunt opes divitibus animos, eosque inflant, ut pulchre sibi sapere videantur, præ- sertim quia à vulgo magni, & excellentes præ- dicantur, & ab adulatoribus prudentes & feli- ces nuncupantur. At homo pauper, sed cor- datus fastum eorum despiciens, per colloquia, quæstiones, & actiones scrutatur, anne vera sa- pientia polleant, facileque divitum deprehen- dit stultitiam: adeoque mavult sapere, & egere, quam opes possidere, & desipere. Confer. Jac. 2. vers. 5.

Quantum vero boni bono publico accedat, cum vere prudentes ac justi ad dignitates evehuntur, vers. 12. docetur : cum exultant (cum extollun- tur, florent & exultandi causam habent, cap. 11. vers. 10.) justi, multa est gloria (multum decus, adeoque etiam causa exultandi est populo, cum justi imperant, & florent cap. 29. vers. 2.) At cum surgunt (vel evehuntur & regnant 2. Reg. 23. vers. 25. Numer. 24. vers. 17.) impii, pervestigatur homo (quia occultare se cogitur, opus est ut investige- tur) ut R. Levi exponit : cum exaltantur impii, pii fugiunt abduntque se in latebras : quare im- pii eos scrutantur, & indagant, ut inde eos in lu- cem ad se educant. Vatablus vertit, & surgenti- bus impiis explorabitur homo, tunc exploratur ho- minis virtus & constantia. Inter malos enim bonum esse, immensæ bonitatis est, dicente Gregorio M. lib. 1. in Job. cap. 1.

Cæterum quum nemo vivat, quin peccet, re- medium etiam ostenditur consequendi gratiam, confessio, & derelictio peccati, h. e. vera & seria pœ- nitentia: vers. 13. Qui tegit scelera sua, non prospe- rabitur (μείωσις : punietur : vel non effugiet pœ- nam, non consequetur misericordiam) qui vero confitetur (& vere pœnitentiam egerit) misericor- diam consequetur. Psalm. 32, 5. Hos. 1, 8. 9. E quibus vero minime confici potest auricularis confessio Papistica, uti quidem Hugo & Cajetanus putarunt: quum in Vet. Testament. Sacramentum pœniten- tiæ, quod fingunt, nondum fuerit, propria ipso- rummet Papistarum confessione: Unde reprobat Hugonis sententiam Cornel. (quamvis eam postea hic prævisam à Sp. S. ἄτεργραφῆς dicat) nec uspiam omnium peccatorum specialis confessio præscripta imo ne possibilis quidem Davidis judicio sit Psal. 19, 13. Ad vitationem autem peccati facit, ut semper in timore Dei vivamus, non quidem servili, qui est infidelium, de gratia Dei dissidentium, vel de- sperantium; sed filiali, qui fidelium proprius est, qui tametsi de remissione peccatorum, & gra- tia Dei certi fiunt, in timore Dei, & vera pie- tate sedulo cavent, ne quid committant, quo Deum offendant, ejusque gratia excidant, Phi- lipp. 2, 12. Jam enim timorem dubitationis & diffi- dentiæ Papisticæ excluserat, promissione indubi- tata misericordiæ pœnitentibus facta: ideoque ti- morem solum cautionis ac reverentiæ, ne gratiam amittamus, postulat Salomo, vers. 14. Beatus, in- quit, homo, qui pavet semper, qui vero indurat cor suum, corruet in malum, ut nempe temerita- tem, audaciam, & duritiem peccatum vilipenden- tem, & justitiæ carnaliter confidentem fugiamus, Nehem. 9. v. 17. Jerem. 7. vers. 25. Ezech. 33. vers. 13. & in timore Dei caveamus, ne torpor aut segni- ties invadat, ne petulantia subrepat, ne caro ad- versus spiritum triumphet, Psalm. 119. vers. 120. 161. ne amittamus gratiam, & excidamus salute æterna Proverb. 8. vers. 12. cap. 14. vers. 16. Addimus & metum pœnæ, utpote quo etiam deterret nos Spiritus Sanctus à peccato Matth. 10. vers. 28. Luc. 12. vers. 4. & bonum quoque est pœnam timere, si modo non solum pœna, sed etiam, & quidem imprimis offensa Dei, & separatio ab illo ceu ami- co, & animæ sponso metuatur. LXX. reddunt: Beatus vir qui timet omnia δι εὐλάβειαν, propter reverentiam Dei, vel ob cautelam, qua declinatur malum, ut Ariasmont. explicat, vel qui veretur omnia, quæ aliquod contagium, vel detrimentum afferre poterant, ut autor Caten. Græc. interpreta- tur. Talis vero timor Dei & cautio à peccatis non destruit fiduciam, sed probe cum ea consistit: quia fiducia confidit contra malum, quod timor Dei formidat. Frustra ergo hoc dicto abutun- tur Papistæ ad adstruendam de remissione pecca- torum diffidentiam. Timor hic, ut Cornelius ipse, non destruit, sed efficit securitatem, fiduci- am & magnanimitatem: allegans Bernhardum E- pist. 87. ad Ogerium, de timore hoc explican- tem, non qui sit laqueus desperationis, sed qui spem acquirat beatitudinis. Cassander in Consult. de A. C. artic. 4. de filiali Dei timore explicat, quo soliciti semper fideles sunt, ne in incursum gratiam Dei receperint, neve à gratia recepta sua injuria & arrogantia rursus cadant in priores sordes, juxta Apostoli monitum, in fide stans noli altum sapere, sed time.

## 28:23
Vers. 23. HE WHO REBUKES A MAN, SHALL FIND THANKS AFTERWARDS FROM HIM, MORE THAN HE WHO DECEIVES BY THE FLATTERIES OF THE TONGUE.

There follow certain moral admonitions, analogous to the preceding sentences: 1. concerning the fruit of correction: He who rebukes a man after me, (Junius, so that he may follow me, or by my example, which pleases Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, as also Mr. Dr. Geier on account of the accentuation, in preference to the Vulgate, Mercerus, Piscator, and the Dutch interpretation, who refer that אחרי to the following words, although at the beginning he who rebukes may be less welcome, yet afterwards he brings back thanks: rendering it AFTERWARDS) shall find thanks more than he who flatters with the tongue. Conf. chap. 27, 6.

2. Concerning the punishment of the son of a spendthrift, vers. 24. He who despoils his father and his mother, saying, it is no transgression, he is a companion of a man who is a destroyer, or a waster, and a robber: worthy of the punishment of death Exod. 12, 23. Ezech. 9, 1. because, to wit, he exhausts his parents with thefts, and brings them to ruin through want and grief. Vulgate, he is a partner of a murderer.

3. Concerning the character of a proud man, vers. 25. He who is broad in spirit (puffed up or elated chap. 21, 4.) stirs up quarrels, while he despises others, nor does he want anyone to be preferred to himself, and thus he is not fattened, but rather wastes away with envy, emulation, and contentions chap. 13, 10.) But he who trusts in the Lord, shall be fattened. Vulgate shall be healed, perhaps for shall be fattened, or shall be satisfied, as Cornelius himself conjectures, although he wishes to save that from the Greek ἐν ἐπιμελείᾳ ἔσαι very ineptly, as if it were the same thing, he will be in care, and shall be healed. The sentence which follows is related: He who trusts in his own heart, (this is a species of elation of mind chap. 3, 5. 6. chap. 23, 4. c. 26, 12.) is a fool, and truly unhappy (because he has not even known himself rightly, let alone God) but he who walks in wisdom, (not trusting in his own heart, but solely in God, Jerem. 9, 23. 24.) he shall escape (dangers, he will be tranquil, safe, and happy.) Author of the Greek Catena LXX. Renders the sense of the interpreters thus: He who places his hope in the audacity of his heart, is a fool: but he who walks prudently and cautiously, shall attain salvation.

4. Concerning beneficence towards the needy, vers. 27. And he who gives to the poor shall not be in want (chap. 19, 17.) and to him who turns away his eyes there shall be a multitude of curses. Jas. 2, 3. Matt. 25, 41. Cyprian, homily on works and alms. If you fear and dread, lest, if you begin to work much, your patrimony being finished by generous work you might be reduced to want, be fearless in this part, be secure: that which is spent for the uses of Christ, from which a heavenly work is celebrated, cannot be finished. I do not promise this to you from my own, but I promise it from the faith of the holy scriptures, and the authority of the divine promise. For the Holy Spirit speaks through Solomon and says: he who gives to the poor, etc. Showing that the merciful and those who work cannot be in need, but rather that the stingy and the barren afterwards arrive at want.

5. On the exaltation and destruction of the wicked, verse 28. While the wicked are exalted, man hides himself (verse 12. The Arab rendered it: in the places of the wicked the status of the just is restricted.) But when they themselves perish, the just are multiplied, chap. 11, 10. The reason is, because the wicked, while they rule, strive to propagate their own impiety: and the whole world is fashioned after the example of the King.

Latin:

Vers. 23. QUI CORRIPIT HOMINEM, GRATIAM POSTEA INVENIET APUD EUM, MA- GIS QUAM ILLE, QUI PER LINGUÆ BLANDIMENTA DECIPIT.

Sequuntur monita quædam moralia, sententiis præcedaneis analoga: 1. de fructu correptionis: Qui increpat hominem post me, (Junius, ut sequatur me, vel meo exemplo, quod Aben-Ezra, Vatablo, ut & Dn. D. Geiero propter accentuationem placet præ Vulgata, Merceri, Piscatoris & Belgarum interpre- tatione, qui illud אחרי referunt ad sequentia ver- ba, etsi initio increpans minus gratus sit, deinceps ta- men gratiam reportat: reddentes POSTEA) gra- tiam inveniet magis quam is, qui blanditur lingua. Conf. cap. 27, 6.

2. De pœna filii decoctoris vers. 24. Qui spoliat patrem suum & matrem suam, dicens, non est præ- varicatio, is socius est viri exterminatoris, vel vasta- toris, & raptoris: pœna mortis dignus Exod. 12, 23. Ezech. 9, 1. quia scil. furtis exhaurit parentes, & ino- pia, ac mœrore eos conficit. Vulgata, particeps est homicidæ.

3. De genio hominis superbi, vers. 25. Latus ani- mo (inflatus vel elatus cap. 21, 4.) miscet jurgia, dum despicit alios, nec quenquam sibi præferri vult, adeoque non impinguatur, sed marcescit po- tius invidia, æmulatione & contentionibus cap. 13, 10.) Sed qui fidit in Domino, impinguabitur. Vul- gata sanabitur, forte pro saginabitur, vel satiabitur, ut Cornelius ipse conjectat, etsi illud è Græco ἐν ἐπιμελείᾳ ἔσαι adhuc salvare perquam inepte velit, quasi idem sit, in cura erit, & sanabitur. Affinis est quæ sequitur sententia: Qui fidit cordi suo, (est hæc species elationis animi cap. 3, 5. 6. cap. 23, 4. c. 26, 12.) est stultus, vereque infelix (quia nec sei- ipsum quidem is recte cognovit, nedum Deum) qui vero ambulat in sapientia, (non suo fidens cor- di, sed Deo unice, Jerem. 9, 23. 24.) is evadet (pe- ricula, tranquillus, tutus & felix erit.) Autor Ca- tenæ Græc. LXX. Interpretum sensum ita reddit: Qui in cordis sui audacia spem ponit, stultus est: qui autem ambulat prudenter & caute, salutem con- sequetur.

4. De beneficentia erga egenos, vers. 27. Et qui dat pauperi non erit inopia (cap. 19, 17.) & averten- ti oculos suos erit multitudo maledictionum. Jac. 2, 3. Matth. 25, 41. Cyprianus homil. de oper. & eleemos. Si vereris, ac metuis, ne, si operari plurimum cœperis, patrimonio tuo larga operatione finito ad inopiam re- digaris, esto in hac parte intrepidus, esto securus: fi- niri non potest, unde in usus Christi impenditur, unde opus cœleste celebratur. Non hoc tibi de meo spondeo, sed de sanctarum scripturarum fide, & divina pollici- tationis autoritate promitto. Loquitur enim per Sa- lomonem Spiritus Sanct. ac dicit: qui dat pauperi- bus, &c. Ostendens misericordes atque operantes ege- re non posse, magis parcos ac steriles ad inopiam post- modum devenire.

5. De evectione & interitu impiorum vers. 28. Dum evehuntur impii, abscondit se homo (vers. 12. Arabs reddidit: in locis impiorum status justorum coarctatur.) Cum vero pereunt ipsi multiplicantur ju- sti cap. 11, 10. Ratio est, quia impii dum regunt, suam impietatem propagare satagunt: & Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis.

## 29:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIX.

Admonitions or proverbs alternate, pertaining to the Republic and to private life, with admonitions concerning children and servants and certain economic morals subjoined.

Ver. 1. A MAN WHO CONTEMNS ONE REPROVING HIM WITH A STIFF NECK, SUDDEN DESTRUCTION SHALL COME UPON HIM, AND HEALTH SHALL NOT FOLLOW HIM.

Because the destruction of dominant wicked men was treated in the last verse of the preceding chapter, now destruction is denounced even to men established in dignity who reject correction: A man of rebukes (or frequently rebuked, both verbally and really) hardening his neck (against God, the word of God, His ministers, and correction made either by words or by blows and scourges, Deuter. 31, 27. Is. 48, 4.) shall suddenly be broken (like an earthen vessel, which once broken cannot be repaired, Jerem. 19, 10. Psalm. 2, 9.) and there shall be no health for him, chap. 4, 15. The punishment of contumacy is therefore set forth here as sudden, very horrible, and irremediable and desperate. Wherefore it is commended to those who are established in dominion or Magistracy, that they act with justice, whence comes common joy; just as, on the contrary, from the dominion of the wicked come common complaints, verse 2. When the just rule, the people rejoice: (Conf. chap. 11, 10.) and when the wicked man rules, (who cares for neither sacred nor profane laws) the people groan, chap. 28, 28.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIX.

Alternant monita, vel paremiæ ad Rempubli- cam & ad vitam privatam pertinentes, sub- junctis monitis de liberis & servis œcono- micis quibusdam moralibus.

Vers. 1. VIRO QUI CORRIPIENTEM DURA CER- VICE CONTEMNIT, REPENTINUS EI SU- PERVENIET INTERITUS, ET SANITAS EUM NON SEQUETUR.

QUia de impiorum dominantium interitu vers. ult. cap. præcedentis actum, jam viris etiam in dignitate constitutis correptionem respuentibus in- teritus denunciatur: Vir increpationum (vel crebro increpatus, cum verbaliter tum realiter) indurans cervicem (adversus Deum, verbum Dei, ejus mini- stros, & correptionem s. verbis s. plagis & verbe- ribus factam, Deuter. 31, 27. Es. 48, 4.) repente con- teretur (instar vasis testacei, quod semel fractum re- parari nequit, Jerem. 19, 10. Psalm. 2, 9.) nec erit ei sanitas, cap. 4, 15. Pœna ergo contumaciæ sistitur hîc tum repentina, tum valde horrenda, tum ine- mendabilis & desperata. Quapropter commen- datur iis, qui in dominio, vel Magistratu consti- tuti, justitia, unde commune gaudium; quemad- modum contra à Dominio impiorum communes querelæ vers. 2. Quando dominantur justi, lætatur populus: (Conf. cap. 11, 10.) & cum dominatur im- pius, (qui neque sacra, neque prophana jura cu- rat) gemit populus, cap. 28, 28.

## 29:3
Ver. 3. A MAN WHO LOVES WISDOM, GLADDENS HIS FATHER: BUT HE WHO FEEDS HARLOTS, SHALL LOSE HIS SUBSTANCE.

To the Political admonitions is subjoined an Economic one concerning a frugal son and one laudable for his study of Wisdom, who in his youthful and manly age exhilarates his parents, and prepares and amplifies wealth: whereas, on the contrary, he who, neglecting the love of wisdom, feeds himself on harlots or any pleasures whatsoever, and nourishes and fosters them, easily squanders the substance and faculties of his parents, after the example of the prodigal son, Luke 15. of whom Chrysologus says: What had been composed by the Father's moderation is dissipated by the son's prodigality.

Latin:

Vers. 3. VIR QUI AMAT SAPIENTIAM, LÆ- TIFICAT PATREM SUUM: QUI AUTEM NUTRIT SCORTA, PERDET SUBSTAN- TIAM.

Monitis Politicis Oeconomicum subjungitur de filio frugi & laudabili Sapientiæ studioso, qui ætate juvenili & virili parentes suos exhilarat, opesque parat & amplificat: quum ex adverso, qui neglecto sapientiæ amore scortis vel voluptatibus quibusvis pascitur, easque nutrit & fovet, substantiam & fa- cultates parentum facile decoquat, exemplo filii prodigi, Luc. 15. de quo Chrysologus: Quæ compo- sita fuerant Patre moderante, prodigente filio dissi- pantur.

## 29:4
Ver. 4. A JUST KING RAISES UP THE LAND, A COVETOUS MAN SHALL DESTROY IT) In the Hebrew: A king in judgment, (that is, who exercises judgment rightly) confirms the dominion. But a man of offerings (who wants gifts to be offered to him, as if he were a priest) destroys the same.

He returns to Political admonitions: In Hebrew, A king in judgment establishes the land, a man of offerings shall tear it down, i.e., who accepts gifts, as Pagninus, Baynus, Cornel. à Lap. and others, and exacts tributes, as Aben-Ezra, just as a man of blood is said to be one who pants for blood, 2. Sam. 16, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 4. REX JVSTVS ERIGIT TERRAM, VIR AVARVS DESTRVET EAM) In Hebræo: Rex in judicio, (id est, qui judicium recte exercet) confirmat ditionem. At vir oblationum (qui munera sibi vult offerri, quasi sacerdos esset) destruit eandem.

Redit ad Politica monita: In Ebr. Rex in judi- cio stabilit terram, vir oblationum diruet eam, h. e. qui accipit munera, ut Pagninus, Baynus, Cornel. à Lap. alii, & exigit tributa, ut Aben-Ezra, quem- admodum vir sanguinis dicitur, qui sanguini in- hiat 2. Sam. 16, 7.

## 29:5
Ver. 5. A MAN WHO SPEAKS WITH SMOOTH AND FEIGNED WORDS TO HIS FRIEND, SPREADS A NET FOR HIS STEPS.

This warning again concerns private individuals, that we should beware of those nearest to us who flatter us, so that they may spread a net for us after the manner of hunters, who imitate the calls of birds—which the birds are accustomed to use when they indulge in their loves to summon their mates—and meanwhile, having thus summoned them, set nets in which they may be entangled and perish. LXX. refer the danger to these smooth-talkers: he who prepares a net for his friend, he surrounds it with his own feet: but this, although Aben-Ezra and R. Levi wish it to be hinted at here in the same way, is explained in the following verse 6. A SNARE, or net, which the treacherous man will spread for another, will wrap up the WICKED SINNER himself: which, however, can also be understood more generally of any transgressor, for so it is held in the Hebrew: in the transgression of an evil man is a snare (insidious, by which the soul is deprived of its happy liberty, and is rendered captive at the will of Satan, 2 Tim. 2:26, so that it cannot sing and rejoice with the righteous, but is wrapped up in the torments of conscience. Conf. ch. 12, 13.) But the righteous (escaping such a snare) will sing and rejoice, enjoying a cheerful conscience in the Lord, ch. 15:15, ch. 17:22, Rom. 14:17. No one, says St. Augustine in his sentences no. 90, can be defrauded of his delights, to whom Christ is joy. For it is eternal exaltation, which rejoices in the eternal good.

Latin:

Vers. 5. HOMO QUI BLANDIS FICTIS- QUE VERBIS LOQUITUR AMICO SUO, RETE EXPANDIT GRESSIBUS EJUS.

Hoc monitum ad privatos iterum spectat, ut pro- ximos caveamus, qui blandiuntur nobis, ut rete nobis pandant more venatorum, qui fistulis avium voces, qui- bus tunc, cum amoribus indulgent, ad socias evo- candas uti solent, imitantur, his interim sic evocatis retia instruunt, quibus implicentur, & pereant. LXX. periculum referunt ad istos blandiloquos: Qui præparat amico rete, circumdat illud suis pedibus : sed hoc, etsi Aben-Ezra & R. Levi hic itidem innui ve- lint, sequenti exponitur vers. 6. LAQUEUS, seu rete, quod perfidus pandet alii, ipsummet INIQUUM PECCANTEM INVOLVET: quod tamen eti- am generalius intelligi potest de quovis transgres- fore, ita enim habetur in Ebr. in prævaricatione viri mali est laqueus (insidiosus, quo anima privatur fe- lici sua libertate, & captiva redditur ad Satanæ lu- bitum, 2. Timoth. 2, 26. ita ut cum justa cantare, ac lætari nequeat, sed angoribus conscientiæ involva- tur. Conf. cap. 12, 13.) Justus autem (laqueum ta- lem effugiens) cantabit & lætabitur, hilari fruens in Domino conscientia, cap. 15, 15. cap. 17, 22. Rom. 14, 17. Non potest, inquit, S. Augustin. in sententiis num. 90. quisquam fraudari delectationibus suis, cui Chri- stus est gaudium. Æterna enim exaltatio est, quæ bo- no lætatur æterno.

## 29:7
Verse 7. THE RIGHTEOUS KNOWS THE CAUSE OF THE POOR: BUT THE WICKED DOES NOT KNOW KNOWLEDGE.

These things pertain to the Polity: namely, that a pious and righteous Magistrate knows the cause of the poor (Deut. 17:8, Jer. 5:28, ch. 22:16, Prov. 2:8, ch. 27:23), but the wicked (and unjust) does not understand (does not investigate causes, especially those of the poor), nor does he attend to knowledge (or those things which he ought to know and attend to, so far is he from judging righteous judgment in their causes, Isa. 1:27, Ps. 82:3, John 7:24). But concerning the loss or gain redounding to the Republic from the profane and unjust, or the pious and wise, it is treated in verse 8: Mocking men inflame (with most serious fires) the city, as the LXX, R. Solomon Jarchi, Junius, Piscator, and the Belgians explain the word יפיחו: because פח is a spark: or rather, as others explain it from Cant. 4:16, they blow vehemently like a whirlwind, and stir up: But the wise turn away fury, or anger, and calm spirits and commotions. That the three following proverbs also tend to this goal is not at all obscure.

Latin:

Vers. 7. NOVIT JUSTUS CAUSAM PAU- PERUM: IMPIUS VERO IGNORAT SCI- ENTIAM.

Hæc ad Politiam pertinent: quod nempe Ma- gistratus pius & justus cognoscat pauperum causam (Deuter. 17, 8. Jerem. 5, 28. cap. 22, 16. Proverb. 2, 8. cap. 27, 23.) impius vero (& injustus) non intelligat, (non investiget causas, imprimis pauperum,) nec attendat scientiam (vel ea, quæ cognoscere & at- tendere debebat, tantum abest, ut rectum judicet judicium in causis eorum Esa. 1, 27. Psalm. 82, 3. Johann. 7, 24.) de damno vero vel commodo à pro- phanis & injustis, aut piis & sapientibus in Rempu- blicam redundante vers. 8. agitur: Homines irriso- res inflammant (incendiis gravissimis) civitatem, ut LXX. R. Salom. Jarchi, Junius, Piscator, Belgæ vo- cem יפיחו exponunt: quia פח est favilla: vel po- tius, ut alii è Cantic. 4, 16. eam explicant, instar tur- binis vehementer præstant, & concitant: Sapientes ve- ro avertunt furorem, vel iram, animos & motus con- sopiunt. Ad quem scopum etiam facere tres se- quentes parœmias, minime obscurum est.

## 29:9
Verse 9. IF A WISE MAN CONTENDS WITH A FOOL, WHETHER HE IS ANGRY OR LAUGHS, HE WILL FIND NO REST.

In private life we are warned 1. to avoid dispute or contention with a fool: because we will never find an end to the arguing, whether we treat him with harsh or gentle ways and words. For obstinate sinners can be recalled from evil habit neither by threats nor by promises; although others are better amended by gentleness, others by severity, Matt. 11:17, 24.

2. That we should not hate the upright, but seek and preserve their soul, verse 10. MEN OF BLOOD (bloodthirsty, unmerciful, and desirous of revenge) HATE THE SIMPLE (in Hebrew, the upright, as being in morals alien to them, so that they even seek to shed his blood, Prov. 1:11, Wis. 2:12), BUT THE RIGHTEOUS SEEK HIS SOUL: that is, they are solicitous about preserving his life, Ps. 142:5, as the Tigurines, Cornel. à Lap., Dn. D. Geier. But R. Aben-Ezra, Salazar, Baynus, Tirinus, and others understand it of revenge: the righteous (judges) seek the soul of the slain, that is, they avenge the death unjustly brought upon him. Ps. 9:13, Ezek. 3:18.

3. That we should restrain our affections, verse 11. A FOOL brings forth all his spirit (everything that is fostered in the mind, that is in the heart, every intention of the mind, and all the affections of the will, he brings into the open, ch. 14:33, ch. 25:28, Sir. 21:29). But the wise man (acting upon him as he tries to break out) makes him quiet, ch. 16:32. Cajetan explains that the fool keeps nothing secret, nothing hidden: the Chaldean and LXX explain it of anger and fury, because fools flare up in fury from any cause: but Solomon comprehends both senses, indeed he embraces not only anger, but other affections as well. But that which is said of the wise man, that HE RESERVES IT FOR LATER, as the Vulgate has it, they take as referring to delay until an opportune time, which is an effective remedy for calming anger.

Latin:

Vers. 9. VIR SAPIENS SI CUM STUL- TO CONTENDERIT, SIVE IRASCATUR, SIVE RIDEAT, NON INVENIET RE- QUIEM.

In vita privata monemur 1. ut caveamus disce- ptionem vel contentionem cum stulto: quia nun- quam disceptandi finem inveniemus, seu asperis seu lenibus modis & verbis ipsum tractemus. Obstina- ti enim peccatores neque minis, neque promissis à prava consuetudine revocari possunt: quum alias alii melius mansuetudine, alii severitate emenden- tur, Matth. 11, 17. 24.

2. Ut ne odio habeamus integros, sed animam eorum quæramus & conservemus, vers. 10. VI- RI SANGUINUM (sanguinolenti, immiseri- cordes & vindictæ cupidi) ODERUNT SIM- PLICEM (in Ebr. integrum, utpote moribus à se alienum, ita ut ejus etiam sanguinem effundere quærant, Proverb. 1, 11. Sap. 2, 12.) JUSTI AU- TEM QUÆRUNT ANIMAM EJUS: id est, soliciti sunt de conservanda ejus vita Psalm. 142, 5. ut Tigurini, Cornel. à Lap. Dn. D. Geier. R. Aben-E- zra vero, Salazar, Baynus, Tirinus & alii de vindicta intelligunt: justi (judices) quærunt animam occisi, id est mortem ipsi injuste illatam vindicant. Psalm. 9, 13. Ezech. 3, 18.

3. Ut affectus cohibeamus, vers. 11. Totum spiritum suum profert STULTUS, (omne quod mente, quod corde fovetur, omnem intentionem animi, omnesque voluntatis affectus in apricum profert cap. 14, 33. c. 25, 28. Sir. 21, 29.) Sapiens autem retror- sum (erumpere conantem agens) quiescere facit eum, c. 16, 32. Cajetanus exponit, nihil intus arcani, nihil secretrans servare stultum: Chald. & LXX. de ira & fu- rore explicant, quod stulti ex quavis causa furore in- ardescant: sed utrumque sensum comprehendit Sa- lomo imo non tantum iram, sed alios etiam affectus simul complectitur. Illud vero de sapiente, quod INPOSTERUM RESERVET, ut habet Vulgata, de dilatione in oportunum tempus accipiunt, quæ se- dandæ iræ efficax est remedium.

## 29:11
Verse 11. A FOOL BRINGS FORTH ALL HIS SPIRIT, A WISE MAN DEFERS AND RESERVES IT FOR LATER) His spirit, that is, whatever he has in his mind. A wise man hides his thoughts until he brings them forth in deeds. Cicero said in more than one place that dissimulation is necessary, especially for those to whom the Republic is entrusted.

Latin:

Vers. 11. TOTVM SPIRITVM SVVM PROFERT STVLTVS, SAPIENS DIFFERT ET RESERVAT IN POSTERVM) Spiritum suum, id est, quicquid in animo habet. Sapiens abscondit cogitata donec rebus ea promat. Iis præsertim, quibus commissa est Respublica, necessariam esse dissimulationem dixit non uno loco Cicero.

## 29:12
Verse 12. A PRINCE WHO GLADLY HEARS WORDS OF LIES HAS ALL HIS MINISTERS WICKED.

These things again look to the Republic: that to the disposition of wicked rulers, who attend to the word שֶׁקֶר, false, empty, deceptive, such as flatteries, detractions, ineptitudes, frauds, all ministers easily adapt themselves to such impiety: and that such rulers delight in wicked ministers, conformable to their own impiety, Sir. 10:2. But understand 'all' synecdochically, that is, most of them.

Furthermore, it is warned in verse 13 that in the Republic the poor and the rich are mixed, and perform mutual services for each other. The poor and the creditor (or rather the rich, who is called a man of usury or frauds, because such are usually the rich, conf. ch. 22:2) have met together; the Lord is the illuminator of both: the Lord deems both worthy of his light: the light of nature, Matt. 5:45, and of grace, John 1:9, showing them temporal and spiritual benefits.

Moreover, the poor are commended especially to Magistrates, ver. 14, of whom usually little account is wont to be taken. As to the King judging in truth (without the disturbance of passions, according to the tenor of the laws) his throne shall be established for ever (periodical eternity is noted, i.e., long-lasting durability). The LXX, who seem to have read לְעֵד instead of לָעַד, translated it 'for a testimony.' But the versions of others confirm the Hebrew reading. While, however, they are commanded to judge the poor in truth, lest they oppress them for the sake of the rich, it is hinted at the same time that the rich likewise are to be judged in truth: mention is made of the former, however, so that they may know that the poor are singularly a care to God, Ps. 10, 14, and that they should not hold their causes in contempt. Aelian, Book 14, Var. Histor. observes that among the Egyptians, the judge wore a sapphire, on which TRUTH was inscribed, from his neck: It was necessary, he says, for him to be the most just and most sincere of all men, who wore around his neck an image fashioned from the gem sapphire, which was called Truth. I, however, would wish a judge not so much to carry around truth carved or expressed in a stone, as to have it implanted and fixed in his soul and mind. Impious, on the contrary, are the axioms of the Machiavellians, who, with Pliny, Epist. 12, book 1, teach: To deceive, according to the customs of the times, is prudence.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PRINCEPS QUI LIBENTER AU- DIT VERBA MENDACII OMNES MINI- STROS HABET IMPIOS.

Hæc iterum ad Rempublicam spectant: quod do- minatorum impiorum ingenio, qui verbo שֶׁקֶר falso, inani, deceptorio attendunt, utputa adulationi- bus, detractionibus, ineptiis, fraudibus, omnes mini- stri tali impietati se facile attemperent: quodque ejusmodi dominatores ministris impiis gaudeant, suæ impietati conformibus Sir. 10, 2. Omnes autem intellige Synecdochice, id est, plerosque.

Porro in Republica mixtos esse, ac mutuas sibi præstare operas pauperes & divites, monetur v. 13. Pauper & creditor (vel potius dives, qui vir usura- rum vel fraudum dicitur, quod tales plerumque esse soleant divites, conf. cap. 22, 2.) obviaverunt si- bi; utriusque illuminator est Dominus: utrosque lu- ce sua dignatur Dominus: luce naturæ Matth. 5, 45. & gratiæ Joh. 1, 9. beneficia ipsis exhibens tempora- lia & spiritualia.

Commendantur autem imprimis Magistratibus pauperes vers. 14. quorum plerumque exigua solet haberi ratio. Quod ad Regem judicantem in verita- te (citra affectuum perturbationem, secundum le- gum tenorem) thronus ejus in æternum (periodica notatur æternitas, h. e. diuturna durabilitas) fir- mabitur. LXX. qui pro לָעַד legisse videntur לְעֵד verterunt, in testimonium. Sed aliorum versiones confirmant Ebræam lectionem. Dum autem pau- peres in veritate judicare jubentur, ne in gratiam divitum illos opprimant, innuitur simul divites iti- dem in veritate judicandos esse: illorum autem pecu- liaris mentio sit, ut sciant Deo pauperes singulariter curæ esse, Ps. 10, 14. nec eorum causas insuper habe- ant. Ælianus L. 14. Var. Histor. observat, apud Æ- gyptios judicem Saphirum, cui VERITAS inscripta à collo gestasse: Eum, inquit, omnium hominum esse ju- stissimum, & sincerissimum oportebat, qui circa collum imaginem ex Saphiro gemma confectam gestabat, quæ vocabatur Veritas. Ego vero judicem non tam in lapi- de sculptam aut expressam veritatem circumferre, quam in animo menteque insitam & infixam habere velim. Impia contra sunt Machiavellistarum axio- mata, qui cum Plinio l. 12. Epist. docent: Decipere pro moribus temporum prudentiam esse.

## 29:14
Ver. 14. THE KING WHO JUDGETH THE POOR IN TRUTH, HIS THRONE SHALL BE ESTABLISHED FOR EVER) Hebraism: King and his, for King's. Truth here signifies justice.

Latin:

Vers. 14. REX QVI JVDICAT IN VERITATE PAV- PERES, THRONVS EJVS IN ÆTERNVM FIRMABI- TVR) Hebraismus: Rex & ejus, pro Regis. Veritas hic ju- stitiam significat.

## 29:15
Ver. 15. THE ROD AND REPROOF GIVETH WISDOM: BUT A CHILD LEFT TO HIS OWN WILL BRINGETH HIS MOTHER TO SHAME.

These pertain to domestic economy 1. Concerning the discipline of children v. 15. The rod (or staff c. 22, 15) and reproof giveth Wisdom: because there is sometimes no less need of blows than of words that are instructing, dissuading, threatening, rebuking c. 5, 10. c. 10, 17. c. 12, 1. c. 13, 10. c. 15, 5. 10. Sirac. 30, 1. so that they may progress in the knowledge of divine and human things, and in the study of true piety and virtue, and may one day be an honor to their parents and friends. But a BOY left to himself (who is restrained neither by the rod nor by correction, he is not imbued with wisdom, and finally) brings shame upon his mother, who is mentioned first because primary education pertains especially to her, and because it is a great thing to become accustomed from tender years, as the saying goes. But because the multitude of the impious is increased from the wicked education of youth, redundant evils are brought on from there, both faults and punishments, v. 16. When the impious have been multiplied, transgression will be multiplied: if indeed the impious provides help to the impious for crimes, and adds courage and boldness; but the just will see their ruins, if not in this, certainly in the future age. Conf. verf. 2. & 6. Ps. 54, 9. 59, 11. 112, 8. 118, 7. Sap. 5, 1. seq. And therefore parents are warned verf. 17. Correct your son, and he will give you rest; (The fruit of the correction of children is the privative one of the tranquility of parents, so that they may be free from cares and sorrows) and he will give delights to your soul (this is the positive fruit, because upright, well-mannered, and wise children, especially when they are raised to honors, are peculiar delights to parents.) Conf. Sir. 30, 1.

What evils redound from multiplied transgression when the Word of God is neglected, is taught regarding the Republic verf. 18: When there is no vision (that is, the Word of God is not observed, which sense consists from the antithesis, or the divinely revealed law is neglected, by which name Holy Scripture is accustomed to be understood: and thus Beda, Hugo, Cajetanus, Vatablus, Mariana, Saa, Estius, Baynus, Menochius, the Belgians, and others explain prophecy here concerning the Word of God and religion as a whole; not only does the Republic not flourish, but it is altogether) the people is dissipated, as the Vulgate and the Chaldean have it, or rather will be laid bare, will be despoiled, as Cajetanus, Junius, Piscator, the Belgians, and others interpret the word פרע from a comparison with Exod. 32, 25. BUT HE WHO KEEPS THE LAW (the people, will not be laid bare of God's protection, or despoiled, but) is blessed himself, he will flourish with every prosperity. Religion alone, says Philo in the Life of Moses, binds together the minds of citizens, and confirms fellowships and society.

Latin:

Vers. 15. VIRGA ATQUE CORRECTIO TRIBUIT SAPIENTIAM: PUER AUTEM QUI DIMITTITUR VOLUNTATI SUÆ CONFUNDIT MATREM SUAM.

Ad œconomiam hæc spectant 1. De disciplina libe- rorum v. 15. Virga (vel baculus c. 22, 15.) & increpa- tio tribuit Sapientiam: quia opus non minus quan- doque est verberibus, quam verbis informanti- bus, dehortantibus, comminantibus, corripien- tibus c. 5, 10. c. 10, 17. c. 12, 1. c. 13, 10. c. 15, 5. 10. Sirac. 30, 1. ut proficiant in rerum divinarum & humana- rum cognitione, ac veræ pietatis & virtutis studio, ac honori sint aliquando suis parentibus & amicis. PUER autem sibi derelictus (qui neque virga, neque correptione coërcetur, is nec sapientia imbuitur, & tandem) pudore afficit matrem suam, quæ imprimis nominatur, quod ad eam prima educatio pertineat maxime, & à teneris, quod dicitur, afuescere mul- tum sit. Quia vero ê prava educatione juventutis augetur impiorum multitudo, adducuntur inde re- dundantia mala, tum culpæ, tum pœnæ, v. 16. Quum multiplicati fuerint impii, multiplicabitur prævari- catio: siquidem impius impio ad scelera auxilium præstet, animosque & audaciam addat; at justi rui- nas eorum videbunt, si non in hoc, certè in futuro seculo. Conf. verf. 2. & 6. Ps. 54, 9. 59, 11. 112, 8. 118, 7. Sap. 5, 1. seq. Ideoque monentur parentes verf. 17. Corripe filium tuum, & requiescere faciet te; (Fructus correptionis liberorum privativus est tranquillatio parentum, ut liberi sint à curis & mœroribus) da- bitque lætitias animæ tuæ (hic est fructus positivus, quia liberi probi, morati & sapientes, imprimis cum ad honores evehuntur, sunt peculiares delitiæ parentibus.) Conf. Sir. 30, 1.

Quæ mala redundent è prævaricatione multipli- cata neglecto Dei verbo, ad Rempublicam verf. 18. docetur: Quum non est visio (id est, non observatur Verbum Dei, qui sensus ex antithesi constat, vel lex divinitus patefacta negligitur, quo nomine Scriptu- ra S. intelligi solet: adeoque Prophetiam hîc de Dei Verbo, & universa religione explicant Beda, Hugo, Cajetanus, Vatablus, Mariana, Saa, Estius, Baynus, Menochius, Belgæ, & alii; non modo non floret Resp. sed omnino) dissipatur populus, ut Vul- gat. & Chaldæus, vel potius nudabitur, spoliabitur, ut Cajetanus, Junius, Piscat. Belgæ & alii vocem פרע ê collatione Exod. 32, 25. interpretantur. CU- STODIENS AUTEM LEGEM (populus, non nudabitur Dei protectione, aut spoliabitur, sed) beatus ipse, omni prosperitate florebit. Religio una, ait Philo in Vit. Mos. civium animos adstringit, & contubernia societatemque confirmat.

## 29:18
Vers. 18. WHEN PROPHECY HAS FAILED, THE PEOPLE WILL BE DISSIPATED) For it was among the other duties of the Prophets to inculcate the precepts of the law to the people.

2. On the discipline of servants v. 19. A servant will not be instructed by words (Sir. 33, 25.) although he understands, yet there is no response, which word is accepted not only concerning the rendering of words, but also of work and obedience, Job 14, 15. chap. 19, 16. Is. 41, 28. Which is to be understood concerning contumacious servants of a servile and refractory disposition: but to others who are tractable, gentleness and kindness are to be shown. Coloss. 4, 1. Ephes. 6, 9.

3. On avoiding precipitation verf. 20. You see a man swift in his words, there is more hope for a fool than for him. Conf. Jacob. 1, 19. Sirac. 4, 34. chap. 19, 28. chap. 20, 5. chap. 23, 1. chap. 28, 19. A similar judgment was brought concerning him who seems wise to himself, Proverbs 26, 12. because precipitation is accustomed to arise from such a persuasion of wisdom. A fool, says R. Levi, having noticed his own stupidity, uses counsel in his affairs, but the precipitate man consults no one, since he seems to himself to be wise enough and more. But just as it is to be avoided elsewhere, so also in the economy, to which inconsiderate precipitation brings many inconveniences.

4. On the education of servants vers. 21. He who delicately nourishes his servant from childhood (the word מפנק occurs only here, but its sense is elicited from the Chaldaism, that it is treating delicately Prov. 4, 3. Cant. 6, 1.) in his end he will be as a son. מנין from the word

נין son Genes. 21, 23. whence also ינון will sprout Ps. 72, 17. Conf. Sirac. 33, 25. The address of the mind, says Plato in Dial. 6 on the Laws, becomes in a certain way a command to servants, and no joking should be had with them: which many do foolishly, while they nourish them delicately, they make the way more difficult both for themselves to command, and for them to obey.

Latin:

Vers. 18. CVM PROPHETIA DEFECERIT, DISSI- PABITVR POPVLVS) Nam Prophetarum inter alia mu- nia erat, legis præcepta inculcare populo.

2. De disciplina servorum v. 19. Verbis non erudie- tur servus (Sir. 33, 25.) quamvis intelligat, non est ta- men responsio, quæ vox non solum de verborum, sed & operis & obsequii redditione accipitur, Job. 14, 15. cap. 19, 16. Es. 41, 28. Quod de servis contu- macibus, servili & refractario ingenio intelligen- dum: aliis autem qui tractabiles sunt, mansuetudo, & benignitas exhibenda. Coloss. 4, 1. Ephes. 6, 9.

3. De præcipitantia vitanda verf. 20. Vides vi- rum velocem in verbis suis, spes est de stulto magis, quam de illo. Conf. Jacob. 1, 19. Sirac. 4, 34. cap. 19, 28. cap. 20, 5. cap. 23, 1. cap. 28, 19. De illo qui sibi sa- piens videtur, simile judicium ferebatur Proverb. 26, 12. quia ê tali sapientiæ persuasione oriri solet præcipitantia. Stultus, inquit R. Levi, sua stolidi- tate animadversa consilio in suis negotiis utitur, sed præceps neminem consulit, cum sibi satis superque sa- pere videatur. Uti autem ea alias, ita & in O経済- mia cavenda, cui inconsiderata præcipitantia mul- ta adfert incommoda.

4. De educatione servorum vers. 21. Qui delicate nutrit à pueritia servum suum (verbum מפנק hîc tantum occurrit, ê Chaldaismo autem ejus sensus eruitur, quod sit delicate habens Prov. 4, 3. Cant. 6, 1.) in novissimo suo erit tanquam filius. מנין à voce

נין filius Genes. 21, 23. unde & ינון sobolescet Ps. 72, 17. Conf. Sirac. 33, 25. Allocutio animi, inquit Plato Dial. 6. de Legib. ad servos quodammodo imperium fit, neque jocus ullus cum illis habeatur: quod multi stulte facientes, dum delicate eos nutriunt, difficilio- rem viam & sibi ad imperandum, & illis ad obedien- dum reddunt.

## 29:22
Verse 22.

A wrathful man stirs up strife: and he who is easy to anger will be more prone to sin.

Ethical admonitions are subjoined (1.) on avoiding wrath: as the cause of strife and various sins. A man of wrath stirs up contention (chap. 15, verse 18) and the master (or possessor) of indignation (which is harsher and more lasting than wrath) is abundant in transgression. See James 1, verse 20. Proverbs 12, verse 16; chap. 14, verses 17, 29. (2.) On avoiding pride, v. 23.

Pride (the affectation of eminence: for the word in Hebrew descends from נאה, to be eminent) of man humbles him (strips him of glory and honor, and places him in an abject seat) but the humble in spirit shall attain glory. Compare chap. 16, verse 18; chap. 18, verse 12; Luke 14, verse 11; chap. 18, verse 14; chap. 1, verses 51, 52; 1 Peter 5, verses 5, 6.

3. On avoiding participation in sins, verse 24. He who participates with a thief (or other sins, and sinners, as such) hates his own soul: (so also he who) hears a curse and does not disclose it (Leviticus 5, verse 1); by communicating in the sins of others, he makes himself a participant in their punishment as well, Psalm 50, verse 18; Romans 1, verse 32. Which communication happens in various ways according to that well-worn saying: I counsel, I command, I consent, I provoke, I praise, I do not uncover the fault, I do not punish, I do not rebuke, I do not oppose, but I protect and defend the deeds of others. The Vulgate renders it: He hears the one adjuring and does not disclose: when, namely, he refuses to disclose the thief to a judge who is lawfully adjuring him, Numbers 5, verse 19, or even when a judge compels him to swear, as with the LXX and the Chaldean, an oath is deferred to him and he does not confess. Grotius has these things on this verse:

Latin:

Vers. 22.

VIR IRACUNDUS PROVOCAT RIXAS: ET QUI AD INDIGNANDUM FACILIS EST ERIT AD PECCANDUM PROCLIVIOR.

Subjiciuntur monita Ethica (1.) de vitanda ira- cundia: ceu causa rixarum, & variorum pec- catorum. Vir iræ excitat litem (cap. 15. vers. 18.) & Dominus (vel possessor) indignationis (quæ aspe- rior & diuturnior est ira) multus (est) prævarica- tione. Vid. Jacob. 1. vers. 20. Proverb. 12. vers. 16. cap. 14. vers. 17. 29. (2.) De superbia fugienda, v. 23.

Superbia (eminentiæ affectatio: vox enim in Ebr. à נאה eminuit, descendit) hominis humiliat eum (gloria & honore eum spoliat, & abjecta sede collocat) at humilis spiritu assequetur gloriam. Conf. cap. 16. vers. 18. cap. 18. vers. 12. Luc. 14. vers. 11. cap. 18. vers. 14. cap. 1. vers. 51. 52. 1. Petr. 5. vers. 5. 6.

3. De peccatorum participatione cavenda vers. 24. Qui participat cum fure (aut aliis peccatis, & pec- catoribus, qua talibus) odio habet animam suam: (ita etiam qui) maledictionem audit, & non indicat Levit. 5. vers. 1.) communicans alienis peccatis pœ- næ etiam aliorum participem se facit, Psalm. 50. vers. 18. Rom. 1. vers. 32. Quæ communicatio variis fit modis juxta tritum illud: Consulo, præcipio, consentio, provoco, laudo, Non retego culpam, non punio, non reprehendo, Non obsto, sed præcipio & defendo aliena. Vulgata reddit: Adjurantem audit, & non indi- cat: cum nempe judici legitime adjuranti furem indicare renuit, Num. 5. vers. 19. vel etiam cum ju- dex ipsum jurare cogit, uti cum LXX. Chald. jusju- randum defertur ei, & non fatetur. Grotius ad hunc versum hæc habet:

## 29:24
Verse 24.

HE WHO PARTICIPATES WITH A THIEF, HATES HIS OWN SOUL: HE HEARS THE ONE ADJURING, AND DOES NOT DISCLOSE) The copula is missing, and he who hears the one adjuring: He is equal to the thief who, when adjured by a magistrate, does not disclose a thief known to him. See the Law of Leviticus 5, 1. Such is that adjuration in Sophocles' Oedipus Rex:

I proclaim these things to you all, Cadmeans, whoever among you knows by whose hand Laius, son of Labdacus, was destroyed, I command him to declare everything to me.

But if you will be silent, and someone, fearing for a friend, shall push aside this word, or keep it to himself, you must hear these things from me. I forbid this man, whoever he is, of this land of which I hold the power and the thrones, that anyone should receive him, or speak to him, or make him a partner in prayers or sacrifices to the gods, or distribute holy water to him.

4. On the harm of anxious fear, and the fruit of courageous confidence, verse 25. The fear of man (trepidation and anxious fear, by which we fear men, is to be taken objectively, as the following clause teaches, since those not trusting in God fear men, so that for their sake they even desert the law of God: whence the LXX and Vulgate render it, 'and fears man,' and B. Luther, 'Für Menschen sich scheuen,' sets a snare (entangles in dangers, and makes the fearful pay, Matt. 10. verse 28). But he who trusts in the Lord shall be exalted: he will not only escape the snares of dangers, but will also be crowned with glory and honor, or in a high and safe place he will be placed in chap. 18, 10. Psalm 18, 3. 17. Prov. 16, 20. The Osiandrine Paraphrase agrees: He who fears men more than GOD, and does not perform his duty because he fears that he might lose the thanks of men or create danger for himself, he will fall into calamity, and what he fears will happen to him. But he who, trusting in the Lord, performs his calling skillfully and strenuously, will be wonderfully defended by the Lord.

5. Concerning the favor not of men, but of God, which is to be sought, ver. 25. Many (having abandoned God) seek the face (or favor. Cf. Psalm 27, 8. Psalm 105, 5.) of the Prince (the ruler). But from the Lord (proceeds) the judgment of individuals (or of every man), that is, lot and fortune, as Vatablus with Aben-Ezra. In which sense this gnome coheres aptly with the preceding: i.e., therefore those who fear men will fall: but those who fear and hope in the Lord will be exalted: because it is not for men, but for God, to distribute to each his own lot, good or bad and miserable.
