To which explanation is subordinated the sense of others, who with R. Levi, R. Solomon, and the LXX Interpreters, understand judgment specifically, because it is God's to direct the heart of the King in judgment, and therefore that the decree in judgment may follow according to a vow, not so much the face of the King is to be sought, as that of God: as Jansenius, Salazar, Osiander, and others explain.

6. Finally, these sentences are concluded by the mutual detestation of the just and the impious, which the extreme disparity of morals and pursuits creates, ver. 27. An abomination to the just is the man of iniquity: but an abomination to the impious is the upright in way. Thus two cities are as it were established, which St. Augustine described: one of God, the other of the Devil: one of the just, the other of the impious, between which there is a perpetual and irreconcilable war, 2 Cor. 6, 14. The just detest and are harassed by the impious, and conversely the impious by the just; the just indeed do not hate the impious, but their impiety, but the impious hate the just just as much as justice and piety. Cf. ch. 21, ver. 8. Job 15, ver. 18. What the Vulgate codices add, The son keeping the word will be outside of destruction, is neither in the Hebrew, nor in the Chaldean Version or the LXX, but at the end of verse 22, ch. 24, among the LXX in the edition. Vatican, are read, and thus they are rashly stitched on, being alien to the sources.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

QVI CVM FVRE PARTICIPAT, ODIT ANI- MAM SVAM: ADJVRANTEM AVDIT, ET NON INDICAT) Deest copula, & qui adjurantem audit: Par furi est qui à Magistratu adjuratus furem sibi notum non indicat. Vide Legem Levitici 5, 1. Talis illa adjuratio in Oedipode rege Sophoclis:

Ὑμῖν προφωνῶ πᾶσι Καδμείοις τάδε, Ὅτις ποθ' ὑμῶν Λάϊον τὸν Λαβδάκου Κάτοιδεν ἀνδρὸς ἐκ τίνος διώλετο, Τῦτον κελεύω πάντα σημαίνειν ἐμοί.

Εἰ δ' αὖ σιωπήσεσθε, καί τις ἢ φίλου Δείσας ἀπώσει τ' ἔπος, ἢ 'χ' αὑτᾶ τόδε Ἁ'κ τῶνδε δράσω ταῦτα χρὴ κλύειν ἐμᾶ. Τὸν ἄνδρ' ἀπαυδῶ τῦτον ὅστις ἐστὶ, γῆς Τῆσδ' ἧς ἐγὼ κράτη τε καὶ θρόνους νέμω, Μήτ' εἰσδέχεσθαι, μήτε προσφωνεῖν τινα, Μήτ' ἐν θεῶν εὐχαῖσι, μήτε θύμασι Κοινὸν ποιεῖσθαι, μήτε χέρνιβας νέμειν.

4. De anxii timoris damno, & animosæ confiden- tiæ fructu vers. 25. Timor hominis (trepidatio & an- xius timor, quo homines metuimus uti objective accipiendum esse sequens membrum docet, cum non fidentes Deo homines metuunt, ut eorum cau- sa etiam legem Dei deserant: unde LXX. & Vulg. reddit, & timet hominem, & B. Luther. Für Men- schen sich scheuen, laqueum ponit (periculis impli- cat, ac pavidos luere facit, Matth. 10. vers. 28.) At qui confidit in Domino, exaltabitur: non tantum laqueos effugiet periculorum, sed etiam gloria & honore coronabitur, vel in loco sublimi & tuto collocabitur cap. 18, 10. Psalm. 18, 3. 17. Prov. 16, 20. Consonat Paraphrasis Osiandrina: Qui homines magis metuit, quam DEUM, & non facit suum offi- cium, propterea quod metuit, ne hominum gratia excidat, aut periculum sibi creet: is ruet in calami- tatem, & quod metuit, eveniet ei. Qui vero in Do- mino confidens, vocationi suae dextre & strenue satisfa- cit, mirabiliter a Domino defendetur.

5. De gratia non hominum, sed Dei quaerenda, vers. 25. Multi (relicto Deo) quaerunt faciem (vel gratiam. Conf. Psalm. 27, 8. Psalm. 105, 5.) Princi- pis (dominatoris.) At a Domino (egreditur) judi- cium singulorum (vel viri cujusque) id est, fors & fortuna, ut Vatabl. cum Aben-Ezra. Quo sensu apte cohaeret haec gnome cum praecedenti: q. d. ideo qui timent homines, corruent: qui vero timent & sperant in Domino, exaltabuntur: quia non ho- minum, sed Dei est cuique suam sortem bonam vel malam miseramque distribuere. Cui explicationi subordinatur aliorum sensus, qui cum R. Levi, R. Salom. & LXX. Interpp. peculiariter judicium intel- ligunt, quia Dei est cor Regis in judicio dirigere, ideoque ut ex voto sequatur decretum in judicio, non tam Regis facies quaerenda, quam Dei: uti exponit Jansenius, Salazar, Osiander, alii.

6. Tandem concluduntur hae sententiae mutua justorum ac impiorum detestatione, quam extrema morum studiorumque creat disparitas, vers. 27. Ab- ominatio justorum est vir iniquitatis: abominatio autem impii est rectus via. Ita duae quasi constituun- tur civitates, quas descripsit S. Augustinus: una Dei, altera Diaboli: una justorum, altera impio- rum, inter quas perpetuum est, & irreconciliabile bellum, 2. Corinth. 6, 14. Justi abominantur & infe- stantur impios, ac vicissim impii justos; justi qui- dem non oderunt impios, sed eorum impietatem, impii vero oderunt justos aeque ac justitiam & pie- tatem. Conf. cap. 21. vers. 8. Job. 15. vers. 18. Quae adjiciunt Vulgati codices, Verbum custodiens filius extra perditionem erit, nec in Ebraeo, nec in Version. Chald. aut LXX. sed in fine vers. 22. cap. 24. apud LXX. in edit. Vatic. leguntur, adeoque temere affu- ta sunt, utpote a fontibus aliena.

## 30:1 Argument
SECTION III. CHAPTER XXX.

The Confession of Agur, in which he confesses his natural ignorance in matters of faith, and especially concerning Christ the God-man, the nature of God, and the divine persons, and designates the Word of God as the sole principle of faith. A prayer for the averting of vanity and false doctrine, and for temporal goods: with certain Rules concerning others, as being wretched, not to be afflicted, and concerning acknowledging our own perversity, and directing our life, through six riddles proposed in as many quaternions concerning four worst vices, four insatiable things, four inscrutable things, four things that move the world, four wisest little animals, four things that walk happily: Finally, concerning doing penance, and restraining anger.

THE WORDS OF THE CONGREGATOR THE SON OF THE VOMITER) He translated names which are proper: Agur the son of Jakeh. He was some Theognis or Phocylides of those times.

What have those gentile poets to do with men full of the Spirit of God? Or will Grotius with Enjedinus call into doubt that Agur was inspired by God? For it was observed before that he did not think or speak worthily enough of the authors of these Proverbs. But since all Scripture of the O.T. is inspired by God, as the Apostle testifies 1 Tim. 3, 16, there is no doubt that these words also acknowledge the Holy Spirit as author, by which name Massa, Prophecy, and Neum, utterance, are designated. For Scripture uses these names when there is talk of Prophecy, or prophetic utterances brought forth by the Holy Spirit as author. Some not without reason hold this Agur the son of Jakeh to be Solomon himself. To whom the name Agur fits, because he COLLECTED sentences serving both spiritual and temporal life, and Ben-Jakeh, son of vomiting or congregation, i.e., the author of the doctrine, which he belched forth abundantly and copiously. Cf. Psalm 45, ver. 2. 1 Kings 4, ver. 32 ff. and he is called Koheleth, congregator, on account of the multitude of Wisdom which he gathered, as R. Solomon testifies, or also on account of the congregation of Ecclesiastical assemblies, which reason R. Abraham ben Ezra gives. The style, indeed, and the matter of these Parables argue for Solomon, since there is a remarkable agreement of both things and words with others. Nor can another be brought forth from the Scriptures who was called by this name. And thus most Jews determine that Solomon is that Agur, the Talmudists, according to R. Solomon in Eccles. 1, R. Levi in this place, who says that Solomon was called Agur, on account of the words which he completed in collecting this book, just as he calls himself Ecclesiastes, on account of the words collected in the book of Ecclesiastes, and the son of vomiting and congregation, because by collecting within himself, and gathering from thoughts in great assemblies, he communicated to others, and wished to propose Prophecy copiously, etc. Similarly R. Solomon notes that Solomon is called Agur the son of the congregation, because he collects all Wisdom and collection. Not inaptly here Cornelius à Lapide: The words of Agur, that is, of Solomon, who was Agur, that is, congregator, and the son of Jakeh, that is, of the vomiter, because he himself gathered his Wisdom here, and contracted it into a few quaternions, and collected his mind and senses into God, so that he might abundantly draw divine things from His light, and full of them, he might then belch them forth to others with a full mouth, with such abundance that he seemed to vomit it, just as a furnace is not absurdly, but elegantly said to vomit sparks and fires, because it ejaculates them copiously, and Virgil says: The golden boss vomits fires. And he vomits his purple soul, Aeneid 9. And Ovid, Epist. 18. Scylla vomits and resorbs the waves. And book 1 of the Fasti. Cacus vomits flames from his mouth. Just as, therefore, whirlpools and fountains gush forth and vomit a quantity of water with force: so Solomon here vomits the waters of Wisdom like an overflowing fountain. The blessed Lord Doctor Cælestinus Mislenta proves this wisdom primarily in his Disputation on the Confession of Agur, chapter 2, Member 1, and for the same he cites St. Augustine, Volume II, Epistle 45, who attributes this chapter to Solomon as the author, as he also cites Lyranus: Which opinion also seems to be confirmed by the fact that in verse 6 he prays for the removal of the temptation of idolatry and falsehood, such as Solomon had previously experienced; and that the description of God and His coeternal Son agrees perfectly with the 8th chapter of Proverbs, and that matters worthy of such great Wisdom, which was in Solomon, are set forth in this chapter; which, because they exhibit the highest mysteries in their principal part, were added to the others under a special title, once the aphorisms or moral sentences were completed. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. The Church, he says, and the Fathers attribute these and the preceding ones equally to Solomon, and cite them by the name of Solomon, not Agur. Thus Bede, Lyranus, Hugo,

Arboreus, Dionysius, Peltanus, & others. Although R. Aben-Ezra indeed understands here a certain man of the time of Solomon of whole life and great wisdom, and most others believe him to be a certain different wise man from Solomon, B. Luther, Philippus Melanchthon, Oecolampad, Theod. Peltanus, Junius, Tremellius, Piscator, Cornelius Jansenius &c. nevertheless easily grant to him that Solomon collected these sayings, which R. Aben-Ezra openly professes. Certainly no one denies that the Holy Spirit acknowledges the author of them, which Grotius scarcely seems to have believed.

Verse of the same.

THE VISION WHICH THE MAN SPOKE, WITH WHOM IS GOD, AND WHO BEING STRENGTHENED BY GOD DWELLING WITH HIM SAYS) Here also he translated proper names, which being preserved, you may translate thus most excellently. For that which is here 'vision', the Hebrew is מַשָּׂא, which elsewhere indeed signifies dire prophecies, but it can also signify a collection or gathering, so that we may understand these to be selected from the writings of Agur. Then 'the man spoke' (supply 'he') to Ithiel, to Ithiel, to Ucal, his disciples namely or his friends: such as Cyrenus to Theognis, and Onomacritus.

By no example did Grotius teach that מַשָּׂא signifies a collection, nor does that meaning suit the word so well. Which he took from נָשָׂא, 'he lifted up', is sometimes rendered by the Greeks as λῆμμα, an accepted enunciation, so that it may indicate something that has proceeded from God, just as prophecies were received from heaven, concerning which this word is used. Nor does the word נְאֻם introduce only a speech, but according to the customary usage of Scripture, which employs the noun derived from it primarily concerning divine revelations, so that it may be noted as a saying divinely implanted and inspired, see Num. 24. v. 3. 2. Sam. 23. verse 1. Furthermore, the particle ל is not necessarily to be explained here by 'TO': so that namely the disciples or friends of Agur may be understood, to whom these sayings were addressed, since it can be rendered 'CONCERNING' and explained about the OBJECT. Thus R. Solomon accepts it, and proves it by a similar example Exod. 14. verse 3. Pharaoh said concerning the children of Israel. See also 1. Kings 10. verse 1. For it was not important to know to whom those sayings were addressed, for they contain no prophecy specifically so called, but they pertain to all in common: nor are persons named Ithel and Uchal found anywhere in Scripture or tradition, and therefore it seems better to define the object, which occurs as something entirely singular and mystical in this utterance or document. However, there is no reason why I should believe with R. Solomon that Solomon himself or his power and Wisdom are insinuated here by those names, as if he had said, 'God is with me through the fullness of Wisdom, God is with me through the fullness of power, and I shall be able to multiply for myself gold, silver, horses and wives, without transgression,' which gloss who does not see to be inept and impious? The faithful are more correctly understood by the LXX Interpreters: 'these things says the man to those who believe in God.' But those who think the object is expressed, explain it concerning Christ the God-man, as if to say: the saying of the man concerning Ithiel is 'GOD IS WITH ME', concerning him, I say, who is Ithiel, God-man, of the same nature as me, and Uchal, i.e., truly omnipotent: to which opinion our B. Myslenta and Cartwright add their vote on this passage, or B. Dn. Gerhard in Exeget. Tom. I. page 1145. This explanation is also added by the Reformed Interpreters in the notes to the Belgian version, and is not disapproved of by the Pontificals. Cornel. à Lapide: Solomon, he says, rises to God and Christ, whom he therefore calls Ithiel, that is, 'God is with me'. Who nevertheless ineptly calls God the Father symbolically the son of the vomiter Agur and says the Holy Spirit is designated by the word Uchal. Indeed if the name איתיאל is compared with the name of the Messiah עמנואל, both agree excellently, and designates Christ

the God-man: since the faithful people confess עמנואל GOD WITH US, but each one of the believers confesses with Agur concerning the same: איתיאל: God is with me. Since therefore that name is proper to Christ Is. 7, 14. ch. 8. Matth. 1. the same will not undeservedly be established concerning this; which therefore seems to be repeated for this reason, that this most distinguished name may be the more deeply impressed upon the mind, and be so connected with the other, that one subject designated by two names may be understood. Nor does the name אוכל fit anyone more correctly than Christ: from יכל 'he was powerful', 'he prevailed in strength', which is used of God Job 42, 2. 'I know indeed that you can do all things' תוכל. Num. 22, 38. אוכל 'I shall be powerful', 'I shall prevail', so that here by the name אוכל the omnipotence of Christ the God-man is noted, which he exercised especially in the work of redemption, when he prevailed over the strong and armed one Is. 44, 24. Luke 11, 22. Rom. 1, 4. indeed also in the work of creation, which this Agur claims here for the Son of God, ὁμοουσίῳ καὶ ὁμοτίμῳ, of the same essence and power with God the Father, verse 4. Since therefore he expressly names the Son of God there, and commands that trust be placed in him, and promises to all who believe in him protection, of which we especially have need against spiritual enemies, indeed he establishes this as the end of Scripture or the word of God, and places the sum of it in this, that recognizing God and his Son from it and placing trust in him, they may have a shield, a safeguard and most certain protection: The object, concerning which Agur had decided to speak in this Spiritual document, is rightly established as the Son of God, Christ the God-man, whom he honors with this name, Ithiel, Vcuchal, MY GOD AND OMNIPOTENT, Ithiel 'God is with me' and Immanuel 'God is with us', who by the assumption of human nature is ὁμοούσιος to us, who from eternity as God is ὁμοούσιος to his Father, and his eternal Son, and truly omnipotent, who gathers the wind in his fists, has bound the waters in a garment, and established all the ends of the earth, of the same incomprehensible virtue, majesty, and essence with the Father: and by his divine virtue he prevailed over our enemies, sin, the Devil, death, and hell, so that we may acknowledge and confess him with Thomas: My Lord and my God Job 20. verse 28. Conf. Apocal. 1. verse 8, 18. ch. 21. verse 6. Cartwright has it thus: that Christ is the subject matter of this prophecy is not surprising, since he is the subject of the whole law and the prophets (I add also the apostles and evangelists), Acts 3, verses 22, 23, 24, Rom. 10, verse 4. Hence therefore we conclude that every doctrine which does not direct toward Christ and does not preach his merit and grace toward us, wanders from the scope of the law and the prophets (and especially of the Gospel). Concerning the appellation of Ithiel, since it is exactly the same as that which is in Matt. 1, verse 23, see what has been annotated by me on that passage. This much only is the difference, that this name exhibits the more consolation, the more it accommodates the benefit of Christ to individual believers separately, more closely and familiarly: That it places the hope of victory to be won over the world, the flesh, and the Devil (for this is the force and sense of the other name) in Christ alone, is a notable doctrine, and abundantly confirmed from other places of Scripture, Psalm 45. and 125. Jerem. 23, verse 24. Job 16, verse 33. Rom. 8, v. 31, 32, 33, etc. Just as therefore, looking at our own strength, we lose heart, so lifting our eyes to Christ, we ought to be confident and cheerful.

Latin:

SECTIO III. CAPUT XXX.

Confessio Aguris, qua ignorantiam naturalem in rebus fidei, & imprimis de Christo θεαν- θρωπῳ, Dei natura, ac personis divinis pro- fitetur ac principium fidei unicum Verbum Dei designat. Oratio pro avertenda vani- tate & falsa doctrina, & pro bonis tempo- ralibus: cum Regulis quibusdam de aliis, utpote abjectis, non affligendis, deque nostra ipsorummet tum perversitate agnoscenda, tum vita dirigenda, per sex gryphos totidem quaternionibus propositos de quatuor pessi- mis vitiis, quatuor insatiabilibus, qua- tuor inscrutabilibus, quatuor orbem com- moventibus, quatuor animalculis sapien- tissimis, quatuor feliciter gradientibus: De- nique de poenitentia agenda, & ira compri- menda.

VERBA CONGREGANTIS FILII VO- MENTIS) Transtulit nomina quae sunt propria: Ag- gur filii Jache. Fuit is aliquis illorum temporum Theognis aut Phocylides.

Quid gentiles illi Poëtæ ad viros Spiritu Dei ple- nos? Aut num Grotius cum Enjedino Agurem θεόπνευσον fuisle in dubium vocabit? Non enim di- gne satis ipsum de auctoribus horum Proverbio- rum sentire, aut loqui, antea observatum. At cum omnis Scriptura V. T. θεόπνευs⅝ sit, teste Apo- stolo 1. Tim. 3, 16. hæc verba etiam autorem Spir. S. agnoscere, dubitandum non est, quo nomine משׂא Prophetia, & נאם dictum, designantur. His enim nominibus utitur Scriptura, cum de Prophetia, vel dictis Propheticis S. S. autore prolatis sermo sit. Agurem etiam hunc filium Jache non abs re pro ipso Salomone habent nonnulli. Cui nomen אגור convenit, quod sententias vitæ cum Spirituali tum temporali inservientes, COLLEGERIT, & בן יקה filii vomitionis vel congregationis, h. e. auctoris do- ctrinæ, quam affatim & copiose eructarit. Conf. Psalm. 45. vers. 2. 1. Reg. 4. vers. 32. seqq. ac קהלת congregans dictus est, ob Sapientiæ multitudinem, quam congregavit, teste R. Salomone, vel etiam ob congregationem cœtuum Ecclesiasticorum, quam rationem reddit R. Abrah. ben Ezr. Stylus certe, ac materia harum Paræmiarum Salomonem arguit, quum & rerum & verborum cum aliis insignis sit convenientia. Neque proferri potest è Sacris alius, qui hoc nomine dictus fuerit. Atque ita statuunt plerique Judæi Salomonem Agurem illum esse, Thalmudistæ, apud R. Salomonem in Eccles. 1. R. Lev. in h. l. qui Salomonem dictum Agur ait, propter verba, quæ complevit in colligendo hoc libro, sicut sei- psum vocat Ecclesiasten, propter verba collecta in li- bro Ecclesiastis, ac filium vomitionis & congregatio- nis, quod colligendo intra seipsum, & congregando de cogitationibus in concionibus magnis, aliis communi- cavit, & voluerit copiose proponere Prophetiam &c. Similiter R. Salomo notat Salomonem vocari Agur filium congregationis, quia colligit omnem Sapien- tiam & collectionem. Non inconcinne hic Cornel. à Lapide: Verba Aguris, id est, Salomonis, qui fuit Agur, id est, congregans & filius Jake, id est, vo- mentis, quia ipse suam Sapientiam hic congregavit, eamque in paucos quaternarios contraxit, ac suam mentem sensusque in Deum collegit, ut ejus lumine di- vina abunde hauriret, eisque plenus illa deinde aliis ple- no ore eructaret, tanta abundantia, ut eam evomere videretur, perinde ac fornax non absurde, sed elegan- ter dicitur vomere scintillas & ignes, quia illas copio- se ejaculatnr, & Virgilius ait: Umbo vomit aureus ignes. Et purpuream vomit ille animam Æneid. 9. & Ovid. Epist. 18. Fluctus vomit atque resorbet scylla. Et lib. 1. Fastor. Flammas ore vomit Cacus. Sicut ergo gurgites & fontes egurgitant vomuntque aquarum copiam cum impetu: Sic Salomon vomit hic aquas Sapientiæ velut fons exuberans. Probat eam sapientiam cumprimis B. Dn. D. Cælestinus Mislenta Disp. de Confess. Agur. cap. 2. Memb. 1. ac pro eadem S. Augustinum Tom. II. Epist. 45. hoc caput Salomoni auctori tribuentem, ut & Ly- ranum adducit: Quæ sententia etiam firmari vi- detur inde, quod vers. 6. precetur, pro remotione tentationis idololatricæ & mendacii, qualem antea expertus fuerat Salomo; & quod descriptio Dei ac coæterni ejus Filii apprime conveniant cum 8. cap. Proverb. & digna tanta imprimis Sapientia quæ in Salomone fuit, in hoc capite tradantur; Quæ quia præcipua sui parte summa mysteria exhibent, pecu- liari titulo cæteris adjecta fuerunt, absolutis nempe aphorismis, vel sententiis moralibus. Cornel. à La- pide in h. l. Ecclesia, inquit, & Patres hæc æque & præcedentia tribuunt Salomoni, citantque nomine Salomonis, non Aguris. Ita Beda, Lyranus, Hugo,

Arboreus, Dionysius, Peltanus, & alii. Etsi vero R. Aben-Ezra virum aliquem tempore Salomonis vi- tæ integræ & magnæ sapientiæ hic intelligit, ac ple- rique alii diversum quendam à Salomone sapien- tem eum esse credant, B. Lutherus, Philippus Me- lancthon, Oecolampad. Theod. Peltanus, Junius, Tre- mellius, Piscator, Cornelius Jansenius &c. facile ta- men illi largiuntur Salomonem dicta hæc collegisse, quod aperte profitetur R. Aben-Ezra. Nullus cer- te negat ea Spiritum Sanctum autorem agnoscere, quod Grotius vix videtur credidisse.

Vers. eod.

VISIO QVAM LOCVTVS EST VIR, CVM QVO EST DEVS, ET QVI DEO SECVM MORANTE CONFORTATVS AIT) Hic quoque nomina propria transtulit, quibus servatis sic vertas optime. Pro eo, quod hic est visio, Hebræum est מַשָּׂא, quod alibi quidem va- ticinia dira significat, sed potest & significare συλλογὴν sive συναγωγὴν, ut intelligamus ex Aguris scriptis hæc esse selecta. Deinde locutus est vir (supple ille) ad Ithiel, ad Ithiel, ad Vcal, discipulos nimirum aut amicos suos: qualis Theognidi Cyr- nus, & Onomacritus.

Nullo exemplo docuit Grotius מַשָּׂא signifi- care συλλογὴν, neque convenit adeo voci illa signi- ficatio. Quæ à נָשָׂא tulit, levavit dicta, Græ- cis quandoque redditur λῆμμα enunciatum acce- ptum, ut à Deo profectum quid indigitetur, quem- admodum Prophetiæ cœlitus accipiebantur, de quibus hæc vox usurpatur. Neque verbum נְאֻם loquutionem tantum infert, sed more Scripturæ usitato, quæ adhibet imprimis nomen inde deriva- tum de revelationibus divinis, uti dictum divinitus inditum & inspiratum notetur, vid. Num. 24. v. 3. 2. Sam. 23. verf. 1. Porro particula ל non est neces- sario hic per AD explicanda: ut nempe intelligan- tur discipuli aut amici Aguris, ad quos hæc dicta sint, quum possit reddi SUPER & de OBJECTO explicari. Sic accipit R. Salomo, & probat ex- emplo simili Exod. 14. vers. 3. dixit Pharao de filiis Israel. Videatur etiam 1. Reg. 10. vers. 1. Siqui- dem non intererat scire, ad quem illa dicta sint, nul- lam enim specialiter ita vocatam Prophetiam con- tinent, sed ad omnes communiter pertinent: neque in Scriptura uspiam, vel traditione reperiuntur per- sonæ ita nuncupatæ Ithel & Uchal, ideoque satius videtur objectum, quod singulare prorsus, ac my- sticum in hoc effato vel documento occurrit, de- finire. Non est autem, quod Salomonem ipsum vel potentiam & Sapientiam ejusdem hic insinuari nominibus illis cum R. Salomone credam, quasi di- xerit, mecum Deus per plenitudinem Sapientiæ, me- cum Deus per plenitudinem potentiæ, & potero mihi multiplicare aurum, argentum, equos & uxores, absque transgressione, quam glossam ineptam atque impiam esse quis non videt? Rectius fideles intel- liguntur à LXX. Interpp. τάδε λέγει ἀνὴρ τοῖς πι- στεύουσι Θεῷ. Sed qui objectum exprimi censent, de Christo Θεανθρώπῳ explicant, q. d. dictum viri de Ithiel est MECUM DEUS, de eo, inquam, qui Ithiel est, Deus homo, ejusdem mecum naturæ, & Uchal, h. e. vere omnipotens: cui sententiæ calcu- lum adjicit B. Myslenta noster & Cartwrightus in h. l. aut B. Dn. Gerhardus in Exeget. Tom. I. pag. 1145. Additur etiam hæc explicatio à Reformatis Interpp. notis ad version. Belgic. neque improba- tur à Pontificiis. Cornel. à Lapide: Salomon, in- quit, assurgit ad Deum & Christum, quem proinde vocat Ithiel, id est, mecum Deus. Qui tamen inepte Deum Patrem symbolice Agurem filium vomentis vocat & Spiritum S. voce Uchal designari dicit. Sane si conferatur nomen איתיאל cum nomine Messiæ עמנואל egregie utrumque convenit, Christumque

θεάνθρωπον designat: quum populus fidelis confi- teatur עמנואל DEUS NOBISCUM, unusquis- que autem credentium cum Agur de eodem profi- teatur: איתיאל: Mecum Deus. Quum ergo illud nomen Christo proprium sit Es. 7, 14. cap. 8. Matth. 1. de hoc idem non immerito statuetur; quod pro- inde videtur ideo repeti, ut hoc tam insigne no- men eo altius menti imprimatur, ac cum altero ita connectatur, ut unum subjectum διώνυμον desi- gnari intelligatur. Neque alii rectius nomen אוכל convenit, quam Christo: à יכל potens fuit, præ- valuit robore, quod de Deo Job. 42, 2. adhibetur: Novi equidem, quod omnia poteris תוכל. Num. 22, 38. אוכל δύνατος ἔσομαι, valebo, ut notetur hic nomine אכל Christi θεανθρώπου omnipoten- tia, quam exercuit præcipue in opere redemtionis, cum prævaluit forti & armato Esa. 44, 24. Luc. 11, 22. Rom. 1, 4. imo & in opere creationis, quod Filio Dei ὁμοουσίῳ καὶ ὁμοτίμῳ ejusdem essentiæ & po- tentiæ cum Deo Patre hic Agur vendicat vers. 4. Quum ergo ibi expresse Filium Dei nominet, & in eum fiduciam collocare jubeat, omnibusque in eum credentibus protectionem, qua adver- sus hostes spirituales imprimis nos egemus, pro- mittat, imo finem hunc Scripturæ vel verbi Dei constituat, ac summam ejusdem in eo collocet, quod Deum ejusque Filium inde agnoscentes ac fidu- ciam in ipsum ponentes, scutum, præsidium & pro- tectionem certissimam habeant: Objectum, de quo in Spirituali hoc documento loqui Agur consti- tuerat, recte statuitur Filius Dei Christus θεάν- θρωπος, quem hoc nomine honorat, Ithiel, Vcu- chal, DEUS MEUS ET OMNIPOTENS, Ithiel Deus meus & Immanuel Deus noster, qui naturæ humanæ assumtione ὁμοούσιος nobis, qui ab æter- no ut Deus, Patri suo ὁμοούσιος, ejusque æternus Filius est, & vere omnipotens, qui colligit verbum velis suis, aquas in vestimento ligavit, omnesque terræ fines constituit, ejusdem incomprehensibilis virtutis, ma- jestatis, & essentiæ cum Patre: suaque divina virtu- te prævaluit hostibus nostris, peccato, Diabolo, morti, & inferno, ut ipsum cum Thoma agnosca- mus & confiteamur: Dominus meus & Deus meus Job. 20. vers. 28. Conf. Apocal. 1. vers. 8, 18. cap. 21. vers. 6. Cartwrightus ita habet: Christum hujus Prophetiæ materiam esse, mirum non est, cum totius legis, & Prophetarum (addo etiam Apostolorum & Evangelistarum) subjectum sit Actor. 3. vers. 22. 23. 24. Rom. 10. vers. 4. Hinc igitur concludimus, omnem doctrinam, quæ ad Christum non dirigit & ejus in nos meritum, & gratiam non prædicat, à legis & Prophetarum (& imprimis Evangelii) scopo aberrare. De Ithielis appellatione, quandoquidem eadem pror- sus est cum illa, quæ est Matth. 1. vers. 23. Vide quæ à me in illum locum annotata sunt. Hoc tantum in- terest, quod hoc nomen eo plus consolationis exhibet, quo Christi beneficium singulis seorsim fidelibus propri- us & familiarius accommodat: Quod spem victoriæ de mundo, carne & Diabolo reportandæ (hæc enim al- terius nominis vis & sensus est) in uno Christo collo- cat, doctrina est insignis, & ex aliis Scripturæ locis ab- unde confirmata Psalm. 45. & 125. Jerem. 23. vers. 24. Job. 16. vers. 33. Rom. 8. v. 31. 32. 33. &c. Quemad- modum igitur lacertos nostros intuentes animum ad- jicimus, sic oculos ad Christum attollentes, confidere, & alacres esse debemus.

## 30:2
Verse 2.

I AM THE MOST FOOLISH OF MEN AND WISDOM IS NOT WITH ME.

In Hebrew, indeed (so the word כי is asseverative, indeed, truly, 1 Chron. 29, verse 14. Job 8, 6. Psalm 10, 14.

Psalm 89, verse 3.) I am brutish more than a man (I am more stupid than it befits a man) and the understanding of a man (אדם, such as the first man had, Adam created in the image of God in true wisdom) is not with me. Verse 3. Neither have I learned wisdom (or could I learn it, apart from the gracious information of the Holy Spirit, both because of the natural dullness and blindness of the mind, and the perversity of the heart and will, and because of the lack of human instruction, since no mortal can hand down divine Wisdom, nor does it consist in anything except the sole revelation of the Spirit of God, 1 Cor. 2, verse 14.) Nor have I known the knowledge of the holy: which is neither φύσει (by nature) in us, nor is it acquired by human μαθήσει (learning) or ἀσκήσει (exercise), but is obtained and procured solely from God, and through the word of God, prayer, meditation, and temptation, and is proper to the holy.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

STULTISSIMUS SUM VIRORUM ET SA- PIENTIA NON EST MECUM.

In Ebr. sane (ita vox כי affeverativa est sane, utique, 1. Paralip. 29. vers. 14. Job. 8, 6. Psalm. 10, 14.

Pfalm. 89. vers. 3.) bardus sum præ viro (stipidior fum quam virum decet) nec est intelligentia hominis (אדם, qualem habuit primus homo, Adam crea- tus ad imaginem Dei in vera sapientia) mihi. vers. 3. Neque didici sapientiam (aut discere potui, extra Spiritus S. gratiosam informationem, tum ob natu- ralem mentis hebetudinem & cæcitatem, ac cordis & voluntatis perversitatem, tum ob defectum hu- manæ institutionis, quum Sapientiam divinam ne- mo mortalium tradere possit, nec nisi sola revela- tione Spiritus Dei ea constet, 1. Cor. 2. vers. 14.) Nec scientiam sanctorum novi : quæ neque φύσει nobis inest, neque μαθήσει vel ἀσκήσει humana acquiri- tur, sed unice à Deo, & per verbum Dei, oratione, meditatione, ac tentatione obtinetur & compara- tur, sanctisque propria est.

## 30:4
Verse 4.

WHO HATH ASCENDED INTO HEAVEN?) Namely of men, so that, for instance, he might dare to change the Laws of God. Which the following things explain. Compare Isa. 40:12.

This question does not only mean that the laws of God are immutable: indeed, it is not about laws here. For what is contained in verse 6 is different, and it is to be understood not only about the law of God, but about the Word of God in general; and he denies not only that anything can be changed in the Word of God, but he asserts the all-encompassing perfection of the Word of God, to which nothing can or ought to be either detracted or added. But here he is occupied with describing the incomprehensible majesty, power, and essence of God. To exalt this all the more, Agur voluntarily confesses his own ignorance in such sublime mysteries. At the same time, however, he recalls us to the one and true principle of Spiritual Wisdom, the Word of God, outside of which he testifies by his own example that we know nothing in spiritual matters. Wherefore he proceeds from the ἄρσις (removal) to the θέσις (position), and removes a false or alien principle, namely that sincere faith in the true God, which it demands, and the reason for salvation, and the institution of the Spiritual life cannot be drawn from human reason: he posits a twofold principle of faith, which arises solely from the Word of God, which principle he teaches in Ps. 119:126 is genuine, because it is most purified and free from all falsehood and stain: most effective, because it is a shield or buckler to all who trust in God: and most sufficient, because it admits no addition or subtraction. He therefore excludes human reason from this axiom, since the nature of man is corrupt, because I have been made בער (brutish), rude, and stupid, foolish and a fool, who excels neither in wisdom nor in morals, as Maimonides explains, by which the blindness of the natural mind in spiritual things, and the dull and brutal perversity of the will and appetite are designated, Psalm 49, verse 21, 1 Corinthians 2, verse 14, Ephesians 4, verse 17 seqq. He adds מאיש (than a man), which our blessed Myslenta does not poorly render, as if I were a man in mystical matters, who might be worth something in them, proving it with similar examples, Psalm 49, verse 3, 1 Sam. 2, v. 2, chap. 26, v. 15, Jer. 5, v. 1, so that at the same time the substantive adjunct דעת חסידים (knowledge of the pious) is understood, as in Exod. 4, verse 18, 1 Samuel 16, verse 18, chap. 17, v. 34, Job 11, verse 2, 2 Sam. 13, verse 3, chap. 18, verse 20. This is confirmed by the added further declaration, from the defect of human intellect, ולא בינת אדם לי (and the understanding of a man is not with me): where Junius and Tremellius understand the understanding divinely implanted in the first man, before he was ashamed. This is certain, that it is understood as the understanding necessary to man for the perception and apprehension of spiritual things, for Agur, the wisest of all men, was abundantly instructed in the wisdom of natural and political things. R. Joseph Albo, book 1, IKKARIM chap. 16, takes the word

בינה (understanding), as knowledge deduced from premises: whence it will be denied that there is a way to arrive at the mysteries of salvation through the discourse of human intellect, 1 Cor. 2, verse 14, 2 Cor. 3, verse 5. Furthermore, he removes human instruction in matters of faith: I have not learned Wisdom: which no Rabbi, however wise he may otherwise be, can have concerning heavenly things by nature, apart from the information and illumination of the Holy Spirit, much less hand it down to others, because this Wisdom is completely hidden from any wise men of the world, 1 Cor. 2, verse 8, whence the LXX Interpreters explain this θετικῶς (affirmatively), and with them Augustine, Vol. 1, Epist. 49, quest. 51, God has taught me Wisdom. Further, Agur adds ודעת קדשים אדע (and I shall know the knowledge of the holy), which they take interrogatively, so that the interrogation responds to a negative, Piscator, Junius and Tremellius: And shall I know the knowledge of the holy? But the Chaldean repeats the particle of negation ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (in common) thus: And I have not known the knowledge of the holy: and thus also R. Levi, R. Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, and B. Luther explain it, since the preceding context demands it entirely. Some render it thus: I have not learned Wisdom (so that) I might know the knowledge of the holy. But the former explanations are simpler and more congruent; because all those things which are accumulated here explain one another, to declare more abundantly our natural ignorance and stupidity in mystical matters. But there is no place for the affirmative translation of the Septuagint Interpreters, καὶ γνῶσιν ἁγίων ἔγνωκα (and I have known the knowledge of the holy), even though the Vulgate translated it similarly, and I have known the knowledge of the holy: It is taught, therefore, that the knowledge of the Holy is so constituted that it proceeds neither from nature nor from the care of any man left to himself, but from God alone; which heavenly, saving knowledge is also otherwise called the knowledge of God, Proverbs 2, verse 5. Isa. 11, verse 9, the knowledge of the Messiah, chap. 53, verse 11, it is called the knowledge of the redeemer, Job 19, verse 25, and it is called the knowledge of God and the Savior conjunctively, John 17, verse 3, and in the parallel place, Proverbs 9, verse 10, it is called the knowledge of the holy, because, namely, it is proper to the faithful and the holy, John 17, verse 19. Raimund, from R. Mos. Hadarsch, understands God by the name of the Holy, so that this word denotes the object, not the subject, of the knowledge.

Solomon illustrates all these things, citing by way of example some mystery from the Wisdom of supernatural things, and the knowledge of the Holy Ones, namely concerning the incomprehensible majesty, power, and essence of God, and of his eternal Son, just as Christ in John 3, when Nicodemus could not grasp the mystery of regeneration with his dull reason as he wished, led him to a similar ὑπακοή (obedience) of faith by other mysteries of sublime Wisdom: And therefore, so that it may be established that he proposed himself as an example to others, the wisest of mortals now openly denies this wisdom to all men in general, with emphatic and most penetrating questions, by which our blindness and stupidity in spiritual matters is displayed before everyone's eyes: In which one must look both to the incomprehensible subject and to the predicate, namely the infinite and incomprehensible works. These things are first set forth in this place, and indeed in four ζητήμασι (questions): The first of which concerns the heaven, the second the winds and the air, the third the waters, the fourth the earth: which among the majestic works of God, if you depart from man, the τῷ μικροκόσμῳ (microcosm), are most to be admired in the macrocosm. Concerning the first, it is thus: Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Which the Jews in Pesikta and R. Solomon in his gloss ineptly interpret concerning Moses, who ascended onto Mount Sinai to God, and from there descended to the people in Exodus 19 and 32: as if Mount Sinai were heaven, or Moses had ever anywhere been said to have ascended into heaven, which the Rabbis themselves deny in the Talmud, Tractate Sukkah: And the Master himself says; the divinity does not descend below forever, and Moses and Elijah did not ascend on high, just as it is said: The heavens of heavens are the Lord's, but the earth He has given to the children of men. Add that the case of Elijah and Moses is different: for the former is read to have been taken up into heaven, which is nowhere found regarding the latter. And how is the name of Moses and his son unnameable and incomprehensible? No less inept is the gloss of the Photinian Enjedinus, that Ithiel and Uchal, the associates of Agur, proposed to him questions about heavenly things and meteors, to which he replies with these words, that he is inept, slow, and dull to resolve those questions; because he neither is wise of himself, nor has learned wisdom, nay, that no mortal can explain such things clearly: For who of men has ascended into heaven, and descended, that he might know the mysteries and secrets of God? Whence is it certain that Ithiel and Uchal were the associates of Agur? Whence, that they proposed such questions to him? And who would believe a man distinguished by the praise of wisdom to be so inept and dull? That he was distinguished for wisdom, these very remarkable and profound proverbs of his prove. He is not, therefore, to be blamed because he was neither wise of himself, nor had learned wisdom. But then, the mysteries and secrets of God are very poorly confused with natural things in the sky and meteors. For there is no need that we ascend into heaven, and thence in turn descend, in order to know those natural things: about which many have philosophized excellently, even though they have not fallen from heaven. Franciscus Junius and Piscator understand the passage as referring to mystical matters, but explain it in terms of local motion: no one can ascend the heavens to know the way of our salvation, and descending, bring it to us. But in this way the following questions will not cohere, since those predicates are denied of others here in such a way that they are vindicated for God alone, and therefore it must be believed that the same is done here as well. Whence the Grotian gloss also must be committed to the sponge. For what will be the continuity: Who of men has ascended into heaven, that he might dare to change the laws of God? Who has held the wind in his palms, etc.? What do those things about the comprehension of the winds, the gathering of the sea, the foundation of the earth have to do with the knowledge of the will of God, by the power of which anyone could presume to change the laws of God? Cartwright interprets it concerning the perversity of the will, and applies it to Christ alone at verse 4. Now he deals with the remaining impotence of the soul, namely the stubbornness of the will, and its aversion from God. Which indeed is so great that, although a man might understand the truth, yet he could no more practice it, and express it in deeds, words, or even thoughts, than, burdened by a terrestrial and heavy body, he could ascend into heaven, or if he were there, descend without falling: Which Ithiel alone can perform, as is also taught more openly in John 3:13. He declares this inability of the will to attain salvation with other comparisons: that this is, namely, as impossible for mortals as to comprehend the wind in one's fist, and to release it where you wish; and to bind water in a garment, as God does with the clouds above, and with sand below: as to establish all the regions of the earth. All these things Christ, as God, can perform most easily, Isaiah 40:12, 15, 16, 17. But he teaches that these things belong to no mortal by the added name, because his name has not yet been heard. Afterwards there seems to be a prolepsis; the silent occupation of which is, perhaps such a one as you seek once existed, but now has departed from the living: The subjection is: Where then is His Son, whom He begat like unto Himself? But just as it is certain that these things fit Christ, so they are also attributed to God the Father, and pertain rather to the incomprehensible majesty and power of both, which far exceeds the grasp of soul and mind, than to the inability of our will. St. Augustine, loc. cit., understands it of the Ascension of Christ into heaven, and His descent; to which interpretation it is an objection that all those questions or predicates seem to be uttered here equally of God the Father and His consubstantial Son, unless perhaps such a distinction is to be established between them, that the first is taken of Ithiel: Who, except Ithiel, has ascended into heaven and descended? The rest, concerning the work of creation and conservation common to God the Father and the Son, are proposed separately. In which manner three doctrines are handed down here: The mystery of Christ's ascension and descent: The infinite power of God in the creation and conservation of things, and also the mystery concerning God the Father and His consubstantial Son. But these things are more correctly referred to God the Father and the Son, and therefore other learned men understand by the ascension into heaven and descent the divine omnipresence, by which God fills heaven and earth, and is present above and below, Psalm 139:8, Jeremiah 23:23, 25, and anthropopathically and by reason of manifestation and works He is said to ascend into heaven and descend, because He is present in heaven and on earth: and He proves His presence there by creation and conservation. Whence also God is said to have descended, Genesis 11:7, chapter 18:24, Exodus 3:8, and to have ascended, Genesis 17:22. Compare Deuteronomy 33:26, Amos 9:6. Thus Lyranus and others think that by this ascension and descent of God is signified the all-encompassing government of God, by which He rules and governs both things above and things below, i.e., as Cornelius à Lapide says in this place: God alone is omniscient and omnipotent, who not by change of place (for He is everywhere and immense) but by His wisdom and operation, as it were, ascends into heaven and descends, while He works in celestial and sublunary creatures, in the highest as well as in the lowest, while, namely, He most wisely establishes the heavens above, orders them, adorns them with stars, moves, rules, and governs them, and below in the air, earth, and sea, creates, feeds, preserves, and makes fruitful all things, animate as well as inanimate, etc. He alludes to Deuteronomy 33:26: The rider of the heaven is your helper: by His magnificence the clouds run: His dwelling is above, and underneath are the everlasting arms. And to that passage in Amos 9:6: Who builds His ascension in heaven. But this omnipresence of God is truly incomprehensible to human reason, so much so that Averroes pronounced the thought of the ancients, who said that God is present in all things, to be childish. The Socinians also, nay, even some Calvinists, because they cannot attain to the divine omnipresence by reason, utterly deny it. Compare Job 38:32, Isaiah 40:12.

The second ζήτημα is: Who gathers the wind in his fists? Which the Jews ridiculously understand as the ashes taken by Moses from the furnace. Augustine explains it strangely regarding the souls of believers contained in a hidden place, and others explain it regarding created spirits, good and evil angels, enclosed in the fists of God: but it is most correctly understood as the wind. Which God not only creates (Job 13:15, Amos 4:3, Rom 4:8, Ps 107:25), but also moderates at his will (Exod 14:21, Job 38:24, Ps 104:4, Ps 147:18, Matt 8:26, ch 14:32), draws forth from his treasuries (Ps 135:7, Jer 10:13, ch 51:16), and impels (Gen 8:1, Exod 10:19, Ps 78:26), and therefore is said to enclose it in his fists, because at his nod the winds blow and execute his commands, or grow quiet. But how incomprehensible this work of divine wisdom and power is, the cited passages testify. Cf. Eccles 11:5 seqq., Job 3:7.

Thirdly Agur asks: Who has gathered the waters in a garment? Which again the Jews ineptly [interpret] concerning the deed

of Moses in the Red Sea, miraculous, Exod. 14. And ἀπροσδιονύσως (irrelevant) and inappropriately Augustine, concerning the effect of Baptism and the putting on of Christ, from the LXX, in a virile but alien interpretation: Who shall turn the waters into garments? Insufficiently Junius concerning the lower waters: But our people most correctly interpret it concerning the waters in general, as much the upper as the lower, as much those in the clouds as those contained in the bed of the sea, which God so restrains that He holds them as if bound in a garment. For He both beams His upper chambers with the upper waters, Ps. 104, v. 3, and sets bounds to the lower waters, that they may not cover the earth, Job 38, v. 8, 9, 10, Ps. 104, v. 9; He Himself binds the water in the clouds, Job 26, v. 7, and gathers the waters of the sea as in a heap, placing the depths in storehouses, Ps. 33, v. 7. Which no mortal can sufficiently attain to and comprehend by reason. See especially Job 37, v. 14, seqq., c. 38, v. 8, seqq., Is. 40, v. 12.

The fourth question is, Who has established all the ends of the earth? Which the Talmudists explain perversely concerning the erection of the Tabernacle, and Augustine understands ἀσκόπως (aimlessly) concerning the apprehension and occupation of all the ends of the earth through the preaching of the Gospel: nor do Junius and Tremellius render it sufficiently conveniently: who has established any ends of the earth? More correctly Aben-Ezra and R. Levi: who has erected all the ends of the earth, that they may not be moved? Which our people rightly accept concerning the ends of the earth, both as to its greater parts and as to the kingdoms themselves in them. Similarly Job 38, v. 5, who has disposed the measures (of the earth) or who has stretched the line upon it? Is. 40, v. 28, Who has created the ends of the earth? Acts 17, v. 26, He has made of one every race of men to inhabit upon the whole face of the earth: defining the bounds of their habitation. That this work is an incomprehensible work of divine power, GOD Himself indicates: Job 38, v. 5. Who has set its measures, if you know? And verse 18, Have you considered the breadth of the earth? Tell me, if you know all things?

These things, therefore, are concerning the predicated works, namely, of the infinite majesty and power of GOD. Now he designates the subject, and that is entirely ἀνεκδιήγητον καὶ ἀνεκφώνητον (inexplicable and unutterable). What is His name, and what is the name of His Son, if you know? He does not ask about just any name, but what fully expresses His nature: and he teaches that this is incomprehensible, partly by this proposed question of a matter inexplicable to us: What is His name? partly by a peculiar interrogation obtaining the force of a negative: If you know? i.e., you by no means know it: or let him come forward who knows and can explain it. For the particle כי here has the force of interrogating, as the preceding things teach, and it is evident from similar places, Job 22, v. 2, c. 31, v. 4, 5, Is. 36, v. 20. And thus the Chaldean, Vulgate Latin, etc. In which manner Damascenus rightly, lib. 1, de Orthod. Fid. cap. 16: The divine is incomprehensible to all and nameless: and Isidorus Pelusiota, lib. 1, Ep. 433. The divine nature is unnameable. And also Varinus: God is nameless and unsignifiable among men. But just as he says the name of this great artificer and governor of things is incomprehensible, so also the name of His Son. What is His name, and what is the name of His Son? By which words he most openly attributes a Son to the creator, preserver, and governor of all things, and teaches that the name and knowledge of Him likewise transcend the entire grasp of our reason by a very long way, and that the name, that is, His nature and attributes, cannot be sufficiently explained by anyone. He names the Son of GOD here peculiarly, not because the name of the Holy Spirit is not equally incomprehensible and ineffable: because these three are one, as John testifies, 1 Epist. 5, v. 7. But partly because he wished to designate here the Wisdom, which He had made the artificer and creator of all things with GOD the Father, in the commemoration of the infinite power and majesty of GOD, shining forth in the work of creation and the preservation of things: partly because His Parent had received a peculiar promise concerning the Son of GOD to be born from His seed, 2 Sam. 7, v. 14, and had published illustrious prophecies concerning His mission and redemption: partly because he was eager to express who that Ithiel and Uchal is, whom he had so called, namely, that He is the Son of GOD, of the same essence, power, and glory as GOD the Father. What of the fact that, with GOD the Father and the Son named, the Holy Spirit also, inasmuch as He is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son, and is breathed, is in the Father and the Son, and is of one essence with the Father and the Son, is comprehended: through whom Agur brought forth this prophecy, and who proposed these sublime, mystical, and most eminent questions through Agur, because holy men of GOD spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, 2 Pet. 1, v. 21. Not to mention that some warn that the inscrutable dispensation of the wind is at the same time an image of the secret progressions of the Holy Spirit, Job 3, v. 8. If anyone desires peculiar and parallel testimonies concerning the name of the Son of GOD being equally ineffable, let him compare Jud. 13, v. 8, where the uncreated Angel said His name was wonderful, hidden, incomprehensible, and Apoc. 19, v. 12: He has a name written, which no one knows but He Himself. Rightly, therefore, Cornel. a Lapide on this place: What is His name, etc. It is a riddle or enigma, i.e., tell me, you who esteem yourself wise and arrogate wisdom to yourself, what is the name of Him who, as I have said, created the heavens, the Spirit, the waters, and the earth, and in His own place has orderly established, regulates, and governs them? You will say His name is God. But what does this name God mean? Whose essence does it signify, what, of what kind, and how great is this essence of His? Certainly you cannot comprehend it. You must confess, therefore, that you do not comprehend the name of GOD, much less the name of His Son: whence he says: If you know. Thus Ignatius explains, Epist. ad Philipp., and August. Ep. 49, ad Deo grat., ad Qv. 8. And some even among the Jews acknowledge this sense: especially R. Moses Hadarsan, whose opinion is praised by Galatinus: There is for us a Father, old and an infant of old age; where is this said? It is written, who has ascended, etc. Father old is His name, and infant of old age is the name of His Son. Whence in this document it is permitted to observe mystically, as the blessed Lord D. Dorscheus notes in his Disputation on Psalm 2, verse 7, in his Pentad, §. 30: (1.) How most closely the name of God and of his Son is coupled by Agur. (2.) That both names, as much of the Son as of the Father, are ineffable and inexplicable, and thus do not fall under human knowledge and wisdom. (3.) That he professes the co-existence of both. (4.) He attributes to both omnipresence through the ascent into heaven and the descent. (5.) Omniscience, through the inscrutable dispensation of the wind. (6.) Omnipotence, through the wonderful binding of the waters. (7.) Creative and conservatory majesty through the establishment of the ends of the earth. Since indeed from the ineffable attributes the ineffability of both names is concluded. (8.) The ὁμοουσίαν of the Son of GOD with the Father, because he is of the same majesty, wisdom, power, and incomprehensible name. (9.) His personal διάκρισιν from the Father. (10.) His natural γέννησιν from the Father. (11.) The ἑνότητα of the adorable majesty with the Father. We add (12.) the equal necessity of the knowledge of the Son and of the Father in saving cognition. Whence how jejune and foreign here is the explanation of Mercerus, who wishes this to be the sense, that it is impossible that any man should be named or designated who might perform these heroic works, is manifest. That the name of him who performs these works—not heroic, but truly divine and of infinite power—cannot be named; that is, of GOD himself, nor of his Son, Agur testifies. Who of sound mind would attribute those divine works to man, or believe that they could be attributed? See more copiously on these matters the Blessed D. Myslenta, my colleague, compater, and brother in Christ, formerly most closely joined, in his Disputation on the Confession of Agur, Giessen, 1619, and in the fuller confession of Agur exhibited in two Disputations at Königsberg in 1622. We profess with a grateful mind that we have been not a little aided in this oracle by his learned examination.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

QVIS ASCENDIT IN COELVM?) Nempe homi- num, ut sc. audeat mutare Dei Leges. Quod sequentia ex- ponunt. Conf. Ef. 40, 12.

Non hæc tantum sibi quæstio illa vult, quod leges Dei sint immutabiles : Imo de legibus hic ni- hil. Quod enim vers. 6. habetur diversum jam est, neque de lege tantum Dei, sed de Verbo Dei in uni- versum accipiendum, nec solum in Verbo Dei quicquam mutari posse negat, sed Verbi Dei perfe- ctionem omnimodam, cui nec detrahi quicquam nec addi possit aut debeat, adstruit. At hic in describen- da incomprehensibili Dei majestate, virtute, ac quidditate occupatur. Quam ut eo magis evehat Agur, suam insipientiam in tam sublimibus myste- riis ultro profitetur. Simul autem nos revocat ad unicum & verum Spiritualis Sapientiæ principium, Verbum Dei, extra quod nihil in Spiritualibus nos sapere exemplo suo testatur. Quapropter procedit ab ἄρσει ad θέσιν, removetque falsum vel alienum principium, quod nempe fides sincera in Deum ve- rum, quam exigit, & salutis ratio, ac vitæ Spiritua- lis institutio ex ratione humana hauriri non possit: ponit geminum fidei principium, quod unice ê Verbo Dei oriatur, quod principium fidei genui- num esse Ps. 119,126. docet, quia purgatissimum omnis falsitatis & maculæ expers: efficacissimum, quia cly- peus vel scutum est omnibus in Deum confidentibus: & sufficientissimum, quia nullam additionem & de- tractionem admittit. Excludit ergo ab hoc axio- mate rationem humanam, siquidem natura hominis corrupta sit, quia factus sum בער rudis, bardus, ac stu- pidus, fatuus ac stultus, qui neque sapientia, neque mo- ribus pollet, ut Maimonides explicat, quo cæcitas mentis naturalis in rebus spiritualibus, & volunta- tis ac appetitus stolida ac bruta perversitas designa- tur Psalm. 49. vers. 21. 1. Corinth. 2. vers. 14. Ephes. 4. vers. 17. seqq. Addit מאיש quod non male B. Mys- lenta noster reddit, quam ut sim vir in rebus mysticis, qui aliquid in illis valeat, similibus exemplis id pro- bans Psalm. 49. vers. 3. 1. Sam. 2. v. 2. cap. 26. v. 15. Jer. 5. v. 1. ita ut simul intelligatur adjunctum sub- stantivum דעת חסידים scientia piorum, ut Exod. 4. vers. 18. 1. Samuel. 16. vers. 18. cap. 17. v. 34. Job. 11. vers. 2. 2. Sam. 13. vers. 3. cap. 18. vers. 20. Quod confirmat addita ulterior declaratio, à defectu intel- lectus humani ולא בינת אדם לי & intelligentia ho- minis non est mihi: ubi Junius & Tremellius intelli- gentiam primo homini divinitus inditam, antequam erubesceret, intelligunt. Id certum, quod intelli- gatur intelligentia homini necessaria ad perceptio- nem, & apprehensionem rerum spiritualium, nam sapientia rerum naturalium, & politicorum affatim instructus fuit Agur omnium hominum sapientissi- mus. R. Joseph Albus l 1. IKKARIM cap. 16. vocem

בינה, de scientia ex præmissis deducta accipit: unde denegabitur ita ratio per discursum intellectus hu- mani perveniendi ad salutis mysteria 1. Cor. 2. verf. 14. 2. Cor.3. verf. 5. Adhæc removet humanam institutionem in rebus fidei : Non didici Sapien- tiam: quam nullus Rabbi quantumcunque alias sapiens sit, per naturam, citra S. S. informationem, & illuminationem de rebus cœlestibus habere pot- est, nedum aliis tradere, quia Sapientia hæc sapien- tibus mundi quibusvis prorsus est abscondita 1.Cor. 2. verf. 8. unde θετικῶς exponunt hoc LXX. In- terpp. & cum iis Augustinus T. 1. Epist. 49. quæst. 51. Deus docuit me Sapientiam. Ulterius addit Agur ודעת קדשים אדע , quæ interrogative accipi- unt, ut interrogatio respondeat negativæ, Piscator, Junius & Tremellius : Et scientiam sanctorum sciam ? Chaldæus vero particulam negandi ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repe- tit h. m. Et non novi scientiam sanctorum: atque ita etiam exponunt R. Levi, R. Aben - Ezra, Vata- blus, B. Lutherus, quum id antecedentia omnino efflagitent. Quidam ita reddunt: Non didici Sa- pientiam (adeo) ut scientiam sanctorum sciam. Sed priores explicationes simpliciores sunt, & magis congruunt; quia mutuo sese illa omnia explicant, quæ hic cumulantur, ad declarandam uberius natu- ralem nostram ignorantiam, & stupiditatem in re- bus mysticis. Translationi vero Septuaginta In- terpp. affirmativæ locus non est καὶ γνῶσιν ἁγίων ἔγνωκα, utut similiter transtulerit Vulgatus, & no- vi scientiam sanctorum : Docetur ergo Sanctorum scientiam ita comparatam esse, ut nec à natura, nec cura hominis cujuspiam sibi relicti proficiscatur, sed ab uno Deo; quæ scientia cœlestis salvifica eti- am alias notitia Dei Proverb. 2. verf. 5. Esa. 11. verf. 9. notitia Messiæ cap. 53. verf. 11. notitia redemtoris dicitur Job. 19. verf. 25. & conjunctim Dei & Sal- vatoris notitia appellatur Johann. 17. verf. 3. ac in loco parallelo Proverb. 9. verf. 10. sanctorum scien- tia vocatur, quia scil. fidelium & sanctorum pro- pria est Joh. 17. verf. 19. Raimund. è R. Mos. Hadarsch. Deum nomine Sanctorum intelligit, ut vox hæc ob- jectum, non subjectum scientiæ notet.

Quæ omnia illustrat Salomo, exempli loco mysterium aliquod è Sapientia rerum supernatura- lium, & scientia Sanctorum, de incomprehensibili nempe majestate, potentia, & effentia Dei, ejusque æterni Filii adducens, non secus atque Christus Johann. 3. Nicodemum cum regenerationis my- sterium stolida ratione affequi, ut volebat, non posset, aliis sublimis Sapientiæ mysteriis ad simi- lem fidei ὑπακοὴν adduxit: Ideoque ut constet, quod se in exemplum proposuerit aliis, morta- lium sapientissimus, nunc omnibus in universum hominibus palam hanc sapientiam derogat, em- phaticis ac maxime penetrantibus quæstionibus, quibus nostra in Spiritualibus cæcitas & stoliditas πρὸς ὄμμα nemini non exhibetur: In quibus tum ad subjectum incomprehensibile, tum ad prædica- tum, opera nempe infinita, & incomprehensibilia, respiciendum. Hæc prius sistuntur hoc in loco, & quidem quatuor ζητήμασι: Quorum primum re- spicit cœlum, alterum ventos & aërem, tertium aquas, quartum terram: quæ inter opera Dei majestati- ca, si ab homine abeas, τῷ μικροκόσμῳ, maxime sunt admiranda in macrocosmo. De primo ita: Quis afcendit in cœlum & descendit ? Quod inepte Judæi in Pefikta & R. Salomo in glossa de Mose, qui ascendit in monte Sinai ad Deum, & inde descendit ad populum Exod. 19. & 32. accipiunt: quasi mons Sinai cœlum sit, aut Moses in cœlum adscendisse uspiam uspiam dicatur, quod negant ipsi Rabbini in Thal- mude Codice Sukka: Et Magister ipse dicit; in æ- ternum non descendit divinitas infra, & non ascen- derunt Moses & Elias in altum, prout dictum est: Cœli cœlorum sunt Domini, & terram dedit filiis hominum. Adde quod Eliæ & Mosis dispar ra- tio sit: ille enim in cœlum transumtus legitur, quod de hoc nuspiam habetur. Et quomodo no- men Mosis & filii ejus innominabile & incomprehen- sibile? Non minus inepta est glossa Enjedini Pho- tiniani, Ithiel & Uchal socios Aguris quæstiones ipsi proposuisse de cælestibus & meteoris, quibus his ver- bis respondeat, se ad quæstiones illas dissolvendas esse ineptum, tardum & stolidum; quia nec per se sa- piat, nec sapientiam didicerit, imo nullum morta- lium talia diserte explicare posse: Quis enim homi- num ascendit in cælum, & descendit, ut mysteria & arcana Dei norit? Undenam constat Ithiel & U- chal socios Aguris fuisse? unde, quod tales quæ- stiones ipsi proposuerint? Et quis virum sapien- tiæ laude insignem, tam ineptum & stolidum cre- det? Sapientiæ certe eum insignis fuisse, hæ ipsæ insignes & profundæ ejus parœmiæ convincunt. Non ergo arguendus, quod neque per se sapuerit, neque sapientiam didicerit. Tum vero pessime confunduntur mysteria & arcana Dei cum rebus naturalibus in cœlo, & meteoris. Neque enim opus est, ut in cœlum adscendamus, atque inde vicissim descendamus, ut res illas naturales cogno- scamus: de quibus multi egregie philosophati sunt, etsi cœlo delapsi non fuerint. Franciscus Junius, & Piscator in notis de rebus mysticis intelli- gunt, sed de motu locali explicant: non potest quis- quam cælos ascendere, ut cognoscat viam salutis no- stræ, & descendens ad nos afferat. Sed ita non co- hærebunt sequentia ζητήματα, quum prædicata ista de aliis hic ita negentur, ut soli Deo vindicen- tur, ideoque idem etiam hic fieri credendum. Unde Grotianam quoque glossam in spongiam in- cumbere oportet. Quæ enim erit συνέχεια: Quis hominum ascendit in cælum, ut audeat mutare leges Dei? Quis continuit ventum palmis suis &c. Ec- quid illa de ventorum comprehensione, maris col- lectione, terræ fundatione ad cognitionem volun- tatis Dei, vi cujus quis præsumere possit leges Dei mutare? Cartwrightus de voluntatis perversitate in- terpretatur, & uni Christo applicat ad v. 4. Jam de reliqua animæ impotentia agit, nempe voluntatis pervicacia, & à Deo aversione. Quæ quidem tanta est, ut quamvis homo veritatem intelligeret, tamen non magis illam exercere poterat, & factis, dictis, aut etiam cogitatis exprimere, quam corpore terrestri & ponderoso gravatus in cælum ascendere, aut si ibi esset, sine lapsu descendere: Quod solus Ithiel præstare potest, sicut etiam apertius docetur Joh. 3, 13. Hanc voluntatis ad salutem consequendum ἀδυναμίαν aliis comparationibus declarat: tam scil. hoc mortalibus im- possibile esse, quam ventum pugno comprehendere, &, ubi velis, emittere; & aquam in veste vincire, ut Deus nubibus superne, & arena inferne: quam omnes terræ plagas firmare. Hæc omnia Christus, qua Deus, facillime præstare potest Esa. 40, 12. 15. 16. 17. Nemi- ni autem mortalium hæc competere docet ab adjun- cto nomine, quia nomen ejus nondum auditum sit. Postea videtur esse prolepsis; cujus tacita occupatio est, forsan talis olim, qualem quæris, extitit, sed nunc è vivis excessit: Subjectio est: Ubi igitur est Filius ejus, quem sibi similem genuit? Sed uti hæc Christo convenire certum est, ita etiam Dei Patri tribuun- tur, & ad incomprehensibilem utriusque majesta- tem & potentiam captum animæ & mentis longe excedentem potius pertinent, quam ad voluntatis nostræ ἀδυναμίαν. S. Augustinus l. c. 2. de Ascen- sione Christi in cœlum, & descensu intelligit; Cui interpretationi id obstat, quod videantur omnia il- la quæsita vel prædicata æque de Deo Patre & Filio ejus ὁμοοσίῳ hic efferri, nisi forte tale discrimen in- ter ea constituendum, ut primum de Ithiele accipia- tur: Quis, nisi Ithiel, ascendit in cœlum & descen- dit? Cætera, opus creationis & conservationis Deo Patri & Filio commune concernentia seorsim pro- ponantur. Quo pacto tria hic documenta traden- tur: Mysterium de Christi ascensu & descensu: In- finita Dei vis in creatione & conservatione rerum, nec non mysterium de Deo Patre & ὁμοοσίῳ ejus Fi- lio. Sed rectius hæc omnia ad Deum Patrem & Fi- lium referuntur, ideoque per ascensum in cœlum & descensum omnipræsentiam divinam alii Dd. intelli- gunt, qua Deus cœlum & terram implet, ac sursum & deorsum præsens est Pf. 139, 8. Jerem. 23, 23. 25. ac ἀνθρωποπαθῶς & ratione manifestationis, & ope- rum ascendere dicitur in cœlum, & descendere, quia in cœlo & in terra præsens est: suamque præsentiam creatione & conservatione ibi probat. Unde etiam descendisse dicitur Deus Genes. 11, 7. cap. 18, 24. Ex. 3, 8. & ascendisse Genes. 17, 22. Conf. Deut. 33, 26. Am. 9, 6. Sic Lyranus, & alii per hunc Dei ascensum & descensum censent significari omnimodam Dei guber- nationem, qua tam supera, quam infera regit, & gubernat, q. d. ut Cornel. à Lapide in h. l. Solus Deus omniscius & omnipotens est, qui non mutatione loci (est enim ubique & immensus) sed sua sapientia & operatione, quasi ascendit in cœlum, & descendit, dum in creaturis cœlestibus, & sublunaribus, summis æque ac imis operatur, dum scil. sursum sapientissime cœlos constituit, ordinat, stellis ornat, movet, regit, guber- nat, ac deorsum in aëre, terra & in mari omnia ani- mata æque ac inanimata creat, pascit, conservat, fœ- cundat &c. Alludit ad Deut. 33, 26. Ascensor cœli auxiliator tuus: magnificentia ejus discurrunt nu- bes: habitaculum ejus sursum, & subter brachia sempiterna. Et ad illud Amos 9, 6. Qui ædificat in cœlo ascensionem suam. Hæc vero omnipræsentia Dei vere incomprehensibilis est humanæ rationi, adeo ut Averrhoës puerilem antiquorum cogitatio- nem pronunciarit, qui Deum omnibus rebus præsen- tem dixere. Sociniani etiam, imo Calviniani quoq; nonnulli, quia ratione assequi non valent divinam omnipræsentiam, penitus eandem negant. Conf. Job. 38, 32. Ef. 40, 12.

Alterum ζήτημα est: Quis colligit ventum in pugillis suis? Quod ridicule Judæi de favillis à Mose in camino acceptis intelligunt. Aliene Augustinus de animabus credentium in occulto loco contentis, aliique de Spiritibus creatis Angelis bonis & malis pugillis Dei conclusis explicant: Rectissime autem de vento accipitur. Quem non creat modo Deus Of. 13. vers. 15. Amos. 4. vers. 3. Rom. 4. vers. 8. Psal. 107. vers. 25. sed & moderatur pro arbitrio Exod. 14. vers. 21. Job. 38. vers. 24. Psalm. 104. v. 4. Ps. 147. vers. 18. Matth. 8. vers. 26. cap. 14. vers. 32. è thesau- ris suis depromit Psalm. 135. vers. 7. Jerem. 10. vers. 53. cap. 51. vers. 16. ac impellit Genes. 8. vers. 1. Exod. 10. vers. 19. Psalm. 78. vers. 26. ideoque pu- gillis suis concludere dicitur, quod ad nutum venti flent & jussa exequantur, aut quiescant. Quam ve- ro incomprehensibile hoc divinæ sapientiæ & po- tentiæ sit opus, loca allegata testantur. Conf. Eccles. 11, 5. seqq. Job. 3, 7.

Tertio quærit Agur: Quis congregavit aquas in vestimento? Quod iterum inepte Judæi de facto

Mosis in mari rubro miraculoso Exod. 14. & ἀπροσδιονύσως ac inconvenienter Augustinus de Baptismi effectu & induitione Christi e LXX. vi- rali, sed aliena interpretatione : Quis convertat aquas in vestimenta ? Insufficienter Junius de aquis inferioribus : Nostrates vero de aquis in univer- sum tam superioribus, quam inferioribus, tam in nubibus, quam maris alveo comprehensis rectis- sime interpretantur, quas ita cohibet Deus, ut ceu ligatas vestimento contineat. Nam & contignat superioribus aquis cœnacula sua Psal. 104. v. 3. & po- nit terminos aquis inferioribus, ne terram operiant Job. 38. v. 8. 9. 10. Psal. 104. v. 9. ipse ligat aquam in nubibus Job. 26. v. 7. & congregat aquas maris velut in acervum ponens in thesauris voragines Psal. 33. v. 7. Quæ ratione satis assequi & comprehendere nemo mortalium potest. Vid. imprimis Job. 37. v. 14. seqq. c. 38. v. 8. seqq. Es. 40. v. 12.

Quarta Quæstio est, Quis stabilivit omnes ter- minos terræ? Quam perverse de Tabernaculi ere- ctione Talmudici explicant, ac ἀσκόπως de appre- hensione & occupatione omnium finium terræ per præ- dicationem Evangelii Augustinus intelligit: neque convenienter satis Junius & Tremellius ita reddunt: quis stabilivit ullos terræ fines? Rectius Aben- Ezra & R. Levi : quis erexit omnes fines terræ, ne dimoveantur ? Quod de terminis terræ, tum qua majores ejus partes, tum qua regna quæque in iis- dem Nostri merito accipiunt. Similiter Job. 38. v. 5. quis disposuit mensuras, (terræ) aut quis extendit in ea regulam Esa. 40. v. 28. Quis creavit terminos terræ Actor. 17. v. 26. Fecit ex uno omne genus homi- num inhabitare super universam faciem terræ : de- finiens terminos habitationis eorum. Quod opus esse incomprehensibile divinæ potentiæ, DEUS ipse indicat: Job. 38. v. 5. Quis posuit mensuras ejus, si nosti. & vers. 18. Nunquid considerasti lati- tudinem terræ? indica mihi, si nosti omnia?

Hæc ergo de prædicatis operibus nempe in- finitæ majestatis & virtutis DEI. Jam subjectum designat, idque prorsus ἀνεκδιήγητον καὶ ἀνεκφώ- νητον. Quod est nomen ejus, & quod est nomen Fi- lii ejus, si nosti? Non de qualicunque nomine, sed quod plene exprimat naturam ejusdem, quæ- rit : idque incomprehensibile esse docet, partim quæstione hac proposita rei nobis inexplicabilis: Quod est nomen ejus? partim interrogatione pe- culiari vim negativæ obtinente? Si nosti? q. d. nequaquam illud scis : aut prodeat qui illud norit atque edisserat. Particulam enim כי hic vim in- terrogandi habere, præcedentia docent, & e locis similibus constat Job. 22. vers. 2. cap. 31. vers. 4. 5. Esa. 36. vers. 20. Atque ita Chald. Vulg. Latin. &c. Quo pacto Damascenus recte lib. 1. de Orthod. Fid. cap. 16. τὸ θεῖον ἀκατάληπτον πάντων καὶ ἀνώνυ- μον : & Isidorus Pelusiota lib. 1. Ep. 433. ἡ θεῖα Φύ- σις ἀκατονόμαστος. Nec non Varinus ἔστιν ὁ Θεὸς ἀνώνυμος, καὶ ἀσήμαντος παρ’ ἀνθρώποις. Ut autem nomen hujus tanti opificis & gubernatoris rerum incomprehensibile dicit, ita etiam nomen Filii ejus. Quod est nomen ejus, & quod est no- men Filii ejus? Quibus verbis apertissime rerum omnium creatori, conservatori, & gubernatori Filium tribuit, ejusdemque nomen & noti- tiam, pariter captum omnem rationis nostræ lon- gissime transcendere, nec a quoquam nomen, hoc est, naturam & attributa ejus satis explicari posse docet. Filium autem DEI hic peculiariter no- minat, non quod Spiritus S. nomen non sit æque incomprehensibile, & ineffabile: quia hi tres unum sunt, teste Johanne 1. Epist. 5. vers. 7. Sed partim quia Sapientiam, quam cum DEO Pa- tre artificem & opificem rerum omnium fecerat, hic designare, in infinitae virtutis & majestatis DEI, relucentis in opere creationis, & conserva- tionis rerum commemoratione voluit: Partim, quia de Filio DEI e semine ejus nascituro peculia- re promissum Parens ejus acceperat 2. Sam. 7. v. 14. ac vaticinia illustria de ejusdem missione & re- demtione ediderat: partim quia exprimere ge- stiit, quis ille Ithiel & Uchal sit, quem ita vocarat, quod nempe sit Filius DEI, ejusdem cum DEO Pa- tre essentiae, potentiae, ac gloriae. Quid, quod no- minato DEO Patre ac Filio Spiritus Sanctus quo- que, utpote qui Patris & Filii Spiritus est, a Patre & Filio procedit, & spiratur, in Patre ac Filio est, & unius cum Patre ac Filio est essentiae, compre- hendatur: per quem prophetiam hanc protulit Agur, & qui per Agurem haec sublimia, mystica & eminentissima ζητήματα proposuit, quia ὑπὸ πνέυμα[τος] ἁγίε φερόμενοι loquuti sint sancti DEI homines 2. Petr. 1. v. 21. Ut taceam, quod nonnulli moneant, quod venti inscrutabilis dispensatio ima- go simul sit arcanorum Spiritum S. progressuum Job. 3. v. 8. Peculiaria & parallela si quis desiderat de nomine Filii DEI aeque ineffabili testimonia, conferat Jud. 13. v. 8. ubi Angelus increatus no- men suum dixit mirabile, occultum, incomprehen- sibile, & Apoc. 19. v. 12. Habet nomen scriptum, quod nemo novit, nisi ipse. Recte ergo Cornel. a Lapide in hunc locum: Quod nomen est ejus &c. Est gryphus sive ænigma, q. d. dic mihi tu, qui te sa- pientem æstimas, & sapientiam tibi arrogas, quod est nomen ejus, qui uti dixi, cælos, Spiritum, aquas & terram creavit, suoque loco ordinate constituit, mode- ratur, & gubernat? Dices nomen ejus esse Deus. At quid sibi vult hoc nomen Deus? cujus essentiam signi- ficat, quæ, qualis & quanta est hæc ejus essentia? uti- que eam comprehendere nequis. Fateare ergo, te nomen DEI non comprehendere, multo minus no- men Filii ejus: unde ait: Si nosti. Sic explicat Ignatius Epist. ad Philipp. & August. Ep. 49. ad Deo grat. ad Qv. 8. Et agnoscunt hunc sensum nonnulli etiam e Judæis: cumprimis R. Moses Hadarsan, cujus hæc a Galatino laudatur sententia: Est no- bis Pater senex & infans senectutum, ubi hoc dici- tur? Scriptum est, quis ascendit &c. Pater senex est nomen ejus, & infans senectutum est nomen Fi- lius ejus. Unde in hoc documento mystice obser- vare licet, notante B. Dn. D. Dorscheo Disp. de Pfal. 2. v. 7. in Pentad. §. 30. (1.) Quam arctissime nomen Dei & Filii ejus ab Agure copuletur. (2.) Quod utrumque nomen tam Filii, quam Patris in- effabile & inexplicabile sit, adeoque non cadat sub scientiam & sapientiam humanam. (3.) Quod utriusque coexistentiam profiteatur. (4.) Utrique tribuat omnipræsentiam per ascensum in cœlum & descensum. (5.) Omnisapientiam, per inscrutabi- lem venti dispensationem. (6.) Omnipotentiam per colligationem aquarum mirabilem. (7.) Crea- toriam & conservatoriam majestatem per constitu- tionem terminorum terræ. Siquidem ex ineffa- bilibus attributis ineffabilitas nominis utriusque concludatur. (8.) Filii DEI cum Patre ὁμοε- σίαν, quia ejusdem est majestatis, sapientiæ, potentiæ, nominisque incomprehensibilis. (9.) Ejusdem personalem a Patre διάκρισιν. (10.) Na- turalem a Patre γέννησιν. (11.) Adorabilis cum Patre majestatis ἑνότητα. Addimus (12.) notitiæ Filii & Patris parilem in cognitione salvifica necessitatem. Unde quam jejuna & aliena hic sit Merceri ex- plicatio, qui hunc vult esse sensum, fieri non posse, ut nominetur ullus hominum aut designetur, qui he- roica hæc opera faciat, manifestum est. Nomina- ri non posse nomen illius, qui ista opera non he- roica, sed vere divina, & infinitæ virtutis faciat; hoc est, DEI ipsius, neque Filii ejus, Agur te- statur. Homini quis sanæ mentis illa divina ope- ra tribuat, aut tribui posse credat? Vid. de his copiosius B. D. Myslenta Collega, Compater & Frater in Christo quondam conjunctissimus, Disp. de Confess. Agur. Giessæ Anno 1619. & con- fessione Aguris pleniori Disputation. duabus Re- giomont. Anno 1622. exhibita. Cujus erudita ἐξετάσει non parum in hoc oraculo nos adjutos grata mente profitemur.

## 30:5
Verse 5. EVERY WORD OF GOD IS REFINED, A SHIELD TO THOSE WHO HOPE IN HIM.

In Hebrew, Every word of GOD is refined (as if by fire, צרופ, liquefied, repurified, pure, like pure silver, Psalm 12, verse 7; Psalm 119, verse 140; Proverbs 15, verse 4. Every impurity, every suspicion of falsehood, error, deceit, simulation, superfluity, and injustice is excluded from the word of GOD, which, like silver or gold repurified from dross and impurities, shines with every kind of purity and sustains every test in the fire of the cross and of any temptation) a shield itself (הוא לו אל GOD) to those who hope in him. Which whole sentence is found in the Davidic hymn, 1 Samuel 22, verse 31; Psalm 18, verse 31: and teaches that the mode of justification is primarily delivered in the word of GOD: inasmuch as it informs us concerning the manner of obtaining salvation: and for that cause it was revealed, 2. Timothy 3, verse 15, in which we are instructed concerning GOD and Christ the God-man, who is that Ithiel and Uchal, whom every one of the faithful ought to acknowledge and profess with true faith, My GOD, the Almighty, in Thee is justice and strength, Isaiah 45, verse 24, who is a shield and buckler, as he was to Abraham, the Father of all believers, Genesis 15, verse 1, by apprehending whom through faith he himself was justified, verse 6; Romans 4:18; so he is to every one of the faithful, that those hoping or confiding in him may be protected from the wrath of GOD, the curse of the law, the power of Satan, the sting of death, and eternal condemnation, and therefore obtain the remission of sins, justice, and eternal salvation. Compare what is said on Genesis 15, verse 1. Whence the purity, sincerity, holiness, and efficacy of Holy Scripture is made manifest.

Latin:

Vers. 5. OMNIS SERMO DEI IGNITUS, CLY- PEUS SPERANTIBUS IN SE.

In Ebr. Omnis sermo DEI purgatus (velut igne, צרופ liquatus, repurgatus, purus, sicut ar- gentum purum Psal. 12. vers. 7. Psal. 119. vers. 140. Proverb. 15. vers. 4. Excluditur omnis impuritas, omnis suspicio falsitatis, erroris, doli, simulationis, superfluitatis, injustitiæ, a verbo DEI, quod in- star argenti, vel auri a scoriis, & impuritatibus re- purgati omnimoda puritate fulget probamque omnem in igne crucis, & tentationis cujusvis su- stinet) Clypeus ipse (הוא לו אל DEUS) sperantibus in ipsum. Quæ tota sententia in hymno Davidico 1. Sam. 22. v. 31. Psal. 18. v. 31. reperitur : & mo- dum justificationis imprimis in verbo DEI tradi docet: utpote quod nos de ratione consequendi salutem informat: ejusque causa revelatum est, 2. Tim. 3. vers. 15. in quo de DEO & Christo θεαν- θρώπῳ, qui Ithiel & Uchal ille est, instruimur, utpote quem quisque fidelium agnoscere, & pro- fiteri vera fide debet, DEUS meus, ὁ παντοκρά- τωρ, in Te justitia, & virtus mihi Esa. 45. v. 24. qui scutum & clypeus uti Abrahæ Patri omnium credentium Gen. 15. vers. 1. quem per fidem ap- prehendendo ipse justificatus est vers. 6. Rom. 4, 18. ita fidelium cuique est, ut sperantes vel confidentes in ipsum protegantur ab ira DEI, maledictione legis, potestate Satanæ, aculeo mortis, & con- demnatione æterna, ideoque remissionem pec- catorum, justitiam, & salutem æternam con- sequantur. Conf. quæ ad Genes. 15. vers. 1. dicta. Unde Scripturæ S. puritas, sinceritas, sanctitas & efficacitas patescit.

## 30:6
Verse 6. DO NOT ADD ANYTHING TO HIS WORDS) He adds, who does otherwise than GOD commands, as stated at Deuteronomy 24, verse 2.
