These things are for the sake of the Papists, who deny the sufficiency and perfection of Holy Scripture, who, when they see this and similar sayings of Scripture standing against them—teaching that nothing is to be added to Scripture, nothing to be taken away or detracted—that is, asserting the perfection of Scripture with a loud voice, they attempt to elide it with a pseudo-interpretation not unlike this: namely, that it is prohibited to add contrary and repugnant things, but not diverse ones, or those which make for the explanation of Scripture. At Deuteronomy 24, verse 2, nothing is annotated concerning this matter: nor is anything held there that makes for this. But Grotius made his exception for the Papists at Deuteronomy 4, verse 8, which is discussed in the Elenctic annotation at the same place. To add to the words of someone, as anyone perceives from the sound of the words, is not to do otherwise than the words command, but to add something over and above to the words, whether they be preceptive or didactic, or of any kind, and to vend this addition as the words of another. Just as it is one thing to perform and execute the words of someone, for example a Prince, which has a place at least in the words of a mandate, not in the words of a promise, or others which do not have the force of a precept: it is another thing to receive and reverently hold the words of some Prince, as they are proposed to us by him, or to acknowledge them as the words of the Prince, and thus to change nothing in them, or to admit that it be changed, lest anything be derogated or detracted from them, or something be added or appended over and above, which is diverse from them: so also it is far different to add something to the words of GOD, the Lord of Lords, and to do otherwise than GOD commands. Not only is the diploma of a King or some prince vitiated when something is added to it by another by private authority, even if he who adds it does not do so in order that it might be contrary in any respect to the diploma of the King or to the contents therein, but acts with the end that he might explain and interpret it, or if he adds something entirely of his own which is not contained in the diploma but is diverse from it, and protests that he adds it without prejudice to the authority of that diploma. The diploma is vitiated by that very fact, and the crime of forgery is committed, because that which is not part of the diploma and did not proceed from the King is vended as part of the diploma and as the King's word. And when a diploma is issued and promulgated in such a way that it is expressly cautioned and prohibited therein that nothing be added by any authority, not only is vitiation committed, but also a violation and transgression by him who adds something. Which the Swedish Ambassador could not have been ignorant of. For he would not have borne it with impunity if he had dared such things, even though he was an Ambassador, by private authority—that is, unless it had been openly granted to him by the King. Nor could he show by any parallel place in the Scriptures that to add, even when the discourse is about precepts, signifies to do otherwise than is commanded. For an addition is not made through repugnant and contrary things, or when something is performed otherwise: but when that which is commanded is performed, and something else is performed over and above that which is commanded. But when something repugnant to the word is done, or otherwise than is commanded, that is not an addition or a fulfillment of the precept, but the precept is derogated from, and thus, as far as lies in him, it is taken away by him who does otherwise, insofar as it is derogated from. While therefore Scripture teaches that nothing is to be added to the Word of GOD, it testifies that it is sufficient, and has need of no supplement or addition, and also bears or admits no πρόσθεσιν. Which is an argument for the perfection of Scripture, for the sake of designating which it is also forbidden elsewhere, that nothing be taken away from the Word of GOD Deut. 4. v. 2. chap. 12. v. 32. inasmuch as that is held to be perfect, to which nothing can be added, nothing taken away. Here indeed only addition is expressly prohibited, concerning which Mercerus says: He does not mention subtraction: because men are more prone to add under the guise of interpretation. It is certain therefore, that the perfection of the Word of GOD is celebrated here: which the preceding and following context also confirms. For the Word of GOD is said to be ignited, or smelted and purified by fire, after the manner of gold and silver smelted and refined in a furnace, as Mercerus observes; whence that Parisian Professor concludes: Therefore we must rely simply on the Word of God, and it behooves us to be content with that knowledge which we can have from it. Cornelius a Lapide has it thus: The Word of God is ignited, that is, smelted, clarified, and pure, for this is what the Hebrew tserupha and the Greek πεπυρωμένοι signify. Whence Symmachus and St. Jerome Ps. 17, 31. translate: The Word of God is proven. For he alludes to chemical vessels, by which gold and silver are purified by fire by smelting out the dross, so that they may become pure and shining. For this is what tserupha signifies. Whence Sarepta was named the city of the Sidonians, because in it there were frequent smelting workshops for smelting metals. The meaning therefore is, as if to say: The words of GOD, that is to say, both the precepts and the promises of GOD, are so true, pure, sincere, and certain, just as if they were gold melted in the fire, refined, and purged from all dross. For in a similar way, or rather far more, the words of God are refined and pure from all contagion, not only of falsehood, fraud, and simulation, but also of vanity and superfluity, so that there is nothing that is lacking in or abounds in the divine utterances, nothing that can be criticized, and therefore it follows: Do not add anything to His words, lest you be reproved. Whence also the Law of God is called immaculate, in Greek ᾱμωμος, that is, irreprehensible; in Hebrew תמימה Themima, that is, integral, blameless, perfect, Psalm 18, v. 8. Cornelius therefore acknowledges that by this epithet the perfection of the word of God is also designated, to which nothing is lacking, nor does anything abound.

What is added, He is a shield to all who hope in Him, Solomon also understands of the Word of GOD: Every word, he says, of divine authority is therefore called an ignited shield, because it both expands the hearts of the elect, who place their hope in GOD, with the fire of charity, and illuminates them with the knowledge of truth, and consumes and purges the filth of vices which it finds in them, and defends them from the snares of enemies and all adversities. Although these words speak of GOD, and the pronoun הוּא refers itself to the name אלוה GOD, as also the suffix in the word בו in Him, not to אמרת the word (since this word is of the feminine gender), it is nevertheless manifest that God, insofar as He has revealed Himself in His word, is regarded, and therefore this is inserted into the purity and perfection of the Word, that the sum of the Word of GOD is situated in it, that it is handed down sincerely and perfectly in the word of GOD, how one must confide in GOD, and that, and how, GOD is a shield to those who hope in Him, and that the power and efficacy of the Word shines in it, so that that faith in GOD and the protection of the promises of faith against spiritual enemies may be obtained. Faith and the Word are related. Since therefore this effect is ascribed to faith, that GOD is to us מגן a buckler and a shield, just as He was a buckler and a shield to Abraham, who believed this Word of GOD, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, Gen. 15, v. 1; and faith apprehends the word, and on our part performs ληπτικω̃ς (receptively) what the Word performs on God's part δοτικω̃ς (donatively), by way of an instrumental cause; it is rightly said that the efficacy of the Word is here simultaneously regarded and insinuated, and Cornelius a Lapide also acknowledges this: It could, however, also be referred to the word of GOD: For this is a shield to man against all temptations: Both because the promise of GOD, especially of life and eternal glory, animates the faithful to repel bravely all the temptations of the world, the flesh, and the Devil: And because the precepts of GOD instill the fear of Him into minds, which dispels all the insults of enemies. Thus Christ, tempted by the Devil, opposed to him the shield of the word of God, saying: It is written: man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of GOD, Matt. 4. S. Paul did the same, as S. Jerome testifies in his life, and other saints. This is what S. Paul says: In all things taking up the shield of faith, in which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one, Eph. 6, v. 16. Because the Word of GOD performs these things sufficiently, there will be no doubt that Papists derogate from the sufficiency and perfection of the same, which we attribute to it.

As for the words which follow in our text, lest you be reproved and found a liar; Cornelius a Lapide indeed thinks that Solomon is explaining himself by them, namely that nothing can be added which opposes or derogates from the Words of GOD: For since the word of GOD is most true, whoever adds anything repugnant to it, it is necessary that he speaks falsely and lies: But that is not a true addition, when someone opposes the word: Then something is rather taken away and derogated from the Word and the truth of the word, when something is added to the Word of GOD, and is sold for the Word of GOD, which is not the word of GOD, as was done by the Pseudo-prophets: and there is no doubt that such are found to be liars, and are reproved by GOD as false speakers, and are noted and refuted by this aphorism. He who adds something, as if from the text, says Alphonsus. Tostatus in Deut. 4, v. 1, 2, either necessary, like other things which are in the text, as if said by the Holy Spirit, this is called PROPERLY TO ADD, and those who do such things incur eternal death. Which Cornelius also had to admit: Again, he says, nothing can be added to them, as if said by GOD, so that you sell your word as the Word of GOD, as the Scribes and Pharisees once did, selling useless traditions, and those contrary to the law of GOD, for the word of GOD, and now heretics do, who vitiate and corrupt heretical words with exposition, while they foist their own dreams and deliriums as the Word of GOD, who therefore will be judged and condemned by God as forgers of Holy Scripture (Jesuits must apply this to themselves, and to their own, no less than to other heretics). For as S. Chrysostom says, hom. 20 in Matt., Do not add to the words of GOD, etc. but he who has dared to do this thinks himself wiser than GOD, and begins to be a false witness, because he says that which neither ear has heard, nor eye has seen. Let the same therefore also be said to the Roman Pontiff, who adds to Holy Scripture traditions and definitions, which he sells as the Word of GOD, and defines that they are to be received with an equal affection of piety, which, however, neither ear has heard from God, nor eye has seen. No one who does not doubt that Holy Scripture is the Word of GOD can doubt that the words of Solomon are to be understood of Holy Scripture; therefore, as being the word of God, nothing is to be added to it. But those things which are sold by the Roman Pontiff besides Scripture as the Word of God, Papists will demonstrate to be the Word of God at the Greek Calends. Since therefore they add them to Scripture, they are reproved by God, and are found to be liars. Cornelius a Lapide rightly paraphrases our words entirely thus: Add nothing to his words, that is to say, one must insist upon the divine words because he who turns away from them wanders into lies: because they themselves are true, pure, polished, and perfect, so that nothing can be added to them or taken away. The words of God, says Procopius, since they exist full and perfect, admit no addition.

Latin:

Vers. 6. NE ADDAS QVICQVAM VERBIS ILLIVS) Addit, qui aliter, quam DEVS imperat, facit, ut dictum ad Deut. 24. v. 2.

Hæc in gratiam Pontificiorum, sufficientiam & perfectionem Scripturæ Sacræ negantium, qui quum videant hoc, & similia Scripturæ dicta sibi obsta- re, Scripturæ nihil addendum, nihil adimendum vel detrahendum esse docentia, hoc est, sonora voce Scripturæ perfectionem adserentia, ψευ- δερμηνείᾳ non absimili ea elidere conantur, adde- re nempe contraria & repugnantia prohibitum esse, non autem diversa, aut ea, quæ ad explicationem Scripturæ faciant. Ad Deut. 24. v. 2. nihil hac de re annotatum : nec quicquam ibi habetur, quod huc faciat. Ad Deuteron. 4. vers. 8. vero Papistarum exceptionem suam fecit Grotius, quæ ad eundem locum annotatione Elenctica discussa. Addere verbis alicujus, ut quivis e sono verborum percipit, non est facere secus, quam verba imperant, sed verbis sive præceptiva sint, sive didactica, seu cujusque generis, ali- quid insuper adjicere, atque hoc additamentum pro verbis alterius venditare. Ut aliud est verba alicujus v. g. Principis præstare & exequi, quod sal- tim in verbis mandati locum habet, non in ver- bis promissi, aut aliis, quæ vim præcepti non ha- bent: aliud est verba Principis alicujus, prout ab ipso nobis proponuntur, suscipere ac reverenter habe- re, vel agnoscere pro verbis Principis, adeoque nihil in illis immutare, aut ut immutetur, admittere, ne quid ipsis derogetur vel detrahatur, aut insuper adjiciatur, vel addatur, quod ab ipsis diversum sit: Sic etiam longe diversa sunt, addere quid verbis DEI, Domini Dominantium, & aliter facere, quam DEUS imperat. Non vitiatur tan- tum diploma Regis, aut principis alicujus, cum ab alio aliquid eidem adjicitur privata auctorita- te, etsi qui adjicit, id non faciat, ut contrarietur ulla in re diplomati Regis, vel contentis in eodem, sed eo fine id agat, ut id explicet, ac interprete- tur, aut si aliquid omnino de suo addat, quod in diplomate non contineatur, sed diversum sit ab eodem, salva auctoritate diplomatis istius, se id adjicere protestetur. Diploma eo ipso vitia- tur, ac crimen falsi committitur, quod pro parte diplomatis, & verbo Regio venditetur, quod pars diplomatis non est, neque a Rege profectum est. Et cum diploma ita editum ac promulgatum, ut diferte insuper eodem cautum ac prohibitum sit, ne quid addatur ulla auctoritate, non vitiatio tan- tum, sed violatio etiam ac transgressio committi- tur ab eo, qui aliquid addit. Quod Legatus Suedicus ignorare non potuit. Neque enim im- pune tulisset, si talia, etsi Legatus fuerit, pri- vata auctoritate, hoc est, nisi a Rege id aperte ipsi concessum, ausus fuisset. Neque ullo e Scripturis parallelo loco ostendere potuit, adde- re, etiam cum de præceptis sermo est, significare aliter facere, quam præcipitur. Additio enim non fit per repugnantia, & contraria: aut cum aliter quid peragitur: Sed cum id præstatur, quod man- datum est, & aliud insuper præter id, quod manda- tum est, peragitur. Gum vero aliquid repugnans verbo fit, aut secus, quam præceptum est, non ea additio, aut impletio est præcepti, sed dero- gatur tum eidem, adeoque tollitur ab eo, qui ali- ter facit, quantum in ipso est, præceptum, in quan- tum scil. eidem derogatur. Dum ergo Verbo DEI nihil addendum esse Scriptura docet, id suf- ficiens esse, nulloque auctario vel additamento opus habere, nullam etiam πρόσθεσιν ferre, vel admittere testatur. Quod est argumentum per- fectionis Scripturæ, cujus designandæ causa alias etiam vetatur, ne quid Verbo DEI dematur Deut. 4. v. 2. cap. 12. v. 32. siquidem id pro perfecto ha- beatur, cui nihil addi, nihil demi potest. Hic vero solum additio expresse prohibetur, quo de Mercerus inquit: Detractionis non meminit: quod homines ad addendum procliviores sint sub specie in- terpretationis. Certum ergo, hic celebrari perfe- ctionem Verbi DEI: quam etiam antecedentia & consequentia firmant. Nam Verbum DEI dici- tur ignitum, vel igne conflatum & purgatum, auri & argenti in fornace conflati & excocti more, ut ob- servat Mercerus; unde concludit Parisiensis ille Professor: Verbo ergo Dei nitendum simpliciter, & contentos nos esse oportet ea notitia, quam ex eo habere possumus. Cornelius a Lapide ita habet: Sermo Dei ignitus, id est, conflatus, defæcatus, & purus, hoc enim significat Ebr. tserupha & Græcum πεπυρωμένοι. Unde Symmachus & S. Hieronymus Ps. 17, 31. vertunt: Sermo Dei probatus. Alludit enim ad vasa Chymi- ca, quibus per ignem aurum & argentum a scoria ex- coquendo purgantur, ut fiant pura & nitida. Hoc enim significat tserupha. Unde Sarepta dicta est urbs Sidoniorum, quod in ea frequentes essent offici- ne conflatoriæ ad conflandum metalla. Sensus ergo est, q. d. Verba DEI, puta tam præcepta, quam pro- missa DEI, adeo sunt vera, pura, sincera, certa, per- inde ac si essent aurum igne colliquatum, conflatum, & ab omni fæce expurgatum. Simili enim modo, imo longe magis verba Dei sunt defecata, & pura ab omni contagione non tantum falsitatis, fraudis & simulatio- nis, sed & vanitatis ac superfluitatis, ut nihil sit, quod eloquiis divinis desit, aut abundet, nihil quod reprehendi possit, ideoque sequitur: Ne addas quid- quam verbis illius, & arguaris. Unde & Lex Dei vocatur immaculata, Græce ᾱμωμος, id est, irre- prehensibilis; Hebr. תמימה Themima, id est, In- tegra, inculpata, perfecta Psal. 18. v. 8. Agnoscit ergo Cornelius, hoc epitheto etiam perfectionem verbi Dei designari, cui nihil desit, aut abundet.

Quod additur, Clypeus est omnibus speranti- bus in se, de Verbo DEI etiam intelligit Salo- mo: Omnis sermo, inquit, divinæ auctoritatis, idcirco ignitus Clypeus dicitur, quia corda electo- rum, qui spem suam in DEO ponunt, & igne cari- tatis extendit, & scientia veritatis illuminat, & sordes vitiorum, quas in eis reperit, consumit & purgat, ac ab insidiis hostium cunctisque defendit ad- versitatibus. Quanquam vero verba hæc de DEO loquantur, ac pronomen הוּא ad nomen אלוה DEUS sese referat, ut & suffixum in voce בו in eo, non ad אמרת sermonem (quum hæc vox fœminini generis sit) manifestum tamen est, Deum quatenus in verbo suo sese revelavit, respi- ci, atque ideo Verbi puritati & perfectioni hoc interseri, quod in eo summa Verbi DEI sita sit, quod verbo DEI hoc sincere, & perfecte traditum sit, quomodo in DEO confidendum, & quod, ac quomodo DEUS Clypeus sit sperantibus in se, quod- que fulgeat in eo vis & efficacia Verbi, quod fi- des illa in DEUM, & promissa fidei protectio adversus hostes spirituales obtineatur. Fides & Verbum relata sunt. Quum ergo fidei adscriba- tur hic effectus, quod DEUS nobis מגן scutum & Clypeus sit, quemadmodum Abrahamo, qui huic DEI Verbo credidit, ac imputatum id ei ad justitiam est, Scutum & Clypeus fuit Gen. 15. v. 1. fides autem apprehendat verbum, & ex parte no- stra præstet ληπτικω̃ς, quod Verbum ex parte Dei præstat δοτικω̃ς, per modum causæ instrumentalis; efficaciam Verbi simul hic respici ac insinuari re- cte dicitur, atque id agnoscit etiam Cornel. a La- pide: Posset tamen quoque ad sermonem DEI refer- ri: Hic enim est Clypeus homini contra omnes ten- tationes: Tum quia promissio DEI, præsertim vitæ & gloriæ æternæ, animat fideles ad omnia tentamen- ta mundi, carnis & Diaboli fortiter repellenda: Tum quia præcepta DEI timorem ejus mentibus induunt, qui omnes hostium insultus dispellit. Sic Christus tentatus a Diabolo objecit ei clypeum sermonem Dei, dicens: Scriptum est: non in solo pane vivit ho- mo, sed in omni verbo, quod procedit de ore DEI Matth. 4. Idem fecit S. Paula, teste S. Hierony- mo in ejus vita, cæterique sancti. Hoc est, quod ait S. Paulus: In omnibus sumentes scutum fidei, in quo possitis omnia tela nequissimi ingnea extin- guere Ephes. 6. v. 16. Hæc ergo quia sufficienter præstat Verbum DEI, de sufficientia & perfectione ejusdem, quam ipsi tribuimus, Papistæ derogant, dubitandum non erit.

Quod ad verba, quæ sequuntur in nostro tex- tu, ne arguaris inveniarisque mendax; Putat qui- dem Cornel. a Lapide illis se explicare Salomo- nem, quod nempe nihil addi possit, quod Verbis DEI repugnet vel deroget: Cum enim verbum DEI sit verissimum, quicunque illi addit aliquid repugnans, necesse est, ut falsum dicat & mentiatur : Sed illa non est vera additio, cum quis verbo contraria- tur : Tum adimitur enim ac derogatur potius ali- quid Verbo ac veritati verbi , cum Verbo DEI aliquid adjicitur, & pro Verbo DEI venditatur, quod verbum DEI non est, uti a Pseudoprophe- tis fiebat: nullumque dubium est, tales mendaces inveniri, & increpari a DEO ceu falsiloquos, atque hoc aphorismo notari ac redargui. Qui ad- dit aliquid, tanquam de textu, ait Alphons. Tosta- tus in Deut. 4. v. 1. 2. vel necessarium, sicut alia, quæ sunt in textu, velut dictum a Spiritu S. hoc vocatur PROPRIE ADDERE, & qui ta- lia agunt, mortem æternam incurrunt. Quod fa- teri etiam oportuit Cornelium : Rursum, inquit, nihil eis addi potest, quasi dictum a DEO, ut vendi- tes verbum tuum esse Verbum DEI, uti faciebant olim Scribæ & Pharisæi traditiones inutiles, & legi DEI contrarias pro verbo DEI venditantes, & nunc faciunt hæretici, qui verba hæretica exposi- tione vitiant & corrumpunt, dum sua somnia & deliria obtrudunt pro Verbo DEI, qui proinde vel- ut falsarii S. Scripturæ a Deo judicabuntur & da- mnabuntur (id sibi applicare debent Jesuitæ, & suis, non minus quam aliis hæreticis) Nam ut ait S. Chrysostomus hom. 20. in Matth. Non ad- das verbis DEI &c. qui autem hoc ausus fuerit, se sapientiorem esse putat, quam DEUM, & incipit esse falsus testis, quia illud dicit, quod nec auris audivit, nec oculus vidit. Idem ergo etiam dictum sit Romano Pontifici, Scripturæ S. addenti traditiones & definitiones, quas pro Ver- bo DEI venditat, parique pietatis affečtu susci- piendas definit, quas vero nec auris audivit a Deo, nec oculus vidit. De Scriptura S. verba Salo- monis intelligenda esse nemo ambigere potest, qui eam Verbum DEI esse non dubitat, illi ergo ut- pote Dei verbo nihil addendum. Ea autem quæ a Pontifice Romano præter Scripturam pro Verbo Dei venditantur, Verbum Dei esse ad Calendas Græcas demonstrabunt Papicolæ. Cum ergo ea addunt Scripturæ, arguuntur a Deo, ac mendaces inveniuntur. Rečte omnino Cornel. a Lapide verba nostra ita παραφράζει : Ne addas quicquam verbis illius, q. d. ideo verbis divinis insistendum est, quia qui ab illis deflectit, in mendacia deerrat : quia ipsa vera, pura, tornata perfecta que sunt, ut nihil addi illis, aut demi possit. Verba Dei, ait Procopius, cum plena & perfecta existant, nullum auctarium admittunt.

## 30:7
Vers. 7. TWO THINGS HAVE I ASKED OF THEE, DENY ME NOT, BEFORE I DIE.

There follows the daily prayer of Solomon for goods both spiritual, or pertaining to the spiritual life, and corporal, pertaining to the animal life. Two things I have asked (with a humble and confident mind, with true devotion or in spirit and truth, John 4:24) that you do not forbid (or withhold from me, do not deny me) before I die, (that is, until I die, while I live: for these things must be prayed for from God throughout one's whole life.) The first is: Remove far from me vanity and lies: that is, preserve me from false doctrine, and keep me in the truth of Thy Word, by meiosis: for the affirmative sense is contained in the negative: the granting of the purity of the word of GOD, of that ignited or refined speech, and the removal or distancing from us of those things which in religion are alien to the same, or contrary to the same, of false dogmas. שָׁוְא denotes vanity, and that which is not such as it seems, or which is false, and heretical, or idolatrous, Lam. 2:14, Ez. 12:24, ch. 21:34, which is declared by way of explanation, by the word of falsehood: or if that refers to idolatry, because idols are mere vanities, it will be permissible to accept this concerning any erroneous dogma whatsoever. Cf. Ez. 13. v. 6. seqq. Job. 17. v. 17. The second thing requested is that by which he first prays against both deficiency and excess in temporal matters, 'Give me neither poverty nor riches': רֵישׁ denotes poverty, by which one does not have the means to support himself and his own honestly: chap. 6. vers. 11. chap. 10. v. 15. chap. 13. v. 18. c. 24. v. 34. עֹשֶׁר riches, or an abundance of wealth, which exceeds the status or condition of the possessor, distracts into various things, induces luxury and wicked confidence, and draws one away from the kingdom of GOD. Psal. 62. vers. 11. Matth. 19. v. 27. 28. Luc. 12. v. 19. seqq. Solomon was indeed the richest of all, and by the strength of the promise 1. Reg. 3. v. 13. he had no need to fear poverty, but because fortune wanders unsteadily, 'He is suddenly an Irus, who was just now a Croesus,' which he had learned from the example of his own exiled father, and there is altogether need for prayers so that we may possess divine promises, therefore he himself also deservedly prayed against poverty, and taught us by his example to pray against the same. Then Solomon prays, and seeks the necessary and convenient sustenance of life: 'FEED ME WITH FOOD CONVENIENT FOR ME.' טָרַף means he tore in pieces, he snatched, and it occurs concerning wild beasts which thus provide for their hunger and that of their cubs, whence he asks that GOD may provide for him as for a helpless cub, and tear and distribute as much as is needed, לֶחֶם חֻקִּי the bread of my statute or my ration. Thus he calls food (for bread in general denotes food, chap. 27. v. 27.) which suffices for sustenance, as if GOD assigns to each his own ration, just as the ration of manna was granted to each one Exod. 16. v. 4. Cf. cap. 8. v. 29. cap. 31. vers. 15. The bread of necessity or indigence is called by the Syrian Interpreter, Matth. 6. v. 11. But it is not to be thought with the Socinians that riches are forbidden, which they nevertheless restrict to the New Testament: because just as Solomon here prays against riches in a qualified sense, which the added words teach, namely, lest being full he deny God by placing confidence in wealth, so the condition of both times under the Old and New Testaments regarding the possession of riches is the same, with no diversity: which we can possess piously and justly, provided that when acquired by legitimate means we do not hold them as an idol, Matth. 6. vers. 24. nor pride ourselves in them, or trust in them 1. Tim. 6. vers. 12. or set our heart upon them Psal. 62. v. 11. but apply and reserve them for the private necessity of ourselves, our neighbor, and especially our own, or even the public necessity of the Church or the Republic, which was done by Solomon: therefore Paul does not command to cast away riches, but teaches how they are to be used 1. Tim. 6. v. 17. 'LEST I BE FULL AND DENY (in Heb. lest I be satisfied with food and wealth, and deny) AND SAY, WHO IS THE LORD?' Cf. Deut. 31. v. 20. c. 32. v. 15. Neh. 9. v. 25. 26. Os. 13. v. 6. Es. 59. v. 13. For there usually follows opulence of mind and pride, confidence in wealth, contempt of God, luxury, security, nay even atheism, Ex. 5. v. 2. 'OR LEST I BE POOR AND STEAL, AND TAKE THE NAME OF MY GOD IN VAIN.' In Heb. & I take (in vain) the name of my God, which happens not only by perjuring, but also by cursing, imprecating, blaspheming, apostasy from the faith and other ways, whence our German version is to be preferred here, as it comprehends everything under a general name. For the consequences of poverty are usually, by the fault of corrupt nature, partly theft and the handling of another's property against the second table, partly the abuse and handling of the divine name against the first table of the divine law.

Latin:

Vers. 7. DUO ROGAVI TE, NE DENEGES MIHI, ANTEQVAM MORIAR.

Sequitur oratio Salomonis quotidiana pro bo- nis tum spiritualibus vel ad vitam spiritualem, tum corporalibus, ad vitam animalem pertinentibus. Duo postulavi (mente humili & fiduciali, vera de- votione vel in spiritu & veritate Joh. 4. v. 24.) ne prohibeas (vel subtrahas a me, ne deneges mihi) antequam moriar, (id est, donec moriar, dum vivo: per totam enim vitam hæc exoranda sunt a Deo.) Primum est : Vanitatem & verbum mendacii longe fac a me: id est, præserva me a falsa dočtrina, & in veritate Verbi tui me conserva, per μείωσιν: nam sensus affirmativus in negativo continetur: puritatis verbi DEI, sermonis illius igniti, vel repurgati concessio, & eorum, quæ in religione ab eodem aliena sunt, aut contraria eidem, falso- rum dogmatum remotio, vel elongatio a nobis. שָׁוְא vanitatem notat, & id, quod tale non est, qua- le videtur, vel quod falsum est, & hæreticum, vel idololatricum Thren. 2. v. 14. Ez. 12. v. 24. c. 21. v. 34. quod κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν declaratur, per verbum men- dacii: aut si illud idololatriam respiciat, quia meræ vanitates sunt idola, hoc de erroneo quo- vis dogmate accipere licebit. Conf. Ez. 13. v. 6. seqq. Job. 17. v. 17. Alterum petitum est, quo primum deprecatur in temporalibus tum defectum tum excessum, Men- dacitatem & divitias ne dederis mihi: ראשׁ pau- pertatem, qua quis non habet unde se & suos ho- neste sustentet, notat: cap. 6. vers. 11. cap. 10. v. 15. cap. 13. v. 18. c. 24. v. 34. עשׁר divitias, vel ab- undantiam opum, quæ statum aut conditionem possessoris excedunt, in varia distrahunt, ad lu- xum & pravam confidentiam inducunt, & a re- gno DEI abstrahunt Psal. 62. vers. 11. Matth. 19. v. 27. 28. Luc. 12. v. 19. seqq. Erat quidem Salo- mo omnium ditissimus, & vi promissionis 1. Reg. 3. v. 13. paupertatem metuere non habebat, sed quia fortuna volubilis errat, Irus & est subito, qui modo Cræsus erat, quod exemplo Patris sui exulis edoctus erat, & precibus omnino opus est, ut promissis divinis potiamur, ideo & ipse pauper- tatem merito deprecatus est, & nos exemplo suo eandem deprecari docuit. Deinde preca- tur Salomo, & expetit necessariam & convenien- tem vitæ sustentationem: TRIBUE TANTUM MIHI NECESSARIA. טרף est discerpsit, ra- puit, & de feris quæ sic fami suæ & catulorum suorum consulunt, occurrit, unde rogat, ut DEUS sibi tanquam imbelli catulo prospiciat, & quantum opus, discerpat, ac distribuat לחם חקי panem statuti aut demensi mei. Sic vocat cibum (panis enim in genere cibum notat, cap. 27. v. 27.) qui sustentationi sufficiat, quasi DEUS cuique suum demensum assignet, uti demensum de manna cuilibet concessum Exod. 16. v. 4. Conf. cap. 8. v. 29. cap. 31. vers. 15. Panis necessitatis vel indigentiæ a Syro Interpr. vocatur, Matth. 6. v. 11. Non autem cum Socinianis existimandum prohibitas esse di- vitias, quod tamen illi ad Nov. Testam. restringunt: quia uti hic secundum quid deprecatur divitias Sa- lomo, quod verba addita docent, ne scil. saturatus Deum abneget fiducia in opibus collocata, ita ea- dem temporis utriusque sub Vet. & Nov. Test. quoad divitiarum possessionem est conditio, nul- la diversitas: quas possidere possumus pie & ju- ste, dum legitimis mediis acquisitas non idoli in- star habemus, Matth. 6. vers. 24. nec iisdem su- perbiamus, aut confidamus 1. Tim. 6. vers. 12. aut cor illis appendamus Psal. 62. v. 11. sed ad priva- tam nostri, proximi, & imprimis nostrorum, vel etiam publicam Ecclesiæ, aut Reip. necessitatem adhibeamus & asservemus, quod a Salomone fa- ctum: ideo divitias non abjicere jubet Paulus, sed quomodo iis utendum sit, docet 1. Tim. 6. v. 17. NE FORTE SATIATUS ILLICIAR AD NEGANDUM (in Ebr. ne forte satier cibo & opibus, & abnegem) ET DI- CAM, QUIS EST DOMINUS? Conf. Deut. 31. v. 20. c. 32. v. 15. Neh. 9. v. 25. 26. Os. 13. v. 6. Es. 59. v. 13. Sequi enim solet opulentia animi ac elatio, confidentia in opi- bus, contemtus Dei, luxus, securitas, imo atheismus, Ex. 5. v. 2. AUT EGESTATE COMPULSUS FURER, ET PERJUREM NOMINE DEI MEI. In Ebr. & assumam (in vanum) nomen Dei mei, quod fit non tantum peje- rando, sed etiam execrando, imprecando, blasphe- mando, apostasia a fide aliisque modis, unde præfe- renda hic Germanica nostra versio, utpote generali nomine omnia comprehendens. Egestatis enim consequentia solent culpa corruptæ naturæ esse partim furtum, & contrectatio rei alienæ adver- sus secundam tabulam, partim nominis divini abu- sus & contrectatio adversus tabulam primam legis divinæ.

## 30:8
Vers. 8. 'GIVE ME NEITHER POVERTY NOR RICHES') Seneca's chorus in Oedipus: 'If it were permitted for me to fashion the fates by my own will, I would temper the sails with a light Zephyr, lest the yards tremble, pressed by a heavy wind; may a gentle breeze, flowing moderately, neither inclining the side, lead the fearless ship. May a safe life carry me, running along the middle path.' Alexis: 'How sweet is everything that is moderate, and not overflowing.' Add what is in Horace concerning the golden mean.

Latin:

Vers. 8. MENDICITATEM ET DIVITIAS NE DE- DERIS MIHI) Senecæ chorus in Oedipo: Fata si liceat mihi Fingere arbitrio meo, Temperem Zephyro levi Vela, ne pressa gravi Spiritu antennæ tremant; Lenis ac modicum fluens Aura, nec vergens latus Ducat intrepidam ratem. Tuta me media vehat Vita decurrens via. Alexis: Ὡς ἡδὺ πᾶν τὸ μέτριον, ἐδ' ὑπεργέμον. Adde quæ apud Horatium de aurea mediocritate.

## 30:10
Vers. 10. 'ACCUSE NOT A SERVANT UNTO HIS MASTER: LEST HE CURSE THEE, AND THOU BE FOUND GUILTY.'

Under the guise of informing against a servant to his Master is insinuated a type of oppression of a lowly neighbor, which is familiar among the rich and powerful: (whence the connection appears with the preceding) namely, that we should not afflict any of the oppressed more; but rather be affected with compassion toward the same. Reference is made, however, to the law in Deut. 23. v. 14. not to deliver up to his Master the servant who has fled to you, etc. We are not therefore forbidden to inform the Master of the servant's fraud and malice, if indeed this is a work of charity, but the informing against an oppressed servant, who takes refuge with us, and the handing over which follows it and is connoted by it, is forbidden, as being too inhumane and contrary to divine law: 'Lest he curse thee,' and imprecate every evil upon us with the just pain of affliction, and we be held guilty, and be compelled to sustain punishment by divine judgment, or even be destroyed and laid waste, as the Hebrew word is taken in Ez. 6. v. 6. Os. 14. v. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 10. NE ACCUSES SERVUM AD DOMINUM SUUM: NE FORTE MALE- DICAT TIBI ET CORRUAS.

Sub specie delationis servi apud Dominum in- sinuatur genus oppressio proximi abjecti, quæ penes divites & potentes familiaris est: (unde συνέχεια apparet cum præcedentibus) ne scil. quenquam oppressorum magis affligamus; sed commisera- tione potius erga eundem afficiamur. Respici- tur autem ad legem Deut. 23. v. 14. ne relegato ser- vum ad Dominum suum, qui ad te confugit, &c. Non ergo prohibemur Domino indicare servi de- fraudationem & malitiam, siquidem hoc opus cha- ritatis sit, sed servi oppressi, & refugium ad nos sumentis delatio, & quæ eam sequitur & ea con- notatur traditio, vetatur, ceu nimis inhumana, & legi divinæ contraria: Ne forte maledicat, & mala quæque imprecetur nobis justo afflictionis dolore, & rei habeamur, ac pœnam, divino judicio sustinere cogamur, vel etiam destruamur, ac desole- mur, ut vox Ebr. Ez. 6. v. 6. Of. 14. v. 1. accipitur.

## 30:11
Vers. 11. 'THERE IS A GENERATION THAT CURSETH THEIR FATHER, AND DOTH NOT BLESS THEIR MOTHER.'

Now how our perversity is both to be acknowledged and to be amended is taught through riddles. In the former quire, therefore, the more significant vices, to which we are prone, are presented to that end, so that we who are prepared to denounce others may take account of ourselves, Matt. 7, verse 5. (1.) Ingratitude toward parents, and those who are in their place, whom we are bound not only to bless but also to benefit, by virtue of the fourth commandment; but, such is the perversity of human nature, not a few are found, indeed an entire generation of them, who do not bless their parents, but curse them, and we are all prone to ingratitude (which kind of vice is insinuated under this species) τῇ Φύσει, verse 11. (2.) Hypocrisy: concerning which verse 12. A GENERATION, WHICH SEEMS CLEAN TO ITSELF (it is clean in its own eyes, as if it lacked stain and filth) AND YET IS NOT WASHED FROM ITS FILTH. Cf. ch. 12, v. 15. which is the kind of hypocrites verse 12. But all are very prone to hypocrisy and simulation, Luke 6, verse 42. Rom. 3, verse 13. (3.) Pride: concerning which verse 13. A GENERATION WHOSE EYES ARE LOFTY, AND WHOSE EYELIDS ARE LIFTED UP ON HIGH. Internal arrogance is described by external gesture, the lifting of the eyes, whereas the humble on the contrary cast their eyes down to the ground, nor dare to lift them up, Luke 18, verse 13. But as pride is the source and beginning of every sin, so it adheres to men by nature. Jerem. 17, v. 9. Syr. 10, verses 14, 15. The fourth kind of sin is injustice and cruelty verse 13. A GENERATION THAT HAS SWORDS FOR TEETH, AND CHEWS WITH ITS MOLARS, TO DEVOUR THE NEEDY (the afflicted) FROM THE EARTH, AND THE POOR FROM AMONG MEN. Such is the beastly rapaciousness and ferocity of men, similarly described in Job 16:9, 29:17, Ps. 35:16, Ps. 57:5. Compare Prov. 25:18, 12:18. A natural propensity toward the same is gathered from Rom. 3:15, 16, 17, where the universal and native corruption of man is described. Let us therefore acknowledge that remarkable corruption of our nature, that perversity, and that congenital and εὐπερίσατον [easily besetting] inclination toward such great vices of ingratitude, hypocrisy, pride, rapaciousness, and injustice, which nevertheless spreads itself in different ways in different people, so that some are more prone to one kind of sin, others to another: whence mention is made here of a diverse generation: so that we may especially crucify and put to death those desires toward which we are more inclined by nature. Col. 3:8, 9; Gal. 4:24.

Latin:

Vers. 11. GENERATIO, QUÆ PATRI SUO MALEDICIT, ET QUÆ MATRI NON BE- NEDICIT.

Jam quomodo nostra perversitas & agnoscen- da, & emendanda sit per gryphos docetur. Prio- ri quaternione itaque vitia potiora, in quæ pro- clives sumus ea fini exhibentur, ut qui alios de- ferre parati sumus, nostri ipsorummet ratio- nem habeamus, Matth. 7. vers. 5. (1.) Ingratitu- do erga parentes, & qui eorum loco sunt, quibus non modo benedicere, sed etiam benefacere te- nemur, vi quarti præcepti; sed, quæ naturæ hu- manæ est perversitas, non pauci reperiuntur, imo integra est eorum generatio, qui parentibus non benedicunt, sed maledicunt, & ad ingratitudinem (quod genus vitii sub hac specie insinuatur) pro- clives sumus omnes τῇ Φύσει, vers. 11. (2.) Hypo- crisis: de qua vers. 12. GENERATIO, QUÆ SIBI MUNDA VIDETUR (munda est in oculis suis, quasi macula, ac sordibus careat) ET TAMEN NON EST LOTA A SORDIBUS SUIS. Conf. c. 12. v. 15. quod est hypocritarum genus vers. 12. Ad hypo- crisin autem & simulationem valde proni sunt omnes, Luc. 6. vers. 42. Rom. 3. vers. 13. (3.) Su- perbia: de qua vers. 13. GENERATIO CORDIS EX- CELSI SUNT OCULI, ET PALPEBRÆ EIUS IN ALTA ERECTÆ. Fastus internus describitur ab externo gestu, oculorum elevatione, quum humiles contra oculos in terram deprimant, nec attollere ausint, Luc. 18. vers. 13. Superbia autem uti fons est & principium omnis pecca- ti, ita hominibus natura adhæret. Jerem. 17. v. 9. Syr. 10. vers. 14. 15. Quartum peccati genus est injustitia & crudelitas vers. 13. GENERATIO QUÆ PRO DENTIBUS GLADIOS HABET, ET COMMANDIT MOLARIBUS SUIS, UT COME- DAT INOPES (afflictos) DE TERRA, ET PAU- PERES EX HOMINIBUS. Qualis bestialis hominum rapacitas, & frocia similiter describitur Job. 16. v. 9. c. 29. v. 17. Psal. 35. v. 16. Psal. 57. v. 5. Conf. Prov. 25. v. 18. c. 12. v. 18. Propensio vero ad ean- dem naturalis è Rom. 3, 15. 16. 17. ubi describitur corruptio universalis & nativa hominis, colligitur. Agnoscamus ergo insignem illam naturæ nostræ corruptionem, perversitatem, & ad tanta vitia, in- gratitudinis, hypocriscos, superbiæ, rapacita- tis, ac injustitiæ proclivitatem congenitam, & εὐπερίσατον, quæ tamen in aliis atque aliis se di- versimode diffundit, ut hi ad illud, isti ad aliud peccati genus propensiores sint : unde genera- tionis diversæ hic mentio facta : ut eas imprimis cupiditates, ad quas natura magis propendemus, erucifigamus, & perimamus. Col. 3. vers. 8. 9. Gal. 4. v. 24.

## 30:12
Verse 12. FOR THREE THINGS THE EARTH IS MOVED, AND THE FOURTH IT CANNOT BEAR: FOR A SERVANT WHEN HE SHALL REIGN: FOR A FOOL WHEN HE SHALL BE FILLED WITH FOOD: FOR AN ODIOUS WOMAN WHEN SHE SHALL BE TAKEN IN MARRIAGE: AND FOR A HANDMAID WHEN SHE SHALL BE HEIR TO HER MISTRESS.

He subjoins Political and Economic matters to the Theological warnings: Under three (so it is in the Hebrew) the earth trembles, and under four (namely, troublesome burdens) it cannot tolerate (the mass or the burden). Which is to be understood concerning the inhabitants of the earth. Moreover, of these four intolerable things, the first pair is of the masculine sex, the servant and the fool; the second pair is of the feminine sex, the odious woman and the handmaid: the former pair causes disturbances in the Republic, the latter in the family are excited. For when a servant has emerged to rule others, who has never learned to govern others, or made trial of it: for according to Claudian there is no beast worse than the rage of a servant raging against free backs: and according to Homer and Plato, Jupiter takes away half the mind of those who are subjected to the yoke of slavery: and a fool, when sated with food, delights, and wine, I add also riches and honors, which are included under food, becomes more foolish. Conf. ch. 14, 24. For since wise men not rarely become foolish from an abundance of riches, Deut. 32, v. 15, it is no wonder if fools become utterly insane and are hostile to all, 1 Sam. 25, 10, seqq. Similarly, a woman hated for her bad morals, if she marries, will be intolerable and most troublesome to her husband. For if anyone marries a bad wife, he ascends a bad cross, from which he hangs perpetually, as Delrio says, Vol. II, adag. p. 333. Cartwright thinks that polygamy customary in the O.T. is being referred to, where one was often dearer than the rest, while the others, being less dear, were called hated. If, therefore, it happens that she who had been hated has won the intimate love of her husband, then she has become intolerable to the rest. But the sentence is more general, and here a woman is referred to who is intolerable not only to others, but even to the husband himself. But most intolerable is a maidservant born in a humble place, accustomed to servitude and misery, when she becomes the heir of her mistress, or succeeds into her place. For since, just as the custody and discipline of daughters is stricter and more severe than that of sons, so the condition of maidservants is harder than that of menservants: it happens that the more they are now cast down, the more insolently they behave when raised to dignity:

See Gen. 16, 4. 9. The sum of the warning, therefore, is that in promoting men to a more honorable condition of life, prudence and caution must be used.

Latin:

Vers. 12. PER TRIA MOVETUR TERRA, ET QUARTUM NON POTEST SUSTINERE: PER SERVUM CUM REGNAVERIT: PER STULTUM CUM SATURATUS FUERIT CIBO: PER ODIOSAM MULIEREM CUM IN MATRIMONIO FUERIT ASSUMTA: ET PER ANCILLAM CUM FUERIT HÆRES DOMINÆ SUÆ.

Theologicis monitis Politica subjungit, & Oeconomica: Sub tribus (ita est in Ebr.) tremit terra, & sub quatuor (oneribus sc. molestis) non potest tolerare (molem, vel onus.) Quod de terræ incolis intelligendum. Intolerabilium autem istorum quatuor par primum sexus est masculini, servus & stultus, par alterum fœminei sexus exosa est, & ancilla: à priori pari turbæ in Republ. à posteriori in familia excitantur. Servus nempe cum emerserit, ut aliis imperet, qui nunquam alios gubernare didicit, aut ejus periculum fecit: nam secundum Claudianum nec bellua deterior ulla est, quam servi rabies in libera terga furentis: & juxta Homerum, ac Platonem dimidium mentis Jupiter illis aufert, qui servitutis forti subjecti sunt: & stultus cum cibo, deliciis, vinoque, addo & opibus, ac honoribus, quæ sub cibo comprehenduntur, saturatus stultior evadit. Conf. cap. 14, 24. Cum enim sapientes præ divitiarum copia non raro stulti evadunt, Deut. 32. v. 15. non mirum, si stulti prorsus insaniant, omnibusque in- festi sint 1. Sam. 25, 10. seqq. Similiter mulier ob mores suos malos exosa, si nubat, viro erit intolerabilis, & molestissima. Siquis enim malam ducat uxorem, in malam ascendit crucem, unde perpetim pendeat, dicente Delrione Tom. II. adag. p. 333. Cartwrightus polygamiam in V. T. usitatam respici putat, ubi una reliquis sæpe charior erat, cæteræ autem minus charæ exosæ dicebantur. Quod si ergo acciderit, ut quæ exosa fuerat, intimum mariti amorem conciliarit, tum illa reliquis intolerabilis extitit. Sed sententia generalior est, & respicitur hic mulier, quæ intolerabilis non solum aliis, sed etiam ipsi marito sit. Maxime autem intolerabilis est ancilla humili loco orta, servituti ac miseriæ assueta, cum hæres dominæ suæ evadit, aut in locum ejus succedit. Quum enim sicut filiarum strictior & severior custodia & disciplina est, quam filiorum, sic ancillarum durior conditio sit, quam servorum: fit ut quanto magis jam deponuntur, tanto ad dignitatem evectæ insolentius se gerant:

Vid. Gen. 16, 4. 9. Moniti ergo summa est, in promovendis hominibus ad honestiorem vitæ conditionem prudentia & cautione utendum esse.

## 30:15
Verse 15.

THE LEECH HAS TWO DAUGHTERS SAYING, GIVE, GIVE] He describes πλεονεξίαν [covetousness] under the image of a leech, which sucks blood with two branches of its tongue.

Grotius, along with Junius and Piscator, wrongly understands the two branches or channels of the tongue by the daughters of the leech, even though the Dutch agree with this interpretation: since, according to Aldrovandus and other naturalists, three corners of the mouth should have been mentioned in this way. Leeches, however, are aquatic insects, most desirous of blood, whence they adhere to the feet of those passing through water and suck blood: whose daughters are called those who, because of an insatiable desire, seem to cry 'give, give,' because they always crave more: which are explained by some as avarice: to which Osiander's paraphrase assents: but because Solomon wished to set these forth by enigmatic quaternions, Jansenius, Saa, Menochius, Delrio, and others more correctly join these with the following in this way: that there are two things that are insatiable, as if they were daughters of the leech: nay, that there are three such things that are not satisfied, or rather four, each of which says, 'give, give': but none (he says) is sufficient: which are enumerated distinctly in this way for the sake of extending the discourse and for emphasis, when at the beginning they could have been simply counted as four: namely 1. שאול [Sheol], by which either the grave or hell is usually understood, namely the receptacle of deceased men, whether by reason of the body or by reason of damned souls: for both the grave cannot be satisfied, and hell is insatiable, ch. 27:20. Yet the grave seems to be understood here rather: because just as the womb receives seed and afterwards brings forth something living, so also the grave receives the bodies of the deceased and afterwards returns them in turn on the day of resurrection: as Menasse Ben Israel has it in 'On the Resurrection of the Dead,' p. 22. 2. The barren womb. Cartwright, along with some others, thinks that the immense desire of a barren woman to conceive is hinted at. Others explain it concerning the narrowness of the womb, understanding the orifice, which greedily gapes to receive seed: as Dr. Gejer, along with Delrio, who refers these in general to incontinent women, whose lust is not satisfied by male seed: which is more appropriate. 3. The earth which is not satisfied with water, but drinks in all water poured upon it or flowing down from heaven, always ready to receive and drink in more. Cartwright takes this concerning the fabled and scorched earth, which, even though it is irrigated by a great abundance of water, after a short interval of time is again as thirsty as if it had drunk nothing. 4. And fire, which will not say, 'it is enough': for whatever wood or material you place upon it, it burns and consumes. Cartwright rightly observes concerning these that there is something underlying these natural things which the Holy Spirit tacitly hinted at through those insatiable things.

For to have proposed these nakedly without any application seems more the work of a natural philosopher than of a prophet divinely inspired, and furthermore occupied with moral matters, nor would it be done consistently with the following comparisons. Therefore, the moral applications which some interpreters hunt for here cannot be disapproved, from which most wish to have anger indicated by Sheol, which is the cause of injuries and murders, and is so similar to Gehenna that an angry man seems to be an infernal demon burning with fury, nor can the desire for vengeance be easily satisfied. Basil, in his homily on anger, says: just as he who has charity has God in himself; so he who has hatred and anger contains a demon in himself. You could, however, not inappropriately understand gluttony by Sheol, which is similarly insatiable, and weakens bodies, makes them putrid and consumes them, and breathes a foul odor, like the grave and hell: concerning which see Nazianzen in his poem on the different kinds of life. I do not attend a banquet, lest I return home late, and like a sleeper, carry back a living belly. Thus does venereal lust, and luxury, marked by the mouth of the vulva, cohere properly with gluttony. The love of a woman, says Jerome against Jovinian, is always insatiable, which when extinguished is kindled, and after abundance is again needy, and it effeminates the manly spirit, and except for the passion which it sustains, it allows one to think of nothing else, nor is it extinguished by the act itself, but rather is inflamed more immoderately and vehemently. Luxury consumes the best blood and the noblest spirits, and makes a man pale, lurid, and bloodless: therefore it is deservedly compared to a bloodsucker, as also by Theocritus in Idyll 2. Alas, cruel love, sated with our blood, fixed to the highest skin, as if a leech had sucked this. in which, and with which wealth perishes, just as water perishes watering sandy ground. (4.) Ambition, which is insatiable beyond others, and never says, it is enough, is like fire, which by burning acquires no wealth, but rather loses all, and tends upward, since ambition is satisfied by no honor, and strives upward, that it may ascend the high summits of dignities.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

SANGVISUGÆ DUÆ SUNT FILIÆ DICENTES, AFFER, AFFER ] πλεονεξίαν describit sub hirudinis ima- gine, quæ duobus linguæ ramis sanguinem fugit.

Perperam cum Junio & Piscatore Grotius per filias sanguisugæ duos ramos, aut canales linguæ in- telligit, etsi annuant huic interpretationi Belgæ: siquidem juxta Aldrovandum aliosque Physicos tres oris anguli sic commemorandi fuissent. San- guisugæ autem insecta aquatilia sunt, sanguinis maxime cupida, unde transeuntium per aquas pedibus adhærescunt, & sanguinem sugunt: cu- jus filiæ ob cupiditatem inexplebilem dicuntur ii, qui videntur clamare affer, affer, quia semper plura appetunt: quæ a nonnullis de avaritia ex- plicantur: quibus adstipulatur paraphrasis Osi- andri: sed quia quaternionibus gryphicis hæc expedire voluit Salomo, rectius Jansenius, Saa, Menochius, Delrio, & alii hæc cum sequenti- bus hoc modo conjungunt: duo esse insatiabilia, ac si filiæ sanguisugæ essent: imo tria esse talia, quæ non satiantur, imo vero quatuor, quorum quodvis ait, affer, affer: nullum vero (ait) sufficit: quæ distincte ita numerantur producendæ orationis & emphaseos causa, quum initio potuissent simpli- citer quatuor numerari: utpote 1. שאול per quod vel sepulcrum vel infernus intelligi solet, re- ceptaculum nempe hominum defunctorum, seu ratione corporis, seu ratione animarum damna- tarum: nam & sepulcrum satiari nequit, & in- fernus inexplebilis est cap. 27. vers. 20. Sepulcrum tamen hic potius intelligi videtur: quia uti vul- va recipit semen, & postea edit aliquid vivens, ita etiam sepulcrum recipit corpora defunctorum, & postea reddit ea vicissim die resurrectionis: ut habet Menasse Ben Israel de resurr. mort. pag. 22. 2. Vulva sterilis. Fœminæ nempe steri- lis immensum concipiendi desiderium innui pu- tat Cartwrightus cum aliis nonnullis. Alii ex- ponunt de angustia uteri, orificium intelligentes, quod semini suspiciendo avide inhiat: ut Dn. D. Gejerus, cum Delrione, qui hæc in universum ad incontinentes mulieres refert, quarum libido non expletur virili semine: quod convenientius est. 3. Terra quæ aquis non satiatur, sed omnem a- quam superfusam vel è cœlo defluentem imbi- bit, semper parata novam suscipere & imbibe- re. De terra fabulosa accipit Cartwrightus, & torrida, quæ tametsi maxima aquarum copia ir- rigetur, exiguo tamen temporis intervallo ite- rum tam sitibunda est, ac si nihil imbibisset. 4. Et ignis, qui non dicet, sat est: quicquid enim lignorum vel materiæ apposueris, comburit, & absumit. Recte autem de his observat Cart- wrightus, aliquid subesse naturalibus istis, quod tacite innuerit Spiritus S. per illa insatiabilia

Hæc enim nude sine aliqua applicatione pro-" posuisse naturalis potius Philosophi videtur," quam prophetæ divinitus inspirati, adhæc in" moralibus occupati, nec comparationibus se-" quentibus congruenter id fieret. Non impro-" bari ergo possunt applicationes morales, quas Interpretes nonnulli hic venantur, e quibus ple- rique per שאול indigitari volunt iram, quæ cau- sa injuriarum & cædium, & ita similis gehennæ est, ut homo iratus videatur esse dæmon infer- nalis furore ardens, nec expleri facile possit vindictæ cupiditas. Basil. hom. de ira, sicut, qui charitatem, inquit, habet DEUM in se habet; ita qui odium & iram habet, dæmonem in se con- tinet. Posses tamen non incommode per שאול gulam intelligere, quæ similiter insatiabilis est, ac corpora labefacit, putrida facit & consumit, ac odorem spirat fœtidum, ut sepulcrum & in- fernus: quo de Nazianz. in carm. de divers. vit. generib. Non epulum adeo, ne sero domum redeam, & ventrem sopitorum ad instar vivus re- feram. Ita cohæret cum gula probe (2) libido Venerea, & luxuria, per os vulvæ notata. Amor mulieris, inquit Hieronymus contra Jovin. semper insatiabilis est, qui extinctus accenditur, & post co- piam rursus inops est, animumque virilem effœmi- nat, & excepta passione, quam sustinet, aliud non sinit cogitare, nec ipso usu extinguitur, sed immo- deratius ac vehementius inflammatur. Luxuria sanguinem optimum-, ac spiritus nobilissimos absumit, hominemque facit pallidum, luridum, exanguem: ideo merito sanguisugæ confertur, uti etiam à Theocrito famum Idyll. 2. Heu cru- delis amor nostro saturate cruore, summæ affixe cu- ti, velut hunc suxiffet hirudo. (3.) Avaritia, quæ similis est terræ sitienti & bibulæ, unde ava- ros hydropicos dixit Chrysost. hom. 15. in 1. Co- rinth. in quibus, & cum quibus pereunt opes, sicut perit aqua rigans terram arenosam. (4.) Ambi- tio, quæ præ cæteris insatiabilis, & nunquam dicit, sufficit, instar ignis est, qui urendo nullas opes acquirit, sed potius omnes perdit, ac fur- sum tendit, siquidem ambitio nullo honore sa- tietur, & sursum nitatur, ut alta dignitatum cul- mina conscendat.

## 30:17
Verse 17.

THE EYE THAT MOCKETH AT HIS FATHER, AND DESPISETH THE OBEDIENCE OF HIS MOTHER, LET THE RAVENS OF THE BROOK PICK IT OUT, AND THE YOUNG EAGLES EAT IT.

In place of 'partus' (birth) in the Hebrew is יקהת (obedience), which is found in Genesis 49, verse 10, nor does the noun 'partus' fit the text. However, a violent death and an ignominious denial of burial are denounced against the mocker of a father and the despiser of the obedience due to a mother, by way of the plucking out of eyes: because birds of prey are accustomed to fly first of all at the eyes of the dead, as being the softest part. They are called ravens of the brook, because ravens are accustomed to live around brooks, 1 Kings 17, v. 3, 4, and they seem to be more savage than those. The sons of the eagle are explained as the younger, or more lively, eagles. Concerning the rapacity of eagles, see Job 9:26, ch. 39:32, 33. Although, however, those hanged by the command of the law of Moses were to be buried, ravens are nevertheless accustomed to fly immediately at the eyes of the dead, and to attack them. But while he mentions particularly the first of the wicked generation, and denounces punishment for it, that, as Mercer interprets, implies that although those four kinds of men are the worst, and worthy of great punishments, yet that first one will be punished most, which curses its parents, or mocks them: or rather, the gravity of the punishment is indicated in one kind of sin, because they deserve all things. For sin is no less grave in the eyes of GOD is hypocrisy, by which we deceive GOD and men, pride, by which we exalt ourselves, and iniquity, by which we oppress our neighbor, than the mockery and disobedience by which we despise our parents: But the mockery of parents is brought forward especially for this reason: because those who are impious toward their parents more easily precipitate themselves into other sins, whence the fourth commandment in the second table was established first by the most wise legislator. But with a certain kind of horrible punishment named, every horrid punishment seems to be comprehended: and this in such a way that the infernal punishment is tacitly hinted at, to be sustained by ravens and rapacious infernal birds, unless perhaps by the ravens of the torrent the black Spirits themselves are immediately understood as being at the torrent of Belial: who are also the degenerate chicks of the celestial Eagle. If, however, these things are also said enigmatically, the allusion to savage, rapacious, black, and ill-omened animals will remain as such.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

OCULUM QUI SUBSANNAT PATREM, ET QUI DESPICIT PARTUM MATRIS SUÆ, EFFODIANT EUM CORVI DE TORRENTIBUS, ET COMEDANT EUM FILII AQUILÆ.

Loco partus in Ebræo est יקהת obsequium, quod habetur Genes. 49. vers. 10. neque conve- nit nomen partus textui. Denuntiatur autem subsannatori patris & comtemtori obedientiæ matris debitæ sub exoculatione mors violenta, & ignominiosa sepulturæ denegatio: quia rapaces vo- lucres omnium primo involare solent defuncto- rum oculos, tanquam partem mollissimam. Corvi torrentis dicuntur, quia corvi circa torrentes dege- re solent 1. Reg. 17. v. 3. 4. illisque sæviores esse viden- tur. Filii Aquilæ de junioribus ceu alacrioribus aqui- lis explicantur. De aquilarum vero capacitate vid. Job. 9, 26. c. 39, 32. 33. Quamvis vero suspensi lege Mosis jubente, humandi fuerint, solent tamen cor- vi statim in mortuorum oculos involare, illosque adoriri. Dum autem peculiariter primum nominatæ generationis pravæ meminit, eique pœnam denunci- ait, id, Mercero interprete, innuit, etsi quatuor illa ho- minum genera pessima sint, magnisq; suppliciis digna, primum tamen illud maxime punitum iri, quod Pa- rentibus maledicit, aut eos subsannat: vel potius in- dicatur in uno peccatorum genere gravitas sup- plicii, quod omnia mereantur. Non minus e- nim grave peccatum in oculis DEI est hypocri- sis, qua DEO & hominibus illudimus, superbia, qua nos ipsos efferimus, & iniquitas, qua proxi- mum opprimimus, quam subsannatio & inobedien- tia, qua parentes despicimus: Sed præcipue ideo pa- rentum subsannatio adducitur: quia qui in Paren- tes impii sunt, in reliqua peccata facilius se præci- pitant, unde quartum præceptum in tabula secunda primum a sapientissimo legislatore constitutum est. Nominato autem certo pœnæ horribilis genere, quodvis horridum comprehendi videtur supplicium: idque ita ut tacite subinnuatur pœ- na infernalis, a corvis & rapacibus volucribus infernalibus sustinenda, nisi forte per corvos tor- rentis ipsi immediate atri Spiritus ad torrentem Be- lial intelligantur: qui & degeneres Aquilæ cælestis pulli. Si tamen & hæc ænigmatice dicta erunt, ma- nebitque ita allusio ad animantia sæva, rapacia, atra & infausta.

## 30:18
Ver. 18.

THERE ARE THREE THINGS DIFFICULT FOR ME AND A FOURTH I UTTERLY DO NOT KNOW: THE WAY OF AN EAGLE IN THE HEAVEN, THE WAY OF A SERPENT UPON A ROCK, THE WAY OF A SHIP IN THE MIDST OF THE SEA, AND THE WAY OF A MAN IN ADOLESCENCE.

In the Hebrew, they are called not difficult, but hidden, or wonderful, as Aquila translates, and Ambrose has in De Vit. Valent.: the Chaldean renders it occult; the LXX, three things are impossible for me to understand: Vatablus, three things are excellent, and above my grasp. In the last member, however, it is expressed not as the way of a man in adolescence, but in a virgin. But those things are wont to be explained by some concerning purely natural things, because neither the flight of an eagle in the heaven, nor the movement of a serpent upon a rock, nor the way or course of a ship in the sea, nor the ways of a man by which he lies in wait for a virgin, leave any trace behind them, so that they can be found or designated by anyone: which sense, however, seems alien to the Solomonic mode of teaching, and especially to these sentences of Agur inculcating a more sublime wisdom. Others therefore seek mysteries in these, but not in one way: concerning which see Cornelius à Lapide. It seems to us now that a progression is made from the sins to which men are liable, and the punishment which they deserve, to the mystery of Redemption, unsearchable to all human reason, which could be said to be done in such a way that those three things hidden to us in nature, in heaven, in earth, in the sea, (and no others) are assumed, not without cause, for the adumbration of the fourth or last of all the most wonderful of wonders, which completely exceeds all nature, all grasp, as if to say: If those things in nature are hidden from us, how much more hidden is this, which is beyond reason, beyond mind, beyond all comprehension, that new thing which the Lord will create, which is the only thing new under the sun, of the Man called thus by way of excellence in Jer. 31. v. 12. (where the same word גבר, who surpasses all others, and the angels themselves designated by a similar name in Psalm 103:20, in strength, authority, and Dominion (which is the emphasis of the word taken in an eminent signification, from which also divine fortitude has its name in Psalm 89:14, Psalm 106:2) the way in that incorrupt virgin, of whom Isaiah 7:14, in whom he himself willed to assume our flesh, and to be conceived, the mighty God Isaiah 9:6, the power of the Most High Luke 1:35. Which way and manner of the incarnation of the Word and of the conception in the womb of the Virgin is truly incomprehensible, and

confessedly a great mystery 1 Tim. 3:16. Whither I also see Cornelius à Lapide going on page 453. The Hebrew word gaber, that is, a robust man, properly belongs to no boy or adolescent, but to Christ alone being born, both because of the strength of his divinity, and because from the instant of his conception according to his soul he was altogether perfect: nor does it seem to lack mystery that it was not said, The way of an adolescent or youth in a young girl, as according to that former literal sense it seemed it should be said, but the way of a man. Certainly, that can truly belong to no other than Christ, and his virgin mother. According to which sense the remaining three ways are rightly understood to be brought forward, so that by the example of them that fourth way, and more wonderful than the others, might be better understood and noted, namely that, just as a bird flies in the air, a serpent creeps upon a rock, a ship passes in the sea without any corruption of the air, or rock, or water, or any sign of division left behind: so also that way of a man happens without the injury and corruption of the virgin. Thus the ancient Rabbis explained this passage concerning Christ incarnate in a Virgin, and among them R. Haccados, that is, the Saint, in Galatinus lib. 7. de Arcanis fidei cap. 15. Lyranus, Jansenius, Franc. Suarez 3. p. q. 28. art. 1. Disp. 5. Sect. 1. and others.

But why does he here compare the way of an eagle flying in the sky to others, unless to intimate, or leave it to be thought, that the Son of God is not undeservedly compared to the eagle, which is the swiftest and most spirited Queen of birds: on account of the sublimity of his heavenly ways, especially regarding the business of our redemption and salvation, for the sake of which he deigned to lower himself from heaven in a way, manner, and mode altogether inscrutable: who is also compared to an eagle in the work of our protection, Exod. 19. v. 14. Deut. 32. vers. 11. Moreover, the way does not only denote a footprint, because it is no wonder here that no visible footprint of a flying eagle remains in the air invisible to us, but rather it is wonderful that the eagle has such swiftness that, which is granted to no other bird, it can seek the sky or the highest air, Job 39. v. 30. Jer. 49. v. 10. 16. Obad. v. 4. and with Oppian saying that it surpasses the air in flight and ascends more sublimely: by which the sublimity of the heavenly mystery of the descent of the Son of GOD, made for the sake of our salvation, is insinuated, as Isidore of Pelusium l. 1. Epist. 416. and especially St. Ambrose tract. on chap. 30. Prov. Tom. 4. pag. 357. intimates: As if it were easy for an eagle suspended on high, by the swift lifting of its wings, to establish manifest traces of its flapping and gliding, or to mark a way in the void, and draw a line of its flight, and fix it in the liquid? -- In this place we ought to accept the eagle as Christ our Lord, who after his venerable resurrection, by which he taught that the human race could return to life after death, flew back like an eagle to the Father, carrying back with him the prey: that is, the man whom he had snatched from the jaws of the enemy. --- As the eagle devours serpents and cooks their poisons with its internal heat, so also Christ our Lord, having struck the dragon, that is, having torn the Devil, while he assumes a human body for himself, extinguished that sin which held man captive, as if it were a pernicious virus, just as the Apostle says: And for sin he condemned sin in his flesh. -- This is therefore what he says: The traces of a flying eagle, because even if after his passion and resurrection our LORD ascended into heaven in the presence of the Apostles, yet whose human understanding is so deep and so great that he can explain how that great majesty deigned either to come from heaven or to return? since it is permitted for us to know only this, that he either came or returned. Who can know how the Word came into the virgin, so that she suddenly conceived, so that she brought forth such a blessed offspring of virginal birth, so that God put on man, whom the whole world can neither endure nor contain? That is what he says, the traces of a flying eagle, that is, of Christ the Lord coming to Thus St. Ambrose.

Furthermore, what is the reason why he makes mention specifically of a serpent on earth, and of its way upon a rock, when the ways of other living creatures on earth, which are equally or more hidden, could have been brought forward? St. Ambrose seems to have explained these things not badly again: since to that mystical Eagle, the Son of God, is opposed the infernal serpent, for whose sake the Son of God wished to descend from heaven, and who laid snares for the same in wondrous ways: who in Christ the Rock tried all ways and methods with whatever art he could, so that he might impede the saving way of the Eagle. This rock, says Ambrose, we ought not to doubt is our Lord. For thus the Apostle says: And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. But the serpent appears from the very name that it is the Devil, just as the more crafty of all the beasts that are upon the earth, that is, the Devil, who is called a serpent for this reason, that he creeps secretly. And that which the sense of man probes by creeping thinly, if it overcomes them, it entangles itself in the marrow and bones of men, and immerses itself. He who could imprint no tracks of his malice upon the body of man, which the omnipotent Christ God had put on, although he dared to attempt it often, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: Behold the prince of the world comes, and finds nothing in me. This therefore is the rock, that is, the flesh of Christ, sprinkled with no iniquity of the enemy, in which no track of a serpent, that is, of any sin, appears, as it is written: who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.

Concerning the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, the same Ambrose left behind different expositions, as Cornelius a Lapide notes (which, however, I do not find in the Basel edition of the year 1538), by which he also judged that Christ is indicated by the ship: as a ship of heavenly goods: which carries all the faithful through the sea of this age to the port of eternal salvation: and he wished his passage through the sea to designate his incarnation and birth from the Virgin Mary, and the Church: which latter exposition seems not inappropriate, and therefore to be preferred. We ought, he says, to accept the ship as the Church established in the salt water of this world, which is fatigued by the frequent gusts of winds, that is, by the blows and lashes of temptations, which the turbulent waves, that is, the power of this age, try to lead to the rocks. Which, even if it is often vexed by the waves or storms of the waters, nevertheless can never suffer shipwreck, because in its mast, that is, in the cross, Christ is raised; in the stern the Father sits as helmsman, the Paraclete Spirit guards the prow. Twelve rowers lead this through the narrow straits of this world into the port, that is, the twelve Apostles, and a similar number of Prophets. This ship therefore is the Church, which, even if it daily encounters this age as some hostile sea, is never dashed against a rock, nor sunk to the depths. But what he says: The ways of a ship sailing, properly signifies that in time it could not be comprehended at all in a wondrous way of persecution. Thus again Ambrose. And those three mysteries, insinuated by the flight of the Eagle in the sky, the way of the serpent on the rock, and the course of the ship in the midst of the sea, or rather, if you prefer, expressly stated, are rightly composed with the unblemished conception of the Son of God in the womb of the Virgin

Mary the Mother of God: because such a conception was necessary for the descent of the Son of God from heaven, and the frustration of the way of the serpent on the rock, so that from then on in the midst of the world, as a sea full of impiety and uncleanness (Isa. 57:20), we might be kept safe in the ship of the Church, until it is permitted to arrive at the port of eternal life, so that we may reach the Eagle in heaven. However, Cornelius a Lapide gathers in vain from this that Christ is the Eagle, and so also the serpent and the ship: and that the Holy Virgin is the sky, and the rock, and the sea. For these comparisons neither suit these mysteries sufficiently, and those things are foreign to the present scope.

Nor do the Jews profit anything when they contend from this passage that the word עלמה does not denote an uncorrupted virgin: For whether the passage is explained concerning the snares usually laid for virgins by men, or concerning the very conception of Christ in the womb of Mary, the force of the word remains intact, implying an uncorrupted virgin: because snares do not argue a corrupted one, but are rather laid for an uncorrupted virgin, for whom men especially lust, and lay snares in all ways, so that they may corrupt them: whence there is no need that we, with Mercerus, concede to the Jews that this word signifies both a married woman and an untouched one, since neither the origin of the word, nor its use, admits anything other than that it denotes a hidden and unblemished virgin.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

TRIA SUNT DIFFICILIA MIHI ET QUARTUM PENITUS IGNORO: VIAM AQUILÆ IN CŒLO, VIAM COLUBRI SUPER PETRAM, VIAM NAVIS IN ME- DIO MARI, ET VIAM VIRI IN ADOLE- SCENTIA.

In Ebr. non difficilia, sed abscondita, vel mi- rabilia, ut Aquila vertit, & Ambrosius habet de Vit. Valent. dicuntur: Chald. reddit occulta; LXX. tria sunt impossibilia mihi intelligere: Vatabl. tria sunt excellentia, ac supra captum meum. In postremo autem membro, non via viri in adolescentia, sed in virgine exprimitur. Explicari autem solent illa a quibusdam de mere naturalibus, quod nec a- quilæ volatus in cœlo, nec colubri incessus super petram, nec navis vel decursus via in mari, nec viæ viri quibus insidiatur virgini, ullum post se relin- quant vestigium, ut a quoquam inveniri aut desi- gnari possint: qui vero sensus alienus videtur a modo docendi Salomoneo, & ab hisce imprimis sen- tentiis Aguris sapientiam sublimiorem inculcan- tis. Alii proinde mysteria in hisce quærunt, sed non uno modo: de quibus vid. Cornel. à Lapide. Nobis videtur nunc à peccatis, quibus obnoxii ho- mines sunt, & pœna quam merentur progressum fieri ad mysterium Redemtionis omni humanæ ra- tioni ἀνεξερεύνητον, quod dici possit ita fieri, ut tria illa nobis abscondita in natura, in cœlo, in terra, in mari, (nec alia) assumantur, non citra causam ad quarti vel ultimi omnium mirabilium maxime mira- bilis, quod omnem naturam, omnem captum pe- nitus excedit, adumbrationem, q. d. Si illa in natu- ra nobis abscondita, quanto magis absconditum est hoc, quod est ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν, novum illud, quod creabit Dominus, quod unicum est sub sole novum, Viri ἐξοχικῶς ita nuncupati Jer. 31. v. 12. (ubi eadem vox גבר qui alios universos, ipsosque angelos simili nomine de- signatos Psal. 103, 20. virtute, autoritate & Dominio exuperat (quæ vocis ἔμφασις est in eminenti signi- ficatione accepta, a qua etiam divina fortitudo no- men habet Psal. 89. verf. 14. Psal. 106. vers. 2.) via בעלמה in virgine illa incorrupta, de qua Es. 7. v. 14 in qua carnem nostram assumere, & concipi vo- luit ipse גבור אל Deus fortis Esa. 9. v. 6. ἡ δύνα- μις τῦ ὑψίςꞵ virtus Altissimi Luc. 1. v. 35. Quæ via & ratio incarnationis τῦ λόγꞵ & conceptionis in utero Virginis vere est incomprehensibilis, &

ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον 1. Tim. 3. v. 16. Quò abire etiam video Cornelium à Lapide pag. 453. Vox Ebræa gaber, idest vir robustus, nulli pro- prie puero vel adolescenti, sed soli Christo nascenti competit, tum ob divinitatis suæ fortitudinem, tum quod ab instanti suæ conceptionis secundum animam omnino fuerit perfectus: nec enim mysterio videtur carere, quod non sit dictum, Via adolescentis sive juvenis in adolescentula, quemadmodum juxta il- lum priorem literalem sensum videbatur dicendum, sed via viri. Certe in nullum alium istud verius competere potest quam in Christum, ejusque matrem virginem. Juxta quem sensum reliquæ tres viæ re- cte intelliguntur adductæ, ut per illarum exemplum quarta illa via, & præ aliis magis mirabilis, me- lius intelligeretur & adverteretur, scilicet quod, quemadmodum avis in aëre volat, serpens super pe- tram repit, navis transit in mari sine aliqua aëris, vel petræ, vel aquæ corruptione, vel divisionis ali- cujus signo relicto: ita & via illa viri contingit sine virginis læsione & corruptione. Ita hunc locum de Christo in Virgine incarnato explicarunt Veteres Rabbini, ac inter eos R. Haccados, id est Sanctus, apud Galatin. lib. 7. de Arcanis fidei cap. 15. Ly- ran. Jansen. Franc. Svarez. 3. p. q. 28. art. 1. Disp. 5. Sect. 1. & alii.

Cur vero aquilæ volantis in cælo viam præ aliis hic comparat, nisi ut Filium Dei aquilæ, quæ avi- um Regina pernicipima, animosissima, non im- merito conferri subinnuat, vel cogitandum re- linquat: ob sublimitatem viarum ejus cælestium, imprimis vero quoad negotium nostræ redemtio- nis & salutis, cujus gratia se de cælo demittere dignatus est via, more, modoque prorsus imper- scrutabili: qui etiam aquilæ in opere nostræ pro- tectionis comparatur, Exod. 19. v. 14. Deut. 32. vers. 11. Non autem tantum via vestigium notat, quia mirum hic non est in aëre invisibili nobis nullum remanere aquilæ volantis vestigium visi- bile, sed id potius mirabile, aquilæ tantam esse pernicitatem, ut quod nulli avium concessum, cælum vel supremum aërem petere possit, Job. 39. v. 30. Jer. 49. v. 10. 16. Obad. v. 4. atque Oppia- no dicente aërem volatu superet, & sublimius eva- dat: quo sublimitas cælestis mysterii descensus Fi- lii DEI de cælo salutis nostræ ergo facti insinua- tur, ut Isidor. Pelusiota l. 1. Epist. 416. & imprimis S. Ambrosius tract. in cap. 30. Prov. Tom. 4. pag. 357. innuit: Quasi vero sit facile, ut suspensa aqui- la in altum celeri elatione pennarum, plausus sui & lapsus vestigia manifesta constituat, aut viam signet in vacuo, & lineam sui volatus ducat, figat in liqui- do? -- Aquilam in hoc loco Christum Dominum no- strum debemus accipere, qui post venerandam resur- rectionem, qua docuit humanum genus in vitam re- dire posse post mortem, velut aquila revolavit ad Pa- trem, prædam secum referens: id est, hominem quem rapuerat de faucibus inimici. --- Ut aquila serpen- tes devorat, & eorum venena calore coquit in- terno, ita & Christus Dominus noster percusso dra- cone, id est, Diabolo lacerato, dum humanum sibi cor- pus assumit, peccatum illud, quod hominem tenebat obnoxium, tanquam perniciosum virus extinxit, sicut Apostolus ait: Et de peccato damnavit peccatum in carne sua. -- Hoc est ergo quod ait: Vestigia aquilæ volantis, quia etsi post passionem & resurrectionem suam præsentibus Apostolis DOMINUS noster ascendit in cælum, tamen cujus hominis tam al- tus sensus & tantus est, ut explicare possit, quo- modo illa tanta majestas de cælo aut venire di- gnata fuerat, aut redire? cum hoc solum nobis scire liceat, quod aut venit aut rediit. Quis enim cognoscere potest, quemadmodum verbum in vir- ginem venerit, ut repente conceperit, ut tam felicem fœtum partus virginalis effunderet, ut hominem Deus indueret, quem totus mundus non potest nec sufferre nec capere? Id est quod ait, vestigia aquilæ volantis, id est, Christi domini advenientis ad terram, ac redeun- tis ad cælos vestigia comprehendi, enarrarique non posse. Hæc S. Ambrosius.

Porro quid causæ est, cur in terris peculiari- ter mentionem colubri faciat, & viæ ejus super pe- tram, quum aliorum in terris animantium viæ æque aut magis absconditæ adduci potuerint? Non ma- le iterum S. Ambrosius hæc exposuisse videtur: si- quidem Aquilæ illi mysticæ Filio DEI serpens infer- nalis, cujus causa Filius DEI de cælo descendere vo- luit, quique eidem miris modis insidiatus est, opponi- tur: qui in Christo Petra omnes vias & rationes tentavit quacunque potuit arte, ut viam Aquilæ σωτήριον impediret. Hanc petram, inquit Am- brosius, dominum nostrum esse ambigere non debe- mus. Sic enim Apostolus ait: Bibebant autem de spi- rituali sequenti petra, petra autem erat Christus.--Ser- pens autem ex ipso nomine quod sit Diabolus apparet, sicut callidior omnium bestiarum, quæ sunt super ter- ram, id est Diabolus, qui ideo serpens dicitur, quod oc- culte serpat. Et quod sensus hominis tenuiter inla- bendo pertentat, quos si convicerit medullis se hominum atque ossibus implicat, & immergit.
