Qui in corpore hominis, quod omnipotens Christus DEUS induerat, nulla malitiæ suæ potuit imprimere vestigia, quamvis illud ausus fuerit sæpe tentare, sicut ipse Dominus in Evangelio ait: Ecce venit princeps mundi, & nihil in me invenit.--Hæc est ergo petra, id est caro Chri- sti, nulla inimici iniquitate respersa, in qua serpentis, id est peccati alicujus vestigium non apparet, ut scri- ptum est: qui peccatum non fecit, nec dolus inventus est in ore ejus.

De navis vero via in medio mari idem Am- brosius diversas reliquit expositiones, Cornelio a Lapide notante, (quas tamen in editione Basiliensi Anno 1538. non invenio) qua & Christum per na- vem indigitari censuit: ceu navem mercium cæle- stium: quæ omnes fideles per mare hujus seculi ve- hit ad portum salutis æternæ: ejusque transitum per mare de ejus incarnatione & nativitate è Maria virgine, & Ecclesiam designari voluit: quæ poste- rior expositio non inconcinna, adeoque præferen- ,,da videtur. Navem, inquit, adæque Ecclesiam ,,debemus accipere in salo mundi istius constitu- ,,tam, quæ crebris ventorum fluctibus, id est ten- ,,tationum plagis & verberibus fatigatur, quam ,,turbidi fluctus, id est, hujus seculi potestas co- ,,natur ad saxa perducere. Quæ etsi undarum ,,fluctibus aut procellis sæpe vexatur, tamen nun- ,,quam potest sustinere naufragium, quia in ar- ,,bore ejus, id est, in cruce Christus erigitur; in ,,puppi pater residet gubernator, proram para- ,,cletus servat spiritus. Hanc per angusta hujus ,,mundi freta duodeni in portum remiges du- ,,cunt, id est, duodecim Apostoli, & similis nume- ,,rus Prophetarum. -- Hæc ergo navis Ecclesia ,,est, quæ etsi quotidie seculum istud tanquam ,,aliquod pelagus sortitur infestum, nunquam eli- ,,ditur ad saxum, nec mergitur ad profundum. ,,--Sed quod ait: Vias navis navigantis, proprie ,,significat quod in tempore miro modo persecu- ,,tionis comprehendi omnino non posset. Hæc iterum Ambrosius. Atque ista tria mysteria per Aquilæ volatum in cælo, serpentis viam in petra, navis decursum in medio maris insinuata, vel po- tius, si malis, ῥητῶς expressa recte componuntur cum conceptione Filii Dei in utero Virginis illibata p

Mariæ θεοτόκꙋ: quia conceptione tali opus erat ad descensum Filii Dei è cælo, & frustrationem viæ serpentis in petra, ut dehinc in mundi medio, ceu maris pleni impietatis & immunditiei Es. 57, 20. tuti servaremur in navigio Ecclesiæ, donec ad portum æternæ vitæ appellere liceat, ut ad Aquilam in cælum perveniamus. Nequicquam autem Cornel. à Lap. hinc colligit, Christum ut Aquilam ita etiam colubrum & navim: Sanctam vero Virginem & cælum, & petram, & mare esse. Hæ enim comparationes nec conveniunt satis hisce mysteriis, & aliena sunt ista a præsenti scopo.

Nec quicquam proficiunt Judæi, cum ex hoc loco vocem עלמה non notare incorruptam virginem contendunt: Nam sive de insidiis Virorum virginibus strui solitis, sive de ipsa Christi in utero Mariæ conceptione locus explicetur, manet integra vocis vis, inferens virginem incorruptam: quia insidiæ non arguunt corruptam, sed struuntur potius incorruptæ virgini, qualibus maxime inhiant, modisque omnibus insidiantur viri, ut eas corrumpant: unde non opus est, ut cum Mercero Judæis concedamus, vocem hanc & nuptam & intactam significare, quum nec origo vocis, nec usus ejusdem aliud admittat, quam ut absconditam & illibatam virginem notet.

## 30:19
Verse 19.

THE WAY OF A MAN IN HIS YOUTH) I think the interpreter wrote 'in his youth' (adolescentula): for so it is in the Hebrew. It signifies that the signs of a virgin or of one corrupted are uncertain.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

VIAM VIRI IN ADOLESCENTIA) Scripsisse interpretem puto in adolescentula: nam sic in Hebræo est. Signisicat incerta esse virginis aut corruptæ indicia.

## 30:20
Verse 20.

SUCH IS ALSO THE WAY OF AN ADULTEROUS WOMAN, WHO EATS AND WIPING HER MOUTH SAYS: I HAVE DONE NO EVIL.

What is understood by the adulterous woman is clear from chapter 2, 17 and chapter 9, 13, 17: namely, depraved concupiscence, which has various ways and arts equally unsearchable to us for tempting and ensnaring us, while Satan, the ὁ μυριοτεχνίτης (master of ten thousand arts), governs and directs the same. Against which arts not even the saints themselves and the wisest of all can sufficiently guard themselves; therefore, the Holy Spirit wished to warn of these same things here after the mystery of Redemption had been enigmatically set forth, and the danger of the little ship of the Church in this world had been insinuated. For the snares that are laid for us in countless ways are most hidden and abstruse, not otherwise than as adulterous women are accustomed to lie in wait with various and wondrous arts for incautious men, whom they desire to solicit to συνꙋσίαν (intercourse), even though afterwards, having obtained their wish, they wipe their mouth as if they had committed no evil at all, and wish to be held most innocent and most honorable.

WIPING HER MOUTH) Affectation of virtue. One thing is said, another is understood. See above 16.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

TALIS EST ET VIA MVLIERIS ADULTERÆ, QUÆ COMEDIT ET TERGENS OS SUUM DICIT: NON SUM OPERATA MALUM.

Quid per mulierem adulteram intelligatur è cap. 2, 17. cap. 9, 13. 17. liquet: nimirum prava concupiscentia, quæ varias vias & artes nobis æque impervestigabiles habet nos tentandi & inescandi, cum Satanas ὁ μυριοτεχνίτης eandem moderatur, & dirigit. A quibus artibus ne sancti quidem ipsi & sapientissimi quique sibi cavere satis possunt, ideo de iisdem monere hic post ænigmatice expositum Redemtionis mysterium, & periculum naviculæ Ecclesiæ in hoc mundo insinuatum voluit Spiritus S. Occultæ enim maximæ & abstrusæ sunt insidiæ, quæ nobis struuntur innumeris modis, non secus atque variis & miris artibus adulteræ insidiari solent incautis hominibus, quos ad συνꙋσίαν solicitatos cupiunt, tametsi postea voti sui compotes factæ, os suum tergant, quasi nihil quicquam mali admiserint, & innocentissimæ, ac honestissimæ haberi velint.

TERGENS OS SVVM) Σεμνολογία. Aliud dicitur, aliud intelligitur. Vide supra 16.

## 30:22
BY A SERVANT WHEN HE SHALL REIGN) It is a saying of Menander: Δούλῳ γενομένῳ δοῦλε δουλεύειν φοβοῦ· Ἀμνημονεῖ γὰρ ταῦρθ· ἀργήσας ζυγῷ. For there is nothing harsher than a base man when he rises to a high position.

Latin:

PER SERVUM CVM REGNAVERIT) Menandri dictum est: Δούλῳ γενομένῳ δοῦλε δουλεύειν φοβοῦ· Ἀμνημονεῖ γὰρ ταῦρθ· ἀργήσας ζυγῷ. nam Asperius nihil est humili cum surgit in altum.

## 30:23
AND BY A MAIDSERVANT WHEN SHE SHALL BE HEIR TO HER MISTRESS) Hesiod: Μήποτε δουλεύσασα γυνὴ εἰς λέκτρον ἵκοιτο.

Now furthermore we are warned to industry and diligence in performing duty, v. 24, by the example of four very small, but most wise, living creatures, and

regarding fortitude and constancy in honest matters, fearless, by the example of four creatures trusting in their own strength, walking fearlessly v. 24. FOUR ARE THE SMALLEST OF THE EARTH (in Hebrew, small of the earth, according to the nature of the language, the smallest of the earth are, as the great nobles of the city 2 Kings 8:6, the rich people, the most wealthy Ps. 45:13) AND THEY ARE WISER THAN THE WISE (their sagacity and skill is understood, which is like wisdom Job 39:20. v. 25. ANTS, A WEAK PEOPLE (not strong; as locusts are called a people because of their number and troop Joel 2:2) WHICH PREPARES FOOD FOR ITSELF IN HARVEST (sagacity in the timeliness of the season, and providence for the future) v. 26. THE CONEY (others, rabbits, such as Tostatus, Pagninus, Arias Montanus, Cajetanus, Mercerus. Jerome, Epist. ad Sun. & Fretell., explain it as an animal which is called ἀρκ[τόμ] in Palestine, and has been accustomed to dwell always in the caverns of rocks and the holes of the earth: Compare Lev. 11:5. Deut. 14:7. Psalm 104:18.) A FEEBLE PEOPLE (a people not strong) WHICH PLACES ITS BED IN THE ROCK (Psalm 104:18, which sagacity pertains to the security and convenience of the place) verse 27.

THE LOCUST HAS NO KING, AND IT GOES FORTH BY ITS TROOPS: (That kind of locust which also served for food Matt. 3:4, unknown to us, has its name from devouring Exod. 10:4, and it used to march in a great troop in Palestine and other Asiatic and African places, but in troops Judg. 6:5, ch. 7:12, Nah. 3:15, not divided, but as if by a given signal joined together, and in certain order Joel 1:7, ch. 2:7, חצץ כלו all of it gathered, the locust, namely. Aben-Ezra, Pagninus, Mercerus, Junius render: Compare all: which regard the order to be observed in the Republic and communion:) Grotius on this passage thus:

Latin:

ET PER ANCILLAM CVM HÆRES FVERIT DOMINÆ SVÆ) Hesiodus: Μήποτε δουλεύσασα γυνὴ εἰς λέκτρον ἵκοιτο.

Jam porro monemur ad industriam, & solertiam in officio præstandam v. 24. exemplo quatuor animantium minimorum, at maxime sapientium, &

ad fortitudinem & constantiam in rebus honestis intrepidam, exemplo quatuor virium suarum fiducia intrepide incedentium v. 24. QVATUOR SUNT MINIMA TERRÆ (in Ebr. parva terræ, juxta linguæ indolem minima terræ sunt, ut magni urbis optimates 2. Reg. 8, 6. divites populi ditissimi Pf. 45. v. 13.) ET IPSA SUNT SAPIENTIORA SAPIENTIBUS (naturalis intelligitur eorum sagacitas, & solertia, quæ sapientiæ instar est Job. 39, 20. v. 25. FORMICÆ, POPULUS INFIRMUS (non fortis; ut locustæ populus ob numerum, & agmen Joel. 2, 2. dicuntur.) QUI PRÆPARAT IN MESSE CIBUM SIBI (sagacitas in temporis oportunitate, & providentia de futuro) v. 26. LEPUSCULUS (alii cuniculi, utpote Tostatus, Pagninus, Ariæmontanus, Cajetanus, Mercerus. Hieron. Epist. ad Sun. & Fretell. de animali, quod ἀρκ[τόμ] in Palæstina dicatur, & semper in cavernis petrarum & terræ foveis habitare consueverit, explicant: Confer. Lev. 11, 5. Deut. 14, 7. Psal. 104. 18.) PLEBS INVALIDA (populus non fortis) QUÆ COLLOCAT IN PETRA CUBILE SUUM (Psalm. 104. versu 18. quæ sagacitas ad loci securitatem & commoditatem pertinet) versu 27.

REGEM LOCUSTA NON HABET, ET EGREDITUR PER TURMAS SUAS: (Lo- custarum genus istud quod etiam esui inserviebat Matth. 3, 4. nobis incognitum a depascendo no- men habet Exod. 10, 4. magnoque agmine incede- bat in Palæstina aliisque locis Asiaticis & Africa- nis, sed turmatim Jud. 6, 5. c. 7, 12. Nah. 3, 15. non divisum, sed velut signo dato conjunctim, certoque ordine Joël. 1, 7. c. 2, 7. חצץ כלו adunata tota ipsa, locusta scil. Aben-Ezra, Pagninus, Mercerus, Junius reddunt: Conferte omnes: quæ ordinem respiciunt in Republ. & communione observandum:) Gro- tius h. l. ita:

## 30:27
Verse 27.

THE LOCUST HAS NO KING, AND IT GOES FORTH ALL TOGETHER BY ITS TROOPS) It is indeed an animal ἀγελαῖον (gregarious), but ἀβασίλευτον (kingless), which we also had concerning the ant above 6:7.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

REGEM LOCUSTA NON HABET, ET EGRE- DITUR VNIVERSA PER TVRMAS SVAS) Est animal ἀγελαῖον quidem, sed ἀβασίλευτον, quod & de formica habui- mus supra 6, 7.

## 30:28
Verse 28. THE LIZARD TAKES HOLD WITH ITS HANDS (others, since the lizard is not found in the palaces of Kings, more correctly with the Chaldean, the spider takes hold with its hands: The word שממית is a ἅπαξ λεγομένη (hapax legomenon), by the Hebrews it is considered the name of a certain insect among the flying things: Concerning the spider also Clarius, Vatablus, Mercerus, Marcus Marinus, Junius, and B. Luther, the Belgians) AND DWELLS IN THE HOUSES OF KINGS (whose sagacity is discovered in its structure and operation, concerning whose thread, straw, and web See Voss. lib. 4 de Idol. cap. 73, & 43, although it may be useless, and cared for by no one, yet it even finds a seat in Royal palaces:) from which it is also evident that wisdom is not situated in the quantity or bulk of the body, but in skill, and skillful action, by which each one provides for himself the necessities: and that divine wisdom shines forth even in the smallest things. Smaller animals, says Tertullian, lib. 1 contr. Marc. cap. 14, the greatest craftsman has increased by industry with talents or virtues. Imitate (if you can) the buildings of the bee, the stables of the ant, the nets of the spider, the threads of the silkworm. We are warned, however, especially here, that we should first provide for ourselves food, then for comfortable housing, and furthermore live in peace and concord with our neighbor, and retain our station, and finally, devoted to some craft, avoid idleness. These are Grotius's words on this verse:

Verse 28.

THE STELLIO LEANS ON ITS HANDS, AND DWELLS IN THE KING'S PALACES) So also the Greeks, καλαβώτης. This animal the Greeks today call σαμιάμινθον. It is clearly from the Hebrew which we have here שממית. He calls the feet hands, which it uses instead of hands. It dwells in the king's palaces, i.e., in the doorways and windows, as Pliny teaches, 30, 3.

There follow therefore at last four that walk well, v. 29. THERE ARE THREE WHICH WALK WELL: (doing their walking well) AND A FOURTH WHICH GOES HAPPILY (or rather four doing well in their gait or going) verse 30. A LION, THE STRONGEST OF BEASTS (Cf. 2 Sam. 17, 10.) SHALL NOT FEAR AT THE MEETING OF ANY (nor does it turn back on account of any, to wit, animal. Cf. Isa. 31, 4. by which we are warned that we should not desist or recede from an honest purpose on account of intervening obstacles, but should break through them with an unconquered and strong spirit) A COCK GIRT ABOUT THE LOINS (thus the Chaldean, LXX, Aquila, and Theodotion explain the word זרזיר as a cock: Junius and Tremellius, Piscator, and Füller, book 5, Miscell. ch. 12, interpret it as a horse: B. Luther, with R. Levi, Pagninus, Vatablus, Mercerus, Marcus Marinus, Lavater, and the Belgians, interpret it as a lelapus, that is, a greyhound: which is slender in the loins, and as it were restricted, or girded, since זרז among the Chaldeans means to gird, to constrain: whence it is not incorrectly said that continence is signified here, by which we restrain carnal desires, and are rendered more apt for the course of piety) AND A RAM (or the he-goat of the goats Gen. 32. verse 14. Who goes before the flock according to that saying: The he-goat himself is the leader of the flock, whence Leaders and Magnates are compared to it Is. 14. verse 9. Ezech. 39. verse 18. Dan. 8. verse 5. 8. Zach. 10. verse 3. The particle וא is not here disjunctive, but copulative, as Lev. 4. verse 22. 23. chap. 16. v. 41. unless it is clearly redundant, as it seemed to Vatablus and Pagninus: But by this figure is noted prudence in predecessors and leaders, that they may happily precede and moderate the flock. Varro says, the ram is the eye of the whole flock. Augustine calls the Apostles the rams of the Lord's flock) AND THERE IS NO KING WHO RESISTS HIM. In Heb. and a King against whom no one rises: who, with the three preceding, is either compared for the sake of imitation, by reason of fortitude, continence or temperance and prudence that he may walk well, or is joined to them, on account of the similarity of an equally excellent gait; by which manner is particularly expressed justice, which most commends his way and government, and strengthens the throne of the same. The word אלקום is not without difficulty, which some as a proper name of Solomon, or of another King, others deny to cohere with the word מלך on account of the Rebia distinction, and say it is a compound word from אל not, and קום to rise, i.e., against whom no one rises, that is, does not dare, or is able to rise, which is the fairly common explanation.

Latin:

Vers. 28. STELLIO MANIBUS NITITUR (alii quum stellio in palatiis Regum non invenia- tur, rectius cum Chaldæo, aranea manibus appre- hendit: Vox שממית ἅπαξ λεγομένη ab Ebræis nomen habetur insecti cujusdam ex volucribus: De aranea etiam Clarius, Vatablus, Mercerus, Mar- cus Marinus, Junius, & B. Lutherus, Belgæ) ET MORATUR IN ÆDIBUS REGUM (cujus sagacitas in structura & operatione deprehenditur, de cujus filo, stramine & trama Vid. Voss. l. 4. de Idol. cap. 73, & 43. etsi inutilis sit, nec curetur ab ullo, tamen etiam sedem invenit in Regiis pala- tiis:) è quibus id etiam constat sapientiam non si- tam esse in quantitate vel mole corporis, sed in so- lertia, & solerti actione, qua quisque sibi de neces- sariis prospicit: ac divinam sapientiam etiam in minimis elucere. Animalia minutiora, ait Ter- tul. l. 1. contr. Marc. cap. 14. maximus artifex de industria ingeniis aut virtutibus ampliavit. Imi- tare (si potes) apis ædificia, formicæ stabula, ara- neæ retia, bombycis stamina. Monemur autem im- primis hic, ut nobis primum de victu, tum de commoda habitatione prospiciamus, ac porro in pace & concordia cum proximo vivamus, ac statio- nem nostram retineamus, denique artificio alicui dediti otium vitemus. Grotii de hoc versu hæc sunt:

Vers. 28.

STELLIO MANIBVS NITITVR, ET MORATVR IN ÆDIBVS REGIS) Sic & Græci, καλαβώτης. Id ani- mal hodie Græci vocant σαμιάμινθον. Id plane est ex He- bræo quod hîc habemus שממית. Manus vocat pedes, quibus ea pro manibus utitur. Moratur in ædibus regis, i. e. in ostiis & fenestris, ut docet Plinius 30, 3.

Sequuntur ergo tandem quatuor bene gradi- entia v. 29. TRIA SUNT QVÆ BENE GRA- DIUNTUR: (gressum bene facientia) ET QUARTUM QUOD INCEDIT FELICI- TER (imo quatuor bene facientia incessu vel eundo) vers. 30. LEO FORTISSIMUS BESTIARUM (Conf. 2. Sam. 17, 10.) AD NULLIUS PAVE- BIT OCCURSUM (nec convertitur propter ullum scil. animal. Conf. Esa. 31, 4. quo monemur ut propter intervenientia obstacula à proposito ho- nesto ne desistamus aut recedamus, sed invicto & forti animo ea perrumpamus) GALLUS SUC- CINCTUS LUMBOS SUOS (ita Chald. LXX. Aquila & Theodot. vocem זרזיר de gallo exponunt: de equo interpretantur Jun. & Tremell. Piscator, Füller l. 5. Miscell. c. 12. de lelape, id est cane lepori- no, B. Luther. cum R. Levi, Pagnino, Vatablo, Mer- cero, Marco Marino, Lavatero, Belgis: qui lum- bis gracilis est, & quasi restrictus, aut præcinctus, quum זרז apud Chald. sit accinxit, constrinxit: unde continentiam hic significari, qua carnales restrin- gimus cupiditates, & habiliores ad cursum pieta- tis reddimur, non inrecte dicitur) ET ARIES (vel hircus caprarum Gen. 32. versu 14. Qui gregem antecedit juxta illud: Dux gregis ipse caper, unde Duces & Magnates ei conferuntur Es. 14. versu 9. Ezech. 39. vers. 18. Dan. 8. vers. 5. 8. Zach. 10. vers. 3. Particula וא non est hic disjunctiva, sed copulativa, ut Lev. 4. vers. 22. 23. cap. 16. v. 41. nisi plane redun- det, ut Vatablo, & Pagnino visum: Notatur autem hac figura prudentia in antecessoribus, & ducibus, ut feliciter gregem præcedant, & moderentur. Varro totius gregis, inquit, oculus est aries. Augustinus Apostolos vocat arietes gregis dominicæ) NEC EST REX QVI RESISTAT EI. In Ebr. & Rex in quem nemo insurgit: qui cum tribus præcedentibus ratione fortitudinis, continentiæ vel temperantiæ & prudentiæ ut bene gradiatur, vel confertur, ad imi- tationem, vel conjungitur, ob similitudinem pari- ter egregii incessus; quo pacto peculiariter expri- mitur justitia, quæ maxime commendat ejus viam & gubernationem, ac firmat thronum ejusdem. Vox אלקום difficultate non caret, quam ceu no- men proprium Salomonis, aut alterius Regis non- nulli, alii ob distinctionem רביע Rebia cohærere cum voce מלך negant, & compositam vocem esse ajunt ex אל non, & קום surgere, q. d. adversus quem non surgit quisquam, id est, non audet, vel valet surgere, quæ sere communis est explicatio.

## 30:32
Vers. 32. THERE IS ONE WHO APPEARS FOOLISH AFTER HE HAS BEEN LIFTED UP ON HIGH: FOR IF HE HAD UNDERSTOOD, HE WOULD HAVE PLACED HIS HAND UPON HIS MOUTH.

To these admonitions concerning the ordering of life, to be observed both in common and in public function, is subjoined a rule concerning penitence, on account of a transgression very common to mortals. For the Hebrew text has it far otherwise here, thus, as Cornelius admits, it is to be rendered: If thou hast acted foolishly in lifting thyself up, and if thou hast thought (of something wicked) hand to mouth (immediately restrain the mouth, or) silently and wisely think, by what reason thou mayest amend and correct that which thou hast foolishly done or thought. Although indeed Cornelius may subjoin another sense for the sake of his Vulgate: and therefore the LXX. Version, although it goes into all other things (since it has it thus: if thou shalt pour thyself out in joy, and shalt extend thy hands with a fight, thou shalt be dishonored (he strives to twist it, yet in the Hebrew, which alone is authentic, as Mr. Dr. Geier most rightly observes, is persuaded the timely amendment and penitence of an error once admitted, refraining oneself from all excuse, and stubborn defense, or altercation: If thou hast acted foolishly not from ignorance, but from pride and stubborn insolence, and hast thought of evil against the love of God or neighbor, or hast plotted it, hand to mouth, do not excuse it, but rather restrain the lip with a finger, acknowledging with serious penitence the sin, which has either already been committed, or thought and deliberated in thy mind, and repenting of it. Conf. Job. 39.

v. 34. Mich. 7, 16. Therefore it is added v. 33. Just as the presser of milk brings forth butter, and the vehement wiper of the nose brings forth blood (Vulg. wrongly substituted breasts in their place, i.e., he who strongly presses the breasts to elicit milk, presses out butter, and he who vehemently wipes the nose, elicits blood) so the presser of wraths brings forth strife. Indeed if anyone wishes to defend his foolishness, not to acknowledge it, quarrels must arise, with stirred-up anger, which seems to be wiped and pressed out by angry words, not otherwise than through the emulsion of milk butter, and through the wiping of the nostrils blood is pressed out: which sense Jansen and Cornel. a Lap do not deny to agree with the Hebrew text. Mercerus: As by pressed milk butter is pressed out, and by the nose being pressed and wiped rather hard blood is elicited, which is often pernicious to the one wiping: So stirred-up anger (which he calls the compression of anger) excites contention: and therefore one must beware, lest thou be stirred to anger against anyone, or move bile in anyone: because from thence arises strife, the cause of many and great evils. Cartwright somewhat differently: One must diligently beware, lest being puffed up in our minds, we defend what is unworthy of us. But many, especially those powerful in authority or talent, under the guise of fortitude and constancy, do not wish to retract whatever they have once decreed (although against right and equity). Nor does this happen only to the wicked Dan. 6, 8. but also to the pious 2. Sam. 19, 29. But of all the fruits of pride, strifes are most to be avoided. For the proud man is easily inflamed with anger, but from anger one comes to quarrels, from quarrels to hands, and thus to slaughter. To which that double comparison of equals looks, which is proposed in the last verse. For just as from the pressure of milk its whole goodness is lost, and by the pressure of the nose blood, in which is life, is pressed out: so by contentions both of mind and body goods are exhausted and consumed. See Galat. 5. verse 15.

SECTION IV. Maternal admonitions given to Solomon concerning those things which are to be avoided and cared for in Government, and concerning the virtuous woman.

Latin:

Vers. 32. EST QVI STULTUS APPAREAT POSTQVAM ELEVATUS EST IN SUBLI- ME: SI ENIM INTELLEXISSET, ORI SUO IMPOSUISSET MANUM.

Monitis istis de vita instituenda, cum in com- muni, tum in functione publica observandis subdi- tur regula de pœnitentia, ob transgressionem mor- talibus valde communem. Ebræus enim textus longe aliter hic habet, ita, fatente Cornelio, red- dendus: Si stulte egisti in elevando te, & si cogitasti (scelerati quid) manum ad os (statim os compefci- to, vel) silenter & sapienter cogita, qua ratione id quod stulte egisti vel cogitasti, emendes, & cor- rigas. Quanquam vero Cornelius alium sensum in gratiam Vulgatæ suæ subjiciat: eoque LXX. Versionem, etsi in alia omnia euntem (quum ita habeat: si profuderis te in lætitia, & extenderis ma- nus tuas cum pugna, inhonoraberis (detorquere sata- gat, in Ebræo tamen, qui solus authenticus, ob- servante rectissime Dn. D. Geiero, suadetur tem- pestiva erroris semel admissi emendatio ac pœnitentia, ab omni excusatione, pertinatique defensione, vel altercatione sibi temperans: Si non ex ignorantia, sed fastu & insolentia pertinaci stulte egisti, & ma- lum adversus dilectionem Dei vel proximi cogi- tasti, aut machinatus es, manum ad os, non excu- sa id, sed digito potius compesce labellum, seria pœnitudine peccatum, quod vel commissum jam, vel cogitatum & deliberatum est apud animum tuum agnoscens, & de eo resipiscens. Conf. Job. 39.

v. 34. Mich. 7, 16. Ideo additur v. 33. Quemadmo- dum expressor lactis educit butyrum, & vehemens emunctor naris educit sanguinem (Vulg. perperam ubera nec suo loco substituit h. m. qui autem forti- ter premit ubera ad eliciendum lac, exprimit buty- rum, & qui vehementer emungit, elicit sanguinem) sic expressor furorum educit litem. Nimirum si quis stultitiam suam defendere, non agnoscere velit, ri- xas oriri oportet, commota iracundia, quæ emun- gi videtur & exprimi verbis iracundis, non secus atque per emulsionem lactis butyrum, & per emun- ctionem narium sanguis exprimitur: quem sensum Ebraico textui convenire Jansen. & Cornel. a Lap haud diffitentur. Mercerus: Ut compresso lacte ex primitur butyrum, & naso compresso & durius emun- cto elicitur sanguis, quod emungenti sæpe perniciosum est : Sic ira concitata (quod compressionem iræ appel- lat) excitatur contentio : ideoque cavendum, ne ira conciteris in quemquam, vel cuiquam bilem moveas : quia inde lis oritur multorum & magnorum malorum causa. Paulo aliter Cartwrightus : Sedulo caven- dum est, ne animis elati, quod nobis indignum sit, defendamus. Multi autem, præsertim auctoritate, vel ingenio pollentes sub specie fortitudinis, & constantiæ quicquid semel (quamvis contra jus, & æquum) de- creverunt, retractare nolunt. Nec solis improbis hoc accidit Dan. 6, 8. sed piis etiam 2. Sam. 19, 29. Sed ex omnibus superbiæ fructibus maxime lites cavendæ sunt. Nam superbus facile ira inflammatur, ex ira vero ad jurgia, ex jurgiis ad manus, atque ita ad cædem devenitur. Quo spectat duplex illa compara- tio parium quæ in postremo versu proponitur. Quem- admodum enim ex pressura lactis bonitas ejus tota de- perditur, & pressura nasi sanguis, in quo vita est, ex- primitur: sic contentionibus tum animi tum corporis bona exhauriuntur, & absumuntur. Vid. Galat. 5. versu 15.

SECTIO IV. Monita materna Salomoni data de iis, quæ in Regimine vitanda, & curanda, deque muliere virtuosa.

## 31:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXXI. & the last.

On avoiding venereal lusts and martial counsels, as also luxurious revelries: and on pursuing beneficence and justice, especially towards the forsaken and the poor. Subjoined are the praises of a virtuous woman by reason of her fidelity to her husband, her diligence in the household, and her proper adornment, especially spiritual, and the reward of praise promised for her life, which is to be preferred above all things, especially on account of the fear of the Lord, and to be celebrated on every side.

Ver. 1.

THE WORDS OF KING LEMUEL ] Most people understand this of Solomon, whom they say had eight names: just as among the poets: Πολυώνυμός ἐστιν Ἀπόλλων. But certainly, since these follow the collection made by the order of Hezekiah, how much more probable is it that these were collected (מַשָּׂא as we have already said at 30, 1) from those things which his mother Abi or Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah, a man undoubtedly wise, had taught him, having received them from his father. WITH WHICH HIS MOTHER TAUGHT HIM ] Thus Euripides: Οὐκ ἐμὸς ὁ μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐμῆς μητρὸς πάρα. For there are also many who are mother-taught.

THERE is no reason why one should depart from the common opinion. Pineda and Cornelius a Lapide say that all Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins declare Lemuel to be Solomon: for no other King is found among the Hebrews or foreigners who is called Lemuel. The reason which Grotius pretends for his new opinion is of no moment: For even if these Proverbs follow those which are said to have been collected by the men of King Hezekiah, yet those also acknowledge Solomon himself as the author, as noted above: Nor did any of the Hebrews, to whom Grotius otherwise attributes much, hold Lemuel to be King Hezekiah: or he wrote these things at his mother's admonitions: all have understood Solomon and his mother Bathsheba. To which the Christians also agree: There is no doubt, says Mercerus, that this Lemuel is Solomon, because we do not read that there was any other King Lemuel in Israel. Furthermore, it is probable that Solomon was taught these things which are said in this place, and similar precepts and admonitions, by his mother Bathsheba, who was pious, whether before he took up the Kingdom or after, just as he said above at the beginning of the book, ch. 4, verse 10, that he was educated by his Father. But since Solomon is called Lemuel or Lamuel, the Hebrews bring forward various reasons, as does Cornelius in this place. Aben-Ezra wishes it to be said as it were למו אל, to them GOD: because the Israelites in his time had and worshipped the one God. But that reason, being rather cold, is deservedly rejected by Mercerus. Others wish למו אל, as it is called in verse 4, to be the same as of God, or to God, who is of God, and pertains to God, because ל is a prefix, to which the expletive syllable מו is accustomed to be added, see Job 27:14, ch. 29:21, namely that Solomon was of God, consecrated to God, and beloved by God, whence he was called Jedidiah, 2 Sam. 12:25, the peculiar treasure of God: Which is the opinion of R. Solomon; also approved by Mercerus. Jansenius wishes it to be signified, to him GOD: or with him GOD: and that he was so called by his mother, when she saw that God was with him. And indeed, since that name is placed in the words of the mother in verse 4, it is likely that Solomon was so named by his mother, with a name that was akin to his own proper name, or with his proper name slightly inflected, as mothers are accustomed to take delight in a certain inflection of the names of their children, and especially where the significance of the inflected name is ominous, pious, and pleasing. That name seemed sweet to her, because she desired this Solomon of hers to be Lemuel, the peculiar treasure of God, and consecrated to God, and according to the name שמואל, who was said to be asked of GOD, which seems to her to have been sacred and very pleasing, because David, having been raised to the pinnacle of the kingdom by Samuel, she alluded to it, and called him by the change of one little letter למואל, that he ought to be of God, and pertain peculiarly to God, in which she also without doubt had respect to the Messiah, of whom Solomon was a notable type; inasmuch as he is of God, in a most eminent manner, the Son of God, beloved of God, consecrated by God. To which it contributes that certain Hebrews wish Solomon to be so called because he sat upon the throne of Immanuel. That Bathsheba taught Solomon these things from his tender years, and thus instructed him concerning the Messiah, the bland appellation of Lemuel (such as are customary for mothers towards children who are still tender) shows, as Cartwright observes in this place.

Latin:

CAPUT XXXI. & ultimum.

De cavendis libidinibus Venereis & consiliis Martialibus, ut & comessationibus luxu- riosis : deque sectanda beneficentia & ju- stitia adversus desertos imprimis atque pauperes. Subjiciuntur mulieris virtuosæ elogia ratione fidelitatis in maritum, stre- nuitatis in familia, ornatusque proprii, maxime spiritualis, & præmii laudis pro- missæ vitæ, imprimis ob timorem Domini omnibus præferendæ, & undique cele- brandæ.

Vers. 1.

VERBA LAMUELIS REGIS ] Plerique de Salomone hoc accipiunt, quem ajunt fuisse octinominem : nimirum sicut apud Poetas : Πολυώνυμός ἐστιν Ἀπόλλων. At certe cum hæc sequantur collectionem Ezechiæ jussu fa- ctam, quanto probabilius est hæc esse collecta (מַשָּׂא ut jam diximus ad 30, 1.) ex iis quæ mater ipsius Abi vel Abiia, Zachariæ viri haud dubie sapientis filia, ipsum docue- rat a patre accepta. QVA ERVDIVIT EVM MATER SUA ] Sic Euri- pides : Οὐκ ἐμὸς ὁ μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐμῆς μητρὸς πάρα. Sunt enim & multi μητροδίδακτοι.

NON est causa, cur discedatur a communi sen- tentia. Omnes Hebræos, Græcos & Latinos La- muelem esse Salomonem dicere, ait Pineda & Corne- lius a Lapide: nec enim ullus alius apud Ebræos, vel exteros invenitur Rex, qui dictus sit Lamuel. Ratio, quam novæ suæ sententiæ prætexit Gro- tius, nullius est momenti : Etsi enim sequantur hæc Proverbia ista, quæ collecta dicuntur a viris Ezechiæ Regis, ista tamen ipsum etiam Salomo- nem auctorem agnoscere supra monitum : Ne- que ullus Ebræorum, quibus alias multum tribuit Grotius, Lemuelem pro Ezechia Rege habuit: aut matris ejus monitis hæc adscripsit: omnes Salo- monem, ejusque matrem Bathsebam intellexere. Quibus etiam Christiani adstipulantur: Non est dubium, inquit Mercerus, hunc Lamuelem Salomo- nem esse, quia non alium legimus fuisse Lamuelem Regem in Israel. Præterea probabile est, a matre Bath- seba, quæ pia fuit, edoctum Salomonem his, quæ hoc loco dicuntur, & consimilibus præceptis ac monitis, si- ve antequam Regnum capesseret, sive post, quemad- modum & supra sub libri initium c. 4. versu 10. dixit a Patre eruditum esse. Cum autem Lemuel vel La- muel dictus sit Salomon, varias afferunt rationes Ebræi, ut & Cornelius in h. l. Aben-Ezra dictum vult quasi למו אל illis DEUS: quod unicum Deum ejus tempore habuerint & coluerint Israeli- tæ. Sed ea ratio, ut frigidior, merito reproba- tur a Mercero. Alii למו אל uti vers. 4. vocatur, idem esse volunt, quod Dei, vel Deo, qui Dei est, & ad Deum pertinet, quia ל præfixum est, cui מו syllaba expletiva addi solet, vid. Job. 27, 14. c. 29, 21. quod nempe Salomo Dei fuerit, Deo consecratus, & dilectus a Deo, unde Jedidiah dictus 2. Sam. 12. v. 25. peculium Dei: Quæ R. Salomonis est sententia; Mercero etiam probata. Jansenius vult significari, ipsi DEUS: vel cum ipso DEUS: atque ita a matre vocatum esse, cum viderit, Deum esse cum eo. Et sane quum in verbis matris nomen illud ponatur vers. 4. verisimile est, Salomonem ita nuncupatum a matre esse, nomine, quod proprio ipsius nomini affine erat, vel proprio nomine paululum inflexo, ut solent matres nominum liberorum quadam in- flexione delectari, ac cumprimis, ubi ominosa, pia, ac grata est nominis inflexi significatio. Suave ipsi id nomen visum fuit, quod ipsum optarrit Le- muel, Dei peculium, Deoque consecratum hunc Salo- monem suum voluerit, & juxta nomen שמואל qui a DEO postulatus dicebatur, quod ipsi videtur sacrum, ac perquam gratum fuisse, quia David a Samuele ad regni fastigium evectus, alluserit, eun- dem unius literulæ commutatione למואל quod Dei esse debeat, & ad Deum peculiariter pertineat, nuncuparit, in quo etiam sine dubio respectum habuit ad Messiam, cujus insignis typus Salomo erat; utpote qui Dei est, eminentissima ratione, Dei Filius, dilectus Dei, consecratus a Deo. Quo facit, quod Ebræi quidam Salomonem ita dictum volunt, quod sederit super solio Immanuel. Bethsebam Salo- monem a teneris annis hæc docuisse, adeoque ita de Messia instituisse, blanda Lamuelis appellatio (quales matribus erga liberos adhuc tenellos usita- tæ sunt) ostendit, observante Cartwrighto in h. l.

## 31:1
THE VISION WITH WHICH HIS MOTHER TAUGHT HIM.

Solomon teaches that these things were received from his mother, which he himself arranged in this way, whence in verse 1 the same words are called those of King Lemuel. Namely, if you look at them materially, they proceeded from his mother Bathsheba; if formally, as they are arranged here, they are to be attributed to Solomon. But they are called משא, a vision or prophecy directed to the instruction of a son: Whence it is gathered that Bathsheba was a Prophetess: which Pineda, Jansenius, Baynus, Cornel. a Lapid., Voetius in part 1, Disp. Sel. page 43, and others establish concerning her.

But first there is a bland address, by which the mother was accustomed to win attention for herself: What, my son, and what, son of my womb, and what, son of my vows? What, I say, shall I most commend to you, my son so beloved, and so sought by vows, and most desired: whence that word בר and the name of son is repeated three times, so that he may listen more attentively, and observe these maternal admonitions more reverently.

Furthermore, before all things, she commends the pursuit of chastity to her son, whom she undoubtedly noticed was most inclined to venereal matters, whose fall she also perhaps foresaw through the Prophetic Spirit.

Latin:

VISIO QVA ERUDIVIT EUM MATER SUA.

A matre hæc accepta docet Salomo, quæ ipse ita digessit, unde vers. 1. dicta eadem verba Lamue- lis Regis. Nimirum si spectes ea materialiter profe- cta a matre Bathseba, si formaliter, prout hic di- gesta Salomoni tribuenda sunt. Dicuntur autem משא visio vel prophetia ad eruditionem filii dire- cta: Unde Prophetissam fuisse Bathsebam colligi- tur: quod de ea Pineda, Jansenius, Baynus Cornel. a Lapid. Voetius p. 1. Disp. Sel. pag. 43, aliique sta- tuunt.

Primum vero blanda compellatio habetur, qua attentionem sibi sueverit conciliare mater: Quid fili mi, & quid fili uteri mei, & quid fili voto- rum meorum? Quid, inquam, maxime tibi com- mendabo tam dilecto, tamque votis expetito, & desideratissimo filio meo: unde trina vice repetitur illud בר & nomen filii, ut eo attentius audiat, & reverentius observet hæcce materna monita.

Porro ante omnia castitatis studium commen- dat filio, quem ad rem Veneream sine dubio ma- xime propensum animadvertit, cujus etiam fors lapsum per Spiritum Propheticum prævidit.

## 31:2
Vers. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

## 31:3
Verse 3. DO NOT GIVE TO WOMEN YOUR SUBSTANCE (in Hebrew it is, your strength) thus prohibiting primarily lust, so that he does not give himself to it, as that by which the strength of mind and body is exhausted: AND YOUR RICHES (in Heb. & your ways) TO DESTROY KINGS. Concerning which he is warned to avoid Martial and warlike counsels: since according to the interpretation of some, two precepts occur here, one about not squandering one's own strength through women, the other about not directing counsels and plans toward the destruction of other Kings, as the mother inculcated in him a zeal partly for chastity, partly for tranquility, peace, and concord. Which does not seem inconsistent: because thus there is no need for any supplement, as is added in the explanation of Mercer. In the latter member, with the prior words repeated ἀπὸ κοινῶ (Do not give to women) your ways: WHICH IS ENOUGH to destroy Kings. Which counsel of peace Solomon followed, and made the kingdom peaceful, opulent, and fortunate, as Cornel. a Lap. has it here. Grotius in this place thus:

DO NOT GIVE TO WOMEN YOUR SUBSTANCE, AND RICHES TO DESTROY KINGS] It seems to be an ellipsis, so that the sense may be, and your riches to those who are very apt to overthrow kings: for certainly Πολλοὶ γυναικῶν δυςυχοῦσιν εἵνεκεν. and I think the errors of Solomon are especially regarded.

The third precept v. 4. concerning avoiding carousing, and thus the pursuit of sobriety and temperance in food, holds it thus: DO NOT TO KINGS O LEMUEL! DO NOT TO KINGS GIVE WINE: BECAUSE THERE IS NO SECRET WHERE DRUNKENNESS REIGNS. Here the Vulgate differs much from the sources: For in Hebrew it is, It is not for Kings O Lemuel, it is not for Kings to drink wine: and it is not for princes to drink Sechar (Strong drink or intoxicating beverage c. 20, 1.) the word אַל not, seems to be placed for אֵין by apocope: as R. Salom. and R. Aben-Ezra note, concerning which see Mercer in this place v. 5. AND LEST PERHAPS THEY DRINK, AND FORGET JUDGMENTS, AND CHANGE THE CAUSE OF THE CHILDREN OF THE POOR. In Heb. it is: lest perhaps he drink, and forget the statute, (that is, lest he drink in such a way that he forgets, or even that any of them should hold the Statute as nothing) and change the judgment of all the children of affliction (that is, of the afflicted.) Indeed, a twofold cause of the precept is handed down, both from the forgetting of laws to be observed, and from the corruption of the administration of justice. For to those who live in drunkenness and luxury (as Chrysostom says) the day is turned into nocturnal darkness, not indeed by the sun being extinguished, but by their own mind being obscured through drunkenness. Drunkenness is the alienation of right reason, and delirium, and according to the soul, the destruction of health. Cf. Lev. 10, 9. Syr. 31, 35.

Latin:

Vers. 3. NE DEDERIS MULIERIBUS SUBSTANTIAM TUAM (in Ebræo est, fortitu- dinem tuam) prohibens ita imprimis libidinem, ne illi se dedat, utpote qua robur animi atque cor- poris exhauritur: ET DIVITIAS TUAS (in Ebr. & vias tuas) AD DELENDOS REGES. Quo de cavendis consiliis Martialibus & bellicis monetur: quum juxta nonnullorum interpreta- tionem duo præcepta hic occurrant, alterum de non profundendo per mulieres robore proprio, alterum de non dirigendis consiliis & rationibus ad aliorum Regum perditionem, ut partim castita- tis, partim tranquillitatis, pacis & concordiæ studium mater ei inculcarit. Quod non inconcinnum vi- detur: quia ita nullo supplemento opus est, quem- admodum in explicatione Merceri additur. In po- steriori membro verbis prioribus ἀπὸ κοινῶ re- petitis (Ne dederis mulieribus) vias tuas: QVOD SATIS EST ad delendum Reges. Quod consi- lium pacis sequutus Salomo, regnum effecit paci- ficum, opulentum, & fortunatum, ut hic habet Cornel. a Lap. Grotius h. l. ita:

NE DEDERIS MULIERIBUS SUBSTANTIAM TUAM, ET DIVITIAS AD DELENDOS REGES] Vi- detur esse ἐλλειψις, ut sensus sit, & divitias tuas illis quæ valde aptæ sunt ad evertendos reges: nam certe Πολλοὶ γυναικῶν δυςυχοῦσιν εἵνεκεν. & puto præcipue respici errores Salomonis.

Tertium præceptum v. 4. de vitandis comes- sationibus, adeoque studio sobrietatis & temperan- tiæ in victu ita habet: NOLI REGIBUS ô LA- MUEL! NOLI REGIBUS DARE VINUM: QVIA NULLUM SECRETUM EST UBI REGNAT EBRIETAS. Multum hic discre- pat Vulgata a fontibus: In Ebræo enim est, Non est Regum ô Lemoel, non est Regum bibere vinum: & principum non est Sechar (Sicera seu potus inebrians c. 20, 1.) vox אַל non, videtur esse posita pro אֵין per apocopen: notantibus R. Salom. & R. Aben- Ezra, de quo vid. Mercer. in h. l. v. 5. ET NE FORTE BIBANT, ET OBLIVISCANTUR JUDICIORUM, ET MUTENT CAUSAM FILIORUM PAUPERIS. In Ebr. est: ne forte bibat, & obliviscatur statuti, (id est, ne ita bibat, ut obliviscatur, vel etiam susque deque habeat quis- quam eorum Statuti) & mutet judicium omnium filiorum afflictionis (id est afflictorum.) Nimirum causa gemina præcepti traditur tum a legum obser- vandarum oblivione, tum a juris dicendi corruptio- ne. Illis enim, qui in Ebrietate, & luxuria vivunt (dicente Chrysostomo) dies in caliginem noctur- nam vertitur, non quidem extincto sole, sed mente ipsorum per ebrietatem obscurata. Ebrietas est rectæ rationis alienatio, & delirium, & secundum animam sanitatis perditio. Conf. Lev. 10, 9. Syr. 31, 35.

## 31:4
Verse 4. DO NOT TO KINGS GIVE WINE) In Hebrew: to drink wine, that is what the Greeks call οἰνοποτεῖν.

Latin:

Vers. 4. NOLI REGIBUS DARE VINUM) In Hebræo: vinum bibere, id est quod Græci dicunt οἰνοποτεῖν.

## 31:6
Verse 6. GIVE STRONG DRINK TO THOSE MOURNING] לְאֹבֵד, that is, to some miserable person. Concerning the word שֵׁכָר see what was said at Luke 1. verse 15.

There follow now those things which were to be pursued by Solomon, namely (1.) Beneficence v. 6. Give strong drink to the perishing, and wine to those who are bitter in soul: so that they may provide some refreshment to one in danger of life, whether because of poverty and the lack of necessary things, or because of labor or some sickness of mind or body, and afflicted by the bitterness of the cross: and that they may not deny drink, which otherwise Kings, and Princes, and Magnates abuse for drunkenness, to those who are to be refreshed, who, being near destruction, may be refreshed by it, and cheered v. 7. that he may drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more. Nehem. 8, 10. Psalm. 104, 15. Wine, says August. ad Virgin. c. 1. removes sadness, deletes all languors of the mind, infuses joy, etc. By which species of beneficence others in the same category, by which the miserable are to be helped, are included. But concerning the rite of the Hebrews, who offered wine to those about to be subjected to capital punishment, deduced from this precept. See Fagius on Exod. 21. 16. Cocus tit. Sanhedr. page 49.

(2.) The administration of justice, regarding the causes of the miserable in courts: Open your mouth for the mute, (to defend innocence, and to confound calumny, for him who does not dare or is not able otherwise to plead his own cause, which is just) for the judgment of all the children of passage (that is, the destruction of neighbors) v. 9. Open your mouth, judge justice, (or in justice, or the judgment of justice, so that there may be an ellipsis) and judge the poor and needy. Conf. Lev. 19, 15. Deut. 16, 18. Job. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 6. DATE SICERAM MOERENTIBUS] לְאֹבֵד, id est, alicui misero. De voce שֵׁכָר vide quæ dicta ad Luc. 1. versu 15.

Sequuntur jam quæ sectanda Salomoni erant, utpote (1.) Beneficentia v. 6. Date Siceram pereunti, & vinum iis, qui amari animo sunt: ut periclitanti de vita sive ob paupertatem, & rerum necessaria- rum defectum, sive ob laborem vel ægritudinem aliquam animi aut corporis, & amaritudine cru- cis afflicto refectionem aliquam præbeant: & po- tum quo alias Reges, & Principes ac Magnates ad inebriationem abutuntur, illis recreandis ne dene- gent, qui exitio propinqui eodem refici queant, & exhilarari v. 7. ut bibat & obliviscatur egestatis suæ, & calamitatis suæ non recordetur amplius. Nehem. 8, 10. Psalm. 104, 15. Vinum, inquit Au- gust. ad Virgin. c. 1. tristitiam removet, omnes animi languores delet, lætitiam infundit &c. Qua benefi- cientiæ specie alia in genere, quibus miseris succur- rendum est, comprehenduntur. De ritu autem Ebræorum, qui capitali afficiendis supplicio vinum propinabant ex hoc præcepto deducto. Vid. Fagius ad Exod. 21. 16. Cocus tit. Sanhedr. pag. 49.

(2.) Justitiæ administratio, quoad causas mise- rorum in judiciis: Aperi os tuum muto, (ad defen- dendam innocentiam, & confundendam calu- mniam, pro eo, qui non audet vel potest causam suam cæteroquin justam agere) ad judicium omnium filiorum transitus (id est interitu vicinorum) v. 9. Aperi os tuum, judica justitiam, (vel in justitia, aut judicium justitiæ, ut ellipsis sit) & judica pauperem & egenum. Conf. Lev. 19, 15. Deut. 16, 18. Job. 29.

## 31:10
Vers. 10. WHO SHALL FIND A VALIANT WOMAN?) That is, a good one. It is called valiant because it excels others in any kind. Thus Nonius noted that a valiant woman is called so now for beautiful, now for dowered. Who shall find? shows it is a rare thing. It is a Greek proverb: It is not easy to find a noble woman. It is an alphabetic poem in praise of a good woman.

Since he received such salutary warnings from his mother for royal sobriety, kindness, and justice, which he deems worthy of the name משׂא Oracle received from God, and judges worthy even of the Canon of Scripture, in honor of his mother, who could be set forth as an example to women for faith, diligence, and piety or the fear of the Lord, he composed a poem according to the letters of the Alphabet, although some things must be accepted conveniently for royal dignity, when they are adapted to the same. With which poem he wished to conclude his Proverbs v. 10. seqq. For R. Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, Jansenius, Cornelius a Lapide, and most other Interpreters believe that Solomon is the author of this, so that the whole book may thus be referred to Solomon as author. For although he received these also from his mother, as to the materials, there is no doubt that the same were arranged by Solomon in the way they are now proposed as if in an alphabetic poem. Moreover, a woman of strength or fortitude is not called so from strength of body or military fortitude, as some render it a woman of an army, nor as Aben-Ezra wishes, from the virtue of acquiring riches, but from the strength and virtue of the mind: who is of a strong mind, and of confirmed virtue: c. 12, 4. who has the fear of the Lord, as is held below v. 29. The LXX render it γυ- ναῖκα ἀνδρείαν a manly woman, who competes with men in virtue. Such a one is called rare, because she is difficult to find. Conf. Eccl. 7, 29. and far (adds Solomon) is her price from pearls, because she far surpasses and exceeds them in price. The Vulgate wrongly renders it far and from the uttermost coasts is her price. The Hebrew, Chaldean, and LXX, as also the Syriac and other Interpreters, agree. Grotius at this place thus: FAR AND FROM THE UTTERMOST COASTS IS HER PRICE] In the Hebrew it is: her price is above gems. The Greeks: and she is more precious than costly stones.

But why such a wife is to be held more precious, Solomon teaches in verse 11 and following, namely both on account of her fidelity and on account of her diligence: because THE HEART OF HER HUSBAND TRUSTS IN HER, that is, the husband can trust in her, and rests securely, certain of the fidelity of his spouse. But this is not the confidence of Religion, or of the first table, for this is owed to God alone, Jer. 17, 5. Psalm 62, 19. Ps. 118, 8. But it is of connubial love, which is required by the force of the second table, not opposed to, nor coordinated with, the trust to be placed in God, as the giver of a faithful and virtuous spouse, and the author of every blessing, Psalm 128, 14. Prov. 18, 12. but subordinated to the same, by which she promises to herself faith, love, and ἰσόψυχον care from the companion of her life and the help divinely granted, and trusts in her as in her own heart, safely entrusting and committing all her things to her. AND SHE SHALL NOT LACK SPOILS: which pertains to her diligence, by which such a wife excels, so that the husband does not lack income or wealth, which are acquired as spoils, not by reason of iniquity or violence, but by reason of pleasantness, and abundant plenty, and the overcoming of the enemies of economic affairs, such as are sloth, lack of curiosity, sleepiness, intemperance: having overcome these, the diligent and energetic matron brings back ample spoils, and with them enriches her house, just as soldiers are accustomed to bring back spoils with joy after defeating enemies, Ps. 68, 13. Is. 9, 3. Others translate, and spoil shall not be lacking: but the word is more correctly referred with Blessed Luther to the person or the husband, than to the thing or the spoil: as is gathered from Proverbs 13, 25, and the following verse refers the suffix to the person: SHE WILL RENDER TO HIM (the husband) GOOD, AND NOT EVIL ALL THE DAYS OF HER LIFE. By which zeal for doing good the former praise of fidelity is declared, nor is the word RETRIBUTION used without cause, but it is hinted that reciprocal and mutual fidelity ought to flourish between spouses. Good is named generally, because she renders all kinds of goods, and indeed with the exclusion of all evil, which she not only does not render or bring upon him, but also in all ways declines and strives to avert from him, by which, namely, anything could be taken away from his honor, health, or resources: nor only at some time, or in a prosperous state, but all the days of her life, and even to the last breath of life: and finally not only through the days of the husband's life, but if he should die first, through the days of her own life, during which she does not neglect to honor the fame of the deceased, to educate the children, and to cherish friends. Cf. Syr. 26. v. 1. 16. Indeed, the strong woman repays her husband, even if he is harsh, with good for evil, soft things for harsh, humble for proud, gentle for angry, and conciliates and earns the favor of her husband in all ways by benefits, duties, and services. On v. 11, Grotius thus:

Latin:

Vers. 10. MULIEREM FORTEM QVIS INVENIET?) Id est, bonam. Forte dicitur quod in ullo genere alia excellit. Sic fortem mulierem dici modo pro pulchra, modo pro dotata notavit Nonius. Quis inveniet? ostendit rem raram. Græcum est proverbium: Γυναικὸς ἐσθλῆς ἐπιτυχεῖν ὀ ῥᾴδιον. Est carmen alphabeticum in laudes bonæ feminæ.

Quum tam salutaria monita a matre accepe- rit ad Regiam sobrietatem, benignitatem, & justi- tiam, quæ nomine משׂא Oraculi a Deo accepti di- gnatur, & Canone etiam Scripturæ digna judicat, in honorem matris, quæ in exemplum fœminis, ob fidem, sedulitatem, & pietatem vel timorem Domini sisti poterat, carmen juxta literas Alphabeti com- posuit, etsi nonnulla convenienter augustæ dignita- ti accipienda sunt, cum eidem aptantur. Quo Car- mine Paræmias suas concludere voluit v. 10. seqq. Hoc enim Salomonem autorem agnoscere R. Aben-Ezra, Vatablus, Jansenius, Cornelius a Lapide, & alii plerique Interpp. credunt, ut ita totus liber ad Salomonem auctorem referatur. Quanquam enim hæc etiam a matre acceperit, quod ad materialia, eo tamen modo, quo illa jam velut in carmine Al- habetico proposita sunt, a Salomone eadem con- cinnata esse dubitandum non est. Cæterum mulier roboris vel fortitudinis non robore corporis vel fortitudine militari, ut nonnulli reddunt mulier exercitus, nec ut Aben-Ezra vult, a virtute compa- randi divitias, sed a robore & virtute animi dicitur: quæ forti animo sit, & virtutis firmatæ: c. 12, 4. cui est timor Domini, ut habetur infra v. 29. LXX. γυ- ναῖκα ἀνδρείαν mulierem virilem reddunt, quæ virtu- te cum viris certet. Rara talis dicitur, quia diffici- lis inventu. Conf. Eccl. 7, 29. & procul est (addit Salomo) a margaritis pretium ejus, quod longe eas pretio superet & excedat. Vulgata perperam reddit procul & de ultimis finibus pretium ejus. Ebræo Chald. & LXX. ut & Syr. aliique Interpp. consonant. Gro- tius h. l. ita: PROCUL ET DE ULTIMIS FINIBUS PRETIVM EJVS] In Hebræo est: præ gemmis pretium ejus. Græci: τιμιωτέρα δὲ ἐστι λιθῶν πολυτελῶν.

Cur autem pretiosior habenda sit uxor talis, docet Salomo v. 11. seqq. nempe tum ob fidem ejus, tum ob strenuitatem: quia CONFIDIT IN EA COR VIRI SUI, id est, confidere potest ei ma- ritus, & secure conquiescit, certus de fidelitate conjugis. Quæ vero non est confidentia Religionis, vel primæ tabulæ, hæc enim soli Deo debetur Jer. 17, 5. Psalm. 62, 19. Ps. 118, 8. Sed connubialis amoris, qui vi secundæ tabulæ requiritur, non opposita, nec coordinata fiduciæ in Deum collocandæ, ceu largi- torem fidelis & virtuosæ conjugis, & autorem omnis benedictionis Psalm. 128, 14. Prov. 18, 12. sed jubor- dinata eidem, qua de vitæ socia & adjutorio divini- tus concesso fidem, amorem, ac curam ἰσόψυχον si- bi pollicetur, eique ut cordi suo confidit, illi omnia sua tuto credens, & committens. ET SPOLIIS NON INDIGEBIT: quod ad strenuitatem ejus pertinet, qua præstat talis uxor, ut vir non indigeat proventibus, vel opibus, quæ spoliis comparantur non ratione iniquitatis aut violentiæ, sed ratione jucunditatis, largæque copiæ, ac devictionis hostium rei œconomicæ, ceu sunt inertia, incuriositas, somno- lentia, intemperantia: quibus superatis spolia am- pla matronæ sedulæ, atque strenuæ reportant, iis- que domum suam locupletant, non secus atque milites devictis hostibus spolia cum gaudio re- portare solent Psal. 68, 13. Es. 9, 3. Alii reddunt, & spolium non deficiet: sed rectius verbum cum B. Lu- thero refertur ad personam vel maritum, quam ad rem vel spolium: ut e Proverb. 13, 25. colligitur, & vers. seq. suffixum personam refert: REDDET EI (viro sc.) BONUM, ET NON MALUM OMNIBUS DIEBUS VITÆ SUÆ. Quo be- nefaciendi studio declaratur prius elogium fide- litatis, nec absque causa RETRIBUTIONIS verbum adhibetur, sed reciprocam & mutuam fi- dem inter conjuges vigere debere innuitur. Bo- num generatim nominatur, quia omnis generis bona, & quidem cum exclusione omnis mali, quod non tantum non reddit, aut conciliat ei, sed omnibus etiam modis declinat, & avertere ab eo studet, quo scil. honori, sanitati, facultatibus ejus quicquam decedere possit: nec id tantum aliquo tempore, aut in statu prospero, sed omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, & usque ad extremum vitæ halitum: ac denique non solum per dies vitæ mariti, sed si ille prius decedat, per dies vitæ suæ, qua defuncti fa- mam cohonestare, liberos educare, amicos fove- re non negligit. Conf. Syr. 26. v. 1. 16. Imo vero mulier fortis viro etiam acerbo bonum pro malo, mollia pro asperis, humilia pro superbis, blanda pro iracundis rependit, virumque sibi beneficiis, officiis & servitiis omnibus modis conciliat & demere- tur. Ad v. 11. ita Grotius:

## 31:11
v. 11. The LXX wrongly understand the Word of God by the mute, open your mouth for the word of God: which Cornelius encrusts with an impious gloss, as if the word of God inscribed in Scripture were tongueless, inanimate, and mute: who nevertheless acknowledges that this concerns protecting the miserable, who do not know how to protect themselves.

Latin:

v. 11. LXX. per mutum perperam Verbum Dei in- telligunt, apri os tuum verbo Dei: quod impia glossa incrustat Cornelius, quasi verbum Dei exa- ratum in Scriptura elingue, inanime & mutum sit: qui tamen agnoscit, de tuendis miseris hic agi, qui se tueri nesciunt.

## 31:11
Vers. 11. AND SHE SHALL NOT LACK SPOIL) Thus she will be rich in furnishings, as a soldier in spoils.

To the other praise, namely of diligence, which is to be further explained, pertain the things that follow concerning laborious assiduity v. 13. SHE HAS SOUGHT WOOL, AND FLAX (she searches, not waiting until the opportunity for working is handed or thrust into her hands, wool from sheep for threads and cloths, flax arising from the earth for undergarments, and other coverings, and domestic utensils, by which kind of domestic labor other works are simultaneously comprehended, according to the condition of the spouse of each. And therefore the genus is added, AND SHE HAS WORKED WITH THE COUNSEL OF HER HANDS. In Hebrew they can be rendered: and she has worked with the delight of her hands without weariness and trouble, as Blessed Luther with Vatablus and the Tigurines rendered: since חפץ is thus used in chapter 3, verse 15, c. 8, verse 11. Whence the fruit and utility of this diligence, namely the increase of the family estate, to explain that, the husband shall not lack spoils, is added in verse 14. SHE HAS BECOME LIKE A SHIP (In Hebrew it is plural Ships, so that she may be compared even to a whole fleet, which brings a huge abundance of merchandise: as if one ship were not sufficient to describe the yields of such a woman) OF A MERCHANT (of a trader) BRINGING HER BREAD FROM AFAR: because ample wealth is brought in by ships 1 Kings 9 verse 26, chapter 10 verse 11, 22. Isaiah 2 verse 16, chapter 33, 2, 3. Truly, a diligent wife, even if she stays at home and does not run to the furthest Indies with merchants, yet like a certain necessary ship bringing from afar, even she herself, by communicating to outsiders what she has worked with her hands, brings her bread from afar. By the name of bread, all things necessary for food and clothing are comprehended, as in chapter 30 verse 25, Matthew 6 verse 11. On verse 13 & 14, Grotius says this:

Latin:

Vers. 11. ET SPOLII NON INDIGEBIT) Ita dives erit fuppellectile, ut miles spoliis.

Ad alterum elogium, strenuitatis nempe, ul- terius explicandum pertinent quæ sequuntur de laboriosa sedulitate v. 13. QVÆSIVIT LANAM, ET LINUM (perquirit, non expectans donec ei in manus tradatur, vel obtrudatur operandi occa- sio, lanam ex ovibus ad fila, & pannos, linum ex terra oriundum ad indusia, & alia tegumenta, & utensilia domestica, qua laboris domestici specie alia opera simul comprehenduntur, pro ratione status conjugis cujusvis. Ideoque additur ge- nus, ET OPERATA EST CONSILIO MA- NUUM. Ebr. reddi possunt: & operata est cum oblectatione manuum suarum absque tædio & mo- lestia, ut Beat. Lutherus cum Vatablo & Tigurinis reddidit: quum ita חפץ adhibeatur cap. 3. vers. 15. c. 8. vers. 11. unde fructus & utilitas hujus sedulita- tis, augmentum nempe rei familiaris, ad expli- candum illud, spoliis non indigebit maritus, addi- tur vers. 14. FACTA EST QVASI NAVIS (In Ebr. plurale est Naves, ut vel classi integræ con- feratur, quæ ingentem mercedum copiam appor- tet: ac si una navis non sufficiat ad proventus ta- lis mulieris describendos) INSTITORIS (mer- catoris) DE LONGE PORTANS PANEM SUUM: quia navibus opes amplæ advehuntur 1. Reg. 9. vers. 26. cap. 10. vers. 11. 22. Esa. 2. versu 16. cap. 33, 2. 3. Nimirum sedula uxor etsi domi ma- neat nec cum mercatoribus extremos currat ad Indos, tamen velut navis quædam necessaria a lon- ge advehens, etiam ipsa sua exteris communican- do, quæ manibus suis operata est, portat de lon- ge panem suum. Nomine panis omnia necessaria ad victum & amictum comprehenduntur, ut cap. 30. versu 25. Matth. 6. versu 11. Ad vers. 13. & 14. hæc Grotius:

## 31:13
Verse 13. SHE SOUGHT WOOL AND FLAX) In Hebrew, linens, that is, various kinds of linens. Verse 14. SHE IS MADE LIKE THE SHIP OF A MERCHANT) More of a seller than a buyer.

To this strenuousness pertains furthermore (2.) Vigilance, especially in the provident care of the family, concerning which in verse 15. AND SHE ROSE BY NIGHT (In Heb. while it is still night), AND GAVE PREY (FOOD) TO HER FAMILY, AND PROVISIONS (a portion, a measured amount or task, as the Chaldean rightly translates, which some understand as the measuring of food, others as the task of labors) TO HER MAIDENS. She does not sleep until broad daylight, but rises before dawn, and while it is still night, so that she may prepare food for her house or family, for servants and handmaids, for sons and daughters (nay, even for her cattle), and provide breakfast earlier, so that she may also assign them their task of labors at the crack of dawn, so that they may thus betake themselves to their works in good time. Cf. chapter 27 verse 27. These are the words of Grotius on this verse:

Latin:

Vers. 13. QVÆSIVIT LANAM ET LINVM) In Hebræo lina, id est, varia genera linorum. Vers. 14. FACTA EST QVASI NAVIS INSTITORIS) Vendax magis quam emax.

Ad hanc strenuitatem pertinet porro (2.) Vigilantia, imprimis in provida familiæ cura, de qua versu 15. ET DE NOCTE (In Ebr. dum adhuc nox est) SURREXIT, DEDITQVE PRÆDAM (CIBUM) FAMILIÆ SUÆ, ET CIBARIA (portionem, dimensum vel pensum, ut recte vertit Chald. quod alii de ciborum dimenso, alii de penso laborum intelligunt) PUELLIS SUIS. Non stertit in multam lucem, sed ante auroram, & dum adhuc nox est surgit, ut domui vel familiæ suæ, servis & ancillis, filiis & filiabus (imo etiam pecudibus suis) cibos præparet, & jentaculum m迴turius præbeat, ut etiam pensum laborum sum- mo mane illis assignet, ut ita tempestive ad operas se conferant. Conf. cap. 27. versu 27. Grotii ad hunc versum hæc sunt:

## 31:15
Verse 15. AND SHE ROSE BY NIGHT, AND GAVE PREY TO HER HOUSEHOLD, AND PROVISIONS TO HER MAIDENS) Prey here is food by metaphor, as spoils were just now. What is provisions here, in Hebrew is a statute, that is, a task. Let us compare with this description of the industrious woman that of Virgil: - - - just as a woman first, whose life is to be sustained by the distaff and the slender Minerva, rouses the ashes and the slumbering fires, adding the night to her work, and keeps her handmaids at their long task by the lights, so that she may be able to preserve the chaste bed of her husband and rear her little children.

To this (3.) also pertains the acquisition & care of estates. For with the price of those things which she has worked with her hands, she buys for herself fields or vineyards, and is devoted to sowing the former and planting and carefully cultivating the latter, so that she may provide for the family as much for drink as for food, and have wherewith she may be able to prepare for them food and drink, no less than garments (concerning the material of which, see verse 13). Verse 15. SHE CONSIDERED A FIELD (she prudently weighs it, not rashly or by chance, but doing this maturely and deliberately) AND BOUGHT IT: FROM THE FRUIT OF HER HANDS (not only did she buy a field, but also) SHE PLANTED A VINEYARD, the yield of which was notable in Judea.

But because for these things there is need of alacrity, therefore (4.) in verse 17 the strenuous woman is described by the same: SHE GIRDED HER LOINS WITH STRENGTH (In Heb. it is in strength, that is, strongly), AND STRENGTHENED HER ARM. For those about to labor strenuously, to set out, or to do battle, gird their loins with a belt, so that they may firm and strengthen them, lest they be weak, soft, and loose, and lest they be a hindrance to those hastening, Exodus 12 verse 11, 1 Kings 8.

verse 46, Psalm 38 verse 3, Ephesians 6 verse 14. But they strengthen their arms so that they may be ready to undertake any labors whatsoever: not by procuring strength for themselves, which arises from God, but by rousing and exercising themselves for labors, by which exercise of strength, strength is increased. For just as by sloth, strength is consumed as if by rust, so by exercise it is increased and confirmed. The cause of this diligence and alacrity is inserted in verse 10. Namely, SHE TASTED AND SAW (the Vulgate adds this 'to see' of its own) THAT HER MERCHANDISE IS GOOD (her own: she perceived this with delight and learned by experience that such diligent operation is useful and wholesome for her). Just as if someone tasting some new and delicate food were so taken by its sweetness that he would spare no labor or expense to satisfy himself with it: so she, having experienced the most sweet fruit of her labor, presses on to her work more alacritously than before, as Cartwright says here: therefore) HER LAMP WILL NOT BE EXTINGUISHED IN THE NIGHT (which he added for the sake of amplification, and so that her assiduity might be commended, because it is not extinguished even in the night itself). It was said before that she rises before light: now it is added that she performs so well in labor that she does not close it with the light, but draws it out until deep into the night.

(5.) Such a woman is praised for the constancy of her labor, ver. 19. SHE HATH PUT FORTH HER HAND TO STRONG THINGS (In Heb. כישור, which is read nowhere else, was from כשר, straight; the LXX render it τὰ συμφέροντα, to those things which are profitable or straight; Vatablus, Mercerus, Pagninus, Junius render it a whorl; Luther, Rocken; AND HER FINGERS (her palms) HAVE TAKEN HOLD OF THE SPINDLE) (by which the former part of the verse is explained: most, with R. Nathan Mardochai & Pagninus, take it of the distaff or staff to which the flax is applied) Since she was said before to assign a task to her maidservants, now it is praised that she herself also applies her hands to the work, and does not disdain even base labors: and indeed in such a way that she applies both hand and palm, with the end also subjoined, namely that she may then both assist the poor, and clothe her family well, and also adorn her house and herself excellently, and thus conveniently provide for the same: which also pertain to the kindness as well as the due solicitude of a virtuous woman. To the former, Grotius says thus:

SHE HATH PUT FORTH HER HANDS TO STRONG THINGS AND HER FINGERS HAVE TAKEN HOLD OF THE SPINDLE) כישור, which he here explains as strong things, is a whorl, as indeed the diligent investigator of words, Rabbi David Kimchi, thinks. The origin is from כשר, which is to shake among the Arabs. פלך, however, which he here translates as spindle, seems rather to be a distaff, from the likeness of a staff or a ship: for that word signifies a staff to the Hebrews, and a ship to the Arabs.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ET DE NOCTE SVRREXIT, DEDITQVE PRÆ- DAM DOMESTICIS SVIS, ET CIBARIA ANCILLIS SVIS) Præda hic est cibus per metaphoram, ut modo spolia. Quod hic est cibaria, in Hebræo est statutum, id est, pensum. Comparemus cum hac gnavæ mulieris notatione similem Virgilii: - - - ceu femina primum Cui tolerare colo vitam, tenuique Minerva Impositum, cinerem & sopitos suscitat ignes. Noctem addens operi, famulasque ad lumina longo Exercet penso, castum ut servare cubile Conjugis, & possit parvos educere natos.

Eo (3.) spectat etiam acquisitio & cura fun- dorum. Pro pretio enim eorum, quæ manibus suis operata est, comparat sibi agros, aut vineas, illisque serendis, his plantandis & solicite colen- dis dedita est, ut tam de potu, quam de cibo fa- miliæ prospiciat, habeatque unde illis cibum ac po- tum, non minus quam vestimenta (de quorum materia vers. 13.) parare possit. vers. 15. CONSI- DERAVIT AGRVM (prudenter expendit, non temere aut fortuito, sed mature & consulto id agens (ET EMIT EUM: DE FRUCTV MA- NUUM SVARVM (non tantum agrum com- paravit, sed etiam) PLANTAVIT VINEAM, quarum proventus in Judæa erat insignis.

Quia vero ad ista opus est alacritate, ideo (4.) versu 17. ab eadem describitur mulier strenua: ACCINXIT FORTITVDINE (In Ebr. est in fortitudine, id est fortiter) LVMBOS SVOS, ET ROBORAVIT BRACHIVM SUUM. Cingulo enim lumbos accingunt strenue laboraturi, profecturi vel præliaturi, ut eos infirmos, molles & fluxos firment atque roborent, ac ne festinanti- bus impedimento sint Exod. 12. versu 11. 1. Reg. 8.

versu 46. Psalm. 38. versu 3. Ephes. 6. versu 14. Brachia autem roborant, ut ad labores quosvis subeundos promtæ sint: non sibi ipsi robur con- ciliando, quod a Deo oritur: sed semet excitando, & exercendo ad labores, quo roboris exercitio robur augetur. Quemadmodum enim desidia, tanquam ærugine vires absumuntur, ita exercita- tione augentur & confirmantur. Causa hujus sedulitatis & alacritatis inseritur vers. 10. Nimi- rum GUSTAVIT ET VIDIT (hoc videre de suo addit Vulgatus) QVIA BONA EST NE- GOTIATIO EJUS (sua: cum oblectatione hoc percepit & experientia didicit, quod sibi uti- lis, & salutaris sit diligens ejusmodi operatio. Quemadmodum si quis cibum aliquem novum, & delicatum degustans usque eo dulcedine ejus capere- tur, ut ad se illo satiandum nulli labori, aut sumtui parceret: ita hæc fructum laboris sui dulcissimum ex- perta alacrius operi, quam ante instat, ut hic Cart- wrightus: ideo) NON EXTINGUETUR IN NOCTE (quod amplificationis causa addi- dit, & ut assiduitas commendetur, quod nec in ipsa nocte extinguatur) LUCERNA EJUS. Dictum est prius, illam ante lucem surgere: nunc additur, ita in labore præstare, ut cum luce illum non claudat, sed ad multam noctem pertrahat.

(5.) Deprædicatur talis mulier a laboris con- stantia, vers. 19. MANUM SUAM MISIT AD FORTIA (In Ebr. כישור, quod alias nuspiam le- gitur, a כשר rectus fuit, LXX. reddunt τὰ συμφέ- ροντα ad ea quæ conducibilia vel recta sunt, Va- tablus, Mercerus, Pagninus, Junius reddunt ver- ticillum, Lutherus Rocken, ET DIGITI EJUS (volæ ejus) APPREHENDERUNT FUSUM) (quo prior pars Versus explicatur: de Colo seu Sci- pione, cui linum applicatur, plerique cum R. Na- than Mardochai & Pagnino accipiunt) Quum an- tea pensum ancillis assignare dicta sit, jam prædi- catur, quod ipsa etiam operi admoveat manus, & ne viles quidem labores aspernari: & quidem ita, ut manum & volam utramque applicet, subjuncto etiam fine, ut nempe tum pauperibus subveniat, tum familiam suam bene vestiat, tum etiam do- mum suam & sese eximie ornet, adeoque commo- de eidem prospiciat: quæ etiam ad mulieris vir- tuosæ tum benignitatem, tum solicitudinem debitam pertinent. Ad priora ita Grotius:

MANVS SVAS MISIT AD FORTIA ET DIGITI EJVS APPREHENDERVNT FVSVM) כישור quod hic explicat fortia, est verticillus, ut quidem censet diligens vo- cum indagator Rabbinus David Kimchi. Origo a כשר quod est quassare Arabibus. פלך autem, quod hic fusum vertit, videtur potius esse colus, a similitudine baculi aut navis: nam vox ista Hebræis baculum, Arabibus navem significat.

## 31:20
Ver. 20. SHE HATH OPENED (extended) HER HAND TO THE NEEDY, (to the afflicted) AND HATH EXTENDED (sent) HER PALMS TO THE POOR. She does not only open when she is asked, but she extends even of her own accord, and that to those who are remote also, Psalm 112. v. 3. 5. Prov. 3, 27. Eph. 4, 28. so that it may be taught how promptly and cheerfully, and how profusely also, and liberally she does this. Concerning solicitude for the family, ver. 21 is treated: SHE SHALL NOT FEAR FOR HER HOUSE (that is, for her domestics, or family) FROM THE COLD OF SNOW: FOR ALL HER HOUSEHOLD (in Heb. all her house) ARE CLOTHED WITH DOUBLE GARMENTS. Heb. שנים, Chald., Pagnin. & others render it scarlet, as it is taken in Is. 1, 18. Num. 4, 8. 2. Sam. 1. 24. but because servants and maidservants are not accustomed to be clothed in scarlet, nor do such garments avail against the cold, more correctly שנים from the root of the word שנה, he repeated, by the Vulgate,

For Luther, Junius, and the Belgians, it is explained regarding the double or necessary and suitable garment against snow and cold: with which the mistress of the house is said to clothe her household, because servants and maids, as slaves at that time, did not provide for themselves regarding clothing. To adornment and proper decoration belong those things which are held in verse 22: SHE HATH MADE HERSELF A COVERING (as Symmachus ἀμφιτάπης, tapestries shaggy on both sides; Aquila and Theodotion, hangings; the Chaldean, bedspreads; Luther, blankets). FINE LINEN AND PURPLE IS HER CLOTHING: which, namely, she made or procured for herself by her own industry. With such garments priests are also clothed: by the fine linen, modesty and innocence are represented by its whiteness, and by the flame-colored dye, fiery love.

Latin:

Vers. 20. MANUM SUAM APERUIT (ex- tendit) INOPI, (ad afflictum) ET PALMAS SUAS EXTENDIT (misit) AD PAUPEREM. Non aperit tantum cum rogatur, sed extendit etiam ultro, idque ad remotos quoque Psalm. 112. v. 3. 5. Prov. 3, 27. Eph. 4, 28. ut quam promte & alacriter, quam prolixe etiam, ac liberaliter hoc faciat, do- ceatur. De solicitudine pro familia vers. 21. agitur: NON TIMEBIT DOMUI SUÆ (id est do- mesticis, vel familiæ) A FRIGORIBUS NIVIS: OMNES ENIM DOMESTICI EJUS (in Ebr. omnis domus ejus) VESTITI SUNT DUPLI- CIBUS. Ebr. שנים Chald. Pagnin. & alii reddunt coccinum, uti accipitur Es. 1, 18. Num. 4, 8. 2. Sam. 1. 24. sed quia servi & ancillæ coccino vestiri non solent, neque vestes tales adversus frigus faciunt, rectius שנים e Radice vocis שנה iteravit a Vulgata,

B. Luthero, Junio & Belgis de indumento duplici seu necessario & idoneo adversus nivem & frigus expli- catur: quo vestire materfamilias domesticos dici- tur, quia servi & servæ, ceu mancipia isto tempore non prospiciebant sibi de vestimentis. Ad mun- dum & ornatum proprium faciunt, quæ vers. 22. ha- bentur: STRAGULATAM VESTEM (uti Sym- machus ἀμφιτάπης tapetia utrinque villosa. A- quila & Theodot. peristromata, Chaldæus strata, Lutherus Decken,) FECIT SIBI. BYSSUS ET PURPURA INDUMENTUM EJUS: quod scil. sua industria sibi fecit, vel comparavit. Qualibus vestibus etiam Sacerdotes amicti sunt: bysso candore suo pudicitiam & innocentiam, flammeo colore amorem igneum referente.

## 31:23
Verse 23.

HER HUSBAND IS NOBLE IN THE GATES, WHEN HE SHALL SIT WITH THE SENATORS OF THE LAND) Namely, on account of a garment worthy of a Senator. Homer also mentions a garment for the court.

The Hebrew נוֹדָע is known and celebrated, Psalm 76, verse 2, in the gates, i.e., in the court or judgment, because judgments were celebrated in the gates so that the judges would always be accessible. The elders of the land (of Israel, 1 Kings 20:7) are called elders from old age, who excel others either in years, or prudence, or experience. Numbers 11:16, Ruth 4:4. This is added concerning the husband, not because she procures authority for her husband with garments, so that he may be raised to dignity, which was the view of R. Solomon and Mariana, nor because she procures an honored husband for herself by her own virtue, because the previous verses dealt with one already married, but because such a wife can deservedly adorn herself with such noble garments, because she herself is noble not only by the nobility of her virtues and actions, but also by the nobility of her husband: and this is explained or confirmed by the following verse 24, because, namely, by the trade of her own handiwork she procures such wealth for herself that she can purchase such precious garments: SHE HATH MADE AND SOLD FINE LINEN (which Greek word Συνδὼν they derive from the Hebrew סָדִין: see Matthew 27:59, perhaps from the city of Sidon, in which a garment of this kind was begun, according to Theophrastus, History of Plants, ch. 9) AND DELIVERED A GIRDLE (made by herself) TO THE CANAANITE (that is, to the merchant, who carried it to foreign regions, Job 40:25). Isaiah 23:8, because the Phoenicians, descendants of Canaan, dwellers by the sea, were famous for trade.

Now he proceeds from bodily adornment to spiritual, as (1) the beauty and adornment of the soul, the fortitude of the mind or courage, verse 25. STRENGTH AND BEAUTY (or glory, that is, glorious strength by hendiadys, although glory or the ornament of various virtues can also be said to be joined with strength) IS HER CLOTHING (Compare Job 40:5, 1 Timothy 2:5, 1 Peter 3:4, 5) IN THE LATTER DAY (or the subsequent, suppose an adverse time or in old age, or even the day of death, Psalm 62:7).

(2) The beauty of the mouth in verse 26, which shines forth in wise and gracious words. SHE HATH OPENED HER MOUTH TO WISDOM (in Wisdom) AND THE LAW OF KINDNESS IS ON HER TONGUE. Mariana tempers wise speech with sweetness.

(3.) The comeliness of the eyes: inasmuch as they do not wander with vain or lustful curiosity, but with due vigilance behold and look upon what is done at home: whence she has no need to eat the bread of idleness because of her diligent inspection and visitation of her family. ver. 17. SHE HATH CONSIDERED (she has looked out) THE PATHS (the ways, that is, the expeditions and steps) OF HER HOUSE (that is, of her household) AND (therefore) SHE HATH NOT EATEN THE BREAD OF IDLENESS, in the Hebrew the bread of negligence or sloth, because she obtains bread by many labors and breaks it for her own: nay, she does not take food unless it is acquired by work strenuously performed.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

NOBILIS IN PORTIS VIR EJUS, QVANDO SE- DERIT CUM SENATORIBUS TERRÆ) Nempe ob vestem Senatore dignam. Vestis ad curiam etiam Home- rus meminit.

Ebr. נוֹדָע est notus & celebris Psalm. 76. v. 2. in portis, i. e. in curia, vel judicio, quia judicia in por- tis celebrabantur, ut obvii semper essent judices. Seniores terræ (Israëliticæ 1. Reg. 20, 7.) Seniores sunt a senio dicti, qui vel annis, vel prudentia, vel expe- rientia alios antecellunt. Num. 11, 16. Ruth. 4, 4. Additur hoc de marito, non quod vestimentis ma- rito conciliet autoritatem, ut ad dignitatem eveha- tur, quod R. Salomoni & Marianæ visum, nec quod virtute sua sibi honoratum conciliet maritum, quia priora de jam maritata egerunt, sed quod uxor talis ideo vestibus ejusmodi nobilioribus se ornare me- rito possit, quia nobilis ipsa non tantum virtutum & actionum nobilitate est, sed etiam nobilitate mariti: idque exponitur, vel confirmatur sequentibus v. 24. quia sc. negotiatione manufactorum suorum e- jusmodi opes sibi conciliat, ut vestes tam pretiosas comparare possit: SINDONEM (quam vocem Græcam Συνδὼν ab Ebræo סָדִין derivant: Vid. Matth. 27, 59. forte a Sidone urbe, in qua amictus hu- jusmodi ceptus, teste Theophrasto Hist. Plant. c. 9.) FECIT ET VENDIDIT: ET CINGULUM (a se factum) TRADIDIT CHANANÆO (hoc est, mercatori, qui ad extraneas regiones deferebat Job. 40, 25.
