Esa. 23, 8. quia Phœnices posteri Canaan ma- ris accolæ ex mercatura celebres fuere.

Jam ab ornatu corporali ad spiritualem pro- cedit, utpote (1.) Decorem & ornatum animi, forti- tudinem mentis seu animositatem v. 25. FORTI- TUDO & DECOR (vel gloria, id est, fortitudo glo- riosa per hendyaden, quanquam etiam cum forti- tudine juncta dici possit gloria vel decus variarum virtutum) INDVMENTVM EJVS (Conf. Job. 40, 5. 1. Tim. 2. 5. 1. Pet. 3, 4. 5.) IN DIE NOVISSIMO (vel posteriori, puta tempore adverso vel in senectu- te, imo die etiam mortis Psalm. 62, 7.

(2.) Decorem oris versu 26. qui effulget in verbis sapientibus & gratiosis. OS SVVM APE- RVIT SAPIENTIÆ (in Sapientia) ET LEX CLEMENTIÆ IN LINGVA EJVS. Mariana sermonem sapientem cum dulcedine temperat.

(3.) Decorem oculorum: utpote qui non va- na aut libidinosa curiositate vagantur, sed debita vigilantia, quæ domi geruntur, intuentur & spe- ctant: unde opus non habet panem pigritiæ co- medere ob diligentem familiæ inspectionem, & visitationem. vers. 17. CONSIDERAVIT (spe- culata est) SEMITAS ((vias, id est, expeditiones, & gressus) DOMUS SUÆ (id est domesticorum suo- rum) ET (ideo) PANEM OTIOSA NON CO- MEDIT, in Ebræo panem incuriæ vel pigritiæ, quia panem multis laboribus capit suisque frangit: imo non sumit cibum nisi strenue facto opere acquisi- tum.

## 31:28
Ver. 28.

HER CHILDREN ROSE UP, AND CALLED HER MOST BLESSED: HER HUSBAND, AND HE PRAISED HER.

The virtues of the strong woman having been set forth, the reward of praise is subjoined, in that she is called blessed by her sons, under whom daughters are also included by synecdoche, and is praised by her husband: they are said to rise who go forth into public, or also who gird themselves for some work, whence public and deliberate, not rash, eulogies are implied, proceeding from those who have most experienced her virtue: Nor do they call her blessed with their tongues only, but also with their works, by which they imitate her virtues, excited and confirmed by the illustrious example of their mother and wife, and by the honors to which they have aspired through her prayers and piety, education and virtue. To which heralds the Holy Spirit himself finally joins his own eulogy: saying v. 29. MANY DAUGHTERS HAVE GATHERED (have prepared) RICHES (thus חיל is taken Deut. 8, 17. 18. Ezech. 28, 4.) BUT THOU HAST SURPASSED THEM ALL. Because she is not only strenuous and industrious, but also adorned with most beautiful virtues, and especially with true faith and piety, of which very many are destitute. Those women, therefore, who lack trust in God and true piety, even though they be faithful to their husbands and very strenuous in domestic affairs, this woman, whom the Holy Scripture extols, leaves at a long interval behind her. And although others may make much of grace and charm of manners and beauty of body, she alone deserves praise from the Spirit of God himself, who with true trust of heart fears GOD, and adheres to Him with sincere piety. Ver. 30. VAIN (falsity itself) IS GRACE (the charm of manners, actions, speech, and gestures) AND VAIN (vanity) IS BEAUTY. Although it is otherwise a notable gift of God Job 42, 15, yet because of inconstancy it is called vanity in the abstract, because form is a most fragile good, and excellent form, as someone says, abounds in many crimes, and according to Ovid, there is a great quarrel between beauty and chastity: hence also Aesop says, do not look at my form, but at my mind. THE WOMAN THAT FEARETH GOD SHE SHALL BE PRAISED. By which name of the fear of the Lord the whole of divine worship is comprehended, and the woman who performs whatever she does of faith toward her husband and diligence in economic matters with true trust in the one God, without which it is impossible to please God Heb. 11, 6, and with unfeigned piety. The pronoun תתהלל emphatically increases this praise, SHE herself shall be praised, i.e., such a one alone, and no others, deserves praise. Which, without virtue, says Bernard, serm. 1. de S. Vict., is glory indeed that comes unmerited, is sought after too hastily, and is captured dangerously. Virtue is the step to glory, virtue is the mother of glory. Vain is grace and vain is beauty, which she did not bring forth: it is virtue alone to which glory is due and is securely bestowed.

Whence, therefore, the Holy Scripture adds a concluding exhortation to all, that they should not deny the due praise to such a woman, and teaches that she is to be celebrated openly by all in verse 31 and last. GIVE HER OF THE FRUIT OF HER OWN HANDS (praise, that is, as appears from the following member and from what precedes. Cf. Jer. 13, 16. Ps. 67, 35. AND LET HER WORKS PRAISE HER IN THE GATES: that is, let her be celebrated publicly on account of her works: nay, her works, she herself being silent, shall publicly celebrate her, even in the very assemblies of magistrates and judges, or generally in a frequent gathering of men, such as was in the gates and in the courts. The LXX wrongly refer it to the husband, and let her husband be praised in the gates. For this whole poem sounds of a woman.

Although these eulogies concerning the strong and virtuous woman treat of the matter according to the letter, the Fathers nevertheless, as they are accustomed, apply them to the Church by way of accommodation and allegorically: such as Augustine, the Author of the Opus imperfectum in Matthaeum, among the Chrysostomian works, Gregory the Great, Bede, and others. Concerning which Cornelius a Lapide may be consulted. Who also adapts them to the Blessed Virgin, and in the place of a colophon loads her with extremely idolatrous eulogies, singing along with Bonaventure to her: To thee every angelic creature proclaims with an ineffable voice: Holy, Holy, Holy Mary Mother of God, mother

Latin:

Vers. 28.

SURREXERUNT FILII EJUS, ET BEA- TISSIMAM PRÆDICAVERUNT : VIR EJUS, ET LAUDAVIT EAM.

Virtutibus mulieris fortis expositis laudis sub- jungitur præmium, quod beata a filiis, sub quibus Synecdochice etiam filiæ comprehenduntur, prædi- cetur, & a viro laudetur : Surgere dicuntur, qui in publicum prodeunt, vel etiam qui operi alicui se accingunt, unde publica & deliberata non temeraria elogia innuuntur, ab iis profecta, qui virtutem ejus maxime experti sunt: Neque Linguis tantum præ- dicant eam beatam, sed etiam operibus, quibus vir- tutes ejus, exemplo illustri matris, & conjugis exci- tati, & confirmati imitantur, & honoribus, ad quos ejus precibus ac pietate, educatione ac virtute adspira- runt. Quibus tandem præconibus jungit se ipse Spiritus Sanctus suo elogio: MULTÆ inquiens v. 29. FILIÆ CONGREGAVERUNT (pararunt) DIVITIAS (fic חיל accipitur Deut. 8, 17. 18. Ezech. 28, 4. ) TU (autem) SUPERGRESSA ES UNIVERSAS. Quia non modo strenua & labo- riosa, sed etiam virtutibus pulcherrimis, & impri- mis vera fide & pietate, quibus plurimæ destituun- tur, ornata. Illas ergo mulieres, quæ fiducia in Deum veraque pietate carent, tametsi maritis fidæ, & strenuæ admodum in re familiari sint, longo post se intervallo hæc relinquit, quam S. S. deprædicat. Et quanquam alii gratiam & venustatem morum ac pul- chritudinem corporis magni faciant, illa tamen unice laudem meretur ab ipso Spiritu Dei, quæ vera cordis fiducia DEUM timet, eique sincera pietate adhæret. Vers. 30. FALLAX (falsitas ipsa) GRATIA (mo- rum, actionum, sermonum ac gestuum venustas) ET VANA (vanitas) EST PULCHRITUDO. Etsi alias insigne donum Dei sit Job. 42, 15. ob incon- stantiam tamen vanitas in abstracto dicitur, quia forma bonum maxime fragile est, & eximia forma, ut nonnemo ait, multis etiam criminibus scatct, ac iuxta Ovidium lis est cum forma magna pudicitiæ: inde & Æsopus, ne mihi, inquit, formam, sed mentem aspice. MULIER TIMENS DEUM IPSA LAU- DABITUR. Quo nomine timoris Domini totus cultus divinus comprehenditur, & mulier, quæ quicquid fidei erga maritum, sedulitatis in re œco- nomica exequitur vera in unum Deum fiducia, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere Ebr. 11, 6. ac infucata pietate facit. Laudem hanc emphaticæ auget pro- nomen תתהלל IPSA laudabitur, q. d. talis sola, non aliæ, laudem meretur. Quæ sine virtute, ait Bern- hard. serm. 1. de S. Vict. est, gloria profecto indebita venit, præpropere affectatur, periculose captatur. Vir- tus gradus ad gloriam, virtus mater gloriæ est. Fal- lax gratia & vana pulchritudo, quam illa non parturi- vit: sola est virtus cui gloria debetur jure & secure im- penditur.

Unde colophonis ergo parænesin addit S. S. ad omnes, ut tali mulieri laudem debitam ne dene- gent, eamque palam ab omnibus celebrandam ita docet versu 31. & ultim. DATE EI DE FRU- CTU MANUUM SUARUM (laudem scil. ut e membro posteriori, & ex antegressis apparet. Conf. Jer. 13, 16. Psal. 67, 35. (ET LAUDENT EAM IN PORTIS OPERA EJUS: id est, celebretur publice ob opera sua: imo opera ejus, ipsa tacente, publice eam celebrabunt, etiam in ipsis Magistratuum judicumque consessibus, vel generatim in frequenti hominum cœtu, qualis in portis, & judiciis erat. LXX. perperam ad virum referunt, & laudetur in portis vir ejus. De muliere enim totum hoc carmen sonat.

Quanquam vero hæc elogia de muliere forti & virtuosa secundum literam agant, per accommo- dationem tamen & allegorice, uti solent, Patres ea- dem Ecclesiæ applicant: utpote Augustinus, Autor Oper. imperfect. in Matth. apud Chrysostom. Gre- gor. M. Beda, alii. Quo de Cornelius a Lapide videri poterit. Qui ea etiam adaptat Virgini Bea- tæ, eamque Colophonis loco perquam idololatri- cis elogiis onerat, e Bonaventura accinens ipsi: Tibi omnis Angelica creatura ineffabili voce proclamat: Sancta, Sancta, Sancta Maria Dei genitrix, mater

# Ecclesiastes

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N TO THE ECCL

Latin:

I. N AD ECCL

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of Grotius
PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

THIS Book קהלת is in Hebrew: the names of its form are usually for the most part feminine; but because the Hebrews lack common ones, they are sometimes used for common ones. And thus it appears to be taken here from the construction with the masculine 1, 1. 2. 12, 8. 9. 10. And for that reason the Greeks translated it εκκλησιαςὴν. It will perhaps be better translated συναθροιστής, in the way the verb קהל is usually translated by συναθροίζειν, so that we may understand that various opinions of men, who were each considered wise among their own people, concerning happiness (περὶ τῆς εὐδαιμονίας) were brought together into this book: clearly just as the book of Job embraces almost all the opinions that have been or can be concerning the divine government of human affairs, or against it. Wherefore we ought not to wonder if we read certain things here that are not to be approved: for it was necessary for one reciting all opinions with their arguments, as Aristotle is accustomed to do before he defines anything, for that to happen: but since both the beginning and the end sufficiently show what the writer's purpose is, for those reasons (as the Hebrews say) it was deservedly received into the canon. I, however, do not think it is Solomon's, but written later under the name of that King, as if led by repentance. I have as an argument for this matter many words which you cannot find elsewhere than in Daniel, Ezra, and the Chaldean interpreters.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTII.

HIC Liber קהלת est in Hebræo: solent nomina ejus formæ plerumque esse muliebria; sed quia He- bræis communia desunt, usurpantur interdum pro com- munibus. Et ita hic sumi apparet ex constructione cum masculino 1, 1. 2. 12, 8. 9. 10. Ac propterea Græci εκκλη- σιαςὴν vertere. Melius forte vertetur συναθροιστής, quomo- do verbum קהל per συναθροίζειν verti solet, ut intelli- gamus redactas in hunc librum varias hominum, qui sapien- tes apud suos quisque habebantur, opiniones περὶ τῆς εὐ- δαιμονίας: plane sicut liber Jobi omnes ferme quæ fuerunt aut esse possunt de divina rerum humanarum gubernatione, aut contra eam sententias complectitur. Quare mirari non debemus, si quædam hic legimus non probanda: omnes enim sententias cum suis argumentis recitanti, ut Aristote- les facere solet priusquam quid definiat, necesse erat id ac- cidere: sed cum & initium & finis satis monstrent quod sit scriptoris propositum, ob eas causas (ut ajunt Hebræi) me- rito in canonem receptus est. Ego tamen Salomonis esse non puto, sed scriptum serius sub illius Regis, tanquam pœni- tentia ducti, nomine. Argumentum ejus rei habeo multa vocabula, quæ non alibi quam in Daniele, Esdra & Chaldæis interpretibus reperias.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations on the Preface of Grotius, with Other Prolegomena
OBSERVATIONS ON THE PREFACE OF GROTIUS, WITH OTHER PROLEGOMENA.

ON the name of the book, whether it denotes a collector of opinions, or indeed a preacher. Whether and how Solomon is the Preacher? On the author of the book, whether Solomon? Whether he performed penance? Arguments of Grotius, by which this book is more recent than Solomon. Whether Chaldean names are contained in it. The source of Grotius's error. The canonical authority of this writing. Not called into doubt by Blessed Luther. Concerning the Papistic abuse of this book, which he severely censured, and virgin, concluding finally with the golden eulogy of the Doctor, whom he calls Angelic, he would have more correctly said leaden delirium: The B. Virgin, from the fact that she is the mother of GOD, has a certain infinite dignity from the infinite good, which is God. How these and countless similar things were to the taste of our Grotius, the intimate advocate and attorney of Papal idolatry, let those see to it who are eager to patronize the same: We, having seen and read these things, could not but grieve at the blindness of men otherwise most sharp-sighted, wonder at the efficacy of errors, and detest the sacrilegious impiety and Roman idolatry: not offering the honor of God to the Theotokos with the Seraphic or Angelic Doctor of the Papists, but devoutly singing with the holy Seraphim themselves and the four mystical living creatures in honor of the one God, the most Holy and most glorious, and the same undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: HOLY, HOLY, HOLY JEHOVAH ZEBAOTH: and, HOLY, HOLY, HOLY Lord God almighty, who was, who is, and who is to come. MAY THE WHOLE EARTH BE FULL OF HIS GLORY. Amen.

Latin:

AD PRAEFATIONEM GROTII OBSERVATIO- NES, CUM ALIIS ΠΡΟΛΕΓΟΜΕΝΟΙΣ.

DE nomine libri, an collecto- rem notet sententiarum, num ve- ro concionatorem. An & quo- modo Salomo Concionator? De au- tore libri, an Salomo? Num is pœ- nitentiam egerit? Argumenta Grotii, quo liber hic Salomone recentior. An Chaldaica nomi- na in eo habeantur. Fons erroris Grotii. Auctoritas scripti hujus Canonica. Non re- vocata in dubium a Beato Luthero. Qu- abusum libri hujus Papisticum graviter taxa- & virgo, concludens denique Doctoris, quem vo- cat, Angelici, aureo elogio, rectius dixisset plumbeo delirio: B. Virgo ex hoc, quod est mater DEI, habet quandam dignitatem infinitam ex bono infinito, quod est Deus. Quomodo haec & similia innumera Je- suitarum intimo idololatriae Papalis advocato, & causidico, Grotio nostro, ad salivam fuerint, de eo viderint, qui patrocinari eidem gestiunt: Nos his- ce visis, & lectis non potuimus non dolere caecita- tem virorum alias oculatissimorum, mirari effica- ciam errorum, & detestari sacrilegam impietatem, ac idololatriam Romanam: non cum Doctore Sera- phico aut Angelico Papistarum honorem Dei Θεοτό- κῳ deferentes, sed cum ipsis Sanctis Seraphim, & quatuor animantibus mysticis in honorem unius Dei, S. S. & gloriosissimae, ejusdemque indivisae Trini- tatis, Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti devote conci- nentes: SANCTUS, SANCTUS, SANCTUS JEHOVAH ZEBAOTH: &, SANCTUS, SAN- CTUS, SANCTUS Dominus Deus omnipotens, qui erat, qui est, & qui venturus est. GLORIA EJUS SIT PLENA UNIVERSA TERRA. Amen.

## 1:1 Introduction: N. J. Lesiasten
N. J. LESIASTEN.

censured, but he valued the book itself most highly. Finally, on the sum, use, and economy of the book.

Grotius, who seeks praise from novelties, is not pleased with the ancient appellation of both the Greek and Latin Church, which called the present book ἐκκλησιαστὴν Ecclesiastes, which the Germans and Belgians also expressed in this way. Perhaps it is better translated, he says, as συναθροιστὴς, in the way the word קֹהֶלֶת is accustomed to be translated by συναθροίζειν, so that we may understand that the various opinions of men, who were each considered wise among their own people, περὶ τῆς ἐυδαιμονίας were gathered into this book, just as the book of Job embraces almost all the opinions that have been or can be regarding the governance of human affairs or against it. Therefore, he might perhaps have preferred it to be called a collector, if it had been in his power, whom the universal Church has hitherto called Ecclesiastes for so many centuries. But he assumes without proof that the author of the book was called by this name (from whom it is undoubted that the book obtained that name) from a collection of opinions: for thus also the book of Job, and Job himself, from whom he likewise says various opinions were collected, ought to have been, or could have been, designated by that name קֹהֶלֶת; most interpreters more correctly derive it from a congregation, from an assembly and people instituted, to whom he not infrequently proposed such things concerning the vanity of all things, except God and the worship of God, which, since it is proper to Ecclesiastes and those preaching, why should he not be rightly called ἐκκλησιαστὴς from that, that is, a Preacher, who speaks words in an assembly: indeed, that ἐκκλησιάζειν also means to congregate is known even from Aristophanes, namely to call into an assembly: both of which things done by Solomon are expressed most conveniently by one word, so that both the convocation itself and the end and scope of the same may be expressed. Conf. 1 Kings 8, 1. 2. 14. And especially Eccles. 12, 9. therefore in the Midrash on this passage it is said thus, that he held his words openly and in a convened assembly. And thus Jerome explains the Greek name in his Commentary on this passage, Tom. VII. of his works. ἐκκλησιαστὴς, however, is called in the Greek language one who gathers a gathering, that is, the Church: whom we can name a preacher, because he speaks to the people, and his discourse is not directed specifically to one, but generally to all.

But that this name is used as a common noun, because it is constructed with the masculine in ch. 12, 12. ch. 8, 28. (which passage is cited incorrectly: he meant to say ch. 7, 28. but in it the masculine construction is not found) ch. 12, 8. 9. 10. Grotius asserts not badly, because the Hebrews lack common nouns; but because it is also constructed with a feminine verb in ch. 7, 28. one must then take it in a feminine sense, and understand a similar substantive, e.g., חָכְמָה wisdom, because it was the wisdom of Solomon, especially by which he drew and gathered assemblies, by which we also know he gathered foreigners to himself 1 Kings 4, 34. Nor indeed, when we interpret the word by 'Preacher', do we mean that Solomon undertook the office of herald of the word and preacher, to which the tribe of Levi was ordinarily destined: in refuting which opinion Cartwright labors in vain, which also, as clearly un-theological, if it be said of Solomon after he had fallen away from the truth once acknowledged, he refutes from Is. 44, 10. 2 Kings 23, 9., disputing without an adversary, as I think. B. Luther, Homily 1 on Ecclesiastes, Preface to Ecclesiastes, Vol. III, Jena Latin, has it thus on page 233: 'I think the title Ecclesiastes, or Preacher, is to be referred more to the name of the book itself than to the author, so that you may understand that these are words spoken publicly by Solomon in some assembly of his princes and others. For since he was King, it was not his duty or office to teach; but that of the Priests and Levites.' Wherefore I think these things were said by Solomon in a certain assembly of his own people, or at a banquet, or even within a banquet, in the presence of some great men and nobles, after he had thought much and long within himself about the condition and vanity of human affairs, or rather of the affections, which he then (as happens) poured out in their presence, and which were then received and collected by those very masters of the community or Church. Whence also at the end they confess that they received these things from one Shepherd and gathered them. Just as any one of us might sit at a banquet and discourse on human affairs, with others receiving what was said. So that, for example, it is a public Sermon, which they heard from Solomon, from which sermon it pleased them to call this book Coheleth, not because Solomon himself was a Preacher, but because this book preaches, as a public discourse. But the new exposition of Cartwright seems more subtle than true: that Solomon is described by this word from the adjunct of a GATHERED soul, and one gathering with the Church, and that Solomon's repentance is thereby insinuated. Concerning which Cartwright says: 'Since it is certain that he repented, as one who is known by many testimonies to have been chosen and loved by God, where at last shall we find this repentance testified to, if we depart from this passage?' He was present, however, so that his repentance might be left testified to posterity, since it was certain that salvation was predicted through the Scriptures, and also so that it might be understood that no one can be saved unless he has repented. From which it is clear that Solomon, wandering away from the Church because of his crimes, received himself back into the bosom or fold of the same Church through repentance (which he sealed as testified in this book).

Furthermore, that the ministerial author of the book is designated by this inscription has been beyond doubt until now. For the initial words of the first chapter are clear: 'The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, King in Jerusalem.' Which is a clear paraphrase of Solomon. Grotius, however, says those are not clear enough to establish that Solomon was the author, which has been believed by the highest consensus of Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins. 'I, however,' he says, 'do not think it is Solomon's, but written later under his name.'

name, as if led by repentance. Thus anything could be invented, and any sense whatsoever could be imposed on any words one pleases. The Holy Spirit himself testifies in the inscription (for Grotius acknowledges its Canonical authority) that these are the words of the son of David, King in Jerusalem: and that he himself is that Ecclesiastes who spoke these words and comprehended them in writing. Grotius, on the contrary, says: 'I, however, do not think it is Solomon's, but written later under his name.' Does piety therefore permit one to attribute to the Holy Spirit as author a certain pseudepigraphical writing, or one bearing a foreign and false title? Is it perhaps unknown to the Holy Spirit whether Solomon was led by repentance or not, so that the book was written by the instinct of the Spirit, because Grotius says it was deservedly received into the Canon, to which only those things belong which were written by the instinct of the Holy Spirit and are God-breathed, under the name of Solomon AS IF led by repentance? Nor indeed is the author mentioned only on the threshold of the book, but frequent repetition of him is made: 'said Ecclesiastes' v. 2. 'I, Ecclesiastes, was King in Jerusalem.' And again chapter 7: 'These things I found, said Ecclesiastes.' Finally, so that no doubt remains, in the conclusion of the book the book is vindicated to the same Ecclesiastes, whom it had called the son of David, King in Jerusalem, at the beginning, chapter 12, 8. 9. 10: 'Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, and all is vanity.' And since Ecclesiastes was most wise, he taught the people, and narrated what he had done, and investigating, he composed many parables. Who is that son of David, King in Jerusalem? Who is that most wise one, if not Solomon? And who narrated those things which this King did, if not Solomon? For he narrates his buildings, which he erected, gardens, pools, and other things to which he had devoted effort, various pleasures to which he was addicted, and the incomparable riches with which he had been endowed. Who among the pious will allow himself to be persuaded that someone falsely assumed the person of Solomon, or narrated lies as if they were done by himself, and attributed them to himself, and that too in a divinely inspired writing? Finally, who, searching out, composed many parables from the Kings in Jerusalem, if not Solomon, who taught the people with many prayers and also many writings which do not exist, and searching out, composed many parables and collected excellent maxims, as Grotius interprets? If another said these same things, simulating the person of Solomon, give me an example where the Holy Spirit inspired supposititious writings, bearing the name and deeds of another, and which such things He brought into the Canon? Therefore, the opinion of Grotius is not to be rejected, but utterly detested, as it is openly opposed to such clear testimonies of Scripture, which also detracts not a little from the authority of the Canonical book. For no book is pseudepigraphical or Spirit. S. can be attributed to an author, or ought to be held as Canonical. There were indeed those who ascribed this book (as also the remaining Solomonic ones) to Isaiah: but these attributed only the collection to Isaiah, while they referred the sentences themselves to the author Solomon. Grotius, however, imagines this book to have been patched together by six various writers, I know not by whom, and asserts that the title of pseudepigraphical was prefixed to it for the sake of gaining authority. Which accusation against a Canonical writing redounds upon the principal author himself, the Holy Spirit.

But concerning the repentance of Solomon, although diverse opinions are read, testimonies are held, not obscure, even in this very book, which Grotius also seems to acknowledge: whence most judge that the book was written by Solomon after he had done penance, for the detestation of the greater vanities of this life, so that by the example of his parent David, who after his grave fall published his confession and consigned it to letters, especially in Psalm 51, in place of a confession he left Ecclesiastes after his most grievous prevarication. For he would not be joined to David with the proclamation of his ways by the Holy Spirit himself if he had died in impenitence: just as 2 Chron. 11, 16. 17. was done: But " and from all the tribes of Israel, whoever had given " their heart to seek the Lord God of Israel, " came to Jerusalem to sacrifice their " victims before the Lord God of their Fathers: And they " strengthened the Kingdom of Judah, and confirmed Re- " hoboam the son of Solomon for three years, for they " walked in the ways of David and Solomon for only " three years. Therefore he made mention of those pleasures Eccl. 2, 1. I said in my heart: I will go and abound in delights and enjoy good things: I did not withhold my heart from enjoying every pleasure: But he acknowledges their vanity v. 2. and especially complains of the danger which threatens from the love of women, taught by his own experience Eccl. 7, 26. I surveyed all things in my mind, to know the impiety of the fool, and the error of the imprudent, and I found A WOMAN MORE BITTER THAN DEATH, who is the SNARE of hunters, and her heart is a net, and her hands are chains; he who pleases God will escape her: But he who is a sinner will be caught by her. Which seems an open indication of repentance and detestation of the impiety into which he was drawn by the love of foreign women as if by a certain snare. Whence Grotius himself at this place admits that Solomon is introduced here as touched by the conscience of evil deeds, of which women themselves had been the principal authors. Certainly that varied experience which the Ecclesiastes attributes to himself in this book does not befit his earlier and youthful years, nor those buildings which he commemorates, constructed within a few years, or the accumulated silver and gold, and the gathered substances of Kings and provinces, of which c. 2, 4. seqq. whence the Rabbis not without reason believe that Ecclesiastes was adorned by Solomon in his old age, which he himself also so graphically describes c. 12, 1. seqq. Which Mercerus proves from Kasvenaki, who reports this opinion of the Hebrews in Prov. Jerome agrees with them in c. 34. Ezech. Solomon, he says, sinned and offended God, although he later did penance, writing the Proverbs, in which he says: " Lately I have done penance, and I looked to choose " discipline. He refers to Prov. 24, 32. Where the Vulgate has it thus: Which when I had seen, I put it in my heart, and by the example I learned discipline. Nor is anything handed down there concerning the penance lately done by Solomon. Mercerus also agrees in this place that Solomon wrote this book at a great and advanced age, when he had made trial of human affairs everywhere. That this book was written by Solomon himself after he had done penance is maintained by our own Jac. Matthiae, B. Waltheri, Dn. D. Geier, by the Reformed Piscator, and others, and by the Pontificals Pineda, although it pleased Bellarmine Tom. I. de V. D. cap. 5. and Bonfrerius otherwise, namely that Ecclesiastes was written before his fall.

The argument of that opinion, that this writing is more recent. Grotius says that he has many words which you cannot find elsewhere than in Daniel, Ezra, and the Chaldean Interpreters. But he does not express what those are: Nor if certain such words occurred in this book, could it be immediately firmly concluded: that it is later than Daniel and Ezra. For must it also be said to be later than the Chaldean Interpreters, because it uses words which are found only in them, by Grotius's opinion? Should it not rather be said that Solomon, not ignorant of the Chaldean language, used them, than that this book does not acknowledge Solomon as its author, whom both the beginning, the conclusion, and the whole treatment of the book so openly attribute to Solomon.

When I unfold the annotations of Grotius, I find no more than four words which he refers to the Chaldeans or Syrians, or explains from Chaldaism. The first is סיר Pots c. 7, 6. which he says is Syriac. But that is already read as used in 2 Kings 4, 39. and also by Moses Exod. 16, 3. Grotius also observed that it was used by David Ps. 60. and 108, 10. Nor do the Hebrews doubt that it is Hebrew.

He noted another in the same c. 7, 31. or rather c. 8, 1., פשר for to solve is a word familiar to the Syrians and Chaldeans. See Dan. 5, 13. 17. the Arabs also use it. But that is taught by R. David Kimchi in the Book of Roots to be the same as פתרון interpretation. Although, however, the meaning of that word, because it does not occur elsewhere in the Hebrew Code, but its root is in use among the Chaldeans, is not undeservedly sought from the Chaldean idiom, it is nevertheless foolishly concluded from this that this book was written in the time of Ezra. For it is not the case that a new meaning of words, whose root is not used in Hebraism, is sought from the Chaldean, or even from the Arabic language, as is established concerning the word אלון, and others, which are not therefore derived from the Chaldean or Arabic language, but had a root in Hebrew, as being the primitive language, even if it is no longer in use among the Hebrews, nor found in the Code, within which almost pure Hebraism is now contained, and therefore its meaning is to be sought from a cognate language which uses that root, and received it from Hebrew as its mother. And Philologists observe that in the first verse of Genesis three words occur, the origin of which is to be sought from Arabism. Yet no one therefore denies that Genesis was written by Moses, or refers it to later times.

He observed a third example in cap. 10, 8.: But גומץ is a Chaldean word, which the Chaldean interpreter often uses, where in the Hebrew there is בור. The reason for this is the same as that of the preceding word. It is read only once in this place: from the root גמץ now unused in Hebraism, from which descends in a cognate language, namely Chaldean, the verb גמץ to dig, and thence the noun גומצא a pit, but who will deny from that that the word גומץ used here is Hebrew, or will admit that it must be held as Chaldean?

Finally, the fourth [point] is held in c. 12, 5: And the caper shall be dissipated. You may translate it very well, he says, from the Hebrew: Lust shall perish: which coheres very well with the preceding. And thus the Chaldeans use this word. The Hebrew word is אביונה, which is derived from אבה, he desired, he willed, and therefore it can be rendered as desire, as Avenarius observes in his Lexicon, and it is rendered thus by the blessed Luther: da elle Lust vergehet.

Thus, therefore, it is clear that Grotius's argument concerning many Chaldean words is vain, since not even one could be brought forth from this book that is only Chaldean and not Hebrew; but the true cause why he willingly transfers the present book to later times seems to be this, namely, that he saw that certain things concerning the future judgment and the other life are contained in it, which, according to his preconceived opinion, he judged did not agree with the time of Solomon: although, so that he might not omit anything to refute them, he attempted to attach another meaning to them as well. He betrayed this opinion of his especially in his preface to the Book of Wisdom: namely, that after Ezra the patience of the pious, the universal judgment, eternal life, and the punishments of Gehenna began to be proposed more explicitly. But how the doctrine concerning the future judgment and the other age did not agree with the time of Solomon, which the Jews themselves acknowledge was handed down by David in the Psalms, and long before by Moses and Job, and prove against the Sadducees, which also Christ proved from Moses against the same in Matthew 22. But these things belong to another place.

Moreover, there was never any doubt in the Church concerning the Canonical authority of this writing, whatever may be the case with the heretics who disparaged it, concerning whom see Sixtus of Siena, book 8. Bibliotheca, heresy 8. Nor is it said with sufficient piety that certain things are read here which are not to be approved, and the reasoning of the sentences in Job is one thing—which are not all Job's, but many are those of Job's friends, who it is established by the judgment of God Himself in chapter 42 sinned in certain matters—and the reasoning of the sentences in this book is another, which are all brought forward by the author Solomon, and from his mind and intention, which the preceding and following context, the scope and summary of the book as well, and especially the final warning, comprising the summary of the whole Scripture in chapters 12, 13, and 14, sufficiently declare; when estimated correctly, they hold themselves to be true and speak of the vanity of worldly things, and they persuade us to joy in the Lord without the approval of worldly joy, so that we may be taught that tranquility and rest for the soul are to be sought in God alone; in whom the faithful can certainly rejoice in prosperous circumstances, without fault or detriment to piety. Nor did the blessed Luther cast Ecclesiastes out of the Canon, as the Papists slander, Bellarmine. Pineda, and others; since he inserted this book among the other Canonical books in the Bibles, and separated it from the Apocrypha, and illustrated the same with a most useful Commentary, which is found in Tom. III. Jena, Tom. IV. Latin Wittenberg, Tom. XII. German Wittenberg, page 81, Tom. V. Altenburg, page 1181. But in the Rhapsody of convivial discourses, let it be said that it is not Ecclesiastes that is destitute of boots and spurs, but Ecclesiasticus, composed in the time of the Maccabees, as he adds, by Siracides, collected from the library of Ptolemy Euergetes. But the blessed Luther more correctly refutes the Papistic distortion of this book and the theology of the religious or monasteries that arose from it, which spread throughout the whole Church, where it was taught that it is Christian to abandon the household, the state, and indeed the episcopal or more truly apostolic ministries, to flee into the deserts, to separate oneself from the society of men, to live in quiet and silence, and that one cannot serve God in the world, as if Solomon calls marriages, governments, offices, and the ministries of the Word vanity, all of which he praises wonderfully here and calls gifts of God: and when Solomon teaches that the men themselves, or their counsels, are also vanities, they, inverting everything, call the things themselves vain, and opine that they themselves and their own counsels are solid and upright, dreaming things beautifully contrary to Solomon, as the blessed Luther gravely and brilliantly warns in his preface to Ecclesiastes, Tom. III. Jena. Latin, folio 230, and thus he teaches that the Papists have produced nothing for us from that MOST BEAUTIFUL and MOST USEFUL book but monsters, and have clearly fashioned abominable idols out of DIVINE GOLD.

Solomon himself grasped the summary of the book of Ecclesiastes immediately at the beginning; which he also repeats towards the conclusion in chapter 12, 8: Vanity of vanities and all is vanity, concerning which the blessed Luther says at chapter 1, 2: He places this at the beginning as the theme of the whole book and the argument of which he wishes to speak. Saying that he speaks of the highest and greatest vanity, that men are most vain in all their pursuits, that they are not content with present things, which they do not use, nor can they enjoy future things, they turn everything, even the best things, into misery and vanity by their own fault, not that of the things. And in another preface to this place: Therefore the summary and scope of this book is that Solomon wishes to make us peaceful and quiet in our minds in the common business and events of this life, so that we may live content with present things without care and desire for future things (just as Paul says, acting without care and anxiety), for to worry about future things is to afflict oneself in vain. But Solomon gathers by a certain perpetual induction that the pursuits and efforts of individual men are vain and fruitless, so that from particulars he may effect a universal conclusion and show that the pursuits of all men are vain. Which the blessed Brentius sets forth thus at chapter 12, 8, p. 120: The whole discourse of this book looks to this, to teach that there is nothing in the whole world in which the mind of man can find rest: But all things, such as wife, children, riches, dignities, the splendid titles of these, power, friends, strength, the form of the body, youth, old age, good health, pleasures, wisdom, poverty, diseases, finally, whatever they may be or can be named, are naked, vain, and empty mockeries: and likewise that all our counsels and thoughts almost never meet with a desirable outcome: but that in the Lord alone, through true and solid faith, the tranquility and peace of souls are found. Whence most correctly the blessed Justus Jonas in the preface in the tract of annotations of the blessed Luther on this place to Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, Tom. V. Altenburg, p. 118, warns that it is evident from this royal discourse that our doctrine concerning faith and true piety is not only Lutheran, but also Solomonic, and has always been and will be the highest Theology, the highest knowledge, the highest and most divine doctrine and religion under the sun.

Moreover, the blessed Luther assigns this use of this book, which is by no means the last, in his former preface, that it counsels one who is occupied in the state or the home in sad circumstances, and instructs and strengthens the mind toward patience in bearing evils, which are infinite there: which he therefore calls the Solomonic Politics and Economics. Thus, therefore, Christian Ethics in the Solomonic Proverbs precedes, Solomonic Politics and Economics succeeds in Ecclesiastes, and Ecclesiastical [theology] concerning the kingdom of Christ is comprised in the Song of Songs. Yet we easily have all these things in this book as well. For we are not only informed in moral Theology, but also concerning the spiritual kingdom, which is righteousness, peace, and joy, Rom. 14, 17, and we are led to that one Shepherd, the author of all wisdom and happiness, c. 12, 11.

The method, however, might appear more heroic than restricted, as employed in this royal sermon. We shall attempt, nevertheless, whether by divine aid we might be able to hunt down the artifice of the arrangement, which is here also truly divine. For having prefixed the title of the book, he himself embraced the sum of the treatment which he undertook to confirm: then he added the arguments of the confirmation from induction: finally, having repeated in chapter 12, verse 8, the sum of the book, he indicated the end of all books.

The treatment is instituted in such a way that the vanity of worldly actions is shown, in which true tranquility and εὐδαιμονία are sought in vain, and from thence is gathered the solidity of faith and piety alone, in which is true rest, joy, and happiness: which inference he institutes from time to time, but especially subjoined it in the last chapter: whence the treatment may be enclosed not inconveniently in this enthymeme; All things in the world are mere vanities; therefore in God alone is true happiness to be sought, and to Him one must uniquely adhere through faith and true piety. It can, however, be divided into two parts: the former is common, the latter proper. In the common part two things are explained: for Ecclesiastes treats both of the vanity of worldly happiness and of the solidity of true and divine happiness. Solomon discourses on the vanity of worldly happiness partly γενικῶς regarding the universal endeavors of man, even the most wise, chapter 1, partly εἰδικῶς, regarding delights and riches, without the εὐδοκίᾳ of God, chapter 2, regarding the anxiety about future things, with divine providence neglected, chapter 3, regarding the favor of men and the desire of having rule without true prudence and piety, chapter 4. Concerning the solidity, however, of true he treats of happiness partly comparatively, partly absolutely. There he institutes an exhortation to prayers, vows, and the fear of God, having made a comparison of the sad misery of the covetous man and the joyful tranquility of true αὐταρκείας [self-sufficiency] resting in the kindness of God, chap. 5. As also a delineation of happiness not using its own good riches, c. 6. Here he commends the pursuit of true εὐδαιμονίας [happiness] first because of the fleeting nature of human life, that we may leave behind a good reputation, the means for which are brought forward, c. 7. Then because of the fruit of divine Wisdom, true cheerfulness, and the debt of obedience, the judgment of disobedience, chap. 8. Thirdly because of the vanity concerning scandals from the equal success of the wicked with the pious in this life, and the end of this life, chap. 9. up to v. 12. And thus far the common part. There follows the proper part of the Solomonic treatment, which 1. concerns public persons, or the Political state, whose happiness depends more upon a wise Ruler and prudent counsels than upon fortitude, chap. 9, 13. seqq. although this evil is also frequent under the sun, that the wicked rule, whose end is nevertheless unhappy, and that there are babblers and fools in councils, whose end is destruction: chap. 10. 2. It looks to private Persons, or to the Economy of each: what kind of person one ought to show oneself to be both toward a needy neighbor, by beneficence, and toward oneself by joy, i.e., lawful [joy], c. 11. and toward God the creator, by true piety, and that from youth, before the evil days of old age come, which is described allegorically: since with the dust returning to the earth, the Spirit may return to God, chap. 12. up to v. 8. To which is subjoined in place of a conclusion the Sum of the book repeated, a description of the author from θεοσδότῳ [God-given] wisdom and a zeal for information, an eulogy of Holy Scripture and a summary of the same, v. 8. seqq.

Latin:

N. J. LESIASTEN.

vit, ipsum vero librum maximi fecit. Denique de summa, usu & οἰκονομίᾳ libri.

Non placet Grotio, laudem ex novitatibus captanti, antiqua Ecclesiae tum Graecae tum Latinae appellatio, quae librum praesentem vocavit ἐκκλη- σιαστὴν Ecclesiasten, quem Germani & Belgae quoque ita expresserunt. Melius forte, inquit, vertitur συν- αθροιστὴς, quomodo verbum קֹהֶלֶת per συναθροί- ζειν verti solet, ut intelligamus redactas in hunc librum varias hominum, qui sapientes apud suos quisque ha- bebantur, opiniones περὶ τῆς ἐυδαιμονίας, plane sicut liber Jobi omnes ferme, quae fuerunt aut esse possunt de rerum humanarum gubernatione aut contra eam sententias complectitur. Collectorem ergo fortassis maluisset dici, si in potestate sua habuisset, quem Ecclesia universa Ecclesiasten hactenus vocavit per tot secula. Sed precario assumit, quod autor li- bri hoc nomine appellatus fuerit (a quo librum id nominis fortitum esse, indubium est) a sententia- rum collectione: Sic enim & Jobi liber, ac Job ipse, a quo pariter sententias varias collectas dicit, eo nomine קֹהֶלֶת indigitari debuisset, aut potuis- set; rectius plerique Interpp. a congregatione, ex aula, populoque instituta, quibus non raro talia de rerum omnium, praeter Deum & cultum Dei, va- nitate, proposuerit, quod quum Ecclesiastarum proprium sit & concionantium, cur non inde ἐκ- κλησιαστὴς recte dicatur, hoc est Concionator, qui in concione verba facit: imo ἐκκλησιάζειν etiam esse congregare vel ex Aristophane notum est, in con- cionem nempe vocare: quod utrumque a Salomo- ne factum una voce exprimitur commodissime, ut cum ipsa convocatio, tum finis & scopus ejusdem exprimatur. Conf. 1. Reg. 8, 1. 2. 14. Et cum- primis Eccles. 12, 9. ideo in Midrasch super h. l. ita dicitur, quod verba sua palam & convocata concio- ne habuerit. Atque ita Hieronymus explicat Grae- cum nomen Comment. in h. l. Tom. VII. oper. ἐκκλησιαστὴς autem Græco sermone appellatur, qui cœ- tum, id est Ecclesiam congregat: quem nos nuncupare possumus concionatorem, eo quod loquatur ad populum, & sermo ejus non specialiter ad unum, sed ad uni- versos generaliter dirigatur.

Cæterum ut commune usurpari hoc nomen, quia cum masculino construitur e cap. 12, 12. c. 8, 28. (qui locus perperam citatur: dicere voluit c. 7, 28. sed in eo non habetur constructio masculina) c. 12, 8. 9. 10. non male asserit Grotius, eo quod Ebræis communia desint; sed quia construitur etiam cum fœminino verbo cap. 7, 28. oportet tum fœminino sensu accipere, ac subintelligere substantivum simi- le, e. g. חָכְמָה sapientia, quia sapientia Salomo- nis fuit, imprimis qua pertraxit collegitque concio- nes, qua etiam exteros collectos ad ipsum novi- mus 1. Reg. 4, 34. Neque vero cum per Conciona- torem vocem inrerpretamur, id volumus, quod Sa- lomo munus præconis verbi & concionatoris, ad quod tribus Levi ordinarie destinata erat, subierit: in qua sententia refellenda frustra sudat Cartwright- tus, quam etiam ut plane ἀθεόλογον, si id dicatur de Salomone, postquam a semel agnita veritate de- fecisset, ex Es. 44, 10. 2. Reg. 23, 9. refellit, sine ad- versario, ut opinor, disputans, homil. 1. in Ecclesiast. B. Lutherus Præfat. in Ecclef. T. III. Jen. Latin. ita habet pag. 233. Titulum Ecclesiasta, sive Conciona- toris, magis referendum puto ad ipsius libri, quam ad autoris nomen, ut intelligas, hæc esse verba per Salomo- nem publice dicta, in concione aliqua suorum Princi- pum & aliorum. Cum enim Rex esset, non erat sui muneris neque officii, docere; Sed Sacerdotum & Levi- tarum. Quare hæc arbitror dicta a Salomone in con- ventu quodam suorum, seu a convivio, vel etiam intra convivium, præsentibus aliquot magnis viris & proce- ribus, postquam apud se multum & diu cogitasset de rerum humanarum, seu potius affectuum conditione & vanitate, quæ sic postea (ut fit) illis præsentibus effude- rit, deinde ab illis ipsis magistris communitatis vel Ec- clesiæ excepta & collecta. Unde & in fine fatentur hæc se accepisse a Pastore uno & congessisse. Sicut nostrûm quispiam posset in convivio sedens, de rebus humanis disputare, aliis, quod diceretur, excipientibus. Ut scil. sit publica Concio, quam ex Salomone audierint, a qua concione placuit librum hunc Coheleth appellare, non quod Salomon ipse Concionator fuerit, sed quod hic liber concionetur, tanquam publicus sermo. No- va autem Cartwrighti expositio subtilior, quam verior videtur: describi hac voce Salomonem ab ad- juncto animæ CONGREGATÆ, & cum Ecclesia col- ligentis, adeoque pœnitentiam Salomonis eadem insi- nuari. Quo de Cartwrightus: Cum certum sit illum resipuisse, ut quem pluribus testimoniis a Deo ele- ctum & amatum esse constat, ubi tandem locorum hanc resipiscentiam testatam esse reperiemus, si ab hoc loco di- sccdatur? Interfuit autem, ut resipiscentia ejus testata posteritati relinqueretur, cum de Salute per Scripturas predicta constaret, tum etiam ut nullum nisi resipiscen- tem salvum fieri posse intelligatur. Ex quo illud li- quet, Salomonem ob sua scelera ex Ecclesia pere- grinantem, in ejusdem Ecclesiæ gremium seu finum per pœnitentiam (quam hoc libro testatam obsignavit) se recepisse.

Porro Auctorem libri ministerialem hac in- scriptione designari, extra dubium fuit hactenus. Verba enim initialia capitis primi diserta sunt: Verba Ecclesiastæ Filii Davidis Regis in Jerusalem. Quæ paraphrasis est luculenta Salomonis. Grotius tamen neque illa satis clara funt, ut quod summo consensu ab Ebræis, Græcis, Latinis, creditum, Salomonem autorem statueret. Ego tamen, inquit, Salomonis esse non puto, sed scriptum serius sub illius Tom. I. V. T.

Regis, tanquam pœnitentia ducti, nomine. Ita quid- vis fingi posset, & verbis quibusvis alius quicunque libuerit, indui sensus. Spiritus Sanctus testatur ipse in ἐπιγραφῇ, (agnoscit enim auctoritatem ejus Canonicam Grotius) hæc esse Filii Davidis Regis in Jerusalem verba: ipsumque esse Ecclesiasten illum, qui hæc verba fecerit, ac scripto comprehenderit. Grotius ex adverso, Ego tamen Salomonis esse non puto, sed serius sub illius nomine scriptum. Num er- go ψευδεπίγραφον quoddam scriptum, vel alie- num, falsumque titulum præ se ferentem Spiritui Sancto auctori tribuere permittit pietas? Num igno- tum forte Spiritui Sancto ductusne pœnitentia Sa- lomo fuerit, nec ne, ut liber ille scriptus fuerit, in- stinctu Spiritus, quia in Canonem merito receptum di- cit Grotius, ad quem non pertinent nisi instinctu S. S. conscripta & θεόπνευσα, sub nomine Salomonis TANQUAM pœnitentia ducti? Nec vero tantum in limine libri auctor commemoratur, sed crebra ejus repetitio fit, dixit Ecclesiastes v. 2. Ego Ecclesia- stes Rex eram in Jerusalem. Et iterum cap. 7. Hæc in- veni, dixit Ecclesiastes. Denique ne dubium ullum supersit, in conclusione libri sonora voce eidem Ecclesiastæ, quem filium Davidis Regem in Jeru- salem initio dixerat, liber vindicatur cap. 12, 8. 9. 10. vanitas vanitatum dixit Ecclesiastes, & omnia va- nitas. Cumque esset sapientissimus Ecclesiastes, do- cuit populum, & enarravit, quæ fecerat, & investigans composuit parabolas multas. Quis ille Davidis fi- lius, Rex in Jerusalem? quis ille sapientissimus, nisi Salomo? Et quisnam ea, quæ hic Rex enarravit, fecit, nisi Salomo? Enarrat enim, ædificia sua, qui extruxerit hortos, piscinas & alia, quibus operam dederat, varias voluptates, quibus deditus, divi- tiasque incomparabiles, quibus præditus fuerat. Quæ aliam personam Salomonis falso assumentem aut mentitum enarrare ac si abs se facta, sibique tribuere, idque in scripto θεοπνεύσῳ, ecquis pius sibi persuaderi patietur? Denique quis investigans parabolas multas composuit e Regibus in Jerusalem, ni- si Salomo, qui docuit populum multis orationibus, multis etiam scriptis, quæ non extant, & investigans composuit parabolas multas, egregias gnomas collegit, ut interpretatur Grotius. Quæ si itidem alius di- xit, Salomonis personam simulans, exemplum ce- do, ubi Spiritus Sanctus Scripta supposititia, alterius nomen, & res gestas præ se ferentia inspiravit, ac quænam talia in Canonem retulerit? Non repro- banda ergo, sed detestanda omnino Grotiana sen- tentia tam perspicuis Scripturæ testimoniis palam opposita, quæ etiam non parum dero gatur auctori- tati libri Canonici. Nullus enim liber ψευδεπί- γραφος vel Spirit. S. autori tribui potest, vel Ca- nonicus haberi debet. Non defuere quidem, qui librum hunc, (ut & reliquos Salomoneos) Esaiæ adscripsere: sed hi Esaiæ tantum collectionem tri- buerunt, sententias autem ipsas ad autorem Salo- monem retulere. Grotius autem sex variis scri- ptoribus nescio a quibus consarcinatum hunc li- brum comminiscitur, eiq; ψευδεπίγραφον titulum autoritatis conciliandæ gratia, præfixum asserit. Quod ἔγκλημα in Canonicum scriptum in ipsum auctorem principalem Spiritum S. redundat.

De pœnitentia vero Salomonea etsi diversæ le- gantur sententiæ, non obscura, vel in hoc ipso libro habentur testimonia, quod agnoscere etiam vide- tur Grotius: Unde plerique censent, a Salomone, postquam egisset pœnitentiam, ad detestationem ma- jorum vanitatum hujus vitæ, librum conscriptum, ut exemplo Parentis Davidis, qui post gravem la- psum confessionem suam edidit ac literis consigna- vit, Psalmo cumprimis 51, confessionis loco Ecclesia- sten post gravissimam prævaricationem reliquerit. Non enim jungeretur Davidi cum præconio viarum suarum ab ipso S. S. si in impœnitentia deces- sisset: quemadmodum 2. Par. 11, 16. 17. factum: Sed „ & de cunctis tribubus Israel, quicunque dederant „ cor suum, ut quærerent Dominum Deum Israel, „ venerunt in Jerusalem ad immolandas victimas „ suas coram Domino Deo Patrum suorum: Et ro- „ boraverunt Regnum Juda, & confirmaverunt Ro- „ boam filium Salomonis per tres annos, ambula- „ verunt enim in viis David & Salomonis annis tan- „ tum tribus. Ideo voluptatum earum mentio- nem fecit Eccl. 2, 1. dixi ego in corde meo: Vadam & affluam deliciis & fruar bonis: Non prohibui cor meum, quin omni voluptate frueretur: Sed vanitatem earum agnoscit v. 2. ac cumprimis conqueritur de pericu- lo, quod a fœminarum amore imminet, propria edo- ctus experientia Eccl. 7, 26. lustravi universa animo, ut cognoscerem impietatem stulti, & errorem impru- dentium, & inveni AMARIOREM MORTE MU- LIEREM, quæ LAQUEUS venatorum est, & sagena cor ejus, vincula sunt manus illius; qui placet Deo, effu- giet illam: Qui autem peccator est, capietur ab illa. Quod apertum videtur indicium pœnitentiæ & de- testationis impietatis, in quam mulierum extera- rum amore ceu laqueo quodam protractus fuit. Unde Grotius ipse ad hunc locum fatetur, introdu- ci hic Salomonem ut tactum conscientia male actorum, quorum præcipue auctores ipsi fœminæ fuerant. Prio- ribus certe ac juvenilibus annis non convenit illa tam varia experientia, quam sibi in hoc libro tribuit Ecclesiastes, neque aut ædificia ista, quæ commemo- rat, intra paucos annos exstructa, aut coacervatum argentum, & aurum, & congestæ substantiæ Regum ac provinciarum, de quibus c. 2, 4. seqq. unde Rab- bini non abs re credunt Ecclesiasten in senectute, quam ipse etiam tam graphice describit c. 12, 1. seqq. a Sa- lomone adornatum esse. Quod ex Kasvenaki pro- bat Mercerus, hanc Ebræorum sententiam in Prov. tradente. Annuit illis Hieronymus in c. 34. Ezech. Salomo, inquit, peccavit & offendit Deum, licet postea egerit pœnitentiam, scribens Proverbia, in quibus ait: „ Novissime ego egi pœnitentiam, & respexi ut eli- „ gerem disciplinam. Respicit Prov. 24, 32. Ubi vulgatus ita habet: Quod cum vidissem, posui in corde meo, & exemplo didici disciplinam. Neque quic- quam de pœnitentia novissime acta a Salomone il- lic traditur. Annuit etiam Mercerus in hunc lo- cum, grandi jam & provecta ætate Salomonem hunc librum scripsisse, quum rerum bumanarum undiquaq; periculum fecisset. Post actam a Salomone pœni- tentiam librum hunc ab ipso scriptum esse e nostris Jac. Matthiæ, B. Waltheri, Dn. D. Geier, e Refor- matis Piscator, & alii, e Pontificiis Pineda statuunt, etsi Bellarmino Tom. I. de V. D. cap. 5. & Bonfrerio aliud placuerit, nimirum ante lapsum conscriptum fuisse Ecclesiasten.

Argumentum opinionis istius, quod recentius sit hoc scriptum. Grotius se habere dicit multa vocabu- la, quæ non alibi quam in Daniele, Esdra, & Chaldæis Interpp. reperias. Sed quænam illa sint, non expri- mit: Neque si vocabula quædam talia in hoc libro occurrerent, statim firmiter concludi posset: Danie- le & Esdra ipsum posteriorem esse. Num enim etiam Chaldæis Interpp. posterior dicendus, quod vocabu- la ea adhibeat, quæ solum in illis reperiuntur, Grotii sententia? Annon dicendum potius foret, Salomo- nem Chaldaicæ linguæ haud ignarum ea adhibuisse, quam librum hunc Salomonem non agnoscere au- torem, quem tam aperte Salomoni tribuit tum in- gressus, tum conclusio, tum tota tractatio libri.

Annotata cum evolvo Grotii, quatuor non plura invenio vocabula, quæ ad Chaldæos vel Syros refert, vel e Chaldaismo explicat. Primum est סיר Ollæ c. 7, 6. quod Syriacum esse, ait. Sed id 2. Reg. 4, 39. jam adhibitum legitur, nec non a Mose Exod. 16, 3. A Davide etiam usurpatum Ps. 60. & 108, 10. observavit Grotius. Neque Ebræi Ebræum esse dubitant.

Alterum eodem c. 7, 31. vel potius c. 8, 1. notavit, פשר pro solvere est vox Syris & Chaldæis familiaris. Vid. Dan. 5, 13. 17. usurpant & Arabes. Verum id a R. David Kimchi in l. Rad. docetur idem esse, quod פתרון interpretamentum. Quamvis autem vocis illius significatio, quia alibi non occurrit in Ebræo Codice, Radix autem ejus apud Chaldæos in usu est, non immerito e Chaldæo idiomate petatur, inepte tamen hinc colligitur, librum hunc tempore Esdræ scriptum. Non enim novam vocum, quarum radix in Ebraismo usitata non est, significationem e Chaldæo peti, vel etiam ex Arabica lingua, uti de voce אלון constat, ac de aliis, quæ vero non derivantur ideo a lingua Chaldaica vel Arabica, sed in Ebræa Radicem habuere, utpote lingua primigenia, utut ea amplius Ebræis in usu non sit, nec in Codice, intra quem pene purus Ebraismus nunc compingitur, reperiatur, ideoque e cognata lingua, quæ eam Radicem usufrequentat, & ab Ebræa ceu matre accepit, petenda ejus significatio. Et observant Philologi in primo versu Geneseos tria occurrere vocabula, quorum origo ex Arabismo petenda. Nemo autem ideo negat Genesin a Mose conscriptam, aut ad posteriora eam refert tempora.

Tertium exemplum cap. 10, 8. observavit: Est autem גומץ vox Chaldaica, quam sæpe usurpat interpres Chaldæus, ubi in Hebræo est בור. Hujus eadem ratio est, quæ præcedentis vocis. Legitur tantum semel hoc in loco: a Radice גמץ in Ebraismo nunc inusitata, a qua descendit in lingua cognata, Chaldæa nempe, verbum גמץ fodere, atque inde nomen גומצא fovea, sed quis inde negabit vocem גומץ hic adhibitam Ebræam, aut Chaldæam eam habendam esse admittet?

Quartum denique c. 12, 5. habetur: Et dissipabitur Capparis. Optime, inquit, vertas ex Hebræo: Peribit libido: quod cum præcedenti optime cohæret. Et sic Chaldæi hanc vocem usurpant. Ebræa vox est: אביונה, quæ ab אבה concupivit, voluit, deducitur, ideoque appetentia reddi potest, ut observat Avenarius in Lex. & a B. Luthero ita redditur: da elle Lust vergehet.

Ita ergo patet vanum esse Grotii argumentum de multis vocabulis Chaldaicis, quum ne unum ex hoc libro proferri potuerit, quod Chaldaicum tantum sit, non Ebraicum, vera autem causa, cur libenter in posteriora tempora trajiciat librum præsentem, hæc esse videtur, quod nempe viderit de judicio futuro, & altera vita quædam in eodem haberi, quæ, pro opinione sua præconcepta, tempori Salomonis non congruere censuit: quamvis, ne nihil ad ea elidenda intermitteret, illis etiam alium sensum affingere conatus fuerit. Quam opinionem suam prodidit imprimis præfat. in librum Sapientiæ: quod nempe post Esdram explicatius proponi ceperit patientia piorum, judicium universale, vita æterna, supplicia gehennæ. Quomodo vero Salomonis tempori doctrina de judicio futuro, & altero ævo non convenirit, quam a Davide in Psalmis, & longe ante a Mose ac Jobo traditam esse, Judæi ipsi agnoscunt, & adversus Sadducæos probant, quam etiam Christus e Mose adversus eosdem probavit Matth. 22. Sed hæc alterius loci sunt.

Cæterum de Canonica Scripti hujus autori- tate nunquam in Ecclesia dubitatum fuit, quicquid sit de hæreticis, qui eam elevarunt, de quibus Sixt. Senenf. l. 8. Bibl. hær. 8. neque satis pie dicitur, quæ- dam hic legi non probanda, & alia est sententiarum in Jobo ratio, quæ omnes non sunt Jobi, sed multæ amicorum Jobi, quos in quibusdam peccasse e Dei ipsius judicio cap. 42. constat, alia sententiarum in hoc libro, quæ omnes ab autore Salomone adferun- tur, & ex ejus mente atque intentione, quam ante- cedentia & consequentia, scopus item & summa li- bri, & imprimis monitum finale, summam Scri- pturæ totius complectens c. 12, 13. 14. satis declarant, æstimatæ rectissimæ se habent, & vanitatem rerum mundanarum loquuntur, gaudiumque in Domino sine approbatione gaudii mundani suadent, ut sic tranquillitatem, & requiem animæ in solo Deo quæ rendam esse doceamur; in quo in rebus prosperis lætari fideles omnino possunt, citra culpam & de- trimentum pietatis. Neque vero B. Lutherus e Canone ejecit Ecclesiasten, ut calumniantur Papi- stæ, Bellarm. Pineda, alii; siquidem librum hunc in Bibliis cæteris Canonicis inseruerit, & ab Apocry- phis separarit, eundemque utilissimo Commentario illustrarit, qui habetur Tom. III. Jen. Tom. IV. Lat. Witeb. Tom. XII. Germ. Witeberg. pag. 81. Tom. V. Altenb. pag. 1181. in Rapsodo autem con- vivalium sermonum ocreis & calcaribus destitutus dicatur non Ecclesiastes, sed Ecclesiasticus, tempore Maccabæorum, ut addit, a Syracide compositus ex Bibliotheca Ptolemæi Evergetæ collatus. Rectius autem Beatus Lutherus redarguit detorsionem hu- jus libri Papisticam & Theologiam religiosorum seu Monasteriorum inde exortam, quæ per totam Ecclesiam grassata fuit, ubi docebatur, hoc esse Christianum dese- rere Oeconomiam, Politiam, imo ministeria Episcopa- lia seu verius Apostolica, fugere in deserta, separare se a societate hominum, vivere in quiete & silentio, in mundo non posse serviri Deo, quasi Salomo vanitatem appellet conjugia, imperia, officia, & Verbi ministeria, quæ omnia mirifice hic laudat, & dona Dei appellat: & cum Salomon ipsos homines, seu consilia eorum etiam vanitates esse doceat, ipsos invertentes omnia, res ipsas vanas appellare, & se suaque consilia solida & recta esse opinari, pulcre contraria Salomoni somniantes, graviter, & præclare monet B. Lutherus in præfat. in Ecclesiast. Tom. III. Jen. Lat. fol. 230. adeoque docet, Papistas nihil nisi monstra nobis ex isto PUL- CHERRIMO & UTILISSIMO libro produxisse, & plane ex AURO DIVINO abominanda idola con- flasse.

Summam libri Ecclesiastes ipse sub initium statim complexus est; quam etiam sub conclusio- nem repetit cap. 12, 8. Vanitas vanitatum & omnia vanitas, de quo B. Luther. ad cap. 1, 2. Ponit hoc exordio tanquam thema totius libri & argumentum, de quo velit dicere. Dicens se de summa & maxima vanitate loqui, quod homines sint vanissimi in omnibus suis studiis, quod non sint contenti præsentibus, quibus non utuntur, neque futuris frui possunt, vertunt omnia, etiam optima in miseriam & vanitatem sua culpa, non rerum. Et in præfat. altera in h. l. Est ergo summa & scopus hujus libri, quod Salomo vult nos reddere pa- catos, & quietos animis in communibus negotiis, & ca- sibus hujus vitæ, ut vivamus contenti præsentibus sine cura & cupiditate futurorum (sicut Paulus ait, sine cura & solicitudine agentes) futurorum enim curam frustra affligere. Colligit autem Sa- lomo inductione quadam perpetua singularium hominum studia, & conatus vanos & irritos esse, ut ex singularibus universalem conclusionem efficiat, & ostendat omnium hominum studia vana esse. Quæ ita effert B. Brentius ad cap. 12, 8. p. 120. Tota hujus libri concio huc spectat, ut doceat, nihil esse in toto mundo, in quo mens hominis acquie- scere possit : Sed omnia, utpote uxorem, liberos, divitias, dignitates, splendidos horum titulos, potentiam, ami- cos, robur, formam corporis, juventutem, senectutem, bonam valetudinem, voluptates, sapientiam, pauper- tatem, morbos, denique, quæcunque tandem sint aut nominari possint, nuda, vana, & inania esse ludibria : omnia item consilia nostra & cogitationes, nunquam fere optabilem eventum sortiri : in solo autem Domino, per fidem veram & solidam animorum tranquillitatem ac pacem inveniri. Unde rectissime B. Justus Jonas præfat. in tract. annot. B. Lutheri in h. l. ad Philipp. Hassiæ Landgr. Tom. V. Altenb. p. 118. monet, ex hac concione Regia constare, quod doctrina nostra de fi- de & pietate vera non Lutherana tantum, sed etiam Salomonea sit, & semper summa Theologia, summa a- gnitio, summa & divinissima doctrina & religio sub sole fuerit, & futura sit.

Usum autem præterea libri hujus hunc mini- me postremum assignat B. Lutherus præfat. priori, quod in Politia vel domo versanti consulat in casibus tristibus, & animum erudiat ac roboret ad patientiam in ferendis malis, quæ sunt ibi infinita : quem proinde Politica & Oeconomica Salomonea vocat. Sic ergo Ethica Christiana in Proverbiis Salomoneis præmis- sæ Politica & Oeconomica Salomonea in Ecclesiaste succedit, Ecclesiastica de regno Christi Cantico Can- ticorum comprehensa. Habemus tamen facile in hoc etiam libro isthæc omnia. Nam non informa- mur tantum in Theologia morali, sed etiam de regno spirituali, quod justitia, pax & gaudium est, Rom. 14, 17. & deducimur ad unum illum Pastorem omnis sa- pientiæ & felicitatis autorem c. 12, 11.

Methodus autem videri possit Heroica magis, quam adstricta in Regia hac concione adhibita. Tentabimus tamen an divina ope, dispositionis arti- ficium, quod hic etiam vere divinum, venari possi- mus. Præmisso enim titulo libri SUMMAM ipse complexus tractationis, quam confirmandam sum- sit : dehinc argumenta confirmationis ex inductione addidit : postremo repetita c. 12, 8. summa libri, fi- nem omnium librorum indicavit.

Tractatio ita instituitur, ut ostendatur actio- num mundanarum vanitas, in quibus vera tranquil- litas, & εὐδαιμονία nequicquam quæratur, atque in- de colligatur solius fidei & pietatis soliditas, in qua vera quies, lætitia, & felicitas : quam illationem sub- inde instituit, sed capite ultimo imprimis subjunxit: unde huic Enthymemati tractatio includetur non incommode ; Omnia in mundo vanitates meræ sunt; in Deo ergo solo quærenda est vera felicitas, eique per fidem, veramque pietatem adhærendum unice. Di- spesci autem potest in duas partes : Prior Communis est, altera Propria. Communi parte duo expedi- untur : agit enim Ecclesiastes tum de vanitate mun- danæ felicitatis, tum de soliditate veræ & divinæ fe- licitatis. De vanitate mundanæ felicitatis disserit Salomo partim γενικῶς quoad conatus universos hominis, etiam maxime sapientis, cap. 1. partim εἰδικῶς, quoad delitias & divitias, fine εὐδοκίᾳ Dei cap. 2. quoad solicitudinem de futuris, postha- bita providentia divina cap. 3. quoad favorem ho- minum, & cupiditatem regimen habendi sine vera prudentia, & pietate c. 4. De soliditate vero veræ felicitatis agit partim comparate, partim absolute. Ibi exhortationem instituit ad preces, vota, & timo- rem Dei, facta tristis miseriæ avari, lætæque tranquilli- tatis veræ αὐταρκείας in Dei benignitate acquie- scentis contentione cap. 5. nec non adumbrationem felicitatis divitiis bonis suis non utentis c. 6. Hic studium veræ εὐδαιμονίας commendat primum ob vitæ hu- manæ fugacitatem, ut bonam relinquamus famam, cujus media adducuntur, c. 7. Deinde ob Sapientiæ divinæ fructum, veram hilaritatem, & obedientiæ de- bitum, inobedientiæ judicium cap. 8. Tertio ob va- nitatem de scandalis ex improborum parili cum piis in hac vita successu, & hujus vitæ exitu cap. 9. usque ad v. 12. Atque hactenus pars communis. Se- quitur pars propria tractationis Salomoneæ, quæ 1. publicas concernit personas, seu statum Politicum, cu- jus felicitas a sapiente Rectore, & consiliis prudentibus magis, quam a fortitudine dependet cap. 9, 13. seqq. etsi malum hoc etiam sub sole frequens, quod impe- rent impii, quorum tamen exitus infelix, quodque a consiliis sint garruli & stolidi, quorum finis est per- nities: cap. 10. 2. Ad Personas privatas spectat, vel ad Oeconomiam cujusque: qualem se præbere debeat tum quoad proximum indigentem, beneficentia, tum quoad seipsum lætitia sc. licita c. 11. tum quoad Deum creatorem, pietate vera, idque inde a juventute, an- tequam dies mali senectutis veniant, quæ allegorice describitur: siquidem pulvere in terram reverten- te, Spiritus ad Deum redeat cap. 12. usque advers. 8. Quibus subjungitur conclusionis loco Summa libri repetita, descriptio autoris a sapientia θεοσδότῳ & informationis studio, elogium Scripturæ S. & summa- rium ejusdem v. 8. seqq.

## 1:1 Argument
COMMON PART On true Εὐδαιμονίᾳ [Happiness] in General. SECTION II. On the vanity of worldly happiness. I. IN GENERAL. CHAPTER I.

The inscription and summary of the Sermon having been premised, he teaches that all the endeavors of natural man are vain, and that the human generation passes away, while on the contrary the earth, Sun, wind, and water always remain in their state and order; that all things among human affairs are full of cares, although nothing new happens under the Sun, and all things are consigned to oblivion; and he testifies that he himself, although a King and endowed with wisdom above others, has experienced that all cares are vain, even those of human wisdom itself.

Latin:

PARS COMMUNIS De vera Εὐδαιμονίᾳ in Communi. SECTIO II. De mundanæ felicitatis vanitate. I. IN GENERE. CAPUT I.

Præmissa inscriptione & summa Concionis, do- cet, universos hominis naturalis conatus va- nos esse, & humanam generationem præter- ire, quum contra terra, Sol, ventus, aqua sem- per in suo statu, & ordine maneant; omnia curarum plena esse in humanis, licet nihil sub Sole novi fiat, & oblivioni tradantur omnia; seque ipsum, etsi Regem, & sapien- tia præ aliis præditum, vanas omnes curas esse, etiam ipsius sapientiæ humanæ, exper- tum esse testatur.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. WHAT HATH MAN MORE OF ALL HIS LABOR WHICH HE LABORETH UNDER THE SUN.

The special argument of this chapter, concerning the vanity of human endeavors and labors in general. What more do they have than vanity, i.e., men are led and drawn by their own counsels and studies, and in such great endeavors what do they have? Nothing but vanity. For they enjoy neither present nor absent things, because the heart is not quiet, thus they are carried suspended between heaven and earth, and they accomplish absolutely nothing: as the Blessed Luther rightly [says] here. Emphatically therefore (he continues) must be taken what he says about his labor. By which word he signifies that he will treat, not of the works of God, in which is holiness and salvation, as are all creatures, but of the works of men, who are driven and carried by their own counsels, so that he may curb their calamities and laborious businesses. Nor does he speak of the labor of the hands, which is commanded divinely, Gen. 3. In labor shalt thou eat thy bread. But of our endeavor and counsels, by which we try to effect what pleases us. For the word Amal signifies hardship and calamity rather than work, namely that labor by which men afflict themselves and torment themselves in vain. For it is a most miserable labor to strive so much in establishing counsels and fulfilling endeavors, and yet to accomplish absolutely nothing. UNDER THE SUN. He is about to describe the kingdom of vanity, and indeed the place of this kingdom, and he calls this whole kingdom of vanity, business under the Sun, a singular phrase, which we do not read elsewhere in Scripture, so that by this he may exclude divine works, which God himself, or even in us, works, and has commanded us to work, which are rather above the sun, and outside of human studies. For the sun rises to this end, that man may go forth to his work Ps. 104. that he may be the light of the world, that he may serve in bodily things. Under that, I say, sun are agitated those vain studies, by which men are afflicted. Drusius refers those words under the sun to the more remote antecedent what profit is there under the sun? But they cohere with the immediately preceding, which he laboreth under the Sun, in the whole world, even if he were to labor in the fortunate isles themselves, as the Lord Dr. Geier has it, and as long as he acts under the Sun, and enjoys the usufruct of light.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QUID HABET AMPLIUS HOMO DE UNIVERSO LABORE SUO QUO LABORAT SUB SOLE.

Speciale argumentum hujus capitis, de vani- tate humanorum conatuum, & laborum in genere. Quid amplius habent, quam vanitatem, b. e. homines suis consiliis & studiis ducuntur & trahuntur, & in tan- tis conatibus quid habent? Nihil quam vanitatem. Neque enim fruuntur præsentibus nec absentibus, quia cor non est quietum, sic inter cælum & terram suspensi feruntur, & plane nihil efficiunt: ut recte hic B. Lu- therus. Emphatice igitur (sic pergit) accipiendum quod dicit de labore suo. Quo verbo significat se actu- rum, non de operibus Dei, in quibus sanctitas & salus est, ut sunt omnes creaturæ, sed de operibus hominum, qui suis consiliis aguntur & feruntur, ut compescat eo- rum calamitates & laboriosa negotia. Nec loquitur de labore manuum, qui est præceptus divinitus, Gen. 3. In labore vescieris pane tuo. Sed de nostro conatu & consiliis, quibus efficere, quæ nobis placent, conamur. Nam vocabulum Amal significat ærumnam & calami- tatem potius quam opus, eum scilicet laborem, quo ho- mines sese adfligunt, & frustra discruciant. Est enim miserrimus labor, tantopere conari in statuendis consiliis & explendis conatibus, & tamen nihil prorsus efficere. SUB SOLE. Descripturus est regnum vanitatis, imo & locum hujus regni, appellatq́; totum hoc vanitatis regnum, negotium sub Sole, singu- lari phrasi, quam alias in Scriptura non legimus, ut per hoc excludat opera divina, quæ Deus ipse, vel etiam in nobis, operatur, & nos operari jussit, quæ potius sunt supra solem, & extra hominum studia. Solem enim ori- tur ad hoc, ut homo egrediatur ad opus suum Psal. 104. ut sit lux mundi, ut serviat in rebus corporalibus. Sub isto, inquam, sole agitantur ista vana studia, quibus af- fliguntur homines. Drusius refert verba illa sub so- le ad remotius antecedens quidnam lucri est sub so- le? Sed cohærent ea cum immediate antecedenti- bus, quo laborat sub Sole, in universo orbe, etiamsi vel in ipsis fortunatis insulis laboraret, ut habet Dn. D. Geierus, & quamdiu sub Sole agit, lucisque usu- ra fruitur.

## 1:4
Vers. 4. VANITY OF VANITIES SAID ECCLESIASTES, VANITY OF VANITIES AND ALL IS VANITY.

IN this summary of the book the Blessed Luther rightly notes the Hebraism: Vanity of vanities, that is, the greatest and highest vanity, and absolutely total vanity: and he observes that this saying refers not to the things themselves, but to the human heart, which abuses things to its own disadvantage. It is a repetition of a vehement assertion and a grave complaint about the vanity of things, and a note of the necessity of this doctrine: because the extreme vanity of worldly things can never be inculcated enough.

Latin:

Vers. 4. VANITAS VANITATUM DIXIT EC- CLESIASTES, VANITAS VANITATUM ET OMNIA VANITAS.

IN hac libri summa recte Ebraïsmum notat B. Lutherus: Vanitas vanitatum, id est, maxima & summa vanitas, & prorsus tota vanitas: idque dictum observat, non in res ipsas, sed in cor humanum, quod rebus abutitur suo incommodo. Repetitio est vehe- mentis asseverationis & gravis querelæ de rerum vanitate, ac necessitatis hujus doctrinæ nota: quia nunquam satis inculcari potest extrema mundano- rum vanitas.

## 1:4
Vers. 4. GENERATION PASSES, AND GENERATION COMES) for they say that human affairs are a circle: Aristotle 4. Physics c. 14. Seneca: All things are linked in a circle, they flee and follow. Tacit. Annal. 3. In all things there is a kind of circle. See also Synesius epistle 374. See the same sentiment treated in Ecclesiasticus 14. v. 18.

Jerome expresses the meaning correctly: As others die, others are born, and those whom you had seen, you do not see; you begin to see those who were not. What is more vain than this vanity, that the earth, which was made for the sake of men, should remain, and man himself, the lord of the earth, should suddenly be dissolved into dust.

Verse of the same. BUT THE EARTH STANDS FOREVER) The issue here is not about the state or the motion of the earth, but about its duration as opposed to the duration of individual men: therefore it is called πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεί.

Although the earth is said to stand, because it endures and perseveres in its state, nevertheless the state of the earth is not badly inferred from this: for that word עמד also implies rest, when something is not moved, Jos. 10, 13. Wherefore it is indicated that the earth stands perpetually immobile, and perseveres in that state, and is not subject to change, as human individuals are. Compare Psalm 119, 91. Therefore Solomon now also compares those things which are moved, and prefers them in a certain respect to man,

The sun, indeed, the air or wind and water, because they ought to be preferred to man not only to the earth, which does not change its place, but always remains unmoved, and persists in the same state, but also to those things which presently change their place, in so far as they remain the same by reason of their essence, whereas man, subject to vanity on account of sin, is such that a generation once departing never returns. For this reason, the mobility of the heavens and the immobility of the earth are also opposed to each other here. The sun rises and sets, and again pants toward its place where it rises. Which, after it has dipped its burning wheel in the ocean, returns through paths unknown to us to the place from whence it went out, and having completed the circle of the night, it rushes forth again from its chamber, as Jerome elegantly puts it here: but of the earth, Ecclesiastes says: The earth, he says, עֹמֶדֶת stands, it does not rise, it does not set, it does not return to its place, but stands unmoved forever.

Latin:

Vers. 4. GENERATIO PRÆTERIT, ET GENERATIO AD- VENIT) φασὶ γὰρ κύκλον εἶναι τὰ ἀνθρώπινα πράγματα: Aristoteles 4. Physicorum c. 14. Seneca: In orbem nexa sunt omnia, fugiunt & sequuntur. Tacit. Annal. 3. Rebus cunctis inest quidam velut orbis. Vide & Sinesium epistola 374. Vi- de eandem sententiam tractatam Ecclesiastici 14. v. 18.

Sensum recte exprimit Hieronymus: Aliis morientibus, nascuntur alii, & quos videras, non vides, incipis videre, qui non erant. Quid hac vanius vani- tate, quam terram manere, quæ hominum causa facta est, & ipsum hominem terræ Dominum in pulverem re- pente dissolvi.

Vers. eod. TERRA AVTEM IN ÆTERNUM STAT) Non hic agitur de terræ aut statu, aut motu, sed de duratione op- posita singulorum hominum durationi: ideo dicitur πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεί.

Etsi terra stare dicatur, quod duret, ac in statu suo perseveret, non male tamen hinc etiam colligi- tur terræ status: Nam vox illa עמד quietem etiam infert, cum quid non movetur Jos. 10, 13.
