Quapro- pter id indicatur, terram perpetuo immobilem stare, atque in eo statu perseverare, nec mutationi, ut hu- mana individua, obnoxiam esse. Conf. Psal. 119, 91. ideo confert nunc etiam Salomo res illas, quæ mo- ventur, ac præfert easdem certa ratione homini,

Solem nempe, aerem vel ventum & aquam, quod non tantum terræ, quæ locum non mutat, sed immota fem- per perstat, & in eodem statu permauet, sed etiam ista, quæ subinde locum mutant, hactenus præferri homini debeant, quod essentiæ ratione eadem ma- neant, quum homo vanitati ob peccatum subjectus ita sit, ut generatio semel abiens nunquam redeat. Hac ergo ratione opponuntur hic quoque sibi cæli mobilitas, & terræ immobilitas. Sol oritur & occi- dit, iterumque ad locum suum aspirat, ubi oritur. Qui postquam ardentem rotam oceano tinxerit, per incogni- tas nobis vias, ad locum unde exierit, regreditur, ex- pletoque noctis circulo rursum de thalamo suo festinans erumpit, ut eleganter hic Hieronymus: de terra ve- ro Ecclesiastes: Terra, inquit, עֹמֶדֶת stat, non oritur, non occidit, non regreditur ad locum suum, sed im- mota stat in seculum.

## 1:5
Verse 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

## 1:6
AND IT TURNS TO THE NORTH) That is, to the places of midnight, from which they call the north and the Germans. This passage shows that the Hebrews believed the earth to be spherical, and the sun to turn around it. It does not show only what was believed by the Hebrews: But what is the opinion of Holy Scripture on that matter; unless perhaps Grotius denied that the Holy Spirit was the principal author of this book. Which is impious. But if it proceeded from the Holy Spirit, who can doubt whether the earth or the sun is moved? Since Holy Scripture itself defined that the sun turns around the earth: Why therefore did Grotius waver at 1 Sam. 2:8, whether the earth moves or rests? Why does he incline to that opinion, that the earth balances itself in motion, bringing forward that the magnet imitates it. See concerning this question Judic. Theol. repet. advers. M. Henr. Nicolai: and Vol. 3. Syst. Theolog. Artic. 5. chap. 2. Qu. 7. p. 1086. seqq.

Verse 6.

SURVEYING ALL THINGS IN A CIRCUIT THE WIND GOES, AND RETURNS INTO ITS CIRCUITS) Some wish the discourse to be continued about the sun, which is called the Spirit, because it has nothing similar to these lower bodies. Others take it concerning the air: of which Pliny 2, 38. The breath of so many animals draws the Spirit from on high. But it strives against it, and the earth, as if into an empty heaven, pours the Spirit: with nature thus moving back and forth, so that by a certain tension of the world's speed, discord is ignited: nor is it allowed for the battle to stand, but it is involved in constant motion: and it stretches around the earth as if in an immense globe of things, presently covering another heaven through the clouds. This is the kingdom of the winds.

Why did he produce those things about the sun, unless he was delighted by Rabbinical trifles of that kind. Just as R. Solomon understands the word Spirit as the appetite of the sun. It is certainly inept that the sun is called a Spirit, but the reason for that appellation is more inept, because it does not have a similar body as these lower things. Thus all those higher things will be Spirits. Nor are Jerome's reasons much more convenient: that the sun is called a Spirit, either because it animates, breathes, and flourishes, and completes its annual courses, or because the Spirit within nourishes both the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, and a mind infused through the limbs moves the whole mass. It is manifest that the wind is designated, or the air, as Aben-Ezra among the Hebrews, Junius, and others understand, since the wind is air impelled, agitated back and forth, whose wonderful circumgyration is described here, which stretches around the earth as if in an immense globe of things, presently covering another heaven through the clouds, which Grotius brought here from Pliny 2, c. 38.

Latin:

ET FLECTITVR AD AQVILONEM) Id est, ad me- dinoctii loca, à quibus septentrionem & Germani appellant. Ostendit hic locus Hebræis terram creditam σφαιροειδῆ, & circa eam verti Solem. Non ostendit solum, quid Ebræis creditum fuerit: Sed quæ sit S. S. ea de re sententia; nisi fortas- sis negarit Grotius, S. S. auctorem principalem hu- jus libri fuisse. Quod impium. Si autem a Sp. S. profecta, ecquis dubitare potest, terrane an Sol mo- veatur? quum circa terram verti Solem, S. S. ipse definierit: Cur ergo fluctuavit Grotius ad 1. Sam. 2, 8. moveaturne terra, an quiescat? Cur propendet in illam sententiam, quod in motu se libret terra, ma- gnetem id imitari, afferens. Vide de hac quæstio- ne judic. Theol. repet. advers. M. Henr. Nicolai: & Tom. 3. Syst. Theolog. Artic. 5. cap. 2. Qu. 7. p. 1086. seqq.

Vers. 6.

LVSTRANS VNIVERSA IN CIRCVITV PERGIT SPIRITVS, ET IN CIRCVLOS SVOS REVERTITVR) De Sole quidam continuari sermonem volunt, qui Spiritus dicatur, quod nihil habeat inferioribus his corporibus simi- le. Alii de aere accipiunt: de quo Plinius 2, 38. Tot ani- malium haustus Spiritum è sublimi trahit. At ille contra niti- tur, tellusque, ut inani cælo, Spiritum infundit: sic ultra citra commeante natura, ut tormento quodam mundi celeritate di- scordia accendatur: nec stare pugnæ licet, sed assiduo raptu in- volvitur: & circa terram immenso rerum quasi globo tendit, subinde per nubes cælum aliud obtexens. Ventorum hoc regnum.

Cur illa de Sole produxit, nisi quod nugis e- jusmodi Rabbinicis delectatus fuerit. Quemad- modum R. Salomo vocem Spiritus de appetitu Solis intelligit. Ineptum certe est, Solem dici Spiritum, at ineptior ejus appellationis ratio, quod non habeat simile corpus ut hæc inferiora. Sic omnia ista supe- riora Spiritus erunt. Neque multo convenientio- res Hieronymi sunt rationes: Solem Spiritum dici, si- ve quod animet, spiretet & vigeat, & annuos cursus ex- pleat, sive quod & Lunæ lucentem globum, & astra Ti- tania Spiritus intus alat, totamque infusa per artus mens agitet molem. Manifestum est ventum designari, vel aerem, uti Aben-Ezra ex Ebræis, Junius, & alii intelligunt, quum ventus sit aër impulsus, ultro ci- troque agitatus, cujus mira circumgyratio hic de- scribitur, quæ circa terram immenso rerum quasi glo- bo tendit, subinde per nubes cælum aliud obtexens, quod e Plinii 2, c. 38. hic adduxit Grotius.

## 1:7
Verse 7.

ALL RIVERS ENTER INTO THE SEA, AND THE SEA DOES NOT OVERFLOW: TO THE PLACE WHENCE THE RIVERS GO OUT, THEY RETURN SO THAT THEY MAY FLOW AGAIN) Namely, with the sea they enter subterranean passages, and there, filtered, they burst forth into springs. That is most evident in the Caspian Sea, which it is now sufficiently established is nowhere connected in the open with the Ocean. Therefore the sea has its channels, just as many rivers absorbed by the lands rise again after a long interval.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

OMNIA FLVMINA INTRANT IN MARE, ET MARE NON REDVNDAT: AD LOCVM VNDE EXEVNT FLVMINA, REVERTVNTVR VT ITERVM FLVANT) Nempe cum mari intrant meatus subterraneos, & ibi colati in fontes erumpunt. Apertissimum id in Ca- spio mari, quod nusquam in aperto cum Oceano esse conti- nens satis jam constat. Habet ergo mare canales suos, sicut multa flumina terris absorpta ex longo intervallo resurgunt

## 1:9
WHAT IS THAT WHICH HAS BEEN? THE VERY THING WHICH IS TO BE: WHAT IS THAT WHICH HAS BEEN DONE? THE VERY THING WHICH IS TO BE DONE) In this sense the Platonists say all things are ἓν καὶ ἕτερον. See below 3. v. 15. M. Antoninus book 12. πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο, καὶ γενήσεται, καὶ νῦν πανταχοῦ γίνεται. and elsewhere πάντα τροποῦ ἐχ ὥσε φοβηθῆναι μήτι καινὸν, πάντα συνήθη.

Latin:

QVID EST QVOD FUIT? IPSUM QVOD FUTU- RUM EST: QVID EST QVOD FACTUM EST? IPSUM QVOD FACIENDUM EST) Hoc sensu Plato- nici omnia dicunt esse ἓν καὶ ἕτερον. Vide infra 3. v. 15. M. Antoninus libro 12. πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο, καὶ γενήσεται, καὶ νῦν πανταχοῦ γίνεται. & alibi πάντα τροποῦ ἐχ ὥσε φοβηθῆναι μήτι καινὸν, πάντα συνήθη.

## 1:13
Verse 13.

I HAVE PROPOSED IN MY MIND TO SEEK AND INVESTIGATE WISELY CONCERNING ALL THINGS WHICH ARE DONE UNDER THE SUN) I have most diligently inquired into the history of animals and fates.

THIS WORST OCCUPATION GOD GAVE TO THE SONS OF MEN) עני The Hebrew, which he translates here as 'worst', often signifies a laborious and troublesome thing, which he will now call the affliction of the spirit. There is labor in those studies, not rest, not happiness itself.

It is not the study of zoology and botany that is referred to here: but Solomon testifies that he applied the cares of his mind and heart to inquire into and investigate with wisdom EVERYTHING THAT IS DONE UNDER HEAVEN. He applied his mind to investigate these worldly things, and especially what pertains to the deeds, pursuits, and events of men, for it is of these that he primarily intends to treat at present. Blessed Luther rightly warned that the Sophists corrupted these words when they thought that the studies of philosophers were being criticized here, by which they scrutinize the natures and causes of things. One must remain, he says, in the theme: We are not speaking of the deeds of GOD, which are not confined under the sun, but are everywhere, but of those things which are done and performed by men under the heavens, which is the place and kingdom committed to us. For divine works are above, below the heaven, and everywhere. There are, therefore, works which we do by our own counsels and strengths, of which he says: I determined in my mind that I would arrange all things in the best way, that I might have the Kingdom established in the best order, but as much as God worked, so much was it ordered. But where God did not add His hand, there I succeeded, urging my own counsels, wisdom, and efforts, so that all things might be managed rightly, but in vain. For I did nothing, except that I miserably twisted and tortured myself (as follows:) THIS EVIL AFFLICTION GOD GAVE TO THE SONS OF MEN, THAT THEY MIGHT BE TORTURED BY IT. That is, God gave me this thought as a punishment, that I might finally learn that I ought not to trust in my own wisdom, and that all things are in vain, even if attempted most wisely, when God does not will it.

Vers. 24.

I HAVE SEEN ALL THINGS THAT ARE UNDER THE SUN, AND BEHOLD, EVERYTHING IS VANITY AND AFFLICTION OF SPIRIT.

The commentary of Blessed Luther pleases here likewise above others, who persists in the theme and present argument: It is a confirmation of the preceding statement. Not only by my own example have I discovered this vanity, but I have contemplated all others, and I have seen their counsels frustrated just as mine were; just as my own counsels did not succeed for me, so I saw them succeed for no one in the whole world. The counsels of the wise are frustrated just as much as those of the foolish. Therefore, that affection which is called 'good intention' is rejected by these words, when people commonly say, 'I meant well.' But there is no good intention except that which is governed by the word of God, and which begins from faith. The rest, even those that are best in appearance, deceive, and even do the greatest harm. Cicero himself, having experienced this, testifies that things thought out in the best way turn out in the worst way. And God acts rightly when He thus frustrates our counsels. Because where even a little succeeds, men are soon puffed up and arrogate glory to themselves, which is against the glory of God, who wishes to be the only one to be glorified. Affliction of spirit, as Jerome [called it] κάκωσις πνεύματος, as Symmachus translated it, is also approved by Junius: and is deservedly preferred to the translation of Aquila, νομὴ ἀνέμε: since both the Chaldean and R. Solomon interpret it as the contraction of the spirit. So also Piscator [translates it] by vexation or trouble, or κακίαν from Matt. 6, last verse, deriving the word רעות from רוע, meaning evil, which others refer to the root רעע, to break or crush, while others refer it to רעה, to graze, so that the grazing or consumption of the spirit is noted.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

PROPOSUI IN ANIMO MEO QVÆRERE ET IN- VESTIGARE SAPIENTER DE OMNIBUS QVÆ FI- VNT SVB SOLE) Historiam animalium & fatorum dili- gentissime inquisivi.

HANC OCCUPATIONEM PESSIMAM DEDIT DEUS FILIIS HOMINUM) עני Hebræum quod hic pessimam vertit, sæpe rem laboriosam ac molestam significat, quod jam nunc dicet afflictionem Spiritus. Labor est in illis studiis, non quies, non ipsa beatitudo.

Non hic ζωολογίας & Φυτολογίας studium respicitur: sed testatur Salomo se animi cordisque curas intendisse ad disquirendum & investigandum cum sapientia OMNE QUOD FIT SUB COE- LO. ad indaganda mundana hæc, & imprimis quod ad facta, studia, & eventus hominum animum ap- plicuerit, de his enim in præsenti agere maxime in- stituit. Recte B. Lutherus monuit, corrupisse hæc Sophistas, cum hic putarunt Philosophorum studia taxari, quibus rerum naturas & causas scrutantur. Manendum, inquit, in themate: Non loquimur de fa- ctis DEI, quæ non coartantur sub sole, sed sunt ubique, sed de his quæ aguntur & fiunt per homines sub cælis, qui est locus & regnum nobis commissum. Nam ope- ra divina sunt supra, infra cælum & ubique. Sunt ergo opera, quæ nostris consiliis & viribus facimus, de quibus dicit: Ego constitui in animo, ut omnia optime disponerem, ut haberem Regnum optimo ordine consti- tutum, sed quantum Deus operabatur, tantum ordi- nabatur. Cæterum ubi Deus non addebat manum, ibi ego successi urgens mea consilia, sapientiam & conatus, ut omnia recte curarentur, sed frustra. Nihil enim egi, nisi quod me misere torsi & excruciavi (ut sequi- tur :) HANC AFFLICTIONEM MALAM DE- DIT DEUS FILIIS HOMINUM, UT HAC CRUCIARENTUR. Id est, Deus dedit mihi hanc cogitationem in pœnam, ut tandem discerem, quod non debeo sapientia mea confidere, & omnia frustra esse, li- cet sapientissime tentata, quando Deus non vult.

Vers. 24.

VIDI CUNCTA QUÆ SUNT SUB SO- LE, ET ECCE UNIVERSA VANITAS ET AFFLICTIO SPIRITUS.

Placet hic itidem præ aliis Commentarius B. Lutheri, qui in themate & argumento præsenti per- sistit: Est confirmatio præcedentis dicti. Non solum meo exemplo comperi vanitatem hanc, sed contempla- tus sum alios omnes, vidique illorum perinde atque mea consilia frustrari, sicut mihi non succedebant propria consilia, sic nulli in toto orbe vidi succedere. Sapien- tum consilia æque frustrantur ut stultorum. Rejici- tur ergo his verbis ille adfectus, qui dicitur bona in- tentio, cum vulgo dicunt, Jch hab es gut gemeynt, Sed nihil est bona intentio, nisi quæ regitur verbo Dei, & quæ a fide incipit. Reliquæ etiam in speciem optimæ fallunt, & vel maxime nocent. Hoc & Cicero ipse expertus testatur, optime cogitata pessime evenire. Et recte facit Deus, cum sic frustratur nostra consilia. Quia ubi vel parum succedit, mox inflantur homines & sibi arrogant gloriam, quod est contra gloriam Dei, qui vult solus gloriari. Afflictio Spiritus, ut Hiero- nymus κάκωσις πνεύματος, ut Symmachus reddi- dit, probatur etiam Junio: & præfertur merito translationi Aquilæ νομὴ ἀνέμε: siquidem & Chal- dæus, & R. Salomo interpretentur contractionem spi- ritus. Sic quoque Piscator per vexationem aut molestiam, vel κακίαν e Matth. 6, ult. a רוע malum esse vocem רעות deducens, quam alii ad radicem רעע confringere, comminuere referunt, alii ad רעה depascere, ut depastio, vel absumtio animi notetur.

## 1:15
Verse 15. THE PERVERSE ARE HARD TO CORRECT, AND THE NUMBER OF FOOLS IS INFINITE.

In Hebrew it is: The perverse cannot be straightened, and the defect cannot be numbered. Where we again acquiesce to the explanation of the Blessed Luther, as being the best: He adds the cause why all things afflict with vain care and anxiety. Because, he says, the defects are infinite, which cannot be corrected, whose magnitude and multitude overcome all human counsels. He wishes therefore to say: I indeed understand wisely enough what is expedient and fitting, but what am I to do about these things? So great is the crookedness and depravity in human affairs that they can never be corrected. -- Wherefore it would be best to commit all things to God, and to follow those who say, Let it go as it goes, because it wants to go as it goes. Which also the German proverb warns, you are much too young for the beak, that you should make old rogues pious. Hence you see Princes, who wish to reform and correct all things in the best way, often do the most harm. It is not possible in human affairs for things to be done so well that all things are done rightly, and that very many evils do not remain. It is therefore most right to walk in Faith, which permits GOD to reign, and prays that the kingdom of God may come, meanwhile tolerating and suffering all things that are evil, but handing this over to Him who judges justly.

Latin:

Vers. 15. PERVERSI DIFFICILE CORRIGUNTUR, ET STULTORUM INFINITUS EST NUMERUS.

In Ebræo est: Perversum non potest dirigi, & defectus non potest numerari. Ubi iterum acquiescimus explicationi B. Lutheri, utpote optimæ: Causam addit, quare omnia affligant frustranea cura & solicitudine. Quia, inquit, defectus infiniti sunt, qui non possunt corrigi, quorum magnitudo & multitudo vincit omnia humana consilia. Vult ergo dicere: Ego quidem sapienter satis intelligo, quid expediat & conveniat, sed quid ad hæc facturus sum? Tanta est curvitas & pravitas in negotiis humanis, ut nunquam possint corrigi. -- Quare optimum fuerit, omnia committere Deo, & sequi illos, qui dicunt, Mitte vadere, sicut vadit, quia vult vadere sicut vadit. Quod etiam Germanicum proverbium monet, du bist viel zu geel umb den Schnabel, daß du soltest alte Schälcke fromm machen. Hinc vides Principes, qui omnia optime reformare & corrigere volunt, sæpe plurimum nocere. Non potest in rebus humanis tam bene agi, ut omnia recte fiant, & non plurima mala restent. Rectissimum ergo est ambulare in Fide, quæ permittat DEUM regnare, & oret, ut adveniat regnum Dei, interim toleret & patiatur omnia male, tradat autem hoc judicanti juste.

## 1:16
Verse 16. I HAVE SURPASSED ALL IN WISDOM.

“For besides the divine wisdom, with which he had been gifted by God, he also excelled in admirable human or political wisdom, to such an extent that even the order of his Ministers was a miracle to the Queen of Arabia, as Luther rightly says here.

Latin:

vers. 16. PRÆCESSI OMNES SAPIENTIA.

„Nam præter sapientiam divinam, qua a „Deo donatus erat, præcellebat etiam admirabili sapientia humana sive politica, in tantum, ut „vel ordo Ministrorum ejus esset miraculo Reginæ Arabiæ, ut recte hic Lutherus.

## 1:17
Verse 17. THAT I MIGHT KNOW PRUDENCE AND DOCTRINE, AND ERRORS AND FOLLY.

He also adds the investigation of insanities and folly: because as Jerome has it, opposites are understood by opposites, and the first wisdom is to have lacked folly: but one cannot lack folly unless one has understood it. The word הוללות denotes a certain notable aberration from wisdom, where the mind, destitute of any guide at all, is snatched by a certain irrational impulse to pursue a thing, but the other, שכלות, denotes a certain foolish levity delighting itself in vain things, and caring little for the true good like children, as Dr. Gejer observes: But Megalander expressed the sentiment best: “Wisdom, he says, is the knowledge by which I see how a Republic is to be constituted and administered, which knowledge or experience afterwards moderates, according to present things and circumstances, with a certain reason and manner, as things and times allow, etc. Folly and imprudence. Namely, that I might remove these from myself and my Kingdom, but promote those. But what happens? I have experienced that this too is an affliction of the Spirit and a useless care, which does not attain its end. Therefore it is most wise to compose oneself so that one can bear all things. Why? Because with great wisdom there is great indignation. He who sees much and knows how it ought to go, cannot help but be vexed

and thinks, Oh how godless, how shamefully things go on in the World. But whence this vexation and indignation? If not from much wisdom. For he who knows much has many causes for anger, as one who daily sees many unworthy things. He who has closed eyes knows nothing, is not indignant. Therefore learn to be silent, to commit the Kingdom to God, and to pray, Lord, thy will be done. Otherwise you weary your heart and body, and waste your time and your life.

Latin:

Vers. 17. UT SCIREM PRUDENTIAM ATQUE DOCTRINAM, ERRORESQUE ET STULTITIAM.

Adjungit etiam indagationem insaniarum & stultitiæ: quia ut Hieronymus habet contrariis contraria intelliguntur, & sapientia prima est stultitia caruisse: stultitia autem carere non potest, nisi qui intellexerit eam. Vox הוללות insignem quandam a sapientia aberrationem, ubi animus omni prorsus rectore destitutus irrationabili quodam impetu rapitur ad rem prosequendam, notat, altera vero שכלות fatuam quandam levitatem in vanis se oblectantem, verumque bonum instar puerorum parum curantem, ut observat Dn. D. Gejerus: Sententiam autem optime expressit Megalander: „Sapientia, inquit, est cognitio, qua video, quomodo sit Respublica constituenda & administranda, quam postea scientia seu experientia „moderatur, secundum res præsentes & circumstantias, ratione quadam & modo, ut res & tempora ferunt &c. Stultitiam & imprudentiam. Sci- „licet, ut hæc amoverem a me & meo Regno, illa „vero promoverem. Sed quid evenit? Expertus „sum etiam hoc esse afflictionem Spiritus & inutilem curam, quæ non assequitur finem. Igitur „sapientissimum est sic se componere, ut omnia „possit ferre. Quare? Quia cum magna sapientia est magna indignatio. Wer viel siehet und weiß wie es gehen soll, non potest facere, quin stomachetur

& cogitat, Ach wie heilos, wie schändlich gehet es zu in Mundo. Unde autem hæc stomachatio ac in- " dignatio? nisi ex multa sapientia. Qui enim mul- " ta sapit, habet causas irascendi multas, ut qui quo- " tidie videat multa indigna. Qui habet clausos " oculos, nihil scit, non indignatur. Itaque disce " tacere, committere Regnum Deo, & orare, Do- " mine fiat voluntas tua. Alioqui fatigas cor & " corpus, ac tempus perdis & vitam tuam. "

## 2:1 Argument
II. IN PARTICULAR. CHAPTER II.

Solomon teaches that the delights of the world are vain, whence he chastised his body with the study of true wisdom, and although he built many things, collected great riches, procured for himself singers and songstresses, and grew above others, and that without neglecting wisdom, yet all things were found to be vain, on account of the equal success of fools in the world, and because it cannot be known what kind of heir there will be; and therefore he concludes that joy in the Lord is to be preferred to all such cares and labors, which does not happen except from the Lord.

Verse 1.

I SAID IN MY HEART: I WILL GO AND ABOUND IN RICHES, AND I WILL ENJOY GOOD THINGS. AND I SAW THAT THIS ALSO WAS VANITY) It did not first occur to Epicurus or the Epicureans that happiness is placed in that pleasure which is perceived by the senses. But that thought has occurred to many men long ago, which nevertheless, by a rightly instituted judgment, is found to be vain.

Latin:

II. IN SPECIE. CAPUT II.

Delitias mundi vanas esse docet Salomo, unde corpus suum castigavit veræ sapientiæ studio, & quamvis multa ædificarit, ma- gnas divitias collegerit, Cantatores & Cantatrices sibi compararit, & præ aliis creverit, idque non posthabita sapientia, vana tamen omnia deprehensa esse, ob parilem stultorum in mundo successum, & quod sciri non possit, qualis futurus sit hæres; ideoque concludit omnibus ejus- modi curis, & laboribus præferendam esse lætitiam in Domino, quæ non contin- git, nisi a Domino.

Vers. 1.

DIXI EGO IN CORDE MEO: VADAM ET AF- FLUAM DIVITIIS, ET FRUAR BONIS. ET VIDI QVOD HOC QVOQVE ESSET VANITAS) Non primo Epicuro aut Epicureis in mentem venit in voluptate ea quæ sensibus percipitur, beatitudinem esse positam. Sed jam olim multis hominibus ea cogitatio incidit, quæ tamen vana recte instituto judicio comperitur.

## 2:2
I HAVE ACCOUNTED LAUGHTER AN ERROR, AND TO JOY I SAID: WHY ART THOU DECEIVED IN VAIN?) Since the better part of man is reason, happiness is wrongly placed in the inferior part. See below 25.

Latin:

RISUM REPUTAVI ERROREM, ET GAUDIO DI- XI: QVID FRUSTRA DECIPERIS?) Cum potior ho- minis pars sit ratio, male felicitas summa ponitur in parte deteriore. Vide infra 25.

## 2:12
Verse 12.

WHAT IS MAN, THAT HE COULD FOLLOW THE KING HIS MAKER) By supplying a slight omission, such as are many among the Hebrews, the sense will thus become optimal: Who is the man who could follow the King in those things which have already been done: namely, in knowing them? Who can compare for himself such a great knowledge of ancient history as a King abounding in resources? But consequently, who will be able to judge better concerning the effects of φρονήσεως καὶ ἀφροσύνης? There is indeed some difference between these, but it is ἐφήμερον. Here in the Hebrew, מֶה is placed not for 'what', but for 'who', as also 1 Sam. 4, v. 6; 2 Kings 1, v. 7.

Mercerus, in his commentary on this passage, reviews various opinions concerning these words, which he confesses to be quite difficult; yet he judges that one to be the simplest which Grotius here sells as new. Mercerus prefers that מה האדם be rendered 'what is man', by way of contempt; not 'who is man'? But, 'what is man', as in Psalm 8:5 and 144:3. Aben-Ezra, however, led the way, explaining the speech thus: Who is he who would wish to follow the King in the magnitude of works and in the experiments of things; that is to say, he will lose his labor: but he who understands the verb יעשׂו, i.e., 'he shall do', at the end, [means] that he will do that which others have already done, where Mercerus prefers to understand לדעת, so that he may know: What is man who would come after (me, so much) the King, so that he may know what (others) have already done or what has already been done, to which new things cannot be added, in which no one can innovate anything, so that he may say or think that he will experience something which the King has not experienced. The translation of Aben-Ezra is nevertheless simpler, even if it produces the same sense, it seems: Who is the man who will come after the King, (who is to experience these things in such a way) Do that which others have already done, that is to say, nothing new will be able to accomplish what others have not accomplished, and consequently, what I have not attempted, and to know nothing else from me. This sense is also presented by Thomas Cartwright, the Cambridge theologian, and the Belgian interpreters. Furthermore, Mercer has indicated yet another sense, that the final words can be referred to Solomon: What is man, that he should wish to test things after the King whom they have already made, that is, whom all have approved, and acknowledged as made both divinely and humanly, whose wisdom and magnificence all admire, to whom all Kings either offer gifts or pay tribute? This explanation commended itself to Ludovicus de Dieu in his animadversions on this passage, interpreting that 'whom they have already made' as referring to GOD and men; or impersonally, 'who has already been made': which could also be understood of the Most Holy Trinity, of whom Scripture loves to speak in the plural, 'whom they have made,' understand אלהים. Which seems to be hinted at by Raimundus Martini in Pugio Fidei, part 3. Dist. 1. c. 3., also bringing forward to this same opinion the Midrash Koheleth on this passage: After the King, that is, after the King of Kings, the holy and blessed GOD, will you be able to stand, etc. He teaches, however, that it must be said, through the fact that it is not written, HE WHO MADE HIM, but THEY WHO MADE HIM, that, since it is written in the law, it can be said, the holy and blessed GOD, and his house of judgment made him: (that is, in the interpretation of Raimundus, GOD the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). But if you say on account of this: therefore there are two principles, it does not follow, for had it not already been said (Deuteronomy 32:6), He made you, and established you? The most simple of all seems to be the translation of B. Luther: 'For who knows what kind of man he will become after the King, whom they have already made ready,' so that a reason is given why he also judged this to be vanity, that he had built buildings with much solicitude, collected riches, and provided for his kingdom with great care, and, having sent such things away, had rather devoted effort to wisdom. For who is that man who is to come after the King, whom you have already thought of, destined, made with minds and counsels, and whom you carry in your eyes (just as we are accustomed to worship the rising sun rather than the setting one), and who can be certain whether he is going to preserve those things and show himself worthy of them? Just as shortly after, Solomon himself explained his mind more fully, v. 18 seqq. I have detested all my 'industry, with which I labored most studiously under the Sun, about to have an heir after me, whom I do not know, whether he will be wise or foolish, and he will rule over my labors, in which I have sweated and been solicitous: and is there anything so vain? Whence I ceased, and my heart renounced laboring further under the Sun. For when another labors in wisdom and doctrine, and solicitude, he leaves what was sought to an idle man: And this therefore is vanity and a great evil. For thus that heir is likewise described with a similar phrase; Because I will leave it (the labor) TO THE MAN, WHO WILL BE AFTER ME, לארם שיהיה אחרי just as in this place שיבוא אחרי המלך הארם THE MAN WHO COMES AFTER THE KING, that is, after me. Compare Osiander on this passage, the Weimar Paraphrast, and Dr. Gejer on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

QVID EST HOMO, UT SEQVI POSSET REGEM FACTOREM SUUM) Suppleto levi defectu, quales mul- ti sunt apud Hebræos, sensus sic optimus fiet: Quis est ho- mo qui insequi Regem posset in iis quæ jam facta sunt: scilicet cognoscendis? Quis tantam sibi potest comparare veteris historiæ cognitionem, quantam Rex facultatibus abundans? At proinde quis melius judicare poterit de effectibus φρο- νήσεως καὶ ἀφροσύνης? Est quidem discrimen inter hæc ali- quod, sed ἐφήμερον. Est hic in Hebræo מֶה positum non pro quid, sed pro quis, ut & 1. Sam. 4. v. 6. 2. Reg. 1. v. 7.

VArias de his verbis, quæ admodum difficilia esse fatetur, recenset sententias Mercerus ad h. l. simplicissimam tamen illam judicat, quam hic pro nova vendit Grotius; Solum mavult Mercerus מה האדם reddi, quid homo, per comtemtum; non quis homo? Sed, quid est homo ut Psalm. 8, 5. & 144, 3. Præivit autem Aben - Ezra, orationem ita explens: Quis est, qui Regem operum magnitudi- ne, & rerum experimentis subsequi velit; q. d. ludet operam: qui vero subintelligit postremis verbum יעשׂו sc. faciet id demum, quod alii jam fecerunt, ubi mavult Mercerus subintelligere לדעת ut sciat: Quid est homo qui post (me, tantum) Regem veniat, ut agnoscat, quæ jam fecerunt (alii) vel quæ jam facta sunt, ad quæ nova non possunt accede- re, in quibus nemo potest quicquam innovare, ut aliquid se dicat aut putet experturum quod Rex non sit expertus. Simplicior tamen Aben - Ezræ translatio, etsi eundem sensum gignat, vide- tur: Quis est homo, qui post Regem veniet, (qui hæc ita experturus sit) Facite id demum, quod alii jam fecerunt, q. d. nihil novi poterit efficere, quod alii non fecerint, ac proinde, quod ego non tentarim, neque aliud a me cognoscere. Hunc sensum exhibent etiam Thom. Cartwrightus Cantabrigiensis Theologus & Belgici Interpp. Cæterum Mercerus alium adhuc sensum indigitavit, quod ad Salomonem referri postrema verba possint: Quid est homo, ut velit res probare post Regem eum, quem jam fecerunt, id est, quem omnes comprobarunt, & cœlitus & humanitus factum agnitum, cujus omnes sapientiam & magnificentiam admirantur, cui Reges omnes aut munera offerunt, aut tributa pensitant? Quæ explicatio sese probavit Ludovico de Dieu animadvers. in hunc locum, illa quem jam fecerunt, de DEO & hominibus interpretanti; vel impersonaliter, qui jam factus est: quod etiam de S. S. Trinitate accipi posset, de qua Scriptura pluraliter loqui amat, quem fecerunt, intellige אלחיו. Quod innui videtur Raimundo Martini in Pugion. Fidei part. 3. Dist. 1. c. 3. in eam etiam sententiam adducenti Midrasch Koheleth ad h. l. Post Regem, id est, post Regem Regum, DEUM sanctum & benedictum tu valebis stare, &c. Docet autem dicendum, per hoc quod non est scriptum, QUI FECIT EUM, sed QUI FECERUNT EUM, quod, ex quo in lege scriptum est, dici potest, DEUS sanctus & benedictus, & domus judicii ejus fecerunt eum: (id est, interprete Raimund. DEUS Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus) Si vero dicis propter hoc: duo igitur principia sunt, non sequitur, nonne enim jam dictum erat (Deuteronom. 32, 6.) Ipse fecit, & aptavit te? Omnium simplicissima videtur B. Lutheri translatio: Denn wer weiß, was der für ein Mensch werden wird nach dem Könige, den sie schon bereit gemacht haben, ut causa reddatur, cur etiam hoc vanitatem judicarit, quod multa folicitudine ædificia extruxerit, divitias collegerit, & regno suo magna cura prospexerit, ac missis talibus potius sapientiæ operam navandam duxerit. Quis enim homo ille, qui post Regem venturus est, quem jam cogitatis, destinatis, animis & consiliis fecerunt, inque oculis suis gerunt, (ut adorare Solem orientem potius, quam occidentem consvevimus,) & quis certus esse potest, utrum illa conservaturus, illisque dignum se præbiturus sit? Quemadmodum paulo post ipse Salomo plenius mentem suam „explicavit v. 18. seqq. Detestatus sum omnem „industriam meam, qua sub Sole studiosissime laboravi, habiturus hæredem post me, quem „ignoro, utrum sapiens an stultus futurus sit, & dominabitur in laboribus meis, quibus desudavi & „solicitus fui: & est quicquam tam vanum? Unde „cessavi, renunciavitque cor meum ultra laborare „sub Sole. Nam cum alius laboret in Sapientia „& doctrina, & solicitudine, homini otioso quæsita dimittit: Et hoc ergo vanitas & magnum malum. Sic enim hæres ille itidem simili phrasi describitur; Quia relinquam illum (laborem) HOMINI, QUI ERIT POST ME, לארם שיהידז אחרי perinde ut hoc in loco שיבוא אחרי המלך הארם HOMO ILLE QUI VENIT POST REGEM, id est, post me. Conf. Osiander in h. l. Paraphrast. Vinariens. & Dn. D. Gejerus in h. l.

## 2:18
Vers. 18.

ABOUT TO HAVE AN HEIR AFTER ME WHOM I DO NOT KNOW WHETHER HE WILL BE WISE OR FOOLISH, AND HE WILL RULE OVER MY LABORS, IN WHICH I HAVE SWEATED AND BEEN SOLLICITOUS: AND IS THERE ANYTHING SO VAIN?) Against those who place happiness in riches. In the Greek epigram it is:

--- But if you guard it for others, from now on it becomes another's.

And in another: O you who are rich for the heirs, but poor for yourself.

See also below 22. and 6, 2. That appears most in childlessness: Childlessness is to be avoided with every effort, which a hostile heir presses with his wishes. But even if one has children, his lineage will nevertheless sometimes fail.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

HABITVRVS HÆREDEM POST ME QVEM IGNORO VTRVM SAPIENS AN STVLTVS FVTVRVS SIT, ET DOMINABITVR IN LABORIBVS MEIS, QVIBVS DESVDAVI ET SOLLICITVS FVI: ET EST QVICQVAM TAM VANVM?) Contra eos qui in divitiis felicitatem collocant. In Epigrammate Græco est:

--- ἂν δὲ φυλάττῃς Ἀλλοτρίοις, ἀπὸ νῦν γίγνεται ἀλλότρια.

Et in altero: Ὦ τοῖς κληρονόμοις πλύσιες, σοὶ δὲ πένης.

Vide & infra 22. & 6, 2. Id maxime apparet in orbis: Orbitas omni fugienda nisu Quam premit votis inimicus heres. Sed etsi quis liberos habeat, aliquando tamen stirps ejus deficiet.

## 2:24
Vers. 24.

IS IT NOT BETTER TO EAT AND DRINK AND SHOW HIS SOUL GOOD THINGS FROM HIS LABORS) In the Hebrew the sense seems to be this: There is no good for man, except that he should eat, and show his soul those things which delight, acquired by his own labor.

AND THIS IS FROM THE HAND OF GOD) It is not always in our power.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

NONNE MELIVS EST COMEDERE ET BIBERE ET OSTENDERE ANIMÆ SVÆ BONA DE LABORIBVS SVIS) In Hebræo sen- sus hic esse videtur: Nullum est homini bonum, nisi ut comedat, & exhibeat animæ suæ ea quæ delectant, labore suo comparata.

ET HOC DE MANV DEI EST) Non est semper in nostra potestate.

## 2:25
Ver. 25.

WHO THEN SHALL DEVOUR) In Hebrew: For who shall eat? That is, who shall more justly enjoy the parts than he who has produced them by his own labor?

AND SHALL ABOUND IN DELIGHTS AS I) In Hebrew: And who has hastened more than I? that is, who has labored more than I? This coheres with the former.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

QVIS ITA DEVORABIT) In Hebræo: Quis enim comedet? Id est, quis justius partis fruetur, quam qui labore suo ea peperit?

ET DELITIIS AFFLVET VT EGO) In Hebræo: Et quis plus festinavit, quam ego? id est, quis plus me labo- ravit? cohæret hoc cum priori.

## 2:26
Ver. 26.

TO THE GOOD MAN IN HIS SIGHT) To him whom God loves.

Ver. the same.

HE GAVE WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE AND JOY) Understand by joy the Democritean τὴν εὐεστώ. See 3. v. 12. 13.

Nay, understand by joy the Christian τὴν εὐεστώ. For true joy, which a man enjoys with a quiet and tranquil conscience, neither Democritus nor any of the Gentiles could have: which is nothing without the acknowledgment and faith of the true God, but is proper and perpetual to the righteous. Prov. 14, 32, chap. 15, 15. 16. chap. 17, 22. Rom. 14, 17. Rightly the Blessed Luther in this place. He divides the world into the pious and the impious. To the pious, besides the gifts common to others, wisdom and prudence are especially added, and also joy, because they are content with present things, and are not vexed by thoughts and desires, as the impious are. Because they know and are wise in administering affairs, etc. In joy and peace they know. But the impious have affliction, so that they always add more, and gather; and are never satisfied. Then, even if they have wisdom and industry, it is nevertheless so mixed with troubles that they are more of a punishment to them, so that they do not enjoy their own labors, so that they cultivate and build, but others enjoy them and derive joy from them. What the impious labor for and build, no one uses rightly, except the pious alone. In sum, the pious truly possess the world, because they enjoy it with joy and tranquility, but the impious, even while having it, do not have it. But it is nothing new that Grotius makes the heathens truly pious and righteous along with the Pelagians: to whom, however, the Catholic Church has always opposed itself. Every life of the infidels, says Prosper, Sentent. 106, from Augustine, is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good. Where the acknowledgment of the eternal and unchangeable truth is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best morals. Gregory the Great, book 2, Moral. c. 15. If faith is not first born in our heart, the rest also cannot be good, although they may seem to be. Bede, book 1, on Canticles. Therefore, what Julian (Grotius) says, that many of the philosophers have patience, chastity, modesty, and other virtues from the good of nature, it is evident that whoever of the philosophers did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, these could have no true virtue, nor any true wisdom.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

HOMINI BONO IN CONSPECTV SVO) Ei quem amat Deus.

Vers. eod.

DEDIT SAPIENTIAM ET SCIENTIAM ET LÆTITIAM) Lætitiam intellige τὴν εὐεστώ Democri- team. Vid. 3. v. 12. 13.

Imo lætitiam intellige τὴν εὐεστώ Christianam. Veram enim lætitiam, qua conscientia quieta, & tranquilla fruitur homo, neque Democrates, ne- que ullus gentilium habere potuit: quæ nulla est si- ne veri Dei agnitione & fide, justorum vero pro- pria ac perpetua est. Prov. 14, 32, cap. 15, 15. 16. cap. 17, 22. Rom. 14, 17. Recte Beat. Lutherus in h. l. Dividit mundum in pios & impios. Piis præter “ dona aliis communia maxime sapientiam & pru- “ dentiam, additur etiam lætitia, quia sunt præsen- “ tibus contenti, non vexantur cogitationibus & “ cupiditatibus, ut impii. Quod cognoscunt & “ sapientes sunt in administrandis rebus &c. In “ lætitia & pace cognoscunt. Impii vero habent “ afflictionem, ut semper plura addant, & congre- “ gent; & nunquam expleantur. Deinde etiamsi “ habent sapientiam ac industriam, tamen sic mo- “ lestiis mixtam, ut magis sint eis pœnæ, suis ut la- “ boribus non fruantur, ut colant, ædificent, alii “ vero fruantur, & gaudium ex illis percipiant. “ Quæ impii laborant & ædificant, nemo recte uti- “ tur, nisi soli pii. Summa, pii vere habent or- “ bem terrarum, quia fruuntur cum lætitia & tran- “ quillitate, impii vero etiam habentes non habent. “ Sed novum non est, Grotium Ethnicos vere pios justosque cum Pelagianis facere: quibus vero Ca- tholica Ecclesia sese nunquam non opposuit. O- mnis infidelium vita, inquit Prosper Sentent. 106. ex Augustino, peccatum est, & nihil est bonum sine sum- mo bono. Ubi deest agnitio æternæ & incommuta- bilis veritatis, falsa virtus etiam est in optimis mori- bus. Gregorius M. libr. 2. Moral. c. 15. Si non prius in corde nostro fides gignitur, reliqua quoque esse bona non possunt, licet esse videantur. Beda lib. 1. in Cant. Quod ergo Julianus (Grotius) dicit mul- tos Philosophorum patientiam, castitatem, modestiam, aliasque de naturæ bono habere virtutes, constat, quia quicunque Philosophorum Christum Dei virtutem & Dei sapientiam nesciverunt, hi nullam veram virtutem, nec ullam veram sapientiam habere potuerunt.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

Anxiety about the future is vain, because all things have a time according to the order of God and nature and divine providence, and nothing is accomplished by that care, and therefore the tranquility and cheerfulness of a good mind is commended, so that all things may be committed to the direction of God, even if by the permission of God the wicked occupy the judgments, and no difference between the end of men and of beasts appears.

Verse 1.

TO EVERYTHING THERE IS A TIME) For just as the earth is cultivated with various and changing seeds, so our minds are cultivated now with this meditation, now with that: Pliny says in Epistles 7, 9. You have similar things in M. Antoninus, book 5.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Solicitudo de futuris vana, quia omnia tem- pus habent secundum Dei & naturæ seriem & divinam providentiam, nihilque cura il- la efficitur, ideoque bonæ mentis tranquilli- tas, & hilaritas commendatur, ut directioni Dei omnia committantur, etsi permissu Dei judicia occupent impii, ac nullum exitus hominum & bestiarum discrimen appareat.

Verf. 1.

OMNIA TEMPVS HABENT) Vt enim terra variis mutatisque feminibus, ita ingenia nostra nunc hæc, nunc illa meditatione recoluntur: ait Plinius in Epistolis 7, 9. Similia habes apud M. Antoninum libro 5.

## 3:5
Verse 5.

A TIME TO EMBRACE AND A TIME TO REFRAIN FROM EMBRACING) Timon: Ὥρα ἐρᾷν· ὥρα δὲ γαμεῖν· ὥρα δὲ πεπαῦσθαι.

Latin:

Verf. 5.

TEMPVS AMPLEXANDI ET TEMPVS LONGVM FIERI AB AMPLEXIBVS) Timon: Ὥρα ἐρᾷν· ὥρα δὲ γαμεῖν· ὥρα δὲ πεπαῦσθαι.

## 3:7
Verse 7.

A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE AND A TIME TO SPEAK) Hesiod: καιρὸς δ' ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

TEMPVS TACENDI ET TEMPVS LOQVENDI) Hesiodus: καιρὸς δ' ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος.

## 3:11
Verse 11.

HE HATH MADE EVERYTHING BEAUTIFUL IN HIS TIME) עשׂה here is 'he ordained'. God has disposed all things in their own times.

AND HE HATH SET THE WORLD IN THEIR HEART) In the Hebrew: Also he has set the world in their heart. Man knows many things that appear in the world, unknown to other living creatures, so that it may appear that the world was created for his sake.

SO THAT NO MAN CAN FIND OUT THE WORK THAT GOD MAKETH FROM THE BEGINNING TO THE END) From the Hebrew: Yet so that man does not know the work of God from head to heel. He sees many things, the purpose of which he does not know for which they were made by God, and what result is to follow: τίς σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο; Rom. 11. v. 34.

Varenius renders this sense not unlike that of Grotius; God implanted in the human heart a study and desire of understanding, He implanted a mind which reasons and more and more gathers the unknown from the better known, and thus shows the age impressed upon it by God Rom. 1, 19. however, man does not attain the work which God has made from the beginning even to the end. We compare with these the explanation of Dn. D. Gejer: that God has given into the heart of men the reason and nature of the present age, which He has offered to us to be perceived in the daily handling of the things of this age.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

CVNCTA FECIT BONA IN TEMPORE SVO) עשׂה hic est ordinavit. Cuncta suis tempo- ribus disposuit Deus.

ET MVNDVM TRADIDIT DIS PVTATIO- NI EORVM) In Hebræo: Etiam mundum dedit in eo- rum corde. Multa quæ in mundo apparent novit homo, aliis animantibus ignota, ut appareat mundum ipsius causa creatum.

VT NON INVENIAT HOMO OPVS QVOD OPERATVS EST DEVS AB INITIO VSQVE AD FINEM) Ex Hebræo: Sic tamen ut non norit homo à capite ad calcem operationem Dei. Multa videt, quæ non scit quo proposito à Deo facta sint, & quis sit secuturus eventus: τίς σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο; Rom. 11. v. 34.

VArenius hunc reddit sensum non absimilem Grotiano; Deus indidit humano cordi stu- dium & desiderium intelligendi, indidit mentem quæ ratiocinatur & magis magisque ex notioribus colligit ignotiora, & ita ostendit impressum sibi a Deo seculum Rom. 1, 19. cæterum homo non as- sequitur opus, quod fecit Deus a principio usque ad finem. Conferimus his Dn. D. Gejeri explica- tionem: quod Deus dederit in cor hominum præ- sentis seculi rationem ac naturam, quam nobis in quo- tidiana rerum hujus seculi tractatione perspiciendam obtulit.

## 3:14
Ver. 14.

I HAVE LEARNED THAT ALL THE WORKS WHICH GOD HAS MADE SHALL ENDURE FOREVER) Think of the great mass of things, heaven, earth, water, then also the kinds of living creatures and other things.

Latin:

Verf. 14.

DIDICI QVOD OMNIA OPERA QVÆ FECIT DEVS PERSEVERENT IN PERPETVVM) Puta ma- gnæ rerum massæ, cœlum, terra, aqua, deinde & animantium rerumque aliarum genera.

## 3:15
Ver. 15.

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ITSELF REMAINS, WHAT IS TO BE HAS ALREADY BEEN, AND GOD RESTORES WHAT HAS PASSED) You may translate it best thus from the Hebrew: What is it that has been? The same thing (which) now (is:) and what is to be, the same thing has been. God seeks that which follows. That is, He as it were calls for that which ought to follow each thing, as winter after autumn has passed. The Chaldean took 'to seek' for 'to avenge', and נרדף for a vexed man, and thinks the sense is that God is an avenger to those who have been unjustly treated badly, so that this may be opposed to human judgments, which are often unjust, of which he will now treat.

Latin:

Verf. 15.

QVOD FACTVM EST IPSVM PERMANET, QVÆ FVTVRA SVNT JAM FVERVNT, ET DE- VS INSTAVRAT QVOD ABIIT) Optime sic vertas ex Hebræo: Quid est quod fuit? idipsum (quod) jam (est:) & quod futurum est idipsum fuit. Deus quærit id quod sequi- tur. Id est, quasi advocat id quod rem quamque sequi de- bet, ut hyemem autumno exacto. Chaldæus requirere sumsit pro ulcisci, & נרדף pro homine vexato, sensumque esse putat, Deum ultorem esse iis, qui injuste male tractati sunt, ut opponatur hoc humanis judiciis, quæ sæpe iniqua sunt, de quibus jam aget.

## 3:18
Ver. 18.

I SAID IN MY HEART CONCERNING THE SONS OF MEN, THAT GOD MIGHT PROVE THEM, AND SHOW THAT THEY ARE LIKE BEASTS) Contrary to that thought about the judgment of the future age, about which the discourse preceded, another thought has arisen for me, that God permits men to live among themselves in a beastly manner, so that He may the better declare and show that men are equal to beasts: to this thought he adds arguments.

Varenius thinks it should be rendered thus: I said in my heart, it is according to the state (condition, reason) of the sons of man, that they themselves should choose God: or that they should acknowledge that they, they themselves, I say, are beasts to themselves, that they may appeal from a corrupt earthly tribunal to a heavenly one, or choose the divine judgment as pure and uncorrupted, or if they deny that, acknowledge that they are plainly beasts to themselves, denying the final judgment and therefore the resurrection of the dead. Cf. Ps. 49, 13. 21. Dn. D. Gejer rendered this passage thus: Because of the condition of the sons of man it will come to pass that GOD will purge them (since in this life there appears almost no difference between man and beasts, as regards life, chance, and death, although man was created in the image and for the worship of God, I concluded that there would be altogether some time of evident discrimination, examination, and repurging) and that He may look upon the fact that they seem to themselves to be beasts (so that at length sometime as supreme judge He may discern, because men themselves seem to themselves as brutes, by hunger, thirst, other troubles, diseases, and death itself, unless such a distinction remained) if the explanation of the word לברם of Mercer, that He might clarify, or openly show them what they are, which he proves from the Rabbis and Eccles. 9, 1., is admitted, the translation of B. Luther is not to be abandoned: That God wished to clarify them, so that they might see that in many things they do not differ from beasts, which Solomon pursues further.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

DIXI IN CORDE MEO DE FILIIS HOMI- NVM, VT PROBARET EOS DEVS, ET OSTEN- DERET SIMILES ESSE BESTIIS) Contra illam cogitationem de judicio futuri ævi, de qua sermo præcessit, alia mihi cogitatio suborta est, permittere Deum homines ferino more inter se vivere, ut eo melius declaret & ostendat homines pares esse bestiis: huic cogitationi addit argumenta.

Varenius ita reddendum censet : dixi ego in corde meo, secundum statum (conditionem, ratio- nem) filiorum hominis est, ut seligant ipsi Deum : aut ut agnoscant, quod illi, illi ipsi, inquam, bestiae sint sibi ipsis, ut corrupto tribunali terrestri appellent ad coe- leste, seu seligant judicium divinum velut purum, & incorruptum, aut si illud abnegant, agnoscant, quod sibi ipsis plane bestiae sint, judicium novissimum ad- eoque resurrectionem mortuorum inficiantes. Conf. Ps. 49, 13. 21. Dn. D. Gejerus sic reddidit hunc locum: Ob conditionem filiorum hominis futurum est, ut purget eos DEUS (quum in hac vita inter homi- nem ac bestias nullum fere discrimen, quoad vitam, casus, mortemque appareat, quum tamen homo ad imaginem, cultumque Dei conditus sit, conclusi fu- turum omnino esse aliquod evidentis discriminis, examinis ac repurgationis tempus) & ut intueatur, quod ipsi jumentum videantur sibi (ut tandem ali- quando ceu supremus judex dispiciat, eo quod ho- mines ipsi sibi ipsis quasi bruta videntur, fame, siti, molestiis aliis, morbis & morte ipsa, nisi restaret ta- lis discretio) si Merceri vocis לברם explicatio, ut dilucidaret, vel aperte ostenderet eos, quales sint, quam e Rabbinis & Eccles. 9, 1. probat, admittatur, B. Lu- theri translatio non deserenda : Dilucidare eos vo- luisse Deum, ut videant, quod in multis non discre- pent a bestiis, quae porro persequitur Salomo.

## 3:21
Ver. 21.

WHO KNOWS IF THE SPIRIT OF THE SONS OF MEN ASCENDS UPWARD?) That is, whether it remains, as the heavenly things. AND IF THE SPIRIT OF BEASTS DESCENDS DOWNWARD?) Perishes, as the bodies themselves buried under the ground? Man by native reason alone has nothing certain about it. The doubts of Socrates, Tully, and Seneca show that.

Varenius rendered it in the contrary sense: Who acknowledges (would that one understood) the Spirit of the sons of man? It ascends, it, I say, itself upward: and (who understands, or discerns from it) the Spirit of the beast. It descends, it, I say, itself downward into the earth. See his Gemmulae Salom. Disput. 1. n. 12. where he proves that exposition at length.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

QVIS NOVIT SI SPIRITVS FILIORVM ASCEN- DAT SVRSVM?) Id est, an permaneat, sicut coelestia. ET SI SPIRITVS JVMENTORVM DE- SCENDAT DEORSVM) Pereat, ut ipsa corpora sub humum defossa? Homo sola nativa ratione nihil de eo comperti habet. Ostendunt id Socratis, Tullii, Senecae dubitationes.

Contrario sensu reddidit Varenius : Quis agno- scit (utinam quis intelligeret) Spiritum filiorum ho- minis? Ascendit ille, ille ipse, inquam, sursum : & (quis intelligit, seu ab illo discernit) Spiritum bestiae. De- scendit ille, ille ipse, inquam, infra in terram. Vid. ejusdem Gemmulae Salom. Disput. 1. n. 12. ubi ex- positionem illam prolixe probat.

## 3:22
Ver. 22.

WHO THEN SHALL BRING HIM?) That is, bring him back into this life.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

QVIS ENIM EVM ADDVCET?) Id est, in hanc vitam reducer.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Worldly vanity from human judgment and favor, envy of labor and skill, as well as the avarice and misery of those who are solitary, as also the folly of rulers, and the inconstancy of fortune.

Ver. 1.

I TURNED MYSELF TO OTHER THINGS] Another thought occurred to me again, that death is better than life.

AND I SAW THE OPPRESSIONS THAT ARE DONE UNDER THE SUN.

IN Hebrew: Oppressions, whether violent or fraudulent. And behold! There were the tears of the oppressed: and there was no comforter for them. And from the hand of the oppressors there was strength for them: and there was no comforter for them. Because the hand or faction of the oppressors was strong, hence those tears without a comforter.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Vanitas mundana ex judicio & favore huma- no, invidia laboris ac peritiae, nec non quod avaritiam & miseriam eorum, qui solitarii sunt, ut & regentium stultitiam, ac fortunae inconstantiam.

Vers. 1.

VERTI ME AD ALIA] Alia rursus mihi cogitatio in- cidit, mortem vita esse meliorem.

ET VIDI CALUMNIAS QUAE SUB SOLE GERUNTUR.

IN Ebraeo : Oppressiones sive violentas, sive frau- dulentas. Et ecce! Lachrymae erant oppressorum: nec existebat eis consolator. Et a manu opprimen- tium illis erat robur: nec erat eis consolator. Quia manus seu factio opprimentium erat valida, hinc illae lacrymae sine consolatore.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

AND I PRAISED THE DEAD MORE THAN THE LIVING: AND HAPPIER THAN BOTH I JUDGED HIM WHO IS NOT YET BORN) Aristotle related that this was said by Satyrus. Chalcidamas expressed it thus: Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον Φύντα δ' ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀῖδαο περῆσαι. Theognis indeed in this manner: Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον, Μηδ' ἐσιδεῖν αὐγὰς ὀξέος ἠελίου Φύντα δ' ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀῖδαο περῆσαι, Καὶ κεῖσθαι πολλὴν γῆν ἐπαμησάμενον. Posidippus indeed in these words: Ἦν ἄρα τῶν πάντων τόδε λώϊον, ἣὲ γενέσθαι Μηδέποτ', ἢρ θανέειν αὐτίκα τικτόμενον.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ET LAVDAVI MAGIS MORTVOS QVAM VIVENTES: ET FELICIOREM VTROQVE JV- DICAVI QVI NEC DVM NATUS EST) Dictum hoc fuisse Satyri narravit Aristoteles. Id sic expressit Chalcidamas: Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον Φύντα δ' ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀῖδαο περῆσαι. Theognis vero in hunc modum: Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον, Μηδ' ἐσιδεῖν αὐγὰς ὀξέος ἠελίου Φύντα δ' ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀῖδαο περῆσαι, Καὶ κεῖσθαι πολλὴν γῆν ἐπαμησάμενον. Posidippus vero his verbis: Ἦν ἄρα τῶν πάντων τόδε λώϊον, ἣὲ γενέσθαι Μηδέποτ', ἢρ θανέειν αὐτίκα τικτόμενον.

## 4:8
Verse 8.

HE IS ONE AND HAS NO SECOND) There is no one related to him by blood for whose sake he might labor.

NOR ARE HIS EYES SATISFIED WITH RICHES) An excellent description of greed. Well said 'eyes': for they alone enjoy riches among the greedy.

AND I DEFRAUD MY SOUL OF GOOD THINGS] I defraud my genius, Terence would say.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

UNUS EST ET SECUNDUM NON HABET) Nemo est ei sanguine propinquus, cujus causa laboret.

NEC SATIANTUR OCULI EJUS DIVITIIS) Aviditatis egregia descriptio. Bene oculi: ii enim soli fruuntur divitiis apud avaros.

ET FRAUDO ANIMAM MEAM BONIS] Genium defraudo, diceret Terentius.

## 4:9
Verse 9.

IT IS BETTER THEREFORE THAT TWO BE TOGETHER THAN ONE) Aristotle praises from Homer, σύντε δύ' ἐρχομένω.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

MELIUS EST ERGO DUOS ESSE SIMUL QVAM UNUM) Ex Homero Aristoteles laudat, σύντε δύ' ἐρχομένω.

## 4:14
Verse 14.

THAT FROM PRISON AND CHAINS SOMETIMES ONE MAY GO FORTH TO A KINGDOM) As Agrippa, King of Judea.

AND ANOTHER BORN IN A KINGDOM MAY BE CONSUMED BY POVERTY) Thus Euripides introduced Telephus begging in a tragedy. In his Helena, Menelaus says thus: Κακῶν δὲ θ' ἡμῖν ἔσχατοι τοῖς ἀθλίοις Ἄλλους Τυράννους αὐτὸν ὄντα βασιλέα, Βίον προσαιτεῖν.

Mr. Varenius thinks the words of the text should be explained according to the counsel of the sources: (just as) he comes forth from prison to reign (sometimes that can happen) so also in his kingdom (a foolish King) he is born (is rendered) poor, through his own folly having ruined the treasures of the kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

QVOD DE CARCERE CATENISQVE INTERDUM QVIS EGREDIATUR AD REGNUM) Ut Agrippa Judææ Rex.

ET ALIUS NATUS IN REGNO INOPIA CONSUMATUR) Sic Telephum mendicantem in Tragœdia introduxit Euripides. In ejusdem Helena sic Menelaus, Κακῶν δὲ θ' ἡμῖν ἔσχατοι τοῖς ἀθλίοις Ἄλλους Τυράννους αὐτὸν ὄντα βασιλέα, Βίον προσαιτεῖν.

Verba textus e consilio fontium ita exponen- da censet Dn. Varenius: (prout) ex carcere prodit ad regnandum (quandoque id fieri potest) ita etiam in regno suo (Rex stultus) nascitur (redditur) pauper, per stultitiam suam thesauris regni pessundatis.

## 4:15
Verse 15.

I SAW ALL THE LIVING WHO WALK WITH THE SECOND YOUTH WHO SHALL RISE UP IN HIS STEAD) By 'second' here understand the heir of the kingdom, as above in 9. The sense is the same as in the old saying, which Pompey usurped, and then Tiberius, that the rising sun is wont to be adored by most. Papinius: And the custom that is to come is loved by the peoples. Thus in kingdoms also there are torments and fears.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

VIDI CVNCTOS VIVENTES QVI AMBVLANT CVM ADOLESCENTE SECVNDO QVI CONSVRGET PRO EO) Secundum hic intellige, hæredem regni, ut supra 9. Sensus est idem, qui in dicto vetere, quod Pompejus usurpavit, deinde Tiberius, à plerisque adorari solem orientem. Papinius: Et qui mos populis venturus amatur. Ita in regnis quoque sunt tormenta & metus.

## 4:16
Ver. 16.

THE NUMBER OF THE PEOPLE IS INFINITE, OF ALL WHO WERE BEFORE HIM) This does not happen through the fault of the King; for from every age the people have been of such a disposition: - - nor ever bearing leaders placed upon a willing neck. As Papinius says.

AND THOSE WHO SHALL BE AFTERWARDS WILL NOT REJOICE IN HIM) In him whom they now wish for themselves as King, whom they love in preference to the reigning King.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

INFINITVS NVMERVS EST POPVLI, OMNIVM QVI FVERVNT ANTE EVM) Non evenit hoc Regis culpa; nam ab omni ætate populi eo fuere ingenio: - - nec impositos unquam cervice volenti Ferre duces. Vt ait Papinius.

ET QVI POSTEA FVTVRI SVNT NON LÆTABVNTVR IN EO) In illo quem nunc Regem sibi optant, quem amant præ Rege regnante.

## 5:1 Argument
SECTION II. Concerning the solidity of true and divine happiness. CHAPTER V. An exhortation to pious prayers and to the fulfilling of vows, and to the fleeing of the seduction of the flesh and injustice: and a comparison of the misery of the covetous man and the man who rests in joyful tranquility through the kindness of God.

Ver. 1. KEEP THY FOOT.

This verse is the last in the Vulgate of chapter 4. But it pertains to chapter 5, where, after having set forth the condition of earthly Kings, Solomon proceeds to the worship to be rendered to the heavenly King: and from theoretical meditations on the vanities of the world he turns himself to certain practical instructions in chapter 5, which is entirely completed by religious counsels. Keep (solicitously out of reverence for the divine majesty) thy foot, when thou shalt go to the house of GOD; and that by approaching to listen, rather than to give the sacrifice of fools (rather than to give with fools, or than when fools give sacrifice) For they do not advert to doing evil. Varenius prefers: For they are not acknowledging so as to do evil. They remain in their blindness and lack of understanding, knowing nothing, so that they may continue to do evil: because the denied knowledge of the heavenly is the cause of the doing of evil, so that they always do evil, persevere in evil, in erroneous worship, in an abominable and impure state.

Ver. same.

THEREFORE LET THY WORDS BE FEW) Contrary to the custom of the pagans, of which we treated in Matt. 6. v. 7.

Latin:

SECTIO II. De veræ & divinæ felicitatis soliditate. CAPUT V. Exhortatio ad pias preces, & vota præstanda, ac fugiendam carnis seductionem & in- justitiam: & comparatio miseriæ avari, hominisque læta tranquillitate benignita- te Dei acquiescentis.

Vers. 1. CUSTODI PEDEM TUUM.

Hic versus in Vulgat. ultimus cap. 4. Sed per- tinet ad cap. 5. ubi post expositam Regum terreno- rum conditionem Salomo progreditur ad cultum Regi cœlesti præstandum: & a theoreticis vani- tatum mundi meditationibus se convertit ad practicas quasdam informationes in cap. 5. quod totum religiosis consiliis absolvitur. Custodi (so- licite præ reverentia majestatis divinæ) pedem tuum, quando ibis ad domum DEI; idque accedendo ad au- scultandum, præ dare stultos sacrificium (potius quam ad dandum cum stultis, vel quam cum dant stulti sa- crificium) Nam illi non advertunt faciendo malum. Varenius mavult: Nam illa non sunt agnoscentes ad faciendum malum. Die bleiben in ihrer Blindheit und Unverstand, wissen nichts, auf daß sie immerhin böses thun: quia negata notitia cœlestis causa est fa- cluræ mali, uti semper faciant malum, perseverent in malo, in erroneo cultu, abominabili impuroque statu.

Vers. eod.

ICCIRCO SINT PAVCI SERMONES TVI) Contra morem paganorum, de quo egimus Matth. 6. v. 7.

## 5:1
Ver. 17.

OBEDIENCE IS BETTER THAN THE SACRIFICES OF FOOLS) I Sam. 15. v. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

MELIOR EST OBEDIENTIA QVAM STVLTORVM VICTIMÆ) I. Sam. 15. v. 22.

## 5:4
Ver. 3. IF YOU HAVE VOWED ANYTHING TO GOD, DO NOT DELAY TO PAY IT) Deuteronomy 23, v. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 3. SI QVID VOVISTI DEO, NE MORERIS REDDERE) Devteron. 23. v. 21.

## 5:6
Ver. 5.

DO NOT GIVE YOUR MOUTH, THAT YOU SHOULD CAUSE YOUR FLESH TO SIN) Do not use flatteries to commit adulteries.

There is nothing here about flatteries, nothing about adultery in the text. Nor do the preceding verses support this sense. For they deal with vows, and therefore Mercer rightly interprets these words: Do not commit yourself by rashly making a vow, and by loosening your mouth, when you do not perform it afterwards, so that you bind yourself or your flesh, that is, your body, to sin, and bring harm, danger, and punishment upon yourself by your own fault. Thus also the Hebrew [scholar] in Jerome: What you cannot do, do not promise, for words do not pass into the wind, but are immediately carried to the Lord by the present Angel, who adheres to everyone as a companion. Similarly Cartwright, the Vinarienses, and others. Blessed Luther, however, took it more generally: Do not speak so carnally, so rashly, so imprudently, that you listen to your flesh, but speak according to the word of God. And Osiander: Beware, lest by speaking rashly before God you sin. (Now he says more explicitly what he means) Nor say before the Angel: This is ignorance. For almost the same reason Jerome: To us, however, the sense seems otherwise, that those are rebuked who complain about the vice of the flesh, and say that they are compelled by the necessity of the body to do things they do not want to do, according to that of the Apostle: For I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate, etc. Do not, therefore (he says), seek vain excuses, and give occasion to your flesh to sin, and say: It is not I who sin, but the sin that dwells in me.

Ver. same.

NOR SAY BEFORE THE ANGEL THERE IS NO PROVIDENCE) In the Hebrew: Nor say before the Angel it is ignorance. In the Greek, μή τε εἴπῃς πρὸ προσώπε τῦ θεῦ, ὅτι ἀγνοιά ἐστι. Before the Angel, that is, the inspector of your actions, and if they are evil, the exactor of punishment: Which Angel the Greeks call the face of God, as in Gen. 32:30, because he acts in the name and person of God. Do not, he says, seek excuses, as if such a sin were light. The avenging Angel stands by.

There is no reason why these things should be understood of an Angel, a created Spirit. For we neither can nor are accustomed to excuse our sins before him under the pretext of ignorance. Nor was a created Angel mentioned in Gen. 32:30, nor is a created Angel indicated by the face of God, the man with whom Jacob wrestled, but the Son of God, which we have shown in its place. The Patriarch therefore said he had seen the face of God himself, not a created Angel, but designating the Son of God. As for this passage, Blessed Luther had indeed understood the ministering Spirit by the Angel in his commentary, which was also Mercer's opinion, but later in a marginal gloss he preferred to understand it as a minister of the word. This interpretation is embraced by Lyranus, Pineda, Dionysius, Piscator likewise, Drusius, and most of our own.

Osiander, the Vinarienses as paraphrasts, etc. Cartwright understands it of Christ: Set before your eyes that you are speaking these specious pretexts before CHRIST, the Angel of the eternal covenant, who knows these evasions and hiding places thoroughly. But with the blessed Luther, we accept it as referring to the minister of the word, who is called the Angel of the Lord in Malachi 2:7, so that if he either demands our vows or reminds us of our sins, we should not lightly excuse them or say they were done through ignorance, lest God, the καρδιογνώσης (knower of hearts), be angry.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

NE DEDERIS OS TVVM, VT PECCARE FACIAS CARNEM TVAM) Noli blanditiis uti ad adulteria perpetranda.

Nihil hic de blanditiis, nihil de adulterio in textu. Nec antecedentia hunc sensum ferunt. De votis enim in illis agitur, ideo Mercerus hæc recte interpretatur: Ne committas temere vovendo votum tuum, & os tuum laxando, quum postea non præstes, ut te ipsum seu carnem tuam, id est, corpus tuum peccato adstringas, & tibi noxam ac periculum & supplicium accersas culpa tua. Sic & Hebræus apud Hierony- mum: Quod non potes facere, ne promittas, non enim in ventum dicta transeunt, sed a præsente Angelo, qui unicuique adhæret comes, statim perferuntur ad Do- minum. Similiter Cartwrightus, Vinarienses, & alii. Generalius tamen accepit B. Lutherus: Ne loquaris tam carnaliter, tam temere, tam imprudenter, ut audias carnem tuam, sed loquaris secundum verbum Dei. Et Osiander: Cave, ne temere loquendo coram Deo pecces. (Jam explicatius dicit, quid velit) Neque dicas coram Angelo: Ignorantia est hæc. Ea- dem pene ratione Hieronymus: Nobis vero aliter sensus videtur, quod arguantur hi, qui de vitio carnis queruntur, & ajunt se corporis necessitate compulsos ea facere, quæ nolunt, secundum illud Apostoli: Non enim quod volo, hoc ago, sed quod nolo &c. Noli itaq; (ait) vanas excusationes quærere, & dare occasionem carni tuæ ad peccandum, & dicere; Non ego pecco, sed quod habitat in me peccatum.

Vers. eod.

NEQVE DICAS CORAM ANGELO NON EST PROVIDENTIA) In Hebræo: Neque dicas coram Angelo est ignorantia. In Græco, μή τε εἴπῃς πρὸ προσώπε τῦ θεῦ, ὅτι ἀγνοιά ἐστι. Coram Angelo inspectore scilicet tua- rum actionum, & si malæ sint, pœnæ exactore: Quem An- gelum πρόσωπον τῦ θεῦ Græci vocant, ut Gen. 32, 30. quia ex nomine ac persona Dei agit. Noli, inquit, excusatio- nes quærere, quasi leve sit tale peccatum. Adstat Angelus vindex.

Non est quod de Angelo, Spiritu creato, hæc accipiantur. Non enim excusare coram eo aut possumus aut solemus peccata nostra prætextu ignorantiæ. Neque Angeli creati Gen. 32. v. 30. facta mentio, aut per πρόσωπον θεῦ creatus indi- gitatur Angelus, vir quicum luctatus Jacob, sed Fi- lius DEI, quod suo loco ostendimus. Faciem ergo ipsius Dei vidisse se dixit Patriarcha, non An- gelum creatum, sed Filium Dei designans. Quod ad hunc locum, per Angelum quidem in commen- tario B. Lutherus etiam intellexerat Spiritum mini- strantem, quæ Merceri quoq; sententia, sed postea in glossa marginali maluit intelligere ministrum verbi. Quam interpretationem amplectuntur Lyran. Pine- da, Dionys. Piscator item, Drusius, & e nostris pleriq;,

Osiander, Vinarienses Paraphraste, &c. Cartwrigh- tus de Christo intelligit: Pone tibi ante oculos, te fu- catos hos prætextus coram CHRISTO æterni fœderis Angelo, hæc effugia & latebras pernosciente, eloqui. Sed cum B. Luthero de ministro verbi, qui Angelus Do- mini dicitur Malach. 2, 7. accipimus, si ipse vel vota nostra exigat, vel de peccatis nos commonefaciat, ne leviter ea excusemus, aut per ignorantiam facta dicamus, ne irascatur Deus καρδιογνώσης.

## 5:7
Verse 6.

WHERE THERE ARE MANY DREAMS, THERE ARE MANY VANITIES AND COUNTLESS WORDS] The sense seems to be more correctly rendered thus: Just as there are many dreams and in dreams vanities, so there are many words—vain ones, of course, especially those by which men extenuate grave sins.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

UBI MULTA SUNT SOMNIA, PLURIMÆ SUNT VANITATES ET SERMONES INNUMERI] Sensus videtur ita rectius reddi : Sicut multa sunt somnia & in so- mniis vanitates, ita multa verba, vana sunt scilicet, ea præ- sertim quibus homines peccata gravia extenuant.

## 5:8
Verse 7.

FOR ONE HIGHER THAN THE HIGH IS, AND ABOVE THESE ALSO THERE ARE HIGHER ONES] The sense here seems to be: Those petty satraps vex others; but greater ones vex them, as Seneca says: Whatever the lesser fears from you, a greater Lord threatens you with this: Every kingdom is under a heavier kingdom. But you would translate that last part more correctly: And the high one of the high ones is above them. For just as the Hebrews say, κατ’ ἔμφασιν (by emphasis) חכמת for חכמות and אלהה for אלהים, בחמת for בהמות and חכמות, so here גבהים is said for גבהי. The sense is that God is above all the highest of men.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVIA EXCELSO EXCELSIOR EST ALIVS, ET SVPER HOS QVOQVE EMINENTIORES SVNT ALII] Hic videtur sensus : Isti minuti Satrapæ alios vexant: ipson vero majores alii ut Seneca ait : Quicquid à vobis minor extimescit, Major hoc vobis Dominus minatur : Omne sub regno graviore regnum est. At postremum illud rectius verteris : Et excelsus excelso- rum super eos. Nam sicut dicunt Hebræi, κατ’ ἔμφασιν חכמת pro חכמות &אלהה pro אלהים, בחמת pro בהמות &חכמות, ita hic dicitur גבהים pro גבהי. Sensus est, Deum esse supra omnes summates hominum.

## 5:9
Verse 8.

AND MOREOVER THE KING OF THE WHOLE EARTH RULES OVER THE SERVANT] The ו here seems to be for כ, so that it is said that God thus rules the universe, just as a king is served from the field, even in land that excels others by a great deal.

Grotius indeed explains this more correctly as referring to God, that He is above all the highest of men, but he translates it thus: And the high one of the high ones is above them. Therefore, he posits an ellipsis in the Hebrew of גבהים (high ones) for גבה גבהים (high one of high ones): But there is no need for that, since the plural noun used can be said to indicate the mystery of the plurality of the divine persons, which was correctly noted by Junius. Similar passages may be seen in Deuteronomy 5:26, Joshua 24:19, Jeremiah 10:10, chapter 23:36, in which sense some also take Hosea 12:1: Judah still rules with אל (God), and is faithful with קדשים (holy ones): because קדשים אלהים (Elohim—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) are holy, Joshua 24:19. But it is much less necessary to invent an ellipsis as often as the noun אלהים occurs, as if a singular were understood, which Grotius indicates here again, but which has already been refuted elsewhere. That the locution is mysterious has been noted even by the Jews themselves. And when not only singulars but also plurals are joined to the noun Elohim in Scripture, how can an ellipsis of the singular number have a place then? The plural adjective of the same meaning, which occurs four times regarding GOD, contributes especially to this passage, Daniel 7:18, 22, 25, 27, where the elect are called קדישי עליונין (Saints of the HIGHER ONES, i.e., Elohim). For thus אלהים can also be understood here, so that גבהים (HIGHER ELOHIM) are indicated, and thus the most high divine persons are hinted at. The gloss or Midrash Koheleth on this passage also explains it regarding GOD, which holds as follows: If you see the oppressor of the poor and the needy, and justice, that is, the just man living forever multiplying goodness and peace, fear the judgment of Gehenna for them, because the high one is watching over the high one: These are the Angels; and the HIGHER ONES are above them: This is GOD, Holy and Blessed. F. Raimundus Martinus observed this mystery in the present passage in his Pugio. Fidei, part 3, Distinction 1, chapter 3, where he also brought forward the passage noted earlier, Hosea 11:12, if indeed according to

Rabbi Solomon, God is to be understood by קדושים (holy ones): as also the passage in Proverbs 30:3, And I do not have the knowledge of the HOLY ONES: which is explained in the Great Exposition on Genesis 44:20 as referring to God, that He is designated by the name קדושים, BECAUSE WHATEVER PERTAINS TO HIM IS IN HOLINESS, as it is said in the last chapter of Joshua, He is a HOLY Elohim. Raimundus understands this of the divine persons. For these pertain to the most holy divine essence and are in the most holy GOD, inasmuch as He subsists in three Holy Hypostases. Mr. Varenius observes yet another proposition of the mystery here: THE HIGH ONE FROM THE HIGH ONE OF THE HIGH ONES (just as גבה is the high Father, from whom עד is the high Son, and from this עד high Son is גבה the high Holy Spirit) IS WATCHING. That the following is to be rendered thus, the counsel of the sources and the accentuation teaches: THE PROFIT OF THE LAND (which, to wit, is not had from plunder, or from an ill-gotten patrimony, not from the oppression of the poor, but from the honest cultivation of the land blessed by God.) IS IN ALL THINGS (above all, it has the likeness of all; nor is that only for the humbler sort, so that it may be permitted to the more powerful to live from what is snatched from the spoils of the humbler or of subjects; not so: For even) THE KING OF THE FIELD IS CULTIVATED (such a King is to be cultivated, who is devoted to the field, and from it provides for his own diet, without the burdens of his subjects. Conf. 2 Kings 10, 18. chap. 21, 25.) the profit from the land goes everywhere, a good king of the field is to be held in honor. Conf. 2 Chron. 26, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ET INSVPER VNIVERSÆ TERRÆ REX IMPE- RAT SERVIENTI] Videtur hic ו effe pro כ, ut dica- tur sic Deus universo imperare, quomodo Regi servitur de agro etiam in terra quæ cæteris plurimum præstat.

Rectius hoc quidem explicat Grotius de Deo, quod sit supra omnes summates hominum, sed ita vertit: Et excelsus excelsorum super eos. In Ebræo ergo statuit ellipsin גבהים excelsi, pro גבה גבהים: Sed ea opus non est, quum nomen plu- rale adhibitum dici possit ad indicandum myste- rium pluralitatis personarum divinarum, quod re- cte notatum Junio. Similia videantur Deuteron. 5, 26. Jos. 24, 19. Jerem. 10, 10. cap. 23, 36. in quam sen- tentiam etiam nonnulli accipiunt Os. 12, 1. Juda ad- huc dominatur cum אל DEO, & cum קדשים sanctis fidelis est : quia קדשים אלהים Elohim (Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus) sancti Jos. 24, 19. Multo vero minus ellipsis toties fingenda, quoties nomen אלהים occurrit, quasi singularis sub- intelligatur, quod hic iterum indicat Grotius, sed alias jam profligatum est. Locutionem illam μυσηριώδη esse etiam Judæis ipsis notatum. Et quum in Scriptura non modo singularia, sed etiam pluralia nomini Elohim adjungantur, quomodo ellipsis singularis numeri tum locum habere potest? Facit ad hunc locum imprimis adjectivum plurale ejusdem significationis, quod quater occurrit de DEO, Dan. 7, 18. 22. 25. 27. ubi electi dicuntur קדישי עליונין Sancti EXCELSIORUM scil. Elo- him. Nam ita hic etiam subintelligi possunt אלהים, ut indigitentur גבהים EXCELSI ELOHIM, adeoque innuantur personæ divinæ ex- celsissimæ. De DEO explicat etiam glossa seu Midrasch Koheleth ad h. l. quæ ita habet: Si vide- ris oppressorem pauperum & egenorum, & justitiam, id est, justum viventem in secula multiplicantem e bonitatem, & pacem, timeto eis judicium gehennæ, quia excelsus desuper excelsum custodiens: Isti sunt Angeli; & EXCELSI super eis : Iste est DEUS Sanctus & Benedictus. Observavit hoc myste- rium in præsenti loco F. Raimundus Martinus Pug. Fid. part. 3. Dist. 1. cap. 3. ubi adduxit quoque lo- cum antea notatum, Hos. 11. v. 12. siquidem juxta

R. Salomonem per קדושים intelligendus sit Deus: ut & locum Prov, 30, 3. Et notitiam SANCTO- RUM nescio: qui in Magna expositione super Gen. 44, 20. de Deo explicatur, quod nomine קדושים defi- gnetur, QUIA QUAECUNQUE AD IPSUM PERTINENT, IN SANCTITATE SUNT, sicut dictum Jos. ult. Elohim SANCTI ipse. Quod de personis divinis intelligit Raimundus. Hæ enim ad divinam essentiam sanctissimam pertinent, & in DEO sanctissimo sunt, utpote qui tribus S. S. hy- postasibus subsistit. Dn. Varenius adhuc aliam mysterii propositionem hic observat, EXCELSUS AB EXCELSO EXCELSI (uti sit גבה excelsus Pater, a quo עד Filius excelsus, & ab hoc עד excelso Filio sit גבה excelsus Spiritus Sanctus) EST OBSERVANS. Sequentia ita reddenda esse e consilio fontium & accentuationis docet: EMOLUMENTUM TERRÆ (quod scil. non habetur ex spolio, vel male conciliato patrimonio, non ex oppressiione pauperum, sed ex honesta terræ cultura a Deo benedicta.) EST IN OMNIBUS (præ omnibus, habet instar omnium; neq; id saltim tenuioribus, ita ut potentioribus liceat ex rapto ex spoliis tenuiorum seu subditorum vivere; non ita: Nam etiam) REX AGRI COLITUR (colen- dus est talis Rex, qui agro est deditus, & ex illo suæ diætæ consulit, sine gravaminibus subditorum. Conf. 2. Reg. 10, 18. cap. 21, 25.) der Vortheil vom Lande gehet überall, ein guter Ackerkönig ist in Ehren zu halten. Conf. 2. Chron. 26, 10.

## 5:10
Verse 9.

THE COVETOUS MAN SHALL NOT BE FILLED WITH MONEY) The poets show this through the fable of Midas: money, unless it is spent, is of no use to anyone.

AND HE WHO LOVES RICHES SHALL NOT RECEIVE FRUIT FROM THEM) In the Hebrew it is המון, which signifies a multitude, and by the force of the subject matter here it ought to be understood of a multitude of moneys. But the Gemara explains: he who loves crowds. Others read: ומי־אהב במעלו תבואה: and he who loves society, shall profit: to wit, in the law. I shall prefer what I said first.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

AVARUS NON IMPLEBITUR PECUNIA) Hoc per Midæ fabulam ostendunt Poetæ: pecunia nisi erogetur, nulli est usui.

ET QVI AMAT DIVITIAS FRUCTUM NON CA- PIET EX EIS) In Hebræo est המון, quod multitudinem fignificat, & ex vi subjectæ materiæ hic de multitudine pe- cuniarum debet intelligi. At Gemara explicat: qui amat tur- bas. Alii legunt: ומי־אהב במעלו תבואה: & qui amat societatem, proficiet: scilicet in lege. Ego quod pri- mum dixi præferam.

## 5:11
AND WHAT PROFIT IS IT TO THE POSSESSOR, EXCEPT THAT HE BEHOLDS THE RICHES WITH HIS EYES) Martial concerning distant villas and fields: O happy janitors and farm-stewards! These things are prepared for the masters, they serve you.

Latin:

ET QVID PRODEST POSSESSORI, NISI QVOD CERNIT DIVITIAS OCULIS SUIS) Martialis de vil- lis & agris longinquis: O janitores villicique felices! Dominis parantur ista, serviunt vobis.

## 5:17
Verse 16.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

## 5:19
Verse 18.

AND LET HIM ENJOY HIS PORTION) Which Horace says: The gods have given you riches, and the art of enjoying them.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ET FRUATUR PARTE SUA) Quod Horatius dicit: Di tibi divitias dederunt, artemque fruendi.

## 5:20
Verse 19.
