FOR HE SHALL NOT MUCH REMEMBER THE DAYS OF HIS LIFE) He does not feel life passing away. O life long to the miserable, short to the happy!

The Hebrew sounds thus, by the interpretation of Junius and Varenius: For if he shall not much (God having given) remember (such a one) the days of his life: because God himself shall answer, (shall grant) to the joy of his heart. The days of life are few, and pass easily: nor do they require so much, if anyone be self-sufficient. But the divine answer through the joy of the heart is to be preferred far above all wealth and riches. GOD, the less He gives of wealth, the more He can give of joys in the heart.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

NON ENIM SATIS RECORDABITUR DIERUM VITÆ SUÆ) Non sentit abire vitam. O vita misero longa, felici brevis!

Ebræa ita sonant, interprete Junio, & Vare- nio: Quod si non multum (Deus dederit) recordabi- tur (talis) dierum vitæ suæ: quia Deus ipse responsurus erit, (annuet) gaudio cordis ejus. Dies vitæ pauci sunt, & facile transeunt: neque adeo multum requi- runt, si quis αὐτάρκης sit. Responsum autem di- vinum per gaudium cordis omnibus opibus & divi- tiis longe anteferendum. DEUS, quo minus dat opum, eo plus dare potest in corde gaudiorum.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. The unhappiness of the rich man who does not use his goods is outlined, who enjoys no joy, always insatiable, whereas on the contrary the wise man, even if poor, knows how to use and enjoy present things, which is certainly better than perpetually panting for greater things.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. Adumbratur infelicitas divitis bonis suis non utentis, qui gaudio nullo fruitur, semper insatiabilis, quum contra sapiens, etsi pauper, præsentibus uti & frui norit, quod utique præstat quam perpetuo amplio- ra anhelare.

## 6:3
Vers. 3. THAT AN ABORTION IS BETTER THAN HE) An improper expression, as in Matt. 26, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 3. QVOD MELIOR ILLO SIT ABORTIVVS) Impro pria locutio, ut Matth. 26, 24.

## 6:6
Verf. 6. DO NOT ALL THINGS HASTEN TO ONE PLACE? Εἰς τὸν ᾅδην. Departure from this life is noted by the word of going away c. I, 4. c. V, 14. 15. c. VI, 4. All, as well the rich as the poor, as well the short-lived as the long-lived, are at length compelled to undergo the same place, namely the grave or the earth, which is the common mother of us all.

Latin:

Verf. 6. NONNE AD UNUM LOCUM PROPE- RANT OMNIA) Εἰς τὸν ᾅδην. Discessus ex hac vita verbo abeundi notatur c. I, 4. c. V, 14. 15. c. VI, 4. Omnes tam divites, quam pau- peres, tam βραχύβιοι, quam vivaces, tandem eun- dem coguntur subire locum, sepulcrum nempe vel terram, quæ communis mater nostrum omnium.

## 6:7
Verf. 7. ALL THE LABOR OF MAN IS IN HIS MOUTH) All use is in food: but nature is content with few things. BUT HIS SOUL SHALL NOT BE FILLED) Desire is insatiable: Solon: Πλέτε δ' ὀδὲν τέρμα πεφασμένον ἀνδράσι κεῖται.

Latin:

Verf. 7. OMNIS LABOR HOMINIS IN ORE EJUS) Usus omnis in victu est : natura autem paucis contenta est. SED ANIMA EJUS NON IMPLEBITUR) Cupiditas est inexplebilis : Solon : Πλέτε δ' ὀδὲν τέρμα πεφασμένον ἀνδράσι κεῖται.

## 6:8
Verf. 8. WHAT HATH THE WISE MAN MORE THAN THE FOOL, AND WHAT THE POOR, EXCEPT THAT HE GOES WHERE THERE IS LIFE?) The sense seems to be: what privilege has the wise man over the fool (in those things which nature desires)? what for the poor (supply: is lacking) if he knows how to walk (to conduct himself well) with the living: with the men of his own age?

Latin:

Verf. 8. QVID HABET AMPLIUS SAPIENS A STUL- TO, ET QVID PAUPER, NISI UT PERGAT ILLUC UBI EST VITA?) Sensus videtur : quod (in iis quæ natura desiderat) privilegium sapientis præ stulto? quid pauperi (sup- ple deest) si norit ambulare (bene se gerere) cum viventibus: cum sui ævi hominibus?

## 6:9
Verf. 9. BETTER IS IT TO SEE WHAT YOU DESIRE, THAN TO DESIRE WHAT YOU DO NOT KNOW) In the Hebrew: Better is the vision of the eyes, than the running of the soul. That is, it is better to enjoy than to hope. It is better to use and enjoy present things than to always wander in mind and pant for greater things. BUT THIS ALSO IS VANITY) Yet even this, to enjoy namely, is a thing not permanent. AND PRESUMPTION OF SPIRIT) In the Hebrew: affliction of spirit. For the more happy a man seems to himself here, the more he fears death.

Latin:

Verf. 9. MELIUS EST VIDERE QVOD CUPIAS, QVAM DESIDERARE QVOD NESCIAS) In Hebræo: Melius est visio ocularis, quam cursus animæ. Id est, præstat frui quam sperare. Præstat uti frui præsentibus, quam divagari sem- per animo & anhelare ampliora. SED ET HOC VANITAS EST) Tamen & hoc, frui scilicet, res est non permanens. ET PRÆSUMTIO SPIRITUS) In Hebræo: afflictio spi- ritus. Nam quo quis hic sibi videtur felicior, eo magis mor- tem metuit.

## 6:10
Verf. 10. HE THAT IS TO BE, HIS NAME IS ALREADY CALLED) In the Hebrew: What is, its name is called: That is, what exists is already known: what is hoped for is unknown. AND IT IS KNOWN THAT HE IS MAN, AND CANNOT CONTEND IN JUDGMENT AGAINST ONE STRONGER THAN HIMSELF) In the Hebrew: It is known that he is made man, and that he cannot contend with one stronger than himself. That is, he cannot be surpassed by him in the changes related to things.

Latin:

Verf. 10. QVI FUTURUS EST JAM VOCATVM EST NOMEN EJUS) In Hebræo: Quod est, vocatum est nomen ejus: Id est, quod existit, notum jam est: quod speratur, ignotum. ET SCITUR QVOD HOMO SIT, ET NON POS- SIT CONTRA FORTIOREM SE IN JVDICIO CON- TENDERE) In Hebræo: Scitur quod fit homo, & quod non possit contendere cum fortiori se. Id est, non posse ab eo supe- rari agnatas rebus vices.

## 6:11
Verf. 11. THERE ARE MANY WORDS, AND THEY HAVE MUCH VANITY IN DISPUTING) In the Hebrew: many are the things which increase vanity: (that is, uncertainty added to future things) what therefore is the utility to man? namely from hope. For these last words, which the Latin attaches to the following Chapter, make the end of this Chapter in the Hebrew. I do not buy hope at a price, says Terence: and another; You do not know what the late Evening may bring.

Latin:

Verf. 11. VERBA SVNT PLVRIMA, MVLTAM- QVE IN DISPVTANDO HABENTIA VANITATEM) In Hebræo: multæ sunt res quæ augent vanitatem: (id est, in- certitudinem rebus futuris additam) quid ergo utilitatis homi- ni? nempe a spe. Nam hæc postrema verba, quæ Latinus Capiti sequenti annectit, finem hujus Capitis in Hebræo fa- ciunt. Spem pretio non emo, ait Terentius : & alter ; Nescis, quid serus Vesper vehat.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

The pursuit of true happiness is commended on account of the fleeting nature of human life, so that we may leave behind a good reputation: and the means for it are handed down, such as the meditation on death, the admission of correction, the restraint of anger, the acquisition of true wisdom which rests in God, the love of justice tempered by equity, the flight from impiety, the prudent dissimulation of injuries, the avoidance of the unchaste woman: which are rare among men, even though God created man upright in the beginning.

Vers. 1. WHICH PASSES LIKE A SHADOW) Pindar: σκιᾶ ἀνθρωπος. See 1 Chronicles 29:15. Job 8:9.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

Commendatur studium veræ εὐδαιμονίας ob vita humanæ fugacitatem, ut bonam relin- quamus famam : ejusque media traduntur, utpote mortis meditatio, correptionis admis- sio, iræ cohibitio, veræ sapientiæ in Deo ac- quiescentis comparatio, justitiæ æquitate temperatæ amor, impietatis fuga, prudens injuriarum dissimulatio, impudicæ mulieris vitatio : quæ rara inter homines, etsi Deus hominem initio rectum condiderit.

Vers. 1. QVOD VELVT VMBRA PRÆTERIT) Pindarus: σκιᾶ ἀνθρωπος. Vide 1. Paralip. XXIX. 15. Job. VIII, 9.

## 7:1
Vers. 2. A GOOD NAME IS BETTER THAN PRECIOUS OINTMENTS) There is here in the Hebrew a paronomasia of the words שמן and שם. The same allusion is in Song of Songs 1:3.

AND THE DAY OF DEATH THAN THE DAY OF BIRTH) Valerius Maximus II. 6. That nation of Thrace indeed deservedly claimed for itself the praise of wisdom, which, celebrating the birthdays of men with weeping, and funerals with hilarity, without any precepts of the learned, perceived the true state of our condition. Mela on the same Thracians: Among some, childbirths are mourned, and the newborn are bewailed: funerals on the contrary are festivals, and are celebrated as if they were sacred rites, with song and play. Solinus on the same: Among many, childbirths are mournful: in short, the parent receives the newborn with weeping: on the contrary, funerals are joyful, so much so that they accompany the departed with rejoicings. Euripides in his Cresphontes translated this sentiment thus: We ought to gather together and lament the one who is born, into how many evils he comes. But the one who has died and has ceased from labors, we ought to send forth from the house rejoicing and speaking well of him.

The Gentiles were ignorant of the true reason why the day of death is to be preferred to the day of birth, namely because the day of death provides for us the beginning of a truer and more blessed life. Revelation 14:13.

Latin:

Vers. 2. MELIVS EST NOMEN BONVM QVAM VNGVENTA PRETIOSA) Est hic in Hebræo παρονομα- σία vocum שמן & שם. Eadem allusio Cant. I, 3.

ET DIES MORTIS DIE NATIVITATIS) Valerius Maximus II. 6. Thraciæ vero illa natio merito sibi sapientiæ laudem vindicavit, quæ natales hominum flebiliter, exequias cum hilaritate celebrans, sine ullis doctorum præceptis, verum conditionis nostræ habitum pervidit. Mela de iisdem Thra- cibus: Lugentur apud quosdam puerperia, natique deflentur: funera contra festa sunt, & veluti sacra, cantu lusuque ce- lebrantur. De iisdem Solinus: Apud plurimos luctuosa sunt puerperia: denique recens natum fletu parens excipit: contra- versum læta sunt funera, adeo ut exentos gaudiis prosequantur. Hanc sententiam Euripides in Cresphontem suam sic trans- tulit: Ἔχρην μὲν ἡμᾶς σύλλογον ποιεμένους Τὸν φύντα θρηνεῖν εἰς ὅσ' ἔρχεται κακά. Τὸν δ' αὖ θανόντα καὶ πόνων πεπαυμένον Χαίροντας εὐφημοῦντας ἐκπέμπειν δόμων.

Gentiles veram causam, cur præferenda dies fatalis diei natali ignorarunt, quod nempe dies mortis nobis verioris & beatioris vitæ exor- dium præbeat. Apoc. XIV, 13.

## 7:2
Vers. 3. IT IS BETTER TO GO TO THE HOUSE OF MOURNING THAN TO THE HOUSE OF FEASTING) Here he comes to better sentiments, which place the good in the mind. Prov. 16, 19.

AND THE LIVING WILL LAY IT TO HIS HEART) As Homer speaks: Τῷ ἐπικάρδιο θυμῷ. That saying also pertains here, γνῶθι σεαυτόν.

Latin:

Vers. 3. MELIUS EST IRE AD DOMUM LUCTUS QVAM AD DOMUM CONVIVII) Hic venit ad melio- res sententias, quæ in animo bonum collocant. Prov. 16, 19.

ET VIVENS DABIT AD COR SUUM) Ut Homerus loquitur: Τῷ ἐπικάρδιο θυμῷ. Pertinet & huc illud, γνῶθι σεαυτόν.

## 7:3
Vers. 4. SORROW IS BETTER THAN LAUGHTER) It is better to have a friend who is angry with you when you sin, than one who smiles at you.

FOR BY THE SADNESS OF THE COUNTENANCE) Of a more severe friend. THE HEART OF THE OFFENDER IS CORRECTED) יוטב let it be better.

The version of B. Luther is to be preferred here, with which the Belgian agrees; since Solomon dwells on the dissipation of the world's joys, and compares penitential or funeral sorrow, arising from the meditation of a sad spectacle in the house of mourning, with the laughter of fools in the house of feasting. Conf. II, Cor. VII, 9. 10. Which the following verse 5 teaches: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. The comparison of the Wise Man's rebuke with the applauding song of fools follows finally in verse 6.

Latin:

Vers. 4. MELIOR EST IRA RISU) Melius est amicum habe- re, qui peccanti tibi succenseat, quam qui arrideat.

QVIA PER TRISTITIAM VULTUS) Amici severioris. CORRIGITUR ANIMUS DELINQVENTIS) יוטב sit melior.

Præferenda hic B. Lutheri versio, cui consonat Belgica; quum commoretur Salomo in profligan- dis mundi gaudiis, & comparet dolorem pœniten- tialem, vel funeralem ortum ex meditatione tristis spectaculi in domo luctus, cum risu stultorum in domo convivii. Conf. II, Cor. VII, 9. 10. Quod do- cet vers. 5. sequens: Cor sapientum est in domo lu- ctus; cor stolidorum autem in domo gaudii. Compa- ratio increpationis Sapientis cum Cantico applauden- te stolidorum sequitur demum vers. 6.

## 7:6
Vers. 7. UNDER THE POT) Under the cauldron, as Ps. LVIII, 10. The word is Syriac. There is also a παρονομασία here. The unstable joy of fools is noted, even if it begins with a great crackling, just as a huge and exulting flame arises from thorns placed under a pot, but which is extinguished immediately once the thorns are consumed.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SUB OLLA) Sub caldario, ut Pf. LVIII, 10. Vox est Syriaca. Est & hic παρονομασία. Notatur instabilis stultorum lætitia, etsi cum magno crepitu incipiat, uti igne e spinis ollæ sup- posito oritur ingens, & exultans quasi flamma, sed quæ absumtis spinis illico extinguitur.

## 7:7
Vers. 8. OPPRESSION TROUBLES A WISE MAN, AND WILL DESTROY THE STRENGTH OF HIS HEART) In the Hebrew: For oppression drives a wise man to madness, and gifts overturn the mind. He continues to show the uncertainty of human affairs, since even the wisest are accustomed to be disturbed from the state of their mind, either by injuries or by benefits.

Latin:

Vers. 8. CALUMNIA CONTURBAT SAPIENTEM, ET PERDET ROBUR CORDIS ILLIUS) In Hebræo: Nam oppressio sapientem ad insaniam redigit, & animum evertunt dona. Pergit ostendere incertitudinem rerum humanarum, cum etiam sapientissimi de statu mentis suæ deturbari sole- ant, aut per injurias, aut per beneficia.

## 7:8
Vers. 9. BETTER IS THE END OF A SPEECH THAN THE BEGINNING) You might more correctly say: the end of a quarrel: for thus the Hebrew word דבר is also taken in Proverbs XVII, 9. And thus the sense will best cohere with what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 9. MELIOR EST FINIS ORATIONIS QVAM PRIN- CIPIUM) Rectius dicas: finis jurgii: nam fic Hebræum דבר sumitur etiam Proverb. XVII, 9. Et fic optime cohæ- rebit sensus cum sequentibus.

## 7:10
Vers. 11. NEITHER SAY, WHAT DO YOU THINK IS THE CAUSE, THAT THE FORMER TIMES WERE BETTER THAN THEY ARE NOW) Do not say, O the morals! O the times! There are many complainers who always accuse the age.

Latin:

Vers. 11. NEC DICAS, QVID PUTAS CAUSÆ EST, QVOD PRIORA TEMPORA MELIORA FUERE QVAM NUNC SUNT) Ne dicas, o mores! o tempora! Multi sunt queruli, qui semper sæculum accusant.

## 7:12
Vers. 13. FOR AS WISDOM PROTECTS, SO MONEY PROTECTS) In the Hebrew is the noun for shadow for protection, as also elsewhere. The Hebrew is to be rendered thus: Although (to be) in the shadow of wisdom is (to be) in the shadow of silver (a most precious thing, and Wisdom itself, even without an inheritance, is for itself a price sufficient and more than the shadow of silver) indeed the excellence of (heavenly) knowledge is (wisdom, that is, or this is what follows) It gives life to its masters, or possessors. Which silver certainly cannot provide.

Latin:

Vers. 13. SICUT ENIM PROTEGIT SAPIENTIA, SIC PRO- TEGIT PECUNIA) In Hebræo est nomen umbræ pro pro- tectione, ut & alibi. Ebræa sic reddenda: Quamvis (esse) in umbra sa- pientiæ sit (esse) in umbra argenti (rei pretiosissi- mæ, & ipsa Sapientia etiam sine patrimonio sit sibi pretium satis & supra argenti umbram) imo excellen- tia notitiæ (cœlestis) est (sapientia sc. vel est hæc, quæ sequitur) Illa vivificat suos Dominos, vel possessores. Quod utique præstare non potest argentum.

## 7:13
Vers. 14. CONSIDER THE WORKS OF GOD) In the Hebrew: see for admire. THAT NO ONE CAN CORRECT WHOM HE HAS DESPISED) In the Hebrew: Whom he has bent, that is, who is born with some bodily defect, who shall heal it? Thus the Chaldean here.

While this may rightly be accepted even concerning such men, the sentiment is nevertheless more general? What he has bent, who shall be able to make straight? He speaks, however, γενικῶς (generally) of the works of God: See the work of God (whatever it is) For who can correct what he (God) has bent? As he had said above in ch. I, 15: that which is crooked cannot be made straight. This, however, is not to be dragged to the perversity of guilt, as is done by some Calvinists: because that is ascribed to the BEST AND MOST HOLY GOD only impiously.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CONSIDERA OPERA DEI) In Hebræo: vide pro admirare. QVOD NEMO POSSIT CORRIGERE QVEM IL- LE DESPEXERIT) In Hebræo: Quem ille curvaverit, id est, eum qui natus sit cum aliquo vitio corporis quis sanabit? Ita hic Chaldæus.

Recte quidem de talibus etiam hominibus hoc accipiatur, sententia tamen generalior est? Quod ille curvaverit quis rectum facere poterit? Loqui- tur autem γενικῶς de operibus Dei: Vide opus Dei (quodcunque) Quis enim possit corrigere, quod ille (Deus) curvaverit? uti supra c. I, 15. dixerat: perver- sum non potest emendari. Non tamen hoc trahendum ad perversitatem culpæ, quemadmodum a Calvi- nianis nonnullis fit: quia ea non nisi impie DEO OPTIMO ET SANCTISSIMO transcribitur.

## 7:14
Verse same. BEWARE OF THE EVIL DAY) Hebrew: and in the evil day see. Seek the outcome. Verse 15. FOR AS HE HATH MADE THIS, SO ALSO HATH GOD MADE THAT, THAT MAN SHOULD NOT FIND AGAINST HIM JUST COMPLAINTS] In the Hebrew: this thing from the opposite of that thing God made, lest man should find anything after it. That is, lest he be able to speak against God, as Ps. LI, 6. He made all things ἀντίσοιχα (corresponding). Does light displease you? behold darkness. Does darkness displease you? behold light. Do you accuse death? life also has been given. Do you not praise life? death will follow. Sirachides XLII. all things are double, one against the other, and He hath made nothing lacking. More correctly B. Luther and the Dutch: lest man should attain anything after Him (of things to come hereafter for man in this life). Conf. Dn. D. Varen. in h. l.

Latin:

Vers. eod. MALAM DIEM PRÆCAVE) Hebræum : & in die mala vide. Quære exitum. Vers. 15. SICUT ENIM HANC, SIC ET ILLAM FECIT DEUS, UT NON INVENIAT HOMO CONTRA EUM JUSTAS QVERIMONIAS] In Hebræo : rem hanc ex adverso rei istius fecit Deus, ne homo quicquam inseniret post eam. Id est, ne obloqui Deo posset, ut Ps. LI, 6. fecit omnia ἀντίσοιχα. Displicet tibi lux ? en tenebræ. Displicent tenebræ ? en lux. Mortem accusas ? data est & vita. Vitam non laudas ? mors sequetur. Sirachides XLII. πάντα δισσὰ, ἓν κατέναντι τῦ ἑνὸς, κὰι ἐκ ἐποίησεν ἐδὲν ἐλλεῖπον. Rectius B. Luther. & Belgæ ne quicquam post se (futurorum deinceps homini in hac vita) assequatur homo. Conf. Dn. D. Varen. in h. l.

## 7:15
Verse 16.

THE JUST MAN PERISHETH IN HIS JUSTICE, AND THE WICKED MAN LIVETH A LONG TIME IN HIS MALICE) Namely, good men are often snatched away from future evils: Whom the gods love, dies young. And on the contrary, for the wicked, life is prolonged for a more severe punishment. See 2 Kings XXII, 20. Is. LVII, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

JUSTUS PERIT IN JUSTITIA SUA, ET IMPIUS MULTO VIVIT TEMPORE IN MALITIA SUA) Nempe viri boni sæpe eripiuntur malis futuris : Ὅν οἱ θεοὶ φιλῦσ’, ἀποθνήσκει νέος. Et contra malis ad graviorem pœnam vita prorogatur. Vide 2. Reg. XXII, 20. Es. LVII, 1.

## 7:16
Verse 17.

BE NOT JUST MUCH) That is, do not arrogate to yourself more of probity, or, what follows, of Wisdom, than is right: be not high-minded Rom. XI, 20. BE NOT ASTONISHED) In the Hebrew it is: Why should you go to ruin? It is indeed Hithpahel, but with the omission of the letter ת.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

NOLI ESSE JUSTUS MULTUM) Id est, noli plus tibi arrogare de probitate, aut, quod sequitur, de Sapientia, quam par est : μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει Roman. XI, 20. NE OBSTUPESCAS) In Hebræo est : Quare te ires perditum? Est enim Hithpahel, sed cum defectu ת literæ.

## 7:19
Verse 20.

WISDOM HATH STRENGTHENED THE WISE MAN ABOVE TEN PRINCES OF THE CITY) Above ten mighty men. Let arms yield to the toga.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

SAPIENTIA CONFORTAVIT SAPIENTEM SUPER DECEM PRINCIPES CIVITATIS) Super decem fortes. Cedant arma togæ.

## 7:20
Verse 21.

FOR THERE IS NO JUST MAN UPON EARTH THAT DOETH GOOD, AND SINNETH NOT) כי which is usually translated 'for', is here placed for 'nevertheless': no one is always wise. Seneca on Clemency, book 6. We have all sinned, some grave things, some light, some by design, some perhaps driven by impulse, or carried away by the wickedness of others, some have stood too weakly in good counsels, and have lost our innocence unwillingly and resisting. See what we have annotated to book II of the Law of War and Peace XX, 19.

He explains this remarkable sentiment concerning the universal corruption of men, that no one is found everywhere just in the whole earth, and who doeth good according to the norm of the Decalogue, so that he does not sin, according to the mind of Seneca on Clemency, ch. 6, who had no knowledge of this corruption of human nature, by adducing a parallel place according to custom, from a Philosophical writing, so that, forsooth, Philosophers are now constituted Interpreters of Scripture in such matters also, of which universal Philosophy knows nothing at all. He therefore renders this very jejune sense: no one is always wise. The cause why he so enervates such remarkable testimonies is the Pelagian and Socinian opinion, by which he was occupied and could not, or more truly would not, see the corruption of human nature and the power of original sin in them. It is indeed certain that, no one is wise at all hours: but not only ignorance, or creeping folly, or error of mind is indicated here: But emphatically all men are concluded under the guilt of sin (1) because there is no just man on earth, namely pure from sin, and just, with regard to the state of men after the fall, as they are viewed according to their natural condition. For by nature we are all children of wrath, and thus subject to sin Eph. II, 3. there is no one just Ps. XIV, 3. (2) Because there is no one who doeth good, who by nature can perform anything good, much less who can fulfill the precepts of the Decalogue, by which the whole Rule of good is exhibited. Which David executes at length in the aforementioned Psalm XIV, and from him Paul Rom. VII. (3) Because there is no man who does not sin: which is so true, that even the justified and the reborn are not entirely ἀναμάρτητοι (sinless): because in many things we all stumble James III, 2. concerning which Paul complained especially Rom. VII, 14. seqq. but of these things elsewhere expressly against the Socinians. He takes it concerning man placed in sins and fixed in the mire of the deep of sin

Jerome. Conf. I Kings VIII, 40. Ps. CXLIII, 12. I John I, 8. Verse 22. BUT ALSO TO ALL WORDS; WHICH ARE SPOKEN DO NOT APPLY THY HEART] Do not inquire too curiously into what each person says. Verse 23. FOR THY CONSCIENCE KNOWS THAT THOU ALSO HAST OFTEN CURSED OTHERS] Seneca: Reflection on ourselves will make us more moderate, if we consult ourselves; have we not ourselves committed something of the sort? have we not erred in this way? is it advantageous for us to be condemned for these things? The passage is from On Anger II. 28. He has similar things in On Anger I. 14. and On Clemency I. 6. Verse 25. MUCH MORE THAN IT WAS, AND A DEEP DEPTH WHO SHALL FIND IT] That which was (that which is past) has departed (that is, flowed away) and the deep, deep (the hidden future) who shall find it? There is great forgetfulness of things past: conjectures about the future are uncertain. These things make the attainment of wisdom difficult. Verse 26. AND THE REASON] The causes of things. For that is חשבון. Verse 27. AND I HAVE FOUND A WOMAN MORE BITTER THAN DEATH] The writer introduces here, as we have said, Solomon, as one touched by the conscience of evil deeds, of which women themselves had been the principal authors. HE THAT PLEASES GOD SHALL ESCAPE HER] For it happens by the favor of God that those snares are avoided. Solomon is not introduced here by another writer, but Solomon himself openly testifies here that he found a woman more bitter than death, just as he also says in v. 29: One woman out of all I have not found, that is, as Grotius interprets, among a thousand women whom I took to myself I found none sincerely upright. If it is permitted to invent another person, as one pleases, what certainty will finally be left in the Scriptures? For not once or only here does the author of the book speak about himself, but throughout the whole book, so that nothing is clearer than that he is the very same Solomon. Indeed, in almost all the chapters he wished to speak in the first person, so that no doubt would remain about the author. In chapter I, four times, in the second thirty times, in the third seven times, and just as often in the fourth, in the fifth, as also in the sixth once, in the seventh eight times, in the eighth nine times, in the ninth six times, in the tenth twice. And shall we still doubt that Solomon himself was the author of the book? Certainly no example of such a masked author can be brought forward in the sacred and Canonical books, and such things are unworthy of the Holy Spirit. Verse 28. THE PREACHER SAID] Thus also the Greeks εἶπεν ὁ ἐκκλησιαστὴς. It is plain that they read אמר הקהלת not as it is now in the Hebrew אמרה קהלת. Whatever the Greeks may have seen or read, it matters little to us: since Grotius himself has not dissented from their frequent errors. But that they had Hebrew Codices at that age, as he wishes them to have read it, that was to be proven, not merely asserted. The modern Hebrew reading is correct: For since the word קהלת is of the feminine, or according to Grotius, of the common gender, why could it not have been constructed with a feminine verb? Others observe, however, that a feminine substantive is understood, and they understand either חכמה wisdom, or נפש soul. It must be said here, says Mercerus, that account is taken of the wisdom which was in Solomon himself, which he also subsequently introduced as speaking in the Proverbs: or certainly of the soul of Solomon himself, which holds the principal part in man, which comes to the same thing. And he adds, that there is great force in it, as if Solomon himself were not saying these things, but wisdom itself. Verse same. TO FIND THE REASON] That is, the cause why most women were worse than men. Verse 29. ONE WOMAN OUT OF ALL I HAVE NOT FOUND] That is, in a thousand women whom I took to myself, I found none sincerely upright. Verse 30. THIS ONLY HAVE I FOUND, THAT GOD MADE MAN UPRIGHT, AND HE HIMSELF HAS MIXED HIMSELF WITH INFINITE QUESTIONS] Upright here signifies simple, just as I think others have rightly explained, and we with them in book II of The Law of War and Peace c. II. §. 2. For that word questions here in the Hebrew is חשבונות. It signifies the many reasons and causes why they should deviate from that primeval simplicity.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

NON EST ENIM HOMO JUSTUS IN TERRA QVI FACIAT BONUM, ET NON PECCET) כי quod verti solet enim, hic positum est pro attamen : nemo semper sapit. Seneca de Clementia l. 6. Peccavimus omnes, alii gravia, alii levia, alii ex destinato, alii forte impulsi, aut aliena nequitia ablati, alii in bonis consiliis parum fortiter stetimus, & innocentiam inviti ac renitentes perdidimus. Vide quæ annotavimus ad libr. II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XX, 19.

Insignem sententiam de universali hominum corruptione, quod nemo in universa terra reperiatur undiquaque justus, & qui faciat bonum juxta normam Decalogi, ita ut non peccet, ad Senecæ mentem de Clement. c. 6. qui nihil de hac corruptione naturæ humanæ cognitum habuit, explicat, locum parallelum pro more, e Scripto Philosophico adducens, ut sc. Philosophi nunc Interpp. Scripturæ in talibus etiam constituantur, de quibus universa Philosophia nihil omnino novit. Sensum ergo perquàm jejunum hunc reddit : nemo semper sapit. Causa cur tam insignia testimonia ita enervet, præcepta est Pelagiana & Sociniana opinio, qua occupatus corruptionem humanæ naturæ & vim peccati originalis in iisdem videre non potuit, aut verius non voluit. Certum est sane illud, nemo sapit omnibus horis : verum non ignorantia tantum, aut subrepens insipientia, vel error mentis hic indigitatur : Sed emphatice omnes homines sub peccati culpa concluduntur (1) quod non sit homo justus in terra, purus nempe a peccato, & justus, quod ad statum hominum post lapsum, qua secundum naturalem conditionem spectantur. Natura enim omnes filii iræ, adeoque peccato obnoxii sumus Eph. II, 3. justus nemo est Ps. XIV, 3. (2) Quod non sit qui faciat bonum, qui natura quid boni præstare possit, nedum qui implere possit præcepta Decalogi, quibus Regula omnis boni exhibetur. Quod prolixe David Psalmo prædicto XIV. exequitur, & ex eo Paulus Rom. VII. (3) Quod non sit homo qui non peccet : quod adeo verum, ut justificati etiam, ac renati non sint prorsus ἀναμάρτητοι : quia in multis labimur omnes Jac. III, 2. quo de conquestus imprimis est Paulus Rom. VII, 14. seqq. sed de his alias contra Socinianos ex professo. De homine posito in peccatis & infixo in limo profundi peccati accipit

Hieronymus. Conf. I. Reg. IIX, 40. Pf. CXLIII, 12. I. Job. I, 8. Vers. 22. SED ET CUNCTIS SERMONIBUS; QVI DICUNTUR NE ACCOMMODES COR TUUM] Noli curiose nimis scrutari, quid quisque dicat. Vers. 23. SCIT ENIM CONSCIENTIA TUA QVIA ET TV CREBRO MALEDIXISTI ALIIS] Seneca: Faciet nos moderatiores respectus nostri, si consuluerimus nos; numquid & ipsi aliquid tale commisimus? numquid sic erravi- mus? expeditne nobis ista damnari? Locus est de Ira II. 28. Similia habet de ira I. 14. & de clementia I. 6. Vers. 25. MULTO MAGIS QVAM ERAT, ET AL- TA PROFUNDITAS QVIS INVENIET EAM] Remo- tum est, (id est, effluxit) id quod fuit (quod præteritum est) & profundum profundum (futurum latens) quis inveniet? Præteritorum magna est oblivio: de futuris conjecturæ in- certæ. Hæc difficilem faciunt sapientiæ adeptionem. Vers. 26. ET RATIONEM] Rerum causas. Id enim est חשבון. Vers. 27. ET INVENI AMARIOREM MORTE MU- LIEREM] Introducit hic Scriptor, ut diximus, Salomonem, ut tactum conscientia male actorum, quorum præcipuæ au- ctores ipsi fœminæ fuerant. QVI PLACET DEO EFFUGIET ILLAM] Nam Dei favore fit, ut illæ decipulæ evitentur. Non Salomo a Scriptore alio hic introducitur, sed Salomo ipse hic palam testatur, se invenisse mu- lierem morte amariorem, quemadmodum etiam v. 29. ait: Mulierem ex omnibus non inveni, id est, ut interpretatur Grotius, in mille mulieribus, quas mi- hi adscivi nullam inveni sincere probam. Si personam aliam fingere liceat, ut libet, quid certi denique re- linquetur in Scripturis? Nam non semel aut hic so- lum ita autor libri de se loquitur, sed per totum li- brum, ut nihil luculentius sit, quam eundem esse ipsummet Salomonem. Imo in omnibus pene ca- pitibus ita loqui voluit in prima persona, ne du- bium superesset de auctore. In cap. I. quater, in se- cundo trigesies, in tertio septies, & toties quoque in quarto, in quinto, ut & in sexto semel, in septi- mo octies, in octavo novies, in nono sexies, in de- cimo bis. Et adhuc dubitabimus Salomonem ipsum libri auctorem fuisse? Exemplum certe per- sonati ejusmodi auctoris in sacris & Canonicis nul- lum proferri potest, & indigna talia sunt Spiritu Sancto. Vers. 28. DIXIT ECCLESIASTES] Sic & Græci εἶπεν ὁ ἐκκλησιαστὴς. Palam est legisse eos אמר הקהלת non ut nunc in Hebræo est אמרה קהלת. Quicquid viderint aut legerint Græci, parum ad nos: cum crebra ipsorum παροράματα ipse Gro- tius dissessus non sit. Sed ita ut legisse eos vult, ha- buisse Codices Ebræos ista ætate, id probandum erat, non nude asserendum. Lectio Ebræa moder- na recte se habet: Quum enim vox קהלת fœmini- ni, aut juxta Grotium, communis generis sit, quid- ni cum fœminino verbo construi potuerit? Subin- telligi autem substantivum fœmininum alii obser- vant, & vel חכמה sapientiam, vel נפש animam subintelligunt. Dicendum hic, inquit Mercerus, sapientiæ, quæ in ipso Salomone erat, rationem haberi, quam & subinde in Proverbiis loquentem induxit: vel certe animæ ipsius Salomonis, quæ in homine præ- cipuas partes tenet, quod eodem recidit. Et addit, ma- gnam in eo esse vim, quasi non ipse Salomon hæc dicat, sed ipsissima sapientia. Vers. eod. UT INVENIREM RATIONEM] Id est, causam cur mulieres pleræque viris essent pejores. Vers. 29. MULIEREM EX OMNIBUS NON INVE- NI] Id est, in mille mulieribus, quas mihi adscivi, nullam inveni sincere probam. Vers. 30. SOLUMMODO HOC INVENI, QVOD FECERIT DEVS HOMINEM RECTUM, ET IPSE SE INFINITIS MISCUERIT QVÆSTIONIBUS] Re- ctum hic significat simplicem, sicut puto & alios recte expo- suisse, & nos cum illis libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis c. II. §. 2. Pro illo quæstionibus hic in Hebræo est חשבונות. id signi- ficat rationes ac causas multas cur à primæva ista simplicitate deflecterent.

## 7:29
WHO IS LIKE THE WISE MAN, AND WHO HAS KNOWN THE SOLUTION OF THE WORD? This πῶσμα seems to be more correctly referred by others to the following chapter: so that the sense may be: Who is to be held in as much esteem as a wise man? And who understands the solution of a matter (of any proposed thing)? פשר for to solve is a word familiar to the Syrians and Chaldeans. See Dan. V, 13, 17. The Arabs also use it.

Who are those others, if not the Socinians, denying original justice, who say that man was made simple like an infant, and not truly holy or just? Smalcius on the nature of God, ch. VII, p. 60. Who does not see how much it differs to be created upright, and to be created with holiness and justice and other supernatural gifts? For he can be called upright, and he is simple, and devoid of all evil. Likewise, he who is only simple and innocent cannot be said to be endowed with holiness or supernatural gifts, as can be seen in infants, whom we rightly call simple and devoid of evil, or innocent; and no one can rightly be called holy as to his morals, since this holiness is not acquired except by actions. But man is said to have been made ישר εὐθύς, upright as to his soul and body, and as to both faculties of the soul, both the intellect and the will. But the uprightness of the intellect consists in this, that it correctly knows objects, without error: if this had a place in the state of integrity, the first man must have been instructed with wisdom: for without it we cannot understand and know things as is proper and correctly. Therefore, created in the image of God, he reflected in himself the wisdom of God the creator: For this holds the primacy in the image of God, Col. III, 9. To the uprightness of the will pertains entirely holiness and justice, or an inclination toward the good, toward doing just and holy things, and thus also the power and faculty of operating justly without impediment: just as conversely, after the fall, he is prone to an evil nature, after he fell from that primordial uprightness. The image of God, who is most holy and most just, shone also in the will, and therefore it is necessary that the will of man also shone in primordial justice and holiness: which the Apostle also clearly asserts, Eph. IV, 23. Furthermore, this moral uprightness, which cannot be imagined without holiness, is the subject here especially, when Solomon says: I found that God made man upright, but they themselves have sought out many thoughts. Which opposition of the primordial created uprightness and the moral perversity contracted by men, teaches again that the first man was created in justice and holiness: because the seeking of many reasonings, in this place, designates not only craftiness and cunning as a defect of the intellect, but also the perversity of the will, which is properly opposed to the upright. In Hebrew they are said to have sought חשבונות, which Grotius explains as many reasons and causes, when they were deviating from primordial simplicity: but the causes why they deviated are not designated, but rather thoughts deviating from the upright, or wicked and oblique ones, alien to that uprightness which God had implanted. For ישר, upright, is opposed to the tortuosity of errors and vices, and other pits of defects. Nor does that word ever denote only simple, but just and good, whence the Greeks render it εὐθῆ, δίκαιον, ἀγαθόν. And here the Jesuit Tirinus confesses: When man was upright, he was devoid of all questions, or quarrels, fights, seditions, rebellions, within and without.

Latin:

QVIS TALIS UT SAPIENS EST, ET QVIS CO- GNOVIT SOLUTIONEM VERBI) Videtur hoc πῶσμα rectius ab aliis referri ad caput sequens : ut sensus sit : Quis tanti habendus est, quanti vir sapiens ? & qui solutionem rei (cujusque propositæ) intelligit ? פשר pro solvere est, vox Sy- ris & Chaldæis familiaris. Vide Dan. V, 13. 17. usurpant & Arabes.

Quinam illi alii sunt, nisi Sociniani, justitiam originalem negantes, qui simplicem dicunt factum hominem instar infantis, non vero sanctum aut ju- stum. Smalcius de nat. Dei c. VII. p. 60. Quis non videt, quantum differat, rectum esse conditum, & con- ditum cum sanctitate, & justitia & aliis donis super- naturalibus ? Nam & is rectus esse dici potest, & sim- plex est, & expers omnis mali. Item qui simplex & in- nocens tantum est, is nec sanctitate, nec donis super- naturalibus præditus esse dici potest, ut in infantibus videre est, quos simplices & expertes mali, vel inno- centes jure appellamus, & sanctus quoad mores sc. ne- mo jure appellari potest, cum hæc sanctitas non nisi actionibus comparetur. Sed homo dicitur factus ישר εὐθύς, rectus quantus est anima, & corpore, & quo- ad animæ facultatem utramque tum intellectum, tum voluntatem. At intellectus rectitudo sita est in eo, quod recte cognoscat objecta, citra errorem : quæ si locum habuit in statu integritatis, sapientia instructus homo primus fuerit, oportet : sine ea enim res, prout par est, ac recte intelligere, & co- gnoscere non possumus. Ideo ad imaginem Dei conditus, sapientiam Dei conditoris in se refere- bat : Hæc enim in imagine Dei τὸ πρωτεῖον obtinet Col. III, 9. Ad rectitudinem voluntatis pertinet omni- no sanctitas & justitia, vel inclinatio ad bonum, ad agendum justa & sancta, adeoque vis etiam ac fa- cultas justa sine impedimento operandi : quemad- modum vice versa post lapsum ad malam naturam propensus est, postquam rectitudine illa primige- nia excidit. Eluxit & in voluntate imago Dei, qui sanctissimus est, & justissimus, ideoque necesse est voluntatem hominis in primæva justitia, & san- ctitate etiam fulsisse : quod clare asserit quoque Apostolus Eph. IV, 23. Porro de hac rectitudine mo- rali, quæ fingi non potest sine sanctitate, hic im- primis sermo est, cum ait Salomo : Inveni Deum fecisse hominem rectum, ipsi autem quæsierunt cogita- tiones multas. Quæ oppositio rectitudinis primige- niæ creatæ, & perversitatis hominum moralis contra- ctæ, iterum docet, hominem primum in justitia & sanctitate creatum esse : quia τὸ quærere ratiocinia plurima, hoc in loco, non solum astutiam & calli- ditatem ad defectum intellectus, sed etiam perver- sitatem voluntatis, quæ proprie recto opponitur, designat. In Ebræo dicuntur quæsisse חשבונות quod Grotius exponit rationes ac causas multas, cum a primæva simplicitate deflecterent : sed non designantur causæ cur deflexerint, verum cogita- tiones potius deflectentes a recto, vel pravæ & obli- quæ, alienæ ab ea, quam Deus indiderat, rectitudi- ne. Opponitur enim ישר rectus, tortuositati errorum ac vitiorum, & aliis defectuum lacunis. Neque no- tat vox illa uspiam simplicem solum, sed justum & bonum, unde Græci reddunt, εὐθῆ, δίκαιον, ἀγαθόν. Et fatetur hic e Jesuita Tirinus : Homo cum rectus esset, expers fuit omnium quæstionum, seu jurgiorum, pugnarum, seditionum, rebellionum, intus & foris.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

The pursuit of true happiness is commended on account of the fruit of divine wisdom, true cheerfulness, and the debt of obedience, which, when neglected, brings evils much greater than disobedience against a King, especially in death, which is inevitable for all, even if the judgment is deferred, and also on account of the reward of piety and the punishment of impiety, even if it seems that the same things happen to the impious for a time as to the pious.

Ver. 1.

THE WISDOM OF MAN APPEARS IN HIS COUNTENANCE) פנים among the Hebrews signifies not only the countenance, but also the gesture, the gait, and the tone of the voice.

AND THE MOST POWERFUL WILL CHANGE HIS FACE) More correctly thus: and he will change the hardness (that is, the arrogance) of his countenance for him. Through Wisdom he will become much more modest even in his countenance.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

Commendatur studium veræ εὐδαιμονίας ob sapientiæ divinæ fructum, veram hila- ritatem, obedientiæ debitum, quod ne- glectum mala affert multo majora, quam inobedientia adversus Regem, imprimis in morte omnibus inevitabili, etiamsi differatur judicium, nec non ob pietatis præmium, & impietatis supplicium, utut ad tempus idem impiis evenire videatur, quod piis.

Vers. 1.

SAPIENTIA HOMINIS APPARET IN VULTU EJUS) פנים apud Hebræos non vultum tantum, sed & ge- stum, gressum, sonumque vocis significat.

ET POTENTISSIMUS FACIEM ILLIUS COMMU- TABIT) Rectius sic: & duritiem (id est, arrogantiam) vul- tus ei immutabit. Per Sapientiam longe fiet etiam in vultu modestior.

## 8:2
Ver. 2.

I KEEP THE MOUTH OF THE KING) It is not 'I keep', but 'keep' that should be read. In the Greek: ςόμα βασιλέως φύλαξον. But in the Hebrew, 'I' precedes, which must be supplied from what follows. I, that is to say, am the King, and therefore I advise you.

AND THE PRECEPTS OF THE OATH OF GOD) You may translate it best from the Hebrew: especially on account of the oath of God. על-דבר or על-דברת means 'on account of', as in Psalm 45:5, 79:9, and elsewhere. The oath of God, just like the 'oath of Jove' for the Latins, is called that which is made by calling upon the name of God.

Otherwise Varenius: As far as I am concerned, keep the mouth (command) of the King (but in such a way that) as far as the Most High (God) is concerned (you observe) the reason of the oath of God; by which you are bound to God, whom one must obey rather than men.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

EGO OS REGIS OBSERVO) Non observo, sed observa legendum est. In Græco: ςόμα βασιλέως φύλαξον. Sed in Hebræo præcedit אני, quod supplendum ex sequentibus. Ego, scilicet Rex sum, & propterea vos moneo.

ET PRÆCEPTA JURAMENTI DEI) Optime ex Hebræo vertas: maxime propter juramentum Dei על-דבר vel על-דברת est propter, ut Psal. XLV, 5. LXXIX, 9. & ali- bi. Juramentum Dei sicut Latinis jusjurandum Jovis, dicitur id quod sit appellato Dei nomine.

ALiter Varenius: Quod ad me attinet, os (man- datum) Regis observa (sed ita uti) quod ad ex- celsum (Deum) attinet (observes) rationem jura- menti Dei; quo obligatus es Deo, cui magis obe- diendum, quam hominibus.

## 8:3
Verse 3.

DO NOT HASTEN TO DEPART FROM HIS FACE) That is, do not do anything by hasty counsel which might offend him by a nod or displease him.

That phrase 'from his face' pertains to the word 'to be disturbed', not to the word 'to depart': Do not be disturbed from his face, depart. Do not be so bold as to approach the King in a very bad cause. Depart rather.

NOR PERSIST IN AN EVIL WORK) If you have offended him in any matter, do not make the fault more serious by stubbornness.

FOR EVERYTHING THAT HE SHALL HAVE WILLED HE WILL DO) As Aeschylus says: Τραχὺς μόναρχος κ᾽ οὐχ ὑπεύθυνος κρατεῖ. Such were the empires in the East.

The right of absolute dominion is not approved: He had previously advised that the King must be obeyed up to the altar. And here the guilty party is supposed, or one placed in a criminal state against whom the King can justly use his power, Romans 13:4.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

NE FESTINES RECEDERE A FACIE EJUS) Id est, noli properato consilio aliquid agere, quod vel nutu offen- derit sibi displicere.

Illud a facie ejus ad verbum perturbandi, non ad verbum abeundi pertinet: Ne perturberis a facie ejus, abito. Noli tam audaculus esse, ut in pessima causa Regem adeas. Abi potius.

NEQVE PERMANEAS IN OPERE MALO) Si qua re eum offendisti, noli pertinacia culpam facere graviorem.

QVIA OMNE QVOD VOLUERIT FACIET) Ut ait Æschylus: Τραχὺς μόναρχος κ᾽ οὐχ ὑπεύθυνος κρατεῖ. Talia erant in Oriente imperia.

Non probatur jus absoluti Dominii: Antea Regi parendum esse usque ad aram monuerat. Et hic supponitur reus, sive in statu criminali positus adversus quem juste potest Rex sua uti potestate Rom. XIII, 4.

## 8:4
Verse 4.

AND HIS WORD IS FULL OF POWER) Whatever kind of word, even prayers. Plato, Epistle VII: Τὰς δὲ τῶν τυράννων δεήσεις ἴσμεν ὅτι μεμιγμέναι ἀνάγκαις εἰσίν.

Verse 4.

NOR CAN ANYONE SAY, WHY DO YOU DO SO?) He cannot be called to account.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ET SERMO ILLIUS POTESTATE PLENUS EST) Qualiscunque sermo, etiam preces. Plato Epistola VII. Τὰς δὲ τῶν τυράννων δεήσεις ἴσμεν ὅτι μεμιγμέναι ἀνάγκαις εἰσίν.

Vers. 4.

NEC DICERE QVISQVAM POTEST, QVARE ITA FACIS?) Non potest ad rationes vocari.

## 8:5
Verse 5.

WHO KEEPS THE COMMANDMENT, SHALL NOT EXPERIENCE ANY EVIL) It is not only most honorable, but also most safe to follow the edicts and decrees of Kings.

THE HEART OF THE WISE UNDERSTANDS TIME AND JUDGMENT) If anything in a King needs correcting, only the Wise know how and when it ought to be done, such as Nathan was.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

QVI CUSTODIT PRÆCEPTUM, NON EXPERIE- TUR QVICQVAM MALI) Non honestissimum modo, sed & tutissimum est sequi edicta & decreta Regum.

TEMPUS ET RESPONSIONEM COR SAPIENTIS INTELLIGIT) Si quid in Rege corrigendum, id quomodo & quando fieri debeat, norunt soli Sapientes, qualis erat Nathan.

## 8:6
Verse 6.

FOR EVERY BUSINESS THERE IS A TIME AND OPPORTUNITY) καιρὸς difficult to find.

AND THE AFFLICTION OF MAN IS GREAT) Much labor is in finding it: κακώσις Symmachus. But the LXX read דעת instead of רעת and translated it γνῶσις.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

OMNI NEGOTIO TEMPUS EST ET OPPORTU- NITAS) καιρὸς inventu difficilis.

ET MULTA HOMINIS AFFLICTIO) Multus in eo reperiendo labor: κακώσις Symmachus. At LXX. pro רעת legerunt דעת & verterunt γνῶσις.

## 8:7
Verse 7.

BECAUSE HE IS IGNORANT OF THINGS PAST, AND CANNOT KNOW THINGS FUTURE BY ANY MESSAGE) He took that שיהיה in the sense of the past, as tenses are often interchanged among the Hebrews, especially after certain particles. See a similar sentiment above VII, 24.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVIA IGNORAT PRÆTERITA, ET FUTURA NULLO SCIRE POTEST NUNTIO) Sumsit illud שיהיה in significatione præteriti, ut sæpe tempora apud Ebræos commutantur, præsertim post particulas quasdam. Vide similem sententiam supra VII, 24.

## 8:8
Verse 8.

IT IS NOT IN THE POWER OF MAN TO RESTRAIN THE SPIRIT) The wrath of the King, as above VII, 10.

NOR HAS HE POWER IN THE DAY OF DEATH] If the King orders him to be killed, there is no escape, see Prov. XVI, 14. NOR IS HE ALLOWED TO REST WHEN WAR BREAKS OUT] That is, if someone has undertaken to fight a war against the King without a discharge: for that is properly מִשְׁלַחַת. NOR SHALL WICKEDNESS SAVE THE WICKED] רֶשַׁע has various meanings. Here it signifies rebellion: he denies that it will go unpunished even for the victors.

This whole verse is perverted by Grotius, and twisted toward the inevitable anger of the King: whereas it is rather about the inevitable end of life here. No man has power over the spirit to restrain the spirit (the soul now departing, as the Chaldean, Kimchi, Jerome, Borrhaus, Drusius; Mr. Dr. Geier, Mr. Dr. Varenius, and others explain) nor is there power in the day of death (to prolong the day of death) nor is there a discharge in that war (nor can anyone delegate or substitute another in that war, so that he might fight with death in his place, who is introduced as an unconquered tyrant, as Mr. Varenius explains: others, nor a dismissal in this battle, such as is wont to befall captives in battle, or after battle) nor shall wicked conflict (by which, namely, someone struggles against invading death) deliver its master (i.e. nor is it permitted to command death, that it might yield, nor to substitute another in that war, nor to struggle or, as it were, with gathered strength, to repel death at the last: as Mr. Varenius holds, noting from Aben-Ezra that רֶשַׁע brings in a multitude of commotion and conflict, and by the force of the passages from Job XXXIV, 29, I Sam. XIV, 49, Psalm LVIII, 22, this is the primary meaning of that word) or as others, nor shall wickedness (indomitable iniquity) deliver its possessor.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

NON EST IN HOMINIS POTESTATE PROHIBE- RE SPIRITUM) Iram Regis, ut supra VII, 10.

NEC HABET POTESTATEM IN DIE MORTIS ] Si eum Rex occidi jusserit, nullum effugium est, Vide Pov. XVI, 14. NEC SINITVR QVIESCERE INGRVENTE BEL- LO] Id est, si bellum quis contra Regem susceperit pugnan- dum sine missione: id enim proprie מִשְׁלַחַת. NEQVE SALVABIT IMPIETAS IMPIVM] רֶשַׁע varias habet significationes. Hic rebellionem significat: eam negat vel victoribus impunitam fore.

Totus hic versus a Grotio pervertitur, & ad iram Regis inevitabilem detorquetur: quum potius de inevitabili vitæ termino hic agatur. Nullus ho- mo imperium habet in spiritum ad continendum spiri- tum (animam jamjam abiturientem, ut Chald. Kimch. Hieronym. Borrhaus, Drusius; Dn. D. Geierus, Dn. D. Varenius alii explicant) neque est potestas in diem mortis (ad prorogandum diem mor- tis) nec est missio ad illud bellum (nec in illo bello alium delegare, vel surrogare potest aliquis, ut nempe sui loco cum morte confligat, qui ut tyran- nus invictus introducitur, uti Dn. Varenius expli- cat: alii, nec dimissio in hoc prælio, qualis in prælio, vel post prælium captivis solet obtingere) neque improba conflictatio (qua sc. aliquis conctaluctatur invadenti morti) eripiet dominum suum (q. d. nec imperare licet morti, ut succedat, nec in bello illo alium surrogare, nec conctaluctari vel collectis qua- si viribus novissime mortem repellere: ut Dn. Vare- nius habet, notans ex Aben - Ezra רֶשַׁע multitudi- nem commotionis ac conflictationis inferre, & vi locorum ex Job. XXXIV, 29. I. Sam. XIV, 49. Psal. XIIX, 22. hanc primariam esse vocis istius significa- tionem) vel ut alii, neque eruet improbitas (nequitia indomita) possessorem suum.

## 8:9
Verse 9. SOMETIMES MAN RULES OVER MAN TO HIS OWN HURT) Indeed. To the son of Ceres, few Kings descend without slaughter and blood, and tyrants by a dry death. Thales: What is difficult? He said, to see a tyrant growing old. Even if this is absent, yet as Tacitus says, They turn their own crimes and outrages into their own punishment. Looking back at both, Silius: How they would wish they had never shone with proud scepters!

Latin:

Vers. 9. INTERDVM DOMINATVR HOMO HO- MINI IN MALVM SVVM) Quippe. Ad generum Cereris sine cæde & sanguine pauci Descendunt Reges, & sicca morte tyranni. Thales: Τὶ δύσκολον; τὸν παθεαμέν@, γέροντα ἔφη Τύραννον. Vt hoc absit, tamen ut Tacitus ait, Fascinora atque flagitia sua ipfis in supplicium vertunt. Vtrumque respiciens Silius: Quam vellent nunquam sceptris fulsisse superbis?

## 8:10
Verse 10. I SAW THE WICKED BURIED, WHO EVEN WHEN THEY WERE STILL LIVING, WERE IN THE HOLY PLACE, AND WERE PRAISED IN THE CITY AS IF THEY HAD DONE RIGHTEOUS WORKS] Praised, as in the Greek ἐπηνέθησαν: it appears they read וישתבחו, for which we have וישתכחו. I do not disapprove of this reading of the Greeks, so that the sense may be: I saw the wicked buried, who when they walked (that is, lived) had come to the holy place. That is, even then they were worshiped with divine honors, like Augustus, of whom Virgil says: For he shall always be a God to me. And Horace: To you present we grant divine honors, and we place altars to be sworn by through your name. And they were praised in the City in which they had done so. That is, in which they had ruled against justice and equity: of whom the discourse preceded. This also is vanity. That glory born of violent empires is of no value.

Nor is the Hebrew source correctly corrected from the Greek version, nor is the divine worship of the living conveniently injected as if it were accepted at that time. The little word כֵּן denotes 'thus' or 'rightly' in Num. XXVII, 17, II Kings VII, 9, Ps. XC, 12, Ps. CXXVII, 2, whence Mr. Varenius rendered the present passage thus: For indeed I truly saw the wicked (with great pomp of funeral rites) after they had killed, buried, as if they had proceeded from the place of the HOLY (as if they had been the greatest saints) & (see the contrary) had been consigned to oblivion in that very virtue, who had done what is right.

Latin:

Vers. 10. VIDI IMPIOS SEPVLTOS, QVI ETIAM CVM ADHVC VIVERENT, IN LOCO SANCTO ERANT, ET LAVDABANTVR IN CIVITATE QVASI JVSTORVM OPERVM] Laudabantur, ut in Græco ἐπηνέθησαν: apparet eos legisse וישתבחו, pro quo nos habemus וישתכחו. Non improbo hanc Græcorum lectionem, ut sensus sit: Vidi ego impios sepultos, qui cum am- bularent, (id est, viverent) venerant ad locum sanctum. Id est, jam tum divinis honoribus colebantur, ut Augustus, de quo Virgilius: Namque erit ille mihi semper Deus. Et Horatius: Præsenti tibi divinos largimur honores, Iurandasque tuum per nomen ponimus aras. Et laudabantur in Civitate in qua sic fecerant. Id est, in qua contra jus & æquum imperaverant: de qualibus sermo præ- cessit. Etiam hoc vanitas. Illa gloria violentis parta im- periis, nullius est pretii.

Nec recte corrigitur fons Ebræus e versione Græca, neque commode injicitur cultus divinus viventium ceu receptus isto tempore. Vocula כֵּן rectum notat Num. XXVII, 17. II. Reg. VII, 9. Pf. XC, 12. Pf. CXXVII, 2. unde ita Dn. Varenius red- didit locum præsentem: Etenim revera vidi impios (magna parentalium pompa) postquam occiderant, sepultos, ac si ex loco SANCTI processissent (als wä- ren sie gewesen die allergrössesten Heiligen) & (vid. contra) oblivioni traditos fuisse in illa ipsa virtute, qui rectum fecerant.

## 8:11
Verse 11. FOR BECAUSE SENTENCE AGAINST EVIL DEEDS IS NOT EXECUTED SPEEDILY, WITHOUT ANY FEAR THE SONS OF MEN COMMIT EVILS] An excellent admonition, which you may see explained more broadly in Psalm XXXVII and LXXIII. Caesar in his reply to the Helvetians, which is in the first book of the Gallic War, truly said, even against himself: That the immortal gods are accustomed, so that men may grieve more heavily from a change of circumstances, whom they wish to punish for their crime, to grant them sometimes more prosperous things and a longer impunity. Theodectes: Whoever blames the divine for mortal affairs, because it does not pursue unjust deeds immediately, but in time, let him hear the reason. For if punishments were immediate, many through fear and piety would have prayed to God; but with punishment being far off, mortals use their nature. But when they are caught, having been seen as evil, they pay penalties in later times. Sallust the Philosopher: If justice immediately followed those who have sinned, men acting justly through fear would not have virtue. I will add also this from Euripides' Electra: -- let no evildoer, if he runs his first step well, think he has conquered justice, until he reaches the end of the line, and turns the goal of life. Tacitly, however, it is given to be understood, if God tolerates tyrants so patiently, how much more ought those to do so who live under their rule.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ETENIM QVIA NON PROFERTVR CITO CON- TRA MALOS SENTENTIA, ABSQVE TIMORE VLLO FILII HOMINVM PERPETRANT MALA] Egregia admonitio, quam latius explicatam videas Psalm. XXXVII. & LXXIII. Cæsar in responso ad Helvetios, quod est belli Gallici libro 1. vere dixit, etiam adversus semet- ipsum: Consuesse Deos immortales, quo gravius homines ex commutatione rerum doleant, quos pro scelere eorum ulcisci velint, his fecundiores interdum res & diuturniorem impunita- tem concedere. Theodectes: Οςις δὲ θνητῶ μέμφετῶν τὰ θεῖ᾽, ὅτι Ουκ ἐυθὺς, ἀλλὰ τῷ χρόνῳ μετέρχεται Τὰς μὴ δικαίας, πρόφασιν εἰσακουσάτω. Εἰ γὰρ παραυτίκ᾽ ἦσαν αἱ τιμωρίαι, Πολὺς διὰ φόβον, κ̉ δὶ ἐυσέβ' τρόποι Θεὸς ἂν ηὔξατο᾽ τὸν δὲ τιμωρίας Απωθεν ὔσης, τῇ φύσῄ χρῶνται βρότοι. Οταν δὲ φωραθῶσιν, ὀφθέντες κακοί, Τίνεσι ποινὰς ὑσέροισιν ἐν χρόνοις. Salustius Philosophus : Ει τοῖς ἡμαρτηκόσιν ἐυθὺς ἠκολέθει αἱ δίκαι, φόβῳ δικαιοπραγῶντες ἄνθρωποι ἀρετὴν ἐκ ἂν εἶχον. Addam & hoc ex Euripidis Electra : - - ὧδε τις κακέργ@- ὤν Μὴ μοὶ τὸ πρῶτον βῆμ᾽ ἐὰν δράμῃ καλῶς, Νικᾶν δοκείτω την δίκην, πρὶν ἂν τέλ Γραμμῆς ἵκηται, κὶ τέλ@- κάμψῃ βίυ. Tacite autem datur intelligi, si Deus tyrannos tam patienter tolerat, quanto magis id eos debere facere, qui sub eorum vi- vunt imperio.

Vers. 17. ET INTELLEXI QVOD OMNIVM OPERVM DEI NVLLAM POSSIT HOMO INVENIRE RA- TIONEM] Sensus est, non omnium Dei operum ratio- nem homini apparere: ἀνεξιχνίασα αἱ ὁδοὶ ἀυτᾶ. Roma- nor. XI, 33.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

The pursuit of true εὐδαιμονία [happiness] is commended on account of the vanity of the scandal arising from the equal success of the wicked with the righteous in this life, and the end of this life: against which is urged the cheerful use of the good things granted, provided we please God (through faith): since success and a blessed outcome are situated not in our cares and labors, but in divine blessing and grace.

Vers. 1. THAT I MIGHT CURIOUSLY UNDERSTAND] ולבר for which the Greeks read: ולב ראה: את־כל־זה: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο σύμπαν εἶδε τοῦτο. THE JUST AND THE WISE AND THEIR WORKS ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD] He attacks another opinion, which attributes all things to fate. Those things in which man can do nothing are said by the Hebrews to be in the hand of God. Therefore, this opinion holds that justice, and wisdom, and all actions are fated. The Chaldean explains כלא במזליא תלי, all things depend on fate, [and] מן שמיא אתגזר: It is ordained from heaven.

Vers. same. AND YET MAN KNOWS NOT WHETHER HE BE WORTHY OF LOVE OR HATRED, BUT ALL THINGS ARE KEPT UNCERTAIN FOR THE FUTURE] In the Hebrew: Even love, even hatred man knows not, all things are before their faces, supply, of men. There is a frequent change of number where genera are discussed. This is what it means: concerning any matter that occurs to a man, the man does not know whether it proceeds from the love of God toward him, or from hatred.

The Vulgate is correctly emended, as we noted in Critic. Sacr. p. 614, but in the explanation, as far as it appears, Grotius follows the Papists, who defend the uncertainty of grace from this passage. Just as Bellarmine lib. III. de Sanctif. c. IV., Tirinus & Menochius in h. l. attempt to prove by this testimony that the grace of God is uncertain in this life. But by that reasoning, it will not be known even to the impious that they are worthy of hatred: which is absurd and contrary to their own conscience, by which they are convicted; therefore Salmero in I. Cor. XII. Disp. 4. writes thus: This passage by no means proves what some take from it, that a man does not know the love of God toward himself, because it follows in the text: He does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred. But the impious, because of their greatest crimes, know that they are most worthy of the hatred of God. Therefore these things are not to be taken simply, but with respect to external events, as is especially apparent from the following verse; namely, that from them a judgment cannot be drawn as to whether one is under grace, just as from external events it is not permitted to know whether the spirit of man ascends upward, or whether he is immortal or not, Eccl. III, 3, which nevertheless is established from elsewhere. Thus Piscator & the Belgian interpreters, who think that the things which follow were added with this intent, interpreting thus: Man does not know either the love or the hatred of God (from) any thing (which is) before their face. Which others render thus: This whole thing, or all those things (indiscriminately) before their face, that is, of the just as well as the impious, so that they cannot, because they see similar things happen to them equally, determine anything certain about the love or hatred of God from such events. Which opinion Tirinus also delivers at verse 2. Because UNIVERSAL THINGS HAPPEN EQUALLY TO THE JUST AND THE IMPIOUS, I think that nothing certain can be gathered from divine benefits and other events, whether prosperous or adverse, as they are common to the unjust as well as the just. Thus Cardinal Cajetan also interprets the present passage: Solomon signifies that from external things we cannot discern good or evil. Nor is it necessary that these words be explained concerning the love or hatred of God toward ourselves, because it cannot be certain to a man concerning that: whether he has God as gracious or angry? since they can be taken concerning others, namely, that it cannot be certain to us from such external things whether they are in grace with God or not? because those external things are common to the pious and the impious, Psal. LXXIII, 15. Thus Osiander & the Vinarienses. And also Dn. D. Franz. tract. de interpret. script. oracul. V. Whether anyone is worthy of the benefits with which each one is heaped by God, he himself will judge most holily, who knows his own heart, whether upright or hypocritical, most exactly; therefore we truly do not know the love or hatred of those things WHICH ARE AROUND US, which last words of the oracle confirm this sense of it. Thus therefore he renders these: Also love, also hatred, man does not know, who is before their faces. Johannes Ferus among the Papists proves this explanation in h. l. You cannot judge from the face of a man whether he is elect or not, neither from external prosperity, nor even from adversity. Ludovicus de Dieu in his animadversions on this passage delivers the same sense, but observes a different punctuation of the text: Thus distinguishing and translating because of the accent Reviah: The just and the wise, and their works are in the hand of God, also love, also hatred: men do not know any of those things which are before them. He says therefore (the words are Dieu's) that love and hatred are in the hand of God, just as the just and their works are, and because God loves whom He wills, and hates whom He wills (which smacks of the absolute decree of Calvin), men do not know any of those things which are before them. They see before them those to whom it is well, they see those to whom it is ill, but they do not know which of them are hateful to God, which are dear. The sense is most plain, and has no scruple. This is he, whom Dn. D. Varenius refutes from the accents. Others explain it concerning the love or hatred of men, so that the sense may be: This is altogether to be pitied, that even the wisest of all do not sufficiently know men, whether they ought to love them and receive them into friendship as pious, or rather hate them as impious. Which opinion the blessed Meisner judges to be conformable to the text and the analogy of faith, Dec. II. Anthrop. Disp. IIX. Q. IV. th. X. And Dn. Varenius embraces it according to the mind of the blessed Luther in the German version, Varenius, yet rendering the last words otherwise, namely in this way: ALL THOSE THINGS (are) BEFORE THEM (i.e., ELOHIM or the divine persons, from the preceding clause). And that explanation concerning the knowledge of the grace or hatred of another, whether this one or that one is loved or rather held in hatred by God, is also proven from the Pontificians by Benedictus Arias Montanus in his Metrical paraphrase, as also by the Jesuit Mariana in his Elegiac paraphrase. But whichever of these interpretations is assumed, the proof of Bellarmine and other Jesuits falls into the sponge. Whom Mercer, the Paris Professor, rightly and deservedly noted here: We can refer love and hatred to God; No one knows either the love of God or His hatred, either in himself or in others, where one must beware lest with the Vulgate interpreter you either err, or take from thence an occasion of erring with the Sophists. Indeed I do not think that the Vulgate interpreter, because he translated this passage thus, man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, understood it in such a way that he wished Solomon to mean, as the Theologasters believe, that one must doubt concerning the love of God toward us, nor that we ought to be certain in our consciences, since this is openly against many passages of Scripture, and notably against that head of our faith, by which we believe the remission of sins, and that the Spirit of the Lord is a witness to our spirit that we are the children of God, and that with confidence we cry Abba Father, and similar things in Paul. Although the interpreter could have omitted the word of worthiness, which is none in us toward God: if however you understand it of external events, as I think he understood it, it will be true that from those external things no one can judge concerning himself or another, whether he is loved by God or held in hatred: and that man as man is ignorant of the cause of both. Because just as the wicked, so also good men suffer calamities: and as the good fare prosperously, so also the wicked: whence it is not to be judged immediately, that whom you see suffering, he is good or evil: nor on the contrary, where you see all things succeeding prosperously for him, is one to be judged from the outcome of events. You may therefore clearly understand what is said here, which becomes most plain in the following verse. Thus Mercerus. Alphonsus de Castro, however much in earlier editions of lib. VII. advers. hæres. tit. Gratias he attributed this passage to the uncertainty of grace, in the newest one, however, being better informed, he felt otherwise, and acceded to our explanation: No one can know anything of these (whether he is elect or not) from the consideration of external things, whether they be prosperous or adverse, because all these things can happen to the just just as well as to the unjust: Therefore, having rejected that testimony because it is doubtful and there is no agreement among all concerning its meaning, it is necessary that we take testimonies from elsewhere. Although indeed we cannot certainly conclude divine grace from external events of this kind, yet it is by no means to be concluded with Tirinus, that we obtain that certainty much less from elsewhere, because other and most certain proofs are available: upon which our faith relies, the promises of the divine word, the sealing of the same through the Sacraments, the sense of faith in our hearts, the internal attestation of the Holy Spirit, concerning which elsewhere. Rightly therefore regarding this passage, Bernard, Sermon V on the Dedication of the Church: 'Who knows; if he is worthy of love or hatred.' Here now it is clearly necessary for faith to assist us; here it is necessary for truth to come to our aid, so that what lies hidden from us in the heart of the Father may be revealed to us through His Spirit, and His Spirit, testifying, may persuade our spirit that we are children of God.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

Commendatur studium vere ἐυδαιμονίας ob vanitatem scandali ex improborum pa- rili cum probis in hac vita successu, & hu- jus vitæ exitu: adversus quod suadetur hilaris bonorum concessorum usus, cum Deo (per fidem) placemus: siquidem successus & eventus beatus non in nostris curis & laboribus, sed divina benedictione, & gratia situs sit.

Vers. 1. VT CVRIOSE INTELLIGEREM] ולבר pro quo Græci legerunt: ולב ראה: את־כל־זה: καὶ διὰ μυ σύμπαν εἶδε τῦτο. SVNT JVSTI ATQVE SAPIENTES ET OPERA EORVM IN MANV DEI] Aliam opinionem aggreditur, quæ fato omnia tribuit. In manu Dei esse dicuntur He- bræis illa in quæ homo nihil potest. Vult ergo hæc opinio & justitiam, & sapientiam, & actiones omnes esse fatales. Chaldæus כלא במזליא תלי omnia a fato pendent, ex- plicat, מן שמיא אתגזר : Cœlitus constitutum est.

Vers. eod. ET TAMEN NESCIT HOMO VTRVM AMORE AN ODIO DIGNVS SIT, SED OMNIA IN FVTV- RVM SERVANTVR INCERTA] In Hebræo: Etiam amorem, etiam odium nescit homo, omnia ad facies eorum, supple, hominum. Est mutatio numeri frequens, ubi de generibus agitur. Hoc vult: de quavis re, quæ ho- mini occurrit, nescit homo, an ea proveniat ex amore Dei in se, an ex odio.

Vulgata rectè emendatur, ut in Critic. Sacr. p. 614. notavimus, in explicatione autem quantum apparet, sequitur Grotius Papistas incertitudinem gratiæ, ex hoc loco propugnantes. Quemadmodum Bellarminus lib. III. de Sanctif. c. IV. Tirinus & Menochius in h. l. probare hoc testimonio conantur, gratiam Dei in hac vita incertam esse. At ea ratione ne impiis quidem notum erit, se odio dignos esse: quod absonum & conscientiæ ipsorum, a qua convincuntur, contrarium; ideo Salmero in I. Cor. XII. Disp. 4. ita scribit: Hic locus nequaquam probat, quod aliqui inde accipiunt, hominem nescire amorem Dei erga se, quia sequitur in textu: Nescit an amore vel odio dignus sit. At impii propter maxima sua scelera norunt, se maxime dignos esse odio Dei. Proinde non simpliciter hæc accipienda, sed respectu externorum eventuum, quemadmodum e versu sequente imprimis apparet; quod nempe ex iis non possit depromi judicium, an sit sub gratia, perinde ut ex eventibus externis non licet cognoscere, an Spiritus hominis ascendat sursum, vel immortalis sit nec ne Eccl. III, 3. quod tamen aliunde constat. Ita Piscator & Belgæ interpp. qui ea quæ sequuntur hac mente addita putant, sic interpretantes: Tam amorem quam odium Dei non cognoscit homo (ex) ulla re (quæ) ante faciem ipsorum. Quæ alii sic reddunt: Universum hoc, vel omnia illa (promiscue) ante faciem ipsorum, puta, tam justorum, quam impiorum, ut non possint, quia vident similia ipsis ex æquo evenire, certi quid de amore vel odio Dei ex ejusmodi eventibus statuere. Quam sententiam etiam Tirinus tradit ad vers. 2. Eo quod UNIVERSA ÆQVE EVENIANT JUSTO ET IMPIO ex beneficiis divinis aliisque eventibus seu prosperis seu adversis nihil certi colligi putem, utpote quæ tam injustis quam justis communia sunt. Sic interpretatur quoque præsentem locum Cardinalis Cajetanus: Significat Salomon ex rebus externis nos non posse discernere bonum aut malum. Neque necessum est, ut explicentur hæc verba de amore vel odio Dei adversus nos ipsos, quod homini de eo constare nequeat: num Deum gratiosum habeat, vel iratum? quum accipi possint de aliis, quod nempe id nobis ex ejusmodi externis constare nequeat, num illi in gratia sint apud Deum, nec ne? quia externa illa piis & impiis communia sunt Psal. LXXIII, 15. Ita Osiander & Vinarienses. Nec non Dn. D. Franz. tract. de interpret. script. oracul. V. An dignus sit aliquis beneficiis, quibus cumulatur a Deo quilibet unus ipse, quam sanctissime judicabit, qui vel rectum vel hypocriticum suum cor novit exactissime, vere igitur nescimus amorem an odium eorum, QUÆ CIRCA NOS SUNT, quæ verba ultima oraculi hunc sensum illius confirmant. Sic ergo reddit hæc: Etiam amorem, etiam odium non novit hominum, qui ad facies eorum. Probat hanc explicationem e Papistis Johannes Ferus in h. l. Non potes ex facie hominis judicare, an electus sit, vel non, nec ex prosperitate externa, nec etiam ex adversitate. Ludovicus de Dieu animadvers. in h. l. sensum eundem tradit, sed aliam textus distinctionem observat: Sic propter accentum Reviah distinguens & vertens: Justi & sapientes, & opera eorum in manu Dei sunt, etiam amor, etiam odium: non norunt homines quicquam eorum, quæ ante se sunt. Dicit ergo (verba Dieu sunt) amorem & odium in manu Dei esse, sicut justos, & opera eorum, & quia Deus amat, quos vult, & odit, quos vult (quod redolet absolutum Calvini decretum) non nosse homines quicquam eorum quæ ante se sunt. Vident ante se, quibus bene est, vident, quibus male est, sed non norunt, quinam ex ipsis Deo exosi, qui- nam chari sint. Planissimus sensus est, nec quicquam scrupuli habet. Hæc ille, quem ex accentibus refu- tat Dn. D. Varenius. Alii de amore vel odio homi- num explicant, ut sensus sit: Hoc omnino miserandum est, quod etiam sapientissimi quique non satis cogno- scunt homines, utrum istos debeant diligere, & in amicitiam recipere tanquam pios, an vero odisse tan- quam impios. Quam sententiam textui & analo- giæ fidei conformem judicat B. Meisnerus Dec. II. Anthrop. Disp. IIX. Q. IV. th. X. Et amplectitur juxta B. Lutheri mentem in versione German. Dn. Varenius, ultima tamen verba aliter reddens, ni- mirum hoc modo: UNIVERSA ILLA (sunt) CORAM ILLIS (ELOHIM sc. seu personis di- vinis, e commate præcedente.) Atque ista explica- tio de cognitione gratiæ vel odii alterius, utrum hic vel ille diligatur, an vero odio habeatur a Deo, etiam probatur e Pontificiis Benedicto Ariæmont. in paraphras. Metric. ut & Mariana Jesuitæ in Ele- giaca paraphrasi. Quæcunque autem ex hisce in- terpretationibus assumatur, in spongiam incum- bit Bellarmini & aliorum Jesuitarum probatio. Quos recte & ex merito hic notavit Mercerus Pa- risiensis Professor: Possumus amorem & odium ad Deum referre; Nec amorem Dei, nec odium scit quisquam, vel in se vel in aliis, ubi cavendum ne cum Vulgato interprete vel erres, vel inde errandi cum Sophistis occasionem sumas. Equidem non existi- mo vulgatum interpretem, quod ita hunc locum ver- tit, nescit homo amorene an odio dignus sit, ita in- tellexisse, ut voluerit Salomon, quod Theologastri credunt, dubitandum esse de Dei amore in nos, nec debere nos in conscientiis nostris certos esse, cum hoc aperte sit contra multa Scripturæ loca, & notan- ter contra illud fidei nostræ caput, quo credimus pecca- torum remissionem, & Spiritum Domini testem esse Spiritui nostro, quod simus filii Dei, & quod cum fi- ducia clamamus Abba Pater, & similia apud Pau- lum. Quanquam nomen dignitatis omittere poterat interpres, quæ nulla est in nobis erga Deum: si tamen de externis eventis intelligas, ut intellexisse eum pu- ro, verum erit, ex istis externis judicare quenquam non posse de se vel alio, an a Deo ametur, an odio ha- beatur: & utriusque causam hominem ut homo est ignorare. Quia ut mali, sic & boniviri calamitates patiuntur: & ut boni prospere habent, sic & mali: un- de non statim, ut quem pati vides, judicandum eum bonum esse vel malum: nec contra, ubi prospere ei vi- des omnia succedere, ex eventu rerum judicandum non est. Sane ergo intelligas quæ hic dicuntur, quæ se- quenti versiculo fiunt planissima. Hæc Mercerus. Alphonsus de Castro utut in prioribus editionibus lib. VII. advers. hæres. tit. Gratias hunc locum pro incertitudine gratiæ attribuit, in novissima tamen rectius informatus secus sensit, & nostræ explica- tioni accessit: Nemo aliquid horum (sitne electus, an- non?) scire potest ex consideratione rerum externa- rum, sive prospera sint, sive adversa, quia hæc omnia possunt justo perinde ac injusto contingere: Rejecto er- go illo testimonio propterea quod dubium est & non convenit inter omnes de sensu illius, oportet aliunde capiamus testimonia. Quanquam vero ex eventibus ejusmodi externis gratiam divinam certo conclu- dere nequeamus, neutiquam tamen cum Tirino concludendum, quod multo minus aliunde eam cer- titudinem obtineamus, quia suppetunt alia, eaque certissima documenta: quibus fides nostra nititur, promissiones verbi divini, obsignatio earundem per Sacramenta, sensus fidei in cordibus nostris at- testatio Spiritus S. interna, de quibus alias. Recte ergo ad hunc locum Bernhardus serm. V. de De- dic. Eccl. Quis scit; si est dignus amore vel odio. Hic jam plane fidem nobis subvenire necesse est, hic opor- tet succurrere veritatem, ut quod de nobis latet in cor- de Patris, nobis per Spiritum ipsius reveletur, & Spi- ritus ejus testificans persuadeat Spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei sumus.

## 9:2
Verse 2.

BECAUSE ALL THINGS HAPPEN ALIKE TO THE JUST AND THE WICKED] Both good and bad things happen to both, death to all: ---- 'One night awaits us all, and the path of death must be trodden once,' says Horace: TO HIM WHO SACRIFICES, AND TO HIM WHO DESPISES SACRIFICES] ---- 'nor will piety bring delay to wrinkles and impending old age, and to indomitable death: Not if you should appease tearless Pluto with three hundred bulls every day, my friend, as they pass,' as the same Horace says, who also says elsewhere: 'neither eloquence nor piety will restore you.' AS THE PERJURER] In the Hebrew: swearing, namely not by design, but rashly. SO ALSO HE WHO FEARS AN OATH] In the Hebrew: he who fears an oath; thus also the Greeks call a good man εὔορκον.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

EO QVOD VNIVERSA ÆQVE EVENIANT JV- STO ET IMPIO] Tam bona quam mala utrisque eveni- unt, mors omnibus: - - - - Omnes una manet nox Et calcanda semel via leti, Ait Horatius: IMMOLANTI VICTIMAS, ET SACRIFICIA CON- TEMNENTI] - - - nec pietas moram Rugis & instanti senectæ Afferet, indomitæque morti: Non si trecenis, quotquot eunt dies, Amice, places illacrimabilem Plutona tauris. Vt idem Horatius, qui & alibi: - - - non te facundia, non te Restituet pietas. VT PERJVRVS) In Hebræo: jurans, nempe non con- silio, sed temere. ITA ET ILLE QVI VERVM DEIERAT) In He- bræo: qui juramentum timet; sic & Græci virum bonum vo- cant εὔορκον.

## 9:3
Verse 3.

AND AFTER THESE THINGS THEY ARE LED TO THE UNDERWORLD] In the Hebrew: and after this to the dead: supply, one must go. Compare Ezek. 32:30 and Isaiah 14:10.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ET POST HÆC AD INFEROS DEDVCENTVR] In Hebræo: & post hoc ad mortuos: supple, eundum est. Confer Ezech. XXXII, 30. & Esaiam XIV, 10.

## 9:4
Verse 4.

THERE IS NO ONE WHO LIVES FOREVER, AND WHO HAS CONFIDENCE IN THIS MATTER] In the Hebrew: כי מי אשר יבחר אל־כל־החיים יש בטחון, but the Hebrews advise us that for יבחר we should write יחבר. Whoever is joined to the living, there is hope for him; namely, that his affairs can be changed for the better. Mr. Dr. Geier taught in this passage that there is no necessity for this change: which, however, he simultaneously showed does not hinder the meaning. A LIVING DOG IS BETTER THAN A DEAD LION] Namely, as Euripides says: Πανταχῆ ζῆν ἡδὺ μᾶλλον ἢ θανεῖν τοῖς σώφροσι. This sentiment conflicts with the other one we had above: but that is not surprising, since, as we said above, everything that is accustomed to come into men's minds is heaped up here. There is no contradiction here, whether you take this from the sense of the Epicureans or whether it was said from the mind of the Holy Scriptures: for a living person can still be of use, even if he is more base, than a dead one, however noble he may otherwise be.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

NEMO EST QVI SEMPER VIVAT, ET QVI HVJVS REI HABEAT FIDVCIAM) In Hebræo: כי מי אשר יבחר אל־כל־החיים יש בטחון, sed monent nos Hebræi pro יבחר refcribendum יחבר Quis- quis sociatur viventibus de eo spes est; nempe posse res ejus in melius mutari. Nullam esse mutationis hujus necessitatem Dn. D. Geier, in h. l. docuit: quam tamen non obesse sensui simul ostendit. MELIOR EST CANIS VIVVS LEONE MORTVO] Nempe, ut ait Euripides: Πανταχῆ ζῆν ἡδὺ μᾶλλον ἢ θανεῖν τοῖς σώφροσι. Hæc sententia pugnat cum altera quam supra habuimus: sed non mirum id, cum, ut supra diximus, cumulentur huc omnia, quæ hominibus in mentem venire solent. Nulla hic ἀντιλογία, sive ex sensu Epicureorum hoc accipias sive e mente S. S. dictum sit: vivus enim adhuc usui esse potest, etsi vilior sit, præ mor- tuo, utut alias nobiliori.

## 9:7
Verse 7.

FOR GOD IS PLEASED WITH YOUR WORKS] You would translate more correctly: for God favors your labors: namely, when He has so prospered them that everything which delights life is abundantly available to you.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

QVIA DEO PLACENT OPERA TVA] Rectius verteris: quia Deus favet laboribus tuis: nempe cum eos ita prosperavit, ut cuncta, quæ vitam delectant, abunde tibi suppetant.

## 9:8
LET OIL NOT BE LACKING FROM YOUR HEAD] Horace: 'Balm pressed upon your hair.' Balaninum oil is the most ancient of ointments according to Pliny 13.1; hence not only here, but also in Cant. 1:1, שמן, that is, oil for ointment, and balsam is בעל שמן, prince of oils, that is, of ointments.
