NOR IS THE RACE TO THE SWIFT] This is what Homer says: Κιχάνη δὲ βραδὺς ὠκύν. NOR THE BATTLE TO THE STRONG) That is, victory. Those who have more virtue do not always win. There is a certain gamble even in wars.

## 9:13
CHAPTER IX. THE LAST PART verse 13. et seqq.

Solomon now proceeds further, to explain specifically upon what the happiness of the Political state depends, namely upon the wisdom of the Ruler, and the prudent counsels of ministers, more than upon fortitude.

Verse 13.

I HAVE ALSO SEEN THIS WISDOM UNDER THE SUN] Political: for he now begins to treat of it. And this is that in which Solomon excelled I Kings 3, 9. 12.

Latin:

CAPITIS IX. PARS VLTIMA vers. 13. seqq.

Progreditur jam Salomo ulterius, ut speciatim exponat, unde status Politici felicitas dependeat, a sapientia nempe Rectoris, & consiliis prudentibus ministrorum magis, quam a fortitudine.

Vers. 13.

HANC QVOQVE SVB SOLE VIDI SAPIENTIAM] Politicam: de ea enim nunc agere incipit. Et hæc est illa qua excelluit Salomo I. Reg. III, 9. 12.

Verse 15.

A POOR AND WISE MAN, AND HE DELIVERED THE CITY BY HIS WISDOM] As that woman did the city of Abel, II Sam. XX, 22.

Vers. 17.

THE WORDS OF THE WISE ARE HEARD IN SILENCE MORE THAN THE CRY OF A PRINCE AMONG FOOLS] In the Hebrew: The submissive words of the wise are to be heard rather than the clamor of a ruler among fools. That is, of some δημαγωγῶ, a turbulent tribune, as Tacitus speaks. See Prov. XXIX, 8. Job XXX, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

VERBA SAPIENTVM AVDIVNTVR IN SILENTIO PLVS QVAM CLAMOR PRINCIPIS INTER STVLTOS] In Hebræo: Verba submissa sapientum audienda potius, quam clamor dominantis inter stultos. Id est, δημαγωγῶ alicujus, turbulenti tribuni, ut Tacitus loquitur. Vide Prov. XXIX, 8. Job. XXX, 8.

## 9:18
Vers. 18.

WISDOM IS BETTER THAN WEAPONS OF WAR) We have had this sense above at VII, 20. Aristotle also treats the same in Politics VII, 13 and 14. Cicero, De Officiis, book 1. But since most people think that military affairs are greater than civil ones, this opinion must be diminished. Where also see what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

MELIOR EST SAPIENTIA QVAM ARMA BELLICA) Sensum hunc & supra habuimus VII, 20. Tractat eundem & Aristoteles Politicorum VII, 13. & 14. Cicero de officiis lib. 1. Sed cum plerique arbitrentur res bellicas majores esse quam urbanas, minuenda est hæc opinio. Vbi & quæ sequuntur vide.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X.

Solomon complains of an evil quite frequent in politics, that the wicked rule, whose end however is unhappy, and that those who are garrulous and foolish are in councils, whose end is destruction: whence public calamity arises when the ruler is a boy: but public happiness, when a noble King rules. Yet one must by no means curse them.

Vers. 1.

DEAD FLIES SPOIL THE SWEETNESS OF THE OINTMENT: WISDOM AND GLORY ARE MORE PRECIOUS, A LITTLE AND FOR A TIME FOLLY] You may translate it correctly thus: As dead flies make the perfumer's ointment stink and putrefy, so does a little folly [outweigh] one who is excellent in wisdom and honor. Those who care for their reputation must take care not to sin even in the slightest.

Latin:

CAPUT X.

Queritur Salomo de malo in Politia admodum frequenti, quod imperent impii, quorum tamen exitus infelix est, quodque a consiliis sint garruli, & stolidi, quorum finis est pernities: unde calamitas publica cum Regens puer est: publica vero felicitas, cum Rex generosus imperat. Illi tamen minime maledicendum.

Vers. 1.

MVSCÆ MORIENTES PERDVNT SVAVITATEM VNGVENTI: PRETIOSIOR EST SAPIENTIA ET GLORIA, PARVA ET AD TEMPVS STVLTITIA] Sic recte vertas: Sicut muscæ immortuæ putere faciunt & fœtere unguentum seplasia, ita egregium sapientia & honore, modicum stoliditatis. Cavendum est iis, qui famæ suæ curam habent, nequid vel minimum peccent.

## 10:2
Vers. 2.

THE HEART OF THE WISE IS AT HIS RIGHT HAND, AND THE HEART OF THE FOOL AT HIS LEFT] The right is the way of virtue, the left the way of vices, as in the letter of Pythagoras. This appears by comparing the passages Deut. I, 29 and Jonah IV, at the end.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

COR SAPIENTIS IN DEXTERA EJVS, ET COR STVLTI IN SINISTRA ILLIVS] Dextera est via virtutis, sinistra via vitiorum, ut in litera Pythagoræ. Apparet id collatis locis Deut. I, 29. & Jonæ IV. in fine.

## 10:3
Vers. 3.

BUT ALSO THE FOOL WALKING IN THE WAY, SINCE HE HIMSELF IS SENSELESS, HE DEEMS ALL MEN FOOLS] In the Hebrew: Even when the fool walks along the ways, his heart is absent, and he says to everyone, behold a fool: that is: He confesses his disease by his countenance and his gait.

IF THE SPIRITS HAVING POWER

ASCENDENT SVPER TE] If you should be in great favor with the King. LOCVM TVVM NE DIMISERIS] Maintain your former modesty. Propertius to Maecenas: Maecenas, knight of Etruscan blood of Kings, who desire to be within your own fortune.

Verse of the same.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SED ET IN VIA STVLTVS AMBVLANS, CVM IPSE INSIPIENS SIT, OMNES STVLTOS ÆSTIMAT] In Hebræo: Etiam cum per vias incedit stultus cor ei abest, dicitque omnibus en stultum: id est: Vultu morbum, incessuque fatetur.

SI SPIRITVS POTESTATEM HABENTES

ASCENDENT SVPER TE] Si apud Regem in magna fueris gratia. LOCVM TVVM NE DIMISERIS] Serva priorem mo- deftiam. Propertius ad Mæcenatem: Mæcenas eques Hetrusco de sanguine Regum Intra fortunam qui cupis esse tuam.

Vers. eod.

## 10:4
QVIA CVRATIO FACIT CESSARE PECCATA MAXIMA] מרפא is indeed a healing: But in this book and in Proverbs it is frequent that א is put for ה. Thus it will signify here leisure or private life, which is less exposed to the occasions of sinning.

Mercerus takes it in a clearly contrary sense, that one should not cease from duty, because such remission leaves in a man and produces great sins. Although these do not agree with the words or the institution, Grotius's explanation is nevertheless no better. For there appears no continuity in the same: If the spirit of him who has power should ascend over you: If you should be in great favor with the King, do not leave your place, that is, maintain your former modesty: Because leisure or private life is less exposed to the occasions of sinning: What coherence is there here? Nor does the explanation agree well with the phrase, by which the spirit ascending על פני over you is explained as grace, since to ascend עליון is to proceed against someone in a hostile manner, even though I am not unaware that Aben-Ezra explains it thus: If it should happen to you to be raised to a trace of honor, do not therefore leave your accustomed modesty and humility of mind, etc. Which sense a certain Hebrew had also handed down to Jerome, but he accepted the reason added concerning the remission from duty and labor, as it is explained by Mercerus: The Hebrew in this place, says Jerome, suspected I know not what: If you should receive any dignity in the world, and be ordained a greater man among the people, do not leave your former works and do not begin to forget your ancient virtues, and not to have your former labor: Because the remedy for your sins is born from good conversation, and not from swelling and superfluous dignity. Jerome, however, interprets it thus: The scripture now signifies the prince of this world and the ruler of these darknesses, and the one working in the children of disobedience, whom the Apostle also mentions. But if he should ascend into our heart, and the mind should receive the wound of an evil thought, we ought not to give place voluntarily, but to fight against the worst thought, and be freed from the greatest sin: lest, namely, we complete the thought with an act, because it is one thing to sin in thought, another in act. But that interpretation is a little more alien. B. Luther renders the sense most simply in the German version, which flows thus from the sources: If the spirit (wrath) of the ruler should ascend against you, do not desert your place, (do not allow yourself to be moved from a tranquil state of mind; Bleibe bey dir selbst, halte still, as B. Luther has in his Commentary on this place, or even from your station. Compare Syr. X, 32. Let the Vinarie Paraphrasts also be seen) for gentleness or remission (from the heat of the passions) makes many sins rest, (both on the part of the offended and on the part of the offender) Verhören und lassen gehen, das sichs selbst stillet, ist grosse Kunst und Tugend, has the marginal gloss of B. Luther. Compare Osiander's Paraphrase. If you resist, says B. Luther in his Commentary on this place, Tom. III. Jen. Lat. f. 274. and you do not wish your counsel to be despised, you will only irritate the hornets, and kick against the goad, because a great part of wisdom is to dissimulate or to yield. For it suppresses the greatest evils which, by thus resting, that is, by yielding, are lulled to sleep, and at length subside by themselves, which otherwise would excite great commotions if you were to continue to oppose yourself. Thus the Romans boast of their Fabius, that by delaying he broke Hannibal. Thus our Frederick the Saxon suppressed the tumultuating Erfurt citizens by silence, and took vengeance. Thus also Virgil: Every fortune is to be overcome by enduring. For these maxims are drawn from the middle of human experience. These are Megalander's words.

Latin:

QVIA CVRATIO FACIT CESSARE PECCATA MAXIMA] Est quidem מרפא curatio: Sed in hoc libro & Proverbiorum frequens est ut א pro ה ponatur. Ita signi- ficabit hic otium sive vitam privatam, quæ minus obnoxia est peccandi occafionibus.

Contrario plane sensu accipit Mercerus, non cessandum ab officio, quia talis remissio relinquit in homine & parit magna peccata. Quæ quamvis non congruunt sive verbis, sive instituto, Grotii tamen explicatio haud melior est. Nam neque ulla appa- ret in eodem συνέχεια: Si Spiritus potestatem haben- tis ascenderit super te: Si apud Regem in magna fue- ris gratia, locum tuum ne dimiseris, id est, serva prio- rem modestiam: Quia otium sive vita privata minus obnoxia peccandi occasionibus: Quæ hic cohæren- tia? Neque phrasi explicatio admodum congruit, qua Spiritus adscendens על פני super te de gratia expo- nitur, cum afcendere עליון sit contra aliquem hostili- ter prodire, etsi non nefciam, quod ita Aben - Ezra explicet: Si te contigerit in vestigium honoris evehi, ne ideo solitam modestam & animi dimissionem re- linque &c. Quem sensum etiam Ebræus quidam Hieronymo tradiderat, sed rationem adjunctam de remissione ab officio & labore accepit, ut a Mercero explicatur: Hebræus in hoc loco, inquit Hieronymus, tale nescio quid suspicatus est: Si ali- quam in mundo acceperis dignitatem, & ordinatus fueris major in populis, noli relinquere priora opera tua & antiquarum virtutum ne incipias oblivisci, laboremque pristinum non habere: Quia peccatorum tuorum remedium ex conversatione bona nascitur, & non ex tumenti & superflua dignitate. Hieronymus vero ita interpretatur: Principem mundi istius & rectorem tenebrarum harum, & operantem in filiis diffidentiæ, cujus & Apostolus meminit, nunc scriptu- ra significat. Quod si in cor nostrum ascenderit, & animus male cogitationis vulnus acceperit, non debe- mus locum ultro tribuere, sed pugnare contra cogita- tionem pessimam, & liberari a peccato maximo: ne sc. cogitationem opere compleamus, quia aliud est cogi- tatione, aliud opere peccare. Sed ea interpretatio paulo alienior. Sensum simplicissime reddit B. Lu- therus in versione Germanica, qui ita e fontibus fluit: Si Spiritus (ira) dominantis adscenderit contra te, locum tuum ne deferito, (ne patiaris te dimoveri a tranquillo mentis statu; Bleibe bey dir selbst, halte still, ut B. Lutherus habet in Comment. ad h. l. vel etiam a statione tua. Conf. Syr. X, 32. Videantur & Vinarienses Paraphrastæ) nam lenitas vel remissio (ab æstu affectuum) quiescere facit peccata multa, (tum penes offensum, tum penes offendentem) Verhören und lassen gehen, das sichs selbst stillet, ist grosse Kunst und Tugend, habet glossa marginalis B. Lutheri. Conf. Ofiandri Paraphrasis. Si resistes, inquit B. Lutherus in Comment. ad h. l. Tom. III. Jen. Lat. f. 274. & nolis contemni consilium tuum, ir- ritabis tantum crabrones, & contra stimulum calci- tras, quia magna sapientia pars est dissimulare seu cedere. Compefcit enim maxima mala quæ sic quie- scendo, id est, cedendo, sopiuntur, & tandem per se- ipsa consilescunt, quæ alioqui excitarent magnos mo- tus, si pergeres te contra opponere. Sic gloriantur Ro- mani de suo Fabio, quod cunctando fregerit Hanni- balem. Sic noster Fridericus Saxo Effordianos tu- multuantes silendo compefcuit, & ultus est. Sic quo- que Virgilius: Superanda omnis fortuna ferendo est. Sunt enim hæ sententiæ ex media rerum humanarum experientia depromtæ. Hæc Megalander.

## 10:6
Verse 6.

POSITVM STVLTVM IN DIGNITATE SVBLIMI, ET DIVITES SEDERE DEORSVM] Those who excel either in wisdom, or nobility, or wealth are suspected by many Kings. Another's virtue is fearful to them, as Sallust says. Therefore they drive away the Professors of Wisdom, and drive all good arts into exile. They have a sinister interpretation toward the eminent, and there is no less danger from great fame than from bad. Nobility and wealth are a crime: all of which Tacitus has. An example in Rehoboam.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

POSITVM STVLTVM IN DIGNITATE SVBLI- MI, ET DIVITES SEDERE DEORSVM] Regibus multis suspecti qui excellunt sive sapientia, sive nobilitate, aut opibus. Aliena illis virtus formidolofa est, ut ait Sallu- stius. Pellunt ergo Sapientiæ Professores, & omnes bonas artes in exsilium agunt. Sinistra illis erga eminentes inter- pretatio, nec minus periculum ex magna fama quam ex mala. Nobilitas, opes pro crimine: quæ omnia habet Tacitus. Ex- emplum in Roboamo.

## 10:7
Verse 7.

VIDI SERVOS SVPER EQVOS] Indeed, it is royal utility neither to prefer a noble, nor a free-born man, nor even a freedman to arms. Thus Tacitus in Germania. ET PRINCIPES AMBVLANTES SVPER TERRAM, QVASI SERVOS] By princes understand noble men.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

VIDI SERVOS SVPER EQVOS] Enimbero neque nobilem, neque ingenuum, nec libertinum quidem armis præpo- nere, regia utilitas est. Sic Tacitus in Germania. ET PRINCIPES AMBVLANTES SVPER TER- RAM, QVASI SERVOS] Principes intellige viros nobiles.

## 10:8
Verse 8.

HE WHO DIGS A PIT SHALL FALL INTO IT] Namely, Bad counsel is worst for the counselor. The same proverb is in Prov. 26:27, 28:10, Ps. 7:16. Moreover, גומץ is a Chaldean word, which the Chaldean interpreter often uses where in the Hebrew there is בור.

HE WHO BREAKS THROUGH A HEDGE, A SERPENT SHALL BITE HIM] Which is accustomed to lie in the thorns. The allegory of the Hebrews adapts this to those who despise the traditions of the wise.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

QVI FODIT FOVEAM INCIDET IN EAM] Nempe Malum Consilium consultori pessimum. Idem proverbium Prov. XXVI, 27. XXVIII, 10. Psal. VII, 16. Est autem גומץ vox Chaldaica, quam sæpe usurpat inter- pres Chaldæus, ubi in Hebræo est בור.

QVI DISSIPAT SEPEM, MORDEBIT EVM COLVBER] Qui in sentibus latere solet. Allegoria Hebræorum hoc aptat ad eos qui sapientum traditiones con- temnunt.

## 10:9
Verse 9.

HE WHO MOVES STONES SHALL BE HURT BY THEM] He who is covetous of another's property, and therefore tears up the boundaries. And this is applied by allegory to those who rashly disturb things once defined. AND HE WHO CLEAVES WOOD SHALL BE WOUNDED BY IT] He who cuts down another's trees. Allegory leads this to those who sow factions and seditions.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

QVI TRANSFERT LAPIDES, AFFLIGETVR IN EIS] Qui alieni est cupidus, & propterea terminos re- vellit. Et hoc per allegoriam applicatur eis, qui semel defi- nita temere commovent. ET QVI SCINDIT LIGNA, VVLNERABITVR AB EIS] Qui alienas arbores cædit Allegoria hoc deducit ad eos qui factiones & seditiones serunt.

## 10:10
Verse 10.

IF THE IRON BE BLUNT, AND THIS NOT AS BEFORE, BUT HAS BECOME DULL, IT SHALL BE SHARPENED WITH MUCH LABOR, AND AFTER INDUSTRY WISDOM SHALL FOLLOW) If the iron has become dull (namely, by long neglect and rust), and he (the master) has not turned its edge (beforehand), then he will excite his strength: (that is, he will strive with all his might to remove the ingrained defect) and much more rectification (that is, polishing) Wisdom: it requires, namely. This is by far the best interpretation of Maimonides.

Dr. D. Geier renders this meaning: if the iron has been dulled and (the cutter, v. 9) does not sharpen its edge, he will be forced to exert his strength (himself, and yet not even so will he cut what needs to be cut sufficiently well), but for profit in directing, there is Wisdom: on the contrary, the profit or excellence of working prosperously and rightly proceeds from nowhere else than from Wisdom. Which explanation we do not hesitate to prefer to the interpretation of Maimonides.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

SI RETVSVM FVERIT FERRVM, ET HOC NON VT PRIVS, SED HEBETATVM FVERIT, MVLTO LABORE EXACVETVR, ET POST INDVSTRIAM SEQVETVR SAPIENTIA) Si hebetatum (nempe longo situ ac rubigine) fuerit ferrum, & ipse (dominus) aciem ejus (pridem) non verserit, tum vires (fuas) excitabit: (id est, omni vi nitetur auferre vitium inolitum) & plus multo rectificatio- nis (id est, polituræ) Sapientia: requirit scilicet. Hæc est in- terpretatio Maimonidæ longe optima.

Dn. D. Geier. hunc reddit sensum: si hebetatum fuerit ferrum & (sissor v. 9.) aciem ejus non exacuat, vires intendere cogetur (ipse, neque sic tamen decen- ter satis secanda dissescabit) at emolumento ad diri- gendum est Sapientia: e contra emolumentum vel excellentia prospere ac recte operandi non aliun- de proficiscitur, quam a Sapientia. Quam explica- tionem Maimonidæ interpretationi præferre non dubitamus.

## 10:15
Verse 15.

THE LABOR OF FOOLS WEARIES THEM, WHO DO NOT KNOW HOW TO GO TO THE CITY) Many fatigue themselves with arduous questions, when they do not even know the obvious: such as the way to the city.

Therefore, clearer than the Vulgate here is Vatablus: the labor of fools wearies them (they torment themselves about difficult things) who nevertheless do not know the way to the city, they are ignorant of a most well-known matter. And this is also the interpretation of Osiander and Aben Ezra. However, that which Dr. D. Geier handed down seems simpler: The labor of fools wearies each one of them, because he does not know how to go into the city: that is to say, just as a traveler must necessarily weary himself if he is to make a journey to the city and is ignorant of the right way, so also the fool, who is ignorant of the right method of completing a business, is forced to weary himself greatly. Which agrees with the version of Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

LABOR STVLTORVM AFFLIGET EOS QVI NE- SCIVNT IN VRBEM PERGERE) Multi quæstionibus arduis se fatigant, cum ne obvia quidem norint: quale est iter ad urbem.

Clarior ergo vulgata hic est Vatablus, labor stul- torum defatigat eos (torquent se circa difficilia) qui tamen nesciunt viam ad urbem, ignorant rem maxi- me notam. Atque hæc etiam Osiandri & Aben- Ezræ est interpretatio. Simplicior tamen videtur ea, quam Dn. D. Geierus tradidit: Labor stultorum fatigat ipsorum quemque, quia nescit ire in civitatem: q. d. uti viator se fatigare necessum habet, si ad ur- bem iter facturus rectam ignoret viam, ita quoque stultus, qui rectam negotii conficiendi rationem ignorat, admodum se fatigare cogitur. Quæ con- gruunt versioni Lutheri.

## 10:16
Verse 16.

WOE TO THEE, O LAND, WHOSE KING IS A CHILD) Many evils are accustomed to happen in kingdoms where the succession has devolved upon a child. For guardians often do not manage affairs in good faith, or they disagree among themselves: nor does the child have enough authority to keep the people in their duty. An example in the times of Joash, 2 Kings 11, and after Ancus Marcius at Rome: in the age of Arcadius and Honorius in the Roman Empire. AND WHOSE PRINCES EAT IN THE MORNING) They hold untimely banquets: for the body burdened with yesterday's vices weighs down the soul as well.

is turned away, so it is drawn away through lack of mercy. For the Prophets testify that famine is often sent for this reason.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

VÆ TIBI TERRA CVJVS REX PVER EST) Multa mala evenire in regnis solent, ubi successio ad puerum devo- luta est. Tutores enim sæpe non ex fide rem gerunt, aut in- ter se discordant: neque puero satis auctoritatis est ad reti- nendos in officio populos. Exemplum in Joasi temporibus II. Reg. XI. & post Ancum Martium Romæ: Arcadii & Ho- norii ætate in Imperio Romano. ET CVJVS PRINCIPES MANE COMEDVNT) Con- vivia intempestiva agitant: nam —— corpus onustum Hesternis vitiis animum quoque prægravat.

do avertitur, ita per immisericordiam attrahitur. Famem enim sæpe ea de causa immitti testantur Prophetæ.

## 10:17
Verse 17.

BLESSED IS THE LAND WHOSE KING IS NOBLE) In Hebrew: son of the bright ones, that is, of the illustrious. For the ancient splendor of a family adds much dignity to a King. There is in the young, there is in horses, the virtue of their fathers. Euripides in Temenus: Alas, alas. To be born from a noble father, how much wisdom and dignity it possesses. And in Hecuba: A terrible character and a mark among mortals to be born of noble parents. AND WHOSE PRINCES EAT IN DUE SEASON, FOR STRENGTH, AND NOT FOR DRUNKENNESS) In the Golden Verses it is: Always make a measure of both food and exercise; and by measure I mean that which will not harm you.

He therefore refers the case to benefits or alms with Aben-Ezra, so that they may be scattered without selection, which, however, Grotius restricts at will to lesser benefits. Mercer and Piscator more conveniently refer it likewise to alms, that in whomever they are bestowed, they are there, they do not perish, but bear fruit, as indicated above in 11:1 by the likeness of bread cast upon flowing waters. And similarly, almost, B. Franzius, De Interp. Script. Orac. 93. A falling tree provides use to those who are in that place, so also the beneficent person will bestow what he has for the use of his neighbor; yet the most convenient is the common interpretation, which refers the case to a man furnished with wealth, who is commanded to bring forth the fruits of beneficence, i.e., as interpreted by B. Luther in this place: You do not know how long you will live and possess things, just as a tree when it is cut down, whether it falls to the South or the North, it will remain there. Thus, however death may oppress you, in whatever place or condition, so you will remain. If the Lord finds you in the South, that is, fruitful and rich in good works, well; but if in the North, that is, not abounding in good works, it is ill for you. As He finds you, so you will be judged, so you will also receive. To which explanation the context or the preceding simile does not object: For as a threat is held here, so there is a promise. If the clouds are full, they pour rain upon the earth, according to the explanation of B. Luther, which is as follows: If you have substance in those who are like a wandering cloud, and have nothing. Fill those clouds, I say, and you will see yourself also being filled. Similarly, almost, Osiander; if you have given liberally, God in turn will pour out upon you a large rain of heavenly blessing, just as a large rain is caused because many and copious vapors have ascended into the middle region of the air. Which agree with the Holy To the explanation of Jerome: Keep your commandments handed down above (concerning beneficence) so that the clouds may pour out their rain upon you. For wherever you have prepared a place for yourself, and a future seat, whether to the South or to the North, there you will remain when you have died. The Vinarians indeed render a slightly different ἀπόδοσιν in their paraphrase, but one which likewise coheres well with the common explanation of the following simile concerning a falling tree: When the clouds are full, they give rain upon the earth; so when a heart is full of the love of God and of one's neighbor, it also does good willingly according to all its ability, 1 John 3:17-18, 4:20, James 2:14-16. This is the conjecture of Dn. D. Geier in a doubtful passage, as to how these declarative things are related to the following words: you do not know what evils will be upon the earth. Undoubtedly, just as the unsearchability of God's judgments is described in the following verses (like the way, the wind, the formation of the fetus, etc.), so here in this place is depicted their immutability, once they are ripe, because they are sent forth like rain from a cloud already filled (just as elsewhere the chastisement of God is compared to rain, Psalm 11:6, Job 20:23, etc.).

Refert ergo casum ad beneficia vel eleemosynas cum Aben-Ezra, ut sine delectu spargantur, quod tamen Grotius pro lubitu restringit ad mi- nora beneficia. Convenientius Mercerus & Pisca- tor ad eleemosynas itidem referens, quod in quem- cunque conferantur, ibi sint, non pereant, sed fructus ferant, ut supra X,1. simili panis in aquas præterfluen- tes projecti indicatum. Et similiter fere B. Franzius de Interp.Script. Orac.XCIII. Arboreum lignum ca- dens ad hunc vel illum locum præstat usum iis, qui isto loco sint, ita quoque beneficus ea, quæ habet, conferet ad usum proximi sui; Convenientißima tamen est communis interpretatio, qua casum ad hominem refert opibus instructum, qui jubetur fructus be- neficentiæ proferre, q. d. Interprete B. Luthero in h. l. Nescis quamdiu victurus sis, & possessurus res, sicut arbor cum succiditur, sive cadat ad Meridiem, sive Aquilonem, ibi manebit. Sic utut mors te oppres- serit, quocunque loco, conditione, ita manebis. Si in- venerit te Dominus in Meridie, id est, fertilem, & in bonis operibus divitem, bene, si vero in Aquilone, id est, non abundantem bonis operibus, male tibi. Ut in- veneris, sic judicaberis, sic recipies etiam. Cui expli- cationi non repugnat contextus, aut antecedens si- mile: Nam ut hic comminatio habetur, ita ibi pro- missio. Si repletæ fuerint nubes, imbrem in terram ef- fundunt, secundum B. Lutheri explicationem, quæ ita habet: Si habes Substantiam in illis qui sunt instar nubis vagæ, & nihil habent. Illas, inquam, nubes re- ple, & te videbis etiam impleri. Similiter fere Osian- der; si liberaliter erogaveris, Deus vicissim largum imbrem cælestis benedictionis in te effundet, quemad- modum largus imber causatur cur multi & copiosi vapores in mediam aeris regionem ascenderint. Quæ consonant S. Hieronymi explicationi: Serva man- data tua superius tradita (de beneficentia) ut nubes super te effundant imbrem suum. Ubicunque enim ti- bi locum præparaveris, futuramque sedem, sive ad Austrum sive ad Boream, ibi cum mortuus fueris permanebis. Vinarienses paulo aliam quidem red- dunt ἀπόδοσιν, in sua paraphrasi, sed quæ iti- dem probe cohæreat cum sequentis similitudi- nis, de arbore cadente, communi explicatione: Wenn die Wolcken voll sind, so geben sie Regen auf Erden; Also wenn ein Hertz voll Liebe GOttes und des Nächsten ist, so thuts auch freywillig Gutes nach allem Vermögen, 1. Joh. III, 17. 18. c. IV, 20. Jac. II, 14. 15. 16. Dn. D. Geieri in loco dubio hæc est conje- ctura, qua ratione similia ista declarativa sint ver- borum proximorum: nescis quæ mala super terram futura. Nimirum sicut versibus sequentibus judi- ciorum Dei describitur imperscrutabilitas ( instar viæ, venti, formationis fœtus &c.) ita h. l. eo- rundem depingi, si matura semel sint, immuta- bilitatem quod eadem dimittantur instar pluviæ, nube jam repleta (sicut alibi castigatio Dei compa- ratur pluviæ Psal. XI, vers. 6. Job. XX, vers. 23. &c.)

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

What kind of person everyone ought to show himself to be toward a needy neighbor in terms of beneficence, both because of its fruit, and because of our ignorance of our future status, and because of testifying to the fullness of love, and because of the impending eternal judgment. Beneficence is to be exercised without curious discussion of opportunity, in the morning and in the evening. Likewise, how everyone ought to conduct himself toward himself, by the right and cheerful use of the present life, when the light of grace shines, when many days are dark, whence from youth immediately joy in the Lord is urged, with the remembrance of divine judgment.

Verse 1.

CAST THY BREAD UPON THE PASSING WATERS) That is, where there is no hope of receiving back. Luke 14:12, 13, 14. FOR AFTER MANY DAYS THOU SHALT FIND IT) God will confer new benefits upon you for that beneficence.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

Qualem se quisque præbere debeat quoad proximum indigentem beneficentia, tum ob fructum ejus, tum ob ignorationem futuri nostri status, tum ob testandam amoris plenitudinem, tum ob imminens æternum judicium. Exercenda benefi- centia sine curiosa oportunitatis discus- sione mane, & vesperi. Qualem item se gerere quisq, debeat, quoad semet ipsum, recta & hilari vita præsentis usurpatio- ne, cum lux gratiæ affulget, quum plures dies sint caliginosi, unde a juventute sta- tim suadetut lætitia in Domino, cum ju- dicii divini recordatione.

## 11:2
Verse 2.

GIVE A PORTION TO SEVEN) Namely, to the poor. FOR THOU KNOWEST WHAT EVIL SHALL BE UPON THE EARTH) Which is to say, just as doing good which, like a tree fallen into a certain place, are not moved. All of which interpretations seem preferable to the explanation of Grotius: If the clouds are filled, they shall pour rain upon the earth: i.e., without any distinction upon all the ground. Thus also do not anxiously inquire what kind of person he is to whom you give. He is a man. What Solomonic sharpness is there in the fact that rain falls upon all the ground? That explanation can, however, be aided if, indeed, it is understood as divine providence and beneficence, of which it teaches us to be imitators, that rain falls upon the ground of the wicked as well as the pious, so that it may correspond to the similitude of Christ in Matthew V, 45. Jerome has now conveniently shown the connection and coherence: Therefore we said above: Cast your bread upon the face of the water, and give to everyone who asks of you: because both the clouds, when they are full, bestow their riches upon mortals, and you, like a tree, however long-lived you may be, will not be so forever, but, overturned by a sudden storm of winds, that is, of death, wherever you have fallen, there you will remain perpetually, whether the final time finds you rigid and cruel, or clement and merciful. Therefore, the tree that has fallen in this life, and has been cut down by the condition of mortality, either sinned before, while it stood, and is afterwards placed in the northern part, or if it brought forth fruits worthy of the south, it will lie in the southern region. Nor is there any tree that is not either toward the North or toward the South.

V, 45. Lignum ergo quod in hac vita corruerit, & conditione mortalitatis fuerit incisum aut pecca- vit ante, dum staret, & in borea parte postea ponitur, aut si dignos austro fructus attulit in plaga jacebit au- strali. Nec est aliquod lignum, quod aut ad Aquilo- nem non sit, aut ad Austrum.

## 11:10
Verse 10.

REMOVE ANGER FROM YOUR HEART] μεμψιμοιρίαν (complaining/grumbling).

Other interpreters explain this as the final judgment: for there an account must be rendered for all things, and the retribution will be universal. Grotius, however, avoids this explanation and prefers to understand it as any other particular judgment, because he does not believe that the doctrine of the final judgment was openly taught in the age of Solomon or perhaps even of Zerubbabel (under whom he wishes these things to have been compiled). Yet it is evident from various places that it was proposed in Moses and the Psalms, Gen. 18:25, Deut. 32:34, Ps. 9:5, Ps. 50:3, 98:9. Indeed, that it was already clearly preached by Enoch, Jude openly teaches in his Epistle, verse 14. And what is clearer than that this is dealt with in this book, ch. 12:4?

Solomon notably warns in this place that we are to be called into judgment FOR ALL THINGS: so that he may designate the universal judgment, where all things will be called into judgment. For then God will bring all things, even those which are hidden and concealed, into judgment, Eccl. 12:14. We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil, II Cor. 5:10. Then men are to be judged from all those things which are written in the books according to their works, Rev. 20:12. Nor is there any judgment that can so greatly recall us from illicit joys as that final one of the day of universal judgment, Luke 22:34, Acts 17:30, II Pet. 3:11, Sir. 7:end. Therefore Gregory the Great, homily 39:11, in the Gospel: If there is any joy of the present time, it should be conducted in such a way that the bitterness of the following judgment never departs from the memory. Which the imperative, AND KNOW, emphatically implies in this place, commanding that for all our joys, both of the heart and of the external senses, it should be kept in memory that we are to be brought into judgment for all things, and thus we should rejoice in such a way that we first examine all the paths of a rejoicing heart, all desires, all refreshment of the eyes and senses, as to how we shall appear with them in that universal judgment before the judge, to whose eyes all things are τετραχηλισμένα (laid bare), even the very counsels of the heart. Finally, since in this life it is not rarely well with the impious, it is manifest that we are recalled here not so much to the judgments that await us in the present life, as to the final judgment. For then it will be rendered to each according to his works, Rev. 22:12.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

AVFER IRAM A CORDE TVO] μεμψιμοιρίαν.

De judicio extremo id explicant alii interpretes: ibi enim de omnibus reddenda erit ratio, & univer- salis erit retributio. Fugit autem hanc explicatio- nem Grotius, ac mavult de alio quovis particulari judicio intelligere, eo quod non credat, Salomo- nis vel etiam fortassis Zorobabelis (sub quo hæc digesta vult) ætate doctrinam de judicio novissi- mo aperte traditam. Quam vero in Mose & Psal- mis propositam fuisse, e variis locis constat Gen. XIIX,25. Deut. XXXII,34. Ps.IX,5. Ps. L,3.XCIIX, 9. Imo ab Enocho jam luculenter eam prædica- tam esse, aperte Judas Epistola sua vers.14. docet. Et quid luculentius, quam quod hoc libro c. XII, 4.

de judicio novissimo agatur? Notanter hoc in loco Salomo monet PRO OMNIBVS nos vocan- dos esse iu judicium: ut universale judicium, ubi omnia in judicium vocabuntur, designet. Tum enim cuncta, etiam quæ sunt occulta & abscondita, DEVS adducet in judicium Eccl. XII, 14. omnes nos oportet manifestari coram tribunali Christi, ut repor- tet unusquisque secundum id quod fecit sive bonum sive malum II. Cor. V, 10. Tum judicandi homines ex omnibus his,quæ scripta sunt in libris secundum ope- ra ipsorum Apoc. XX, 12. Nec ullum est judicium, quod tantopere nos ab illicitis gaudiis revocare pos- sit, atque novissimum illud diei pantocriticæ Luc. XXII,34. Act.XVII, 30. II.Petr.III, 11. Syr.VII,ult. Ideo Gregorius M.homil. XXXIX, 11. inEvang. Si quæ est præsentis temporis, ita agenda lætitia,ut nunquam amaritudo sequentis judicii recedat a memoria. Quod emphatice innuit hoc in loco Imperativus, ET SCITO, præcipiens, ut ad omnia gaudia nostra tam cordis, quam externorum sensuum in memoria versetur, propter omnia nos adductum iri in judi- cium, adeoque ita lætemur, ut prius omnes cordis lætabundi vias, omnia desideria, omnem oculorum ac sensuum refocillationem examinemus, quomo- do in illo universali judicio coram judice, cujus oculis cuncta sunt τετραχηλισμένα, etiam ipsa cor- dis consilia, cum iisdem comparituri simus. De- nique quum in hac vita impiis non raro bene sit, non tam ad judicia, quæ nos manent in præsenti vita, quam ad novissimum judicium hic nos revo- cari, manifestum est. Tum enim reddetur cuique secundum opera sua Ap. XXII, 12.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII.

How everyone ought to conduct himself toward GOD the creator from youth and before the evil days of old age come, which is inept and very troublesome: since death is altogether to be feared, and the body is to be dissolved, but the Spirit is to return to God. The conclusion of the whole discourse: the summary of which is repeated, the author's Wisdom and care in instruction are asserted, Holy Scripture is commended, and a summary of it is exhibited, by which our duty, that God is to be feared and His precepts kept, and the chief argument for performing it, that all things are to be brought into judgment.

Verse 1.

REMEMBER THY CREATOR. In Hebrew there is the plural number בוראיך, by which the mystery of the plurality of the divine persons is insinuated. For that consultation in Gen. I, 26, LET US MAKE man in OUR image, after OUR likeness, openly teaches that several divine persons created man: and this form of speaking is wont to insinuate this mystery in the O. T., as for instance when several who made us are introduced by the plural name עשי, Job XXXV, 10, Ps. CXLIX, 2, Is. LIV, 5, concerning which passages it has been treated elsewhere: which are plainly similar to this one of ours. Not undeservedly, therefore, did Raymundus Martinus observe this mystery in the present passage already 400 years ago in Pugio Fidei part. III. dist. 1. c. III, where after having adduced the passages Gen. I, 26, c. XI, 7, c. XXXV, 7, Deut. IV, 7, Jos. XXIV, 19, II. Sam. VII, 23, Jer. XXIII, 36, Eccl. II, 12. thus he adds. A similar mode of speaking about God is in Eccl. XII, 1. Remember thy creators: where the Gloss or Midrash says: This is the King of Kings, God holy and blessed. Moreover, all those passages have been ignored by Grotius: who recognizes no mysterious expression in them. Vers. 2. BEFORE THE SUN AND THE LIGHT AND THE MOON BE DARKENED) With many poetic expressions and metaphors interspersed, he describes the inconveniences of old age. The sun and moon are said to fail for those to whom even those things which are by nature most pleasing to men cease to be pleasing. See what we have said at Matt. XXIV, 29. Others, not inappropriately, having regard to the subsequent circumlocutions of the vigor of the inner mind, of the intelligence of the sharpness of judgment, of the power of counseling, think that the weakening of these is signified by this darkening. See B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 487. AND THE CLOUDS RETURN AFTER THE RAIN) The general description of evils still continues. Clouds after rain, as elsewhere deep calleth unto deep, and a perpetual succession of inconveniences. B. D. Gerhard, in his Commonplaces on death §. 71, has accepted this description concerning the exhalations and vapors, which are more frequent and almost continuous in old age due to the weakness of the stomach and a defect of digestion, which supply material for the distillations of the brain, from which further follow catarrhs, coughs, difficulty of breathing, etc. Vers. 3. WHEN THE KEEPERS OF THE HOUSE SHALL TREMBLE) The hands tremble. AND THE STRONG MEN SHALL BOW THEMSELVES) The legs, the Atlases of the body. AND THE GRINDERS SHALL BE IDLE IN A SMALL NUMBER) In the Hebrew: And the grinding women (that is, the molar teeth) shall cease, because even if they are few, they are weary. They are said to be diminished for both reasons, both in number and also in their strength. AND THOSE THAT LOOK OUT OF THE WINDOWS SHALL BE DARKENED) Properly through the windows: those who look out. He understands the eyes, for which the intervals of the eyelids are as it were windows. Vers. 4. AND THEY SHALL SHUT THE DOORS IN THE STREET IN THE HUMBLING OF THE VOICE OF THE GRINDING) And the exits toward the forum shall be shut because of the weakness of the voice, which before sounded like a mill. LXX. And they shall shut the doors in the market, (active for passive) in the weakness of the voice of the grinding, (supply 'of') Symmachus, the voice having become useless. The forum will be closed to him, because of the thinness of the voice. More correctly, these things are commonly explained concerning the lips: old men do not willingly open their lips, they are weary of speaking: for the two lips are as it were doors, through which the heart goes out, as it were while a man speaks, and expresses the sentiment of his mind. In the humbling of the voice of the grinding, that is, according to Osiander's interpretation, the voice (which is so formed by the teeth and tongue that it becomes articulated) is no longer loud and clear, but humble and feeble. AND THEY SHALL RISE UP AT THE VOICE OF THE BIRD, AND ALL THE DAUGHTERS OF SONG SHALL BE BROUGHT LOW) In the Hebrew: And (man, that is) shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of song shall be brought low. He shall be awakened from sleep at the sound of the smallest bird, and the Muses will be of no value to him. This latter member is best explained by the passage concerning Barzillai in II Sam. XIX, 35. Regarding the awakening from sleep, also Jac. Matthiae, Dn. D. Gejerus, and others with Osiander explain it in this way: sleep is rendered worse because of the dryness of the body, so that old men are awakened by the song of a little bird. But what is added, and all the daughters of song are bowed down, Osiander has interpreted thus: the ears become flaccid and pendulous, and no longer perform their duty. Daughters of song, it seems more correct to understand as the ears, being destined for distinguishing songs and sounds, than the Muses, which are humbled, become flaccid, weak, and inept among old men, so that they must often even be bent outwardly toward the mouth of the speaker, (as Jerome, Lyranus, B. Luther, Pineda, Ferus, Delrio, and others have explained the daughters of song. For not only are musical concerts despised by old men, but they are also perceived with difficulty due to the deafness of the ears.

Latin:

CAPUT XII.

Qualem se quisque gerere debeat erga DEVM conditorem inde a juventute & antequam dies mali veniant sene- ctutis, quæ inepta & perquam molesta est: siquidem mors omnino metuenda, & corpus dissolvendum,Spiritui autem revertendum sit ad Deum. Conclusio totius concionis: quæ repetitur summa ejusdem, asseritur autoris Sapientia & in informatione cura, commenda- tur Scriptura Sacra, ejusdemque sum- marium exhibetur, qua nostrum debi- tum, quod Deus timendus, ejusque præcepta servanda, & ejus præstandi argumentum præcipuum, quod omnia proferenda sint in judicium.

Vers. 1.

MEMENTO CREATORIS TUI. IN Ebræo est pluralis numerus בוראיך quo myste- rium pluralitatis personarum divinarum insinua- tur. Plures enim divinas personas hominem creaf- se consultatio illa Gen. I, 26. FACIAMVS homi- nem ad imaginem NOSTRAM secundum similitu- dinem NOSTRAM, aperte docet : Soletque hæc forma loquendi hoc mysterium in V. T. insinua- ri, utputa cum plures qui fecerunt nos plurali no- mine עשי introducuntur Job.XXXV,10.Ps.CXLIX, 2. Es.LIV, 5. de quibus locis alias actum est : Quæ huic nostro plane similia sunt. Non immerito ita- que observavit hoc mysterium in præsenti loco jam ante CCCC. annos Raymundus Martinus in Pu- gione Fidei part. III. dist. 1. c. III. ubi post adducta loca Gen.I, 26. c. XI, 7. c. XXXV, 7. Deut. IV,7. Jos. XXIV,19. II. Sam. VII,23. Jer. XXIII, 36. Eccl.II,12. ita subjungit. Similis modus loquendi de Deo est Eccl. XII, 1. Memento creatorum tuorum: ubi Glos- sa sive Midrasch: Hic est Rex Regum Deus sanctus & benedictus. Omnia autem illa loca a Grotio insu- per habita sunt: qui nullam loquutionem μυςη- ριώδη in iis agnoscit. Vers. 2. ANTEQVAM TENEBRESCAT SOL ET LUMEN ET LUNA) Poeticis locutionibus multis inter- fertis Metaphoris, describit senectutis incommoda. Sol & Lu- na deficere illis dicuntur, quibus etiam illa quæ per naturam gratissima sunt hominibus, grata esse desinunt. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXIV, 29. Alii non incommode respectu habito subse- quentium περιφράσεων interioris animi vigoris, in- telligentiæ judicandi acuminis, consulendi δυνά- μεως debilitationem hac obtenebratione significari putant. Vid. B. D. Glass. Rhet. S. p. 487. ET REVERTUNTUR NUBES POST PLUVIAM) Durat adhuc generalis malorum descriptio. Nubes post plu- viam, ut alibi abyssus post abyssum, & perpetua successio in- commodorum. De exhalationibus ac vaporibus ex imbecillita- te ventriculi & vitio concoctionis in senili ætate crebrioribus, ac fere continuis, quæ materiam suppeditant destillationibus cerebri, ex quibus porro sequuntur catarri, tussis, difficultas respira- tionis &c. B. D. Gerhard. LL. CC. de morte §. 71. hanc descriptionem accepit. Vers. 3. QVANDO COMMOVEBUNTUR CUSTO- DES DOMUS) Manus trement. ET NUTABUNT VIRI FORTISSIMI] Crura Adlantes corporis. ET OTIOSÆ ERUNT MOLENTES IN MINUTO NUMERO) In Hebræo: Et cessabunt molitrices, (id est, mo- lares dentes) quia & si sua defessi sunt. Imminuti dicuntur utraque ratione tum nume- ro, tum etiam viribus suis. ET TENEBRESCENT VIDENTES PER FORAMI- NA) Proprie per fenestras: Οἱ παρακύπτοντες. Intelligit oculos quibus intervalla palpebrarum sunt quasi fenestræ. Vers. 4. ET CLAUDENT OSTIA IN PLATEA IN HVMI- LITATE VOCIS MOLENTIS) Et claudentur egressus fo- rum versus ob infirmitatem vocis, quæ ante ut mola sonabat. LXX. Καὶ κλείσουσι θύρας ἐν ἀγορᾷ, (activum pro passivo) ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ φωνῆς τῆς ἀληθούσης, (supple περι) Symmachus, ἀχρειωθείσης τῆς φωνῆς. Occlusum illi erit forum, ob vocis tenuitatem. Rectius de labiis communiter hæc explicantur: labia non libenter aperiunt senes, tædet eos lo- qui: sunt enim labia duo quasi ostia, per quæ cor egreditur, quasi dum loquitur homo, & animi sui sententiam exprimit. In humilitate vocis molentis, id est, interprete Osiandro, vox (quæ per dentes & linguam ita formatur, ut fiat articulata) non am- plius est alta, & clara, sed humilis, & imbe- cillis. ET CONSURGENT AD VOCEM VOLUCRIS, ET OBSURDESCENT OMNES FILIÆ CARMINIS) In He- bræo: Et surget (homo scilicet) ad vocem avis, & deprimentur filiæ omnes carminis. Excitabitur ex somno ad sonum mini- mæ avis, & nullo in pretio illi erunt Musæ. Posterius hoc membrum optime explicat locus de Barzillajo II. Sam. XIX, 35. De excitatione a somno etiam Jac. Matthiæ, Dn. D. Gejerus, & alii cum Osiandro h. m. explican- te: somnus redditur deterior propter corporis sic- citatem, ita ut aviculæ cantu senes excitentur. Quæ vero subjunguntur, & incurvantur omnes filiæ car- minis, ita interpretatus Osiander est: aures fiunt flaccidæ & pendulæ, nec amplius officium suum faciunt. Filiæ carminis, rectius videntur aures in- telligi utpote canticis sonisque dignoscendis desti- natæ, quam Musæ, quæ humiliantur, flaccescunt debiles atque ineptæ fiunt apud senes, ita ut sæpius etiam incurvandæ sint exterius ad os loquentis, (ut cum Hieronymo, Lyrano, B. Luther. Pineda, Fe- rus, Delrio & alii filias cantici exposuere. Non enim tantum concentus Musici contemnuntur a senibus, sed & difficulter ob aurium surditatem percipiuntur.

## 12:5
Vers. 5. THEY SHALL ALSO BE AFRAID OF THAT WHICH IS HIGH, AND FEARS SHALL BE IN THE WAY) In the Hebrew: They shall fear both those things which are eminent, and those which are broken in the way. If they set themselves on the road, they will fear lest they stumble on things that are protruding or depressed. For there is danger to old men from both.

THE ALMOND TREE SHALL FLOURISH) The head shall grow white, like the flowers of the almond tree.

THE LOCUST SHALL BE A BURDEN) In the Hebrew: The locust shall be a burden: that is, the lustful part shall contract a hernia.

The customary explanation of B. Luther, Philippus, Piscator, and others is to be preferred to that new gloss, which Osiander's paraphrase succinctly exhibits: The locust shall be burdened, that is, old men walk with slender legs and a depressed body, as if you were to see a locust carrying a heavy burden under which it is bent, so that these things are referred to the legs and the spine of the back.

AND THE CAPER BERRY SHALL FAIL) You may best translate from the Hebrew: Lust shall perish: which coheres best with the preceding. And thus the Chaldeans use this word.

Others more correctly take this concerning the desire and appetite for food and drink, and other similar things.

FOR MAN GOETH TO HIS ETERNAL HOME) As Catullus says: One perpetual night must be slept. He goeth, that is, he shall approach more and more.

AND THEY SHALL GO ABOUT IN THE STREET MOURNING) Hired mourners shall go about the funeral on all sides, as was the custom then. See what is at Matt. XI, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 5. EXCELSA QVOQVE TIMEBUNT ET FOR- MIDABUNT IN VIA) In Hebræo: Timebunt & quæ emi- nent, & quæ fracta sunt in via. Si in viam se dent, metuent, ne offendant in exstantia aut depressa. Ab utrisque enim periculum est senibus.

FLOREBIT AMYGDALUS) Albescet caput, ut flores amygdali.

IMPINGUABITUR LOCUSTA) In Hebræo: Oneri erit locusta: id est, particula salax herniam contrahet.

Glossæ illi novæ præferenda consueta B. Luthe- ri, Philippi, Piscat. & aliorum explicatio, quam succincte exhibet Osiandr. paraphrasis: Onerabi- tur locusta, id est, gracilibus cruribus, & depresso corpore senes incedunt, quasi videas locustam gra- ve onus ferentem sub quo incurvetur, ut ita hæc ad crura, & spinam dorsi referantur.

ET DISSIPABITUR CAPPARIS) Optime vertas ex He- bræo: Peribit libido: quod cum præcedenti optime cohærer. Et sic Chaldæi hanc vocem usurpant.

Rectius hoc alii de desiderio & appetitu cibi & potus, aliarumque rerum similium accipiunt.

QVONIAM IBIT HOMO IN DOMUM ÆTERNI- TATIS SUÆ) Sicut Catullus ait: Nox est perpetua una dormienda. Ibit, id est magis magisque accedet.

ET CIRCUIBUNT IN PLATEA PLANGENTES) Præficæ funus undique ambibunt, ut tunc erat moris. Vide quæ ad Matth. XI, 17.

## 12:6
Vers. 6. OR EVER THE SILVER CORD BE LOOSED) In the Hebrew: before the silver cord is not lengthened (that is, contracted): that is, the marrow of the back withers, whence it happens that the back is bent; for time has bent me, says Crates. Thus the Hebrews.

OR THE GOLDEN BOWL BE BROKEN) In the Hebrew: And the golden bowl be broken: it seems to be understood of the bile which in old age is less accustomed to be contained in its vessels.

Others explain the golden spring as the radical moisture: Mr. D. Gejer not unaptly understands by the silver cord the attractive, retentive, and expulsive force of the nutritive faculty, and by the golden bucket the veins as vessels receiving blood, and the arteries as vessels receiving spirits.

OR THE PITCHER BE BROKEN AT THE FOUNTAIN) The bladder may less contain the humor entrusted to it.

Others more correctly adapt the pitcher to those members which receive from the veins and arteries the liquid brought to them: Osiander wishes the stomach to be compared to a pitcher, just as the liver to a wheel, by whose aid water is drawn from a well to refresh a man: which in old men at length neither the stomach nor the liver perform their duty in digesting and distributing nourishment.

OR THE WHEEL BROKEN AT THE CISTERN) The bowels may less respond at their proper times, now more rapid, now more constricted.

Mr. D. Gejer more conveniently refers it to the heart, which moves continuously like a wheel, and is in a certain way the principle and cause of motion in the other members. He who indeed not without reason warned that the general scope of the metaphor suffices here, even if one does not scrupulously inquire into each of these things handed down in v. 6, praising for the same opinion Jerome, Mercer, Jacob Matthias, D. Glassius, and the Weimar Bible. There are almost infinite varieties of opinions if those things are discussed more specifically: so that it is difficult to choose which explanation is to be preferred. But just as in the preceding verses the old man has been described regarding the various inconveniences of old age, so now the life of man itself and its cessation are depicted metaphorically, that we may be warned of the remembrance of the Creator before life ends: which is therefore compared with the drawing of water from a well, where there is need of a cord from which the urn hangs, and the urn itself, or bucket, and the pitcher into which the drawn water is poured: and a spring is required, from which the water flows; and also a wheel, around which the drawing-rope is wound, and the well itself, or pit. These individual things, therefore, as long as they are kept in their integrity, that is, (according to metaphorical application) as long as spirits gush forth in the heart, and are equally drawn from the arteries and distributed, and also are elaborated by the brain, as long as the lungs also draw in and give back air, as long as the stomach rightly receives nourishment and gives back chyle, as long as the liver receives it carried through the mesenteric veins and gives back blood, as long as these are safe and are in good condition, for so long is man preserved. He speaks of life as of a fountain, says Dr. Glassius, by which water is drawn in a pitcher hanging from a chain: its dissolution and breaking signifies life ceasing or death and destruction. The epithets of silver and gold denote the preciousness of life. And therefore these things seem to be referred to death rather than to the inconveniences of old age alone, which were sufficiently depicted in the preceding verses, since the silver cord may be dissolved and the golden bowl broken even in the young, etc., and mention of death has already been made before in verse 5. Which also pleased Jerome, that these are enigmas of death. For how, he says, the pitcher which is broken ceases to draw, and the wheel, through which waters are lifted from the lake and wells, if it has been broken, the use of water is intercepted: so also when the silver cord has been interrupted and the stream of the soul has returned to the fountain, man will perish. Whence finally in verse 7, in proper words, a periphrasis of death is added concerning the reversion of the dust into the earth and the spirit or soul to God: as that by which the corruptibility of the body, and the separation of the soul from the body, and immortality is clearly expressed.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ANTEQVAM RUMPATUR FUNICULUS ARGENTEVS) In Hebræo: antequam non elongetur (id est, contrahatur) argenteus funis: id est, marcescat medulla dorsi, unde sit, ut dorsum curvetur ὁ γὰρ χρόνος μ' ἔκαμψε, ait Cra- tes. Sic Hebræi.

ET RECURRAT VITTA AUREA) In Hebræo: Et fran- gatur phiala aurea: intelligendum videtur de bile quæ in se- necta minus solet vasis suis contineri.

Alii scaturiginem auream de humido radicali explicant: Dn. D. Gejerus per funem argenteum vim nutritivæ facultatis attractricem, retentricem ac expultricem per situlam vero auream venas ceu sanguinis, & arterias ceu spirituum vasa exceptoria non inconcinne intelligit.

ET CONTERATUR HYDRIA SUPER FONTEM) Vesica minus contineat sibi creditum humorem.

Rectius hydriam accommodant alii ad membra illa, quæ a venis & arteriis excipiunt delatum liquo- rem: Stomachum hydriæ comparari vult Osiander, uti jecur rotæ, cujus ope aqua extrahitur e puteo, ut hominem reficiat: quod in senibus tandem ne- que ventriculus, neque epar suum faciant officium in concoquendo, & distribuendo alimento.

ET CONFRINGATUR ROTA SUPER CISTER- NAM) Alvus minus respondeat temporibus suis, modo ci- tatior, modo adstrictior.

Commodius ad cor refert Dn. D. Gejerus, quod instar rotæ continuo movetur, motusque in mem- bris cæteris est principium certo modo, ac causa. Qui vero non præter rem monuit, generalem me- taphoræ scopum hic sufficere, etiam si de singulis hisce v. 6. traditis scrupulose non disquiratur, lau- dans in eandem sententiam Hieronymum, Mer- cerum, Jacobum Matthiam, D. Glassium, Bibl. Vi- nariens. Infinitæ fere sunt varietates, si specialius illa discutiantur, sententiarum: ut difficile sit elige- re, quænam præferenda sit explicatio. Uti autem in præcedentibus senex quoad incommoda senectu- tis varia descriptus est, ita nunc vita ipsa hominis, ejusque cessatio depingitur metaphorice, ut mo- neamur de creatoris recordatione, antequam vita desinat: quæ comparatur proinde cum hau- stione aquæ ex puteo, ubi opus fune, ex quo pen- det urna, & urna ipsa, sive situla, & hydria in quam hausta aqua effunditur: ac scaturigo requi- ritur, unde aqua promanat; nec non rota, circ quam volvitur funis ductarius & puteus ipse, seu fo- vea. Hæc ergo singula, quamdiu in integritate sua servantur, hoc est, (juxta metaphoricam applica- tionem) quamdiu in corde scaturiunt spiritus, re- &eque ab arteriis hauriuntur ac distribuuntur, nec non a cerebro elaborantur, quamdiu etiam pul- mones attrahunt,redduntque aerem,quamdiu ven- triculus recte excipit alimenta, redditque chylum, quamdiu eum per venas mesaraicas delatum exci- pit epar, redditque sanguinem, quamdiu hæc salva sunt, & recte se habent, tamdiu conservatur homo. De vita ut de fonte loquitur, inquit D. Glassius, qua hydria de catena pendente hauritur: ejus dissolutio & fractio vitam cessantem seu mortem & interitum significat. Argentei vero & aurei Epitheta vitæ pre- tiositatem notant. Ideoque hæc ad mortem potius referenda videntur, quam ad incommoda solum se- nectutis, quæ in præcedentibus depicta satis erant, siquidem etiam in juvenibus funis argenteus dis- solvatur, & phiala aurea confringatur &c. ac de morte jam antea v. 5. mentio facta sit. Quod etiam placuit Hieronymo, quod hæc mortis sint ænigma- ta. Quomodo enim, inquit, hydria quæ conteritur,ces- sat haurire, & rota, per quam de lacu, & puteis levan- tur aquæ, si confracta fuerit, aquæ usus intercipitur: ita & cum funiculus argenti fuerit interruptus & ani- mæ rivus recurrerit ad fontem, interibit homo. Un- de tandem verbis propriis v. 7. de reversione pulve- ris in terram & spiritus vel animæ ad Deum mortis περίφρασις subjuncta: utpote qua corporis corru- ptibilitas, ac animæ a corpore separatio, & immor- talitas clare expressa est.

## 12:7
Vers. 7. AND THE DUST SHALL RETURN TO ITS EARTH, FROM WHENCE IT WAS] The body to the earth, says Euripides in the Suppliants. Lucretius: The same thing yields back to the earth what it was before. See what we have said in book II of the Law of War and Peace, chapter XIX, § 11, and on Genesis III, 9.

AND THE SPIRIT SHALL RETURN TO GOD, WHO GAVE IT] Euripides in the said tragedy: the spirit to the ether. See what we have said on Job XXXIV, 14.

That passage is as follows: God will draw to Himself his spirit and breath: upon which Grotius annotates these things: the life of all living creatures is from God, if He recalls it, all things die. The same kind of speaking is in Ps. CIV, 9. Nothing is there about the manner in which the Spirit returns to God. But if the passage is compared for the purpose of teaching that by the Spirit nothing else is understood than life, how will life be said to return to God, and indeed in opposition, when the body is converted into dust? Does life remain with God and does the soul, from which life is, not remain? Does not the very opposition of the Spirit remaining and returning to God, and the body, which is converted into the dust of the earth and corrupted, sufficiently teach that by the Spirit is designated the immortal and incorruptible soul, which is opposed to the corruptible body? For as Solomon previously proposed a very ingenious description of old age, so now he describes death from the dissolution of the soul and body, and the state of each after dissolution: namely, that the dust or the body formed from dust returns to the earth, from whence it was: but the Spirit or soul returns to God, who had given it, i.e., it is not reduced to nothing, or vanishes into air, but returns to God, the Lord of the spirits of all flesh, Num. XVI, 22, who produced it not from the dust of the earth as the body, but breathed it into man when the body was made from the dust of the earth into a living soul; since there is here openly a discourse concerning the first origin of both. Since therefore the soul returns to Him, to whom it is about to render an account of how it presided over the palace of the body entrusted to it, so that it may either be crowned with eternal rewards or punished with eternal torments, Ecclesiastes warns us to remember our Creator God in time and in the days of our youth, before old age and death creep upon us. However, Euripides contributes nothing to this opinion concerning the state of our soul with God, who had no knowledge of God from the light of nature, and therefore could by no means define the Spirit migrating to the ether with the same mind and sentiment as the divinely inspired writers have handed it down. For what is established to us by nature, whether concerning the first origin of the soul breathed into Adam, or concerning the return of the same to God? But such glosses smack of the instruction of the School of the Socinians: which by no means believes in the life of the soul after this life, but if souls survive, it makes them devoid of operation in a separated state, and judges that the lot or state of another life never entered into the mind of Solomon. Certainly in the same way Socinus corrupted this saying in his Response and Defense of Puccius concerning the first state of man, chapter I, p. 79, explaining the Spirit as a thing not subsisting by itself, as a thing of living animal life, which, since it neither subsists in any way by itself, nor yet can vanish, returns to God, who had given it, as to the fountain of all life, when it departs from him to whom it had been given. But this gloss is so putrid that even the disciples of Socinus themselves were ashamed of it, and Smalcius himself, otherwise closely adhering to his master, the ill-fated Socinus, acknowledged that the passage must be accepted concerning the rational soul, and openly confirmed that the soul of man survives after death, in his refutation of Franz, p. 409, 410. See what we have said against Socinus in Socinism Overthrown concerning this passage, Sect. X, cited 1, Contr. II, p. 1023. Molineus, Arminius, Bellarminus, Fequernekinus, Bucanus, Calixtus, Hornejus, and Dreierus strive to prove the creation of souls from this, which opinion Hackspan in this place professes is very pleasing to him, but we have refuted it expressly in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony, Sect. II, c. III, p. 461, seqq. And St. Augustine rightly observed in book X of the Literal Commentary on Genesis, c. IX, that the ancient Doctors of the Church had already answered that the Spirit returns to God, who gave it to the first man when He breathed into his face, the dust, that is, the human body, having been turned into its earth from whence it was originally made. Add also Epistle CLVII, as well as XXIX to Jerome, where Augustine teaches that that saying favors the propagation of the soul more. See what we have said in the cited place, p. 546.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ET REVERTATUR PULVIS IN TERRAM SUAM, UNDE ERAT] Τὸ σῶμα δ’ εἰς γῆν, ait Euripides in Supplicibus. Lucretius: Cedit idem retro de terra quod fuit ante. Vide quæ diximus libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. XIX. §. 11. & ad Genes. III, 9.

ET SPIRITUS REDEAT AD DEUM, QVI DEDIT ILLUM] Euripides dicta Tragoedia: πνεῦμα μὲν πρὸς αἰθέρα. Vide quæ diximus ad Job. XXXIV, 14.

Locus ille ita habet: Spiritum illius & flatum ad se trahet Deus: ad quem Grotius hæc annotat: vita omnium animantium a Deo est, si revocet, cuncta moriuntur. Idem loquendi genus Ps. CIV, 9. Nihil ibi de eo quo modo ad Deum redeat Spiritus. Si vero confertur ideo locus, ut doceatur, per Spiri- tum nihil aliud intelligi quam vitam, quomodo vi- ta ad Deum redire dicetur, & quidem in opposi- tione, cum nempe corpus in pulverem convertitur? num remanet vita apud Deum & non remanet ani- ma, a qua est vita? Annon ipsa oppositio Spiritus remanentis & ad Deum redeuntis, ac coporis, quod in pulverem terræ convertitur & corrumpi- tur satis docet, per Spiritum animam immortalem & incorruptibilem, quæ corpori corruptibili op- ponitur designari? Nam ut antea admodum inge- niosam senectutis descriptionem proposuit Salo- mo, ita nunc mortem a dissolutione animæ & cor- poris, & statum utrumque post dissolutionem de- scribit: quod nempe revertatur pulvis vel corpus e pulvere formatum, in terram,unde erat: Spiritus ve- ro vel anima revertatur ad Deum, qui eandem de- derat, h.e. non in nihilum redigatur, aut in auram evanscat, sed ad Deum Spirituum universæ carnis Dominum Num. XVI, 22. redeat, qui eam non ex pulvere terræ ut corpus produxit, sed inspiravit ho- mini cum corpus e pulvere terræ in animam viven- tem factum est; Siquidem de utriusque prima ori- gine hic aperte sermo fit. Quum ergo ad eum re- vertatur anima, cui rationem redditura est, quo- modo corporis Palatio sibi credito præfuerit, ut vel æternis præmiis coronetur, vel æternis fuppli- ciis plectatur monet Ecclesiastes, recordemur in tempore & in diebus juventutis nostræ Dei creatoris, priusquam senectus & mors nobis subrepat. Nihil au- tem ad hanc de animæ nostræ statu apud Deum sen- tentiam Euripides facit qui de Deo nihil e naturæ lumine cognitum habuit, ideoque Spiritum πρὸς αἰθέρα migrare eadem mente ac sententia neuti- quam definire potuit, qua id tradidere Scriptores θεόπνευςοι. Quid enim per naturam nobis constat sive de prima origine animæ Adamo inspiratæ, sive de reditu ejusdem ad Deum? Sapiunt autem tales glossæ Scholæ Socinianorum informationem: quæ animæ vitam post hanc vitam haudquaquam cre- dit, sed si animæ supersint, easdem operationis in statu separato expertes facit, ac Salomoni neuti- quam in mentem venisse vitæ alterius sortem aut statum censet. Eodem certe modo dictum hoc corrupit Socinus Respons. ac Defens. Puccii de stat. prim. hom. cap. I. p. 79. Spiritum de re per se non sub- sistente, de re animalem vitam vivendi explicans, quæ cum nec per se aliquo modo subsistat, nec tamen eva- nescere possit, ad Deum, qui eam dederat, tanquam ad omnis vitæ fontem, cum ab eo, cui data fuerat re- cedit, revertatur. Quæ vero glossa adeo putida est, ut puduerit ejusdem jam ipsos Socini discipulos, ac Smalcius ipse presse alias adhærens magistro suo insausto Socino agnoverit, de anima rationali locum accipiendum esse, ac aperte confirmare, animam ho- minis post mortem superstitem esse in refut. Franz. p. 409. 410. Vide quæ contra Socinum in Socinismo profligato de hoc loco diximus Sect. X. cit. 1. Contr. II. p. 1023. Creationem animarum hinc probare sa- tagunt Molineus, Arminius, Bellarminus, Fequer- nekinus, Bucanus, Calixtus, Hornejus, Dreierus, quam sententiam plurimum sibi arridere profite- tur h. l. Hackspan. sed refutavimus eam ex professo in Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica Sect. II. c. III. p. 461. seqq. Et recte observavit S. August. lib. X. de Gen. ad liter. c. IX. respondisse jam veteres Eccle- siæ Doctores redire Spiritum ad Deum, qui eum dedit homini primo, quando in ejus faciem suffla- vit, converso pulvere, id est, humano corpore in terram suam unde primitus factum est. Adde & Epist. CLVII. ut & XXIX. ad Hieron. ubi docet August. magis dictum illud favere propagationi animæ. Vid. quæ diximus l. c. p. 546.

## 12:8
Verse 8. VANITY OF VANITIES, SAID ECCLESIASTES, AND ALL IS VANITY) The Writer returns to that from which he had made his beginning, and having unfolded all the opinions which can come into a man's mind, he says that we can indeed use other things with moderation: but that he deserves the name of blessed, as far as this life admits, who in all things acts so as to please God: for in that is the sum of both wisdom and tranquility: follow God, the Pythagoreans used to say.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VANITAS VANITATUM, DIXIT EC- CLESIASTES, ET OMNIA VANITAS) Redit Scriptor ad id unde initium fecerat, evolutisque opinionibus omni- bus, quæ homini in mentem venire possunt, ait cæteris qui- dem rebus uti nos posse cum modo: eum autem beati nomen, quatenus hæc vita capit mereri, qui in omnibus id agit, ut Deo placeat: in eo enim esse summam tam sapientiæ, quam tran- quillitatis: θεῶ ἕπε dicebant Pythagorici.

## 12:9
HE TAUGHT THE PEOPLE] With many speeches, and also with many writings, which do not exist.

AND SEARCHING OUT HE COMPOSED MANY PARABLES] He collected excellent maxims from various writers, and added some himself from his own experience.

Verse 31. THE WORDS OF THE WISE ARE LIKE GOADS] Like goads they leave behind, which was once said of Pericles. The words of the wise, the useful teachings.

Latin:

DOCUIT POPULUM] Multis orationibus, multis et- iam scriptis, quæ non extant.

ET INVESTIGANS COMPOSUIT PARABOLAS MULTAS] Egregias γνώμας collegit ex variis scriptoribus, quasdam & ipse de sua experientia addidit.

Vers. 31. VERBA SAPIENTUM TANQVAM STI- MULI] Κέντροις ἐγκαταλείπεσι, quod de Pericle dictum olim. Verba sapientum, αἱ χρηςομάθειαι.

## 12:11
AND AS NAILS DRIVEN DEEP) Thus they stick in the memory because of their brevity and authority.

Verse of the same. WHICH BY THE COUNSELS OF MASTERS ARE GIVEN BY ONE SHEPHERD] In the Hebrew: The authors of the collections (the collectors) were given by one Shepherd: that is, those who were to collect these things, and under the person of Solomon heap them into one body, had a mandate from one shepherd, that is, as I think, Zerubbabel, who because of the meager circumstances of the Jews and the reverence for the Persian Empire, not daring to call himself King, although among his own he was held as King, usurped the more modest name of shepherd.

Latin:

ET QVASI CLAVI IN ALTUM DEFIXI) Ita hæ- rent memoriæ ob breviloquentiam & auctoritatem.

Vers. eod. QVÆ PER MAGISTRORUM CONSILIA DATA SUNT A PASTORE UNO] In Hebræo: Aucto- res collectionum (οἱ συλλογεῖς) dati sunt à Pastore uno: id est, qui hæc colligerent, ac sub persona Salomonis in unum cor- pus congererent mandatum habuere ab uno pastore, id est, ut puto Zorobabele, qui ob res tenues Judæorum & Persici Imperii reverentiam, Regem se dicere non ausus, quanquam inter suos pro Rege habebatur, nomen usurpavit modestius pastoris.

## 12:12
Verse 12. OF THESE MORE, MY SON, DO NOT SEEK) In the Hebrew: beware; but it is understood, do not seek. Let these suffice for you. He seems here to address Zerubbabel.

OF MAKING MANY BOOKS THERE IS NO END) If he said this in that age, what would he say now, if he were to inspect our libraries?

AND MUCH STUDY) Reading.

WEARINESS OF THE FLESH) If it is excessive, it harms health.

Latin:

Vers. 12. HIS AMPLIUS FILI MI NE REQVIRAS) In Hebræo: cave; sed intelligitur, ne quæras. Hæc tibi sufficiant. Abjudem videtur hic alloqui Zorobabel.

FACIENDI LIBROS NULLUS EST FINIS) Si hoc ea ætate dixit, quid nunc diceret, si nostras bibliothecas in- spiceret?

FREQVENSQVE MEDITATIO) Lectio.

CARNIS AFFLICTIO) Si nimia est, nocet sanitati.

## 12:13
Ver. 13. LET US HEAR THE CONCLUSION OF THE WHOLE MATTER) In the Hebrew: The end of the whole matter, which has now been heard (from you) is: this, namely, which follows. This is the sum, to which such a rambling dissertation will lead you.

FEAR GOD) That is, worship and revere him.

What is commonly said, that Africa always brings forth something new, you may most rightly apply to Grotius, though he is not an African but a Dutchman: of which same native soil Heinsius sang not inappropriately: whom Batavia, the mother, rightly shudders at and hardly believes she bore for herself. It was not enough to invent that the Ecclesiastes was written as eclogues of various writers, collected from diverse authors. He even dared to feign that these did not proceed from Solomon, whose name they bear on the front, but were proposed under the person of Solomon, as if the Holy Spirit had employed masked writers or pseudepigrapha for the Sacred Canon. Now he even invents various collectors, who, namely, reduced the book of Ecclesiastes into one body from various writers, which, as far as I know, has hitherto come into no one's mind regarding this book, since although diverse opinions about happiness are ventilated in it, the thing itself teaches that their discussion was not adorned here by diverse people, but by one writer. Finally, so that nothing should be lacking in his inventions, by a new and for so many centuries unheard-of discovery, which I believe never even entered the minds of the most fabulous Jews, he makes Zerubbabel the author of the book of Ecclesiastes, and feigns that he is the one shepherd indicated here, and that he is addressing his son Abjud. But if, against such open testimonies of Scripture as are read here—that these things proceeded from the King in Jerusalem, the son of David, who also speaks of himself throughout the whole book—it is permitted to fable that not Solomon but Zerubbabel speaks under the person of Solomon, what will finally be so clear in Scripture that it cannot be evaded by some invention? The author here has expressed himself most clearly, if in any sacred writing, at the beginning of the book, throughout the whole book, and finally now at the conclusion of the same, where it is proclaimed that Ecclesiastes was a wise man; which eulogy belongs to Solomon κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν (pre-eminently) 1 Kings 3:12, and that he taught the people the Scripture, i.e., he propagated wisdom to the whole people of Israel, both by living voice and by writings, and that he pondered and searched out (most accurately) and thus accumulated many parables: therefore, the same is the author of Ecclesiastes, to whom the continuation of the Parables or the book of Proverbs belongs, and neither are different collectors of the Parables established, but one author of them is designated, who is also called Ecclesiastes. By what right, therefore, can it be feigned that there were other collectors of Ecclesiastes, and another author, or even other authors of the book of Proverbs: It is proclaimed of Ecclesiastes that he studied to find acceptable words, and upright writings, and true words, and thus with the greatest zeal he searched out the Sacred Scriptures of Moses, Job, Samuel, and David, with which Solomon not only enriched his Wisdom, but also studied to propagate acceptable, upright, and true words, which he therefore included in books written by divine inspiration, for his God-given Wisdom, and those most wholesome and useful. And hence the words of those wise, God-breathed writers are celebrated, which Solomon studied to find, so that he might rightly investigate their meaning, and adapt them concisely to the Canonical use of the Church, and comprehend them in writings, because they are as sharp goads, by which our sloth is excited, and as nails fastened, since they not only penetrate hearts, but also remain firmly and most tenaciously fixed in them, and cling to our mind. Added are בעלי אספות, which some explain by apposition regarding the words of the wise, that they are called nails fastened, masters of collections, since the word בעל extends itself to any things whatsoever, among other eminent ones, because they obtain pre-eminence among other sentences, that is, most choice, as Junius interprets, or instruments or means, firmly gathering together things otherwise separated from one another, which exposition seems most simple to our Dr. Geier. Which Ludov. de Dieu also approves: What if בעלי אספות were an attribute of nails, which are called masters of collections: because by them things are gathered and joined together, which otherwise would remain separated? In this sense I would translate, and as nails driven in, by which joinings are made. Certainly those who do not attend to the words of the wise have a scattered mind, dissipated affections, and disturbed morals. All of which are gathered and joined together as if by driven nails, by the words of the wise. In which way nothing will be held here concerning collectors, whom Grotius imagines were appointed by Zerubbabel. Most, however, either refer these things to the wise, who are called masters or authors of collections, or to the nails driven in by the masters of collections, so that the preposition מ from is understood, which comes to the same thing: nor will Grotius's translation be bad if it is taken this way, taking these words absolutely, so that they neither adhere to the former by apposition, nor is there a need to understand any preposition, but they are connected with the following: the authors of collections were given by one Shepherd, here the same meaning can remain: Namely, that the authors who collected the sacred letters were given by one Shepherd; so that not Zerubbabel, who did not live in that age in which these things were written, but God is understood, by whom those authors were divinely appointed and inspired. But in truth the accent Athnach on the word אספות prevents these things from being construed in this way, whence no room is left for the translation, much less for the meaning, from that translation newly carved out by Grotius. The French version presents another interpretation. And the masters of congregations (that is, the Doctors of the Church) are as nails driven in. But Ecclesiastes is still engaged in the commendation of the Word of God, which even the things that are added prove: by which he teaches that those words of the Wise proceeded from God. Wherefore either a preposition is to be understood, which is not infrequent in the Hebrew text: that the words of the wise are as nails driven in, because namely they proceeded not by human work, but from the θεοπνεύστοις authors of collections; or whether those authors are now called given by one Shepherd through apposition, or this is referred to the words themselves, so that consequently along with the principal cause the ministerial authors are designated as Masters of collections: through whom, however, the Prophets can also be understood, although they are called masters of collections, because they taught the Church: although the opinion of those is simpler, who understand a collection of sentences, and thus wish the Prophets to be described by the collection of sacred monuments, not by the collection of the Church. Therefore the last words can be explained in three ways: either so that they cohere thus: the words of the wise are as nails driven in by the Masters of collections, given by one Shepherd; or they are simply connected thus; the Masters of collections (were, to wit) those wise men, whose words are as goads. But they were given by one Shepherd: they did not undertake that office of their own accord, but were divinely given and instructed for it: or finally so that these last words explain the authority of the words of the wise, they were given (those words) by one Shepherd. Which also pleased Ludovicus de Dieu: I construe the following נתנו מרעה אחד with דברי חכמים so that three things are said about the words of the Wise. 1. That they are like goads, 2. That they are like nails &c. 3. That they are given by one Shepherd. The first two convey the utility and efficacy, the third the authority of the words of the wise. Although interpreters vary here (without the sense being varied), yet almost all understand by the one Shepherd the supreme author of the Holy Scriptures himself ὁμοθυμαδὸν: namely, the Son of God, who came specifically by the name of Shepherd, Ezek. 34:23, Zech. 13:7, John 10, or the Triune God; for thus not only the ancients, Gregory Neo-Caesariensis and Jerome, explain it, but also more recent ones of our own, especially Osiander, the Vinarians, Mr. Dr. Gejer, etc., then among the Calvinists, Junius and the Belgian interpreters; and also among the Papists, Lyranus, Vatablus, Titelmannus, Saa, Ferus, Pineda, Menochius, Tirinus. Mercerus joins these to the preceding in this way: although there are many individual authors of the words of wisdom and of heavenly doctrine, yet there is one author of them all, namely the Lord, all things having been dictated by the Holy Spirit.
