He notes that the name of Shepherd is used so that the metaphor may be persisted in, because he had mentioned goads, with which shepherds goad their flocks. Where Zerubbabel is called ONE SHEPHERD, the place will not be shown. But Christ is openly called ONE SHEPHERD, Ezek. 34:23, ch. 37:24. Some indeed among the Hebrews understand Moses: but how could all the θεόπνευσα writings, which Solomon investigated, be referred to Moses, how will he be set over the masters of the collections, the θεοπνεύστοις writers, as the supreme author and one Shepherd, by whom the others were directed? But no one has been found who understood Zerubbabel and judged that he was called Shepherd for the sake of modesty: no one who dreamed that in v. 12 Abjudem the son of Zerubbabel was designated. Ecclesiastes speaks without doubt in this v. 12: Beyond these, MY SON, do not require. But shall we believe that Zerubbabel was Ecclesiastes? Grotius himself distinguishes Ecclesiastes or the author of this book, or rather the authors (because he makes several συλλογεῖς), from Zerubbabel, by whose command he says the book was collected: for I do not think Grotius believed that Zerubbabel spoke through the whole book and assumed the person of Solomon, although he was most prepared to invent everything, even the most πα- ράδοξα. Nor indeed does Ecclesiastes address his own son properly so called, or his natural son, but under the name of son he addresses a disciple, a hearer, and a reader, for whom he wishes to provide with fatherly affection, as a Doctor and spiritual Father, capturing benevolence with that very gentle name, which was customary for Solomon, Prov. 1:8, as also for other sacred writers, especially St. John, 1 Ep. 2:1, etc. But since Grotius confesses that those words, for beyond these, my son, require nothing, must be explained from the Hebrew in this way: beware, so that it is understood, do not seek. These will suffice for you: it is manifest that by these the sufficiency and perfection of the sacred letters is indicated, which Mercerus also observed: that one must acquiesce in them, so that you do not require others, i.e., be admonished, my son (to whom the apostrophe is directed, as is common in Proverbs), from those words of the wise: from these you will abundantly derive admonition, from here you will take in abundance those things by which you may be informed about any matters whatsoever. Allow yourself, therefore, to be abundantly admonished, taught, and instructed from the sacred books: acquiesce in them. For there is no end to other books being written daily, the reading of which does nothing but weary man. There are those who wish the Sanhedrin to be designated by these verses 13, 14, 15, by which the collection of the Biblical books was made. Indeed, since the Targum rendered that בעלי אספות as Masters of the Sanhedrin; as Jerome has it, the words of the Wise, which were given by the counsel of the MASTERS by one Shepherd. They judge, therefore, that that great Council is indicated, by which the Crown of the Law was restored and the Canon of the O.T. was constituted. And for that reason they think a παραίνεσιν is added, concerning other books not to be referred into

the Canon. But since Ecclesiastes has Solomon as its author, and thus was adorned long before the Babylonian captivity and the Synagogue by which the Canon is believed to have been constituted, that opinion does not deserve to be counted: yet perhaps the conjecture of our blessed Luther in his commentary on this place is not to be rejected, that long before that Sanhedrin and the times of Ezra, even Sacred Critics were constituted, who would select the books pertaining to the Canon, who are to be considered their predecessors, through whom the Canon of the O.T. was then completed in the time of Ezra; whence it is added here: See therefore, my son, whether you adhere to these books which have been received, but despise the rest (do not hold them in such a place that they are to be compared to these), nay, they were even despised by those wise men. We have spoken more fully about these in Crit. Sacr. p. 381, which can be compared here.

Vers. 13. AND KEEP HIS COMMANDMENTS) Do what he commanded either in that primeval law or in the law of Moses.

He brings in again the Noachian precepts, about which not a jot is found in the Scriptures. But the commandments are understood to be not only those which exhibit the legal will of God, but also those which exhibit the evangelical, without which there is no filial fear of God, nor can there be a true method of worshipping God. Cf. Ps. 19:9, 119:6, 19, 73, 86. For the Gospel teaches that nothing pleases God except faith in Christ, Gal. 5:6, Heb. 11:6. But the Law, having brought man to the knowledge of himself and justified him through faith, instructs him how he ought to fear God, and to live piously, justly, and soberly.

Vers. eod. FOR THIS IS EVERY MAN) In this is the whole of man, i.e., his good.

AND ALL THINGS THAT SHALL BE DONE) In the Hebrew, every work.

Latin:

Vers. 13. FINEM LOQVVENDI PARITER OMNES AUDIAMUS) In Hebræo: Finis rei totius, quæ nunc audita est (abs te) est: hoc sc. quod sequitur. Hæc summa est, quo tam vaga dissertatio te ducet.

DEUM TIME) Id est, cole, ac reverere.

Quod Vulgo dicitur Africa semper aliquid no- vi, rectissime Grotio etsi non Afro, sed Batavo ap- plices: de quo vero eodem natus solo Heinsius non præter rem cecinit: quem jure Batavia mater horret & haud credit se peperisse sibi. Non satis erat comminisci, scriptum Ecclesiastis eclogas esse va- riorum scriptorum, ex auctoribus diversis collectas. Fingere etiam ausus est, hæc non a Salomone profecta, cujus nomen in fronte gerunt, sed sub persona Sa- lomonis proposita, ac si personatos scriptores aut ψευδεπίγραφα ad Sacrum Canonem adhibuisset Spiritus Sanctus. Nunc etiam varios συλλογεῖς & collectores, qui sc. ex variis scriptoribus in unum cor- pus redegerunt librum Ecclesiastis, comminiscitur, quod hactenus nemini de hoc libro quantum sciam, in mentem venit, quum opiniones quidem diversæ de felicitate in eodem ventilentur, sed res ipsa do- ceat, eorum discussionem, non ab diversis hic ad- ornatum esse, sed ab uno scriptore. Denique ne quid commentis desit, novo & per tot secula inau- dito εὑρήματι, quod ne fabulosissimis Judæis qui- dem, credo, unquam in mentem venit, Zorobabe- lem auctorem libri Ecclesiastis facit, eumque pasto- rem unum hic indigitari, ac filium suum Abjudem alloqui fingit. Sed si contra tam aperta testimonia Scripturæ, qualia hic leguntur, quod a Rege in Je- rusalem, Davidis filio hæc profecta, qui etiam per totum librum de sese loquitur, fabulari licet, non Salomonem sed Zorobabelem sub persona Salo- monis loqui, quid tam apertum denique in Scriptu- ra erit, quod non commento aliquo eludi queat? Autor hic luculentissime, si in ullo scripto sacro, expsessus est, sub initium libri, per totum librum ac denique nunc sub conclusionem ejusdem, ubi prædi- catur, quod Ecclesiastes sapiens fuerit; quod elo- gium κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν Salomoni congruit I. Reg. III, 12. ac Scripturam populum docuerit, h. e. ad totum Israelis populum, tum voce viva, tum scriptis sapientiam propagavit, & perpenderit ac pervestigarit, (accu- ratissime) adeoque cumulavit parabolas multas: Idem ergo auctor est Ecclesiastes, cui continuatio Parabolarum vel liber Proverbiorum convenit, ne- que diversi συλλογεῖς constituuntur Parabolarum, sed unus earum auctor designatur, qui etiam Ec- clesiastes vocatur. Quo ergo jure fingi potest alios collectores fuisse Ecclesiastis, alium auctorem, vel au- ctores etiam alios libri Proverbiorum: Prædicatur Ecclesiastes, quod studuerit invenire verba desidera- bilia, & scripta recta, veraque verba, adeoque sum- mo studio indagarit Sacra scripta Mosis, Jobi, Sa- muelis, Davidis, quibus non tantum locupletavit Sapientiam suam Salomo, sed verba desiderabilia, recta, veraque etiam propagare studuerit, quæ pro- inde libris inspiratione divina scriptis complexus fuit, pro Sapientia sua θεοσδότῳ, iisque longe salu- berrimis atque utilissimis. Atque hinc celebrantur verba sapientum illorum Scriptorum θεοπνεύσων, quæ invenire studuit Salomo, ut sensum eorum re- cte investigaret, eaque ad usum Canonicum Ec- clesiæ concinne adaptaret, ac scriptis comprehen- deret, quod sint tanquam stimuli acuti, quibus no- stra desidia excitatur, & tanquam clavi infixi, quum non modo penetrant corda, sed firmiter ac tenacif- fime etiam iisdem infixa maneant, mentique no- stræ hæreant. Additur בעלי אספות quæ explicant nonnulli per appositionem de verbis sapientum, quod clavi infixi, domini collectionum dicantur, quum vox בעל ad res quasvis sese extendat, inter alias eminentes, quod inter alias sententias prædo- minium obtineant, id est, lectissima, ut interpreta- tur Junius, vel instrumenta aut media, firmiter res, alioquin disjunctas invicem colligentia, quæ exposi- tio simplicissima videtur Dn. D. Geiero nostro. Quam probat etiam Ludov. de Dieu: Quid si בעלי אספות sit attributum clavorum, qui dicantur domini col- lectionum: quia illis colliguntur & coagmentantur, quæ alias separata manerent? hoc sensu verterem, & sicut clavi infixi, quibus fiunt coagmentationes. Utique qui ad verba sapientum non attendunt, disper- sam habent mentem, dissipatos affectus, & disturba- tos mores. Quæ omnia colliguntur & coagmentantur quasi infixis clavis, verbis sapientum. Quo pacto ni- hil hic de collectoribus habebitur, quos a Zoro- babele constitutos fingit Grotius. Plerique tamen aut ad sapientes hæc referunt, qui domini vel aucto- res collectionum dicantur, aut ad clavos infixos a Do- minis collectionum ut subaudiatur præpositio מ ab quod eodem recidit: neque male Grotii sic habe- bit translatio, absolute hæc verba accipientis, ut neque per appositionem prioribus hæreant, neque opus sit subintelligere aliquam præpositionem, sed cum sequentibus connectantur: autores collectio- num dati sunt a Pastore uno, hic eadem manere po- test sententia: Quod nempe auctores, qui sacras li- teras collegerunt, a pastore uno dati sint; ut non Ze- rubabel, qui ista ætate non vixit, qua hæc scripta sunt, sed Deus intelligatur, a quo autores illi cæli- tus constituti, & inspirati sunt. Verum enimvero obstat accentus Athnach in voce אספות quo mi- nus hæc ita construi possint, unde locus non relin- quitur translationi, nedum sententiæ, ex illa trans- latione noviter exsculptæ Grotii. Aliam interpre- tationem exhibet Gallica versio. Et Domini con- gregationum (id est, Doctores Ecclesiæ) sunt tan- quam clavi fixi. Sed versatur Ecclesiastes adhuc in commendatione Verbi Dei, quod etiam ea, quæ adduntur, probant: quibus verba illa Sapientum a Deo profecta esse docet. Quapropter vel præpo- sitio subaudienda, quod non infrequens est in textu Ebræo: quod verba sapientum clavi infixi sint, quia nempe non humana opera, sed ab aucto- ribus collectionum θεοπνεύστοις profecta; sive jam per appositionem auctores illi dicantur a pastore uno dati, sive ad verba ipsa hoc referatur, ut proinde juxta cum causa principali autores ministeriales Magistri collectionum designentur: per quos tamen etiam intelligi poterunt Prophetæ, licet Domini col- lectionum dicantur, quod Ecclesiam docuerint: quanquam simplicior eorum sit sententia, qui col- lectionem sententiarum intelligunt, adeoque Pro- phetas a congregatione monumentorum sacrorum de- scribi volunt, non a collectione Ecclesiæ. Tribus mo- dis ergo postrema verba exponi possunt: vel ut ita cohæreant: verba sapientum clavi infixi a Magistris collectionum, datis a pastore uno; aut simpliciter ita connectantur; Magistri collectionum (fuerunt sc.) sapientes illi, quorum verba sunt tanquam stimuli. Dati autem sunt illi a Pastore uno: non suapte spon- te id suscepere munus, sed divinitus ad id dati & instructi sunt: aut denique ut postrema hæc verba auctoritatem verborum sapientum exponant, data sunt (verba illa) a Pastore uno. Quod etiam Lu- dovico de Dieu placuit: Quæ sequuntur נתנו מרעה אחד construo cum דברי חכמים adeo, ut de verbis Sapientum tria dicantur. 1. Quod sint sicut- stimuli, 2. Quod sint sicut clavi &c. 3. Quod data sint a Pastore uno. Duo priora utilitatem & efficaciam, tertium autoritatem tradit verborum sapientum. Etsi autem hic varient Interpp. (sensu non variato) Per pastorem tamen unum plerique omnes ipsum au- ctorem summum S. literarum ὁμοθυμαδὸν intelli- gunt: scil. Filium Dei, qui peculiariter Pastoris no- mine venit Ezech. 34, 23. Zach. 13, 7. Joh. 10. sive Deum Triunum, sic enim explicant non tantum veteres Gregorius Neo-Cæsar. & Hieronym. sed etiam recen- tiores Nostrates, imprimis Osiander, Vinarienses, Dn. D. Gejerus, &c. tum e Calvinianis Junius, & Belgæ Interpretes: nec non e Pontificiis Lyranus, Vatablus, Titelmannus, Saa, Ferus, Pineda, Menochius, Tirinus. Mercerus hæc ita superioribus jungit: etsi plures sint singuli sapientiæ verborum autores, & doctrinæ cælestis, est tamen omnium unus autor, nempe Dominus, omnia a Spiritu Sancto dictata. Pastor is autem nomen ad- hiberi notat, ut in metaphora persistatur, quia stimu- lorum meminerat, quibus Pastores pecora stimulant. Ubi Zorobabel UNUS PASTOR dicatur, non monstrabitur locus. Christus autem UNUS PA- STOR aperte vocatur Ez. 34, 23. cap. 37, 24. Non- nulli quidem ex Ebræis Mosen intelligunt: sed quo- modo omnia θεόπνευσα scripta, quæ indagavit Sa- lomo, ad Mosen referri poterunt, quomodo ille Ma- gistris collectionum scriptoribus θεοπνεύστοις præ- ficietur, tanquam autor summus, ac Pastor unus, a quo cæteri directi sunt? Nemo autem inventus est, qui Zorobabelem intellexerit, & modestiæ causa Pa- storem dictum censuerit: nemo, qui v. 12. Abjudem filium Zorobabelis designari somniarit. Loquitur sine dubio hoc v. 12. Ecclesiastes: His amplius FILI MI ne requiras. Num autem Zorobabelem fuisse Ec- clesiasten credemus? Distinguit ipse Grotius Eccle- siasten vel auctorem hujus libri, aut potius auctores (quia plures συλλογεῖς facit) a Zorobabele, cujus mandato librum collectum dicit: neque enim opi- nor credidit Grotius, Zorobabelem per totum li- brum loqui, & personam Salomonis affumsisse, quanquam ad omnia fingenda, etiam maxime πα- ράδοξα paratissimus fuerit. Nec vero Filium suum proprie ita dictum, aut naturalem alloquitur Eccle- siastes, sed filii nomine compellat discipulum, audi- torem, & lectorem, cui paterno affectu consultum cupit, ceu Doctor ac Pater spiritualis, nomine isto admodum blando benevolentiam captans, quod Salomoni solenne fuit Prov. 1, 8. ut & aliis sacris Scri- ptoribus, cumprimis S. Joh. 1. Ep. 2, 1. &c. Quum au- tem fateatur Grotius verba illa, his enim amplius, fili mi, nihil requiras, ita ex Hebræo explicanda esse: ca- ve, ut subintelligatur, ne quæras. Hæc tibi sufficient: manifestum est, istis sufficientiam & perfectionem sa- crarum literarum indigitari, quod etiam Mercerus observavit: acquiescendum esse iisdem, ita ut non alia requiras, q. d. satis superque ex illis verbis sapientum, fili mi, (ad quem apostrophe dirigetur, ut passim in Proverbiis) admonitus esto: ex his abunde referes ad- monitionem, hinc sumes affatim, quibus informeris de quibusvis rebus. Sine ergo te abunde ex libris sacris admoneri, & doceri ac erudiri: in illis acquiesce. Nam aliorum librorum quotidie scribendorum non est finis, quorum lectio nihil nisi hominem fatigat. Sunt, qui his vers. 13. 14. 15. designatum volunt Synedrium, a quo facta sit librorum Biblicorum collectio. Si- quidem Targum illud בעלי אספות reddiderit רבני סנהדרין Magistri Synedrii; uti Hieronymus habet, verba Sapientum, quæ per MAGISTRO- RUM consilium data sunt a Pastore uno. Censent ergo Concilium illud magnum indigitari, a quo Co- rona legis restituta ac Canon V. T. constitutus. Et ob eam causam addi putant παραίνεσιν, de aliis libris in

Canonem non referendis. At quum Ecclesiastes autorem habeat Salomonem, adeoque longe ante ca- ptivitatem Babylonicam, & Synagogam, a qua con- stitutus creditur Canon, adornatus sit, Sententia illa calculum non meretur: non tamen respuenda for- tassis conjectura B. Lutheri nostri in comment. ad h.l. quod longe ante illud Synedrium, & Esdræ tem- pora Critici etiam Sacri constituti fuerint, qui seli- gerent libros ad Canonem spectantes, qui anteces- fores eorum habendi, per quos deinde Esdræ tem- pore completus fuerit Canon V. Test. unde hic ad- datur: Vide ergo, mi fili, an adhæreas istis libris, qui sunt recepti, reliquos autem contemnas, (non habeas eo lo- co, ut istis comparandi sint) quin & a Viris istis sapi- entibus comtemti sunt. Diximus de his uberius Crit. Sacr. p. 381. qui hic conferri poterit.

Vers. 13. ET MANDATA EJVS CVSTODI) Fac quæ jussit aut in primæva illa lege, aut in lege Mosis.

Ingerit iterum præcepta Noachdata, de quibus ne gry in Sacris habetur. Mandata autem intelli- guntur non solum, quæ voluntatem Dei legalem, sed etiam quæ Evangelicam exhibent, sine qua timor Dei filialis nullus est, nec vera colendi Deum ratio habe- ri potest. Conf. Ps. 19, 9. 119, 6. 19. 73. 86. Evange- lium enim docet, non placere Deo quicquam nisi fidem in Christum, Gal. 5, 6. Ebr. 11, 6. Lex autem hominem ad sui agnitionem adductum & per fidem justificatum erudit, quomodo Deum timere, pie, ju- ste ac sobrie vivere debeat.

Vers. eod. HOC EST ENIM OMNIS HOMO) In eo est totum hominis, scil. bonum.

ET CVNCTA QVÆ FIENT) In Hebr. opus omne.

## 12:14
GOD WILL BRING INTO JUDGMENT) Sooner or later, as it shall seem good to him, see above 11:9.

FOR EVERY ERROR, WHETHER THAT BE GOOD OR EVIL) In the Hebrew, Also every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil. Thales, being asked whether anyone could hide from God while doing something, or even thinking it, said: He is the overseer of us, according to Epicharmus.

Thus he also explains this statement concerning the particular judgment, which speaks most clearly of the universal judgment of God, and is explained by the interpreters. For he teaches that not certain things, but all things, everything that will be done, or as in the Hebrew, EVERY WORK, will be brought into judgment, even every hidden thing, whether it be good or evil: which will happen on that day of universal judgment, when even the hidden counsels of the heart will be made manifest. 1 Cor. 4, 5. St. Augustine, book 20, On the City of God, ch. 3. What could have been said more briefly, more truly, more wholesomely? Fear God, he says, and keep his commandments, because this is the whole man. For whoever is a man is a keeper of the commandments of God, since he who is not this, is nothing. For he is not reformed to the image of truth, remaining in the likeness of vanity. Because God will bring every such work, that is, everything that is done by man in this life whether good or evil, into judgment. Jerome notes in this place that the Hebrews also interpret this concerning the final and universal judgment. But also concerning this book. In every kind of our life, Hilary warns in his commentary on Psalm 118, the memory of the divine judgment must be implanted and contained within us, so that when we do anything, with the memory of judgment residing in us, or rather never departing, our works may serve the commandments of God. BLESSED will he be, whoever has done all things not without the memory of the divine judgment. BEHOLD I COME AS A THIEF. BLESSED IS HE THAT WATCHETH (Rev. 16, 15.) BEHOLD I COME QUICKLY, AND MY REWARD IS WITH ME, TO RENDER TO EVERY MAN ACCORDING TO HIS WORKS (Rev. 22, 12.) I conclude with St. Augustine: Lord, thy coming is horrible, and thy Majesty is formidable; I too would fear thy justice and judgment, unless mercy and truth went before thy face. Thy mercy blots out my sins, thy truth grants the grace which thou hast promised to the sinner RESTING IN THY WOUNDS. AMEN, Lord JESUS, Amen.

Latin:

ADDVCET DEVS IN-JVDICIVM) Citius aut tar- dius, ut ipsi videbitur, vid. supra 11, 9.

PRO OMNI ERRATO, SIVE BONVM, SIVE MA- LVM ILLVD SIT) In Hebr. Etiam omne occultum, sive bonum, sive malum sit. Thales interrogatus, an quis latere Deo posset aliquid faciens, ne cogitans quidem, inquit. αὐτὸς ἴσθ᾽ ἁμῶν ἐπόπτης, juxta Epicharmum.

Ita hoc etiam dictum de particulari Judicio ex- plicat, quod de judicio Dei universali apertissime lo- quitur, & ab Interpp. explicatur. Docet enim non quædam, sed omnia, cuncta quæ fient, vel ut in Ebræo, OPUS OMNE, adductum iri in judicium, etiam omne occultum, sive bonum, sive malum sit: quod fiet in die illo Pantocritico, cum occulta etiam consilia cordis patefient. 1. Cor. 4, 5. S. August. l. 20. de Civit. Dei c. 3. Quid brevius, verius, salubrius dici potuit? Deum, inquit, time, & mandata ejus custodi, quia hoc est omnis sermo. Quicunque enim est homo, est custos mandatorum Dei, quoniam qui hoc non est, nihil est. Non enim ad veritatis imaginem reformatur, remanens in similitudine vanitatis. Quia omne hoc opus, h. e. omne quod fit ab homine in hac vita sive bonum sive ma- lum, Deus adducet in judicium. De extremo & uni- versali judicio etiam exponere Ebræos notat Hieron. in h. l. Sed etiam de hoc libro. In omni vitæ no- stræ genere monet Hilar. in enar. Ps. 118. memoria divini judicii nobis inserenda, & continenda est, ut cum aliquid agimus residente in nobis judicii memoria, vel nunquam potius abeunte præceptis Dei opera nostra famulentur. BEATUS erit, quisquis non sine memoria divini judicii omnia gesserit. ECCE VENIO SICUT FUR. BEA- TUS QUI VIGILAT (Ap. 16, 15.) ECCE VENIO CITO, ET MERCES MEA MECUM EST, RED- DERE UNICUIQUE SECUNDUM OPERA SUA (Ap. 22, 12.) Finio cum S. August. Domine, hor- ribilis est adventus tuus, & formidabilis est Majestas tua, Ego quoq; tuam timerem justitiam, & judicium, nisi fa- ciem tuam antecederet misericordia, & veritas. Miseri- cordia tua delet peccata mea, veritas tua præstat, quam peccatori in VULNERIBUS TUIS RECUMBENTI promisisti gratiam. AMEN, Domine JESU, Amen.

# Song of Songs

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. ON THE SONG OF SONGS, ANNOTATIONS BY D. ABRAHAM CALOVIUS, REFUTING GROTIUS

Latin:

I. IN A CANTICUM C ANNOTATA ET GROTIANOR D. ABRAHAM

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface of Grotius
PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

This poem is called by the Hebrews the most excellent poem, on account of many elegances which, when translated into another language, do not taste the same. It is, however, an ὀαριστὺς between Solomon and the daughter of the King of Egypt, with two choirs also speaking in turn, both of young men and of virgins, who were sleeping in the places nearest to the bridal chamber. The secrets of the marriage lie hidden here under honest coverings of words: which is also the reason why the ancient Hebrews did not want this book to be read except by those already close to marriage. It is believed, however, that Solomon, the more to perpetuate this writing, composed it with such art that, without much distortion, there could be found in it by ἀλληγορίᾳ those things which expressed God's love toward the Israelite people: which the Chaldean Paraphrast here both sensed and showed: nor did Maimonides accept it otherwise. But since that love was a type of the love of Christ toward the Church, Christians have exercised their talents in applying the words of this poem to that matter, with praiseworthy zeal. For the Apostles also had compared the union of Christ with the Church to a marriage. Eph. 5, 32. 2 Cor. 11, 2. Rev. 19, 7. 9.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTII.

CArmen hoc vocatur Ebræis excellentissimum carmen, ob multas elegantias, quæ in alium sermonem translatæ non idem sapiunt. Est autem ὀαριστὺς inter Salomonem & filiam Regis Ægypti, interloquentibus etiam choris duobus tum juvenum, tum virginum, qui in proximis thalamo locis ex- cubabant. Nuptiarum arcana sub honestis verborum in- volucris hîc latent: quæ etiam causa est, cur Hebræi veteres hunc librum legi noluerint, nisi à jam conjugio proximis. Creditur autem Salomon, quo magis perennaret hoc scri- ptum, ea arte id composuisse, ut sine multa distortione ἀλλη- γορίᾳ in eo inveniri possent, quæ Dei amorem adversus po- pulum Israëliticum exprimerent: quod & sensit, & ostendit Chaldæus hic Paraphrastes: nec aliter accepit Maimonides. Ille autem amor typus cum fuerit amoris Christi erga Eccle- siam, Christiani ingenia sua ad applicanda ad eam rem hujus carminis verba exercuerunt, landabili studio. Nam & Apo- stoli Christi cum Ecclesia conjunctionem matrimonio com- paraverant. Ephes. 5, 32. 2. Cor. 11, 2. Apocal. 19, 7. 9.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations on the Preface of Grotius
OBSERVATIONS ON THE PREFACE OF GROTIUS.

That this poem is called by the Hebrews the most excellent poem on account of many elegances, Grotius does not say badly: but that is not the chief, much less the only, reason for the naming of this Song. Nor is it called the most excellent poem in the inscription, but the Song of Songs: and that not only because it abounds in many elegances, beyond others, but because it is simply the chief and most excellent among all the Songs in the Holy Scriptures. Of which the Targum here lists ten from the whole Scripture, although more are found altogether, besides the Psalms, Ex. 15, 1. Num. 21, 17. 18. Deut. 32, 1. seqq. Josh. 10, 12. (which the Chaldean observes was sung by Joshua when, for his sake, the Sun and Moon stood still for thirty-six hours) Jud. 5, 2. 1 Sam. 2, 1. 2 Sam. 22, 3. 1 Chron. 16, 8. Is. 12, 1. c. 26, 1. c. 30, 29. c. 42, 10. &c.

Nor indeed does the present Song excel only among all the songs of Solomon, who is read to have written a thousand and five, 1 Kings 4, 32, because it was adopted into the number of Canonical books above all the rest, but it must deservedly be held the most eminent Song among all that have ever been written; and that not so much on account of the elegance of the words and the charm of the artifice, as on account of the richness of the mysteries which it contains, because the highest and most eminent mysteries are brought forth in this Song with most excellent artifice, and in words breathing the most profound wisdom of things, so that no song has ever been found that deserves to be compared with this, much less to be preferred to it, whether we look at the hidden riches of the mysteries, or the most sweet and most effective mystical veils of the words, or the most convenient and elegant manner of proposing and singing the things which it exhibits. Concerning which Mercerus judged not without reason: If you weigh the other songs of Scripture more diligently, you will find almost individual mysteries in them, but here you will find all the mysteries of both the Old and the New Law covered under figures and similitudes, both those which have happened and those which are to happen. The Hebrews certainly in the Midrash say

N. 7. ON THE GROTIAN [ANNOTATIONS] OF THE SONG OF SONGS, REFUTING THEM BY CALOVIUS.

that before Solomon the law was not sufficiently understood, until he came along to illustrate it with his parables and similitudes: which, although it is not to be believed concerning the holy Patriarchs, concerning Moses and Aaron, concerning Samuel and David, it appears nevertheless that the hidden wisdom of this book is highly valued among the Rabbis themselves, who otherwise are vehemently blind in the Prophetic Writings. And the ancient Doctors of the Church honor this book with distinguished eulogies, celebrating it above other sacred books on account of the mysteries which are hidden in it, and for that reason pronouncing with unanimous opinion that this title of the Song of Songs is attributed to it. Whom Grotius ought deservedly to have heard here. Dionysius, Epist. 9 to Titus, says that the book of the Song of Songs contains mysteries full of the divine light of hidden Theology, yet veiled by various metaphors and similitudes, by which he most excellently indicates such mysteries. Gregor. Nyssenus Homil. 1. in Cantic. As in the holy of holies we are reminded by that superlative appellation of a certain abundance and amplitude of holiness: so also by the appellation of the Song of Songs, this sublime book promises that it will deliver to us certain most secret mysteries. Justus Orgelitanus, Preface to Commentary on the Canticles. The sacraments of this book are recognized as being very inscrutable and involved, not without reason in the very prefixing of the title. The Song of Songs is prescribed, because it is produced without any doubt as more eminent than the others. For it is veiled by very many and almost unusual mysteries, beyond the custom of other Scriptures, so that unless Christ presides over the senses, they cannot be investigated even by the most subtle inner chambers of the intellects. Bernhard. serm. 1. in Cantic. There is bread in Solomon, and that very splendid and tasty: I mean the book which is inscribed the Song of Songs, etc. Similar praises are read in Origen, homil. in Cant., Cassiodorus in Cant. Comment., Gregory the Great, Prologue in Cant., Isidore of Seville, book 6, Etymol. ch. 2, and others.

That Solomon is the author is certain from the title. Nor does Grotius deny this; who, although he adjudges Ecclesiastes away from Solomon, as has been said, on account of frivolous conjectures, nevertheless ascribes this Song to Solomon as author. The author of the Midrash explains לשלמה as concerning Solomon, but he wishes this name to be sacred, in this sense: concerning the Lord Messiah, or the King, whose is peace: or the peacemaker. But just as מזמור לדוד is a Song not about David, but of David, so also here the author is indicated, and not the object of this Song: which Grotius also acknowledges. For the genitive case is accustomed to be expressed in Hebrew also by ל, as Psalm 90:1, Hab. 3:1. Compare Gen. 7:11, Job 30:24, Psal. 120:1, Ezra 10:3, Mal. 3:8. Although some in the Psalms wish the dative case to imply at the same time the principal cause of the Holy Spirit, as if to say, a Psalm inspired to David by God, such as Lipomanus, Titelmannus, Genebrardus, Bellarminus; thus this Song will be implied as inspired by the Holy Spirit to Solomon.

But the Midrash most correctly makes the Messiah the object, approaching the interpretation of the Christians, whereas on the contrary Grotius constitutes Solomon himself as the object and argument, being of the same mind as the opinions of certain other Rabbis, and throughout this whole Song remarkably Judaizing with them.

He establishes, however, as it appears, a triple sense of the Canticle: The first is the literal one, concerning King Solomon himself and the daughter of the King of Egypt, the Bride. The second is the allegorical one, concerning the love of God toward the Israelite people, which he maintains was expressed under the words of the Canticle with study and not without singular artifice, and thus was even intended by Solomon himself. The third is the typical one, concerning the love of Christ toward the Church, which he does not disapprove of, insofar as Christians have endeavored to apply the words of this song to that matter. But how can not only a double, but a triple sense of the same statement be established, intended by the Holy Spirit? If it is to be believed that all those things were intended and signified by the same words, will the Holy Spirit not have spoken ambiguously on purpose with the same words, designating not one, but three distinct objects—for example, by the Bridegroom, Solomon, God, and Christ; by the Bride, the daughter of Pharaoh, the Israelite people, and the Church of the New Testament or of all times—so that he has played with mere ambiguities through all the words of the Canticle? Nor is there any reason for Grotius to say that there is only one sense, concerning Solomon, but that the words were composed by Solomon with such art that the love of God toward the people would be expressed, yet that this sense was not precisely intended by the Holy Spirit. For thus Solomon, the ministerial author, would have intended one thing, and the Holy Spirit, the principal author, another. And shall we believe that the Holy Spirit wished to consecrate for the canonical and perpetual use of the Church a Canticle so prolixly adorned concerning the love of Solomon and an exotic Bride, or that Solomon labored with peculiar art to that end, or rather that the Holy Spirit himself did so, in order that the Israelites might be persuaded that it was sung concerning the love of God toward the people, when it was sung not of divine love, but of the mutual human loves of a Bridegroom and Bride, and that thus, by the simulation of another sense, he sought the favor of the Israelites, and for this end, as Grotius trifles, that the Canticle of Solomonic love toward his Bride might endure? The Holy Spirit had no need of peculiar artifice so that the books which He destined for the perpetual Canon of the Church might endure.

Thus, while Grotius conceived everything in a profane manner concerning this most holy Canticle, he slipped into that profane opinion regarding the intention, scope, and argument of the Canticle, by which its divine authority is utterly overturned. And what else did he do in his annotations than to profane the most holy Canticle thoroughly, with a mind certainly by no means pious or Christian? For example, while at verse 6, 'lest I begin to wander after the flocks of thy companions': this, he says, is said in jest like that of Catullus: 'Lest she go to be sought elsewhere': and at verse 7, 'feed thy kids, satisfy thy appetite,' whence the word τραγίζειν. Horace, 'To play like a wanton she-goat'; of which kind more occur in these annotations on the most holy Canticle. What do those things proclaim, if not the profane mind of the Annotator? Who also does not appoint as interpreters of this divine Canticle the Prophets or Apostles, or the Prophetic Spirit, according to the Petrine prescription in 2 Epistle 1, but profane poets: Catullus, Horace, Theocritus, Claudian, Virgil, Tibullus, Martial, Silentiarius, Ovid, who in almost all these annotations tinkle with their amatory and other verses. Not undeservedly, therefore, is Grotius to be noted with a similar censure to that with which Antonio Possevino, along with Del Rio, in Tom. 2 of the Apparatus Sacer, p. 372, noted Sebastian Castellio: 'Castellio (Grotius), an enemy to holy things, has dared with his wanton and prurient interpretations to clamor against those who establish the Canticle of Canticles as a precious treasure of divine mysteries.' And we certainly use with better right concerning Grotius what Sixtus Senensis wrote in Bibliotheca, book 6, heresy 13, p. 664, concerning Castellio: 'It is no wonder if Castellio (Grotius) has played so immoderately in divine matters, as if with Catullus concerning Lesbia's sparrow and the girl's swelling little eyes and the golden apple, because, as he himself indicated in his little glosses, he never believed that the mystical loves of Christ and the Church were described in that divine Canticle, but that he wove an amatory dialogue concerning the venereal and profane loves of Solomon and his Sulamite friend, and the loves of her women.'

Now, as regards the allegorical explanation of the love of God toward the Israelite polity, since it, according to Grotius, presupposes the literal sense concerning the love of Solomon and the Bride, but this is destitute of any foundation and is in no way to be admitted in so holy and divine a Canticle, that allegory also collapses. Nor do the things that occur in the Canticle sufficiently agree with the Jewish polity, unless there is need of a distorted explanation, which is not to be borne in the Holy Scriptures. Wherefore it remains that it be explained concerning the love of Christ and the Church, which has been done by the common consent of the ancient and modern Doctors of the Church until now: not merely by some accommodation—for no one will deny that that is worthy of praise even in histories and any oracles whatsoever, where something at least occurs that can be accommodated or has the nature of a type—but because they believed that this is the true and genuine sense of the Canticle intended by the Holy Spirit.

The opinion of Grotius, however, is woven together from diverse interpretations, both of Jews, and of heretics, and of the orthodox, as he loves to join together things that are inconsistent in religion just as in the interpretation of Scripture everywhere. For that certain heretics explained the Canticle concerning Solomon and the daughter of the King of Egypt, Theodoret is the author in his preface to the Canticle, whom Philastrius refutes in his work on heresies, chapter 131, and compares to unlearned Jews in chapter 145. And that heresy is attributed to Theodore of Mopsuestia in the Second Council of Constantinople, Collation 4, which the Anabaptists renewed, as witnessed by Jodocus Coccius, Vol. 1, Thesaurus, chapter 6, article 8, and Sixtus Senensis, book 8, Bibliotheca Sancta, heresy 8, p. 645. The first sense, therefore, which he calls literal, Grotius owes to heretics.

The second [interpretation], which is allegorical to the same, he received from the Jews, who explain it only concerning God and the Synagogue, or the Israelite people, because they do not acknowledge Christ and his new people, which Lyranus and Mercerus note. Although indeed the blessed Luther thinks that in this Canticle also God is established as the Bridegroom and his people as the Bride, Tom. 4. Jen. Lat. in comment. of the year 1536, p. 268, yet he teaches that the spiritual kingdom of Christ is also regarded in the same, at the words of chapter 1, 'Our little sister,' and he explained the Bride as the Church of the New Testament in Tesseradec. Consol. Tab. 1. cap. 11. Tom. 1. Jenens. Lat. fol. 399. Finally, the heart must be lifted up and one must ascend into the mountain of Myrrh with the Bride. This is Jesus Christ crucified, the head of all the saints, the Prince of all who suffer, of whom many have written many things, and all have written everything, as is fitting. The memory of him is commended to the Bride, where it is said: 'Set me as a seal upon your heart, and as a seal upon your arm.' The blood of this lamb, marked in the light, wards off the striking Angel. By this the Bride is commended, that her hair is like the purple of the King (i. e., her meditation is red with the memory of the passion of Christ). This is the wood which Moses was commanded to cast into the waters of Mara, i. e., bitter passions, and they were made sweet. There is nothing that this passion does not sweeten, even death, as the Bride says: 'His lips are lilies dropping the first myrrh.' What is the proportion of lilies and lips, when the latter are red and the former are white? Certainly she speaks mystically, that the words are most white and most pure, in which there is nothing of muddy bitterness or malice, but they are sweet and mild, by which nevertheless he may drop and persuade the first and chosen myrrh, i. e., most bitter death; these most pure and most sweet lips are powerful, [to make] most bitter death (which is like the first myrrh removes all the stench of sin at once) sweet, bright, white, and acceptable. Add to these things which are read in Vol. 2 of the Jena German [edition], fol. 338, on ch. 2 of the first Epistle of Peter: 'But the breasts that give forth this milk and suckle the young children are the preachers in Christendom, as the Bridegroom says to the Bride, Cant. 3: Thou hast two breasts, like two young roes, which shall have a bundle of myrrh hanging about them, as the Bride says, Cant. 1.' 'My beloved is like a bundle of myrrh that hangs between my breasts,' that is, that one must always preach Christ; the Bridegroom must be mingled in the midst of the breasts, otherwise it is wrong, and the milk is falsified if one does not preach Christ purely. This happens, then, in this way: when one preaches that Christ died for us and has saved us from sin, death, and hell, that is pleasant and sweet like milk.

Grotius adopted a third sense from the Christians, which, however, if we weigh the matter correctly, he himself does not hold as the sense of Solomon's text, but as an application to the Church of Christ of those things which he judges to have been said literally about the people of God under an allegory, or more truly about the Bride of Solomon.

Moreover, that this is not treated here according to the letter concerning the earthly or external love of Solomon and his Egyptian Bride, or some virgin of Shulam or Jerusalem (as others wish), but concerning the love of Christ toward the Church, many things in the New Testament teach. (1) The Bridegroom here is also King, ch. 1, 4, 12; ch. 3, 9, 11; and at the same time Shepherd, ch. 1, 7, which fits Christ perfectly, Ps. 2, 5; John 10, 12; Ezek. 34; but Solomon by no means (who was never a Shepherd, let alone when he was King). (2) The Bride is both Queen and keeper of the vineyard, Cant. 1, 7, and she feeds the flock of sheep, v. 8; then she is struck and wounded by the watchmen of the city, the keepers of the walls take away her mantle, ch. 5, 6; how can these things be taken literally concerning the Bride and wife of the King and most powerful Queen? (3) The brother of this Bride is Solomon, sucking the breasts of her mother, whom he himself desires to kiss, ch. 8, 1, and she is called his sister, ch. 3, 12, 'A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse!' ch. 8, 8. What shall we do for our sister? which in no way fits the spouse of Solomon. (4) Who will believe that Solomon so praised himself: that he is white and ruddy, the chosen one out of thousands, ch. 5, 10? (5) The beauty of the Bride is described in such a way that it shines more brightly than the midday sun, [so that it] cannot be understood literally concerning bodily and external beauty. For those things which are celebrated here concerning the head, nose, eyes, teeth, neck, breasts, and belly of the Bride do not imply bodily beauty, but remarkable deformity, see ch. 4, 2; ch. 5, 7; ch. 6, 5; ch. 7, 2, 4; 8, 10. E.g., when Solomon gives her a head like Carmel, a nose like a tower, eyes like a pool, teeth like flocks of shorn sheep, etc. (6) It does not fit the Bride of Solomon, which is held in ch. 1, 5: 'I am black, but comely, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon; do not consider me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me,' etc. (7) If they are explained according to the letter concerning the Bride of Solomon, many conflicting and inconsistent things will occur, v. 9, that she herself is the daughter of a prince, ch. 7, 1, and is described as the daughter of a shepherd, ch. 1, 6; that she is terrible as an army of camps, ch. 6, 9; and that she was wounded by the watchmen, ch. 6, 7; and other things of this kind that occur. (8) Loves and pleasures are described here in such a way that it would be a matter of conscience to take them literally concerning bodily and external love and temporal pleasures. For such things would not be ascribed to a sacred Canticle, or a divine and Canonical writing, without impiety. Concerning which Lyra warned most correctly in the Preface to his Commentary on this place: 'Although this love of Solomon and the daughter of Pharaoh could have been lawful, as being contained within the limits of marriage, nevertheless it was carnal, and such love frequently has something dishonest and illicit attached to it.' on account of which such a description of love does not seem to pertain to the Canonical books of Holy Scripture: especially because books of this kind were written by the dictation of the Holy Spirit, etc.

(9) Who the Bridegroom is, and who the Bride is, about whom it is sung here, cannot be judged more correctly than from the interpretation of the Holy Spirit, who everywhere testifies that Christ is the Bridegroom, and the Church, and especially that which is of the New Testament, is the bride, and celebrates their marriage and mutual and mystical loves. Ps. 68, 13; Isa. 54, 5; ch. 61, 10, 11, 12; ch. 62, 4, 5; Jer. 1, 21; ch. 2, 32, 38, 41; Ezek. 16, 8; Hos. 2, 16, 19; ch. 14, 1; Matt. 9, 15; ch. 22, 2; ch. 25, 1; John 3, 28, 29, 30; 2 Cor. 11, 2; Eph. 5, 23, 25, 31, 32; Rev. 19, 7; ch. 21, 2; ch. 22, 17, 20.

(10) That remarkable harmony which exists between this canticle and Ps. 45, which the blessed Gerhard exhibited as a type in his preface to the Postilla on Solomon ch. 5, sufficiently teaches that it is sung here of no other Bridegroom than the Messiah, of whom it is treated in the aforementioned Psalm: so much so that it could appear that Solomon decided here to adorn a commentary on that spiritual epithalamium of his father.

(11.) Since the Holy Spirit everywhere in other Scriptures explains those things which are contained in this Canticle concerning spiritual love, in such a way that He even uses the same or similar words, that parallelism and harmony is no obscure indication that the same love is treated in this Canticle, and since on the contrary it is nowhere explained as concerning any other secular or external love, what else can be concluded from this than that it by no means treats of secular love, but only of mystical and spiritual love. For the interpretation of Scripture is not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, 2 Pet. 1, 21. Who will believe that a typical accommodation is so frequently handed down in the Scriptures with the same and analogous words, but that a historical, literal sense, properly and directly intended by the Holy Spirit, is not proposed even once in the Holy Scriptures? That the matter may be more manifest, let one compare the places previously cited with this Canticle, and it will be in the open that not a few things from it are repeated elsewhere in the Scriptures and explained concerning spiritual love. Thus, what is held in Cant. 4, 7 concerning the beauty of the Bride is explained in Eph. 5, 27 concerning the spiritual beauty of the Church. Similar to the invitation of the bridegroom and the response of the same in Cant. 5, 1 is the invitation and response in Apoc. 22, 17. 20. What is held concerning the Bridegroom knocking at the door in Cant. 5, 2, corresponds to those things which are read in Apoc. 3, 20, etc.

(12) All things which are said in this Canticle most openly agree with the spiritual love of Christ and the Church, or of a faithful soul, according to the emphasis of the words, the phraseology of Scripture, and the analogy of other places, just as interpreters show everywhere. But not all things agree with the love of Solomon toward the daughter of Pharaoh, whether you look to the proper sense of the words or the parallelism of other places according to hermeneutical laws. Then indeed, even if some things perhaps agree, that nevertheless by no means suffices for it to be concluded that the love of Solomon is sung here. For it would be necessary that all things agree with it. Nor indeed is the question whether things similar to those which are held in the Canticle regarding the proper sense are found in marriage and connubial love? Or whether Solomon, on the occasion and in the sense of the sweetness of his own connubial love, sang of the most sweet and chaste love of the mystical bridegroom? which could be conceded without detriment to the true and genuine sense intended by the Holy Spirit in this Canticle, just as any believer, while in the reading and meditation of the Canticle, sets before his mind the sweetness of that ineffable love, considers the chaste and modest love which a Bridegroom and Bride mutually cherish between themselves, and in his own marriage and love can constitute for himself a type and a certain image of the same, with the Apostle leading the way in Eph. 5:25 ff. But the question is concerning this: whether the Holy Spirit intended by these words to describe directly the earthly or external love of Solomon and his Bride? Or whether this sense is the proper and literal one, properly intended in this Song? That is, whether the Holy Spirit here intended to write an epithalamium for Solomon, or rather for the Messiah, or for both, so that it describes the love of Solomon indeed properly and directly, but at the same time typically designates the love of Christ, of whom Solomon was a type? We do not entirely deny that Solomon was a type of Christ in his love also toward his spouse in a certain respect, but we deny that that type or the love of Solomon is described here. It is one thing by far for a thing expressed by words to be a type: it is another thing for the words themselves to contain a typical sense, and besides the literal sense, to also need to be explained typically. Nor do we deny that, in order for the parabolic sense—which we believe to be the literal one here, and the one primarily intended by the Holy Spirit—to be elicited, it is required that one be concerned first with the husk of the letter, if that is said to be done at least for this end, that the kernel, once that is opened, may be elicited, which the Holy Spirit exhibits for us to taste under that husk. We concede an allegory here entirely, which, since it has a foundation in the thing, and therefore such things can be found in connubial love, and some things can also be found in some bride that occur here, can be admitted: but they are assumed and supposed here rather than signified by the words, as those are taken in this place by the Holy Spirit, and in the present Song they ought not to be compared otherwise than for the sake of unfolding an allegory or a parabolic signification: but by no means so urged as if the Holy Spirit had properly intended to treat of them here, and wished the words themselves to be taken without trope, metaphor, or allegory, and intended here the sense which they render without a trope. Although some things are also so constituted that, if understood in a rhetorically proper sense—that is, without figures—they would render a false, absurd, and paradoxical meaning, which therefore it is openly evident cannot in any way be understood here according to such a proper sense. The matter can be declared by similarities: for just as it is not necessary that those things which are said about the weddings in Matt. 22 and the ten virgins in ch. 25, should agree in a literal and historical sense with weddings that were once celebrated on earth in such a way and no other, so that they might then be accommodated to mystical weddings and the heavenly Bridegroom, and be more correctly understood from such earthly weddings. For history is not recounted there, but a parable: Similarly, neither is it necessary here that we should think that there existed some bride to whom all those predicates applied, and in whom those things were found to shadow forth the Bride of Christ. For who was ever such a one? Therefore, Mercer rightly says in the preface to this place: I truly think that Solomon, when he wrote these things, so tempered his style and pen that he did not think of external and earthly weddings, but of all things sublime, mystical, spiritual, and heavenly.

13. Christian interpreters with unanimous consent have explained the Song of Songs solely concerning the spiritual love of God or Christ, and not concerning the love of Solomon, or both. From the Greeks, Dionysius, produced earlier; with whom Origen agrees in Homily 1 of the two on the Song: understand Christ as the Bridegroom, the Church as the Bride without spot or wrinkle. Athanasius in the Synopsis: This little book is full of the addresses of the old people, and generally of the human race, and of the Church from the Gentiles to the Word, and again of the Word to the same and to the human race. Epiphanius, heresy 33: my dove, my perfect one, that is, the holy Bride herself, the Catholic Church. Theodoret in the preface to his Commentary on the Song appeals to the holy Fathers of the earlier centuries: Those who maintain that Solomon speaks of his own Bride, the daughter of Pharaoh, ought to acknowledge that the holy Fathers, who placed this book among the divine Scriptures, were far superior to them either in wisdom or in spirit. Likewise: approaching from the old to the new Bride, let us interpret the Song of Songs in this way, and let us imitate the holy Fathers, and let us acknowledge one Bride speaking with one Bridegroom, and let us learn from the holy Apostles who the Bridegroom is and who the Bride is. Basil the Great, homily 12 in the beginning of the Proem: The Song of Songs contains the concord of the Bridegroom and the Bride, that is, the familiarity of the soul with God the Word. ψυχῆς οἰκείωσιν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν λόγον. Gregory of Nyssa in the preface to the Song: Through those things which are here, the soul is adorned in a certain way as a Bride for an incorporeal, spiritual, and immaterial conjunction with GOD. Psellus in Theodoret: The Song of Songs wisely proposes Christ as the Bridegroom, and likewise the soul as the Bride, languishing and entangled with the love of the Bridegroom. To these add Philo of Carpathus, as well as three anonymous Fathers in Theodoret. From the Latins, Tertullian, book 4 against Marcion, ch. 2. Christ also summoned this Bride to Himself through Solomon from the calling of the Gentiles, since you have read, come, Bride, from Lebanon. Cyprian, book 1, Epistle 6: That the Church is one, the Holy Spirit declares in the Song of Songs, saying from the person of Christ, one is my dove, my perfect one. Optatus of Milevis, book 1 against Parmenianus: Christ is the one Bridegroom of the Church, as He Himself testifies in the Song of Songs. Jerome, Epistle to Paulinus: Solomon, the peaceful and lovable one, corrects the morals of the Lord, teaches nature, joins the Church, and sings the epithalamium of holy weddings. Augustine, book on Pastors, ch. 15: We know the Song of Songs, holy songs, songs of love, songs of holy love, of holy charity, of holy sweetness: I clearly wish to hear from there the voice of the Shepherd, the voice of the sweetest Bridegroom. And book 17 of The City of God, ch. 20. The Song of Songs is a certain spiritual holy pleasure of minds, in the marriage of that King and Queen of the City, which is Christ and the Church, but this pleasure is wrapped in allegorical coverings, so that it may be desired more ardently, and seen more pleasantly. Justus Orgelit. in the preface to the Commentary. The sacraments of this book are known to be very inscrutable and involved. Cassiodorus in the preface. Solomon, inspired by the divine Spirit, composed this little book concerning the nuptials of Christ and the Church. Gregory the Great in the Prologue. It must be noted that this book is called not Songs, but the Song of Songs. For it is as much more sublime than all songs as it is offered in the nuptials of a more sublime festivity. Isidore of Seville, book 6, Etymologies, ch. 1. Solomon entitled the third book the Song of Songs, where through an epithalamium poem he mystically sings of the union of Christ and the Church. Bede, book 2, on the Canticles, ch. 1. Whoever desires to read the Song of Songs, in which the wisest of Kings, Solomon, described the mysteries of Christ and the King forever, and of his city under the figure of the Bridegroom and the Bride, ought to remember first of all that the whole congregation of the elect is generally called the Church. Alcuin, his disciple, is of the same mind as Bede; Aponius, praised by Bede; and Angelomus, the abbreviator of Aponius; Haymo, the epitomizer of Bede; as also Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. Theodulf, Bishop of Orleans, singing of the books of Solomon, says, The third adorns the bridal chamber of the Church and of Christ. Honorius of Autun in the Prologue. The subject matter of the book is the Bridegroom and the Bride, that is, Christ and the Church. Bernard, sermon 1 on the Canticles. Solomon, divinely inspired, [describes] the praises of Christ and the Church, and the grace of sacred love, and the eternal marriage he sang of the Sacraments, and at the same time expressed the desire of a holy soul, and composed praises in the form of an Epithalamium, exulting in a joyful Spirit, though figuratively. And in sermon 13 on the Canticles: Although no one among us should presume to arrogate to himself that he dares to call his own soul the Bride of the Lord, yet because we are of the Church, which deservedly glories in this name and the reality of the name, we do not undeservedly usurp a share of this glory. For what we all possess together fully and integrally, this we share individually without contradiction. Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London, equal in age to Bernard, in the prologue to his Commentary on the Canticle: In the Song of Songs, Solomon, passing over all things, stands before the divine majesty, embracing this as a Bridegroom, and representing to Him all that can be of love, out of affection. He indicates, therefore, that the soul or the Church, kindled by the fire of love, does not seek these visible things, but sighs for invisible things with the whole affection of the heart and the whole intention of the mind. We refrain from citing the Doctors of later centuries. For what would be the end of these testimonies? In short, all agree in this opinion, that this Canticle treats of the love of GOD and the Church, both the ancient and the more recent Doctors of the Church, except that some writers of recent ages have either applied what is said in the Canticle to the Blessed Virgin Mary, or, where Mariolatry has already begun to prevail, have directly and adequately claimed the occurring praises for the same Mary, who are indeed unworthy to be counted in the holy Catalogue of the Fathers. What of the fact that they were reprobated by the Church as heretics who explained it otherwise than of Christ? Concerning which Philastrius, heresy 131. There is a heresy which doubts concerning the Song of Songs, judging it likewise not to have been proclaimed to men by the divine Spirit, but for the sake of human affairs and pleasures. Theodoret, Preface to the Canticle: Most of those who slander the Song of Songs and deny that it is a spiritual book, bring forward certain fables not worthy even of raving old women, namely, that the wise Solomon wrote it about himself and the daughter of Pharaoh, while others, related to the same folly, have feigned that the daughter of Pharaoh is the Bride, Abishag the Shunammite. Which error we previously observed was also condemned in Theodore of Mopsuestia by the 2nd Council of Constantinople.

Not only do Christian Interpreters agree here, but the Jews themselves explain it concerning the love of God and the Church; and that not according to accommodation only, or in such a way that they admit another literal sense and hold this only as mystical, which Grotius could not prove from them, nor did he attribute it to them except rashly, but so that they believed the literal sense and the one properly intended by the Holy Spirit to convey the spiritual love of GOD toward His people. The Chaldean paraphrase, which is held in great esteem among the Jews, teaches that the book was written by a Prophetic Spirit. It does not, therefore, wish for it to be taken in a historical sense. For its inscription reads thus: These are the Canticles and Songs which Solomon the Prophet and King of Israel spoke before the Lord God of the universe through the Prophetic Spirit. The ancient Jews are read to have said: Far be it, far be it, that this Canticle should be about obscene matters, but it is a Metaphor; otherwise, if it were not of great authority, it would not be written in the Catalogue of the holy Scriptures. The most ancient of the Rabbis also assert that the name of Solomon in this Canticle is not a proper name, but an appellative, derived, namely, from peace, to express God the author of peace, which Galatinus confirms with many testimonies, book 3, On the Arcane Truths of the Catholic Faith, ch. 26. Nor did those of the Hebrews think otherwise, who warned that no one should read this book before the 30th year of age, lest, namely, youth, when mystical love is sung, should conceive indecent loves in their heart, as witnessed by

Origen, homily 1 on the Canticle, from two of Gregory Nazianzen in his Apology, Jerome in the preface to the homilies on the Canticle, concerning which Mercerus in the preface to this place. They especially permit this book to be read only by those whose affections of wickedness have already cooled, lest they take what is said here in a worse sense. For there is nothing here that is not holy, chaste, modest, and immaculate. The same is also the opinion of those who have illustrated the Canticle with commentaries from the Rabbis. The author of the Midrash, R. Aben-Ezra, R. Solomon Jarchi, R. David Kimchi, and others. Aben-Ezra observes that it is not the custom, nor decorous in the city, for a man to address a girl or woman openly about amorous matters as is done in this book. In the Midrash, however, it is noted that there was indeed a controversy among the wise concerning the Church, but that NO ONE EVER IN ISRAEL controverted concerning this book, that it does not defile the hands, nor is it profane. Indeed, while the Hebrews call the other books Holy, they call this the holy of holies, as the apex of the others, whence they are accustomed to attribute to it this name קדש קדשים, holiness of holinesses. Some of the Hebrews warn that in the Canticles of Scripture either Israel praises the Lord, as in Ex. 15, or the Lord praises Israel, Deut. 32, but here both are done; the Bridegroom praises the Bride, and in turn the Bride the Bridegroom.

It is helpful here to note the Interpreters who have endeavored to illustrate this Canticle with their commentaries in the Christian Church. Origen's two homilies on the Canticle are extant from around the year of Christ 226, as well as four homilies: concerning which Jerome in the Prologue to Damasus. Origen, while he surpassed everyone in other books, in the Song of Songs he surpassed himself. Concerning those four, however, whether they are Origen's, Emsm. raised a doubt in his censure of the books of Origen. PHILO of Carpathus wrote on the Canticle in the year 346: AMBROSE in the year 375, in his book on Isaac and the soul and in his sermons on Psalm 118, expounded almost the entire Canticle. GREGORY OF NYSSA in the year 380 wrote 15 Homilies on the Canticle up to chapter 6, verse 8. THEODORET, Bishop of Cyrus, in the year 430, adorned a commentary on the whole Canticle: in which is involved the exposition of three Fathers, Nyssenus, Nilus, and Maximus: as well as the interpretation of PSELLUS. Around the year of Christ 540. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS illustrated the Canticle, which was composed at the same time by JUSTUS OF URGEL, Bishop; in the year 600 GREGORY THE GREAT compiled an excellent Commentary. In the year 731 the Venerable BEDE expounded it in seven books, and ALBINUS or Alcuin around the year 780 wrote five books on the Canticle, a Compendium of which appeared in London in the year 1638. In the year 812 APONIUS illustrated the Canticle in six books. In the year 850 HAYMO, Bishop of Halberstadt, reduced Bede's commentary almost into a compendium: In the year 853 ANGELOMUS, an abbreviator of Aponius, appeared. In the year 1070 Abbot WILLERAM in the Monastery of St. Peter near Merseburg illustrated the Canticle in verse. In the year 1106 ANSELM, whether of Canterbury or Laon, adorned a succinct commentary: In the year 1119 RUPERT of Deutz wrote seven books on the Canticle, but adapted almost everything to Mary the Mother of God. In the year 1130 Abbot BERNARD of Clairvaux 24. Sermons on the Canticle expounded the first two chapters: which Abbot GILBERT continued with 48 sermons, but only up to chapter 5, 8. RICHARD of St. Victor, a Scot, in the year 1132 expounded the whole Canticle: which was also done in the 50th year of the same century by WOLBERO, Abbot of St. Pantaleon in Cologne, and in the year 56 by GILBERT FOLIOT, Abbot of Leicester, afterwards Bishop of London: and in the year 1220.

by Honorius of Autun, A.D. 1240; by William, Bishop of Paris, A.D. 1264; by Hugh of Saint-Cher, Cardinal, A.D. 1270; by Thomas Aquinas, A.D. 1320; by Nicholas of Lyra, a converted Jew, A.D. 1349; by Robert Holcot, A.D. 1350; by Nicholas Gorran, A.D. 1419; by John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, A.D. 1471; by Dionysius the Carthusian, A.D. 1490; by James of Valencia, Bishop of Christopolis. And these are the more important among the ancients. If anyone desires more, along with the moderns, let him consult B. Gerhard in his Prolegomena to the Postilla on Solomon, chapter XI. Some will also be brought forward in these annotations as the occasion arises. No one has so defiled this most holy song as Grotius. We, intending to follow the pious ancients and, among the moderns, especially OUR OWN, will both cleanse the song of Grotian filth and draw out its most sacred meanings, as the Holy Spirit shall grant grace.

It remains that we say something about the order and arrangement of this song. We cannot, however, entirely approve the opinion of those who think that the state of the Church is described in general, both first or incipient, which are the changed desires of Christ and the Church, and the first cradles, as it were, of love; then the middle or adolescent, which is its progress and growth; then the third or the fullness of perfect age and the peak of love, and as it were around the goals, because the fullness is exhibited when all the flocks of the sheepfold have been received: or those who wish the state of the Church to be exhibited as Thomas Broughton does in his preface, partly legal before the captivity, chapter 1, in the captivity itself, chapter 2, to verse 15, after the captivity until the birth of Christ, chapters 3, 6. and death, chapters 4, 6; partly Evangelical, and its state both incipient to chapter 4, verse 16, and consummated, so that it treats also of the elder born, the same being first pure, then obscured by mist and darkness, chapter 5, finally restored to chapter 6; then of the younger born, namely either the prince, at his birth and confirmed age, thence chapters 7 and 8 to verse 5, or the two inferior ones, etc. Nor does the opinion of Lyranus deserve to be counted, who wishes the times of the Old Testament to be described in the first 6 chapters: (1) until the departure from Egypt, chapter 1, to verse 12; (2) the progress through the desert from verse 12 to chapter 4, verse 6; (3) the approach to the boundary, the rest of the fourth chapter: and furthermore the state of the land possessed under Joshua and the Judges, chapter 5; under David, chapter 6, to verse 10; Solomon, verse 10. He wishes the following kings until the Babylonian captivity to be described in verse 11, and after the captivity in verse 12: and that in the remaining chapters the state of the Church of the New Testament is exhibited regarding its inception, chapter VII to verse 11; the expansion of the incipient, verse 11 and following; the tranquility of the expanded, chapter VIII, which is the desire for this peace until verse 8, and the completion of the same from verse 8 to the end. Nor can we add our vote to the almost similar distribution of Georg Eder, who in Oeconom. Bibl. book II, table 113, assumes that the state of the ancient Church until the times of Christ is described through 10 Dramas, so that (1) it treats of the pilgrimage of the fathers, Terah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, chapter I, 1-12; (2) of the multiplication of the people, chapter 1, 12-14; (3) of the oppression of the same in Egypt, verse 15 and following, chapter 2, 12; (4) of God's defense and appearance to Moses in the bush, chapter 2, 3 and following; (5) of the exodus of Israel from Egypt, verse 8 and following. (6) Of the pilgrimage through the desert, chapters 3 and 4; (7) of the introduction into the holy land, chapter 5; (8) of the exaltation, persecution, and liberation of the people under the Judges, chapter 5; (9) of the wisdom of Israel, chapter 8, 10; (10) of the eternal dwelling of the bridegroom in the people, the other nations having been left behind, verse 14. No better is the speculation of James of Valencia, Bishop of Christopolis, concerning the state of the Israelite Church from then until the times of the Solomonic reign, prefiguring the state of the Christian Church until the times of Constantine the Great, described here in ten particular songs; or that of Cornelius a Lapide, who with others makes five parts: I. From the birth and preaching of Christ until Pentecost, chapter 1 to chapter 2, 8. And the infancy of the Church. II. The adolescent from Pentecost until the Emperor Constantine, to chapter 3, 6. III. The virile age in the time of Constantine until chapter 4, 2. IV. Of the Church growing old and inclining toward senility until chapter 6, 3, with the Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, and Pelagians, to be sure, raging. V. Of the Church that began to be renewed by Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril, Augustine, Jerome, and continued by the successors of the renewal until the end of the world, when on the day of judgment a full renewal and glorification will take place. Or that of John Cocceius, who, just as he investigates and finds his seven periods of the New Testament Church frequently there in the Scriptures, in Moses, in the Prophets, and in the Apocalypse, where neither the Holy Spirit placed them, nor has anyone instructed by the Spirit of God been able to see or find them until now, so in this Song he has attempted to designate them in his Synopsis, and Medulla Prophetiæ, and thoughts on the Song as an icon of the kingdom of Christ: namely the First, which he makes that of the preaching among the Jews and the nations before the intensifying persecutions and the destroyed temple, chapters 1 and 2. The Second, of the testing and refining of the Church in the most grave, long-lasting, and various persecutions until, the tyrants having been destroyed, peace was granted to it by earthly princes, chapters 3 and 4. The Third, of the Church pacified from persecutions and nourished by the nations, but beginning to conflict with the false Church and with the domination of men and certain calamities, but yielding to the amplification of the Church and ending in rest, chapters 5 and 6 to verse 9. The Fourth, of the true Church shining forth and showing itself in the midst of the false Church until the division from verse 9 of chapter 6 to chapter 7, 11. The Fifth, of the Church after peace was sought in vain and the conversion of the opposing multitude was expected, or the Reformation, receding from the great city, and in that recession agitated until its peace, chapter 7, 11, 12, 13, and 8, 1, 2, 3. The sixth of the Church established in new distress after the peace which it had obtained from the secession, c. 8, 4. 5. 6. Finally, the seventh of the Church aspiring after many struggles to the kingdom of Christ, and the preaching of it in the whole world.

Setting aside these and similar not so much explanations as voluntary and violent distortions of the Song of Songs, although one must admit that Osiander warned not without merit that a rhetorical arrangement is not to be sought in this love poem; since everything is full of affections which snatch the mind of the lover now here, now there, yet the investigation of every arrangement is not to be despised or despaired of, nor do some, praised by the blessed Gerhard in the preface to the Postilla on Solomon, c. 7, § 10, describe it inaptly, saying that the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church is first described by the treatment of the betrothal, where the first act is joyful, namely the conversation of the Church and Christ c. 1, of Christ and the Church c. 2, the intermediate act is then joyful, namely the discourse of the Church c. 3, the discourse of Christ c. 4, then sad, where the Church is saddened on account of the departure of the Bridegroom c. 5, and the last concerning the return of the Bridegroom c. 6. Then from the expedition of the nuptials, which the Church seeks first for itself c. 7, secondly for its sister, that is, the Church of the Gentiles c. 8. Doubtless, as Osiander rightly says, there are vicissitudes of joy and complaints in this Song: because the Church is exposed to the cross, to afflictions, and to various temptations, nor is it yet perfect in the knowledge of God and in charity.

Moreover, it pleases me especially, as the Paraphrase, so also the partition handed down in the Ernestine Bibles, which is said to have the blessed GERHARD as its author, and according to his mind the blessed GLASSIUS, to whose better understanding the excellent explanation of the principal sayings in this Canticle, presented in the Gerhardian Postilla on Solomon, will contribute not a little. For this man of God was, if any other theologian of our century was, instructed by the Spirit of God in a rich measure, which his truly God-breathed writings abundantly testify: Who, just as he had warned, following the example of Thomas Aquinas and John Gerson, and the judgment of other Christian interpreters, and indeed even of the Jews, in his Exegesis on Holy Scripture § 149, that the explanation of this Canticle is not to be approached in youth, but reserved for the consolation of Christian old age and as a viaticum for pious emigration, so in his own old age, and toward the close of a truly holy life, he devoted himself to the meditations of the Canticle.

It will be permissible to establish three parts: The first presents the desire of the bride, the Church, longing for the advent of the Bridegroom into the flesh, explained by the dialogue of the Church with Christ in chapter 1: with the promise of the Bridegroom explaining his advent and his benefits, and the reciprocal invitation of the bride to the joyful enjoyment of them, testifying to their reciprocal desire and affection in chapter 2. The second [presents] the solicitude and grief of the bride concerning

THE DESIRE OF CHRIST IS FULFILLED

Latin:

AD PRÆFATIONEM GROTII OBSERVATIONES.

CArmen hoc vocari Hebræis ex- cellentissimum carmen ob multas elegan- tias, Grotius non male dicit: sed ea præcipua non est appellationis Cantici hujus, nedum unica ratio. Neque id carmen excellentissimum in inscri- ptione, sed Canticum Canticorum vocatur: idque non tantum quod elegantiis multis, præ aliis, scateat, sed quod simpliciter inter Cantica omnia in sacris literis hoc præcipuum ac præstantissimum sit. Quo- rum decem e Scriptura universa hic recenset Thar- gum, quamvis plura omnino, præter Psalmos, repe- riantur Ex. 15, 1. Num. 21, 17. 18. Deut. 32, 1. seqq. Jos. 10, 12. (quod a Josua cantatum fuisse, cum in ejus gratiam Sol & Luna triginta sex horis stetissent, Chaldæus observat) Jud. 5, 2. 1. Sam. 2, 1. 2. Sam. 22, 3. 1. Paral. 16, 8. Es. 12, 1. c. 26, 1. c. 30, 29. c. 42, 10. &c.

Nec vero tantum inter omnia Salomonis can- tica, qui mille & quinque legitur scripsisse 1. Reg. 4, 32. Canticum præsens excellit, quod præ reliquis o- mnibus in librorum Canonicorum numerum ado- ptatum est, sed inter omnia, quæ unquam scripta sunt, Canticum merito habendum eminentissimum; idque non tam ob verborum elegantiam, & artificii venustatem, quam ob mysteriorum, quæ continet, u- bertatem, quia summa & eminentissima mysteria ex- cellentissimo artificio in hoc Cantico, verbisque pro- fundissimâ rerum sapientiam spirantibus efferuntur, ut nullum unquam Canticum repertum sit, quod cum hoc conferri mereatur, nedum eidem præferri de- beat, sive mysteriorum reconditas divitias, sive ver- borum suavissimorum & efficacissimorum mystic velamina, seu modum proponendi ac decantandi rebus, quas exhibet, convenientissimum & elegan- tissimum respiciamus. De quo haud præter rem Mercerus judicavit: Si cætera Scripturæ cantica dili- gentius perpendas, singula fere in illis mysteria reperies at hic omnia tam veteris, quam novæ legis mysteria sub f- guris & similitudinibq tecta invenies, & quæ evenerunt & quæ eventura sunt. Ebræi certe in Midrasch di-

N. 7. D CANTICORUM GROTIANA, RUM ELENCTICA MI CALOVII.

cunt, ante Salomonem legem non satis intellectam fuisse, donec ille supervenerit suis parabolis, & similitudinibus eam illustraret: quod etsi de sanctis Patriarchis de Mose & Aarone, de Samuele & Davide credendum non sit, apparet tamen, sapientiam libri hujus reconditam magni fieri apud Rabbinos ipsos, qui alias in Scriptis Propheticis vehementer cæcutiunt. Et insignibus mactant veteres Ecclesiæ Dd. hunc librum elogiis, præ aliis sacris libris, ob mysteria, quæ in eo recondita sunt, eundem imprimis celebrantes, atque ea de causa hunc titulum Cantici Canticorum ipsi tributum esse, unanimi sententia pronunciantes. Quos hic audire merito debuisset Grotius. Dionysius Epist. 9. ad Tit. Librum Canticorum, dicit, mysteria continere divino reconditæ Theologiæ lumine plena, velata tamen variis metaphoris & similitudinibus, quibus excellentissime talia mysteria indicat. Gregor. Nyssenus Homil. 1. in Cantic. Ut in sancto sanctorum per appellationem illam superlativam de abundantia quadam, & amplitudine sanctitatis monemur: Sic & per appellationem Cantici Canticorum arcanissima quædam arcana traditurum se nobis sublimis hic liber pollicetur. Justus Orgelitanus Præfat. Comment. in Cantic. Sacramenta libri hujus quam multum inscrutabilia & involuta dignoscuntur non immerito in ipsa prænotatione tituli. Cantica Canticorum præscribuntur, quia cæteris eminentiora sine dubitatione aliqua producuntur. Sunt enim plurimis & pene insolitis, ultra aliarum Scripturarum consuetudinem velata mysteriis, ita ut nisi Christus præsit sensibus, nec subtilissimis intelligentiarum adytis valeant investigari. Bernhard. serm. 1. in Cantic. Est panis apud Salomonem, isque admodum splendidus, sapidusque: Librum dico, qui Cantica Canticorum inscribitur &c. Similia elogia leguntur apud Origen. homil. in Cant. Cassiodorum in Cant. Comment. Gregorium M. Prolog. in Cant. Isidor. Hispal. l. 6. Etymol. c. 2. & alios.

Salomonem autorem esse, e titulo certum est. Neque id negat Grotius; Qui etsi Ecclesiasten Salomoni, uti dictum, ob frivolas conjecturas abjudicet, Canticum tamen hoc Salomoni auctori adscribit. Autor Midrasch לשלמה exponit de Salomone, sed nomen hoc sacrum esse vult, hoc sensu: de Domino Messia, vel Rege, cujus est pax: vel pacifico. Verum uti מזמור לדוד est Canticum non de Davide, sed Davidis, ita etiam hic indicatur autor, non vero objectum hujus Cantici: quod agnoscit quoque Grotius. Exprimi enim Hebræis etiam casus gignendi consuevit per ל, ut Psalm. 90, 1. Hab. 3, 1. Conf. Gen. 7, 11. Job. 30, 24. Psal. 120, 1. Efr. 10, 3. Mal. 3, 8. Quanquam nonnulli in Psalmis Dativo casu velint innui simul causam principalem S. S. q. d. Psalmus Davidi inspiratus a Deo, utpote Lipomanus, Titelmannus, Genebrardus, Bellarminus; sic Canticum hoc innuetur a Spiritu S. inspiratum Salomoni.

Rectissime autem Midras objectum facit Messiam accedens Christianorum interpretationi, ut ex adverso Grotius Salomonem ipsum objectum & argumentum constituit, aliorum quorundam Rabbinorum sententiæ ὁμόψηφος, ac per totum hoc Canticum cum iisdem insigniter Judaizans.

Triplicem autem ut apparet, sensum Cantici constituit: Primus literalis ipsi est de Rege Salomone, & filia Regis Aegypti Sponsa. Secundus est allegoricus de amore Dei adversus populum Israeliticum, quem sub verbis Cantici studio, nec absque artificio singulari expressum, adeoque ab ipso Salomone etiam inten- tum fuisse autumat. Tertius typicus est de amore Christi erga Ecclesiam, quem non improbat, quatenus nempe Christiani ad eam rem verba hujus carminis applicare studuerunt.
