Sed quomodo ejusdem dicti non geminus tantum, sed triplex sensus constitue- tur, a Spiritu S. intentus? Si omnes illos verbis iis- dem intentos ac significatos esse credendum, annon data opera S. S. ambigue loquutus erit iisdem ver- bis, non unum, sed tria distincta objecta designans, verbi gratia, per Sponsum Salomonem, Deum, & Chri- stum, per Sponsam filiam Pharaonis, populum Israeliti- cum, & Ecclesiam N. T. vel omnium temporum, ut ita per omnia verba Cantici meris ambiguitatibus lu- serit? Nec est, quod dicat Grotius, unum tantum es- se sensum de Salomone, verba autem ea arte a Salomo- ne quidem esse composita, ut amor Dei exprimeretur er- ga populum, non tamen præcise hunc sensum a Spiritu S. intendi. Sic enim aliud intendisset Salomo, au- tor ministerialis, aliud Spiritus S. autor principalis. Et num credemus, Spiritum S. in usum Ecclesiæ Ca- nonice & perpetuum consecrare voluisse Canticum, tam prolixe adornatum, de amore Salomonis & Spon- sæ exoticæ, aut arte peculiari in id elaborasse Salomo- nem, imo ipsum Spiritum S. ut persuaderetur Israeli- tis, de amore Dei erga populum decantatum esse, quod non de amore divino, sed de amoribus mutuis humanis Sponsi & Sponsæ decantatum erat, adeo- que simulatione alterius sensus Israelitarum favo- rem aucupatum esse, idque hac fini, ut nugatur Grotius, ut Canticum amoris Salomonei adversus Sponsam suam perennaret? Non opus habuit Spiritus S. artificio peculiari, ut libri, quos Canoni perpetuo Ecclesiæ destinavit, perennarent.

Ita dum prophana omnia de hoc sanctissimo Cantico concepit Grotius, in prophanam istam o- pinionem de intentione, scopo & argumento Cantici dilapsus est, qua divina ejusdem auctoritas prorsus evertitur. Et quid aliud annotatis suis egit, quam ut penitus prophanaret sanctissimum Canticum, ani- mo certe neutiquam pio, aut Christiano? Exempli gratia, dum ad v. 6. ne vagari incipiam post greges so- dalium: hoc joco, ait, dicitur ut illud Catulli: Ne quæ- situm aliunde eat: & ad v. 7. pasce hædos tuos, exple appetitum, unde verbum τραγίζειν. Horatius, Lascivæ similem ludere capreæ; cujusmodi plura occurrunt in hisce ad Canticum sanctissimum annotatis. Quid illa aliud, nisi animum prophanum Annotatoris proclamant? Qui etiam interpretes divini hujus Cantici non Prophetas aut Apostolos, vel Spiritum Propheticum constituit, ex præscripto Petrino 2. Ep. 1. sed Poetas prophanos Catullum, Horatium, Theocri- tum, Claudianum, Virgilium, Tibullum, Martialem, Silentiarium, Ovidium, qui in omnibus pene anno- tatis istis versibus suis amatoriis, aliisque tinniunt. Non immerito ergo parili censura notandus Gro- tius, qua Antonius Possevinus cum Del-Rione Tom. 2. Appar. Sacr. p. 372. Sebast. Castalionem notavit: Castis sacris inimicus Castalio (Grotius) petulcis, & pruriginosis suis interpretationibus ausus est obstrepere illis, qui Canticum Canticorum divinorum mysteriorum pretiosum thesaurum statuunt. Et potiori certe jure de Grotio usurpamus, quod Sixtus Senensis Bibl. l. 6. hær. 13. p. 664. de Castalione scripsit: Non mirum si Castalio (Grotius) tam immodice in re divina veluti cum Catullo de Lesbiæ passerculo & turgidulis puellæ o- cellis, & aureolo malo luserit, quia ut ipsemet in glossulis indicavit, nunquam credidit in illo divino Cantico my- sticos Christi & Ecclesiæ amores describi, sed de Vene- reis atque prophanis Salomonis, ejusque amicæ Sulami- tis, atque ejusdem fœminarum amoribus amatorium colloquium texi.

Jam quod ad allegoricam amoris Dei erga Israe- liticam politiam, explicationem attinet, quum ea, juxta Grotium, sensum literalem de amore Salomonis & Sponsæ supponat, hic vero fundamento omni de- stituatur, nec ullatenus in tam sancto ac divino Can- tico admittenda sit, allegoria etiam illa labitur. Nec vero satis conveniunt, quæ in Cantico occurrunt, politiæ Judaicæ, quin distorta explicatione opus sit, quæ in Scripturis S. ferenda non est. Quapropter superest, ut de amore Christi & Ecclesiæ explicetur, quod ab Ecclesiæ antiquis & modernis Dd. com- muni hactenus consensu factum: non per aliquam accommodationem tantum; Eam enim etiam in Hi- storiis & oraculis quibusvis, ubi aliquid saltem, quod accommodari, aut typi rationem habere possit, oc- currit, laude dignam esse, nemo inficiabitur; sed quod hunc verum & germanum sensum a Spiritu S. intentum Cantici esse crediderint.

Contexta autem Grotii sententia est e diversis interpretamentis tum Judæorum, tum hæreticorum, tum orthodoxorum, ut amat ille ἀσύγκλωσα in reli- gione pariter ac Scripturæ interpretatione passim conjungere. Nam de Salomone & Filia Regis Æ- gyptii quosdam hæreticos Canticum exposuisse Theo- doretus autor est præfat. in Cantic. quos refellit Phi- lastrius de hæresibus c. 131. & Judæis ineruditis com- parat cap. 145. Et tribuitur illa hæresis Theodoro Mopsuestano in Synodo Constantinopol. 2. Colla- tion. 4. quam renovarunt Anabaptistæ, teste Jodoco Coccio T. I. Thesaur. c. 6. art. 8. & Sixto Senensi lib. 8. Bibl. S. hæres. 8. p. 645. Primum ergo sensum, quem literalem vocat, hæreticis debet Grotius.

Alterum, qui eidem est allegoricus, a Judæis ac- cepit, de Deo & Synagoga tantum, vel populo Israe- litico explicantibus, quia Christum & novum ejus populum non agnoscunt, quod notat Lyranus & Mercerus. Quanquam vero B. Lutherus in hoc Cantico quoque Deum Sponsum & populum ejus Sponsam constitui putat Tom. 4. Jen. Lat. in com- ment. de Anno 1536. p. 268. respici tamen eodem spirituale etiam regnum Christi, ad verba c. 1. Soror nostra parvula docet: & Sponsam de Ecclesia N. T. exposuit in Tesseradec. Consol. Tab. 1. cap. 11. Tom. 1. Jenens. Lat. fol. 399. Ultimo levandum est cor sursum & ascendendum in montem Myrrhæ cum Spon- sa. Hic est Jesus Christus crucifixus, caput omnium sanctorum, Princeps omnium patientium, de quo multi multa, & omnes omnia, sicut decet, scripserunt. Hujus memoria Sponsæ commendatur, ubi dicitur: Pone me ad signum super cor tuum, & sicut signa- culum super brachium tuum. Hujus agni sanguis in lumine signatus arcet percussorem Angelum. Ab hoc commendatur Sponsa, quod coma ejus sit, sicut purpuræ Regis (i. e. meditatio ejus rubet passionis Chri- sti memoria) Hoc est lignum, quod Moses jussus est mit- tere in aquas Mara, i. e. amaras passiones, & dulces fa- ctæ sunt. Nihil est, quod hæc passio non dulcoret, etiam mortem, sicut dicit Sponsa; Labia ejus lilia stillantia myrrham primam. Quæ proportio liliorum & la- biorum, cum hæc rubeant, & illa albicent? Utique my- stica loquitur, quod verba candidissima sint & purissi- ma, in quibus nihil culentæ amaritudinis, aut livoris, sed suavia & mitia, quibus tamen stillet ac persuadeat primam & electam myrrham, i. e. amarissimam mor- tem; Potentia sunt hæc purissima labia ac dulcissi- ma, amarissimam mortem (quæ sicut prima myrrha omnem peccati putorem semel tollit) dulcem. nitidam, candidam, acceptabilemque reddere. Adde his, quæ leguntur Tom. 2. Jen. Germ. f. 338. super c. 2. prior. Petrinæ Epist. Die Brüste aber, die diese Milch von sich geben, und die jungen Kindlein säugen, sind die Prediger in der Christenheit, wie der Bräutigam zur Braut sagt Cant. 3. Du hast zwo Brüste, wie zwey junge Hinnlein, die sollen haben ein Püschel Myrrhen umb sich hangen, wie die Braut spricht, Cant. 1. Mein Lieber ist wie ein PüschelMyrrhen, das mir zwischen meinen Brüsten hanget, das ist, daß man immer Christum sol predigen, der Bräutigam muß mitten in den Brüsten seyn gemenget, sonst ists unrecht, und wird die Milch gefälscht, wenn man nicht lauter Christum prediget, das gehet nun also zu, wenn man prediget, daß Christus für uns gestorben ist, und uns errettet hat von Sünden, Tod und Höll, das ist lustig und süß, wie die Milch. Quæ observanda duximus, ne quis B. Lutherum nostrum Grotianæ sententiæ omnino patrocinari falso opinetur.

Tertium sensum a Christianis assumsit Grotius, quem tamen, si rem recte æstimemus, ipse non pro sensu textus Salomonis habet, sed pro applicatione eorum, quæ de populo Dei sub allegoria, aut verius de Sponsa Salomonis secundum literam, dicta censet, ad Ecclesiam Christi.

Non agi autem hîc secundum literam de amore terreno, vel externo Salomonis, & Sponsæ ejus Ægyptiæ, vel virginis cujusdam Sulamitahæ, vel Hierosolymitanæ (ut alii volunt) sed de Christi amore erga Ecclesiam, cumprimis N. T. multa docent. (1) Sponsus hîc & Rex est c. 1, 4. 12. c. 3, 9. 11. & simul Pastor c. 1, 7. quod Christo optime convenit Ps. 2, 5. Job. 10, 12. Ezech. 34. Salomoni autem neutiquam (qui nunquam Pastor fuit, nedum cum Rex esset (2) Sponsa est & Regina, & custos vineæ Cant. 1, 7. gregemque pascit ovium v. 8. tum a vigilibus civitatis percutitur & vulneratur, custodes murorum auferunt ei pallium c. 5, 6. quæ quomodo de Sponsa & uxore Regis, Reginaque potentissima ad literam accipi possunt? (3) Sponsæ hujus frater Salomo est, ubera matris ejus fugens, quem osculari optat ipse cap, 8, 1. & soror vocatur ejusdem c. 3, 12. Hortus conclusus soror mea Sponsa! c. 8, 8. Quid faciemus sorori nostræ? quæ nullatenus conjugi Salomonis congruunt. (4.) Ecquis credet Salomonem seipsum ita deprædicasse: quod sit candidus & rubicundus, electus ex millibus c. 5, 10. (5) Pulchritudo Sponsæ ita describitur, ut Sole meridiano clarius effulgeat, non posse ad literam intelligi, de corporali & externa pulchritudine. Non enim illa pulchritudinem corporalem inferunt, sed insignem deformitatem, quæ hic celebrantur de capite, naso, oculis, dentibus, collo, mammis, ventre Sponsæ, vid. cap. 4, 2. c. 5, 7. c. 6, 5. c. 7, 2. 4. 8, 10. E. g. cum dat ei Salomo caput instar carmeli, nasum instar turris, oculos instar piscinæ, dentes instar gregum ovium detonfarum &c. (6) Sponsæ Salomonis non convenit, quod c. 1, 5. habetur: Nigra sum, sed formosa sicut tabernacula Cedar, sicut pellis Salomonis, nolite me considerare, quod fusca sim, quia decoloravit me Sol &c. (7.) Si secundum literam de Sponsa Salomonis explicentur, multa occurrent pugnantia, & ἀsýsata v. 9. quod ipsa sit filia principis c. 7, 1. & describatur ceu filia pastoris cap. 1, 6. quod sit terribilis, sicut castrorum acies c. 6, 9. & quod vulnerata fuerit a custodibus c. 6, 7. & quæ hujusmodi alia occurrunt. (8) Amores ac voluptates hic ita describuntur, ut de corporali & externo amore ac voluptatibus temporalibus secundum literam accipere, religio sit. Neque enim talia sacro Cantico, aut scripto divino & Canonico, citra impietatem ad- scribentur. Quo de monuit rectissime Lyranus in Præf. Comment. in h. l. Licet hic amor Salomonis & filiæ Pharaonis potuerit esse licitus, utpote intra li- mites matrimonii contentus, tamen carnalis fuit, & frequenter habet talis amor aliquid inhonestum & illi- citum adjunctum. propter quod descriptio talis amoris non videtur ad libros S.Scripturæ Canonicos pertinere: maxime quia hujusmodi libri dictante S. S. sint con- scripti &c.

(9.) Quis sit Sponsus, quæ Sponsa, de quibus hic canitur, non rectius judicari potest, quam ex in- terpretatione Spiritus S. qui passim Christum spon- sum, Ecclesiam & cumprimis eam, quæ Novi est Te- stam. sponsam esse testatur, eorumque conjugium & mutuos ac mysticos amores celebrat. Psalm. 68, 13. Esa. 54, 5. c. 61, 10. 11. 12. c. 62, 4. 5. Jer. 1, 21. c. 2, 32. 38. 41. Ezech. 16, 8. Hos. 2, 16. 19. c. 14, 1. Matth. 9, 15. c. 22, 2. c. 25, 1. Joh. 3, 28. 29. 30. 2. Cor. 11, 2. Eph. 5, 23. 25. 31. 32. Apoc. 19, 7. c. 21, 2. c. 22, 17. 20.

(10) Insignis illa harmonia, quæ huic cantico cum Psalm. 45. inter- cedit, quam ὡς ἐν τύπῳ exhibuit B. Gerhardus præ- fat. in Postill. Salomoneam c. 5. satis docet, de nullo alio Sponso hic cani, quam de Messia, de quo in præ- dicto Psalmo agitur: adeo, ut videri possit, Salomo- nem constituisse hic commentarium in Epithalamium illud Spirituale parentis sui adornare.

(11.) Quum Spiritus S. passim in aliis Scripturis ea, quæ hoc Can- tico habentur, de spirituali amore explicet, ita ut verbis etiam iisdem aut similibus utatur, paralleli- smus & consonantia illa non obscurum indicium est, de eodem amore in hoc Cantico agi, & quum ex adverso nuspiam de amore alio seculari, vel externo id explicetur, quid aliud inde concludi potest, quam quod illud neutiquam de amore seculari, sed de amore mystico, ac spirituali solum agat. Non enim interpretatio Scripturæ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως est 2. Pet. 1, 21. Ecquis credet, typicam accommodatio- nem tam frequenter ac verbis iisdem & analogis in Scripturis traditam, historicum autem, literalem, ac a Spiritu S. proprie & directe intentum sensum ne se- mel quidem in S.literis propositum esse? Ut res ma- nifestior sit, conferat quis loca antea citata cum hoc Cantico, & in aprico erit, non pauca ex eodem alibi in scripturis repetita esse, ac de spirituali amore expli- cata. Ita quod Cant. 4, 7. de pulchritudine Spon- sæ habetur, Eph. 5, 27. de spirituali pulchritudine Ec- clesiæ explicatur. Invitationi sponsi & responsorio ejusdem Cant. 5, 1. similis est invitatio & responsio Apoc. 22, 17. 20. Quod de Sponso januam pulsan- te habetur Cant. 5, 2. ei respondent, quæ Apoc. 3, 20. leguntur &c.

(12) Omnia, quæ in hoc Cantico dicuntur, apertissime congruunt amori Christi & Ecclesiæ, vel animæ fidelis spirituali juxta verborum emphasin, Scripturæ phrasin, & analogiam aliorum locorum, quemadmodum Interpp. passim ostendunt. At amori Salomonis adversus Pharaonis filiam non conveniunt omnia, sive verborum sensum propri- um, sive aliorum locorum parallelismum respicias juxta leges herminevticas. Tum vero etsi quæ- dam fortassis congruant, id tamen neutiquam suffi- cit, ut concludatur Salomonis amorem hic decan- tari. Nam necessum esset, ut omnia illi conveniant. Neque vero id quæritur, utrum similia istis, quæ quoad sensum proprium in Cantico habentur, in Con- jugio & amore connubiali reperiantur? aut an Salomo occasione & sensu suavitatis amoris sui connubialis de suavissimo & castissimo amore sponsimystici cecinerit? quod citra detrimentum veri & genuini sensus a Spiritu Sancto in hoc Cantico intenti concedi pof- set, perinde uti quivis fidelis, dum in lectione ac meditatione Cantici, amoris istius ineffabilis sua- vitatem animo suo sistit, castum & pudicum amo- rem, quem Sponsi & Sponsæ inter se mutuo fovent, cogitat, ac in suo ipsius conjugio, & amore typum & imaginem quandam ejusdem sibi constituere po- test, præeunte Apostolo Eph. 5, 25. seqq. Sed de eo quæstio est, utrum his verbis directe intenderit S. S. amorem terrenum vel externum describere Salo- monis & Sponsæ ejus ? vel utrum hic sensus sit pro- prius, & literalis in hoc Cantico proprie intentus ? h. e. an Spiritus S. hic constituerit Epithalamium Sa- lomoni, an vero Messiæ conscribere, aut utrique, ut Sa- lomonis amorem quidem proprie & directe describat, sed eodem simul typice amorem Christi designet, cujus typus Salomo fuit ? Neque vero id prorsus negamus, typum fuisse Salomonem Christi in amore etiam erga conjugem suam certa ratione, sed hic typum illum vel Salomonis amorem describi, negamus. Aliud longe est rem per verba expressam typum esse: Aliud vero, verba ipsa typicum sensum continere, ac præter literalem sensum typice etiam explicari debere. Neque id inficiamur, ut parabolicus sensus, quem hic lite- ralem esse, ac primum intendi a Spiritu S. credimus, eruatur, requiri, ut primum de cortice literæ soli- citus quis sit, si id saltem hoc fini dicatur fieri, quo nucleus, illo aperto, eruatur, quem sub illo cortice nobis degustandum exhibet Spiritus S. Allegoriam hic omnino concedimus, quæ quum fundamentum in re habeat, ideoque in amore connubiali reperiri talia, nonnulla etiam in Sponsa aliqua inveniri pos- se, quæ hic occurrunt, admitti potest: sed ea assu- muntur hic potius, ac supponuntur, quam per ver- ba, prout illa hoc loco a Spiritu S. accipiuntur, si- gnificantur, & in præsenti Cantico non aliter, quam evolvendæ allegoriæ, aut parabolicæ significationis causa conferri debent: neutiquam vero ita urgeri, ac si proprie constituerit Spiritus Sanctus de illis hic tractare, ac verba ipsa sine tropo, metaphora, aut allegoria accipi vellet, eumque, quem sine tropo reddunt, sensum hic intenderet. Quamvis non- nulla etiam sic comparata sint, ut sensu Rhetorice proprio, h.e. absque figuris intellecto, falsam, abso- nam & paradoxam sententiam reddant, quæ proin- de palam constat, non posse secundum talem sen- sum proprium ullatenus hic intelligi. Declarari res similibus potest: uti enim necessum non est, ea quæ de nuptiis Matth. 22. & decem virginibus c. 25. dicuntur, sensu literali & historico convenire nu- ptiis, quæ aliquando in terris ita, ac non aliter ce- lebratæ sint, quo deinde accommodari ad nuptias mysticas & Sponsum cœlestem queant, rectiusque e nuptiis ejusmodi terrenis intelligi. Non enim hi- storia ibi recensetur, sed parabola: Similiter neque hic necessum est, ut existimemus aliquam Sponsam extitisse, cui omnia illa prædicata convenerint, & in qua illa ad adumbrandam Christi Sponsam inventa fuerint. Quænam enim unquam talis fuit? Proin- de recte Mercerus in præf. in h. l. Ego sane Salomo- nem, cum hæc scriberet, ita stylum suum & calamum temperasse puto, ut externas nuptias & terrestres non cogitaret, sed omnia sublimia, mystica, spiritualia & cœlestia.

13. Interpretes Christiani unanimi consensu exposuere Canticum Canticorum unice de amore Spirituali Dei vel Christi, non vero de amore Salo- monis, aut de utroque. E Græcis Dionysius antea pro- ductus; cui Origenes consonat Hom. 1. ex duabus in Cantic. Christum Sponsum intellige, Ecclesiam Sponsam sine macula & ruga. Athanasius in Syno- psi: Libellus hic plenus est alloquiorum veteris populi, & generaliter generis humani, Ecclesiæque ex gentibus ad Verbum, & rursus Verbi ad eandem & ad genus humanum. Epiphanius hæref. 33. columba mea, perfecta mea, hoc est, ipsa sancta Sponsa, Catholica Ecclesia. Theodoretiis præf. Comment. in Cantic. provocat ad sanctos Patres priorum seculorum: Debebant isti, qui statuunt Salomonem de sua Sponsa, Pharaonis filia loqui, se longe vel Sapientia vel Spiritu præstantiores agnoscere sanctos Patres, qui librum hunc inter divinas Scripturas collocarunt. Item: a veteri ad novam Sponsam accedentes, hac ratione Can- tica Canticorum interpretemur, ac sanctos imitemur Patres, atque unam Sponsam cum uno Sponso loquen- tem agnoscamus, & qui sit Sponsus, quæque sit Sponsa, e sanctis discamus Apostolis. Basil. M. hom. 12. in Princ. Prooem. Cantica Canticorum Sponsi & Spon- sæ concordiam continent, hoc est, animæ cum Deo Ver- bo familiaritatem. ψυχῆς οἰκείωσιν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν λόγον. Greg. Nyss. in præf. Cantic. Per ea, quæ hic sunt, ornatur quodammodo anima tanquam Sponsa ad incorpoream, Spiritualem, materiæque expertem DEI conjunctionem. Psellus apud Theodoret. Canticum Canticorum sapienter proponit Christum Sponsum, Sponsamque itidem animam, amore Sponsi languentem, atque implicatam. His adde Philon. Carpathium, ut & tres Patres Anonymos apud Theo- doretum. E Latinis Tertullianus l. 4. adv. Marc. c. 2. Hanc Sponsam Christus sibi etiam per Salomo- nem e vocatione gentium accersivit, siquidem legisti, veni Sponsa de Libano. Cyprianus libr. 1. Epist. 6. Quod autem Ecclesia una sit, declarat in Cantico Canti- corum Spiritus Sanctus ex persona Christi dicens, una est columba mea, perfecta mea. Optatus Milevit. l. 1. adv. Parm. Christus est Sponsus unus Ecclesiæ, sicut in Canticis Canticorum ipse testatur. Hieronymus Epist. ad Paulin. Salomo pacificus & amabilis Domi- ni mores corrigit, naturam docet, Ecclesiam jungit, & Christum, sanctarumque nuptiarum canit Epitha- lamium. August. lib. de Pastorib. cap. 15. No- vimus Cantica Canticorum sancta, Cantica amatoria, Cantica sancti amoris, sanctæ caritatis, sanctæ dul- cedinis: plane volo inde audire vocem Pastoris, vocem dulcissimi Sponsi. Et lib. 17. de Civit. Dei cap. 20. Canticum Canticorum spiritualis quædam est sancta- rum voluptas mentium, in conjugio illius Regis & Re- ginæ Civitatis, quod est Christus & Ecclesia, sed hæc voluptas allegoricis tegminibus involuta est, ut desi- deretur ardentius, videaturque jucundius. Justus Orgelit. in præfat. Comment. Sacramenta libri hujus multum inscrutabilia & involuta dignoscuntur. Cas- siodorus in præfat. Salomo inspiratus divino Spiritu composuit hunc libellum de nuptiis Christi & Ecclesiæ. Gregorius M. in Prolog. Attendendum est, quod liber hic non Cantica, sed Canticorum Cantica dicitur. Tanto est enim omnibus Canticis sublimior, quan- to in nuptiis sublimioris festivitatis offertur. Isidorus Hispalens. lib. 6. Etym. c. 1. Salomon Tertium li- brum Canticum Canticorum prænotavit, ubi per Epi- thalamium carmen conjunctionem Christi & Ecclesiæ mystice canit. Beda lib. 2. in Cant. cap. 1. Cantica Canticorum, in quibus sapientissimus Regum Salomo mysteria Christi & Regis in æternum, & civitatis ejus sub figura Sponsi & Sponsæ descripsit, quisquis legere cupit, meminisse debet imprimis, quod omnis electorum congregatio generaliter Ecclesia vocatur. Bedæ ὁμόψηφος est Alcuinus ejus discipulus, Aponius Bedæ laudatus, & Angelomus, Aponii abbrevia- tor, Haymo Bedæ Epitomator, ut & Anshelmus Cantuar. Archi-Episcopus. Theodulphus Aure- lian. Episcop. de libris Salomonis canens, Tertius, inquit, Ecclesiæ thalamum Christique perornat. Hono- rius Augustodunensis in Prol. Materia libri est Spon- sus & Sponsa, id est, Christus & Ecclesia. Bernhar- dus serm. 1. in Cant. Salomo divinitus inspiratus Chri- sti & Ecclesiæ laudes, & sacri amoris gratiam, & æterni connubii cecinit Sacramenta, simulque expressit sanctæ desiderium animæ, & Epithalamii carmen exultans in Spiritu jucundo, composuit elogia, figurate tamen. Et serm. 13. in Cantic. Etsi nemo nostrûm sibi arrogare præsumat, ut animam suam quis audeat Sponsam Do- mini appellare, quia tamen de Ecclesia sumus, qui me- rito hoc nomine & re nominis gloriantur, non immerito gloriæ hujus participium usurpamus. Quod enim simul omnes plene integreque possidemus, hoc singuli sine con- tradictione participamus. Gilbertus Foljot Episco- pus Londinensis, Bernardo ætate suppar, in prol. Comment. in Canticum: In Cantico Canticorum Sa- lomo cuncta prætervolans divinæ majestati assistit, hanc ut Sponsum amplectens, huic totum quod amoris esse potest, ex affectu repræsentans. Animam igitur vel Ecclesiam amoris igne succensam non hæc visibilia quæ- rentem, sed ad invisibilia toto cordis affectu, tota men- tis intentione suspirantem indicat. Sequiorum secu- lorum Dd. adducere supersedemus. Quis enim finis esset horum testimoniorum? Verbo; consen- tiunt omnes in hac sententia, quod de amore DEI & Ecclesiæ hoc Cantico agatur, cum veteres tum recentiores Dd. Ecclesiæ, nisi quod nonnulli proxi- marum ætatum Scriptores B. virgini Mariæ aut ap- plicarint, quæ in Cantico dicuntur, aut ubi Mario- latria obtinere jam cœpit, directe & adæquate elogia occurrentia eidem Mariæ vindicarint, qui vero in- digni sunt, qui sancto Patrum accenseantur Catalo- go. Quid quod ab Ecclesia ceu hæretici reproba- ti fuerint, qui secus explicarunt, quam de Christo. Quo de Philastrius hæres. 131. Est hæresis, quæ de Cantico Canticorum ambigit, ipsa itidem æstimans non Spiritu divino, sed humanarum rerum causa ac volu- ptatum hominibus ab eodem prædicata. Theodoret. Præfat. in Cantic. Plerique ex iis, qui Canticum Can- ticorum calumniantur, ac spiritualem esse librum ne- gant, fabulas quasdam ne aniculis quidem deliranti- bus dignas, conferunt, alii nimirum, quod sapiens Sa- lomo de seipso, deque Pharaonis filia præscripserit, non- nulli autem eidem affines stultitiæ Pharaonis filiam Sponsam esse Abisag Sunemitiden confinxerunt. Quem errorem etiam in Theodoro Mopsuesteno damnasse Concilium 2. Constantin. antea observavimus.

Nec Christiani tantum Interpretes hic consen- tiunt, Judæi ipsi de amore Dei & Ecclesiæ explicant; idque non secundum accommodationem tantum, aut ita, ut alium admittant sensum literalem, hunc tan- tum pro mystico habeant, quod ex ipsis probare non potuit Grotius, nec nisi temere iisdem impu- tavit, sed ut crediderint, sensum literalem ac proprie a Spiritu Sancto intentum amorem spiritualem DEI adversus populum suum inferre. Chaldaica para- phrasis, quæ in magno penes Judæos est pretio, Spi- ritu Prophetico librum scriptum esse docet. Non er- go historico sensu eundem accipi vult. Sic enim habet inscriptio ejusdem: Hæc sunt Cantica & Car- mina, quæ dixit Salomo Propheta & Rex ipsius Israel coram Domino Deo universi orbis per Spiritum Pro- pheticum. Antiqui Judæi dixisse leguntur: Absit, absit, ut Canticum hoc sit de rebus obscænis, sed est Metaphora, alioqui nisi magnæ esset autoritatis, non scriberetur in Catalogo sanctarum Scripturarum. Asserunt etiam Rabbinorum antiquissimi, nomen Salomonis in hoc Cantico non esse proprium, sed appellativum, a pace scil. derivatum, ad Deum pacis autorem exprimendum, quod multis testimoniis confirmat Galatin. lib. 3. de Arcan. Cath. Verit. c. 26. Neque aliter senserunt, qui ex Ebræis monue- runt, ne ante 30. ætatis annum librum hunc quis le- geret, ne scil. juventus cum decantatur mysticus amor, amores indecentes corde conciperet, teste

Orig. hom. 1. in Cantic. ex duab. Gregor. Nazianz. in Apolog. Hieronymo praefat. homil. in Cantic. de quo Mercerus in praef. ad h. l. Maxime hunc li- brum non nisi iis legendum permittunt, quibus jam de- ferbuerint affectus nequitiae, ne quae hic dicuntur, in de- teriorem partem rapiant. Nihil enim hic est, quod sanctum, castum, pudicum & immaculatum non sit. Eadem quoque illorum sententia est, qui e Rabbi- nis Canticum commentariis illustrarunt. Autor Midrasch, R. Aben-Ezra, R. Salomon Jarchi, R. Da- vid Kimchi, & alii. Aben-Ezra observat, non esse moris, nec decorum in civitate, ut palam vir puellam aut mulierem ita de rebus amatoriis compellet, ut in hoc libro fit. In Midrasch vero notatur, de Ecclesia. ste quidem inter sapientes controversiam fuisse, sed de hoc libro NEMINEM UNQUAM IN ISRAELE controvertisse, quod manus non coinquinet, nec profa- nus sit. Imo quum caeteros quidem libros Sanctos dicant Ebraei, hunc sanctum sanctorum vocant, vel- ut caeterorum apicem, unde ei hoc nomen tribuere solent קדש קדשים sanctitas sanctitatum. Non- nulli ex Ebraeis monent in Canticis Scripturae vel Is- raelem laudare Dominum, ut Ex. 15. vel Dominum laudare Israelem Deut. 32. hic vero utrumque fieri; Sponsus laudat Sponsam, & vicissim Sponsa Sponsum.

Juvat hic annotare Interpretes, qui Canticum hoc commentationibus suis illustrare conati sunt in Christiana Ecclesia, Origenis circa Annum Christi 226. extant homiliae duae in Cantic. ut & homiliae quatuor: de quo Hieronym. in Prolog. ad Damas. Origenes cum in caeteris libris omnes vicerit, in Cantico Canticorum ipse se vicit. De quatuor tamen illis, an sint Origenis, dubium movit Emsm. in censur. de libris Origen. Atque hi potiores sunt e veteribus. Plures si quis desideret, una cum recentioribus adeat B. Gerhard. in Pro- œm. in Postill. Salom. cap. XI. Adducentur etiam nonnulli in hisce annotatis pro re nata. Nemo ita sanctissimum canticum conspurcavit, uti Grotius. Nos pios veteres, nec non e recentioribus imprimis NOSTROS sequuturi & a Grotiana spurcitie canti- cum repurgabimus, & sensus ejus sacratissimos e- ruemus, prout gratiam concesserit Spiritus S.

Superest, ut de ordine ac dispositione hujus can- tici aliquid dicamus. Non possumus autem eo- rum omnino probare sententiam, qui vel in genere statum Ecclesiæ describi putant, tum primum seu in- choatum, quod mutata Christi & Ecclesiæ desideria, & prima amoris quasi incunabula; tum medium vel adolescentis, qua progressum & incrementa; tum ter- tium vel plenitudinem perfectæ ætatis & culmen amo- ris, & quasi circa metas, quod ovilis gregibus cun- ctis receptis plenitudo exhibeatur: vel ita Ecclesiæ statum cum Thoma Brugthon. in præfat. exhiberi volunt, partim legalis ante captivitatem cap. 1. in ipsa captivitate c. 2. ad v. 15. post captivitatem usque ad Christi natales cap. 3, 6. & mortem cap. 4, 6. partim Evangelicæ, ejusque tum inchoatæ ad cap. 4, 16. tum consummatæ, ut agatur & de natu majori eademque primo pura, deinde caligine & tenebris obscurata cap. 5. denique restaurata ad cap. 6. tum de natu minoribus, videlicet vel principe, nascenti, & confir- mata ætate, inde cap. 7. & 8. ad v. 5. vel inferioribus duabus &c. Neque calculum meretur sententia Lyrani, qui V. T. tempora capp. 6. prioribus (1.) usque ad egressum ex Ægypto cap. 1. ad v. 12. (2.) progressum per desertum a v. 12. ad c. 4, 6. (3.) acces- sum termini c. quarto reliquo: & porro statum pos- sessæ terræ sub Josua & Judicibus c. 5. sub Davide c. 6. ad v. 10. Salomone v. 10. Regibus sequentibus us- que ad captivitatem Babylonicam v. 11. post captivi- tatem v. 12. describi vult: ac cæteris capitibus exhi- beri statum Ecclesiæ N. T. quoad inchoationem c. VII. usque ad v. 11. inchoati dilatationem v. 11. seqq. dila- tati tranquillitatem cap. VIII. qua pacis hujus de- siderium usque ad v. 8. & ejusdem complementum v. 8. usque ad finem. Neque suffragium addere pos- sumus consimili fere distributioni Georgii Ederi, qui in Oeconom. Bibl. libr. II. tab. 113. statum Ecclesiæ antiquæ usque ad Christi tempora per 10. Dramata describi autumat, ut (1.) agatur de peregrinatione patrum, Thare, Abrahami, Isaaci, Jacobi cap. I, 1. 12. (2.) de multiplicatione populi c. 1, 12. 13. 14. (3.) De oppressione ejusdem in Ægypto v. 15. seqq. c. 2, 12. (4.) De Dei defensione & apparitione Mosi in rubo facta c. 2, 3. seqq. (5.) De exitu Israelis ex Ægy- pto v. 8. seqq. (6.) De peregrinatione per deser- tum cap. 3. & 4. (7.) De introductione in terram sanctam c. 5. (8.) De exaltatione, persequutione, & liberatione populi sub Judicibus cap. 5. (9.) De sapientia Israelis cap. 8, 10. (10.) De æterna ha- bitatione sponsi in populo, relictis cæteris gentibus v. 14. Nihilo melior est vel Jacobi de Valentia Epi- scopi Christopolitani speculatio de statu Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ inde usque ad tempora regiminis Sa- lomonei præfigurante statum Ecclesiæ Chri- stianæ usque ad Constantini M. tempora decem par- ticularibus canticis hic descripto; vel Cornel. a Lap. qui cum aliis quinque partes facit: I. Ab ortu & præ- dicatione Christi usque ad Pentecosten c. 1. usque ad c. 2, 8. Et infantiæ Ecclesiæ. II. Adolescentis a Pentecoste usque ad Constantinum Imperat. ad c. 3, 6. III. Virilis ætatis tempore Constantini usque ad c. 4, 2. IV. Ecclesiæ veterascentis in senium in- clinatus usque ad c. 6, 3. grassantibus nempe Aria- nis, Nestorianis, Eutychianis, Pelagianis. V. Ec- clesiæ renovari cœptæ a Basilio, Chrysost. Cyrill. Au- gust. Hieron. & continuatæ a successoribus renovatio- nis usque ad finem mundi, quando in die judicii plena fiet renovatio, & glorificatio. Vel Johann. Cocceji, qui uti septem suas Ecclesiæ N. T. perio- dos ibi frequenter in Scripturis, in Mose, in Prophe- tis, in Apocalypsi & investigat, & invenit, ubi nec Spi- ritus S. easdem posuit, nec ullus Spiritu Dei instru- ctus hactenus eas videre aut invenire potuit, ita in Cantico hocce ordine easdem designare conatus est in Synopsi, & Medulla Prophetiæ cantici, & cogitationi- bus de Cantico ut icone regni Christi: utpote Primam, quam facit prædicationis inter Judæos & gentes ante ingravescentes persecutiones, & destructum templum c. 1. & 2. Secundam probationis, & conflationis Eccle- siæ in gravissimis, diuturnis, ac variis persequutio- nibus usque dum, destructis tyrannis, per principes terrenos pax ei concederetur cap. 3. & 4. Tertiam Ecclesiæ pacatæ a persecutionibus, & nutritæ a gentibus, sed incipientis conflictari cum falsa Ecclesia & cum ho- minum dominatione & calamitatibus quibusdam, sed cedentibus ad Ecclesiæ amplificationem, & in quietem definentibus c. 5. & 6. usque ad v. 9. Quar- tam Ecclesiæ veræ in medio falsæ Ecclesiæ emicantis & se ostendentis usque ad divisionem a v. 9. c. 6. ad c. 7, 11. Quintam Ecclesiæ post frustra petitam pacem & expectatam conversionem multitudinis adversariæ, sive Reformationem, recedentis ab urbe magna, & in ea recessione exagitatæ usque ad pacem ejus cap. 7, 11. 12. 13. & 8, 1. 2. 3. Sextam Ecclesiæ in nova angu- stia constitutæ post pacem, quam a secessione conse- quuta erat c. 8, 4. 5. 6. Septimam denique Ecclesiæ aspirantis post multa certamina ad regnum Christi, & prædicationem ejus in toto mundo.

Missis his & similibus non tam explicationi- bus, quam voluntariis & violentis detorsionibus Cantici Canticorum, etsi fateri oporteat, non im- merito monuisse Osiandrum, non quærendam esse in hoc amatorio carmine dispositionem Rhetoricam; si- quidem omnia plena sint affectibus, qui animum aman- tis jam huc jam illuc rapiant, haud spernenda tamen, aut desperanda omnis dispositionis indagatio, nec inconcinne nonnulli a B. Gerhardo in Postill. Sa- lom. præfat. c. 7. §. 10. laudati, describi ajunt spiri- tuale conjugium Christi & Ecclesiæ primum a sponsa- lium tractatione, ubi actus primus lætus, videlicet colloquium Ecclesiæ & Christi c. 1. Christi & Eccle- siæ, c. 2. intermedius tum lætus, videlicet sermo Ec- clesiæ c. 3. sermo Christi c. 4. tum tristis, ubi Ecclesia tristatur ob discessum Sponsi cap. 5. & ultimus de re- ditu Sponsi c, 6. Deinde a nuptiarum expeditione, quas Ecclesia expetit primo pro se c. 7. secundo pro sorore sua, h. e. gentium Ecclesia c. 8. Nimirum, ut recte Osiander, vicissitudines sunt in hoc Cantico gau- dii & querelarum: quia Ecclesia exposita est cruci, af- flictionibus, & variis tentationibus, nec perfecta adhuc est in agnitione Dei & charitate.

Placet autem imprimis ut Paraphrasis, ita & partitio in Bibliis Ernestinis tradita, quæ autorem ha- bere dicitur B. GERHARDUM, & ex ejus mente B. GLASSIUM, ad cujus proinde meliorem intellectum non parum conducet præclara explica- tio præcipuorum dictorum in hoc Cantico in Postil- la Salomonea Gerhardina exhibita. Fuit enim Vir hic Dei, si quisquam alius Theologorum nostri se- culi, Spiritu Dei πίόνι μέτρῳ instructus, quod scri- pta vere Enthea affatim testantur : Qui uti exemplo Thomæ Aquinatis, & Joh. Gersonis, & judicio alio- rum Christianum Interpretum, imo etiam Judæo- rum monuerat in Exegesi de Scriptura S. §. 149. ex- plicationem hujus Cantici non esse in juventute at- tingendam, sed in solatium Christianæ senectutis, ac piæ emigrationis viaticum reservandam, ita in se- nectute, & sub clausulam veræ sanctæ vitæ medita- tionibus Cantici vacavit.

Partes autem tres licebit constituere: Prima desiderium sponsæ, Ecclesiæ, sistit, exoptantis adven- tum Sponsi in carnem, dialogismo Ecclesiæ cum Christo cap. 1. expositum: cum promisso Sponsi ad- ventum suum, & beneficia exponentis, & reci- proca invitatione sponsæ ad lætam eorum fruitio- nem desiderium & affectum reciprocum testantis cap. 2. Altera solicitudinem & dolorem sponsæ de

PAR DESIDERIU TUS CHRI PLET

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

The Bride desires the kiss of Christ's mouth at his advent, captivated by declarations of love as if by his breasts, more than by the pleasures of the world, so that thus the odor of his recognition may spread more widely, and exultant, as if he were already present, about to lead her into his chamber: she protests before her companions concerning the darkness of her calamity, and adjures the bridegroom to show her the place of pasture: From whom, having been informed about his tracks and in what place he keeps her, and cheered by the promise of greater adornment, perceiving the odor of his saving passion, she makes him a bundle of myrrh and a cluster of Copher, and from the beauty of her eyes proclaimed by him, and in turn proclaiming him for his beauty, she congratulates herself greatly on the fruitfulness and happiness of the bridal chamber.

Ver. 1. LET HIM KISS.

The Bride, the Church, and every faithful soul in her, speaks of the Bridegroom, the Son of God, Ps. 45:12, Isa. 54:5, 6, 62:5, Hos. 2:19, John 3:29, 2 Cor. 11:2, Eph. 5:31, 32, Rev. 21:9. For the attached [verses] testify that it is the speech of the bride:

Beginning abruptly, however, she immediately seeks the kisses of the bridegroom, which is a sign of supreme desire and love: concerning which Ambrose speaks beautifully in Sermon 1 on Ps. 116. Imagine a virgin betrothed for a long time, and burning with righteous love, who has known many excellent works of her beloved through the assertion of credible witnesses: suspended by desires, delayed frequently, now unable to bear the delays, who would have done everything to see the bridegroom, having finally obtained her wishes, troubled with joy at the sudden advent of the Bridegroom, not seeking the beginnings of a greeting, not the exchange of words, but immediately [seeking] the loss of the Bridegroom in temptations, with the joy of the same upon the finding of the Bridegroom: and furthermore, he depicts the bridegroom's solicitude for the tranquility of the Bride, along with his delight in the same declaration, with the Bride exulting over the bed of rest, well guarded, and the diadem of the Bridegroom on the day of his betrothal, c. 3, and the Bridegroom reciprocally congratulating himself on the beauty of his bride, with a declaration of his most ardent love and desire, c. 4. The third [part] comprises the Bride's invitation into the garden, and the Bridegroom's response with the Bride's joy at having heard the Bridegroom's voice, but mixed with grief at his departure, and the cause of that grief, set forth in a dialogue, namely the supreme beauty of this bridegroom, chap. 5. who in turn depicts the charm of his Bride, chap. 6. & 7. and is invited by the bride to go out into the field, so that the nations might also be made partakers of that joy, towards the end of chap. 7. And he responds to the Bride's desires in reality, presenting to her a multitude of nations, and sustains her, desiring the permanence of love, with a promise of grace concerning the strengthening of the walls, and the preservation of the vineyard, c. 8.

RS I. UM ADVEN- [TUM]

which she had desired to demand. Thus therefore also the holy Church, which, betrothed in the beginning of the world in Paradise, prefigured in the flood, announced through the law, called through the Prophets, had long awaited the redemption of men, the beauty of the Gospel, the coming of the beloved, impatient of delay, rushes into kisses saying: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. She does not express the name of him whom she desires, but simply says LET HIM KISS. For there was none but the ONE, whom they carried in their heart, whom they so greatly desired, whose kisses the faithful sought. She exults in kisses, she asks for what she desires, says Bernard, serm. 7. on the Canticles, yet she does not name him whom she loves, because she does not doubt that they know him, inasmuch as frequent conversation with them is wont to be had about him. Conf. Job 20, 15.

LET HIM KISS ME WITH THE KISS OF HIS MOUTH.

Would that at last HE, whom I carry in my heart, might appear, and be manifested in the flesh! Would that he might exhilarate me present with the kisses of love! Would that he might address me from mouth to mouth! Would that he might deign to breathe into me the spirit of his lips! For by this vow the bride testifies to her desire 1. Concerning the act of incarnation: that the Son of God might at last descend from heaven, betroth human nature to himself, and manifest himself in it 1. Tim. 3, 16. These are the words of the ancient people, says Athanasius in the Synopsis, praying the Lord that he would descend, and be joined to flesh. So also Ambrose in the book on Isaac and the soul, chap. 3. Consider either the Church, suspended for many ages by the Lord's coming so long promised to her through the Prophets, or the soul which, raising itself from the body, having renounced the delights of luxury and carnal pleasures, and having also stripped off the anxiety of secular vanities, has long desired for itself the infusion of the divine presence and the grace of the saving word, to be worn away because he comes late, and to be afflicted. And therefore as if wounded with love, since she cannot bear his delays, she turns to the Father to ask that he send to her God the Word: II. As a sign of love: Because the Bride seeks the kisses of the incarnate Son of God, the most desired Bridegroom, as a sign of intimate love, Rom. 16, 15. If he wishes to be convinced, it is a paraphrase of Bernard, sermon 2 on the Canticles, that he promises by the pleasure of his will through such frequent embassy now, yet does not exhibit it, let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, and thus by an equal sign make her secure of peace. III. As an oral address: namely, that the Son may deign to address her not through others, but directly from mouth to mouth: and just as he has addressed the Bride through the Prophets until now, Hos. 12, 10, and as if kissing her and testifying to his love, so at last he may address her in person, Is. 52, 6, Heb. 1, 1, and announce to her the word of grace, John 1, 17, 18. Tim. 1, 9. 10. which is like a sweet kiss, Prov. 24, 26, of his most graceful lips, Ps. 45, 3, Zeph. 3, 9. Thus Jerome, Ep. 146. The Church prays for the coming of the Bridegroom, saying: I do not want him to speak to me through Moses, I do not want him to speak through the Prophets. Let him assume my body himself, let him kiss me in the flesh. And Origen, hom. 1 from the two on the Canticles: The Church, inflamed by love and desire from the promises and benefits of God, asks that the Messiah be sent, so that she may hear him speaking in the flesh, and see him teaching. And also Gregory of Nyssa, hom. 1 on the Canticles: Because the words of the Bridegroom are spirit and life, and whoever is joined to the spirit becomes spirit; and he who is joined to life passes from death to life, in accordance with the voice of the Lord, therefore the virgin soul desires to approach the fountain of spiritual life. Now the fountain is the mouth of the Bridegroom, from which the words of eternal life flowing forth fill the mouth that draws them in. That the Jews themselves interpret it thus, Galatinus observes, book 3, de arcan. Cath. verit. c. 7. The ancient Talmudists explained it thus: Let the Messiah, the Son of God, kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, that is, let him instruct and teach me with his own mouth, and when I ask about the way of Salvation, let him not despise the touch of my mouth. Let him no longer send Moses, who had a stammering tongue; let him not send Isaiah, who said he was polluted in his lips; let him not send Jeremiah, who said he did not know how to speak, but let the Son of God himself, who is the wisdom and power of the Father, come and teach me with his mouth. 4. As the breath of the Holy Spirit. When the Bridegroom kisses the Bride out of love, he as it were breathes his Spirit into her, which she eagerly draws in: Thus the Bride seeks to drink in the Spirit of the lips and mouth of her Bridegroom, and prays that he may deign to breathe the same into her. Cf. John 20, 22. 23. A kiss, says Ambrose, l. c., is that by which lovers adhere to one another, and as it were enjoy the sweetness of interior grace. Through this kiss the soul adheres to God the Word, through which the spirit of the one kissing is transfused into her: just as those who kiss one another are not content with the mere tasting of lips, but seem to infuse their spirit into each other.

It is said, however, in the plural number: WITH THE KISSES of his mouth: concerning which Ambrose also warned in the loc. cit.: She does not seek one kiss, but many kisses, so that she may satisfy her desire. For she who loves is not content with the sparingness of one kiss, but demands more, claims more, and thus is accustomed to commend herself more to her beloved. Finally, she in the Gospel was approved thus: Because she did not cease, he says, to kiss my feet: and therefore many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. Therefore this soul also desired many kisses of the Word, so that she might be illuminated by the light of divine knowledge. Kisses in the plural signify vehement desire and supreme love toward the Bridegroom, so that the Bride cannot be satiated by his presence, and desires it to be continuous. For true love knows no measure: and as Bernard says, the measure of loving God is to love without measure.

verf. eod. BECAUSE THY BREASTS ARE BETTER THAN WINE.

In the Hebrew it is: Because thy loves are better than wine: as Vatablus says, thy loves surpass wine in goodness. The interpreters understand the declarations and consolations of love, Ps. 94, 19, especially those to be perceived under the coming of Christ and the gathering of the Church throughout the world, Is. 66, 11. 13, 1 Pet. 2, 2. 3, which are sweeter than wine, i.e., than all worldly pleasure, Eccles. 10, 19, Ps. 104, 15. Similarly Corn. a Lap. says: Because I have tasted the sweetness of milk, that is, of spiritual consolations flowing as if from thy breast from thy love: therefore breasts giving milk denote love giving consolations and wondrous sweetnesses, with Haymo and Thomas preceding: By the breasts of Christ is understood the sweetness of the Gospel, by which the infancy of believers is nourished as if by milk. The breasts of Christ, as Cornelius says again, are his very wisdom and beneficence, from which honey-speaking and the sweetness of doctrines and words flow like honeyed milk, which is sweeter than all the wine of carnal pleasures, as being sharp and biting. But because דֹּדִים, not דַּדִּים is found in the source, of which the former signifies loves, the latter breasts, as Marc. Marinus admits, there is no place here for a comparison with breasts, nor for the long discussion of Cornelius, how breasts, which are proper to women, can be attributed to the Bridegroom as a man?

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Osculum oris Christi sub adventum ejus desiderat Sponsa, amoris declarationibus ceu uberibus ejus præ voluptatibus mundi capta, ut sic odor agnitionis ejus amplius se diffundat, & exul- tabunda, quasi jam adsit, in cameram suam ipsam adducturus: protestatur coram consor- tibus de atroré calamitatis, & obtestatur sponsum, ut locum pasturæ sibi monstret: A quo de vestigiis suis & quo loco ipsam habeat, informata, & promisso majori ornatu exhi- larata odorem passionis salutiferæ percipi- ens, fasciculum myrrhæ, & botrum Copher ipsum facit, & a venustate oculorum ab ipso deprædicata, eumque vicissim ob pulchritudi- nem deprædicans de fœcunditate & felici- tate thalami sibi oppido gratulatur.

Vers. 1. OSCULETUR.

DE Sponso Filio Dei loquitur Sponsa Ecclesia, & quævis in ea fidelis anima, Ps. 45, 12. Esa. 54, 5. 6. 62, 5. Os. 2, 19. Joh. 3, 29. 2. Cor. 11, 2. Eph. 5, 31. 32. Apoc. 21, 9. Sponsæ enim sermonem esse affixa te- stantur:

Ex abrupto autem incipiens oscula sta- tim sponsi expetit, quod signum est summi desi- derii & amoris: de quo pulcre Ambros. serm. 1. in Ps. 116. Constitue virginem desponsatam multo tempo- re, & justo ferventem amore, quæ multa præclara opera dilecti probabilium testium assertione cognoverit: de- sideriis suspensis dilatam frequenter, jam non fe- rentem moras, quæ omnia fecisset ut sponsum videret, aliquando votis potitam suis, ad improvisum Sponsi adventum gaudio turbatam, non quærere pri- mordia salutationis, non verborum vices, sed statim amissione Sponsi in tentationibus, cum gaudio ejus- dem ob inventionem Sponsi: & porro sponsi solici- tudinem de tranquillitate Sponsae, cum oblectatio- nis suae in eadem declaratione depingit, exultante Sponsa de lecto quietis, probe custodito & diade- mate Sponsi in die desponsationis suae, c. 3. ac reci- proce gratulante sibi Sponso de pulchritudine sponsae suae, cum amoris ac desiderii sui ardentissimi conte- statione c. 4. Tertia invitationem Sponsae complectitur in hortum, & responsum Sponsi cum gaudio Sponsae ob auditam vocem Sponsi, sed mixto luctui ob disces- sum, ejusque luctus causa, dialogo exposita, summa nempe sponsi hujus pulchritudine cap. 5. qui vicis- sim Sponsae suae venustatem depingit cap. 6. & 7. & a sponsa invitatur ad egressum in agrum, ut gen- tes etiam gaudii istius participes reddantur, sub fi- nem cap. 7. Sponsaeque desideriis respondet reapse, sistens ei multitudinem gentium, ac dilectionis peren- nitatem exoptantem gratiae promissione de confir- matione murorum, & vineae conservatione susten- tat, c. 8.

RS I. UM ADVEN- STI ADIM- TUM.

quod desiderasset exigere. Ita ergo & sancta Eccle- sia, quae in primordiis mundi desponsata in Paradiso, praefigurata in diluvio, annunciata per legem, vo- cata per Prophetas, diu redemtionem hominum, Evan- gelii decorem, dilecti expectasset adventum, impatiens morae, in oscula ruit dicens: Osculetur me ab osculo oris sui. Non exprimit nomen ejus, quem desi- derat, sed simpliciter OSCULETUR inquit. Erat enim non nisi UNUS, quem in corde gerebant, quem tantopere desiderabant, cujus oscula expete- bant fideles. Gestit in oscula, petit quod cupit, in- quit Bernhard. serm. 7. in Cantic. non tamen nomi- nat, quem amet, quia illos nosse non dubitat, utpote de quo frequens sibi cum illis soleat esse confabulatio. Conf. Job. 20, 15.

OSCULETUR ME OSCULO ORIS SUI.

Utinam tandem ILLE, quem in corde gero appareat, & manifestetur in carne! utinam praesens amoris osculis me exhílaret! utinam de ore ad os me alloquatur! utinam spiritum labiorum suorum mihi insufflare dignetur! voto enim hoc sponsa te- statur desiderium suum 1. Qua incarnationis actum: ut de coelo tandem descendat Filius Dei, humanam sibi desponset naturam, & in ea se manifestet 1. Tim. 3,16. Sunt verba ista veteris populi, ait Athanasius in Synopsi, precantis Dominum, ut descenderet, & carni conjungeretur. Ita & Ambrosius libro de Isaac & anima cap. 3. Confidera vel Ecclesiam tam diu pro- misso sibi per Prophetas dominico adventu per tempo- ra multa suspensam, vel animam quae elevans se a corpore, abdicatis luxuriae delitiis, voluptatibusque carnalibus, exuta quoque solicitudine secularium va- nitatum, jam dudum infusionem sibi divinae praesentiae, & gratiam verbi salutaris exoptet, commacerari quod sero veniat, & affligi. Ideoque quasi vul- neratam charitate, cum moras ejus ferre non possit, con- versam ad patrem rogare, ut mittat sibi Deum verbum: II. Qua amoris fignum: Quia expetit Sponsa oscula Filii Dei incarnati, Sponsi desideratissimi, in signum amoris intimi, Rom. 16, 15. Si mihi vult esse persuasum, Paraphrasis est Bernhardi serm. 2. in Cantic. quod de suæ beneplacito voluntatis tam crebra jam legatione spondet nec exhibet, osculetur me osculo oris sui, sicque signo pari faciat de pace securam. III. Qua orale al- loquium: ut nempe non per alios, sed ἀμέσως ab o- re ad os se alloqui dignetur Filius: & quemadmo- dum per Prophetas hactenus Sponsam alloquutus est Hos. 12, 10. eamque veluti osculatus, & amores suos testatus, ita tandem αὐτοπροσώπως ipsam al- loquatur Es. 52, 6. Ebr. 1, 1. & verbum gratiæ ei an- nunciet, Joh. 1, 17. 18. 2. Tim. 1, 9. 10. quod est instar suavis osculi Prov. 24, 26. labiorum ipsius gratiofif- simorum Ps. 45, 3. Zeph. 3, 9. Sic Hieron. Ep. 146. Ec- clesia de sponsi precatur adventu: Nolo mihi, dicens, per Mosen, nolo per Prophetas loquatur. Ipse meum corpus assumat, ipse me osculetur in carne. Et Origenes hom. 1. ex duabus in Cantic. Ecclesia ex Dei promissis, & beneficiis amore & desiderio succensa petit mitti Messiam, ut eum audiat in carne loquentem, ipsum videat docentem. Nec non Gregor. Nyssenus hom. 1. in Cantic. Quia verba sponsi spiritus sunt & vita, quicunque autem conglutinatur spiritui, fit spiri- tus: & qui vitæ conjungitur, transit a morte ad vitam, congruenter voci Domini, propterea desiderat appro- pinquare animam fonti vitæ spiritualis virgo anima. Fons autem est os sponsi, unde scaturientia verba vitæ æternæ implent os ea attrahens. Sic etiam Judæos ipsos interpretari observat Galatinus l. 3. de arcan. Cath. verit. c. 7. Veteres Thalmudistæ sic exposuerunt: Osculetur me Messias Filius Dei osculis oris sui, id est, ipse ore proprio instruat & erudiat me, atque oris mei tactum, cum de via Salutis interrogavero, non con- temnat. Non jam Mosen mittat, qui linguam impe- ditam habebat; non Esaiam, qui se labiis pollutum di- cebat: non Jeremiam, qui se loqui nescire ajebat, sed ipse Dei Filius, qui Patris sapientia & virtus est veniat, & ore suo me doceat. 4. Qua Spiritus S. afflatum. Cum ex amore Sponsus osculatur Sponsam, ei veluti Spiritum suum inspirat, quem illa avide attrahit: Ita Sponsa expetit Spiritum labiorum & oris sponsi sui haurire, & ut eundem sibi insufflare dignetur, orat. Conf. Joh. 20, 22. 23. Osculum est, inquit Ambros. l. c. quo invicem amantes sibi adhærent, & velut gratiæ in- terioris suavitate potiuntur. Per hoc osculum adhæ- ret anima Deo Verbo, per quod sibi transfunditur spi- ritus osculantis: sicut etiam hi, qui se osculantur, non sunt labiorum prælibatione contenti, sed spiritum suum sibi invicem videntur infundere.

Dicitur autem in plurali numero: OSCULIS oris sui: de quo itidem monuit loc. cit. Ambrosius: Non unum osculum quærit, sed plura oscula, ut deside- rium suum possit explere. Quæ enim diligit, non est unius osculi parcitate contenta, sed plura exigit, plura vendicat, & ita se amplius dilecto commendare consue- vit. Denique illa in Evangelio sic probata est: Quia non cessavit, inquit, osculari pedes meos: & ideo remif- sa sunt ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multum. Ergo & hæc anima oscula verbi multa desiderabat, ut illumi- netur divinæ cognitionis lumine. Oscula in plurali significant vehemens desiderium & amorem sum- mum erga Sponsum, ut ejus præsentia satiari ne- queat Sponsa, eamque continuam exoptet. Nam verus amor nullum novit habere modum: & Bernhar- do dicente, modus amandi Deum est amare sine modo.

verf. eod. QUIA MELIORA SUNT UBERA TUA VINO.

In Ebræo est: Quia meliores sunt amores tui vino: ut Vatabl. amores tui vinum bonitate superant. Vinarienses amoris declarationes & consolationes Pf. 94, 19. maxime sub adventum Christi, & congrega- tionem Ecclesiæ per orbem percipiendas intelli- gunt Ef. 66,11. 13. 1. Pet. 2, 2. 3. quæ vino, i.e. omni mun- dana voluptate suaviores sunt Ecclef. 10,19. Pf. 104,15. Similiter Corn. a Lap. q. d. Quia dulcorem lactis, id est, consolationum spiritualium a tuo amore quasi ubere manantem gustavi: ubera ergo lac dantia notant amorem dantem consolationes, & suavitates mirificas, præeunte Haymone & Thoma: Per ubera Christi dul- cedo Evangelii intelligitur, qua velut lacte nutritur in- fantia credentium. Ubera Christi, ut iterum Cornel. sunt ipsa ejus sapientia, & beneficentia, ex quibus melli- loquentia & doctrinæ verborumque suavitas quasi mel- leum lac profluit, quod omni vino voluptatum carna- lium, utpote acri & mordaci suavius est. Sed quia דֹּדִים, non דַּדִּים habetur in fonte, quorum illud a- mores, hoc ubera significat, fatente Marc. Marino, comparationi cum uberibus hic locus non est, neque disputationi prolixæ Cornelii, quomodo Sponso utpo- te viro tribuantur ubera, quæ sunt propria fœminarum?

## 1:2
verf. 2. FRAGRANT WITH THE BEST OINTMENTS.

In the Hebrew, these do not cohere with the preceding, but by the force of the accentuation, they cohere with the following: At, or because of the fragrance of thy best ointments, thy name is as oil poured out. As before she proclaimed the sweetness of the loves of the Bridegroom, so now the Bride proclaims the fragrance and odor of his name, which, like oil poured out, spreads from itself the most sweet odor of his best ointments of life-giving knowledge, 2 Cor. 2, 14 ff., by which faithful souls are more refreshed than the heart and head of a man with oil and balsam of the most excellent fragrance.

Ps. 23:5. Ps. 92:11. For in the name of Jesus is the highest power of life-giving knowledge, Acts 4:12, which upon the coming of Christ was to spread itself through the whole world, through the proclamation of the Gospel: As when precious nard or balsam is poured out, the whole house is filled with fragrance, Mark 14:3. John 12:3. Bernard explains this in sermon 15: O blessed name! O oil poured out everywhere! As far as it runs from heaven into Judea, and thence into all the earth, the Church cries out from the whole world, thy name is oil poured out. And further: Oil, he says, shines, feeds, and anoints. It fosters fire, nourishes the flesh, soothes pain; it is light, food, and medicine. See the same now also concerning the name of the Bridegroom: preached, it shines; meditated upon, it feeds; invoked, it soothes and anoints. Moreover, the preceding words teach that we should look primarily to the εὐωδίαν or fragrance of the oil, which is commended most highly in balsam, Ps. 133:2. Ps. 141:5. as well as in that holy and precious oil, Ex. 30, with which the High Priest was to be anointed, in which the most excellent myrrh was used, having the power both of preserving from putrefaction and of healing wounds: concerning the application of which to this place see the Postilla of Salomon on the feast of the Circumcision. Furthermore, it is not said, thy name is like oil, but oil itself, for the sake of emphasis, as if to say it spreads such an odor from itself that thy name must be considered precious oil itself: so that the highest fragrance may thus be denoted. Mention is made, however, of oil poured out: and the pouring out of this oil was made

(1) in the incarnation of the Word, concerning which Anselm says on this place: while oil is in the vessel, it neither gives off an odor nor soothes pains, so also the name of God, while he himself was still held enclosed in the bosom of the Father, was little or not at all recognized, but after he assumed flesh, visiting the world with his presence, he exposed himself to be known by all, he sent forth an odor, that is, fame and a good reputation concerning himself:

(2) in the passion of Christ, where the shrub of the most noble balsam, having been wounded as if by a sharp knife, poured out most wholesome balsam, Luke 22:44, Isaiah 53:5. Just as in Judea shrubs of balsam cut by a knife are said to pour out balsam: In his passion Christ was made as a broken vessel, Psalm 22:16, then (3.) especially in the universal promulgation of the Gospel, concerning which Theodoret in this place: Just as an ointment enclosed in a vessel contains the fragrance of the scent itself, but if it be poured out, it fills the air itself also: So the Lord Christ was known to few before his passion, but after he sustained the cross and death, the blessed Apostles were immediately filled with that sweetness, running through the earth and crossing the seas, and announcing the Gospel to all, they filled the whole world with the sweetness of the scent.

Verse of the same.

THEREFORE THE YOUNG MAIDENS HAVE LOVED THEE.

It is a discourse concerning the faithful souls after the universal preaching of the Gospel: עַל־כֵּן young maidens, or virgins are of a younger age, which force of the word Jerome observes in chapter 7 of Isaiah. Therefore the faithful from the nations converted to Christ in the time of the New Testament are designated, 2 Corinthians 11:2, Revelation 14:4, who, perceiving the scent of the name of Jesus from the herald of the Gospel, acknowledged Christ by true faith as the bridegroom of their souls, and loved him intimately, and so always desired to follow him.

Latin:

verf. 2. FRAGRANTIA UNGUENTIS OPTIMIS.

In Ebræo non cum præcedentibus, sed vi ac- centuationis, cum sequentibus hæc cohærent, Ad, vel propter odorem unguentorum tuorum optimorum oleum effusum nomen tuum. Ut ante suavitatem amo- rum sponsi, sic jam fragrantiam & odorem nominis ejus deprædicat Sponsa, quod instar olei effusi un- guentorum ejus optimorum odorem suavissimum de se spargit vivificæ cognitionis, 2. Cor. 2, 14. feqq. qua fideles animæ magis refocillantur, quam cor & caput hominis oleo & balsamo odoris præstantissimi

Pf. 23, 5. Pf. 92, 11. In nomine enim Jesu summa vi- vificæ notitiæ est, Actor. 4, 12, quæ sub adventum Christi se diffusura erat per totum orbem, per præ- conium Evangelii: Sicut nardo vel balsamo pretio- so effuso, tota domus fragrantia repletur Marc. 14, 3. Joh. 12, 3. Explicat id Bernhard. ferm. 15. O nomen be- nedictum! o oleum undiquaque effusum! Quousque de cælo in Judæam, & inde in omnem terram excurrit, de toto orbe clamat Ecclesia, oleum effusum nomen tuum. Et porro: Oleum, inquit, lucet, pascit, & ungit. Fovet ignem, nutrit carnem, lenit dolorem, lux, cibus, medicina. Vide idem nunc & de Sponsi no- mine, lucet prædicatum, pascit recogitatum, invocatum lenit, & ungit. Respici autem imprimis εὐωδίαν seu fragrantiam olei antecedentia docent, quæ com- mendatur maxime in balsamo Pf. 133, 2. Pf. 141, 5. nec non in sancto illo & pretioso oleo, Ex. 30. quo Pontifex ungendus erat, in quo myrrha præstantis- sima adhibita & preservandi a putredine vim habens, & curandi vulnera: de quorum applicatione ad h. l. vid. Postill. Salomon. in fest. Circumcis. Cæterum non dicitur, nomen tuum est sicut oleum, sed ipsum oleum, emphaseos causa, q. d. tantum odorem de se spargit, ut ipsum oleum pretiosum habendum sit nomen tuum: ut summa fragrantia ita denotetur. Mentio autem fit olei effusi: & effusio olei hujus facta

(1) in verbi incarnatione, de qua Anshelmus in h. l. oleum dum in vase est, neque odorem profert, neque dolores sedat, ita & nomen Dei dum ipse adhuc in sinu Patris conclusus teneretur, parum vel nihil agnosceba- tur, postquam vero carnem assumsit, presentia mun- dum visitans, seipsum omnibus cognoscendum expo- suit, odorem, hoc est, famam & bonam opinio- nem de se emisit:

(2) in Christi passione, ubi frutex balsami nobilissimi velut cultro acuto vulneratus balsamum saluberrimum effudit, Luc. 22, 44. Es. 53, 5. Sicut in Judæa frutices balsami cultro incisi balsamum fundere dicuntur: In passione Christus factus est ut vas confractum, Ps. 22, 16. tum (3.) imprimis in universali Evangelii promulgatione, de qua Theodor. h. l. Quemadmodum unguentum in vase conclusum inclusam continet & ipsam odoris fragrantiam, sin autem effundatur, ipsum quoque replet aerem: Sic Dominus Christus ante passionem paucis notus erat, at postquam crucem mortemque sustinuit, continuo B. Apostoli suavitate illa repleti sunt terram percurrentes, & maria trajicientes, omnibusque Evangelium nunciantes.odoris suavitate mundum universum compleverunt.

Vers. eod.

IDEO ADOLESCENTULÆ DILEXERUNT TE.

De fidelibus animabus post universalem prædicationem Evangelii sermo est: עַל־כֵּן adolescentulæ, vel virgines sunt junioris ætatis, quam vocis vim Hieron. observat. in c. 7. Esa. Ideo fideles è gentibus ad Christum conversis tempore N. T. designantur 2. Cor. 11, 2. Apoc. 14, 4. qui odorem nominis Jesu e præcone Evangelii percipientes, Christum vera fide ceu sponsum animarum agnoverunt, eumque intime amarunt, adeoque eum sequi semper optarunt.

## 1:3
Verse 3.

DRAW ME AFTER THEE: WE WILL RUN IN THE FRAGRANCE OF THY OINTMENTS.

He speaks first in the singular, draw me, because every faithful soul desires this sweet drawing for itself, and has need of it individually: then in the plural, we will run, because they wish to follow Christ in groups and in competition. Moreover, another reading and punctuation occurs in Ambrose concerning those who are initiated into the mysteries, chapter 6: they have drawn thee, likewise draw us after thee. But in the source and among the Chaldean, Aquila, and Symmachus, the Vulgate reading is held, however much the codices of the Seventy Interpreters vary. Aponius, Justus Orgel, Bernard, and others also distinguish it thus: draw me after thee. However, that phrase, in the fragrance of thy ointments, is not held in the Hebrew text: but the Vulgate preferred to follow the Seventy Interpreters (however erroneously) than the authentic text. That sigh, Draw me, indicates both the impotence of the bride, who cannot follow the bridegroom unless she is drawn by him, and the efficacy of the divine drawing, John 6:44. Whence Bernard: draw me in a way unwilling, that you may make me willing; draw me sluggish, that you may render me running. Here the Jesuit Cornelius also praises these words of Bernard, convinced by the power of truth, as it appears: We will run, we will run, but in the fragrance of thy ointments, not in the confidence of our own merits. Nor do we trust that we run in the magnitude of our own strengths, but in the multitude of thy mercies. For even if we were willing when we ran, it was not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy. And even the reborn are compelled to acknowledge their own infirmity in this race, Romans 7:14, 23. I would wish to follow thee, O bridegroom, but with concupiscence resisting I am not able, as Cornelius a Lapide confesses. We have, says St. Ambrose concerning Isaac and the soul, chapter 3, the desire of following, which the grace of thy ointments inspires, but because we cannot equal thy courses, draw us, that supported by thy aid, we may be able to insist upon thy footsteps.

How Christ drew men through the incarnation, through the function of his ecclesiastical office, by divine oracles and miracles, and also by examples of meekness and other virtues, Matthew 11:29, as if by a triple cord of charity, Hosea 11:4, as also through his passion, John 12:32, and finally through the universal preaching of the Gospel, Romans 10:18; how likewise he still draws through the Word and Sacraments, through benefits both bestowed and promised, and through the scourges of the cross, Psalm 32:3, when the evils that press upon us compel us to go to God; how finally God is to draw us through the blessed emigration, Psalm 142:8, Luke 2:29, where we shall follow the Lamb whithersoever he shall go, Revelation 14:4, the blessed Gerhard has expounded in his Postils on Solomon, Sunday 24 after Trinity. We only append the sentiment of Gregory the Great on this place: The pious soul asks that it be drawn by God through grace, by which it may be able to follow him through imitation. For no one is able to run through the way of the commandments of God unless he be drawn by grace. He draws us, that we may adhere to him by faith, John 6:44, that we may follow him by obedience, John 15:5, 10, Psalm 119:33, and that we may insist upon his footsteps by patience, 1 Peter 2:21, and at length remain with him eternally, John 14:3, 1 Thessalonians 4:16. But we run in the way of his commandments, Psalm 54:31, and in the proposed stadium, 1 Corinthians 9:24 ff., Philippians 3:12, Hebrews 12:1, etc.

verse of the same. THE KING HATH BROUGHT ME INTO HIS CELLARS.

Now the Bridegroom is expressed by the name of KING, from Ps. 45, 2. 12. Ps. 2, 6. who is about to lead the bride into the storehouses, [Hebrew text], ταμιεῖα, as the Vulgate and LXX. or as Luther, into his private room and chamber, the house of his Father after the course is finished John 14, 2. where there is pleasure, rest, and security, Ps. 16, 11. Isa. 32, 17. 18. which we now possess in hope Rom. 8, 24. Eph. 2, 6. whence we rejoice and are glad in our bridegroom the savior Luke 1, 47. Isa. 61, 10. and we prefer his loves to wine and all pleasures Matt. 6, 33. Ps. 33, 9. THE UPRIGHT (in heart) love thee O King Bridegroom Ps. 32, 11. חֲדָרָיו signifies inner sanctuaries, such as are private rooms and bedchambers, in which the master himself dwells in secret, and stores up his wealth and treasures. Arabic: renders, into a secret chamber. Syrian, into a bridal chamber. But Cassiodorus, Aponius, Anselm, and Bede understand it of heaven: Concerning which introduction of the King and the same bridegroom at the end of the world, see Matt. 25, 1. 34. seqq. Rev. 19. and 21, 9. whence Bede gives this reason for the connection: Therefore I beseech the bridegroom, that he himself, having given his hand, may help us running after him, lest we fail, because I have already tasted the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, I have already tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet, I have already known the good things which are prepared for me in heaven, he himself revealing them. And being turned to him immediately and giving him thanks, she says, we will exult and be glad in thee, as if she were saying: we are by no means lifted up by the gifts received, but in all that we live well we exult, nay we will exult and be glad in thy mercy. This exhilaration indeed happens even in this life, but inchoatively, namely through the feeding of the word Psalm 23, 5. and 19, 11. Heb. 5, 12. 14. whence Jerome Epist. 142. to Damasus. Theodoret. Greg. Just. Orgelit. and Rupert. in this place, the storehouses are the Holy Scriptures, as well as through the consolation of the Holy Spirit Ps. 94, 19. 119, 92. and through the foretaste of heavenly joy Heb. 6, 5. but it will be consummately in the soul by the translation into Paradise Luke 23, 45. 16, 25. and by the glorious assumption of the whole composite being Matt. 25, 34. and therefore the joy, which is not even half-full in this life Ps. 84, 3. will then be consummated and plenary in the other 1 Pet. 1, 8. Rev. 19, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

TRAHE ME POST TE: CURREMUS IN ODOREM UNGUENTORUM TUORUM.

Loquitur primum in singulari trahe me, quod unaquæque fidelis anima hunc suavem tractum pro se appetat, eoque sigillatim opus habeat: deinde in plurali, curremus, quod catervatim, & certatim sequi Christum velint. Cæterum & lectio & distinctio alia occurrit apud Ambrosium de iis, qui initiantur mysteriis c. 6. attraxerunt te, item attrahe nos post te. Sed in fonte & apud Chald. Aquilam & Symmachum lectio vulgata habetur, utut Cod. LXX. Interpp. varient. Aponius, Justus Orgel. Bernhardus & alii sic etiam distinguunt: trahe me post te. Non habetur autem illud in odorem unguentorum tuorum, in textu Ebræo: sed maluit vulgatus sequi LXX. Interpp. (utut perperam) quam textum authenticum. Suspirium autem illud Trahe me, cum impotentiam sponsæ innuit, quæ sponsum sequi nequeat, nisi ab eo trahatur, tum efficaciam tractus divini Joh. 6, 44. Unde Bernhardus: trahe quodammodo invitam, ut facias voluntariam, trahe torpentem, ut reddas currentem. Laudat hic Jesuita Cornelius etiam hæc Bernhardi, vi veritatis, ut apparet, convictus: Curremus, curremus, sed in odore unguentorum tuorum, non in nostrorum fiducia meritorum. Nec in magnitudine virium nostrarum currere nos confidimus, sed in multitudine miserationum tuarum. Nam etsi quando cucurrimus, voluntarii fuimus, non fuit volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Et agnoscere coguntur etiam renati suam infirmitatem in hoc cursu Rom. 7, 14. 23. Vellem te sequi, o sponse, sed concupiscentia reluctante non valeo, ut fatetur Cornel. a Lap. Habemus, inquit S. Ambrof. de Isaac & anima c. 3. cupiditatem sequendi, quam unguentorum tuorum inspirat gratia, sed quia cursus tuos æquare non possumus, attrahe nos, ut auxilio tuo fultæ, vestigiis tuis possimus insistere.

Quomodo Christus attraxerit homines per incarnationem, per muneris sui Ecclesiastici functionem, divinis oraculis & miraculis, nec non mansuetudinis & aliarum virtutum exemplis Matth. 11, 29. ceu triplici funiculo charitatis Os. 11, 4. ut & per passionem Joh. 12, 32. ac denique per universalem Evangelii prædicationem Rom. 10, 18. quomodo item adhuc attrahat per verbum & Sacramenta, per beneficia tum præstita tum pro- missa, & per crucis flagella Psal. 32, 3. cum mala, quæ nos premunt, ad Deum ire compellunt, quomodo denique tracturus Deus nos sit per beatam emigra- tionem Psal. 142, 8. Luc. 2, 29. ubi sequemur agnum, quorsum iverit Apoc. 14, 4. exposuit B. Gerhardus Post. Salom. Dom. 24. post Trin. Subjungimus tan- tum Gregorii M. sententiam ad h. l. Pia anima petit, ut a Deo trahatur, per gratiam, quo sequi eum possit per imitationem. Neque enim currere quis valet per viam mandatorum Dei nisi per gratiam trahatur. Tra- hit nos, ut fide ipsi adhæreamus Joh. 6, 44. obedientia ipsum seqvamur Joh. 15, 5. 10. Psal. 119, 33. & patien- tia vestigiis ejus insistamus 1. Pet. 2, 21. ac tandem pe- nes ipsum æternum maneamus, Joh. 14, 3. 1. Thessal. 4, 16. Currimus autem in via mandatorum ejus Psal. 54, 31. & in stadio proposito 1. Cor. 9, 24. seqq. Phil. 3, 12. Ebr. 12, 1. &c.

vers. eod. INTRODUXIT ME REX IN CELLARIA SUA.

Jam exprimitur Sponsus REGIS nomine, e Pf. XLV, 2. 12. Ps. 2, 6. qui sponsam in cellaria, [Hebrew text], ταμιεῖα, ut vulgat. & LXX. vel ut Lutherus, in conclave & ca- meram suam, domum Patris sui post exantlatum cursum Joh. 14, 2. ducturus est, ubi voluptas, quies, & securitas, Ps. 16, 11. Esa. 32, 17. 18. quam jam pos- sidemus in spe Rom. 8, 24. Eph. 2, 6. unde gaudemus & lætamur de sponso salvatore nostro Luc. 1, 47. Es. 61, 10. & amores ejus vino, & voluptatibus omnibus præferimus Matth. 6, 33. Ps. 33, 9. RECTI (corde) diligunt te o Rex Sponse Ps. 32, 11. חֲדָרָיו significat in- tima penetralia, qualia sunt conclavia, & cubicula, in quibus herus ipse secreto degit, ac suas opes, & thesauros recondit. Arab: reddit, in cubiculum se- cretum. Syrus, in thalamum. De cælo autem in- telligit Cassiodorus, Aponius, Anshelmus, & Beda: De qua introductione Regis ejusdemque sponsi in fine mundi futura vid. Matth. 25, 1. 34. seqq. Apoc. 19. & 21, 9. unde Beda hanc dat συνεχείας rationem: Ideo deprecor sponsum, ut nos post se currentes data ma- nu ipse, ne deficiamus, adjuvet, quia jam dulcedinem regni cælestis prælibavi, jam gustavi, & vidi, quoniam suavis est Dominus, jam bona quæ mihi in cælis sunt præparata, ipso revelante cognovi. Moxque ad ipsum conversa ei gratias agens, exultabimus, inquit, & læta- bimur in te, ac si diceret: nequaquam ipsi de perceptis muneribus extollimur, sed in omni quod bene vivimus exultamus, imo exultabimus & lætabimur in tua mise- ricordia. Fit quidem hæc exhilaratio etiam in hac vita, sed inchoative, per verbi nempe cibationem Psalm. 23, 5. & 19, 11. Ebr. 5, 12. 14. unde Hieron. Epist. 142. ad Damas. Theodorei. Greg. Just. Orgelit. & Ru- pert. in h. l. cellaria sunt Scripturæ S. nec non per S. S. consolationem Ps. 94. 19. 119, 92. & per gaudii cælestis prægustationem Ebr. 6, 5. sed consummative ea fiet in anima in Paradisum translatione Luc. 23, 45. 16, 25. & totius compositi gloriosa assumtione Matth. 25, 34. id- eoque gaudium, quod ne quidem semiplenum est in hac vita Ps. 84, 3. tum consummatum erit & ple- narium in altera 1. Pet. 1, 8. Apoc. 19, 7.

## 1:4
Verse 4. AS THE TENTS OF KEDAR) Egypt draws much from neighboring Arabia; and perhaps the mother of this Queen was an Arab woman.

These things are from the preconceived opinion that this is sung about the daughter of the Egyptian King. To which he now adds another divination, about the mother of the same, an Arab woman. But could not the comparison be drawn from the tents of Kedar, even if the person who institutes the same was not from Arabia, or the vicinity of Arabia? But the discourse is about the mystical Bride according to the interpretation of all the Doctors: who while she says, I am black, but desirable and beautiful as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains

Of Solomon, Gregory of Nyssa indeed and Aponius, as well as Mercer, refer both the likeness of the tents of Kedar and the curtains of Solomon to the blackness as well as the beauty of the Bride: But others more conveniently, with Origen, Theodoret, Cassiodorus, Gregory the Great, Anselm, Rupert, and Bernard, refer the former likeness to the blackness, the latter to the beauty, so that by way of anthypophora she responds: If anyone should say that I, as a pastoral and rustic woman, living like the Kedarenes in the tents for the sake of feeding the flock, am scorched and blackened by the heat of the Sun, and unworthy of the love of the King: I confess indeed that I am black in external appearance, yet I am beautiful within, just as the curtains of Solomon, gleaming with gold, gems, and precious paintings, are exceedingly beautiful and lovely. As to the blackness, Origen in Homily I of the four on the Canticles thinks that it alludes to the Ethiopian wife of Moses, a type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Nor do some others deny this; however, the likeness of the tents of the Kedarenes excellently suits the state of the Church: For just as those were the tents not only of those who were discolored—which the name itself also implies—but also of those who were continually wandering and also warring: So the Church, because of the heat of temptations and persecutions, is discolored and black, and is perpetually wandering in these lands, and is exposed to continuous battles. But here, the blackness arising from the heat of the Sun is primarily regarded, as the explanation subjoined teaches: because the Sun has discolored me. Which the Bride of Solomon did not have to complain of, even if she had been a neighbor to the Arabs, or born of an Arab mother. The Church, however, rightly complains of her blackness, both because of the sin that clings to her, and especially because of the heat of the cross: yet she rejoices at the same time because of her internal beauty, with which she shines like the curtains of Solomon, with which she has been adorned by her Solomon, Christ the Bridegroom. Thus, Ambrose, in Book II of De Spiritu Sancto, ch. 2, explains it concerning the deformity of sin: Black through fault, beautiful through grace; black through condition, beautiful through redemption. Similarly, in Psalm 119: Dusky through fault, beautiful through grace; dusky through vice, beautiful through the washing. I am dusky because I have sinned; beautiful, because Christ now loves me. And Augustine, Sermon 86 on the Season: Black by nature, beautiful by grace; black by original sin, beautiful by the Sacrament of Baptism. And from the Greeks, Nyssenus: When I was black through sin, and through my works was akin and joined to darkness, He made me beautiful through His love, having exchanged beauty with my foulness, and having transferred the filth of my sins to Himself, He imparts His beauty to me. To this effect is the fact that Theodoret understands by the skins of Solomon the precious skins with which Solomon was clothed, as if to say: I am the Bride of the true Solomon, that is, of Christ, and therefore I am beautiful because I walk clothed in Him and in His garments. This explanation is approved in this place by Cornelius a Lapide, the Jesuit, even if it is manifest that it favors the imputed righteousness of Christ. Beda interprets it concerning the deformation of the cross: I am black through the adversity of pressures, but beautiful through the beauty of virtues; the heat of tribulations is signified by the name of the Sun. And St. Bernard, Sermon 26 on the Canticles. The bride does not blush at the blackness, which she knows to have been present even in the bridegroom, to whom it is also a great glory to be likened. It is blackness, but the form and likeness of the Lord. Why do you reproach the blackness which the fervor of persecution, not the shame of conduct, has induced? Ambrose also looks to this in De Spiritu Sancto, ch. 11: She is black, he says, with the dust of her exercise while she battles, beautiful while she is adorned with the insignia of her victory. Similarly, Alcuin on this passage: I am black in the pressures of persecutions, but beautiful in the beauty of virtues, which is: I appear black indeed in the eyes of the persecutors, but before God I shine adorned with the beauty of virtues. The holy Church says, namely, that she is black like Kedar, because she is so obscured by the afflictions of the infidels that she becomes as if an enemy to the whole world. Solomon was peaceful in both life and name, who made for himself tents from the skins of dead animals, and the Lord creates for Himself a Church from those animals which mortify the desire of the flesh within themselves. Therefore, the Church is like the skins of Solomon. Gilbert Foliot joins both: For the Church of God is black either by the passion of the body, or by the maceration of the flesh, and the attrition of the Spirit.
