The Church, therefore, or any perfect soul, says that she is black, like the tents of Kedar, because just as these could not be conquered by any incursions, so also these could not be turned away from the love of God and the worship of His justice by any threats, by any furies and scourges of adversaries, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 4. SICVT TABERNACVLA CEDAR) Ægyptus multum trahit de Arabia finitima; & forte mater hujus Re- ginæ fuerit Arabissa.

Hæc ex præconcepta opinione, quod hic ca- natur de filia Regis Ægyptii. Cui nunc aliam divi- nationem adjicit, de matre ejusdem Arabissa. Sed annon comparatio a tabernaculis Cedar depromi poterat, etiamsi persona, quæ eandem instituit, non fuerit ex Arabia, aut Arabiæ vicinia? Sermo autem est de Sponsa mystica secundum interpretationem Dd. omnium: quæ dum ait, nigra sum, sed desidera- bilis & formosa sicut tabernacula Cedar, sicut aulæa

Salomonis, Gregorius Nyssenus quidem & Aponius, nec non Mercerus utramque similitudinem taber- naculorum Cedar & aulæorum Salomonis refe- runt tam ad nigredinem, quam ad formositatem Spon- sæ: Sed convenientius alii cum Origene, Theodoreto, Cassiodoro, Gregorio M. Anshelmo, Ruperto, & Bern- hardo referunt priorem similitudinem ad nigredi- nem, posteriorem ad formositatem q. per ἀνθυποφο- ρὰν respondeat: Si quis dicat, me ceu pastoritiam & rusticanam instar Cedarenorum in tabernaculis pascen- di gregis ergo degentem, æstu Solis adustam & denigra- tam, amore Regis indignam: Fateor sane, nigram me esse externo aspectu, formosa tamen sum interius, quemadmodum Salomonis aulæa, auro, gemmis, pi- cturisque pretiosis micantia, perquam pulchra & venu- sta sunt. Quod ad nigredinem, alludi ad Æthio- pissam uxorem Mosis, typum Ecclesiæ e gentibus colle- ctæ, censet Origenes hom. I. ex quatuor in Cantic. Neque abnuunt alii nonnulli; Similitudo autem ta- bernaculorum Cedarenorum egregie convenit statui Ecclesiæ: Nam ut illa erant non modo decolorato- rum, quod nomen etiam ipsum importat, sed con- tinue quoque peregrinantium, nec non belligeran- tium tabernacula: Ita Ecclesia ob æstus tentationum & persequutionum decolor & nigra est, ac perpe- tuo peregrinatur in his terris, pugnisque continuis exposita est. Sed hic respicitur imprimis nigredo a Solis æstu oriunda, ut explicatio subjuncta docet: quia Sol me decoloravit. Quod Salomonis Sponsa conqueri necessum non habuit, etiamsi vicina fuis- set Arabibus, aut ex Matre Arabissa procreata. Ec- clesia autem merito queritur de nigredine sua tum ob adhærens peccatum, tum imprimis ob crucis æstum: gaudet tamen simul ob internam pulchritudinem, qua instar aulæorum Salomonis nitet, qua a Salomo- ne suo Christo Sponso ornata est. Sic de peccati deformitate explicat Ambrosius lib. II. de S. S. cap. 2. Nigra per culpam, decora per gratiam, nigra per condi- tionem, decora per redemtionem. Similiter in Psal. 119. Fusca per culpam, decora per gratiam, fusca per vitium, decora per lavacrum. Fusca sum, quia pecca- vi, decora, quia jam me diligit Christus. Et Augu- stinus serm. 86. de Tempore: Nigra per naturam, formosa per gratiam, nigra originali peccato, formosa Baptismi Sacramento. Et e Græcis Nyssenus: Cum nigra essem peccato, & per opera affinis essem & con- juncta tenebris, me pulcram fecit per dilectionem suam pulchritudine commutata cum mea turpitudine, in se translatis fordibus meorum peccatorum suam mihi impertit pulchritudinem. Quo facit, quod Theo- doretus per pelles Salomonis intelligit pelles pretiosas, quibus vestiebatur Salomo q. d. Ego sum Sponsa veri Salomonis, id est, Christi, ideoque sum formosa, quia eo, ejusque vestibus vestita incedo. Quam ex- plicationem probat hoc loco Cornelius a Lapide, Je- suita, etsi imputatæ justitiæ Christi eam favere in a- prico sit. De crucis deformatione interpretatur Beda: Nigra sum adversitate pressurarum, sed formo- sa decore virtutum, tribulationum ardor Solis appella- tione signatur. Et S. Bernhard. serm. 26. in Cantic. Non erubescit sponsa nigredinem, quam novit præces- sisse etiam in sponso, cui similari quanta etiam gloria est. Nigredo est, sed forma & similitudo Domini. Quid exprobratis nigredinem, quam fervor persequu- tionis, non pudor conversationis induxit. Eo etiam respicit Ambrosius de S. S. c. 11. Nigra est, inquiens, exercitii sui pulvere, dum præliatur, decora, dum victo- riæ suæ insignibus decoratur. Similiter Alcuinus in h. l. Nigra sum in pressuris persecutionum, sed formo- sa in decore virtutum, quod est, nigra quidem in ocu- lis persequentium appareo, sed ante Deum ornata de- core virtutum refulgeo. Dicit scil. sancta Ecclesia se nigram ut Kedar, quia afflictionibus infidelium ita est obscurata quasi totius mundi fieret inimica. Salomon & vita & nomine pacificus erat, qui sibi tentoria de mortuorum animalium pellibus faciebat, & Dominus Ecclesiam de illis animalibus sibi creat, quæ desiderium carnis in se mortificant. Ergo Ecclesia est similis pel- libus Salomonis. Gilbertus Foljoth utrumque con- jungit: Ecclesia enim Dei nigra est vel passione corporis, vel maceratione carnis, & Spiritus attritione. Ait igitur Ecclesia, vel anima quævis perfecta se nigram es- se, sicut tabernacula Cedar, quia sicut hæc nullis pote- rant excursionibus expugnari, sic & hæ ab amore Dei, & cultu justitiæ illius nullis poterant minis, nullis pote- rant adversariorum furoribus ac flagellis averti &c.

## 1:5
Verse 5. THEY HAVE MADE ME A KEEPER IN THE VINEYARDS, MY OWN VINEYARD I HAVE NOT KEPT] They destined me for celibacy: But I preferred marriage.

A gloss entirely arbitrary, nay, inept. How shall we understand by the keeper in the vineyards a celibate woman, and by one who does not keep her own vineyard, a married woman? Who does not see that these things are inept? And whence is it certain to Grotius that the daughter of Pharaoh was destined for celibacy? The explanation concerning the spiritual Bride holds itself much more correctly: that a cause may be rendered why the sun discolored her, because the persecuting brothers compelled her to act as a keeper in foreign vineyards, so that she could not keep her own vineyard, and wandering about while inspecting those, she was darkened by the rays of the Sun: because the Jews, obstinate in Judaism, attacked the Apostles and the first Christians, and compelled them to flee to the Gentiles, whence they could not keep the native Jewish Church, having endured various heats of persecutions through the vineyards of the Gentiles. Thus Alcuin: The bitterness of the persecution of the sons of the Synagogue causes her not to keep the vineyard at Jerusalem, but to be the keeper of many vineyards, that is, of Churches throughout the world: The primitive Mother Church is the Synagogue, to which God says through the Prophet (Zech. 8), Zion, you shall be called the city and Mother of cities. Thus also Origen, Cassiodorus, Justus Orgelitanus, Beda: and also Willeramus. And of our own, Dürfeldius; of the Papists, Cornelius a Lapide, and others. If, however, it pleases one to accept these more generally, as it seemed to others, by the sons of the brother, false brothers can be understood: And the Bride will attribute to them the blame for why she could not guard her vineyard, as if to say, this office was indeed entrusted to me, that I should cultivate and guard the vineyard of the Lord, but false brothers hinder me, so that I cannot fully obtain that which I would wish, which is the paraphrase of Osiander: or she may also confess her own fault here, that she did not perform her office as is fitting, as the Vinarienses interpret. Although Gilbert Foliot wishes this to be said only regarding the opinion of men, in this way, that she seemed not to guard the vineyard, because she did not or could not prevent the saints from undertaking torments for Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 5. POSVERVNT ME CVSTODEM IN VINE- IS, VINEAM MEAM NON CVSTODIVI] Destinave- runt me cœlibatui: Ego vero matrimonium prætuli.

Glossa prorsus arbitraria, imo inepta. Quo- modo per custodem in vineis cœlibem, & quæ vineam suam non custodit, conjugatam intelligemus? Inepta hæc esse, quis non videt? Et unde constat Grotio, quod filia Pharaonis cœlibatui destinata fuerit? Longe rectius sese habet explicatio de Sponsa spiri- tuali: ut causa reddatur, cur sol eam decolorarit, quia fratres persequentes cœgerint eam custodem agere in vineis alienis, ut propriam vineam custodire nequive- rit, ac illas lustrando oberrans radiis Solis obsuscata sit: quod Judæi obstinati in Judaismo oppugnarint Apostolos & primos Christianos, & cœgerint ad gentes fugere, unde Ecclesiam nativam Judaicam custodire non potuerint, varios per vineas gentium persequutionum æstus perpessi. Sic Alcuinus: A- cerbitas persecutionis filiorum Synagogæ facit vineam Hierosolymis non custodire, sed multarum vinearum, id est Ecclesiarum per orbem custodem: Mater primi- tiva Ecclesia est Synagoga, cui per Prophetam Deus, (Zach. 8.) Zion tu vocaberis civitas & Mater civita- tum. Sic etiam Origen. Cassiodor. Justus Orgelit. Beda: nec non Willeramus. Et e nostris Dürfeldius; e Pontificiis Cornelius a Lapide, aliique. Si tamen hæc placeat accipere generalius, quod aliis visum, per filios fratris falsi fratres intelligi possunt: Et Sponsa illis culpam tribuet, cur vineam suam custo- dire non potuerit, q. d. commissum quidem mihi est hoc officium, ut vineam Domini excolerem, & custodi- rem, sed impediunt me falsi fratres, ut non possim id, quod vellem, plene obtinere, quæ Osiandri est paraphra- sis: aut culpam etiam propriam hic profiteatur, quod officio suo prout par est, functa non fuerit, uti inter- pretantur Vinariensis. Quanquam Gilbertus Fol- joth hoc ad opinionem hominum tantum dictum velit, hoc modo, quod visa sit vineam non custodire, quia sanctos a suscipiendis pro Christo tormentis non prohibuit aut prohibere potuit.

## 1:6
Verse 6.

LEST I BEGIN TO WANDER AFTER THE FLOCKS OF THY COMPANIONS] This is said in jest, like that of Catullus: Lest what is sought go elsewhere.

Who would not detest the obscene joke, or rather the profane taunt of Grotius? For without impiety such a joke cannot be attributed to the breath and inspiration of the Holy Spirit. And if the Bride wishes most of all to avoid the companions of the Bridegroom and his rivals and adversaries, and desires uniquely to be nourished in peace and pasture by the shadow of her Bridegroom, what has this to do with a Catullian joke? These are entirely serious matters, not jocular: since we can very easily be seduced from the seat of the Bridegroom to heretical flocks, or to the conventicles of hypocrites, so that we may enjoy the alien fodder of errors or vices, who sell themselves as companions of Christ, as Theodoret, Philo Carpathius, Nyssenus, Bede, Alcuin, Foliot, and other ancients explain. In the Hebrew it is not 'as one who wanders,' which word Grotius thought to be of lasciviousness, but 'as one covered,' as Jerome rendered it in the version of Origen. LXX.

they have περιβαλλομένη. The word כְּעֹטְיָה, which the Vulgate rendered in the common way, is from עָטָה, to clothe by covering: which some, along with Origen, explain as referring to modesty, honesty, and virginal shame: Unless you tell me, I begin to be tossed about as a wanderer, and while I seek you, I run into the flocks of others, and because I am ashamed of the face of others, I begin to cover my own without delay. Cf. Tertullian, de virgin. veland. Others interpret it as sadness, on account of which the face is accustomed to be covered with a veil, with R. Solomon preceding, in which manner Lucas Osiander: since you sometimes seem (among so many temptations, persecutions, and sects) to have withdrawn far from the Church, and cannot be found, we ask you to let yourself be found, lest we turn aside to other unwholesome shepherds (who nevertheless boast that they are shepherds of the Church) and seek you in vain, sorrowful. Even if you should take this word in the highest degree concerning her who wanders about like a harlot, as Vatablus and Mercerus explain, by the example of Tamar in Gen. 38:14, it will not, however, be a matter of jest, but a most serious one, so that she may generate an opinion of jealousy in the Bridegroom and expose him to danger while she wanders here and there for the sake of seeking him.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

NE VAGARI INCIPIAM POST GREGES SODA- LIVM TVORVM] Hoc joco dicitur, ut illud Catulli: Ne quæsitum aliunde eat.

Obscœnum jocum, vel scomma potius pro- phanum Grotii quis non detestetur? Nam absque impietate talis jocus afflatui & inspirationi Sancti Spiritus tribui non potest. Et si maxime cavere vult Sponsa sodales Sponsi æmulosque ejusdem ri- vales, & adversarios, optatque Sponsi sui umbra quiete & pastu ali unice, quid hoc ad jocum Catul- lianum? Seria hæc prorsus sunt, non jocosa: quando- quidem facillime seduci possimus a Sponsi sede ad hæreticos greges, vel hypocritarum conventicula, ut a- lienis pabulis errorum vel vitiorum fruamur, qui se sodales Christi venditant, ut Theodoretus, Philo Carpa- thius, Nyssenus, Beda, Alcuinus, Foljoth, aliiq; Veteres exponunt. In Ebræo non est sicut vaga, quam vocem lasciviæ esse putavit Grotius, sed sicut cooperta, ut Hieronymus in versione Origenis reddidit. LXX.

habent περιβαλλομένη. Vox כְּעֹטְיָה quam vu- gari reddidit vulgatus, est ab עָטָה induit operien- do: quam de modestia, honestate, & pudore virginali exponunt nonnulli cum Origene: Nisi tu mihi an- nunciaveris, incipio errabunda jactari, & dum te quæ- ro, in aliorum greges incurro, & quia aliorum erubesco faciem, meam absque mora mox contegere incipio. Conf. Tertull. de virgin. veland. alii de tristitia in- terpretantur, præ qua solet facies velo operiri, præ- eunte R. Salomone, quo pacto Lucas Osiander : cum interdum videaris, (inter tot tentationes, persequutio- nes & sectas) ab Ecclesia longe recessisse, nec inveniri posse, rogamus te ut reperiri sinas, ne ad alios non salu- tares pastores declinemus (qui tamen jactans se esse pa- stores Ecclesiæ) & te frustra mæsti quæramus. Si etiam maxime verbum hoc de ea, quæ meretricis instar pal- tiolata, ut Vatablus & Mercerus exponunt, exemplo Tamar Gen. 38, 14. oberrat, accipias, non tamen jo- ci res erit, sed maxime seria, ut Sponso Zelotypiæ opi- nionem ingeneret, ac periculum exponat, dum huc illuc ejus quærendi causa oberrat.

## 1:7
Verse 7. IF YOU DO NOT KNOW YOURSELF.

Te is a Hebrew pleonasm: If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, where I feed, where you may be able to find me, go forth after the tracks of your feet (this pronoun is redundant) among so many crowds and afflictions, follow the tracks of pious men who were my sheep, imitate them insofar as they were my imitators; by their wholesome labors you will be led to find me, as Osiander has it here.

Verse of the same. FEED YOUR KIDS) Satisfy your appetite, whence the word τραγίζειν. Horace: 'Wanton, to play like a she-goat.' NEAR THE SHEPHERDS' TENTS) τῶν διδάμων. See also 3, 3. But would the Bridegroom command the Bride to τραγίζειν, and to satisfy her appetite among his companions, and to play like a wanton she-goat? Away with such a profane and obscene, nay, blasphemous thought in such a Holy Song, and indeed concerning such a holy Bridegroom, who is himself the Holy of Holies! Nor is there any room for irony, if it is feigned to be so with Titelmann. Because the Bridegroom would not play with such an obscene and impure irony, and the Bride had to be answered as to where the Bridegroom was feeding, lest she wander about as a vagabond. Furthermore, whence will it be taught from the Scriptures that the force of this phrase 'to feed kids' is 'to satisfy one's appetite'? Then indeed, not without merit, Mercerus warns that it must be diligently observed here from the Hebrews in the Midrash, that in the Song all things sound in praise, and not in disgrace, and that not even the slightest thing is said on either side that could offend the other, but all are words of reconciliation, encomiums, blandishments, and sweetness. Bernard, although he understands the senses of the body by the wandering and petulant kids, thinks it is a warning if she does not recognize herself, and does not value the heavenly goods given or promised, because she could easily be entangled by the senses of the flesh. Ambrose, in 'On the Soul and Isaac,' chapter 4, wishes a warning to be instituted here: feed your kids, that is, rule those things which are on your left. For if they are not ruled, they easily slip; restrain the petulance and lasciviousness of your body. Subdue light motions: feed them not in those bodily tents, but in the tents of the shepherds who know how to rule the flock. But it is not for us to take 'kids' in a bad sense, and explain it either as wicked concupiscences, or with others as reprobate men: for those are not the kids of the mystical Bride, to whom it is said: Feed your kids. Which was the cause for most to slip into a foreign sense here, primarily because they did not understand the Hebrew phrase (if you do not know yourself), that is, that לָךְ is accustomed to be redundant, and following the versions they explained it as 'if you do not know yourself,' and inculcated that γνῶθι σεαυτὸν: whereas the question had been instituted concerning the seat and place where the Bridegroom now sits, and the response ought to correspond to him now: if you do not know this, O most beautiful of women, go forth by the tracks of the flock (in the Vulgate 'Your' is wrongly added) and feed your she-goats, near the tents of the shepherds. He teaches, therefore, where she ought to feed her she-goats; otherwise he would not have satisfied the Bride's request, and he persists in the begun similitude taken from pastoral life. As, therefore, 'to feed' was taken when she was asking about the Bridegroom, where he feeds (which can in no way be taken there as satisfying an appetite), so here also it must be understood in the response, when, having indicated the place, he commands, 'feed your she-goats.' The Hebrew word גדית does not denote adult and petulant kids, which are expressed by other words, thejaschim and Zephirim, but implies a tender age and she-goats, nor is the name of kids always used in a bad sense, but it also occurs concerning the faithful in Isaiah 11:6, who are also called ἀρνία in John 21:16, whence they are committed to the Church, not as stinking he-goats here, but as delightful lambs, any who are weak, or it refers (which pleases Mercerus) to the little flock of the Church, despised and rejected by the judgment of the world. She is therefore commanded to go forth by the tracks of the flock that went before, that is, of the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles. For thus Christ is to be sought: namely, in his word, handed down from the very beginning of the world to the Fathers, the Prophets, and finally to the Apostles: these tracks must be followed, from these one must not recede even a nail's breadth. More fully, by the tracks of the flock you may understand the holy tracks of all the saints who have gone before, in the way of the word of GOD, or Holy Scripture, Psalm 25:4, 27:11, 119:9, in the path of faith and justice, Rom. 4:10, Prov. 4:18, in the path of piety and holiness, Ps. 143:11, Prov. 2:8, 20, ch. 15:29. But because the tracks of the faith and piety of the Saints shine uniquely in the way of the word of God, and cannot be distinguished from the tracks of hypocrites and false companions of the Bridegroom, nor can we avoid those, unless through the way which is shown in Holy Scripture, therefore the tracks of all the Saints of the universal flock of the faithful, shown in the Holy Scriptures, indeed according to the way prescribed in Holy Scripture, concerning which Psalm 119. & according to the light, type, & Rule of Holy Scripture shining before here are designated: so that the very word of God set forth in the Holy Scriptures, and holily observed by the flock of the faithful, may be established as the mark and κριτήριον of the true Church. This is the way by which one must go, and by no means turn aside from the same, either to the right or to the left Isa. 30, 21. Josh. 1, 6. Gal. 6, 16. And therefore the Bride is commanded to feed her flock, and especially the tender kids, the weak in faith, her little goats BESIDE THE TENTS OF THE SHEPHERDS: that is, of the heralds of the word of God, just as shepherdesses feed their little goats beside their huts and rear them with milk, so that infants in faith and more tender souls may be fed and nourished with the pure milk of the word and the beginnings of Christian doctrine 1 Cor. 3, 2. 1 Pet. 2. Heb. 3. & just as flocks are fed beside the tents in green pastures, so let them be refreshed in the green pastures of Scripture with the fodder of the word of God Ps. 23, 3. To some it seems to be an allusion to the Priests of the O. T. who taught and fed the people in the courts of the Lord beside the temple & tabernacle of the Lord Ps. 27, 4. Ps. 26, 8. but the simpler explanation is that which persists in the simile begun: the matter however comes to the same thing.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SI IGNORAS TE.

Te est Pleonasmus Ebraicus: Si ignoras, o pul- cherrima inter mulieres, ubi pascam, ubi me reperire queas, egredere post vestigia pedum tuorum (hoc pro- nomen redundat) inter tot turbas & afflictiones in- siste vestigiis piorum hominum, qui fuerunt oves meæ, hos imitare quatenus illi fuerunt mei imitato- res, illorum salutaribus laboribus eo deduceris, ut me invenias, ut hic habet Osiander.

Vers. eod. PASCE HÆDOS TUOS) Exple appetitum, unde verbum τραγίζειν. Horatius. Lasciva similem ludere capreæ. JVXTA TABERNACVLA PASTORVM) τῶν διδά- μων. Vide & 3, 3. Qui vero Sponsus juberet Sponsam τραγίζειν, & appetitum suum implere, apud Sodales suos, ac lasciva similem ludere capreæ? Apage prophanam & obscœnam, imo blasphemam ejusmodi cogita- tionem in tam Sancto Cantico, imo de tam sancto Sponso, qui est ipse Sanctus sanctorum! Neque iro- niæ locus est, fi cum Titelmanno ea fingatur. Quia neque luderet Sponsus tam obscœna & impura Iro- nia, & respondendum erat Sponsæ, ubi pasceret Sponsus, ne illa vagabunda oberret. Porro unde e Scripturis phraseos istius hanc vim esse docebitur pascere hædos esse explere appetitum suum? Tum ve- ro non immerito ex Ebræis in Midras diligenter hic observandum esse monet Mercerus, quod in Canti- co omnia in laudem sonent, non vero in dedecus, ac ne tantillum quidem ab alterutra parte dicatur, quod al- teram possit offendere, sed omnia conciliationis & en- comiorum ac blanditiarum suavitatisque sint verba. Bernhardus etsi per hædos vagos & petulantes corpo- ris sensus intelligat, comminationem esse putat, si non agnoscat se, ac bona cœlestia data, aut promissa non æstimet, quod nempe carnis sensibus facile intricari pos- sit. Ambrosius de anima & Isaac cap. 4. admonitio- nem hic institui vult: pasce hædos tuos, id est, rege quæ in sinistra tua sunt. Nam si non regantur, facile la- buntur; coerce petulantiam & lasciviam corporis tui. Edoma leves motus: pasce eos non in eis corporeis taber- naculis, sed in tabernaculis pastorum, qui regere gre- gem norunt. Sed non est ut hædos in malam partem accipiamus, ac vel de concupiscentiis pravis, vel cum aliis de reprobis hominibus, explicemus: illi enim non sunt Sponsæ mysticæ hædi, cui dicitur: Pasce hædos tuos. Quæ causa plerisque fuit, ut ad alienum sen- sum hic delaberentur, imprimis quia etiam phrasin Ebræam (si nescis tibi) non intellexere, quod nempe לָךְ redundare soleat, ac versiones sequuti exposue- rint, si te ignoras, ac illud γνῶθι σεαυτὸν inculcarint: quū quæstio fuerit instituta de sede ac loco, ubi nempe scat nunc Sponsus, eique nunc responsio congruere debeat, si hoc nescis, o mulierum pulcherrima, egrede- re per vestigia gregis (in vulgata perperam additur Tui) & pasce capellas tuas, juxta tabernacula pasto- rum. Docet ergo, ubi capellas suas pascere debeat, alias non satis fecisset quæsito Sponsæ, ac persistit in cœpta similitudine ex vita pastoritia desumta. Ut ergo pascere sumebatur, cum de Sponso quæreba- tur, ubinam pascat (quod nullatenus de appetitu ex- plendo ibi accipi potest) ita hic etiam intelligi de- bet in responso, quum indicato loco jubet, pasce ca- pellas tuas. Vox Ebræa גדית non notat hædos adultos, & petulcos, qui aliis vocibus thejaschim, & Zephirim exprimuntur, sed ætatem teneram & capel- las infert, neque semper in malam partem hædorum nomen adhibetur, sed occurrit etiam de fidelibus Esa. 11, 6. qui & ἀρνία dicuntur Job. 21, 16. unde Ec- clesiæ committuntur peculiariter hic non olentes hirci, sed delectabiles agnelli, quilibet infirmi, aut re- spicitur (quod Mercero placet) ad pusillum gregem Ecclesiæ, mundi judicio contemtum & abjectum. Ju- betur itaque egredi per vestigia gregis, qui præcessit, hoc est, Patriarcharum, Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Sic enim Christus quærendus est : nimirum in verbo suo, tradito jam inde ab orbis initio, Patribus, Pro- phetis, tandem & Apostolis: his vestigiis insisten- dum, ab his ne latum quidem unguem recedendum. Plenius per vestigia gregis intelligas sanctorum omni- um, qui præcesserunt, sancta vestigia in via verbi DEI, vel Scripturæ Sacræ Psalm. 25, 4. 27, 11. 119, 9. in semita fidei & justitiæ Rom. 4, 10. Prov. 4, 18. in semita pietatis & sanctitatis Ps. 143, 11. Prov. 2, 8. 20. c. 15, 29. Quia vero vestigia fidei & pietatis Sanctorum in via ver- bi Dei unice effulgent, neque a vestigiis hypocrita- rum & falsorum Sponsi sodalium dignosci possunt, nec illa evitare nos possumus, nisi per viam, quæ monstratur in Scriptura Sacra, ideo vestigia Sancto- rum omnium gregis universi fidelium, in Scripturis Sacris monstrata, imo juxta viam in sacra Scriptura præscriptam, de qua Psalm. 119. & juxta lucem, ty- pum, & Regulam Scripturæ Sacræ prælucentia hic designantur: ut nota ac κριτήριον Ecclesiæ veræ consti- tuatur ipsummet Dei verbum in Scripturis Sacris expositum, & a grege fidelium sancte observatum. Hæc est via, qua eundum, nec ullatenus ab eadêm, sive ad dextram, sive ad sinistram deflectendum Esa. 30, 21. Jos. 1, 6. Gal. 6, 16. Ideoque pascere jubetur Sponsa gregem suum, & cumprimis hædos tenellos, in- firmos in fide, capellas suas JUXTA TABERNA- CULA PASTORUM: hoc est, præconum verbi Dei, uti pastrices capellas suas juxta tuguriola enutriunt & lacte educant, ut infantes in fide ac teneriores ani- mæ lacte puro verbi & initiis doctrinæ Christianæ pascantur ac nutriantur 1. Cor. 3, 2. 1. Petr. 2. Ebr. 3. & uti juxta tabernacula in pratis viridibus greges pascuntur, sic illi in pratis viridibus Scripturæ pabu- lo verbi Dei reficiantur Ps. 23, 3. Nonnullis videtur alludi ad Sacerdotes V. T. qui docebant & populum pascebant in atriis Domini juxta templum & taber- naculum Domini Ps. 27, 4. Ps. 26, 8. sed simplicior est explicatio in cœpta similitudine persistens: res ta- men eodem redit.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

I HAVE LIKENED THEE, O MY LOVE, TO MY COMPANY OF HORSES IN PHARAOH'S CHARIOTS] You might more correctly say Equitio. Which like a three-year-old mare in broad fields plays leaping about, says Horace.

The Osiandrine and Ernestine paraphrase understands this of the company of horses of Solomon in the chariots, which he had received from Pharaoh King of Egypt 1 Kings 10, 26. 28, to which the bride is compared on account of her beauty, virtue, and strength in war, alacrity and speed, patience, and the spirit to break through. Job 39:22. Psalm 20:8. But the one who speaks here is Christ; therefore, his cavalry is understood, not Solomon's: for he says to my cavalry: not to Solomon's cavalry. Wherefore the ancients more correctly understand the cavalry of God as set against the chariots of Pharaoh, which he overthrew in the Red Sea, because in a similar way he wishes to defeat all enemies through the Church; as Origen, Cassiodorus, Bede, Aponius, Gregory the Great, Anselm, Bernard, and others explain, when they compare Hab. 3:15, 8 and Ps. 68:18, concerning which Gilbert Foliot [speaks]. But who is understood here as the cavalry of the bridegroom, if not the one who fights bravely everywhere for the bridegroom, and spreads his victories in heaven, in the air, on land, and on the sea: this is the multitude of the Angels. This, therefore, is what the Holy Spirit says: My love, I have likened thee to my cavalry, in the chariots of Pharaoh: that is, while the angelic company was occupied in overturning the chariots of Pharaoh, I established thee as similar to that company of mine, acting thus for thee, fighting thus for thee, rescuing thee thus, as if wishing to have thee always as a participant in my cavalry. Thus also the paraphrase of Alcuin has it: as I freed the former people from Egyptian fear, so I will free thee, my bride, from the hands of those who pursue thee, if thou trustest in me.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

EQVITATUI MEO IN CVRRIBVS PHARAONIS ASSIMILAVI TE AMICA MEA] Rectius dicas Equitio. Quæ velut latis equa trima campis Ludit exultim. ait Horatius.

De equitatu Salomonis in curribus, quos a Pha- raone Rege Ægypti acceperat 1. Reg. 10, 26. 28. para- phrasis Osiandrina & Ernestina intelligit, cui com- paretur sponsa ob pulchritudinem, virtutem, & for- titudinem in bello, alacritatem & celeritatem, pati- entiam, & animositatem perrumpendi. Hiob. 39, 22. Psalm. 20, 8. sed qui hic loquitur Christus est; hu- jus ergo, non Salomonis equitatus intelligitur: Equi- tatui enim inquit meo: non Equitatui Salomonis. Quapropter rectius veteres equitatum Dei intelli- gunt curribus Pharaonis oppositum, quos in mari ru- bro prostravit, quod simili modo per Ecclesiam ho- stes omnes profligare velit; uti cum Chaldæo, Ori- genes, Cassiodorus, Beda, Aponius, Gregor. M. Ans- helmus, Bernhardus, & alii explicant, conferentes Hab. 3, 15. 8. & Ps. 68, 18. de quo Gilb. Foljoth. Hic vero quis equitatus sponsi intelligitur, nisi qui pro sponso fortiter ubique pugnat, & victorias ejus cœlo, aë- re, terra marique dilatat: Hæc Angelorum multitudo est. Hoc itaque est, quod Spiritus S. ait: Amica mea assimilavi te equitatui meo, in curribus Pharaonis: id est, dum angelicus comitatus in subvertendis curri- bus Pharaonis occuparétur, te illi meo comitatui simi- lem constitui sic agens pro te, sic pugnans pro te, sic eru- ens te, tanquam equitatui meo participem semper ha- bere volens te. Sic etiam habet paraphrasis Alcuini: sicut priorem populum de Ægyptio liberavi timore, sic te, sponsa mea, de persequentium, si in me confideris, liberabo manibus.

## 1:10
Verse 10. THY CHEEKS ARE BEAUTIFUL AS THE TURTLE DOVE'S.

Vatablus translates, thy cheeks are lovely among the little women. Thus also the Chaldean and the Rabbis explain תּוֹרִים as earrings, gems, and necklaces. Osiander [translates] among gems, among ornaments distinguished by gems. Similarly with Blessed Luther, the Ernestine paraphrase: to which interpretation that which follows, thy neck as necklaces, is more suitable. Therefore, chastity and modesty, which shine forth on cheeks worthy of ornament, are joined to fortitude, namely in their blush and shame.

Verse same. THY NECK AS NECKLACES. By the neck, which is subjected to a burden and a yoke just as much as the head, the subjection and obedience of the Church, which is devoted to Christ her bridegroom and head, is noted; which is compared to necklaces, Proverbs 1:8. The Septuagint translate it as ὁρμίσκυς, which Ambrose in Psalm 118 renders as 'redimicula' (bands/fillets): because obedience does not so much depress the neck as it redeems it, just as religion binds and couples to God the mind that was torn away from God. Thy neck, says Ambrose, is like bands; it is sweet to carry the yoke of Christ, if you think they are ornaments of your neck, not burdens: therefore lift up your eyes to the Lord your God, and seek God, and you will find. Raise your neck, you wear bands, not chains.

Latin:

Vers. 10. PULCHRÆ SUNT GENÆ TUÆ SICUT TURTURIS.

Vatabl. vertit, venustæ sunt genæ tuæ inter mulier- culas. Sic etiam תּוֹרִים Chald. & Rabb. per inau- res, gemmas & monilia explicant. Osiander inter gemmas, inter ornamenta gemmis distincta. Simili- ter cum B. Luth. Ernestina paraphrasis: cui inter- pretationi magis convenit quod sequitur, collum tuum sicut monilia. Fortitudini ergo castitas & ve- recundia quæ in genis emicat ornatu dignis subjun- gitur, in earum nempe rubore & pudore.

Vers. eod. COLLUM TUUM SICUT MO- NILIA. Per collum quod oneri & jugo æque ac capiti subjicitur, subjectio & obedientia Ecclesiæ, quæ Christo sponso & capiti suo dedita est, notatur; quæ monilibus confertur Proverb. 1, 8. LXX. vertunt ὁρμίσκυς quod Ambros. in Ps. 118. reddit redimicula: quia obedientia collum non tam deprimit quam redimit, uti religio mentem à Deo avulsam Deo re- ligat, & copulat. Cervix tua, inquit Ambros. sicut redimicula; portare Christi jugum suave est, si orna- menta putes cervicis tuæ esse non onera: attolle ergo oculos tuos ad Dominum Deum tuum, & quære De- um, & invenies. Erige cervicem, redimicula, non vin- cula geris.

## 1:11
Verse 11. WE WILL MAKE THEE CHAINS OF GOLD, STUDDED WITH SILVER.

In Hebrew: Chains of gold we will make for thee, dotted with silver. Symmachus: golden insignia, with varieties of silver. Vatablus: suitable ornaments of gold we will make for thee, with marks or studs of silver. Cassiodorus says 'murenulae' are ornaments of a virginal and girlish neck, namely little golden rods intertwined with very fine silver threads sometimes mixed in with beautiful variety. They are called 'murenulae' from the likeness of a sea fish, which is called a 'murena'. Osiander and the Vinarienses explain this as the more ample gifts of the Holy Spirit to be conferred upon the bride, Phil. 1:6, 9; Col. 1:9; 1 Cor. 1:5; and the Vinarienses and others note the mystery of the Holy Trinity, that Christ here joins himself with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the word WE WILL MAKE. Gilbert Foliot preceded them. It is to be noted, he says, the very change of speaking, that whereas the bridegroom has used singular speech until now, now speaking to the same bride he says in the plural number, we will make thee chains of gold; thus he shows the mystery of the Trinity, which fits better than if you were to attribute these things to the Angels with Psellus. For the bridegroom is speaking, not the Angels. Compare Gen. 1:26, John 14:13.

Latin:

Vers. 11. MURENULAS AUREAS FACIEMUS TI- BI, VERMICULATAS ARGENTO.

In Ebr. Catenulas auri faciemus tibi punctatas ar- gento. Symmachus insignia aurea, cum varietatibus argenti. Vatabl. ornamenta convenientia ex auro fa- ciemus tibi, cum notis vel clavis argenteis. Cassio- dorus murenulæ, ait ornamenta sunt colli virginalis & puellaris, videlicet virgulæ auri perplexæ intermix- tis nonnunquam pulchra varietate subtilissimis argen- ti filis. Dicuntur murenulæ à similitudine piscis mari- ni, qui murena vocatur. De amplioribus donis Spi- ritus S. conferendis sponsæ explicant Osiand. & Vi- nariens. Phil. 1, 6. 9. Col. 1, 9. 1. Cor. 1, 5. & mysterium S. S. Trin. quod Christus se cum Patre & Spir. S. hic conjungat in verbo FACIEMUS notant Vinarien- ses, aliique. Præivit Gilb. Foljoth. Notanda, inquit, est ipsa dicendi mutatio, quod cum hucusq; sponsus singu- lari sit usus eloquio, nunc eidem sponsæ verba faciens plurali numero dicit, murenulas aureas faciemus tibi sic Trinitatis monstrat arcanum, quæ magis congru- unt, quam si cum Psello hæc Angelis tribuas. Loqui- tur enim sponsus, non Angeli. Conf. Genes. 1, 26. Joh. 14, 13.

## 1:12
Verse 12. MY SPIKENARD GAVE ITS ODOR. It seems that נרדי is not 'my spikenard', but 'nardinum' (spikenard ointment): so that he may say that the breath of her husband breathing in his sleep is even sweeter than spikenard.

But what is that sweetness of Solomon's breath when he breathed in his sleep? For Grotius understands it concerning that. But in the text there is nothing about sleep. While the King is in his 'mesibbo', in his reclining place, that is, he reclines in the circle of those reclining. For the Hebrew word signifies a circuit or a crown or the place of those reclining, who were accustomed to be arranged in a circle. Avenarius in his Lexicon notes that it can also be taken as a Hiphil participle: Until the King shall be among the surrounding ministers; but the former sense is more suitable: which the Greeks express as ἐν ἀνακλίσει. And the word נרד is nard (spikenard), Cant. 4:13, 14, whence the Greek νάρδος and the Latin nardus: therefore with the suffix here it is 'my spikenard'. Therefore the Bride is speaking about herself, not about the Bridegroom, and since that peculiar custom existed among the delights of Judea, that those reclining were sprinkled with ointments, Mark 14:3, it fits the Bride perfectly, sprinkling the Bridegroom with the odor of spikenard in the reclining place. Which Mercer explains not badly: meanwhile, while Christ is present to his Church, feeding her with his word, the Bride renders the good odor of her faith, and of virtues and good works. Compare John 12:5, 2 Cor. 2:15. Osiander understands this concerning the odor of prayers in this way: the Church, having heard the sweetest consolation which she obtained through prayers, says; while my King and Bridegroom Christ was in his reclining place, cheerful at the table with his friends, my spikenard gave its odor; at the opportune time the prayers of the Church (which are like the best odors) come before the face of Christ, and move him to hear, and to console the Church effectively with his word. Somewhat more alien are the things which Cornelius à Lapide and Franciscus [prolixly] discuss here concerning the reclining place of Christ, in the throne of divinity, in the incarnation, in preaching, in death, in resurrection, in heavenly glory. Junius indeed also renders nardinum: and attributes it to the Bridegroom, but he understands the reclining to be in heaven: 'Meanwhile while the King is in his reclining place,' in heaven, 'nard gives forth its scent,' I am perfumed with most sweet odors, how much more when, life having been revealed, I shall be revealed with him in glory. But the interpretation is more alien: for no comparison is instituted here between the state of the Church in this and the future life. The reclining of Christ in the kingdom of the Church is indicated in Matt. 8:11 and in the hearts of the faithful in Apoc. 3:20, who smells the nard of faith and good works, Phil. 4:18, and of prayers, and is delighted by that odor: indeed he perfumes us ourselves with oil, when he prepares a table for us in his kingdom, so that we may render a good odor, Ps. 23. For here in the present life he still prepares for us golden chains, and adorns us little by little more and more by the H. Trinity, as in the preceding verse Christ the Bridegroom [says], 'We will make golden chains,' I, with the Father, and the H. S. (cf. John 14:23. Foljoth, along with other Fathers, observed that the mystery of the Trinity is shown here) for you with silver points.

Latin:

Vers. 12. NARDVS MEA DEDIT ODOREM SVVM) Videtur נרדי non esse nardus mea, sed nardinum: ut dicat mariti sui in somno respirantis halitum etiam nardino esse suaviorem.

Quænam vero illa suavitas halitus Salomonei cum in somno respiravit? De eo enim intelligit Grotius. At in textu nihil de somno. Dum Rex במסבו in ac- cubitu suo, id est, in corona discumbentium recumbit. Vox enim Ebræa circuitum seu coronam aut locum discumbentium, qui in orbem disponi solebant, signi- ficat. Avenarius in Lexico notat accipi etiam posse, ut participium Hiphil: Donec Rex fuerit inter cir- cumdantes ministros; sed prior sensus convenientior est: quem Græci exprimunt ἐν ἀνακλίσει. Et vox נרד est nardus Cant. 4, 13. 14. unde Græcum νάρδος & Latinum nardus: ideo cum suffixo hic est nardus mea. De se ergo Sponsa loquitur, non de Sponso, & quum inter delicias Judææ mos ille peculiaris fue- rit, ut discumbentes unguentis perfunderentur Marc. 14, 3. optime id convenit Sponsæ nardi odore perfundenti Sponsum in accubitu. Quod non male explicat Mercer. interim dum præsens Ecclesiæ suæ ad- est Christus, verbo suo pascens eam, bonum odorem fi- dei suæ, & virtutum ac bonorum operum reddere Spon- sam. Conf. Joh. 12, 5. 2. Cor. 2, 15. Osiander de odore precum intelligit hoc pacto: Ecclesia, audita suavissi- ma consolatione, quam precibus impetravit, ait; dum esset Rex & Sponsus meus Christus in accubitu suo, in mensa hilaris cum amicis suis, nardus mea dedit odo- rem suum, in tempore oportuno veniunt preces Ecclesiæ (quæ sunt instar optimorum odorum) ante faciem Christi, eumq; permovent, ut exaudiat, & verbo suo ef- ficaciter consoletur Ecclesiam. Paulo alieniora sunt, quæ de accubitu Christi, in throno divinitatis, in incar- natione, in prædicatione, in morte, in resurrectione, in gloria cœlesti prolixe hic Cornel. à Lap. Franc. Junius reddit quidem etiam nardinum: ac Sponso tribuit, sed accubitum in cælis intelligit: Interea dum Rex in accubitu suo est, in cælis, nardinum edit odorem suum, perfundor odoribus suavissimis, quanto magis cum patefacta vita revelabor cum ipso in gloria. Sed alie- nior est interpretatio: nulla enim hic comparatio instituitur status Ecclesiæ in hac & futura vita. Ac- cubitus Christi in regno Ecclesiæ indigitatur Matth. 8, 11. & in fidelium cordibus Apoc. 3, 20. qui nardum fi- dei & bonorum operum Phil. 4, 18. ac precum odora- tur, ac odore isto delectatur: imo nos ipsos oleo per- fundit, cum mensam nobis in regno suo parat, ut odorem bonum reddamus Ps. 23. Hic enim in præ- senti vita adhuc nobis parat murenulas aureas, nos- que subinde magis magisque ornat S. S. Trin. ceu versu præcedente Christus Sponsus, Murenulas au- reas faciemus, Ego, cum Patre, & S. S. (conf. Joh. 14, 23. Trinitatis hic monstrari arcanum Foljoth cum aliis Patribus observavit) tibi cum punctis argenteis.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. A BUNDLE OF MYRRH IS MY BELOVED TO ME, HE SHALL ABIDE BETWEEN MY BREASTS.

That the Bride spreads from herself a good odor of faith and virtues is primarily because she has her beloved bridegroom as a bundle of myrrh abiding between her breasts, whence Nyssen, hom. 3: 'My brother is to me a binding, which I hang from my neck over my chest, through which I offer a good odor to the body.' The name דוד denotes both friend, and bridegroom, and kinsman, דוד what? cousin, sister's son. The LXX have ἀδελφὸς: Jerome, 'fraternus': concerning which Origen, 'The Church which speaks three times about the cousin, we are gathered from the Gentiles. Our Savior is the son of the sister, that is, of the Synagogue.'

This signification of the bridegroom is simpler and more convenient: yet it can well be connoted with the dispensation of faith, because the bridegroom is a brother, a kinship of nature. A bundle of myrrh is said to hang between the breasts, both because of the continual meditation on the passion, as Bede rightly explained: Christ as a bundle of myrrh then dwells between the breasts of the bride, when the Church meditates on the death of her Redeemer without intermission with her inmost heart: and who does not know that the heart is located between the breasts? and also because of the studious imitation of virtues: because as Gregory the Great holds, while the holy mind considers the life of CHRIST in every part, it gathers against all vices the virtues that resist through his imitation, from which it fits for itself a bundle of myrrh, by which it may wipe away the eternal rot of its own flesh. Myrrh is described partly by its odor Sirac. 24, 20. whence the beds of myrrh applied Proverb. 7. 17. partly by its bitter taste, Mark 15, 23. partly by its power of preserving from rot: as Anselm says in this place, myrrh, he says, is a most bitter thing, and therefore bodies anointed with it remain intact, because on account of the excessive bitterness worms do not approach. Therefore it befits the passion of Christ, which offered a pleasing odor Ephes. 5, 2. was very bitter, and can preserve us from rot. Therefore, so that the bride may prepare this bundle of myrrh for herself, let her ascend the mountain of myrrh, Canticles 4. and harvest myrrh there chapter 5. let her meditate on the passion of Christ, and thus she also always carries this bundle in her heart, so that it may dwell in the midst of the breasts, i.e., according to Theodoret, in the principal part of the soul, namely the heart, which is situated between the breasts. Blessed Gerhard in Post. Salomon. Dom. Quinquages. notes here that Israelite virgins especially carried bundles of myrrh in their hearts, who writes more fully about these. You also if you are wise, says St. Bernard, you will imitate the prudence of the bride, and you will not suffer this bundle of myrrh, so dear, to be torn from the principality of your breast even for an hour, always retaining in memory all those bitter things which he endured for you, and revolving them in assiduous meditation, so that you too may be able to say, a bundle of myrrh &c. And I, brothers (continues Bernard), from the beginning of my conversion, instead of a heap of merits, which I knew I lacked, took care to bind this bundle for myself, and to place it between my breasts, collected from all the anxieties and bitternesses of my Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 13. FASCICULUS MYRRHÆ DILE- CTUS MEUS MIHI, INTER UBERA MEA COMMORABITUR.

Quod bonum odorem fidei & virtutum Sponsa de se spargit, inde imprimis est, quod dilectum spon- sum suum ceu fasciculum myrrhæ habet inter ubera commorantem unde Nyssen. hom. 3. Fraternus meus mihi est alligamentum, quod collo suspendo supra pe- ctus, per quod bonum odorem præbeo corpori. Nomen דוד & amicum, & sponsum notat, & consanguineum, דוד quid? consobrinum, sororis filium. LXX. ἀδελφὸς habent: Hieronym. fraternus: de quo Origenes, Ecclesia quæ ter loquitur de fratruele nos sumus ex gentibus congre- gati. Salvator noster sororis est filius, hoc est, Synagogæ.

Simplicior autem est & convenientior hic sponsi si- gnificatio: bene tamen connotari potest cum fidei dispensatione, quia sponsus est fraternus, naturæ co- gnatio. Fasciculus autem myrrhæ dicitur inter ube- ra pendens tum ob jugem passionis meditationem, ut recte Beda exposuit: Christus tanquam myrrhæ fa- sciculus tunc inter ubera sponsæ commoratur, cum Ec- clesia mortem sui Redemptoris sine intermissione inti- mo corde meditatur: inter ubera autem cordis locum esse quis nescit? tum ob studiosam virtutum imitatio- nem: quia ut Gregor. M. habet, dum sancta mens CHRISTI vitam ex omni parte considerat, contra omnia vitia ex ejus imitatione repugnantes virtutes congregat, ex quibus sibi fasciculum myrrhæ aptat, quo carnis suæ putredinem sempiternam abstergat. Describitur myrrha partim ab odore Sirac. 24, 20. unde lectis myrrhæ adhibitæ Proverb. 7. 17. partim ab amaro sapore, Marc. 15, 23. partim à virtute præ- servandi à putredine: uti Anshelm. h. l. myrrha, in- quit, est res amarissima, & ideo ea uncta corpora ma- nent integra, quia præ nimia amaritudine vermes non accedunt. Passioni ergo Christi convenit, quæ gra- tum odorem præbuit Ephes. 5, 2. perquam amara fuit, nosque à putredine præservare potest. Ideo ut hunc fasciculum myrrhæ sibi conficiat sponsa, myrrhæ montem conscendat, Cantic. 4. myrrham- que ibi demetat cap. 5. passionem Christi medite- tur, atque ita etiam fasciculum hunc in corde suo semper gestat, ut in medio uberum commoretur, h. e. juxta Theodor. in præcipua animæ parte, corde nempe, quod inter ubera situm. Israëlíticas virgines imprimis desponsatas gestasse fasciculos myrrhæ in corde hic notat B. Gerhard. in Post. Salomon. Do- min. Quinquages. qui de his fusius. Tu quoque si sa- pis, inquit S. Bernhard. imitaberis sponsæ prudentiam, atque hunc myrrhæ tam carum fasciculum de princi- patu tui pectoris nec ad horam patieris avelli, amara illa omnia, quæ pro te pertulit, semper in memoria re- tinens, & assidua meditatione revolvens, quo possis dicere & tu, fasciculus myrrhæ &c. Et ego fratres (pergit Bernhardus) ab ineunte mea conversione, pro acervo meritorum, quæ mihi deesse sciebam, hunc mihi fasciculum colligare, & inter ubera mea colloca- re curavi, collectum ex omnibus anxietatibus & ama- ritudinibus Domini mei.

## 1:14
Vers. 14.

A CLUSTER OF CYPRUS IS MY BELOVED TO ME IN THE VINEYARDS OF ENGEDI.

Cophar or Cyprus is the fruit of the Cyprus tree, which St. Jerome teaches is fragrant, and blooms like a flowering grape, from which Cyprus oil is made. In Engedi Solomon had most excellent vineyards, both of vines, and of Cyprus, and of balsam. Thus Cassiodorus and Philo Carpathius explain it. Dioscorides describes the virtues of Cyprus in book 1, chapter 4, and among other things, that it is a remedy against the stings of scorpions. Compare Cornelius à Lapide in this place. The bride calls Christ a cluster of Cyprus: because he is most sweet to her in smell and taste like it, who like a cluster was pressed in the winepress of the passion, according to Ambrose in Psalm 118, where he also speaks of Engedi, It is a place, he says, in Judea in which opobalsam is produced &c. concerning which see Jerome, Tradit. in Gen. chapter 14.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

BOTRUS CYPRI DILECTUS MEUS MI- HI IN VINEIS ENGEDDI.

Cophar sive Cyprus est fructus arboris Cypri, quem S. Hieronymus docet odoratum esse, & in- star efflorescentis uvæ florere, ex quo Cyprinum fit oleum. In Engaddi Salomo vineas habebat tum vitium, tum Cypri, tum balsami præstantissimas. Ita explicat Cassiod. & Philo Carpath. Cypri virtutes de- scribit Dioscor. l. 1. c. 4. & inter alia, quod adversus scorpionum ictus remedio sit. Conf. Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l. Botrum Cypri Christum vocat sponsa: quia ejus instar ipsi odoratu & gustu est suavissimus, qui velut botrus in passionis torculari expressus, secundum Ambrof. in Psalm. 118. ubi etiam de Engaddi, Locus, inquit, est in Judæa in quo opobalsamum gignitur &c. de quo Hieron. vid. Tradit. in Gen. c. 14.

## 1:15
Vers. 15.

BEHOLD YOU ARE FAIR, MY LOVE, BEHOLD YOU ARE FAIR: YOUR EYES ARE DOVES.

She is called fair twice either because of her remarkable beauty, or because of the beauty of both soul and body: or rather because of the beauty of justice both imputed 2 Cor. 5, 21. and begun, Coloss. 3, 12. whose eyes are well said to be of doves, according to Gregory, because while she groans in temporal things and is snatched toward eternal desires, she guards her senses in simplicity and detests carnal concupiscences. Moreover, Gregory adds: By the eyes of doves can also be understood the preachers of the Churches, who preserve the simplicity which they preach, and despising visible things, pant after eternal things with great groans. Dove-like eyes are introduced here because of beauty, simplicity, chastity, because according to Pliny doves do not violate the faith of marriage, as Blessed Gerhard deduced in Dom. 15 post Trin. because of their brightness and mobility.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ECCE TU PULCRA ES, AMICA MEA, ECCE TU PULCRA ES: OCULI TUI CO- LUMBARUM.

Bis pulcra dicitur sive ob venustatem insignem, sive ob pulcritudinem tum animæ tum corporis: seu potius ob pulchritudinem justitiæ tum imputa- tæ 2. Cor. 5, 21. tum inchoatæ, Coloss. 3, 12. cujus oculi bene columbarum esse perhibentur, secundum Gre- gor. quia dum in temporalibus gemit & ad æterna de- sideria rapitur, in simplicitate sensus suos custodit & carnales concupiscentias detestatur. Addit autem Gregorius: Possunt etiam per oculos columbarum Ecclesiarum prædicatores intelligi, qui simplicitatem, quam prædicant, servant, & visibilia contemnentes ad æterna cum magnis gemitibus anhelant. Oculos co- lumbinos hic introduci propter formositatem, sim- plicitatem, castitatem, quia Plinio teste columbæ con- jugii fidem non violant, ut propter luciditatem, & vo- lubilitatem B. Gerhard. Dom. 15. post Trin. deduxit.

## 1:16
Ver. 16. OUR FLOWERING BED.

What Bede notes here and Bernard, the bride indicates to the Bridegroom that the bridal chamber is adorned, and she silently invites him to it. Our bed is green, or covered with green flowers, and thus it is verdant, flowering, and blooming. The LXX, according to Origen and Theodoret, have κλίνη ἡμῶν σύσκιος, our shady bed. The sense according to Osiander is: Our churches are now flourishing by the benefit of God: the beams of our houses are cedar, not feeling decay: they are incorruptible, and our ceilings are cypress. Our churches are well built by the word of God, so that we may hope they will be long-lasting, and they offer a good reputation for themselves, just as cypress wood emits a sweet odor. The Weimar theologians explain the flowering bed thus, that many children of God are generated by the power of the gracious operation of the Bridegroom, Ps. 45, 17. John 1, 12. 13. through the word and Sacraments 1. Pet. 1, 23. John 3, 3. and may the Church flourish as if blooming most sweetly, Isa. 35, 1. in which the bridegroom has his rest as if in a bedchamber, Ps. 132, 14. and affects his faithful ones with heavenly rest and peace, Ps. 149, 5. Phil. 4, 7. They take the cedar beams and cypress ceilings to mean that those children are regenerated to a living hope, to an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance in the house of God, or in heaven, 1. Pet. 1, 3. just as cedar wood does not rot, is beautiful, uniform, and always green: but cypress wood emits a sweet odor. Gilbert Foliot: Just as it is pleasant to rest in a flowering bed, so also it is safe and secure to rest under a roof that is covered with cedar beams. For cedar and cypress are of an incorruptible nature, they do not know how to be corrupted, they preserve their greenness and likewise their odor; they also put serpents to flight with their odor, and kill them, and thus provide security for those resting under them. The ceilings provide protection for the beams, and strength, they also preserve their greenness, and odor, by which serpents are killed. By the beams, however, he understands the angels, by the ceilings the Archangels. More suitable is the commentary of Wolbero, Abbot of St. Pantaleon of Cologne, around the year of Christ 1150, understanding by the beams and ceilings the Rectors and Doctors of the Churches, who in the individual churches committed to them are for protection and ornament by their words and examples, and spreading the odor of their holiness and doctrine far and wide, they also protect and adorn the universal Church itself. The cedar, he says, has three things memorable about its nature: height, odor, and incorruptibility: which rightly correspond to the Holy Doctors, because they are lifted up by the contemplation of divinity, they are spread all around by the odor of doctrine and good action, they are not corrupted by any rot of infidelity or depravity, nay, by their odor they even put serpents to flight, because by their doctrine they are able to repel evil thoughts creeping secretly in the heart, and to put to flight the ancient serpent suggesting those same things, that is, the Devil with the thoughts themselves. The cypress also in its nature has the grace of odor and incorruption, which also befit the Doctors on account of the odor of their doctrine and life and the incorruption of their faith.

Latin:

Vers. 16. LECTULUS NOSTER FLORI- DUS.

Quod Beda hic notat & Bernhardus, sponsa indicat Sponso thalamum esse ornatum, eumque tacite ad illum invitat. Lectulus noster viridis, seu viridibus floribus coopertus, adeoque virens, flo- rens & vernans est. LXX. apud Orig. & Theodoret. habent κλίνη ἡμῶν σύσκιος, lectulus noster umbrosus. Sensus juxta Osiandrum est: Ecclesiæ nostræ Dei be- neficio nunc florent: tigna domorum nostrarum sunt Cedrina non sentientia cariem: sunt incorrupti- bilia, & laquearia nostra sunt cypresfina. Ecclesiæ nostræ bene sunt ædificatæ verbo Dei, ut diuturnas fo- re speremus, & bonam de se famam præbent, sicut cy- pressina ligna suavem odorem emittunt. Vinarien- ses floridum lectum ita explicant, quod multi libe- ri Dei vi gratiosæ operationis Sponsi generentur Ps. 45, 17. Johann. 1, 12. 13. per verbum & Sacramenta 1. Petr. 1, 23. Joh. 3, 3. & vireat quasi ac floreat Ecclesia suavissime Esa. 35, 1. in qua sponsus tanquam in cu- bili suam habet requiem Ps. 132, 14. & fideles suos cœlesti requie, & pace afficit, Ps. 149, 5. Phil. 4, 7. Tigna autem cedrina, & laquearia cypressina eo acci- piunt, quod liberi illi ad vivam spem regenerentur, ad incorruptibilem, immaculatam, & immarcescibilem hæreditatem in domo Dei, vel in cœlo, 1. Petr. 1, 3. uti lignum cedrinum non putrescit, pulcrum, æquabile est, & semper viret: Cypressinum vero lignum sua- vem odorem emittit. Gilbertus Foljoth: Sicut in le- cto florido quiescere amœnum est, sic & sub tecto, quod tignis cedrinis opertum est, quiescere tutum & secu- rum. Cedrus enim & cupressus imputribilis naturæ sunt, corrumpi nesciunt, viriditatem suam conservant pariter & odorem; odore quoq; suo serpentes fugant, & enecant & sub iis quiescentibus securitatem sic parant. Laquearia tignis munimen parant, & fortitudinem, viriditatem suam etiam conservant, & odorem, quibus serpentes enecantur. Per tigna autem angelos, per laquearia Archangelos intelligit. Convenientior est Wolberonis Abbatis S. Pantaleonis Coloniensis circa annum Christi 1150. commentarius, per tigna & laquearia Rectores & Doctores Ecclesiarum intelli- gens, qui in singulis sibi commissis Ecclesiis pro munimento & ornamento sunt verbis & exemplis, ac longe lateque sanctitatis & doctrinæ suæ odorem spargentes ipsam quoque universalem Ecclesiam muniunt, & ornant. Cedrus, inquit, tria habet natu- ræ suæ memorabilia, proceritatem, odorem, imputribi- litatem: quæ recte S. Doctoribus congruunt, quia di- vinitatis contemplatione sublevantur, doctrinæ & bo- næ actionis odore circum quaque sparguntur, nulla in- fidelitatis vel pravitatis putredine corrumpuntur, imo odore suo fugant etiam serpentes, quia doctrina sua malas cogitationes occulte in corde serpentes valent re- pellere, & easdem suggerentem antiquum serpentem, hoc est, Diabolum cum ipsis cogitationibus fugare. Cy- pressus quoque in sua natura gratiam habet odoris & incorruptionis, quæ etiam Doctoribus conveniunt pro- pter doctrinæ & vitæ odorem & fidei incor- ruptionem.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

The Bridegroom, promising that he would sprout like a flower, is recognized by the Bride—who is like a lily among thorns—in the midst of the forest trees, as the one whose shade and fruit she delights in, and by whom she, languishing with love, is refreshed: and having heard his most sweet voice concerning the quiet of his beloved not being disturbed, she rejoices at his arrival, and proclaims his promptness: and being invited by him to come, as the past winter is over, spring is arriving, the flowers are now appearing, the time of pruning is present, and the voice of the turtledove is now heard, she is exhilarated by the scent and sweetness of the fruits, and in turn testifies her desire and love to him.

I AM THE FLOWER OF THE FIELD) Rose of Sharon. Sharon is a most fertile land. Is. 65, 10. ἁ ῥοδόχρως Ἐλένα, in Theocritus.

Thus also the Tigurines [translate] Rose of Sharon. Pagninus, Marinus, and Vatablus also interpret the Hebrew word חבצלת as rose. B. Luther retains a general name: Ich bin eine Blum in Saron: because the Hebrew names of trees, flowers, and gems are too polysemous. That word occurs only here and in Is. 35, 1, denoting a beautiful, purple, and very fragrant flower. Sharon, according to Adrichom, is a city and a level region, rich and most fertile. Cf. 1 Chron. 5, 16; ch. 28, 29; Is. 33, 9; ch. 29, 1, 2; ch. 25, 10, in which region Nazareth is situated, the city of the Lord's conception. It is added: and the lily of the valleys. שושנת, although some with the Chaldean and Galatians translate it as rose, is a lily, as the LXX, Aquila, Symmachus, Jerome, Aben-Ezra, R. Solomon, the Tigurines, Vatablus, and others hold, from שש, six, because it is adorned with six petals: just as the Phoenicians and Arabs call the lily Susanna.

Theodoret, Nyssen, Ambrose, Philo Carpathius, Osorius, Genebrard, and Vatablus attribute these words to the Bride, along with the Chaldean and the Hebrews in the Midrash: but Origen, Theodoret, Aponius, Cassiodorus, Bede, Anselm, Bernard, Rupert, Honorius, and others in this place more correctly recognize them as being the Bridegroom's (as is evident from v. 2), as do Ambrose in his book *On the Soul* and Isaac ch. 4, 5, and Cyril *On the Incarnation* ch. 9, saying, as Wolbero has it: You rightly feel, O beloved, that you ascribe all your beauty to me, because I am in truth the flower of the field, that is, the honor and beauty and ornament of the whole universal Church diffused throughout the world as a most joyful field. I am also the lily of the valleys, that is, the cleansing, refreshment, and medicine of the humble or of those depressed by some sorrow and affliction of this world for the sake of my name. For the nature of the lily has three things in itself that are delightful: whiteness, fragrance, and medicine against burning. Cornelius, with Bede, gives this reason for the connection: You have spoken rightly, O Bride, that our bed is flowery. But know that it is flowery not from you, but from me: For I am the flower of the field. Just as a flower is the ornament of the field, so is Christ the ornament of the world, as Origen, Ambrose, and Bede [say], a flower that never withers, whose beauty never fails, whose color never diminishes, whose vigor never perishes: A flower, however, of the field, which is not enclosed in a garden, but is exposed to be plucked by all. Cf. Is. 11, 2; Jer. 23, 6. The lily of the valleys, that is, as some explain, of those who are humble and depressed in heart. In the lily, according to Honorius, five things are considered: because it is white, having a prominent golden color, and is fragrant, and hanging, and always curved: Thus Christ is white in his humanity, golden in his Deity, fragrant in his preaching, hanging in receiving the penitent, and curved in condescending to sinners and lifting them up. Beautifully, says Bede, in the lily the exterior whiteness gradually opens itself first, and thus finally the grace of the golden color, which was hidden within, is revealed, because the Lord, born into the world, was first a man sublime to those who truly believed in him, but in the preceding time he was known as the true God. Christ was a flower in his conception and birth, a flower in his holy conversation, a flower in his resurrection, as Ambrose, book 2 *On the Psalms* ch. 5, [and] a flower in his ascension, or translation into heaven. See B. Gerhard, *On the Feast of the Purification of Mary*. That Christ is called a lily by reason of his figure, not unlike a royal crown, whence in Pierius's *Hieroglyphics* he is called a royal flower; by reason of his beauty, Matt. 6, 28; Is. 35, 1; by reason of his color, both white, by which the purity of human nature is noted, and golden, by which the Deity of Christ is noted: as also by reason of his fragrance, Sir. 40, 18, and his virtue, because the root of the lily is conducive against inflammation, and the leaves against the bite of a serpent, Num. 21, 9; John 3, 14. But the lily of the valleys [is so called] on account of the humility which he shows in the entrance, progress, and exit of his life, teaches B. Gerhard, *On the 17th Sunday after Trinity*. As all these things fit Christ most excellently, so since this dialogue still concerns the desire for the coming of Christ and its fulfillment, which Christ here promises to his Bride, the Ernestine Paraphrase is not inappropriate: that Christ testifies that he is a flower in Sharon, that is, that he would sprout from the earth in the region of Nazareth in the fullness of time, like a most pleasant flower, Ps. 132, 12, 18; Is. 11, 1; ch. 53, 2; Jer. 23, 5; ch. 33, 15; Zech. 3, 8; ch. 6, 19; afterwards to diffuse his fragrance through the world by the preaching of the Gospel, 2 Cor. 2, 15, 16; and that as the lily of the valleys, he would arise in the humble and dark valley of the world like a most white lily, and would humble himself for the sake of the Bride, Phil. 2, 8.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

Sponsus promittens se floris instar germinatu- rum, sponsæ, quæ instar lilii est inter spinas, se adfuturum, agnoscitur à Sponsa in medio arborum sylvestrium, cujus umbra & fru- ctu delectatur, à quo refocillatur amore lan- guida: auditaque voce ipsius suavissima de quiete amicæ non turbanda, ob adventum ejus gaudet, ejusque promtitudinem depræ- dicat: & ab ipso invitata, ut præterita hye- me, vere adveniente, floribus jam apparen- tibus, tempore putationis præsente, voce turturis jam audita, veniat & odore ac sua- vitate fructuum se exhilarat, vicissim deside- rium & amorem suum ipsi testatur.

EGO FLOS CAMPI) Rosa Saron. Saron terra est fe- racissima. Es. 65, 10. ἁ ῥοδόχρως Ἐλένα, apud Theocritum.

Sic etiam Tigurini Rosa Saron. Pagninus, Mari- nus & Vatablus interpretantur quoque vocem Ebr. חבצלת rosa. B. Lutherus nomen generale retinet: Ich bin eine Blum in Saron: quia Ebræa nomina arborum, florum & gemmarum nimis sunt πολύσημα. Vox illa solum hîc & Es. 35, 1. occurrit, pulcrum, purpureum, & valde odoriferum florem notans. Saron juxta Adrichom. urbs est, & Regio campestris, pinguis & fertilissima. Conf. 1. Paral. 5, 16. c. 28, 29. Es. 33, 9. c. 29, 1. 2. c. 25, 10. in qua re- gione Nazareth sita, urbs conceptionis Dominicæ. Additur: & lilium convallium. שושנת etsi non- nulli cum Chald. & Galat. rosam vertant, lilium est, ut LXX. Aquila, Symmachus, Hieronymus, Aben- Ezra, R. Salomon, Tigurini, Vatablus, alii habent, à שש sex, quia sex ornatur foliis: quemadmodum & Phœnices, Arabesque lilium Susanna nuncupant.

Verba hæc Sponsæ tribuit Theodor. Nyssen. Ambros. Philo Carpath. Osorius, Genebrard. Vatabl. Osian- der cum Chald. & Ebræis in Midrasch: sed Sponsi ea esse rectius agnoscunt (ut è v. 2. patet) Origenes, Theod. Aponius, Cassiodor. Beda, Anshelm. Bern- hard. Rupertus, Honorius & alii in h. l. ut & Am- bros. lib. de anima & Isaac c. 4, 5. Cyrill. de incarnat. c. 9. q. d. ut Wolbero habet: Recte ô dilecta sentis, quæ omnem tuam pulchritudinem mihi adscribis, quia ego revera sum flos campi, hoc est honor & pul- chritudo & ornatus totius universalis Ecclesiæ per to- tum mundum ceu lætissimum campum diffusæ. Ego quoque sum lilium convallium, id est, emundatio, re- fectio & medicina humilium sive aliquo mœrore & afflictione hujus mundi mei nominis causa depresso- rum. Lilii quippe natura tria habet in se delectabilia, candorem, odorem, medicinam contra adustionem. Cornelius cum Beda hanc reddit connexionis ratio- nem: Recte dixisti ô Sponsa, lectulus noster flori- dus. At scias eum esse floridum non ex te, sed ex me: Ego enim sum flos campi. Sicut flos est ornamen- tum campi, sic Christus mundi, ut Origenes, Am- brosius, Beda, flos nunquam marcescens, cujus pul- chritudo nunquam deficit, nunquam minuitur co- lor, nunquam deperit vigor: Flos autem campi, qui horto non concluditur, sed omnibus carpen- dus exponitur. Conf. Esa. 11, 2. Jerem. 23, 6. Lilium convallium, id est, ut nonnulli explicant, humilium, & depressorum corde. In lilio juxta Honorium quin- que considerantur: quia est candidum, habens au- reum colorem prominentem, & est odoriferum, & pendulum, & semper incurvum: Sic Christus can- didus est in humanitate, aureus in Deitate, odorife- rus in prædicatione, pendulus in suscipiendo pœniten- tes, incurvus in condescendendo peccatoribus & eos sublevando. Pulcre, inquit Beda, in lilio prius se candor exterior paulatim aperit, & sic demum aurei coloris, quæ latebat intus, gratia patescit, quia natus in mundo Dominus prius homo sublimis his, qui in eum vere credebant, at tempore præcedente Deus verus innotuit. Flos fuit Christus in conceptione, & nativitate, flos fuit in sancta conversatione, flos in resurrectione, ut Ambrof. l. 2. de Pf. c. 5. flos in ascensione, seu translatione in cœlum. Vid. B. Gerhard. Festo purific. Mar. Lilium dici Christum ratione figuræ, coronæ Regiæ non absimilis, unde Pierio in Hierogl. flos regius dicitur, ratione decoris Matth. 6, 28. Ef. 35, 1. ratione coloris tum candidi, quo humanæ naturæ puritas, tum aurei, quo Deitas Christi notatur: ut & ratione odoris Syr. 40, 18. & virtutis, quia radix contra inflammationem, folia lilii contra morsus serpentis conducunt, Numer. 21, 9. Joh. 3, 14. Lilium vero convallium ob humilitatem quam in vitæ ingressu, progressu & egressu ostendit, docet B. Gerhard. Dn. 17. post. Trinit. Quæ uti optime Christo conveniunt omnia, ita quum hic dialogismus adhuc concernat adventus Christi desiderium, ejusque adimpletionem, quam Christus hîc pollicetur Sponsæ suæ, non inconcinna est Paraphrasis Ernestina: quod Christus se testetur esse florem in Saron, hoc est, in plenitudine temporum è terris progerminaturum in regione Nazareth, instar floris amœnissimi, Pf. 132, 12. 18. Ef. 11, 1. c. 53, 2. Jer. 23, 5. c. 33, 15. Zach. 3, 8. c. 6, 19. postea odorem suum per orbem prædicatione Evangelii diffusurum 2. Cor. 2, 15. 16. quodque ut lilium convallium, in humili, & opaca mundi valle instar lilii candidissimi oriturus, ac semetipsum Sponsæ causa humiliaturus sit, Phil. 2, 8.

## 2:2
Verse 2.

AS THE LILY AMONG THORNS, SO IS MY LOVE AMONG THE DAUGHTERS.

Τῶν δ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἄν τις ἄμωμο, ἐπείχ᾽ Ἐλένᾳ παρισωθῇ.

Lilies sometimes grow, or are placed, even among briars and thorns: thus the Church flourishes in the midst of heretics and the wicked, who prick and lacerate her, while she herself, like the lily, remains in her whiteness, fragrance, and splendor of doctrine and holiness, nay, even shines more and more. Honorius on this passage says: Just as I, the Bridegroom, am the lily of the valleys, that is, the ornament of the humble, so you, my love, will be the lily of the thorns, that is, the glory of the nations. The Bride of Christ is called a lily by reason of her vigor, Hos. 14:6; her beauty, Matt. 6:28, Isa. 35:1, Sirach 5:8; her fragrance, Sirach 50:18. The wicked, however, are compared to thorns on account of their barrenness, Matt. 7:16; their intractability, 2 Sam. 23:6; the wickedness of the serpents and vipers lurking within them, Matt. 3:7; the unhappiness of their outcome, Heb. 6:8, 2 Sam. 23. How likewise the pious are pricked by the thorns of temptation, Luke 8:14, of seduction, and of persecutions, see B. Gerh. in the cited place, Dn. Exaudi.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SICVT LILIVM INTER SPINAS, SIC AMICA MEA INTER FILIAS.

Τῶν δ᾽ οὐδ᾽ ἄν τις ἄμωμο, ἐπείχ᾽ Ἐλένᾳ παρισωθῇ.

Lilia etiam inter sentes & spinas quandoque nascuntur, vel constituta sunt: ita Ecclesia in medio hæreticorum & impiorum floret, qui illam pungunt & lacerant, ipsa, lilii instar, in suo candore, odore, & splendore doctrinæ & sanctitatis permanente, imo magis magisque coruscante. Honorius in h. l. Sicut ego, inquit Sponsus, sum lilium tonvallium, videl. ornatus humilium, sic eris tu amica mea lilium spinarum, id est, decus gentium. Lilium dicitur Sponsa Christi ratione vigoris Of. 14, 6. decoris Matth. 6, 28. Efa. 35, 1. Sirac. 5, 8. odoris Syrac. 50, 18. Spinis vero comparantur impii propter sterilitatem Matth. 7, 16. intractabilitatem 2. Sam. 23, 6. Serpentum & viperarum in illis latentium pravitatem, Matth. 3, 27. eventus infelicitatem Ebr. 6, 8. 2. Sam. 23. Quomodo item pii pungantur à spinis tentationis Luc. 8, 14. seductionis, & persequutionum, vid. B. Gerh. l. c. Dn. Exaudi.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

AS THE APPLE TREE AMONG THE TREES OF THE WOOD, SO IS MY BELOVED AMONG THE SONS) That comparison in Theocritus pertaining to Helen is similar:

- - - ἅτ᾽ ἀνέδραμεν ὄγμον ἀρούρα, Ἡ κάπῳ κυπάρισσο...

Beautifully by Wolbero: As the apple tree is a fruit-bearing tree having three useful things in itself, by which it refreshes, that is, fruit, fragrance, and shade; and among the trees of the woods, which are certainly unfruitful, it is considered incomparable; so my beloved, by the fruit and fragrance of holiness, and justice, and doctrine, and by the shade of his protection, by which he refreshes, teaches, and defends those believing in him, stood among the sons, that is, the Jews, who indeed were sons at first, and now wish to be, but are not, because God said of them, I have brought up and exalted sons, but they have despised me Joh. 8. Isa. 1. and therefore they are unfruitful and useless trees, and for this reason to be cut down and cast into the fire. The rest of men, therefore, are wild trees, on account of natural sterility Matth. 7, 17. on account of darkness Isa. 9, 2. Luke 1, 79. and the certainty of destruction Matth. 3, 10. Christ, however, is compared to a fruit-bearing tree Rev. 22, 2. 14. Cf. Ezek. 17, 22. Sirach 24, 22. by reason of fruitfulness, Cant. 2, 3. Rev. 2, 7. who according to Nyssenus came into the world for this purpose, and was made a tree of the forest of the same essence as the human forest, yet fruit-bearing, so that he might render men, however depraved and wild, from wild ones fruit-bearing. Likewise: Christ in that he is a tree is of the same essence as the human forest. For he was tempted in likeness without sin, but in that he bears such fruit, that through him the senses of the soul are rendered sweet, he has a greater difference from the forest than that which the lily has from thorns. He is also compared to a fruit-bearing tree by reason of shade, of which later, and also by reason of grafting, which we have need of, if we also ought to bear fruit Joh. 15, 4. Rom. 11, 23. See if you please B. Gerhard. Dom. 16. after Trinity. The Bridegroom therefore insinuates the fruit of his conception and humiliation, that indeed the Bride by the virtue of his incarnation and passion will also beautifully germinate like a white and golden lily, on account of the gold of faith and the whiteness of love, and will scatter from herself the most fragrant scent of knowledge and virtues Ps. 92, 1. Isa. 35, 1. Sirach 39, 17. 18. although she must persevere among the thorns of many calamities, temptations, and persecutions Ezek. 2, 6. ch. 29, 21. Joh. 16, 33. Acts 14, 22.

Verse same. UNDER THE SHADOW OF HIM WHOM I HAD DESIRED I SAT, AND HIS FRUIT WAS SWEET TO MY TASTE.

Fruit-bearing trees, such as the apple tree, as they are in themselves more temperate and sweeter than the unfruitful and wild ones: so also they emit a more temperate and sweeter shadow than them. To Chrysostom, shadow is providence, the care and protection of the Church Isa. 51, 16. Ps. 36, 2. Ps. 91, 12. To Gregory the Great, the shadow of Christ is the protection of the Holy Spirit, of which later. Christ, however, offers us a shadow or remedy against the heat of conscience, divine wrath, and eternal damnation, Deut. 4, 24. ch. 32, 22. Luke 16, 24. as also a safe refuge against the persecutions of enemies Ps. 17, 8. Ps. 91, 1. seqq. Isa. 4, 5. ch. 25, 4. This tree of life also offers to our taste sweet fruit for nourishment, the refreshment and healing of spirits, Rev. 22, 2. 14. provided we desire it through faith and enjoy it. See B. Gerhard. Dom. 7. Trin. St. Bernard therefore, he says, had desired the shadow of Christ above all, because he alone is the one who not only cools from the heat of vices, but also fills with the delight of virtues. The bride therefore answers the bridegroom in return, proclaiming the same, that he is not only like a flower, but a most sweet tree, that he not only delights and refreshes with his scent and color, but also feeds with his fruit, and profits in many ways, and with his shadow cherishes, protects, and refreshes in the heat: and that this tree of life in the midst of men, who are sons by reason of creation, even if they have degenerated into a wild nature, is to be planted in its time Ezek. 17, 22. 23. so that those unfruitful trees, having deserved nothing but destruction, Jude v. 12. Matth. 3, 10. ch. 7, 18. may be able to turn out fruit-bearing, Matth. 12, 32. and that under the shadow of this most desired tree, which the Bride was awaiting with great desire, until in the fullness of time that shoot should go forth from the root of Jesse Isa. 11, 1. about to turn out a green and fruit-bearing tree, which was indeed to be cut down for us Luke 23, 31. Isa. 53, 2. 8. but then it will be the true tree of life, Rev. 22, 2. under whose shadow alone refreshment can be had in the heat of divine wrath, and protection against all adversities, whose fruits alone will bring sweetness, with all bitterness arising from the fruit of the forbidden tree dispelled; namely, the fruits of his love, which this tree of life brought forth in the PASSION Rev. 2, 7. for recreation, and spiritual and heavenly healing ch. 22, 3. 14. which are offered to us in the word of the Gospel, as that in which we taste the sweetness of the Lord Ps. 34, 9. and which is sweeter to our taste than honey and any honeycomb Ps. 19, 11. Ps. 119, 103. Hence the bride congratulates herself, and rejoices greatly, that she is to be led by the bridegroom into the wine cellar, where the sweetness and pleasantness of that fruit is stored, which gladdens the heart of man Psalm 104, 15. And although the bride must still fight even unto blood Heb. 12, 1. seqq. yet under the love of the bridegroom as a banner, she can be secure, and conquer, and triumph in all adversities Rom. 8, 37. Ps. 60, 6. Although she may also be affected by some languor, she is nevertheless to be refreshed by the bridegroom himself with fruits that comfort the heart, and to be sustained by his hand supporting and embracing most sweetly, Isa. 62, 4. 5. On account of which confidence of the bride, behold the most desired bridegroom is present, and adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to disturb the rest of the bride, and the arrival, presence, and voice of the bridegroom are recognized by the bride with the greatest pleasure, as is evident from v. 2. seqq.

Verse same. TO MY THROAT) See Prov. 30, 20. Verse 4. HE BROUGHT ME INTO THE WINE CELLAR) That I might drink. See Prov. 5, 15. Verse 5. HE ORDAINED CHARITY IN ME) In the Hebrew: His banner over me is love: as if he were to say, I serve as a soldier under his banner, upon which is inscribed, love.

Grotius seems to be inebriated with mere venereal loves when he cast these notes onto paper. For he dreams of nothing but loves of this kind in this most holy Song: Therefore he even brings in a Nymph from Theocritus at verse 5. BECAUSE I LANGUISH WITH LOVE. The Nymph in Theocritus says Ναρκῶ νὴ τὸν Πᾶνα. And when at verse 11 there is talk of the passing of winter, that one gloss explains everything: Spring is the time of loves. When the Bridegroom at verse 14 says, SHOW ME THY FACE, Grotius tastes nothing but bodily beauty and the symmetry of the body. But what analogy or connection does the passage Prov. 30, 20, Such is also the way of an adulterous woman, who eats, and wiping her mouth says, I have done no evil, have with this of ours, ch. 2. 3. HIS FRUIT IS SWEET TO MY THROAT, or Prov. 5, 15, Drink water from thy cistern and the streams of thy well, with these of the Bride, HE BROUGHT ME INTO THE WINE CELLAR, that the Annotator should have ordered these to be compared with one another? What is more manifest than that the discourse is about the fruit of the tree of life, Christ, which is by far the sweetest to the throat of the faithful. For of him the Bride says in verse 2, as the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. Therefore from the apple tree, because it gives a better shade than the plane tree, even though the shade of this one is most pleasant, the mystical Bride has the shade of protection and refreshment, and from its fruits sweetness and sustenance, concerning which Gregory the Great beautifully says on this passage: Rightly is Christ figured by the apple tree, but other men by the trees of the wood, because in Christ alone, as often as we seek, we find the food of salvation; in his words and examples we refresh our souls with sweet and wholesome fruit.
