He is indeed the tree of life, which he bestows upon us. He is the one who, while he breathes himself into us, feeds the soul. But in other things, if we find any refreshment, we take it from them not because it is theirs, but because it is Christ's: because whatever is in them besides God is without doubt deadly to us as we find. And concerning the shadow of this evil: The shadow of Christ is the protection of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit overshadows the mind which He fills; because He tempers the heat of all temptations, and while the breeze of His inspiration gently touches the mind, He expels whatever harmful heat it was sustaining, and the mind, which perhaps had already been made withered by the excessive heat of vices, the shadow of the Holy Spirit protects and refreshes. Concerning the sweetness of the fruits, Gregory the Great likewise speaks sweetly: Christ Himself, the fruit-bearing tree, exists planted in our heart through faith, which if our mind loves worthily and diligently cultivates, it brings forth fruits that are inwardly beautiful and useful. While the mind, taking these, eats them greedily, it puts aside all the pleasures of the world in comparison to their sweetness. For it is very sweet to meditate upon heavenly things for oneself, to fix the inner eye upon eternity, so that at times, even in tears, the mind may be kindled and pricked with compunction, and, lifted up among tears by the food of Angels, may feed all the more greedily upon wisdom itself, the sweeter it is. Hence it is that it is added: He brought me into the wine cellar. And St. Bernard, Serm. 48: Deservedly had she desired his shadow, from which she was to receive both refreshment and, at the same time, sustenance. For the other trees of the woods, although they may have the shadow of comfort, yet do not have the sustenance of life, nor the perpetual fruits of salvation. By the wine cellar, others understand Holy Scripture, with Gregory of Nyssa and Aponius, because this offers us the wine of wisdom: others, with Theodoret, Cassiodorus, Bede, and Anselm, the Church, in which we draw that wine of wisdom and divine love from the Word of God: others, with Gregory the Great, Bernard, and Haymo, the house of prayer and contemplation. What, says Gregory, do we accept as more fitting for the wine cellar than the very secret contemplation of eternity? In this eternity, the holy Angels are inebriated with the wine of wisdom, while, seeing God Himself face to face, they are satisfied with every spiritual pleasure; this, the holy mind, if it be brought in by the Bridegroom, enters after putting aside all temporal things, in which it tastes, as much as is granted to it, of those angelic delights. Those interpretations can be joined by a certain reasoning: so that the Church is indeed the wine cellar, but because of Holy Scripture, inasmuch as it alone offers the wine of heavenly wisdom, just as the word of God and the Gospel is compared to wine, Isa. 55, 1. Prov. 8, 5. Matt. 9, 17. which we do not enjoy more sweetly than if we enter into the secret contemplation of eternity in the word, and in the Church, see Psalm 34, 9. 1 Pet. 2, 2. Psalm 36, 9. Alcuin on this place: The wine cellar ought to be understood as the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is accustomed to be given and received; whose grace is designated here by the name of wine. His fruits are sweet to my throat, who refreshes me with the heavenly sweetness of His grace. Foljoth, the King brought me into the wine cellar, that is, a certain storehouse of divine Scriptures, by which He draws me away from the world, by which He permits me now to have a dwelling place for those things which are above. Mercerus: He brought me into the house of wine, i.e., into the house of feasting and joy, namely, into the sacred mystery, by which I might be exhilarated and inebriated as if with wine.

The things that are added are rightly explained from the Hebrew thus: and his banner over me is love. But it is not the case that we should interpret it with Grotius, I serve as a soldier under his banner: for they do not express the action of the Bride, but rather the affection of the Bridegroom, which the Bride celebrates here in him: i.e., he sets before me, as if in the place of a banner, the love by which he draws me to himself, just as soldiers are gathered and drawn by a banner, so that they may always cast their eyes upon it. For the love with which Christ loves us ought to be a banner for us, by which we may be admonished never to turn our eyes away from him: indeed, when he brought me into the house of feasting and of all kinds of delights and joy, he showed me love as a banner. For it is the charity of the Lord that makes us penetrate into such great mysteries, as the most learned Mercerus holds in this place. Similarly Osiander: Christ exhilarates the heart of the Church with spiritual joy; and declares most manifestly that He loves us with ardent love. His love raises up our dismayed minds, just as an erected banner excites soldiers to alacrity. For we do not deny that we are also raised up by the love of Christ to fight under his banner: which the Vinarian Paraphrasts also look to here.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SICVT MALVS INTER LIGNA SYLVARVM, SIC DILECTVS MEVS INTER FILIOS) Similis illa apud Theocritum comparatio ad Helenam pertinens:

- - - ἅτ᾽ ἀνέδραμεν ὄγμον ἀρούρα, Ἡ κάπῳ κυπάρισσο...

Pulcre Wolbero: Sicut malus arbor fructifera tria in se habens utilia, quibus reficit, hoc est fructum, odorem, & umbram; inter ligna sylvarum quoque, quæ utique infructuosa sunt, incomparabilis habetur; ita dilectus meus fructu & odore sanctitatis, & justitiæ, & doctrinæ, atq; umbra protectionis suæ, quibus in se credentes reficit, docet, & defendit, inter filios, id est, Judæos extitit, qui primo quidem fi- lii fuerunt, & nunc esse volunt, sed non sunt, quia de eis Deus dixit, filios enutrivi, & exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me Joh. 8. Esa. 1. & ideo sunt ligna in- fructuosa, & inutilia, atque ob hoc succidenda & in ignem mittenda. Cæteri ergo homines sylvestres arbores sunt, ob naturalem sterilitatem Matth. 7, 17. ob opacitatem Ef. 9, 2. Luc. 1, 79. & excidii parita- tem Matth. 3, 10. Christus autem arbori pomiferæ confertur Apoc. 22, 2. 14. Conf. Ezech. 17, 22. Sirac. 24, 22. ratione fructificationis, Cant. 2, 3. Apoc. 2, 7. qui secundum Nyssenum ad hoc in mundum venit, & factus est lignum sylvæ ejusdem essentiæ cum sylva humana, fructiferum tamen, ut homines quantumli- bet pravos & sylvestres è sylvestribus redderet fru- ctiferos. Item: Christus in eo quod est lignum est ejusdem essentiæ cum sylva humana. Tentatus enim est in similitudinem absque peccato, in eo autem quod talem fert fructum, ut per eum dulces reddantur sen- sus animæ, habet majorem à sylva differentiam, quam est ea quam habet lilium à spinis. Confertur etiam ar- bori pomiferæ ratione obumbrationis, de qua post- ea, nec non ratione insitionis, qua opus habemus, si fructus etiam nos ferre debeamus Joh. 15, 4. Rom. 11, 23. Vid. si placet B. Gerhard. Dom. 16. post Tri- nit. Fructum ergo conceptionis & humiliationis suæ Sponsus insinuat, quod nempe Sponsa virtute incarnationis & passionis suæ etiam pulcre pro- germinatura sit instar lilii candidi, & aurei, ob au- rum fidei & candorem amoris, & odorem cognitionis & virtutum fragrantissimum de se sparsura Pf. 92, 1. Ef. 35, 1. Sirac. 39, 17. 18. tametsi inter spinas multa- rum calamitatum, tentationum & persecutionum ipsi perseverandum sit Ezech. 2, 6. c. 29, 21. Joh. 16, 33. Actor. 14, 22.

Vers. eod. SUB UMBRA ILLIUS QUEM DESIDE- RAVERAM SEDI, ET FRUCTUS EJUS DULCIS GUTTURI MEO.

Arbores frugiferæ, qualis est malus, uti in se tem- peratiores & suaviores sunt, quam infrugiferæ, & agrestes: ita & temperatiorem suavioremque præ illis emittunt umbram. Umbra Chrysostomo pro- videntia est, cura & protectio Ecclesiæ Esa. 51, 16. Pf. 36, 2. Pf. 91, 12. Gregorio M. umbra Christi prote- ctio est Spiritus Sancti, de quo postea. Præbet au- tem Christus nobis umbram sive remedium contra æstum conscientiæ, iræ divinæ, & damnationis æter- næ, Deut. 4, 24. c. 32, 22. Luc. 16, 24. ut & tutum re- fugium contra persequutiones hostium Pf. 17, 8. Pf. 91, 1. seqq. Ef. 4, 5. cap. 25, 4. Præbet etiam hæc arbor vitæ gutturi nostro dulcem fructum ad cibationem, spirituum refectionem & sanationem, Apoc. 22, 2. 14. modo per fidem id desideremus eodemque fruamur. Vid. B. Gerhard. Dom. 7. Trin. S. Bernhardus pro- pterea, inquit, Christi potissimum desideraverat um- bram, quod solus sit, qui non solum ab æstu refrigerat vitiorum, sed & replet delectatione virtutum. Respon- det itaque sponso sponsa κατ᾽ ἀμοιβὴν eundem de- prædicans, quod ipse non tantum instar floris, sed arboris sit suavissimæ, non odore & colore suo tantum delectet, & reficiat, sed fructu quoque pascat, & mul- tis modis prosit, umbraq; sua foveat, protegat, & in æ- stu refocillet: quodque hæc arbor vitæ in medio ho- minum, qui filii sunt ratione creationis, etsi in sylve- strem naturam degenerarint, suo tempore ita plan- tanda sit Ezech. 17, 22. 23. ut infrugiferæ illæ arbo- res, nil nisi excidium promeritæ, Jud. v. 12. Matth. 3, 10. c. 7, 18. frugiferæ evadere possint, Matth. 12, 32. utque sub umbra arboris hujus desideratissimæ, quam magno desiderio expectabat Sponsa, donec in plenitudine temporis surculus ille de radice Jes- se egrederetur Es. 11, 1. arbor viridis & frugifera evasurus, quæ exscindenda quidem pro nobis Luc. 23, 31. Es. 53, 2. 8. at vera arbor vitæ tum erit, Apoc. 22, 2. sub cujus umbra unice in æstu iræ divinæ ha- beri poterit refocillatio, & adversus omnes adversi- tates protectio, cujus fructus unice dulcedinem ad- ferent, amarore omni è fructu ligni vetiti oriundo discusso; fructus nempe amoris ejus, quos in PAS- SIONE protulit hæc arbor vitæ Apoc. 2, 7. ad recrea- tionem, & sanitatem spiritualem & cœlestem c. 22, 3. 14. qui in verbo Evangelii nobis præbentur, ut- pote in quo suavitatem Domini gustamus Psal. 34, 9. quodque gutturi nostro præ melle ac favo omni dul- cius est Ps. 19, 11. Psal. 119, 103. Inde gratulatur sibi sponsa, & gaudet oppido, quod à sponso deducen- da sit in cellam vinariam, ubi fructus illius dulce- do & suavitas recondita est, quæ cor hominis læti- ficat Psalm. 104, 15. Et quamvis pugnandum sponsæ adhuc sit etiam usque ad sanguinem Ebr. 12, 1. seqq. sub amore tamen sponsi ceu vexillo, secura ea esse potest, atque vincere, & triumphare in omnibus ad- versitatibus Rom. 8, 37. Ps. 60, 6. Quamvis etiam lan- guore aliquo afficiatur, reficienda tamen ab ipso sponso est pomis cor confortantibus, & sustentanda manu ejus fulciente, & amplexante suavissime, Esa. 62, 4. 5. Ob quam sponsæ fiduciam, ecce adest spon- sus desideratissimus, & adjurat filias Jerusalem, ut ne requiem sponsæ turbent, & agnoscitur adventus, præsentia & vox sponsi à sponsa, cum summa volu- ptate, uti è v. 2. seqq. constat.

Vers. eod. GVTTVRI MEO) Vide Prov. 30, 20. Vers. 4. INTRODVXIT ME IN CELLAM VINA- RIAM) Vt biberem. Vide Prov. 5, 15. Vers. 5. ORDINAVIT IN ME CHARITATEM) In Hebræo: Vexillum ejus super me est dilectio: quasi dicat, mi- lito sub ejus vexillo, cui inscriptum est, amor.

Inebriatus videtur Grotius meris amoribus Ve- nereis, cum has notas in chartam projiceret. Nil enim nisi amores ejusmodi somniat in Cantico hoc sanctissimo: Ideo Nympham etiam apud Theocri- tum adducit ad vers. 5. QVIA AMORE LAN- GUEO. Nympha apud Theocritum Ναρκῶ νὴ τὸν Πᾶνα. Et cum vers. 11. de transitu hyemis sermo est, unica illa glossa expedit omnia: Ver tempus amorum. Cum Sponsus vers. 14. OSTENDE MIHI FACI- EM TUAM, nihil aliud Grotius nisi corporalem venustatem sapit & συμμετρίαν corporis. Sed quid analogiæ aut commercii loco Proverb. 30, 20. Talis est & via adulteræ mulieris, quæ comedit, & os suum tergens dicit, non sum operata malum, cum hoc no- stro, c. 2. 3. FRUCTUS EJUS DULCIS GUTTU- RI MEO, aut Prov. 5, 15. Bibe aquam de cisterna tua & fluenta putei tui cum hisce Sponsæ, INTRO- DUXIT ME IN CELLAM VINARIAM, ut hæc inter se conferre jusserit Annotator? Quid manifestius, quam quod sermo sit de fructu arboris vitæ Christi, qui gutturi fidelium longe dulcissimus est. Nam de illo Sponsa vers. 2. sicut malus inter ligna sylvæ, sic dilectus meus inter filios. A malo er- go, quia meliorem dat umbram quam platanus, etsi umbra hujus jucundissima sit, umbram protectionis & refocillationis, à fructibus ejus suavitatem & refe- ctionem habet Sponsa mystica, de quo Gregor. M. pulchre ad hunc locum: Merito per malum Christus, per Sylvestria vero ligna cæteri homines figurantur, quia in solo Christo cibum salutis, quoties quærimus, invenimus; in ejus verbis & exemplis animas nostras fructu suavi & salubri reficimus. Ipse est quippe li- gnum vitæ, quam nobis tribuit. Ipse est, qui dum nobis semet ipsum inspirat, animam pascit. In cæteris vero si quid refocillationis invenimus, non quod illorum, sed quod Christi est, ab illis sumimus: quia quicquid in eis præter Deum est, mortificum nobis procul dubio invenimus. Et de umbra hujus mali: Umbra Chri- sti protectio est Spiritus Sancti. Spiritus quippe San- ctus mentem, quam replet, obumbrat; quia omnium tentationum fervorem temperat, & dum aura sua inspirationis suaviter mentem tangit, quicquid no- xii caloris sustinebat, expellit, & quam jam forsitan nimius vitiorum æstus marcidam fecerat, umbra san- „cti Spiritus protegens recreat. De suavitate vero „fructuum suaviter itidem Gregorius M. Arbor „fructifera ipse Christus in corde nostro plantatus „per fidem existit, quam si mens nostra digne di- „ligit, & instanter excolit, fructus nimirum in- „terius pulcros & utiles gignit. Quas dum mens „capiens avide comedit, omnes mundi volupta- „tes præ ejus dulcedine postponit. Dulce enim „est valde sibi cœlestia cogitare, in æternitate ocu- „lum intimum figere, ut aliquando in fletibus eti- „am mens accensa compungatur, & inter lacry- „mas sublevata Angelorum cibo, ipsa vid. sapi- „entia quanto dulcius, tanto avidius pascatur. „Inde est quod subditur: Introduxit me in cellam „vinariam. Et S. Bernhardus Serm. 48. Merito „ejus desideraverat umbram, de qua & refrigeri- „um esset, & refectionem pariter acceptura. Nam „cætera quidem Sylvarum ligna etsi umbram sola- „tii habeant, sed non vitæ refectionem, non fru- „ctus perpetuos salutis. Per cellam vinariam alii intelligunt Scripturam Sacram cum Gregorio Nysse- no & Aponio, quia hæc propinat nobis vinum sapi- entiæ: alii cum Theodoreto, Cassiodoro, Beda, & Anshelmo Ecclesiam, in qua vinum illud sapientiæ & amoris divini haurimus è Verbo Dei: alii cum Gregorio M. Bernhardo, & Haymone domum ora- tionis & contemplationis. Quid, inquit Grego- rius, per cellam vinariam congruentius, quam ipsam arcanam æternitatis contemplationem accipimus, in hac æternitate S. Angeli vino sapientiæ inebriantur, dum ipsum Deum facie ad faciem videntes omni Spiri- tuali voluptate satiantur; Hanc sancta mens, si à Spon- so introducatur, postpositis omnibus temporalibus in- trat, in qua ex illis Angelicis deliciis, quantum sibi conceditur, gustat. Conjungi possunt certa ratio- ne illæ interpretationes: Ita ut Ecclesia quidem sit cella vinaria, sed ob Scripturam S. utpote quæ sola propinat vinum sapientiæ cælestis, quemadmodum verbum Dei & Evangelium vino comparatur Esa. 55, 1. Prov. 8, 5. Matth. 9, 17. quo non fruimur sua- vius, quam si arcanam æternitatis contemplationem ingrediamur in verbo, & in Ecclesia, vid. Psalm. 34, 9. 1. Petr. 2, 2. Psalm. 36, 9. Alcuinus in hunc locum: Cella vinaria Ecclesia debet intelligi, in cujus unitate solummodo S. S. dari solet & accipi; cujus gratia h.l. vini nomine designatur. Fructus ejus dulces gutturi meo, qui gratiæ suæ cælesti dulcedine me reficit. Fol- joth, introduxit me Rex in cellam vinariam, id est, A- pothecam quandam Scripturarum divinarum, qua me à mundo abstrahit, qua me ad ea quæ sursum sunt habitaculum habere nunc permittit. Mercerus in- troduxit me in domum vini q. d. in domum convivii & lætitiæ, in mysterium scil. Sacrum, quibus velut vino exhilararer, & inebriarer.

Quæ adduntur, ex Ebræo ita recte exponun- tur: & vexillum ejus super me amor. Ea vero non est, quod cum Grotio interpretemur, milito sub ejus vexillo: Non enim actum Sponsæ, sed affectum potius Sponsi exprimunt, quem hic celebrat in eo Sponsa: q. d. præfert mihi tanquam vexilli loco amo- rem, quo me ad se attrahit, ut vexillo congregantur & attrahuntur milites, ut eo semper oculos conjiciant. Amor enim, quo nos amat Christus, vexillum nobis ef- se debet, quo admoneamur, ne ab eo unquam oculos avertamus: imo quum me in epularum & omnis gene- ris delitiarum & gaudii domum adduxit, oftentavit mihi amorem pro vexillo. Charitas enim Domini est, quæ nos in mysteria tanta penetrare facit, ut habet hoc in loco Doctissimus Mercerus. Similiter Osiander: Christus Spirituali lætitia exhilarat cor Ecclesiæ; & de- clarat manifestissime, se ardenti amore nos diligere. Ejus dilectio erigit consternatas mentes nostras, sicut vexillum erectum milites ad alacritatem excitat. Erigi enim amore Christi nos etiam ad pugnandum sub ve- xillo ejus non diffitemur: Quod hic respiciunt etiam Paraphrastæ Vinarienses.

## 2:5
Verse 5. SUPPORT ME WITH FLOWERS) With flagons of the best wine, as is accustomed to be done for those who are fainting.

STRENGTHEN ME WITH APPLES) Strengthen me with apples, namely Punic ones, or similar.

Verse same. FOR I AM SICK WITH LOVE) A nymph in Theocritus: Ναρκῶ μὴ τὸν Πᾶνα.

What has this Venus-like [expression] to do with the most chaste love of the mystical Bride? Alcuin in his Compendium explains it as a languor arising from the weariness of this pilgrimage and the love of the heavenly vision. Bernard understands it as a deficiency of love, which could easily grow tepid. But without doubt, the discourse is about a languor arising from the vehemence of love and desire: which is a holy desire for perennial communion with Christ, and therefore primarily also for the blessed Conjunction in heaven. The LXX translate: I am wounded by charity, because the pious are as if pierced by the dart of the love of Christ, and almost faint from desire for Christ the Bridegroom. Augustine in Psalm 37: She says she is wounded by charity. For she loved indeed and did not possess; she grieved because she did not yet have [Him]. Therefore, because she grieved, she was wounded, but she was receiving this wound for true salvation. He who has not been wounded by this wound cannot arrive at true health. So great is the affection of my love toward the Bridegroom that I almost languish in spirit from desire for Him: therefore I have need of refreshment, food, and drink, that I may be recreated with grapes and apples. This verse shows how great the ardor of charity toward the Son of God ought to be in all Christians, as Osiander warns on this passage. For a more prolix explanation of it, see Gerhard, [Sermon for] Laetare Sunday.

Latin:

Vers. 5. FULCITE ME FLORIBUS) Lagenis vini opti- mi, ut fieri solet τοῖς λιποθυμοῦσι.

STIPATE ME MALIS) Roborate me malis, nempe Punicis, aut similibus.

Vers. eod. QUIA AMORE LANGVEO) Nympha apud Theocritum: Ναρκῶ μὴ τὸν Πᾶνα.

Quid hæc Venerea ad castissimum amorem Spon- sæ mysticæ? Alcuinus in Compend. de languore ex hujus peregrinationis tædio & supernæ visionis amore explicat. Bernhardus defectum amoris, qui tepe- scere facile possit, intelligit. Sed de languore ex vehementia amoris & desiderii sine dubio sermo est: quod est sanctum desiderium perennis communio- nis cum Christo, adeoque imprimis etiam beatæ Conjunctionis in cælo. LXX. vertunt: Vulnerata sum charitate, quia amore Christi quasi telo transfixi languent pii, ac pene deficiunt præ desiderio Chri- sti Sponsi. Augustinus in Psalm. 37. Vulneratam se dicit charitate. Amabat enim quidem & non tenebat; dolebat, quia nondum habebat. Ergo quia dolebat, vulnerata erat, sed hoc vulnus ad veram salutem capie- bat. Qui hoc vulnere non fuerit vulneratus, ad ve- ram sanitatem non potest pervenire. Tantus est affe- ctus amoris mei erga Sponsum, ut ejus desiderio fe- re animo langueam: itaque refectione, cibo & po- tu opus habeo, ut uvis ac pomis recreer. Osten- dit hic versus, quantus ardor charitatis erga Fili- um Dei in omnibus Christianis esse debeat, ut mo- net Osiander in hunc locum. Prolixiorem ejus ex- plicationem vid. apud. Gerh. Dom. Lætare.

## 2:7
I ADJURE YOU, O DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, BY THE ROES AND THE HINDS OF THE FIELDS, THAT YOU DO NOT STIR UP, NOR MAKE THE BELOVED AWAKE, UNTIL SHE HERSELF WISHES) ἔγειρετε δὲ πρὸς ὧν, Theocritus, See also 3, 5.

The Bride, languishing with love, fell into a sleep and a swoon of the spirit, entirely carried away into the desire of the Bridegroom, wherefore, having been carried into the little bed by the young maidens, she fell asleep in it. The Bridegroom, therefore, adjures her companions not to stir her from this holy and sweet sleep, but to let her rest in it until she herself wakes of her own accord. By which adjuration he shows how much this sleep of love pleases him. Thus Cornelius à Lapide with Origen, Aponius, and others. It is a hunting oath, by which the bridegroom, like a rural shepherd, adjures the hunters by the hinds and roes, which they themselves hunt in the fields in the manner of the daughters, that is, the virgins of Tyre, to whom those of Judea are neighbors, who were given to hunting, according to that of Virg. Aen. 1: It is the custom for the virgins of Tyre to carry a quiver. For we are accustomed to swear by things most highly beloved, such as hinds are to hunters, as this same Cornelius says, i.e. If you violate this execratory adjuration of mine, O Jews, by persecuting the Church and the faithful Christians, it will come to pass that the hind will perish for you, the roes will be sterile, the fields will likewise become sterile and turn to stone, and finally your whole region will be laid waste and overturned, as was done by Titus and the Romans, as the Commentator also holds. Who, even if he understands mystically by the hinds and roes the angels with Origen, Phil. Carpath., and Nyssenus, and souls stripped of bodies with Bernard, does not, however, reject the explanation of Theodoret and Rupert, who understand the Prophets and Patriarchs, or of Aponius, who understands the Apostles and Doctors: which is altogether to be preferred. To Wolbero, the daughters of Jerusalem are souls tending toward the vision of supernal Peace, but, because the infirmity of the mind still hinders them, they are less able to arrive. The roe and the hinds. For it is said that the roe has four notable natures: that when it has been wounded, it is healed by tasting dittany; that it discerns wholesome herbs with the sharpness of its sight; that it ruminates; that it feeds in mountainous places and always seeks higher things. And this is the life and doctrine of the saints: to heal their excesses by humble confession, to discern the better meanings of the holy scriptures with the sharpness of their own sense, to take the food of divine commands by reading, and to resume it by committing it to a tenacious memory, to rise from virtues to virtues by daily progress. In the hind also, three probable things of nature are noted: that, namely, when it has swallowed a serpent, having drunk at a fountain, it casts off all poison with the hairs of its whole body; that when driven by dogs, it opens a way for itself to flee in the densest woods with its horns; that when changing pastures, having formed a line, one supports the other by placing its head on the other's back because of the weight of the horns. These things are also fitting for the faithful to do and to teach, so that whoever has been infected by some poison of sin may run back to Christ, the fountain of mercy, by whose infusion of piety and grace he may be able to be free from that sin and from other vices of the soul. If he is agitated in his soul by malignant spirits, as if by certain dogs, in the woods of secular affairs, which are full of sins and vices, let him make a way for himself to flee them by a strong repulsion of the spirit, or, having renounced all such occupations, let him study to be at leisure for God alone in the love of the contemplative life, which is also to open a way of salvation for oneself with horns. For the horn, since it is born from the flesh, exceeds the flesh, and he who adheres to the contemplative life, although he is in the flesh, is nevertheless lifted up in mind outside the flesh. Let them study to tolerate the infirmities of morals or of bodies equably with one another, and to serve one another with dutiful charity; just as the Apostle says, bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. Gal. 6. The Bridegroom is afterwards said to be like the roe and the fawn of the hinds, who was the leader of the Prophets and the prince of the Apostles. Deut. 18, 18. Heb. 3, 1.

Latin:

ADJVRO VOS FILIÆ JERVSALEM PER CAPREAS CERVOSQVE CAMPORVM, NE SVSCITETIS, NEQVE EVIGILARE FACIATIS DILECTAM, QVOADVSQVE IPSA VELIT) ἔγειρετε δὲ πρὸς ὧν, Theocritus, Vide & 3, 5.

Sponsa amore languens incidit in somnum, & animi deliquium, tota abrepta in desiderium Sponsi, quare ab adolescentulis in lectulum delata in eo obdormiit. Sponsus ergo socias ejus adjurat, ne ab hoc sancto suavique somno eam suscitent, sed in eo conquiescere sinant, donec ipsa sponte evigilet. Qua adjuratione ostendit, quam sibi hic amoris somnus placeat. Sic Cornelius à Lapide cum Origene, Aponio, & aliis. Juramentum est venatorium, quo sponsus velut pastor ruralis venatores adjurat, per cervos & capreas, quas ipsi in agris venantur more filiarum, id est, virginum Tyri, quibus Judææ vicinæ sunt, quæ venationi vacabant, juxta illud Virg. Æn. 1. Virginibus Tyriis mos est gestare pharetram. Solemus enim jurare per res summe dilectas, quales venatoribus sunt cervi, ut iterum hoc Cornelius, q. d. Si adjurationem hanc meam execratoriam violaveritis ô Judæi persequendo Ecclesiam, & fideles Christianos, fiet ut vobis cervus pereat, steriles sint capreæ, agri pariter sterilescant, & lapidescant, denique tota regio vestra vastetur & evertatur, uti per Titum & Romanos factum, ut item Commentator habet. Qui etsi mystice per cervos & capreas angelos cum Origene, Phil. Carpath. & Nysseno, animasque exutas corporibus cum Bernhardo intelligat, non tamen vel Theodoreti & Ruperti, qui Prophetas & Patriarchas, vel Aponii qui Apostolos & Doctores intelligit, explicationem respuit: quæ omnino præferenda. Wolberoni filiæ Jerusalem sunt animæ ad supernæ Pacis visionem tendentes, sed adhuc præpediente mentis infirmi- tate minus pervenire valentes. Caprea & cervi Quatuor enim, inquit, naturæ notabi- lia dicitur habere Caprea; quod cum vulnerata fuerit gustato diptamno sanatur, quod herbas salubres visus acumine discernit, quod ruminat, quod in montuo- sis pascitur & semper altiora petit. Et hæc est vita & doctrina sanctorum, excessus suos humili confessio- ne sanare, sententias meliores sanctarum scriptura- rum sensus sui acumine discernere, divinorum man- datorum cibaria legendo sumere, & tenaci memoriæ commendando resumere, de virtutibus ad virtutes profectu quotidiano assurgere. In Cervo quoque tria attenduntur naturæ probabilia, quod scilicet ser- pentem deglutiens potato fonte cum pilis totius corpo- ris omne venenum deponit; quod à canibus agitatus in densissimis sylvis viam sibi fugiendi cornibus ape- rit; quod in mutandis pascuis facto agmine alter al- terius dorso capite imposito invicem propter pondus cornuum sustentantur. Hæc quoque fidelibus con- venit agere & docere, ut qui aliquo peccati veneno in- fectus fuerit, ad fontem misericordiæ Christum re- currat, cujus pietatis & gratiæ infusione, possit & illo peccato, & cæteris animi vitiis carere. Si à mali- gnis spiritibus veluti quibusdam canibus in sylvis sæ- cularium negotiorum, quæ plena sunt peccatis & vi- tiis, animo agitatur, viam sibi aufugendi ea faciat forti repulsione spiritus, sive abrenuntiatis omnibus hujusmodi occupationibus soli Deo vacare studeat in contemplativæ vitæ amore, quod est etiam cornibus viam sibi salutis aperire. Cornu quippe cum de car- ne nascatur, carnem excedit, & ille qui contemplati- væ vitæ inhæret, quamvis in carne sit, extra carnem tamen mente sublevatur. Infirmitates morum sive corporum studeant invicem æquanimiter tolerare, & officiofa sibi obsequi charitate; sicut dicit Apostolus, alter alterius onera portate, & sic adimplebitis le- gem Christi. Gal. 6. Sponsus postea similis Capreæ hinnuloque cervorum dicitur, qui Prophetarum coryphæus, & Apostolorum princeps fuit. Deut. 18, 18. Ebr. 3, 1.

## 2:8
Verse 8.

THE VOICE OF MY BELOVED, BEHOLD HE COMETH LEAPING UPON THE MOUNTAINS, SKIPPING OVER THE HILLS.

As the Bridegroom with the greatest eagerness: Behold I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me, testified Psalm 40:8. Thus the bride, perceiving that coming from the voice of her beloved, exclaims for joy: Behold he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills. Which was done in his coming into the flesh. The bride heard confusedly and faintly the voice of the Bridegroom coming and skipping over the mountains, so that he might hasten to the bride languishing with love, whence this voice was sent from afar, as Ambrose teaches in Psalm 118, when silence was proclaimed at his coming in Zechariah 2:13, or when his voice was heard, St. John the Baptist, who calls himself so in John 1:23. The bridegroom then came leaping upon the mountains, when he was carried in the womb of his mother treading through the mountains, or as St. Ambrose more fully [explains] in the place cited. Let us see him leaping; he leaps from heaven into the virgin, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the Jordan, from the Jordan into the cross, from the cross into the tomb, from the tomb into heaven; and in his hymn: His departure from the Father, his return to the Father, his excursion even to the lower regions, his recurrence to the seat of God: and also Bernard, Sermon IV on the Ascension, recounting the mountains upon which he leaped, namely that one on which he taught, Matthew 5, that one on which he prayed, John 6, that one on which he was glorified, Matthew 17, that one on which he was crucified, Matthew 27, that one from which he ascended into heaven, Luke 24.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

VOX DILECTI MEI, ECCE ISTE VE- NIET SALIENS IN MONTIBUS, TRANSI- LIENS COLLES.

Ut Sponsus cum προθυμίᾳ summa: Ecce ego ve- nio, in volumine libri scriptum est de me, testabatur Psalm. 40, 8. Ita sponsa adventum illum è voce di- lecti sui percipiens, præ gaudio exclamat: Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles. Quod in adventu in carnem factum est. Sponsa audiit confuse & tenuiter vocem Sponsi advenientis & transilientis montes, ut ad sponsam amore languen- tem festinanter accurreret, unde vox hæc fuit emi- nus missa, docente Ambros. in Psalm. 118. cum indi- ceretur silentium sub adventum ejus Zachar. 2, 13. aut cum audiretur vox ejus S. Johannes Baptista, qui se ita vocat Joh. 1, 23. Venit tum sponsus saliens in montibus, cum in utero matris per montana cal- cantis portabatur, vel ut plenius S. Ambrosius l. c. Videamus salientem, salit de cælo in virginem, de ute- ro in præsepe, de præsepi in Jordanem, de Jordane in crucem, de cruce in tumulum, de tumulo in cælum; & in hymno suo: Egressus ejus à Patre, regressus ejus ad Patrem, excursus ejus usq; ad inferos, recursus ad sedem Dei: nec non Bernhard. Serm. IV. Ascens. recensens montes, in quos saliit, illum nempe in quo docuit Matth. 5. illum in quo oravit Joh. 6. il- lum in quo glorificatus fuit Matth. 17. illum in quo crucifixus fuit, Matth. 27. illum ex quo in cælum ascendit Luc. 24.

## 2:9
Verse 9. MY BELOVED IS LIKE A ROE, OR A YOUNG HART.

He is like a roe and a young hart because of their speed, 2 Sam. 2:18, in the work of redemption, the course of the ministry, the propagation of the Gospel, and the swiftness of his aid, Ps. 19:6, Matt. 18:20, ch. 28:20; to which he is also similar because of the sharpness of his sight; whence the roe (caprea) is called by the Greeks δόρκαδες from δέρκειν (to see), and because of the virtue of extracting serpents, which, once drawn from their caverns, the harts devour, whence they are called ἔλαφοι from ἐλᾶν ὄφιν (to extract the serpent): because Christ extracted the infernal serpent from the human race, and devoured and destroyed him in victory, Isa. 25:8. This was done when he came into the flesh as the seed of the woman who would crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15, and when the infernal hunter pursued and hunted him like a morning hind with his hunting dogs, Ps. 22:1.

Verse same. BEHOLD HE STANDETH BEHIND OUR WALL, LOOKING FORTH AT THE WINDOWS, SHEWING HIMSELF THROUGH THE LATTICE.

Thus he stood behind the wall at the time of his advent in the flesh, when he did not manifest the rays of his majesty, but emptied himself and appeared in a humble and servile form: concerning which Gregory the Great says: Christ incarnate stood as if behind our wall, because the divinity lay hidden in the assumed humility: and because human infirmity could not bear his immensity if he were to show it, he placed the obstacle of the flesh, and whatever great things he did among men, he did as if lurking behind a wall. But he who looks through the windows and lattice is partly seen and partly hides himself: thus also the Lord Jesus Christ, while he both performed miracles through the power of his divinity and endured abject things through the weakness of the flesh, looked forth as if through a window and lattice: because in one thing he was hidden, in another he appeared as to who he was. Which sentiment, however, can also be applied not inappropriately to other actions of Christ, because he also observes the same manner at other times, when he hides himself from his own, to whom, however, he is present and assists: as Aponius says, he stands as if hidden and watches the struggle of the faithful soul: and he does not show himself only so that, with the enemies completely put to flight and the battle ceasing, the soul might not perish through the torpor of idleness, but he looks on as if through windows, delaying the aid of his vision so that the soul may receive strength to resist, and the enemy's assault, diminished by his terror, may rest a little. This is what Anthony experienced in his struggle, according to Athanasius in his life. How the affection of love, the affection of the associate, the affection of the contemplator, and the affection of the liberator are thus expressed, the blessed Gerhard sets forth on Monday of Easter.

Latin:

Verf. 9. SIMILIS EST DILECTUS MEUS CAPREÆ, HINNULOQUE CERVORUM.

Similis capreæ & hinnulo cervorum ob velocita- tem 2. Sam. 2, 18. in opere redemptionis, cursu mi- nisterii, propagatione Evangelii, & celeritate au- xilii Pfal. 19, 6. Matth. 18, 20. c. 28, 20. quibus etiam similis, ob visus perspicacitatem; unde Caprea Græ- cis δόρκαδες ὰ δέρκειν vivendo, & ob extrahendi ser- pentes virtutem, quos è cavernis extractos cervi vo- rant, unde dicti ἔλαφοι ἀπὸ τῦ ἐλᾶν ὄφιν extrahere serpentem: quia Christus serpentem infernalem è genere humano extraxit, eumque in victoriam de- voravit, & peremit, Efa. 25, 8. Quod factum est, cum in carnem veniret ceu semen mulieris caput serpentis contriturum Genes. 3, 15. & cum ipsum in- star cervæ matutinæ venator infernalis per canes suos venaticos insectaretur, & venaretur Pf. 22, 1.

Verf. eod. EN IPSE STAT POST PARIETEM) Crura. RESPICIENS PER FENESTRAS, PROSPI- CIENS PER CANCELLOS.

Sic post parietem stetit sub adventum in car- nem, cum non manifestavit radios majestatis, sed exinanivit se, & in forma humili ac servili apparuit: de quo Gregor. M. Quasi post parietem nostrum Christus incarnatus stetit, quia in humilitate assum- ta divinitas latuit: & quia ejus immensitatem, si ostenderet, infirmitas humana ferre non posset, carnis obstaculum objecit, & quicquid magni inter homines operatus est, quasi post parietem latitans fecit. Per fenestras autem & cancellos qui aspicit, partim vide- tur, partim vero se abscondit: Sic & Dominus Jesus Christus dum & miracula per divinitatis potentiam fe- cit, & abjecta per carnis infirmitatem pertulit, qua- si per fenestram & cancellos prospexit: quia in alio latens, in alio quis esset apparuit. Quæ tamen sen- tentia applicari etiam ad alias Christi actiones nonTx incommode potest, quia eundem morem etiam alias non raro observat, cum se suis abscondit, qui- bus tamen præsto est, & assistit: cum Aponio dicen- te quasi occultus stat, & spectat luctamen animæ fide- lis: & tantum se non ostendit, ne omnino fugatis hosti- bus cessante pugna, otii torpore illa depereat, sed vel- ut per fenestras aspicit, suæ visionis adjutorium com- morando, ut anima vires recipiat resistendi, & hostis impugnatio diminuta ejus terrore aliquantulum con- quiescat. Quod Antonius in lucta sua expertus est apud Athanas. in vita ejus. Quomodo ita expri- matur affectus amoris, affectus associantis, affectus contemplantis, affectus liberantis, exequitur B. Ger- hard. in Fer. 2. Pasch.

## 2:11
Vers. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

## 2:11
Verse 11. FOR LO, THE WINTER IS PAST) The snows flee away, the grasses now return to the fields. THE FLOWERS APPEAR) Virgil: And now every field, now every tree is budding, now the woods are leafing, now the year is most beautiful. Spring is the time of loves.

Grotius Judaizes in this, that he takes the words here according to the letter: and he savors of nothing but carnal loves. But why would the Holy Spirit describe the time of Spring so prolixly for the sole purpose of teaching that it was convenient for the earthly and bodily loves of Solomon? The Doctors of the Church refer this to the time of the advent of Christ: some indeed to the first advent; others, however, to the second: because both are a time of joy and salvation, which, begun here, is to be consummated in the other advent. Ambrose, book 4, On Isaac and the Soul, chapter 4: Before the advent of Christ is winter, after his advent are flowers. Where there were thorns before, there are now flowers. Bede on this passage: Where the Sun of righteousness shone upon the world, and with the perfidy of winter-like infidelity soon receding and driven away, the flowers appeared on the earth, because the beginnings of the now-nascent Church shone in the faithful and pious devotion of the Saints. Alcuin in the Compendium: Arise, make haste my love, my beautiful one, and come. Arise from the bed of rest, in which you seek to take care of yourself alone. Make haste and come to fulfill the care of salvation also for your neighbors through the zeal of diligent preaching. For lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Now the cold of infidelity and the rain of iniquity have receded, which covered the whole world until the time of the Lord's incarnation. The flowers appeared on the earth, i.e., the beginnings of faith and justice flourished in the world, as the Church grew. The time of pruning has arrived: i.e., with the useless branches of vain religion pruned away, the hearts of men are prepared for the future fruit of faith. The voice of the turtle dove has been heard in our land. That is, of Christ our Savior saying, repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. The fig tree has brought forth her green figs: The precepts of the old law have fallen. The vines in blossom have given their scent: i.e., the Evangelical people, like flowering vines, have given the scent of holy conversation far and wide. And thus do most of the Fathers, as well as more recent interpreters. Which sense the Vinariean Paraphrasts explain, as does the blessed Gerhard in his Postils on Solomon, Sunday 4 of Advent, as well as the Sunday after the Nativity of Christ. That these things can likewise be explained of the second advent of Christ, the blessed Gerhard taught on the 26th Sunday after Trinity, along with Origen, Homily 4 of the four on the Canticles, Ambrose, Sermon on Psalm 68, and Gregory and others. The former interpretation, however, seems more convenient for this place: because there is no place for the warning about catching the little foxes and the danger of the vines being laid waste in the second advent of Christ; which things, however, look to the same time, as appears from a comparison of verses 13 and 15. At the time of the advent of Christ, the voice of the turtle dove of John the Baptist was heard and the flowers appeared: concerning which Ambrose, loc. cit. The good flowers are the Apostles; who poured forth the scent of their various writings and works. Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 5 on the Canticles. The turtledove here, he says, is John, the forerunner of this broad Spring; he himself shows these lovely flowers of virtue to men, and offers them to those wishing to gather flowers by pointing out that flower from the root of Jesse. Thus also three Fathers in Theodoret, bringing forward testimony of His coming into the flesh, say, the voice of the Turtledove has been heard in our land. He names the Turtledove the Prophet and forerunner of His Advent, inasmuch as he is solitary and modest, whose voice is the preaching of repentance. Osiander in his Paraphrase hands down another meaning, concerning a time of peace and quiet after any persecution whatsoever. For he explains it generally, even if he declares it with special examples, h. m. that is, the time of persecutions has now ceased and peace and happiness have returned, a pleasant and welcome time. Such a Spring (after the most savage winter of persecutions) God granted to His Church under the pious Emperor Constantine the Great. Ecclesiastical History testifies at length how many benefits that pious Emperor conferred upon the Church of God. Our own age has also seen such a change from sad times into much happier ones, which benefits I wish we may not lose through ingratitude. Mercerus also explains it generally concerning a time of salvation and happiness. However, no one will easily be found who wishes the time of love to be indicated in the Grotius sense. And if it pleases to press the letter, the Bridegroom seems rather to be calling the Bride back from her little bed into the fields and vineyards for their cultivation, as Cornelius à Lapide has noted.

Latin:

Verf. 11. JAM ENIM HIEMS TRANSIT) Diffugere nives, redeunt jam gramina campis. FLORES APPARVERVNT) Virgilius: Et nunc omnis ager, nunc omnis parturit arbor, Nunc frondent silvæ, nunc formosissimus annus. Ver tempus amorum.

Grotius in eo Judaizat, quod verba secundum literam hîc accipit: Nec nisi Venereos amores sa- pit. Cur autem Spiritus S. tam prolixe Veris tem- pus describeret eâ solum fini, ut amoribus Salomo- nis terrenis & corporalibus commodum id esse do- ceret? Dd. Ecclesiæ referunt hoc ad tempus adven- tus Christi: alii quidem ad adventum primum; alii vero ad secundum: quia uterque tempus lætitiæ ac salutis est, quæ hic inchoata, in altero adventu con- fummanda est. Ambrosius lib. 4. de Isaac & anim. cap. 4. Ante adventum Christi hyems est, post adven- tum ejus flores sunt. Ubi ante spinæ, ibi nunc flores. Beda in h. l. Ubi Sol justitiæ mundo illuxit, ac sece- dente ac depulsa mox brumalis infidelitatis perfidia, flores apparuerunt in terra, quia initia jam nascentis Ecclesiæ in Sanctorum fideli ac pia devotione claruerunt. Alcuinus in Compendio: Surge, propera amica mea, formosa mea, & veni. Surge de strato quietis, in quo tuimet solius curam agere quæris. Propera & veni ad implendam etiam proximis curam salutis per studium sedulæ prædicationis. Jam enim hyems transiit, imber abiit, & recessit. Jam frigus infidelitatis & imber iniquitatis recesserunt, quæ totum orbem usque ad tempus Dominicæ incarnationis tegebant. Flores apparuerunt in terra, i. e. initio fidei & justitiæ floruerunt in mundo, crescente Ecclesia. Tempus putationis advenit: i. e. Amputatis inutilibus vanæ religionis sarmentis, futuro fidei fructui præparantur corda hominum. Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra. Id est, Christi Salvatoris nostri dicentis, pœnitentiam agite: appropinquavit enim regnum cœlorum. Ficus protulit grossos suos: Veteris legis præcepta ceciderunt. Vineæ florentes odorem dederunt: i. e. Evangelicus populus ceu vites florentes sanctæ conversationis odorem longe lateque dederunt. Atque ita plerique Patres, nec non recentiores Interpp. Quem sensum explicant Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, ac B. Gerhardus in Postill. Salomon. Domin. 4. Advent. ut & Dominic. post Nativitat. Christi. De secundo vero adventu Christi cum Origene Homil. 4. ex quatuor in Cant. Ambros. Serm. in Psalm. 68. & Gregorio & aliis explicari pariter hæc posse B. Gerhardus Dominic. 26. Trinit. docuit. Videtur tamen prior interpretatio huic loco convenientior: quia monito de vulpeculis capiendis & periculo vastandarum vinearum locus non est in adventu secundo Christi; quæ tamen idem tempus respiciunt, ut è collatione vers. 13. & 15. apparet. Tempore adventus Christi vox turturis Johannis Baptistæ audita & flores apparuerunt: de quo Ambrosius l. c. Boni flores Apostoli; qui diversorum scriptorum atque operum suorum fuderunt odorem. Gregor. Nyssenus Hom. 5. in Cantic. Turtur hic, inquit, Johannes est, lati hujus Veris præcursor, ipse venustos hosce virtutis flores hominibus ostendit, ac flores legere volentibus offert commonstrando illum è Jesseæ radice florem. Sic etiam tres Patres apud Theodoret. Adventus sui in carnem testimonium afferens, vox, inquit, Turturis audita est in terra nostra. Turturem nominat Adventus sui Prophetam, & præcursorem, utpote solitarium & pudicum, cujus vox est pœnitentiæ prædicatio. Alium sensum tradit Osiander in Paraphrasi, de tempore pacis & quietis post persequutionem quamcunque. Nam generaliter explicat, etsi specialibus exemplis declaret, h. m. id est, tempus persecutionum jam cessavit & rediit pax & felicitas, tempus jucundum & gratum. Tale Ver (post sævissimam hyemem persecutionum) concessit Deus Ecclesiæ suæ pio Cæsare Constantino Magno. Ecclesiastica Historia prolixe testatur, quanta beneficia in Ecclesiam Dei pius ille Imperator contulerit. Talem tristium temporum commutationem in multo lætiora etiam nostra ætas vidit, quæ beneficia utinam non per ingratitudinem amittamus. De tempore salutis & felicitatis in genere etiam explicat Mercerus. Nemo autem facile invenietur, qui tempus amorum sensu Grotiano indicari velit. Et premere si libeat literam, revocare potius Sponsam videtur Sponsus è lectulo in agros & vineas ad earum culturam, uti Cornelius à Lapid. notavit.

## 2:14
Vers. 14.

SHOW ME THY FACE) Thy beauty, the symmetry of the body. CATCH FOR US THE LITTLE FOXES) The young ones.

The discussion here is not about external beauty, not about the symmetry of the body, but about internal beauty, about the decorum of the soul. Just as in the Sacred Davidic Epithalamium, Ps. 45: The glory of the King's daughter is internal. Thus, before v. 14, he had called her his dove, his beautiful one: concerning which Gregory the Great says, Christ calls his Spouse a friend because of faith, a dove because of simplicity, beautiful because of action: Gregory of Nyssa says she is beautiful because, approaching God like a mirror, she received into herself the image of divine beauty. She is also called a dove not only because of simplicity (Matt. 10:16), purity, fecundity, and amiability, but also because of beauty (Ps. 68:14), as the interpreters observe. Concerning this dove, the Spouse says that she is hidden in the clefts of the rock. These things do not accord with the carnal thoughts of Grotius, but refer to the spiritual rock, Christ (Isa. 28:16; Matt. 16:18). 1 Cor. 10:4, and his wounds (Zech. 3:9). Concerning which Gregory the Great says: I would willingly understand by the clefts of the rock the wounds of the hands and feet of Christ hanging on the cross, but I would call the cavern of the wall the wound of the side, which was made by the lance, in the same sense. Thus also Cassiodorus: The Spouse dwells in these clefts, because she has placed all the hope of her salvation in the passion of her Redeemer. There she hides, secure from the snares of malignant spirits, as if from the snatching of a hawk. Similarly Bede, Justus Orgelitanus, Anselm, Aponius, Bernard, and others. Cf. B. Gerhard, Dom. Quasimodogeniti. Furthermore, the face of the soul, which the Spouse desires to see and by which he is delighted, is true confidence (Jer. 5:3; Heb. 11:6). Concerning which Gregory the Great says: What do we understand by the face, if not faith, by which we are known by God? And what by the voice, if not preaching? But the Spouse commands that the Spouse show him her face; because whoever says he has faith, it is necessary that he exercise himself in good works, so that in external works the internal faith may shine forth; but it is also necessary that the voice of preaching follow the works, because whoever perfectly expands himself in holy works, it follows that he should also exhort his neighbors to do the same. Therefore it follows: Thy voice is sweet and thy face is comely: For then both the voice is pleasing and the face is adorned, when works follow preaching and, in turn, good works accompany preaching. Similarly Theodoret, Origen, Cassiodorus, Bede, Anselm, and others. This sense is approved even by the Papists themselves. Cornelius à Lapide says: The Spouse here asks the Church to exhibit to him the purity of faith and works, as a comely face, and the preaching of heavenly doctrine, as a sweet voice. Therefore it is added, take for us the little foxes that demolish the vineyards; so that the sincere heavenly doctrine may be propagated. For foxes, as Augustine has it in Psalm 40, signify insidious and most fraudulent heretics, deceitful, lurking in cavernous windings, and stinking with a foul odor. Bernard in this place: When deceit is betrayed, when fraud is uncovered, when falsehood is convicted, then the little fox that was demolishing the vineyards is most rightly said to be caught. And thus almost all interpreters understand heretics by the foxes. Ignatius, Epist. ad Philad., Origen, Theodoret, Cassiodorus, Aponius, Bede, Bernard, Anselm, Nazianzen, orat. 2 de Eccles., Chrysostom in Ps. 70, Ambrose l. 2 de S. S., Augustine in Ps. 80 and serm. 107 de tempore, and others. For the comparison deduced by reason of dwelling, by reason of deceit, by reason of damage, and by reason of companionship, see B. Gerhard, Dom. 8 Trinit. Thus Ezek. 13:4, concerning false prophets it is said: Thy prophets, O Israel, were like foxes in the deserts, etc. He calls them little foxes, however, because they are accustomed to be more troublesome to vineyards and more spirited in inflicting damage, as Gregory the Great says; or out of contempt, so that he may diminish the strength of the adversaries of the Church, and because, even if they seem most powerful to themselves, they are only small and contemptible if the Lord wishes to take up arms against them, which Mercerus notes here. Grotius here tastes nothing but the earthly: Take for us the little foxes, that is, the little fleas. What is added: For our vineyard has blossomed, sounds thus in Hebrew: And our vineyard has small grapes: for the Spouse wishes the little foxes to be warded off before the grapes ripen, lest the vineyards later feel a more serious loss when the grapes have matured, so that heretics, above all, may be warded off from those churches in which the beginnings of virtues begin to germinate after the first rudiments of faith. Heresies are of great value among those who are not of value in the faith, says Tertullian, l. de praescript. c. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

OSTENDE MIHI FACIEM TVAM) Pulchritudinem tuam, συμμετρίαν corporis. CAPITE NOBIS VULPES PARVVLAS) Pulcellos.

Non hîc de externa pulchritudine, non de Cor- poris συμμετρία, sed de interna pulchritudine, de animæ decore sermo est. Perinde, uti in Sacro Epi- thalamio Davidico Ps. 45. Gloria filiæ Regis intrinse- cus est. Sic ante v. 14. dixerat eam columbam suam, formosam suam: de quo Gregor. M. propter fidem Christus Sponsam suam amicam vocat, columbam propter simplicitatem, formosam propter operatio- nem: Gregor. Nyssenus, pulcra, inquit, quia ap- propinquans ad Deum instar speculi imaginem in se suscepit divinæ pulchritudinis. Columbam quoque vocari non solum ob simplicitatem Matth. 10, 16. puritatem, fœcunditatem, amabilitatem, sed etiam ob speciositatem Psal. 68, 14. observant Interpp. De hac columba ait Sponsus, quod in foraminibus pe- træ abscondita sit. Quæ non congruunt carnalibus Grotii cogitationibus, sed petram spiritualem Christum respiciunt Esa. 28, 16. Matth. 16, 18. 1. Cor. 10, 4. ejusdemque vulnera Zach. 3, 9. Quo de Gre- gor. M. per foramina petræ vulnera manuum & pe- dum Christi in cruce pendentis libenter intellexerim, cavernam vero maceriæ vulnus lateris, quod lancea factum est, eodem sensu dixerim. Sic & Cassiod. in his foraminibus Sponsa moratur, quia totam spem suæ sa- lutis in passione sui Redemptoris constituit. Ibi ab insi- diis malignorum spirituum, quasi à raptu accipitris se- cura delitescit. Similiter Beda, Just. Orgelit. Ans- helmus, Aponius, Bernhard. alii. Conf. B. Gerh. Do- min. Quasimodog. Porro Facies animæ, quam vi- dere cupit, & qua delectatur Sponsus, est vera fidu- cia Jerem. 5, 3. Ebr. 11, 6. Quo de Gregorius M. Quid per faciem, nisi fidem, qua à Deo cognoscimur, acci- pimus? Et quid per vocem, nisi prædicationem intel- ligamus? Sed præcipit Sponsus, ut ei Sponsa faciem suam ostendat; quia quicunque se fidem dicit habere, necesse est, ut in bonis operibus se exerceat, ut in ope- ribus exterioribus fides interior illucescat, sed & ope- ra necesse est, ut Vox prædicationis sequatur, quia qui- cunque in Sanctis operibus perfecte se dilatat, conse- quens est, ut ad eadem facienda proximos quoque ex- hortetur. Ideo sequitur: Vox tua dulcis & facies tua decora: Tunc enim & vox placet & facies decoratur, quando & opera prædicatio sequitur & rursum prædi- cationem bona opera comitantur. Similiter Theodore- tus, Origenes, Cassiodorus, Beda, Anshelmus, aliique. Quem sensum ipsi etiam Pontificii probant. Spon- sus, inquit Cornelius à Lapide, ab Ecclesia hîc po- scit sibi exhiberi puritatem fidei & operum, quasi fa- ciem decoram, & prædicationem cœlestis doctrinæ, quasi vocem dulcem. Ideo additur, capite nobis vul- peculas, quæ demoliuntur vineas; quo doctrina cœ- lestis sincera propagetur. Vulpes enim, ut habet Au- gustinus in Psalm. 40. insidiosos maximeq; Hæreticos fraudulentos significant, dolosos, cavernosis anfracti- bus latentes & decipientes, & odore tetro putentes. Bernhardus in h. l. Cum proditur dolus, cum fraus aperitur, cum convincitur falsitas, rectissime tunc dicitur capta vulpes pusilla, quæ demoliebatur vi- neas. Atque ita Hæreticos per Vulpes intelligunt ple- rique omnes interpp. Ignat. Epist. ad Philad. Ori- genes, Theodoret. Cassiodorus, Aponius, Beda, Bern- hard. Anshelmus, Nazianz. orat. 2. de Eccles. Chry- sost. in Ps. 70. Ambrof. l. 2. de S. S. August. in Ps. 80. & serm. 107. de tempore, alii. Comparationem ratione domicilii, ratione doli, ratione damni, ra- tione consortii deductam, vid. apud B. Gerh. Dom. 8. Trinit. Sic Ezech. 13, 4. de falsis Prophetis dicitur, quasi vulpes in deserto Prophetæ tui Israel erant &c. Parvas autem vulpes appellat, quia illæ infestiores esse vineis solent, & animosiores in damno infe- rendo, ut Gregor. M. vel per contemtum, ut adver- sariorum Ecclesiæ robur extenuet, & quod, etsi sibi potentissimi videantur, pusilli tantum sint, & con- temti, si in illos arma sumere velit Dominus, quod hic Mercerus notat. Grotius hic nil nisi terrenum sapit: Capite nobis vulpes parvulas, id est, pulicellos. Quod additur: Nam vinea nostra floruit, in Ebræo ita sonat: Et vinea nostræ uvæ minutæ: vult enim Sponsus, ut vulpeculæ arceantur, priusquam matu- rescant uvæ, ne postmodum gravius damnum senti- ant vineæ, cum uvæ maturuerint, ut hæretici præ- primis arceantur ab illis Ecclesiis, in quibus post prima fidei rudimenta progerminare incipiunt vir- tutum initia. Hæreses apud illos multum valent, qui in fide non valent, ait Tertull. l. de præscript. c. 2.

## 2:16
Verse 16. HIS LEFT HAND UNDER MY HEAD, AND HIS RIGHT HAND SHALL EMBRACE ME) Let the arms grow black with the binding: Claudian.

If you listen to Junius, you will believe that it refers not to the embrace of the Bridegroom, but to the manner of reclining, which he explains thus: The Bridegroom himself moves both hands to support me in this my infirmity, and in the expectation of that future most blessed meeting, He sustains me with His power. Moreover, this form of supporting is taken from the ancient manner of reclining at banquets: just as the Ancients used to dine reclining, not sitting (as today). But that is Junius's singular interpretation. Interpreters commonly refer it to an embrace: which, however, is to be learned not from Claudian or another profane writer, but from the Holy Scriptures. Furthermore, some establish distinct benefits here in the left and right hand; whether because the left provides the grace of this life, and the right the glory of the future life, as Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, and Bede wish; as well as Bernard, who [writes] in Sermon 4 on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. The left hand indeed lifts, the right hand receives: The left hand heals and justifies, the right hand embraces and beatifies. Or, because the left hand provides temporal goods, the right hand spiritual ones, as seemed to Ambrose in Psalm 118, Sermon 14, on verse 5, and to Alcuin, who says: In the left hand of Christ, His temporal gifts are signified; in the right, the beatitude of perpetual life. Or because it designates the left hand in mourning; but the right hand in consolation and refreshment, to which the Osiandrian Paraphrase of these words seems to incline. Even if He seems to have deserted me, yet afterwards he embraces me most lovingly, consoles me with his word, protects me, and demonstrates to me the most certain signs of his love. Cornel. à Lapide says: The left hand indicates adverse things; the right, however, prosperous ones. But the things he adds about prelates, whom he makes the Head of the Church, just as he constitutes the rest of the faithful as the body, that the former should be exercised by adverse things, the latter soothed by prosperous ones, are very inept. The adversities of the prelates of the Roman Church are known to the world, but they are such as Monastic Poverty is among most of them. However, Mercerus's opinion is pleasing: That this is placed simply to express the gesture of those embracing, so that we may understand the extraordinary love of Christ for the Church, which is described in the manner of the love of a Bridegroom for a Bride. But nothing earthly, nothing carnal is to be thought of here, but all things spiritual and sublime. Although the explanation of Ambrose and Alcuin does not displease, according to which such a connection of the following is presented by Wolbero: Therefore, the beloved, delighted by the sleep of the beloved, under whose head, that is, mind, he had placed his left hand, that is, temporal utility, but had embraced her with his right hand, that is, the love of eternal life, thus addresses the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, faithful souls, saying: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the fields, that you do not stir up, nor make the beloved awake, until she herself wishes. What is this sleep so sweet and so wholesome, that because of it such an adjuration of the beloved is made? Is it not that in which the beloved, resting in sweet and desirable quiet, had said above, his left hand under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me. For she had put all temporal things behind her, but was intent upon eternal and indefectible goods with that contemplative eye of the desirable soul, and in this desirable vision of the mind she was sleeping, as it were, delightfully.

Latin:

Vers. 16. LÆVA EJUS SUB CAPITE MEO, ET DEXTRA ILLIUS AMPLEXABITUR ME) Livescant brachia nexu: Claudianus.

Si Junium audias non amplexum Sponsi, sed accubitus modum respici credes, qui sic explicat: Sponsus ipse manum utramque admovet ad sustentan- dum me in hac infirmitate mea, & in expectatione fu- turi illius beatissimi congressus sua virtute sustinet. Est autem hæc sustentandi forma sumta ab antiqua ratione accumbendi in Conviviis: prout Veteres ac- cumbentes, non sedentes (ut hodie) epulabantur. Sed ea singularis Junii est interpretatio. Com- muniter ad amplexum referunt interpretes: qui ve- ro non è Claudiano, aut alio prophano Scriptore, sed è Sacris Scripturis discendus est. Cæterum in læva & dextra hic distincta beneficia statuunt non- nulli; Sive quod leva gratiam hujus vitæ, dextra gloriam futuræ vitæ præstet, uti vult Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, Beda; nec non Bernhardus, qui Serm. 4. de Vigil. Nativit. Domin. Læva quidem le- vat, dextra suscipit: Læva medetur & justificat, dex- tra amplexatur, & beatificat. Sive, quod læva bona temporalia, dextra spiritualia præstet, ut Ambrosio vi- sum in Psalm. 118. Serm. 14. ad v. 5. & Alcuino, qui, in læva, inquit, Christo temporalia ejus dona, in dex- tra perpetuæ vitæ beatitudo signatur. Sive quod læ- vam designet in luctu; dextram vero in consolatione & refectione, quo abire videtur Osiandrina horum verborum Paraphrasis. Etsi me interdum deseruisse videatur, tamen postea me amantissime complectitur, consolatur verbo suo, meque tuetur & amoris sui signa certissima mihi demonstrat. Cornel. à Lapid. Læva, inquit, indicat adversa; dextra vero prospera. Quæ vero subjungit de prælatis, quos Ecclesiæ Caput efficit, uti fideles cæteros corpus constituit, quod illi exerceantur adversis, hi demulceantur prosperis, perquam inepta sunt. Adversa Prælatorum Romanæ Ecclesiæ orbi nota sunt, sed talia, qualis est apud plerosque Paupertas Monastica. Placet autem Merceri sententia: Simpliciter ad exprimendum amplectentium gestum hoc esse positum, ut eximium intelligamus Christi in Ecclesiam amorem, qui, more amoris Sponsi in Sponsam describitur. Sed nihil hic terrenum, nihil carnale cogitandum, sed omnia spiritualia, & sublimia. Quamvis nec displiceat Ambrosii & Alcuini explicatio, juxta quam à Wolberone talis sequentium nexus exhibetur: Igitur dilectus dilectæ delectatus dormitione, cujus capiti, id est, menti sinistram suam, hoc est temporalem utilitatem supposuerat, dextra vero sua hoc est æternæ vitæ dilectione amplexatus fuerat, taliter filias Jerusalem, hoc est animas fideles alloquitur dicens: Adjuro vos filiæ Jerusalem per capreas aervosque camporum ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, quoad usque ipsa velit. Quæ est ista tam suavis tamque salubris dormitio, ut propter eam talis fiat dilecti adjuratio? Nonne illa est in qua dulci & optabili quiete dilecta requiescens supra dixerat, læva ejus sub capite meo, & dextera illius amplexabitur me. Omnia enim temporalia postposuerat, æternalia vero & indeficientia bona illo contemplatorio concupiscibilis animæ oculo intendebat, & in hac desiderabili mentis visione delectabiliter quasi dormiebat.

## 2:16
Verse 16. MY BELOVED IS MINE, AND I AM HIS, WHO FEEDS AMONG THE LILIES.

A mutual attestation here of the Spouse and the Spouse because of mutual betrothal (Hos. 2:19), mutual union (John 6:56; 1 Cor. 6:17; Eph. 5:32), mutual love (Eph. 5:1; John 15:14; Cant. 1:13, 15; and c. 3:4), mutual placement (Ps. 19:15), and mutual collation (Isa. 61:10; c. 62:4, 5). But specifically the Spouse says of the Spouse: My beloved is mine through faith (1 Cor. 6:17) and through possession (Cant. 3:4); and of herself: And I am his through acquisition: because he has purchased me for himself as a peculiar treasure, and thus I am entirely his (1 Cor. 6:20). Or if you prefer: My beloved gives himself to me through the communication of himself and all his goods and honors (John 17:19, 23; 1 John 1:3; Rom. 8:32; 1 Cor. 1:30; 2 Pet. 1:3. Cf. Ezek. 16:10; Zech. 2:8). And I consecrate myself entirely to him (Luke 1:69; Rom. 12:1). Tit. 2, 14. of his honor, on account of due thanksgiving and glorification. My beloved is mine through the guidance of the Spirit Rom. 8, 14. and I am his through prompt observance. Just as he, says Theodoret, preferred me to all, so I prefer him to all. He is mine, says St. Bernard, because he is kind and merciful; I am his, because I am not ungrateful. He gives me grace upon grace: I give him thanks for grace. He [is devoted] to my liberation, I to his honor: He to my salvation, I to his will. He is mine, and not another's: since I am his one dove: I am his and not another's. Moreover, he is said to feed (not as the Vulgate has it, to be fed) among the lilies. The LXX [says] ποιμένων, acting as a shepherd among the lilies. Cf. c. 1, 7. where Origen: It is shown by these things that this Bridegroom is also a Shepherd, Psalm 23, 1. 2. Moreover, he performs this office among the lilies, that is, among the faithful, who are compared to lilies v. 2. among pure and holy souls, whom he feeds with doctrine, sacraments, and example. What is designated by the lilies, says Gregory the Great, if not clean souls, which, while they retain the whiteness of chastity, smell sweetly to all their neighbors through the reputation of a good name.

Latin:

Vers. 16. DILECTUS MEUS MIHI, ET EGO ILLI, QUI PASCITUR INTER LILIA.

Mutua hîc contestatio Sponsi & Sponsæ ob mu- tuam desponsationem Hos. 2, 19. mutuam unionem Joh. 6, 56. 1. Cor. 6, 17. Ephes. 5, 32. mutuam dilectio- nem Ephes. 5, 1. Joh. 15, 14. Cantic. 1, 13, 15. & c. 3, 4. mutuam collocationem Ps. 19, 15. mutuamque colla- tationem Es. 61, 10. c. 62, 4. 5. Speciatim autem Spon- sa de Sponso dilectus, inquit, meus mihi per fidem 1. Cor. 6, 17. & per possessionem Cant. 3, 4. & de semet- ipsa, & ego illi per acquisitionem: quia me ceu pe- culium sibi comparavit, adeoque ita ego illius sum tota 1. Cor. 6, 20. vel si mavis: Dilectus meus mihi se donat per sui ipsius, & omnium bonorum & hono- rum suorum communicationem Johann. 17, 19. 23. 1. Joh. 1, 3. Rom. 8, 32. 1. Cor. 1, 30. 2. Petr. 1, 3. Conf. Ezech. 16, 10. Zach. 2, 8. Et ego ipsi me totam con- secro, Luc. 1, 69. Rom. 12, 1. Tit. 2, 14. ejusdem ho- nori, ob debitam gratiarum actionem & glorifica- tionem. Dilectus meus mihi per Spiritus guberna- tionem Rom. 8, 14. & ego ipsi per promptam observa- tionem. Sicut ipse, inquit Theodorec. me omnibus prætulit, sic ego ipsum omnibus antepono. Ille mihi, inquit S. Bernh. quia benignus & misericors est, ego illi, quia non sum ingrata. Ille mihi gratiam ex gra- tia: ego illi gratiam pro gratia. Ille meæ liberationi, ego illius honori: Ille saluti meæ, ego illius voluntati. Ille mihi, & non alteri: quoniam una sum columba ejus: Ego illi & non alteri. Pascere autem dicitur (non ut Vulg. habet pasci) inter lilia. LXX. ποι- μένον, pastorem agens in liliis. Conf. c. 1, 7. ubi Ori- genes: Ostenditur per hæc, quod Sponsus hic etiam Pastor sit, Psalm. 23, 1. 2. Inter lilia autem hoc officio fungitur, h. e. inter fideles, qui liliis comparantur v. 2. inter puras, & sanctas animas, quas pascit do- ctrina, Sacramentis, exemplo. Quid per lilia, ait Gregor. M. nisi mundæ animæ designantur, quæ dum castitatis candorem retinent, per bonæ famæ opinionem proximis quibusque suaviter olent.

## 2:17
Vers. 17. UNTIL THE DAY BREATHES AND THE SHADOWS INCLINE, RETURN, BE LIKE, MY BELOVED, TO A ROE, AND TO A YOUNG HART UPON THE MOUNTAINS OF BETHEL.

It is expressed until when he feeds among the lilies in the Church; namely, until the end of the world Matth. 28, 20. 1. Corinth. 11, 26. when the heat of tribulations will cease 1. Petr. 4, 12. Apoc. 7, 16. c. 21, 4. and the time of ἀναψύξεως (refreshment) will arrive Act. 3, 20. The latter part, Return, be like a roe, etc., explains the hastening of the return and second coming Tit. 2, 13., as the Bride groans Apoc. 22, 20., just as the Ernestine paraphrase also interprets the conclusion of the Canticle 8, 14.: But Osiander explained it concerning the visitation of the Church to be repeated often until the consummation of the age: Return, O dearest Bridegroom, often to us, that by your grace you may visit in the meantime your Churches scattered here and there in the world: Be like, my beloved, to a roe and to a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel, i. e., of division: But B. Gerhard in

After Solomon. Sunday 23 after Trinity, he most conveniently understands the circular journeying of Judea in the days of the flesh of Christ, and he wishes the mountains בָּתֶר to be mountains in the region of Gilead divided from the rest of Judea by the Jordan, from 2 Sam. 2:29, so that it may be indicated that Christ would perform his ministry in Judea with great speed, just as the roe is especially proclaimed for its speed in chapter 2:9, mention also being made of those who accepted these things concerning the conversion of the Jews toward the end of the world: which, however, he rightly dismisses. The word סָבַב is he went around, he circled, which Christ applies to circular preaching in Acts 10:38, and he derives it from Bunting's itinerary: just as in Mark 6:6 it is said of him περιῆγε τὰς κώμας κύκλῳ: in which manifold journeying he himself came into Mount Tabor, into Mount Zion, into the Mount of Olives, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 17. DONEC ASPIRET DIES ET IN- CLINENTUR UMBRÆ REVERTERE, SI- MILIS ESTO DILECTE MI CAPREÆ, HINNULOQUE CERVORUM SUPER MON- TES BETHEL.

Exprimitur quousque pascat inter lilia in Eccle- sia; nimirum usque ad finem mundi Matth. 28, 20. 1. Corinth. 11, 26. cum æstus tribulationum cessabit 1. Petr. 4, 12. Apoc. 7, 16. c. 21, 4. & tempus ἀναψύξε- ως adveniet Act. 3, 20. Posteriora Revertere, similis esto capreæ, &c. de reditu & adventu secundo Tit. 2, 13. maturando, uti Sponsa gemit Apoc. 22, 20. explicat Ernestina paraphrasis, quemadmodum etiam Can- tici conclusionem 8, 14. interpretatur: Osiander vero de visitatione Ecclesiæ sæpius iteranda usque ad consummationem seculi exposuit: Revertere ô cha- rissime Sponse, sæpe ad nos, ut gratia tua visites interea Ecclesias tuas hinc inde sparsas in mundo: Similis esto, dilecte mi, capreæ hinnuloque cervorum super montes Bethel, i. e. divisionis: B. Gerhardus autem in

Post Salom. Domin. 23. post Trinit. commodissime de circulari peragratione Judææ in diebus carnis Chri- sti intelligit, & montes בָּתֶר montes in regione Gilead per Jordanem a reliqua Judæa divisos esse vult e 2. Sam. 2, 29. ut indicetur magna celeritate Christum ministerium suum in Judæa peracturum, quemad- modum caprea imprimis ob celeritatem prædica- tur cap. 2, 9. facta etiam eorum mentione, qui hæc de conversione Judæorum sub finem mundi accepe- re: quam vero merito dimittit. Verbum סָבַב est circuivit, circumgyravit, quod applicat prædicationi Christus circulari Actor. 10, 38. eamque e Buntingii itinerario deducit: quemadmodum Marc. 6, 6. de ipso dicitur περιῆγε τὰς κώμας κύκλῳ: in qua mul- tipliciprofectione ipse in montem Thabor, in montem Sion, in montem oliveti venit, &c.

## 3:1 Argument
PART II. A SIGHING OVER THE LOSS OF THE BRIDEGROOM CONVERTED INTO THANKSGIVING. CHAPTER III.

The Bride seeks the lost Bridegroom in bed, in the streets and at the crossroads, groaning greatly before the watchmen, and she does not wish to let him go once found, until she arrives with him at her mother's house: the Bridegroom, solicitous about the Bride's rest, is exhilarated by her perfumes: and her bed, as safe and splendid, is described by him from the diadem with which he is crowned on the day of his espousals.

Verse 1.

ON MY BED BY NIGHTS I SOUGHT HIM WHOM MY SOUL LOVETH: I SOUGHT HIM, AND I FOUND HIM NOT.

Alcuin accepts this concerning the Church of the Gentiles: Long ago with much zeal I sought the Lord, but because I was still subject to the allurements of my flesh, and blinded by the darkness of profound ignorance, I did not find the light of truth, i.e., the Lord. But most, such as Ambrose, Gregory the Great, and others, understand it concerning the Bride abandoned on the cross in the darkness of calamity, anxiously seeking the Bridegroom. By nights, during the time of affliction, when mere darkness appears, Ps. 44:10, Eph. 10:10, Lam. 3:2, 6, I was meditating on rest in my beds, but because of anxiety I did not find him, Psalm 6:7, I was insistent in prayers, and I was seeking my beloved, but I did not find him. The Bridegroom hides himself, says Gregory the Great, lib. 5 Moral. c. 4, so that, not being found, he may be sought more ardently. Ambrose in Psalm 119: I sought in the nights, i.e., in persecutions and adversities. For it is night for all to whom there is not perfect security.

Latin:

PARS II. SUSPIRIUM DE AMISSIONE SPONSI IN GRATULATIONEM CONVERSUM. CAPUT III.

Sponsa quærit Sponsum amissum in lecto, plateis & compitis, valde gemens penes custodes, & inventum dimittere non vult, donec in do- mum maternam cum ipso perveniat: Sponsus de quiete Sponsæ solicitus exhilaratur ejus odoramentis: ejusque cubile ceu tutum & splendidum, ipse a diademate, quo in die de- sponsationis suæ coronatur, describitur.

Vers. 1.

IN LECTULO MEO PER NOCTES QUÆ- SIVI, QUEM DILIGIT ANIMA MEA: QUÆ- SIVI ILLUM, ET NON INVENI.

DE Ecclesia gentium Alcuinus accipit: Jam- dudum multo studio quæsivi Dominum, sed quæ adhuc illecebris carnis meæ subdita fui, & tenebris profundæ ignorantiæ obcæcata, non inveni lumen ve- ritatis, i. e. Dominum. Sed de Sponsa in cruce dere- licta in tenebris calamitatis Sponsum anxie quæ- rente plerique intelligunt, Ambros, Gregor. M. alii. Per noctes tempore afflictionis, cum meræ tenebræ apparent, Ps. 44, 10. Ef. 10, 10. Thr. 3, 2. 6. in lecto- rum requiem meditabar, sed præ anxietate non in- veniebam Psalm. 6, 7. precibus instabam, & quære- bam dilectum meum, sed non inveniebam eum. Abscondit se Sponsus, inquit Gregor. M. l. 5. Mo- ral. c. 4. ut non inventus ardentius quæratur. Am- bros. in Psalm. 119. Quæsivi in noctibus, i. e. in persecu- tionibus & adversis. Nox enim est omnibus, quibus non est perfecta securitas.

## 3:2
Verse 2.

I WILL RISE AND GO ABOUT THE CITY) Allegorically, the Paraphrast explains this concerning the Israelites, mutually exciting one another to go to the tabernacle of the congregation.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

SVRGAM ET CIRCVIBO CIVITATEM) Allegorice Paraphrastes hoc explicat de Israëlitis, mutuo se excitanti- bus, ut eant ad tabernaculum conventus.

## 3:4
Verse 4. INTO THE HOUSE OF MY MOTHER AND INTO THE CHAMBER OF HER THAT CONCEIVED ME) Thus Theocritus: κᾀγὼ ἐς τὸν ἄντρον ἱκοίμαν.

Latin:

Vers. 4. IN DOMVM MATRIS MEÆ ET IN CVBI- CVLVM GENITRICIS MEÆ) Sic Theocritus: κᾀγὼ ἐς τὸν ἄντρον ἱκοίμαν.

## 3:6
Verse 6. WHO IS THIS THAT COMETH UP OUT OF THE WILDERNESS LIKE PILLARS OF SMOKE) It is a transposition. For he wishes to say, whose perfumes ascend here like vapor from a field. For מִדְבָּר is accustomed to be translated both as ἀγρὸς, and πεδίον and ὄρος.

He is now silent about the literal sense which he himself attributes to the Song. For he saw well that it does not befit the Royal Bride to go around through the city, and to seek the Bridegroom, and to be wounded by the watchmen. Whence it is evidently gathered that an allegorical sense underlies the words: which Grotius ought to have acknowledged throughout the whole Song. For the reason for the whole Song is the same as for this part. But the Chaldean sense does not agree at all: for if the Israelites excite themselves to frequent the assemblies in the tabernacle, why do they have need to go around through the City and seek the Bridegroom? Were they ignorant of the place of the tabernacle? Why is it that they ask of the watchmen whether they have seen the Bridegroom? Why is it that they suffer blows and are instructed by the watchmen? If you desire to know the opinion of the Jews more fully, Mercerus proposes it thus: The Hebrews, he says, refer all these things more narrowly to the ancient people, when in the desert the Lord threatened that He would not go up with them, because they were a stiff-necked people, Exod. 33. When the Israelites had finally fallen in with the watchmen Moses and Aaron, they found God in the time of Joshua, when He, having become propitious to them after the extinction of the generation of the desert of twenty years and above, from which none entered into the promised land, except Joshua and Caleb, on account of the sin of the calf and of the spies and other things, introduced them into the land, where, now placed, they profess that they will not let Him go until they have brought Him into the maternal house, that is, into the tabernacle, where the ark, to be fixed in Shiloh, Gilgal, Nob, and other places, and finally in the temple of Solomon, which the Hebrews call בית עולמים, the perpetual house; because now that the ark was placed there, it would no longer change its place or seat, as before. Therefore, it is a discourse about the mystical Bride, who in the Cross and calamity anxiously seeks the Bridegroom through the streets of the City, while she searches the Scriptures and seeks the same in His word; but in temptations and the afflictions of the cross she does not immediately find Him, Isa. 49:14, or she simply indicates that she leaves nothing untried so that she may find Him and obtain His consolation and help. She asks the watchmen, therefore, the heralds of the word of God, Isa. 62:6, Ezek. 3:17 (or if you prefer, those who sell themselves as watchmen; who, however, had neither seen the Bridegroom nor could show Him. Which happened to our ancestors under the Papacy, and still happens to Christians afflicted and tempted there, who do not have suitable Ministers of the Church from whom they can receive true and solid consolation concerning the grace of Christ), and finally she finds the sweetest Bridegroom and, having found Him, she retains Him and does not wish to let Him go, Ps. 116:3, 4, 5, Gen. 32:26. Furthermore, what she suffers on the cross, while she anxiously seeks the Bridegroom, from the watchmen who sell themselves as true Ministers of God, is hatred and persecution, Cant. 5:7, Job 15:19, Heb. 11:13, 15. Grotius could have learned this meaning in Paris from a certain Parisian Royal Professor, if he did not deign to consult our own, or at least from the Jesuits, Cornelius a Lapide, Menochius, and others. But it was enough for Grotius to cite Theocritus, or other poets, or at most the Chaldean Paraphrast and the Rabbis, from whom he wished to reconcile light to the Canticle.

Vers. 6. WHO IS THIS THAT COMETH UP OUT OF THE WILDERNESS LIKE PILLARS OF SMOKE, PERFUMED WITH MYRRH AND FRANKINCENSE, WITH ALL POWDERS OF THE MERCHANT?

Alcuin thinks that the Synagogue is wondering how the people of the nations suddenly ascended from the lowest pleasures through the wilderness of gentility and idolatry to the high summits of virtues, kindled by the fire of divine love, striving with every effort of virtues toward heavenly things, through the mortification of carnal pleasures, the purity of works, and the odor of all virtues. In general, he takes it concerning the bride of Foljoth, understanding by the wilderness the world, which brings forth the thorns of sins, receives the poisons of unclean spirits, and sends those who receive these to the caverns of the underworld. Smoke, he says, born from fire and ascending on high, gradually withdraws itself from human sight: thus the Church, kindled by the fire, namely, of the Holy Spirit, into the love of God, ascending, does not cease until, abstracted from earthly things, she is snatched to the invisible things of heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 6. QVÆ EST ISTA, QVÆ ASCENDIT PER DESERTVM SICVT VIRGVLA FVMI) Est transposi- tio. Vult enim dicere, cujus odores hic adscendunt ut vapor ex agro. Nam מִדְבָּר verti solet & ἀγρὸς, & πεδίον & ὄρος.
