Tacet jam de sensu literali, quem ipse Cantico tribuit. Vidit enim probe, non convenire hæc Sponsæ Regiæ circuire per civitatem, & quærere Sponsum, ac vulnerari a custodibus. Unde evidenter colligitur, subesse verbis sensum allegoricum: quod agnoscere debuisset Grotius per totum Can- ticum. Eadem enim ratio est totius Cantici, quæ hujus partis. Chaldæi autem sensus neutiquam con- gruit: nam si se excitant Israëlitæ ad frequentan- dos conventus in tabernaculo, cur opus habent circuire per Civitatem & quærere Sponsum? num locum tabernaculi ignorabant? Quid est, quod quærant ex custodibus, anne viderint Sponsum? quid, quod verbera patiantur & instruantur a cu- stodibus? Judæorum sententiam si plenius scire cupias, ita eam proponit Mercerus: Hebræi, inquit, angustius hæc omnia ad veterem populum referunt, quum in deserto Dominus minaretur, se cum illis non adscensurum, quod duræ cervicis essent Exod. 33. Israelitas tandem quum in custodes Mosen & Aa- ronem incidissent, illis demortuis Deum tempore Jo- suæ invenisse, quum ille propitius illis factus post ex- tinctam generationem deserti ab annis viginti & supra, ex qua nullus in terram promissam ingressus, præter Josua & Caleb, ob peccatum vituli & explo- ratorum & alia, eos in terram introduxit, ubi jam positi se profitentur illum non missum facturos, donec in ædes maternas adduxerint, id est, in tabernaculum, ubi arca, figendum in Silo, Ghilgal, Nob & aliis locis & tandem in templo Salomonis, quod Ebræis בית עולמים domum perpetuam appellant; quod jam ibi arca collocata, non ultra locum mutaret, aut sedes, ut ante. De Sponsa ergo mystica sermo est, quæ in Cru- ce & calamitate anxie quærit Sponsum per Civita- tis plateas, dum Scripturas indagat & in verbo suo eundem quærit; Sed in tentationibus & crucis af- flictionibus non actutum eundem invenit Esa. 49, 14. vel simpliciter indicat, se nihil intentatum re- linquere, ut eum reperiat, & consolationem & opem ejus consequatur. Custodes ergo rogat, verbi Dei præcones Es. 62, 6. Ezech. 3, 17. (aut si mavis, eos, quæ se pro custodibus venditant; qui vero Sponsum neque viderant, neque ostendere poterant. Quod majo- ribus nostris accidit sub Papatu, & adhuc accidit Christianis ibi afflictis & tentatis, qui non habent idoneos Ecclesiæ Ministros, a quibus veram & so- lidam consolationem de gratia Christi accipere pos- sint,) tandemque invenit Sponsum dulcissimum inventumque retinet, nec dimittere vult Ps. 116, 3. 4. 5. Genes. 32, 20. Quæ insuper in cruce, dum anxie Sponsum quærit, a custodibus, sese pro veris Dei Ministris venditantibus, odium & persecutionem pa- titur Cantic. 5, 7. Job. 15, 19. Ebr. 11, 13. 15. Didicisse hunc sensum poterat Parisiis Grotius e Parisiensi quodam Professore Regio, si nostros consulere di- gnatus non fuit, aut saltem e Jesuïtis, Cornel. a La- pide, Menochio & aliis. Sed Grotio satis fuit Theo- critum, aut alios Poëtas, vel ad summum Paraphra- stem Chaldæum ac Rabbinos adducere, e quibus lu- cem Cantico voluit conciliare.

Vers. 6. QUÆ EST ISTA, QUÆ ASCEN- DIT PER DESERTUM SICUT VIRGULA FUMI EX AROMATIBUS MYRRHÆ ET THURIS, ET UNIVERSI PULVERIS PI- GMENTARII?

Alcuinus mirari Synagogam censet, quomodo gentium populus subito ab infimis voluptatibus per de- sertum gentilitatis & idololatriæ ad alta virtutum culmina adscenderit, igne amoris divini accensa omni nisu virtutum ad cælestia tenderit, per mortificatio- nem carnalium voluptatum, puritatem operationum, & odorem virtutum omnium? In genere de sponsa Foljoth accipit per desertum mundum intelligens, qui spinas parturit peccatorum, venena suscipit im- mundorum spirituum, & suscipientes hæc ad cavernas mittit inferorum. Fumus, inquit, ex igne natus in alta conscendens paulatim humanis se subtrahit conspectibus: sic Ecclesia igne scil. S. S. in amorem Dei accensa, adscendens non desinit, donec a terrenis ab- stracta ad invisibilia cæli rapiatur.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. BEHOLD THE BED OF SOLOMON) A bedchamber. The magnificence of the new bridegroom is proclaimed.

Latin:

Vers. 7. EN LECTVLVM SALOMONIS) Cubiculum. Magnificentia novi mariti prædicatur.

## 3:9
Verse 9. HE MADE HIMSELF A LITTER) In Hebrew אפריון, Jerome believed that to be the Greek φορει̃ον: and the LXX translate it thus. φορει̃ον is a litter, or something similar.

Latin:

Vers. 9. FERCVLVM SIBI FECIT) In Hebr. אפריון, id effe Græcum φορει̃ον credidit Hieronymus: & fic vertunt LXX. φορει̃ον est lectica, aut simile quid.

## 3:10
Verse 10. A GOLDEN RECLINING-PLACE) The floor. A PURPLE ASCENT) The canopy of the litter.

He accepts these things concerning Solomon the new husband according to the proper and direct sense of Holy Scripture. Although it may be conceded that there is an allusion to the Majesty of Solomon, the Holy Spirit does not primarily intend to describe it here, but wished to present the heavenly Solomon and his axioms: to depict whom, just as He used various colors, so we do not wish to deny that some things were also transferred here from Solomonic Majesty, but so that the allegorical sense, which others call mystical, may here remain the proper one and the one primarily intended by the Holy Spirit. If anyone also establishes some type in the Majesty of Solomon, we do not object: just as this bed of Solomon is accepted here by the Weimar Paraphrasts as a certain image of the bed of Christ. Thus Osiander on this passage. King Solomon has very strong bodyguards, who also keep watch at night, so that no harm may befall him and his Queen. It is certain, however, that Solomon in his Majesty was a type of Christ: and that the places where Religion is practiced are called beds and couches by the Prophets, Isaiah 57, because there Christ must be most holily joined with the Church. He wishes therefore to say: God protects those places where the Gospel is purely taught with the protection of the strongest Angels, so that the Churches may not be dissipated in various afflictions and dangers. Furthermore, lest there be any doubt that the Majesty and state of the earthly Solomon is not being celebrated here, but the Majesty of Christ, the heavenly Solomon, and the condition of his Church is being described, those things are added which openly teach that the discourse here is about the Magnificence of Christ and the perfection of his Church. For if one wishes to explain verse 7 concerning Solomon, the last verse certainly cannot be understood of him, but it treats clearly of Christ: Go forth and see, O daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of his gladness. For Solomon was not crowned by his mother with a diadem on the day of his espousals. Therefore Cassiodorus, Theodoret, Philo Carpathius, Gregory the Great, Bede, and almost all other Interpreters understand by the bed of Solomon the Church, especially of the Gentiles, in which, as in a bed, Christ the true Solomon, the King of peace, rests. To which opinion Cornelius à Lapide, ineptly claiming that the Roman see is the bed, opposes in vain that the Church is the Bride herself, and not the bed: for who does not know that in such parables and figures one thing is often compared to many, on account of different respects, and that all things signified cannot be expressed by one comparison? Just as Christ is Priest, altar, sacrifice, and the one to whom the sacrifice is offered, in different respects. The litter, says Cornelius, signifies the Roman Church, now ample and magnificent and [ruling] over other Churches scattered throughout the whole world, through the Roman Pontiff, presiding and ruling like Solomon. An excellent litter, and sufficiently sumptuous! But the litter, which is in the Hebrew, has been changed in the Vulgate into a litter [ferculum]. Therefore Rome will be the litter, but not of Christ the Bridegroom, but rather of the Anti-Christ; indeed, divine oracles teach that it is the litter of the Babylonian harlot. Cornelius acknowledges that the Hebrew אפריון is a marriage bed or couch, so called from פרה to be fruitful, because offspring is generated in it. He acknowledges that the Vatican LXX and St. Ambrose in book 3 on Virgins read: King Solomon made himself a bed: that R. David translates it as a bed on which brides are carried: R. Solomon as an honorable throne, the Syrian as a throne, the Arabic as a building: He acknowledges that Loyfius and Sanchez, and Genebrard rightly understand it as a litter. For the text demands that: King Solomon made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon, he made its columns of silver, a golden reclining-place: and yet he still talks nonsense about his litter [ferculum]: King Solomon made himself a litter [ferculum] of the woods of Lebanon etc. But they have the necessity of admitting such a slip and error of the Vulgate, which has been canonized by the Roman Pontiffs. Grotius, however, rightly notes that a litter or something similar ought to be understood by the Hebrew word, and that this also signifies the Φορεῖον (which Jerome thinks is the very Hebrew word אפריון used here). But setting those things aside, so that we may return to our Solomon, the ancients Gregory of Nyssa, Philo Carpathius, Cassiodorus, Justus Orgelitanus, Gregory the Great, Aponius, Bede, and others acknowledge with great consensus that it designates Christ, and they accept the litter as being about the Church. Gregory the Great: King Solomon made himself a litter [ferculum] of the woods of Lebanon, because according to the grace of his foreknowledge Christ constructed the holy Church from saints who are to remain forever. He made its columns of silver, because he gave Preachers to the same Church, whom, so that they might support it with examples, he strengthened with great rectitude of justice, and so that they might instruct with preachings, he adorned with the brightness of eloquence, as if with the splendor of silver. He made a golden reclining-place, because while he shone in the hearts of the perfect, he showed them the power of his divinity through contemplation, in which contemplation, while he showed them the beauty of heavenly joys, he composed for them a reclining-place as if of gold, because he provided a place in which they might rest, refreshing themselves. Which reclining-place is well said to be golden, because wisdom is better than all riches, and all things that are desired cannot be compared to it. Other Interpreters explain those parts of Solomon's litter a little differently: But they unanimously understand by Solomon Christ himself. Psellus, in Theodoret, on the words: King Solomon made himself a litter; the proposed discourse, he says, most wisely indicates the Church collected from the Gentiles. For King Solomon, i.e. The Bridegroom, who is the frankincense of the nations once rejected, is also to be venerated and is Holy, of whom David, the composer of the Psalms, makes mention; saying, the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon. By the columns and bases, however, understand for me the Apostles and Prophets, who supported the Church of Christ, etc. Three Fathers in the same Theodoret have it thus: From those who had been cut out from that wicked root and built upon Christ as the foundation of faith, Christ himself, that peaceful king, made a litter for himself: since upon these, brought to perfection, he was carried as if in a chariot to instruct men. But narrating the equipment of the litter in detail, he says, he made its columns of silver, which indeed are the utterances of the Lord, of which David says; The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver refined in the fire. Upon which, as if upon certain columns, the Bridegroom drew the Bride, who had been lifted up, to himself, establishing her as his own vehicle, who in herself would bear the true conjunction of these utterances. And its golden reclining-place, i.e., the tranquility of her mind, he established as the chief seat for himself, where he might rest: for he shows this by gold, which excels all things consisting of matter. Its purple ascent, the royal palace of God, to be sure. For if Solomon signifies the peaceful one and indicates Christ, who has pacified all things in himself: but Peace is the joy of the mind removed from all disturbance: this true joy is the royal palace of God, alien to all sedition. The royal palace of God is indeed the ascent of the soul, which, like a litter, receives the peaceful king. The things which Theodoret himself hands down in his own exposition are almost identical. All agree that by Solomon, Christ is to be understood. The little bed of Solomon, says Cassiodorus, is called the holy Church, because in it the Saints of God are delighted amidst many troublesome vices by the embrace of true piety. Therefore, as for those sixty mighty men, by whom the bed of the Lord is surrounded, they are rightly understood as the legions of Angels, which He has in His hand, by whom He protects His Church; or the Doctors and Ministers of the word, who by their vigilance and arms defend the Church of the Lord against snares, girded with the sword of the word, so that they may repel the adversary, and ward off the terrors of the night, the errors of darkness and ignorance, and whatever other dangers. As R. Solomon advises, that disciples studious of wisdom are compared to mighty men having a sword in their hands. Cons. Ps. 127, 4. 5. Ephes. 6, 17. A certain number for an uncertain, which is frequently placed in Scripture. But it is not read anywhere in the history of Solomon about such a splendid litter of Solomon, and about a guard of such a kind, by which the same was surrounded, when other things, which are not of such importance, have not been omitted in the history. Whence Gregory of Nyssa concludes that this is not about a material litter of Solomon: That this narrative about the bed is by no means readily available from history, it will be able to be clear to anyone from those things which have been produced in a corporeal manner about Solomon, whose palace and table and the rest of the order of the kingdom have been described most accurately, while in the meantime nothing new and unusual exists about the bed. Wherefore it is altogether necessary that the explanation of this passage should not cling to the letters, but these things must be accepted by a certain more diligent consideration, with the mind turned away from the gross signification of the words to spiritual contemplation. Nyssenus adds another reason, which I am pleased to subjoin: What adornment could have come to the bridal bed from 60 adorned soldiers, whose skill is to know the terrible works of war, whose adornment is to have a sword as a protection for the body, and who, finally, are girded during the night-time? Thus Nyssenus. And what was the point of singing in such a distinguished Canticle about the chamberlains and guards of Solomon in his bedchamber, of whom everyone was aware, and about whom Solomon would boast from his couch, exalting himself so greatly, seeking I know not what laurel wreath in this mustaceo? That is certainly not to be presumed of Solomonic wisdom in this most holy and excellent Canticle. Whence the Jews themselves seek mysteries in these things, even if, on account of the veil which is still placed upon their hearts, they are unable to perceive them.

Verse of the same.

HE PAVED THE MIDDLE WITH LOVE FOR THE DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM) The middle of it was paved with love by the women of Jerusalem. That is, the middle parts of the litter have histories of loves, embroidered by the needle of Jewish women.

This gloss, like all the others, savors only of Solomon the son of David, and his litter: which, as I have said, it is by no means likely to have been celebrated here so laboriously by Solomon himself. And who will believe that the Holy Spirit wished to commemorate in such a distinguished Canticle the histories of loves, which, as Grotius divines, were embroidered with a needle on the litter of Solomon, so that, forsooth, it might not escape us that the pavement of the Solomonic litter was adorned with histories of loves embroidered with a needle? Cornelius à Lapide brings forward various interpretations of the Vulgate version, various ones of the Hebrew text; which can be rendered thus: He paved the middle of it with stones of love, for instance burning gems, such as pyropes and carbuncles, which are a symbol of love: which Sottomajor translates thus: The middle of it paved with the love of the most dear Bride: which others with the LXX render: The middle of it paved with gems to conciliate love from the daughters of Jerusalem, etc. According to Mercer you may render it thus: The middle, that is, THE INTERIOR PARTS OF IT (the litter) paved (as if depicted and figured on all sides) with love, with love, I say, of the daughters of Jerusalem, i.e.

of one of the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, the Bride. Others with the Vulgate and B. Luther render: FOR THE DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM: so that, forsooth, all these things may yield to them for honor, pleasure, and salvation. Now as for the proper sense, which is contained under the bark of the letter, and under the grammatical sense, some indeed wish for a description of heavenly glory in verses 9 and 10, which the Belgian Interpreters note at this place. Most interpret it concerning the glory and dignity of the Church in this age, and Mercer does not badly present the sense thus: that indeed all these things tend to this, that we may understand that the Church shines forth with all endowments, graces, and ornaments, and abounds in gold, silver, and purple, all of which the Word of the Lord equals, nay, far surpasses. That its interior burns with love and charity is not obscure to understand from the fact that Christ, whose this most magnificent work is, burned with such love for her that He laid down His life for her. Similarly our Osiander explained: that Christ knows how to hold and, as it were, delicately treat His Church according to the measure of time and infirmity, so that not only the mother herself may not be in danger, but also afterwards her tender little children may be sweetly carried, lest they perish. And the Weimar Paraphrasts: whose paraphrase I append here, since it illustrates the B. Luther version and the text itself not incongruously: The King Solomon had a litter made for him of wood from Lebanon (of the very best cedars), the pillars of which were silver, the covering golden, the seat purple, the floor in the middle was lovingly paved (and prepared) for the sake of the daughters of Jerusalem (to show them and all the people his royal splendor and power herewith, verse 11, and therein to bring his royal spouse lovingly and gloriously from one place to another: But much more graciously and gloriously does the heavenly Solomon deal with his own spiritual bride, the Christian Church, whom He graciously and gently leads through this world by his holy Word, as if on a beautiful litter, and finally brings to himself into eternal joy and glory: He guides her according to his counsel, and finally receives her with honor, Psalm 73, 24, where she will be with him eternally, and will see his glory, which his Father gave him. John 17, 24.) We observe only this, that by King Solomon named in the text, Christ is to be understood immediately, which is manifest from v. 11, and is proven by the common reckoning of the Fathers, even though an allusion to the litter of the earthly Solomon could have been made, concerning which, however, as Gregory of Nyssa previously warned, nothing certain is known. For in the following words v. 14, the Weimar Paraphrasts themselves, with the blessed Osiander, understand Christ immediately by King Solomon, the King and Prince of peace Heb. 7, 2. Ps. 110, 6. crowned with glory and honor Heb. 2, 9. and appointed head, Bridegroom and Savior of his Church Eph. 1, 21. c. 5, 23. Over whom, as his Bride, he rejoices greatly Is. 62, 5. and will rejoice eternally Apoc. 19, 7. of whom also the aforementioned verse 11 was understood by the Ancients, although they explained the same either concerning the human nature of Christ, by which the Son of God was as it were crowned in the incarnation: which is the opinion of Ambrose in his book on Isaac, ch. 5, Athanasius in his Synopsis, Philo of Carpasia, Cassiodorus, Gregory the Great, Bede, Anselm, Honorius, and Bernard in Sermon 2. Epiphanius is the exposition; Or concerning the crown of thorns, which some also call the crown of charity, because out of charity he willed to wear it, with which he was crowned at the time of his passion by his mother the Jewish Synagogue, as Tertullian, Cyprian, Gregory of Nyssa, and Bernard interpret in this place, concerning which both explanations Gerhard speaks at length in his Postilla Salomonis on the 1st Sunday of Advent and Palm Sunday. Theodoret calls Judea the mother, as far as it pertains to the humanity of Christ, who placed the crown of charity upon him in life: for he crowned him with thorns for the sake of contempt, but he himself through the thorns received the diadem of charity: for he endured ignominy on his brow and willingly approached the torments of death; for which reason the betrothal of the joy of his heart. For then indeed the communion of the wedding took place, namely at the Last Supper, when he instituted the Eucharistic nuptial banquet. Similarly three anonymous Fathers in Theodoret. Observe the reason for the betrothal in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal, namely in the crown of thorns which the Synagogue of the Jews, from which he himself is according to the flesh, placed upon Christ's head: on the day of his saving death, in which he betrothed the Church to himself with his own blood: And on the day of the joy of his heart, in which, indeed, meeting a saving death for us, he freed us from the slavery of the enemy, and thus, obeying the will of the Father, he rejoiced in the Spirit, although he was vexed by the torments of the flesh. Whence three opinions are found concerning the day of the betrothal and the crown. The first refers to the incarnation of the Son of God and his mother the Θεοτόκον; the second to the passion of the same and the Jewish Synagogue, which is called his mother; the third refers to the glorification of Christ; concerning which, however, a doubt arises: why is he said to be crowned with honor by his mother? where it may be said: that the mother, while she crowned him through contempt with a crown of thorns, because he entered into glory through the passion, promoted his glory, albeit unwillingly and beyond her intention. Others, however, with Mercerus leading, add a fourth explanation, by which these things are referred to the celebration of Christ: if indeed he is glorified and celebrated by his mother, that is, by the Church, and the faithful are his glory, praise, and crown. 1 Thess. 2:19. For what, says Mercerus, he commands to observe as the crown with which he was crowned by his mother, understand as the highest glory, nay, all and most absolute beauty, which Christ received from the Church, that is, which she bestowed upon him, having placed all her hope and salvation in him, not that he did not have all his glory from the Father, but that through the Church, by the preaching of the Gospel, the glory of Christ was acknowledged in the whole world, and his kingdom promulgated and propagated, which was of the greatest joy to Christ, that, namely, the Church had bestowed such beauty upon him, acknowledging that she was redeemed by him. But the Church is indeed called a mother, but of the faithful, and not the mother of Christ. Here, however, the discourse is about the mother of Christ; as the Bride of Christ, the Church is exhibited here, not as a mother. And the simpler explanation seems to be about the crown of thorns of the passion, according to which are the three Fathers in Theodoret. they render this reason for the συνεχείας: Because the Mistress notices that the disciples are hesitant on account of her, and full of admiration, to explain those things which pertain to her; in the Bridegroom Christ she wishes them henceforth to contemplate the manner of our salvation and deservedly to doubt and admire how he himself, through his saving torments and death, has bestowed tranquility and life upon us. Therefore, go forth, she says, and see, O daughters of Zion, cease to consider what pertains to me, the handmaid, and fix the gaze of your mind on the peaceful Lord, contemplating how he has acquired salvation for us here. Or concerning the crown of exultation and glory, with which he himself, διὰ τὸ πάθημα, was crowned by his mother according to the flesh, the Jewish Synagogue, because he is descended from the Jews, even though she uniquely intended his destruction and excision. In which way the crown of glory was indeed received from the Father, but through the intervention of the mother and the crown of thorns, because through the bitter coronation of the mother he brought back the glorious crown of eternal majesty, Phil. 2:9, Heb. 2:9. Which explanation Psellus approves from the Ancients in Theodoret, although he does not understand the Father's charity through the mother of the Bridegroom so conveniently, and Osiander followed him, as did the Vinarienses.

Latin:

Vers. 10. RECLINATORIVM AVREVM) Pavimentum. ASCENSVM PVRPVREVM) Camera lecticæ.

De Salomone novo marito hæc accipit secun- dum proprium & directum S. S. sensum. Quamvis vero concedi possit, alludi ad Majestatem Salomo- nis, non tamen eam hîc describere primo intendit Spiritus S. sed cœlestem Salomonem, ejusque axio- mata sistere voluit: ad quem depingendum uti va- riis usus est coloribus, ita diffiteri nolumus, etiam nonnullos à Salomonæa Majestate hic transfumtos es- se, sed ut allegoricus sensus, quem alii mysticum vo- cant, hic maneat proprius & primo à Spiritu S. in- tentus. Si quis etiam in Majestate Salomonis typum aliquem constituat, non refragamur: uti à Para- phrastis Vinariensibus hic lectulus Salomonis acci- pitur, ceu imago quædam lecti Christi. Ita Ofian- der in h. l. Habet Rex Salomon fortissimos corporis cu- stodes, qui etiam noctu vigilant, ne ipsi & Reginæ ipsius quicquam mali contingat. Certum est autem, Salomonem in sua Majestate fuisse typum Christi: & loca, ubi exercetur Religio, vocari à Prophetis le- ctos & strata Esa. 57. quippe ubi Christus debet cum Ecclesia sanctissime conjungi. Vult igitur dicere: Deus ea loca, ubi pure docetur Evangelium, fortissi- morum Angelorum præsidio tuetur, ut in variis affli- ctionibus & periculis non dissipentur Ecclesiæ. Cæte- rum ne dubium sit, hîc non Salomonis terreni Ma- jestatem & statum celebrari, sed Majestatem de- scribi Christi, cœlestis Salomonis, & conditio- nem Ecclesiæ ejus, subjunguntur ea, quæ aperte docent, de Christi Magnificentia, & Ecclesiæ ejus perfectione hîc sermonem esse. Nam si v. 7. de Salomone quis velit explicare, ultimus certe versus de eo intelligi nequit, sed de Christo lucu- lenter agit: Egredimini & videte filiæ Sion Regem Salomonem in Diademate, quo coronavit illum ma- ter sua in die desponsationis illius, & in die lætitiæ ejus. Salomon enim à matre sua coronatus non fuit dia- demate, in die desponsationis suæ. Ideo Cassiodorus, Theodoretus, Philo Carpathius, Gregorius M. Beda, & alii Interpp. pene omnes per lectulum Salomonis intelligunt Ecclesiam, præsertim gentium, in qua velut in lectulo Christus verus Salomon Rex pacifi- cus requiescit. Cui sententiæ frustra Cornelius à La- pide, Romanam sedem lectulum esse, inepte afferens, opponit, quod Ecclesia sit ipsa Sponsa, non vero le- ctulus: quis enim nescit, in talibus parabolis & fi- guris rem unam sæpe multis comparari, ob diver- sos respectus, & quod una comparatione omnia si- gnificata non possint exprimi? uti Christus est Sa- cerdos, ara, sacrificium, is cui offertur sacrificium, diverso respectu. Ferculum, inquit Cornelius, si- gnificat Ecclesiam Romanam jam amplam & magni- ficam cæterisque Ecclesiis toto orbe sparsis, per Roma- num Pontificem, præsidentem & instar Salomonis do- minantem. Eximium ferculum, satisque lautum! Sed lectica, quæ in Ebræo est, in Vulgata in fercu- lum commutata est. Lectica ergo Roma erit, non autem Christi Sponsi, verum Anti-Christi; imo meretricis Babylonicæ lecticam eam esse oracula divina docent. Agnoscit Cornelius Ebræum אפריון esse torum, vel lectulum genialem, ita dictum à פרה fructificare, quod in eo proles generetur. Agno- scit, LXX. Vaticanos, & S. Ambrosium in lib. 3. de Virginib. legere, lectum sibi fecit Rex Salomo: R. Davidem vertere lectum, quo deferuntur Sponsæ: R. Salomonem thronum honorificum, Syrum thro- num, Arabicum ædificium: Agnofcit, recte Loy- fium & Sanchiezem, ac Genebrardum intelligere le- cticam. Id enim textus pofcit: Lecticam fecit fibi Rex Salomo de lignis Libani, columnas ejus fecit argen- teas, Reclinatorium aureum: & tamen ineptit ad- huc de ferculo fuo: ferculum fecit fibi Rex Salomo de lignis Libani &c. Sed ita lapfum & errorem Vul- gatæ à Pontificibus Rom. canonizatæ fateri necef- fum habent. Bene autem Grotius lecticam aut fi- mile quid per Ebræam vocem intelligi debere, idque etiam Φορεῖον (quod efse ipfum Ebræum hic adhi- bitum vocabulum אפריון Hieronymus putat) fignifi- care, notat. Misfis vero iftis, ut ad Salomonem no- strum redeamus, magno confenfu veteres Gregor. Nyffenus, Philo Carpathius, Caffiodorus, Justus Orge- litanus, Gregorius M. Aponius, Beda & alii Chri- ftum defignare agnofcunt, ac lecticam de Ecclefia accipiunt. Gregorius M. Ferculum (lecticam) fe- cit fibi Rex Salomo de lignis Libani, quia fecundum præfcientiæ fuæ gratiam Chriftus fanctam Ecclefiam de fanctis in æternum permanfuris conftruxit. Colu- mnas ejus fecit argenteas, quia eidem Ecclefiæ Prædi- catores dedit, quos, ut eam exemplis fuftentarent, ma- gna justitiæ rectitudine roboravit, & ut prædicationi- bus erudirent, nitore eloquii, quafi fplendore argenti decoravit. Reclinatorium aureum fecit, quia dum in cordibus perfectorum refplenduit, ei divinitatis fuæ potentiam per contemplationem oftendit, in qua con- templatione dum eis pulchritudinem cæleftium gau- diorum monftravit, quafi reclinatorium ex auro eis compofuit, quia locum, in quo refocillantes requie- fcant, appofuit. Quod reclinatorium bene aureum effe dicitur, quia melior est fapientia cunctis opibus, & omnia, quæ defiderantur, ei non pofsunt comparari. Paulo aliter explicant illas lecticæ Salomonis par- tes Interpp. alii: Sed unanimiter per Salomonem ipfummet Chriftum intelligunt. Pfellus apud Theo- doretum ad verba: Ferculum fecit fibi Rex Salo- mo; Sermo propofitus, inquit, fapientiffime Ecclefi- am ex Gentibus collectam innuit. Rex enim Salomo, i. e. Sponfus, qui est gentium olim rejectarum libanus, etiam eft venerandus & Sanctus, de quo Pfalmorum Conditor David meminit; justus, inquiens, ut palma florebit, ficut Cedrus Libani multiplicabitur. Per co- lumnas & bafes tamen mihi Apoftolos & Prophetas intellige, qui Chrifti Ecclefiam fuftinuerunt &c. Tres Patres apud eundem Theodoretum ita habent: Ex his, qui ex improba ifta radice excifi fuerant & super Chriftum fidei fundamentum ædificati, fercu- lum fibi fecit ipfe Christus, rex ille pacificus: cum fu- per his ad perfectionem adductis, tanquam curru, ad erudiendos homines veheretur. Sigillatim autem fer- culi apparatum enarrantes, columnas ejus, inquit, fe- cit argenteas, quæ quidem funt eloquia Domini, de quibus David; Eloquia, inquit, Domini eloquia ca- fta argentum igne examinatum. Super quibus tan- quam columnis quibusdam Sponfus fublatam Spon- fam ad fe traxit, proprium ipfam vehiculum confti- tuens, quæ in feipfa ferret veram horum eloquiorum conjunctionem. Et Reclinatorium ejus aureum, i. e. mentis ipfius tranquillitatem, præcipuam fibi, ubi quiefceret, fedem conftituit: id enim per aurum often- dit, quod rebus omnibus ex materia conftantibus an- tecellit. Afcenfum ejus purpureum, regiam nimirum Dei. Nam fi Salomo fignificat pacificum & Chriftum indicat, qui in fe cuncta pacificavit: Pax autem est animi lætitia ab omni turbatione remota: hæc vera lætitia est Dei regia ab omni feditione aliena. Regia utique Dei est afcenfus animæ, quæ ferculi inftar fufci- pit regem pacificum. Gemina fere funt, quæ Theodo- ret. ipfe tradit in propria expofitione. Confentiunt omnes, per Salomonem Chriftum intelligendum- esse. Lectulus Salomonis, inquit Cassiodorus, dicta est Ecclesia sancta, quia in illa Sancti Dei multis tu- multibus vitiosis amplexu veræ pietatis delectantur. Quod ergo ad fortes illos sexaginta, quibus stipatus est lectus Domini, legiones Angelorum, quas in ma- nu sua habet, recte intelliguntur, quibus suam tue- tur Ecclesiam; vel Doctores ac Ministri verbi, qui vigilantia sua & armis Ecclesiam Domini adversus insidias defendunt, gladio verbi accincti, ut adver- sarium repellant, & pavores nocturnos, errores te- nebrarum & ignorantiæ & quæcunque alia pericula arceant. Uti R. Salomo monet, Discipulos sapientiæ studiosos viris fortibus gladium præ manibus habenti- bus comparari. Cons. Ps. 127, 4. 5. Ephes. 6, 17. Nu- merus certus pro incerto, quod frequens in Scri- ptura ponitur. Neque vero legitur uspiam in histo- ria Salomonis de lectica tam splendida Salomonis, ac de custodia ejusmodi, qua eadem stipata fuerit, quum alia, quæ tanti momenti non sunt, in histo- ria prætermissa haud sint. Unde Gregorius Nyssenus concludit, non agi hîc de Salomonis lectica mate- riali: De historia quidem minime promtam esse hanc de cubili narrationem, cuivis esse perspicuum poterit ex illis, quæ more corporeo de Salomone prodita sunt, cujus & regia & mensa & reliqua regni ratio accura- tissime descripta sunt, cum interim novi quiddam & inusitati de cubili nihil extet. Quapropter omnino necessarium est, ut enarratio hujus loci non literis inhæ- reat, sed consideratione quadam diligentiori hæc ac- cipienda sunt, aversa mente ad contemplationem spi- ritualem à significatione vocum crassa. Addit & ali- liam rationem Nyssenus, quam subjungere placet: Quis ornatus Sponsali toro accesserit de 60. militibus ornatis, quorum scientia sit nosse terribilia belli opera, ornatus ensem habere pro munimento corporis, qui denique nocturno tempore cincti sint? Hæc Nyssenus. Et quid attinebat canere in tam insigni Cantico de Cubiculariis & Præsidiariis Salomonis in cubiculo ejus, de quibus constabat omnibus, & qui Salomo de lectulo suo gloriaretur, seque eodem tantopere efferret, nescio quam laureolam quærens in hoc mustaceo? Ne præsumendum id quidem de sapien- tia Salomonea in hoc tam sancto & excellenti Can- tico. Unde Judæi ipsi mysteria in hisce quærunt, etsi ob velamen, quod cordibus ipsorum adhuc im- positum, perspicere ea non valeant.

Vers. eod.

MEDIA CHARITATE CONSTRAVIT PROPTER FILIAS JERUSALEM) Media eius strata amore à mulieri- bus Hierosolymitanis. Id est, media lecticæ amorum histo- rias habent, mulierum Judæarum acu pictas.

Hæc glossa, uti cæteræ omnes, Salomonem Davidis filium tantum sapit, & lecticam ejusdem: quam, uti dixi, tam operose hîc celebratam esse ab ipso Salomone nequaquam sit verisimile. Et quis credet, Spiritum S. amorum historias, quæ in lecti- ca, ut Grotius divinat, Salomonis acu fuerint pi- ctæ, commemorare peculiariter in tam insigni Can- tico voluisse, ne scil. nos lateret, historiis amorum acu pictis strata lecticæ Salomoneæ ornata fuisse? Cornelius à Lapide adfert varias interpretationes vulgatæ versionis, varias textus Ebræi; quod ita reddi possit: Medium ejus constravit lapidibus amo- ris, puta gemmis ardentibus, quales sunt pyropi, & carbunculi, qui symbolum sunt amoris: quod Sot- tomajor ita vertat: Medium ejus stratum amore Sponsæ summæ charæ: quod alii cum LXX. reddant: Medium ejus gemmis constratum ad amorem à filia- bus Jerusalem conciliandum &c. Juxta Mercerum ita reddas: Medium, id est, INTERIORA EJUS (lecticæ) constrata (velut depicta & figurata undi- que) amore, amore, inquam, filiarum Jerusalem, i. e.

unius ex filiabus Jerusalem, id est, Sponsæ. Alii cum Vulgata & B. Luthero reddunt : PROPTER FI- LIAS Jerusalem : ut scil. illis honori, voluptati & saluti hæc omnia cedant. Jam quod ad sensum pro- prium, qui sub cortice literæ, & sub sensu Gramma- ticali continetur, nonnulli quidem v. 9. & 10. de- scriptionem cœlestis gloriæ haberi volunt, quod no- tant Belgici Interpp. ad h. l. Plerique de gloria & di- gnitate Ecclesiæ in hoc seculo interpretantur, sensum- que non male Mercerus ita exhibet: quod nem- pe hæc omnia eo tendant, ut intelligamus, omnibus dotibus, gratiis, & ornamentis præfulgere Ecclesiam, auro, argento, purpuraque abundare, quæ omnia exæ- quat, imo longe superat Verbum Domini. Ejus inti- ma amore ardere & charitate, non est obscurum intel- ligere ex eo, quod Christus, cujus est hoc tam ma- gnificum opus, tanto ejus amore exarserit, ut vitam pro ea exposuerit. Similiter Osiander noster expo- suit: quod noverit Christus pro ratione temporis & infirmitatis Ecclesiam suam tenere & quasi delicate tractare, ut non modo ipsa mater non periclitetur, sed & postea etiam tenelli ejus filioli suaviter vehantur, ne pereant. Et Paraphrastæ Vinarienses: quorum paraphrasin hic adscribo, quum egregie B. Lutheri versionem textumque ipsum non incongrue illu- stret: Der König Salomon ließ ihm eine Sänffte machen von Holtz aus Libanon (von den allerbesten Cedern) derselben Seulen waren silbern, die Decke gülden, der Sitz purpurn, der Boden mitten inne war lieblich gepflastert (und zubereitet) um der Töchter willen zu Jerusalem (denenselben und al- lem Volck seine Königliche Pracht und Macht hie- mit zu zeigen, verf. 11. und darinnen seine Königliche Gemahlin lieblich und herrlich von einem Ort zum andern fortzubringen: Aber viel holdseliger und herr- licher gehet der himmlische Salomo um mit seiner ei- nigen geistlichen Braut, der Christlichen Kirchen, die Er gnädiglich und sanfft durch sein heiliges Wort, als auf einer schönen Sänffte, in dieser Welt füh- ret, und endlich zu sich in die ewige Freude und Herr- lichkeit bringet: Er leitet sie nach seinem Rath, und nimmt sie endlich mit Ehren an, Psalm 73, 24. da sie ewiglich bey ihm seyn, und seine Herrlichkeit, die ihm sein Vater gegeben, sehen wird. Joh. 17, 24.) Id so- lum observamus, per Regem Salomonem in textu denominatum intelligendum esse immediate Chri- stum, quod è v. 11. manifestum est, & communi Pa- trum calculo probatur, etsi ad Salomonis terreni le- cticam allusio facta esse potuerit, quo de tamen, ut Gregorius Nyssenus antea monuit, nihil certi con- stat. Nam in verbis sequentibus v. 14. ipsimet Para- phrastæ Vinarienses, cum B. Osiandro immediate per Regem Salomonem Christum intelligunt, Regem & Principem pacis Ebr. 7, 2. Ps. 110, 6. gloria & ho- nore coronatum Ebr. 2, 9. & caput, Sponsum & Sal- vatorem Ecclesiæ suæ constitutum Ephes. 1, 21. c. 5, 23. De qua, tanquam Sponsa sua, oppido gaudet Es. 62, 5. & æternum gaudebit Apocal. 19, 7. de quo etiam ver- sum prædictum 11. accepere Veteres, quamvis eun- dem vel de humana Christi natura, qua Filius Dei in incarnatione veluti coronatus fuerit, explica- rint: quæ Ambrosii lib. de Isaac. cap. 5. Athanasii in Synops. Philonis Carpathii, Cassiodori, Gregorii M. Bedæ, Anshelmi, Honorii & Bernhardi Serm. 2. Epi- phan. est expositio; Vel de corona spinea, quam & charitatis coronam etiam nonnulli dicunt, quia ex charitate illam gestare voluit, qua tempore passio- nis à matre Synagoga Judaica coronatus est, uti in- terpretatur Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Gregorius Nys- senus, & Bernhardus in h. l. de qua utraque explica- tione prolixe Gerhardus Postill. Salomon. ad Do- min. 1. Advent. & Dom. Palmarum. Theodoretius matrem appellat Judæam, quantum pertinet ad Christi humanitatem, quæ charitatis coronam illi in vita imposuit: Spinis enim illum contemtus causa coronavit, ipse vero per spinas suscepit diadema charitatis: fronte enim ignominiam pertulit atq; ultro ad mortis cruciatus accessit; quamobrem desponsationis diem illam vocavit & diem lætitiæ cordis ejus. Tunc quippe nuptiarum communio facta est, in Cœna nempe ultima, quando nuptiale convivium Eucharisticum instituit. Similiter tres Patres Anonymi apud Theodoret. Spectate desponsationis rationem in diademate, quo coronavit eum mater sua in die desponsationis ejus, in spinea nimirum Corona, quam Christi capiti imposuit Judæorum Synagoga, ex qua ipse est secundum carnem: in die salutiferæ mortis ejus, in qua proprio sanguine Ecclesiam sibi desponsavit: Et in die lætitiæ cordis ejus, qua quidem salutarem pro nobis mortem oppetens, nos ab hostis servitute liberavit, atque ita Patris obtemperans voluntati lætatus est Spiritu, licet carnis cruciatibus vexaretur. Unde tres reperiuntur sententiæ de die desponsationis & de corona. Prima ad incarnationem Filii Dei ac matrem Θεοτόκον; altera ad passionem ejusdem & Synagogam Judaicam, quæ mater ejus dicitur; Tertia ad glorificationem Christi refertur; circa quam vero dubium oritur, cur à matre dicatur honore coronatus? ubi dici poterit; quod mater, dum coronavit eum per contemptum spinea corona, quia per passionem intravit in gloriam, ejusdem gloriam, licet invita ac præter intentionem promoverit. Addunt tamen alii, præeunte Mercero, quartam explicationem, qua hæc referuntur ad Christi celebrationem: siquidem à matre, hoc est, ab Ecclesia glorificetur, ac celebretur, ac fideles sint ipsius gloria, laus & corona. 1. Thessal. 2, 19. Quod enim, inquit Mercerus, jubet spectare coronam, qua à matre sit coronatus, intellige summam gloriam, imo omnem & absolutissimum decorem, quem ab Ecclesia acceperit Christus, id est, quem ei detulerit, in eum spe omni & salute collocata, non quod à Patre omnem suam gloriam non haberet, sed quod per Ecclesiam Evangelii prædicatione toto orbe agnita fuerit Christi gloria, & regnum ejus promulgatum ac propagatum, id quod summæ fuit lætitiæ Christo, quod scil. tantum decorem sibi detulisset Ecclesia, agnoscens se ab eo redemtam. Sed Ecclesia mater quidem dicitur, at fidelium, non autem mater Christi. Hic vero de Christi matre sermo est; ut Sponsa Christi hîc exhibetur Ecclesia, non vero ut mater. Et simplicior explicatio videtur de corona vel passionis spinea, juxta quam tres Patres apud Theodor. hanc reddunt συνεχείας rationem: Quia Magistra animadvertit discipulas hæsitabundas propter se, atque admiratione plenas, ea quæ ad se pertinent explicare; in Sponso Christo vult eas deinceps salutis nostræ modum contueri & merito dubitare, atque admirari, quomodo ipse salutiferis cruciatibus, ac morte sua tranquillitatem, & vitam nobis largitus sit. Proinde egredimini, inquit, & videte filiæ Sion, omittite, quæ ad me ancillam attinent, considerare, & in Domino pacifico mentis aciem defigite, contemplantes, quomodo salutem hic nobis acquisiverit. Vel de corona exultationis & gloriæ, qua ipse διὰ τὸ πάθημα à matre secundum carnem, Synagoga Judaica, quia ex Judæis oriundus est, etsi interitum ejus & excisionem unice intendente, coronatus est. Quo pacto corona gloriæ à Patre accepta quidem, sed interventu matris & coronæ spineæ, quia per coronationem matris acerbam coronam reportavit æternæ majestatis gloriosam, Phil. 2, 9. Ebr. 2, 9. Quam explicationem è Veteribus Psellus probat apud Theodoretum, quamvis per matrem Sponsi Patris charitatem non adeo commode intelligat, eamque sequutus est Osiander, ut & Vinarienses.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

The Bridegroom proclaims the beauty of the Bride, by which he testifies to her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, cheeks, neck, and breasts, and the promptness of his own passion (by which she is compared to him), inviting her to himself, with a declaration of love, resting in the breasts of his love, and the sweetness of her lips, and the fragrance of the odors of her garments, comparing her to a fragrant garden, which he commands the North and South winds to blow through.

Ver. 1.

APART FROM THAT WHICH LIES WITHIN) The Greeks seem to have read both here and twice below עַלְמַתֵךְ. But in our Hebrew, within your hair: for the hair almost reaches to the eyes. YOUR HAIR, AS A FLOCK OF GOATS) In the Hebrew: Which rise in the morning from Mount Gilead; thus also among the Arabs גלש is taken. The head is compared to the most beautiful Mount Gilead: the goats leaping with hair on the head.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Sponsus pulchritudinem Sponsæ prædicat, qua oculos, capillos, dentes, labia, genas, collum, & ubera, suæq; passionis (qua illa ei comparata) promtitudinem testatur, eandem ad se invitans, cum declaratione amoris, acquiescentis uberibus amoris ejus, & dulcedine labiorum, ac suavitate odorum vestimentorum ipsius, comparans eandem horto odorifero, quem ventum Borealem & Austrinum perflare jubet.

Vers. 1.

ABSQVE EO, QVOD INTRINSECUS LATET) Videntur legisse Græci & hic & bis infra עַלְמַתֵךְ. At in Hebræo nostro, intra comam tuam: Coma enim ferme ad oculos pervenit. CAPILLUS TUUS, UT GREX CAPRARUM) In Hebræo: Quæ mane surgunt de monte Galaad; sic & Arabibus גלש sumitur. Monti pulcherrimo Galaad confertur caput: capreis capillisubsultantes in capite.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

ALL WITH TWIN OFFSPRING, AND THERE IS NO BARREN ONE AMONG THEM) In the Hebrew: All twins, and there is no aborting one among them. The teeth correspond to each other in equal order, nor is any part missing.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

OMNES GEMELLIS FOETIBUS, ET STERILIS NON EST INTER EAS) In Hebræo: Omnes geminæ, & abortiens non est inter eas. Dentes æquali ordine inter se respondent, nec ulla pars vacat.

## 4:3
Ver. 3.

AS A PIECE OF A POMEGRANATE) So are thy cheeks. BESIDES THAT WHICH IS HIDDEN WITHIN) In the Hebrew again: between thy hair. This means: thy cheeks are red, like the kernels in a pomegranate.

Grotius interprets this whole description of the beauty of the Bride literally concerning the Bride of Solomon, and he puts forward this sense as the proper one, and the one intended here by the Holy Spirit. But that these things cannot be understood literally is taught by the very similes employed in the description, which little accord with external beauty; yet they serve excellently for illustrating spiritual grace in a parabolic and figurative sense. And whence is it certain that she was of such beauty and συμμετρίαν (symmetry) in all parts as the daughter of Pharaoh, if external beauty is expressed here? The eyes of doves designate the enlightened eyes of the understanding, Eph. 1:14, because they are simple, ingenuous, modest, and bland. Thy eyes are as doves, i.e., according to the interpretation of Bede, the eyes of thy heart are simple and pure and entirely immune from all duplicity of deceiving and feigning. Likewise: Thy eyes are as doves; because thy senses are endowed with spiritual understanding. Likewise: The friend of Christ has the eyes of doves, because everyone who truly loves Him inwardly is not inflamed by any appetite for external things after the manner of kites, nor does he meditate on inflicting anything against any living being; which is said to be of dove-like meekness, for he contemplates all things that occur with a simple, mild, and humble heart. It can also be said that by the eyes are understood the Doctors, who are the eyes of the Church. Which explanation is approved by Mercer and others: just as the hair, within which the eyes are celebrated, according to the same are the sayings of Scripture, which like most beautiful hair adorn the Doctors of the Church, so that they may stand out more beautifully among the hair of the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. Thy hair is as a flock of goats that have ascended from Mount Gilead; here the hair is understood, according to Alcuin, as the faithful people, who provide the greatest ornament to the Church by their multitude: Gilead is explained as a heap of testimony, which fits well with the ordered multitude of the Saints. Similarly Gregory the Great and Philo of Carpathus interpret, as does Mercer: Blessed Luther rendered it, 'die beschoren sind auf dem Berge Gilead' (which are shorn on Mount Gilead), because גלש in the Targum is to be shorn, Lev. 13:41, and R. Joseph Kimchi, as his son reports, interpreted it thus: which are shorn and placed among the trees of the forest and appear so beautiful, as if they were combed with a comb; In the Weimar Paraphrase, with B. Luther leading, they are explained concerning the testimonies of Scripture in this way: Thy hair is like a flock of goats, which are shorn (as it were combed among the shrubs in the wood, and made fine and smooth) on Mount Gilead, which name signifies a house of witness, Gen. 31, 47. 48. and signifies the Holy Scripture, where many testimonies of God are abundantly contained, as is also indicated there in Luther's little gloss, and these are a glorious ornament of Christendom, at the same time also a means and instrument of spiritual fruitfulness in the rebirth and renewal of men, just as whole beautiful flocks adorn a mountain where they graze, and at the same time are very fruitful. Thy teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing, all with twin offspring and there is not a barren one among them. Or as others prefer, like the FLOCKS of shorn sheep, which have come up, etc. which, according to the literal sense, Cornelius a Lapide explains thus: The teeth of the Bride are compared not to flocks, but to the teeth of flocks or of shorn sheep, which nourish twin offspring, because the teeth of those seem sharper and stronger than the rest, inasmuch as they must both satisfy their own hunger, which they feel more on account of the cold of shearing, and in addition must sustain and suckle the twin offspring which they have brought forth; that is to say, the Bride has teeth so strong that she can pluck and digest food with them, sufficient not only for herself, but also for her twin offspring. As for the marrow of the meaning, most interpreters understand by teeth the Doctors of the Church, with Origen leading the way, hom. 17 on Gen. They are teeth, who provide the food of the Scriptures to those worthy of interpretation. explaining their understanding, they provide it to the body of the Church. These teeth ought to be white and pure, lest perhaps it be said to them: you who teach others, do not teach yourself. And according to Gregory of Nyssa, who observes in Homily 7, it is required in these mystical teeth, the preachers, that they be shorn, i.e., stripped of earthly weight, and that they be pure and bright by the washing of conscience, and that they ascend through just progress, and that they be not barren in any kind of virtue and exercise, but fruitful and fertile in any one. Gregory the Great has it thus: Holy preachers are well called teeth, because while they elucidate the Holy Scripture by explaining it to the lesser brethren, they chew it as if it were bread for little ones, like mothers for their children, by which the weak may grow strong for stronger things. These, indeed, are said to be like a flock of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing, because, while they remember that they have been washed from all sins in Baptism, they willingly lay down the burdens of the world; so that they may walk the more easily the more freely they proceed to attain and preach heavenly things. Similarly Cassiodorus, Justus of Urgel, Theodoret, Aponius, Carpathius, Jerome book 3 on Jer. ch. 3, Augustine, book 2 on Christian doctrine, Bede, Anselm, as also Alcuin, whose paraphrase I submit: In the hair they are designated as more fragile, but in the teeth as more perfect and also apt for ruling the Church, who are both shorn and washed, stripped by renouncing the world and cleansed by the washing of life, fruitful with twin charity. There is no one who does not bring forth the offspring of good work. The latter pertain to the fruit which they bear, and to the multitude of souls which they win for Christ and beget. 2 Cor. 4, 15. 1 Pet. 1, 23. B. Luther Vol. 2. Jena. Lat. f. 25. The Bride of Christ also has teeth, Cant. 4 and 6, i.e., rebukes, by which the Church chews and reproves sinners, and in turn converts and incorporates them into herself; they are like shorn sheep, i.e., meek, rebuking without fury and zeal, then shorn, that is, empty of the care of things, not seeking the gains and wool of the sheep. These teeth are figured in the jawbone, which Samson lifted and struck a thousand men with it, Jud. 15. But let us proceed in the words of the Canticle: v. 3 it has: Like a scarlet ribbon are thy lips and thy speech is sweet, which words Alcuin explains neatly with the following: By the scarlet ribbon the doctrine of truth is understood: The lips of the Bride are likened to scarlet, because the Church does not cease to preach the price of the Lord's blood (by which she was redeemed): or because holy preaching flames with the ardor of charity.

Like a piece of a pomegranate, so are thy cheeks. In the cheeks, modesty is expressed; in the pomegranate, the passion of Christ. The Bride therefore has the redness of the pomegranate in her cheeks, when she confesses the Sacrament of the Lord's passion with words and proves it with deeds. Cassiodorus and Bede again understand by the cheeks the preachers, who, while they announce the passion of Christ, exhibit a redness as it were outwardly; but when they demonstrate how great a utility of our redemption has resulted from it, and that man is not only justified from sins through the passion of Christ, but also attains divine fellowship, it is as if it were white, which lies hidden inwardly, just as when a pomegranate is broken, redness appears outwardly, but whiteness inwardly.

It follows in the Canticle: Thy neck is like the tower of David, which is built with battlements, a thousand shields hang from it and the armor of the strong. Philo Carpathius, Eugenius, Justus of Urgel, as also Gregory the Great, Hom. 15 on Ezech., interpret this tower of David as the Holy Scripture, from which the panoply of weapons is drawn to defeat all errors and depraved morals. Gregory the Great says: The miracles and the tremendous works of God, which Scripture commemorates, are the battlements, because they testify to the truth of God, protect them, and add strength against enemies, yet we are not able to imitate them. But the precepts of God and the examples of the Saints, which Scripture commemorates, are the shields, by which we are fortified, if we hold them in our hand and put them into practice. Justus of Urgel: A thousand shields hang from it. This tower can fittingly be understood as the Canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testament, which has been established as an exalted tower by the Holy Spirit. A thousand shields hang from it; this number is taken as the fullness of power, as in the Psalm: The word which he commanded, to a thousand generations. Therefore, in this Holy Scripture all the armor of the strong is found, from which one fights bravely either against the Devil or against his ministers. This is Justus: Which are also held by Philo of Carpathos. Nor do the Papists deny it, otherwise they would be μισόγραφοι: Alphonsus a Castro, book 3 against heretics, title Script. Scripture is the mystical tower of David, from which all the armor of the strong and of Catholic men hangs, therefore Heretics attempt to detract from the Holy Scriptures. Albertus Hungerus, Disput. Ingolstad. Year 82, under the title Defense of Scripture against Pseudo-Scripturarians, Conclusion 14. Holy Scripture is that tower of David, which was built with bulwarks, from which a thousand shields hang, and all the armor of the strong. Others say that the spiritual neck of the Bride is the Preachers, even though they have also been compared to teeth: because the same thing is sometimes accustomed to be figured by various similitudes. This interpretation does not depart much from the former: for the preacher of the word is compared to the tower of David only on account of the Word which he preaches, nor is he equipped with armor or shields except through Holy Scripture, in which the spiritual panoply is held: and it can only be called the neck of the Church when it belches forth the Word of GOD. Whence Gregory the Great on this passage: in the neck is the throat, in the throat is the voice. What then is designated by the neck of the Church, if not its sacred utterances? Psellus in Theodoret: But you, holy Church, understand for me the great neck to be Paul, who bore Christ the head of all, and if you have learned of any others similar to him. Theodoret himself: Your neck, which supports your head and face, holds all the doctrines of others, with which, as if with javelins, it pierces all adversaries.

It also has many shields, by which you are protected and extinguish the fiery darts of the enemy. For you are fortified with the armor of the Spirit, and you easily wound the enemies, since you abound with all the arrows of the strong: And you refute them now through the Prophets, now through the Apostles, and uncover their weakness. That the Doctors of the Church are designated by the neck, is taught especially by Gregory of Nyssa, Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, Aponius, Bede, Anselm, to which explanation the Chaldean paraphrase also seems to agree. Because just as the neck is the middle between the head and the members, connecting the latter to the head, so that the head also infuses Spirit and life through the neck into it, and conveys food into the stomach: So the preachers of the word are as it were the middle between Christ and the rest of the faithful, through whom Christ as the head derives his doctrine, spirit, and strength into the remaining faithful, and from whom these receive the spiritual food of the soul. Such a neck, says Nyssenus, was Paul, who indeed carried the name of the Lord, having been made a vessel of election for the Lord, and the Head was accurately adapted to him so that whatever he said, it was no longer he himself speaking, but his head was speaking, just as he indicated to the Corinthians, that it was Christ who was speaking in him, and who was directing the word of truth by the Spirit. Thus Alcuin also paraphrases in his Compendium: The neck is the Preachers, by whose faith and constancy, the same City is firm and everywhere impregnable. The bulwarks of the same city are the fortifications of the sacred Scriptures, or the examples of the preceding Fathers. A thousand shields hang from it, because as many as there are precepts in the divine books, so many are the defenses of our breast, by which we are defended against all snares. All the armor of the strong; all instruction is either of operation or of heavenly doctrine, through which we not only escape, but also overcome. The former explanation, that Holy Scripture is designated by the neck, is embraced by our Gerhard, and pursued at length in his Postilla on Solomon for the Sunday Invocavit, which the Weimar Paraphrasts also retain.

Finally, the breasts of the Bride are treated in v. 5. Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies. Since that comparison of breasts and young roes appears remote and incongruous, about which Interpreters labor in various ways, Titelmannus posits a hypallage: But it may seem that the words can be most simply explained thus: thy two breasts are (like) those of two twin roes, which feed among the lilies (the breasts, namely, which they suck and by which they are nourished: and thus perhaps the preceding things can also be explained not inconveniently: For the authentic text does not object: as it is said in v. 1. Thy eyes are like (the eyes of) a Dove; so let the rest also be explained in the same manner.) Thy hair (not as a flock, but) as a flock of goats (hair) which arise from Mount Gilead, (as R. Jonah explains from the Arabic language, as R. Kimchi testifies, which explanation is approved by Grotius) or which have been washed and placed between the trees of the Forest and thus appear beautiful, as if they were combed with a comb, as B. Luther explains with R. Kimchi. And that these can be explained in this way is also observed by Mercerus: thy hair is like the hair of a flock of goats, (so that the word hair is repeated) which stand out and are seen from Mount Gilead, where the pastures were most joyful and abundant, just as he himself interpreted the later words with R. Aben-Ezra: Thy teeth (not as a flock of shorn ones, but) as the teeth of a flock (of sheep) that have come up from the washing: thy two breasts (not like two young roes, but) like (the breasts) of two twin roes, (by which they were nourished) of a goat (or such as they have in a goat and suck from her two twin young) which feed among the lilies. For as the goat nourishes the young, so the Church nourishes the Jews and

Gentiles. However, Interpreters teach at length that the breasts are compared to the young roes themselves; and this opinion seems to be confirmed by the description in chapter 7, 3, although the interpretation I mentioned can also have a place there. By the breasts, however, most Fathers understand the two Testaments or the doctrine of the O. and N. Testament, Justus Orgelit, Philo Carpathius, Aponius, Gregory the Great, book 24 of the Morals, ch. 10, Anselm, etc., which mutually regard each other, where also lilies or the sweetest sayings, by which the mind may be refreshed, are found. Theodoret on this passage: By the breasts, he says, we again receive the fountains of doctrine, which provide things suitable for each age, to some indeed milk, but to others solid food. Gilbert Folliot: These are the breasts which we suck, from which we receive growth, so that we may please Christ the King, the two Testaments, of which one is preparatory, the other consummating. Some Doctors wish for the breasts to denote the Doctors, namely Gregory of Nyssa, Cassiodorus, Bede, as those who feed the people with the milk of doctrine: so that the twins designate concord in doctrine and preaching, as St. Gregory notes. The Weimar Paraphrasts understand the two Sacraments, the explanation of which, whoever wishes, will be able to compare. Nor does it stand in the way that other things have been compared to the Doctors, the Word, and divine doctrine, and Holy Scripture; for in many ways, as Bede says, and in many modes of figures, the same mysteries of Christ and the Church are repeated, but when repeated they always bring something new, by which it either procures an increase for the same mysteries, or through the very novelty delights the minds of the hearers more. Thus St. Gregory applies all these to the Doctors of the Church, but for different reasons, so that they are indeed called the eyes of the Church, because they accurately observe everything; teeth, because they rebuke the wicked, and cast those consumed by the tooth of chastisement into the body of the Church; the Neck, because they supply the vital Spirit of grace and spiritual foods to the rest of the body; Breasts, because they exhibit milk to the little ones in Christ. Which diverse comparison can be applied also to the diverse gifts and virtues, in which some excel others in the Church: so that some are eyes, because of the sharpness of contemplation; others teeth, because of the power of rebuke; others lips, because of the sweetness of preaching; others the neck, because of the strength, fortitude, and virtue of support; others breasts, because of the peculiar faculty of the nourishment of the little ones. For the Holy Spirit distributes his gifts to each one as he wills, so that one may be an eye in the mystical body of the Church, another an ear, another may perform the function of another member, 1 Cor. 12, 11. et seqq. If anyone wishes for regard to be had for the diverse offices of teachers in the Church, we shall not object, provided he does not distribute the offices according to the autonomy of the Pope, but according to the norm of Holy Scripture and the form of the ancient Church. Thus the eyes of the Bride will be Bishops or Superintendents; the Teeth, Pastors rebuking heretical and wicked men; the Neck, Doctors defending the Church; the scarlet Lips, Preachers, because they ought above all to be red with the blood of Christ; the breasts, Catechists, who instill milk into the little ones in Christ. It does not, however, seem necessary that we refer everything to the ministers of the word, since in the mystical body of the Church various members are found, and various are the gifts of the Church, by which she is beautiful, so that it may not inconveniently be said that this or that is designated. To pursue all of these would be the work of a proper commentary; let it suffice here to have tasted a few, so that it may be clear that a sense consistent with the marrow can be given, and there is no need that we understand these according to the bark of the letter, much less that we believe with Grotius that they were said of the Bride of Solomon. To whom we must now return.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

SICUT FRAGMEN MALI PUNICI) Ita genæ tuæ. ABSQVE EO, QVOD INTRINSECUS LATET) In Hebræo iterum: inter comam tuam. Hoc vult: genæ tuæ rubent, ut acini in malo punico.

Totam hanc descriptionem pulchritudinis Sponsæ Grotius secundum literam de Sponsa Salomonis interpretatur, eumque sensum ceu proprium, & à Spiritu S. hîc intentum venditat. At secundum literam hæc intelligi non posse, vel ipsa in descriptione adhibita similia edocent, quæ externæ pulchritudini parum congruunt; spirituali autem venustati sensu parabolico & figurato illustrandæ eximie inserviunt. Et unde constat, eam quoad omnes partes pulchritudinem & συμμετρίαν fuisse Pharaonidæ, si pulchritudo externa hîc exprimatur? Oculi columbarum oculos illuminatos intellectus designant Ephes. 1, 14. quia illi simplices, ingenui, pudici, blandi. Oculi tui columbarum, i. e. interprete Beda, oculi cordis tui simplices & mundi atque ab omni duplicitate fallendi ac simulandi prorsus immunes. Item: Oculi tui Columbarum; quia sensus tui spirituali sunt intellectu præditi. Item: Oculos columbarum habet amica Christi, quia omnis, qui illum veraciter intus amat, nullo externarum rerum appetitu, milvorum more accenditur, nulli viventium adversum quid inferre meditatur; quod columbinæ fertur esse mansuetudinis, qui cuncta, quæ occurrunt, simplici, miti & humili corde contemplatur. Dici etiam potest, per oculos intelligi Doctores, qui Ecclesiæ sunt oculi. Quæ explicatio Mercero & aliis probata: uti Coma, intra quas oculi celebrantur, secundum eosdem sunt dicta Scripturæ, quæ comarum pulcherrimarum instar ornant Doctores Ecclesiæ, ut inter comas testimoniorum S. literarum pulchrius emineant. Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum, quæ adscenderunt de monte Galaad; Hîc intelliguntur capilli secundum Alcuinum populi fideles, qui maximum decus sua numerositate præbent Ecclesiæ: Galaad acervus testimonii explicatur, qui bene convenit ordinatæ multitudini Sanctorum. Similiter Gregor. M. & Philo Carpathius interpretantur, ut & Mercerus: B. Lutherus reddidit, die beschoren sind auf dem Berge Gilead, quia גלש in Thargum est decalvari Levit. 13, 41. & R. Joseph. Kimchi, referente ejus filio, sic interpretatus est: quæ detersæ sunt funt & positæ inter arbores sylvæ & ita speciosæ appa- rent, quasi essent pectæ pectine; In Paraphrasi Vina- riensi præeunte B. Luthero exponuntur de testi- moniis Scripturæ hoc pacto : Deine Haar ist wie die Ziegen = Heerde, die beschoren (zwischen dem Ge- sträuch im Holze gleichsam gekämet, und fein schlecht gemacht) sind auf dem Berge Gilead, welcher Na- me heiffet ein Zeugenhausse, Genes. 31, 47. 48. und bedeutet die H. Schrifft, da viel Zeugniß von GOtt häuffig innen sind, wie daselbst auch in Lutheri Glößlein angedeutet wird, und sind diese eine herr- liche Zierde der Christenheit, zugleich auch ein Mittel und Werckzeug der geistlichen Fruchtbarkeit in der Wiedergebuhrt und Erneurung der Menschen, gleich wie gantze schöne Heerden einen Berg zieren, da sie weiden, und zugleich sehr fruchtbar sind. Dentes tui sicut greges tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, omnes gemellis fœtibus & sterilis non est inter eas. Vel quod alii malunt, sicut GREGVM tonsarum, quæ adscenderunt &c. quod juxta literæ corticem Cornelius a Lapide ita explicat: Dentes Sponsæ com- parari non gregibus, sed dentibus gregum sive ovium tonsarum, quæ gemellos nutriunt fœtus, quia dentes illorum videntur cæteris acutiores & validiores, ut- pote quibus & famem suam, quam ob frigus tonsionis majorem sentiunt, satiare, & insuper gemellos fœtus, quos genuerunt, sustentare & lactare debent; q. d. Sponsa adeo validos habet dentes, ut iis cibum car- pere & digerere possit non sibi tantum, sed & suis gemellis fœtibus sufficientem. Quoad medullam sensus plerique Interpp. per dentes intelligunt Docto- res Ecclesiæ, præeunte Origene hom. 17. in Gen. Den- tes sunt, qui Scripturarum cibos dignis interpretation. explanantes earum intellectum Ecclesiæ corpori submi- nistrant. Hi dentes candidi debent esse & puri, ne forte illis dicatur: qui alios doces, te ipsum non doces. Et Gregorio Nysseno, qui Homil. 7. observat, in dentibus hisce mysticis prædicatoribus requiri, ut sint tonsi, h. e. nudati pondere terreno, & ut lavacro conscientiæ sint puri & nitidi, & justum per profectum adscen- dant, & ut in nullo genere virtutis & exercitio sint steriles, sed in quolibet fœcundi & fertiles. Greg. M. ita habet: Dentes bene sancti Prædicatores vocantur, quia dum sanctam Scripturam exponendo minoribus fratribus elucidant, quasi panem parvulis, tanquam matres filiis commasticant, quo infirmi ad fortiora convalescant. Hi nimirum sicut grex tonsarum, quæ ascenderunt de lavacro, esse dicuntur, quia, dum se a peccatis omnibus in Baptismo ablutos esse recordan- tur, libenter onera mundi deponunt; ut ad cælestia consequenda & prædicanda, quo liberius, eo facilius gradiantur. Similiter Cassiodorus, Justus Orgelita- nus, Theodoretus, Aponius, Carpathius, Hieronymus lib. 3. in Jer. c. 3. Augustinus, lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. Beda, Anshelmus, ut & Alcuinus, cujus subjicio pa- raphrasin: In capillis fragiliores, in dentibus vero perfectiores quoque & ad regendam Ecclesiam apti de- signantur, qui & tonsi & loti sunt, nudati renuncian- do seculo & vitæ lavacro mundati, gemina charita- te fœcundi. Non est, qui fœtus boni operis non agat. Posteriora ad fructum, quem ferunt, & ad anima- rum multitudinem, quas Christo lucrifaciunt & gignunt, pertinent. 2. Cor. 4, 15. 1. Petr. 1, 23. B. Lu- therus Tom. 2. Jen. Lat. f. 25. Sponsa Christi dentes quoque habet Cant. 4. & 6. h. e. increpationes, quibus Ecclesia mandit & arguit peccatores, rursusque con- vertit & sibi incorporat; sunt sicut oves detonsæ, mi- tes scil. arguentes sine furia & Zelo, tum tonsæ, id est, rerum cura inanes, non quærentes lucra & lanas ovium. Hi dentes figurati sunt in maxilla, quam Sam- son levavit & percussit in ea mille viros Jud. 15. Sed pergamus in verbis Cantici: v. 3. ita habet: Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua & eloquium tuum dulce, quæ verba concinne explicat cum feqq. Alcuinus; Vit- ta coccinea doctrina veritatis intelligitur : Labia Sponsæ cocco afsimilantur, quia Dominici fanguinis, (quo redemta est) pretium prædicare non cefsat Ec- clesia : vel quia prædicatio sancta charitatis ardore flammefcit.

Sicut fragmen mali punici, ita genæ tuæ. Ingenis verecundia, in malo punico passio Chri- sti exprimitur. Habet ergo ruborem in genis Sponsa mali punici, cum Sacramentum Dominicæ passionis verbis fatetur & factis probat. Cassiodorus & Beda per genas iterum prædicatores intelligunt, qui dum passionem Christi annunciant, quasi ruborem exte- rius exhibent; cum autem demonstrant, quanta uti- litas nostræ redemtionis inde provenerit, & quod ho- mo per passionem Christi non solum a peccatis justifi- cetur, sed & divinum consortium adipiscatur, quasi candidum est, quod intrinfecus latet, ficuti malum punicum cum frangitur, exterius rubor, interius au- tem candor apparet.

Sequitur in Cantico: Sicut turris David collum tuum, quæ ædificata est cum pro- pugnaculis, mille clypei pendent ex ea & armatura fortium. Turrim hanc Davidis Philo Carpathius, Eugenius, Justus Orgelitanus, ut & Gregorius M. Hom. 15. in Ezech. de Scriptura S. ex qua depro- mitur armorum panoplia ad debellandos omnes errores & pravos mores, interpretantur. Greg. M. Miracula inquit, & opera Dei tremenda, quæ Scri- ptura commemorat, sunt propugnacula, quia verita- tem Dei testantur, protegunt illos, & contra hostes vi- res addunt, ea tamen non valemus imitari. Præcepta autem Dei & exempla Sanctorum, quæ Scriptura commemorat, sunt clypei, quibus munimur, si manu ea tenemus & in opera redigimus. Justus Orgelitan. Mille clypei pendent ex ea. Potest hæc turris Scri- ptura Canonica V. & N. Test. convenienter intelligi, quæ per Spir. S. turris excelsa constituta est. Mille clypei pendent ex ea; hic numerus per plenitudinem potestatis accipitur, ut in Psalmo: Verbum quod man- davit, in mille generationes. Itaque in hac S. Scriptura omnis armatura fortium reperitur, ex qua vel con- tra Diabolum, vel contra ministros ejus fortiter pu- gnatur. Hæc Justus : Quæ etiam habentur apud Philonem Carpathium. Neque abnuunt Papistæ, alioqui μισόγραφοι: Alphonsus a Castro lib. 3. ad- vers. hæretic. tit. Script. Scriptura est mystica turris David, ex qua omnis armatura fortium & Catholico- rum Virorum pendet, ideo Hæretici conantur Sacris Scripturis detrahere. Albertus Hungerus Disput. Ingolstad. Anno 82. sub titulo Defens. Script. contra Pseudo-Scripturarios Concl. 14. Scriptura Sacr. est turris illa Davidis, quæ ædificata est, cum propugnaculis, ex qua mille clypei pendent, omnisque armatura fortium. Alii collum spirituale Sponsæ Prædicatores esse dicunt, etsi iidem etiam dentibus comparati fuerint : quia res eadem variis similitu- dinibus figurari quandoque solet. Quæ interpre- tatio a priori non multum abit : nam turri David Prædicator verbi comparatur non nisi ob Ver- bum, quod prædicat, neque armatura aut clypeis instructus est, nisi per Scripturam Sacram, in qua spiritualis panoplia habetur : & collum Eccle- siæ tum solum dici potest, cum Verbum DEI eructat. Unde Gregorius M. in h. l. in collo gut- tur, in gutture vox est. Quid ergo per collum Ec- clesiæ, nisi sacra ejus eloquia designantur? Psellus apud Theodoretum: Tu vero mihi sancta Ecclesia collum magnum Paulum intellige, qui caput omnium Christum gestavit, & si quos alios, similes illi didicisti. Theodoretus ipse: Habet collum tuum, quod caput tuum & faciem sustinet, omnes aliorum doctrinas, qui- bus tanquam jaculis cunctos adversarios transigit.

Habet item clypeos multos, quibus protegeris & ignita hostis tela extinguis. Munitus enim es Spiritus armatura, & facile hostes vulneras, cum omnibus fortium sagittis abundes : Eosque modo per Prophetas, modo per Apostolos redarguis, atq; ipsorum retegis imbecillitatem. Doctores autem Ecclesiæ per collum designari, cumprimis docent Gregorius Nyssenus, Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, Aponius, Beda, Anshelmus, cui explicationi congruere etiam Chaldæa paraphrasis videtur. Quia sicut collum medium est inter caput & membra, illa capiti connectens, ita ut caput etiam Spiritum & vitam per collum in ea influat, & cibum in stomachum trajiciat : Sic prædicatores verbi quasi medii sunt inter Christum & cæteros fideles, per quos Christus ceu caput, doctrinam suam, spiritum & robur in fideles reliquos derivat, & a quibus hi cibum animæ spiritualem accipiunt. Tale collum, inquit Nyssenus, erat Paulus, qui portavit quidem nomen Domini, factus Domino vas electionis, & ei accurate adaptatum fuit Caput ut & quodcunque diceret, non amplius esset ipse loquens, sed caput ejus loqueretur, prout indicavit Corinthiis, Christum esse, qui in se loquebatur, & qui Spiritu verbum dirigebat veritatis. Sic παραφράζει etiam in Compendio Alcuinus : Collum sunt Prædicatores, quorum fide & constantia, in eadem Civitate firma est & undique inexpugnabilis. Propugnacula autem ejusdem civitatis Scripturarum sacrarum munimina sunt, vel Patrum præcedentium exempla. Mille clypei pendent ex ea, quia quot in divinis libris præcepta sunt, tot sunt nostri pectoris munimina, quibus contra omnes insidias defendimur. Omnis armatura fortium ; omnis instructio est vel operationis vel doctrinæ cælestis, per quam non solum evadimus, sed & superamus. Priorem explicationem, quod S. Scriptura per collum designetur, amplectitur Gerhardus noster, ac late prosequitur in Postill. Salomon. ad Domin. Invocavit, quam etiam retinent Paraphrastæ Vinarienses.

Tandem de uberibus Sponsæ agitur v. 5. Duo ubera tua sunt duo hinnuli capreæ gemelli, qui pascuntur in liliis. Quum remota & inconcinna appareat illa comparatio uberum & hinnulorum, de qua laborant varie Interpp. Titelmannus hypallagen statuit : Sed videri queat, simplicissime ita exponi posse verba : duo ubera tua sunt (velut) duorum hinnulorum gemellorum capreæ, qui pascuntur in liliis (ubera, quæ scil. illi sugunt & quibus lactantur : atque ita fortassis non inconvenienter præcedentia etiam explicari poterunt : Textus enim authenticus non repugnat : ut quemadmodum dicitur v. 1. Oculi tui sicut (oculi) Columbæ ; sic cætera etiam ad eundem modum exponantur.) Capillus tuus (non ut grex, sed) ut gregis caprarum (capillus) quæ mane surgunt de monte Galaad, (ut R. Jona ex lingua Arabica, teste R. Kimchio explicat, quæ expositio Grotio probatur) vel quæ detersæ sunt & positæ inter arbores Sylvæ & ita speciosæ apparent, quasi essent pexe pectine, uti cum R. Kimchi explicat B. Lutherus. Atque ita exponi hæc posse observat quoque Mercerus : pilus tuus pilo similis est gregis caprarum, (ut שער pilus repetatur) quæ prominent & conspiciuntur ex monte Galaad, ubi lætissima & uberrima erant pascua, quemadmodum posteriora verba ipse cum R. Aben-Ezra interpretatus est : Dentes tui (non ut grex tonsarum, sed) ut dentes gregis (ovium) tonsarum, quæ adscenderunt de lavacro : duo ubera tua (non sicut duo hinnuli, sed) sicut (ubera) duorum hinnulorum gemellorum, (quibus illi lactabantur) capreæ (vel qualia in caprea habent & sugunt duo hinnuli ejus gemelli) qui pascuntur inter lilia. Ut enim caprea lactat hinnulos, ita Ecclesia lactat Judæos &

gentes. Hinnulis tamen ipsis ubera comparari In- terpp. prolixe docent; ac videtur hæc sententia e descriptione cap. 7, 3. confirmari, quamvis & ibi ea, quam dixi, interpretatio locum habere possit. Per ubera autem duo Testamenta vel doctrinam V. & N. Testamenti plerique Patres intelligunt, Justus Or- gelit. Philo Carpathius, Aponius, Gregorius M. lib. 24. moral. cap. 10. Anshelmus &c. quæ se invicem mutuo respiciunt, ubi etiam lilia vel suavissima di- cta, quibus animus reficiatur, inveniuntur. Theo- doretus in h. l. Per ubera, inquit, rursus doctrinæ fon- tes accipimus, qui singulis ætatibus congruentia sub- ministrant, aliis quidem lac, aliis autem solidum ci- bum. Gilbertus Foljoth: Hæc sunt ubera, quæ su- gimus, a quibus incrementa suscipimus, ut Christo Regi placeamus, duo Testamenta, quorum unum præ- paratorium est, alterum consummans. Nonnulli Doctores per ubera notari volunt, nimirum Grego- rius Nyssenus, Cassiodorus, Beda, utpote qui populum doctrinæ lacte pascunt: ut gemelli designent concor- diam in doctrina & prædicatione, notante S. Gre- gorio. Paraphrastæ Vinarienses duo Sacramenta intelligunt, quorum explicationem, qui volet, con- ferre poterit. Nec vero obstat, quod Doctoribus, Verbo, & doctrinæ divinæ, ac Scripturæ S. alia com- parata fuerint; multisarie enim, ut Beda ait, & mul- tis figurarum modis eadem Christi & Ecclesiæ myste- ria repetuntur, sed repetita semper aliquid novi affe- runt, quo vel eisdem mysteriis augmentum procuret, vel per ipsam novitatem animos audientium amplius delectet. Ita S.
