Gregorius hæc omnia Doctoribus Ecclesiæ, sed ob diversos respectus applicat, ut nempe iidem dicantur oculi Ecclesiæ, quia accura- te omnia observant; dentes, quia improbos corri- piunt, & castigationis dente confectos in Ecclesiæ corpus ingerunt; Collum, quia vitalem gratiæ Spi- ritum & spirituales cibos reliquo corpori submi- nistrant; Ubera, quia lac parvulis in Christo exhi- bent. Quæ diversa comparatio adhiberi potest etiam diversis donis & virtutibus, quibus alii præ aliis in Ecclesia pollent: ut alii sint oculi, ob acri- moniam contemplationis; alii dentes, ob vim corre- ptionis; alii labia ob suavitatem prædicationis; alii collum ob robur, fortitudinem & virtutem sustenta- tionis; alii ubera, ob peculiarem facultatem nutritio- nis parvulorum. Distribuit enim S. S. unicuique sua dona, sicut vult, ut alius in Ecclesiæ corpore mysti- co sit oculus, alius auris, alius alterius membri vi- cem præstet 1. Cor. 12, 11. seqq. Si quis ad munia di- versa doctorum in Ecclesia respectum haberi velit, non refragabimur, modo non distribuat munia, juxta Papæ αὐτονομίαν, sed juxta Scripturæ S. nor- mam & antiquæ Ecclesiæ formam. Sic oculi Spon- sæ erunt Episcopi vel Superintendentes; Dentes Pastores Hæreticos atque improbos corripientes; Collum Doctores Ecclesiam propugnantes; Labia coccinea Concionatores, quia rubere imprimis de- bent sanguine Christi, ubera Catechetæ, qui lac in- stillant parvulis in Christo. Non tamen necessum videtur, ut ad ministros verbi referamus omnia, quum in corpore mystico Ecclesiæ varia reperian- tur membra, ac varia sint Ecclesiæ dona, quibus illa speciosa est, ut vel ista vel hæc designata esse non in- commode dicatur. Quæ persequi omnia justi foret Commentarii; sufficiant hic quædam delibasse, ut constet, dari posse sensum medullæ convenientem, nec opus esse, ut secundum corticem literæ hæc in- telligamus, nedum ut de Sponsa Salomonis dicta esse cum Grotio credamus. Ad quem nunc nobis revertendum erit.

## 4:4
Vers. 4. A THOUSAND SHIELDS HANG FROM IT] He compares the pearls hanging from the neck to those shields hanging from the tower.

An overly arbitrary, overly jejune gloss. And what will become of all the armor of the mighty, what of the bulwarks? Was the neck of the Bride adorned with such ornaments, which were like bulwarks, or did they represent all the armor of the mighty? Who does not see that these things are mystical: and that the neck of the mystical Bride is compared to the tower of David, and by that description of the Davidic tower is designated the strength of Holy Scripture, in which we have bulwarks, a thousand shields, i.e., as many as are sufficient, and all the armor of the mighty, which are drawn from Scripture, as from a sacred panoply, for the defense of the Church and the defeat of its enemies. Concerning which we have already spoken, and have brought forward the very confession of the Papist adversaries.

Latin:

Vers. 4. MILLE CLYPEI PENDENT EX EA] Clypeis illis de turre pendentibus confert uniones pendentes de collo.

Nimis arbitraria, nimis jejuna glossa. Et quid fiet omni armaturæ fortium, quid propugnaculis? Num collum Sponsæ vest ebatur talibus ornamen- tis, quæ erant similia prœpugnaculis, aut omnem ar- maturam fortium referebant? Quis non videt hæc mystica esse: ac Sponsæ mysticæ collum turri com- parari Davidis, eaque descriptione turris Davidicæ designari robur Scripturæ Sacræ, in qua propugna- cula habemus mille clypeos h. e. tot, quot sufficiunt, & omnem armaturam fortium, quæ e Scriptura, tanquam e sacra panoplia, ad defensionem Eccle- siæ & debellationem hostium ejusdem depromun- tur. Quo de jam diximus, ipsamque adversariorum Papistarum confessionem adduximus.

## 4:6
Ver. 6.

TO THE MOUNTAIN OF MYRRH AND TO THE HILL OF FRANKINCENSE] Thus he calls the breasts because of their most sweet odor.

But this gloss is again both too frivolous, and entirely new and unheard of: that by the mountain of Myrrh and the hill of frankincense the breasts of the Bride, the daughter of Pharaoh, are denoted. And the matter of the breasts and teats had already been dealt with under another comparison in v. 5, of fawns, or of the breasts which they suck. Although indeed various opinions are read concerning the sense of these words, yet, so far as I know, the Grotius invention has never come into anyone's mind.

In the Hebrew text, in the same verse, there precede those things which the Fathers and most Interpreters refer to the preceding verse, since the reason for the accents in the Poetic books is not always observed: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, whence a double Interpretation: The former is this: Who feed among the lilies, until the day breathes, etc., which most explain concerning the consummation of the age: until the shadows of the sorrow of this age flee, and the day of eternal happiness breathes and shines forth. For here is night, says Gregory the Great, but there will be day, because here we are dim-sighted in the brightness of truth, there God himself, the whole truth, will shine upon our minds. Alcuin: Who feed among the lilies, i.e., the most pure examples of the Holy Fathers, until we pass through the shadows of present mortality, as the eternal day breathes. And this is according to the former connection. But as regards the other connection, Mercerus embraces it, and thinks it looks to the shadow of the Old Testament and the day of the New Testament. Therefore the Lord says, according to him, that until the day breathes and shines brighter, and the legal shadows have fled, the light having now arisen for the world with his advent, he will act in the house of the sanctuary, and will dwell there with the ancient people, because the temple was built on Mount Moriah. In which manner Mercerus had also explained a similar expression in chap. 2, 17: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee; return, be like, my beloved, to a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether, so that meanwhile, while the clear day shines and fuller salvation is shown to the world through Christ, when the shadow of the Old Testament and the sorrow and trouble will flee, he may be present with his Church, and come to help it with wondrous speed from those scented mountains, supplying scents by which it may be refreshed and strengthened. But in both places most other Interpreters, neglecting the distinction of the accents, refer that description of feeding among the lilies to the preceding words, both where there was speech about the Bridegroom in chap. 2, 16: My beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the lilies in the most pleasant and most fragrant pastures, until the day breathes, etc., and here concerning the Bride and the twin fawns of the faithful Jews and Gentiles, who feed among the lilies until the consummation of the age.

Now therefore, as to the present words; I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense, seven interpretations of them are found: The first, concerning the house of the Sanctuary on Mount Moriah, we have already indicated: where incense, prayers, and sacrifices were offered to God. The second is of those who think the Bride is now being called back by the Bridegroom, so that she may go with him to the mountain of Myrrh through mortification, and to the hill of frankincense through devotion; Or also that the Bride promises that she wishes to visit those who are devoted to the mortification of the flesh and the devotion of prayer. Thus Gilbert Foliot: I will go to the mountain of Myrrh, i.e., I myself will presently visit the Church, which is a mountain of myrrh and a hill of frankincense. But the mountain of Myrrh is the height of mortification, of which the Apostle says, mortify your members which are upon the earth. But the Church mortifies these things by considering the things which are above. But the hill of frankincense is the humility of prayer, by which the Church suspends itself on high, and as if from the censer of the heart, the smoke of incense ascends. Alcuin in Compend.: In myrrh the mortification of the flesh is expressed, in incense the devotion of prayer; as if the Bride were saying, I will frequent them and will glorify with pious illumination those whom I suspect to be sublime in the virtue of passion or prayer. And so also Gregory the Great and Bede in this place. A third explanation seems akin, that of B. Osiander: I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of frankincense, that is, I will approach with chaste and spiritual and holy love to my Church, whose summit is like a mountain, in which Myrrh is born; or hills, in which Frankincense grows: for all things in her are elegant, pleasing, pure, clean, she has nothing of filth or impurity. The fourth exposition is more common and that of most of the Fathers, Gregory. Nyssenus, Theodoret, three Anonymous authors, and Psellus in the same, and others, who refer the mountain of Myrrh to the passion, and the hill of frankincense to the resurrection of Christ. Theodoret: when you are so beautiful and wounded by the wound of love for me, I will suffer death for you, and will willingly ascend the mountain of myrrh: but I will rise again, and return to the hill of frankincense. See Cornelius a Lapide in this place. Fifth, B. Gerhard understands by the mountain of myrrh, as also by the hill of frankincense, the mountain of Golgotha and the passion of Christ, Postill. Salomon. Hom. on the day of the great passion, page 660. Which opinion is also approved by the authors of the Weimar Paraphrase. Sixth, concerning the departure of Christ into Heaven, Piscator, Junius, and Tremellius understand it as if to say: until the evening of the world arrives, that I may take you to myself, I shall meanwhile depart into Heaven and shall be delighted by the fragrance of the Angels and of the spirits of the just and perfect; into the heavenly Jerusalem, where those friends who cherish me have already been received, and whose services are most fragrant. Seventh, Dürfeldius accepts these words of the Bride in such a way that by the mountain of myrrh and frankincense, Hermon and Lebanon are noted as if they were mountains of myrrh and incense; and by the former, indeed, are designated purity, beauty, holiness, and the sweet-smelling fragrance and gifts redundant to the Church from the merit of Christ's passion; by the latter, however, the prayers of the Saints are designated; so that the Bride, awakened from the sleep of sin, may ascend full of confidence to the mountain of myrrh and frankincense. But it is manifest that here the words of the Bridegroom are continued, who also in the following verse weaves together the speech begun concerning the beauty of the Bride. Therefore, that interpretation seems to be preferred which wishes to refer here to the passion of Christ (by which that beauty of the Church had to be compared) or, if you still insist on persisting in the description of the beauty of the Bride, I would say that her breast and belly are designated as pleasing to the Bridegroom by the incense of devotion and the mortification of the flesh. This will be the eighth exposition, but one born from the conjunction of the second and third, or certainly not much different from them. And thus, through the breasts of the Bride, the belly is celebrated, because it becomes like a mountain of myrrh on account of the mortification of the flesh, and her breast, because it is like the hills of frankincense on account of the devotion of the heart: because it is subjoined: You are so beautiful, my friend, and there is no spot in you: and, as all things are drawn together into a summary, after a review of most of the members, the beauty of the Bride is proclaimed in these words. Theodoret rightly interprets what is said concerning imputed beauty: The Bride became immaculate and beautiful, because she was made near to the Bridegroom, and thus she received all splendors and was rendered luminous from the Light itself. Concerning the beauty also, which comes to us through renewal, three Anonymous Fathers explain not inappropriately: She is all beautiful; because she is beautiful in mind and soul and flesh: And indeed in flesh, inasmuch as it is purged here from the force and efficacy of perturbations, and adorned with the habits of virtues; in soul, however, as one who is freed here from every vice of concupiscence, and adorned with the discourses or reasons of the precepts: in mind, however, as one who is freed from base thoughts, and shines forth in the Holy Spirit through the grace of Deification. And for that reason there is no spot in you, because you have been made near to me on account of perfection. But we seek and expect this beauty here more truly than we obtain it in this life Rom. 7, 24. 2. Cor. 7, 1. which indeed we are about to attain in the other life Ephes. 5, 14. 1. Cor. 13. Alcuin says she is all beautiful, in all those who fear God, small and great, so that he seems to have understood it not of the perfection of degrees (of beauty), but of parts.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

AD MONTEM MYRRHÆ ET AD COLLEM THURIS] Sic vocat mammas ob suavissimum odorem.

Hæc vero iterum & frivola nimis, & nova pror- sus atque inaudita est glossa: per montem Myrrhæ & Collem thuris mammas Sponsæ, filiæ Pharaonis no- tari. Et de mammis atque uberibus jam actum erat sub alia comparatione v. 5. hinnulorum, vel ube- rum, quæ illi sugunt. Quanquam vero de verborum istorum sensu variæ legantur sententiæ, nemini ta- men, quod sciam, unquam in mentem venit Gro- tianum commentum.

Præcedunt in Ebræo textu, in eodem versu, quæ Patres & Interpp. plerique ad versum præce- dentem referunt, siquidem ratio accentuum in li- bris Poeticis non semper habita: Donec adspiret dies & fugiant umbræ, unde gemina Interpretatio: Prior hæc est: Qui pascuntur in liliis, donec dies aspiret &c. quod de consummatione seculi plerique exponunt: donec fugiant umbræ mœroris seculi hujus, & adspiret atque illucescat dies felicitatis æternæ. Hic quippe nox est, ait Gregorius M. ibi vero dies erit, quia hic in nitore veritatis caligamus, ibi Deus ipse tota veritas mentibus illucebit. Alcuinus: Qui pascuntur in liliis, h. e. candidissimis Sancto- rum Patrum exemplis, donec præsentis mortalitatis umbræ,æterno die adspirante, transeamus. Atque hæc juxta priorem συνέχειαν. Alteram vero connexio- nem quod attinet, amplectitur eam Mercerus, & ummbram V. Testamenti ac diem N. Testamenti respi- ci censet. Inquit ergo Dominus, secundum ipsum, se donec dies spiret & affulgeat clarior, & fugerint umbræ legales luce jam pleniore orbi exorta adventu suo, acturum in æde sanctuarii, atque ibi cum veteri populo versaturum, quia in monte Moria constru- ctum fuit templum. Quo pacto etiam similem lo- cutionem cap. 2, 17. exposuerat Mercerus: Donec adspiret dies & fugiant umbræ; revertere, similis esto, dilecte mi, capreæ vel hinnulo Cervorum super mon- tes Bether, ut interim dum dies clarus affulget, & plenior salus per Christum ostenditur orbi, quum umbra Vet. Testamenti & mœror ac molestia fu- gient, Ecclesiæ suæ adsit, & eam mira celeritate adju- tum veniat ex montibus illis odoratis suppeditans odoramenta, quibus reficiatur & roboretur. Sed in utroque loco plerique alii Interpp. neglecta distin- ctione accentuum referunt illam descriptionem de pastu inter lilia ad verba præcedentia, tum ubi de Sponso sermo erat cap. 2, 16. Dilectus meus mihi & ego illi, qui pascit inter lilia in pascuis amœnioribus & odoratissimis, donec spiret dies &c. tum hic de Sponsa & de hinnulis gemellis fidelium Judæorum & gentium, qui inter lilia pascuntur usque ad consum- mationem seculi.

Jam ergo, quod ad verba præsentia; ibo ad montem myrrhæ & ad collem thuris, septem eorum reperiuntur interpretationes: Primam de æde San- ctuarii in monte Moria jam indicavimus: ubi thura, orationes & facrificia Deo offerebantur. Altera eorum est, qui revocari nunc Sponsam a Sponso putant, ut nempe secum vadat ad montem Myrrhæ per mortificationem, & ad collem thuris per devotio- nem; Vel etiam promittere Sponsam, quod eos vi- fitare velit, qui mortificationi carnis & devotioni sunt dediti orationis. Sic Gilbertus Foljoth: Vadam ad montem Myrrhæ i. e. præsens ipse visitabo Eccle- siam, quæ est mons myrrhæ & collis thuris. Mons ve- ro Myrrhæ altitudo est mortificationis, de qua Apo- stolus, mortificate membra, quæ sunt super terram. Hæc vero mortificat Ecclesia considerando, quæ sur- sum sunt, Collis vero thuris humilitas est orationis, qua se Ecclesia in alta suspendit, & velut e thuribulo cordis quasi fumus thuris adscendit. Alcuin. in Com- pend. In Myrrha mortificatio carnis, in thure devo- tio orationis exprimitur; quasi diceret Sponsa, fre- quentabo eos & pia propitius illustratione glorificabo, quos in passionis sive orationis virtute sublimes esse su- spicio. Atque ita etiam Gregorius M. & Beda in h. l. Tertio affinis videtur explicatio B. Osiandri: Va- dam ad montem myrrhæ & ad colles thuris, id est, accedam casto & spirituali ac sancto amore ad Eccle- siam meam, cujus vertex est instar montis, in quo na- scitur Myrrha; aut colles, in quo Thus provenit: omnia enim in ea sunt elegantia, grata, pura, munda, nihil habet fœditatis aut spurcitiei. Quarta expositio communior est ac plerorumque Patrum, Gregor. Nysseni, Theodoreti, trium Anonymorum, & Pselli apud eundem & aliorum, qui montem Myrrhæ ad passionem; collem thuris ad resurrectionem Christi referunt. Theodoretus: quando adeo decora es & amoris erga me vulnere sauciata, pro te mortem op- petam, & myrrhæ montem sponte conscendam: sed iterum resurgam, & revertar ad collem thuris. Vid. Cornel. a Lapide in h. l. Quinto B. Gerhardus ut per montem myrrhæ, sic etiam per collem thuris in- telligit montem Golgatha & passionis Christi, Postill. Salomon. Hom. ad diem passion. magnæ pag. 660. Quæ sententia probata quoque Paraphr. Vinarien- sis autoribus. Sexto de profectione Christi in Cœlum Piscator, Junius & Tremellius intelligunt, q. d. do- nec vespera mundi adveniat, ut te assumam, ego interea in Cœlum proficiscar & odore Angelarum & spiri- tuum justorum & perfectorum delectabor; in Hieru- salem cœlestem, ubi recepti jam sunt amici, qui me co- lunt, & quorum officia sunt odoratissima. Septimo sic verba Sponsæ hæc accipit Dürfeldius, ut per montem myrrhæ & thuris Hermon & Libanus, ceu montes myrrhini & thurei notentur; & per illum quidem puritas, pulchritudo, sanctitas, suaveolens- que dulcedo & dona ex merito passionis Christi ad Ecclesiam redundantia; per hunc vero preces San- ctorum designentur; ut ita Sponsa excitata a so- mno peccati plena fiduciæ ad montem myrrhæ & thuris adscendat. Sed manifestum est, hic verba Sponsi continuari, qui etiam versu sequenti cœptam orationem pertexit de pulchritudine Sponsæ. Præ- ferenda itaque videtur illa interpretatio, quæ passio- nem Christi hic respici vult (qua comparanda fuit illa pulchritudo Ecclesiæ) aut, si adhuc persisti in pulchritudinis Sponsæ descriptione urgeas, pectus ejus ac ventrem thure devotionis & mortificatione carnis Sponso gratum, designari dixerim. Quæ expositio octava erit, sed e secunda & tertiæ con- junctione enata, vel certe non multum ab iis diver- sa. Atque ita per ubera Sponsæ venter celebratur, quod instar montis myrrhini fit ob carnis mortifica- tionem, & pectus ejusdem, quod instar collium thuris sit ob devotionem cordis: quia subjungitur: Ita pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te: ac, ut in com- pendium contrahuntur omnia, post membrorum plerorumque recensionem, summatim pulchritudo Sponsæ verbis istis deprædicatur. Quæ de imputata pulchritudine recte interpretatur Theodoretus : Im- maculata & pulchra evasit Sponsa, quia propinqua Sponso effecta est, atque ita omnes splendores suscepit & lucida ex ipsa luce reddita est. De pulchritudine etiam, quæ per renovationem nobis obtingit, tres Patres Anonymi non inconvenienter explicant: Tota pulchra est; quia pulchra est mente & anima & carne: Et quidem carne, quippe quæ repurgatur hic a vi & efficacia perturbationum, & ornata virtu- tum moribus; anima vero, ut quæ liberata est hic ab omni concupiscentiæ vitio, & sermonibus vel rationi- bus decorata præceptorum: mente vero, ut quæ vilibus cogitationibus liberata, & splendenti in Spiritu S. per gratiam Deificatione refulgeat. Ac ob id macula non est in te, quæ propter perfectionem mihi proxima effecta sis. Sed hanc pulchritudinem hic affectamus verius & expectamus, quam impetramus in hac vi- ta Rom. 7, 24. 2. Cor. 7, 1. quam vero in altera vita consecuturi sumus Ephes. 5, 14. 1. Cor. 13. Alcuinus totam pulchram dicit, in omnibus scil. timentibus Deum, pusillis & magnis, ut non de perfectione (pulchritudinis) graduum, sed partium intellexisse videatur.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. COME FROM LEBANON MY BRIDE, COME] He wishes to say this: I will lead you through the most pleasant places of my kingdom: from Lebanon to Amana, thence to Hermon, a part of which is Sanir Deut. 3, 9. Solomon had a forest in Lebanon 1. Kings 7, 2. 2. Chron. 8, 6. Concerning the pleasantness of Hermon see Ps. 83. From all sides we will pluck garlands for you. Thus in the Epithalamium of Helen: We, in the morning, to the running track and to the meadow leaves, will go, plucking sweet-smelling garlands, remembering you much, O Helen. Grotius sticks again in the bark, and leaves the marrow and the kernel. He does not wish to lead the Bride into Lebanon, but calls her, so that she may come from Lebanon: nor are the other mountains proposed here as the terminus to which the Bride is to be led, but rather as the terminus from which her calling is proposed, nor finally are they celebrated here for the pleasantness of the place, since they are rather described as mountains of leopards and dens of lions. More rightly, therefore, the ancient Fathers understand by the mountains of Lebanon, Amanah, Senir, and Hermon, situated in Phoenicia outside Judea, the Gentiles; so that the Bride may come from those horrid and wooded mountains from infidelity and Gentilism, where she had to live among fierce lions and leopards, to the Church, and arrive at the Bridegroom. See Is. 11, 16. as Athanasius observes in the Synopsis, that the Church of the Gentiles is designated by these mountains, and the nations are called away from idolatry and Gentilism to faith and Christianity. Similarly Tertullian lib. 4. against Marc. cap. 11. Let the Paraphrase of Osiander and the Vinarienses be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 7. VENI DE LIBANO SPONSA MEA, VENI] Hoc vult dicere: Deducam te per amœnissima regni mei: à Libano in Amana, inde in Hermonem, cujus pars Sanir Deut. 3, 9. Saltum in Libano habebat Salomon 1. Reg. 7, 2. 2. Par. 8, 6. De Hermonis amœnitate vide Pf. 83. Vndique corollas tibi decerpemus. Sic in Ephithalamio Helenæ: Ἀμμες δ᾽ ἐς δρόμον ἦρι καὶ ἐς λειμώνια φύλλα Ἑρψοῦμες, στεφάνως δρεψεύμεναι ἁδὺ πνέοντας, Πολλᾶτεῦ ὦ Ἑλένα μεμναμίναι. Hæret iterum in cortice Grotius, & medullam atque nucleum relinquit. Non in Libanum deducere vult Sponsam, sed vocat eam, ut de Libano veniat: neque cæteri montes ut terminus ad quem deducen- da Sponsa, sed potius ut terminus à quo vocationis ejusdem hic proponuntur, Nec denique ab amœni- tate loci hic celebrantur, siquidem potius ut montes pardorum & cubilia leonum describantur. Rectius ergo Patres antiqui per Libanum, Amanah, Senir, & Hermon montes in Phœnicia extra Judæam sitos Gentiles intelligunt; ut veniat Sponsa de horridis sylvosisque istis montibus ab infidelitate & Genti- lismo, ubi inter fævos leones & pardos agendum, ad Ecclesiam, & perveniat ad Sponsum. Vid. Es. 11, 16. uti Athanasius in Synops. observat, Ecclesiam gen- tium his montibus designari, gentesque evocari ab ido- lolatria & gentilismo ad fidem & Christianismum. Similiter Tertullianus lib. 4. contra Marc. cap. 11. Conferatur Paraphr. Osiandri & Vinariensium.

## 4:9
Vers. 9. YOU HAVE WOUNDED MY HEART] Theocritus concerning love: and what wounds you make! MY SISTER] Thus also the Latins called their friends. Tibullus, Martial, and others mention this.

Excellent Interpreters of the Song of Solomon! The Bride of Christ is truly his sister: because we are from one Father Adam according to the flesh; indeed, just as Christ is the only-begotten Son of God by nature, so we are sons of God by grace: And therefore he himself is our brother, in a double respect, both by the communion of nature, and by the relationship of the same Father. Who nevertheless deigns to betroth us to himself, and to take us as his Bride out of singular love and affection Hos. 2. Bede in this place calls the Church sister and Bride, because he joined her to himself by the covenant of the heavenly bridal chamber, because he also deigned to become man, and to exist as her natural brother. Three Fathers in Theodoret: On account of the conjunction of the flesh you are a Sister to me; but on account of the voluntary bond of charity, and the union of the Spirit, you are betrothed to me.

Vers. eod. IN ONE OF YOUR EYES] Meleager concerning Love: You have not escaped me, Archer, hiding in the eyes of Zenophila. AND IN ONE HAIR OF YOUR NECK] Silentiarius: Having snatched one golden hair from the tresses of Doris, she bound my hands like a captive. Vers. 10. HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE YOUR BREASTS MY SISTER MY BRIDE] In the Greek Epigram: And milk-white breasts, well-matched, desirable, shapely, more delightful than any bud.

Truly worthy, whom he summons here to explain the Song of most holy and most chaste love! But if we look to the sense of the Holy Scripture itself, which he intends here, it is a discourse concerning the faith and the spiritual eye of the Bride, by which the Bridegroom is delighted above all Jer. 5, 1. Heb. 11, 6.: and concerning charity, and obedience, as a most noble necklace of the neck. Theodoret in this place: But he says this: both of your eyes are indeed to be admired, and deservedly named like a dove's; but one of them, which contemplates divine things, which philosophizes about God, which gazes upon the hidden mysteries of God, strikes my heart with amazement. Let us seek, however, what that one ornament is, which, placed around the neck of the Bride, excels the others, and let us learn from St. Paul; who says, there remain faith, hope, charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity. And again: love is therefore the fulfillment of the law. Gregory of Nyssa Hom. 8. in the Song. By the necklace of the neck is understood the yoke of Christ, which the soul has taken upon itself.

Latin:

Vers. 9. VVLNERASTI COR MEVM] Theocritus de amore: τὰ δὲ τραύματα ἀλίκα ποιεῖς; SOROR MEA] Sic & Latini amicos vocabant. Memi- nit Tibullus, Martialis, & alii.

Egregii Interpp. Cantici Salomonei! Sponsa Christi vere soror ejus est: quia ab uno Patre Ada- mo sumus secundum carnem; imo ut Christus est Filius Dei unigenitus per naturam, ita nos filii Dei sumus per gratiam: Ideoque ipse frater noster est, gemino respectu, & naturæ communione, & Patris ejusdem habitudine. Qui tamen nos sibi desponsare dignatur, & in Sponsam assumere ex singulari amo- re & dilectione Hos. 2. Beda in h. l. Ecclesiam soro- rem cognominat & Sponsam, quia cælestis eam thala- mi sibi fœdere conjunxit, quia & ipse homo fieri, ac frater ei naturalis existere dignatus est. Tres Patres apud Theodoretum: Propter carnis conjunctionem es mihi Soror; propter voluntarium autem charitatis vinculum, atque unionem Spiritus desponsata es mihi.

Vers. eod. IN UNO OCULORUM TUORUM] Meleager de Amore: - - - οὔ με λέληθας Τοξότα, Ζηνοφίλας ὄμμασι κρυπτόμενος. ET IN UNO CRINE COLLI TVI] Silentiarius: Χρυσῆς εὑρύσασα μίαν τρίχα Δωρὶς ἐθείρης Οἷα δαμυκτύτυς δῆσεν ἐμὰς παλάμας. Vers. 10. QVAM PVLCHRÆ SVNT MAMMÆ TVÆ SOROR MEA SPONSA] In Epigrammate Græco: Καὶ μαζοὶ γλαγοέντες, εὐζυγες, ἱμεροέντες, Εὐφυέες, πάσης τερπνότεροι κάλυκος.

Digni profecto, quos hic accersat ad sanctissimi & castissimi amoris Canticum explanandum! Cæterum si sensum ipsius S. S. quem hic intendit, respiciamus, de fide & oculo spirituali Sponsæ, quo delectatur imprimis Sponsus Jer. 5, 1. Ebr. 11, 6. sermo est: & de charitate, atque obedientia, ceu torque colli nobilissimo. Theodor. in h. l. Hoc autem dicit: ambo quidem oculi tui sunt admirandi, ac similes columbæ merito nominati; sed alter eorum, qui divina contemplatur, qui philosophatur de Deo, qui de Deo recondita mysteria contuetur, Cor meum stupore afficit. Quæramus autem, quidnam sit unum ornamentum illud, quod Sponsæ collo circumdatum, cæteris antecellit, discamusque a S. Paulo; qui, manent, inquit, fides, spes, charitas, tria hæc: major autem horum est charitas. Et rursum: plenitudo ergo legis est dilectio. Gregorius Nyssenus Hom. 8. in Cantic. Per torquem colli intelligitur jugum Christi, quod anima in se suscepit.

## 4:10
Vers. eod. THE SCENT OF YOUR OINTMENTS] That is, your breath is better than ointment.

Forsooth, the Holy Spirit will be occupied in celebrating the breath of the daughter of Pharaoh! And whence were there for her breaths of such fragrance, that they were better than precious ointment? The LXX and Ambrose interpreted it as the scent of garments; since the garments received the scent from the ointments. If you distinguish them from one another: as in the following verse 11 in the Hebrew it is said concerning the scent of the garments, that it is like the scent of Lebanon, by the scent of the ointments it will be possible to understand the good fame of the Church, which is spread far and wide, not otherwise than the scent of aromatics, just as it is said concerning Josiah Sir. 46, 1. The memory of Josiah is made into the composition of a scent, the work of a perfumer. By the name of garments, however, the graces and gifts, with which the Church is adorned, which are a most fragrant scent to Christ the Bridegroom, in the manner of trees in Lebanon, can be understood. Thus Alcuin. The scent of your ointments is above all aromatics: The most sweet fame diffused through the whole world is clearer than that of the old law and the Fathers, which is confined to Judea alone. And the scent of your garments, like the scent of incense. The garments of the Church are her works, which are compared to the scent of incense, because all things which the Church does holy for the Lord render in their place the function of prayers.

Latin:

Vers. eod. ODOR VNGVENTORVM TVORVM] Id est, halitus tui meliores unguento.

Scilicet in halitu filiæ Pharaonis celebrando occupabitur Spiritus Sanctus! Et unde illi halitus tantæ fragrantiæ erant, ut unguento pretioso meliores fuerint? LXX. & Ambros. per odorem vestimentorum interpretati sunt; quum ab unguentis vestimenta acceperint odorem. Si distinguas ea ab invicem: uti versu sequenti 11. in Ebræo de odore vestimentorum dicitur, quod sit velut odor Libani, per unguentorum odorem famam bonam Ecclesiæ, quæ late spargitur, non secus atque odor aromatum, intelligere licebit, quemadmodum de Josia dicitur Sir. 46, 1. Memoria Josiæ in compositionem odoris facta, opus pigmentarii. Vestimentorum autem nomine gratiæ & dona, quibus ornata est Ecclesia, quæ Christo Sponso sunt odor fragrantissimus, more arborum in Libano, intelligi possunt. Sic Alcuin. Odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata: Fama suavissima diffusa per orbem totum fidei clarior est, quam veteris legis & Patrum, quæ in sola Judæa coangustatur. Et odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris. Vestimenta Ecclesiæ opera sunt ejus, quæ odori thuris comparantur, quia cuncta, quæ sancta pro Domino agit Ecclesia per ea orationum vicem reddunt.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. YOUR LIPS ARE A DISTILLING HONEYCOMB) Thus lips in a Greek Epigram: The nectar-flowing portals of the mouth. HONEY AND MILK UNDER YOUR TONGUE] Hence the tasting of milk and honey after baptism. Tertullian mentions this in De Corona, and against Marcion 1.

Concerning the sweetness of the lips and speech of the Bride, that her lips imitate a distilling honeycomb, Gregory, Cassiodorus, Bede, Theodoret, Aponius, and others: Conf. Psalm 119, 103. Proverbs 10, 10. chap. 24, 13. Theodoret: the honeycombs which are carried on the lips of Doctors are the divine Scriptures, which contain the bees that seek honey, the Prophets and Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 11. FAVVS DISTILLANS LABIA TVA) Sic labia in Græco Epigrammate: Στόματος νεκταρέη πρόθυρα. MEL ET LAC SVB LINGVA TVA] Hinc post baptismum lactis & mellis prægustatio. Meminit Tertullianus de Corona, & adversus Marcionem 1.

De labiorum & sermonis Sponsæ suavitate, quod labia favum stillantem imitentur Gregorius, Cassiodor. Beda, Theodor. Aponius, alii: Conf. Psal. 119, 103. Proverb. 10, 10. cap. 24, 13. Theodor. favi mellis, qui in Doctorum gestantur labiis, sunt divinæ Scripturæ, quæ continent apes mellis affectrices, Prophetas & Apostolos.

## 4:12
Vers. 12. A GARDEN ENCLOSED] In this sense the Greeks also say κῆπος. See Diogenes on Stilpo. Thus also 5, 1. and a garden in the Lampsacene poem, and a little garden in Apuleius. It signifies, however, that she was of well-guarded virginity. And in this sense the Jews use these words.

Grotius therefore seeks the meaning here from the Heathens and Jews, having abandoned the monuments of the Holy Fathers, not unknown to him. Because he wished to adhere only to the bark of the letter; which is to Judaize, and this in the Canticle indeed more than to Judaize. As if the Holy Spirit had spoken here only of the virginity of the daughter of Pharaoh well guarded. And what does the denomination of a sealed fountain mean for itself, if the daughter of Pharaoh is indicated? Theodoret. He calls the Bride a garden, as one who bears not one fruit of piety and virtue, but many and various. Enclosed, however, because it is fortified, and not exposed to snares. For the gates, he says, of hell shall not prevail against it. If Grotius had wished to hear the Doctors of the Church, he would not have denied that the Church is elegantly compared in this place to a garden blooming with all graces and virtues as if with heavenly plants, which the provident care of God fortifies, and which is sealed and enclosed by faith, hope, and charity. See Gilbert Folliot, and others. A garden, says Gregory the Great, is the holy Church, because while it begets many peoples in faith, it sends forth good earth as if they were beautiful flowers. Which garden is well said to be enclosed, because it is fortified on all sides by a wall of charity, lest any reprobate enter within the number of the Elect. Alcuin: The garden enclosed is the Church, because it brings forth the manifold germs of spiritual works: It is a fountain, which overflows with saving doctrine: Enclosed, because it persists fortified by the protection of the Lord: sealed by the word of faith. Compare the Weimar and Osiander Paraphrases.

Latin:

Vers. 12. HORTVS CONCLVSVS] Hoc sensu & Græci κῆπος dicunt. Vide Diogenem Stilpone. Sic & 5, 1. & hortus in Lampsaceno carmine, & hortulus apud Apulejum. Significat autem eam fuisse bene custoditæ virginitatis. Et hunc in sensum Judæi hæc verba usurpant.

Ab Ethnicis ergo & Judæis sensum Grotius hic petit, relictis S. Patrum monumentis, sibi non in- cognitum. Quia inhærere literæ cortici solum vo- luit; quod est Judaizare, & hoc in Cantico quidem plus quam Judaizare. Quasi Spiritus S. solum de virginitate filiæ Pharaonis bene custoditæ hic locutus fuerit. Et quid sibi vult denominatio fontis signati, si Pharaonis filia indigitata? Theodoret. Hortum nominat Sponsam, ut quæ non unum pietatis virtutis- que fructum, sed multos & varios ferat. Conclusum autem, quod munitus sit, nec insidiis expositus. Nam portæ, inquit, inferni non prævalebunt adversus eam. Patres Ecclesiæ Doctores audire si voluisset Grotius, eleganter hoc in loco Ecclesiam horto conferri omnibus gratiis & virtutibus velut plantis cœlestibus vernanti, quem Dei provida cura mu- nit, quique fide, spe & charitate signatus & conclu- sus est, non abnuisset. Vid. Gilbertus Foljoth, & alii. Hortus, inquit Gregorius M. sancta Ecclesia existit, quia dum populos multos in fide gignit, quasi flores pul- chros bona terra emittit. Qui hortus conclusus bene esse dicitur, quia charitatis vallo circumquaque muni- tur, ne intra numerum Electorum reprobus aliquis ingrediatur. Alcuinus: Hortus conclusus Ecclesia est, quia multivaria spiritualium operum germina profert: Fons est, qui doctrina salutari redundat: Conclusus, quia Domini protectione munita persistit: signatus sermone fidei. Confer. Paraphr. Vina- riens. & Osiandrina.

## 4:13
Ver. 13. THY SHOOTS ARE A PARADISE OF POMEGRANATES.

According to Folliot, the shoots are good words and works, by which the Church begets and nourishes martyrs, and transmits them to heaven: others living holily she proposes as an example to their neighbors, and thus sends forth the fruits of pomegranates. The pomegranate encloses a multitude of grains under a red rind, its fruit refreshes sweetly: thus those who shed their blood for Christ gather to themselves a multitude of virtues and, flourishing in peace, perform good works, instruct and refresh their neighbors, and both send forth the odor of virtues, like a Paradise, of sweetness.

Latin:

Vers. 13. EMISSIONES TUÆ PARADISUS MALORUM PUNICORUM.

Emissiones Foljotho verba sunt bona & opera, quibus Ecclesia gignit & nutrit martyres, & ad cælum transmittit: alios sancte viventes proximis in exem- plum proponit, & sic malorum punicorum fructus emittit. Malum punicum sub rubeo cortice multi- tudinem granorum claudit, fructus ejus dulciter re- ficit: sic qui pro Christo sanguinem fundunt, congre- gant sibi multitudinem virtutum atque in pace viren- tes bona operantur, proximos instruunt & reficiunt, & utrique odorem virtutum, tanquam Paradisum, suavitatis emittunt.

## 4:14
Ver. 14. CAMPHIRE WITH SPIKENARD, SPIKENARD AND SAFFRON.

Camphire, says Alcuin, is an aromatic tree, signifying the blessing of heavenly grace: Spikenard expresses the type of the Lord's passion; Saffron expresses the fervor of charity. CALAMUS AND CINNAMON. Calamus, which is also Cassia, is an aromatic tree, but small, and therefore designates those humble in Spirit. Likewise Cinnamon, which signifies those who despise themselves, which is also a short tree, but fragrant, and sweet; but humility has great praise and sweetness before God. WITH ALL THE TREES OF LEBANON. Just as calamus and cinnamon demonstrate the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon demonstrate their sublime actions. MYRRH AND ALOES WITH ALL THE CHIEF SPICES. These are aromatic trees, which express the continence of the flesh with all the chief spices, that is, with the more excellent charisms of virtues. And the conjunction of these trees with the spices is beautiful, because while we restrain the flesh from lasciviousness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 14. CYPRI CUM NARDO, NARDUS ET CROCUS.

Cyprus, inquit Alcuin. arbor aromatica est, si- gnificans cælestis gratiæ benedictionem: Nardus Do- minicæ passionis typum; Crocus charitatis fervorem exprimit. FISTULA ET CINNAMOMUM. Fistula, quæ & Cassia, arbor aromatica, sed modica, & ideo humiles Spiritu designat. Item Cinnamo- mum, qui se ipsos despiciunt, signat, quæ & ipsa brevis est arbor, sed odorifera, & dulcis; sed humilitas ma- gnam habet laudem, & dulcedinem apud Deum. CUM UNIVERSIS LIGNIS LIBANI. Sicut fistula & cinnamomum humiles sanctorum cogitatio- nes, sic ligna Libani sublimes eorum actiones demon- strant. MYRRHA ET ALOE CUM OMNI- BUS PRIMIS UNGUENTIS. Arbores sunt aromaticæ, quæ continentiam carnis exprimunt cum omnibus primis unguentis, id est, charismatibus virtutum excellentioribus. Et pulchra est conjunctio harum arborum cum unguentis, quia dum carnem a lascivia refrenamus, consequens est, ut majora spiritus dona percipiamus.

## 4:15
Ver. 15. A FOUNTAIN OF GARDENS, A WELL OF LIVING WATERS, WHICH FLOW WITH IMPETUS.

Alcuin must be heard again. Both, he says, is the Church, both a fountain of gardens, because it begets spiritual fruits, and a well of living waters, on account of the hidden mysteries, which are revealed to the saints alone through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Of living waters on account of the divine utterances, which proceed from the invisible treasures of divine grace. FROM LEBANON. He speaks of the Church itself, which is both white through the purity of faith, and high through the glory of virtues. Through Lebanon others understand Christ, along with Aponius and Richard, to whom the Weimar Paraphrasts accede, comparing Christ to Lebanon on account of its height, beauty, and fruitfulness.

Latin:

Vers. 15. FONS HORTORUM PUTEUS AQUARUM VIVENTIUM, QUÆ FLUUNT IMPETU.

Audiendus iterum Alcuinus. Utrumque, inquit, Ecclesia est, & fons hortorum, quia spirituales gi- gnit fructus, & puteus aquarum viventium, propter occulta mysteria, quæ sanctis per Spir. S. revelatio- nem solis panduntur. Aquarum viventium propter eloquia divina, quæ de invisibilibus divinæ gratiæ thesauris procedunt. DE LIBANO. De ipsa Eccle- sia dicit, quæ & candida est per munditiem fidei, & alta per virtutum gloriam. Per Libanum alii Chri- stum intelligunt cum Aponio & Richardo, quibus accedunt Paraphr. Vinar. Christum Libano com- parantes ob altitudinem, pulchritudinem, & fœ- cunditatem.

## 4:16
Ver. 16. AWAKE, O NORTH WIND, AND COME, O SOUTH WIND] For this is useful for the beneficial, as follows.

Grotius savors merely carnal things. Theodoret reveals the meaning: He commands that the contrary wind ascend: and that divine grace may blow, so that (the Bridegroom) may gather the ripe fruits of his aromatics, and none of them be corrupted by the wind, or fall before maturity. Thus also Psellus wishes the blast of the north wind, which extinguishes the beauty of flowers with ice, to be driven away: but that the most wholesome south wind be present, which, blowing in Scripture, once instilled the flow of words into the Apostles. Three Fathers in Theodoret: Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Depart, most wicked Spirit, who afflict the souls that are instructed by me with perturbations, as if with the blasts of the north wind, and come, most holy Spirit, who warm them with the gifts of your grace, as if with the wholesome breezes of the south. Others, however, wish both winds to be summoned for the sake of testing. Alcuin: In the north wind are designated the adversities of the world, in the south wind the blandishments: because the Church is tested by a double assault. Awake, is the voice of one permitting, not of one commanding. And let its aromatics flow, that is, let the constancy of virtues disperse wonderful odors. And this is another explanation, which also pleased Osiander, as well as the Weimar commentators. A third takes those two contrary winds as the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit according to Justus Orgelit. North wind and South wind are different words, but they insinuate the gifts of one Holy Spirit. North wind, while it offers refreshment to those who are burning. South wind, while it resolves those who are hard to believing or doing good. And since one is noted in two, he does not say, blow through, but blow through my garden and let its aromatics flow. Inspire the believing people and let its good works abound, which explanation B. Gerhard embraced in his Postil on Solomon for Sunday. Sing, he teaches, that the Holy Spirit is called wind on account of the symbol of his appearance, on account of his hidden origin, and also on account of his saving effect. But he is compared to both the South and North wind, on account of the filling of the whole Church, on account of the exposition of the Old and New Testament, on account of the administration of the Ecclesiastical Ministry, and on account of the diverse government of the Church. Mercer’s fourth exposition is not very foreign: The Church desires the fame of its works, and to reach Christ by faith and the divine inspiration of the Spirit (for this is what it means for this garden to be blown upon by the wind) so that he, perceiving this fruit as it were from there, may be delighted. He mentions contrary winds, the cold North and the warm South, so that one may be tempered by the other, and furthermore so that the scent of the spices may be spread more widely, that is, that the fame of its good works and thanksgivings may resound in every direction. Junius’s explanation is more foreign, who wishes these to be referred to Christ, not to the Spirit. S. There is no reason why we should review it. They are the words of the Bridegroom himself, according to Gregory the Great, Anselm, and Rupert, who has continued his discourse up to this point concerning the beauty of the Bride; now therefore, since he has compared her to a most fragrant garden, he seems to call upon the Holy Spirit, so that he may blow through the garden, so that its spices may give forth their scent; although they may also be taken as the sigh and Vow of the Bride, as Ambrose, Nyssen, Augustine, Psellus, Theodoret, and others teach: which is favored by the fact that the following words of the Bridegroom’s invitation, let my beloved come into my garden, are joined in one verse with these words; by which means, excited by such praise of the Bride, she will vow that by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit the spices of her garden may breathe forth, and delight the Bridegroom,

Latin:

Vers. 16. SVRGE AQVILO, ET VENI AVSTER] Ωφελεῖ γὰρ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ εὐεργετικὸν, ut sequitur.

Mere carnalia sapit Grotius. Theodoretus sensum aperit: Præcipit, ut ventus adscendat con- trarius: & gratia divina spirei, quo maturos aro- matum ipsius fructus colligat (Sponsus) nec ullus eo- rum vento corrumpatur, aut decidat ante maturi- tatem. Sic etiam Psellus flatum aquilonis pessimum glacie florum pulchritudinem extinguentem pelli vult: austrum autem saluberrimum adesse, qui spi- rans in Scriptura Apostolis olim verborum fluxus in- stillavit. Tres Patres apud Theodoretum: Surge aquilo & veni auster. Fatesse Spiritus improbissime, qui animas, quæ a me instituuntur, perturbationibus, quasi aquilonis flatibus affligis, & veni sanctissime Spiritus, qui eas gratiæ tuæ donis, tanquam auris au- stri salutaribus calefacis. Alii tamen utrumque ven- tum explorationis causa accersi volunt. Alcuinus: In aquilone adversa mundi, in austro blandimenta designantur: quia gemina oppugnatione probatur Ec- clesia. Surge, permittentis vox, non imperantis est. Et fluant aromata illius, id est, virtutum constantia miros odores dispergat. Atque hæc altera est explica- tio, quæ Osiandro etiam placuit, ut & Vinariensibus. Tertia duos illos contrarios ventos de S. S. diver- sis donis accipit juxta Justum Orgelit. Aquilo & Au- ster diversa sunt vocabula, sed unius S. S. insinuant dona. Aquilo, dum æstuantibus refrigeria præbet. Anster, dum duros ad credendum vel benefaciendum resolvit. Et quoniam in duobus unus advertitur, non ait, perflate, sed perfla hortum meum & fluant aromata illius. Inspira credentem populum & redun- dent bona opera ejus, Quam explicationem ample- xus B. Gerhardus Postill. Salom. Dom. Cantate, do- cet, Spiritum S. ventum dici propter apparitionis Symbolum, propter occultum ortum, nec non pro- pter salutarem effectum. Austro vero simul & Aqui- loni comparari, propter totius Ecclesiæ impletionem, propter V. & N. Test. expositionem, propter Eccle- siastici Ministerii administrationem, & propter di- versam Ecclesiæ gubernationem. Non multum alie- na est quarta Merceri expositio: Optat Ecclesia suo- rum operum famam, & ad Christum pervenire fide & divino Spiritus afflatu (hoc enim est vento afflari hunc hortum) ut ille inde velut hunc fructum perci- piens oblectetur. Ventos contrarios memorat, Aqui- lonem frigidum & Austrum calidum, ut alter altero temperetur, præterea ut ita latius aromatum odor spargatur, id est, in omnem partem percrebescat fama bonorum suorum operum & gratiarum. Alienior est Junii explicatio, qui hæc ad Christum referri vult, non ad Spir. S. Non est, quod eam recenseamus. Verba ipsiusmet Sponsi sunt, secundum Gregor. M. Anshelmum & Rupertum, qui continuavit hucusque sermonem suum de pulchritudine Sponsæ; Nunc ergo quum horto eandem comparavit fragrantif- fimo, vocare Spiritum S. videtur, ut hortum perflet, ut odorem dent aromata ejus; quanquam ea etiam accipi possint, ut suspirium ac Votum Sponsæ, uti docent Ambrosius, Nyssenus, Augustinus, Psellus, Theodoretus, & alii: quibus favet, quod verba se- quentia invitatoria Sponsi, veniat dilectus meus in hortum meum, uno versu conjungantur cum hisce verbis; quo pacto Sponsæ elogio tanto excitata vo- vebit, ut Spiritus Sancti afflatu aromata horti sui spirent, Sponsumque oblectent,

## 5:1 Argument
PART III. THE JOY OF THE BRIDE AND BRIDEGROOM CONFIRMED IN THE GARDEN OF THE CHURCH. CHAPTER V.

The Bride invites the Bridegroom into the garden, who arrives promptly, after he has harvested the myrrh, and after his passion, refreshed, he has prepared a banquet of gladness for his friends; he also awakens the sleeping Bride by the shadowing forth of his passions, and soon hiding himself, he is sought by the Bride, languid for love because of his remarkable beauty, by which [he shows] the whiteness and redness, and the comeliness of his head, hair, eyes, cheeks, lips, hands, belly, legs, appearance, and the sweetness of his throat.

Ver. 1. LET HIM EAT THE FRUIT OF HIS FRUITS) To eat and to drink is frequent among the Hebrews for enjoying any thing whatsoever. COME INTO MY GARDEN) The husband speaks: nor is it that of one calling, but of one congratulating himself: εὐπάθων. EAT, O FRIENDS, AND DRINK, AND BE DRUNKEN, O BELOVED) The husband invites his companions, that they may imitate him.

Therefore, by the same reasoning, he explains these things, and those which precede, concerning the Bridegroom and his friends. But since the Bridegroom is Christ himself, those things must be understood of him in another way; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey, and I have drunk my wine with my milk: these things [must be understood] in another way concerning the friends of Christ; Eat and drink, and be drunken. The Vinarienses Paraphrasts wish for the passion of Christ to be noted by the myrrh and aromatics, and the joy which followed thereafter to be noted by the honeycomb and honey, milk and wine: But it seems rather to be indicated that Christ enjoys our repentance, faith, and confession, as well as our charity and other virtues with singular pleasure. That these are the aromatics which he smells with pleasure, that this is the honey which he enjoys so greedily that he eats the honeycomb at the same time: that this is his wine and milk, with which he is delighted in his garden; when the faithful bring forth sweet fruits to the glory of God and the increase of the Church, honey and honeycomb, milk and wine proceed from them, or those things which are so sweet to him that he enjoys and is refreshed by them as by most sweet food and drink. As the Bridegroom is said to have gathered myrrh and aromatics from his garden, which are pleasing to the smell: so he enjoys honey, milk, and wine, which are sweet to the taste. By myrrh, repentance, faith, and the mortification of the flesh are noted; by aromatics, invocation and other good works are noted: Honey with the honeycomb denotes the preaching of the word of God, which is to us like honey and the honeycomb, Ps. 19, 11 and 119, 102; nay, it is sweet even to Christ, because he is delighted by the propagation and fruit of the word. As in mystical banquets heavenly doctrine is not only like food to us, but also like drink, and therefore is wont to be compared to wine and milk; to the former because of the more tender, to the latter because of the more adult: So Christ also has his food, he has his drink, with which he is delighted: nay, he himself is exhilarated by the joy of the faithful, and as it were feasts with us, Apoc. 3, 30; therefore he himself is also said to enjoy wine and milk, especially because he perceives singular pleasure from it when the faithful, whether they be little ones or more adult, are fed by the word of God. My food is, he says himself, John 4, 34, to do the will of him who sent me. Mercerus says, the Bridegroom signifies mystically that he holds the works of his Church as most acceptable, and that he is delighted by her faith, confession, and invocation, which are the fruits of the Church, no otherwise than any man is wont to be by plucking most fragrant aromatics, such as myrrh, or honey, eating so greedily as to devour the honeycomb at the same time. I have drunk my wine with my milk. The doctrine of the Church and the Word is compared now to wine, now to milk, here to both, because it both exhilarates the heart after the manner of wine, and strengthens the weaker after the manner of milk. He compares the communion of the Church with himself to a banquet and feasts. This is Mercerus. But in the invitation of the faithful, it is signified that the faithful enjoy the grace and spiritual benefits of God, righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. 14, 17, unto spiritual drunkenness, when they are filled with the Spirit, Ephes. 5, 18, and are made drunk from the abundance of the house of the Lord, and are given to drink from the torrent of pleasure, Ps. 36, 9. Which spiritual drunkenness is an alienation of the mind from the love of the flesh and the world, and its translation to heavenly and celestial things, so that they may be Christ's, and may adhere to him, and be uniquely delighted by him; concerning which Ambrose in Ps. 118, Serm. 13. A good drunkenness, which makes a certain ecstasy of mind toward better and pleasant things, so that our mind, unmindful of anxieties, is exhilarated by the wine of gladness, concerning which St. Bernard also treats in his work on loving God; that sober drunkenness, indeed, not gorging on unmixed wine, not dripping with wine, but burning for God.

Latin:

PARS III. GAUDIUM SPONSÆ ET SPONSI IN HORTO ECCLESIÆ CONFIR- MATUM. CAPUT V.

Sponsa invitat Sponsum in hortum, qui promtus adventat, postquam myrrham demessuit, & post passionem suam recreatus amicis suis con- vivium hilaritatis apparavit, Sponsam etiam dormientem adumbratione passionum sua- rum excitat, & mox sese abscondens quæri- tur a Sponsa præ amore languida ob insignem ejus pulchritudinem, qua candorem & rubo- rem, ac decorem capitis, comarum, oculorum, genarum, labiorum, manuum, ventris, cru- rum, speciei, & suavitatem gutturis ejus.

Vers. 1. COMEDAT FRVCTVM POMORVM SVO- RVM) Comedere & bibere pro re quavis frui frequens Hebræis. VENI IN HORTVM MEVM) Loquitur maritus: nec est vocantis, sed sibi gratulantis: εὐπάθων. COMEDITE AMICI, ET BIBITE, ET INEBRIAMINI CHARISSIMI) Invitat maritus sodales suos, ut ipsum imitentur.

EAdem ergo ratione de Sponso & amicis hæc, & quæ præcedunt, explicat. At quum Sponsus sit ipse Christus, aliter de ipso accipienda ista erunt; Comedi favum meum cum melle meo, & bibi vinum meum cum lacte meo: aliter hæc de amicis Christi; Comedite & bibite, & inebriamini. Ibi notari per myrrham & aromata passionem Christi, per favum & mel, lac & vinum gaudium, quod deinde secutum est, Paraphrastæ Vinariens. volunt: Sed indicari potius videtur, Christum frui nostra pœnitentia, fide & confessione, nec non charitate, aliisque virtutibus nostris cum singulari voluptate. Hæc esse aromata, quæ cum voluptate odoratur, hoc esse mel, quo tam avide fruatur, ut favum simul comedat: hoc esse vinum & lac ipsius, quo delectatur in horto suo; cum fideles fructus suaves ad Dei gloriam & Ecclesiæ incrementum proferunt, ab illis prodire mel & favum, lac & vinum, vel ea, quæ ita dulcia ipsi sint, ut iisdem ceu cibo ac potu suavissimo fruatur ac recreetur. Ut myrrham & aromata collegisse ex horto suo Sponsus dicitur, quæ grata ad odorem: sic frui melle, lacte & vino, quæ suavia ad saporem. Per myrrham pœnitentia, fides & carnis mortificatio; per aromata invocatio & opera alia bona notantur: Mel cum favo verbi Dei præconium notat, quod nobis instar mellis & favi est Ps. 19, 11. & 119, 102. imo dulce etiam Christo est, quia delectatur verbi propagatione & fructu. Ut in mysticis epulis doctrina cœlestis nobis non tantum instar cibi est, sed etiam instar potus, atque ideo vino & lacti conferri solet; huic ob teneriores, illi ob adulteriores: Sic habet & Christus cibum, habet potum suum, quo delectatur: imo lætitia fidelium exhilaratur ipse, ac quasi convivatur nobiscum Apoc. 3, 30. ideo & ipse frui vino & lacte dicitur, maxime, quia voluptatem inde percipit singularem, cum fideles seu parvuli sint, seu adultiores, verbo Dei pascuntur. Meus cibus est, inquit ipse Joh. 4, 34. ut faciam voluntatem ejus, qui misit me. Significat, inquit Mercerus, mystice Sponsus, se acceptissima habere Ecclesiæ suæ opera, & ejus fide, confessione, ac invocatione, qui fructus sunt Ecclesiæ, non aliter oblectari, quam quis hominum soleat odoratissima decerpens aromata, ut myrrham, aut mel, usque adeo comedens avide, ut favum simul devoret. Bibi vinum meum cum lacte meo. Doctrina Ecclesiæ & Verbum nunc vino, nunc lacti comparatur, hic utrique, quod & vini more cor exhilaret, & infirmiores lactis more corroboret. Com- municationem Ecclesiae secum convivio comparat, & epulis. Haec Mercerus. In invitatione vero fidelium significatur, fideles frui gratia & beneficiis Dei spi- ritualibus, justitia, pace & gaudio in S. S. Rom. 14, 17. ad spiritualem inebriationem, cum spiritu pleni fiunt Ephes. 5, 18. & inebriantur ab ubertate domus Domini, ac torrente voluptatis potantur Ps. 36, 9. Quae spiritualis ebrietas est alienatio mentis ab amore carnis & mundi, ejusque traductio ad superna & coele- stia, ut sint Christi, adhaereantque illi, eoque unice dele- ctentur; de qua Ambrosius in Ps. 118. Serm. 13. Bona ebrietas, quae ad meliora & jucunda facit quendam mentis excessum, ut immemor solicitudinum animus noster vino jucunditatis hilaretur, de qua etiam S. Bernhardus tractat. de diligendo Deo; Sobria illa ebrietas, vero, non mero ingurgitans, non madens vi- no, sed ardens Deo.

## 5:2
Vers. 2. I SLEEP, AND MY HEART WAKETH]. It is a certain half-waking and half-sleep.

He sticks again only in the bark of the letter. Furthermore, since the Bride is the Church, three Fathers according to Theodoret say that she sleeps, with worldly things and the senses lulled to the contempt of them, but that she watches in mind and hears Christ knocking: others say that she sleeps when the ministry is negligent, and the watchmen sleep with a great part of the congregation. Since sleep is wont to be taken in a bad sense concerning the sleep of sin and the neglect of duty, Matt. 13, 25, Apoc. 3, 2, 1 Thess. 5, 6. But the heart of the Church itself, which according to Gregory the Great are the elect, watches, because there always remain some who persist in faith and watch. They judge that this sleep should be explained as a certain torpor of faith, with Piscator and Junius; as if the Church were saying, I was indeed torpid as if oppressed by sleep, but my faith was by no means extinguished. And thus generally the Vinarienses, that the flesh is indeed oppressed by sleep through infirmity, but the Spirit watches toward Christ: which later interpretations seem to agree more with those things which follow in the text than the former, or the expositions of others: which, as being more alien, I forbear to recount. For here the Church confesses her infirmity and drowsiness, that she did not let in Christ who was knocking and gently calling, nay, graciously awakening, and all but nearly lost him. See here Junius in the notes. For he knocks, as Augustine says in Sermon 57 on John, that he may shake the quiet from the idle saints, and cries: Open to me, my sister, from my blood, my nearest one, from my approach, my dove, from my Spirit, my perfect one, from my word, which you have learned more fully from leisure. Ambros. book on Isaac and the soul, chapter 6. Even if you sleep, if only Christ finds the devotion of your soul, He comes and knocks at its door and says, open to me, my sister. Those who embrace the opinion of the former of the three Fathers, along with Ambrose in his exhortation to a Virgin, Augustine in the cited passage, and Gregory the Great in book 5 of his Morals, chapter 22, teach that the Church or the holy soul is called to greater holiness, so that it may open the depths of the heart to Christ and be filled with a fuller knowledge and love.

OPEN TO ME] Admit me. MY HEAD IS FULL OF DEW] We have spoken of this dew elsewhere.

It has not been possible to find thus far where he has treated of this dew, except at Psalm 110:3. By the name of dew (I cite his words), the Hebrews call seed by an elegant metaphor; hence that venerable κρύψις, Canticles 5:3. See also Isaiah 26:9. But that meaning does not fit at all. For if seed is to be understood, the sense will be this: Open to me. Admit me. My head is full of seed. Who will tolerate this interpretation? And how will it fit with those things which are added: And my locks with the drops of the night? Not to mention that it cannot be shown where by the word of the dew the seed is understood: just as we have said at Psalm 110, 2. Therefore, as regards the meaning of these words of the Canticle; some take them in a good sense, others in a worse. Those who take them in a good sense understand the head full of dew and the locks with the drops of the night in such a way that the Bridegroom says that refreshment is found in him against the heat, and that he abounds in the dew of blessing and of all graces, and that he bedews souls with the sweet irrigation of his Word, such as is wont to be at night, in the greatest heat. This is the explanation of Mercerus: who also adds these things: He says head, because he himself is the head of the Church, or having regard to his divinity, which is the head in Christ. For as Christ is the head of the Church, so also God is the head of Christ: and persisting in the metaphor he says locks, indicating that he is filled and imbued with graces on every side. For moisture adheres most to the hair. Most, however, interpret them in a worse sense; some wish this to be the meaning, as if the Bridegroom were saying that he is wet with the night rain for the sake of visiting the Bride, and that on her account he has endured the cold and the injury of the air and the inclemency of the night. Which is to be understood concerning the sufferings in his afflicted members, just as Osiander explains. Tirinus paraphrases thus: For I am in the world as if in the deepest and coldest night, in which those who provoke me with their crimes heap dew, frost, and hail upon my head, while they chill me and cause me not to love them, but to hate them. He also explains it concerning those things which Christ sustained for our sake in his passion: that his head was burdened with the cold dew, and the drops of all our crimes, of all the miseries, reproaches, blasphemies, spittings, and torments which he sustained for our sake. Which is also the interpretation of Junius: I shunned no evil or inconvenience, but I took it upon myself for your sake. This pleased the Belgian interpreters as well as the Weimar paraphrasts, who intimate that the night of the great passion is especially looked to here. And this explanation seems to us most suitable. To which it is vainly objected that dew is nowhere taken in a bad sense; for who will deny that night drops and dew bring inconveniences with them, Gen. 31, v. 42, Dan. 4, 22. And what can be a more effective argument for rousing us than the passion of Christ our Bridegroom endured for us? Although the first interpretation concerning the dew of grace is not unsuitable. For just as the heavenly Bridegroom wins the Bride to himself and soothes her with his benefits, so he proclaims their abundance and fruitfulness when he seeks to have them opened to him.

Latin:

Vers. 2. EGO DORMIO, ET COR MEVM VIGI- LAT]. Est quaedam semivigilia & semisomnus.

Haeret iterum tantum in cortice literae. Caete- rum quum Sponsa Ecclesia sit, tres Patres apud Theo- doretum dormire eam dicunt, rebus mundanis, sensi- bus ad contemptum illorum sopitis, sed mente vigilare & audire pulsantem Christum: alii dormire ipsam ajunt, cum ministerium negligens est, vigiles cum magna coetus parte dormiunt. Siquidem somnus in malam partem accipi soleat de somno peccati & neglectu officii Matth. 13, 25. Apoc. 3, 2. 1. Thess. 5, 6. Cor autem ipsum Ecclesiae, quod secundum Grego- rium M. electi sunt, vigilat, quia semper aliqui su- perfunt, qui in fide persistant ac vigilent. Somnum hunc de torpore quodam fidei, cum Piscatore ac Junio, explicandam esse censent; ac si diceret Ec- clesia, torpebam sane velut somno oppressa, fide vero minime extincta. Atque ita fere Vinarienses, quod caro somno quidem opprimatur per infirmitatem, Spi- ritus autem vigilet ad Christum: quae posteriores interpretationes iis, quae in textu sequuntur, magis congruere videntur, quam prior, aut aliorum expo- sitiones: quas, ut alieniores, recensere supersedeo. Confitetur enim hic infirmitatem atque oscitantiam suam Ecclesia, quod Christum pulsantem ac blande compellantem, imo gratiose excitantem non in- tromiserit, ac tantum non pene amiserit. Videatur hic Junius in notis. Pulsat enim, dicente Augustino Serm. 57. in Joh. ut excutiat quietem Sanctis otiosis & clamat: Aperi mihi, de sanguine meo Soror mea, de accessu meo proxima mea, de Spiritu meo columba mea, de sermone meo, quem plenius ex otio didicisti, perfecta mea. Ambros. lib. de Isaac & anima cap. 6. Etsi dormias, si modo devotionem animae tuae invene- rit Christus, venit, & pulsat ejus januam & dicit, aperi mihi Soror mea. Qui priorem trium Patrum sententiam amplectuntur cum Ambrosio exhort. ad Virginem, Augustino loco cit. Greg. M. lib. 5. mora- lium c. 22. Ecclesiam vel animam sanctam ad majorem sanctitatem vocari docent, ut intima cordis Christo aperiat, & pleniori cognitione & amore repleatur.

APERI MIHI] Admitte. CAPVT MEVM PLENVM EST RORE] De hoc rore diximus alibi.

Non invenire licuit hactenus, ubi de hoc rore egerit, nisi ad Ps. 110, 3. Roris nomine (verba ejus re- cito) semen eleganti translatione appellant Hebraei; inde σεμνὴ illa κρύψις, Cant 5, 3. Vide etiam Es. 26, 9. At illa significatio nullatenus congruit. Nam si semen intelligendum sit, sensus erit hic: Aperi mihi. Admitte. Caput meum plenum est semine. Quis hanc interpretationem feret? Et quomodo congruent illi, quae adduntur: Et cincinni mei guttis noctium? ut taceam, quod ostendi non possit, ubi per vocem roris semen intelligatur: quemadmodum ad Psal. 110, 2. diximus. Quod ergo ad sententiam horum verborum Cantici; alii in bonam, alii in sequiorem partem ea accipiunt. Qui in bonam, rore plenum caput & cincinnis guttis nocturnis ita intelligunt, quod in se refrigerium inveniri dicat Sponsus adversus æstum, ac se rore benedictionis & gratiarum omnium abundare, ac dulci irrigatione Verbi sui, qualis esse solet noctis, summo æstu, animos perfundere. Quæ Merceri explicatio est: qui hæc etiam subjungit: Caput dicit, quia ipse caput est Ecclesiæ, vel divinitatis suæ rationem habens, quæ in Christo caput est. Ut enim Christus Ecclesiæ, sic & Deus Christi caput est: ac in Metaphora persistens cincinnos dicit, indicans, se undiquaque gratiis esse refertum & imbutum. Humor enim capillis maxime inhæret. Plerique tamen in sequiorem partem interpretantur; Alii hanc volunt esse sententiam, quasi dicat Sponsus, se visendæ Sponsæ causa imbre nocturno madere, & ejus nomine frigus & injuriam aeris ac intemperiem noctis esse perpessum. Quod de passionibus in membris suis afflictiis intelligendum, sicuti Osiander explicat. Tirinus ita παραφράζει: Sum enim in mundo velut in altissima & frigidissima nocte, in quo qui me suis sceleribus lacessunt, congerunt rorem, gelu & grandinem super caput meum, dum me infrigidant & efficiunt, ne eos amem, sed oderim. Explicat etiam de iis, quæ Christus in passione nostri causa sustinuit: quod caput ejus gravatum fuerit frigido rore, & guttis omnium scelerum nostrorum, omnium ærumnarum,probrorum, blasphemiarum, sputorum, tormentorum, quæ nostri causa sustinuit. Quæ Junii quoque est Interpretatio: Nullum malum aut incommodum defugi, quin susceperim propter te. Hæc Belgis Interpp. ut & Paraphrastis Vinariensibus etiam placuit, qui ad noctem passionis magnæ hic imprimis respici, innuunt. Atque hæc explicatio nobis commodissima videtur. Cui frustra opponitur, quod nusquam ros in malam partem accipiatur; nam quis negabit nocturnas guttas, roremque incommoda secum ferre Gen. 31. v. 42. Dan. 4, 22. Et quod efficacius argumentum nos excitandi esse potest, quam Christi Sponsi nostri passio pro nobis exantlata? Quanquam nec prima Interpretatio de rore gratiæ sit incommoda. Nam uti beneficiis suis Sponsam sibi conciliat, ac demulcet Sponsus cœlestis, ita eorum abundantiam & ubertatem prædicat, cum aperiri sibi expetit.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. I HAVE PUT OFF MY TUNIC, HOW SHALL I PUT IT ON] These are the words of one refusing: by the tunic understand the habit of the night, which is put off when women take their daily garments: Propertius: Who when she was loosening the night-fastenings of her Sidonian mitre. I HAVE WASHED MY FEET] I have taken water, Roman women would say. You have that in Ovid quite often. In what sense feet are spoken of here you will see at Gen. 49, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 3. EXPOLIAVI ME TVNICA MEA, QVO MODO INDVAR ILLA] Sunt hæc verba ἀποκιζομένης: per tunicam intellige noctis habitum, qui exuitur, ubi diurna vestimenta sumunt mulieres: Propertius: Quæ cum Sidoniæ nocturna ligamina mitræ Solveret. LAVI PEDES MEOS] Sumsi aquam dicerent fœminæ Romanæ. Habes id apud Ovidium sæpius. Pedes quo sensu hic dicantur videbis ad Gen. 49, 10.

## 5:4
Vers. 4. HE TREMBLED] He was moved.

It does not appear to be the words of one feigning, nor of one feignedly refusing, as Grotius wishes, but of one hesitating, excusing, and struggling with flesh and blood. But when the Bride, oppressed by the torpor of sin, desires to indulge in her pleasure and rest, and dreads the afflictions and adversities that await the faithful, she struggles with herself in this way, and signifies how difficult it is for the flesh to be drawn away from the pleasures of the world and to adhere to Christ alone. Junius renders the sense thus: I debated with my mind, I wavered in faith, and hindered by my infirmity I hesitated, as if I could not open the doors without the damage of cold or the inconvenience of filth; finally, like a fool, I valued such a small inconvenience in performing my duty more than so many evils and inconveniences which the Bridegroom had voluntarily undertaken for my sake. Which explanation is confirmed by the following: Inasmuch as she offended the Bridegroom by this refusal, so that he withdrew himself and the Bride had need to seek him. Confer. Theodoret on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 4. INTREMvit] Commotus est.

Non apparet esse verba simulantis, nec simulate recusantis, uti vult Grotius, sed cunctantis, excusantis, & luctantis cum carne & sanguine. Quum autem Sponsa peccati torpore oppressa voluptati suæ, & quieti indulgere cupiat, ac afflictiones & adversitates, quæ fideles manent, horreat, secum ita luctantur & quam difficile carni sit abstrahi a voluptatibus mundi, unique Christo adhærescere, significat. Sensum ita reddit Junius: disceptavi cum animo meo, titubavi fide & præpedita infirmitate mea ita sum cunctata, quasi non potuissem sine frigoris damno aut sordium incommodo fores aperire, denique stulta pluris feci tam exiguum incommodum in fungendo officio meo, quam tot mala & incommoda, quæ Sponsus propter me voluntarie susceperat. Quæ explicatio firmatur e sequentibus: Siquidem hoc re- cre- sponso offenderit Sponsum, ut se subduxerit ac quærere ipsum Sponsa necessum habuerit. Confer. Theodor. in h. l.

## 5:5
Vers. 5. MY HANDS DRIPPED WITH MYRRH.

From the contact of the Bridegroom, her hands were strengthened to perform works pleasing to him, as the Weimar interpreters rendered; a most sweet odor, as Osiander; Alcuin understands continence and passions by myrrh: others, the mortification of the flesh, Gregory the Great, penance: all of which can be joined in a certain respect. Dürfeld takes it concerning the false imagination of purity of the Synagogue, but irrelevantly.

Latin:

Vers. 5. MANUS MEÆ STILLAVERUNT MYRRHAM.

Ex contactu Sponsi confortatæ sunt manus opera ipsi grata præstandi, ut Vinariens. red- diderunt; odorem suavissimum ut Osiander: continen- tiam & passiones per myrrham Alcuin. intelligit: mortificationem carnis Gregor. M. pœnitentiam alii: quæ omnia certo respectu conjungi possunt. De falsa puritatis imaginatione Synagogæ accipit Dürfeld. sed aliene.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. THE KEEPERS FOUND ME, WHO GO ABOUT THE CITY) Hands, which go about the whole body by feeling, they grope, they steal. THEY WOUNDED ME] They boast that they are naked, he says. THEY TOOK AWAY MY MANTLE FROM ME] Sulpitia: as if I were stripped of my Cadurcian bands.

A strange and inept interpretation, and hitherto, I believe, entirely unheard of. For who ever dreamed that by these keepers hands are indicated, and that to go about the city is the hands going about the whole body by feeling? And how did the hands find the Bride? That these things are inept, everyone sees. But it is consistent with the truth that pastors, who ought to be the keepers of the holy city, and who sell themselves as such, are understood, 2 Cor. 11, 13. 15. Which Mercerus also proves: They are keepers, who take them in a good sense, to whom the Church is committed, who with the word of God, which is a sword cutting on both sides, wound consciences, cutting away vices, and by the mantle is understood the corrupt and vicious life which they were leading before, whom they seriously lead to the Lord. But it is better to understand the bad guardians, and false Prophets and Doctors, into whom the Church sometimes falls, while for some time the Bridegroom withdraws himself from her, who most grievously wound consciences; and they tear away from her that saving veil with which she was previously covered, namely, the purity and sincerity of doctrine. Thus we have understood the garment stripped off above. Furthermore, because even if the Church is ruled by Pseudo-Prophets, she is not, however, so abandoned by the Lord that she does not recognize her state, and wish to return to her Bridegroom, and find him, who sometimes withdraws himself because of our sleepiness: therefore the following adjuration is added by the Church to the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, to individuals from the body of the Church, who are faithful, and have persisted in the purity of the Word. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I am sick with love. So also the Weimar Paraphrase. Junius understands it generally; all were hostile to me, even those by whom I ought to have been guarded. Osiander explains it concerning the preachers of the law, who know only how to argue and exaggerate sins, but not how to console afflicted consciences. Tirinus's explanation concerning the Doctors and Prelates of the Church, who are wounded by the arrows of divine love, is foreign.

Latin:

Vers. 7. INVENERVNT ME CVSTODES, QVI CIRCVMEVNT CIVITATEM) Manus, quæ totum cor- pus palpando circumeunt, ψηλαφῶσι, κλεπτορίζυσι. VV LNERAVERUNT ME] Vdam se jactant dicit. TVLERVNT PALLIVM MEVM MIHI] Sulpitia: ut me cadurcis destitutam fasciis.

Mira & inepta interpretatio, atque hactenus, ut credo, prorsus inaudita, Quis enim unquam so- mniavit, per custodes hos manus indigitari, & cir- cuire civitatem esse, manuum totum corpus palpan- do circumeuntium? Et quomodo manus invene- runt Sponsam? Inepta hæc esse, nemo non videt. Pastores autem, qui custodes sanctæ civitatis esse debent, atque pro talibus sese venditant, intelligi, vero consentaneum est 2. Cor. 11, 13. 15. Quod pro- bat etiam Mercerus: Custodes sunt, qui in bonam partem intelligunt eos, quibus commissa est Ecclesia, qui verbo Dei, qui gladius est utrinque scindens, vulne- rant conscientias, resecantes vitia, & per peplum in- telligitur corrupta & vitiosa vita, quam ante duce- bant, quos illi serio ad Dominum adducunt. Sed præ- stat malos custodes, falsosq́; Prophetas & Doctores in- telligere, in quos interdum incidit Ecclesia, dum per aliquod tempus sese ab ea Sponsus subducit, qui con- scientias gravissime vulnerant; ac peplum illud salu- tare, quo prius velata erat, ei detrahunt, puritatem scilicet, & sinceritatem doctrinæ. Sic fere supra tuni- cam spoliatam intelleximus. Cæterum quia etsi Ec- clesia per Pseudo - Prophetas regatur, non tamen ita a Domino destituitur, quin statum suum agnoscat, & ad suum Sponsum redire velit, eumque invenire, qui nostra somnolentia nonnunquam sese subtrahit: ideo sequens adjuratio subjungitur Ecclesiæ ad filios Jeru- salem, id est, singulos de corpore Ecclesiæ, qui fideles sunt, & in puritate Verbi perstiterunt. Adjuro vos filiæ Jerusalem, si inveneritis dilectum meum, ut nuncietis ei, quia amore langueo. Sic etiam Pa- raphr. Vinarienses. Junius generaliter intelligit; omnes infesti fuerunt mihi, etiam illi, a quibus fue- ram custodienda. Osiander de legis Concionatoribus explicat, qui tantum peccata arguere & exaggera- re, non autem afflictas conscientias consolari norunt. Aliena est Tirini explicatio de Doctoribus & Præ- latis Ecclesiæ, qui vulnerati sunt sagittis amoris divini.

## 5:8
Verse 8. I ADJURE YOU] New odes often begin, as in this place.

There is no reason why a new ode should be invented here, since the anxious search for the lost Bridegroom is continued, and the daughters of Jerusalem are even adjured to announce the Bride's love to the Bridegroom: to declare which, a notable description of the Bridegroom is added. As to what this may contain in its depths, let us hear Alcuin from the ancients, illustrating the same with a brief, but not inappropriate, paraphrase: My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands. White, because without sin; ruddy, by the blood of his passion: chosen out of thousands, because he alone is the Mediator of God and men. His head is the most fine gold: the head of Christ is God, who alone is good and best; his locks are as the branches of palm trees, black as a raven: the locks are the multitude of the saints, which

They adhere to God with faithful service: palms raised because of their eminence before God; black because of their contempt before men: Or raised because of victory, black because of pressures. His eyes are like doves by the streams of waters, they are the holy Doctors, through whom the Church sees what is right, who are well compared to doves because of innocence and simplicity, and to streams of waters because of divine charisms. Which are washed with milk, and reside near the fullest streams. He says washed with milk, i.e., cleansed by the sweetest grace: and reside near the fullest streams, i.e., the abundance of all spiritual gifts. In the streams can be designated the erudition of the old law, and in the fullest streams the perfection of Evangelical doctrine, because holy preachers bring forth from their treasures things old and new. Her cheeks are like beds of spices. In the cheeks of our Savior his modest piety and severity are expressed: in the beds of spices his virtues and sweetness and the fame of his glory are designated. Planted by the perfumers: his lips are lilies distilling the first myrrh. To the Prophets and Apostles; the former narrating the mysteries of his future incarnation, the latter the deeds: his lips are the words of his doctrine; Lilies because they promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom; distilling the first myrrh, because they preach that through the contempt of present pleasures, one must arrive at this. His hands are turned gold.
