Hands, that is, works, because what he taught in words, he fulfilled in deeds: Turned, because they hold in themselves every rule of justice; as it is said, it behooves me to fulfill all justice. They are also golden hands, because all that he did in man, he perfected with the glory of divinity. Full of hyacinths. Which excite us to the hope and love of heavenly things, because the hyacinth is a gem of the color of the air. His belly is ivory. The belly of the beloved therefore designates the fragility of his humanity, ivory the beauty of chastity, Sapphire the sublimity of heavenly virtues. Distinct with Sapphires. Because partly human fragility is understood by hunger, temptation, fatigue, death; partly divine loftiness by miracles, resurrection, and the glory of the ascension. His legs are marble columns. By the term of legs, the journeys of the incarnation of Christ are insinuated, which are compared to marble columns because of firmness and uprightness. Which are founded upon golden bases. Because whatever was done by him, or about him, all things were disposed by the counsel of divine foreknowledge before the secular times. His appearance, as of Lebanon, chosen as cedars. As Lebanon surpasses other mountains in the height and grace of its trees, so the Lord Christ surpasses all saints in the height of merits and the grace of virtues. Chosen as cedars. As he surpasses other trees, which are born in Lebanon, by his dignity, so Christ transcends all who are born to life in the Church by his glory. His throat is most sweet. In the throat is remembered the internal sweetness of his words, which he who tastes, does not hunger. And he is all desirable. What more do you seek? He is all desirable, because he is all God, and all man, into whom the Angels desire to look, God in the majesty of the Father, man in the virginity of the mother; in him the Creator, in her the Savior. Such is my beloved, and such is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. The more devoutly anyone loves God, the more familiarly he has God as a friend; and it is necessary that you understand him as such, if you wish to have him as a friend. Thus Alcuin. Mercerus says that by the head likewise is designated the divinity: by the hair the fullness of graces gathered in Christ: by the eyes pure and white the perspicacity and purity of the judgments of the Lord: by the cheeks and beds of spices the sweetness and fruitfulness of the gifts: by the lips distilling myrrh diffusing its odor everywhere the words of the Lord full of the highest sweetness and fruitfulness, exhilarating the mind and diffusing their sweetness far and wide, in the manner of lilies and the best myrrh: by the hands, which are like golden orbs filled with precious stones, the purest and most beautiful works of the Lord: by the belly referring to the whiteness of ivory, with the ornament of Sapphire, the interior senses of the divine word, and the intimate mysteries, in which there is the highest brightness and evenness: by the legs similar to marble columns the firmness and stability of the works and sermons of the Lord. The Weimar Paraphrasts explain all these members as the members of the human nature of Christ, and at the same time wish to designate the passion, which he endured in the same, who can be compared here.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ADJVRO VOS] Sæpe incipiunt novæ odæ, ut hoc loco.

Non est, cur hic nova oda fingatur, cum con- tinuetur sollicita inquisitio Sponsi amissi, atque adeo adjurentur filiæ Jerusalem, ut Sponso nuncient amorem Sponsæ: ob quem declarandum subjungi- tur insignis Sponsi descriptio. Quæ quid in recessu habeat, e Veteribus Alcuinum audiamus, brevi pa- raphrasi, sed non incongrua eandem ita illustran- tem: Dilectus meus candidus, & rubicundus, electus ex millibus. Candidus, quia sine peccato, rubicun- dus, sanguine passionis: electus ex millibus, quia so- lus Mediator Dei & hominum. Caput ejus aurum optimum: Caput Christi Deus, qui solus bonus, & optimus, Comæ ejus, sicut elatæ palmarum, nigræ, quasi corvus: Comæ caterva sunt sanctorum, quæ

Deo fideli famulatu adhærent: elatæ palmæ propter eminentiam apud Deum; nigræ propter despectio- nem apud homines: Vel elatæ ob victoriam, nigræ ob pressuras. Oculi ejus sicut columbæ super rivulos aquarum, sancti Doctores sunt, per quos Ecclesia vi- det, quæ recta sunt, qui bene columbæ propter inno- centiam & simplicitatem, & rivulis aquarum propter charismata divina comparantur. Quæ lacte sunt lo- tæ, & resident juxta fluenta plenissima. Lacte lotas di- cit, i. e. gratia dulcissima mundatas: & resident juxta fluenta plenissima i. e. omnium donorum spiritualium abundantiam. Potest in rivulis veteris legis eru- ditio, & in fluentis plenissimis perfectio Evangelicæ doctrinæ designari, quia sancti prædicatores de thesauris suis proferunt vetera & nova. Genæ illius sicut areolæ aromatum. In genis Salvatoris nostri ejus modesta pietas simul & severitas exprimitur: in areolis aromatum virtutes & dulcedo & fama glo- riæ ejus designantur. Consitæ a pigmentariis: labia ejus lilia distillantia myrrham primam. Prophetis & Apostolis; illi futuræ incarnationis ejus arcana, hi facta narrantes: labia illius verba sunt doctrinæ ejus; Lilia quia claritatem cœlestis regni promit- tunt; distillantia myrrham primam, quia per con- temptum voluptatum præsentium, ad hanc perve- niendum esse prædicant. Manus illius tornatiles aureæ. Manus, id est, opera, quia quæ verbis do- cuit, factis implevit: Tornatiles, quia in se omnem regulam justitiæ tenent; ut dicitur, oportet me omnem justitiam implere. Sunt & manus aureæ, quia omnia quæ in homine gessit, divinitatis gloria perfecit. Plenæ hyacinthis. Quæ ad spem nos cœlestium at- que amorem excitant, quia hyacinthus aeri colo- ris gemma est. Venter ejus eburneus. Venter ergo dilecti fragilitatem humanitatis ejus designat, ebur decorem castitatis, Saphirus sublimitatem cœle- stium virtutum. Distinctus Saphiris. Quia partim hu- mana fragilitas esurie, tentatione, fatigatione, mor- te; partim divina celsitudo miraculis, resurrectio- ne, & ascensionis gloria intelligitur. Crura illius columnæ marmoreæ. Crurum vocabulo, itinera in- carnationis Christi insinuantur, quæ columnis mar- moreis propter firmitatem & rectitudinem com- parantur. Quæ fundatæ sunt super bases aureas. Quia quicquid per eum, vel de eo gestum est, omnia divinæ prævisionis consilio ante tempora secularia disposita sunt. Species ejus, ut Libani, electus ut ce- dri. Ut Libanus celsitudine & gratia arborum alios montes, sic Dominus Christus omnes sanctos meritorum celsitudine, & gratia virtutum antecel- lit. Electus ut cedri. Sicut alias arbores, quæ in Libano nascuntur, superat dignitate sua, ita Christus omnes qui in Ecclesia ad vitam nascuntur, sua tran- scendit gloria. Guttur illius suavissimum. In gutture interna dulcedo verborum illius memoratur, quam qui sapit, non esurit. Et totus desiderabilis. Quid amplius quæris? Totus desiderabilis est, quia totus Deus, & totus homo, in quem desiderant & Ange- li prospicere, Deus in majestate Patris, homo in virginitate matris; in illo Creator, in hac Salvator. Talis est dilectus meus, & talis est amicus meus, filiæ Jerusalem. Quanto devotius quisque diligit Deum, tanto familiarius habet amicum Deum; & talem necesse ut intelligas eum, si vis eum habere amicum. Hæc Alcuinus. Mercerus per caput itidem divini- tatem: per capillos plenitudinem gratiarum in Chri- sto confertam: per oculos puros & candidos perspi- cacitatem & puritatem judiciorum Domini: per maxillas & areolas suavitatem & ubertatem dono- rum: per labia stillantia myrrham undiquaque odo- re se diffundentem verba Domini summa suavitate & ubertate plena, animum exhilarantia & longe lateque suam dulcedinem diffundentia, liliorum & myrrhæ optimæ more: per manus, quæ ut orbes au- rei repleti lapidibus pretiosis, opera Domini puriffi- ma & pulcherrima: per intestinanitorem eboris re- ferentia, cum ornamento Sapphiri sensus interiores verbi divini, & intima mysteria, in quibus summus nitor & æquabilitas: per crura similia columnis marmoreis firmitatem & stabilitatem operum & sermonum Domini designari ait. Paraphrastæ Vinarienses membra hæc omnia de membris huma- næ Christi naturæ explicant, simulque passionem, quam in iisdem exantlavit, designari volunt, qui hic conferri poterunt.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

The bride, having professed that the bridegroom is staying in the garden and is hers, is overwhelmed by that eulogy of beauty which kindles the flame of love; which she describes by reason of the hair, teeth, and cheeks, having instituted a comparison with others, indeed with the Moon, and the Sun: and having signified her entry into the vineyard, she recalls the Shulamite to repentance.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Sponsa in horto morari sponsum, eumque suum professa mactatur ab eo elogio pulchritudinis flammam amoris accendentis; quam ratione capillorum, dentium & genarum describit, comparatione cum aliis instituta, imo cum Luna, & Sole: ac significato in vineam in- gressu Sulamitida revocat ad pœnitentiam.

## 6:4
Ver. 3. THOU ART BEAUTIFUL MY FRIEND SWEET] In Hebrew: As Tirzah, the name of a city. TERRIBLE AS AN ARMY SET IN ARRAY] The Greeks would say blosyra or sobara. Ver. 6. BESIDE THY HIDDEN THINGS] Again in Hebrew: Within the hair.

The LXX and the Vulgate took the name Tirzah as an appellative. Thou art beautiful as COMPLACENCY or as sweetness itself: but the fact that Jerusalem is added shows it to be a proper name. TIRZAH was the seat of the Kings of Israel, as Jerusalem was of the Kings of Judah, both beautiful and illustrious cities: to which, because of beauty and excellence, the bride is compared, the Church, which is also called the city of God Ps. 46 and 48. But because of her majesty she is compared to an army set in array, terrible to enemies. Terrible AS BANNERED, i.e., as cohorts distributed under distinct banners into certain ranks and instructed for fighting, concerning whose spiritual armor and strength in the Lord Eph. 6, 10. to which pertains especially firm trust, united concord, and religious obedience: Bernard. Serm. 41. on the manner of living blessedly. As enemies fear when they see armies of camps set in order for war, so the Devil is terrified at the sight of concord. She is terrible, says Bede, because she has the whole army of virtues set in order within herself.

Latin:

Vers. 3. PVLCHRA ES AMICA MEA SVAVIS] In Hebræo: Ut Thirsa, nomen urbis. TERRIBILIS VT CASTRORVM ACIES ORDINA- TA] βλοσυρὰ aut σοβαρὰ dicerent Græci. Vers. 6. ABSQVE OCCVLTIS TVIS] Rursum in He- bræo: Intra comam.

NOmen תרצה ceu appellativum accepere LXX. & Vulg. Pulcra es sicut COMPLA- CENTIA vel ceu ipsa suavitas: sed nomen pro- prium esse adjuncta Hierosolyma docet. TIRSA Regum Israelis sedes fuit, ut Hierosolyma Regum Judæ, utraque pulcra & præclara civitas: cui ob pul- chritudinem & præstantiam sponsa confertur, Ec- clesia, quæ etiam civitas Dei dicitur Pf. 46. & 48. ob majestatem vero hostibus terribilem castrorum aciei ordinatæ comparatur. Terribilis UT VE- XILLATÆ, h. e. ut cohortes sub distinctis vexillis in certos ordines distributæ & ad pugnandum in- structæ, de quarum spirituali armatura & fortitudi- ne in Domino Eph. 6, 10. ad quam imprimis firma fi- ducia, unita concordia, & religiosa obedientia perti- net: Bernhard. Serm. 41. de mod. beate viv. Ut hostes timent quando acies castrorum ordinatas ad bellum vident, sic Diabolus ad concordiæ intuitum expavescit. Terribilis est ait Beda, quia universam virtutum aciem habet in se instructam.

## 6:8
Verse 7. THERE ARE SIXTY QUEENS, AND EIGHTY CONCUBINES, AND OF THE YOUNG MAIDENS THERE IS NO NUMBER: ONE IS MY DOVE] It is lacking, however. The sense is, although in my women's quarters there are so many legitimate wives taken, so many others less solemnly admitted, and many maidens besides, who are kept for me, yet there is one uniquely beloved.

Again he understands Solomon, and his wives, concubines, and maidens. But history does not teach that he had as many as are numbered here: indeed, it teaches the contrary, namely that he had more wives than concubines, 1 Kings 11:3. And who will admit that Solomon had innumerable young maidens who were kept for him? These things must be understood mystically, as the whole Canticle. The Weimar theologians explain this as the multitude of particular churches, both great and small, and of faithful converts, who are called maidens. Compare Psalm 45:15. Osiander also indicated this sense: It is signified that many churches will indeed be planted here and there in the world, some of greater estimation and fame, others of less; but from all these is gathered one Church, namely that of the Elect: This is the one most dear to Christ, which He cannot hate: This is that one, of which we speak in the Apostles' Creed;

I believe in the Catholic Church, the Communion of Saints. Mercerus explains it similarly, and rightly observes that a certain number is put for an uncertain one, as above, when the 60 of Solomon were named in chapter 3. But the ancient Doctors wish for the orders of the pious and the diversity of gifts in one elect [body] to be regarded here, with Queens, concubines, and young maidens distinctly designated. Theodoret in this place: We are not ignorant that there are many and various orders of the pious, which the Lord also teaching, says, there are many mansions in my Father's house. And in the distribution of talents, they did not each receive five talents, but one five, another two, the third one, each according to his own ability. Also in the parable of the women, he says, some fell on good ground, and brought forth fruit, some thirty, some sixty, and some an hundred. By the Bride, therefore, he understands souls, which, moved solely by the love of the Bridegroom, embrace the labors of cultivating virtue, and are willing both to do and to suffer all things. Queens, however, are those who, incited by the desire for the Kingdom, bear the labors of piety: Concubines are those who obey divine laws out of fear of hell: since the Bridegroom joins himself even to them, having become all things to all men: finally, young maidens, who are sluggish and slothful, neither burning with love for the Bridegroom, nor drawn by the desire for the kingdom, nor moved (as is fitting) by the fear of hell, but pass their lives negligently, although they nevertheless retain an immovable faith and maintain the institutions of piety, and abhor heretical and foreign discipline: and living more sluggishly, they seem now to care for themselves, now again to return to sloth, now to involve themselves in sins, now to repent, and to pour forth tears through penance. Which explanation seems very appropriate, analogous to the exposition of Psellus and the other three Fathers in Theodoret; but worked out a little more neatly.

Latin:

Vers. 7. SEXAGINTA SVNT REGINÆ, ET OCTO- GINTA CONCVBINÆ, ET ADOLESCENTVLARVM NON EST NVMERVS: VNA EST COLVMBA MEA] Deest attamen. Sensus est, quamvis in gynæconitide mea tot sunt uxores legitimæ ductæ, tot aliæ minus solemniter adscitæ, multæ præterea Virgines, quæ mihi servantur, una tamen est unice dilecta.

Iterum intelligit Salomonem, ejusque uxores, concubinas & virgines. Sed eum totidem habuisse, quod hic numerantur, historia non docet: imo contrarium docet, quod nempe plures habuerit uxores, quam concubinas 1. Reg. 11, 3. Et quis ad- mittet, Salomonem innumeras habuisse virgines adolescentulas, quæ ipsi servatæ fuerint? Mystice hæc intelligenda, ut totum Canticum. De multitu- dine Ecclesiarum particularium, cum magnarum, tum parvarum & fidelium conversorum, qui vir- gines dicuntur, Vinarienses Theologi explicant. Con- fer. Pf. 45, 15. Quem sensum Osiander etiam indica- vit: Significatur autem multas quidem passim in orbe terrarum plantatum iri Ecclesias, alias majoris existi- mationis & famæ, alias minoris; ex his autem omni- bus colligi unam Ecclesiam, nimirum Electorum: Hæc est, Christo charissima, quam non potest odisse: Hæc illa est, de qua dicimus in Symbolo Apostolico;

Credo Ecclesiam Catholicam, Sanctorum Com- munionem. Similiter explicat Mercerus, nume- rumque certum pro incerto, uti supra, cum 60. Sa- lomonis nominabantur cap. 3. poni, recte obser- vat. At Doctores Veteres ordines piorum donorum- que diversitatem in una electa, Reginis, concubinis, & adolescentulis distincte hic designatis, respici volunt. Theodoretus in h. l. Multos ac varios esse piorum or- dines non ignoramus, quod Dominus etiam docens, multæ, inquit, mansiones sunt apud Patrem meum. Et in distributione talentorum non quina singuli ta- lenta acceperunt, sed unus quinque, alter duo, tertius unum pro sua quisque virtute. In feminis etiam pa- rabola, aliud, inquit, cecidit in terram bonam, & fe- cit fructum tricesimum & sexagesimum & centesi- mum. Per Sponsam igitur animas intelligit, quæ sola Sponsi charitate impulsæ labores excolendæ vir- tutis amplectuntur, omniaque & facere & pati vo- lunt. Reginas autem, quæ Regni cupiditate irritatæ pietatis labores ferunt: Concubinas, quæ gehennæ formidine divinis legibus parent: quum Sponsus cum ipsas quoque conjungatur, omnibus factus omnia: adolescentulas denique, quæ inertes ac ignavæ, nec Sponsi amore flagrant, nec regni trahuntur cupidita- te, nec gehennæ metu (prout par est) commoventur, sed vitam traducunt negligenter, quum tamen & fi- dem immobilem retineant & pietatis instituta tuean- tur, & ab hæretica ac peregrina disciplina abhor- reant: ac fegnius quidem viventes modo videantur seipsos curare, modo rursus ad ignaviam redire, mo- do se peccatis involvere, nunc resipiscere, & per pœ- nitentiam lacrymas fundere. Quæ explicatio per- quam congrua videtur, Pselli & aliorum trium Pa- trum apud Theodoret. expositioni analoga; at paulo concinnius elaborata.

## 6:10
Verse 9. WHO IS SHE THAT LOOKETH FORTH AS THE MORNING RISING] Thus the Latin Poet: I had stood by chance greeting the rising dawn, When suddenly from the left Roscius arises: With your permission, may I say, O heavenly ones, A mortal seemed more beautiful than a God. Grotius compares the Latin Poet: we the Doctors of the Church. Alcuin says this voice is that of the Synagogue, wondering at the Church; and explains it thus: The Church proceeds like the dawn, because now the Sun of true light is shown in her to the world after the darkness of long ignorance. Foljoth: The Church, desiring the eternal, shines with supernal brightness and the light of justice, she rises like the dawn, because having abandoned the depravity of the age, she turns herself into the radiance of a new light. Cassiodorus and Bede explain these praises of the Church thus: Who is she that, like the dawn, the darkness of infidelity having passed, shows that she has the light of truth, progressing from virtue to virtue and occupying the whole world with heavenly preaching. Fair as the Moon, because she is illuminated by the grace of Christ the true Sun, and because in the present life she sometimes grows when peace is granted, and sometimes seems to decrease through adversities. Elect as the Sun, in the other life, where she will shine forever with joy from the vision of her creator, and also in the present life, because she imitates Christ the true Sun, and being united by the union of charity, she is terrible to the Demons, as an army set in array. These are the ancient Doctors, to whom our contemporaries are now compared, entirely of one mind as to the sense of the words: Osiander in particular, and the Weimar Paraphrasts.

Latin:

Vers. 9. QVÆ EST ISTA, QVÆ PROGREDITVR QVASI AVRORA CONSVRGENS] Sic Latinus Poëta: Adstiteram exorientem auroram forte salutans, Cum subito à læva Roscius exoritur: Pace mihi liceat cælestes dicere vestra, Mortalis visus pulchrior esse Deo. Grotius Latinum Poëtam confert: nos Docto- res Ecclesiæ. Alcuinus vocem hanc Synagogæ esse dicit, mirantis Ecclesiam; atque ita explicat: Progre- ditur Ecclesia quasi aurora, quia jam veri luminis in ea Sol ortus mundo post tenebras longæ ignorantiæ monstratur. Foljoth: Ecclesia æterna appetens, su- perna claritate & luce justitiæ fulgescit, quasi aurora consurgit, quia derelicta pravitate seculi sese in novi luminis fulgorem convertit. Elogia hæc Ecclesiæ ita explicant Cassiodorus & Beda: Quæ est ista, quæ quasi aurora, transactis tenebris infidelitatis, lumen veritatis habere ostendit, proficiens de virtute in virtu- tem totumque orbem cœlesti occupans prædicatione. Pulchra ut Luna, quia Christi veri Solis gratia illu- minatur, & quia in vita præsenti aliquando, concessa pace crescit, aliquando per adversitates decrescere vide- tur. Electa ut Sol, in alia vita, ubi perpetuo resplende- bit gaudio de visione conditoris sui, atque etiam in vita præsenti, quia Christum verum imitatur Solem, quæ- que charitatis unione unita, terribilis Dæmonibus est, ut castrorum acies ordinata. Hæc veteres Dd. quibus nunc conferantur Nostrates, prorsus ὁμό- ψηφοι quod ad verborum sensum: Osiander impri- mis, & Paraphrastæ Vinarienses.

## 6:11
Verse 10.

AND I WENT DOWN INTO THE GARDEN OF NUTS, TO SEE THE FRUITS OF THE VALLEYS, AND TO SEE IF THE VINE FLOURISHED, AND THE POMEGRANATES BUDDED] Whether she were in her flow. A similar allegory, and tending to the same end in the book Kethub: Every vine produces wine: that in which there is no wine is sterile. But that word 'wine' is explained by 'blood of virginity.' Away with such obscene thoughts from the style, matter, and scope of this most holy Canticle, which are most alien to it, and savor of nothing but a carnal mind, in no way responding to the most holy affection of the Bridegroom. Theodoret, three Anonymi in the Catena of the same, Cassiodorus, Mercerus, and others think this voice is not the Bridegroom's, but the Bride's. But let us grant that it is the Bridegroom's, as Jerome does in Chapter XII of Zechariah. Philo Carpathius, Gregory the Great, and Anselm teach: who does not see that, according to this opinion, he himself persists in the allegory: and when he says he went down into the garden, these things tend to this, that he might inspect the fruits of the garden, and especially, whether the vine flourished and the pomegranates budded? Where the interpreters believe that the nuts of penance and patience, and the apples of the valleys or the fruits of humility; then the grapes and wines of devotion, and also the pomegranates of charity are required, according to the sense contained under the bark of the letter. But no one, even in a fever, dreamed of those obscene things, which do not fit the garden, nor the nuts, or apples, or pomegranates in that way. Alcuin: that I might see if the vines had flourished: to see if the studies of virtues had flourished. And the pomegranates had budded: If any were prepared after the example of the Lord's passion to shed their blood.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ET INSPICEREM, SI FLORVISSET VINEA ET GERMINASSENT MALA PVNICA] An nupta esset ἐν ῥύσει. Similis allegoria, & eodem tendens in libro Kethub: Omnis vitis producit vinum: in qua non est vinum, ea est sterilis. Explicatur autem illud יין per דם בתולים. Facesseant obscænæ ejusmodi cogitationes ab hujus sanctissimi Cantici stylo, materia & scopo alie- niffime, nec nisi animum carnalem sapientes, neu- tiquam sanctissimo affectui Sponsi respondente. Vocem hanc non Sponsi, sed Sponsae esse Theodore- tus, tres Anonymi, in Catena apud eundem, Cassio- dorus, Mercerus, alii putant. Sed largiamur, Spon- si ea esse, ut Hieronymus in Cap. XII. Zach. Philo Carpathius, Gregorius M. & Anshelmus docent: ecquis non videt, juxta hanc sententiam persistere ipsum in allegoria: & quum in hortum se descen- disse dicat, haec eo tendere, ut scil. horti fructus in- spiceret, & cumprimis, an vinea floreret ac germi- narent mala punica? Ubi nuces poenitentiae & pa- tientiae, & poma convallium seu fructus humilitatis; tum uvas & vina devotionis, nec non mala punica charitatis requiri, juxta sensum sub literae cortice comprehensum Interpp. credunt. Nemo autem ista obscoena, quae neque horto, neque nucibus, aut pomis malisque punicis eo pacto conveniunt, vel per febrim somniavit. Alcuinus; ut inspicerem, si floruissent vineae: inspicere, si virtutum studia flo- ruissent. Et germinassent mala punica: Si qui ad exemplum Dominicae passionis praeparati essent suum fundere sanguinem.

## 6:12
Verse 11.

I KNEW NOT] I had not thought. MY SOUL MADE ME LIKE THE CHARIOTS OF AMMINADIB] For the chariots of Amminadab. The name seems to have been that of a well-known leader, to whom a purple chariot belonged.

Nowhere is such a prefect read of, whose name is Amminadab. Some wish these words to be the Bridegroom's, to whom they attribute the whole discourse of this Chapter, such as Osiander, and the Weimar [theologians], as also Junius, and others. That 'I knew not' is therefore spoken in the human manner, because the Bridegroom was wondering at the course of the Gospel among the nations, even though nothing can escape him or be hidden from him. Others prefer that it is the voice of the Synagogue, which was troubled because of the chariots of Amminadab, seeing, that is, the chariot and course of the Gospel opposing Judaism: which sense Cornelius a Lapide says is common to the Fathers, Gregory the Great, Cassiodorus, Bede, Justus of Urgell, Philo Carpathius, Anselm, Rupert, and others. The chariot and course of the Gospel are noted by the four-horse chariots from Ezekiel: by which many also think that the four-horse chariot of the Evangelists, carried most swiftly through the world by the ministry of the holy Apostles through the preaching of the Gospel, is signified: but some take the word עמי נדיב appellatively, on account of the chariots of my willing or liberal people. As the Syriac translates it by the chariot of a prepared people. And because that word can also be rendered Leader or Prince of my people, as the Fifth edition translated it, you have placed me in the chariot of the people of the Leader: some think that Christ is thus pointed out. But the sense comes to the same thing. For it could seem wonderful to the Jews that among the nations the chariots of Christ the Prince of his people had made such progress. I will add one or two paraphrases. Alcuin makes this the voice of the Synagogue: I knew not, my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab. I knew not, the gifts of spiritual grace to be in you, O Bride. But my soul troubled me because of the introduction of the New Testament and the Evangelical Chariot, which Aminadab (which is interpreted, the Willing one of my people) that is, Christ, is carried through the whole world: to whom the Church soon responds by consoling: Return, return, O Shulamite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Do not be troubled, but return to the acknowledgment of your redeemer, who was promised to you so often in the Prophets and the law. Return with purity of faith, with perfection of works, O Shulamite (so some of the Ancients read in the Latin text; the Hebrew has Shulamite) that is, with the bond of infidelity now thoroughly scraped away, return to your Redeemer, that you may be saved. Similarly Gilbert Foljoth: The Synagogue stands, is stunned, and trembles, and at length having returned to itself says, I did not know, that is, I was ignorant of such great grace and gifts of your Spirit bestowed, and so my soul has troubled me, because I wandered in darkness. Because of the chariots of Aminadab it signifies Christ. For Aminadab is interpreted as the Willing one of my people. For he himself stood as the head of the whole people, born willingly, given willingly unto death, etc. Whose chariots indeed are the four Gospels, which are drawn through the world, while they are preached to the peoples and believed, and are received with all veneration, etc. Whoever wishes may now compare with these the Paraphrase of Osiander and of the Weimar Theologians.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

NESCIVI] Non cogitaveram. ANIMA MEA CONTVRBAVIT ME PROPTER QVADRIGAS AMINADABI] Propter currus Aminadab. Nomen videtur fuisse Ducis bene noti, cui currus esset pur- pureus.

Nuspiam legitur praefectus talis, cui nomen Aminadab. Verba quidam haec volunt esse Sponsi, cui totam orationem hujus Capitis tribuunt, utpote Osiander, & Vinarienses, ut & Junius, aliique. Il- lud ergo nescivi more humano dictum, quod mira- retur Sponsus cursum Evangelii inter gentes, etsi eum nihil fugiat aut latere possit. Alii vocem Syna- gogae esse malunt, quae conturbata fuerit propter qua- drigas Aminadab, videns scil. currum cursumque Evangelii adversari Judaismo: quem sensum com- munem esse Patrum, Gregorii M. Cassiodori, Bedae, Justi Orgelit. Philon. Carpathii, Anshelmi, Ruperti, aliorum, Cornelius a Lapide dicit. Quadrigis no- tari currum & cursum Evangelii ex Ezechiele no- tum: quibus etiam quadrigam Evangelistarum ce- lerrime per praedicationem Evangelii S. Apostolo- rum ministerio per orbem vectam innui, plerique censent: Vocem vero עמי נדיב appellative acci- piunt nonnulli, propter quadrigas populi mei spon- tanei vel liberalis. Uti Syrus vertit per currum po- puli parati. Et quia vox illa reddi etiam potest po- puli mei Dux vel Princeps, uti Quinta editio transtu- lit, posuisti me in currum populi Ducis: Christum ita indigitari, nonnulli putant. Sensus autem eo- dem recidit. Id enim mirum videri poterat Judaeis, quod inter gentes quadrigae Christi Principis populi sui talem progressum fecerant. Adscribam unam atque alteram paraphrasin. Alcuinus vocem Syna- gogae hanc facit: Nescivi, anima mea conturbavit me propter quadrigas Aminadab. Nescivi, dona gratiae spiritualis in te esse Sponsa. Sed anima mea conturbavit me propter introductionem Novi Testa- menti & Evangelicae Quadrigae, quae Aminadab (qui interpretatur, populi mei Spontaneus) id est, Chri- stus per totum vehitur mundum: cui Ecclesia conso- lando mox respondet: Revertere, revertere Sunami- tis, revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te. Noli tur- bata esse, sed revertere ad agnitionem tui redemtoris, qui tibi toties in Prophetis & lege promissus est. Re- vertere puritate fidei, operum perfectione, o Suna- mitis (ita legeruut nonnulli Veteres in Latino tex- tu; Ebraeus habet Sulamitis) id est, captiva jam vinculo infidelitatis penitus abraso, revertere ad tuum Redemtorem, ut salveris. Similiter Gilbertus Foljoth: Synagoga stat, stupet, & contremiscit, & in se tandem reversa ait, Nescivi, id est, Tantarn gratiam & dona Spiritus tui collata ignoravi, adeoque anima mea conturbavit me, quia in tenebris aberravi. Pro- pter quadrigas Aminadab Christum significat. Ami- nadab enim Spontaneus populi mei interpretatur. Ipse enim totius populi caput extitit, sponte natus, sponte in mortem datus &c. Cujus quidem quadrigae sunt quatuor Evangelia, quae per mundum trahuntur, dum praedicantur populis & creduntur, & omni veneratione digna suscipiuntur &c. Conferre nunc, qui volet, cum istis poterit Paraphrasin Osiandrinam, & Vina- riensium Theologorum.

## 6:13
Verse 12.

RETURN, RETURN, O SHULAMITE) He calls back the one fleeing. Shulamite, that is, the wife of Solomon.

Whither would the wife of Solomon have fled, that she had to be called back with such contention? And how do those things which we have hitherto had concerning the Shulamite, and which occur in the remaining chapters, suit her? The Latin reads Shunammite, as if Abishag the Shunammite were signified, but the Hebrew codices have Shulamith, which the interpreters, led by the Chaldean, deduce not from Solomon, but from Salem: i.e., Jerusalemite. Whence Mercerus rightly concluded that she was not the daughter of Pharaoh, of whom this epithalamium was published: but he observes that this name suits the Church, because it began from Jerusalem. Theodoret on this passage: Just as in this book our Lord is Solomon, that is, peaceful: so also his Bride, as having obtained peace from him, and having been delivered from the old war, is called peaceful.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

REVERTERE, REVERTERE SULAMITIS) Refu- gientem revocat. Sulamitis, id est, Salomonis uxor.

Quorsum fugisset uxor Salomonis, ut tanta contentione revocanda fuerit? & quomodo illi ea praedicata, quae hactenus de Sulamith habuimus, quaeque in reliquis Capp. occurrunt, conveniunt? Latinus legit Sunamitis, quasi significaretur Abisag Sunamitis, sed Ebraei Codd. habent Sulamith, quod non a Salomone, sed a Salem deducunt Interpp. prae- eunte Chaldaeo: q. d. Hierosolymitana. Unde recte collegit Mercerus, non fuisse filiam Pharaonis eam, de qua hoc Epithalamion editum: Ecclesiae autem hoc nomen convenire observat, quia a Jerusalem cepit. Theodoretus in h. l. Quemadmodum in hoc li- bro Dominus noster Salomon, id est, pacificus: sic etiam ejus Sponsa, ut ab illo pacem assecuta, & a veteri libe- rata bello pacifica nominatur.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

The Bridegroom commends the bride for her origin, gait, limbs, stature, and speech; the bride desires to wander with the bridegroom into the field and the vineyard, offering him all that is hers.

Verse 1. WHAT WILL YOU SEE IN THE SHULAMITE, AS IT WERE THE COMPANY OF TWO ARMIES] It coheres with the preceding. She denies that she wishes to be inspected. For this spectacle would not be more pleasant than a bloody army.

But how do these things suit the wife of Solomon? Furthermore, this does not only cohere with the preceding by reason of the sense, but it also pertains to the previous chapter in the Hebrew text. Grotius assumes that the words are those of the bride herself; which most deny, and attribute them rather to the Bridegroom. Gregory the Great, Philo Carpathius, Cassiodorus, Aponius, Honorius, Alcuin, Anselm, Haymo, and others. However, there is nothing in the Hebrew about a BLOODY Army. The companies are indicated by מחנים, which name Junius wishes to be a proper noun, calling it an apostrophe of the Bridegroom to his friends, whom he excites by questioning, so that they may be spectators and witnesses of the greatness of the glory which is in the Church, and the response either of the friends, or rather of the Bridegroom himself to the question: Do you see how glorious and with what a spectacular and strong retinue the Church is! Clearly when I behold this crowd coming to meet me, I seem to see that joyful day, when the Israelites returning to David received him with the greatest joy and gladness at Mahanaim, and were graciously received by him. See the history in 2 Sam. 19. Most, however, take the rest as an appellative: as military troops, and two battle lines marching in order as if in a chorus to join battle. Theodoret says, The Bride, composed of many of the saints, is like a camp because of her fortitude and high strength of spirit and military arms: then also she exists as a chorus bearing divine praises in her mouth. Some observe that two peoples are designated by the dual number, from whom the Church is collected, and they think that an allusion is made here besides to the heavenly angelic hosts in Gen. 31, with whom the Church will one day constitute one chorus, namely, when it is to triumph in the heavens. Alcuin specifically hints that these things pertain to the Jews, whom the Church was calling back, rendering this sense: You grieve for the hardened Synagogue: the time is near when you will see in her the choruses of those warring against malignant spirits and praising God. So that it is the voice of the Bridegroom, responding to the Church concerning the Synagogue. And not a few of the ancients explain this concerning the conversion of the Jews; yet Theodoret, Justus Orgelitanus, and St. Ambrose in his work on the death of Valentinian wish these things to be said of the Church in general, which opinion is also that of Osiander and the Weimar theologians, and seems to be preferred. The Papists here [say] many things about the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world and about the return of Enoch and Elijah, without Scripture.

Verse same. HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THY FEET IN SHOES, O PRINCE'S DAUGHTER] The Hebrews refer these to the Sanhedrin by way of allegory.

Grotius, however, admires the shoes of the daughter of Pharaoh, and has his eyes fixed on the beautiful entry in them. The Holy Fathers explain them with a unanimous opinion concerning the Church, and understand the modest steps as the gait of virtues, the steps by which she walks to God, or even to preach the Gospel. Alcuin notes that the constancy of works and the mortification of pleasures are praised here in her; Theodoret and three anonymous authors, as well as Ambrose, understand them as the modesty, gravity, and piety of her gait and external actions. Gregory the Great, Cassiodorus, Beda, and Anselm understand them as steps directed toward propagating the Gospel. The Weimar theologians combine both in their paraphrase, the gait for defending the Word of peace, Isa. 52:7, Eph. 6:26, and according to the rule of the word, Gal. 6:14, 16. But how these things suit the Sanhedrin does not appear. Does it come under the name of the Prince's daughter, or is it shadowed forth through her? or were the Queen's shoes or feet the assessors of the Sanhedrin? R. Solomon more fittingly refers the feet to the ascent of the Israelites and the stated festivals, which were three in a year, according to God's commandment in Exod. 13. Grotius for the most part chooses all the worst things when he consults the Jews. But it is certain that the daughter of the Prince is the Church of God the Father Almighty, who governs the whole world, a daughter noble through Christ in the endowments and mighty works and thanks of the Holy Spirit.

Verse same. THE JOINTS OF YOUR THIGHS] The circumference of the thigh.

The word חמוקי is rightly rendered circumference or circuit. But it had to be explained what is understood by the circumference of the thighs, and why they are compared to jewels, the work of the hands of an excellent craftsman? Mercerus maintains that the thighs refer to the generation of children, whom the Church daily brings forth for Christ, and that the most beautiful and artful method of generating through the preaching of the Word is designated, where there is the highest adornment, the excellent art of Christ the craftsman. Therefore Osiander paraphrases thus: You have loins not distorted, but most aptly disposed for fruitfulness and generation. The Weimar theologians intimate that the truth of the loins signifies the stability of all in the faith Eph. 6. v. 14. Rom. 15, 2. with the readiness to resist enemies 1. Pet. 5. v. 8. and perpetual vigilance, as indicated in Luke 12. v. 35.

Latin:

CAPUT VII.

Sponsus commendat sponsam ab origine, incessu, membris, statura & sermone, sponsa cum sponso exspatiari desiderat in agrum, & vi- neam, ei sua omnia offerens.

Vers. 1. QVID VIDEBIS IN SULAMITE, NISI CHOROS CASTRORUM] Cohaeret cum superioribus. Negat se velle inspectari. Neque enim hoc spectaculum sua- vius fore quam cruenti exercitus.

QUi vero haec Salomonis uxori conveniunt? Caeterum non tantum sensus ratione hoc co- haeret cum superioribus, sed ad caput etiam praece- dens pertinet in Ebraeo textu. Assumit Grotius, ver- ba esse ipsius sponsae; quod plerique negant, & Sponso potius ea tribuunt. Gregorius Magnus, Philo Carpathius, Cassiodorus, Aponius, Honorius, Alcuinus, Anshelmus, Haymo, alii. Nihil autem in Ebraeo habetur de CRUENTO Exercitu. Chori מחנים indigitantur, quod nomen proprium esse vult Junius, apostrophen Sponsi ad amicos dicens, quos interrogando excitet, ut amplitudinis gloriae, quae in Ecclesia est, Spectatores sint, & testes, ac respon- sionem sive amicorum, seu potius ipsius Sponsi ad quae- stionem: Videtis quam gloriosa & quam spectato, fortique comitatu sit Ecclesia! Plane quum hanc tur- bam occurfantem mihi conspicio, videri mihi videor laetum illum diem, quo Israelitae revertentes ad Davi- dem maximo gaudio & laetitia omnium exceperunt eum Machanaymis, & gratiose ab eo excepti sunt. Vide Histor. 2. Sam. 19. Plerique tamen reliqui ut ap- pellativum accipiunt: tanquam turmas militares, & binas acies ordine incedentes velut in choro ad pu- gnam committendam. Theodoretus, Sponsa, inquit, multis e sanctis conflata, cum propter fortitudinem atque excelsum animi robur armaque militaria castris est similis: tum etiam chorus existit divinas laudes in ore gerens. Duali numero designari duos populos, e quibus collecta est Ecclesia, nonnulli observant, & allusionem praeterea ad coelestes exercitus an- gelicos Gen. 31. hic fieri putant, cum quibus unum chorum olim conftituet Ecclesia, in cœlis nempe triumphatura. Alcuinus peculiariter ad Judæos, quos revocabat Ecclesia, hæc pertinere innuit, hunc reddens senfum: Tu doles Synagogam obdura- tam: prope est tempus, quo choros bellantium adver- sus malignos Spiritus, & laudantium Deum videbis in ea. Ut sit vox Sponsi, respondentis Ecclesiæ dę Synagoga. Et de conversione Judæorum non pauci exponunt e Veteribus; Theodoretus tamen, Justus Orgelitanus, & S. Ambros. de obitu Valent. de Eccle- sia in genere hæc dicta volunt, quæ sententia etiam Ofiandri & Vinariens. est, & præferenda videtur. Papistæ hic multa de conversione Judæorum sub fi- nem mundi & de reditu Enochi & Eliæ, ἄτερ γρα- φῆς.

Vers. eod. QVAM PULCHRI SUNT GRESSUS TUI IN CALCEAMENTIS FILIA PRINCIPIS] Hæc ad Sy- nedrium κατ' ἀλληγορίαν referunt Ebræi.

Grotius vero calceamenta miratur Filiæ Pha- raonis, & in ingressum in iisdem pulchrum defixos habet oculos. S. Patres de Ecclesia unanimi senten- tia explicant, & pudicos gressus de incessu virtutum, de gressibus, quibus ad Deum ambulat, vel etiam ad prædicandum Evangelium, intelligunt. Operum constantiam, & mortificationem voluptatum hic in ea laudari notat Alcuinus, Theodoretus, & tres Ano- nymi, nec non Ambrosius de modestia, gravitate & pietate incessus & actionum exteriorum intelligunt. Gregorius M. Cassiodorus, Beda, Anshelmus de gressi- bus ad propagandum Evangelium directis. Vinarien- ses utrumque conjunguut in paraphrasi, incessum ad propugnandum Verbum pacis Esa. 52, 7. Eph. 6. v. 26. & juxta regulam verbi Gal. 6, 14. 16. quomo- do autem hæc Synedrio conveniant, non apparet. Num id filiæ Principis nomine venit, aut per eam ad- umbratur? aut num calceamenta Regina vel pedes erant assessores Synedrii? Convenientius R. Salomo pedes ad ascensum Israelitarum & statas ferias, quæ trinæ erant in anno, juxta Dei præceptum Exod. 13. refert. Grotius plerumque pessima quæque eligit, cum Judæos consulit. Certum autem est, filiam Principis Ecclesiam esse Dei Patris Omnipotentis, qui orbem totum moderatur, filiam per Christum doti- bus & virtutibus gratiisque Spiritus Sancti nobilem.

Vers. eod. JUNCTURÆ FEMORUM TUORUM] Fe- moris ambitus.

Vox חמוקי recte ambitus vel circuitus reddi- tur. Sed explicandum erat quid per ambitum femo- rum intelligatur, & cur monilibus, operi manuum egregii artificis comparentur? Femora ad generatio- nem filiorum, quos quotidie Ecclesia Christo gi- gnit, referri, ac rationem generandi pulcherrimam & artificiosissimam per Verbi prædicationem de- signari, Mercerus vult, ubi summus ornatus, ars exi- mia Christi opificis. Ideo Osiander sic παραφράζει: Habes lumbos non distortos, sed aptissime dispositos ad fœcunditatem & generationem. Vinarienses lumbo- rum veritate cunctorum in fide stabilitatem Eph. 6. v. 14. Rom. 15, 2. cum promtitudine resistendi hosti- bus 1. Pet. 5. v. 8. & vigilantia perpetua significari, innuunt Luc. 12. v. 35.

## 7:2
Verse 2. YOUR NAVEL IS A ROUNDED GOBLET] A good comparison, for the navel is round like a goblet, and hollow; and inside it has certain small circles.

NEVER LACKING CUPS] For the navel was accustomed to be anointed with balsam and similar things, partly for the sake of health, partly for pleasure.

According to Mercerus, it is signified that the navel of the Church, that is, the intimate seat, from which, as from a navel the fetus in the womb, the whole flock is nourished, which the ministers of the word hold, never lacks the juice of saving doctrine, which is abundantly distributed to all. Corn. a Lapide explains it thus: as if to say, the vital parts of the Bride are full of moisture and juice, by which they are abundantly irrigated and nourished, and kept vigorous, lively, and succulent. Theodoret compares what is said in Ezek. 16 about the navel of Judea: your navel was not cut. Because here it is said in contrast: your navel is a rounded goblet, not lacking a cup. For she, he says, originating from Egypt, did not cut her navel: but simply cut her navel, but amputated it so deeply that she plucked out every root of idolatry, and seemed like a rounded goblet, which always has a cup of gladness, and never lacks the joy that proceeds from piety. For the reborn draw the wine of saving doctrine from the Church, just as a fetus in the womb draws through the mother's navel, nor does the navel of the Church ever fail, because the doctrine of the Church is inexhaustible, flowing from the perennial fountain of Holy Scripture. It is clear that this does not refer to delights or the preservation of health, nor to balsam and other things, but to the preservation of the more tender fetus in the womb of the Church, which draws drink through the navel as if from a goblet.

Verse same. YOUR BELLY IS LIKE A HEAP OF WHEAT SET ABOUT WITH LILIES] Bushels of wheat are accustomed to be leveled. Thus, How flat the belly under the chastened breast. As the master of such things says. The lilies here are the sides.

Let there be no mention of a bushel, but of a heap of wheat. Others therefore note that the belly is called wide below and narrow above like a heap: but that this is primarily referred to here, that as in the Church drink does not fail, so neither does food, whence it is compared to a goblet full of mixed wine and a heap of wheat, fenced about everywhere with lilies, because the food of the Church is full of sweetness and abounds with thanks. Theodoret: Your belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies, that is, the storehouse of your soul is full of secret mysteries, which emit fragrance on all sides. Cornelius a Lapide wishes the same, or almost the same, to be said as what was said about the navel, but through another metaphor: because he had said that the belly is also included under the navel, so that it may be signified that it is filled with every nourishment, as much food as drink; and that a heap of wheat is a symbol of fertility and fruitfulness: but lilies of chastity, so that it may be hinted that the belly of the Bride is so fruitful for nourishing the other members that it is nevertheless pure and chaste, because according to Pliny, nothing is more fruitful than wheat. Gregory the Great wishes preachers to be designated by the navel, and the people by the belly. The navel, he says, is the order of holy preachers, which is well called a goblet, because while the people are instructed by them, they are inebriated with spiritual wine by their office. Which is well called rounded, because according to the customs of all men it is necessary that the tongue of the preacher be turned; who does not need cups, because it is necessary that he drink more abundantly what he offers to others, and contain more fully what he gives. And further: by the belly is designated the breadth of the people, which is well fenced about with lilies like a heap of wheat, because while it intends holy works and is prepared for the heavenly barn, it is fortified on all sides by the examples of the saints, so that it may persevere. The Church, says Delrio from St. Ambrose, and Menochius in this place, produces many grains, that is, many faithful to be stored in the barn of the Lord, whose multitude is a heap gathered into one by the bond of charity, leveled by the cylinder of justice, and fenced about by examples of modesty and other virtues.

Latin:

Vers. 2. UMBILICUS TUUS CRATER TORNATILIS] Bona comparatio, nam umbilicus rotundus est ut crater, & cavus; & intus orbiculos quosdam habet.

NUNQVAM INDIGENS POCULIS] Nam umbilicus balsamo & rebus similibus perfundi solebat, partim valetu- dinis, partim deliciarum causa.

Juxta Mercerum significatur, Ecclesiæ umbili- cum, id est, sedem intimam, unde tanquam ex umbi- lico fœtus in utero, sic totus grex alatur, quam mi- nistri verbi tenent, nunquam carere succo doctri- næ salutaris, qui ubertim omnibus tribuatur. Corn. a Lapide ita explicat: q. d. vitalia Sponsæ plena sunt humore & succo, quo abunde irrigantur, & aluntur, ac vegeta, vivida & fucculenta confervantur. Theo- doretus confert, quæ Ezech. 16. de Judææ umbilico dicuntur: non est præcisus umbilicus tuus. Quia hic ex adverfo dicitur: umbilicus tuus crater tornatilis, non indigens poculo. Illa enim, inquit, ex Ægypto ori- unda non præcidit umbilicum suum: sed veluti per radicem quandam ex Ægypto impiæ doctrinæ traxit improbitatem. Hæc autem non simpliciter modo præ- cidit umbilicum suum, sed ita penitus amputavit, ut omnem idololatriæ radicem evelleret, & crateri tor- natili similis videretur, qui lætitiæ poculum semper habet, nec gaudio, quod ex pietate proficiscatur, un- quam indiget. Renati enim vinum salutaris doctri- næ ab Ecclesia, non secus atque fœtus in utero per umbilicum matris hauriunt, neque deficit umbili- cus Ecclesiæ unquam, quia doctrina Ecclesiæ inex- haufta est, de perenni fonte Scripturæ S. profluens. Non hic ad delicias aut valetudinis conservatio- nem, nec ad balsamum, aliaque, sed ad fœtus tene- rioris in utero Ecclesiæ conservationem, qui per umbilicum potum quasi ex cratere haurit, respici, in aprico est.

Vers. eod. VENTER TVVS SICVT ACERVVS TRITICI VALLATVS LILIIS] Modii tritici applanari solent. Sic Quam castigato planus sub pectore venter. Vt ait talium Magister. Lilia hîcc sunt latera.

Non sit modii mentio, sed acervi tritici. Alii ergo latum infra, angustum superne instar acervi, ventrem dici notant: at respici hic id imprimis, quod ut in Ecclesia potus non deficit, sic nec cibus, unde & crateri pleno vino mixto ac acervo tritici con- feratur, septo undiquaq́, liliis, quia fuavitate plenum est Ecclesiæ pabulum, gratiisque abundat. Theodo- retus: Venter tuus sicut acervus tritici vallatus liliis, id est, animæ tuæ penu arcanis plenum mysteriis, quæ undiquaque fragrantiam emittunt. Idem, vel quasi idem dici cum eo, quod de umbilico dicebatur, Cor- nelius a Lapide vult, sed per aliam Metaphoram: quia sub umbilico etiam ventrem comprehendi di- xerat, ut significetur, quolibet alimento, tam cibo, quam potu refertum esse; ac acervus tritici ferti- litatis & fœcunditatis Symbolum sit: lilia vero castitatis, ut innuatur, ventrem Sponsæ ita esse fœcundum ad nutriendum cætera membra, ut ta- men sit purus & castus, quia secundum Plinium, tri- tico nihil fœcundius. Gregorius M. per umbilicum praedicatores, per ventrem populum designari vult. Umbilicus, inquit, sanctorum prædicatorum ordo est, qui bene crater esse dicitur, quia dum per eos populus eruditur, vino spirituali, ipsorum officio, inebriatur. Qui bene tornatilis nuncupatur, quia juxta mores hominum universos necesse est, ut lingua prædicatoris volvatur; qui poculis non indiget, quia quod aliis pro- pinat necesse est, ut cætera abundantius bibat & ple- nius, quod dat, contineat. Et porro: per ventrem po- puli latitudo designatur, qui bene sicut acervus tritici liliis vallatur, quia dum operibus sanctis intendens in cœleste horreum præparatur, exemplis sanctorum, ut perseveret, undiq́, munitur. Ecclesia, inquit ex S. Am- brosio Delrio, & Menochius in h. l. multa grana, id est, multos fideles in horreo Domini reponendos produ- cit, quorum multitudo est cumulus in unum vinculo charitatis coacervatus, cylindro justitiæ æquatus, & pudicitiæ, cæterarumque virtutum exemplis vallatus.

## 7:4
Verse 4. YOUR EYES ARE LIKE THE POOLS IN HESHBON] Serene, not turbid.

It was spoken of before concerning the other members of the Bride, the neck is now called an ivory tower. The Vinarienses understand Holy Scripture, and wish its purity, strength, and virtue and majesty to be designated in this way. Other doctors understand the word with Gregory the Great.

that the neck of the Bride is called like an ivory tower, because the preachers of the Church are held to be both high through contemplation, and strong through the exercise of holy works, and precious through divine wisdom. Aben-Ezra understands this of the Messiah. Now as far as the eyes are concerned, by the symbol of the pool not only their serenity, or triple beauty is noted, as Luysius observes; inasmuch as with serenity there is also the amplitude of the eyes, but a just and decent size, and also quiet and stability, which in eyes full of gravity and decorum is an indication of a constant and simple mind. For those whose eyelids and eyes are moved with great speed are either timid, or altogether crafty and deceitful. Moreover, the wisdom of the Church is signified, not small, but as much as is altogether necessary; whence it is compared to a pool, because it is diffused like a river, Sir. 24:43, and both its perspicacity and its constancy; and by the name Heshbon, which denotes art, Eccl. 7:30, that most excellent art is hinted at the same time, which is uniquely found in the Church, of believing rightly, living piously, and dying happily: by the gate of Bath-rabbim, named from the multitude of those entering, the multitude of the faithful is designated in the spiritual Jerusalem. Mercerus says the pools of the Church are most abundant, to which peoples from everywhere flow for the sake of drawing water, i.e., doctrine; whence not undeservedly mention was made of the populous gate, at which these pools are situated, so that the Church might be secretly denoted by this populous gate, which opens its bosom to all. It is added: your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. For by that likeness is noted the exact providence, perception, and discretion of the Church, by which it smells from afar, and the Spirit discerns, nay, judges all things. Theodoret: It is high, he says, and sublime, and looks up to the heavenly sweetness of odor, and perceiving the ointment of the Bridegroom, cries out; because of the odor of your ointments we will run. Whence it is compared to a tower, which is situated in Lebanon, which looks toward the face of Damascus. For because the Devil is transfigured into an angel of light, and takes the appearance of spiritual ointment, the nose of the Bride necessarily erect and vigilant looks toward the face of Damascus, lest being deceived and omitting the true ointment, she follow the false and deceptive one. But divine Scripture frequently puts Damascus for the Gentiles and the impiety which flourished at that time. Meanwhile, those things which Mercerus has here are worthy to be brought forward: They understand the house of the forest of Lebanon, which Solomon built, as it is 3 Kings 7. They understand 'looking toward the face of Damascus' as meaning that whoever was upon it could look from there as far as Damascus and count its houses. But I understand it simply as looking toward Damascus. Her nose is compared to a tower, because it was straight and equal on all sides, having nothing twisted. A nose is praised for being erect and flat, not twisted. Aben-Ezra understands the High Priest, because he would bring incense to the nose of the Lord, as is in the blessing of Moses, Deut. 33. Our people understand the ministers of the word, not without cause, because they stand out and are a strength. What is added, 'looking toward Damascus,' is added for the sake of describing the tower, and does not contribute much to the mystery, as is the case with many things in this Song: which our people often, and sometimes the Hebrews, twist too curiously toward allegories. Unless perhaps that allegory of the Hebrews pleases, that it is expected that Jerusalem will be extended as far as Damascus, just as Zechariah prophesied in his new chapter, but understanding mystically the propagation of the Church and the kingdom of Christ. It is also worth observing, as Mercerus notes there, that Solomon chose in these praises for comparison whatever places of the land of Israel he could, having something notable, so that the comparisons might be more notable. Therefore they ought not to seem harsh. Add that the affection of lovers brought this about, who choose huge things for comparison: for they never think the form of the beloved has been praised enough.

Latin:

Vers. 4. OCULI TUI SICUT PISCINÆ IN HESE- BON] Sereni, non turbidi.

De membris aliis Sponsæ antea dictum, Col- lum nunc dicitur turris eburnea. Scripturam S. in- telligunt Vinarienses, ejusque puritatem, fortitudi- nem, & virtutem ac majestatem ita designari vo- lunt. Alii Dd. verbi intelligunt cum Gregorio M.

id collum Sponsæ instar turris eburneæ dici, quia Prædi- catores Ecclesiæ & alti per contemplationem, & for- tes per sanctorum operum exercitationem, & pretiosi per divinam sapientiam habentur. Aben-Ezra id de Messia intelligit. Jam quod ad oculos attinet, per Symbolum piscinæ non tantum serenitas eorum, seu triplex pulchritudo notatur, observante Luysio; utpote cum serenitate simul oculorum amplitudo, sed justa & decens magnitudo, nec non quies & sta- bilitas, quæ in oculis gravitatis & decoris plena, & constantis, & simplicis animi indicium est. Nam quorum crebro palpebræ, atq; oculi magna celeri- tate moventur, aut timidi sunt, aut omnino vafri atq; fallaces. Significatur autem Ecclesiæ sapientia non exigua, sed quanta omnino necessaria est; unde pi- scinæ comparatur, quia diffusa est instar fluminis Sir. 24, 43. ejusque tum perspicacitas, tum constantia; & per nomen Hesbon, quòd artem notat Eccl. 7, 30. innuitur simul ars illa præstantissima, quæ in Eccle- sia unice reperitur, recte credendi, pie vivendi, bea- te moriendi: per portam Bath Rabbim a multitudi- ne ingredientium nuncupatam multitudo fidelium designatur in spirituali Hierosolyma. Mercerus Dd. Ecclesiæ dicit piscinas esse uberrimas, quo undique populi confluant hauriendæ aquæ, i. e. doctrinæ cau- sa; unde non immerito portæ populosæ fuerit facta mentio, ad quam hæ piscinæ sint sitæ, ut occulte per hanc portam populosam Ecclesia denotaretur, quæ omnibus gremium aperit. Additur; nasus tuus sicut turris Libani, quæ respicit contra Damascum. Notatur enim ea similitudine exacta providentia, perspectio, & discretio Ecclesiæ, qua longe odoratur, & Spiritus discernit, imo dijudicat omnia. Theodoretius: Cel- sus est, inquit, & sublimis, & cœlestem suspicit odoris suavitatem, Sponsique unguentum percipiens, clamat; propter odorem unguentorum tuorum curramus. Unde comparatur turri, quæ in Libano sita est, quæ respicit faciem Damasci. Nam quia Diabolus in angelum lucis transfiguratur, unguentique spiritualis speciem sumit, necessario Sponsæ nasus erectus ac vi- gilans respicit faciem Damasci, ne decepta verum omit- tens unguentum, fallax ac deceptorium sequatur. Damascum autem pro Gentilibus atque impietate, quæ eo tempore vigebat, frequenter ponit divina Scri- ptura. Digna interim sunt, quæ hic adferantur, quæ hic Mercerus habet: Intelligunt domum saltus Li- bani, quam construxit Salomon, ut est 3. Reg. 7. Prospi- cere faciem Damasci intelligunt, quod qui super eam esset, inde in Damascum usque prospicere & numerare posset ejus domos. Sed simpliciter intelligo quod Da- mascum versus spectaret. Nasus illi turri compara- tur, quod ea recta esset, & undiquaq; æqualis, nihil ha- bens obtortum. Nasus laudatur erectus & planus, non obtortus. Aben-Ezra summum Sacerdotem intelligit, quod nari Domini incensum admoveret, ut est in be- nedictione Mosis Deut. 33. Nostri verbi Ministros in- telligunt, non sine causa, quod emineant & robori sint. Quod subditur, spectans versus Damascum, designan- dæ turris gratia est additum, nec ad mysterium admo- dum facit, qualia multa sunt in hoc Cantico: quæ no- stri sæpe curiose nimium & interdum Hebræi ad al- legorias contorquent. Nisi forte illa placet Hebræo- rum allegoria, quod expectetur, fore, ut Hierosolyma Damascum usque protendatur, sicut Zacharias no- vo capite est vaticinatus, sed mystice intelligens Ec- clesiæ & regni Christi propagationem. Observari etiam meretur, quod ibi notat Mercerus, delegis- se Salomonem in his encomiis ad comparationem, quæcunque loca potuit terræ Israel, insigne aliquid habentia, ut insigniores essent comparationes. Ita- que duræ videri non debent. Adde, quod affectus amantium huc adduxit, qui ingentia ad compara- tionem deligunt: nunquam enim satis putant lau- datam esse amantis formam.

## 7:5
Ver. 5. THE HAIR OF THY HEAD, AS THE KING'S PURPLE BOUND IN THE CHANNELS) Thus among the Poets, the purple hair of Nisus. Bound in the channels, namely of the dyers, that is, dyed a second time, δίβαφος. If the words were to be explained in that way, certainly neither should the distinctive accent be fixed on the word כארגמן, nor should this word be placed in the construct state. Wherefore the Vulgate, according to the Hebrew truth, with which the LXX Interpreters agree, is to be corrected thus: And the hair of thy head, as purple, the King bound in the channels, as Pagninus and Arias-Montanus [have it], or in the rafters, as Mercer has it. There had preceded: Thy head upon thee כרמל as Carmel, to wit, the highest mountain of Phoenicia: Which Bride's head is Christ himself, compared to this mountain for its eminence and the fruitfulness of its gifts and graces: but so that at the same time regard is had to the passion of Christ, because כרמל brings in a crimson color. Now therefore it is subjoined: And the hair of thy head as purple: by which some understand the multitude of the faithful having [it] from Christ, so that it may shine, like purple, with graces: others understand the graces of Christ the head. The Weimar Paraphrasts wish the thoughts chiefly intent upon the passion of Christ, and thus abstracted from worldly things and involved in meditations, to be designated by the hair. Some of the ancient Doctors think the heralds of the Word are denoted. But Corn. a Lap. is very inept. The Jesuit [thinks] that by the head is meant Elijah, whom he imagines will return from heaven at the last time, as the head of the Church to be converted from the Jews; that by the hair are to be understood the religious and particularly the Jesuitical society (you would more correctly call it Esauitical), by which, however, he later wishes the Cardinals of the Roman Church also to be designated, as if Elijah were also to be attended by Cardinals, or as if there were to be two heads of the Church then, Elijah and the Roman Pontiff, unless they prefer to hold this one as the Anti-Christ, against whom he is otherwise to fight. But as to the fact that the King is said to be bound in the channels, that, omitting other and those Elian interpretations which Cornelius collected, you should understand most simply with Mercer concerning the Messiah (whom R. Aben-Ezra also confesses is indicated here) according to that Psalm 45:12: And the King shall desire thy beauty. The King so burns with love for thee, because of thy remarkable beauty, that he does not refuse to be bound to the rafters or even the channels of the houses for the sake of contemplating thy form, through which the drops of rain fall down from the roof, or that we may understand the dyeing channels (which also pleases Grotius), so that because he had compared her hair to purple, he says the King is attached to the channels from which that purple is washed, because of his desire for her. Piscator explains it similarly, that the King is detained as if bound in the walks, having seen that beauty: as also Junius in his notes, although he refers this to the King, whoever he may be, because there is no one of such glory who could be satisfied by the sight of that glory.

Latin:

Vers. 5. COMA CAPITIS TVI, SICVT PVRPVRA REGIS VINCTA CANALIBVS) Sic apud Poetas purpu- rea Nisi coma. Vincta in canalibus, nempe purpurariorum, id est, iterum tincta, δίβαφος. Si eo modo explicanda forent verba, utiq; nec ac- centus distinctivus in voce כארגמן figi deberet, & vox hæc in regimine poneretur. Quapropter vulga- ta ad Ebraicam veritatem, cui consonant LXX. In- terpp. ita corrigenda: Et coma capitis tui, sicut purpu- ra, Rex ligatus in canalibus, uti Pagninus & Arias- Montanus, vel in tignis, ut Mercerus habet. Præcesse- rat: Caput tuum super te כרמל sicut Carmelus, mons scil. Phœnicis altissimus: Quod Sponsæ caput Chri- stus ipse est, monti huic ob eminentiam & donorum ac gratiarum fœcunditatem comparatus: sed ita ut simul respectus ad passionem Christi habeatur, quia כרמל colorem puniceum infert. Nunc ergo subjun- gitur: Et coma capitis tui sicut purpura: per quam alii fidelium multitudinem a Christo habentem, ut gratiis, purpuræ more, fulgeat: alii Christi capitis gratias in- telligunt. Vinarienses Paraphrastæ cogitationes in passionem Christi præcipue intentas atque adeo a mun- danis abstractas, & meditationibus implicatas per co- mam designari volunt. Veterum nonnulli Doctores, vel præcones Verbi denotatos censent. Perquam in- eptus vero est Corn. a Lap. Jesuita per caput Eliam, quem e cœlo rediturum fingit novissimo tempore, ceu caput Ecclesiæ e Judæis convertendæ; per comam religiosos & peculiariter societatem Jesuiticam (Esa- viticam rectius vocares) intelligi debere, per quas tamen postea Cardinales Ecclesiæ Rom. etiam desi- gnari vult, quasi Elias etiam Cardinalibus stipandus sit, aut duo capita tum futura sint Ecclesiæ, Elias, & Pontifex Romanus, nisi hunc pro Anti-Christo, adversus quem alias pugnaturus sit, habere malint. Quod autem Rex dicitur ligatus in canalibus, id missis aliis, iisque Elienis interpretationibus, quas Cornelius collegit, simplicissime cum Mercero intel- ligas de Messia (quem hic indigitari etiam R. Aben- Ezra fatetur) juxta illud Psalm. 45, 13. Et tuæ for- mæ desiderio Rex capietur. Rex ita tui amore ardet, ob insignem tuam speciem, ut tignis aut etiam ædium canalibus alligatus esse contemplandæ formæ tuæ cau- sa non recuset, per quos e tecto foras guttæ pluviæ de- cidunt, vel ut canales infectorios intelligamus (quod Grotiovetiam placet) ut quia purpuræ comam ejus compararat, dicat Regem canalibus, e quibus abluitur illa purpura, annexum esse præ ejus desiderio. Simili- ter fere exponit Piscator, quod Rex detineatur velu- ti alligatus in ambulacris, conspecta illa pulchritudi- ne: ut & Junius in notis, quamvis hæc ad Regem, quemcunque referat, quod nullus tanta gloria sit, qui aspectu istius gloriæ expleri possit.

## 7:8
Ver. 8. I WILL ASCEND INTO THE PALM TREE) Ἐπιβήσω.

I do not investigate what Grotius means by this word. But that the Bridegroom is speaking these things, and that they are said about that Bride, the feminine gender affixed teaches. Corn. a Lap. notes that Cassiodorus, Phil. Honor., Greg. M., Apon., Bed., Ansb., Ruper., and many others accept these things concerning Christ about to ascend the cross, which many think was made from a palm tree, Cyprian, tract. on the passion: Thou hast ascended, O Lord, the palm tree, because the wood of the cross portended triumph. But the Bride had been compared to a palm tree in the preceding verse: and the mention of the breasts subjoined teaches that the same is looked at here. Furthermore, there is no discourse in these words about conjunction for unfruitfulness in spiritual marriage: which rather presuppose a fruit-bearing palm tree and spiritual offspring. I will ascend into the palm tree, I will apprehend the fruits (in the Hebrew, branches) of it, I will embrace with love and cherish and sustain them. Thy breasts are as clusters of the vine, and the odor of thy [nose] as the odor of most sweetly fragrant apples, i.e. for others children with heavenly doctrine, which by its odor will wonderfully refresh thee and them. Whence Junius paraphrases thus: I will dwell with thee, I will purge thee and I will recognize and perceive singular fruits from thee, just as palm branches are tended in palm trees: which produce flowers and buds from the branches of the palm trees for fruit. See Plin. lib. 3. c. 4. By this presence of mine, he says, it will come to pass that thou art entirely vigorous, fragrant, pleasing, and to all who shall approach thee, salutary by thy eloquence: all of which are attributed humanly, compared to breasts, face, and palate under certain conditions. Mercer, however, because he thinks the choir of Jerusalemite maidens had spoken from the beginning of the chapter, believes these things are said in the person of each of them, so that when the Church had been compared to a palm tree, each one of those to whom it is a pleasure to join themselves to the Church says what follows: I will ascend the palm tree, and I will reach out to the branches of it, i.e., I will pluck its fruits; when I possess [it], I will join myself to my Church, so that I may enjoy its fruits, i.e., gifts and graces, I may communicate with them, I may be a participant of them. In the word I will ascend, the simile is taken from gardeners, who climb trees and pluck ripe fruits. What are added further: And thy breasts shall now be as clusters of the vine, and the odor of thy nostrils as apples, the Weimar [theologians] take thus, as if the Bridegroom were saying: now may thy breasts, i.e., the Sacraments, be pleasing to thee, so that many may be refreshed by them and sustained unto salvation. And the scent of your nostrils, i.e., a diligent inquiry into the Scriptures and a scrutiny of doctrines, may be like the apples of the heavenly fruit, Cant. 2:3, so that the scent of my knowledge may be propagated far and wide, 2 Cor. 2:14. Others similarly accept it in this way, that the breasts or loves of the bride bring pleasure to the Bridegroom himself.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ADSCENDAM IN PALMAM) Ἐπιβήσω.

Non indago, quid Grotius hac voce velit. Spon- sum autem hæc loqui, & de Sponsa ista dici affixa fœ- min. generis docent. Corn. a Lap. notat Cassiodorum Phil. Honor. Greg. M. Apon. Bed. Ansb. Ruper. & alios plures hæc de Christo accipere in crucem ascensu- ro, quam multi putant ex palma confectam fuisse, Cyprian. tract. de passione: Adscendisti, Domine, pal- mam, quia crucis lignum portendebat triumphum. Sed palmæ comparata erat versu præcedenti Sponsa: & eandem hic respici uberum mentio subjuncta docet Cæterum de conjunctione ad infœcunditatem in conju- gio spirituali his verbis sermo non est: quæ frugife- ram palmam, & fœtus spirituales potius præsuppo- nunt. Ascendam in palmam apprehendam fructus(inE- bræo ramos) ejus, amore complectar ac fovebo, & su- stentabo eosdem. Ubera tua sunt botri vineæ, & odo tuę sicut odor malorum suavissime fragrantium, i.e. ali- tibi filios cœlesti doctrinâ, quæ odore suo te & illos mire recreabit. Unde Junius ita παραφράζει: Versabor tecum, purgabo te & singulares fructus recognoscam, ac percipiam ex te, quemadmodum in palmis curantur palmites: qui ex ramis palmarum prodeuntes flores, germinaque ad fructum perficiunt. Vid. Plin. lib. 3. c. 4. Hac mea præsentia, inquit, futurum est, ut vegeta sis tota, odora, grata & omnibus, qui ad te accedent, salu- taris facundia tua: quæ omnia humanitus uberibus, vultui & palato certis conditionibus comparata tri- buuntur. Mercer. tamen, quia inde ab initio capitis chorum puellarum Hierofolymitanarum loquutum ef- se censet, in persona cujusque earum hæc dici existi- mat, ut quum palmæ Ecclesia comparata fuerat, unaquæque ex iis, quibus se Ecclesiæ jungere volupe est, dicat, quæ sequuntur: Conscendam palmam, & protendam ramos ejus i. e. fructus ejus decerpam; cum potiar, Ecclesiæ meæ me adjungam, ut ejus fructibus, i. e. donis & gratiis fruar, cum illis communicem, earum siam particeps. In voce ascendam similitudo est ab hortulanis petita, qui arbores conscendunt, fru- ctusque maturos decerpunt. Quæ porro adduntur; Et erunt nunc ubera tua sicut racemi vitis, & odor na- rium tuarum, sicut malorum, Vinarienses ita acci- piunt, quasi dicat Sponsus: modo ubera tua, i. e. Sa- cramenta tibi grata sint, ut multi iisdem recreentur & ad salutem sustententur. Et odor narium tuarum, i. e. diligens inquisitio in Scripturis & scrutinium doctri- narum sit instar malorum cœlestis pomi Cant. 2, 3. ut ita odor cognitionis meæ longe lateque propagetur 2. Cor. 2, 14. Alii similiter ita accipiunt, quod ubera vel amores grati Sponso ipsi voluptatem adferant.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. YOUR THROAT IS LIKE THE BEST WINE WORTHY OF MY BELOVED FOR DRINKING, AND FOR HIS LIPS AND TEETH FOR RUMINATING) That indicates what Tibullus says: 'From which envy might depart, which mutual Venus makes with pressed tooth.' Likewise: 'And to fix marks on the neck with a tooth.' The Greeks read these last words far differently than what is now in the Hebrew: namely, thus למשתים דובר שפת ושנים. For דבר is translated by ἱκανῶν in 1 Kings 20:11, and the LXX here have ἱκανόμενον. But Symmachus has προστίθεμενον. He therefore reads דובק, not badly. In the Hebrew that we have, the sense is strange: 'making the lips of those who are asleep speak to rectitudes.'

Those lascivious things of Tibullus are unworthy to be compared here. ἑκάς ἑκάς ἔςε βέβηλοι. We are engaged in a most holy Epithalamium. The sweetness of the Bride's throat is from nowhere else than the divine Word, which she proclaims, which is accustomed to be compared to the best wine. But since the Bridegroom seems to speak these things, what is the meaning of those words, 'wine worthy of MY BELOVED'? Osiander and the Vinarienses, Alcasar, and others think that by 'my beloved' one should understand Christ the Bridegroom as a friend to oneself. Franciscus Junius takes the word adverbially, rendering it 'most lovingly,' of which more later. But the ancients, as well as Almonacurius and others, attribute these words to the Bride. For the Bride, says Alcuinus, snatched the word from the mouth of the Bridegroom, because he compared her to the best wine: and she added, 'worthy of my beloved,' i.e., such is the sublimity of the Evangelical preaching that my beloved himself, appearing first through this in the flesh, opened the heavenly way to the world: 'and for his lips and teeth to ruminate,' i.e., he gave it especially to the Apostles and Preachers to meditate upon. 'And his turning is toward me,' i.e., he alone loves and helps me, so that I do not fail on the way. Mercerus explains these things thus; namely, that each of the girls of Jerusalem says this, as also Corn. a Lap. and Cosmus Damianus says this voice is that of the choir of young women in v. 8; which the ancients also, Chrysostom in Homily XXII to the people of Antioch, and others, assign to the holy soul. Furthermore, Grotius took the opportunity from the Vulgate to slip into that lascivious interpretation; for which there is absolutely no place according to the Hebrew truth. Which he himself desires to be corrected from the translations in an inverted, nay, perverse order: since these are to be examined according to the original text, and they desire the norm of the Hebrew truth. But it is sought in vain, that there is a wonderful meaning in the Hebrew: whose words κατὰ πόδα [word for word] are thus: And thy throat like the best wine going to my beloved: or which goes to my beloved. למישרים to rectitudes, or as Pagninus, because of goodness; making the lips of those who are asleep to speak. This wine is said to go to the beloved and to tend straight, according to Mercerus, because it behaves itself rightly in the cup, because it shows itself generous to the beloved when it is seen in the goblet, and in the bowl as if it shows its goodness, as in Prov. 23:31 such a kind of speaking occurs: look not upon the wine when it is red, and shows its color in the cup, יתהלך במישרים showing itself straight: which others there explain, moving itself properly. The Vulgate, however, renders it, that it enters smoothly. Ludovicus de Dieu, it enters most easily: word for word, in rectitudes, adverbially, i.e., rightly and plainly, from ישר he was plain, equal, according to which comparison here the generous wine is said to enter to the beloved straight and smoothly; because the preposition ל is accustomed to be used for ב, as Luther rightly: Der meinem Freund glatt eingehe. Franciscus Junius interprets it thus: thy palate as wine of the best odor, (i.e., most fragrant, most sweet, and exciting the dormant senses by the pure administration of the word) moving itself most lovingly, and most rightly, (Hebrew: going to manners, to rectitudes: as Prov. 23:21. But the former noun of loves is truncated for the sake of euphony by the final letter through apocope, as 2 Kings 11:19 and Ps. 144:2. & below 7:6.) causing the lips of those who are asleep to speak: (a hyperbolic expression, if you look at the simile, but nevertheless most true, if we shall consider the preaching of the Gospel, which is the word of life, and the incorruptible seed of salvation.) These are Junius's words. But that wine is said to make the lips of those who are asleep speak, either in this sense, that it makes those who are asleep speak, or excites dormant senses, and refreshes the mind: Or it will be explained thus: that it speaks with the lips of those who are asleep: as speech is attributed to wine, just as walking is also; according to that: Fruitful cups, whom have they not made eloquent? Thus Nigidius Siculus says the Sicilians call the best wine the wine of the dead, because, namely, it as it were raises the dead, and makes them speak. But those things are wrongly joined by Grotius, which are separated by the distinctive accent Athnach: by the power of which that למישרים pertains to the preceding verb הולך and not to the following דובב, also the words are wrongly changed, and other letters are substituted, so that the Greek and Latin text may be carved out, by which method the authentic text is truly rendered a waxen nose. Gregory the Great explains the meaning thus: Such, he says, is the wine of the Bride, that it is worthy for the beloved to drink; because while the holy Church preaches the true faith, while it excites its hearers to holy works, while it demonstrates by words and works that to love, imitate, and embrace Christ alone is good, what else does it do than make its wine worthy, so that it may taste sweet in the mouth of the Bridegroom? Osiander's paraphrase pleases: Hebrew: which enters into my beloved sweetly, so that it may speak to the lips of those who are asleep, that is, your discourses will exhilarate my friends (Christians: for Christ calls these his friends, John 15), as the most sweet wine, and will spiritually inebriate them, so that they may speak (from that spiritual joy) those things which seem absurd and foolish to the sons of this world. For the wisdom of the world laughs at the mysteries of the Christian Religion, and the zeal of Christians in the confession of pure doctrine. Cf. Acts 2:13, Eph. 5:18. What if by the word MY BELOVED the Bridegroom the Son of God understands God his Father, so that the best wine goes to the Father because of his goodness, or according to his rectitude, and is testified to be approved by him?

Latin:

Vers. 9. GVTTVR TVVM SICVT VINVM OPTI- MVM DIGNVM DILECTO MEO AD POTANDVM, LABIISQVE ET DENTIBVS ILLIVS AD RVMINAN- DVM) Illud indicat, quod Tibullus: Queis livor abiret, Quem facit impresso mutua dente Venus. Item: Et in collo figere dente notas. Longe aliter hæc ultima legerunt Græci, quam nunc in He- bræo est: nempe sic למשתים דובר שפת ושנים. Nam דבר per ἱκανῶν vertitur 1. Reg. 20, 11. & LXX. hic ha- bent ἱκανόμενον. At Symmachus, προστίθεμενον. Legit igitur is דובק non male. In Hebræo, quod nos habemus, mirus est sensus: ad rectitudines faciens loqui labia dormientium.

Venerea illa Tibulli indigna sunt, quæ hic confe- rantur. ἑκάς ἑκάς ἔςε βέβηλοι. In sacrosancto versa- mur Epithalamio. Gutturis Sponsæ suavitas non ali- unde est, quam a Verbo divino, quod illa prædicat, quod vino optimo conferri solet.
