Sed quum Sponsus hæc loqui videatur, quid sibi volunt illa, vinum di- gnum DILECTO MEO? Per dilectum meum quem- cunq; sibi amicum intelligereChristum Sponsum Osi- ander & Vinarienses, Alcasar, aliiq; existimant. Franc. Junius vocem adverbialiter accipit, reddens aman- tissime, de quo postea. Veteres vero, ut & Almonacu- rius aliiq; Sponsæ hæc verba tribuunt. Arripuit enim, inquit Alcuinus, Sponsa verbum ex ore Sponsi, quia ille vino optimo eam comparavit: & subjecit, dignum di- lecto meo, i. e. tanta sublimitas est Evangelicæ prædi- cationis, ut ipse dilectus meus primus per hanc in carne apparens, mundo iter cœleste aperuerit: labiisq; & den- tibus illius ruminandum, i. e. Apostolis, Prædicatori- busq; maxime dedit ad meditandum. Et ad me con- versio ejus, i. e. me solum diligit & adjuvat, ne deficiam in via. Mercerus hæc ita explicat; nempe quod hæc loquatur unaquæque e puellis Hierofolymitanis, uti etiam Corn. a Lap. nec non Cosmus Damianus vocem hanc chori adolescentularum v. 8. esse ait; quam Veteres quoque Chrysost. Hom. XXII. ad popul. Antioch. & alii animæ sanctæ assignant. Cæterum in illa Venerea, ut prolaberetur Grotius, e vulgata an- sam sumsit; quibus per Ebraicam veritatem nullus prorsus locus est. Quam inverso, imo perverso or- dine ipse e translationibus correctam cupit: quum hi ad textum originalem examinandi sint, ac nor- mam desiderentEbraicam veritatem.Frustra autem queritur, mirum in Ebræo esse sensum: cujus verba κατὰ πόδα sic habent: Et guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum vadens ad dilectum meum: vel quod it dile- cto meo.למישרים ad rectitudines, vel ut Pagnin.pro- pter bonitatem; loquifaciens labia dormientium. Ad dilectum ire ac recta tendere hoc vinum dicitur se- cundum Mercerum, quod recte se gerat in cyatho, quod dilecto se generosum exhibeat, quum in cali- ce conspicitur, & in scypho velut ostendat bonita- tem suam,uti Prov. 23,31. tale loquendi genus occur- rit:ne respicias vinum,quum rubet, & colorem suum in cyatho demonstrat, יתהלך במישרים sese rectum ex- hibens: quod alii ibi exponunt, agitans sese probe. Vulgata autem reddit, quodingreditur blande. Lu- dovicus de Dieu, subit facillime: ad verbum, in recti- tudinibus, adverbialiter,i.e.recte & plane,à ישר pla- nus, æqualis fuit, juxta quam collationem hic vinum generosum dilecto recta blandeque ingredi dicitur; quia præpositio ל pro ב usurpari solet,utLuth.recte: Der meinem Freund glatt eingehe. Franc.Jun. ita in- terpretatur: palatum tuum ut vinum odoris optimi, (i. e. odoratissimum, suavissimum, & sopitos sensus excitans pura administratione verbi) movens se a- mantissime,rectissimeq;, (Hebr. iens ad mores, ad recti- tudines: ut Prov. 23, 21. Est autem prius nomen amo- rum Euphoniæ causa truncatum postrema litera per apocopen, ut 2. Reg. 11, 19. & Ps. 144, 2. & infr. 7, 6.) efficiens, ut loquantur labia dormientium : (hyper- bolica locutio, si spectes similitudinem, sed tamen verissima, si prædicationem Evangelii, quod est verbum vitæ, & incorruptum salutis semen, consi- derabimus.) Hæc Junius. Dicitur autem vinum il- lud loqui facere labia dormientium, vel hoc sensu, quod dormientes loqui faciat, aut sensus sopitos exci- tet, & animum recreet: Vel ita exponetur: quod lo- quatur labiis dormientium: ut sermo vino, sicut & ambulatio tribuatur; juxta illud. Fœcundi calices, quem non fecere disertum. Sic Siculi ait Nigidius Siculus, vinum optimum vocant vinum mortuorum, quod scil. mortuos quasi suscitet, & loqui faciat. Male autem à Grotio illa conjun- guntur, quæ per accentum distinctivum Athnach separata sunt: vi cujus illud למישרים pertinet ad præcedens verbum הולך non ad sequens דובב,male etiam immutantur verba, literæque aliæ substituun- tur,ut exsculpatur Græcus & Latinus textus, quo pacto vere naseus cereus redditur textus authenticus. Sensum ita exponit Gregor. M. Tale, inquit, est Sponsæ vinum,ut dignum sit dilecto ad potandum; quia dum sancta Ecclesia fidem veram prædicat, dum au- ditores suos ad sancta opera excitat, dum solum Chri- stum diligere, imitari,amplecti, bonum esse, verbis & operibus demonstrat, quid aliud quam vinum suum dignum facit, ut in ore Sponsi dulce sapiat? Placet O- siandri paraphrasis: Hebr. quod ingreditur in dile- ctum meum suaviter, ut loquatur labiis dormiturien- tium, id est, tui sermones amicos meos (Christianos: hos enim Christus amicos suos vocat Joh. 15.) ex- hilarabunt, ut vinum suavissimum, & spiritualiter eos inebriabunt, ut ea loquantur (ex illa spirituali læ- titia) quæ filiis hujus mundi videntur absurda & stulta. Ridet enim mundi sapientia Religionis Chri- stianæ mysteria, & Christianorum Zelum in confessio- ne puræ doctrinæ. Conf. Act. 2,13. Eph. 5,18. Quid si verbo DILECTUM MEUM Sponsus Filius Dei Deum Patrem suum intelligat, ut vinum optimum ire ad Patrem propter bonitatem suam, vel secundum rectitudinem suam testetur, eidemque probari?

## 7:10
Verse 10. I AM MY BELOVED'S, AND HIS CONVERSION IS TOWARD ME.

- Vatablus. I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me. I am, he says, wholly his: and he in turn desires me uniquely. Beautifully Gregory the Great: Since by faith and love I adhere to Christ alone, I follow him alone, I desire to see him alone as one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, I joyfully experience the sweetness of his regard, the kindness of his visitation, the sweetness of his conversation, and experiencing it, I proclaim it.

Latin:

Vers. 10. EGO DILECTO MEO, ET AD ME CONVERSIO EJUS.

- Vatabl. Ego dilecti mei sum, & ad me desiderium ejus. Ego, inquit tota illius sum: & ille vicissim u- nice me desiderat. Pulcre Gregor. M. Quoniam fide ac dilectione soli Christo adhæreo, solum sequor, solum cum Patre & S. S. unum Deum videre concu- pisco, respectionis ejus suavitatem, visitationis beni- gnitatem, conversationis dulcedinem gaudenter ex- perior, experiens proclamo.

## 7:11
Verse 11. COME MY BELOVED, LET US GO FORTH INTO THE FIELD, AND LET US REMAIN IN THE VILLAGES.

Let the Gospel be communicated also to the Gentiles, so that Christ and the true Church may be among them also. LET US RISE EARLY TO THE VINEYARDS (to inspect them) IF THE FLOWERS BRING FORTH FRUIT (Hebrew: whether the clusters are opening: whether good ones can already be seen) IF THE POMEGRANATES HAVE FLOURISHED (more correctly: whether they are flourishing): THERE WILL I GIVE THEE MY BREASTS: there you will perceive the fruit of our mutual love. (i.e., the Churches are to be visited, whether they are progressing, and growing in the knowledge of God, and in good works. Where this is, Christ is vehemently delighted over his Church) as the Osiandrian paraphrase has it here. Thus Gregory, Justus Orgel, and others take these things concerning the Church inviting Christ, so that he may visit her particular Churches. The Hebrew את-דודַי Vatablus, Pagninus, and Arias Montanus more correctly translate as my loves. Breasts are expressed by the noun שדי.

Latin:

Vers. 11. VENI DILECTE MI, EGREDIA- MUR IN AGRUM, ET COMMOREMUR IN VILLIS.

Communicetur Evangelium etiam gentibus, ut & apud ipsos sint Christus & vera Ecclesia. MA- NE SURGAMUS AD VINEAS (inspiciendas) SI FLORES FRUCTUS PARTURIUNT (Ebr. num aperiantur botri: an jam conspici possint boni) SI FLORUERUNT rectius an floreant) MALA PUNICA: IBI DABO TIBI UBERA MEA: ibi fructum percipies nostri mutui amo- ris. (i. e. visitandæ sunt Ecclesiæ, an proficiant, & crescant in agnitione Dei, & in bonis operibus. Quod ubi sit, Christus vehementer delectatur super Ecclesia sua) ut hic habet Osiandrina paraphrasis. Ita Gregorius, Justus Orgel. & alii hæc accipiunt de Ecclesia invitante Christum, ut particulares suas Ecclesias visitet. Ebr. את-דודַי Vatabl. Pagn. & Ariæmont. rectius vertunt Amores meos. Ubera exprimuntur nomine שדי.

## 7:13
Verse 13. THE MANDRAKES HAVE GIVEN THEIR ODOR) That is, I see signs of conception. For the mandrake is useful for that, as we said in Genesis 30:14. What follows pertains to the same thing. Nor am I ignorant of what the Greeks write about the mandrake: but there are many kinds of herbs of the same name: and the same ones born in different soil, and with different preparation, have different value.

These are more correctly taken as signs of Spring, as is manifest from the comparison of verse 12 with chapter 2:12, 13. That the word דודאים denotes mandrakes is still vehemently doubtful: Dürfeldus laboriously collected reasons in this place, that the mandrake agrees with Dudaim neither in nobility nor in sweetness nor in beauty. What kind of fruits Dudaim are (which word the interpreter translates as Mandrake) is uncertain. But it can be gathered from this place and from Genesis 30:14 that it was a most excellent flower or fruit, says Osiander in this place. Which is also the opinion of the Belgian Interpreters on Genesis 30:14; therefore they retain the name Dudaim in the version, and in the notes to this place they deny that mandrakes are understood. Junius generally renders it thus: those lovely flowers giving forth odor: And so also Piscator: Die lieblichen Blumen geben Geruch. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that certain flowers are designated, or a certain species of herb or shrub. Luther explained it by the appearance of a flower known to us that gives off a pleasant scent, the lilies. But at Gen. 30:14, he retained in his version the name Dudaim: because there a special designation was involved, but here the name of a pleasant and fragrant flower sufficed. And regarding that passage he has it thus: Ask yourself what Dudaim are. They should be lilies, they should be berries, and no one knows what they should be. Some call them winter cherries, which become ripe in the wheat harvest. The Weimar editors add: Without doubt it was a sweet-smelling flower or a sweet-tasting fruit. But if we suppose that the mandrake is indicated; whence will the scents of the mandrake be considered as signs of conception? The mandrake is believed not to benefit, but rather to hinder conception on account of its extreme coldness, which we leave to its own place. If it were to benefit conception at all, is the scent of the mandrake therefore to be considered a sign of conception? But the opinion of those is to be approved who think that a spring sprout is indicated, and that a description of the spring season is had here. For as far as the more intimate sense of the parabolic expression is concerned, various opinions are read again. Some understand this of the signs of the wedding day and the glorious advent, to which opinion Junius has inclined his explanation and analysis: others of the signs of the imminent time of the conversion of the nations, to which the Weimar theologians accede: others explain it of the signs of the fruitfulness of the Gospel in general, toward which Osiander's paraphrase tends. And so also Alcuin: The mandrake is compared to the virtues of the saints on account of the manifold kinds of remedies: the gates of the Church are the saints, the Doctors. In such gates the mandrakes give a scent, when all spiritual persons scatter far and wide the fame of their virtues from themselves. But Augustine, book 22, chapter 56 of The City of God, understands by the scent of the mandrake the good fame of the saints: Cassiodorus wishes the fruitfulness of virtues to be designated here. Gregory the Great says: What is understood by the mandrake, that is, a medicinal and fragrant herb, if not the virtue of the perfect, who, while they distribute the examples of good works all around through holy fame, sprinkle them as if it were a scent by which the sick may be healed. Philo Carpathius wishes to look particularly at the Doctors here: because while they diligently search the sacred Scriptures, and from them produce and provide for the children of the Church a good and sweetly smelling fruit, they diffuse the most sweet scent and fruit of the true faith. Truly inept are the Papists, who by the mandrake understand the royal maiden lying in the field without a head, the multitude of the faithful, whose head was the Antichrist, by whose amputation she is without a head, who, lulled to sleep in sins, is to awaken at the voice of the Preachers and exhale a sweet scent of piety. Such comments Cornelius a Lapide pursues at length, also appealing to the dream of the Jews, just as he praised here the comments of the Chaldeans about the Jews who were to recognize their Messiah (namely, through Elijah at the end of the world), illustrating Jewish comments with Papist comments.

Latin:

Vers. 13. MANDRAGORÆ DEDERVNT ODOREM SVVM) Id est, figna video conceptus. Nam ad eum utilis mandragora, ut diximus Genes. 30, 14. Eodem pertinent, quæ sequuntur. Neque ignoro, quæ de mandragora scribant Græci: sed multa sunt herbarum genera nominis ejusdem: & eædem in alio natæ solo, & alio paratu, aliud valent.

Rectius hæc ut signa Veris accipiuntur, ut è collatione v. 12. cum c. 2, 12. 13. manifestum est. Vo- cem דודאים mandragoras notare, adhuc vehemen- ter dubium: rationes collegit operose Dürfeldus in h. l. quod mandragora nec nobilitate nec suavitate nec pulchritudine cum Dudaim conveniat. Qua- les fructus sint Dudaim (quod vocabulum interpres vertit Mandragora) incertum est. Colligi autem po- test ex hoc loco & ex Genes. 30, 14. quod fuerit flos aut fructus præstantissimus, inquit Osiander in h. l. Quæ etiam Belg. Interpp. sententia est ad Genes. 30, 14. ideo retinent in versione nomen Dudaim, & in no- tis ad hunc locum negant Mandragoras intelligi. Junius generaliter ita reddit, amabiles istos flores edentes odorem: Atque ita etiam Piscator: Die liebli- chen Blumen geben Geruch. Certos tamen flores de- signari dubitandum non est, aut certam herbæ vel arbusculi speciem. Lutherus per speciem noti nobis floris odorem gratum reddentis exposuit, die Lilien. At Gen. 30, 14. retinuit in versione sua nomen Du- daim: quia ibi intererat specialis designatio, hic ve- ro sufficiebat grati & odoriferi floris nomen. Et ad locum illum ita habet: Frage du selbst, was Du- daim seyn. Es sollen Lilien, es sollen Beer seyn, und niemand weiß, was es seyn sollen. Es heissens etliche Jüden-Kirschen, die in der Weitzen-Erndt reiff wer- den. Vinarienses addunt: Sonder Zweiffel ist es ei- ne wohlriechende Blume, oder wohl-schmeckende Frucht gewesen. Sed si ponamus, mandragoram in- digitari; unde odores mandragoræ pro signis conceptus habebuntur? Conceptioni non prodes- se, sed obesse potius ob summam frigiditatem cre- ditur mandragora, quod suo loco relinquimus. Si omnino prodesset conceptioni, num ideo odor mandragoræ signum conceptionis habendus est? Probanda autem illorum sententia, qui vernum germen notari, ac verni temporis descriptionem hic haberi censent. Nam quod ad sensum intimiorera parabolicæ locutionis attinet, variæ iterum legun- tur sententiae. Nonnulli de signis diei nuptialis & gloriosi adventus intelligunt, ad quam sententiam, explicationem & analysin suam inflexit Junius: alii de signis imminentis temporis conversionis gentium, quibus Vinarienses accedunt: alii de signis fructificationis Evangelii in genere explicant, quo Osiandri tendit paraphrasis. Atque ita etiam Alcuinus: Mandragora propter multimoda medicaminum genera sanctorum virtutibus comparatur: Portae Ecclesiae Doctores sunt sancti. In hujusmodi portis mandragorae dant odorem, cum Spirituales quique ex se virtutum famam longe lateq́; spargunt. Sed August. l. de C. D. 22. c. 56. per mandragora odorem bonam sanctorum famam: Cassiodor. virtutum foecunditatem hic designari vult. Gregor. M. Quid, inquit, per mandragoram, herbam scil. medicinalem & odoriferam, nisi virtus perfectorum intelligitur, qui dum exempla bonorum operum circumquaque per sanctam famam tribuunt, quasi odorem, quo aegroti sanentur, adspergunt. Philo Carpathius peculiariter Doctores hic respici vult: quia dum bene scrutantur sacras Scripturas, & ex iis bonam & suaviter olentem frugem Ecclesiae filiis pariunt ac mandunt, verae fidei suavissimum odorem fructumque diffundunt. Inepti vere sunt Papistae, qui per mandragoram regiam puellam sine capite in agro jacentem multitudinem fidelium intelligunt, cujus caput erat Anti-Christus, quo amputato sine capite est, quae in peccatis sopita ad vocem Praedicatorum evigilatura, suavem pietatis odorem exhalatura sit. Qualia commenta prolixe persequitur Corn. a Lap. etiam ad Judaeorum somnium provocans, quemadmodum hic Chaldaeorum de Judaeis Messiam suum agnituris (scil. per Eliam in fine mundi) commenta Judaica commentis Papisticis illustrans, laudavit.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

The bridegroom satisfies the repeated desires of the Bride, and a multitude of nations is presented to him, leaning upon him from the wilderness, just as the Israelite Church was once awakened: the Bride asks to be placed as a seal upon the heart and arm of the bridegroom, desiring his perennial love, and inquiring about her younger sister, she is made certain of the confirmation of the walls and the preservation of the spiritual vineyard: and with mutual desire declared, and the voice of the bride to be heard, and the flight of the bridegroom over the mountains of spices, so that he may carry the bride with him there, the whole colloquy is concluded.

Verse 1. O THAT THOU WERT AS MY BROTHER) That is, I wish you were my brother. THAT SUCKED THE BREASTS OF MY MOTHER) A brother still a little child, to whom sisters are accustomed to offer kisses. THAT I SHOULD FIND THEE WITHOUT, I WOULD KISS THEE; YEA, SHOULD NO MAN DESPISE ME) That I might also openly, with no one disapproving, give you kisses.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

Desideriis Sponsae iteratis satisfacit sponsus, sistiturque eidem gentium multitudo e deserto ipsi innixa, sicut Ecclesia Israelitica excitata quondam fuit: Sponsa petit ceu signaculum super cor & brachium sponsi poni, perennem ejus amorem desiderans, & de minori sorore quaerens de confirmatione murorum & conservatione vineae spiritualis certior redditur: mutuoq́; desiderio declarato, & audiendae vocis sponsae, & fugae sponsi super montes aromatum, ut sponsam secum eo vehat, totum concluditur colloquium.

Vers. 1. QVIS MIHI DET TE FRATREM MEUM) Id est, utinam frater meus esses. SUGENTEM UBERA MATRIS MEAE) Frater parvulus adhuc, qualibus solent sorores libare oscula. UT INVENIAM FORIS, ET DEOSCULER TE ET JAM ME NEMO DESPICIAT) Ut etiam palam nemine improbante oscula tibi dem.

## 8:2
Verse 2. INTO MY MOTHER'S HOUSE) See above 3, 4.

Grotius dreams of mere carnal kisses. He ineptly understands this most holy vow of the most holy Bride concerning the desire for the Pharaoh's daughter, as always and everywhere kissing Solomon even openly, which he imagines was so much in her that she wished him to be the same little brother to whom she, as a sister, could offer kisses, with no one disapproving, as often as she wished. Which gloss, savoring of a carnal and lustful mind, is unworthy of being laboriously refuted: even though Cornelius a Lapide approves the same, as far as the sense of the letter is concerned. What can this be of women, says Bede, that she should suddenly desire her beloved and chosen one not to be a young man, as he had been, but to be born again to her as a brother in infantile age and to be nourished as a little child at her mother's breasts, whom she had been accustomed to find as an adult? Interpreters commonly explain this of the holier desire of the Bride of Christ. Some indeed [explain it] of the desire for the consummation of the marriage in Heaven; as do three anonymous authors in Theodoret, Junius, and Cornelius a Lapide, who takes that 'that I should find thee without' in this way, i.e., outside the earth: others of the desire for the incarnation of the Son of God: St. Athanasius in the Synopsis, Cassiodorus, Theodoret, Philo Carpathius, Gregory the Great, and Bede, so that the desires of the faithful of the Old Testament are expressed here, awaiting the advent of the Messiah and the incarnation, through which the Son of God came forth as it were from the bosom of the Father. Concerning which Ambrose, On the Institution of Virgins, chapter 2: He was made 'without' who was 'within.' See him 'within' when you read that he is in the bosom of the Father: Recognize him 'without' when he seeks us, that he may redeem us. Thus Alcuin: 'O that thou wert as my brother': that voice is of the ancient righteous ones desiring the advent of Christ in the flesh. 'That sucked the breasts of my mother,' that is, to be born in the Synagogue, and to be nourished according to the nature of human generation. 'That I should find thee without, and kiss thee.' The beloved was 'within' while in the beginning was the Word: 'without' while the Word was made flesh. 'Kiss thee,' i.e., I may see face to face, and speak mouth to mouth. 'And should no man despise me.' Before the advent of Christ the Church was only within the straits of Judea; after the ascension it was spread throughout the whole world and became venerable. Others interpret it of the desire for the conversion of the nations, which opinion seems the simplest and agrees more with the text. 'I wish,' says the ancient Church, 'without,' i.e., outside Judea (because those outside the faith are said to be 'without,' Eph. 2:13, 1 Cor. 5:12, Prov. 8:1, Luke 14:13), 'I would find thee as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother,' i.e., of the Catholic Church (for the whole is accustomed to come under the name of the mother, and a part under the name of the daughter among the Hebrews). Which the Weimar theologians accept concerning the reception of the Sacraments, Circumcision, and Baptism. Christ is said more simply to have sucked the breasts of the mother Sulamith when he was instructed and increased in wisdom in the days of his flesh, in the Jewish Church, to which were entrusted the oracles of God, Rom. 3:2. Some explain that he is said to suck the same breasts in his members, with Justus Orgelit, when the Doctors refresh us with spiritual Sacraments and most pious exposition as if with true milk. 'That I may kiss thee among the nations': that I may worship thee with the nations, in the way we are commanded to kiss the son, Ps. 2:12. 'Lest I be despised,' or lest they despise me, to whom I was previously a contempt. 'I would lead thee into my mother's house, there thou wouldst teach me': I would devote effort that I might be received and rejoice to remain in the Church as in my mother's house: I will procure for thee a lodging, which may be by prayer, faith, and the study of piety, so that I may be informed by thee, and hear thy word. While indeed We grant hospitality to Christ and his Gospel, and in return we receive this benefit, that we may be instructed and make progress in the saving knowledge of God. As Osiander rightly says here: And I will give you a cup of wine spiced (with aromatics), and the must of my pomegranates (expressed from pomegranates), that is to say, you shall be refreshed in turn by my fruits, and you shall be exhilarated with most sweet wine. By the name of pomegranates, charity is primarily designated, which is most sweet to our Bridegroom. Some understand by wine the doctrine, which is accustomed to be compared to wine. See Is. 55, 5. ch. 55, 1. Prov. 9, 5. which wine is indeed offered to us, but it also delights the Bridegroom when the doctrine of the word is propagated. The former explanation is simpler, however, which Osiander also embraces in his Paraphrase. riensis, and Mercerus: who, by spiced wine, he says here, with which she says she will give him to drink, and the juice of pomegranates, understand the fragrance of good works and the sweet juice of faith, with which the Church will delight him when she has been taught by him. Some of the ancients referred the must of pomegranates particularly to the charity which shone forth in the Martyrs. Thus Alcuin: I will give you a cup of spiced wine, i.e., fervent love adorned with various pigments of virtues: and the must of my pomegranates: i.e., the glorious triumph of the holy martyrs, who, through most fervent charity, do not hesitate to go to you through iron and flames.

Latin:

Vers. 2. IN DOMUM MATRIS MEAE) Vid. sup. 3, 4.

MEra oscula carnalia somniat Grotius. Votum hoc Sponsae sanctissimae sanctissimum de desiderio Pharaonidae, inepte carnaliter intelligit, semper & ubique etiam palam osculandi Salomonem, quod tantum in ipsa fuisse fingit, ut fratrem parvulum eundem esse optarit, cui libare ipsa tanquam Soror, oscula, nemine improbante, possit, quotiescunque velit. Quae Glossa animum carnalem Venereumque resipiens, indigna est, quae operose confutetur: etsi, qua literae sensum, eandem probet Lapideus Cornelius. Quae potest esse foeminarum, inquit Beda, quae dilectorem dilectumque suum repente desideret non esse juvenem, uti fuerat, sed in infantili aetate fratrem sibi denuo nasci suaque genitricis uberibus parvulum nutriri, quem adultum reperire consueverat? De Sponsae Christi sanctiori desiderio communiter Interpp. explicant. Nonnulli quidem de desiderio consummationis nu- ptiarum in Cœlis; uti apud Theodoretum tres Ano- nymi, Jun. Corn. à Lap. qui illud ut inveniam te foris; ita accipit, i. e. extra terram: Alii de desiderio incar- nationis Filii Dei: S. Athanas. in Synopsi, Cassiodor. Theodor. Philo Carpath. Greg. M. Beda, ut desideria hic exprimantur fidelium V. T. expectantium ad- ventum Meffiæ & incarnationem, per quam Filius Dei e sinu Patris quasi foras prodiit. Quo de Ambr. de Instit. Virgin. c. 2. Foris factus est, qui erat intus. Vide illum intus, quando legis, quod in sinu Patris est: Cognosce illum foris, quando nos quærit, ut redimat. Sic Alcuinus: Quis mihi te det fratrem meum: vox ista est antiquorum justorum optantium adventum Christi in carne. Sugentem ubera matris meæ, id est, in Synagoga nasci, ac nutriri juxta humanæ genera- tionis naturam. Ut inveniam te foris, & osculer. In- tus erat dilectus, dum in principio erat Verbum: foris, dum Verbum caro factum est. Osculer, i. e. facie ad faciem videam, & ore ad os loquar. Et jam ne nemo despiciat. Ante adventum Christi intra angustias Ju- dææ tantum fuit Ecclesia, post ascensionem in toto mun- do dilatata fuit & venerabilis. Alii de desiderio con- versionis gentium interpretantur, quæ sententia sim- plicissima videtur, textuiq; magis convenit. Utinam, inquit Vetus Ecclesia, foris, i. e. extra Judæam, (quia extra esse dicuntur extranei a fide Eph. 2, 13. 1. Cor. 5, 12. Prov. 8, 1. Luc. 14, 13. inveniam te fratrem meum, su- gentem ubera matris meæ, h. e. Catholicæ Ecclesiæ (nam totum matris, pars filiæ nomine venire apud E- bræos solet.) Quod de Sacramentorum, Circumcisio- nis & Baptismi susceptione Vinarienses accipiunt. Simplicius suxisse ubera matris Sulamithæ Christus di- citur cum informatus est, & profecit sapientia in di- ebus carnis, in Ecclesia Judaica, cui credita erant τὰ λόγια τꭈ̃ θεꭈ̃ Rom. 3, 2. Nonnulli in membris suis eun- dem sugere dici ubera, cum Justo Orgelit. explicant, cum spiritualibus Sacramentis & piissima expositio- ne tanquam vero lacte Doctores nos reficiunt. Ut osculer te inter gentes: ut cum gentibus te colam, quomodo osculari jubemur filium Ps. 2, 12. Ne con- temnar, vel ne despiciant me, quibus antea contemtui fui. Ducam te in domum matris meæ, ibi docebis me: operam navarem, ut in Ecclesia ceu matris meæ do- mo susceptus gestias permanere: procurabo tibi hospitium, quod sit prece, fide ac pietatis studio, ut abs te informer, & audiam verbum tuum. Dum n. Christo ejusque Evangelio hospitium apud nos con- cedimus, vicissim hoc beneficii reportamus, ut in salvifica Dei agnitione erudiamur & proficiamus. Ut hic recte Osiand. Et dabo tibi poculum ex vino (aromatibus) condito, & mustum malorum granato- rum meorum (e malis granatis expressum) q. d. fru- ctibus meis vicissim reficieris, & exhilaraberis cum vino suavissimo. Malorum granatorum nomine charitas cumprimis designatur, quæ Sponso nostro suavissima est. Nonnulli per vinum doctrinam intel- ligunt, quæ vino comparari solet. Vid. Es. 55, 5. c. 55, 1. Prov. 9, 5. quod vinum nobis quidem propina- tur, sed Sponsum etiam oblectat, cum doctrina ver- bi propagatur. Simplicior tamen prior est explica- tio, quam etiam amplectitur Osiand. Paraphr. Vina- riensis, & Mercerus: qui, vinum odoratum, inquit hic, quo se potaturam eum dicit, & succum malorum granatorum intellige odorem bonorum operum & sua- vem fidei succum, quo Ecclesia sit oblectatura, ubi ab eo edocta fuerit. Malorum granatorum mustum non- nulli veterum peculiariter ad charitatem, quæ in Martyribus eluxit, retulere. Sic Alcuinus: Dabo tibi poculum ex vino condito, i. e. ferventem amorem va- riis virtutum pigmentis ornatum: & mustum malo- rum granatorum meorum: i. e. gloriosum sancto- rum martyrum triumphum, qui ferventissima charitate per ferrum flammasque ad te ire non dubitant.

## 8:5
WHO ASCENDS FROM THE DESERT) Which breathes as sweetly as a field fresh from the rain.

Who has ever heard such a wonderful gloss? The Bride is not compared to a field here, nor is anything said about her breath: not to mention how inept and foreign this commentary about the sweet breath of the Solomonic Bride is. It is very well known that by the desert in the Prophetic books, paganism is designated. Therefore, Alcuin, along with other ancients, is correct: The voice of the Synagogue wondering how the Church had suddenly ascended from the desert of Gentilism into the embraces of the Bridegroom, overflowing with delights (which is added in the Vulgate; but it is not held in the Hebrew, unless perhaps the Vulgate expressed the following Hebrew word with this periphrasis), i.e., with the beauty of all gifts! Most, however, prefer that this voice be the Bridegroom's: to whom the Vinarienses accede, as does Osiander. How beautiful is the Church (thus her paraphrase has it), having indeed arisen in arid and uncultivated places, where no fruit of the Gospel could be hoped for, but now she proceeds excellently, and leans sweetly by faith upon Christ the Bridegroom, just as if a beloved woman were walking joined beside her dearest husband, and they were mutually wrapping their arms around each other's necks. From the desert, says Mercerus, of darkness and ignorance, where there is a scarcity of all things, the Church ascends to the knowledge of Christ and God, from whence all graces are poured out, so that she may join herself to her Bridegroom Christ, and lean upon him, and depend on him, and cast all her own things upon him, and commit all things to him. This is what he says: LEANING UPON HER FRIEND. He had explained that word מתרפקת from the Hebrews by מתחברת, joining herself to her friend, just as in the Arabic language a companion is called Rephac, and מתענגעת, taking delights upon her friend; he judges that both are thus comprehended in the Greek and Latin text, overflowing with delights, and leaning upon her companion. But Ludov. de Dievius on this passage thinks that the Greek word ἐπιστηριζομένη and the Latin INNIXA should be sought rather from the Ethiopian language, where רפק is to recline, to lie down, which is used for ἀνακλίνεσθαι in Matthew 8:11, Reclining upon her beloved. The Jesuit Corn. à Lap. can be seen here to have dipped his pen into Lutheran ink: while he says that the 'leaning upon her beloved' signifies that the Church is climbing into Heaven, not by her own powers, but by the grace of Christ. For no one ascends into Heaven, except he who descended from Heaven, the Son of man, who is in Heaven (John 3), and whom he has deigned to lead with him into Heaven.

UNDER THE APPLE TREE I AWAKENED YOU: THERE YOUR MOTHER WAS CORRUPTED: THERE YOUR PROGENITRESS WAS VIOLATED) In the Hebrew: Under the apple tree I uncovered you: (that is, I deflowered you) there your mother conceived you, there your progenitress conceived you: that is, in the same way. What he understands by the apple is not obscure from 2:3, 4. See Servius on that line of Virgil: I myself will gather the apples with their soft down. Thus also the Greeks say, ἰσοβόλα.

A gloss no less foreign than it is shameless. It is not 'I uncovered you' in the Hebrew, so far is it from being able to be snatched away to mean defloration. For the verb עוררתיך is I AWAKENED YOU, from עור, he awakened, he was awake, in Piel he aroused, he awakened (Zech. 9:13, Ps. 8:3, Prov. 10:12), which nowhere signifies 'I uncovered.' And although most attribute those words to the Bridegroom, the masculine suffixes in the Hebrew teach that they are the Bride's, who is speaking these things to the Bridegroom. For that bold rashness of Corn. Lapid. will be approved by no sensible person: by which, for dictatorial authority, he decrees that the Hebrew text must be corrected. I say these are the words of the Bridegroom, not the Bride, and therefore in the Hebrew, points should be substituted which signify feminine pronouns instead of masculine, so that for חבלתך and אמך and עוררתיך you read עוררתיך and חבלתך and so on in the others that follow. What, I ask, is the cause of such great audacity? For St. Greg., Theod., teach by unanimous consent that these are the words of the Bridegroom. Cassiod., Philo, Apollonius, Beda, Justus, Anshel., Rupert., Angelomus, Haymo, Alcuin, Thomas, and all the other Fathers, Greeks as well as Latins. Thus, therefore, the text of Scripture was to be corrected according to the interpretation of the Fathers. Beautiful, excellent, than which there is nothing higher. What wonder that the Fathers, who could not consult the Hebrew text, attributed these to the Bridegroom: since the later words were erroneously rendered in the Vulgate version, 'there your mother was corrupted, there your progenitress was violated,' which Grotius himself corrected here from the Hebrew. And Grot. himself acknowledges that the Bride speaks these things: who accepts the sixth verse, by which the speech is continued, as the words of the Bride: 'Let me be near to your heart, and as a necklace, which is placed upon the heart.' Cornelius admits at v. 6 that the Chaldean, the Arabic, the Rabbis, and certain Catholics also attribute those to the Bride. Therefore, as to the genuine sense, the Bride is said to have awakened the Bridegroom with prayers, under the apple tree, under the shadow and grace of the Bridegroom himself (for she herself compares him to an apple tree in ch. 2:13), in the garden of the Church; where Christ is conceived by the Church as mother, from the communion of faithful Saints, in their hearts. She asks, therefore, that the Bridegroom place her as a seal upon his heart, since she has awakened him with prayers (Ps. 44:24) and bound him to his love in the bosom of the Church; where Christ is generated with great pain in the hearts of the faithful (Gal. 4:19), just as the LXX used the verb ὠδίνεῖν here, which brings about a painful birth. Mercerus is almost similar: Under the apple tree I awakened you (because the apple tree is also consecrated to love), I awakened you, I say, so that you might favor me, and receive me under the shadow of it, that is, YOUR shadow: and there, just as your mother gave birth to you, because there, when I had received myself under the shadow, and had fled to your protection, you were as if born, and became a safeguard to me. Thus I would feel about this whole passage, for it is difficult to adapt the individual parts otherwise. The mother of the Bridegroom can be called, as above at the end of ch. 3, the congregation of the faithful, which as it were gives birth to Christ, for when it flees to him with its prayers, it leads him to bring help to itself. Cf. the Notes of the Belgian Interpreters on this passage. Vatablus interprets this in this way concerning the cross of Christ: By believing under the cross that you have suffered, I will awaken you with frequent prayers, so that your cross may be to me one of pardon, grace, and salvation.

Latin:

Verf. 5. QVAE ASCENDIT E DESERTO) Quæ tam dulce halat, quam ager à pluvia recens.

Quis unquam tam mirabilem glosam fando accepit? Nec agro hic Sponsa comparatur, nec de halitu ejus quicquam habetur: ne dicam, quam in- eptum & alienum hoc sit commentum de dulci ha- litu Sponsæ Salomoneæ. Per desertum in libris Pro- pheticis gentilismum designari, notissimum est. Pro- inde recte Alcuinus cum aliis veteribus; Vox Syna- gogæ mirantis, quomodo Ecclesia de deserto Gentilita- tis in Sponsi subito amplexus ascendisset, deliciis afflu- ens (quod additur in vulgata; in Ebræo autem non habetur, nisi forte Vulgatus hac περιφράσει vocem Ebræam sequentem expressit) i. e. omnium donorum pulchritudine! Plerique tamen vocem hanc Sponsi esse malunt: quibus accedunt Vinarienses, ut & Osian- der. Quam pulchra est Ecclesia (sic habet ejus para- phrasis) orta quidem in locis aridis & incultis, ubi nul- lus Evangelii fructus sperari poterat, sed nunc egregie incedit, & innititur fide suaviter Christo Sponso, ac si dilecta conjuncta juxta maritum charissimum ince- dat, & mutuo brachia collis circumdent. Ex deserto, inquit Mercerus, tenebrarum & ignorantiæ, ubi o- mnium rerum penuria, ascendit Ecclesia ad Christi & Dei cognitionem, unde omnes gratiæ infunduntur, ut se Sponso suo Christo adjungat, & ei innitatur, & ex eo pendeat, in eum omnia sua conjiciat, ei omnia commit- tat. Hoc est, quod dicit: INNITENS AMICO SUO. Vocem illam מתרפקת ex Ebræis exposuerat per מתחברת adjungens sese amico suo, uti lingua Arabi- ca Socius appellatur Rephac, & מתענגעת delicias a- gens super amicum suum, utrumque in Græco & La- tino textu ita comprehendi censet, deliciis affluens, & innixa socio suo. At Ludov. de Dievius ad h. l. Græ- cam vocem ἐπιστηριζομένη & Latina INNIXA ex lingua Æthiopica potius petendam existimat, ubi רפק est recumbere, accumbere, quod pro ἀνακλίνεσθαι ponitur Matth. 8, 11, Recumbens super dilectum suum. Jesuita Corn. à Lap. hic calamum tinxisse in atra- mentum Lutheranum videre potest: dum τὸ innixa super dilectum, inquit, significat, Ecclesiam scandere in Cœlum, viribus non suis, sed gratiæ Christi. Nemo enim ascendit in Cœlum, nisi qui descendit de Cœlo Filius ho- minis, qui est in Cœlo Joh. 3. & quem ille secum in Cœ- lum ducere dignatus sit.

SVB ARBORE MALO SVSCITAVI TE: IBI COR- RVPTA EST MATER TVA: IBI VIOLATA EST GENITRIX TVA) In Hebræo: Sub arbore malo nudavi te: (id est, devirginavi) ibi concepit te mater tua, ibi concepit te ge- nitrix tua: id est, eodem modo. Malum quid intelligat, non obscurum ex 2, 3. 4. Vide Servium ad illud Virgilii: Ipse ego cana legam tenera lanugine mala. Sic & Græci dicunt, ἰσοβόλα.

Glossa non minus aliena, quam impudica. Non est in Hebræo nudavi te, tantum abest, ut ad deflo- rationem abripi queat. Nam verbum עוררתיך est EXCITAVI TE, ab עור excitavit, evigilavit, in Piel exuscitavit, excitavit Zach. 9, 13. Psal. 8. 3. Prov. 10, 12. quod nuspiam significat NUDAVIT. Et quan- quam verba illa plerique Sponso tribuant, suffixa ta- men masculina in Hebræo docent Sponsæ ea esse, quæ hæc ad Sponsum loquatur. Nemini enim corda- to probabitur audax illa Corn. Lapid. temeritas: qua pro autoritate dictatoria decernit, corrigendum esse textum Hebræum. Dico hæc esse verba Sponsi, non Spon- sæ, ac proinde in Heb. substituenda esse puncta, quæ signi- ficent pronomina fœminina pro masculinis, ut pro חבלתך pro אמך אמך pro עוררתיך legas עוררתיך חבלתך & ita in cæteris, quæ sequuntur. Quæ obsecro tantæ audaciæ causa? Nam verba hæc esse Sponsi una- nimi consensu docent S. Greg. Theod. Cassiod. Philo, A- polonius, Beda, Justus, Anshel. Rupert. Angelomus, Hay- mo, Alcuinus, Thomas, cæterique omnes Patres, Græ- ci æque ac Latini. Sic ergo è Patrum interpretatione corrigendus erat textus Scripturae. Belle, praeclare, ut nihil supra. Quid mirum, Patres, qui Ebraeum tex- tum consulere non potuere, Sponso haec tribuisse : quum in vulgata versione erronee reddita fuerint posteriora verba, ibi corrupta est mater tua, ibi viola- ta est genitrix tua, quae hic ex Ebraeo Grotius ipse correxit. Et agnoscit ipse Grot. Sponsam haec loqui : qui versum sextum, quo continuatur sermo, ut Sponsae verba accipit: Sim proxima cordi tuo, & mo- nile, quod super cor ponitur. Sponsae illa Chaldaeum etiam, Arabicum, Rabbinos & Catholicos quosdam tri- buere, fatetur Cornelius ad v. 6. Quod ergo ad sensum genuinum, Sponsa excitasse Sponsum dicitur preci- bus, sub malo, sub ipsius Sponsi (hunc n. malo com- parat ipsa c. 2, 13.) umbra ac gratia, in horto Ecclesiae; ubi concipitur Christus ab Ecclesia matre, a com- munione Sanctorum fidelium, in cordibus ipsorum. Rogat ergo Sponsum, ut se ponat super cor suum si- gnaculum, quandoquidem excitavit ipsum precibus Psal. 44, 24. suoque amori alligaverit in gremio Ec- clesiae; ubi magno dolore generatur Christus in cor- dibus fidelium Gal. 4, 19. uti hic LXX. verbum ὠδί- νεῖν, quod dolorosum partum infert, adhibuere. Si- militer fere Mercerus: Sub pomo excitavi te (quia & pomus amori consecrata est,) excitavi, inquam, ut mihi faveres, me sub umbram illius, id est, TUAM reciperes: atque illic velut mater tua te genuit, quia il- lic, quum me sub umbram recepisssem, & ad tuam cli- entelam confugissem, velut genitus es, & mihi factus in praesidium. Ita de toto hoc loco senserim, nam singula a- lioqui accommodare, difficile est. Mater Sponsi dici po- test, ut supra in fine c. 3. fidelium congregatio, quae velut Christum enitatur, quum enim suis precibus ad illum confugiens, ad sibi opem ferendam, adducit. Conf. No- tae Belgar. Interpp. ad hunc locum. Vatablus de cruce Christi interpretatur h. m. Sub cruce credendo, te esse passum, excitabo te frequentibus precibus, ut crux tua mihi sit veniae, gratiae & salutis.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. SET ME AS A SEAL UPON YOUR HEART) Let me be so near to your heart, as a necklace, which is placed upon the heart.

AS A SEAL UPON YOUR ARM) Let me adhere to you, as a ring to the hand.

The sense is too thin and meager for words of such weight and such emphasis. We remove above all Solomon, whom Grotius alone had in mind. The Bride therefore addresses the mystical Bridegroom: and desires to be placed upon his heart. Cornelius proves from the Hebrew text that these are the words of the Bride, not the Bridegroom: For it has the masculine שִׂימֵנִי, 'place me,' O Bridegroom; for if they were the words of the bridegroom, it should have been said שִׂימִינִי, that is, 'place me,' O woman, O bride. Add that the suffix is masculine in the word לִבֶּךָ, 'your heart,' and זְרוֹעֶךָ, 'your arm,' O Bridegroom. Cornelius also acknowledges that that sense is plain, and yet, having abandoned it, he laboriously pursues another, more obscure one, by which the Fathers judge these words to be the Bridegroom's, and he is nothing or little concerned about the true and proper sense, even though Rupert accepted those words as the Bride's, which was also done by the Chaldean. Although some posit an enallage of gender here, it is not easily to be admitted in the Canticle, for thus it will not rarely be entirely ambiguous whether the Bridegroom or the Bride is speaking in this Canticle. But that the Holy Spirit wished to speak ambiguously and to employ an enallage, so that we might be left in doubt as to whose words they are, is not likely. Nor do those things which are said about the insuperable power of love suit the Bride in such a way that it is more certain than certain that they suit the Bridegroom's love and affection. Wherefore the Weimar Paraphrase rightly accepted the words as the Bride's and excellently expressed their sense. The Bride asks for this, that she may not only be close to his heart like a necklace, but that she may be imprinted upon the heart itself as a seal, and thus also be imprinted upon the arm of Christ as a seal. That it may always be carried in the mind, that he may be mindful of her, Neh. 13, 13. and may love her, always on the arm, that he may do well to her, Hag. 2, 24. Is. 49. Mal. 3. Such a sense Cornelius himself acknowledged here: namely, that the Bride asks that the Bridegroom may seal his heart and arm and love of a Bride so miserable and corrupted by sin. And how does Grotius carve a necklace out of a seal? He understands by the seal a ring in the words subjoined: AS A SEAL UPON THINE ARM, that I may cling to thee, as a ring to the hand. But is a ring usually placed upon the heart or breast? Although neither is a ring placed upon the arm, nor was it right for Grotius to change hand into arm. But a seal can conveniently be taken for the thing impressed by the seal; namely, that the Bride and her image may be impressed upon the mind of the Bridegroom, and also impressed upon his arm, so that he may never put aside the memory of her from his mind, and she may always be before his eyes. For a seal can be taken for the thing sealed, says Cornelius, and he confirms that sense (concerning the image of the Bride) from Ambrose, Honorius, Hugo, and others. LOVE IS STRONG AS DEATH) My love is insuperable. JEALOUSY IS HARD AS HELL) In Greek ζῆλο. But that signifies ardent love. THE LAMPS THEREOF ARE LAMPS OF FIRE AND FLAMES) In Hebrew: Its coals, coals of fire, (as) the flame of God, that is, of a burnt offering: in this name שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה the שׁ abounds, as often among the Chaldeans. The Bride does not speak of her own love, but rather celebrates the love of the Bridegroom: although indeed these things can also be accommodated to the love of the Bride in a certain way, because she herself imitates the affection of the Bridegroom, and fashions herself and her mind toward him, and the affection and love of the Bridegroom and Bride is correlative; as they are explained by the Blessed Gerhard concerning the mutual love of both, both of the Bridegroom toward the Bride, and of the Bride toward the Bridegroom in Postill. Salomon. Dom. 13. post Trin.: Without doubt, however, all the predicates, if the emphases which they import are accepted, are too eminent to suit the love of the Bride, and they belong in a far more sublime way to the immense and insuperable love of Christ, concerning which let the Blessed Gerhard and the Vinarieans be seen there in the paraphrase to this place. Grotius was here again captured by carnal and venereal thoughts: when he explained the love of the Solomonic Bride from Antipater, Zenodotus the Greeks, and Aedituus the Latin poet, namely how many waters could not extinguish it. But against this fire of Venus, unless it be Venus herself, there is no other force that can suppress it; as the verses cited from Aedituus have. Similarly, the words which follow; IF A MAN GIVETH ALL THE SUBSTANCE OF HIS HOUSE FOR LOVE HE WILL DESPISE IT AS NOTHING; he illustrated from nowhere else than from Tibullus, Go under the command and under the title of the household gods. Behold a famous interpreter of the divinely inspired Song! But the genuine sense of this whole address, of this Chapter up to verse 8, unless I am mistaken, is now in the open from these things which have been said. Indeed the Bride had wished that she might soon find the Bridegroom her brother outside of Judea through the incarnation, sucking the breasts of his mother, whether through education or through the enjoyment of the milk of heavenly doctrine, according to the nature and progress of the human condition, and that it might be permitted to her to fix there the kiss of faith, devotion, and charity, so that he might no longer be held in contempt, but might be held venerable in and outside of Judea, throughout the whole world: promising with all readiness to receive and apprehend the same with the joyful arms of faith, and to lead him to the house of her mother, the universal Church, and so far to devote all effort, that she might be able to unfold her loves in the same, and enjoy the fruits of love in return: there she also hopes to be taught by her Bridegroom, and promises in turn that she will offer him pleasant cups of spiced wine and must of pomegranates, which can be expected from the spiritual vineyard and garden from the branches clinging to the spiritual vine, and filled with the sweetest grapes, and from the pomegranates most acceptable in odor and taste: so that he may be exhilarated by faith, and the various fragrances of virtues, and the charity of the Bride as if by spiced wine and must of pomegranates. Nor does the Bride doubt that she will be successful in her vow. For she says, His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me; that is to say, he embraces me with the highest love. And therefore he will not deny me what I vow: thus I can rest with joyful hope in his embraces, and await that longed-for time with confidence. The Bridegroom, however, confirms her in this hope of hers, adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem, all who belong to the people of God, not to disturb the Bride: reminding the Bride, however, for that reason, that she should rest in the meantime, and not allow herself to be disturbed by anyone in this conceived hope, until the desired time shines forth. Soon also, as if the Church from the Gentiles were already seen and beheld from afar coming forth with joyful and distinguished beauty, he says with admiration and joy, Who is this that ascendeth from the barren desert of the Gentiles, horrible with the thorns and briars of sins, who reclines upon her beloved with true confidence of heart and undivided charity, and relies and delights solely in the Bridegroom of faithful souls? To whom therefore the Bride arising from the Gentiles answers: Under the apple tree I awakened thee, there thy mother brought thee forth, there she bore thee who brought thee forth, that is to say, dost thou not know me? I am she who under the apple tree, under Thee thyself (for the Bride compares him to an apple tree in ch. 2, 2.) am thy sweetest shade (in the garden of the Church) I awakened thee by faith and prayer, and by the virtue of thy grace, when I was enjoying that sweetest shade of grace, I provoked thee to the embrace of sweetest love. There the Church brought thee forth (in the hearts of the faithful Jews) there she bore thee, who gave birth to thee, (in the hearts of the faithful Gentiles) for under the shade of the grace of the tree of life the Church Mother brings forth Christ through the ministry, so that he may be conceived, and in the hearts of the faithful, so that he may be formed, and cherished in the womb of our heart, there thou art equally formed in my heart, O Bridegroom chosen from the Gentiles, as thou art formed through the sacred ministry in the heart of the faithful from the Jewish people, thy peculiar treasure. Therefore he adds a most fervent prayer: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, that I may always be before your heart and eyes, that I may enjoy your love and power, and rejoice, so that you may never forget me, never abandon me with your grace and power. Thus I shall be able to lean upon you, my Bridegroom, by a perennial and most constant cohesion of faith and charity. For your love is strong as death, and jealousy is hard as hell. Death, as a powerful and invincible tyrant, rules over the whole human race because of sin, nor is there anything that can break its force; hell encloses those bound as if in a most hard prison, nor is there anyone who can snatch them from it, or release us from its hard chains. But your love, most dear Bridegroom, Hero of dual Substance, is no less strong than death, by which you overcame the force of death itself; your jealousy is no less hard than hell, by which you broke through even the most hard prison of hell itself. Since you surround and embrace me with this love, I am certain that neither death nor hell can separate me from your charity; just as death and hell allow no one to be snatched from them. The coals of your love are burning coals, the fire of a most blazing flame, the flames of the Lord, of divine love, truly infinite and immense; and so many waters will not be able to extinguish charity, nor will rivers overwhelm it: Many waters are many peoples (Rev. 17) who, even if they inundated Christ in a dense throng, especially at the time of the passion, by the crowd of priests, people, soldiers, and all men (Is. 53, 6.) nay, even of all demons, the flames of that immense love could not be extinguished; nor could rivers of tribulations and anxieties, of passions of soul and body, have been able to overwhelm them: therefore, much less now shall the flames of his love against me, his chosen Bride, be extinguished by waters or any rivers. Christ was all kindled with love (thus Osiander paraphrases) toward the Church, and that love has dominated him to such an extent that he did not hesitate to undergo the dire and most bitter death of the cross for the Church, nor could the love of Christ be extinguished by those waters of tribulations and passions. With the same love he embraces his own most constantly, John 13. Therefore, no creature shall separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus, our Lord, Rom. 8. If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it with contempt, i.e., it will be despised and rejected: If one were to give all the goods in his house for love (of the sweet Savior, and the effect of the same), it would all be worth nothing (Silver and gold and everything that is precious in the world is far too little, nay, nothing for this. 1 Pet. 1:18, Ps. 49:8-9, Matt. 15:76), as the Weimar paraphrasts beautifully [say] with the Blessed Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 6. PONE ME UT SIGNACULUM SVPER COR TVVM) Ita cordi tuo sim proxima, ut monile, quod super cor ponitur.

VT SIGNACLVM SVPRA BRACHIVM TVVM) Ita tibi adhaeream, ut annulus manui.

Sensus nimis tenuis & exilis ad verba tanti ponderis, tantaeque Emphaseos. Removemus ante omnia Salomonem, quem solum in mente habuit Grotius. Sponsum ergo mysticum alloquitur Spon- sa: & super cor ejus poni exoptat. Verba Sponsae haec esse, non Sponsi, ex Ebraeo textu probat Cornelius: Habet enim masculine שִׂימֵנִי pone me ô vir Sponse; si enim essent verba sponsi, dicendum fuisset, שִׂימִינִי id est, pone me, ô foemina, o sponsa. Adde, quod affixum Masculin. sit in voce לִבֶּךָ cor TUUM, & זְרוֹעֶךָ brachium tuum, ô Sponse. Agnoscit etiam Cornelius, sensum illum planum esse, & tamen relicto illo, alterum obscuriorem, quo verba haec Sponsi esse censent Patres, persequi- tur operose, ac de vero proprioque sensu nihil, aut parum sollicitus est, utut Rupertus verba ea ut Spon- sae acceperit, quod etiam a Chaldeo factum. Quan- quam v, nonnulli hic enallagen generis ponant, ea ta- men in Cantico non facile admittenda, nam ita pror- sus ambiguum erit non raro, loquaturne Sponsus, an Sponsa in hoc Cantico? Voluisse autem Spiritum S. ambigue loqui, atque Enallagen adhibere, ut in du- bio relinqueremur, cujusnam verbi sint, verisimile non est. Neque ita conveniunt ea, quae de amoris vi insuperabili dicuntur Sponsae, uti Sponsi amori & dilectioni ea convenire, certo certius est. Quapro- pter recte de Sponsa verba accepit, sensumq; eorum eximie expressit Paraphrasis Vinariensis. Id petit Sponsa, ut non tantum instar monilis cordi sit pro- xima, sed ut cordi ipsi imprimatur ut signaculum, atq; ita etiam brachio imprimatur Christi ceu signa- culum. Ut semper geratur in animo, ut ipsius me- mor sit Nehem. 13, 13. ipsamq; amet, semper in brachio, ut ei bene faciat, Hag. 2, 24. Ef. 49. Mal. 3. Qualem sensum Cornelius ipse hic agnovit: quod nempe petat Sponsa, ut Sponsus cor suum & brachium jugi memoria, & amore Sponsæ tam miseræ & peccato corruptæ velut signaculo obsignet. Et quomodo e signaculo exsculpet Grotius monile? Intelligit per signaculum annulum in verbis subjunctis: UT SIGNACULUM SUPER BRACHIUM TUUM, ita tibi adhæream, ut annu- lus manui. Num vero annulus poni solet super cor vel pectus? Quanquam nec super brachium pona- tur annulus, neque Grotio integrum fuerit manum in brachium commutare. Signaculum autem com- mode accipi potest pro re signaculo impressa; uti nempe Sponsa ejusque effigies imprimatur animo Sponsi, imprimatur etiam brachio ejus, ut nunquam ejus memoriam animo deponat, ac semper ea verse- tur ipsi ante oculos. Signaculum n. potest sumi pro re si- gnata, ait Cornelius, eumq; sensum (de Sponsi effigie) ex Ambrosio, Honorio, Hugone, aliisque confirmat. FORTIS EST VT MORS DILECTIO) Insuperabilis amor meus. DVRA SICVT INFERNVS ÆMVLATIO) In Græco ζῆλο. Id autem significat amorem ardentem. LAMPADES EJVS LAMPADES IGNIS ATQVE FLAMMARVM) In Hebræo: Pruna ejus, pruna ignita, (ut) flamma Dei, id est, holocausti: in nomine hoc שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה abundat שׁ, ut apud Chaldæos sæpe. Non de amore suo Sponsa loquitur, sed amo- rem potius Sponsi celebrat: quamvis vero etiam pos- sint Sponsæ amori certa ratione hæc accommodari, quia ipsa imitatur affectum Sponsi, & ad eum se, ani- mumq; suum fingit & affectus amorq; Sponsi & Spon- sæ correlativus est; uti a B. Gerh. de utriusque mutuo amore, tum Sponsi erga Sponsam, tum Sponsæ erga Sponsum in Postill. Salomon. Dom. 13. post Trin. ex- plicantur: Sine dubio tamen prædicata omnia, si ea quam important, ἐμφάσεις accipiantur, eminentio- ra sunt, quam uti Sponsæ amori conveniant, atq; im- mensæ, & insuperabili Christi dilectioni longe subli- miori ratione competunt, de quibus illic B. Gerh. & Vinarienses in paraphrasi ad h. l. videantur. Grot. carnalibus & Venereis cogitationibus hic iterum ca- ptus fuit: cum amorem Sponsæ Salomoneæ ex Anti- patro, Zenodoto Græcis, & Ædituo Latino Poëta, quo- modo nempe aquæ multæ extinguere illum non po- tuerint, explicavit. At contra hunc ignem Veneris, nisi si Venus ipsa, nulla est, quem possit vis alia opprimere; uti versus ex Ædituo adducti habent. Similiter verba, quæ sequuntur; Si DEDERIT HOMO SUBSTAN- TIAM OMNEM DOMUS SUÆ PRÆ DILECTI- ONE QUASI NIHIL DESPICIET EAM; non ali- unde, quam e Tibullo, Ite sub imperium sub titulumq; lares; illustravit. Hem præclarum Cantici θεοπνεύστ sanctissimi Interpretem! Sensus autem hujus alloquii integri, hujus Capit. ad v. 8. usque germanus, nisi fal- lor, jam in aprico est ex his, quæ dicta sunt. Nimirum optarat Sponsa, ut Sponsum fratrem suum per incar- nationem, sugentem ubera matris suæ, sive per edu- cationem, sive per lactis doctrinæ cœlestis fruitio- nem, juxta humanæ conditionis naturam, & profe- ctum, foris mox inveniat extra Judæam, eique illic o- sculum fidei, devotionis, charitatis figere liceat, ne ita despectui amplius, sed in & extra Judæam, per totum orbem venerabilis habeatur: promissa omni prom- titudine eundem suscipiendi & apprehendendi lætis fidei ulnis, ac deducendi ad domum matris suæ, uni- versalis Ecclesiæ, adeouq; operam omnem impenden di, ut in eadem explicare amores suos, fructibusque amoris κατ' ἀμοιβὴν frui possit: ibi & sese edoctum iri abs Sponso suo sperat, & pollicetur vicissim, se præbiturum ipsi grata pocula vini conditi & musti malorum granatorum, quæ è vinea & horto spiri- tuali ab palmitibus adhærentibus viti spirituali, & uvis suavissimis repletis, & a malis odore & sapore acceptissimis expectari possunt: ut fide, variisq; vir- tutum odoramentis, & charitate Sponsæ veluti vino condito, & musto malorum granatorum exhilare- tur. Neq; dubitat Sponsa, se voti sui compotem fu- turam. Læva n. inquit, ejus sub capite meo, & dextra illius amplexabitur me; q. d. summo me amore com- plectitur. Ideoq; non denegabit mihi, quod voveo: læta sic spe quiescere in amplexibus ejus possum, & expectare tempus illud exoptatum cum fiducia. Sponsus vero confirmat eam in hac spe sua, adjurans filias Jerusalem, omnes qui ad populum Dei pertinent, ne Sponsam turbent: Sponsam autem ea ratione com- monefaciens, ut quiescat interea, nec a quoquam se turbari patiatur in hac concepta spe, donec opta- tum tempus affulgeat. Mox etiam quasi visa jam & conspecta eminus Ecclesia de Gentilitate læta pul- chritudine insigni prodeunte, cum admiratione & gaudio, quæ est ista, inquit, quæ afcendit de sterili, spi- nisque & vepribus peccatorum horrido gentilitatis deserto, quæ recumbit super dilectum suum vera cordis fiducia & charitate indivulsa, inque animarum fide- lium Sponso unice nititur ac delectatur? Cui proin- de respondet Sponsa è Gentilitate oriunda: Sub arbo- re malo excitavi te, ibi enixa est te mater tua, ibi peperit Genitrix tua, q. d. non nosti me? Ego illa sum, quæ sub arbore malo, sub Te ipso (hunc n. malo comparat Spousa c. 2, 2.) sum umbra tua suavissima (in horto Ecclesiæ) fide & prece te excitavi, & gratiæ tuæ vir- tute, cum umbra illa gratiæ suavissima fruerer, ad amoris suavissimi amplexum te provocavi. Ibi Ec- clesia te enixa est (in cordibus fidelium Judæorum) ibi peperit, quæ genuit te, (in cordibus fidelium gentilium) sub umbra enim gratiæ arboris vitæ Ec- clesia Mater parturit Christum per ministerium, ut concipiatur, ac in cordibus fidelium, ut formetur, & foveatur in utero cordis nostri, ibi æque formatus es in corde meo, Sponse e gentilibus electe ut formatus es per sacrum ministerium in corde fidelium e populo Ju- daico, peculio tuo. Ideo subjungit votum calidissi- mum: Pone me in signaculum super cor tuum, ut signa- culum super brachium tuum, ut semper corde atque oculis tuis obverser, amore ac virtute tua fruar, at- que gaudeam, quo nunquam mei obliviscaris, nun- quam me destituas gratia ac virtute tua. Ita inniti ti- bi Sponso meo potero, fidei & charitatis cohæsione perenni, ac constantissima. Nam amor tuus fortis est, ut mors, & Zelus durus, sicut infernus. Mors tanquam potens & invictus tyrannus dominatur ob peccatum toti humano generi, nec quicquam ejus vim infrin- gere valet; infernus concludit durissimo veluti car- cere vinctos, nec est, qui illi eosdem eripere, aut nos duris ejus vinculis exolvere queat. At amor tuus, Sponse charissime, Heros geminæ Substantiæ, non minus fortis, quam mors, quo mortis ipsius vim su- perasti; Zelus tuus non minus durus, quam infernus, quo ipsum etiam inferni carcerem durissimum per- rupisti. Hoc ergo amore quum me ambias ac complectaris, certus sum, quod neque mors neque infernus à charitate tua me separare valeat; perin- de ut mors ac infernus neminem sibi eripi patitur. Prunæ amoris tui ardentis prunæ (sunt) ignis flagran- tissimi, flammæ Domini, amoris divini, vere infiniti, & immensi; itaque aquæ multæ non poterunt extin- guere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam : Aquæ multæ populi multi sunt (Apoc. 17.) qui etsi den- so agmine inundarint Christum, maxime tempore passionis, a turba tamen Sacerdotum, populi, mili- tum hominum universorum (Es. 53, 6.) imo Dæmo- num etiam universorum amoris illius immensi flam- mæ extingui non potuere; neque flumina tribu- lationum & anxietatum, passionum animæ atq; cor- poris, obruere easdem valuerint : proinde multo minus nunc amoris ejus flammas adversus me Spon- sam suam electam aquæ, aut flumina ulla extinguent. Christus totus amore accensus fuit (ita παραφράζει Osiand.) erga Ecclesiam, atq; illi amor usque adeo est dominatus, ut pro Ecclesia diram & acerbissimam mortem crucis subire non dubitaverit, neque illis tri- bulationum & passionum aquis potuerit Christi amor extingui. Eodem amore suos complectitur constantissi- me Joh. 13. itaque nulla creatura nos separabit à dile- ctione Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu, Domino nostro Rom. 8. Si dederit homo omnem substantiam domus suæ pro dilectione, contemnendo contemnet eam, i. e. contemnetur ac reprobabitur ea: Wenn einer alles Gut in seinem Hause um die Liebe (deß süssen Hey- landes, und derselben Würckung) geben wolte, so gülte es alles nichts, (Silber und Gold und alles, was köstlich ist in der Welt, ist viel zu gering, ja nichts hierzu. 1. Pet. 1, 18. Psal. 49, 8. 9. Matth. 15, 76.) ut pulchre cum B. Luth. Vinarienses Paraphrastræ.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. MANY WATERS SHALL NOT BE ABLE TO EXTINGUISH CHARITY] They could not extinguish this love. Antipater: A torch of love is always eternal; yet it was extinguished, not even then, when born in a great sea. Zenodotus: Who carved Love and placed him by the springs, thinking he would stop this fire with water? Ædituus, a Latin poet: Why do you bring a torch, Phileros, for which we have no need? We shall go: this flame shines sufficiently in the heart. For the savage force of winds can extinguish that, or a bright shower falling from the sky: But on the contrary, no other force can suppress this fire of Venus, unless it be Venus herself. IF A MAN SHOULD GIVE ALL THE SUBSTANCE OF HIS HOUSE FOR LOVE, HE WILL DESPISE IT AS NOTHING) Tibullus: Go under command and under the title of the household gods.

Latin:

Vers. 7. AQVÆ MVLTÆ NON POTVERVNT EX- STINGVERE CARITATEM] Non possent exstinguere hunc amorem. Antipater: Πυρσὸς ἔρωτος ἀεὶ αἰώνιος· ἐσβέσθη δὲ Οὐδὲ τότ᾽ ἐν πολλῷ τικτόμενος πελάγει. Zenodotus: Τίς γλύψας τὸν Ἔρωτα παρὰ κρήνῃσιν ἔθηκεν, Οἰόμενος παύσει τοῦτο τὸ πῦρ ὕδατι; Ædituus Poeta Latinus: Quid faculam præfers, Phileros, qua nihil opus nobis? Ibimus: hoc lucet pectore flamma satis. Istam nam potis est vis sæva exstinguere venti, Aut imber cœlo candidus præcipitans: At contra hunc ignem Veneris, nisi si Venus ipsa, Nulla est quæ possit vis alia opprimere. SI DEDERIT HOMO OMNEM SVBSTANTIAM DOMVS SVÆ PRÆ DILECTIONE QVASI NIHIL DESPICIET EAM) Tibullus: Ite sub imperium sub titulumque lares.

## 8:8
Vers. 8. SHE HAS NO BREASTS) Her breasts are not yet budding.

WHAT SHALL WE DO FOR OUR SISTER IN THE DAY WHEN SHE IS TO BE SPOKEN TO) In Hebrew, when speech will be made about her: when it will be a matter of her being married.

If these things are said about the daughter of Pharaoh, how is she called Sister either by Solomon or by the girls of Jerusalem? But dismissing that fiction, we are concerned with the true sense. That these things are said about the Church to be gathered from the Gentiles is clear from the preceding: And most of the Ancients acknowledge: Our sister is still small, and has no breasts yet. Alcuin says: It designates the first times of the nascent Church from the Gentiles, when it was still small in number and less fit to preach the word. What then seems to you, O Synagogue, to be done about our sister, when she is to be spoken to, that is, to be led into the faith through the ministry of the word. Osiander makes the Church speak these things thus: I would wish that tender churches, my little sisters, were also more fully betrothed to Christ, but I see that they are still quite weak in faith, and as it were not yet mature enough for marriage; what then shall I do about them? Cassiodorus, Gregory the Great, and others judge that these are the words of the Bridegroom; with whom Alcuin agrees. The Hebrews and Greeks, such as Theodoret, three anonymous authors, Philo Carpathius, and others, judge better that they are the words of the adult Bride about the novice Bride, as Cornelius notes here, even though he twists it to the conversion of the Synagogue of the Jews at the end of the world with Hortulanus and Delrio, and thus, as with the Chaldean here, he judaizes in this as in many other things. It is believed more correctly, therefore, that the adult Jewish Bride is speaking here about the novice Gentile Church. Our people, says Mercerus, (Christian interpreters) think these are the words of the Synagogue converted to Christ about the Gentile people, whom she calls her sister, because she was finally called to Christ: just as the Jews themselves are said to lack breasts; because she lacked the knowledge of the law, and having nothing from which she might nourish and teach others, nor having true doctrine in herself, like a girl not yet nubile or fit for a husband: Thus she was in no way fit to receive Christ and God, since divine miracles had not been handed down to the Gentiles as they had to the Jews. The Synagogue, therefore, wishing that the Gentiles also be brought to the knowledge of Christ, asks what is to be done for her, at what time she will marry Christ, will be brought to Christ, and speech will be made about the Gentiles being brought to Christ. For this is the time of her betrothal. These are the words of Mercerus.

Latin:

Vers. 8. VBERA NON HABET) Mammæ ejus non- dum fororiant.

QVID FACIEMVS SORORI NOSTRÆ IN DIE, QVO ALLOQVENDA EST) In Hebræo cum de ea sermo fiet: cum de ea maritanda agetur.

Si hæc de Pharaonis filia dicuntur, quomodo ea Soror vocatur sive a Salomone sive à puellis Hie- rosolymitanis? Sed misso commento illo, de vero sensu solliciti sumus. De Ecclesia è gentibus colligenda hæc dici, è superioribus liquet: Et agnoscunt pleri- que Veterum: Soror nostra parva adhuc est, & ube- ra nondum habet. Alcuinus: Prima, inquit, nascen- tis Ecclesiæ de Gentibus tempora designat, quando ad- huc & parva fuit numero, & minus idonea prædicare verbum. Quid ergo tibi videtur, ô Synagoga, de Sorore faciendum nostra, quando alloquenda est, id est, per verbi ministerium ducenda in fidem. Osian- der Ecclesiam hæc ita loquentem facit: Vellem tene- ras Ecclesias, Sororculas meas, etiam Christo plenius desponsari, sed video, adhuc eas infirmas admodum esse in fide, & quasi nondum satis matrimonio maturas; quid igitur agam de illis? Cassiodorus, Greg. M. & alii censent, hæc esse verba Sponsi; cum quibus Alcuinus facit. Melius Ebræi & Græci, ut Theodoretus, tres Anonymi, Philo Carpath. & alii censent, esse verba Sponsæ adultæ de Sponsa novella, uti hic notat Cor- nelius, etsi ad Synagogam Judæorum convertendam in fine mundi cum Hortulano & Delrione detor- queat, adeoque cum Chaldæo hic, ut in aliis plerique judaizet. Rectius ergo Sponsam adultam Judaicam Ecclesiam, de novella Gentium Ecclesia hic loqui creditur. Nostri, inquit Merc. (Christiani Interpp.) Synagogæ verba esse putant ad Christum conversæ de gentili populo, quem Sororem suam appellat, quod ad Christum tandem sit vocata: ut & ipsi Judæi mammis carere dicuntur; quod legis cognitione careret, nec habens, unde alios aleret, & doceret, nec veram do- ctrinam in se habens, ut puella nondum nubilis aut apta viro: Sic ad Christum & Deum recipiendum minime idoneus, quum gentibus divina miracula, ut Judæis, tradita non fuissent. Optans ergo Syna- goga, gentes etiam ad Christi cognitionem adduci, rogat, quid ei faciendum sit, quo tempore Christo nubet, ad Christum adducetur, fiet Sermo de genti- bus ad Christum adducendis. Nam hoc tempus est elocationis ejus. Hæc Mercerus.

## 8:9
Vers. 9. IF SHE IS A WALL, LET US BUILD UPON HER SILVER BATTLEMENTS: IF SHE IS A DOOR, LET US JOIN HER WITH CEDAR BOARDS) The sense is: we shall find her an excellent husband. That is elegantly illustrated by a double similitude. For battlements are wont to be placed upon walls; and a door to be closed by inserting planks.

Who then, or which ones are they who presume to find a husband for the daughter of Pharaoh? And who ever dreamed that these things sound as Grotius, through a fever, I believe, thought of? Moreover, others take these similitudes in an antithetical sense, while others take them in almost the same sense. The antithesis of Cornelius a Lapide pleases me; since almost all the Fathers and interpreters judge that by the wall is denoted the firmness, perseverance, and constancy of the Bride, it is necessary that we take her infirmity, mobility, and inconstancy by the door placed against and opposite the wall. He applies this to the double class of Jews to be converted at the end of the world, foolishly [claiming] that this voice is that of the followers of Elijah. Similarly the Hebrews, except that they twist it to the construction of the city and temple, which they expect. If she is a wall, that is, if she persists constantly in her faith and in the fear of the Lord, we shall build for her a holy city and a chosen house; But if she is a door, that is, opening herself and offering herself to all, we shall apply to her wooden planks, etc. Although the Fathers recognized some diversity in these similitudes regarding the different members of the Church, they did not admit an opposite sense. Alcuin: If she is a wall, if she has in herself some who are strong in faith, or clear in intellect, or instructed in philosophy, let us add to them silver battlements, that is, the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, so that they may be able to protect the weak and unlearned all the more easily. If she is a door, if they are simple, yet eager for the study of teaching, let us propose to them the examples of pious just men, so that they may be able to fulfill the work of teaching more surely and effectively. Cedar designates the virtues of the Saints, and the boards designate the breadth of charity. In almost the same way Mercerus: If it is a wall, that is, if she be constant in the fear of me, and in worship, not allowing herself to be torn away, but resisting most constantly all who attempt to call her away, we shall build upon her a palace, a silver tower, that is to say, we shall add to her moreover strength, and we shall adorn her with many graces and gifts. But if it be a door; understand that another degree of the Elect is brought forward, so that the first is of those who are most constant in the fear and sincere worship of the Lord: the next is of the weaker ones, who have indeed taken up the worship and fear of the Lord, but are not yet fully confirmed; these, however, he says, will not lack his gifts either. If it be a gate, so that, namely, the Word and the gifts of the Holy Spirit may be introduced into her as into a certain door, not resisting the Spirit of God, but opening the door of the heart (c. 5, 2.) we shall enclose upon her a cedar board, that is, we shall apply to her moreover for her more ample adornment and strength, a cedar board, that is to say, we shall join other gifts to her. Osiander judged that this diversity of the faithful is referred to here: If she is a wall (that is, if the Church, our little sister, is constant in faith, not casting away the confession of the Gospel) let us build upon her bulwarks, or more correctly: silver palaces: If she is a door: and has sincerely admitted me with my Gospel into her heart: Let us join together, or, let us adorn that door with cedar boards

(that is, Christ wishes to dwell, as in a palace, in those who retain the confession of the Gospel, according to that; I and the Father will make our abode with him, John 14. And those who receive Christ by faith, their infirmities are covered, and they themselves are so confirmed that there is no danger that they might rot and perish. For the cedar tree does not feel decay. Piscator also assumes the same diversity, because a gate is not as strong as a wall. However, the similarities can also be understood concerning the same subjects, whether they come down to the same thing, or whether they designate only different respects. Thus, it does not displease Mercer that both similarities pertain to the same thing: since gates also ward off adversaries, so that the sense may be: we will besiege it, or we will fortify it with a cedar board, so that it may be firmer. To which also Theodoret's exposition goes: Since she is to be joined to the great King, and is to be as a wall for his house, so that she may guard and keep those things which are within, and as a door may preserve those things which have been stored away; let us build upon the wall, indeed, silver battlements, that is, utterances shining with reason: For the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver examined by fire, proven to the earth, so that standing upon them she may attack enemies with arrows, and pursue those who are laying snares. But as for the door, let us place upon it boards, and those of cedar, which cannot receive the corruption of sin. If you prefer different respects to be indicated, with Honorius leading the way, it can be said that by the wall, stability is designated, and by the door, an open access to the conversion of others, to whom she is a door, by word and example, so that the Church may be excited by this notable promise, so that she may be constant and stable like a wall, and may lie open like an open door both to the doctrine of the Holy Scriptures and to the admission of others: since the Bridegroom wishes to place silver battlements upon her as a wall, so that she may be fortified against temptations by the most lucid utterances of Holy Scripture, and to join her together as a door with cedar boards by the examples of the Saints (or if you prefer, by the incorruptible word of God), so that an entrance to life may lie open through it to many, and she herself may be immune from rot, and incorrupt; just as the cedar tree is not subject to rot. The Weimar Paraphrasts agree with this explanation, as do the Belgian Interpreters. as well as Vitus Dietericus in his Summaries: At the same time she will be like a wall, upon which are silver towers and bulwarks, that is, she will be built upon such a foundation that the gates of hell can do nothing against it. Item. She will be a beautiful cedar door, through which all the Gentiles will enter into the kingdom of heaven. To which finally also the explanation of Franc. Junius goes, even if he thinks that simply a new form of the city is indicated, as if, with the middle wall torn down, a new wall and new gates are provided to enlarge the city, and that by the name of wall and gate the city is designated synecdochically, and in it a silver palace, i.e., a most precious royal residence, so that it may be the house of the great King. But no one has been found thus far who has taken these things as referring to the finding of the husband of Pharaoh's daughter.

Latin:

Vers. 9. SI MVRVS EST, ÆDIFICEMVS SVPER EVM PROPVGNACVLA ARGENTEA: SI OSTIVM EST, COMPINGAMVS ILLVD TABVLIS CEDRINIS) Sensus est: egregium illi inveniemus maritum. Id gemina similitudine lepide illustratur. Nam pinnæ superponi mu- ris solent; & ostium claudi immissa fore.

Quinam ergo, aut quænam illæ, quæ invenire maritum Pharaonis filiæ præsumunt? & quis un- quam somniavit, hæc id sonare, quod Grotio per fe- brim, ut credo, in mentem venit? Cæterum simili- tudines istas alii sensu accipiunt antithetico, alii vero pene eodem. Antithesis Corn. a Lap. placet; Cum o- mnes fere Patres & Interpp. censeant, per murum no- tari firmitatem, perseverantiam, & constantiam Sponsæ, necesse est, ut per ostium muro contrapositum & oppo- situm accipiamus ejusdem infirmitatem, mobilitatem & constantiam. Quæ ad geminam classem Judæorum in fine mundi convertendorum applicat, ineptiens, hanc vocem esse asseclarum Eliæ. Similiter Ebræi, ni- si quod ad constructionem urbis & templi, quam ex- pectant, detorqueant. Si murus est, id est, si constan- ter in fide sua, & timore Domini persistat, construe- mus ei urbem sanctam & domum electam; Sin sit ja- nua, aperiens scil. sese & prostans omnibus, adhibe- bimus ei asseres ligneos &c. Quanquam vero Patres aliquam diversitatem agnoverint in hisce similitu- dinibus, quoad diversa Ecclesiæ membra, opposi- tum tamen sensum non admisere. Alcuinus: Si mu- rus est, si aliquos habet in se fortes in fide, vel claros ingenio, vel Philosophia instructos, addamus illis propugnacula argentea, id est scientiam divi- narum Scripturarum, ut eo facilius possint tuta- ri infirmos atque indoctos. Si ostium est, si sint simplices, tamen docendi studio inhiantes, pro- ponamus illis piorum exempla justorum, quo cer- tius & efficacius docendi opus implere possint. Ce- dri virtutes Sanctorum, & tabulæ latitudinem chari- tatis designant. Eodem fere modo Mercerus: Si est murus, id est, si constans sit in timore mei, & cultu, non sinens se avelli, sed omnibus avocare eam co- nantibus resistens constantissime, superstruemus ei palatium, arcem argenteam, q. d. addemus ei insu- per robur, & eam ornabimus multis gratiis & do- nis. Quod si sit ostium; intellige, gradum alium Ele- ctorum afferri, ut primus sit eorum, qui sunt con- stantissimi in timore & sincero cultu Domini: pro- ximus infirmiorum, qui cultum quidem & timo- rem Domini susceperunt, sed nondum plane con- firmati sunt; hos tamen etiam donis suis, inquit, non carituros. Si sit janua, ut scil. in eam tanquam in ostium quoddam intromittatur Verbum & Spir.
