Sancti dona, Spiritui Dei non resistens, sed cordis ostium aperiens (c. 5, 2.) aretabimus super eam tabulam Cedrinam, id est, ei adhibebimus insuper ad ejus ornatum ampliorem & robur, cedrinam tabulam, q. d. alia dona ei adjungemus. Ad quam diversitatem fidelium hic respici censuit Osiander: Si murus est (id est, si in fide constans est Ecclesia, Sororcula nostra, non abjiciens confessionem Ev- angelii) ædificemus super eam propugnacula, rectius: palatia argentea: Si ostium est: atque me sincere cum Evangelio meo in cor suum admiserit: Compin- gamus, seu, exornemus illud ostium tabulis cedrinis

(id est, Christus vult habitare, tanquam in palatio in iis, qui confessionem Evangelii retinent, juxta il- lud; Ego, & Pater mansionem apud eum faciemus Joh. 14. Et qui Christum fide recipiunt, eorum in- firmitates teguntur, & ipsi ita confirmantur, ut non sit periculum, ne computrescant & pereant. Cedrus enim arbor cariem non sentit. Eandem diversita- tem assumit quoque Piscator, quia janua tam fortis non est, uti murus. Possunt autem similitudines de iisdem etiam subjectis intelligi, sive ut eodem reci- dant, sive ut diversos solum respectus designent. Ita non displicet Mercero, ut eodem pertineat utraque similitudo: siquidem & portæ adversarios arceant, ut sensus sit: obsidebimus eam, vel muniemus ce- drina tabula, ut sit firmior. Quo abit quoque Theo- doreti expositio: Cum magno Regi copulanda sit, & tanquam murus futura domus ipsius, ut caret & cu- stodiat ea, quæ intus sunt, & tanquam ostium ea, quæ recondita fuerint, conservet; tanquam super muro quidem ædificemus argentea propugnacula, h. e. elo- quia ratione splendentia: Eloquia enim Domini elo- quia casta, argentum igne examinatum, probatum terræ, ut in ipsis consistens hostes sagittis petat, & insi- dias struentes persequatur. Ipsi autem ut ostio tabulas, easq́; cedrinas, quæ peccati corruptionem suscipere ne- queant, imponamus. Si diversos respectus indigitari malis, præeunte Honorio, dici poterit, per murum stabilitatem, per ostium aditum apertum ad conver- sionem aliorum, quibus ostium est, verbo & exem- plo designari, ut promissione hac insigni excitetur Ecclesia, quo constans & stabilis sit instar muri, & ceu ostium apertum pateat tum doctrinæ S. S. tum aliorum intromissioni: siquidem ipsi tanquam mu- ro Sponsus imponere velit argentea propugnacula, ut eloquiis S. Scripturæ lucidissimis adversus ten- tationes muniatur, eamque tanquam ostium tabulis cedrinis exemplis Sanctorum (vel si mavis verbo Dei incorruptibili) compingere, ut multis introi- tus per illud ad vitam pateat, atque ipsa a putredine immunis sit, ac incorrupta; sicut Cedrus arbor ob- noxia non est putredini. Cui explicationi accedunt Paraphrastæ Vinarienses, ut & Belgici Interpp. nec non Vitus Dietericus in Summariis: Zur selbigen Zeit wird sie seyn wie eine Mauer, da silbern Thürme und Bollwerck auff sind, das ist, Sie wird auf ein solch Fundament gebauet seyn, da die Pforten der Höllen nichts wider können. It. Sie wird eine schöne Cedern-Thüre seyn, durch welche alle Heyden zum Himmelreich werden eingehen. Quo denique etiam abit Franc. Junii explicatio, etsi simpliciter novam civitatis formam, ut diruto muro mediano novus quasi murus & novæ quasi portæ ad ampliamdam civitatem curentur, indicari, & appellatione muri ac portæ Sy- necdochice civitatem designari putet, inque ea pala- tium argenteum, i. e. Regia pretiosissima, ut sit domus magni Regis. Nemo vero inventus hactenus, qui hæc de inventione mariti filiæ Pharaonis acceperit.

## 8:10
Vers. 10.

I AM A WALL) The bride says that she is now such a wall. AND MY BREASTS ARE LIKE A TOWER) Which protrudes from the wall. FROM WHICH I WAS MADE BEFORE HIM, AS IF FINDING PEACE) I am, she says, a wall, for the use not of war, but of love.

These things are twin to the above, and unworthy of laborious refutation. Alcuin expressed the sense best: I am a wall, I am compacted of living stones, joined together by the glue of charity, and built upon an immovable foundation. And my breasts are like a tower, from which I was made before him, as if finding peace, that is, having most strong teachers, like towers, who know both how to nourish the little ones, and to expel all the darts of the wicked one. And this happened to me from the time when Christ reconciled me to himself, because he is the true peace, making both one. Similarly, Mercer, explaining the breasts as the Word of God; he hints that she is stable in the doctrine and word of the Lord, by which she is nourished and nourishes others, and that the divine utterances, by which she suckles her own, are to her like towers and battlements, by which she remains invincible. Nor is the explanation of Vitus Theodoricus any different; Such a promise the bride accepts with thanks, and says: I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers, for the Word teaches and defends. Therefore, those who have such words find peace, and have a gracious God, so that even the devil and the world can gain nothing against them. The explanation of the Weimar authors and other recent ones comes to the same thing; nor do Theodoret, Honorius, and other ancients disagree. Concerning a wall for the use not of war, but of conjugal love, I do not remember reading anyone.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

EGO MVRVS) Ait nupta se jam talem esse murum. ET VBERA MEA SICVT TVRRIS) Quæ de muro prominet. EX QVO FACTA SVM CORAM EO, QVASI PA- CEM REPERIENS) Sum, inquit, murus, ad usum non belli, sed amoris.

Gemina hæc superioribus, & indigna operosa confutatione. Sensum optime expressit Alcuinus: Ego murus, ego de vivis compacta sum lapidibus, glutine charitatis adunata, & super fundamentum immobile ædificata. Et ubera mea sicut turris, ex quo facta sum coram eo, quasi pacem reperiens, id est, Doctores habens fortissimos, ceu turres, qui & parva nutrire sciunt, & omnia maligni jacula expel- lere. Et hoc mihi accidit ex eo tempore, quo Chri- stus me reconciliavit, quia ipse pax vera, faciens u- na traq; unum. Similiter Mercerus ubera de Verbo Dei explicans; Innuit, se in doctrina & verbo Domini, quo alitur, & alios alit, stabilem esse, & divina elo- quia, quibus suos lactet, sibi esse velut turres ac pro- pugnacula, quibus invicta permaneat. Neque alia est explicatio Viti Theodorici; Solche Verheissung nimmt die Braut mit Gnaden an, und spricht: Ich bin eine Mauer, und meine Brüste sind wie Thür- me, denn das Wort lehret und wehret. Darum, die solche Wort haben, finden Friede, und haben einen gnädigen GOtt, dass auch der Teuffel und die Welt ihnen nichts kan angewinnen. Eodem redit Vina- riensium, & aliorum recentium explicatio; neque discrepant Theodoretius, Honorius, aliique Veteres. De muro ad usum non belli, sed amoris conjugalis, qui explicet, neminem me legere memini.

## 8:11
Vers. 11. A VINEYARD WAS TO THE PEACEFUL ONE IN THAT WHICH HAS PEOPLES) From the Hebrew thus: A vineyard is to Solomon in Baalhamon. That place was not far from Jerusalem. HE DELIVERED IT TO KEEPERS) He let it out to those who would diligently guard it. A MAN BRINGS FOR ITS FRUIT A THOUSAND PIECES OF SILVER) Each tenant gives a thousand shekels for the use of the vineyard.

Latin:

Vers. 11. VINEA FVIT PACIFICO IN EA, QVÆ HABET POPVLOS) Ex Hebræo sic: Vinea est Salomoni in Bahalamon. Is locus erat non longe ab Hierosolymis. TRADIDIT EAM CVSTODIBVS) Elocavit eam iis, qui eam diligenter asservarent. VIR AFFERT PRO FRVCTV EJVS MILLE AR- GENTEOS) Quisque conductor dat pro usu vineæ Siclos mille.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. MY VINEYARD IS BEFORE ME) Vineyard here, what garden was above. I do not let out my own.

He takes these things concerning Solomon literally: following Aben-Ezra, who nevertheless understands the rest, which follow, concerning the Messiah, which Grotius also wishes to be said concerning Solomon. Although indeed these things, which are in verse 11, could be understood concerning Solomon, so that the comparison of Christ's spiritual vineyard with this vineyard of Solomon might then be subjoined, as Mercer thinks; and Piscator, who wish it to be said antithetically in verse 12: My vineyard is before me, i.e., I wish to have it before me, or to reserve it for myself, not to commit it to others, or to let it out. Nevertheless, the opinion of others is to be preferred, that all these things are said concerning Christ, the sacred Solomon; since throughout the whole Canticle no one else than Christ is understood by this name, nor is there read anywhere in Scripture a vineyard of such a kind of Solomon, which is situated in Baalhamon, or concerning a place of that name. Whence Mercerus himself thinks that name was invented by Solomon to show the frequency of the Church, which is understood by this vineyard. With what rashness, therefore, does Grotius invent that Baalhamon was a place not far from Jerusalem? And whence is it certain to him that Solomon received a thousand shekels for the use of that vineyard? Since, therefore, most all Christian interpreters, as Mercerus admits, understand these things of Christ, one should not rashly depart from them: for the sense flows very well, as the Vinarienses Paraphrasts, among others, have taught. The vineyard was to Solomon, to Christ, in Baal-Hamon, in a populous place, inasmuch as the Church is gathered from all peoples. The vineyard, says Alcuin, i.e., the Catholic Church abounding in the fruit of faith, belonged to the Peacemaker, that is, to Christ, who made peace for all things in heaven and on earth, in that congregation which possessed many peoples from the whole world, not in Judea alone. With this agree Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, Just. Orgelit., Ambrose, Bede, Anselm, and others. He delivered it to the keepers, the teachers of the word, who are the keepers of the spiritual vineyard, Ezek. 3:17, Isa. 61:5, Heb. 13:17. A man brings for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver: Everyone, for the fruits which he can enjoy in the vineyard, such as the grace of God, heavenly wisdom, saving faith, peace of conscience, hope of glory, joy on account of the success and efficacy of the Word, the foretaste of the future age, the fruits of righteousness, etc., brings and pays, as if in a due and perfect census (signified by a thousand shekels), thanksgiving, praise, and celebration of the divine name, attributing all things to the heavenly Solomon, directing all things to his praise, and consecrating all his own things to his honor and glorification, because whatever of increase and successes proceeds, is to be attributed solely to His grace, merits, care, and blessing: many thousands of souls are also to be brought to this Solomon, as fruits of the vineyard to the glory of His name. Whence Christ; my vineyard, He says, is before me: I myself take care of my vineyard, and I bless the labors of my ministers. They plant and water, but I give the increase 1 Cor. 3:6. This is the voice of the Bridegroom, says Alcuin: Truly, even if I commend you to other guardians, yet I always have you in my presence, seeing and rewarding the devotion of your labor in all things. Three Fathers in Theodoret: although I have appointed some guardians of my Church, yet I am the Lord and its Bridegroom, and the zeal of the guardians rests upon my care and providence.

Verse same. A THOUSAND ARE THINE, O SOLOMON, AND TWO HUNDRED FOR THOSE WHO GUARD ITS FRUITS) In the Hebrew: A thousand for you, O Solomon, and two hundred (supply, I will give for) those who guard its fruit. I will give you much dowry money, from which you may hire ministers and guardians for the son who will be born to me. She says this after she had conceived.

A merely arbitrary, utterly unheard-of, and extremely inept gloss! There is nothing here about dowry money, of which there is neither trace nor vestige in the text, nothing about the guardians of a son: nothing about his conception. Nor did Solomon need dowry money to hire ministers and guardians for a son about to be born, he being the richest of all the Kings whom the Sun has seen. And why should the Vineyard be cared for by Solomon alone, not by the guardians, as Grotius wishes, in commerce with the Solomonic wife? What similarity or analogy is here? The Bride speaks, therefore, but a mystical one, and she speaks of the heavenly Solomon, and also of the spiritual vineyard. A thousand silver pieces are owed to the Bridegroom himself, that is, the entire yield: yet two hundred are to be granted to those who guard its fruit, because he is to expect a hundredfold remuneration in double, in this and the future life out of the mere grace of the heavenly Solomon, Matt. 19. Holy Doctors (so Alcuin's paraphrase has it) are endowed with a double remuneration, which is designated by the two hundred, by me. To Solomon (my Lord and King) belongs the (aforementioned) substance (all praise, honor, and glory). But to those guardians (who have proven themselves faithful and zealous in the spiritual work of the vineyard until the end, to them are given out of grace) two hundred. (A beautiful praise will also befall them from the mouth of their Lord, whom they have faithfully served, on the Last Day, 1 Cor. 4:5, Matt. 25:21, 23. They will have a hundredfold reward, Matt. 19:29. Twofold and doubled, Is. 61:7, that is, unspeakable joy and glory, Dan. 12:3, 1 Cor. 3:8. Luke 10:35) together with its fruits (besides that which, according to the preceding report in v. 11, they have received in this life not only as true Christians, but also as servants of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God 1 Cor. 4:1, from the mild hand of God, albeit under many crosses and persecutions Mark 10:30, 2 Cor. 4:8, 9, 10), as the Vinarian paraphrasts have explained, with whom the Osiandrian Paraphrase agrees. Those who wish to compare the yield of the Solomonic vineyard and the vineyard of Christ here with Mercer, Junius, Piscator, and the Belgian Interpreters, render this meaning: the one to whom his vineyard is let out returns a very great fruit indeed to Solomon (so that a certain number is put for an uncertain one), or he reserves some part for himself, namely two hundred shekels. But I enjoy my vineyard alone: all things redound to me. But the reasons adduced are why it is necessary to understand these things solely of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 12. VINEA MEA PENES ME EST) Vinea hic, quod hortus supra. Ego meam non eloco.

Hæc de Salomone ad literam accipit: sequutus Aben-Ezram, qui tamen cætera, quæ sequuntur, de Messia intelligit, quæ Grotius etiam de Salomone dicta vult. Quanquam vero hæc, quæ in vers. 11. ha- bentur, de Salomone intelligi possent, ut compara- tio deinde subjungatur vineæ Christi spiritualis cum ista Salomonis vinea, uti Mercerus putat; & Piscator, qui ἀντιθετικῶς v. 12. dictum volunt: Vinea mea penes me est, i. e. eam volo coram me habere, vel mihi reservare, non aliis committere, aut elocare. Præferenda tamen aliorum sententia, quod hæc o- mnia de Christo, sacro Salomone, dicta sint; siqui- dem per totum Canticum nemo alius, quam Chri- stus hoc nomine intelligatur, neque uspiam in Scri- ptura de vinea ejusmodi Salomonis legatur, quæ in Baalhamon sita, aut de loco ejus nominis. Unde Mercerus ipse putat, nomen illud confictum esse à Salomone ad ostendendam Ecclesiæ frequentiam, quæ per hanc vineam intelligitur. Qua ergo teme- ritate fingit Grotius, Baalhamon locum fuisse non longe ab Hierosolymis? Et unde constat ipsi, quod mille Siclos acceperit Salomo pro vineæ istius usu? Quum ergo plerique omnes Interpp. Christiani, fa- tente Mercero, de Christo hæc intelligant, temere non est ab iisdem recedendum: Sensus enim opti- me fluit, ut præter alios Paraphrastæ Vinarienses docuere. Vinea fuit Salomoni Christo in Baal-Ha- mon in loco populoso, siquidem ex omnibus popu- lis Ecclesia colligatur. Vinea, inquit Alcuinus, i. e. Catholica Ecclesia fructu abundans fidei, fuit Pacifi- co, id est, Christo, qui omnia pacificavit in Cœlis & in terris, in ea congregatione, quæ multos populos possedit ex toto orbe, non in Judæa solum. Cui consonant Cassiodorus, Philo Carpathius, Just. Orgelit. Ambros. Beda, Anshelmus & alii. Tradidit eam custodibus, verbi Doctoribus, qui custodes vineæ spiritualis sunt Ezech. 3, 17. Es. 61, 5. Ebr. 13, 17. Vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos: Unusquisque pro fructi- bus, quibus in vinea frui potest, quales sunt gratia Dei, sapientia cœlestis, fides salvifica, pax conscien- tiæ, spes gloriæ, gaudium, ob successum & efficaci- am Verbi, prægustus futuri seculi, fructus justi- tiæ &c. affert, ac pendit veluti in censum debitum ac perfectum (mille siclis significatum) gratiarum actio- nem, laudem & celebrationem divini nominis, Salomoni cœlesti omnia accepta referens, omnia ad laudem ejus dirigens, omnia sua ipsius honori, & glorificationi consecrans, quia quicquid pro- ventuum & successuum prodit, ipsius gratiæ, meri- tis, curæ & benedictioni tribuendum unice: adfe- renda etiam Salomoni huic multa animarum mil- lia, ceu fructus vineæ ad nominis ipsius gloriam. Vnde Christus; vinea, inquit, mea est coram me: Ego ipse curam ago vineæ meæ, & laboribus mini- strorum meorum benedico. Ipsi plantant & rigant, ego vero do incrementum 1. Corinth. 3, 6. Hæc vox Sponsi est, inquit Alcuinus: Verum etsi te aliis com- mendem custodibus, tamen te semper in mea habeo prasentia, videns & remunerans laboris tui devotio- nem in omnibus. Tres Patres apud Theodoretum: quamvis custodes aliquos Ecclesiæ meæ constituerim, tamen ego Dominus, ejusque Sponsus sum, & custo- dum studium mea nititur cura & providentia.

Vers. eod. MILLE TVI PACIFICI, ET DVCENTI HIS, QVI CVSTODIVNT FRVCTVS EJVS) In Hebræo: Mille tibi, o Salomon, & ducentos (supple, dabo ego pro) cu- stodientibus fructum ejus. Ego tibi plurimam dotalem pe- cuniam dabo, unde filio, qui mihi nascetur, ministros & cu- stodes conducas. Hæc dicit, postquam conceperat.

Mere arbitraria, inaudita prorfus, & perquam inepta Glossa! Nihil hic de pecunia dotali, cujus nec vola nec vestigium in textu, nihil de custodibus filii: nihil de ejus conceptione. Neque Salomo in- diguit dotali pecunia, ut filio nascituro ministros & custodes conduceret, ipse Regum omnium, quos Sol vidit, ditissimus. Et quid Vinea a solo Salomone, non a custodibus curandæ, uti vult Grotius, com- mercii cum uxore Salomonea? quæ similitudo hic aut analogia? Loquitur ergo Sponsa quidem, sed mystica, & de Salomone cœlesti loquitur, nec non de vinea spirituali. Mille argenteos deberi ipsi Spon- so, id est, omnem proventum: ducentos tamen custo- dientibus fructum ejus concedendum, quia centu- plam remunerationem in duplo expectare habeat, in hac & futura vita ex mera Salomonis cœlestis gratia Matth. 19. Doctores Sancti (ita habet Alcui- ni paraphrasis) duplici remuneratione, quæ ducente- nario designatur, donantur apud me. Dir Salomon (mein Herr und König) gebühren die (vorgedachte) substantz (alles Lob, Ehr und Preis) Aber denen Hütern (welche sich treu und eiferig in der geistlichen Wein-Arbeit biß ans Ende erwiesen, denen werden aus Gnaden geschencket) zweyhundert. (Es wird ihnen auch ein schönes Lob aus dem Munde ihres HErrn, dem sie treulich gedienet, am Jüngsten Ta- ge wiederfahren, 1. Cor. 4, 5. Matth. 52/21. 23. Sie werden hundertfältige Vergeltung haben, Matth. 19, 29. Zweyfältig und gedoppelt, Es. 61, 7. das ist, unaussprechliche Freude und Herrlichkeit, Dan. 12, 3. 1. Cor. 3, 8. Luc. 10, 35.) samt seinen Früchten (nebenst dem, was sie dem vorgeschehenen Bericht nach v. 11. in diesem Leben nicht allein als wahre Christen, son- dern auch als Diener Christi, und Haußhalter über GOttes Geheimniß 1. Corinth. 4, 1. aus der milden Hand GOttes, wiewohl unter vielen Creutz und Ver- folgungen Marc. 10, 30. 2. Cor. 4, 8. 9. 10. empfan- gen,) uti Paraphrastæ Vinarienses exposuere, qui- bus consonat Paraphrasis Osiandrina. Qui compa- ratum hic vineæ Salomoneæ & vineæ Christi pro- ventum volunt cum Mercero, Junio, Piscatore, In- terpp. Belgic. hunc reddunt sensum: permagnum quidem fructum reddit Salomoni is, cui vinea ejus elocata (ut numerus certus pro incerto ponatur)sea aliquam sibi reservat partem, utpote ducentenos si- clos. Sed ego vinea mea solus fruor: omnia ad me re- dundant. Sed adductæ causæ sunt, cur unice de Christo hæc intelligere oporteat.

## 8:13
Verse 13. O YOU WHO DWELL IN THE GARDENS) There is indeed a Hebrew word ending in ית, but we have said at the inscription of Ecclesiastes that such are often taken commonly. Solomon addresses the infant lying in the womb: and says that all the Jews greatly desire to hear its voice.

A wonderful and again monstrous gloss. First, the feminine gender is transformed into the masculine. Then it is imagined that Solomon is addressing an infant lying in the womb, when the Dialogism in the whole Colloquy is instituted only between the Bridegroom and the Bride, or, as others wish, also with the companions of the Bridegroom or the Bride. But where the speech was directed to an infant is nowhere found. And who, even in a fever, ever dreamed that Solomon's son lying in the womb was designated by this paraphrase, O YOU WHO DWELL IN THE GARDENS? Nor did such a thing ever come into the minds of the Rabbis themselves, the masters of ineptitudes. Furthermore, by what reason is the womb of the Solomonic wife understood by GARDENS in the plural, or even by a vineyard? For Grotius takes vineyard and garden here as the same. Add that it is not read that Pharaoh's daughter bore any son to Solomon. Finally, how do those words, THE FRIENDS LISTEN, MAKE ME HEAR YOUR VOICE, agree either with a fetus lying in the womb, or with Jews desiring its happy exit from the womb? It is manifest that the Bridegroom speaks to the Bride here; who is said to dwell in the gardens, because the gardens of the Churches are entrusted to her, and she is occupied in cultivating them with the word of the Lord, and in conferring a various kind of plants, graces, and gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Church, says Cornelius not badly, is itself the most grateful garden, and she is busy with all the Elect and each of the Elect, as if they were gardens. The Church dwells fixedly in the gardens, i.e., she is assiduously engaged in the pleasantness of the Scriptures, in cultivating the Paradises of virtues that are perpetually green, beautifully flowering, and sweetly smelling. He had already proclaimed the sweetness of her voice before; now he testifies that her companions also desire to hear it themselves. By companions, Piscator understands the remaining Persons of the Holy Trinity, the Father and the Holy Spirit; but more correctly the FRIENDS are understood as the Saints, although others wish for the Saints and Angels to be designated at the same time. So sweet (thus Mercer paraphrases) is your voice of one confessing, celebrating, and invoking the Lord and announcing the word, that even the Companions, i.e., the Angels and saints, gladly hear your voice. He calls them his companions, because he uses their work and ministry in defending or teaching the Church. Cassiodorus, Theodoret, Aponius, Bede, and Anselm also understand the Angels. This Osiandrian paraphrase is pleasing: O my dearest Spouse the Church, who indeed seemest to dwell in a valley of tears, but in reality dwellest in Paradise, on account of the internal joy and consolation of thy conscience, come, celebrate me with the confession of the Gospel, that other Churches, having heard thy confession, may be confirmed in the faith, and by thy example may set forth a pious confession of their own faith before the world, to the glory of my name and their own salvation. B. Gerhard, Postill. on Solomon, 9th Sunday after Trinity, understands by the voice the voice of the confession of our sins: the voice of devout prayer: the voice of glorification and thanksgiving: the voice of the preaching and confession of the Gospel: the voice of obedience and holy conversation. The Weimar theologians think the choir of the Apostles is addressed, and that the other faithful who are their companions are called. But the praised paraphrase seems simpler.

Latin:

Vers. 13. QVÆ HABITAS IN HORTIS) Est quidem Hebr. vox in ית desinens, sed tales sæpe communiter sumi, diximus ad inscriptionem Ecclesiastæ. Alloquitur Salomo infantem in utero latentem: dicitque, omnes Judæos valde optare, ut vocem ejus exaudiant.

Mirabilis iterum ac portentosa glossa. Primo genus fœmininum in Mascutinum transformatur. Tum fingitur, Salomonem alloqui infantem in utero latentem, cum Dialogismus in toto Colloquio Sponsi solum cum Sponsa institutus sit, aut, ut alii volunt, etiam cum Sodalibus Sponsi, vel Sponsæ. Ubi autem ad infantem directus sermo fuerit, nu- spiam invenitur. Et quis vel per febrim fomniavit unquam, Salomonis filium in utero latentem, hac paraphrasi designatum, QUÆ HABITAT IN HORTIS? Nec ipsis quidem ineptiarum Magistris Rabbinis tale quid in mentem unquam venit. Porro qua ra- tione per HORTOS in plurali uterus uxoris Salomo- neæ intelligitur, aut etiam per vineam? nam vineam & hortum hic pro eodem habet Grot. Adde, quod Pharaonis filia Salomoni nullum filium peperisse legatur. Denique quomodo illa, AUSCULTANT AMI- CI, FAC ME AUDIRE VOCEM TUAM, conveniunt vel fœtui in utero latenti, vel Judæis desiderantibus felicem ejus ex utero egressum? Sponsum ad Spon- fam hic loqui manifestum est; quæ in hortis habita- re dicitur, quia horti Ecclesiarum ipsi concrediti sunt, & in excolendis illis verbo Domini, varioque plantarum, gratiarum & donorum S. S. genere con- ferendis occupatur. Ecclesia, inquit non male Cor- nelius, Catholica & ipsa est hortus gratissimus, & omnium Electorum & singulorum Electorum, velut hortorum satagit. Ecclesia fixe habitat in hortis, i. e. assidue versatur in amœnitate Scripturarum, in ex- colendis Paradisis jugiter virentium, pulchre floren- tium, & suaviter olentium virtutum. Vocis ejus sua- vitatem jam antea prædicaverat; jam socios etiam ejusdem sese audire discupere, testatur. Per socios Piscator reliquas Personas SS. Trinitatis, Patrem & Spiritum S. intelligit; sed rectius AMICI intelligun- tur Sancti, quamvis alii Sanctos simul & Angelos de- signari velint. Tam suavis (ita παραφράζει Merc.) est vox tua confitentis, celebrantis & invocantis Do- minum ac verbum annunciantis, ut etiam Socii, An- geli scil. & sancti libenter vocem tuam audiant. So- cios suos appellat, quod eorum opera utatur, & mi- nisterio, in propugnanda vel docenda Ecclesia. An- gelos etiam Cassiodor. Theodor. Aponius, Beda, Ans- helmus intelligunt. Placet hæc Osiandrina Paraphra- sis: ô charissima mea Sponsa Ecclesia, quæ videris qui- dem habitare in valle lachrymarum, sed revera habi- tas in Paradiso, propter internam conscientiæ tuæ læ- titiam, & consolationem, age, celebra me confessione Evangelii, ut aliæ Ecclesiæ audita tua confessione in fide confirmentur, & tuo exemplo piam confessionem fidei suæ coram mundo edant, ad nominis mei gloriam, & ipsorum salutem. B. Gerhard. Postill. Salom. Do- min. 9. Trinit. per vocem intelligit vocem confes- sionis peccatorum nostrorum: vocem devotæ oratio- nis: vocem glorificationis & gratiarum actionis: vo- cem prædicationis & confessionis Evangelii: vocem obedientiæ & sanctæ conversationis. Vinarienses compellari chorum Apostolorum, eorumque so- cios cæteros fideles vocari censent. Sed laudata Paraphrasis simplicior videtur.

## 8:14
FLEE MY BELOVED) Flee quickly from the womb. Such is that: Be born, O promised name of Dardanus, to Iulus. This, forsooth, still remained for the heap of various absurdities, lest the epilogue should not correspond to the beginning and to the whole text of the Grotian commentaries. By the beloved, the BRIDEGROOM in the Canticle is noted, and not indeed the son of the Bride. And who of sound mind will admit that those words; Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of spices, are the same as flee quickly from the womb? But we do not wish here to answer a fool a word further according to his folly, mindful of the Solomonic warning. It is certain that the Church vows and prays for this. Which others declare regarding the coming of the saving incarnation; others regarding the coming of the kingdom and the propagation of the word; others regarding the coming of blessed glorification, desired and sought by the faithful. Piscator wishes the ancient Church to seek the coming into the flesh; we, however, the coming to final redemption. Regarding the propagation of the word, Osiander: O dearest Spouse, quickly divulge and most widely propagate your sweetest Gospel, so that kingdoms converted to you may offer the sweet and fragrant odor of your praises and of pious works from themselves, and show themselves grateful to you, and refresh your Church (with their good reputation). Similarly Mercerus: he desires the Lord's coming and presence to himself, knowing how grievous it is for Him to be absent from him even for a little while. Although Alcuin understands the flight as the ascension into Heaven, he nevertheless wishes the Spouse to be likened to a roe because of the frequent visitation of grace; as if he were saying openly: since, appearing in the flesh, you brought me the precepts and gifts of life, now that these are accomplished, return to the bosom of the Father, and let this be my consolation, that since I cannot behold you with continuous vision, you might at least deign to console me with frequent visitation. The Dutch Interpreters do not disapprove of this sense. Most Fathers embrace it: Cassiodorus, Philo, Justus, Beda, Bernard. Junius joins the coming of grace and glory; i.e., It is certain for me to do what you command. But do you yourself be present and grant what you command, and hasten to fulfill your promises by your glorious coming. So also the Dutch Interpreters. But it seems more appropriate to accept it as the sighing of the Church to the Spouse Christ for the hastening of the glorious coming. Because the universal Church, such as it is to be in the time of the N.T., is already introduced through the vineyard in Baalhamon, and its fruit, which the ministers of the Word, as keepers of the vineyard in the N.T. propagated throughout the whole world and all peoples, bring to the heavenly Solomon, and will bring until the end of the world, is designated. This vow and desire is made by her who dwells in the gardens, i.e., in the Churches diffused throughout the world, whose voice of preaching

Latin:

FUGE DILECTE MI) Effuge ex utero velociter. Tale illud: Nascere Dardaniæ promissum nomen Iülo. Id scil. adhuc restabat ad variarum ineptia- rum cumulum, ne non Epilogus responderet exor- dio, totique textui commentorum Grotianorum. Per dilectum SPONSUS in Cantico, non vero Sponsæ filius notatur. Et quis sanæ mentis verba illa; Fuge, dilecte mi, & assimilare capreæ hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum, idem esse, admittet, quod effuge ex utero velociter? Sed nolumus hic stulto verbum amplius respondere secundum stultitiam, memores moniti Salomonei. Certum est, quod Ecclesia hoc voveat, ac precetur. Quod alii de adventu salutiferæ incarnationis; alii de adventu regni, & propagationis verbi; alii de adventu beatæ glorificationis, à fidelibus desiderato, at- que expetito declarant. Piscator veterem Eccle- siam adventum in carnem; nos autem adventum ad finalem redemtionem expetere vult. De propagatio- ne verbi Osiander: ô Sponse charissime, celeriter divulga, & latissime propaga dulcissimum Evange- lium tuum, ut regna ad te conversa suavem & fra- grantem odorem laudum tuarum, & piorum operum de se præbeant, tibique se gratos exhibeant, & Ecclesiam tuam (bona sua fama) recreent. Similiter Mercerus: optat Domini ad se adventum & præsentiam, cogno- scens, quam grave sit, eum vel tantillum a se abesse. Alcuinus etsi fugam de adscensu in Cælum intelli- gat, assimilari tamen Capreæ vult Sponsum ob fre- quentem gratiæ visitationem; ac si aperte dicat; quo- niam in carne apparens, præcepta ac dona vitæ mihi tulisti, nunc his peractis, revertere in sinum Patris, & hoc mihi sit solatium, quod cum continua visione non queam te cernere, saltim crebra visitatione me conso- lari dignari velis. Quem sensum non improbant Belgici Interpp. Amplectuntur eum plerique Patres, Cassiodorus, Philo, Justus, Beda, Bernhardus. Junius adventum gratiæ & gloriæ conjungit; q. d. Certum est mihi facere, quod jubes. Sed tu ipse adesto & dato, quod jubes, promissaque perficere glorioso adventu tuo festinato. Sic etiam Belgæ Interpretes. Sed conve- nientius videtur accipi ut suspirium Ecclesiæ ad Spon- sum Christum ad maturandum adventum gloriosum. Quia universalis Ecclesia, qualis tempore N. T. fu- tura, jam introducta est per vineam in Baalhamon, & fructus ejus, quem ministri Verbi, ceu custodes vineæ in N. T. per totum orbem omnesq; populos propagatæ, Salomoni cœlesti ferunt, & ad finem us- que mundi laturi sunt, designatus. Votum hoc at- que desiderium ab ea fit, quæ in hortis, h. e. Ecclesiis per orbem diffusis, habitat, cujus vocem prædica-

# Lamentations

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Veteris Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. PREFACE OF GROTIUS TO THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH.

This book also must be added to the Poetic ones. For it is written in meters, which are all arranged by Alphabet, except for the last chapter: but even in the former ones there is this difference, that the first, second, and fifth chapters give single verses to single letters: the third chapter gives three. Jeremiah was very apt for treating τὰ παθητικα (the pathetic things). This is apparent both from his Prophetic writings, and from the fact that he made a lament for the death of King Josiah, as we learned in 2 Chronicles 35:24. The subject matter of these θρηνῶν (laments), as the LXX also noted in the heading, is the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the deportation carried out by Nebuchadnezzar. It should be noted, however, that in the second, third, and fourth chapters the order of the letters Phe and Ayn is inverted. For since it is customary among the Hebrews for Ayn to precede and Phe to follow, here on the contrary it happens that Phe precedes and Ayn follows: for which matter I can conjecture no other reason than that the Chaldeans used a different order than the Hebrews, just as the Arabs also arrange the order of letters differently. Therefore, in the first chapter Jeremiah speaks as a Hebrew: in the following ones, as a subject of the Chaldeans.

Latin:

I. N ANNO AD LAMEN JERE PRÆFATIO GROTIANA.

Hic quoque liber Poëticis addendus. Scriptus est enim metris, quæ & per Alphabetum digesta sunt omnia, ex- cepto ultimo capite: sed & in prioribus hæc est differentia, quod primum, secundum & quintum caput singulis literis singulos dant versus: caput tertium ternos. Valde fuit aptus ad tractanda τὰ παθητικα Jeremias. Apparet id & ex scriptis ejus Propheticis, & inde quod in Josiæ regis mortem lessum fecit, ut didicimus 2. Paralip. 35, 24. Est autem ho- rum θρηνῶν argumentum, ut & LXX. in capite annota- runt, excidium urbis Hierosolymorum & deportatio per Nabuchodonosorem facta. Notandum autem in secundo tertio & quarto capite inversum ordinem litterarum Phe & Ayn. Nam cum soleat apud Hebræos Ayn præcedere, Phe sequi, hîc contra sit ut Phe præcedat, Ayn sequatur: cujus rei non aliam conjectare possum rationem, quam quod Chal- dæi alio ordine sunt usi quam Hebræi, sicut & Arabes ali- ter digerunt litterarum ordinem. Itaque primo capite loquitur Jeremias, ut Hebræus: sequentibus, ut Chaldaeo- rum subditus.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations on the Preface of Grotius, with Other Prolegomena
OBSERVATIONS ON THE PREFACE OF GROTIUS, with other prolegomena.

of the preaching and confession of the divine name the Spouse wishes to sound perpetually; then indeed the mountains of spices are indicated κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν (pre-eminently) as the mountains of the heavenly Jerusalem, in which mere most fragrant spices, with no stench admitted, breathe. And it is consistent that this sweetest Canticle should be concluded with the sigh of desire for that most desired time of the consummation of the nuptials, which the Spouse also uses in the conclusion of the Apocalypse, chapter 22, 21. But Mercerus and the Dutch rightly note that the word for fleeing is not to be taken as to flee, but as to contend with great speed, as one who flees is accustomed to do. Cornelius admits that by the mountains of spices the hills of blessed eternity, the seats of the Angels, are understood; where all things are fragrant with incense and the perfume of praises and jubilation, to which the Church also wishes to be transferred, just as roes and fawns are accustomed to carry off their young with them, nay, without them they do not wish to snatch themselves alone from the hunters and be transferred to the mountains redolent with spices. And the Ancients also interpret this concerning the second coming of Christ, by which He will snatch the Elect with Him; Ambrose on the Good of Death, ch. 5, Theodoret, Aponius, Bernard, Sermon 9 on Psalm 'He who dwells', etc., Honorius, and others. Similarly, among the more recent, the Weimar Paraphrasts understand it concerning the high and great mountains of the heavenly Jerusalem, Apoc. 21, 10, Ps. 15, 1, Ps. 121, 1. There the mountains of separation, ch. 2, 17, must become fragrant spice-mountains, from whose refreshing scent of life all stench of sin and death will be driven away for all eternity, Apoc. 21, 4. In sum, the Spirit and the bride say, Come. He who testifies to these things says, Yes, I am coming soon, Amen, Yes come Lord Jesus! Apoc. 22, 17, 20. Which vow we also make our own, concluding this most excellent Canticle with these pious desires, the hidden mysteries of which we shall then finally understand fully when we are led to the marriage of the Lamb and shall sing that heavenly HALLELUJAH, Apoc. 19, 1 ff., thus: FLEE, MY BELOVED, AND BE LIKENED TO A ROE AND A FAWN OF THE DEER UPON THE MOUNTAINS OF SPICES. COME, LORD JESUS, AMEN! HALLELUJAH!

Latin:

AD PRÆFATIONEM GROTII OBSERVATIONES, cum aliis προλεγομένοις.

tionis & confessionis nominis divini Sponsus perpe- tuo sonare vult; tum vero montes aromatum κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν indigitantur montes cœlestis Hierosolymæ, in quibus mera aromata odoratissima, nullo fœtore admisso, spirant. Et consentaneum est, suavissimum hoc Canticum suspirio desiderii temporis illius de- sideratissimi consummationis nuptiarum concludi, quo Sponso eadem etiam in Apocalypseos conclu- sione utitur cap. 22, 21. Recte autem notant Merce- rus & Belgæ, fugiendi verbum non pro fugere, sed pro magna celeritate contendere, uti solet, qui fugit, accipi. Per montes aromatum colles beatæ æternitatis, sedes Angelorum intelligi fatetur Cornelius; ubi omnia fragrant thure & incenso laudum & jubilo- rum, quo se etiam transferri optet Ecclesia, uti so- lent capreæ & hinnuli fœtus suos secum eripere, imo sine iis nolunt se solos eripere à venatoribus, & transferre in montes aromatibus redolentes. Ac de secundo Christi adventu, quo secum rapiet Ele- ctos, interpretantur etiam Veteres; Ambrosius de bono mortis cap. 5. Theodoretus, Aponius, Bernhar- dus Serm. 9. in Psal. Qui habitat &c. Honorius, alii. Similiter è recentioribus Paraphrastæ Vinarienses intelligunt de altis & magnis montibus cœlestis Hie- rosolymæ Apoc. 21, 10. Ps. 15, 1. Ps. 121, 1. Da müssen die Scheideberg cap. 2, 17. wohlriechende Würtzber- ge werden, von derer erquickendem Lebens-Geruch, aller Sünden- uud Todes-Stanck wird in alle E- wigkeit vertrieben seyn, Apocal. 21, 4. Summa, der Geist und die Braut sprechen, komm, Es spricht, der solches zeuget, Ja, ich komme bald, Amen, Ja komm Herr JEsu! Apoc. 22, 17. 20. Quod votum etiam nostrum facimus, piis his desideriis Canticum ex- cellentissimum, cujus abscondita mysteria tum de- mum intelligemus plene, cum ad nuptias agni de- ducemur, & cœleste illud HALLELUJAH decan- tabimus, Apoc. 19, 1. seqq. ita concludentes: FUGE, DILECTE MI, ET ASSIMILARE CAPREÆ HINNULO- QUE CERVORUM SUPER MONTES AROMATUM. VE- NI, DOMINE JESU, AMEN! HALLELUIAH!

## 1:1 Introduction: N. 7. Annotations on the Lamentations of Jeremiah
N. 7. ANNOTATIONS ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH.

We must speak here first concerning the order of the Books. Grotius loves to be singular here, as he does not rarely elsewhere: neither appending the Book of Lamentations to the Prophecy of Jeremiah, which is done by Christians, and which, since he had followed the customary order throughout the rest of the whole Scripture, ought by all means to have been observed by him, nor referring it with the Jews among the five small volumes, which they call [Megillot], but establishing a new order; so that it follows the Solomonic books, and precedes the writings of the Prophets. Which is to be disapproved of in more than one way. First, because the writings of Jeremiah are thus torn apart; then, because the Lamentations are placed before the Prophecy of Jeremiah itself, and indeed even before the prophecies of Isaiah, and are eliminated from the number and class of the Prophetic writings and of the so-called Major Prophets. Finally, because he departs from the judgment and custom of all antiquity and of the Christian Church. The reason which is alleged is less cogent: namely, that this book also is to be added to the Poetical [books], inasmuch as it is written in meter. For the Doctors of the ancient Church did not value this so highly, nor did other more recent ones, that they should separate his lamentations from the volume of Jeremiah; indeed, if this were to be held a sufficient reason, why did he not also bring hither other Canticles, which he thinks were written in meter, for example the Canticle of Moses, of Hannah, and of others, torn away from their own body, or why at least did he not separate the last chapter of Habakkuk, which he likewise makes metrical, from the rest, and transfer it hither?

But whether this book was written in meter, which is the second chapter of the prolegomena, not a few doubt. Jerome indeed in Epistle 115 to Paulinus of Urbino asserted it, whom others follow, but in what the rationale of that meter consists, and its difference from other books which are confessed by all not to be poetic, no one has hitherto explained. And that it seemed incredible already in Jerome's time appears from the Preface to Job, namely, whether there are any meters in the Bible? Who indeed appeals there to Philo and Josephus, and compares sacred things with the poems of Flaccus, Pindar, and Alcaeus, but no analogy can be shown with them, and that Fr. Gomarus was in vain here with his Davidic Lyre, we have already long ago observed in the Critico Sacro, which we later discovered was noted also by Rivet and by others. Let those who invent an erratic ode, which consists not of one or another certain kind of meter, but of variously intercurrent ones, and of countless numbers, such as Ausonius does in Pindar, in biblical hymns, put forward a μέτρον ἄμετρον if they like, that is, a free poem or one ἀντικείμενον ἐν προσκειμένῳ. If, however, something analogous to meter is to be sought in the sacred Canticles, it will perhaps be found more easily in these Lamentations than indiscriminately in any Davidic Psalms, especially regarding the number of syllables observed in the verses. According to Jerome, the first two chapters and the alphabet in the Lamentations, as also the last chapter, are written in Sapphic meter, but the third chapter in Trimeter. Maldonatus in the Preface to the Commentary on Lamentations. Jeremiah thus assigns the numbers in the Lamentations in the first Alphabet; under each letter, he says, three dodecasyllabic verses are contained, but in the second alphabet three verses each are concluded under one letter, of which the first is of sixteen, the others of twelve syllables: In the third, three verses are not only placed under one letter, but also begin with the same, of which one, without the order being kept, is usually of fourteen, the others of twelve syllables: the fourth is similar to the first. Cornelius à Lapide and others follow Maldonatus. But let the reader test whether the numbers agree in all respects; I doubt that this number of syllables is found precisely in all the verses. Nor is there time or inclination to inquire curiously now. I have also spoken about the poetry of the Hebrews more fully in the Prolegomena of my separate Commentary on Genesis.

Therefore, these being dismissed, we shall investigate the subject matter: which is more useful and more necessary. And this will be for us the third chapter of the Prolegomena. Grotius, according to the title prefixed in the Edition of the LXX, constitutes the subject matter as the destruction of the city of Jerusalem and the devastation made by Nebuchadnezzar. For there is found in Greek and Latin Codices a title of this kind, or rather an opening of the book: And it came to pass, after Israel was led into captivity, and Jerusalem was desolate, Jeremiah sat weeping, and lamented with this lamentation over Jerusalem and sighing with a bitter soul and wailing, he said. But that title is very suspect, indeed it is of no authority at all. Since not only do some Greek and Latin Interpreters not report the same, concerning which Christopher à Castro in his Isagoge, as also Cornel. à Lapide: But also it is missing in the Hebrew text; or to speak more correctly, it was never added. For if it had existed in the Hebrew, this book would by no means have been named by the Hebrews from the initial word איכה. The Chaldean prefixes another title, but of the same authority: Jeremiah the Prophet and great Priest said.

But that the book was written after the destruction of the city, not a few doctors, and those of no obscure authority, deny, both among the Hebrews and among the Christians, who wish not the history of a past event to be described, but a lamentable Prophecy of a future calamity. Nor is that opinion perhaps to be disapproved, if indeed it be said that, on the occasion of the death of Josiah, when Jeremiah was singing his dirge, and foresaw by the Spirit what and how great evils were impending over Jerusalem, in order to move τὰ πάθη, he had to deplore the future calamity in these lamentations, and that they were therefore to be repeated annually among the people of God, so that the people of the Lord might be turned to repentance even by that mournful lamentation. And it could seem that the use of the Lamentations was greater then, if those evils were so graphically predicted, so mournfully deplored, and placed as it were before the eyes annually, than if they are said to have been composed after the devastation had already been completed. They would thus be twins to the Canticle of Solomon; for as in this Canticle, which excels among all Canticles, the joys are described prophetically, which for the most part were still to come, as if they had provided the matter for the poem as most present, so in the Lamentations of Lamentations, to which no equals are read, future evils are announced by a Prophetic Spirit, as if they were moving before the eyes, or had already happened, and had provided the cause for reading, and had expressed the lamentations and tears to the Prophet who was looking upon them. Which opinion is also favored by what is in 2 Chronicles 35:25.

it is held, Jeremiah lamented Josiah greatly, and all the singing men and singing women UNTO THIS DAY repeat the lamentations over Josiah, and it became as it were a law in Israel. Behold, it is reported as written in the lamentations. Where also the name קִינֹות is held, by which the present book is distinguished. And since that book of Lamentations still existed when the Paralipomena were written, which was always a constant tradition among the Hebrews that they were written by Ezra, as witnessed by Grotius in the Preface to the First Paralipomena, either it must be said that Ezra did not wish to add the book of Lamentations, which he himself indicated in the second of Chronicles, to the other Canonical books, and allowed it to perish, which is not likely, or it will have to be confessed that these Lamentations, which we now have in our hands, are the same as those which were written on the occasion of the death of Josiah. Maldonatus thinks this is also confirmed by the fact that in Lamentations 4:20 Jeremiah complains: The breath of our nostrils, the Lord Christ, was taken in our sins, to whom we said, in your shadow we shall live among the nations. For the Hebrews interpret this concerning the death of Josiah (although others explain this more correctly as referring to the captivity of Zedekiah, and wish for it to be predicted here, and the complaint in chapter 5:16, The crown of our head has fallen, woe to us, because we have sinned, seems to be more relevant to this). Josephus certainly in Antiquities book 10, chapter 6, seems to hint at this opinion, as do Jerome in Zechariah 12 and in the preface to Lamentations, and also the Chaldean Paraphrast in chapter 1:18, and Tarnovius in the prolegomena to his commentary does not think it improbable. since it is expressly stated (so B. Tarnovius has it on p. 4) that those Lamentations exist today, and it is also likely that such artifice was employed in their composition so that they might endure all the better for posterity: and that there is no need to assert, without necessity and a certain foundation, that two lamentations were written by Jeremiah: the former concerning the death of Josiah, which has perished; the latter concerning the destruction of Jerusalem and Judea, which is this one that exists. This is also the opinion of Rabanus, Maldonatus, Junius and Tremellius, and among our own, B. D. Quistorpius: although other interpreters believe the Lamentations were written after the destruction of Jerusalem, whom Cornelius à Lapide follows in his prolegomena, as well as Menochius and Tirinus; while others, with Origen and Eusebius, interpret them as referring to the evils brought about by the captivity of Jeconiah.

In this disagreement of opinions, Grotius ought not to have assumed so simply, as if it were undoubted, that the argument is the destruction of the city and the deportation carried out by Nebuchadnezzar, and that these things are described historically as having happened: But that had to be proven, since it is established that it is denied by others. For that Pythagorean αὐτὸς ἔφα does not hold here. Junius and Tremellius assign such an argument: The Book of Lamentations contains mournful complaints about the miserable state of the Jews from the time of the death of King Josiah, by which, as the beginning of all calamities, Jeremiah was led to lament the present and impending miseries of the Church and the whole Kingdom. Wherefore he complains, both in his own name and in the name of all the pious, about the most grievous evils received, confesses public and private sins, calls everyone to repentance, faith, and prayer, deprecates the wrath of God, seeks grace, and implores mercy according to the covenant. And in the notes they have it thus: Although this book of lamentations does not lament only one calamity of the Jews, but multiple ones, which have arisen from time to time since the days of Josiah until the destruction of the whole kingdom and almost the people, there is no doubt, however (as is the author Ezra 2 Chron. 35, 25), that it was written by the Prophet on the occasion of the death of Josiah, and delivered to the Church. For when the Prophet (who had previously heard prophecies about the destruction of the kingdom, and had himself prophesied through the mercy of the revelations of God) saw Josiah killed by Necho, and consequently the kingdom slipping into reliance on the King of the Egyptians, as sacred history shows, he wrote a lament from these beginnings of most grievous evils, in which he comprehended both present matters and others that were to follow: so that the Church, having been forewarned, might then repent, or at least the future remnants of the Church of God might be more confirmed in the faith and truth of God after that, might confess their sins, renounce themselves, approach God chastely, proclaim his justice, and implore mercy. By such a vivid representation, the people could certainly be moved more vehemently to repentance: nor does the Prophet seem to have had the convenience of composing the threnody after the city was destroyed, since he was an exile in Egypt, and the threnodies were always annexed to the Prophets, as containing prophecy, and did not constitute a separate volume in antiquity.

However, this could raise a doubt, that in the Threnodies the lamentation is not instituted only about the death of Josiah, ch. 5, but also about the captivity of Zedekiah, who was carried away long after, with other Kings intervening, ch. 4. And B. Hülsemann judges it more likely that the Threnodies were written during the very siege of the city, alleging to that effect also Athanasius in the Synopsis, Epiphanius in the Life of Jeremiah, and B. Luther. That is certainly not to be conceded to Hugo the Cardinal and Dionysius the Carthusian, that these lamentations concern nothing other than the death of Josiah: since reading alone teaches the contrary; nor do R. Solomon, Lyranus, Isidorus, Vatablus, Sixtus Senensis, Menochius, and Trinus deserve any assent in that, that this book is the one which King Jehoiakim burned, Jer. 36, 32.

The fourth and last thing, which must be premised from the occasion of the Grotian preface, concerns the alphabetical series in the second, third, and fourth chapters. For since the order of the letters Pe and Ayin is inverted there, and Pe precedes, Grotius gives this reason by conjecture, that the Chaldeans used a different order than the Hebrews, just as the Arabs also stated the order of the letters differently, and thus in the first chapter Jeremiah speaks as a Hebrew, in the following ones as a subject of the Chaldeans. Which would not be inelegant, if that conjecture could be confirmed from the order of the Chaldean Alphabet. Which, however, seems little probable for the very reason that the Chaldeans, retaining all and only the Hebrew letters, recount all the others in the same order as the Hebrews. Hence the reason for this is far different from that of the Arabic language. For this has a very different alphabet. It is enough that there was a peculiar reason for the Holy Spirit, both that an acrostic, and a varied one, was observed, and that the order of these letters was varied, even if we do not know it, and we willingly profess our ignorance. To wish not to know certain things in such matters, which the best Master wished us not to know, is learned ignorance.

The book of Threnodies can be divided into a Lamentation and a Prayer: The former is held in the first four chapters, the latter in the last, the fifth. The Lamentation deplores first, under the form of a mourning widow, both the bereavement of Jerusalem, ch. I, and the calamity of the whole Jewish land, ch. II. Then, under the person of an afflicted man, it deplores the evils sent in, ch. III, and specifically laments the devastation of the sanctuary, the horrible famine, the unexpected occupation of the city, and the abduction of the King, ch. IV. Finally, in ch. V, by a prayer, it presents to God the misery of the prophet and the people, and seeks their restoration.

Latin:

N. 7. OTATA ITATIONES EMIÆ.

DIcendum hic primum de ordine Li- brorum. Grotius singularis hic esse amat, ut alias non raro: Librum Thre- norum neque Prophetiæ Jeremiæ sub- jungens, quod à Christianis fit, & ab ipso, quum de cætero per totam Scripturam sequutus fuerit usi- tatum ordinem, observandum omnino erat, neque cum Judæis inter volumina quinque parva, quæ vo- cant, referens, sed novum ordinem constituens; Ut Salomoneos libros sequatur, & scripta Propheta- rum antecedat. Quod non uno modo improban- dum. Primo quod discerpantur ita scripta Jeremiæ; Tum quod Threni ante ipsam Prophetiam Jeremiæ, imo etiam ante Esaiæ vaticinia præfigantur, & è numero ac classe Scriptorum Propheticorum ac Prophetarum majorum, qui vocantur, eliminentur. Deniq; quod a totius antiquitatis, & Ecclesiæ Chri- stianæ judicio, & consuetudine discedatur. Ratio, quæ prætexitur, minus prægnans est: Quod nem- pe hic liber quoque Poeticis addendus, utpote me- tris scriptus. Non enim hoc tanti fecere Veteres Ec- clesiæ Dd. non alii recentiores, ut a volumine Jere- miæ lamentationes ejus sequestrarent, imo si hæc ratio sufficiens habenda, cur non etiam alia Canti- ca, quæ metro scripta putat, verbi gratia Mosis Can- ticum, Hannæ, & aliorum a corpore suo avulsa huc retulit, aut cur saltem non caput ultimum Habacuc, quod pariter metricum facit, a reliquis separavit, & huc transtulit?

Sed an metro scriptus hic liber sit, quod alterum est τῶν προλεγομένων caput, non pauci dubitant. Hie- ronymus sane Epist. 115. ad Paul. Urb. id asseruit, quem sequuntur alii, sed in quonam metri istius ratio, & ab aliis libris, quos non esse Poeticos apud omnes in confesso est, differentia sita sit, nemo hactenus explicavit. Et incredibile id Hieronymi tempore jam visum fuisse apparet ex Præfat. in Job. anne nempe ulla in Bibliis sint metra? Qui ad Philonem quidem & Josephum ibi provocat, & cum Flacci, Pindari, & Alcæi carminibus sacra comparat, sed cum illis nul- la ostendi potest Analogia, & frustra hic fuisse Fr. Go- marum cum Lyra sua Davidica, jam pridem in Criti- co sacro observavimus, quod à Riveto etiam & ab aliis notatum postea deprehendimus. Qui oden errati- cam, quæ non uno aut altero, certo metrorum genere, sed ex varie intercurrentibus constet, & numeris in- numeris, quales Ausonius in Pindaro, in hymnis Bi- blicis fingunt, μέτρον ἄμετρον si lubet, simul ponant, h. e. carmen solutum vel ἀντικείμενον ἐν προσκειμένῳ. Si tamen aliquid metro analogum in Canticis sacris quærendum, facilius fortassis in Threnis hisce, quam promiscue in Psalmis quibusvis Davidicis invenietur, maxime quoad Syllabarum numerum in versibus observatum. Secundum Hieronymum duo prima capita & alphabeti in Threnis, ut & ultimum caput scripta sunt sapphico metro, tertium autem caput Trimetro. Maldonatus in Præf. Comment. in La- ment. Jerem. ita numeros in Threnis assignat in pri- mo Alphabeto; sub singulis, inquit, literis terni do- decasyllabi versus continentur, in secundo autem alpha- beto terni quique versus sub una litera concluduntur, quorum primus sexdecim, reliqui duodecim syllabarum sunt: In tertio terni versus non solum sub una litera po- nuntur, sed etiam ab eadem inchoantur, quorum unus non servato ordine quatuordecim, alii duodecim syl- labarum esse solent: quartum simile est primo. Mal- donatum sequuntur Cornelius à Lapide & alii. Pe- riclitetur autem lector, an numeri per omnia con- sentiant, ego hunc syllabarum numerum, præcise in versibus omnibus inveniri, ambigo. Neque vacat aut lubet nunc inquirere curiose. Dixi etiam de Poesi Ebræorum fusius in Prolegomen. Com- mentarii peculiaris in Genesin.

Proinde missis hisce, argumentum indagabi- mus: quod utilius, magisq; necessarium. Atque hoc tertium nobis erit τῶν Προλεγομένων caput. Argu- mentum vero constituit Grotius juxta titulum in E- ditione LXX. præfixum excidium urbis Hierosolymio- rum & devastationem per Nabuchodonosorem factam. Reperitur enim in Græcis & Latinis Codicibus ejus- modi titulus, vel potius ingressus libri: Et factum est, postquam in captivitatem redactus est Israel, & Jerusalem deserta est, sedit Jeremias flens, & planxit lamentatione hac in Jerusalem & amaro animo suspi- rans & ejulans dixit. Sed titulus ille valde suspe- ctus, imo nullius plane autoritatis est. Siquidem non modo Græci & Latini Interpretes nonnulli eundem haud referant, de quo Christophorus à Ca- stro in Isagog. ut & Cornel. à Lapide: Sed etiam in Ebræo textu is desideretur; vel ut rectius dicam, nunquam additus fuerit. Nam si in Ebræo exti- tisset, liber hic nequaquam ab initiali voce איכה nominatus Ebræis fuisset. Chaldæus alium titulum præmittit, sed ejusdem autoritatis: Dixit Jeremias Propheta & Sacerdos magnus.

Scriptum autem esse librum post excidium ur- bis, non pauci, nec obscuræ auctoritatis Doctores negant, cum inter Ebræos, tum inter Christianos, qui non rei præteritæ historiam, sed futuræ calamitatis lamentabilem Prophetiam describi volunt. Neque improbanda fortassis illa sententia, si nempe dica- tur, quod occasione mortis Josiæ, quum lessum ejus cantaret Jeremias, & Spiritu prævideret, quæ & quanta mala imminerent Hierosolymæ, ut τὰ πάθη moveret, threnis hisce calamitatem futuram de- plorare debuerit, illique ideo quotannis in populo Dei repetendi fuerint, ut vel lugubri illa lamenta- tione ad pœnitentiam flecteretur populus Domini. Et videri posset, majorem ita usum fuisse Threno- rum, tum, si προφητικῶς illa mala tam graphice præ- dicta, tam lugubriter deplorata, & quotannis velut ob oculos posita fuerint, quam si peracta jam deva- statione concinnati dicantur. Gemini sic forent Cantico Salomonis; Ut enim in hoc Cantico, quod inter omnia Cantica eminet, prophetice gaudia de- scribuntur, quæ maximam partem adhuc futura e- rant, ac si præsentissima materiam carmini præbuis- sent, ita Prophetico Spiritu prænunciantur in Thre- nis Threnorum, quibus pariles non leguntur, mala futura, ac si ob oculos versarentur, aut jam evenis- sent, ac legendi causam subministrassent, Threnos- que ac lachrymas Prophetæ inspectanti expressif- sent. Cui sententiæ etiam favet, quod 2. Chron. 35, 25.

habetur, Jeremias maxime luxit Josiam, cujus omnes Cantores, atq́; Cantatrices usque IN PRÆSENTEM DIEM lamentationes super Josiam replicant, & qua- si lex obtinuit in Israel. Ecce scriptum fertur in lamen- tationibus. Ubi etiam nomen קִינֹות habetur, quo liber præsens insignitur. Et quum liber ille Lamen- tationum tum adhuc extiterit, cum Paralipomena conscriberentur, quæ ab Esdra scripta, constans semper fuit apud Ebræos fama, teste Grotio Præfat. ad Prior. Paralip. aut dicendum, quod Esdras librum Lamentationum, quem ipse indigitavit in secundo Chronicorum, noluerit Canonicis cæteris adjun- gere, ac interire passus sit, quod verisimile non est, aut fateri oportebit, quod hi Threni, quos nunc sub manibus habemus, iidem sint, qui mortis Josiæ oc- casione scripti sunt. Quod confirmari etiam inde putat Maldonatus, quod Thren. 4, 20. queratur Je- remias: Spiritus oris nostri Dominus Christus captus est in peccatis nostris, cui diximus, in umbra tua vi- vimus in gentibus. Id enim de Josiæ morte Hebræi ac- cipiunt, (quanquam hoc alii de captivitate Sedeciæ rectius explicent, eamque hic prædictam velint, ac magis huc facere videatur quærela cap. 5, 16. Cecidit corona capitis nostri, væ nobis, quia peccavimus) Jo- sephus certe lib. 10. Antiqu. c. 6. innuere hanc sen- tentiam videtur, ut & Hieron. in Zach. 12. & Procœm. in Threnos, nec non Chaldæus Paraphrastes in cap. 1, 18. neque improbabilem eam esse putat Tarnov. in Prolegom. comment. cum expresse (sic habet B. Tarnovius p. 4.) dicatur, quod extent illi Threni ho- die, etiamque sit verisimile, propterea adhibitum esse tantum in compositione artificium, ut tanto melius du- rarent ad posteros: quodque ita opus non sit, ut citra necessitatem & fundamentum certum asseramus, fu- isse duas lamentationes à Jeremia conscriptas: prio- rem super mortem Josiæ, quæ perierit: posteriorem super excidio Hierosolymæ & Judææ, quæ sit hæc, quæ extat. Quæ etiam Rabani, Maldonati, Junii & Tre- mellii, & è nostris B. D. Quistorpii est sententia: Tametsi alii Interpp. credant post excidium Hiero- solymitatum Threnos conscriptos esse, quos sequitur Cornel. à Lapide in prolegom. Menochius, Tirinus: alii vero de malis per captivitatem Jechoniæ illatis accipiant cum Origene, & Eusebio.

In hoc sententiarum divortio non ita simplici- ter quasi indubitato certum debuit Grotius assu- mere, quod argumentum sit excidium urbis & de- portatio per Nebucadnezarem facta, & quod ea ut fa- cta historice describantur: Sed probandum id erat, quum ab aliis negari constet. Non enim hic valet illud Pythagoricum αὐτὸς ἔφα. Junius & Tremellius argumentum tale assignant: Liber Lamentationum querimonias lugubres continet de miserabili Judæo- rum statu inde a morte Josiæ Regis, quo tanquam ca- lamitatum omnium primordio Jirmeja adductus est ad deflendum præsentes, & instantes Ecclesiæ Regnique totius miserias. Quapropter ipse tum suo, tum piorum omnium nomine conqueritur de malis gravissimis ac- ceptis, peccata publica privataque confitetur, omnes ad resipiscentiam, fidem & orationem revocat, iram Dei deprecatur, gratiam petit, & misericordiam im- plorat ex fœdere. Et in notis ita habent: Etsi hic la- mentationum liber non unam tantum calamitatem Judæorum deflet, sed multiplices, quæ inde à Joschijæ temporibus coortæ sunt subinde usque ad excidium to- tius regni, ac ferme populi, non dubium est tamen (ut auctor est Hezra 2. Chron. 35, 25.) quin occasione mor- tis Joschijæ à Propheta fuerit conscriptus, & Ecclesiæ traditus. Nam quum vidit Propheta (qui prius Pro- phetias de excidio regni audiverat, & ipse propheta- verat per misericordiam revelationes Dei) Joschija à Necone occisum, ac proinde regnum delabi in fidu- ciam Regis Ægyptiorum, ut historia sacra ostendit, ex istis malorum gravissimorum primordiis lamentum conscripsit, quo tum res præsentes, tum etiam successu- ras alias comprehendit: ut præmonita Ecclesia tunc resipisceret, aut saltim futuræ Ecclesiæ Dei reliquiæ post istum in fide & veritate Dei magis confirmaren- tur, peccata confiterentur, sibi renunciarent, Deum castè accederent, justitiam ejus prædicarent, & implo- rarent misericordiam. Viva certe ejusmodi ὑποτυ- πώσει vehementius commoveri poterat populus ad pœnitentiam: neque post urbem excisam videtur commoditatem habuisse Propheta threnodiam concinnandi, cum in Ægypto exularet, & annexi semper fuere threni Prophetis, ceu prophetiam continentes, neque peculiare volumen constitue- runt in antiquitate.

Id tamen dubium movere posset, quod in Thre- nis non de Josiæ tantum morte lamentatio institua- tur c. 5. sed etiam de captivitate Zedekiæ, qui mul- to post, aliisq; intervenientibus Regibus abductus est, c. 4. & verosimilius censet B. Hülsemann. Thre- nos ipsa obsidione urbis conscriptos esse, allegans in eam sententiam etiam Athanasium in Synopsi, Epiphan. in Vit. Jerem. & B. Lutherum. Id utique minime concedendum Hugoni Cardin. & Diony- sio Carthuf. quod lamentationes hæ nihil aliud quam Josiæ mortem concernant: cum contrari- um sola lectio doceat; nec in eo assensum ullum merentur R. Salomo, Lyranus, Isidorus, Vatablus, Sixtus Senens. Menoch. Trinus, quod liber hic ille sit, quem Rex Jojakim combussit Jer. 36, 32.

Quartum & ultimum, quod ex occasione præ- faminis Grotiani præmittendum, concernit alpha- beticam seriem, in secundo, tertio & quarto capite Quum enim ibi inversus ordo literarum Phe & Ajn sit, ac Phe præcedat, rationem conjectando han dat Grotius, quod Chaldæi alio ordine sint usi, quam Hœbræi, sicut & Arabes aliter dixerunt ordinem lite- rarum, adeoque primo cap. loquatur Jeremias ut He bræus, sequentibus ut Chaldæorum subditus. Quæ no inconcinna esset, si conjectura illa firmari poslit d ordine Chaldaici Alphabeti. Quæ vero vel ideo pa rum probabilis videtur, quod Chaldæi Ebræas lite ras omnes & solas retinentes, cæteras omnes parit ordine recenseant cum Ebræis. Inde longe alia hu- jus, quam Arabicæ linguæ est ratio. Hæc enim al- phabetum maxime diversum habet. Satis est, pecu- liarem fuisse Spiritui S. rationem, tum quod Acro- stichis, eaque varia observata, tum quod harum li- terarum ordo variatus sit, utut eam nesciamus, & ignorantiam nostram ultro profiteamur. Nescire quædam velle in talibus, quæ Magister optimus nesci- re nos voluit, erudita est inscitia.

Dispesci potest Threnorum liber in Lamenta- tionem, & Orationem: Illa prioribus quatuor Capp. hæc postremo Quinto habetur. Lamentatio deplorat primum sub forma viduæ lugentis tum orbitatem Hierosolymæ cap. I. tum totius terræ Judaicæ calamitatem cap. II. Deinde sub persona viri afflicti mala immissa deplorat cap. III. ac spe- ciatim sanctuarii devastationem, famem horren- dam, insperatam urbis occupationem, & Regis ab- ductionem deflet cap. IV. Tandem cap. V. oratio- ne sistit Deo Prophetæ miseriam populi, ejusque reductionem petit.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

Jerusalem, once a Queen, now a widow weeping, a servant, despised, miserable, carried away into captivity with her children, acknowledges her disobedience, complains about the malice of her enemies.

Vers. 1. HOW DOTH THE CITY SIT SOLITARY) A coin made in similar times, that is, of Vespasian, responds to this description, where Judea sits weeping under a palm tree, in the form of a captive.

The word 'solitary' denotes not only deserted by allies, but desolate and abandoned: and extreme solitude and devastation is opposed to the former frequency. Cf. Jer. 18, 16. ch. 19, 8.

PRINCEPS PROVINCIARUM) That city which had ruled over the Ammonites, Moabites, and others.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

Hierosolyma olim Regina jam vidua plorans, ser- va, contemta, miserabilis, cum liberis in ca- ptivitatem abducta, agnoscit suam inobedi- entiam, queritur de hostium malitia.

Vers. 1. QVOMODO SEDET SOLA ILLA URBS) Respondet huic descriptioni nummus temporibus factus similibus, id est, Vespasiani, ubi Judæa sedet plorans sub pal- ma, in forma captivæ.

VOx sola non desertam tantum a sociis, sed de- solatam, & dereliCtam notat: & opponitur pristinæ frequentiæ summa solitudo, & vastitas. Conf. Jer. 18, 16. c. 19, 8.

PRINCEPS PROVINCIARUM) Illa urbs quæ Ammo- nitis, Moabitis, aliisque imperaverat.

Vers. 2. OMNES AMICI EJUS SPREVERVNT EAM) As the Idumeans. See Ps. 137, 7, and what is said there.

Vers. 5.

FACTI SUNT HOSTES EJUS IN CAPITE] Deuter. 28, 45.

Vers. 5.

FACTI SUNT HOSTES EJUS IN CAPITE] Deuter. 28, 45.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. RECORDATA EST) She remembers.

DIERUM AFFLICTIONIS SVÆ) Which she now suffers.

ET PRÆVARICATIONIS) Which is the cause of the evils.

DESIDERABILIUM SUORUM) One must supply here &, that is, she compares the times of her happiness with these times.

CUM CADERET) You may rightly translate it now, while the people falls &c.

THE ENEMIES SAW HER, AND MOCKED HER SABBATHS) As Agatharchides in his former book against Apion, where he calls it a worthless custom: Seneca in Augustine, City of God, book 6, chapter 2, who says that the seventh part of life is lost by resting: Plutarch on superstition, and Rutilius in his Itinerary. It is truly a wonder that they did not understand how great the utility was of having certain assemblies for teaching true piety, when elsewhere there were temples without any instruction, and schools without any piety.

Grotius, with Rabbi Solomon, understands this as the Sabbaths of sanctification and of rest sacred to God, which were a mockery to the Gentiles. But others understand it as sorrowful Sabbaths, or of cessation in a hostile land: where the temple, altars, prophets, the worship of God, and other things ceased and were lacking to the people. Thus the Chaldean renders it משבתה, of its cessation, namely that all its goods ceased, by which it had previously excelled over other peoples. Similarly Tremellius and Junius; that all that beauty which was named before had ceased, namely the princes and all desirable things.

The Vulgate translation, however, which B. Luther also retained, can be kept. But that they did not mock them for the sake of the rest sacred to God, but because of the miserably sad and mournful celebration of the Sabbaths in captivity. For the celebration of the Sabbath or the seventh day was so far from being a laughingstock to the Chaldeans or to most other nations, that they imitated the custom everywhere, as Josephus testifies in book 2 against Apion, that there is no Greek city, no barbarian one, to which the custom of the seventh day, on which the Jews rest, has not reached. And Philo concerning the seventh day affirms: ἑορτὴ γὰρ ἐστὶν οὐ μιᾶς πόλεως ἢ χώρας ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ τοῦ παντὸς. For it is a feast day not for one city or region, but for the universe. Theophilus of Antioch in book 2 to Autolycus: περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης ἡμέρας ἣν πάντες ἄνθρωποι ὀνομάζουσι. Concerning the seventh day, which all men celebrate. Clement of Alexandria brings forward from Hesiod in Stromata 5: ἕβδομον ἱερὸν ἦμαρ. The seventh day is holy, and other similar things from Homer and Callimachus.

Latin:

Vers. 7. RECORDATA EST) Recordatur.

DIERUM AFFLICTIONIS SVÆ) Quam nunc patitur.

ET PRÆVARICATIONIS) Quæ causa malorum.

DESIDERABILIUM SUORUM) Supplendum hic &:, id est, simul tempora felicitatis suæ cum his temporibus comparat.

CUM CADERET) Vertas recte nunc, dum cadit po- pulus &c.

VIDERUNT EAM HOSTES, ET DERISERUNT SAB- BATA EJUS) Ut Agatharchides libro priore contra Ap- pionem, ubi vocat φαῦλον ἐθισμόν: Seneca apud Augusti- num de Civitate Dei lib. 6. cap. 2. qui septimam partem sie ait perdi vacando: Plutarchus de superstitione, & Rutilius in Itinerario. Mirum vero non intellexisse eos quantæ es- set utilitatis aliquos esse conventus ad docendam veram pie- tatem, cum alibi Templa essent sine ulla institutione, scholæ sine ulla pietate.

Intelligit Grotius cum R. Salomone de Sabba- this sanctificationis, & quietis Deo sacris, quæ derisui fuerunt gentilibus. Sed alii tristia Sabbatha, vel cessa- tionis in terra hostili intelligunt: ubi cessabant & deerant populo templum, altaria, Prophetæ cultus Dei & alia. Sic Chaldæus משבתה reddit, cessatio- nis ejus, quod nempe omnia ejus bona cessarent, quibus præ aliis populis antea eminuerant. Simi- liter Tremellius & Junius; cessasse totum decorem il- lum, qui nominatus est ante, nempe principes & omnes res desiderabiles.

Retineri tamen potest Vulgata interpretati quam etiam B. Lutherus retinuit. Sed ut non qu dem ob quietem Deo sacram, verum ob miserabile tristem & luctuosam Sabbatorum celebrationem captivitate ipsis illuserint. Nam Sabbati vel septim diei celebratio adeo non fuit Chaldæis, aut aliis e am gentibus plerisque deridiculo, ut morem imit passim sint, uti testatur Josephus lib. 2. contra Ap nullam esse urbem Græcam, nullam barbaram, qua non pervenerit mos septimæ diei, qua Judæi feriantu Et Philo de die septima affirmat: ἑορτὴ γὰρ ἐ μια πόλεως ἡ χώρας ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τῶ παντὸς. Est enim f stus dies non uni Urbi, aut Regioni, sed universo. The philus Antiochenus lib. 2. ad Autol. περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμ ἡμέρας ἣν πάντες ἄνθρωποι ὀνομάζεσι. De septim die, quam omnes homines celebrant. Clemens Al xandr. adfert ex Hesiodo Stromat. 5. ἕβδομον ἱερ ἡμῶν. Lux septima sancta, & alia his similia ex H mero & Callimacho.

IPSA AVTEM GEMENS CONVERSA EST RE TRORSVM) Vt solent feminæ verecundæ.

## 1:9
HER FILTH IS IN HER FEET. The Hebrew has: in her fringes. That is, her discharge flows from everywhere and gives itself to be seen. He persists in the comparison.

Others explain it concerning the filth of sins, with the Chaldean and Aben-Ezra, which appeared from afar and as if on the edges of her garments. It is added: She did not remember her latter end, i.e., what kind of outcome her sins would have, as the Chaldean, Hugo, Isidore, Vatablus, Luther, and others explain.

SEE, O LORD, MY AFFLICTION. He says that 'me' is to be supplied here, as often elsewhere. So also below in chapter 2.

Latin:

SORDES EJVS IN PEDIBVS EJVS) In fimbriis ejus habet Hebræum. Id est, undequaque manat, & conspici se dat profluvium ejus, Perstat in comparatione.

Alii de peccatorum sordibus exponunt cum Chald. & Aben-Ezr. quæ eminus, & quasi in oris vestium apparuerint. Additur: Posteriorum suorum non est recordata, i. e. qualem eventum habitura es sent peccata, ut Chald. Hugo, Isidorus, Vatabl. Luth. & alii explicant.

VIDE DOMINE AFFLICTIONEM MEAM) Sup- plendum hic ait, ut sæpe alibi. Sic & infra c. 2.

Verse 10. THE ENEMY HAS STRETCHED OUT HIS HAND TO ALL HER DESIRABLE THINGS. That is, to the offerings of the Temple.

BECAUSE SHE SAW THE GENTILES ENTER HER SANCTUARY. She was forced to see it.

OF WHOM YOU HAD COMMANDED THAT THEY SHOULD NOT ENTER INTO YOUR CHURCH. Who did not even have the right of marriage with us. See what is said in Deuteronomy 23:1.

QVIA VIDIT GENTES INGRESSAS SANCTVA RIVM SVVM) Coacta videre fuit.

DE QVIBVS PRÆCEPERAS NE INTRARENT IN ECCLESIAM TVAM] Qui nec connubii jus nobiscum ha- bebant. Vide quæ dicta Deut. 23, 1.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. O ALL YOU) לוא is not always of one entreating, but often of one wishing, as appears in Genesis 17:18.

Some, with Vatablus and Piscator, translate by way of deprecation; may this great evil not reach you, God forbid: Grotius seems to think that לוא should be read as 'would that, O all you, you would perceive my vows!' But thus it would not be אליכם, but rather אתם, as Tarnovius observes, who therefore thinks לוא is said for הלוא: 'It is nothing to you, O travelers!' And thus also Junius.

HE HAS VINTAGED ME) In Hebrew: He has afflicted me with pain.

Latin:

Vers. 12. O VOS OMNES) לוא non semper est depre- cantis, sed sæpe optantis, ut apparet Genes. 17, 18.

Nonnulli cum Vatablo, Piscat. vertunt per mo- dum deprecationis; ne ad vos pertingat hoc tantum malum, Deus prohibeat: Grotius putare videtur, legendum esse לוא utinam ô vos omnes percipiatis vota mea! Sed ita non esset אליכם, verum אתם, ut observat Tarn. qui proinde לוא pro הלוא dictum pu- tat: Nihil ad vos, ô Viatores! Atque sic etiam Junius.

VINDEMIAVIT ME) In Hebr. Dolore me affecit.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. FROM ON HIGH) From heaven, as the Chaldean has it here. For the Assyrian is the rod of God's fury.

Vers. 13. DE EXCELSO) E cœlo, ut hic habet Chal- dæus. Nam Assyrius virga furoris Dei.

## 1:14
Vers. 14. HE HAS WATCHED THE YOKE) He reads with a right-hand dot. But in the Hebrew text which we use, it is better with a left-hand dot, so that the sense is, the yoke is impressed.

The Vulgate is rightly corrected from the Hebrew. Which Grotius ought always to have observed. The word נשקד is among the hapax legomena, and as Aben-Ezra says, such a word that in the Bible has neither father nor mother: according to Avenarius in his Lexicon, it signifies, it is impressed into the skin like a stigma, as a point is fixed into flesh: and it has an affinity with נקד, he pointed. B. Luther followed the Greeks and Latins: whom it is not necessary to say read otherwise; since they could have expressed the sense (as is often done) even if they did not render the word itself word-for-word. For when the yoke of sins is firmly impressed by the hand of a punishing God, and fixed like a stigma, it will rightly be called 'watched,' and you will have significantly expressed the thing itself: 'My heavy sins are awakened through his punishment.'

THEY ARE WRAPPED TOGETHER) Twisted like ropes, which press heavily upon the neck.

Latin:

Vers. 14. VIGILAVIT JVGV M) Legit Schin dextratum. At in textu Hebræo, quo utimur, melius est sinistratum, ut sensus sit, impressum est jugum.

Recte corrigitur Vulgata ex Hebræo. Quod semper observare debuisset Grotius. Vox נשקד est ἐκ τῶν ἅπαξ λεγομένων, & ut Aben-Esdra ait, tale ver- bum, quod in Bibliis nec Patrem nec Matrem habet: secundum Avenarium in Lexic. significat, impressus est in cutem tanquam stigma, ceu punctum carni infigitur: & affinitatem habet cum נקד punctavit. Græcos & Latinos sequutus est B. Lutherus: quos non neces- sum est dicamus aliter legisse; quum sensum po- tuerint exprimere (ut sæpius factum) etsi non κατὰ πόδα verbum ipsum reddiderint. Quum enim jugum peccatorum manu Dei punientis im- primitur firmiter, & ceu stigma infigitur, recte di- cetur xeris, & fignificanter rem ipsam ita expresseris: Meine schwere Sünden sind durch seine Straff er- wachet.

CONVOLVTÆ SVNT) Contortæ ut funes, qui gravi- ter colli infidunt.
