VT CONTERERET ELECTOS MEOS) Juvenes.

TORCVLAR CALCAVIT DOMINVS VIRGINI FILIÆ JVDÆ) Id est, expressit ei sanguinem, ut vinum so- let exprimi in torculari.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. MY BELLY IS TROUBLED) In Hebrew: My bowels are troubled.

WITHOUT THE SWORD BEREAVETH, AND AT HOME THERE IS DEATH LIKE UNTO IT) As it were death, that is, famine is in the city: a description of the time in which the city of Jerusalem was besieged, 2 Kings 25:3, Jeremiah 52:6, wherefore these things will be more correctly translated in the past tense.

Latin:

Vers. 20. CONTVRBATVS EST VENTER MEVS) In Hebræo: Viscera mea conturbata sunt.

FORIS INTERFICIT GLADIVS, ET DOMI MORS SIMILIS EST) Quasi mors, id est, fames est in urbe: de- scriptio temporis ejus, quo obsessa fuit urbs Hierosolyma 2. Reg. 25, 3. Jerem. 52, 6. quare rectius hæc per præteritum vertentur.

## 1:21
Vers. 21. THEY HAVE REJOICED: FOR THOU HAST DONE IT) Here כי is more correctly translated as 'but': as if he were to say: thy judgments must be borne by me.

THOU HAST BROUGHT THE DAY OF CONSOLATION) Thou shalt bring also the day of consolation, to wit, of mine.

In Hebrew: Thou hast brought, thou hast called the day; in which they shall be as I, as the explanation is added, what kind of day is understood, to wit, of vengeance upon the enemies: as most interpreters explain.

THEY SHALL BECOME LIKE UNTO ME) Captivity also hangs over Babylon. Ps. 137:9, Jer. 51:20, 30, 31, 32. Add what we have produced from Herodotus in the Annotations to book 3 of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

Latin:

Vers. 21. LÆTATI SVNT: QVONIAM TV FECISTI) Rectius כי hic vertitur per sed: quasi dicat: ferenda mihi sunt tua judicia.

ADDVXISTI DIEM CONSOLATIONIS) Adduces & diem consolationis, scil. meæ.

In Ebr. Adduxisti, diem vocasti; qua erunt sicut ego, uti additur explicatio, qualis intelligatur dies, vindictæ scil. in hostes: ut plerique Interpp. exponunt.

FIENT SIMILES MEI) Imminet & Babyloni captivi- tas. Pf. 137, 9. Jer. 51, 20. 30. 31. 32. Adde, quæ ex Herodoto produximus Annotatis ad librum 3. de Veritate Religionis Christianæ.

## 1:22
Vers. 22. VINTAGE THEM, AS THOU HAST VINTAGED ME] It can also be translated: Do unto them, as thou hast done unto me. For the word is ambiguous.

To vintage for to punish, v. 12 and chap. 2:20.

Latin:

Vers. 22. VINDEMIA EOS, SICVT VINDEMIASTI ME] Potest etiam verti: Fac eis, ut mihi fecisti. Est enim verbum ambiguum.

Vindemiare pro punire v. 12. & cap. 2, 20.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

A lamentation concerning the glory of Israel cast down, the habitation of Jacob laid waste, the bulwarks and palaces of Judah destroyed, and all the power of Israel broken in the wrath of the Lord, and concerning the evils which the Kings, Prophets, Elders, Virgins, and infants sustained, as well as the derision and joy of the enemies, whence all are provoked to the profusion of tears and wailing.

Vers. 1.

HE HATH CAST DOWN FROM HEAVEN UNTO THE EARTH THE BEAUTY OF ISRAEL) From the highest to the lowest. Compare Matt. 11:23.

FOOTSTOOL OF HIS FEET) The Ark is often called this in respect to the rest of the land of Judea. But also all of Judea can be called this in respect to other lands.

Where Judea is so called, it does not show. The Ark is indeed sometimes called this, but not in respect to the rest of Judea, but in respect to the gracious presence of God, who manifested Himself particularly at the Ark. It is to be observed, however, that the footstool of the feet of the Lord is called either the whole orb of the lands, Isa. 66:1, or the temple of the Lord, 1 Chron. 28:2, Isa. 43:7, or the Ark, which stood out in the temple, toward which it was customary to worship, Ps. 99 and 132:7. Here the temple seems to be regarded, because God did not even spare His own temple, as Jonathan and R. Solomon interpret: and also among the Christians, Theodoret, Olympiodorus, Thomas, Lyranus.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

De Israelis gloria dejecta, Jacobi habitatione de- solata, Judæ propugnaculis & palatiis destru- ctis, omniq; potentia Israelis confracta in ira Domini lamentatio, & de malis, quæ Reges, Prophetas, Seniores, Virgines, infantes susti- nuerunt, nec non de hostium irrisione, & gau- dio, unde ad profusionem lachrymarum & planctum provocantur omnes.

Vers. 1.

PROJECTT DE COELO IN TERRAM INCLYTAM ISRAEL) A summis ad ima. Confer Matth. 11, 23.

SCABELLI PEDVM SVORVM) Arca sæpe sic voca- tur respectu cæteræ terræ Judææ. Sed & Judæa tota sic vo- cari potest respectu aliarum terrarum.

UBi Judæa ita vocetur, non ostendit. Arca qui- dem sic interdum vocatur, verum non respectu Judææ cæteræ, sed respectu gratiosæ Dei præsentiæ, qui ad arcam peculiariter se manifestavit. Obser- vandum autem, quod scabellum pedum Domini, vel totus terrarum orbis dicatur Ef. 66, 1. vel templum Domini 1. Chron. 28, 2. Ef. 43, 7. vel arca, quæ emi- nebat in templo, ad quam adorari solebat Pf. 99. & 132, 7. Hic templum videtur respici, quod ne qui- dem templo suo pepercerit Deus, ut Jonathan & R. Salomo interpretantur: Nec non è Christianis Theodoret. Olympiod. Thomas, Lyranus.

## 2:2
Ver. 2. ALL THE BEAUTIFUL THINGS OF JACOB] In the Hebrew: dwellings.

HE HAS POLLUTED THE KINGDOM AND ITS PRINCES) He has disgraced, delivering both the land and the people into the dominion of profane nations.

Latin:

Vers. 2. OMNIA SPECIOSA JACOB] In Hebræo : habitacula.

POLLVIT REGNVM ET PRINCIPES EJVS) Infama- vit, tradens & terram & populum in ditionem profanarum gentium.

## 2:3
Ver. 3. HE HAS BROKEN IN THE WRATH OF HIS FURY EVERY HORN OF ISRAEL) Horn, i.e., glory, as 1 Sam. 2:1; especially royal majesty is indicated by this name.

Latin:

Vers. 3. CONFREGIT IN IRA FVRORIS SVI OMNE CORNV ISRAEL) Cornu, i. e. gloriam, ut 1. Sam. 2, 1. præcipue regia majestas hoc nomine indicatur.

## 2:5
Ver. 5. HE HAS FILLED IN THE DAUGHTER OF JUDAH HUMILIATION AND HUMILIATED) He followed the Greek version. Others translate from the Hebrew, mourning and sorrow.

Why does he not pretend here to have read the Greeks or another Latin [text] again? The sense in the Vulgate, however, is almost non-existent; it has filled [the text] with 'humiliated' [masculine] and 'humiliated' [feminine]. Which, however, Maldonatus tries to introduce, so that it may harmonize with the Hebrew, in this way: he caused there to be a great abundance of men and women, of the miserable and the weeping. Nor does it harmonize with the Greek version: indeed, the Greek version recedes even further from the sources, and disagrees with itself. For in the Basel edition of the year 1545, it is held: καὶ ἐπλήθυνε τῇ θυγατρὶ Ἰᾄδα ταπεινώσενα, καὶ τεταπεινωμένην: but in the Vatican copy, the latter words are held thus: ταπεινωμένην καὶ τεταπεινωμένην. Without doubt, therefore, B. Luther is more correct: 'Er hat der Tochter Juda viel klagens und leidens gemacht' [He has caused the daughter of Judah much lamenting and suffering], in which manner also Junius, and from the Jews R. Aben-Ezra: 'multiplicavit in Israel fletum & luctum' [he multiplied in Israel weeping and mourning]. The Chaldean Paraphrast also agrees.

Latin:

Vers. 5. REPLEVIT IN FILIA JVDA HVMILIA- TVM ET HVMILIATAM) Secutus est Græcam versionem. Alii ex Hebræo vertunt, luctum & mœrorem.

Cur non hic iterum Græcos aut Latinum aliud legisse fingit? Sensus autem in Vulgata ferme nul- lus, replevit humiliatum & humiliatam. Quem ta- men inferre conatur Maldonatus, ut Hebræo con- sonet, hoc modo: fecit ut magna esset copia virorum ac mulierum, miserorum ac plorantium. Neque Græcæ versioni consonat: imo versio Græca adhuc lon- gius recedit à fontibus, & à seipsa discrepat. Nam in Basiliensi editione de Anno 1545. habetur καὶ ἐπλή- θυνε τῇ θυγατρὶ Ἰᾄδα ταπεινώσενα, καὶ τεταπεινω- μένην: in Vaticano vero exemplari habent verba po- steriora ita: ταπεινωμένην καὶ τεταπεινωμένην. Sine dubio ergo rectius B. Lutherus: Er hat der Tochter Juda viel klagens und leidens gemacht, quo pacto etiam Junius, & è Judæis R. Aben-Ezra: multipli- cavit in Israel fletum & luctum. Consonat etiam Chaldæus Paraphrastes.

## 2:8
Verse 8. HE HAS STRETCHED HIS LINE] In the Hebrew.

he stretched the rule: i.e., he leveled everything to the ground as if by a plumb line. If one wishes to listen to the Hebrews, to whom Grotius otherwise attributes much in explaining idioms, it must be explained: he brought forth a sentence, as to how they are to be punished: as R. Solomon explains that Hebraism from 2 Sam. 8:2, 2 Kings 21:13. Others render it: he designed the demolition in his mind beforehand, as architects are accustomed to stretch a line when they design something: which agrees with the preceding words: 'The Lord thought to destroy the wall of the Daughter of Zion, he stretched his line': Confer Cornelius a Lapide here.

Latin:

Vers. 8. TETENDIT FVNICVLVM SVVM] In Hebr.

tetendit regulam: i. e. omnia solo æquavit quasi ad libellam. Si Ebræos, quibus in explicandis idiotismis alias multum tribuit Grotius, audire libeat, expo- nendum, protulit sententiam, quomodo puniendi sint: uti R. Salomo Ebraismum istum explicat è 2. Sam. 8, 2. 2. Reg. 21, 13. Alii reddunt, designavit animo prius demolitionem, uti solent funiculum extendere architecti, cum aliquid designant: quod convenit verbis antecedentibus: cogitavit Dominus dissipa- re murum Filiæ Sion, tetendit funiculum suum: Confer Cornelium à Lapide hic.

THE VIRGINS OF JERUSALEM HAVE CAST THEIR HEADS TO THE GROUND] This is what the Greeks call κατηφεῖν or κατηφᾶν. Caesar: 'sad, with head bowed, to look at the ground'.

Vers. 10.

ABJECERVNT IN TERRAM CAPITA SVA VIR- GINES JERVSALEM] Hoc est, quod Græci dicunt κατη- φεῖν vel κατηφᾶν. Cæsar: tristes capite demisso terram intueri.

Verse 11.

MY LIVER IS POURED OUT UPON THE GROUND) That is, all my desires have collapsed. For the liver is their seat.

WHEN THE LITTLE ONE WAS FAILING From hunger, as follows.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

EFFVNDITVR IN TERRAM JECVR MEVM) Id est, desideria mea omnia conciderunt. Eorum enim sedes jecur.

CVM DEFICERET PARVVLVSI Præ fame, ut sequitur.

## 2:13
Ver. 13. FOR GREAT IS AS THE SEA THY DESTRUCTION] He reads, as we have in the Hebrew, כים. But the LXX read כוס, a cup of thy destruction.

Whatever the LXX may have read or seen, the Hebrew is correct, and the Vulgate text which agrees with it. To what shall I compare thee, that I may bring a similar example to comfort thee? For it is a comfort of some sort to the miserable to have had companions in misfortune. Thus the Chaldean and the Hebrew interpreters: Great is thy destruction as the sea; Lyranus, Corn. a Lapide, Maldonatus: just as no abundance of waters can be compared to the sea, so there is no grief that can be compared with thy grief. The Chaldean: thy breaking is multiplied, according to the multitude of the breaking of the waves of the great sea, in the time of its tempest. The translation of the Syrians and the Arab tends to this, as also Vatablus, Tarnovius, and other interpreters.

Latin:

Vers. 13. MAGNA EST ENIM VELVT MARE CON- TRITIO TVA] Legit, ut nos in Hebræo habemus, כים. At LXX. legerunt כוס, ποτήριον συντριβῆς σε.

Quicquid legerint aut viderint LXX. recte se habet Ebræus, & qui ei consonat Vulgatus textus. Cui comparabo te, quod simile exemplum adducam, ut te consoler? Solamen enim qualecunque esse mise- ris solet, socios habuisse malorum. Sic Chaldæus & In- terpp. Ebræi: Magna est contritio tua velut mare; Lyranus, Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus: sicut nulla aquarum copia mari potest comparari, ita nullus est dolor, qui cum dolore tuo conferri possit. Chaldæus, multiplicata est confractio tua, secundum multitudi- nem confractionis fluctuurn maris magni, tempore tempestatis ejus. Eo & Syri & Arabis translatio ten- dit, ut & Vatablus, Tarnovius, & alii Interpp.

## 2:14
Ver. 14. THY PROPHETS] Not God's prophets, but thine, flattering thee Jer. 23, 16.

BUT THEY HAVE SEEN FOR THEE FALSE ASSUMPTIONS) In Hebrew משאות, which is wont to be said of sad prophecies. Such things they sang against Babylon.

AND EJECTIONS] They prophesied that it would come to pass for thee that thou wouldst drive the Babylonians far away.

Hugo Cardinalis, Thomas, and Bonaventura had preceded Hugo Grotius, as also Corn. a Lapide: Maldonatus, however, interprets it otherwise: namely, that the Pseudo-Prophets, so that they might not always seem to prophesy pleasant things, occasionally mixed in some light adverse things.

But since a denomination is usually made from the more important part, the gloss of Maldonatus is by no means to be approved. B. Luther follows the explanation of the ancients most excellently: They have preached to thee loose sermons, by which they preached thee out of the land. Because it was relevant to relate here not so much what the false prophets threatened to the Chaldeans, as what they promised to the Jews, and it escapes no one that the word משאות is used generally of any sermon: they have seen for thee prophecies of falsehood, and of ejections: where Olympiodorus and Theodoretus imply, from God: because they preached those things which drove the Jews away from God and the right path. Lyranus and Dionysius render ejections in almost the same way, because they prophesied those things which in reality were ejections, which B. Luther expressed more clearly. Ver. 15. THEY HAVE MOVED THEIR HEAD] In mockery, as 2 Kings 19, 21. Ver. 16. THEY HAVE OPENED THEIR MOUTH UPON THEE] Like gaping wild beasts, Ps. 22, 14. Ver. 17. WHICH HE HAD COMMANDED FROM DAYS OF OLD) Which He had threatened in the sanction of His law, Lev. 26, 25. Deut. 28, 36. 48. Ver. 19. ARISE, PRAISE IN THE NIGHT) In Hebrew: Cry out. LIFT UP THY HANDS TO HIM FOR THE SOUL OF THY LITTLE ONES) That God may preserve them, if not thee, at least in life. Ver. 20. SHALL WOMEN EAT THEIR FRUIT TO THE MEASURE OF A PALM) This also happened according to the threats of the law Deut. 28, 53. Ver. 22. THOU HAST CALLED AS TO A SOLEMN DAY, THOSE THAT HELD ME ROUND ABOUT) Thou hast called enemies upon me from every region, no otherwise than men are wont to be summoned to a feast day.

Latin:

Vers. 14. PROPHETÆ TVI] Non Dei Prophetæ, sed tui, tibi adulantes Jer. 23, 16.

VIDERVNT AVTEM TIBI ASSVMTIONES FAL- SAS) In Hebr. משאות, quod de vaticiniis tristibus dici solet. Talia illi canebant adversus Babylonem.

ET EJECTIONES] Vaticinabantur tibi fore ut Babylo- nios longe dispelleres.

Præiverat Hugoni Grotio Hugo Cardinalis, Thomas, & Bonaventura, ut & Corn. à Lapide: Ali- ter tamen Maldonatus interpretatur: nimirum Pseudo-Prophetæ, ne semper jucunda viderentur va- ticinari, subinde levia quædam adversa miscebant.

Sed quum a potiori fieri soleat denominatio, mini- me probanda Maldonati glossa. Optime B. Luthe- rus veterum explicationem sequitur: Haben dir gepredigt lose Predigt, damit sie dich zum Land hin- aus predigten. Quia non tam quod Chaldaeis mina- ti, quam quod Judaeis polliciti falsi Prophetae fue- rint, hic referri attinebat, & neminem fugit, vocem משאות generaliter usurpari de quavis concione: vi- derunt tibi Prophetias mendacii, & expulsionum: ubi Olympiodor. & Theodoretius subintelligunt, a Deo: quod ea praedicarint, quae a Deo & via recta Judaeos expellebant. Lyranus & Dionysius similiter fere reddunt ejectiones, quod ea prophetarint, quae revera fuerunt ejectiones, quae B. Lutherus lucu- lentius expressit. Vers. 15. MOVERUNT CAPVT SVVM] Per ludibri- um, ut 2. Reg. 19, 21. Vers. 16. APERVERVNT SVPER TE OS SVVM] Vt hiantes ferae, Pf. 22, 14. Vers. 17. QVEM PRAECEPERAT A DIEBVS ANTI- QVIS) Quem minatus erat in sanctione legis suae, Lev. 26, 25. Deuter. 28, 36. 48. Vers. 19. CONSVRGE, LAVDA IN NOCTE) In He- braeo: Clama. LEVA AD EVM MANVS TVAS PRO ANIMA PARVVLORVM TVORVM) Vt Deus si non te, illos sal- tem in vita conservet. Vers. 20. ERGONE COMEDENT MVLIERES FRV- CTVM SVVM AD MENSVRAM PALMAE) Factum & hoc secundum minas legis Deut. 28, 53. Vers. 22. VOCASTI QVASI AD DIEM SOLEN- NEM, QVI TENERENT ME DE CIRCVITV] Ab omni regione hostes in me advocasti, non aliter quam ad fe- stum diem homines convocari solent.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III.

A sad complaint under the person of a man vehemently afflicted, concerning the denial of divine grace, who, however, raises himself in turn by the mercy of the Lord, to be shown again to those who patiently wait for it, provided that serious repentance is practiced, guilt acknowledged, and trust placed in God: therefore a formula of penitential prayer precedes here from the Prophet.

Ver. 1. I AM THE MAN SEEING MY POVERTY] Jeremiah laments his own along with public evils, especially when, with the city besieged, he was shut up in a dire prison.

Thus with the Hebrews and with Origen, and the Jesuit Christoph. a Castro, Grotius. But others assert that Jeremiah utters these things in the name of the whole people: or they think that just as he has hitherto introduced the Church of the Jews under the guise of some woman, so now he presents it under the person of some man, who sets forth the evils sent upon him by God. Which opinion is to be embraced. Since the manner of speaking testifies that Jeremiah did not say these things about himself, both because he could not speak of himself alone in the plural, and because of the subject matter itself: For many things are said here which do not fit the afflictions of Jeremiah himself v. 3. v. 6. as the Lord has turned himself against me, and turned his hand; he has placed me in dark places AS THOSE DEAD FOREVER, which are explained too coldly as referring to the harsher imprisonment of Jeremiah v. 10. seqq. He has become to me a bear lying in wait, and a lion in secret (lurking) he has bent his bow, and set me as a mark, my soul is cast off from peace etc. That he himself, moved by the Holy Spirit, uttered these words in these θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) lamentations, is hardly likely. Therefore Theodoret, Rabanus, Hugo, Thomas, Lyranus, Isidorus, Sanctius, Geisler, Vatablus, B. Luther, both Osianders, Hutter, Tarnovius, Cramer, and others understand these things of the people: let verses 22, 33, and following be seen, which certainly cannot be explained of Jeremiah alone. And Grotius admits at v. 45 that there the Prophet is not speaking specifically of himself, but of the whole people. Vers. 5. HE HAS BUILT AGAINST ME) He has enclosed me on every side. See below 9. He understands these things of the prison. But more serious evils are indicated. Therefore Osiander, even though he understands it of Jeremiah, explains: he built a certain rampart of the miserable, so that I can nowhere break out or escape. Which some interpreters, along with Maldonatus, also think is explained by the things that are added: And he has surrounded me with gall and labor: namely, that he was surrounded on every side by dangers and labors, so that he could not flee from one evil without running into another. Thus also the Hebrews, the author of the Midrash, R. Solomon, as well as the Chaldean interpreter. But they interpret it not of Jeremiah, but of the city of Jerusalem. Similarly, Origen and Theodoret explain it of the rampart and mounds with which the Chaldeans devastated the city. R. Solomon also refers to this in verse 9. He has blocked my ways: although Maldonatus not badly explains it metaphorically, that God has blocked the ways with squared stone, that is, he has surrounded the people with such great dangers on all sides that they could not break through.

Latin:

CAPUT III.

Tristis querela sub persona viri vehementer affli- cti, de gratia divina denegatione, qui vero se erigit vicissim misericordia Domini, illis, qui patienter eam expectant, iterum exhibenda, modo seria agatur poenitentia, agnita culpa, & fiducia in Deum locata: ideo formula pre- cationis poenitentialis hic praeit Propheta.

Vers. 1. EGO VIR VIDENS PAVPERTATEM ME- AM] Cum publicis malis simul & sua deplorat Jeremias, praecipue cum obsessa urbe in diro carcere conclusus fuit.

ITa cum Ebraeis & cum Origene, ac Jesuita Chri- stoph. a Castro Grotius. Sed alii Jeremiam totius populi nomine haec proferre asserunt: aut sicut in- troduxit hactenus Ecclesiam Judaeorum sub specie alicujus faeminae, ita nunc sub viri alicujus persona, qui mala a Deo sibi immissa exponat, sistere existi- mant. Quae sententia amplectenda est. Siquidem Je- remiam haec de seipso non dixisse tum loquendi mo- dus testetur, quum in plurali de se solo loqui non potuerit, tum materia ipsa: Multa enim hic dicun- tur, quae non conveniunt ipsius Jeremiae afflictioni- bus v. 3. v. 6. tanquam contra me vertit se Dominus, & convertit manum suam; in tenebricosis collocavit me QUASI MORTUOS SEMPITERNOS, quae nimis frigide de carcere duriori Jeremiae explican- tur v. 10. seqq. Ursus insidians factus est mihi, & Leo in abscondito (delitescens) tetendit arcum suum, & posuit me, quasi signum, repulsa est a pace anima mea &c. Quas voces ipsum a Spir. S. agitatum in threnis hisce θεοπνεύστοις emisisse, vix est verisimile. Ideo de populo haec intelligunt Theodoret. Rabanus, Hugo, Thomas, Lyran. Isidorus, Sanctius, Geisler. Va- tablus, B. Lutherus, Osiander uterque, Hutterus, Tar- novius, Cramerus, & alii: videantur vers. 22. 33. & seqq. qui certe de solo Jeremia explicari non pos- sunt. Et fatetur ad v. 45. Grotius, ibi non specialiter de se, sed de toto populo loqui Prophetam. Vers. 5. AEDIFICAVIT IN GTRO MEO) Vndique me inclusit. Vide infra 9. De carcere haec accipit. Sed graviora mala indi- cantur. Ideo Osiander, etsi de Jeremia intelligat, explicat: aedificavit q. vallum quoddam miserorum, ut nusquam erumpere aut evadere queam. Quod ex- plicari etiam censent Interpp. nonnulli cum Mal- donato, iis quae adduntur: Et circumdedit me felle, & labore: quod nempe omni ex parte circumdatus fuerit periculis & laboribus, ut non potuerit ex uno malo fugere, quin incurreret in aliud. Sic Ebraei quoque, Autor Midrasch, R. Salom. ut & Interpres Chaldaeus. Sed interpretantur non de Jeremia, ve- rum de civitate Hierusalem. Similiter Origenes, & Theodoretus explicant de vallo & aggeribus, quibus Chaldaei urbem vastarunt. Eo etiam refert R. Salo- mo vers. 9. Conclusit vias meas: quamvis non male Maldon. metaphorice exponat, Deum quadro la- pide vias conclusisse, id est, tam magnis undique pericu- lis circumsepsisse populum, ut perrumpere non posset.

## 3:8
Verse 8. WHEN I HAVE CRIED AND PRAYED] When I cried and prayed.

Latin:

Vers. 8. CVM CLAMAVERO ET ROGAVERO] Cum clamarem, & rogarem.

## 3:11
Verse 11. HE HAS SUBVERTED MY PATHS] He has taken away from me the freedom of walking.

Too thinly. More correctly Maldonatus explains from the preceding phrase: He has blocked my ways with squared stones, he has subverted my paths, that is, he has cut them off, so that I do not see any path by which I can escape, just as when farmers cut through paths with a plow, so that they do not appear, so that it may be signified by this metaphor that God has cut off from the Jews every hope of help, and has snatched away from them every plan. Similarly Cornelius a Lapide.

HE HAS SET ME DESOLATE] In Hebrew it is desolate.

Latin:

Vers. 11. SEMITAS MEAS SVBVERTIT] Ademit mi- hi ambulandi libertatem.

Nimis tenuiter. Rectius Maldonatus e phrasi praecedente explicat: Conclusit vias meas lapidibus quadris, semitas meas subvertit, id est, excidit, ita ut non videam ullam semitam, qua possim effugere, quemadmodum cum aratro agricolae vias perscin- dunt, ita ut non appareant, ut significetur hac me- taphora Deum Judaeis omnem spem auxilii prae- cidisse, omneque illis consilium eripuisse. Simi- liter Cornelius a Lapide.

POSVIT ME DESOLATAM] In Hebraeo est desolatum.

## 3:16
Verse 16. HE HAS BROKEN MY TEETH TO THE NUMBER] Because in Greek it is ἐξέβαλε ψήφῳ ὀδόντας με, this interpreter thought that ψῆφον was a pebble. But the Greeks understood by ψῆφον a small stone. And so it is in the Hebrew, he caused my teeth to be broken with small stones: that is, with stony bread, as Seneca speaks.

HE HAS FED ME WITH ASHES] In Hebrew: he immersed me in ashes. But the Hebrews often take ashes for mud. See the history in Jer. 38, 6.

Rightly the Greek is explained and the Latin is corrected from the Hebrew text. But why did Grotius not observe the same in other places? The Papists are foolish, who labor for the sake of the Vulgate version concerning its ψευδερμηνείαν, which they ought rather to have corrected. To the number, that is, one by one, says Maldonatus, that is, not all at once, so that the pain might be more severe and longer-lasting, which he then explains by a metaphor from the Hebrew: He broke my teeth with a stone, that is, he caused me the greatest pain: to which Hector Pintus does not disagree. Others among Corn. a Lapide explain it thus: With a stone, that is, with a decisive and condemnatory pebble he condemned all the teeth, that is, all the members. But that Cornelius a Lapide thinks the fullest meaning is, he broke my teeth in a pebble, or to a pebble, that is, to the number in order and one by one: and yet he paraphrases thus: he broke all my teeth to one, while namely he mixed pebbles or small stones into my bread, which while I bite, I break my teeth. He acknowledges therefore that the Chaldean and the LXX rightly translated, he broke my teeth with a stone, which he explains thus, that pebbles were actually mixed into the breads, whether out of malice, or rather out of hunger and scarcity. Which is also the opinion of R. Solomon, and of Joh. Piscator, Tremellius and Junius render this sense of the Hebrew phrase; He disturbs and prostrates me to the ground with such force that my teeth are crushed and broken by grit. Luther explained the sense of the phrase very well: He has beaten my teeth into small pieces, because when they are broken with a stone, they are crushed into parts. Thus therefore he rendered it, so that the emphasis of the metaphorical locution, which Pintus and Maldonatus also acknowledge here, could be understood more easily. Which receives some light from Ps. 3, 9.

Prov. 20, 87. Therefore the Vinarians explain: He has indeed treated me too terribly. Osiander deduces this version from the Hebrew thus: he broke my teeth into fragments. Which does not seem inconvenient, because גָרַס has a relationship with גָרַשׁ he divided. And the following words, he fed me, he corrects from the Hebrew, he fed me in ashes, as B. Luther, He rolls me in the ashes. הִכְפִּישׁ is he turned, or rolled: he inverted me in ashes, R. Solomon has, he defiled me with dust, Aben-Ezra: he humbled me in ashes, the Chaldean. Where Osiander not badly subjoined this explanation: that is, he treated me violently, as if someone were not only to loosen the teeth of a miserable man with a fist, but also to break them, and prostrate him to the ground, and trample him with his feet in the dust: Grotius HE FED ME WITH ASHES. In Hebrew he immersed me in ashes. But the Hebrews often take ashes for mud. See the history in Jer. 38.16. We have now given the true sense, which is without doubt more suitable here. Grotius gratuitously assumes that Jeremiah is speaking of himself, having followed the Tigurine version here, as it appears, which has, he precipitated me into the mud.

Latin:

Vers. 16. FREGIT AD NVMERVM DENTES MEOS] Quia in Graeco est ἐξέβαλε ψήφῳ ὀδόντας με, putavit hic interpres ψῆφον esse calculum. At Graeci per ψῆφον intellexere lapillum. Et sic in Hebraeo est, fecit confringi lapillis dentes meos: id est, pane lapidoso, ut Seneca loquitur.

CIBAVIT ME CINERE] In Hebraeo: immersit me ci- neri. Sed cinerem pro luto saepe sumunt Hebraei. Histo- riam vide Jerem. 38, 6.

Recte ex Ebraeo textu Graecus explicatur, La- tinus emendatur. Sed cur in aliis locis idem non observavit Grotius? Inepti sunt Papistae, qui in gratiam Vulgatae versionis laborant circa ψευδερ- μηνείαν ejus, quam corrigere potius debebant. Ad numerum, id est, sigillatim, ait Maldonatus, id est, non omnes simul, quo dolor gravior ac diuturnior esset, quod deinde per metaphoram ex Hebraeo explicat: Confregit lapide dentes meos, id est, maxi- mum mihi dolorem fecit: Cui non abnuit Hector Pintus. Alii apud Corn. a Lapide ita explicant: La- pide, id est, calculo decretorio & condemnatorio ad mortem damnavit omnes dentes, id est, omnia mem- bramea. Cornelius autem ille Lapideus plenissi- mum sensum esse putat, fregit dentes meos in calculo, vel ad calculum, id est, ad numerum ordine & sigilla- tim: & tamen ita παραφράζει ad unum omnes dentes meos fregit, dum videl. calculos vel lapillos pani meo miscuit, quos dum mordeo, confringo dentes meos. A- gnoscit ergo Chaldeum, & LXX. recte vertisse, con- fregit lapide dentes meos, quod explicat ita, quod mi- sti reipsa lapilli fuerint panibus, sive ex malitia, seu potius ex fame & penuria. Quae etiam R. Salomonis est sententia, & Joh. Piscatoris, Tremellius & Junius Phraseos Ebraeae hunc reddunt sensum; Tanta vi me deturbat, ac prosternit in terram, ut elisi dentes comminuantur scrupis. Lutherus optime sensum phraseos exposuit: Er hat meine Zähne zu kleinen Stücken geschlagen, quia cum lapide franguntur, in partes comminuuntur. Sic ergo reddidit, ut metaphoricae loquutionis, quam hic etiam Pintus & Maldonatus agnoscunt, emphasis intelligi faci- lius posset. Quae lucem aliquam accipit e Ps. 3, 9.

Prov. 20, 87. Ideo exponunt Vinarienses : Er hat mich ja zu schrecklich zugerichtet. Osiander ex He- bræo hanc versionem ita deducit: fregit ad frustu- la dentes meos. Quod non inconveniens videtur, quia גָרַס cognationem habet cum גָרַשׁ divisit. Et verba sequentia, cibavit me, ex Ebræo corrigit, convalvit me in cinere, uti B. Lutherus, Er wälzet mich in der Aschen. הִכְפִּישׁ est versavit, seu volvit : in- vertit me in cinere, habet R. Salomo, inquinavit me pulvere, Aben-Ezra: humiliavit me in cinere, Chal- dæus. Ubi non male subjunxit Osiander hanc ex- plicationem: id est, violenter me tractavit, ac si quis homini misero dentes non modo pugno labefaciat, sed etiam confringat, eumque in terram prosternat, atq; pe- dibus in pulvere conculcet : Grotius CIBAVIT ME CINERE. In Hebræo immersit me cineri. Sed cinerem præ luto sæpe sumunt Hebræi. Historiam vide Jerem. 38.16. Verum sensum jam dedimus, qui sine dubio hic commodior. De seipso Jerem. loqui gratis assumit Grotius, Tigurinam hic, ut apparet, sequutus, quæ habet, precipitavit me in lutum.

## 3:17
Vers. 17. AND MY SOUL IS REMOVED FAR FROM PEACE] The scribes placed נַפְשִׁי, but it had been נַפְשׁוֹ, with the discourse turned to God, whose thoughts Jeremiah complained had been far from his prosperity.

But whence did this become known to Grotius? By what document or evidence? We see the itch of the man and his ἀυθάδειαν in correcting the sources, even though he has no reason to bring forward, except that it pleases him so. That the discourse is not about God, the words subjoined by way of explanation teach: I have forgotten good things. The Papists themselves acknowledge this: Maldonatus: My soul is removed far from peace. It must be read so, he says, because it is so in Hebrew, and so some of our Latin codices have it, and so the Chaldean and the LXX read. The sense, however, is, my soul was far from having any peace and tranquility, or תִּזַּח it removed itself from peace, that is, it could not rest, Ps. 38, 4. And Cornelius à Lapide: My soul is removed far from peace: so the Roman, Hebrew, and Septuagint read. He calls peace rest, prosperity, and joy, whence follows I have forgotten good things, to wit, of former happiness. That is to say, my soul lacks all accustomed tranquility.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ET REPULSA EST A PACE ANIMA MEA] Scribæ posuerunt נַפְשִׁי, fed fuerat נַפְשׁוֹ, ad Deum verso sermone, cujus cogitationes longe à sua prosperitate abfuisse, querebatur Jeremias.

Unde vero hoc innotuit Grotio? Quo docu- mento, aut indicio? Videmus pruritum hominis & ἀυθάδειαν in corrigendis fontibus, etsi nullam ad- ferre habeat causam, nisi quod ita placeat. Non de Deo sermonem esse, verba κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν subjun- cta docent: oblitus bonorum. Agnoscunt id ipsimet Papistæ: Maldonatus: Repulsa est à pace anima mea. Sic legendum, inquit, quia sic Ebraice est, & sic ali- qui nostri Latini codices habent, & sic Chaldæus & LXX. legerunt. Sensus autem est, longe abfuit animus meus, ut ullam pacem & tranquillitatem haberet, vel תִּזַּח elongavit se a pace, id est, non potuit conquie- scere Ps. 38, 4. Et Cornelius à Lapide: Repulsa est à pace anima mea : ita legunt Roman. Hebr. & Se- ptuaginta. Pacem vocat quietem, prosperitatem, & gaudium, unde sequitur oblitus sum bonorum scil. felicitatis pristinæ. q. d. anima mea caret omni solita tranquillitate.

## 3:20
Vers. 20. I WILL BE MINDFUL AND MY SOUL SHALL LANGUISH IN ME] In the Hebrew: by remembering it will remember: that is, as often as my soul calls that time to mind, it wastes away entirely.

Others more correctly refer these things to God: by remembering it will remember: because he had said before, remember my poverty and my transgression; therefore now he raises himself up, because the Lord will remember, that is to say, I know for certain that it will come to pass that you will remember: which (even though the Vulgate has it otherwise) this Jesuit Maldonatus acknowledges here. And thus Blessed Luther: You will indeed remember it. As also Osiander, who also explains the following word תָשׁוּחַ with the Chaldean rendering it, my soul will pray over me, my soul, the LXX καταδολεχήσει ἐπ’ ἐμὲ will converse with me, Tremellius, it meditates; and this my soul meditates in me: For my soul tells me, as if it were Schin sinistratum תָשׂוּחַ, although that also can be explained by metalepsis, IT WILL ASSERT or IT WILL CONCLUDE, after various bowing down, to wit; when the mind twists itself in all directions, and at length concludes: For תָשׁוּחַ is otherwise it bowed down: as is added: This I recall to my mind, and therefore I hope. Maldonatus renders it thus: I know for certain that it will come to pass that you will remember, O Lord, yet in the meantime my soul is humbled and afflicted.

Latin:

Vers. 20. MEMORIA MEMOR ERO ET TABESCET IN-ME ANIMA MEA] In Hebræo: recordando recorda- bitur: id est, quotiescunque animus meus illius temporis re- miniscitur, totus contabescit.

Alii rectius hæc ad Deum referunt: recordan- do recordabitur: quia dixerat antea, recordare pau- pertatis, & transgressionis meæ; ideo nunc se erigit, quod recordaturus sit Dominus q. d. certo scio fo- re, ut recorderis: quod (etsi secus Vulgata habeat) agnoscit hic Jesuita Maldonatus. Atque ita B. Lu- therus: Du wirst ja daran gedencken. Ut & Osiander, qui etiam sequentem vocem תָשׁוּחַ cum Chaldæo reddente, orabit anima super me, anima mea, LXX. καταδολεχήσει ἐπ’ ἐμὲ confabulabitur mecum, Tre- mellio, meditatur exponunt; & hoc meditatur ani- ma mea in me: Denn meine Seele saget mirs, quasi esset Schin sinistratum תָשׂוּחַ, quamvis & illud per metalepsin exponi possit, ASSERET vel CON- CLUDET, post variam scil. incurvationem; cum mens in omnes partes se torquet, ac tandem con- cludit: Nam תָשׁוּחַ alias est incurvavit: uti additur: Hoc revoco in animum meum, & propterea spero. Maldonatus ita reddit: Certo scio fore, ut recorderis Domine, tamen interim humiliatur & affligitur ani- mus meus.

## 3:21
Vers. 21.

THESE THINGS RECALLING IN MY HEART, I WILL HOPE IN GOD] These things, that is, the present state, my deliverance from the miry pit, placing them at the same time before my eyes, I will have that as an argument by which I may trust in God in the future as well.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

HÆC RECOLENS IN CORDE MEO, IN DEO SPERABO] Hæc, id est, statum præsentem, liberatio- nem meam ex lacu lutoso, simul mihi ob oculos ponens, id argumentum habebo, quo in posterum quoque Deo con- fidam.

## 3:22
Ver. 22. THE MERCIES OF THE LORD BECAUSE WE ARE NOT CONSUMED) Better: because the mercies of God are not consumed: For תמנו through the epenthesis of the letter נ for תמו is a Chaldean form, and the Chaldean Interpreter has taken it so here. Also the LXX: ὅτι ἐκ ἐξέλιπέ με.

He prefers without doubt this interpretation and preconceived opinion, that Jeremiah is speaking only of himself. But there is no need for that epenthesis and Chaldean form. And the order is inverted thus: which has it so in the sources; the mercy of the Lord, BECAUSE we are not consumed. Therefore the causal BECAUSE is not to be placed first. And תמנו in Num. 17, v. last, is we are consumed. Whence the Vulgate Version is correct here, with which the Tremellian and B. Luther's German also agree.

Latin:

Vers. 22. MISERICORDIAE DOMINI QVIA NON SVMVS CONSVMTI) Melius: quia misericordia Dei non sunt consumta: Nam תמנו per epenthesin literæ נ pro תמו est forma Chaldaica, & hic ita sumsit Chaldæus Interpres. Etiam LXX. ὅτι ἐκ ἐξέλιπέ με.

Præfert sine dubio hanc interpretationem & præconceptam opinionem, quod de se loquatur solum Jeremias. Sed illa ἐπενθέσει & forma Chaldaica non est opus. Et invertitur ita ordo: qui sic in fontibus habet; misericordia Domini, QVIA non consumti. Non ergo præmittenda causalis QVIA. Et תמנו Num. 17. v. ult. est consumti sumus. Unde recte hic se habet Versio Vulgata, cui consonat etiam Tremelliana, & B. Lutheri Germanica.

## 3:23
Ver. 23. NEW IN THE MORNING) Write New [feminine], and refer it to the mercies: daily, he says, one follows another.

The Latin is deservedly corrected: Maldonatus even acknowledges this, adding the reason, because the Hebrews read it so (therefore the Latin text must be corrected from the Hebrew). And corrected copies have it so, and the LXX also translated it so. This is what he says. Where then is the authority of the Vulgate?

We dealt with v. 25 up to 33 in the Memory of the Just, presented at Wittenberg as an image of Christian patience and divine Mercy, Conc. 17.

Latin:

Ver. 23. NOVI DILVCVLO) Scribe Novæ, & refer ad miserationes: quotidie, inquit, aliæ alias sequuntur.

Merito corrigitur Latina: agnoscit etiam id Maldonatus !addita causa, quia sic Hebræi legunt (Ex Ebræo ergo corrigendus Latinus textus) Et sic emendata habent exemplaria, & sic LXX. quoque transtulerunt. Hæc ille. Ubi ergo Vulgatæ αὐθεντία?

De v. 25. usq; ad 33. egimus in Memoria justor. Witteberg. exhibita effigie patientiæ Christianæ & Misericordiæ divinæ Conc. 17.

## 3:26
Ver. 26. WITH SILENCE) That is, patience.

Latin:

Vers. 26. CVM SILENTIO) Id est, patientia.

## 3:28
Ver. 28. BECAUSE HE HATH LIFTED UP UPON HIM) He accommodates himself to the yoke. He does not throw off the yoke, or fight against the yoke.

Others explain it more correctly as referring to God, when He cast it upon him, in whose hand, namely, are all things, which Luther [expresses] by metalepsis, when something befalls him. Which B. Tarnovius observed in his Commentary on this passage. In the Hebrew it is כי נטל עליו which seems to be most conveniently rendered: Because He (God) laid upon him, the yoke, namely, of which mention had been made before. For נטל also signifies He laid upon, 2 Sam. 24:12. Three things I lay upon thee: whence נטל is a weight, a burden, which is laid upon someone. Prov. 27, v. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 28. QVIA LEVAVIT SVPER SE) Jugo se accommodat. Non jactat jugum, ε ζυγομαχεῖ.

Rectius de Deo id explicant alii, quando projecit super eum ille, in cujus scil. manu omnia, quod Lutherus per metalepsin, wenn ihn etwas überfällt. Quod observavit B. Tarnovius Comm. in h. l. In Ebræo est כי נטל עליו quod videtur commodissime reddi: Quia imposuit (Deus) super ipsum, jugum sc. cujus antea mentio facta erat. Nam נטל significat etiam imposuit 2. Sam. 24, 12. Tria ego impono super te: unde נטל pondus, onus, quod imponitur alicui. Prov. 27. v. 3.

## 3:29
Ver. 29. HE PUTTETH HIS MOUTH IN THE DUST] He worships God prostrate on the ground. Thus 1 Cor. 14, v. 25.

Not adequately. For that phrase imports something more: namely, humiliation, by which he acknowledges himself to be dust, and patience, that before he would speak against God, he would rather put his mouth in the dust.

Latin:

Vers. 29. PONIT IN PVLVERE OS SVVM] Deum adorat in terram pronus. Sic 1. Cor. 14. v. 25.

Non adæquate. Amplius enim quid phrasis illa importat: humiliationem nempe, qua se pulverem esse agnoscit & patientiam, quod priusquam Deo obloqui velit, potius in pulverem os suum ponat.

## 3:30
Ver. 30. HE GIVETH HIS CHEEK TO HIM THAT SMITETH HIM) Tacitus, Histories 3, spoke of offering one's face to insults. See what [is said] on Matt. 5:39, and on the Law of War and Peace, book 1, ch. 2, § 8.

Latin:

Vers. 30. DABIT PERCVTIENTI SE MAXILLAM) Os præbere contumeliis dixit Tacitus Histor. 3. Vide quæ ad Matth. 5, 39. & de Jure Belli & Pacis l. 1. c. 2. §. 8.

## 3:33
Ver. 33. FOR HE HATH NOT AFFLICTED) He hath afflicted.

FROM HIS HEART) Not that He wishes evil to the good, but that He may either test them or set them forth as an example of patience. See the following.

Latin:

Vers. 33. NON ENIM HVMILIAVIT) Afflixit.

EX CORDE SVO) Non quod bonis male velit, sed ut eos aut exploret, aut in exemplum patientiæ proponat. Vide sequentia.

## 3:38
Ver. 38. OUT OF THE MOUTH OF THE MOST HIGH SHALL NOT PROCEED BOTH GOOD AND EVIL) You may better connect it with those things above: Who shall say that out of the mouth of the Most High do not proceed both evil (that is, adversities) and good (that is, prosperities).

He corrects the Vulgate again. Blessed Luther also approves of that connection in his German translation. Maldonatus also agrees, as does Corn. a Lapide: This interrogation, he says, depends on the preceding verse, i.e., who is so impious as to say that neither adversities nor prosperities happen to us from the mouth, that is, the command and ordination of God. But concerning the Calvinist abuse of this aphorism, see Tarnov. Comm. in h. l. and the writers of the cited places. The sense is, as B. Hülsem. rightly says here, that nothing happens without divine providence, Is. 44, 6. 7. Am. 3, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 38. EX ORE ALTISSIMI NON EGREDIENTVR NEC BONA NEC MALA) Melius connectas cum illis superioribus: Quis dixerit ex ore Altissimi non procedere & mala i(d est,adversa) & bona, (id est, prospera.)

Iterum corrigit Vulgatam. Probat eam connexionem etiam B. Lutherus in translatione Germanica. Annuit etiam Maldonatus, ut & Corn. a Lapide: Pendet, inquit, hæc interrogatio ex versu præcedente, q. d. quis tam impius sit, ut dixerit, nec adversa, nec prospera evenire nobis ex ore, id est, præcepto & ordinatione Dei. De abusu autem hujus aphorismi Calviniano vid. Tarnov. Comm. in h. l. & LL. CC. Scriptores. Sensus est, ut hic recte B. Hülsem. nihil fieri citra providentiam divinam Es. 44, 6. 7. Am. 3, 6.

## 3:39
Ver. 39. WHY HATH A LIVING MAN MURMURED, A MAN FOR HIS SINS) Why should any man murmur because of his sins? that is, the punishments of his sins: if he is afflicted because of sins, let him correct himself.

He follows R. Solomon and Maldonatus here. You might translate more correctly from the Hebrew: Why, or what does a living man (to whom God still grants time for repentance) complain about? A man, or everyone (should murmur) against his sins, by which he drew upon himself those evils for which he grieves. And so also B. Luther. Thus there is no need to take sin metonymically for the punishment of sin.

Latin:

Vers. 39. QVID MVRMVRAVIT HOMO VIVENS, VIR PRO PECCATIS SVIS) Cur murmuret homo quisquam ob peccata sua? id est, pœnas peccatorum suorum: si ob peccata affligitur, corrigat se.

Sequitur hic R. Salomonem, & Maldonatum. Rectius ex Ebræo vertas: Cur, aut quid homo vivens (cui Deus adhuc pœnitentiæ tempus indulget) queritur? Vir seu unusquisque (murmuret) contra peccata sua, quibus mala illa, ob quæ dolet, sibi attraxit. Atq; ita etiam B. Lutherus. Sic opus non est peccatum accipere metonymice pro pœna peccati.

## 3:44
Ver. 44. THOU HAST SET A CLOUD FOR THYSELF THAT PRAYER MAY NOT PASS) The recent memory of sins.

God is said to cover Himself with a cloud when He does not open heaven to prayers: Cf. Syrac. 35. v. 19. Lam. 2. v. 1. c. 3. v. 8, Luther elegantly: you have covered yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer could pass through. Tarnovius notes from Kyber that these things are in Midrash Tillim: R. Chanina asked R. Nachmanni himself: what is that in Lam. 3. v. 44, you have covered yourself with a cloud, that prayer may not pass? He answered him: The gates of prayer are sometimes open, but sometimes they are closed. But the gates of repentance are never closed, because it is said in Ps. 65. v. 6, the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of the far-off sea. The sea is never closed forever, but whoever wishes to be washed in it can be washed, at whatever hour he wishes to do so. So also it is with repentance: for at any hour that he wishes to repent seriously, let him do so, and God will receive him. Others interpret it as a cloud of sins, hindering the hearing, Origen, Theodoret, Rabanus, Hugo, Lyranus from Is. 59. v. 2. Ps. 109. v. 18. But men interpose it, not God.

Latin:

Vers. 44. OPPOSVISTI NVBEM TIBI NE TRANSEAT ORATIO) Peccatorum recentem memoriam.

Dicitur se Deus nube operire, cum cælum pre- cibus non aperit: Conf. Syrac. 35. v. 19. Thren. 2. v. 1. c. 3. v. 8, Lutherus eleganter du hast dich mit einer Wolcken bedeckt, daß kein Gebet hindurch konte. Notat ex Kybero Tarnovius, quod in Midrasch Tillim hæc habeantur: Rogavit R. Chanina ipsum R. Nachmanni: quid est illud Thren. 3. v. 44. ob- duxisti tibi nubem, ne transeat oratio? Respondit illi: Portæ orationis quandoque sunt apertæ, quando- que vero clausæ. At portæ pœnitentiæ nunquam sunt clausæ, quia dicitur Psal. 65. v. 6. fiducia omni- um extremitatum terræ, & maris longinquarum. Mare nunquam in æternum clausum est, sed quicun- que vult lavari in illo, lavari potest, quacunque hora id facere voluerit. Sic etiam pœnitentia se habet: omni enim hora, qua voluerit serio facere pœnitenti- am, faciat, & Deus suscipiet eum. Alii de nube peccatorum interpretantur, impediente exaudi- tionem, Origenes, Theodor. Raban. Hugo, Lyran. ex Es. 59. v. 2. Ps. 109. v. 18. Sed eam homines inter- ponunt, non Deus.

## 3:45
Ver. 45. THOU HAST MADE ME AN ERADICATION AND AN ABJECTION IN THE MIDST OF THE PEOPLES] In the Hebrew: Thou hast made us (for the Prophet is not speaking specially about himself here, but about the whole people) an outcasting and filth among the peoples. סחי is properly what the Apostle Paul called περίψημα 1 Cor. 4. v. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ERADICATIONEM ET ABJECTIONEM POSVISTI ME IN MEDIO POPVLORVM] In Hebræo: Ejectamentum & sordes posuisti nos (non enim specialiter de se hic, sed toto de populo Propheta loquitur) inter populos. סחי proprie est quod Paulus Apostolus dixit περίψημα 1. Cor. 4. v. 13.

## 3:46
Ver. 46. THEY HAVE OPENED THEIR MOUTH UPON US] Above 2. v. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 46. APERVERVNT SVPER NOS OS SVVM] Supra 2. v. 16.

## 3:47
Ver. 47.

FEAR AND A SNARE IS BECOME UPON US, PROPHECY AND DESTRUCTION] Better from the Hebrew: Fear and a pit has happened to us, devastation and destruction.

The version of B. Luther also returns to this; the Papists themselves acknowledge that the error of the Vulgate is either from the scribes, who wrote 'prophecy' instead of 'devastation', or from a παροράματι of the author. See Maldonatus on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 47.

FORMIDO ET LAQVEVS FACTA EST NOBIS VATICINATIO ET CONTRITIO] Melius ex Hebræo: Formido & fovea evenit nobis, vastatio & contritio.

Huc etiam B. Lutheri versio redit, Vulgatæ errorem vel a librariis, qui loco vastationis va- ticinationem scripserunt, vel a παροράματι auto- ris esse, agnoscunt ipsimet Papistæ. Vid. Maldo- nat. in h. l.

## 3:48
Ver. 48. MY EYE HATH BROUGHT DOWN DIVISIONS OF WATERS] Better: My eye flows with rivers of waters.

Luther elegantly: 'my eyes run down with water-brooks over the misery': For the eye is placed in the singular for the plural. Tarnovius posits a hypallage, 'my eye descends in rivers of waters', that is, my eyes almost descend and flow down from my head, with so many tears that the moisture flows everywhere in rivers.

Latin:

Vers. 48. DIVISIONES AQVARVM DEDVXIT OCVLVS MEVS] Melius: Rivis aquarum manat oculus meus.

Eleganter Lutherus: meine Augen rinnen mit Wasser-Bächen über den Jammer: Singulare enim oculus positus est pro plurali. Hypallagen ponit Tarnovius, rivis aquarum descendit oculus meus, id est, oculi mei fere descendunt ac defluunt ex capite, cum lacrymis tam multis, ut humor defluat un- dique rivis.

## 3:49
Ver. 49.

AND HATH NOT BEEN SILENT) Nor has it rested: For thus דמת is often taken.

The Latin version is rightly explained or rather corrected in this way, according to the sources. B. Luther: 'For there is no ceasing there.'

Latin:

Vers. 49.

NEC TACVIT) Nec quievit: Ita enim דמת sæpe sumitur.

Recte ita explicatur vel emendatur potius Latina versio, juxta fontes. B. Lutherus: Denn es ist kein aufhören da.

## 3:51
Ver. 51. MY EYE HATH SPOILED MY SOUL] The Chaldean rightly explains: My weeping was so great that it harmed my life (that is, my health).

IN ALL THE DAUGHTERS OF MY CITY) When the towns situated around Jerusalem were being captured on all sides.

Latin:

Vers. 51. OCVLVS MEVS DEPRÆDATVS EST ANI- MAM MEAM] Chaldæus recte explicat: Tantus fuit fletus meus, ut noceret vitæ (id est, valetudini) meæ.

IN CVNCTIS FILIABVS VRBIS MEÆ) Cum oppida circum Hierosolyma sita undique caperentur.

## 3:52
Ver. 52. THEY HAVE TAKEN ME IN HUNTING) Jer. 37, 12. 13. WITHOUT CAUSE) Without any crime of mine.

Grotius takes these and the following things concerning Jeremiah, but the context teaches that they are to be understood concerning the Church. And the prayer, which is held in the last verses, agrees more if it is said that the afflictions of the Church are being described. For the Holy Spirit is accustomed to express all sorts of dire things through such imprecations against the enemies of the Church. Osiander himself, although he applied certain things in this chapter to Jeremiah, explains these latter things concerning the whole Church or the Jewish people. Nevertheless, Jeremiah could have alluded with metaphorical expressions to those things which he himself suffered: which is also customary in the Psalms of David. Cornelius acknowledges that Theodoret, indeed, Hugo, Thomas, and Lyranus explain it concerning the people captured by the Chaldeans, who are called hunters in Jer. 16, 16, for these hunted the Jews without cause, even if he thinks that Jeremiah returns here to himself and his own miseries.

Latin:

Vers. 52. VENATIONE CEPERVNT ME) Jer. 37, 12. 13. GRATIS) Sine ullo meo crimine.

De Jeremia hæc & sequentia accipit Grotius, sed ea de Ecclesia intelligenda esse, contextus docet. Et votum, quod versibus ultimis habetur, magis congruit, si dicatur afflictiones Ecclesiæ describi. So- let enim Ecclesiæ hostibus talibus imprecationi- bus dira quæq; mirari Sp. S. Osiander ipse, etsi quæ- dam in hoc capite Jeremiæ applicarit, hæc poste- riora de tota Ecclesia vel populo Judaico explicat. Potuit tamen Jeremias metaphoricis loquutionibus allufisse ad ea, quæ ipse passus est: quod in Davidis quoq; Psalmis solemne est. Theodore tum sane, Hugo- nem, Thomam, & Lyranum exponere de populo capto a Chaldæis, qui vocentur Venatores Jer. 16, 16. hi e- nim venati sunt Judæos gratis, agnoscit Cornelius, etsi redire hic Jeremiam ad se & suas ærumnas putet.

## 3:53
Vers. 53. MY LIFE HAS FALLEN INTO THE PIT) See Jeremiah 37:6. AND THEY HAVE PLACED A STONE OVER ME) By which the pit was obstructed. See a similar instance in the History of Daniel. Osiander, reading from the Hebrew, more correctly says: They have blotted out my life in the pit. They have cast a stone over me: that is, they killed and threw me into the pit, and cast stones over me, as those do who wickedly commit murder. By these words, he says, the Prophet describes the virulence and cruelty of the enemies of the Church of God: for they desire the Church to be utterly extinguished and destroyed. They covered my head with waters: so that I could not emerge: then I said to myself: I have perished, it is all over with me. By these various figurative speeches, the Prophet teaches with what great evils the Church is overwhelmed: so that at times it seems to have perished entirely: But the Lord meanwhile sustains it miraculously. Maldonatus says that it at least alludes to the pit into which the Prophet was thrown: and he admits that by metaphor, waters are called adverse things, the waves of fortune, as in Ps. 69:2. Vers. 54. WATERS HAVE OVERFLOWED OVER MY HEAD) He said water for mud. Vers. 55. FROM THE LOWEST PIT) More correctly, the deepest. Vers. 56. DO NOT TURN AWAY THINE EAR) More correctly: Thou hast not turned away. Vers. 63. SEE THEIR SITTING AND THEIR RISING) By sitting and rising, the Hebrews understand all the leisure and business of men. See Ps. 139:2. Vers. 65. THOU SHALT GIVE THEM THE SHIELD OF THE HEART THY LABOR) Better, the covering of the heart. For הגין is to cover. Thou shalt cause their heart to flee from them. But what is here 'labor', in the Hebrew is 'execration', תאלתך. But the Greeks and the Latin read תלאתך with the letters transposed. We do not labor over the mistranslation of the Vulgate, whose errors are obvious everywhere. In the former clause, however, it can still be defended: where Grotius explains מגנת as covering. R. Kimchi, Pagninus, and Vatablus explain it as anguish, affliction, sorrow, sighs. Piscator as the obsession of the heart, that is, extreme anxiety. Schindler as the covering and pain of the heart. Which the Vulgate renders as 'shield'. Regarding which, Luc. Bacmeister the elder says: as a shield covers the body, so miseries and sorrows surround the heart, and press upon it as if most heavily, so that it struggles with perpetual dread and torture. Thus the curse will be as a shield: Cf. Ps. 109:18-19. In the Hebrew there is a neat wordplay: Give them to whom I am my shield (v. 63) pain of heart was מגנת and may thy execration come upon them. Corn. a Lapide as the encircling of the heart, that is, sorrow and ardor, which encircles, closes, anguishes, and oppresses the heart, as do Vatablus and the Chaldean. B. Luther elegantly: let it terrify the heart, and feel thy curse.

Latin:

Vers. 53. LAPSA EST IN LACVM VITA MEA) Vide Jeremiæ 37, 6. ET POSUERUNT LAPIDEM SUPER ME) Quo pu- teus obstruebatur. Vide simile in Historia Danielis. Rectius Osiander ex Ebræo ita legens: De- leverunt vitam meam in puteo. Conjecerunt lapidem super me: id est, occiderunt & abjecerunt, me in puteum, & lapides super me conjecerunt, ut fa- ciunt, qui sceleste cædem committunt. His verbis, inquit, Propheta virulentiam & crudelitatem hostium Ec- clesiæ Dei describit: quippe qui Ecclesiam plane extin- ctam & deletam cupiunt. Operuerunt aquis caput meum: ut emergere non potuerim: tum apud me dixi: Perii, actum est omnino de me. Variis hisce fi- guratis sermonibus docet Propheta, quantis malis Ec- clesia obruatur: ut quandoque plane videatur periisse: Sed Dominus interim eam mirabiliter sustentat. Allu- dere saltem ad lacum ait Maldonatus, in quem pro- jectus fuit Propheta: & per metaphoram aquas vocari res adversas fluctusῦ fortune, admittit, ut Pf. 69, 2. Vers. 54. INUNDAVERUNT AQVÆ SUPER CAPUT MEUM) Aquam dixit pro luto. Vers. 55. DE LACU NOVISSIMO) Rectius profundissimo. Vers. 56. NE AVERTAS AUREM) Rectius: non aver- tisti. Vers. 63. SESSIONEM EORUM ET RESURRECTIO- NEM EORUM VIDE) Per sedere & surgere Hebræi omnia hominum otia & negotia intelligunt. Vide Pf. 139. v. 2. Vers. 65. DABIS EIS SCUTUM CORDIS LABOREM TUUM) Melius absconsionem cordis. Nam הגין est ab- scondere. Facies, ut cor ipsis refugiat. Quod vero hic est labo- rem, in Hebræo est, exsecrationem, תאלתך. At Græci & Latinus legerunt תלאתך transpositis litteris. Non laboramus de παρερμηνείᾳ Vulgati, cujus παροράματα passim obvia sunt. In priori tamen in- cisu defendi adhuc potest: ubi מגנת absconsionem explicat Grotius. R. Kimchi, Pagninus, Vatablus ex- ponunt angustiam, afflictionem, mærorem, suspiria. Piscator obsessionem cordis, hoc est, anxietatem sum- mam. Schindlerus operimentum atq; dolorem cordis. Quod Vulgata reddit scutum. Quod de Luc. Bacmei- sterus senior: ut scutum contegit corpus, ita miseria & dolores cor circumdant, & quasi gravissime premunt, ut cum perpetuo pavore & cruciatu luctetur. Ita ma- ledictio erit quasi Clypeus: Conf. Pf. 109, 18. 19. In Ebræo est παρονομασία concinna: Da illis quibus ego sum מגיני (v. 63.) dolorem cordis fuit מגנת & execratio tua obveniat illis. Corn. a Lapide circumcin- Etionem cordis, id est, mærorem & ardorem, qui cor cingat, claudat, angat, opprimat, uti Vatabl. & Chal- dæus. B. Lutherus eleganter laß ihn das Herz er- schrecken, und deinen Fluch fühlen.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

The Prophet deplores the desolation of the sanctuary, the horrible famine, and the occupation of the city, and the cause of these evils, the shedding of innocent blood, and the vanity of the hope of foreign aid, which led the King into captivity, with the addition of some consolation that the guilt of Zion will cease, and the malice of the daughter of Edom will be visited.

Vers. 1. HOW IS THE GOLD DARKENED, THE FINE COLOR CHANGED) By gold, the Princes are to be understood. THE STONES OF THE SANCTUARY ARE DISPERSED) That is, the Priests and Levites.

So indeed with Olympiodorus, Lyranus, Dionysius, Vatablus, Emanuel Saa: But more correctly according to the letter, from which one should not depart without necessity, most others understand it of the gold of the temple (1 Kings 6:20, 1 Chron. 7:4) and the stones of the sanctuary, of which the temple consisted, skillfully sanctified, hewn, and polished (1 Kings 5:17, ch. 6, 7), and they say the devastation of the temple is designated, with the Chaldean, Rabanus, and Hugo. The former explanation of Grotius agrees neither with the phrase of Scripture nor sufficiently with the text; since here in verse 1 the destruction of the temple is deplored, but in the following second verse, the unworthy estimation of the sons or inhabitants of Zion is described; as the words themselves clearly teach, and most Interpreters, Osiander and Vinariensis in their paraphrase, Cramer in his summaries, Tarnovius in his Commentary, Corn. à Lapide, Maldonatus in this place, and others explain. Vers. 2. IN EARTHEN VESSELS] In pottery of no value. Vers. 3. BUT EVEN THE SEA MONSTERS HAVE DRAWN OUT THE BREAST, THEY HAVE SUCKLED THEIR YOUNG] תנין which is here in the Hebrew, sometimes signifies a dragon, sometimes any sea monster, and is translated in Greek elsewhere as κῆτος, elsewhere as σειρὴν, as also here by Symmachus. DAUGHTER OF MY PEOPLE] Jerusalem. LIKE THE OSTRICH IN THE DESERT] So also the Greeks στρουθίον. And the Scholiasts interpret it as στρουθοκάμηλον. It seems that in the Hebrew, through a fault of the writer, the י has slipped out, for יענים are ostriches, or little ostriches, Lev. 11:16, ch. 14:15, Job 30:29, Isaiah 43:20, ch. 34:13. Ostriches neglect their eggs. See Job 39:15. It seems to Grotius here that in the Hebrew, through a fault of the Scribe, the י has slipped out, because יענים are ostriches. But what Grotius may have seen, I cannot see. For it is read in all the copies I have been able to inspect, nor do I find any omission of it observed by the Interpreters. Vers. 4. THE TONGUE OF THE SUCKLING HAS CLEAVED TO HIS PALATE FOR THIRST] Because the women, exhausted by famine, had no milk. THEY HAVE EMBRACED DUNG] They sought whether there was any food in the dunghills. See 2 Kings 18:27. Vers. 6. THE INIQUITY OF THE DAUGHTER OF MY PEOPLE IS MADE GREATER THAN THE SIN OF SODOM] Because no prophets had been sent to the citizens of Sodom, as the Chaldean notes here. Cf. Matthew 11:23. IT WAS OVERTHROWN IN A MOMENT, AND HANDS DID NOT TAKE HOLD IN IT) In the Hebrew: Hands did not sit in it: it did not suffer a siege by a hostile army before it was destroyed. Vers. 7. HER NAZARITES WERE WHITER THAN SNOW] Because of frequent washings. CLEANER THAN MILK] Well-fed. REDDER THAN ANCIENT IVORY] פנינים, which is here in the Hebrew, is usually translated as precious stones. Here, carbuncles or rubies are to be understood: whence the Greeks here rightly translated it as 'they were reddened'. MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN SAPPHIRE] In the Hebrew: Sapphire was their cutting: their polishing was like that of sapphire. Vers. 9. IT WAS BETTER FOR THOSE KILLED BY THE SWORD THAN FOR THOSE KILLED BY FAMINE] Happier were those who perished by the sword, and not by a slow and agonizing death, which Homer called the worst of all. Verse 10. THE HANDS OF MERCIFUL WOMEN COOKED THEIR OWN CHILDREN] See above 2, 20. Similar to 2 Kings 6, 28. 29. and in the history of Josephus concerning the siege by Titus Vespasian. Verse 13. BECAUSE OF THE SINS OF HIS PROPHETS) Note again 'his'. For he indicates the false prophets, whom the people had chosen for themselves. AND THE INIQUITIES OF HIS PRIESTS) That is, even of the priests: to such an extent had the corruption of morals invaded all orders. Verse 14. THEY WANDERED BLIND IN THE STREETS) That is, like the blind. The priests who had shed innocent blood were sprinkled with blood on all sides when the city was captured. They wandered like the blind, they ran hither and thither, uncertain where to turn themselves because of the multitude of corpses. I shall append to this passage, which is difficult enough, the interpretation of Ludov. de Dieu, but reduced to a summary. It is as follows: It contains the punishment which, on account of the sins of the prophets and priests shedding blood in the midst of the holy city, befell the whole people: The punishment, however, is threefold: 1. They wandered blind through the streets, that is, they ran about here and there like blind men because of the cruelty of the enemies. 2. They defiled themselves with blood. They rushed through the very blood of the slain, and thus defiled themselves. 3. That which was not permitted to them, they touched with their garments: that is, corpses, which it was forbidden by law to touch. But they could not find a firm resting place elsewhere either. For 'depart, you unclean' was said to them, 'depart, depart, do not touch.' Because they fled away, or rather wandered, (or for that reason they flew away.) Although they could not remain long where they entered. For it was said among the nations, they shall not continue to dwell.

THEY ARE POLLUTED WITH BLOOD, AND SINCE THEY COULD NOT, THEY HELD THEIR SKIRTS Since they could not otherwise avoid the blood, they held the hem of their garments with their hands.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

Deplorat Propheta desolationem sanctuarii, hor- ribilem famem, & occupationem urbis, ac malorum istorum causam, effusionem innocui sanguinis, & vanitatem spei exteri auxilii, quæ Regem in captivitatem egit, addito ali- quo solatio cessaturæ culpæ Zionis, & visitan- dæ ἐπιχαιρεκακίας filiæ Edom.

Vers. 1. QVOMODO OBSCURATUM EST AURUM MUTATUS EST COLOR OPTIMUS) Per aurum Princi- pes intelligendi. DISPERSI SUNT LAPIDES SANCTUARII) Id est, Sacerdotes & Levitæ.

ITa quidem cum Olympiodoro, Lyranus, Diony- sius, Vatablus, Emanuel Saa: Sed rectius ad lite- ram, a qua præter necessitatem discedendum non est, de auro templi 1. Reg. 6, 20. 1. Chron. 7, 4. & la- pidibus sanctuarii, ex quibus templum constabat, affabre sanctis, dolatis, & perpolitis 1. Reg. 5, 17. c. 6. 7. alii plerique intelligunt, ac templi devastationem designari ajunt, cum Chaldæo, Rabano, Hugone. Pri- or Grotii explicatio neque phrasi Scripturæ, neque textui satis congruit: quum hic vers. 1. deploretur templi destructio, versu autem secundo sequenti, filiorum vel incolarum Sion præstantissimorum indigna æstimatio describatur; Uti verba ipsa luculenter docent, ac plerique Interpp. Osiander & Vinariens. in paraphr. Cramerus in sumariis, Tarnovius in Comm. Corn. à Lap. Maldonatus in h. l. & alii explicant. Vers. 2. IN VASA TESTEA] In fictilia nullius pretii. Vers. 3. SED ET LAMIÆ NUDAVERUNT MAMMAM, LACTAVERUNT CATULOS SUOS] תנין quod hic est in Hebræo, modo Draconem, modo quodvis monstrum marinum significat, vertiturque Græce alibi κῆτος, alibi σειρὴν, ut & hic à Symmacho. FILIA POPULI MEI] Hierosolyma. QUASI STRUTHIO IN DESERTO] Sic & Græci στρουθίον. Et Scholiastæ interpretantur στρουθοκάμηλον. Videtur hic in Hebræo per scriptoris vitium elapsum י, nam יענים sunt στρουθοὶ, vel στρουθία, Lev. 11, 16. c. 14, 15. Job. 30, 29. Esaiæ 43, 20. c. 34, 13. Struthiones ova sua negligunt. Vid. Job. 39, 15. Videtur hic Grotio in Ebræo vitio Scriptoris elapsum י, quia יענים sunt στρουθοὶ. Sed quid Grotius viderit, videre non possum. Legitur enim in omnibus, quæ contigit inspicere exemplaribus, neque ἔκπτωσιν ejus ab Interpretibus observatam reperio. Vers. 4. ADHÆSIT LINGVA LACTENTIS AD PALATUM EJUS IN SITI] Quia fœminæ fame exhaustæ lac non habebant. AMPLEXATI SUNT STERCORA] Quæsierunt an in fimetis aliquid esset alimenti. Vide 2. Reg. 18, 27. Vers. 6. MAJOR EFFECTA EST INIQVITAS FILIÆ POPULI MEI PECCATO SODOMORVM] Quia Prophetæ nulli ad Sodomorum cives missi fuerant, ut hic notat Chaldæus. Conf. Matth. 11, 23. SUBVERSA EST IN MOMENTO, ET NON CEPERUNT IN EA MANUS) In Hebræo: Non sederunt in eam manus: non passa est obsidionem ab hostili exercitu antequam diureretur. Vers. 7. CANDIDIORES NAZARÆI EJUS NIVE] Ob crebras lotiones. NITIDIORES LACTE] Bene habiti. RUBICUNDIORES EBORE ANTIQVO] פנינים, quod hic est in Hebræo verti solet, λίθοι πολυτελεῖς. Hic intelligendi pyropi, sive carbunculi: unde Græci hic bene ἐπυῤῥώθησαν. SAPPHIRO PULCHRIORES] In Hebræo: Sapphyrus excisio eorum: erat polities eorum qualis Sapphiri. Vers. 9. MELIUS FUIT OCCISIS GLADIO, QVAM INTERFECTIS FAME] Feliciores fuere qui gladio perierunt, non autem lenta ac cruciabili morte quam pessimam omnium dixit Homerus. Vers. 10. MANUS MULIERUM MISERICORDIUM COXERUNT FILIOS SUOS] Vide supra 2, 20. Simile 2. Reg. 6, 28. 29. & in historia Josephi de obsidione per Titum Vespasianum. Vers. 13. PROPTER PECCATA PROPHETARUM EJUS) Nota iterum ejus. Falsos enim Prophetas indicat, quos populus sibi asciverat. ET INIQVITATES SACERDOTUM EJUS) Id est, etiam Sacerdotum: adeo omnes ordines invaserat morum corruptio. Vers. 14. ERRAVERUNT CÆCI IN PLATEIS) Id est, ut cæci. Sacerdotes qui sanguinem injustum effuderant, undique sanguine aspersi fuere cum urbs caperetur. Erraverunt ut cæci, cursitarunt huc illuc, incerti quo se verterent præ multitudine cadaverum. Adscribam ad hunc locum, qui difficilis satis Ludov. de Dieu interpretationem, sed in compendium redactam. Ea ita habet: Pœnam continet, quæ ob peccata Prophetarum & Sacerdotum effundentium sanguinem in medio sanctæ urbis toti populo evenit: Pœna autem triplex: 1. Vagati cæci sunt per plateas, id est, hinc inde cæcorum instar ob hostium crudelitatem, discurrerunt. 2. Contaminarunt se sanguine. Ruerunt per ipsum interfectorum sanguinem, atque ita se contaminarunt. 3. Quod non licebat ipsis, attingebant vestimentis: id est, cadavera, quæ attingere lege prohibitum erat. Sed nec alibi firmam sedem invenire potuere. Nam recedite immundi dictum est illis, recedite, recedite, ne attingite. Quia avolarunt, imo vagati sunt, (vel ideo avolarunt.) Etsi quo intrarunt, diu hæ- rere non potuerunt. Nam dictum est inter gentes, non pergent commorari.

POLLVTI SVNT IN SANGVINE, CVMQV NON POSSENT TENVERVNT LACINIAS SVAS Cum aliter sanguinem vitare non possent, oram vestium ma- nibus tenuere.

## 4:15
Ver. 15. DEPART, YE POLLUTED, THEY CRIED UNTO THEM) By the very nations, they were held to be polluted, those who ought to have avoided all pollutions most religiously. For it was the opinion of the nations that those to whom blood adhered were polluted.

FOR THEY HAVE QUARRELED, AND HAVE BEEN MOVED AMONG THE NATIONS) That is, many of the nations, moved by grave anger against such miserable people, said.

Ver. same. HE SHALL NOT ADD ANY MORE TO DWELL AMONG THEM) Namely, God does not wish to dwell among those so polluted. They read לא יוסיף. But our Hebrew Codices have לא יוסיפו they shall not dwell any more, namely, the Jews in their own land.

Our Codices are correct: whatever the Vulgate may have seen. D. Backmeisterus renders the sense in this way: the simpler meaning seems to be that these murderers were so foul and polluted with blood that they even warned everyone they met not to approach them and be polluted by their touch, and therefore they fled from others and said openly that they could not dwell any longer with such murderers. Cf. Tarnovius on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 15. RECEDITE POLLVTI, CLAMAVERVN EIS) Illis qui omnes pollutiones religiosissime vitare debe- bant, ab ipsis gentibus habiti sunt pro pollutis. Nam gentium erat opinio, pollutos esse quibus adhæreret sanguis.

JVRGATI QVIPPE SVNT, ET COMMOTI IN TER GENTES) Id est, multi ex gentibus gravi ira in tan miseros commoti dixerunt.

Vers. eod. NON ADDIT VLTRA VT HABITE IN EIS) Nempe, Deus apud tam pollutos versari nolet. Le- gerunt לא יוסיף. At nostri Codices Hebræi haben לא יוסיפו non habitabunt ultra, nempe Judæi in Patri sua.

Recte se habent nostri Codices: quidquid vide- rit Vulgatus. Sensum reddit D. Backmeisterus hoc modo: simplicior sententia esse videtur, quod tam fœ- di & polluti sanguine fuerint homicidæ isti, ut etiam obvios quosq́; monuerint, ne sibi appropinquarent, & attactu suo polluerentur, ideoque alios fugisse, & dixisse se palam, quod cum talibus homicidis diutius habita- re non possint. Conf. Tarnovium in hunc locum.

## 4:16
Ver. 16. THE FACE OF THE LORD HATH DIVIDED THEM) The anger of God scattered them. But the Greeks read חלקם with different vowel points. For they translate it μερὶς αὐτῶν.

Grotius acknowledges that the Greeks read it wrongly in this way: preferring the Hebrew, as is proper, and the sense is plain, which B. Luther correctly expressed, Darum hat sie dess HErrn Zorn zerstreuet.

THEY DID NOT REVERENCE THE FACE OF THE PRIESTS) The nations reproached the Hebrews with these things: they said there is no hope of return for them: They even raged against good priests. See the example in 2 Chron. 24:22.

NOR DID THEY HAVE COMPASSION ON THE OLD) Not regarding the gods in their hearts, nor having pity. As Homer says in Odyssey Ξ.

Latin:

Vers. 16. FACIES DOMINI DIVISIT EOS) Ira Dei dispersit eos. At Græci חלקם legerunt cum aliis pun- ctis. Vertunt enim μερὶς αὐτῶν.

Male legisse ita Græcos agnoscit Grotius: E- bræum præferens, uti par est, sensusque planus est, quem recte expressit B. Lutherus, Darum hat sie dess HErrn Zorn zerstreuet.

FACIES SACERDOTVM NON ERVBVERVNT) Hæc gentes exprobrabant Hebræis: nulla dicebant spes est il- lis reditus: Etiam in bonos Sacerdotes sævierunt. Vide ex- emplum 2. Paral. 24, 22.

NEQVE SENVM MISERTI SVNT) ἐκ ὄπιδα φρονέοντες ἐπὶ φρεσὶν, ὐδ᾽ ἐλεητύν. Ut ait Homerus Odysseæ Ξ.

## 4:17
Ver. 17. WHILE WE WERE YET STANDING, OUR EYES FAILED FOR OUR VAIN HELP: WHEN WE LOOKED ATTENTIVELY TO A NATION THAT COULD NOT SAVE) That is, while our affairs were still standing, we looked to the Egyptians, but in vain. See 2 Kings 18:21.

Latin:

Vers. 17. CVM ADHVC SVBSISTEREMVS, DEFE- CERVNT OCVLI NOSTRI AD AVXILIVM NO- STRVM VANVM: CVM RESPICEREMVS ATTENTI AD GENTEM QVÆ SALVARE NON POTERAT) Id est, cum adhuc starent res nostræ, respeximus ad Ægyptios, sed frustra. Vide 2. Reg. 18, 21.

## 4:18
Ver. 18. OUR STEPS SLIPPED) I do not see clearly how the Latin interpreter read it. But there was a double reading from antiquity, צרו and צדו. Aben-Ezra and others follow the latter, interpreting: they narrowed our steps: that is, they had closed all exits: the Chaldean follows the former: They hunted our footsteps. See 2 Kings 24:5. The Greeks depart further, for they read צערינו, ἐσμικρυναν μικρὺς ἡμῶν.

He sweats much in thinking up various readings: but no necessity compels us to acknowledge them, since there could have been an error in the translation, even if the same reading prevailed, or the sense was expressed in other words. For they did not always render word for word. The Hebrew text has צדו which is 'they hunted': as the Chaldean, Pagninus, and Arias Montanus rendered it, and because hunters do not only observe, but also narrow the steps of wild beasts, therefore Aben-Ezra rendered it according to the sense, 'they narrowed our steps.' Which the Latin also explains in some way: 'They made our footsteps slippery,' that is, we could not walk safely in the middle of our streets, because the enemies placed snares not only outside, but also in the middle of the streets, as is explained by R. Solomon. From the Greek version, nothing else can be concluded, if it be sincere, as it came from the hand of the LXX Interpreters, than a παρόραμα of the translators. B. Luther rightly and clearly: One hunted us, so that we might not walk in our streets.

OUR END HAS DRAWN NEAR) Of the city and the civil state.

OUR DAYS ARE COMPLETED BECAUSE OUR END HAS COME) That is, that time destined for the destruction of the nation.

Latin:

Vers. 18. LVBRICAVERVNT VESTIGIA NOSTRA) Non satis video, quomodo legerit Latinus Interpres. At duplex ab antiquo fuit lectio צרו & צדו. Hanc sequun- tur Aben-Esdra & alii interpretantes: arctaverunt gressus no- stros: id est, egressus omnes clauserant: illam Chaldæus: Venatice institerunt vestigiis nostris. Vid. 2. Reg. 24, 5. Græci longius abeunt, legerunt enim צרנו צערינו, ἐσμικ- ρυναν μικρὺς ἡμῶν.

Multum sudat in excogitandis variis lectioni- bus: quas vero ut agnoscamus, nulla cogit neces- sitas, quum erratum esse potuerit in translatione, utut eadem obtinuerit lectio, aut verbis aliis ex- pressus sensus. Non enim semper verbum verbo reddidere. Ebræus textus habet צדו quod est vena- ti sunt: ut Chaldæus, Pagninus, Ariæmontanus red- didere, & quia venatores non observant tantum, sed etiam coarctant gressus ferarum, ideo ad sen- sum reddidit Aben-Ezra, arctaverunt gressus nostros. Quem etiam exponit aliqua ratione Latinus: Lu- bricaverunt vestigia nostra, hoc est, in mediis plateis nostris non poteramus tuto ambulare, quia insidias po- fuerunt hostes non solum foris, sed etiam in plateis me- diis, ut exponitur R. Salomo. E Græca versione nil aliud nisi παρόραμα, si illa sincera sit, ut a manu LXX. Interpretum prodiit, translatorum conclu- di potest. B. Lutherus recte & perspicue: Man jagte uns, daß wir auf unsern Gassen nicht gehen durfften.

APPROPINQVAVIT FINIS NOSTER) Vrbis & sta- tus civilis.

COMPLETI SVNT DIES NOSTRI QVIA VENIT FINIS NOSTER) Id est, tempus illud exitio gentis desti- natum.

## 4:19
Vers. 19. OUR PURSUERS WERE SWIFTER

THAN THE EAGLES OF THE HEAVENS] It represents those last times which preceded the time of the captured city. There was nowhere an escape; in the mountains, in the plains, everywhere there were those who would intercept those wishing to flee because of famine.

Latin:

Vers. 19. VELOCIORES FVERVNT PERSECVTORES

NOSTRI AQVILIS COELI] Repræsentat ultima illa tem- pora, quæ antecesferunt captæ urbis tempus. Nusquam erat ef- fugium, in montibus, in planis, ubique erant, qui intercipe- rent ob famem fugere volentes.

## 4:20
Vers. 20. THE BREATH OF OUR MOUTHS CHRIST THE LORD WAS CAPTURED IN OUR SINS) The King, he says, was captured because of our sins. Some of the Hebrews trace this back to Josiah: But whoever has rightly considered the preceding things will see that these are much more rightly applied to Zedekiah.

Not only do some Hebrews, along with the Chaldean, take this concerning Josiah, but also Jerome in ch. 12 of Zechariah, Rabanus, Hugo, Vatablus, Sanchez, and others, i.e., from the slaughter of Josiah our calamity and ruin began: But we grant that these are more conveniently understood concerning Zedekiah, whether we look at the antecedents and consequents, or the native meaning of the words, because Josiah was not captured, but wounded. Many, however, of the Fathers—Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Tertullian, Ambrose, Theodoret, Olympiodorus, Eusebius in book 4 of the Demonstratio ch. 24, Rufinus in the Symbolum, Prosper part 3 of the Praedicta 21, Fulgentius book 3 to Thrasimund, Paschasius, the Author of the marginal gloss, and in part and hesitantly Jerome in this place—understand it concerning Christ, which explanation most Papists embrace, because of the Vulgate version. For in it is held 'Christ the Lord was captured in our sins,' as if the name יהוה should be rendered in the nominative case, and flies to Christ, whom Jeremiah loved most and lamented, whose type Zedekiah was, in a prophetic manner, who is the Breath of our mouths, that is, our soul and life, as Origen, Rupert, and Lyranus interpret. Concerning whom see at length Christoph. a Castro, and Corn. à Lapide. But that transition to Christ would be foreign here, where the Prophet in Lamentations deplores the calamities of his own time, and speaks openly of the insidious hunting of the Chaldeans, and their swift pursuit, which not even the King could escape without falling into their hands. Therefore it should be rendered: the anointed of the Lord, not the Lord: For the name משיח is placed in the status of regimen, which error of the Vulgate version and the LXX Interpreters, who likewise rendered it by apposition χρισὸς κύριος, Grotius passes over with a dry foot. But the Jews say the King is the Breath of their mouth, because he preserved life for them, just as the air which we draw: under whose protection they were able to breathe and breathe well, and to despise the spirit and threats of the enemies: or because he was as dear to them as the vital spirit, as the Chaldean explained. Therefore B. Luther according to the sense, 'He who was our comfort': who in the marginal note explains it concerning the King of the Jews, and as it appears, concerning Zedekiah, of whom Franc. Junius, Piscator, Osiander, the Vinarieans, Bacmeister, Tarnovius, and others of our side also interpret; yet B. Joh. Henricus Ursinus, in his Adversaria, explained it concerning Christ our Lord, captured in our sins, or rather cast into the pit of the Jews, who is the shade of the faithful. Sacr. 1. p. 210. in the words, 'he was captured in their pits,' as Lyranus and Arias Montanus translated, that it is a proverbial metaphor, explaining it thus: the princes of the Jews dug a pit for the Lord, in which they themselves perished.

TO WHOM WE SAID: IN THY SHADOW WE SHALL LIVE AMONG THE NATIONS) Under whose protection we had hoped we would live safely, even against the will of the nations.

Latin:

Vers. 20. SPIRITUS ORIS NOSTRI CHRISTVS DO- MINVS CAPTVS EST IN PECCATIS NOSTRIS) Rex, ait, captus est ob peccata nostra. Retro trahunt hoc ad Josiam Hebræorum nonnulli: Sed qui præcedentia recte considera- verit, videbit multo hæc rectius ad Sedeciam aptari.

De Josia non tantum Ebræi nonnulli cum Chal- dæo, sed etiam Hieronymus in c. 12. Zach. Rabanus, Hugo, Vatablus, Sanchez & alii accipiunt, q. d. a cæ- de Josiæ cœpit calamitas & ruina nostra: Sed largi- mur, convenientius hæc de Zedekia accipi, sive antecedentia & consequentia spectemus, sive si- gnificationem nativam verborum, quia Josias non est captus, sed vulneratus. Multi tamen è Patribus Justinus, Ireneus, Origenes, Tertullianus, Ambrosius, Theodoretus, Olympiodorus, Eusebius l. 4. demonstr. c. 24. Ruffin. in Symbol. Prosper part. 3. prædict. 21. Fulgent. l. 3. ad Thrasim. Paschasius, Autor gloss. margin. ex parte etiam ac dubitanter Hieronymus in h. l. de Christo intelligunt, quam explicationem Papistæ plerique amplectuntur, ob versionem vulga- tam. In ea enim habetur Christus Dominus captus est in peccatis nostris, quasi nomen יהוה in casu re- cto reddendum sit, & ad Christum, quem maxime amabat, & plangebat Jeremias, cujus typus erat Zedekias, more Prophetico, avolet, qui est Spiritus oris nostri, id est, anima & vita nostra, ut Origenes, Rupertus, Lyranus interpretantur. De quo vide prolixe Christoph. a Castro, & Corn. à Lapide.
